## Complete Course of Patrology

Or a universal, complete, uniform, convenient, economical library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each individual volume or each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the work itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the material treated below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority or influence in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: the first, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a single glance; the second, of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers have commented on the individual biblical books and in what passages of their works.

A most accurate edition, and one easily preferred to all others if the following are taken into consideration: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection, which is unified, methodical, and chronological, and which for the first time in our library brings together six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

**SECOND SERIES**

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III, under the direction of J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. Two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; three hundred of the Greek-Latin edition for one thousand eight hundred. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; in the latter case, however, they are provided only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of Our Lord 840

# Saint Agobard, Bishop of Lyons

[Column 0009]

## Historical Notice on Saint Agobard

*[Galland, Library of the Ancient Fathers]*

[Column 0009A]

Authors have handed down to us quite a good deal about Agobard. He was a Gaul by nationality and was born in the year 779, as Mabillon informs us. [Note: [Column 0009C] *Italian Journey*, section XIV, p. 68.] He soon went to Spain; leaving there in 783, he came to Narbonese Gaul. In 813, when Leidrad withdrew to the monastery of Soissons, Agobard was appointed to administer the see of Lyons, which in the following year, 814, after Leidrad’s death, he obtained as his own and held until the year 840 or 841, when, on the eighth day before the Ides of June, [Note: [Column 0009C] Ado, *Chronicle*, under the year 815; Hugh of Flavigny, *Chronicle*, under the year 841; and the *Chronicle of Saint Remigius of Dijon.] he exchanged life for death at Saintes. In 818, by publishing a book addressed to the emperor Louis, he refuted the errors of Felix of Urgell. He attacked the insolence of the Jews with particular severity, also sending a supplicatory letter to the emperor himself from the Council of Lyons in the year 829.

When Lothair and Pepin, Louis’s sons, openly took up arms against their father, [Note: [Column 0009C] Uspergensis, *Chronicle*.] Agobard experienced varying fortunes from the year 833 onward. “For Agobard, having been torn away from the prince’s allegiance, inflamed the youthful mind of Lothair by his counsel. A council was summoned, where each man contended with the utmost boldness for stripping [Column 0009B] the father of his diadem.” [Note: [Column 0009C] Papirius Masson, *Life of Agobard*.]

In 834, when Lothair had been expelled from Gaul by his father Louis, Agobard joined himself to him as a companion in his error. Neither an apology for his action, adorned with every rhetorical embellishment, nor the integrity of a man otherwise distinguished by his virtues could prevent him from being deposed [Note: [Column 0010C] Aventinus, *Bavarian Annals*, book IV.] at the assembly at Thionville in 835, although no one else was appointed in his place. In 837, having abandoned Lothair, he returned to Gaul and was reconciled once more with Louis. He followed Louis to the Rhine in the year 840 or 841 and died at Saintes.

There is no one who does not praise Agobard’s knowledge and learning: Masson, Fabricius, Baluze, Cave, and others. By a fortunate accident Masson discovered his works at the home of a certain Lyons bookbinder. They were about to be torn apart, unless the learned man had snatched them from his hands; he later published them at Paris in 1605. Stephen Baluze subsequently followed his example and in 1666 most diligently prepared a new edition of the same works, furnished with notes. [Column 0010A] We have resolved to reprint the Baluze edition.

Du Pin and Cave list Agobard’s writings. Cave, however, is somewhat unfair to him on account of his little book on Paintings and Images. While all the others—Masson, Baluze, Raynaud, Mabillon, Coint, and other men certainly of keen judgment—maintain that Agobard’s statements can be softened and understood in a favorable sense, Cave alone preferred to go entirely in the opposite direction.

Yet Hercules himself could do nothing against two. For the following points are sufficiently clear:

1. During that period the Gauls were divided on this matter according to different tendencies. [Note: [Column 0010C] See Berardus on Gratian’s *Canon*, part I, chapter 43, and part II, chapter 71, concerning canon 6 of distinction 37.]

2. The second canon of the Council of Frankfurt in 794, in which those Fathers seem to have condemned the Second Council of Nicaea, is found nowhere except in the codex of Saint Remigius, in which it also appears to have been inserted by another hand. [Note: [Column 0010C] Baluze, notes to the *Capitularies*, vol. II, p. 753.]

3. The Franks were especially afraid that the empire, which had come to them because—as historians universally acknowledge—they had vigorously defended and supported the veneration of images, might fall back again to the Greeks [Column 0010B] if the veneration of images were restored among them.

The intention of the Franks, therefore, was not to attack iconoduly in the sense understood by Western Catholics. Rather, they pursued their own cause by whatever means they could, even by representing the veneration of images as having been recalled by the Greek council to true worship (*latria*). Thus there were some who wished Nicaea not to be accepted for political reasons, and others who wished it rejected for religious reasons, although those reasons departed from the truth.

What wonder, then, if Agobard—otherwise vehement in his religious convictions—perhaps believing that the worship of latria had truly been decreed for images by the Council of Nicaea, and wishing to serve the interests of the Frankish empire, went somewhat farther in his words than was proper? See more on this in the aforementioned Berardus.

There is therefore nothing astonishing in Agobard’s being counted among the saints in the ancient Martyrologies, since he was in fact a very devout man and did not hold opinions against the true worship of images; he did, however, offend humanly against the prince.

[Column 0009C]

# Baluze’s Preface Placed at the Beginning of His Edition of the Works of Saint Agobard

[Column 0009D]

Last year, when the works of Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, were being published, I complained somewhat about the lack of diligence and care shown by Papirius Masson in editing [Column 0010D] the studies of ancient writers. Now, at the beginning of this preface, I wish to lament my lot, since I am once again compelled to complain about a most distinguished man, [Column 0011A] and this more sharply and vigorously than I did in the preface to Lupus.

For if any writer was ever treated carelessly, this certainly happened to Agobard. It is beyond question that scarcely a single line in Masson’s edition—the first in which Agobard was published—does not contain something different from the ancient codex that Masson used. So much so that Lupus, although otherwise extremely defiled, appears most carefully edited in comparison with Agobard.

Thus, since this man enjoys great fame and learned men daily declare that they owe him very much, I seem to have undertaken a work full of risk and plainly dangerous, since I have decided to expose his negligence and carelessness. Nevertheless, one hope consoles me: you, learned reader, and those like you, will readily pardon my boldness and judge this labor of mine fairly and favorably once you understand that my care was entirely necessary. You will easily convince yourself of this, reader, after recognizing from a comparison of our edition with Masson’s how deformed and discolored Agobard had previously been, and after seeing him corrected in almost innumerable places. [Column 0011B]

I therefore offer you a new edition of Agobard, corrected according to the codex used by Masson, which the illustrious Nicolaus Colbert, bishop of Luçon, supplied to us from the Royal Library. And lest anyone doubt that this is precisely Masson’s book, the following words are written on the front of the codex in the hand of the illustrious Jacques-Auguste de Thou: “From the books of Papirius Masson.”

Then, in the hand of Jean-Baptiste Masson, who donated that book to the Royal Library, these words were added in the same lettering:

“These manuscript works of Agobard, brought to light by Papirius Masson, I, Jean-Baptiste Masson, almoner to the king and brother of Papirius, have given as a gift to the Royal Library, for the greater fidelity of that edition, on 16 July in the year of salvation 1618. LE MASSON.”

I thought it appropriate to record this so that everyone might know that our edition was prepared according to that very codex which Masson used. [Column 0011C]

Moreover, we all owe Masson great gratitude for preserving Agobard. For when he, as he himself writes in his letter to the Church of Lyons, was looking for books in Lyons in the Merchants’ district, and was visiting a bookbinder for that purpose, the binder was ready to tear apart Agobard’s codex, written on parchment in ancient script. He already held a knife in his hand for that slaughter, but Masson saved its life by paying the price of the book.

Furthermore, reader, you should be warned that I was not so scrupulous in this edition that I did not sometimes correct our author by conjecture, whenever the occasion required it—that is, whenever Agobard’s meaning seemed disturbed in the ancient codex and the correction was easy and obvious.

When I saw that these errors belonged to the scribes and not to Agobard, I thought it best to remove them. Nor do I think that anyone of sound mind will take this badly. Yet if any attempted correction [Column 0011D] seemed to be of some importance, I did not conceal that it was my own correction, lest the authority of the ancient codex deceive anyone here.

Above all, I observed this rule consistently and with the utmost fidelity in the books published concerning the dispute between the emperor Louis the Pious and his sons. I corrected those books according to the manuscript codex; or, if I changed anything from the received reading on my own authority, I did not conceal it in the notes. The matter seemed to be of great importance.

Besides Agobard’s works that had long been published, this edition presents his previously unpublished book against [Column 0012A] Amalarius’s four books *On the Divine Offices*. I shall briefly explain how it came into my possession.

By chance the distinguished Antonius Vion Herovallius, being favorably disposed toward these studies, shared with me a sheet containing a list of certain works by ancient writers that had not yet been published and were said to be in the possession of the distinguished Peter Francis Chifflet, a priest of the Society of Jesus, who now resides at Dijon. The list had been written in Chifflet’s own hand.

Trusting greatly in the man’s courtesy, I wrote him a letter and asked him to send me a copy of that work of Agobard, so that it might be published along with the other works of the distinguished writer. He willingly complied and sent it at once.

Meanwhile I wrote concerning the matter to the distinguished man whom I was proud to call my friend, Francis Solleisel Clapier, a patrician of Lyons, who recently died near Lyons. When he learned that the ancient codex from which [Column 0012B] Chifflet had copied this book was in the library of Peter Marnaesius, senator of Grenoble and canon of Vienne, a most distinguished and noble man, and, as Clapier wrote, most skilled in divine and human law, he arranged for it to be brought to him at Lyons and then immediately sent it to me in Paris, out of his friendship for me, as I shall soon explain.

Indeed, I had thought that this edition could begin immediately after Easter and be completed by June. But the hope of obtaining the Marnaesian codex, which Clapier made certain, brought delay to this undertaking.

To this inconvenience was added a far more serious misfortune: a grave illness of the eyes, so severe that I even feared I might lose my sight, or at least one of my eyes. But by God’s providence this misfortune too was brought to a favorable end.

Thus, after I emerged from this illness—for I do not dare say that I recovered—the book of Marnaesius was brought to me, clearly the very one that Chifflet had seen. [Column 0012C] For it contained a statement that the book had come from the library of the monastery of Bonneval in the diocese of Vienne.

My first care, therefore, was to collate Agobard’s book against Amalarius with Chifflet’s copy; then, similarly, to collate the book *On the Privilege and Right of the Priesthood*, which was also written in that codex, with Masson’s edition.

I also collated—and let me mention this in passing—the letters of Avitus, bishop of Vienne, with Sirmond’s edition, perhaps to be presented in a better light at some future time. Not long afterward the book was returned to Clapier, to be restored in good faith to its owner.

I also added to this edition, so that you could not complain that anything was lacking here, reader, Papirius Masson’s letter to the Church of Lyons, his preface to Agobard, and a synopsis of Agobard’s works.

But I wish to warn you that there are many things in these works of Masson’s which neither accord with the customs of Agobard’s age nor fit the history [Column 0012D] of those times. We did not wish to examine these matters in detail. If, nevertheless, you should find anything there contrary to our notes, you must consider the whole of that material contrary to the truth.

These are the matters about which I thought you should be warned, reader. You see that I am taking pains not to disappoint your expectations. For last year I promised new editions of several ancient writers, including Agobard, and I have wished by this edition at least to discharge the obligation I knew I owed you.

[Column 0013]

## The Ancient Author of the Life of the Emperor Louis the Pious, under the Year 835

[Column 0013C]

The emperor therefore spent the greater part of the winter at Aachen, and from there departed for Thionville before Christmas, where the people who had been ordered to attend also arrived.

When he had taken his seat there, he complained against certain bishops concerning his deposition. But since some had fled to Italy and others, when summoned, had refused to obey, only Ebbo appeared among those accused.

When he was pressed to give an account of such matters, he claimed that he alone was being pressed after all the others, in whose presence these things had been done, had been left behind. But the other bishops, while pleading the necessity of their presence, excused themselves on the ground of their innocence.

At last Ebbo, distressed at being wearied by such matters, after seeking the advice of certain bishops, pronounced a kind of confession against himself. He affirmed that he was unworthy of the priesthood and judged that he should irrevocably abstain from it; and he communicated this decision both to the bishops and, through them, to the emperor.

[Column 0013D] After this had been done, Agobard, archbishop of Lyons, who had delayed coming when summoned to make satisfaction, was removed from the episcopal office after being summoned three times, while the others, as we have said, fled to Italy.

## The Same Author, under the Year 836

The emperor held the next assembly after this judgment in the district of Lyons during the summer, at a place called Stramiacus, with his sons Pepin and Louis. Lothair’s absence was caused by the severity of the illness mentioned above.

At this assembly he ordered the case of the vacant Churches of Lyons and Vienne to be examined, because their former bishops—Agobard had been ordered to come and give an account but had not come, [Column 0014A] while Bernard of Vienne had indeed appeared but had again taken flight—were absent.

The matter, however, remained unfinished because of the absence of the bishops, as has been stated.

## Verses of Walafrid Strabo to Agobard, Bishop of Lyons

When I had scarcely completed three times six years of life,

my name came to you, revered Father.

I know that it reached you, since I received your reply,

which was for us the equivalent of great love.

For if you remember—for how could you not remember?—

I rejoice, and I ask that you remember everywhere.

Love itself still burns in our hearts;

the desire itself remains strong

to see you and enjoy your speech.

If the queen left the hot [or: cultivated] kingdoms of the Ethiopians

and the fields of Sheba in order to seek Solomon,

why should we not, for whom another kingdom is being prepared,

remain solely in the love of the Creator?

[Column 0014B] For, I confess, if I were now given a definite choice,

whether to receive the gifts of the world or of intellect,

I would pursue the secure leisure of knowing the truth more freely

rather than golden ages that perish.

But concerning the new flower whose fragrance,

born among you, spreads its scent everywhere,

rumor nourishes these places.

Flora once came,

when the several gods addressed the hills,

bearing thyme and meadows.

To this Florus the judgment of Christ’s worshipers

more fittingly attributes whatever flourishes in teaching and speech.

For this Florus follows the flower sprung from the shoot of Jesse,

and hands on what that lover brought to humanity.

What bee would be so sluggish,

so ungrateful for heavenly gifts,

as not willingly to feed itself on this nectar?

May this flower bloom without withering,

and, fragrant with flowers, always send its breath

everywhere to God,

until it raises its summits extended

toward the starry abodes

and already possesses fruit without end.

Let ambrosia, roses, lilies, ears of grain, and crocus yield—

[Column 0014C] all sweet things together.

May love of this flower be pleasing.

May I enjoy it, use it, be warmed by it,

delight in it, and abound in it;

may I be nourished and instructed

by hearing and seeing it.

May God one day grant us to impart

mutual gifts to one another.

Let each part gather something of the harvest.

By the divine gift, I pray, farewell without end,

sending your sweet writings in return.

## Ado of Vienne in His Chronicle, under the Year 810

Bernard was bishop of Vienne, and Leidrad was bishop of Lyons. At the beginning of the emperor Louis’s reign, Leidrad sought the monastery of Soissons; in his place Agobard, a chorepiscopus of the same Church, was substituted as bishop, with the consent of the emperor and the entire synod of the bishops of Gaul.

Some, wishing to defend this action, said that the venerable Agobard had been ordained in the see of Lyons by three bishops at Leidrad’s command. But canonical authority declares that there are not to be two bishops [Column 0014D] in one city, and that while a bishop is alive he ought not to choose a successor for himself. For this reason, rules established in so great an order by the Church must not be bypassed for any reason whatsoever.

## The Same Author, under the Year 815

Bernard and Agobard still governed the Church of Vienne. Both were accused before the emperor; abandoning their Churches, they went to Italy to Lothair, the other emperor. Later, through the efforts of the devout emperors, Agobard recovered the see of Lyons and Bernard that of Vienne.

A few years later Agobard died at Saintes while stationed on a royal expedition.

[Column 0015A]

## Flodoard, Book II of the *History of Rheims*, Chapter 20

In the year 834 from the Lord’s incarnation, Lothair, terrified by the assembly of his brothers and of many faithful men of his father the emperor, slipped away in flight and left his father, who was still excluded from entering the church.

Among those who accompanied him were certain bishops who had supported him in his father’s adversity and, contrary to the sacred rules, returned to their sees: Jesse of Amiens, Herehold of Auxerre, Agobard of Lyons, and Bartholomew, bishop of Narbonne.

## From the Chronicle of Hugh of Flavigny

At the beginning of the emperor Louis’s reign, Leidrad sought the monastery of Soissons; in his place Agobard was substituted as chorepiscopus of the same Church, with the consent of the emperor and the whole synod of the bishops of Gaul.

Some, wishing to defend this action, said that he had been ordained in the see of Lyons by three bishops at Leidrad’s command.

Thus Agobard and Bernard of Vienne, accused before Louis [Column 0016A], abandoned their Churches and went to Lothair in Italy. But through the efforts of the devout emperors, both recovered their sees. A few years later Agobard died at Cénates while on a royal expedition.

# Papirius Masson’s Preface to Agobard, Published in the Year 1605

Papirius Masson, jurisconsult, sends greetings to the holy and illustrious Church of Lyons.

Under the Emperor Antoninus Verus, the principal cities of Gaul, and those said to excel all the others, were Lugdunum and Vienna, situated at the confluence of the Rhone and Saone, the most famous of rivers. There, Suetonius—and before him Seneca—declares that the Emperor Claudius was born. At Lugdunum, indeed, fairs were held which, because of the crowds of people traveling there from every nation, were accustomed to be praised and celebrated everywhere as being of great renown.

Eusebius of Caesarea, in the fifth book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, records the foregoing; at the same time he says that Photinus, a most blessed man and bishop of that city, after reaching his ninetieth year and more, endured much for Christ and died in prison, into which he had been thrown by soldiers. Not long afterward God gave him a distinguished successor, Irenaeus, admirable for the sanctity of his life and his learning, as his works demonstrate; the same writer narrates many distinguished things about him. After him, Verissimus was a man of great name: he alone among the bishops of Gaul attended the Council of Sardica and subscribed its decrees with the others.

Now I come to Eucherius, whose writings still survive and who was famous to John Cassian, who lived in the time of Leo the Great, pontiff of the Roman Church. Cassian speaks of him most honorably in two places, as does Hilary of Arles in the *Life of Honoratus*, his predecessor, and, much later, Florus of Lugdunum, an exceptionally learned man, whose letter to Bartholomew, bishop of Narbonne, together with one of Agobard’s letters, is extant. Viventiolus follows, a most outstanding and holy man. Agobard says of him:

> “He was bishop of Lugdunum; what his learning was, not only his own writings but also what others have written about him bears witness.”

Since these writings have perished, or perhaps still lie hidden somewhere, I must speak of his successors. Thus Agobard, a Gaul by birth, succeeded Leidrada, a Norican and learned man, in the bishopric of Lugdunum, in the time of the Emperor Louis the Pious and king of the Franks. He presided over the emperor’s deposition at Soissons, among the peoples of Belgica Secunda, in the monastery of Saint Medard, in the year 833, as he himself writes. Thegan, his fellow bishop of Trier, also wrote about this at the same period. Curious readers will be able to compare the two accounts.

Agobard speaks of King Childebert and of Pepin; of Charlemagne, for whom he wrote an epitaph at his funeral; of Louis’s wives, Ermengard and Judith, the most beautiful woman of that age, although he does not mention them by name; of the sons of that emperor, Lothair, Louis, and the boy Charles; and of the Burgundian kings Gundobad and Sigismund. He utterly overthrows, by the firmest reasoning, arguments, and testimonies of the ancients, Gundobad’s most unjust law, devised for the destruction of mankind. The laws of the Burgundians survive, from which one may extract that most disastrous statute.

He lived under Gregory IV, Roman pontiff, whose cause and that of the designated Emperor Lothair he perhaps defended too zealously, or more sharply than was either fitting or proper, especially against his most kindly father, the king, than whom no one was ever better or more just. Nevertheless, those who had followed Lothair’s cause against his father were eventually restored to favor, among them Agobard. The emperor employed him in the great affairs of the kingdom, while occupied with which he died among the Santones, near the Ocean.

Endowed with great judgment and most richly instructed in divine learning, Agobard wrote with gravity and extreme force, as his works attest. He left behind, because of his holiness and learning, an immortal glory for his name, especially among the sons and pupils of the Church, whose morals and discipline, almost fallen and dying out, he revived.

He wrote against Felix, bishop of Urgell, as did Paulinus of Aquileia and another, a man of most profound learning whose name is uncertain, who composed seven books against Felix. I recently read these books in manuscript and admired them.

He also wrote letters to the bishops Bernard of Vienne, Nibridius of Narbonne, and his successor Bartholomew, whom we mentioned above; to Ebbo of Reims, whom he calls “the most magnificent and most longed-for lord, father and son”; to Eaor, whose see, because of the scarcity of authors, I have not yet been able to discover; to Hilduin, prelate of the imperial palace; and to Wala, most holy and blessed abbots; and to Adalard and Helis, dear and most venerable men. He calls those men abbots: one of them presided over the distinguished monastery of Dionysius in the territory of the Parisii, and he also took care to make known, through the publication of his books, what manner of man he was and how great.

He wrote against the Jewish people, who were entirely offensive and hostile to him, attacking them and brilliantly refuting many of their unheard-of fabrications against Christ Jesus. He also replied to Matfred, a most distinguished and illustrious man, attacking and accusing Gerricus, Frederic, and Evrard because they had shown themselves formidable to Christians but lenient toward Jews. The time of Matfred’s death is recorded in the *Life of Louis*.

He reports that several synods were held in Gaul, and in two places complains about Roman clerics and certain others who presented the Gallican canons as useless and superfluous, and who asserted that those synods had been convened in the absence of the legates of the Roman see and without the emperor’s command.

He most clearly exposes the errors of the Greeks concerning images and paintings and denies that they ought to be worshiped. We Catholics all approve this position and follow the testimony of Gregory the Great concerning them.

He also gives a full account of the division of the empire made by Louis; this is explained by Walafrid Strabo, though not in the same words. He treats of thunder and storms and of the false opinion of the mad populace, just as Maximus of Turin had done before him in a sermon and homily during the time of Theodosius the Younger.

In argument he uses testimonies from the divine books, from the ancient sacred translation, and sometimes from Jerome. We wish to give this warning so that no one may be needlessly disturbed or suppose that anything has been added or altered by me. I have always considered such a thing impious, holding that good faith is owed to authors as a matter of the strictest justice.

When necessary, he brings forward and displays the testimonies of the Fathers: of Saint Cyprian, Hilary, Jerome, Ambrose—whom he himself calls pre-eminent in learning and holiness—Augustine, Leo, Symmachus, Vigilius, Pelagius II, Gregory the Great, Gregory II, and Alcimus Avitus, bishop of Vienne, whom he says was an orthodox and eloquent teacher; finally, Bede, whom he declares to have been, in his own time, a man of no ordinary learning among the English people.

Among the Greeks he cites Athanasius, Cyril, Theodoret, Proclus, John Chrysostom, Eusebius of Caesarea, and others. We do not wish to pass over Clement, Roman pontiff, and Sylvester, whom he cites, although the same books are judged apocryphal; nevertheless, many testimonies from them are found to have been used by the doctors.

Among secular writers he uses the testimony of no one except the grammarian Priscian.

Therefore, holy and illustrious Church of Lugdunum—for this is how Eusebius calls you, indeed calling you most illustrious—show me your gratitude, and crown me as a citizen honored with the civic crown. For when I was looking for books among you in the district of the Merchants, and Stephen Verdier was with me—he is now dead—and we were visiting a bookbinder for this purpose, that man was about to cut up Agobard’s codex, written on parchment in ancient script, and held a knife in his hand for that butchery. We bought the manuscript its life, which proved fortunate and auspicious.

Farewell. Paris, 1 January 1605.

## Papirius Masson’s Brief Synopsis of the Life of Agobard and of His Doctrine

The life of this bishop remained obscure for many centuries—obscure, I say, not because of any lack of talent or acumen, nor because of the lowliness of his office, but because of the darkness of the times. Amandus has his witnesses; Engilbert, Jonas, Walafrid, and the other contemporaries have their lights. This man, however, has few, indeed almost none, except what historical necessity inserts or what his own volumes furtively and, as it were, inadvertently reveal.

We nevertheless learn from Ado that he was initiated into the presbyterate at an early age and, because of the integrity of his life and doctrine, raised to the dignity of chorepiscopus. Soon afterward, when Leidrada withdrew to the monastery at Soissons, Agobard was elevated to the summit of the primacy of Lugdunum, with the emperor’s consent and that of the entire synod of the bishops of Gaul. There, bearing the vesture and burden of so great an eminence, he spent many years without reproach, engaging in continual contests of school and tongue against the synagogues of the Jews.

But a single blemish darkened an old age shining with so much glory.

[Note: [Col. 0017D] Conrad, abbot of Usperg, in his *Chronicle*.]

When Clotarius was being removed from the helm of the entire empire through hatred and the fury of his stepmother Judith, daughter of Count Welf, he secretly and openly plotted against his father and seized the minds of both orders, lay and ecclesiastical, for the destruction of his father’s scepter. Among them, Agobard, torn away from the prince’s allegiance, inflamed the youthful mind of Clotarius by his counsel.

A council was summoned, where everyone contended most boldly for taking the diadem from the father. Under this pretext he attacked the emperor and, after stripping him of his crown, cast him into monastic solitude. The Gauls raged and could not endure such an injury to the father. They took up arms, restored the emperor, and summoned his sons, Pepin and Bernard, through whose help Clotarius was compelled to beg and plead for forgiveness.

The authors of the plot were sought for punishment. The ecclesiastical instigators of the disturbance were discovered, and they fled into Italy.

> “The emperor compelled Ebbo to go among the Saxons. He nevertheless removed Agobert of Lugdunum from the assembly of bishops: he was deposed. He also condemned the others who had escaped into Italy by the religious authority of all the priests. After this, on the first Sunday of Lent, as though he had not yet been released from the unjust curse of the sacrificers, he was again solemnly blessed by seven archmystes, who offered good prayers, after the petitions had been read from the book, with the greatest joy of all who were present and with the people acclaiming him. Thus he was happily purified. As though that eternal majesty were subject to human power, or were shut up in a box or glass, like a dark spirit held by a magical whisper, so that at our nod it might close or open the heavens.”

[Note: [Col. 0017D] Aventinus, book IV of the *Annals of Bavaria*.]

Dangers of this kind and the disturbances of a peaceful life turned his mind away from writing, so that thereafter he might devote himself to the light of the Gospel, the restoration of the Church, and the discharge of his office.

The year of his birth is unknown. It is known that he was born in the golden age of Charlemagne, that nurse of illustrious and most learned Apollos; that he flourished in the silver age of Louis; and that he died amid the iron conflicts of Louis’s sons, at Saintes, during the royal expedition, while every kind of destruction was tearing apart the ruins of the collapsing empire.

He excelled in an oratorical style of speech and especially in his memory of Scripture. He had illustrious contemporaries renowned in philosophy and theology, whose books we wear out through use: Hincmar, archbishop of Reims; Haimo, bishop of Halberstadt; Rabanus; Walafrid Strabo; Claudius of Turin, on the worship of images; Jonas of Orléans; Halitgar; Amalarius; Heliprand, bishop of Toledo; Engilbert; and many others whom we omit.

He treated serious subjects, whose synopses we set out below.

## Synopsis of the First Volume, Against the Doctrine of Felix

Under the empire of Charlemagne and Louis, a certain bishop of Urgell in Aragon emerged from the highest peaks of the Pyrenees. He was otherwise a prudent man and not lacking in Spanish subtlety. He revived from the underworld the seeds of the Nestorian sect, long since extinguished by the splendor of the Gospel.

First he was rebuked and convicted by Heliprand, bishop of Toledo. Then, to restrain his insolence, a council was summoned at Regensburg by the emperor. Third, he was brought to Rome, where, prostrate at the threshold of Saint Peter, he acknowledged his heresy before Pope Adrian. Finally, after he had again written down his fabrications, he was confronted by Agobard, defeated, and compelled to confess his error.

After Felix’s death, Agobard demolished the foundations of his doctrine by the authority of the Fathers and of Scripture. These are the foundations of Felix’s teaching.

### I

It derives from Nestorius: there are two separate persons in Christ, constituting a double Son, or double Christ—one in the flesh, the other in the Word. The latter was not crucified but is the Son of God by nature, truth, proper identity, kind, birth, and substance; the former, namely the incarnate one, suffered and is the Son of God by grace, election, will, good pleasure, predestination, assumption, and adoption.

### II

As the natural Son of God, he possesses everything essentially—eternity, wisdom, and so forth. As man, everything that belongs to him is accidental: a child, a prophet, and so on. These are accidental to him according to the dispensation of the flesh, not proper to him according to the power of divinity. In humanity he is only a priest; in divinity, a giver of life.

### III

It follows that the Virgin is, in one manner, the mother of the divine nature and, in another manner, the mother of the human nature: properly of humanity, but by grace of divinity.

### IV

Just as Christ and the Church are called one but are not one person or one suppositum, so, although it is said that the Word became flesh and is one, they are nevertheless not a single hypostasis.

These are the foul expressions with which that Spanish darkling dared to obscure the light of Christ; our fellow Gaul weakens them with excellent arguments.

### I

In Christ there are indeed two natures, but substantially united in one hypostasis and one person. Hence not merely the humanity but the whole Christ suffered, while the divinity was, in its own impassible manner, nailed to the cross, without sensation or passion.

Therefore there are not two sons but one, in two natures, hypostatically and without confusion: the Son of God by nature, proper identity, and substance, but not by grace, since he is coeternal with the Father. Nor is he the Son by predestination, since the Father is not prior to him in time or nature, but only in origin. Nor by adoption, since otherwise he would at some time have been alien from God. Nor by assumption, since the one who assumes and the one assumed are the same. He is therefore the one natural Son of God.

And just as every human being, soul and flesh, is one person, so Christ is one person, the Word and man.

### II

From such a union it follows that the things belonging to the flesh become those of the divinity. For if the flesh is proper to the Word, why should the names belonging to the flesh not be proper to him? Therefore, when he assumed flesh, he made all things proper to the flesh his own, so that according to both natures he is both giver of life and high priest, and so forth. Just as, according to both soul and body, the whole human being is called rational, a child, and a philosopher.

### III

Consequently, the Virgin was the mother of both natures, including the divine nature, without which the flesh was never incarnate; and she gave birth to the whole incarnate Christ.

### IV

As regards Christ’s union with the Church, it is unlike the incarnation. For that union occurs at least in spirit, not in body; in faith, not in flesh; in speech, not in action; in love, not in copulation. It arises from an infinite number of persons joined to some mystical head and therefore cannot be called a true union—the union, I mean, of the incarnation—which is formed from two natures and substances in one person.

These are the arguments by which Agobard shattered the force and sinew of Felix’s doctrine.

## Volume II: On the Insolence of the Jews

In adversity no nation is more degraded than the Jews; in prosperity, none is more insolent. By the favor of the imperial majesty, a place of peace and residence had been granted to them in Gaul, especially at Lugdunum. But when the sweetness of peace somewhat released them from the hardships of flight, they devised schemes, flattered the most distinguished courtiers, and bound them to themselves with money.

Thus, through crooked frauds, they secretly extorted from the most merciful emperor measures against the bishop of the Church of Lugdunum, who was turning the people away from them:

That they should not sell Christian slaves to Jews.

That Christian women should not keep the Sabbath with them.

That they should not work on Sundays.

That during Lent they should not dine with them or eat the same meats.

That they should not buy meat sacrificed by them or drink their wine.

They attacked him and drew individual Christians into their synagogues by flattery and inflated praises of patriarchal dignity. They grew insolent and, contrary to Christian custom, bought Christian slaves.

Agobard complains to the emperor, exposes their schemes, reveals the authors of the plot, and asks for a remedy for so great a ruin. He promises to portray, by testimonies from Scripture, their life, customs, and superstitious manner of living.

## Volume III: On Jewish Superstitions

[Note: [Col. 0019D] In this chapter, read “Ebbo,” not “Eaor.”]

Here Agobard argues at length that the obstinacy of the detestable Jewish nation and its rites, alien from the path of truth, caused the ancient Fathers to compose canons warning against association, shared meals, and intercourse with them. Indeed, he says that they were so hated that the illustrious Ambrose preferred death to rebuilding the wall of the Jewish temple.

### I

Let senior clerics who have attended a Jewish banquet be excommunicated for one year. If younger clerics presume to do so, let them be beaten.

### II

From supper until the first [day of] Passover, let them not walk through the streets. Otherwise, let them be restrained by the judges.

### III

No Christian shall be a slave to a Jew; instead, let him be freed upon payment of twelve solidi.

### IV

If anyone has enticed a Christian slave toward Jewish doctrine, let him be punished by the loss of the slave and by legal condemnation.

### V

Let no Jew meet with Christians during the season of Passover.

The cause of this severity is found in their fury, obstinacy, and corruption of doctrine. Those Pharisaic *Deuteroseis* have concealed the truth under so many clouds that scarcely any light remains among them.

They say:

- That God is corporeal, and hears and sees.
- That the human body was made in the image of God.
- That demons were created from vain thoughts about God.
- That the letters of the alphabet are eternal.
- That the Law of Moses was written before the world.
- That there are many heavens, many earths, and many hells.
- That God has seven trumpets.
- That the apostle Peter was called Cephas, that is, “Rock,” because of the dullness of his understanding.
- That Jesus Christ was hanged on a fork by the judgment of Tiberius, buried beside an aqueduct, carried away by an inundation of water, and sought by Pilate for twelve lunar months.
- They call Christians idolaters because they invoke the saints.
- They have heads of their synagogues who distinguish, by sight and taste, the blood of a menstruating virgin as clean or unclean.
- They may walk two thousand feet on the Sabbath.

Hence it is concluded that, if separation from heretics and schismatics was commanded, then separation from Jews was commanded all the more—from the concision, in whom the evangelical light was utterly extinguished. This follows the custom of the apostles, who shook the dust from their feet at the threshold and condemned them with a dreadful anathema.

## To Adalard, Wala, and Others

Because of frequent complaints about the madness of the Jewish populace, the Emperor Louis compelled a gathering of bishops, where Agobard pleaded the cause of the Christian Church, but wrongly, etc., being hindered by fear. He now writes to the noble Fathers and attributes the weakness of his mind to fear.

Then, in a concise letter, he asks those bishops what he ought to do concerning Jewish slaves who are drawn by love of Christ to Christian baptism: whether he should receive them or reject them.

## Letter to Nibridius

He connects this with the preceding complaint and stirs up that father and all the bishops so that, by unanimous agreement, they may extinguish the Jewish contamination which daily creeps forward, lest their Church itself be extinguished.

## To the Emperor

Because this treatise is ἀκέφαλος, “headless” or “without a beginning,” I thought this title ought to be attached to it.

### On the Impiety of Trial by Combat, Against the Gundobadic Law, Which Wishes Cases to Be Settled by Swords Rather Than Judgment

[Note: [Col. 0021D] See the *History of Burgundy*.]

Since we are all one in Christ, in unity of faith, affection, and religion, it is impious to break unanimous peace by battle and, in legal disputes, to attack life with swords when the equity of judgments, the eyes of witnesses, and integrity can supply what is needed.

Moreover, that law is neither Mosaic nor evangelical. Rather, it was devised by the most foul and hostile enemy of Christ, so that disputes might be investigated not by witnesses or the testimony of truthful men but by iron and fire.

Agobard therefore appeals to the most merciful emperor to take care that so wicked a custom be abolished from the kingdom.

## Volume VII: On the Right of the Priesthood

Agobard speaks with great eloquence to his fellow bishop Bernard, drawing much from the Fathers and still more from Scripture.

### I

The priesthood belongs to all who are members by faith of the supreme Priest.

### II

Although that expression is very broad, when used of the ministry it properly refers to designated priests. Its beginning was in Abel, Cain, Noah, Abraham, and the other Nazirites of the Levitical tribe, without distinction between the good and the bad.

### III

For what is considered in a priest is not merit but the power of the ministry; not the person but the dignity of the person; not integrity but office.

### IV

Thus a good layman cannot perform what a wicked bishop can perform—namely, the sacraments and ecclesiastical functions—without danger to his soul, as in the case of Uzzah.

### V

These functions include baptism and the consecration of the body and blood of Christ, and so forth. Since these things cannot be improved or degraded either by the merits of the good or by the fraud of the wicked, but are accomplished by the power of the Spirit, they must be honored equally by all, whether received from good or wicked priests.

There are four classes of priests:

1. The first are to be loved: those who both live and teach well.
2. The second are to be tolerated: those who teach well but do not live especially well. These are to be heard, not imitated.
3. The third are to be despised: those who live badly and are ignorant.
4. The fourth are to be anathematized: those who live either well or badly but teach badly. They must be abandoned altogether.

## On Hail and Thunder

A grim and superstitious opinion about hail and storms had become widespread among the people. They thought that these were stirred up by a magician’s incantations. They called this “the levitational air.” Agobard refutes it with many reasons and arguments, by which he surrounds and exposes such darklings and sorcerers.

1. From the most shameful lie of men, who attribute to human beings what belongs to God alone.
2. From the intrinsic nature of the lie on which they relied.
3. From the testimonies of Scripture. The scriptural passages attribute the stirring of storms to God, not to Moses, Samuel, or the sorcerers Jamnes and Mambres. Therefore these men falsely attribute the movement of storms to magicians.
4. From the interpretation of the same Scripture. For although God pours out storms, whether through angels or through Moses and Elisha, it does not follow that those men stirred them up independently of him, but rather through ministerial agency.
6. From the harmony and testimony of the entire universe. The whole universe recognizes God alone as its author and mover; therefore created beings do not possess this power.
7. If the good Israelites could hurl hailstones upon the wicked, the wicked too could have hurled them upon the good; yet the kings of Canaan never accomplished this.
8. If wicked men could do this, they could overwhelm anyone they hated with sudden storms.
9. From the nature of scourges and heavenly bodies, whose proper function is to obey not man but the author of nature.
10. From the nature of man, who is ignorant of the secrets of the ether.
11. From the unstable faith of sorcerers, who for this reason ask nothing from God.

He attempts to erase many other fabrications from the heart of the people, long impressed upon it by custom, especially the story circulated about Grimoald, duke of Benevento, who allegedly caused all the oxen to die by sending men through the dust. His aim is to impress upon the people the genuine mark of the Gospel.

## To Fredegisus, Abbot

The abbot Fredegisus asserted the following doctrines against Agobard.

### I

That Christ was truly humble and, insofar as he was humble, knew himself to be in error.

### II

That all Scripture, together with all its interpreters, is canonical, and that they had never erred in grammar.

### III

That the Holy Spirit inspired in the prophets and apostles their inward thoughts and formed the very external words in their mouths, as in the case of Balaam’s she-ass.

### IV

That souls were created in some definite place and then descended into bodies.

### V

That God is one thing and Truth another.

### VI

That none of the ancient patriarchs were Christians and that Christ was not present in the Old Testament.

Agobard’s responses are as follows.

### To I

Christ possesses the nature of our bodies but not their origin, and therefore possesses impeccability. Although he made himself humble, he did so by an inclination of mercy, not by emptying himself of power: he abolished the sins of others rather than confessing sins of his own.

### To II

The authority of Scripture is beyond doubt—namely, of the canonical Scriptures. Among the interpreters, first come the Seventy-Two, then Jerome. Certain Jewish interpreters are to be rejected: Aquila, Theodotion, Symmachus, and Didymus.

Interpreters should be read in such a way that Scripture takes precedence—not with the freedom to judge, but with the necessity of believing. Interpreters, however, should be read not with the necessity of believing but with the freedom to judge.

They erred in grammar, not through malice or incompetence but as a form of accommodation.

### To III

This is shown by the example of Moses and Aaron: one of them, the prophet, had a more impeded voice than Aaron, who was not a prophet. It is also shown by the apostles, who proclaimed the Gospel not with the pomp of eloquence but in the power of the Spirit.

### To IV

The fourth proposition is refuted by passages from Scripture and philosophy.

### To V

The fifth is refuted by the nature of God, which has nothing divided in it but is wholly what it is.

### To VI

Christ was not manifestly revealed but was known by the patriarchs under the Levitical vesture, through faith. This is shown by Scripture, the Fathers, reason, and the unity of the Church, from Adam’s origin down to Christ.

Thus, although the sacraments were different, the substance of the sacraments was nevertheless the same.

And although the Old and New Testaments are spoken of, this is not because the latter was recently invented, but because what had lain hidden under the bark of the Levitical cloud from the beginning of the law was manifested to the whole world.

## To Hilduin and Wala, Prelates, on the Baptism of Jewish Slaves

[Note: [Col. 0023D] Hilduin was abbot of the monastery of Saint Dionysius near Paris and archchaplain of the sacred palace; Conrad, abbot of Usperg.]

The Jews, partly through deceit and partly through money, had extorted many measures from the emperor hostile to the peace of the Church. Among other things, they obtained that no Jewish slave should be baptized without the consent of his Jewish master.

Hence dreadful disturbances arose between the two peoples. In this letter Agobard depicts the matter to a noble courtier and prelate, highly favored by the emperor. He complains about the novelty of the edict and argues that it must not be permitted for the following reasons:

1. Because of the insolence of the Jews, who would deter every slave from the baptismal bath.
2. Because of God’s command, for he wishes all to be saved, including slaves, who share with all others the bond of nature and origin. Although they serve the world in body, God wishes them bound to him in the worship of the mind, against every coercive violence.
3. Because Christ is all in all, and through baptism they are freed from every yoke of servitude.
4. Because of the clearest passages of Scripture.

Finally, he asks Hilduin to prevail upon the emperor either to repeal the edict or, at least, to grant slaves the freedom to come to the faith without violence.

## On the Deception of Signs

A certain epilepsy was becoming more severe, so that people fell as though possessed by demons. Indeed, a kind of pustular burning and marks appeared on their bodies. As a result, the terrified populace, following pagan custom, made offerings to avert such ulcers.

Bartholomew asks the cause of this anger sent down from heaven. Agobard replies that these things occur by God’s will and through the ministry of an angel, in order to instruct the faithful and torment the reprobate, just as in former times God struck the Egyptians and Philistines through swollen blisters and hemorrhoids. He adds many other things, which we leave to the leisure of the reader.

## To Matfred

This letter depicts nothing other than the miseries of his age, stirred up by the Jews, who had utterly overturned the integrity of morals, religion, and public harmony. He asks Matfred, who possessed great influence with the emperor, to remedy disturbances of this kind.

## To the Clergy of Lugdunum, on the Manner of Ecclesiastical Government

Quarrels arose among the clergy of Lugdunum concerning the administration of the Church, and they moved Agobard to write on this subject. First, beginning with the unity of the Church, both of its members and of its head, he urges each person to make peace with the others.

These are his axioms.

### I

The one bride has one bridegroom. Since he is essentially truth, peace, justice, and every good, he must be loved for his own sake, not for the sake of anything else.

### II

The members of that Church are not those who quarrel with one another but those who agree with one another and build one another up in love and worship of him.

### III

Hence, from that mutual bond and connection of love, Christ and the Church are called one lamb and one bride.

### IV

Moreover, from that inward and eternal marriage of the lamb and the ewe, lambs and sheep are generated. They form one lamb, inseparable and indissoluble by an eternal bond—that is, the Church.

### V

From that generation it follows that she who is called the bride of Christ is also called Christ’s daughter. For those whom he took together and once for all from eternity as his bride, he generates individually and in time through the Word.

He is called “brother” because of the common fellowship of nature and flesh with man.

She is called a vineyard because of the multitude of her children; a garden because of her variety and beauty; a fountain because of the overflowing abundance of heavenly waters everywhere; a sealed fountain because of her marvelous and hidden mysteries; a queen because of her dominion over the synagogue, demons, and all sects; a maidservant because of her obedience; and a mother because of the generation of her children.

This diversity of names does not make anything divided, but constitutes one bridegroom and one bride.

This unity of affection ought to draw the clergy away from every disagreement, so that they may devote themselves to their appointed office, which is to be God’s helper, not the Antichrist’s.

Those who dissolve unity are of many kinds:

- The corrupt, who disturb the unity of the Church by open scandal.
- Hypocrites, through simulated justice.
- Adulterers, by corrupting the truth openly and deceptively.
- The ambitious, for the sake of honor.
- Mercenaries, through the sweetness of petty gain.
- Φίλαυτοι, “self-lovers,” who draw hearts not toward love and praise of the bridegroom but toward love and praise of themselves, and so sever the unity of the Church.

But the true shepherd and guardian of true peace rejects such monsters from the ministry, watches over the flock without negligence, domination, pretense, or scandal, and feeds it according to all the regulations prescribed for him by the heavenly Emperor.

He urges all shepherds, priests, and abbots to become such men if they wish to be members of the one head and to govern the Church according to the divine commandments.

## On Images

Taking up the second commandment of the Decalogue, Agobard here treats expressly of the worship of images. In his age the superstition surrounding images was astonishing, and dreadful disputes raged concerning the worship of statues. The First Council of Nicaea prescribed that images be worshiped; the Second confirmed this. Disputes arose throughout the East and spread into Gaul. A council was assembled at Frankfurt, where Nicaea was openly condemned.

### I

The one God is to be worshiped without an image, and so forth.

### II

There is no example anywhere, throughout all the Testaments and the Fathers, of an image being worshiped.

### III

An image ought to serve as an ornament and delight the eyes, not instruct the people, and so forth.

In that period Claudius of Turin wrote on the worship of images. Jonas of Orléans wrote against him. Many others joined in treating the same subject, including kings themselves.

Agobard speaks with the greatest clarity. The following are his principal points, drawn from Saint Augustine and the other Fathers.

### I

There is no other image of God than that which is God himself and according to which he is himself. It cannot be painted and therefore cannot be worshiped in an image, except in the image that he himself prescribed for us—namely, Christ.

### II

There are indeed two kinds of worship, external and internal. Both are called religion. By both, inwardly and outwardly, we are bound eternally and exclusively to God. To this belong δουλεία (*douleia*) and λατρεία (*latreia*), together with the other forms of worship, insofar as they are names of religion.

### III

Where, however, the terms refer to human office and servitude, δουλεία (*douleia*) may be used of slaves and subjects; εὐσέβεια (*eusebeia*), of all people; honor, of saints and martyrs; piety, of parents. But only religion is used of God, because it is owed absolutely to God alone.

### IV

Hence it is clear that neither angels nor saints are to be worshiped with any religious worship, apart from the eternal image of God, which places itself between human beings and God.

### V

Angels are not to be worshiped:

1. Because they are blessed with a blessedness that is not their own.
2. Because they do not wish such worship to be offered to them.
3. Because this distinguishes them from demons.

### VI

Saints are not to be worshiped because they are holy only through the holiness of the Spirit, lights only from the supreme Light, and gods only from God. They perform miracles not as causes but as means and instruments. Therefore, leaving them behind, one must fly farther onward toward the eternal Light.

### VII

Nevertheless, we honor their memorials and traces, wherever they exist, whether in writings or in bodily remains; indeed, we honor their tombs because of the resurrection, life, and imitation of their example. We do not, however, build temples or altars to them, but to God alone.

### VIII

For this is the law of worship: no creature, no phantom formed by the mind concerning God, no human work, neither the rising nor setting sun, neither cloud nor fire nor trees, nor the works of human beings such as images, is to be worshiped. For if the works of God are not to be worshiped, how much less the works of human beings—that is, images of God, angels, and saints!

IX. Nor should you object that you worship not the image but the thing represented by the image. For the object determines the worship. Add that this is a fraud of Satan, who, under the appearance of honoring the saints, leads the mind over to idols and drags us down from the true and eternal one to carnal things.

X. Paintings are to be viewed with the external eye, as inanimate things. God is to be worshiped inwardly. Those images are for the sake of history and memory, not religion; God is for *latria*, *dulia* [Col. 0027A], and everlasting religion. The images are to be regarded without care and without honor, since they can do neither harm nor good. God is to be approached with hope, love, honor, and joy without end.

XI. Add that, so that every superstition may be cast away, no image is to be painted on the walls of a church and no statue is to be erected; nor should such images be called holy, because nothing is holy except the temple of God (1 Cor.), so that the one true God may be worshiped forever and ever. Amen.

## On the administration of the entire ecclesiastical order

*(We have prefixed this title, following the author’s intention.)*

The emperor Louis had convened a very large assembly of the ecclesiastical and lay orders concerning the reform of the Church. Among the others, Adalard [Col. 0027B] and Helisachar shone forth like the brightest torches: the former by the integrity of his life and the splendor of his office, the latter by the light of his learning. With one heart, they all loudly proclaimed that the dignity of the Church must be restored. Agobard welcomed their eager expressions; he pleaded and acted on behalf of the Church, turning the minds of each toward the glory of the Church, which was almost collapsing. Let them build and raise up the walls of Jerusalem, already falling into ruin.

From there he attacks the sacrilege of lay fraudsters who live off ecclesiastical embezzlement and make God’s property the property of sacrilegious men. He proves from the earliest beginnings, growth, and increase of the nascent Church—by which it began to become wealthy under the guidance of the Spirit—that canons had been established prohibiting the seizure of ecclesiastical property and allowing no one to depart from those canons without the ruin of his conscience. He asks the emperor to provide a remedy and the assembly to plead against the sacrilegious Gauls [Col. 0027C].

The speech of Agobard was received eagerly by the aged Helisachar and Adalard. They advise the emperor on this matter; and he, having summoned a council of the political and Levitical orders, extinguished the mutual disagreements that had disturbed laymen and bishops over the possession of ecclesiastical property. Since, however, there were certain detractors who were spreading rumors everywhere about Agobard’s audacity and ignorance and proclaiming him the author of the dissension, Agobard dispelled this stain. He presented a likeness of the truth to a certain friend who had questioned him about the matter.

From this occasion he found an opportunity to write about ecclesiastical affairs and their administration, drawing testimonies from both Testaments. Its principal headings are these: On priests. On the payment of tithes. On the punishment of sacrilege. On the honor paid to bishops throughout all ages. On not alienating churches; and he inserts perpetual denunciations against the Simonians. Since all these matters rest on passages rather than arguments, I leave them to the reader.

## Book Arranged from Divine Judgments

### On divine judgments against those who think that God’s judgment is revealed by water, fire, or weapons

The title of this volume does not seem to me entirely appropriate. For this is its subject. [Col. 0027D]

There were two methods of purging hidden fraud and crime: iron and fire. The first belonged to Gundobad, who ordered disputes, where there were no witnesses, to be settled by iron and weapons. The second arose from an old-established custom. When witnesses were lacking, the popular ordeal was employed, namely, cold water or red-hot iron [Col. 0028A]. Agobard attacks these practices as abominable, showing that hidden matters are never brought to light by such contests. He exhorts people to peace and embraces almost the whole of Christian ethics.

*[Note: Institut. juris canon., I. IV, tit. 2. In the History of Burgundy.]*

## A Sermon of Agobard

This discourse is exceptionally elegant, varied, and illuminated on every side by divine figures. Its subject is Christ. But from that starting point it spreads out and wanders into various fields: the Church, its merits, and the Antichrist. Since these matters are somewhat *ἀμεθοδικά*—lacking orderly method—I leave them aside.

## On the Division of the Empire

Mindful of the peace of the empire and of the uncertain outcome of life, the emperor Louis, having summoned an assembly of all Gaul, divided the empire into three kingdoms and conferred the chief portion [Col. 0028B] upon Lothar, after requiring, as was customary, oaths of fidelity and obedience from everyone. Lothar revolted and attacked his father. The ecclesiastics favored this emperor, to whose service they had been bound by a solemn oath. When his father wished to inflict penalties upon them, Agobard boldly replied that he himself had been the cause of that upheaval and public dissension, because he had divided the empire. And, more boldly still, he openly declared that he would obey Lothar because of the bond of his oath, and so forth.

## On the Comparison of the Two Governments

Two letters dealing with the same subject are contained here. The first is addressed to the emperor Louis, in which our bishop sets forth the reasons for his flight and delay: the public disturbances. From there he attacks the summit of imperial splendor [Col. 0028C], proving that it is subject to pontifical majesty, both from the authority of the canons and from certain testimonies of the Latin Fathers. He therefore advises the emperor to receive Pope Gregory kindly when he comes into Gaul as a mediator of domestic peace, and to submit himself to him with the greatest humility.

The sense of the second is as follows. Lothar’s revolt had carried away almost all Italy, the pope, and also many Gallic bishops, with whose help he intended to take the empire from his father. The true Gauls resisted and summoned Agobard; he refused. They held an assembly, whose chief points against his contumacy, and in support of Gallic liberty, were these:

1. The Roman bishop is to be called pope and brother, not father or pontiff.

[Col. 0028D]

2. Imperial majesty has greater power in administering the Church than pontifical authority.

3. The emperor is not to be dishonored by a presumptuous excommunication.

4. A single pontiff may be rejected without injury to the apostolic see.

5. In matters of faith, bishops are accustomed to swear an oath to the emperor.

6. Agobard, primate of Aquitaine, if he obeyed the pontiff rather than the emperor, would henceforth possess no authority to excommunicate and no jurisdiction over the other parishes.

7. A bishop who obeyed the pontiff rather than the council of the Gallic Church would be deprived of fellowship and honor [Col. 0029A].

Agobard responds to each point in detail. As far as he can, he breaks down these privileges because of their common alliance with the pontiff and Lothar. He strives to prove that the emperor and the Gallic Churches depend upon the episcopal see. Then he attributes all the disturbances and burning upheavals of the empire both to Louis’s inactivity and to the hidden frauds of the queens whom he had married. With the greatest boldness he favors the policy Lothar had pursued against his stepmothers. Finally, he rouses Louis’s mind to repentance and humility, so that by recovering his senses thereafter the affairs of the empire might be more secure.

## The Public Penance of the Emperor Louis

When affairs had been pacified, the emperor Louis was compelled in a public assembly [Col. 0029B] to undertake public penance because of the luxury, inactivity, and cowardice of his former life. He acknowledged his fault, asked forgiveness, and prostrated himself before the altar. Having confessed three or four times, shedding tears, and having laid aside his weapons and scepter, he received penance through the imposition of the bishops’ hands, and so forth.

## On the Ancient Rite of Singing Psalms in the Church, and on the Correction of the Antiphonary

*(These two headings should not have been separated but joined into one, since they treat precisely the same subject.)*

A certain sectarian arose at Lyons who brought astonishing calumnies against the ecclesiastical rites and bespattered them with blemishes. These were his claims:

1. The Church of Lyons had departed from the genuine manner of singing [Col. 0029C].

[Col. 0030A]

2. The ancient Fathers had been accustomed to sing in poetic form.

3. There was no reason why nocturnal vigils should be held.

4. There were many other songs that were not found in Scripture.

In his Antiphonary and Responsory he also added the following blasphemies and monstrosities:

5. Christ had brought human nature down from heaven.

6. The two natures were mixed into one.

7. Human beings had received Christ, whom previously they had known and desired by natural impulse.

8. Christ had slipped through the Virgin’s ear into the place of birth.

Agobard refutes each point.

On the first: the Church of Lyons had adhered firmly to the statutes of the Levitical and apostolic law [Col. 0030B] and therefore could not err.

On the second: the ancient Church had strongly rejected the poetic manner of singing.

On the third: David had established daily and nightly vigils in the Levitical choir.

On the fourth: Scripture is so complete that nothing is to be added to it or taken away; whatever is found in it is to be sung, but nothing else.

He tears apart the remaining monstrosities in the same manner and restores both the Antiphonary and the Responsory entirely to their former clarity.

These, then, are the principal doctrines of Agobard: certainly clear, profound, and shining with every beauty. May the reader enjoy them.

[Col. 0029C]

# The Book of Saint Agobard, Bishop of Lyons, Against the Dogma of Felix of Urgell, to the Emperor Louis the Pious

*[Note: Saint Agobard. We give Agobard the designation “saint” following the edition of Masson and because divine honors are paid to him in the Church of Lyons, where he is commonly called Saint Agobo. He is also called a saint in the martyrologies of those regions. We have little to say about Agobard beyond what is found among the eulogies. Nevertheless, following our customary practice, we shall here give a brief account of his life. They say that he was a Gaul by birth, although this is not sufficiently established. He was initially co-bishop with Leidrad, archbishop of Lyons—the office we now call coadjutor, though, as I believe, not with the title of future succession. For Leidrad could not have done this by private authority, nor without the knowledge of the prince, nor anywhere except in a synod, whether provincial or general. Later, when Leidrad withdrew and retired to the monastery of Soissons, Agobard ascended that see in the year 813, “with the consent,” as Ado says, “of the emperor and the entire synod of the bishops of Gaul,” or, as Hugh of Flavigny says more explicitly, “with the consent of the emperor and the entire synod of the Gallic bishops.” I had been inclined to interpret that synod as the one celebrated in the same year at Chalon by the bishops and abbots of the whole of Lyonnaise Gaul. But Ado and Hugh of Flavigny sufficiently indicate that Agobard’s substitution took place in the presence of the emperor and in the universal or entire synod of the Gallic bishops—that is, in the general and plenary synod of the bishops of the Frankish kingdom. This cannot apply to the synod of Chalon, which was merely provincial. Therefore it can refer to no other synod than that of Mainz, held in the same year; and that the emperor Louis was present at it is shown by Ivo of Chartres, part IX, chapter 82. Agobard’s substitution gave rise to discussion because the ancient canons appeared to have been violated; some insisted that they had to be preserved intact and could not be violated for any reason. The canons seemed to have been infringed in two ways. First, it was established that two persons could not occupy a single see. Second, it was forbidden for any bishop to choose his own successor. The opponents nevertheless yielded, though the reason for their yielding is unknown. I readily believe that Agobard, aided by his own virtues and by the efforts of the excellent prince, prevailed over his envious opponents; also because Leidrad had inclined toward him—a man highly distinguished at court, who seemed to have won great authority for himself by his final deed. There were also many examples from antiquity that allowed such a substitution to take place.

Agobard fell upon the worst and most embittered times, as he himself complains more than once. Yet amid these evils of the age he retained a constancy worthy of a bishop, although otherwise he was timid and scarcely dared to speak before the great. For he frequently emphasizes his own modesty and timidity. Above all, he burned with hostility toward the Jews: he both detested their impious rites and profane ceremonies and wished them abolished. Hence arose serious storms and tempests against Agobard. He also sharpened his pen—indeed, very sharply and in more than one place—against the law of Gundobad, which he considered strongly opposed to Christian piety and simplicity. He likewise directed his strength robustly and learnedly against the error of Felix, bishop of Urgell, who had died shortly before at the city of Lyons. Above all, he was a perpetual and steadfast defender of the canons, so much so that he severely rebuked even the Romans of his own time for despising the Gallic canons on the—if Heaven wills—sole ground that the modern Romans had not approved them or that Roman legates had not been present at their enactment.

It would be surprising if a man of such character had not incurred the envy of his contemporaries. Accordingly, he had to write an apology for himself against the slanders and attacks of the abbot Fredegis, otherwise a very distinguished man, and also against certain men of Provence and Septimania who were highly hostile to the name of Agobard. Meanwhile, as the question of the adoration and worship of images grew heated, it occupied the efforts of learned men. Agobard too expressed his opinion on the matter: he was sharp and vehement against the adoration of images, yet pious and religious toward the saints, whose imitation he urges upon all Christians.

Thus he became a principal enemy of superstitions and vigorously attacked the folly of those who thought that hail, thunder, and the other storms of heaven could be raised by magicians and enchanters, whom that age for this very reason called *tempestarii*. I am convinced that he was truly a great man. Yet by one very wicked deed—whatever some may think to the contrary—he stained his illustrious deeds and great virtues. For when Lothar Augustus dared in the year 833 to suppress his father Louis to such an extent that he even confined him in prison and arranged for him to be subjected to public penance, Agobard, I say, went over to Lothar’s side and defended it with such intensity and stubbornness of mind that for this very reason he was counted among the principal leaders of the Lotharian faction.

For that reason he was removed from the episcopal office [Col. 0032C] by the authority of the synod held at Thionville in the year 835. The matter was again brought forward the following year at Stramiacum, not far from Lyons, but without result because of Agobard’s absence. Finally, when harmony had been restored between Louis and Lothar, Agobard was permitted to return to his see.

At last he died among the people of Saintonge in Second Aquitaine, during a royal expedition, in the year 840, as I believe. For in that year, as is written in the Bertinian Annals, the emperor Louis was in Aquitaine, attempting to settle the Aquitanian disturbances. The author of the Shorter Chronicle of Saint Benignus of Dijon likewise records that Agobard died in that year, on the eighth day before the Ides of July.

From his surviving writings it appears that he was known to and familiar with the most distinguished men of that age: Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims; Bernard of Vienne; Nibridius and Bartholomew of Narbonne; the abbots Adalard, Wala, Helisachar, and Hilduin; Matfrid, count of Orléans, who then held the foremost position with Louis the Pious; and Walahfrid Strabo, abbot of Reichenau. Whether he was abbot of the monastery of Saint Medard of Soissons for three years, as some have maintained—namely, from the year 830, when Hilduin the abbot was sent into exile by Louis the Pious—I leave to others to investigate.

This is sufficient to say about Agobard’s life. Let us now return to our subject.]*

*[Note: Against the Dogma of Felix. We have taken this title from the list of Agobard’s books prefixed to Masson’s manuscript codex, where it reads: “Book I of Agobard, bishop, Against the Dogma of Felix, to the Emperor.” For this book had no other title in the old codex. One must marvel at Masson’s audacity: not content with the old inscription of the letter to Louis the Pious, he added another of his own as though it came from the old codex. Thus, at the very beginning of Agobard’s works, he printed: “Agobard, bishop of Lyons, sends greetings to the Emperor Louis.” Who would not believe that Masson had seen this written in the old codex? Yet nothing of the sort is found there.]*

To the most religious of Christians, the kindest of the kind, the most tranquil of the gentle, the lover of Christ, and therefore the most pious Augustus, victor and triumphant, the most glorious lord Louis, emperor, Agobard, one of the least of your faithful servants, has sent the little work appended below for your most sincere, subtle, and sacred judgment: a work which I have published, or rather compiled, against a new—or rather revived from an ancient source—heresy [Col. 0030D], on account of certain people, for whom I thought it useful, as is explained more fully there.

*[Note: The Revived Heresy. The Felician heresy was propagated from the Nestorian heresy, as Agobard will show below; Pope Adrian I also writes this to the Spanish bishops in the *Caroline Code*, title 97.]*

Therefore, pious ruler and lord, head of the world, glory of the earth, distinguished boast of all Catholics, you who illuminate the faith and extend peace [Col. 0031A], I beseech your gentleness to deign to read through the aforesaid little work in contemplation of the Son of God, who assists your empire, so that it may be approved or rejected by your keen judgment [Col. 0032A].

*[Note: I beseech your gentleness.
