This was undoubtedly imitated from the booklet of Prayers by the presbyters Marcellinus and Faustinus, which begins: “We beseech your gentleness, most pious emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, that you may tirelessly deign to read these things in contemplation of Christ, the Son of God, who aids your empire.”]*

For if it is approved, it is commended by you for reading to those whom it will benefit; but if it is rejected, its author is corrected through you. For apostolic teaching urges everyone to grow in knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ and commands everyone to be ready to give an answer to those who ask for an account of the hope that is in us. It also requires a priest to embrace the faithful word that accords with the teaching, so that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and rebuke those who contradict it. If this was always to be pursued, how much more now, when we see that the time is already near of which the Lord says: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you suppose that he will find faith upon the earth?” [Col. 0033A]

## I

After the death of that Felix who had once been bishop in the see of Urgell, we found a certain document issued by him in the form of questions and answers. As we read and considered it, we carefully observed that the man had, as far as he could, craftily and deceitfully restored the whole corruption of his doctrine, in which he had formerly been exposed and convicted and on account of which he had been deposed from the episcopal dignity [Col. 0033B]. Although he later suppressed some words that he had previously uttered rashly, he nevertheless now added others that he had then kept silent.

*[Note: The See of Urgell. It still retains that name today. It is commonly called La Seu d’Urgell, that is, “the See of Urgell.” It is a famous city of Tarraconian Spain, situated on the ridge of the Pyrenees. Einhard writes in the Annals under the year 792: “Urgell is a city situated on the ridge of the Pyrenees. Its bishop, named Felix, a Spaniard by nationality, had been consulted by Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, by letter about what he ought to think concerning the humanity of our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ: whether he should believe and call him, insofar as he is man, the proper or adopted Son of God. Felix, with great rashness and lack of consideration and contrary to the ancient teaching of the Catholic Church, not only declared him to be adopted, but also took the greatest pains to defend his perverse opinion in books written to the aforesaid bishop. For this reason he was brought to the royal palace, where the king then resided at Regensburg, a city of Bavaria in which he had also wintered. There, when a council of bishops had been assembled, Felix was heard; and, having been convicted of error, he was sent to Rome into the presence of Pope Adrian. There, in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, he confessed and renounced his heresy before the pope himself. Having done this, he returned to his own city.”]*

*[Note: Deposed. Until now it had remained uncertain at what time Felix, bishop of Urgell, was finally deposed from his episcopal dignity. Nor do I agree with Juan de Mariana, otherwise a very learned man, who infers from a corrupt passage in Ado of Vienne that this deposition took place at the Council of Frankfurt, which was convened by order of Charlemagne in the year 794. “After the matter had been discussed,” Mariana writes (*History of Spain*, book VII, chapter 8), “the wicked opinion was condemned along with its authors; and, unless they changed, Felix and Elipandus were forbidden to celebrate the sacred rites. Felix, as Ado of Vienne reports, was banished by the judgment of the Fathers and ended his life at Lyons without ever abandoning his error.”

I would more readily believe that the synod granted Felix pardon if he repented, and that he renounced his error and thus remained in his episcopal dignity. But since he returned once more to his former errors, he was undoubtedly brought to Aachen before Charlemagne and deposed at the synod held there in the year 799. That this deed was carried out at that time is clear from the letter he wrote immediately after that synod to the clergy and people of Urgell. He indicates plainly that he was not then a bishop, since he begins: “In the name of God. Felix, formerly an unworthy bishop,” and so forth. He had indeed once been a bishop—that is, before he was deposed from his episcopal dignity at that synod. Then, by order of the prince, not of the bishops, as Mariana incorrectly writes, he was exiled to Lyons, the most illustrious city of Gaul.]*

I, for my part, having refuted that document as best I could according to the truth of the faith—or having published it as something that ought to be refuted—learned that certain of the brethren had taken offense. Not, as I think, through perversity of mind, but through simplicity of understanding, they supposed that I had not done this out of zeal for the faith but out of the zeal of envy, as is customary among those who, desirous of empty glory, disparage good men in order to try to raise themselves above them; and, if by their slanders they succeed in preventing those men from being admired, obtain the glory of admiration for themselves.

Since among us there are people who need both to know the integrity of the faith, by which they may be able to avoid the evil of unbelief, and to obey right judgments, so that they may deserve to advance in the doctrine of piety, I considered it appropriate to take up and amplify what the aforesaid man thought wrongly and to set against his words—wherein he departed from the truth of the faith—the judgments of the holy Fathers. Thus, whoever deigns to read may recognize with what caution he should follow the purest understanding of Catholic truth.

## II

I am not addressing these remarks to learned and eloquent men who, by judging all these matters perfectly, are capable of showing what should be approved or rejected, and who perhaps will not even deign to read this work, composed in rustic simplicity [Col. 0034B]. I address them instead to people like myself, whom I truly know to benefit from correcting their faith with the greatest care. These people, admiring the life of the aforesaid Felix, think that everything he said must be approved.

*[Note: Admiration of Felix’s Former Life. It was therefore established in those times that Felix was a bishop of the old school and that his conduct was beyond reproach. For not only does Agobard teach this [Col. 0034C], but so does Alcuin, a writer of the same period. These are his words in his letter to Elipandus, bishop of Toledo: “For we read in the letters of blessed Felix—a man outstanding in religious life and conspicuous for holiness—that he should wish to love and preach the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical unity, without which no one can please God.” And below: “Although the aforesaid servant of God, Felix, lives a praiseworthy life before men, nevertheless, as it seems, in many respects he does not wholly and fully follow the judgment of the Fathers in his profession of the Catholic faith.” Again: “I have also thought it right to urge your most holy will most earnestly to endeavor, by your holy prayers and most gentle exhortations, to convert that venerable man Felix to the unity and truth of the Catholic faith. For God is faithful, gracious, and merciful, and will in no way forget his many good deeds, his religious life, and the labors in which he toils day and night with untiring will. Consider and reflect more diligently how great will be your glory and reward before God and his saints in the salvation of your brother—of so great a man, of such outstanding rank and holiness, a servant of Christ” [Col. 0034D]. Again: “That Felix, whom you declare to be supreme in charity, chaste, and adorned with good character, we have in the camp of Christ.” Then, in the epilogue of Book IV against Elipandus, he sets before those who seem to doubt the grounds of the Catholic faith the example of Felix, converted from error to Catholicism: “Instructed by the example of that religious man, of great renown among his own people,” and so forth. Finally, in letter 76 (now 4), he praises Felix for his piety and asks his prayers before God as those of a holy man. Thus he is not without reason called saint in the ancient records of the Church of Urgell. Nothing, therefore, is more deceptive than corrupt religion. From this it may meanwhile be inferred that sound doctrine does not immediately follow from a bishop’s holy life. For God sometimes tests us, so that it may become clear whether we love him or not. “The reason is clearer than light,” says Vincent of Lérins, “why divine providence sometimes permits certain teachers of the Churches to preach certain new doctrines: ‘that the Lord your God may test you.’ And indeed it is a great trial when one whom you think a prophet, a disciple of prophets, a teacher and defender of truth, whom you have embraced with the highest reverence and love, suddenly and secretly introduces harmful errors,” and so forth. He then adduces the examples of Nestorius, Photinus, and Apollinaris, who were known to have been great men and very powerful opponents of heretics.]*

Not knowing that faith is not to be measured by a man’s life, but that life is to be tested by the faith [Col. 0035A].

*[Note: Life Is to Be Tested by Faith. This is evidently in accordance with Tertullian’s thought, who says in chapter 3 of *On the Prescription Against Heretics*: “Do we test faith by persons, or persons by faith?”]*

For although many who believe rightly perish because they live wrongly, no one who believes wrongly is saved by living well. For only almighty God knows the hidden things of human beings: who, despite a blameworthy life, carries a humble mind, or who [Col. 0035D], despite a praiseworthy life, carries a proud one.

*[Note: With a Praiseworthy Life, That Is, a Proud Mind. Thus arrogance can exist even in rags. Thus even those who are said to be saints can sometimes be proud. Optatus of Milevis states this admirably and very appropriately to Agobard’s thought in the second book Against Parmenian: “Sins with humility have been found better than innocence with pride.” Likewise, in Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 5, when a certain boy had seized a viper unharmed and the brothers of the monastery were exalting the deed as a miracle, the abbot restrained him with rods so that his immature age would not become insolent, repeatedly saying “that consciousness of weakness was better than vanity about virtues.” See Saint Gregory, book IV, *Pastoral Care*.]*

Neither person is perfect. But which of the two displeases the author more is known only to him. For we know that those who are rightly conscious of their weakness do not believe themselves to be saints, even when others call them so. But those who, because of their good conduct, trust themselves to be saints when others praise them, and consider themselves qualified to judge and despise some on account of their carnal life and others on account of the foolishness of their understanding—indeed, who disparage everyone alike—cannot please the one who said: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart.”

Whoever truly strives to please God should subject his soul to God with complete humility. For faith is the first thing that subjugates the soul to God; then come the precepts of living. When these are observed, our hope is strengthened and charity is nourished. Since knowledge and action together make a person blessed, just as error must be avoided in knowledge, so wickedness must be guarded against in action.

## III

Therefore I beseech you, beloved people, to whom I say that this work is necessary: do not let simple words weary you; rather, let the purity of the faith delight you [Col. 0035C]. For, as one of the Fathers says (Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book IV, chapter 11), in the words of those who discuss matters, truth is to be loved, not the words:

> “For what good is a golden key if it cannot open what we wish to open? Or what harm is there in a wooden one if it can do so, when we seek nothing except that what is closed may lie open?”

Whoever entirely scorns reading our work will nevertheless find here, sufficiently set forth, the judgments of the holy Fathers, with which he may compare Felix’s understanding. Let him only not neglect to purify his faith according to their rule. For, as blessed Athanasius says: “Unless someone preserves the Catholic faith whole and inviolate, he will without doubt perish forever” [Col. 0036A].

And as another teacher says (Augustine, on Psalm 147): “Just as bodily virginity is an untouched body, so the virginity of the soul is an incorrupt faith.”

He also says (Augustine, *Tractate VIII on the Gospel of John*):

> “Christ is the truth in such a way that everything true is understood in Christ: the true Word of God, God equal to the Father, a true soul, true flesh, a true man, true God, a true birth, true suffering. If you call any one of these things false, corruption enters; worms of lies are born from the serpent’s poison, and nothing will remain whole. For wherever there is the corruption of some falsehood, there the integrity of truth will not exist.”

*[Note: True Suffering. In Augustine’s Tractate VIII on the Gospel of John and in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences* from Augustine, chapter 326, the following is found: “A true birth, true suffering, a true death, a true resurrection. If you call any one of these things false,” and so forth. But these words do not occur in Augustine. The sentence “For wherever there is the corruption of some falsehood, there the integrity of truth will not exist,” however, is found in Prosper.]*

These statements are very useful for assessing the subtlety of the truth that I am about to discuss here, provided that I have been capable of explaining what I say adequately.

[Col. 0036B]

## IV

The heretic Nestorius divides and separates the two natures in the one Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, so completely that in setting forth his doctrine he speaks of one as though he were speaking of two—as though he supposed that the Word of God was one and Emmanuel another—even though he often confesses that they are one person.

Eutyches, on the other hand, speaks in his doctrine of the one Son of God in his single person as though he were one substance. Although he confesses the eternal birth of his divinity and does not deny the temporal birth of his humanity, he nevertheless mixes and confuses the two substances so completely that he seems to proclaim only one.

Since, then, the truth of the faith rejects both Nestorius and Eutyches and holds the middle position between them, blessed Cyril, defender of that same truth and bishop of Alexandria, while wishing to correct Nestorius’s depravity, offended blessed John, bishop of the Church of Antioch, and those who were with him because of the obscurity of his words, dealing as he was with an exceedingly subtle matter. A division consequently arose between the Antiochene and Alexandrian Churches.

The Antiochenes asked Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, to act against blessed Cyril. And, remarkably, although both parties were Catholic—both the Antiochenes and the Alexandrians—because blessed Cyril was thought to be a heretic, though he was not, Theodoret found a middle position between the heretic Nestorius and the Catholic Cyril. From it Theodoret himself, while fighting for the truth, acted against the truth: while pleasing these Catholics, he displeased those. Yet this was corrected, with God’s help, through the efforts of John and Cyril.

### V

I have brought these matters forward for this reason: so that we may carefully consider how subtly, humbly, truthfully, and cautiously the truth of the faith must be sought. Therefore, before we discuss what the aforementioned Felix left in writing, I think I should first explain how, while still alive, he attempted, in his own words, to persuade certain people of several propositions that ought to be rejected.

As I have said, he once began teaching certain persons to believe that our Lord Jesus Christ, according to the flesh, truly did not know where Lazarus’s tomb was, since he said to his sisters, “Where have you laid him?” [Col. 0037B] (John 11:34), and that he truly did not know the day of judgment [Col. 0037C].

[Note: *To be ignorant of the day of judgment.* Alcuin also reproaches Felix with this same offense in Book V against Felix himself: “At last,” he says, “you came to the point where the same Lord speaks about the day of the final judgment—a day whose knowledge you labor to deny to Christ insofar as he is man, as can be recognized from your own words.” He then quotes Felix’s words, in which he seemed to have written as follows: “For he himself, you say, is the one who, according to the foreknowledge of his divinity, foretold the day of judgment through the prophet: ‘The day of vengeance is in my heart; the year of my redemption has come.’ Nevertheless, because of the nature of his humanity, he is the one who declares in the Gospel according to Mark: ‘But concerning that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, except the Father alone.’”]

He also truly did not know what the two disciples walking along the road were discussing concerning the things that had happened in Jerusalem; and he likewise truly did not know whether Peter loved him more than the other disciples when he said, “Simon Peter, do you love me more than these?” (John 21:16).

When I learned this, I approached him [Note: *I approached him.* That is, in the city of Lyon, where Ado records that he lived in exile in the following words: “Felix, the heretical bishop of Urgell, was detected dogmatizing that our Lord Jesus Christ was the adoptive, not the proper, Son of God. He was brought into the presence of Adrian, the Roman pontiff, and renounced the heresy merely in words. A synod was again held against this heresy at Frankfurt, with the legates of the Apostolic See, Bishops Theophylact and Stephen, presiding; and, convicted and condemned by the authority of the holy Fathers, Felix was again banished with his error into perpetual exile at Lyon. He is said to have died in that very error.” Thus reads the old edition, and indeed it is better than the edition printed at Paris by the Sonnian press in 1583 under the care of Laurentius de la Barre. In that edition the final words of this passage read: “Felix, convicted and condemned, was again sent into perpetual exile with his error,” and so forth. This wording misled the most learned Joannes Mariana.]

in the presence of those to whom he was making these assertions, and asked him whether he really held this opinion. When he attempted to affirm it, I rebuked him and denounced his perverse statements. I showed the others, as best I could, with what vigilance they ought to reject these views and in what sense they should understand those passages of Scripture. I also sent Felix for reading certain statements of the holy Fathers that contradicted his blasphemies. After reading them [Col. 0038A], he promised that he would diligently apply himself to every correction.

For this reason, when I dismissed him quietly, I did not think it necessary to publish his same blasphemies abroad, because they did not concern me [Col. 0037D].

[Note: *Nor did it concern me.* Felix was a bishop in another province, namely in Narbonensis. For at that time, after the Moors’ arrival in Spain and the destruction of Tarragona, the bishops of those regions were under the metropolitan of Narbonensis, as has been explained more fully in the notes to the Council of Narbonne held against Felix. Thus Faustinus, bishop of Lyon, refused to judge the case of Marcianus, bishop of Arles, because he was a bishop in another province—namely, Narbonensis—as the illustrious Petrus de Marca, archbishop of Paris, explains more fully in Book I, chapter 10, section 8, and Book VII, chapter 1, section 5, of *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire.]

### VI

After his death [Col. 0038C], I learned from certain faithful brothers who had heard it from him that he had said that God, the Son of God the Father, ought in no way to be called one who suffered or was crucified; rather, the man assumed by him suffered and was crucified. He tried to confirm this by the example of Isaac, who was led by his father to be sacrificed, but was not himself sacrificed: a ram was sacrificed in his place. Thus, as he imagined, the son of God was represented in Isaac and the son of man in the ram.

[Note: *After his death.* From this it may be inferred—and Ado also reports it—that Felix died at Lyon. This is also evident from the very beginning of this book, where Agobard says that after Felix’s death he found a document composed by him in the form of questions and answers. I think that the letter concerning the confession of faith, written from Lyon—where I believe he was exiled by Charlemagne in 799 after the Council of Aachen—to the clergy and people of Urgell was composed by Felix; it was published among the works of Alcuin. Felix therefore appears to have survived his deposition for a long time, namely until the beginning of the reign of Louis the Pious.]

The aforementioned Felix acted in this way because he utterly refused to accept, or was unable to persuade himself to believe, that in our one Lord Jesus Christ the union of two natures had been substantially accomplished, and that God the Word had been united to the flesh according to subsistence, as will clearly appear below from his own words. Against these views we too, with God’s help, shall set the corresponding testimonies of the holy Fathers.

For, fearing that he might fall into the confusion of Eutyches, he collapsed into the division of Nestorius [Col. 0038D].

[Note: *The division of Nestorius.* Alcuin writes in Book I against Felix: “We follow neither the Nestorian division, which wished to introduce two persons in Christ on account of the two natures, nor the confusion of Eutyches, who, on account of the one person, wished to weave one nature into Christ. Both deviated from the Catholic faith and were equal in impiety, because they did not hold the right faith; yet they were unequal in their error, because the one confuses and the other divides.”]

But since we have said that the subject of our discussion fell into Nestorius’s worst division, I think it appropriate to set down here the statements of Nestorius before we proceed to examine Felix’s words. Thus the prudent reader may recognize how consonantly Felix thought with Nestorius, and, wherever he wickedly divides the two substances in the one Lord and again takes refuge, as it were, in the unity of the person by saying, “Nevertheless, one in both, not two,” how closely he imitates Nestorius in this as well.

### VII

Nestorius says that the Lord was “formed by the power of the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb, made from a woman and made under the law, so that he might redeem us all from slavery to the law; already predestined, receiving adoption, living ineffably for himself, causing him to die according to human law, but raising him from the dead and leading him into heaven, and making him sit at the right hand of God. From there, having been placed above all principalities, powers, virtues, dominions, and every name that is named—not only in this age but also in the age to come—he received worship from every creature, [Col. 0039B] as one possessing an inseparable conjunction with the divine nature, with every creature offering worship through reference to God and through its understanding.

“And we do not say that there are two sons or two Lords, because there is one Son of the Father according to the Word, God the only-begotten Son of the Father; and, having been joined to and made a participant in the Son, this man shares the name and honor, while the Lord according to essence is God the Word, with whom this man, being joined, shares honor. Therefore we do not call these two sons or two Lords, because, with the Lord and Son established according to substance, he maintains an inseparable conjunction with him; assumed for the sake of our salvation, he is granted the name and honor of Son and Lord.

“This is not like one who, established according to himself, is a son—hence, according to blessed Paul, we too are called sons—but he alone possesses this distinction: participating in conjunction, adoption, and lordship with God the Word, he removes every suspicion of two sons and two Lords, while, through his conjunction with God the Word, he receives from every creature all the faith, understanding, and contemplation belonging to him, and, by reference to God, worship as well.

“Therefore we call Jesus Christ the true Son and Lord, through whom all things were made, understanding primarily God the Word as substantially the Son of God.”

Again the same Nestorius says: “If anyone says that he who is Emmanuel is true God, and not rather ‘God with us’—that is, that he dwelt in the nature that is ours, because he was united to our nature, which he assumed from the Virgin Mary”—and after some intervening words he adds, “let him be anathema.”

Again he says: “If anyone dares to say that after the assumption of man the Son of God is naturally one, although he is Emmanuel, let him be anathema.”

Again he says: “If anyone, after the incarnation, names God the Word as someone other than Christ,” and after a few words adds, “let him be anathema.”

And again: “If anyone says that the man created in the Virgin is the only-begotten Son,” [Col. 0040A] and after a few words adds, “let him be anathema.”

There you have the statements of Nestorius. If you compare them with Felix’s words, both in the conjunction of the person and in the division of the natures, you will find that they proceed with one and the same meaning.

### VIII

I think that your charity should also be warned concerning the fact that Felix frequently takes pleasure in saying “the assumed man” or “the form of a servant.” Although these expressions can be used piously, as they are very frequently found in the holy Fathers, it must nevertheless be considered that they can also be used impiously, as these words displeased us in Nestorius.

To this blessed Cyril replied as follows (*Defense of the Twelve Anathemas against Theodoret*, chapter 7): “Accustomed to hold what is better and truer, and attaining the more subtle understandings necessary for explaining the mystery and for perfect knowledge, in accordance with the intention of the sacred Scriptures and the gentleness of the holy Fathers, we do not say that a man was assumed by God the Word and joined to him externally according to a mode of inhabitation; rather, we determine that he was made man. For this reason we say that those who presume to speak of an assumed man, and affirm that he ought to be co-worshiped with the Son of God as one alongside another, have departed from the piety of the doctrines.”

Again he says: “Thus he became man; he did not assume a man, as Nestorius prefers. And so that it might be believed that he became man while remaining what he was—namely, God according to nature—he is therefore also said to hunger and, from the weariness of travel, to grow weary” [Col. 0040B].

[Note: *To grow weary.* Thus the old manuscript reads throughout; Masson had printed *flacessere* instead. It ought to be written *lassescere*, following the ancient and excellent spelling. We have nevertheless chosen in good faith to reproduce the reading of the old manuscript. Alcuin, in Book I against Elipandus, speaking of the devil, says: “He wished to test whether he was the Son of God, whom he saw hunger, thirst, and grow weary.”]

—and so forth.

### IX

In the document mentioned above, Felix said, after some preceding material, asking as though in question form: “Did God the almighty Father beget the Son by will or by necessity?”

He answers: “With respect to the essence of his divinity, neither by will nor by necessity, but by nature. For in the true Son begotten from the substance of the Father, will cannot precede birth, where nature comes first. Yet neither was it by necessity, since necessity certainly does not exist in God.

“But with respect to the substance of his humanity, he begot that same Son of his not from himself, but created him from the substance of the virgin mother and willed him to be born. For this reason, with respect to our redemption, he is believed to be his Son by will, not by any necessity.”

### X

In this statement Felix first prepares for himself, by means of a superfluous and empty question—whether the Father begot the Son by will or by necessity—the opportunity to arrive at what he thinks wrongly but does not dare to explain openly.

For when he says, “In the true Son begotten from the substance of the Father,” he divides the divinity from the humanity in the Lord in such a way that he calls him the true Son only according to his divinity, in which he was begotten from the substance of the Father. According to his humanity, however, in which he says that he was created from the substance of the virgin mother, he considers him not to be true, although he does not dare to explain this openly.

This deception is apparent in the fact that he speaks of the substance of the divinity as though it belonged to another person apart from the humanity. By speaking only of the substance of the divinity—“In the true Son”—he wishes to demonstrate that he is not the true Son in both substances.

But when he adds, “Will cannot precede birth where nature comes first,” he openly professes a falsehood. For in the almighty and eternal God all things are eternal, and nothing accrued to him in time who created time. For a nature without beginning and requiring no increase to have is to be, and to be is everlasting; just as it admits no end, so it admits no change.

Therefore, in him nature does not precede will, nor will counsel, nor counsel the Word; for just as he was never without the Word, so he was never without wisdom, counsel, will, or anything else that can truthfully be said of God.

### XI

We confess our Lord, the only Son of God, to be true God, and likewise believe him to be the true Son. For he is not one son from the Father and another from the mother. Although divinity is one thing and humanity another, he is the same one and true Son in both, as blessed Cyril teaches us:

“One, therefore, is the Son; one is the Lord Jesus Christ, both before the incarnation and after the incarnation. For the Son who is the Word of God the Father is not one, and the one born again from the holy Virgin another; rather, the very same one who is God before the ages is believed to have been brought forth according to the flesh from a woman [Col. 0041C]. This does not mean that his divinity received from her its beginning of being, or that he took from the holy Virgin the principle of his subsistence; rather, as I have said, it means that the Word who subsists before the ages is said to have been born from her according to the flesh. His flesh became his own, just as each of us has his own body.”

### XII

That he is believed to be wholly true God, blessed Cyril himself teaches as follows (*Anathema I*): “If anyone does not confess that Emmanuel is God in truth, and therefore that the holy Virgin is Mother of God because she bore bodily the Word from God made flesh, let him be anathema.”

Again, in the *Declaration of the Twelve Anathemas*: “We say that the Word was united to flesh possessing a rational soul, beyond understanding and ineffably, in the manner known to him alone. Therefore he remained God both in the assumption of the flesh, and there is one Son of God and of the Father, our Lord Jesus Christ—the very same one both before every age and time, insofar as he is understood as the Word and radiance of his substance, and in the last times, by the economy, man because of us.”

Again he says: “The Word became flesh from God the Father, not by a transition or conversion of his nature, but by making his own the flesh taken from the holy Virgin. One and the same is called Son: before the becoming human, still the Word without flesh; after the becoming human, the same one embodied.”

Again, in the *Defense of the Twelve Anathemas against Theodoret*, chapter 2:

“Since Nestorius everywhere destroys the birth according to the flesh of God the Word, and introduces for us only a unity of dignities, saying that the man united to God was honored with sonship by homonymy—that is, by the use of the same name—we must necessarily oppose his statements and say that a unity according to subsistence was accomplished. By ‘according to subsistence’ we declare nothing other than this: that by the sole nature or subsistence of the Word, the Word himself, truly united to human nature, without any change or confusion, as we have often said, is understood to be one Christ, and is one Christ, the same God and man.”

Again he says:

“We worship one and the same, because his body is not foreign to the Word but rather belongs to him, with which he sits with the Father—not as two sons sitting together, but as one with the flesh because of the unity. If we reject unity according to subsistence, we fall into proclaiming two sons. For we must divide everything and say that the man is specifically called the son, while God the Word, again specifically, naturally possesses the name and designation of Son.

“Therefore the one Lord Jesus Christ must not be divided into two sons. The reasoning of the true faith must in no way be understood in this way, nor should the unity of persons be understood as some have supposed.”

Again:

“A man proceeded from a woman without ceasing to be God, and was begotten from God the Father; but in the assumption of the flesh he remained what he had been. This is what the reasoning of subtle faith everywhere teaches.”

Again he says:

“Since divinely inspired Scripture speaks of one Son and Lord, after the ineffable unity, if you name Emmanuel God, we understand him as incarnate and made man, the Word from God the Father. Whether you call him man, we nevertheless recognize him as that very same one, participating economically in the conditions of humanity. We say that the one who is intangible became tangible, and that the one who is invisible became visible.

“For the body united to him was not foreign to him; we also say that it is tangible and visible. But those who do not believe in this way, and who, as I have said, distinguish subsistences after the unity and understand a mere conjunction between them according to dignity or authority alone, are excluded by the present anathema from those accustomed to think rightly.”

### XIII

Felix asks: “Did the Virgin Mary give birth to God and man in the same way and equally, or is she to be believed to be Mother of the divinity in one way and Mother of the humanity in another?”

He answers himself, saying: “Although the same glorious Virgin is faithfully believed to be the Mother of God and man, she is rightly confessed to be Mother of God in one way and Mother of man in another.”

### XIV

To these words we reply that they are not only blasphemous and worthy of every hatred, but also novel and unheard-of. For how could she be Mother of God in one way and Mother of man in another? Certainly she gave birth to God incarnate; and she is his mother in one single way, not in two—namely, in that God became and was born man in her and from her.

It is not the Catholic custom to call her “Mother of man”; she is always called Mother of God. If God became man and was born from her, he was certainly not born in two ways. For if he were born in two ways, he would also be born on two occasions—which it is impious to say.

Indeed, if God was born from her in one way and man in another, there are two: one God and another man; that is, the same one is not both God and man, nor is the same one man and God.

The heretic Nestorius, who held this view, did not say that God was born from Mary, but that a man was born from the seed of David. If this man were Catholic, he would believe that the same one is both God and man, and that he was born once and in one way only.

But since he says that the holy Virgin is Mother of God in one way and Mother of man in another, I think that, just as he does not speak according to customary usage, so he does not speak in a Catholic manner. Catholics certainly teach that the Lord has neither a mother in his divinity nor a father in his humanity.

But this man, by separating divinity from humanity, believes that she is Mother of God in one way and Mother of man in another. He partly reveals this when he says: “For the nature of the assumed humanity holds her to be its proper mother, while she was made Mother of God by the grace and condescension of the divinity.” In what follows he will reveal this even more fully and clearly, and then we shall reply to it at a more appropriate point.

### XV

Now, since he says that she is Mother of God in one way and Mother of man in another, although it has never been customary in the formulation of the faith to call her Mother of man—for it is hardly surprising that the mothers of all human beings are mothers of human beings—let us hear from the statements of the holy Fathers how she is to be proclaimed Mother of the man who was made, that is, of the Word made flesh.

For that eminent champion against Nestorian impiety, the most learned and blessed Cyril, says:

“We affirm, therefore, that the Word from God the Father became man in the assumption, was united to holy and living flesh, and truly proceeded from that very womb as man, without confusion, while remaining also the Word. Therefore the holy Virgin is also Mother of God.

“But I think it should be regarded as superfluous to say that she ought to be called Mother of man. For if there were some so exceedingly mad as to say that the nature of God the Word had flesh as a kind of source and beginning of its own essence, perhaps there would at some point have been a reason neither absurd nor contemptible for those who wished her also to be called Mother of man.

“But since this opinion is abominable and hateful to everyone, the holy Virgin is understood to be Mother of God only when one first accepts the faith—namely, that the Word from God the Father became flesh, that is, man. For the Virgin did not give birth, as I have said, to bare divinity.

“What advantage, then, is there in those who say that she ought also to be called Mother of man? As is clear, this is an invention devised by them against Christ. For they cannot bear to think or say that the one who was the Son from God the Father before the ages was, in the last times of the world, united without confusion and without change from the womb to flesh possessing a rational soul, and thus became ours according to manhood.”

### XVI

Again, after some intervening material, Felix asks in question form: “Is Christ the Lord, in both natures, equally the Son of God, or unequally?”

He then answers: “Not equally, but unequally.”

Next he asks in what manner this occurs, and answers affirmatively: “Since he contains within himself two natures, that is, the nature of his divinity and of our humanity, in the same way he is believed to be the Son of God in two ways.”

Here I beg and urge the reader—if indeed there is one willing to read—to weigh carefully what is being said. Above he said that the holy Virgin is Mother of God in one way and Mother of man in another. Now he says that our Lord is the Son of God in two ways, and unequally in those ways.

Behold four modes, distinct from one another, by which he says that the Lord is the Son of God the Father and of his human mother. Perhaps someone who has read more than I have has found something similar to this. I nevertheless do not know of having read anything of this sort in either Catholic or heretical doctrine.

But let us examine what follows, to see whether he adds still more modes to these four.

### XVII

Felix therefore asks: “Proceed with the modes implied.”

He answers: “According to the essence of the divinity: by nature, truth, propriety, kind, birth, and substance; but according to the humanity, he says, not by nature, but by grace, election, will, good pleasure, predestination, assumption, and other things similar to these.”

Although he had proclaimed four modes of the Lord’s birth—two from the virgin mother and two from God the Father—twelve have now been found: six from the Father and six from the mother.

The intention with which he does this is clear to those who consider it carefully: everything that he attributes to the birth of the divinity, he removes from the humanity. If he had done this merely to show that humanity is one thing and divinity another, he would certainly have had an easier and more customary way of speaking by which he could have demonstrated it. Had he followed that method, he would have said neither anything novel nor anything false.

For by saying that, according to the essence of his divinity, he is Son in truth, by proper relation, and by the other attributes he joins to these, he wants him, according to his humanity, to be neither true nor proper, but the opposite in every respect.

### XVIII

But since he discloses these matters more clearly below, let us now consider why he wants him, according to his humanity, to be the Son of the Father—not by nature, birth, origin, or truth, but by grace, election, will, good pleasure, predestination, and assumption.

Anyone who knows his earlier errors understands what he now intends. For he had said that our Lord Jesus Christ was, according to his humanity, an adoptive son of the Father.

And although he still said and thought other, even worse things, for some reason unknown to me he was examined only concerning the word “adoration” [Baluz., “adoption” [Col. 0045C]]; and, once convicted, he was compelled to deny it—not merely three or four times, but after being convicted of this many times [Col. 0046D], he was forced to deny what he had perversely dared to teach.

[Note: *Convicted of this many times.* Namely, at the Council of Narbonne in 788, at Regensburg in 792, before Pope Adrian in Rome, at the Synod of Frankfurt in 794, at the Roman synod in 799, and at Urgell and Aachen in the same year. It is therefore clear that Agobard’s observation is entirely true: Felix was convicted not merely three or four times, but many times.]

[Note: *Concerning the sole name “adoption.”* From this we learn that Felix’s error did not remain confined to the nature of Christ, but that he was also entangled in other errors. Nevertheless, his other errors were not examined in the synods; only the heresy concerning the adoption of the Son of God was examined. This is evident from the wording used at the Council of Narbonne: “Especially because of the pestilential doctrine of Felix of Urgell.” They do not say “on behalf of Felix’s doctrines,” but “on behalf of the doctrine.”

Indeed, from Dungal’s prologue it can be concluded that Felix held the same opinion concerning images as Claudius of Turin. These are Dungal’s words: “For when the Lord Charles, of blessed memory, the most ardent and vigilant protector and champion of the Catholic faith, broke with the mighty rod of apostolic authority the head of the most wicked viper in Felix, the master of this error, hissing against the unity of the Church,” and so forth.

This may also be inferred from the first book of Jonah of Orléans against that same Claudius of Turin. Hence you may understand that the annotator of the Council of Elvira is mistaken when, in order to show that his fellow Spaniards were never hostile to images, he argues that Felix was not entangled in these opinions [Col. 0046D].]

But because he did not do this from the innermost conviction of his heart and from a willing mind, he judged within himself that he had previously held the right opinion and had later made a wrong denial.

[Note: *From the innermost conviction of his heart.* The outcome therefore showed that Felix had falsely written the following to the people of Urgell: “With God’s favor we have returned wholeheartedly to the universal Church, not with any pretense or veil of falsehood, as formerly, God knows, but, as I have said, with true credulity of heart and confession of the mouth.” Unless, perhaps, Felix then really held this view but later changed it.]

And so, because he trembled with fear where there was no fear, he now labors in this letter to show that the Lord, according to his humanity, is neither true God nor the true Son of God, nor the proper Son.

But since, with God’s help, we shall set against all these claims the statements of the holy Fathers, by which it may be recognized how far he departed from Catholic truth, let us now set down his following words, so that all his perversity may be exposed and his falsehoods later refuted by true arguments.

### XIX

Felix again asks: “Is Christ the Lord and our Redeemer believed to be the true and proper Son of God in his divinity, and likewise in his humanity, or otherwise?”

He then answers: “That one is truly believed to be the true and proper Son who was begotten from the substance of the Father, not assumed from elsewhere; generation gives him the name of Son, not election, grace, adoption, or will.”

Here he has now exposed the whole error that he had concealed in his heart. For by saying, “That one is truly believed to be the true and proper Son who was begotten from the substance of the Father, not assumed from elsewhere,” he reveals that he believes in two sons: one begotten and the other assumed; one to whom generation gives the name of Son, and the other to whom election, grace, or adoption gives it.

Perhaps someone favoring his party might say: “Felix did not believe in two, as you claim, since he immediately added: ‘Nevertheless, one in both, not two.’”

To this I reply that it is never customary to use *ille* (‘that one’) and *cui* (‘to whom’), as Felix wrote here, except when persons are being discussed; and the one whom he held divided in his heart he could not properly unite with empty words.

We have already shown above from the words of Nestorius that this was also his manner of speaking: that the same one is “one in both, not two.” But blessed Cyril and the others who proved capable of exposing his deception and overthrowing his madness certainly did not believe that this man could hold one Lord in the faith, since he spoke so plainly about him as though he were two.

## XX

But let us suppose that we agree with the one who tries to assert that Felix understood there to be one Son, not two. What, then, does it mean when he says that one and the same person is true and not true, proper and not proper, by birth and by adoption, by origin and by election, by substance and by assumption? Certainly such unity is not unity but duality; to join in this way is to divide, and to unite in this manner is to separate.

I ask: where have you ever read in the divine [Col. 0046B] Scriptures, or in the doctrines of the catholic Fathers, that our Lord, according to his humanity, is called the Son of God the Father by assumption, election, or grace? Certainly, I have never read it. And if Scripture says, “Blessed is he whom you have chosen and taken up” (Ps. 64:5), or, “I have exalted the chosen one from my people” (Ps. 88:20), does it introduce such a meaning that we should call and confess him the elect or assumed son of God the Father?

[Note: [Col. 0046D] “Confess.” The manuscript had *conferi*; Masson wrongly printed *conferri* in its place. Since it is evident that *confiteri* must be read, we did not doubt that Masson’s emendation should be rejected.]

And if the evangelist says that he was full of grace and truth, does he teach that we ought to confess him, according to his humanity, to be the Son of God the Father by grace? Therefore, since the Apostle says of him, “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” shall we say that, according to his humanity, he was an “acceptive” son of God the Father?

[Col. 0046C] Let whoever can do so carefully consider who assumed—or took up—what, and why. Certainly the Word of God, coeternal with the Father, assumed our substance; but not so that he himself might be a son to himself; not so that he might begin to be a son to God the Father in a manner different from that in which he had been a son before the incarnation; not so that he might multiply the modes and names of sonship—for he did not duplicate himself by a union of duality.

For the one who assumes is not one person and the one assumed another. It is not another who became poor for us, but he who was rich before assuming poverty. It is not another who became sin for us, but he who previously knew no sin. Thus, as the Apostle [Col. 0047A] explains, the heavenly physician took from us that by which he might apply contrary remedies to us: namely, that, while preserving his impassibility, immortality, and immutability, he might give us life by his death, enrich us by his poverty, honor us by his insults, heal us by his wounds, and accomplish other things of this kind.

[Note: [Col. 0047D] “Give us life by his death.” From sermon 75 in the appendix to the sermons of Saint Augustine: “Our Lord Jesus Christ did this: enriching us by his poverty, raising us by his humility, healing us by his weakness, giving us life by his death.”]

Thus also blessed Jerome writes in a certain passage:

> “What greater madness can there be than that the Son of God should be born the son of a human being, should endure the discomforts of ten months, await the coming of birth, be wrapped in swaddling clothes, be subjected to his parents, grow through successive ages, and, after insults, words, slaps, and scourges, even become a curse for us upon the cross, so that he might free us from the curse of the law, having become obedient to the Father unto death?”

But since we must refute all the badly understood statements of Felix written above by the words of the Fathers, let anyone who wishes read the passages of the Fathers appended below. [Col. 0047B]

Meanwhile, since I remember having said above that Felix could in no way persuade himself to believe that the union of two natures had been made naturally and substantially in one Lord, and since we have shown by the words of blessed Cyril how it is believed to have been made naturally, the reader has, on this same subject, a sufficiently polished and lucid statement of blessed Jerome, when he was discussing that passage of divine Scripture where it is said:

[Note: [Col. 0047D] A statement of blessed Jerome. This passage is taken from letter 7, *To a Sick Friend, on the Perfect Man*, printed in volume IX of Jerome’s works. Learned men, however, maintain that this letter is not Jerome’s; Agobard had no doubt that it was Jerome’s.]

> “I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and the seed of the woman. She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. 3:15).

> “Do you not see,” he says, “do you not consider that already then he was threatening him in Christ? For I understand no other seed of the woman at all except him [Col. 0047C] whom the Apostle says was made from a woman, made in the flesh; him who, as the evangelist reports, was thought to be the son of Joseph, but was not; him, certainly, who is the Word made flesh. For if we look to the ordinary and natural manner of generation, women do not have seed. Indeed, no woman conceives without a man. And so, since the seed of human generation had already been corrupted in Adam by transgression, heavenly seed is promised, as the Apostle understands it—not from the corruption of a man, but from God—which nevertheless would become flesh in a woman, and would naturally unite within that little vessel itself, in which those elements are situated, the first bodily elements of substance, that is, fluid and blood.”

Blessed Augustine likewise:

[Col. 0047D]

> “For that nature which remains eternally begotten from the Father assumed our nature without sin, so that it might be born from a virgin. For eternal and divine nature could in no way be conceived and born temporally from human nature unless, through the assumption of true humanity, the ineffable divinity in itself had received a true [Col. 0048A] conception and birth in time. Thus God is eternal and true, truly conceived and born in time from the Virgin. For when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons—that God, namely, who was naturally made the son of a human being, while he is uniquely, naturally, the only-begotten Son of God the Father.”

[Note: Blessed Augustine, namely, in the book *On Faith to Peter*. But learned men have already shown that this book is not Augustine’s, but that of Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe.]

## XXI

But against what Felix says—that the one Son is the son of God the Father in two ways, and of his mother in two ways—he thereby aims to show that according to his divinity he is true, but according to his humanity he is not true. How false this is has already been shown by the statements of blessed Cyril set out above. Now testimonies from him and from others must be presented, [Col. 0048B] by which it may be shown that our one and only Lord is wholly God and Son of God, and also a human being and the son of a human being, while the proper character of each substance remains intact; and that he is wholly true in what he is. Thus, whoever wishes to introduce into our faith different modes of divine sonship may see whether he can find any place for them.

Blessed Cyril:

> “I am willing to ask him whether he says that the union of the Word with the humanity of the Word, or with the holy animated body, was intelligibly made according to truth, or rather that he himself, together with others, understands it according to a conjunction which is a relation—the teachable discourse and form of an existent thing with an existent and divine form. For unity has demonstrated one, and we [Col. 0048C] refuse to divide into two. Although, according to the Scriptures, the Word became flesh, nevertheless he is still also the only-begotten Son according to the true unity that lies beyond mind and reason. Therefore that one and true Christ Jesus himself worked divine signs as through an instrument, his own body, and did not merely have them worked in him.”

Again Cyril:

> “Our Lord Jesus Christ is one and alone, truly existing as the Son of God the Father. Having become flesh, he rules all things together with his own begetter; every knee of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings bends to him, and every tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father. He himself, therefore, is indeed Lord of all, insofar as he is understood and is God, although after the incarnation he is not without flesh. But to say in turn that he is neither God nor Lord is utterly absurd—indeed, truly filled with every impiety.”

Again he says:

> “The mystery of the dispensation of the Only-begotten with flesh, now that we have already been brought into these matters, is nevertheless worthy of being joined together in our statements, and of being displayed with no lack of propriety.” [Col. 0048D]

A little later:

> “Since Nestorius, then, wrote of Christ: ‘Therefore he who suffered is the merciful high priest, for the God who suffered is his life-giver,’ and called the God of Christ the Word of God, adding also: ‘But he himself was both an infant and the Lord of the infant,’ we do not affirm this, because his words were uttered not with greater propriety, but with excessive impiety. [Col. 0049A] For if the Word from God the Father is the God of Christ, there will be two in every respect, and unquestionably so. But how can he himself be understood to be both an infant and the Lord of the infant? Therefore he is not called both the God of himself and the Lord of Emmanuel, if the same person is at once God and human, as the incarnate and enfleshed Word of God.”

## XXII

Blessed Augustine likewise: [Col. 0049B]

> “For I do not divide our Savior, nor do I confuse him, lest I either proclaim an incorporeal and imaginary flesh or a carnal and mortal divinity. I do not separate him, lest I appear to introduce one offspring of God the Father according to the flesh and another according to majesty; for the same Son of God proceeded from the Father without beginning, and deigned to be born in time from the Virgin. Impassible in what belongs to him, suffering in what belongs to us, he deigned from the womb to clothe the incomprehensible majesty as with a garment of flesh. There is one person of the Mediator, not one substance; one person, I say, lest there be not one Christ; not one substance, lest, once the Mediator’s dispensation had been removed, he should be called either only the Son of God or the son of a human being.”

A little later: [Col. 0049C]

> “When these were joined into one person through the incomprehensible dispensation of the Mediator, he preserved for each its own properties, but joined foreign properties to their proper ones. He preserved what was proper, since he did not lose the immensity of divinity and did not reject the weakness of flesh. He joined foreign properties to their proper ones, since the same and inseparable Christ is killed by the proper property of flesh, while by the proper property of divinity he is not held in the lower world. By the proper property of flesh he tasted the death of life; by the proper property of divinity he rendered the flesh everlasting. Therefore it is not rightly said, ‘In the Son the Father suffered,’ since the Son suffered in flesh that he does not share with the Father. Thus the flesh was glorified by majesty, while majesty is taught to have been humbled in the flesh. But we are certain that both are to be proclaimed not of two Christs, as you think, but of one and the same person, whom after the Virgin’s childbirth we know as God and human being.” [Col. 0049D]

Behold, blessed Augustine asserts that whoever confuses our Savior either proclaims an incorporeal and imaginary flesh or a carnal and mortal divinity; while whoever separates him appears to introduce one offspring of God the Father according to the flesh and another according to majesty. It is therefore certain that you separate our Savior, since you maintain two modes of sonship, so that he is Son in one way according to divinity and in another way according to flesh. But if the one and same inseparable God and human being is killed by the proper property of flesh and remains inseparably so by the proper property of divinity, where will your modes have any place? [Col. 0050A]

## XXIII

Again blessed Augustine:

> “For some sons are adoptive,” he says, “and others natural. The latter, because they are begotten from the beginning, are always sons and proper sons. The former, at first strangers, become sons afterward, when they are seen to be brought into the family through adoption. With which, then, should the Son of God be compared? If with adoptive sons, he will be like us before the Father. If with proper sons, he must be said to have come forth from the substance of the begetter.”

[Note: [Col. 0049D] “To be adopted in the Son.” Thus the old codex; Masson’s emendation, *in Filium* (“into the Son”), is plainly legitimate. But because Agobard frequently violates grammatical rules, we judged that these errors too should be retained out of respect for the man.]

Behold, blessed Augustine plainly teaches that no one can be adopted as a son who was not previously a stranger; nor can anyone receive a father by adoption unless he had his own proper father. You, who proclaim that the one Lord is the Son of the Father in two ways, namely by propriety and by adoption, must show, on that side by which he is adoptive, whom he had as his proper father, or show that he existed before he was adopted—just as blessed Augustine distinguished adoptive sons from proper sons.

Again blessed Augustine (*Enchiridion*, chap. 35): [Col. 0050B]

> “Accordingly, Christ Jesus, the Son of God, is God and human being. God before all ages, human being in our age; God, because he is the Word of God—for the Word was God. Human being, because a rational soul and flesh came into union of person with the Word. Therefore, insofar as he is God, he and the Father are one; but insofar as he is human, the Father is greater than he. For although he was the only Son of God, not by grace but by nature, so that he might also be full of grace, he was made the son of a human being as well: the same person, both things from both, one Christ.”

If blessed Augustine had ever needed to proclaim that our Lord was the Son of the Father by grace according to his humanity, this statement would have provided the most important and appropriate [Col. 0050C] place for it. When he says, “Although he was the only Son of God, not by grace but by nature,” he could have added, “so that he might also become a son by grace, he was made the son of a human being.” But he did not say this. Rather, he said, “so that he might also be full of grace, he was made the son of a human being.”

For what reason he says that he was made the son of a human being so that he might be full of grace, he carefully explains in the following statement:

> “Here the grace of God is commended in a truly grand and evident manner. For what did human nature merit in the man Christ, that it should be singularly assumed into union of person with the only Son of God? What good will, what zeal for a good purpose, what good deeds preceded by which this man might merit [Col. 0050D] becoming one person with God? Was he previously a human being, and was this singular benefit bestowed upon him when he had singularly merited God? Surely, from the moment he began to be human, he began to be nothing other than the Son of God—and this uniquely—because of the Word of God, who, after assuming him, became flesh, and was certainly God; so that, just as every human being is one person, namely rational soul and flesh, so Christ might be one person, the Word and the human being. Whence came such glory to human nature—without any preceding merits, undoubtedly gratuitous—unless because here the great and singular grace of God is clearly shown to those who consider it faithfully and soberly, so that human beings may understand that they are justified from sins by the same grace by which it came about that the human Christ could have no sin?” [Col. 0051A]

Thus the angel greeted his mother when he announced this future birth:

> “Hail,” he said, “full of grace”; and shortly afterward: “You have found grace,” he said, “with the Lord.”

She is called full of grace and said to have found grace with God so that, while preserving her virginity, she might be the mother of her Lord, indeed of the Lord of all.

A little later:

> “For Truth itself, the only-begotten Son of God, not by grace but by nature, assumed a human being by grace with such unity of person that he himself might also be the son of a human being.”

Here too, where he says that the Son of God is not by grace but by nature, [Col. 0051B] he could have added that he also became the Son of God by grace, by assuming a human being, if we ought to believe him to be the Son of God the Father by grace according to his humanity. But he said nothing of the sort. Rather, he said, “By grace he assumed a human being.”

The one who assumed was certainly the Son of God, the Word of God. Certainly, by grace he assumed a human being. He became human through mercy, because he was born through mercy, not by necessity; he died through mercy, not by debt. Do we here refer anything to the Father, so that we can say that he is the Son of God the Father by grace?

For if we ought to believe that, by grace, adoption, assumption, or whatever else may be said in accordance with these terms, he was the Son of God according to his humanity, there would have been no more suitable place above for blessed Augustine to express it than where he said of the assumed human being, “Surely, from the moment he began to be human, he began to be nothing other than the Son of God.” He could have added “by grace,” “by adoption,” “by election,” or something of this kind. But he did not do so.

Let us therefore see whether what he did add can refer to these matters. [Col. 0051C] He says:

> “Surely, from the moment he began to be human, he began to be nothing other than the Son of God—and this uniquely—and because of the Word of God, who, after assuming him, became flesh, certainly God.”

Behold, blessed Augustine says that the human being was made one person with God, that he is the unique Son of God, and that he is God. Did he here signify to us that we ought to believe him not to be the true Son of God and not true God, as Felix teaches? Certainly, I think that when he said, “From the moment he began to be, he began to be nothing other than the Son of God,” he added “and this uniquely” for the very reason that we should believe him to be the true Son of God, wholly true and wholly proper—not partly proper and partly adoptive. [Col. 0051D]

## XXIV

But if, in this unusual manner, I seem to speak to anyone because I say “the whole Lord,” let whoever he is listen to a similar statement by Pope Symmachus addressed to the emperor Anastasius:

[Note: A statement of Pope Symmachus in his *Apology* addressed to the emperor Anastasius. This passage is read somewhat differently in Symmachus than in Agobard. For the words “Therefore he is the least,” etc., which Agobard has, Symmachus’s letter reads: “Therefore he is the least who believes in Christ in this way; but he believes in Christ in this way who believes in Christ in his entirety,” etc.]

> “Christ, therefore, is truly wholly God and wholly human: thus conceived, thus born, thus living in the world, thus suffering, thus among the dead, thus raised again, thus appearing to the disciples, thus taken up into heaven, thus said thereafter to be coming, thus even today remaining in the realm of heaven, as the Apostle says: ‘In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.’ And certainly he says of him what he now is. Therefore he is the least who believes in Christ; he believes in such a Christ who believes in the whole Christ—not in a half-Christ, and therefore not in Christ, since Christ is whole only when entire, and entire only in this manner.” [Col. 0052A]

Behold, blessed Pope Symmachus too says that the whole Christ is truly God and wholly human. If, therefore, he is wholly truly God, he is certainly wholly true God and the proper Son of God, because the whole act of generation gave him the name “son,” not a half-son, as Felix wishes—although neither is humanity from the substance of the Father, nor divinity from the substance of the mother. [Col. 0052B]

But because the Word of God, of one substance with the Father, assumed our substance into the unity of his person, he will not be a son in another manner after the assumption of humanity than he was before the incarnation.

## XXV

Again blessed Augustine:

> “He was on earth, and said that he was in heaven; and, what is greater, the Son of Man was in heaven, the Son of God was in heaven, in order to demonstrate one person in both natures. And insofar as he was the Son of God, he was equal to the Father, the Word of God, in the beginning God with God; while insofar as he was the son of a human being, he assumed a human soul and human flesh, and, having put on humanity, went out among human beings. [Col. 0052C] For in these two aspects there are not two Christs, nor two sons of God, but one person, one Christ, the Son of God; the same one Christ, not one son of a human being and another Son of God, but the Son of God according to divinity and the son of a human being according to flesh.

> “But who among us, who understand little or possess little wisdom, would not rather wish to distinguish it in this way: the Son of God in heaven, and the son of a human being on earth? But lest we divide him in this way and, by dividing him, introduce two persons, only he ascended into heaven who descended from heaven. Who? The Son of Man. Therefore the Son of Man descended from heaven. Was not the Son of Man made on earth? Was not the Son of Man made through Mary? But, human being, do not separate the one whom I wish to unite. It is not enough that the Son of Man descended. Christ descended, for the same Son who is the Son of God descended. Yet he is in heaven who walks on earth. He was in heaven because Christ is everywhere; and the same Christ is both the Son of God and the son of a human being.”

Again blessed Augustine says:

> “Jesus was therefore predestined, so that he who was destined to be the son of David according to the flesh might nevertheless be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, because he was born from the Holy Spirit; and through the Virgin Mary there took place that singular and ineffable assumption of a human being by God the Word, so that the Son of God might at the same time be the son of a human being, and the son of a human being because of the human being assumed, and he is truly and properly called the son of a human being on account of the human being assumed, and the Son of God on account of the only-begotten God who assumed him, lest a quaternity rather than a Trinity be believed. [Col. 0052D] This elevation of human nature was predestined to be so great, lofty, and supreme that it could not be raised any higher, just as divinity itself, for our sake, could not lower itself any further.” [Col. 0053A]

Again blessed Augustine (*City of God*, book I, chapter 15):

> “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God, but by grace, not by nature. For the only Son of God by nature, because of his mercy toward us, became the son of a human being, so that we, who by nature are sons of human beings, might through him become sons of God by grace. Remaining immutable, he assumed from us the nature in which he would receive us, and, holding fast to his divinity, became a sharer in our weakness, so that, changed for the better, we might lose what we are—sinners and mortal—through participation in his immortality and righteousness, and preserve what he made good in our nature when we are filled with the highest good in the goodness of his nature. For just as through one sinful human being we came into this exceedingly grave evil, so through one and the same human being who is God and justifies us we have come to that exceedingly sublime good.”

Again blessed Jerome: [Col. 0053B]

> “The prophet says: ‘Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me.’ The rod is the mother of the Lord, from whom this staff came forth to sustain the world, already wearied by age. When he descended into the Virgin’s womb, therefore, let us retrace the whole history of our redemption: poured forth in birth, he displayed himself as a human being for the sake of the human being, and made his own creature from the Creator; he assumed the form of a servant; he emptied himself by an act of will and power, not by a change in the nature of divinity, through which he could not fail to be [Col. 0053C] what he had been; he endured curses in exchange for saving miracles, spitting, blows, a crown of thorns, and finally the cross for our sake; he entered the underworld; on the third day he rose again in the body that had been fastened to the cross; after death, as a human being and God, he sought heaven as the victor over death; he sat at the right hand of God; he will come at the appointed time to render judgment; and he is daily celebrated as the Spirit of God through the mouths of his saints.

> “To think upon these things is to live; this meditation is the soul’s birth. To fall back or return to these things is to be joined to the Lord; through these things to be humbled with him is to suffer with him; to die with him; and with him also to be raised.”

## XXVI

[Note: Blessed Vigilius was a bishop of Thapsus in Africa. I willingly agree with the most learned man, the priest Peter Francis Chifflet of the Society of Jesus, who, having recently published and vindicated the works of this Vigilius, demonstrated that he was bishop of Thapsus, a city in Africa in the province of Byzacena. See Sirmond’s notes on Theodulf, p. 277.]

Blessed Vigilius likewise: [Col. 0053D]

> “We confess one and the same Christ, the Son of God and the son of a human being, not two. Thus the Word sowed for himself the beginnings of flesh within the hidden recesses of the Virgin’s womb—that is, he truly became incarnate—yet the nature of the Word was not changed into flesh. Likewise, the nature of flesh passed into the person of the Word through the union of the one who assumed it, yet it was not thereby consumed in the Word. For both remain: the nature of the Word and of flesh. From these two, which remain even today, there is one Christ and one person. [Col. 0054A]

> “Who, clothed in sacrilegious opinion, could be so foolish; who could cast himself into so precipitous an abyss of error, as to deny that the Son of God now sits at the right hand of the Father and will come to judge the living and the dead, though he knows that the Lord himself said: ‘When the Son of Man comes in the glory of his Father’?”

Again he says: [Col. 0054B]

> “Although Jesus Christ is properly the name of flesh, not of the Word, and God is properly the designation of the Word, not of flesh, nevertheless the Word, because of his flesh, is the human being Jesus Christ; and the flesh, because of God the Word, is God the Word.”

Again he says: [Col. 0054C]

> “It is one thing not to have a beginning, and another to subsist from a beginning; one thing to die, and another not to be able to die. Yet, just as both are proper to Christ himself, so both are common not to him but in him. For if we say that it is common to him, it is necessary that we be required to give and identify another with whom this same thing is common to him; the necessity of such a confession leads toward the impious doctrine of Nestorius.

> “It is therefore better and more catholic to say that what is common is in him, not to him; and better to say that what is proper is proper to him, not in him. Thus it is proper to him to die who, because of the nature of the Word, cannot die.

> “Likewise, because of the ineffable mystery of one person, the mortality of the flesh was common in him to the nature of the Word, which could not die; and the immortality of the nature of the Word is common in him to the flesh, which succumbed to death. Therefore, just as dying and not dying are proper to him from both natures, so what belongs properly to each of those natures is common in him to both natures.”

## XXVII

Saint Hilary the Confessor: [Col. 0054D]

> “Born, therefore, from the Virgin as a human being, the only-begotten God, at the fullness of time, in order to raise the human being in himself to God, maintained throughout the whole manner of evangelical speech that he might teach himself to be believed to be the Son of God and might instruct that he be proclaimed the son of a human being. He spoke and acted as a human being in all that belongs to God, and then spoke and acted as God in all that belongs to the human being; yet throughout that twofold mode of speech he never spoke except with an indication both of the human being and of God.”

Behold, blessed Hilary plainly says that our Lord Jesus Christ, teaching in the synagogues and everywhere, maintained this manner of speech throughout: he taught that he was to be believed the Son of God, and certainly the true one. But if true, then also proper. Otherwise, why were four modes not found from that time onward by which he might be believed—namely, two pertaining to the Father and two to the mother?

But blessed Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, when explaining the Apostle’s words concerning the Jews (Rom. 9:5), says: [Col. 0055A]

[Note: Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, in his letter to the Armenians, from which Alcuin also quotes this passage in book IV *Against Felix*. “Concerning this statement,” he says, “blessed Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, says in his letter to the Armenians as follows: ‘The Apostle called him Christ, to show that according to truth he was made human by God. He called him “the one who is,” to declare that he is without beginning. He called him “above all,” to proclaim him Lord of all creation. He called him “blessed,” so that we may humbly adore him as omnipotent and not attack him with accusations as a fellow servant.’” Moreover, John of Antioch, together with the Eastern Council, approved this letter of Proclus, as Facundus teaches in book I *For the Defense of the Three Chapters*, chapters 1 and 3, and book VIII, chapter 1. In book II, chapter 2, he also teaches that Justinian received and confirmed this same letter of Proclus, and that it was received and confirmed by the Council of Chalcedon. Alcuin again cites the same letter in book II *Against Felix*, and Theodulf of Orléans cites it near the end of his book *On the Holy Spirit*.]

> “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever.”

He says:

> “How these words of Paul frustrate the deception of those who love wickedness! For he called him Christ, to show that according to truth God was made human. He says that he is from the Jews according to the flesh, to make clear that he did not begin to exist from the time when he was incarnate. He called him ‘the one who is,’ to declare him without beginning. He called him ‘above all,’ to proclaim him Lord of all creation. He called him ‘God,’ lest, carried away by his sufferings and appearance, we dare deny his undefiled substance. He called him ‘blessed,’ so that we may humbly adore him as omnipotent and not attack him with accusations as a fellow servant. He called him ‘forever,’ to show that the one who created us by his word is continually honored by us on account of his divinity.

> “Since, therefore, we possess Christ as existing, as God, and as blessed forever, let us venerate him [Col. 0055B] as God and Lord, saying to the defenders of foreign doctrines: ‘If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.’”

## XXVIII

Again Felix asks:

> “What difference is there between the proper and natural names of divinity in the one Son of God and those names added to his humanity?”

He answers, adding:

> “The difference is that in divinity, just as he is the true Son of God, so also he is true God. In humanity, just as he is truly human, so also he is truly the son of a human being.”

It seems to me that Felix has made a ridiculous move here. He asked about the differences [Col. 0055C] between the names of divinity and humanity, and replied that the difference is that in divinity he is true God, and in humanity true human being. This is not a difference of names, but rather a separation of substances.
