For if, as he says, “God” is the name of divinity and “human being” the name of humanity, he ought certainly to have said what difference there is between the two names, namely “God” and “human being.” And since he says below “only-begotten” in divinity and “first-born” in humanity, he ought certainly to have said what difference there is between “only-begotten” and “first-born.”

But let us set out Felix’s own words as he continues, so that the reader may recognize from them how, by separating the names, he divides the substances: [Col. 0055D]

> “In the one,” he says, “he is God above all; in the other, a human being within all. And, to gather many things together in a brief summary: in the one—that is, in the essence of divinity—he is God, Lord, the Word of the Father, the truth of the Father, wisdom, power, the image of the Father, the invisible splendor [Col. 0056A] of the Father, light from light, consubstantial with the Father, like him, equal in all things, invisible as the Father, immeasurable, uncircumscribed, omnipotent, creating all things with the Father and the Holy Spirit, maker, giving life to whom he wills, as does the Father, choosing with the Father whom he wills, predestining with the Father those whom he foreknows, sanctifying, deifying, glorifying whom he wills, and many other things similar to these.

> “Those things added to him, however, are: human being, infant, child, adolescent, young man, minister of the law, servant of the Father, less than the Father, subject, brother of the elect, participant with them, fellow heir, their kinsman, conformed to them, like them in all things except sin, mediator between God and human beings, prophet, evangelist, apostle, priest, high priest. All these things, and things similar to them, are added to him according to the dispensation of the flesh, not proper to him according to the power of divinity.”

## XXIX

[Col. 0056B] As the text itself demonstrates, Felix plainly testifies that these names are according to the dispensation of the flesh and are not proper according to the power of divinity.

If the flesh itself is called proper and belongs to the Word, why will the names of the flesh not be proper to the one whose flesh itself is proper? It seems to me that Felix understood that these names—“human being,” “infant,” “child,” “apostle,” and “high priest”—would not belong to our Lord and Savior unless he became incarnate. This is certainly true.

Yet he did not understand that after he became incarnate these names became proper to God, because God himself became these things: God the Word became a human being, an infant, and a child; he himself became an apostle; he himself became a high priest. [Col. 0056C]

But because, as I have said, Felix could rightly say that these names do not belong to the Lord from the nature of divinity, but from humanity, he nevertheless did not speak rightly in saying that they are not proper. They became proper because of the proper flesh that he assumed.

XXX. Nevertheless, let us demonstrate from the words of the Fathers what caution regarding sound faith we ought to maintain in this matter. Thus the blessed Bishop Vigilius [Note: [Col. 0056D] In *The Refutation of the Acephali*, that is, in Book V *Against Eutyches*, ch. 8, where he defends the Council of Chalcedon. The Acephali, in the age of the Emperor Justinian, were hostile to the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon. The Acephali were identical with the Eutychians, as Facundus of Hermiane teaches in the letter published by Dom Luc d’Achery. Although they did not wholly follow Eutyches’ doctrine, Facundus calls them Semi-Eutychians in Book I, ch. 5, and Book IV, ch. 3, of his *Defense of the Three Chapters*. See Sirmond’s notes on Book II of Facundus.] in his *Refutation of the Acephali Heretics*, said as follows:

> “Just as it is proper to both natures that He should die and not die, so what is proper to those natures is common in Him to both. To give an example: it is proper to me to bear upon my body, by the nature of my flesh, the mark of the bruise caused by every blow; and it is proper to me not to bear that same mark upon my spirit, by the nature of my soul. Likewise, it is proper to me to bear in my mind, by the nature of my soul, the wound of a word—that is, a harsh expression—and it is proper to me not to carry that same wound in my body, by the nature of my flesh. Although each is proper to me, and proper to my body and soul respectively, each is foreign to them individually, since neither does the body understand a harsh or pleasant word, nor does the soul become livid from the wound of a whip. Yet both are common in me to my soul and body: for neither does the soul feel apart from the body, to which feeling was proper for it, nor does the body bear the marks of blows without the participation of the soul. Therefore, what is proper to me in each part and foreign to each part is common in me itself to each part, as what is proper to each. Yet I myself am one in both, in what they have in common in me; and I myself am one in each of the things proper to me individually. Since this is so, we must pass through the sequence of the divine writings and gather very many testimonies, by which it may be demonstrated how impious and sacrilegious it is to refer by the property of nature to the Word the things proper to Christ’s flesh, and by the property of nature to ascribe to the nature of the flesh the things proper to the Word; and how no less impious it is, under the pretext of distinguishing properties, to alienate from the Word the things proper to the flesh, and under the same rule of distinction to alienate from the flesh the things proper to the Word, when both are common to them in Christ, and Christ is both.”

XXXI. Felix says that the Lord was an apostle and high priest in His humanity alone. But the blessed Cyril teaches against this as follows:

> “For the divinely inspired Scriptures proclaim to us God made human, Emmanuel, and affirm that the Word of God and Father, who has shared in flesh and blood, has become very near to us—that is, a human being—not by conversion or change, but by the ineffable power of union. Therefore we also confess one Lord Jesus Christ, one faith, and one holy baptism. But those who depart in this way from sound doctrines, and raise against the sacred Scriptures a harsh and arrogant interpretation, observing only what they think is correct, say that a human being was assumed by God the Word, according to what, I suppose, was said by one of the holy prophets: ‘I was not a prophet, nor a prophet’s son, but I was a tavern-keeper rubbing sycamores, and He took me from the sheep.’ And as the blessed David says: ‘The Lord receives the meek.’ For through habit and spiritual familiarity, as though through will, grace, and sanctification—just as we ourselves, cleaving to the Lord, are one spirit, according to what is written. But this is not the Lord’s becoming human, nor is it His sharing very near to us in flesh and blood; rather, it is making a human being His own, and not in any different way from that in which prophets, apostles, and all the other saints may be so called. Do you suppose that Saint Paul was misleading those sanctified by faith when he said most openly of the Only-Begotten: ‘Although He was rich, He became poor for our sake’? Far from it. For the herald of truth truly says that He is rich. And how did He become poor? Let this statement also now be examined by us. If, as they themselves presume to think and say, a human being was assumed by God, how did the one who was assumed become poor, having been declared glorious and exalted beyond nature? For He was glorified; or, if this is not true, they will disparage the assumption as bringing Him down to a lesser and more dishonorable measure of humanity. But such an opinion is absurd. Therefore the one who was assumed did not become poor. It remains to say that He who is rich as God was made in our poverty.”

And again:

> “We must therefore attend not to their many words, but to the upright and undefiled faith of the evangelical and apostolic ordinance. God is in flesh and blood, and through the things that are human we recognize the measure of His humanity. Thousands upon thousands of holy angels minister to Him, and seraphim surround His sacred seat. But because He became human and was called the high priest, He does not offer sacrifice to a God greater than Himself, but to Himself and to the Father, thereby securing the confession of our faith.”

And again:

> “Observe, then, that He sacrifices according to His humanity, but sits as God. For what does the blessed Paul say? ‘We have such a high priest, who sits at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens.’ Knowing, therefore, that although He was God He became human, and that the Son is one and the same, we attribute everything to Him as to one person, and we do not fail to recognize the modes of the dispensation, always directing, with skill and prudence, the force of the expressions toward His obedience.”

XXXII. Felix attributes vivification to the divinity alone, saying that the Lord, according to His divinity, gives life to whomever He wills. He does not remember that the flesh of the vivifying Word must also be believed to be life-giving, as the blessed Cyril teaches:

> “We therefore say that the body was made the proper body of the Word, and not the body of some human being existing separately and apart from Him who is understood to be Christ and the Son. Just as each person’s body is called his own when considered separately from the one to whom it belongs, so in the one Christ it must certainly be understood to exist as kindred and consubstantial with our bodies. Since it was made from a woman, it is understood and called His own in the manner I have described. But because the Word is by nature from God the Father, He displayed His flesh as life-giving; therefore it became a blessing for us. The life-giving Christ said: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: I am the living bread that came down from heaven, and I gave life to the world.’ And again: ‘The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world.’ And again: ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.’”

The blessed Cyril likewise says:

> “So that I may not seem to be the only one who calls the body of the Word His own, I have also wished to set forth testimonies of the holy Fathers, so that our opponents may know that they accuse us pointlessly when we follow their voices everywhere. Thus our most renowned father and bishop Athanasius says in his book *On the Holy Trinity*: ‘And it was evident that it was not an apparition, but that He truly had a body.’ For he taught that Christ, when He put on human flesh, put it on in its entirety together with its proper sufferings, so that, just as we say that the whole body is His own, so also the sufferings of the body alone are called His own, although they did not affect Him according to His divinity.”

XXXIII. Felix asks:

> “Do proper names revert to accidents, or accidents to proper names, or not?”

He answers:

> “They do revert.”

He asks:

> “In what order?”

He answers:

> “Because of the singularity of the person, in whom the divinity of the Son of God and His humanity have actions in common. For this reason, sometimes the things that are divine are referred to the human, and at times the things that are human are ascribed to the divine. In this manner the Son of God sometimes deigns to be called the son of man in the Son of Man, and the son of man is called the Son of God in the Son of God.”

Here I warn the reader to compare this reversion of Felix’s names with the statement of Nestorius, and to consider whether they may perhaps be similar. For, as we set forth above (ch. 7), Nestorius says:

> “Having an inseparable conjunction with the divine nature, through the relation of God and with every creature offering worship in its understanding; and we do not say there are two sons or two Lords.”

And shortly afterward Nestorius again says:

> “But He alone, possessing this distinction above all others—that He participates in the conjunction with God the Word through adoption and lordship—removing every suspicion of a duality of sons and lords, would nevertheless have, in the conjunction with God the Word granted to us, the whole faith, understanding, and contemplation belonging to Him, on account of which He also received worship from every creature by relation to God.”

Behold, Nestorius says that the Lord received contemplation—that is, divinity and worship—by relation to God. Felix, however, says that the names revert because of the unity of the person, and that for this reason the Son of God is called the son of man, and the son of man is named the Son of God. It seems to me that although the words of both Nestorius and Felix are novel, unusual, and confused, the sense of one of them—or a similar sense—is nevertheless found here.

Furthermore, we must carefully consider what Felix said:

> “Sometimes the Son of God deigns to be called the son of man in the Son of Man.”

What does this mean? Is it only sometimes, and not always? Is He merely called, and does He not exist as such? Then he says:

> “And the son of man is named the Son of God in the Son of God.”

Is He merely named, and does He not exist as such?

XXXIV. But because I know that there is a certain similarity between these words and statements of the blessed Jerome, which Felix used to expound in a perverse sense in his first dispute, let us see whether Felix’s meaning and words do not differ from Jerome’s. For the blessed Jerome says (see the complete passage of Jerome below, ch. 39):

> “This son of man, through the Son of God, is deemed worthy to be the Son of God in the Son of God.”

Behold, the blessed Jerome says “is deemed worthy to be.” Felix says “is called” and “is named.” Certainly there is a great difference between “is deemed worthy to be” and “is called” or “is named.” He says: “The son of man in the Son of God is deemed worthy to be the Son of God.” Certainly the entire Catholic Church believes and confesses this in precisely this way.

The one who is deemed worthy to be truly and properly began to be, because, as has already been said above, from the moment He began to be, He began to be nothing other than the Son of God, and this Son is unique. Those who are called and named received the spirit of adoption so that they might be called sons of God. For from the time they began to exist, they were sons of Adam, sons of wrath, and sons of this age. While they were such, the mercy of God anticipated them before they could will or choose anything good. Just as He foreknew and predestined them before the foundation of the world, He called them at the appointed time and justified them through the adoption and redemption of souls; afterward He will glorify them through the adoption and redemption of bodies at the final resurrection.

These things take place in those who by the grace of adoption are made and called sons of God, through Him who was naturally born before the ages and naturally made in the world as the only Son of God. He is the Son of God by being born, not by being reborn; generation, not regeneration, gave Him the name of Son. From that substance in which He began to be, from the moment He began to be, He is not merely named the Son of God at some point, as Felix wishes, but is always the Son, as Catholics believe.

Thus, as the blessed Jerome says, by joining God and humanity, we hold both the son of man in Jesus and the Son of God in Christ. Here wisdom will turn, as the Apocalypse says. Here the power of the promised antidote must be revealed. Here the poison of the Manichaeans and the earthly offspring of the Arians must be overcome by the divine seed, if one may so speak.

[Col. 0060C]

XXXV. Felix also recalls the Lord’s saying:

> “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.”

He adds:

> “Certainly, when He was saying these things, the Son of Man was not yet in heaven by nature in the one receiving Him, that is, in the Son of God.”

But because I cannot discern from these words what he intended to say or what he meant, they must be left undiscussed, and we must proceed to his other statements—especially since above we set forth the blessed Augustine’s exposition of the Lord’s words just mentioned.

XXXVI. Felix likewise says:

> “Certainly, the Catholic faith believes that it was not the proper Son of God, who was begotten from the substance of the Father and is in every respect like the Father, who was delivered up for us, but a human being assumed by Him.”

These are Felix’s words. But we say: Far be it, far be it, that the Catholic faith should believe this faith, which continually chants:

> “I believe in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ, His only Son, our Lord, born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, who suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified and buried.”

For the Catholic faith believes that the one who is the Son of God the almighty Father, and who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin, is Himself the one delivered up for us, Himself the one who suffered, Himself the one crucified, dead, and buried; and that He Himself rose again, ascended into heaven, now sits at the right hand of the Father, and from there—that is, from the Father’s right hand—will come to judge the living and the dead.

But since, as was said above in the words of the blessed Jerome (ch. 25), to have thought about these things is to have lived; this meditation is a birth of the soul; to fall back or return to them is to be joined to the Lord; through them to be humbled with Him is to suffer with Him; to die with Him is also to be raised with Him—it is good and fitting to append here the judgments of the Fathers on this matter as well.

The blessed Augustine says as follows:

*(On the Faith, to Peter the Deacon, ch. 12):*

> “The law and the prophets never ceased to foretell His future birth according to the flesh, His death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, in accordance with what He Himself commanded, obeying both in words and deeds. For even by the sacrifices of bodily victims, which the Holy Trinity itself—one God of the New and Old Testament—commanded our fathers to offer to Him, the most welcome gift of that sacrifice was signified which God the Son alone, according to the flesh, would mercifully offer for us. For, according to apostolic teaching, He offered Himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, as a fragrant aroma. He is the true God and true high priest who once entered the holy places for us, not in the blood of bulls and goats, but in His own blood—just as that priest prefigured who entered the Holy of Holies each year with blood. This, then, is the one who in Himself alone displayed what He knew to be necessary for the effecting of our redemption: the same priest and sacrifice, the same God and human being; priest, through whom we have been reconciled; sacrifice, by which we have been reconciled; temple, in which we have been reconciled; God, to whom we have been reconciled. Yet He alone is priest, sacrifice, and temple, because all these things are God according to the form of a servant. He is not God alone, because according to the form of God He is this together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Therefore we have been reconciled through the Son alone according to the flesh, but not to the Son alone according to His divinity.”

The blessed Vigilius likewise says:

*(Against Eutyches, book II, ch. 9):*

> “Thus we rightly say that the Word of God endured the injuries of suffering, yet did not in any way experience suffering. I shall state it even more clearly. The divinity was pierced by nails; but it could not itself be penetrated, as His flesh could. For the flesh, once opened, made a place for the wound. The indivisible and impenetrable deity therefore remained so. By receiving sufferings, then, but not yielding to their effects, the Word of God is shown to have suffered impassibly. But because His flesh not only endured all these things but also felt them and yielded to them, we rightly and deservedly say that God was sensibly affected by all these conditions of suffering in His flesh, without sensation or change in His divinity. See, then: enduring suffering belongs to both natures; but yielding to suffering does not belong to both natures, since they belong to one and the same person.”

The blessed Athanasius likewise says:

> “And it was shown to all that the Word was not a body, but that the body was the body of the Word. Thomas touched it after he saw Him risen from the dead, and he saw in Him the marks of the nails which He had endured, looking upon the Word Himself in His body while He was being crucified. Although He could have prevented it, He did not prevent it; rather, He also made His own the things that were proper to the body, as His own. Thus the incorporeal Word, when the body was struck by the attendant, said as one suffering: ‘I gave my back to blows, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting.’ Whatever the humanity of the Word suffered, the indwelling Word referred to Himself, so that we might become participants in the divinity of the Word. And it was wondrous that He Himself was suffering and not suffering: suffering, because His own body was suffering; and in the one who suffered there was also no suffering, because, remaining God by nature, the Word is impassible. He Himself was incorporeal in a passible body, while the body had within itself the impassible Word, destroying the body’s weaknesses.”

XXXVII. Felix says:

> “Divine Scripture speaks in such a way that the things belonging to the head—that is, Christ—are referred to the body, that is, the Church, and the things belonging to the body are ascribed to the head.”

This may be true in part. But he would have spoken more truly if he had said: Sometimes the head speaks in the voice of the body, as in the words, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” and, “I was hungry and you gave me food,” and other things of this kind.

But the things that properly belong to the excellence of the head are not referred to the body in the way he says, because this communion of head and body occurs more in the words of Scripture than in actions and realities, as in the psalm:

> “Far from my salvation are the words of my offenses.”

And:

> “O God, You know my foolishness, and my offenses are not hidden from You.”

In these passages the Lord took upon Himself on behalf of His body only the voice, not the action or reality.

This man, however, as it seems to me, strives so greatly to join the head and the body that he even says they are one person. From this he appears to confirm his opinion: that he believes the Lord, according to His humanity, to be the Son of God the Father only in the same ways in which the other saints become sons of God—that is, by grace, adoption, election, predestination, and the rest—as he openly said above concerning the Lord. For this reason it appears in his words that, in a certain sense, he joins the Savior’s body to the Church more closely than to the Holy Trinity.

Accordingly, at the conclusion of his work he adds these words:

> “For the Church cannot have anything pertaining to life and godliness except what it has received from its head, that is, Christ, as the Apostle testifies when, writing to the Ephesians, he says: ‘Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, who chose us in Him before the foundation of the world, who predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ in Him.’”

It is entirely true that Christ and the Church are frequently called head and body by the Apostle. And therefore they are one person, that is, Christ and the Church.

[Note: “And therefore they are one person, that is, Christ and the Church.” Thus it is read in book VI of the *Capitularies*, ch. 302: “Moreover, we do not fail to know that Christ and the Church are one person. Therefore the things that belong to the Church belong to Christ; what is offered to the Church is offered to Christ; and what is taken away from His Church is undoubtedly taken away from Christ.” Likewise, in ch. 305: “And because we truly recognize that Christ and the Church are one person, whatever belongs to the Church belongs to Christ.” How this should be understood is clearly explained by Saint Pope Gregory in book XIX of the *Moralia on Job*, ch. 11, where we read: “Because we have often already said that Christ and the Church are one person—He, namely, the head of this body, and she the body of that head, and so forth.”]

They are one person because the body is called the body of the head, and the head is certainly the head of the body. For the head is not said in relation to itself, but in relation to the body.

Nevertheless, the manner and distinction of how they are called one person must be maintained. For we do not believe that Christ and the Church are one person in the same way that we believe the Word and flesh in the Son of God to be altogether one person—not joined from two persons, but constituted from two substances. The same manner does not apply to Christ and the Church, which are joined from many persons. The unity of person—that is, of Christ and the Church—is spiritual, not bodily.

Thus the Apostle carefully teaches, saying:

> “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit. There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; divisions of activities, but the same God, who works all things in all. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. To one, through the Spirit, is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healing in the one Spirit; to another, the working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of tongues. But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as He wills. For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, slaves or free, and we were all given to drink of one Spirit. For the body is not one member, but many” (1 Cor. 12:3–14).

Behold, the Apostle clearly shows how Christ and the Church are believed to be one person: namely, because, having drunk of one Spirit and been baptized in one Spirit, we have been made one body through the Spirit of Christ according to that same Spirit; and in that same Spirit different graces are given to individual people, so that one person belonging to the body does not possess all the graces, all the ministries, or all the activities infused into the body through the one head, Christ.

For this reason he says elsewhere:

> “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Him. But if Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin, while the Spirit lives because of justification.”

Behold, through the Spirit of Christ we become His members. Having become His members, Christ is in us, and in this way He is our head—that is, the head of the Church—who works all things not in each individual, but in all.

[Note: [Col. 0064D] “He is our head.” In the manuscript it is read thus: *caput est Xpm*; this should be read as *caput est Christum*, as Masson also printed it. But in his *Errata* he himself warned that *nostrum* should be read. This correction is certainly necessary. We have therefore judged that it should be printed thus.]

Thus in individuals He does not work all things, but some things, while in all He works not some things, but all things. The divine [perhaps: “distributes”] Spirit distributes the graces; the Lord distributes the ministries; God distributes the activities. The Holy Trinity, namely the one God, both now works all things in all and in the future will be all things in all and in each.

But because all things are done through the mediator of God and human beings, who is certainly God and human, therefore Christ the mediator is said to be, and is, the head of the Church. The Apostle says: “Christ is the head of every man”—that is, of every man from whom the whole Church is constituted—“and the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3).

In this way, then, let us confess that Christ and the Church are one person. But Felix, because he says in an improper manner that the things belonging to the head are referred to the body, attempts to establish that the things the Church receives from Christ are those which he asserts belong to Christ—namely, grace, adoption, election, and the rest.

For this reason he confirms and concludes his argument with apostolic testimony, saying:

> “He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world, and predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ in Him” (Eph. 1:4).

As though the Apostle were saying: God chose us in Christ when He chose Him; in Him and through Him He predestined us for adoption as sons when He also predestined Him for adoption as a son, so that according to His humanity He might be an adopted son.

This was entirely Felix’s meaning. Therefore, speaking of the unity of Christ and the Church, he said that the things belonging to the head are referred to the body. We have already discussed these matters sufficiently above, adding suitable testimonies of the Fathers that would show that they must be understood differently wherever grace, election, predestination, assumption, or adoption is mentioned in the sayings of the holy Fathers.

XXXVIII. To demonstrate this once again more easily, let us give an example. Felix read in the blessed Augustine:

> “The Word of God received a human being by grace.”

But he did not know how to distinguish whose grace this was, from whom it came, or to whom it was granted. It is granted by God, through the Word of God, to human nature, so that it might be received in the Son, so that there might be one Son with the Son, and so that we might have in Him the firstfruits of our substance, who is the true and proper Son.

For those firstfruits of ours were not received into the person of the Word on account of the merit of the humanity that was assumed, but by His mercy and grace for our redemption. This is the grace commended by the Catholic teacher.

Felix, however, did not understand it in this way. On the contrary, he thought that this grace was granted by the Father to the Son, so that He might deign, through the assumption of humanity, graciously to adopt Him as a son.

This error necessarily required him to fall into one of two evils: either to believe in two sons, one human and the other divine, or, while saying that there was one Son, to confess that He was the Father’s Son in two ways—true and not true, proper and adoptive, by nature and by grace.

These two evils are discerned in his writings. They would certainly not be discerned unless, by the most hidden judgment of God permitting it, his heart sometimes inclined toward one position and sometimes toward the other.

And because error knows no limit, he was brought to the point that, just as he said that Christ was the Father’s Son in two ways, so he would say that the holy Mother of God gave birth to God in one way and to a human being in another—as though she had given birth to a human being outside God.

[Col. 0065B]

XXXIX. Felix also read in the books of the holy Fathers Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, Hilary, and Avitus, when they were discussing the Savior’s incarnation, the word “adoption,” which they used according to the manner of assumption or reception. He, however, drew from it a different and contrary meaning.

So that we may express our understanding of this matter more appropriately, let us set forth one of their statements so complete that, wherever adoption is mentioned, the way in which it should be understood may be gathered from what precedes and follows.

The blessed Jerome says in his brief and elegant treatise *Against the Manichaeans, On the Likeness of Sinful Flesh*:

> “Finally, the very statement proposed confirms this: it testifies that the first Adam was made into a living soul, and the last Adam into a life-giving spirit. Behold why, after so many years and the incomprehensible courses of the ages, He is separated from all mortals, from whom, as one born according to the flesh, He is separated [the syntax is uncertain]: the former was first and living, the latter last and life-giving; the former scarcely possessed what had been given him, while the latter grants what is to be possessed.
>
> “The Psalmist also explained this in two verses, saying: ‘What is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You visit him?’ ‘Man’ must be understood as Adam; ‘the son of man’ must be understood as the Lord, who is visited in remembrance of the old man and filled with the spirit of greeting in remembrance of the dead. The very words express this, so that it is not surprising to see the matter plainly: remembrance is joined to man, and visitation is joined to the son of man.
>
> “What else could remain for that mortal man? What else ought to be infused into this life-giving one? For remembrance is owed to the dead, while visitation is shown to the living. Both were accomplished in the Lord through the incarnation: the last is visited for the sake of remembrance of the first, and through the visitation of the last the first is saved.
>
> “This sense has as its close counterpart the statement: ‘The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second from heaven, heavenly.’ Who is this heavenly one? Without doubt, He who, in the baptism of the one whom He bore, caused him to hear what no one before Him had heard: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’
>
> “And how is ‘today’ to be understood if, in the beginning, the Word was, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word? It is because this is not the Word who must be believed always to have been in the Father, and with the Father, and together with the Father; rather, it is the human being whom God the Word had received into the grace of salvation who heard these words.
>
> “This son of man, through the Son of God, is deemed worthy to be the Son of God in the Son of God. Adoption is not separated from nature, but nature is joined with adoption. For when the Word became flesh, the one who assumes was not diminished through what was assumed; rather, in the one who assumes, the assumption grew.
>
> “For the substance of weakness belonging to a creature could be changed through the Creator, but the nature of eternity belonging to the Creator could not be changed into a creature. And therefore, when it is said, ‘The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second from heaven, heavenly,’ the material of the body is not separated, but the life-giving form; the flesh is not removed, but the one who received the flesh is shown—namely, the one who says in the Gospel: ‘You are from below; I am from above.’ He says ‘from above,’ not with reference to starry flesh, but to divine power.”

Behold, after the blessed Jerome said, “Adoption is not separated from nature, but nature is joined with adoption,” he added, to show what this adoption was:

> “For when the Word became flesh, the one who assumes was not diminished through what was assumed, but in the one who assumes the assumption grew.”

What he called “adoption” above, he called “assumption” below; and what he had called “nature” above, he explained by adding “the one who assumes” and “the one who is assuming.” Therefore adoption signifies here nothing other than assumption.

Nor does the entire statement of the blessed Jerome demonstrate anything at all from which we could suspect that he believed or taught that our Lord Jesus Christ, according to His humanity, should be regarded as the adopted son of God the Father.

For when he says “adoption,” “nature assuming,” “assumption,” “the one assumed,” and “the one who assumes,” none of these seems to be referred to the Father. Rather, the discussion is recognized as concerning only the two substances from which the one person of the unique and true Son of God is constituted.

To state more fully what we believe: human nature was adopted—that is, received or assumed—in the person of the Son by the Son, so that although He Himself was the Son, He was not a son in another way, but in the same way in which He was already the Son. This is what is meant by:

> “The one who assumes was not diminished through what was assumed, but in the one who assumes the assumption grew.”

XL. Accordingly, we believe that Hilary and the other teachers spoke and thought in this way wherever they inserted the name or verb “adoption” into the doctrines of the faith.

The blessed Hilary says:

*(Book II of the *On the Trinity*, near the end):*

> “The Virgin gives birth; the birth is from God. The infant cries; angels praising are heard. The swaddling clothes are dirty; God is worshiped. Thus the dignity of power is not lost while the humility of the flesh is adopted.”

Shortly afterward he adds that in the assumption of the flesh He exists as a human being, but in His deeds as God.

A little earlier he had said:

> “Finally, let those same heretics, together with the Jews, be angry that Christ, confessing the Father as His own, made Himself equal to God; and together with them let them hear: ‘Believe my works, because I am in the Father and the Father is in me.’ There is therefore one immovable foundation, one blessed rock of faith, confessed by the voice of Peter: ‘You are the Son of the living God.’”

Behold, the admirable teacher says that Christ confesses God as His own Father. Indeed, if He has a proper Father—not one who adopts, but one who begets—then He is a proper son, not one adopted, but one born.

## XLI

[Note: [Col. 0067D] Blessed Avitus, bishop of Vienne. See Sirmond in his notes to Avitus’s Letter 28, where he also cites this passage of Agobard. But this passage of Avitus is read somewhat differently in Sirmond’s edition than in Agobard. Agobard’s edition, however, agrees with a manuscript codex belonging to the distinguished senator of Grenoble, Petrus Marnaesius.]

Blessed Avitus also, the most vigorous conqueror of the heretical Photinians, wrote as follows:

“Certainly, when the Jews were howling around and brandishing against our Lord the weapons of their blasphemies, whom we believe to have replied, ‘Amen, I say to you: before Abraham was, I am’—unless, through the concord of the begetter and the offspring, he himself descended through the succession of maternal ancestors from Abraham’s seed, [Col. 0067B] he who preceded Abraham in eternity without any reckoning of years. That greatest of the patriarchs, when he saw that day in which God remains without end, desired to see him in whom man was united to God. ‘He saw,’ he says, ‘and rejoiced’; for just as he beheld him in whom there was innate majesty, so also he had conceived in his desire this one in whom adopted humility was illuminated.”

But since, in saying these things, he neither believed nor taught that our Lord was an adoptive son according to his humanity, this is apparent from what he had said earlier in the same work:

[Note: [Col. 0067D] From what he stated beforehand. Either Avitus’s work has perished, in which these fragments were connected, or Agobard must be acknowledged to have suffered a lapse of memory. For the earlier fragment is taken from Avitus’s Second Letter, whereas the later one comes from Letter 28.]

“But the Apostle says: ‘When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son.’ Indeed, he who is sent existed before he was sent. For if he had not existed before Mary, adoption would have made him, like the others, a son of God, not nature. Nor would he himself have said in the Gospels: ‘God so loved the world that he gave his only Son.’ He was therefore not chosen by that ineffable fatherhood, but begotten; a Son truly and faithfully proper to him in each nature, both as God and as man: [Col. 0067C] in his divinity proceeding from the Father, in his body beginning from his mother.”

“Behold, the catholic teacher testifies truthfully against Felix that our Lord is the Father’s Son neither by adoption nor by election, but by descent and proper sonship.”

## XLII

When blessed Pope Gregory was explaining the words of Elihu, where he says, “Behold, God is exalted in his strength, and none is like him among the legislators,” he said:

[Note: [Col. 0067D] *Moral.* Book XXVII, chapter 1.]

“We can call all those legislators whom we know to have admonished the people rightly from the law. But none among the legislators is like this mediator. For those men, called freely, return from sins to innocence; and by preaching they lead others back from the things they themselves have experienced. But our Redeemer is a man without sin, a Son without adoption.”

Behold, this eminent teacher says that our Lord is a Son without adoption. Certainly, if he had known him to be the Father’s Son in two ways—that is, by adoption according to his humanity and by nature according to his divinity—he would never have called him a Son without adoption.

[Col. 0068A]

## XLIII

[Note: [Col. 0068D] Fidentius. He perhaps means Fidentius the bishop and martyr, who is mentioned in Augustine’s Sermon 30, among those sermons published by Sirmond.]

A certain catholic teacher, Fidentius, likewise taught that our Lord is the proper and true Son of God. Explaining the passage in the Gospel where, after the Lord had been transfigured on the mountain, the Father’s voice came to the apostles, saying, “This is my beloved Son,” he says:

“For this reason, when the apostles raised their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus alone: so that he too, the Son of Man, might not be thought to be merely a man of God like Moses and Elijah or the other saints, and the Lord of majesty might not be placed on the same level as adoptive sons.”

Here also this teacher of piety, saying that he must not be equated with adoptive sons, calls him the Son of Man. If he had known him to be adoptive according to the flesh, he would not, by calling him the Son of Man, have distinguished him from adoptive sons in this way as the Lord of majesty.

[Col. 0068B]

## XLIV

When blessed Augustine was explaining the Epistle of blessed Paul the Apostle to the Galatians and had reached the passage that says, “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, in order to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons,” after several remarks pertinent to the explanation of these words, he added:

“The same Apostle did not say that we should receive adoption as sons, but that we should receive it again, so that he might signify that we had lost it in Adam, from whom we are mortal. Here we receive adoption again; and the Only-Begotten did not disdain this by sharing in our nature, being made of a woman.”

But if the aforementioned teacher had wished us to understand from these words that our Lord, the Only-Begotten Son of God, should be confessed as the Father’s son in two [Col. 0068C] ways—that is, by nature and by adoption—he would never again have taught in the following manner, as he did in his exposition of Psalm 88:

“Who among the clouds shall be compared with the Lord? And who shall be like the Lord among the sons of God? Therefore no one among the sons of God shall be like the Son of God. He himself is called the Son of God, and we are called sons of God. But who shall be like the Lord among the sons of God? He is one and only; we are many. He is one, and in him we are one. He is born; we are adopted. He is the Son begotten from eternity by nature; we are made in time by grace. He is without any sin; through him we have been freed from sin. Who, then, among the clouds shall be compared with the Lord, or who shall be like the Lord among the sons of God?”

Behold, the illustrious teacher proclaims that our Lord is Son by birth, not by adoption, [Col. 0068D] saying: “He is born; we are adopted. He is the Son begotten from eternity by nature; we are made in time by grace.”

For unquestionably, one who is born is not adopted by the one from whom he is born; and one who is adopted is not born from the one by whom he is adopted. Yet unless one is born, he cannot be adopted. One is born from one person and adopted by another. Our Lord, however, because he was not [Col. 0069A] born from another father, is not adopted by God the Father. And because he is born from God the Father, he is not adopted by the Father even though he is man; for in the assumption of flesh he does not become another being. Rather, the one who was God becomes man: God born without beginning for his own sake, man born at a definite beginning for our sake—one and only, proper and true.

Nor, because he deigned to become a participant in our substance and mortality, should he therefore be believed to have become a participant also in our condition. We are born by condition, as has already been said above; he was born through mercy. We die under obligation; he through power. By his power we are made, from sons of wrath, sons of God. [Col. 0070A] He, however, never subject to such conditions, can be nothing other than the proper and true Son by eternal birth.

For this reason also, even with the humanity he assumed, he is one true God with the Father: not later than the Father, not less than the Father or the Holy Spirit, not differing in majesty, not unequal in power, not differing in operation. For this holy Trinity, distinct in persons but inseparable, is one. He is one—not in one essence, but one essence; one substance, one name, one nature—living and reigning throughout all ages of ages, without recollection of past things and without expectation of future things. Amen.

[Col. 0069A]

[Note: [Col. 0069C] *To the same emperor, concerning the insolence of the Jews.* This is undoubtedly the title of the book in an old codex, and it seemed that it ought to be retained. But we did not divide this book, or rather this letter, into chapters, because the brevity of the letter did not permit it.]

# TO THE SAME EMPEROR, CONCERNING THE INSOLENCE OF THE JEWS

[Col. 0069B]

## I

To the most Christian, truly most devout, victorious and triumphant in Christ, the most fortunate Emperor Louis, ever Augustus: Agobard, the least of all your servants.

Since almighty God, who foreknew and predestined you before the ages to be a devout ruler in times of great necessity, has exalted your prudence and zeal for religion above those of the other mortals of your time, there is no doubt that you have been prepared as a remedy for dangerous times. Of these the Apostle speaks: “In the last days perilous times shall come, and men shall be lovers of themselves, covetous, boastful,” and so forth, “having indeed the appearance of piety, but denying its power.” From such times nothing remains to be expected that is not already visible, except the release of Satan and the public trampling of the holy city [Col. 0069C] for forty-two months, which is to come through the head of all the wicked, the Antichrist.

Since these things are so, I beseech your most tranquil patience to lend your most patient ear to the words by which I, the lowest of your servants, think your most holy [Col. 0070B] solicitude ought to be admonished concerning a matter of such necessity—one which is either the only matter, or at least the chief matter, to which your government ought to extend aid above all others. If I could relate it while concealing the names of its authors, I certainly would. But since that cannot be done, I entrust myself to your goodness and patience, exposing myself to dangers and making known to you what it would be harmful to conceal.

[Note: [Col. 0069D] *Making known*, that is, indicating or explaining, in the active sense, as it was then commonly used. Thus in royal ordinances and in the books of the *Capitularies*: “He made known to us,” that is, “he signified.” Saint Pope Gregory also used the word in this way in several places, specifically Book II, Indiction 11, Letter 87; Book III, Indiction 12, Letter 2; and many other places.]

## II

Gerricus and Fredericus came; Evrardus preceded them.

[Note: [Col. 0069D] Gerricus, called Capis in the *Life of Louis the Pious*, where it is written that in the year 813 he was sent from Aquitaine into Germany by Louis to Charlemagne, to consult him about certain necessary matters.]

[Note: [Col. 0069D] Fredericus, a royal agent, as Agobard teaches. He may perhaps be the same man who, after the death of Louis the Pious, joined Lothair and was sent by him to Louis and Charles, the brothers of Lothair, as Nithard writes at the end of his second book. In the capitularies of Charles the Bald, title 43, chapter 17, there is also mention of a certain magnate named Fredricus, who may likewise be the same as this Fredericus.]

[Note: [Col. 0070D] Evrardus. Perhaps the same man who is called Eberardus in Einhard’s *Annals*, and who was Charlemagne’s chief cupbearer; Charlemagne sent him in the year 781 to Tassilo, duke of Bavaria.]

[Note: [Col. 0070D] *Your agents*, that is, envoys, who were then commonly called *missi dominici*, because they were sent by the prince. “The royal agents,” Sirmond says in his notes to the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, “were those whom the prince dispatched outside the ordinary order to various parts of the kingdom, with the greatest authority, to administer justice—for that is how they expressed it.”]

These men were indeed your agents, though they were not acting entirely on your behalf, but partly on behalf of another. They showed themselves terrifying to Christians and gentle toward the Jews, especially at Lyon, where they portrayed a form of persecution against the Church and aggravated it with many groans, sighs, and tears.

[Col. 0070C]

Since this persecution was directed especially against me, I need not disclose it all, unless perhaps your most merciful solicitude wishes to know. Nevertheless, insofar as it is harmful to the Church of Christ, if your gentleness permits, I shall begin briefly to make it known.

When the Jews first came, they gave me a written order in your name, and another to the man who governs the county of Lyon as vice-count, commanding him to offer assistance to the Jews against me.

[Note: [Col. 0070D] *Persecution against the Church.* Not a new persecution of some kind—lest anyone be misled by this obscure manner of writing—but the old persecution that afflicted the Church for approximately three hundred years at the beginnings of Christianity.]

[Note: [Col. 0071C] *Vice-count.* Since counties were entrusted to men of great dignity, who rarely left the prince’s side, those men appointed others in the counties committed to them to govern the people in their place; hence they were called vice-counts. In our own time we see, for example, that the cardinal-nephew of the supreme pontiff is always legate of Avignon, while a prelate appointed at Avignon in his place exercises the legate’s authority there and is therefore called vice-legate.]

[Col. 0071A]

Although the Jews recited these written orders as bearing your sacred name and although they were sealed with your ring, we nevertheless utterly refuse to believe that such documents proceeded from your judgment.

The Jews then began to become insolent with hateful arrogance, threatening that we would be subjected to every kind of injury through the agents whom they had obtained to exact vengeance from the Christians. After them came Evrardus, repeating the same things and saying that your majesty was greatly angered against me because of the Jews.

Then the aforementioned agents also came, carrying in their hands a stipendary *tractoria* and capitularies of decrees, which we do not believe existed by your command.

[Note: [Col. 0071C] A stipendary *tractoria*, that is, a letter by whose benefit agents were received and received their *conjectum*, namely, the payment and levy that were undoubtedly demanded from those on whose behalf the envoys were sent. In *tractoriae* it was customary to record how much ought to be supplied to each agent according to his rank; hence Agobard calls it a stipendary *tractoria*. See what we said the previous year in the notes to Lupus of Ferrières’s Letter 63.]

[Note: [Col. 0071D] *Capitularies of decrees*, that is, instructions given to the agents concerning the case of the Jews. These were highly favorable to the Jews and unjust toward the Christians. For this reason Agobard, who knew Louis’s piety well, cannot be induced to believe that these capitularies were genuine.]

For these reasons the Jews rejoiced beyond [Col. 0071B] measure, while the Christians were saddened—not only those who had fled, or who had gone into hiding, or who had been subjected to coercion, but also the others who saw or heard what was happening. This was especially so because the Jews’ judgment had been confirmed in such a way that they dared irreverently to preach to Christians what they ought rather to believe and hold, blaspheming [Col. 0072A] before them the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ.

## III

This perversity was also strengthened by the words of the agents, who whispered into the ears of certain people that the Jews were not, as most suppose, objects of abhorrence, but were dear in your eyes; and, according to what their men said, that they were considered in some respects better than Christians.

I, your unworthy servant, was not at Lyon, but was far away because of the monks of Nantua, who were suffering from a certain disagreement among themselves.

[Note: [Col. 0071D] The monks of Nantua, in the territory of Lyon, commonly called Nantua. Hugh of Flavigny writes in his *Chronicle*: “Thus the Emperor Charles, called the Bald, died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 877, Indiction 11, on the day before the Nones of October, in the territory of Lyon, and was buried at Nantua in the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul. But, following an angelic warning, he was transferred to Paris and royally entombed at Saint-Denis.” The *Chronicle of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon* and the *Chronicle of Bèze* say: “Charles, having returned to Gaul and reached the territory of Lyon, died there and was buried in the monastery of the Apostles Peter and Paul, at a place called Nantoide because of the abundance of waters flowing together there. Afterwards, following an angelic admonition, he was transferred from there to Paris and buried with royal burial in the church of Saint-Denis.” Thus, in a charter of King Louis the Stammerer for the church of Lyon, part of which was published by Severtius, the monastery of Nantua is said to be in the county of Lyon. Today, however, it lies outside the kingdom of France, in the domain of the duke of Savoy, approximately halfway between Lyon and Geneva, in the county of Bugey.]

Nevertheless, I sent our agents and a little letter to them, so that they might command whatever they wished or had been ordered to command, and we would obey. But we obtained no pardon, so that even some of our priests, whom they specifically threatened, [Col. 0072B] did not dare to present themselves before them.

We suffered these things at the hands of the Jews’ supporters for no other reason than that we had preached to Christians that they should not sell Christian slaves to the Jews, should not permit the Jews themselves to sell Christians into Spain, and that the Jews should not have hired household servants, lest Christian women observe the Sabbath with them, [Col. 0073A] work on Sundays, dine with them during the days of Lent, and their hired servants eat meat on those same days. Nor should any Christian buy meat slaughtered and skinned by Jews and sell it to other Christians; nor should they drink the Jews’ wine; and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0072C] *That they should not sell Christian slaves to them.* Agobard had done nothing wrong here. The same decree had previously been issued by Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, Book VI of the *Capitularies*, chapter 117: “It has been decided that Christian slaves shall not serve or remain attached to Jews.” And chapter 318: “We generally command that Christian slaves not be handed over to pagans or Jews.” This had also been preceded by a law of Constantine the Great, mentioned by Eusebius in Book IV, chapter 27, of his *Life of Constantine*: “Likewise the constitution of the Augusti Honorius and Theodosius, which appears in the Theodosian Code, states: ‘No one shall dare to purchase Christian slaves belonging to Jews. For we consider it impious that the most devout servants should be polluted by the ownership of the most impious buyers.’” Valentinian Augustus likewise says in an appendix to the Theodosian Code: “We deny Jews and pagans the right to conduct lawsuits or serve in the military. We do not wish persons subject to Christian law to serve them, lest, under the pretext of ownership, they change the confession of the venerable religion.” See Saint Pope Gregory, Book II, Letters 75 and 76; Book III, Letter 21; Book XII, Letter 18; Ivo of Chartres, Part I, chapter 281 and following, and Part XIII, chapter 98; the Collection of Bernard of Pavia, Book V, title 5; Innocent Cironius in the Fifth Compilation, Book V, title 3; and Gregory IX’s *Decretals*, Book V, title 6.]

For it is the custom of the Jews that, whenever they slaughter an animal for food, if the animal has not been killed with three cuts; if, after its entrails have been opened, the liver appears injured; if the lung has adhered to the side or air has penetrated it; if the gallbladder has not been found; and in other such cases, these things, rejected by the Jews as unclean, are sold to Christians, and in an insulting expression they call them “Christian animals.”

[Col. 0073B]

## IV

As for the wine, which they themselves admit to be unclean and which they use only to sell to Christians, if it happens to spill onto the ground anywhere, even in a filthy place, they hasten to draw it up again from the earth and put it back into vessels for preservation. Many witnesses, not only Christians but also Jews, testify to the other reprehensible practices they carry on concerning it.

That they daily curse our Lord Jesus Christ and Christians in all their prayers under the name of the Nazarenes is testified not only by blessed Jerome, who writes that he knew them inwardly and outwardly, but also by many of the Jews themselves.

Taking an example from this matter, I spoke to the Christians in the following way:

[Note: [Col. 0073C] “If any man.” This is a fragment of the address that Agobard delivered at Lyon against the Jews, continuing to the words “we ought to be human.”]

“If any man is faithful and loving toward his elder or master, and perceives that someone is his enemy, slanderer, reviler, and threatener, he does not wish to be that person’s friend, table-companion, or sharer in his food. If he were such a person and his elder or master discovered it, the latter would not consider him faithful to himself.

[Note: [Col. 0073C] *Elder*, that is, lord; in the vernacular, *Seigneur*. See the notes of Jérôme Bignon to Marculf, pages 443 and 458, and David Blondel’s *Dissertation on the Right of the People in Ecclesiastical Government*, page 49.]

Therefore, since we unquestionably know that the Jews are blasphemers and, so to speak, cursers of the Lord God of Christ and of his faithful Christians, we ought not to join ourselves to them in the sharing of food and drink, at least according to the measure established by the holy Fathers through examples and prescribed by their words.

[Col. 0074A]

Nevertheless, since they live among us, we ought not to be malicious toward them, nor hostile to their life, health, or wealth. We should observe the measure established by the Church, not one that is obscure, but one plainly set forth, concerning how we ought to be cautious and humane toward them.”

[Note: [Col. 0073D] *Their wealth*, that is, the wealth of the Jews. This reputation has always accompanied the Jews since Christians began to prevail. Albert Krantzius also notes in Book VIII, chapter 23, of his *Metropolis of Salzburg* that they accumulated great wealth everywhere. In 1098, when Jews were secretly carrying their wealth from Bohemia into Poland and Pannonia, and the report of their flight reached Duke Břetislav, he ordered them detained and their treasures confiscated for the treasury. Cosmas of Prague, who records these events, adds: “Oh, how much money was taken from the wretched Jews on that day! Not even from burning Troy was so much wealth carried to the shores of Euboea.” Hence, even in our own age, whenever we wish to say that someone is very wealthy, we commonly say, “He is rich like a Jew,” *Il est riche comme un Juif*; and this expression is used even where Jews are known only by name.]

## V

These things, most devout lord, are a few of the many things I have said concerning the treachery of the Jews, our admonition, and the injury inflicted upon Christianity by the Jews’ supporters. I do not know whether this can reach your knowledge.

Nevertheless, it is supremely necessary that your most devout solicitude should know how the Christian faith is harmed by the Jews in certain respects. For while they boast, lying to simple Christians, that they are dear to you because of the patriarchs; that they enter honorably into your presence and depart from it; that persons of the highest rank desire their prayers and blessings, and confess that they wish to have a lawgiver such as the Jews have; while they say that your counselors have been angered against us on their account because we forbid Christians to drink their wine; while, in their attempt to affirm this, they boast that they have received many pounds of silver from them for the purchase of wine; while they claim that, after the canons have been searched, no reason can be found why Christians ought to abstain from their food and drink; while they display commands issued in your name and sealed with golden seals, containing words which we believe are not genuine; while they display women’s garments as though they had been sent to their wives by your female relatives or by ladies of the palace; while they display the glory of their ancestors; and while they are unlawfully permitted to build new synagogues—

[Note: [Col. 0074C] *New synagogues.* Agobard is indignant that the Jews were then permitted to construct new synagogues, as though in contempt of the Christian religion. He says that this is contrary to the law. The law appears in the Theodosian Code, Book XVI, title 8, *On Those Who Dispute Concerning Religion*, where the Augusti Honorius and Theodosius decree: “What we recently established concerning the Jews and their synagogues shall remain firm: namely, that they shall never be permitted to build new synagogues, nor fear that their old ones will be taken away.” Saint Gregory mentions this law in Book VII, Indiction 2, Letter 5: “For just as the legal definition does not allow the Jews to erect new synagogues, so it permits them to retain their old ones without disturbance.” He mentions the same law again in Letter 58 of the same book. Alexander III also appears to have referred to it when he wrote: “You must not allow Jews to build new synagogues where they have not previously had them. But if the old ones have collapsed or threaten to collapse, you may tolerate their rebuilding with equanimity—not, however, so that they may raise them higher or make them larger or more splendid than they are known to have been before. They ought certainly to consider it a great privilege that they are tolerated in their old synagogues and religious observances.”]

—the matter has reached the point that ignorant [Col. 0075A] Christians say that the Jews preach better than our priests. This is especially so since the aforementioned agents, in order not to impede the Jews’ observance of the Sabbath, ordered the markets that customarily took place on Saturdays to be moved, and left it to the Jews’ discretion on which days thereafter they should be held. They said that this suited the interests of Christians because of the Sunday rest, although it was shown to be more disadvantageous to the Jews. Those who live nearby purchase the necessities of life on the Sabbath and then devote themselves more freely to the solemnities of Mass and preaching on Sunday; and those who come from far away, taking advantage of the market, attend the offices both in the evening and in the morning and, once the solemnity of Mass has been completed, return home spiritually edified.

[Note: [Col. 0075B] *Markets on Saturdays.* It is therefore an ancient practice that markets are held on the day of the Sabbath. Shortly afterward Agobard gives the reason for this arrangement: namely, that Christians, having bought the necessities on that day, might serve God more freely on the following day. For throughout the entire day, whenever it was a feast, the Christians of old devoted themselves to prayer, as is clear from Facundus of Hermiane in the preface to the books he published in defense of the Three Chapters: “I was scarcely granted a respite of seven days,” he says, “among which there were also two feast days.” Thus Bishop Jean Monluc of Valence rightly says in chapter 35 of *On the Reformation of the Clergy of Valence and Die*: “Our ancestors did not wish those greater days to be days of idleness so that we should do nothing on them and merely cease from all activity. Rather, the purpose of feast days among Christians is chiefly the cessation of labor and work, so that on those days the people may attend sacred rites, offer worship, honor, and prayers to God, and remain devoted to sermons, the public prayers of the Church, and vows. For these reasons, therefore, we have decreed that Sundays and the other days listed in our catalogue should all be observed carefully and religiously throughout our dioceses, and especially that on those days no gatherings for games, theatrical performances, or other entertainments of that kind should take place.” In support of this chapter he then cites, among other things, a decree of the provincial Council of Cologne, which reads: “The people must also be diligently admonished concerning why holidays, and especially Sunday—which has always been celebrated in the Church of God since the time of the Apostles—were instituted. It was so that all might gather together in unity to hear the word of the Lord, to hear the Mass also, and to receive Communion; in short, to devote themselves to God alone, so that the day might be spent entirely in prayers, hymns, psalms, and spiritual songs. For this is what it means to sanctify the Sabbath.” Would that the Christians of our own time understood these things, they who now publicly do all the things that the Council of Cologne and Jean Monluc forbade Christians to do. For as charity grows colder day by day, iniquity abounds, as Christ Jesus foretold in the Gospel according to Matthew.]

Now, if it pleases your most benevolent gentleness to hear, let us say what the churches of Gaul and their rulers—both kings and bishops—have held, handed down as something to be held, and left written for posterity concerning the distinction between the two religions, namely the Christian and the Jewish; and how this accords with apostolic authority and apostolic actions, drawing its origin from the Old Testament.

[Note: [Col. 0076B] *Both kings.* He divides the government of the Gallican Church between kings and bishops. For the Church has been entrusted to princes for governance, as Charlemagne says in the preface to his books *On Not Worshipping Images*, and as the synod held at Thionville in the year 849 states in canon 1. Thus the bishops gathered at the Council of Paris in the year 824, writing to the emperors Louis and Lothair, say that these princes, by God’s dispensation and entrustment, govern the entire holy Church of God. Louis the Pious, writing to the Roman pontiff, says that the Holy Spirit had been given to him, Louis. Nothing, however, is clearer or more consistent with Agobard’s view than what the bishops say in canon 2 of the same council at Thionville: “For you know well,” they say, “that the one who alone could rightly become both king and priest arranged the Church in such a way that it would be governed by pontifical authority and royal power.” See Marca, Book II, chapter 1, of *On Concord*.”]

From these things it is demonstrated [Col. 0076A] how detestable the enemies of truth must be considered, how they are worse than all unbelievers, as the divine Scriptures teach, and how they think of God and heavenly things in a manner more unworthy than all unbelievers.

We discussed all these matters with our fellow bishops and sent them for presentation to your most exalted Excellence.

[Note: [Col. 0076C] *We discussed with our fellow bishops*, that is, with the bishops. From this I think it may be inferred that the following letter was written by some synod in which Agobard took part. This appears to be indicated by the letter written in the name of three bishops and sent by Agobard together with this one to the Emperor Louis the Pious. It may be that these three bishops wrote in the name of the entire synod and that Agobard was entrusted with sending the synodical letter to the prince; but he declined to do so without adding his own report as well. Perhaps this took place at the synod held at Lyon in the year 821, which Agobard and Bernard attended.]

## VI

After the preceding memorandum had been dictated, a certain man arrived, fleeing from Spain, from Córdoba.

[Note: [Col. 0076D] Córdoba, or Corduba, which was the seat of the Saracens in Spain, as Lucas of Tuy teaches; this may also be inferred from the letter of Eulogius of Córdoba to Wiliesind, bishop of Pamplona.]

He said that he had been stolen by a certain Jew at Lyon twenty-four years earlier, when he was still a small boy, and sold; and that in the present year he had fled with another man who had likewise been stolen at Arles by another Jew six years earlier.

When we searched for acquaintances of this man who had come from Lyon and found them, some people reported that others, too, had been stolen by the same Jew, while others had been bought and sold; and that in the present year another boy had been stolen and sold by another Jew.

At that point it was discovered that many Christians were being sold by Christians and purchased by Jews, and that the Jews were perpetrating many unspeakable acts too shameful to write down.

[Col. 0077]

[Note: [Col. 0077A] *Letter of Agobard.* This title is taken from an old manuscript; nor could there have been any reason why it should have been omitted in Papirius Masson’s edition.]

# LETTER OF SAINT AGOBARD, BERNARD, AND EAOF, BISHOPS, TO THE SAME EMPEROR, CONCERNING JEWISH SUPERSTITIONS

[Note: [Col. 0077A] *Of Bernard, archbishop of Vienne:* to whom letters of Paschal I and Eugenius II, Roman pontiffs, are extant and have been published in volume IX of Cardinal Baronius. Later, in the year 833, when Lothair Augustus rebelled against Louis the Pious and drew many bishops over to his side—including Agobard—Bernard of Vienne also defected to that party. Lothair’s faction consequently became so powerful that Louis was deposed from the empire and imprisoned. When Louis was finally restored, Agobard and Bernard were expelled from their sees because of that treachery: Agobard because he delayed attending the assembly at Thionville, although he had been summoned three times; Bernard because, after appearing at that assembly, he fled again to Italy to Lothair. Their case was reconsidered at the assembly of Crémieu, not far from Lyons, in 836, as the author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* relates: “At that assembly, he caused the case of the vacant churches of Lyons and Vienne to be examined, because their former bishops—Agobard, who had been ordered to come and give an account but had not come, and Bernard of Vienne, who had indeed appeared but had fled again—were absent. But this matter remained unfinished because of the absence, as stated above, of the bishops.” It was therefore decided to suspend judgment, since no one absent and unheard ought to be condemned. Meanwhile they were reconciled with Louis, namely at the time when Lothair was reconciled with his father. Each then recovered his see, as Ado of Vienne records.]

[Note: [Col. 0077C] *Eaof.* Thus the manuscript expressly reads, although another manuscript also clearly writes *Eaor* a little later. The former reading is undoubtedly the more accurate. For I think Eaof was none other than the man called Faova in the Chronicle of Bèze, who was bishop of Chalon in 830, precisely the time when Agobard governed the church of Lyons, and who subscribed about the year 834 to the privilege of Aldric, archbishop of Sens, for the monastery of Saint-Remi, where he is called Fova, in volume II of the *Spicilegium*, p. 584. Hincmar, too, in his later work against Gottschalk, chapter 36, lists among the bishops who condemned Ebbo “Favo, bishop,” that is, this same man from Chalon. Faova, Fova, and Favo could have been written incorrectly for Eaof through an easy scribal error, as everyone can see, since the letter E differs little from F. The fact that the form is *Faova*, not *Faof*, should not trouble anyone. For the letter F was sometimes used by ancient scribes in place of V. Thus Fulrad, abbot of Saint-Denis and chief chaplain and counsellor of King Pippin, is called Vvolradus in Pope Stephen III’s letter to Pippin in Baronius under the year 756, although it is certain that his name was Fulrad; and in the edition of the same letter found in the *Codex Carolinus*, title 8, it is expressly written: “through the diligent service of the God-beloved man Folrad, your faithful servant.” Likewise, the monastery of Saint Boniface, Fulda, is called Volda in the account of the clergy of Rheims concerning the deposition of Ebbo: “He ordered him to be led under guard to Volda, the monastery of Saint Boniface.” It is also called Vulda in the Council of Rheims against Arnulf, chapter 23: “Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims, while attempting the same things, endured similar treatment for similar reasons at the monastery of Vuldense, through Rothad of Soissons and Erchenrad, bishop of Paris.” Likewise, in the Hildesheim Chronicle under the year 1093, Vratislaus, duke of Bohemia, is called Fratislaus. Nor do I doubt that, if anyone wished to pursue the matter, he would find many more examples. Moreover, Papirius Masson is mistaken when, in his *Synopsis of Agobard’s Works*, he thinks that *Ebon* ought to be read here instead of *Eaor*.]

[Col. 0077A]

## I

To our most Christian and glorious lord, Louis, perpetual Augustus and emperor: Agobard, Bernard, and Eaof, unworthy bishops, your suppliant servants.

As was briefly indicated in the preceding memorandum—

[Note: [Col. 0078C] The preceding memorandum, namely Agobard’s letter, which was sent together with the letters of the bishops Agobard, Bernard, and Eaof.]

—the insolence and importunity of the Jews, by which the tranquillity of faith has been driven from the hearts of certain simple Christians, compelled us to write to your most gentle and prudent solicitude concerning the caution Christians ought to exercise toward Jewish perfidy, superstitions, and innumerable errors, insofar as our lowliness has been able to discover them through the practice and institutions of the earlier rulers of the Gallican churches.

[Note: [Col. 0078C] *Our lowliness*, that is, our insignificance. The most modest men call themselves the lowest of human beings, just as Paul calls himself “the refuse of all” and the least of the apostles, considering himself unworthy to be called an apostle. Thus Jonah, bishop of Orléans, writes in a letter to Pippin, king of Aquitaine: “By diabolical cunning they have slandered my lowliness before your serenity.” The same writer says in a letter to Matfrid: “You have reminded me of my lowliness.” The supplied text is corrupt or incomplete here: “This is how it should be read, not *extremitatem*,” as the distinguished Lucas Dacherius rightly pointed out. Likewise, in the privilege of Landeric, bishop of Paris, for the monastery of Saint-Denis: “The most glorious lord Clovis, king of the Franks, illumined by divine light, requested the lowliness of our humility through a pious petition,” etc.]

Indeed, if, as the present great necessity demands, we had dared or been able to bring before your ears the injuries to souls inflicted upon the faithful by the vessels of the devil, namely the minds of the Jews, your piety would certainly have commanded that a remedy be applied.

But now—because it is extremely dangerous for us to say and make known that, just as at the time of his Passion our Lord Jesus Christ, intending to reconcile all things through the blood of his cross, was sold by a false disciple and purchased by his true persecutors for mockery and crucifixion—

[Col. 0079A]

[Note: [Col. 0079C] *Purchased*, that is, bought.]

—so now he is, in a certain manner, purchased by wicked Jews so that they may insult and blaspheme him more freely—we shall write only a few things about the examples and decrees of the Fathers, and then about the Acts of the Apostles, the Gospels, and the Scriptures of the Old Testament, in order to confirm the pious vigilance of good shepherds in governing.

## II

The blessed confessor Hilary—of whom Saint Jerome speaks as follows in his letter to Laeta on instruction: “Let her always keep Cyprian’s little works in her hands. Let her run with unhindered step through the letters of Athanasius and the books of Hilary. Let her delight in the treatises and talents of those whose books do not waver in the piety of faith. Let her read the others in such a way that she judges them more than she follows them”—his Life acknowledges how carefully he always avoided the profane companionship of Jews and heretics.

[Note: [Col. 0079D] Namely, the Life of Hilary, bishop of Poitiers. These details do not occur in the Life now circulated under Fortunatus’s name. Thus another Life of Saint Hilary must once have been in people’s hands.]

He so detested such enemies of the Church that not only did he not share a meal with them, but he would not even share the common greeting of a passerby.

The sacred history of the Life of Saint Ambrose likewise records what is worthy of insertion here and what Christians ought religiously to know:

[Note: [Col. 0079D] *The grove of the Valentinians.* Agobard reproduced this entire passage from the Life of Saint Ambrose written by Paulinus. When Rhabanus wrote against the Jews, he was content to report the burning of the synagogue and therefore omitted what is related about the burning of the Valentinians’ shrine. Ambrose himself also mentions the latter burning in Letter 29, writing to the emperor Theodosius: “Shall the shrine of the Valentinians, which was burned, also be avenged? For what is it except a shrine in which a gathering of Gentiles takes place?
