Although the Gentiles call twelve gods gods, these people worship thirty-two aeons, whom they call gods.” Concerning this Valentinian error, see Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 33; he also wrote a separate book against them.]

“‘In the regions of the East,’ he says, ‘in a certain town, a Jewish synagogue and a grove of the Valentinians were burned by Christian men, because the Jews or Valentinians had insulted Christian monks. The Valentinians’ heresy worships thirty gods. But the governor of the East sent a report concerning this matter to the emperor, because the emperor had ordered the synagogue to be rebuilt by the bishop.

“When the substance of this command reached the ears of the venerable bishop Ambrose, he sent a letter to the emperor—for he himself could not hasten there at the time—in which he urged him to revoke what he had ordered and declared that he ought to be granted a hearing by him. If he were not worthy to be heard by the emperor, then the emperor was not worthy to be heard on his behalf, nor to whom he should entrust his prayers or vows. He also declared himself ready to undergo death in such a matter, lest through his silence he make the emperor a transgressor, since the emperor had issued so unjust an order against the Church.

“Later, when he returned to Milan, he dealt publicly with the same matter while the emperor was seated in the church. In that discourse he introduced the person of the Lord speaking” (Sozomen, *Tripartite History*, book VII, chapter 8; book IX, chapter 30):

‘I made you emperor from the lowest position. I delivered your enemy’s army into your hands. I gave you the forces that he had prepared against you for his army. I reduced your enemy to your power. From your offspring I established one above the throne of the kingdom. I made you triumph without labour. And you grant triumphs over me to my enemies?’

“When the emperor descended from the tribunal, he said to him: ‘Today, bishop, you have spoken against us.’ But he replied that he had spoken not against the emperor but for him.

“Then the emperor said: ‘Truly, I had issued harsh orders against the bishop concerning the rebuilding of the synagogue.’ It was said that vengeance should be taken upon the monks by the counts who were present at the time.

“To them the bishop said: ‘I am dealing with the emperor now; with you I must deal differently.’

“And so he obtained the revocation of what had been decreed. He was unwilling to approach the altar until the emperor testified that he ought to act in accordance with his faith.

“The bishop said to him: ‘Then I act by your faith.’

“The emperor replied: ‘Act by my faith.’

“After this pledge had been repeated, the priest, now secure, celebrated the divine mysteries.”

Behold the two greatest pillars of the churches of God: Hilary and Ambrose. The first teaches us by his example that we must carefully abstain not only from the food of the Jews but also from their greetings, which all people commonly exchange with one another. The second, because the synagogue of the Jews had been burned by Christians and the emperor had ordered it to be restored through the labour of the bishop, did not hesitate to offer himself to death; and the holy man was so horrified and disgusted by this—something that might perhaps be considered trivial if it happened today—that he did not doubt that death undertaken for such a matter would be reckoned to him as martyrdom.

He also declared the emperor a transgressor for issuing so unjust a command against the Church; and unless the emperor had preserved for him a place of hearing, Ambrose testified that he would interrupt his customary intercession on his behalf.

[Col. 0081A]

[Note: [Col. 0080C] *His customary intercession on his behalf*, that is, on behalf of the emperor.

[Col. 0080D] It was customary to mention the ruler’s name during the mysteries. Tertullian says in chapter 30 of the *Apology*: “For we invoke the eternal God for the safety of the emperors.” A little farther on: “We pray for all the emperors: for them a long life, secure rule, a safe household, strong armies, a faithful senate, an upright people, a peaceful world, and whatever are the vows of a human being and of Caesar.” Soon afterward the author teaches, on the authority of blessed Paul in the First Letter to Timothy, that this is a Christian obligation.

At that time it did not yet seem necessary to pronounce the emperor’s name during the mysteries, since the whole world obeyed one ruler and that holy simplicity of the ancient Christians still remained in the Church. But after the world began to be divided, and fraud and deceit began to intrude among Christians in place of innocence and simplicity, it could become doubtful, for these reasons, for which king the priest was praying if the ruler’s name were omitted and the Church prayed for him only in general terms. Then it seemed necessary to pronounce the ruler’s name, so that frauds might be prevented and peoples might understand that the Church’s mind, proceeding from divine command and apostolic tradition, was that they should preserve inviolate their holy faith toward the king who then ruled, and pray for him to have a long life, secure rule, a safe household, and all the other wishes appropriate to a human being and a king.

Thus in the *Book of Sacraments*, usually attributed to Gregory the Great, it is expressly commanded that the king’s name be pronounced during the mysteries: “Together with your servant, our pope N., and our king N., and all orthodox worshipers of the Catholic and apostolic faith.” Various examples of this custom could also be produced.

But, leaving the others aside, we shall take an example from our own age. About twenty years ago, when the Catalans, for just and necessary reasons, placed themselves under the protection and patronage of Louis XIII, king of France, and willingly and gladly subjected themselves to his rule, hatred of the French nevertheless remained implanted in some hearts, together with a concealed inclination toward the Spaniards. The Spaniards therefore used these feelings to disturb the condition of Catalonia.

It seemed especially opportune and highly useful to exploit the influence of the monks, to whom almost all responsibility for sacred preaching in those regions had then fallen, since that class of men possesses great authority among the common people, and especially among the Catalans, a deeply religious nation.

At that time the most distinguished Pierre de Marca, later archbishop of Toulouse and Paris, was sent to Catalonia with very broad authority, so that by his prudence, wisdom, and other good qualities—of which he possessed an abundance—he might retain for the most Christian king the province that had recently turned to us and accustom it to obey French rule.

When he arrived at Barcelona and had been informed of these matters, he summoned to his residence the heads of the monasteries of that city, whom they call provincials or superiors. On the Ides of July in the year 1644, he delivered to them a speech in Latin concerning the merits of King Louis XIII and of his son, who now reigns, toward Catalonia, and concerning the faith owed to the ruler, not only because of anger but also because of conscience, as the Apostle says. He laid before them four provisions to be observed by all the monks throughout the province. One of them was this:

“Third, what I require of you is that during the solemn celebration of Mass, in accordance with the command of Saint Paul, the tradition of the ancient Fathers already attested by Tertullian himself, and the text of the Roman Missal, a special and explicit commemoration of the most Christian king be made by all priests; so that not merely a general mention of the king be introduced, but the name of Louis be expressly pronounced, as the Church’s daily practice requires, lest otherwise suspicion arise that one thing is being intended in the mind and another being feigned in words.”

Finally, he warned that the royal magistrates would not fail in their duty if the monks transgressed in this matter. But lest penalties appear to have been established only against the monks, as though suspicion rested upon them alone, he afterward sent letters to the vicars general of each diocese containing the same commands. A letter of his to the vicars general of the diocese of Elne is extant, in which it is written:

“In the prayers also recited for the king’s welfare during the solemn celebration of Mass, let them expressly and specifically pronounce the name of Louis.”

Against this speech of Marca’s, a very childish little declamation was published that same year at Tarragona by Brother Pierre Moliner, a Trinitarian master, doctor of theology, and professor of the afternoon chair at the academy of Lleida. These are the titles with which the man, learned and eloquent in his own opinion, adorned himself; but, so far as may be inferred from his little declamation, he was not so much disliked by the Muses as unknown to them.]

What, then, must this man of God be thought likely to have done if he had seen the canonical statutes overturned in his own day on account of the unbelieving Jews?

## III

Nor did the most holy Cyprian and the man of God Athanasius abominate them with less hatred. Indeed, as their writings testify, they execrate the obstinate impiety of Jewish unbelief above every error of the Gentiles.

All the most reverent rulers of the Gallican churches followed their deeply religious faith and devotion to Christ and decreed that the entire, utterly polluted society of the Jews must be completely shunned by all Christians. We have therefore decided to set forth their judgments on this matter and immediately demonstrate from them how detestable Jewish association is.

[Col. 0082A]

## IV

Almost the whole Church of Christ knows how outstanding a doctor of orthodoxy and how eloquent Alchimus Avitus, bishop of the church of Vienne, was. The deeds written about Saint Apollinaris, bishop of the church of Valence, and his frequent miracles, which continue to this day, testify gloriously to how great he was and is. The written Life of Saint Gregory, bishop of the church of Langres, together with the end of his life and the honour bestowed upon him by the Church, still testifies to the holiness and truthfulness he possessed. Both his own writings and others’ writings concerning Viventiolus, bishop of the church of Lyons, testify to the character of his teaching.

These men, therefore, assembled with twenty other most reverend bishops in the name of the Lord for the defence and preservation of the Church and decreed, concerning the matter mentioned above, among other things:

[Note: [Col. 0082B] Together with twenty others, namely at the Council of Epaon, held in the year 517 under the presidency of Avitus, bishop of Vienne. But here Agobard says that only twenty-four bishops attended that council, whereas twenty-five are found in the commonly circulated editions, unless he intended to give a round number—a supposition I would readily accept.

There is also disagreement concerning the place where that council was held, and this question has drawn learned men’s opinions in different directions. I do not wish to settle that dispute. I should nevertheless not remain silent about having recently seen an old manuscript of Avitus’s letters, which also contains a letter to Quintianus, bishop—one which Sirmond and others after him think was a summons to the bishops of the province of Vienne to attend the Council of Epaon. Yet the name Epaon is entirely absent from that manuscript. The passage concerning the convening of the council reads:

“Therefore we ask all the brethren together that, with God’s favour, a central and suitable place in the parish of your bishopric has been selected for the eighth day before the Ides of September, as has the time, etc.”

From this passage, though it is very corrupt, it may perhaps be possible to infer the site of Epaon, since it was located on the borders of several dioceses in the kingdom of Burgundy. Avitus says that it was central to Quintianus’s bishopric. I am fully convinced—incidentally—that this Quintianus was distinct from the bishop of Clermont and held some otherwise unknown see in the Burgundian kingdom, perhaps in the province of Vienne.]

[Col. 0082D]

“If a cleric of higher rank has attended the banquet of any heretic, he shall not have peace for a year; if younger clerics presume to do so, they shall be beaten. Our decree has also prohibited laymen from the banquets of Jews, and no one of our clergy shall eat bread with any person who has been defiled by a Jewish banquet.”

And in the conclusion of their decrees, trusting in the presence of the Lord, as he himself says, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them,” they decreed as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0082D] *Among other things they decreed.* Rhabanus says the same in chapter 55 of his book against the Jews. To state my own opinion, it is sufficiently clear that this book was excerpted from the bishops’ letter. Since that letter, as we said above, had been sent from some council and therefore possessed the force of public authority, it must have circulated widely, so that everyone might understand the judgment of the region of Lyons concerning this matter. When it later came into Rhabanus’s hands and gave him an occasion to write against the Jews, he excerpted his work from that synodal letter. That is our view. Certainly he presents the same observations and authorities of the ancients, generally in the same words used by the bishops in writing to the emperor Louis the Pious.]

“Therefore, if any of the holy bishops who, by their own subscriptions, have confirmed the decrees made by divine inspiration and common agreement, or any of those whom God may appoint as their successors, after reading them in their entirety, should transgress the rule of observance, let him know that he will be held guilty alike by divine judgment and by the judgment of the brotherhood.”

## V

Much testimony in the distinguished writings of Saint Caesarius, bishop of the church of Arles, indicates what his merit and learning were. When he had assembled thirty-five bishops and the representatives of bishops in one body in the name of the Lord, for the defence and confirmation of Catholic truth, he decreed among other things:

[Note: [Col. 0083D] With thirty-five bishops at the Council of Agde, held in the year 506 under Caesarius of Arles. We shall discuss this council at greater length in our notes on Ruricius of Limoges and shall offer several observations that may perhaps not be unworthy of learned men’s curiosity. See Rhabanus, *Book Against the Jews*, chapter 56.]

“From now on let all clergy and laymen avoid the banquets of Jews, and let no one receive them at a banquet. Since they do not use the common foods of Christians, it is unworthy and sacrilegious for Christians to consume their foods, when they judge unclean the things that we consume with the Apostle’s permission. In this way Catholics would begin to be inferior to Jews, if we used what they set before us while they despised what is offered by us.”

## VI

Priscus, bishop of the church of Lyons; Artemius, of Sens; Remedius, of Bourges; and Saint Siagrius, bishop of the Aedui, together with many others, renewed the ecclesiastical statutes and defined as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0083D] They defined this at the First Council of Mâcon, held in the year 581 under the presidency of Priscus, bishop of Lyons. See Rhabanus, chapter 57 of the same book.]

“Let Jews not be appointed judges over Christian peoples, nor be permitted to serve as tax collectors, lest thereby—God forbid—Christians appear to be subject to them. Let Jews, from the Lord’s Supper until the first day of Easter, in accordance with the edict of King Childebert of blessed memory, be denied permission to walk through the streets or marketplace as though for the purpose of insult; and let them show reverence to all the Lord’s priests and clerics, nor presume to take a seat before priests unless they have been ordained. If they should perhaps presume to do so, let them be restrained by the local judges according to their rank.

“Let no Christian presume to participate in Jewish banquets. If any cleric or layman should presume to do what is impious even to say, let him know that whoever has been defiled by their impiety is to be excluded from the fellowship of all Christians.

“And although what ought to be observed concerning Christians who, whether through captivity or through any frauds, have become involved in the service of Jews was long ago established not only by canonical but also by legal protections, nevertheless, since a complaint has now arisen that certain Jews residing in cities or towns have burst into such insolence and arrogance that even when Christians protest, they do not permit them to be freed from their servitude at a price, we therefore decree by the present council, with God as our author, that no Christian henceforth ought to serve a Jew. Instead, upon payment of twelve solidi for each good slave, any Christian shall have permission to redeem that slave either into freedom or into service.

“For it is impious that those whom Christ the Lord redeemed by the shedding of his blood should remain entangled in the bonds of persecutors.

“If any Jew should refuse to comply with what we have decreed, then, for as long as he delays accepting the stipulated payment, the slave himself shall be permitted to live with Christians wherever he wishes.

“We further decree specifically that if any Jew is convicted of having persuaded a Christian slave to adopt Jewish error, he shall both lose that slave and suffer legal punishment.”

[Note: [Col. 0083D] *The edict of Childebert.* It may seem strange that the Fathers of the Council of Mâcon should use Childebert’s law against the Jews, since the authority of the Third Council of Orléans ought seemingly to have carried greater weight with them, as that council enacted precisely what was contained in King Childebert’s edict. Yet they do not even mention the canon of Orléans. Nevertheless, the memory of that council was not so old that some of those present might not still have survived. It therefore seems possible to infer that the canons of councils did not have the force of law before they had been confirmed by the ruler. This confirmation was made through a public edict. And because the enforcement of royal constitutions is more prompt, especially among magistrates, who are charged with protecting and executing the laws, the Fathers of Mâcon, in order to win the favour of the magistrates, declare that they are decreeing in accordance with King Childebert’s edict and, in the meantime, approve the ruler’s act by this procedure. Agobard will transcribe this canon of the Council of Orléans below, in chapter seven of this book.]

## VII

[Note: [Col. 0084D] Saint Lupus, bishop of Lyons, who presided over the Third Council of Orléans in the year 538. Rhabanus is mistaken when, copying this passage from Agobard, he says that Lupus was bishop of Troyes. For he says in chapter 58 of his book against the Jews: “Saint Lupus, bishop of Troyes, and with him twenty-four other bishops or representatives of bishops, etc.” But Lupus, bishop of Troyes, had died long before that Council of Orléans was held.]

Saint Lupus, together with twenty-four other bishops or representatives of bishops, likewise assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ for the concerns of his body, which is the Church, and decreed among many other things:

“Since, by God’s favour, we live under the rule of Catholic kings, from the day of the Lord’s Supper until the second day of the week at Easter—that is, during those four days—they shall not go out among Christians, nor presume to mingle with Catholic peoples in any place or on any occasion.”

## VIII

The Council of Laodicea (chapters 37 and 58) decreed:

“It is not proper to accept from Jews or heretics the festive gifts that are sent, nor to celebrate festivals with them; it is not proper to receive unleavened bread from Jews or to share in their impieties.”

And another council—the First Council of Orléans, chapter 19, and the First Council of Clermont, chapter 6—decreed:

“If anyone enters into marital union with Jewish depravity—that is, if either a Christian woman unites in bodily intercourse with a Jew or a Jewish woman with a Christian—whoever is known to have committed such a great crime shall immediately be separated from the Christian assembly and banquet, and from communion with the Church.”

## IX

And since ecclesiastical statutes must be confirmed by apostolic acts, and new things by old things, let us see what Irenaeus says concerning blessed John, whom Jesus loved greatly—apostle and evangelist, the most ancient apostolic teacher and martyr of Christ, and bishop of the church of Lyons.

[Note: [Col. 0085D] *Ecclesiastical statutes.* The bishops rightly insist that ecclesiastical statutes must be strengthened by apostolic acts; that is, ecclesiastical rules cannot be regarded as equitable unless it is clear that they correspond to tradition. Thus my excellent patron rightly observed in book V, chapter 9, §3, of *On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire* that whatever was formerly brought forward in councils was customarily approved not absolutely, but only after investigation—namely, if it agreed with the interpretation and teaching of the Fathers. Therefore, as the same author says in chapter 8 of that book, it was once anxiously investigated in councils whether a new letter of any Roman pontiff agreed with the Scriptures and the canons, so that only then would everyone be bound by its authority and be confirmed in the faith, as though by two bonds: the pontiff’s definition and the council’s declaration. This is the meaning of Marcian Augustus when he wrote that what Pope Leo I defined according to the ecclesiastical canons would be declared by the council.]

[Note: [Col. 0086D] *New things by old.* For, as Marca writes there, “since one must cling to the faith once delivered, as the apostle Jude teaches, it follows that the character of Christian faith is that ancient things should be brought forth, not new things created,” as Vincent of Lérins rightly warned. Thus the emperor Claudius said in Tacitus, *Annals*, book XI: “Everything, Conscript Fathers, that is now believed to be most ancient was once new. This too will grow old, and what we defend today by examples will itself become an example.”]

Irenaeus says this in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 14; see Baronius under the year 74:

“Polycarp, moreover, was not only instructed in the companionship of the apostles and associated with many who had seen the Lord, but was also appointed bishop of the church at Smyrna in Asia by the apostles. We saw him ourselves in our earliest youth, for he lived a very long time and, in extreme old age, bore glorious and radiant witness through his life and died.

“He always taught the things he had learned from the apostles, which he also handed on to the Church and which alone are true. There are people who heard him say that John, the Lord’s disciple, went to Ephesus to bathe, and when he saw Cerinthus inside, sprang out of the bath without washing, saying that he feared the bathhouse might collapse while Cerinthus, the enemy of the truth, was within it.

“Polycarp himself, when Marcion once met him face to face and said, ‘Recognize us,’ replied, ‘I recognize you, I recognize the firstborn of Satan.’

“So much reverence did the apostles and their disciples have that they would not even exchange a word with anyone who corrupted the truth.”

If someone should perhaps say that Cerinthus was a heretic, not a Jew, let him know that in the apostolic age there were no heretics except those who came from Jews and Samaritans, such as Simon and Menander, Ebion and Nicolaus. From the errors of the aforementioned Cerinthus, however, let him recognize that everything he asserted was Jewish.

(See Epiphanius, book I, heresy 28, and Irenaeus, book I, chapter 25.)

He preached that our Lord Jesus Christ was merely human and had not risen, and that circumcision was necessary. After the resurrection, he said, Christ’s kingdom would be earthly and would be established in Jerusalem; human beings would again live in the flesh, subject to desires and vices, in order to celebrate the legal festivals once more and slaughter fleshly sacrifices again.

From the statutes written above, one should also observe that Jewish association is to be detested and avoided much more than the association of other heretics. For if all heretics are to be detested because they are enemies of the truth, then those who exercise the greater enmity must be detested much more.

For, in truth, it is characteristic of heretics to agree with the Church on some matters and disagree with it on others—that is, to blaspheme partly and partly harmonize with the truth. But the Jews lie about our Lord and God Jesus Christ and his Church wholly and blaspheme them wholly, believing nothing true about him except his death.

Even in this they do not believe what is true, since they say that his death was like the deaths of other human beings—that is, imposed by the necessity of nature, not undertaken by the will of mercy.

For this reason they curse the Lord and his body in all their prayers, just as was foretold in the Lord’s voice when he said to the Father: “They will curse, and you will bless.”

Therefore, if the enemies of the Catholic faith are to be detested and avoided because they are enemies of the truth, then above all unbelievers, disbelievers, and heretics the Jews must be detested, because no class of human beings is found that takes such pleasure in cursing the Lord.

This is by no means unknown to us, since, speaking with them almost every day, we hear the mysteries of their error.

### X

Finally, they say that their God is corporeal and distinguished by bodily features among his limbs, hearing with one part as we do, seeing with another, speaking with another, or performing some other action; and consequently that the human body was made in the image of God—except that he has fingers on his hands which are inflexible and rigid, since he does nothing with his hands. They say that he sits, after the manner of some earthly king, on a throne carried by four beasts and contained within a great palace, however large it may be.

They also think that he entertains many superfluous and empty thoughts; and because all of these cannot come to fulfillment, they are turned into demons. They proclaim innumerable other abominations about their god, as we have said, and worship such an image as they themselves have fashioned and established in the likenesses of their hearts—not the true, unchanging, and immutable God, whom they utterly fail to know.

They also believe that the letters of their alphabet exist eternally and, before the beginning of the world, obtained various offices over which they ought to preside in this age. They say that the Mosaic Law was written many years before the world. Nor do they fail to affirm that there are several earths, several underworlds, and several heavens. One of these they call *Racha* (*Rakiah*, “firmament”), that is, the firmament; they assert that it supports God’s mills, in which manna is ground for the angels as food. Another they call *Araboth*, in which they maintain that the Lord dwells; and they claim that this is what the Psalm says: “Make a way for him who rides upon Araboth” (Psalm 67:5).

For this reason they say that God has seven trumpets, one of which measures a thousand cubits for him. And why say more? There is no page or sentence of the Old Testament about which they either do not possess fabricated and written lies handed down by their ancestors, or which they themselves do not continually fabricate with ever-new superstition and presume to repeat when questioned.

For in the teachings of their ancestors they also read that Jesus was a certain young man held in honor among them and instructed under the teaching of John the Baptist; that he had very many disciples, and gave one of them, because of the hardness and dullness of his understanding, the name Cephas, that is, “Rock.” When the people were awaiting him for the festival day, certain boys from his school are said to have gone out to meet him and, in honor and reverence for their teacher, sung to him, “Hosanna to the Son of David.”

Finally, accused because of his many lies, he was thrown into prison by the judgment of Tiberius, because Tiberius’s daughter—to whom Jesus had promised the birth of a male child without a husband—had conceived a stone. Thereafter, as a detestable magician, he was hanged on a forked stake; there he was struck on the head with a stone and killed in this manner. He was buried beside a certain aqueduct and entrusted to a Jew for guarding. At night, however, he was swept away by a sudden flooding of the aqueduct. By Pilate’s command he was sought for twelve lunar months, but was never found.

Then Pilate is said to have proclaimed this law to them:

> “It is evident,” he said, “that he has risen, as he promised—the one whom you killed through envy—and that he is found neither in the tomb nor anywhere else. For this reason I order you to worship him. Whoever refuses to do so shall know that his portion will be in hell.”

Their elders fabricated all these things, and they themselves read them with foolish obstinacy, so that by such fictions the whole truth both of Christ’s virtue and of his Passion might be emptied of meaning, and so that worship might not truly be offered to him as God, but might appear to have been conferred upon him solely by Pilate’s law.

They also assert that Peter was not brought out of prison by an angel, according to our faith, but by Herod’s mercy, since Peter’s wisdom had been greatly praised in his presence. Finally, they claim that Christians worship idols, and do not shrink from saying that the miracles obtained among us through the intercession of the saints are performed by the devil.

Who could doubt that, for all these things, they deserve the greatest hatred? Scripture itself shows that they are to be hated when it says, plainly according to the Hebrew truth:

> “Those who oppose you have risen up wickedly in vain; your enemies have opposed you” (Psalm 82:3).
>
> “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord? And do I not waste away because of your adversaries? I hated them with perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me” (Psalm 139:21–22).

Burning with this zeal for God, blessed Jerome says of them in one place:

> “If it is right to hate human beings and detest some nation, I turn away with extraordinary hatred from the circumcision. To this day they persecute our Lord Jesus Christ in the synagogues of Satan.”

Likewise, elsewhere (Letter 151, Question 10):

> “I cannot review the many traditions of the Pharisees, which today they call *deuteroseis*, nor how much they resemble old women’s tales. Many of them are so shameful that I blush to mention them. I shall mention one thing, however, to the disgrace of the hostile nation. They appoint to their synagogues men of great wisdom, assigning them to a foul task: if they cannot discern by sight whether the blood of a virgin or menstruating woman is clean or unclean, they test it by taste.
>
> “Furthermore, when they have been commanded that on Sabbaths each person should remain seated in his own house and not go out or walk from the place where he lives, if we press them according to the letter so that they may neither walk, lie down, nor stand, but only sit if they wish to observe the commandments, they commonly answer:
>
> “Rab Achibas, Simeon, and Hillel, our teachers, handed down to us that we should walk two thousand feet on the Sabbath—and other teachings of this kind—putting human doctrines before the doctrine of God.”

> **Note:** In the royal manuscript it is written *Barachibas*, for which Masson printed *Barachias*. But in Jerome, whose passage this is, it reads *Rab Akibas*. Therefore, so as not to abandon the reading of the ancient manuscript, we printed *Rab Achibas*. The error had arisen through a transposition of letters.

> **Note:** Hillel was a man of great renown, from whose school eighty distinguished men emerged. The most famous of them, as Genebrard notes, were Jonathan son of Uzziel and Simeon the Just, who received Christ into his arms. That they were great men is also evident from the fact that Johanan ben Zakkai, the least learned of Hillel’s disciples, is nevertheless said to have mastered the entire body of the Kabbalah and the Scriptures, as well as every branch of philosophy, with the greatest precision, and to have presided over the school of the scribes and Pharisees with great distinction. Hillel lived for one hundred and twenty years.

### XI

Since they are defiled by so many and such great impurities of both thought and conduct, the saying of the prophet Haggai is completely fulfilled in them. At the Lord’s command he questioned the priests in this manner:

> “If one who is unclean in soul touches any of these things—bread, or stew, or wine, or oil, or any food—will it be contaminated?”

And the priests answered and said, “It will be contaminated.”

Then Haggai answered and said:

> “So is this people, and so is this nation before my face, says the Lord; and so is every work of their hands” (Haggai 2:4).

That a necessary division must be made because of all these things between the carnal Israelites and the spiritual Jews, the Lord mystically indicates through the prophet Zechariah, saying:

> “And I cut off my second staff, which is called Cord, in order to dissolve the brotherhood between Judah and Israel” (Zechariah 11:14).

For, according to the Apostle, “What partnership has the faithful with the unfaithful? What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial?”

Here we must observe that, just as unbelievers voluntarily separate themselves from ecclesiastical communion, refusing to share in any mysteries with the faithful, so the faithful ought devoutly to separate themselves both in daily association and in companionship from unbelievers. And if they cannot yet separate themselves from them geographically, they should do so in time, until they are also separated in place. Thus the faithful—who constitute the Church—cry out to God, saying:

> “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation.”

This will then be perfectly fulfilled when what John the Baptist foretold that the Lord would do comes to pass:

> “His winnowing fan is in his hand; he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor, gather his wheat into the granary, and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

Before his Passion, the Lord, not yet willing to take the children’s bread from the table and throw it to the dogs, said to his disciples:

> “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel.”

And he said to the Canaanite woman:

> “Let the children first be satisfied.”

> **Note:** These are Christ’s words to the Canaanite woman. A certain man who, at the end of the last age, published theses used this among other arguments to demonstrate that women are not human beings. I thought it worth noting this so that the reader may understand that the question was not first raised at that time, nor merely as an amusement, but was seriously proposed by a certain Gallican bishop at the Synod of Mâcon in the year 585, as Gregory of Tours relates in Book VIII, chapter 20, of his *History of the Franks*.

As if he were saying:

> “Let the bread that descended from heaven first be offered to the children who are to be nourished unto life. After they have received it, let the others who remain behind in disgust—when they say, ‘This is a hard saying; who can hear it?’ and, ‘How can this man give us his flesh to eat?’—let the servants of the Lord’s table pass to the hungry dogs, that is, let the apostles pass to the Gentiles.”

As blessed Mary, the Mother of God, filled with the Holy Spirit, had foretold:

> “He has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty” (Luke 1:53).

And much earlier Hannah, the mother of Samuel:

> “Those who were filled beforehand hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry were satisfied.”

Between these two, the prophet Isaiah says:

> “Behold, the Lord, the ruler of hosts, will take away from Jerusalem and from Judah every support of bread” (Isaiah 3:1).

### XII

This began to be fulfilled in the following order. First the Lord said to his preachers:

> “Do not go into the roads of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans.”

But as he was about to ascend into heaven, he said:

> “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature.”

Thus, after the preaching of the apostles had first been rejected by Judea, it might then come to our aid when Judea had proudly rejected it as a testimony to its own condemnation.

When this had begun to be fulfilled, and the time had arrived for the prophecies concerning the reception of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews to be fulfilled, Paul and Barnabas were preaching, and crowds were gathering to hear the word of the Lord, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “When the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and contradicted what was spoken by Paul, blaspheming. Then Paul and Barnabas spoke boldly: ‘It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first. But since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. For thus the Lord has commanded us: “I have appointed you as a light to the Gentiles, so that you may be for salvation to the ends of the earth.”’”
>
> “When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord; and all who were appointed to eternal life believed. The word of the Lord was spread throughout the whole region. But the Jews stirred up devout and respectable women and the leading men of the city, raised a persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and expelled them from their territories. But they shook the dust from their feet against them and came to Iconium. The disciples, meanwhile, were filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.”

Again, in the same book:

> “Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ. But when they opposed him and blasphemed, he shook out his garments and said to them, ‘Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.’ And departing from there, he entered the house of a certain man named Titus Justus.”

> **Note:** The word *Justus* is not found in the manuscript. Masson’s edition nevertheless contains it, while omitting the name *Titus*, which is found in the ancient manuscript. Both names, however, occur here in the Acts of the Apostles. Therefore we retained both on that account.

There also:

> “Paul entered the synagogue and spoke boldly for three months, arguing and persuading them about the kingdom of God. But when some became hardened and did not believe, reviling the Way of the Lord before the crowd, he withdrew from them and separated the disciples.”

In these words we must carefully consider that, as the number of believers from the Gentiles gradually increased and the Jews became more hostile to the word of the Lord and ceased to believe, the separation of the preachers from them was likewise gradually revealed. For they shook out both their garments and the dust of their feet against them, fulfilling the Lord’s command. When he sent his disciples to preach, he said:

> “Whoever does not receive you or hear your words, when you leave that house or city, shake the dust from your feet. Amen, I say to you: it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city.”

They are commanded to shake the dust from their feet as a testimony to their labor: they entered the city, and the apostolic preaching reached the inhabitants. Or the dust is shaken off so that they may receive nothing from them—not even what is necessary for food—because they rejected the Gospel. Thus the teachers explain the shaking off of the dust, not only in the Gospel where it is commanded, but also in the Acts of the Apostles where it is carried out.

### XIII

For this reason, at first, when Paul and Barnabas were set apart for the work, they are read to have entered the synagogues of the Jews in each city and argued on the Sabbaths about the kingdom of God—that is, when the Jews gathered.

On the second circuit (*circumcisione*; F., *circumitione*), Paul and Silas are again read to have been received by the brothers in each place and to have stayed with the brothers. Thus, when Paul and his companions went up to Jerusalem, some of the disciples from Caesarea went with them, bringing with them, to lodge with him, a certain Mnason of Cyprus, an ancient disciple. When they arrived in Jerusalem, the brothers welcomed them.

> **Note:** *Bringing with them.* In the manuscript this passage reads: “bringing them to lodge with Jason,” and so forth. Masson printed: “bringing with them, to lodge with Mnason.” But in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 21, it reads: “bringing with them Mnason, with whom they were to lodge.” Therefore, on the authority of Acts, we established the reading that now appears in the edition of Agobard’s works.

### XIV

The chosen vessel and teacher of the Gentiles, Paul, everywhere observes the strictness of this rule. Any attentive reader or hearer can easily recognize this from his own acts.

Thus, when he preached at Philippi, he is not read to have entered or stayed in the house of Lydia the seller of purple, although she worshiped God, until she and her entire household believed in Christ and were baptized. Likewise, he did not enter the house of the man who was guardian of the prison, nor accept his hospitality, until the man himself had believed in the Lord and had been baptized with his entire household, becoming worthy to have so great an apostle as his guest.

When he came to Tyre, it is written that he stayed no more than seven days with the disciples. Similarly, at Caesarea he is said to have stayed in the house of Philip the evangelist, who had four virgin daughters who prophesied. While Paul was detained there under guard for some time, only his own companions are read to have ministered to him.

At Sidon, too, although he was treated kindly by Julius the centurion, he is said to have gone only to friends—who were certainly believers—and to have cared for his own needs. Likewise, when he came to Puteoli, he is reported to have stayed seven days with the brothers. In Rome itself he lived for two years in lodgings of his own.

He also always acknowledges that he and those who were with him supplied their necessities by the labor of their own hands. When he laid the foundations of the word of God among others, he is found to have received support from the churches of the faithful.

As for the necessities said to have been provided for him and his companions by Publius’s father and the other inhabitants of the island of Mytilene, who does not see that these were accepted not from unbelievers but from believers? Paul also healed Publius’s father and performed so many cures of illnesses on that same island that there can be no doubt that very many of its inhabitants were brought under the faith of Christ and honored the messenger of their salvation with countless honors.

Thus it is established that the apostle Paul observed these things in this manner.

### XV

If anyone also considers the deeds of Peter, the foremost of the apostles, he will see that Peter did indeed enter at one time into the house of Cornelius and those who were with him, but did not remain with them or take food there until they had been filled with the Holy Spirit and baptized in the name of Christ, becoming worthy of the fellowship and companionship of the faithful.

Likewise, at Joppa he lodged in the house of a certain faithful man named Simon the tanner. While hungry, he wished to taste food there, and saw a linen vessel full of various animals descending from heaven. A voice was made to him:

> “What God has cleansed, you must not call common.”

This is said to have happened three times, so that, through faith in the Holy Trinity, the future cleansing of all nations might be foreshadowed, just as the Lord had long before commanded the apostles to go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Those Gentiles, then, were already believers, baptized, and cleansed. With them Peter ate when those who had believed from the circumcision were absent, but when they were present he refrained from eating, so that they might not be scandalized.

Here we must also faithfully consider that if such a great apostle withdrew from the table of faithful Gentiles so as not to scandalize Jewish believers who still observed the carnal practices of the Law, lest, by dining with Gentiles, he should appear to act contrary to Jewish custom, with how much greater zeal ought Christians now to withdraw from the companionship of unbelieving Jews? Otherwise, by the example of this unlawful communion, they might scandalize their companions and fellow members of the Christian religion, and by such conduct either appear to favor Jewish superstitions or be convicted of dissolving ecclesiastical statutes.

### XVI

> **Note:** *In the books of Clement*, namely at the end of Book II of the *Recognitions*. Agobard plainly considered this work of Clement apocryphal. There is therefore no doubt that, in Agobard’s judgment, the *Itinerary of Blessed Peter*, written by Clement, is the very work that still appears under the title *Recognitions*—a view Bellarmine also considered probable.

In the books of Clement, bishop of the Roman Church, certain statements are also found in which the aforementioned Apostle speaks about observing this matter. We have thought it appropriate to insert them here. Although these books are judged apocryphal, many testimonies from them are nevertheless found to have been used by teachers.

Clement therefore introduces the Apostle speaking to him when Clement had not yet been purified by the grace of baptism and, for that reason, had been separated from Peter’s table along with others like him:

> “It is not out of pride, O Clement, that I do not dine with those who have not yet been purified. Rather, I fear that I might harm myself while benefiting them in no way.”

A little later:

> “Let none of you, he says, be saddened at being separated from our meal. The one who wishes to be baptized quickly is separated only for a short time, but the one who delays is separated for much longer. Therefore, it depends on you when you wish to come to our table, not on us, for we are not permitted to eat with anyone unless he has first been baptized.”

We have necessarily quoted these passages from Clement’s writings because we wished to show clearly that the apostles handed down this very ancient observance. These statements must indeed be regarded as true, especially since they appear in no respect to differ from the acts of the apostles.

### XVII

Are we to think that Christ’s chosen apostles wished to share a table with unbelieving Jews, or could enjoy a pleasant meal with them, when Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, speaks to the Thessalonians as follows?

> “You became imitators, brothers, of the churches of God that are in Judea in Christ Jesus, because you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews, who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, persecuted us, do not please God, and are hostile to all people. They forbid us to speak to the Gentiles so that they may be saved, thereby always filling up the measure of their sins. But the wrath of God has come upon them to the end.”

With such people—whom the chosen vessel calls killers of Jesus and the prophets, persecutors of the apostles, displeasing to God, hostile to all people, always filling up their sins, and groaning under God’s wrath until the end of the age—are we to believe that either the apostles shared a common meal, or that any of the faithful ought to maintain their companionship?

> **Note:** *Shared a common meal.* This seemed the correct reading instead of the *commune cavisse convivium* found in Masson’s edition. The manuscript reads exactly: *vel apostoli credendis commune anisse convivium*. From this reading we established the true text.

### XVIII

But since the Apostle mentioned the churches in Judea that were in Christ—that is, those who had believed from among the Jews—we must also consider whether they, while living among their fellow countrymen, observed these things among themselves.

We can easily recognize this from the words of Saint Luke, who says:

> “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and no one claimed that any of his possessions was his own, but they held everything in common.”

A little later he says:

> “All who owned houses or fields sold them, brought the proceeds of what they had sold, and laid them at the apostles’ feet. Distribution was made to each according to his need.”

And again, after some intervening material:

> “They were all united in Solomon’s portico. None of the others dared to join them, but the people magnified them.”

Therefore they did not share a common meal with those with whom they did not even share a common dwelling. Everything they held in common had not been obtained from just anywhere, but had been received solely from the contributions and offerings of the faithful.

Even during the great famine said to have occurred under Claudius, they are reported to have neither sought nor received anything from the unbelieving Jews among whom they lived. Instead, they received supplies from those who had come to faith in Christ among the Gentiles, when the ministers of the faithful brought them their offerings.

> **Note:** *Under Claudius.* Eusebius mentions this famine in Book II, chapter 8, of his *Ecclesiastical History* and in his *Chronicle*, where he says, as Baronius understood it, that it occurred in the fourth year of the reign of Claudius Augustus. In fact, Eusebius’s *Chronicle* says nothing about the year in which the famine occurred. Like the *History*, it says only that it occurred under Claudius. Baronius therefore incorrectly corrects Eusebius here by assigning the famine to the second year of Claudius, on the authority of Cassius Dio. Josephus Scaliger, however, in his notes on Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, thinks that it occurred in the year of the world 2061, that is, the fifth year of Claudius’s reign. It is not our task to settle this dispute between such eminent men.

The time was already approaching when it would be said to all the faithful concerning all the enemies of the Christian faith:

> “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, and do not say ‘Hail’ to him. For whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works.”

According to this statement, if the person who says “Hail” to one who is alien to apostolic doctrine shares in his evil works, how much more does the person share in Jewish wickedness who celebrates a common meal with them?

### XIX

Furthermore, so that Christians might become more cautious concerning the defilements of heretics or Jews, it was said—and is still said—to them:

> “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world. By this the Spirit of God is known: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God. This is Antichrist.”

And there:

> “Who is a liar except the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? He is the Antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son. Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father; whoever confesses the Son also has the Father.”

These words make it entirely clear that the Jews are not merely liars but also Antichrists. Although they deny the Son, they confess the Father in vain; because they do not confess the Son, they do not deserve to have the Father. Above all, by denying that Jesus, who was born of the Virgin Mary, is the Christ, they have claimed for themselves both the name and the language of Antichrist.

For what else will Antichrist say except that Jesus was not the Christ, while he himself is what Jesus was falsely believed to be? In this one respect Antichrist surpasses the blasphemy of the Jews: he presumes to call himself Christ. But in this respect the Jews equal the wickedness of Antichrist: they dare to deny that Jesus was the Christ. They are therefore Antichrists to the extent that their blasphemies agree with the blasphemies of Antichrist.

Who, then, would share a table with Antichrist and claim to preserve faith in Christ? Or who would not gladly avoid the company of those whom he sees blaspheming their own Savior, and to whom he hears him solemnly proclaiming:

> “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. Nevertheless I say to you, it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.
>
> “And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will descend to hell. For if the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Sodom, it would perhaps have remained to this day. Nevertheless I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you” (Matthew 11:21–22).

### XX

Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum—cities of Galilee—are lamented by the Savior because, after so many signs and miracles, they did not repent. Tyre and Sidon are preferred to them because those cities merely trampled upon the natural law, whereas these cities, after transgressing the natural law, also devoted themselves to idolatry and vices.

They are preferred for another reason: Tyre and Sidon [the text reads *et scriptae*, apparently corrupt] made little account even of the signs that were performed among them. For although it is harmful both not to hear the truth and to despise it once heard, it is much worse—indeed incomparably worse—to despise what has been heard and known, and then to persecute and blaspheme it.

Blessed Peter shows this most clearly when he says of such people:

> “It would have been better for them not to know the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back.”

This is demonstrated even more clearly by the Lord’s words in the following parable:

> “When an unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it wanders through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it. Then it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds it empty, swept, and decorated. Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself; they enter and dwell there, and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first. So will it be with this most wicked generation.”

From this it is evident that the unclean spirit of idolatry withdrew from the heart of the former Jewish people when the Law was given to them and wandered for a long time through dry places—that is, through the unfruitful hearts of the Gentiles—seeking to establish a secure dwelling among them.

But at the coming of Christ, when all the nations believed in him, it was expelled from there and returned to its former house. It found that house empty of God but adorned with carnal observances of the Law, as though cleansed by Pharisaic traditions. Because it saw the house as especially suitable for its habitation, it took with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself. Entering with them into its innermost parts, it made its last state worse than its first.

That house of the Jewish people is now possessed by a greater number of demons than it had been in Egypt before it knew the Law, for it blasphemes Christ in its synagogues.

### XXI

In vain, therefore, do the supporters of the Jews—grieving us and making them rejoice—think that they ought to be honored on account of the patriarchs, and dare to say to Christians that the Jews are better than they are. We read that even the Hagarenes—now called Saracens by a corrupted form of the name—along with the Amalekites, Midianites, and Africans, derive their origin from Abraham. Yet no one should therefore think that they ought to be honored or that they are better than Christians.

> **Note:** *They are called Saracens.* Eusebius writes in his *Chronicle*: “Abraham begot Ishmael from the slave woman Hagar; from Ishmael came the nation of the Ishmaelites, who were later called Hagarenes and then Saracens.” Saint Jerome thinks that the Saracens were so called from Sarah, Abraham’s wife, just as the Hagarenes were called from Hagar, the slave woman. Joseph Scaliger rejects this, however, in his notes on Eusebius’s *Chronicle*. He thinks instead that the origin of the word should be derived from *sarak*, which in Arabic means “thieves”: “Such,” he says, “are those called by the Turks the Cossack Tartars, such as the *Martolossi*, and such as the *Bandolieri* in the Pyrenees.” Innocentius Cironius nevertheless prefers Jerome’s opinion to Scaliger’s in Book V of the *Decretals*, title 6. Genebrardus, however, thinks that the Saracens were more likely named from Mount Sara, which they once inhabited.

Not only can the Jews not be better than us, but they are found to be worse than the nations listed above. Those nations did not receive the Law, whereas the Jews, after the Law had been given to them and prophets had been sent to them, also killed the Son of God.

But if, according to the Apostle, “not the children of the flesh are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as the seed,” then, to the degree that the Jews are alienated from the seed promised to Abraham—that is, from Christ—they are likewise shown to be unworthy of the glory of God’s children. They have not received the heavenly Jerusalem as their mother, but have remained children of the earthly Jerusalem and of Hagar the slave woman, who gives birth into slavery.

### XXII

But what does Scripture say?

> “Cast out the slave woman and her son. For the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman.”

The Jewish people, therefore, were expelled from their father’s house and separated from the inheritance of the children of the Church, which was made free through Christ. For, as the Lord says:

> “The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever.”

Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin, and cannot be released from this yoke of slavery unless he deserves to be set free through the Son of God.

The Jews, although the Lord says, “If the Son makes you free, you will truly be free,” do not believe in him, while boasting that they are Abraham’s seed and have never been slaves to anyone. Thus they are not only excluded from the freedom of the spirit, but are also found to be subject to carnal slavery.

Nor is this all: they remain children of the devil, as the Lord also shows when he says to them:

> “You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father.”

Do they not daily satisfy their father’s desire by despising the Law, rejecting the prophets, persecuting the Church, and blaspheming the very Son of God?

Since these things are so, by what reasoning should slaves of sin be preferred to God’s servants, children of the slave woman to the children of the free woman, the disinherited to the heirs, and children of the devil to the children of God?

Through the prophet Isaiah, the Lord separates them from his servants with such a great division that he shows both that they have lost their former name and that they have already been numbered among the dead. He says:

> “Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall hunger.
>
> “Behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall thirst.
>
> “Behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame.
>
> “Behold, my servants shall cry out because of the joy of their heart, but you shall howl because of the anguish of your heart; and because of the contrition of your spirit you shall howl.
>
> “You shall leave your name as a curse to my chosen ones; and the Lord God will kill you, but he will call his servants by another name. Whoever is blessed upon the earth shall be blessed by the God of Amen; and whoever swears upon the earth shall swear by the God of Amen.”

Thus the Jewish people, stripped of their former name and slain by the sword of their unbelief, while God’s chosen are called by another name, blessed with the Christian name, and sworn into the sacraments of Christ, can neither be regarded as their equals nor even share bodily sustenance with them. They have not deserved to be joined to them by the very designation of servitude.

### XXIII

But if we also consider by what virtues the dwelling in God’s tabernacle and the ascent of his holy mountain may be attained, that virtue is by no means insignificant among them by which the just man is worthy to be praised in these words: “The wicked is reduced to nothing in his sight, but he glorifies those who fear [God].” Therefore the faithful and those who fear God must everywhere be glorified and honored.

But that people which is wholly placed in the Evil One, which did not recognize God’s power and God’s wisdom and consequently remained in the antiquity of wickedness and error, must be regarded as nothing in the sight of all believers. No one should honor them on account of their money or wealth; rather, because of their greed for these things, they, sprinkled with Naaman’s leprosy, are to be abominated as truly most filthy and unclean, while the whole people of the faithful has been cleansed in the waters of baptism by the true Elisha. Moreover, the Apostle’s voice must always and everywhere pronounce an anathema against them: “If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema. Maranatha.”

For if the one who does not love the Son of God is anathema, then the one who hates, persecutes, or blasphemes him must be anathematized as far more detestable. Furthermore, if anyone willingly indulges in friendship with such a person and is not ashamed to offer assistance to his impious association, he too will rightly hear what King Jehoshaphat heard when he was rebuked by the Lord’s prophet: “You offer assistance to the impious, and you join friendship with those who hate the Lord; and for this reason you deserve the Lord’s anger.”

That king indeed received testimony to his righteousness in every other respect; but in this one matter alone he offended and incurred God’s anger: he did not shrink from offering assistance to the impious and to those who hated God, nor from joining them in friendship. Scripture plainly indicates that these were none other than those who had cut themselves off from the house of David. In the same way, these impious people, the Jews who are always enemies of the Son of God, separate themselves from the house of the true David, which is the Church. Cut off from the kingdom of Christ, they await and desire the kingdom of Antichrist, whom the Lord Jesus will kill “with the breath of his mouth” and destroy “by the manifestation of his coming.”

Nor will he order only Antichrist himself to be killed, but also those who wanted him to reign over them. According to the Gospel parable, after receiving the kingdom of heaven, when he returns he will order them to be killed in his presence.

### XXIV

Therefore, as Christians have been rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of God’s beloved Son, we must in no way be polluted by the company and association of those from whose errors we have been proved wholly liberated.

We ought to remember how that prophet who had been sent from Judah to Bethel—where King Jeroboam of Samaria worshiped a golden calf—was forbidden by God to eat or drink there and replied even when the king invited him: “If you were to give me half of your house, I would not eat bread or drink water in this place.” Moreover, he refused to accept the gifts offered him by that same king.

But afterward, having been deceived by a certain false prophet, he ate and drank in the same place contrary to the Lord’s command. Delivered over to a lion by God’s judgment, he was killed by it and died.

For although it is not easily discerned where, in the Old Testament, religious Jews were carefully forbidden by the Lord to abstain from the food and drink of unbelievers, examples of the saints nevertheless provide evidence. Thus it is written concerning Daniel: “Daniel resolved in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s table or with the wine that he drank,” and he asked the chief of the eunuchs not to defile him. Permission was granted to Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael while the other Israelite boys ate the royal food.

This observance became so deeply established among the Jews that at the time of the Lord’s coming it was common to all, so that the impious Jews said to the Lord’s disciples: “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” Not only they, but also unbelievers, argued against Peter—those who were of the circumcision—saying: “Why did you enter among men who had the foreskin, and eat with them?”

After giving them an account, Peter added that a voice from heaven had spoken to him a second time: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common.” From that time it began to be made clear what blessed Paul wrote: “All things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean” (Titus 1:15).

Although many use this testimony in the opposite sense—that is, they think that it is therefore permitted them to eat the food of unbelievers—it entirely confirms our observance, so that we may know that the tables of the unclean are unclean, because their minds and consciences are polluted. How could the tables of those whose storehouses and shops are accursed not be unclean?

### XXV

But since, in writing, we have reached the curses imposed by God upon the unbelieving Jews, let us review them somewhat more carefully from the preceding passages.

Moses said to the whole Israelite people beyond the Jordan, in the plain of the wilderness: “Behold, today I set before you a blessing and a curse: a blessing if you obey the commandments of the Lord; a curse if you do not heed the commandments of your God. When the Lord your God brings you into the land which you are entering to possess, you shall place the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal, which are beyond the Jordan.”

Although these words are filled with very great meanings, they could not be fulfilled until the Jordan had been crossed—that is, until the sacrament of baptism had been consecrated by the waters of the Jordan touched by Christ’s body.

Gerizim, which is interpreted as “division,” signifies the apostolic people, divided from the synagogue of unbelievers, just as Paul says of himself: “When it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb to reveal his Son in me, I did not yield to flesh and blood.”

Ebal, however, which is interpreted as “the ancient abyss,” signifies the carnal and unbelieving Synagogue, which did not consent to pass over into the newness of the life-giving Spirit, but preferred to remain in the antiquity of the killing letter.

While they persevered there, an immense river of curses came upon them, in accordance with what is written: “The princes of Judah became like those who remove a boundary. I will pour out my anger upon them like water.”

And just as all promises and blessings altogether rested upon the apostolic people, so all threats and curses were confirmed upon the synagogue of Satan, in the very order of events that Moses had foretold when he said: “You shall be cursed in the city”—that is, Jerusalem—“cursed in the field,” scattered throughout the world; “cursed shall be your storehouse.”

Another translation reads: “Cursed are your storerooms and all that remains of you; cursed is the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your land. Cursed shall be the one entering”—that is, being born into this life—“and cursed the one going out” (Deuteronomy 28:17–19), namely, dying from this life.

And after much else he says: “The stranger who dwells with you in the land”—that is, the people of the nations—“shall rise above you and become higher,” having been made a son of the patriarchs and a companion of the root and richness of the olive tree. “But you shall descend and be lower, cut off from the olive tree and lying dry upon the earth, destined for fire. He shall be the head, and you shall be the tail.”

Even now some people come, attempting by their own efforts to raise them to the head from which they fell, as though they ought not to be the tail. Yet they will always be the tail until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel is saved—that is, all who are to be saved.

For the Lord will increase the plagues of those among them who are now unbelieving: great and enduring plagues, the worst and perpetual diseases. Another translation says: “most genuine plagues and true diseases.”

Again, in the same passage: “He will bring upon you all the afflictions of Egypt which you feared, and they will cling to you. Moreover, every sickness and every plague that is not written in the book of this law, the Lord will bring upon you until he destroys you.”

This is plainly what we quoted above from the Gospel: “The last state of that man”—that is, of the man into whom the unclean spirit has entered with seven other spirits more wicked than itself—“will be worse than the first.”

### XXVI

We have said these things briefly and have sampled only a little from many matters. We wished merely to show in outline with how many gifts of blessing God prepared the apostolic people to be worthy, and with how many curses, deservedly, he rejected the unbelieving synagogue; so that what had been foretold might also be fulfilled in the elect.

For the one who gave the law will give blessings, blessing them, according to the Apostle, “with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ.”

And upon those who believed neither the letters of Moses nor the words of Christ, and who were therefore rejected by God’s just judgment, would come the curse that had been foretold by Moses himself in these words: “Cursed is everyone who does not remain in the words of this law, to do them,” refusing to hear what is written in it: “The word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, so that you may do it.”

The Apostle explains this as follows: “This is the word of faith which we preach: that if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.”

### XXVII

Let these matters, then, have been briefly touched upon by us. For we must yield to those who are greater, more penetrating, and more eloquent, to whom it is very easy to disclose the deeper and more hidden aspects of this subject.

This ought to be done immediately, since the love of many is growing cold, iniquity is abounding everywhere, the wickedness of unbelievers is growing stronger, and the deceit of Antichrist is approaching.

Would that the diligence of the most religious Emperor might command one of his people to collect everything that the teachers of the Churches have written, explained, or indicated in the Holy Scriptures concerning what is to be understood about Antichrist. It would certainly serve to guard the faith, to raise up hope, and to strengthen and commend the sweetness of the love of Christ. Amen.

[Col. 0099C]

## CONSULTATION AND PETITION OF AGOBARD, BISHOP, TO THE GREAT MEN OF THE PALACE, CONCERNING THE BAPTISM OF JEWISH SLAVES

[Note: Consultation. In the royal manuscript there was no title at this place. But in the very ancient catalogue of Agobard’s works, which is copied at the beginning of the volume, the title of this work is written as we have published it.]

To the most reverend and most blessed lords and masters, and holy fathers, Adalard, Wala, and Helisachar.

[Note: Adalard, abbot of Old Corbie, in the diocese of Amiens. He was the son of Bernard, the brother of King Pippin, as Paschasius Radbertus relates in his Life. He was therefore raised at Pippin’s court, as Agobard teaches, among others, in chapter 2 of his book *On the Administration of Ecclesiastical Affairs*. After Pippin’s death, Adalard was admitted among the closest members of the household of King Charlemagne. In 809 the king sent him to Pope Leo III, together with Bernhari, bishop of Cologne, and Asio of Worms, to consult concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, a question that had recently arisen in Gaul.

Later, in 817, he is believed to have gone over to the side of King Pippin of Italy, who was rebelling against his father Louis. When the conspiracy failed and its leaders were punished, Adalard was exiled to the monastery of Saint Philibert in Aquitaine—that is, to the island of Herio, where the monastery of Saint Philibert was located—as is clear from the Life of Philibert preserved by Duchesne and from Ademar of Chabannes.

That monastery is now called the Black Monastery, commonly Noirmoutier, in the diocese of Luçon. Adalard was confined on this island until 821, when he was recalled from exile and restored to the monastery of Corbie, as Einhard relates: “He also summoned Adalard from Aquitaine, where he was in exile, and ordered him to be abbot and head of the monastery of Corbie, as he had been before.”

The author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* says: “He also restored Adalard, formerly abbot of the monastery of Corbie but then residing in the monastery of Saint Philibert, to his former office.”

The author of the *Annals of Saint Bertin*, under the year 822, writes: “The lord emperor, after holding counsel with his bishops and nobles, was reconciled with his brothers, whom he had ordered to be tonsured against their will; and concerning this deed, as well as what had been done regarding Bernard, the son of his brother Pippin, and also what had occurred concerning Adalard the abbot and his brother Wala, he made a public confession and performed penance.”

But the author of the book *On the Construction of New Corbie* complains that the accusation against Adalard was false: “Then pestilential men approached him”—that is, Louis the Pious, the emperor—“and expelled him from his office without fault, and exiled him without cause.”

Adalard therefore again became a participant in Louis’s counsels and held the leading place among them, as may be gathered from Hincmar, in letter 14 to the nobles of the kingdom, chapter 12: “I saw the old and wise Adalard, a relative of the lord Emperor Charlemagne and abbot of the monastery of Corbie, first among the foremost counselors in my youth; I read and copied his little book on the order of the palace.”

He died in 823, on the day after the Kalends of January, having in the preceding year composed a brief or little book concerning what he wished thereafter to be observed in the monastery of Corbie. This work was published in volume IV of the *Spicilegium* of Dom Luc d’Achery, Benedictine monk.

Wala, Adalard’s brother, succeeded him as abbot of Corbie. In the *Life of Louis the Pious*, Wala is therefore called a relative of that emperor. And lest anyone doubt that this is the same Wala, we have the authority of Einhard, whose words in the *Annals* under the year 823 are these: “He sent his son Lothair to Italy, and with him he sent Wala the monk, his relative—that is, the brother of Adalard the abbot—and Gerung, master of the doorkeepers.”

Wala died in 835 in the presence of Emperor Lothair, as is written in the *Life of Louis the Pious*. Paschasius Radbertus gives him this encomium in the *Life of Adalard*: “Then Wala, a most distinguished man, who succeeded him, afterward an outstanding father of monks, at that time first among the foremost and alone more beloved than all others, closely attached to the king through an excessive intimacy and raised to the highest dignity of prefect, more illustrious than all in the senate and, in military matters, stronger than all through his prudent courage. Such praise followed him in every affair of life that he was considered able to accomplish far more through love than all the arrogance and even tyranny of the others. For he was a guardian of justice and an ornament of honor, and also a just oppressor of the oppressed.”

He is called Walo in the book *On the Construction of New Corbie* and in Einhard’s *Annals* under the year 812.]

Adalard, Wala,

[Note: Helisachar, priest and abbot of the monastery of Centula, situated in the diocese of Amiens, as Ariulfus teaches in book III, chapter 4, of the *Chronicle of Centula*. Ariulfus adds that he was also head of the monastery of Gemmeticum.

That he was a man of great distinction is clear even from the title of this little work, where he is named among the nobles of the palace. We also have the authority of Einhard, who writes under the year 827: “The emperor sent the priest and abbot Helisachar, together with the counts Hildebrand and Donatus, to settle the disturbances in the Spanish March, and so forth.”

Abbot Amalarius likewise testifies in his book *On the Order of the Antiphonary* that this Helisachar was first among the foremost men of Emperor Louis’s palace. That he was Louis the Pious’s chancellor is clear from the fact that in several charters of Louis, the deacon Durandus subscribed in place of Helisachar.

He also attended blessed Benedict of Aniane when the abbot was dying, as Smaragdus relates in his Life.]

Helisachar.

[Col. 0101A]

Recently, when we had already been granted time to return from the palace, your most gracious affection sat down and heard me murmuring rather than speaking against those who were supporting the Jews’ complaints.

When you had heard and moderated what was being said on the other side, you rose, and I followed you. You entered into the presence of the prince; I remained before the door. Shortly afterward you arranged for me to enter. But I heard nothing except permission to depart.

[Note: “Permission to depart,” that is, leave to go away. In those times they used the verb *to absolve* for what Latins would call granting permission to depart. For example: “To absolve ambassadors.”]

What you said to the most gracious prince about the aforementioned matter, however, and how he received it or what he replied, I did not hear.

Afterward I did not approach you, hindered by cowardly shame and weariness that exhausted me. This weariness came upon me not so much from the entanglement of affairs as from the baseness of my mind.

Therefore I departed troubled, set out uncertainly, reached home confused, and sat down afflicted.
