I would write the causes of this affliction. But I fear imposing a burden upon your gentleness. Nevertheless, the bearer of this letter can tell you about them, if your patience permits.

There are, however, certain matters which I do not think should be kept silent, on account of which I make them known to your prudence and address them to your most faithful fatherhood.

The first matter, which it is most necessary for me—and, as I think, for everyone—to know, so that you may deign to give counsel corresponding to God’s work, is what should be done concerning the pagan slaves of the Jews whom the Jews have purchased and raised, and who, living among us, are learning our language.

They hear about the faith and see the celebration of the solemn festivals. Through these things they are pierced with love for Christianity, desire to become members of Christ in the body of the Church, and flee to the Church,

[Note: “Asking for baptism.” These were the slaves or servants of the Jews who were not themselves Jews but pagans. While living at Lyons among Christians and approving their customs and religion, they approached the church asking for baptism. The Jews objected, so as not to lose slaves who had cost them money. But Agobard offers the purchase price, in accordance with the canons, provided that they may be made Christian slaves.

There may indeed have been bad faith among those slaves: perhaps they merely pretended to wish to embrace the Christian faith in order to be claimed for freedom. For the law provided that Christian slaves must not serve or remain attached to Jews, as we noted in the book *On the Insolence of the Jews*.

Nor was this cunning of slaves new at that time. Already during the time of the Council of Gangra, some were withdrawing from the service of their masters because those masters were not Christians. Hence Dionysius Exiguus expressed the heading of the third canon of Gangra as follows: “Concerning slaves who cast off the yoke of servitude under pretext of Christianity.” The canon itself reads: “If anyone, under pretext of divine worship, teaches a slave to despise his own master, to withdraw from his service, and not to serve him with goodwill and all honor, let him be anathema.”

In the age of Gregory the Great, too, this activity of male and female slaves seemed harsh to the Jews. Gregory writes in book III, indiction 12, letter 9: “It has also come to our attention that slaves and female servants of Jews, fleeing to the church on account of the faith, are either being restored to unbelieving masters or having their price paid so that they may not be restored,” and so forth.

See the same Gregory, book V, indiction 14, letter 31, and the letter of Pope Gelasius to Siracusius, Constantius, and Laurentius, bishops, in Ivo, part XIII, chapter 113.

These passages of Gregory also support Agobard’s position. For Gregory orders absolutely that the slaves of Jews who flee to the church be claimed for freedom in every possible way, whether they had formerly been Christians or had recently been baptized.]

asking for baptism. The question is whether we ought to deny this to them or provide it wherever we can.

For my part, I hold the following position. Every human being is certainly God’s creature, and in every human being, even a slave, the Lord God who created him in the womb, brought him forth into the light of this life, granted him life, and preserved his health has a greater share than the man who, after paying twenty or thirty solidi, enjoys the service of his body.

No one doubts that although every slave owes the work of his bodily limbs to a carnal master, he owes the religion of his mind to the Creator alone.

For this reason all the holy preachers, companions of the apostles, teaching all nations and baptizing them, did not await permission from carnal masters in order to baptize slaves, as though slaves ought not to be baptized unless their masters permitted it. Rather, knowing and preaching that slaves and masters have one Lord God in heaven, they baptized them all, gathered them all into one body, and taught them all to be brothers and sons of God.

Nevertheless, each person was to remain in the condition in which he had been called,

[Note: “He should remain in this condition,” that is, no one was liberated from servitude after receiving baptism, in accordance with Paul’s teaching in chapter 7 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians. The canon of Gangra cited above also refers to this.]

not by choice but by necessity; and if any could become free, they were rather to make use of that opportunity.

It is also easy to infer by reasoning that if pagans flee to Christ and we do not receive them but reject them on account of their carnal masters,

[Note: “Carnal masters.” Salvian, in book III of *On the Government of God*, page 58: “Although we do not despise God by this injury alone, by which carnal masters are accustomed to be despised by their servants.”]

this is impious and cruel, since no one can be master of a human soul except its Creator.

We also think that this should be considered: if a religious emperor takes up arms against nations alien to the name of Christ and, having become victorious,

[Note: “Subjects them to Christ,” that is, the pagans whom he conquered in war. The same expression is also used by Stephen of Tournai in letter 170 to Canute, king of the Danes: “We ask that you, who so often overcome idolaters by arms and subject them to the Christian yoke,” and so forth.

Thus Charlemagne, distressed that the Saxons were not Christians, took up arms against them, determining not to end the war until they had been subjected to Christ. Einhard writes in the *Annals* under the year 776: “When the king was wintering at Quierzy, he resolved to attack the treacherous and oath-breaking nation of the Saxons in war and to persist until either, having been defeated, they were subjected to the Christian religion, or they were utterly destroyed.”

Einhard and the other Frankish annalists testify that what Charlemagne had conceived in his mind succeeded. Yet the chief authority must be attributed to the testimony of Louis the Pious, who says in a charter ordered to be issued to invite pagans to Christianity: “Our father also, the glorious Charles of blessed memory, subjected all Saxony to ecclesiastical religion and, subduing their fierce hearts by the sword, taught the yoke of Christ as far as the borders of the Danes and Slavs.”

As for the methods Charles used against the Saxons in order to subject them to Christ, no witness can be clearer than Charles himself, who enacted a law decreeing that no Saxon might be permitted not to be a Christian, under penalty of death. These are his words from the *Capitulation concerning the Regions of Saxony*, published by Holstenius, chapter 7: “If henceforth anyone among the Saxon people, hiding among them, wishes to remain unbaptized and refuses to come to baptism and wishes to remain a pagan, let him be put to death.”

For this reason the ancient author of the book *On the Construction of New Corbie* in Saxony thinks that Charles was more powerful in war than all Christian kings. “After the death,” he says, “of the most noble King Pippin, his son Charles obtained the entire kingdom of the Franks. The Lord granted him such strength and power that he not only ably governed the kingdom of the Franks but also subjugated many barbarian peoples all around.

Thus it came about that he not only subjected the Saxon people, which formerly rebelled against the Franks, to his own rule, but also deserved to dedicate it to the sweet name of Christ. For we believe that he was therefore more powerful in wars than all Christian kings: those whom he subjected to his rule, he dedicated to the name of Christ.”

Add to these the passages collected by the learned theologian John Launoy of Paris in chapter 5 of his book *On the Ancient Custom of Baptizing Jews and Infidels*.

Moreover, when you read in *On the Construction of New Corbie* that Charlemagne dedicated to the name of Christ the peoples whom he subjected to his rule, you must remember, reader, that not only the Saxons were converted to the Christian faith through his efforts, but also the Huns and Avars, as Sirmond observes in his note to Theodulf, page 287.

Long before Charlemagne there had also been the example of Clovis, king of the Franks, the first of the Frankish rulers to give his name to Christ. For, if any credence is due to the unpublished author of the Life of Saint Domninus, the hermit of Limoges, Clovis sent an edict throughout all the provinces of the Frankish empire ordering everyone, after abandoning the worship of idols, to turn to the religion of Christ.

These are the words of that author: “At that time King Clovis ruled Gaul and Germany, a man brave in arms and eloquent in speech; and all the Franks, both Christians and pagans, were subject to his rule. The king himself, from the beginning of his lineage, was a gentile. But through the divine inspiration of the Redeemer’s mercy, after the admonition of Saint Remigius, archbishop of Reims, he became a Christian, with the Lord’s favor, in the catholic faith.

After this king had been raised from the sacred font, he sent messengers through all the provinces subject to his authority and commanded that all temples of false gods be destroyed and burned, and that they should believe in the one true and omnipotent God and serve him alone. If anyone should presume to despise this royal decree, let him acknowledge himself guilty of offending royal majesty.”]

subjects them to Christ and joins them to the religion, this is a work of piety and worthy of praise. How, then, can we neglect it if there are among those who have been subjected people who desire baptism?

Nor do we say this so that the Jews may lose the prices they paid for such persons. Rather, we offer the prices,

[Note: “According to the statutes of the fathers,” namely, in accordance with canon 16 of the First Council of Mâcon, which is transcribed above in book 6 of *On Jewish Superstitions*.]

according to the statutes of the fathers; but they do not accept them, thinking that the officials of the palace favor them and wish them better treatment than those who assert the matters stated above.

These are the matters concerning which we ask your counsel or, through you, the command of the lord emperor.

This would certainly not be necessary if the man who is the master of the Jews

[Note: “Master of the Jews,” namely Evrard, as is clear from the following letter addressed to Nibridius, bishop of Narbonne: “Some envoys attempted it,” he says, “and especially Evrard, who is now the master of the Jews,” and so forth.]

would pay attention in the way you told him he ought to act.

For if, according to your command, he faithfully considered our office, just as we wish to show him honor in his own office, there would be no need to cause offense by questioning him except for the advancement of instruction.

Furthermore, there would be no dispute or disagreement concerning the Jews’ affairs if he had wished to act reasonably.

Now act toward us according to the love which the Holy Spirit has poured into your hearts, and bring consolation to your servant, because I am tormented by great fear and various anxieties.

For if we deny baptism to Jews or to their slaves when they ask for it, I fear divine condemnation; if we grant it, I fear human offense and such hostile injuries to our household.

Since I considered it unworthy to write about these injuries and disagreements in this little letter, I have sent your piety a small inventory,

[Note: “A little brief,” that is, an inventory, as we noted concerning the first letter of Lupus of Ferrières. Antiquity called a brief what we call today an inventory.

Thus Eusebius retained this word in the Greek text of book X, chapter 6, of his *Ecclesiastical History*. The word is also used in the same sense in the *Theodosian Code*, book III, *On Remission of Debts*, and book I, *On Liberal Studies in the City of Rome and Constantinople*.

Hence the passage of Optatus in book I *Against Parmenian*: “A brief of the gold and silver entrusted to Caecilian, as had been assigned by Mensurius, was handed over.” On this passage see the notes of Balduinus, although he does not seem to have sufficiently grasped the true meaning of the word.

From the same root come *inbreviate* in the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald* and in Hincmar, in the preface to book IV of the *Capitularies*.]

through which you may learn what the matters are.

Nor should your fortunate gentleness be displeased with me because I am importunate toward you in demanding such things. Rather, consider that this is the cause of the Church, the concern of the faith, and a divine work.

Moreover, all my confidence rests in your holiness. Therefore undertake this holy labor for the sake of eternal recompense and assist our Church by giving help and instruction, since you are debtors because of the great confidence it places in you.

[Col. 0107]

## LETTER OF SAINT AGOBARD, BISHOP, OF EXHORTATION TO NIBRIDIUS, BISHOP OF NARBONNE, CONCERNING AVOIDING JEWISH COMPANY AND ASSOCIATION

[Col. 0107A]

To the Most Blessed Father Nibridius, Archbishop of Narbonne [Note: Nibridius, archbishop of Narbonne, formerly abbot of the monastery of Crassus in the diocese of Carcassonne. I gladly embrace the conjecture of the distinguished man Guillaume Catel, who thinks that Nibridius and Nifridius are one and the same name. Nifridius was abbot of Crassus during Charlemagne’s reign. Catel would have adhered more firmly to this opinion if he had known that this archbishop of ours is called not Nibridius but Nifridius in the oldest copy of the charter of Louis the Pious mentioned above, and Nefridius in Alcuin’s preface to his books against Elipandus. From being abbot of Crassus, therefore, he became archbishop of Narbonne after Daniel, around the year 799. For it is certain that he was already a bishop before the Council of Aachen was held against Felix, bishop of Urgell. That he took part in the Council of Urgell, held against Felix before the Council of Aachen, may be inferred from the preface to Alcuin’s books against Elipandus of Toledo. Moreover, Nibridius was a man of great distinction in those times, as appears from this letter of Agobard to him. He was an envoy of Charlemagne in 813 at the Sixth Council of Arles, together with John, archbishop of that city. That he was still alive under Louis the Pious is clear from the charter mentioned above, as well as from another charter of the same ruler for the monastery of Aniane, published by the distinguished Benedictine monk Dom Luc d’Achery in his notes to Guibert, abbot of Notre-Dame de Nogent, p. 623.]

Agobard to Nibridius, in God the Father and the Lord Jesus, everlasting salvation.

If the nearness of our places and the tranquility of circumstances allowed it [Note: The nearness of the places. For the road from Lyon to Narbonne is extremely long, extending for 230 miles. Nevertheless, Agobard went there several times, as is clear from Louis’s charter for the monastery of Aniane.], I should indeed wish to speak with your fatherhood more frequently face to face, and, both in private and in public needs, always to be instructed by the counsel of your holiness. But since the great distances of the lands lying between us prevent this, I endeavor to accomplish by letter what I cannot accomplish by speech [Col. 0108A], bringing to your knowledge my own—indeed, the Church of God’s—not inconsiderable need, and desiring that where I find myself weak, I may be fortified by the support of your virtue as by a most powerful shield and an impregnable wall.

Let the venerable gray hairs of your fatherhood therefore know that this present year [Note: In the present year. I believe that this letter was written at the beginning of the reign of Louis the Pious, shortly [Col. 0107D] after Agobard became archbishop of Lyon.] while I was going through the people of our parish [Note: With due diligence. Bishops are bound to go throughout their parishes, that is, their dioceses. The Council of Tarragona, canon 8: “Through experience as our guide, we have discovered that some diocesan churches have been left deserted. For this reason we have decreed by this constitution that the order of ancient custom be maintained, and that the dioceses be visited annually by the bishop. And if any basilica should happen to be found abandoned, it must be ordered to be restored under his direction.” The Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 35: “The bishop ought to travel through all his dioceses and parishes each year, to inquire what each basilica requires for its restoration. But if he himself, whether detained by illness or entangled in other occupations, cannot fulfill this, let him send suitable priests or deacons, who shall investigate both the revenues of the basilicas, their repairs, and the conduct of those who serve in them.” Although this latter law was excessively favorable to the negligence of certain bishops, the Council of Trent renewed it, session 24, chapter 3, on Reform. Nor is there any doubt that, if the canon of the Council of Tarragona had been enacted everywhere in all provinces, and if later regulations had not moderated it, certain bishops who plead their occupations as an excuse for their negligence and ignorance would have labored with all their strength to avoid offending against the canons. For if they had not been ignorant of the canons, they would have understood what punishment threatens those who despise them. The prudence and religious concern of the kings of Agobard’s age therefore deserve great praise: they imposed upon bishops, who alone at that time possessed the power of confirming Christians, the obligation of traveling through their dioceses each year. Book VII of the Capitularies, chapter [Col. 0108C] 94: “We decree that each bishop shall diligently travel through his parish every year, endeavoring to confirm the people, teach the congregations, investigate and prohibit pagan observances, diviners, sorcerers, auguries, amulets, incantations, and every impurity of the pagans.” See also chapters 109 and 265 of the same book, as well as the Capitula of Charles the Bald, title 5, chapters 4, 5, and 6; title 6, chapter 28; and title 41, chapter 6. An edict of the ruler Carloman had preceded this, at the synod attended by the martyr Boniface. At that synod the ruler ordered as follows: “And whenever, according to canon law, the bishop goes around the parish to confirm the people, the priest must always be ready to receive the bishop.” Nevertheless, I do not wish anyone to infer from what has been said that I think there are no legitimate reasons for which a bishop may be excused from personally visiting his diocese. For if, for example, he is seriously ill, there is no doubt that he may refrain from a personal visitation: “For it is not the fault of sloth when pitiable misfortune excuses a man,” as Cassiodorus says in Book V of the Variæ, letter 36. Moreover, if he is compelled to be absent from his diocese on the business of the Church or of the state; if a soldier ravages the region, sparing neither sacred nor profane places; or if the person in power orders the bishop to leave the province, I would not deny that these too are legitimate reasons for not visiting the diocese. In that case one should follow the example of Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, who, although in exile, nevertheless governed his diocese through his priests. For he himself teaches this in the book he wrote to Constantius Augustus: “I am a bishop, remaining in the communion of all the Gallic Churches and bishops, although in exile, and still distributing the Church’s communion through my priests.” But once those causes have ceased, once the bishop—whether ill or absent—has again been granted free power to visit his diocese, then let him travel through the parishes of his diocese. When the necessity has ceased, let what was done for the sake of necessity also cease, to use the words of Urban II, taken from the canons of the Council of Clermont. Nor would I deny that the law of the Toledan canon is just and holy. But just as the Council of Nicaea committed some rules to writing and others to oral tradition, as Bishop Faustinus of Potentia, the legate of Pope Zosimus, argued at the Council of Carthage, so perhaps it would have been wiser and better not to insert any exception into the canons, lest it provide a pretext for the sloth of certain bishops. For laws are enacted with the intention that they should benefit, not harm, as Pope Symmachus writes to Avitus, bishop of Vienne.] with due diligence, and if anything in them appeared to be corrupt [Col. 0109A], I corrected it, insofar as the grace of God granted me strength, in accordance with the rule of truth. I announced and commanded to everyone, according to the law of God and the ordinances of the holy canons, that, as true worshipers of the Christian faith, they should separate themselves with every form of observance from the company of unbelievers—not, of course, from pagans, who by no means dwell among us [Note: But from the Jews. For canon 12 of the Council of Vannes, held in 465, had forbidden clerics to attend Jewish banquets: “Henceforth let all clerics avoid the banquets of the Jews, and let no one receive them at a banquet, because, since they do not use common foods with Christians, it is unworthy and sacrilegious for Christians to eat their food; for what we consume with the Apostle’s permission is judged unclean by them. Thus clerics would begin to be inferior to the Jews if we used what they set before us while they despised what was offered them by us.” But since this law seemed to include clerics alone, and there was great fear that such familiarity with Jews would also harm laypeople, canon 40 of Agde next extended the rule against laypeople. Agobard copied this canon in chapter 5 of his book On Jewish Superstitions. Agobard himself, however, enlarged the law by an edict forbidding any Christian to live with Jews. The most holy Ferreolus, bishop of Uzès in Narbonnese Gaul, had held a different view. He ate and drank with Jews, even criminals, in order to win them for Christ. This aroused against him the suspicion of Childebert, king of the Franks, who feared that such familiarity with Jews and Saracens might turn to the ruin of the kingdom. An ancient author of the Life of Ferreolus—until now unpublished—which I once copied at Toulouse from a very old manuscript of the college of Foix, relates the event as follows: “He was so concerned for the Jews—even for those whom public opinion condemned—that, eating and drinking with them, he mingled sweet admonitions with the bitterness of their character and softened it; and by converting many of them to the faith of Christ, they obtained the grace of baptism, while he made those lifted up by pride humble before Christ. He brought forward the accusation of the Pharisees, who blamed the Lord for eating and drinking with publicans and sinners; and he recalled the Lord’s answer, saying: ‘Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.’ And: ‘I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance.’” This was indeed excellent and in accord with Augustine’s mind. Thus he says, quoted by Gratian, 23, question 4: “We cannot win unbelievers for Christ if we avoid their conversation and their table. Hence the Lord also ate and drank with publicans and sinners.” From this it may be inferred that the same practices were not pleasing to all provinces: sometimes rules prevailed in Africa that were less approved by the Gauls; and again, within Gaul, certain practices pleased one bishop that did not please all. Yet meanwhile the bond of fraternal concord remained, and the peace of the Church was preserved. For in matters of discipline each Church may retain its own particular customs, provided they are not contrary to the faith, as Marca noted from Augustine and Gregory the Great in Book III of On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire, chapter 9, § 2, and Book VII, chapter 18, § 6. This may also be confirmed by the authority of Augustine, who wrote to Januarius in Letter 119, chapter 18: “I am indeed surprised that you wished me to write something for you concerning those matters that are observed differently in different places, since this is unnecessary and one most salutary rule must be retained in such matters: wherever we see or learn that practices have been established which are not contrary to the faith or to good morals and which contribute something toward the encouragement of a better life, we should not merely refrain from condemning them, but should pursue them with praise and imitation.” It may likewise be confirmed by the authority of Alcuin, who, speaking of the Church in Part III, chapter 17, of his Confession of Faith, says: “Although the whole Church is bound by the universal tradition of the ancestors, each Church nevertheless exists and is governed by private constitutions and particular instructions, whether according to the variety of places or as each has thought best. Customs, indeed, are diverse; but the integrity of orthodox faith within it is one and the same.” Thus Charlemagne, in the Capitular on Not Worshiping Images, Book I, chapter 6, excuses the Gallican Church’s disagreement with the Roman Church in the celebration of offices on the ground that the custom of the Gallican Church was not contrary to the faith. And Lupus of Ferrières, writing to Pope Benedict III, mentions ecclesiastical customs maintained variously in different places and asks the pontiff to instruct carefully Adulfus and Acaricus, monks of Ferrières, whom Lupus was sending to Rome for this reason, “so that through them,” he says, “the Roman institution may reach us and all others who piously seek such things. For in whatever pertains to religion or moral conduct, variety creates uncertainty.” It is therefore clear that Lupus did not disapprove of those differing customs, but nevertheless wished all the Churches to be uniform, namely, in order to avoid uncertainty. Accordingly, Stephen, bishop of Tournai, says splendidly in Letter 104: “The holy Roman Church has been accustomed either to approve the ancient customs of the Churches that conflict neither with reason nor with law, or has not judged them worthy of disapproval.” See Ratramnus, Book IV Against the Greeks, chapter 1, and Ruzeus, Treatise on the Preeminence of the Archiepiscopal Dignity, privilege 13. But to return our discourse to the point from which it digressed, the author of the Life of Saint Ferreolus adds: “Hence he was accused before Hildebert, king of the Franks, because he ate and drank with Jews and Saracens and gave them gifts. Then the aforementioned king, fearing that he was plotting some deception against him, ordered him to be sent from the city of Paris in France into exile; and there he remained in exile for three years.”] but from the Jews, who appear to be spread throughout this city of ours and several other neighboring cities.

For it seemed both very unworthy and inconsistent with our faith that the children of light should be darkened by association with darkness, and that the Church of Christ—whom it is fitting to prepare, without spot or wrinkle, for the embrace of the heavenly Bridegroom—should be disfigured by companionship with the spotted, wrinkled, and rejected Synagogue. And truly it is absurd that a chaste virgin, betrothed to one man, Christ [Note: Betrothed to one man, Christ. This was the universal conviction of the ancients concerning Christ and the Church: they called Christ the Bridegroom of the Church and the Church his bride, and none of them ever thought that the Church was not a bride of one husband. Thus Cyprian, in his book On the Unity of the Church, calling the Church the bride of Christ and our mother, says: “The bride of Christ cannot be adulterated. She is undefiled and chaste. She knows one house and, with chaste modesty, guards the sanctity of one chamber.” Augustine likewise expressed his opinion so plainly in Sermon 20 of those published by Sirmond that it is unnecessary to guess what he thought in this matter: “As he was about to ascend into heaven,” he says, “he entrusted the Church herself anew. The Bridegroom, as he was departing, entrusted his bride to his friends—not so that she should love any one of them, but that she should love him as Bridegroom and them as the Bridegroom’s friends, and that they should not allow her to be corrupted by wanton love.” Hence Pope Leo IX, writing to Robert, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu in Auvergne, stated that Christ is the true and only Bridegroom of the holy Church. Finally, Saint Bernard wrote as follows to Eugene III in Letter 237: “It remains that, after this transformation of yourself, she also who has been entrusted to you, the bride of your Lord, should be transformed for the better, and should henceforth be called not Sarai but Sarah. Understand what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding. If you are the Bridegroom’s friend, do not call his beloved ‘my princess,’ but simply ‘the princess,’ claiming nothing in her as your own except that, if necessary, you ought even to give your life for her.” Nevertheless, at the Council of Lyon under Gregory X, the Roman pontiff is called the Bridegroom of the Church, in the chapter “Ubi periculum,” On Elections, in the Sixth Book.] should seek the banquets of a prostitute and, through sharing food and drink, should not only fall into various sins but also endure danger to the faith. For through excessive familiarity and continuous cohabitation, some of the Christian flock observe the Sabbath with the Jews while violating the Lord’s Day by unlawful work; and they also violate the appointed fasts. Many women are held by them in the status of female slaves; others are kept as hirelings; some are even corrupted. All such women are collectively given over to their domination, lust, or deception, with the sons of the devil aiding this very purpose by concealed hatred and deceptive flatteries. They loudly proclaim that they are descended from the patriarchs, the race of the righteous, the offspring of the prophets [Note: The offspring of the patriarchs. See what we said in the book On the Insolence of the Jews.], while the wretched people who hear this do not know that their own prophets commonly call them a sinful nation, a people weighed down with iniquity, a wicked seed, criminal children, their father an Amorite, their mother a Hittite, the rulers of Sodom, and the people of Gomorrah. Nor do they know that John the Lord’s forerunner called them broods of vipers, and that the Lord himself frequently called them serpents, a wicked, crooked, perverse, and adulterous generation. Thus some among the common and rustic people are led into such a sea of error that they are persuaded in mind and impiously confess among their peers and equals that this alone is God’s people, that among them is the observance of true religion, and that their faith is far more certain than ours.

[Col. 0111C]

When we saw this evil growing among the people entrusted to us and spreading day by day through the force of habit, we endeavored with all our strength to extend a hand to those who had fallen and to recall wandering minds to the line of truth. We considered it right that, just as the law of God once commanded them not to enter into marriage with the nations or to share a common banquet with them, lest through matrimonial association and the sharing of food they should fall away from divine worship and bend the freedom of their minds beneath the yoke of idolatry, so now our people too should be forbidden to presume to share food with unbelieving Jews, to share drink with them, or to have the companionship of living together [Col. 0112A]. This is so that under the pretext of such association they may not depart from the simplicity of the Christian faith, while, attending to Jewish fables, they become entangled in inextricable snares of error; and so that, since we cannot lead any of them to the spiritual virtue of our faith by the great humanity and kindness we show them, some portion of our own people may not be captured by spiritual banquets while willingly sharing their fleshly feasts.

Our fathers appear to have followed this providence of the divine law in their canonical ordinances. We have obeyed their commands with devoted hearts, insofar as we could: fearing the danger to the souls entrusted to us and dreading that their blood would be required from our hands at the divine judgment [Note: Their blood from our hands. Agobard fears that if he does not exercise vigilant and diligent care over the souls entrusted to him, and if they perish through his sloth and negligence, God will require their destruction from his hand at the divine judgment. See the notes to Letter 79 of Lupus of Ferrières.].

Some emissaries, especially Evrard [Note: Evrard, the royal emissary. See the notes to the book On the Baptism of Jewish Slaves.], who is now master of the Jews, nevertheless attempted to destroy this religious work of ours and to weaken it under the pretext of imperial edicts. We did not yield to them even for an hour, so that the truth of the divine law and the venerable constitution of the holy Fathers might continue among us in immovable and unshaken observance. Nor did we dare to submit to commands so savage, nor could we believe that the most religious and God-worthy prince had ordered anything contrary to the divine law, opposed to the sacred canons, or dangerous to the salvation of the Church. His faithful diligence and admirable piety are always vigilant for this purpose: that the law of God may be observed everywhere, that canonical institutions may endure with perpetual firmness, and that the salvation and strength of the Church may grow more gloriously throughout the whole world with every passing day.

Therefore you too, most blessed Father, who are now believed to be a pillar in all things and the support of the house of God, stand upon the rock of ecclesiastical observance—immovable, fearless, unshaken—despising the winds, rains, and floods of the opposing storm. They may batter the foundation of the house of God, but they cannot overthrow it, because the gates of hell cannot prevail against it [Note: Against it—that is, against the Church, according to Agobard’s interpretation of the passage from the Gospel of Matthew: “Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” This passage has been variously interpreted: some refer it to the rock, that is, Peter and his Roman successors, the pontiffs; others to the rock, that is, Peter’s confession. Some have referred it to the Church, which Christ founded upon the rock, that is, upon himself. For Christ was the rock, as Saint Paul says in chapter 10 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians. Agobard, however, had no doubt that Christ’s promise referred to the Church, against which the gates of hell would not prevail. John XXI also embraced this interpretation in a letter written to James, king of Majorca, which we published last year after the notes to Lupus of Ferrières.].

Knowing, therefore, venerable Father, that all who are under the law are under a curse and clothed with a curse as with a garment; that it has entered their inward parts like water and their bones like oil; that they are cursed in the city and cursed in the field, cursed when they enter and cursed when they leave; that the fruit of their womb, their land, and their livestock is cursed; that their storehouses, granaries, warehouses, food, and even the remnants of their food are cursed; and that none of them can be rescued from this so savage and dreadful curse of the law except through him who was made a curse for us; knowing also that no one who refuses apostolic preaching is to be used at all, but that even the dust of the city and of their house must be shaken from one’s feet, and that it will be more tolerable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for them—remain steadfast in observance of the divine law, persist in the canonical institutions, hold those whom you can hold, frighten those whom you can frighten. Do not say [so], nor permit any of the faithful, through profane association with those who are cursed and condemned, to share in such great curses and such dreadful condemnations.

Rather, send the defenses of your exhortations also to your neighboring fellow bishops and brothers, so that by the common agreement and shared labor of all this great evil may be removed from the Churches of Christ. Let us fulfill the joy of Mother Church, all saying one thing, thinking one thing, feeling one thing—that is, being united in the struggle—for we know that this too is the desire of our most gracious Redeemer, according to what he himself prays to the Father for us: “I do not pray for these alone, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they too may be one in us.”

Our confidence in you is so great that we believe this work will stand either through your effort or—God forbid—fall through your neglect. May the God of patience and consolation grant us to think the same thing toward one another, according to Jesus Christ, so that with one mind and one voice we may glorify God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

[Col. 0113B]

BOOK OF THE SAME AUTHOR TO THE AFOREMENTIONED EMPEROR, AGAINST THE LAW OF GUNDOBAD AND THE UNGODLY DISPUTES CONDUCTED UNDER IT

### I

I beseech your unshakable gentleness and your most tranquil wisdom, most benevolent lord emperor [Col. 0113C], not to disdain reading without weariness these little pages that I offer, in contemplation of that highest and unchangeable Truth which is Christ our Lord. From his sayings and laws these words have been taken, and he lovingly and watchfully protects and assists your empire. Let not your tranquility, which deserves praise, be offended that the least of all men presents these things for the most excellent of men to read. For they contain nothing other than what you know better and more profoundly.

[Col. 0113D]

### II

God, the Son of God, made man for the sake of human beings, showing the way of salvation and entrusting the teaching of life to his chosen disciples, as he was about to ascend into heaven, said to them: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.” And again: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you.”

They went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them. Through them, to every creature—that is, to all the nations of the world—was announced one faith bestowed by God; one hope was spread by the Holy Spirit in the hearts of believers; one charity was born in all; one will arose, one desire was kindled; one prayer was handed down. Thus all people, from different nations, of different conditions, of different sexes, of different nobility and dignity, and of different forms of servitude [Col. 0114C], might together say to the one God and Father of all: “Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.” Calling upon one Father, they seek one sanctification; they ask for one kingdom; they desire the fulfillment of his will, as it is done in heaven; they pray that one daily bread be given them and that debts be forgiven to all.

For the teachers of the world, the light of the world, the holy apostles, could not teach anyone to say, “Forgive me my debts,” or “Do not lead me into temptation, but deliver me from evil”; rather, they taught one person to cry out for all and all for each one. O heavenly brotherhood, O everlasting concord, O indivisible unity, derived from one Author and referred back to one end of all things! Through it the heavens rejoice, the earth exults, the sea and its fullness are stirred, the fields rejoice together with all that is in them, and all nations clap their hands and shout to God with a voice of rejoicing!

### III

And how fitting it is that, having all become brothers, they invoke one God as Father: servant and master, poor and rich, unlearned and educated, weak and strong, humble laborer and exalted emperor. No one now disdains another; no one despises himself beneath another; no one exalts himself above another.

For we are one bread and one body of Christ—indeed, according to the Apostle, one Christ—stripping off the old man with his deeds and putting on the new, the one who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of his Creator. There “is neither Gentile nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, Aquitanian nor Lombard, Burgundian nor Alamannian, slave nor free,” but Christ is all and in all [Note: Aquitanian and Lombard. All these peoples whom Agobard lists here, and many others besides, were at that time subject to the Frankish empire. Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 281: “We wish and command that all who, with God’s help, are subject to our authority—Romans as well as Franks, Alamanni, Bavarians, Saxons, Thuringians, Frisians, Gauls, Burgundians, Bretons, Lombards, Basques, Beneventans, Goths, Spaniards, and all the rest subject to us—although they may appear to be bound by whatever bond of law or connected by customary practice, observe this judgment,” and so forth. All these peoples therefore used their own laws. See below, in the notes to chapter 14 of this book.].

For all things are theirs, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come. For all things, it is said to them, are yours; but you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.

And again: “Just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, whether slaves or free, and we were all given to drink of one Spirit.” And lest anyone should unbelievingly suppose that only a very few had drunk of one Spirit, he says: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit.”

There are indeed diversities of gifts and of works, but it is the same Lord and the same God who works all things in all, and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills. None of these, therefore, is a stranger or an alien; rather, they are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone. In him every structure joined together grows into a holy temple in the Lord. Those who were far away have been brought near by the blood of Christ.

For he is our peace, who made both one. Indeed, we can truly say that he made all things one, breaking down the dividing wall of hostility in his flesh, abolishing the law of commandments in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace, and reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, killing the hostility in himself. Coming, he preached peace to those who were far away and peace to those who were near, for through him both have access in one Spirit to the Father.

### IV

If, then, the Lord suffered for this purpose—that in his blood he might bring near those who were far away; if the dividing wall has already been broken down and hostility has been killed in him; if all have been reconciled to God in one body; and if they have become so completely one body in one Spirit that they are called Christ rather than Christians, as the apostolic statement quoted above declares: “Although all the members of the body are many, they are one body; so also is Christ” (for it does not say, “So also are Christians,” but “Christ”)—I desire through your piety to know whether such a diversity of laws does not obstruct this great unity of divine action—a diversity existing not only in individual regions or cities but even in many households.

For it often happens that five men travel or sit together, and none of them outwardly shares a common law with another in transitory matters, while inwardly they are held by the one law of Christ in eternal matters. And when it happens that all of them are truly Christians, loving the truth of the faith, and believing one another to be most dear brothers; when none rejects the testimony of another, and they build one another up with good words; if suddenly a dispute in court should arise for one of them, he cannot have any of his dearest companions with whom he was traveling as a witness, because no one’s testimony is accepted against a Gundobad [Note: Gundobad—that is, a Burgundian living under the law of Gundobad. This cannot refer to King Gundobad, who had died many centuries earlier. Accordingly, below, in chapter 10, he will call the Burgundians collectively Gundobads.], and so forth.

### V

Here, I beseech you, most benevolent and sacred emperor, let your patience come to my aid; and let your magnanimity not be indignant that I, unworthy though I am, speak of worthy things, and that a small man speaks of great matters. Through these matters—which perhaps cannot be corrected—I wish to reach those that are necessary and especially suited to your generosity.

But if what I say is inappropriate, let the just one correct me in mercy—that is, let your goodness correct me—and let him not expose the one whom he corrects.

To me, your servant—though the least, yet faithful—it nevertheless seems incongruous that a Christian should not be able to give testimony concerning a Christian, and therefore that a brother should not be able to testify concerning a brother. For, as was said above, all who have one God as Father are brothers and children of God. The Gospel also speaks plainly of this.

Hence it happens that when a just man is not permitted to testify against an unjust man because, according to the world, they belong to different laws, although according to God they ought to belong to one law, this is done to the injury of that unity and incorporation demonstrated above by the apostolic statements. For if someone is to be rejected as a witness, let the one who belongs to another faith or sect be rejected instead—also the one with whom the Apostle teaches that no food is to be eaten, saying: “If anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, with such a one do not even eat.” And again: “If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, mark that man and do not associate with him”—certainly not at table.

Unless all such people return to the body of Christ through penitential satisfaction, they will undoubtedly remain in the body of the devil, and consequently will belong to his kingdom and city.

## VI

Here there must certainly be discernment and separation between kingdom and kingdom—that is, between Christ’s and the devil’s—and between the city of God and the city of the devil, which constitute two peoples. For the city of God contains the people of acquisition, while the city of the devil contains the people of perdition. But if it is impossible for human beings to distinguish all who belong to the city of God from those who belong to the city of the devil, at least let them exclude from testimony those whom they recognize most clearly from their own fruits, and whom the apostolic writings teach to have been separated from the body of Christ. But those whom one bodily structure holds together, and who for the most part are not merely members of one body but members of one member, why are they excluded from giving testimony against one another? What advantage is there in making it impossible for one Christian to testify against another because of the law they call Gundobad’s law, whose author was a heretical man, and a vehement enemy of the Catholic faith (there are very few people who follow this law)? [Col. 0117B] From this arises a very absurd situation: if one of them commits some wrongdoing in a public gathering or even in the marketplace, he is not convicted by witnesses but is allowed to perjure himself, as though there were no one through whom the truth could be discovered. Here it plainly becomes evident that the law is harmful and condemnable.

[Col. 0117C] **The law of Gundobad**, whose author was Gundobad, king of the Burgundians in Gaul and a contemporary of the great Clovis. For, according to Gregory of Tours, “He established milder laws for the Burgundians, so that they would not oppress the Romans.” Yet the law of Gundobad, which perhaps at that time had appeared good, seemed unjust to certain pious men of Agobard’s age.

[Col. 0117D] **A heretical man.** Gundobad was an Arian. Nevertheless, at one point he was troubled by a desire to renounce his error, to such an extent that, persuaded by Avitus, bishop of Vienne, that the Arian sect was impious, he secretly sought to be anointed. Fear of the people prevailed, however. Thus, as Gregory of Tours says in Book II, chapter 34 of *The History of the Franks*, “he persisted in this madness until the end of his life, and refused publicly to confess the equality of the Trinity.”

[Col. 0117D] **There are very few.** Therefore the perfidy of the Arians had not yet been entirely extinguished in those regions, although they were extremely few.

## VII

But if it pleased our most wise lord, the emperor, to transfer them to the law of the Franks, they would themselves become more noble, and this region would be lifted, however slightly, from the squalor of its miseries. For because of them it has happened that not only the strong but also the weak and the elderly are frequently challenged to single combat and fighting—even over the most worthless matters. From these deadly contests arise unjust homicides and cruel and perverse outcomes of judgments, not without the loss of faith, charity, and compassion, while they suppose that God is on the side of the one who has been able to overcome his brother and cast him into the depths of misery. This is the worst kind of error and a confused order: that, on account of such perversities, the Scripture of truth should be despised, Christian harmony should perish, and such unworthy notions should be held about God, who is good by nature, that he favors the rapacious and opposes the afflicted.

[Col. 0118C] **This region: Lugdunensis.** For it used Gundobad’s law, since Lyons was a city of the Burgundian kingdom.

[Col. 0118D] **Are challenged to single combat.** He condemns single combat—that is, the private duel established by Gundobad for deciding disputes.

## VIII

Christ’s teaching says: “Whoever wishes to bring you to judgment and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well.” And again: “It is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits. Why not rather suffer injustice? Why not rather endure fraud?” Their opponents, by contrast, say: “Fight without fear; for you will certainly overcome the one who claims what is yours or brings an action against you.” And they promise divine assistance to men who are so opposed to evangelical compassion.

Thus they proceed boldly to combat, where two men come face to face, prepared to strike one another repeatedly over matters which they ought to have loved far less than they ought to have loved one another. For the man whom one wishes to kill or overcome, one has been commanded to love as oneself; and the trifling objects over which he contends he ought to regard as refuse, in order to gain Christ.

[Col. 0118D] **Those trifling objects.** We already noted in the preface to Lupus that Masson’s edition is corrupt at this point: it reads *recusias* instead of *reiculas*. Yet the ancient manuscript used by Masson clearly has *reiculas*, as the distinguished François Juret first pointed out to me in his notes on Letter 91 of Ivo of Chartres. This word is written in various ways in ancient books. Here, in Agobard, and also in the *Life of Saint Licinius, Bishop of Angers*, edited by Duchesne, as well as elsewhere, it is written *reiculas*; in Salvian and others, in more than one passage, *resculas*; and elsewhere *reculas*. See Juret, if desired, on the letter of Ivo mentioned above.

Where then is charity—the charity without which the perfect interpreter of all the languages of angels and human beings becomes like a sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal; without which the perfect prophet, the most learned teacher, and the man who shines with miracles through faith is nothing; without which generosity in almsgiving and the severity of martyrdom profit nothing? The soldiers of Christ who truly possessed this charity subjected the world to Christ through faith, but by dying, not by killing.

## IX

When there was a public dispute concerning the truth of religion, with some believing that any creature whatsoever should be worshiped in place of God, while others taught that only the Creator should be worshiped, those who were killed—not those who killed—were victorious. Truth was manifested by dying, not by killing. The witnesses of truth increased through death, whereas the defenders of iniquity perished by killing.

For if in this life the innocent were always victorious and the guilty were defeated, Pharaoh would not have killed Josiah; Josiah would have killed Pharaoh. Herod would not have killed John; John would have killed Herod. Nor would that holy city, Jerusalem, illustrious in the age of grace through innumerable throngs of monks, clerics, and other faithful people, have been subjected to the Saracens, as were other cities and regions; nor would Rome have been subjected to the Goths, simultaneously pagans and heretics; nor Italy to the Lombards—and many things of this kind.

[Col. 0118D] **To the Saracens, namely Jerusalem.** This had occurred approximately two hundred years before the book was written. The distinguished Cardinal Baronius, consulting Theophanes and others, has shown that Omar, leader of the Saracens, captured the holy city in the year 636.

[Col. 0119D] **Rome to the Goths.** That is, Rome was captured by Alaric, king of the Goths, who entered the victorious city on 24 August 410, as the same Baronius demonstrates.

[Col. 0119D] **Pagans and heretics.** He is speaking of the Goths. Since Radagaisus, king of the Goths, was a pagan, and after he was killed the remnants of his army—undoubtedly consisting of pagans—passed over to Alaric, who was indeed a Christian but a follower of the Arian perfidy, it is clear that the Goths who shortly afterward captured Rome were partly pagans and partly heretics.

[Col. 0120D] **Italy to the Lombards.** Baronius proves that this happened in the year of Christ 568, under Alboin, king of the Lombards.

We do not say these things in order to deny that God sometimes acquits the innocent and condemns the guilty, but because God has in no way ordained that this should occur in every case before the final judgment. And because such contests are vehemently opposed to Christian simplicity and compassion, and exceedingly contrary to evangelical teaching, let it be far from a Christian mind to seek escape from the adversities of this world through conflicts or to obtain its joys by means of fighting.

On the contrary, during the sacred solemnities of Mass we frequently pray to the Lord to grant us, for love of him, to despise the prosperity of the world and fear none of its adversities. Therefore it is altogether fitting that the Christian mind should, with fear and trembling, “work out its salvation,” according to the Apostle, and pass in thought to things to come, without fixing its understanding upon present affairs. For, by God’s most hidden dispensation, the outcomes of events in the present age are various, as Holy Scripture also testifies:

“There are righteous people to whom many things happen as though they had done the works of the wicked; and there are wicked people who are as secure as though they possessed the deeds of the righteous. And again: Because sentence against evil deeds is not quickly carried out, the hearts of human beings are filled with the determination to do evil without fear. And again: There are righteous and wise people, and their works are in the hand of God; yet no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred. Everything remains uncertain for the future, since all things come alike to the righteous and the wicked, to the good and the bad, to the clean and the unclean, to the one who sacrifices and the one who despises sacrifice. As it is with the good, so with the sinner; as with the perjurer, so with the one who swears truthfully. This is the worst thing among all that happens under the sun: that the same things happen to everyone. Therefore the hearts of the children of men are filled with evil and contempt during their life, and afterward they descend to the dead” (Ecclesiastes 9:1–3).

And again:

“I turned and saw that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the learned, nor favor to the skilled, but time and chance happen to them all. No one knows his own end. For as fish are caught on a hook, and as birds are seized in a snare, so human beings are caught at an evil time, when it suddenly overtakes them” (ibid., vv. 11–12).

There is no repayment of merits in the present life, but in the future. The faithful mind ought not to suspect that almighty God wishes the hidden deeds of human beings to be revealed in the present life through boiling water or red-hot iron—much less through cruel contests.

[Col. 0120D] **Boiling water.** On the judgment by boiling water and by heated iron, see François Pithou in his *Glossary to the Books of the Capitularies*, Juret in his observations on Letter 74 of Ivo of Chartres, and Sirmond in his notes on Geoffrey of Vendôme, Book III, Letter 38.

For this reason the Apostle commands that judgment concerning hidden matters be withheld “until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the things hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts.” Yet he permits judgment between brothers, so that disputes may be brought to an end.

## X

The usefulness of judgments, however, consists in the examination of cases and the carefulness of investigation, just as Solomon is recorded to have acted in the dispute between the two prostitutes. His request was pleasing to God for this very reason: he did not ask for riches or long life, but for wisdom to discern judgment.

So also Daniel, still a boy, when God stirred up his spirit, judged two wicked judges with wise discernment, through which the blessed Susanna was delivered from unjust condemnation. If these two judgments had occurred in our own times, it is easy to imagine what judges would say—before whom perjuries or bribes most often bring matters to an end.

How necessary the integrity of judgments is to kingdoms and peoples Scripture testifies, saying: “A kingdom is transferred from one nation to another because of injustices, wrongs, insults, and various deceits” (Ecclesiasticus 10:8). All these things abound more than among any other peoples among the Gundobads, under whose law it is not permitted to settle cases through examination or the testimony of truthful witnesses. Instead, whoever wishes may threaten with arms, so that the weaker person does not dare to retain what is his or to reclaim it—as though truth needed to be revealed by weapons. No authority and no reason permits anyone to believe this.

[Col. 0120D] **The Gundobads**, that is, the Burgundians, as was said in the fourth chapter of this book.

## XI

There is another matter that is useful for examining this question carefully, as reported in the Book of Judges. Certain men in the city of Gibeah, from the tribe of Benjamin, had committed an outrageous crime against the wife of a Levite. All the tribes of Israel assembled to punish this deed, while the entire tribe of Benjamin also gathered in the aforementioned city of Gibeah to defend the wrongdoing of its people.

The children of Israel first consulted the Lord at Shiloh and asked who should be commander of the battle. The Lord answered them: “Let Judah be your leader.” As soon as they began to attack the city, twenty-two thousand men of their number were killed.

Then they wept before the Lord until evening, and asked him whether they should proceed to fight against the children of Benjamin or not. The Lord answered them: “Go up against them and engage in battle.” When the battle was joined, eighteen thousand of them were struck down.

Therefore they came again to the house of God, sat weeping before the Lord, fasted until evening, and offered sacrifices. Then, proceeding once more to battle, they killed the entire tribe of Benjamin except those six hundred men.

Who would not be astonished at such an event? Who would not be terrified at the judgment of God, often hidden but never unjust? Certainly the children of Israel had the command of the law to punish crimes and avenge wrongdoing. Nor did they rely on the command of the law alone: they also asked the Lord while praying, and proceeded to battle at his command. Yet many more of them were killed beforehand, and afterward they punished the criminals—if, indeed, those six hundred did not include some of themselves.

[Col. 0121B] **For one mill-ass.** That is, an ass that works at a mill, as he will say at the end of the book *On the Method of Ecclesiastical Government*.

Since all these things are so, who is so reckless as to believe that, if two people contend over one mill-ass—or over anything even more worthless—the other person cannot fall, the one who is thought to be the rightful owner, when perhaps he has many or greater sins than the other, for which he ought to be punished?

This truly is not law but death. It is especially to be despised because it was devised by people who not only did not pray but also blasphemed the wisdom of God.

[Col. 0121B] **Blasphemed**, that is, reviled. Augustine, in Book *On the Work of Monks*, chapter 28: “Under the general name of monks, your profession is blasphemed.” Gregory of Tours, Book VI, chapter 46, speaking of King Chilperic: “He hated the causes of the poor and continually blasphemed the priests of the Lord.” The *Life of Saint Leodegarius*, edited by Duchesne, chapter 12: “For when the cruel Ebroin had satisfied his fury concerning the matters mentioned above, he again began to seek opportunities by which he might remove the blasphemy of his cruelty from human eyes.” The *Deeds of Dagobert I, King of the Franks*, chapter 46, where the great virtues of Ega are discussed: “He was nevertheless blasphemed by many because he was devoted to avarice.” Book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 170: “We exhort all to honor and venerate greatly the bishops and priests, before whom the whole earth bows its head, and through whom our empire also flourishes; nor do we wish them to be attacked, blasphemed, or slandered by anyone.” Book VII, chapter 142: “The one who composes songs for the blasphemy of another, or who sings them, shall be punished outside the ordinary legal procedure.” The *Annals of Metz* for the year 865: “They added many other things, blaspheming that same pope.”

From this comes the French word *blamer*, meaning “to revile”; later it too came to be used for insulting God. For formerly we saw an ancient manuscript at Tulle containing the record of a lawsuit concerning the see of Tulle between Guichard of Comborn, abbot of Uzerche, and Louis of Albuçon, prior of Mortagne, in the year 1457. Charles Petit, a royal sergeant, says in the proceedings he then drew up that the nephew of the same Guichard greatly obstructed him from making public a decree of the Parliament of Paris issued against Guichard, even threatening and blaspheming the Creator by saying that Charles’s deed and those of his assistants would not go unpunished but would have to be expiated by their slaughter. These are Charles’s words: “The said nephew of that abbot, dressed as a squire, reviling our Creator, said that there would be dead and slain upon the paving-stones.”

## XII

To this may be added another matter that seems worthy of pious consideration: namely, the Gallican canons, which some reject as almost superfluous or useless, because modern Romans have not commended them, although the ancient Romans venerated them devoutly. For they were issued by venerable and holy men whose lives and holiness were commended by frequent miracles. No one who has been able to hear of the many holy bishops throughout Gaul could ever have failed to find an account of them recorded in writing and handed down by report to posterity in each place.

[Col. 0121D] **Concerning the Gallican canons.** Our ancestors always held the Gallican canons in great reverence—not only the Gauls but also the Spaniards, as the most learned men have observed. Indeed, the name “Gallican canons” also included Spanish canons, as is clear from Hincmar in chapter 36 of his later work against Gottschalk: “It is also clearly recognized in the Gallican canons, concerning Potamius, archbishop of Braga, and the Council of Valencia.” It is evident that this refers to the Tenth Council of Toledo, at which Potamius, bishop of Braga, was deposed. For when he mentions the Council of Valencia, he is referring to the fourth canon of the Council of Valencia, held in the province of Vienne in the year 374.

England once used these same Gallican canons as well, since it was nearby; this may be inferred from the Council of Herford, held in the year 672. I am convinced that the book of canons produced at that council was none other than the code of the canons of the Gallican Church, and I possess reliable evidence by which this could be demonstrated, as I may perhaps show more fully elsewhere.

And truly, if, according to the Lord’s saying, “where two or three are gathered in his name, there he is in the midst of them,” how much more is he present where twenty or thirty, or many more, have gathered—not only in the Lord’s name but also endowed with faith, distinguished by wisdom, renowned for their life, revered for their holiness, and fearsome through signs and wonders?

[Col. 0123B] **With equal authority.** He says that regional or provincial councils, such as the Gallican councils, do not possess authority equal to that of general councils of the whole world, but that they should nevertheless be received with appropriate reverence. This may be taken from Augustine, Book II *On Baptism*, chapter 3: “The councils held in individual regions or provinces yield without any hesitation to the authority of plenary councils held from the whole Christian world.”

An ancient author, in the preface to his *Collection of Canons*, after speaking of the four ecumenical councils, says: “But if there are any councils which the holy Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, have decreed, they remain established after the authority of these four.” After him, Jesse, bishop of Amiens, says in a letter to his diocesan clergy: “If any other councils of the holy Fathers, gathered together out of necessity and filled with the Spirit of God, have decreed anything, they are to be observed and received.”

Hincmar, in his *Fifty-Fifth Opusculum*, chapter 25, says: “But if there are any councils instituted by the holy Fathers, he decreed that they should be guarded and observed after the authority of the four councils”—that is, Pope Gelasius, whose words these are: “If there are also any councils instituted up to the present by the holy Fathers, we command and decree that, after the authority of these four, they too are to be guarded and received.”

See Marca, Book III of *On the Concord of the Priesthood and Empire*, chapter 4, section 6, and Book VI, chapter 21, section 6.

Nor is this said so that the decrees of all episcopal assemblies everywhere should be thought worthy of reception with equal authority, as are the decrees of Nicaea, Chalcedon, and the other general councils assembled and received with the consent of the whole world. Rather, because of necessary matters whose definitions are not found in those general councils, faith should be given to these regional councils with the appropriate religious reverence. It is better for each person to follow their authority than his own opinion. It ought not to be possible to pass without grief when the definitions of many holy and Catholic men are neglected, while the law of one heretical king, Gundobad, is carefully observed as though it had been given by God.

[Col. 0122C] **Modern Romans.** Agobard ridicules and reproves the Romans of his own time, who wished to twist the customs of the ancient Church toward their own practices and therefore despised the Gallican canons because modern Romans had not commended them. Agobard answers this accusation by saying that the ancient Romans had held a different view and had devoutly venerated those canons.

He could therefore with excellent right have used against them the same weapon later wielded against the Greeks by Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie, in Book IV *Against the Greeks*, chapter 3: “It is therefore astonishing what sort of prudence this is among the new wise men: not to accept what their own ancestors are shown to have accepted.”

Thus the customs of the Romans, once holy and having won the reverence of the whole world for that people, had now been turned into contempt. Gerbertus likewise complains of his own age in Letter 40: “The customs of the Romans are an object of horror to the world.” In my opinion this happened because those who ought to have served as an example to all Christians throughout the world in observing the canons were trampling upon them more shamelessly than anyone else.

Nor do I say this myself; Rather of Verona, bishop of Verona, says it in Part II of *On Contempt for the Canons*, in volume II of Dom Luca D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 188: “Let someone also ask why, more than other nations reborn through baptism, the Italians are despisers of canonical law and scorners of the clergy.” And below, p. 190: “Why, then, should the envy of rivals, eager to disparage, inquire into these matters? Surely so that what could not become known through the preceding evidence might be demonstrated by what follows. Namely, so that anyone seeking the source of this present universal contempt for the holy canons might discover it. Our inquiry has reached and established this: it undoubtedly happened through the fault of those who, although they read and understand them, consider them worthless.”

See also the notes on chapter 20 of the book *On the Dispensation of Ecclesiastical Affairs*.

Nor is this said so that the sanctions of all episcopal assemblies everywhere should be believed receivable with equal authority, as are those of Nicaea, Chalcedon, and the other general councils convened and accepted by the agreement of the whole world. Rather, since matters necessary to be settled are often not found in the definitions of those general councils, faith should be given to regional councils with due religious reverence. It is better for each person to follow their authority than his own judgment. Nor can one pass without grief when the definitions of many holy and Catholic men are disregarded while the law of the one heretical king Gundobad is diligently observed as though given by God.

## XIII

In the time of the aforementioned Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, there was in the city of Vienne a holy bishop named Avitus. He was Catholic in faith, most eloquent in speech, keen in intellect, a most pleasing expositor of the Holy Scriptures, highly learned in secular literature, and extremely skilled in meter, as his works also testify.

He frequently disputed about the faith with Gundobad, composing dialogues with him when present and answering him through letters when absent. He left behind many distinguished works of intellect and virtue.

[Col. 0123C] **Disputing about the faith.** Of the disputes Agobard calls by this name, Dom Luca D’Achery recently published one in volume V of the *Spicilegium*, pp. 110ff. Avitus himself mentions another dispute with Gundobad in Letter 21, addressed to Lord Sigismund, Gundobad’s son: “When, by God’s favor, I have been granted your presence, I shall explain to you the entire course of the dispute.”

[Col. 0123C] **Dialogues.** We possess another fragment of one of these dialogues, preserved by Agobard in his book *On Paintings or Images*, chapter 9.

[Col. 0123D] **Answering him by letters when absent.** There are altogether eight letters of Avitus to King Gundobad, almost all concerning the cause of religion. Recently I also found another in an old manuscript belonging to the distinguished Peter Marnaesius, senator of Grenoble. Since it has not yet been published and may be useful against the distorted interpretations of certain people, I thought it appropriate to publish it after my notes in the appendix to the *Acts of the Ancients*, title 2.

[Col. 0123D] **With Gundobad himself lost in his perfidy.** Gregory of Tours, Book II, chapter 34, speaking of Gundobad: “Confounded by this reasoning, he persisted in this madness until the end of his life.”

[Col. 0123D] **King Sigismund, Gundobad’s son**, a man whom the following age regarded as most holy, and indeed publicly consecrated. Thus, in an ancient historical fragment published by Christian Ursinus and, after him, Duchesne, he is called a saint: “For Leudegisus, when he was mayor of the palace, had taken a wife from the lineage of Saint Sigismund, king of Burgundy.” Recently, however, the distinguished Adrien de Valois published the *Passion of Saint Sigismund*, composed, as he thinks, by a contemporary author and perhaps a monk of Agaune. From it it appears that, when his circumstances had been utterly ruined, this prince fled from Burgundy to a mountain called Veresallis and became a monk there, in order to withdraw himself from the savagery of his enemies; but that the treachery of certain Burgundians caused him to be drawn back from his flight under a pretext of piety. I shall give the author’s own words:

> “Therefore, when the Franks were devastating almost countless kingdoms and laying waste with great violence the cities of Gaul, so that a very great multitude of Burgundians joined themselves to the Franks, then Saint Sigismund, seeing himself hemmed in on every side, sought Mount Veresallis; and, after the manner of Elijah the Tishbite, chose to live alone, in order to escape the barbarous ferocity of a most cruel people, because his life was in danger, according to what the excellent preacher, writing of his tribulations, says: ‘In perils among false brethren.’ Then the Burgundians, more from necessity than willingness, surrendered themselves wholly to the Franks in a different manner, promising to seek out their most holy man Sigismund, their prince, and deliver him to them bound. When this promise was heard, Saint Sigismund, learning of their wickedness, cut off the hair of his head and exchanged lay clothing for the habit of religion. While he rested in the aforesaid place, almost worn away by fasts and vigils, a few Burgundians came to him, ostensibly out of affection, and promised secretly to lead him under some guard to the tombs of the holy martyrs. But when the bands of Burgundians together with the Franks had reached the enclosure of the monastery of Agaune itself, the Burgundians, like Judas the betrayer of Christ, laid hands on him and delivered him, bound in chains, to the Franks and to their king Clodomir.”

[Col. 0124D] But this author leaves unknown where in the world that mountain was situated, on which Sigismund wished to hide. It is probable that Sigismund sought foreign lands far removed from Gaul, lest he be discovered if he remained nearby. Accordingly, there is a constant local tradition, even consecrated in a certain poem, that he withdrew into Tarraconensian Spain, not far from Barcelona, to Mount Signium. Although that poem departs considerably from historical fact, it nevertheless seems to prove that Sigismund lived in this retreat until he was brought back by his own people. It is worthwhile, however, not to transcribe that poem, written in the vernacular Catalan tongue, but to relate in our own words the history described in it.

It says that the holy martyr Sigismund—or Sagimund, as he is now called—son of the king of the Burgundians, when in his fifteenth year he received a wound from a thorn, judged that no remedy was more suitable than to leave the world and hide himself in the wilderness. For this reason he came alone to the Pyrenees, where they divide Narbonensian Gaul from Tarraconensian Spain; having crossed the mountain passes joining the Spains to Gaul, he reached the town of Ficarias, which still today is the first place encountered by travellers on that road after they have crossed the mountains, and thence proceeded straight to the city of Ausona. There he met a certain Domarius—that is, I suppose, a canon of the church of Ausona—a man of most holy life, who pointed out to him Mount Signium, where he could work out his salvation far from the dangers of the world. Taking the road to a very high mountain called *a media die*, he came to a lodging called Podium-Vallis; learning that hermits lived in those mountains, he immediately went there and soon encountered a hermit, by whom he was taught what followers of that way of life ought to know. Then, bidding the man farewell, he withdrew into the wilderness, living on the herbs that grew there and drinking water.

Meanwhile Sigismund’s father, while seeking his son, went into those regions. When he reached the church of Saint Martial, situated on Mount Signium, he happened to find his son there. For every Friday Sigismund went there to receive barley bread, which it was customary to give in alms at that place. Yet the son was not recognized by his father, although they conversed together. Nature nevertheless prevailed, and he confessed that he was Sigismund. The father begged his son to abandon that life and return with him to Burgundy. Sigismund resisted, proclaiming the glory of this world vain and foolish and saying that eternal riches should rather be considered. Yet his father did not depart, but attempted by the same exhortation to bend his son’s mind, now through the filial affection owed to a father, now by invoking the tender name of his mother. Why delay longer? The father prevailed, and both returned to Burgundy, becoming a cause of great joy to their subjects. Thus far from that poem.

[Col. 0126C] These things agree sufficiently with the foregoing account, except for that youthful age and the father’s journey. How Sigismund ended his life may be learned from Gregory of Tours and other writers of Frankish history. And doubtless he made good use of death. Consequently, because of this deed and because he had built the monastery of Agaune, he was thereafter counted among the saints.

Avitus converted Gundobad’s successor, King Sigismund, to the Catholic faith. At this conversion he delivered before the people a homily filled with the greatest sweetness of thought and the most pleasing composition of words.
