[Col. 0123D] **King Sigismund**, namely, converted him from Arianism to Catholicism. That this happened while Gundobad was still alive is clear from the letters of Avitus.

[Col. 0126C] **He delivered a homily.** It no longer survives. See Sirmond on Letter 40 of Avitus.

What this venerable and holy man replied to the aforementioned Gundobad concerning these contests, let your graciousness hear, if it pleases you.

When they were discussing these matters with one another and blessed Avitus was condemning such contests, Gundobad replied to him:

> “Why is it that among kingdoms and nations, and even among individual persons, cases to be settled are so often entrusted to battle as to a divine judgment, and victory goes especially to the side to which justice belongs?”

To this blessed Avitus replied:

> “If, I say, kingdoms or nations were seeking divine judgment, they would first fear what is written by the Psalmist: ‘Scatter the nations that desire war’; and they would love what is likewise said: ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay,’ says the Lord. Or does heavenly justice not judge the movement of cases without weapons and swords? For often, as we see, the party that holds something justly or claims what is just suffers in battle, while either superior strength or secret deceit gives victory to the unjust party.”

### XIV

I do not say these things as though the varied outcomes of war were not governed by the judgment of the heavenly will. But it sometimes happens that, when people assemble for conflict under invocation of divine judgment, and the lot concerning the matter at issue falls against the defeated party, those sins which that party does not remember are punished instead, and it loses the merit of the present cause because of the debt of its sins.

What happens when an innocent traveler encounters an armed robber, and, without any formal declaration of judgment, either yields and is stripped, or resists and is punished—until the robber himself, in another conflict, in which he hopes that his cause will be judged favorable to him, perishes under judgment all the more because of this earlier deed?

What shall we say, then, about the uncertainty of single combats, which personal fury so often carries out among peaceful peoples, when, over some matter of dispute, both combatants sometimes justly lay down their lives, preferring the vilest gains to human and precious lives, and invoking God’s judgment in anger while impatience refuses to wait?

Here I ask whether the cause for which both combatants fall was bad for both of them. And would that it might please almighty God that, under one most pious king, all should be governed by one law—the very law by which he himself lives and by which his neighbors are ruled.

[Note: **One law should govern all.** He says that it is greatly to be desired that so many peoples as are subject to Louis’s rule should be ordered to live under one law, and that there should not be as many laws as there are peoples. For the Lombards lived by their own law, the Burgundians by theirs, the Saxons likewise by theirs, and the Goths by theirs, and so with the others. It is greatly to be desired that, just as all these peoples obey one prince, so they should also be governed by one law, not by different laws. But since that is difficult and almost impossible for a human being, at least the Gundobad law, which is exceedingly inhuman, should be removed. See the notes on chapter 3 of this book, and Ivo, part VIII, chapter 213, from the Council of Tribur, chapter 39.]

This would certainly contribute greatly to the harmony of the city of God and to the equity of peoples. But since this is a great undertaking and perhaps impossible for a human being, at least this one law of which we are speaking should be removed—not merely as useless, but even as harmful.

[Col. 0127]

## TO BERNARD, BISHOP: ON THE PRIVILEGE AND RIGHT OF THE PRIESTHOOD

[Note: **This is unquestionably the title of this book** in the codex of Papirius Masson and in the body of the book. In the old manuscript codex of the most distinguished man Peter Marnaesius, senator of Grenoble, however, the book is entitled as follows: *Bishop Agobard of Lyon’s Letter on the Dignity of the Priesthood to Barnard, Archbishop of Vienne*—which amounts to the same thing.]

[Col. 0127A]

### I

Agobard, to Bernard, his venerable brother in Christ and fellow bishop, everlasting salvation in the Lord.

Recently, while we were conversing together, especially about the pressures, hatred, and contempt directed against the churches [Note: **And against the clergy.** In the following century Ratherius, bishop of Verona, also grievously lamented the same conditions in part II of *On Contempt for the Canons*, in volume II of the *Spicilegium*, p. 188.] and the clergy—which have now begun to intensify in a manner unknown and unprecedented in past ages—your holiness saw fit to instruct me to excerpt from the sacred Scriptures or from the sayings of the holy Fathers certain passages that might provide us with material for investigating, considering, and lamenting the evils of our own time, evils unknown to our predecessors and fathers.

Although the Holy Spirit, speaking through the prophets, did not remain silent about them, saying: “And it shall be as with the people, so with the priest,” and many things of this kind.

It therefore seemed appropriate to me to comply with your holy devotion by setting aside, on the right and on the left, the matters that the Fathers have carefully and abundantly written concerning the reward of good priests and the condemnation of wicked ones, and by attempting, through writing, not to explain but to touch briefly and examine more closely something intermediate that is common to both: namely, the privilege and right of the priesthood.

[Col. 0127B]

### II

It should first be stated very briefly that all truly faithful people have been made members of the supreme priest—the priest who is God and our Lord Jesus Christ, mediator between God and human beings—by whom they have been made a kingdom and priests for the Father. They are called “a chosen race, a royal priesthood,” and under the supreme head there is one priest.

[Note: **One priest.** Agobard maintains that there is one priesthood in the Church of Christ, whose supreme head is Christ, who is the supreme priest; and that all the faithful are one priest under Christ as their one head, because of the passage in the First Epistle of blessed Peter where the faithful are called “a chosen race, a royal priesthood.”

Cyprian understood the matter differently when he wrote in Epistle 55: “Heresies have arisen from no other source, nor have schisms been born from any other cause, than that the priest of God is not obeyed, and that one priest at a given time and one judge at a given time, acting in Christ’s place, is not considered in the Church.” According to the observation of Rigaltius, Cyprian’s meaning here is simply that each church—which is a portion of the universal Church—ought to have one bishop-priest, who is priest of his own church for a time and judge in Christ’s place for a time.

“For these,” Cyprian says in Epistle 65, “are the beginnings of heretics and the origins and attempts of schismatics who think wickedly: that they may please themselves and, in proud arrogance, despise the one set over them”—that is, the bishop.

Baronius, however, in the year of Christ 34, §203, maintains that the one priest in Cyprian is Peter’s successor, the Roman pontiff, and he does so in terms that seem plainly to exclude the other bishops from that passage, and consequently to wish only the Roman pontiff to preside in the Church in Christ’s place. Yet Rigaltius also inferred from this passage that individual bishops are vicars of Christ.]

For this reason, those legal disqualifications that prevent a person from being a priest also exclude him from the body and kingdom of the supreme Priest, as the reliable exposition of the Fathers demonstrates.

Thus, when the sacred law began to be given through Moses, that sacred lamb whose blood, sprinkled on the lintels and doorposts of the houses, prevented the destroyer from entering the houses of those celebrating Passover, was not commanded to be taken by the priests, or by the people for the priests, or offered to God by the priests. Rather, it was to be taken by the entire assembly of the children of Israel, by families and households, according to the number of persons sufficient to consume it.

Nor are any excluded as unworthy or unclean; this is prescribed in common for all, with foreigners alone separated, while resident aliens and hired servants are included.

Finally, although the lamb is commanded to be without blemish, it is nevertheless ordered, according to the ancient translation, to be eaten from sheep and goats, and to be eaten with bitterness.

[Note: **The unworthy and the unclean.** He seems to admit even these to the eating of the lamb. Paul likewise admits them, but declares that they eat and drink judgment upon themselves.]

### III

To make clear the eminence or dignity of the priesthood as a whole, let us consider its ranks from the beginning of the world.

The firstborn—if that term may be used—of the first human being are the first said to have performed priestly ministry: Cain and Abel, that is, to have offered sacrifices to God. One of them was rejected, and his sacrifices were not regarded. This may have happened because he offered his own vows, not those of the people, although another cause of his rejection also existed.

For in what follows one will never find that offerings made on behalf of others were rejected, even if the one who offered them was unworthy, provided that he belonged by faith to the household, or offered within the household in which the lamb was to be eaten, as the law commands, saying: “It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not take any of its flesh outside.”

Rather, the hearts of those who offer through priests, whatever those priests may be, are weighed, as can be shown in many passages.

Thus the Lord says concerning good priests: “Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, my soul would not be toward this people.” And again: “I have no pleasure in you, and I will not accept an offering from your hand.”

Conversely, we have learned by human hearing and sight that offerings made to God through priests of reprehensible life have been accepted in such a way that they even healed bodily illnesses.

[Note: **They healed bodily illnesses.** From the fact that certain people healed bodily illnesses in the Lord’s name and became famous for miracles, it does not immediately follow that they were holy men, unless the other circumstances are equal, as we said in our letter to Lupus of Ferrières. Miracles, therefore, are not the most certain signs of a holy life.

For if we attend to miracles, Herodotus relates in Book I that Croesus was thrown into the fire by order of Cyrus, king of the Persians. Then, moved by remorse, Cyrus sent men to rescue him from the flames. But the blaze was so widespread that those sent by Cyrus could not extinguish it. Then, when Croesus had already recognized Cyrus’s repentance, a sudden rain burst forth at Croesus’s prayers and extinguished the fire.

Tacitus, in Book IV of the *Histories*, records that through Vespasian’s agency, without any human remedy, daylight returned to a blind man. To lend credibility to this account, he adds: “Both those who were present still relate the matter, now that falsehood has no reward.”

Spartianus recounts miracles performed by the emperor Hadrian in his *Life*; there is also an ancient Roman inscription concerning Aesculapius, published by Lipsius and Baronius; and Flavius Vopiscus, in his *Life of the Divine Aurelian*, reports that Apollonius of Tyana restored the dead to life.

In short, the books of the ancients are full of such narratives. One should consult Livy, Book I; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book VII; Plutarch, *Life of Coriolanus*, chapter 11; Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, chapter 11; Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book I, chapter 7; and others.

I know that Baronius diminishes the credibility of these prodigies, and rightly so. Far be it from anyone to suppose that such things could truly have been done by men who did not know the true God.

But if someone who was neither a pagan nor a Christian, but entirely free from religious commitments and human passions, were seriously to examine such narratives, he might perhaps give equal credence to the histories of pagans and Christians. Why should Christ have greater authority for him than Jupiter?

And lest anyone cry out that I am going farther than necessary, saying that no one could deny that so many great Christian miracles, which are commonly read about, actually occurred, I shall cite the testimony of Joseph Albo, a Jew, from his disputation against Christians, which Gilbert Genebrard translated into Latin. Thus this Jew speaks:

“The demonstration of true faith consists in the continuation of signs, as they continued in Israel when the Israelites lived in their own land; you will not find this among those devoted to the Christian or Ishmaelite religion.”

For pagans too insist that their miracles are true, as we have seen in Tacitus. Caecilius, defending pagan religion in Minucius Felix, says among other things:

“Even in sleep we see, hear, and recognize the gods whom during the day we impiously deny, reject, and perjure ourselves against.”

A little earlier he had said that, through the help of the gods who protect the Roman state, there are given “protection amid dangers, healing for diseases, hope for the afflicted, and assistance for the wretched.”

What, then, shall we say about heretics, who also wish their faith to be confirmed by miracles? For it is clear from Tertullian that Montanus attributed his new discipline to the Paraclete and to revelations, and from Augustine that the Donatists boasted of visions and portents in order to establish their error concerning baptism.

Sulpicius Severus also records that Valens, an extremely Arian man, if one may speak in that way, when announcing to the emperor Constantius the victory won over Magnentius at Mursa, dared to say that an angel had announced the event to him, so as to increase the reverence in which he was held, being confident that his hearer would readily believe him.

Moreover, in Letter 135 of Boniface of Mainz, we read that Adalbert, an impostor and heretic, became famous among his followers through miracles as well, and that they raised a serious complaint against Boniface because he had taken away from them the worker of wonders and exhibitor of signs.

Miracles, then, to return to the point from which we digressed, are not always the most certain signs of a holy life, since wicked men too can become famous through prodigies—or rather, have become famous in this way—as Agobard teaches.

There is an especially notable passage on this subject from blessed Pope Gregory, in Homily 29 on the Gospels:

“For those bodily miracles,” he says, “sometimes reveal holiness, but do not produce it. The spiritual miracles that take place in the mind, however, do not reveal the virtue of life but produce it. The wicked can possess the former; only the good can enjoy the latter.

Thus Truth says of certain people: ‘Many will say to me on that day, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?” And then I will declare to them, “I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity.”’

Therefore, dearest brothers, do not love signs that can be shared with the rejected; love instead the miracles of charity and piety that we have just mentioned. They are all the safer because they are hidden.”

Let us now hear the illustrious star of the Gallican Church, Charlemagne, subscribing to blessed Gregory’s judgment. Thus he speaks in the *Capitulary on Not Worshiping Images*, Book III, chapter 25:

“For many signs and many miracles are performed by apostate angels and even by their followers. Although they are spiritual powers—or, as I might say, spiritual wickednesses—they bestow prophecies upon certain wretched people and perform many mighty works through their satellites. Among these will be those who say: ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works in your name?’ To them the eternal Judge will say: ‘I do not know you.’

Since signs are often performed at the devil’s instigation, therefore blessed Gregory, bishop of the holy Roman Church, said: ‘Do not love, my brothers, signs that can be shared with the rejected.’

The most holy Augustine likewise testifies in these words that miracles are performed by demons, resembling the miracles performed through God’s holy servants. For he says: ‘One ought not to be disturbed when miracles are often performed through magical arts that resemble the miracles performed through God’s holy servants,’ and so forth.”

An ancient unknown author, whose manuscript I possess, writes:

“We have learned from God himself that even sinners can perform signs, prodigies, and healings in the Lord’s name. While by this presumption they help others, they harm themselves through their ambition for human glory, because they glory in a gift falsely attributed to them, not in merits deserving of it.

We rightly believe that a Christian may become famous through signs and prodigies without thereby becoming holy, if he lives with intemperate and harsh behavior; but that through temperate and peaceful conduct, even without the power to perform signs, a person may become holy, perfect, and a man of God.”

Peter Damian, in chapter 28 of the book called *The Most Pleasing*, writes:

“What is surprising,” he says, “if almighty God permits the priestly office to be propagated in his Church through wicked ministers, since through those same men he frequently also displays signs of power—not on account of the merit of a religious life, but because of the sacrament of the priestly mystery that they have received?”

Finally, we must carefully consider Augustine’s statement that miracles had already ceased in his own age because they were no longer necessary, though they had been necessary at the beginning of Christianity.

These are Augustine’s words in chapter 25 of *On True Religion*:

“We have learned that our ancestors, at that stage of faith by which one ascends from temporal things to eternal things, followed visible miracles—for otherwise they could not have done so. Through them it was accomplished that such miracles would not be necessary for later generations.

For when the Catholic Church had been spread and established throughout the whole world, those miracles were not permitted to continue into our times, lest the human mind should always seek visible things and, through familiarity with them, the human race should grow cold toward the things whose novelty had inflamed it.”

Charlemagne, Book IV, chapter 15:

“For the Catholic Church,” he says, “in order to grow in faith, had to be nourished by miracles; and, so that its young plantation might grow strong, it had to be refreshed by continual irrigations.”

Thus Aymo of Fleury, in the prologue to his *Life of Saint Abbo*, openly declares that those miracles raise no one up and that people can be holy without them:

“If someone should therefore think that Abbo’s reputation ought to be diminished because during his life he scarcely performed any remarkable sign, let him read the lives of the outstanding teachers Augustine and Jerome. In them he will find praised not the prodigies of temporal signs—which wicked people often perform—but purity of life, eloquence in salutary teaching, and constancy of faith.”

How little importance should be attached to the fame of prodigies is taught by the author of the appendix to the *Annals of Heinrich Stero*. Speaking of a certain Armannus, who because of his renown was held in great honor among the people of Ferrara, he writes under the year 1302:

“Then the body of a certain man named Armannus, which for thirty-one years had been venerated as that of a saint in the church of Ferrara, was exhumed and burned, by the diligence and command of the inquisitors of heretical depravity in those regions, as the body of a condemned heretic; and his precious altar was destroyed.”

[Note: **The whirlpool of human affairs!**]

They perhaps will say to God, “Lord, Lord, in your name we cast out demons and performed many mighty works,” and so forth.

Something similar is also read in the Book of Judges concerning Micah. He had a carved image and a cast image, a separate shrine, and made an ephod and teraphim. He received a certain young man of Levitical descent to serve as his priest. Although he was plainly a priest of the images, contrary to the law, he nevertheless consulted the Lord on behalf of the sons of Dan, and received a favorable answer concerning what was to happen.

### IV

The same principle also helps confirm the position that priestly services are dispensed according to the merits of peoples. The Lord says to the holy prophet Ezekiel:

“I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, and you shall be mute, unable to act as a reproving man, because the house is rebellious.”

Conversely, concerning Caiaphas it is said:

“He did not say this of himself. But, because he was high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was about to die for the nation.”

But why seek examples elsewhere, when the evangelist says even of the Lord himself:

“He could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them, and he marveled because of their unbelief.”

Another evangelist expresses the matter more clearly, saying:

“He did not perform many mighty works there because of their unbelief.”

In these people, then, the merit of unbelief meant that many miracles were not performed among them; and even the few who were healed were cured not by the power of the word alone, but by the laying on of hands.

The centurion’s paralyzed servant and the daughter of the Canaanite woman, who was grievously troubled by a demon, he restored to health by the word alone.

[Col. 0131C]

This was plainly required by the greatness of their faith. The one had said: “Only say the word, and my servant will be healed.” The other had not doubted that even little dogs could receive crumbs falling from their masters’ table.

The Savior praised her with remarkable commendation, saying of the centurion: “I have not found such faith in Israel”; and to the Canaanite woman: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.”

Conversely, among the other true disciples, he also bestowed a great grace of miracles upon Judas, a false disciple and genuine betrayer.

[Note: **A genuine betrayer.** He is speaking of Judas Iscariot, who was one of the Twelve. The emperor Otto and the Roman synod, in their letter to Pope John XII, preserved by Luitprand in Book VI, chapter 10, write:

“Judas, the betrayer—or rather seller—of our Lord Jesus Christ, had first received from his master, together with the others, the power of binding and loosing, in these words: ‘Truly I say to you, whatever you bind on earth…’ For as long as he was good among the disciples, he was able to bind and loose. But after he became a murderer through the poison of greed and wished to kill life, who could afterward loose him when bound or bind him when loosed, except the man who strangled himself with the most wretched noose?”]

As the Gospel relates:

“Jesus summoned his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to heal every disease and every sickness.”

It then adds:

“Now the names of the twelve apostles are these: first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother”; and after all the others have been listed, Judas Iscariot is placed last, “who also betrayed him.”

Then it continues:

“These twelve Jesus sent out.”

And shortly afterward:

“As you go, preach, saying that the kingdom of heaven has drawn near. Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons.”

Another evangelist adds:

“And going out, they preached that people should repent; and they cast out many demons, anointed many sick people with oil, and healed them.”

Speaking of such people—both good and wicked preachers—the Apostle says:

“What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, and I will rejoice.”

### V

From the matters mentioned above it is therefore gathered that priests, when they are heard or are beneficial through preaching, ought not to attribute this to their own merits, but to the merits of those for whom they act.

[Note: **Nor should the people attribute it to the priest’s fault.** He is noting the opinion of the ignorant common people, who judge a priest’s life solely by miracles and suppose that a priest is not righteous if his prayers, offered for the public welfare, are not heard by God. Rather, this should be attributed to the people’s own wicked conduct and serious offenses against God.]

Nor should the people attribute the failure to the priest’s fault, but to their own, when the priest is effective neither in prayer nor in speech. This may happen in different ways, as blessed Pope Gregory affirms, saying in Homily 17 on the Gospels:

“Often, because of their own wickedness, the tongue of preachers is restrained; often, however, it happens because of the fault of those subject to them that the word of preaching is taken away from those who preside.”

We say these things in order to show that good things can be administered through both good and wicked men; but that good men are often unable to benefit the wicked and are prevented from exercising the usefulness of their ministry.

Thus the Lord, speaking of the unfaithful vineyard, says:

“I will command the clouds not to rain upon it.”

And likewise, when forbidding Jeremiah, the same Lord says:

“Do not pray for this people, nor take up praise and prayer on their behalf, because I will not hear you.”

As for what we said earlier about Cain: if he had offered sacrifice on behalf of others—which cannot be done without charity—it would in no way have been said that the Lord did not regard Cain and his offerings. This will be demonstrated more clearly below, if the Lord sees fit to grant it.

For now, let us continue with what we have begun concerning the excellence and dignity of the priesthood and of priests.

### VI

Noah, through whom the human race was restored, built an altar to the Lord after the flood and offered burnt offerings. The Lord smelled the pleasing odor and said to him:

“I will never again curse the ground because of human beings.”

Melchizedek, king of Salem, is written to have been priest of God Most High. Concerning him the Apostle says:

“Consider how great this man was, to whom even Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth from the choicest things.”

The chosen patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, of whom the Lord says to David, “I have made your name like that of one of the great ones who are celebrated on earth”—are read to have built altars.

Blessed Job too is written to have offered burnt offerings every day. As blessed Jerome says:

“It is an ancient tradition of the Jews that before the law all the firstborn were priests and sacrificed victims to God.”

Under the law, however, the tribe of Levi is taken in place of every firstborn who opens the womb among the children of Israel. The Levites become God’s own, and Moses is told:

“Take the Levites in place of all the firstborn among the children of Israel, and the cattle of the Levites in place of their cattle; and the Levites shall be mine. I am the Lord. Any outsider who approaches to minister shall die.”

A remarkable and exceedingly astonishing thing! All the Levites whom Moses and Aaron counted, according to the Lord’s command, by their families, every male from one month old and upward, numbered twenty-two thousand—just as there are twenty-two letters among the Hebrews and twenty-two books of divine authority in the Old Testament.

This corresponds to what is said in Deuteronomy:

“Moses therefore wrote this law and delivered it to the priests, the sons of Levi, who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and to all the elders of Israel.”

### VII

It is also worthy of complete wonder that the firstborn males of the children of Israel, in whose place the sons of Levi were given, numbered by name, from one month old and upward, twenty-two thousand two hundred and seventy-three.

For the number twenty-two, as stated, corresponds to the number of letters and books; above it are a double hundred, a sevenfold ten, and a single three—numbers most sacred in the divine writings.

[Note: Thus the royal codex reads. The Marnaesian codex, however, has “in the divine books.”]

From this time onward, it was no longer appropriate for every firstborn to be a priest, but only the Levites, the sons of Aaron, who were separated from the people, as it is written:

“You shall not number the tribe of Levi, nor include their total among the children of Israel, but appoint them over the tabernacle of the testimony.”

And shortly afterward:

“When the camp is to set out, the Levites shall take down the tabernacle; and when the camp is to be established, they shall set it up. Whoever among outsiders approaches shall be put to death.”

They were so separated from and placed above the people that the Lord commanded Moses to say to them—to Aaron, that is, and his sons:

“Thus shall you bless the children of Israel.”

And after the blessing:

“They shall invoke my name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them.”

They will not bless; I will bless. Their task is to invoke; mine is to bless.

In these words he does not exclude the wicked, but speaks collectively of all, both good and wicked. By “wicked” I mean men such as Hophni and Phinehas, Somna and Phadassur, and others of that kind, although these received punishment in the present life.

It was not only the priests’ task to pray for the people, but also that of all the Levites, as the Lord himself says:

“I took the Levites in place of all the firstborn of the children of Israel, and I gave them as a gift to Aaron and his sons from among the people, so that they might serve me for Israel in the tent of the covenant and pray for them, lest there be a plague among the people if they dare to approach the sanctuary.”

Here it should be observed that, just as not all priests and Levites could be holy and righteous, so not all the other Israelites were wicked and sinful. Nevertheless, through sinful priests and Levites the saving rites of the people were accomplished—rites that could not be performed through righteous members of the people.

And although righteous members of the people are more worthy of eternal life than unrighteous priests, unrighteous priests can perform the sacraments on which the salvation of the people rests, whereas righteous members of the people cannot. This is because the power of the ministry itself remains effective in whatever sort of minister performs it, while righteousness is ineffective in one who has not been granted the authority to minister.

Moses repeatedly impresses this also upon the people, saying:

“The Lord separated the tribe of Levi, so that it might carry the ark of the covenant of the Lord, stand before him in ministry, and bless in his name.”

### VIII

The sacraments of the altar must be attempted only by those appointed for them, to such an extent that the Lord says to Aaron:

“You and your sons and your father’s house with you shall bear the iniquity of the sanctuary; and you and your sons with you shall bear the sins of your priesthood.”

And afterward:

“If any outsider approaches, he shall be put to death.”

This is read as having been terribly fulfilled in Uzzah, when David was bringing the ark of the Lord from the house of Abinadab. It is written:

“They placed the ark of the Lord on a new cart and brought it from the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill. Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were driving the new cart.”

And shortly afterward:

“When they came to the threshing floor of Nachon, Uzzah stretched out his hand toward the ark of God and held it, because the oxen were kicking and had caused it to tilt. The Lord was angry with Uzzah and struck him for his rashness, and he died there beside the ark of God.”

Certainly Uzzah was carrying out the task assigned to him: he was driving the cart. It seemed to belong to his service to support the ark of God, which the unruly oxen had caused to incline.

But because it was not his office to touch it, what he seemed to have done out of devotion was terribly reckoned by God as rashness—a rashness so great that it was immediately punished by the penalty of death.

Blessed David was so terrified by this that Scripture continues:

“David was afraid of the Lord that day, saying, ‘How shall the ark of the Lord come to me?’ And David was unwilling to take the ark of the Lord into the city of David, but turned it aside into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.”

After some time, when he heard that the Lord had blessed the house of Obed-edom the Gittite because of the ark of God, he summoned the chief priests and Levites and is read to have given this command:

“You who are the heads of the Levitical families, sanctify yourselves together with your brothers, and bring up the ark of the Lord God of Israel to the place prepared for it, lest, as at the beginning, when you were not present, the Lord struck us, so now, while we act, something unlawful occur.”

Conversely, King Uzziah—of whom it is written that he sought the Lord and loved him in all things—when he had grown strong, became proud to his destruction and neglected the Lord his God.

He entered the temple of the Lord and wished to burn incense upon the altar of incense. At once Azariah the priest entered after him, accompanied by eighty priests of the Lord, men of great courage. They resisted the king and said:

“It is not your office, Uzziah, to burn incense to the Lord, but that of the priests, that is, the sons of Aaron, who have been consecrated for this ministry. Go out of the sanctuary; do not despise it. This will not be counted to you as glory by the Lord God.”

Uzziah became angry. Holding the censer in his hand so that he might burn incense, he threatened the priests. Immediately leprosy appeared on his forehead before the priests in the house of the Lord, above the altar of incense.

When Azariah the high priest and all the other priests looked at him, they saw the leprosy on his forehead and quickly expelled him. Terrified, he himself hastened to leave, because he had immediately felt the Lord’s blow. (2 Chronicles 26:16ff.)

Thus are those who despise priests struck by such vengeance, and such strength and steadfastness are proclaimed in priests.

For this reason that same Azariah is raised up with singular praise, as it is written concerning him:

“Azariah the priest, of the family of Aaron, was the one who exercised the priesthood in the house that Solomon built in Jerusalem.”

## IX

Since such great dignity of priesthood has therefore been bestowed upon priests, the people are commanded to obey them in all things. Moses says:

> “Then the priests, the sons of Levi, whom the Lord your God has chosen to minister to him and to bless in his name, shall come forward; and every matter and whatever is clean or unclean shall be decided according to their word.”

How dangerous it is not to obey priests is also declared in a remarkable way through Moses:

> “Take careful heed lest you incur the plague of leprosy; but do according to everything that the priests of the Levitical order teach you, in accordance with what I commanded them, and diligently carry it out.”

Since leprosy is a bodily illness, why does he command obedience not to physicians but to priests? Unless it is because, by listening humbly to priests, one avoids impurity of mind, especially error—provided, however, that the priest teaches what the Lord commanded. For this is what he says: “You shall do everything that the priests teach you, according to what I commanded them.”

[Note: **If a priest teaches something else.** Therefore, if priests teach heresy or propose anything contrary to good morals, it is lawful for the people to resist and reject their preaching. Subjects may consequently examine the words of their superiors, at least whenever they command something that agrees neither with sacred Scripture nor with tradition. D. Erasmus treats this argument elegantly, as is his custom, in his discussion of the words from chapter 23 of the Gospel according to Matthew, “Upon the seat of Moses,” and so forth. He speaks as follows:

> “Some twist this passage to mean that everything commanded by bishops or superiors must be obeyed, even when they are wicked, because of the authority of their office. But Christ is speaking of those who correctly taught the Mosaic law, not of those who ensnared people with their own petty regulations. Thus even now a bishop who correctly teaches the Gospel should perhaps be heard, although he himself lives little in accordance with the Gospel. But who could endure those who, against Christ’s teaching, exercise sheer tyranny over the people through laws repeatedly made and unmade for their own advantage, measuring everything by their profit and dignity? Those who entangle the people with petty regulations devised for gain and tyranny do not sit in the evangelical chair, but in the chair of Simon Magus or Caiaphas.”

Goffrid of Vendôme likewise solemnly warns of this in Letter 27 of Book III, writing to Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, that prelates are not to be obeyed if they command anything against Scripture or the canons:

> “A prelate must indeed be obeyed, but not in everything he suggests—only in those things that God commands. For if prelates command anything against the constitution of God or of the Fathers, they immediately lose the authority to command, and in that matter they must in no way be obeyed.”

This has always been the mind of the Church: peoples ought to be subject to bishops and carry out their commands, so that the bond of fraternal concord may remain. But if superiors impose something burdensome and harsh upon their subjects, patience must be maintained, and one must not immediately rage against them. Even if they are disorderly, they must be obeyed so that division may not arise—provided that they do not compel anyone to impiety.

I hear some saying that patience accomplishes nothing except that heavier burdens are imposed upon those who tolerate everything too easily. I admit that this is sometimes so. But an evil that one cannot remove must be endured with equanimity. I do not, however, demand servile patience, from which those enrolled among the adopted children of God ought to remain far away. Rather, I desire a kind of patience worthy of the followers of Christ: one that is neither abject nor, on the other hand, rebellious, but steadfast and generous. In this way the fierce spirits of superiors may perhaps be softened.

And if other remedies are lacking, subjects may sometimes admonish those who rule, when the matter is of some importance or when they offend against the public good. Gregory the Great offers an outstanding passage on this subject in Book XXV of his *Moralia on Job*, chapter 21:

> “Therefore, while the matter is conducted with faith preserved, it is a mark of virtue if whatever belongs to a superior is endured. Yet one should humbly suggest that what displeases might perhaps be corrected, if it can be corrected. But one must take the greatest care that an unregulated defense of justice does not turn into pride; that, while rectitude is loved without caution, humility—the very teacher of rectitude—is lost; and that no one despise as his superior one whom he may happen to criticize in some action. Against this swelling of pride, the minds of subjects are subdued for the preservation of humility when their own weakness is constantly considered.”

See the same Gregory in Book II of *Pastoral Care*, chapter 8.

Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, follows Gregory. In Book II of *On Consideration*, chapter 1, he writes thus to Pope Eugene III:

> “It is not my humility to dictate to you that anything should be done in this way or that. It is enough to have indicated that something ought to be done by which the Church may be consoled and the mouths of those speaking wickedly may be stopped.”

Nevertheless, subjects must above all take care not to despise their superiors merely because the latter’s life appears blameworthy in some respect.

> “For a subtle path of rectitude and humility must be followed, so that the blameworthy deeds of teachers may displease in such a way that the minds of subjects do not withdraw from preserving reverence toward their teaching authority,”

as Saint Gregory warns in the same Book XXV, chapter 22.]

For if a priest teaches something other than what the Lord commanded, a leper follows a leper and a blind man a blind man; consequently, both will be expelled from the camp, and both will fall into the pit. Therefore, a priest should teach nothing except what the Lord commands, so that he may be heard for salvation.

Thus also the Lord speaks to Ezekiel:

> “You shall hear a word from my mouth, and you shall announce it to them from me.”

He says, “You shall hear”—not from elsewhere, but “from my mouth”—and “you shall announce it from me,” not from yourself; for whoever speaks falsehood speaks from his own resources. On the other hand, every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and the light of truth comes from the Father of lights. There is no good or truth except from him who alone is good by nature and truly so.

## X

But let us see whether the apostolic writings also teach these things in harmony with the Law.

The blessed Apostle Paul, writing to the Hebrews, says:

> “Obey your superiors and be subject to them. For they keep watch, as those who must render an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning.”

Writing also to Timothy, he says:

> “Let the presbyters who preside well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching. For Scripture says, ‘You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain’; and, ‘The laborer is worthy of his wage.’”

“On this matter,” says blessed Pope Gregory (*Homily 17 on the Gospels*), “one must consider that two rewards are owed for the same work: one on the way, the other in the homeland; one that sustains us in our labor, the other that rewards us in the resurrection.”

Likewise, writing to the Corinthians, he says, among many other things relevant to this subject:

> “Who feeds a flock and does not eat of the flock’s milk? Do I say this merely from a human point of view? Or does the law not say the same? For it is written in the law of Moses: ‘You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain.’ Does God care about oxen? Or does he certainly say this for our sake? Indeed, it was written for our sake, because the one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes in hope of receiving the harvest. If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?”

And shortly afterward:

> “Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary, and that those who serve at the altar share with the altar? So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel.”

And again in the same place:

> “I appeal to you, brothers: you know the household of Stephanas and Fortunatus, that they are the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints. You also should submit to such people, and to everyone who cooperates and labors. I rejoice at the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they supplied what was lacking in you. For they refreshed my spirit and yours. Therefore acknowledge people of this kind.”

Likewise, to the Thessalonians:

> “We ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you, preside over you in the Lord, and admonish you; esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.”

## XI

We have gathered these few testimonies from the Old and New Testaments in which we may behold, as in a mirror, the disgrace of our own age—a disgrace that ought to be lamented with every source of tears—now that the impious custom has grown so strong that scarcely anyone is found who, panting after and making even the slightest progress toward temporal honors and glory, does not have a domestic priest.

[Note: **A domestic priest.** In the age of Agobard, that custom had become widespread by which leading men kept domestic priests who celebrated the divine offices and mysteries for them on their estates and in their fields. In earlier times this had been permitted by the indulgence of bishops, as is clear from canon 21 of the Council of Agde. In Agobard’s age, however, that episcopal indulgence had turned into a necessity. For there exists a law against rejecting clerics whom laymen presented to bishops to be made presbyters, in Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 90, and Book V, chapter 178. See also Hincmar’s *Capitula given to presbyters* in the year 874, chapter 5.

Thus, because those presbyters remained with the magnates, they came to be called their presbyters. Pope Nicholas I took this very seriously, as is clear from his letter to a certain Gallic bishop, preserved in Hugh, abbot of Flavigny’s *Chronicle*:

> “It sounded ridiculous, dearest brother, when, recommending to us the bearer of your letter, you stated that he was the presbyter of the illustrious Count Gerard. But what your prudence intended to say by writing this, and what you understood by such a phrase, I confess that we do not know. Did Count Gerard consecrate him as a presbyter? Does he belong to Gerard’s diocese? Where did you read this? Where did you learn it? Unless it is because presbyters are not ordained, according to the sacred Scriptures, specifically for a church, estate, or martyr-shrine, but are established in the houses of laymen and associate with secular persons, so that they are now said to belong neither to God nor to any church, but to that count and that duke.”

The eighteenth canon of the synod of Pavia, held under the emperors Lothair and Louis around the year 850, calls clerics of this kind—those who remain in the households of magnates—“acephalous”:

> “Clerics or priests who are governed under the discipline and care of no bishop are in no way to be regarded as such. The ancient custom of the Church has called such men acephalous, that is, ‘without a head.’ Secular men must therefore be taught that, if divine mysteries are to be continually celebrated in their houses—which is highly commendable—they must nevertheless be handled by those who have been examined by bishops and are proved to be accompanied by commendatory letters from their ordainers when they happen to migrate to foreign places.”

Urban II says the same in canon 9 of the Council of Melphi:

> “Because a new kind of acephalous cleric has arisen in our time—men who remain in courts and are subject to men and women, to the disgrace of their order, although the canons provide that no cleric may approach a court without the bishop’s permission, nor a bishop without the metropolitan’s—we strictly command and prohibit that anyone retain men of this kind.”

]

Such a person does not have a domestic priest in order to obey him, but in order to demand from him continually both lawful and unlawful obedience—not only in divine offices but also in human affairs—so that many are found who either serve at their tables, mix filtered wines, lead dogs, or manage the horses ridden by women, or provide for little estates.

[Note: **Filtered wines.** This is how the royal codex reads, and likewise the Marnaesian codex; it is not *sacrata* (“consecrated”), as it was wrongly printed in Masson’s edition. *Saccata vina* means “wines strained through a sack,” perhaps what we today call Hippocratic wine. This kind of drink is greatly favored by those who spend their lives in pleasures and luxury.]

[Note: **Provide for little estates.** That is, they take charge of fields and become collectors of fiscal property, revenues, or taxes. Agobard disapproved of this, as did the Fathers of the synod of Pavia held around the year 850. They speak thus in canon 19:

> “That abuse must also be prohibited by which certain secular men appoint presbyters or other clerics as tenants, stewards, or collectors of fiscal property, revenues, or taxes. Therefore, if anyone henceforth is found guilty of this transgression, both parties shall be excommunicated: the one who appointed him and the one who disgracefully obeyed.”

This very practice was later gravely prohibited in the synods of subsequent centuries. Yet the evils prevailed over the remedies.]

And since such people, of whom we are speaking, cannot have good priests in their houses—for what good cleric would endure having his name and life dishonored by association with such men?—they care nothing at all what sort of clerics these are, how blind they are through ignorance, or how entangled in crimes. They care only to have their own presbyters, on whose account they abandon the churches, the elders, and public offices.

[Note: **Elders.** This is how both codices read. Masson, however, printed *sermones* (“discourses”).]

That they do not have them for the honor of religion is evident from the fact that they do not honor them. Thus, when they want these men ordained presbyters, they speak of them contemptuously and ask or order us, saying:

> “I have a little cleric whom I raised from my own slaves,”

or from my beneficiaries,

[Note: **Beneficiaries.** That is, vassals or feudal tenants. *Beneficium* was then the term for what was later called a fief, as we noted in the letter of Lupus of Ferrières, no. 119.]

or from my peasants,

[Note: **District inhabitants (*pagenses*).** That is, from those who live in the district entrusted to me to govern. From the bishops’ admonition to King Louis the German, chapter 12:

> “Appoint counts and ministers of the commonwealth who do not love gifts, who hate avarice, who detest pride, and who do not oppress or dishonor the district inhabitants.”

See Bignonius in his notes on Marculf, p. 518, and Sirmond in his notes on the *Capitula* of Charles the Bald, p. 47.]

or, “I obtained him from this or that man, or from this or that district. I want you to ordain him my presbyter.”

And when this has been done, they suppose that, because of it, presbyters of the higher order are no longer necessary for them, and they frequently abandon the public offices and preaching.

[Note: **Presbyters of the higher order.** That is, the presbyters whom we now call rectors of parish churches. Gregory the Great calls them “cardinal presbyters” in Book II, Letter 9, in order to distinguish them from the others; Walter, bishop of Orléans, does likewise in chapter 2 of his *Capitula*. The passage of Pope Leo concerning cardinal presbyters, cited in Book I of the *Decretals*, title 24, chapter 2, must be understood in the same way. Nor do I agree with Duaren, who, in Book I, chapter 13 of *On the Sacred Ministries of the Church*, interprets this passage as referring to presbyters who celebrate the divine service together with their bishop in the greater church—which we call the cathedral—and whom people today commonly call canons.]

Thus what the prophet said has also been fulfilled among us:

> “Your people are like those who dispute with the priest. You shall fall today, and the prophet shall fall with you.”  
> And shortly afterward: “I will change their glory into disgrace. They eat the sins of my people, and they lift up their souls toward their iniquity. And it shall be: as the people, so the priest; I will visit his ways upon him and repay him for his thoughts.”

Or there is the other passage in Scripture, which says:

> “After these words Jeroboam did not return from his evil way; on the contrary, he made priests of the high places from the lowest of the people. Whoever wished filled his hand, and became a priest of the high places. Because of this the house of Jeroboam sinned, and it was overthrown and destroyed from the face of the earth” (III Kings [1 Kings] 13:33–34).

## XII

Perhaps someone will resist these two statements, saying:

“These things were spoken about the ten tribes of Israel, which under Jeroboam withdrew from the house of David, the holy city, the temple and altar, and the ministry of the chosen priests. Therefore they should be understood of heretics, who withdraw from the true house of David, that is, Christ, and from communion with or the teaching of Catholic priests. We have not withdrawn from the Church, nor do we despise the mother churches; but we have priests such as we can obtain.”

[Note: **Mother churches.** That is, parish churches in which we have been incorporated into the body of Christ and in which we were educated. They were likewise called “matrix churches” at the Council of Chalon-sur-Saône, held in the year 915, a fragment of which was published by Severtius, and also in Ivo’s Letter 173. At the Council of Carthage held in 418, however, canon 33 uses “matrix church” to mean the cathedral.]

Let whoever says this consider the many ways in which one may withdraw from the house and body of David, and he will undoubtedly find that all the deeds deserving condemnation correspond very closely to this matter, just as our teachers understood it.

There are, moreover, many other statements of divine authority in which such great profanation is condemned without ambiguity. Such is the passage of the prophet Malachi (1:8):

> “If you offer the blind for sacrifice, is that not evil? And if you offer the lame and the sick, is that not evil?”

This statement can indeed be understood specifically of carnal or spiritual sacrifices, but it may also plausibly be understood of those who make the offerings.

But since there are many sayings of the Fathers about what sort of men these ought or ought not to be, we must discuss the matter with complete contrition of heart, we who in these very evil times have received the ministry of ordaining and governing churches. If we cannot avoid the danger altogether, let us at least strive to help ourselves to some degree, lest we share in the sins of others—for our own sins are already abundant.

Although our iniquities have risen above our heads and have weighed heavily upon us like a heavy burden, let us not despise the Apostle’s pious admonition:

> “Lay hands hastily on no one, and do not share in the sins of others.”

## XIII

Ever since the faith of Christ was announced and received throughout the world, the rulers of churches have not been surrounded by dangers so numerous, so serious, and so unavoidable. For, as we remember having already said, the world flourished in earlier years as though in its youth. But now it is weighed down by its own old age and, as though death were near, is pressed by increasing troubles.

We can say the same without hesitation about the Church. In earlier years she was strong for enduring sufferings, upright in the perfection of truth, powerful in the display of signs, girded by devotion to wondrous continence and abstinence, vigilant against the rage of wolves, and free to resist the wicked. But now she is so weakened by every infirmity of mind—

[Note: **So weakened.** The subject is the Church. Salvian says at the beginning of Book I of *Against the Catholic Church*:

> “For when the peoples of the faith were multiplied, faith was diminished; and as her children increased, the mother became sick. Thus, Church, you have become weaker through the growth of your fruitfulness, and by advancing you have slipped backward, as though less strong in your powers.”

]

that it is neither safe nor possible to speak, while it is neither ready nor easy to take precautions.

[Note: **Neither safe for speaking.** The misfortune of Agobard’s age was such that priests were not permitted to say what they wished, but had to handle gently the vices of their subjects. This is the final stage of calamity. Accordingly, that great man, Saint Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, says splendidly in his book *On the Lapsed*:

> “Whoever flatters a sinner with soothing caresses supplies fuel for sinning; he does not suppress sins but nourishes them. But whoever rebukes and instructs his brother with stronger counsel advances him toward salvation. ‘Those whom I love,’ says the Lord, ‘I rebuke and discipline.’ Thus the priest of God ought not to deceive people through misleading attentions, but to provide salutary remedies. The physician is unskilled who, sparing the hand, touches the swollen openings of wounds and, preserving the poison enclosed in the deeper recesses of the organs, allows it to increase. The wound must be opened and cut, and, after the corruption has been removed, treated with stronger medicine. Let the patient cry out, shout, and complain in impatience because of the pain; later, when he has felt the healing, he will give thanks. For, dearest brothers, a new kind of disaster has arisen; and as though the storm of persecution had raged too little, there has been added to the accumulation of evils a deceptive harm under the name of mercy and a flattering destruction.”

]

Would that we could at least grieve worthily over these years of famine and sterility that Pharaoh saw in a dream and the holy man Joseph understood and explained.

For the river of this age, from which seven beautiful and exceedingly fat cows seemed to rise, grazing in marshy places, signifies earlier times, which had teachers exalted in doctrine, radiant in holiness, firm in defending the truth, and ready to resist the fury of wolves.

But now—and this cannot be said without profound sorrow—other cows, ugly and wasted by emaciation, are already emerging from that same river. If we attempt to say something about this matter according to the meagerness of our speech, we may perhaps offend one another. Nevertheless, if, with God’s help, we come together,

[Note: **Come together.** He warns Bernard, bishop of Vienne, that this matter is so serious that it deserves to be treated in a synod of several provinces, and that, should the occasion arise, it must not be neglected.]

we ought to discuss it carefully and faithfully. For it is customary even among those whose health is failing and whose sickness is gaining strength to think and inquire about such matters, so that they may arrive at an understanding of them.

## XIV

Let us also ask whether that which is terrifyingly proclaimed through the prophet may already be near, and fear lest it involve us in destruction:

> “On that day, says the Lord of hosts, the peg that was fixed in a secure place shall be removed; it shall be broken and fall, and what hung upon it shall perish, because the Lord has spoken.”

So that what the Truth says may consequently be fulfilled:

> “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith upon the earth?”

Yet because the Truth itself says again:

> “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age,”

there will undoubtedly always be people in the Church with whom he is present. There will be exceedingly strong and robust warriors of God, against whom the one who is now bound in the abyss will be released and permitted to wage war with all his strength. Divine grace will make them capable of fighting so monstrous a beast and of emerging victorious over it.

Let us therefore exhort one another day by day, not abandoning our assembly. Let us hear the Lord warning through the prophet:

> “Gather the wheat into my granary, and let there be food in my house.”

This is the evangelical wheat of which it is said:

> “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord appoints over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time?”

Blessed is that servant whom, when the Lord comes, he finds doing this.

But if this was always necessary, how much more now, when that time is already nearer, about which the Lord says:

> “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will send a famine upon the earth—not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God—and the good virgins will fail.”

Meanwhile, as another prophet says:

> “What is its goodness, and what is its beauty, except the grain of the chosen and the wine that causes virgins to flourish?”

In these words each of us must above all undergo the strictness of judgment against himself and demand from himself a confession of the truth: whether he is more concerned to gather wine in which there is luxury, or wine that causes virgins to flourish.

## XV

Let these few remarks about ourselves suffice, insofar as they concern our office and ministry.

Let us next tell the faithful laity with what faith and hope they should strive to venerate the divine sacraments when administered by priests generally, whether those priests are diligent or negligent, watchful or sluggish.

For the divine sacraments—namely baptism, the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood, and the other rites in which the salvation and life of the faithful consist—are so great and holy that they can neither be improved by the merits of good men nor be made worse by the perversity of bad men. By the invocation of the High Priest,

[Note: **The High Priest.** That is, Christ.]

they are ineffably accomplished by the majesty of the Holy Spirit, not by human power.

Therefore, as blessed Augustine teaches:

> “The sacrament of Christ is not to be approved in good ministers and rejected in bad ones, as though it belonged to one or the other, since it is the same in both and belongs only to God. And although it is good in the worst men, even if one of the men who perform it is worse than another, what they perform is not therefore worse in one than in the other. For even among two bad Catholics, if one is worse than the other, he does not bear a worse baptism; nor, if one of them is good and the other bad, is baptism bad in the bad man and good in the good man. Rather, it is good in both—just as the light of the sun, or even of a lamp, is not worse in worse eyes than in better eyes, but is the same in both, although according to their differing condition it either gladdens or torments them.”

[Note: **By the perversity of bad men.** Agobard therefore holds that the sacraments are effected even through the sacrifice of an impious priest. Cyprian held another view. In Letter 68, as Erasmus notes there, he seems altogether to think that nothing is effected through the sacrifice of an impious priest; indeed, that the people are more greatly defiled.

Optatus, however, clearly writes in Book VI that something can be sanctified even when the invocation of the divine name is made through the work of a sinner:

> “Therefore it is now plainly evident that something can be sanctified through the invocation of the name of God, even if a sinner invokes God.”

Anastasius the pope held the same view in the case of Acacius, in his letter to the Emperor Anastasius, chapters 7 and 8; Agobard cites it below in chapter 17 of this book. Hincmar of Rheims also uses this authority in Letter 26, written to Pope Nicholas. Liutprand of Pavia seems likewise to have drawn from it in Book I, chapter 8:

> “For even those who had received apostolic salvation or blessing from Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, before the betrayal were not deprived of it after the betrayal and the hanging of his own body, except insofar as some shameful crimes may have defiled them. For the blessing bestowed by Christ’s ministers is poured out not through the one who is seen, but through the priest who is unseen. For neither the one who waters nor the one who plants is anything, but God who gives the growth.”

In the time of Alexander III, the Church plainly believed that the Lord’s body was consecrated equally by a bad priest and by a good one. This is clear from the judgment against the “Good Men” pronounced by Gaucelin, bishop of Lodève, in the name of the entire synod, preserved in Roger of Hoveden’s later part of the *Annals*.]

## XVI

Similarly, blessed Pope Gregory admonishes us, by means of an apt example, not to despise the divine sacraments when administered by ministers of God of any kind. He says:

> “It often happens, my brothers, as I am saying, that a powerful person has a despised servant. Yet when he perhaps sends some reply through that servant to his own people or to strangers, the person of the speaking servant is not despised, because reverence for the lord who sent him is preserved in the heart. Those who hear do not consider through whom they hear, but what they hear and from whom they hear it. So, brothers, so should you act. Even if you perhaps rightly despise us, preserve in your minds reverence for the Lord who calls.”

The same Father speaks of these matters in an exhortation to bishops (*Homily 17 on the Gospels*):

> “Through us, indeed, the faithful come to holy baptism; through our prayers they are blessed; through the laying on of our hands they receive the Holy Spirit from God; and they themselves attain the heavenly kingdom. And behold, through our negligence we are heading downward. The elect enter the heavenly homeland, purified by the hands of priests, while the priests themselves, through a reprobate life, hurry toward the punishments of hell. To what, then, or to what thing should I compare bad priests, except to baptismal water, which washes away the sins of those baptized, sends them to the heavenly kingdom, and itself flows down into the sewers? Let us fear this, brothers. Let our conduct correspond to our ministry. Let us think daily about the remission of our sins, lest our life remain bound by sin, through which almighty God daily frees others.”

## XVII

In agreement with this, blessed Pope Anastasius also teaches about these matters (*Decrees*, chapters 7 and 8), saying:

[Note: **Pope Anastasius, in the Decrees, chapters 7 and 8.** Agobard abridged Anastasius’s words.]

> “Even baptism that is administered far from the Church, whether it is given by an adulterer or by a thief, reaches the recipient as an undefiled gift, because that voice which sounded through the dove excludes every stain of human pollution. It declares and says: ‘This is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’

> “Indeed, although Judas was sacrilegious and a thief, whatever he performed among the apostles by virtue of the office entrusted to him, the benefits bestowed through that unworthy man suffered no harm on that account. Whatever any minister in the Church appears to perform according to his office for the advancement of human beings is wholly contained in and completed by the effect of the Godhead. Paul, through whom Christ speaks, affirms this:

> “‘I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.’ Therefore neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth.

> “God does not ask who or what sort of person preaches, but whom he preaches; thus he confirms that even the envious may preach Christ well.

> “Bad men, therefore, by administering good things, harm only themselves and do not defile the mysteries of the Church. Consequently, those who receive the mysteries entrusted to them either in consecrations or in baptism should in no way fear that the divine gifts may appear invalid. Since the mysteries possess their own power, the person who is guilty in himself does not harm others in this matter.”

### XVIII

We have therefore set forth these opinions and definitions of the Fathers so that the faithful may know that they suffer no harm from the crimes of priests in receiving the sacraments, provided that the sacraments are celebrated according to the rule established by the Lord or according to ecclesiastical tradition.

For the rest, it is supremely necessary to take the greatest care that, when ordaining or appointing ministers, we do not share, as was said above, in the sins of others,

> **[Note: “In appointing or offering.” This was added from the Marnaesian manuscript.]**

namely, by promoting criminals to the priesthood, or,

> **[Note: “The blind through ignorance.” Agobard says that it is much worse if those who are uneducated are advanced to the priesthood than if criminals are. Indeed, among the virtues necessary for a bishop, Paul lists learning, so that he may be able, as he says, “to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict.” Thus the ancients entirely excluded from the priesthood anyone who was not learned. For Pope Hilary decreed in the Roman synod of 465: “Those ignorant of letters, as well as those who have suffered the loss of any limb, and those who are penitents, should not dare aspire to sacred orders.” Likewise Gelasius, in the Decrees, chapter 16: “We have learned that illiterate persons and those impaired in some part of the body have been admitted without any consideration to ecclesiastical service; but ancient tradition and the old practice of the Apostolic See do not accept this, because one lacking sacred learning cannot be suited to sacred offices, and the legal precepts have decreed that nothing defective is to be offered to God at all. Therefore, henceforth let such things be avoided in every way, and let no such person be received into the clergy.” See the notes on letter 79 of Lupus of Ferrières.]**

> **[Note: “By promoting criminals.” This is prohibited. For the person promoted to the priesthood must have an unimpaired reputation, according to the Apostle’s command. Hence the ancient Church kept those stained by scandals far from the company of the clergy, as is clear from Pope Gelasius’s Decrees, chapter 18. Alcuin also grievously laments this in *Confession of Faith*, book III, chapter 36, because this ancient law had already fallen into disuse: “O unhappy times of ours,” he says, “which neither fear God nor revere the force of the sacred canons! Nowadays no sacrilegious or criminal person is forbidden to approach the office of the sacred order.”]**

or—and this is far worse—by promoting to the priesthood those blinded by ignorance, who do not know how to perform the mysteries themselves according to ecclesiastical order, which must be wholly condemned and admitted in no way, or who lead the blind toward the pit of eternal damnation.

The Lord also shows that he sternly rejects this, saying through the prophet: “Because you rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you may not serve me as priest.” And again: “The priests despised my law and profaned my sanctuaries; they made no distinction between the sacred and the profane, and they did not understand the difference between the polluted and the clean.”

On the contrary, according to the apostolic commands, we ought always to be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks us for an account of the hope that is in us, and a preacher ought to embrace the faithful word that accords with sound doctrine, so that he may be able to exhort in sound teaching and refute those who contradict.

Although a priest ought to be irreproachable both in life and in teaching, so that he may rightly be heard and imitated, nevertheless, if one of these qualities is lacking, it is more tolerable to obey one who teaches well but lives reprehensibly than one who both lives wickedly and does not know what he should teach.

The former were like those concerning whom the Lord commanded, saying: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do.” Clearly, by observing these instructions, people could endure such rulers without danger to themselves.

But concerning the other man, since he is wholly useless and wholly harmful, and cannot be heard or imitated without danger, certain people rightly understand the saying in the Gospel: “If your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness.”

Again, in Proverbs: “Luxury is not fitting for a fool, nor for a servant to rule over princes.” And there also: “The lips of the righteous instruct many, but those who are uneducated will die in poverty of heart.” And again: “As one who throws a stone into a heap of Mercury, so is one who gives honor to a fool.”

Although this statement applies especially to those who presume to ordain such men.

### XIX

And since our subject now concerns the dignity of the priesthood, as well as priests—provided that their conduct agrees with their ministry—we must carefully understand, at the end of this little work, that there are four kinds of them: one to be loved, another to be tolerated, a third to be despised, and a fourth to be anathematized.

The kind of rulers to be loved consists of those who live well and teach well.

The kind to be tolerated consists of those who teach well but live reprehensibly, or who live well but, because of simplicity of understanding, are unable to teach others. The former of this class are to be heard, but not imitated, just as the Lord says when speaking of such men: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do.”

The latter, if their life is subject to piety and adheres to teachers of piety, are undoubtedly striving toward the goal of the commandment, which is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfaked faith. Their life can indeed be instruction to some. Nevertheless, they cannot be counted among perfect preachers, because they have no basis from which to bring forth things new and old.

And as the Fathers said:

> “By the barking of dogs and the shepherd’s staff, the rage of wolves must be driven off.”

The kind to be despised, as we said above, consists of those who live reprehensibly and do not know what they should teach.

The last kind, which we said must also be anathematized, consists of those living in any manner whatsoever—that is, whether well or badly—but teaching badly.

> **[Note: “Those living in any manner whatsoever.” He says that those priests are to be anathematized whose life, even if in some respect irreproachable, is nevertheless accompanied by bad teaching. We saw an example of this above in the book against Felix, bishop of Urgell.]**

For they are heretics, even if they live well.

### XX

Since, then, we are caught amid such great and such difficult straits, from which we cannot escape by our own strength, it is supremely necessary that we beseech with our whole heart him who is able to do all things beyond what we ask or understand, so that, by the abundance of his mercy, holding our right hand, he may direct us according to his will and receive us into glory.

May he himself govern those who govern; may he himself direct those who direct; so that we may pasture his flock with discipline and not in the vessels of an inexperienced shepherd.

> **[Note: “His flock,” that is, Christ’s. Although the faithful of each diocese are sometimes called the flock of the bishop who governs that diocese, this is by a figure of speech. Properly speaking, the flock does not belong to the bishop but to Christ. Hence, in the Gospel, he himself calls Christians his sheep and lambs when he entrusts them to Peter and the other apostles, that is, to bishops.]**

May he himself grant strength and power to the people, and present to himself a clean, radiant, wholly unblemished flock, worthy of the heavenly sheep, where there is a dwelling place for those who rejoice in the splendors of the saints.

> **[Note: “In his temple.” Everything from this point through the word “Amen” is absent from Masson’s edition. Nevertheless, it is present in the manuscript used by Masson, and likewise in the Marnaesian manuscript.]**

In his temple let all of us, flock and shepherds together, give glory in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong honor and power forever and ever. Amen.

I wish you, most reverend and most beloved Father and brother in Christ, always good health, and I ask you to remember us.

[Col. 0147A]

## A BOOK AGAINST THE FOOLISH OPINION OF THE COMMON PEOPLE CONCERNING HAIL AND THUNDER

### I

In these regions,

> **[Note: “In these regions,” namely, in the territory of Lyon and the regions surrounding it.]**

almost everyone—nobles and commoners, townspeople and peasants, old and young—believes that hail and thunder can be produced at human will.

For as soon as they hear thunder and see flashes of lightning, they say: “It is a levitating wind.” When asked what a levitating wind is, some, with embarrassment and a conscience that stings them only slightly, and others confidently, as uneducated people commonly do, assert that it is produced by the incantations of men called Tempestarii.

> **[Note: “Tempestarii.” Elsewhere they are called *sortiarii*: men who claim that by means of their art they can arouse lightning, thunder, and other storms of the air. Charlemagne says: “Therefore we order that diviners, enchanters, tempestarii, or binders are not to be made; and wherever they are found, let them be corrected or condemned.” He also says: “Concerning incantations, auguries, divinations, and those who produce storms or other acts of magic, the holy council has decreed that wherever they are discovered, the archpriest of that diocese must see that they are subjected to the most diligent examination, in case they confess the evils they have committed. But let this discipline be imposed with such moderation that they do not lose their lives, but may be saved, afflicted in prison until, by God’s inspiration, they promise to amend their sins.” Herard, archbishop of Tours, also calls them *tempestuarii* in chapter 3 of his *Capitularies*: “Concerning sorcerers, enchanters, diviners, fortune-tellers, dreamers, tempestuarii, and charms against cold, and concerning women who practice magic and those who invent various portents: let them be prohibited and punished with public penance.”]**

They say that the wind has been “raised,” and for that reason call it a levitating wind.

Whether this is true, as the common people believe, must be established from the authority of divine Scripture. But if it is false, as we believe beyond any doubt, it must be emphasized with the greatest force how guilty of falsehood is the person who attributes a divine work to a human being.

By this claim he is trapped between two greatest and most deadly lies: he testifies that a human being can do what belongs to God alone, and that God does not do what he does.

Even if, concerning lies about lesser matters, we must truthfully hold to what is written—“An obscure utterance will not go forth into emptiness, but the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11)—and again, “You will destroy all who speak lies,” and, “A lying witness will perish,” or, “A false witness will not go unpunished,” or even what we read in the Apocalypse of the apostle John:

> “Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have authority over the tree of life and may enter the city by its gates. Outside are dogs, sorcerers, the sexually immoral, murderers, those who serve idols, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.”
