How much more must this be said of so grave a lie as the one we have undertaken to discuss, which is no less serious than the lies of certain heretics.

The blessed apostle Paul says:

> “But if the dead are not raised, we are found to be false witnesses of God, because we testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise; for if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ risen.”

Thus, just as all who proclaim that Christ the Lord was raised by the Father would be found false witnesses of God if the dead were not raised, so also this man, who takes God’s wondrous and exceedingly terrifying work away from God in order to attribute it to a human being, is without doubt a false witness of God.

[Col. 0148B]

### II

We have seen and heard many people so buried in madness and so estranged by stupidity that they believe and say that there is a certain region called Magonia, from which ships come through the clouds. In these ships the crops that fall through hail and perish in storms are carried back to that same region, while the aerial sailors supposedly pay the Tempestarii for them and receive grain or other crops in return.

Because of this deep stupidity, which has blinded those who believe that such things can happen, we saw several people, at a certain gathering, bring forward four bound persons—three men and one woman—as though they had fallen from those very ships. After keeping them in chains for several days, they finally brought them before an assembled crowd, as I have said, in our presence, as though they were to be stoned.

Yet truth prevailed. After much argument, those who had brought them forward were themselves confounded, in accordance with the prophetic saying: “As a thief is ashamed when he is caught.”

### III

But because this error, which so generally possesses the minds of almost everyone in this region, must be judged by all rational people, let us produce the testimonies of Scripture by which it can be judged. When these have been examined, it will not be we ourselves but truth itself that will overthrow the most foolish error and rebuke all who agree with it as vessels of error, saying with the Apostle: “Every lie is not from the truth.”

What is not from the truth is certainly not from God; and what is not from God does not hear his words, just as Truth itself says:

> “Whoever is from God hears the words of God. The reason you do not hear is that you are not from God.”

In another place he says the same thing in different words:

> “My sheep hear my voice. The reason you do not hear is that you are not of my sheep.”

And elsewhere:

> “Everyone who is from the truth hears my voice.”

Therefore, anyone who believes or speaks a lie, or asserts something that is not, and by holding to whatever is not, toward what else does he tend except toward nonbeing? For he tends toward nonbeing because he withdraws from him who is, who said to Moses:

> “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you.’”

And of him blessed Job speaks:

> “For he alone is.”

To speak more plainly: truth possesses essence—or rather, it is essence in its own substance, because it subsists. A lie, however, since it has no essence—for it is nothing—does not subsist.

God alone therefore is, because he alone has true being, having received being from no one. All things created by him do indeed exist, but they do not possess that true and supreme being, because they received being in order to exist.

Lies, on the other hand, because they did not receive being in order to exist, possess no being at all. Thus the person who clings to a lie clings to something that is not—although it should not even be called a thing.

Whoever clings to what is not withdraws not only from the one who made him, but also from what he himself was made to be, since there are no more than two kinds of being: one supreme, which did not receive its being from another, and the other great, which received its being from God—that is, the Creator and the creature.

A lie, therefore, because it is not the Creator, is not supreme being; because it is not a creature, it is not great being; because it possesses no essence, it is no being at all.

Whoever wishes to persist in what is, therefore, should not withdraw from him who gave him being. Whoever does not wish to withdraw from him who truly is should flee what entirely is not—that is, a lie.

### IV

Since every liar is an advocate of falsehood, and every advocate of falsehood is a false witness acting against the truth, let us now see whether these men who say that a divine work is performed by human agency have any authority to support them.

In the sacred Scriptures, the first place where hail is introduced is found among those plagues by which Egypt was struck. This was the seventh plague of Egypt.

The Lord said:

> “Behold, tomorrow at this very hour I will rain down exceedingly great hail, such as has not been in Egypt from the day it was founded until the present time” (Exodus 9:18).

In these words the Lord says that he himself will send hail on the following day—not some human being, certainly not Moses or Aaron, who were righteous men of God, and not Jannes and Jambres, the Egyptian enchanters who are called Pharaoh’s magicians, whom the Apostle says resisted Moses just as these men resist the truth.

Those magicians had already, as it is written, cast down each of their staffs before Pharaoh by Egyptian incantations and certain secret arts, and the staffs had become serpents, although Aaron’s staff swallowed their staffs. They had already turned water into blood and had brought frogs up from the rivers, although they were unable to restrain them, as Moses did by the word of the Lord, so that they remained only in the river.

But when the matter came to gnats and they could do nothing, they said that the finger of God was opposing them, and they attempted nothing further of that kind.

Certainly, if any human being could send hail, Jannes and Jambres would have sent it, since they turned water into blood and brought frogs up from the rivers—things that those who are now called Tempestarii cannot do.

### V

Scripture continues in the same passage:

> “Moses stretched out his staff toward heaven, and the Lord gave thunder and hail, and lightning flashing across the earth; and the Lord rained hail upon the land of Egypt, and hail and fire mingled together” (ibid., verse 23).

Here too the passage shows that the Lord alone is the creator and author of hail, not any human being.

Perhaps those who attribute this power to human beings will say that Moses stretched out his staff toward heaven, and that therefore the storm was sent through a human being.

Certainly Moses was a good and righteous servant of the Lord. But these people whom they call Tempestarii do not dare to confess that they are good and righteous; rather, they call them evil and wicked, deserving temporal and eternal condemnation. Nor do they call them servants of God, except perhaps in the sense of being under compulsion, not in voluntary service.

For if, in imitation of Moses, human beings were the authors of hail, they would surely be servants of God, not servants of the devil.

Yet the sentence cited above does not show even Moses to be its author, but only almighty God.

The Psalmist, who also mentions this hail, says of God:

> “He killed their vines with hail, and their mulberry trees with frost; he delivered their cattle to hail and their possessions to fire” (Psalm 77:47–48).

But because in the present passage the Psalmist adds that the affliction was sent through evil angels, we must understand that God exercises the scourges of vengeance or testing through evil ministers. They possess the will to harm from themselves, but receive the power to do so from him.

Just as the will to harm is their own, so the power to do what they will belongs to the Lord alone. The power belongs neither to human beings, whether good or evil, nor to opposing forces, but to the Lord alone, who grants power to their evil will insofar as he wishes and withdraws it insofar as he does not wish them to be able to act.

In another psalm the Psalmist likewise says of God:

> “He made their rains hail, and flaming fire upon their land; he struck their vines and crushed the trees of their borders.”

He truly struck them, and truly crushed them—but it was not a human being or an evil angel, only God, without whom the legion of evil angels could not even harm the pigs or cast them into the sea.

It was plainly God of whom it is said:

> “At the brightness before him his clouds passed away, hail and coals of fire. The Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice: hail and coals of fire.”

And to him we sang:

> “Flash forth lightning and scatter them; send out your arrows and confuse them.”

He “covers the heavens with clouds and prepares rain for the earth; he gives snow like wool and sends his ice like morsels. He sends his word and melts them; he breathes his spirit, and the waters flow.”

The one whom the creatures of the earth praise is not praised only by the dragons of the abyss, but also by fire, hail, snow, ice, and the spirit of storms, which fulfill his word—not the word of a human being, nor the word of an evil angel.

### VI

We also read about hail in the book of Joshua:

> “Therefore the five kings of the Amorites gathered together—the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon—together with their armies, and they encamped against Gibeon, attacking it.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The Lord said to Joshua: ‘Do not fear them, for I have delivered them into your hands.’”

And shortly afterward:

> “As they were fleeing from the children of Israel and were on the descent toward Beth-horon, the Lord cast great stones upon them from heaven as far as Azekah, and many more died from the hailstones than the children of Israel killed with the sword” (Joshua 10:5, 8ff.).

Here too it is evident that, without any human imprecation, the Lord sent hail upon those whom he judged worthy of such a scourge.

For if evil human beings, such as those whom these deluded people call Tempestarii, could do this, hail would certainly have fallen upon the children of Israel, not upon their enemies.

But because neither evil people against the good nor good people against the evil can do this, the statement makes the matter entirely clear.

The Book of Wisdom also bears witness to this, saying to the Lord:

> “It is impossible to escape your hand. For when the ungodly denied that they knew you, they were scourged by the strength of your arm with strange waters, and suffered persecution through hail and rains, and were consumed by fire. For what was extraordinary was that, in water, which extinguishes everything, fire had greater force. The world is the avenger of the righteous.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Snow and ice endured the force of the fire and did not melt, so that they might know that the fire burning in hail and rain, flashing forth, destroyed the harvests of their enemies” (Wisdom 16:15ff.).

### VII

If, therefore, almighty God scourges the enemies of the righteous with strange waters, hail, and rains by the strength of his arm—his hand being impossible to escape—then those who believe that human beings can do these things are entirely ignorant of God.

For if human beings could send hail, they could also send rain. No one has ever seen hail without rain.

They could also avenge themselves upon their enemies, not merely by taking away their crops but by taking away their lives. Whenever the enemies of the Tempestarii happened to be traveling or working in the fields, they could heap up a mass of hail over them and bury them beneath it.

Some people even say that they know such Tempestarii who can cause hail falling over a wide area to flow together into one place—into a river or an unfruitful forest, or onto a single, supposedly, cask beneath which the man himself is hiding.

We have often heard many people say that they certainly knew such things to have been done in particular places, but we have not yet heard anyone testify that he had actually seen them.

Someone once told me about a certain man who claimed to have seen such things. I took great pains to see him, and I did so. When I spoke with him and he attempted to say that he had seen it happen, I bound him with many entreaties and solemn adjurations, including divine threats, begging him not to say anything except what was true.

He then affirmed that what he was saying was true, naming the person, the time, and the place; yet he confessed that he had not been present at the time.

Likewise, in the book of Ecclesiasticus, which bears the title *Jesus son of Sirach*, it is written:

> “There are spirits created for vengeance, and in their fury they confirmed their scourges; at the time of consummation they will pour forth their power and will confound the fury of him who made them. Fire, hail, famine, and death: all these were created for vengeance. The teeth of beasts, scorpions, and serpents, and the avenging sword, for the destruction of the ungodly” (Ecclesiasticus 39:33ff.).

If hail was created, like the other things mentioned here, then it was certainly created by God, not by a human being.

Again, in the same book we read:

> “Look at the rainbow and bless him who made it. It is exceedingly beautiful in its splendor. It encircled the heavens with the circle of its glory; the hands of the Most High opened it. By his command he hastened the snow, and he hastens to send forth the flashes of his judgment. Therefore the treasuries were opened, and the clouds flew out like birds. In his greatness he placed the clouds, and the hailstones were broken apart. At his sight the mountains will be shaken, and at his will the south wind will blow. The voice of his thunder will strike the earth; the storm of the north wind and the gathering of the spirit. As a bird settling down to sit, so it scatters snow; and as a locust descends, so is its descent. The eye will admire the beauty of its color, and the heart will be terrified at its rain. He will pour out frost like salt upon the earth; and when it freezes, it will become like the tops of thistles. The cold north wind will blow, and the ice will freeze upon the water. It will rest upon every gathering of waters and clothe itself over the waters like a breastplate. It will devour the mountains, burn up the wilderness, and extinguish the green things like fire. The mist is the medicine of all things in its haste, and the dew that meets the coming heat will humble it. At his word the wind was silent; by his thought he calmed the abyss, and the Lord Jesus planted it.”

> **[Note: “The Lord Jesus planted it.” This is exactly how the royal manuscript reads. Nevertheless, I have no doubt that the reading of the Vulgate is more correct: “The Lord planted islands in it.”]**

(Ecclesiasticus 43:12–25.)

### VIII

Behold, in this long and profound passage from Ecclesiasticus, everything that takes place in the air, everything that descends from the air to the earth, and everything concerning the sea and the winds is attributed, with the most refined wonder, to God’s command: the appearance, brilliance, and circuit of the rainbow; the hastening of snow; the terror of lightning; the speed of clouds; the suspension of winds; the striking of the earth; the conflict of breezes; the freezing of water—not only in the clouds, as with hail and snow, but also on the earth, in snow, rain, standing waters, and flowing rivers; the drying up of green things by frost, as we often see; and also the dissolution of all these things, which occurs in the season of dewy mists and through the blowing of the south wind and the west wind.

It also says that all these things grow still and are calmed at God’s word.

Therefore, no human helper should be sought in such matters, because none will be found—except perhaps the saints of God, who have obtained and will obtain many things. Some of them will have power to shut the heavens so that it does not rain during the days of their prophecy, like Elijah, and to turn waters into blood and strike the earth with every plague as often as they wish, like Moses and Aaron in Egypt.

Truly, no one sends hail in summer except the one who also sends snow in winter. The reason for both events is the same: in both seasons the clouds are customarily raised higher than usual.

### IX

We also read in the book of blessed Job:

> “From the inner regions the storm proceeds, and from the Bear comes the cold. When God blows, frost condenses, and again the waters are poured out far and wide. The cloud desires grain, and the clouds scatter their light; they illuminate all things around, wherever the will of the governing God leads them, toward everything he has commanded them over the face of the world” (Job 37:9ff.).

We must listen attentively to what is said: “The clouds illuminate all things around, but wherever the will of the governing God leads them.”

If, therefore, God governs them, an unjust human being cannot turn them in another direction, because he can neither command God nor deserve to obtain such a thing by prayers.

What follows—“toward everything he has commanded them over the face of the earth”—what else should it mean except toward everything God commands the clouds, whether for the scourging or the assistance of human beings: for snow, hail, rain, lightning, flashes, or thunder, by which lofty buildings are often thrown down?

Certainly this happens not at a human command but at God’s command, as the passage says. Shortly afterward it adds:

> “Do you know when God commanded the rains to show the light of his clouds? Do you know the paths of the great clouds and the perfect knowledge of them?”

Here too we must observe that if a human being does not know the paths of the clouds or their perfect workings, he knows even less how, through their function, they benefit or harm human beings.

The exception, as was said, is the saints, who can accomplish many things through him according to God’s will, by his own gift—not by their own power or by any opposing power, but by the will of the Creator. Thus many servants of God have often obtained through their prayers that the Lord should graciously grant rain during a time of drought.

### X

Thus the blessed apostle James, setting before us the deed of the prophet Elijah as an example, urges us to turn to prayer in sadness, illness, and for the remission of sins, saying:

> “Pray for one another, so that you may be saved. The continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful. Elijah was a human being like us, subject to suffering; and he prayed that it might not rain, and it did not rain for three years and six months. And again he prayed, and the heaven gave rain, and the earth produced its fruit.”

Elijah therefore prayed that it might not rain, and it did not rain for three years and six months.

He did this for the rebuke and correction of his people: that they might first be reproved for their turning away of mind, because they had abandoned the worship of almighty God and followed the filth of idols; and that afterward, having been scourged and wearied by the expectation of rain, they might be corrected and return to the Lord God whom they had abandoned.

### XI

Likewise, when Samuel the prophet and leader of the people of Israel reproved that same people for their frequent transgressions, recounting to them the benefits of almighty God and, in contrast, their own turning away, the people understood that they had committed a great evil and had offended God by asking for a king.

By praying, Samuel obtained that, at an unaccustomed time, rain should fall terribly with thunder and flashes of lightning.

Thus it is written that Samuel said to the people:

> “Stand and see this great thing that the Lord will do before your eyes. Is it not wheat harvest today? I will call upon the Lord, and he will give thunder and rain; and you will know and see that you have committed a great evil before the Lord by asking for a king over you.”

And Samuel cried out to the Lord, and the Lord gave thunder and rain on that day. All the people greatly feared the Lord and Samuel.

The whole people said to Samuel:

> “Pray for your servants to the Lord your God, so that we may not die. For we have added to all our sins the evil of asking for a king” (1 Samuel 12:16ff.).

Terrified by the sound of thunder and the flashing of lightning, they asked for the intercession of the holy prophet. Although they were sinners, they asked as faithful people—not like these half-believers of ours, who, as soon as they hear thunder or even a slight breath of wind, say: “It is a levitating wind,” and curse, saying:

> “Cursed be that tongue, and may it wither; it should already have been cut off—the tongue that does this.”

Tell me, I ask you: whom are you cursing, a righteous person or a sinner?

A sinner—and one partly unbelieving like yourself—could not, as you say, raise the wind, because he could neither do so by his own power nor command evil angels. Indeed, even the evil angels have no power in this matter.

He did not entreat the Lord to obtain it through prayer, because, like you, those whom you consider Tempestarii believe that such things happen through evil magic, not through the will of God.

Even if they asked the Lord God for this, they would not deserve to obtain it. Such things belong to the righteous, not to the wicked; for when the wicked ask the Lord for something in such matters, they ask unbelievingly and with a divided mind, not with the certainty of faith.

### XII

Furthermore, at the time when the land of Israel was suffering drought because of Elijah’s prayer, even pasture was denied to the animals.

For it is written:

> “Ahab said to Obadiah: ‘Go through the land to all the springs of water and into all the valleys, if perhaps we can find grass and preserve the horses and mules, so that the animals may not perish entirely’” (1 Kings 18:5).

As is evident, despairing of rain—since there would be none except according to Elijah’s word—they searched for grass for the animals near springs and streams. They were already learning that what Elijah had said to Ahab was true:

> “As the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there will be neither dew nor rain during these years except according to the word of my mouth.”

And certainly Elijah stated how many years there would be.

Why, then, did this Ahab, as I said, not ask the Tempestarii to raise storms and, as you commonly say, levitating winds, by which the earth might be watered and grass provided for his horses, mules, and other animals, for which he was concerned—especially since he was not afraid of losing the crops in the fields or the vineyards, because at that time there were none at all?

### XIII

In our own times too we sometimes see that, after the harvests and grape-gatherings have been collected, farmers are unable to sow because of drought. Why do you not prevail upon your Tempestarii to send the “lifting breezes” by which the earth may be watered and you may afterward sow? But since you have neither done this nor ever seen or heard it done, listen now to what the Lord himself—the creator, ruler, governor, arranger, and dispenser of all things—says to his servant, blessed Job, among other matters also concerning things of this kind.

For when the devil—the inventor, prince, and head of every evil, the accuser of the brethren—had accused blessed Job before the Lord, saying that he served him not with a right intention, that is, not merely to please him and enjoy him alone, but for the increase and protection of earthly possessions; and when he had requested that Job be put to the test, so that by testing him he might demonstrate this to be true—the wicked, proud, and most foolish one, as though he knew the mind of God’s man better than his creator—the Lord, both just and merciful, just in order to confound the devil and merciful in order to exalt his faithful servant, granted him power, first over all his possessions, then over his children, afterward over the health of his body, next over the persuasion of his wife, and finally over the reproaches and manifold contempt of his servants.

But the devil, defeated and confounded, withdrew; and the Lord’s servant, victorious and triumphant, grew stronger. Therefore, wishing to humble him, just as the Apostle says of himself, lest the greatness of revelations should exalt him, so also lest the greatness of victory should make Job elated, the merciful Lord did not humble him by removing the possessions he had lost, nor by striking his body, through which he had already been tested like gold in a furnace, nor by comparing him with some great man—for on earth there was no one like him, since among the men of the East he was great. Nevertheless, he began to humble him profoundly by magnificently displaying to him the immensity of his power, so that the faithful servant, recognizing the ineffable greatness of his immeasurable and uncircumscribed creator, might despise himself and, by despising himself, bow low. And so it happened.

For this appears in his words, when he says: “Therefore I reproach myself and do penance in dust and ashes” (Job 42:6). Another translation makes this clearer, saying: “I have despised myself, and have wasted away, and have regarded myself as earth and ashes.”

In this humiliation, when almighty God was questioning his faithful servant about who had made or knew how to make these things, and where he had been when they were made, he asks him about matters which no one but almighty God alone can accomplish. He says:

“Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?”

And:

“Who set its measurements, or upon what were its bases established?”

“Who shut up the sea with doors?”

And:

“Can you perhaps join together the shining stars, the Pleiades, or can you disperse the circle of Arcturus?”

“Do you perhaps know the order of heaven?”

“Will you perhaps send forth lightning, and will it go?”

—and many things of this kind.

Among these many and such great matters, he also asks him:

“Have you entered the storehouses of snow, or have you looked upon the storehouses of hail, which I have prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war?”

“By what way is light distributed, and heat divided over the earth?”

“Who gave the most violent rain its course, and a way to the resounding thunder,”

“so that it might rain upon the earth where no human being is, in the wilderness where no mortal dwells,”

“so that it might fill the impassable and desolate land and bring forth green plants?”

“Who is the father of rain? Or who begot the drops of dew?”

“From whose womb did ice come forth? And who begot frost from heaven?”

“Waters are hardened into the likeness of a stone, and the surface of the abyss is congealed” (Job 38:4 ff.).

### XIV

Behold, then, the great works of God, whose ordering even blessed Job himself had previously been unable to admire so loftily and so precisely. If the Lord has storehouses of hail, and he alone sees them—storehouses which blessed Job had not yet seen—where did these Tempestarii find them, whom blessed Job did not find and whom we cannot find either, nor even estimate where they might be?

The Lord asks his faithful servant whether he knows who gave the most violent rain its course and a way to the resounding thunder. But those against whom this discourse is directed show us little men alien to holiness, justice, and wisdom, stripped of faith and truth, hateful even to their neighbors, from whom they claim that the most violent rains, the thundering noises of waters, and the “lifting breezes” can be produced.

The Lord says that he prepared these things for the time of the enemy, that is, for vengeance. But these very enemies and adversaries of righteousness—against whom vengeance must be taken, especially after those who move boundary markers, seize a widow’s ox as a pledge, crush the arms of orphans, leave naked those who have no covering, drive the needy from their houses, and distress people—they say possess power over the things which the Lord prepared for vengeance upon his enemies.

The Lord says that he is the father of rain and confirms that he himself generated frost from heaven. These wretched men say that the most miserable of human beings possess a large share in this dispensation.

God presents to us as something marvelous that waters are hardened into the likeness of a stone. If this could ever happen at the pleasure of these most wretched men, it would certainly not be marvelous.

### XV

This folly is no small portion of unbelief; and this evil has now grown so great that in many places there are wretched men who say that they do not indeed know how to bring on storms, but nevertheless know how to protect the inhabitants of a place from a storm.

They have fixed how much of their crops they should give to these men, and they call this a *canonicum*.

> **Note:** They call this a *canonicum*, namely, that portion of the crops which was annually assigned by landowners to the Tempestarii so that they would drive storms away from their fields.

There are many who willingly never give a tithe to priests, nor distribute alms to widows, orphans, and other needy people—alms which are frequently preached to them, repeatedly read aloud, and continually urged upon them—and they do not comply. But the *canonicum* which they call this, they willingly pay to their protectors, by whom they believe themselves protected from storms, although no one preaches, admonishes, or exhorts them to do so, and the devil entices them.

Finally, in such matters they place a large part of their hope for life, as though they lived through those men. This is not a portion, but almost the fullness of unbelief; and if we consider it carefully, we shall pronounce without ambiguity that it is the fullness of unbelief.

For, according to the divine Scriptures, there are three virtues in which the whole of worship is comprised, through which God is worshiped: faith, hope, and charity. Whoever, therefore, divides his faith and hope, so that he believes partly in God and partly believes that the things belonging to God belong to human beings, and partly hopes in God but partly hopes in a human being, God certainly does not accept such divided faith and hope. Consequently, such a person cannot be counted among the faithful. And one whom divided faith and hope separates from the number of the faithful is undoubtedly swallowed up by the abyss of unbelief. Rightly, therefore, such a person incurs that curse of the prophet:

“Cursed is the man who places his hope in man.”

Nor should he flatter himself by saying, “I hope more in God than in man,” because hope cannot be divided into portions. Either it will be whole and secure, or it will be insecure and nonexistent.

### XVI

A few years ago a certain folly was disseminated, when there was a mortality among cattle. People said that Duke Grimald of Benevento had sent men with powders to scatter them through the fields, mountains, meadows, and springs, because he was an enemy of the most Christian Emperor Charles; and that, when this powder had been scattered, the oxen died.

> **Note:** Grimald, Duke of Benevento. During that period there were two dukes of Benevento, both named Grimald, and one succeeded the other. The *Chronicle of Saint Vincent of Vulturno* says: “After Arichis had died at Benevento, Grimoald was recalled through the prayers of the Beneventans, having been received back by Charles, and he himself assumed his father’s duchy. He bestowed many gifts upon churches and monasteries of God’s servants, but especially upon that of the most blessed Vincent. When our Grimoald had died, another Grimoald, his kinsman, succeeded him; and when this one departed, Sico was substituted.” I think the former is the one meant by what Einhard records under the year 802: “Grimoald, Duke of the Beneventans,” he says, “besieged at Nuceria Winigis, Count of Spoleto, who was in command of the garrison and was exhausted by ill health; he received him into surrender and treated him honorably after capturing him.” The author of the *Annals of Saint Bertin* records the same. The latter, however, was killed in the year 818, as the same Einhard says: “When the Emperor had come to Heristal, he encountered envoys of Sico, Duke of the Beneventans, bringing gifts and excusing him concerning the death of Grimoald, his predecessor.” The *Life of Louis the Pious* says: “The Emperor proceeded by the direct route through Rouen and Amiens to Aachen for the winter quarters. When he was returning and entering the palace at Heristal, envoys of Sico, Duke of Benevento, were sent to meet him, bringing very large gifts and clearing their lord of the death of Grimoald, his predecessor.” Which of these two is to be understood as the subject of the history Agobard narrates here cannot be affirmed. I would nevertheless more readily believe that these rumors were spread among the populace under the earlier Grimoald. For these events took place under Charlemagne. He had succeeded Arichis, who died in 787, as Einhard records in the *Annals*, and others succeeded him thereafter.

Because he was an enemy of the most Christian Emperor Charles; and when this powder had been scattered, the oxen died.

> **Note:** Enemy of Emperor Charles. This makes clear that this book was written at the beginning of the reign of Louis the Pious, when the memory was recent of the war successfully waged by Charlemagne against Grimald, Duke of Benevento. Einhard, under the year 812: “Peace was made with Abubaz, king of the Saracens; likewise with Grimald, Duke of the Beneventans; and the Beneventans paid twenty-five thousand gold solidi as tribute.” Louis the Pious afterward confirmed this peace, as Einhard teaches under the year 814: “He made and confirmed a treaty with Grimald, Duke of the Beneventans, on the same terms as his father: namely, that the Beneventans should pay a tribute of seven thousand solidi each year.”

Because of this, we heard and saw many people arrested, and some killed, while most were fastened to planks, thrown into a river, and drowned. And what is very astonishing, those who were arrested themselves gave testimony against themselves, saying that they possessed such powder and scattered it.

Thus the devil, by God’s hidden and just judgment, having received power over them, was able to succeed against them to such an extent that they themselves became false witnesses against themselves unto death. Neither discipline, nor torture, nor death itself deterred them from daring to speak falsely against themselves.

This was believed by everyone, so that there were scarcely any who considered it utterly absurd. Nor did they reasonably consider how such powder could exist—powder from which only oxen would die, and no other animals—or how it could be carried across such extensive regions, over which men could not scatter powder, not even if the men and women, old and young, of Benevento had set out from their region with three carts each loaded with powder.

Such folly has now oppressed the wretched world that Christians presently believe things as absurd as no one previously could have persuaded pagans, who were ignorant of the creator of all things, to believe.

We have therefore brought this matter forward because it is similar to the matter about which we are speaking, and it could at least provide an example of empty deception and the genuine diminution of reason.

---

## ALSO, A BOOK AGAINST THE OBJECTIONS OF ABBOT FREDEGIS.

### I

To the most reverend and most blessed lord and father, Fredegis, abbot.

> **Note:** Fredegis, abbot of Saint Martin of Tours after Alcuin, whose disciple he had been, as is clear from Alcuin’s life. He was also chancellor of the Emperor Louis the Pious. His name is written in various ways. Here, and likewise in the charter of that same Louis for Hildebold, bishop of Mâcon, he is called Fredegisus. In Charlemagne’s Testament, as reported by Einhard, he is called Fridugisus, and rightly so, in my opinion. He is likewise named in the charters of Louis the Pious for the church of Paris, and in that prince’s charter for the church of Saint Lambert of Utrecht, published in volume one of the *History of the Bishops of Liège*, p. 154, and finally in the charters of the same Louis for the monastery of Arles in the diocese of Elne and for the monastery of Saint Grata in the diocese of Urgell. He is nevertheless called Fregedis by Theodulf, bishop of Orléans—meaning the same as Fredegisus—from whom we also learn that he was a deacon. See Sirmond’s notes on Theodulf, p. 292.

Some time ago the kindness of your modesty, moved against us by the demands of our sins, struck us with such attacks that they seemed to exceed the measure of your gentleness and sincerity—unless, in refuting us, you were using such a rebuke only in words, while not approving it in your heart.

For if all those things which you brought forward against us, and partly fabricated, had been understood by you as they were expressed, you would have transgressed not only your modesty but also the truth. Therefore, most wise man, if your greatness deigns to permit it, we endeavor through this little letter to clear ourselves of those charges which we find written against us in your letter.

Deign to remember the letter which you most recently sent against us, and recognize the charges to which we now undertake to respond.

### II

You wrote in your preface, saying:

> “If we judged that we should respond to everything which we found written in the little letter of your affection, we would seem to exceed not merely the length of a little letter but even the proportions of a longer book. But since, for the sake of brevity, we have chosen to touch summarily upon a few things out of many…”

From these words of yours it appears that you criticized everything which you found written in our little letter. But those who criticize everything praise nothing; those who refute everything accept nothing. Consider from these matters which you have touched upon summarily, for the sake of brevity, how justly you do this. If you criticized these matters so unjustly, how much more unjustly did you treat those which you omitted?

First, among the matters which you chose to touch upon, you take up for refutation our statement in which we said:

> “For whoever is truly humble thinks lowly of himself; and whoever thinks lowly of himself does not doubt that he has erred.”

To make it appear that this statement is not true, you prove that the Lord Jesus Christ was truly humble and say:

> “Because he was truly humble according to us, he thinks lowly of himself and did not doubt that he had erred.”

We ask you to consider how calumniously this has been said by you. For which of the faithful is unaware that when we speak of the humility of self-abasement and confession of sin—things which unquestionably ought to be true in everyone—we must never mix our Lord Jesus Christ together with other human beings? Nor ought you, because the Lord Jesus Christ did not think lowly of himself and never recognized that he had erred, defend other human beings from the humility of self-abasement and confession of sin to such an extent that you wish to prove from this—as is apparent in your letter—that no truly humble person thinks lowly of himself and that no one ought to confess himself a sinner.

### III

Indeed, venerable master, our foolishness thought and thinks that when a person speaks about such matters, he ought not to group our Lord Jesus Christ together with other human beings. For the humanity assumed by the Word, although it possesses the nature of our bodies, does not possess their origin. We are formed from human seed; he was born of the Holy Spirit. Although he became man for our salvation, he did not cease to be God; and although he is truly human, he is nevertheless the one true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

That humility by which our Lord Jesus Christ, though he existed in the form of God the Father, emptied himself in order to receive the form of a servant was an inclination of mercy, not an emptying of power. Although he endured the lowliness of suffering, he nevertheless made it known that he was equal to God the Father.

He is altogether equal to the Father: he is not lesser in glory, later in time, or inferior in power. He became man not in order to err, but in order to carry upon his shoulders the wandering sheep once it had been found and lead it to the house of the heavenly homeland, that is, to the vision of the Father.

Therefore it does not follow—indeed, it is very unjust—that when someone speaks truthfully about things belonging to human beings, another should nullify that speech by comparison with the Lord.

Again and again we say that it is the mark of an obstinate person to attack, by the example of the Lord, things which are truthfully said about mere human beings, none of whom exists without sin, as it is written:

> “There is no just person who does good and does not sin.”

And again:

> “No one is clean from defilement, even if his life upon earth is only one day.”

The Apostle Peter bears witness concerning the Lord, saying:

> “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth.”

Will what Paul says therefore not be true because this is true?

> “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God.”

### IV

Because you say, “When these things have been properly considered, it will appear that your reasoning is not true,” we cannot determine how you intended these words. We dare, however, to affirm that whoever denies this reasoning to be true has not yet understood how it ought to be known.

What, then, does the Apostle mean when, speaking about the Lord and saying, “Who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” he first says:

> “Think among yourselves what was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5–6).

And shortly before he had said:

> “Do nothing through rivalry or vain glory, but in humility let each consider the other superior to himself” (ibid., v. 3).

If it is not true that one who is truly humble thinks lowly of himself, why did Abraham, speaking with the Lord, confess that he was ashes and dust?

Moses also testified that he was not eloquent, and from the time when the Lord began to speak with him he said that he was still more impeded and slow of tongue.

Concerning himself and Aaron he said to the people:

> “For what are we?”

Gideon, whom the angel called the strongest of men, by contrast thought so lowly of himself that he said he was the least in his father’s house and that his family was the lowest in Manasseh.

Saul, too, when he said almost in these words that he belonged to the smallest tribe and recognized himself as the least in that tribe, so that he confessed himself unworthy of royal honor, was chosen as king. Therefore the Lord says to him:

> “When you were little in your own eyes, you became head among the tribes of Israel.”

David also—of whom the Lord says, “I have found a man according to my heart,” because he was truly humble—thought so lowly of himself that he testified not only that he was unworthy to reign but also became the king’s son-in-law. Later he cried out to Saul:

> “Whom are you pursuing, king of Israel? A dead dog and a single flea.”

Thus he complained that Saul was pursuing him as though he were pursuing a partridge in the mountains.

Later, when he was in the great glory of kingship and suffered no adversary, he said:

> “I shall play, and I shall become still more contemptible than I have become, and I shall be humble in my own eyes.”

And again:

> “Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up; I have not walked in great matters or in things too wonderful for me,”

and so forth.

Nor did he doubt that he had erred, because he very frequently confesses not only his errors but also his iniquities, sins, offenses, crimes, weaknesses, disturbances, fear, trembling, and anxiety of heart. If we wished to set down all their testimonies, an extensive work would be required.

### V

You say that it is not true reasoning that one who is truly humble should think lowly of himself or believe without doubt that he has sinned. We, on the contrary, know through this reasoning that all the saints were heard by the Lord in their prayers, as Daniel was in his confession, where he confessed not only his own sins and those of his people, but also the sins of kings, princes, and priests.

The three youths in the fiery furnace cried out in truth and judgment:

> “You have brought all these things upon us because of our sins. For we have sinned and acted wickedly by departing from you.”

The Lord also testifies in the Gospel that the tax collector who had gone up with the Pharisee into the temple to pray therefore descended to his house justified: knowing himself to be lowly, he stood at a distance and did not wish even to lift his eyes toward heaven; and, not doubting that he had sinned, he struck his breast, saying:

> “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”

Why else did the Lord say of the centurion that he had not found such faith even in Israel, unless because that centurion, thinking lowly of himself and having a lofty understanding of the Lord, considered himself unworthy, as he said, to go and ask the Lord to heal his child? Instead he sent his friends and again sent word to the Lord through a messenger, saying:

> “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.”

The Canaanite woman, to whom the Lord, as she cried out, replied, “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs,” immediately agreeing said:

> “Yes, Lord; for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from the tables of their masters.”

And therefore she deserved to hear:

> “O woman, great is your faith.”

### VI

If someone should object to us with the words of the truly humble just man who says:

> “I have not sinned, and my eye remains in bitterness” (Job 17:2),

and again:

> “I have suffered these things without iniquity in my hand,”

let him hear that same just man humbly confessing again:

> “I have sinned. What shall I do to you, O guardian of men?”

And again:

> “How many iniquities, sins, crimes, and offenses I have—show me” (Job 13:23).

Again Scripture says that the one whom God therefore scourges so that, instructed by sufferings, he may recognize his lowliness and his sins, looks upon human beings and says:

> “I have sinned; truly I have done wrong; I have not received what I deserved.”

Why, then, do you say that it is not true for a truly humble person to think lowly of himself or believe that he has sinned, when it is perfectly clear that this belongs to the saints, not to the proud?

Why does the Apostle John say:

> “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins”?

If, according to you, he had wished to think great things about himself rather than lowly things, he had grounds for boasting, since he reclined upon the Lord’s breast and was loved by him more than the other disciples.

The Apostle James also says:

> “For we all offend in many things.”

If anyone thinks that these words were not spoken truthfully but only humbly, let him know that in this understanding he follows Pelagius. Therefore, if he wishes to be corrected, let him read the books of blessed Augustine against the Pelagians, and let him know that all the saints truly accused themselves of sins, so that they necessarily had to say for themselves:

> “Forgive us our debts.”

But concerning these matters, we do not doubt that you know how much could be said.

### VII

You also say that with your entire purpose you are defending divine Scripture, together with its editors, interpreters, and commentators, against the calumnies of our ignorance.

We shall not answer you on this matter, because just as it is said of certain people, “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear,” so it can be said to you: “There you prepared your whole defense where there was absolutely no need for defense.”

For who among us has ever slandered any editor or interpreter of the divine Scriptures?

You say that we criticized the apostles and interpreters, whom we thought should be criticized only as much as we now think that those who disparage the truth should be praised.

For we said that the interpreters or commentators of the divine books did not take care to hold unalterably to the rule of grammatical art. They did this neither through ignorance nor through malice, but for the reason of accommodation: just as the usage of Holy Scripture accommodates itself to human words, so that, speaking in human fashion, it might bring the force of an ineffable matter to human understanding and display unfamiliar mysteries through familiar things; so its interpreters, following it, strove above all to render that which would provide readers with a clearer meaning, even when it was contrary to grammar to the extent that it agreed with the sacramental meaning of the matter.

We have therefore taken this as a defense of our own position. Just as no one ought to criticize those who could, if they wished, express everything according to grammatical discipline but were not afraid to speak against that discipline in order to accommodate themselves to us and not abandon the simplicity of truth, so everyone ought to spare us, who, even if we wished to speak everything according to grammar, could not do so, provided that we hold the right faith and catholic understanding.

In those words which we can use, we say—as you also demonstrate by the testimony of Priscian—

> “For I believe that nothing in human inventions can be perfect in every respect.”

> **Note:** This is testified by Priscian, the distinguished grammarian, whose work was especially handled by learned men in those times. Lupus of Ferrières also cites this passage in Letter 34 and in his *Book on Three Questions*, p. 235.

### VIII

You undertook a great and unnecessary labor, as though defending the evangelist or interpreter, arguing that the evangelist did not publish in vain, nor the interpreter translate in vain, the word “bloods” in the plural, as a definite reason demanded.

We not only did not criticize this matter, but never even heard it criticized by the impious. And although you labored so greatly in this defense, your labor revealed nothing new to us.

We had already read that the holy teachers explained that the interpreter translated “bloods” in the plural in this passage because he could not otherwise transfer into Latin the meaning of the evangelist, which the evangelist had expressed in Greek—not, as you say, because he found it in the plural in Greek.

For there are many nouns which are found in Hebrew or Greek in a different gender or number from that which they have in Latin. Yet the interpreter did not take care to translate them in the same gender in which he found them, because no necessity compelled him.

For example, among the Hebrews *spirit* is expressed in the feminine gender, whereas in Latin it is masculine. None of the interpreters, following the Hebrew, attempted to put it in the feminine gender in Latin, even when necessity demanded it. For in Scripture the Holy Spirit is at times signified through the feminine gender, yet Latin writers do not therefore use the feminine gender.

Likewise, *sin* is masculine in Hebrew, feminine in Greek, and neuter in Latin. Although it is signified by many things in Scripture, no Latin writer changed its gender, because no advantage required it.

We have said this because you claim that the interpreter translated “bloods” in the plural because it is expressed in the plural among the Greeks, whereas this is not so.

Interpreters or commentators of the divine utterances were not afraid to speak contrary to grammar in order to display the integrity of the meaning; we not only do not criticize them, but wish to be defended by them against criticism.

For just as they are to be praised for words uttered contrary to grammar, so we are to be tolerated. They, rich in words, spoke as they wished; we, poor in words, signify what we wish as best we can through the narrowness of our language.

And if we are their children and do not stray from their understanding and faith, let what is loved in them be tolerated in us also. Let the person to whom we speak attend to the meaning, not the words, so that he may hear the Apostle’s counsel:

> “Do not contend about words.”

And:

> “Do not be sickly preoccupied with questions and disputes about words, from which arise envy, contention, blasphemy, and evil suspicions.”

### IX

But after the words of the teachers you added the following in your own words:

> “Thus, in this one manner, the apostles and evangelists and the interpreters of all divine Scripture, together with its catholic commentators, can reasonably be defended against the charge of ignorance. For they said absolutely nothing contrary to the rule of grammar which some reason or some cause of the mystery did not require to be said in that way.”

The ecclesiastical teachers differ greatly from these words of yours. In our smallness, it seems to us that neither you nor we ought to think or say anything about this matter except what we read that orthodox teachers thought or said.

Nevertheless, the authority of those authors is unshaken and firm through whom the Holy Spirit composed the books of the New and Old Testaments. No human being was ever permitted, or is permitted, to think that they ought to have said even one letter differently from the way they said it, because their authority is firmer than heaven and earth, according to what the Lord says:

> “It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one tittle of the law to fall.”

After these comes the firm authority of the Seventy Translators, who, as is established, translated the Old Testament from Hebrew into Greek before the Lord’s coming.

There is also the faithful edition of our interpreter, the presbyter Jerome, who magnificently translated it from Hebrew into Latin.

There were also certain venerable catholic Latin interpreters who translated the edition of the Seventy into Latin.

Apart from these, however, there were many interpreters open to criticism, and rightly criticized, such as those most famous Judaizing and heretical interpreters—namely Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus. One of them produced two editions differing from each other.

> **Note:** Aquila. In Charlemagne’s *Capitulary on Images Not to Be Worshiped*, book I, chapter 13: “A new translation of the law is to be sought after the Seventy Translators, Theodotion, Symmachus, Aquila, and even blessed Jerome.” Concerning Theodotion and the period in which he lived, see the most distinguished scholar Henri Valois in his annotations on Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 8.

There were also certain Latin interpreters whom the presbyter Jerome criticized in the prefaces which he placed before the books that he either translated from Greek into Latin or revised. Thus, in the preface which he composed for the book of blessed Job in accordance with the Greek revision, he asserted that that book among the Latins had been so shortened and mutilated that it displayed its ugliness publicly to its readers. He likewise criticized certain interpreters in other places.

### X

We speak in this way about the interpreters because the special teachers did not all receive or praise them equally and indiscriminately, as you seem to do; nor did they place equal trust in all of them.

Concerning commentators also, blessed Father Augustine handed down a rule quite different from what you say is to be held. In the book which he wrote against Faustus the Manichaean, he speaks not only of those who were criticized by teachers but also of the most approved commentators:

> “This kind of writing, that is, commentaries, should be read not with the necessity of believing but with the freedom of judging. For only books possessing divine authority are to be read not with the freedom of judging but with the necessity of believing. The Apostle handed down this form when he said: ‘Do not extinguish the Spirit; do not despise prophecies; test everything, hold fast to what is good, and abstain from every appearance of evil.’ In this passage the Apostle Paul called the teachings and commentaries of teachers ‘prophecies,’ as he indicates elsewhere when he says: ‘Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge’ (1 Corinthians 14:29). He did not mean the prophecy of which the Apostle Peter says: ‘For prophecy was never brought forth by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were inspired by the Holy Spirit.’”

### XI

We say all these things so that it may appear that just as you accuse us unjustly when you say that we are critics of the apostles and of the divine Scriptures, so—or rather much more unjustly—you equate any interpreters and commentators whatsoever with the apostles and evangelists, when you regard Symmachus, Paul, Didymus, and John as worthy of one and the same defense and indiscriminate praise.

> **Note:** “Much more unjustly.” Massonus rightly indicated in his list of errors that it ought to be read this way. For in the manuscript it is expressly written, “many unjust [men].”

It is good to remember the words of the Lord, when he says:

> “If you offer rightly but do not judge rightly, have you not sinned?”

Whoever rightly believes the catholic faith appears to offer rightly. But if he grants any teachers or interpreters equal veneration with the apostles and evangelists, he does not divide rightly, and therefore he sins.

## XII

After the words of our statement set forth above, you added, saying:

> “For it is shameful to believe that the Holy Spirit, who poured the languages of all nations into the minds of the apostles, spoke through them rusticity rather than the nobility of each language.” [Col. 0166A]

No one who fears speaking idly will understand with what intention you said this—unless, perhaps, you add this accusation against us as well, as though we were censuring the Holy Spirit for rusticity. But if that is so—that is, if you say these things with such an intention—what can we reply to this except: May the omnipotent God himself, knower of hidden things, witness of hearts, and searcher of kidneys, see and hear it.

Apart from the fact that you seem to charge us with such sacrilege, it is also apparent from these words of yours that you think concerning the prophets and apostles not only that the Holy Spirit inspired in them the meaning of their preaching and the forms or arguments of their expressions, but also that he himself formed the very bodily words externally in their mouths. If you think this, who could enumerate the absurdities that would follow?

First of all, speaking cautiously to your learned understanding, remember what Moses says to the Lord when he excused himself from being sent to Pharaoh, asserting that he was weak of voice and impeded in speech. The Lord did not reply to him, “You are lying”; but, assenting to his entreaty, said:

> “Behold, Aaron your brother; I know that he is eloquent. He shall be your prophet. You shall speak to him, and he shall speak to Pharaoh.”

Observe: if, according to you, the very bodily words sounding in Moses’ mouth belonged to him, and the voice that sounded was his, why then was his voice weak? Why then was his speech impeded? Aaron was Moses’ prophet; Moses was God’s prophet. Why, then, was a stronger voice and more fluent speech found in Moses’ prophet than in God’s prophet? Will you also attribute this defect—namely, weakness of voice and impediment of tongue—to the Holy Spirit?

It remains, then, that just as an articulate voice was formed by angelic agency in the mouth of the she-ass, so you should say that it is formed in the mouths of the prophets. And then another such absurdity would follow: if they received words and the sounds of words in this manner, they would have been ignorant of their meaning. But far be it from us to entertain such ravings.

If we said anything about the eloquence of the apostle Paul, we quoted the words of the teacher Jerome, in which he says in one place:

> “Let those who think that Paul spoke according to humility, and did not speak truthfully when he said, ‘Though I am unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge,’ defend the coherence of this passage.”

And again:

> “But if someone can also demonstrate, on the basis of the eloquence of his speech, that the Apostle was perfect and did not fall into the faults of grammatical art, then he should rather be heard.”

Whenever we note solecisms or anything of that kind, we do not assail the Apostle, as malicious people accuse us of doing; rather, we are the Apostle’s defenders. For a Hebrew of Hebrews, lacking the polish of rhetorical speech, the arrangement of words, and the beauty of eloquence, would never have been able to lead the whole world to the faith of Christ unless he had evangelized it “not in the wisdom of speech, but in the power of God.” [Col. 0166D–0167A]

Consider carefully also what he says in the prefaces to Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel concerning the difference in the speech of those prophets. You will find that the nobility of divine eloquence does not consist, as you assert, in the manner of philosophers, in swelling and pomp of words, but in the power of its meanings, according to what the Apostle himself says:

> “For the kingdom of God is not in speech, but in power.”

[Note: [Col. 0167D] “Isaiah also, the prophet.” In the manuscript and likewise in Masson’s edition, the reading was “Isaiah also, the philosopher,” etc. Since this was evidently a scribal error, not Agobard’s, we have freely corrected that passage.]

The prophet Isaiah also says that the people are of profound speech, so that the eloquence of its language cannot be understood, and that there is no wisdom in it. And the Lord says to Ezekiel:

> “For you are not being sent to a people of profound speech and an unknown language, whose speech you would be unable to understand.” [Col. 0167A]

From these passages it is clear that the nobility of Holy Scripture does not consist, according to the philosophers, in eloquence of words—in which there is no wisdom—but in the power and skill of its meanings and in the force of its sentences. The Apostle demonstrates this when he says:

> “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, destroying counsels and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every understanding into captivity in obedience to Christ.”

And again:

> “Christ did not send me to baptize, but to evangelize—not in the wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.”

And again, after some intervening words:

> “When I came to you, brothers, I did not come with sublimity of speech or wisdom, announcing to you the testimony of Christ.”

And again:

> “We speak wisdom among the perfect—not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed—but we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the wisdom that has been hidden.”

And shortly afterward:

> “These things also we speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit.”

## XIII

Behold, then: praise of divine wisdom is found in the sacred mysteries and in the teaching of the Spirit, not in inventions of words.

You have collected many testimonies of blessed Augustine in praise of Scripture; but you do not praise it in the way Augustine praised it, nor in the way Jerome, Ambrose, and Gregory did. For they admired the majesty of divine speech, yet, unable to express in words what is ineffable, were overcome by its glory and faltered in praising it, since their wonder was more sufficient than their speech.

You praise it in such a way that your praise diminishes rather than increases it. For in those things that are external, you say that the Holy Spirit supplied the apostles with the nobility of languages, so that you may praise and defend all interpreters and every kind of expositor indiscriminately and on the same level as the apostles.

For if, according to you, the Holy Spirit supplied all the authors of the divine books equally with external nobility, why is one apostle—Paul—found to be more eloquent in the Hebrew language than in Greek, just as the aforementioned Jerome writes in the preface to the Epistle entitled “To the Hebrews,” saying:

> “It is certainly not surprising if he appears more eloquent in his own language, that is, Hebrew, than in a foreign language, that is, Greek, in which the other Epistles were written.” [Col. 0167D–0168A]

There you have Paul more eloquent in one Epistle than in the others. Yet the other Epistles, although they may seem to possess somewhat less in the matter of language than that one, are nevertheless not of lesser power in their hidden meanings, secret mysteries, and figures of speech, in which they surpass all the wisdom of this world incomparably.

## XIV

After the many serious accusations with which you burdened us, calling us censors of divine speech, you defend the claim that you spoke correctly when you said, “When the soul reaches the body.” You bring forward testimonies from Scripture, saying:

> “Let the spirit return to him who gave it.” (Ecclesiastes 12:7.)

And:

> “Let the soul of the child return within him.” (3 Kings 17:21.) [Col. 0168A–B]

These testimonies in no way fit the matter for which they are introduced in defense. For who is unaware that the soul, once created by God, thereafter exists as a substance, and is eternal and immortal in its substance? Accordingly, after the dissolution of the body, it can return to him if it is just, descend below if it is unjust, and return within the body to restore it to this life. No one is unaware that these things happen to souls already released from bodies.

But we criticize the statement you made concerning souls being infused into bodies: “When the soul reaches the body.” It is as though you knew from what region it comes—or perhaps you know in what region that unknown material lies from which you say souls are created: in the void over which the north wind is stretched, or in the inner regions of the south, or perhaps at the rising or setting of the sun; or from wherever you say the soul reaches the body.

They can, of course, come from the place where they are created, so that they may be sent into bodies. But when you say that they reach them, you do not believe that they are created in those very bodies, but somewhere far away. We therefore asked you whether that place is in the heavens, in some part of the world, or outside the world.

But let this matter be as you wish, provided only that you do not set the testimony of some person disputing with Augustine against us as though it were the testimony of Augustine himself.

Nevertheless, we think that this especially must be held: what divine Scripture teaches concerning this matter:

> “Just as you do not know the way of the spirit, or how the bones are joined together in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you do not know the works of God, who is the maker of all things.” [Col. 0168C–D]

The ecclesiastical teachers likewise taught in their doctrines that the soul is not a part of the divine substance or nature, and that it does not exist before it is mingled with the body; rather, it is created at the same time as the body with which it appears to be mingled.

The opinions of the philosophers say that the soul exists before it is born in the body. But no evidence confirms this as true. For whether we existed before, we ourselves do not know, nor do we have any human being who can say so. Therefore, what ought rather to be mocked than investigated must not be investigated.

[Col. 0169A]

## XV

Next you asked us whether God is one thing and truth another, so that God himself is not truth. We are so astonished at this question of yours that we think you dictated it joking and laughing. Who has ever heard such a question?

If truth were something else, would God no longer be truth? Tell us: whenever truth is named in Holy Scripture, must God always be understood? Certainly, we say that Scripture frequently names truth as the opposite of falsehood, just as it also commonly names human charity and love, which are opposed to hatred, and concord, which is opposed to discord.

Therefore, when Paul says, “I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie,” do you understand him as though he were saying, “I speak God,” or “I speak Christ,” “in Christ Jesus”? Or when he says, “Putting away falsehood, speak truth, each one with his neighbor,” do you understand God himself as the truth?

Again, where it is written, “The king who judges the poor in truth—his throne shall be established forever.” And again, “The lip of truth shall be firm.” And again, “He who speaks truth in his heart.” Also in Jeremiah:

> “Every friend will walk deceitfully and will not speak truth.”

And in Hosea:

> “For there is no truth, no justice, and no mercy of God in the land.”

And in Zechariah:

> “Judge truth and the judgment of peace in your gates.”

Could this be understood as though he were saying, “Judge God in your gates”? Behold: Scripture frequently speaks of truth, not of God himself, but of that virtue which is opposed to injustice [Col. 0169B–C] and falsehood.

Nevertheless, this does not mean, as you wish, that God himself is not truth; rather, it means that God is also truth.

## XVI

Then, with your syllogisms, you attempt to assert that all the holy patriarchs and prophets, kings and priests, in the Old Testament were not Christians. You say to us:

> “If, by calling them Christians, you wish to affirm that they were Christians, it is exceedingly absurd that they should have been Christians before Christ.”

Behold the words by which you deny that the saints of the Old Testament were Christians. But you deny something far worse when you say that Christ did not exist at that time.

Believe me, venerable master: if you had said, “They were not called Christians,” your blasphemy might perhaps have been slight. But when you say, “They were not Christians,” you unjustly blaspheme such a great multitude of saints. Likewise, if you said of the Lord Jesus Christ, “He was not yet openly called Christ by all the faithful,” that would be tolerable. But when you say, “He was not Christ,” it is so great a blasphemy that it is not far removed from the preaching of Paul of Samosata.

## XVII

Then you add, as though exhorting us, saying:

> “But how was Christ not yet [Christ]?”

You read the book of the aforementioned blessed Father Augustine, chapter 6, and quote the chapter as containing a meaning quite different from what you think. For in that chapter it is written:

> “Since, then, Christ’s name derives from what is written, ‘God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions,’ it pertains to the fact that he became man—that is, that, taking the form of a servant, he was found in appearance as a man. This appearance certainly began in time. Yet it was of this same Christ that it was said, when he was in the form of God.” [Col. 0169D–0170A]

And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore Christ was not yet what he began to be when he emptied himself—not losing the form of God, but taking the form of a servant.”

These are the words of blessed Augustine. You wish to use them to assert that God the Word did not have the name Christ before he became flesh, whereas Augustine, in the sentence quoted above, says the contrary:

> “It was of this same Christ that it was said, when he was in the form of God.”

There you have Christ existing in the form of God and then taking the form of a servant. Before he took it, he was certainly not yet the son of man, but the Son of God—yet Christ.

Again Augustine says:

> “Therefore Christ was not yet what he began to be when he emptied himself.”

Here too Christ is named as one who was not yet what he began to be when he emptied himself—that is, man. For what else did he begin to be except man, when he took the form of a servant?

Certainly Augustine does not say, “Christ did not exist, who began to be”; rather, he says, “He was not what he began to be.”

## XVIII

For if Christ did not exist before Mary, what does the Apostle’s statement mean:

> “Jesus Christ, yesterday and today, the same also forever.” (Hebrews 13:8.) [Col. 0170B]

If Christ did not exist, and the saints of the Old Testament were not Christians, why does the Apostle again say:

> “Remember that you were once Gentiles in the flesh, who are called the uncircumcision by that which is called the circumcision, made in the flesh by human hands; because at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the citizenship of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world.” (Ephesians 2:11–12.)

The Apostle teaches that the Gentiles were without Christ at the time when Israel possessed the hope of the promise. And what does it mean to say, “You were without Christ, alienated from the citizenship of Israel,” except indirectly to show that Israel was not without Christ in the time of the promise?

If Christ did not exist, and neither did Christians, why does the same Apostle say of Moses:

> “He refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to have the enjoyment of sin for a time, considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt; for he looked toward the reward.” (Hebrews 11:24–25.)

If those under the Law did not worship Christ when they were good, and did not tempt him when they were evil, why does he again say of those who worshiped him:

> “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them. And the rock was Christ.”

And of those who tempted him:

> “Nor let us tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him and perished by serpents.”

And so that you may know that under the Law there were not only Christians but also sons of Christ, hear the Apostle again:

> “It was fitting that he for whom and through whom all things exist, who had brought many sons into glory, should perfect the author of their salvation through sufferings.”

Hannah, the mother of Samuel, praying in the temple, says:

> “The Lord will judge the ends of the earth; he will give power to his king and exalt the horn of his Christ.”

This was even at the time when there was not yet a king in Israel, before Saul was anointed or even born—the man whom you considered worthy to choose for denying Christians. [Col. 0170D–0171A]

Of David it is written:

> “The man to whom the Christ of the God of Jacob was appointed, the excellent psalmist of Israel.”

David himself says:

> “Exalting the salvation of his king and showing mercy to his Christ.”

Ethan also says:

> “But you have rejected and despised; you have delayed your Christ.”

Habakkuk says:

> “You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ.”

Jeremiah laments, saying:

> “The breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord, has been captured in our sins.”

## XIX

Then you add, saying:

> “Not everyone anointed with chrism should therefore be called a Christian. Rather, they were called Christs rather than Christians, as in the Psalms: ‘Do not touch my Christs.’” [Col. 0171A–B]

In these words you deny that the anointed—namely, kings and priests—were Christians. You offer a psalmic testimony that Scripture speaks not of priests or kings, but only of the patriarchs, namely Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob:

> “They passed from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people”—that is, from Chaldea to Mesopotamia, then to the land of Canaan and Egypt, and again to Gerar.

For their sake kings were rebuked—namely, Abimelech, Pharaoh, Hamor, Shechem, and others. Concerning them the Lord commanded, “Do not touch my Christs,” saying this not so much in words as through the certainty of his defense.

Behold: you have patriarchs called “Christs,” whom you will in no way be able to prove to have been anointed with any bodily anointing. Why, then, are they called Christs, if they were not anointed?

You say, therefore, that they were “many Christs” by virtue of anointing, although you never read that several kings, or even two priests, existed simultaneously at that time. For kings and priests were anointed only when one died and another succeeded him, as a representation of the one true Christ. These men were indeed called Christs.

## XX

But concerning the patriarchs we ask: how do you believe that they were anointed without visible chrism and without the water of baptism, but only with invisible and spiritual chrism?

Likewise, in the Old Testament we believe that not only all the holy patriarchs but also many situated among the Gentiles were anointed with invisible chrism. Through this anointing they became members of Christ and one body with all those predestined to eternal life.

Accordingly, when the Apostle had enumerated all the gifts of grace distributed through the Holy Spirit to the faithful of both the Old Testament and the New, he added:

> “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, slaves or free; and we were all made to drink of one Spirit.”

[Col. 0171D] “We were all made to drink.” This is Paul’s passage from the First Epistle to the Corinthians. In Paul’s text—as Agobard also quotes it in chapter 37 of his book Against Felix, in chapter 7 of his book On the Manner of Ecclesiastical Government, and in chapter 7 of his Exhortatory Sermon to the People—the reading is: “and we were all made to drink of one Spirit.” In the royal manuscript, however, and in Masson’s edition, it reads: “and we were all baptized in one Spirit.” It seemed that this should be changed. For shortly afterward Agobard, repeating that passage and asking what that drink is, says: “We were made to drink of one Spirit.”

With this Spirit the patriarchs were anointed; with this Spirit, many martyrs, who passed into eternal life without bodily baptism. [Col. 0171D–0172A]

[Col. 0171D] “Many martyrs.” Agobard therefore held that those who suffered the disgrace of death for the name of Christ were carried directly to heaven, even if they had not been baptized. The same was the view of the ancient author of the book On the Singularity of the Clergy, commonly attributed to Cyprian:

> “For this reason martyrdom is called both a crown and a baptism, because it equally baptizes and crowns.”

Likewise, Alcuin, in his Confession of Faith, book III, chapter 28:

> “We do not say that any catechumen, even if he dies in good works, possesses eternal life—except through martyrdom, where the whole sacrament of baptism is completed. For confessors are baptized by blood, or by fire, or by other sufferings.”

The ancient author mentioned above, likewise, and hitherto unpublished, says in his Confession of Faith:
