> “We do not believe that any catechumen, even if he dies in good works, possesses eternal life—except through martyrdom, where the whole sacrament of baptism is completed. The one who is to be baptized confesses his faith before the priest and, when questioned, responds. The martyr does the same before the persecutor: he confesses his faith and, when questioned, responds. After confession, the one is sprinkled with water or immersed in it; the other is sprinkled with blood or immersed in fire. The one receives the Holy Spirit through the laying on of the bishop’s hands; the other becomes a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit.”

How, then, were all these—patriarchs and martyrs, together with the other faithful of the Old and New Testaments—baptized into one body and in one Spirit? Hear the same Apostle again:

> “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink.”

What drink? The one he mentioned in the preceding statement: “We were made to drink of one Spirit.” And what spiritual food, unless participation in the body of Christ?

Finally, the Apostle says:

> “For you are all one in Christ Jesus. And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring.”

And you say that Abraham was not a Christian, although we cannot be Christians unless we become Abraham’s offspring.

The Apostle says:

> “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring,” who is Christ.

And you say that Abraham was without Christ. The Apostle says:

> “Therefore those who are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham.”

And again:

> “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.”

And you say that Abraham and we were blessed with blessings so different, and anointed with spirits so different, that he could be Christ but not a Christian, while we could be Christians but not Christ.

## XXI

The Apostle says that God the almighty Father subjected all things beneath the feet of his Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, and gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body and his fullness, who fills all things in all.

And again:

> “For he is our peace, who made both one and broke down the middle wall of the barrier, abolishing enmity in his flesh, annulling the law of commandments by decrees, so that he might create the two in himself into one new man, making peace, and might reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, killing the enmity in himself. And coming, he preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near, because through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father. Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone. In him the whole structure, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in him you also are built together into a dwelling place of God in the Holy Spirit.”

And why do you wish to divide this Church, this body that is the fullness of its head, this unity that he made from both, these people created in himself, these two reconciled in one body to God through the cross, this structure that has been built, this holy temple in the Lord, this dwelling place of God in the Spirit, so that they should be one thing and we another?

What, then, was the benefit of our both having access through the head to the Father in one Spirit, if the root of the olive has no communion with the wild olive grafted into it?

The tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh built an altar beyond the Jordan because they already feared you, lest, when they had crossed the Jordan, you should say to them:

> “You do not belong to us; you are not Christians; you are without Christ, because Christ did not yet exist.”

[Col. 0173D] “You are not Christians.” Here Agobard gravely refutes Fredegisus, who had said that the patriarchs of the Old Testament were not Christians. Agobard has Justin Martyr and Augustine in agreement with him; Baronius praises them at the beginning of his Apparatus to the Ecclesiastical Annals. See also the book Against Amalarius, chapter 15.

There is absolutely no other difference between them and us except that the sacraments of salvation, which were effected through the Mediator for our sake and theirs, save us as things past, while they were saved as things future. What we believe and hold as past, they believed and held as future; they had it only in conscience and in figures of future things, whereas we have it also in public profession, vows, and proclamation of past events, together with the tangible signs of the sacraments.

It is like those two men who carried one cluster of grapes on a pole: they performed one and the same work without distinction, except that one carried the same cluster behind him and the other before him. It is also like those who preceded and followed the Lord as he entered Jerusalem, crying, “Hosanna.”

[Col. 0174A]

## XXII

If anyone should think to object to these things with what is said in Isaiah or in the Apocalypse about a “new name,” which undoubtedly is understood to mean “Christian,” let him know that the holy teachers understood it to be called new because it had recently been dispersed, not because it had recently been invented.

Therefore the religion of the Christians is not novel or newly arisen, but descends from the very origin of the world, with the same Christ as its teacher and founder. For from the beginning it looked toward his image and form.

Moreover, concerning the unity of the faithful of the Old and New Testaments, blessed Jerome says:

> “For just as all who were not yet born die in the first-formed Adam, so all—even those who were born before Christ’s coming—are made alive in the second Adam. Thus it comes about that we have served the Law in the fathers, and they are saved by grace in the sons.”

This understanding accords with the Catholic Church, which asserts one providence for the Old and New Testaments and does not distinguish in time those whom it joined together in origin.

Let us all be built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, held together by the cornerstone, Jesus Christ our Lord, who made both one and, destroying the dividing wall, abolished in his flesh the enmity between the two peoples; he changed the difficulty of the ancient Law through the integrity of evangelical doctrines.

Truly, in Christ we are one bread, and the two of us have agreed upon the earth. Just as we are founded upon the prophets, so the patriarchs already stood upon the foundation of the apostles.

Concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, the aforementioned teacher also says:

> “After he deigned to be born from a Virgin’s womb for our salvation, Christ Jesus, the man between God and men, was called the mediator.”

Before, however, he assumed the body of a man, while he was with the Father and all the saints whom Scripture mentions, without the addition of the man whom he had not yet assumed, he was called mediator only.

For by his precious blood he redeemed both us and them—namely, the patriarchs and prophets—from the curse of the Law. For all were justified by faith in Christ. Abraham saw Christ’s day and rejoiced; and Moses considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, for he looked toward the reward.

[Col. 0173D]

# LETTER TO THE DIGNITARIES OF THE PALACE AGAINST THE IMPIOUS DECREE CONCERNING THE BAPTISM OF JEWISH SLAVES

To the lords and most holy, most blessed, illustrious men, Hilduin, prelate of the sacred palace [Alternatively: archchaplain], and Wala, abbot, Agobard, your little servant.

[Col. 0173D] “To Hilduin, prelate of the sacred palace,” that is, archchaplain or chief chaplain, as he is called in Louis the Pious’s decree concerning Hildebold, bishop of Mâcon, which is preserved in the library of Cluny. For our princes had in their palace a member of the ecclesiastical order who held precedence over the others and was therefore called the prelate of the sacred palace; or “archbishop of the sacred palace” if he was a bishop.

Thus Hildebold, archbishop of Cologne, is called “archbishop of the sacred palace” in the preface to the council held at Mainz in the year 813. This is evidently the same Hildebold whom Charlemagne wished to retain in his palace after Angilram, as is clear from canon 56 of the Council of Frankfurt.

Agobard therefore calls Hilduin the prelate of the sacred palace because he was the chief chaplain. For the same reason Lupus of Ferrières calls this same Hilduin “master of the clergy” in Letter 101. We have already noted, in connection with the Council of Verneuil, that abbots, if they held supreme authority in affairs, were formerly superior to bishops, even in synods. Nor is this so ancient that it was not still practiced in the time of Suger, as is clear from chapter 2 of his Life.

[Col. 0175A] “And to Wala, abbot,” [Col. 0175D] Wala, abbot of Corbie in the diocese of Amiens, as we said in connection with the book On the Baptism of Jewish Slaves.

Your very prudent Mildness should know that I have ventured to write what follows to both of you because I know without ambiguity that you are the principal, and almost the only, assistants of the most Christian emperor [Note: [Col. 0175D] Louis the Pious] in the way of God, and therefore that one of you is always present in the palace [Note: [Col. 0176C] One always, namely Hilduin. For he necessarily had to remain in the palace on ecclesiastical business. See what we said concerning the office of archchaplain [Col. 0176D] in the notes to Lupus of Ferrières.] and the other frequently [Note: [Col. 0176D] The other frequently, namely Wala, whom Louis used extensively in administering the state, as is clear from Paschasius Radbertus, Life of Adalhard.]—so that in works of piety, which must be sought, found, and held without any error, you may be his exhorters through your very prudent suggestions and, as I have said, his assistants.

I have written several brief notices to your sincerity, informing you that a certain woman, transferred by Christ’s grace from Judaism to Christianity, is suffering severe persecutions because of the faith in Christ that she has embraced. You can learn about these through the brief statement of that woman; and in this matter an almsgiving so excellent awaits you that no greater one could exist.

Now, since I am informing you of the cause of this persecution—which may also be the fuel of impious error—you should deign to learn it. The Jews carry about a certain decree, which they boast was given to them by the emperor, containing the following [Note: [Col. 0176D] “That no one may baptize a Jewish slave without the consent of his master.” Agobard rightly grows indignant against that decree, since it was contrary to ancient canons and the laws of the rulers. For even in our Gaul the First Council of Mâcon had granted slaves the power to receive baptism, even against the wishes of their masters. The Emperor Constantine Augustus, writing to Pope Felix, likewise permitted Jews generally to embrace the Christian religion, and forbade that anyone who had given his name to Christ should, on that account, suffer any disturbance or harassment from the Jews. Thus Agobard did not find it plausible that that decree had been issued by the Emperor Louis, who was called “the Pious” par excellence, since it inflicted manifest insult upon the Christian name.] that no one may baptize a Jewish slave without the will of his master.

We do not believe this at all, since it is impossible that such a sentence, so contrary to ecclesiastical rule, should have proceeded from the presence of the most Christian and most pious emperor. For your God-loving prudence knows very well how, from the beginning, the holy apostles received from Truth itself a command concerning this matter: without any distinction of persons and without any exception based on status, they were told universally: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” And again: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.”

Observing this with complete faith and constancy, those apostles and all ecclesiastical rulers thereafter did not hesitate not only to preach and convert to the faith slaves belonging to every kind of person, but also the wives and children of emperors and consuls, and, once converted, to baptize them without awaiting anyone’s permission.

This can readily be recognized in the deeds of others, but it is demonstrated with especial clarity in the apostolic letters. For we read at the end of the Epistle to the Philippians (4:22): “All the saints greet you, especially those who are of Caesar’s household.” No one, surely, doubts that this was the most impious Nero. No one doubts that his household members and palace servants, converted by apostolic preaching, could never have been sanctified by baptism if his will or permission in this matter had been awaited. By the greatest terror of persecution he not only deterred unbelievers from coming to the faith but also strove to drive believers away from it. Hence, in the final atrocity of his fury, he slaughtered the very leaders and teachers of the Christian faith, whose teaching he saw bringing almost the whole world under the faith of Christ against his own decrees.

In the Epistle to Timothy, after the Apostle had commanded prayers and supplications to be offered for all human beings, he concluded: “For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.”

And in the Epistle to Titus, after showing that old men and old women, young women, young men, and slaves must be instructed by appropriate commands, he concluded in this way: “For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people, instructing us,” and so forth.

Therefore, if—as these examples most clearly prove—it is the will of God our Savior that all people be saved, come to the knowledge of the truth, and be reconciled through the one mediator between God and human beings, who gave himself as a ransom for all; if the grace of this reconciliation and salvation has shone upon all without distinction, who would dare to injure God’s goodness so greatly by placing a restriction upon his mercy and decreeing that it be bestowed upon those who implore it at the discretion of impious people, whose most obstinate unbelief not only permits none of their own people to approach the faith of Christ but also never ceases publicly and secretly to blaspheme and detest those who believe?

Finally, it is clear to those who consider the matter piously that the one almighty God, the creator of all and their most just governor, who first formed the human being from the dust of the earth and made for him from his rib a helper like himself, and who propagated the whole human race from them as from one fountain and one root, made all people of one condition.

Although, because sins demanded it and by his most just and inscrutable judgment, some have been raised to various honors while others have been oppressed beneath the yoke of slavery, he nevertheless ordained that bodily service be rendered by slaves to their masters in such a way that [Note: [Col. 0177C] “The inner person in his image.” Agobard therefore places the likeness of God that exists in the human being in the soul, not in the body. See the notes to Epistle 30 of Lupus of Ferrières and to the book On Three Questions, p. 471. The Jews held other absurdities, believing that the human body had been made in the image of God, as Agobard writes in his book On Jewish Superstitions, chapter 10. In that place Masson noted in the margin that these Jewish fabrications are also found in the Kabbalah.] he willed the inner person, created in his image, to be subject to no human being, no angel, and no creature whatever, but to himself alone.

Hence, in his law, concerning this slavery of the mind—which is owed to him alone—he commanded: “You shall fear the Lord your God, and you shall serve him alone.” And the Apostle, showing that this same inner person is free from every distinction of sex and every difference of creator and origin, teaches as follows: “Stripping off the old person with his deeds and putting on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of his creator; where there is neither Gentile nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all.”

Since, therefore, those who come to baptism are renewed through knowledge of the Creator in the inner person, who is free from every condition of slavery, what reason can there be for preventing slaves from attaining this without their masters’ permission, and for denying them the right to serve God unless they have obtained permission from human beings?

Certainly, in the Epistle to Timothy the same Apostle commanded: “Let all who are under the yoke as slaves consider their masters worthy of all honor, lest the name of the Lord and the teaching be blasphemed. Those who have believing masters must not despise them because they are brothers; rather, they should serve them all the more because they are believers,” and so forth (1 Tim. 6:1).

In these words he clearly speaks of all Christian slaves, some of whom served believing masters and others unbelieving ones. Yet he established commands for the slaves of unbelieving masters—who would of course still have been bound by the chain of unbelief if, in this matter, they had followed the will of those whom they served.

Philemon was wronged by the slave Onesimus, whom the Apostle Paul, while imprisoned, converted to the faith of Christ and washed in the font of sacred baptism. Yet Philemon does not complain about this; indeed, he is instructed to receive him, now believing and baptized, as the Apostle’s own heart.

Because we desire to follow these authorities, while fearing to transgress the decree that is produced as though by imperial authority, we find ourselves caught between two dangers. If we observe that decree and neglect ecclesiastical regulations, we offend God; if we follow these regulations, we fear the emperor’s displeasure—especially since [Note: [Col. 0177D] “The teacher of the unbelieving Jews.” Evrardus. See above in the notes to the book On the Baptism of Jewish Slaves.] the teacher of the unbelieving Jews continually threatens us that he will bring [Note: [Col. 0177D] “Envoys from the palace,” that is, the emperor’s envoys.] envoys from the palace, who will judge and punish us for matters of this kind.

You should judge how much this not only disturbs us but also places an obstacle before those who could easily have been converted to the faith.

Therefore, most holy and God-loving Fathers, weighing these dangers of ours in your pious hearts as though they were your own, intercede with the most Christian and merciful emperor so that this impediment may be removed from holy Church and so that, among the many great matters that he piously and justly administers within the empire entrusted and preserved for him by Christ, he may also come to the aid of this matter through the most merciful and customary goodness prompted by love of Christ.

Let it not happen that souls—souls through which the flock of the faithful could have been increased, and for whose salvation the universal Church publicly supplicates God during the days of the Lord’s Passion [Note: [Col. 0178C] Publicly, namely for the Jews, for whose conversion the Church prays every year during the days of the Lord’s Passion, as Agobard says—that is, on the Wednesday of Holy Week. There exists a prayer that priests publicly recite in the Church at that time for this purpose. Rabanus, in his book Against the Jews, chapter 4, speaking of the Jews, says: “Indeed, even worse than heretics, as the Catholic Church judges them to be; for during the days of the Lord’s Passion, after heretics and schismatics, and almost after the pagans, the Church prays for them.” Likewise, chapter 59: “Indeed, sincerely seeking their true salvation, for which the Church is accustomed solemnly to pray, let us preserve ecclesiastical sincerity toward them.”]—should, because of the hardness of unbelievers and those hostile to God, remain entangled in the devil’s snares on account of this decree as well.

Certainly, the sacred canons have established that if any of them come to baptism, the bishop or any of the faithful who wishes to do so has the power to redeem them (see the book On Jewish Superstitions, chapter 6). We very gladly desire to do this, asking only that they be granted free opportunity to come to the faith. We do not say that their children or slaves should be forcibly taken away from them, but that unbelievers should not be permitted to deny permission to those who come to the faith.

[Col. 0179]

## Letter to Bartholomew, Bishop of Narbonne, Concerning the Deception of Certain Signs

[Col. 0179A]

### I.

To the most reverend and beloved lord and brother Bartholomew, bishop of Narbonne [Note: [Col. 0179B] After Nibridius. He attended the council held at Toulouse in 828, together with Nothon, archbishop of Arles, [Col. 0179C] and Agiulf of Bourges. Then, around the year 834, he subscribed the privilege of Aldric, archbishop of Sens, for the monastery of Saint Remigius of Sens, which is found in volume 2 of Dom Luc d’Achery’s Spicilegium. Later, when Emperor Lothair rebelled against his father Louis, Bartholomew supported Lothair’s party. When Lothair departed for Italy in 834, Bartholomew, abandoning his see contrary to the sacred regulations, accompanied him, as Flodoard records in book 2, chapter 20, of his History of Rheims. Bartholomew therefore remained in Italy until 844. Then, when Louis, Lothair’s son, went to Rome to carry his father’s instructions to the pope and the Roman nobles concerning the ordinations of the Roman pontiffs, Bartholomew accompanied Louis there as well. When Louis had been anointed king of the Lombards, Bartholomew took the opportunity to ask Pope Sergius II, together with Ebbo of Rheims, “to deign to reconcile them and grant them the pallium.” The same prelate said that they were not even worthy to receive communion among the clergy, but should have permission to communicate only among the common people. Thus teaches the author of the Book of the Deeds of the Pontiffs, cited by Hincmar, in chapter 36 of the latter’s work Against Gottschalk, p. 326. Accordingly, after Bartholomew was deposed, Berarius was appointed in his place. I find that Berarius occupied the see of Narbonne in 844, on 20 June, in a charter of King Charles the Bald issued on that day for the church of Narbonne; Catellus published part of it, but we possess the complete document copied from the original. Moreover, Amulo of Lyon mentions this book, or letter, of his to Bartholomew, bishop of Narbonne, in his letter to Theobald of Langres.] Bartholomew, bishop, Agobard, [Note: [Col. 0180C] Hildigisus. From this it is clear that this Hildigisus belonged to the clergy of Lyon. He was doubtless a priest, since Florus, who was only a deacon, is named after him.] Hildigisus, and [Note: [Col. 0180C] Florus. A deacon of the church of Lyon, and, for that age, a very learned man, also famous for his published writings. We discussed these in the notes to Lupus of Ferrières. There exists a small work by Florus on the election of bishops, published by Masson at the end of Agobard’s works; for that very reason we wished it to appear together with those works.] Florus, eternal salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ.

We have learned that your prudent mind is concerned about how one should understand what has begun to happen in a certain place: certain people are struck so that they fall, like epileptics or those whom the common people think or call possessed by demons. A venerable brother [Note: [Col. 0180C] A certain venerable brother, namely the bishop of Ucetia in Narbonensis Prima, as I suppose. Elephantus was then bishop at Ucetia, as is clear from the Manual of Dhuoda.] also reported this to us, especially [Note: [Col. 0180C] In a church situated in the city of Ucetia, as is established by Amulo’s letter to Theobald, [Col. 0180D] p. 142.] in a certain church where the body of a saint named Firminus is venerated [Note: [Col. 0180D] Firminus, bishop of Ucetia, who occupied that see in 540 and 555, and whom Arator the subdeacon mentions in his letter to Parthenius, published by Sirmond after the notes to Ennodius. We possess his Life, praised by learned men but not yet published, which we once copied at Toulouse from a very ancient manuscript of the College of Foix.] And now, through you, we have learned that another kind of phenomenon also occurs: marks resembling burns appear and are felt on human bodies, as though sulfur had burned in those places. Yet we were not told that anyone had died from these things, nor that anyone who had previously been ill had been cured.

When people of both sexes and different ages see these things, they make offerings at the place—or, as you say, at the places. Indeed, offerings of another kind now also appear to be made elsewhere: each person gives whatever he can, whether gold or silver, livestock, or any other commodities, without anyone’s urging and without being instructed for any rational reason, but terrified by irrational fear.

This seems to us exceedingly foolish, since no signs of healings and no hope of divine favor are demonstrated there. For this reason it could more easily have been understood what precaution ought to be taken.

Certainly, just as it is most true that these blows cannot occur except by God’s permission, so it is most certain that they are administered by no other power than that of an angel striking. Who is so foolish as not to know that almighty God scourges human beings, visibly and invisibly, for instruction and conversion—not only through human beings but also through beasts and through the smallest and most worthless living creatures? He does so not only through fiery serpents but also through frogs, flies, gnats, and locusts; not only through living creatures but also through inanimate things, such as hail, rivers, rains, and droughts.

Your prudence knows, of course, the source of what we are saying: holy Scripture is our authority. And if we mention lions, hornets, caterpillars, worms, rust, and devouring—that is, a curse [Col. 0180B] (a single name under which many things can be understood)—we shall have the same authority. If we add bears, wolves, swine, and wild stags, examples will nevertheless not be lacking, even if it cannot easily be demonstrated from Scripture.

### II.

Although these burns about which you are troubled are not very different from swollen blisters—or, as another edition says, the Egyptian “boils” brought upon the Egyptians—and from the blows inflicted upon the Philistines, which the Book of Samuel explicitly records, and from other such protruding afflictions, who can be permitted to remain ignorant of how sufferers, hearers, and spectators ought to act in all these matters, since there is one Lord of all, who scourges and heals, strikes and cures, leads down to the underworld and brings back?

The blessed Job confessed this concerning him, saying: “Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you, my friends, because the hand of the Lord has touched me,” although that same Scripture says: “Satan struck him with a most grievous ulcer.” Yet although the striker struck, he is said to have touched Job because he possessed the striker under his power—not only in the body but also in the loss of possessions. Thus Job says again: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away,” while the Lord had said to the devil himself: “Behold, all that he has is in your hand.”

But since the striker can never have this power unless he receives it from the one under whose power he himself also is, the power must be ascribed to the one who grants and restrains, permits and checks.

The Scriptures are full of examples of this kind, including the passage concerning Saul, where we read that an evil spirit seized him. In these words divine Scripture wonderfully shows both that power must be attributed to the Lord and that malice must be attributed to the devil. The devil does not receive his malice, but has it from himself; what he does not have, however, he receives—that is, power.

### III.

We do not need to write these things to you, since you possess many sublime statements of sublime teachers. Nevertheless, two kinds of phenomena seem to us worth bringing to your attention, and we think that they must be investigated equally by you and by us.

The first is this: we do not know whether it should be called a correction, an infirmity, or rather a virtue. We think we know only this about the matter: that it is not brought about through the ministry of any hostile power.

So it was with the blessed priest Zechariah, who walked blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord. Because he was unbelieving concerning the promise made to him by the archangel Gabriel, he was punished with silence.

The blessed Daniel, “the man of desires,” also acknowledges this, saying: “Lord, at the sight of you my bones were loosened”; and he says that afterward he languished for many days. The blessed Jacob, moreover, wrestling with the angel, became lame.

### IV.

We do not say this as though the devil, having received no power, could not inflict corrections upon the saints, since the Apostle plainly says that a thorn in the flesh was given to him, an angel of Satan. But these afflictions can be distinguished from other blows, including that by which Mary, the sister of Moses and Aaron, and King Uzziah were struck with leprosy: she because of the sin of slander, he because of the pride of presumption.

If there is uncertainty whether these things occurred solely by God’s command or through the ministry of good or evil angels, we do not know whether the same uncertainty can apply to Nadab and Abihu, of whom it is written that fire went out from the Lord and killed them.

Something similar appears to have happened to Uzzah, who, presuming to support the ark of the Lord, is said to have been struck and killed by the Lord.

### V.

Since the judgments of the Lord are always just but frequently hidden, they seem even more obscure to us in the death of the Beth-shemites. There, apart from the seventy men who perhaps had tried either to sacrifice or to handle the ark of the Lord with their hands, fifty thousand of the common people are said to have been struck by the Lord, although they must be believed to have done none of these things.

Even if they were killed through the agency of a striking angel, they are rightly said to have been struck by the Lord, according to the principle set forth above.

### VI.

Perhaps someone might similarly question the two companies of fifty, each with its fifty men, sent to Elijah, asking whether they were killed through angelic agency. Scripture therefore says that fire descended from heaven and consumed them.

But one should likewise consider what is said concerning the sheep of blessed Job: “The fire of God fell from heaven and consumed the sheep and the servants who were tending them,” although no one doubts that this was done through Satan’s agency.

### VII.

The second kind is that in which the devil appears to prevail over certain people, not so much in order to strike them as to mock them. We have heard of and known many who were beaten by demons with stones and clubs but were harmed in no way; some, however, were both mocked and injured.

No other cause seems to account for this except either emptiness of faith or delight in vanity. We cannot easily produce examples of this from Scripture, yet scarcely anyone exists who has not heard or seen such things, since many, stunned by empty fear or empty wonder, lose their understanding and strength of mind.

For the devil knows, as the blessed Leo says (Sermon 7, On the Nativity of the Lord), whom to cast down through sorrow, whom to deceive through joy, whom to overwhelm through fear, and whom to seduce through wonder.

Hence the Apostle urges: “Resist him, strong in faith.” He is always eager to do harm, both when he shows himself as what he is and when he transforms himself into an angel of light and displays what appear to be signs of healings.

He must truly be resisted in both circumstances, so that we neither fear empty terrors nor take delight in empty miracles.

### VIII.

We have inserted these remarks about two kinds of phenomena: one in which the devil’s agency has no part, as we said concerning the blessed Zechariah, Daniel, and Job; and another in which weakness of faith, emptiness of reason, or dullness of understanding is the cause.

It is fitting here to add those great and terrible events that the Lord willed to occur for the instruction of the faithful. Through them we are taught that even the devil, the rebel against light, serves God and is a minister of divine action, since through him scourges and tribulations are inflicted not only upon the wicked but also upon the good.

That blows are inflicted upon the impious and unbelieving by evil angels is plainly declared by the Psalmist when he speaks of the plagues with which Egypt was struck: “He sent upon them the anger of his indignation, indignation, anger, and tribulation, a sending of evil angels” (Ps. 77:49).

In the Book of Ecclesiasticus we read (39:33): “There are spirits created for vengeance, and in their fury they have confirmed their torments.”

Hence in the Book of Tobit (3:8) we read concerning Sarah, daughter of Raguel, that she had been given to seven men, and that the demon named Asmodeus had killed them as soon as they entered to her.

Concerning the impious King Ahaz, Scripture testifies in the Book of Chronicles: “King Ahaz himself sacrificed victims to the gods of Damascus, his smiters, and said: ‘The gods of the kings of Syria help them; I will appease them with sacrifices, and they will help me.’” Yet, on the contrary, they became his ruin and the ruin of all Israel.

The Psalmist shows who the gods of the nations are when he says: “All the gods of the nations are demons.” The Apostle likewise says in his First Epistle to the Corinthians: “What the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God.”

### IX.

That both the impious and the faithful are sometimes handed over to evil spirits to be struck is demonstrated more clearly than daylight by the history of blessed Job. There the devil’s undertaking and God’s permission are plainly described.

Finally, after the loss of his possessions and the death of his children, when Satan had demanded that Job’s bone and flesh be touched by God’s hand, and the Lord had permitted it, saying, “Behold, he is in your hand,” it is said of him: “Then Satan went out from the presence of the Lord and struck Job with a most grievous ulcer, from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head” (Job 2:7).

The Lord also shows in the Gospel that illnesses and afflictions by which the pious or impious are tormented for a long time may be inflicted by evil angels. When he answered the ruler of the synagogue, who criticized him concerning the woman whom he himself had healed from a spirit of infirmity, he added afterward: “And ought not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound for eighteen years, to be released from this bond on the Sabbath day?”

Hence the blessed Peter, speaking in the Acts of the Apostles about the Lord’s miracles, says of him: “He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.”

The Apostle Paul also says that he handed Philetus and Hermogenes over to Satan so that they might learn not to blaspheme.

Concerning the man who had his father’s wife, he speaks to the Corinthians as follows: “Although absent in body, I am present in spirit, and I have already judged, as though present, the one who has acted in this way. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are assembled, and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus, hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus.”

Regarding himself he says what we have already mentioned: “And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to strike me with blows.”

### X.

We read in the Book of Wisdom that the terrors of tribulations are also caused by demons. When Scripture recounts the plagues of Egypt, which the Psalmist shows were sent through evil angels, it says among other things: “Nor did the cave that held them keep them without fear, because a descending sound troubled them, and gloomy faces appearing brought them terror” (Wis. 17:4).

Hence the Prophet promises God’s protection to the just person, saying: “His truth will surround you with a shield. You will not fear the terror of the night, the arrow flying by day, the affair that walks in darkness, the attack, and the demon at noon.”

The Lord also shows in the Gospel that these hostile powers seek and desire from God the power to strike and harm, when he says to his disciples: “This night Satan has demanded you, that he may sift you like wheat.”

The Psalmist says likewise: “In it”—that is, in the night—“all the beasts of the forest will pass through, the young lions roaring to seize and seek their food from God,” and in many other passages of divine Scripture.

### XI.

Although, as we said above, the devil does not always and in every case receive power, he nevertheless always has, in everyone and through everything, an entirely complete desire to do harm. He especially thirsts for those over whom he sees that he can prevail, because they are weak in faith and empty of the weight of reason.

That is why he appears to cast down children, girls, and all sorts of dull-minded people, and to mark them with burn-like spots.

Whenever a faithful and rational person sees or hears this, he raises his heart to the fear of God alone, who does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear. The same should be done when we are scourged by the teeth of beasts, or by whatever means and wherever we may be scourged, or when we see others being scourged.

### XII.

As for those about whom you have informed us, who run to the same churches in which they are struck and give whatever they can, we believe that they do this entirely because they have been deceived by terrors and have lost their better judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0183D] They would do better. He seems to condemn those who enrich the memorials of martyrs with offerings, saying that they would do better if they spent their possessions on the poor and on guests. These are the living temples of Christ. Nevertheless, I do not think Erasmus derived his statement from this passage when, in his Colloquy On a Religious Pilgrimage, he says that very many people visit the temples of the saints but give nothing, or very little, claiming that the money would be more rightly applied to the needy. Certainly the needs of the poor must be relieved—who denies it? Yet the house of God must not meanwhile be neglected, as we said in the notes to book 6 of Salvian, On the Government of God. See also Erasmus’s Antidote to Jerome’s Epitaph of Paula, and Launoi on chapter 6 of the book On the Care of the Church for the Wretched and Poor.]

They would do better if they distributed their possessions to the poor and [Note: [Col. 0183D] Guests. Hospitality was then greatly practiced in the Church. Book 1 of the Capitularies, chapter 75: “It also seems fitting and venerable to us that guests, pilgrims, and the poor should have regular and canonical hospitality in various places.” See the capitularies of Charles the Bald, title 6, chapter 40, and title 23, chapter 10; Lupus of Ferrières, letters 11, 42, 45, 55, and 71; Jonas of Orléans, book 2 of On Lay Instruction, chapter 29; and others. Hildebert moreover recounts the praises of hospitality in several letters. See Launoi, chapter 8 of the book just cited.] guests, and ran to the priests of the Church to be anointed with oil [Note: [Col. 0184D] With oil, namely the oil with which the lamps hung at the martyrs’ tombs were burning. Baronius, commenting on the year of Christ 55, notes from Augustine, Theodoret, and others that many miracles were customarily performed through such oil. I shall cite only Augustine, from chapter 8 of book 22 of The City of God: “Again, among us, the son of a certain Irenaeus, a collector, died of illness. While his lifeless body lay there and his funeral was being prepared amid the groans and lamentations of others, one of his friends, among the words of those offering consolation, suggested that the body should be anointed with the oil of that same martyr, Stephen. This was done, and he came back to life.”] according to the evangelical and apostolic command, together with fasting and prayers, to which almsgiving must be joined.

For if there were signs of healings that appeared to be granted by God through the merits of the saints, a crowd would rightly gather at those places; and if offerings were made there according to ecclesiastical custom and the arrangements of the Fathers, their use would indeed be fruitful because of the exercise of mercy.

But now, because these things serve the greed and avarice of certain people, God is not honored, [Note: [Col. 0185B] Nor are the poor helped. Agobard therefore held that offerings made at the memorials of martyrs were a matter belonging to the poor, and had not been devised to nourish the avarice or luxury of those in charge, or to make life more comfortable. Accordingly, such offerings were to be converted into relief for the poor; otherwise their use was extremely bad. But today, how many of those who sit at the altars of the saints are there who are not convinced that nothing from the offerings ought to fall to the poor, and who do not labor to preserve those gifts as though they were their household altars? Finally, there are many places, certainly renowned among natives and visitors, for which no more reliable or splendid revenue exists than that which comes from offerings. I praise the piety of these people. Yet it would be greatly desirable that those entrusted with collecting the offerings should have some charity toward the poor and not convert them only into the adornment of dead temples.]

nor are the poor helped.

If they conducted this matter according to God’s will, in accordance with what God has wished to make known to human beings throughout all the holy Scriptures, they would know how sublimely and wonderfully the Lord has deigned to show the path of this matter through the prophet Micah, who says:

“Shall I offer holocausts to God and year-old calves? Can the Lord be appeased by thousands of rams or by many thousands of fat goats? Shall I give my firstborn for my crime, the fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul?”

And although all these things are rejected, Scripture immediately adds in what way the Lord may be appeased, saying:

“I shall show you, O human being, what is good and what the Lord seeks from you: certainly, to do justice, to love mercy, and to walk attentively with your God.”

For just as it is blameworthy not to distribute what belongs to the poor to the poor, so it is fruitless if things that ought to be distributed to those who show the Church due reverence are given, amid the burning breath of greed, either to be hoarded avariciously or to be squandered abusively.

[Col. 0185B]

## To Matfredus, Nobleman of the Palace: A Lament Concerning Injustices

[Col. 0185C]

To the Most Distinguished and Illustrious Man, Matfredus

[Note: “Matfredus.” Even from the title of this letter alone it is clear that he was a man of great rank and authority at the palace of Louis the Pious. Louis himself calls him an illustrious man in a charter for the monastery of Grata in the diocese of Urgell, part of which we published the previous year in the notes to Letter 29 of Lupus of Ferrières. Thus the emperor says: “Count Matfredus, an illustrious man, having approached the serenity of our eminence, etc.” That he was Count of Orléans is established by Adrevald of Fleury, Book I, chapter 20, On the Miracles of Saint Benedict, and by the Life of Louis the Pious under the year 829. At that time, therefore, Jonas, bishop of Orléans, sent him three books On Lay Instruction, edited by Dom Luc d’Achery in the first volume of the Spicilegium; they had previously been published at Douai in 1645 from an old manuscript codex of Saint-Amand at Pabula, under the care of D. Ildephonse Goetghebuer, librarian of that monastery. Then, in the year 830—as Thegan relates in chapter 36—he conspired with Pippin, king of Aquitaine, and the palace nobles against Louis the Pious, whom they wished to expel from the kingdom. But Louis, the son of Louis, opposed this most wicked deed. Again, in the year 833, he defected with the other rebels to the party of Lothar, and, following him as he fled to Italy, died there in 835, as the author of the Life of Louis the Pious reports. See Sirmond’s notes on Theodulf, p. 301.]

Agobard to Matfredus, in Christ our Lord, the giver of life and our savior, wishes life and eternal salvation.

I beg your most excellent dignity patiently and kindly to deign to hear what your faithful little servant suggests, because, with God as my witness—he who searches hearts and kidneys—I say this with no other intention than concern for the advancement of your prosperity, both present and future. The almighty, eternal, and merciful God, before whom there is neither past nor future, but all the successive ages that revolve among mortals and temporal beings remain eternally present before him, chose you before the foundation of the world to be, in these dangerous times of ours,

[Note: [Col. 0186D] “Minister of the emperor and empire,” that is, minister of the palace and realm: minister of the palace because Matfredus did not leave the prince’s side and held the foremost place with him, sharing his secrets and counsels; minister of the empire or realm because, besides the county of Orléans, over which he was bound to keep special watch, the greater part of Louis’s responsibilities in governing the empire rested with Matfredus.]

the minister of the emperor and of the empire, and honored and enriched you above all others, not only outwardly but also inwardly—namely, with prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance, than which, according to the Scriptures, nothing is more useful in human life.

He established you at the side of the ruler of affairs,

[Note: “At the side of the ruler of affairs,” that is, Louis the Pious, emperor, from whose side Matfredus did not depart, as we have already said.]

so that you might be both his supporter in arranging equity and a participant in the reward of blessedness.

What, then, is most necessary for your most devoted purpose except that, with every effort and exertion of mind, you should watch most keenly over the ordering of affairs, so that iniquity may be crushed, fraud and deceit destroyed, wickedness dispersed, cruelty shattered, justice raised up, humility consoled,

[Col. 0187A]

faith strengthened, and the Church brought into serenity?

For your prudence should know that in these regions, in which we are neighbors, impiety has advanced to such a degree of security that scarcely anyone is found who loves justice and withdraws from injustice, except one whose mind divine inspiration touches and whose will it guides; so that wherever traces of goodness are seen, they are regarded as a free gift.

[Note: “The fear of kings has ceased.” Thus Lupus of Ferrières complains in Letter 126 that in his own age vices had burst forth into such freedom that, once impunity had been secured, no one feared God, king, or bishop, even in the most open matters. Our notes on that letter should certainly be consulted.]

The fear of kings and laws has ceased among many, to such an extent that most people now think that no one need be feared, reasoning within themselves and saying in their hearts: “If a complaint against me reaches the palace, the case will be referred to advocates.”

[Note: “To advocates,” that is, to those who report cases to the prince; consequently, the publication or concealment in silence of provincial offenses lies in their power.]

“There I shall find”

[Note: “Relatives,” that is, blood relations or connections by marriage. I had thought this belonged to the lowest Latin usage, and that formerly the word “parents” included only father and mother, as was stated in the notes to Book III of Salvian’s To the Catholic Church. But Sallust’s authority now leads me to think otherwise. In Sallust, Sulla addresses Bocchus, king of Mauretania, as follows: “Besides, we have relatives in abundance; of friends, neither we nor anyone at all has had enough.”]

“many relatives or friends, through whom I shall certainly ensure that I incur no royal displeasure, because a hidden gift will extinguish anger, and the one who ought to be feared, with others interposed, will not see our follies.”

By such opportunities, excellent sir, nearly the whole of that condition flourished in our wretched age which the blessed martyr Cyprian, in his own time, claimed that Christians had indeed escaped but lamented in a most mournful and sorrowful voice as raging more violently among pagans:

[Note: In the Letter to Donatus. As is his custom, Agobard greatly abridged the passage from that letter.]

“Among the laws themselves, wrongdoing is committed; amid legal rights, sin is practiced: innocence is preserved nowhere, not even where it is defended. Who, then, will help in such circumstances? An advocate? But he betrays and deceives. A judge? But he sells his judgment: the man who sits to punish crimes commits them; and, in order that the innocent defendant may perish, the guilty judge himself becomes guilty. There is no fear of the laws; no dread of the quaestor or the judge. What can be bought off is not feared to be committed. The laws have agreed with sins,

[Col. 0187C]

and”

[Note: “It began to be lawful.” Cyprian says elegantly in the same letter: “The world is wet with mutual blood; when individuals commit murder, it is a crime, but when it is done publicly, it is called valor.” Thus in the Pseudo-Plautine Querolus it is said that whatever is common—that is, whatever is generally done—is lawful: “Lar. What shall we say about falsehood? Querolus. Well, who tells the truth? That is common; go away. Lar. Is it therefore not a crime? What about adultery? Quer. Indeed, even that is not a crime. Lar. When did it begin to be lawful? Quer. Do you ask me, as though you did not know? It is something that can neither be permitted nor prohibited.”]

“what is public began to be lawful. What sense of shame, what integrity, can exist there, where those who condemn the wicked are absent, and only those appear for you to condemn?”

And something I cannot say without danger: many such people think that you are a wall between themselves and the emperor, by which they may be defended

[Col. 0188A]

from correction. Rather, most excellent of men, strive to be a wall that increases blessings: one that assaults the harmful, protects the innocent, agrees with God, differs from the enemy, and amasses a heavenly reward.

Although the intention of our mind is already sufficiently clear from the foregoing words, so that you may know without any doubt that I am not lamenting personal grievances, let your prudent kindness understand that I could not be saying these things against

[Note: “Our count Bertmund,” prefect of the province of Lyon, as Nithard calls him in Book I.]

our count Bertmund, since he has organized his county quite well with regard to justice; for he has appointed someone of such character to act on his behalf in these matters,

[Note: “Such a man,” that is, a viscount. It is therefore clear that in those times the institution of viscounts lay within the discretion of counts.]

who performs the task energetically not merely out of love and fear of his superior,

[Note: “His superior,” that is, his lord, the count of Lyon.]

but also—which is more exalted and praiseworthy—out of love of God and love of equity and justice itself, so that it seems to us that nowhere in these regions is the work done with greater diligence and attention.

But we say all these things wholly because of the faith that, under God, we owe also to the emperor our lord, and for the sake of attaining your eternal blessedness and the happiness of your present life. For, as you yourself do not doubt, the great familiarity that God has granted you with the lord emperor will be reckoned by the almighty Lord as a great spiritual talent entrusted to you. We desire that you expend it so energetically that you may deservedly hear the Lord say at his judgment: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things,” and so forth. May that harsh and irrevocable reproach be turned away from you which will fall upon the negligent, when the Lord says: “You wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I did not sow and gather where I did not scatter,” and so forth.

Nor should I name specifically the persons who greatly need correction, lest I seem to be an accuser, since that

[Note: “Is not my office,” namely, accusation. Bishops ought not to be accusers. Arcadius and Honorius, emperors, to Theodorus, prefect of the praetorium: “Let the governor of the province know that injury to priests, the ministers of the Catholic Church, and the place itself and divine worship must be punished, once the guilty have been convicted or confessed, by a capital sentence. Nor should he wait for the bishop to demand vengeance for an injury to himself, since holiness has been left solely the glory of forgiving.” This law appears in the Theodosian Code I.31, On Bishops, and was later incorporated into Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 304. Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, writes in Letter 42: “I am indeed distressed and deeply grieved that I am compelled to write against a man whose offenses, because of the dignity of his priesthood, ought properly to have been concealed. Yet I write in order to vindicate the poor whom he has oppressed.”]

is not my office; rather, I desire you to be as concerned as a most devoted minister of God and a fitting helper of a good emperor, so that, found worthy and faithful by both Lords, you may deservedly receive recompense from both.

[Col. 0189A]

LETTER TO THE CLERICS AND MONKS OF LYON, ON THE FORM OF ECCLESIASTICAL GOVERNMENT

I. Because I have learned that various rumors and suspicions exist among certain people, I have written what follows, so that you may deign to learn what I think should be observed in the exercise of ecclesiastical government, and so that the murmuring of the few may cease once my intention has been disclosed to all.

[Col. 0189B]

[Note: [Col. 0189D] “There is one bridegroom,” that is, Christ, the true and sole bridegroom of the holy Church. See above in the notes to the letter to Nibridius.]

There is one bridegroom who has a bride. He is to be loved for his own sake, not for anything else, since he himself is peace, truth, justice, sanctification, redemption, every good thing, and without him there is no good. He came from heaven and is above all; those whom he rescues from earth he raises to heaven. The friends of the bridegroom are those who, seeing and hearing one another, build one another up in love and worship of the bridegroom; the children of the bridegroom are both those who build and those who are built up.

There is one Lamb who has a bride, of whom it is said to the apostle John: “Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.” And there was shown to him the holy city Jerusalem descending from heaven from God, possessing the glory of God.

II. Concerning this bride and city it is sung in heaven: “Alleluia, for the Lord our almighty God has reigned.

[Col. 0189C]

Let us rejoice and exult, and let us give him glory, because the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself; and it has been granted to her to clothe herself in linen.”

Concerning this wife and city the evangelist John says that she is also the tabernacle of God. For he says: “And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying: Behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and he himself, their God, will be with them as their God; and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death shall be no more, nor shall there be mourning, crying, or pain any longer.”

From this city and virgin wife the Lamb of God, the God-Lamb, the almighty Lamb, the Lamb of the Almighty, begets the lambs

[Col. 0189D]

and sheep whom he commends to the blessed apostle Peter,

[Note: “Whom he commends to the blessed Peter,” that is, to bishops, as the ancient writers explain. See the notes to Letter 84 of Lupus of Ferrières.]

saying: “Feed my lambs.” And again: “Feed my sheep.”

This bridegroom and almighty Lamb says to his bride and wife: “Your hair is like flocks of goats that have come up from Mount Gilead. Your teeth are like a flock of sheep that have come up from the washing, all bearing twins, and none is barren among them.” And again: “Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, feeding among the lilies.”

This woman is both wife and daughter of her husband, the Lamb and prince, to whom he himself says: “How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of a prince!”

III. He himself is the prince, the father of his bride, and her brother. For he says to this wife and sister of his: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck. How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride!”

Nor is it surprising if a wife is a sister, since her breasts and bosom are also a tower, and she herself is a wall. For the father and bridegroom speaks of her thus: “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed? If she is a wall, let us build silver battlements upon her; if she is a door, let us panel her with cedar boards.”

And she replied: “I am a wall, and my breasts are towers, from the time when I became in his sight as one finding peace.”

Why should it be surprising that she is a wall and a city, when she is also a vineyard that has a husband? “A vineyard,” he says, “belonged to the Peaceful One; in it she has peoples. He entrusted it to guardians; a man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.” Concerning it the husband and father himself immediately adds: “My vineyard is before me.”

This same vineyard is also a virgin and a wife, of whom it is sung in the nuptial song to the king and bridegroom: “The wife stood at your right hand, in a golden diadem.”

And the bridegroom and father himself says to that wife: “Hear, daughter, and see.” The singer of this song says to her: “And, daughter of the most mighty, the rich peoples will entreat your face with gifts.”

This is according to the Hebrew text. The older translation, however, in order to show the same woman as queen and daughter of the king, says to the king: “The queen stood at your right hand.” And shortly afterward: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within.”

This queen is not only a vineyard, but also a garden and a spring: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed spring.”

She is also called a woman, as it is written: “Who will find a strong woman?” And afterward: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land.”

In her person Paul also writes to certain believers: “For I have betrothed you to one man, to present a chaste virgin to Christ.”

To her the Lord Christ himself speaks: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.”

And she says of him: “Let my beloved come into his garden and eat the fruit of his trees.”

IV. This bride is queen, wife, and servant. But this is not surprising. What is surprising, and full of every mercy, is that her husband and lord is also her lady, as the Psalmist sings: “As the eyes of a servant girl look to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes look to the Lord our God.”

She is also called a woman who has ten drachmas and, after losing one, lights a lamp, sweeps the house, searches, and finds it.

She is also called a mother, as he himself speaks through Isaiah, saying: “As one whom a mother comforts, so I will comfort you.”

For truly she is both mother and mistress: virtue and wisdom, strength and glory, resurrection and life, the way and truth, illumination and salvation, and other things of this kind.

V. It is no less remarkable that a servant and friend can also be the mother of her lord, in the manner in which the Lord says: “For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.”

The Apostle says the same of himself: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.”

VI. These various names of the bridegroom and bride, Christ and the Church, are not taken from particular historical events—such as when Scripture speaks of Sarah, Rebecca, and Rachel, in whom the union of Christ and the Church was prefigured—nor from that kind of expression in which, through a meaningful foreshadowing, they are applied to perceptible realities—such as “the mountain of the house of the Lord,” where the mountain signifies the Lord and the house the Church—and many similar examples.

Rather, they are taken from those passages where Scripture, within an orderly account of events, proceeds in this way, but simply indicates Christ and the Church by various such names, and where no one is so foolish as to think that anything other than Christ and the Church should be sought.

VII. The wondrous kindness of the Creator is displayed when the body clings to the head with such unity,

[Note: “The body to the head,” that is, Christ to the Church. Christ is the head of the Church. Bishops, however, are members of the body of Christ, which is the Church. Thus Pope Gregory I writes to Januarius, archbishop of Cagliari, Book I, Letter 60: “If our Lord himself, according to the testimony of Holy Scripture, declares himself the husband of widows and the father of orphans, then we, too, as members of his body, ought with the greatest devotion of mind to direct ourselves toward imitating the head.” See the same Gregory, Book II, Letter 37, and Book VII, Letter 110.]

and the head presides over the body, as the Prophet sings: “He clothed me with garments of salvation and surrounded me with the robe of justice, as a bridegroom adorned with a crown and as a bride adorned with her jewels.”

And shortly afterward: “For the young man will dwell with the virgin,

[Col. 0192A]

and your children will dwell in you. And as a bridegroom rejoices over a bride, so your God will rejoice over you.”

The Apostle plainly demonstrates this, saying: “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, slaves or free, and we were all given to drink of one Spirit.”

For it is the Spirit of Christ that creates this unity.

VIII. These are the things that provide the pious and faithful soul with an ineffably delightful diversion, and with such a diversion as cannot exist in the present life from contemplation of created things; indeed, to speak confidently, no similar diversion can be found in any of God’s visible or invisible works.

Concerning this diversion the Lord commands through the Prophet: “Speak to the heart of Israel and divert her.”

Concerning it also the man with whom God is present, in the vision by which his mother instructed him, commands in mystical speech: “Give strong drink to those who are grieving, and wine to those who are bitter in spirit. Let them drink and forget their poverty, and remember their sorrow no more.”

Concerning this the Psalmist also, after calling blessed the one who did not look upon vanity and false insanities—or, as it is read in Hebrew, upon the proud spectacles and displays of falsehood, in which lie the diversions of carnal minds—adds: “You have done many wonderful things, O Lord my God, and in your thoughts there is none like you.”

IX. Therefore, whoever has undertaken the office of preaching and the place of governance,

[Note: “Has undertaken the office of preaching and the place of governance.” Let bishops listen. Agobard says that anyone who has undertaken the office of preaching and the place of governance, yet neglects it in these highest matters and devotes himself to hunting, bird-catching, fishing, and other worldly pleasures, is not a bishop but a destroyer of God’s work and therefore an assistant of Antichrist. Arnulf, bishop of Orléans, did not differ greatly from Agobard’s judgment when he spoke these words against the Roman bishop at the synod of Reims against Arnulf, chapter 28: “What, reverend fathers, do you think this man is who sits on a lofty throne, radiant in purple and gold? What, I ask, do you think he is? Surely, if he is deprived of charity and is puffed up and exalted by knowledge alone, he is Antichrist, sitting in the temple of God and displaying himself as though he were God.” It has always seemed foreign to priestly dignity to be occupied with secular business and worldly anxieties. The bishops assembled at the Synod of Paris in 829 likewise blamed this in themselves when they wrote to Louis the Pious: “The priests, partly through negligence, partly through ignorance, and partly through greed, have occupied themselves with secular business and worldly anxieties beyond what they ought.”]

and neglects in these supreme matters what is the supreme work of God’s mercy—the diversion of the friends of the faithful—and seeks consolation and diversion

[Note: “In riches.” He condemns riches in a bishop, since the bishop occupies the place in the Church of the poor Christ. But, I think, he means that the bishop is to be blamed when he uses riches badly, namely, for luxury, lust, greed, and other vices of wicked minds. For the one who feeds the poor, builds churches, and sends people to instruct the nations in the faith will never be rich enough, even if he possesses immense treasures.]

in riches, in

[Note: “In metallic ornaments.” Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, gravely reproaches the same thing in wicked bishops when writing to Henry, archbishop of Sens: “The naked cry out, the hungry cry out, they complain and say: Tell us, pontiffs, what does gold do on a bridle? Does gold drive away cold or hunger from a bridle? The beasts walk laden with gems, while you do not care about our bare legs in little shoes. Rings, chains, bells, and certain studded straps, and many such things, as splendid in color as they are precious in weight, hang from the necks of mules; yet you do not show pity by placing even half-belts upon the sides of your brothers.” Nor does Peter of Clairvaux differ from his teacher and father in a letter that he wrote under the name of Jesus Christ to Pope Innocent VI and the Roman Curia in 1353. In chapter 30 he says: “We exhort you not to be excessively concerned to make yourselves conspicuous by your riding; let there not run about you ranks of neighing, champing horses; let bridles not be elaborately dyed with gold, nor reins made of silken threads; let spurs not gleam with silver; let saddles not be covered with scarlet or conspicuous purple; let precious hanging clasps not fasten belts with nails glittering in gold; let the ornament of those same straps, fragrant with purple dye, not give off its scent; let the coverings of saddles not be studded with knobs of ivory, refined gold, silver, or any other precious metal; let shining breastplates not be covered with purple; do not carry feverish golden bridles; let proud steeds not be burdened with radiant gems, and so forth.” From our very old manuscript codex, from which another fragment was published the previous year in the notes to Lupus of Ferrières, p. 478.]

metallic ornaments,

[Col. 0193A]

in hunting,

[Note: “In hunting.” Bishops were forbidden to keep dogs or practice hunting. On this subject canon 55 of the Synod of Agde is especially famous: “Bishops, priests, and deacons may not keep dogs for hunting or hawks. If any such person is discovered engaging in this pleasure, if he is a bishop, let him abstain from communion for three months; a priest shall abstain for two months; a deacon shall cease from every office or communion.” See also canon 4 of the Council of Epaon and canon 13 of the Second Council of Mâcon. Prince Carloman, at the synod attended by the martyr Boniface, said: “We have also forbidden all servants of God those hunts and woodland wanderings with dogs, and likewise the keeping of hawks and falcons.” Nicholas I also severely reproves hunting in a bishop, in Gratian, Distinction 34, chapter “Quorumdam.” Likewise Nicholas II, in the Decrees, chapter 6: “Let bishops and clerics carry no weapons, and let them devote themselves neither to hunting nor to bird-catching.” I would therefore gladly recall those who delight in hunting to what Prosper says to all Christians in the peroration of his book On the Glory and Kingdom of the Saints: “If you have a desire to hunt,” he says, “you have the highest mountains, through which the sayings of the apostles and prophets run like swift deer. You also have in the fields the rock, a refuge for hedgehogs and hares, which the Lord Christ hunts through his dogs in simplicity of heart, so that they may be free from the thorns of sins.” See Jonas of Orléans, Book II, On Lay Instruction, chapter 23.]

in hunting, bird-catching, and fishing, and, what is worse, in

[Note: “In banquets.” It is remarkable how concerned the ancients were about this, never missing an opportunity to admonish bishops to abstain from banquets and drunkenness, in accordance with Paul’s command that a bishop must not be a drunkard. Jerome’s notable passage from his Commentary on the Prophet Micah is quoted by Gratian, Distinction 35, chapter 4: “The leaders of the churches who abound in delicacies and believe that they preserve chastity amid feasts and revelries are described by the prophetic word as destined to be cast out of spacious houses and lavish banquets, and of meals procured with much labor, and cast out because of their wicked thoughts and deeds. And if you wish to know where they are to be cast out, read the Gospel: into the outer darkness, namely, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Is it not confusion and disgrace to preach Jesus crucified, the teacher of the poor and the hungry, with stuffed bodies, and to proclaim the teaching of fasting with flushed cheeks and protruding jaws?” The great Gregory likewise sharply rebukes Natalis, bishop of Salona, in Book II, Letter 14, because, having abandoned pastoral care, he occupied himself solely with banquets. Therefore he later admonished the same Natalis—who had turned Gregory’s rebuke into a joke, citing Abraham and Isaac as examples, one of whom had received angels at a banquet and the other, after being satisfied, had given his son a blessing—to abstain from banquets, in an elegant letter written to him, which is Letter 37 of the same book. It is clear that those banquets were not especially Christian, since, besides drunkenness and gluttony, the participants also refrained neither from defaming Christians nor from mocking anyone who reproved them. Episcopal banquets ought to be serious.]

banquets, drunkenness, and musical performances, as the Lord condemns through the Prophet, saying: “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that they may burn with wine. Harp, lyre, tambourine, flute, and wine are in your banquets; but you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands.”

Such a person is not a helper of God, as Paul says: “For we are God’s helpers. You are God’s agriculture; you are God’s building.”

Rather, he is a destroyer of God’s work and therefore an assistant of Antichrist;

[Col. 0194A]

and although in human eyes he may appear to be a priest,

[Note: “Yet in the eyes of God he is not.” He therefore says that a man called to the episcopate, if he indulges in worldly pleasures, is not a priest in God’s eyes, even though he bears the appearance of a bishop before human beings and thus seems to be a bishop. Thus Saint Ambrose, in chapter 3 of On the Dignity of the Priesthood, speaking of a bad bishop, says: “Such a bishop declares to the people: Peace be with you. To carnal eyes he appears to be a great bishop, but to divine scrutiny he is seen to be a great leper.” Likewise Marcellinus and Faustinus, in the Book of Petitions, p. 46, say that certain bishops subscribed to the treachery of the Arians “so that they might appear to retain the episcopal name among human beings, which they certainly no longer possessed before God after their impious subscriptions.” Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, in chapter 1 of Against the Sermon of Fastidiosus, likewise says that a man, although he had received the honor of the presbyterate in the sight of human beings, did not possess it before the Lord. The Albigensian heretics held the same view; Roger of Hoveden reports that they said “that bishops and priests should be ordained in the Church, and that if such persons were not ordained as the command required, they were not bishops or priests but ravening wolves, hypocrites, and deceivers.” Yet the most learned men have rightly observed that the constant judgment of the Catholic Church, descending from apostolic teaching and tradition, is that even an evil man, canonically ordained, is truly a priest and helper of God. For if this rule were not certain, terrible confusion would have disturbed the Church even in the beginnings of Christianity. Judas was evil, yet he was an apostle of Christ. Nor can anyone deny that many evil bishops existed at various times thereafter. Finally, Christ says that the scribes and Pharisees sat upon Moses’ seat. Thus Agobard seems to have written so forcefully in order to admonish bishops of their duty and to make them understand how displeasing an evil bishop’s life is to God.]

yet in the eyes of God he is not; because, when the Lord comes for judgment, he will be separated, and his portion will be placed with the unbelievers. Concerning such people it is written: “I saw the wicked buried: they were even in the holy place while they were still alive, and they were praised in the city as though for righteous deeds.”

Therefore none of these should be a leader of God’s people, lest, while seeking the heavenly kingdoms, he plunge them into the pit where he himself has been plunged by God’s judgment, as the Lord demonstrates to blessed Job, saying: “Do you have an arm like God?” And after some intervening words: “Hide them,” he says—that is, the proud and wicked—“together in the dust, and plunge their faces into the pit.”

X. There are others who, like these, do not appear impious to human beings, but through simulated righteousness become, in human eyes, whitewashed tombs; in God’s eyes, that is, inwardly, they are full of the bones of the dead and every impurity.

The blessed apostle Paul says: “For we are not like the many, adulterating the word of God, but in sincerity, as from God, before God, in Christ we speak.”

And again: “Having this ministry, according as we have received mercy, we do not fail; rather, we renounce the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness nor adulterating the word of God, but by the manifestation of truth.”

For just as an adulterer does not seek the fruit of offspring, but only seeks to satisfy his own will and fulfill his lust, so everyone who has undertaken the ministry of the word, if he does not sincerely seek the salvation of his hearers and the edification of the Church, but speaks the word of God for the sake of something else that is less important than the salvation of his hearers, in order to obey his own will—in short, he is an adulterer.

### XI

Therefore it is not only heretics who adulterate the word of God by mixing in their own deceits. So too do all who hasten through the sacred ministry to attain temporal honors and riches; and also those who cannot be elevated to honors and riches, but desire to obtain their daily food or covering from the sacred ministry—for they do not receive support in order to preach, but preach in order to receive it.

[Note: [Col. 0195C] They preach in order to receive. For there were then, as Agobard rightly condemns, certain men who preached the word of God for the sake of profit, being less concerned with the care of souls than with collecting money. Agobard appears to have taken this entirely from Saint Pope Gregory, whose words are these, from Book XIX on Job, chapter 11: “The feet are washed with butter when the stipends owed by their hearers are bestowed upon holy preachers; and those whom the labor imposed by preaching fatigues are refreshed by the richness of good works supplied by their disciples—not because they preach in order to be fed, but because they are fed in order to preach, that is, in order that they may continue preaching; not so that the activity of preaching may be diverted toward the intention of obtaining food, but so that the means of support may serve the usefulness of preaching. Hence good preachers do not preach for the sake of food, but receive food for the sake of preaching.” Nor would I say that preachers should receive nothing from their hearers. For “the laborer is worthy of his wages,” and it is just that those who sow spiritual things for us should reap our material things, as the Apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians. Gregory himself cited this passage in Homily 17 on the Gospels, to show that it is right for the Christian people to supply preachers with the necessities of support. For this, as I have said, is just and entirely equitable. But who could tolerate certain preachers who leave nothing undone in order to occupy the greater sees, from which a larger salary proceeds—as though the word of God were not effective except in proportion to the price placed upon it?] They do not speak with sincerity, as from God and before God; rather, they walk in cunning and do not renounce the hidden things of shame, but embrace them. They are adulterers.
