Whoever, therefore, is set over others—whether cleric or monk—if he appears so kind, gentle, and affable that he turns the hearts of his subjects toward love of himself and [Note: [Col. 0196D] Toward his own praise. He censures another equally detestable class of preachers: those whose sole concern is to appear to preach elegantly. There are far too many of this sort; would that there were none! He then warns that this must be avoided. Saint Gregory states the matter splendidly in the homily cited shortly before: “Whoever preaches,” he says, “in order to receive here the reward either of praise or of payment unquestionably deprives himself of the eternal reward.” See the same Gregory again, Homily 21 on Ezekiel.] his own praise, he is an adulterer and ought never to undertake the governance of souls.

But whoever is so prudent, gentle, and gracious that those who see and hear him are turned and kindled toward love and praise of the Bridegroom is the Bridegroom’s friend. He seeks the bride’s chastity and rightly assumes the governance of souls.

Every cleric or monk who has been given even the smallest measure of the word of wisdom or the word of knowledge, and who, while speaking, desires to turn and inflame his hearers toward love and praise of himself, preaches himself, not the Bridegroom. For this reason he must be expelled from the inner bridal chamber, because he is an adulterer. He presides outside, in the courtyard, not at the bride’s command but by permission of her patience; for whether the Bridegroom is proclaimed by occasion or in truth, there is reason for rejoicing. A faithful soul, indeed, is kindled toward love of the Bridegroom by hearing his praises from anyone whatsoever, not toward love of the person who praises negligently. It loves the diligent praiser as a neighbor, not as the Bridegroom; it loves him in the Bridegroom, not in place of the Bridegroom.

Walking in the undefiled way, [Col. 0196B] this man ministers to the Lord, not to himself, and may be placed over others. But the one who does not walk and instead lies inert in sloth, and who in this manner ministers to himself rather than to the Lord, ought not to be placed over others.

Whoever assigns the guardians of observances according to his own desire and not for the benefit of those in his household administers to himself, not to the Lord. He is not the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord should set over his household.

The labor of fools will afflict those who do not know how to travel to the Bridegroom’s city; therefore they ought not to be made leaders of others. The labor of the wise heals them. For they are led by the Bridegroom onto the right path, so that they may go to the city of habitation. Such men should be made leaders of those who have here no abiding city but seek the one that is to come, among the flock that ascends from the washing.

The fruitful are to be loved, and the barren endured; the healthy are to be guarded, and the sick healed. For the Bridegroom came from heaven to seek what had perished, to bring back what had been cast away, to bind up what was broken, to strengthen what was weak, and to guard what was fat and strong.

### XII

These things are to be observed in the sheep under one’s care. But the condition of prelates and shepherds is different. For just as blessed is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord has appointed over his household, to give them food at the proper time, who imitates the Shepherd [Note: [Col. 0196D] The Shepherd of shepherds, that is, Christ. Prosper, Peter Chrysologus, Julianus Pomerius, Ruricius of Limoges, Gregory the Great, Hincmar, and others also call him by this name. In the same sense he is elsewhere called the prince of shepherds, priest of priests, pontiff of pontiffs, and bishop of bishops. In later centuries the Roman bishop, too, was called “bishop of bishops.” This should be understood in the following way: since he is the head of all the Lord’s priests and the principal bishop of the whole world, by the privilege of his see he is understood to have been appointed over the other bishops of the world; consequently, in a certain sense, he becomes bishop of bishops, especially since the care and solicitude of the universal Church belong to him. Nevertheless, one must not suppose that this title was anciently bestowed upon the Roman bishop, although some think they can infer this from Tertullian’s book On Modesty and from Cyprian’s preface to the Council of Carthage. For, if I understand these matters correctly, Tertullian here attacks the Roman pontiff with satirical wit; certainly he does not flatter him. And it is clear that they are mistaken about Cyprian’s meaning. Cyprian does not say that the presumption of the Roman bishop, who called himself “bishop of bishops,” should be removed. Rather, he says: “For none of us has appointed himself bishop of bishops”—that is: I do not think that any of the bishops who are present here would go so far in presumption as to exalt himself above all his colleagues and insist that his own single opinion, as tyrants are accustomed to do, ought to prevail against the opinion of the majority, especially whenever the matter under discussion concerns the faith. I believe this to be the genuine meaning of Cyprian’s words. This way of speaking, moreover, was taken from the discipline of rhetoric. Otherwise, if those who are above bishops ought to be called bishops of bishops, there is no doubt that the leading bishop of Africa, namely the bishop of Carthage, ought to have been called bishop of bishops. For if this expression had any authority, it would greatly diminish the dignity of the Roman bishop, since certain bishops would appear to equal him. Sidonius, in Book VI, Letter 1, calls Lupus, bishop of Troyes, “father of fathers” and “bishop of bishops.” Ennodius, in Book I, Poem 15, calls Ambrose, bishop of Milan, “shepherd of prelates.” Yet no one would say that the Roman pontiffs who flourished in the age of Lupus and Ambrose were subject to Lupus or Ambrose. Indeed, Charlemagne himself is called “bishop of bishops” by the monk of Saint Gall in Book I, chapter 27, of his work On the Ecclesiastical Care of that same Charles. Edgar, king of England, who was alive in the year 966, is called “shepherd of shepherds” by the provincial synod of England held under Dunstan. Likewise, Eusebius, in Book I, chapter 44, of The Life of Constantine, calls Constantine “the common bishop of all,” and calls King Clovis “the prelate of the peoples and regions.” Remigius, bishop of Reims, calls him so, although it has never occurred to anyone until now to regard these men as bishops. I have thought it worthwhile to note this so that it might be clear to everyone how Tertullian’s and Cyprian’s words are to be understood. For “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.”] of shepherds in the administration of pasture, so, conversely, with regard to shepherds who feed themselves—who do not strengthen what is weak, heal what is sick, bind up what is broken, bring back what has been cast away, or seek what has perished—the Shepherd of shepherds should rescue his sheep from their mouth and feed them in the richest pastures, including those who in this present life continually endure a wicked shepherd for their own sake.

Indeed, the devout sheep always seeks a good shepherd. But if such a shepherd is lacking in this mortal life, the one who laid down his life for his sheep is not lacking. Therefore, where correction is impossible, the sheep must tolerate the shepherd as a hireling sitting in Moses’ seat. For the devout Bridegroom, the true Shepherd, commanded that the sheep do what such men say, but not do what they do.

### XIII

I have said these things at the end so that no one may think that I regard the faithful sheep who prudently tolerates a wicked shepherd as lost. Above all, I urge that every shepherd nourish, instruct, and correct those subject to him—not for himself but for the Lord—in the discipline and fear of the Lord, just as the chief Shepherd commanded blessed Peter, saying: “Feed my lambs,” he says, “not yours”; and therefore, “for me, not for you.”

This is certain evidence that you truly love me: if you diligently feed my lambs, for which you will receive the crown of righteousness.

So too a certain ancient shepherd expressed the care of vigilant solicitude in mystical words, saying: “It is not yet time for the sheep to be shut into the folds. First give the sheep drink,” and thus he leads them back to pasture.

When this is not done, there comes what the prophet laments, saying: “Therefore my people have been led away captive, because they had no knowledge; and their nobles have perished from hunger, and their multitude has dried up from thirst.” And another says: “The little ones asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them.”

### XIV

These words, though not unlearned, have nevertheless been arranged unskillfully by an unlearned man, and are necessary for everyone, from him who sits on the throne [Col. 0198C]—that is, the bishop. For he sits on a throne in the church, that is, in a higher seat. Sulpicius Severus also calls that episcopal chair a throne, in the first chapter of the second Dialogue, exaggerating the matter in order to provoke envy: “Recently,” he says, “I saw, not without embarrassment, a certain man seated on a lofty throne, as though on a royal tribunal, in an elevated seat.” I shall add a passage from the distinguished Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, who, explaining canon 53 of the African Collection, says: “It signifies the worldly arrogance and swelling pride of certain bishops who exercised domination over the clergy; and, raised onto a chair as though it were some royal throne and a fortress of empire, they claimed tyrannical domination for themselves.” Almost immediately he continues: “Certainly the episcopal chair was elevated and set, as it were, at the summit, so that the bishops could admonish the faithful from a higher place.” This seems to have been taken from Augustine, whose words in his exposition of Psalm 126 are: “For this reason a higher place has been assigned to bishops, so that they may oversee and, as it were, guard the people.” Shortly afterward: “Just as a higher place is made for the vinedresser to guard the vineyard, so a higher place has been made for bishops.” See Henri Valois’s annotations on Eusebius’s Ecclesiastical History, Book VII, chapter 30.] down to him [Col. 0198D] who labors at the mill—that is, down to shepherds and superiors of the lower orders, so that no one might think that these words are spoken only to bishops. Shortly afterward he adds that these writings were composed not only for bishops, but also for abbots, superiors, and priests, whom, he says, are to be understood under the names “shepherds” and “rulers.” Thus he also excludes deacons from the office of shepherd. Yet Cyprian and other ancients recognized priesthood in them as well.] who labors at the mill.

I am writing not so much to those to whom I owe nothing except charity, but to those who have been entrusted to us; nevertheless, by the names “shepherds” and “rulers” I understand abbots, superiors, and priests. I earnestly beg them to devote themselves wholeheartedly to the exhortation and supplication of the blessed Apostle Peter, who says:

“Therefore I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and also a sharer in the glory that is to be revealed: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion but willingly according to God; not for shameful gain but eagerly; not as domineering over those entrusted to you, but becoming examples to the flock from the heart. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.” Amen.

[Col. 0199A]

## Book Against the Superstition of Those Who Think That the Worshipful Service of Adoration Should Be Offered to the Paintings and Images of the Saints

[Note: [Col. 0199C] In Agobard’s age a most wicked superstition had gained strength: certain people thought that service or adoration should be offered to images of the saints in the same way as to the divine Trinity. This seemed so impious to the Gallican Church that the bishops assembled at the Council of Frankfurt condemned the Second Council of Nicaea, which appeared to have ordered that adoration of images, and Charlemagne himself is thought to have taken up his pen against it. Later, during the reign of Louis the Pious, son of Charles, the fervor of the bishops of Gaul on this subject again became conspicuous. Since they could not tolerate that adoration of images, they left nothing unattempted in order to recall the minds of the faithful from this error. Indeed, while they were striving for the truth, they seemed to insult the images, so that one might think they had asserted that no worship at all was owed to them; nevertheless, they retained them so that, through looking at them, the faithful might be stirred to imitate holy men. Agobard was one of many who devoted himself to this work, but he did so with such vehemence that some consequently thought this book insufficiently Catholic. Yet certain devout and learned men, after carefully examining the matter, judged that it contained nothing that openly violated the faith of the Church, and accordingly deprived the Spanish Censure and Cardinal Baronius of authority against Agobard. I would believe that Agobard wrote what everyone in Gaul at that time thought, as Sirmond also observed. Certainly it is not my task to pronounce upon these difficult questions. Nevertheless, I cannot remain silent about the fact that I greatly approve the decrees of the Council of Cambrai, held in 1565 under Maximilian de Berghes, archbishop of Cambrai, which ruled as follows concerning images:

“Let no images be erected in churches except with the bishop’s consent and judgment. If any have been erected and display anything unbecoming or inconsistent with the prototype, order that they be removed or altered. Moreover, let the people be taught that no worship is owed to an image because of its material, its elegance, the price of its workmanship, or anything else belonging to the craft or substance of the image; rather, worship and honor are principally referred to the thing signified. Thus one must admonish the person praying or venerating to direct his mind to the thing signified, and not to the sign, which neither hears, sees, nor feels.”

See William Durand, Book II, On the Manner of Celebrating a General Council, chapter 57.] (G)*

[Col. 0199B]

The first commandment of the Decalogue is spoken by God:

“I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery. You shall have no foreign gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor the likeness of anything that is in heaven above or that moves in the waters beneath the earth. You shall not adore them or worship them.”

To these words blessed Augustine adds very briefly, saying (Homily on Exodus, chapter 1):

“In the first commandment, some likeness of God in human fabrications is forbidden—not because God has no image, but because no image of him ought to be worshiped except that which is also what he himself is, and not that image in place of him, but together with him.”

In saying this, blessed Augustine briefly teaches us how we ought to understand the other commandments of this kind. For since it is distinctly said that no likeness is to be made of anything in heaven or on earth, this is not understood as referring only to likenesses of foreign gods, but also to heavenly creatures and to whatever the human mind has been able to devise in honor of the Creator.

Therefore Moses also speaks openly to the people, saying:

“The Lord spoke to you from the midst of the fire. You heard the sound of his words, but you saw no form at all.” And shortly afterward:

“Therefore guard your souls carefully. You saw no likeness on the day when the Lord spoke to you at Horeb from the midst of the fire, lest, deceived, you make for yourselves a carved likeness or an image of male or female, the likeness of any beast that is on the earth, or of birds flying beneath heaven, or of reptiles that move upon the earth, or of fish that dwell in the waters beneath the earth; lest, raising your eyes to heaven, you see the sun and all the stars of heaven and, deceived by error, adore and worship them.”

In these words it must be especially noted that if the works of God’s hands are not to be adored and worshiped, even in honor of God, how much less are the works of human hands to be adored and worshiped, even in honor of those whose likenesses they are said to be.

### II. From Book X of Saint Augustine’s *City of God*: The Various Meanings of Worship

“We must consider and discuss, as much as God grants, how the immortals and blessed, established in heavenly seats, dominions, principalities, and powers—those whom these people call gods, and of whom they call some good demons and others angels like ourselves—are to be believed to wish religion and piety to be preserved by us. That is, to speak more plainly: do they wish us to perform sacred rites and sacrifices for them also, or only for their God, who is also ours, or to consecrate some of our possessions, or ourselves, through the rites of religion?

For this is the worship owed to divinity—or, if it must be expressed more precisely, to deity. Since I have no sufficiently suitable Latin word with which to signify it in a single term, whenever necessary I indicate what I mean with a Greek word. Our writers, wherever *latria* occurs in the sacred Scriptures, have translated it as ‘service.’ But the service owed to human beings, according to which the Apostle commands servants to be subject to their masters, is ordinarily called by another Greek name. According to the usage of those who composed the divine writings for us, *latria* either always, or so frequently that it is almost always so understood, means the service that pertains to the worship of God.

Accordingly, if worship is simply named, it does not appear to be owed to God alone. For we are also said to worship human beings whom we regularly visit either with honor in remembrance or by our presence. Not only are those things said to be worshiped to which we subject ourselves with religious humility; certain things that are subject to us are also said to be worshiped. From this word come the terms for farmers, tenants, and inhabitants. The gods themselves are called heavenly inhabitants for no other reason than that they inhabit heaven—not, of course, by venerating it, but by dwelling in it, as though they were certain tenants of heaven. They are not like those tenants who are bound, for cultivation, to their native soil under the dominion of its possessors, but like the great author of Latin eloquence says (*Virgil, Aeneid* I, 16):

> There was an ancient city, Tyrian settlers held it.

He called them settlers from inhabiting, not from agriculture. Hence cities founded by larger cities, as though by swarms of peoples, are also called colonies.

Yet, in a certain proper sense of this word, it is entirely true that worship is owed to God alone. But because worship is also spoken of with regard to other things, the worship owed to God cannot be expressed by a single Latin word. Even religion, although it seems more distinctly to signify not just any worship but the worship of God—for this reason our writers translated by that name what is called *thrēskeia* in Greek—is nevertheless not free from ambiguity when the question concerns the worship of the deity. In ordinary Latin usage, not only among the uneducated but also among the most learned, religion is said to be owed to human relationships, kinships, affinities, and every sort of connection; so we cannot confidently say that religion means nothing but the worship of God, since this word seems improperly to be removed from its meaning of observance toward human relationships.

Piety is also commonly understood properly as the worship of God, which the Greeks call *eusebeia*. Yet piety is also said to be shown dutifully toward parents. In popular usage, this word is also frequently used of works of mercy. I believe this happened because God chiefly commands these works and testifies that they please him either in place of sacrifices or before sacrifices. From this usage it has come about that God himself is called pious. The Greeks, however, do not use any expression of their language to say that God ‘practices *eusebeia*,’ although even their common people use *eusebeia* for mercy. Therefore, in certain passages of Scripture, wishing the distinction to be clearer, they preferred to say *theosebeia*, which is formed from the worship of God, rather than *eusebeia*, which derives from good worship.

We cannot express either of these in a single word. What is called *latreia* in Greek and translated into Latin as ‘service,’ but specifically the service by which we worship God; or what is called *thrēskeia* in Greek and *religio* in Latin, but specifically that which we practice toward God; or what they call *theosebeia*, which we cannot express in one word but may call the worship of God—we say that this is owed only to that God who is the true God and who makes his worshipers gods. Therefore, whoever are the immortal and blessed beings in heavenly dwellings, if they do not love us and do not wish us to be blessed, they certainly ought not to be worshiped. But if they love us and wish us to be blessed, then surely they wish this from the same source from which they themselves are blessed.”

In the same book, shortly afterward (chapter 4):

“To him we owe the service called *latria* in Greek, whether in the various sacraments or in ourselves. For together we are his temple, and each of us individually is a temple, because he deigns to inhabit both the harmony of all and each individual—not greater in all than in each, since he is neither enlarged by bulk nor diminished by division.

When our heart is raised upward toward him, it is his altar. Through his only-begotten Priest we appease him. We slaughter bloody victims for him when we contend for his truth even unto blood. We burn the sweetest incense for him when we blaze with pious and holy love in his sight. To him we vow and return his gifts in us, and ourselves as well. On the solemn festivals and appointed days of his benefits we dedicate a sacred commemoration to him, lest ungrateful forgetfulness creep in through the passage of time. We sacrifice to him the victim of humility and praise upon the altar of the heart, burning with the fire of charity.

In order to see him as he may be seen, and to cling to him, we are cleansed from every stain of sins and evil desires and consecrated in his name. For he himself is the fountain of our blessedness; he himself is the end of every desire. Choosing—or rather choosing again—him whom we had lost by neglect, we tend toward him in love, so that by reaching him we may rest. We are blessed because we are perfected in that end.”

### III. From Book IX of the Same Work of Saint Augustine, That No Other Mediator Is to Be Sought between God and Human Beings Except the One Who Is God and Man

“The multitude that is blessed becomes blessed through participation in the one God. Deprived of that participation, the miserable multitude of evil angels opposes it as an impediment rather than intervening as an aid to blessedness; even by its multitude it somehow makes such an uproar that it prevents access to that one source of blessedness. To lead us to it, we needed not many mediators but one, and that one precisely through whose participation we are blessed: the Word of God—not a thing made, but the one through whom all things were made.

Yet he is not mediator merely because he is the Word—for the Word, supremely immortal and supremely blessed, is far removed from miserable mortals—but mediator through the fact that he became human. By this very fact he shows that, for reaching that good which is not merely blessed but makes blessed, we ought not to seek other mediators through whom we might suppose that we must construct stages of approach. For the blessed and peaceful God, becoming a sharer in our humanity, provided a shortcut to participation in his divinity.

In freeing us from mortality and misery, he does not lead us to immortal and blessed angels so that through participation in them we too may be immortal and blessed, but to that Trinity through participation in which the angels also are blessed. Therefore, when in the form of a servant he wished to be lower than the angels in order to be mediator, in the form of God he remained above the angels: the same one who in the lower realm is the way of life, and in the higher realm is life itself.”

### IV. From Book X of the Same Work: Saint Augustine Clearly Teaches by the Example of the Lord Jesus Christ That Sacrifice Is to Be Offered to No Creature

“Those who think that these visible sacrifices are appropriate for other gods, but that invisible and greater sacrifices are appropriate for the supreme God as invisible—greater things for the greater, better things for the better, such as the services of a pure mind and good will—certainly do not understand that these are signs of those things, just as spoken words are signs of things.

Therefore, just as in praying and praising we direct meaningful words toward him to whom we offer in our hearts the realities signified by those words, so in offering sacrifice let us understand that a visible sacrifice must be offered to no one other than the one whose invisible sacrifice we ourselves ought to be in our hearts.

Then all the angels and higher powers, who are more powerful through goodness and piety, favor us, rejoice with us, and help us according to their ability toward this very end. But if we wish to offer these things to them, they do not gladly accept them; and when they are sent to human beings in such a way that their presence can be perceived, they expressly forbid it.

There are examples of this in the sacred writings. Some thought that the honor owed to God should be offered to angels, either by adoring them or by sacrificing to them; they were prevented from doing so by the angels’ admonition and commanded to offer it to the one to whom alone they knew it was lawful to offer it.

Holy men of God also imitated the holy angels. For when Paul and Barnabas performed a miracle of healing in Lycaonia, the Lycaonians thought them gods and wished to sacrifice victims to them. With humble piety they rejected this from themselves and announced to them the God in whom they should believe.

The deceitful spirits arrogantly demand this for themselves for no other reason than that they know it is owed to the true God. For, as Porphyry says, and as some suppose, they do not actually delight in the odors of corpses but in divine honors. They have a great abundance of odors everywhere, and if they wanted more, they could provide them for themselves.

Therefore the spirits that arrogate divinity to themselves are pleased not by the smoke of any body but by the mind of a suppliant whom they deceive and subject to themselves, exercising dominion over him and blocking the way to the true God, so that the human being may not be his sacrifice while sacrifice is offered to anyone other than him.

For this reason the true Mediator, insofar as, taking the form of a servant, he became mediator between God and human beings—the human being Christ Jesus—although in the form of God he receives sacrifice with the Father, with whom he is one God, nevertheless in the form of a servant preferred to be a sacrifice rather than to receive one, so that no one might on this account suppose that sacrifice should be offered to any creature.”

[Col. 0204A]

### V. Again from Book X of the Forementioned Work: No Creature That Worships God Wishes to Be Worshiped in Place of Him to Whom Itself Is Subject

“Therefore, whatever immortal power, endowed with however great a virtue, loves us as itself, wishes us to be subject to the one to whom it is itself blessedly subject, so that we may be blessed. If, then, it does not worship God, it is miserable because it is deprived of God.

It rather supports that divine judgment and favors the power of love in accordance with which it is written: ‘Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be destroyed, unless it be to the Lord alone.’

To say nothing for the moment of the other matters belonging to the religious service by which God is worshiped, there is certainly no human being who would dare say that sacrifice is owed to anyone except God. Many things belonging to divine worship have been appropriated and are offered as honors to human beings, whether through excessive humility or pernicious flattery. Nevertheless, those to whom these things are offered are regarded as human beings, and they are said to be objects of worship and veneration; if much more is added, they are also said to be objects of adoration.

But who has judged that sacrifice should be offered except to one whom he knew, thought, or imagined to be God?”

### VI. From Saint Augustine’s *On True Religion*: Among Whom Above All the True God Is to Be Sought

“Therefore,” he says, “we must first follow those who say that there is one supreme and only true God, and that he alone is to be worshiped. If the truth does not shine forth among them, only then should we depart.

For just as, in the very nature of things, the authority of one who brings everything back to one is greater, and in the human race no power belongs to a multitude except a consenting one, so in religion those who call us to the One ought to have the greater and more trustworthy authority.”

### VII. From Homily XXV of Saint Gregory the Pope on the Gospels: How God Is Also to Be Sought among the Saints

“Yet while we are seeking, the watchmen who guard the city find us, because the holy Fathers who guard the condition of the Church come to meet our good efforts, so that by word or writing they may teach us. When we pass beyond them a little, we find the one whom we love.

For our Redeemer, although in his humility he was human among human beings, was nevertheless, in his divinity, above human beings. Thus, when the watchmen are passed by, the Beloved is found: for when we see that the prophets and apostles are beneath him, we consider him who by nature is God to be above human beings.”

From these words of the Song of Songs (where, speaking in the person [Col. 0204D] of Holy Church, he says: “The watchmen who guard the city found me. Have you seen him whom my soul loves?”—“A little while after I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves”), having briefly noted the foregoing from that homily, let us now see what the same Father says of these words in Book XVIII of his Explanation of Job. He says therefore (chap. 33):

“When the Church was seeking her Redeemer, she did not wish to place her hope in those ancient preachers, as she says: ‘A little while after I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves.’ For she could not find him if she had not wished to pass beyond them.”

Blessed Augustine speaks in harmony with this interpretation in the first homily on the Gospel according to John, saying (Tractate I):

“John is one of those mountains [Col. 0205A] of which we sang a little earlier, saying: ‘I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me.’ Therefore, dearest brothers, if you wish to understand, lift your eyes to this mountain—that is, raise yourselves to the evangelist; raise yourselves to his meaning. But because these mountains receive peace, and no one can be in peace who places his hope in man, do not raise your eyes to the mountain in such a way that you think your hope ought to be placed in man. Rather, say: ‘I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me,’ so that you may immediately add: ‘My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.’

“Therefore let us lift our eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to us. Yet the mountains themselves are not those in which our hope ought to be placed. For they receive what they may minister to you. [Col. 0205B] From whom, then, do the mountains receive what they are to minister, when we lift our eyes to the Scriptures? From this: the Scriptures were ministered through human beings. We have lifted our eyes to the mountains, from which help will come. But because the very human beings who wrote the Scriptures did not shine from themselves—for he was their light who enlightens every human being coming into this world—and because that mountain was John the Baptist, who said, ‘I am not the Christ,’ lest anyone placing his hope in the mountain should fall away from him who illumines the mountains; and he himself, having confessed, said: ‘For from his fullness we have all received’—thus you ought to say: ‘I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me.’

“Do not attribute the help that comes to you to the mountains, but follow on and say: ‘My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and [Col. 0205C] earth.’ Therefore, brothers, I have given you this warning so that, when you have raised your heart to the Scriptures, while the Gospel was being proclaimed—‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word,’ and the rest of the passage that was read—you may understand that you have lifted your eyes to the mountains. Unless those words had been spoken, what would you have had from which even to form a thought? You would not have found it. Therefore help came to you from the mountains, so that you might at least hear these things. If you are not yet able to understand what you have heard, invoke help from the Lord, who made heaven and earth, because the mountains were able to speak in such a way that they themselves could not illumine: they too were illumined by hearing.

“From there the one who said these things received them—John, brothers, the one who reclined upon the breast of the Lord and drank from the breast of the Lord what he might offer us. But he offered words. [Col. 0205D] You must receive understanding from the place from which he too drank, the one who offered it to you.”

The same teacher speaks similarly here in the twelfth homily of the aforementioned work, when he was expounding the words of John the Baptist, who replied to his disciples:

“‘A human being cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven. You yourselves bear me witness that I said: “I am not the Christ.”’ It is as though he were saying: ‘Why are you deceiving yourselves? How did you yourselves put this question to me? What did you say to me? “Rabbi, the one who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore witness”’?

“You know, therefore, what witness I have just borne to him. Am I to say that he is not what I said he was? I, who received something from heaven so that I might be something? You want me to be nothing, so that I might speak against the truth. ‘A human being cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven. You yourselves bear me witness that I said: “I am not the Christ.”’ ‘You are not the Christ!’ ‘But what if I am greater than he, because you baptized him? I was sent. I am the herald; he is the judge.

“And hear testimony much stronger and much clearer. See what is happening among us. See what we ought to love. See that to love some human being above Christ is adultery. Why do I say this? Let us attend to John’s voice. One could have gone astray concerning him; he himself could have been thought to be what he was not. He rejected false honor from himself in order to hold fast to solid truth. See what he says of Christ and what he says of himself: ‘He who has the bride is the bridegroom.’ Be chaste; love the bridegroom.

“But what are you? What do you say to us? ‘He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice.’”

And a little later:

“See,” he says, “how he stands on solid ground: ‘I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal.’ You humble yourself well; rightly you stand, rightly you do not fall, rightly you hear, and you rejoice with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice.

“Thus also the Apostle, the friend of the bridegroom, is jealous, and he is jealous not for himself but for the bridegroom. Let him hear the voice of one jealous with the jealousy of God. He said, ‘I have been jealous for you,’ not with my jealousy, not for me, but with the jealousy of God. How so? For whom are you jealous, and for whom do you show jealousy? ‘For I betrothed you to one husband, to present a chaste virgin to Christ.’

“What, then, are you afraid of? Why are you jealous? ‘I am afraid,’ he says, ‘that just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the chastity that is in Christ.’

“The whole Church has been called a virgin. You see and rejoice that the members of the Church are diverse and endowed with diverse gifts. Some are married men, others married women; some are widowers and seek no further wives; others are widows and seek no further husbands; some preserve bodily integrity from their earliest age; others have vowed their virginity to God. The gifts are diverse, but all these together are one virgin.

“Where is this virginity? It is not in the body—for bodily virginity exists in only a few women. Although virginity can also be spoken of in men, it is the holiness of only a few. Bodily integrity too exists in the Church, and it is an honorable member. But there are other members in the body, and all preserve virginity in the mind.

“What is the virginity of the mind? Whole faith, firm hope, sincere charity. This is the virginity which the one who was jealous feared might be corrupted by the serpent, for just as a bodily member is violated in some particular place, so the seduction of the tongue violates the virginity of the heart.” [Col. 0206D]

## VIII

From Book IX of Saint Augustine’s *City of God* (chap. 23): Although holy angels and human beings are called gods, those same holy angels can in no way be called “gods of gods,” that is, gods of holy human beings. From this consideration it follows that, if holy angels cannot be called gods of human beings, human beings can much less be so called.

The same teacher says:

“Yet when we are asked whether human beings are called gods because there are gods in the people whom God addresses through angels or human beings, how much more worthy are the immortals of that name, since they enjoy that blessedness to which human beings desire to attain by worshipping God—what shall we answer? We must answer that it was not without reason that human beings were called gods more explicitly in the Holy Scriptures than those immortal and blessed beings who, we are promised, will be our equals in the resurrection; this was so lest unbelieving weakness, because of their excellence, dare to appoint one of them as our god. Such a thing is easily avoided in the case of a human being.

“And human beings ought more clearly to have been called gods in the people of God, so that they might become certain and confident that he is their God who is called God of gods. For although those immortal and blessed beings who are in heaven are called gods, they were not called gods of gods—that is, gods of the human beings established among the people of God—to whom it was said: ‘I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.’

“This is why the Apostle says: ‘Although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we are in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we are through him.’” [Col. 0207B]

## IX

These matters being so, there is a proper measure of divine, evangelical, and even human glory, as Bishop Alcimus Avitus of Vienne says in his *Dialogue*, where he speaks with King Gundobad:

“Yet in what you say—that by excluding the Father and the Son from equality with heavenly glory, as though they were an angelic creature, you bring against me a kind of envy on account of the honor unlawfully bestowed upon the heavenly powers, saying, ‘Then we ought also to render glory to angels, archangels, and whatever beings are in the heavens’—although this has little to do with the case, even at present I do not altogether reject it, as though we were afraid to render glory to a sublime and excellent creature.

“For there is a measure of divine glory, a measure of angelic glory, and also a measure of human glory, which we find in many places in the Scriptures attributed without the fault of flattery both to the merits of the saints and to the distinctions of kings. For what is the first glory among human beings? ‘This is the glory of all his saints.’ And in the Gospel the Lord says that even Solomon, in all his glory, was not clothed like the flower of the lily.” [Col. 0207C]

## X

Let us now hear blessed Jerome proclaiming similar things. For in the letter which he sent to the presbyter Riparius concerning the schism of Vigilantius, he says:

“We, however, worship and venerate not only the relics of martyrs—I do not say merely those—but not even the sun and moon, angels and archangels, seraphim and cherubim, or every name that is named in the present age and in the age to come, lest we serve the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. We honor the relics of the martyrs so that we may adore the one whose martyrs they are. We honor you so that the honor shown to servants may redound to the Lord, who says: ‘Whoever receives you receives me.’”

**[Note: [Col. 0207D] Concerning the Schism of Vigilantius. This man is famous for Jerome’s sharply pointed writings against him. It is certain that he was a very great heretic and deserved that Jerome should blaze against him. It is commonly thought that he was a Spaniard. But the most illustrious man, Petrus de Marca, Archbishop of Paris, proves that opinion false in his *Dissertation on the Homeland of Vigilantius*, which we shall one day publish. He proves that Vigilantius was an Aquitanian.]**

Blessed Augustine agrees with this in Book I [Col. 0208A] of *The City of God* (chap. 13), speaking as follows:

“The bodies of deceased righteous people are not to be despised and cast aside; the Holy Spirit used them as instruments and vessels for every good work. For if a father’s garment, ring, or anything of that kind is dearer to descendants in proportion as their affection for their parents is greater, then by no means should the bodies themselves be spurned, since we wear them much more familiarly and intimately than any clothing. For these bodies belong not to adornment or assistance applied from without, but to the very nature of the human being.

“Hence the funerals of the righteous of old were attended with dutiful care, their obsequies were celebrated, and burial was provided. While they were alive, they themselves entrusted to their children instructions concerning the burial or even transfer of their bodies. The Lord himself, who was to rise on the third day, praises and commends for proclamation the good work of the devout woman who poured expensive ointment over his limbs and did this for his burial. Those who carefully and honorably took his body down from the cross and arranged for its burial are also rightly remembered in the Gospel.

“Nevertheless, these authorities do not teach that any awareness exists in corpses; rather, they indicate that the bodies of the dead also belong to the providence of God, to whom even such duties of piety are pleasing, on account of establishing belief in the resurrection.” [Col. 0208B]

Augustine likewise says in Book VIII of the same work (chap. 27):

“Yet we do not establish temples, priesthoods, sacred rites, or sacrifices for martyrs, because it is not they but their God who is our God. We honor their memorials as those of holy human beings of God, who struggled for the truth even to the death of their bodies, so that true religion might become known after false and fabricated religions had been convicted. Even those who previously held such beliefs restrained them out of fear.

“But who has ever heard a priest standing at an altar—even one constructed for the honor and worship of God over the holy body of a martyr—say in his prayers: ‘I offer sacrifice to you, Peter, or Paul, or Cyprian’? Rather, the sacrifice is offered at their memorials to God, who made them both human beings and martyrs and joined them to his holy angels in heavenly honor. Thus, by that celebration, we give thanks to the true God for their victories, and, calling upon him for help, we exhort ourselves, through the renewal of their memory, to imitate such crowns and palms.

“Therefore, whatever religious observances are performed at the places of the martyrs are ornaments of their memorials, not sacred rites or sacrifices offered to the dead as though they were gods. Those who bring their meals there as well—for better Christians do not do this, and in many regions no such custom exists—intend, when they have set out the food and pray, then remove it to eat or distribute some of it to the needy, that it should be sanctified there through the merits of the martyrs in the name of the Lord of the martyrs.

“But the one who knows the one sacrifice of Christians, which is offered there also, knows that these are not sacrifices to the martyrs. We therefore honor our martyrs neither with divine honors nor with human insults, as the pagans honor their gods; we offer them no sacrifices, nor do we turn their reproaches into sacred rites for them.” [Col. 0209A]

He also says in the book he wrote on the work of the six days (*Questions on Genesis*, Book I, question 84) that Jacob, when he set up the stone which he had placed under his head and made it into a monument and poured oil over it, did not do anything resembling idolatry. Neither then nor afterward did he frequently worship the stone or sacrifice to it; rather, it was a sign most clearly established in prophecy, relating to anointing. Hence the name “Christ” comes from *chrism*.

For sacrifice is not to be offered not only to a stone, but to no bodily or incorporeal creature, [Note: [Col. 0209D] Nor in honor of anyone. Agobard says that no one may dedicate a church in honor of any saint, but only to God alone. I think, however, that he would have changed his opinion had he lived in our age, in which it has become customary for churches to be dedicated in honor of the saints. In former times churches were dedicated in honor of God, and memorials of martyrs were in them.] nor is a temple to be built in honor of anyone except the one living God. Blessed Augustine proves this not only elsewhere, but also in the disputation he held face to face with Maximus the Manichaean, in these words:

“If the Holy Spirit were not God, he would certainly not make us ourselves his temple. For it is written in the Apostle: ‘Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?’ And again: ‘Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?’

“Now, if we were to build a temple of wood and stone for some most excellent holy angel, would we not be condemned by the truth of Christ and excluded from the Church of God, because we would be offering to a creature that service which is owed to God alone?” [Col. 0209C]

## XII

God alone, therefore, is he—as we have already demonstrated many times above—in whom we ought to place the hope of our blessedness, as the same Father intimates in the first book *On Christian Doctrine*, saying (Book I, chapters 32–33):

“Whatever person we pity and assist, we do this for that person’s benefit and have that benefit in view. Yet somehow it also follows that the benefit is ours, since God does not leave unrewarded the mercy we extend to the needy. This reward is supreme: that we may enjoy him himself, and that all who enjoy him may also enjoy one another in him.

“For if we do this in ourselves, we remain on the way and place the hope of our blessedness in a human being or in an angel. Both the proud human being and the proud angel arrogate this to themselves and rejoice that the hope of others is established in them. But a holy human being and a holy angel, when we are weary and desire to rest in them and remain in them, refresh us instead—either by the provision they have received on our account or by that which they have received on their own account. Yet they have received it, and, having thus refreshed us, they compel us to go to him, so that, enjoying him together, we may be blessed.

“For the Apostle also cries out: ‘Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?’ And again: ‘Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.’ And the angel warns the human being who worships him to worship him instead under whom, in relation to the Lord, he himself is also a fellow servant.

“When you enjoy a human being in God, you enjoy God rather than the human being. For you enjoy the one by whom you will be made blessed, and you rejoice that you have reached the one in whom you place your hope, so that you may come to him. Hence Paul says to Philemon: ‘Yes, brother, let me enjoy you in the Lord.’ If he had not added ‘in the Lord,’ but had merely said ‘let me enjoy you,’ he would have placed the hope of his blessedness in him.” [Col. 0210B]

## XIII

That only a rational creature can become blessed, and that it has this very good only from God, the same teacher testifies in Book XII of *The City of God* (chap. 1), speaking as follows:

“There is no good of a rational or intellectual creature by which it may be blessed except God. Thus, although not every creature can be blessed—for wild animals, wood, stones, and anything of that kind neither attain nor receive this gift—the creature that can be blessed cannot do so from itself, because it was created from nothing, but from him by whom it was created.

“For when it has attained this good, it is blessed; when it has lost it, it is miserable. But he who is blessed not by another good but by himself cannot be miserable, because he cannot lose himself. We therefore say that there is only one immutable good, the one true blessed God; whereas the things he made are indeed good because they are from him, but mutable because they were made not from him but from nothing.

“Although, therefore, the things for which God is the greater good are not supreme, those mutable goods are nevertheless great which can cling to the immutable good and thereby be blessed. That immutable good is their good to such a degree that without it they must be miserable.” [Col. 0210C]

From *On True Religion* (chap. 55):

“Let our religion, then, not be the worship of airy and heavenly bodies, but of the one by whose contemplation they are blessed. For we are not blessed by seeing an angel, but by seeing the truth, through which we also love the angels and rejoice with them. We do not envy them because they enjoy that truth more readily and without any hindering troubles; rather, we love them all the more, since we too have been commanded by our common Lord to hope for something of this kind.

“Therefore we honor them with love, not with servitude. Nor do we establish temples for them. They do not wish to be honored by us in this way, because, when we are good, they know that we ourselves are temples of the Most High God.” [Col. 0210D]

Indeed, when angels answer prayers, God answers, as in his true and unmade temple, as in all his saints; and his eternal commands are fulfilled in time without a visible law.

Nor should it disturb us that, although he is invisible, he is often said to have appeared visibly to the fathers. For just as an audible sound is not the thought established in the silence of understanding itself, so the form in which God was seen was not the invisible nature constituted in itself. Nevertheless, he himself is seen in that bodily form, just as the thought itself is heard in the sound of the voice. They did not fail to understand that, in the bodily form—which was not God himself—they were seeing the invisible God.

For Moses was speaking with one who spoke, and yet he said to him: “If I have found favor before you, show yourself clearly to me, so that I may see you.”

## XIV

Augustine likewise says in Book V of *On the Trinity* (chap. 1):

“Things that are said about the immutable and invisible nature, about the supreme living being who is self-sufficient, are not to be measured by the customary standards of visible, mutable, mortal, or needy things. Yet even in those things,” he says, “which lie close to our bodily senses, or in which we ourselves are in the inner human being, let us strive to grasp knowledge, even though we do not suffice to do so. Nevertheless, faithful piety is not impudently inflamed toward those divine and ineffable things that are above us—not by the arrogance that puffs up its own powers, but by the grace of the Creator and Savior himself.

“For by what understanding can a human being grasp God, when he does not yet grasp the understanding itself by which he wishes to grasp him? But if he already grasps this understanding, let him carefully consider that nothing in his nature is better than it, and let him see whether there are in it any outlines of forms, gleams of colors, spacious magnitude, separation of parts, distinctions of mass, movements across intervals of place, or anything of that sort.

“Certainly we find none of these things in that by which we find nothing better in our nature—that is, in our understanding, by which we grasp wisdom insofar as we are capable. What, then, we do not find in what is better in us, we ought not to seek in him who is far better than what is better in us.

“Thus, if we can and insofar as we can, let us understand God as great without quantity, as creator without need, as present without position, as containing all things without having a form, as wholly present everywhere without a place, as eternal without time, as making mutable things without any change in himself, and as suffering nothing.

“Whoever thinks of God in this way, even if he cannot yet discover in every respect what he is, nevertheless piously guards, insofar as he can, against thinking of him as something he is not.” [Col. 0211D]

## XV

How much visible things hinder the apprehension of invisible things, and how much love of corporeal things—even good ones—hinders the contemplation of spiritual things, the Lord himself demonstrates when he says: “I tell you the truth: it is better for you that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you” (John 16:7).

The often-mentioned Father Augustine teaches that this is the meaning of these words (Tractate XCV on John, chap. 16):

“It is better for you that this form of a servant be taken away from you. The Word made flesh dwells among you, but I do not want you still to love me carnally and, content with this milk, always desire to remain infants. If I do not withdraw the tender food with which I nourished you, you will not hunger for solid food; and if you do not cease hungering carnally, you will not be capable of the Spirit.

“For what does ‘If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you’ mean? Could he not send him while he was present here? Who would say that? For the one was not absent from the place where the other was. What, then, does ‘If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you’ mean, except: ‘You cannot receive the Spirit unless you cease to love Christ carnally’?

“Hence the one who had already received the Spirit says: ‘Although we knew Christ according to the flesh, now we no longer know him in that way.’ For he called Christ’s very flesh ‘not according to the flesh’ who spiritually knew the Word made flesh.

“This is surely what the good teacher wished to signify when he said: ‘For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come. But if I go away, I will send him to you.’ When Christ descended bodily, not only the Holy Spirit but also the Father and the Son were spiritually present with them. And so, when they were about to become spiritual from being carnal, they were destined to possess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit more capaciously.” [Col. 0212B]

## XVI

No wise person, therefore, is unaware that a faithful human being, in order to advance from external things, must be drawn inward, not driven outward from interior things so as to decline. One must pass from flesh to soul, from body to spirit, from visible things to invisible things, from the world to God. And this is called progress if one passes to better things, not to worse.

**[Note: [Col. 0211D] To better things one should pass. Thus Polycarp says in Eusebius, Book IV, chap. 15: “For our mind is not changeable from better things to worse. We consider it beautiful and honorable to run from vices to virtue.” From the translation of the most distinguished Henry Valesius.]**

The person who has read and understood the words of Saint Augustine set out a little earlier knows that the soul is better and the body worse, the spirit more exalted and the flesh most lowly. Even fools agree that the things human and carnal presumption fabricates are far worse than these.

Among such things are also those images which not only sacrilegious people call holy, because they offer divine worship to the works of their own hands, but which foolish people also call holy, attributing holiness to images without a soul; and not only that, but irrationally granting sanctification—which, the Apostle testifies, takes place through the Word of God—to likenesses that have never spoken.

**[Note: [Col. 0211D] They call them holy images. Agobard rightly expresses indignation that they should call images holy, attributing sanctity to inanimate things and to the works of their own hands. Nevertheless, there is nothing to prevent their being called holy in some sense, with reference to the persons painted or fashioned on those panels. For this reason Bede calls them holy in his recently published *History of the Abbots of Wearmouth*.]**

Finally, Gideon—who, according to the angel, was a most valiant man and is said to have died in a good old age—requested, as the divine Scripture relates, gold earrings from his companions from the spoil, and received them. He made an ephod from them and placed it in his city of Ophrah, and all Israel prostituted themselves after it; and it became a ruin to Gideon and to his whole household.

Although he did this in honor of God, nevertheless, because he wanted to place it not in the place which the Lord had chosen but in his own city—something which the law had forbidden—his household did not, as he supposed, attain elevation through it, but destruction.

And so that we may know that Gideon did not make it for foreign gods, the text immediately continues: “After Gideon died, the children of Israel turned away and prostituted themselves with the Baals.” When they prostituted themselves after the ephod, they are not said to have turned away, so that we may understand “from God”; nor are the Baals, Astaroth, or any idol named. But when they went after foreign gods, the Baals are immediately specified. *Baalim* is the plural in Hebrew and commonly signifies idols in the divine Scripture.

Likewise, when the erring people made one calf in the wilderness, it was said: “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” [Col. 0213B]

## XVII

It is blameworthy not only to render divine honor where it is not permitted, but also to honor the memorials of the saints ostentatiously in order to seek popular glory.

**[Note: [Col. 0213D] Memorials of the saints—that is, temples in which the bodies of saints lie buried, or where their solemn memory is celebrated.]**

The Lord, as blessed Jerome testifies, rebukes the Pharisees for this in the Gospel in these words:

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous, and say: ‘If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their partners in the blood of the prophets’” (Matthew 23:29–30).

The aforementioned teacher therefore, by a most prudent syllogism, proves them to be sons of murderers, since they themselves, for the reputation of goodness and glory among the people, build the tombs of the prophets whom their ancestors killed, and say (on Matthew, chap. 23):

“‘If we had been in that time, we would not have done what our fathers did.’ Even if they do not say this in words, they say it by their actions, in that they ostentatiously and magnificently build memorials for those who were killed, while they do not deny that these were slaughtered by their fathers.” [Col. 0213C]

## XVIII

But lest anyone think that the testimony of individual saints should be disregarded, I wish to insert here not the testimony of one person but that of one Church, from which it may plainly be seen who was honored with divine worship by the faithful of old, and what love they bore toward the memorials of the saints.

Thus the Church of God, which speaks to Catholics concerning the passion of Polycarp, says among other things about the veneration of holy martyrs (Eusebius, Book IV, chap. 15):

“But that enemy of all good and adversary of all the righteous, when he saw that Polycarp had been crowned both with the glory of martyrdom and for the virtues of his distinguished life, and had obtained through death the rewards of immortality, began to take great pains that his remains should not be granted for burial to those who desired them.

“Accordingly, Nicetas, the father of Herod and brother of Dalcus, was urged to approach the magistrate and ask him not to permit the body to be buried, lest, he said, ‘leaving the one who was crucified, the Christians should begin to worship this man.’ The Jews were especially contriving this, for they watched our people closely lest they should seize him while the flames were still burning.

“Those most wretched people did not understand that we can never abandon Christ, who endured death for the salvation of the whole world, nor worship anyone else, since we know the true God, who alone is to be worshiped. But we love and venerate the martyrs as disciples of the Lord, as those who faithfully preserved their allegiance to the teacher and Lord; and we too desire to share in their faith and perseverance in love.

“When the centurion saw the Jews persisting so obstinately in their contention, he himself placed the body in the midst and burned it. Afterwards we gathered his bones, made more precious than the most costly gems and more esteemed than all gold by the fire, and, as was proper according to custom, laid them away.

“At that place, by the Lord’s favor, we still assemble in solemn and celebrated gatherings, especially on the day of his passion. But when we celebrate the memorials of those who suffered earlier, we do so so that the minds of those who come afterward may be stirred up by distinguished examples to follow the way of their predecessors.” [Col. 0214B]

These things are taken from Book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, so that they may hold their place among the other authorities of the divine law and of the holy Fathers.

Since the judgment of all is one—that religious worship is owed to God alone—what remains for the faithful except that, with our minds cleansed of every profane servitude to fabrications, we should strive with all our strength so that we may truthfully say what is written:

“For it was not human invention of evil skill that led us into error, nor the fruitless labor of a painting’s shadow, nor a sculpted image fashioned with varied colors, whose appearance gives desire to the senseless; and he loves the likeness of a dead image without a soul. Lovers of evil are those who place their hope in such things, and those who make them, those who love them, and those who worship them.

“Again: ‘No human being can fashion God to resemble himself. Since he is mortal, with wicked hands he fashions a dead thing. For he himself is better than the things he worships: he has lived, though he was mortal, but they have never lived’” (Wisdom 15:4 ff.). [Col. 0214D]

## XIX

Someone may perhaps say that he does not think there is anything divine in the image he worships, but that he grants it such veneration solely in honor of the one whose likeness it is.

The answer is readily given: if the image he worships is not God, it is in no way to be venerated as though this were in honor of the saints, who in no way claim divine honors for themselves, as has already been shown by many testimonies above.

It is also worth remembering that, as the eleventh book of the aforementioned history relates, after the shrines and images of the idols had been destroyed at Alexandria, such ardor for Christianity inflamed those converted from demons to Christ that each person painted the sign of the Lord’s cross on doorposts, entrances, windows, walls, and columns.

O what sincere religion! The banner of the cross was painted everywhere, not some likeness of a human face. God was evidently arranging this wonderfully, perhaps even without their knowing it. For if those who had abandoned the worship of demons had been ordered to venerate images of the saints, I think it would have seemed to them that they had not so much abandoned idols as changed their images.

## XX.

That images of the apostles and of the Lord himself were produced or preserved by the ancients rather for love and remembrance than for the honor of religion or any veneration in the manner of the Gentiles is shown by Eusebius of Caesarea in Book Seven, chapter 18, of his *Ecclesiastical History*. He inserts the following account after briefly mentioning some of the events that he had learned had taken place at Caesarea Philippi:

> “Since, then, we have mentioned this city, it seems right also to recall what occurred there and what we have judged worthy of historical record. The woman whom the Gospels report to have been healed by the Savior from an issue of blood is known to have been a citizen of this city; her house is still shown there. Before the entrance of her house, a certain elevated base is displayed, on which an image in bronze of the woman herself, as though fallen on her knees and extending her palms in supplication, appears to have been fashioned. Beside it stands another statue, likewise cast in bronze, in the form of a man, elegantly draped in a robe, extending his right hand toward the woman. At the foot of this statue, from the base, a plant of a novel kind grows. When it has sprung up, it habitually grows until it reaches the hem of that bronze garment; when, growing upward, it touches the very top of the bronze fringe, it acquires from that point the power to drive away all diseases and infirmities, so that whatever the bodily ailment may be, it is removed by a small drink made from the moistened healing herb. The herb has no power at all if it is plucked before it has grown up and touched the top of the bronze fringe.

> “They said that this statue had been formed in the likeness of the face of Jesus, and it remained down to our own times, as we ourselves saw it with our own eyes. Nor is it surprising if those who had believed from among the Gentiles seemed to offer such a gift in return for the benefits they had received from the Savior, since even now we see images of the apostles Peter and Paul and of the Savior himself being represented and painted on panels; indeed, we have also seen ancient images of them preserved by certain people.

> “This seems to me to have been observed indifferently from a Gentile custom, according to which they are accustomed to honor those whom they have judged worthy of honor. For the preservation of the insignia of the ancients for the memory of posterity is a sign of honor toward the former and of love toward the latter.

> “Finally, the chair of James—who was chosen by the Savior himself and by the apostles as the first bishop on earth, in Jerusalem, and whom the books designate as the brother of Christ—is preserved there even to the present day. Thus all those who, down to the present time, receive the priesthood of that see sit upon it.”

Thus far Eusebius.

## XXI.

Bede too, an Englishman and, in his time, by no means inadequately versed in the divine Scriptures, when he was discussing the sea that Solomon made in the temple of the Lord, added the following after these words:

> “It should certainly be noted that there are some who think that the law of God forbids us to sculpt or paint likenesses of human beings, or of any animals or things whatsoever, in a church or in any other place, because in the Decalogue of the law it says: ‘You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness that is in heaven above, or on earth beneath, or of those things that are in the waters under the earth.’ They would by no means think this if they recalled Solomon’s work, by which he made palms and cherubim inside the temple, together with various carvings; on its columns, pomegranates and networks; in the bronze sea, twelve oxen and carved scenes; and also, as is read below, on the sides of the vessels, lions with oxen, palms, axles, and wheels, together with cherubim and various kinds of paintings.

> “Or certainly, they should have considered the works of Moses himself, who, at the Lord’s command, first made cherubim on the mercy seat and afterward made a bronze serpent in the wilderness, by looking upon which the people were saved from the venom of the fiery serpents. If it was permitted for a bronze serpent to be raised on wood, by looking upon which the children of Israel would live, why is it not permitted to recall for the faithful, by painting it, the exaltation of the Lord Savior on the cross, by which he conquered death? Or why may one not recall his other miracles and healings, by which he wonderfully triumphed over the same author of death, when the sight of these things often brings great compunction to those who look upon them and also unfolds, as it were, a living reading of the Lord’s history to those who do not know letters? For painting is called in Greek ζωγραφία, that is, ‘living writing.’

> “If it was permitted to make twelve bronze oxen, each group of three facing the four regions of the world while carrying the sea placed upon them, what prevents the twelve apostles from being painted, going forth and baptizing all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, represented, so to speak, before the eyes of all in living writing?

> “If it was not contrary to the law to make carved scenes in a circle ten cubits wide in that same sea, how will it be thought contrary to the law if we sculpt or paint on panels the histories of the saints and martyrs of Christ, who, by keeping the divine law, deserved to attain the glory of eternal recompense?

> “But if we attend more carefully to the words of the law, it may perhaps become clear that it is not forbidden to make images of things or animals, but that making these things for the sake of idolatry is altogether prohibited. For when the Lord was about to say on the holy mountain, ‘You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness,’ he first said: ‘You shall have no other gods before me.’ Then he added: ‘You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness that is in heaven above, or on earth beneath, or of those things that are in the waters under the earth.’ And he concluded: ‘You shall not worship them, nor serve them’ (Deut. 5:8–9).

> “By these words it is openly declared that those likenesses are forbidden to be made by human beings which the impious customarily make for the veneration of foreign gods, and which wandering paganism devised for serving and worshiping them. Apart from this, no letter of the divine law, as I think, forbids such things from simply being made.

> “Otherwise, when the Pharisees tested the Lord about paying tribute to Caesar, saying that Caesar’s name and image were stamped upon it, he would certainly not have answered: ‘Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.’ Rather, he would have corrected their error by saying: ‘It is not lawful for you to make an image of Caesar on the impression of your gold, because the divine law forbids such a sculpture.’ For this would have been the place for him to say so, after the census coin had been shown to him, if Caesar’s image had been fashioned upon it for the sake of his idolatry and not rather as a sign of royal power.”

It is enough to have taken these passages from the booklet of the aforementioned man.

## XXII.

We read in the *Acts of Blessed Sylvester the Pope* that Constantine the emperor, who had not yet been reborn in the font of life, recognized and immediately adored the faces of the holy apostles Peter and Paul when the aforementioned pope showed him panels in which the likenesses of both apostles had been fashioned from ancient times for remembrance, just as they had been shown to him in a nocturnal vision.

[Note: [Col. 0217D] *In the Acts of Blessed Sylvester.* This passage is also cited by Charlemagne in the *Capitulary on Not Worshiping Images*, Book II, chapter 13, as well as by the Council of Paris held in the year 824 and by Walafrid Strabo in chapter 8 of his book *On Matters Pertaining to the Church*. Charlemagne, however, judges that the book of the *Acts of Blessed Sylvester*, where the account of the images brought before Emperor Constantine is written, has no authority, because it is not included among the Catholic books listed in the *Decree of Gelasius*.]

But should we, on the authority of Constantine, be obliged to adore the image of any saint, when that emperor did this more from the noxious custom of idolatry than from the truest consideration of reason, which he himself had not yet understood?

And lest we seem to assert this presumptuously, we insert the authority of blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan, a man outstanding in learning and holiness. In the revelation shown to him concerning the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, he relates that he recognized the blessed apostle Paul from his recollection of Paul’s portrait, while Paul spoke and the other two remained silent. Yet nowhere does he write that Paul adored—not to mention a painting of him—even the apostle himself, present and speaking with him.

Blessed Paulinus also sharply rebuked a certain presbyter by letter because he had requested that a portrait of Paulinus and his wife be sent to him, so that he might always have with him, in this way, those whom he loved while they were absent.

[Note: [Col. 0217D] *A certain presbyter.* Sulpitius Severus, presbyter of Primuliacum, as is clear from the eighth letter of Paulinus to Severus, where it is written: “What answer should I give you concerning that request by which you ordered our portraits to be painted and sent to you? I beg you, by the bowels of charity: what solace of true love are you seeking from empty forms?” This, however, does nothing against those who adore images. Severus had requested portraits of Paulinus and Therasia, not as though he intended to adore them, but so that he might always have present in that manner those whom he loved while absent, as Agobard also acknowledges. Nor do I think anyone would wish to condemn this affection.]

It is also read that blessed Pope Gregory rebuked the bishop of Forojulium because he had erased images of the apostles from his basilica on account of the superstition of the common people, who were adoring them contrary to the rule of faith; yet he corrected such an error by rational authority while leaving the painting intact for the memory of posterity.

[Note: [Col. 0218D] *The bishop of Forojulium.* I think Agobard’s memory failed him: instead of the bishop of Forojulium, he probably meant Serenus, bishop of Massilia, whom Gregory rebuked in various letters because he had broken images. See St. Gregory, Book VII, indiction 2, letter 109, and Book IX, indiction 4, letter 9.]

## XXIII.

Blessed Augustine, in Book Ten, chapter 8, of *The City of God*, said among other things:

> “We read that deadly bites of serpents, inflicted as the most just punishment of sins, were healed when a bronze serpent was raised on wood and looked upon, so that relief might be given to the afflicted people and so that death, destroyed by death, might be signified by the likeness of crucified death. This serpent, preserved in memory of the event, the people afterward began to worship as an idol; therefore King Hezekiah, serving God with religious authority, crushed it with great praise for his devotion.”

The same Father also discusses, in Book One, chapter 10, of *The Harmony of the Gospels*, which he composed against the pagans, those who said that the Lord Jesus Christ had written a book in epistolary form and handed it over to Peter and Paul. He says:

> “When they wished to invent something of this kind—that Christ had written to his disciples—they considered to whom he could most plausibly be thought to have written, as though to those who had clung to him more familiarly, to whom such a secret might suitably be entrusted. Peter and Paul occurred to them. I believe they saw them painted together with him in many places, because Rome celebrates the merits of Peter and Paul with more solemnity also on account of the same day of their passion. Thus they deserved to fall altogether into error, seeking Christ and his apostles not in the sacred books but on painted walls.”

Thus far Saint Augustine. From these words it is manifestly inferred that if Hezekiah, the religious king, crushed the bronze serpent that God had commanded to be made, because the wandering people had begun to worship it as an idol, then the images of the saints ought, with far greater religious seriousness, to be destroyed in every way and scraped away down to the dust—although the saints themselves too favor this, since they most indignantly endure having images adored for their honor in contempt of divine worship—especially since God did not command them to be made, but human understanding devised them.

## XXIV.

That God is to be worshiped more chastely without images is also testified by Quintus Lucilius Balbus, a pagan philosopher, as the aforementioned teacher inserts him arguing in Book Four, chapter 30, of *The City of God*, in these words:

> “Do you not see, then, how reason has been led from natural things, well and usefully discovered, to imaginary and fictitious gods? This has produced false opinions, turbulent errors, and superstitions almost worthy of old women. For the forms of the gods, their age, clothing, and adornment are known to us; moreover, their kinds, marriages, relationships, and everything else have been transferred to the likeness of human weakness. For they too are represented as having disturbed minds. We have even learned of the desires, illnesses, and anger of the gods.

> “Nor, as the stories relate, were the gods free from wars and battles.
