Not only—as with Homer—when different gods defended two opposing armies on opposite sides, but also when they waged their own wars against the Titans or the Giants. These things are both said and believed most foolishly, and are full of vanity and extreme frivolity.

> “Meanwhile, consider what those who defend the gods of the nations confess. Then, when he says that these things belong to superstition, he turns to the religion which he himself seems, according to the Stoics, to affirm. ‘For not only philosophers,’ he says, ‘but also our ancestors separated superstition from religion. Those who prayed and sacrificed all day so that their children might survive were called superstitious.’

> “Who does not understand that, while fearing the custom of the state, he is trying to praise the religion of his ancestors and separate it from superstition, but cannot find a way to do so? For if those who prayed and sacrificed all day were called superstitious by their ancestors, were not those also superstitious who instituted what this man criticizes—the images of gods distinguished by different ages and clothing, the kinds of gods, their marriages, and their relationships? When these things are condemned as superstitious, that condemnation necessarily implicates the ancestors who instituted and worshiped such images.”

And shortly afterward, in chapter 31:

> “The same extremely acute and learned author,” he says, “also declares that only those seem to him to have understood what God is who believed him to be a soul governing the universe by motion and reason. Consequently, although he did not yet hold what the truth contains—for the true God is not a soul but the maker and creator even of the soul—nevertheless, if he could be free from the prejudices of custom, he would acknowledge and urge that one God should be worshiped, governing the universe by motion and reason. The remaining question between him and us would then be whether he called God a soul rather than the creator of the soul.

> “He also says that the ancient Romans worshiped the gods without images for more than one hundred and seventy years. If this practice had continued, the gods would have been observed more chastely. Among other witnesses to this opinion he would also summon the Jewish people. Nor does he hesitate to conclude the matter by saying that those who first set up images of the gods for peoples removed fear from their cities and added error, wisely judging that the gods could easily be despised in the stupidity of images.”

## XXV.

Blessed Augustine also says in his booklet *On True Religion* that nothing impedes the apprehension of truth more than a life devoted to lust and false imaginings of sensible things, which, impressed upon us through the body by this sensible world, generate various opinions and errors. No error, he says, could have existed in religion if the soul had not worshiped as its god a soul, or a body, or its own phantasms—things that are nothing other than fabrications drawn from the appearance of a body through bodily sense.

Therefore, let us not serve the creature rather than the Creator, and let us not become empty in our thoughts. This is perfect religion.

He also says, in chapter 25:

> “Since the Catholic Church has been spread and established throughout the whole world, those miracles were not permitted to continue into our times, lest the soul should always seek visible things and the human race grow cold through familiarity with those things whose novelty had once inflamed it.”

Likewise, in chapters 33 and 34:

> “The mind judges perversely when the intellect, not the eye, has been made to contemplate the highest beauty. It wishes to turn the mind toward bodies and the eyes toward God. For it seeks to understand bodily things and to see spiritual things, which cannot be done.

> “Therefore this perversity must be corrected, because unless one makes what is above below and what is below above, one will not be suited to the kingdom of heaven. Let us not seek the highest things among the lowest, nor cling to the lowest things themselves. Let us judge them, lest we be judged together with them—that is, let us assign them only as much value as their outward appearance deserves, lest, while we seek first things among the last, we be numbered among the last by the First.”

Likewise, in chapter 55:

> “Let the worship of dead human beings not be our religion. For if they lived piously, they are not treated in such a way as to seek honors of this kind; rather, they wish him to be worshiped by us by whose illumination they rejoice that we are sharers in their merit.

> “They are therefore to be honored for imitation, not adored for religion. Let the worship of human works not be our religion. The craftsmen who make such things are better than the things themselves, yet we must not worship even the craftsmen. Let the worship of our phantasms not be our religion. For any truth whatsoever is better than everything that can be fabricated according to one’s will. Yet even the soul itself, although it is a true soul, must not be worshiped when it imagines false things.

> “A real piece of straw is better than a light formed in empty thought according to the conjecture of the one imagining it. Yet it is the belief of a madman that the straw we perceive and touch should be worshiped.”

The same author says in his letter to Consentius, letter 85:

> “When the composition of carnal thought and the empty fabrication begin to undermine veneration, let us hasten, with the one who inwardly assists and illuminates us—who does not wish to dwell in our hearts with such idols—to shatter these things and, in a certain sense, shake them out of our faith, so that we do not permit even a particle of such phantasms to remain there.”

## XXVI.

That one incurs the offense of genuine rashness when one appropriates something divine for sacrilegious rites is testified by the same teacher in his letter to Januarius, where he says, letter 119, chapter 20:

> “Those who draw lots from the pages of the Gospels—although it is preferable that they do this rather than run to consult demons—nevertheless this custom also displeases me: to wish to turn toward worldly business and the vanity of this life the divine oracles that speak for the sake of another life.”

Blessed Jerome speaks similarly when he interprets the Lord’s words, which are as follows:

> “For they enlarge their phylacteries and magnify their fringes. They called those little tablets, he says, ‘phylacteries’ of the Decalogue, thinking that whoever possessed them had them as a protection and defense for himself. The Pharisees did not understand that these things are to be carried in the heart, not on the body. Otherwise, chests and coffers also have books, but they do not have knowledge of God.

> “Among us, superstitious little women continue to do this to the present day with tiny Gospels, with the wood of the cross, and with things of this kind—women who indeed have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.”

## XXVII.

> “From such practices,” says blessed Pope Leo—let us also quote his words, from Sermon 7 on the Nativity of the Lord—“that impiety also arises whereby, when the sun rises at the beginning of the daylight, it is worshiped by certain more foolish people from elevated places.

> “Some Christians even think that they perform this so religiously that, before they reach the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, which is dedicated to the one true and living God, after climbing the steps by which one ascends to the platform of the upper altar, they turn their bodies toward the rising sun and, bowing their necks, incline themselves in honor of the shining orb. We are deeply distressed and grieved that this is done, partly through the fault of ignorance and partly through the spirit of paganism.

> “For even if some perhaps worship the Creator of the beautiful light rather than the light itself, which is a creature, one must nevertheless abstain from the very outward form of this observance. When the person who has abandoned the worship of the gods finds it among us, will he not retain with himself as plausible a part of his former belief, seeing that it is common to Christians and impious people alike?

> “Therefore let condemned perversity be cast away from the custom of the faithful, and let the honor due to the one God not be mingled with the rites of those who serve creatures. For divine Scripture says: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’

> “And blessed Job, a blameless man, as the Lord says, and one who kept himself from every evil thing, says: ‘Have I looked upon the sun when it shone, and the moon proceeding brightly, and my heart rejoiced in secret, and I kissed my hand? This is the greatest iniquity and denial against the most high God.’

> “What, then, is the sun, or what is the moon, except the elements of visible and bodily light, one of greater brightness and the other of lesser light? For just as some periods are diurnal and others nocturnal, so the Creator established a different quality in the heavenly lights. Yet before these things were made, days had already passed without the service of the sun and nights without the ministry of the moon.

> “These things were created for the benefit of human beings, so that the rational animal would not be deceived in the division of months, the recurrence of years, or the reckoning of times; for by the unequal lengths of unequal hours and the manifest signs of dissimilar risings, the sun completes the years and the moon renews the months.

> “For, as we read, on the fourth day God said: ‘Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them shine upon the earth, and let them divide the day and the night, and let them be for signs and seasons, for days and years; and let them be in the firmament of heaven and shine upon the earth.’

> “Awaken, O human being, and recognize the dignity of your nature. Remember that you were made in the image of God, which, although corrupted in Adam, has nevertheless been restored in Christ.

> “Use visible creatures as they ought to be used, just as you use the earth, sea, sky, air, springs, and rivers. Whatever is beautiful and wondrous in them, refer to the praise and glory of the Creator.

> “Do not devote yourself to that light in which birds and serpents, beasts and cattle, flies and worms delight. Touch bodily light with bodily sense, but embrace with the whole affection of your mind that true light which enlightens every human being coming into this world, concerning which the Prophet says: ‘Come to him, and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed.’

> “For if we are the temple of God and the Spirit of God dwells in us, then each faithful person possesses more in his own soul than he admires in heaven.

> “Therefore, beloved, we neither command nor advise you to despise the works of God or to judge anything contrary to your faith in the things that the good God created good. Rather, we urge you to use every form of creature and the entire adornment of this world rationally and temperately.

> “For the things that are seen, as the Apostle says, are temporal; but the things that are not seen are eternal. Therefore, since we were born for present things but reborn for future things, let us not be devoted to temporal goods but attentive to eternal ones.

> “And so that we may be able to contemplate our hope more closely, let us consider, in the very mystery of the Lord’s birth, what divine grace has bestowed upon our nature. Let us hear the Apostle saying: ‘For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.’”

## XXVIII.

In these words of the blessed pope and orthodox teacher, one must carefully consider that if the works of God’s hands are not to be adored and worshiped, even in honor of God, how much less are the works of human hands to be adored and worshiped, even in honor of those whose likenesses they are said to be?

For if any image were to be adored or worshiped, it would more properly be the image of the Creator than of the creature. God made the human being in the image and likeness of God. A human being, however, cannot make anything in which there is the likeness of the human being in mind and reason. If, by sculpting or painting, one somehow represents a likeness of the body or limbs, one represents precisely what is least in the human being, not what is greatest.

Certainly, if human beings were to be adored, living human beings should be adored rather than painted ones—that is, where they possess the likeness of God, not where they resemble animals or, more truly, stones or pieces of wood, which lack life, sense, and reason.

Blessed Augustine speaks of these matters in this way in Book Five, chapter 5, of *On True Religion*:

> “Righteous human beings, who have all their joys in the one God, rejoice with those who praise them when God is blessed through their deeds. But when they themselves are praised as though they were the objects of praise, they correct those who are in error, if they can; and when they cannot, they do not rejoice with them but desire that they be corrected from that fault.

> “If good angels and all the holy ministries of God are like these people, or even purer and holier, what do we fear—that we might offend one of them if we are not superstitious? With their help, let us strive toward the one God and bind our souls to him alone, from which act religion is believed to have received its name; thus let us remain free from every superstition.”

And after some intervening material:

> “Let religion therefore bind us to the one almighty God, because between our mind, by which we understand him as Father and Truth—that is, the inner light—and him, no creature is interposed.”

## XXIX.

From Book Twenty-two, chapter 10, of *The City of God*:

> “Martyrs perform miracles—or rather, God performs them, whether they cooperate or pray—so that the faith may advance by which we believe that they are not our gods, but share with us the one God.

> “In the end, the pagans both established temples for their gods, built altars, appointed priests, and offered sacrifices. We, however, do not build temples for our martyrs as for gods, but memorials as for dead human beings whose spirits live with God.

> “Nor do we erect altars there on which to sacrifice to the martyrs. Rather, we offer sacrifice to the one God, both of the martyrs and of ourselves. In that sacrifice, the martyrs, as human beings of God who conquered the world by confessing him, are named in their proper place and order; yet they are not invoked by the priest who offers the sacrifice.

> “For he sacrifices to God, not to them, although he sacrifices in their memory, because he is God’s priest, not theirs. The sacrifice itself is the body of Christ, which is not offered to them, because they themselves are that.”

Thus far blessed Augustine.

## XXX.

This is sincere religion, this is the Catholic custom, this is the ancient tradition of the Fathers, as is also easily proved from the *Book of Sacraments*, which the Roman Church preserves.

[Note: [Col. 0223C] *From the Book of Sacraments.* He means the *Book of Sacraments* of Saint Gregory, a copy of which we have in the one published in this city of Paris about twenty years ago by the most distinguished man, Hugo Menard, a Benedictine monk. Menard himself thought that it was the very *Book of Sacraments* of Saint Gregory. We, however, have been persuaded of something quite different. For in the office of the Wednesday after Palm Sunday there is an explicit mention of the empire of the Franks, which proves that this codex was written after the year 800 and therefore is not Saint Gregory’s book. I am surprised that Menard overlooked this, since in his preface he also tries to confer authority upon this codex from the fact that, as he says, it was written before the empire of Charlemagne, even though there is no mention of an emperor in it.

The ancient use of this book of Sacraments already existed in the Roman Church and consequently in the Gallican Church. For Pope Gelasius had written a book of this kind, later reduced to an epitome by Gregory the Great, as John the Deacon teaches in the Life of that same Gregory, as he is cited by Berno of Reichenau in chapter 1 of *On Certain Matters Relating to the Mass*:

> “He also abridged into a single little volume the Gelasian book on the solemnities of the Mass, removing much, changing a little, and adding some things. He entitled that volume the *Book of Sacraments*.”

Moreover, in an old manuscript codex of the monastery of Ripoll in Catalonia, it is read as follows:

> “Here begins the *Book of Sacraments*, edited by Saint Gelasius, Roman pope, and corrected and abridged by blessed Gregory, pope of the apostolic see.”

See Menard’s preface to the *Book of Sacraments* mentioned above. It is called a *Sacramentary* in Book Seven, chapter 305, of the *Capitularies*.]

Whoever goes beyond or abandons this manner of veneration despises the discipline of his father and abandons the law of his mother. Therefore neither grace shall be added to his head nor a necklace to his neck. Let the royal road, then, be held.

The apostles, the teachers of the Church, taught this road; the leaders of the flock held to it. For God’s sheep, abandoning its shepherd and wandering from the path along which the leader goes before it, becomes entangled in thorns and is devoured by wolves.

Let us offer glory and honor to the Lord alone, and let us not commit fornication with images, becoming like those of whom God says: “I also crushed their adulterous heart, which departed from me, and their eyes, which committed fornication through various things.” And the apostle Peter says: “Having eyes full of adultery and unceasing sin.”

Jerusalem too is said to have committed fornication with the sons of the Chaldeans when she saw them depicted on the wall.

Let God be adored, worshiped, and venerated by the faithful; let sacrifice be offered to him alone, either in the mystery of the body and blood by which we were redeemed or in the sacrifice of a contrite and humbled heart.

Let angels and holy human beings be loved and honored with charity, not with servitude. Let the body of Christ not be offered to them, since they themselves are that body.

[Note: [Col. 0224C] *Let us not place our hope in a human being.* What does this mean? Does he condemn the invocation of the saints? I do not think so. At that time everyone was persuaded that the saints ought to be invoked and that they had very great power on our behalf before God; Agobard himself writes this in the following chapter. He therefore means that the saints are not to be adored, since they too are human beings—clearly following the example of the apostle Peter. When Cornelius fell at Peter’s feet in order to adore him, Peter became angry and said: “Rise, for I too am a human being.”

Jerome also adduces this passage against Vigilantius, the principal enemy of the martyrs:

> “For who, O madman, ever adored martyrs? Who considered a human being to be God? Did not Paul and Barnabas, when the Lycaonians thought them to be Jupiter and Mercury and wished to sacrifice victims to them, tear their garments and declare that they were human beings? This was not because they had not once been better than the dead men Jupiter and Mercury, but because, under the error of paganism, the honor due to God was being offered to them. We also read this concerning Peter, who raised up Cornelius, who wished to adore him, with his hand and said: ‘Rise, for I too am a human being.’”

See Hincmar, Letter Two to King Charles the Bald, chapter 8.]

Let us not place our hope in a human being but in God, lest that prophetic saying perhaps rebound upon us: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord.”

Catholic teachers of the Church also affirm that this applied to those who believed that the Lord Jesus Christ was a mere human being and not also God; for that reason they trusted in a human being and were therefore accursed.

## XXXI.

Let no one deceive himself; let no one mislead himself; let no one circumvent himself. Whoever adores any painting, or any cast or molded statue, does not offer worship to God; he does not honor angels or holy human beings, but venerates images.

The crafty and cunning enemy of the human race does this, so that under the pretext of honoring the saints he may introduce idols again and once more be worshiped through various likenesses; so that he may turn us away from spiritual things and plunge us into bodily things, and so that in every respect we may deserve to hear from the Apostle: “O foolish people, who has bewitched you?” And: “Are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being completed by the flesh?”

For Satan, as the same Apostle says, “transforms himself into an angel of light.” Finally, he introduces feasting and drunkenness under the name of charity; he pretends that pride and inflexible harshness are the steadfastness of an undisturbed spirit; and he calls blind fury zeal for righteousness.

Therefore the apostle John says: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God.”

Let us look at a painting as a painting, lacking life, sense, and reason. Let the eye be nourished by this sight. But let the mind venerate God, who grants both the crown of victory to his saints and the assistance of their intercession to us.

## XXXII.

The ancients too possessed images of the saints, either painted or sculpted, as was also shown above—but for the sake of historical record and remembrance, not for worship. For example:

[Note: [Col. 0225D] *Synodal proceedings.* From this we learn that assemblies of bishops were once customarily painted in the places where councils had been held, so that the memory of so great an event might remain fixed in the minds of mortals and provide evidence of the defeat of error.]

Synodal proceedings were painted with the Catholics supported by the truth and victorious, while the heretics, exposed and convicted by the falsehoods of their perverse doctrine, were expelled. This was done in remembrance of the firmness of the Catholic faith, according to the custom of depicting both foreign and civil wars, so that the event might be remembered, as we also see in many places.

But none of the ancient Catholics ever thought that these images ought to be worshiped or adored.

### XXXIII

Now, however, error has become so conspicuous as it gains strength that it is close or akin to the heresy of the Anthropomorphites to adore images and place one’s hope in them.

[Note: **The Anthropomorphite heresy.** Epiphanius, in heresy 70, calls these people Audianists. He does not number them among heretics, but among schismatics, making allowance for their rustic simplicity. Their error was that they imagined God in human form, according to which form, they said, he had created the human being in his image and likeness. They also maintained that Passover ought to be celebrated on the fourteenth day of the moon, after the Jewish manner. The founder of that sect was Audaeus of Mesopotamia, a thoroughly holy man and one who adhered to ancient custom, as is clear from the same Epiphanius. See the *Praedestinatus*, book I, chapter 50.]

But what is the cause of this error? Faith has been removed from the heart, and complete trust has been placed in visible things. Just as, when we see men painted in armor, or engaged in agriculture—harvesting or gathering grapes—or fishermen standing in boats and casting their nets, or hunters with extended spears, pursuing does and stags with dogs, we do not hope to receive from them an increase of the army, assistance for the year’s work, heaps of wheat, streams of new wine, or fish, does, and pigs; so likewise, if we see winged angels painted, apostles preaching, or martyrs suffering torments, we ought to hope for no assistance from the images we behold, since they can do neither harm nor good.

It was rightly determined, for the purpose of emptying out this superstition, by the orthodox fathers that paintings ought not to be made in a church:

> “Let nothing that is worshiped and adored be painted on the walls.”

[Note: **The orthodox fathers** were the bishops assembled in the Council of Eliberitanum around the year 305. They decreed that paintings ought not to be in a church: “Let nothing that is worshiped and adored be painted on the walls.” This canon has remarkably exercised the ingenuity of learned men.]

### XXXIV

But with what presumption is it done that, without a basilica, without an altar, and without the relics of saints, Masses are celebrated over such fabrications? The holy Fathers, assembled in the Council of Carthage, determined as follows (*Codex of the Canons of the African Church*, title 83):

> “Let the altars that are constructed here and there in fields or along roads, as memorials of martyrs, where no body or relics of martyrs are proved to have been buried, be destroyed by the bishops who preside over those places, if this can be done. But if popular disturbances do not permit it, let the peoples nevertheless be admonished not to frequent those places, so that those who think rightly may not be held captive by any superstition of their own. In general, let no memorial of martyrs be accepted as credible except where there is a body or some relics, or where the origin of some dwelling, possession, or martyrdom is transmitted with the fullest certainty. For altars established anywhere on the basis of dreams and empty revelations, as it were, of various people, are to be rejected altogether.”

These statutes were sufficient for those times. For the error had not yet arisen by which images fashioned from charcoal, vermilion, or sinople were called holy images and proclaimed worthy of adoration.

[Col. 0226C]

### XXXV

Nor should cunning again retreat to its hiding places of deceit and say that it does not adore images of the saints, but the saints themselves. For God cries out:

> “I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to graven images.”

And the Apostle, speaking of our Lord, the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, says:

> “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name.”

He then explains what this name is:

> “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.”

No holy angel, no holy human being, lays claim to this power, praise, dominion, or name that is above every name. For the angel who claimed it, or the human being whom the angel persuaded to claim it, each fell.

If any human being or angel is worshiped besides the one who is proclaimed to be both God and human being, and the angel of the highest counsel—as the Prophet testifies—there is no other name that is or can be above this name, which is above every name, nor is there any name equal to it. But since no one is equal to God, and no one else exists essentially as Jesus—that is, as Savior—let us believe the Apostle and yield to divine authority. Let us bend the knee at the name of Jesus alone, which is above every name, lest, if we grant this honor to another, we be judged alienated from God and be abandoned to follow the desires of our heart in our own inventions.

*Here ends Agobard, bishop, on Images.*

[Col. 0227A]

# BOOK ON THE ADMINISTRATION OF ECCLESIASTICAL PROPERTY

### I

Your faithful and venerable affection has informed me that distinguished and honored men residing throughout Septimania and Provence speak continually against me in slander; although they do not spare others either, saying that we—and especially I—have stirred up an unheard-of contention and discord over ecclesiastical property. They claim that this matter is being pursued among them in every way and without interruption, not only by defamation but also by threats and the devising of cunning plots.

You also say that they are unwilling to accept any satisfaction or defense; but if anyone offers them a reasonable explanation in order to make amends, they accuse it of being late and recently invented. Since your fraternity wishes to know the unvarnished truth about this matter—namely, how the alleged movement and agitation arose, especially concerning me, and how far or in what way I took part in such an administration, heard about it, or made suggestions—I write these things truthfully to you, as you have requested.

First, you yourself can know that I was never among our greater and better men in such a position of place or honor that I could have been either an instigator of discord or a reconciler of peace. Indeed, being inexperienced and timid, I can rarely speak among such men. Nevertheless, insofar as I can remember, I shall explain what you are asking about, as I myself know it, so that you too may know it.

[Note: **Septimania.** By the name Septimania here, as also in Jonas of Orléans, I think is meant not only the first Narbonensis but also the diocese of Urgell, which was then under the metropolitan of Narbonne. For in the charters of Louis the Pious and Charles the Bald, the churches and monasteries of that region are counted as belonging to Septimania, as we have said elsewhere. It is certain that Felix, bishop of Urgell, a man of very holy life, labored more to instruct the peoples subject to him in what he believed to be the true faith than the other peoples of Narbonese Gaul. Yet Jonas says in book I of *On the Worship of Images*: “Felix, having given the same poisonous draught to many in Septimania, nevertheless wished, insofar as it lay within his power, to give it also to Gaul and Germany.” The name Septimania is recent and was coined late, certainly after the Romans had been expelled by the Goths. It did not originate, as many think, from Biterræ of the Septimani, but from that portion of the Seven Provinces which had fallen to the Goths by right of war. Sidonius, the author of this name, therefore calls it “the Septimania of the Goths.” The illustrious Peter de Marca himself has extensively developed this new opinion concerning the name Septimania in book I of the *Marca Hispanica*.]

[Note: **Provence**, that is, the second Narbonensis, which is still called Provence. From Cyprian’s letter 67 it might perhaps be argued that it was already called by this name at that time.]

### II

In those days, when our sacred and religious lord the emperor, having summoned an assembly, was holding court at Attigny and energetically providing for every advantage of the peoples entrusted to him, he arrived at the more elevated consideration of a matter requiring very necessary counsel. He desired, naturally, to discover how he might commend to the priests and to all his distinguished men the most suitable advancement of instruction and the abolition of negligence. He sought this commendably, under the inspiration of God’s grace; he found it elegantly; and he announced it faithfully with his own lips.

It would now be too lengthy to repeat all these matters, since they were then set out in distinct chapters and ought to be known to everyone.

[Note: **At Attigny.** Eginhard reports that this synod was held in August of the year 822; the author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* says the same.]

[Note: **Set out in distinct chapters**, twenty-eight in number, published at Attigny and still extant. I agree with Sirmond, who thinks that these chapters are being discussed here.]

### III

When our teachers were then extolling this matter, still in its beginnings, with marvelous praises—and especially the venerable old man Adalardus, who also said that from the time of King Pippin to that day he had never seen or considered a matter concerning the advancement of the common good undertaken with greater elevation or glory—he and the other leading men added this, lest the negligence of those who were to respond and obey should be discouraged. They said to the whole council:

> “Whatever your wisdom may discover that is useful for avoiding sins, escaping dangers, elevating religion, illuminating doctrine, strengthening faith, and cultivating zeal for holiness, declare it confidently, and do not doubt that the lord emperor, in obedience to God, will be ready to carry these things out. For, as the sacred Scriptures teach, sins bring misfortunes, disturbances, disasters, and sterility upon peoples. He takes every care that, by establishing good things and destroying evil ones, they may obtain with you before the Lord—once adverse circumstances have been removed—the ability, with God’s favor, to govern prosperously the kingdom entrusted to him.”

[Note: **Adalardus**, abbot of Corbie; see what we said about him in the book *On the Baptism of Jewish Slaves*.]

[Note: **From the time of King Pippin.** Adalardus was raised at Pippin’s court, as we said above. It is therefore entirely true what Agobard says: Adalardus was very old when that synod was held at Attigny. Agobard calls him “the venerable old man,” an epithet not ordinarily given to the aged except those who have lived to advanced years. King Pippin died in 768.]

### IV

When our leading men were speaking of these and similar matters with the greatest pleasure, I, as the humblest and least important of all, began gradually to offer the following suggestion to such great men:

“Behold, almighty God has prepared the mind of the lord emperor so that he earnestly wishes to recognize the powers of the age, whether they agree or disagree with equity. It is expedient that whatever is discordant should be corrected, if possibility permits; but insofar as possibility does not assist us, it should be endured with fear of God. Thus, when something unlawful is done out of necessity and cannot be avoided, fear may at least make excusable the person whom the execution of the act does not render innocent.

“Therefore your diligence must point out to his magnanimity the dangers concerning ecclesiastical property, which laymen handle contrary to prohibition and the canons and spend for their own uses.”

[Note: **Ecclesiastical property.** This was the universal complaint in those times, which Agobard repeatedly emphasizes in this book: that ecclesiastical property was unjustly possessed by laymen, although the canons had forbidden it. Besides the Gallican canons, he is referring, I think, to the Roman synod under Pope Symmachus, which prohibited the alienation of ecclesiastical property and decreed that it should not be handed over to laymen.]

“For after the Church of God had spread throughout the whole world and had begun to be exalted and magnified in every region and nation; after churches began to be built by faithful emperors, kings, bishops, and other powerful men, and to be enriched with property and furnished with treasures, it necessarily followed that, through the providence of princes, laws were promulgated and, through the solicitude of bishops, canons were established concerning consecrated property—that is, property assigned to sacred places—so that it might be protected from wicked men and from administrators, or properly put to use.

“Bishops, holy men, of whom the Church then had an abundance, assembled. They determined that the sacred canons ought to be preserved inviolate, since they had been confirmed by the Spirit of God, by the consent of the whole world, by the obedience of princes, and by the harmony of the Scriptures.”

[Note: **The canons must be preserved inviolate.** I recognize in Agobard a fervent devotion to antiquity. He wishes everything to be restored to the standard of the earlier rules. It is clear that he was well versed in the canons and ecclesiastical discipline. No one is more eager for the canons to be preserved intact than those who devote their study and labor to learning the judgments of the sacred canons.

Agobard gives a very serious reason why the canons ought to remain inviolate and undefiled: “Because,” he says, “they have been confirmed by the Spirit of God, by the consent of the whole world, by the obedience of princes, and by the harmony of the Scriptures.” From this we learn what our fathers’ view was in those times regarding the legitimate authority of councils. First, it was necessary for canons to be decreed with such moderation that nothing contrary to sacred Scripture should be sanctioned in them. Next, the consent of the faithful and the authority of princes—an authority that Agobard calls “obedience” in a more modest term—were necessary so that the execution of what had been defined might follow. In disciplinary matters, the authority of princes and the consent of peoples were always considered highly important.

Finally, many later synods, at which Roman pontiffs also presided, established provisions that were not observed even by those in whose age they had been established, as we have noted elsewhere. As for the age of Agobard, it is clear that the Gallican canons observed were only those that pleased the princes, while the others were not admitted. This can be demonstrated, no one would deny, by the single example of the synod of Meaux held under Charles the Bald.]

“From that time it has been accepted and established that to act against the canons is nothing other than to act against God and against his universal Church; and no faithful person has ever understood that such statutes could be violated without danger to religion. Therefore what was established by God’s authority cannot be excused by a new necessity that did not exist at the time. For all times and all the ages of the world are present and standing before almighty God; he cannot remember anything as past or await anything as future.

[Note: **These necessities.** The princes used to say that they were compelled by a kind of necessity to grant ecclesiastical property to laymen, so that, assisted by these goods, they might more easily remain in the service of the princes—that is, perform military duty. We have said a little about this matter in the notes to Lupus of Ferrières. See book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 181; the *Capitula of Charles the Bald*, title 23, chapter 7; Lupus of Ferrières, letter 71; and Flodoard, book III, chapter 4 of the *History of Reims*.]

“Accordingly, these necessities that people now allege, on account of which they think themselves free to convert sacred property to common uses, although they were still future for human beings, were nevertheless present to God. What the Church established through his Spirit, he wished all people to preserve and observe throughout every day until the end of the age.

“But since what we say about sacred property unlawfully transferred to lay uses was not done by this lord emperor but by his predecessors, and since it is therefore impossible for him to correct everything that his predecessors left behind after wrongly usurping it,

[Note: **His predecessors**, namely Charles Martel, the discoverer of this new legal practice, and then Pippin and Charlemagne.]

“at least, when you admonish him, may he deign to consider the danger which, even if he cannot avoid it, may nevertheless make him excusable before the merciful Lord when he weighs, fears, and grieves over it.

“And you should share the burden of the danger and lighten the burden of the one carrying it, insofar as possible. If you share the dangers with him and he shows compassion toward you in times of sorrow and acts as your defender in persuasion; if you share one judgment and bear so great a danger together, may the punishment for such transgression be turned away both from him and from you.”

When I had said these things, the most reverend men, the abbots Adalardus and Helisachar, replied piously. Whether they reported what they had heard to the lord emperor, I do not know.

### V

In the following year, when they had been ordered to be present at the palace of Compiègne and discussion was being held among them concerning these matters, after much conversation the reasoning, insofar as I understood it, was brought to this point: first, that the offenses involved in the unlawful use of sacred property should be impressed upon everyone’s understanding; afterward, that, having become more cautious through fear of God concerning what laymen possess, they should also become more faithful and merciful concerning what has remained with the churches.

Thus they would show piety toward their own possessions and protection toward the churches; concord, joined with compassion, would become capable of remedy and pardon; and, with piety accompanying the offense, it would also be secure in the hope of indulgence.

[Note: **At the palace of Compiègne.** In the year following the assembly at Attigny, that is, in 823, a synod was held at Compiègne, in which the matter of sacred property unlawfully used was again treated. I am surprised that no one has hitherto recognized this synod. Eginhard certainly mentions an assembly held at the palace of Compiègne in November 823, as had been ordered at the assembly of Frankfurt, and says that Pope Paschal’s legates were heard there. The author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* and the author of the *Annals of Saint-Bertin* also mention this.

No one should object that the assembly was purely political and not ecclesiastical, and therefore not a synod. Agobard is a witness in the following chapter that bishops also attended it. In those times it was customary for bishops, at such royal assemblies, to discuss sacred and religious matters separately from the laymen when the matter was purely spiritual, and together with them when it concerned ecclesiastical discipline. Consequently, decrees were later published that possessed the authority and dignity of an episcopal council, as Marca demonstrates at greater length in book VI of *On Concord*, chapter 25. There is therefore no doubt that this assembly at Compiègne, in which Agobard says that the unlawful use of sacred property was discussed, ought to be counted among the ecclesiastical synods, just like the others celebrated in that century.]

### VI

When the lord emperor heard and considered this matter, wishing to bring it to the tranquillity of peace, which had been disturbed to some degree, he did everything within his power to unite the bishops and counts in agreement and peace.

From this I concluded that, in the same way that the lord emperor had weighed and understood the matter and caused the dissension to subside, all his counts and distinguished men had also understood and desired the same thing. But, on the contrary, as I hear, these men of whom we are speaking magnify the discord that had begun, and say that they had heard or understood nothing of any discord in the presence of the lord emperor.

But since in this matter we neither can nor wish to soothe or exasperate any of them, let us leave the case to God, who orders all things, and to the one entrusted with governing, so that he may do what the outcome of events, inspired by God, brings about.

[Note: **Let us leave the case to God**, that is: Since they refuse to yield to the truth, let us yield to time. God, to whom all things are known, will disclose the truth when he sees that this is expedient for human affairs.]

Leaving aside what does not concern us, let us proceed to matters that concern all the faithful—how they ought to be believed or understood—and, insofar as the weakness of our understanding reaches, let us set before our eyes for consideration, on the authority of the Scriptures and the canons, what you have requested.

### VII

Although it may be considered unfitting for us to suggest to our betters what should be thought about the administration of ecclesiastical property, and although the powerful of this world may not think that they should inquire about such matters from people like us, nevertheless, since we live among such men whether we wish it or not and hear and speak about this frequently, it seemed right to you, dearest brother, as I think, that we should draw authority from the sacred books and the canons, and likewise bring forward the examples of the saints, so that we may avoid the human errors that must be avoided above all and hold fast to God’s truth, from which anyone who departs must remain in darkness.

Certainly, since we have drawn many examples from the Old Testament to strengthen this position, there may perhaps be those who say that these are figures of other matters and that the dispute cannot be settled by them. If there are such people, it seems to me that you should ask them where the Fathers teach that no one can be advanced to the priesthood if he has taken a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute—and, to put it more briefly, a non-virgin—as his wife, even though, according to the Apostle, he is shown to be the husband of one wife.

[Note: **If a widow.** This is taken from apostolic canon 18, which reads: “If anyone takes a widow who has been cast out, or a prostitute, or a female slave, or any woman from among those who are devoted to public spectacles, he cannot be a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or belong to the number of those who serve in the sacred ministry.”

Innocent I, in his letter to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, writes: “A cleric must not take a widow as wife, because it is written: Let a priest take a virgin as wife, not a widow, not one who has been cast out. Certainly, one who strives for the priesthood through his labor and uprightness of life must take care that he not be prevented from attaining it by this impediment.”

Pope Hilary, in a Roman synod, says: “Above all, therefore, care must be taken that no one who has married a woman who was not a virgin should aspire to the sacred orders, as was prescribed in the earlier acts.”

Gregory the Great, book II, letter 25: “We command you never to perform unlawful ordinations: neither of a bigamist nor of one who has not taken a virgin as wife.”]

And since they cannot demonstrate this from the New Testament, they must admit that it is contained in the ancient decree—

[Note: **The ancient decree**, that is, in the Old Testament, where these precepts are found, not in the New. Leviticus, chapter 21: “He shall take a virgin as wife,” namely, the priest. “He shall not take a widow, a divorced woman, a defiled woman, or a prostitute, but a maiden from his own people.” Ezekiel, chapter 44: “They shall not take widows or divorced women as wives, but virgins from the seed of the house of Israel.” For nothing else is prescribed in the New Testament except that a bishop be the husband of one wife, as Agobard has correctly noted.]

—and not only this, but perhaps many things of the same kind. Consequently, I think, they will have to concede that these lines of reasoning, begun in the Old Testament, can and ought to derive their force from that same source, especially since the evangelical and apostolic writings confirm that wherever the law teaches a moral principle, it is to be understood and maintained in that sense.

Moreover, since all the testimonies drawn from there for resolving the present question do not correspond in every respect to the matters to which they are applied in defense, it seems to me that we should touch on them so briefly that they appear sufficient to devout people, while those who are prepared to serve controversy more than edification may reserve laborious verbosity for their own pleasure.

### VIII

It is known to all who read the Scriptures that from the beginning of the human race there were priests and altars, victims and sacrifices—not only those offered to God, but also tithes that were vowed and paid to the priests. First fruits were diligently given again to the priests themselves, and tithes of all things were contributed by the whole people to the other ministers, who also paid tithes from the tithes they received to the priests.

It is also clear that, besides the tithes the people paid to the ministers—that is, the Levites—they were commanded by the Lord to take another tenth of their possessions in the third year and eat it in sacred places, that is, near the altar of the Lord, together with widows, wards, orphans, and Levites.

The Lord also commanded that cities be given by all the children of Israel to the priests and Levites for habitation. Forty-two were given, together with six cities of refuge—that is, forty-eight cities in all—and around each city a space of two thousand cubits for the grazing of livestock.

This remained undisturbed throughout the entire period of the judges and kings, so that neither the impious Ahab nor the wicked Manasseh nor his son Amon dared violate it. But after Israel was separated from the house of David by Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin, then for the first time the priests of the Lord were expelled, as King Abijah of Judah reproached Jeroboam himself for doing.

### IX

After the death of Moses, Joshua took the entire multitude of the children of Israel and came to Gilgal. When they had surrounded the city of Jericho, Joshua said to all Israel:

> “The Lord has handed the city over to you, and let this city and everything in it be accursed and devoted to the Lord.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Beware lest you touch anything that has been commanded, and become liable to transgression, and all the camp of Israel fall under sin and be troubled. Whatever gold and silver there is, and the vessels of bronze and iron, shall be consecrated to the Lord and placed in his treasury.”

And again:

> “They burned the city and everything found in it, except the silver, gold, and vessels of bronze and iron, which they consecrated to the treasury of the Lord.”

In a remarkable way, when one man had transgressed this command, all are said to have transgressed and taken for themselves what was devoted to destruction, and the Lord is reported to have become angry against the children of Israel.

### X

The Lord commanded through Moses that an animal suitable for sacrifice, if anyone vowed it to the Lord, should be holy and could not be exchanged—that is, neither a better animal for a worse nor a worse for a better. But if it were exchanged, he says, both the animal exchanged and the animal for which it was exchanged would be consecrated to the Lord.

The same is said concerning houses and fields:

> “If anyone vows his house and consecrates it to the Lord, the priest shall consider it, and it shall be sold according to the price established by him. But if the one who made the vow wishes to redeem it, he shall add a fifth part to the valuation.”

Likewise, concerning a field, if the one who vowed it does not wish to redeem it but it is sold to another, he cannot redeem it afterward, because, when the day of Jubilee comes, it will be sanctified to the Lord, and the consecrated possession will belong to his priest.

And shortly afterward:

> “Everything that is consecrated to the Lord, whether it is a human being, an animal, or a field, shall not be sold or redeemed. Whatever has once been consecrated shall be holy to the Lord.”

If almighty God did not wish human beings, animals, fields, or houses to be consecrated to him, he would never have commanded this in the Old Testament or permitted it to be done in the New Testament.

### XI

How great the reverence with which things consecrated to the Lord ought to be guarded can be gathered from many passages of Scripture and from the countless punishments of divine defense that could ever have been recorded throughout the world. A prudent reader can understand this especially clearly from the words of the Lord proclaimed through the prophets. For example, through Jeremiah, as is customary when hidden things are signified by comparison with things better known, it is said proverbially:

> “Israel is holy to the Lord, the first fruits of his produce. All who devour him are guilty; evils will come upon them, says the Lord.”

As blessed Jerome says, the sense of these words is:

> “Just as those who devour the first fruits, though by no means of the priestly lineage, are guilty of crime, so those who defile Israel will be subjected to evils.”

Malachi likewise, while exhorting people concerning tithes, sets before both the diligent and the negligent the reward and vengeance proclaimed in the Lord’s words. When they ask God, “In what do we pierce you?” he answers:

> “In tithes and first fruits. You are cursed with want, and you pierce me—you, the whole nation. Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, so that there may be food in my house; and test me in this, says the Lord, whether I will not open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out a blessing upon you in abundance,”

and so forth.

Similar things are read in the book of Ezra. It says:

> “We established ordinances for ourselves, to give a third part of a shekel each year for the service of the house of our God, and for the bread of the presence, and for the perpetual sacrifice.”

And again:

> “We cast lots concerning the offering of wood among the priests, the Levites, and the people, so that it might be brought into the house of our God by the houses of our fathers, at appointed times, year by year, to burn upon the altar of our God, as it is written in the law of Moses. We also determined to bring the first fruits of our land and the first fruits of every fruit of every tree, year by year, into the house of the Lord; the first fruits of our sons and of our livestock, as it is written in the law; and the first fruits of our cattle and sheep, so that they might be offered in the house of our God to the priests who minister in the house of our God; and the first fruits of our food, drink offerings, and the fruit of every tree, as well as wine and oil, we would bring to the priests in the storeroom of our God, and a tenth part of our land to the Levites. The Levites themselves shall receive tithes in all the cities where we labor. The priest, a son of Aaron, shall be with the Levites in the tithes of the Levites, and the Levites shall offer a tenth part of their tithe in the house of our God, in the storeroom of the treasury. For the children of Israel and the children of Levi shall bring to the storeroom the first fruits of grain, wine, and oil. There shall be the consecrated vessels, and the priests, singers, gatekeepers, and ministers; and we shall not abandon the house of our God.”

These words clearly show how great the care and diligence of that people were toward the house of God and toward sacrifices and gifts of every kind. Fervent with every religious zeal, they took care to pay not only tithes and first fruits but also a third part of a shekel, surely fulfilling the command of the law, which says:

> “When you make a vow to the Lord your God, you shall not delay in paying it, because the Lord your God will require it of you; and if you delay, it will be counted against you as sin.”

### XII

I thought it right to set these words down here so that every faithful person might consider religiously that, if delay itself is counted as sin for one who makes a vow and pays it late, much more guilty is the person who does not fulfill what he has vowed even belatedly.

If one who does not fulfill his own vows is shown to be faithless—according to Ecclesiastes, which says that God is displeased with a faithless and foolish promise, and that it is better not to vow than, after making a vow, not to fulfill it—how much greater is the impiety of one who usurps, invades, plunders, and authorizes the plundering of what others have vowed and paid; and who, by perverse judgment, deceitful testimony, and impious perjury, hastens to alienate it from the house of God, where it was vowed, paid, and assigned by others?

### XIII

We read in the Books of Kings that not only praiseworthy but also blameworthy kings brought into the house of the Lord and into its treasuries what their fathers had vowed but had not paid.

If, therefore, the piety of sons who fulfill their fathers’ vows is praised, then, conversely, it is worthy of every curse if a son withholds his father’s vow and does not fear to take away what his father contributed.

It is read in the book of the prophet Jeremiah that at that time the rulers and the whole people made a covenant that each person would release his slave—namely, a Hebrew man or Hebrew woman—who nevertheless are later called their companions, neighbors, and brothers, and would no longer rule over them. But afterward they turned back and brought again into subjection their male and female slaves whom they had released to freedom, and made them servants and maidservants.

For this reason God’s anger was kindled fiercely against them, and he struck them with the following storm of threats:

> “You have turned back and profaned my name, and each of you has brought back his male slave and his female slave whom you had released to be free, and you have subjected them. Therefore thus says the Lord: You have not listened to me, to proclaim freedom, each one to his brother and his neighbor. Behold, I proclaim freedom for you, says the Lord, to the sword, pestilence, and famine, and I will make you a terror to all the kingdoms of the earth.”

And shortly afterward he adds:

> “Their corpses shall be food for the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth.”

XIV. Therefore, if those who took Hebrew slaves who had been released according to the law and made free, and then brought them back into slavery—[Col. 0236A] their own slaves, certainly, not someone else’s—are said to have profaned the Lord’s name and are punished for this with the gravest retribution, let every religious person consider faithfully how much more irreparably deserving of fury are those who not only bring back into slavery their own former slaves, whom they or their parents had once granted freedom, [Note: [Col. 0235D] “They bring back into slavery.” That is forbidden. For it is not permitted to return a slave who has been granted freedom to slavery, except under the title of ingratitude. But that those who have been entrusted to the Church cannot in any way be reclaimed, the First Council of Orange decreed in canon 7: “If anyone attempts to force those manumitted in the Church, or commended to the Church by testament, into slavery, service, or the condition of a tenant, let him be restrained by ecclesiastical punishment”; this canon was later repeated at the Second Council of Arles. Moreover, canon 34 of that same Council of Arles teaches that a person manumitted in the Church could not be returned by his master to slavery, even on the ground of ingratitude. For it is impious that what is released from the bonds of slavery in the Church of God, out of regard for God, should be treated as void, as canon 7 of the Fifth Council of Orléans puts it. See also the Second Council of Mâcon.] but also cruelly oppress in manifold ways people made free by others and entrusted to the Church by their liberators for protection and defense, crushing them under every form of slavery, while leaving the Church and its priests no authority to protect them in the place of their patrons, as they ought to have done.

The Lord’s name is utterly profaned by such people; his house, which is the Church, is violently plundered; and the mother of the faithful is dishonored. Without doubt, an injury to her is also an injury to God. On this matter, perhaps, we cannot speak without offending others. Nevertheless, if anyone wishes to consider the matter patiently, he can see how much worse these times are than even those that passed under unbelievers. For those people honored their gods—which were not gods, but the works of their hands—and did not dare violate their sacred things. Now, however, those to whom it has been said, “Honor the Lord from your substance,” in turn dishonor the Lord from what belongs to him, since they not only abuse the services of the ecclesiastical household but also press his freedmen into pitiable slavery.

XV. Furthermore, that those who did not know the true God and worshiped false gods showed greater care toward their sacred things and priests than many do now is demonstrated most clearly in sacred history, [Col. 0236C] which relates that blessed Joseph subjected the whole land of Egypt to Pharaoh, except the land of the priests, which had been given to them by the king. They were supplied with fixed rations from the public granaries and were therefore not compelled to sell their possessions.

In this matter we must consider with what great diligence they honored their priests: they not only supplied them with sacred offerings but also provided them with ordinary food so carefully that they would not even allow them to purchase it. Yet now, in certain places, no class of people—whether free or enslaved—is so insecure in its dwelling as priests are, since they cannot in any way be secure or know for how many days they will be permitted to retain the Church or their own dwelling.

Certainly, when the Jewish people conducted not only sacred activities in the Lord’s temple but also ordinary commerce, placing various merchandise in the consecrated courts—although they thought that even this was lawfully done for the sake of sacred things, so that those who were about to offer sacrifices and lacked the means from their own resources might easily find what they needed—the Lord nevertheless, to show that he cared for his house and his Father’s house, drove such people from the temple with whips. We should therefore judge from the Lord’s deeds and words, if it is not permitted to sell anything else in his house, how much more wicked it is to make the house itself available for sale.

The priests of the Egyptians, during a time of famine, were supported by public subsidies so that they were not compelled to sell their possessions. Now not only ecclesiastical possessions, but even the churches themselves [Note: [Col. 0237D] “The churches, together with their possessions, are sold.” The origin of this evil must be sought in the granting of ecclesiastical property that had been made to secular men. For they retained the churches given to them together with their possessions and transferred them to their heirs, as is clear from Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 110, and Book V, chapter 44. Once this right had been accepted, there was no doubt that, just as these properties could be divided among heirs, they could also be alienated and sold if circumstances required. This still occurs today in Gaul with regard to what are called enfeoffed tithes. Their possessors transmit them to their heirs or sell them to others, as they wish.] are sold together with their possessions.

Nor do we dare say as much as we should about those whose great-grandfathers or great-great-grandfathers built and endowed churches and, in written and duly confirmed testaments, declared that they would have no heirs except the Church and its rectors. Now these descendants, contrary to the piety of their ancestors, if they are able to claim the walls as their own, think it permissible to sell with the churches not only what was bestowed by their founders [Col. 0237B] but also much that many of the faithful [Note: [Col. 0237D] “For burials.” Most possessions, estates, and fields from which the Church was enriched and enlarged arose from this source. The faithful believed that their condition after this life would be better if they were aided by the prayers of ecclesiastical men. To obtain this from them, they especially arranged for their bodies to be buried near churches through which ecclesiastical men regularly passed, so that the memory of the deceased might be renewed daily in their minds. Meanwhile, they entrusted their property to the Church, so that people might more readily be moved by this temporal recompense to implore God’s mercy for those who had given and who had already died. See Book VI of the Capitularies, chapters 285, 293, and 322, and Book VII, chapter 199.] consecrated there for burials or any other devotion, with no one prohibiting them.

XVI. But since the house of the Lord that stood in Jerusalem seems to have given us the occasion to speak of these matters concerning churches, lest anyone think that what is related about that house does not apply to the buildings of basilicas, let anyone who has entertained such a thought understand that churches are made for the same reason as that house itself was made: namely, to praise God, to entreat him, and to offer sacrifice.

Solomon himself, its builder and dedicator, says to the Lord in his prayer of consecration:

“If heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house that I have built? [Col. 0237C] Yet it was made only that you might regard the prayer and supplication of your servant, Lord my God, and that you might open your eyes over this house day and night. Hear the prayers of your servant and of your people Israel, whoever prays to you in this place.”

Therefore, with complete faith and for every reasonable consideration, whatever was lawfully or unlawfully done in it by worshipers or despisers, and whatever is recorded concerning it—whether concerning the diligence of those who built it, the negligence of those who ceased to care for it, or the wickedness of those who destroyed it—must be regarded as an example, authority, and pattern for the basilicas that have been built.

It will consequently be necessary for us to weigh religiously how the Lord, in restoring that same temple, condemns the negligent and rewards the devoted, according to the words that he speaks through the prophet Haggai:

“This people says: ‘The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built.’ Is it then time for you to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies deserted? And now this is what the Lord of hosts says: Set your hearts upon your ways. You have sown much and brought in little; you have eaten and have not been satisfied; you have drunk and have not been intoxicated; you have clothed yourselves and have not been warmed; and whoever gathered wages put them into a purse with holes. Thus says the Lord of hosts: Set your hearts upon your ways; go up to the mountain, bring wood, and build the house, and I will accept it, and I will be glorified, says the Lord. You looked for more, and behold, it became less; you brought it into the house, and I blew it away. Why? says the Lord of hosts. Because my house is deserted while each of you hastens to his own house. Therefore the heavens over you have been restrained from giving dew, and the earth has been restrained from giving its produce. I summoned drought upon the land, upon the mountains, upon the grain, upon the wine, upon the oil, and upon everything that the soil produces, and upon human beings, animals, and every labor of human hands.”

And later:

“Set your hearts from this day and henceforth, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, from the day on which the foundations of the temple of the Lord were laid; set your hearts upon it. Is the seed still in the granary? And have the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive tree not yet blossomed? From this day I will bless.”

If the children of Israel, recently returned from captivity, were struck with such barrenness because they neglected to restore the temple of the Lord, and if, once its foundations had been laid, they were immediately filled with every blessing and the fruitfulness of all things, it is altogether clear that the greatest religious duty is to show care for God’s house, and that neglecting it becomes a cause of misery and unhappiness.

XVII. We must also consider more attentively what is read in this prophecy: “And God stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel the governor, and the spirit of Jesus the priest, and the spirit of all the rest of the people.” From this it is plainly understood that anyone who obeys and loves the temple of God is a house of the Holy Spirit.

For it is evident that at that time God stirred up not only the spirit of the faithful, so that they desired to restore the house of God with complete joy and eagerness, but also that of unbelieving kings—namely Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes. They not only granted permission to build but also supplied assistance in the form of wood, grain, wine, oil, salt, livestock, and gifts of gold and silver, together with their rulers.

In the Books of the Maccabees, too, several kings are remembered as generous toward the temple of God; in the same books God’s vengeance is also recorded against those who plundered or attempted to plunder the sacred vessels. It is readily recalled in the case of King Antiochus and of Heliodorus, who had been sent by Seleucus.

Behold: once the foundations of the temple had been laid, the children of Israel were immediately blessed in everything; those who delayed the work were severely punished for their negligence; and the plunderers of sacred things were condemned by an irrevocable sentence. Since this example is not enough for us, even though throughout the Scriptures we read and recognize in so many ways that loving the house of God is religious, neglecting it irreligious, and plundering it impious, and that everyone received his due deserts, as did all the rulers who said, “Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as an inheritance,” being made or destined to be “like a wheel and like straw before the face of the wind”? [Col. 0239B]

XVIII. But perhaps someone may argue that these things ought to have been done under the Old Testament, whereas they need not be observed so strictly under the New. Whoever he may be, let him remember the example of the Lord, which the holy Fathers understood from the evangelical words.

The evangelist relates that a certain woman approached the Lord and anointed his feet. At this, the traitor Judas complained: “Why this waste of ointment? It could have been sold for much and given to the poor.” The evangelist immediately adds: “He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief and, having the money box, carried away what was put into it.”

What the Lord did with the money box is shown in part by the fact that, when Judas was going out from him and Satan had already entered into him, the Lord said, “What you are going to do, do quickly.” The disciples who heard this thought that he was ordering Judas either to buy what was necessary for the feast or to give something to the poor. They certainly would not have thought this unless they had previously seen it done.

But since the question has been raised why the Lord, who had said to his disciples, “Do not carry gold, silver, or copper in your belts,” and had not allowed them to take anything else on the road except a staff, himself had treasures in a money box, blessed Augustine discusses the matter, as far as I remember, in *In John*, Tractate 50, chapter 12. He says that our Lord Jesus Christ, who preceded the form and instruction of his Church by deeds and words, as it is written, “What Jesus began to do and teach,” foresaw that treasures would in the future be faithfully and commendably deposited and guarded by the faithful and religious in the churches, and most disastrously stolen by thieves.

By “thieves,” I mean the term generally, as we understand it in the Apostle, where he says, “Let the one who was stealing steal no longer”—that is, from every kind of dishonorable profit. The Lord therefore wished, as I have said, to establish in this matter a pattern for his Church: for what purposes such treasures should be used, with what faith they should be handled, and what condemnation those who defrauded them deserved, since Judas ended in such a fate.

In this discussion, the aforementioned Father distinguishes, unless I am mistaken, three kinds of theft and thieves: theft from private, public, and divine property. For although stealing something from another person’s private treasury is unquestionably a crime, the crime is much greater when it is from public property, which [Note: [Col. 0239D] “The laws of the secular world,” that is, civil laws. Such a law is found in the *Digest*, Book 9, concerning the Julian law on embezzlement, where these words of the jurist Paulus are cited from his single book *On Public Trials*: “Sacrilegious persons are punished capitally. They are sacrilegious who have plundered public sacred things. But those who have attacked private sacred things or unattended shrines deserve more than thieves but less than sacrilegious persons. Therefore it must be carefully considered what is sacred and what offense falls under the charge of sacrilege. Labeo, in the thirty-eighth book of his *Later Works*, defines embezzlement as the theft of public or sacred money, when committed not by the person entrusted with its custody; and therefore a sacristan does not commit embezzlement with regard to the things entrusted to him.” Augustine appears to have had this passage in mind in his fiftieth *Tractate on John*: “Behold, Judas is among the saints; behold, Judas is a thief; and, lest you despise it, he is a sacrilegious thief, not an ordinary thief; a thief of the money box, but the Lord’s money box; of the money box, but the sacred money box. If crimes are distinguished in court between ordinary theft and embezzlement—for embezzlement is theft from the public treasury, and theft of private property is not judged in the same way as theft of public property—how much more severely must a sacrilegious thief be judged, who takes not from just anywhere but from the Church.” This passage is praised in Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 302.] secular laws have called sacrilege.

To defraud the Lord’s treasures—that is, ecclesiastical treasures—of anything, which among us is specifically regarded as sacrilege [Note: [Col. 0240D] “Is regarded by us under the name of sacrilege.” There is indeed a law on this matter in Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 323: “Everyone must know that it is sacrilege to remove unjustly, in any manner, anything belonging to the Church from the churches to which it is lawfully due and transfer it elsewhere.” See the same book, chapters 285 and 305.] is plainly so enormous a crime that there can be no doubt that those who commit it must be assigned to the fate of Judas.

Since these things are so, and since to usurp, steal, give, receive, or retain anything unlawfully from the aforesaid properties is theft, let the devout mind consider how much caution the matter requires.

XIX. It has also been asked, or could have been asked, why the Lord did not give the public collectors, who said to Peter, “Does your teacher not pay the didrachma from the money box?” a stater from the money box, but sent Peter to the sea to take one from the mouth of a fish.

The teachers of the Church have answered that the Lord’s money box was spent on the poor and on feast days. When necessity required that it be used for the food of the Lord’s disciples—as it is written, “The disciples went into the city to buy food”—the Lord did not wish to put what belonged to the poor toward a public exaction. Instead, by his almighty power, he wished to take from the sea what did not belong to the poor and return it to the treasury, thereby giving his disciples an example to commend to the Church.

Following this pattern, the sacred canons established the manner in which ecclesiastical property was to be distributed: namely, that it should be spent on feeding the poor, supporting the clergy, repairing buildings, and meeting the needs of rectors, as the examples of the saints commend. There is no doubt that this practice was preserved until very recent times.

Finally, they do not permit laymen to be not only owners of sacred property [Note: [Col. 0241B] “Nor even administrators.” Book VI of the *Capitularies*, chapter 294: “No authority is ever recorded as having been granted to laymen, however religious, to dispose of anything from ecclesiastical resources.”] but even administrators. Rather, they order that stewards be chosen from the clergy itself [Note: [Col. 0241B] “Stewards from the clergy itself.” This is taken from canon 26 of the Council of Chalcedon. That canon was later confirmed by the emperors and accepted in practice throughout all the provinces, as Marca shows in Book VIII of *On Concord*, chapter 18.], and they allow fields, vineyards, and slaves to be assigned for use only to clerics, monks, and pilgrims.

Anyone who wishes to learn more carefully what is said on this subject and in which councils may discover it by reading and reviewing the relevant texts.

XX. But since there are people who think that Gallican canons or those of other regions should not be accepted because Roman legates, or the emperor’s legates, were not present when they were established, it remains for them also to teach that the doctrines, expositions, and various treatises of the most illustrious holy Fathers—such as Cyprian, Athanasius, Hilary, Jerome, and Augustine—should not be accepted, because when they discussed or explained these matters, neither Roman nor imperial legates were present.

Those seem to me to think more soundly who, in accordance with the Lord’s saying that he is present wherever two or three are gathered in his name, do not doubt that the Lord was also among them, and who believe that anyone who does not listen to the Church should be regarded as a pagan and a publican.

Wherever Catholic rulers of the churches meet, in the fear of God and in his name and honor, for the benefit of the churches, whatever they establish in agreement with the holy Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0241D] “In agreement with the holy Scriptures.” They were convinced that ecclesiastical rules, even those issued in synods, were worthless unless they agreed with the holy Scriptures. Consequently, whenever Roman pontiffs sent letters to synods concerning matters of faith, the assembled bishops examined whether those letters agreed with the sacred Scriptures, as Marca shows at length in Book V of *On Concord*.] must unquestionably be rejected by no one; indeed, it must be revered by everyone, since it is supported by the greatest authority. For the Roman pontiffs themselves both decreed that two councils should be held each year and earnestly commended the great councils.

The person who acts more correctly is surely the one who, whenever the statutes of great synods do not address unusual circumstances that arise, deliberates to follow the statutes of the ancients, which are not reasonably to be criticized, rather than one who places his own opinions above theirs [Note: [Col. 0241D] “Places them above their opinions.” Agobard agrees with an ancient author of a collection of canons, hitherto unpublished, which I possess. After speaking in his preface about dividing his collection into three books, he adds: “If anyone finds in them something concerning councils that he judges should be despised or not accepted, let him pardon the poverty of our understanding. Nevertheless, we consider it proper to prefer the judgment of many to the suspicions of individuals, and in whatever matters we do not possess the authority of general councils, to follow the judgments of those synods held in the various provinces rather than our own opinion.
