Finally, the sacred and general decrees of the canons themselves prescribe that a council of bishops be held twice each year in every province, and they call that a plenary synod where the metropolitan bishop is present with his diocesan bishops. Since particular councils are therefore held by the authority of general councils, it is clear that no one can disapprove of anything in their statutes unless he can prove by unmistakable evidence that they established something contrary to faith or good morals.” Thus far the ancient collector. If I say that he was a contemporary of Agobard, I may perhaps not be mistaken. For he cites no canons except those that Agobard himself could have praised—namely, the canons and decrees of the pontiffs that then existed in the Code of the Canons of the Gallican Church. As for Agobard’s and this ancient collector’s claim that, in order to add authority to regional and provincial councils, their celebration was commanded by great and general councils and was to occur twice a year, this was taken from canon 5 of Nicaea, canon 20 of Antioch, and canon 19 of Chalcedon. The ancient collector adds another reason: that a synod is plenary when the metropolitan bishop has attended with his diocesan bishops. This was taken from canon 16 of Antioch, where it is written: “That is a complete council where the metropolitan bishop is present.” Ferrandus also mentions it in his *Summary of the Canons*, title 144, as do Gratian, Burchard, Ivo, and others. It is therefore very surprising that R. P. Louis Cellot did not notice this when, in his notes on chapter 25 of the Council of Douzy, he repeatedly criticized Hincmar, as he himself says, for citing this canon of Antioch, although it does not appear in express words in the Antiochene synod. That synod indeed wisely decreed many things in various canons concerning the dignity and rights of metropolitans, but nowhere declared that a council was complete when the metropolitan was present. Thus far Cellot. From this it is clear that even the smallest matters sometimes escape the notice of those who think themselves wise. They had only to read the Antiochene canons. But because Cellot was then extremely busy, he was content to reread the titles of the canons of that synod. This caused his error. For Dionysius gives the heading of canon 16 merely as: “Concerning vacant bishoprics.” It says nothing about a complete council.] .

I am entirely convinced that all orthodox rulers who, in any place or time, established something concerning the conduct and preservation of ecclesiastical affairs earnestly sought to make it agree with the statutes of their predecessors and with the authority of the divine Scriptures.

Now, nothing has ever been established in synods, nor publicly preached by the holy Fathers, concerning the giving of property or the arrangement of churches. No necessity compelled them to do so, since religious devotion was everywhere burning and the desire to adorn churches was spontaneously aflame. Who would not have been stirred to these things by the deed and saying of the Lord that the Gospel reports—namely, that the Lord sat opposite the treasury and watched how the crowd cast money into the treasury, and praised the poor widow above all because she had cast in only two small coins?

Behold, the Lord sits and watches those who offer, to show that the offerings of the faithful are pleasing to him. It necessarily follows that, while watching those who give, he looks with disapproval on those who take away; while praising the one who gives everything, he condemns the one who does not give—or rather, the one who defrauds or steals anything.

XXI. Everyone should consider with all the greater attention, and care with all the greater devotion, the command to render to Caesar what is Caesar’s and to God what is God’s. The Apostle also commends this command as something to be fulfilled, saying: “Render to all what is owed: tribute to whom tribute, tax to whom tax, fear to whom fear, honor to whom honor.”

For we do not owe fear to human beings, since the Prophet commands us: “Do not fear the reproach of human beings, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies.” It is also written: “Whoever fears man will quickly fall,” and: “Do not fear those who kill the body.”

But we certainly owe fear to God, and honor to God, to his house, and to all its members. Scripture, showing who is righteous, says: “The wicked is despised in his sight, but he glorifies those who fear the Lord.”

Fear, then, must be shown to God, lest he be offended by our conduct; and honor must be shown to him, so that he may be glorified by offerings. Thus the Fathers understand the saying, “Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s,” namely, tributes and taxes; and “what is God’s to God,” namely, tithes, firstfruits, and other offerings, whether vowed or voluntary.

Indeed, the Jewish claim regarded it as unlawful to pay tribute to Caesar precisely because they had been commanded to pay the aforesaid things to God. The Lord commends both obligations when he says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin and every herb, and abandon the weightier matters of the law—judgment, mercy, and faith,” immediately adding: “These you ought to have done, and not omitted the others.”

XXII. Therefore what the Lord testifies ought to be done must be done and will always have to be done. What the Lord either commanded to be done or commended when done out of devotion was not, and never will be, something to be regarded lightly.

Certainly, the law did not forbid subjects either to drink wine or to live in houses. Yet Jonadab, son of Rechab, forbade both to his sons as an exhortation. After many years, when they were compelled by enemies to enter a city and remain there, they could not in any way be compelled to drink wine—not even by a prophet. For this reason they were praised by the Lord for their obedience, and he also promised that a man of Jonadab’s line would never be lacking before him.

If what one man commanded his descendants was observed so carefully and religiously for so long that it was even considered worthy of God’s praise—something he had commanded not by the force of law but from the fervor of religion—what should we think of the people of our own time, whom almighty God and the universal Church, under the names of father and mother, never cease to instruct? They must surely be reproached by comparison with those people, just as the Jewish people were when the Lord said: “The words of Jonadab have prevailed over my words,” and so forth.

Conversely, we must believe that whatever any superior commands in the exercise of authority cannot be despised without the danger of disobedience, as is made entirely clear by the deeds of Saul.

When his son Jonathan, armed with faith and the strength of his protector, had gone to the Philistine outpost and their camp was thrown into confusion, Saul pursued the enemies with his companions, chasing and striking them down. Seeing that the matter was going well, he charged the people, saying: “Cursed be the man who eats bread today, until I have taken vengeance on my enemies.”

Jonathan, who did not know of this, tasted a little honey. For this reason the Lord became angry, so that he would not answer when the people asked what they should do. Unless the good deeds already accomplished had delivered Jonathan, he might have been discovered and put to death without appeal.

Here we must consider with complete fear that, although ignorance could not excuse him and the virtue of such great faith did not turn away divine indignation until the hour of death had arrived, we might still marvel if some did not observe that he had eaten honey, not bread. But because, according to the manner of sacred speech, “bread” includes whatever can be eaten, we must consider how carefully the Lord wishes whatever a superior has not irreligiously commanded to be observed, since he did not allow Saul’s command, transgressed unknowingly, to pass without punishment.

Who today would believe himself guilty if he did not obey an order given by someone in authority? Yet, according to the inward rule of God’s judgments, we see that sins are investigated more subtly and more harshly than we are able to guard against or fear.

XXIII. These things have been said so that an opportunity may be offered for more careful and prudent consideration: if one person who is obeyed by many is so beneficial, and one person who disobeys in ignorance is so harmful to all, how much recompense, good or evil, does one deserve who obeys or despises the concordant commands of many—especially since the Lord is understood to have said not only to the apostles but to all who undertake the ministry of teaching in the Church: “Whoever hears you hears me; whoever despises you despises me.”

Who could adequately magnify the hidden deed of Ananias and Sapphira, so exaltedly discovered and so terribly punished? From this arose so enormous a crime that they were convicted of testing the Holy Spirit and lying to God, even though they are reported to have preferred to keep for themselves only part of the price of the field, which was still in their own power.

It had not yet been placed at the apostles’ feet, nor had it yet been brought into the fellowship of the brethren. With what severity would someone be judged who took something from the apostles’ money box or from the resources already offered to the whole Church, if the one who took from what was still to be offered was judged in this way?

If someone stole anything from another person’s ordinary property, the command of the law would impose a penalty requiring him to restore double or quadruple the amount. But because Ananias defrauded sacred property assigned—or rather, destined to be assigned—to holy preachers and holy poor people, he was punished with death. That death was not inflicted by a sword or by the hands of officials; it was inflicted by the power of sacred speech.

Thus the first fraud committed in the Church concerning ecclesiastical property was punished. Adam was condemned to such punishment in paradise: by touching what was forbidden, he became subject to death and unworthy of dwelling in paradise. Ananias, together with his wife, by committing fraud in the Church, was deprived both of ecclesiastical fellowship and of earthly habitation.

The Lord had said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor.” Aspiring to perfection in accordance with this command and selling everything they possessed, the believers distributed the proceeds of their property not to any poor persons other than the holy faithful; and above all, they offered them to the holy preachers for distribution to the poor.

They understood such people to be the poor meant by the Lord’s words. Thus blessed Paul also testifies that he accepted responsibility for this ministry when the others gave their right hands to him and Barnabas, so that they might preach among the circumcised while Paul and Barnabas preached among the Gentiles, saying: “Only that we should remember the poor.”

## XXIV

Thus, in agreement with these sacred canons, they wished ecclesiastical property to belong also to the poor. For the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel. From this, among the faithful, there arose the most sacred and praiseworthy practice that churches should be endowed, so that the Church herself might feed her preachers, the choirs of ministers, the crowds of the poor, and the multitude of pilgrims who flock to her.

How much reverence, faith, and care ought to be applied to these possessions, God’s will demonstrated through the multitude of miracles that took place throughout the world, in its various regions, places, and churches. For it was not merely one Ananias, together with his wife Sapphira, who was punished by death for fraud committed against sacred possessions, but countless others—almost a thousand—who were struck with illness, tormented by demons, or condemned to blindness. If some diligent person had wished, or been able, to collect into one account what has been written about them, he would have composed enormous volumes. How much more, then, must be the number of things that were done, made known, and handed down but not written down, because they were too numerous?

## XXV

We say these things not because we threaten all who act rashly with temporal divine punishment, but rather to show that the care, preservation, and stewardship of these possessions belong to God. Through so many miracles and over so long a period he terrified the wicked—not only unbelievers but also believers—lest they rashly dare to commit unlawful acts against sacred places. He wished at least that punishment might restrain like brute animals those whom reason or the carrying out of the divine commandments could not restrain as human beings.

For they ought to have known, since they were created by God as rational beings, that if it is not lawful to covet one’s neighbor’s property, then much less is it lawful to covet the Lord’s.

## XXVI

Nor should this be understood as though the bestowal of divine gifts, the forgiveness of sins, and the gift of the heavenly kingdom were not to be desired; these things certainly belong to the Lord. But since our subject is the sacred possessions of the churches, we are now speaking according to what the Lord commanded in the Law, saying:

“You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his house, nor his field, nor his male slave, nor his female slave, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that belongs to him.”

In these words we must carefully consider that, if it is wrong to be or to produce a false witness against any neighbor for any reason, then it is much less lawful to act falsely against the Lord concerning the resources of his Church, consecrated to his name. Likewise, if one ought not to covet a neighbor’s house, field, male slave, female slave, or anything else belonging to him, then much more must one not covet what has been handed over to the Lord for the support of the poor.

## XXVII

In possessions of this kind the abundance of God’s mercy becomes apparent: he graciously deigns to receive from human beings what he himself has given. Hence David faithfully confesses to him, saying:

“For all things are yours, and what we have received from your hand, we have given you.”

Therefore, things consecrated to God must not be coveted or taken away. Rather, they must be weighed with such a disposition of mind and guarded intact, set apart from every common use, as the Lord himself indicates in Deuteronomy, saying:

“You shall speak in the presence of the Lord your God: ‘I have brought what was sanctified from my house, and I have given it to the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, and the widow, just as you commanded me. I have not passed over your commandments, nor have I forgotten your instruction. I have not eaten any of it in my mourning, nor have I separated any of it in my uncleanness, nor have I spent any of it on a funeral. I have obeyed the voice of the Lord my God and have done everything as you commanded me. Look down from your sanctuary and from your lofty heavenly dwelling, and bless your people and the land that you have given us.’”

Thus, as has been said, the firstfruits and tithes must be regarded with this devotion of heart, preserved untouched with such reverence, and offered to the Lord with such purity of confession, that God’s regard from his lofty heavenly dwelling and the blessing of the people and the land may more readily be obtained.

## XXVIII

To this confession commanded by the Lord for the faithful, the following saying of the Apostle may appropriately be added. To his faithful disciple he gave this command:

“If any faithful man”—or, “if any faithful woman” [Note: [Col. 0247C] “Or, if any faithful woman.” These words do not occur in Paul. I therefore believe it to be a copyist’s error: unable to determine which reading ought rather to be adopted, “if any faithful man” or “if any faithful woman,” he included both, leaving the judgment to the reader. We have observed that this frequently happened among ancient copyists [Col. 0247D], as we noted in our work addressed to Salvianus and Lupus of Ferrières.] “has widows, let him provide for them and not burden the Church, so that it may be sufficient for those who are truly widows.”

“Let the presbyters who preside well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and teaching.” For Scripture says:

“You shall not muzzle the ox while it is threshing.”

And:

“The laborer is worthy of his wages.”

In these words, I believe the following point especially deserves consideration: if the widow of any faithful person must be supported by him, so that the Church may not be burdened, then much more must provision be supplied from elsewhere for dogs and horses [Note: [Col. 0247D] “For dogs and horses.” From this it is clear that laymen who possessed ecclesiastical property used it for luxury, not necessity—without doubt without the knowledge of the princes; otherwise they would not have tolerated it.], and for the other servants, whether human or animal, who are maintained by the rich for pleasure, display, and shameful amusements.

This is so that they may not merely burden the Church of God, but also devastate and utterly plunder it. That this is exceedingly unlawful is demonstrated not only by this one saying but in many ways throughout the whole body of divine Scripture, where not only the punishments of transgressors but also the rewards of those who faithfully administer possessions consecrated to the Lord are described in many forms.

## XXIX

Whoever considers this work worthy of reading and reflection should know that we are speaking these things not only about laymen [Note: [Col. 0247D] “But also about bishops.” He censures bishops and the prelates who follow them, who use ecclesiastical possessions for luxury and do not consider what the Fathers have established concerning things dedicated to God. Nor does he strike only at prelates, but also at clerics generally. We should therefore understand that all of us who have been enrolled in the Lord’s portion have received from the Lord and the Church the stewardship of ecclesiastical revenues, but are to use them as the Law commands—not for the empty displays or entertainments of the world, but for feeding the needy, repairing churches, and purchasing books necessary or useful for acquiring piety and learning, as well as other things of this kind. Above all, however, the Church’s intention has always been that a cleric should first take from ecclesiastical revenues only as much as is needed for his support. I say this lest anyone distort what was said above into an occasion of envy.], but also about bishops, abbots, [Note: [Col. 0248C] “Or certain clerics.” For the term “clerics” includes all who have been enrolled in the clergy, including presbyters and deacons. Gregory the Great, Book XI, Indiction 6, Letter 54: “Lest it be objected that he is speaking of the same cleric, not of a presbyter, it should be known that in the same constitution, chapter 19, it is read that under the designation ‘clerics’ presbyters and deacons are included.” He then cites words from Novel 123 of the emperor Justinian, where chapter 19 reads: “Presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, singers, and readers, all of whom we call clerics.” Nevertheless, long after these times, the people of Ruscinon in Narbonese Gaul continued to dispute whether bishops, abbots, and the other ecclesiastical ranks were included under the term “clerics.” This uncertainty was removed when Guido, bishop of Elne, issued a constitution at his diocesan synod, held on 8 April 1339.]

or certain clerics who do something other than what ought to be done with the sacred possessions mentioned above, or who handle them differently from what God, the holy Fathers, and the authorities have established.

There is no need for us to labor over many examples concerning this matter, since it is plainly evident to rational people how many reprehensible and unbecoming things are done by those whom the sacred order admits to ecclesiastical governance. They ought to weigh and dread with the utmost attention the saying in which blessed Job speaks in their person:

“If my land cries out against me, and its furrows weep with it; if I have eaten its fruits without payment and afflicted the souls of its farmers; let thistles spring up for me instead of wheat, and thorns instead of barley.”

Although these words can also bear another interpretation, referring to the complaint of a subjected people when it rightly complains against its shepherd because of negligence in preaching or because of the impediment caused by bad examples, they can also appropriately be applied to the person of the ecclesiastical household. When a wicked and perverse shepherd oppresses it unjustly and abuses things consecrated to God unworthily, and when he adorns—or rather disgraces—his own condition and unlawful desires, as well as those of his associates, with ostentation and the pomp of falsehood, not only the Church over which he presides but also all who recognize the ugliness of his conduct are stirred to murmur and speak against such a ruler.

Such a man, even if he spends money on preaching, nevertheless, because of his carnal desires and indecent acts, cannot escape the appointed punishment. Instead, for the pleasures of the present life, the stings of eternal punishment will arise against him. [Note: [Col. 0248D] “Such a man.” He says that a bishop, even if learned and diligent in instructing the people, will be consigned to eternal punishments if he devotes himself to worldly display and abuses sacred possessions.]

## XXX

Yet this sentence does not strike only wicked bishops, presbyters, or abbots while leaving laymen who improperly use ecclesiastical possessions secure. They must carefully consider the following here: if a man accompanied to some degree by an accepted ecclesiastical rank or by expenditure on preaching spends those same possessions, to his own detriment, on common uses because of lust and desire for shameful gain, how much greater will be the harm to the man who neither holds nor performs ecclesiastical ministry, nor spends money on the word, but who hastens all the more freely toward whatever belongs to display or lust and uses sacred possessions?

With how much greater self-inflicted harm does he feast sumptuously from sacred possessions—possessions with which the groaning and grieving, in the tribulation of poverty, ought to have been consoled—while he eats with the rich who feast, rejoicing and laughing, refusing to undertake the Lord’s work and enjoying himself as though he were doing what pleases God? Moreover, he feeds and intoxicates actors, mimes, and the most shameful and frivolous jesters [Note: [Col. 0249B] “Jesters.” A class of actors who also sang with pipes, strings, or other instruments. A later age, using the word then adopted from French, called them *jongleurs*. They were called *joculares* from the jokes and games they performed for the people.], while the Church’s poor perish, tormented by hunger.

We offer this matter for the consideration of the prudent rather than explain it openly. For although it has been said to the rich:

“Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up treasure in the last days.”

And again:

“You have feasted upon the earth and nourished your hearts in luxury.”

Yet they were not commanded to devote themselves to daily banquets and to clothe themselves in the most costly garments, lest their riches perhaps remain to rot or their clothes be eaten by moths. Rather, just as they are struck by the threat of the present judgment because of greed, so also they are struck because of feasting and luxury.

## XXXI

If these words were spoken to those who perhaps did such things with their own possessions, they may be addressed with much greater force to certain rich men of the present time:

“Howl over the miseries that are coming, because while you feast on possessions that are not yours and store up treasure from what has been entrusted for the support of the Church’s poor, the poor themselves and the ecclesiastical household are tormented by hunger. Whoever among them has been defrauded or oppressed by you cries out, and their cry has entered the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth, who said: ‘You shall not withhold the wages of the needy and the poor; rather, on that same day you shall give him the price of his labor before sunset, lest he cry out against you to the Lord and it become sin for you.’”

Many such things are said in the divine books concerning this matter and concerning everything discussed above; no human being can neglect them without suffering the gravest harm.

[Col. 0249B]

# A BOOK OF DIVINE SAYINGS, COMPILED WITH VERY BRIEF NOTES, AGAINST THE DAMNABLE OPINION OF THOSE WHO THINK THAT THE TRUTH OF DIVINE JUDGMENT IS REVEALED BY FIRE, WATER, OR ARMED COMBAT

[Note: [Col. 0249D] Agobard, distressed by the injustice of the Gundobad law, which commanded that cases be brought to an end by single combat or duel—something they foolishly and wrongly called the Judgment of God—gathers in this book sayings from both Testaments to show that this law is impious and entirely contrary to Christian piety and simplicity. The book is altogether learned and worthy of Agobard. Masson had made two books from it and had separated the sayings from this little work, contrary to the evidence of the title and to Agobard’s testimony. Since the matter required it, we have joined them together again. I should also point out to you, reader, that Agobard’s notes corresponding to the sayings were placed in the margin of the manuscript of Agobard’s works. Consequently, the copyist used by Masson, not understanding which note belonged to which passage, threw everything into confusion. We have restored each note to its proper place.]

[Col. 0249C]

## I

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, who is our peace and who made both peoples one, breaking down the dividing wall of hostility in his flesh, abolishing the law of commandments in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace and reconciling both in one body to God through the cross, killing the hostility in himself; and coming, he proclaimed peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near. For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:14–18).

Here begin the divine testimonies from the Gospel, apostolic, and prophetic writings, by which it is demonstrated more clearly than daylight that domestic combats and fraternal conflicts are contrary to the reconciliation of the human race and to Christ the reconciler—those conflicts undertaken by people who think that uncertain and hidden matters concerning perishable things can be revealed and that, through means contrary to truth, hidden truth can be displayed.

For if almighty God, creator and ruler of the world, had wished—or permitted—the truth of judgment concerning hidden matters to be discovered through mutual slaughter, he would not have commanded judges or magistrates [Note: [Col. 0250D] “Masters,” that is, magistrates; the word is used in this sense also below, in chapter six of this book.] to be appointed in each city. Nor would he have commanded that deniers be convicted by witnesses, or that, where witnesses are lacking, a dispute be settled by an oath.

Nor would he have given that law concerning husband and wife, if a spirit of jealousy should stir up the husband, by which the woman was to be proved adulterous [Col. 0251A] or innocent through the bitterest waters [Note: [Col. 0250D] “She was to be proved adulterous,” namely, through the ordeal of cold water. This ordeal was nevertheless forbidden by Charlemagne, as is clear from a capitulary issued in his sixteenth year. Hincmar mentions this law in his work on the divorce of Lothair and Theutberga and also in Letter 39 to Hildegarius, bishop of Meaux, in which he treats the ordeal of cold water at length. See the distinguished Francis Juretus in his notes on Letter 74 of Ivo of Chartres, where you will find much concerning the examination by cold or hot water. Here we present an illustrious example of this ordeal, conducted not upon a lowly person—as Juretus thought such judgments were customarily used only against common and plebeian persons—but upon a woman of high rank, who cleared herself of the accusation of having procured an abortion through this crude experiment for discovering the truth. We owe our knowledge of this event to the author of the book on the miracles of Blessed Mary of Rocamadour near Cahors, to whom the woman had vowed herself in this danger to her life and reputation. The book exists in Paris, in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and was shared with me, with singular kindness, by Dom Lucas Dacherius, librarian of that monastery. Thus the author speaks in Book I, chapter 36:

“After Gaston of Béarn had died, his wife, Leofas by name, the sister of the king of Navarre, remained pregnant; but not long after her husband’s death she suffered a miscarriage. Nobles, commoners, and the whole mixed multitude of both sexes made excessive lamentation over it and foretold, as though it had already occurred, the future slaughter of the people, the destruction of the churches, and finally the devastation of the entire region. And, as the outcome proved, the conjecture about what had occurred was false: Sancho, king of Pamplona, and the king’s council falsely brought the woman to trial and charged her with the crime of having delivered a child before its natural time. Therefore they decreed that she should be subjected to various tortures, burned by fire, or thrown bound beneath the waves. But she, facing imminent death and innocent of this crime, entreated our Lady of Rocamadour to come to her aid. Nor was she lacking in response to her petition. Indeed, bound as she was to undergo the water ordeal, she was thrown from the lofty bridge of the castle called Salvaterra into the depths of a raging torrent. More than three thousand men and women had gathered for that spectacle of grief—or rather of savagery—awaiting the shipwreck of one who was not shipwrecked; some jeering, others moved by compassion and praying to the Lord on her behalf. But she, through the Lord’s mercy and the assistance of his most glorious mother, was borne upon the waves of the deepest torrent and came to rest upon the sands without sinking, at a distance greater than an archer could shoot his bow three times. Her people then joyfully carried her home, delivered from danger. Thereafter, in praise and glory of her deliverer, she made an elaborate cloth and sent it to the church through G., abbot of Rocamadour.”]

It would not have ordered, concerning the discovered corpse of a murdered man, that the leaders of the nearest city assemble, wash their hands, and declare before God that their hands had not shed innocent blood.

Nor would the holy and innocent man David have said to his persecutor Saul, “If God stirs you up against me, let him accept the sacrifice,” and so forth. Rather, he would have said: “Send one of your men to fight me in single combat and prove that I am guilty toward you if he kills me”; or at least: “Command iron or water to be heated, so that I may touch it with unharmed hands”; or: “Set up crosses [Note: [Col. 0252C] “Set up crosses.” This too was one of the common purgations then in use. It is called the ordeal of the cross in the charter of the division of the Frankish empire made by Charlemagne: “We wish that, for the clarification of a doubtful matter, the will of God and the truth of the matter be sought through the ordeal of the cross.” Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 108: “It has been decreed that no one henceforth presume to perform any examination by the cross, lest the passion of Christ, which is his glorification, be held in contempt through anyone’s rashness.” Book V, chapter 125: “Concerning one who has committed perjury, so that he pays no redemption but loses his hand. If the accuser wishes to contest the perjury, let him stand at the cross. If the swearer prevails, let the accuser make amends according to his law.”], and let me stand immovable before them.”

## II

Since neither divine nor human law has sanctioned anything of this kind, and foolish men call these things the Judgment of God [Note: [Col. 0252C] “The Judgment of God.” It is also called this by Gregory of Tours, Book VII, chapter 14: “You, most pious king, placing this in the judgment of God, so that he may decide when he sees us fighting on the level ground of a single field.” But the matter is so well known that it needs no testimony. Here Agobard argues forcefully against that impious and murderous custom.], how can it be proved that something is the judgment of God which God never commanded, never wished, and which is not shown to have been introduced by the examples of the saints or of any of the faithful?

It would be as though almighty God ought to serve human anger or human inventions [Note: [Col. 0252D] “Inventions of men.” Pope Stephen V, writing to Lambert, bishop of Mainz, also calls this kind of purgation a superstitious invention: “What has not been established by the teaching of the holy Fathers must not be undertaken through superstitious invention.”], or as though he acted against himself. He commanded in the Law and in the Gospel that a person should love his neighbor as himself; yet, as though he had changed his will, when people begin to quarrel among themselves over insensible things—over a portion of a small field, for example, or over brute animals, such as horses or pigs, or over whatever else people dispute when moved by greed, which is characteristic of those outside the Church, not religious people [Note: [Col. 0252D] “Which is characteristic of secular litigants.” I do not think that those who litigate in court are meant here, but those who are outside the Church, that is, non-Christians. For he contrasts secular people with the religious, that is, Christians. He does not prohibit these people from engaging in litigation, provided that it takes place before judges and magistrates. A little later he will say that judgments among human beings are necessary.], would the invoked Lord reveal a temporal—or rather, a most contemptible—justice?

It cannot properly be called justice, since no one is thereby made just. When one man stands against another, one man against his neighbor, whom he certainly ought to love as himself, would God cause one to fall before the other, and cause a neighbor to kill or overthrow by the law of greed the person whom he had commanded to be loved through the holy Law?

The Apostle clearly shows that there is a law of sin, a law of the flesh, and a law of death, and that these things are contrary to the law of the Spirit and the law of life. For those who are led by the Spirit of God and are therefore sons of God hear the Apostle teaching:

“It is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather suffer injustice? Why do you not rather endure fraud?”

## III

Nor do we say this as though judgments among human beings were unnecessary. They are not only necessary but also good—those judgments of which the Lord speaks to Solomon:

“Because you asked for wisdom to discern judgment, behold, I have done according to your words and have given you a wise and understanding heart.”

And elsewhere:

“The multitude of the wise is the health of the world, and a wise king is the stability of the people.”

And again:

“Wisdom is better than strength, and a prudent man is better than a strong one. Hear, therefore, O kings, and understand; learn, O judges of the ends of the earth.”

Likewise:

“Because of this”—clearly, because of wisdom—“I shall have honor among the crowds and esteem among the elders, though young, and I shall be found discerning in judgment.”

Blessed Job also acknowledges this, saying:

“If I rejected judgment with my male slave or with my female slave when they disputed against me.”

For holy Job did not fight with his slaves and female servants using swords or clubs. He knew that equity was to be settled not by slaughter but by wisdom and mercy, which speaks of itself:

“Counsel is mine, and equity; prudence is mine, and strength. Through me kings reign, and lawmakers decree what is just. Through me princes rule, and the powerful determine justice.”

Therefore eternal divine Wisdom must be sought with unwavering faith and obtained through constant prayers and reading. The Apostle James declares:

“If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach, and it will be given to him. But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing.”

That this same wisdom must be sought through persistent reading, the Lord himself makes clear when he charges Joshua:

“Be strong, therefore, and very courageous, so that you may keep and do the whole law that Moses my servant commanded you. Do not turn away from it to the right or to the left, so that you may understand everything you do. Let the scroll of this law not depart from your mouth, but meditate on it day and night, so that you may keep and do everything written in it.”

## IV

Nor should it be thought that a person falls in these domestic wars, in the ambushes of robbers, or in any civil or domestic quarrels unless God delivers him into the hand of his neighbor, as he himself speaks through the Prophet against wicked shepherds:

“Their shepherds did not spare them, and I will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land, says the Lord. Behold, I will deliver human beings, each one into the hand of his neighbor and into the hand of his king; they will strike the land, and I will not rescue it from their hand. And I will feed the sheep of slaughter because of this, O poor ones of the flock.”

This too must be noted in that saying: the elect are called sheep of slaughter, just as the Apostle, taking his testimony from the Psalm, says:

“For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter.”

And in the Law it is commanded:

“Whoever strikes a person intending to kill him shall be put to death. But if he did not lie in wait for him, and God delivered him into his hand, I will appoint for you a place to which he may flee.”

## V

We must believe with complete faith that nothing happens in the world except as God either orders or permits it. All the hairs of the heads of the faithful are numbered, and not one of two or five sparrows falls to the ground without God. As one of the saints says—Augustine, *Sermon 6 on Matthew*:

“Not even a leaf falls from a tree without God’s will.”

Nevertheless, since it is well known that the good are killed by the wicked, but the wicked never by the good except in public wars and lawful judgments, this belongs to the hidden judgments of God, which are like a great abyss. Human beings have not been granted knowledge of why the Almighty permits such things to happen.

That the righteous are often killed by the wicked David also testifies concerning the death of Abner:

“Abner did not die as fools commonly die; rather, he fell as people fall before the sons of wickedness.”

But, as we have said, no one has been permitted to investigate these matters. Paul himself, who was caught up to the third heaven and again, in wonder, into Paradise, exclaims that the judgments of God are incomprehensible and his ways unsearchable:

“Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?”

## VI

To those who consider these matters piously and humbly, it becomes clear that hidden and concealed things cannot be discovered through slaughter, iron, or water. For if they could, where would the hidden judgments of God be?

Truth, then, ought to be sought between Catholics and heretics through such an examination, as the proud and foolish heretic Gundobadus, king of the Burgundians, attempted to demand from blessed Avitus, an outstanding and orthodox preacher. Avitus most wisely and commendably restrained and rebuked his madness. [Note: [Col. 0253D] “The heretic Gundobadus.” See above, in Book 13 of the work against the law of Gundobadus.]

If hidden faults could be discovered by inventions of this kind, as we have often said, neither wisdom nor wise men, neither judges nor magistrates, would be necessary. But since what is said about God is most true—“With him are strength and wisdom; he knows both the deceiver and the one who is deceived”—the truth of matters and judgments must be sought from him and according to him.

The divine sayings themselves must now be set forth [Note: [Col. 0253D] “Must be set forth.” This single passage shows that the sayings which follow are not to be separated from this book. Nevertheless, Masson did so, adding this title of his own: “Agobard’s Expositions Here and There from Scripture, on Peace, on Calming the Affections of the Heart, and Especially on the Whole of Christian Ethics, on Antichrist, on Hell, and on Persecutions.” Nothing of this sort is found in the ancient manuscript, nor was it necessary. Nevertheless, to smooth the way for the reader, we have added the words: “The Sayings Follow.”], and it must be perceived from them what their author wishes the reconciled people of God’s possession, the children of the resurrection, and the sheep of the supreme Shepherd to be like, and how they ought to act both toward one another and toward the wolves and beasts lying in wait.

# THE SAYINGS FOLLOW

[Col. 0254D]

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

When two people stand on opposite sides, prepared for mutual slaughter, they do not possess this good will. Therefore the angels of peace are not present among them, offering eternal joys.

“Great peace have those who love your law, and for them there is no stumbling block.”

For those to whom great peace does not exclude stumbling do not yet possess the fullness of the Law, which is love.

“Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.”

Perhaps contentious people will say that meekness is necessary for possessing the land of the living, but fraternal combat for defending the land of the dying. Let them hear the Apostle saying:

“We have no such custom, nor do the churches of Christ.”

“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.”

Eternal mercy and the honor of being God’s children are not offered to the unmerciful or to those who break the peace, but to those who make peace.

[Col. 0255B]

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not kill.’ Whoever kills shall be liable to judgment. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ shall be liable to the council. Whoever says, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna,” and so forth.

“You have heard that it was said: ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I say to you: Do not resist evil. If anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also. And to the one who wishes to go to court with you and take your tunic, surrender your cloak as well,” and so forth.

The ancient people were commanded that whoever inflicted a particular injury on another should be compelled to suffer the same injury. The new people, however, are commanded to inflict no evil but to endure patiently the evil inflicted upon them.

Therefore, whoever not only does not resist but even goes beyond and surpasses the measure of retaliation belongs neither to the ancient people nor to the new. We are commanded to love those whom we are not permitted to harm, even when they harm us.

There are three ways in which one sins: in thought, in speech, and in action. It is therefore clear that the root of evils lies in thought, while the fruit lies in action.

Accordingly, the ancient people were forbidden the fruits of evil, whereas in the new people we are commanded to uproot its roots. Thus, among them homicide constituted guilt; among us, hidden anger and insulting speech do so.

Therefore, whoever does not cleanse his mind of fury, restrain his hands from slaughter, and is subject neither to the Law with the ancients nor endowed with the freedom of evangelical grace with the new, belongs to neither.

[Col. 0255D]

“You have heard that it was said: ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust.

“For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this? And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing? Do not even the Gentiles do this?

“Therefore, be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect. For if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses. But if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your sins.

“Therefore, whatever you wish people to do to you, you also do to them. For this is the Law and the Prophets.”

[Col. 0256A]

No one can in any way be a son of God unless he imitates him. Whoever degenerates from such great nobility by refusing to imitate him does not truthfully but falsely say, “Our Father, who are in heaven.” Therefore he is condemned not only for cruelty but also for falsehood.

If we shall not enter the kingdom of heaven unless our righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, how much less shall we enter unless it exceeds that of tax collectors and Gentiles?

He who rewards perfection reserves nothing for corruption except condemnation. Consider, O lover of perishable things and neglecter of yourself: you can forgive another who sins against you, but you cannot forgive yourself.

And because no greater remedy for so grave an evil can be found than to forgive what you are able to forgive, so that what you are able to commit may be forgiven you, you cannot erase it yourself.

“Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me.”

If one who loves father or mother more than God is unworthy of him, how much more unworthy is one who loves earth or a pig more than God? Such a person is shown to love these things more because, for their sake, he does not hesitate to offend love, which is God.

Amen I say to you: Unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.

[Col. 0256C]

The neglect of this command will be followed by an irremediable and endless torment. The gate of the heavenly kingdom is narrow: it admits the little ones but excludes the enormous. Whoever, therefore, stands ready for slaughter, wishing to appear terrifying not through the humility of little children’s simplicity but through the ostentation of a giant, is altogether rejected from this entrance.

Hasten to fulfill it while you have your hands and feet unbound, for days will come of which you will say, “I do not like them”; when, with feet and hands bound, you will be sent into the outer darkness—that is, the freedom to flee and to act will be taken away.

“Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times?” Jesus says to him: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.”

[Col. 0256D]

“Wicked servant, I forgave you the whole debt because you begged me”—up to this point. “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts. Put your sword back in its place. For all who take up the sword will perish by the sword. Have salt among yourselves, and keep peace among yourselves.”

For it is a grave evil for one who has sinned not to forgive his brother from the heart. Hence it happens that sins once forgiven through repentance are recalled for punishment.

As the soul is better than the body, so the sword by which the soul is destroyed eternally is worse than the sword by which the body is killed for a time.

Just as any dish without salt is not [Col. 0257A] suitable or useful, so every virtue—even faith itself—is of no avail for a person’s salvation without peace.

“Which of these three seems to you to have been neighbor to the man who fell among robbers?” And he said: “The one who showed mercy to him.” “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth that I heard from God. Abraham did not do this. You do the works of your father. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.”

If the priest and the Levite, who did not inflict wounds upon the man wounded by robbers, but were not his neighbors because they did not help him, were not neighbors, how much less are those who inflict wounds? Whoever, therefore, makes himself estranged from neighborliness by not showing mercy is also estranged [Col. 0257B] from the medicine that the heavenly Samaritan mercifully poured into the wounds of the man lying there.

Whoever seeks to kill a member of the household of faith is not a son of Abraham, because Abraham did not do this. Rather, he does the works of his father—that is, of the devil, who was a murderer from the beginning. Those who follow the supremely good shepherd are sheep; but those who pursue him in his members are wolves.

“If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also will my servant be.”

Whoever serves follows; whoever opposes pursues hostilely.

[Note: [Col. 0257C] “I give you a new commandment.” No statement seems to me more fitting or more appropriate for commending mutual concord and love among Christians than those final words of Christ the Lord that Agobardus records here. Christ regarded the matter as so important that he wished it to be commended to his apostles and disciples as though on the tablets of his final will. He repeated and impressed it upon them so often for no other reason than to show that it was especially his desire that the apostles and disciples—among whom, as Saint Leo says in his fourth letter, all the bishops of the Churches were represented—should live in concord and, by their example, urge the people toward mutual love.

For that divine mind foresaw what he clearly predicted through the evangelists: that, once he had left the earth, when the enemy of humanity had sown weeds among the wheat, controversies and quarrels would arise among Christians—not only among the people but also among the ministers. And why not, since the apostles themselves, men filled with that spirit of Christ and still warm from Christ, who breathed and preached nothing but peace and concord in accordance with their Lord’s example, nevertheless fell so far backward that they stirred up something like enmity against one another?

Nor am I speaking of some ordinary member of the apostolic company—far be envy from my words—but of those two leaders of the apostles, Peter and Paul, the latter of whom boasts in a remarkable manner that he is an imitator of Christ. Yet this very imitator of Christ, Paul himself, teaches us that when Peter came to Antioch, and indeed after receiving the Holy Spirit, he opposed him to his face because he was blameworthy.

Did the dispute between Paul and Barnabas also become so inflamed, likewise at Antioch, that it ended in separation? And were the Corinthians, still a young planting of Christ, not reproved by Paul because even then there were among them dissensions, divisions, rivalry, and quarrels?

Heresies then arose, and schisms arose, which tore that seamless tunic, disturbed the peace of the Church, and nearly destroyed the concord of the brethren. This happened while Christianity was still fervent, while the innocent Church was still wandering in its cradle, while the flock was still small, while it was counted glorious to suffer reproach for the name of Christ.

But after the Church had put away its swaddling bands and, laying aside its childish garment, had become stronger and entered adolescence, the innocent Church no longer crying in its cradle, the love of brotherhood gradually slipped from Christian hearts, and a stubborn eagerness to harm and deceive one another crept in. Hence arose lawsuits, hence quarrels, hence wars and killings, and everything that can be destructive to Christian concord.

From this source came the Gundobad law, which prescribed that disputes be ended by single combat when other proofs were lacking. Agobardus attacks it vigorously, as the matter required, because it was profoundly contrary to Christian piety and simplicity. Yet such is the changeability of human affairs that this law was afterward received throughout all the provinces everywhere, to such an extent that even cases involving churches and monasteries, when obscure, were settled by single combat, with champions appointed by both sides; for that is what the fighters were called.

At last, by God’s providence, this most evil law was abolished by the edicts of princes and the canons of councils. But as evils are more persistent in their victory, it is retained today—not indeed for ending lawsuits, but for ending quarrels and disputes. Although the sternest edicts have been issued against this savage custom, and most recently the wisest of kings, Louis XIV, renewed them, this stubborn and unconquerable madness for fighting nevertheless persists, and no one yields to the laws.

If people could be recalled from that savagery by warnings and exhortations, they should be reminded that fraternal concord and sincere, wholly unfeigned love are very dear to Christ, and that he commanded his followers to love one another just as he had loved them. For this is the true mark of the Lord’s disciples: that they have love for one another. This was Christ the Lord’s new and final commandment.]

“I give you a new commandment: that you love one another, [Col. 0258A] as I have loved you, so that you also may love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

“I ask not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, so that they also may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me.” Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger. For human anger does not accomplish the righteousness of God.

If the Lord’s disciples are recognized by love, the devil’s disciples are recognized by quarrels and disputes.

If unity draws the world to faith, disagreement drives the world to unbelief.

But if you have bitter zeal and disputes in [Col. 0258B] your hearts, do not boast and become liars against the truth. This is not wisdom descending from above, but earthly, natural, demonic. For where there is jealousy and contention, there are instability and every evil work.

And the apostle Paul says: “Do not contend with words, for it is useful for nothing except the ruin of the hearers”—speaking of that wisdom which is not from above but earthly and demonic. And blessed Paul indicates the same when he says: “Avoid profane and empty talk. For they advance greatly toward ungodliness, and their speech spreads like gangrene.”

If, then, contention of heart shows people to be liars against the truth, and contention of words subverts [Col. 0259A] the hearers, how much more does contention of hands and weapons?

Not one evil work, or merely a part of evil works, but every evil work, as Paul also shows: “For those who are contentious and do not obey the truth but obey iniquity, there will be wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress upon every human soul that works evil.”

But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, compliant, consenting to what is good, full of mercy and good fruits, judging without hypocrisy. The fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

Consider, O judge, that the wisdom which judges without hypocrisy, deceit, or fraud is peaceable and full of mercy.

[Col. 0259B]

“From where do wars and disputes arise among you? Is it not from this—from your desires that wage war in your members? You desire and do not have; you kill and are jealous, and you cannot obtain; you dispute and wage war, and you do not have because you have not asked. You ask and do not receive because you ask wrongly, so that you may spend it on your desires. Adulterers, do you not know that friendship with this world is enmity with God?”

Here it is plainly shown from where wars and disputes arise.

Whoever, therefore, wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God. “Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that will come upon you.”

Since he does not say, “Whoever is a friend,” but “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world,” he clearly shows that, just as the Lord declares in the Gospel that the man who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in [Col. 0259C] his heart, even if he has not reached the completion of the wicked act, so whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is already an adulterer, even if he has not attained the honors and riches of the world. Thus the apostle Paul says not, “Those who become rich,” but, “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and a snare of the devil,” and thereby become enemies of God.

For it is better, if such is the will of God, to suffer while doing good than while doing evil.

This statement shows that even those who do good suffer the evils of this world, not—as many suppose—only those who do evil.

[Col. 0259D]

Therefore be prudent and watchful in your prayers. Above all, maintain continual mutual love among yourselves, because love covers a multitude of sins. For your part, applying every effort, supply virtue in your faith, knowledge in virtue, self-control in knowledge, endurance in self-control, godliness in endurance, brotherly affection in godliness, and love in brotherly affection.

The person who rises up to fight against his neighbor does not have continual love. But this too must be noted: if love covers a multitude of sins, quarrels and disputes heap up an abundance of crimes.

[Col. 0260A]

If all these qualities are present and abound in you, they will make you neither idle nor fruitless in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For whoever lacks these things is blind and gropes with his hand, having forgotten the cleansing of his former sins. “By this the children of God and the children of the devil are revealed. Everyone who is not righteous is not from God, nor is the one who does not love his brother; for this is the message that you heard from the beginning: that we should love one another. Not like Cain, who was from the evil one and killed his brother. And why did he kill him? Because his works were evil, but his brother’s were righteous. Do not marvel, brothers, if the world hates you. We know that we have passed from death to life because we love the brethren. Whoever does not love his brother is a murderer. [Col. 0260B] And you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him. By this we have known the love of God: that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.”

Here the Apostle clearly shows that the person in whom these virtues are present is not unfruitful or empty, whereas the one in whom they are absent is blind and walks in darkness.

“Bless those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse. Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep. Have the same mind toward one another; do not set your mind on high things, but associate with the lowly. Do not be wise in your own sight. Repay no one evil for evil; provide what is good, not only before God but also before all people. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live in peace with all people; do not [Col. 0260C] defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath. For it is written: ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay,’ says the Lord. But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. For by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Love does no evil to one’s neighbor. Therefore love is the fullness of the law.”

We must not only refrain from persecuting those who persecute us, but also from cursing them; on the contrary, we must bless them from the heart.

Woe to the world because of scandals! Great blindness and profound misery! We have not yet learned that our neighbor has done us harm, and by our own evil we try to portray as an evildoer the person who may perhaps be innocent. [Col. 0260D]

We must not only refrain from making people weep; on the contrary, whenever we see anyone weeping, we ourselves ought to weep with them.

We, who are stronger, ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak and not please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor for the good, for edification. For Christ did not please himself, but, as it is written: “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me.” For whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope.

You do not wish to please for his good the person against whom, with arm extended [Col. 0261A] and sword brandished—or [Note: [Col. 0261D] holding a *matarus*. The copyist whom Masson employed did not understand what *matarus* was. He therefore thought the foreign, or rather corrupt, word was at fault; this caused him to print *manum tenens* (“holding the hand”) instead of *matarum tenens* (“holding a matarus”). A *matarus* is a kind of weapon, smaller than a spear; I think it is what is called a missile in the *Life of Louis the Pious*. Even today the Gascons, or at least the Basques, who form part of the Gascon people, carry weapons of this sort on journeys and elsewhere.] holding a *matarus*—you stand ready to strike so savagely that, stripped of every virtue, he is thrown to the ground and confesses himself guilty, even if he is not.

May the God of patience and consolation grant you to have the same mind toward one another according to Jesus Christ, so that with one accord and one mouth you may glorify God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore welcome one another, just as Christ also welcomed you, for the glory of God.

Where people oppose one another with their mouths—that is, with words—in disputes, there can be no unity of mind; consequently, God is not glorified by such people but is continually dishonored.

“Love is patient; love is kind. Love does not envy; it does not act improperly; it is not puffed up; it is not [Col. 0261B] ambitious; it does not seek its own; it is not provoked; it does not think evil; it does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails.”

If, compelled by the love of Christ, we ought to be harmonious and attuned to our neighbors, it must be considered who rises up to quarrels and dissensions. Certainly, the servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, correcting with modesty those who resist.

Love is patient and kind because it tolerates through patience those whom it loves through kindness. If the person who tolerates someone but does not love him does not perform the work of love, how much more is this true of the person who does not even tolerate him? If love does not provoke, if it is not stirred to anger, and does not rejoice over iniquity, [Col. 0261C] it must be considered how far from love are those who provoke one another and fight for earthly desire. Love never fails because it is always progressing and never comes to decline.

“For whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you. For the love of Christ urges us, because we judge this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose for them.”

Those for whom Christ died ought not to live for themselves but for Christ. Whoever lives for Christ in no way wishes to harm his neighbor. Therefore it must be asked [Col. 0261D] for whom the person who prepares to harm his neighbor—[Col. 0262A] by killing him or striking him down—is living: for himself or for the devil, since it is certain that he is not living for Christ.

“Brothers, rejoice; be perfect; encourage one another; have the same mind; live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you. Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice. Be kind and compassionate toward one another, forgiving one another, just as God forgave us.”

It belongs to the perfect to have the same mind—that is, to think as one, not in diverse and opposing ways—and therefore to have peace. But those who act contrary to this by quarreling and disputing should consider whether the God of peace is with them. Since it is certain that the person who does not have God, who is the life of souls, is dead, it follows without doubt that it belongs to the dead to put others to death and to wish that their neighbor should not live.

[Col. 0262B]

Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us. Our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers and authorities, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

This statement is a rule for Christians, and it is so clear that anyone can examine himself in it as in a mirror.

“Brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is holy, whatever is lovable, whatever is of good repute—if there is any virtue or any praise of discipline—think about these things. What you have learned, received, heard, and seen in me, do; and the God of peace will be with you.”

[Col. 0262C]

Whoever wishes to have the God of peace with him—that is, to be his temple—should do what this statement teaches, so that he may glorify and bear God in his body. For whoever does not bear God in his life will, willingly or unwillingly, bear the enemy to his own death.

“We urge you, brothers: correct the unruly, console the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient toward all. See that no one repays evil to anyone with evil; but always pursue what is good toward one another and toward all. Rejoice always. Pray without ceasing. Give thanks in everything. For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for all of you.”

This statement too is a rule of Christianity. But it must be carefully noted that [Note: [Col. 0261D] he commands a person to be patient, in imitation of Christ, whose imitators we must be if we wish to appear to be his true disciples. For he certainly gave a great example of patience when he returned nothing for wrongs and injuries and did not wish to raise a hand against anyone in order to avenge insults. He did this so that we might all understand with what zeal and care we ought to swallow injuries and endure the insults of wicked people, since the Lord and our God himself left his enemies unavenged.

Cyprian speaks very aptly in Letter 65 about the slanders that Christ endured from the Jewish priests: “All these things were done by him humbly and patiently, so that we might have an example of humility and patience.” Thus he was shaping us for peace and for maintaining patience amid slanders and contradictions; this, as the same Cyprian says in his book *On the Good of Patience*, is the good of Christ. Hence Tertullian, in his book *On Patience*, calls Christ “the lord of patience and its teacher.”] to be patient [Col. 0262D] toward all, not only toward friends. For patience is especially necessary toward enemies.

[Col. 0263A]

“I saw beneath the altar the souls of those slain because of the word of God and because of the testimony that they held, and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, O holy and true Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?’ And white robes were given to each of them, and they were told to rest for a little while longer, until their fellow servants and their brothers, who were to be killed as they had been, should be completed.”

This statement teaches that the time for vengeance upon the faithful is not in the present. For if the saints who suffered for the faith seek vengeance upon their persecutors—upon whom, naturally, vengeance is to be taken—and do not obtain it, how do these men, whenever they become angry with their neighbors and rush into hand-to-hand conflict, suppose that God serves [Col. 0263B] them and ministers to their most bitter passions?

“Woe, woe, that great city Babylon, that mighty city! For in one hour your judgment has come.”

If Babylon’s judgment will come in one hour, how do its citizens so frequently suppose that God judges on their behalf? This statement shows that God’s judgments are hidden and impenetrable. Hence it is clear that those who suppose that God’s impenetrable judgments are plainly revealed through wars and killings are foolish and presumptuous.

“For I will require the blood of your souls from the hand of every beast and from the hand of humanity; from the hand of a man and of his brother I will require the human soul. Whoever sheds human blood, his blood will be shed, [Col. 0263C] for humanity was made in the image of God.”

This first law, given by God to humanity, most emphatically forbids the shedding of human blood.

Not everyone who kills a person will be killed bodily. Rather, it must be understood according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “For everyone who takes up the sword will perish.” And the Apostle says: “No murderer has eternal life abiding in him.” The reason why such guilt is followed by so great a punishment is that humanity was made in the image of God.

“The tents of robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God, although he has placed everything in their hands. Why, then, do the wicked live, and why are they exalted and strengthened [Col. 0263D] by riches? Their offspring remain before them, a throng of relatives and grandchildren in their sight. Their houses are secure and peaceful, and God’s rod is not upon them. Their ox conceives and does not miscarry; their cow gives birth and is not deprived of its offspring. Their little ones go out like flocks, and their children leap about in play. They hold the tambourine and the lyre and rejoice at the sound of the organ. They spend their days in prosperity and in a moment descend to the underworld.”

This statement indicates that the prosperity of the wicked is temporary. Therefore those who suppose that each person here receives what he deserves are mistaken.

“If you have an arm like God, and if you thunder with a voice like his, gird yourself with splendor, lift yourself up on high, and [Col. 0264A] be glorious, and clothe yourself in splendid garments. Scatter the proud in your anger; look upon every arrogant person and humble him. Look upon all the proud, confound them, and crush the wicked where they stand. Hide them together in the dust and plunge their faces into the pit. Then I too will confess that your right hand can save you.”

Those who think they can discover people’s merits through conflicts and encounters should have an arm like God, thunder with a voice like his, gird themselves with splendor, lift themselves up on high, and be glorious; then they may be their own saviors, scattering, humbling, crushing, and plunging the wicked and proud into the pit.

“For I will not trust in my bow, nor will my sword save me, because you saved us from our enemies and confounded those who hate us. In God we will praise all day long, and we will confess your name forever. Yet you have confounded and cast us away, and you do not go out with our armies. You have turned our backs before the enemy, and those who hate us have plundered [Col. 0264B] themselves from us. You gave us like sheep to be devoured, and you scattered us among the nations.”

This statement suggests that no one is saved, or shown to be righteous or innocent, through bodily armor, and that God himself does not always repay the merits of the good with rewards in this life. Hence Paul, who fought the good fight, completed his course, and kept the faith, says that the crown of righteousness is laid up for him, not that he has received it. For in the present he received five times forty lashes less one, was beaten with rods three times, [Col. 0264C] stoned once, suffered shipwreck three times, and endured all the dangers that he himself lists.

“O God, the nations have entered your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem a heap of stones. They gave the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, and the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth. They poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them. We have become a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those around us.”

This statement demonstrates exactly the same thing as the preceding one.

“Who will ascend the mountain of the Lord? Or who will stand in his holy place? The one innocent in hands and pure [Col. 0264D] in heart, who enters without blemish and practices righteousness, who speaks truth in his heart, who is not quick with his tongue, who has done no evil to his friend, and has not endured reproach against his neighbor. Whoever overlooks loss for the sake of his friend is righteous; but the way of the wicked will deceive them. The patient person is better than the strong, and the one who rules his spirit is better than the conqueror of cities. Weapons and swords are on the way of the perverse; but the guardian of his soul keeps far away from them. When your enemy falls, do not rejoice, and when he is ruined, do not let your heart exult, lest the Lord see it, be displeased, and turn his anger away from him.”

Let the brotherly warrior see whether he is innocent in his hands and pure in heart, [Col. 0265A] and whether he does everything that the following statement enumerates.

The person who does not rule his spirit through patience does not merely refuse to be better; he does not even wish to be good. When he contends with his neighbor over a brute animal, he is unwilling to overlook even a small loss for God’s sake.

“Rescue those who are being led to death, and do not cease to free those who are being dragged to destruction. If you say, ‘Our strength is insufficient,’ the one who examines the heart understands; nothing escapes the one who saves your soul, and he will repay each person according to his works. I saw wickedness under the sun in the place of judgment, and in the place of justice, iniquity. And I said in my heart: ‘God will judge the righteous and the wicked, and there will then be a time for every matter.’ I turned to other things and saw the calumnies committed under the sun, the tears [Col. 0265B] of the innocent, and no one to console them; nor could they resist, deprived of everyone’s help, the violence done to them.”

You must not only refrain from leading people to death; you must also rescue those who are being led away, if you do not want the Lord to repay you according to your works.

When the Lord distinguishes between the righteous and the wicked, then there will be a time for every matter—not now. The Church, longing for that time, asks the Lord, saying: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation.” If people had at least been able to administer justice in this matter, the evils enumerated by the following statements would not exist.

“If you see the oppression of the needy, violent judgments, and justice overturned in a province, do not marvel at [Col. 0265C] this matter, because one who is higher than the high is above it, and there are others still more eminent above these.”

For God, who is exalted above the exalted, observes these things. He has placed his angels over the judges and kings of the earth; they can certainly prohibit injustice and have greater power on earth than any human authorities. But because he preserves judgment and the consummation of the world for the end, when the harvest has ripened and the reapers have come, he will command that the wheat be separated and the weeds handed over to the fire. Therefore he now waits and delays the sentence until the field of this world has been more fully cultivated.

“The righteous person perishes in his righteousness, and the wicked lives for a long time in his wickedness.”

It is God’s hidden wisdom to afflict the saints [Col. 0265D] now, so that they receive evil during their life, and not to visit sinners for their crime, but to reserve them as though for punishment, so that he may restore eternal good to the former and inflict everlasting evil upon the latter.

It is better, according to God’s will, that the righteous perish in his righteousness than that he kill the wicked because of his wickedness. And because this is what happens, the following statement comes to pass:

“There are righteous people to whom many things happen as though they had done the deeds of the wicked, and there are wicked people who are so secure as though they possessed the deeds of the righteous.”

Among the other vanities that occur in the world with varied outcomes, I also discovered this: that what ought to happen to the wicked frequently happens to the righteous, [Col. 0266A] while the wicked live so happily in this world that you would think them supremely righteous.

“No one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred; but everything is kept uncertain for the future, since all things happen alike to the righteous and the wicked, to the good and the bad, to the pure and the impure, to the one who sacrifices victims and the one who despises sacrifices. As with the good, so with the sinner; as with the perjurer, so with the one who swears truly.” This is the worst thing among all that happens under the sun, because the same things happen to everyone.

If everything is kept uncertain for the future, the folly of some people is astonishing: by accursed combats they think they can make certain what is uncertain.

“I turned to something else and saw under the sun that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor [Col. 0266B] bread to the wise, nor riches to the learned, nor favor to the skilled, but time and chance in everything. No one knows his end. But just as fish are caught by a hook and birds are seized in a snare, so human beings are caught in an evil time when it suddenly overtakes them.”
