This statement does not deny providence but teaches that the outcomes of things are uncertain to human beings. The Epistle to the Romans agrees with this passage: “It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy.” The statement “There is no bread for the wise” is confirmed daily by the example of many who, although they are exceedingly wise, lack necessities; an educated man may remain hidden in obscurity, suffer persecution, and not only fail to enjoy favor among the people but waste away in poverty and destitution. These things happen because everything flows in an uncertain condition, [Col. 0266C] and merits are not repaid in the present but in the future.

“There is an evil that I saw under the sun, as though proceeding by error from the face of a ruler: a fool placed in high dignity, while the rich sit below. I saw servants on horses and princes walking on the ground like servants.”

He therefore recalls that he observed this injustice in the world: that God’s judgment appears unjust, and that, whether through ignorance or without God’s will, in the powers of the world or in the leadership of the Church, those who are rich in speech and wisdom, and rich also in good works, often sit in obscurity, while some imprudent person holds the chief place in the Church. This occurs through the agency of the one who possesses power [Col. 0266D] in the world, while he suppresses the powerful and learned and does not permit them to appear among the peoples; but those whom he knows to be imprudent he appoints as superiors in the Churches, so that the blind may be led by the blind into the pit.

“Why have you shown me iniquity and labor, to see plunder and injustice against me? Judgment and contradiction have become stronger. Therefore the law has been torn apart, and judgment does not reach its conclusion; because the wicked prevail against the righteous, therefore perverse judgment goes forth.”

These words are spoken by people who do not know that God’s judgments are unsearchable, nor the depth of his riches, wisdom, and knowledge, and that God does not see as a human being sees. Human beings look only at present things; God knows what is future and eternal.

The saints’ common complaint to God is why an unjust judgment is made against them and innocent blood is shed in persecutions—as when, if they stand before the tribunal of secular judges, a judge who has accepted gifts condemns the innocent and frees the guilty. This may be said not only of the judges of the world but sometimes also of [Note: [Col. 0267C] the leaders of the Church, that is, bishops. Thus bishops are called by the ancients and by the Roman pontiffs themselves, as was stated in the letter to Lupus of Ferrières.] the leaders of the Church: that because of gifts they tear the law apart, do not bring judgment to its conclusion, and allow the wicked to prevail against the righteous; and that in judgment the sin of the rich is defended more than the truth of the poor. Hence the complaint is that perverse judgment goes forth.

We must not be troubled by this inequality of affairs, seeing that at the beginning of the world the righteous Abel was killed by the wicked [Col. 0267B] Cain, and later Esau reigned in his father’s house while Jacob was in exile. The Egyptians afflict the children of Israel with mud and bricks.

Why do you look upon those who act unjustly and remain silent while the wicked devours one more righteous than himself? And do you make human beings like the fish of the sea, and like a creeping creature that has no ruler?

Our Lord, knowing the weight and measures of his mercy, sometimes does not hear the one who cries out, in order to test him, provoke him more earnestly to prayer, and, as though refined by fire, make him more righteous and pure. Understanding this, the Apostle—according to what he says after having obtained mercy [Col. 0267C] from the Lord—says, “We do not grow weary”; and he blesses God at all times and knows that “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

[Col. 0268A]

“From Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem; and he will judge among many peoples and rebuke strong nations even at a distance. And they will beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into pruning-hooks. Nation will not take up the sword against nation, nor will they learn war any longer. Come and see the works of the Lord, what wonders he has done upon the earth, removing wars to the ends of the earth. He will break the bow, shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire.”

Alas, what grief! Among many nations it has already happened that, when the passion for warfare ceased, people devoted themselves to agriculture, on account of which weapons too were turned into implements. Yet the Burgundians still have need, because of their continual domestic wars, to forge sickles, pruning-hooks, and ploughshares into swords.

[Col. 0268B]

“Be still and know that I am God.” But my feet had almost stumbled; my steps had nearly slipped. For I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners, because they gave no thought to their death and their vestibules stood firm. They do not share in the labor of human beings, nor are they scourged along with humanity. Therefore they were nourished for arrogance; they clothed themselves in iniquity; their eyes advanced from abundance; the thoughts of their hearts overflowed. They mocked and spoke wickedly, uttering slander against the Most High.

This statement too says that these things would have been partly fulfilled in bodily reality, if the Burgundians had consented.

[Col. 0267C]

## EXHORTATORY SERMON TO THE PEOPLE ON THE TRUTH OF THE FAITH AND INSTRUCTION IN EVERY GOOD

### I

Listen, our brothers, household of Christ, flock of the supreme shepherd, people of his pasture, and sheep of his hand. Enter the gates of the eternal king with confession, and his courts with hymns, so that it may be said to you: “Behold, now bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord, who stand [Col. 0267D] in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near.” And how near he is! For “in him we live and move and have our being.” He is interior to all minds, interior to all bodies; he fills within, surrounds without, carries below, and protects above.

He who is now so near will come at a time when he cannot be found. And why will he not be found, since he is everywhere and absent nowhere? Because then there will no longer be time to seek the Lord, but only to undergo punishment—for those who do not find him now.

Do what the psalm says: “Let all your works give thanks to you, O Lord, and let your holy ones bless you.” Bless him together with them, or give thanks to the Lord together with all his works.

### II

You do not need to travel from place to place, from one kingdom to another people, in order to seek the Lord. He offers himself to you freely and says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter in to him, and dine [Col. 0268D] with him, and he with me.” What has ever been so sweet? What so delightful?

He adds also and says: “Whoever conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne.” Behold, he wishes to enter to you, so that you may dine with him; do not be reluctant to open. He wishes not only to dine with you in your mind, but also to raise you to his throne, so that you may sit with him. To one promised such things, what more ought to be desired?

The Lord still makes this promise and says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

Therefore let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands, and be like people waiting for their lord when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks they may immediately open to him. Blessed are those [Col. 0269A] servants to whom the Father and the Son come and with whom they make their dwelling.

But woe to those who drive such a guest away from themselves, for wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul, nor will it dwell in a body subjected to sins. The Holy Spirit of discipline flees deceit and withdraws from thoughts that lack understanding. Therefore do not think about empty things; do not desire what perishes. Avoid foolish and old-womanish tales, and train yourselves in godliness.

Open to the Lord who knocks, so that he may enter to you, dine with you, and make his dwelling with you. Nor does he knock silently; as he knocks, he speaks to every soul: “Open to me, my sister, my beloved, my dove, my undefiled one.”

But, bringing every diligence to bear, minister virtue in your faith, and in virtue [Col. 0269B] knowledge. For if, by meditating upon your faith and hope, you grow in knowledge and understanding of God, you do not live empty or without fruit, and thus you retain the Lord as your guest.

### III

Faith is that by which we believe in one almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: the true Trinity, the true Unity. O how true is the Trinity, in which no one is born from himself and no one proceeds from himself, but one from another! The Son is born from the Father, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Without doubt, therefore, it is evident that one is he who begets, another he who is begotten, and another he who proceeds from both. O how true is the Unity, in which there is not one Spirit of the Father and another of the Son, but one Spirit of both! Nor does he first proceed from the Father into the Son and then from the Son to spread [Col. 0269C] the gift of charity in the hearts of the faithful; rather, he proceeds simultaneously from both.

The Father’s deity is not one, the Son’s another, and the Holy Spirit’s another, but the deity of the three is one; and therefore there is truly one God. For if it were one and another, there would not be one God.

There is therefore one deity, one eternity, one majesty, one power, one will, one operation, one piety, and one glory. And because the three are altogether distinct from one another, there is Trinity; and because they are not different things, there is Unity. Because the Father is not the Son, nor the Son the Father, nor either of them the Holy Spirit, there is true Trinity. But because the Father is what the Son is, and the Son is what the Father and the Spirit are, there is true Trinity [editorial correction: Unity].

No power or will of the Father preceded the Son’s birth. Likewise, nothing preceded the procession of the Holy Spirit.

We confess the Father as the begetter [Col. 0269D] of the Son, but the maker of heaven and earth and of all visible and invisible things. We confess the Son as unbegotten of the Father, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, born, not made, *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιον) with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth; through whom the angels praise the majesty of the Father, the dominions adore it, the powers tremble before it, and the forces of heaven and of the heavens of heaven attend upon it.

We confess the Holy Spirit as life-giving, proceeding from the Father and the Son, to be adored and glorified with the Father and the Son, who spoke through the prophets.

We confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the three together bestowing the gift—as undivided without confusion, eternal without time, and equal without distinction.

[Col. 0270A]

One is the great and exceedingly praiseworthy Lord, whose greatness has no end and whose wisdom cannot be numbered. He is certainly great, not in bulk but in power: although through the bulk of a body he is nowhere, through his uncircumscribed substance he is absent nowhere.

### IV

This true Trinity and true Unity, the one Lord, all the angels praise from the heavens and in the heights; so do all the powers, the sun and moon, the stars and light, the heavens of heavens, and the waters that are above the heavens. For “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.”

From the earth, dragons and all the abysses praise him; so do fire, hail, snow, ice, and the storm winds; mountains and hills, fruit-bearing trees and all cedars; beasts and all cattle, reptiles and winged [Col. 0270B] birds; kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth; young men and maidens, old men with the young—for his name alone has been exalted.

His praise is above heaven and earth, and his glory is in the assembly of the holy ones. For he is praised in his holy places, in the firmament of his power, in his mighty deeds, according to the abundance of his greatness; with the sound of the trumpet, with psalter and lyre, with tambourine and dance, with strings and organ, with well-sounding cymbals, with cymbals of jubilation.

### V

Since all these things together—rational and irrational—unceasingly praise God, how ought human beings, created in the image and likeness of God and called to the praise of his glory, to be sluggish, slow, or idle? Those creatures indeed praise the Lord [Col. 0270C] always. We, even if we cannot do so always, should at least praise him frequently. To us it is said through the Apostle: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession, so that you may proclaim the mighty deeds of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light.”

And through the prophets: “Tell of all his wonders; proclaim his purposes among the nations; make known his inventions among the peoples.”

Of these mighty deeds and wonders, and of their character, Scripture proclaims in the following words:

“He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire. He founded the earth upon its foundation; it will not be shaken forever and ever. He set its cornerstone when the morning stars praised him together and all the sons of God shouted for joy. In his strength the seas [Col. 0270D] were suddenly gathered together, and by his wisdom he struck down the proud. He stretched out the north over the void and suspended the earth upon nothing. He binds the waters in his clouds, so that they do not burst forth together below. He takes away the drops of rain”—and, as another translation says, “his innumerable showers.”

“He measured the waters in the hollow of his hand and weighed the heavens with a span. He suspended the mass of the earth with three fingers and set the mountains by weight and the hills on a balance. His throne is a flame of fire, and his wheels are burning fire. A fiery and rushing stream goes forth from before him. Thousands of thousands minister to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stand before him.”

For all the armies of heaven attend him, not only on his right but also on his left. Of these the prophet saw one come forth, [Col. 0271A] saying: “I will go, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets”—that is, of the king who was deceived and destined to be deceived—“so that he might ascend to the place where his destruction had been prepared.”

### VI

The prince or great one of this left-hand army, out of envy for the holy man Job, demanded him, so that he might be granted to him by the Lord—not in order to test him, which was accomplished through that evil one against his will, but in order to condemn him, as the abundance of his wickedness desired.

The prince of this left-hand army [Col. 0271B] approached the first human being, created good and well by the good God, inflamed by the fire of envy. He deceived him, made him a transgressor, and subjected him to every kind of corruption. He made him, cast down from the fellowship of the angels, his companion; and, snatched away from angelic light, he subjected him to his own darkness and made him liable to eternal death.

But the supremely good and merciful Lord, in order to restore so great a ruin and heal so great a wound, sent his Son, God the Word, so that he might become flesh—that is, a true human being—and dwell among us, that is, in the perfect humanity which he assumed for us (Augustine, *On John*, Tractate IV), from us—that is, from the holy Virgin, prepared and preserved for this purpose.

He dwelt bodily, not spiritually as in the other saints—that is, by the gift of grace—as it is written: “Whoever adheres to the Lord is one spirit.” Although they adhere to the Lord and God dwells in them, this does not thereby make them gods by nature, as in Christ “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily,” so that he is God substantially.

This humanity, from the moment it began to exist, [Col. 0271C] could be nothing other than God and the only Son, because the Only-Begotten became flesh, so that he might be true God, true human being, and one God. And although flesh is one thing and divinity another, he himself is not one person in the flesh and another in divinity; rather, from both there is one Christ, God and human being, with the truth and integrity of both natures remaining—namely, with humanity not changed into divinity, nor divinity transformed into humanity.

He who is one Christ, God, from both natures, is adored with the Father and the Son by every creature, as we said above, just as he was adored before the Word became flesh. For the unchangeable deity, which in its incarnation unchangeably assumed our weakness, in which it could die, could neither be diminished nor increased.

[Col. 0271D]

### VII

Therefore our one Lord Jesus Christ, true God and true human being, came to suffer, in order to endure all those things that had been foretold about him through the Scriptures. Thus, after being seized, bound, scourged, mocked, and suspended on the cross, when the hour came for him by his own power to lay down his life—being about to take it up again by his own power—he cried out in a loud voice, saying: “It is finished.” And, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.

Born by a true birth, he endured the true suffering of true flesh, underwent a true death, and, by a true resurrection of the flesh, presented himself alive to his disciples with many proofs. For forty days he appeared to them and spoke about the kingdom of God. He ate and drank in their presence, not from necessity but by his power.

[Col. 0272A]

While they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes. And as they gazed toward heaven while he was going, behold, two men stood beside them in white garments, and they said: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.”

Therefore he sits in the flesh that he assumed for us at the right hand of the Father, and he will come in glory to judge the living and the dead; his kingdom will have no end.

He himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth—the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. He is praised with the Father by the angels in this way: “To him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb be blessing, honor, glory, and power forever and ever.”

[Col. 0272B]

And when he comes in the majesty of himself and of the Father, he will be so feared by those whom he is about to judge that they will say to the mountains and rocks: “Fall upon us and hide us from the face of him who sits upon the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb; for the great day of his wrath has come, and who will be able to stand?”

After this, all the elect from every nation, tribe, people, and language will stand before the throne in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palms in their hands. They will cry out in a loud voice, saying: “Salvation belongs to our God who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb.”

Of them it is said: “These are those who have come out of the great tribulation, who washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.” Therefore they are before the throne of God and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits upon the throne will dwell over them.

They will hunger no more and thirst [Col. 0272C] no more; neither will the sun fall upon them, nor any heat, because the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne will shepherd them and lead them to springs of the waters of life, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.

Everlasting joy will be upon their heads; they will obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and groaning will flee away.

This city of God—that is, the whole assembly of all the saints—does not need the sun or the moon to shine upon it. For the glory of God has illumined it, and its lamp is the Lamb.

And it will be said to it: “No longer will iniquity be heard in your land; devastation and destruction will not be within your borders. Salvation will occupy your walls, and praise your gates. The sun will no longer be your light by day, nor will the brightness of the moon illumine you; but the Lord will be your everlasting light, and your God your glory. Your sun will no longer [Col. 0272D] set, and your moon will not wane, because the Lord will be your everlasting light, and the days of your mourning will be complete.”

Your people—all the righteous—will inherit the land forever. The nations will see your righteous one, and all kings your glorious one. You will be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord has named. You will be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord and a royal diadem in the hand of your God.

You will no longer be called “Forsaken,” nor will your land any longer be called “Desolate.” Rather, you will be called “My delight is in her,” and your land “Inhabited,” because the Lord has taken delight in you, and your land will be inhabited.

For a young man will dwell with a virgin, and your sons will dwell in you. As a bridegroom rejoices over a bride, so your God will rejoice over you.

[Col. 0273A]

Nothing defiled or that practices abomination and falsehood will enter it, nor foolish virgins who did not take oil with them—only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life. And they will reign forever and ever.

### VIII

These illustrious testimonies of Holy Scripture display the unity and equality of the one seated upon the throne and of the Lamb—that is, of the Father and the Son—since one great day of their wrath is spoken of.

He remained equal to the Father even after he became less than the Father. Therefore the holy Fathers, namely, the teachers of the Church, handed down this brief hymn to be sung after the Psalms, Antiphons, and Responsories:

“Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit; as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end.”

And when the elect from every people [Col. 0273B] and language are said to stand before the throne in the sight of the Lamb, and one salvation is sung to him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb, and they together illumine their city, this very point is shown, so that we may know that the Father and the Son are one, even after the Son became less and proved obedient unto death, even death on a cross.

For this reason God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.

He also shows how the exalted head raises its body to such sublimity, and shows the unity of the head and the body, namely, of the bridegroom and the bride. Hence it is said: “He clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness, [Col. 0273C] like a bridegroom adorned with a crown and like a bride adorned with her jewels.” He called himself both bridegroom and bride.

This is that great unity, the immeasurable and ineffable good that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart,” which God has prepared for those who love him. The Lamb is the bridegroom of his flock and the shepherd of his sheep; he is a lamb in his passion, a lion in his resurrection, an eagle in his ascension, a cornerstone, and also the stone cut from the mountain without hands, which became a great mountain filling the whole earth.

This is the kingdom that will never be destroyed and will not be handed over to another people; it will itself stand forever.

Of this unity and ineffable sublimity of the head and body, the prophet Daniel says: “I was watching in a vision of the night, and behold, one like [Col. 0273D] a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven. He came to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him. And he gave him power, honor, and a kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and languages will serve him. His power is an eternal power that will not be taken away, and his kingdom will not be destroyed.”

### IX

This unity and sublimity of the head and body, which will one day exist in appearance and reality, must already now be held with every devotion in faith and hope.

The Apostle commends it sublimely when he says: “He who descended is the same one who ascended above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things. And he gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers, for the completion [Col. 0274A] of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all attain the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature humanity, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ; so that we may no longer be children, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine, by the wickedness of human beings, by cunning directed toward the deception of error.”

“But practising the truth in love, let us grow in every way into him who is the head, Christ: whose whole body, joined together through every joint of supply, according to the working in the measure of each individual member, produces the body’s growth for its own building up in love.”

And again: “The head, from whom the whole body, supplied and constructed through its bonds and connections, grows into its increase.”

And elsewhere: “Be diligent [Col. 0274B] to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling. There is one Lord, one faith, one baptism. There is one God and Father of all, who is above all, through all, and in us all.”

Likewise, concerning the unity of the members: “For just as the body is one,” he says, “and has many members, while all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or gentiles, slaves or free, and we were all given to drink of one Spirit. For the body is not one member but many.”

### X

That the mediation of the mediator between God and human beings, our Lord Jesus Christ, joins every elect creature to the Father, so that in this ineffable unity [Col. 0274C] of spirit there is no difference of race, condition, or sex, but that from angels as well as human beings one household and one city of God may be formed, and that Christ may be the one head of so great and wondrous a unity, the Apostle teaches as follows:

“Do not lie to one another. Strip off the old human being with his deeds, and put on the new, the one being renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who created him. Here there is no gentile and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian and Scythian, slave and free, but Christ is all and in all.”

And again: “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus.”

And elsewhere: “I want you to know [Col. 0274D] that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a woman is man, and the head of Christ is God.”

Likewise: “All things are yours; but you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.”

And elsewhere: “He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, because in him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers. All things were created through him and in him; and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him.

“He is also the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he himself might hold first place in everything. For in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, [Col. 0275A] whether the things on earth or the things in heaven.”

And again: “In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power.”

### XI

For this ineffable unity, the mediator between God and human beings himself, God and human being, Christ Jesus, prayed to the Father at the time of his passion, saying:

“Sanctify them in the truth. Your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, so I sent them into the world. And for them I sanctify myself, so that they too may be sanctified in truth. I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, so that all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I am in you, that they too may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me.

“And I have given them the glory that you gave [Col. 0275B] me, so that they may be one, just as we are one. I in them and you in me, so that they may be perfected into one, and the world may know that you sent me and loved them as you loved me.

“Father, I desire that those whom you gave me may be with me where I am, so that they may see my glory, which you gave me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world.”

When this great and sublime unity will be completed, the Apostle shows most carefully, saying:

“As all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ, but each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ’s, who believed at his coming. Then the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when he has abolished every principality, power, and force. For he must reign [Col. 0275C] until he places his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death. For he has subjected all things beneath his feet.”

And again: “Behold, I tell you a mystery. We will all rise, but we will not all be changed. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we will be changed. For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality.

“When this mortal body has put on immortality, then the saying written will come to pass: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?’ The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

This victory is not reached without struggle, [Col. 0275D] for no one ought to be crowned unless he has competed lawfully.

### XII

That part of this unity which still journeys on earth has adversaries against whom it must fight without ceasing, because “all who desire to live devoutly in Christ Jesus suffer persecution.”

First there are the devil and his angels, our enemies, against whom the Apostle wishes us to arm ourselves, saying:

“Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil. For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.

“Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist in the evil [Col. 0276A] day and, having perfected everything, stand firm. Stand therefore, with your loins girded in truth, and clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, and with your feet shod for the preparation of the Gospel of peace. In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, praying at all times in the Spirit with every prayer and supplication.”

There are also human beings who persecute openly, of whom the Lord himself says:

“Behold, I am sending you like sheep among wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. Beware of human beings. For they will hand you over to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you. You will be led before governors and kings because of me, as a testimony to them and to the nations.”

[Col. 0276B]

There are also other persecutors who pursue people with enmity, hatred, slander, accusations, losses, quarrels, and various harshnesses. Against these one must not fight with weapons, but with patience and endurance, as the Apostle teaches that we should be patient toward all, and as the Lord commands us not to resist evil.

“If anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also.” And again: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven.”

And again: “For if you forgive human beings their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses. But if you do not forgive human beings, neither will your Father forgive your sins.”

There are also enemies of the faith, to whom the Apostle says: “In the last times some will depart from the faith, attending to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy.”

Against these one must fight not with bodily weapons, but with spiritual ones: namely, by examples, the authority of Scripture, and arguments founded upon faith and truth.

There are also daily enemies [Col. 0276C] whom we cannot avoid either by place or by time. The Apostle enumerates them, saying: “Do not fulfill the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. These oppose one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish. But if you are led by the spirit, you are not under the law.

“The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, debauchery, the service of idols, sorcery, enmities, quarrels, jealousies, anger, strife, [Col. 0276D] dissensions, factions, envy, murder, drunkenness, revelry, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.”

Against these one must fight not only by reason but also by labor, abstinence, self-control, and vigils, as the Apostle instructs us by his own example, saying: “I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected.”

Therefore, instructing his disciple and already confident concerning himself near the end of his life, he exults in this way:

“But you, be watchful in all things, labor, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry. For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight; I have completed the course; I have kept the faith. Henceforth [Col. 0277A] a crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day—not only to me, but also to all who love his coming.”

### XIII

Amid all these things, let the faithful take care not to presume entirely, or even in the least, upon their own strength, but rather upon God’s help, so that they may reach the end of good works or persevere in a good work. For the Lord says: “Without me you can do nothing.”

And the Apostle says: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure.”

And again: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves.”

And again: “Not that we are competent to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves; our sufficiency is from God.”

And the Lord says: “No one can come to me unless the Father, who sent me, draws [Col. 0277B] him.”

God does many good things in a human being that the human being does not do; but a human being does no good thing unless God grants that the human being may do it.

For human beings do their own will, not God’s, when they do what displeases God. But when they act according to their will in such a way that they serve the divine will, although they willingly do what they do, the will nevertheless belongs to him by whom what they will is both prepared and commanded.

God loves us as those whom we will become by his gift, not as those whom we are by our own merit. God foresees, knows beforehand, assists, and rewards his own good works in us.

No one is good except God alone, who is not good by another’s goodness. Human beings, however, are good not by their own goodness but by God’s goodness. He is the source and origin of goodness—indeed, he is goodness itself—from whom comes every good thing, and without whom there is nothing [Col. 0277C] good.

## XIV.

This is the faith and hope of the Catholic Church, which is the pillar and foundation of the truth, proclaimed in the Law and the Prophets, in psalms and hymns, evangelized by the apostles, attested by the martyrs, and expounded by the teachers. Whatever is found contrary to this faith, and whatever is discordant and contradictory, is inept and profane, empty talk that greatly advances ungodliness, and therefore the doctrine of demons and of antichrists, concerning whom the Apostle says:

“Little children, it is the last hour; and just as you heard that the Antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have arisen.”

Of these another apostle says:

“These are grumblers, complainers, walking according to their own desires; and their mouth speaks arrogance.”

The Antichrist is the head of them all. Concerning him the Apostle says:

“But we ask you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering to him, that you not be quickly shaken from your understanding, nor terrified, either by spirit, or by word, or by a letter supposedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were imminent. Let no one deceive you in any way. For unless the apostasy first comes, and the man of sin, the son of perdition, is revealed—he who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God—do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you these things? And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time. [Col. 0278A] For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work; only let him who now restrains it continue to restrain it, until he is removed from the midst. And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the manifestation of his coming. His coming is according to the working of Satan, with every power, signs, and lying wonders, and with every deceit of unrighteousness for those who are perishing, because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved. Therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie and all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to unrighteousness.”

Concerning this time the Lord also says in the Gospel:

“Then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor will be. And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened. [Col. 0278B] Then, if anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is the Christ,’ or ‘There,’ do not believe it. For false Christs and false prophets will arise, and they will give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led astray. Behold, I have foretold it to you.”

Concerning the Antichrist the prophet Daniel says:

“He will speak words against the Most High, and will wear down the saints of the Most High; and he will intend to change times and laws. They will be delivered into his hand for a time, times, and half a time. Then judgment will sit, so that his power may be taken away, crushed, and destroyed to the end. But the kingdom, the power, and the greatness of the kingdom under the whole heaven will be given to the people of the saints of the Most High, whose kingdom is everlasting.”

And again:

“From one of them there came forth one little horn; and it became great toward the south, toward the east, and toward the Strength; and it was magnified even to the Strength of heaven. It cast down some of the host and of the stars, and trampled them. It was magnified even against the Prince of the host; from him it took away the continual sacrifice and cast down the place of his sanctuary. Strength was given against the continual sacrifice because of sins; truth was cast down to the ground, and it acted and prospered.”

And again:

“After their kingdom, when iniquities have increased, a king of shameless countenance and understanding riddles will arise. His strength will be reinforced, but not by his own power; and, beyond what can be believed, he will lay everything waste, prosper, and act. He will destroy the mighty and the people of the saints according to his will. Deceit will prosper in his hand; he will magnify his heart, and in the abundance of all things he will destroy many. He will rise up against the Prince of princes, and without a hand he will be crushed.”

And again:

“The king will act according to his will; he will exalt and magnify himself against every god, and he will speak grand things against the God of gods. He will prosper until wrath is completed, for the appointed end has been fixed. He will pay no regard to the God of his fathers; he will be in the desires of women, and he will care for no god, because he will rise up against all things.”

In the book of Revelation:

“I saw a beast rising from the sea, having seven horns, ten heads, and upon its horns ten diadems; and upon its heads the name of blasphemy. [Col. 0279A] The beast that I saw was like a leopard, its feet like those of a bear, and its mouth like the mouth of a lion. And the dragon gave it his power and great authority. I saw one of its heads as though it had been mortally wounded, but its mortal wound was healed. The whole earth marveled after the beast. They worshiped the dragon that gave authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying: ‘Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?’ It was given a mouth speaking great things and blasphemy, and it was given authority to act for forty-two months. It opened its mouth in blasphemies against God, to blaspheme his name, his tabernacle, and those who dwell in heaven. It was given power to make war with the saints and to conquer them.”

And again:

“I saw another beast rising from the earth; it had two horns like a lamb, and it spoke like a dragon. It exercised all the authority of the first beast in its presence. It made the earth and those who dwell in it worship the first beast, whose mortal wound had been healed. It performed great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in the sight of human beings. It deceived those who dwell on the earth because of the signs it was given to perform in the presence of the beast.”

And again:

“I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, which has seven heads and ten horns. The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the abyss, and it will go into destruction. The inhabitants of the earth will marvel—those whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world—when they see the beast that was and is not. Here is the meaning that has wisdom. The seven heads are seven mountains upon which the woman sits, and they are seven kings. Five have fallen, one is, and another has not yet come; and when he comes, he must remain for a short time. The beast that was and is not is itself the eighth, and is one of the seven, and goes into destruction. The ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom, but receive authority as kings for one hour after the beast. These have one purpose, and they will give their power and authority to the beast. These will fight with the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called, chosen, and faithful.”

And again:

“I saw the beast and the kings of the earth and their armies gathered to make war against him who sat upon the horse and against his army. [Col. 0279D] The beast was seized, and with it the false prophet who had performed signs before it, by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. These two were thrown alive into the lake of burning sulphur and fire, and the rest were killed by the sword of him who sat upon the horse, which proceeds from his mouth.”

And again:

“When the thousand years are completed, Satan will be released from his prison. He will go out and deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, and gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea. They went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city. Fire came down from God out of heaven and devoured them; and the devil who deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulphur, [Col. 0280A] where the beast and the false prophets will be tormented day and night forever and ever.”

## XV.

Three are mentioned here: namely, the devil, the beast—which is the Antichrist—and the false prophet, who will display all the power of the Antichrist in lying signs and wonders. The two beasts, through the activity of the devil, are the most prominent members in the whole body of the lost.

The devil is indeed the inventor and cause of every evil, invisible to human beings as they live mortal lives. He has been a murderer from the beginning. All the evils he has carried out and continues to carry out he has exercised chiefly through human beings. He brought about that first evil, perpetrated through the deception of the first human beings, by means of the serpent, because there was no human being through whom the first human beings could be deceived. He spoke to Eve through the serpent, and to Adam through Eve. Then through Cain he killed Abel. Afterward all evils sprouted, iniquities increased and continue to increase, until they reach the summit of evil, when, with God permitting and ordering it, the devil will take for himself a most suitable vessel: namely, that condemned and ruined human being, the head of the lost. He will grow to such wickedness that the worst of all human beings will be able to display himself and be heard as though he were God, and will rise up against all things, exalting and boasting himself above everything called God and everything worshiped.

Thus it has already been said of him by the Lord:

“There is no power upon earth that can be compared with him who was made so as to fear nothing. He sees every lofty thing. He is king over all the sons of pride.”

That this was said of him is shown above, where it is said:

“When the sword seizes him, he will not be able to stand; neither spear nor breastplate.”

## XVI.

That all the lost constitute one body, whose head is this same Antichrist, is shown above, where it was said:

“The members of his flesh adhere to one another.”

And again:

“His body is like cast shields, compacted with scales pressing upon one another. One is joined to another, and not even a breath passes through them; one adheres to another, and those holding fast to one another are in no way separated.”

Concerning this body and its head—that is, the devil or the Antichrist—the prophet Ezekiel also says:

“Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh, king of Egypt, great dragon, who lie in the midst of your rivers and say: ‘The river is mine, and I made myself.’ And I will put a bridle in your jaws, and fasten the fish of your rivers to your scales; and I will draw you out from the midst of your rivers, and all the fish of your river will cling to your scales, and I will cast you into the desert, you and all the fish of your river.”

Concerning his power, in a psalm—but according to the Hebrew translation—it is said:

“‘The wicked, according to the height of his anger, does not seek; there is no God in all his thoughts. His ways bring forth labor at all times. Your judgments are far from his face. He despises all his enemies. He speaks in his heart: “I shall not be moved from generation to generation; I shall be without evil.” His mouth is full of cursing, deceit, and greed; under his tongue are deceit and iniquity. He also lies in wait beside the vestibules, in hidden places, to kill the innocent. His eyes watch the strong; he lies in wait in secret like a lion in his lair. He lies in wait to seize the poor; when he has drawn him into his net, he crushes him and throws him down, and he rushes upon him powerfully with his strength.’”

## XVII.

What this body of the devil and the Antichrist is in the present, and what awaits it in the future, is shown in another psalm, where it is said:

“Why do you boast in evil, you who are mighty in iniquity?” and so forth.

The book entitled *Wisdom* also speaks of this body of the lost: how, at the end of time, overwhelmed by eternal miseries, it will undergo late and fruitless repentance, saying:

“Then the righteous will stand with great confidence,” and the rest that follows:

“Therefore we have gone astray from the way of truth; the light of justice did not shine for us, and the sun of understanding did not rise for us. We grew weary in the way of iniquity and perdition, and we traveled difficult roads, but we did not know the way of the Lord. What did pride profit us, or what did the boasting of riches bring us? All those things passed like a shadow, like a messenger running past, and like a ship that crossed through the moving water.”

That angels and human beings who are lost constitute one body, assigned to one torment, the Lord shows in the Gospel, where he says that he will declare in judgment:

“Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”

Concerning the torment of wicked angels and human beings, the prophet Isaiah says at the end of his book:

“They will go out”—there is no doubt that the holy will do so—“and they will see the corpses of the men who transgressed against me. Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished, and they will be, to the satiety of the sight, for all flesh.”

This punishment and place of punishments is called in the Gospel “outer darkness.” There the servant who is not accused of fraud but of uselessness is thrown, because he did not multiply by trading the talent he had received; and there the other man who did not attend the wedding dressed in a wedding garment is thrown after his hands and feet have been bound.

This place is frequently called *infernus*—the underworld—in Scripture. Thus there is the saying in Proverbs:

“The path of life is above the instructed, so that you may turn aside from the lowest underworld.”

And the righteous king Hezekiah says to the Lord:

“The underworld will not confess to you, nor will death praise you.”

And in the psalm:

“In the underworld, who will confess to you?”

And again:

“The dead will not praise you, Lord, nor all who descend into the underworld.”

And blessed Job says:

“All that is mine descends into the deepest underworld.”

It is also designated by other names, as the same blessed Job again says to the Lord:

“Release me, then, so that I may mourn a little before I go and do not return to a land of darkness covered with the gloom of death; a land of misery and darkness, where the shadow of death and no order dwell, but everlasting horror.”

For what is signified by the name “dark land” except the closed land of Tartarus? The underworld is not without reason called a land, because whoever has been seized by it is held firmly. Thus whoever is held, expelled from the sight of the strict Judge, is confined in the land of misery and darkness: for outside, pain torments those whom blindness, separated from the true light, darkens within. The avenging flame of past vices burns there, but it has no light.

## XVIII.

It must nevertheless be understood that, just as in the house of the Father there are many dwellings according to the diversity of virtue, so the inequality of crimes subjects the condemned to different punishments in the fires of Gehenna. Although Gehenna is one for all, it does not burn all with one and the same intensity. Yet its punishments torment those immersed in them beyond their strength, and preserve them while extinguishing in them every support of life, so that the end of life punishes them in such a way that their torment always lives without end; for through torments it hastens toward an end, yet, continually failing, endures without end. [Col. 0282B]

Thus for the wretched there is death without death, an end without end, failure without failing, because death lives, the end always begins, and failure does not know how to fail.

[Note: [Col. 0281D] “Death without death.” This is taken from Saint Gregory, *Moralia on Job*, Book IX, chapter 48. [Col. 0282D] See our notes on Book III of Salvian’s *On the Governance of God*.]

Although the fire there does not shine even for consolation, it nevertheless shines to some degree so that it may torment them more greatly. For the wicked will also see their followers with them in torment, illuminated by the flame, those for whose love they sinned; so that those who carnally loved their life contrary to the commands of the Creator may also be afflicted by their destruction, thereby increasing their own damnation.

This place of punishments is also called a lake, but one in which there is no water, as it is said through Zechariah:

“You too, by the blood of your covenant, have sent out your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water.”

And through the righteous king Hezekiah:

“Those who descend into the pit will not await your truth.”

It is called the lowest part of the lake, the foundations of the lake, and the lowest part of the abyss.

## XIX.

You, then, washed with the water of baptism, honored with the Christian name, and marked with the sign of salvation, consider carefully and weigh diligently whether we have reason to fear, whether there is anything that we must guard against with every concern of mind. Let us in no way neglect to think about this, as the sacred psalm also teaches, saying:

“I will declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin.”

And again:

“For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me.”

Let us occupy not only our minds by thinking about these things, but also our tongues by speaking of them. The other temporal dangers, the smaller they are, should trouble us less. These dangers, however, the greater they are, should disturb and grieve us all the more, and pierce us with profound pains, sighs, and groanings, so that what is written may be fulfilled in us:

“Pierce my flesh, Lord, with your fear, for I have feared your judgments.”

Faithfully consider what blessed Job confesses about himself, saying:

“I have always feared God as though waves were swelling over me, and I could not bear his weight.”

If he who feared in this way could ever allow his mind to be occupied with vain thoughts or his tongue with idle words, then turn the eyes of your mind through the neighboring regions and consider mortals in our own times. What do you see them devoting themselves to? What do they think, say, and do? How many strive to do what the Apostle commands, saying:

“Let no evil word proceed from your mouth, but only such as is good for the building up of faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear.”

And again:

“Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to God. Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.”

And again:

“What then, brothers? When you come together, each of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has a tongue, has an interpretation. Let everything be done for edification.”

And again:

“Whether you eat or drink, or do anything else, do everything to the glory of God.”

Truly, exactly as the Lord says:

“A good person brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart.”

Just as it is entirely true that one who has a treasure of goodness in his heart cannot do otherwise than think and speak good things, so one who speaks empty and useless things demonstrates that he is empty and devoid of spiritual grace. For if he were not, he would run forward and undoubtedly build up those who hear him in faith and thanksgiving to the glory of God.

## XX.

Behold, you have now heard the good things that you ought to love and desire with your whole heart, and you have heard the evils that you ought to flee with all your strength and every effort. [Col. 0283C] Therefore consider what place the love of perishable things and the fear of passing loss and danger can rightly have between the two.

It must be understood altogether that, just as it is a sin to love unlawful or immoderate temporal goods, so it is entirely a sin to fear them in a disordered manner—and so great a sin that it is counted among the other sins, excludes one from the kingdom of heaven, and condemns one to eternal punishments, as it is read in Revelation:

“But for the fearful, the unbelieving, the accursed, murderers, fornicators, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake burning with fire and sulphur, which is the second death.”

Blessed Peter the Apostle teaches not only that persecutors must not be feared, but also that whatever harm persecutors can inflict must not be considered an injury. He joins together two testimonies, from the psalm and from the prophet Isaiah, saying:

“The eyes of God are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”

And:

“Who is there who can harm you if you are zealous for what is good?”

The Lord also commanded this through the prophet, saying:

“Do not fear the reproaches of human beings, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies. For as a garment, so the worm will eat them; and as wool, so the moth will consume them. But my salvation will be forever.”

Similarly, he commands through himself in the Gospel:

“Do not fear those who kill the body, and after this have nothing more that they can do.”

## XXI.

That not fearing persecutors of the body is a great gift from God the Lord shows when he speaks to Jeremiah, saying:

“Therefore gird your loins, and rise and speak to them everything that I command you. Do not be afraid before them, for I will not make you fear their face. For I have made you today a fortified city, an iron pillar, and a bronze wall against the whole land.”

Similarly, to Ezekiel:

“Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces, and your forehead harder than their foreheads. Like adamant and flint I have made your face. Do not fear them or be afraid before them, because they are a rebellious house.”

And because fearing an enemy who can inflict only bodily harm is a grave crime, the psalm instructs us to pray in this way:

“Hear, O God, my prayer when I entreat you; rescue my soul from the fear of the enemy.”

As though it said: “Free me from the fear of the enemy and subject me to your fear.”

The same is expressed in another psalm:

“Because many fight against me, I will fear from the height of the day; but I will hope in you.”

This should be understood as though he were saying: “Many indeed fight against me. But, strengthened by the help of your grace and hoping in you, I will fear not their multitude but your exalted light.”

Those who fight against me cannot penetrate the height of the day, whose twelve apostles shine “by the mouth” (*ore*; F.: *horae*, “hours”).

## XXII.

Those who truly trust in the Lord confidently say in God:

“I will praise my words; in God I have hoped. I will not fear what flesh can do to me.”

And again:

“The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me.”

For who will bring an accusation against God’s elect, as the Apostle says? And again:

“Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword—as it is written: ‘For your sake we are killed all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter’? But in all these things we conquer through him who loved us.”

Perfect Christians, therefore, not only do not fear tribulations; they even glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, testing produces hope, and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into their hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to them. They regard it as complete joy when they fall into various trials. Beyond all doubt, they know that through tribulations and distresses they are forged, tested, and purified like gold and silver in a furnace of fire, not like straw or hay. For the heavenly Father applies the fire of tribulation to them for this purpose: to wash away impurities, not to turn them into ashes.

Thus the voice of the saints is found in the psalm:

“For you have tested us, O God; you have examined us by fire, as silver is examined. You brought us into a snare; you placed tribulations upon our backs; you set human beings over our heads. We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment.”

They endure all these things through various persecutions. Often they tolerate superiors whom they know to be worse, as though such people had been placed upon their heads. They tolerate not only tribulations but also temptations, like fire and water, through adversities and prosperities. They take every care that neither fire burn them nor water corrupt them. Passing through fire and water—that is, through prosperity and adversity—they are brought out into refreshment, where they fear no enemy and endure no distress, because perpetual refreshment and perpetual rest remain.

## XXIII.

But in order to reach this, what must all the faithful do amid so many evils—some passing away, some remaining; some to be endured, others to be fled—except what the Lord and our Redeemer, liberator and governor, commanded when he instructed his disciples concerning the final tribulations, saying:

“Watch at all times, praying that you may be considered worthy to escape all these things that are about to happen and to stand before the Son of Man.”

Similarly, when he warned them of his passion, already at hand, he said:

“Pray that you do not enter into temptation.”

Earlier, when the Pharisees asked him when the kingdom of God would come, after answering he added:

“One must always pray and not grow weary.”

He showed this through the parable of the harsh judge and the widow who persistently appealed to him. In another place, when he said through a parable that someone who persistently asked obtained from another the convenience of having bread given to him, he added:

“And I say to you: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.”

And shortly afterward:

“If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him?”

## XXIV.

Concerning this matter—that is, the constancy, or rather the persistence, with which the faithful ought to be concerned and attentive in prayer—the whole sacred Scripture of the New and Old Testament is full of examples and commands. In them, in a way incomprehensible to human beings, certain things that almighty God promised would happen were delayed by him so that they might be obtained through prayers.

Thus, when the Apostle Peter was detained by Herod and thrown into prison, prayer was made to God by the Church without interruption.

Paul also exhorts his hearers, saying:

“Pray at all times in the Spirit, and remain watchful in it with all perseverance and supplication for all the saints, and for me, so that speech may be given to me when I open my mouth with confidence, to make known the mystery of the Gospel, for which I am an ambassador in this chain, so that in it I may dare to speak as I ought.”

And similarly in another place:

“Devote yourselves to prayer,” he says, “remaining watchful in it with thanksgiving; praying at the same time for us also, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also imprisoned, so that I may make it manifest as I ought to speak.”

## XXV.

That each person ought not to be concerned in prayer only for himself or for the saints, but also for all human beings, the same blessed Paul shows by commanding:

“I urge, then, first of all, that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and for all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and chastity.”

That this should be done not only at all times but also in every place he shows by adding shortly afterward:

“I desire, therefore, that men pray in every place, lifting up pure hands without anger or disputation.”

Similarly, women should pray in an adorned manner, with modesty and sobriety.

## XXVI.

Above all, it must be understood that prayer ought to be without anger and disputation, and likewise without hesitation, with complete confidence and faith. This is shown in many places, but especially where Peter says to the Lord:

“Rabbi, behold, the fig tree that you cursed has withered.”

And Jesus answered and said to them:

“Have faith in God. Truly I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, ‘Lift yourself up and throw yourself into the sea,’ and does not hesitate in his heart but believes that whatever he says will happen, it will be done for him. Therefore I say to you: Whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you will receive it, and it will come to you.”

Blessed James the Apostle also admonishes us to pray in this way, saying:

“If anyone asks God for wisdom, who gives generously to all and does not reproach, it will be given to him. But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing. For whoever doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind. Therefore let that person not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord. A man of divided mind is unstable in all his ways.”

The great abundance of God’s sweetness grants such faith and confidence; to him it is said in another psalm:

“For you, Lord, are gentle and mild, and of great mercy toward all who call upon you.”

And through the prophet it is said to us:

“Dissolve the bonds of wickedness; loosen the bundles that oppress; set free those who are broken; and tear apart every burden. Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor and homeless into your house. Then your light will break forth like the morning, your healing will quickly arise, your justice will go before your face, and the glory of the Lord will gather you. Then you will call, and the Lord will answer you; you will cry out, and he will say: ‘Behold, here I am.’”

These verses clearly demonstrate that the one who devoutly hears the Lord is mercifully heard by the Lord. But another translation begins these prophetic verses in this way:

“Dissolve the obligations of violent sureties; release the broken into remission; tear up every unjust document; and at the end, while you are still speaking, he will say: ‘Behold, here I am.’”

This is something that must be preached, heard, and fulfilled.

## XXVII.

The almighty and merciful Lord graciously announces this abundance of his sweetness through the prophet Ezekiel, saying:

“Turn and repent from all your iniquities, and iniquity will not be your ruin. Cast away from you all your transgressions by which you have transgressed, and make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why will you die, house of Israel? For I do not desire the death of the dying, says the Lord. Turn back and live.”

The same is shown through Isaiah, when he says:

“Let the wicked abandon his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him, and to our God, for he is abundant in forgiveness.”

The Lord offers us this sweetness of his mercy through the same prophet, saying:

“Remember these things, Jacob and Israel, for you are my servant. I formed you; you are my servant, Israel; you will not forget me. I have wiped away your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. Return to me, for I have redeemed you.”

And again:

“I am, I am he himself, who wipes away your iniquities for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins.”

## XXVIII.

Those who have neglected these sweetest calls of God in the present time, while he may be found and while he is near, and when the time has come not for working but for each person’s receiving according to his works, will hear bitter reproaches:

“I called, and you refused; I stretched out my hands, and there was no one who looked. You despised all my counsel and neglected my rebukes. I too will laugh at your destruction.”

Then there will be for them that fruitless conversion of which the Lord speaks through the prophet to all, saying:

“Turn back, and you will see what there is between the righteous and the wicked, and between one who serves God and one who does not serve him. For behold, the day will come, burning like a furnace; and all the proud and all who commit ungodliness will be straw. The coming day will set them ablaze, says the Lord of hosts, and it will leave them neither root nor shoot. But for you who fear my name the sun of justice will rise, and healing will be in its wings; you will go out and leap like calves from the herd, and you will trample the wicked when they are ashes beneath the soles of your feet, on the day that I act, says the Lord of hosts.” [Col. 0288B]

[Col. 0287B]

# Agobard’s Lamenting Letter [Note: [Col. 0287D] There is no title at this point in the royal manuscript. We have therefore retained the one found by Masson, although we had intended to change this as well. But because this title has now prevailed, and this little book is accustomed to being cited under the name *Lamenting Letter*, it seemed that it ought not to be changed.]

## Concerning the Division of the Frankish Empire among the Sons of the Emperor Louis

### I. To the most glorious lord Louis, emperor: Agobard, his little servant.

Since every faithful person owes the sincerity of faith to every other faithful person, there is no doubt that faith must especially be kept by all who are faithfully subject to the divine ordering toward a faithful prelate entrusted with the governance of the commonwealth. This is taught by the Apostle:

“Let every soul,” he says, “be subject to the higher authorities.”

Although no one should be treated unfaithfully, another apostle therefore also says:

“Be subject to every human creature for God’s sake.”

And we are taught to pray for all human beings, for kings and for those who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety.

And elsewhere it is said:

“Therefore be subject, not only because of wrath, but also for the sake of conscience.”

## II.

Since these things are so, and all who are faithful ought to be faithful to you, how can anyone be faithful to you if, seeing or understanding your danger, he does not intervene as far as he can, so as to point it out and make it known to you—provided, of course, that an opportunity or the means to do so is not entirely denied him? I call almighty God to witness, he who searches hearts and reins, that no other reason exists for which I presume to write these things except that I grieve, beyond what I can express, over the dangers that seem to threaten you, especially the danger to your soul. For just as the soul is a substance far more excellent than the body, so we ought to care for the soul with far greater solicitude than for the body, as the Lord himself teaches in the Gospels, as you know very well.

## III.

[Note: The present year, that is, the year 833. For at that time Louis was planning to suppress the rebellion of his sons and gathered an army against them, with an altogether disastrous outcome, as the writers of that period relate.]

In the present year, then, amid the crushing, disturbance, agitation, and affliction of the earth and of those who dwell upon it, such great evils have multiplied that no human being could enumerate them. Yet no cause demanded, and no necessity compelled, the conflicts in which we are engaged to take place as they have. For if you had wished, you could have lived a peaceful and tranquil life with your sons, no less than your father and your grandfather.

[Note: Your father and grandfather, Charlemagne and Pippin.]

May almighty and merciful God, who dwells in your heart, be present; and may your patience also be present, by which you surpass other men, so that you may deign to hear and weigh calmly what I suggest.

## IV.

At the time when you took care to make your son a participant in your name,

[Note: A participant in your name. This occurred in the year 817, as Einhard relates. “The emperor Louis,” he says, “held at Aachen the customary general assembly of his people, at which he crowned his first-born son Lothar and made him his associate in name and empire.” But the author of the Chronicle of Moissac relates these matters at greater length and also confirms the events that Agobard recounts here: “In the year 817 the emperor Louis celebrated Easter at the palace of Aachen. That same summer he ordered an assembly of the people from his entire kingdom or empire to be held there, at Aachen, the royal seat—that is, of bishops, abbots, counts, and the elders of the Franks. He disclosed to them the plan of his counsel, which he had conceived: to establish one of his sons as emperor. For he had three sons by his wife, Queen Ermengard: the first was named Lothar, the second Pippin, and the third Louis. Then the whole people approved that, while he was still alive, he should make one of his sons emperor, just as his father Charles had made him. Then the entire people fasted for three days, and litanies were performed. After this the aforementioned emperor chose Lothar, who was the eldest, as emperor, and by means of a golden crown bestowed the empire upon him, while the people acclaimed him, saying, ‘Long live the emperor Lothar.’ Great rejoicing took place among the people on that day. The emperor himself blessed the Lord, saying: ‘Blessed are you, Lord our God, who today have granted that one sprung from my seed should sit upon my throne while my eyes behold it.’” An unpublished author of the Annals of Aniane writes that this took place on 30 July.]

you began the matter publicly by asking this question, saying:

[Col. 0289A]

“Does a man have to postpone what concerns the stability of the kingdom and the strength of government, or does he not?”

When everyone had answered that it was useful and necessary, that it should not be postponed but rather hastened, you immediately disclosed to all what you had discussed with only a very few. You said that, because of the frailty of life, whose end is uncertain, you wished, while you still had the strength, to bestow the imperial name upon one of your three sons, in whom you might in some way discern the will of God.

To discover that will, you ordered everyone to undertake a three-day fast, and the priests to offer sacrifices to almighty God, who is gracious, gentle, and abundantly merciful toward all who call upon him. You also ordered that everyone should give alms throughout those three days more generously than usual, so that almighty God, who in supreme kindness governs the hearts of those who hope in him, might pour his will into your heart and not allow your will to incline toward anyone except him whom he approved.

Thus you completed everything that ought to be done in such a matter, with such faith and hope that no one could doubt that this had been infused and inspired in you by God. You assigned portions of your kingdom to your other sons,

[Note: You designated portions of the kingdom—Aquitaine to Pippin and Bavaria to Louis.]

but, so that there might be one kingdom and not three,

[Note: So that there might be one kingdom, not three. Yet matters later turned out differently. After Louis’s death, one kingdom of the Franks became three, as has been stated in the note to the letter of Lupus of Ferrières.]

you preferred the one whom you had made a participant in your name above them. Thereafter you ordered the proceedings to be written down, the written document to be signed and confirmed, and, once he had become a participant in your name,

[Note: You sent him to Rome. No one should suppose that this happened immediately after the assembly at Aachen, or that Lothar was sent in order to receive the imperial crown from the Roman pontiff, as though the approval of the supreme pontiff had then been necessary for the new emperor. I shall quote Einhard, a man raised at court, well acquainted with public affairs, and a highly skilled and judicious writer concerning the rights of majesty. After saying that Lothar was sent by his father to Italy in the year 822 to administer the government there, he finally says under the year 823: “While Lothar was administering justice in Italy according to his father’s command, and was already hastening to return from Italy, at the request of Pope Paschal he came to Rome. Received honorably by him, on holy Easter day at Saint Peter’s he received the crown of the kingdom and the name of emperor and Augustus. From there he returned to Pavia, and in June came to the emperor.” The author of the Life of Louis the Pious writes the same, as do others.]

you sent him to Rome so that the deeds you had performed might be approved

[Col. 0290A]

and confirmed by the supreme pontiff. Thereafter,

[Note: You ordered everyone to swear. It is chiefly from this passage that Father Theophilus Raynaud attempts to prove that Agobard should be freed from blame, even though he supported Lothar’s rebellion against his father. “The insolence and shamelessness of recent writers,” he says, “who measure others by their own character, cannot in any way be tolerated. They portray Agobard as a factionalist and rebel and adorn him with such flowers that, if we believe them, he acted in the matter under discussion with an entirely malicious and wicked intention.
