Yet the opposite is plainly established by Agobard’s own letter to the emperor Louis, from which it is clear that Agobard undertook his actions rather through fear of violating the divine majesty and profaning the oath sworn at Louis’s own command by his son than through any ill will toward Louis.” As though it were not well known that no one admits himself guilty, and that those who begin or support a rebellion do not claim that they act for just reasons. In the end, if the pretext of the public good is lacking, they allege the breach of agreements, the violation of an oath, or something similar. If Theophilus Raynaud’s argument were valid, I could easily show that all the bishops who carried out Louis’s deposition were free from blame. For what could appear holier, more religious, or more worthy of episcopal gravity than the proceedings of that impious and abominable deposition? Yet posterity blamed those men, and none of those who lived after them has so far attempted to excuse that infamous overthrow of an excellent prince. Agobard alone will serve as an example that Lothar’s party was not without learned men who supported the rebellion with hand and tongue. I venerate Agobard from my heart, but I believe that he was a human being; and what he did wrongly I neither approve nor attempt to excuse.]

you ordered everyone to swear that all should follow and preserve such an election and division. No one considered this oath contemptible or superfluous; rather, it seemed timely and legitimate, because it appeared to pertain to peace and concord.

As time went on, whenever and wherever imperial letters were sent, they contained the names of both emperors.

[Note: The names of both emperors. The beginning of those letters was: “Louis and Lothar, emperors Augustus by divine providence.”]

But afterward, when your will had changed, the established arrangements were overturned, the name was omitted from the letters,

[Note: The name was omitted. That insult undoubtedly inflamed Lothar’s spirit. For why would his father have made him a partner in the empire if he later refused to admit his name into the partnership of the paternal empire, a partnership that had been maintained for many years?]

and attempts were made in every matter to do the opposite. Yet neither God himself, nor an angel, nor a prophet has told you, “I regret that I established it thus,” as Samuel said to Saul. Even now you do not know how the matter has been determined in the secret counsels of God.

[Col. 0290B]

And behold: without any reason or deliberation, you reject without God the one whom you chose with God; and, without awaiting the outcome of his will, you repudiate a matter that you approved when you sought his will in choosing. Your prudence does not fail to know that God must be followed, not preceded. For whoever wishes to precede him tests what is not of faith, as the Lord himself says: “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.”

## V.

I beg you, my lord, not to receive these words with disdain. Rather, enter with God into the sanctuary of your mind and speak with him through the piety of faith. There you will find that you have said to God—not in words but in deeds:

[Col. 0291A]

“Lord, we have asked and entreated the face of your regard, humbly requesting that, through your illumination and governance, we might choose a participant in the empire. But because we did not act well with you, we have found better counsel without you.”

Far be this from us—far be it! May God turn you away from rejecting God’s inspiration and establishing the will of men who think only in carnal terms, so that you are led into error and carried away.

I beg your clemency to consider, according to the prudence granted you by God, how the blessed Apostle James reproves those who, moved by their own impulses, propose to do something without regard for divine permission. He says:

“Come now, you who say: ‘Today or tomorrow we shall go into that city, spend a year there, engage in trade, and make a profit’—you who do not know what tomorrow will bring. For what is your life? It is a vapor that appears for a little while and then will vanish. Instead, you ought to say: ‘If the Lord wills, and if we live, we shall do this or that.’”

And beware of those who follow their own spirit, for faith does not belong to everyone.

## VI.

The Lord knows those who are his. And all of us who are his, however small the light of truth that we enjoy, sincerely love you through the illumination of truth and faithfully desire your everlasting happiness. For this reason we grieve over the many evils and great crimes perpetrated this year on this account, and we greatly fear that God’s fury may be roused against you.

We remember your most ardent religious devotion, which we have always known in the constancy of your prayers: singing and chanting psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to God with a pure heart; in heartfelt contrition; in the compunction of a peaceful mind; in concern for acts of mercy; and in energetic pursuit of every good work.

Therefore, as has been said, we think it necessary to fear lest this devotion grow lukewarm or grow cold. Rather, we ought to hope that it will burn more fervently and increase by persevering to the end, so that eternal salvation may follow.

## VII.

And because mention has been made above of a lawful and timely oath, it seems to me that it should not be concealed from your Excellency that there is now much murmuring among men because of the contrary and divergent oaths, and not murmuring only, but also sorrow and disparagement directed against you. This displeases me in every way. Their murmuring seems to them to bear upon what blessed Jerome says in his exposition of Jeremiah, at the place where the prophet says: “And you shall swear, ‘As the Lord lives,’ in truth, judgment, and righteousness.” The aforesaid teacher therefore says: “At the same time it must be observed that truth, judgment, and righteousness are the companions of an oath. If these are absent, it will by no means be an oath, but perjury.”

[Col. 0291B]

[Note: In other editions this book contained, besides this letter of Agobard to the Emperor Louis, also the letter of Gregory IV to the bishops of the kingdom of the Franks and the Apologetic Book on behalf of the sons of the same Louis. But both the matter itself and the authority of the ancient manuscript have persuaded us to distinguish these three works. For it is certain that the letter written to Louis ends with these words: “May the merits of your deeds enable the endeavours of this matter to approach apostolic merits.” There should then follow, though not in the same book, the letter—or rather the fragment of a letter—of Gregory IV to the bishops of Louis’s party; and it ought not to have been bound in the same fascicle for this very reason, that no mention of it occurs in the letter to Louis. Finally, the Apologetic Book undoubtedly ought to have been separated from both letters. For it is nothing other than a book issued publicly and, as is clear, circulated everywhere throughout all the provinces, to prove that the reasons which moved Lothar and his brothers to take up arms against their father were just—what we should today call in French a *manifeste*. Moreover, and this is decisive, those three compositions are separate and divided in the royal manuscript, and each begins with a capital letter, as the beginnings of books ordinarily do. But because Agobard’s later compositions have no title in the old manuscript, the copyist on whose authority the edition of Masson appeared thought that they ought to be joined. Besides, this little book too had no title in the old manuscript. We have therefore retained the title made by Masson, for no other reason than that it has already prevailed, so that learned persons cite it by that title.]

# ON THE COMPARISON OF ECCLESIASTICAL AND POLITICAL GOVERNMENT, AND ON THE WAYS IN WHICH THE DIGNITY OF THE CHURCH EXCELS IMPERIAL MAJESTY

[Col. 0291C]

## I.

Agobard to his most clement and most Christian lord, the Emperor Louis, and therefore most worthy of every praise.

Your most prudent diligence commands that both orders be ready against the disturbances of this time: the military order, namely, and the ecclesiastical—that is, both those who serve in secular warfare and those who serve in sacred ministries; the former indeed to contend with the sword, the latter to dispute with the word—so that like may be able to oppose like. In this matter it must especially be known that in a clash of arms justice from the government above is more to be expected than strength of arms; but in a contest of words truth is more to be expected than abundance of words. For this reason all must pray with the whole intention of their minds that he of whom you say, “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation,” may, because he is your illumination, shine his face upon you; and, because he is your salvation, save you in his mercy, so that in keeping with this prayer you may add: “Lord, let me not be confounded, for I have called upon you.”

[Note: The disturbances of this time, that is, the wars and dissensions which existed in the Frankish kingdom in the year 833 because of the division between Louis and his sons, as we said above.]

## II.

Therefore I, your little servant, when I learned from your sacred command that I had been ordered to hasten to your presence so equipped that, together with the other ecclesiastical men, I might be able to offer opposition by just reproof against the unjust reprovers of just reproof, thought it fitting, in the service of God and of you, to send these words appended below, drawn from the deeds and judgments of the Fathers of old, to your most glorious Excellency, so that your holy religious devotion may deign devoutly to consider the reverence which you owe, for your daily advancement, toward the apostolic see.

[Note: Debtors of this reverence. Agobard instructs Louis concerning the reverence owed to the apostolic see. Yet perhaps Agobard’s work was not necessary. For I think that no one in all Gaul hitherto—at least none of those who have been joined in communion with the apostolic see—has supposed that great reverence is not owed to the apostolic see. Certainly, in Agobard’s age, the bishops writing from the Synod of Paris in 824 to the emperors Louis and Lothar speak thus: “We do not doubt that fitting reverence of honour ought rightly to be rendered to those who sit in the sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter.”]

Finally, when blessed Pope Pelagius rebuked certain bishops because they omitted his name in the celebration of the sacred mystery—that is, in the solemnities of the Masses, namely at the beginning, where we are accustomed to say, “First of all, which we offer to you for your holy catholic Church, which may you deign to grant peace to, guard, unite, and rule throughout the whole world, together with your servant our pope”—he said to those bishops:

“I am exceedingly astonished at your separation from the universal Church, which I cannot bear with equanimity. For since the most blessed Augustine, mindful of the Lord’s saying, which placed the foundation of the Church in the apostolic sees, says that whoever withdraws himself from the authority or communion of the prelates of those sees is in schism, and declares that there is no Church other than that which is established upon the episcopal roots of the apostolic sees, how do you not believe yourselves separated from the communion of the whole world, if in the sacred mysteries you omit the customary remembrance of my name, in whom, though unworthy, you see the stability of the apostolic see at the present time to reside through succession in the episcopate?”

[Note: Pope Pelagius I. That letter was sent to the bishops of Tuscany and is found in the volumes of councils.]

[Note: Together with your servant our pope. It is an ancient custom in the Church that Catholic bishops, and especially the Roman bishop, are named during the mysteries, so that the faithful may thereby know that the pontiffs are joined in communion with the apostolic see. Pelagius complained, and rightly, that those bishops had omitted this observance. For it belongs to a good bishop to bear impatiently any attempt to make schism and division in the Church of God. But a manifest indication of schism is when someone withdraws himself from communion with the apostolic see, from which the rights of venerable communion flow to all, as the Fathers of the Council of Aquileia say in their letter to the Emperor Gratian.]

[Note: The foundation of the Church in the apostolic sees. Since in the notes to Lupus of Ferrières we promised to say more in connection with Agobard concerning the dignity and authority of the apostolic sees, the matter seems to require that we fulfil our promise, particularly because it is of such importance that scarcely any subject seems more worthy to occupy the eyes and minds of devout and learned readers. By apostolic Churches I mean, in Augustine’s sense, those which merited to possess apostolic sees and to receive epistles: that is, those both founded by apostles and to which extant apostolic epistles were written. They were several in number: Corinth in Achaia; Thessalonica and Philippi in Macedonia; Ephesus in Asia; and Rome in Italy. Tertullian lists these apostolic Churches in his book *On the Prescription against Heretics*. Besides these, Gelasius also counts Alexandria and Antioch among the apostolic sees in his decree on canonical books. Nor is it doubtful that they too were apostolic; Jerusalem and Ancyra, and also Colossae in Greater Phrygia, belong to this number. Indeed, the ancients considered the dignity of these Churches so weighty that they thought no serious matter in the Church could be decided without the knowledge of the bishops presiding over those sees, especially the Roman, Alexandrian, and Antiochene bishops; and they judged a person heretical and schismatic if he was not joined to those Churches in communion.

Thus, when Eastern councils, without consulting the Roman bishop, condemned Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and Marcellus of Ancyra, Julius sent them a rebuking letter, complaining of this procedure and maintaining that the judgment was invalid, since those bishops were not bishops of ordinary Churches but of Churches which the apostles themselves had instructed in the faith by their own labour. Hence Athanasius’s and Marcellus’s case could not have been judged without consulting him and the Roman synod; rather, it had above all been necessary to write to the Westerners about the matter, so that the great Churches might afterwards be reconciled by the common agreement of all. Marca shows that this is the true and genuine sense of Julius’s letter to the Easterners.

Augustine also acknowledges that prerogative of the apostolic Churches in Letter 162. There, discussing Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, and his colleagues, against whom a synod of Donatists had pronounced a sentence of condemnation although they were absent, he says that this judgment was invalid and that those bishops could reserve their cause for the judgment of other colleagues, especially those presiding over apostolic Churches. Thus Caecilian was safe from the attacks of his enemies, since he was joined in communion with the Roman Church and the other Churches from which the faith of the Gospel had flowed—that is, the apostolic Churches. This again is Marca’s statement. For we gladly use his authority, robbing no one of his honour, much less the man to whom I profess, always and everywhere, that I owe as much as one student of these matters can owe to another.

Pope Pelagius I also, in his letter to the patrician Valerian, when dealing with the bishops of Aquileia and Milan, reserves to his own see nothing special in matters of the universal Church except insofar as it is one of the apostolic sees. Thus he says that if any doubt arises against the decrees of universal synods, recourse must be had to the apostolic sees to receive an explanation: “But whenever some doubt about a universal synod arises for some persons, either those who desire the salvation of their souls should of their own accord come to the apostolic sees to receive an explanation of what they do not understand, etc.” A little later he adds that one separated from the apostolic sees is without question schismatic: “Whoever, therefore, is divided from the apostolic sees is undoubtedly in schism and attempts to set up an altar against the universal Church.” From this it is clear that the apostolic Churches formerly possessed great dignity and authority. And not without reason: for, as Pope Pelagius teaches after Augustine, the foundation of the Church is in the apostolic sees.

Because of this authority, Eutyches, condemned by Flavian in the Synod of Constantinople in 448, appealed indeed to a Roman synod, but not to that alone. He also appealed to the synods of Alexandria, Jerusalem, and Thessalonica, as has been excellently demonstrated in Book VII, chapter 6, of *On the Harmony of Priesthood and Empire*. Nevertheless, the Roman Church was always preferred to the other apostolic Churches because Peter and Paul consecrated it with their blood and were consecrated in martyrdom for Christ at Rome. For this same reason it was called, by antonomasia, the apostolic see, even by the ancients. Above all, when the Fathers of the Western Church say simply “the apostolic see,” they always mean Rome, because it alone was apostolic in the West.

Yet I do not therefore agree with the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius, who thinks that the Churches of Tours and Bordeaux—called apostolic sees in Gregory of Tours, Book IV, chapter 26, where the Council of Saintes, held in 566, is discussed—were called apostolic not because they had been established by apostles, “but because apostolic authority granted by the apostolic see of Peter through the pallium resided in them.” Baronius plainly had later centuries in view. For afterwards it was believed that the honour of the pallium had been decreed for metropolitans on account of the apostolic office—that is, so that by receiving the pallium metropolitans might understand that they were vicars of the apostolic see, as Marca observed from Rabanus. But this could not hold at the time of that Council of Saintes, when no Gallican bishop, except the bishop of Arles, had yet received the pallium from the Roman bishop. Baronius would certainly have been embarrassed if he had been compelled to prove that it had been sent before this time to the archbishops of Tours and Bordeaux.

They were instead called apostolic because in those times all episcopal Churches were called apostolic, in accordance with Tertullian’s observation, because they had received their faith from that first apostolic see which the apostles had founded. Therefore, when you see Ruricius, bishop of Limoges, called by Faustus of Riez “most worthy of an apostolic see,” you must understand not the Roman see but Limoges, over which Ruricius most worthily presided and was therefore most worthy of that see. See also our notes to Vincent of Lérins.]

## III.

The most blessed Pope Leo also writes thus to all the bishops of the province of Vienne concerning the authority and privilege of the apostolic see:

“Our Lord Jesus Christ, the Saviour of humankind, so established the worship of divine religion, which God’s grace willed to shine forth among all peoples and all nations, that the truth previously contained in the proclamation of the law and prophets might go forth through the apostolic trumpet for the salvation of the whole world, as it is written: ‘Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.’ But the Lord willed that the mystery of this office should belong to the duty of all the apostles in such a way that he placed it principally in the most blessed Peter, chief of all the apostles, so that from him, as from a certain head, he might pour out his gifts into the whole body; and so that anyone who dared to withdraw from Peter’s solidity might understand himself to be excluded from the divine mystery. For, having received him into partnership in indivisible unity, he willed that he be called what he himself was, saying: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church,’ so that by the wonderful gift of God’s grace the building of the eternal temple might rest upon Peter’s solidity, strengthening this Church of his by such firmness that neither human rashness could assail it nor the gates of hell prevail against it. But whoever attempts to infringe its authority, yielding to his own desires and not following what he received from the ancients, wishes with a most impious presumption to violate the most sacred firmness of this rock, which, as we have said, God himself has built.”

These are the words of blessed Leo; and many others teach likewise, so that the everlasting solidity of that steadfast rock, upon which the Lord our Saviour founded his own Church, might firmly retain the summit of its primacy from the rising of the sun to its setting, through the authority of its successors both directly and through his vicars.

[Note: Through his vicars—that is, through the Roman pontiffs, who are frequently called vicars of the apostolic see. Pope Gelasius, in his letter to the Emperor Anastasius, says: “And, however unworthy a vicar of the apostolic see I may be, whatever I discover to be lacking in the full Catholic faith, I strive, according to my capacity, to supply by appropriate representations.” Likewise Symmachus, in his *Apology* to the same Anastasius: “Where I do not cease to call you to witness by my voice, O ruler of human affairs, however unworthy a vicar of the apostolic see I may be, etc.” The bishops assembled in a Roman synod in 800, in the cause of Pope Leo, say: “We do not dare to judge the apostolic see, which is the head of all God’s Churches. For we are all judged by it and by its vicar.” And similarly in many other places. They are also called vicars of blessed Peter and vicars of the apostles Peter and Paul, as we have stated more fully elsewhere. Indeed, Cyprian in Letter 67 calls Pope Stephen the vicar and successor of the Roman pontiffs Cornelius and Lucius.]

From these authorities blessed Pope Anastasius, writing to the emperor, teaches that he acts as Christ’s ambassador who prays for the Church’s peace; and he admonishes the emperor himself to obey the ordinances of the apostolic see.

## IV.

Certainly, most clement lord, if Pope Gregory has now come unreasonably and to fight, he will deservedly depart having been fought and repulsed. But if he is striving to labour for the tranquillity and peace of the people and of you, he ought properly and reasonably to be obeyed, not resisted. For if he wishes to restore to its former state what was done by your will and authority with the consent of your whole empire, and was afterwards confirmed in the apostolic see, his arrival is quite reasonable and timely. For you ought in no way to change what has thus been established by you; nor can this be done without grave danger and guilt of soul.

[Note: Pope Gregory IV, who had then come into Gaul with Lothar after joining his party against the latter’s father, as we shall say below.]

[Note: He will depart having been fought and repulsed. That what Agobard here foretold occurred is clear from Hincmar, who speaks thus in Letter 41 written to Adrian II: “And how Gregory, carried away with Lothar while his father resisted, came into Francia, and peace afterwards was not in Francia as before; and the pope himself did not return to Rome with such honour as was fitting and as his predecessors had done.”]

[Note: Confirmed in the apostolic see. Not because the approval of the Roman pontiff was necessary, but because Pope Paschal greatly desired this, as we said above in the notes to the Tearful Letter.]

## V.

During these most sacred Easter days, letters of this Apostolic One were brought to me, commanding that we should observe fasts and prayers with abstinence, in case the almighty Lord might deign to grant success to his endeavour, so that it might be obtained from you that the former peace and concord be restored to your household and kingdom. Hearing this, I was moved to compunction and, as far as I could, raised the countenance of my heart to Jesus Christ our Lord, ardently desiring that this so unjust tumult might be calmed by his most gracious omnipotence without the shedding of blood.

[Note: “The Apostolic One,” that is, the Roman pontiff, who was then Gregory IV. For in those times this appellation belonged to the Roman pontiff alone. Formerly, however, individual bishops were called apostolic, for the reason that, being successors of the apostles, they governed their sees endowed with apostolic virtues, to use the words of Julianus Pomerius in chapter 25 of Book I of *The Contemplative Life*; and also because, when all sees were called apostolic, those presiding over them were consequently called apostolic. Subsequently the title was gradually taken away from ordinary bishops and became peculiar to metropolitans. At last it was taken away from them too, and the whole dignity of this name was transferred to the bishop of Rome. Thus for several centuries now he alone has been called apostolic.]

## VI.

May your exalted prudence deign devoutly to consider what the Apostle says: “In the last days perilous times shall come.” Blessed Pope Gregory lamented these dangers even in his own time, when the state of affairs was still far and incomparably better than it is now, saying:

“For I am so buffeted in this place by the waves of this world that I cannot at all direct to harbour the old and decaying ship which I undertook, by God’s hidden dispensation, to govern. Now waves rush upon it from the front; now foaming masses of sea swell up from its side; now a tempest presses on from behind. Amid all this turmoil, I am compelled now to steer the helm directly into adversity itself, now to turn the ship’s side and evade obliquely the threats of the waves. I groan because I perceive that through my negligence the bilge-water of vices increases; and, while the tempest strikes with force, the decaying planks are already, already sounding the onset of shipwreck.”

Alas, alas! If the ship of the Church was already decaying then, and if its planks were already rotten, what is it now?

VII. I have ventured, most pious lord, to recall to your memory these words of the most blessed doctor so that, since no one doubts that you are far more—and immeasurably more—a lover of the heavenly kingdom than of the earthly, of what will remain than of what will pass away, and since, in accordance with your holy faith, hope, and charity, you can please God by no other work so dearly as by concern for and administration of the peace and unity of the Church, your most diligent piety may strive to ensure that every faithful soul may advance in faith and in the knowledge of God—for this is dearer to God than all other things. May the merits of your efforts on behalf of this cause bring your merits near to those of the apostles.

[Col. 0297B] [Note: [Col. 0297C] This letter—or, more accurately, fragment of a letter—is of great importance; and from the first time it appeared publicly, it engaged the industry of learned men. Masson, who was the first to publish it, indeed thought that it had been written by Agobard, whom he calls primate of Aquitaine, against the bishops of Louis’s party. Following the same line, Goldast gave it this title: *Reply to the synodal letter of the Frankish bishops assembled from Germany and Gaul on behalf of the emperor Louis the Pious.* Finally, the man of divine genius, Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, discovered that the letter was not by Agobard but by Gregory IV, Roman pontiff. He proved this with so many arguments that anyone who does not see the light of truth here must be exceedingly bleary-eyed. For this reason we gave that letter the following title: *Letter of Pope Gregory IV to the Bishops of the Frankish Kingdom.* Since it was corrupt in many places, we carefully [Col. 0297D] and faithfully corrected it against the evidence of the manuscript.] 

# LETTER OF POPE GREGORY IV TO THE BISHOPS OF THE FRANKISH KINGDOM

[Col. 0297C]

Writing to the Roman pontiff, you addressed him in the preface by contradictory titles, [Note: [Col. 0297D] “Brother,” according to the ancient custom, of which Cyprian is an especially faithful representative; nor did the African councils, or Augustine himself, use any other form. But the examples were too ancient to have retained validity in these times. Baronius, moreover, speaking under the year 419 of Augustine’s books against Julian, acknowledges that the custom formerly prevailed whereby individual bishops called the Roman pontiff “brother,” without detracting anything from his dignity and majesty. And I entirely approve Erasmus’s observation: in his Commentary on Cyprian’s Letter to Antonianus, he suspects that the title “brother” here does not imply equality of rank, but partnership in communion.] namely, “brother” and “pope,” whereas it would have been more appropriate to show him only paternal reverence.

When you learned of his arrival, [Col. 0298C] you say that you rejoiced, [Note: [Col. 0298C] You say that you rejoiced. The old manuscript has this exactly. But because the word *laetari* is written [la et ari], the copyist thought that a letter had been omitted and that one should read *lamentari* (“to lament”), as Masson’s edition has it. That this emendation is unnecessary is clear from what Gregory says below: “Then, after you said that you had rejoiced at our arrival,” etc. A little later Masson’s edition likewise read, “namely, it would be subject to the prince,” which makes no sense. The royal manuscript is therefore more correct, explicitly reading *profuturum* (“would be beneficial”).] believing and hoping that it would benefit all subjects of the prince, and that our meeting with you would not be denied unless the sacred imperial command should forestall it. These statements are blameworthy [Col. 0299A] in one respect because the command of the apostolic see ought to have appeared no less sacred to you than the one you call imperial; and in another because what you say about its having been forestalled is untrue. It was not that command which forestalled ours, but ours—that is, the pontifical command. Nor ought you to have been unaware that the government of souls, which is pontifical, is greater than the imperial government, which is temporal.

Blessed Gregory of Nazianzus did not hesitate to proclaim this in the Church before emperors. Thus he addresses the emperors themselves, saying (On the Words of Jeremiah): “Do you accept freedom of speech, and willingly receive what the law of Christ imposes upon you, through our priestly authority, under our jurisdiction and subject to these tribunals? For he has given us authority also; he has given us a sovereignty much more perfect than your sovereignties. Or does it seem just to you that spirit should yield to flesh, that heavenly things should be surpassed by earthly things, or that human things should be preferred to divine things?”

Why, then, do you, as true priests—ministers of divine, not human, worship—not answer the emperor, whom you say you were forestalled by his sacred command, just as that same blessed Gregory addresses the emperor who was present, saying: “Patiently, I beg you, accept our freedom. I know that you are a sheep of my flock, numbered by Christ, the supreme shepherd, among his sheep and sealed by the Holy Spirit. I know that amid the sacred altars you are reverently subjected to the hands of the priest. I know that you preserve the worship and faith of the blessed Trinity not by your own preaching, but by ours.”

And afterward: “Always remember that you share one and the same nature with all who are subject to you. Nevertheless, in spirit be with God, and glory not so much in ruling the world as in having Christ rule you.”

Why, too, while you remain with the emperor, do you not abandon your most foolish flatteries and preach to him, saying with blessed Augustine (The City of God, book V, chapter 24):

“We call emperors happy if they rule justly; if, amid the tongues of those who exalt them with lofty honors and the excessively humble greetings of those who salute them, they are not puffed up, and remember that they are human beings; if they make their power the servant of God’s majesty, so as to extend God’s worship as far as possible; if they fear, love, and worship God; if they love that kingdom more in which they do not fear having partners; if they are slow to punish and quick to forgive; if they exercise punishment for the needs of governing and protecting the state, not to satisfy the hatred of enmities; if they grant forgiveness not to provide impunity for wickedness, but in hope of correction; if what they are often compelled harshly to decree they compensate with the gentleness of mercy and the generosity of benefits; if their luxury is restrained in proportion to the freedom they might otherwise enjoy; if they prefer to rule their desires rather than any nations.

“And if they do all these things not out of a passion for empty glory, but out of love for eternal happiness; if they do not neglect to offer to their true God, for their own sins, the sacrifice of humility, compassion, and prayer—such Christian emperors, we say, are happy for the present in hope, and afterward will be happy in reality, when what we await has come.”

But you, on the contrary, [Col. 0300B] because you do not wish to be true builders, are undoubtedly true deceivers, as it is written: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your steps.”

Then, after saying that you had rejoiced at our arrival, you added that, according to the report of certain persons, you had again been deeply grieved. This is surely the mark of an unstable mind. It is entirely true that “the one who hesitates is like a wave of the sea driven and tossed by the wind.” Yet amid these hesitations you judge us, with great foolishness, to be forgetful of pastoral duty and the strictest moderation.

Then, as it is written, “Since wickedness is cowardly, it bears witness against itself” (Wisdom 17:10), you add something deserving of every kind of shame, saying that we have come to carry out some presumptuous and wholly unreasonable [Col. 0300C] excommunication. [Note: [Col. 0299D] Excommunication. At that time it was rumored that Gregory had come in order to excommunicate both Louis and the bishops supporting him, unless they promptly obeyed his commands. But Gregory found the bishops anything but cowardly, and mindful of their rank. They therefore openly declared that such an excommunication would be void and would rebound upon its author. A notable passage on this subject, often praised by learned men, occurs in the Life of Louis the Pious, which says:

“Since the rumor spread everywhere that what was said about the others was true, but that the Roman pope was present for the purpose of ensnaring both the emperor and the bishops in the bonds of excommunication, if any should prove disobedient to the will of the emperor and his sons, the emperor’s presumptuousness somewhat diminished the bishops’ boldness; nevertheless, they asserted that they would by no means submit to his will; but that, if he came intending to excommunicate, he would depart excommunicated, since the authority of the ancient canons held otherwise.”

Quite rightly, indeed. For that excommunication would have lacked all rational basis; indeed, it would have been carried out contrary to reason.]

And you admonish us, in excessively obscure and confused words and thoughts, not to break out into presumption either by our own will or at another’s urging, since, as you say, this would constitute an injury and dishonor to the imperial power, and a [Note: [Col. 0300D] Diminution. Masson’s edition reads *domini rationem*, which, in my judgment, has no meaning. The royal manuscript has *diminurationem*, from which we have reconstructed the correct reading; if anyone does not approve it, *diminutionem* (“diminution”) may be substituted for *minorationem*. One or the other must necessarily be read.] diminution and reproach of our authority.

Tell me, please, what are these monstrous expressions? And what more properly belongs to the dishonor of imperial power: actions deserving excommunication, or excommunication itself?

But because it would be laborious to enlarge upon these statements of yours, since they are full of nausea, I ask only this: tell me how it can happen that, [Note: [Col. 0300D] While the honor of the apostolic see remains. Thus already at that time they distinguished between the see and the one seated upon it—that is, between the Roman chair and the pontiff presiding over that chair. Nor is this distinction new. Clear and manifest evidence of it exists in Leo the Great’s Letter 53: “For the sees are one thing, those presiding over them another.” Likewise, in Letter 62: “Although the merits of prelates are sometimes different, the rights of the sees nevertheless remain.”

The bishops assembled at the Council of Paris in 824 held the same view. Writing to the emperors Louis and Lothair, and speaking of the Roman pontiff, who was rumored to favor those who believed that images ought to be worshiped, they say: “We certainly believe that, although in some respect they may perhaps wish to claim for themselves a superstitious custom, they will in no way presume to command anything from that same see except as authority and truth require. For he will respect your power, the authority of the see, and the testimony of truth.”

Auxilius, who flourished under Pope Formosus, says in book II of On His Ordination, chapter 18: “Pontifical sees are one thing; those presiding over them another.”

Baronius also recognized this distinction in the case of Pope Marcellinus, when he says that, however much his lapse may be thought to have occurred, it brings no prejudice against Catholic truth; and he cites a passage from Tertullian’s On the Prescription Against Heretics, where it is written: “Do we prove faith from persons, or persons from faith?”

Baronius’s statement would be absurd and empty unless it were established that the rights of the sees remain even though the merits of those presiding over them are sometimes different—that is, unless the see were distinguished [Col. 0301D] from the one seated upon it.

For this reason Ferrerius, the legate of the king of France at the Council of Trent, while complaining about Pope Pius IV, nevertheless separates the dignity and authority of the Roman see from Pius. These are his words:

“We venerate, revere, esteem, and extol to heaven with the greatest praises the apostolic see, the supreme pontiff, and the holy Roman Church, for whose dignity our ancestors shed their blood and for which even today fierce fighting is taking place in France. But we reject, repudiate, and despise the authority of Pius IV, whatever his judgments and decisions may be.”]

while the honor of the apostolic see remains, only my person should remain [Col. 0301A] subject to reproach and disgrace? For it is entirely impossible that, if the one who occupies the place of blessed Peter is dishonored, [Note: [Col. 0301D] Without fault alone. The old manuscript has this exact wording. Masson instead published: “If he is dishonored without fault, while his chair is honored,” etc. Apart from the fact that Masson’s boldness cannot be tolerated in a matter of such importance, the author’s actual meaning clearly contradicts that emendation. The letter’s author is playing on the words *honoratur* (“is honored”) and *honorata* (“honored”). He says: “It is entirely impossible that, if the one who occupies the place of blessed Peter is dishonored, his chair should remain honored.” But he adds the highly important qualification, “without fault alone,” as though he were saying: “Especially when the one who is dishonored is without fault.” For even if the pontiff were wicked, the chair would nevertheless always have to be honored, and on account of the chair, the one seated upon it—as the example of Caiaphas proves.] his chair should remain honored, if he is without fault.

The pontifical chair must be honored to such an extent, and the one seated upon it on account of the chair, that the Evangelist even says of Caiaphas, despite his cruelty, unbelief, and impiety: “But this he did not say of himself; but, being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus should die for the nation.” Thus it is clear that even the impious Caiaphas was honored with prophecy on account of the chair.

Yet you proclaim that a faithful pontiff and worshiper of piety should be dishonored without injury to the see. This is entirely false.

You rightly add that I ought to remember [Note: [Col. 0302C] The oath concerning the pledge of fidelity. The Frankish bishops were therefore maintaining that Pope Gregory, at the beginning of his pontificate, had made Louis a pledge of fidelity, sealed also by an oath. The pontiff neither denies nor admits that this was true. We shall shortly show that it is highly probable that Gregory did in fact do so. The otherwise very learned Franciscus Florens, however, wrongly interprets this passage as referring to Agobard, under title 6, On Election and the Authority of the Elected.] the pledge of fidelity made [Col. 0301B] to the emperor under oath.

If I did so, I wish to avoid perjury by announcing to him everything that he commits against the unity and peace of the Church and the kingdom; but if I do not, I shall be perjured—as you will also be, if indeed I swore.

But you, since without doubt you swore and swore again, promising him that you would act faithfully toward him in everything, now see him acting contrary to the faith and rushing toward destruction, yet do not recall him as far as lies within your power. [Note: [Col. 0302C] You are perjured. What? Did the oath of fidelity that bishops at that time gave to the prince also include the obligation that bishops should understand themselves to be bound by oath not to allow anything contrary to the faith of Christ to be done by the prince?

John of Salisbury, in Letter 170, says: “Do you think those faithful who point out to the lord king the paths of sin, and labor to ensure his success in those things presumed against the justice of the Lord? Which seems more faithful to you: the one who, at the command of an erring man, ministers to his faults, or the one who drives away his destructive pleasures? Let each person judge as he wishes. I shall never regard as a faithful friend of the lord king [this is exactly how it must be read, not “the Lord and”] one who obeys his pleasure in such a way as to bring loss of health and life.”

Juret’s observations on Letter 35 of Ivo of Chartres should also certainly be consulted.]

Then you promise me a venerable reception, provided that I come to him as he wishes.

You read this not in the divine books, but in your own consciences, because you do everything for temporal reward, being reeds shaken by the wind, bent by every breeze.

Consider, consider, brothers, how far your mind is from that petition which, during the celebration of Mass, you customarily address to God not in your will but with your voice: “Grant us, for love of you, to despise the prosperity of the world and to fear none of its adversities.” For if you made this petition from the heart, he who says, “Ask, and it shall be given you,” would already have granted it.

Then you say that the first division of the kingdom, which the emperor had made among his sons, has now been altered according to [Note: [Col. 0302D] The opportunity of circumstances. The old manuscript and Masson’s edition both read “according to the opportunity of the kings.” But the corruption of this passage is demonstrated by its meaning. Moreover, shortly afterward, when these matters are reconsidered, Gregory says: “For this alteration, which you say was made according to the opportunity of circumstances,” etc. It therefore seemed necessary to emend the text.] the opportunity of circumstances. This is entirely false in two ways.

First, it is not an opportunity but an inopportune measure, since it is the cause and origin of disturbance and dissension, upheaval and plunder, and of all the evils that it would take too long to enumerate individually—not to mention countless perjuries and the expulsion of faith and peace.

Second, you do not yet know whether it has been altered or whether, through the true King and Lord, it remains inviolate.

This alteration, which you say was made according to the opportunity of circumstances, is recognized not to have been made through God because it is the source of many sins. For what is done by God’s will is often the cause of oppression and persecution, as happened to the holy apostles and martyrs, [Col. 0303A] who suffered for no other reason than the defense and confirmation of evangelical truth. But it could not have been the cause of sins and crimes, as your division is, which you say was opportune.

Then, when you say with great arrogance that, if we come reverently to the emperor, we shall learn from him the whole truth of the matter and why the division was altered opportunely and beneficially, the magnitude of your pride compels you to speak thus, as though you alone were able to understand the causes of events.

I tell you truly that the one who does not understand how many and what kinds of fruits of evil your alteration has produced is not merely foolish but also wretched; nor does he understand from whose treasury of an evil heart it proceeded, or for what reason you are the praisers and defenders of this wickedness.

Then you add [Col. 0303B] that, unless I come according to your will, I do not have your churches in agreement with me, but so opposed that I may do or arrange nothing in your parishes, and may excommunicate no one because you will resist me. [Note: [Col. 0303C] In your parishes—that is, dioceses—as we have explained at greater length in the notes to Lupus of Ferrières.

Who would not be astonished here at the freedom of the Gallican bishops, threatening the Roman pontiff that they would prevent him from doing anything in their dioceses if he withdrew from their communion?

It is also highly noteworthy that they even dared to say openly and plainly, in a letter to the Roman pontiff, that they would not tolerate it if Pope Gregory wished to excommunicate anyone subject or faithful to the prince. This passage may be useful in defending Gaul against a sentence of interdict, should such a sentence happen to be issued.]

Truly true is what Truth says: “The evil man brings forth evil things from the evil treasure of his heart.”

Why, then, ought you to be opposed to me and to your churches in a mission of peace and unity, which is Christ’s gift and ministry? Do you not know that peace on earth was promised to people of good will by the song of the angels, while through the Apostle tribulation and anguish are promised to every soul that works evil?

Here it becomes clear that the saying of Scripture applies to you: “Weapons and swords are in the way of the perverse.”

You strive to oppose us with your perversities, although we are carrying out a mission of peace. For whoever among you are members of Christ cannot sever him from the body of the head, which is Christ.

Even if you strive to separate yourselves from the body, nevertheless, as it always has been, is, and will be, that anointing—the Holy Spirit—preserves the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace among all the faithful everywhere. [Note: [Col. 0303D] The Gallican and German Church. He joins the two Churches for the reason that, since the kingdom of the Franks consisted of both peoples, whenever a synod was convened, bishops from both peoples assembled for it. This had occurred at the synod from which the letter of the bishops of Louis’s party to Pope Gregory was sent, and to which this letter is the response.]

The Holy Spirit descends from Christ the Head into the beard, which is the company of the apostles, and from this beard onto the edge of the garment, which is the collar of the tunic—that is, the Church of Christ, which receives the Head so that Christ may dwell in its heart through faith.

We say these things so that you may know that you cannot divide [Note: [Col. 0303D] The Gallican and German Church from the unity of the tunic that lies beneath the collar—that is, from the more exalted members of the Church who are nearest to the beard, namely the apostles, and consequently to the apostolic sees, just as there can be no beard except on a head.] the Gallican and German Church from the unity of the tunic lying beneath the collar, that is, from the more exalted members of the Church who are nearest to the beard, namely the apostles and, through them, the apostolic sees, just as the beard cannot exist except on the head.

Then [Col. 0304B] you add, introducing something ridiculous, and something we preferred to keep silent rather than say: “If you do not act, if you do not give your assent to our counsel, you will be exposed to danger to your honor.”

If you preferred—that is, if you wanted more—to keep silent rather than speak, why did you not keep silent?

It is customary among you that the lesser should prevail over the greater. Your greater desire was to remain silent, and the lesser desire was to speak; yet the lesser conquered the greater. We must surely believe that among lovers of discord desire is victorious and self-restraint defeated.

But as for what we recognize you to be threatening—danger to my rank—[Note: [Col. 0303D] Danger to the rank: that is, deposition and expulsion from the Roman chair. Gregory rightly marvels at the confidence of these Gallican bishops, who threaten the Roman pontiff with deposition.] who can explain how absurd, inappropriate, and foolish it is, since your threat is not on account of a crime, [Note: [Col. 0304C] On account of murder. He refers to Apostolic Canon 25, which, as Gregory of Tours cites it, reads: “A bishop discovered in murder, adultery, or perjury shall be removed from the priesthood.” But in Dionysius Exiguus and other ancient collectors there is nothing about murder. Hence de Marca was forced to suspect that this canon had been corrupted in order to press the case of Praetextatus, bishop of Rouen, who had confessed at the Council of Paris that he was guilty of an intended murder, in hope of pardon.

It may be that this clause too, because it seemed entirely just in later times, was subsequently received generally into new editions of the Apostolic Canons, with the addition also of the term “sacrilege.” Gregory likewise appears to have had this clause in his copy. Thus the Roman correctors are seriously mistaken when they suppose that the clause concerning murder was first added by the bishops assembled at the Council of Tribur in 895, and that this was why Gratian, who lived after that time, added the clause to this Apostolic Canon, Distinction 81, chapter “Presbyter.”]

namely, murder, sacrilege, theft, or anything of that kind, but because we do not come in the way you yourselves wish; and to this matter you add an oath.

And you do not remember, though ashamed, that [Note: [Col. 0304D] *Perjuri pejeratum* [“the perjured, the perjurer”; a fragmentary heading]. By a law accepted among all peoples everywhere, bishops who violate the faith pledged by oath to the prince are to be deposed. For a bishop discovered in perjury is ordered to be deposed by Apostolic Canon 25.

Those ancient founders of Christian laws wisely and justly saw that “the punishment of bishops who have violated their oath must be all the more severe because they stand out by a greater dignity, and by their example others can more easily be provoked to similar acts,” to use the words of Urban III in his letter to the archbishop of Pisa, in book III of the Decretals.

If bishops are never permitted to commit perjury, still less are they permitted to violate the faith pledged by oath to princes, whom God commanded us to honor and respect. It was therefore never doubtful that a bishop convicted of violating his pledged fidelity to the prince had to be removed from his rank.

This law also bound the Roman bishop while the pope was merely the bishop of the city—that is, before the lordship of the city of Rome was transferred to him. Thus, in ancient times, the ordinations of Roman bishops, like those of other bishops, could not take place without the consent of those who at various times ruled in Rome. For it is very much in the interest of rulers that in cities subject to their empire bishops should be appointed who teach the people by word and example that the rights of majesty must not be violated.

From this universally accepted law it also followed that a new Roman pontiff should make a pledge of fidelity to the prince. Ancient histories speak of the Roman pontiffs themselves regularly doing this.

As for the Frankish kings, there is an illustrious testimony to the matter in Alcuin’s Letter 84 (Patrologia Latina, volume 98, column 907), which is Charlemagne’s letter to Pope Leo III. After Leo became pontiff, he informed Charlemagne by letter of his ordination; the letter also contained an oath of fidelity. These are Charlemagne’s words:

“Having read through your Excellency’s letter and heard the decretal document, we rejoiced greatly, I confess, both in the unanimity of the election, in our obedience in humility, and in the fidelity promised to us.”

Before Leo, Pope Constantine, who occupied the Roman see after Paul I, likewise wrote to King Pepin:

“We, with God our God as our witness, he to whom the hidden things of the heart are manifest, shall remain with firm constancy—indeed, more than our aforesaid predecessors the pontiffs—in the charity, love, and sincere fidelity of your kingdom, protected by God, and of your Franks, together with all our people.”

Thus it happened that Paschal I, fearing that, if the allegations brought against him to the emperor Louis the Pious were shown to be true—namely, that Theodore, primicerius of the Roman Church, and Leo the nomenclator had been killed at his instigation because of their fidelity to Lothair, whom Louis had recently made partner in the empire—would be removed from his rank, immediately judged that the prince must be appeased.

Sending legates to him, Paschal asserted that he would clear himself of the suspicions raised against him. Shortly afterward he did so at Rome before Louis’s legates. The author of the Life of Louis the Pious says that Paschal cleared himself, together with many bishops, of the murder of the slain men—that is, by obtaining, as Thegan reports, the oath of thirty-four bishops, who testified that Paschal was not guilty of that killing. The author of the Bertinian Annals also relates this history.

When Paschal finally died, Eugene II succeeded him. Following ancestral custom, Eugene swore an oath of fidelity to the emperors Louis and Lothair; moreover, he required the Roman clergy and people to be bound by an oath that included the following, undoubtedly on the basis of agreements:

“And that I shall not consent that the election of a pontiff in this Roman see be conducted otherwise than canonically and justly, according to the limits and understanding of my authority; and that the one who has been elected shall not, with my consent, be consecrated pontiff before he has made such an oath in the presence of the lord emperor’s envoy and the people, with an oath of the kind that Lord Pope Eugene has willingly put in writing for the preservation of all.”

So teaches the continuator of Paul the Deacon, published by Marquard Freher.

It must not, however, be thought that this oath was invented only then. [Col. 0306A] That it had been customary earlier is evident from Einhard under the year 817, where we read:

“To him”—that is, to Pope Stephen—“Paschal, elected as his successor, after solemnly completing his ordination, sent both gifts and an explanatory letter to the emperor. In it he asserted that the honor of the pontificate had been imposed upon him, though he had not wished it and had resisted it vigorously.”

He was evidently excusing the haste of his ordination, because it had taken place unexpectedly, without waiting for the emperor’s envoy or legate.

But because Eugene had been ordained with the same haste, the emperor, wishing to counter this boldness and establish a precedent for the future, “decided to send his son Lothair, partner in the empire”—these are Einhard’s words—“to Rome, so that, acting in his place, he might attend with the new pontiff and the Romans to whatever the necessity of affairs appeared to demand [the following printed words, *extra conscientiam principis*, are corrupt in context], and apparently obtain from Pope Eugene an oath of fidelity.”

It is highly probable that the pontiffs who followed and lived during Louis’s lifetime did not omit this part of their obedience, and that what the Gallican bishops charged Gregory IV was true: at the beginning of his pontificate he made Louis a pledge of fidelity, sealed also by an oath. Gregory neither admits nor denies that he did so, but leaves the matter uncertain.

But why pursue conjectures in a manifest matter? Consider how the Bertinian Annals speak of Gregory’s election and ordination:

“Pope Eugene died in the month of August. In his place, the deacon Valentine was elected and ordained by the Romans, but he completed scarcely one month in the pontificate. After his death, Gregory, priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, was elected; but he was not ordained until the emperor’s legate came to Rome and examined what kind of election had been made by the people.”

It is clear, unless I am mistaken, that the legate did not consent to Gregory’s ordination until Gregory had given a written oath concerning his fidelity to the prince, following Eugene’s example.

Therefore, when Gregory understood that his defense was tottering on this point, yet wished to retain his rank, he resorted to other devices—namely, to the incompetence of the judges.

For—and this must be observed above all—he did not say that he could not be degraded because he had violated the faith pledged to the prince; rather, he said that those bishops who were perjured were incompetent judges. Gregory maintained that the bishops of Louis’s party were perjured.

If there had been no fault at all in those bishops, Gregory would not have denied that the investigation of the crime charged against him belonged to them.

So certain was this right of princes that, even one hundred and thirty years later, John XII was deposed at a Roman synod for the crime of violating the fidelity he had pledged to the emperor Otto, as the continuator of Liutprand teaches, book VI, chapter 10.

But after the authority of the emperors declined, and imperial power passed to the Germans, the Roman pontiffs began to flex their muscles and cast off from themselves the authority of princes—a thing that had not happened under the Frankish emperors.

Then, gradually, kingship entered the Church, and those who for a long age had been subject to princes afterward mocked them, even trampling the necks of their lords underfoot.

What a whirlpool (*Euripus*) of human affairs!

But before I leave this subject, it seems necessary, since we have said that the ordinations of Roman pontiffs once could not take place without the presence of the emperor’s legates, to support this observation with several examples from later times.

An illustrious testimony to the matter appears in the Bertinian Annals under the year 844:

“Gregory, pontiff of the Roman Church, died. Sergius succeeded him and was installed in the same see. After he had been ordained in the apostolic see, Lothair sent his son Louis to Rome with Drogo, bishop of Metz, to act so that henceforth, when an apostolic pontiff died, no one there should be ordained bishop except by his command and in the presence of his envoys. When they came to Rome, they were honorably received. When the business had been completed, the Roman pontiff consecrated Louis king by anointing him and girded him with a belt.”

Nevertheless, the Romans always regarded this law as burdensome and harsh; [Col. 0307B] and therefore at various times they attempted to violate it.

Not long afterward, when the Roman see was vacant following the death of Nicholas I, Adrian II was substituted for him, with the emperor’s envoys neither summoned nor consulted. The emperor at that time was Louis II, the grandson of the Pious.

When Louis’s envoys heard this, they took it badly, indignant that, although they were present, they had not been invited and had not been deemed worthy to participate in the election of the future prelate, whom they themselves had desired.

When they were given the explanation that this had been omitted not out of contempt for Augustus but with a view to the future—namely, to prevent the custom of waiting for the princes’ envoys at the election of Roman prelates from becoming established through such a precedent—they calmed all their indignation from the depths of their hearts, and themselves approached the elected man humbly to offer their greetings.

[“In Gratian, Distinction 63, chapter ‘When Adrian’; and in Ivo, part V, chapter 16. But, to add this incidental warning, this account has little or no credibility in my judgment. For how could the envoys have completely calmed their indignation when the Romans said that this had been done so that the presence of the emperor’s envoys would not turn into a requirement, when precisely this was the foundation of their complaint? Are we to suppose that men raised at court and steeped in the long tradition of the Caesars were so careless of, and so ready to abandon, the rights of majesty that they would allow them to be overturned and erased so easily?

It is more probable that the Romans excused the haste of the ordination by saying that Adrian had been seized rather than elected, and that it had not been possible to restrain the zeal of the clergy and people.

They undoubtedly added that they knew what right the emperor possessed in the election and did not despise it, and that they would ensure that such attempts were not tolerated in the future—provided only that the envoys tolerated Adrian’s election and came to offer him their greetings.

I believe that the envoys were mollified by these words, full of obedience and reverence toward Augustus, and therefore approached Adrian to greet him.

Then the emperor Louis, lest he create a schism in the Church of God, approved and praised this election.

This is my conjecture.]

But because after these events the Romans frequently passed over the emperors’ envoys in silence during the election of pontiffs, it pleased them to suppress this boldness at the Council of Ravenna, held in the year 904. Baronio published its acts, in which Pope John IX promulgated this decree:

“Because the holy Roman Church over which we preside suffers many acts of violence when a pontiff dies, which are inflicted for this reason: that, without the emperor’s knowledge and the presence of his envoys, …”
in [his] presence, the consecration of the pontiff takes place, and—contrary to canonical rite and custom—there are no envoys sent by the emperor present, who might prevent violence and scandals from occurring at his consecration. We wish this henceforth to be abolished; and that the pontiff who is to be appointed [Col. 0308C], with the bishops and the entire clergy assembled, be elected at the request of the senate and the people who have been appointed; and that he, elected by all in the sight of everyone with the greatest solemnity, in the presence of the imperial legates, be consecrated.”]

Perjurers cannot depose a perjurer [Col. 0305A], even if I were one. Finally, you do not know that I am perjured. But concerning you, there is no one who doubts that this is so. In this matter your cleverness ought to have remembered that whoever stirs up a sewer, the more he stirs it, [Col. 0306A] the greater the stench he causes to be emitted.

But in promising similarly that action will be taken against the brothers and fellow bishops who follow me, and in adding “irrevocably,” your astonishing presumption in this matter [Col. 0307A] is made evident. Can something done in part not be reconsidered by the community as a whole? Can something done among people who have deviated from righteousness not be reconsidered among better people—namely, those who hold fast to what is right? Or will something maliciously judged in the present not have to be reconsidered at God’s [Col. 0308A] judgment?

What your threats contain has never yet been done since the beginning of the Church. For even if I had been perjured, you ought to have applied to yourselves that Gospel saying: “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same condemnation?”

[Col. 0307A]

# AGOBARD’S APOLOGETIC BOOK [Note: This book has no title in the old manuscript. I have therefore thought it appropriate to supply one. It is in fact an Apologia for Lothar and his brothers against Louis the Pious.] FOR THE SONS OF THE EMPEROR LOUIS THE PIOUS, AGAINST THEIR FATHER

## I

Hear this, all nations; let the earth and its fullness hear, from the rising of the sun to its setting, from the north and the sea. Let them know and consider together that the sons of Lord Emperor Louis were and are justly indignant, and that they rightly think and strive to cleanse their father’s palace from the filth of crimes and wicked factions, and the kingdom from its most bitter and turbulent disturbances—provided only that sincere faith among them and fraternal good faith, worthy of God and pleasing to every faithful people, remain and endure inviolate.

## II

When, therefore, the aforesaid lord and emperor was living peacefully at home and flourishing in his palace, while he still kept under his protection his young wife [Note: Judith, the young wife and last wife of Louis the Pious, and mother of Charles the Bald. Louis married her in 819.] and, according to the Apostle [Note: According to the Apostle. This exhortation of Paul to husbands appears in chapter 7 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians. This passage was held in such high authority that it was later decreed at the Synod of Leptines that a marriage should be dissolved if the husband were impotent and unable to render the marital debt to his wife, as was noted in connection with Letter 81 of Lupus of Ferrières.] rendered her the marital debt, in the course of time these relations first began to grow lukewarm and then cold. As a result, the woman, having abandoned lawful conduct, turned—or rather was turned—toward unlawful behavior [Note: A woman dissolving into wantonness. This was the occasion of the civil wars. Judith Augusta possessed very great influence with Louis as his wife. This aroused Lothar’s anger, since he impatiently endured his stepmother’s favor. Causes for complaint were therefore sought, and the woman was charged with adultery. Count Bernard perhaps enjoyed her greatest favor. Hence the rumor that he was the man who had polluted the emperor’s bed. Since slander and envy are readily received by willing ears, as Tacitus observed, this opinion, first spread among a few, immediately grew into a great public report. Arms were taken up. The woman was captured and confined in a monastery; Bernard saved himself by flight. Thegan, in chapter 36 of his *Deeds of Louis the Pious*, says: “And they wished to expel the lord emperor from the kingdom, which his beloved namesake son prevented. The impious men mentioned above, bringing many accusations against him, said that Queen Judith had been violated by a certain Duke Bernard, who was of royal descent and the son of the lord emperor through sacred baptism. Lying in every respect, they seized Queen Judith, forcibly veiled her, and sent her into a monastery.”], and took to herself suitable persons for carrying out shameful acts, first secretly and then openly.

At first only a few knew of this, then more, and finally the entire palace, the kingdom, and the ends of the earth. The lower people mocked it, the greater grieved over it, and all distinguished men judged it intolerable. Accordingly the spirits of the emperor’s sons were stirred by a reasonable zeal: they saw their father’s bed stained, the palace defiled, the kingdom thrown into confusion, and the name of the Franks—which had until then been renowned throughout the world—brought into darkness.

Rising, therefore, each of them with one pious agreement to cleanse away the crimes, they assembled together. After some had been arrested [Note: Namely Conrad and Rudolf, the queen’s brothers, as Thegan reports. Also Heribert, Bernard’s brother, and Odo, his cousin, as stated in the *Life of Louis the Pious*.], and others had fled [Note: Especially Duke Bernard, who, saving himself by flight, withdrew to the Spanish March, whose defense had been entrusted to him. The *Annals of Fulda*, under the year 830, say: “A movement against the emperor arose at Compiègne among the leading Franks because they did not wish Bernard to remain in the palace. After he had been driven away and put to flight, they were reconciled with him.” The author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* says: “Bernard was also present; by fleeing in the manner described, he saved himself and had long been an exile in the regions of Spain.” By “the regions of Spain” he means the Spanish March, now called Catalonia. It was called the frontier of Spain because at that time this part of Spain belonged to the Frankish kingdom, as we have said elsewhere.

Since the occasion has arisen, it seems appropriate to say something about Bernard, so that the man who caused so many disturbances and wars may not remain hidden in obscurity. That he was of great nobility is clear from Thegan’s statement that he was descended from the royal line and was the son of Emperor Louis the Pious through sacred baptism. He was evidently the son of Count William, who founded the monastery of Gellone in First Narbonensis, now called, after its founder, the monastery of Saint William of the Desert.

In the year 820, after Count Bera of Barcelona had been deposed for the crime of treason, Bernard was appointed by Emperor Louis the Pious to govern that county. In the eleventh year of Louis’s reign—that is, in 824, as is plainly established by Einhard—on the Kalends of July, he married Duodena, a most noble woman, in the palace at Aachen. Two years later she bore him a son, William, born on the third day before the Kalends of December.

Meanwhile, while Louis’s sons were raging against Queen Judith and her son Charles and plotting civil wars, Louis, “in order to have some support at court”—here I gladly transcribe the words of the great man Peter de Marca, Archbishop of Paris, from Book Three of his *Spanish March*—“taking as his associate in his counsels and administrator of his kingdom a certain Duke Bernard of Septimania, as Nithard says, appointed him chamberlain and entrusted Charles to him, placing him second to himself in the empire. But certain treacherous courtiers drove three brothers to such a degree of wickedness that, having gathered a strong band of rebels, they began to consider expelling their father from the kingdom. Hatred sought a pretext: the familiarity of Count Bernard with Judith, which they interpreted perversely, although it followed from the necessity of his palace office, and also because Bernard had been appointed Charles’s guardian.” Thus far de Marca.

Bernard, therefore, driven out, went to Barcelona in 830. The following year Louis recalled him and restored him to his former honor. In 842 he was blessed with another child, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April; on that day Duodena bore Bernard a second son at the city of Uzès in First Narbonensis.

When war broke out among Louis’s sons, Bernard refused to take sides. This aroused Charles’s anger. Finally, when Charles came to Toulouse in 844, he summoned Bernard to him and killed him, though Bernard suspected no harm from him, as the author of the *Annals of Fulda* reports. Odo Aribertus gives a fuller account of this murder. The most distinguished senator of Toulouse, William Masnavius, with singular kindness, supplied us with the following fragment from an old manuscript:

“After peace had been separately confirmed and sealed by the king and the count with eucharistic blood, Count Bernard of Toulouse came from Barcelona to Toulouse and paid homage to King Charles in the monastery of Saint Saturninus near Toulouse. When the king had grasped the count with his left hand, as though to help him rise, he drove a dagger into his side with the other hand and cruelly killed him—not without violating faith and religion, nor without suspicion of parricide. For he was commonly believed to be Bernard’s son, and his face bore a striking resemblance to Bernard’s, nature revealing the mother’s adultery. After this abominable murder, the king, leaving the blood-stained throne and striking the corpse with his foot, cried out: ‘Woe to you, who defiled the bedchamber of my father and lord!’”

See Catellus, *History of the Counts of Toulouse*, chapter 8.]

After others had escaped, the instigator of these evils, Queen Judith [Note: The author of the evils: Judith Augusta.], was excluded from the palace, placed under guard, and, after changing her royal clothing [Note: Dressed in the habit of a nun. This occurred in 830, as is clear from the *Life of Louis the Pious*. It should nevertheless be noted that, although she placed a veil over her head—whether willingly, as the author of the *Life of Louis* says, or by force, as Thegan writes—she was not tonsured. She was confined in the monastery of Saint Radegund at Poitiers. There she displayed so many and such great proofs of piety to the nuns that they publicly declared their wish to follow the empress’s example. The author of the *Annals of Metz* says: “She was forced to go to the city of Poitiers and was confined there in the monastery of the Holy Cross. There she herself strove day and night with all her strength to serve our Lord Jesus Christ most diligently; and she so pleased those serving the Lord there that all declared their desire to imitate her.”], was dressed in the habit of a nun; they restored the father to peace and to some degree of respectability [Note: Some degree of honor. This was the pretext for the civil war: the palace was dishonored by the empress’s adultery with Bernard—an affair so public that it could not be concealed even by silence or dissimulation. The palace had to be cleansed of the filth of crimes, and Louis restored to his senses and dignity, as though he had been driven mad by his wife’s sorcery. Moreover, Lothar was not to endure such disgrace inflicted upon his father’s name. The author of the *Life of Louis* says: “They therefore said that a good son ought not to endure his father’s disgrace, but should remove the offending persons and restore his father to his reason and dignity. If he did this, not only would the reputation of virtue follow him, but the enlargement of his earthly kingdom as well; under this pretext they concealed their guilt. Attracted by these incentives, the young man, and so forth.”].

When, however, through the excessive leniency of the sons, what had been well done was undone—through the blandishments of the flesh, the wicked favors of those driven by desire, and disgraceful flatteries—the woman was again recalled as legitimate mistress [Note: She was recalled to the palace in 831, as the author of the *Life of Louis* and the author of the *Annals of Saint-Bertin* report. It was entirely just that Judith, “who had been taken from him unjustly and without law or judgment,” as the author of those *Annals* says, should be restored to Louis. He therefore sent men to bring her back from Aquitaine.

“She was nevertheless not honored as his wife,” says the author of her *Life*, “until she had legally cleared herself of the charges brought against her.” A synod was therefore convened at Nijmegen on the River Waal by the emperor’s command and with apostolic authority, in October. Since no accuser appeared against her and she had purged herself by oath according to Frankish law, the bishops judged that she ought to be restored to her husband as his legitimate wife.

The author of the *Annals of Saint-Bertin*, under the year 831, says: “To that assembly the lady empress came, as she had been ordered, and, standing in the presence of the lord emperor and his sons, declared that she wished to clear herself of all the charges brought against her. The people were then questioned whether anyone wished to accuse her of any crime. When no one was found who could bring any harm against her, she cleared herself, according to Frankish judgment, of everything of which she had been accused.”

The author of the *Annals of Metz* says: “Afterward, in October, the emperor held his assembly at the estate of Nijmegen. At that assembly, by apostolic authority and with the consent of the bishops, it was considered and canonically determined that the emperor should receive back his wife.” Further on: “When the assembly at Nijmegen had been completed, the emperor returned from there and reached the palace at Aachen to spend the winter. There he received the aforesaid Judith, his empress, as his wife and restored her to her former honor.”

Thegan, chapter 37: “From there the lord emperor came to Aachen, to his own seat; and the aforesaid wife came there to meet him. He received her honorably, at the command of Gregory, the Roman pontiff, and by the just judgment of the other bishops.”

The illustrious Archbishop of Paris praises this passage of Thegan in Book Three of his *Spanish March* to show that Judith was restored to her husband by ecclesiastical judgment, not by decree of a public assembly. These are his words:

“Since she had been forced into a monastery after the veil was placed upon her, for the purpose of public penance, once the crime had been cleansed by oaths, it was necessary that the unjust imposition of penance be rescinded. This could not be done by royal authority or by decree of a public assembly, but by ecclesiastical judgment and power. Thegan also observed this, when he says that the queen was honorably received at Aachen by the emperor at the command of Gregory, the Roman pontiff, and by the just judgment of the other bishops.”

Then, lest anyone should think from this event that in every ecclesiastical case involving princes the intervention of the Roman pontiff’s authority was necessary, the same archbishop prudently and learnedly adds, as is his custom:

“The authority of the Roman pontiff was joined to the judgment of the bishops of France solely out of regard for the Augusti, whose dignity made this case more important. As for more serious cases, Innocent I once taught that the apostolic see should be consulted. It was because of the same dignity of the persons involved that the divorce of King Lothar and Theutberga was handled before Nicholas I.
