Thus the references made today in ecclesiastical cases concerning kings to the supreme pontiff are not without precedents of their own—references that became more frequent after princes were exempted from ordinary jurisdiction by papal rescripts. Yet neither legal reasoning nor precedent permits us to doubt that, when circumstances require it, princes may renounce those privileges for a time.

In former times, too, it was not always the case that the authority of the supreme pontiff had to be awaited in every ecclesiastical case involving princes, as is clear from the public penance forcibly imposed upon Emperor Louis the Pious by certain bishops. Other bishops released him from it without consulting the Roman pontiff, restoring to the prince the arms, crown, and royal garments of which he had been deprived because of the penance. This restoration was confirmed by the full synod of 835, as the author of the *Life of Louis*, Nithard, and the *Annals of Saint-Bertin* report.”

Thus far de Marca.

Moreover, at this same synod of Nijmegen, by whose authority Judith was restored to her husband, Jesse, bishop of Amiens, was, as Thegan reports, “deposed by the just judgment of the bishops.” Flodoard, Book II of his *History of Reims*, chapter 20, shows that this deposition of Jesse was carried out by Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, “because of disloyalty to the emperor.”]

was restored to the palace and preferred above counsels and counselors. Through her instigations the ruler’s mind was changed, and he began to gore his sons with hard horns and disturb the peoples.

Thus there occurred something previously unheard of among mortals: the persecuted did not so much endure persecution unjustly as the persecutors exercised it unwillingly and under compulsion; and the persecutors not only exercised it but also suffered it, while being forced with extreme violence into conflicting and contradictory oaths.

## III

Consider and see whether anything of this kind has ever happened. An oath was first sworn to the senior emperor; then, at that same emperor’s command, those very men swore to the junior emperor. Again, at his direction, some of them swore to the brother-king [Note: The king-brother, namely Louis the German, who was Lothar’s brother.]; and finally almost all were compelled to swear to the boy [Note: The boy Charles, surnamed the Bald, who was then still very young, as is clear from the *Life of Louis the Pious* under the year 833: “Lothar led him back to his own territories together with Charles, then a very young boy.” Charles was born in June 823, as the same author of the *Life of Louis* reports.].

Nor did the matter end there. As though none of this had happened, further oaths arose. “Shall I not visit these things,” says the Lord? Shall contempt for God and pollution of his name remain unpunished? As it is written: “You shall not swear falsely, nor profane the name of the Lord your God.”

Behold, after the abysses of folly had been laid open, to what has the matter come? When armies ought to be sent against foreign peoples, and the emperor himself ought to fight against barbarian nations in order to subject them to the faith and enlarge the boundaries of the kingdom of the faithful—for the universal Church prays precisely this in those solemn prayers on the days of the Lord’s Passion for the emperors: “May God subject the barbarian nations to them”—now, on the contrary, the whole kingdom with all its extremities is gathered together into its own midst, though with differing intentions. Some prepare to tear open their own inward organs; others to pacify, if possible, the most unjust discord.

All of them ought to have considered with pious minds what is said in the aforesaid prayers, where the priest exhorts them, saying: “Let us pray also for our most Christian emperor, that God and our Lord may subject all barbarian nations to him, for our perpetual peace.” The house of God, therefore, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth, prays that barbarians be subjected to the most Christian emperor—not that those already subject should be disturbed and turned barbarous. For it is not the task of a most Christian emperor to drive out his subjects and divide those who are united.

## IV

O Lord God of heaven and earth, why have you permitted your most faithful and most Christian servant, our emperor, to fall into such negligence that he does not wish to see the evils by which he is surrounded? [Note: So that he does not wish to see the evils. These things were then being spread among the populace. The author of the *Life of Louis* says: “Moreover, his father was so deceived by certain illusions that he could neither avenge these matters nor even perceive them.”]

For he loves those who hate him and hates those who love him. What if it is true that many who seem to understand matters more subtly assert that there are certain people at his side eagerly awaiting the destruction of his sons? And what if, once they have seen it, they have agreed among themselves to lay hands upon the emperor and divide the kingdom among themselves? [Note: Divide the kingdom among themselves. Thus Capito Cossutianus, a man whose spirit was prone to crimes, said the following among other things to Nero while urging him to have Thrasea killed, according to Tacitus in Book XVI of the *Annals*: “They prefer liberty in order to overthrow the empire. If they overturn it, they will attack liberty itself.” It is characteristic of human nature to pursue vices under the name of virtues and to conceal evil counsels under the appearance of good. Those who stir up civil wars always put forward the public good as their pretext. Sallust, in *Catiline*, says: “For, to state the truth briefly, during those times whoever disturbed the republic fought each according to his own power under honorable names: some pretending that they were defending the rights of the people, others that the authority of the senate should be greatest, while all feigned the public good.”]

Whether this is true, they themselves know. Yet there are many who do not doubt that those of whom we speak press upon the kingdom as upon a leaning wall or a tottering fence. Hence it is clear that, unless God comes to its aid, the kingdom will either be handed over to foreigners or divided among many tyrants.

This is analogous to the present situation, because the emperor, who ought to be preparing just wars against the kings of the barbarians, is preparing to act unjustly against his beloved sons.

## V

Some also say that the mistress of the senior palace [Note: The mistress of the senior palace—that is, the palace of Louis the Pious, who shortly before was called the senior emperor; Lothar was the junior emperor. After Louis made Lothar his associate in the empire and joined him to the empress Irmingard, the ruling family was divided. Louis remained on this side of the Alps, while he ordered Lothar to govern Italy. Hence there were two households, or palaces: the senior palace, the house of Louis, and the house or palace of Lothar. Judith, therefore, who was Louis’s wife, was mistress of the senior palace.]—apart from what is said about her hidden and open conduct—plays childishly, even while certain members of the priestly order watch, and while most of them play along with her [Note: Most playing along with her. Agobard condemns the bishops who played childish games with Judith, as well as those who watched and perhaps praised such childish amusements. At this same period the Roman synod held under Eugenius II condemned the same behavior among priests. It decreed in chapter 11: “A priest ought diligently to search out and teach the divine words, so that he may be found blessed, of whom the Psalmist says: ‘He will meditate on his law day and night.’ Therefore he should not take pleasure in having games performed before him. If he is found to transgress, he must cease after the bishop’s admonition; otherwise he is to be judged canonically.”].

They ought, according to the rule that the Apostle gives concerning the choice of bishops—“one who rules his own household well, having children subject to him with all chastity; for if anyone does not know how to rule his own household, how will he care for the Church of God?”—to have said to the playing mistress: “If a queen does not know how to govern herself, how will she care for the propriety of the palace? Or how will she diligently exercise the reins of the kingdom?”

They ought also to have recalled to her what can suitably be applied to the preceding statement, at least with regard to its outward sense, which Holy Scripture says elsewhere: “A diligent woman is a crown to her husband; but she is rottenness in his bones when she does things worthy of disgrace.” And again: “A dripping roof on a cold day and a contentious woman are alike. Whoever restrains her is like one who restrains the wind and empties the oil from his right hand.”

But perhaps someone will say: “She is not contentious, but gentle and pleasant” [Note: Gentle and pleasant. This shows that Judith was a woman of remarkable friendliness and courtesy, not fierce or proud, as often happens to women raised to the highest fortune. Yet Agobard seems to mention this in order to increase hostility toward her, as though it could be inferred from it that Judith was an adulteress and prostitute. Seneca, *Controversies* I.2, records Junius Gallio saying of a certain girl who had been in a brothel: “If anyone doubts whether she was a prostitute, let him hear how pleasing she is.” Hence Juvenal’s line:

“A pleasing voice—and wicked fingers.”

]. The answer to these words is that there is no greater quarrel than to provoke, embitter, dishonor, and wish completely to estrange good sons from a good father.

And because she is said to be loved by her husband for her beauty alone [Note: Because of beauty alone. Judith was therefore beautiful. Thegan, speaking of her in chapter 26, says: “For she was exceedingly beautiful.” The *Annals of Metz*, under the year 829, say: “Emperor Louis had a certain queen, exceedingly beautiful, named Judith, well instructed in the flowers of wisdom, whom he had taken as his wife.” This passage shows that she was not cherished by her husband solely for her beauty, as Agobard says, but also for the outstanding virtues with which she was adorned. That pointed remark should be excused as the product of partisan zeal.

It is generally acknowledged everywhere among all peoples that beauty is a great and particular glory of women. No one, therefore, has yet condemned bodily beauty in women. Tertullian writes admirably in Book II of *On the Apparel of Women*: “Although beauty is not to be condemned—as bodily happiness, as an addition to God’s creative work, as a kind of good garment for the soul—it must nevertheless be feared because of the injury and violence of its pursuers, which even Abraham, the father of faith, feared in the appearance of his wife.”

Beauty should not, therefore, be put on display, as the same Tertullian had just taught in these words: “First, because the desire to please through beauty does not come from an undivided conscience; and we know that beauty naturally invites lust.”

I do not know by what fate it has always happened that whenever a woman has appeared beautiful, she has fallen under suspicion of having a promiscuous body. Thus, when Bias was asked whether he should marry or live a celibate life, he replied: “Either you will marry a beautiful woman or an ugly one. If she is beautiful, you will have her in common with others; if she is ugly, you will have punishment.” This is recorded by Aulus Gellius in Book V, chapter 11 of the *Attic Nights*. Diogenes Laertius, however, relates the same saying of Bion and Antisthenes in their *Lives*, and Valerius Maximus attributes it to Socrates in Book VII, chapter 2.]

it should have been impressed upon both of them that the same Scripture says again: “Grace is deceitful, and beauty is vain; the woman who fears the Lord is the one who will be praised.”

## VI

Now, therefore, all who fear and love God, and who love the king and the kingdom, using the things of this world in peaceful fellowship and enjoying divine things, must strive with all their strength to squeeze out the wound of iniquity and draw over it the scar of healing—without the shedding of blood, without the slaughter of killing, without the bitterness of quarrels, and without the turbulent and foul mingling of unclean spirits.

Then it may truly be said of the Church of this kingdom: “This is the house of God and the gate of heaven. The gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” And again: “The Lord your God is mighty in your midst; he himself will save you. He will rejoice over you with gladness, he will be silent in his love, and he will exult over you with praise. I will gather those who had departed from the law, because they were from you, so that you may no longer bear reproach on their account.” And let all the people say: “Amen, amen,” and a hymn to God [Note: Let all the people say. This is certainly how it should be read, not “the apostle,” as it was printed by Masson. Two years ago we corrected a similar error in Salvian, Book III of *The Government of God*.].

## VII

Just as truth is found not only in words but also in deeds—for the Apostle demonstrates this when he says: “Practicing the truth in love, let us grow in every respect into him who is the head, Christ”; and another Apostle says: “My little children, let us not love in word or speech, but in deed and truth”; and again: “If we say that we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth”—so too falsehood consists not only in words but also in deeds.

Thus the Lord speaks in the Apocalypse, saying: “Nothing defiled shall enter it”—clearly meaning the heavenly city—“nor anyone who practices abomination and falsehood.” And shortly afterward: “Everyone who loves and practices falsehood.”

In the Gospel the Lord says of the inventor of all evils: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth.” If that truth—which we also sing in the Psalms, “Draw near, Lord, and all your ways are truth”—possessed the minds of all human beings, the affairs of the world would remain peaceful in harmonious fellowship even without rulers and princes.

But now, because he who did not stand in the truth never ceases to act against the truth, and does not cease sowing the weeds of scandals while people sleep, finding enough hearts suited to warm and nourish his seeds, the evil of disturbance overflows and throws the peace and unity of quiet into disorder through insane fury.

For this reason one must watch carefully and act shrewdly, with tongue and hand, against the corrupters of truth and peace, so that they may either be restrained or suppressed.

## VIII

The disturbance of this time and these regions, which through the wondrous gentleness and sweetness of Almighty God was calmed without armed conflict, must not be remembered sluggishly or carelessly. Rather, it ought to kindle the hearts of the faithful eagerly in praise and thanksgiving to God, and make them attentive to prudent vigilance.

The character and origin of this disturbance and confusion should not be passed over in complete silence. When the most Christian and most pious emperor, Lord Louis, had lost the companionship of a good wife whose faith and character suited him [Note: His good wife: Irmingard, who died in 818, on the fifth day before the Nones of October.], it was necessary for him to take another who could assist him in governing and administering the palace and the kingdom.

But by God’s hidden judgment such a woman was taken—one who, although during the first years she was kept under the authority and power of her husband and lord and remained submissive, was eventually found to be capable of becoming a great source of turbulent waves and a rich treasury of confusion. She afflicted, saddened, disturbed, and almost crushed and destroyed not only the common people and the nations and princes, but also the emperor’s most distinguished sons, even those who were married and who possessed the reins of kingdoms [Note: Those who possessed the reins of kingdoms: Lothar, of Italy; Louis, of Bavaria; and Pippin, of Aquitaine.].

When those concerned for the condition and honor of the kingdom, the tranquility of peace, and the quiet of the people saw these things increasing—when they saw the palace dishonored, the kingdom’s glory darkened, and the name of its rulers brought to shame—they began to complain, murmur, grieve, and lament.

Meanwhile the spirits of honored men and of the king’s sons were stirred. As the conspiracy grew and counsel was added, each came from his own place; joining together, they approached the palace, drove out the ministers of crime, and expelled from the household and honor of the kingdom the queen who was the cause of all the evil. They established her in confinement as an exile [Note: In confinement as an exile: they transported her to Aquitaine and shut her up in the monastery at Poitiers, as we have already said.].

Afterward, as though they had now freed their good father from the snare of ruin, they rejoiced that they had fulfilled what is written: “Cast out the scoffer, and strife will go out with him; quarrels and insults will cease.”

When the sons had completed this entirely blameless deed, worthy of all praise, they returned to their own territories, having restored their father to his honor and glory.

## IX

When these matters had thus been concluded, the enemy of every good thing and author of every evil, who had not left the hearts he had possessed, set about restoring and renewing his evil; and the queen—who, after changing her royal attire, was thought to be continuing in the dress of a nun, as both the proper order demanded and [Col. 0316D] the rectitude of judgment taught—was brought back

[Note: [Col. 0316D] The rectitude of judgment demanded it. Agobard’s objection would be entirely just if Judith had been judged an adulteress and, for that very reason, assigned to public penance in a monastery. But we have already seen that this was done by force and without law or judgment.]
 [Col. 0317A] into the palace and taken into the partnership of marriage as though she were a legitimate wife,

[Note: [Col. 0317B] This could in no way be so. There is indeed a law in the fifth book of the Capitularies which provides that a woman who has taken the sacred veil upon her head, whether willingly or unwillingly, must never lay it aside. These are the words of chapter 113 of that same book: “In whatever manner a woman, with her husband’s canonical permission or after his death, has taken the sacred veil upon her head, whether willingly or unwillingly, she must remain in it altogether and must not lay it aside.” But this, I think, must be understood of a widow who veiled herself willingly, not of a woman veiled by force. For when the law says that she who has been veiled even unwillingly cannot withdraw, it is plainly necessary to understand it of one who has been convicted of adultery and, for that very reason, ordered to be confined in a monastery at her husband’s wish. No law, however, permits chaste wives to be taken away from their husbands except with the consent of both parties, so that they may devote themselves to prayer, in accordance with the Apostle’s counsel.

But even if we granted that the law was unambiguous, it would do nothing to support the emperor’s case. Judith had neither received the veil canonically nor with her husband’s consent, but by force and fear. Therefore there was no doubt that her husband could reclaim her if he wished.

The situation was different with widows. They were not permitted to lay aside the sacred veil, [Col. 0317D] especially among the Lombards, for which matter clear evidence exists. Since the occasion has arisen, I shall give an example from approximately this period, concerning a certain Lombard woman who, during the reign of Louis II, the pious grandson, was punished by the loss of her property because, after receiving the religious veil, she had presumed to marry.

The matter was as follows. Justus, a gastald by office and a Frank by nation, lived among the Lombards, and there married a woman named Gundi. He was certainly permitted to live according to the law of his homeland, had he declared before the judges at the beginning of his residence among the Lombards that he wished to live according to Frankish law. But he preferred to choose Lombard law, perhaps overcome by the force of love because Gundi would not otherwise have married him. For Lombard law was highly favorable to wives.

When she had therefore buried her husband and could not endure her longing for the deceased, she put on the habit of a nun in the monastery of Saint Mary and placed the veil upon her head, with the consent of Grimald, bishop of Penne, in accordance with the law of the emperor Lothair, which appears in Book II of the Lombard Law, title 6, chapter 4.

Meanwhile Sisenand, a Frank, began to seek this woman’s hand and afterward married her. When news of this matter reached the imperial judges, a lawsuit was brought against Sisenand and his wife by Maio, advocate of the Emperor Louis. He accused the woman of adultery under Lombard law, on the ground that after receiving the sacred veil she had again joined herself to a man, and therefore asserted that her person and property ought, according to the law, to belong to the palace. That law appears in Book II of the Lombard Law, title 6, chapter 1, and Book II, title 37, chapter 1.

Sisenand, however, denied that she had assumed the religious habit. But when Maio later proved that she had been veiled, the imperial judges pronounced both Gundi herself and her property forfeit to the fisc. They also imposed a fine of six hundred solidi upon Sisenand, and one of one hundred and fifty solidi upon Amelfred, son of Justus and Gundi, who had consented to the marriage. The fine imposed upon Amelfred was according to the law of Liutprand, which appears in Book II of the Lombard Law, title [Col. 0318D] 37, chapter 1.

This judgment against Gundi was issued in the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Casauria in the twenty-fourth year of the Emperor Louis II, in the month of December. Then Louis gave Gundi’s property to the monastery of Casauria on the third day before the Kalends of May, in the twenty-fifth year of his reign—that is, in the year 875.

But because the property that Justus had given to his wife had not been properly distinguished from the property of their children, the matter was again contested before the judges at Teate in August 877. The estate of Monactianus was adjudicated to the monastery, and, in addition, Justus’s property was divided between his sons and the monastery.

I have chosen to recount briefly this history, which contains many matters worthy of notice. I extracted it from the ancient records of that period preserved in the cartulary of the same monastery; after the notes, reader, you will find it published through the good offices of the most distinguished man Antonius Vion of Hérouval, born for the benefit of these studies.]

—which by then could in no way be the case. Thus shamefully and indecorously placed upon the royal throne, she increased and multiplied the former evil.

What ought the good son to have done? Was he to dissemble? Was he to remain silent? Was he to keep quiet? This did not please that sleepless eye which guards its Israel. Rather, it stirred up the spirits of the sons, and they gathered again to cut down the renewed stock of evils.

For they feared that what Holy Scripture says concerning a certain king might befall their father: “There was none like Ahab, who sold himself to do evil in the sight of the Lord. For Jezebel his wife incited him, and he became abominable.”

[Col. 0317B]

## X

But perhaps someone of a contrary disposition may try to remove these words of Holy Scripture as inappropriate, because it follows that he “followed the idols of the Amorites.” Whoever he may be should know that the fittingness of the passage cannot be annulled. For, in the time of the Law among the ancient people, idols and images signified all errors among the new people, that is, in the time of grace.

The order of these words itself must be understood in this way: “He became abominable through various desires and enticements, so that he even openly rushed into the worship of idols.” Whoever wishes to think otherwise here should consider how he contradicts the Apostle, who says: “And covetousness, which is the service of idols”; and should observe how truthfully it is said: “The root of all evils is desire; and by desiring it, some have wandered from the faith.”

If, then, desire causes one to wander from the faith, and covetousness is the service of idols, what evil remains that does not arise from the root of desire? Therefore it must faithfully be concluded that all who desire riches, glory, secular honor, and precedence are not far removed from the worship of idols.

## XI

We say these things for the purpose of showing that the evils and virtues of the ancients are appropriately applicable to the evils and virtues of those who go astray among the new people.

Although Ahab, incited by his wife, wandered from the faith and, at her urging, committed that crime involving the death of Naboth the Jezreelite, yet, when rebuked by the prophet Elijah, though he was not reformed, he was compelled to perform penance. By that act of penance he postponed the evils threatening him; he did not remove them.

If this is properly considered, it clearly demonstrates how greatly evil wives harm their husbands. Jehu, whom the Lord raised up as king to punish the house of Ahab and his deceptive wife, did not merit eternal life because he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam. Yet because he zealously carried out the Lord’s vengeance against Jezebel and against the house [Col. 0319A] that she had incited, it was granted to him that his sons should reign to the fourth generation.

After him, blessed Jehoiada, the holy high priest who ordered the utterly impious Athaliah to be killed, placed Joash upon his father’s throne, and cleansed Jerusalem of its filth and impurities, is adorned by divine Scripture with this praise:

“Jehoiada grew old, full of days, and died when he was one hundred and thirty years old; and they buried him in the city of David among the kings, because he had done good in Israel and with his household.”

Behold: this devout priest was rewarded both with temporal and with eternal recompense; Jehu, however, only with temporal recompense.

## XII

Let us also see what happened to Samson, whom the Apostle numbers among the catalogue of righteous men.

He loved a woman who did not love him, and who obeyed his enemies more than the friend who loved her. Because that righteous man trusted an unfaithful woman, he lost both the light of his eyes and the leadership of the Israelite nation.

Although his former strength was later restored and he ended his dishonorable life with a glorious death, he did not lack eternal life; nevertheless, he did not recover his former leadership.

Thus may the lord who was formerly emperor [Note: [Col. 0319C] The former emperor. This passage also shows that this apologetic book was written not long after the deposition of Louis the Pious, that is, in the year 833. For in the following year the emperor was restored at an assembly of bishops held on the Kalends of March [Col. 0320D] in the monastery of Saint-Denis.] piously consider this, lest he lose the heavenly and everlasting kingdom—he who, deceived by a woman, lost an earthly and temporal one.

Let him submit to divine judgments, since nothing on earth occurs without cause. Let him vow and repay his vows to the Lord God, the terrible one, and to him who takes away the spirit of princes.

For it is characteristic of good kings to say: “I always feared God as though waves were swelling over me.” Blessed Job says this. He did not consent to his wife when she attempted to deceive him, but rebuked her sharply, saying: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women.”

In another passage he says of God: “With him are strength and wisdom. He knows both the deceiver and the one who is deceived.” And: “He loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a cord.” And again: “He changes the heart of the rulers of the earth’s people and deceives them, so that they wander uselessly along an impassable road.”

The same thing would have happened to blessed Job himself had he willingly listened to his wife’s persuasion.

The Lord, therefore, is terrible not only to the peoples of the earth but also to the rulers of the people. Concerning him, a certain proud king, humbled, confesses under compulsion:

“I blessed the Most High, and I praised and glorified him who lives forever, because his power is an everlasting power and his kingdom is from generation to generation. All the inhabitants of the earth are regarded as nothing before him. According to his will he acts both among the powers of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and there is no one who can resist his hand or say to him, ‘Why have you done this?’”

And shortly afterward:

“Now therefore I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise, magnify, and glorify the King of heaven, because all his works are true and his ways are judgments, and those who walk in pride he is able to humble.”

## XIII

We do not say these things in order to compare our former lord the emperor with impious and unbelieving kings. Rather, because he allowed himself to be deceived by an evil woman, what is written happened to him: “He who troubles his own house shall possess the winds.”

Through this troubling and possession of the winds, countless perjuries and immense acts of plunder were committed, together with murders, adulteries, and incest. For all these things, the formerly most religious emperor must undertake penance: he must return to his heart and perform penance, humbled beneath the powerful hand of God, to whom it is not impossible to grant him the exaltation of eternal life.

For the exaltation of temporal life is no longer appropriate to him who, after his house and mind had been troubled, yielded to another by divine dispensation and judgment, and gave place not to some enemy or stranger but to his beloved son.

Therefore, amid all the joy and exultation of his heart, he ought continually to offer the highest thanks to the supreme and almighty God. For, as he always desired, an enemy conqueror did not succeed him in the kingdom; rather, a loving son did.

Now, therefore, let all alike—the turbulent and the quiet—hear the Prophet say: “Let all the earth be silent before the face of the Lord.” And let them hear the Psalmist: “Let all the earth fear the Lord, and let all who dwell in the world be moved before him. For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created,” and so forth.

[Col. 0319D]

# AGOBARD’S CHARTULA PRESENTED TO THE EMPEROR LOTHair IN THE COUNCIL OF COMPIÈGNE, IN THE YEAR 832

[Note: [Col. 0319D] We supplied this title for the little book because Masson’s edition had the following: “The public penance of Emperor Louis before the most distinguished assembly of bishops, with Agobard presiding.” That title is not found in the old manuscript. It is certainly misleading even for the reason that it says Agobard presided over this assembly.

We have therefore entitled this book the Chartula, on account of the authority of the Acts of Louis’s deposition. After recounting what was done against the excellent prince at the Council of Compiègne, those Acts finally say: “After these things had been done, it pleased each of the bishops to insert in his own chartula how this matter had been conducted, to confirm it with his own writing, and to offer the confirmed document to the aforesaid prince Lothair as a memorial of this event. Finally, it seemed good to all of us who were present to gather together briefly and concisely in one document the substance of all the chartulae—in fact, of so great a matter—and so forth.”

From this it is clear that each bishop presented his chartula to Lothair before the council was dissolved. We have also indicated in the title of this little book that Agobard did so.]

In the name of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ.

In the year 833 of his incarnation, I, Agobard, unworthy bishop of the Church of Lyon, was present at the venerable assembly held at the palace called [Col. 0321A] Compiègne,

[Note: [Col. 0321C] Compiègne, situated in the diocese of Soissons, on the River Oise.]

—which assembly consisted of most reverend bishops, most magnificent and illustrious men, and a college of abbots and counts, together with people of every age and rank. It was presided over by the serene and most glorious Emperor Lothair, a lover of Christ the Lord. Under his protection and with his assistance, the matters set out below were arranged in the first year of his reign, [Col. 0321C] in the fourth month,

[Note: [Col. 0321C] The fourth month, that is, October, in which the wicked deposition of the excellent prince took place. [Col. 0321D]]

because all these people were under a very pressing necessity to deliberate carefully about the danger facing the kingdom in the present and about its future condition. For the kingdom had long been wavering and was being driven toward ruin through negligence—or, to speak more accurately,

[Note: [Col. 0321D] Through the idleness of Lord Louis. This was the complaint of the traitors: that the Frankish kingdom, which had been greatly enlarged under Charlemagne, was collapsing under Louis’s reign. The Acts of his deposition state: “And how, in the course of time, through his lack of foresight or negligence, it came into such disgrace and degradation that it became a source not only of sorrow to its friends but also of ridicule to its enemies.”]

—through the idleness of the former venerable emperor Lord Louis. He had become entangled in these matters through corrupt minds that were both corrupted and corrupting others, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “For they themselves were wandering and leading others into error.”

Whatever was discovered through useful and praiseworthy deliberation and discussion by this assembly, whatever had to be established, I approved in agreement with its judgments and, in agreeing, judged it myself.

First, there were matters that appeared to concern the welfare and stability of the kingdom and king; then those that were plainly recognized as concerning the rescue and purification of Lord Louis’s soul. These matters were faithfully sought, truthfully discovered, and orderly carried out at the aforesaid assembly, particularly in the decision of that assembly that Lord Louis should be admonished by envoys and messengers concerning his errors and exhorted to return to his heart, according to the prophetic saying,

[Note: [Col. 0321D] By envoys and messengers. For the bishops say in the same Acts: “Yet, mindful of God’s commands, of our ministry, and of his benefits, we judged it fitting, with the permission of the aforesaid prince Lothair, to send an embassy to him by the authority of the sacred assembly, to admonish him concerning his offenses.”]

[Col. 0321C]

and to recognize his deeds, which he had carried out against God by running along the paths of wickedness and injustice, and thereafter to accept counsel for his life and salvation. Thus he might obtain indulgence and remission of his iniquities from the almighty Judge and Lord,

[Col. 0322A]

who is most merciful in pardoning crimes; so that he who had lost the earthly kingdom through multiplied negligences might, through the supplications of his confessions, attain the heavenly kingdom through him with whom there is mercy and abundant redemption.

[Note: [Col. 0321D] A little book was issued. The Acts of the deposition say: “On these matters they gave him a chartula containing a summary of his offenses, by which they might specifically rebuke him; he carried it in his hands.” The same chartula, or little book, as Agobard calls it, is preserved in those Acts, where it is divided into eight chapters.]

For this reason a little book was also prepared by the more diligent men and presented to him, setting out his crimes. In it he could plainly see, as in a mirror, the foulness of his deeds, and what was said perfectly of the penitent could be fulfilled in him: “I acknowledge my iniquity; my sin is always before me.”

For this reason all the bishops who had been present at the aforesaid assembly approached him again, grieving and sympathizing with his weaknesses and miseries, exhorting, imploring, and asking that almighty God, by the hand of his mercy, bring him out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth.

The most merciful Lord not only did not withhold this, but did not delay it. As soon as contrition of humbled heart had been revived in his mind, he prostrated himself before them—not once or twice, but three times or more—acknowledged his crimes, asked pardon, begged the assistance of their prayers, received counsel, and requested penance. He promised that he would most willingly fulfill the humility imposed upon him.

The law and order of public penance were made known to him. He did not reject them but consented to everything. Finally,

[Note: [Col. 0322C] He entered the church. The Acts of the deposition say: “Then the same Lord Louis came to the basilica of Saint Mary, the holy mother of God, where the bodies of the saints rest—namely, Medard, confessor and bishop of Christ, and also the most excellent martyr Sebastian, and so forth.”

But, lest anyone err on this point, this was not carried out at Compiègne, although that predatory council was held there. It took place in the city of Soissons, in the monastery of Saint Medard, [Col. 0322D] where Louis was being held in custody by order of Lothair.]

he came into the church before the assembly of the faithful, before the altar and the tombs of the saints,

[Note: [Col. 0322D] Namely, the tombs of Medard and Sebastian.]

and, prostrated upon sackcloth, confessed everything two, three, and four times in a clear voice with an abundant outpouring of tears. Having laid aside his weapons with his own hand and cast them at the steps of the altar, he received public penance with a contrite mind,

[Note: [Col. 0322D] Through the imposition of the bishops’ hands. The Acts of the deposition say: “Then he laid aside the military belt and placed it upon the altar; and, stripping off his secular clothing, he received the habit of a penitent through the imposition of the bishops’ hands.”

This deed was performed by Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, as is clear from the Account of the Clerics of Reims Concerning the Deposition and Restoration of Ebbo: “Lothair, traveling through the imperial palaces, brought his father with him to Soissons, to the monastery of Saint Medard. There, at the urging and command of the other bishops and leading men of the kingdom, Ebbo was compelled—because it was in his diocese—to impose public penance upon him. For this reason he incurred Louis’s excessive and lasting hostility.” See also Thegan, chapter 44.]

through the imposition of episcopal hands, [Col. 0323A] with psalms and prayers.

After laying aside his former clothing and assuming the habit of a penitent, rejoicing and confident, he asked to be carried back upon the shoulders of the most merciful shepherd into the unity of the sheep that had been found and redeemed.

[Col. 0324A]

After these events I, Agobard, an unworthy bishop, was present; I judged in agreement and consent with the better men, and, signing with my own hand, subscribed.

[Col. 0323A]

# AGOBARD’S LETTER TO EBBO, BISHOP OF REIMS, ON HOPE AND FEAR

To the most magnificent and most desired lord father and brother Ebbo, bishop of the Church of Reims, Agobard sends eternal salvation in the Lord God.

One day, when your devotion—greatly to be cherished, honored, and praised—was especially carrying in your hands and expressing with your mouth matters pertaining to the edification of good minds, your devotion toward me being wholly gratuitous, that is, without merit on my part and prompted solely by your own kindness, those who were present recognized your most diligent intention: you wished always to keep with you, from the divine Scriptures, certain passages in which you might meditate day and night upon what was appropriate to the places and times, in accordance with the blessed man who “did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly,” whether ascending a horse or descending from it, and with passages of suitable length.

Thus you might truly be like a tree planted beside the streams of the Scriptures, whose every work prospers. And what are its works? Clearly, fruits and leaves, which are understood as deeds and words: fruits in actions and leaves in speech. The leaf of this tree does not fall, because, in accordance with what is written of Samuel—“Not one of all his words falls to the ground”—he carefully takes care not to utter anything frivolous or empty, something more worthy of oblivion than of remembrance.

Thus the Apostle instructs his like-minded companion, saying: “Avoid foolish and old-womanish fables”; and again he commands certain people to be warned “not to devote themselves to fables and endless genealogies, which provide questions rather than the edification that is in faith.” And again: “Avoid profane and empty talk. For they advance greatly toward ungodliness, and their speech spreads like a cancer.”

Therefore, when your God-devoted and faithful holiness deigned to disclose such matters to me, I suggested [Col. 0323D] that you should first order difficult and arduous passages from the divine books to be written in the same Enchiridion that you carried with you—passages especially suited to restraining minds through fear, lest they be lifted up into empty presumption—and, after considering these attentively and for a long time, you should finally order whatever seemed appropriate

[Note: [Col. 0323D] To insert into your own manual, that is, a book that is always in one’s hands. Thus Agobard himself says at the end of this letter: “Especially since you also ordered a work of this kind to be made, one that could be carried in the hand for a little while, not one to be kept in a cupboard or chest.”

For this reason Duodena, wife of Duke Bernard, when she wrote admonitions to her son William, entitled the book of admonitions Manual, in this manner: “The Manual Book of Duodena, which she herself sent to her son William.” The most distinguished man William Catellus, senator of Toulouse, had seen one copy of this book. We ourselves long possessed another, during the lifetime of the most illustrious Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, who afterward gave it as a gift to the most distinguished lord Luke D’Achery, a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur.]

to be inserted in your own manual.

When I had made this suggestion, you deigned to command me to begin as seemed appropriate to me and to send the work to your holiness for judgment.

All Scripture, then, is divinely inspired, as the Apostle says, and is useful for teaching, reproving, and instructing in righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect and equipped for every good work.

This Scripture possesses such permanence that its author, eternal Truth, the Word and Wisdom of the Father, our Lord and Redeemer, bears witness concerning it, saying: “It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one iota of the Law to fall.” And again: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”

Since these enduring words are full of rules of morality, discipline, virtues, works, and faith, among other things there are two matters absolutely necessary for the moderation of human minds: hope and fear. Concerning these the Lord mystically commands priests and teachers of all peoples through the Law, saying: “You shall not take away the upper and lower millstone as a pledge.”

Although these millstones can rightly figure the two Testaments, they are usefully understood as hope and fear: the lower being called fear, the upper hope. If either one is lacking, a person cannot make flour, because he cannot work anything sound in his mind when fear without hope weighs him down, or hope without fear lifts him up.

Therefore the Psalmist, joining the two together, says: “The Lord is pleased with those who fear him and with those who hope in his mercy.”

Finally, Judas the traitor, after the Lord’s betrayal, because he feared without hope, saying, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood,” went away and hanged himself, and his body burst open and his entrails were poured out.

Conversely, because those who answered the Lord, “We are Abraham’s seed, and we have never been slaves to anyone,” were lifted up by hope alone without fear, they disdained to believe in the Savior. They presumed that they were not to be saved but were already saved. Divine Scripture is entirely filled with examples of this kind.

It is always necessary, however, that these two millstones be continually present in the minds of the faithful: hope always raises the spirit, while fear weighs it down; fear must temper hope, and hope must temper fear. Lest hope lift the mind into pride, fear, constantly accompanying it, must weigh it down; and, again, lest immoderate fear bury the spirit in despair, hope must immediately raise it up.

For fear, if it is without hope, is more properly called despair. Hope, if it is without fear, is shown to be empty presumption.

The heavenly Physician wishes us to use such a balance, as a kind of antidote. He alone searches out and knows inner illnesses, and to him it is said: “You alone know the hearts of the children of men.” He also says: “I am he who searches the kidneys and hearts.”

His word is living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. He knows that the human mind can be kept securely at its center by these two virtues.

Since this is so, it seemed to me that I should first set down some of those passages belonging to the lower millstone—that is, to the unspeakable terror of minds—because they are exceedingly difficult. Since we have been commanded to work out our own salvation with fear and trembling, and all the faithful desire salvation, those things by which salvation is wrought—fear and trembling—should first be founded in our studies, so that the things to be placed above them, being easier, may necessarily be sought through their impetus.

It is also natural to the human soul that, while enduring fear with a certain distress, it should hasten of its own accord to return to hope, which is thought more joyful, although fear is no less necessary and useful.

Because, then, if we excerpt such passages from all the divine books, the work becomes too long, it is enough for us now to take up those that are readily available and more commonly used—especially since you ordered a work of this kind to be made, one that could be carried in the hand for a little while, not one to be kept in a cupboard or chest.

As I was beginning, therefore, the first passage of the seventh Psalm presented itself to me, the one we sing, saying:

“Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands, if I have rendered evil to those who rendered it to me, then may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies. May my enemy pursue my soul, seize it, and trample my life upon the earth, and bring my glory down into the dust.”

[Note: [Col. 0325B] It presented itself to me as I was beginning. From this passage it is also evident that much is missing here, and that this is rather the beginning of the book than the whole book. For this reason, at the end, we decided to add the words that do not appear in the manuscript: “Many things are missing.”]

Many things are missing.

[Col. 0325B]

# AGOBARD’S BOOK ON DIVINE PSALMODY

[Col. 0325C]

Because [Note: [Col. 0325D] Recently a foolish and wicked man. Unless I am greatly mistaken, he means Amalarius the deacon. Hence it happened that, when Amalarius later published four books on the Divine Offices, Agobard bit him in return, dissecting those books down to the quick. Moreover, this hostile feeling toward Amalarius was inspired in Florus of the Church of Lyon by our bishop. For after Agobard’s death, Florus attacked Amalarius fiercely in a letter written in the name of the Church of Lyon concerning predestination. These are Florus’s words, truly full of barbs: “We receive with great displeasure and sorrow the news that ecclesiastical and prudent men were consulting Amalarius about matters of faith; for by his words and books, full of lies, errors, and fantastical and heretical arguments, he infected and corrupted, so far as he could, nearly all the Churches in Gaul and even some in other regions; so that it was not he himself who should have been questioned about the faith, but all his writings, at least after his death, should have been consumed by fire.” Amalarius, then, had criticized certain features of the Church’s singing—undoubtedly through intemperance of speech and style, or because it is sometimes the pastime of great talents to carp at the words and deeds of others. This audacity stung Agobard, and he did not conceal it. Thus it was the cause and occasion of his writing this book.] recently a foolish and wicked slanderer, notorious to all for that very foolishness and wickedness, broke out against us. He does not cease to tear apart our holy Church, that is, the Church of Lyon, not only in speech but also in writing, as though it did not celebrate the solemn rites of divine song correctly, or according to ancestral custom and usage. It was therefore necessary to collect and arrange more carefully and fully, in a little book commonly called an *Antiphonary*, the entire series of sacred offices which, through the customary service of the singers, is presented throughout the whole year in ecclesiastical assemblies, just as, by God’s favor, it is preserved in that same Church; [Col. 0325D] with a preface, of course, [Note: [Col. 0326D] Of the pious and orthodox Father Leidrard, archbishop of Lyon, who had organized the singing in the Church of Lyon, as is clear from a letter he wrote to Charlemagne.] by the pious and orthodox Father, [Col. 0326C] whose thoroughly approved faith and teaching, exercised and publicly demonstrated in the service of our Lord God, became known to all; so that all peaceful and prudent sons of the Church into whose hands the text of this little book should come might recognize most truly and clearly that the aforesaid Church of Christ, under the governance and protection of the same Christ the Lord, had neither departed from the straight path of faith nor failed faithfully to preserve the ancestral custom declared by ecclesiastical statutes, and consequently differed in no respect from the ancient usage of the Church of God, [Note: [Col. 0326D] “Nor despise another’s different custom.” This is exceedingly well said. For each Church may have its own particular customs, provided that they are not contrary to the faith, as we have explained more fully in our remarks on the letter to Nibridius of Narbonne. See Gratian, Distinction 12.] nor despised another’s different custom, if it was shown to be legitimate; but, in accordance with the Apostle, [Col. 0326D] followed the things that are more useful and more excellent. For he says: [Col. 0327A] “And this I pray, that your charity may abound more and more in knowledge and all discernment, so that you may approve the things that are excellent, and may be sincere and without offense for the day of Christ.” And elsewhere: “So that you may approve what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.” And again: “But earnestly desire the better gifts.” And once more: “Do not become children in understanding.” The venerable councils of the Fathers also decree that in no way should [Note: [Col. 0327D] “Common psalms.” This is taken from the final canon of the Council of Laodicea, where it is written: “That common psalms should not be sung in the Church, nor books other than the canon be read, but only the sacred volumes of the New or Old Testament.” The canon therefore prohibits the recitation in church of “common psalms,” that is, those composed by private and unlearned persons. For this custom had become widespread—as Justellus observed concerning this Laodicean canon, and Henri Valois concerning Book VII, chapter 24, of Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*—so that many composed psalms and hymns in honor of Christ and had them sung in the Church, as they prove from various passages of Eusebius. The Laodicean synod therefore subsequently forbade such psalms to be sung in the Church, judging it unworthy of God’s majesty for the Christian people to praise God with words other than those of the sacred books.] common psalms be sung in the Church, and [Note: [Col. 0327D] “Nothing poetically composed.” Agobard holds that light songs and easy verses, such as those we now call motets, should not be sung in the Church. Nor was Agobard alone displeased by that practice. It also displeased the great man William Durand, bishop of Mende, whose words are these, from Book II, chapter 19, of *On the General Manner of Celebrating a Council*: “It would seem very fitting that undevout and disorderly songs of motets and the like should not be performed in church, since Distinction 92, ‘Cantors,’ condemns them.” Yet that custom still endures in the Church, although those great men thought it ought to be removed and abolished. For what is more common than for light songs, suited to melody, to be sung in the Church? And not merely occasionally, so that it might seem accidental, but every year, on the feast of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ. Hence those songs have long been called by the established name *Noëls*, that is, songs of the Nativity.] nothing poetically composed be used in the divine praises.

Among them, blessed Pope Gregory also teaches that places should not be loved for the sake of places, but places for the sake of good things. And, commending this to us even more forcefully—that just as we should not pursue things for the sake of places, so neither should we pursue them for the sake of particular persons or the customs of times—he was not afraid, even in the Roman Church itself, to remove certain reprehensible matters from the sacred offices and ministries, imposing even the penalty of anathema, as his decrees openly demonstrate (see *Book on the Correction of the Antiphonary*, chapter 15, below).

If the aforesaid slanderer had humbly and obediently considered this, he would never have fallen into such folly as to defend the words of random people, whose names, meaning, and faith he does not know, as though they were the divine Scriptures, and to attempt to explain them through fantastical and laughable allegories. Certainly, if he had been willing to think anything soundly, it would have been enough for every correction and silence that, just as during the daytime at Mass only divine utterances are generally sung, so at night, when sacred vigils are offered to God, the same rule should undoubtedly be observed. One almighty Lord is praised at both times; both times serve the one Lord, to whom it is said: “The day is yours, O Lord, and the night is yours. You made the dawn and the sun.”

But his foolish and fruitless labor causes prudent people, who are not at all contentious and who fear God, greater concern, so that, in order to avoid such blemishes and errors, they may cling more vigorously and attentively to divine authority and ecclesiastical statutes. This precaution of faith, and this most sincere discipline of observance—that in the temple of God and before the divine altar only the melody of divine utterances should be celebrated—is also most firmly commended to us by the authority and examples of the Old Testament. There, in the Book of Chronicles, [Col. 0328A] we read that blessed David, king and prophet of God, first established choirs of Levites praising the Lord in the tabernacle or temple, and entrusted to them psalms, hymns, and songs divinely inspired to him and to the others who prophesied with him; and that he decreed that they should be sung morning and evening amid the divine burnt offerings and sacrifices.

It is clear that this custom, handed down by the holy prophets and most diligently preserved by succeeding Fathers, was carried on with religious observance until the time of the New Testament, when that temple had to be destroyed. Therefore, if we truly desire to celebrate divine praises without offense or hesitation, it is supremely necessary that we conform ourselves entirely to the divine words, in which there is no error and no ambiguity.

Thus the same Book of Chronicles, repeating its account of the Levites, the ancient singers of divine praise, says: “The Levites were to stand in the morning to give thanks and sing to the Lord, and likewise in the evening, both at the offering of the Lord’s burnt offerings and on Sabbaths, new moons, and the other solemnities.”

Again, at the dedication of the temple under Solomon, it says: “The king and all the people dedicated the house of the Lord. The priests stood at their offices, and the Levites with the instruments of the songs of the Lord, which King David had made to praise the Lord, for his mercy endures forever, singing the hymns of David through their hands.”

Likewise, in the restoration and purification of the same temple under Hezekiah, it is written: “Hezekiah and the leaders commanded the Levites to praise the Lord with the words of David [Col. 0328C] and of Asaph the seer, and they praised him with great joy.” The same occurred under Josiah, in the celebration of the Passover: “The singers, the sons of Asaph, stood in their order according to the command of David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, the king’s prophets.”

How holy and religiously this whole institution was, and how sweetly and reverently it should be imitated, the Book of Ecclesiasticus, among other magnificent praises of blessed David, continues in these words: “In every work he gave thanks to the Holy and Most High in words of glory. With all his heart he praised the Lord and loved God, who made him, and gave him power against his enemies. He established singers before the altar, and by their sound he made the melodies sweet. He gave beauty to the festivals, and adorned the appointed times until the completion of his life, so that they might praise the holy name of the Lord and magnify the holiness of God in the morning.”

The spiritual grace of singing psalms is also praised in the same most holy king in the Book of Samuel, where we read: “David, son of Jesse, said: The man to whom the Christ of the God of Jacob was appointed, the excellent psalmist of Israel, said: The Spirit of God spoke through me, and his word was on my tongue.”

There is no doubt that every faithful and disciplined person will willingly submit to such holy authority and such evident truth. But if some contentious and obstinate person tries to contradict it, and prefers to drink from a muddy stream rather than from the purest spring, let him beware lest he suffer from that exceedingly harmful illness which one of the ancient Fathers wisely and briefly warned us to avoid, saying: “One who, having despised the truth, presumes to follow custom is either envious and malicious toward the brethren to whom the truth is revealed, or ungrateful toward God, by whose inspiration his Church is instructed.”

[Col. 0329A]

# AGOBARD’S BOOK ON THE CORRECTION OF THE ANTIPHONARY

[Col. 0329B]

## I

To his beloved brothers in Christ, and especially [Note: [Col. 0329D] To the singers of the Church of Lyon. This commendation was added because of Leidrard’s care. As he himself writes to Charlemagne, he took such care in arranging the sacred ministries in the Church of Lyon that he even established schools for singers, so well trained that they could instruct others as well.] the singers of the Church of Lyon, Agobard sends eternal greetings in the same Christ our Lord and Savior.

We have often suggested to your Charity in our mutual conversations how carefully levity must be avoided and seriousness pursued in offering the divine praises—namely, so that, with reasonable consideration, like prudent sons of the Church and those nourished from infancy on its reasonable milk, you might reject what displeases God and, with united zeal, pursue in word as well as deed what is pleasing and acceptable to him.

For if among serious and wise men not only levity of conduct but also levity of speech is judged blameworthy, how much more is it so before God, the author of all holy seriousness [Col. 0329C] and wisdom, to whom the Psalmist says: “In a grave people I will praise you,” and to whom the Apostle urges us to offer rational worship.

Nor should whatever seems suitable to anyone be employed indiscriminately and without careful examination in the praises of God, since the Apostle says: “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought. But the Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings. He who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he pleads for the saints according to God.”

Therefore the apostles, conscious of human ignorance, asked God for a form of prayer, saying: “Lord, teach us to pray.” It is certainly evident that it is greater to offer worthy praise to God than to entreat him for one’s own weakness—especially since the latter ends with the close of this present life, while the former begins here and is perfected in the future, according to what the Psalmist says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; throughout the ages of ages they will praise you.”

## II

If, then, we need the teaching of the Holy Spirit when we pray, [Col. 0330B] much more do we need it when we offer praises to God. For just as no one pleads according to God except by his inspiration, so no one praises God worthily except by his instruction.

The divine majesty must therefore be praised not with anyone’s inventions, but with the utterances of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, the sons of Aaron, when they offered strange fire to the Lord, experienced not the reward of obedience but the condemnation of presumption.

Therefore, avoiding this example with the greatest care, let us attend diligently to what is written in Proverbs: “Every word of God is a fire-tested shield to those who hope in him. Do not add anything to his words, lest you be rebuked and found a liar.”

Adding nothing, then, to God’s words, and fearing to be rebuked and found liars, let us be inflamed and defended together during prayer and praise by the fire-tested word of God, which is the shield of hope.

And since the Lord says: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life,” let us reject all human inventions, which must be judged dead because of their vanity, and let us sound forth in his service with the living utterances of Christ, so that our voices may not be rejected as alien to him, but may deserve to be admitted as his own, together with the heavenly powers that, trembling before God’s majesty, adore and praise him.

## III

For this reason we have also corrected the Antiphonary, as far as our abilities allowed, for the most part, cutting out what seemed either superfluous, frivolous, or false, [Note: [Col. 0329D] “Or blasphemous.” Some have accused Agobard of excessive scrupulousness in this matter, because he too readily condemned certain antiphons and responsories which, although not taken from the sacred books, are nevertheless more pious than impious. I hear that the same antiphons which Agobard condemns here still exist today in the Breviary of Lyon. They certainly exist in the Breviary of the Church of Paris. It is therefore clear that things once received in the Church are not easily changed, and that bishops ought to be cautious in such matters, lest their ministry be blamed. Why not? Agobard’s own efforts were ineffective. Urban VIII likewise corrected the hymns. Yet the ancient hymns are still always sung in the Church, and no one has yet been found who would append notes to the hymns corrected by Urban.] or blasphemous.

We have often admonished you, and, because of the present or future complaints of certain people, deemed it necessary to place the substance of our admonition at the front of this same little book [Col. 0330D]. We are not establishing anything universal, but, according to the modest measure of our understanding, offering what we can in the house of God, whose care has been entrusted to us. We presume nothing on the basis of our own judgment, but follow the authority of Holy Scripture, the decrees of the sacred canons, and the institutions and examples of the catholic Fathers.

Before saying anything about these, it seems fitting, by way of example, to point out briefly and lightly refute certain absurdities contained in the aforesaid book, so that from these very few examples it may become clearer how necessary are the things we shall say below, since they were established by the Fathers, and with how much fear and care it is useful for us to observe their decisions.

## IV

First of all, what can one say of this? At the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, in the choir of the faithful and of the more learned faithful, the following was sung:

“When the sun has arisen from heaven, you will see the King of kings proceeding from the Father like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber.”

Certainly the catholic faith holds that the Word of God, who in the beginning was with the Father, joined a bride to himself in the bridal chamber of the virgin womb. Assuming her nature in the unity of his person, he became flesh so that he might dwell among us.

United to our nature, he proceeded from the virginal womb like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber; he did not bring that nature from heaven, as heretics have dared to assert. Consequently, he did not proceed from the Father like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber.

The Word of God, the Son of God, proceeded from the Father and came into the world. To come into the world meant nothing other than to assume the truth of human nature in the Virgin’s womb, in which he would make himself visible to the world.

He therefore did not draw this nature of our humanity, to which he was united as the Bridegroom of the Church, from the Father’s bosom [Col. 0331C], but took it from the Virgin’s flesh.

## V

Moreover, the aforesaid antiphon displays both rashness and manifest falsehood, since it adapts the words of Holy Scripture to the perversity of its own meaning and confuses the Savior’s births—whether from the Father before the ages or from his mother in the fullness of time—so thoroughly that it is entirely impossible to understand which birth it wishes to discuss.

This must be avoided everywhere with the greatest care: the order of the divine words must not be altered, lest a labyrinth of error be woven from the Scripture of truth.

## VI

Consider also how rigorously that responsory sung at the same vigils must be rejected. In it that vain presumptuous person says:

“From that hidden dwelling of his the Son of God went forth; he descended to visit and console all who desired him with their whole heart.”

It is disfigured both by ignorance of language and by the absurdity and falsity of its meaning. For he spoke with extreme levity of the Son’s hidden dwelling, and falsely asserted that he visited and consoled all who desired him, when rather those whom he deigned to visit he himself made capable of recognizing and desiring him.

## VII

Consider also the words of another responsory, composed as though on the mystery of Christ’s birth, but, contrary to the custom of the nocturnal office, pompously shouted from an elevated place:

“He descended from heaven, sent from the citadel of the Father [Note: [Col. 0331D] ‘He entered through the Virgin’s ear.’ The words of this responsory were changed in later editions of the Paris Breviary, where it now reads: ‘He descended from heaven, sent from the citadel of the Father; he entered through the virgin mother into our region, clothed in a purple robe, and came forth through a closed gate, the light and glory of the whole fabric of the world.’], he entered through the Virgin’s ear into our region, clothed in a purple robe, and came forth through a golden gate, the light and glory of the whole fabric of the world.”

First, it does not identify who descended. As for what he meant by “the citadel of the Father,” he himself utterly failed to understand. Is there some heavenly or super-heavenly structure that was made by him, or something else that is not the same as the Father, or that is the Father himself? If it exists, how is it his citadel?

Nor do catholic ears tolerate the claim that the Word of God entered through the Virgin’s ear, since, being incorporeal and wholly present everywhere, he neither approaches locally nor needs a bodily entrance. Unless perhaps he wished to persuade us that the holy Virgin conceived the Son of God through the sound of angelic words.

How far this differs from the truth of the faith is clear from the words of the angel himself. When the Virgin asked him, “How will this happen, since I do not know man?” he answered: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

How, moreover, can the virginal womb be understood as “our region,” since that virgin is the mother of the only Son, while all of us are born not from virgin flesh but from flesh corrupted by sin? This cannot be discovered at all.

Next, when he says that the Son, clothed in a purple robe, entered through the Virgin’s ear—whether he imagined him clothed in royal dress according to human custom, or supposed that the Word of God did not receive human form from the Virgin but brought it from heaven, calling that form a purple robe—he is guilty of the clearest blasphemy.

And how frivolously he dared to say that he came forth through a golden gate! Christ’s birth from the Virgin ought not to be sketched with superfluous words, but declared through a simple confession. He is not, as that man says, the light of the whole fabric of the world, but, according to the truth of the Gospel, the light only of rational creation.

## VIII

Someone also composed another responsory from the words of the Gospel, though not in the Gospel’s order; it is now sung after being corrected by your Charity. It says:

“Darkness came upon them when the Jews had crucified Jesus; and about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice: ‘God, God, why have you forsaken me?’ Then one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.”

It is certain to all the faithful that our Savior died for us not compelled by any violence of pain, but voluntarily; nor did he lose his soul by necessity, but laid it down by his own authority, as he himself says: “No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, so that I may take it up again.”

But this man, ignorant of the Gospel’s order and of the truth of the faith, first said that the Lord’s side was pierced by the soldiers with a spear, and then that he gave up his spirit. It is entirely pagan to suppose that Christ died not through the kindness of his own will but through the force of pain.

On the contrary, the Gospel reports that the Lord cried out with a loud voice: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit”; and, saying this, he expired.

The soldiers who were present were so astonished at Christ’s death that they are reported immediately to have glorified God and confessed him to be the Son of God. Later, when the Jews requested that the legs of the robbers crucified with him be broken, Pilate granted their request; but Jesus was already dead, and the Gospel reports not that his legs were broken, but that his side was opened by the soldier’s spear—not, as this ignorant writer put it, “pierced through.”

## IX

What of those many false prophecies, if one may call them that, found in the responsories and antiphonaries and pronounced as though from the Lord’s own voice, although they occur in none of the divine Scriptures?

For example:

“On the eighteenth day of the tenth month you shall fast, says the Lord, and I will send you a Savior and defender, who will go before you and lead you into the land that I swore to your fathers.”

And again:

“I will place a crown of glory upon his head, says the Lord, and I will clothe him in a white robe, because he kept my commandments and because his blood was poured out upon the earth for my name.”

And again:

“You are holy, says the Lord; I will multiply your number, so that you may pray for my people in this place.”

And many other ridiculous and fantastical sayings of this kind.

The words that the Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel against false prophets seem appropriate to their inventors:

“Woe to the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit and see nothing.”

And shortly afterward:

“They see empty visions and prophesy lies, saying, ‘The Lord says,’ when the Lord has not sent them, and they persist in confirming their word. Have you not seen an empty vision and spoken a lying divination? You say, ‘The Lord says,’ though I have not spoken.

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have spoken vanity and uttered lies, behold, I am against you, says the Lord God. My hand will be against the prophets who see empty things and prophesy lies. They shall not be in the council of my people, nor shall they be written in the writing of the house of Israel, nor shall they enter the land of Israel.”

## X

But these and similar matters, of which the aforesaid book contained an infinite supply, can be judged more easily through conversation and faithful examination, since it is unworthy to write them down and tedious for your wisdom to hear them.

It now remains for us to expound, as we promised above, the decrees of the sacred canons and the opinions of the catholic Fathers, so that it may be clearly shown by them with what caution the inventions of the light-minded must be avoided: inventions founded on no truth, adorned by no reason, and exposed to contempt.

## XI

[Note: [Col. 0333C] In the African Council. This canon appears in the African Council, chapter 70, and in the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, title 103. In both places, however, it differs slightly from Agobard’s edition. For there it reads as follows: “It was also resolved that prayers which have been approved in council—whether prefaces, commendations, or the laying on of hands—should be celebrated by all, and that no others at all should be used contrary to the faith, but that whatever has been collected by the more prudent should be said.”]

The following decree was promulgated in the African Council:

“That prayers and supplications are not to be said unless they have been approved in council; nor should any of them at all be sung in the Church except those which have been examined and approved in synod by the more prudent, lest something contrary to the faith should have been composed either through ignorance or through zeal.”

Here we should briefly consider that not only those things composed through the zeal of unbelief, but also those which have been composed through [Note: [Col. 0334C] “Simplicity.” The manuscript reads *inplacitate*, for which Masson printed *imbecillitate*. We have restored *simplicitate*, as the matter seemed to require.] the simplicity of ignorance against the rule of faith, are rejected with equal severity.

## XII

When blessed Jerome was explaining the Apostle’s command in his Commentary on chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Ephesians—where he says, “Be filled with the Spirit, speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord”—he did not remain silent about what he saw as blameworthy in the singers of the Church.

“Therefore,” he says, “we ought to sing, make melody, and praise the Lord more with the mind than with the voice. This is what is meant by the words: ‘Singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord.’

“Let young men hear this; let those hear it whose duty it is to sing psalms in the Church: God is to be sung not with the voice but with the heart. Nor should the throat and jaws be smeared with a sweet medicinal preparation after the manner of tragedians, so that theatrical melodies and songs may be heard in the Church, but rather with fear, with works, and with knowledge of the Scriptures.

“Even if someone is, as they commonly call it, cacophonous, if he has good works he is a sweet singer before God. Let Christ’s servant sing in such a way that it is not the singer’s voice but the words being read that please; so that the evil spirit which was in Saul may be driven out from those who are similarly possessed by it, and not introduced into those who have made a theater for the crowds out of the house of God.”

In these words we should carefully consider that Jerome confirms that those who sing, like David the psalmist, with fear and spiritual seriousness can drive the evil spirit even from their hearers. But those who take excessive delight in theatrical sounds and stage-like melodies, even when the words are divine, he testifies not only to fail to drive that spirit from others but, what is terrifying, to introduce it into themselves.

Hence, elsewhere, when the same teacher was explaining Isaiah’s statement, “Your assemblies are wicked” (chapter 1), he says:

“Every assembly that does not offer spiritual sacrifices, and does not hear what is sung in the fiftieth psalm—‘A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit; God does not despise a broken and humbled heart’—is abominable to God.”

The free mind, therefore—that is, the mind not subject to the bodily senses—must resist vain and harmful delight of the ears just as it resists the delights of the other senses: sight, smell, taste, and touch. The soul is weighed down and captured by the disturbances of these senses.

Finally, how greatly the pleasures of the ears weaken the mind’s strength is attested by the same teacher, who says:

“Hearing is soothed by the varied singing of instruments and the inflections of voices; by the song of poets and the wit, turns, and whatever else enters through the ears in comedies and mimes, and weakens the manliness of the mind.”

## XIII

Blessed martyr Cyprian also speaks in a similar way in his sermon *On Jealousy and Envy*, explaining the Apostle’s statement, “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around seeking someone to devour.”

He says:

“He prowls around each one of us, and, like an enemy besieging an enclosed place, examines the walls and tests whether some part of the members is less stable and less trustworthy, through whose entrance he might penetrate into the interior.

“He presents alluring forms and easy pleasures to the eyes, so that through sight he may destroy chastity. He tests the ears through melodious music, so that by hearing a sweeter sound he may loosen and soften Christian vigor.”

## XIV
