Understanding this also as belonging to the devil’s temptation, blessed Augustine gives thanks to God in Book X, chapter 33, of his *Confessions* for having been freed from this vice.

“Pleasures of the ears,” he says, “had entangled and subjected me more tenaciously, but you have loosened and freed me. Now, in the sounds animated by your words, when they are sung with a sweet and skillful voice, I confess that I rest somewhat, while through those holy words themselves our souls feel themselves moved more religiously and fervently into the flame of devotion when they are sung in this way than if they were not sung so.”

And again, after saying several things about the usefulness of singing psalms in the Church, he offers a measured judgment:

“It seems safer to me—I remember having often been told this concerning Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria—that he made the reader of the psalm sound his voice with so slight a modulation that it was closer to recitation than to singing.

“Nevertheless, when I remember the tears I shed at the songs of your Church at the beginning of the recovery of my faith, and now when I am moved not by the singing but by the things that are sung, when they are sung with a clear voice and the most fitting melody, I recognize again the great usefulness of this institution. I am more inclined—not indeed pronouncing an irrevocable judgment—to approve the custom of singing in the Church, so that through the pleasures of the ears the weaker mind may rise into an affection of devotion.

“Yet when it happens to me that the singing moves me more than the thing that is sung, I confess that I sin in a manner deserving punishment, and then I would rather not hear the singer.”

Behold how this most holy and learned man both approves the practice of singing for the sake of the weak, whom it makes rise into an affection of devotion, and yet says that, when the singing moves the mind more than the thing sung, the sin is deserving of punishment—so much so that it would be better not to hear the singer, even when the singing and sounds are animated and enlivened by divine utterances, so that the life of the songs and sounds lies in the meanings of the divine utterances.

But if, in his own days, he had heard people singing not divine utterances but human inventions, would he not have judged such singing dead and lifeless?

## XV

But because the title of the aforementioned little book displays the name of Bishop Gregory [Note: The title bears Gregory’s name. For there exists among the works of Saint Gregory the Pope an *Antiphonary*, or *Gradual*, arranged according to the cycle of the year. Agobard, however, maintains that this book is not Gregory’s—unless it truly belonged to Gregory but was corrupted over the course of time.], and some, adopting this opinion, consequently think that it was composed by the blessed Gregory, Roman pontiff and most illustrious teacher, let us see what that holy man established concerning ecclesiastical chant, or what the Roman Church sang in his time.

Thus he says in his *Decrees* (Book IV, indiction 13, letter 44):

> “In this holy Roman Church, over which divine providence has willed that I preside, a very reprehensible custom arose some time ago: certain men are chosen as singers for the ministry of the sacred altar, and, having been constituted in the order of deacons, devote themselves to the modulation of the voice, though it would have been fitting for them to be free for the office of preaching and for the pursuit of almsgiving. Hence it frequently happens that, while a pleasing voice is sought for the sacred ministry, a suitable life is neglected; and the singer, as a minister of the Lord, provokes Him by his conduct while delighting the people with his voice. Therefore, by the present decree I establish that, in this see, the ministers of the sacred altar must not sing, but are to perform only the office of reading the Gospel during the solemn celebrations of Mass. I decree, however, that the psalms [Col. 0336C] and the other readings be presented by subdeacons or, if necessity demands, by the lesser orders. But if anyone should attempt to act against this decree of mine, let him be anathema.” And they all replied, “Let him be anathema.”

Behold, the apostolic man censures the custom by which the duty of singing was imposed upon deacons; and he says that what must be sought in them is not a pleasing voice but a suitable life. He asserts that God is provoked by the conduct of such ministers, even if they delight the people with their voices. Once such a custom has been condemned, he decrees that the psalms and the other readings be presented by subdeacons or by the lesser orders, with only the office of reading the Gospel assigned to the deacons. From this it is plainly demonstrated that the psalms were then customarily sung in the Church, and that even now the greater part of the divine offices is composed from them; it was not composed from the inventions of just anyone. No one doubts that such inventions were not composed by so great a man, unless he is ignorant of his most sincere faith and outstanding learning.

## XVI

Since the sayings of the holy Fathers have sufficiently shown how greatly human frivolity and falsehood must be avoided, and how greatly the truth and sincerity of the divine utterances must be embraced, I gladly append a few words of the blessed martyr Cyprian, by which it may be shown with what seriousness and moderation the divine offices ought to be celebrated:

> “Let speech and prayer among those who pray,” he says (*Sermon on the Lord’s Prayer*), “be disciplined, containing quietness and modesty. Let us consider that we stand in the sight of God. We must please the divine eyes both by the bearing of our bodies and by the manner of our voice. For just as it is characteristic of the shameless to make a din with shouting, so it is fitting for the modest to pray with restrained petitions. And when we assemble together with the brethren and celebrate the divine sacrifices with the priest of the Lord, we must remember modesty and discipline: we must not scatter our prayers indiscriminately in disorderly utterances, nor loudly parade before God, with tumultuous loquacity, a petition that ought to be commended modestly. For God is the hearer not of the voice but of the heart; nor must He be admonished by shouting, since He sees our thoughts, as the Lord testifies and says: ‘And all the churches shall know that I am He who searches the kidneys and hearts.’ Let the psalm resound. Let our banquet be sober spiritual hearing; let religious sweetness delight our ears.”

## XVII

Instructed, therefore, by these and similar admonitions of the Fathers, and following in the footsteps of those whom we do not doubt have gone before us to the Lord, let us reject all human inventions as superfluous things and resound in His praises with the words of the Lord, which suffice for everything, so that with blessed David we may be able to say: “What we have received from Your hand, we have given You.” For, as blessed Augustine says, “Nothing is rightly offered to God except what is received from Him.”

In another passage he likewise instructed his own people: “Do not sing anything except what you have read should be sung.” Certain religious men, following this, gave the following command to the brethren subject to them:

> “Let no one presume, in this congregation, either to meditate upon or to recite responsories or antiphons which some people customarily sing in an arranged melody according to their own pleasure, without having taken them from canonical Scripture.”

For we ought to imitate the sound and simple apostolic teaching and that of our fathers, to establish grace, and to subject the heart and conduct to discipline. We ought, therefore, to sing those things which, as blessed Augustine says, have been written in such a way that they are sung.

> “But what has not been written in this manner, let us not sing; for such things must not be made known to human beings in any other way than the way in which the Lord Himself commanded them to be manifested through His prophets and apostles. From us He seeks obedience rather than the sacrifice of victims; He is pleased not by the studied artistry of song but by the observance of His commandments and purity of heart.”

## XVIII

These most sincere ordinances of the Fathers must be observed with every diligence and reverence. For by this means the purity of faith and the discipline of religion are most beneficially preserved, and two evils utterly opposed to piety are usefully cut away: first, the presumption of the most foolish people, who dare to sing in churches not only inept and superfluous things but also profane and heretical ones, is completely excluded; second, a great occasion for foolish and harmful occupation is removed from boys and from all generally upon whom the duty of singing has been imposed.

Among them, very many spend all the days of their lives, from early childhood to the gray hairs of old age, preparing and perfecting their singing. They consume in such occupation the whole time that ought to be devoted to useful and spiritual studies—namely, reading and searching the divine utterances. What is undoubtedly highly harmful to their souls is that, ignorant of their faith, unversed in the holy Scriptures, and empty and devoid of divine understanding, they think this alone sufficient for themselves. For this reason they also walk about puffed up and inflated if they appear to have learned, however imperfectly, the sound and voice of singing and to have been counted among the singers.

Such people must fear lest they be struck by that very rebuke of God which blessed Gregory mentioned above: while they delight the people with their voices, they provoke God by their conduct. He says: “This people honors Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me.” And again: “Take away from Me the tumult of your songs; I will not hear the songs of your lyre.”

Blessed Jerome also, as mentioned above, plainly says of people of this kind that they have made the Church of God into a theater for the crowds. Avoiding this superfluous occupation in the same sacred offices, the ancients—although they certainly had at their disposal an abundant variety of praise from the divine books, as well as skill in musical modulation—nevertheless preferred to repeat the same things often rather than occupy or burden the minds of those who sing with innumerable and unnecessary matters.

## XIX

Therefore, with the help of God’s grace, we must strive and take every pious care that, just as the Church possesses, for the celebration of the solemn rites of Mass, a *Book of Mysteries* [Note: The *Book of Mysteries*, that is, the *Book of Sacraments*, concerning which we spoke above in chapter 30 of the book *On Images*.], arranged with the purest faith and elegant brevity; and just as it possesses a *Book of Readings*, suitably collected from the divine books, so also we may possess this third official little book—that is, the *Antiphonary*—cleansed of all human inventions and falsehoods [Note: “Human inventions.” Perhaps Alcuin was referring to the very things Agobard censures here when he wrote the following to the brethren of Lyon in letter 69: “Do not cherish in ecclesiastical offices traditions unheard of in former times.”], and sufficiently ordered throughout the entire cycle of the year from the purest words of holy Scripture.

Thus, in carrying out the sacred offices, according to the most approved rule of faith and the venerable discipline of paternal authority, one uniform and identical form of prayers, one form of readings, and one form of ecclesiastical melodies may be observed by us. Once these have been learned as quickly as possible by boys of good ability, they will make them sufficiently and seriously competent to sing the divine praises, while not hindering them from more important and spiritual studies.

For who is so contentious—or rather so insane and so opposed to every consideration of truth—as not to acknowledge that it is more right, appropriate, and beneficial to sing in the praises of God what one sees to be faithfully taken from the divine sayings and books? Thus, just as in the Catholic Creed we profess our faith not in our own words but in those of the apostles, and in the Lord’s Prayer we make our supplication not in our own words but in the words of the Lord and our Savior Himself, so also, in honoring the divine praise, let us resound not with human but with divine and spiritual psalms, hymns, and songs, according to the Apostle.

For other things are sought in vain where these are known to suffice and to abound beyond measure.

[Col. 0339A]

# HERE BEGINS [Note: We already pointed out, in the book *On Divine Psalmody*, that in this book Agobard repays Amalarius in kind. I do not alter my judgment. Moreover, this book is now being published for the first time from an old manuscript belonging to the distinguished Peter Marnaesius, senator of Grenoble, as was stated in the preface. There is nothing in it particularly noteworthy.] THE BOOK OF THE VENERABLE AGOBARD, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS, AGAINST THE FOUR BOOKS OF AMALARIUS, ABBOT [Note: “Amalarius, abbot.” The old manuscript explicitly reads this way. This is confirmed by the authority of a very ancient manuscript of the Thuane Library, which contains the same Amalarius’s books *On the Divine Offices*. In that manuscript it reads as follows: “The book of Amalarius, abbot, on the divine offices.” Again: “The contents of the following treatise of Amalarius the abbot’s writing on the divine offices begins.” It must therefore be investigated of what monastery he was abbot. Elsewhere he is called a chorepiscopus. For there is preserved in the library of the monastery of Echternach, in the Duchy of Luxembourg, an old manuscript written more than six hundred years ago, from which the Reverend Father Alexander Wilthemius of the Society of Jesus copied this material and sent it to Paris to the Reverend Father Philippe Labbe, who, out of friendship for me, willingly shared it with me. It begins: “The official book of Amelarius the chorepiscopus—that is, concerning ecclesiastical order and the other offices—in four books, addressed to the emperor Louis.” Besides Amalarius’s published works, five of his letters are preserved in Paris in two very ancient manuscripts of the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; they will shortly be brought to light in volume VII of Dom Luc d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*. The first is addressed to Jeremiah, archbishop of Sens, concerning the name of Jesus and how it ought to be written, together with Jeremiah the archbishop’s reply. The second is addressed to Jonah, bishop of Orléans, on the same matter, together with Jonah’s reply. The third is addressed to Rantgarius, bishop of Noyon, on how the words from the Gospel should be understood: “This is the cup of my blood of the new and eternal covenant,” and so forth. The fourth is addressed to Hetto the monk—presumably the one who was abbot of Fulda after Hrabanus—concerning the name *Seraphim*, when it is neuter and when masculine. Finally, the fifth is addressed to Guntard: whether it is permissible to spit immediately after the sacrifice has been consumed. The first letters, together with Jeremiah’s and Jonah’s replies, are also preserved in the manuscript of the monastery of Echternach and are in the possession of the distinguished Philippe Labbe.] (G)*

## I

In his first book, chapter thirty-seven, Amalarius says:

> “The Roman custom inserts one day, namely the seventh day before the Kalends of May [25 April], which it calls the Greater Litany, not a fast. A litany, as we said earlier, is a supplication among us. A tranquil mind, free from evil desire, can pray to God even if it eats meat soberly at midday and rejoices in the Lord’s resurrection. Nevertheless, the practice of the greater Fathers—that is, of the apostles—must be followed. Perhaps from the office itself we shall be able to understand what ought to be requested at such a time.
>
> “The first prayer at Mass says: ‘Grant, we beseech You, almighty God, that we who trust in Your mercy in our affliction may always be protected against every adversity by Your defense.’ The offertory agrees with this, saying: ‘Help me, Lord my God; save me for the sake of Your mercy. Let those who rise up against me be put to shame.’
>
> “At that time, namely on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, enemies may stir up wars against neighboring kingdoms. As I think, holy Church prudently provided that God should be asked to destroy now the plans of those who wish to attack His peace, just as formerly He destroyed the counsel of Ahithophel. The Epistle also directs its attention to this when it says: ‘For the continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful.’
>
> “The Gospel gives voice to another petition, saying: ‘Which of you asks a father for bread, and again for a fish, and again, if he asks for an egg?’ In these three things we can understand temporal matters that are to be requested: by bread, all good things that grow from the earth; by fish, those that come from the fields; by egg, the animals that mate with one another. These things are making progress at the time mentioned: the shoots of the crops are sprouting; the fruits of the trees are emerging from the blossom; the liquid of the vines and of the olive is bursting forth from its trees; and the young animals are beating the fields with their feet.
>
> “Since these things are necessary for our use, they ought to be requested from the Lord so that they may be preserved.”

## II

In these words of Amalarius anyone can easily detect what is useless and what is harmful. For he says that litanies—that is, Rogation prayers—can be performed without fasting and abstinence from meat, something never stated even by people of little wisdom.

The Ninevites, certainly, when they were converted by the preaching of the prophet Jonah, had no teachers to instruct them that the sacrifice pleasing to God is a contrite spirit and a broken and humbled heart. Yet, understanding by natural reason that God’s mercy was to be bent by such things, and recognizing what weapons they should take up against the destruction threatening them, the same Scripture says:

> “And Jonah began to enter the city, traveling one day’s journey, and he cried out and said: ‘Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.’”

> “And the men of Nineveh believed in the Lord, and they proclaimed a fast, and clothed themselves in sackcloth, from the greatest to the least”—that is, even to the nursing infant, as those understood who wished to write about this praiseworthy repentance. Among them was Prudentius, a learned man, who says:
>
> “No one remembered drinking; no one remembered eating.
>
> All the young had abandoned their fasting tables.
>
> Indeed, when milk was denied,
>
> the cradles of the wailing infants were drenched with tears.
>
> The sparing nurse withheld the nourishment of her breast.”

The same Scripture continues:

> “And the word reached the king of Nineveh, and he rose from his throne, cast off his garment, clothed himself in sackcloth, and sat in ashes. And he cried out and said in Nineveh, by decree of the king and his nobles: ‘Let neither human beings nor animals, cattle nor sheep, taste anything; let them not feed, and let them not drink water. Let human beings and animals be covered with sackcloth, and let them cry mightily to God. Let each person turn from his evil way and from the iniquity that is in his hands. Who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and turn back from the fury of His anger, so that we shall not perish?’
>
> “And God saw their works, that they had turned from their evil way; and He had mercy concerning the evil which He had said He would do to them, and He did not do it.”

But through the prophet Joel the Lord Himself shows what sort of rogations He wishes to be offered to Him, saying:

> “Turn to Me with all your heart, in fasting, weeping, and mourning; and rend your hearts and not your garments. Turn to the Lord your God, for He is gracious and merciful, patient and abundant in mercy, and ready to relent concerning evil.”

Moreover, as for what he adds—that on the seventh day before the Kalends of May the Gospel lesson concerning the example of bread, egg, and fish should be read because they prosper at that time, and that the Lord should then be entreated on their behalf so that they may be preserved for our use—who does not see how worthy of laughter this is, since the Lord never commanded public prayers to be made for these things? On the contrary, He commanded:

> “Do not seek what you shall eat or what you shall drink, and do not be lifted up. For all these things the nations of the world seek. But your Father knows that you need them. Nevertheless, seek the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you.”

For even if God is to be entreated on behalf of the crops of the earth and of every kind of animal, are Rogation prayers also to be made on behalf of fish, so that they may be preserved for us?

## III

Again, in his first book, chapter twenty-seven, Amalarius says:

> “The one whom the bishop earlier prayed to send the Holy Spirit, in what follows he asks to deign to seal the recipient unto eternal life—that is, that the recipient may not lose the same Spirit until He brings His guest to eternal life.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Without this seal we ought not to appear before God. Concerning it, as though concerning a garment, Paul said to the Corinthians: ‘For we who are in this body groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be stripped but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.’ Of what garment he is speaking, he shows subsequently: ‘Now He who prepares us for this very thing is God, who has given us the pledge of the Spirit.’”

## IV

Everyone who is concerned for the sincerity of the faith can judge what sort of words these of Amalarius are. Yet this which he adds, saying:

> “Concerning this seal, as though concerning a garment, Paul said to the Corinthians: ‘For we who are in this body groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be stripped but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life,’”

if he read somewhere that this passage has the meaning he introduces, is perhaps the error of the person who wrote it. But if he devised it himself, it is excessive presumption.

For what is he burdened by which makes him groan? Certainly by the fact that he does not wish to be stripped but to be clothed over. And if he does not wish to be stripped of the garment of the Holy Spirit, with what does he wish to clothe himself over the Spirit of God?

But since it is laborious to refute his interpretation, it is enough for us to say that the Catholic teacher blessed Augustine declares this garment to be the mortality of the flesh which we bear while living in this body. Therefore we groan, being burdened, because we fear that through temporal death we may be stripped of the garment of the flesh; and, if it were possible, we would wish to be clothed over with immortal life—not laying aside that mortality through death, but rather having it swallowed up by life.

[Col. 0342B]

## V

Again, in his first book, chapter forty, Amalarius says:

> “It is customary for ordinary people to ask for how long they ought to preserve the anointing of chrism on the head, so that those who receive the laying on of hands may not wash, apart from the time of the baptistery. They may be answered that the anointing should be celebrated for as long as the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles is generally celebrated by the Church—that is, for seven days.
>
> “And not without reason. Since He came to His guest in seven women, it is proper that each woman’s banquet be prepared for Him on successive days. Concerning these women Isaiah says: ‘Seven women shall take hold of one man.’ Their banquet is when they themselves satisfy their guest from their own resources. Christ held such banquets among His guests, and the Holy Spirit likewise holds such banquets.
>
> “The guest of the Holy Spirit is the human mind. The mind is satisfied by the richness of the Holy Spirit all the more abundantly the less it has been devoted to carnal pleasures.
>
> “Let the recipient observe the time of the coming of the Holy Spirit as a dear friend is accustomed to behave toward a dear friend. When a dear person comes to a dear friend, the one who receives him does not wish to offend him in anything; rather, whatever he knows to be pleasing to him, he offers him from a kindly heart. In the same way, whatever the recipient of the Holy Spirit recognizes as pleasing to Him, let him offer it to Him for as long as He is with him. If he does this, perhaps he will be reconciled to Him more quickly when some offense has caused Him to depart from him.
>
> “When Christ remembers that the anointing of chrism is present to Him, then above all He remembers that He ought to be under the discipline of the Holy Spirit. That anointing is performed so that we may know that the Holy Spirit works invisibly within us.
>
> “Oil is accustomed to comfort the limbs of the weary; balsam is accustomed to give off a fragrance. The limbs of our soul are weary when it regrets having done what is contrary to God’s will. To such a soul the Holy Spirit is accustomed to come and show it sins that have been forgiven or are to be forgiven. Hence the Spirit Himself is also called the Comforter.”

Let everyone who hears these confused and useless words of Amalarius see how he should correct or ridicule them, since they do not build up faith but destroy it; nor do they plant virtues in the minds of their hearers, but uproot them—especially where, at the end, he says:

> “When Christ remembers that the anointing of chrism is present to Him, then above all He remembers that He ought to be under the discipline of the Holy Spirit.”

## VI

Again, Amalarius says in the same chapter:

> “For it was not without reason that the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost in wind and fiery tongues. He wished to demonstrate to the future Church what He had accomplished in the apostles through His coming.
>
> “He came in a mighty wind to show that He would shake every earthly desire from the hearts of the apostles. For just as a violent wind throws dust from the face of the earth, so the coming of the Holy Spirit drives every earthly desire from the human heart.
>
> “He appeared in fiery tongues to demonstrate what sort of tongues He would make the tongues of the apostles—that is, tongues speaking and pouring fiery words into the hearts of believers. For these fiery words consume sins and kindle hearts to love of the eternal homeland.
>
> “This is the charity that is poured into the hearts of believers and makes them one heart, in imitation of its own substance—that is, so that they will one thing, just as the Holy Trinity wills one thing.”

## VII

Let prudent people weigh what judgment they should form concerning these words of Amalarius. It is nevertheless clear that what he says—that the Spirit came in a mighty wind to show that He would shake every earthly desire from the hearts of the apostles—must be challenged.

If, at the very hour when they were filled with the Holy Spirit, all earthly desires still had to be shaken from the hearts of the apostles, what had the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, accomplished in them during three years? And why did He say to them: “Now you are clean, because of the word which I have spoken to you”? And again: “You are clean, but not all”?

Were they not already new wineskins, prepared and capable of receiving the new wine—that is, the Holy Spirit, who would lead them into all truth?

But in what he adds, saying:

> “He appeared in fiery tongues to demonstrate what sort of tongues He would make the tongues of the apostles—that is, speaking and pouring fiery words into the hearts of believers. For these fiery words consume sins,”

he does not sufficiently attend to what he is saying. The apostles had long since been speaking; they had already preached and had already performed many great signs, so that they said to the Lord: “Even the demons are subject to us in Your name.”

But words do not consume sins, as this man says. Rather, they administer faith and build up faith, which prepares those who hear for the grace of baptism, from that time onward.

As for what he adds, saying that the fiery words of the apostles kindle hearts to love of the eternal homeland—“This is the charity that is poured into the hearts of believers and makes them one heart, in imitation of its own substance—that is, so that they will one thing, just as the Holy Trinity wills one thing”—if he thinks correctly, he does not speak correctly about what is good.

For there is a great difference between the words of preachers and the anointing of the Holy Spirit. If the apostles’ words had been able to accomplish in the hearts of their hearers what this man dreams, then the words of the Lord would rather have accomplished it in the hearts of the Jews.

But since this is not the work of words but of the divine inner gift, the teacher ought to make this known in his teaching. Amalarius, on the contrary, teaching not according to sound doctrine, is recognized as holding the view that, just as charity—that is, the Holy Spirit—by grace makes the hearts of the faithful one and makes them will one thing, so in the Holy Trinity the grace of the same Spirit makes the Holy Trinity itself one and makes it will one thing, just as the Arians were accustomed to teach.

## VIII

Again, in his first book, chapter thirteen, Amalarius says:

> “Our Lord is the lamb who was handed over at the beginning of the fifteenth lunar day, and He ascended the cross on the Parasceve. A responsory follows with four verses. There can be no doubt that Christ the man consisted of the four elements. It is natural for a human being to consist of earth, water, air, and fire. When He assumed human nature, He assumed these four elements. They hung on the cross between the two thieves. Hence one verse: ‘You shall be known in the midst of two animals,’ as Jerome says in his commentary on Habakkuk.”

## IX

Let the prudent carefully consider how wildly Amalarius ranges in these words, while he wishes to cure the errors of a deranged mind through charity.

Those who composed chant from the words of Scripture made it according to their own judgment, in whatever way seemed suitable to them—and in different ways in different regions. They were not moved by the Spirit of God, as blessed Peter speaks concerning the prophets and the prophecy of future events, saying:

> “For prophecy was never brought forth by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were inspired by the Holy Spirit.”

Therefore, if a person adds four verses to one responsory, this is not the shadow of any riddle, as this man thinks and most falsely compels others to think.

But concerning what he says:

> “A responsory follows with four verses. There can be no doubt that Christ the man consisted of the four elements. It is natural for a human being to consist of earth, water, air, and fire. When He assumed human nature, He assumed these four elements,”

the Apostle’s statement must be set against these most foolish and blasphemous words:

> “See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ.”

Let Amalarius say how Christ the man consists of the four elements. True believers—that is, Catholics—hold Christ in the manner in which blessed Augustine confesses Him, saying (*Sermon 8 on Various Matters*):

> “Let us acknowledge the twofold substance of Christ: the divine, by which He is equal to the Father; and the human, by which the Father is greater than He. Yet the two together are not two but one Christ, lest God be a quaternity rather than a Trinity. For just as one human being consists of rational soul and flesh, so one Christ is God and man. And therefore Christ is God, rational soul, and flesh.”

We confess Christ in all these things and Christ in each of them.

Who, then, is He through whom the world was made? Christ Jesus—but in the form of God.

Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate? Christ Jesus—but in the form of a servant.

Again, concerning the individual components of which a human being consists:

Who was not abandoned in hell? Christ Jesus—but in the soul alone.

Who, destined to rise again, lay for three days in the tomb? Christ Jesus—but in the flesh alone.

Amalarius goes on to say:

> “It is natural for a human being to consist of earth, water, air, and fire.”

This is far removed from a clear-minded understanding. It is a philosophical invention. Although ecclesiastical teachers do not wholly reject it, they do not agree with it in every respect, nor do they say that this is natural at the beginning of creation.

It is inappropriate to speak at greater length about this matter now, since the authority of Scripture demonstrates that it must be understood otherwise—namely, in the passage where the almighty Creator says to the human being whom He had formed from the mud of the earth—or, as another translation has it, from dust:

> “You are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

Water, air, and fire cannot do this; nor can the soul which the Creator breathed into the face of the human being formed from dust. Rather, it happens as Scripture says elsewhere:

> “Let the dust return to its earth, from which it came, and let the spirit return to God who gave it.”

If it is said with excessive foolishness of any human being that he naturally subsists from the elements, how much more so must this be rejected when said of Christ the Lord, whose flesh has no origin except the operation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and the assumption by the Word alone?

> “For the Word became flesh in order to dwell among us.”

Therefore, as blessed Augustine says, Christ is God, soul, and flesh. But God is not from the elements, nor is the soul. The reality of the flesh was taken from the Virgin’s body without any human or angelic work, but, as has been said, solely by divine action.

As for what Amalarius says—“When Christ assumed human nature, He assumed these four elements”—he must be answered that the elements did not need to be redeemed from the death of sin, as did the human being who was held captive under the devil through transgression.

Humanity had gone astray like a sheep that was lost. For its sake the good shepherd came, to seek, find, and lead it back to the heavenly homeland, where it may live without the administration of bodily elements, enjoying God through that same Redeemer, as it is written:

> “And let us be in His true Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.”

Concerning the elements, however, we must believe what the chief of the apostles, blessed Peter, says:

> “But the day of the Lord will come like a thief; on it the heavens will pass away with great violence, and the elements will be dissolved by heat.”

Amalarius adds:

> “They”—that is, the elements—“hung on the cross between the two thieves. Hence one verse: ‘You shall be known in the midst of two animals.’”

What more ridiculous thing could he have said than that air and fire hung from the cross, when their nature is to be carried upward?

And he adds that Jerome says this in his commentary on Habakkuk. Tell me, I beg you, what have Jerome and Habakkuk to do with this? Does he say that the elements will be known to hang in the midst of two animals?

## X

Again, in his first book, chapter twelve, Amalarius says:

> “If He emptied Himself, according to the Apostle, after He had assumed the form of a servant, how much more when He became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross?”

Amalarius must be told that the Apostle does not speak as he says—that is, “After He had assumed the form of a servant, He emptied Himself”—but rather: “He emptied Himself, assuming the form of a servant”; that is, He became obedient unto death in the very assumption of the form of a servant, and not afterward.

## XI

Again, in his third book, chapter twenty-three, Amalarius says:

> “Now we must speak about the *Te igitur*. From the beginning of the prayer up to the place where it says, ‘and command us to be numbered among Your chosen flock,’ the sacrifice of the chosen is celebrated—of those who have nothing in the flesh that resists them, nor anything in the conscience that disturbs them. For just as there were two altars in the tabernacle of Moses, or in Solomon’s temple—one for incense and the other for burnt offerings—so there are two sacrifices of the holy Church.”

A little later, again in chapter twenty-four, he adds:

> “After the first sacrifice has been offered, which consists of the prayers of the perfect and is joined to the sacrifice of the angels, one descends to the universal sacrifice, namely the immolation of Christ, which is celebrated before ‘Nobis quoque peccatoribus.’”

And shortly afterward he adds:

> “For one victim, Christ, was offered for the just and the unjust.”

## XII

Against these confused words and turbulent ideas of Amalarius, the answer must be given that neither Pelagius nor Coelestius dared to preach their heresy so irreverently.

They asserted only the possibility, saying that a human being could be without sin if he wished; yet they did not dare to say that they themselves were without sin. Amalarius, however, dares to say something much worse, asserting that there are many who have nothing in the body that resists them, nor anything in the conscience that disturbs them.

Although this man is worse than they, both groups contradict the apostle John in common, who says:

> “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

They also contradict the apostle Paul, who says:

> “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin which is in my members.”

There, troubled, he adds:

> “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?”

The Psalmist likewise, speaking in the voice of the perfect—those who can say, “As the deer longs for the fountains of water, so my soul longs for You, O God”—adds:

> “My soul is troubled within me.”

And again:

> “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?”

### XIII.

The same Amalarius further says: “For just as there were two altars in the tabernacle of Moses, or in Solomon’s temple—one for incense and the other for burnt offerings—so there are two sacrifices of the holy Church.”

To this one must reply that, just as the Catholic Church does not have two faiths or two baptisms, so it does not have two altars or two sacrifices. Thus blessed Jerome also teaches in his exposition of the prophet Isaiah, where it says, “On that day there shall be an altar of the Lord in the land of Egypt,” saying:

“Now one altar is spoken of in the same way as one faith, one baptism, and one Church.”

And again:

“But one altar of Egypt—that is, of this world—is spoken of, so that we may know that all the altars erected against the altar of the Church do not belong to the Lord.”

Let Amalarius also hear this: just as there is one altar of the Church, so there is one bread of Christ’s body and one cup of his blood. For the Apostle received this from the Lord and handed it on to the Church:

“Because our Lord Jesus Christ, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and, giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘This is my body, which will be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this whenever you drink it in remembrance of me.’”

Accordingly, the Church, following the tradition of the apostles and consecrating the mystery of the Lord’s sacred body and blood with these words, expressly says that the Lord told the apostles: “Take and eat, all of you, from this. For this is my body.” Likewise afterward, when the meal had been completed, taking this splendid cup also.

Let every believer pay attention to what is meant by “this.” Clearly, the cup which the priest offers in sacrifice is none other than the very cup which the Lord handed to the apostles. Thus, just as one must understand the matter concerning the blood, so also must one understand it concerning the body.

### XIV.

Amalarius then adds, saying:

“After the first sacrifice has been offered, which consists of the prayers of the saints and is joined to the sacrifice of the angels, one descends to the universal sacrifice.”

These words of Amalarius do not accord with Catholic truth. For when he says “the first sacrifice,” he shows that he has in mind another sacrifice which is later. But when he adds that it consists of the prayers of the perfect and is joined to the sacrifice of the angels, it is astonishing if he himself understands what he is saying.

For how does a sacrifice consist of the prayers of the perfect? Does another consist of the prayers of sinners? And if the sacrifice which consists of the prayers of the perfect is joined to the sacrifice of the angels, which consists of the prayers of sinners, is it then joined to the sacrifice of demons?

Next he proceeds, saying: “One descends to the universal sacrifice,” namely, the sacrifice of Christ. What is he saying? From where does one descend? And to where does one descend?

He plainly says: “One descends to the universal sacrifice.” If one descends to the universal—that is, the catholic—for what is called *universale* in Latin is called *catholicum* in Greek—then one descends from something non-Catholic to the Catholic, namely, to the sacrifice of Christ.

If the later sacrifice is itself universal and the immolation of Christ, then the earlier sacrifice is neither universal nor the immolation of Christ. And how can it consist of the prayers of the perfect and be joined to the sacrifice of the angels if it is neither universal nor the immolation of Christ?

Tell us, then, which sacrifice is better: the earlier one, consisting of the prayers of the perfect, but nevertheless neither universal nor the immolation of Christ; or the later one, consisting of the prayers of sinners, not joined to the sacrifice of the angels, and yet universal and the immolation of Christ? Who has ever heard of such a thing? Or what heresy has ever plunged itself into such an irrational confusion?

### XV.

He further adds these words:

“Because Christ, one victim, was offered for the just and the unjust.”

The first apostles, Peter and Paul, do not speak in this way. The former says: “Christ died once for our sins, the just for the unjust.” The latter says: “For why, while we were still weak, did Christ die for the ungodly at the appointed time?” And shortly afterward:

“For if, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, much more, now that we have been justified by his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him. For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.”

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have not come to call the just, but sinners to repentance.”

For although there were many just people before the Lord’s passion, they were saved by that faith in which they believed that Christ would die for the unjust and the ungodly; and that very faith freed them from injustice and ungodliness.

### XVI.

Amalarius says again, in the fourth book, chapter four:

“There is a priest on earth who must intercede daily for himself and for the people of God. There is a priest in heaven who does not need to intercede, but nevertheless wills to do so and intercedes for us every day.

“The priest who is on earth neither wishes nor is able to say that he is without sin, since John says: ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.’ Yet although he is a sinner, he ought not to be so tormented by his conscience that he is as great a sinner as he knows many people in the earthly community to be.”

### XVII.

Among these wandering, frantic, and wholly contemptible words of Amalarius, the worst are those in which he says:

“Yet although he—the priest—is a sinner, he ought not to be so tormented by his conscience that he is as great a sinner as he knows many people in the earthly community to be.”

These words are not merely useless; they are very harmful and contrary to the truth. For the Catholic faith holds that God accepts no one’s sacrifice or prayer unless that person has acknowledged his own iniquity, as David clearly demonstrates in his prayer of repentance, saying:

“Wash me yet more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me.”

It is as though he were saying: “I deserve your forgiveness because I have acknowledged my iniquity. For if I do not acknowledge it, you will not forgive.”

Thus also the Lord commands through Moses, saying:

“If a ruler sins and, through ignorance, does one of the things prohibited by the Lord’s law, and afterward understands his sin, let him offer a sacrifice to the Lord.”

And shortly afterward:

“The priest shall pray for him and for his sin, and it shall be forgiven him.”

And again:

“If a person sins through ignorance and does one of the things prohibited by the Lord’s law, and, having become guilty of sin, understands his iniquity, let him offer an unblemished ram from the flocks to the priest, according to the measure and assessment of the sin. The priest shall pray for what he did unknowingly, and it shall be forgiven him who sinned through error against the Lord.”

Solomon also says in his prayer at the dedication of the temple:

“If anyone recognizes the plague of his heart and stretches out his hands in this house, you will hear in the place of your dwelling and will be reconciled.”

Let the prudent believer weigh how contrary Amalarius’s counsel is to divine truth, and how closely it accords with the persuasion of the devil.

### XVIII.

In the fourth book, the final chapter, Amalarius says:

“Very recently, as I think, it was shown to me by him who opens and no one shuts what may reasonably be said concerning the Lord’s body placed on the altar and concerning the cup from his side, without prejudice to the teaching of those who wish to explain to me elsewhere and more fully how and why the bread should be placed differently on the altar and the cup beside it.

“The altar is the cross of Christ, from the place where it is written in the canon, ‘Therefore, remembering,’ until the cup is wrapped in the deacon’s cloth, after the manner of Joseph, who wrapped the Lord’s body in a linen cloth and a shroud.”

And shortly afterward:

“The bread spread out upon the altar shows the Lord’s body stretched out on the cross, which we eat. The wine and water in the cup show the sacraments that flowed from Christ’s side on the cross—that is, blood and water—with which our Lord gives us drink.”

### XIX.

To these words of Amalarius one must reply: if he thinks that this was shown to him by him who opens and no one shuts, to whom he adds, saying, “without prejudice to the teaching of those who wish to explain to me elsewhere and more fully,” where does he think he can find someone who could explain it to him better than the Lord, who opens and no one shuts?

Why did he not remember the evangelical saying:

“Do not be called teachers, because your one teacher is Christ.”

[Col. 0349B]

## THE POEMS OF SAINT AGOBARD

### I. [Note: [Col. 0349D] Epitaph of Charles. We supplied this poem with its title, following the authority of the Chronicle of Novalesa, in which it is found inserted. With its help we also corrected the errors that had crept into Masson’s edition.]

## Epitaph of the Emperor Charles the Great

After Christ, from the Virgin, had taken for himself  
Golden heavenly limbs, suitable for the world’s sin,  
The fourteenth year had already flown  
After eight times a hundred years;  
Charles, the glory of the Frankish people,  
Deserved to cross the fiery waters  
Of the billowing ethereal heavens  
And reach the peaceful harbor.

He who for fourteen times six years  
Successfully held the scepters of the kingdom  
And, as king, joined kingdoms once more to his kingdom,  
Departed from the world on the fifth day before the Kalends of February,  
An old man who brought his life to an end  
At seventy years.

Therefore I ask—if you are moved by any prayers—  
And you, reader, who read these verses of the epitaph:  
Say that Charles’s spirit may possess  
The starry citadel.

### II. [Note: [Col. 0349D] On the translation. The history of this translation is found in the Martyrology of Ado of Vienne, from which it was published among the Eulogies. But we supplied the following twenty-four verses, which were missing from earlier editions, from Pamelius’s edition, where he published them among the Prolegomena to the works of Saint Cyprian.]

## On the Translation of the Relics of the Holy Martyrs Cyprian, Speratus, and Pantaleon to the City of Lyon

The glorious and pious ruler,  
Charles, adorned with imperial majesty,  
Ruled the noble scepter of the Franks,  
Govern­ing his subject peoples with piety.

He had ordered chosen men to cleave the waters,  
And now, with the thunderer propitious to him,  
After many labors of an arduous journey,  
They sought the returning sea on their way home.

Suddenly they entered the Libyan regions,  
Where Carthage, lying in grievous ruin,  
Mourns the vanished glory  
Of her former youth.

While they entered the basilicas dedicated to God  
And the venerable temples of Christ,  
They saw, martyr Cyprian,  
That a neglected tomb preserved your bones.

Then, moved by immense grief  
And gazing toward heaven with a great sigh,  
They asked the aid of the everlasting God,  
For whom your head was piously severed.

Soon, with knees bent in prayer,  
They opened the sarcophagus  
And carefully enclosed the sacred limbs  
In prepared linen cloths;  
They committed the body to a sacred coffin.

They quickly took away together  
All the bones of the blessed martyr Speratus  
And also those of Pantaleon,  
And bound them in cloths.

They swiftly boarded the prepared ship  
And did not fear the dangers of the savage sea.

As they departed, prosperous Arles, rich in harbor,  
Met them with a peaceful haven  
And, with a welcoming bay,  
Received and kindly comforted the weary.

As soon as the excellent priest heard this,  
He who held the peaceful see at Lyon,  
Burning with extraordinary zeal for the saints  
And devoted everywhere to sacred things,  
Ledradus, the glory and distinction of the clergy,  
Prayed, pleaded, and quickly obtained  
That the most holy bones of the pious martyrs  
Should be laid within our walls,  
At Lyon, beside the peaceful altar of John,  
Who watered Christ with a glass-clear stream.

There, flourishing with your companions  
In glorious honor, illustrious Cyprian, you sleep.  
But, I ask, keep watch, and, as you watch,  
Attend to our prayers;  
Become for us a merciful and powerful patron of God;  
Release us from our crimes and grant our prayers.

Thus, I ask, mindful of that tongue of yours  
Which confessed the everlasting Word of God  
And gave its neck to be cut by the sword,  
But sang of Christ and knows not how to be silent.

Christ, ever merciful, continually hears it,  
As it rouses holy peoples by its pen  
And utterly burns away wicked heresies  
And false gods with the thunderbolt of the Word.

May he also always hear it praying  
For the people and for our patron;  
May he cherish the shepherd and enlarge the flock;  
May he grant the gift of faith and the glory of salvation.

O holy teacher, O blessed martyr,  
In your piety preserve Bishop Agobard,  
Who has raised up your name, merit, and feast  
In his words and adorned them with honor.

O threefold honor, O threefold summit!  
O three magnificent and pious witnesses!  
May the one Trinity, mighty through the ages,  
Be favorable to us through a threefold prayer.

[Col. 0351B]

## In the Year of the Lord 840

## EGINHARD, ABBOT

[Col. 0351B]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE ON EGINHARD

From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca of Middle and Late Latin Literature*.

[Col. 0351C]

Eginhard—also Eynardus, Einartus, Aeginardus, Agenardus, Egvinardus, Einchardus, Emchardus, Heinardus, and Eginerius [Note: [Col. 0351D] See the distinguished Leibniz’s *Letters to Various Persons*, p. 391]—was a German from the Odenwald [Note: [Col. 0351D] D. Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling, *Leisure Works*, vol. II, p. 302 ff.], surnamed “the Wise” [Note: [Col. 0351D] He is so called by Odilo in the history of the translation of Saint Sebastian the martyr]. After Charlemagne died in 814, Eginhard—who had been his son-in-law, archchaplain, chancellor, and notary of the royal palace [Note: [Col. 0351D] D. Teulet, in his edition of Eginhard’s works, published at Paris in two volumes in 1840, denies that Eginhard was ever Charlemagne’s son-in-law, archchaplain, chancellor, or notary of the royal palace, but considers him director of public works (*chef des travaux publics*). See, if you please, the *Notice on Eginhard* in vol. II of the edition mentioned above, p. V. EDIT.]—survived him for many years. He educated Lothar, the son of Louis the Pious, and held various abbacies: those of Blandin, Fontenelle, Saint John of Pavia, Ghent, and others. He died after the year 840.

His epitaph, composed by Rabanus Maurus, is read among Rabanus’s works, vol. VI, p. 228. More about Eginhard is found, besides the editors and especially C. V. Johann Hermann Schminckius, in Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, century IV, part I; in Johann Weinskens, [Note: [Col. 0352D] *Acta Eruditorum*, published in German, parts 26 and 27, vol. III, pp. 143, 210] in the *Seligenstadt Navigation* and in *Eginhard Illustrated and Vindicated*, Frankfurt, 1714, folio; in Franciscus Dionysius Camusatus, in the *Library of Alfonso Ciacconius* [Note: [Col. 0352D] *Bibliothèque Raisonnée*, vol. VII, p. 114 ff.]; and in Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling, second volume of the *Leisure Works*, chapter 5.

[Col. 0351D]

Among his writings, first place belongs to the *Life of Charlemagne*, written no less accurately and faithfully than in a polished style, so that one readily recognizes him as an imitator of Suetonius and the better writers. It was first published and dedicated to Emperor Charles V by Count Hermann of Nuenar, Cologne, 1521, quarto, together with the *Annals* from the year 741 to 829.

There are very few passages—and these seem to have arisen rather from variants in the manuscript [Note: [Col. 0352D] Compare the aforementioned Gundling, *Leisure Works*, vol. II, p. 213 ff.]—in which he presents the text differently, so that he can justly be accused neither of assuming the role of an interpolator nor of wishing to diminish the authority or credibility of his author.

From there it appeared in the very ancient collection of Hervagius’s historians, an account of which may appropriately be added here for the reader’s benefit. The following works are therefore offered in that collection:

- Three books by Widukind the Saxon, Benedictine monk, on the deeds performed by Emperors Henry and Otto I, together with annotations on the same written by Martin Frechtus, p. 1.
- The *Life of Emperor Henry IV Augustus*, written by a certain contemporary, p. 53.
- Seven letters of the Duke of Bavaria, and several letters of Henry IV to the Roman pontiff and other princes, p. 73.
- A little book by Conrad Vecerius, royal secretary, on the deeds of Emperor Henry VII, p. 84.
- A brief account by Hermann, Count of Nuenar, concerning the origin and settlements of the ancient Franks, addressed to Caesar Charles V, p. 102.
- The *Life and Deeds of Charlemagne, Most Powerful King of the Franks and Enlightener of His Germany, and Most Deserving Emperor*, by Eginhard—or, as some copies have it, by Alcuin [Note: [Col. 0352D] “There are some,” says the aforementioned Schminkius, “who deny this *Life* to Eginhard and attribute it to Alcuin, such as the manuscript of Cag-Gonville, Alberic the monk under the year 770, Blondus, Petrarch, and others. But they seem to have been led into error because Alcuin also wrote an account of Charlemagne’s deeds, as the most learned Duchesne noted from the Moissiac manuscript at the end of this book. Ignorance exchanged and confused these offspring with one another. For so many manuscripts survive bearing Eginhard’s name, and so many writers follow him step by step (*κατὰ πόδα*, “foot by foot”) in matters concerning Charlemagne and acknowledge him as their author, that no doubt remains about the true parent of this little book. To these witnesses is added Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, a witness beyond reproach, who in his first letter to Eginhard most certainly vindicates this book for its true author.”], p. 107.
- Aeneas Sylvius, Cardinal of Saint Sabina of Siena, on the origin and deeds of the Bohemians and, among them, of several emperors. The work is enriched with complete periods and cleansed of countless errors, on the authority of a manuscript of good quality. Addressed to Alfonso, King of Aragon, p. 126.
- Six books by Liutprand, deacon of the Church of Pavia, on the deeds of the emperors and kings of Europe. Addressed to Raymond, bishop of the Church of Lérida in Spain, p. 219.
- *Chronological Epitome of the German Emperors*, composed by Jacob Wimpheling of Sélestat and his associates, and recently revised by a certain learned man. Addressed to Thomas Wolphius the younger, interpreter of pontifical law, p. 315.
- *Chronicle of Mainz*, written by Bishop Conrad, with a preface by Johann Hervagius. Addressed to Blessed Arnoald of Sélestat, secretary of Caesar Charles V. Basel, 1532, folio, published by Johann Hervagius, with an index of notable events prefixed.

From that time Eginhard’s *Life of Charlemagne* was repeatedly sent to press: with the three books of Beatus Rhenanus’s *German History*, who died in 1542, Basel, 1551, folio; with the anonymous Benedictine’s *Annals of the Kings of the Franks—Pippin, Charlemagne, and Louis the Pious—from 751 to 829*, Cologne, 1561 and 1562, duodecimo; and also at the beginning of the writings on German affairs edited by Justus Reuber, Frankfurt, 1584, and reprinted at Hanover, 1619.

It was also published by Georg Christian Johann, who adorned Reuber’s collection with various appendices and added to Eginhard various readings from Schminck’s edition, Frankfurt, 1726, folio. Several copies of Johann’s edition are nevertheless said to have perished in the Frankfurt fire of that same year, 1726 [Note: [Col. 0353D] *Scholarly Newspapers*, 1726, pp. 533 and 741].

*The Life and Deeds of Charlemagne by Eginhard*, at one time his pupil and sworn secretary, appears in Marquard Freher’s *Corpus of Ancient and Authentic Frankish History*, p. 435, Hanover, 1613, folio, besides the Leipzig edition of 1616, quarto, with the *Annals* from 741 to 829 and the preface of Count Nuenar.

Christophorus Helwich, vicar of Mainz, who died in 1632, is also said to have published and illustrated Eginhard with commentary in 1631. He published at Frankfurt in 1631, quarto, the *Antiquities of the Monastery of Lorsch*, reprinted in the new volume of Georg Christian Johann’s *Writings Serving the History of Mainz*, Frankfurt, 1727, folio.

Eginhard’s *Life of Charlemagne* is found in André du Chesne’s *Writers of Frankish Affairs*, vol. II, p. 93, Paris, 1636, folio, revised against five manuscript codices:

*The Life and Conduct of the Most Glorious Emperor Charles, Great King and Most Invincible Augustus*, published by Eginhard, the most learned man of his time and highly accomplished in the liberal arts, educated by the aforesaid prince and a promoter and defender of the Christian religion.

It was also published with the notes of Johann Bolland in the *Acts of the Saints*, 28 January, vol. II, p. 877, Antwerp, 1643, folio, collated with two manuscripts and various editions.

Johann Joachim Frantzius of Strasbourg also added Eginhard’s account of Charlemagne, without notes, p. 97, to his history of Charlemagne, which he himself had composed while still young from the writers of that period. Strasbourg, 1644, quarto, with a preface by Johann Heinrich Boeclerus.

Especially deserving of praise is the diligence of Johann Friedrich Besselius of Filzen in Prussia, who published Eginhard with learned annotations at Helmstedt in 1667, quarto. The excellent Meibomius afterward sent him readings from the Florentine manuscript, whose variants V. C. Tobias Eckartus also noted in the *Life of Albert of Stade*, pp. 54 ff. Eckartus observes that Albert repeated many passages from Eginhard word for word, so that this work can sometimes usefully serve either to emend Albert or to establish the genuine reading.

An accessible *Life and Deeds of Charlemagne, with Eginhard as author*, is also found in the *Writers of German Affairs* by Johann Michael Heineccius and Johann Georg Leuckfeld, Frankfurt, 1707, folio.

Finally, we owe the best edition of this *Life* to the distinguished Johann Hermann Schminckius [Note: [Col. 0353D] *Acta Eruditorum*, 1711, p. 529; *Memoirs of Literature*, vol. I, p. 229; *History of the Works of the Learned*, 1711, p. 429], finely and accurately printed at Utrecht, 1711, quarto.

After a historical dissertation on the life and writings of Eginhard, Eginhard himself follows, divided into thirty-four chapters, with the complete notes of Besselius, Bolland, and the editor. Then, after previously unpublished observations by Goldast and Marquard Freher’s dissertation on the stature of Charlemagne, concerning chapter 22 of Eginhard, with floral excerpts and notes by Heinrich Günther Thulemarius from the 1682 edition, the volume concludes with Count Hermann of Nuenar’s brief account of the origin and settlements of the ancient Franks, the preface he prefixed to the first edition of Eginhard in 1521 addressed to Charles V, and variant readings of Eginhard from various manuscripts.

In the Hohendorf Library, recently transferred to the Imperial Library, Eginhard is mentioned in part III, p. 282, with manuscript notes; and on p. 269 appears “Letter of M. Pean to M. Schmincke concerning his edition of Eginhard,” written in 1712, together with “Notes and Observations of Sr. Pean on the said edition of Eginhard.”

In the same Imperial Library are Eginhard’s manuscript codices, from which Lambecius emended several passages in vol. II, pp. 263, 323 ff., 390, and elsewhere.

The dissertation of the distinguished Johann David Koelec on the library of Charlemagne, concerning chapter 33 of Eginhard, was published at Altdorf, 1727, quarto.

Johann Augustinus Egenolf furnished Eginhard with a German translation, Leipzig, 1728, duodecimo [Note: [Col. 0354D] A German paraphrase of the *Life of Charlemagne* in Teutonic verse, but made from a different Latin writer than Eginhard, was composed four hundred years ago. It survives in manuscript in the Imperial Library, according to Lambecius, vol. II, p. 385 ff. In the Gotha Library, see the Reverend D. Ernst Salomon Cyprian’s *Catalogue of Manuscripts*, p. 104 ff. The title of the book is: “This is the King Charles, whom Rome and Arles serve.”].

The rest of Eginhard’s writings are as follows:

### Letters

Sixty-two letters, edited from the Laon manuscript by André du Chesne, vol. II of the *Writers on Frankish Affairs*, p. 695 ff., and in Johann Weinkens’s *Eginhard Vindicated and Illustrated*, Frankfurt, 1714, folio.

### On the Translation of the Holy Martyrs Marcellinus and Peter

Four books in prose concerning the translation of the bodies of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, who are said to have suffered under Diocletian and Maximian around the year 303 and whose bodies were brought from Rome to the Benedictine abbey of Seligenstadt in the diocese of Mainz around the year 826.

Surius published them on 2 June; from there they were reproduced in the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. I for June, p. 181, collated with the manuscript of Christina, Queen of Sweden. The same *Acts*, vol. VI, pp. 1 ff., should also be consulted, as well as the work of Johann Weinckens, who rendered Eginhard’s four books in epic verse, Frankfurt, 1714, folio.

### Acts of the Martyrdom of the Same Saints

The acts of their martyrdom are expressed in trochaic verse, beginning:

“There was a certain exorcist, Peter by name.”

Surius attributed this work to Eginhard, although it was found in the same codex without an author’s name. From Surius it is also offered in the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. I for June, p. 174.

### Annals from 741 to 829

These *Annals*, which some attribute to the *Chronicle of Lorsch*, were published by Nuenar and others without an author’s name together with Eginhard’s *Life of Charlemagne*. André du Chesne, on a scarcely plausible conjecture, attributes them to Eginhard as author.

### Chronological Breviary

The *Chronological Breviary*, or *Abridgment of the Chronicle from Bede*, from the creation of the world to the year 809 of Christ, runs briefly and summarily through events. Lambecius published it from an imperial codex, vol. II, pp. 395, 398, and afterward attempted to vindicate it for Eginhard with arguments to which each person will grant or deny credibility according to his judgment.

### On the Miracles of Saint Alexander

A book by Rudolf the monk concerning the miracles of Saint Alexander, son of Saint Felicitas, completed by M. Eginhard, together with a letter of that same Eginhard to Sundrolt the priest. It is preserved in manuscript by Frederick Pacius at Leiden, and is of such antiquity that he has no doubt it is the autograph of Meginhart—for that is how the name is written in the memorandum published in this very year, 1734—and was written in the ninth century.

### Charter of Donation

A charter granting a place in the Odenwald forest, dated 815, from Louis the Pious to Eginhard, is found in Reuber’s preface and in the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. I for June, p. 177.

### Lost Works of Eginhard

A book *On the Arrival, Customs, Wars, and Superstition of the Saxons*, from which certain fragments are found in Adam of Bremen, book I of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 6 and following.

A little book *On the Adoration of the Cross*, addressed to Lupus of Ferrières. In the fourth letter to Eginhard, Lupus says:

“I have embraced, as was fitting, the little book *On the Adoration of the Cross*, which in my judgment is most useful and which you dedicated to my name.”
