No one has yet revealed what kind of work Eginhard’s little book on the Psalms may be. It is listed in the ancient catalogue of the Bobbio Library, published by Muratori, *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, vol. III, p. 822, in these words: “Little book of Einard on the Psalms.”

In the Imperial Library I myself saw a little book of Psalms sent as a gift by King Charlemagne to Pope Adrian I, preceded by a certain apparatus on the books of Sacred Scripture. Everything is preceded by verses in the manner of a letter, which we call dedicatory. Could all of this, apart from the verses dictated by some other author, perhaps be attributed to Alcuin? Let the learned decide.

[Col. 0355C]

# THE LIFE AND CONDUCT OF THE MOST GLORIOUS EMPEROR CHARLES, GREAT KING

(See among the works of blessed Charlemagne, volume XCVII of this *Patrology*, column 25.)

[Col. 0355C]

# NOTICE ON THE LAURISSENSES AND EGINHARD’S ANNALS

(In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*.)

The Annals of Lorsch and of Einhard are so closely connected with one another that they cannot be investigated separately. Both extend from the year 741 all the way to 829, and they narrate nearly the same events, in an order of statements not greatly different and, for the greater part—namely, from the final decade of the eighth century onward—in precisely the same words, with only very few exceptions. Thus it is evident either that one was derived from the other, or that both derive from a common source. [Col. 0356D]

We have given the name *Annals of Lorsch* to those annals which, first published by Canisius and later by Chesnius and Bouquet, had until now circulated under the designation “Plebeian” or “Loiselian,” because not only their relationship to the Lesser Annals of Lorsch, but also the fact that their most ancient copy was found in that monastery, clearly shows that the original beginning of the work must be referred to the monastery of Lorsch. In the work itself they continue up to the year 788, which appears to be the point beyond which the first author did not proceed, since from that point two continuations follow: one, also found in the Annals of Lorsch, from the years 789–793 in the Lorsch manuscript; the other, from the year 788 to 829, in the remaining manuscripts.

The character of the two parts is very different. The style of the first is unpolished and crude, and its scribal technique so entirely lacking that it formerly gave rise to the name “Plebeian” or “rustic annals.” Moreover, its concern for truth—at least in matters relating to Saxony—is sufficiently suspect that it has not secured complete confidence among learned men. The second part, on the contrary, is ennobled by the same style and the same outlook as Einhard’s *Annals*. Nevertheless, there can be no doubt that the author of the first part was contemporary with him, if not in every matter, at least in his account of events after the year 768. For although he never gives King Pippin the titles “Great” or “Most Glorious,” as he does his son, the whole arrangement of the work—begun about the year 768 and enlarged year by year—persuades us of this; and in the year 774 he calls Saint Boniface the latest martyr, while in 776 he testifies that many people still remained who said that they had seen those events. [Col. 0357B]

Einhard’s *Annals*, since throughout the seventy-nine years they encompass they display one and the same style and everywhere the same manner of observing and writing, must have proceeded from one author, Einhard himself. His name was disclosed by the anonymous author—whom Mabillon thinks to have been Odilo, a monk of Saint-Medard—of the book on the translation and miracles of Saint Sebastian, published at the beginning of the tenth century. In his preface to Ingramnus, abbot of Saint-Medard of Soissons, he speaks as follows:

> “Agenard, surnamed the Wise, who was regarded as eminent in that age, mentioning this most revered fellow-citizen of heaven in the deeds of the emperors Charles the Great and his son Louis, among the other matters that he dictated in the course of each year, did not consider it labor wasted to strengthen mortal deeds with immortal testimony, saying as follows:
>
> “ ‘While these things were taking place, Hilduin, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Denis, sent to Rome and, with Eugene, then bishop of the holy apostolic see, consenting to his petitions, received the bones of the most blessed martyr of Christ, Sebastian. He placed them at the city of Soissons, in the basilica of Saint-Medard. While they lay unburied there, in the chest in which they had been brought, beside the tomb of Saint-Medard, such a multitude of signs and prodigies became manifest, and such power of miracles in every kind of healing shone forth by divine grace in the name of that same most blessed martyr, that no mortal could either comprehend the number of those miracles or explain their variety in words. Some of them are said to have been so astonishing that they would exceed human credulity—unless it were certain that our Lord Jesus Christ, for whom that same most blessed martyr is known to have suffered, can accomplish by divine omnipotence everything that he wills, since every creature in heaven and on earth is subject to him.’ ”

Since these words are found in precisely the same form in our *Annals* near the end of the year 826, everyone will understand that there can no longer be doubt either about the author or about the general reliability of the work. [Note: Nuenarius identified the author as a monk of the Benedictine order; Freherus, apparently guided by the preface to the anonymous *Life of Louis the Pious*, had proclaimed Adelmus or Adhemar to be the author.] Mabillon, who had allowed himself to be drawn by Cointius’s arguments to the opposing side in the *Benedictine Annals* under the year 774, began to compose the history of the year 826 on the basis of the force of this testimony, first brought forward by Chesnius, and treated it in such a way that he too acknowledged Einhard as the author of the work. [Col. 0357D]

On the other hand, the passage of Trithemius in which Einhard is said to have written “the Life and deeds of the emperor Charles the Great, in three books; also the translation of the aforesaid martyrs, in one book; the history of past times, in one book; and certain other works,” although it was not even attacked by his opponents, is nevertheless uselessly brought forward by Chesnius. For the beginning of the sentence—“the Life and deeds of Charles … three books”—plainly shows that Trithemius’s opinion rests on no solid basis and should rather be called an error. It is evident that Trithemius had obtained a manuscript—of the kind that still survive at Hanover, Vienna, Munich, Kassel, and Modena—in which Einhard’s *Life of Charles*, our *Annals*, and the two books of the monk of Saint Gall on the deeds of Charles had been appended one after another, and that he transferred all these works, confused together, under the single name of Einhard. [Col. 0358A]

Nor, however, do we possess only Odilo’s testimony, by which Einhard is asserted to be the author of the work. To refute briefly the objections first raised by Cointius, the leader of the opposing view, in the *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks* under the year 774, §§ 127–133: the account of the consecration of the monastery of Lorsch in the year 774, to which he attached the greatest weight and which had initially carried Mabillon away as well, appears in all editions to date—the Nuenarian, Freherian, Chesnian, Bouquetian, and those derived from them—but is acknowledged by no manuscript whatsoever. It was inserted into the Nuenarian book by some monk of Lorsch. Indeed, we do not even fail to know the source from which he received it, since we remember that precisely the same account is given above in the Lesser Annals of Lorsch. [Col. 0358B]

The other statement composed in praise of Einhard—“Heinardus, the wisest of the men of his time, stirred by the ardor of holy devotion, etc.”—which we read in Reuber’s edition under the year 827, was taken from the anonymous *Life of Louis the Pious*. Once Cointius’s principal argument has thus been overturned, it is easy to judge what weight his remaining evidence possesses. It amounts to this: the author of the *Life* says that Pippin was crowned by Pope Stephen, that he himself knew nothing about Charles’s childhood, that Carloman died two years after the beginning of his reign, and that the Saxon-Lombard war began two years later; whereas the annalist declares Pope Zacharias to have been the author of Pippin’s elevation to royal dignity, does not fail to mention that Charles, as a boy, was crowned together with his father, and knows that Carloman died in the year 771, and assigns the beginning of the Lombard war to 773. It is readily understood that these differences are of no importance. [Col. 0358C]

On the contrary, the modesty worthy of such a man—with which the annalist in 827 conceals the author of the translation of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, although in a similar matter in 826 he had named Hilduin, and by which in 806 he almost entirely allows his own name to disappear—together with the entire conception of the work; its much purer style, comparable only with the *Life of Charles*; its same manner of observing and narrating, wholly alien to the other writers of its age but especially fitting for a historian (compare, for example, the passage under 778 concerning the battle with the Basques, which will immediately recall to you chapter 9 of the *Life of Charles*; and under 787, 789, 792, and 793, the account of Tassilo’s downfall, the war against the Wiltzi, which is also found in chapter 12 of the *Life of Charles*, the conspiracy aroused by Fastrada’s cruelty, and the Felician heresy); and, finally, its incorruptible love of truth—all these vindicate these annals, as well as the *Life of Charles the Great*, for Einhard.

Since this is so, there will be no need to investigate the sources of the work for long. The first part, from the year 741 to 788, rests upon the *Annals of Lorsch*, but in such a way that, after errors and incorrectly stated matters had been corrected, small details omitted, and major ones added, the whole work emerged far more perfect, having been carefully reviewed, amended, and better arranged by such a man. For the years 789–829, during which he had been employed by Charles and Louis in the affairs of the kingdom and was living at nearly the highest level of influence, he completed the history under his own direction. Whether he did so amid the actual business of administering the state or during leisure at Seligenstadt is not sufficiently clear. I am nevertheless more inclined to think that he wrote year by year while he himself was largely in charge of affairs. For although we know that even after his voluntary renunciation of secular matters he continued to concern himself with public affairs, both while Louis Augustus was alive and after his death—and therefore he should be thought not to have abstained from writing history—the remarks under the year 806 about eclipses, and under the years 825 and 823 about the girl from Commercy, appear to have been composed in those very years. [Col. 0359A]

We also understand that he wrote somewhere near the Rhine because, under the year 821, when speaking of the freezing of the rivers in Gaul and Germany—the Rhine, Danube, Elbe, and Seine—he adds: “the thawing of which inflicted no small damage on the villages situated beside the banks of the Rhine.” This, together with his consistent description of Germany as lying beyond the Rhine (for example, under 795 and 826), persuades us that he was not at Seligenstadt. I therefore propose that the second part of the work was composed by Einhard year by year while he remained attached to the imperial court, especially at Aachen. This also explains his profound silence concerning the downfall of the abbots Adalhard and Wala—for he does mention their restoration—and why the work did not extend beyond the year 829.

To conclude my opinion about both works in a few words: I believe that the *Annals of Lorsch*, composed in the monastery of Saint Nazarius up to the year 788, came into the hands of Einhard, the great friend of the men of Lorsch, during the final decade of the eighth century. He supplied them with a continuation for the years 788–829, of the kind displayed by the manuscripts of the *Annals of Lorsch*. Once the work had been brought to completion, he also revised the earlier part, which he understood to require his assistance greatly, and published it under his own name together with the continuation, altering it only in a few words. If this opinion pleases anyone less, let him not fail to teach us otherwise.

As for the reckoning of time: the monk of Lorsch and Einhard begin their year from the Nativity of the Lord. This is beyond doubt in those years in which events also took place during the winter—for example, at the beginning and end of 768, 776, 781, 785, 787, 800, 801, 802, 806, and in 807. Nevertheless, after spending the winter in repose, both appear to begin the new year only after the beginning of spring, and to attach Christmas and Easter to the year immediately past. This cannot lead anyone into error. [Col. 0359C]

I arranged the edition in such a way that, since the two *Annals* agree almost word for word from the year 801 onward, I printed from that point only the second edition, which I believe was the last one approved by the author, while preserving the differing readings of the other edition and inserting them into the text with brackets. It remains to explain that in the notes for the years 801–829, the letter A signifies the manuscripts of Einhard’s *Annals*, and the letter B the manuscripts of the *Annals of Lorsch*.

All earlier editions rest on the Lorsch, Loiselian, and Baron de Crassier manuscripts, as well as on the Nuenarian, Cardinal d’Armagnac, and Kassel manuscripts. If I had obtained no other aids besides these, I intended to call upon those writers who in later centuries adapted our annals for their own use. But I gained much better resources, since through the generosity of the Society I was able to inspect excellent manuscripts throughout Germany and Italy and to use the readings of others. The resources for our edition of the *Annals of Lorsch* were therefore as follows:

1. A copy of the Lorsch manuscript, “very ancient and on parchment,” published by Canisius, *Lectures of Antiquity*, vol. III, pp. 187 ff. It extends to the end of the year 788, with a continuation for the years 789, 790, 791, 792, and 795 appended. Since this continuation is wholly different from the other continuation, and can be found in the Annals of Lorsch, only its final and sufficiently corrupt words need be presented here:

   > “But it was also very powerful in Burgundy and Francia. And when Lord King Pippin departed from there, the Saracens who were in Spain, thinking that the Avars had fought against the king, came out from their territories into some part of India; joining themselves together toward our region, many fell there on both sides.”

   Since the reliability of Canisius’s editions is already sufficiently established in other respects, we should not be surprised that the style and many other things were altered by that man, who was excessively devoted to good Latin—if indeed we are guided by a sound conjecture. A few examples taken from the single year 787 will make this clearer. Where the manuscripts read:

   > “And then the Saxons rebelled again. When the aforesaid son of Lord King Charles heard this, he went to meet them, so that he had not entered Benevento, and they wished to fulfill all the wishes of the aforesaid lord king; wherefore the apostolic lord, greatly intervening, was already entreating the said lord king. And the lord king replied to the apostolic that this was what he had wished; but when the apostolic had learned of their instability or lies, he immediately placed an anathema upon their duke and his supporters,”

   Canisius published:

   > “The Saxons rebelled again. When the aforesaid son of Lord King Charles heard this, he went to meet them, so that he might not enter Benevento, because he wished to fulfill all the wishes of the king. Therefore the apostolic lord, greatly intervening, entreated the lord king, who replied that he had wished this. But when the apostolic had learned of the instability of their message, he immediately struck the aforesaid duke and his supporters with anathema.”

   Since this is the case, I have followed this edition less closely, although, out of respect for the name of Lorsch, it certainly deserves to be placed first. [Col. 0360B]

2. Much greater weight had to be assigned, on the other hand, to the manuscript numbered 617 in the library of Queen Christina, which I obtained for our use through the discovery of the most excellent Lord Baron de Stein at Rome. It is a parchment manuscript, in what is called octavo format, from the ninth century, written in a reliable and careful hand that rarely deviates from the truth, as the facsimile appended to this page testifies. Its beginning is missing up to the word *placitum* in the year 777; then one leaf is missing in the year 787, another for the years 791–794, and the end of the *Annals* after the word *recesserunt* in the year 813. That the work began in 741 is evident from the number attached to each year, since, for example, the year 778 is counted as chapter 37; the same numbers occur in manuscripts 5 and 7. Nothing is known about the manuscript’s origin; I have—

3. I am convinced that the Petavian manuscript, from which Chesnius excerpted several readings in the margin of his edition, is no other than this one. For all those readings agree most exactly with the Vatican manuscripts, and no doubt should be raised by the statement that it begins in the year 778, since Chesnius may have neglected the final words extant from the preceding year. It is sufficiently established that most of Alexander Petavius’s books passed into Queen Christina’s library, and manuscript 617 is inscribed with Petavius’s name. In Chesnius’s time, however, the leaf that is now missing for the years 791–794 had not yet fallen out. [Col. 0360D]

4. It is evident from what they report under the years 792 and 804 that the first author of the *Annals of Fulda* drew from a manuscript of the *Annals* that was closely related to manuscript 2 or 3. Since, however, their work is wholly different from ours in plan and diction, we rarely have recourse to their authority.

5. A manuscript of the Imperial Library at Vienna, numbered 90 in the catalogue of ecclesiastical history and written toward the end of the ninth century, contains, besides our *Annals*, the deeds of the Roman pontiffs, the deeds of the Frankish kings with a continuation to the year 741, and several other less important matters. The scribe joined these works by means of rubricated headings, intending thereby to compose both ecclesiastical and secular history from the origin of the Roman Church and the Frankish people to the time of the emperor Lothar. Thus, since the death of Charles, mayor of the palace, had already been reported at the end of Fredegar’s *Continuation*, the year 741 was omitted from the *Annals*, where no other subject is discussed. In the year 768, to which at the beginning the same material was assigned as in the other manuscripts of the *Annals*, one line was erased and the rubric “Here begins the Deeds of Charles the Great, king, and of his brother Carloman” was inserted. In the year 814, the word *excessit* is followed by the rubric “Here end the Deeds of Lord Charles the Great and most excellent emperor of the Franks.” Then follows the second part of the *Life* written by Einhard, and the remaining part of the *Annals*, marked by the rubric “Here begins the Deeds of Louis, emperor, son of Charles the Great, emperor.” [Col. 0363A]

6. Another Viennese manuscript, no. 989 in the catalogue of secular history, likewise on parchment and in quarto format, from the eleventh century, omits the years 741–770 and prefixes to the rest the title “Here begin the struggles of the great king Charles against the Saxons and many other peoples.” It belongs to the same group as the fifth manuscript. Both, together with Einhard’s and the Fulda annals, record the conspiracy of Hardrad in 785, which all the others omit, and place Pippin’s conspiracy in 793 at the same point as those manuscripts. In its spelling and orthography it sometimes faithfully reports the reading of the second manuscript, though at other times it departs from it more substantially.

7. No one who knows that both manuscripts fail at the word *recesserunt* in the year 813 will doubt that the ancient manuscript obtained by Chesnius, formerly belonging to Antonius Loisel and later to François de Thou, is a copy of the second manuscript. Consequently, the authority of Chesnius’s edition is virtually nil for us, especially since he does not present his manuscript in full but, following Canisius’s rashness, frequently borrows new patches from him and sews them onto an old garment. Examples are the words *adhuc* under 776, *grassati* under 778, and *reliqui* at the end of 778, which occur in no manuscript and were wrongly introduced by Canisius, who abandoned the ancient order of the words without understanding the author’s meaning.

7b. Since in the manuscripts already enumerated the account of the siege of Büraburg—entirely absent from the Lorsch manuscript—is assigned to the year 774, whereas in the others it is assigned to 773, it is necessary to touch at this point upon the chronicle of Regino, which follows those manuscripts. [Col. 0363B]

8. The very few readings of the manuscript of the Baron de Crassier published by Bouquet prove that it is extremely similar to our manuscripts 2, 5, and 6.

9. The *Annals of Bertin* transcribe ours almost in full, with very few additions. Thus, for example, under the year 807 they retain the words concerning the star called Mercury, and therefore, where Chesnius’s hands have failed us, they help confirm the genuine reading as it is preserved in manuscripts 2, 5, 6, and 8.

9b. The same applies to the *Annals of Metz*, which derive from the *Annals of Bertin* and from Regino.

10. The *Life of Charles the Great*, published by Chesnius from an old manuscript of the Thuani library, vol. II, pp. 50–67;

11. The *Life of Charles the Great*, by a monk of the monastery of Saint Eparchius of Angoulême, published by Chesnius from a very ancient manuscript of the Thuani library, vol. II, pp. 68–87; [Col. 0363D]

12. The *Saxon Annalist*, in Eckhard, *Corpus of Medieval Writers*, vol. I, pp. 133 ff.

We were also able to use three fragments:

13. A parchment manuscript from the end of the tenth century, the Chisian manuscript. Fragments for the years 760–764, 766–768, 773, 774–776, 780, 781, 783, 786–788, 794, 796, 799, 804, 805, 808, 810, 814, 815–824, 826, 827, and 829 have been inserted into the chronicle of Benedict, a monk of Saint Andrew, with its wording rendered into very poor form.

14. A Florentine parchment manuscript in large folio, from the eleventh century. It is an appendix to the *Deeds of the Frankish Kings* and covers the years 741–749. A copy of it exists.

14b. A manuscript of the Imperial Library at Vienna, no. 477 in the catalogue of secular history, from the fifteenth century.

15. A Viennese parchment manuscript from the beginning of the twelfth century, in quarto format. It is another appendix to the *Deeds of the Frankish Kings*, covering the years 741–755, 758–759, and 775.

Let the reader judge whether, with the aid of these materials, we have restored the genuine reading of the work. [Col. 0364A]

In editing Einhard’s *Annals*, the following manuscripts and editions were at hand:

1. A manuscript of the Imperial Library at Vienna, numbered 654 in the catalogue of secular history, on parchment, in quarto format, from the tenth century. It places the *Life of Charles* before the *Annals*. Of all the manuscripts I was able to see, it is the most outstanding in age, craftsmanship, and the diligence of its scribe. We have therefore either always adopted its reading or reported it in the notes. It generally writes *adspirare*, *adgredi*, etc.; *conpono*, *contemno* or *contempno*, *inmaturus*, etc.; *operiri*, *opidum*, *incolomis*, *hii*, and more often *regi* instead of *rei*; *privare* instead of *carere* in 777; *revertisset* in 779; and *verteretur* and *versio* instead of *reverteretur* and *reversio* in 798–799. Two leaves fell out in 822 and 823; we encountered another lacuna in 824 and 825. I learned nothing about the manuscript’s origin. A copy of it exists in the Imperial Library, catalogue of secular history no. 154, on paper and in folio format.

2. A manuscript formerly belonging to the famous monastery of Bec, now Paris, Royal Library no. 5924, whose very careful collation we owe to D. Charles Weber. Its beginning is missing up to the words in the year 743, “Carloman and Pippin, with their forces joined”; then one leaf is missing in 773, 774, and 775, and the words *graviter fuerant desolati* in 824. Since these omissions occur both in the Bec manuscript—whose paper copies I compared with the printed editions, one in the Imperial Library at Vienna, catalogue of theology no. 269, from the year 1540, and another in the Vatican Library, no. 3849, from the sixteenth century—and in the Royal Paris manuscript, as well as in Duchesne’s readings excerpted from the manuscript of Cardinal d’Armagnac, we conjecture that the Bec manuscript was transferred first to the cardinal’s library and then to the royal library. All its other readings support this opinion, except for a few cited by Chesnius, which should be charged to the editor’s fault. The manuscript itself, written in the tenth or eleventh century, rarely departs from the Viennese manuscript and only in minor matters. [Col. 0364B]

3. A manuscript of the Public Library of Trier, whose collation we owe to the distinguished Wyttenbach, librarian of Trier and a most devoted associate in our work. It is on parchment and from the eleventh century. In general it agrees with the preceding manuscripts, although it sometimes offers a less trustworthy reading. Under the years 751 and 752, in a blank space, it reports the dedication of the monastery of Lorsch, which took place much later. [Col. 0364C]

4. A manuscript of the Royal Library of Hanover, on parchment, in quarto format, from the twelfth century. It contains the *Life of Charles*, the *Annals*, and the monk of Saint Gall. It follows the first manuscript. Its spelling differs slightly in such words as *iustitia*, *opportunus*, *sollempnis*, and similar forms.

5–6. The same material is presented by two fourteenth-century parchment manuscripts in quarto format from the Imperial Library at Vienna: no. 110 in the catalogue of ecclesiastical history and no. 990 in that of secular history. They follow the traces of the Hanover manuscript so closely that they must be judged to have derived from it, or at least from the same source. For although, in fourteenth-century manuscripts, readings would naturally be expected to deteriorate, the fourth agrees for the most part with the fifth, the fifth with the sixth, and the sixth with the fourth, even in their errors. In this matter, compare, for example, what we reported in the readings under the years 800, 813, 819, 820, 822, 824, and 826. [Col. 0364D]

7. Freher’s edition in the *Corpus of Frankish History*, vol. II, pp. 381 ff., rests upon a manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Germain in Paris. It belongs to the same group as manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and 4, but contains several interpolations, both concerning matters relating to Saint-Germain and taken from the anonymous *Life of Louis the Pious*. Either the scribe or the editor altered the diction in several places. Moreover, as appears from the manuscript of the Guelferbytana Library communicated to me by our Ebert, Freher sometimes preserved Nuenarian readings and at other times substituted others from his own manuscript; thus, for example, the marginal reading under 768, “or Orowicus,” belongs to the manuscript of Saint-Germain, while under 733, “or Viburg,” belongs to the first edition.

8. A manuscript of the Royal Library of Munich had indeed been collated by our associates, but through an extraordinary turn of fortune we have so far been unable to obtain possession of the collation itself. Nevertheless, it did not seem right to suppress the edition because it would derive too little benefit from that source. According to Docen (*Archives of Germany*, vol. II, pp. 89 ff.), the book formerly belonged to the monastery of Saint Mang in Stadt-am-Hof; it is from the twelfth century, in quarto format, and contains 167 leaves. It contains, in four books, Einhard’s *Life of Charles*, the *Annals*, the *Deeds of Charles* by the monk of Saint Gall, and several other works. I therefore believe that the readings of the *Annals* differ no more from manuscripts 4, 5, and especially 6 than do those of the monk of Saint Gall.

9. Nuenarius’s first edition, published at Cologne in quarto format in 1524, adds under the year 774 from the Lesser Annals of Lorsch the same account of the monastery of Lorsch that is appended in the Trier manuscript under the years 751 and 752. In other respects, apart from the diction, which Nuenarius reshaped according to his own will, they are not far apart. For example, in both the count Bernard is absent under 811, and in both under 820 the Carniolans who inhabit the river Carcaso are mentioned. [Col. 0367B]

10. The Amberg fragment, copied by the distinguished Moritz, professor and public librarian, and communicated to us with the greatest courtesy, consistently follows manuscripts 1 and 2. It is on parchment and extends from the words “into the land of the Slavs who are called Sorbs” in 806 to “his sons of the kingdom” in 821.

11. A fifteenth-century paper manuscript that I examined in the Modena Library in 1823 contains the *Life of Charles*, the *Annals*, and the monk of Saint Gall, counted as four books. A single reading in the year 743, “Ochsenburg,” was sufficient to prevent me from wasting further effort on its collation. [Col. 0368A]

12. A manuscript of the Electoral Library of Kassel, numbered 5 among the historical works, presents the same four books in the same order, written in 1498; nor is the word “Ochsenburg” absent. Several of its readings were added to the margin of Reuber’s second edition.

The remaining editions—the Cologne edition of 1561 (1562) in duodecimo, the Leipzig edition of 1616 in quarto, Reuber’s first and second editions of 1584 and 1726, Chesnius’s edition of 1636, Leukfeld’s of 1707, and Bouquet’s of 1744—reprint the Nuenarian edition. Bouquet inserted into the text several readings of the manuscript of Cardinal d’Armagnac, first excerpted by Chesnius, though he rarely used them to correct the text. The principle of our edition is to restore the genuine text on the authority of the manuscripts we have reviewed, and to present the principal readings both of the Nuenarian and Freherian editions and those peculiar to manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, while disregarding changes introduced at the editors’ discretion. In accordance with the plan of our institution, we have added only a few notes. [Col. 0368B]

Among the medieval writers—many of whom used our work in the form in which it appears in the continuation of the *Annals of Lorsch* down to the year 829—we mention here, besides Einhard, only the author of the *Annals of Fulda* down to the year 838, when he is thought to have died, and the nearly contemporary author of the *Life of Louis the Pious*, who plainly followed our account in his narration of the years 814–829. The Saxon poet of Lamspringe rendered Einhard’s *Annals* in verse during the reign of Arnulf.

[Col. 0367B]

(8.) 9.] in the villa called Dura [Note: [Col. 0382C] the villa which 1. 7. (8.) 9.] [Note: [Col. 0382C] Duria 7 b. 12.], it was announced to him that Waipharius had lied in everything. Karolus 12., likewise hereafter.], with him, and he captured many fortresses [Note: [Col. 0382D] captured 1. 7. (8.) 9. 12. 13. “everywhere”]. (8.) 9.] by battle, and in Auvergne [Note: [Col. 0382D] Auernen 1.] he captured many other fortresses [Note: [Col. 0382D] many others 7.] by agreement; they submitted themselves to his rule. Limodicas 13.], devastating and laying waste [Note: [Col. 0382D] destroying 1. 7.] the aforesaid province because of the negligence [Note: [Col. 0382D] negligence 1. negligences 7. 9.] of Duke Waifarius. ## DCCLXIII

King Pippinus held his assembly at Nevers and, making his fourth campaign in Aquitania, was there [Note: [Col. 0382D] there 1. 7. (8.) 9.] when Tassilo [Note: [Col. 0383C] thessilo, likewise hereafter 1.] duke of the Bavarians abandoned his oaths and everything he had promised. By evil design he withdrew himself from it and set aside all the benefactions that his uncle, King Pippinus, had bestowed upon him. By fraudulent devices he withdrew and made for Bavaria, wishing never again to see the face of the aforesaid king. King Pippinus, campaigning through Aquitania [Note: [Col. 0383C] “through Aquitania up to the city” is absent 5.], reached Cahors [Note: [Col. 0383C] “to Durcia” 13.], ravaging Aquitania; returning by way of Limoges [Note: [Col. 0383C] Lemovicas 7. [Col. 0383D] 9.] [Note: [Col. 0383D] Longlaar 1. Longolare 12.] and likewise Easter. And the reckoning of the years changed in

## DCCLXVII

Then Lord King Pippinus [Note: [Col. 0386C] “king” is absent 1. “King Pippinus” 7. 9.] held a great synod in the aforesaid villa concerning the Holy Trinity [Note: [Col. 0386C] “the holy city” 1.] between the Romans and the Greeks, and concerning the holy images. Galvuldanum 13.]. He returned safely to his homeland and celebrated Easter in the city of Vienne [Note: [Col. 0386C] Bienna 13.].

From there he proceeded until he reached the Garonne [Note: [Col. 0386C] “reached the city up to the Garonne” 13.], captured many rocky strongholds [Note: [Col. 0386C] rockas 1.] and caves [Note: [Col. 0385D] *Rocca* is still used in Italy for a mountain fortress, for example Rocca del Papa on Mount Albanus, and many such places in the Apennines.], including the fortress of Scoralia [Note: [Col. 0386D] Scora 1.] [Note: [Col. 0385D] Scorailles, Turenne. Peyrusse. Bouquet.], Torinna [Note: [Col. 0386D] Torvina 12.], and Petrocia [Note: [Col. 0386D] Perotia 1.]. He returned to Bourges, and there news was announced of the death of Pope Paul. ## DCCLXVIII

Lord King Pippinus made a campaign and captured Remistagnum [Note: [Col. 0386D] “the lake of the Rhine” 1. Herimstagnum 13.], reaching the city of Saintes [Note: [Col. 0386C] and [Note: [Col. 0386D] “and” is absent 7. 9. 12.]. There he captured [Note: [Col. 0386D] he captures 1. 12.] the mother of Waipharius, his sister, and his nieces [Note: [Col. 0386D] “having captured the mother . . . the sister . . . the niece” 7. 9.] [Note: [Col. 0386D] “his” and “he came” 1. 7.] as far as the Garonne. From there he went to the place called Montis [Note: [Col. 0386D] Montis, or according to others Mortis 1.] [Note: [Col. 0385D] A place unknown to Valesius and Bouquet.]. There Herowicus [Note: [Col. 0386D] Heronicus 1. Herovicus 7. Hibi Erohunicus 13.] came with another sister of Waipharius the duke. Returning safely from there, he celebrated Easter in the fortress called Sels [Note: [Col. 0386D] “in the fortress which” 1. 7. (8.) 9.] [Note: [Col. 0385D] Either Seltz in Alsace or some place in Aquitania. The distinguished Guizot, in his French translation of our annals (*Collection des mémoires relatifs à l’histoire de France. Annales d’Eginhard*, p. 11), translates it as Selles. Valesius lists two places of that name: Selles in Berry, or rather Celle, Cella of Saint Eusicus, and Selles-sur-Nahon, or rather Celle, Cella of Saint Genulfus. Since, however, Sels does not derive its name from *Cella*, we cannot agree with this highly distinguished historian on this point.].

Again setting out on campaign [Note: [Col. 0386D] assuming 1. 7. 9. 12.] with Queen Lady Bertradana, he reached the city of Saintes [Note: [Col. 0386D] Xanctones 1.]. There Lady Queen Bertradana [Col. 0387A] [Note: [Col. 0387C] “there he left the said queen” 1. 7. “there Lady Bertrada the queen” 9.] was left with her household, while he went into the region of Périgord [Note: [Col. 0387C] Petragoricum 9.]. After Waipharius had been killed, he returned triumphantly to Saintes [Note: [Col. 0387C] the city of Xanctones 1. the city of Saintes 7.]. Remaining there for several days [Note: [Col. 0387C] several days 1. 7. (8.) 9. 12.], he began to fall ill. He proceeded toward the region of Tours [Note: [Col. 0387C] of the Turones 1.] on his return [Note: [Col. 0387C] “he went to Orcerus, to Saint Martin” 1.], prayed to Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 0387C] Martinus 5.] [Note: [Col. 0387C] “he prayed, and to Saint” 7.], and reached Saint-Denis [Note: [Col. 0387C] Dionysius 5.], where he ended his days on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 0387C] “he died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October” 1. “the seventh day before the Kalends” 7.].

Lord Charles and Carlomannus were raised to the kingship: Lord Charles on the seventh day before the Ides of October in the city of Noyon [Note: [Col. 0387C] Noviomis 1.], and Carlomannus likewise in the city of Soissons. ## 772

There was a great drought, so that water failed [Note: [Col. 0394C] “great and so severe that it failed” in 1; *it failed* placed after *so* in 5.] at the place mentioned above, where the Irminsul stood [Note: [Col. 0394C] *Ermenstil* in 1; *Hermensul* in 10]. And when the aforesaid glorious king wished to remain there for two or three [Note: [Col. 0394C] *Glorious* is absent in 6.] days [Note: [Col. 0394C] *Days* is absent in 1.] in order to destroy the shrine completely [Note: [Col. 0394C] *Perdestruendum*; *perdistruendum* in 5.], and they had no water, then suddenly, by the generosity of divine grace, at midday, while the entire army was resting, waters poured forth most abundantly in a certain torrent, although all the men were unaware of it [Note: [Col. 0394C] *Men* is absent in 6.], so that the entire army had sufficient water [Note: [Col. 0394C] *Suffitienter* in 6.].

Then the aforesaid great king [Note: [Col. 0394C] “The aforesaid great” is absent in 6.] [Note: [Col. 0394C] “The great king” in 1.] came to the river Wisora [Note: [Col. 0394C] *Wiseram* in 9; *Wisaram* in 10 and thereafter], and there held an assembly with the Saxons and received twelve hostages [Note: [Col. 0394C] *Twelve* is absent in 7.]. He returned to Francia [Note: [Col. 0394C] *Frantia* in 5.] and celebrated Christmas at Haristallium [Note: [Col. 0394C] *Haristalho* in 1; one manuscript reads: “Christmas and Easter at Herstal, and the year of the Lord changed to 773” in 9.], and likewise Easter. And the reckoning of the years changed to

## 773

Then Lord King Charles [Note: [Col. 0394C] “Then King Charles” in 6.] [Note: [Col. 0394C] “Charles the most gentle king” in 7.] went to winter at the estate called Theodone [Note: [Col. 0394C] *Teodone* in 6.] [Note: [Col. 0394C] *Estate* is absent in 1.]. While he was there, a messenger of Lord Pope Hadrian, named Peter, came by sea as far as Marseille [Note: [Col. 0394C] *Maxiliam* in 5; *Arelatum* in 11.], and from there reached Lord [Note: [Col. 0394C] *Lord* is absent in 6.] King Charles [Note: [Col. 0394C] *King* is absent in 1, 7, and 10.] by land [Note: [Col. 0394C] “from there by the Rhône” in 1; “from there by land” in 9; “by land travel” in 10; “by a land route” in 11.] [Note: [Col. 0394C] *As far as* is absent in 1 and 6.] [Note: [Col. 0394C] *Reaching*; *joining* in 1; *arriving* in 6; *he arrived* in 9.] to invite the above-mentioned glorious king [Note: [Col. 0394C] *Glorious* is absent in 6.] together with the Franks, for the service of God and the rights of Saint Peter, and for the relief of the Church [Note: [Col. 0394C–D] “For the service of God and the rights of Saint Peter, or for the relief” in 6.], against King Desiderius and the Lombards [Note: [Col. 0394D] *Longibardi* in 1.].

For this reason he came by sea, because the roads had been closed to the Romans by the Lombards [Note: [Col. 0394D] “And from there” in one witness; “because the roads were closed” in 6.]. Then Lord and most exalted King Charles took counsel with the Franks about what he should do [Note: [Col. 0394D] *He entered into counsel with* in 1; *he took counsel together with* in 6; *he held counsel together with* in 10.]. After taking counsel [Note: [Col. 0394D] “He ordered, following counsel, that” in 1; “he ordered that, just as” in 7.], so that, just as the messenger of the apostolic lord [Note: [Col. 0394D] “The messenger of Pope Hadrian” in 7 and 9; “the messenger of Lord Pope Hadrian, through his word” in 6.] had requested in the word of Lord Pope Hadrian [Col. 0395A], so it should be done [Note: [Col. 0395C] *To be done* in 1; *that it be done* in 6.], then the aforesaid glorious king held a general synod [Note: [Col. 0395C] *Sinodum*; *synodum* in manuscripts 1, 7, and others.] [Note: [Col. 0395C] *Postulatum* in 1; *postulavit* in 6, 7, and 9; *postulaverat* in 10. *Aforesaid* in 1; absent in 6 and 9. “The glorious king” in 7. *General* is absent in 1.] with the Franks in the city of Genoa [Note: [Col. 0395C] “In the city of Genoa” in 1; “in the Genoese city” in 6; “at the city of Genoa” in 7 and 9; “in the city of Genoa” in 10; *Genua* in 11; *Iebam* in 13.].

There dividing the army [Note: [Col. 0395C] “Dividing and then proceeding, the king divided” in 1; “dividing, he himself proceeded” in 7, 9, 10, and 11. *Lord* is absent in 6.], the said lord king proceeded over Mount Cenis [Note: [Col. 0395C] *Canisium* in 1; *Cenisium* in 7, 8, and 9; *Cinisium* in 10; *Cesusium* in 11.], and sent his uncle Bernard over Mount Jovis [Note: [Col. 0395C] *Iovis* in 1, 7, 10, and 12.] with some of his [Note: [Col. 0395C] “With his other faithful men” in 1, 7, 8, and 10.] faithful men.

Then both armies joined one another at the passes [Note: [Col. 0395C] *Sclusas* consistently in 9; *coniugentes* in 5.], and Desiderius himself came to meet Lord King Charles [Note: [Col. 0395C] “Desiderius went to meet Lord King Charles” in 1; “Desiderius went to meet Lord King Charles” in 7, 8, and 9; *king* is absent in 9; “Desiderius came to meet Lord King Charles” in 10 and 11.].

Then Lord King Charles [Note: [Col. 0395C] *Lord* is absent in 1 and 6.] together with the Franks pitched his camp at those same passes. [Note: [Col. 0395C–D] The conjunction *et* (“and”) is absent in manuscript 7.] And he sent his troop-detachment (*scara*) through the mountains [Note: [Col. 0395D] *Mountains* in 1 and 7; *mountain districts* in 8 and 9.]. When Desiderius learned this [Note: [Col. 0395D] “Following them” in 1.], he [Note: [Col. 0395D] “King Desiderius” in 7, 8, and 9.] abandoned the passes [Note: [Col. 0395D] *Closed passes* in 5; *he abandoned* in 7, 8, 9, and 10.]. The aforesaid Lord King Charles [Note: [Col. 0395D] *The aforesaid lord* is absent in 6; “the aforesaid lord, however” in 7 and 9.] together with the Franks, with the Lord’s help and through the intercession of the blessed Apostle Peter, entered Italy through the open passes without injury or disturbance, he and all his faithful men. And he reached the city of Pavia [Note: [Col. 0395D] Pavia. Here manuscripts 8, 9, 9b, 10, and 11 insert the passage printed below under 774, “And when … he had wished.”], and, after Desiderius had been shut inside, laid siege to that city.

There Lord Charles celebrated Christmas in his camp [Note: [Col. 0395D] “In his camps” in 1 and 6; “in those camps” in 7; “in the same camp” in 9; “inside his camp” in 10.] and Easter at Rome [Note: [Col. 0395D] “Easter in Rome” in 1.]. And the reckoning of the years changed to

## 774

And when [Note: [Col. 0395D] “And when … he wished” is absent in 1 and 13; it occurs under the year 773 in 8, 9, 9b, 10, and 11.] in that same year he had gone to defend the holy Roman Church of God, at the invitation of the supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. 0395D] “At the urging” in 7; “at the prayer” in 10.], leaving a frontier force behind against the Saxons, without having entered into any treaty whatsoever [Note: [Col. 0395D] “The treaty having been accepted, the Saxons themselves” in 7; “they accepted no treaty. The Saxons themselves” in 9.], the Saxons themselves came forth with a great army against the borders of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0395D] “Against the borders of the Franks and the Picts” in 7 and 9; “and they reached the Franks” in 11.]. They advanced as far as the fortress called Buriaburg [Note: [Col. 0395D] Mons Bierberg, on the right bank of the Eder, near the village of Ungedanken opposite Fritzlar; today deserted. *Chronicon Gottwicense*, from Schmink’s dissertation on the bishopric of Büraburg.]

Nevertheless, the inhabitants of the border region, troubled by this matter, seeing it, entered the fortress. When therefore that Saxon people [Note: [Col. 0398C] *Saxon people* in 6–12.] began savagely to burn the houses outside with fire [Note: [Col. 0398C] *Houses* is absent in 6.], they came to a certain basilica at a place called Friedislar [Note: [Col. 0398C] *Fridislar* in 7 and 12; *Fredislar* in 9; *Friedislar* in 10 and 11.], which Boniface, the last martyr of blessed memory, had consecrated, and through the spirit of prophecy had foretold would never be burned by fire [Note: [Col. 0398C] *Fires* in 6.].

The same aforesaid Saxons began with great determination to attack that basilica, seeking by every possible means to burn it with fire [Note: [Col. 0398C] *With fire* in 7 and 9; *with fire* is absent in 6.] or burn it completely [Note: [Col. 0398C] *Concremare* in 6.]. While this was happening, two young men in white appeared to certain Christians who were in the fortress, and likewise to certain pagans who were present in that army. They protected that basilica from the fire [Note: [Col. 0398C] “They protected it for that reason” in 7.], and for that reason the attackers could not set fire to it either inside or outside, nor inflict any damage on that same basilica [Note: [Col. 0398C–D] “Nor inflict any damage on this basilica” in 5; “on the same basilica” in 9, 10, and 11.]. But, terrified by fear at the sign of divine majesty, they turned to flight, although no one pursued them.

Later, one of those same Saxons was found dead beside the basilica, kneeling with bent knees and leaning over his feet [Note: [Col. 0398D] “Above his feet” in 7 and 9.], holding fire and wood in his hands, as though by blowing with his mouth he had wished to set the same basilica on fire [Note: [Col. 0398D] *He had wished*; “When Lord King Charles returned …” in 7.].

When Lord King Charles returned from Rome, he again reached Pavia [Note: [Col. 0398D] *Reached* in 1, 7, 9, and 10.], captured that city [Note: [Col. 0398D] “And captured that city” in 7 and 9.], and took King Desiderius with his wife and daughter, together with all the treasure of his palace [Note: [Col. 0398D] “His palace” in 1, 7, 10, and 11.].

There all the Lombards from every city of Italy came and submitted themselves to the rule of the glorious Lord King Charles and the Franks. Adalgisus [Note: [Col. 0398D] *Adaigulfus* in 1; *Adalgisus* in 6 and 10; *Adalgisus, however,* in 7, 8, 9, and 11.], son of King Desiderius, fled and entered the sea [Note: [Col. 0398D] *Entered* in 1; *entered the sea* in 7, 9, and 11.], and went to Constantinople.

Then glorious Lord King Charles [Note: [Col. 0398D] *Lord* is absent in 6.], after Italy had been subdued and organized, left a Frankish guard in the city of Pavia [Note: [Col. 0398D] *A guard* in 1 and 7; *guards* in 5; “an organized guard” in 9 and 10; “a guard having been left” in 11.], and, with his wife and the remaining Franks, returned to Francia with a great triumph, God helping him.

When he had reached the place called Ingilinhaim [Note: [Col. 0398D] *Ingelheim* in 1; *Ingilinheim* in 6; *Ingelhaim* in 7 and 9; *Ingilheim* in 11.] [Note: [Col. 0397D] Concerning the imperial palace at Ingelheim, see Schoepflin’s dissertation in the *Commentationes Academiae Theodoro-Palatinae*, vol. I, p. 300.], he sent four troop-detachments (*quatuor scaras*) into Saxony [Note: [Col. 0398D] *Misit* (“he sent”) in manuscripts 1, 7, 10, and 11; manuscript 5 repeats *quatuor* (“four”).] Three of them engaged in battle with the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0398D] “Into Saxony, three of which” in manuscripts 1 and 7; “into Saxony; but those three” in manuscript 9.] [Col. 0399A], and, with the Lord’s help, were victorious; the fourth detachment did not fight, but returned unharmed [Note: [Col. 0399B] *Inlaesi* in 1; *illaesi* in 7 and elsewhere.] to its own territory with much booty.

And the aforesaid glorious king [Note: [Col. 0399B] *Glorious* is absent in 6.] celebrated Christmas [Note: [Col. 0399B] [Col. 0399C] “Christmas and Easter at the estate of Carisiacum, in the year 775” in 9.] at the estate called Carisiacum, and likewise Easter [Note: [Col. 0399C] From this point onward, manuscript 5 writes *Karolus*.]. And the reckoning of the years changed to

## 775

Then the pious and illustrious Lord [Note: [Col. 0399C] *Lord* is absent in 6; “Lord King Charles” in 15; “King Charles” in 6.] King Charles held a synod [Note: [Col. 0399C] *Synod* in 1 and 6.] at the estate called Duria [Note: [Col. 0399C] “Düren, while traveling onward” in 1.], and from there proceeded into Saxony. He captured the fortress of Sigiburg [Note: [Col. 0399C] *Sigisburgum* in 7 and 10.], rebuilt Aeresburg [Note: [Col. 0399C] *Heresburgum* in 7, 9, and 11; *reaedificavit* with an orthographic variation in 6.], and came to the river Weser [Note: [Col. 0399C] *Wisaram* in 10 and 15; *Wiseram* in 9.] at the place called Brunsberg [Note: [Col. 0399C] *Brunisberc* in 15; *Brunisburg* in 10; *Brunisburgo* in 11.].

There the Saxons were preparing for battle, wishing to defend the bank of the aforesaid river [Note: [Col. 0399B] “The Saxons were preparing themselves for battle” in 15.]. With the Lord’s help, and while the Franks were fighting, the Saxons were put to flight [Note: [Col. 0399C] “The Saxons fled” in 1, 7, and 9; “the Saxons were routed” in 5; “the Saxons wandered” in 6; “the Saxons were driven off” in 8; “the Saxons having been routed” in 10; “the Saxons having been wearied” in 15.]. The Franks gained possession of both banks, and many Saxons were killed there [Note: [Col. 0399C] “Many Saxons were killed there. With the Lord’s help, the Franks were victorious. Amen.” Manuscript 15 ends here.]

Then Lord King Charles divided his army, took with him whom he wished, and proceeded as far as the river Obaccrus [Note: [Col. 0399C] *Obacerum* in 1; *Aboccrum*, corrected to *Abodcrum*, in 5; *Obaccrum* in 6; *Obacrum* in 7, 9, 10, and 11.].

There all the Eastphalian Saxons [Note: [Col. 0399C] “The Eastphalian Saxons” in 7; “the Saxony of the Eastphalians” in 10.] came with Hassio [Note: [Col. 0399C] *Bassione* in 5; *Hasione* in 6; *Mansione* in 9; *Assione* in 11; *Hassion* in 10; *Hussinon* in 12.] and gave hostages according to what pleased him [Note: [Col. 0399D] “According to what pleased the king” in 9.]. They swore oaths that they would be faithful to the territory of the aforesaid Lord King Charles [Note: [Col. 0399D] *Charles* is absent in 1; “King Charles” in 6.].

Likewise, when the aforesaid most gentle king [Note: [Col. 0399D] “The most gentle king” in 6.] was already returning [Note: [Col. 0399D] “Already returning from there” in 1; “while returning” in 6.], the Angrarii [Note: [Col. 0399D] *Angarii* in 6 and 11.] came to the district [Note: [Col. 0399D] *Bago* in 5.] called Bucki [Note: [Col. 0399D] *Buckhi* in 1; *Buki* in 7; *Bocki* in 8; *Bachim* in 10; *Bocensi* in 11.] together with Bruno and their other nobles [Note: [Col. 0399D] *Optimates* with an orthographic variant in 6.], and there gave hostages [Note: [Col. 0399D] “They gave hostages there” in 1; “they gave hostages there” in 7.] just as the Austrasians had done.

When the aforesaid king was returning from there [Note: [Col. 0402C] *While returning* in 6.], he found another part of his army on the river Weser, holding the bank that they had been ordered to hold [Note: [Col. 0402C] This phrase is absent in 6.]. The Saxons fought with them at a place called Lidbach [Note: [Col. 0402C] *Lidpach* in 1; *Liddach* in 5; *Diddach*, corrected to *Lidbach*, in 6; *Lidbad* in 7; *Lidbah* in 8, 9, and 10; *Litca* in 11.], and the Franks, by God’s will, won the victory, and killed many of those Saxons [Note: [Col. 0402C] *Of them* is absent in 1, 7, and 11; *of the Saxons* in 9 and 11.].

When Lord King Charles heard this, he again attacked the Saxons with an army, inflicted no smaller slaughter upon them [Note: [Col. 0402C] *Upon those men* in 1 and 7.], and acquired much booty from the Westphalians [Note: [Col. 0402C] *Westphaleos* in 1; *Westfalos* in 6.]. They gave hostages, as the other Saxons had done [Note: [Col. 0402C] “As those other Saxons” in 7 and 9.]. After receiving the hostages, taking much booty [Note: [Col. 0402C] *Assumpta* in 1, 6, and 9; *sumpta* in 7.], and after a third slaughter had been inflicted upon the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0402C] “And likewise after the slaughter of the Saxons had been carried out” in 1 and 7; “and after the Saxons had been slaughtered three times” in 6; “and after a third slaughter of the Saxons” in 11; the word *ter* is absent in 10; the syllable *ter* is absent in 5.], the aforesaid Lord King Charles returned to his own territory in Francia, with the Lord’s help.

Then he heard that Hrodgaudus [Note: [Col. 0402C] *Ruodgandus* in 1; *Rodhgaudus* and *Rodgaudus* in 5; *Roigaudus* in 7, 9, and 11; *Rodgaudus* in 10, and likewise below.], a Lombard [Note: [Col. 0402C] *Longibardus* in 1.], had betrayed his loyalty, broken all his sworn agreements, and wished to make Italy rebel [Note: [Col. 0402C] “And, breaking his oath, wished to revolt” in 7 and 9.]. While Lord King Charles was traveling in those regions with some Franks [Note: [Col. 0402C] “Then Charles with the Franks” in 1.], he celebrated Christmas at the estate called Scladdistat [Note: [Col. 0402C] *Scladistat* in 7 and 9; *Scladdistath* in 8; *Sclezistat* in *Elisatio* in 9b; *Selexeistat* [Col. 0402D] and Easter at *Elizatio* in 12; “Lord” and similar words are absent here and elsewhere in 6.] [Note: [Col. 0401D] Schlettstadt in Alsace.] And the reckoning of the years changed to

## 776

Then Lord [Note: [Col. 0402D] *Lord* is absent in 1. “As we said above, the king came to the city of Pavia and hurriedly directed his journey into the region of Friuli.” *Annales Mettenses*; in the account of the assault on Aeresburg, the *Annales Mettenses* follow Regino.] King Charles entered Italy, seeking the region of Friuli [Note: [Col. 0402D] “Proceeding through the region of Friuli” in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0402D] *Proceeding* in 6 and 7; “having traversed the region of Friuli” in 10.]. Hrodgaudus was killed, and the aforesaid Lord [Note: [Col. 0402D] *Aforesaid lord* is absent in 1 and 6.] King Charles celebrated Easter at the city of Tarvisium [Note: [Col. 0402D] *Taravisium* here and below in 7 and 11; *Tarwisium* in 9; *Tharvisum* in 10.]. He captured the cities of Friuli and Tarvisium [Note: [Col. 0402D] “After capturing the city of Friuli and Tarvisium” in 1; “the Friulian city” in 7; *Foroiulium* in 10.] together with the other cities that had rebelled [Note: [Col. 0402D] “And the cities that” in 5.] [Note: [Col. 0402D] “That had rebelled” in 1; “that had been rebellious” in 6.]. He placed Franks in charge of all of them and again returned to Francia in prosperity [Col. 0402C] and victory.

Then a messenger arrived and said [Note: [Col. 0402D] *Who* is absent in 1, 7, 9, and elsewhere.] [Note: [Col. 0402D] “He came and said” in 5.] that the Saxons were rebelling [Note: [Col. 0402D] *To rebel* in 1; *had rebelled* in 5 and 10; *having been rebelled against* in 6 and 9.], had released all their hostages [Note: [Col. 0402D] *Dulgtos* and *dulgtos* is absent in 1; *dultos* in 6; *tultos* in 9.], and had broken their oaths [Col. 0403A] [Note: [Col. 0403C] “To break their oaths” in 1.], and that they had persuaded the Franks to leave Aeresburg fortress by evil devices and unjust agreements [Note: [Col. 0403C] *Evil device* in 6.] [Note: [Col. 0403C] “Persuading the Franks to leave them” in 1.]. Thus, after Aeresburg had been abandoned by the Franks [Note: [Col. 0403C] “With Aeresburg abandoned” in 7.], they destroyed its walls and fortifications [Note: [Col. 0403C] “The Saxons destroyed the works” in 7 and 9.].

From there they wished to do the same to Sigiburg [Note: [Col. 0403C] *Sigiburgo* in 1; *Sigisburgo* in 7, 8, 9, and 10.], but, with the Lord’s help, the Franks resisting them bravely [Note: [Col. 0403C] *Them* is absent in 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11], they achieved nothing.

[Note: [Col. 0403C–D] The passage beginning “For when …” and ending “his servants” is absent from manuscript 1 and from the Annals of Einhard, Fulda, and Tiliani. This shows that the entire narrative—which is moreover placed at different points in different manuscripts—should not be regarded as part of the genuine text. Rather, after the year 788 someone knowledgeable about these events added it in the margin of the exemplar from which manuscripts 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12 descended. In manuscripts 5, 6, and 7 it is inserted not after the second *inde* (“from there”) but after the first: “They destroyed them. From there, for when … proceeding, his servants. From there they wished …” [Col. 0403D] In manuscripts 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12 it is inserted after “to do the same,” incorrectly in both placements. Separately, manuscript 13 omits everything for this year after “he returned to Francia,” together with the years 777, 778, and 779.]

For when they could not deceive by agreements those who were guards inside the fortress, as they had deceived others who had been in another fortress [Note: [Col. 0403D] “Another fortress” in 7; “in another castle” in 6.], they began to prepare battles and siege engines, so that by force they might capture it. And, by God’s will, the stone-throwing engines [Note: [Col. 0403D] Engines for throwing stones.] that they had prepared [Note: [Col. 0403D] *Had prepared* in 6.] caused more damage to them [Note: [Col. 0403D] *Damage* in 6.] than to those who lived inside the fortress.

When they saw that this was of no use to them [Col. 0403B], they also prepared *clidae* [Note: [Col. 0403D] *Clidos* in manuscript 7; the term denotes wicker screens.] in order to attack the fortress by force. But the power of God, as was right, overcame their power. One day, when they had prepared for battle against the Christians who lived in that fortress, the glory of God visibly appeared above the church building inside the fortress [Note: [Col. 0403D] “The basilica situated inside the fortress” in 6.], seen by those who were outside as well as by those inside [Note: [Col. 0403D] *Also* is absent in 6; “seen by many” in 6, 7, and 9; “seen by all” in 10.], many of whom remain to this day. They say that they saw something like two shields, blazing and moving with a red color above that church.

When the pagans who were outside saw this sign, they were immediately thrown into confusion and, terrified by great fear, began to flee to their camp [Note: [Col. 0403D] “To the fortress” in 5.]. Their entire multitude, shaken with terror, took flight [Note: [Col. 0403D] “Taking flight” in 7; “flight having been taken” in 5.], and some killed one another. Those who looked back because of fear thrust themselves upon the spears of those who were fleeing ahead of them [Note: [Col. 0403D] “They thrust the spears of those whom they carried on their shoulders into the bodies of those in front” in 9; “They were pierced by the spears of those ahead because of fear” in 11; *they fled* in 5.] and were carrying them on their shoulders; others were struck by various blows among themselves [Col. 0406A] [Note: [Col. 0406C] “They suffered various blows” in 6, 7, 8, and 9.] and were punished by divine vengeance.

No one can recount how greatly the power of God worked against them for the salvation of the Christians [Note: [Col. 0406C] “How greatly the power of God worked for the salvation of the Christians against them” in 7.]. Nevertheless, the more terrified they were by fear, the more the Christians were strengthened, and they praised almighty God, who had deigned to reveal his power over his servants.]

The Saxons then took flight, and the Franks pursued them, killing them as far as the river Lippe [Note: [Col. 0406C] “As far as the river” in 5; *the river* in 1, 7, and 8.], while the fortress was saved; and the Franks returned victorious.

When Lord King Charles reached Worms and heard all these matters [Note: [Col. 0406C] “These matters” in 5.] [Note: [Col. 0406C] “Having heard” in 6.], he convened a synod in that same city. There he held a public assembly, and, after counsel had been taken [Note: [Col. 0406C] *Council* in 1 and 7.], with God’s help and with great haste [Note: [Col. 0406C] *Haste* is absent in 6.] he suddenly entered the Saxon fortifications made of felled trees [Note: [Col. 0405D] Defensive works made of trees laid across one another.] [Note: [Col. 0406C] *Houses* in 7 and 9; *lands* in 10.].

The terrified Saxons [Note: [Col. 0406C] “The Saxons through the lands” in 1.] came from every direction to the place where the Lippe rises [Note: [Col. 0406C] *And* is absent in 7.] and surrendered the entire homeland into their hands by pledge [Note: [Col. 0406C–D] *Waidium*; “by a pledge” in 1; *wadimoniam*, “by a guarantee,” in 9.] [Note: [Col. 0406D] *All* in 1 and 7; *the whole* in 9.], promised that they would be Christians, and submitted themselves to the authority [Note: [Col. 0406D] *Jurisdiction* in 1, 6, 7–9, and elsewhere.] of Lord King Charles and the Franks.

Then Lord King Charles, together with the Franks, rebuilt the fortress of Aeresburg [Note: [Col. 0406D] *Restored* in 1; *rebuilt* in 6.] anew [Note: [Col. 0406D] *Anew* is absent in 1.] and another fortress on the Lippe. There Saxons came with their wives and children, an innumerable multitude [Note: [Col. 0406D] “An innumerable” in 6; “innumerable” in 1.], and were baptized [Note: [Col. 0406D] “The multitude was baptized” in 6.]. They gave as many hostages as the aforesaid lord king requested [Note: [Col. 0406D] *To them* is absent in 1; *from them* in 6; *by them* in 7, 9, and 10.]. After the aforesaid fortresses had been completed and arranged [Note: [Col. 0406D] “After the aforesaid fortresses had been completed and arranged” in 1, 7, 9, and 10.], Frankish detachments [Note: [Col. 0405D] *Scara*, our *Schaar*, a troop or company.] remained there and guarded them [Note: [Col. 0406D] “With the detachments remaining there and guarding them” in 7 and 10.].

Lord King Charles returned to Francia and celebrated Christmas at Haristallium [Note: [Col. 0406D] *Haristalho* in 1; *Aristallio* in 5.] and Easter at the estate called Niumaga [Note: [Col. 0406D] *Niomaga* in 1; *Neumaga* in 7.] [Note: [Col. 0406D] Nijmegen.]. And the reckoning of the years changed to

## 777

Then Lord King Charles held a public synod [Note: [Col. 0406D] *Public* feminine in 1 and 5.] at Paderborn [Note: [Col. 0406D] “At Paderborn” in 1.] for the first time. All the Franks gathered there [Note: [Col. 0406D] *Venientes* (“coming”) in manuscript 1; *convenientesque ibi* (“and gathering there”) in manuscript 6.], and Saxons from every part of Saxony gathered from all directions [Note: [Col. 0406D] This phrase is absent in 1.]—except that Widukind [Note: [Col. 0406D] *Vindobundis* in 1; *Witochindis* in 7; *Windochinus* in 9; *Widochindus* in 8.] remained in rebellion with a few others [Note: [Col. 0406D] *Others* is absent in 1.]. He fled for refuge into the region of the Northmen [Note: [Col. 0407C] *Nordmannia* in 5; *Normannia* in 7 and 9.] together with his companions.

Saracens from the regions of Spain also came to the same assembly [Note: [Col. 0407C] “To the same” in 1, 7, and 10; the word *placitum* begins manuscript 2.] [Note: [Col. 0407C] “From Spain, namely *Ibinalakabe*” in 1.]. These were Ibn al-Arabi and the son of Deiuzefi [Note: [Col. 0407C] *de Vizosi* in 1; *Diuzefi* in 5; *Deiuzevi* in 6.], who is likewise called Joseph in Latin, and likewise his son-in-law [Note: [Col. 0407C] “And likewise his son-in-law Alaruiz” in 11. The editor states: “I am convinced that the name *Alarviz* is nothing other than a repeated form of *Alarabi*. I regard the reading of manuscript 2 as similar and corrupt.”].

There a multitude of Saxons was baptized [Note: [Col. 0407C] “The multitude was baptized” in 1.]. According to their custom, they made over all their free status and allodial property [Note: [Col. 0407C] *Allod* in 7 and 9; *inheritance* in 9b.] into *dulgtum* hands [Note: [Col. 0407C] *Dulgium* in 1; *dultum* in 7.], should they thereafter change according to their evil custom unless they preserved Christianity in all things, or fidelity to the aforesaid Lord King Charles, his sons, and the Franks [Note: [Col. 0407D] *Aforesaid* is absent in 1.].

And he celebrated Christmas at the estate called Dotciacum [Note: [Col. 0407D] *Doriacum* in 1; *Dorciacum* in 7; *Dociacum* in 9.] [Note: [Col. 0407D] Douzy, in the district of Mosomagus, near Sedan. See Valesius, cited above, pp. 182–183.], and Easter in Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0407D] *Equitania* in 6.], at the estate called Cassinogilum [Note: [Col. 0407D] “The estate called Cassivogila” in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0408D] Casseneuil, in the district of Agen. Ibid., p. 131.]. And the reckoning of the years changed to

## 778
