Then [Note: [Col. 0407D] Here codex 3 begins.] Lord King Charles [Note: [Col. 0407C] Moved by the prayers and complaints of the Christians who were in Spain under the yoke of the Saracens, he entered Spain with an army.] proceeded on his march through the regions of Spain [Note: [Col. 0407D] *agens*, “conducting,” in 6.] [Note: [Col. 0407D] *in partes*, “into the regions,” in 1.] by two routes: one [Note: [Col. 0407D] *unam*, “one,” in 7.] through Pamplona [Note: [Col. 0407D] *pampilonen*, “Pamplona,” in 1 and 6], by which the aforesaid great king himself advanced as far as Zaragoza. There, forces coming from the regions of Burgundy and Austrasia [Note: [Col. 0407D] *Austrasia*, in 9], or Bavaria, Provence [Note: [Col. 0407D] *Provincia*, “Provincia,” in 5], and Septimania [Note: [Col. 0407D] *Septimana*, “Septimana,” in 1], and part of the Lombards [Note: [Col. 0407C] “All Spain trembled before these innumerable legions.”], joining themselves to the aforesaid city from both sides [Note: [Col. 0407D] *et ex*, “and from,” in 7] of the army [Note: [Col. 0407D] *unaque*, “from one side,” in 1] [Note: [Col. 0407D] “the Lombards joining themselves,” in 7], received hostages there from Ibn al-Arabi and Abu Thawr [Note: [Col. 0407D] “hostages from Derbanalambi and Drabatauro,” in 1], and from many Saracens. Pamplona was destroyed [Note: [Col. 0407D] *pampilonea*, “Pamplona,” in 2; “destroyed” in 1, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and others], and the Hispani [Note: [Col. 0407D] “the Hispani and Vascones subjected … the Navarri,” in 1], the Vascones [Note: [Col. 0407D] “the Hispani and Vascones,” in 7 and 9], and also the Navarri [Note: [Col. 0407D] “Navarri,” in 7] were subjected. He returned to the regions [Note: [Col. 0407D] “into the regions,” in 1] of Francia. And when the Saxons heard that Lord King Charles and the Franks [Col. 0407C] had gone so far into the regions of Spain [Note: [Col. 0407D] “were,” in 6], through the persuasion [Note: [Col. 0410C] “persuasion,” in 2] of the aforesaid Widukind [Note: [Col. 0410C] *Vindekindi*, in 1; *Widokindi*, corrected to *Widokingi*, in 2; *Widokingi*, in 3; *Widukindi*, in 4; *Widochindi*, in 5; *Widichindi*, in 6; *Withochindi*, in 7; *Widechinni*, in 9; *Widochindi*, in 10 and 11; *Widikindi*, in 12.] and his companions [Note: [Col. 0410C] “Widukind and his companions,” in 1, 7, and others], they again rebelled according to their evil custom [Note: [Col. 0410C] “revolted,” in 5], and this was reported [Note: [Col. 0410C] *hoc* is absent in 5] to Lord King Charles [Note: [Col. 0410C] *regi*, “to the king,” in 1, 5, 6, and 7] at the city of Auxerre [Note: [Col. 0410C] *Annasiodorum*, in 1; *Authisiodorum*, in 5; *Autisiodorum*, in 6, 7, and others].

Then the aforesaid lord king sent a *scara* [Note: [Col. 0410C] “a Frankish *scara*, quickly and hastily, to resist the aforesaid Saxons,” in 1] of Franks to hasten swiftly to resist the aforesaid Saxons [Note: [Col. 0410C] “a *scara* of Franks, so that it might run in haste to resist the Saxons, but those rebels reached Deutz,” in 6]. But those rebels reached the Rhine as far as Divicia [Note: [Col. 0410C] *Diuca*, in 1; *Diuicia*, in 2 and 3; *Diutia*, corrected to *Dutia*, in 5; *Diucia*, in 6; *Durecia*, in 7; *Duitia*, in 8; *Duitium*, in 9], plundering along the Rhine [Note: [Col. 0410C] *Rhenum*, “the Rhine,” consistently in the manuscripts examined: 2, 5, and 6], committing many atrocities, burning the churches of God among the convents of holy women [Note: [Col. 0410C] “they ravaged among the nuns,” in 1 and 7; “with the nuns,” in 9], and doing things too loathsome to enumerate [Note: [Col. 0410C] “to number”; [Col. 0410D] “to number,” in 6].

When they suddenly heard of the return of Lord King Charles and of his *scara*, which he had sent to meet them [Note: [Col. 0410D] “his. He sent it to meet them,” in 2], they abandoned the Rhine and returned through Logenehi [Note: [Col. 0410D] *Longenhri*, in 1; *Loinahi*, in 5; *Loginahi*, in 6; *Longenehi*, in 7; *Longene*, in 8 and 11; *Lingonem*, in 9; *Logene*, in 10] [Note: [Col. 0410D] A district along the Lahn, the Lahngau.] into the regions [Note: [Col. 0410D] *partes*, “regions,” in 1] of Saxony. The *scara* [Note: [Col. 0410D] *scara*, in 2] [Col. 0410B] of the Franks did not meet them there [Note: [Col. 0410D] *non* is absent in 9], but, following their tracks [Note: [Col. 0410D] *ipsorum*, “of them,” in 1], overtook them on the river called the Adarna [Note: [Col. 0410D] *Adarnia*, in 7], at a place called Lihesi [Note: [Col. 0410D] *Liesi*, in 5; *Liesu*, in 6] [Note: [Col. 0410D] The Saxon Poet calls this place Battenfeld in this year.].

There battle was begun and very successfully concluded [Note: [Col. 0410D] *valde*, “very,” is absent in 6]. With the Lord’s help, the Franks were victorious. A multitude of Saxons were killed there [Note: [Col. 0410D] “were killed, and the rest,” in 1], and those who fled [Note: [Col. 0410D] “and the rest,” in 7] returned to Saxony in great disgrace [Note: [Col. 0410D] “with great disgrace,” in 5; “with great shame,” in 1 and 6]. The aforesaid most merciful king celebrated Christmas in the villa called Heristal [Note: [Col. 0410D] *Haristalhio*, in 1], and Easter likewise. And the number of the years changed to

## 779

Then Lord King Charles proceeded on his march through the regions of Neustria [Note: [Col. 0410D] *Neustriae*, in 7; *Niustriae*, corrected to *Austriae*, in 6], and reached the villa [Note: [Col. 0410D] *villam*, “the villa,” in 5 and 6] called Compiègne [Col. 0410C] [Note: [Col. 0410D] *Compendium*, in 1]. Then, returning toward the regions [Note: [Col. 0410D] *per partes*, “through the regions,” in 1] of Austrasia, Duke Hildebrand [Note: [Col. 0411C] *Hiltibrandus*, in 6], Duke of Spoleto [Col. 0411A] [Note: [Col. 0411C] *Spoletanus*, in 1; *Spolitanus*, in 6, 7, and 9], presented himself with many gifts [Note: [Col. 0411C] “with many presents,” in 1, 5, 6, 7, and others] before the aforesaid great king, at the villa called Virciniacum [Note: [Col. 0411C] *Wirciniacum*, in 1, 5, 7, and others; *Irciniacum*, in 6].

A synod was held at a villa called Düren [Note: [Col. 0411C] “at the villa called,” in 1; “at a villa called,” in 5 and 7; “a villa called,” in 6], and the march was undertaken [Note: [Col. 0411C] “he proceeded,” in 1 and 6; “the march was completed,” in 6; “he proceeded,” in 7] into the regions [Note: [Col. 0411C] *in* is absent in 1, 5, 6, 7, and others] of Saxony. At Lippeham [Note: [Col. 0411C] *Lippeam*, in 5; *Lippaham*, in 7] the river Rhine was crossed [Note: [Col. 0411C] “after crossing the river Rhine,” in 1; “at the crossing,” in 2; “crossing,” in 5; “the crossing of the Rhine river” is absent in 6]. The Saxons wished to resist at a place called Bohholt [Note: [Col. 0411C] *Buoholz*, in 1; *Bobholz*, in 5; *Bohholtz*, in 6; *Bohholz*, in 8; *Hocholz*, in 9; *Bolhoz*, in 10; *Botolz*, in 11] [Note: [Col. 0411D] Bocholt, on the river Aa, north of Lippeham.].

With the Lord’s help, they did not prevail. Fleeing from there, they abandoned all their strongholds, and the way was opened to the Franks. Entering Westphalia [Note: [Col. 0411C] *Westualahos*, in 1; *Westfaluos*, in 2; *Westualos*, in 6], they conquered them all [Note: [Col. 0411C] “conquered,” in 1, 5, 7, and others]. Those who were beyond the Weser [Note: [Col. 0411C] *Wisora* is absent in 2; *Wisoram*, in 6 and 7; [Col. 0411D] “the remaining people who were beyond the Weser,” in 1], when Lord King Charles had come to a place called Medofulli [Note: [Col. 0411D] *Medofuldi*, in 1] [Note: [Col. 0411D] Throughout the course of the Weser, only Mülbeck near Rinteln and Polle, a fortress of the kingdom of Hanover, show any resemblance to the name *Medofulii*.], gave hostages and again confirmed their oaths [Note: [Col. 0411D] “and then,” in 1; “and thereafter,” in 5 and 6; “again” is absent in 7]. Then the aforesaid glorious king returned to Francia [Note: [Col. 0411D] “to France,” in 1 and 7; *Frantiam*, in 6]. He celebrated Christmas in the city of Worms [Note: [Col. 0411D] “in the city of Wormatia,” in 1, 6, 7, and others], and Easter likewise. And the number of the years changed to

## 780

Then Lord King Charles proceeded on his march to organize Saxony and reached Heresburg. From there he went to the place where the Lippe rises. Holding a synod there, he proceeded toward the regions of the river Elbe, and on that very march all the Bardengau people [Note: [Col. 0411D] *Bardoganenses*, in 1; *Bardogauenses*, in 7] [Note: [Col. 0411D] The inhabitants of the Bardengau, which comprised a large part of the duchy of Lüneburg; its principal settlement at that time was Bardenwich.] and many of the Nordleudi [Note: [Col. 0411D] *Nordilendis*, in 1; *Nortleudi*, in 5; *Nortelendi*, in 6] [Note: [Col. 0412D] That is, the Saxons beyond the Elbe, the Nordalbingi.] were baptized at a place called Orhaim [Note: [Col. 0411D] *Orcheim*, in 1; *Orthaïm*, in 5; *Orahim*, in 7], beyond the river Obacrum.

He reached the aforesaid river, where the Ora flows into the Elbe [Note: [Col. 0411D] “where the Obacrum flows,” in 7] [Note: [Col. 0412D] The river Ohre; not far from its confluence with the Elbe stands the town of Wolmirstedt today.]. There, having organized everything both in Saxony and among the Slavs [Note: [Col. 0411D] “both Slavia and Saxony,” in 1], the aforesaid illustrious king returned to Francia [Note: [Col. 0411D] “to France,” in 1, 5, 6, and 7].

Then, after taking counsel [Col. 0411C] to proceed on a pilgrimage for the sake of prayer [Note: [Col. 0411D] *perageret*, “he should proceed,” in 1, 5, and 7; *ageret*, “he should conduct,” in 6] to the regions of Rome [Note: [Col. 0411D] *causa*, “for the sake,” in 1, 5, 6, and others], together with his wife, Lady Queen Hildegard [Note: [Col. 0411D] *Hildegarda*, in 6]. He celebrated Christmas in the city of Pavia [Note: [Col. 0411D] “in the city of Pavia,” in 1 and 6]. And the number of the years changed to

[Col. 0414A]

## 781

Having proceeded on the aforesaid journey [Note: [Col. 0414C] “And King Charles, having proceeded,” in 1 and 7], he celebrated Easter in Rome. There Lord Pippin, son of the aforesaid Lord Charles the Great, was baptized [Note: [Col. 0414C] *est*, “was,” is absent in 2] by Pope Hadrian, who himself received him from the sacred font [Note: [Col. 0414C] *eum*, “him,” is absent in 2]. The two sons of the aforesaid Lord King Charles were anointed as kings [Note: [Col. 0414D] “anointed,” in 1] by the aforesaid pontiff. They were Lord Pippin and Lord Louis [Note: [Col. 0414D] *Hlodowicus*, in 6; *Lodouicus*, in 1], kings: Lord Pippin king in Italy [Note: [Col. 0414D] *rex* through the second occurrence of *rex* is absent in 1], and Lord Louis king in Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0414D] “Louis in Aquitaine,” in 2; “King Louis in Aquitaine,” in 7].

When Lord King Charles was returning from there, he reached the city of Milan [Note: [Col. 0414D] “Milan, the city,” in 1]. There his daughter, Lady Gisola [Note: [Col. 0414D] *Gistola*, in 1; *Gisola*, in 7], was baptized by an archbishop named Thomas [Note: [Col. 0414D] *Dioma*, in 1], who himself received her from the sacred baptismal font [Note: [Col. 0414D] “from the sacred font,” in 6 and 7; “from baptism,” in 1 and 5; “lifted her from the font,” in 6]. From there he returned to Francia.

Then two envoys were sent by the aforesaid apostolic lord: namely, the bishops Formosus [Note: [Col. 0414D] *Formosus*, in 5] and Damasus [Note: [Col. 0414D] *Damansus*, in 1], to Duke Tassilo [Note: [Col. 0414D] *Thassilonem*, in 1; *Tessilonem*, in 6], together with envoys of Lord King Charles—namely, the deacon Riculfus [Note: [Col. 0414D] *Ruculfum*, in 6] and Eberhard [Note: [Col. 0414D] *Eberaldum*, in 7], master of the cupbearers [Note: [Col. 0414D] *magistrum*, “master,” in 5, 6, and 7]—to admonish and charge him to remember his former oaths, and not to act otherwise than he had long ago promised on oath to Lord King Pippin and Lord Charles the Great and the Franks [Note: [Col. 0414D] “and so that he should not otherwise act,” in 1, 5, 6, and 7; “unless as,” in 1 and 6; *ad partem*, “on behalf of,” is absent in 5; “Lord King Pippin and Lord Charles the Great” is absent in 6; *vel*, “or,” is absent in 1].

Then Tassilo, duke of the Bavarians [Note: [Col. 0414D] *Tesilo*, in 6], agreed that, after receiving hostages from Lord King Charles, he would come into his presence [Note: [Col. 0414D] “would come,” in 2; “would come” is absent in 6]. The aforesaid king did not refuse this [Note: [Col. 0414D] *renuit*, “did not refuse,” in 1 and 7].

The aforesaid duke came into the presence of the most pious king at the city of Worms [Col. 0414C] [Note: [Col. 0414D] *Vurmatia*, in 5; *Vurmatica*, in 6; *Warmacia*, in 7], renewed his oaths, and gave twelve chosen hostages, promising to preserve everything that he had sworn to Lord King Pippin, in the interest of the aforesaid Lord King Charles and his faithful men. These hostages too were received at the villa of Quierzy [Note: [Col. 0414D] *Carisiaca villa*, in 1] from the hand of Bishop Sinbert [Note: [Col. 0414D] *Simbert*, in 1; *Sinberti*, in 2, 3, 5, and 6; *Ingberti*, in 7]. But the aforesaid Duke Tassilo did not long preserve the promises he had made. The aforesaid glorious lord king celebrated Christmas in the aforesaid villa of Quierzy [Note: [Col. 0414D] “the villa” is absent in 2; “the aforesaid city of Quierzy,” in 1], and Easter likewise. And the number of the years changed to

[Col. 0415A]

## 782

Then Lord King Charles proceeded on his march, crossing the Rhine to Cologne [Note: [Col. 0415C] *pertransiens*, “crossing over,” in 6]. He held a synod where the Lippe rises. There all the Saxons came together [Note: [Col. 0415C] “came,” except the rebel Widukind, in 1], except the rebel Widukind [Note: [Col. 0415C] “the rebel Widochind,” in 5; “Windochindus,” in 7]. The Northmen also assembled there, envoys of King Sigifrid [Note: [Col. 0415C] *Sifridi*, in 1; *Sigifredi*, in 5 and 7; *Godefridi*, in 7b and 9b]—namely Halfdan [Note: [Col. 0415D] *Haltani*, in 5; *Haltoni*, in 7; *Halptani*, in 2, 3, and 6] with his companions. Likewise the Avars assembled there, sent by the Cagan and Jugur [Note: [Col. 0415D] *Vigerio*, in 1; *Vigurro*, in 7; *Iugurno*, in 5]. When the assembly had been completed, Lord King Charles returned to Francia.

When he had returned, the Saxons immediately rebelled again according to their accustomed practice, at the urging of Widukind [Note: [Col. 0415D] *Vindekindo*, in 1; *Widichindo*, in 2]. Without Lord King Charles knowing this, he sent his envoys Adalgisus [Note: [Col. 0415D] *Adalgisum*, in 1, 5, 6, and 7], Gailo [Note: [Col. 0415D] *Algonem*, in 1; *Galonem*, in 5; *Gaiolonem*, in 6; *Wailonem*, in 7], and Woradus to raise the army of Franks and Saxons against a few Slavs who had rebelled [Note: [Col. 0415D] “who were rebels,” in 1].

The aforesaid envoys, hearing on the way that the Saxons had rebelled [Note: [Col. 0415D] *rebellassent*, “had revolted,” in 1 and 5], joined the aforesaid *scara*, attacked the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0415D] “fell upon the Saxons,” in 1], and sent no report of the matter to Lord King Charles [Note: [Col. 0415D] *regi*, “to the king,” in 1, 5, 6, and 7].

They engaged the Saxons in battle, fought bravely, and killed many Saxons [Note: [Col. 0415D] “killing many Saxons,” in 1, 5, 6, and 7]. The Franks were victorious [Note: [Col. 0415D] “were victorious,” in 1]. Two of those envoys, Adalgisus and Gailo, fell there on the mountain called Suntel [Note: [Col. 0415D] *Suntal*, in 1; *Sumptdal*, in 5; *Sümtal*, in 6; *Suntdal*, in 7] [Note: [Col. 0415D] The Sündel or Süntel, on the northern bank of the Weser between Münden and Rinteln; on its northern side lies the Dachtelfeld, that is, “the field where someone was beaten.”].

When Lord King Charles heard this [Note: [Col. 0415D] “hearing that,” in 2; “hearing this,” with the remainder omitted, in the others], he went there with the Franks whom he was able to gather quickly, and reached the place where the Alara flows into the Weser [Note: [Col. 0415D] *Alacra*, in 6].

Then all the Saxons assembled again and submitted themselves to the authority of the aforesaid lord king [Note: [Col. 0415D] “of the lord king,” in 1, 5, 6, and 7]. They handed over all the malefactors who had been chiefly responsible for that rebellion, to be killed—four thousand five hundred [Note: [Col. 0415D] “those rebels, and they killed them, except Widukind,” in 1]. And so it was done, except for Widukind [Note: [Col. 0415D] *Widochindus*, in 5, 6, 7, and others], who escaped by flight [Note: [Col. 0415D] *elapsus*, “having escaped,” in 1 and 7] to the regions [Note: [Col. 0415D] *ad partes*, “to the regions,” in 1] of Northmannia [Note: [Col. 0415D] *Normannia*, in 7].

When all this had been accomplished [Note: [Col. 0415D] “these things having been accomplished,” in 1], the aforesaid lord king returned to Francia. He celebrated Christmas in the villa called Thionville [Note: [Col. 0415D] *Theodonis*, in 1; *Theodone*, in 7], and Easter likewise. And the number of the years changed to

[Col. 0418C]

## 783

Then Lady Hildegard, the queen, who had deserved well, died on the day before the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 0418D] “of May, which was the vigil,” in 1]. This occurred on the day that was then the vigil of the Ascension of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0417D] Correctly so, because Easter fell on March 23.] [Note: [Col. 0419B] “And she was buried near the city of Metz in the basilica of the apostles and of Saint Arnulf.”]

Lord King Charles went into the regions [Note: [Col. 0418D] *per partes*, “through the regions,” consistently, apparently by Canisius’s conjecture, in 1] of Saxony because the Saxons had again become rebels [Note: [Col. 0418D] “had rebelled again,” in 1]. With a few Franks he reached Detmold [Note: [Col. 0418D] *Theotwaldi*, in 1; *Theodmali*, in 6; *Theotmallim*, in 7] [Note: [Col. 0418D] Detmold.]. There the Saxons prepared a battle [Note: [Col. 0418D] *pugnam*, “a battle,” in 1, 5, 6, and 7] in a field, where Lord King Charles and the Franks attacked them bravely in their accustomed manner, and the Saxons turned their backs [Note: [Col. 0418D] “and the Saxons turning their backs” is absent in 2]. With the Lord’s help, the Franks were victorious. A very great multitude of Saxons fell there [Note: [Col. 0419C] *maxime*, “very greatly,” in 2], so that only a few escaped by flight [Note: [Col. 0419C] *fuga*, “flight,” in 5 and 7].

From there the aforesaid glorious king came in victory to Paderborn [Note: [Col. 0419C] *Padenbrun*, in 1], where he joined his army. He proceeded to the place where the Saxons had again gathered at the river called the Hase [Note: [Col. 0419D] On whose bank lies Osnabrück.]. There, after battle had again been joined [Note: [Col. 0419D] *ibi*, “there,” is absent in 1 and 7], no smaller number of Saxons fell, and, with the Lord’s help, the Franks were victorious.

The aforesaid lord, proceeding on his march [Note: [Col. 0419D] “the lord king,” in 1 and 7], crossed the river Weser and reached the river Elbe [Note: [Col. 0419D] *Albium*, in 5]. From there the aforesaid great king returned to Francia.

In the same year Lady Berta, the queen, died on the fourth day before the Ides of July. [Note: [Col. 0419B] “And she was buried at Causiacum. But from there she was transferred to Paris and buried beside her husband in the church of Saint Denis the martyr.”]

When Lord King Charles had reached Worms [Note: [Col. 0419D] *Wurmaciam*, in 5; *Warmaciam*, in 7], he took Lady Queen Fastrada [Note: [Col. 0419D] “Lady Fastrada the queen,” in 1; “Lady Fastradana the queen,” in 7] as his wife. He celebrated Christmas in the villa called Heristal [Note: [Col. 0419D] *Haristalh*, in 1], and Easter likewise. And the number of the years changed to

[Col. 0419C]

## 784

Then the Saxons again rebelled according to their accustomed practice [Note: [Col. 0419D] “The Saxons then rebelled again,” in 1; “revolted,” in 5], and part of the Frisians joined them [Note: [Col. 0419D] *Fresonum*, in 5; *Forisonum*, in 6].

Then Lord King Charles proceeded on his march, crossed the Rhine at Lippeham [Note: [Col. 0419D] *Lippiam*, in 1 and 2 and 7; *Lippiaham*, in 5; *Lippiham*, in 6], and entered Saxony, ravaging and laying it waste as he went, until he reached Huculvi [Note: [Col. 0419D] *Huculum*, in 1; *Huculin*, in 7; *Hucului*, in 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, and 9] [Note: [Col. 0419D] The town of Petershagen, formerly Hockeleve, which received its present name and civic rights.].

There, having taken counsel, because the floods of water were exceedingly great [Note: [Col. 0419D] *eo* is absent in 6; one copy reads “because they were not at all great”], he decided to enter through Thuringia [Note: [Col. 0419D] *Thuringiam*, in 1; *Durringiam*, in 6; *Thoringiam*, in 7] from the eastern side against the Ostphalians [Note: [Col. 0419D] *Hostfalaos*, in 5; *Ostualaos*, in 1], while leaving his son Lord Charles with a *scara* against the Westphalians [Note: [Col. 0419D] *Westualos*, in 1; *Wetfalaos*, in 5]. And so it was done [Note: [Col. 0419D] *quod ita*, in 1, 2, and 7; *et quod ita*, in 6].

King Charles proceeded through Thuringia [Note: [Col. 0419D] *Turingiam*, in 1; *Toringam*, in 2; *Durringam*, in 6; *Thoringiam*, in 7] as far as the river Elbe, and from there to Stagnfurt [Note: [Col. 0422C] *Stainfurt*, in 1; *Stagnfrud*, in 2; *Stangfurt*, in 5; *Stagnfurt*, in 6; *Stangfurd*, in 7; *Stagnfurd*, in 8; *Stangford*, in 9] [Note: [Col. 0421D] “Stasfurt on the Bode?” The place, at a ford of some river between the Hercynian Forest and the Elbe, remains to be identified. No other site appears so suitable, since Pippin also seems in 748 to have gone by the same route through Hochseeburg and Stagnfurt to the districts of Scahaningi and Orhaim.] [Col. 0422A] and from there to Scahiningi [Note: [Col. 0422C] *Schalingi*, in 1; *Scainingi*, in 5 and 6; *Scaingi*, in 7; *Scaningi*, in 9].

There, after an assembly had been held [Note: [Col. 0422C] “after the assembly had been held,” in 1, 5, 6, 7, and others], the aforesaid glorious king returned to Francia [Note: [Col. 0422C] *Frantiam*, in 5 and 6]. The Westphalians, however, wished to gather at the Lippe [Note: [Col. 0422C] “at Philippia,” in 6].

When the aforesaid son of Lord King Charles heard this [Note: [Col. 0422C] The expression *auditu co* arose from the form then used for the letter *t*; 2 reads *auditu co*, while 1, 5, 6, and 7 and others read *audito a*], he went to meet them with the *scara* that had been left with him, in the district called Dragini [Note: [Col. 0422C] *Oragmi*, in 1; *Dragani*, in 6], and they joined battle.

With the Lord’s help, Lord Charles, son of the great King Charles, was victorious together with the Franks, and many Saxons were killed. By God’s will he returned unharmed to his father in the city of Worms. There, after taking counsel with the Franks, it was decided that the aforesaid lord king should again march into Saxony during the winter [Note: [Col. 0422C] “in winter,” in 1 and 7]. And so it was done.

He celebrated Christmas near Skidrioburg [Note: [Col. 0422C] *Kidrioburg*, in 1; *Kydrioburg*, in 6; *Hidrioburg*, in 9], in the district of Waizzagau [Note: [Col. 0422C] *Vuazzagawi*, in 1; *Waizzagawi*, in 2 and 3; *Waizzagavi*, in 5; *Wazzagaiwu*, in 6; *Wauzanaga*, in 7; *Waizzgawi*, in 8; *Waisagawi*, in 9], on the river Ambra [Note: [Col. 0422C] *Ambram*, the accusative, in 1], in the villa of Liudihi [Note: [Col. 0422C] *Lutundi*, in 1; *Liudihi*, in 2 and 3; *Liuhidi*, in 5 and 8; *Liuthildi*, in 6; *Luidi*, in 7; *Luichidi*, in 9] [Note: [Col. 0422D] Old Lüde, now deserted, according to Falke, p. 349. He maintains that the existing village of Lüde near Pyrmont was built later; this is supported by the fact that Schieder lies too far from Lüde for it to have stood beside that place.]. ## 785

Then Lord King Charles, proceeding on the aforementioned journey. [Note: “the aforementioned journey” (1); “proceeding on the journey in this manner” (6).] [Note: While he was proceeding, a solar eclipse occurred: “A solar eclipse occurred on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, from the first hour of the day until the fifth hour. He came to Rome and was received with great honor, etc.” (6).] He came to Rome and was received with great honor by the lord apostolic Adrian. [Note: “by the lord” (1, 5, 6, 7); “Hadrian” (7).] He remained there several days with the lord apostolic.

Duke Arichis of Benevento sent his son Romuald with great gifts, asking that, upon the arrival of the aforementioned lord king, he not enter Benevento, since they wished to fulfill all the king’s commands. [Note: “to enter Benevento, since he wished to fulfill all the king’s wishes” (1).] But the apostolic did not at all believe this, nor did the Frankish nobles; and they made an agreement with the aforementioned Lord King Charles that he should come into the Beneventan territories to establish their rights. And so it was done.

When he had reached Capua, Duke Arichis abandoned the city of Benevento and shut himself up in Salerno. [Note: “the Beneventan city” (2); “when he reached Capua, Duke Arichis withdrew” (6).] Terrified by fear, he did not dare to look Lord King Charles in the face in person. Instead, he sent envoys and presented both his sons: Romuald, whom Lord King Charles had with him, and Grimoald, whom the aforementioned Arichis had with him. [Note: “whom the aforementioned Arichis retained in his keeping” (7).] He offered many gifts and other hostages, so that the king might comply with his request. [Note: “might comply with his petition” (1, 6, 7); “might comply” (1).]

Then the lord and glorious King Charles, together with his priests and other nobles, considered that that land should not be destroyed and that its bishoprics and monasteries should not be abandoned. [Note: “that its monasteries should not be laid waste” (1); the words “and that its bishoprics and monasteries should not be abandoned” are absent in (2).] He chose twelve hostages, and a thirteenth, the son of the aforementioned duke, named Grimoald. [Note: “namely, the son of the aforementioned duke” (1).] After accepting the gifts, all the Beneventans swore an oath, both the aforementioned duke and Romuald. [Note: “Romuald” (5, 6).]

And the oft-mentioned most pious king returned and celebrated Easter with the lord apostolic in Rome. [Note: “And the most pious King Charles returned and celebrated Easter at Rome with the lord apostolic. Behold, during the days of the Easter festival a dispute arose between the Roman and Gallican singers. The Gauls said that they sang better and more beautifully than the Romans. The Romans said that they rendered the ecclesiastical melodies with the greatest skill, as they had been taught by Saint Pope Gregory; they said that the Gauls sang corruptly, mangling and destroying the sound melody. This dispute came before Lord King Charles. The Gauls, relying on the protection of Lord King Charles, greatly reproached the Roman singers. The Romans, relying on the authority of their great learning, called them fools, rustics, and ignoramuses, like brute animals, and preferred Saint Gregory’s teaching to their rusticity. When the quarrel could not be settled by either side, the most pious Lord King Charles said to his singers: ‘Tell me openly which is purer and which is better: a living spring, or its streams flowing far away?’ They all answered with one voice that the spring, as the head and source, was purer, whereas its streams, the farther they withdrew from the spring, became increasingly turbid and corrupted by filth and uncleanness. And Lord King Charles said: ‘Return to the spring of Saint Gregory, for you have plainly corrupted the ecclesiastical melody.’ Immediately Lord King Charles asked Pope Adrian for singers who could correct the singing in Francia. He gave him Theodore and Benedict, the most learned singers of the Roman Church, who had been instructed by Saint Gregory; and he also gave him the antiphonaries of Saint Gregory, which he himself had notated in Roman notation. When Lord King Charles returned to Francia, he sent one singer to the city of Metz and another to the city of Soissons, ordering the schoolmasters of all the cities of Francia to hand over their antiphonaries to them for correction and to learn singing from them. The antiphonaries of the Franks were therefore corrected, for each person had corrupted them according to his own discretion, adding or subtracting material; and all the singers of Francia learned the Roman notation, which they now call Frankish notation. The Franks, however, could not perfectly express in song the trembling, quivering, flexible, or sharply articulated sounds, breaking the sounds in their throats with their naturally barbarous voice rather than expressing them. *Vinnolata* voice is gentle, soft, and flexible; *vinnolata* is derived from *vinno*, that is, a curl softly bent. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book III, chapter 19. The greater school of singing remained in the city of Metz; and to the extent that Roman instruction surpasses that of Metz in the art of melody, to that extent the Metz melody surpasses the other schools of Francia. In the same way the aforementioned Roman singers instructed the Frankish singers in the art of organum. Lord King Charles also brought with him from Rome to Francia teachers of grammar and computation, and ordered the study of letters to be spread everywhere. Before Lord King Charles, there had been no study of the liberal arts in Gaul. During those Easter days envoys of Duke Tassilo came to Rome to the most pious Lord King Charles, etc. When these words had been completed, Tassilo’s envoys were released. Then the lord apostolic and the glorious Lord King Charles bade one another farewell; having received the blessing and completed the prayer, he returned gloriously to Francia, bringing with him Roman singers, highly skilled grammarians, and calculators. The same most gentle King Charles reached his wife, the lady Queen Fastrada, in the city of Worms, and there they rejoiced together, giving thanks and praise for God’s mercy.” (11).]

There the envoys of Duke Tassilo arrived, namely Bishop Arnus and Abbot Hunricus, and requested that the apostolic settle the peace between Lord King Charles and Duke Tassilo. [Note: “Hunricus the abbot, so that they might bring the matter before the apostolic” (1).] The lord apostolic strongly intervened, entreating the aforesaid lord king. [Note: “entreating” (6, 7); “beseeching” (1).] The lord king himself replied to the apostolic that he had wanted and sought this for a long time but had been unable to find it. [Note: “had been unable to” (1, 6, 7).] He said that he wanted it done immediately.

The aforesaid lord king wished to establish peace with those envoys in the presence of the lord apostolic. But the aforementioned envoys refused, saying that they would not have dared to make any firm agreement on their side. [Note: “the envoys refused, saying that …” (7).] When the apostolic learned of the instability—or falsehood—of their position, he immediately placed their duke and his supporters under anathema if he failed to fulfill the oaths that he had promised to King Pippin and likewise to King Charles. [Note: “the aforementioned duke and his supporters were struck with anathema” (1).]

He adjured the aforementioned envoys to warn Tassilo not to act otherwise, but to be obedient in every respect to Lord King Charles, his sons, and the Frankish people, lest bloodshed or injury to that land should occur. [Note: “lest bloodshed should come about” (1, 7); “lest injury to that land should occur.”] If the duke, with hardened heart, should refuse to obey the words of the apostolic, then Lord King Charles and his army would be released from all danger of sin; and whatever happened in that land—through fires, murders, or any kind of evil—would fall upon Tassilo and his supporters, while Lord King Charles and the Franks would thereafter remain innocent of every fault. [Note: “whatever happened in that land” (1, 5, 6, 7); “whatever might happen” (7); “fires” is supported by (2); “Tassilo” is spelled “Thassilo” in (1, 7); “his supporters” appears as “his supporters” in (6).]

When these words had been completed, Tassilo’s envoys were released. Then the lord apostolic and the glorious Lord King Charles bade one another farewell; having received the blessing and completed the prayer, the aforementioned most excellent king returned to Francia.

The same most gentle king reached his wife, the lady Queen Fastrada, in the city of Worms. There they rejoiced and made each other happy, praising together the mercy of God. [Note: “mercy” appears as “mercy” in (1, 5, 6, 7); the word “city” is added in the note.]

The aforementioned lord king then assembled a synod in that same city and announced to his priests and other nobles how everything had proceeded on his journey. When he had come to this place and explained everything concerning Tassilo’s side, just as it had happened, [Note: “when he had reached the place” (1); “just as it had been done” (1, 5, 6, 7); “as he recounts” (2), a reading that sufficiently indicates the correct text.] the same king then decided to send envoys and ordered Tassilo to fulfill everything according to the command of the apostolic and according to justice. [Note: “to hasten to fulfill it” (7).] They had promised under oath to be obedient and faithful in every respect to Lord King Charles, his sons, and the Franks, and to come into his presence. But Tassilo refused and scorned to come. [Note: After “scorned to come,” one leaf of manuscript 2 is missing; the next surviving text begins, “Then again …” (7).]

Then Lord King Charles, together with the Franks, seeing that his cause was just, began to proceed with his army toward Baioaria. He himself came to the place called Lechfeld, above the city of Augsburg. [Note: “to the place called Lechfeld” (1); “to the place called Lechfel” (7).] [Note: “Das Lechfeld near Augsburg.”] He ordered another army to be assembled, namely Franks, Austrasians, Thuringians, and Saxons, and to join him on the Danube at a place called Faringa. [Note: “Phoring, or Pförring, between Ingolstadt.”]

He ordered a third army to be assembled in the Italian territories, so that King Pippin might come with his army as far as Trento and remain there, while sending his army forward in full strength as far as Bolzano. [Note: “as far as … as far as” is absent in (2); “Trento, Trident”; “Bolzano, or Bozen, a celebrated town likewise in the county of Tyrol.”]

Then, perceiving that he was surrounded on every side, and seeing that all the Baioarians were more faithful to Lord King Charles than to him, and that they had recognized the justice of the aforementioned lord king and preferred to support justice rather than oppose it, Tassilo, hemmed in on every side, came in person, surrendering himself into the hands of Lord King Charles as his vassal, returning to him the duchy entrusted to him by King Pippin, and acknowledging that he had sinned and acted wrongly in every respect. [Note: “surrendering himself into the hands” (1, 5, 7); “into his hands as a servant” (9b); “and he acknowledged” (1, 7).]

Then, renewing his oaths, he gave twelve chosen hostages and a thirteenth, his son Theodo. [Note: “twelve” is absent in (6).] After receiving the hostages and the oaths, the aforesaid glorious king returned to Francia. He celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at the estate called Ingelheim, and likewise Easter. And the number of the years changed to

## 788

Then Lord King Charles assembled a synod at the aforementioned estate of Ingelheim. Tassilo came there by order of the lord king, like his other vassals. [Note: “vassals” (1).] The faithful Baioarians began to say that Tassilo had not kept his faith, but had subsequently appeared deceitful, after giving his son together with the other hostages and the oaths, at the urging of his wife Liutberga. [Note: “Liutburga” (1).]

Tassilo could not deny this either, but confessed that he had afterward sent [envoys; object unstated] to the Avars, had incited the vassals of the aforementioned lord king against him, and had plotted against their lives. When his own men swore their oaths, he ordered them to hold something else in mind and to swear deceitfully. And what is more, he confessed that he had said that, even if he had ten sons, he would have wished to lose them all rather than let the agreements remain in such a condition or permit them to stand firm as he had sworn. [Note: “as he had sworn” (2, 3, 5, 6); “as had been agreed” (1); “as he swore” (7).] He also said that he would rather be dead than live in this manner. [Note: “that it was better to be dead” (6); “the woman [said] that he was dead” (2); “that he would die” (7).]

When all these matters had been established, the Franks, Baioarians, Lombards, and Saxons, together with those gathered from all the provinces for the same synod, recalling his earlier crimes and how he had abandoned King Pippin in the army—an act called *harisliz* in the German language [Note: “harislig” (1); “haristalliz” (2, 3); “herisliz” (6); “harislit” (7)]—seem to have judged that the same Tassilo should be put to death.

But when all cried out with one voice that a capital sentence should be carried out against him, the aforementioned most pious Lord King Charles, moved by mercy, out of love for God and because Tassilo was his kinsman, prevailed upon God’s faithful and his own faithful that he should not die. [Note: “out of love” (1); “because he was his kinsman” (1, 5, 6, 7); “restrained” appears as “prevailed” in (1, 5, 6).]

The aforementioned Tassilo was asked by the most clement lord king what he wished to do. He requested permission to have himself tonsured, enter a monastery, and perform penance for such great sins, in order to save his soul. His son Theodo was likewise judged, tonsured, and sent into a monastery. A few Baioarians who wished to persist in opposition to Lord King Charles were sent into exile. [Note: “who wished” (5, 6, 7).]

In the same year a battle was fought between the Greeks and the Lombards: on one side under a duke named Hildebrand of Spoleto, and on the other under Duke Grimoald, whom Lord King Charles had appointed duke over the Beneventans. Wineghisus was sent with a few Franks to observe everything they did. [Note: “Winegisus” (1); absent in (2); “Winechisus” (7); “together” is absent in (7).] With the Lord’s help, victory was won by the Franks and the aforementioned Lombards.

Likewise, another battle was fought between the Avars, at a place whose name is [lacuna], and the Franks who were living in Italy. [Note: “at a place whose name is …” is absent in (2); “the Franks” appears as *francos* in (7); “who are seen to dwell in Italy” (1); “who occupied Italy” (7).] With the Lord’s help, the Franks won the victory, and the Avars returned in disgrace, fleeing without victory.

A third battle was fought between the Baioarians and the Avars in the field of Ibose. [Note: “Ibose” (6, 8); “Hibose” (7).] [Note: “A town of Austria on the Danube, above Pöchlarn, and the monastery of Melk.”] There were sent there by Lord King Charles Grahamannus and Audacrus, together with some Franks. With the Lord’s help, victory belonged to the Franks and Baioarians.

All these events were plotted through deceit by the aforementioned Duke Tassilo and his wicked wife Liutberga, hateful to God. [Note: “Tassilo together with his evil wife Liutberga” (1); “they plotted and carried them out” (7).]

A fourth battle was fought by the Avars, who wished to take revenge against the Baioarians. Envoys of Lord King Charles were likewise sent there, and, with the Lord’s protection, victory came to the Christians. When the Avars began to flee, a great slaughter took place there as they were killed; others lost their lives by drowning in the Danube River. [Note: “many dead bodies” (1, 5, 7); “and they drowned others in the Danube” (1). The material added by the remaining manuscripts is not recognized by the Lorsch manuscript (1). Since its continuation consists almost entirely of the same words as the Chronicle of Moissac for the years 789, 790, 791, 792, and part of 793, whose author followed it, we have thought it should be attached to them.]

## Continuation of the Lorsch Annals up to the Year 829, by Einhard

After all these events, Lord King Charles himself reached Regensburg. There he arranged the boundaries and marches of the Baioarians, so that, with the Lord’s protection, they might be safe against the aforementioned Avars.

Returning from there, he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at the palace of Aachen, and likewise Easter. And the number of the years changed to

## 789

From there he set out on a journey toward the territories of the Slavs, whose name is Wiltze, with the Lord’s help. [Note: “Sclavinia” (5); “whose name” (7); “Wiltze” (5, 6, 7).] Together with the counsel of the Franks and Saxons, he proceeded, crossing the Rhine at Cologne and passing through Saxony. He reached the Elbe River, and there built two bridges, at one of which he constructed, on both ends, a wooden-and-earthen fortress. [Note: “a fortress of wood and earth”; one witness reads “of linen.”] From there he advanced farther and, by the Lord’s favor, brought the aforementioned Slavs under his dominion.

Franks and Saxons were with him in the same army. The Frisians, traveling by ship along the River Havel, joined him there with certain Franks. [Note: “Havel” (7); “the Havel.”] Slavs were also with him, whose names were the Sorabi, [Note: “Sorabi” (7); “Sorabi” (2); “Sorabi.”] and the Abotriti, whose prince was Witzan. [Note: “Wintzan” (5); “Wizzan” (7).] There, having received hostages and many oaths, and under the Lord’s guidance, he reached Francia.

He celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Worms, and likewise Easter. [Note: “Worms, Easter” (5); “Worms, Easter” (6); “Worms” (7); “likewise Easter” is absent in (2).] And the number of the years changed to

## 790

[Note: At the beginning of this year King Charles sent his first-born son Charles beyond the Seine, giving him the duchy of Maine. In the summer of that same year he returned to his father. The king held an assembly of the Franks in the city of Worms and arranged what seemed useful for his kingdom. In that year, etc. (9b).]

In the following year he made no expedition, but again celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in the aforesaid city, and likewise Easter. And the number of the years changed to

## 791

From there he set out on a journey toward Baioaria and reached Regensburg. [Note: “Regensburg” (5); “Regensburg” (6); “reached” is absent in (7).] There he joined his army. After the council of the Franks, Saxons, and Frisians had been held there, they decided to undertake an expedition because of the excessive and intolerable wickedness that the Avars had committed against the holy Church and the Christian people, since they had been unable to obtain justice through envoys. [Note: “the expedition was resolved upon” (7); “to undertake a journey,” that is, “a journey was to be undertaken.”]

With God’s help they proceeded into the aforementioned territories of the Avars. As they hurried toward the River Enns, [Note: “the Enns.”] they arranged there to perform litanies for three days. Celebrating the solemnities of the Mass, they sought God’s comfort for the safety of the army, for the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, and for victory and vengeance against the Avars. [Note: “to celebrate” (5, 6); “they awaited assistance” (6).]

The aforementioned prince proceeded from the southern side of the Danube. The Saxons, together with certain Franks and a very large number of Frisians, likewise proceeded from the northern side of the Danube. [Note: “from the north” (5, 6, 7); “a very large number of Frisians” (9b).] They reached the places where the aforementioned Avars had prepared their fortifications.

From the southern side of the Danube they went toward Cumeoberg. [Note: “Cummeoberg” (7); “Comeoberg” (9).]

[Note: An ancient city mentioned several times in the *Life of Saint Severinus*, now entirely destroyed. Its site and the mountain Cumeoberg are disputed. The village now called Kaumberg lies at least five German miles from the Danube in a straight line and stands among the mountains. It must therefore be supposed either that the military road of that age crossed the mountains—as the broad road now does from the Field of Lilies (Lilienfeld) through Kaumberg to Heiligenkreuz—or that the name Cumeoberg once extended farther, as far as the outermost mountains on the bank of the Danube. This view is more consistent both with our passage and with the ancient course of the military road following the Danube. It is confirmed by a charter of King Louis of Germany from the year 836, published by the illustrious Franz Ulrich Kopp in *Tachygraphia*, vol. I, pp. 394–395, and by the configuration of the places themselves, which I explored, together with that mountain road, in 1821. Continuous mountains extend from the borders of Styria all the way to the Danube. Only a narrow road remains open toward the river, with Greifenstein Castle looming above it; defended by fortifications either on the last mountain or near Königsstädten—which I identify with Commagenis—it blocks travelers from passing through. The Fulda Annals likewise record, under the year 884, a meeting between Emperor Charles and Zwentibold at Mount Comianus, that is, Cumeoberg, near Tulln. This does not fit the village of Kaumberg, separated by mountains from the source of the Tulln, but fits Königsstädten very well.]

On the other bank they went to a place called Kamp, because that is the name of the river which flows there into the Danube. [Note: “Kampa” (6).] [Note: The Kamp, rising in the mountains of Bohemia, flows past Zwettl and joins the Danube somewhat below Krems.]

When the Avars saw armies occupying both banks and ships coming through the middle of the river, terror from the Lord came upon them. They abandoned the fortified places mentioned above and left behind their fortifications and engines. They fled, and, with Christ leading his people, both armies were brought in without injury. [Note: “The aforementioned army entered Pannonia without injury” (9b).]

The aforementioned army proceeded in this way as far as the river called the Rába. [Note: “whose name is” (5, 7).] From there both armies returned from the two banks to their own regions, glorifying God for so great a victory.

Lord King Charles celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Regensburg, and likewise Easter. [Note: After “celebrated,” a leaf is missing in manuscript 2; the text resumes with the year 794, beginning in the middle of a word.] And the number of the years changed to

## 792

[Note: The passage concerning the conspiracy discovered is absent from (7, 8, 9, 9b, 10, and 11). In Einhard’s Annals and the Fulda Annals (5, 6, and 12), it follows the account of the heresy. Where it was placed in manuscript 2 cannot be known, since a leaf has been cut out. Chesnius was the first to receive it into the text from manuscript 3 and to place it before the entire narrative, wrongly in my opinion. This, indeed, caused him to insert the word “Regensburg” into the following sentence and to alter other things as well.]

The Felician heresy was first condemned there. [Note: “It was first heard and first condemned at Regensburg” (3).] Anghilbertus brought him into the presence of Adrian the apostolic, and after making his confession he again renounced his heresy. [Note: “Anghilbertus” (6); “Angilbertus” (7); “renounced him” (6).]

A conspiracy against the king, made by his son Pippin, was discovered and suppressed. No military expedition was undertaken in that year. A bridge was built over vessels crossing the river, fastened with anchors and ropes so that it could be joined and dismantled. Lord King Charles celebrated the Nativity of the Lord there, and Easter was likewise celebrated. [Note: “He celebrated the Nativity of the Lord and Easter there, King Charles” (7).] And the number of the years changed to

## 793

In the autumn the king traveled by ship from Regensburg as far as the great trench between the Altmühl and the Rednitz. [Note: “Altmühl” (6); “Altmühl” (7); “the Altmühl.”] There the apostolic envoys appeared with great gifts. There an envoy announced that the Saxons had again broken faith.

From there, traveling by ship along the Rednitz and then the Main, he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Saint Kilian’s in Würzburg. [Note: “Würzburg” (5, 6, 7, 8).] And the number of the years changed to

Easter was celebrated at Franconofurt [Note: [Col. 0443D] *fracnofurd* 5; *franchenfurd* 6; *francnofurt* 7], and there a great synod of the bishops of Gaul, Germany, and Italy [Note: [Col. 0443D] Manuscript 6 has *Italiorum* (“of the Italians”) for the printed *Italiae* (“of Italy”).] was assembled [Note: [Col. 0443D] *est* is absent in 6] in the presence of the aforesaid prince and of the envoys of the lord apostolic Adrian, whose names are these: the bishops Theophylact and Stephen [Note: [Col. 0443D] *sthefanus* 2]. There the Felician heresy [Note: [Col. 0443D] *eresis* 2] was condemned for the third time [Note: [Col. 0443D] *condempnata* 5, 6]; they committed that condemnation [Note: [Col. 0443D] *dampnationem* 6] to writing in a book on the authority of the holy Fathers, and all the priests signed that book with their own hands [Note: [Col. 0443D] Manuscript 5 has *conscripserunt* (“they wrote it down”) for the printed singular *conscripsit* (“he wrote it down”).]. There Queen Fastrada [Note: [Col. 0443D] *fastradana* 6; *fastradane* 7] died and was honorably buried at Saint Alban [Note: [Col. 0443D] The epitaph that is seen there today is more recent and will be included among our inscriptions]. The pseudo-synod of the Greeks [Note: [Col. 0443D] *pseudasinodus* 2], which they falsely called the seventh and held in favor of venerating images [Note: [Col. 0443D] Manuscripts 2, 5, and 6 have *vocabant pro* (“they called [it] in favor of”) for the printed *vocabant, quam pro* (“which they called … in favor of”).], was rejected by the pontiffs.

From there the army was moved into the regions of Saxony [Col. 0443D] in two divisions. In one [Note: [Col. 0443D] Manuscript 7 has *unam* (“one,” accusative) for the printed *una* (“in one”).] was the most glorious lord King Charles himself [Note: [Col. 0443D] *Fuit ipse* (“he himself was”) is absent in manuscript 7.]; into the other he sent his most noble son, the lord Charles [Note: [Col. 0443D] Manuscript 2 has *alium* (“the other,” masculine) for the printed *aliam* (“the other,” feminine, referring to the division).], by way of Cologne [Col. 0446A]. The Saxons, however, gathering in the field called Sinitfelt [Note: [Col. 0446D] *sinistfelt* 5, 9; *sinitsfelt* 6; *sinasifelt* 7; *sinitfelt* 2, 8] and preparing themselves as though for battle, when they heard that they were surrounded from two sides, God scattered their plans. Although deceitfully, they promised that they would be Christians [Note: [Col. 0446D] Manuscripts 5 and 7 read *fraudulenter Christianos* (“deceitfully, Christians”) rather than the printed promise *fraudulenter se Christianos* (“deceitfully, that they would be Christians”).] and faithful [Note: [Col. 0446D] Manuscript 2 has singular *fidele* (“faithful”) for printed plural *fideles*.] to the lord king [Note: [Col. 0446D] Manuscripts 2 and 6 have ablative *rege* (“king”) for dative *regi* (“to the king”).]. The king returned to the palace called Aquis [Note: [Col. 0446D] *Aquisgrani* in manuscript 7.] [Note: [Col. 0446D] Manuscript 2 has present *reddit* (“returns”) for printed *rediit* (“returned”).], and there celebrated Christmas and Easter. And the reckoning of the years changed to

## 795

In this year the king also came to the place called Cuffinstang [Note: [Col. 0446D] *cussinstang* in 5; *chusstagn* in 6; *cuffinstain* in 8], and into the suburb [Note: [Col. 0446D] et in (“and into”), 2; for suburbium (“suburb,” accusative), 7 has suburbio (ablative)] of the city of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0446D] *mogontiacensis* 5, 6; *moguntiacensis* 7], and held his assembly there. When he heard that the Saxons, as usual, had rendered void the promise they had made concerning embracing Christianity and maintaining faith toward the king [Note: [Col. 0446D] For habenda (“to be maintained,” ablative feminine), 2 has habendi (genitive); for regis (“of the king”), 7 has regi (“to the king”); for fecerant (“they had made”), 2 has fecebant (“they were making,” nonstandard spelling).], he entered Saxony with an army and reached the river Elbe, at the place called Hliuni [Note: [Col. 0446D] *libum* 5; *lunis* 7] [Note: [Col. 0446D] Lüne near Lüneburg], where Witzin [Note: [Col. 0446D] *wizzin* 5, 6; *wizin* 7], king of the Abodrites [Note: [Col. 0446D] *abadritorum* 5], had then been killed by the Saxons. There also came envoys of Tudun, who held great power among the Avars and in their kingdom [Note: [Col. 0446D] Manuscript 2 has present *habeat* (“he may have”) for printed imperfect *habebat* (“he held”).]. They said that this same Tudun [Note: [Col. 0446D] *isdem* 7; *Tudun* is a title, not a personal name, as our author also indicates. Cf. *Historia miscella*, p. 144], together with his land and people, wished to surrender to the king [Note: [Col. 0446D] Manuscript 2 has ablative *rege* (“king”) for dative *regi* (“to the king”).] and to receive the Christian faith through his direction [Note: [Col. 0446D] Manuscripts 2 and 6 have accusative *ordinationem* (“direction”) for ablative *ordinatione* (“through his direction”); manuscript 7 punctuates *suscipere. Rex* (“to receive. The king …”).].

But after afflicting the Saxons to a great extent, laying waste their land [Note: [Col. 0446D] *Eorum* (“their”) is absent in manuscript 7.], and receiving their hostages, the king returned to Gaul. At the palace called Aquis [Note: [Col. 0446D] *Aquisgrani* in manuscript 7; manuscripts 2, 6, and 7 read *qui vocatur* (“which is called”) for printed neuter *quod vocatur*.] he celebrated Christmas [Col. 0447A] and likewise Easter. And the reckoning of the years changed to

## 796

Pope Adrian [Note: [Col. 0447D] *Hadrianus* 7] died, and Leo, as soon as he succeeded to his place [Note: [Col. 0447D] Manuscript 2 has *ut ad locum* (“as soon as [he came] to the place”) for printed *ut in locum* (“as soon as [he succeeded] to the place”).], sent envoys with gifts to the king. He also sent him the keys of the confession [Note: [Col. 0447D] Manuscript 2 has plural *confessiones* for singular *confessionis*, the “confession” or shrine of Saint Peter.] of Saint Peter and the banner of the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0447D] *rome* 2].

Duke Henry [Note: [Col. 0447D] *Heirichus* 5; *heinricus* 6], duke of Friuli [Note: [Col. 0447D] *furinlensis* 6; *foroiuliensis* 7], also sent his men, together with Wonomyro [Note: [Col. 0447D] *uunomyro* 5; *wonomiro* 7], a Slav, into Pannonia [Note: [Col. 0447D] Manuscript 2 has the corrupt *Sclavo cum Pannonias* (“a Slav with Pannonias”) for the printed *Sclavo in Pannonias* (“a Slav into Pannonia”).]. He plundered the *hring* [Note: [Col. 0447D] *hrigun* 7; *hirigum*, “prince of the Avars,” 7b] of the Avar people, which had remained peaceful for a long time, while its princes were exhausted by civil war among themselves—Chagan [Note: [Col. 0447D] *clagan* 2] or Jugurro [Note: [Col. 0447D] *iuguro* 5, 6], having been subjected to internal slaughter [Note: [Col. 0447D] Manuscript 6 has the anomalous *ac dictis* (“and the things said”) for printed *ac interfectis* (“and killed”).] and killed by his own men—and he sent to the lord king Charles at the palace of Aquis the treasure of the ancient kings, accumulated over the long span of many centuries [Note: [Col. 0447D] Manuscript 2 has the corrupt reading *prolixitate quetum* at “accumulated over the long span.”]. Having received it and completed thanksgiving to God, the giver of all good things [Note: [Col. 0447D] Manuscript 5 has singular *peracto* (“having been completed”); manuscript 7 has plural *peractis … actionibus* (“the acts … having been completed”) for the printed phrase about completed thanksgiving.], that most prudent and most generous man, the steward of God, sent a large part of it to Rome, to the thresholds of the apostles, through Angilbert [Note: [Col. 0447D] *anghibertum* 6], his beloved abbot; he distributed the remaining part to his nobles, clergy and laymen, and his other faithful.

In the same year Tudun [Note: [Col. 0447D] *thudun* 2], in accordance with his promise, came to the king with a large part of the Avars [Note: [Col. 0447D] *avarum* 5, 6]. He surrendered himself, his people, and his homeland to the king; [Note: [Col. 0447D] manuscript 7 has *ipseque et* (“and he also”) for printed *ipse* (“he”)] he and the people were baptized, and, honorably presented with gifts, returned.

The king gathered his armies and entered Saxony, sending his son Pippin, king of Italy, into Pannonia with his army [Note: [Col. 0447D] *Suo* (“his”) is absent in manuscripts 5, 6, and 7; manuscript 7 has finite *misit* (“he sent”) for participial *mittens* (“sending”).]. Reports from him came to the king in that same Saxony: one said that the Kagan, whom the Avars had appointed for themselves after the killing of the former rulers, had come to meet him with the other nobles [Note: [Col. 0447D] manuscript 2 spells *occurrisse* (“had come to meet”) as *hoccurrisse*]; another said that Pippin was sitting with his army in the *hring* [Note: [Col. 0447D] *ringo* 7]. The lord king, having traversed Saxony, returned to Gaul with his army intact [Col. 0447D] [Note: [Col. 0447D] manuscript 2 has present *recipit* (“returns/receives himself”) for printed *recepit*] [Note: [Col. 0447D] Manuscript 2 has *recepit* (“he received”) for printed *rediit* (“he returned”).], and at the palace of Aquis, joyfully saw his son Pippin returning from Pannonia and bringing the part of the treasure that had remained [Col. 0450A] [Note: [Col. 0447D] Manuscript 2 has plural *remanserant* (“had remained”) for printed singular *remanserat* (“had remained,” agreeing with the part).]. There [Note: [Col. 0450D] *ibidem* (“in that same place”) in manuscripts 5, 6, and 7] he celebrated Christmas and Easter. And the reckoning of the years changed to

## 797

The city of Barcelona [Note: [Col. 0450D] *Parcinona* in manuscript 6; *Barzinona* in 7] in Hispania, which had defected from us some time previously, was restored to us through its governor Zatus [Note: [Col. 0450D] Manuscript 2 has the corrupt *per iatim in prefectum* at the phrase “through its governor.”]. For he came to the palace and commended himself and the city to the lord king [Note: [Col. 0450D] Manuscript 2 has ablative *rege* for dative *regi* (“to the king”) and the corrupt *cum vitate commandavit* at “commended himself and the city.”].

An expedition was made into Saxony [Note: [Col. 0450D] manuscript 7 has ablative *expeditione* (“on an expedition”) for nominative *expeditio* (“an expedition”)], and passage was forced as far as the ocean, across all the marshes and trackless places [Col. 0450B] [Note: [Col. 0450D] Manuscript 2 has *plaudes* for printed *paludes* (“marshes”).]. The king returned [Note: [Col. 0450D] manuscript 5 makes the verb explicit as *regressus est* (“returned”)] from Haduloha [Note: [Col. 0450D] *baduloha* 5; *hadulocha* 6; *hadulobar* 7; *haduloa* 9]—this is the name of the place where the ocean washes Saxony [Note: [Col. 0450D] Manuscript 7 has *adluit* (“washes against”) for printed *alluit* (“washes”).]—and, having received the whole Saxon people into submission through hostages, crossed the Rhine and returned to Gaul. At the palace of Aquis he received Abdallah the Saracen, son of Ibn-Mauga [Note: [Col. 0450D] *ibinmaugae* 2, 3, 5, 6; *ibimaugae* 7], a king who, driven from his kingdom by his brother [Note: [Col. 0450D] Manuscript 2 adds *est in* (“is in”) in the clause concerning his brother.], was living in exile in Mauretania, since he had commended himself to him [Note: [Col. 0450D] Manuscript 2 has *ipsorum* (“of them”) for printed *ipsum* (“him”); manuscript 6 has accusative participle *commendantem* (“commending”) for *commendasset* (“had commended”).].

There also came the envoy of Nicetas, who then governed Sicily, named Theoctistus [Note: [Col. 0450D] *theoctis* 5], bearing a letter from the emperor. The king received him magnificently and dismissed him after a few days. In the middle of November he entered Saxony with the army for winter quarters. Having pitched camp beside the river Weser [Note: [Col. 0450D] *wisuram* 5, 6], he ordered the camp to be called Heristelli [Note: [Col. 0450D] Herstelle, or so called today; it lies below Karlshafen and above Höxter]. Envoys of the Avar people [Note: [Col. 0450D] *avarorum* 5, 6, 7] came there with great gifts [Col. 0450C].

From there he caused Abdallah the Saracen, with his son Illudowic [Note: [Col. 0450D] *luduwicho* 5; *ludwico* 6], to return to Hispania, and sent his son Pippin to Italy [Note: [Col. 0450D] Manuscripts 5, 6, and 7 have *ad Italam* (“to the Italian [land],” corrupt or elliptical) for *ad Italiam* (“to Italy”).]. He himself spent the whole winter there arranging Saxony; there he celebrated Christmas, and there Easter [Note: [Col. 0450D] Manuscript 7 reads “he celebrated the Lord’s [Nativity] and Easter.”]. And the reckoning of the years changed to

## 798

There also came an envoy of King Alfonso of Galicia and Asturias [Note: [Col. 0451C] *austriae* 2, 5; *austuriae* 6], named Froia [Note: [Col. 0451C] *flora* 2; *frola* 3, 5; *flola* 6; *froia* 7, 9], presenting a tent of extraordinary beauty.

But [Note: [Col. 0451C] Sed (“but”) is absent in 7] at that very time of Easter [Note: [Col. 0451C] For printed *ipso* (“that very”), manuscript 2 has *ipsa*. The latter form is anomalous beside neuter *tempore* and could be feminine nominative or ablative, or neuter plural; the intended construction is uncertain.] the Nordliudi [Note: [Col. 0451C] *noridluidi* 3; *nordludi* 6; *nurliudi* 7], who were settled beyond the Elbe, stirred up a revolt and seized the royal envoys who were then staying among them to administer justice [Note: [Col. 0451C] Manuscript 7 has *apud regem* (“with the king”) at the phrase about administering justice among them.]. They immediately slaughtered some of them [Note: [Col. 0451C] Manuscript 7 adds *et quosdam* (“and some”) before the slaughtered envoys.], while [Note: [Col. 0451C] manuscript 7 reads *ceteri vero* (“the others, however”) for printed accusative *ceteros* (“the rest”)] keeping the rest for ransom; some of these escaped, and the others were ransomed.

The king gathered an army at Haristallium [Note: [Col. 0451C] *haristalli* 6; *heristallio* 7] and proceeded to the place called Minda [Note: [Col. 0451C] *mimda* 5; *munda* 6] [Note: [Col. 0451D] Minden]. After taking counsel, he took up arms against the deserters [Note: [Col. 0451C] Manuscripts 5 and 7 have *inde in* (“from there against”) at the transition to taking up arms.] and traversed all Saxony between the Elbe and Weser, laying it waste [Note: [Col. 0451D] Manuscript 7 has gerundive *populandam* (“to be laid waste”) for printed participle *populando* (“laying waste”).].

The Nordliudi [Note: [Col. 0451D] Manuscript 7 reads *Nordliudi autem* (“the Nordliudi, however”).], engaging in battle against Thrasucon [Note: [Col. 0451D] *tarsochonem* 5; *thrasuchorem* 6; *trasuconem* 7], duke of the Abodrites, and Eburisus [Note: [Col. 0451D] *eborisum* 5, 6, 7] [Note: [Col. 0451D] Our form is *Ebers*, *Evers*], our envoy, were defeated in battle. Four thousand of them were killed at the site of the battle. The remainder who fled and escaped, although many of those too had fallen [Note: [Col. 0451D] Manuscript 2 has the corrupt *cecidissem de pauci* at “although many of those too had fallen.”], negotiated terms of peace.

The king received hostages, including those whom they identified as the most treacherous of the Saxon leaders, and returned to Francia. Proceeding to the palace at Aquisgrani [Note: [Col. 0451D] *aquisgrani* 7], he received the embassy of the Greeks sent from Constantinople. The envoys were Michael, formerly patrician of Phrygia [Col. 0451C] [Note: [Col. 0451D] *phrigiae* 7], and the presbyter Theophilus, bearing a letter from the empress Irene [Note: [Col. 0451D] *erene* 2]. Her son, the emperor Constantine, had been seized and blinded by his own people in the preceding year [Note: [Col. 0451D] Manuscript 7 has *superiori* (“preceding”) for printed *superiore* in the phrase “preceding year.”]. This embassy, however, concerned peace alone.

After dismissing them, he also released with them Sisinnius [Note: [Col. 0451D] *sisinnum* 5], the brother [Note: [Col. 0451D] *fremen* 5] of Tarasius [Note: [Col. 0451D] *trasii* 3], bishop of Constantinople, who had long before been captured in battle in Italy.

In this year the star called Mars [Note: [Col. 0451D] *sydus* 7] could nowhere be seen in the whole sky, from July of the preceding year until July of this year. The Balearic Islands were plundered by the Moors and Saracens.

King Alfonso of Galicia [Note: [Col. 0454D] *gallatiae* 5; *gallaciae* 6] and Asturias [Note: [Col. 0454D] *austrie* 2], after plundering Lisbon [Note: [Col. 0454D] *olysipona* 7], the farthest city of Hispania, sent to the lord king during the winter, through his envoys Froia and Basiliscus [Note: [Col. 0454D] Manuscript 5 has *Basilicum*, an accusative form of the envoy’s name Basiliscus.], the tokens of his victory: cuirasses, mules [Note: [Col. 0454D] Manuscript 5 has *multos* (“many”) for printed *mulos* (“mules”).], and captive Moors [Note: [Col. 0454D] Manuscript 7 adds *rege Carolo* (“to King Charles”) after the captive Moors.]. Thus, in this palace, both Christmas [Note: [Col. 0454D] Manuscripts 2 and 6 have *Natalem* (“Christmas”) without printed *Domini* (“of the Lord”); *et* (“and”) is absent in manuscript 7.] and Easter [Note: [Col. 0454D] Manuscript 7 reads *Pascha similiter a* (“Easter likewise by …”).] were celebrated by the lord king. And the reckoning of the years changed to

## 799

The Romans seized Pope Leo during the greater litany, blinded him, and cut out his tongue [Note: [Col. 0454D] “They cut off his tongue” 7]. Placed in custody [Note: [Col. 0454D] Manuscripts 2 and 6 have accusative *custodiam* (“custody”) for ablative *custodia* (“in custody”).], he escaped by night [Note: [Col. 0454D] Manuscripts 5, 6, and 7 have *noctu* (“by night”) for printed *nocte*.] over a wall. He came to the envoys of the lord king who were then at the basilica of Saint Peter—namely, Wirundus, the abbot [Note: [Col. 0454D] of Stavelot], and Winigisus, duke of Spoleto [Note: [Col. 0454D] *winichisum spolitanum* 7]—and was taken to Spoleto [Col. 0454C] [Note: [Col. 0454D] *spoletum* 7].

The lord king set out for Saxony, crossed the Rhine at the Lippe [Note: [Col. 0454D] The words from *Rhenum* (“Rhine”) through *et* (“and”) are absent in manuscript 2; manuscript 6 has *Lippeham* for Lippe.], and pitched camp at the place called Paderborn [Note: [Col. 0454D] *paderbrunno* 2; *padabrunno* 7]. From there, having divided the army, he sent his son Charles with half of it to meet the Slavs and to receive [Note: [Col. 0454D] For Sclavorum, adque recipiendos (“of the Slavs, and to receive”), 2 has sclavorum que recipendos (“of the Slavs and to receive,” with altered conjunction and spelling); 5, 6, 7 have scl. et ad rec. (“of the Slavs, and to receive,” abbreviated by the editor)] the Saxons who had come from the Nordliudi [Note: [Col. 0454D] *nortliudis* 7] at Bardengauwi [Note: [Col. 0454D] *bardingauwi* 5; *bardingawini* 6; *bardingauni* 7]. He himself kept the other half with him and received Pope Leo at the same place with the greatest honor.

There, while awaiting the return of his son Charles [Note: [Col. 0454D] Manuscript 5 has present participle *exspectans* (“awaiting”) for printed *exspectando* (“while awaiting”).], he dismissed Pope Leo with the same honor with which he had received him. Leo immediately set out for Rome, and the king returned to his palace at Aquisgrani. During the same expedition an envoy of Michael, governor of Sicily, named Daniel [Note: [Col. 0454D] *daniel* 2], came to the lord king and was again dismissed from there with great honor [Col. 0455A] [Note: [Col. 0454D] Manuscripts 5, 6, and 7 have *atque* (“and”) at the dismissal.].

In the same year the people of the Avars [Note: [Col. 0455D] *avarorum* 7] defected from the faith they had promised. Duke Eric of Friuli [Note: [Col. 0455D] *heiricus dux foroiuliensis* 7; *foroiuliensis* 5, 6], after accomplishing so many successful deeds, was ambushed and overwhelmed by the townsmen near Tarsatica [Note: [Col. 0455D] Tersatto, for Fiume (Fiume of Saint Vitus)]. Count Gerold [Note: [Col. 0455D] *geraldus* 7], governor of Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0455D] Manuscript 5 has *comis* for *comes* (“count”).], fell in battle against the Avars [Note: [Col. 0455D] Manuscript 2 has the corrupt *ceciditatem insule*; manuscripts 5, 6, and 7 read *cecidit insulae* (“he fell, of the island”) at the statement that Gerold fell in battle.] [Note: [Col. 0455C] “He fell and was buried at Reichenau. Concerning him it is read in the *Vision of Wettin* that he is numbered among the martyrs.” 9b].

The Balearic Islands, which had been plundered by the Moors and Saracens in the preceding year, sought and received aid from our people, surrendered to us, and, with God’s help, were defended by our people against the incursions of the raiders. The standards of the Moors that had been taken in battle were also presented to the lord king [Note: [Col. 0455D] Manuscript 2 has ablative *rege* (“king”) for dative *regi* (“to the king”).].

Count Wido [Note: [Col. 0455D] *comis* 2], who governed the Breton March [Note: [Col. 0455D] *brittanniae* 6, 7, and so thereafter] [Note: [Col. 0455D] Manuscript 2 has *presentabat* (“was presenting”) at the description of Wido’s government of the Breton March, an anomalous placement.], entered Brittany with his fellow counts and, traversing the whole region, received it into submission. To the king, who had returned from Saxony, he presented the weapons of the leaders who had surrendered, with each man’s name inscribed on them. For each of them [Note: [Col. 0455D] manuscript 7 has genitive *uniuscuiusque* (“of each one”) for nominative *unusquisque* (“each one”)] had handed himself, his land, and his people over to him, and the entire province of the Bretons, something that had never previously happened, was subjugated by the Franks [Note: [Col. 0455D] Manuscript 7 redundantly reads *antea a Francis fuerat a Francis* (“previously had been by the Franks by the Franks”).].

In the same year a certain monk came from Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0455D] *hierusolimis* 5; *hierosolimis* 7] and brought a blessing and relics from the Lord’s tomb, which the patriarch of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0455D] *hierosolimitanus* 5, 6] had sent to the lord king [Note: [Col. 0455D] Manuscript 2 has ablative *rege* (“king”) for dative *regi* (“to the king”).]. Azan, governor of the city called Osca [Note: [Col. 0455D] Manuscript 2 adds *qui dicitur* (“which is called”) before Osca.], sent the keys of the city through his envoy, together with gifts [Note: [Col. 0455D] *Transmisit* (“sent”) is absent in manuscript 2.]. Christmas Day was celebrated in the same palace [Note: [Col. 0455D] Manuscript 2 reads the anomalous *est in die Natalem* (“is on the day Christmas”); *dies* (“day”) is absent in manuscript 5.]. And the reckoning of the years changed to

## 800

The king caused the released Jerusalem monk [Note: [Col. 0458D] *hierosolimitanum* 6 (7)] to return, sending with him Zacharias [Note: [Col. 0458D] *zachariam* 5], a presbyter from his palace, to carry his gifts through those holy places.

In the middle of March he departed from the palace at Aquisgrani and traveled along the shore of the Gallic Ocean. In the sea itself, which was then infested with pirates [Col. 0458B], he established a fleet and arranged garrisons. He celebrated Easter at Centulum, at Saint Richarius. From there [Note: [Col. 0458D] manuscript 7 reads *ibique* (“and there”) for printed *ibi* (“there”)] he again proceeded along the ocean shore to the city of Rouen [Note: [Col. 0458D] *rotumagam* 5; *ratumagnum* 6]. There, after crossing the river Seine, he reached Tours, to Saint Martin, for the sake of prayer [Note: [Col. 0458D] “There all the Breton leaders and counts came to him with gifts.” 9b].

He remained there several days because of the serious illness of Lady Liutgard, his wife [Note: [Col. 0458D] *domna* 2], who both died and was buried there. She died on the second day before the Nones of June. From there, returning through Orléans and Paris [Note: [Col. 0458D] *perisios* 2], he returned to Aquisgrani.

On the day before the Nones of July there was an unusually severe frost, and likewise on the seventh day before the Ides of July, though it caused no harm to the crops. At the beginning of August he came to Mainz [Note: [Col. 0458D] *mogontiam* 6; *mogunciacum* 7] and arranged an expedition to Italy [Note: [Col. 0458D] Manuscripts 5 and 7 have *conduxit* (“he assembled”) for printed *constituit* (“he arranged”); manuscript 6 has *Italia* for accusative *Italiam*.]. Setting out from there with the army, he came to Ravenna.

There, after arranging an expedition against the Beneventans, he turned his journey toward Rome after a seven-day truce and ordered the army, together with his son Pippin, to go plundering through the lands of the Beneventans [Note: [Col. 0458D] Manuscripts 5, 6, and 7 place *in* after *filio* (“son”) in the order *filio in Beneventanorum fines*.].

When he reached Rome, Pope Leo and the Romans with him met him on the day before, at Nomentum, twelve miles from the city, and received him with the greatest humility and honor. After dining [Note: [Col. 0458D] manuscript 2 has participle *prandens* (“dining”) for printed finite *prandit* (“he dined”)] with him in that place, Leo immediately went ahead of him to the city.

On the following day, standing on the steps of the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter [Note: [Col. 0458D] Manuscript 7 has *in basilica* (“in the basilica”) for printed *in basilicae gradibus* (“on the basilica’s steps”).], Leo sent out to meet him the banners of the city of Rome. He also arranged and stationed in suitable places groups of both pilgrims and citizens who would sing praises as he came. Then, with the clergy and bishops, he received the king as he dismounted from his horse and ascended the steps. After prayer had been offered [Note: [Col. 0458D] Manuscript 2 has the corrupt *ascendentem sub dataque* at the words concerning his ascent and the prayer offered.], he led him into the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter while everyone sang psalms.

This took place on the eighth day before the Kalends of December [Note: [Col. 0459D] Manuscript 7 reads *sunt autem haec* (“these things, however, took place”).]. After seven days the king summoned an assembly and made known to everyone why he had come to Rome [Note: [Col. 0459D] Manuscript 2 has corrupt *vocato quur* at “summoned an assembly … why.”]. From then on, every day he devoted himself to the matters for which he had come [Note: [Col. 0459D] Manuscripts 5 and 6 have *ad ea quae* (“to those things which”), manuscript 7 *ad quae* (“to which”), and manuscript 2 plural *venerant* (“they had come”) for singular *venerat* (“he had come”).].

Among these, the greatest or most difficult matter [Note: [Col. 0459D] manuscript 2 has superlative *difficillimum* (“most difficult”) for printed comparative *difficilius* (“more difficult”)] was the first undertaken: the investigation of the crimes brought against the pontiff [Note: [Col. 0459D] Manuscript 2 has plural *discutientibus* (“as [they] investigated”) for the printed investigation phrase.]. Since no one, however, was willing to act as a prosecutor of the crimes, Leo carried the Gospel, climbed the ambo in the presence of all the people in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter [Note: [Col. 0459D] Manuscript 5 has present participle *conscendens* (“climbing”) for printed finite *conscendit* (“he climbed”).], invoked the name of the Holy Trinity, and cleared himself by oath of the crimes brought against him.

On the same day Zacharias [Note: [Col. 0459D] *zaccharias* 5; *zachariam* 2] returned from the East and came to Rome with two monks, one from the Mount of Olives and the other from Saint Sabas [Note: [Col. 0459D] *sancta* 2, 5; *sancta*, corrected to *sancto*, 6; *sancto* 7] [Note: [Col. 0459D] That is, the *laura*, or monastery, of Saint Sabas the presbyter]. The patriarch of Jerusalem had sent them, together with Zacharias, to the king. For the sake of blessing they brought the keys of the Lord’s tomb [Note: [Col. 0459D] Manuscript 2 has the corrupt *claves se pulchritudo minici* at the list of keys brought as a blessing.], as well as the keys of the place of Calvary, and also the keys of the city and of the mountain, together with a banner.

The king received them kindly [Note: [Col. 0459D] “He received one of them but did not keep him with himself” 2], kept them with him for several days [Note: [Col. 0459D] Manuscripts 5 and 7 have singular *detinuit* (“he kept”) for printed plural *detinuit eos* in this clause.], and dismissed them in April after rewarding them. He celebrated Christmas at Rome. And the reckoning of the years changed [Note: [Col. 0459D] Manuscripts 5, 6, and 7 have singular *inmutatus est* (“was changed”) for the printed year-transition wording.] to

## 801

On that most sacred day of the Nativity of the Lord, when the king rose from prayer before the confession of the blessed apostle Peter in order to attend Mass [Note: [Col. 0459D] Manuscript 2 has *surrexit* (“rose”) for printed *surgens* (“rising”).], Pope Leo placed a crown on his head [Note: [Col. 0459D] Manuscript 2 has nominative/ablative *corona* for accusative *coronam* (“a crown”); *eius* (“his”) is absent there.], and the entire Roman people acclaimed:

“Life and victory to Charles Augustus, crowned by God, the great and peaceful emperor of the Romans!”

After the praises, he was worshiped by the apostolicus according to the custom of the ancient rulers; and, the title of Patrician having been removed [Note: [Col. 0459D] Manuscript 2 has *ablatu* for ablative absolute *ablato* (“having been removed”).], he was called Emperor and Augustus.

A few days later he ordered those who had deposed the pontiff in the preceding year [Note: [Col. 0459D] Manuscript 5 has *superiori* (“preceding”) for printed *superiore* in “preceding year.”] to be brought before him. After an inquiry had been held concerning them, they were condemned to death [Note: [Col. 0459D] Manuscripts 5 and 7 have *capite* (“by the head,” hence capitally) at the death sentence.] under Roman law [Note: [Col. 0459D] Manuscript 7 has *Romanorum* (“of the Romans”) for printed *Romana* (“Roman”) law.] as guilty of treason [Note: [Col. 0459D] *Ut* is absent in manuscript 2, which has *maiestatis ei* (“of majesty to him”) at the charge of treason.].

*(The remainder through the year 829 agrees with Einhard’s Annals so closely that I have judged that only their variant readings should be added and marked with the sigla A and L.)*
