[Col. 0368C]

# THE ANNALS OF EINHARD

## 741

In this year Charles [Note: [Col. 0368D] Thus almost everywhere in codices 1, 2, 3; the others have *Karolus* or *Carolus*, and occasionally *carlus*] the mayor of the palace died, leaving three sons as heirs: namely Carloman [Note: [Col. 0368D] So, or consistently with *c*, in codices 1, 2, 5; *carlomannum* 3, 4; *karolomannum* 6, 7], Pippin [Note: [Col. 0368D] *pipinum* 5, 7], and Grifo [Note: [Col. 0368D] *griffonem* 6]. Grifo, who was younger than the others, had as his mother a woman named Swanahilde [Note: [Col. 0368D] *suaniehild* 3; *swanahildem* 4, 6; *swanihildem* 5; *suanihildem* 7], the niece [Note: [Col. 0368D] *neptim* 7] of Odilo [Note: [Col. 0368D] *odilosis* 3; *udilonis* 5, 6, and likewise at 743], duke of the Bavarians [Note: [Col. 0368D] *bauariorum* 5]. She stirred him, through an evil plan [Note: [Col. 0368D] The abbreviation *m. c.* for *malo consilio* (“through an evil plan”) is absent in manuscript 7.], to hope for the whole kingdom, so far that he immediately seized the city of Laon [Note: [Col. 0367D] Laon] and declared war on his brothers.

They quickly gathered an army, besieged Laon, and received their brother into submission. Then they directed their energies toward organizing the kingdom and recovering the provinces that, after their father’s death, had withdrawn from the alliance of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0368D] manuscript 1 reads *ita* (“thus”); the remaining manuscripts have *recuperandas* (“to be recovered”)] [Note: [Col. 0368D] “and directed their energies toward recovering those provinces that had withdrawn from the community of the Franks after their father’s death,” 7].

To ensure that, when they set out abroad [Note: [Col. 0368D] manuscript 3 has *extrema* (“the outermost things”) for printed *externa* (“foreign parts”)], they might leave everything secure at home [Note: [Col. 0368D] manuscript 7 has *profecturi*, followed by abbreviated *o. d.* (“being about to set out …”), instead of printed *profecti* (“having set out”)] [Col. 0369A], Carloman took Grifo and had him kept under guard at Novum Castellum [Note: [Col. 0369D] This seems to be Neufchâteau in the duchy of Luxembourg, east of the towns of Charleville and Mézières]. He is said to have remained in that custody until the time when Carloman himself departed for Rome [Note: [Col. 0369C] The word Roman (“to Rome,” as printed) is absent in 7 and perhaps 3.]. [Note: [Col. 0369D] This appears to have been derived from the same source as the Metz Annals for this year.]

## 742

[Note: [Col. 0369C] Since the number of the year 741 is missing above, codex 1 reads here DCCXLI; for the year 743, DCCXLII; for 745, DCCXLIII; and for 746, 747, and 748, DCCXLVIII.]

Carloman and Pippin, having gained possession of the kingdom of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0369C] Manuscript 7, and perhaps 3, abbreviates *regnum Francorum* (“kingdom of the Franks”) as *r. F.*.], wishing first to recover Aquitaine, entered that same Aquitaine with an army against Hunold [Note: [Col. 0369C] *honoldum* 6], duke of that province [Note: [Col. 0369C] Manuscript 7, and perhaps 3, has *ipsius* (“of that same one”) for printed *illius* (“of that one”).]. They captured a certain castle called Luccas [Note: [Col. 0369D] Loches, in the territory of the Turones Transligerini, at the Andria or Angers; Valesius, *Notitia Galliae*, p. 288] [Note: [Col. 0369C] “to which the name Lucas belongs,” 7; “which is called L.” 6].

Before withdrawing from that province [Note: [Col. 0369C] *Ea* (“that [province]”) is absent in manuscript 7.], they divided between themselves the kingdom that they held jointly [Note: [Col. 0369C] For habuerunt (“they held”), 4 has habuerant (“they had held”), and 7 administrabant (“they were administering”).] at the place called Old Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0369C] “They divided it between themselves at the place called Old Poitiers,” 7] [Note: [Col. 0369D] Vieux-Poitiers on the Clain, not far from its confluence with the Vienne; the same work, p. 601.]. In the same year, after they had returned home [Note: [Col. 0369B] Manuscript 6 has *domi* (“at home”) for printed *ad propria* (“to their own territory”).], Carloman entered Alamannia [Note: [Col. 0369D] *alemanniam* 7, perhaps 3], which too had withdrawn from the alliance of the Franks, with an army and devastated it with sword and fire [Note: [Col. 0369D] Manuscript 7 has *igne* (“fire”) for printed *incendio* (“conflagration”).].

## 743

Carloman and Pippin set out with their forces joined together against Odilo, duke of the Bavarians, and, after battle had been joined, routed his army. After they had returned from there [Note: [Col. 0369D] Manuscript 4 reads *in caede* (“in the slaughter”), manuscript 5 *a caede* (“from the slaughter”), for the printed *inde* (“from there”).], Carloman alone set out for Saxony and received into submission the castle called Hohseoburg [Note: [Col. 0369D] Thus 1, 3, 6; *hohseburg* 2, whose Viennese copy reads *herochseburg*; *hohseobur* 4; *hohseburc* 5; *hochsigburg* 7] [Note: [Col. 0369D] Hoch-Seeburg in the district of Hohsi, now Seeburg in the county of Mansfeld, on the border of Saxony and Frankish Thuringia, between the west and south of Halle].

In it he also received Theoderic [Note: [Col. 0369D] *thedericum* 7; *theodoricum* 2], a Saxon, the leading man of that place, into submission.

## 744

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0369D] *Item* (“likewise”) is absent in manuscript 7.] the same brothers, Carloman and Pippin [Col. 0369C], entered Saxony with united forces and again received the aforementioned Theoderic [Note: [Col. 0369D] *teodericum* 4; *theodoricum* 5; *thedericum* 7] into submission [Note: [Col. 0369D] The phrase “into submission” is absent in manuscript 7.].

## 745

[Note: [Col. 0370D] The account of the year 745 seems to have fallen out, since what now follows should not be assigned to the years 745, 746, 747, 748, 749, and 750, but to the following years 746, 747, 748, 749, 750, and 751. Cf. the short annals and the account of the translation of Saint Germanus in Bouquet V, 426, where the sequence of events is accurately established.]

In this year Carloman revealed to his brother Pippin what he had long been considering [Note: [Col. 0369D] Witness 7 has k. id quod dudum secum p. est, “Carloman, that which he had long pondered with himself,” with the author’s name and verb abbreviated in the apparatus]: that he wished to abandon secular life and serve God in the monastic habit. For this reason, the expedition of the present year having been abandoned [Note: [Col. 0369D] “He dismissed the expedition,” 7], Pippin was free to fulfill Carloman’s vows [Col. 0372A] and arrange his journey—for Carloman had decided to go to Rome—taking care that his brother might arrive honorably and fittingly at the place he desired [Note: [Col. 0372C] Manuscript 7, and perhaps 3, has *frater suus* (“his brother”) for printed *fratrem suum* (“his brother,” accusative).].

## 746

Carloman set out for Rome, abandoned secular glory, and changed his clothing. On Mount Soracte [Note: [Col. 0372C] *soracte* 7] he built a monastery in honor of Saint Sylvester [Note: [Col. 0371D] The monastery of San Silvestro on Mount Soracte, which the Romans call Monte Oreste, still exists today], where Saint Sylvester is said once to have hidden during the persecution that took place under the emperor Constantine [Note: [Col. 0372C] The clause about Saint Sylvester’s hiding during the persecution is absent in manuscript 7.].

After staying there for some time, he left that place on better advice and came to the monastery of Saint Benedict in the province of Samnium, beside the fortress of Cassino [Note: [Col. 0372C] *cassinum* 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Among all experts in the affairs of Cassino, it is established that the famous name is written with only one *s*] [Note: [Col. 0372D] I found the chapel built in honor of Saint Carloman in the church of the monastery of Monte Cassino, splendid with paintings and mosaic work, intact and reverently preserved by the Fathers in 1822], intending to serve God [Note: [Col. 0372D] Manuscript 7 has *Cassinam arcem* (“the fortress of Cassino”) at the statement that Carloman intended to serve God.]. There he received the monastic habit [Col. 0372B].

## 747

Grifo, the brother of Carloman and Pippin [Note: [Col. 0372D] Here and thereafter 1 has *Gripho*; the others *Grifo*], unwilling to be subject to his brother Pippin, although he lived honorably under him, fled to Saxony with a band of men. Having gathered an army of Saxons, he settled beside the river Ovacra [Note: [Col. 0372D] Manuscript 7 reads *super fluvio Obacro* (“on the river Ovacra”); the others read as above, except manuscript 5, *Onacra*.], at the place called Orheim [Note: [Col. 0372D] *horheim* 7] [Note: [Col. 0372D] Now Orum on the Oker, above Wolfenbüttel].

Pippin [Note: [Col. 0372D] Witness 7 has c. pipinus autem cum, “but Pippin, with …,” as abbreviated in the apparatus], with an army of Franks, proceeding through Thuringia [Note: [Col. 0372D] *turingiam* 3? 4, 7], entered Saxony against his brother’s schemes and settled beside the river Missaha [Note: [Col. 0372D] *missaham* 7], at the place called Skahningi [Note: [Col. 0372D] *scahningi* 4, 5; *skachningi* 6; *schaninge* 7] [Note: [Col. 0372D] Schöningen on the stream Meissau, in the duchy of Brunswick]. No battle, however, was fought between them [Note: [Col. 0372D] Manuscript 6 reads *non est tamen inter eos* (“nevertheless there is not between them”); manuscripts 3?, 5, and 7 read *inter eos non est* (“between them there is not”), varying the order of the printed no-battle clause.], but they withdrew from the meeting after an agreement had been made.

## 748

Grifo, distrustful of the loyalty of the Saxons, went to Bavaria. With the forces that flocked to him from Francia [Note: [Col. 0372D] Manuscript 7 reads *ad eum de Francia* (“to him from Francia”) for the troops flocking to Grifo.], he brought the duchy itself under his power. He received Tassilo [Note: [Col. 0372D] *thassilonem* 5] and Hiltrude [Note: [Col. 0372D] *hildrudem* 5; *hiltthrudim* 7] into submission and welcomed Swithger [Note: [Col. 0372D] *suidgerum* 4; *swikerum* 5], who came to aid him [Note: [Col. 0372D] Manuscripts 3? and 7 read *sibi in auxilium* (“to aid him”).].

When this was reported to Pippin, he set out for Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0372D] manuscript 7 adds *in* before *Baioariam* (“into Bavaria”)] with a very large army [Note: [Col. 0372D] Manuscript 3 has *magno* (“large”) for printed superlative *maximo* (“very large”).], captured his brother Grifo together with all who had come with him or to him [Note: [Col. 0372D] Manuscript 7 has *cum eo* (“with him”) and also the abbreviated, textually uncertain *ipsum eo v.* at the capture of Grifo and his followers.], restored Tassilo to the duchy, and, returning home, bestowed twelve counties on Grifo in the manner of dukes [Note: [Col. 0372D] Manuscript 5 has *ducatum* (“duchy”); manuscripts 4, 5, and 6 have *comitibus* (“to counts”) for the printed statement about twelve counties bestowed in the manner of dukes.].

But he was not satisfied with such a benefaction, for in the same year he fled to Waifarius [Note: [Col. 0373C] *wifarium* 5], duke of Aquitaine.

## 749

Burchard [Note: [Col. 0373C] *burkardus* 2; *burckhardus* 5], bishop of Würzburg [Note: [Col. 0373C] *wirziburgensis* 2, 5; *wirciburgensis* 4; *wirtziburgensis* 7, perhaps 3], and the presbyter Folrad [Note: [Col. 0373C] Manuscript 7 adds *presbyter* (“presbyter”) to Folrad.], chaplain [Note: [Col. 0373C] It should have been written *cappellanus*; it occurs in none of the codices], were sent to Rome to consult Pope Zacharias about the case of the kings who at that time existed in Francia: they bore only the name of king, but possessed no royal power [Note: [Col. 0373D] The clause that the kings possessed no royal power is absent in manuscript 3.].

Through them the aforesaid pontiff declared that it was better for the man to be called king in whom the highest power resided [Note: [Col. 0373D] The pontiff’s declaration that the holder of supreme power should be called king is absent in manuscript 7.]. By his authority he ordered that Pippin be made king.

## 750

In this year, according to the decree of the Roman pontiff, Pippin was called king of the Franks. He was anointed for this dignity and honor with sacred unction by the hand of Boniface, of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0373D] *bonifacii* here and at 754; the others, except 1], archbishop and martyr [Note: [Col. 0373D] Manuscript 7 adds *martyris* (“martyr”) to Boniface’s title.], and, according to Frankish custom, was raised onto the throne of the kingdom in the city of Soissons [Note: [Col. 0373D] *suessiona* 7].

Hilderic [Note: [Col. 0373D] *hidericus* 5; *hyldericus* 6], who falsely bore the name of king, was tonsured and sent to a monastery.

## 751. 752. 753.

[Note: [Col. 0373D] Charles, returning from Italy, celebrated the dedication of the church of Saint Nazarius the martyr and the translation of his body at our monastery of Lorsch in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 774, on the Kalends of September, codex 3. The same manuscript assigns the numbers 752 and 753 to the years 753 and 754.]

This year King Pippin entered Saxony with a large army [Note: *cum* (“with”) is omitted in witness 1]. Although the Saxons resisted him with the utmost stubbornness, they were nevertheless driven back and withdrew; and he himself advanced as far as the place called Rimi [Note: Remen above Minden], which lies on the river Weser [Note: *Wisaram* in witnesses 5 and 6; *Wiseram* perhaps in 3 and 7]. In this expedition Archbishop Hildigarius [Note: of Cologne] was killed, on the mountain called Iuburg [Note: *Viburg* perhaps in 3, 5, and 6; *Duburg* in 7]. As the king was returning [Note: “with the king returning,” witnesses 5 and 6], a messenger came from Saxony [Note: “he received news,” witness 7] concerning the death of his brother Grifo and by whom and in what manner he had been killed [Note: “slain,” witness 6].

In the same year Pope Stephen came to King Pippin at the estate called Carisiacus [Note: Quiersy on the Oise], urging him to defend himself and the Roman Church from the attacks [Note: “afflictions,” witness 7] of the Lombards [Note: *Longobardorum* in witnesses 1, 4, 5, and 6; afterward, however, manuscript 1 gives the better reading]. Pippin’s brother Karlomannus, who had already become a monk, also came at the command of his abbot, in order to oppose his brother [Note: omitted in witness 7] at the request of the Roman pontiff. It is thought, however, that he did this unwillingly, because neither did he dare disregard the orders of his abbot, nor did that abbot [Note: “his,” witness 7; “that abbot,” witness 6] dare resist the commands of the king of the Lombards, who had ordered him to do this [Note: “had ordered,” perhaps witnesses 7 and 3].

### 754

After Pope Stephen had received from King Pippin a guarantee of the defense of the Roman Church [Note: *aecclesiae* in witness 4, and frequently so; “of the Church” is omitted in witness 6], he consecrated Pippin by sacred anointing to the dignity and honor of kingship, and together with him his two sons, Karlus and Karlomannus. He remained in Francia during the winter.

In the same year [Note: The dispute concerning the death of Saint Boniface was examined by Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, year 755; he supports Willibald, Boniface’s contemporary, who gives the year 755 and the eighth indiction], Boniface, archbishop of Mainz [Note: *Mogontiacensis* in witnesses 2 and 5; *Mogonciacensis* in 3 and 6; *Moguntiacensis* in 7], while preaching the word of God in Frisia, was killed by pagans and crowned with martyrdom.

### 755

King Pippin, at the invitation and urging of the aforesaid Roman pontiff, entered Italy with a strong force [Note: “with a strong hand,” witness 4; *cum* is omitted in witness 6], in order to exact from the king of the Lombards what was owed to the blessed apostle Peter [Note: “Italy, on account of the territories taken from the Roman Church by the king of the Lombards,” witness 7]. When the Lombards resisted and defended the passes of Italy, the fiercest fighting took place at the mountain defiles themselves [Note: “the narrow mountain passes called defiles,” witnesses 3 and 6; “the narrow places of the mountains which they call defiles,” witness 7]. When the Lombards gave way, all the Frankish forces overcame the difficult route without great exertion [Note: “the route, although difficult,” witness 7].

Heistulfus, however, king of the Lombards [Note: *Haistulfus* in witness 5; *Haistolfus* in witness 7, and likewise below], unwilling to join battle, was besieged by King Pippin in the city of Pavia. Pippin did not lift the siege until he had received forty hostages as security for the restoration of what was owed to the holy Roman Church [Note: “for restoring what had been taken from the Roman Church,” witness 7]. After the forty hostages had been given and the promises confirmed by oath, Heistulfus returned to his own kingdom [Note: “went back,” witness 6], while he sent Pope Stephen back to Rome with the priest and chaplain Folradus [Note: *Floradus* in witnesses 5 and 6] and a considerable Frankish force.

Karlomannus, the king’s brother and a monk [Note: omitted in witness 7], who had remained in the city of Vienne with Queen Berthrada [Note: *Berhtrada* in witness 5; *Berchtrada* in witness 6; *Bertrada* in witness 7], was seized by a fever before the king returned from Italy and died. By the king’s command his body was carried back to the monastery of Saint Benedict, where he had received the monastic habit.

### 756

Although Heistulfus, king of the Lombards, had given hostages in the preceding year [Note: “the preceding year,” witness 5] and had bound both himself and his nobles by oath to restore what was owed to the holy Roman Church [Note: “and to return what he had taken from the Roman Church,” witness 7], he fulfilled none of his promises in practice [Note: “none of the promised things,” witness 7]. For this reason King Pippin again entered Italy with an army and besieged Heistulfus, who had shut himself up in the city of Pavia, compelling him by the siege to fulfill his promises.

Pippin handed over to Saint Peter Ravenna, restored to him, the Pentapolis, and the whole Exarchate belonging to Ravenna; and when these matters had been completed [Note: *iis* for *his* in witness 7], he returned to Gaul [Note: “returned,” witness 2].

After Pippin’s departure, Heistulfus began considering how he might not so much fulfill his promises as deceitfully alter what had already been fulfilled. By chance he fell from his horse while hunting [Note: “from his horse” is omitted in witness 6]; as a result, he contracted an illness and within a few days brought his life to an end [Note: “his final end,” witness 7]. Desiderius, who had been his master of the horse, succeeded him in the kingdom.

### 757

The emperor Constantine sent King Pippin many gifts [Note: *multa* is omitted in witness 2; “the emperor sent many gifts to King Pippin,” witness 7], among them an organ [Note: plural *organa* perhaps in witnesses 7 and 3]. These gifts reached him at the estate of Compendium, where he was then holding a general assembly of his people.

Tassilo, duke of the Bavarians [Note: *Thassilo* in witness 5], also came there with the leading men of his people and, according to Frankish custom [Note: “of the Franks,” witness 4], commended himself into the king’s hands as a vassal, placing himself in the king’s hands [Note: “in his hands,” witness 4]. He promised by oath, over the body of Saint Denis, fidelity both to King Pippin himself and to his sons Karlus and Karlomannus [Note: “over,” perhaps witnesses 7 and 3]. And [Note: “But,” perhaps witnesses 7 and 3] not only there, but also over the body of Saint Martin and Saint Germanus, he likewise promised by oath that he would preserve faith with the aforesaid lords of his [Note: omitted in witnesses 5 and 6] throughout the days of his life.

Similarly also [Note: “also” is omitted in witness 7], all the leading men and elders of Bavaria who had come with him into the king’s presence [Note: “came,” witness 6] promised at the aforesaid venerable places that they would preserve faith with the king and his sons [Note: “his son,” witness 6].

### 758

King Pippin attacked Saxony with an army [Note: “entered Saxony,” witness 4]. Although the Saxons resisted most vigorously and defended their fortifications, the defenders were driven out in battle, and Pippin entered the rampart by which they had been attempting to defend their homeland. After battles had been fought everywhere, he killed a very large number of them [Note: witness 1 reads *ita*; the other witnesses read *cecidit*], compelled them to promise that they would do his entire will [Note: “do his will,” witness 7], and that every year, as a mark of honor, they would give three hundred horses as a gift at the general assembly [Note: “each year,” witness 7]. After these arrangements had been made and confirmed according to Saxon custom so that they would be binding, he withdrew into Gaul with his army [Note: “with his army,” witness 2].

### 759

A son was born to King Pippin, whom he wished to be called Pippin after himself. But the boy was overtaken by an untimely death and died in the third year after his birth. That year the king celebrated Christmas at Lonclare [Note: *Longlare* in witness 7] and Easter at Iopila; nor did he undertake any journey beyond the boundaries of his kingdom.

### 760

Waifarius, duke of Aquitaine, had refused to return to the rulers of the venerable churches the property that was in his power and belonged to churches established under the authority of King Pippin. He also scorned to listen when the king, through his envoys, warned him about these matters [Note: “warned the king concerning these things,” witness 7]. By his obstinacy he provoked the king to undertake war against him.

For the king, having gathered forces from every direction, entered Aquitaine and declared that he would exact by war the property and rights of the churches [Note: “he would exact the property of the churches by war,” witness 7]. When he had encamped at the place called Tedoad [Note: *Tedo* in witness 4; *Thedoad* perhaps in witnesses 3, 5, 6, and 7], Waifarius, not daring to fight, sent an embassy to the king and promised that he would do what was commanded, return the rights of the churches [Note: “return their rights to the churches,” witness 7], and give whatever hostages were demanded. He also gave two of the leading men of his people, Adalgarius and Itherius [Note: *Iterius* in witnesses 5 and 6].

By this action he so mitigated the king’s anger against him [Note: “the anger thus aroused against him,” witness 7; *adeo* is omitted in witness 7] that the king immediately abandoned the war. After receiving the hostages who had been given to guarantee the promises, the king refrained from war and, returning home, dismissed his army and spent the winter at the estate of Carisiacus [Note: *Carisiaca* in witness 6], where he also celebrated Christmas and Easter.

### 761

Although Waifarius had given hostages and sworn oaths [Note: “oaths as well,” witness 7], he nevertheless judged it preferable to exact vengeance for the war waged against him in the preceding year [Note: “to exact it,” witness 7]. He therefore sent his army to ravage Frankish possessions as far as the city of Chalon.

When this was reported to King Pippin, who was holding the general assembly at the estate of Duria [Note: Düren, between Cologne and Aachen], he gathered auxiliary forces from every direction [Note: “counselors,” witness 4; “neighboring forces,” witness 6], entered Aquitaine with a great military force, and captured several towns and fortified places by assault [Note: *oppida* for *opida* in witnesses 2–7]. Among the chief of these were Bourbon, Chantelle, and Clermont [Note: “Bourbon, Chantelle-le-Chastel, and Clermont”].

Some [Note: *quae* for *quaedam* in witness 1] surrendered voluntarily to the victor [Note: “surrendered,” perhaps witnesses 3, 5, 6, and 7], especially the fortresses of the Arverni [Note: *Arvenorum* in witness 4; *Aruennorum* in witnesses 5 and 6; *Avernorum* in witness 7], which were then under the pressure of war.

The king, however, devastating with sword and fire everything he found outside the fortifications [Note: witness 7 has “with fire”], turned back after reaching the town of Limoges [Note: *Lemovicas* in witnesses 5 and 6; *Limovicam* in witness 7]. After spending the winter at the estate of Carisiacus, he celebrated Christmas and Easter there. His eldest son Karlus was with the king on this expedition [Note: omitted in witnesses 5 and 6]; after his father’s death, supreme authority over the entire empire passed to him [Note: “came to him,” witness 7].

### 762

King Pippin, wishing to bring the war he had undertaken to an end, entered the province of Aquitaine again with large forces. After capturing the city of Bourges [Note: *Beturica* in witness 4] and the fortress of Thouars, he returned. He spent the winter at the estate of Gentilly [Note: near Paris] and celebrated there Christmas and the solemn rites of the Easter feast [Note: variant spellings include *sollempnia*, *solempnia*, *solennia*, and “the solemnity,” as recorded in the witnesses].

### 763

When the appropriate season of the year returned, the king held an assembly at Nevers [Note: *Niversis* in witness 3] and, having gathered forces from every direction, King Pippin again entered Aquitaine. He devastated with sword and fire everything outside the fortifications and advanced as far as the town of Cahors [Note: “He came,” witness 4].

From there, intending to withdraw into Francia with his army intact [Note: “with his entire army,” witness 7], he returned through Limoges [Note: *Limovicam* in witness 7]. On this expedition Tassilo, duke of Bavaria [Note: “duke of Bavaria,” witness 4; *Thassilo* in witness 5], pretending illness out of deceit, returned to his homeland [Note: “into his homeland,” witness 7]. After firmly resolving to rebel, he swore that he would no longer come into the king’s presence [Note: “appearance,” perhaps witnesses 7 and 3; *se* is omitted in witness 7].

The king dismissed his army into winter quarters [Note: “the army into winter quarters,” perhaps witnesses 7 and 3] and settled at the estate of Lonclare [Note: *Longlare* in witness 7] to spend the winter. There he celebrated Christmas and Easter. At that time [Note: “this,” witness 7] there was such a severe and harsh winter that, because of the intensity of the cold, it seemed impossible to compare it with any winter of preceding years [Note: “none,” witness 7; *posse* is omitted in witness 2].

### 764

King Pippin [Note: *dictracto* in witness 4], with his attention divided because of two wars—the Aquitanian war [Note: “that is, the Aquitanian [war],” perhaps witnesses 7 and 3] already undertaken long before, and the Bavarian war that had to be undertaken because of the rebellion of Duke Tassilo [Note: “the Bavarians,” witness 2]—held a general assembly of his people in the city of Worms. He postponed the expedition to the future and remained at home that year. He spent the winter at the estate of Carisiacus and celebrated there Christmas and the holy solemnity of the Easter feast [Note: “holy Easter,” witness 7; “the holy solemnity of the Easter feast,” witnesses 5 and 6].

In the same year [Note: omitted in witness 2] a solar eclipse occurred on the first day [Note: “the second day before the Nones of June,” witnesses 3, 4, and 5; “the first day” is omitted in witness 2] at the sixth hour.

### 765

That year King Pippin remained at home and, although the Aquitanian war was not yet finished, did not leave the boundaries of his kingdom on account of it. Instead, he held a general assembly of his people at the estate of Attiniacus [Note: *Atiniacus* in witness 2], and spent the winter at Aachen [Note: “He held it at the estate of Attiniacus; the winter season was at Aachen,” witness 5]. There he celebrated both Christmas and Easter [Note: “where,” witnesses 3 and 5; “there also,” witness 6].

### 766

To bring the Aquitanian war to completion, King Pippin held an assembly at Orléans [Note: “at the assembly,” perhaps witnesses 7 and 3] and set out for Aquitaine. He rebuilt the fortress of Argentomagus [Note: “Argentum Magnum,” witness 5], which Waifarius had destroyed [Note: *Destructum* in witnesses 2–7; “repaired,” perhaps witnesses 7 and 5]. After placing Frankish garrisons there and in the city of Bourges [Note: *depositoque*, “after placing,” is *dispositoque*, “after arranging,” in witnesses 2–7; *in* is omitted in witnesses 2 and 4; “both there and in,” witness 7], he returned. He celebrated Christmas at Salmonciacus [Note: *natalem* for *natalemque* in witness 7; *Salmontiacus* in witness 4; *Salmontiaco* in witnesses 5 and 6] and Easter at Gentilly [Note: *Gentiliacus* in witnesses 5 and 6].

### 767

A dispute arose concerning the Holy Trinity and the images of the saints between the Eastern and Western Churches—that is, between the Romans and the Greeks. King Pippin convened a synod on this question at the estate of Gentilly [Note: *in* is omitted in witness 5; “Pippin’s assembly at the estate of Gentilly,” witness 6]. When it had been completed [Note: “when the matter had been completed,” witness 4], he set out for Aquitaine after Christmas to bring the aforesaid war to an end.

Traveling through Narbonne, he attacked and captured Toulouse, and received the districts of Albi and Gévaudan into submission [Note: “Gévaudan, the ancient district of the Gabali in the Auvergne,” Valesius, p. 213; *Gavuldianum* in witness 3; *Gavuldensem* in witness 7]. Returning to Vienne, after performing there the sacred rites of Easter and restoring the army after its labors, he set out for the remaining operations of the war in August, when summer was already nearly over.

Coming to Bourges, he held an assembly in the Frankish manner in the open field [Note: *Franciaco* in witnesses 5 and 6; “held,” witness 4]. From there he advanced to the river Garonne [Note: *Garonam* in witness 2; *Garongam* in witness 4], and captured many fortresses, rocky strongholds, and caves in which large numbers of the enemy were defending themselves. Among the chief were Scoralia [Note: *Scolaria* in witnesses 3 and 4], Torinna [Note: *Turinna* in witness 4; *Torrinna* in witnesses 5 and 6], and Petrocia [Note: “and,” witness 4; omitted in witness 7].

Returning [Note: *reversus* for *reversusque* in witness 4] to Bourges, he dismissed the army into winter quarters [Note: *Hybernia* in witness 7] and settled there [Note: “but remained there,” witnesses 3 and 6; “tarried,” witness 7], celebrating Christmas. That year Pope Paul of Rome died, and news of the event reached the king there.

### 768

As soon as King Pippin saw that the proper time for conducting the war had arrived, he summoned an army from every direction and hastened to the city of Saintes [Note: *Sattonica* in witness 4]. After capturing Rimistain on the way [Note: *Rimastamo* in witness 6], he reached the aforesaid city, where Waifarius’s mother, sister, and nieces [Note: “and his nieces,” perhaps witnesses 7 and 3; “the king’s nieces,” witness 6] were brought into his presence. He received them kindly [Note: omitted in witness 6] and ordered that they be kept safe.

He then set out for the river Garonne. There Erowicus [Note: *Eberwicus* in witness 7; *Eworwicus* in witness 3] met him with another sister of the aforesaid duke, at the place called Montes, and surrendered himself and her to the king. After several matters had gone favorably, the king returned [Note: omitted in witness 3] and celebrated Easter in the fortress called Sels [Note: *Fels* in witness 2].

[Col. 0388A]

Taking his wife and household with him, he came again to the city of Saintes [Note: *Santonicum* in witnesses 1, 2, 5, and 6; *Sattonicam* in witness 4]. He left his wife and household there [Note: “and,” perhaps witness 7; “his wife and household,” witness 6] and devoted himself with all his forces to pursuing Duke Waifarius. He did not desist until he had either captured or killed the rebel [Note: “until he had both captured him and killed the rebel,” witness 7].

After Duke Waifarius had been killed [Note: “Waifarius the duke,” perhaps witnesses 7 and 3] in the territory of Périgueux [Note: *territurium* in witness 2; Perigueux], and, as it seemed to him, the Aquitanian war had been brought to an end, he returned to Saintes. After remaining there for some time, he fell ill. Nevertheless, while suffering from this illness [Note: *illa* for *ipsa* in witnesses 5 and 6; *invalitudine* in witnesses 5 and 6; *valetudine* in witness 7], he was carried to Tours and prayed at the shrine of Saint Martin.

From there, when he had reached Paris [Note: *veniset* in witness 2], he died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October. His body was buried in the basilica of the blessed martyr Denis.

His sons Karlus and Karlomannus were made kings by the consent of all the Franks. Karlus received the royal insignia in the city of Noyon [Note: *Noviomago* in witnesses 4, 5, 6, and 7], and Karlomannus at Soissons [Note: *Suessona civitate* in witnesses 4, 5, and 6; *Suessiona* in witness 7].

[Note: Karlus received the northern portion of the Frankish kingdom, apart from half of Aquitaine; his brother received the southern portion. In Karlus’s share were, for example, Angers, Rouen, Noyon, the estate of Audriaca, the monasteries of Saint Bertin and Corbie, Valenciennes, Liège, Herstal, Aachen, Düren, Lower Maastricht, Gorzia, Mainz, and Worms; accordingly, the northern parts of Neustria and Austrasia, Frisia, and certainly Thuringia together with Bavaria fell to him. In Carlomannus’s territory were, for example, the monastery of Argenteuil, Paris, Soissons, Salmonciacus, Corbonacum, Attiniacum, Pontio, Theodonis villa, Metz, Verdun, Calmuntiacum, Brocomagum, the southern parts of Neustria and Austrasia, Septimania, Burgundy, Provence, Alsace, and Alamannia.]

Karlus, who was the elder by birth, went to Aachen [Note: “Karlus at Aachen,” witness 7], where he celebrated Christmas, and celebrated Easter in the city of Rouen [Note: *Ratumago* in witness 6; *Rotoimago* in witness 2; *Rotomago* in witness 7].

### 769

After these two brothers succeeded their father and divided the kingdom between themselves, the province of Aquitaine, which had fallen by lot to the elder King Karlus, could not remain at peace, since the remnants of the war still remained there [Note: “could not,” witness 5]. For a certain Hunoldus [Note: *Hunholtus* in witness 7, and likewise below], aspiring to kingship, stirred the minds of the provincials to undertake new enterprises.

Against him King Karlus himself, to whom that province had fallen by lot, set out with an army. But he could not obtain his brother’s assistance, because the latter was prevented by the evil counsel of his nobles from doing so. After merely holding a conference with him at a place called Duasdives [Note: Its location is unknown. It seems to have been beyond the Rhine, in the kingdom of Carlomannus, not in the territory of the Pictones], while his brother returned to his own kingdom, Karlus set out for the Aquitanian city of Angoulême [Note: *Egolisenam*; *Ergo lisenam* in witness 6; *Lisenam* in witness 5].

From there, having gathered forces from every direction [Note: “with forces gathered from every direction,” witness 7; “from every direction” is omitted in witness 3], he pursued the fleeing Hunoldus [Note: “followed,” perhaps witnesses 7, 3, and 2] and came very close to capturing him [Note: “was not far from capturing him,” witness 1]. But Hunoldus was saved by his knowledge of the places where he could conceal himself from the king’s army. He abandoned Aquitaine and sought refuge in Gascony [Note: *Vasconiam* in witness 7 throughout], believing that he would be safe there.

At that time the duke of the Gascons was a man named Lupus, to whose protection Hunoldus did not hesitate to entrust himself. The king sent an embassy [Note: *missa ocius*, “sent more quickly,” in witness 7] to him and ordered that the fugitive be handed over. He added this condition: if Lupus did not obey him, he should know that the king would enter Gascony by war and would not withdraw from it until he had brought his disobedience to an end [Note: “and would not withdraw until he had put an end to it, unless he obeyed,” witness 7; “obeying him,” witness 4].

Terrified by the king’s threats [Note: *nimis*, “excessively,” in witness 1; *minas*, “threats,” in witness 2], Lupus handed over Hunoldus and his wife without delay and promised that he too would do whatever was commanded.

The king, while waiting for the envoys he had sent to return, built a certain fortress [Note: *quoddam* is omitted in witness 7; “a certain fortress,” witness 3] near the river Dordogne [Note: *Dornoniam* in witness 5; *Dordoniam* in witness 2], called Fronsac [Note: *Franciacum* in witnesses 1 and 3; *Fronctiacum* in witness 5; the name is omitted in witness 2]. When the envoys returned, the fugitive was brought back, and the fortress had been built [Note: “and the fortress having been built,” witnesses 4, 5, and 6]; the king returned to his own kingdom [Note: “went back,” witnesses 2 and 5].

He celebrated Christmas at the estate of Düren and Easter at Saint Lambert in the district of Liège [Note: *Lanbertum* in witness 2; Liège].

### 770

Lord King Karlus [Note: *Domnus* rather than *dominus* in witness 7 and 3, and likewise below] held a general assembly of his people in the city of Worms [Note: *Worcia* in witness 4]. Berthrada, mother of the kings [Note: *Berhtrada* in witness 5; *Berchtrada* in witness 6; *Bertharda* in witness 1; *Bertrada* in witness 7], having spoken with her younger son Karlomannus at Salusia [Note: Seltz in Alsace. Although Schöpflin, in *Alsatia Illustrata*, vol. I, pp. 706–707, attacks Valesius, who held the same view, and understands the place to be somewhere in the Worms district on the river Salus near Ingelheim—since it might seem that Karlus, after holding an assembly at Worms, did not travel as far as Alsace—the place must nevertheless be sought not below Worms and in Karlus’s kingdom, but in Karlomannus’s kingdom, to which Alsace belonged. All who have carefully examined our annals agree on this point; for here the subject is not Karlus’s assembly, but Karlomannus’s departure with his mother for Italy], set out for Italy for the sake of peace [Note: The comma in the edition is not placed here but, incorrectly, only after *causa*, producing a very different meaning. The reading adopted here is supported by the authority of all the manuscripts I have examined and, as I am convinced, of the remaining manuscripts as well].

After completing the business for which she had gone there [Note: “had been,” witness 7], and after also venerating in Rome the thresholds of the holy apostles, she returned to her sons in Gaul [Note: “to her sons in Gaul,” witnesses 4 and 5; “she returned to her sons in Gaul,” witness 6]. King Karlus celebrated Christmas at Mainz [Note: *Mogonciaci* in witness 2; *Mogonciaco* in witnesses 3, 5, and 6; *Mogontiaci* in witness 4; *Moguntiaco* in witness 7] and Holy Easter at the estate of Herstal.

### 771

After holding the customary general assembly at the estate of Valenciennes on the river Scheldt [Note: *Scaldim* in witness 7; *Vallentiana* in witness 7; *Valenciana* in witnesses 5 and 6], King Karlus set out to spend the winter.

While he remained there for some time, his brother Karlomannus died at the estate of Salmonciacus on the second day before the Nones of December [Note: The witnesses read variously: “on the day before the Nones,” “on the day before the …,” “on the second day before the Nones,” “on the sixth day before the Nones,” and “on the day before the Nones.” We have therefore altered *ad* to *a* and restored what we believe to be the true reading: “he died on the second day before the Nones of December”].

The king, turning his attention to taking possession of the whole kingdom, came to the estate of Carbonacum [Note: *Carboniacum* in witness 2; “he came to the estate,” witness 4]. There he received Bishop Wilharius of Sion [Note: *Wlharium Sedunensem* in witness 6], the priest Folradus [Note: an abbreviated and corrupt form in witness 1], and many other priests [Note: “very many,” witness 5], as well as the counts and leading men of his brother [Note: *Primatos* in witnesses 1, 2, and 3; *Primates* in witnesses 4–7], who came to him. Among them the most distinguished [Note: “especially,” witness 6] were Warinus and Adalhardus [Note: *Adelhardus* in witness 7].

For his brother’s wife and sons had gone to Italy with part of the nobles [Note: *Patre*, “with their father,” in witness 5; “their departure to Italy,” witness 7]. The king patiently endured their departure to Italy, as though it were unnecessary [Note: “impatiently,” witness 7]. He celebrated Christmas at Attiniacus [Note: “at Attiniacus,” witness 7; *Antiniacus* in witness 4] and Easter at Herstal [Note: “at Herstal,” witness 7].

### 772

After Pope Stephen died at Rome, Hadrianus [Note: *Adrianus* in witnesses 3–7, and likewise below] succeeded him in the pontificate [Note: “to the pontificate,” witnesses 3–7].

King Karlus, having convened a general assembly at Worms [Note: “the city of Worms,” witness 4], resolved to attack Saxony by war. He entered it without delay, devastated everything with sword and fire [Note: “after devastating everything,” witnesses 4 and 5; “with everything devastated,” witness 6], captured the fortress of Eresburg [Note: “this time Eresburg,” witness 1; elsewhere as in the text], and overthrew the idol [Note: *idolumque*, “and the idol,” in witness 7] called Irminsul by the Saxons [Note: *Irminsula Saxonibus* in witness 1; *Yrminsul Saxonibus* in witness 6; “which is called,” witnesses 5 and 6].

While he remained in the same place for three days during its destruction, it happened that, because the sky remained continuously clear and all the streams and springs of that place had dried up [Note: *exiccatis* in witness 7; *exsiccatus* in witness 2], no water could be found for drinking. But so that the army, exhausted by thirst, would not suffer longer, it is believed that this happened by divine action: one day, while everyone was resting at midday according to custom, such a great quantity of water burst forth beside the mountain adjoining the camp [Note: “near the mountain,” witnesses 7 and 3], from a hollow [Note: “from the concavity,” witness 7] of a certain torrent [Note: Concerning this torrent near the village of Oldenbeke, not far from the sources of the Lippe, which is now called the resonant spring of the Bullerborn, see Fürstenberg, *Monumenta Paderbornensia*, p. 216 and following. Since the nature of this spring is such that there can be no doubt that it is the very torrent mentioned in our account, it is also clear that Irminsul stood not at Eresburg but several thousand paces east and south of the sources of the Lippe. From this we seem to learn both that Irminsul, or Ermensul, was a column of Irmin or Arminius, and the true site of the Varian disaster. That the image of the immortal hero and the shrine in which it stood were of enormous size, so that even today their foundations might remain, may be inferred from the fact that Karlus spent at least three days with his entire army in destroying it], that it was sufficient for the whole army [Note: “for the entire army,” perhaps witnesses 7 and 3].

Then [Note: “then,” perhaps witnesses 2, 3, and 7] the king, after destroying the idol, advanced to the river Weser and there received twelve hostages from the Saxons [Note: *ibi*, “there,” in witness 1]. From there he returned to Francia and celebrated both Christmas and the holy solemnity of the Easter feast at the estate of Herstal [Note: *Haristallio* in witness 7; “holy Easter,” witness 7].

### 773

Because Pope Hadrianus could not endure the arrogance of King Desiderius and the oppression [Note: omitted perhaps in witnesses 7 and 3] of the Lombards [Note: *Longobardorum* in witnesses 4, 5, and 6; “could not endure” in witness 2], he decided [Note: *ut* is omitted perhaps in witnesses 7 and 3; *mittere* for *mitteret* perhaps in witnesses 7 and 3] to send an embassy to Karlus, king of the Franks, and ask him to bring aid to himself and the Romans against the Lombards [Note: *ut sibi* for *eumque sibi*, and *ferret rogare* for *opem ferre rogaret*, perhaps witnesses 7 and 3]. Since this could not be done by a land route through Italy, he made the envoy he had sent, a man named Petrus, board a ship at Rome [Note: *navim* in witnesses 7 and 3] and travel by sea as far as Marseille [Note: “as far as Marseille,” witnesses 4, 5, and 6], and from there reach Francia by land.

When Petrus reached the king at the estate of Thionville [Note: *Theodone* in witness 5; *Thedonis* in witness 7; Thionville, Diedenhofen], where Karlus had then spent the winter, and explained to him the purpose of his embassy, he returned to Rome by the route on which he had come [Note: “went back,” witness 6].

After carefully considering the matters being conducted between the Romans and the Lombards, the king [Note: omitted in witness 7] judged that he ought to undertake war against the Lombards in defense of the Romans. He came with the entire Frankish army to Geneva [Note: *Gebennam* in witness 7; *Geneuam civitatem* in witness 3; Geneva, a city of Burgundy situated beside the Rhône].

There, while deliberating about undertaking the war, he divided the forces he had brought with him [Note: The text from here through the words “of the year 775” is absent because one leaf was cut out; witness 2 supplies the missing passage]. He ordered one part, under his paternal uncle Bernhardus [Note: *Bernhartus* in witness 7], to travel over the Mount of Jupiter [Note: the Great Saint Bernard, formerly the Pennine summit]; leading the other himself [Note: omitted in witness 3], he hastened to enter Italy by the Mount of Cenis [Note: *Cynisium* in witness 6; *Cinisum* in witness 7; “to enter Italy” is omitted in witness 7].

After crossing the Alpine ridge, he put to flight, without coming to battle [Note: *congressum*, “engagement,” in witness 7], King Desiderius, who was vainly trying to resist him. He besieged Desiderius, shut up in Pavia [Note: *Ticino* in witness 7; *Ticinio* in witness 4; *Tycino* in witness 6], and, because the assault on the city was difficult, spent the entire winter season in numerous efforts to capture it.

### 774
While these events were taking place in Italy, the Saxons, having found what seemed an exceedingly favorable opportunity [Note: [Col. 0396D] “favorable”: *oportunam* in 7 and 3?], because of the king’s absence [Note: [Col. 0396D] “having found”: *nacti* in 7 and 3?], ravaged the neighboring territories of the Hessi with sword and fire [Note: [Col. 0396D] “Hassorum”: *assorum* in 5]. When they were attempting to burn the basilica dedicated by the blessed martyr Boniface, at the place now called Frideslar by its inhabitants [Note: [Col. 0396D] Fritzlar], and were trying in vain to accomplish this, a sudden divinely sent fear seized them [Col. 0396C]; thrown into confusion by shameful panic [Note: [Col. 0396D] *turpi* was changed by a later hand to *a* in 3], they returned home in flight.

But the king, leaving an army to besiege and storm Ticenum [Note: [Col. 0396D] *tyceni* in 6], set out for Rome to pray. After fulfilling his vows, he returned from there to the army [Note: [Col. 0396D] *regressus* in 3], and compelled the city, exhausted by its long siege, to surrender [Note: [Col. 0396D] *in* for *ad* in 7]. The other cities followed its example, and all submitted themselves to the authority of the king and the Franks [Note: [Col. 0396D] omitted in 7]. And [Note: [Col. 0396D] *At* in 7 and 3?] the king, having subdued Italy and organized it for the time being, returned to Francia, taking King Desiderius captive.

For his son Adalgis [Note: [Col. 0396D] *Adalgisus* in 5, 6, and 7], in whom the Langobards [Note: [Col. 0396D] *langoberdi* in 1] appeared to place great hope, when the affairs of his homeland had been despaired of [Note: [Col. 0396D] *desperatis* in 5–7], abandoned Italy and went to Greece to the emperor Constantine; there he grew old in the rank and dignity of the patriciate [Note: [Col. 0396D] *patriatus* in 1; *permansit*—“he remained”—was added by a recent hand in codex 3].

When the king had returned home, before the Saxons realized that he had arrived, he sent an army divided into three parts into their territories. It devastated everything with fire and plunder, killed many Saxons who attempted to resist, and returned with enormous booty [Note: [Col. 0397D] *reversus*—“returned”—in 6]. [Note: [Col. 0397D] “He returned. As Charles was returning from Italy, he celebrated the dedication of the church of the holy martyr Nazarius and the translation of his body in our monastery of Lorsch, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 774, on the seventh day before the Kalends of September.”]

## 775

While the king was wintering at the villa of Carisiacum, he resolved to attack the treacherous and treaty-breaking Saxon people in war and to persevere until either they were defeated and subjected to the Christian religion [Note: [Col. 0400C] This reading is found consistently in nearly all medieval manuscripts; the editors have introduced *subiicere*, *traiicere*, and similar forms on their own authority], or they were utterly destroyed.

After holding a general assembly at the villa of Dura, and after also crossing the Rhine [Note: [Col. 0400C] *renoque* in 4], he marched into Saxony with all the forces of the kingdom. At the very first assault, he began to attack the fortress of Sigiburgum by fighting. It contained a Saxon garrison [Note: [Col. 0400C] *arx*—“fortress”—in 7; *in qua*—“in which”—in 7; *erat praesidium*—“there was a garrison”—in 6].

[Note: [Col. 0399D] Sigiburgum is neither Sigeberg nor, as the distinguished Wigand wishes in his book *Die Vorzeit. Ein Taschenbuch für 1824*, pp. 79 ff., Sigburg or Segburg on the Diemel, but a now-destroyed fortress on a sheer crag at the confluence of the Ruhr and Lenne. I learned from D. Moller’s essay *Über Hohensyberg*, Dortmund, 1804, that ancient ditches can still be seen there.]

He fortified Aeresburgum, another fortress destroyed by the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0400C] *muniunt*—“they fortify”—in 4], and placed a Frankish garrison in it. From there, coming to the river Wisura, he encountered at the place called Brunesberg a large force of Saxons assembled there, attempting to prevent his crossing the river [Note: [Col. 0400C] *a transitu*—“from crossing”—in 7].

[Note: [Col. 0400C] *Brunesberg*: *brunesberc* in 4; *brunnesberg* in 5 and 7.]

[Note: [Col. 0399D] Near Huxara; compare the *Monumenta Paderbornensia* and D. Wigand’s dissertation cited above. In 1295 it was completely destroyed by Bishop Otto of Paderborn and Counts Adolf and Albert of Schwalenberg, although until then it had sometimes been the fortress and residence of the abbots of Corvey. It is a high, precipitous mountain, fortified with several ditches, some of which are called *Sachsengraben*, that is, “ditches of the Saxons.”]

But in vain. For they were routed and put to flight at the first encounter, and a great number of them were killed there. And [Note: [Col. 0400C] *tunc rex*—“then the king”—in 6] the king, having crossed the river, hurried with part of the army to the river Ovacrum [Note: [Col. 0400C] *ouacerum* in 4 and 5; *obacrum* in 6 and 7]. There Hesso [Note: [Col. 0400C] *hesso* in 7; *hesuuinus* in 4; *esswinus* in 5; *hessumus* in 6], one of the leading Saxons [Note: [Col. 0400D] *ex*—“from among”—in 7 and 3?], met him with all the Ostfalai [Note: [Col. 0400D] *ostfalis* in 3? and 7; *ostflais* in 5; the remaining witnesses agree with the text]. He gave the hostages whom the king had demanded and swore an oath of loyalty.

When the king had returned from there [Note: [Col. 0400D] *reversus* in 7], and had reached the district called Bucki [Note: [Col. 0400D] *buchi* in 3?, 5, 6, and 7], the Angrarii [Note: [Col. 0400D] *angarii* in 4, 5, and 6; *ungarii* in 3] came to meet him with their leaders, and, like the Ostfalai, gave hostages and oaths as he had commanded [Note: [Col. 0400D] “gave hostages and swore oaths” in 7].

[Note: [Col. 0400D] In this district are the Bükkeberg mountain and the principal town of Bückeburg, made famous even among foreign peoples by its count Wilhelm.]

Meanwhile, the part of the army which he had left at the Wisura, having established a camp at the place called Hlidbeki [Note: [Col. 0400D] *hudbeki* in 1, 2, 3, 4, and 7; *hudbechi* in 5 and 6. It is clear that both forms derive from *hlidbeki*], was caught and deceived by a Saxon stratagem because of its careless conduct [Note: [Col. 0400D] *incaute agens*—“acting carelessly”—in 5 and 7].

[Note: [Col. 0400D] Today Lidbach, west of Minda.]

For when the Frankish foragers were returning to the camp around the ninth hour of the day, the Saxons mingled with them as though they too were their companions [Note: [Col. 0400D] “as though they were their companions” in 3? and 7], and thus entered the Frankish camp. They attacked the sleeping and half-awake men and are said to have slaughtered a considerable number of the unsuspecting multitude [Note: [Col. 0401D] “and, having attacked the sleeping men” in 7]. But they were driven back by the courage of those who were alert and resisted bravely [Note: [Col. 0401D] *compulsi*—“forced back”—in 3 and 7], withdrew from the camp, and departed under the agreement that could be made between them in such an emergency [Note: [Col. 0401D] *ex pacto* in 3? and 7].

When this was reported to the king, he hastened forward with all possible speed and pursued the rear of the fugitives [Note: [Col. 0401D] *insecutus* in 2–7], striking down a great multitude of them [Note: [Col. 0401D] “a great multitude from them” in 7; “he struck down a great multitude from them” in 3]. Then at last, after receiving hostages from the Westfalai [Note: [Col. 0401D] “Westfalorum” here, but in the following passages as in the text], he returned to Francia to winter [Note: [Col. 0401D] *franciam* in 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7].

## 776

As the king was returning home, he was informed that the Langobard Hruodgaud [Note: [Col. 0401D] *hyuodgaudum* in 3; *ruodgaudum* in 4; *hrudgaudum* in 5; *rodgaudum* in 6; *rotgaudum* in 7]—whom he himself had appointed duke of the people of Foroiulium [Note: [Col. 0401D] *foroviniensibus* in 6]—was plotting a revolution in Italy and that already several cities had defected to him [Note: [Col. 0401D] *cum plures*—“when more”—in 5].

Judging that he must hasten to suppress this movement, he set out for Italy at speed, taking with him the most energetic of his men [Note: [Col. 0401D] *quendam*—“a certain one”—in 4, 5, and 6]. After killing Hruodgaud [Note: [Col. 0401D] variant spellings: *hyuodgaudoque* in 3; *ruotgaudoque* in 4; *rudgaudoque* in 6; *rotgaudoque* in 7], who was aspiring to the kingship, and promptly receiving the cities that had defected to him, he appointed Frankish counts in them and returned with the same speed with which he had come [Note: [Col. 0401D] *velocitate venerat* in 4; *veloci* in 2].

Hardly had he crossed the Alps when messengers met him and announced that the fortress of Aeresburgum had been stormed by the Saxons and that the Frankish garrison which he had placed there had been expelled [Note: [Col. 0401D] “the fortress … stormed … and the garrison … expelled” in 3? and 7]. Another fortress, Sigiburgum, had indeed been attacked but had not been captured, because those who had been stationed there for the defense of the place made a sortie and attacked the Saxons from behind while they were off guard and intent on the assault [Note: [Col. 0401D] *praesidii causa*—“for the sake of the garrison”—in 3–7]. After killing many, they forced the rest not only to abandon the attack but also to flee; they pursued them, wandering and scattered, as far as the river Lippia [Note: [Col. 0401D] *lipiam* in 1 and 5; *libiam* in 2].

When this had been reported to the king [Note: [Col. 0404A] “when it had been announced to the king” in 7], he held an assembly at Wormacia and resolved that Saxony must be invaded without delay. Having gathered immense forces [Note: [Col. 0404D] “he resolved to march into Saxony, and, having gathered forces” in 7], he reached the place he had chosen in Saxony with such speed that he forestalled, by that haste, all the enemy’s preparations with which they were preparing to resist him [Note: [Col. 0404D] *conabantur*—“they were attempting”—in 7; *perverteret*—“overturn”—in 3?, 5, 6, and 7].

For when he came to the source of the Lippia, he found an immense multitude of that treacherous people as though devoted and suppliant, repenting of their error [Note: [Col. 0404D] *et*—“and”—in 7], and asking pardon [Note: [Col. 0404D] “and as though asking pardon for their error” in 7 and 3?]. He mercifully forgave them, and caused those who claimed that they wished to become Christians to be baptized. After they had given and received fraudulent promises concerning the preservation of their faith, and after he had received the hostages he had demanded, he restored the fortress of Aeresburgum, which had been demolished, built another fortress over the Lippia [Note: [Col. 0404D] The editor thinks it was at the site of modern Lippstadt], and left a substantial garrison in each. He himself returned to Callia and wintered at the villa of Heristallium [Note: [Col. 0404D] *haristallio* in 3? and 7].

## 777

As spring weather began to appear, the king set out for Noviomagus. After celebrating the solemnity of the Easter festival there, he marched into Saxony with a huge army to hold a general assembly of his people at the place called Padrabrun [Note: [Col. 0405D] *padrabrunno* in 2; *padabrunno* in 3; *patherbrunno* in 4; *padrabunno* in 5 and 6; *padrabrunna* in 7]. He did this because of the fraudulent promises of the Saxons, which he could not trust.

When he arrived there, he found the entire council and people of the treacherous nation, whom he had ordered to come to him, obedient but deceitfully devoted [Note: [Col. 0405D] *faclaciter* in 2]. For all came to him [Note: [Col. 0405D] *venerant* in 4] except Widichind [Note: [Col. 0405D] *winichindum* in 4; *windichinum* in 6; *widikindum* in 7], one of the leaders [Note: [Col. 0405D] *e*—“from among”—in 3? and 7] of the Westfalai. Conscious of many crimes and therefore afraid of the king [Note: [Col. 0405D] *veritus regem* in 4, 5, and 6], he had fled to Sigifrid, king of the Danes [Note: [Col. 0405D] *sigefridum* in 2].

The others who had come submitted themselves so completely to the king’s authority [Note: [Col. 0405D] *potestate*—“authority”—in 3] that they deserved to receive pardon on the condition that, if they ever again violated his decrees, they would be deprived of both homeland and freedom [Note: [Col. 0408C] *ut si*—“if”—in 7; *privarent*—“they would deprive”—in 1 and 2; *carerent*—“they would lack”—in 3, apparently an emendation; *privarentur*—“they would be deprived”—in 4–7]. A very large number of them, who had promised—though falsely—that they wished to become Christians, were baptized there [Note: [Col. 0408C] *baptisata* in 2?, 3?, and 7; *cum*—“with”—in 5].

At the same place and time, a certain Saracen named Ibinalarabi [Note: [Col. 0408C] *Ebinalarabi* in 5 and 6; *Abenalarabi* in 9; see the same volume, p. 170, line 18, a reference that escaped both Chesnius and Bouquet] came from Spain into the king’s presence with other Saracen companions. He surrendered himself and the cities over which the Saracen king had placed him.

Therefore, after completing the aforementioned assembly, the king returned to Gaul [Note: [Col. 0408C] “returned to Gaul” in 2, 3, and 7; “turned toward Gaul” in 4, 5, and 6; “returned to Francia” in 9] and celebrated Christmas at the villa of Dutciacum [Note: [Col. 0408D] *ducciaco* in 5; *duciaco* in 2, 3, and 9; *duniaco*, alternatively *ducciaco*, in one manuscript; *dutcia* in 7]. He celebrated Easter in Aquitania at Cassinoilum [Note: [Col. 0408D] *cassinoilum* in 2, 3, and 7; *cassinoildum* in 6; *cassinogilum* in 9]. [Note: [Col. 0408D] “In this villa a son was born to him by Queen Hildegard; they named him Hludouicus from the sacred font” in 7.]

## 778

Then, encouraged by the aforementioned Saracen, he formed—by no means without reason—the hope of capturing certain cities in Spain. Having gathered an army, he set out. After crossing the Pyrenean range in the region of the Vascones [Note: [Col. 0408D] *pyrenei* in 3?, 6, and 9; *pirynei* in 4; *pyrenaei montis*—“of the Pyrenean mountain”—in 7], he first attacked and took by surrender the town of Pamplona [Note: [Col. 0408D] *pampelonem* in 2? and 9] of the Navarri [Note: [Col. 0408D] *navarnorum* in 3; *navarorum* in 6].

From there, crossing the river Ebro at a ford [Note: [Col. 0408D] *iberum* in 7 and 9; *hyberum* in 5], he approached Caesaraugusta, the principal city of that region [Note: [Col. 0408D] *caesaraugustanam* in 5]. After receiving hostages offered by Ibinalarabi [Note: [Col. 0408D] *sibinalarabi* in 2; *abenalarabi* in 9; *ibnalarabi* in 7], by Abuthaur [Note: [Col. 0408D] *abithaur* in 9; *abittahur* in 6], and by certain other Saracens [Note: [Col. 0408D] *dederunt*—“gave”—in 7], he returned to Pamplona [Note: [Col. 0408D] *pampelonem* in 2? and 9]. He destroyed its walls down to the ground [Note: [Col. 0408D] *murum*—singular, “wall”—in 9 and 3] so that it could not rebel, and, intending to return, entered the pass of the Pyrenees.

At its summit the Vascones, having laid an ambush [Note: [Col. 0408C] *W. s.* in 4, 5, and 6], attacked the rear column and threw the entire army into great confusion [Note: [Col. 0408D] “they were throwing it into confusion with great tumult” in 9]. Although the Franks appeared superior to the Vascones both in arms and in courage, they were nevertheless defeated by the unfavorable terrain and by the unequal nature of the battle.

In this engagement most of the courtiers whom the king had placed in command of the forces were killed [Note: [Col. 0408D] *plurimi*—“very many”—in 7]. The baggage was plundered [Note: [Col. 0408D] *et dir. imp.*—“and the baggage was plundered”—in 7], and, because of their knowledge of the terrain, the enemy immediately dispersed in different directions [Note: [Col. 0408D] *statim*—“immediately”—is omitted in 9].

The reception of this wound [Note: [Col. 0409C] *accepti* in 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6; *accepti dolor*—“the pain of the wound”—in 7; *accepti recordatio*—“the memory of the wound”—in 3? and 9; since a noun is required here, I judged that the sense should be restored by adding one letter, rejecting the conjectures of manuscripts 7 and 9] clouded in the king’s heart a large part of the successes that had been achieved in Spain [Note: [Col. 0409C] *in inspania* in 2].

Meanwhile, the Saxons, as though they had found an opportunity [Note: [Col. 0409C] *nacti* in 3–10], took up arms and advanced as far as the Rhine. But since they could not cross the river, they devastated with sword and fire everything consisting of villages and estates from the city of Diutia [Note: [Col. 0409C] *diucia* in 6; *duicia* in 5 and 9; *duitia* in 7] to the stream [Note: [Col. 0409D] “the river” in 7] of the Moselle.

[Note: [Col. 0409D] Duitz, opposite Cologne.]

In the same way they destroyed sacred and profane things alike. The enemy’s anger had spared neither age nor sex [Note: [Col. 0409C] *sexus seu*—“sex, or”—in 7; *sacrarum virginum*—“of sacred virgins”—in the note], so that it was plainly evident that they had entered Frankish territory not to plunder but to exact vengeance [Note: [Col. 0409D] “to exercise vengeance” in 9].

When the king received news of this at the city of Autesiodorum [Note: [Col. 0409D] *antesiodorum* in 1 and 9; *autisiodorum* in 4, 5, and 6; *autefioderum* in 3; *altissiodorum* in 7], he immediately ordered the eastern Franks [Note: [Col. 0409D] “eastern Franks” in 4, 5, and 6] and the Alamanni [Note: [Col. 0409D] *alemannos* in 7 and 9] to hasten to repel the enemy. After dismissing the rest of the forces, he himself went to the villa of Heristallium [Note: [Col. 0409D] *haristallium* in 3 and 9; so consistently], where he had decided to winter [Note: [Col. 0409D] *hyemaret*—“would winter”—in 9].

But the Franks and Alamanni who had been sent against the Saxons hurried toward them by forced marches, hoping that perhaps they might find them in their own territories. The Saxons, however, having already completed their undertaking, were returning to their homes. The men sent by the king followed their tracks and found them traveling through the district of the Hessi above the river Aderna [Note: [Col. 0409D] *repererunt* in 9; *reppererunt* in 3]. They attacked them immediately at the very ford of the river and struck them down in such a slaughter [Note: [Col. 0409D] *cecidere* in 7] that, from their immense multitude, scarcely a few are said to have reached home by flight [Note: [Col. 0409D] *fuendo* in 1].

## 779

The king, moving from Heristallium, where he had wintered and where he had celebrated Christmas and holy Easter, at the first mildness of spring, came to Compendium [Note: [Col. 0409D] Compiègne]. After completing the business for which he had come and returning [Note: [Col. 0409D] *reverteretur* in 3? and 9], he was met by Hildibrand [Note: [Col. 0409D] *hildebrandus* in 2, 3, 6, 7, and 9; *hiltibrandus* in 5], duke of Spoletium [Note: [Col. 0409D] *spoletanus* in 3, 5, 7, and 9; *spolitanus* in 6], with splendid gifts at the villa of Wirciniacum [Note: [Col. 0409D] *wirtiniaco* in 3].

[Note: [Col. 0409D] Neither Valesius nor Bouquet investigated its location. If it is not Virisiacum, modern Verzy near Rheims, it must certainly be sought on the route from Compendium to Dura.]

He received him kindly [Note: [Col. 0409D] *benignissime*—“most kindly”—in 3 and 9; *recepit*—“received”—in 3 and 9], gave him gifts, and sent him back to his duchy.

With his mind intent on the Saxon expedition, he went to Dura. After holding a general assembly there according to custom, he crossed the Rhine with the army at the place called Lippeham [Note: [Col. 0409D] *lippehan* in 2; *lipphean* in 3; *lippiam* in 4; *lippia* in 5, 6, and 7].

[Note: [Col. 0410D] At the confluence of the Lippia and the Rhine.]

When the Saxons, led by a vain hope, attempted to resist him at a place called Buocholt [Note: [Col. 0412C] *bucholt* in 6 and 9], they were routed and put to flight [Note: [Col. 0412C] *fagati* in 1; *fatigati* in 5].

The king entered the territory of the Westfalai and received them all into submission. From there he came to the Wisura and, having set up camp at a place called Midufulli [Note: [Col. 0412C] *medufulli* in 9; *nudufulli*, alternatively *midufulli*; *medufulli* in 7], maintained a permanent camp there for several days. There the Angrarii [Note: [Col. 0412C] *angarii* in 2 and 7; *angeri* in 9; *ungarii* in 3] and the Ostfalai came, gave hostages, and swore oaths.

After completing this, the king crossed the Rhine and withdrew to the city of Wormacia for winter quarters [Note: [Col. 0412D] “to Wormacia” in 7; “to winter at Wormacia” in 9].

## 780

Then, as soon as a favorable opportunity in the season seemed to smile upon him [Note: [Col. 0412D] *arridere* in 3, 4, 5, and 6; *addesse* in 9], he again set out with a large army into Saxony [Note: [Col. 0412D] “into Saxony” in 7 and 9]. Passing by the fortress of Aeresburgum [Note: [Col. 0412D] *arx*—“fortress”—in 9], he came to the source of the Lippia, where he established a camp and stayed for several days.

From there he turned his route eastward and approached the river Ovacrum [Note: [Col. 0412D] *obacrum* in 9]. When all the Saxons of the eastern regions had met him there, as he had ordered [Note: [Col. 0412D] *omnes*—“all”—is absent in 6; *omnium* in 3? and 9], a very large number of them were baptized at a place called Orheim [Note: [Col. 0412D] *horheim* in 6 and 9; *oreheim*, alternatively *horheim*, in 7], according to their customary pretense.

From there he proceeded to the Elbe. Having established a camp at the place where the Ora [Note: [Col. 0412D] *hora* in 3, 5, 6, and 9] and the Elbe meet, he devoted his efforts to settling matters both among the Saxons who inhabit this side of the river [Note: [Col. 0412D] *ceteriorem*—“nearer”—in 1; *exteriorem*—“outer”—in 9] and among the Slavs [Note: [Col. 0412D] “and among the Slavs” in 7; “and of the Slavs” in 4; *sicavorum* in 6] who inhabit the farther bank.

After arranging and ordering these matters for the time being, he returned to Francia. He then took counsel and resolved to go to Rome to pray and fulfill his vows. Taking his wife and children with him, he set out for Italy without delay. He celebrated Christmas at Ticenum [Note: [Col. 0412D] *ticini* in 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 9] and completed the remainder of the winter by staying there [Note: [Col. 0412D] *mansit*—“he stayed”—in 3? and 9].

## 781

From there he came to Rome and was received with honor by Pope Hadrian. [Note: [Col. 0413D] Omitted in 7.] While he was celebrating holy Easter there, the same pontiff baptized his son Pippin [Note: [Col. 0413D] “his son Pippin” in 7] and anointed him king [Note: [Col. 0413D] omitted in 3 and 9]. He also anointed Hludewicus [Note: [Col. 0413D] *hludowicum* in 7; *lovdewicum* in 5; *ludewicum* in 4 and 6; *ludovicum* in 9, and likewise almost consistently in what follows], his brother, and placed a crown upon him [Note: [Col. 0413D] *corona*—“a crown”—in 1].

The elder, Pippin, was established as king in Langobardia, while the younger, Hludewicus [Note: [Col. 0413D] the words “that is Hludewicus” are absent in 9; *idem ... idem*—“the same ... the same”—in 3], was established as king in Aquitania.

When the king had left Rome and arrived at Mediolanum, Thomas, archbishop of that city [Note: [Col. 0413D] “bishop” in 9], baptized his daughter there, naming her Gisla [Note: [Col. 0413D] *gisilam* in 5 and 6], and received her from the sacred font. After these events, he returned to Francia.

While he was still at Rome, an agreement was reached between him and Pope Hadrian that they should jointly send envoys to Tassilo, duke of Baioaria [Note: [Col. 0413D] “duke of Baioaria” in 3, 4, 6, and 9], to remind him of the oath which he had sworn to King Pippin, his sons, and the Franks [Note: [Col. 0413D] *filii*—“sons”—in 1]: namely, that he ought to be subject and obedient to them [Note: [Col. 0413D] “so that he would be subject to them and obedient” in 3; “so that he would be subject and obedient” in 9; “so that he would be subject to them and obedient” in Bouquet].

For this embassy, Formosus [Note: [Col. 0413D] *formosus* in 5, 6, 7, and 9] and Damasus [Note: [Col. 0413D] *damasius* in 6], bishops, were chosen and sent on the pope’s behalf; on the king’s behalf, the deacon Richolfus [Note: [Col. 0413D] *ricolphus* in 3] and Eberhardus [Note: [Col. 0413D] *eburhardus* in 2, 3, and 4; *eberhartus* in 9], master of the household cupbearers, were chosen.

When they had spoken with the aforesaid duke as they had been ordered [Note: [Col. 0413D] *cum quae iussi* in 7], his heart was so softened that he said he wished to hasten immediately into the king’s presence, provided that such hostages were given to him that he would have no reason to fear for his safety [Note: [Col. 0413D] *darentur*—“were given”—in 5 and 7; “hostages be given” in 3? and 9].

After these hostages had been given, he came without delay to the king at Wormacia, swore the oath that had been commanded [Note: [Col. 0413D] the words “he swore the oath that had been commanded” are absent in 1], and immediately gave the twelve hostages that had been demanded. Sindbertus [Note: [Col. 0413D] *sindberdus* in 1; *suidbertus* in Bouquet], bishop of Reginum in Baioaria, brought them to the king’s presence at Carisiacum.

But the same duke, after returning home, did not remain long in the faith he had promised. The king spent the winter at the same villa [Note: [Col. 0413D] *transiens* is identical in the manuscripts 3?, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 9; *transigens*—“spending”—is another reading], celebrating Christmas and Easter in the same place [Note: [Col. 0413D] “in the same place” is absent in 7]. [Note: [Col. 0413D] “During these same days, when Guichard, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Germain, had died, Robert was appointed in his place as its head” in 7.]

## 782

At the beginning of summer, when the army could already be led forth because of the abundance of fodder, he judged that they should go into Saxony and hold there, as he did every year in Francia [Note: [Col. 0416C] omitted in 5], a general assembly.

After crossing the Rhine at Cologne, he came with the entire Frankish army to the source of the Lippia and, having set up camp there [Note: [Col. 0416C] omitted in 2, 4, 5, 6, and 7], remained there for many days. Among other matters, he both heard and dismissed the envoys of Sigifrid [Note: [Col. 0416D] *sigefridi* in 7 and 9], king of the Danes, and those whom Caganus and Iugurrus, princes of the Huns, had sent to him as though for the sake of peace [Note: [Col. 0416D] *princeps*—singular— in 2; *solvit*—“dismissed”—in 9].

When the assembly had been completed and he had withdrawn across the Rhine into Gaul, Widokindus [Note: [Col. 0416D] *widochindus* in 5; *widocindus* in 6; *widikindus* in 3, 7, and 9], who had fled to the Nordmanni [Note: [Col. 0416D] *normannos* in 2, written by a second hand; 7], returned to his homeland and stirred the minds of the Saxons to revolt with false hopes [Col. 0416B] [Note: [Col. 0416D] “the minds of the Saxons” in 3? and 9].

Meanwhile, the king was informed [Note: [Col. 0416D] “was notified” in 7] that the Sorabi, Slavs who inhabit the plains lying between the Elbe [Note: [Col. 0416D] *albino* in 1] and the Sala, had entered the territories of the Thuringi [Note: [Col. 0416D] *euringorum*, a typographical error, according to Chesnius] and the Saxons bordering them, in order to plunder, and had ravaged certain places with plundering and fire [Note: [Col. 0416D] *et*—“and”—in 7].

He immediately summoned three of his officials, Adalgis the chamberlain [Note: [Col. 0416D] *camerario suo*—“his chamberlain”—in 4, 5, and 6; *cubiculario*—“bedchamber officer”—in 9], Geilo the count of the stable [Note: [Col. 0416D] omitted in 9], and Worado the count of the palace [Note: [Col. 0416D] omitted in 7], and ordered them, taking with them the eastern Franks and Saxons, to suppress the audacity of the rebellious Slavs with all possible speed [Note: [Col. 0416D] “with whatever speed they could” in 3 and 7; “as quickly as possible” in 9].

When they had entered Saxon territory to carry out the king’s orders [Note: [Col. 0416D] “had entered the territories with the boundaries reversed” in 7], they discovered that the Saxons, following Widukind’s counsel [Note: [Col. 0416D] *widokindi* in 4; *widikindi* in 3, 7, and 9], had prepared to wage war against the Franks [Note: [Col. 0416D] *paratos*—“prepared”—in 3, 5, 6, and 9].

Abandoning the route by which they had intended to go to the Slavs, they hurried with the forces of the eastern Franks to the place where they had heard that the Saxons were assembled [Note: [Col. 0416D] “where they had heard the Saxons were assembled” in 9; “where they had heard that they were assembled” in Bouquet].

In Saxony they were met by Count Theoderic [Note: [Col. 0416D] *teodericus* in 4; *thederichus* in 9; *thedericus* in Bouquet, and likewise hereafter], a relative of the king, with the forces which, after hearing of the Saxon revolt, he had been able to gather hurriedly in Ribuaria [Note: [Col. 0416D] *ripuaria* in 2, 3, and 9]. He advised the hastening envoys first to learn through scouts, as quickly as possible, where the Saxons were and what they were doing; then, if the nature of the place permitted, they should attack them all together.

They praised this advice and reached with him the mountain called Suntal [Note: [Col. 0416D] *sunttal* in 2; *sultal* in 4; *sontal* in 9], on whose northern side the Saxon camp had been established [Col. 0417A]. There Theoderic set up camp. The others, as they had agreed with him [Note: [Col. 0417D] *convenerant* in 3–9], crossed the Wisura and encamped on the very bank of the river so that they might more easily go around the mountain [Note: [Col. 0417D] *circuire* in 3, 4, 7, and 9].

After conferring among themselves, they feared that the fame of victory would be attributed to Theoderic if they had him with them in the same battle. Therefore, without him [Note: [Col. 0417D] *eo*—“him”—in 3 and 9], they decided to engage the Saxons. Taking up their arms, each one hurried with the utmost speed toward the place where the Saxons stood in battle before their camp—not as against an enemy standing in a battle line, but as though pursuing fugitives and plundering spoils, each according to the speed of his horse [Note: [Col. 0417D] “they hastened toward the fugitive, pursuing the rear and plundering the spoils” in 9].

When they had arrived there badly [Note: [Col. 0417D] omitted in 3 and 9], they fought badly as well. For when battle had been joined [Note: [Col. 0417D] *cum misso* in 1], they were surrounded by the Saxons and almost all were killed. Those who were able to escape did not reach their own camp, from which they had set out, but fled to Theoderic’s camp, which lay beyond the mountain.

The loss was nevertheless greater for the Franks than their numbers would suggest, because two of the envoys, Adalgis and Geilo, four counts [Note: [Col. 0417D] *quatuor* in 2–9], and as many as twenty other distinguished and noble men were killed, besides the others who followed them and preferred to perish with them rather than live after them.

When the king received news of this [Note: [Col. 0417D] *suscepisset*—“had received”—in 9], he judged that he must delay nothing. He hastily gathered an army and set out for Saxony. Summoning all the Saxon leaders to him, he investigated the authors of the revolt. Although they all proclaimed Widokind [Note: [Col. 0417D] *widikindum* in 3, 5, and 9] to be the author of this crime [Note: [Col. 0417D] *cuius*—“of which”—in 1], they could not hand him over, because, after the deed had been committed, he had gone to the Nordmanni [Note: [Col. 0417C] *his*—“these”—in 2; omitted in 3 and 9].

The others, however, who had followed his persuasion and committed so great a crime [Note: [Col. 0417D] *peregere* in 7], were handed over, up to the number of 4,500. At the river Alara [Note: [Col. 0417D] *alarum* in 2 and 7], at the place called Ferdi [Note: [Col. 0417D] *ferdia* in 2; *fredi* in 7], they were all beheaded on the same day by order of the king.

[Note: [Col. 0417D] Verden.]

After carrying out this vengeance [Note: [Col. 0417D] *patrata*—“carried out”—in 6 and 7], the king withdrew to the villa of Theodone for winter quarters [Note: [Col. 0417D] *in theodonem villam* in 7; *theodonis villam* in 9].
