There he celebrated Christmas and Easter in the customary manner [Note: [Col. 0417D] *ibique et*—“there also”—in 3 and 9; “there” is omitted in 7 and 9].

## 783

When spring weather smiled upon him and he had prepared himself for the Saxon expedition—for news had reached him of their complete revolt [Note: [Col. 0417D] omitted in 4; omitted after *ad eum* in 9]—before he moved from the aforementioned villa [Note: [Col. 0420D] *se moveret*—“moved”—in 9], Queen Hildigardis [Note: [Col. 0417D] *hiltigardis* in 5; *hildegardis* in 7], his wife, died on the second day before the Kalends of May.

After he had performed the customary rites at her funeral [Note: [Col. 0420D] *postquam*—“after”—in 7; *persolverat*—“had performed”—in 7; *persolvisset*—“had performed”—in 9], he led the army into Saxony, as he had planned.

When he learned that the Saxons were preparing for battle at the place called Theotmelli [Note: [Col. 0420D] *teotmelli* in 4; *theothmelli* in 7; *theotinelli* in 6; *thietmelle* in 9], he hastened toward them with all possible speed [Note: [Col. 0420D] “with the utmost speed” in 9]. When battle had been joined, he struck them down in so great a slaughter that, from their innumerable multitude, very few are said to have escaped [Note: [Col. 0420D] *praeparasse*—“had prepared”—in 7; *cognovisset*—“had learned”—in 9].

When he had withdrawn with the army from the battlefield to Padrabrunnon [Note: [Col. 0420D] *patherbrunnon* in 4; *padrabrunnam* in 9; *padrabunnum* in 7], and had set up camp there to await the part of the army that still had to come from Francia, he heard that the Saxons were gathering in the territory of the Westfalai above the river Hasa, so that they might engage him there in battle if he came.

Moved by this report, he united the Frankish forces that had then come to him with those that he already had with him [Col. 0420B] and set out without delay for the place where they were assembled [Note: [Col. 0420D] *quo*—“to which”—in 7]. He engaged them and fought with the same success as before. An immeasurable number of them were killed, their spoils were plundered, and a great number of captives was also led away.

From there, victorious, he turned his route eastward [Note: [Col. 0420D] omitted in 3? and 9] and traversed everything, devastating it, first as far as the Wisura and then as far as the Elbe [Note: [Col. 0420D] *albim* in Bouquet].

Returning from there to Francia, he married Fastrada, daughter of Count Radolfus [Note: [Col. 0420D] *radulfi* in 3 and 7; *radoldi* in 4; *rudolfi* in 5], a Frank by nationality. By her he had two daughters.

In the same year, the king’s mother, Berhtrada, of good memory [Note: [Col. 0420D] *berthrada* in 3, 5, and 9; *bertrada* in 4 and 7; *berchtrada* in 6], died on the fourth day before the Ides of July. He himself settled at the villa of Heristallium to winter there [Note: [Col. 0420D] omitted in 5], and celebrated Christmas and holy Easter there.

## 784
Source/review notes: All 269 printed apparatus notes are retained as separately associated year-and-lemma entries with exact readings, sigla, and source-specific English explanations; corrupt or abbreviated readings remain explicit.

[Col. 0420D]

As soon as the opportunity of the season arose, the king, intent on completing the remnants of the Saxon war, crossed the Rhine with his army at the place called Lippeham [Note: lippeam; lippea; lippia; lippeheim], having devastated the districts of the Westphalians, and came to the Weser. When he had settled in the place called Huculbi, with his camp established beside the river, he saw that he could not cross into the northern parts of Saxony, as he had planned, because of the excessive flooding of the waters, which had then suddenly resulted from the continual rains. Therefore he turned his route toward Thuringia and ordered his son Charles to remain with part of the army in the territory of the Westphalians. He himself, traveling through Thuringia, came into the plains of Saxony adjoining the rivers Elbe and Saale; after laying waste the fields of the eastern Saxons and burning their villages, he returned to Francia from Scahningi [Note: Schoningen; variants: scaningi, scanigni, schaningi, schannico, schahningi, schaninge]—this was the name of the place [Note: in this place the name was; absent in one witness; in witness 3 it is read only as *loco*, “place”; for this was the name of the place].

But his son Charles, when a Saxon army had met him as he was traveling in the district of Draigni [Note: daigno] beside the river Lippe [Note: according to Falk, *Traditiones Corbeienses*, pp. 318–319, these places were Hertfeld, Lisborn, Werne, and even Cappenberg], engaged them in a cavalry battle and fought with a fortunate and successful outcome [Note: “fought with the outcome”; absent in witnesses 3, 4, and 9]. For after a great number of them had been killed and the rest scattered in different directions, he returned victorious to his father at Worms.

The king, however, having again assembled an army, set out for Saxony. After celebrating the day of the Lord’s Nativity in camp beside the river Ambra [Note: the Emmer], in the district of Huettagoe [Note: wettagoe; manuscript: huthagoe; Huettagoe; in the counties of Pyrmont and Schwalenberg and the neighboring lands; compare Falke, cited work, p. 6], near the Saxon fortress called Skidroburg [Note: “which is called Kidroburg”; “which is called Skidroburc”; “which is called Skridoburg”; “which is called Dekidroburg”; Schieder beside the Ambra], he advanced in a campaign of devastation to a place called Rimi [Note: rum]. There the Weser and the Waharna [Note: warharna; waharnna; vagarna] come together. When both the harshness of the winter season and the flooding of the waters prevented him from advancing farther, he withdrew into the fortress of Aeresburg for winter quarters [Note: “into Aeresburg”; “into the fortress of Aeresburg”].

## 785

[Col. 0421D]

Since he had decided to winter there, he summoned and brought to himself his wife and children, and, leaving with them in the same fortress a sufficiently trustworthy and strong garrison [Note: “camp” or “within the same camp”; “in the same fortress”], he himself went out with a mobile force to lay waste the Saxon districts and plunder the villages. By ranging everywhere and mingling everything with slaughter and fire, both personally and through the commanders whom he had sent, he made the winter sufficiently troubled for the Saxons.

After he had inflicted enormous destruction on nearly all the regions of the Saxons by such devastations throughout the whole winter season [Note: “throughout the whole period of winter”], the winter at last having passed and supplies having been brought from Francia [Note: “brought”], he held the public assembly of his people, according to the customary solemnity, at the place called Paderborn [Note: patherbrunn; padrabunno; padrabrunna]. When he had completed the matters that belonged to the business of that assembly [Note: “those matters”], he set out for the district called Bardengau [Note: bardengo; bardengoum; bardengau]. There, hearing that Widukind [Note: Widogind; widikind] and Abbio [Note: “and” is omitted in several witnesses; one editor reads “against all except Abbio,” but *ad Abbionem* cannot apparently mean “against Abbio,” so *ac* should be retained; the Saxon Poet likewise seems to have read either *ac* or *et*] were in the trans-Elbian region of the Saxons [Note: transalbiona; “the trans-Elbian region”], he first began, through Saxon intermediaries, to urge them not to hesitate to come over to his allegiance, abandoning their treachery [Note: “to come to their allegiance”; “they might come”].

Since they, conscious of their crimes [Note: this is absent in one witness], hesitated to entrust themselves to the king’s faith [Note: “to entrust themselves to the king”], they finally received from him the pledge of immunity that they desired and obtained the hostages for their safety whom they had requested. Amalwin, one of the courtiers, had brought these hostages to them after being sent by the king. They came with that same Amalwin into the king’s presence at the villa of Attigny [Note: attinico], and there they were baptized [Note: baptised].

For after the king had sent the aforementioned Amalwin to summon them [Note: to bring them], he returned to Francia. The obstinacy of Saxon treachery [Note: “perversity”] then subsided for several years [Note: “several years”] chiefly because they could not find suitable opportunities for revolt.

In the same year, beyond the Rhine among the eastern Franks, an excessive conspiracy was formed against the king. Its author was known to have been Count Hardrad [Note: hartrad]. But news of this was quickly brought to the king, and through his skill so powerful a conspiracy soon subsided without any great danger. Its authors were condemned, some to the deprivation of their eyesight and others to exile [Note: “punishment”].

## 786

[Col. 0424D]

When the winter season had ended and the king had celebrated holy Easter at the villa of Attigny, he decided to send an army into Cisalpine Brittany [Note: “the maritime region”]. For when the island of Brittany had been invaded by Angles and Saxons [Note: “occupied”], a large part of its inhabitants, crossing the sea, seized territories on the farthest borders of Gaul, those of the Veneti and the Coriosolitae [Note: corosolitae]. That people, having been subdued and made tributary by the kings of the Franks, used to pay, though unwillingly, the tax imposed upon it.

Since at that time they were not obedient to orders, Audulf, superintendent of the royal table, was sent there and suppressed the insolence of that faithless people with remarkable speed [Note: “in anger”; the reading is uncertain]. He brought to the king at Worms both the hostages whom he had received and several of the leading men of the people.

When peace had been established everywhere, the king decided to go to Rome and attack the part of Italy now called Benevento [Note: Beneventan; “in which Benevento is situated”]. He judged it appropriate to bring under his authority the remaining portion of that kingdom, whose head he held in the person of the captured King Desiderius, and whose greater part he had already subdued in Lombardy [Note: “the greater part”].

He did not delay long but quickly gathered the Frankish forces and entered Italy in the very harshness of winter. After celebrating the Lord’s Nativity at Florence, a city of Tuscany, he hastened toward Rome with all possible speed [Note: “with the greatest speed”]. When he had arrived there and had deliberated with Pope Hadrian and with his own nobles about his expedition into Benevento [Note: this phrase is absent in some witnesses], Aragisus [Note: aragissus], duke of the Beneventans, heard of his arrival and learned of his intention to enter his territory. He tried to divert the king from his purpose.

He sent his elder son Rumold [Note: rumoald; rumuldo; runoldo] with gifts to the king and began to ask him not to enter the land of the Beneventans. But the king, judging that he ought to act very differently in the matter he had begun, kept Rumold with him and advanced with his entire army to Capua, a city of Campania [Note: “Capua, a city of Campania”; the phrase is absent in one witness]. Having established his camp there, he settled in it [Note: this clause is absent in two witnesses], intending from there to wage war [Note: “to begin war”; “to wage war”], unless the aforementioned duke had forestalled the king’s intention by prudent counsel [Note: “purpose”].

For, abandoning Benevento [Note: “the city of Benevento”], which is regarded as the capital of that land, he withdrew with his people to Salerno, a coastal city, as though it were more strongly fortified [Note: “a stronger fortification”]. He sent an embassy and offered both his sons to the king, promising that he would willingly obey everything that was commanded.

The king accepted his requests and, out of regard also for fear of God, refrained from war. He received the duke’s younger son, named Grimoald [Note: grimoaldus], as a hostage [Note: “in place of a hostage”], and sent the elder son back to his father. In addition, he received eleven hostages from the people [Note: “eleven hostages”] and sent envoys to bind both the duke himself and the entire Beneventan people by oaths [Note: “to obligate them”].

After this he spoke with the envoys of Emperor Constantine [Note: “Constantine”], who had been sent to him to request his daughter in marriage. After dismissing them, he returned to Rome and celebrated the holy Easter feast with great joy [Note: “Easter”; “the paschal feast”].

## 787

[Col. 0425D]

While the king was still staying at Rome [Note: “the king” is absent in one witness; several witnesses add “still”], Tassilo, duke of Bavaria [Note: “of the Bavarians”], sent his envoys, namely Bishop Arn [Note: of Salzburg] and Abbot Hunric [Note: Hunrich; Heinrich; Hainrich; of Lunaelacus, or Mondsee], to Pope Hadrian, asking that he deign to become a mediator of peace between the king and himself.

The pontiff did not think that his request should be refused. Instead, with as much persistence as he could, he took care to intercede with the king so that peace and concord might arise between them through the admonition and intervention of his apostolic authority [Note: “with very assiduous persistence”].

When the king replied that he greatly desired this as well, and at the same time asked the envoys of the aforementioned duke what security they ought to provide for this pacification [Note: “peace”], they answered that nothing had been entrusted to them concerning this matter and that they would do nothing else in this affair except carry the king’s and the pontiff’s replies back to their lord [Note: “would become”; variant: “would do”].

Moved by their words, the pope decided that, as deceitful and fraudulent men, they should be struck with the sword of anathema if they abandoned the faith formerly promised to the king. Thus they returned with the peace negotiations unfinished [Note: “the matter of peace unfinished”].

The king, having venerated the thresholds of the holy apostles [Note: absent in one witness] and fulfilled his vows [Note: “of salvation”], received the apostolic blessing and returned to Francia. When he found his wife Fastrada, his sons and daughters, and the whole company that he had left with them at Worms, he decided to hold his general assembly there.

At that assembly he recounted before his nobles everything he had done in Italy. Finally, when mention was made of the envoys of Tassilo who had come to him at Rome, he formed the plan of testing what Tassilo intended to do concerning the loyalty he had promised [Note: “what he wished to offer in fulfillment of his promised faith”]. He therefore assembled a huge army, divided it into three parts, and decided to march against Bavaria [Note: “against Bavaria and Tassilo himself”].

He ordered his son Pippin to come with the Italian forces into the Tridentine valley [Note: tridentine], while the eastern Franks and the Saxons, as they had been ordered, approached the Danube at the place called Pferinga [Note: feringa]. He himself, with the army he had brought with him, settled above the river Lech, which separates the Alamanni and the Bavarians [Note: “divides them”], in the suburb of the city of Augsburg. From there he was certainly going to advance against Bavaria with so powerful a force, unless Tassilo had taken counsel for himself and his people by coming to the king [Note: “had taken counsel”].

For, seeing himself surrounded on every side, Tassilo came as a suppliant and begged to be forgiven for his former deeds [Note: “prayed”]. The king, however, being naturally very merciful, spared the suppliant and petitioner. He received from him, besides his son Theodo, twelve other hostages whom he himself demanded [Note: this phrase is absent in one witness; another reads “whom he had demanded”], secured the people of the land by oaths, and returned to Francia.

In the suburb of Mainz, at the villa called Ingelheim [Note: ingilumheim; ingillunheim; ingilinheim; ingelheim], because he had wintered there, he celebrated both the Lord’s Nativity and Easter.

## 788

[Col. 0429A]

Since the king had decided to hold a general assembly of his people in the same villa, and had ordered Duke Tassilo, like his other vassals, to be present at that assembly [Note: the phrase is absent in one witness], when Tassilo had arrived in the king’s presence as he had been commanded, he was accused by the Bavarians of lèse-majesté [Note: “high treason”; “the crime of lèse-majesté”].

They charged him with having, after he had given his son as a hostage to the king, at the urging of his wife Liutberga [Note: the name was altered by a later corrector in one witness to Litberga; variants: Liuthburga, Lutberga, Luitburga, Luitkarda], who was the daughter of King Desiderius of the Lombards and had always been most hostile to the Franks after her father’s exile, stirred up the Hunnic people against the king and persuaded them to undertake war against the Franks [Note: “had stirred up”].

The events of that same year proved that this was true. Many other statements and deeds were also charged against him, things that could have been done or uttered only by an enemy and an angry man [Note: absent in one witness]. He did not begin to deny even one of them.

Convicted of wrongdoing [Note: *noxae*; variant *noxiae*], by unanimous agreement he was condemned as guilty of lèse-majesté to capital punishment [Note: “the crime of lèse-majesté”]. But the king’s clemency took care to free him, although he had been sentenced to death. For, after his clothing had been changed, he was sent to a monastery, where he lived as religiously as willingly as he had entered it [Note: “as willingly as he entered it”; “willingly”].

Likewise his son Theodo [Note: teodo] was tonsured and devoted to monastic life [Note: this clause is absent in one witness]. The Bavarians who were found to have been aware of and accomplices in their treachery and fraud [Note: “associates”; “were reported to have been”; “are reported to be”] were confined in exile in various places [Note: “were exiled”].

The Huns, as they had promised Tassilo [Note: “had promised”], gathered two armies: with one they attacked the March of Friuli [Note: “the March”; “the Marchland”], and with the other Bavaria. But in vain. For they were defeated and put to flight in both places, and after losing many of their men they withdrew to their own territories at great cost.

As though intending to avenge this injury, they attacked Bavaria again with larger forces. But in the first encounter [Note: “at the first battle”] they were driven back by the Bavarians, and an innumerable multitude of them was killed [Note: “their innumerable multitude”]. Many of those who, attempting to escape by flight, wished to swim across the Danube [Note: one witness reads “did not wish to swim across it”] were swallowed by the river’s currents [Note: absent in one witness].

Meanwhile Emperor Constantine, angry because the king had refused him his daughter, ordered the patrician Theodore [Note: teodoro], prefect of Sicily, together with his other commanders, to lay waste the territory of the Beneventans.

While they were carrying out their orders, Grimoald [Note: grimoaldus], whom the king had appointed duke of the Beneventans in that same year after his father’s death [Note: “duke Beneventan”; variant “Beneventan”], and Hildebrand [Note: hildebrandus], duke of the Spoletans [Note: “of the Spoleto people”], met them in Calabria with the forces they had been able to assemble. With them was the king’s envoy Winigis [Note: winnigis], who later succeeded Hildebrand in the duchy of Spoleto [Note: “Spoletan duchy”; “duchy of Spoleto”].

They joined battle and killed an enormous number of the enemy. Victorious without serious loss to themselves or their men, they brought a large number of captives and spoils back to their camp.

The king, however, set out for Bavaria and organized and arranged that province together with its boundaries. Returning from there, he celebrated at his palace in Aachen, where he had wintered, both the Lord’s Nativity [Note: “the day of the Lord’s Nativity”; one witness omits the phrase] and holy Easter according to the customary solemnity.

## 789

[Col. 0433C]

There is a nation of Slavs [Note: Sclavi; Sclavonians] in Germania, settled along the shore of the ocean. In their own language it is called Welatabi, but in Frankish Wiltzi [Note: Uultzi; in the margin: Wilsi]. That people was always hostile to the Franks. It used to persecute with hatred, oppress by war, and provoke its neighbors who were either subject to or allied with the Franks [Note: “challenge them”].

The king, judging that he could no longer endure its insolence [Note: “for a longer time”; “being angry”], decided to attack it in war. Having assembled a huge army, he crossed the Rhine at Cologne. From there, traveling through Saxony, when he reached the Elbe he established a camp on its bank and joined the river with two bridges. He fortified one of them at both ends with a rampart and strengthened it with a garrison.

After crossing the river, he led the army where he had decided and, entering the land of the Wiltzi, ordered everything to be laid waste with sword and fire.

Although that people was warlike and confident in its own numbers [Note: absent in one witness], it could not long withstand the attack of the royal army [Note: “was not able”]. Accordingly, as soon as the city of Dragawiti was reached [Note: *dragamutina*; margin: “the manuscript has *Dragawiti*”]—for he far surpassed all the other rulers of the Wiltzi in both nobility of birth and the authority of age [Note: witness 7 reads “he who [surpassed] the others”; it omits *longe* (“far”), reads *senatus* (“of the senate”) for *senectutis* (“of age”), and has *praeeminebat*; witnesses 9 and perhaps 3 likewise omit *longe* and read *praeeminebat*. Witness 9 has *est, Wiltzan, nam-is*; the editor judges *Wiltzan*, a German rendering of *Wiltzi*, to be a gloss accidentally admitted into the text, and rejects the historical and critical arguments built on that corruption]—he immediately came out from the city with all his people to the king, gave the hostages that were demanded, and promised by oath that he would preserve his loyalty to the king and the Franks.

All the other leading men and petty kings of the Slavs followed him [Note: the phrase is absent in several witnesses; variant: “following him”] and submitted themselves to the king’s authority.

Then, after that people had been subdued and after he had received the hostages whom he had ordered them to give [Note: “ordered”], the king returned by the same route by which he had come to the Elbe [Note: albiam]. After bringing the army back across the bridge and arranging in due course the matters that concerned the Saxons, he returned to Francia. At the city of Worms [Note: Warmatia, as also in several passages below] he celebrated both the Lord’s Nativity and Easter.

## 790

[Col. 0437D]

In this year the king undertook no military expedition [Note: “no expedition was made”]. But while residing at Worms, he both received envoys from the Huns and in turn sent his own to their leaders.

They were negotiating about the borders of their kingdoms and where those borders ought to lie [Note: “about the boundaries between their kingdoms”; “concerning the boundaries between them”]. This dispute and quarrel [Note: “and” is absent in one witness] became the seed and origin of the war that was later waged against the Huns.

The king, however, so that he might not seem to grow sluggish and waste time in idleness [Note: “to become sluggish”], sailed along the river Main to Saltz [Note: salz; salzt; Sala] [Note: Königshofen, at the headwaters of the Frankish Saale], his palace in Germania built beside the river Saale. From there he returned to Worms by the same river, carried downstream by the current [Note: “through Worms”; “into Worms”].

While he was wintering there, the palace in which he was staying was accidentally consumed by a nighttime fire. Nevertheless, remaining there, he celebrated both the Lord’s Nativity and Easter according to the customary solemnity [Note: “and celebrated holy Easter”].

## 791

[Col. 0437C]

When the mildness of spring had passed [Note: “of spring”; “spring having passed”], around the beginning of summer the king departed from Worms and set out for Bavaria, with the intention of repaying the Huns for their deeds and bringing war upon them as quickly as he could [Note: “as soon as possible”].

Therefore, having assembled for this purpose the strongest forces possible from his entire kingdom and gathered supplies [Note: absent in one witness], he began his march with the army divided into two parts [Note: “bipartite”; variants “divided in two”].

He entrusted one part to Count Theodoric [Note: compare the note at the year 782] and his chamberlain Meginfrid [Note: “bedchamber official”], ordering them to travel along the northern bank of the Danube [Note: “the north bank”].

He himself, with the other part, which he retained with him [Note: “retained”], occupied the southern bank of the same river, intending to attack Pannonia. He ordered the Bavarians to descend along the Danube with the army’s supplies, which were transported by ships [Note: “conveyed”], carried downstream by the current.

Thus, once the march had begun [Note: variant spelling], the first camp was established beside the Anesus [Note: Anisus]. This river, flowing between the territories of the Bavarians and the Huns, was regarded as the fixed boundary of the two kingdoms.

There prayers were offered for three days so that the war might have prosperous and happy outcomes [Note: *supplicatio*, a solemn prayer or supplication; variant *subplantatio*, “replacement”].

Then at last the camp was moved, and war was declared by the Franks against the Hunnic people. After the Hunnic garrisons had been driven out and the fortifications destroyed [Note: “demolished”], one of which had been built above the river Cambus [Note: “there was a river”; “the other”], while the other stood near the city of Comagena on Mount Cumeoberg [Note: cumeberg; quioberg], constructed with a very strong rampart [Note: “a rampart had been constructed,”], everything was laid waste with sword and fire.

When the king and the army he was leading had reached the waters of the Arrabo [Note: the Raab], he crossed that river and advanced along its bank to the place where it joins the Danube [Note: the phrase is absent in two witnesses]. After remaining there in a stationary camp for several days [Note: “having held a stationary camp there for several days”], he decided to return by way of Sabaria [Note: sabania; sarabia; baioaria; Sarvar].

He ordered the other forces, which he had placed under Theodoric and Meginfrid, to return through the Bohemians [Note: bohemos; begaminos; behamannos] by the route along which they had come [Note: “by the route they had traveled”].

Thus, after traversing and devastating a large part of Pannonia, he withdrew into Bavaria with the Frankish army unharmed. The Saxons and Frisians, with Theodoric and Meginfrid, returned home through the Bohemians, as had been ordered [Note: “as he had ordered”].

This expedition was accomplished without any mishap or loss [Note: “without any disadvantage”], except that in the army which the king was leading such a plague arose among the horses that it is said scarcely a tenth part of so many thousands of horses survived [Note: “so great a plague of horses”].

After dismissing his forces, he came to the city of Reginum [Note: “in Regiminum”; Reginum], now called Reganesburg [Note: reganeburg; Ratisbon], and settled there to winter. There he celebrated both the Lord’s Nativity and Easter.

## 792

[Col. 0441A]

Orgellis [Note: La Seu d’Urgell] is a city situated on the ridge of the Pyrenees [Note: “there is a city”]. Its bishop, named Felix, a Spaniard by birth, was consulted by letter by Elipand, bishop of Toledo, about what he ought to think concerning the humanity of our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ: whether, according to that by which he is man, he should be believed and called the proper or adoptive Son of God.

Felix, very rashly and inconsiderately, and contrary to the ancient teaching of the Catholic Church [Note: absent in one witness], not only pronounced him adoptive, but also took care, in books written to the aforementioned bishop, to defend his perverse position [Note: “opinion”] with all possible obstinacy [Note: “most obstinately”].

For this reason he was brought to the king’s palace [Note: “he was brought”; “he was brought to the king”]. At that time the king was residing at Reginum, a city of Bavaria, where he had wintered [Note: “where he had also wintered”]. There, after a council of bishops had been assembled [Note: “counsel”], Felix was heard and convicted of error. He was sent to Rome into the presence of Pope Hadrian [Note: “the Roman”], and there, before the pope himself [Note: absent in several witnesses], in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, he condemned and repudiated his heresy [Note: “confessed it”]. After this he returned to his own city.

While the king was spending the summer there, a conspiracy was formed against him by his elder son, named Pippin, and by certain Franks who declared that they could not endure the cruelty of Queen Fastrada [Note: fastradana]. For that reason they had conspired to kill the king.

When the conspiracy had been exposed by Fardulf, the Lombard [Note: ardulf], he himself was rewarded for preserving his loyalty with the monastery of Saint-Denis. The authors of the conspiracy, however, as guilty of high treason [Note: “guilty of lèse-majesté”], were partly slain by the sword and partly hanged on gallows. For the crime they had contemplated, they were punished by such a death.

The king, however, because of the war undertaken against the Huns, remained in Bavaria and built a bridge of boats on the Danube for use in that war. There he celebrated both the Lord’s Nativity and holy Easter.

## 793

[Col. 0441C]

Since the king desired to complete the war he had begun [Note: “the war that was to be begun”; “complete”], and had decided to attack Pannonia again [Note: “resolved”; “determined”], he was informed that the forces which Count Theodoric was leading through Frisia [Note: phrisiam] had been intercepted and destroyed by the Saxons in the district of Hriustri [Note: hruistri; hiriustri; riustri; rustri; hrinstri; hriusti; rhiustri] [Note: Rustringen, on the left bank of the Weser where it flows into the sea], beside the river Weser [Note: absent in one witness].

When he received this news, he concealed the magnitude of the disaster and abandoned his march into Pannonia [Note: “he abandoned it. The king was then persuaded that, if…”].

When certain men who said that they had learned the matter assured him that, if a ditch capable of carrying ships were dug between the rivers Radantia [Note: radantia; adantia] and Alomona [Note: alamon; alimon; alomonea; almonum], it would be entirely practicable to sail from the Danube to the Rhine, since one of these rivers joins the Danube and the other the Main, he immediately came with his entire retinue to the place [Note: “to that place”]. After gathering a great multitude of people [Note: “and a great multitude of people had been gathered”; another version: “after gathering a multitude of people”], he spent the whole autumn on this undertaking [Note: one witness has a corrupt sequence concerning the ditch and the rivers].

A ditch was therefore dug between the aforesaid rivers, two thousand paces in length and three hundred feet in width. But it was in vain. For, because of the continual rains and because the earth was marshy [Note: *plaustris*, “wagons,” an obvious grammatical corruption for *palustris*, “marshy”], naturally saturated with excessive moisture [Note: “imbued with moisture by its own nature”; “naturally infected”; “infected”], the work being undertaken [Note: “the work begun”] could not hold. As much earth as the diggers had removed during the day sank back at night when the soil slid again into its place [Note: “sliding back”; “as it slid back”].

While he was occupied with this work [Note: “the king being occupied”], two extremely unwelcome reports were brought from different parts of the earth. One was the complete defection of the Saxons; the other was that the Saracens, having entered Septimania, joined battle with the guardians and counts of that frontier, killed many Franks, and returned victorious to their own territory [Note: “were victorious and returned”; “might return victorious”].

Moved by these events, he returned to Francia. He celebrated the Lord’s Nativity at Saint Kilian [Note: Kilian; Kylian] beside the river Main, and the paschal feast on the same river at the villa of Franconofurd [Note: Franconouurt; Franconouuro; Franconofurt], where he had also wintered [Note: “the solemnity of the paschal feast”].

## Complete textual apparatus

The following entries preserve every supplied note separately. Each is tied to its Latin lemma and year; exact readings and witness sigla follow the English explanation. The narrative above supplies the translated context.

### 789

- **N145, at *celebravit DCCLXXXIX Natio quaedam Sclavenorum*.** [Col. 0436C] The apparatus records the following witness spelling or inflection of the Slavs; it does not change the translated sense. Source reading: `sclauorum 4. 5. 6. 7. sclauonorum 9.`

- **N152, at *longius sibi non ferendam ratus*.** [Col. 0436D] Printed ratus means “thinking/judging”; witness 3 instead reads iratus, “angry.” Source reading: `iratus 3.`

- **N156, at *proinde cum primum civitatem Dragawiti*.** [Col. 0436D] Witness 7 reads dragamutinam; the margin states, “the manuscript has Dragawiti.” Source reading: `dragamutinam 7. in marg. « dragawiti habet MS. »`
- **N157, at *civitatem Dragawiti ventum est nam*.** [Col. 0436D] Witness 7 omits the phrase. Witnesses 9 and perhaps 3 contain “Wiltzan.” The editor explains that Wiltzan is a German rendering of Wiltzi, probably inserted above the line in Nuenarius’s codex and then admitted into the text; even if the Trier manuscript contains it, the error is merely older. Arguments built on the corrupt passage collapse once the manuscript reading is restored. Source reading: `deest 7. est, Wiltzan, nam-is 9. 3 (?) Vocem Wiltzan, theotiscam vocabuli Wiltzorum versionem, huic a scriba aliquo in Nuenarii codice superpositam, editoris vitio in textum irrepsisse, eo confidentius contendam, quod in nullo eam codice offenderim; quod si in Trevirensi forte legatur, vitium certe antiquius foret, sed eodem modo coepisse constaret. Ceterum omnia criticorum historicorumve argumenta loco hucusque corrupto superstructa, vera lectione codicum auctoritate restituta, concidunt.`
- **N158, at *Dragawiti ventum est nam is*.** [Col. 0436D] Witness 7 reads “he who [surpassed] the others.” Source reading: `is qui ceteris 7.`

- **N164, at *primores ac reguli omnes secuti*.** [Col. 0437D] Witnesses 1, 2, perhaps 3, 5, and 6 omit the words; witness 4 reads “following”; witness 9 reads “all followed.” Source reading: `deest 1. 2. 3 ? 5. 6. sequentes 4. secuti omnes 9.`

- **N168, at *reversus est et in Wormacia*.** [Col. 0437D] The apparatus records the following witness spelling or inflection of Worms; it does not change the translated sense. Source reading: `warmatia 7. ita aliquotiens in sequentibus.`

## 794

[Col. 0444C]

The king, in order to condemn the Felician heresy, at the beginning of summer—when he also held the general assembly of his people—assembled a council of bishops from all the provinces of his kingdom in the same estate. The envoys of the holy Roman Church were also present at this synod, namely the bishops Theophylact and Stephen, acting as representatives of Pope Hadrian, by whom they had been sent. At this council the aforementioned heresy was condemned, and a book against it was composed with the common authority of the bishops; in it they all subscribed with their own hands.

The synod that, a few years earlier, had been assembled at Constantinople under Irene and her son Constantine, and had been called by them not only the Seventh but also the Universal Synod, was renounced by everyone, so that it should neither be regarded nor called the Seventh or Universal, as wholly superfluous.

Queen Fastrada also died there and was buried at Mainz, at St. Alban’s. When these matters had been completed, the king decided to enter Saxony with a divided army, in such a way that he himself would enter from the south with half the forces, while his son Charles would cross the Rhine at Cologne with the other half and come into the same region from the west.

When this had been done, although the Saxons had taken up position in the field called Sinotfeld, as though intending to join battle with the king and awaiting his arrival there, they abandoned the hope of victory that shortly before they had falsely promised themselves and all turned to surrender. Defeated without a battle, they submitted themselves to the power of the victorious king. They therefore gave hostages and promised under oath that they wished to keep faith with the king.

Thus, with the battle abandoned, the Saxons returned home, while the king, crossing the Rhine, withdrew into Gaul; and when he had reached Aachen, he spent the winter there and celebrated both the Nativity of the Lord and Easter.

[Notes on Col. 0444D–0445D: At *condemnandam*, witness 9 reads “ad”; witness 2 has *condempnationem*. Witness 6 reads *consilium* rather than *concilium*. Witness 7 reads “summoned the same estate.” Witness 1 has *synodo*; *et* is absent in witnesses 3 and 9. Witness 9 reads “the envoys of the Roman pontiff.” Theophylact appears as *theophilactus* in witness 6 and *teophilactus* in witnesses 4 and 5. Witness 9 reads *fuerant* (“had been”) rather than *sunt* (“have been”). Witness 7 reads *eo* (“in it”) rather than *in quo* (“in which”). *Propriis manibus* (“with their own hands”) is absent in witness 9; *in* is absent in witness 7. Irene’s name appears as *harena* in witness 5, *helena* in witnesses 3, 4, 6, and 7, and *irene* in witness 9. Witness 7 reads *tantum* (“only”) rather than *solum*; witnesses 3 and 9 have *erat* (“was”) rather than *est* (“is”). Witness 7 reads “so that it should be neither called nor regarded.” *Et* (“and”) is absent in witnesses 3, 4, and 9. Mainz appears as *moguntiaci* in witnesses 2 and 9, *mogontia* in witness 3, *magontiaci* in witness 4, *mogonciaco* in witness 5, and *monciaco* in witness 6. Charles appears as *Carolus* in witnesses 1, 4, and 7. *Sinotfeld* occurs as *sinotfeldus* in witness 2, *sinotfeldum* in witnesses 5 and 6, *sinofeld* in witness 4, *smetfeldus* in the manuscript, *sinotfeld* in witness 7, and *sintfelt* in witness 9. The field of Sendfeld is near Wünnenberg, south of Paderborn and north of Eresburg; compare Fürstenberg, *Monumenta Paderbornensia*, p. 185. Witnesses 5 and 6 read *operirentur* (“were awaited”) rather than *opperirentur*. Witness 7 has *falso paulo ante* (“shortly before, falsely”). Witness 7 reads *dederuntque* (“and they gave”). Witnesses 3 and 9 read *velle servare* (“to wish to keep”), while witness 7 has *regi servare se velle* (“that they wished to keep faith with the king”).]

## DCCXCV

Although the Saxons had given hostages the previous summer and had sworn the oaths they had been ordered to swear, the king nevertheless, not forgetting their treachery, held the general assembly beyond the Rhine at the estate called Cuffesstein, which lies on the Main opposite the city of Mainz, according to customary practice. From there he entered Saxony with his army and traversed almost the whole country, laying it waste.

When he had reached the district of Bardengoi and, having set up camp near the place called Bardenwih, was awaiting the arrival of the Slavs whom he had ordered to come to him, he was suddenly informed that Witzin, king of the Abodrites, while crossing the Elbe, had fallen in the very river into an ambush arranged by the Saxons and had been killed by them.

This event added what were virtually spurs to the king’s resolve to subdue the Saxons more quickly and stirred him still more deeply against the treacherous people. After a large part of the land had therefore been laid waste, and after receiving the hostages whom he had ordered them to give, he returned to Francia.

During this expedition, while he was encamped above the Elbe, envoys came to him from Pannonia, sent by one of the leading men of the Huns, who was called Tudun among his people. He announced his own arrival and promised that he wished to become a Christian.

The king, coming to Aachen, celebrated there, as in the preceding year, both the Nativity of the Lord and Easter at their appointed times.

[Notes on Col. 0445D–0446D: Cuffesstein is identified as Kostheim. *Contra* may mean “opposite,” “near,” or “beside.” Bardenwih is identified as Bardowik, near Lüneburg. *Abodritorum* is uncertain in witnesses 2 and 9. *Albiam* means “the Elbe.” Tudun appears as *thudun*, *tudum*, *tudmi*, and *tridun* in variant witnesses. Witnesses 4, 5, and 6 read *vocatur* (“is called”) rather than *vocabatur* (“was called”).]

## DCCXCVI

At Rome, after Hadrian’s death, Leo assumed the pontificate. He immediately sent the king, through his envoys, the keys of the confession of St. Peter and the banner of the Roman city, together with other gifts, and asked him to send one of his leading men to Rome who could bind the Roman people to his allegiance and submission by oaths.

For this purpose Angilbert, abbot of the monastery of St. Richarius, was sent. Through him the king also sent to St. Peter a large part of the treasure that Duke Eric of Friuli had brought to the king from Pannonia in that same year, after plundering the royal residence of the Huns called Hringus. He distributed the rest with a generous hand among his leading men, courtiers, and the other soldiers serving in his palace.

When these matters had been completed, he himself marched into Saxony with the Frankish army, while he ordered his son Pippin to go to Pannonia with the Italian and Bavarian forces.

He, after laying waste a large part of Saxony, returned to Aachen to spend the winter. Pippin, however, having driven the Huns beyond the river Tisza and completely destroyed their royal residence—which, as has been said, was called Hringus, but by the Lombards was called the Camp—and having plundered nearly all the wealth of the Huns, came to his father at Aachen, where he was spending the winter, and presented to him the spoils of the kingdom that he had brought with him.

That Tudun, too, of whom mention was made above, trusting in his stated intentions, came there to the king and was baptized together with all who had come with him, and was rewarded. After giving the oath of loyalty, he returned home; but he did not wish to remain long in the fidelity he had promised, and not long afterward paid the penalty for his treachery.

The king, as has been said, remaining at Aachen for the winter, celebrated there both the Nativity of the Lord and Easter according to custom.

[Notes on Col. 0447D–0449D: *Hringus* appears in variant forms including *rhingus*, *hritigus*, and *ringus*. “Ring” in our language means “circle” or “ring.” Concerning the region of the Avars, compare the Monk of Saint Gall, Book II, chapter 1. *Tiza* is the river now called the Theiss. Witnesses vary between *Hringus*, *Ring*, and related forms. The residence is called *Campus* (“the Camp”) by the Lombards; in witnesses 4, 5, and 7 the words “but the Camp” are absent. *Baptisatus* is a variant spelling of “baptized.” The readings *remuneratus* (“rewarded”) and *remuneratus est* (“was rewarded”) vary among witnesses. The forms of *Aquisgrani* (“Aachen”) also vary.]

## DCCXCVII

The city of Barcelona, situated on the Spanish frontier and, as fortune alternated, now subject to the power of the Franks and now to that of the Saracens, was at last restored to the king by the Saracen Zatu, who had then seized it. For at the beginning of summer he came to the king at Aachen and voluntarily surrendered himself, together with the city mentioned, to his authority.

After receiving it, the king sent his son Louis with an army into Spain to besiege Huesca. He himself, as usual, entered Saxony to crush the obstinacy of that treacherous people, and did not stop until he had traversed all its boundaries. For he advanced as far as its remotest borders, where the land is washed by the ocean between the Elbe and the Weser.

Returning from there, when he had reached Aachen and had received there Abdella the Saracen, son of Ibn-Mauge, king of Mauritania, who had come to him, and had heard Theoctistus, the envoy of the patrician Nicetas, who then governed Sicily, bearing letters from the emperor sent from Constantinople, he resolved to winter in that region in order to complete the Saxon war.

Taking his retinue with him, he marched into Saxony, set up camp above the Weser, and settled there. He ordered the camp to be called Heristelli; the inhabitants still call the place by that name.

He distributed the army that he had brought with him throughout Saxony into winter quarters. He ordered Pippin, returning from Italy, and Louis, returning from the expedition in Spain, to come to him there. There he received and dismissed the envoys of the Huns who had been sent to him with great gifts. He also received the envoy of Alfonso, king of Asturias and Galicia, who brought him gifts.

From there he sent Pippin back to Italy and Louis to Aquitaine. He ordered Abdella the Saracen to go with Louis; afterward, as he wished, Abdella was taken into Spain and entrusted to those in whom he had no hesitation in placing his confidence.

The king, remaining in Saxony, celebrated there both the Nativity of the Lord and Easter.

[Notes on Col. 0449D–0452A: Huesca is identified in the apparatus. The note on Heristelli identifies the place with the land of Hadein, part of the kingdom of Hanover, to which in former times Ritzebüttel, a prefecture of Hamburg’s territory at the extreme edge of the land, also belonged. The forms of Ibn-Mauge’s name include *Ibin-Mauge*, *Ibiinmauge*, *Ibimmauge*, and *Ibiminaugae*. Alfonso’s name appears as *Hadefonsi*, *Haidefonse*, and *Adelfonsi*. The geographical readings vary among Asturias, Galicia, Austria, and Calabria. The readings concerning Abdella include *Abdella* and *Adbellum*. Witness 9 omits *ad se* (“to him”) after “sent.”]

## DCCXCVIII

When spring was now approaching, although the army could not yet be brought out of its winter quarters because of a shortage of fodder, the Saxons beyond the Elbe, finding an opportunity, seized and killed the king’s envoys who had been sent to them to administer justice. They spared only a few of them, apparently in order to ransom them, and slaughtered the rest together with Godescalcus, the king’s envoy whom he had sent a few days earlier to Sigifrid, king of the Danes.

As Godescalcus was returning at the same time after completing his embassy, he was intercepted and killed by the authors of this revolt.

[Note on Col. 0451D: Witnesses 1, 2, and 3, as well as the Saxon poet, read “by the Huns.” Nevertheless, I prefer “by these men,” since in writing *hujus* (“of this man” or “of these men”) and *Hunis* (“by the Huns”) are very easily confused, and the connection of the sentences does not admit *Hunis*. For if Einhard had wished to say that the Huns sent envoys into Saxony to stir up the people to revolt, and that they had arranged Godescalcus’s murder so as to make their wish more certain of success, he would certainly have expressed so important a matter in another way. Although manuscripts 1, 2, and 3 are the best of all, they derive from a single source; this is shown not only by this passage but also by the readings cited above under *redimendum* (“to ransom”). The Saxon poet appears to have followed the same authority. Even if one assumes that this authority itself was authentic, every expert in the matter will concede that things could also have been written in it contrary to the author’s intention.]

When these events became known, the king was gravely angered. He gathered an army, set up camp above the Weser at the place called Mimda, took up arms against the breakers of their treaty and the deserters, and, as avenger of the murder of his envoys, laid waste with sword and fire all the territory of Saxony lying between the Elbe and the Weser.

The Saxons beyond the Elbe, elated by pride because they had been able to kill the king’s envoys with impunity, took up arms and marched against the Abodrites. The Abodrites had always been allies of the Franks, ever since they had once been received by them into their alliance.

Their leader Thasco, learning of the movement of the Saxons beyond the Elbe, met them with all his forces at the place called Suentana. Battle was joined, and he struck them down in a great slaughter. The king’s envoy, named Eburis, who had been present at the battle and held the right wing in the Abodrite line, reported that four thousand of them had fallen in the first encounter.

Thus routed and put to flight, and having lost many of their men, they returned to their own territory in great distress.

The king, meanwhile, returned to Francia. When he had reached Aachen, he first received the envoys of the empress Irene, sent to him from Constantinople. For her son Constantine had been seized and blinded by his own people because of his insolent behavior.

At their request he permitted Sisinnius, brother of Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople, who had formerly been captured in battle, to return home. The envoys were Michael, surnamed Ganglianos, and Theophilus, a presbyter from Blachernae.

[Notes on Col. 0452C–0453D: *Suentana* appears to be the place called Schwan, in the district of the grand duchy of Mecklenburg, situated on the Warnow. The name Thasco occurs as *Tascho*, *Tasco*, and *Thrasico*. Eburis appears as *Eberwinus*. The readings include *necis* (“of the death”) and *necess* (“necessary”) in the apparatus. Witness 9 calls the Saxons beyond the Elbe “those who are called Northmen.” The reading *fuere* (“have been”) and the alternative *fuerant* (“had been”) vary. *Auxiliatores* (“helpers”) is read as *auxiliares* (“allies”) in some witnesses. *Suscepti* (“received”) appears as *recepti* (“admitted”) in another. The place-name occurs as *Mimda*, *Minda*, *Mindam*, *Munda*, and *Mitidam*.]

After their release, envoys came from Spain, from Alfonso, king of Asturias and Galicia: Basiliscus and Froia. They brought gifts that Alfonso had arranged to send to the king from the spoils he had taken as victor at Lisbon, a city he had conquered. They were seven Moors, with an equal number of mules and coats of mail. Although they were sent as a gift, they appeared rather to be insignia of victory. The king received them kindly and, after rewarding them honorably, dismissed them.

The Balearic Islands—which their inhabitants now call Majorca and Minorca—were plundered by Moors engaged in piracy.

The king spent the winter at Aachen and celebrated there both the Nativity of the Lord and Easter.

[Notes on Col. 0453D: Lisbon is identified as *Olisipona*. The city’s name appears as *Olisiponam*, *Olisipononam*, *Olipononam*, *Olisipinam*, and *Olysseponam*. *Manubiae* means “spoils”; *manibus* is an alternative reading. The passage means that Alfonso sent seven Moors, with seven mules and seven coats of mail. The readings *donum* (“gift”) and *donu* vary. *Remuneratos dimisit* means “dismissed them after rewarding them”; one witness reads *remisit* (“sent them back”).]

## DCCXCIX

At Rome, while Pope Leo was preparing to proceed in a litany from the Lateran to the church of blessed Lawrence, which is called *ad Graticulam*, he was riding on horseback when he fell into an ambush arranged by the Romans near that same basilica.

There he was thrown from his horse and, as some thought, had his eyes torn out and his tongue cut off as well. Naked and half dead, he was left in the street.

Then, at the command of those who had been responsible for this deed, he was sent to the monastery of the martyr St. Erasmus, supposedly for treatment. During the night, through the care of a certain Albinus, his chamberlain, he was lowered over the wall. He was received by Winigis, duke of Spoleto, who had hurried to Rome after hearing of such a crime, and was taken to Spoleto.

[Notes on Col. 0453D: *Ad Graticulam* appears to refer to San Lorenzo in Lucina; compare the Life of Leo III by Stabulensis. *Letaniam* is used here instead of *ad* or *in letaniam*; this is evidently an expression familiar from the *Liber Pontificalis*. Compare Vignoli’s edition, II, 93, 243, 244. In manuscript 7 the wording is: “At Rome, while Pope Leo was proceeding with a litany …” The readings include *laterano* (“from the Lateran”), *craticulam* (“Graticula”), and variants of *Spolitino* and *Spoletium*.]

When the king received news of this, he ordered that Leo, as the vicar of St. Peter and Roman pontiff, should be brought to him with the greatest honor. Nevertheless, he did not abandon the journey that he had decided to make into Saxony.

He therefore held a general assembly beyond the Rhine at the place called Lippeham. After crossing the river there, he advanced with his entire army to Paderborn and, settling in camp, awaited the arrival of the pontiff, who was hastening to him.

Meanwhile he sent his son Charles to the Elbe with part of the army to settle certain matters with the Wiltzes and Abodrites and to receive some Saxons from Nordliudis. While he was awaiting Charles’s return, the pontiff arrived and was received by him with great honor. He remained with the king for several days.

When he had disclosed to the king everything on account of which he had come, he was sent back to Rome with great honor, accompanied by the king’s envoys who had been sent with him, and was restored to his position.

After dismissing him, the king remained there for a few days and released the envoy of Michael, the patrician of Sicily, named Daniel.

He also received the sad news of the deaths of Gerold and Eric. One of them, Gerold, prefect of Bavaria, fell in battle against the Huns; the other, Eric, after many battles and notable victories, was intercepted and killed by an ambush laid by the townspeople at Tarsatica, a city of Liburnia.

[Notes on Col. 0455D–0456D: Tarsatica is identified as Tersat, in place of Fiume, “Fiume of St. Vitus.” Compare Einhard, *Life of Charles*, chapter 13. The names Gerold and Eric occur in numerous variant forms, including *Gerholtus*, *Gerholti*, *Herici*, *Herrici*, and *Heinrici*.]

Having arranged the affairs of the Saxons as circumstances required, the king returned to Francia.

While he was spending the winter at Aachen, Count Wido, prefect of the Breton frontier, who in that same year had traversed the whole province of the Bretons with the counts accompanying him, brought the weapons of the leaders who had surrendered, with each man’s name inscribed on them. It seemed that the province had then been completely subdued and would have remained so, unless the instability of that treacherous people had soon changed the situation in another direction, as usual.

The standards that had been seized from pirate Moors killed at Majorca were also brought. The Saracen Azan, prefect of Huesca, sent the keys of the city, together with other gifts, to the king, promising that he would surrender it if an opportunity arose.

A certain monk also came from Jerusalem and brought a blessing and relics from the place of the Lord’s resurrection, which the patriarch had sent to the king. The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord while remaining in the same palace. When the monk wished to return, the king released him and ordered a certain Zacharias, a priest from his palace, to go with him; he entrusted his gifts to Zacharias to be carried to those holy places.

[Notes on Col. 0456D–0457C: The readings *signa* (“standards”) and *claves* (“keys”) vary among the manuscripts. Jerusalem appears as *Hierosolima*, *Hierosolyma*, and *Hierosolimis*. The note identifies the blessing and relics as those sent by the patriarch from the place of the Lord’s resurrection. The readings concerning the Breton province include *Brittonum*, *Britonum*, and *Brittaniam*.]

## DCCC

As spring weather returned, around the middle of March the king departed from Aachen and traversed the shore of the Gallic Ocean. In the sea itself, which was then being ravaged by Northmen pirates, he established a fleet and arranged defensive positions. He celebrated Easter at Centula, at St. Richarius.

From there, proceeding again along the seacoast, he came to the city of Rouen. After crossing the Seine there, he went to Tours, to St. Martin, for the sake of prayer. He remained there for several days because of the serious illness of his wife Liutgard, who died and was buried there. She died on 4 June (2 Non. Jun.).

From there he returned through Orléans and Paris to Aachen. At the beginning of August he came to Mainz, held the general assembly there, and announced his journey into Italy.

Departing from there with his army, he came to Ravenna. After remaining there no more than seven days, he ordered his son Pippin to proceed with the same army into the land of the Beneventans. Moving from Ravenna together with his son, he reached Ancona. Leaving Pippin there, he set out for Rome.

The day before he arrived, Pope Leo had met him at Nomentum and received him there with great reverence. After they had dined together, the king remained there while the pontiff went ahead to the city.

On the following day the pontiff stood on the steps of the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter with the bishops and the whole clergy. He received the king as he approached and dismounted from his horse, singing God’s praises and giving thanks. While everyone sang psalms, he led him into the church of that most blessed apostle, glorifying and magnifying God.

These events took place on 24 November.

[Note on Col. 0457D: Nomentum is identified as Nomento. In the Middle Ages, emperors, imitating the magistrates of antiquity, usually entered through the Angelic Gate by the Triumphal Way over Monte Mario, where they could rejoice at the first and most joyful sight of the city subject to them. They did not approach Rome by the Via Flaminia, the Flaminian Gate, and the Milvian Bridge, as we do. In the year 800, however, the basilica of St. Peter still stood outside the city. An accurate description of it, such as Charles then found it, will be useful to read in the printed reference “W. CII. Caroli Bunsen et Ernesti Plattner” (its precise bibliographic expansion is uncertain) by Charles Bunsen and Ernst Platner.]

After seven days the king called an assembly and made clear to everyone why he had come to Rome. From then on he devoted himself each day to the matters for which he had come. Among these, the greatest and most difficult was the first undertaking: investigating the crimes charged against the pontiff.

When no one wished to come forward as a witness to those crimes, however, Leo carried the Gospel before the whole people, mounted the ambo in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, invoked the name of the Holy Trinity, and cleared himself by swearing an oath concerning the accusations brought against him.

On the same day Zacharias, the priest whom the king had sent to Jerusalem, arrived in Rome with two monks whom the patriarch had sent with him to the king. They brought, as a blessing, the keys of the Lord’s tomb and of the place of Calvary, together with a banner.

The king received them kindly, kept them with him for several days, and, when they wished to return, dismissed them after rewarding them.

[Notes on Col. 0460D: *Claves sepulcri dominici* means “the keys of the Lord’s tomb”; witnesses vary in the wording. The readings concerning the number of days and the monks’ release vary among the witnesses. Witnesses 3 and 9 omit certain repeated words; witness 1 reads *aliquot* (“several”), while witness 2 omits *dies* (“days”).]

## DCCCI

## Complete supplied manuscript apparatus

The following source-ordered apparatus translates every printed note and preserves each witness association. Each entry is tied to the immediately preceding Latin anchor from the canonical source. Pure spelling variants retain their printed forms; differences of wording, syntax, tense, number, omission, and editorial interpretation are stated in English without silently regularizing uncertain or corrupt readings.

### Opening council and Saxon expedition

- [Col. 0444D] After *Rex propter*: `ad 9.` Witness 9 has `ad condemnandam`, “in order to condemn,” in place of `propter condemnandam`, “for the purpose of condemning.”
- [Col. 0444D] After *Rex propter ... condemnandam*: `condempnationem 2.` Witness 2 substitutes the noun “condemnation” (spelled `condempnationem`) for “condemning.”
- [Col. 0444D] After *concilium*: `consilium 6.` Witness 6 reads “counsel/advice” instead of “council.”
- [Col. 0444D] After *in eadem villa congregavit*: `eandem villam convocavit 7.` Witness 7 literally reads “he summoned the same estate/villa,” rather than “he assembled [the council] in the same estate”; the reading is awkward as transmitted.
- [Col. 0444D] After *in eadem synodo*: `synodo 1.` Witness 1 has the same word “synod” with a different case/form.
- [Col. 0444D] After *in eadem synodo et*: `deest 3. 9.` Witnesses 3 and 9 omit `et`, “also/and.”
- [Col. 0444D] After *legati sanctae Romanae ecclesiae*: `legati romani pontificis 9.` Witness 9 reads “envoys of the Roman pontiff” instead of “envoys of the holy Roman Church.”
- [Col. 0444D] At *Theophylactus*: `theophilactus 6. teophilactus 4. 5.` Witnesses give the name spellings *Theophilactus* (6) and *Teophilactus* (4, 5).
- [Col. 0444D] After *a quo missi sunt*: `fuerant 9.` Witness 9 reads “by whom they had been sent” rather than “by whom they have/were sent.”
- [Col. 0444D] At *In quo*: `eo 7.` Witness 7 reads “in it” instead of “in which.”
- [Col. 0445C] After *omnes propriis manibus*: `p. m. deest 9.` Witness 9 omits `propriis manibus`, “with their own hands.”
- [Col. 0445C] After *ante paucos annos in*: `deest 7.` Witness 7 omits `in`, “at/in,” before Constantinople.
- [Col. 0445C] At *Herena*: `harena 5. helena 3. 4. 6. 7. irene 9.` The empress's name appears as *Harena* (5), *Helena* (3, 4, 6, 7), and *Irene* (9).
- [Col. 0445C] At *non solum*: `tantum 7.` Witness 7 reads `tantum`, “only,” for `solum`, with no material change of sense.
- [Col. 0445C] At *universalis est*: `erat 3. 9.` Witnesses 3 and 9 read “was” rather than “is.”
- [Col. 0445C] At *haberetur dicereturve*: `diceretur habereturque 7.` Witness 7 reverses the order: “should be called or regarded,” rather than “regarded or called.”

- [Col. 0445D] At *Sinotfeld*: `sinotfeldus 2. sinotfeldum 5. 6. sinofeld 4. smetfeldus ms. sinotfeld 7. sintfelt 9.` The field-name has the listed witness forms; the manuscript itself has *Smetfeldus*.
- [Col. 0445D] At *Sinotfeld*: `Campus Sendfeld prope Wunnenberg, a meridie Paderbornae et septentrione Eresburgi. Cf Fürsten bergii Mon. Pad. p. 185.` This is the field of Sendfeld near Wünnenberg, south of Paderborn and north of Eresburg; compare Fürstenberg, *Monumenta Paderbornensia*, p. 185.
- [Col. 0445D] At *opperirentur*: `operirentur 5. 6.` Printed `opperirentur` means “they awaited”; witnesses 5 and 6 read `operirentur`, “they were covered.”

- [Col. 0449D] At *Asturiae*: `asturicae 2 ? 9. austrie 6.` Witness 9, and perhaps 2, reads “Asturian”; witness 6 reads “Austria” instead of Asturias.

### DCCXCVIII

- [Col. 0452C] At *ver adpeteret*: `appareret 4. 5. 6. accederet 9.` The printed text says “spring was approaching”; witnesses 4–6 read “spring was appearing,” and witness 9 “spring was drawing near.”
- [Col. 0452C] At *propter inopiam*: `p. i. 3. 9.` Witnesses 3 and 9 reverse the order to `inopiam propter`, “because of the shortage.”
- [Col. 0452C] At *nancti*: `nacti 1. 3 - 9.` These witnesses use the spelling `nacti`, with the same sense “having found/obtained.”
- [Col. 0452C] At *missi erant*: `fuerant 2.` Witness 2 reads “had been sent” (`missi fuerant`) instead of “were sent.”
- [Col. 0452C] At *ad redimendum*: `remendum 1. remedium 2. remeandum 3. nunciandum 9.` In place of “for ransom,” witness 1 has corrupt `remendum`; witness 2 reads “for a remedy,” witness 3 “for returning,” and witness 9 “for reporting/announcing.”
- [Col. 0452C] At *Godescalcum*: `godessclacum 1. godesscalcum 2. godeschalcum 9. goteschalchum 5. godeschalchum 6.` These are witness spellings of Godescalcus's name.
- [Col. 0452C] At *Sigifridum*: `sigefridum 7. sifridum 6.` Witnesses 7 and 6 spell the king's name *Sigefridum* and *Sifridum*.
- [Col. 0452C] At *Is cum eodem tempore reverteretur*: `cum legatione functus r. 9.` Witness 9 reads “when, after discharging his embassy, he was returning,” with `r.` abbreviating the repeated verb.
- [Col. 0452C] At *reverteretur*: `verteretur 1.` Witness 1 reads “was turning” rather than “was returning.”
- [Col. 0451D] At *ab hujus seditionis auctoribus*: `Ab Hunis 1, 2, 3, et poeta Saxo; ...` Witnesses 1–3 and the Saxon Poet read “by the Huns.” The editor prefers `hujus`, “by the authors of this revolt,” because *hujus* and *Hunis* are easily confused in writing and the connection does not admit “Huns.” Had Einhard meant that the Huns sent envoys into Saxony to incite revolt and arranged Godescalcus's murder to ensure success, he would have stated so important a matter differently. Although manuscripts 1–3 are the best, this passage and the readings above at *redimendum* show that they derive from one source; the Saxon Poet followed that authority. Even if that source was itself authentic, an expert will concede that material contrary to the author's intention could have been written in it.
- [Col. 0452C–D] At *Mimda*: `mimda 1. mindam 2. minda 3. 4. 6. munda 5. 9. mitidam ms. minda 7.` The place-name has the listed forms; the manuscript reads *Mitidam*.
- [Col. 0452D] At *necis*: `neces 1.` Witness 1 has the form `neces` for “death/killing,” apparently a corrupt or differently inflected reading.
- [Col. 0452D] At *Albiam ac Wisuram*: `et 2.` Witness 2 reads “the Elbe and the Weser” instead of “the Elbe and/also the Weser.”
- [Col. 0452D] At *Transalbiani autem*: `autem qui nordmanni vocantur 9.` Witness 9 expands this to “those beyond the Elbe, however, who are called Northmen.”
- [Col. 0452D] At *regis legatos*: `l. r. 3. 9.` Witnesses 3 and 9 reverse the order to `legatos regis`, “the king's envoys.”
- [Col. 0452D] From *Nam Abodriti* through *recepti sunt*: `deest 9.` Witness 9 omits: “For the Abodrites had always been helpers of the Franks, ever since they had once been received by them into alliance.”
- [Col. 0452D] At *auxiliatores*: `auxiliares 2. 3. 7.` Witnesses 2, 3, and 7 call the Abodrites “auxiliaries/allies” instead of “helpers.”
- [Col. 0452D] At *semper fuerunt*: `fuere 7. fuerant 4.` Witness 7 gives the contracted “were”; witness 4 reads “had been.”
- [Col. 0452D] At *ex quo*: `abs 4.` Witness 4 reads `abs quo`, another form of “from/since which [time].”
- [Col. 0452D] At *recepti*: `suscepti 6.` Witness 6 reads “taken up/accepted” instead of “received.”
- [Col. 0452D] At *Thasco*: `tascho 2. tasco 3. thrasico 9.` The leader's name appears as *Tascho*, *Tasco*, and *Thrasico*.
- [Col. 0452D] At *Suentana*: `Videtur esse locus Swante, in districtu magni ducatus Meklenburgici Schwan, ad Warnowam sito.` This appears to be the place Swante, Schwan in the district of the grand duchy of Mecklenburg, situated on the Warnow.
- [Col. 0452D] At *Eburis*: `eberwinus 9.` Witness 9 calls the king's envoy *Eberwinus*.
- [Col. 0452D] At *At rex*: `ad 2.` Witness 2 has `ad` (“to”), a corrupt reading for adversative `At`, “but.”
- [Col. 0453C] At *Aquasgrani*: `aquisgrani 5. 6. aquisgranum 7.` Witnesses give the Aachen forms *Aquisgrani* and *Aquisgranum*.
- [Col. 0453C] At *Herenae*: `helenae 3. 4. 5. 6. hirenae 7. irenes 9.` The empress's name appears as *Helenae*, *Hirenae*, and *Irenes*.
- [Col. 0453C] At *ad se de Constantinopoli*: `deest 7. a se de 4. 5. 6.` Witness 7 omits `de`, “from,” before Constantinople; witnesses 4–6 read `a se de`, “from himself, from,” instead of `ad se de`, “to him from,” producing an awkward construction.

- [Col. 0453D] At *venerunt*: `venere 3. 9.` Witnesses 3 and 9 use the contracted form with the same sense “came.”
- [Col. 0453D] At *de Hispania*: `hispaniis 2.` Witness 2 reads the plural/form `Hispaniis`, literally “from the Spains,” instead of “from Spain.”
- [Col. 0453D] At *Hadefonsi*: `adefonsi 5. adelfonsi 9.` Alfonso's name appears as *Adefonsi* and *Adelfonsi*.
- [Col. 0453D] At *Basiliscus et Froia*: `basilicus scilicet et 7.` Witness 7 reads “Basilicus, namely, and [Froia].”
- [Col. 0453D] At *manubiis*: `manibus 5. 6.` Witnesses 5 and 6 read “hands” instead of “spoils.”
- [Col. 0453D] At *quas*: `quasi 4.` Witness 4 reads `quasi`, “as if/about,” instead of the relative “which”; the resulting construction is problematic.
- [Col. 0453D] At *Olisiponam*: `olisipononam 1. 5. olipononam 2. olisipinam 6. olysseponam 7. olisipponam 9.` The city-name Lisbon has the listed witness spellings.
- [Col. 0453D] At *Olisiponam*: `Lissabon.` The place is Lisbon.
- [Col. 0453D] At *coeperat*: `acceperat 4.` In context the printed form is used for what Alfonso had taken at the conquered city; witness 4 reads `acceperat`, “had received.”
- [Col. 0453D] At *dono*: `donu 1.` Witness 1 gives a spelling/form of “gift.”
- [Col. 0453D] At *Quos et*: `q. rex et 7.` Witness 7 expands this to `quos rex et`, “whom/them the king also.”
- [Col. 0453D] At *dimisit*: `remisit 3.` Witness 3 reads “sent back” instead of “dismissed/sent away.”
- [Col. 0453D] At *pascha*: `p. more solito 9.` Witness 9 reads `pascha more solito`, “Easter according to custom.”

### DCCXCIX

- [Col. 0453D] At *letaniam*: `laetania 3. 4. 5. letania 6. 7. litania 9. ...` The word “litany” has the listed spellings. Here `letaniam` plainly stands for `ad letaniam` or `in letaniam`, a usage common in the *Liber Pontificalis*; compare Vignoli's edition II, pp. 93, 243, 244. Witness 7 reads: “At Rome, while Pope Leo was proceeding with a litany ...”
- [Col. 0453D] At *de Lateranis*: `laterano 7.` Witness 7 reads singular “from the Lateran.”
- [Col. 0453D] At *Graticulam*: `craticulam 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 9.` These witnesses spell the title *Craticulam* (“the Gridiron”).

- [Col. 0453D] At *dimissus*: `demissus 2. 9.` Witnesses 2 and 9 use the spelling/form *demissus*, with the same sense “lowered down.”

- [Col. 0456D] At *ab illo*: `eo 7.` Witness 7 reads “by him” using `eo` instead of `illo`, with no material change.

- [Col. 0456D] At *Tharsaticam*: `tarsathicam 5. tarsaticam 4. 7. 9. tharsicam 3.` The Liburnian city-name has the listed witness forms.

- [Col. 0456D] At *Hierosolima*: `hierosolyma 7. hieresolymis 9.` Witness 7 gives another spelling of Jerusalem; witness 9 uses the plural/locative form “from Jerusalem.”
- [Col. 0457C] At *Et rex*: `Deest I.` Witness 1 omits `Et`, “and.”

- [Col. 0457C] At *verna temperie*: `veris 4. 5. 6.` Witnesses 4–6 read “with the weather/season of spring returning” instead of “with spring weather returning.”

- [Col. 0457D] At the king's approach to Saint Peter's: `Medio aevo imperatores ...` In the Middle Ages emperors, imitating the magistrates of antiquity, customarily entered the Angelic Gate by the Triumphal Way over Monte Mario, where they first rejoiced in the very happy view of the city subject to them. They did not approach Rome by the Via and Gate Flaminia and the Milvian Bridge, as people do now. In 800, however, Saint Peter's basilica still stood outside the city. A precise description of it as Charles found it may be read in the forthcoming work cited in print as `W. CII. Caroli Bunsen et Ernesti Plattner`; the exact expansion of that citation is uncertain.
- [Col. 0457D] At *eiusdem beatissimi apostoli*: `b. petri a. 2.` Witness 2 explicitly reads `beati Petri apostoli`, “of the blessed apostle Peter.”
- [Col. 0460D] At *cotidie*: `quotidie iis 9.` Witness 9 spells “daily” `quotidie` and adds `iis`, “to those matters,” linking it to the purposes for which he had come.

- [Col. 0460D] At *iurando*: `iureiurando 4. 5. 6. 9.` These witnesses read “by an oath” instead of “by swearing.”
- [Col. 0460D] At *Hierosolimam*: `ierosolymas 9.` Witness 9 gives the plural/place form “to Jerusalem.”
- [Col. 0460D] At *qui*: `ii 9.` Witness 9 reads “they” instead of relative “who.”
- [Col. 0460D] At *sepulcri dominici*: `d. sepulchri 2. 7.` Witnesses 2 and 7 reverse the order to `dominici sepulchri`, “of the Lord's tomb.”
- [Col. 0460D] At *receptos*: `susceptos 3. 9.` Witnesses 3 and 9 read “welcomed/accepted” instead of “received.”
- [Col. 0460D] At *aliquot*: `aliquos 1.` Witness 1 uses a differently inflected form of “several,” agreeing with “days.”
- [Col. 0460D] At *dies*: `deest 2.` Witness 2 omits `dies`, “days.”
- [Col. 0460D] At *redire volentes*: `v. r. 2.` Witness 2 reverses the order to `volentes redire`, “wishing to return.”

He himself, having entered the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on the most sacred day of the Lord’s Nativity to celebrate the solemn Masses [9 omits *celebranda*, “to be celebrated”], and standing before the altar where he had bowed in prayer, Pope Leo placed a crown upon his head, while all the Roman people acclaimed:

“Life and victory to Charles Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor of the Romans!”

After these praises he was worshiped by the same pontiff according to the custom of the ancient rulers; then, with the title of Patrician omitted, he was called Emperor and Augustus.

A few days later, those who had deposed the same pontiff in the previous year [*deposuerant*, “had deposed,” 9; *deposuere*, “deposed,” 2] were brought to trial. After an inquiry had been held concerning them, they were condemned to death according to Roman law, as guilty of treason [9: “as guilty of the crime of lese-majesty”; *Romanorum* (“of the Romans”) in the Roman reading]. For their sake, however, the pope interceded with the emperor out of pious feeling, and their lives and bodily integrity were spared; nevertheless, because of the magnitude of their crime [B 2: *factioni*, “of the faction”], they were deported into exile.

The leaders of this faction were Paschalis the nomenclator [B 5: *nomenculator*; the nomenclator followed the pontiff on horseback in processions and, at his command, summoned guests to the papal table] and Campulus the sacellarius [2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, B 2 and following: *sacellarius*; keeper of the treasury], along with many other noble inhabitants of the city of Rome, all of whom were condemned by the same sentence.

Afterward he organized the affairs of the city of Rome, of the apostolic see, and of all Italy—not only public affairs but also ecclesiastical and private matters—for throughout the whole winter the emperor did nothing else [B 2: *toti*, “of the whole”]. He also sent an expedition against the Beneventans with his son Pippin. After Easter, on 7 Kalends of May [25 April], he left Rome and came to Spoleto [4, 5, 6: *Spoletum*].

While he was there, on 2 Kalends of May [30 April], at the second hour of the night, a very great earthquake occurred [B 2 omits this], by which all Italy was severely shaken. As a result, the roof of the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul, the most beautiful of all the basilicas [which, alas, burned down completely in July 1823], fell for the greater part together with its beams [B 5: *cecidit*, “fell”; B 2: *urbis montes*, “the mountains of the city”; B 7: *et montes*, “and mountains”]. In certain places cities and mountains collapsed. In the same year certain places around the river Rhine, in Gaul, and in Germany also trembled.

A pestilence arose because of the mildness of the winter season [B 2, 5: *molliciem*, “softness”; B 2: *Hiberni tempore*, “in the winter season”]. The emperor went from Spoleto [4, 5, 6: *Spoleto*] to Ravenna and, after staying there for several days [B 2: *aliquod*, “some”; R.: “having arrived at Ravenna”; A.L.: uncertain fragment, *a.*], proceeded to Pavia. There he was informed [B 2: *nunciator*, “he was announced”] that the envoys of Aaron, king of the Persians [Aaron, Amīr al-Muʾminīn, king of the Persians], had entered the port of Pisa [B 7: “entered into Pisa harbor”]. He sent to meet them and had them presented to him between Vercelli [B 2, 7: *Vercellis*] and Ivrea [B 2, 5, 6, 7: *Eporeia*; Ivrea; A.L.: *Eporeiam*].

One of them was a Persian from the East, envoy of the aforesaid king [A.L.: “envoy of the king of the Persians”—for there were two]. The other was a Saracen from Africa, envoy of Amir Abraham, who governed at Fossato on the borders of Africa [the kingdom of Fez]. They reported that Isaac the Jew, whom the emperor had sent four years earlier to the aforesaid king of Persia with his envoys Lantfrid and Sigimund [5: *Sigismund*; A.L.: *Sigimund*], had returned with great gifts. Lantfrid and Sigimund, however, had both died on that journey [A.L.: “both had died”].

Then he sent Erchanbald the notary [2: *Erchembauldum*; 5: *Erchinboldum*; 6: *Erchanboldum*; B 6: *Erchanbaldum*] to Liguria to prepare a fleet by which the elephant and the things being brought with it might be transported [B 2: *quae*, “which”; B 5, 6: *quae deferabantur*, “which were being transported”; A.L.: *deferebantur*, “were being carried”].

He himself, after celebrating the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist at Ivrea, crossed the Alps [B 5: *transgressus est*, “he crossed”] and returned to Gaul.

That summer Barcelona, a city in Spain [B 5: *in Spania*; B 6: *in Ispania*; B 7: *Hispaniae*], which had already been besieged for two years, was captured. Its governor Zatun [B 7: *Zatum*; 4: *Zatus*, and likewise below] and many other Saracens were taken prisoner.

In Italy, too, the city of Teate [11: *Reate*; Chieti, not far from Ortona] was likewise captured and burned, and its governor Roselmus was taken prisoner [2, 4, 5, B 7 add *est*, “was captured”; B 7: *eius*, “its”]. The castles belonging to that city were received into submission. Zatun and Roselmus were brought into the emperor’s presence on the same day [B 5, 6: *perducti*, “brought”] and condemned to exile.

In October of that year [B 2: *octubrio*], Isaac the Jew returned from Africa with the elephant and entered the port of Venus [Porto Venere, at the mouth of the Gulf of La Spezia]. Since he could not cross the Alps because of the snow [1 omits this], he wintered at Vercelli. The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at the palace of Aachen [1: *natalem*, “the Nativity”; A.L.: “the number of years is changed”].

## 802

The empress Irene sent from Constantinople an envoy named Leo, a *spatharius*, to confirm peace between the Franks and the Greeks [A.L.: “concerning the confirmation of peace”].
