In turn, after releasing him, the emperor sent Jesse, bishop of Amiens, and Count Helmgaud [5: *Helmgandum*; 4, 6, 7, 9, B 6, 8: *Helingaudum*; 3: *Heligaudum*; B 7: *Heingaldum*] to Constantinople, so that they might establish peace with her [B 2: *statuerint*, “might have established”].

Easter was celebrated at the palace of Aachen. In July of that year, on 13 Kalends of August [20 July], Isaac arrived with the elephant and the other gifts sent by the king of the Persians, and delivered everything to the emperor at Aachen. The elephant’s name was Abul-Abbas [A.L.: *elefanti*, “of the elephant”; B 7: *Abulabat*; B 6: *Ambulabaz*].

The city of Ortona in Italy [on the Upper Sea, not far from the river Sagrus] was received into submission. Luceria [between the south and west of Sipontum], exhausted by a frequent siege, also surrendered, and a garrison of our men was placed there.

During the summer the emperor devoted himself to hunting in the Ardennes [A.L.: “he devoted himself to hunting”]. Having sent an army [7: “having sent an army into Saxony”; 9: “having sent the army”], he ravaged the Saxons beyond the Elbe.

Grimald, duke of the Beneventans [4, 5, 6: *Grimoldus*; 9: *Grimoaldus*], besieged Winigis, count of Spoleto, who was in command of the garrison at Luceria [B 6: *Lucerna*], weakened by ill health [B 2: “the fatigued forces besieged him”], and took him by surrender; after capturing him, he treated him honorably.

The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Aachen [A.L.: “the number of years is changed”].

## 803

That winter an earthquake occurred around the palace itself and the neighboring regions, and a mortality followed [B 2: *subsequata*, “followed”].

[9 b.: “After Easter the emperor left Aachen, came to Mainz, and there held the assembly of the Franks in the customary manner.”]

Winigis [B 2: *Winegisus*; B 6: *Winighisus*] was released by Grimald [B 2, 5: *Grimaldo*; 9: *Grimoaldo*], and the emperor’s envoys [B 5, 6: “the envoys of the lord emperor”] returned from Constantinople. With them came the envoys of the emperor Nikephoros, who at that time governed the empire—for Irene had been deposed after the arrival of the Frankish embassy [3, 4: *Heienam*; 5: *Harenam*; 4: *Franticae*; 8, B 7, 11: *Franciae*; B 2: “after the embassy of the Franks”]. Their names were Michael [1, 3, 9, B 7: *Michael*], bishop; Peter, abbot; and Callistus [B 7: *Callistus*], a *candidatus* [*candidati*: members of the palace corps employed to guard the emperors].

They came to the emperor in Germany, at the river Saale, at a place called Saltz [B 2: *Salz*; B 6: *Saliz*; 5: *Salzt*; 6: *Saltzt*; Königshofen]. There they received in writing the terms of the peace to be made [B 2: *paciendae*; B 2: *susciperunt*, “received”]. From there they were dismissed with a letter from the emperor; they returned to Rome and then went back to Constantinople [B 7: “And from there they were dismissed”; B 2: *Et hic*, “and here”].

[9 b.: “Fortunatus, patriarch of the Greeks, also arrived, bringing with him, among other gifts, two ivory doors carved with marvelous workmanship.”]

The emperor then set out for Bavaria.

[9 b.: “He hunted buffaloes and other wild beasts through the Hercynian Forest. From there he came to Regensburg and, having arranged what seemed useful, awaited the return of the army from Pannonia. When they had returned, he went out to meet them at Regensburg. There Zodan, prince of Pannonia, also came with them and surrendered himself to the emperor. Many Slavs and Huns were also present at the same assembly, and they submitted themselves, together with everything they possessed, to the emperor’s rule. After all necessary arrangements had been made for those regions, he came through Alemannia and Worms, during the winter, to the palace at Aachen, and there celebrated the Nativity of the Lord.”]

After arranging the affairs of Pannonia, he returned to Aachen in December and there celebrated the Nativity of the Lord [A.L.: “the number of years is changed”].

## 804

The emperor wintered at Aachen [B 5: *Aquasgrani*].

[9 b.: “Leaving Aachen, he came to the palace called Nijmegen. Remaining there during spring, he also celebrated Easter there. As summer began, he returned to the palace at Aachen and sent an army into Saxony. After crossing the Rhine, he held a general assembly of the Franks near the source of the Lippe. From there he proceeded through Saxony and established a camp at a place called Boldonstat (Holdonstat). Princes of the Slavs were also present in that camp. After investigating their affairs and arranging them according to his judgment, he appointed Trasicon as their king. From there he sent his armies through various parts of Saxony and, with God’s help, by a most prudent plan, completely exterminated both those treacherous people whom he had crossed the Elbe to reach and those who remained in Wigmoti and, through their frequent crimes, were turning the Saxon people away from the path of truth. He sent them, women and children included, out of Saxony by various routes and dispersed them throughout Gaul and the other regions of his kingdom without any injury to his army. At the same time, Godefrid, etc.”]

During the summer, after an army had been led into Saxony, he transferred all the Saxons who lived beyond the Elbe and in Wihmuodi [B 2: *Albiam in Wihcmuodi*; 3, 7: *Wihinuodi*; 4: *Wimodi*; 5: *Winuodi*; 6: *Wimuodi*; B 6: *Wichmuodi*; B 7: *Wimuadi*]—women and children included [B 2 omits *cum*, “with”; B 2: *mueribus*]—to Francia, and gave the trans-Elbian districts to the Abodrites.

At the same time Godofrid, king of the Danes, came with his fleet and with all the cavalry of his kingdom to a place called Sliesthorp [5: *Sliestorf*; 6: *Snesthorp*; 4: *Scliesthorp*; 3: *Suesthor*; B 7: *Liesthorp*] [Schleswig; *wig* means “city,” while *thorp* means “village”], on the border of his kingdom and Saxony. He had promised that he would come to a conference with the emperor, but, dissuaded by the counsel of his men [A.L.: “terrified by the counsel of his men”], he did not approach nearer [B 2: *si*, “if”; B 2: *propicius*, “more favorable”].

The emperor, however, was seated above the river Elbe at a place called Holdunsteti [4: *Holdunesteti*; 9: *Holdunstetin*; B 6: *Holdunstein*; B 7: *Hodumsteti*] [Hollenstedt, two German miles from the Elbe, south of the town of Harburg; above, under the year 795, we saw Lüne joining the river Elbe]. He sent an embassy to Godofrid concerning the return of the fugitives [A.L.: “but communicated through envoys whatever he wished”; 9, B 7: “the return of the fugitives in mid-September”], and in mid-September came to Cologne.

After dismissing the army, he first made for Aachen and then for the Ardennes [B 2: “he went to the Ardennes”], and, devoting himself to hunting, returned to Aachen.

In mid-November he was informed that Pope Leo wished to celebrate the Nativity of the Lord with him wherever this might be possible. He immediately sent his son Charles to Saint Maurice and ordered him to receive the pope honorably. He himself went out to meet him at the city of Reims [9 b.: “in the basilica of the blessed bishop and confessor Remigius”]. Having received him there [B 2: “having first received him at Carisiacum”], he led him first to the estate of Carisiacum, where he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord [9 b.: “From there they proceeded together and reached the city of Soissons. Leaving the pope there, he went to the monastery of Celles to confer with his sister Gisla, who was ill in those days. After enjoying her conversation, he had Pope Leo, whom he had left at Saint-Medard, come to meet him at Carisiacum. Then …”], and afterward to Aachen [B 9: “then to Aachen”].

After giving him great gifts, he had him escorted as far as Ravenna, since the pope wished to travel through Bavaria.

The reason for his arrival was this: During the preceding summer it had been reported to the emperor that the blood of Christ had been found in the city of Mantua. For this reason he sent to the pope, asking him to investigate the truth of the report. Seizing this opportunity to leave Rome, the pope first went to Lombardy, supposedly to conduct the investigation mentioned above; then, taking the road, he suddenly proceeded all the way to the emperor. He stayed with him for eight days and, as has been said, returned to Rome.

[A.L.: “The number of years is changed.”]

[9 b.: “The king, spending the remainder of the winter in the palace already mentioned, celebrated Easter with joy.”]

[Rigbodo, bishop of Trier, died on 1 October. B 2, 3. This notice is also found in the Annals of Fulda.]

## 805

Not long afterward, Capcanus [1, 2, 3, 4, 7, B 2, 6, 8, 9: *Capcanus*; B 5: *Captanus*; 5, 6: *Capanus*; 9: *Cacanus*; 7, B 7: *Caganus*], prince of the Huns, approached the emperor because of the needs of his people, asking that a place be given to him for habitation between Sabaria [Sarvar] and Carnuntum [6: *Carnutum*; B 5: *Carnotum*; 3: *Cornuntum*; B 7: *Carnontum*] [Heimburg, a town on the Danube on the borders of Austria and Hungary], since, because of the attacks of the Slavs, he could not remain in his former settlements [4, 5, 6: *poterant*, “they could not remain”].

The emperor received him kindly—for Capcanus was a Christian, named Theodore—and, granting his request, allowed him to return with gifts. After returning to his people [B 2: *reddiens*], he died a short time later [B 2: *paucos*, “a few”].

Caganus [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, B 2, 5, 6, 7, 8: *Caganus*; 9: *Cacanus*] then sent one of his nobles [B 2: *obtimatibus*, “nobles”], asking that the ancient dignity which Caganus had customarily held among the Huns [B 6 omits “among the Huns”] be granted to him. The emperor granted his request and ordered Caganus to hold the supreme authority over the entire kingdom according to their ancient custom [B 2: *Caganum*, corrected to *Cagano*].

In the same year [9 b.: “while the emperor was at the palace situated at Aachen”], he sent his army with his son Charles into the land of the Slavic people called the Bohemians [4: *vocatur Beheim*, “is called Beheim”; 7: *vocantur Beheimi*; 7: *Beheimi*; 9: *Behemanni*; B 7: *Behehuni*].

[9 b.: “He ordered the army to penetrate that same region by three routes. He ordered part of the army, with Charles, his son and king, to proceed through the eastern part of Francia and Germany so that, after crossing the Hercynian Forest, it might attack the aforesaid Slavs. He directed another part through Saxony so that, from the other side, it might burst upon the Slavs together with the Saxons and countless Slavs, after crossing the aforesaid forest from the north. He also ordered an expedition of all Bavaria to enter the same region from a third direction. When they came from every side into the plain of Bohemia, the princes of all the different peoples appeared before King Charles. Those countless armies encamped not far from one another. Acting under the command of King Charles and the princes who were with him, the entire army invaded that region. But the Slavs, penetrating trackless places and forests, did not prepare themselves for battle. After the region had been ravaged and burned for forty days, he killed their duke, named Lecho. When no fodder for the horses or provisions for the army remained, he returned home, the aforesaid region having been devastated and reduced to nothing. The emperor, meanwhile, spending the summer in hunting and pleasure, traveled through the Vosges Forest and came to a place called Campus. After staying there several days, he joyfully received his beloved son, King Charles, returning from the expedition. From there, in July, he left Aachen, came to Theodonis Villa, and proceeded through Metz, etc.”]

He devastated their entire country [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7: *omnem*; B 6: *omne*; B 7: “all of it and its people”], killed their duke, named Becho [1–7: *Bechonem*; 9, B 2, 5, 6, 7, 8: *Iechonem*; A.L.: *Lechonem*], and, returning from there, came to his father in the Vosges Forest [1, 3, 4, 5, 6, B 2, 5, 6, 8: *Vosego*; 2: *Vosega*; 7: *Vosegum*; 9: *Vogesum*; B 7: *Wosago* and likewise below], at a place called Camp [Champs in Lorraine, a small estate near Bruyères on the Velogne stream, north of the mountain of Remiremont and east of Épinal].

For the emperor had left Aachen in July, passed through Theodonis Villa and Metz [A.L.: “having left Theodonis Villa, he proceeded through Metz”], and made for the Vosges [B 6: *Vosagum*]. There, devoting himself to hunting [B 2: *venationibus*, “to hunts”; A.L.: “applying himself to hunting”], after the army’s return he proceeded to the castle of Rumericus [B 6: *Romerici*; 7: *Rumorici*; 9: *Rumrichi*; 4: *Numerici*] [Remiremont]. After staying there for some time [B 6: *aliquantulum*, “somewhat”], he settled in his palace at Theodonis Villa to spend the winter. There both his sons, Pippin and Louis, came to him, and there he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord [A.L.: “the number of years is changed”].

## 806

Immediately after the Nativity of the Lord, Willeri [9: *Wilharius*] and Beatus, dukes of Venice, and Paul, duke of Iadera [B 7: *Ioderae*; Zara], together with Donatus, bishop of the same city, envoys of the Dalmatians [B 7: *Dalmatiarum*], came into the emperor’s presence with great gifts. The emperor then made arrangements concerning the dukes and peoples both of Venice and of Dalmatia [B 2: *populi*, “of the people”].

After dismissing them, the emperor held a conference with the leading men and nobles of the Franks concerning the establishment and preservation of peace among his sons and the division of the kingdom into three parts, so that each of them might know which part he ought to defend and govern if it should fall to him while he survived [B 2: *superestes*, “if he should survive”; A.L.: *eveniret*, “if it should happen”].

A testament concerning this division was drawn up; it was confirmed by oath by the nobles of the Franks; and provisions were made for preserving the peace [B 2: *constitutione*, “a provision”; B 2: *cause*, “of the cause”]. All these matters were committed to writing and sent through Einhard to Pope Leo, so that he might sign them with his own hand [1, 2, 4, 7, B 5, 7: *Einhardum*; B 2: *Einardum*; B 6: *Heinhardum*; 3: *Heinlardum*; 9: *Eginhardum*; 6: *Pernhardum*; 5 omits “through Einhard”].

After reading them, the pontiff gave his assent and subscribed them with his own hand.

The emperor dismissed both sons to the kingdoms assigned to them, namely Pippin and Louis. From Theodonis Villa [A.L.: “the palace of Theodonis Villa”] he sailed down the Moselle and the Rhine with the current toward Nijmegen [5: *Naviomagum*], and there celebrated the holy Lenten fast and the most sacred feast of Easter [B 5: “his son, so that he might have the kingdom”]. A few days later he came to Aachen.

From there he sent his son Charles with an army into the land of the Slavs called the Sorabi, who dwell [A.L.: “the Sorabi who dwell”] on the river Elbe [B 2: *Albiam*]. During that expedition Miliduoch [4: *Miliduohc*; 5: *Miliduch*; 6: *Miliduoh*; B 2: *Mihi Duohc*; B 6: *Mibduoch*], duke of the Slavs, was killed. Two forts were also built by the army, one on the bank of the river Saale and the other beside the river Elbe [one at Halle and the other opposite Magdeburg; compare the Chronicle of Moissac for this year]. After the Slavs had been pacified, Charles returned with the army and came to the emperor at a place called Silli [B 8: *Sylli*] [Selle, on the right bank of the Meuse near Dinant].

An army was also sent from Bavaria, Alemannia, and Burgundy, as in the preceding year, into the land of the Bohemians [1: *Beeheim*, corrected to *Beheim*; 4, 5, B 6: *Beheim*; 9: “the land of the Behemanni”]. After ravaging a considerable part of the country, it returned without any serious mishap.

In the same year Pippin sent a fleet from Italy against the Moors who were ravaging the island of Corsica. The Moors, not awaiting its arrival, withdrew. Nevertheless, one of our men, Hadumar, count of the city of Genoa [B 2, 5: *comis*, “count”], imprudently fighting against them, was killed.

In Spain, the Navarri [B 5: *Navari*] and the people of Pamplona [9: *Pompelonenses*], who in earlier years had defected to the Saracens [B 7: “had defected from the Saracens”], were received into allegiance.

A fleet was sent by the emperor Nikephoros, commanded by the patrician Nicetas, to recover Dalmatia [1, 2, 3, 10: “to recover”; 4, 5, 6, B 2, 5, 6: “to receive”; 7, 9, B 7: “to regain”]. The envoys who had been sent to the king of the Persians nearly four years earlier [A.L.: “who had previously been sent”] were transported past the stations of the Greek ships and returned to the harbor of Tarvisium [B 7: *Tarvisiani*; 7: *Tarvisani*] without any of the enemy perceiving them.

The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Aachen [A.L.: “the number of years is changed”].

## 807

In the preceding year, on 4 Nones of September [2 September], there was an eclipse of the moon. At that time the sun stood in the sixteenth degree of Virgo, while the moon was in the sixteenth degree of Pisces.

In the present year, on the day before the Kalends of February [31 January], the moon was in the seventeenth degree [1: “the moon was”], when the star of Jupiter seemed to pass across it. On 3 Ides of February [11 February] there was a solar eclipse at midday, with both heavenly bodies standing in the twenty-fifth degree of Aquarius.

Again, on 4 Kalends of March [26 February], there was a lunar eclipse, and that same night blades or rays of marvelous size appeared. The sun stood in the eleventh degree of Pisces and the moon in the eleventh degree of Virgo.

Moreover, on 16 Kalends of April [17 March], the star Mercury was seen in the sun like a small black spot, slightly above the middle [3?, 5, 7, 9, 10: *medio*, “middle”; A.L.: “a black spot, nevertheless slightly above the middle”] of the same heavenly body. It was visible to us for eight days [B 9: “which was seen by us for eight days”]. But, because clouds obstructed our view, we could not observe when it first entered or when it departed [A.L.: “we could not observe”; 9: “it could not be observed”; 9 b.: “we could not observe it”].

Again, on 11 Kalends of September [22 August], a lunar eclipse occurred at the third hour of the night [B 2 adds *hora*, “at the hour”], with the sun in the fifth degree of Virgo and the moon in the fifth degree of Pisces. Thus, from September of the preceding year until September of the present year, the moon was darkened three times and the sun once.

Radbertus [1: *Radberdus*; 7, 9, B 7: *Ratbertus*], the emperor’s envoy, who was returning from the East, died. The envoy of the king of the Persians, named Abdella, also reached the emperor together with monks from Jerusalem, who were acting as the envoys of Thomas the patriarch. Their names were George and Felix [“This George is abbot on the Mount of Olives; his homeland is Germany, and he is also called by his proper name Egilbaldus”; 6: *Georius*; B 5, 6: *Egelbaldus*; B 7: *Engelbaldus*; Annals of Lorsch].

They brought gifts which the aforesaid king had sent to the emperor: a pavilion and tents of the atrium (*tentoria atrii*) of extraordinary size and beauty [A.L.: “tents of the atrium made in various colors”]. Everything was made of byssus, or fine linen, both the tents and their ropes, and dyed in different colors.

Among the gifts of the aforesaid king there were also many costly silken cloaks [1, 2, 3, B 2, 5, 6: *sirica*], perfumes, ointments, and balsam. There was also a water-clock of brass, marvelously constructed by mechanical art. In it, the passage of the twelve hours was marked by a water mechanism, with an equal number of bronze balls that fell when the hours were completed and, by their fall, caused a cymbal placed beneath them to ring. In addition, the clock contained an equal number of horsemen who emerged through twelve windows when the hours were complete and, by their exit, closed the same number of windows that had previously been open. There were also many other things in that clock which it would take too long to enumerate.

Among the aforesaid gifts were also two brass candelabra of extraordinary size and height. All these things were brought to the emperor at the palace of Aachen [A.L.: “all these things to Aachen”].

The emperor kept the envoy and the monks with him for some time, then sent them to Italy and ordered them to await the proper season for navigation. In the same year he sent Burchard [B 2: *Burghardus], count of his stable, with a fleet to Corsica, so that he might defend it against the Moors, who in preceding years had been accustomed to come there for plunder.

As was their custom, they came out from Spain and first landed on Sardinia [B 2: *in Sardiniam impulsi*, “were driven onto Sardinia”]. There, after engaging the Sardinians in battle and losing many of their own—for it is reported that three thousand fell there—they reached Corsica by a direct course.

There, in a certain harbor of the island, they again fought a battle with the fleet commanded by Burchard [B 2: *Burghardus*]. They were defeated and put to flight, losing thirteen ships, while very many of their men were killed.

That year they were so harassed by adverse fortune in every place that they themselves declared that this had happened to them because, in the preceding year, contrary to all justice, they had carried sixty monks away from the island of Pantelleria [situated between Sicily and Africa] and sold them in Spain [B 7: *Hispaniam*]. Some of these monks, through the emperor’s generosity [B 7: *libertatem*, “liberation”; A.L.: “returned again to their own places”], returned once more to their own places.

The patrician Nicetas, who was stationed in Venice with the fleet of Constantinople, made peace with King Pippin and established a truce lasting until August. He then broke camp and returned to Constantinople.

In this year [B 2: “in this year”] the emperor celebrated Easter at Aachen, as well as the Nativity of the Lord [A.L.: “the number of years is changed”].

## 808

[The supplied source ends here, with no further text.]

The winter was exceedingly mild and pestilential in that year. As spring began, the emperor set out for Nijmegen; after completing the Lenten fast there and celebrating holy Easter, he returned again to Aachen [Note: Aquis in B 7.]. And because it was reported that Godfrey, king of the Danes, had crossed over into the territory of the Obodrites with an army, he sent his son Charles to the Elbe with a strong force of Franks and Saxons, ordering him to resist the mad king if he attempted to attack the borders of Saxony. But after remaining for several days in camp on the shore, and after storming and capturing by force several Slavic strongholds, he returned with great loss to his forces. For although he had driven out Drasco [Note: drasoconem in B 8; trasconem in B 7; thrasiconem in 9.], duke of the Obodrites, because he distrusted the loyalty of his people, and had captured the other duke, Godelaib [Note: godolaibum in 3.], by treachery and hanged him on the gallows, and had made two parts of the Obodrites tributary to himself, nevertheless he lost the best and most warlike of his soldiers, and with them the son of his brother, Reginold by name, who was killed, together with many leading Danes, in the assault on a certain town.

The emperor’s son Charles [Note: lord Charles in B 7.] joined the Elbe by a bridge [Note: iuncxit in B 2.] and transferred the army under his command across it, with all possible speed, against the Linones [Note: lilones in 3; hilinones in 9.] and Smeldingos [Note: smeldignos in B 5.], who likewise had defected to King Godfrey [Note: They lived beyond the Elbe between the Wilzi and the Obodrites; the Smeldingi were nearer the Elbe. Compare *Chronici Gottwicensis Prodr.*, II, 660.]. After devastating their fields all around, he crossed the river again and withdrew safely with his army into Saxony.

There were with Godfrey on the expedition mentioned above Slavs called Wiltzi [Note: wilzzi in B 5; wilzi in B 7.]. Because of the ancient enmities that they customarily had with the Obodrites [Note: quam abodritis in 1.], they willingly joined themselves to his forces; and when he returned to his kingdom, they too went home with the booty that they had been able to seize from the Obodrites.

Before returning, however, Godfrey destroyed the trading settlement which had been established on the shore of the ocean and was called, in the Danish language, Reric [Note: According to Gebhard, *Hist. Daniae*, p. 381, it is Rorich, a small village near Wismar, although I cannot find it on geographical maps.], and which provided great advantage to his kingdom through the payment of customs [Col. 0470B]. Having transferred the merchants from there, he put out with his fleet and came with his entire army to the harbor called Sliesthorp [Note: suesthorp in 3; fliesthorp in 4; sliestorph in 5; siliestorph in 6; liesthor in others; sliesthorp in 7; sliestorff in 9; sliesthrop in B 5; sbestorb in B 6; sciesthrop in B 7; liesthorp in B 9; slieswic in B 12.].

After remaining there for several days, he decided to fortify with a rampart the boundary of his kingdom facing Saxony, in such a way that, from the eastern inlet of the sea—which they call Ostarsalt [Note: ostharsalt in 2; orstalsalt in 3; ostersaltus in 5; ostersalt in 6 and 9; ostarhsalt in others; Iestarhsalt in 7; ostarsalz in B 2; ostarsal in B 5; estarsalt in B 7; ostarsaltz in B 8; etc.] [Note: The Baltic Sea.]—to the western ocean, a rampart would extend along the whole northern bank of the River Eider [Note: The Eider; compare “Kieler Blätter,” vol. IV, p. 403.]. Only one gate was left open [Note: tamen in B 7; “with only one harbor left open through which carts could be sent out and brought in” in 4, 5, and 6.], through which wagons and horsemen could pass out and return [Note: per quem in 1 and 2.]. He therefore divided the work among the commanders of the forces and returned home.

Meanwhile, the king of the Northumbrians [Note: nordidanhumbrorum in 2; nordhumbrorum in 3 and 9; nordanimbrorum in 4; northanimbrorum in 5; nordanumbrorum in 6; norddanhumbrorum in 7.] from the island of Britain, Eardulf by name [Note: earduf in 1; eardulfus in 3 and 7 and B 7; ardulf in 9.], expelled from his kingdom and country [Col. 0470C], came to the emperor while he was still staying at Nijmegen. After explaining the circumstances of his arrival, he set out for Rome; and, returning from Rome, he was restored to his kingdom through the agency of the legates of the Roman pontiff and the lord emperor [Note: deducitur in B 2.].

At that time Leo III presided over the Roman Church. His legate sent to Britain was Aldulfus [Note: addulfus in B 7; adolphus in 9.], a deacon from Britain itself [Note: de ipsa brisinia in B 2.], of Saxon nationality. Together with him, the emperor sent two abbots: Hrotfridus [Note: ruotfridus in 3 and 4; hortfridus in 5 and 6; rotfridus in 7; rutfridus in 9; hruotfridus in B 2 and 7; hrodfridus in B 5 and 6.] the notary [Note: Abbot of Saint-Amand.] and Nantharius [Note: mantarius in 3; nantarius in 4; mancharius in 6.], abbot of Saint-Omer [Note: audomaro in 2 and 7 and B 2 and 5; audemauro in 5; sancti audemauri in 6; otmaro in 3 and B 7; othmaro in 9.].

The emperor, however, after having two forts built by his legates above the River Elbe [Col. 0471A] and placing garrisons in them against Slavic incursions, wintered at Aachen and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord and holy Easter there [Note: natalem in 1, 2, etc., and B 6. — The phrase “And” is altered in the numbering of the years in A and L.; the alteration is absent in B 5, 6, and 7; mutatus in B 8.].

## DCCCIX.

A fleet sent from Constantinople first reached Dalmatia and then Venice [Note: Veneciam in 1 and B 2 and 6; other witnesses have Venetiam here and below.]. While it was wintering there, part of it approached the island of Comacchio [Note: Comacchio.]. After a battle had been joined against the garrison stationed there, it was defeated and routed and withdrew to Venice.

The commander of the fleet, Paulus by name, attempted to negotiate with Pippin [Note: with lord Pippin in B 7; perhaps B 2.] the king of Italy concerning the establishment of peace between the Franks and Greeks, as though this had been entrusted to him. But when Wilharenus [Note: wilhario in 9.] and Beatus, dukes of Venice, obstructed all his initiatives [Note: eius is absent in 1.] and were even preparing an ambush for him [Note: parentibus in 1, 2, and B 5; paraverunt in B 2.], he learned of their treachery and departed [Col. 0471B].

In the western regions [Note: “western lands” in 9.], the lord King Louis entered Spain with an army and laid siege to the city of Tortosa [Note: desertosam in B 2; Tortosa.], situated on the bank of the River Ebro [Note: hiberis in 1, 4, 5, and 6; iberi in 7 and 9.]. After spending a considerable time in its assault [Note: expugnatione in A and L.], when he saw that it could not be captured so quickly, he abandoned the siege and withdrew safely with his army into Aquitaine.

After Aldulfus [Note: nordanimbrorum in 4 and 6; nordamhumbrorum in B 5.] king of the Northumbrians [Note: ardulfus in 1 and B 6; adolphus in 9; addulfus in B 7; adulfus in 4.] had been restored to his kingdom and the emperor’s and pontiff’s legates had returned, one of them—namely Aldulfus the deacon [Note: Ardulf, deacon, in A and L.]—was captured by pirates while the others crossed without danger. He was taken by them to Britain [Note: brittania in 10.] and redeemed by a certain man of King Coenulf [Note: quadam in B 2; cenulfi in 4 and B 2.], and returned to Rome [Note: reversus est in B 2.].

In Tuscany, Populonia, a coastal city [Note: popolonium in B 6.], was plundered by Greeks called Orobiotae [Note: Greek: Οροβιωται; “inhabitants of the mountains.”]. The Moors likewise entered Corsica from Spain and, on the very Saturday of holy Easter, plundered a certain city, leaving nothing in it except the bishop and a few old and infirm people.

Meanwhile, Godfrey, king of the Danes, sent word through certain merchants that he had heard that the emperor was angry with him because he had led an army against the Obodrites in the preceding year and had avenged his wrongs [Note: suum ultus in B 2.]. He added that he wished to clear himself of the charge brought against him: the breaking of the treaty [Note: inrumptionem in B 2.] had first been begun by them [Note: illo primis in 1, 2, 3, and 10 and B 2, 5, and 6; ab eis primum in 4, 5, and 6; prius in 7 and 9; primitus in B 7.].

He also requested that a meeting of the emperor’s counts and his own should be held beyond the Elbe, near the borders of his kingdom, at which the deeds performed on both sides could be brought forward and the matters deserving correction enumerated between the parties [Note: “the matters between the parties corrected” in 7 and 9.]. The emperor did not refuse. A conference was held beyond the Elbe with the leading Danes at a place called Badenfliot [Note: badenfliot in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 7 and B 5 and 6; badenflioth in 5; badenfliet in 9; batenfliot in 10; melac in B 7; the place is left blank in B 2 and 8.] [Note: The place is unknown, certainly situated near the Eider.]. After many matters had been brought forward and enumerated on both sides, they departed with the business entirely unresolved.

Thrasco [Note: thrasco in 1, 2, 5 and B 2, 5, and 6; trasco in 4, 6, 7, and others.], duke of the Obodrites, after giving his son as a hostage to Godfrey when Godfrey demanded him, gathered a force of his people and, having received aid from the Saxons, attacked his neighbors the Wiltzi. He devastated their lands with fire and sword [Note: vastavit in 4, 5, and 6.] and returned home with immense booty. Then, having again received stronger aid from the Saxons, he stormed the largest city of the Smeldingi [Note: “the largest city” in B 2.] and, as a result of these successes, compelled all who had defected from him to return to his alliance.

After these events, the emperor returned from the Ardennes to Aachen and held a council in November concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, a question first raised by a certain monk, John [Note: iohannis in B 2.], from Jerusalem. To settle it, Bernharius [Note: bernarius in B 7; bernhardus in 4 and 5; bernardus in 6; bernhartus in 9.] bishop of Worms [Note: wormacensis in 1, 2, 3, and 7 and B 2; uurmacensis in B 5 and 6; the other witnesses have wormaciensis and similar forms.] and Adalhardus [Note: adalradus in 4; adelhardus in 5; alahardus in 7; adelhartus in 9; adhardus in B 6.] abbot of the monastery of Corbie [Note: corbiae in 1 and 5; corbeia in B 2.] were sent to Rome to Pope Leo.

The same council also discussed the condition of the churches and the conduct of those who are said to serve God in them. Yet nothing was decided, apparently because of the magnitude of the matters involved.

When the emperor was informed of many things concerning the arrogance and pride of the king of the Danes [Col. 0472C], he decided to build a city beyond the River Elbe and place a Frankish garrison in it. After gathering men for this purpose throughout Gaul and Germany [Note: “having gathered a man” in 2.], and ordering that they be led through Frisia to the designated place, equipped with weapons and the other necessities [Note: “weapons and the other things” in 2; “necessaries” in 2.], Thrasco [Note: thrarco in B 2.], duke of the Obodrites, was treacherously killed in the trading settlement of Reric by Godfrey’s men [Note: “in the Obodrite trading settlement of Reric” in B 2; rerich in 5, 6, and B 6.].

But after the emperor had reconnoitered the site where the city was to be established [Note: “where the city was to be built” in 3, 5, and 6; “where it was to be constructed” in 4.], he appointed Count Egbert [Note: aegbertum in B 2; egibertum in 3 and 6; “to cross over” in 2.] to carry out this undertaking and ordered him to cross the Elbe and occupy the place.

The site lies on the bank of the River Sturia [Note: The River Stor in Holstein.] and is called Esesfelth [Note: esfelth in 1; esfelt in 4, 5, and 6; esesfelth in 2 and 10 and B 2 and 5; esesfelt in B 6; essesfelt in 9; essesfelth in B 8; esfelt in 4; eselfelth in 3 and 7; esselfelt in B 7.] [Note: Itzehoe.]. It was occupied by Egbert [Note: ab egiberto in 3 and 6.] and the Saxon counts around the Ides of March, and fortification was begun [Note: caeptus in 1.].

Count Aureolus [Note: auriolus comis in B 2.], who was stationed in the commercial district of Spain and Gaul beyond the Pyrenees, opposite Huesca and Zaragoza [Note: caesaraugustum … caestaraugustus in B 2.], died. Amoroz [Note: amaroz in 3 and 9 and B 8.], prefect of Zaragoza and Huesca, took his place [Note: “his office” in A and L.] and stationed garrisons in his forts [Note: “and in the forts” in B 2.]. He sent an embassy to the emperor [Note: “from the emperor” in B 2; “In DCCCX” in B 5.] and promised that he wished to come over to him in submission, together with everything he possessed.

An eclipse of the moon occurred on 26 December.

## DCCCX.

Amoroz [Note: Amaroz in 3; Armoroz in B 6.], prefect of Zaragoza [Note: caesaraugusto in B 2.], after the emperor’s legates had reached him, requested that a conference be held between himself and the guardians of the Spanish frontier [Col. 0473B], promising that at the conference he would come over, together with all his men, under the emperor’s authority. Although the emperor agreed that it should take place, the matter remained unresolved because of numerous intervening causes.

The Moors, having assembled a very large fleet from all Spain [Note: classe is omitted in 1.], first landed in Sardinia and then in Corsica. Finding no garrison there, they brought almost the whole island under their control [Note: subigerunt in B 2, 5, and 6; subiecerunt in B 7.].

Meanwhile, King Pippin, provoked by the treachery of the Venetian leaders, ordered Venice to be attacked by land and sea. After Venice had been subjected [Note: A note states that Pippin did not obtain all the Venetian islands, but attacked Rialto by a naval bridge and was compelled to abandon the attempt when a sudden storm arose; this is established from Venetian chronicles.], and its leaders had submitted, he sent the same fleet to ravage the shores of Dalmatia.

But when Paulus, prefect of Cephallenia [Note: cefalagiae in 5; cefalaiae in 6; cephaleniae in 7; celalaniae in B 5; celafaniae in Bouqu.], arrived with the eastern fleet to bring aid to the Dalmatians, the royal fleet returned to its own territory.

Hruodtrud [Note: hruodtrut in B 5; hruottrud in 2; hruodrud in 3; rhodtrudis in 7; rotdrudis in 9.], the emperor’s elder daughter [Note: “younger” in 3.] died on 6 June [Note: 3 June in B 5.].

While the emperor was still staying at Aachen and planning an expedition against King Godfrey, he received news that a fleet of two hundred ships from Nordmannia [Note: nordmannia in 1 and 3, 4, 6, and 9 and B 5; nordusmannia in 2; northmannia in 5; nortdmannia in 7; nortmannia in B 2 and 7; normania in B 6. The great variety of the form sufficiently indicates that the reading of manuscript 1 is genuine.] had landed in Frisia, that all the islands adjoining the Frisian coast had been devastated, and that the army was already on the mainland and had fought three battles with the Frisians. The Danes had conquered and imposed tribute on the defeated, and one hundred pounds of silver had already been paid by the Frisians as tribute; but King Godfrey was at home. And so it was.

This report so stirred the emperor that, after sending messengers throughout all the surrounding regions to gather an army, he himself left the palace without delay [Note: In manuscript B 2, the folio is lost after these words; the text resumes below at “his king of Italy.”]. First he intended to meet the fleet [Note: occurreret in B 7.]; then, after crossing the Rhine, he decided to await at a place called Lippeham [Note: lippeha in 5 and 6; lippeam in B 7; lippenheim in 9.] the forces that had not yet assembled.

While he remained there for several days, that elephant which Aaron, king of the Saracens, had sent him died a sudden death.

When the forces had finally assembled, he hastened with all possible speed to the River Aller [Note: alraram in 1; araram in 9; alacram in B 6.]. Having pitched camp beside its confluence with the River Weser, he awaited the outcome of King Godfrey’s threats. For that king, puffed up with the most empty hope of victory, boasted that he wished to meet the emperor in battle [Col. 0474B].

But while the emperor remained in camp at the place mentioned, reports of various events were brought to him [Note: deferunt in 1, 3, and B 7; venerunt in 5; devenerunt in 6; perferuntur in 9; deferuntur in 2, 7, and B 5; “they report to him” in B 6.]. He learned that the fleet which had ravaged Frisia had returned home; that King Godfrey had been killed by one of his own retainers; that the fortress called Hohbuoki [Note: hohbuochi in 3.] [Note: Much has been debated about this place. Some think it was Hamburg, although the fact that Hamburg lay somewhat farther from the Wiltzi seems to oppose this. Others propose Boitzenburg, though the name is quite different. It was more likely Büchen in the duchy of Lauenburg, no farther from Holdunsteti and Hliuni on the opposite bank than from the Elbe.] on the River Elbe, in which Odo, the emperor’s legate, and the garrison of the eastern Saxons were stationed, had been captured by the Wiltzi [Note: wilzzis in B 5 and 6.]; that Pippin, his son and king of Italy, had died on 8 July; and that two embassies from different parts of the world—one from Constantinople and the other from Córdoba [Note: cordoba in B 5.]—were said to be approaching to make peace.

After receiving these reports, he arranged the affairs of Saxony as circumstances required and returned home.

So great was the pestilence among the cattle during that expedition that scarcely any remained for so large an army, for all perished to the last one [Note: perirent in B 7.]. And not only there: throughout all the provinces subject to the emperor, a most devastating mortality of that kind of animal raged [Note: “also through all” in A and L.; “through all” in 10.].

The emperor came to Aachen in October [Note: octubrio in B 7; octimbrio in B 6.], heard the aforementioned embassies, and made peace with the emperor Nicephorus and with Abulaz, king of Spain. He restored Venice to Nicephorus [Note: reddit in 1.] [Note: We know the terms of this peace from the pact of the emperor Lothar I with the Venetians. We shall present them to readers later, transcribed from the parchments of the archive formerly belonging to the Venetian republic and now to the imperial archive at Vienna.], and received back Count Haimricus [Note: hamricum in 1, 4, and 10; amricum in 2; hanricum in 3; amri in 5; hamri in 6; henricum in 7; heimrichum in 9; haimricum in B 2, 5, and 8; heimricum in B 6; adimricum in B 7.], formerly captured by the Saracens, when Abulaz sent him back.

In that year the sun and moon were eclipsed twice [Note: bis is absent in B 7]: the sun on 7 June [Note: 7 June in 1, 7, and 10 and B 2, 5, 8, 9, and 12; 6 June in 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, and B 7; 7 July in B 6; 6 July in 6.], and on 30 November; the moon on 21 June and on 15 December [Note: 14 December in 2 and B 7.].

The island of Corsica was again ravaged by the Moors.

Amoroz [Note: amaroz in B 6.] was expelled from Zaragoza by Abdiraman [Note: abdirama in B 5.], the son of Abulaz [Note: repulsus in B 7.], and was forced to enter Huesca.

After Godfrey, king of the Danes, died, Hemming, the son of his brother, succeeded to the kingdom and made peace with the emperor.

## DCCCXI.

After Arsafius the *spatharius*—that was the name of the ambassador of the emperor Nicephorus—had been released and dismissed, ambassadors were sent by the emperor to Constantinople to confirm that same peace [Note: gratie in B 2; greciae in B 5.]: Haido [Note: hatto in 9.] bishop of Basel [Note: basilensis in 3; bassensis in 5; basiliensis in 9; balensis in B 6.], Count Hugus [Note: hugo in 6, 7, and 8; hug in B 2, 5, and 7.] of Tours [Note: comis in B 2; toronicus in 1, 2, 4, and 10 and B 6; toringus in B 5; turonicus in the remaining witnesses.], Aio the Lombard from Friuli [Note: foro Iuli in 10 and B 5; fori Iuli in B 6.], and with them a certain Leo, a *spatharius*, a Sicilian by nationality, and Willeri, duke of the Venetians.

One of the latter two had fled from Sicily to the emperor in Rome ten years earlier, when the emperor was there; wishing to return, he was sent back to his homeland. The other, deprived of his office because of treachery, was ordered to be taken to Constantinople to his lord.

The peace agreed upon between the emperor and Hemming, king of the Danes, was maintained under arms alone by oath, because the severity of winter closed the road for travel between the two parties. This continued until the return of milder spring weather [Note: veris tempore in B 7.] and the opening of the roads that had been closed by the violence of the cold [Note: fuerant in B 7.]. Then twelve leading men from each side, that is, Franks and Danes, met above the River Eider at a place called … [Note: In 1: “at the place called …, oaths being given in turn”; in 2 and 7: “at the place called …, being raised in turn”; manuscripts 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, B 2, 5, and 6 read *datis*, “given,” with no lacuna; in 9 the phrase “at the place called” is absent.] [Col. 0475C] and, according to their rite and custom, the peace was confirmed by oaths.

The leading men on the Frankish side were:

Walach [Note: walah in B 2; wala in B 7; walachus in 7.], count, son of Bernhard [Note: bernardi in B 2 and 7.];

Burchard [Note: purchardus in B 6.], count [Note: *comis* throughout in B 2];

Unroch, count [Note: unrocus in 4 and B 2, 5, and 7; mirocus in 7.];

Uodo, count [Note: vado in 7; wado in 10.] [Note: Manuscript B 2 continues after “Meginhardus count” with four blank lines and then “Bernhardus count, Egbertus count,” etc.; B 5 omits *Meginhardus count* but indicates a lacuna; B 6 omits it; manuscripts B 3, 8, 10, and 11 read *Meginhardus comes*; B 9 reads *Meinhardus comes*.] [Meginhardus, count, in A and L.];

Bernhard, count [Note: absent in 3 and 9; Bernard in 7 and B 7.];

Egbert, count [Note: egberdus in 1; egibertus in 3; egebertus in 5 and 6; egilbertus in B 6.];

Theotheri, count [Note: thiotheri in 10 and B 5; teotheri in 2; theoderi in 3; theodorus in 5 and 6; thothericus in B 2; theodoricus in 7; theodericus in B 7; thederichus in 9.];

Abo, count [Note: abbo in 4; absent in 5.];

Ostdag, count [Note: ostdagus in 7; ostdach in 9; estagi in B 6; osdag in 4 and B 2, 7, and 8.];

Wigman, count [Note: wigmannus in 7; wigman in B 7.].

On the Danish side were, first of all, Hemming’s brothers, Hancwin [Note: hancvin in 2; hancum in 7; hancwinc in 9; hancwihe in B 6.] and Angandeo [Note: agadeo in 5; agandeo in 6; agantheo in B 2.]; then the other honorable men among their people: Osfred [Note: osfrid in B 2 and 7; offredus in 7, and likewise below.], surnamed Turdimulus [Note: tardimulo in B 2.]; Warstein [Note: warsteinus in 7; warsten in 9; warsein in B 7.]; Suomi; Urm [Note: urni in B 2; urim in B 7; urmus in 7; urin in 9.]; another Osfrid, son of Heiligen [Note: heligen in B 5; heiligeni in 7; heiligon in 9.]; Osfred of Sconaowe [Note: sconaouuae in B 5.]; Hebbi [Note: heibi in B 6; heppi in 6.]; and Aowin [Note: awin in 9; aouus in 7; awin in 10.].

After the emperor had made peace with Hemming and held the customary general assembly at Aachen, he sent three armies into three parts of his kingdom: one beyond the Elbe against the Linones [Note: hilinones in 9; liuones in 7.], which ravaged them and restored on the bank of the River Elbe the fortress of Hohbuoki [Note: hohbuozi in 4; hohbuochi in 5.] that the Wiltzi had destroyed in the preceding year [Note: distructum in 1 and B 2 and 5.]; another into Pannonia to settle the disputes between the Huns and Slavs; and a third into Britain to punish their treachery. All of them, having achieved success, returned unharmed [Col. 0476B].

Meanwhile, the emperor went to Boulogne, a coastal city, to inspect the fleet that he had ordered to be built in the preceding year [Note: “on land, because of the fleet” in B 2 and 5; *classes*, “fleets,” in parentheses.], where the same ships had been assembled [Note: eadem naves in 1 and 2 and B 2 and 6.]. He restored the lighthouse which had been established there in ancient times to guide the courses of sailors [Note: constitutum in B 2; constitutos in 5 and 6.] and lit a fire at its summit during the night [Note: “and restored it there,” *earumque ibi*, in 2 and 5; “and the temple there,” *fanumque ibi*, in 9.].

From there he came to the River Scheldt and, at the place called Ghent [Note: granda in 4; gand in 7 and B 7.] [Note: Ghent, in French *Gand*.], inspected the ships built for the same fleet [Note: aedificatos in B 2.]. He arrived at Aachen around the middle of November.

As he approached, envoys of King Hemming, Aowin [Note: aouun in B 6.] and Hebbi, met him, bringing the king’s gifts and peaceful words [Note: “bringing the king and peaceful words” in B 2.]. Also at Aachen, awaiting his arrival, were those who had come from Pannonia: Canizauci [Note: camzanci in 7; cani, zauci in 9.], prince [Note: plural “princes” in B 7.] of the Avars, and Tudun, together with other leading men and dukes of the Slavs living along the Danube [Col. 0476C]. They had been ordered by the commanders of the forces sent into Pannonia to come into the ruler’s presence [Note: *fuerant* in B 7; “they were seen” in B 2.].

Meanwhile, Charles, the emperor’s elder son [Note: “the son of the lord emperor” in A and L.], died on 4 December [Note: 3 December in B 5.]. The emperor wintered at Aachen.

## DCCCXII.

Not long afterward, it was reported that Hemming, king of the Danes, had died [Col. 0477A]. When Sigifrid, the nephew of King Godfrey, and Anulo [Note: Anolo in B 5 and 8; amilo in 7 and 9; in 2 the words “and Anulo, grandson of the king” are absent.] [Note: “grandson” is written with a lacuna in B 2.] the nephew of the former King Heriold [Note: “of Heriold and of the king himself” in A and L.; *pas* in 1.], wished to succeed him, but could not agree which of them should rule, they gathered their forces and joined battle, and both died. The faction of Anulo nevertheless gained the victory [Note: victoria in 3, 4, 6, 7, 10, and B 2, 5, 6, 8, and 9.]. His brothers Heriold and Reginfrid [Note: reginfredus in B 7; reginfridus in 5 and 6; ragenfridus in 7.] were established as kings by their party; the defeated faction, necessarily following them, did not refuse to acknowledge the same men as their rulers. In that battle, 10,940 men are said to have fallen [Note: “10,840 men” in B 5.].

The emperor Nicephorus, after many notable victories, died in a battle fought against the Bulgarians in the province of Moesia. His son-in-law Michael became emperor and received and released the emperor Charles’s envoys, who had been sent to Nicephorus, in Constantinople [Note: “to Constantinople” in 2 and B 5.] [Col. 0477B]. He also sent his own envoys with them: Michael the bishop, Arsafius [Note: arfasium in 2 and B 2.], and Theognostus [Note: adque teognostrum in B 2; theognistum in 9.], *protospatharii*. Through them he confirmed the peace begun with Nicephorus.

At Aachen, where they came to the emperor, they received from him in the church the written treaty. According to their custom—that is, in the Greek language—they sang praises to him, calling him Emperor and *Basileus* [Note: Greek: βασίλεα, “Basileus,” calling him so; and then they returned, in 9.]. On their return, when they came to Rome, they again received the same written treaty or pact from Pope Leo in the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle.

After dismissing them, the emperor held a solemn general assembly at Aachen and sent Bernhard, Pippin’s son and his own grandson, into Italy. Because of the report that a fleet was coming from both Africa and Spain to ravage Italy, he ordered Walan [Note: wallonem in 9.], the son of his paternal cousin Bernhard, to remain with him until the outcome of events brought security to our people.

This fleet came partly to Corsica and partly to Sardinia; and the part that reached Sardinia was almost entirely destroyed.

The fleet of the Northmen [Note: nordusmannorum in 2; nord-mannorum in 3, 7, and 9 and B 2, 5, and 6; nordamannorum in 4; nortmannorum in B 7; northanimbrorum in 5; nordanumbrorum in 6.] attacked the island of Ireland of the Scots [Note: scotorum in 1, 6, and 9 and B 7; scotthorum in 2.]. After joining battle with the Scots [Note: scottis in 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, and 10 and B 2, 5, and 6.], a considerable number of the Northmen were killed, and the fleet shamefully fled home.

Peace was made with Abulaz [Note: abulax in 2.] king of the Saracens, and likewise with Grimoald, duke of the Beneventans; and the Beneventans paid twenty-five thousand gold solidi as tribute.

An expedition was made against the Wiltzi, and hostages were received from them.

Hariold [Note: herioldus in 3 and 10 and B 7; heriholdus in 9.] and Reginfrid [Note: regenfridus in B 6; ragenfridus in 7; reinfridus in 2.], kings of the Danes, sent an embassy to the emperor, asking for peace and requesting that their brother Hemming be sent back to them [Note: “Robert, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Germain, died. The exceptionally wise man Iruuno (Irmino) succeeded him” in 7.].

In this year there was an eclipse of the sun in the afternoon of 15 May.

## DCCCXIII.

The emperor wintered at Aachen, and, as spring weather began, he sent Amalarius, bishop of Trier, and Peter, abbot of the monastery of Nonantula, to Constantinople to confirm peace with the emperor Michael. A bridge at Mainz burned down in May; after this, while the emperor was hunting in the Ardennes, he took to his bed because of pain in his feet. On recovering, he returned to Aachen. Then, after holding a general assembly, he summoned his son Louis, king of Aquitaine, to Aachen, placed the crown upon him, and made him his associate in the imperial dignity. He appointed his grandson Bernard, son of his son Pippin, over Italy and ordered him to be called king.

Councils were also held throughout Gaul by order of the emperor, by the bishops, for the correction of the condition of the churches. One was convened at Mainz, another at Rheims, a third at Tours, a fourth at Chalon, and a fifth at Arles. At that assembly, in the emperor’s presence, the constitutions enacted at each council were compared. Whoever wishes to know them will be able to find them in the five cities mentioned above, although copies of them are also kept in the palace archive.

[Note: The manuscripts read *veris* (“of spring”) in 4, 5, and 6; *verna* (“spring”) in 7; and *verno tempore* (“in springtime”) in 9 and B 7, instead of *verni temperie* (“spring weather”). *Almaharium* is read in manuscript 3 instead of *Amalharium*. *Novantulas* occurs in manuscript 6 and B 2; *nantulas* in B 2.]

From this assembly certain Frankish and Saxon nobles were sent across the River Elbe to the borders of the Northmen, to make peace with them according to the request of their kings and to return their brother. When an equal number—namely sixteen—of Danish nobles met them at the appointed place, peace was confirmed after oaths had been exchanged on both sides, and the kings’ brother was returned to them.

[Note: Manuscript 6 reads *nam XV* (“namely fifteen”) and B 7 *nam VI* (“namely six”), instead of *nam 16*.]

At that time, however, the kings were not at home. They had gone with an army to Westarfold, a region situated at the farthest end of their kingdom between north and west, facing the northern extremity of Britain. Its rulers and people had refused to submit to them.

[Note: The name appears as *Westarfoldam* in the principal text, *werstarfoldam* in manuscript 4, *westerfoldam* in B 6, and *westerfoeldam* in 9. Westarfold was in the western part of the Cimbrian peninsula, in southern Jutland. See Gebhardi, *History of Denmark*, p. 382.]

After they had subdued the region and returned, and had received from the emperor the brother who had been sent to them, the sons of King Godfred and many of the Danish nobles—who had long before abandoned their homeland and lived in exile among the Swedes—assembled forces from every direction, made war upon them, and, as bands of their countrymen streamed to them from every part of Danish territory, engaged them in battle and drove them from the kingdom with little difficulty.

[Note: The manuscripts read *Sueones* in the main text; *soeones* in 2, *suueones* in 3, *suenes* in 4, *suenones* in B 2, and *suones* in B 5.]

When the Moors were returning from Corsica to Spain with much booty, Irmingarius, count of Emporiae, laid an ambush for them at Majorca and captured eight of their ships. In them he found five hundred Corsican captives and more.

[Note: Manuscript B 5 reads *Sorsica* instead of *Corsica*. The town of Emporiae is today called Ampurias.]

Wishing to avenge this, the Moors ravaged Centumcellae, a city of Tuscia, and Nice, in the province of Narbonensis.

[Note: Centumcellae is Civita Vecchia; Nice is Nizza.]

They also attacked Sardinia, but after engaging the Sardinians in battle, they were driven back and defeated. Having lost many of their men, they withdrew.

[Note: In B 2, 3, and 7, the text ends with the word *recesserunt* (“they withdrew”).]

Meanwhile the emperor Michael, attacking the Bulgarians in war, met with little success. Accordingly, he returned home, laid aside the diadem, and became a monk. Leo, son of the patrician Bardas, was appointed emperor in his place.

[Note: The manuscripts read *Leo, Bardae patricii filius* in the main text; manuscript 3 has *leo eabdae patricius*, 9 *leo bapdae*, and Chesn. *leo papdae*.]

Crum, king of the Bulgarians, who two years earlier had killed the emperor Nicephorus and driven Michael from Moesia, elated by his success, advanced with his army as far as Constantinople itself and pitched camp beside the city gate. When he was riding around the city walls, the emperor Leo made a sortie, caught him off guard, and forced him, seriously wounded, to save himself by flight and return shamefully to his homeland.

## DCCCXIV

The lord Charles the emperor, while wintering at Aachen, in approximately the seventy-first year of his life, the forty-seventh of his reign, the forty-third since the conquest of Italy, and the fourteenth since he had been called emperor and Augustus, departed this life on the fifth day before the Kalends of February.

[Note: Manuscript 2 reads XLIIII (“forty-fourth”) instead of XLVII (“forty-seventh”). In manuscripts 10 and 11, *excessit* (“departed this life”) concludes the account; manuscript 11 adds the following brief description of the emperor’s burial.]

[Note: He was buried at Aachen in the basilica of the holy Mother of God, which he himself had built. His body was embalmed and placed seated on a golden throne in the vaulted part of the tomb, girded with a golden sword and holding a golden Gospel book in his hands and upon his knees. His shoulders rested against a chair, and his head was honorably raised and fastened by a golden chain to the diadem. A piece of the holy cross was placed in the diadem. They filled his tomb with spices, perfumes, balm, musk, and many golden treasures. His body was clothed in imperial garments, and his face was covered beneath the diadem with a cloth. A hair shirt was placed against his flesh, which he had always secretly worn; over the imperial garments they placed a golden pilgrim’s pouch, which he had been accustomed to carry to Rome. A golden scepter and a golden shield consecrated by Pope Leo were placed before him, hanging down. Then his tomb was closed and sealed. No one can tell how great the lamentation and mourning for him was throughout the whole earth; even among the pagans he was mourned as though he were the father of the world. The greatest mourning, however, was among Christians, especially throughout his entire kingdom. After he had been anointed with holy oil by the bishops, had received the viaticum, and had arranged all his affairs, he commended his spirit to the Lord and died in peace in the year 814 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. His most glorious son Louis reigned after him, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. 11.]

When his son Louis received news of this at the estate called Theodoadus in Aquitaine, where he too was then wintering, he came to Aachen on the thirtieth day after the event and, with the unanimous consent and favor of all the Franks, succeeded his father.

[Note: *Aequitania* occurs in B 6 and likewise frequently elsewhere. Theodoadus was Doué, near Saumur; see Valesius, *Notitia Galliarum*, p. 552.]

Turning his attention to the administration of the kingdom he had assumed, he first heard and dismissed the embassies of the peoples who had come to his father. He then received, in the same manner, other embassies that had been sent to his father but were now coming to him.

Among these the chief was an embassy sent from Constantinople. For the emperor Leo, who had succeeded Michael, sent his envoys—Christophorus the spatharius and Gregory the deacon—with Amalarius the bishop and Peter the abbot, who had been sent to Michael but had come to Leo, to the lord Charles; through them he sent a written statement and confirmation of the pact and alliance.

[Note: Manuscript 9 reads *de const missa* (“the embassy from Constantinople was sent”) instead of *de Constantinopoli directa* (“sent from Constantinople”). Manuscript B 2 reads *michaheli* instead of *Michaeli*. The principal text has *venerunt* (“came”); Chesn. reads *venerant* (“had come”).]

After receiving and dismissing these envoys, the lord Louis sent his own envoys to the emperor Leo to renew their friendship and confirm the aforesaid pact: Norbert, bishop of Reggio, and Richowinus, count of Poitiers.

[Note: The manuscripts read *Nordbertum* in the principal text; *norbertum* in 4 and 5; *nordus bertum* in 2. For Richowinus they read *richoinum* in 2, 4, and B 5; *richonium* in 3 and 7; *richwinum* in 9. *Patavinum* occurs in the principal text; *pitavinum* in 4, *pictavinum* in B 6, *pictavium* in 7, and *pictavensem* in Bouq.]

After holding a general assembly of his people at Aachen to administer justice and relieve the oppression of the common people, he sent envoys to every part of his kingdom. He summoned his grandson Bernard, king of Italy, to him and, after presenting him with gifts, sent him back to his kingdom.

He made and confirmed a pact with Grimoald, duke of the Beneventans, on the same terms as his father had done: namely, that the Beneventans should pay an annual tribute of seven thousand solidi. Then he sent two of his sons, Lothar to Bavaria and Pippin to Aquitaine.

[Note: The name Lothar appears as *Hlotharium* in the principal text, *hlutharium* in 4, *lutharium* in 6, and *lotharium* in 9.]

The Danish kings Hariold and Reginfrid, who in the preceding year had been defeated by the sons of Godfred and driven from the kingdom, having restored their strength, again made war upon them. In this conflict Reginfrid and one of the sons of Godfred, the elder by birth, were killed.

Thereafter Heriold, distrustful of his own position, came to the emperor and commended himself into his hands. The emperor received him and ordered him to go into Saxony and await a suitable opportunity at which he could provide the assistance he had requested.

[Note: The manuscripts give various forms of the names: *Herioldus*, *heriholtus*, *harioldus*, and *heriholtus*. Manuscript 9 reads *ei quemadmodum petierat* (“to assist him as he had requested”) instead of *sicut petierat*.]

## DCCCXV

The emperor ordered the Saxons and Abodrites to prepare for this expedition. Twice during that winter they attempted to cross the Elbe, but a sudden change in the weather softened and dissolved the river’s ice, and the undertaking remained unfinished.

[Note: The manuscripts read *Albis transiri posset* in the principal text; *albis transire posset* in 1, 2, 3, 6, and 9; *albia transire posset* in B 5; *albia transire potuisset* in B 6; *albis transiri posset* in 4, 5, and 10; and *albia transiri potuisset* in 7. Manuscript 9 has *ac glacie* (“and the ice”) instead of *glacie*. A. L. reads *imperfectum* (“incomplete”) instead of *infectum* (“unfinished”).]

At last, when winter had passed, around the middle of May an opportune time for departure appeared. Then all the Saxon counts and all the forces of the Abodrites, together with the emperor’s envoy Baldrich, as had been ordered, crossed the River Eider and reached the land of the Northmen called Sinlendi.

[Note: The name appears as *Sinlendi* in the principal text, *nomine sinlendi* in 9, *sindlendi* in 5, and *sialandiam* in 7. According to Othere, it lay in the eastern part of the Cimbrian peninsula, south of Jutland. See Dahlmann, *Researches in the Field of History*, vol. I, p. 439.]

From there they set out and, on the seventh day, finally pitched camp at a place called [lacuna] on the shore of the ocean.

[Note: Manuscript 9 reads *dicitur Littus oceani* (“it is called the Shore of the Ocean”). In manuscripts 2, 10, B 5, and 9, a space of four or six letters is left blank after *dicitur* (“is called”). Manuscript 7 omits *in loco qui dicitur* (“at a place called”). Manuscript B 5 reads *ponuntur* (“are placed”) instead of *ponunt* (“they place”).]

They remained there in a permanent camp for three days. The sons of Godfred had gathered a large force and a fleet of two hundred ships against them and were stationed on an island three miles from the mainland, but the Saxons and Abodrites did not dare to engage them. They ravaged the neighboring settlements on every side, took forty hostages from the inhabitants, and returned to the emperor in Saxony.

At that time the emperor was holding a general assembly of his people at a place called Paderborn.

[Note: The place-name appears as *Padrabrunno* in the principal text; *padrabundo* in 5, *padrebunno* in B 5, *poderbrunno* in B 6, *patherbrunno* in 4, *padrabrunna* in 9, and *padrebrunno* in 7.]

There all the leading men and envoys of the eastern Slavs came to him. But before he reached that place—that is, while he was still at home—news was brought to him that certain leading Romans had conspired to kill Pope Leo in Rome itself, and that, after information about this plot had reached the pope, all the leaders of that faction had been slaughtered by his order.

[Note: One version reads *priusquam tamen illuc veniret, sed domi adhuc* (“before he came there, when he was still at home”).]

The emperor was distressed by this. After arranging the affairs of the Slavs and of Heriold, and leaving Heriold in Saxony, he went to the palace at Frankfurt. There he sent Bernard, king of Italy and his grandson, who had himself been with him in Saxony, to Rome to investigate the reported events.

When Bernard reached Rome, he fell ill and took to his bed. Nevertheless, through Count Gerold, who had been assigned to him as envoy for this purpose, he reported to the emperor what he had discovered.

[Note: Manuscript 9 reads *ipse secum* (“he with him”) instead of *ipse* (“he himself”). Manuscript 9 reads *Is cum eo* (“when he came there”) instead of *Is cum Romam venisset* (“when he reached Rome”). The name appears as *Geroldus* in the principal text and *gerholtus* in 9. The envoy was *legatus* (“envoy”) in the principal text; manuscript 9 reads *nunciavit* (“reported”) instead of *mandavit* (“sent word”).]

The pope’s envoys—John, bishop of Silva Candida, Theodore the nomenclator, and Sergius the duke—followed him and fully satisfied the emperor concerning the charges brought against their lord.

Envoys from Sardinia, from the city of Caralis, came bearing gifts.

[Note: Caralis is Cagliari. The manuscripts read *de Carali* in the principal text, *de karoli* in 5, 6, and B 6.]

The peace that had been made with Abulaz, king of the Saracens, and had been maintained for three years, was broken as though it were useless, and war was again undertaken against him.

[Note: The manuscripts read *irrupta* in the principal text; *erepta* in 1, *erupta* in 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 10, *rupta* in 7 and 9, and *rupta* in B 5 and B 6.]

Bishop Nordbert and Count Richowinus returned from Constantinople, bringing the written pact that the emperor Leo had given them. Among other things, they reported that a very severe earthquake had occurred there in August for five continuous days. They testified that many buildings of the city itself had collapsed and that the inhabitants of other cities had been overwhelmed by the ruins.

[Note: The manuscripts read *Nordbertus* in the principal text and *nordberdus* in 1 and 4; *Richoinus* in the principal text and *richwinus* in 9.]

It is also said that in Gaul, Santones, a city of Aquitaine, trembled in September.

[Note: The name appears as *Santones* in the principal text, *sanctonas* in 4 and 6, and *santonis* in 7. The month appears as *Septembrio* in the principal text and *septembri* in 7 and 9.]

The River Rhine, swollen by Alpine rains, overflowed beyond its usual level.

[Note: Manuscript B 5 reads *imbrio* (“by a rainstorm”) instead of *imbribus* (“by rains”).]

When the Romans saw that Pope Leo had fallen ill, they gathered a band of men and first plundered all the estates that the pontiff had recently built in the territories of the several cities. Then they set them on fire. Finally, they decided to go to Rome and violently seize what they complained had been taken from them.

[Note: Manuscript 4 reads *idem episcopus* (“the same bishop”) instead of *idem pontifex* (“the same pontiff”); manuscript 9 omits *idem pontifex*. Manuscript 9 reads *ditionibus* (“jurisdictions”) instead of *territoriis* (“territories”). Manuscript 9 reads *exstruxerat* (“had built”) instead of *exstruxit* (“built”). Manuscript 1 reads *viderunt* (“they saw”) instead of *viderent* (“they saw” in the subjunctive).]

When Bernard learned of this, he sent troops under Winigis, duke of Spoleto, suppressed the revolt, and forced them to abandon their undertaking. Through his envoys he informed the emperor of what had occurred.

[Note: The manuscripts read *ab incepto* in the principal text; B 5 has *ab coepto* and 9 *a coepto*. A. L. reads *a cepto*.]

## DCCCXVI

When winter had passed, the Saxons and the eastern Franks were ordered to make an expedition against the Sorbian Slavs, who were not obedient to orders. They vigorously fulfilled what had been commanded and suppressed the boldness of the rebellious people without great difficulty. For after one city had been captured, whatever in that people appeared rebellious became quiet upon promising submission.

The Basques who live beyond the Garonne and around the Pyrenean mountain, angered by the removal of their duke Sigwin—whom the emperor had removed because of his excessive arrogance and depravity of character—were stirred by their customary fickleness. Having formed a conspiracy, they revolted in every respect.

[Note: The name appears as *Sigwinus* in the principal text and 9 and B 6; *sigewinus* in 4; *siguwinus* in 3; and *sigivinus* in B 5.]

But they were so thoroughly subdued by two expeditions that their surrender and attainment of peace seemed late in coming.

Meanwhile, in the twenty-first year of his pontificate, around the eighth day before the Kalends of June, Pope Leo departed this life.

[Note: The principal text reads *VIII Kal. Iun.*; B 5 reads *VIII kal. Iul.* (“the eighth day before the Kalends of July”); B 8 reads *V kal. Iun.* (“the fifth day before the Kalends of June”). Bouq. reads *a seculo migravit* (“departed from the world”) instead of *de corpore migravit* (“departed from the body”).]

The deacon Stephen was elected and ordained in his place. Before two months had elapsed after his consecration, he hastened to come to the emperor by the fastest journeys he could make, sending two envoys ahead to present his case to the emperor as though on behalf of his consecration.

When the emperor heard this, he decided to meet him at Rheims. He sent men to escort him there and, arriving before him, received him with great honor.

Stephen immediately explained the reason for his arrival to the emperor. After the customary solemn celebration of Mass, he crowned him by placing the diadem upon his head. Many gifts were then given and received between them, lavish banquets were celebrated, and their friendship was established with the strongest firmness. Other measures beneficial to the holy Church of God were arranged as circumstances permitted. The pontiff set out for Rome, while the emperor went to the palace at Compiègne.

[Note: The manuscripts read *oppipare* in 1, 4, and B 6; *opipare* in 2, 3, 7, and B 5; *oppidare* in 5 and 6; and *opime* in 9, meaning respectively “lavishly,” “sumptuously,” “richly,” or “very well.” Manuscript 9 reads *fortissimo* (“with the firmest”) instead of *firmissimo* (“with the strongest”).]

While staying there, he received envoys from the Abodrites and envoys from Spain sent to him by Abdirahman, son of Abulaz, king of the Saracens. After spending twenty days or more there, he departed for Aachen to winter.

[Note: The name appears as *Abdirahman* in the principal text, *abdirahaman* in B 5, and *abdirachman* in 9.]

## DCCCXVII

The envoys of Abdirahman, son of Abulaz, king of the Saracens, sent from Zaragoza, came to request peace. The emperor heard them at Compiègne and ordered them to precede him to Aachen.

When he arrived there, he received an envoy of the emperor Leo from Constantinople, named Nicephorus, who had been sent concerning the Dalmatians. Since Cadolah, to whom responsibility for that border had been entrusted, was absent but was expected shortly, he ordered Nicephorus to await his arrival.

[Note: The principal text reads *Dalmatinorum* (“of/concerning the Dalmatians”); the manuscripts read *dalmaticorum* in 4 and B 5, *dalmantinorum* in B 6, *delmaticorum* in 7, and *dalmatarum* in 9. The name Cadolah appears as *Cadolah* in the principal text, *cadolaus* in 6, *cadolachus* in 7, *cadolach* in 9, and *cadolon* in B 5.]

When Cadolah arrived, a discussion was held between him and the emperor’s envoy concerning the matters that the latter had brought forward. Since the matter concerned many Romans and Slavs and seemed unable to be settled without their presence, its determination was postponed. Albgarius, grandson of Unroch, was sent to Dalmatia for this purpose with Cadolah and the aforesaid envoy.

[Note: The manuscripts read *cum Cadolane* in the principal text; *cum cadolach* in 9, *kadolone* in 5, *cadolone* in 6, and *cadelane* in B 6. The name Albgarius appears as *Albgarius* in the principal text, *abgarius* in 2 and 3, *albagarius* in 5 and 6, and *albigarius* in 7 and 9. For Unroch, manuscript 7 reads *mirochi*.]

The envoys of Abdirahman, after being detained for three months and beginning to despair of returning, were sent back.

The sons of King Godfred of the Danes, disturbed by Heriold’s continual attacks, sent an embassy to the emperor, requested peace, and promised that they would observe it. But since this appeared more deceitful than truthful, it was disregarded as empty, and assistance was given to Heriold against them.

The moon was eclipsed on the Nones of February at the second hour of the night, and a comet appeared in the constellation of the Charioteer.

[Note: The manuscripts read *Agitatoris* (“the Charioteer” or “Driver”) in 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, B 5, and B 6; in manuscript 5 a second hand wrote *Sagitatoris* (“the Archer”); manuscripts 7 and 9 read *Sagittarii* (“Sagittarius”).]

Meanwhile, in the third month after Pope Stephen had come to Rome, though that month had not yet been completed, around the eighth day before the Kalends of February, he died.

Paschal was elected as his successor. After his ordination had been solemnly completed, he sent the emperor gifts and an explanatory letter, in which he asserted that the honor of the pontificate had been imposed upon him even though he did not wish it and had resisted it most strongly.

[Note: The manuscripts read *inpactum* in 1, 2, 3, 7, 9, 10, B 5, and B 6; *impositum intimavit* in 4, 5, and 6.]

Nevertheless, he sent another embassy and requested that the pact made with his predecessors be made and confirmed with him as well. Theodore the nomenclator conveyed this embassy and obtained what had been requested.

On the Thursday on which the Lord’s Supper is celebrated, as the emperor was returning from church after completing the sacred service, the wooden portico through which he was walking suddenly collapsed. It had been built of fragile material, and the beams and planks supporting the structure, already rotten and decayed, were unable to bear any weight. The collapse brought the emperor down to the ground together with more than twenty men who were walking with him.

[Note: Manuscript 9 omits *tunc* (“then”). Manuscript 9 reads *depressit* (“crushed”) instead of *deposuit* (“brought down”).]

Although this accident seriously injured most of those who fell with him, it caused him no injury except that the left side of his lower chest was bruised by the hilt of the sword with which he was girded, the back of his right ear was wounded, and his right thigh near the groin was crushed by the weight of a piece of wood.

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *aliut* (“anything else”) instead of *aliud* (“anything else”); the other reading is *reliqui aliud* (“the rest suffered something else”). Manuscript 9 reads *Qui cum casus* (“when this accident”) instead of *Qui casus* (“this accident”).]

Through the diligent care of the physicians attending him, he recovered with great speed. On the twentieth day after the accident he departed for Nijmegen and exercised himself by hunting.

[Note: Manuscript 9 reads *sed opera* (“but through the efforts”) instead of *sed instantia* (“through the diligence”) of the physicians.]

After returning from there, he held his customary general assembly of his people at Aachen. At it he crowned his firstborn son Lothar and made him his associate in name and imperial power. He appointed his other sons, who had been called kings, one over Aquitaine and the other over Bavaria.

After the assembly had ended, he went toward the Vosges forest to hunt. There he encountered envoys of the emperor Leo. He heard them at the palace at Ingelheim, near the city of Mainz, and discovered that their embassy concerned nothing other than what Nicephorus, the same emperor’s envoy, had recently brought. He therefore dismissed them promptly and continued on his journey.

[Note: The manuscripts give variants of Ingelheim: *Ingilenhaim* in 10 and B 5 and B 6, *ingilinheim* in 4, and *ingelheim* in 9. For Mainz they read *Mogontiacum* in the principal text, *mogon ciacum* in 1, 5, and 6, *magontiam* in B 6, *moguntiacum* in 9, and *magontiacam* in 7.]

When the revolt of the Abodrites and Sclaomir was reported, he sent word through an envoy that only the counts who customarily remained on garrison duty beside the Elbe should stay there to protect the borders entrusted to them.

The cause of the revolt was that Sclaomir, who since the death of Thrasco had alone held royal power over the Abodrites, was ordered to share it with Ceadrago, Thrasco’s son. This so greatly enraged him that he declared that he would never again cross the River Elbe or come to the palace.

He immediately sent an embassy across the sea, joined friendship with the sons of Godfred, and obtained from them a promise that an army would be sent into Saxony beyond the Elbe. Their fleet came up the Elbe as far as the fortress of Esesfeld and devastated the entire bank of the River Stör. Gluomi, guardian of the Northmen’s frontier, led infantry forces and, together with the Abodrites, approached the fortress by land.

[Note: The place-name appears as *Esesfeld* in the principal text; *eselsfeld* in 2, *essefeld* in 3, *esesflet* in 4, *esefeld* in 6, *eselfeldem* in 7, *essesfeld* in 9, *essesfeldum* in B 5, and *esesfeldum* in B 6. The name Gluomi appears as *gluomicusto* in 1 and *gluomus* in 7. Manuscript 2 reads *nordmannici* for “of the Northmen.”]

When our men resisted them bravely, they abandoned the siege of the fortress and withdrew.

Meanwhile, as the emperor was returning from the Vosges to Aachen after finishing his hunt, he was informed that his grandson Bernard, king of Italy, had, on the advice of certain wicked men, contemplated tyranny. He had already fortified all the entrances by which Italy is entered—that is, the mountain passes—with garrisons, and all the cities of Italy had sworn allegiance to him. This was partly true and partly false.

When the emperor hastened to enter Italy against this movement with a large army gathered from all Gaul and Germany with the greatest speed, Bernard, distrustful of his own position, especially because he saw his supporters abandoning him daily, laid down his arms and surrendered to the emperor at Chalon.
