[Note: The manuscripts read *Cavillionem* in the principal text, *gavillonem* in B 5, *cavillonem* in 3 and B 6, and *cabillonem* in 7 and 9.]

The others followed him. They not only surrendered after laying down their arms but also voluntarily disclosed, at the first questioning, everything exactly as it had happened.

The leaders of this conspiracy were Eggideo, the foremost among the king’s friends; Reginhardus, his chamberlain; and Reginharius, son of Count Meginharius, whose maternal grandfather Hardradus had once conspired in Germany with many nobles of that province against the emperor Charles.

[Note: The name appears as *Eggideo* in the principal text and *egiddeo* in 3. Manuscript 9 reads *inter omnes amicos* (“first among all his friends”) instead of *inter amicos regis primus* (“the foremost among the king’s friends”). The names appear as *Reginhardus*, *reginhartus* in 9, and *Reginhardus* in the apparatus; *Reginharius* and *reginhardus* in the variants. Manuscript 1 reads *meginharii* for *Meginharii*. Manuscript 9 reads *cubicularius* (“chamberlain”) instead of *camerarius* (“chamberlain”).]

There were also many other distinguished and noble men who were discovered to have taken part in the same crime, among them several bishops: Anshelm of Milan, Wolfoldus of Cremona, and Theodulfus of Orléans.

[Note: Manuscript 3 reads *theodolfus* instead of *Theodulfus*.]

## DCCCXVIII

After the fraud had been discovered and the conspiracy exposed, and all the rebels had been brought under his authority, the emperor returned to Aachen. When the Lenten fast had ended, a few days after Holy Easter, he ordered the leaders of the conspiracy named above, together with the king, to be condemned by the judgment of the Franks to capital punishment, but commanded that they be deprived only of their sight.

The bishops, deposed by synodal decree, were handed over to monasteries. The others, according as each appeared more or less guilty, were either sent into exile or tonsured and confined to monasteries.

[Note: Manuscript 9 reads *exilio proscribi* (“to be proscribed into exile”) instead of *exilio deportari* (“to be deported into exile”).]

After these matters had been arranged, the emperor himself attacked Brittany with a very large army and held a general assembly at Vannes. From there he entered the province and, after capturing the rebels’ fortifications, quickly brought the whole region under his power without great difficulty.

For after Mormanus, who had claimed royal power for himself in that land, contrary to the customary practice of the Britons, was killed by the emperor’s army, no Briton could be found who would resist, carry out the orders given, or refuse to surrender the hostages demanded.

[Note: The manuscripts give *Mormanus* in the principal text and *marmamus* in B 6. Manuscript 4 reads *bretto* for “Briton.” B g reads *faceret* (“would carry out”) instead of *facere* (“to carry out”).]

When the expedition had been completed, the emperor dismissed the army and returned to the city of Angers. His queen and wife Irmingard, whom he had left there sick when he departed, died two days after he came to her, as her illness grew worse, on the fifth day before the Nones of October.

[Note: The city-name appears as *Andecavos* in the principal text, *andecaos* in 3, *andecavis* in B 5, *andegovis* in 6, and *andegavos* in 7 and 9. The name Irmingard appears as *Irmingardis* in the principal text and *irmengardis* in 2. Manuscripts 4 and 6 read *regia coniux* (“royal wife”) instead of *coniux* (“wife”). The *Codex Arman* reads *VI non. oct.* (“the sixth day before the Nones of October”) instead of *V Nonas Octob.*]

A solar eclipse occurred on the eighth day before the Ides of July.

The emperor returned to Aachen to winter, traveling through Rouen, Amiens, and Cambrai. When he reached Heristal, he encountered envoys of Sigo, duke of the Beneventans, bearing gifts and exonerating him concerning the killing of his predecessor, Duke Grimoald.

[Note: The manuscripts give *Ratumagum* in the principal text, *rothomagum* in 7, and *rotomagum* in 9 for Rouen; and *Camaracum* in the principal text and *cameracum* in 1 and 5 for Cambrai.]

There were also envoys from other peoples: from the Abodrites; from Borna, duke of the Guduscani and Timociani, who had recently defected from the alliance of the Bulgarians and come over to our borders; and from Liudewit, duke of Lower Pannonia, who, fomenting revolution, was attempting to accuse Cadolah, count and prefect of the march of Friuli, of cruelty and arrogance.

[Note: The name of the Timociani appears as *Timocianorum* in the principal text and *timacianorum* in 2. The name Liudewit appears as *Liudewiti* in the principal text, *ludewici* in 4 and 5, *liudewiti* in B 5, *ludowiti* in 6, and *liudewici* in 10 and B 6. Manuscript B 5 reads *calolaum* instead of *Cadolaum*, and *foroiulensis* instead of *Foroiuliensis*. Manuscript B 6 reads *conabant* (“they attempted”) instead of *conabatur* (“he was attempting”).]

After hearing and dismissing them there, the emperor went to Aachen to winter.

[Supplementary apparatus for the preceding passages: In manuscripts 7 and B 2 (3), the passage from *Pons* (“a bridge”) through *reversus est* (“he returned”) is absent. For Chalon, manuscript 3 reads *cabillonis*, 7 *cabilloni*, 9 *cabillone*, and 5, 6, and B 7 *cabillone*; B 5 reads *potuit* (“was able”) for *poterit* (“will be able”). B 5 and 6 have *princeps* (“ruler”) for *principes* (“rulers”), and manuscripts 1, 5, and 6 have *turbis* (“crowds”) for *turmis* (“bands”). For Irmingarius, manuscript 2 reads *irmigarius*, B 2 has an uncertain lacunose form ending *-ingarius*, and B 7 *herminguarius*. For Crum, manuscript 4 reads *crimas* and 6 *brumas*.

For Louis, B 2 reads *hludouuicum* and B 5 *hlodowicum*. Manuscript 9 reads *patrem ante quidem* (“indeed, to his father before”) for *ad patrem quidem*; it also reads *confirmandum misit* (“sent [them] to confirm”) for *confirmandum direxit*, *sui fines misit* (“sent [them] into his own territories”) for *in omnes regni sui partes dimisit*, and *donavit et in regnum remisit* for the wording concerning Bernard’s gifts and return. For Grimoald, manuscripts 4, 5, and 6 read *grimoldo*. The forms of Heriold’s name are: *facto herioldus* in 1, 2, (3), 10, B 5, and B 6; *harioldus* in 4, 5, 6, and 7; and *heriholtus* in 9. Manuscript 9 reads *posset* (“could”) for *potuisset* (“might have been able”).

For the Danish expedition, *Abodriti* appears as *abotriti* in 2, 9, and B 6; manuscript 9 omits *fere* (“nearly/about”); Baldrich appears as *baldericho* in 9 and *balderico* in 7. The forms of Hariold’s name at this point are *harioldo* in 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10, and B 5; *hairioldo* in 6; *harialdo* in B 6; and *heriholto* in 9. Manuscript 9 omits *qui* (“who”), has *residerent* (“were stationed”) for *residebant*, and *ipsique cum eis* (“and they themselves with them”) for *cum eis*. Its alternative wording for the emperor’s situation is *priusquam tamen illuc veniret, sed domi adhuc* (“but before he came there, while he was still at home”). B 5 reads *renhus* for *Rhenus* (“Rhine”).

For the following year, manuscripts 4, 5, and 6 read *domiti* (“subdued”) for *edomiti* (“thoroughly subdued”); manuscript 9 reads *potuit* (“could”) for *poterat* (“was able”) of Stephen’s speed of travel. Manuscripts 3, 4, 5, 6, and 9 read *ibi cum moraretur* (“while he was staying there”); 2 and B 6, *ibi cum moratur*; and 1, 7, 10, and B 5, *ibi conmoratus*. At the opening of DCCCXVII, B 5 reads *abdirahaman* and B 6 *abdiracman* for *Abdirahman*. B 5 reads *et firmare* (“and to confirm”) for *et firmari* (“to be confirmed”); Bouq. reads *vero peracto* (“indeed having been completed”) for *peracto*; and manuscript 9 reads *exercitus trans Albim* (“an army across the Elbe”) for *in Saxoniam transalbianam* (“into Saxony beyond the Elbe”).

In the Bernard conspiracy passage, manuscripts 3, 4, 5, and 6 read *clausas* (“closed [passes]”) for *clusas* (“mountain passes”), and manuscript 9 reads *congregato cum summa* (“having been assembled with the greatest”) for *congregato summa*. Finally, manuscript 9 reads *sunt et Bernhartum regem* (“were [named], and King Bernard”) for *sunt, simul et regem* (“were [named], together with the king”).]

## DCCCXIX
Sclaomir, king of the Abodrites, on account of whose treachery an army of Saxons and East Franks had been sent across the Elbe that same year to avenge it, was brought to Aachen by the commanders of the Saxon frontier and the emperor’s envoys who were in charge of the army. When the leading men of his people, who had likewise been ordered to come, accused him of many crimes, and he was unable to refute the charges brought against him with a reasonable defense, he was condemned to exile, and the kingdom was given to Ceadragus, son of Thrasco.

In a similar manner, Lupus Centulli, a Basque, who had fought in battle that same year with Berengar at Toulouse and with Warinus, count of the Auvergne [Col. 0486D]—during which engagement he also lost his brother Garsandus [Note: *garuhandum* in 9; *garhardum* in 3.], a man of singular madness [Note: “he lost the man” in 9.]—and who himself came close to destruction unless he saved himself by fleeing [Note: “had saved himself” in 9.] [Col. 0487A], when he had come into the emperor’s presence and could not clear himself of the treachery of which he was monstrously accused by the aforesaid counts [Note: *inmane* is absent in 9; *immaniter* in 7.], was likewise carried away into temporary exile [Note: “condemned to exile” in 9.].

A council was held at Aachen [Note: *aquasgrani* in 1.] after the Nativity of the Lord. At it many matters concerning the condition of churches and monasteries were discussed and arranged; certain highly necessary chapters were also written out and added to the laws, since they were lacking [Note: *legimus* (“we read”) in 1; *necessaria* (“necessary”) in 9.]. When this had been completed, the emperor, after inspecting the daughters of many nobles, took as his wife Judith, daughter of Count Welf [Note: *huelpi* in 1–7 and B 5–6; *welpi* in 9.].

Again, a council was held in July at the palace of Ingelheim [Note: *ingilumheim* in 2; *ingilenheim* in 4; *gilenheim* in 6; *in ingilenhaim* in B 5; *ingilheim* in B 6; *ingelheim* in 9.], and an army was sent from Italy into Pannonia on account of Liudewit’s rebellion. After achieving little success, it returned with its task almost unfinished [Col. 0487B]. And Liudewit [Note: “but Liudewit is” in 9.], puffed up with pride, sent envoys to the emperor as though seeking peace, proposing certain conditions and promising that he would do whatever was ordered if those conditions were granted [Note: “proposing certain conditions, in return for whose concession” in 1.]. When the emperor did not accept them but proposed other terms to him through his own envoys, Liudewit judged it best to persist in the treachery he had begun. He therefore sent envoys in every direction and arranged to incite the neighboring peoples near him to war [Note: “near him” is absent in 9.].

He also intercepted the people of the Timociani, who, having abandoned their alliance with the Bulgars, were trying to come to the emperor and place themselves under his authority; and he so ensnared them with false persuasions that, abandoning what they had intended to do, they became partners and accomplices in his treachery [Note: “so that this might not happen” in 9.].

When the army had returned from Pannonia, Cadolah, duke of the Friuli March, was seized by fever and died in the march itself. Baldric was appointed in his place. When he had entered the region of the Carantani, which had been assigned to his care, he encountered there Liudewit’s army, which was marching beside the river Drava [Note: “The Drave, or Drau.”]. Attacking it with a small force, he killed many men, turned the army back, and drove it from that province.

Borna, duke of Dalmatia, met Liudewit, who was coming against him with large forces, at the river Colapis [Note: *colampium* in 4 and 6.] [Note: “The Culpa.”]. In the first engagement he was deserted by the Guduscani; nevertheless, protected by the assistance of his household troops, he escaped. Dragamosus [Note: *dramagosus* in 5 and 6; *dragomosus* in 9.], Liudewit’s father-in-law, was killed in that battle. At the beginning of the defection he had abandoned his son-in-law and joined Borna.

The Guduscani returned home and were again subdued by Borna [Note: “by Borna” is absent in 1.]. But Liudewit [Note: “But Liudewit” in 1.], finding an opportunity [Col. 0487D], entered Dalmatia with a strong force in December and devastated it with sword and fire [Note: “he devastated everything with fire” in A and L.]. When Borna saw that he was entirely unequal to him [Note: *p. imperam* in 1.], he shut up all his possessions in fortresses. He himself, with a picked force, attacking now from the rear and now from the flank [Note: “now from the altar” in 1.], harassed Liudewit’s troops [Note: *liudewit copias* in 1.] by night and day wherever he could. He did not allow Liudewit to move about his province with impunity; finally, after inflicting heavy losses, he forced him to leave his territory. Three thousand men of Liudewit’s army were killed, and three hundred or more horses were captured, besides baggage and plunder of various kinds. Borna arranged to report the whole course of these events to the emperor through his envoys [Note: “after being stricken, he seized his own region and expelled him” in 4, 5, and 6.].

In the western regions, Pippin, the emperor’s son, entered Gascony with an army at his father’s command. After removing the rebels from it, he so pacified the entire province [Note: *paccavit* in 1 and 5.] that no rebel or disobedient person seemed to remain there.

Harioldus, likewise, was escorted back to his ships by the Abodrites at the emperor’s command and sailed to his homeland, as though he were going to receive the kingdom there. Two of Godofrid’s sons are said to have joined themselves to him, as though they were going to hold the kingdom together with him, while two other sons were expelled from their homeland. But this is thought to have been done by deception.

After dismissing the council, the emperor came first to Kreuznach [Note: *crucianacum* in B 5; *crucianiacum* in 6.] [Note: “Creuznach.”], then to Bingen [Note: “Bingen.”]. From there he sailed down the Rhine with the current as far as Koblenz. He then departed for the Ardennes for the sake of hunting. After completing the hunt there according to the customary practice, he returned to Aachen for the winter.

## DCCCXX.

In January a council was held there [Note: “there was held” in 6.], at which deliberation was made concerning Liudewit’s defection. It was decided that three armies should be sent simultaneously from three directions to devastate his region and restrain his boldness [Col. 0488C]. Borna first made recommendations through envoys and then came in person, presenting what he thought ought to be done.

At this council Bera, count of Barcelona [Note: “of Barcelona also” in 4, 5, and 6.], who had long been accused by his neighbors of fraud and disloyalty [Note: *infelicitatis* (“unhappiness”) in B 5.], attempted to fight his accuser in mounted combat and was defeated [Note: *simulabatur* (“was being accused”) in 4, 5, and 6.]. Although he was to be condemned as guilty of treason to death, the emperor spared him out of mercy and sent him into exile at Rouen [Note: “proscribed into exile” in 9.].

When the winter had passed, as soon as the grass could provide fodder for the animals, those three armies were sent against Liudewit. One entered from Italy through the Noric Alps, another through the province of the Carantani, and the third through Bavaria and Upper Pannonia. Two of them—the right and the left—entered more slowly, because one was prevented from crossing the Alps by an enemy force resisting it, while the other was impeded both by the length of the journey and by the river Drava, which had to be crossed. The middle army, however, which entered through the Carantani, although resistance was offered to it in three places, enjoyed better fortune: after defeating the enemy three times and crossing the Drava as well, it reached its appointed places more quickly [Col. 0489A].

Liudewit undertook nothing against these forces. He merely kept himself and his men inside the fortification of a castle that he had built on a steep mountain, and is said to have had no communication with them, whether concerning war or peace, either in person or through envoys [Note: “to have had communication with them” in 1; “with them” is absent in 9.].

After the armies had assembled in one place, they devastated almost the entire region with sword and fire [Note: “devastating with fire” in 9.] and returned home without suffering any serious loss. The army that had traveled through Upper Pannonia, however, was seriously afflicted while crossing the Drava by an intestinal illness caused by the unhealthy character of the places and waters; a considerable part of it was consumed by this disease.

These three armies had been assembled from Saxony, East Francia, and Alamannia [Note: *alimannia* in 1.], as well as Bavaria and Italy. When they had returned home, the Carniolans who live around the river Sava [Note: “who live around the river Carcasavus” in 3 and 9.] and are almost adjacent to the men of Friuli surrendered to Baldric. A part of the Carantani, which had defected from us to Liudewit’s side, likewise took care to do the same.

The treaty between us and Abulaz, king of Spain [Note: “king of the Saracens” in the constant reading of 9.], which had been established and was sufficiently advantageous to neither party, was deliberately broken, and war was undertaken against him.

In the Italian Sea, eight merchant ships returning from Sardinia to Italy were captured and sunk by pirates. From Nordmannia thirteen pirate ships set out. They first attempted to plunder on the Flemish coast, but were driven back by those who were stationed there [Note: “by those who were there on guard” in 9.]. Nevertheless, because of the negligence of the guards, they burned several poor cottages and drove away a small number of livestock [Col. 0489C]. When they attempted similar actions at the mouth of the Seine, the coast guards resisted them; after five of their men had been killed, they withdrew unsuccessfully. Finally, having met with success on the Aquitanian coast, they completely plundered a certain village called Bundium [Note: “An unidentified village. For Valesius, loc. cit., p. 103, understands by it St. Paul de Born, situated across the Garonne near a lake close to the sea; but this rests on conjecture. It should be read Born, which is entirely unsuitable to the place.”] [Note: *Buynbundium* in A and L.] and returned home with enormous booty.

That year, because of continuous rains and air saturated with excessive moisture [Note: *umore* in 1, 2, and 10; *humore* in 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, B 5, and B 6.], great hardships occurred. A plague among both human beings and cattle spread so terribly and so widely that scarcely any part of the entire Frankish kingdom could be found free and untouched by it. Grain and legumes were also spoiled by the continual rains: they either could not be gathered or rotted after being gathered.

Wine, too, whose yield was small that year, became sour [Col. 0489D] [Note: *aceruum* in 1, 2, 10, and B 6; the other witnesses read *acerbum*.] and unpleasant [Col. 0490A] because of the lack of heat. In certain places, moreover, because rivers had overflowed and water stood stagnant on the plain, autumn sowing was so impeded that absolutely no crops were sown before the spring weather.

The moon was eclipsed on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, at the second hour of the night [Note: *ora* (“hour”) in 1.]. After completing the autumnal council at Quierzy and finishing the customary autumn hunt, the emperor returned to Aachen [Note: *inmaniter … et intacta … ex inundatione … vernum tempus … aquas* in 9.].

## DCCCXXI.

A council was held at Aachen in February. At it the war against Liudewit was discussed, and three armies were organized to devastate the fields of the treacherous men in succession during the coming summer. A similar decision was made concerning the Spanish March [Note: *hispana* in 1, 2, 3, 7, and 10; *hispania* in 4 and B 5–6; *hyspania* in 5–6; *hispanica* in 9.], and this was also commanded to the commanders of that frontier.

Again, it was decreed that a council should be held at Nijmegen in May [Col. 0490B], and counts who were to come there were appointed.

Then [Note: “that year” in 9; “at the same time” in B 5.], after completing the Easter festival, the lord emperor sailed along the Meuse. There he reviewed the division of the kingdom among his sons, which had been established and written down in earlier years [Note: *regni* is lacking at this point in codex 10.], and confirmed it by the oaths of the leading men who had been able to be present at that time. He also received there the envoys of Paschal, the Roman pontiff—namely Peter, bishop of Centumcellae, and Leo the nomenclator—and, after quickly dismissing them [Note: *iesdemque* in 1.], sent the counts who were present on the Pannonian expedition. He himself remained there for a short time [Note: “remained” in B 6.] and then returned to Aachen.

A few days later, traveling through the Ardennes, he came to Trier and Metz. From there, making for the castle of Rumeric, he spent the remainder of the summer heat and half of autumn in hunting exercises in the forested and secluded regions of the Vosges [Note: “he spent” in B 5.].

Meanwhile Borna, duke of Dalmatia and Liburnia, died. At the request of the people and with the emperor’s consent, his nephew, named Ladasclavus [Note: *ladosclavus* in 6; *ladasclao* in B 8–9.], was appointed his successor.

News was also brought of the death of Leo, the emperor of Constantinople: he had been killed in the palace itself through a conspiracy of certain of his leading men, especially through the plots of Michael, count of the household troops [Note: “through the plots of the household troops” in 9.]. Michael is said to have assumed the imperial insignia through the support of the citizens and the enthusiasm of the palace soldiers [Note: the clause *infulas imperii suscepisse dicebatur* is absent in 2; *dicebatur* (“was said”) in 9.].

Fortunatus, patriarch of Grado, had been accused before the emperor by one of his own priests, named Tiberius, on the charge that he was encouraging Liudewit to persist in the treachery he had begun and was assisting him by sending artisans and masons to strengthen his castles. For this reason he was ordered to go to the palace. At first, as though intending to fulfill the order, he departed for Istria [Note: *histria* in 1; the other witnesses read *histriam* or *hystriam*]. From there, pretending to return to the city of Grado, while none of his people suspected anything except those with whom he had planned it, he found an opportunity to sail away secretly. He came to the Dalmatian city of Zadar and disclosed the reasons for his flight to John, the commander of that province; John immediately put him on a ship and sent him to Constantinople.

In the middle of October [Note: “in October” in 9.] a general council was celebrated at the village of Theodon with a large attendance of the Frankish people. There the lord Hlotharius, firstborn son of the lord emperor Hludovicus [Note: “lord” is absent twice in 9.], solemnly took as his wife Irmingard [Note: *irmingartham* in B 6; *yrmingardam* in 6; *irmingardim* in 9; *irmengardam* in 2.], daughter of Count Hugh.

Envoys of the holy Roman Church also came there with great gifts: Theodorus, the first secretary, and Florus, the *superista* [Note: *superista* is absent in 9.] [Note: *superista* properly means a sacristan; the term occurs several times among the offices of the papal court.].

Counts who had already returned from Pannonia were also present at the same council. After devastating the entire region of the deserters and those adhering to Liudewit, and since no one had given them an opportunity to fight, they had returned home [Col. 0491B].

At this assembly the singular mercy of the most pious emperor shone forth. He showed it toward those who had conspired in Italy with his nephew Bernhard against his person and kingdom. He ordered them to appear before him there and not only granted them life and limb [Note: *menbra* in B 5.] but, with great generosity, restored to them the possessions that by judgment of the law had been confiscated into the fisc [Note: *libertate* (“liberty”) in 1, 5, and 6.].

He also summoned Adalhard from Aquitaine [Note: *equitania … chorbeiae* in B 6.], where he was living in exile, and ordered him to be abbot and rector of the monastery of Corbie, as he had been before. Together with him he restored his brother Bernharius [Note: *bernarium* in B 5; *berenharium* in B 6.], reconciled to that same monastery, to it [Col. 0491C].

After completing these matters that he had begun for the welfare of the kingdom [Note: “those matters that concerned the welfare of the kingdom” in 9.] and generally completing the oath that part of the leading men had sworn at Nijmegen [Note: *sacramenta* (“oaths”) in B 5.], he returned to Aachen. After the solemn celebration of the wedding, he sent his son Hlotharius to Worms for the winter [Note: *uurmatiam* in B 5; *warmatiam* in B 6.].

All was quiet that year on the Danish side. Harioldus was received by Godofrid’s sons into partnership in the kingdom, and this is thought to have brought about a peaceful condition among them at that time [Note: “was thought” in 4, 5, and 6.].

But because Ceadragus, prince of the Abodrites, was being marked with treachery and with a certain alliance made with Godofrid’s sons, his rival Sclaomir was sent back to his homeland. When he had come into Saxony, he fell ill and, after receiving the sacrament of baptism [Note: *baptissimi* in 1; *baptismo* in B 6; *baptismatis* in 9 and 7.], died.

Autumn sowing was hindered in certain places by the continual rains. Winter followed it, so long and severe that not only small streams and moderate rivers but even the greatest and most famous rivers—the Rhine, the Danube, the Elbe, and the Seine, as well as the other rivers flowing through Gaul and Germany [Note: *germania* in 1.] toward the ocean—were so tightly bound by solid ice that for thirty days or more they supported wagons traveling back and forth as though joined by bridges [Note: *tricenis eo* in B 5.]. The thaw caused considerable damage to the villages situated along the banks of the Rhine.

## DCCCXXII.

In the land of the Thuringians [Note: *thoringorum* in 2.], at a certain place beside a river [Note: “beside a certain river” in Bouq.], a turf fifty feet long, fourteen feet wide, and one and a half feet high was cut and lifted from the earth without human hands. It was found twenty-five feet away from the place from which it had been taken [Col. 0492B].

Likewise, in the eastern part of Saxony adjoining the territory of the Sorabs [Note: *saraborum* in 5; *solaborum* in B 5; *sarabarorum* in 6.], in a deserted place beside a lake called Arnseo [Note: “Lake Arendsee, in the Old March.”], the earth swelled up in the form of a mound and, extending for the length of one league [Note: *leucae* in 9.], rose within the space of a single night into something like a rampart without any human labor [Note: “raised it like a rampart” in 9.].

Winigisus, duke of Spoleto [Note: *spoletanus* in 7 and 9; *spolitanus* in 4 and 6.], already worn down by old age, laid aside his secular clothing and devoted himself to the monastic way of life. Not long afterward, stricken by bodily illness, he died. Suppo, count of the city of Brescia [Note: “Brescia.”] [Note: “of the city” is absent in 9.], was appointed in his place [Note: the phrase “Suppo, count of Brescia, was appointed in his place” is absent in 4 and 6.].

The lord emperor, after holding counsel with his bishops [Col. 0492C] and leading men, was reconciled with his brothers, whom he had ordered to be forcibly tonsured [Note: *tonderi* in 7 and 9.]. He made a public confession and performed penance both for this act and for what had been done concerning Bernhard, the son of his brother Pippin, as well as concerning Adalhard the abbot and his brother Walah [Note: *uualahun* in 4; *uualaum* in 5 and 6; *uualachum* in 3 and 9; *gualachum* in 7; *uualahuum* in B 5.]. This, however, he carried out at the council that he held at Attigny in August of the same year, in the presence of all his people. There he took the greatest care to make amends for whatever similar acts he could discover had been done either by himself or by his father [Note: “acts done by his father” in 9.].

An army was sent from Italy into Pannonia to finish the war against Liudewit. At its arrival Liudewit abandoned the city of Siscia [Note: *sicia* in 2; *sua* in the codex of Arman; *scissia* in B 9; *scisia* in B 5; *sciscia* in B 6.] [Note: “Sissek.”] and fled to the Sorabs, a people said to possess a large part of Dalmatia [Col. 0492D]. After deceitfully killing one of their dukes, by whom he had been received, he brought that man’s city under his own authority [Note: “brought it under his domination” in B 5.]. Nevertheless, he sent his envoys to the emperor’s army and promised that he wished to come into the emperor’s presence.

Meanwhile, at the emperor’s command, the Saxons built a certain castle across the Elbe at a place called Delbende [Note: Delvunda is a river, called the Stecknitz in German, in the duchy of Lauenburg. From the town of Mölln it flows to the Elbe; at its headwaters there is also a forest of the same name, now called Sachsenwald, which Adam of Bremen recognizes in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 9. Since Einhard makes no mention of the Elbe, I think that the castle was built on the river Stecknitz, on the border of the Saxon frontier, near Mölln, or at Mölln itself.]. They drove out the Slavs who had previously occupied it [Note: the readings are *illum* (“it,” masculine) in the text, *illud* (“it,” neuter) in 3, 7, and 9, and *eum* (“him/it,” masculine) in 6.] and placed a Saxon garrison there against their incursions.

The counts of the Spanish March crossed the river Segre in Spain [Note: “The Segre, which flows into the Ebro near Mequinenza.”]. After devastating the fields, burning many villages, and taking considerable booty, they returned.

In a similar manner, after the autumnal equinox, an expedition was made by the counts of the Breton March against the property of a certain Breton named Wihomarcus [Note: *wihomarchus* in 9.] who at that time was in rebellion [Note: “who was then a rebel” in 9; “who was then rebellious” in 4 and 7.] [Col. 0493B]; everything was devastated with sword and fire.

After the council that was being held at Attigny had been completed [Note: “the council that was held” in 7 and 9.], the lord emperor went to the Ardennes for the sake of hunting. He sent his son Hlotharius to Italy [Note: after the words “his son,” two folios of codex 1 are missing; the text resumes in the year 823 with the fragment “his own [man] had been killed. It was reported.”] and sent with him Walah, a monk and his kinsman, namely the brother of Adalhard the abbot, and Gerungus, master of the doorkeepers [Note: “sent with him” in 9.], so that he might use their counsel both in household matters and in affairs pertaining to the interests of the kingdom.

He ordered Pippin to go to Aquitaine. First, however, he made him take in marriage the daughter of Count Theotbert of Madrie [Note: *theoberti* in 2 and B 6; *theodberti* in 6; *thietberti* in 9; *teutberti* in 7.], and after the wedding had been celebrated, depart for the western regions [Note: “western lands” in 9.].

After completing the autumn hunt, he himself crossed the Rhine and went to winter at a place called Frankfurt [Note: “to winter beyond the Rhine at Frankfurt” in 9.]. There he assembled a general council and, according to customary practice, took care to discuss with the leading men whom he had ordered to be summoned everything necessary for the welfare of the eastern parts of his kingdom [Note: “the eastern borders of his kingdom” in 9.].

At this council he heard the envoys of all the eastern Slavs—that is, of the Abodrites, Sorabs [Note: *saraborum* in 2, 4, 5, 6, B 5, and B 6.], Wiltzes [Note: *uuilzzorum* in B 5; *wilsorum* in 9; *uuilzorum* in 5 and 6; *uultzorum* in 1.], Bohemians [Note: *behemannorum* in 9; *boheimorum* in 6; *bohemiorum* in 7.], Moravians [Note: *moramorum* in 7; absent in 4; *maritanorum* in 3.], and Praedenecenti [Note: *praedevecentorum* in B 6; *predenescentorum* in 5 and 7.] [Note: their settlements are identified below, under the year 824.]—and of the Avars living in Pannonia, who had been sent to him with gifts [Note: “who had been sent to him” in 9.].

There were also at the same council envoys from Nordmannia, both from Harioldus’s side and from Godofrid’s sons. After hearing and dismissing all of them [Note: “after hearing them and dismissing them” in 9.], he wintered in the same place, having built there the new buildings that he had arranged for this purpose [Note: “with new buildings recently constructed” in B 5; “having built new buildings as he had determined with himself” in 9.].

## DCCCXXIII.

In the month of May an assembly was held at the same place (Note: “an assembly was held there, that is, on the ninth [day]” in 9). At it, not only all the leading men of Francia (Note: “not only all” in 5, 6), but also those of East Francia and Saxony, Bavaria (Note: “Bavaria” in B 6), Alamannia (Note: “Alamannia”; “of Alamannia”; B 6), Burgundy bordering on Alamannia (Note: “bordering Burgundy and from” in 5, 6), and the regions adjoining the Rhine were ordered to be present. Among the embassies of barbarians who came either because they had been summoned or of their own accord, two brothers—namely, kings of the Wiltzi—who were engaged in a dispute with one another over the kingdom, came into the emperor’s presence. Their names were Milegastus (Note: “Millegastus” in 4, 5, 6; “Meligastus” in 3, 9; “Milegatus” in 2) and Cealadragus (Note: “Cealagragus” in 5; “Cealadargus” in B 6; “Celeadragus” in 7, 9).

These men were the sons of Liub, king of the Wiltzi. Although he held his kingdom divided together with his brothers (Note: “his kingdom” in d, 9), nevertheless, because he was the eldest, supreme authority over the whole kingdom belonged to him. When he died after engaging in battle with the eastern Abodrites (Note: “when, after engaging” in 9) (Note: “had fallen in battle against the Wiltzi” in 9), the people of the Wiltzi made his son Milegastus (Note: “Milegastus” in 2, 4, 7, B 5, 6; “Millegastus” in 5, 6; “Meligastus” in 3, 9) their king, because he was the eldest (Note: “who was the elder” in 9). But when he administered the kingdom entrusted to him with insufficient dignity according to the custom of the people, they deposed him and conferred royal honor upon his younger brother (Note: “they conferred it” in 9). For this reason both men came into the emperor’s presence.

After hearing them, and recognizing that the will of the people inclined more favorably toward the honor of the younger brother, the emperor decided that the latter should retain the authority conferred upon him by his people (apparatus: “populo potestatem,” ‘authority [by] the people,’ A. L.); nevertheless, he sent both men, after presenting them with gifts and binding them by oath, back to their homeland.

At the same assembly Ceadragus, prince of the Abodrites, was accused before the emperor of acting insufficiently loyally toward the Frankish party and of having for a long time evaded coming into the emperor’s presence. For this reason envoys were sent to him; with them he again sent some of the leading men of his people to the emperor, and through their spokesman promised that he would come into the emperor’s presence by the next winter.

Hlotharius, meanwhile, while administering justice in Italy according to his father’s command and already preparing to return from Italy, came to Rome at the request of Pope Paschal. Received honorably by him, on Holy Easter Day at Saint Peter’s he received both the crown of the kingdom and the title of Emperor and Augustus. From there he returned to Pavia and came to the emperor in the month of June.

When he had given the emperor a report concerning the judicial affairs that he had partly completed and partly begun in Italy (Note: “partly completed” is absent in 5, 6), Count Adalhard of the palace was sent to Italy, and was ordered to take with him Mauringus (Note: “Mauningus” in 4; “Magringus,” corrected to “Maringus,” in B 5; “Maringus” in 3), count of Brescia, and to see to the completion of the judicial proceedings that had been begun.

He appointed his brother Drogo (Note: “Drago” in 4), who was living under canonical discipline, rector of the church of Metz, with the consent and election of the clergy of that city, and judged that he should be advanced to the rank of bishop (Note: “to be advanced” in 9).

At the same assembly the time and place for holding another assembly were arranged: namely, the month of November and the palace of Compendium (Note: “were announced” in 9). When the assembly had been concluded and the leading men had been dismissed (Note: “the nobles” in 9), and the emperor had decided to depart from there, news was brought to him of the death of Liudewit. After abandoning the Sorabs, he had reached Dalmatia (Note: “into Dalmatia” in 9; “into Delmatia” in 7) and Liudemuhsl, the uncle of Duke Borna (Note: “Ludemuhsl” in 4; “Ludemuslum” in 6; “to Liudemisl” in B 5; “Liudemuslum” in 9, B 6; “Liudewislum” in 7), and, after staying with him for some time, had been killed through his treachery.

It was also reported that Theodorus, primicerius of the holy Roman Church, and Leo the nomenclator (Note: “clator” in 1, 2), his son-in-law, had first been blinded and then beheaded in the Lateran patriarchate (Note: “in the Lateran” in 4, 5, 6, 7, 9), and that this had happened to them because they had acted faithfully in every respect toward the party of Hlotharius, the young emperor (Note: “because they supported the emperor” in 6). There were also those who said that the deed had been carried out either by order or on the advice of Pope Paschal.

To investigate and examine this matter carefully, Adalungus (Note: “Adalangus” in 3; “Adalingus” in 4; “Adalgundus” in 6), abbot of the monastery of Saint Vedastus, and Hunfridus (Note: “Humfridus” in B 5; “Huntfridus” in 6), count of Chur, were sent.

But before they had departed, envoys (Note: “ligati,” ‘bound men,’ in 1) of Pope Paschal arrived: John, bishop of Silva Candida, and Benedict, archdeacon of the apostolic see (Note: “of the pontiff” is absent in 9). They asked the emperor to remove from the pontiff the disgrace by which he was believed to have consented to the death of the men mentioned above. After he had answered them as reason required and dismissed them, he ordered his aforesaid envoys to go to Rome to investigate the truth of the matter (Note: the neuter “investigandum” in B 5), as he had previously arranged.

He himself (Note: “himself” is absent in 9) spent the remainder of the summer in the district of Worms (Note: “Wurmacense” in B 5; “Wuormacensi” in 4, 6; “Wormaciensi” in 9; “Warmacensi” in 7), and afterward in the Ardennes (Note: “transiens,” ‘spending time/passing through,’ in 3, 5, 6, B 5, 6). After completing the autumn hunt, he came to Compendium on the Kalends of November, as had been agreed.

The envoys who came to Rome could not ascertain the certainty of what had occurred (Note: “could not do so” in 9), because Pope Paschal, together with a large number of bishops, purified himself by oath (Note: “cleared himself” in 9) from any participation in this deed. And, vigorously defending the killers of the men mentioned above, because they belonged to the household of Saint Peter, he condemned the dead as though they were guilty of treason and declared that they had been rightly killed (Note: “he condemned” in 9; “and rightly” in 7, 9, 3; “he pronounced” in 9). For this reason, together with the aforesaid envoys who had been sent to him, he sent John, bishop of Silva Candida, Sergius the librarian (Note: “Serius the librarian” in B 6), Quirinus the subdeacon, and Leo the master of the soldiers to the emperor.

When the emperor had learned, both through them and through his own envoys, of the pontiff’s oath and of the defense of the accused, he judged that there was nothing more for him to do in this affair. Having given John the bishop and his companions a suitable reply, he sent them back to the pontiff.

Ceadragus (Note: “Cedragus” in 1, 3, B 5), prince of the Abodrites, making his promises good, came to Compendium with some of the leading men of his people and gave before the emperor a not implausible account of the reason for his arrival, which had been delayed for so many years. Although he appeared blameworthy in certain matters (Note: “although” is written “libet” in 1), nevertheless, on account of the merits of his parents, he was not only pardoned but also presented with gifts and permitted to return to his kingdom.

Hariold also came from Nordmannia, seeking help against the sons of Godofrid, who threatened to drive him from his homeland. To investigate the reason for this more carefully, the counts Theotharius (Note: “Teotharius” in 2; “Theodarius” in 3; “Theotarius” in B 5; “Theosarius” in B 6) and Hruodmundus (Note: “Rodtmundus” in 9; “Rovdmundus” in B 6; “Hariolthmundus” in 4, 5, 6; “Ruodinandus” in 7) were sent to the sons of Godofrid. They carefully investigated both the cause of the sons of Godofrid and the condition of the whole kingdom of the Nordmanns; they preceded Hariold’s arrival and disclosed to the emperor everything they had been able to learn in those regions.

Ebo, archbishop of Rheims, also returned with them. On the advice of the emperor and by the authority of the Roman pontiff, he had gone to the borders of the Danes for the sake of preaching, and during the preceding summer had baptized many of them as they came to the faith.

This year, it is reported, certain portents occurred (Note: “portents of various kinds”; a gloss from the margin has entered the text in 1). Among the chief were earthquakes in the palace at Aachen; in the territory of Toul (Note: “Tullense” in 1; “Tulense” in B 5; “Tullense” in B 6; some have “Tullensi”), near the village of Commerciacum (Note: “Commercy on the Meuse”), a certain girl of about twelve years who abstained from all food for ten months; and, in Saxony, in the district called Firihsazi (Note: “Firihsazi” in 1, 3; “Firihsati” in B 5; “Fiuhsazi,” and in others “Strihsazi,” in 7; “Strihsazi” in 4, 6; “Strisazi” in 5; “Frihsazi” in 2, 9, B 6; “Firichsare” in the Saxon Annalist; “Firicsaze” in the Saxon Chronographer; “Virsedi” in the Quedlinburg Chronicle. Note: “I prefer to call it unknown rather than, with some more recent writers who follow the reading Wirsedi of the Quedlinburg Chronicle, to sell it as Wolsatia or Wursatia. Among the names of Saxon districts, Flethihi comes closest to our word, but it is nevertheless so much farther away that it cannot be regarded as the same name.”).

Twenty-three villages were burned by celestial fire, and flashes of lightning were seen falling from the sky in clear weather and during the day.

(Note: “And” [“But” in 7] in the territory of the Italian city of Como (Note: “Comense” in 7; “Italio” in B 6; “in the village” is absent in B 6), in the village of Grabadona (Note: “Grabbadona” in B 6; “potestatem” in B 6), on the western shore of Lake Larius, near its beginning (Muratori, *SS.*, vol. X, p. CXXXI), in the church of Saint John the Baptist, an image of Saint Mary holding the child Jesus in her lap and of the Magi offering gifts was painted in the apse of the same church. Because of extreme age it had grown dark and had almost been effaced (Note: “Ippolita” in B 6; “Obolita” in B 5; “by age, already almost effaced” in 7). It shone for two whole days with such brilliance (Note: “celebrity” in B 6) that, to those who saw it, it seemed entirely to surpass every splendour of a new painting by the beauty of its age (Note: “new” in B 5, 6; “the gracefulness of its beauty to beholders” in 7; “vincere diceretur vel vinceretur maiorum,” ‘it was said to surpass, or to be surpassed by, [the] elders,’ in B 6). Nevertheless, that radiance did not illuminate the images of the Magi, apart from the gifts they were offering. 9, B 5, 6, 9.)

In many regions the crops were destroyed by the devastation of hail (Note: “destroyed” in 1), and in some places, together with the hail itself, real stones of enormous weight seemed to fall (Note: “stones, and these also” in 1; “stones, and they” in 9). Houses too are said to have been struck from heaven, and human beings and other animals in various places were unusually and frequently killed by lightning strikes.

A great pestilence and mortality then followed. It spread savagely everywhere throughout Francia and, raging with terrible force, consumed an innumerable multitude of people of every sex and age.

## 824

King Omortag of the Bulgars (Note: “King of the Bulgars, N., as if” in B 5—the printed “Non” is evidently uncertain/OCR-corrupt; “King of the Bulgars, N., as if” in B 6; Omortag is absent in 7, 9, 9b) sent envoys with letters to the emperor, as if for the purpose of making peace. After hearing them and reading the letters that had been brought, the emperor, reasonably disturbed by the novelty of the affair (Note: “the king’s novelty” in 1), sent a certain Machelmus from Bavaria (Note: “Michelinus” in 9; “Machelinus” in 7; “Machalmus” in 2), together with the envoys, to the aforementioned king of the Bulgars, in order to investigate more carefully the reason for this unusual embassy, which had never before come to Francia.

Meanwhile a harsh and very prolonged winter set in. Its severe cold killed not only other animals but also some human beings.

The moon was eclipsed on the third day before the Nones of March, in the second hour of the night.

It was announced that Suppo, duke of Spoleto, had died. The envoys of the Roman pontiff returned to Rome and found him suffering from a serious illness and already near death (Note: “and even near death” in B 5). A few days after their arrival he also departed this life.

When two men had been elected to replace him amid a dispute among the people, Eugenius, archpriest of the title of Saint Sabina (Note: “then archpriest” in 9), was nevertheless substituted and ordained, the party of the nobles prevailing.

When Quirinus the subdeacon, one of those who had served on the earlier embassy, brought news of this to the emperor, an assembly was announced for approximately the eighth day before the Kalends of July. The assembly was held at Compendium (Note: “of Compendium” in 3, 7, 9; in place of the words “announced and held at Compendium, he [was intent] on a Breton” in manuscripts 4 and 6, with the intervening text omitted, only “pronicam” is read; in 5 the words “announced and at Compendium” are absent). The emperor, intent on personally undertaking an expedition to Brittany, decided to send his son Hlotharius, his associate in the empire, to Rome, so that, acting in his place, he might settle and confirm with the new pontiff and the Roman people whatever the needs of the situation seemed to demand.

Hlotharius departed for Italy after the middle of August to carry this out. The emperor, however, delayed undertaking the journey he had prepared to make into Brittany (Note: “had planned to make” in 9) until the beginning of autumn, because the famine was still extremely severe. Then, after gathering troops from every quarter, he came to the city of Rennes, which lay next to the borders of Brittany. From there, dividing the army into three parts, assigning two parts to his sons Pippin and Hludowic (Note: “Hludewiho” in 1; “Ludewico” in B 5), and retaining the third with himself, he entered Brittany and devastated the whole country with fire and sword (Note: “ravaged” in 9).

After spending forty days or more on this expedition (Note: “sixty,” through a typographical error, in Bouq.), and receiving the hostages he had demanded from the treacherous Breton people (Note: “Brantonum” in B 6), he returned on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December to the city of Rouen, where he had ordered his wife to await him (Note: “where he had ordered her to await him on the fifteenth day before the Kalends” in 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 9, B 5, 6; “ad” is absent in 5, 6; an easy conjecture is “a. d. XV Kal.”; “on the twelfth day before the Kalends” in the Arman manuscript).

For he had also ordered the envoys of the emperor Michael, who were being sent to him (Note: this clause is absent in 9), to meet him there. With them Fortunatus, patriarch of the Venetians (Note: “patriarch of Grado” in 9), returned and came into his presence.

But the emperor’s envoys, who were carrying letters and gifts and declaring that they had been sent to confirm peace, said nothing concerning Fortunatus. Nevertheless, among other matters belonging to their embassy, they brought forward certain questions concerning the veneration of images, on account of which they said that they ought to go to Rome and consult the bishop of the apostolic see.

After hearing their embassy and giving them his reply, the emperor dismissed them and ordered them to be taken to Rome, as they said they wished (Note: “he ordered them to go to Rome so that they might be examined by the pontiff” in 9). He also questioned Fortunatus about the reason for his flight and sent him to the Roman pontiff for examination. He himself departed for Aachen, where he had decided to spend the winter.

When he arrived there and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord, news was brought to him that the envoys of the king of the Bulgars were in Bavaria. He sent to meet them and ordered them to remain there until a suitable time (Note: “he ordered them to stay there” in 9).

He immediately permitted the envoys of the Abodrites, commonly called Praedenecenti, who lived next to the Bulgars in Dacia beside the Danube, and whose arrival had likewise been announced, to come. When they complained of the unjust aggression of the Bulgars (Note: “hostility” in 1) and demanded that assistance be brought to them against them (Note: “that they were being unjustly attacked by the Bulgars” in 9), they were ordered to return home and then come back at the time appointed for the Bulgar envoys.

After Suppo had died at Spoleto, as had been reported, the same duchy was received by Adalhard, count of the palace, who was called the Younger. He held that office for scarcely five months (Note: “a month” in 1) before being seized by fever and dying.

When Moringus, count of Brescia, was elected as his successor, he fell ill upon receiving the announcement of the honor assigned to him and died a few days later.

The counts Aeblus (Note: “Elbus” twice in 5, 6) and Asinarius were sent with forces of Basques to Pamplona (Note: “Pampilon” in 2, 7; “Pompelon” in 9). After completing the task assigned to them and returning, they were led into an ambush and surrounded through the treachery of the mountaineers on the very crest of the Pyrenees (Note: “Perineus” in 1). They were captured, and the forces they had with them were almost wiped out. Aeblus was sent to Córdoba (Note: in 1 the text from “and Aeblus indeed” through “harass his neighbors with fires and plundering” in the entry for 825 is absent), while Asinarius, through the mercy of those who had captured him, was permitted to return home as one who was related to them by blood.

Hlotharius, in accordance with his father’s command (Note: “father’s instruction” in 9; “order” in 5), departed for Rome and was honorably received by Pope Eugenius. When he disclosed to him the matters entrusted to him, he corrected, with the benevolent consent of the aforesaid pontiff, the condition of the Roman people, which had long been corrupted by the wickedness of certain bishops (Note: “benevolent” in 3), so that all who had been grievously despoiled and left destitute by the seizure of their property (Note: “despoiled by seizure” in 4, 6; “by ransom” in 5; “by restoration” in 9) were magnificently consoled by the recovery of their goods, which had come about through his arrival, by God’s gift (Note: “the phrase concerning the recovery of their goods is absent in 2”).

This year, a few days before the summer solstice, after the air had suddenly changed into stormy weather in the territory of Autun (Note: “Augustodunense” in B 5), an enormous fragment of ice is said to have fallen together with hail. It is said to have been fifteen feet long, seven feet wide, and two feet thick (Note: “thickness” is “grossitude” in 6).

## 825

After the holy Easter festival had been solemnly celebrated at Aachen, with spring weather also smiling favorably (Note: “of spring” in 5, 6; “in springtime” in 9), the emperor went to Nijmegen for the sake of hunting and ordered the envoys of the Bulgars to come to Aachen around the middle of May.

For he decided to return there in this way (Note: “for then he decided to return there” in 9), intending to hold there an assembly which he had indicated to the nobles that, after returning from Brittany, he wished to hold there at that time (Note: “would hold” in 9; *quem* in 7, 9, but *quod* in the remaining witnesses).

When he had returned after completing the hunt, he heard the Bulgar embassy. Its subject was the establishment of the boundaries and frontiers between the Bulgars and the Franks.

At the same assembly nearly all the leading men of Brittany were present. Among them was Wihomarcus (Note: “Wiomarcus” in 3; “Wihomarchus” in 9), who by his treachery had thrown all Brittany into confusion and, through his utterly foolish obstinacy, had provoked the emperor’s resolve to undertake the expedition mentioned above. At last, adopting wiser counsel, he did not hesitate to come to the emperor’s faith, as he himself put it.

The emperor both forgave him and, after presenting him with gifts, permitted him to return home together with the other leading men of his people. But he exchanged the faith he had promised, as he had done previously, for the treachery of his people. He did not cease, as far as he could, to harass his neighbors with fires and plundering (Note: “ac” is absent in 7, 9), until he was surrounded and killed in his own house by the men of Count Lantbertus (Note: “Lambertus” in 4, 5, 6).

After hearing the Bulgar embassy, the emperor sent letters to their king through the same envoys who had been sent to him and replied as he thought appropriate. Having dismissed the assembly, he went to the Vosges, to Mount Rumericus (Note: “the fortress of Rumericus” in 9; “Rumericus” in 7), for the sake of hunting. There he received his son Hlotharius, who had returned from Italy and had come to him.

After completing the hunt and returning to Aachen, he held a general assembly of his people in the customary manner in the month of August (Note: “the month” is absent in B 5). At this assembly, among the other embassies that came from various regions (Note: “from various countries” in 9), he also heard envoys of the sons of Godofrid from Nordmannia (Note: “Godefrid” in 1; “Godifrid” in B 6), and ordered the peace they had requested to be confirmed with them in their borderland in the month of October (Note: “he caused it to be confirmed” in 9).

When all the affairs that seemed to belong to the business of that assembly had been completed, he withdrew to Nijmegen with his elder son, while he sent his younger son Hludowic to Bavaria (Note: “his son Hludowic” is absent in 9). He himself, after completing the autumn hunt, returned to Aachen around the beginning of winter (Note: “the clause ‘he himself returned’ is absent in 2; ‘however’ is absent in 9).

In the territory of Toul, near the village of Commerciacum (Note: “the village of Cummarciacum” in 2; “Cummertiacum” in B 5; “Comerciacum” in B 6), a certain girl, whose name was …, about twelve years old (Note: a gloss concerning “the name, the three-year fast of the girl” entered the text in 1; “named N.” in 2, B 6), is reported to have fasted after receiving Holy Communion, which she had received from the hand of a priest at Easter. First she abstained from bread, then from all other food and drink, to such an extent that, taking no bodily nourishment whatsoever and without any desire for sustenance, she completed a full three years (Note: “an entire three years” in 9).

She began to fast in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 823, as was noted above in the account of that year, and in this year, that is, 825, around the beginning of November, after completing her fast, she began to take food and live by eating like the rest of mortals.

## 826
When his envoys had reported to the king of the Bulgars what they had accomplished [Note: *had done*; *were reporting*, 9], he again sent the man whom he had first dispatched to the emperor, with a letter, asking that the boundaries be defined without delay [Note: *without delay concerning the boundaries*, 9], or, if this was not acceptable, that each party should defend its own boundaries without a peace treaty [Note: *might defend*, 9]. Since there was a report that the Bulgarian king had either been expelled from his kingdom or killed by one of his own nobles, the emperor delayed answering him [Note: *but he*, 9]. He ordered the envoy to wait and, in order to establish the truth of the report, sent Bertricus, count of the palace, to the counts Baldricus [Note: *Baldericus*, 9] and Geroldus [Note: *Gerholtus*, 9], guardians of the Avar frontier, in the province of the Carantani [Note: *province*, 1]. When Bertricus returned without bringing back anything certain about what the rumor had spread, the emperor summoned the envoy and sent him back without a letter [Col. 0501B].

Meanwhile King Pippin, the emperor’s son, as he had been ordered, came to Aachen around the Kalends of February with his nobles and the guardians of the Spanish frontier—for the emperor had then wintered there. After discussing and arranging with them [Note: witness 9 reads *cum quibus ubi de* ("with whom, where, concerning") for *cum quibus cum de* ("with whom, concerning")] the defense against the Saracens of the western regions [Note: *discussed and concluded*, 9], Pippin returned to Aquitaine and spent the summer in the place assigned to him [Note: *returned and spent the whole following summer there*, 9].

The emperor, however, left Aachen in the middle of May [Note: *in the month* is absent in 9; *Aquisgrano* ("from Aachen"), 9] and came around the Kalends of June to Ingelheim [Note: the witnesses read *Ingeleheim* 3, *Ingilinheim* 4, *Gilenheim* 6, *Ingilenheim* 7 and B 6, *Ingilenhaim* B 5, and *Ingelheim* 9]. After holding a considerable assembly there, he heard and dismissed many embassies sent from various parts of the earth [Note: *and he heard and dismissed them*, 9].

Among these, the chief and preeminent [Note: *praeeminens*, 9] embassy [Note: *the embassy of the Roman pontiff*, 9] was that of the apostolic Holy See, namely the Roman Church, represented by Leo, bishop of Centumcellae, and Theophylactus, the nomenclator. From overseas [Note: *from the regions beyond the sea*, 9] came Dominic, abbot of Mount Olivet. There were also envoys of the sons of Godofrid, king of the Danes, sent concerning peace and a treaty [Note: *sent for that purpose*, 9]. From the regions of the Slavs came certain leading men of the Abodrites, accusing their duke Ceadragus [Note: *the princes of the Abodrites*, 9].

Tunglo also [Note: *Tungo*, 7], one of the leading men of the Sorabi, was accused, because he too was not obedient. Both men were warned that, if they delayed coming to the emperor’s general assembly in mid-October [Note: *if they delay*, 9; *had delayed*, 7], they would suffer punishment worthy of their treachery [Note: *would suffer*, 7, 9].

Some of the leading men of the Britons also came, whom the guardians of that frontier had chosen to bring. At the same time Herioldus arrived with his wife and a large multitude of Danes. At Mainz, at Saint Alban’s, he was baptized with those whom he had brought with him. After receiving many gifts from the emperor, he returned through Frisia by the road along which he had come. In that province he was given a county called Hriustri [Note: *unus* ("one") is absent in 9; *Riustri*, 9], so that, if necessity required, he might withdraw there with his possessions [Note: “The most pious emperor feared that, because of such an act, he might be denied a place of residence in his native land; therefore he gave him a county in Frisia called Ruistri,” 7].

Baldricus and Geroldus, counts and prefects of the Pannonian frontier, were present at the same assembly [Note: “Baldericus and Gerholtus, counts and prefects of the Pannonian frontier, were also present at the same assembly,” 9]. They declared that, as yet, they had been unable to detect any movement of the Bulgars against us [Col. 0502B].

With Baldricus came a priest from Venice named Georgius, who claimed that he could make an organ [Note: “could construct an organ in the Greek manner. The emperor received him gladly, and because God was granting him things previously unknown in the Frankish kingdom, he gave thanks and commended Georgius to Tanculfus, superintendent of the sacred treasury. He ordered that he be supported from public funds and commanded that everything necessary for this work be prepared,” 7; an interpolation from *The Life of Louis the Pious*, chapter 40]. The emperor sent him to Aachen with Thancolfus, the treasurer [Note: the witnesses read *Tancolfus* 4 and 6, *Thamcolfus* 2, *Tanculfus* 7 and B 5, and *Thangolfus* B 6], and ordered that everything necessary for making the instrument be supplied to him [Note: *for that instrument*, 9; cf. Einhard, *History of the Translation of Saints Marcellinus and Peter*, book IV, no. 75, in the Bollandists’ *Acta Sanctorum*, June 2, p. 201. There Georgius is said to have “constructed in the palace at Aachen, with marvelous skill, an organ which in Greek is called *hydraulica* (a water-organ)”; afterward he was appointed head of the monastery of Saint Salvus in the town of Valentiana].

After a general assembly had been agreed upon and announced for mid-October, and all other matters had been settled according to solemn custom, the emperor himself crossed the Rhine with his entourage to a villa called Saltz [Note: the witnesses read *Saltzuo* B 5, *Salz* 2, 3, and 4, *Satz* 5 and 6, and *Sels* 9]. Envoys of the Neapolitans came to him there, and, after receiving his reply, returned home.

There he was informed of Aizo’s flight and treachery [Note: *the treachery of Wuizo*, B 5; *of Iaco*, B 6]: how he had deceitfully entered Ausona [Note: the witnesses read *Ausonia* 4, *Auzona* 6, and *Ausolla* B 6; Note: “the Ausonensian settlement, called Vich”], and, having been received by the people whom he had deceived, destroyed the city of Roda [Note: “Roda, on the river Ter, west of Gerunda”; the witnesses read *the whole city* 2, 3, 7, and 9; *Roda* corrected to *tota* in 5; *rodam* in Bouq., from *The Life of Louis*; *Rotam* in 1, 4, 6, and B 5–6], fortified the castles of that region that seemed stronger [Note: *had fortified [lacuna] had received*, 9], and, having sent his brother to Abdiraman, king of the Saracens [Note: *Abdirachman*, 9; *Thraman*, B 6], received from that king, at his command, the assistance he had requested.

Although the emperor took the news of this affair seriously, he nevertheless judged that nothing should be undertaken rashly and decided to await the arrival of his counselors. After completing the autumn hunt, around the Kalends of October he sailed down the River Main with the current as far as Frankfurt [Note: the witnesses read *Franconofurd* 5, 6, and B 5, and *Franchonefurt* B 6] [Col. 0503A].

Coming from there to Ingelheim [Note: the witnesses read *Ingilumhaim* 2, *Ingelenheim* 3, *Ingilinheim* 4, 5, and 7, *Gilenheim* 6, *Ingelheim* 9, *Inginlinhaim* B 5, and *Ingulunheim* B 6] in mid-October, he held there the general assembly, as had been agreed [Note: *announced*, 9]. At it he heard both Ceadragus, duke of the Abodrites, and Tunglo, who had been accused before him of treachery. He allowed Tunglo to return home after receiving his son as a hostage. But he retained Ceadragus with him, dismissing the other Abodrites, and sent envoys to the Abodrite people, ordering them to inquire whether the common people wished him to rule them. The emperor himself then departed for Aachen, where he had decided to winter.

When the envoys whom he had sent to the Abodrites returned and reported that the people held differing opinions about receiving their king, but that the better and more distinguished men agreed about receiving him [Note: *the best and most distinguished*, 9], the emperor accepted the hostages whom he had demanded and had Ceadragus restored to his kingdom [Col. 0503B].

While these things were taking place, Hildoinus [Note: *Hilduinus*, 9], abbot of the monastery [Note: *of the monastery* is absent in 9] of the martyr Saint Dionysius, sent to Rome and, with the approval of Eugenius, then prelate of the apostolic Holy See [Note: *with the bishop’s approval*, with intervening material missing in witnesses 4, 5, and 6], obtained the bones of the most blessed martyr of Christ, Sebastian. He placed them in the city of Soissons [Note: the witnesses read *Vessona* 1 and 4, *Vessonem* 2, *Vesona* 3, *Suessona* 5, 6, 7, B 5, and B 6, *Suessiona* 9 and B 9, and *Suessionia* in Chesn. and Bouq.], in the basilica of Saint Medard.

While they still lay unburied beside the tomb of Saint Medard, in the coffin in which they had been brought [Note: *with the traveling coffin, just as they had been brought*, 7; a reading derived from the anonymous *Life of Louis*, chapter 40; Semler], such a multitude of signs and miracles became manifest, and such power of healing in every [Note: *omne* ("every"), 4] kind of illness shone forth through divine grace in the name of that most blessed martyr [Note: *flashed forth*, 9], that no mortal could either comprehend the number of those miracles or express their variety in words. Some are said to have been so astonishing that they would exceed the capacity of human weakness to believe, unless it were certain that our Lord Jesus Christ, for whose sake that most blessed martyr is known to have suffered [Note: *the most blessed martyr* is absent in 9], can do through divine omnipotence whatever he wills [Note: *who suffered, can do all things*, 9; *through divine power*, and related wording, 9].

The aforesaid venerable abbot Hildoinus, among the many monasteries entrusted to him by imperial generosity, also had charge of the noble monastery visible from the city of Soissons. Clothar, once king of the Franks, and his son Sigibert had built it at great expense in honor of the most blessed confessor of Christ, Medard, and had buried his most sacred remains there. In the same way, after the death of Irmino, the aforesaid abbot governed the place of Saint Vincent the Levite and Martyr in the suburb of Paris, where the precious confessor of Christ, Germanus, rests. Childebert, once the illustrious king of the Franks and brother of the aforementioned King Clothar, built it [Note: the whole passage from “The aforesaid venerable abbot” is an interpolation from *The Life of Louis the Pious*, chapter 40, 7]. To him every creature in heaven and on earth is subject.

## 827

The emperor sent Helisachar, priest and abbot, together with the counts Hildibrandus [Note: *Ildebrandus* 2; *Hildebrandus* 7 and 9] and Donatus, to settle the disturbances in the Spanish March. Before their arrival, Aizo, relying on the aid of the Saracens, inflicted many hardships on the guardians of that frontier and wearied them so greatly with continual raids [Note: *wearied them exceedingly*, 9] that some of them abandoned the castles they ought to have defended and withdrew.

The son of Berani [Note: the witnesses read *Berani* 1–6, B 5, B 6, and 9; *Beronis*, 9; *Berae*, 7], named Willemundus [Note: *Willimundus*, B 6], also [Note: *necnon* ("and also") is absent in 9] defected to him, as did many others, eager for revolution with the fickleness characteristic of their people. Joining themselves to the Saracens and Moors [Note: *and Moors* is absent in 9], they daily ravaged Ceretania [Note: *Cerdagne*] and the Vallis [Note: “Vallès, a very fertile valley 28,000 paces long and 16,000 paces wide, east of the River Llobregat and north of Barcelona”; Petrus de Marca, *Marca Hispanica*, p. 166] with plunder and fires.

While Abbot Helisachar, sent by the emperor with others [Note: *missis* ("sent"), 9] to calm and appease the minds of the Goths and Hispanics living in those regions, had acted prudently with great personal industry and the counsel of his companions [Note: *might act*, 9], and while Bernhardus, count of Barcelona, resisted with the greatest determination the ambushes of Aizo and the cunning and fraudulent schemes of those who had defected to him [Note: *who had made them defect*, 5 and B 5], and rendered their reckless attempts fruitless, it was reported that an army sent by Abdiraman, king of the Saracens, to bring aid to Aizo had arrived at Zaragoza. Abumarvan, a relative of the king, had been appointed commander over it and, persuaded by Aizo [Note: *by Aizo’s persuasion*, 9], confidently promised himself victory.

Against him the emperor sent his son Pippin, king of Aquitaine, with a very large Frankish force, and ordered him to defend the boundaries of his kingdom. This would indeed have been done, had not the commanders whom he had placed over the Frankish army, through their negligence, arrived at the March later than the circumstances required, bringing the army under their command [Note: *which he was leading*, 3].

That delay was so harmful that Abumarvan [Note: *Abumaruam*, 2], after laying waste the fields of Barcelona and Gerona, burning the villages, and plundering everything he found outside the cities, withdrew safely with his army to Zaragoza before he could even have been seen by our army.

The omens of this disaster were thought to be the battle-lines repeatedly seen in the sky and that terrifying passage of nocturnal flashes through the air. The emperor, after holding two assemblies—one at Nijmegen [Note: the witnesses read *Niumagam* 2, 5, 7, B 5, and B 6; *Mogiogam* 6; *Noviomagum* 3 and 9], because of the false promises of Hohricus [Note: *Horicus*, 6 and 9; *Honricus*, 7], son of Godofrid, king of the Danes, who had promised that he would come there into the emperor’s presence; and the other at Compiègne, where he received the annual gifts and ordered those who were to be sent to the Spanish March what they should do and how they should act—spent the remainder of the time between Compiègne, Quierzy, and the other neighboring palaces until the beginning of winter.

Meanwhile the Danish kings, namely the sons of Godofrid [Note: *the sons, that is*, 9], expelled Herioldus from their joint rule and compelled him to leave the territory of the Northmen [Note: witness 2 reads *Nordusmannorum*; therefore the printed text is to be read *Nordmannorum*, "of the Northmen"]. The Bulgars too devastated with sword and fire the Slavs settled in Pannonia [Note: *Pannia*, 1], sending a naval force along the Drava. After expelling their dukes, they appointed Bulgar rulers over them [Note: *Bulgarian rulers over them*, 9].

Pope Eugenius died in August. In his place Valentinus, a deacon, was elected and ordained by the Romans [Note: *elected by the Romans and ordained*, 7 and 9], but completed scarcely one month in the pontificate [Note: *one month* is absent in 9]. After his death, Gregorius, a priest of the title of Saint Mark [Note: *of the title* is absent in 9], was elected, but he was not ordained until the emperor’s envoy came to Rome and examined what the people’s election had been like [Note: *came … and examined*, 9].

Envoys of the emperor Michael from Constantinople, sent supposedly to confirm the treaty [Note: the surrounding phrase is absent in B 5], came to the emperor at Compiègne in September [Note: *to the emperor* is absent in 9]. He received them there kindly, heard them, and dismissed them [Note: *the emperor received and dismissed them kindly*, 9]. At the same time Einhard, the wisest man of his age, stirred by the ardor of holy devotion, sent to Rome and, with the pope’s approval, had the bodies of Saints Marcellinus and Peter conveyed into Francia; he laid them to rest very fittingly on his own estate and at his own expense. By their merits the Lord still works there many miraculous acts of power [Note: 7; an interpolation from *The Life of Louis the Pious*, chapter 41].

The bodies of the most blessed martyrs Marcellinus and Peter were taken from Rome, transferred to Francia in October [Note: “to the German part of Francia”], and there glorified by many signs and miracles [Note: The history of the translation was written by our own Einhard, who arranged for the bodies to be transferred. See the Bollandists’ *Acta Sanctorum*, June 2. He reports that part of the relics had already been transferred by him near the end of the preceding year to Michilinstadt, and from there, on January 17, 827, to Mulinheim; the remainder was delivered there by Abbot Hildoinus eight days after Easter and kept at Aachen through the summer. Finally, after he had received permission from the emperor, who had departed for the solemn hunt, to leave, it was brought to Mulinheim and reunited with the sacred bodies. Since, therefore, the translation was completed in October, as stated above, Einhard returned to Aachen to winter there. Anyone can see how well the account of the event, as read in the annals and in the history of the translation, coheres; and it is surprising that learned men who denied the annals to Einhard could have rejected the work for the sole reason that the history of the translation gives January 17, while the annals place the translation in October].

## 828

An assembly was held at Aachen in February [Note: *Aquasgrani* in witness 1 and B 5–6; the other witnesses read *Aquisgrani*]. At it, among many other matters, particular attention was given to what had happened in the Spanish March. The men who had commanded the army were found culpable and, according to their deserts, were punished by the loss of their offices [Note: *found and, according to their deserts, punished by loss of their offices*, 9].

Likewise Baldricus [Note: *Baldericus also*, 9], duke of Friuli, was deprived of the offices he held [Note: *the offices which he held* is absent in 9] because, through his negligence, the Bulgarian army had ravaged the borders of Upper Pannonia with impunity [Note: *the Bulgars ravaged the borders of Pannonia*, 9]. The March that he alone had held [Note: this phrase is absent in 9] was divided among four counts.

Halitgarius, bishop of Cambrai, and Ansfridus, abbot of the monastery of Nonantola [Note: *abbot*, B 5], were sent to Constantinople and, as they themselves reported upon their return, were honorably received by the emperor Michael.

In June the emperor came to the villa of Ingelheim [Note: *villa* is absent in 9]. There he held a court for several days. After taking counsel about sending his sons Lothar and Pippin with an army to the Spanish March and arranging how this should be done, he dismissed the envoys of the Roman pontiff—Quirinus, the primicerius, and Theophylactus, the nomenclator—who had come to him there, after hearing their embassy [Note: *after hearing their embassy*, 9]. He then departed for the villa of Frankfurt [Note: the witnesses read *Franconouurd* 4, *Franchonofurth* B 6, and *Franconofurt* 9], stayed there for some time, and came to Worms. From there [Note: *et inde* ("and from there"), 9] he proceeded to the villa of Theodonis, from which place he sent his son Lothar [Note: *filium cum* ("his son with"), 9] with a large Frankish force to the Spanish March.

When Lothar had reached Lyons, he settled there and awaited a messenger who would inform him of the Saracens’ arrival. While waiting, he conferred with his brother Pippin. When he learned that the Saracens either feared or did not wish to come to the March, his brother returned to Aquitaine, while he himself returned to his father at Aachen.

Meanwhile, since matters had to be discussed on the borders of the Northmen both concerning confirmation of the treaty between them and the Franks and concerning Herioldus [Note: *tractatum* ("discussed"), B 5], and since almost all [Note: *poene* ("almost"), 1] the counts of Saxony, together with the margraves [Note: the witnesses read *markionibus* 1, 2, 3, and B 5; *marcionibus*, B 6; *marchionibus*, the other witnesses], had assembled there, Herioldus, excessively eager to take action, violated the peace that had been agreed and secured by hostages by burning and plundering several small villages of the Northmen [Note: *he broke the peace by burning … the villages*, 9].

When the sons of Godofrid heard this, they immediately gathered their forces and came to the March. They crossed the River Eider and attacked our men, who were encamped on its bank and expected no such thing. They stripped them of their camp [Note: against *castris exuunt* ("they strip them of their camp"), the witnesses read *castris exciunt* ("they destroy/clear the camp"), 1, and *castris exeunt* ("they leave the camp"), 4], put them to flight, plundered everything, and withdrew with all their forces to their own camp.

Then, after taking counsel to forestall retaliation for this deed, they sent an embassy to the emperor. They explained how unwillingly and under what great necessity they had done this [Note: *they did it*, 9], but declared themselves ready to make amends, leaving it to the emperor’s judgment how the matter should be settled [Note: *to what extent*, 9] so that firm peace might remain between the parties thereafter.

Count Bonifacius, to whom the protection of Corsica had then been entrusted, took with him his brother Bereharius [Note: the witnesses read *Beretharius* 3, *Bercharius* 7 and 9, *Bernharius* 4, *Berenharius* B 6, and *Bernhardus* 5 and 6] and several other counts from Tuscany. After sailing around Corsica and Sardinia with a small fleet, and finding no pirate at sea, he crossed to Africa [Note: the phrase from “finding no pirate” through “crossed to Africa” is absent in B 6]. Landing between Utica and Carthage [Note: the witnesses read *and Carthage* 9, *and Chartage* 2, and *and Cartagine* B 6], he encountered an innumerable multitude of inhabitants suddenly gathered together. He engaged them in battle, defeated and routed them five times or more, and, after many Africans had been struck down and some of his own companions had also been lost through recklessness [Note: *some*, 9], withdrew to his ships. By this deed he inspired the Africans with great fear.
