The moon failed at daybreak on the Kalends of July, while setting [Note: 9 reads *on the Kalends of June*]. Likewise, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January—that is, on the Nativity of the Lord—it was darkened at midnight [Note: *and on the eighth day before the Kalends of January*, 9].

It is reported that in the region of Gascony, beyond the River Garonne, in the county of Agen, grain resembling wheat rained from the sky, though the grains were somewhat shorter and rounder; some of it was brought to the emperor’s palace at Aachen [Note: 7, B 8, 9, and 12].

Around the feast of Saint Martin the emperor came to Aachen to winter [Note: *around the solemnity of Saint Martin*, 9]. After settling there, he spent the whole winter in various assemblies convened for the necessary business of the kingdom.

## 829

After the winter had ended, during the very holy fast of Lent, a few days before Easter, an earthquake occurred at night at Aachen [Note: *holy* is absent in 9], and a wind arose so violent [Note: *arose*, 9] that it stripped the roofs from not only the humbler houses but also, to no small extent, the very basilica of the holy Mother of God, which they call the chapel and which was roofed with lead tiles.

The emperor [Note: *vero* ("however") is absent in 9] remained at Aachen amid various occupations until the Kalends of July [Note: witnesses 4 and 6 read *June*]. Finally, in August, he decided to depart with his entourage for a general assembly to be held at Worms. But before he moved from there [Note: *departed*, 9], he received news that the Northmen intended to invade the region of Saxony beyond the Elbe and that their army, which was preparing to do this, was approaching our borders.

Disturbed by this report, he sent messengers throughout every part of Francia [Note: *the regions of Francia*, 9] and ordered the entire body of his people to come after him into Saxony with the utmost haste [Note: *the whole multitude of his people*, 9]. At the same time he announced that he intended to cross the Rhine at Neuss [Note: “Neuss, opposite Düsseldorf”] around the middle [Note: *circiter* ("about") is absent in 9] of July.

When he discovered, however, that the report spread about the Northmen was false [Note: *that the rumor about the Northmen had been spread falsely*, 9], he came to Worms in mid-August, as he had previously arranged [Note: *as he had decided*, 9]. After holding the general assembly there, he received the annual gifts offered to him according to solemn custom [Note: *according to solemn custom* is absent in 9] and heard and dismissed the many embassies that had come to him from Rome, Benevento, and other distant lands [Note: *from distant regions*, 9].

After that assembly had ended [Note: *illo* ("that") is absent in 9], he sent his son Lothar [Note: *suum* ("his") is absent in 9] to Italy [Note: *sent him to Italy*, 9] and appointed Bernhardus, count of Barcelona, who until then had governed the Spanish March, as his chamberlain [Note: *camararius* in witnesses 1, 2, 4, 6, B 5, and B 6].

Having suitably arranged and completed the other matters that appeared to belong to the conclusion of that court [Note: “He assigned a portion of the kingdom to his son Charles. Cf. Thegan, chapter 35”], and having dismissed the people to return home, the emperor himself went to the villa of Frankfurt to hunt in autumn [Note: the witnesses read *Franconovurdum* 2, *Franconouuardum* 2, *Franconouurd* 4, *Franconofurdum* 6 and B 5, *Franchonofurdum* B 6, *Francofurdum* 5, *ad Franconofurt* 9, and *in Franconofurd* 7]. After the hunt he returned to Aachen to winter there [Note: witness 9 reads *reversus ibidem sancti Martini atque beati Andreae* ("having returned there, [he celebrated] Saint Martin and blessed Andrew")], where he celebrated with great joy and exultation the Mass of Saint Martin, the feast of the blessed apostle Andrew, and the very sacred day of the Lord’s Nativity [Note: “These were Einhard’s last visits to Aachen; for in March of the following year, after the rebellion that arose at Compiègne, he asked for and received permission to withdraw to Seligenstadt. Thus the public end of the *Annals* and of his *Life* is the same”].

## The Letters of Einhard

[Note: These letters were first published from an old manuscript of Laon by Andreas Chesnius, volume II of the *Scriptores Francici*, p. 695. In their publication no chronological order is observed. Einhard, who maintained celibacy with his wife Imma, governed several abbeys. He is believed to have died in 839.]

## Letter I. To Ansgisus

[Note: Ansegisus, descended from a noble Frankish family, received the monastery of Saint Geremar at Flavigny from Charlemagne in 807 on a precarious grant. In 817 the monastery of Luxeuil was entrusted to him, and in 823 that of Fontenelle, when Einhard resigned it. He died in 833.]

To my most beloved brother in Christ, the venerable Ansgisus: everlasting salvation in the Lord.

I ask your affection not to take it harshly, but rather mercifully and amicably, that I intercede with you on behalf of a former dependent of ours, now a dependent of Lord Lothar, asking that you allow him to retain the benefice which I gave him, under whatever terms you think appropriate, until, with the help of the Lord, we are able to provide him with some other support from the generosity of our lords.

You will find me more ready and devoted to carrying out your will and advantage if you deign to grant my requests in this matter. I pray that you may always prosper in the Lord.

[Note: The manuscript and edition read “with you”; Dom Teulet considers these words redundant, since they are repeated after only a few intervening words.]

## Letter II. To Gozbertus, Abbot

[Note: Gozbertus was elected abbot of Saint Gall in 816 and died in 837 or the following year.]

To Gozbertus, religious servant of Christ and venerable abbot: Einhard, a sinner.

I ask that your holiness deign to learn about the case of a man named Bebo, to whom I granted a benefice from the monastery of Saint Chlodowald [Note: This can scarcely be understood as the monastery of Saint Clodoald near Paris] because he served me faithfully. But after I commended him to Lord Lothar, I obtained from the emperor that he confirm the same benefice to him for the length of his life.

For this reason I ask and beg your affection not to allow any impediment to be placed in his way concerning that benefice, until, if the Lord wills, we can discuss the matter with you. I give you this instruction because I know the perverse will and boundless greed of certain men, who care nothing about the losses of their neighbors so long as they can satisfy their own most voracious desire. I pray that you may always prosper [in the Lord].

## Letter III. To Amalarius

[Note: This appears to be Amalarius, a priest of Metz, who wrote four books on the divine or ecclesiastical Offices and another on the order of the psalms or antiphonary.]

To Amalarius, most reverend servant of Christ: Einhard, a sinner.

I do not know who anticipated the arrival of your servant, who brought me your letter and caused him to inform you [Note: Or rather, “caused me to write.” Dom Teulet supplied the word “quickly” for the lacuna] [lacuna] that you should come to the emperor on the Sunday before Palm Sunday.

But after I received your letter [Note: Before the words “your letter,” Teulet adds these words from the manuscript] and questioned the emperor about what you had requested, he ordered me to write to you that you should celebrate Holy Easter at home and order the rest of your retinue to follow you afterward, so that, when he had come to you at the palace, you could receive his instructions and, after the purpose of your embassy had been explained to you, undertake your journey without delay.

I pray that you may always prosper in the Lord.

[Note: Amalarius was sent by Louis the Pious to Pope Gregory IV in 827, as he himself writes in the preface to his *Antiphonary*.]

## Letter IV. To Otgarius, Archbishop

[Note: Otgarius, also called Autcarius, was made archbishop of Mainz in 826 after having been abbot of Weissenburg. He died in 847.]

To the holy and deservedly venerable Lord Otgarius, reverend archbishop: Einhard, a sinner.

This cleric, named Werdricus, belongs to the congregation of Saint Boniface [Note: That is, to the monastery of Fulda] and is staying with us by permission of his abbot, because he is our relative. We are therefore now sending him to you, so that you may order him to be ordained to the diaconate, if you see that this can be done canonically on the basis of the circumstances set out in the letter of his abbot. The abbot recently sent that letter to me when I consulted and questioned him about this matter, and I have sent it to you through this same brother for your reading. In it, as I believe, you can immediately understand whether that ordination can now take place or must be deferred to another time.

I pray and desire that heavenly grace may always and everywhere guard your holiness, who serves it devotedly, most holy and reverend father.

## Letter V. To Jacobus, Bishop

[Note: From the Laon manuscript, Teulet added this title to the fifth letter: “Concerning ordination.”]

To Jacobus, venerable in Christ and most reverend bishop: Einhard, a sinner.

This cleric, named Otmarus, brought me a letter from your holiness in which you asked me to give that cleric permission to remain with you, since he was born and raised in this region.

After considering the circumstances of the case, I decided to grant your request in such a way that the cleric, together with his brothers and mother, may remain with you as you asked, and may pay his annual rent to Saint Servatius [Note: That is, to the monastery of Saint Servatius at Maastricht on the Meuse], as our brothers have arranged for them.

As for the ordination of that cleric, it is in your power to do whatever you think best, since you know both his character and his manner of life and know whether he is suitable to receive any sacred order [Note: Dom Teulet reads, “to receive any sacred ordination”].

I pray that your holiness, mindful of me, may always prosper in Christ.

## Letter VI. To Egilolfus and Hunbertus

[Note: Perhaps we should read *Heistolphus*, who was archbishop of Mainz and whose suffragan was Humbertus, bishop of Würzburg.]

To the most beloved brothers in Christ and devoted servants of Christ [Col. 0511B], Egilolf and Hunbert, eternal salvation in the Lord.

I know that you are not unaware that Bishop Wolfgar of blessed memory [Note: He was the Bishop of Würzburg, whom Hunbert perhaps succeeded.]—at my request—granted our man Gerbert, in the district of Dubargawe, at a place called Asgbah, from the property of Saint Kilian, three hides and twelve dependants. But since he was unable to retain this any longer than the lifetime of that bishop, I ask your kindness to permit the aforesaid Gerbert to hold that benefice as he has held it until now, until he has been ordained bishop in this see and an agreement has been reached between me and him about what should be done with that benefice in the future. I wish you always good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0511C]

## LETTER VII. TO COUNT POPPO.

To the magnificent, honourable, illustrious, and glorious man Poppo, count [Note: D. Teulet has *gracious* in place of *glorious*], Eginhard sends greetings in the Lord.

Some men [Note: Teulet inserts before *men*: “two poor men.”] fled for refuge to the threshold of the blessed martyrs of Christ, Marcellinus and Peter, confessing themselves guilty. In your presence they were convicted of a certain theft [Note: The same learned editor adds *of* before *a certain*] which they had committed by stealing iron implements in the lord’s forest [Note: So the manuscript; Teulet has *forest* in the feminine form]. They have already paid part of the composition and are still to pay [Note: Teulet supplies “ought to pay”; the manuscript has *debberent*. The printed editions omit this word]; but, as they claim, they have no means of paying because of their poverty.

Therefore we ask your kindness to deign, for love of the martyrs of Christ to whom they have fled, to spare them as far as possible, lest they perish utterly through such an offence; rather, may they find [Col. 0511D] that it has benefited them in your regard that they fled to the tombs of the holy martyrs. I wish you always good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0512A]

## LETTER VIII. TO OTGAR, ARCHBISHOP.

To the holy and deservedly venerable lord Otgar [Note: Following D. Bouquet and Teulet, we have judged that this letter was addressed to Otgar. The former published it as the manuscript reads: “To the holy lord R. G. R. O., reverend …”], most reverend bishop.

A certain priest named Hruodrad came to me, saying that he belonged to your fiscal estate of Manniacum, and that he had received permission from your chorepiscopus and the other brothers to travel to Rome, in the month of March. But afterward, when he had reached Mainz, he was unable to find men with whom he could make that journey. For this reason he turned aside to one of our countrymen whom he knew, named Hildebert, and remained with him until he found men travelling to Rome. He says that he has now found them, and asked me to obtain from you permission for him to undertake that journey.

For, as he himself says, he wishes to complete the journey as quickly as he can and return to his place. Therefore I ask your holiness to deign, as he requests, to grant him permission, and not to let it harm him that he has remained so long on the road, since, because many obstacles arose, he unwillingly did what he was unable to remedy. We wish your holiness, mindful of our weakness, always good health in Christ, most holy and most reverend father.

[Col. 0512B]

## LETTER IX. TO GEBOIN, COUNT OF THE PALACE.

To our most beloved brother Geboin, glorious count of the palace, Eginhard sends greetings in the Lord.

I ask your affection to deign to hear this countryman of ours, David by name, who wishes to present his needs to you; and, if you recognize that his case is reasonable, make it possible for him to appeal to our lord emperor. He is a man of Lord Lothar [Note: Teulet has *Hlothar*]. Therefore you ought to help him not only because of my request, but also out of honour and love for his lord. I hope soon to be worthy to see you safe and unharmed.

[Col. 0512C]

## LETTER X. TO HETTI, ARCHBISHOP.

To the holy and deservedly venerable lord Hetti, most reverend archbishop, Eginhard the sinner.

Just as we learned from your holiness’s letter that you wished, so we took care to do without delay, namely by sending you the relics which you wrote that you wished to have for the dedication of your new basilica. We did this willingly, since we have such confidence in you that whatever fragment of the sacred ashes of the blessed martyrs reaches you will receive such honour as we ought to have shown to their entire bodies, had sloth and negligence not held us back from the honour due to them.

But concerning what you wished to learn from us, we are scarcely able to make you better informed, since almost nothing about these matters reaches our knowledge; nor are we especially curious about things from whose knowledge we gain no benefit and little pleasure. We wish your holiness, mindful of our weakness, always good health in Christ, most holy and most reverend father.

[Col. 0513A]

## LETTER XI. TO COUNT HRUOTBERT.

To the magnificent, honourable, illustrious, and glorious man Hruotbert, count, eternal salvation in the Lord.

I ask your kindness to deign to inform me what you wish, or [Note: The manuscript and Teulet do not have the comma or the word *or*], what should now be done concerning the case of Alahfrid, our man: whether it should be dismissed entirely, or whether he should still hope that, through your assistance, he may be worthy to obtain his rightful claim [Note: Teulet reads *so that*].

For I reported the entire case to our lord emperor, together with Counts Adalhard and Geboin of the palace, including how it had been investigated by you through truthful men. He replied that he was surprised that the case had not already been settled. Therefore I ask your affection not to disdain informing me [Note: Teulet has the better reading: “that you now deign to inform me”] what the aforesaid man of ours ought to do regarding his case. I wish you always good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0513C]

## LETTER XII. TO THE PRIEST LIUTHARD AND THE VICEDOMINUS EREMBERT.

In the name of Christ, Eginhard, abbot, sends greetings in the Lord to Liuthard, priest, and Erembert, vicedominus, our faithful men.

Let it be known to you that we have instructed the priest Willibald, whom we believe to be our faithful man, to receive our census from our men, both at Saint Bavo’s and in the monastery of Blandinium. For this reason we are sending him to you, because we wish you to assist him so that he may receive that census both in full and in good silver [Note: D. Teulet restores this passage, which was confused in the printed editions and omitted by D. Bouquet, as follows: “And when it has been received, we wish you to assist him in this, so that he may be able to bring it to us.”]. I wish you always good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0513D]

## LETTER XIII. TO COUNT POPPO.

To the magnificent, honourable, illustrious, and glorious man Poppo, count, Eginhard sends eternal greetings in the Lord.

I have been told that you asked me to give you certainty about three matters. It is difficult for me to do so concerning one of them, namely the woman whom you know better than I do: whether she can be taken by you in marriage without guilt.

As for the provisions which you received at Aachen, I desire no other return than your friendship. Concerning Jopila, when we have spoken together, I am ready to act according to what we then agree between us; and therefore I cannot now indicate more to you in my letter. I wish you always good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0514A]

## LETTER XIV. TO GERWARD, LIBRARIAN.

To my most beloved brother Gerward, Eginhard sends eternal greetings in the Lord.

I am uncertain what I ought to think about you: whether you failed to understand my letters, or whether you did not care about my danger. But I am more easily led to suppose that, because of certain occupations, my writings were read and understood by you with too little attention [Note: The manuscript reads *I am led*], than to believe that your affection failed to care about the danger threatened to me.

For you urge—or rather, you give the advice—that, abandoning the vigils of the martyrs, which I have been ordered constantly to attend and participate in, I should go to the palace, although I have been warned that an absence of seven days will incur punishment. This cannot be avoided merely during the delay to be spent at the palace, but not even on the journey which must be made to the palace—especially by me, who, because both of the difficulty of the road and of my bodily weakness, have rarely been able to travel from Aachen to the threshold of the martyrs in less than seven days.

But now I ask and earnestly entreat you to reread and understand the writing which I sent you [Note: D. Teulet adds “if you are willing”], and, as I asked you long ago in my letters, do not hesitate to write back to me what you think about that revelation and the commands by which I am bound. There will be no shortage of carriers if you wish to send what you write to Bonotto, our vicedominus. I wish you always good health in the Lord [Note: Teulet has, from the manuscript, “I wish you always good health”], dearest and most affectionate brother and lord.

[Col. 0514C]

## LETTER XV. IN THE PERSON OF BOMA, TO BLIDTHRUT.

To my most beloved sister Blidthrut, Boma [Note: Petzius thinks that *Imma*, the name of Eginhard’s wife, should be read here instead of *Boma*], your friend and well-wisher, sends eternal greetings in the Lord.

A certain servant of yours from Makesbah, named Wenilo, took a free woman in marriage. Now, fearing your anger and that of his lord Albinus as well, he has fled for refuge to the threshold of the holy Marcellinus and Peter. Therefore I ask your affection to deign to intercede for him on my behalf, so that, with the favour of both his lord and yourself, he may be permitted to keep the woman whom he has taken. I wish you always good health [Note: Teulet adds “in the Lord”].

[Col. 0515A]

## LETTER XVI. TO COUNT HATTO.

To our most beloved friend Hatto, glorious count, Eginhard sends eternal greetings in the Lord.

A certain man of yours, named Hunno, has come to the threshold of the holy Marcellinus and Peter, seeking pardon because he had taken your female servant, his fellow-servant, in marriage without your command. Therefore we ask your kindness that he may be worthy to receive your forgiveness for this act, if his offence is found deserving of pardon. I wish you always good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0515A]

## LETTER XVII. TO HRABAN, ABBOT.

To the most reverend servant of Christ, Hraban, venerable abbot [Note: Hraban became abbot of Fulda in 822 and succeeded Otgar in the episcopate of Mainz in 847], Eginhard the sinner.

A certain man of yours, named Gundhart, asked us to intercede for him with your holiness, so that, without offending you—or rather, with your favour—he might be permitted to omit the military expedition which must be undertaken at the present time and remain at home [Note: Teulet reads “stay behind”]. He asserts that he is compelled by great necessity to remain, because he is involved in a feud and dares not undertake this journey with his enemies and those who lie in wait for his life, especially with the count with whom he has been ordered to go, whom he says is his bitterest enemy.

Therefore he asks that the authority of your command not drive him into such danger. He says that he will take care of it and make arrangements to settle matters without troubling you with the collector of the military levy, if he comes and compels him. I would not ask you about this matter if I had not learned of his distress and dangers. I wish you always good health.

[Col. 0515C]

## LETTER XVIII. TO MARCHRAD, VICEDOMINUS.

To our beloved friend Marchrad, vicedominus [Note: Teulet adds “glorious”], Eginhard sends eternal greetings in the Lord.

Two servants of Saint Martin from the estate of Hedabach, named Willirannus and Otbertus, fled [Note: Teulet reads “fled for refuge”] to the threshold of the blessed martyrs of Christ, Marcellinus and Peter, because their brother had killed one of his companions. They ask to be permitted to pay the wergeld for their brother and that his limbs be spared.

Therefore we ask your affection to deign, as far as possible, to spare him for the love of God and his saints, to whose threshold they have fled. I wish you always good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0515D]

## LETTER XIX. IN THE PERSON OF THE EMPEROR LOUIS, TO COUNT G.

In the name of the Lord God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, august emperor, to Count G.

[Col. 0516A]

Let it be known to you that we wish, when this letter of ours reaches you, that you immediately, without any delay, prepare yourself to come on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January—that is, six days before Christmas—to meet our envoy H. at our estate called Heilambrunno.

Whatever he, together with the other counts and our faithful men, orders you to do in our name, strive to do; and act in such a way that we may have good confidence in your loyalty. Farewell.

[Col. 0516A]

## LETTER XX. IN THE PERSON OF THE EMPEROR LOUIS, TO H., HIS FAITHFUL MAN.

In the name of the Lord God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, august emperor, to H., our faithful man.

Let it be known to you that we wish you to order one of your sons, our vassals—whichever you know to be best able to do this—to be prepared, so that whenever Count R. and our envoy H. wish to send us a message through him, he may be able to travel without delay or slowness to Tours. For there he will find either us ourselves or our beloved wife, if it is the Lord’s will. See that you show no negligence in this matter, if you wish to have our favour. I wish you always good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0516B]

## LETTER XXI. IN THE PERSON OF THE EMPEROR LOUIS, TO T., HIS FAITHFUL MAN.

In the name of the Lord God and our Saviour Jesus [Col. 0516C] Christ, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, august emperor, to T., our faithful man.

Let it be known to you that we wish you to prepare yourself so that, whenever Count HRT. [Note: So the manuscript; Teulet has *Hrotbertus*] and our envoy II. wish to send us any message through you, you may immediately, without delay or slowness, travel with that message to Tours [Note: Teulet’s reading is better: *Turones*]. For there you will find either us ourselves or our beloved wife, if it is the Lord’s will. See that you show no negligence in this matter, if you wish to have our favour.

[Col. 0516C]

## LETTER XXII. TO A., HIS DOMINICAL ENVOY.

To our beloved brother and friend A., dominical envoy, Eginhard sends eternal greetings in the Lord.

I thought it was well known to you that our men whom we have in these regions were assigned to coastal guard duty according to the arrangement and command of our lord emperor, not only at the time when he departed for [lacuna]oriam [Note: Teulet thinks that these letters are the ending of the name of some city or region and that *Bajo* should be supplied, so that it would read *Bajoaria*], but also when he went to Orléans.

Therefore it does not seem just to me that they should have to pay the military levy, since they were nowhere else except where the emperor himself ordered them to be. For this reason I ask your affection to grant us a postponement in this matter until our lord emperor comes. We will then remind him of his command, and he will order whatever pleases him. I wish you always good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0517A]

## LETTER XXIII. TO HIS VICEDOMINUS.

In the name of Christ, Eginhard, abbot, sends greetings in the Lord to his vicedominus and faithful man.

Let it be known that we wish you to send some men to Aachen to repair and restore our lodgings, and, according to custom, to arrange for what we need to have there—namely flour, malt, wine, cheese, and other things—to be brought there at the proper time.

As for the oxen which are to be slaughtered, we wish you to have them brought to Ludinaca and slaughtered there. We wish you to have one of them given to Hruotlouge; and the small portions and entrails which cannot be kept for our use, we wish given to the household that is there.

For our part, with the Lord’s help, if life permits, we intend to come to the palace around the feast of Saint Martin. Therefore we wish you to make all this known also to the younger men, and to command them in our name to provide for our expenses in the same way as we have commanded you. Farewell.

[Col. 0517B]

## LETTER XXIV. TO A CERTAIN OFFICIAL OF HIS.

In the name of Christ, Eginhard, called abbot, sends greetings in the Lord to N.

We inform you that we need wax for our service, and that we cannot obtain it in these regions because there has been little honey-production in these lands during the past two years. Therefore we wish you to discuss and consider with N. how, if possible, you might together prepare one pack-load [Note: Teulet adds “to come to us”] with our vassals who are returning to us from these regions after the feast of Saint Bavo. Farewell and pray for us.

[Col. 0517C]

## LETTER XXV. TO N., BISHOP.

To the holy and deservedly venerable lord N., reverend priest of the Most High God, Eginhard the sinner sends greetings.

A certain servant of Saint Mary, named N., belonging to the authority of your holiness, has come to the threshold of the blessed martyrs of Christ, Marcellinus and Peter, because of the crime he committed in killing his companion on account of a quarrel that had arisen between them.

Therefore we ask your holiness, out of reverence for those same martyrs to whose threshold he has fled, to deign to spare him, so that, with both the integrity of his limbs and the penalty of blows remitted, he may be permitted to settle and make amends for what he committed in evil intent by payment of money. We wish your holiness always good health in Christ, most holy and most reverend father.

[Col. 0518A]

## LETTER XXVI. TO HIS FRIEND U.

Ev. SS. [Note: So D. Bouquet; Teulet has: “Einhard sends greetings to his U.”]

Frumold, son of Count N., whose sister N. has as his wife, is worn down more by illness than by old age—for he is continually afflicted by severe pain in his feet. He has a modest benefice in Burgundy, in the district of Geneva, where his father was count, and he fears losing it unless your kindness assists him, because, owing to the illness that weighs upon him [Note: The manuscript and Teulet read “because of the illness”], he cannot come to the palace.

Therefore he asks that, in this necessity, you deign to petition our lord emperor to permit him to retain the benefice which his grandfather granted him and which his father permitted him to hold, until, having recovered his strength, he comes into the emperor’s presence and commends himself to him in the customary manner.

Farewell, most loving of my little ones, as your old and infirm little one wishes [Note: Teulet reads “wishes”].

[Col. 0518B]

## LETTER XXVII. TO N., COUNT.

To the magnificent, honourable, illustrious, and glorious man N., count, Eginhard sends eternal greetings in the Lord.

N., a royal vassal and the brother of Count N.’s wife, weighed down by disease of the feet and old age, wished to come to our lord emperor, but was unable to do so because of his illness. As soon as he can, he will come to his service.

Meanwhile he asks to be permitted to retain his benefice, which Emperor Charles gave him in Burgundy, in the district of Geneva, until he comes into the emperor’s presence and commends himself into his hands.

It seems right and useful to me that this should happen as he desires, because he is a good and prudent man and of good reputation among his neighbours. You will do well if you deign to assist him in this matter. I wish you always good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0518C]

## LETTER XXVIII. TO N., COUNT.

To the magnificent, honourable, illustrious, and glorious N., count, Eginhard sends eternal greetings in the Lord.

I ask your kindness to deign to assist this young man N. with our lord emperor, so that he and his brother may not lose the benefice which they possess. For they have fifteen hides in the district of Tournai [Note: So the manuscript; Teulet has “in the district of Tornacum”], and five hides beyond the Rhine.

He wishes to serve our lord emperor with the benefice situated in the district of Tournai, and he wants his brother, with the benefice beyond the Rhine, to commend himself to N., while nevertheless they jointly retain the entire benefice. But the brother will not consent to this unless our lord emperor commands him to do so.

For, unless this is done, they will lose the benefice which they possess beyond the Rhine. Therefore he asks your goodness to deign to petition our lord emperor about this, so that he may order his brother to act in this way. He himself is ready to provide whatever guarantee pleases our lord emperor, that he does not wish always to retain his benefice jointly with his brother [Note: Teulet reads: “that he does wish always to retain it”; he deletes the word *not* from the printed text]. I wish you always good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0519A]

## LETTER XXIX. TO N., PRIEST.

To the holy and deservedly venerable lord N., priest of the Most High God, Eginhard the sinner sends greetings.

We received Eburon, your kinsman and faithful man, who came to us, with joyful affection, thinking that he would remain with us for a longer time. But since he is hastening to return to you, we did not wish to send him away without our letter, lest, if he returned empty-handed, it should be thought that he had not come to us.

Nevertheless, concerning the matters about which he thought he would bring you reliable information, I can neither communicate anything certain to you nor indicate it through him, because the change in affairs which has recently taken place in this kingdom has so disturbed us that we utterly do not know what we ought to do, except, in accordance with the words of Jehoshaphat, to direct our eyes toward the Lord; and, in accordance with the words of Philo, to implore divine help when human assistance ceases.

We commend to your affection the bearer of this letter, Eburon himself, though he is our kinsman [Note: Teulet reads “your kinsman”], as a man most dear to us [Note: The same editor reads “to your affection” as “to your choice”]. For we trust in God that, even if it cannot happen now, with the help of divine mercy we shall send him back to you again, joyful and cheerful, at a suitable time. We wish divine grace always and everywhere to preserve your holiness in good health and mindful of us.

[Col. 0519C]

## LETTER XXX. TO VUSSIN, HIS SON.

To his most beloved son Vussin [Note: Eginhard had Vussin by his wife Imma], greetings in the Lord.

I fear, my son, and greatly dread that, having left the sheepfold, you may be mindful neither of yourself nor of me. For immature youth, unless restrained by the reins of discipline, does not easily walk in the paths of justice.

Therefore, my son, strive to imitate upright conduct, and do not wish in any way to offend the one whom I always urged you to follow. Rather, mindful of your profession, attend to learning his commands, insofar as he himself permits, since you have entrusted yourself wholly to him.

Once instructed in these matters and accustomed to putting them into practice, you will lack none of the benefits of life-giving knowledge. As I warned you when I was present, exercise yourself in the pursuit of learning, and whatever noble knowledge you may be able to acquire from the luminous and abundant genius of that great orator, leave nothing untouched.

Above all, remember to imitate his upright conduct, in which he excels. For grammar and rhetoric, and the other studies of the liberal arts, are vain and very harmful to the servants of God unless they are understood to be subordinate to good morals through divine grace: “knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.”

It would be better for me to happen to see you dead than puffed up and teeming with vices. For the Saviour did not command us to learn from him the performance of miracles, but meekness and humility of heart.

What more can I say? You have often heard these and similar things from me. Would that it might someday happen that you delight in those things by which, with God’s help, purity of heart and body is attained.

I have therefore sent you obscure words and names from the books of Vitruvius which might occur to me at present, so that you may seek out their meaning there. And I believe that most of them can be shown to you in the little chest which Lord E. fashioned with ivory columns, in the manner of ancient works.

And concerning what Vitruvius calls *scenographia*, ask what Virgil means when he calls something a *scene* in Book III of the *Georgics*. For he says:

[Note: Teulet adds the following verse:

“Now it pleases to lead forth solemn processions.”]

“It delights to go to the temples and see the slaughtered bullocks,

or how the scene, its fronts turned aside, may withdraw, and how

the Britons, woven into purple, may lift the curtains.”

Farewell.

[Col. 0520B]

## LETTER XXXI. TO N., BISHOP.

To the holy and deservedly venerable lord N., bishop, Eginhard sends eternal greetings in the Lord.

Although it greatly grieves me to hear, through [lacuna], that you, most beloved lord, are in this most grievous bodily suffering [Note: D. Teulet supplies *letters* and we follow his punctuation as more suitable to the sense], nevertheless I receive no small consolation from knowing that this suffering benefits you and pertains to the cleansing of your soul.

For I believe that divine mercy permits you to be afflicted for so long by this bodily illness so that, when you depart from this body, it may receive you purified.

As for prayers to be offered for you, I assure your affection that, insofar as God deigns to grant me strength and ability, I shall strive through those whom I can judge worthy to be heard, just as I know that you have confidence in me regarding my weakness.

Although one must never despair of recovering bodily health, since God is powerful to do whatever he wishes with his creature, nevertheless it is better for each of us to prepare himself for certainties than, because of uncertainties, to neglect what is necessary while hoping for better things [Note: Teulet reads “while hoping for what must be hoped for”]. I wish you always good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0520D]

## LETTER XXXII. TO A FRIEND.

To my most beloved, Eginhard the sinner—now placed at the very end, yet, while breath remains, faithful before God to you and yours.

[Col. 0521A]

My dearest, I commend to your affection my soul, which has departed from a body subjected to sins, so that you may deign to enroll it among the company of your faithful and yours. Thus, aided in its misery by the devotion of holy prayers and the prayers of pious brothers, may it be worthy to receive some place of refreshment [Note: So the manuscript; Teulet corrects the manuscript’s error by printing “a certain place”].

Having briefly touched on these matters because of the excessive and great distress of body and spirit, I beg you, my dearest, for the love of God and out of friendship for my unworthiness, to exercise the utmost care over the churches entrusted to my smallness, lest after my death rapacious wolves invade the place of holiness and scatter the most humble flock. Rather, may a ruler be granted to them who knows how to love or fear God and to help mercifully those subject to him.

Our brothers, and your most faithful men, from the monastery of N., wished a certain brother [Note: D. Teulet, following Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, prints “a certain brother” rather than following the faulty manuscript] among them, one close to me, to preside over them: young in age, but, as I think, old in character. You know his lineage well [Note: Teulet adds, as a paraphrase, “for he is”]: the son of N., brother of N., and a kinsman of many nobles.

They sent him to Worms and, while I was still alive, when N. deigned to visit me, they commended him in his presence. In the presence of Count N., he promised me and my relatives, with great emotion and many tears, [lacuna] [Note: After the dots Teulet also prints the word “saying,” explaining in a note that the word can clearly be read in the manuscript, although the printed editions omit it]. Compelled by N.’s prayers, he agreed that, if it should be brought about by God, they wished that he should take my place.

Therefore, dearest, remember to strive earnestly that this not be delayed but be carried out above all. I am sending one cloak, which I ask you to order given to the brothers at Saint Servatius, so that they may mention me [Note: So the manuscript; Teulet reads “which,” following D. Bouquet, who retained the manuscript reading in the text]. I have ordered my mule to be given to your affection. Let Imma, my most beloved sister, be your helper in these matters; and I commend my soul to you! Distress does not permit me to say more, yet I commend my soul once again to your prayers.

[Col. 0521C]

## LETTER XXXIII. TO N., COUNT, AND N., JUDGE, DOMINICAL ENVOYS.

To the beloved brothers and friends in Christ, N., count, and N., judge, glorious envoys of our lord emperor, Eginhard sends greetings in the Lord.

Our men who come to us from these regions regularly tell us of your good will and kindness toward us, in that you protect our men and spare them wherever you are able to spare them—both in matters of the military levy and in other cases belonging to your assigned jurisdiction.

Therefore we give you great thanks, as is fitting, and pray God and his saints that he may deign to repay you with a reward corresponding to your deeds, not only here in the present life but also in the future. We also promise that you may regard our smallness as ready to fulfil your wishes. Farewell.

[Col. 0522A]

## LETTER XXXIV. TO LOTHAR, PARTNER IN THE EMPIRE.

May my lord, the most pious Augustus, live forever.

How great a care and solicitude my insignificance feels for your greatness, I cannot easily explain in words. Since I have always loved you as much as my most pious lord, your father, and have wished both of you equally to remain safe, after he assumed you into the fellowship of his name and kingdom, with the consent of all his people, and instructed my humble self to care for you and diligently admonish you concerning the correction of your conduct and the pursuit of honorable and useful things. But although in these matters you have found my service less useful to you than it ought to have been, nevertheless faithful goodwill has not been lacking, nor is it lacking even now; it does not permit me to remain silent, but rather compels me to make you aware of your [Note: [Col. 0522D] After the words “to make you aware of your,” the learned editor Teulet added nearly three lines from a more recent manuscript, hitherto unknown in printed editions, which complete the sense. The learned editor of Eginhard will not be displeased if we reproduce the passage here as he restored it: “It compels me to make you aware of your [safety and briefly explain the dangers against which you ought to guard. Let your greatness know] …”]. . . . . let you know that certain men, seeking their own advantage rather than yours, are troubling your gentleness and attempting to persuade you that, setting aside your father’s counsel and abandoning the obedience owed to him, you should leave the place entrusted to you by your most pious father to govern and guard, and go to him against his will, when he neither wishes nor commands it, and remain with him although it displeases him.

What could be imagined more perverse or indecent than this! Consider what sort of thing this persuasion is and how much evil it contains. First, as it seems to my insignificance, it urges you to disregard God’s commandment by which honor is ordered to be shown to parents, and to regard as worthless the long life promised as the reward for keeping that commandment. Then it urges you, having cast aside obedience, to assume disobedience in its place, and through arrogance to rise up rebelliously against him under whom you ought humbly to have lived in submission. Finally, it urges you, by contempt and disobedience driving out charity, to let discord—which ought never even to have been named between you—grow so greatly that hatred should arise where love ought to have been. You must take the greatest care that this does not happen.

I believe your prudence is not unaware how great an abomination in God’s sight is a rebellious and disobedient son, since God, as you can read in Deuteronomy, commanded through Moses that such a son be stoned by all the people. Therefore I judged it necessary to admonish your *neptitas* [uncertain; Teulet reads “piety”] [Note: [Col. 0523D] From these words Mabillon concludes that Imma, Eginhard’s wife, was the daughter of Charlemagne, in the fourth century of the Benedictine history, part I, in the historical eulogy of Angilbert, abbot of Centula: “If Lothair,” he says, “was Eginhard’s grandson, then [this was] through his wife, who therefore must have been Charlemagne’s daughter.” Pagi, however, in the year 792, considers that the matter is not proved by these words, since the terms “niece,” “uncle,” and similar expressions had considerable breadth in those times and admitted various explanations. Indeed, Mabillon himself, in book XXVII of the Benedictine Annals, no. 51, thinks that this relationship could have arisen from another source, and considers that the little story—or rather fable—of the chronicler of Lorsch, who makes Imma Charlemagne’s daughter, is overthrown by this one argument alone: that Eginhard had a wife. The learned abbot Lebeuf, in a dissertation that in 1740 won the prize offered by the Academy of Soissons, understands *neptitatem* to mean primacy or pre-eminence; he derives the word from the German *nempt* or *nept*, meaning “pre-eminent.” He likewise maintains that the word *Neustria*, which the ancients called *Neptrecum* or *Neptricum*, means the same as “the pre-eminent kingdom,” from *nept*, “pre-eminent,” and *rich* or *reich*, “kingdom.” — Thus D. Bouquet. But the most recent editor of Eginhard, D. Teulet, has substituted *pietatem* (“piety”) for *neptitatem*, which he proves by many arguments to be wholly unusual, devoid of meaning in every sense, and attributable to a copyist’s negligence. EDIT.] so that, through the prudence granted you by God, you may guard against your danger, and not suppose that this divine judgment can be disregarded by anyone merely because it was written in the old law. For it is one of many commandments that our elders and teachers—the holy Fathers, that is—have judged must be observed by both present and former generations, by Christians as well as Jews [Note: [Col. 0524D] Teulet: “ancient.”].

I love you, God knows, and therefore admonish you so frankly. You should consider not the lowliness of the person giving the warning, but the soundness of the counsel. I wish you well, etc.

[Col. 0523A]

## LETTER XXXV. TO N., ABBOT

To the holy and deservedly venerable lord N., most reverend abbot, N. [that is, Eginhard], a sinner.

From the report of my friends I have learned concerning N.—whether I ought to call him abbot or bishop I do not know; you know best who he is—that he is accustomed to use your wholesome and most prudent counsel in matters relating to his advancement. Therefore it seemed proper to me to ask your holiness to speak to the man mentioned above on behalf of his nephew Eburon, who is now staying at Metz, and to beg him not to defraud him of the hope he had given him, but rather to continue in the kindness toward him that he had promised.

Specifically, may he deign to assist him, who is in poverty, from his own resources, so that through lack and want of necessary things he may not be compelled to abandon the position in which he himself placed him. This will certainly happen unless he makes provision beforehand to prevent it. The matter can easily be provided for if he is willing to remain faithful to his promises, by which he compelled him to agree with him.

I wish your holiness, ever mindful of my insignificance in Christ, good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0523C]

## LETTER XXXVI. TO A FRIEND

To my beloved brother and dearest friend N., Eginhard sends eternal salvation in the Lord.

Count N. asked me to entreat you concerning those pigs which you sent to be pastured for his service: that you might permit him to keep the same pigs until they became fatter and better, and he could purchase them at a fair price for the lord’s use. Knowing of our friendship, he thought that I might obtain this from you. And I, trusting in your affection, ask that you not hesitate to fulfill his wish in this matter.

I wish you always good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0524A]

## LETTER XXXVII. TO HIS STEWARD

In the name of Christ, Eginhard to N., his steward.

We are greatly surprised that everything could have remained as it has concerning the matters we entrusted to you. For, as we have heard, of the grain which you were to send to Mulinheim, whether for making flour or brewing malt, you sent nothing—not anything else except thirty pigs, and those not good but mediocre, and three measures of legumes. Apart from that, nothing.

And not only this, but throughout this entire winter we were unable to see either you or any messenger of yours who might bring us news from those regions. If we can obtain no greater benefit from Frideslar than you have caused us to obtain from it, we do not know why we ought to have that benefice.

Now, therefore, if you have any concern for our favor, we ask that you strive to correct your negligence and quickly make us certain what we ought to expect from you.

[Col. 0524B]

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO BROTHER N.

To my beloved brother N., Eginhard sends greetings in the Lord.

We wish you to instruct Egmunel, in our name, to make us sixty square bricks, measuring two manual feet on every side and four fingers in thickness, and another two hundred smaller ones, likewise square, measuring one and a half [manual feet] and four fingers on every side, and three fingers in thickness [Note: [Col. 0524D] Manuscript: *Lapitu*; Teulet: *Lapathi*.].

We have sent you through this man some seed of lapathum [dock] which we wish you to have sown in a spacious place; it usually grows into a large herb.

Farewell.

[Col. 0524C]

## LETTER XXXIX. TO THE PEOPLE OF MÉRIDA, IN THE PERSON OF THE EMPEROR LOUIS

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, N. [that is, Louis], by the divinely ordained providence of God emperor Augustus, sends greetings in the Lord to all the nobles and to the entire people of Mérida [Note: [Col. 0524D] Mérida lies on the river Guadiana in Lusitania and is therefore distant from the Spanish March. For this reason Cointius, under the year 826, no. 37, thinks that instead of “to the people of Mérida” one should read “to the people of Zaragoza.”].

[Col. 0525A]

We have heard of your tribulation and the manifold hardships you suffer through the cruelty of King Abdirhaman, who, driven by excessive greed for your possessions, which he attempted to take from you, has very often violently oppressed you. We have learned that his father Abolaz acted in the same way: by unjust impositions he compelled you to pay him a tribute of which you were not debtors, and on account of this he turned friends into enemies and those obedient to him into opponents and disobedient subjects. For he also attempted to deprive you of your freedom and to burden and humiliate you with unjust taxes and tributes.

But, as we have heard, you have always, like brave men, bravely repelled the injuries inflicted upon you by unjust kings and manfully resisted their cruelty and greed. We have learned from the reports of many people that you are doing the same now.

Therefore it has pleased us to send you this letter, to console and exhort you to persevere in defending your freedom against the most cruel king, in the cause that you have begun, and not to yield to his fury and savagery, as you have not done until now. Since this same king is a most certain adversary and enemy both of us and of you, let us fight against his savagery by common counsel.

For, with the help of almighty God, we wish to send our army next summer to your March [Note: [Col. 0525D] Teulet: “our March.”], so that it may be stationed there and wait until you inform us when it should advance, if it seems good to you that, in order to assist you, we should direct that same army against our common enemies who reside in our March. Thus, if Abdirhaman or his army should wish to come against you, they may be hindered by our army, so that he and his army may be unable to come against you in support.

For we assure you that, if you wish to turn away from him and turn to us, we grant you the full and undiminished use of your ancient freedom; we permit you to remain exempt from tribute and taxation; and we command you to live under no law other than the one under which you yourselves wish to live. Nor do we wish to treat you otherwise than by honoring you as friends and allies in the defense of our kingdom.

We wish you always good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0525C]

## LETTER XL. TO THE EMPRESS

Let our most pious lady know that I, your servant, after leaving Aachen, have been afflicted by such severe bodily ailments that I could scarcely have reached Valenciennes from Utrecht even on the tenth day. There I was seized by such a great pain in my kidneys and spleen at once that I was unable to cover even a single mile on horseback during an entire day.

Therefore I beseech your piety to permit me, with your favor, to travel by boat to Saint N. [Note: [Col. 0525D] That is, to Saint Bavo, or to the monastery of Saint Bavo.] and to lie there until almighty God deigns to give me the strength to make the journey. [Col. 0526A] For as soon as I am able to ride, I shall hasten to come either to you or to the lord emperor, whichever you prefer me to do.

Now I humbly beg your piety to deign, when you come to him, to excuse me to my most merciful lord for not coming to you. God is my witness that I have written nothing false to you about my health. Indeed, there are certain other ailments I suffer within myself that are much more serious, about which I can speak only with one who is utterly faithful.

Know this, however: you cannot acquire a greater reward before God at present than by arranging that I may hasten to the service of the holy martyrs of Christ as soon as I recover. [Col. 0526B] For I can reach that place from Saint N. by boat in fifteen days. If bodily weakness did not hinder me, I would not send this letter, but would come in person and share with you in the affairs being conducted among you.

[Col. 0526B]

## LETTER XLI. TO A FRIEND

Now, placed in great distress, I beg your kindness to deign to intercede for me with my most pious lord and emperor. For when the queen left Aachen, she ordered me—since I was unable to go with her—to follow her to Compiègne. Obeying her commands, I came to Valenciennes with great difficulty, scarcely in ten days.

From there, because I could no longer ride [Note: [Col. 0526D] The manuscript and Teulet read *qui* (“who”).], I traveled by boat as far as Saint N. [Col. 0526C] For excessive diarrhea and kidney pain alternate within me and follow one another so severely that, from the time I set out from Aachen, there has not been a single day on which I have not suffered from one illness or the other.

In addition to these are other ailments that arose from that illness during which I lay sick last year—namely, constant numbness in my right thigh and an almost unbearable pain in my spleen. Afflicted by these sufferings, I lead a very sad life, almost devoid of every pleasure, especially because I fear that I may die somewhere other than I wish, engaged in something other than serving the holy martyrs of Christ.

Therefore I adjure and beseech you, by the blessed martyrs of Christ Marcellinus and Peter, to deign to intercede for my insignificance with the most pious emperor, so that he may not be angry with me because I did not go to meet him as those who were able to do so did [Col. 0526D] [Note: Teulet adds *utique certe* (“certainly indeed”) before *venissem* (“I would have come”).]. I would have come if I had been able, and I shall come as soon as I can; whether absent or present, I shall remain faithful to him.

I therefore ask your charity to deign, by your letters, to inform me as quickly as you can both about what has been done and about what is to be done among you. I wish you always good health in the Lord.

Everything now taking place in this kingdom was foretold as future two years ago, when the martyrs of Christ revealed it.

[Col. 0527A]

## LETTER XLII. TO THE EMPEROR LOUIS

To the great lord, a humble servant.

I do not doubt that my most pious lord remembers how you gave me permission that, when my lady proceeded to you, I should depart to perform the service of the blessed martyrs of Christ. I wished to do this. But my lady ordered me to follow her to Compiègne, and, obeying her commands, as soon as I was able to obtain my horses I began to travel after her to Compiègne.

On this journey I was seized at once by pain in my spleen and kidneys and so afflicted that I scarcely reached Valenciennes from Utrecht in ten days. When I realized there that I could no longer ride, I came in the morning by boat to Saint N., and now, placed there in great distress and pain, I ask and beg that your piety deign to grant me permission to proceed to the place where the sacred bodies of your pious patrons rest.

For I can travel there by boat from Saint N. in fifteen days. You can acquire a great reward before God if you permit me to go to the service of his saints, provided I am able to reach that place alive. I believe that those holy martyrs ought to intercede for you before God if you are willing to put their service before your own. For nowhere else in your kingdom can I render you greater benefit than there, if you are willing to help me in this.

[Col. 0527C]

## LETTER XLIII. TO N., BISHOP

To the holy and deservedly venerable lord N., most reverend bishop, Eginhard, a sinner.

I never cease giving as many thanks as I can to almighty God and our Lord Jesus Christ, because I have learned that my most glorious and God-preserved, and ever-to-be-preserved, lord Lothair Augustus has come safely and unharmed from Italy, and that you, dearest to me, have come with him. I wish and pray that he may soon permit me to come there, where I may be worthy to enjoy your bodily presence.

Meanwhile I commend my insignificance to your charity, and through you to his piety, and I beg you not to deign, through anyone’s persuasion, to suspect anything sinister concerning my humble self. I call God and the holy martyrs Marcellinus [Col. 0527D] and Peter to witness that I cannot express to you the love and devotion with which I know myself to be devoted to you [Note: [Col. 0528D] Teulet: “in words.”].

Therefore I confidently ask that, when I come, I may be worthy to find you toward me as I do not doubt that I have deserved you to be toward me. I wish your holiness, mindful of my weakness, always good health in Christ.

[Col. 0527D]

## LETTER XLIV. TO HIS FRIEND E.

To the holy and deservedly venerable lord E., E. S. S.

[Col. 0528A]

Although there are very many things about which I may reasonably wish to be informed, two in particular now occupy me with greater curiosity. The first is where and when that general assembly is to be held; the second, whether the lord Lothair ought to return to Italy or remain with his father. May your charity not hesitate to make me certain about these two matters.

For I need knowledge of them more than of the other affairs taking place among you, since from these matters depends what I ought to do, if divine mercy deigns to favor me so that I may be able to accomplish something useful. I wish, dearest of my friends, soon to be worthy to see you in good health.

[Col. 0528A]

## LETTER XLV. TO COUNT G.

[Col. 0528B]

To my dearest brother, G., glorious count and nobleman, Eginhard sends eternal salvation in the Lord.

I have always felt your affection toward me to be benevolent, but never more than now, when you obtained permission for me to proceed to the service of the saints Marcellinus and Peter, who on account of this deed will intercede for you before God. Therefore I give your kindness as many thanks as I can and earnestly beg you, in keeping with your good custom, always to be willing to support me both with the lord emperor and with his sons, especially with the lord Lothair [Note: [Col. 0528D] Teulet adds “the young man.”], Augustus, in whose piety, although undeserving, I have great confidence.

Furthermore, I ask you to be willing to obtain a reward for N. the painter, your devoted young man, and to help him and deign to intercede for him with the lord emperor, if you see a suitable opportunity, so that through anyone’s envy he may not lose the benefice he acquired by serving his lords well. It is unnecessary for me to name for you those whom he fears in this matter, since they are as well known to me as to you. I ask only that, insofar as you can, you deign to help him.

I wish you always good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0528C]

## LETTER XLVI. TO ABBOT N.

To the most venerable N., most reverend abbot, Eginhard, a sinner.

Just as I do not suppose that I have forgotten my request, so I do not suppose that you have forgotten your promise, although afterward many and varied obstacles arose which could have caused our conversation not merely to lie dormant for a time but to be consigned to perpetual oblivion.

I mean the conversation we had when we were together in the palace, concerning the roof of the basilica of the blessed martyrs of Christ Marcellinus and Peter, which I am now laboring to build, although with great difficulty, and when we agreed upon purchasing lead for the price of fifty pounds.

Although the work on the basilica has not yet reached the point at which the need for roofing compels me to make provision, nevertheless, because the end of mortal life is uncertain, it always seems necessary to hasten, so that the good work begun by us may, with the Lord’s help, be completed.

Therefore I ask your kindness to deign to inform me by letter about the purchase of that same lead, so that I may know whether anything has yet been undertaken in the matter; and, if it has not yet been undertaken, when that business ought to be begun and, with the Lord’s help, completed.

For this reason I beg your great charity not to hesitate to make me certain about this matter by your letters. I wish you, mindful of me, always good health in the Lord.

[Col. 0529A]

## LETTER XLVII. TO A FRIEND

I ask you to write me nothing about the state of affairs at the palace, because I take no pleasure in hearing about anything that is being done there [Note: [Col. 0529B] The bracketed word *illic* (“there”) is supplied editorially.]. Concerning my other friends—if anyone besides you remains—I am very eager to learn where you are and what you are doing.

Therefore I have taken care to send you this letter, to remind you to write to me about what is happening with you: namely, what health you enjoy, and whether and when it may be possible, life permitting, for us to see one another. I have often desired to see you and speak with you, but never more ardently than now, because never has a greater need come upon me to discuss and consider the conduct of life with a friend. I do this willingly with no one more than with you, since I place greater confidence in no one’s loyalty.

I have sent through this boy a letter to Abbot N. I ask that, if he is able to go, you have him escorted by one of your men as far as the abbot. Or, if perhaps, because of the weariness of his pack animals, he is unable to travel farther than he usually does, I beg you to receive from him the letter I am sending to Folco, and to forward it to him through someone, asking him to reply to me and to send back to you whatever answer he wishes to give him. Then, as soon as you find a suitable bearer, have that reply delivered to me.

I wish you, dearest lover of my friends, always good health in Christ and that you remain mindful of me.

[Col. 0529C]

## LETTER XLVIII. TO N., BISHOP

To the holy and deservedly venerable lord N., most reverend [bishop], Eginhard, a sinner.

This priest, named N., earnestly asked me to intercede for him with you, so that you might deign to deal mercifully with him. As he himself asserts, he is in great poverty, especially now that the small benefice he had in Bavaria has been taken away from him and given to another.

Now he does not know what to do or how he ought to serve his lord, unless the lord Hl., through your intercession, deigns to give him some support for sustaining his present life. I wish you, mindful of me, always good health in the Lord, and I ask that you deign to commend my insignificance to the most pious emperor.

[Col. 0529D]

## LETTER XLIX. TO N., A NOBLEMAN AND HIS FRIEND

To my dearest brother and most faithful friend N., glorious nobleman, Eginhard sends eternal salvation in the Lord.

Because I have found your loyalty so well proven that I can have no doubt that in all the needs of myself and my people I should flee to the help of your charity, I have now sent to you, with this letter, these countrymen and dependents of mine, Am . . . . . and Theothoum, asking you to receive them affectionately, as is your custom, and to assist them in the needs they have made known to you, both with the lord Hl. Augustus and with his most pious father, so that they may have as great a confidence in you as I do.

I wish you always good health, best and dearest of friends.

[Col. 0530B]

## LETTER L. TO LOTHAIR

My lord, your most pious father, ordered that men from the monastery of N. should be our assistants and fellow workers in the construction of the basilica [Note: [Col. 0529D] The word “basilica” is missing from the manuscript, with no blank space.] of the blessed martyrs of Christ, Marcellinus and Peter, your patrons.

But, as it seems to me, they will do nothing concerning that work unless an order from your clemency reaches them, instructing them anew to assist us in the aforesaid work according to the arrangement of our lord and your father.

Therefore, in order to make the cause of the work mentioned above known to you, I have taken care to send these supplicatory letters of my humble self to your greatness. Through them I ask and humbly beg you, for the love and honor of Christ’s martyrs, your patrons, to deign to take care for the construction of their basilica, so that through your assistance it may be completed, and to send us to the bishops mentioned above your sacred command in letters of your most glorious authority, which they would not dare disregard.

Thus your reward before God may increase, and the blessed martyrs may intercede for you, so that your kingdom may always grow and be strengthened and remain safe and defended from the plots and attacks of evil spirits and malevolent men.

I wish and pray that my lord the king may be well and live forever.

[Col. 0530C]

## LETTER LI. TO THE SAME

On behalf of a certain friend and dependent of mine, N., namely, your faithful servant, I wish to beseech your piety to deign to receive him and, when he has commended himself into your hands, to give him some consolation from the benefices here in our neighborhood that are known to be vacant and available.

For he is a nobleman and a man of good faith, and he is also well educated, so as to serve most usefully in whatever business may be entrusted to him. He served your grandfather and father faithfully and energetically, and he is likewise prepared to serve you, if God is willing to grant him life and health.

For he is still very ill and therefore cannot come into your presence; he will come as soon as he can. Therefore I beg your piety to permit me to know what I may promise him from your goodness [Col. 0531A], so that he may live in good hope until he reaches your presence.

[Col. 0531A]

## LETTER LII. TO N., PRIEST, AND N., STEWARD

In the name of Christ, Eginhard, abbot, sends greetings in the Lord to N. the priest and N. the steward, our faithful men.

Let it be known to you that we wish you to have the gift-offerings (*eulogiae*) prepared according to custom, as a man usually prepares them for the service of his lord, both for the service of the lord Hl. and of N., his wife. When he has returned from the estate of Audriaca to Compiègne, we wish them then to be presented there. Afterward we wish you to inform us by a brief note how those gift-offerings . . . [Col. 0531B] had been received by him or by her. Farewell.

[Col. 0531B]

## LETTER LIII. TO A CERTAIN FAITHFUL SERVANT

In the name of Christ, Eginhard, abbot, sends greetings to that faithful servant of ours.

You know that, insofar as we were able, we took care to fulfill your wish in arranging for your daughter to be returned to you. Therefore we ask you, for the honor and love of Saint N. and of us, to consent to this: if we arrange for that man to obtain his freedom, permit him to take your daughter in marriage. For it seems better to us that she should again be married to that man, if he is made free, than that she should be rejected by everyone.

Farewell.

[Col. 0531C]

## LETTER LIV. TO N., ABBOT

In the name of Christ, Eginhard, humble abbot, sends eternal salvation in Christ to N., abbot, faithful and beloved.

I do not doubt that you remember how you entrusted both yourself and your people to me. Since matters stand as your own will has determined, it is henceforth my duty to provide you and yours, wherever it may be suitable, with worthy assistance in every way, insofar as knowledge and ability permit.

Therefore let your affection know that our vassal and your daughter desire, through marital love, to possess each other, with the Lord’s favor and your consent. For this reason I have decided to send you a message, making it known that, if it pleases you that the marriage take place, it seems suitable both to the mother and brother and to all the relatives.

Moreover, I do not merely wish the matter to be confirmed; if you give me the power to complete it, I wish to provide honorably and as quickly as possible whatever is suitable, both in benefices and in other matters.

Furthermore, the aforementioned vassal himself will provide the dowry and increase the gifts. The only thing remaining for this matter is either that you yourselves not delay coming in person to complete it, or that you grant permission for us to complete it.

For we know what we can accomplish at present, with the Lord’s favor; but we do not know what the coming day may bring. Therefore it is written: “Let not your hand cease, let not your foot cease, [Col. 0532A] but whatever you do.”

With these matters set forth, we ask you to strive to make us certain about this matter both through this messenger and through your letters.

Farewell.

[Col. 0532A]

## LETTER LV. TO N., BISHOP

To the deservedly venerable lord N. E.

Because of the shortage of ministers at the altar, necessity compels me to beg your holiness to deign to ordain this cleric, named N., to the order of the diaconate. He is suitable for this not only in age but also in learning.

Therefore we have sent him into the presence of your kindness, so that we may be worthy to receive him back from you consecrated to the aforesaid order.

I wish you always good health in Christ.

[Col. 0532B]

## LETTER LVI. TO THE EMPEROR

The authority of nearly all the ancients has judged that the novel and unusual rising of stars signifies to wretched mortals the arrival of things ill-fated and sad rather than joyful or prosperous. Only the sacred Scripture of the Gospel testifies that the appearance of a new star was salutary; it relates that the wise men of the Chaldeans saw it and, inferring from its brilliant radiance the recent birth of the eternal king, reverently offered gifts fitting for such majesty.

But the star that recently appeared is reported by all who testified that they had seen it to have had a dreadful and scarcely joyful appearance and to have burned threateningly. It made, as I think, omens appropriate to our deserts and indicated the calamity of which we are worthy. For what difference does it make whether the approaching wrath against the human race is announced by a human being or by a star?

This alone is necessary to understand: the appearance of the star was not pointless, but warned mortals to strive, by repenting and turning the Lord’s mercy toward themselves, to avert the danger that was to come. Thus, in Jonah’s preaching, the destruction of the city of Nineveh, which had been foretold to its people through him, was postponed by divine mercy.

And God . . . [lacuna; surviving “-turum” is uncertain] permitted through the prophet Jeremiah, when him into the potter’s house . . . . . [lacuna].

[Col. 0532C]

## LETTER LVII. TO COUNT N.

[Col. 0532D]

To the magnificent, honorable, and illustrious man N., glorious count, Eginhard sends eternal salvation in the Lord.

The lord emperor sent word through Dagolf the huntsman [that] Count N. should bring together in one place those counts who are in Austria—namely Hatto, Poppo, and Gebehard—and their other associates, so that they might consider among themselves what should be done if anything new had arisen in the region of Bavaria.

Then it seemed good to them that both you and Atto should be present at the same assembly. Therefore they ask you to consider and inform them at what place their conference seems most suitable to be held. For H. thinks that this could work well.

[Col. 0533A]

## LETTER LVIII. TO N., BISHOP

The letters of your most humble little dependents strive to present themselves before the eyes of the most excellent bishop, declaring their devotion, insofar as their ability permits, to be ready if the benevolence of your eminence does not disdain to give orders.

In every service to you and yours, both now and henceforth, whether they are situated near the clemency of your presence or appear wherever they may be, they have willingly professed themselves obedient to your honey-sweet commands.

Now, although they have deserved nothing, nevertheless trusting in the utterance of your promise, they do not hesitate to remind the piety of your charity.

May your blessedness remain in good health.

[Col. 0533A]

## LETTER LIX. TO THE EMPRESS’S CHIEF CHAPLAIN

To the honorable, exalted, and spirit-filled-with-wisdom . . . . . . . . . master and chief chaplain of the lady empress, your faithful little dependents, through this note of our insignificance, wish perpetual salvation to your blessedness.

May your goodness remember the matter about which we once spoke, so that, just as you encouraged us and generously promised, you may diligently arrange for it to be successfully fulfilled with the person whom you know. And inquire whether we should go to him or proceed in another direction, and deign quickly to send us word through a faithful messenger or through your letters.

Because of the great confidence we have in you, we have written to you so boldly about our need. We ask you also to deign to inform us about your well-being, because your health is our joy, and your joy is our gladness. This is what we hope, desire, and wish to hear: may it come to pass happily for many years.

Farewell now and always, most glorious man, in Christ Jesus and in all his saints. Amen.

[Col. 0533C]

## LETTER LX. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS LORD M.

[Col. 0533D]

To the illustrious man M., a lord of most noble eminence, V., and glorious: your most faithful and devoted little servants, ready in every respect to serve your excellence, approach you with faithful and desirable service.

We return the greatest thanks possible to the eminence of your highness, because, granting assent to our petition, you brought to completion the matter concerning the chapel established at the estate of Lens. Yet you sent [lacuna], who came to clothe us from that place; he would have done precisely as you ordered, had not the men of V., your brother, opposed it. Nevertheless, that place has been utterly devastated, so that no covering of the buildings at all remains there which has not been sold, alienated, or destroyed, except for the basilica, which has also partly collapsed.

For the sake of the reward owed to you, however, we had firmly resolved in our mind that whatever we could acquire in the present year we would spend on restoring the place; and we wish to do so, if he has so decided and decreed through the estate [lacuna]. Your messenger [lacuna] found nothing there, despite your labours, because everything had been destroyed, except the demesne tithe, which, on your instruction, he ordered to be preserved. Whether this should be so or not is entirely unknown to us.

We have therefore reported these matters to your eminence so that your highness may consider and determine how the place can be restored, and so that no danger may arise if a house dedicated to God is neglected and brought to ruin. Whatever, therefore, your excellence may wish concerning this matter, may you kindly make known to our smallness through your messenger. May Christ protect your eminence for a long time and likewise lead you to eternal life. Amen.

[Col. 0534A]

## LETTER LXI. TO THE SAME

To the foremost, distinguished, and excellent man of noble birth, N., W., and G., wholly devoted and dedicated to your eminence, we wish faithful obedience and service in all things.

Since your eminence wished to impose some service upon our lowliness, and since it has not yet been brought to completion, we make the reason known to your highness. The cleric of your brother A., whom at your command we received into A.’s service, took away with him the memorandum which you sent to our smallness, so that on our behalf he might offer your brother an explanation for the work of that same man remaining unfinished on account of your service. The measurements which you sent us were also taken away in that memorandum, and we have so far been entirely unable to find them.

Therefore send us those measurements, and we shall endeavor, as far as we are able, to carry out your service. We continually desire that your eminence may be well in the Lord.

[Col. 0534C]

## LETTER LXII. TO HLOTHAR

Although I firmly believe that my most pious lord always remembers his patrons, the most blessed martyrs of Christ Marcellinus and Peter, who, by the hidden judgment of God, left Rome and came into Francia for the exaltation and protection of your kingdom, and who, for some reason unknown to me, deigned to lodge with me, a sinner, I nevertheless have a great obligation frequently to remind you of matters pertaining to their honor, lest I incur danger and loss to my soul if I prove more negligent in giving that reminder than I ought. And although they are most merciful—even sparing their own executioner—I fear offending their king, our Lord Jesus Christ, for whose love they did not hesitate to die, if he should find me acting sluggishly in providing the honors appropriate to their worship.

Therefore, most pious lord, I humbly admonish and ask your excellence to deign to remember that exchange of the place in which the venerable bodies of the martyrs rest, which was made with Bishop Otgar, and to make that place their own, for the freeing of which you gave your own property to Saint Martin.

I also presume to remind your mercy of those petitions of mine which, when I was terrified by the approach of imminent death, I laid before you: that you might deign to give something from our benefices to support those who are to serve God beside the most sacred bodies of the holy martyrs, your most gentle patrons. At that time, by your most gracious promises, you gave me hope that I should not be defrauded of my desire—not only in this matter, but also in the matter of granting your mercy to those whom I had brought up for your service, and of assisting them from those same benefices.

I have the firmest confidence that by doing this you will merit both God and his saints, if you deign to make me attain my vow in this matter.
