I also ask you to deign to consider and weigh what reward awaits you with God, and how your praise will increase before the world, if through you and in your days the resting place of the holy martyrs is enlarged, adorned, and cultivated, both in its buildings and in its other necessities, so that its construction may also be attributed to your name, and so that both your memory and that of the martyrs may be celebrated by all peoples in perpetual remembrance.

Finally, I ask and earnestly beseech your great gentleness to deign to look mercifully and piously upon me, a wretched and sinful man, now old and very infirm; to have me released and freed from worldly cares; and to permit me to remain in peace and tranquility beside the tombs of the blessed martyrs of Christ—namely, your patrons—under your protection, in the service of those same saints and in the service of God and our Lord Jesus Christ. Thus that unavoidable and final day, which usually follows the age in which I now stand, may find me not occupied with passing and empty cares, but rather free for prayer and reading, and exercising my thoughts in meditation on the divine law.

[Col. 0535C]

## LETTER LXIII. TO HIS FRIEND LUPUS

Eginhard sends greetings to his Lupus.

All my occupations and all my cares, whether concerning my own affairs or those of my friends, have been removed and shaken from me by the grief which I suffered at the death first of my most faithful wife, and now of my dearest sister and companion. Nor does it seem capable of ending, since memory retains the nature of her extinction so tenaciously that it cannot be wholly torn away from it.

To this is added the fact that the grief itself repeatedly grows and festers the wound once received, because our vows were allowed to accomplish nothing, and the hope which we placed in the merits and intercession of the martyrs has utterly frustrated our expectation. Hence it happens that words of consolation, which usually heal the sorrow of others, instead make the wound in our heart break open and bleed afresh, when they order me to bear calmly the troubles of misfortune which they themselves do not feel, and think that I should rejoice in a situation in which they cannot show any trace of joy or gladness.

For what mortal is there who is of sound mind and sound judgment, who would not lament his fate and judge himself unhappy and most wretched when, placed in affliction, he finds turned away and inexorable the one whom he had believed would favor his prayers?

Do such things seem to you capable of stirring sighs and tears in so insignificant a little man, of driving him to groaning and lamentation, and even of casting him into the abyss of despair? They certainly would have done so, had I not, supported by the aid of divine mercy, immediately turned to investigate what our greater and better predecessors had decreed should be held and preserved in such causes and circumstances.

There were eminent teachers at hand—indeed, not merely teachers who should not be despised, but teachers whom all ought to hear and follow: the glorious martyr Cyprian, and the most illustrious interpreters of sacred and divine literature, Augustine and Jerome.

Encouraged by their judgments and most salutary counsels, I tried to raise upward the heart weighed down by deep sorrow. I began diligently to consider within myself what I ought to think about the death of my dearest companion, whose mortality I saw to have come to an end more than her life. I also tried, if I could, to compel myself to make reason produce within me what a long passage of time usually produces: namely, that the wound which a sudden disaster inflicted upon our spirit through an unexpected death might begin to form a scar and to heal through the medicine of voluntary consolation.

But the magnitude of the wound resists ease. And although the remedies offered by the teachers mentioned above for alleviating deep grief are most health-giving, as though offered by the most skilled and also most gentle physicians, the wound that still draws blood does not yet permit the time of healing.

Perhaps at this point you wonder and say that grief arising from such an occasion ought not to have been so long and enduring—as though it lay within the power of the grieving person to bring to an end what he had neither been able to control nor foresee when it began.

The magnitude or duration of grief, however, seems capable of being measured by the extent of the losses that have occurred. Since I feel these losses horribly every day—in every action, every undertaking, the entire administration of the household and family, and in arranging and ordering everything pertaining either to divine or human duty—how can it happen that a wound which has caused so many and such great troubles, whenever it is repeatedly touched, does not break open and renew itself rather than heal or become firm?

For I believe—and I do not fear that this opinion will prove false in my case—that this grief and anxiety, which arose in me from the death of my dearest companion, will remain with me forever, until the span of time which God may grant me for this wretched and temporal life reaches its appointed end.

Yet so far I find it more beneficial than harmful, since it restrains and holds back the spirit hastening toward joys and prosperity, as though with certain bridles and reins, and recalls my mind to the remembrance of death—whereas hatred of old age and forgetfulness had drawn it toward hope in and love of long life.

I see that not much time remains for me to live, although I entirely do not know how much that may be. But this I hold as absolutely certain: one who has only recently been born can quickly die, and an old man cannot live long. Therefore I judge it far more useful and blessed to pass the brief span of uncertain time in mourning than in joy. For if, according to the Lord’s word, those who lament and mourn will be blessed and happy (Matthew V, 5), then, conversely, those who do not fear to end their days in perpetual and unbroken joy will become unhappy and wretched.

[Col. 0538A]

I give and offer thanks to your affection because you have deigned to console me through your letters. For you could not have given a greater or more certain sign of your love toward me than by extending the hand of encouragement to one who was sick and lying prostrate, and by admonishing me to rise—one whom you could not fail to know was cast down in mind and weighed down by grief.

Farewell in good health, dearest and most longed-for son.

[Col. 0537A]

# EGINHARD’S HISTORY OF THE TRANSLATION OF THE BLESSED MARTYRS OF CHRIST, MARCELLINUS AND PETER

*(Acta Sanctorum of the Bollandists, volume I, June)*

[Col. 0537B]

## PROLOGUE

### 1

Eginhard, a sinner, to the true worshipers of the true God and the sincere lovers of Jesus Christ our Lord and his saints.

Those who committed to writing and memory the lives and deeds of the righteous, and of people who lived according to the divine commandments, seem to me to have intended nothing other than to stir the minds of all people, through such examples, toward correcting corrupt morals and praising the omnipotence of God. They did this not only because they were free from envy, but because they abounded greatly in charity, which desires that all should be cared for.

Since their praiseworthy purpose is so evident that it is perfectly clear, apart from what I have said, that they intended no other undertaking, I do not at all see why many should not imitate them. Therefore, because I am conscious that the books which I have composed, to the best of my ability, concerning the translation of the bodies of the blessed martyrs of Christ Marcellinus and Peter, and concerning the signs and miracles which the Lord willed to perform through them for the salvation of believers, have been written with the same will and intention, I have resolved to publish them and offer them for reading to the lovers of God.

For I believe that this work ought not to appear to any of the faithful merely empty and superfluous; rather, I presume that I shall have labored fruitfully and usefully if I can bring it about that the mind of the reader rises in praise of its Creator.

[Col. 0537C]

## CHAPTER ONE

### Envoys sent by Eginhard to Rome to obtain relics. The relics of Saints Marcellinus and Peter obtained

[Col. 0537D]

### 2

While I was still living at the palace and occupied with worldly affairs, I was reflecting with many thoughts upon the leisure which I longed eventually to enjoy. I obtained a certain secluded place, very far removed from the crowds, through the generosity of the prince whom I was then serving, Hludowic.

This place lies in the forest of Germania, situated between the rivers Neckar and Main. In modern times it is called by the inhabitants and surrounding peoples Odanwald.

[Note: The manuscript has *Hodanuhuald*; elsewhere, *Odonowald*.]

There, according to the extent of my means and expenditures, I built not only houses and dwellings for living in, but also a basilica suitable for the celebration of divine offices, constructed with work that was not unbecoming. I began to wonder in whose name and honor, above all, it ought to be dedicated—whether to which saint or martyr.

When much time had passed amid this uncertainty of mind, it happened that a certain deacon of the Roman Church, named Deusdona, came to the palace to seek the king’s assistance in his own affairs. After staying there for some time, when he was preparing to return to Rome, having completed the business for which he had come, we invited him one day, as a matter of courtesy and as though he were a pilgrim, to dine with our humble household.

While dining, we discussed many matters, and our conversation eventually reached the subject of the translation of the body of the blessed Sebastian and of the neglected tombs of the martyrs, of which there is a great abundance at Rome.

[Note: The translation had not yet taken place; it was still to be requested.]

From there the conversation turned to the dedication of our new basilica. I began to ask how I might obtain some of the genuine relics of the saints who rest at Rome.

At first he hesitated and replied that he did not know how this could be done. Then, when he noticed that I was both concerned and curious about the matter, he promised that he would answer my question on the following day.

[Col. 0538D]

### 3

After this, when I had again invited him, he immediately handed me a little book from his bosom, asking me to read it alone and not to disdain telling him what I thought of what was written in it.

I received the book and, as he requested, read it privately by myself. It contained the following: he had a great many relics of saints at home, and he wished to give them to me if, supported by my assistance, he could return to Rome. He knew that I had two mules, and that if I gave him one of them and sent with him one of my faithful men to receive those relics from him and bring them to me, he would immediately send them to me.

[Manuscript: *esse* (“to be”) occurs in the phrase “he would immediately send them to me.”]

I approved the proposal of the man who was advising me and decided to put the promise, whose reliability was uncertain, to the test without delay. Accordingly, after giving him the animal he requested and adding money for his journey, I ordered my notary, named Ratleicus—who himself had a vow to go to Rome for the sake of prayer—to travel with him.

Thus they departed from the palace at Aachen—for the emperor and his retinue were there at that time—and came to Augusta Suessionum.

[Note: Surius has *Augusta Suessorum*, by which name it is also called in Fortunatus, *Life of Saint Medard*, 8 June, no. 36.]

There they spoke with Abbot Hildoinus at the monastery of Saint Medard, because the deacon mentioned above had promised him that he could arrange for the body of the blessed martyr Tiburtius to come into his possession.

Attracted by these promises, Hildoinus sent with them a certain priest, a clever man named Hunus, ordering him to bring back to him the body of the aforementioned martyr once he had received it from the deacon. From there they set out and proceeded toward Rome with all possible speed.

[Note: Hilduinus became abbot in 817, but was driven into exile in 830, recalled in 833, and died and was buried in the abbey of Saint Medard in 842. He was also abbot of Saint Denis and Saint Germain at Paris.]

### 4

After they had entered Italy, it happened that my notary’s boy, named Reginbaldus, was seized by a tertian fever and caused no small hindrance to their journey through his suffering. During the hours when he was held by the heat of the fever, they were unable to travel. They were few in number and therefore did not wish to separate from one another.

Although this inconvenience had considerably delayed their journey, they nevertheless tried to hasten it as much as they could. Three days before they reached the City, a man in the dress of a deacon appeared in a vision to the boy suffering from the fever and asked him why his master was hastening to go to Rome.

When the boy explained to him, as far as he knew them, both the deacon’s promises to send me the relics of the saints and the things he had promised Abbot Hildoinus, the man said:

“It will not happen that way, but quite otherwise. The outcome of the matters on account of which you have come will be fulfilled. For this deacon, who asked you to come to Rome, will do little or nothing of what he promised you. Therefore I want you to follow me and to attend carefully, with an anxious mind, to what I shall show and tell you.”

### 5

Then, taking him by the hand, as it seemed to him, he made him climb with him to the summit of a very high mountain. When they were standing there together, he said:

“Turn toward the east and look upon the fields lying beneath your eyes.”

When he had done so and looked upon the fields of which the man had spoken, he saw in them structures of immense size, built in the form of a great city. When the man asked him whether he knew what this was, he replied that he did not know.

Then the man said:

“It is Rome, which you see.”

Immediately he added:

“Direct your eyes into the inner parts of the city, and observe whether some church appears to you in those places.”

[Manuscript: *ulteriora*, “the farther parts,” instead of *interiora*, “the inner parts.”]

When he said that a certain church had appeared to him:

[Note: [Col. 0540D] Baronius maintains, under the year 826, no. 16, that this was the church of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, built by Constantine the Great, and visible from afar because of its breadth and height.]

the man said:

“Go and tell Ratleicus that in the church which you have just seen there is hidden the object which he must bring to his master. Therefore let him take care to receive it as quickly as possible and return to his master.”

When the boy said that none of those who had come with him would believe what he said about such a matter, the man replied:

“You know that all who are making this journey with you are aware that you have suffered from a tertian fever for many days and have not yet had any remission from it.”

And he replied:

“It is as you say.”

“Therefore,” said the man, “I want this to serve as a sign for you and for those to whom you will report the words I have spoken: from this hour, by God’s mercy, you will be free from the fever which has held you until now, so that it will not affect you again on this journey.”

After these words the boy awoke and took care to report to Ratleicus everything which he seemed to have seen or heard. When he had related it to the priest traveling with him, both of them thought that they should test the dream (*somni*; manuscript *somnii*) by the truth of the promised recovery. For, according to the pattern of the fevers from which he had usually suffered, the one who had seen the dream ought to have become feverish that same day.

To show that this had been not an empty delusion but rather a true revelation, he felt no sign of his usual fever either that day or on any of the days that followed it. Thus they believed the vision, but did not trust the deacon’s promises.

### 6

Accordingly, when they reached Rome, they obtained lodging beside the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter called *ad Vincula*, in the house of the deacon with whom they had come. They stayed with him for several days, awaiting the fulfillment of his promises.

But since he was unable to fulfill his promises, he concealed his inability beneath various delays. At last they spoke with him and asked why he wished to deceive them in this way, while also begging him not to detain them any longer by deceiving them and to avoid hindering their return with empty hopes.

When he heard this, and realized that by such cunning he could no longer impose upon them, he first informed my notary that he could not possess the relics promised to me. His brother, to whom he had entrusted both his house and everything he possessed when he departed, had gone to Beneventum for the sake of trade; he himself did not know at all when his brother would return. Since he had entrusted the relics to him for safekeeping, just as he had entrusted his other belongings, he could not possibly know what had become of them, because he had found them nowhere in the same house. Therefore, Ratleicus should consider what he would do, since nothing remained on the deacon’s part which he could hope for.

After he had said this to my notary, and Ratleicus complained that he had been deceived and badly misled by him, the deacon addressed Hildoinus’s priest as well with certain empty and frivolous excuses. Having inspired him with a similar hope, he made him withdraw.

The next day, however, when he saw them very sad, he urged them to go with him to the cemeteries of the saints. He thought that something of the kind might be found there to satisfy their wishes, and that there would be no need for them to return empty-handed to their homeland.

They liked this proposal and wanted to begin as quickly as possible what he was urging them to do. But, following his usual practice, he postponed the undertaking and, by this delay, cast those whose spirits had then been somewhat raised into such despair that they abandoned him and resolved to return to their homeland, even though the matter had not been accomplished.

### 7

My notary, however, recalling the dream which his boy had seen, began to urge his companion to go without their host to the cemeteries which the deacon had promised to show them.

Accordingly, after finding and hiring a guide and local informant, they first came to the basilica of the blessed martyr Tiburtius on the Via Labicana, three miles from the City. They examined the martyr’s tomb with as much care as possible and cautiously considered whether it might be opened in such a way that others would not notice.

Then they descended into the crypt adjoining the same basilica, in which the bodies of the blessed martyrs of Christ Marcellinus and Peter had been buried. After examining the character of that monument as well, they departed, thinking that their host might remain unaware of what they had done.

But events turned out differently from what they had supposed. Although they themselves did not know by what indications, information about the deed soon reached their host. Fearing that they might satisfy their wishes without him, he resolved (*consilio*; manuscript *consilium*) to forestall them by hastening ahead.

Since he had complete and thorough knowledge of those places, he addressed them kindly and urged them to go there together. If God deigned to favor their prayers, he said, they could, by common counsel, do whatever seemed necessary.

### 8

They agreed to his proposal and, with mutual consent, fixed a time for undertaking it. After completing a three-day fast, they reached the place by night, without any Roman citizen knowing.

Having entered the basilica of Saint Tiburtius, they first tried to open the altar beneath which his sacred body was believed to lie. But their effort met with little success: the monument, built of extremely hard marble, easily repelled the unarmed hands of those trying to open it.

Therefore, abandoning the tomb of that martyr, they descended to the tomb of the blessed Marcellinus and Peter. There they invoked our Lord Jesus Christ and worshiped the holy martyrs, then attempted to lift from its place the stone covering the top of the tomb.

When it had been lifted, they saw the most sacred body of Saint Marcellinus lying in the upper part of the same tomb. A marble tablet placed at his head, bearing an inscription, gave clear evidence of which martyr’s limbs had lain in that place.

They received the body with the utmost veneration, as was fitting, lifted it, wrapped it in a clean shroud, and handed it over to the deacon to carry and preserve. To ensure that no indication of the removed body remained, they replaced the stone in its place and returned to their lodgings in the City.

The deacon affirmed that he wished and was able to preserve the body of the most blessed martyr beside the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter called *ad Vincula*, where he also had a house. He entrusted it to his brother, named Luniso, for safekeeping. Thinking that this satisfied my notary, he began to urge him to return to his homeland with the body of the blessed Marcellinus.

[Col. 0542B]

### 9

But my notary was meditating upon and turning over in his mind something quite different. As he later told me, it seemed to him that he was by no means permitted to return to his homeland with only the body of the blessed Marcellinus—as though it were a sacrilege for the body of the blessed martyr Peter, who had shared his companion’s passion and had rested with him in the same tomb for more than five hundred years, to remain there while Marcellinus departed.

Once this thought had taken shape in his mind, he suffered such labor and disturbance of spirit that he found neither eating nor sleeping sweet or pleasant unless the bodies of the martyrs, just as they had been joined in passion and in the tomb, should also be joined in setting out abroad.

But he was greatly uncertain how this could be done. He knew that he could find no Roman who would offer him any assistance for such a matter, nor even anyone to whom he would dare disclose this secret of his mind.

While he was in this anxiety of heart, he encountered a foreign monk named Basil, who had come to Rome from Constantinople two years earlier. On the Palatine Hill he was lodging among other Greeks of the same profession, together with his four disciples.

The notary approached him and disclosed to him the concern from which he was suffering. Encouraged by his counsels and relying upon his prayers, he received such firmness of heart that he resolved to attempt the matter as quickly as possible, even at the risk of his life.

He summoned his companion, Hildoinus’s priest, and began to discuss with him the possibility of secretly returning to the basilica of the blessed Tiburtius, as they had done before, and again attempting to open the tomb in which the martyr’s body was believed to be enclosed.

### 10

The proposal was approved. Taking with them the boys whom they had brought, they secretly set out by night, while their host had no knowledge of where they were going.

When they reached the place, they made prayers before the door of the church for a favorable outcome, then entered. Dividing their companions among themselves, the priest remained in the basilica with some of them to search for the body of the blessed Tiburtius, while Ratleicus approached the body of the blessed Peter in the crypt attached to the same church.

He opened the tomb without any difficulty and, with no one preventing him, removed the sacred limbs of the holy martyr. He carefully enclosed them in a silk cushion which he had prepared for this purpose.

Meanwhile, the priest who was searching for the body of the blessed Tiburtius, after expending great effort in vain, saw that he could make no progress. He abandoned the work, descended into the crypt to Ratleicus, and began to ask him what should be done.

Ratleicus said that he thought the relics of Saint Tiburtius had been found, and showed him the object of which he was speaking. Shortly before the priest had come down to him in the crypt, Ratleicus had found, in the same tomb in which the sacred bodies of Marcellinus and Peter had lain, a hole of rounded shape, excavated inward to a length of approximately three feet and open to a width of one foot. A considerable quantity of fine dust had been placed in it.

It seemed to both of them that this dust might have remained from the body of the blessed Tiburtius after his bones had been removed, and that, to make it more difficult to find, it had been placed midway between the blessed Marcellinus and Peter in the same tomb.

They therefore agreed that the priest should take it and carry it with him as the relics of the blessed Tiburtius.

### 11

After these matters had been completed and arranged, they returned to their lodgings with the objects they had found.

Afterward Ratleicus spoke with his host and asked him to return the sacred ashes of the blessed Marcellinus, which he had entrusted to him for safekeeping, and not to detain him any longer than necessity required, since he wished to return to his homeland.

The host not only returned without delay what Ratleicus had requested, but also offered him a considerable portion of the relics of the saints, collected in a single bundle, to be brought to me. When asked their names, he replied that he would tell me when he came to me.

He nevertheless warned me to venerate them with the same devotion with which the other relics of the holy martyrs were venerated, because they were no less worthy in God’s sight than the blessed Marcellinus and Peter. He said that I would believe this as soon as knowledge of their names reached me.

Ratleicus accepted the offered gift and, as he was convinced, joined it to the bodies of the holy martyrs.

[Col. 0543C]

## CHAPTER TWO

### The sacred relics carried through various places to Michilinstadt, and, after various visions, to Mulinheim, later called Seligenstadt

[Col. 0543D]

### 12

After taking counsel with his host, he had that sacred and desirable treasure, stored and sealed in chests, transported as far as Pavia by Luniso, his brother, whom we mentioned above, and by Hildoinus’s priest, who had come with him.

He himself remained in Rome with his host, waiting and listening continuously for seven days to learn whether anything concerning the removal of the bodies of the saints had come to the knowledge of the citizens.

When he saw that no outsider mentioned the deed at all, he concluded that it remained concealed. He then set out after those whom he had sent ahead, taking his host with him.

When they found them at Ticinum, beside the basilica of the blessed John the Baptist, which is commonly called Domnana and at that time belonged to my authority through a royal benefice, they decided to remain there for several days, both for the recovery of the animals on which they had traveled and to prepare themselves for the longer journey.

[Note: The printed text has *Donnarum*, or *Dominarum*. For there were two churches of Saint John the Baptist at Pavia, one of which was magnificently built and endowed by Queen Theodelinda. Bernardus Scaccus discusses it in *History of Ticinum*, book IX, chapter 5; Stephanus Breventanus, book III, chapter 2, says that it was also called by the name “Burgus,” because it stood outside the first circuit of the walls, or perhaps “Palude.” It had, however, another ancient name. For Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book IV, chapter 49, speaking of Queen Gundiberga, Theodelinda’s daughter, says: “Following the example of her mother—just as her mother did at Modicia, so she built within the city of Ticinum a basilica in honor of the blessed John the Baptist.” Scaccus adds in book IX, chapter 9, that she “named it in honor of her sex, Domnarum—that is, of women.” How and when this church was given to the monks, and thus came under Eginhard’s jurisdiction, I leave to the people of Ticinum to investigate. In the meantime, Scaccus rightly corrects Platina, who in his *Life of John IV* assigned that church to Terracina and drew Sabellicus into the same error, although no occasion for it appears anywhere.]

### 13

While they were thus delaying, a report went abroad that envoys of the holy Roman Church had been sent by the pontiff to the emperor [Note: The author of the *Deeds of Louis the Pious*, under the year 826, mentions this embassy and says that it was heard at Ingelheim on the Kalends of June. Those who carried it out were Leo, bishop of Centumcellae, and Theophylact, the *nomenclator*, on behalf of Pope Eugene II at that time.], and that they would soon arrive. Fearing, therefore, that their arrival might cause them some difficulty or even obstruction if the envoys found them there, they decided that some of their number should depart and, by hastening their journey, forestall the envoys [Manuscript: “outstrip”]; while the others should remain where they were and, after carefully investigating the matter that concerned them, hasten to follow their companions whom they had sent ahead once the same envoys had departed.

When this arrangement had been agreed upon among them, Deusdona, together with Hildoin’s priest, went ahead of the envoys coming from Rome and hastened with all possible speed to Augusta Suessionum, where he supposed Hildoin to be. Ratleicus, however, remained at Pavia with the treasure he had with him, waiting until the envoys of the Apostolic See had passed by, so that, once they had crossed the Alps, he might pursue his journey more safely.

Fearing, therefore, that Hildoin’s priest—who had gone ahead with Deusdona and possessed full and exact knowledge of everything that had been done or discussed among them, and who seemed cunning and untrustworthy—might contrive some obstacle for him on the road he had decided to take, Ratleicus judged that he should travel by another route. He sent to me a servant of our procurator Ascolf, bearing a letter in which he assured me both of his return and of the delivery of the treasure that, with divine assistance [Col. 0544D], he had obtained.

Then, after he had inferred from the lodging arrangements being prepared for the Romans that they had crossed the Alps, he left Pavia and on the sixth day came to [Note: He means Agaunum, where Saint Maurice was crowned with martyrdom together with the Theban Legion and gave his name to the place, as will be said on 22 September. It is a place in Savoy on the Rhône, about nine leagues from Sion of the Helvetians, which lies east of it.] Saint Maurice.

There, having obtained what seemed necessary for the purpose, he placed those sacred bodies, enclosed in a small coffin, upon a bier. Then he proceeded from there and began to carry them openly and publicly, with the assistance of the people who came to meet him.

### 14

When he had passed the place called Caput-Laci [Note: Lake Leman, or Lake Geneva, begins at the town of Neuville; perhaps the place is called here by a changed form of that name. It lies five leagues below Saint Maurice.] and reached a fork in the road [Note: I suppose this fork to have been not far beyond the lake, where the roads leading into France diverge; I would gladly receive more precise information from those familiar with the region], he entered the right-hand road and came through the territory of the Alamanni as far as Solodorum [Note: At this time Solodorum, or Solodurum, is a city of the Swiss Confederates, whose entire territory was formerly divided between the Alamanni and the Burgundians, so that the latter’s portion was also called Lesser Burgundy. Solodorum lies more than forty leagues north of the town of Saint Maurice.], a Burgundian town.

There he encountered those whom, after I had been informed of his arrival, I had ordered to go out from Trajectum to meet him [Note: Trajectum on the Meuse below Liège is meant]. At that time I was near the River Scheldt, in the monastery of Saint Bavo [Note: The monastery of Saint Bavo was in the city of Ghent, on the site where the castle now stands. Eginhard held both this abbey and the nearby abbey of Saint Peter on Mount Blandinium, and he mentions both in his letters.], when a letter from my notary was delivered to me by the servant of our procurator whom I mentioned above.

After reading it and being informed of the arrival of the saints, I immediately ordered one of our household to go to Trajectum, take with him priests and other clerics as well as laymen, and hasten to meet the approaching saints wherever he could first do so.

He lost no time. With those whom he had brought with him, he met, after a few days, the men who were carrying the saints at the place mentioned. They joined together, and, accompanied by choirs of people singing hymns who were now assembling from every direction, they came swiftly, amid the immense joy of all, to the city of Argentoratum, now called Strasbourg [Note: The journey from Solodorum to Strasbourg, a city situated on the Rhine and the metropolis of Alsace, is reckoned at about fifty leagues.].

From there they sailed downstream on the Rhine. When they had reached a place called the Port [Note: This appears to have been a harbor found somewhat below the confluence of the Neckar and the Rhine—that is, below Mannheim, from which the marked place is about eight leagues distant. The “stations” mentioned here are what the Germans call *Rast*, places of rest, situated about an hour and a half from one another and furnished with supports, about four feet above the ground, for the convenience of those carrying burdens.], they disembarked on the eastern bank of the river [Manuscript adds: “in”]. On the fifth station they reached a place called Michilinstadt [Note: Michelstadt, or Michelstad, in the present county of Erbach], amid an immense multitude of people exulting in the praises of God.

That place lies in the German forest which in modern times is called Odanwald [Note: Today, the Odenwald], about six leagues from the River Main. Since they found there a basilica newly built by me but not yet dedicated, they carried the sacred remains into it and deposited them as though they were destined to remain there forever.

### 15

When this had been reported to me, I immediately hastened there with all possible speed [Note: After covering a journey of about 120 leagues—the distance from Ghent, where Eginhard then was, to Michelstadt—so that, if the relics were brought there in October, Ratleicus may be believed to have arrived in November or even December.].

After three days had elapsed since our arrival, one of Ratleicus’s servants, at his command, remained alone in the church after the office of vespers had been completed and the others had gone out. Having closed the doors, he withdrew beside the sacred bodies into a small cell, as though to keep vigil there. Overcome by sudden sleep, he seemed to see two doves fly in through the window on the right side of the apse and settle on the ridge of the bed directly above the bodies of the saints. One was entirely white; the other appeared to have a varied mixture of gray and white.

As they walked about on the ridge for some time and uttered in turn the customary cooing of doves, as though conversing with one another, they went out again through the same window and disappeared. Then a voice sounded above the boy’s head:

“Go,” it said, “and tell Ratleicus to inform his master that these holy Martyrs do not wish their bodies to rest in this place. They have chosen another, and intend to migrate there quickly.”

The boy could not see who had spoken these words. When the voice had ceased, he awoke, and, roused from sleep, returned to the basilica. When Ratleicus came back, he told him what he had seen.

The next day, as soon as he could meet me, Ratleicus took care to report what his servant had related to him. Although I did not dare to disregard the mystery of this vision, I nevertheless decided to await some more certain sign. Meanwhile I had those sacred remains removed from the cloths in which they had arrived wrapped and sewn into silks and new cushions.

When I examined them and observed that the relics of blessed Marcellinus were smaller in quantity than those of Saint Peter, I supposed that Marcellinus had been smaller in bodily stature than Saint Peter. But the truth, later revealed, proved that the matter was otherwise: where, when, by whom, and in what manner the theft was committed and disclosed, I shall relate in its proper place. For now, the sequence of the narrative already begun must be continued and maintained.

### 16

After I had inspected that great and marvelous treasure, more precious than all gold, the small coffin in which it was contained began greatly to displease me because of the poor quality of the material from which it had been made. Wishing to improve it, one day, after the evening office had been completed, I ordered one of the church attendants to bring me the measurement of the coffin, taken with a rod.

As he was lighting a candle in order to do this and lifting the hanging cloths with which the coffin was covered, he noticed that the coffin was dripping everywhere with a liquid resembling blood. Terrified by the novelty of the sight, he hastened to report to me what he had seen.

I then went with the priests who were present and looked upon that astonishing miracle, worthy of every wonder. Just as marble columns, capitals, or images tend to sweat and stream when rain is imminent, so that coffin, which contained the most sacred bodies, was found wet with real blood and covered with it on every side.

The unprecedented and previously unheard-of nature of the miracle terrified us. Therefore, after taking counsel, we decided to observe a three-day fast [Col. 0547B] with supplications, so that through divine revelation we might be worthy to learn what that great and ineffable portent meant and what it urged us to do.

When the three-day fast had been completed and evening was approaching, that dreadful bloody liquid suddenly began to dry. In a marvelous manner, although it had dripped continuously for seven full days without interruption like a perpetual stream of water, within a very few hours it became so completely dry that, at the hour of night—for it was Sunday—when we entered the church at the appointed signal to celebrate the office before dawn, no trace of it could be found on the coffin.

I ordered the linens hanging around the coffin—sprinkled with the same liquid and stained as they were with blood-colored marks—to be preserved [Manuscript adds: “and” after *ut* (“as”)]. They still display a great indication of that unheard-of portent [Col. 0547C]. It is certain that the liquid had a slightly salty taste, like that of tears, and the thinness of water, but the color of true blood.

### 17

That same night, one of our servants named Ruodland dreamed that two young men had appeared before him. As he himself testified, they entrusted him with many things to tell me about transferring the bodies of the saints, and showed him to what place and in what manner this should be done. They also commanded him, with terrible threats, to report it to me without delay.

As soon as he was able to approach me, he took care to tell me everything he had been ordered to report. When I heard this, I began to be consumed by immense anxiety and to consider in my mind what I ought to do: whether fasts and supplications should again be celebrated and God once more troubled on account of our curiosity; or whether we should seek someone who served God devoutly and perfectly, to whom we could disclose the anxiety of our hearts and the complaints of our cares, and ask him to obtain from God through his prayers a revelation of this matter for us.

But where or when could such a servant of Christ be found by us, especially in that region? Although it was known that certain monasteries were situated not far from the place where we were, because the discipline of monastic life was still in its infancy in those areas, there was either rarely or never anyone of whose holiness even the faintest report was heard.

Meanwhile, while I was distressed by these anxieties and imploring the assistance of the holy martyrs, and while I earnestly urged all who were with us to do the same, it happened that for consecutive days [Manuscript adds: “twelve”] no night passed without one, two, or even three of our companions receiving in dreams the revelation that the bodies of the saints had to be transferred from that place to another.

Finally, one of the priests who were with us, named Hildfrid, saw in a vision—as he himself confessed—a certain man dressed as a priest, distinguished by venerable gray hair and clothed in a white garment. He addressed him in these words:

“Why,” he said, “is Eginhard so hard-hearted and so obstinate that he does not believe so many revelations and thinks that so many warnings sent to him by God should be disregarded? Go and tell him that what the blessed martyrs desire to be done with their bodies cannot remain undone.

“Although until now he has delayed doing their will in this matter, even now, if he does not wish the merit of this deed to pass to another, let him hasten to fulfill their command and not neglect to carry their bodies to the place they themselves have chosen.”

### 18

After these and many other varied warnings had been reported to me, it seemed that the transfer of the sacred remains should no longer be delayed. Accordingly, after taking counsel, we resolved to strive to complete it as quickly as possible.

We therefore hastily and with the utmost diligence prepared everything that seemed necessary for transporting them. At first light, after the morning office had been completed, we lifted that sacred and priceless treasure and began to carry it on our journey, amid the great grief and sorrow of those who were to remain behind at the place.

A crowd of poor people accompanied us; during those days they had flocked there from every direction to receive alms. The people living nearby were completely unaware of what was happening among us.

The sky was heavy with filthy clouds, which could quickly have dissolved into an immense rainfall had divine power not prevented it. Indeed, throughout that night it had rained so continuously that it seemed altogether impossible for us to begin our journey that day.

But heavenly grace, acting through the merits of its saints, brought about our doubt—which arose from weakness of faith—in a way very different from what we had expected. We saw that the road on which we traveled had been changed into a condition different from what had been expected: we found little mud, and the streams, which ordinarily would have risen greatly in such heavy and continuous rain as had fallen that night, had scarcely risen at all.

When we had left the forest and approached the nearest villages, we were welcomed by frequent crowds of people who came out to meet us and sing praises to God. They accompanied us for nearly eight leagues and, devotedly assisting us and our companions in carrying the sacred burden, eagerly joined us in singing the divine praises.

### 19

When we saw that we could not reach the appointed place that day, we turned aside to a village called Ostheim [Note: Ostheim is recorded at the edge of the Ottenwald forest, about three leagues before reaching Seligenstadt], which lay beside our road. As evening was already approaching, we carried those holy bodies into the basilica of Saint Martin, which is in the same village.

I left our companions there to keep watch, while I went ahead with a few others, hastening toward the place to which we were heading. During the night I prepared everything required for receiving the saints.

At the basilica in which we had left their most sacred treasure, a paralyzed religious woman named Ruodlang from the monastery of Makesbah—which was separated from that church by a distance of one league—was brought by her friends and relatives in a cart. While she spent the night keeping vigil and praying among the others beside the saints’ bier, she recovered the health of all her limbs. The next day she returned to the place from which she had come, walking on her own feet, without anyone supporting her or assisting her in any way.

### 20

At dawn we rose and went out to meet our companions as they approached. With us was an immense multitude of our neighbors, who had been stirred by the report of the saints’ arrival and had assembled outside our doors at first light so that they might go with us to meet them.

We encountered them at the place where the little stream called the Gaspentia flows into the Main [Note: Certainly somewhere between Seligenstadt and Aschaffenburg, although the topographical maps indicate no stream there, still less one called Gaspentia].

Proceeding together from there and praising the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, we carried the sacred remains of the most blessed Martyrs to Upper Mulinheim—which is what that place is called in modern times [Note: Mulinheim is Seligenstadt]—amid the great joy and rejoicing of all who were able to be present.

But because of the excessive multitude of people, which had filled everything ahead of us, we could neither approach the church nor carry the bier into it. We therefore erected an altar in the adjacent field, in a somewhat elevated place, under the open sky. After placing the bier behind the altar, we celebrated the solemnities of Mass.

When these had been completed and the multitude had returned to their homes, we carried the sacred bodies into the church chosen for them by the blessed Martyrs. We placed the bier beside the altar and arranged for Mass to be celebrated again.

During that celebration, a boy of about fifteen years, named Daniel, from the district of Portianus, who had come there begging among the other poor, approached the bier. He was so bent over that he could not look at the sky except while lying on his back. Suddenly, as though pushed by someone, he fell.

After he had lain there for a long time as though asleep, all his limbs were restored and his nerves regained their strength. He rose sound before our eyes.

These things occurred on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February [Note: That is, on the feast of Saint Anthony, which in that year, 827, fell on a Thursday]. The sky was so clear and bright that day that its brilliance equaled the splendor of the summer sun. The air itself was so mild and pleasantly tranquil that its gentle warmth anticipated the temperate serenity of spring.

### 21

The next day we placed the sacred bodies of the blessed Martyrs in a new coffin and set it in the apse of the basilica. As is customary in France, we covered it with a wooden canopy and draped it with linen and silken cloths for adornment. We added an altar and erected on either side the two banners of the Lord’s Passion that had usually preceded the bier on the journey.

We took care, according to the measure of our poverty, to make the place suitable and appropriate for the celebration of the divine offices. We appointed clerics [Note: Mabillon thinks that Eginhard here means monks by the term “clerics”; or, he says, one must conclude that clerics were first established there and monks afterward. The latter conjecture seems more genuine to me. It was not so easy immediately to found a monastery as to appoint several clerics to serve there in the meantime. Nevertheless, Mabillon infers from Eginhard’s fourth letter that the monastery was established while Eginhard was still alive. In that letter a certain Werdricus, a monk of Fulda, is said to have lived at Seligenstadt with the permission of his abbot; such permission would scarcely have been granted if the place had then had no monks.] to keep continual vigils there and to devote themselves diligently to the singing of the divine praises.

We ourselves, summoned not only at our own initiative but also by a royal diploma that had met us on the road, returned to the palace [Note: The palace at Aachen is meant, where Emperor Louis the Pious was then residing] with great rejoicing.

## CHAPTER III

### Some relics of Saint Marcellinus, formerly removed, are recovered and transferred to other places. Miracles performed.

### 22

Only a very few days had passed since I had come to the court [Note: Baronius judged that these events occurred in the year 827 and reported them accordingly. “County” here means the imperial court, which, as I have said, was then residing at Aachen] when, rising early in the morning according to the custom of courtiers, I went to the palace.

When I entered, I found Hildoin—the man whom I mentioned in the preceding book—sitting before the door of the imperial bedchamber and waiting for the prince to come out. I greeted him in the customary manner, asked him to rise, and invited him to accompany me to a certain window from which there was a view over the lower part of the palace.

Standing side by side and leaning against the window, we spoke at length about the translation of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, as well as about the miracle displayed when their coffin dripped with blood, as I have related, for seven days.

As our conversation reached the point where we also mentioned the garments found with their bodies, I said that Saint Marcellinus had been clothed in a garment of remarkable fineness. Hildoin, as though he knew the matter as well as I did, replied that I had spoken truthfully about the garments.

I was astonished and began to ask how he could have acquired knowledge of garments he had never seen. He looked at me, remained silent for a little while, and then said:

“I think it better that you should learn from me what, even if I remain silent, you will soon learn through others, and that I should be the simple betrayer of this matter, rather than that someone else should reveal it and perhaps not state it simply. For it is naturally impossible for anyone to report truthfully something of which he has learned not through personal knowledge but through the report of others.

“I entrust only to your discretion how you will deal with me after you have learned from my account the whole truth of what happened.”

### 23

I briefly replied that I would do nothing to him except what we should agree between ourselves. Then he said:

“The priest who went to Rome at my command to bring back the relics of Saint Tiburtius was unable to accomplish as he wished the purpose for which he had gone there. Meanwhile, your notary, having received the relics of the holy martyrs about which we are speaking, had decided to return home.

“The priest therefore made an arrangement with him: while your notary remained in Rome for a short time, the priest would go ahead as far as Pavia with Junizo [Note: Here the name is written Junizo four times, continuing through section 25, where Lunizo occurs again], the brother of Deusdona, and with his men, who were to carry the sacred remains. He would wait there for the arrival of the notary and Deusdona.

“Both agreed to this plan. While they remained in Rome [Manuscript: ‘while they stayed behind’], the priest set out for Pavia with Lunizo and the servants carrying the relics.

“When they arrived there, the chests containing the sacred remains were placed in your church before the altar and carefully guarded by the clerics and laymen keeping watch in the same basilica.

“One night, when he himself was keeping watch in the church among the others, it happened—as he claims—around midnight that, as sleep gradually overcame them, everyone who had assembled inside the basilica to keep vigil fell asleep except him.

“Then it occurred to him, or seemed to occur to him, that it could not have happened without some significant reason that so many people had been overtaken by such sudden sleep. Thinking that he should take advantage of the opportunity, he rose, lit a lamp, and silently approached the chests.

“He burned through the threads attached to the seals by applying the flame of the candle. He quickly opened the chests without a key and took from each body the portion that seemed appropriate to him. Then he fastened the seals, which remained intact, to the ends of the burned threads and returned to his place, without anyone perceiving what he had done.

“After stealing the relics of the saints in this manner, he returned to me and brought them. At first he insisted that they were not the relics of Saint Marcellinus or Saint Peter but of Saint Tiburtius. Then, when he became apprehensive for some reason, he spoke with me privately and openly revealed whose relics they were and how he had obtained them.

“We have placed them honorably at Saint Medard in a celebrated shrine, where they are venerated by all the people with great devotion. But whether we may retain them lies within your discretion.”

### 24

When I heard this, I remembered what I had heard from one of my hosts while I was recently traveling to the palace. Among other things he had said to me:

“Do you know what report about the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter has spread throughout this region?”

When I replied that I did not, he said:

“Those who come from Saint Sebastian [Note: That is, from the monastery and church of Saint Medard, where the relics of Saint Sebastian had been deposited; similarly below, in section 87, someone is said to have been led to Saint Sebastian] say that a certain priest of Abbot Hildoin, who traveled to Rome together with your notary, on their return—when they were staying together in a common lodging—opened the chests containing the bodies of the saints while all your men were overcome by drunkenness and sleep and completely unaware of what was happening.

“He removed the bodies, carried them away, and delivered them to Hildoin, and they are now at Saint Medard. Only a small amount of sacred dust remained in your chests, and this was brought to you by your notary.”

As I recalled this and compared it with what Hildoin had told me, I was deeply disturbed. This was especially because I had not yet found a plan by which I could extinguish that detestable report, spread everywhere by the devil’s cunning, and drive it from the hearts of the deceived multitude.

Nevertheless, I judged it best to ask Hildoin to return to me the very thing that he could not deny had been taken from my chests, delivered to him, and received by him after his spontaneous confession.

I pursued this request with all possible insistence. Although he was somewhat more obstinate and reluctant to agree than I had hoped, he was nevertheless overcome by my persistent pleas and yielded to my importunity, even though shortly before he had declared that, especially in this matter, he would yield to no one’s command.

### 25

Meanwhile, I sent letters to Ratleicus and Lunizo—they were at the place where I had deposited the bodies of the Martyrs—and informed them what sort of report about those same holy martyrs was circulating throughout almost all Gaul. I urged them to consider whether they could observe or recall anything like, or resembling, what Hildoin alleged had been done by his priest during their journey.

They immediately came to me at the palace and brought a story very different from Hildoin’s account. First of all, they testified that everything the priest had reported to Hildoin was false. After they had left Rome, they had given neither that priest nor anyone else any opportunity by which he could have gained access to commit such a crime.

They said, however, that the fact that something had happened to the sacred remains of the Martyrs otherwise than it should have occurred had taken place at Rome, in Deusdona’s house, through the greed of Lunizo and the cunning of the priest mentioned above. This was at the time when the body of Saint Marcellinus, removed from its tomb, was being kept in Deusdona’s house. They described the manner of the deed as follows.

The priest of Hildoin mentioned above, frustrated in the hope he had conceived of obtaining the body of Saint Tiburtius, resolved not to return to his master completely empty-handed and to secure by fraud what he could not obtain honestly.

He approached Lunizo, whom he knew to be poor and therefore covetous. By offering him four gold coins and five silver solidi, he enticed him into committing the betrayal.

After accepting the money that had been offered, Lunizo opened the chest in which Deusdona had placed and enclosed the body of Saint Marcellinus, and gave that most wicked scoundrel permission to take from it whatever he wished, in whatever quantity he desired.

Nor was the priest sparing in this robbery. He removed from the sacred remains of the blessed Martyr as much as a vessel holding a sextarius seemed capable of containing.

Lunizo himself, who had contrived this with the priest mentioned above, fell at my feet and testified through tears that it had been done in this manner.

### 26

When I had learned the truth of the matter, I ordered Ratleicus and Lunizo to return to the place from which they had come.

Then, after speaking with Hildoin and reaching an agreement with him about the time when the sacred relics would be returned to me, I ordered two clerics from our household—Hiltfrid and Filimar, one a priest and the other a subdeacon [Note: Some call him a deacon]—to go to Augusta Suessionum [Note: Surius has “Suessorum”] to receive them.

Through them I sent one hundred gold coins to the place from which the relics were to be taken, as an offering of blessing.

When they arrived at the monastery of Saint Medard on Palm Sunday [Note: Therefore 14 April, since Easter in that year, 827, was to be celebrated on the 21st], they remained there for three days. After receiving the incomparable treasure for which they had been sent, they returned to the palace with all possible speed, accompanied by two brothers from the same monastery.

They did not, however, bring the relics to me but to Hildoin. After receiving them, he had them guarded in the oratory of his house until, once the business of the Easter festival had passed, he had leisure to show me what was to be returned before actually returning it.

When eight days or more had elapsed after Holy Easter, the king went out from the palace to hunt. Hildoin, in accordance with our agreement, removed the relics from his oratory, where they had been kept, carried them into the basilica of the holy Mother of God, and placed them upon the altar. He then had me summoned to receive them.

Opening the chest in which the relics were contained, he showed it to me so that I might see what he was returning and what I was receiving.

### 27

Then he lifted the same chest from the altar and placed it in my hands. After offering the appropriate prayer and also performing the duties of precentor, he assigned to the clerics prepared to sing an antiphon suited to the praise of the Martyrs.

As we departed with that priceless treasure, he accompanied us with singing as far as the door of the basilica.

From there we proceeded slowly with crosses and candles, praising the mercy of the Lord, until we reached the oratory in our house, which was built with humble workmanship. Since no other place was available there, we carried the sacred relics into it.

I think I should not remain silent about the miracle that occurred during this procession, which, as I have said, we made from the basilica to our oratory.

As we were leaving the church and singing praise to our Lord God in a loud voice, such a powerful and exceedingly sweet fragrance filled that part of the village of Aachen which lies west of the church that almost all the inhabitants of that quarter, as well as everyone who happened to be there for any reason or business, were divinely moved.

Abandoning the tasks they had in hand, they all hurried at the fastest possible pace—first to the church, and then, as though following its trail, to our oratory, where they had heard that the relics had been carried.

An immense crowd of rejoicing and astonished people gathered within our enclosure. Although many of those who had assembled did not know what was happening, they were nevertheless filled with joy and exultation and joined in praising the mercy of almighty God.

### 28

After the report became increasingly widespread that the relics of the martyr Saint Marcellinus had been brought to that place, a crowd so large and so overwhelming gathered not only from the same village of Aachen and from the neighboring and adjacent villages, but also from more distant places and districts, that it was scarcely possible for us to enter the oratory to celebrate the office there, except during the evening and night hours.

The sick and the infirm, afflicted with various illnesses, were brought from every direction and placed by their relatives and friends around the walls of the oratory.

There one could see almost every kind of illness being cured, through the power of Christ the Lord and through the merits of the most blessed Martyr, in people of every sex and age.

Sight was restored to the blind, walking to the lame, hearing to the deaf, and speech to the mute. Paralytics and those deprived of the strength of their entire bodies, who had been carried there on the hands of others, recovered their health and returned home on their own feet [Note: Some of the miracles are reported below in full in Chapter Six].

29. When these things had been reported to the royal ears through Hildoinus, he first decided that, after returning to the palace, he would approach our oratory, where these events had occurred, in order to venerate the martyr. But, at Hildoinus’s urging, he was prevented from doing so and ordered the relics to be carried to the larger basilica; when they had been brought there, he venerated them with humble supplication. After the solemn celebration of Mass, he offered to the blessed martyrs Marcellinus [Col. 0554D] and Peter a certain small estate situated beside the river Ara, called Ludovesdorf [Note: [Col. 0553D] Surius reads *Ludovestropf*. The river Ara, which rises beside it in the Duchy of Jülich, enters the diocese of Cologne through the Eifel and flows into the Rhine between Cologne and Confluentia, at the town of Zunichium.], comprising fifteen *mansi* and nine *aripennes* of vineyards. The queen likewise offered her belt, made of gold and gems, weighing three pounds.

When these offerings had been completed, the relics were brought back to their place, namely our oratory, and remained there for forty days or more [Note: [Col. 0554D] Thus, until the end of May or the beginning of June.], until the emperor, leaving the palace, customarily sought the forests for hunting. After this had happened, and we had prepared whatever seemed necessary for our departure, we set out from the village of Aachen with those same relics.

At the very moment of our departure, while the solemn Mass was being celebrated, an old woman, very well known at the palace and about eighty years of age, who suffered from contracted tendons, was cured in our presence. As we learned from her own account, she had been afflicted with this illness for fifty years and had performed the function of walking by crawling on hands and knees, like a four-footed animal.

30. We then set out on the journey and, with the merits of the saints assisting us, reached on the sixteenth day [Ms.: “on the sixth day at last”] the village of Mulinheim, where, with the Lord’s help, we had left the sacred ashes of the blessed martyrs when we departed for the court [Col. 0555B]. I must not remain silent about how much joy and gladness came to the peoples settled along that road at the arrival of those relics; yet it cannot be fully described or expressed as it actually was. Still, it must be told, lest something of such great importance for the praise of God appear to have been suppressed through negligence.

First of all, my mind eagerly recalls what we remember seeing after leaving the palace, in the presence of many people. There is said to be a small river called the Vurmius [Note: [Col. 0555D] Commonly called Worm, rising not far above the city and flowing into the Rur near Hensberg. Mabillon, I do not know through what error, reads *Wimiobum* and places the village of Mulinheim near it, contrary to the explicit sense of this passage.], with a bridge about two miles from the palace of Aachen. When we came to it, we stopped there briefly, because of the crowd that had followed us from the palace as far as that point and was already wishing to return, so that it might have a place for prayer.

There one of the people praying approached the relics with another man and, looking at his companion, said: “For the love and honor of this saint, I release you from the debt for which, as you know, you are bound to me.” For, as he himself admitted, the other owed him half a pound of silver.

Likewise, another man took his companion by the hand and drew him toward the relics, saying: “You killed my father, and therefore we were enemies toward one another. But now, for the love and honor of God and of this saint, I wish, having laid aside our hostility, to establish and enter into a covenant with you, so that henceforth perpetual friendship may remain between us. Let this saint be witness to the love agreed upon between us, and let him avenge the one who first attempts to violate this peace!”

31. Here that crowd which had left the palace with us, after worshiping and kissing the sacred relics, returned home with many tears, which it could not restrain because of its excessive joy. Another crowd, which had come to meet us there, accompanied us, singing *Kyrie eleison* without interruption until we reached the place where we were similarly received by others coming to meet us. These people, after making a supplication in the same manner as the first group, likewise returned home.

In this way, on each successive day, from first light until evening, accompanied by crowds of people who praised the Lord Christ [Col. 0556A], we proceeded from the palace of Aachen to the aforementioned village of Mulinheim, with the Lord prospering our journey. There we placed the relics on the altar, behind which stood the small shrine containing the sacred ashes of the martyrs, having enclosed them in a jeweled reliquary.

They remained placed there until, in the month of November, as we were preparing to go to the palace, we were warned through a revelation that we should not depart from that place before joining them to the body from which they had been taken. How it was revealed that this ought to be done must not be passed over in silence, because it was shown not only in a dream, as usually happens, but also through certain signs and terrors belonging to the vigilance of waking persons: the blessed martyrs had in every respect wished their command in this matter to be fulfilled [Col. 0556B].

32. There was one of the clerics assigned to keep watch over the basilica, named Landolphus. At that time he had been entrusted with the duty of striking the signal, and his bed stood beside the southern door of the basilica. When, according to the custom of the nocturnal and morning office, he rose in the customary manner and moved the signal, and, after completing that office before dawn, wished to sleep again, he closed the church doors and prostrated himself before the sacred ashes of the martyrs in order to pray.

There, when he began to recite the fiftieth psalm, as he himself states, he heard near him on the pavement what sounded like the footsteps of a man walking back and forth in that place. Terrified with no small fear, he raised himself slightly onto his knees and began to look around in every direction [Col. 0556C], thinking that one of the poor people, with the church doors closed, might have hidden in some corner.

When he saw that there was no one else inside the walls of the basilica but himself, he again bent down to pray and repeated the psalm he had begun earlier. But before he could complete even one of its verses, the reliquary placed upon the altar, which contained the sacred relics of the blessed Marcellinus, suddenly made such a violent cracking sound that it seemed to have burst apart as if struck by a hammer.

The basilica’s two doors, which were already closed—the western and the southern—also made a similar sound, as though someone were striking and pushing against them.

33. Terrified and astonished by these things, and utterly unaware of what he ought to do, he rose from the altar [Col. 0556D] and threw himself in fear upon his bed. Suddenly overcome by sleep, he saw a man of unfamiliar appearance standing before him, addressing him in these words:

“Is it certain,” he said, “that Eginhard wishes to hasten to the palace in such a way that he will not first return the relics of Saint Marcellinus, which he brought here, to the place from which they had been taken?”

When Landolphus replied that he knew nothing about this matter, the man said: “Rise at first light, and, by the authority of the Martyrs, command him not to presume to leave here or go anywhere before he restores those relics to their proper place.”

He awoke, rose, and, as soon as he was able to meet me [Col. 0557A], took care to report to me what he had been commanded. I, however, did not think that anything in such a matter should be done sluggishly; rather, I judged that what had been commanded must be fulfilled without inserting any delay. Accordingly, I ordered whatever seemed necessary for this to be prepared that very day. On the following day I took care, with the greatest diligence, to unite those sacred relics to the body from which they had been taken.

How pleasing this action was to the most blessed martyrs is clearly demonstrated by the miracle that followed. For on the following night, when we were solemnly seated in the basilica for the morning office, an old man deprived of the use of his legs, crawling on knees and hands, entered to pray. In the presence of all of us, through the power of God and the merits of the most blessed martyrs [Col. 0557B], he was so perfectly cured at the very hour at which he had entered that he no longer needed even the support of a staff in order to walk. He also affirmed that he had been deaf for five continuous years and that his hearing had been restored at the same time as the use of his feet.

When these things had been accomplished, I departed for the court, as I had reported above that I intended to do, in order to spend the winter there, pondering many matters within myself.

[Col. 0557B]

## CHAPTER IV

Miracles performed at Mulinheim among the deaf and mute, the contracted, and other sick persons. — Beer changed into wine. — A candle lit of its own accord.

34. I am about to write of the powers and miracles which the most blessed martyrs of Christ, Marcellinus and Peter, performed in various places after their most sacred bodies had been brought from Rome to Francia—or rather, of those works which the King of Martyrs, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, deigned to perform for the salvation of human beings through their blessed merits and devout prayers. I have judged it necessary to touch briefly in a preface upon the fact that most of what I intend to write reached my knowledge through the reports of others.

Nevertheless, my confidence in these reports has been so firmly established by what I myself saw and recognized while present that, without any hesitation, I believed the things reported by those who testified that they had seen them to be true, even though until then I had had little or no acquaintance with the persons from whom I heard these accounts.

In any case, the first things that seem to require writing are those performed and seen by me in the place to which those most blessed martyrs ordered their most sacred ashes to be transferred [Col. 0557D]. Next will come those reported to have occurred in the palace at Aachen, before the very eyes of the courtiers. Then I have judged that we should set down those events reported to have occurred in the various places to which, at the request of religious men and with my permission, their sacred relics were carried. By preserving this order in the account, nothing will remain omitted from all the signs and miracles that could come to the knowledge of our littleness.

But now that the preface has been completed, let us bring forward the miracles themselves that must be told.

[Col. 0558A]

35. After the sacred bodies of the most blessed martyrs, as has already been demonstrated above, had been brought—at their command and with our compliance—to the place where they now rest, amid the immense rejoicing of the faithful peoples, and after the solemn Mass had been celebrated in the field, they were carried into the basilica by the hands of the priests, of whom a considerable number had then gathered there. The bier on which they had been carried was placed beside the altar, and another office began to be celebrated there.

Suddenly a certain young man, afflicted with a loosening of the loins and therefore bent over and leaning on staffs, burst from the middle of the surrounding crowd. Wishing to bend down in worship, he fell upon his knees; but, in a wondrous manner, as though someone were tearing him away—or rather pulling him backward [Col. 0558B]—he fell onto his back and lay for a very long time like someone asleep.

Then, as if awakening, he raised himself into a sitting position. A little later, without anyone supporting him, he rose. Standing in the midst of the crowd gathered around him, he joined the others in giving thanks for his restored health and praising God’s mercy.

When we questioned him, he told us that he had come there from the district of Portianus [Note: [Col. 0557D] We have already read of this above, in no. 20; but we are still investigating which place the district of Portianus was.], together with other poor people and pilgrims, and that he was called Daniel.

At almost the same hour, indeed at the same moment, so to speak, at which the man just mentioned obtained health inside the church and before the very altar through the power of Christ and the intercession of the martyrs, a certain paralytic woman, deprived of the use of almost all her limbs, lay before the church doors and called upon the holy martyrs for help.

Immediately, in the sight of all who stood nearby, she began to be shaken with convulsions, as though nauseated, and then vomited and expelled a great quantity of phlegm and bile [Col. 0558C]. After this, she took a little cold water, asked to be lifted from the place where she lay, and, leaning on a staff, entered the basilica. After worshiping the martyrs and regaining strength in her limbs, she returned home.

36. Meanwhile, a man named Vuillibertus, who had a house not far from the basilica where the bodies of the blessed martyrs now rest, approached the bier among the others who had gathered to offer veneration to the saints and presented, as though as a gift, forty denarii.

When we asked him who he was and what he intended by this offering, he reported that a few days earlier he had been seized by a very serious illness and brought to the point of death, so that everyone who saw him had given up hope for him and advised him quickly to distribute all his possessions for the remedy of his soul. He said that he had done so.

After he had arranged for everything he possessed to be given to pious places, one of his servants complained with a great groan that they had acted wrongly and very negligently in failing to give anything from his goods to the saints who had recently come from Rome.

Then he asked those standing around whether they knew of anything belonging to him that still remained and could be sent to the martyrs. [Col. 0559A] At that time they were still at Michilinstadt, and it had not yet become famous through any signs that they were to depart from there.

Someone then replied that, since only one pig remained of all his possessions and no recipient had been designated to whom it should be given, it had pleased him to order that it be sold and that, after his death, its price be sent for the martyrs’ lamps.

When these words had been spoken, he stated that he had felt such a sudden cure that immediately, with all pain driven away, he even desired to eat. After taking food, he recovered so quickly that by the next day he could go about quite comfortably attending to or performing whatever work the needs of his household required.

Afterward, that pig was sold, and this was its price, which he was offering by vow to the blessed martyrs [Col. 0559B].

37. As for the remaining powers and miracles which the Lord performed through them for the salvation of human beings, since I see no importance in the order in which they are told, I have judged that they should be described as they come to mind. In reporting them, one must consider more what happened and why than when something happened.

After the relics of the blessed martyrs had been solemnly placed in the same basilica, and the sacred solemnities of Mass were celebrated daily according to the custom established by the Church, it happened one day, while the divine service was being performed and we were stationed in the upper parts of the same church, looking down upon the people below, that a certain half-naked cleric who had come to the same service with the others and was standing in the middle of the crowd suddenly collapsed in so violent a fall that he lay for a very long time on the pavement, like a dead man [Col. 0559C].

When some of those standing nearby tried to lift and raise him as he snored, such a quantity of blood burst from his mouth and nostrils that the entire front of his body—that is, his chest and belly, down to the garment covering his groin—was drenched by the outpouring.

After water had been brought and he had been revived, he recovered his strength and spoke clearly. Later, when we questioned him, he testified that from childhood until the present he had been unable either to hear anything or to speak.

He said that his homeland was Britain and that he was English by birth. He had undertaken the journey in order to visit his mother, who was living as a pilgrim in Rome, and had thus arrived at that place among the other pilgrims who wished to travel together to Rome. But when his companions departed, he had remained behind. The day on which he was cured, he said, was the seventh since he had come to that place.

When we asked his name, he replied that he knew his name not at all, because from the time when he had become deaf he had never heard his own name.

38. Several days later, when we had gathered in the church for the evening office according to custom, a certain deaf and mute girl was brought there. Her father and brother had led her through many holy places in search of healing and had finally brought her to that place from the district of the Bituriges [Note: [Col. 0559D] Namely, in Aquitania Prima, to which the fame of the miracles had reached.]. They made her stand with the others in the same church.
