Suddenly, as though seized by a kind of madness, she shook with all her strength the boards whose noise she used when begging for alms and, in a frenzy, threw them into the crowd standing before her. Then she ran to the church’s left wall and, as though intending to climb it, leaped upward three feet or more, fell backward, and lay there for a while more like a dead person than someone asleep. Since she was almost entirely spattered with blood pouring excessively from her mouth and nostrils, those standing nearby lifted her and carried her into the middle of the basilica.

After she had lain there for some time, she sat up as though awakening from deep sleep. Then she stretched out her hands to those standing nearby and begged with whatever gestures she could make that she be raised to her feet.

Once she had been raised, she was led to the altar. There, when she saw Ratleicus standing among the other clerics near the altar and looking at her, she immediately burst out with these words:

“You are Ratleicus,” she said; “you are called by this name; you are the servant of these saints.”

When he asked her how she knew this, or who had told her his name, she replied:

“These saints who rest here, when I was lying as though asleep, came to me and put their fingers into my ears and said to me: ‘When you rise and approach the altar, know that the young cleric whom you will see standing before you and looking at you is called Ratleicus, and he is our servant [Col. 0560C], for he is the one who brought our bodies to this place.’”

And so it truly was. For he was the very man whom, as we recorded in the first book, we had sent to Rome to receive the relics of the saints from a certain deacon and bring them to us.

In this manner, before us, through the power of the most blessed martyrs, the spirit of illness having been driven away, she obtained complete bodily health. Her father and brother, who had brought her there, testified that she had always been deaf and mute from the time of her birth.

39. I myself did not see the miracle that I am now about to recount. But I can believe the words of those through whose report it became known to me no less than if I had seen it with my own eyes. Therefore I have decided to present it without hesitation and without any doubt, not merely as something heard, but rather as something seen by me personally [Col. 0560D].

Certain merchants from the city of Mainz, who used to buy grain in the upper regions of Germany [Note: [Col. 0560D] Namely, from the margraviate of Kulmbach, the bishopric of Bamberg, and the neighboring regions of Bohemia.] and transport it down the river Main to the city, took aboard their ship, at his own request, a certain blind man of Aquitanian birth named Albricus, so that he might earn a reward from God, and brought him to the basilica of the blessed martyrs.

When he had disembarked there and been received as a guest in the house of the church’s custodian, he remained there for seven days or more. In addition to his blindness—which, since he lacked eyes, already appeared to be congenital—he had a horrible and loathsome illness affecting his entire body.

All his limbs trembled violently, shaking him with such severe distress that he was completely unable to bring food to his mouth with his own hands.

One day, while lying in his lodging during the morning hours, he fell asleep. In his sleep he saw someone standing beside him and urging him to rise quickly and hurry to the church, saying that the time had come when, through the power of the saints, he was to be freed from that wretched affliction.

He awoke and was led to the church, where he sat before the doors on a certain stone. The divine office was then being celebrated in the church according to custom. After the prayers that ordinarily precede the reading of the Gospel had been completed, the Gospel itself began to be read.

When scarcely two verses had been completed [Col. 0561B], behold, suddenly, as though suffering some violent force, the trembling man cried out: “Help me, Saint Marcellinus!”

Although all who were in the church were greatly disturbed by this cry, most of them remained in place out of reverence for the Gospel reading. Nevertheless, many ran to see what had caused the outcry. They found him, as they later testified, lying in the place where he had been sitting, stretched out on his back, with his chin and chest flooded by blood flowing from his nostrils.

When they raised him and revived him with a little cold water, he reported that, at the moment when he had uttered that cry, he had seemed to himself to have been struck in the neck by someone’s fist, and that for this reason he had invoked the help of the blessed martyr.

It is certain, however, that this blow was so beneficial to him that from that moment onward no trace of that loathsome trembling ever again appeared in his body.

He afterward remained in the same place for nearly two years. As he himself testified, during that two-year period there was no night in which he did not see in a dream the same martyrs who had saved him. He also heard many things from them, which he was ordered to tell others. Of these, we now see that most of what he then predicted would happen is being fulfilled.

40. A few days later we saw another man afflicted with a similar illness cured in the same basilica, through the merits of those same saints, in a similar manner [Col. 0561D].

One night, when we were seated in the church to celebrate the morning office and hear the readings from divine law, a man in clerical dress entered. His limbs trembled, and, leaning on a staff, he could scarcely guide his staggering steps.

When he bent down beside the wall to pray, he let out a great cry, suddenly fell headfirst, and, after a brief interval, rose cured of the affliction by which he had been held.

When we asked him whether he had seen anything besides what we had all been able to observe at the hour when he received his healing, he said that shortly before entering the basilica he had come to the old church, which lay a short distance west of the new basilica where the martyrs were then resting [Col. 0562A], in order to pray. Finding it closed, he had prayed before its doors.

Then, after rising and beginning to go toward the church, he saw a cleric of venerable gray hair, dressed in a white stole, walking ahead of him in the direction in which he too wished to go. As he himself states, he followed him all the way to the door of the basilica.

When the two of them arrived there, the one who was walking ahead stopped and pressed himself against the left doorpost, as though he wished the other—whom he had shortly before preceded—to enter first. When the man hesitated, the cleric nodded and ordered him to enter before him.

After the man had entered and bent down to pray, the cleric stood behind him, struck him in the neck with his fist, and knocked him down; then he immediately vanished. No one else, however, was able to see him except the man who had been healed.

[Col. 0562B]

41. At almost the same time, one night when we rose and were going to the church, we found before the church doors a certain boy lying in the portico, so miserably contracted that his chin touched his knees.

He asked one of those following us to carry him into the church. Moved by compassion, the man lifted him and laid him in the church beside the chancel screen.

Immediately overcome by sleep, the boy fell asleep where he had been laid. He did not fully awaken until, through the saints’ intercession, he had been so perfectly cured of that wretched contraction that, upon waking, he rose by himself from the place to which someone else had carried him and approached the altar to give thanks to God.

When day had broken and we were able to speak with him, he reported that, three times before the church signal had sounded, he had been awakened by an unknown cleric and admonished not to fail in coming to the church at the time of the morning office [Col. 0562C]. He said that he had done so and afterward, as we had seen, recovered the complete health of his body while sleeping in the church.

He appeared to be about fifteen years old.

42. We likewise saw another man—not a boy, as this one had been, but very old and decrepit—afflicted with the same illness and cured in the same place, in a similar manner and at a similar time.

One night, when we had come to the church doors to celebrate the morning office, we found him on the very threshold. Leaning on his knees, he supported himself with two staffs and, by this extremely slow movement, delayed our entry.

When we stood behind him and waited for his sluggish advance, such a fragrance of the sweetest odor came forth from the basilica and filled our nostrils that, in its excellence, it surpassed the skillful composition of all perfumes and incense.

At last he entered and fell down before us beside the chancel screen, as though to sleep. We too entered the basilica, took our places, and, together with the others, sang the psalms that were being recited in the customary manner.

When the first reading began, we heard the old man groaning and imploring help as though he were suffering violence. Then, after a short interval, we saw him raise himself into a sitting position and immediately, taking up the staffs with which he had been accustomed to guide his walking [Col. 0563A], stand on his feet.

We saw these things ourselves. He, however, stated that it had seemed to him that two men had seized him as he lay there: one by the shoulders and [Ms.: “and”] arms, the other by the thighs and feet, and that, by pulling him, they had stretched out the tendons that had been contracted [Ms.: “in this way”].

Since, besides the affliction of contraction, he also claimed to have been deaf, he said that, when he had been raised into a sitting position, something like the blow of a fist striking his head with great force had come upon him [Ms.: “had come from above”]. At the same time, he heard a voice commanding that he should hear in the future.

This old man, thus healed, testified that he had come from the district of the Helvetii, now called Aragaovin [Note: [Col. 0563D] Now Argow, the district so called from the river Ara flowing through it; it occupies, as it were, the center of all Helvetia and is subject to the people of Lucerne.], and that he was Alamannian by birth.

43. Another man, weakened in a similar manner by contraction of the tendons [Col. 0563B], who said that he had come from the village of Liège, where Saint Lambert rests in body [Note: [Col. 0564D] Saint Lambert, bishop of Maastricht, is commemorated on 17 September.], fell onto the pavement before all who were present on a certain Sunday night, after the morning office had been completed and we had already returned from the church.

At that time, because of those who had come from far away and were hurrying to return home, a priest was customarily celebrating the sacrament of the saving host. The man lay there for a short while as though asleep; then, as if awakened from sleep, he rose without anyone lifting him.

When one of those standing nearby picked up the staffs which he had previously used and which, when he fell, had slipped from his hands and lay some distance away, and offered them to him, he refused, saying: “Far be it from me ever to touch them again.”

This man too, healed in this manner, returned to his homeland, from which he had reached the threshold of the martyrs by crawling rather than walking.

44. Not long afterward, when in the month of November I was preparing to go to the court, as was customary, in order to spend the winter at the palace, I had already begun the journey. After crossing the Rhine, I came to the royal estate called Sinciacus [Note: [Col. 0564D] Sinciacus, commonly Zinsich, a town in the diocese of Cologne, four leagues above Bonn.] to spend the night.

After supper, which had occupied part of the night, I withdrew with my attendants into the privacy of the chamber where I was to rest. The servant who usually brought us drink entered hurriedly, as though about to announce something new.

When I looked at him, I said: “What do you wish to report? For, as I see, you have something you want to bring to our knowledge [Col. 0563D].”

Then he said: “Two signs have just taken place before us, and I have come to report them to you.”

When I ordered him to say whatever he wished, he continued:

“Just now, when you rose from supper and entered this chamber, I went down with my companions into the cellar beneath this dining room. When we began distributing beer to the servants who were asking for it, a boy sent by one of our fellow servants arrived, carrying a flask, which he asked us to fill.

“When it had been filled, he also asked that he be given a little of the same beer to drink. It was given to him in a vessel that by chance had been placed empty above the barrel in which the beer was stored. But when he brought it to his mouth to drink, he cried out with great astonishment that this was wine, not beer.

“When the man who had filled the flask—and who had drawn the very drink given to the boy through the same opening—began to accuse him of lying, the boy said: ‘Take it and taste it; then you will prove that I have spoken not falsely but truly.’

“The man took and tasted it, and likewise testified that it tasted of wine, not beer. Then a third and a fourth man, and the others who were present, tasted it one by one, astonished, and drank all that had been in the vessel. Everyone who tasted it testified that it had the flavor of pure wine, not beer.”

[Col. 0564B]

45. While they were stunned with astonishment at this sign, it happened that the candle whose light they were using there, and which was then burning fastened to the wall beside the barrel, fell onto the pavement wet with moisture without anyone touching it. It was extinguished so completely that not even the smallest spark remained in it.

One of them seized it and ran to the door. But, overcome by the horror of the darkness, before going out he stood on the threshold and said: “Holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, help us!”

At this invocation, the candle which he held in his hand was lit.

When I heard this, I immediately gave praise and thanks, as was fitting, to almighty God, who always and everywhere glorifies his saints and who had deigned to make us, his servants, joyful through such great powers, while we then had their sacred relics with us [Col. 0564C].

After the man who had reported these things to me had finished his account, I ordered him to withdraw to his lodging. When I had placed myself on my bed to rest, I began to turn many matters over in my mind and to wonder what that change of beer into wine— that is, the transformation of an inferior drink into a better one—might signify or foreshadow.

I also wondered why such a miracle had occurred in that place, namely in the royal residence, and not rather in the place where the most sacred bodies of the blessed martyrs who had performed these wonders through the power of Christ were deposited.

Although, through long and anxious thought, I was unable to arrive at a certain investigation of this question, I nevertheless held, and shall always hold, as certain that the divine and heavenly power through which these and other miracles of this kind are believed to occur never does anything, or permits anything to be done, without a reason among creatures whom I do not doubt belong to its providence and governance.

[Col. 0564D]

## CHAPTER V

Other miracles performed at Mulinheim: the deaf and mute, paralytics, and the mad healed. — Light granted to travelers by night. — A booklet presented to the emperor.

46. Accordingly, having departed from there, as I said above, I proceeded to the assembly [Col. 0565A]. For at that time Emperor Louis, residing at the palace of Aachen, had ordered a gathering of the nobles to be held there in the middle of winter [Note: [Col. 0565D] Einhard, in the *Annals of the Deeds of Louis the Pious*, states that an assembly was held at Aachen in February of the year 828.]. I too was ordered to be present among the others; and because I was compelled to be away from the vicinity of the blessed martyrs, I spent a not very pleasant stay at the palace. Therefore, after a month had elapsed since I had gone there, I sent one of our men, named Ellenhard, instructing him to hasten with all possible speed to the shrine of the blessed martyrs. After visiting our brothers whom, when departing, I had left there to perform divine service, and carefully investigating everything that was being done there, he was to return quickly to us.

When he had arrived there, he remained for three days. On the fourth day, when he was already preparing to return to us, that blind man named Albricus, whom we mentioned earlier [Note: [Col. 0565D] See above, no. 39.], detained him as he was preparing to leave. He insisted that Ellenhard would not begin his journey until he had seen a certain sign, the report of which would make me glad and exceedingly joyful. He also added that the most blessed martyrs had appeared to him in a dream during the preceding night and had instructed him to seek out a certain poor man named Gisalbert, weighed down by an enormous hump and consequently bent over and supported by short sticks; and, once he had been found, to place him in the upper room above the basilica’s portico at the time of the morning office, beside the relics that were there. For there, through the merits and power of the saints whose relics they were, he was to be freed from the deformity of his hump and the affliction of his curvature [Col. 0565C].

The man obeyed the advice and postponed until the following day the journey he had been preparing to undertake. The blind man, meanwhile, searched for the poor man as he had been ordered and found him; and, as he had been instructed, he placed him in the upper part of the church beside the aforesaid relics at the time of the morning office.

Those relics, as we did not yet know [Note: [Col. 0565D] We discussed these matters at length under 19 January, the day on which these martyrs—Marius, Martha, Audifax, and Habacuc—are commemorated.], were those of the blessed martyr Marius and of his wife and children, namely Martha, Audifax, and Habacuc. They had been brought to us together with the bodies of the saints Marcellinus and Peter, in the same reliquary. But the man who brought them did not know whose relics they were. For the man who had sent them to me had promised that he would come to me and identify personally the names of the saints whose relics they were; and this was later done [Col. 0565D].

The poor man who had been placed beside them by the aforementioned blind man, when the second lesson was being read according to custom during the nocturnal office, uttered a tremendous cry and caused no little terror among those who heard it. Several clerics, together with the man who had been ordered to remain there awaiting this event, hurried to him and found him lying face down and stretched out near the altar [Col. 0566A], while the pavement beneath his mouth was soaked with a great quantity of blood. They lifted him, revived him with water that had been brought, and led him joyfully into the lower part of the church, sound and upright, retaining no trace whatsoever of that camel-like crookedness.

When this miracle had thus been accomplished, the man whom I had sent there returned to me with the greatest haste. After reporting what he had seen, he filled us with great joy and exultation.

47. Not long afterward Ratleicus, who, as we demonstrated earlier, had brought the sacred ashes of the martyrs from Rome, came as he himself asserted he had been ordered to come, carrying a little book containing several chapters. He reported that its contents were as follows. The blind man whom we have just mentioned had commanded him, by the authority of the martyrs, to write out those chapters and bring them to me, and to tell me to receive them and present them to the emperor for reading.

I received the little book from him, read it, had it corrected and newly written, and presented it to the emperor as he had ordered. The emperor received and read it; but of the things that he had been ordered or admonished to do through this little book, he took care to fulfill very few. What those chapters contained, and what he did or left undone, should be related elsewhere rather than here.

One matter, however, must not merely be passed over; indeed, I think it should be written down openly and clearly: namely, how it was revealed and commanded that this little book should be produced and given to the king. Ratleicus reported that the matter occurred as follows:

“Several days ago,” he said, “when we had gathered in the church according to custom to celebrate the nocturnal office, that blind man whom you know approached me and asked me to withdraw with him to some more secluded place. I did as he wished and entered with him the little cell in which I usually rested. Then he began:

“‘This night, a little before we arose after being awakened by the sound of the bells, a certain man appeared to me in a vision. He was venerable with gray hair, clothed in a white garment, and holding a golden staff in his hand. He addressed me in these words:

“‘“See to it, Albricus, that you understand well everything I shall tell you, and retain it in such a tenacious memory that you can explain it also to others who are to write it down. For I wish these things to be written and shown to Emperor Louis for reading by your elder [Col. 0566D]. They are exceedingly necessary [Note: [Col. 0566D] The author of the *Annals of Fulda*, under the year 874, thinks that if Louis had taken care to observe these things, perhaps he would not have suffered in purgatory for thirty-four years what he revealed himself to be suffering to his son Louis, who was holding an assembly at Seligenstadt, asking to be freed from it through the prayers of his own people.]—not only for the prince to know, but also for him to do—in whose kingdom these martyrs came by divine command.”’”

48. “Then he began and pronounced, in order, twelve or somewhat more chapters. He commanded me to enumerate and explain them to you and to four others whom I shall name to you; and afterward you were to make a little book and bring it to your elder, who is now staying at the palace, and command him by the authority of the martyrs to present it to the emperor as quickly as possible.

“Then he added:

“‘Do you know who I am, who command you to do these things?’

“I, without hesitation, replied that he was Saint Marcellinus.

“And he said:

“‘It is not as you suppose. I am the archangel Gabriel. I have assumed the person and appearance of Marcellinus because the Lord God has entrusted me with the care of all things and causes pertaining to these martyrs. I have now come to inform you of these matters, which I command you to write, because it is the divine will that, by their authority, they reach the king’s knowledge without the interposition of delay.

“‘As I have commanded you, at first light, after the morning office has been completed, announce what you have heard to those to whom I have ordered you to announce it.’

“Then I said:

“‘No one will believe that an angel has spoken with me or commanded me to announce these things.’

“He replied:

“‘It will not be so. But I shall give you a sign, which you are to perform before them. When they have seen it, they will no longer have any doubt about the things you have conveyed to them at my command. Therefore, tell Ratleicus to provide you with two new candles that have not yet been lit. Holding one in your right hand and the other in your left, stand before the altar. When you have finished narrating everything I have commanded you, tell those who hear these things to believe that what you have said is true and was commanded by an angel of God, if these candles in your hands are illuminated before their eyes without any visible application of fire.’”

After this had occurred, the little book was written and brought to me, and through me was presented to the king. He too received and read it. For this reason I decided to mention the little book among the other miracles: because on the occasion when it was commanded that the book be written, that marvelous and unusual lighting of the candles took place, which the angel himself—he who illuminated them—had foretold would occur through the merits of the blessed martyrs.

49. At approximately the same time, when Ratleicus had returned from us to the basilica of the martyrs, another little book was brought to us from there. It contained the words and reasoning of a certain demon who called himself Wiggo [Col. 0567D]. These statements were made by him before many witnesses, beside the altar near which the sacred ashes of the martyrs had been placed, in response to the questions of a priest who had read the exorcism over a possessed person. The event is reported to have occurred as follows.

There is an estate in the district of Nithagome [Note: [Col. 0567D] I think that here and below, in no. 53, *Nithagouve* should be read. It is a tract so called from the river Nitha, commonly called the Nid, which flows into the Main below Frankfurt, at the place where the town of Höchst now stands. I would not venture to suggest by conjecture that the place mentioned here as *Heccostat* is that town, since among the places in the diocese of Mainz I find one called *Hetstat*, a not entirely dissimilar name, though omitted from the topographical map.], named Hecgstat, belonging to the monastery of Saint Nazarius [Note: [Col. 0568D] The monastery of Saint Nazarius beyond the Rhine, commonly called Lorsch or Lorishaim, where we stated in the Life of Saint Godegrand, under 6 March, that the body of Saint Nazarius had been deposited by Bishop Godegrand. The matter is treated more fully in the Life of Saint Nazarius, under 12 June. Consult Marquard Freher, part I of *On Palatine Origins*, chapter 6.]. From there a girl of about sixteen years of age, possessed by that same wandering spirit [Col. 0568A], was brought by her parents to the basilica of the martyrs.

When she came before the tomb containing the sacred bodies, and the priest had read the exorcism over her head according to custom, he then began to ask the demon how and when he had entered her. The demon answered the priest not in the barbarian language, which alone the girl knew, but in Roman speech. The priest was astonished and asked how she knew the Latin language, when her parents, who were standing there present, entirely understood no such speech.

“‘You have never seen my parents,’” he replied.

Then the priest said:

“‘Who, then, are you, if these are not your parents?’”

50. And the demon, speaking through the girl, said:

“‘I am a subordinate and disciple of Satan, and for a long time I was a gatekeeper among the inhabitants of hell. But for several years now, together with eleven companions, I have ravaged the kingdom of the Franks. We destroyed grain and wine, and all other crops that grow from the earth for human use, by killing them as we had been ordered. We killed the livestock with diseases and sent pestilence and plague upon the people themselves. All the adversities and every evil that they have long been suffering on account of their merits came upon them through our actions and infliction.’”

Here the priest asked him for what reason such power had been granted to him.

“‘Because of the wickedness of this people and the manifold iniquities of those set over it. They love gifts rather than justice; they fear human beings more than God; they oppress the poor and refuse to listen to widows and orphans who cry out to them; they administer justice to no one unless he pays for it.

“‘In addition to these things, there are many others, almost beyond counting, committed daily both by the people themselves and by their rulers: perjuries, drunkenness, adulteries, murders, thefts, and robberies. No one prevents them from being committed, and once they have been committed, no one punishes them.

“‘The more powerful devote themselves to shameful profits, and abuse the higher position they received for governing their inferiors for pride and empty glory. They practice hatred and envy not so much among strangers as among relatives and those joined by kinship. Friend does not trust friend; brother hates brother; father does not love son.

“‘Few are those who give tithes faithfully and devoutly; fewer still are those who give alms. This is because whatever they are commanded to give to God or to the poor, they think is lost to themselves.

“‘They do not fear to possess unjust measures and false weights, contrary to God’s command. By fraud they deceive one another; they are not ashamed to give false testimony; they do not observe Sundays and feast days [Col. 0569A], but work on them, as on other days, according to whatever their will dictates.

“‘Because of these and many other things which God either commanded human beings to do or prohibited them from doing, and because this people has become disobedient to his commands through its obstinacy, we have been permitted—indeed, ordered—to do to human affairs the things I have listed above, so that they may pay the penalty for their faithlessness. For they are faithless and deceitful, since they do not take care to keep what they promised at baptism.’”

The demon spoke all these things in Latin through the mouth of the barbarian girl.

51. When the priest began to press him with commands to leave, he said:

“‘I shall leave, not because of your command, but because of the power of the saints, who do not permit me to remain in her any longer.’”

After saying this, he threw the girl onto the pavement and made her lie there for a short while face down, as though sleeping. Shortly afterward, when he had departed, the girl seemed to awaken from sleep. Through the power of Christ and the merits of the blessed martyrs, she rose sound before the eyes of all who were present and marveled. After the demon had been expelled from her, she could no longer speak Latin, so that it could plainly be understood that it was not she herself who had spoken, but the demon through her mouth.

Alas, what misery has overtaken our times, in which not good men but evil demons are teachers, and inciters of vice and persuaders to crime admonish us concerning our correction.

52. At approximately the same time, a certain nun named Marethrudis, from the district of Wetareiba [Note: [Col. 0569D] I am also afraid that this name is not correctly written, since I suspect that *Wetteravia* should be read: a region watered by the river Wettera, between the town of Lich, where that river rises, and Assenheim, where it joins the Nitha.], was held for ten years by a dreadful paralytic illness so severely that during all that time she scarcely had the use of any bodily function for human purposes. Her parents had already despaired of her, since they had taken her to all the holy places to which they could reach.

At last they brought her to the basilica of the martyrs and placed her beside the chancel screen during the nocturnal office. Through the merits and intercession of those same saints, she was immediately granted the long-desired health—so fully and perfectly that, having recovered the strength of all her limbs, she who had arrived there on a litter returned home on foot.

But when she began to go back home, she was seized on the very journey by the same illness from which she had rejoiced to have been freed. Therefore, repenting of her return, she asked to be taken back once more to the threshold of the martyrs. As soon as she had been brought back, she received without any delay the health she had lost by departing.

Having therefore made a vow that she would no longer leave the service of the saints of her own accord, she built herself a small cell not far from the church in which to live. From then on, conducting herself religiously in the service of the blessed martyrs, she remained there with great devotion.

53. It is also established that, not long afterward, another woman was freed by the same most blessed martyrs from a serious affliction [Col. 0570A]. The event is known to have occurred as follows.

In the district of Nithagowe there is an estate called Ursella, about six leagues distant from the basilica of the martyrs. There a woman, having awakened in the morning and sat up in her bed, stretched herself according to the custom of those who awaken, extending her arms and yawning repeatedly in order to dispel her sluggishness. She opened her mouth somewhat wider than she should have, and when the joints of her jaws beside her ears had become dislocated, her gaping mouth remained fixed and immobile. No longer able to close it, she had become more like a mask than a human being and was paying the gravest penalty for her careless yawn [Note: [Col. 0570D] *Persona* properly and in Latin means “mask”; hence *personatus*, that is, “masked.”].

When this became known to the women living on the same estate, they hurried to her and attempted to help the afflicted woman with herbs and foolish incantations [Col. 0570B]. But their vain and superstitious presumption had no effect; rather, whatever the ignorant hands of these women applied to her under the pretense of treating her tormented and harmed her.

Meanwhile, the brother of the woman’s husband arrived and, with sound advice, urged that she be taken without delay to the basilica of the martyrs. He asserted that she would be healed there, if she was ever to recover her health.

They immediately placed her on an animal and began to lead her there. As they approached the basilica, however, they took her down from the animal and made her proceed on foot. When they had come to the point where the little tower containing the basilica’s bells could already be seen, those leading her ordered her to raise her eyes so that she might look at it. She looked, saw it, and without any intervening delay recovered her health.

There they all fell together to the ground, praising the divine mercy with whatever praises they could offer. Then they rose and hastened to the basilica. After venerating the most holy martyrs and fulfilling vows according to their means, they returned home with great rejoicing.

We saw this same woman and spoke with her; and from her own account we learned what had happened to her.

54. I now wish to relate what I myself saw occur on the feast day of the blessed martyrs.

A certain boy who was deaf and mute had come there three years earlier and had been appointed by the church’s custodian as doorkeeper in the custodian’s house. On the feast day, after the day had ended and the evening office had been completed, he was sitting beside the door when he suddenly rose, entered the basilica, and fell face down on the right side of the altar [Col. 0570D].

The sacristan, who was placing a candelabrum with a candle before the altar, found him lying there and immediately took care to inform me. We, who were then together, quickly entered the church and found him lying there just as the sacristan had found him.

When we ordered him to be lifted up, he could not be roused, as though overcome by a very deep sleep. At last, as if awakening, he raised himself. Seeing us standing around him, he rose and spoke in Latin to those who were standing nearby.

Some of our people say that about six months earlier, when he had slept at night in the house of one of our men, he had spoken two words in his sleep, and that at that moment he had received hearing, which until then he likewise lacked as much as speech. This was inferred from the fact that, after awakening from that sleep, he carried out everything that anyone commanded him, as though he understood.

But this seems especially remarkable in the present miracle: he understood someone speaking to him not in Latin but in his barbarian language, yet once cured he spoke not in the barbarian tongue but in Latin.

He also reported that he had seen the blessed martyrs and heard from them many things that he was to tell others. But because he postponed reporting them at that time, as though he would speak of them on the following day, they were so completely erased from him through forgetfulness [Col. 0571B] that he remembered nothing at all of having heard them.

Since he did not know his own name, I ordered him to be called Prosper, on account of the favorable outcome of the miracle. He still survives and continues in the same office as before, in the house of the church’s custodian.

55. On the day before Prosper received his speech—that is, on the vigil of the same feast—a certain young man, likewise deaf and mute, came to the basilica. As he implored the help of the saints with a suppliant gesture, he too, with the Lord’s assistance, deserved to receive complete healing from both illnesses.

Like the earlier boy, I called him Godescalc, since he had never heard his own name. Yet unlike Prosper, he spoke, after the saints’ merits had granted him the power of speech [Col. 0571C], not in Latin but in the barbarian language, as was natural to him by birth.

56. When a certain necessity, as usual, compelled me to visit the king’s assembly in the month of December—if I remember correctly, on the Kalends—I departed from the place of the martyrs and arrived the following day at the fortress now called Wisibada [Note: [Col. 0571D] Commonly Wiesbaden, that is, “white baths,” in the Rheingau, almost opposite Mainz and about a league and a half from that city], intending to lodge there.

Because the forest adjoining that place made it more convenient to travel through it, we rose earlier than usual. The servants who were to go ahead of us with the baggage set out. But after they had left the village in which we had stayed and begun their journey, such a dreadful darkness surrounded them that they could not know at all where they ought to turn.

There was also a severe cold, and the earth, covered with frost, prevented them from seeing the road. The mountain ridges over which they had to travel were themselves hidden by clouds, so that they could not see how far away or how near they were. In addition, fog lay in the valleys; by its density it obstructed their vision and delayed those wishing to make their way forward.

When they saw themselves blocked by so many obstacles and had no clear idea what to do, they dismounted from their horses and tried to find the road by touch, since they could not see it. But when this attempt had little success, they mounted their horses again and decided that they would rather entrust themselves to the error they dreaded than cause delay [Col. 0572A].

Proceeding a short distance through the darkness, they reached a cross that had been placed beside the road on which they were to travel in memory of the blessed Marcellinus.

The reason for placing that cross there was that, two years earlier, when I was returning from the palace and carrying the relics of the blessed martyr Marcellinus that had then been restored to me, the inhabitants of the village where we had stayed that night had met me at that place. In memory of this event, and in honor of the blessed martyr, they had arranged for the cross to be set up there as a kind of title or memorial.

When the aforementioned servants reached it—more by wandering than by traveling—they decided that they should wait there for their companions who were following. To prevent them from losing their way, they gathered them to themselves by the sound of a trumpet. Then, once they were together, they invoked the blessed martyrs to bring them help, and, raising their voices, they sang “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*) three times.

57. When this had been done, a flash of light sent down from heaven shone over them the same number of times, so brightly that it equaled the radiance of daylight. This flashing brought them such assistance in making their journey that, once the fog had vanished and the darkness had been dispelled, they could clearly see the road they had to take. Thus, even though they traveled through forests and mountains darkened by woods, they completed their journey without the hindrance of error until sunrise.

Indeed, during the first flash, such heat came together with the light that they confessed they felt it like the vapor of a furnace that had been set alight. Through its breath not only was the fog consumed, but also the frost that at that time covered the mountains and the entire forest, so completely that after the third flash no trace whatsoever of that chill remained.

Those who had seen and experienced these things related them to us in the evening of that same day, after we had arrived at our lodging. Believing their words, we praised with thanksgiving the mercy of almighty God, because he had deigned, through the merits of his saints, to help and console us in all our necessities.

58. Although all the things we have learned to have been accomplished through the merits of the blessed martyrs are great and must be attributed to divine power for the salvation of mortals, nevertheless, in the miracle that I have now decided to commit to memory, the power of almighty God is so plainly and clearly recognized [Col. 0572D; Ms. reads *clarere*, “to shine clearly”] that no one can doubt that he can most easily accomplish whatever he wills in every creature of his.

There is a village called Suntiligua [Note: [Col. 0571D] Perhaps *Suntilinga*, with the ending familiar among the Alamanni; nevertheless, the maps nowhere show it.], in the district of Nithagonne. A certain priest named Waltbertus held a church there. He became mentally deranged and was brought to the basilica of the martyrs, to the great sorrow of his relatives.

Three of those relatives were his brothers, one a priest and two laymen; the fourth was a monk, his kinsman, from the monastery of Hornbach [Note: [Col. 0572D] Horenbach, two leagues from the city of Deux-Ponts, a town under the diocese of Metz on the borders of the Palatinate, somewhat nearer the city. Adjacent to it is Alt Horenbach, that is, “Old Horenbach.” Perhaps a monastery once stood there; later, when heresy prevailed in that place, it was converted to secular uses, according to Bucelinus.]. He himself had also been educated there from childhood.

I asked them whether any further medical treatment had yet been given to him by any physician.

“‘As soon as we discovered that he had been seized by this affliction,’ they said, ‘we brought him to the monastery where he had been raised. There, although physicians treated him extensively according to their medical skill, they could not drive the illness from him. Our friends then advised us to bring him to the mercy of these saints. For we trust that they can save him, just as we have learned that many others have been saved here.’”

After this, they were received as guests and remained with us for four days, taking him to the church each day and making him lie before the sacred ashes of the martyrs.

On the fifth day, his brother the priest and the monk who had come with him asked me to receive him, together with his two lay brothers [Ms., “to order him to be received”], until they themselves returned; for they said that they would return after three days.

I did as they wished and entrusted him to our priest Hiltfrid. After the priest had received him and led him into the cell where he himself stayed, toward evening of that same day the madness by which he was held became violently agitated. He seized a knife, which chance had placed within the reach of a madman, and attempted to kill one of his brothers who was guarding him. That man avoided death by fleeing and informed our people, who were nearby, of his madness.

Then the priest whom we had charged with guarding him suggested to me, and at the same time persuaded me, to permit him to be bound. He was therefore bound with iron chains and placed on a bed. The doors were secured, and he was left alone in the room [Col. 0573C]. His brothers kept watch before the door and guarded him with vigilant care, as though he might break out.

The bonds with which he was fastened were such that, while held in them, he could not turn onto his right or left side, nor lie in any position other than on his back.

59. He slept, therefore, as he himself testifies, and did not awaken before midnight. But when he awoke at the crowing of the roosters, he saw that he had been released not only from the bonds of his chains but also from the madness by which he had suffered.

Immediately he turned his whole mind toward offering praise to God. He sang psalms and hymns, loudly enough—despite being alone, and out of excessive joy—to awaken everyone sleeping in the vicinity of the cell.

Then he rose, approached the door, and asked his brothers, who were keeping watch there, to permit him to go outside to attend to the needs of nature. They, however, thinking this a trick of a madman, did not dare to agree. Instead, they summoned their host, who had confined him there, and begged him to speak with him.

After speaking with him and understanding from the rational character of his answers that he was of sound mind, the host opened the door and permitted him to go wherever he wished. When he returned, he asked what had happened to the chains with which he had bound and confined him.

The priest replied:

“‘The chain with which you bound me is safe. If you wish to know where it is, search for it and you will find it.’”

They therefore lit a lamp and found it lying before the bed on which they had made him rest. It was arranged in the same manner and fastened with the same knots as when they had placed him on that bed with it and left him alone in the room.

Who should be believed to have done this except the one who created all things from nothing, and who can perform in the things he created such deeds as cannot be grasped by the mind or explained in human speech?

For who could conjecture in thought or recount in words how that priest had been released from those bonds, when we know with absolute certainty that no one could free himself alone from such bonds if he had been fastened in the same way as that priest was when he was shut alone in the room?

Those who had left him there, when they returned and found him sound and in possession of his mind and memory, went back home with him, rejoicing and praising God.

We learned that this had happened not from the report of just any witnesses, but from our own experience, because by God’s will we were there at the time. Therefore we write with confidence that we came to know the event, as they say, by eyewitness testimony.

But since all the things we have undertaken to write about the powers of the martyrs cannot possibly be completed in the present discourse, let this book now come to an end, so that what remains may more suitably be begun again from another starting point.

[Col. 0574C]

## CHAPTER VI

Miracles performed at the emperor’s palace through the relics of these saints: blindness, contraction, paralysis, and fever removed.

60. In the account of the signs and powers that I have resolved to write in this book, those seem deserving of first place which occurred at the palace and came to the knowledge not only of the common people but also of the prince himself, his nobles, and all, so to speak, the members of his court. They deserve this place not only for that reason, but also because at that time our little oratory, where these same miracles occurred [Note: [Col. 0574D] This refers to what is related above, nos. 21 and 22, concerning the relics brought to the oratory.], contained no relics other than those of the blessed Marcellinus and Peter. Thus whatever healings and signs are known to have occurred there must be attributed and referred particularly and exclusively to those whose relics alone are known to have been present there.

As we shall demonstrate below, those most blessed martyrs performed many works of power and miracles at places belonging to other saints. These may reasonably appear to some to have been performed jointly by the martyrs and the saints in whose basilicas they occurred, especially because those believed to possess equal merit before God may rightly be thought to cooperate jointly in the performance of miracles.

But the contrary is demonstrated by the fact that it is clearly established that no powers were performed in those places before the relics of the blessed martyrs mentioned above had been brought there.

Now, as we promised, let us set forth the miracles that occurred at the aforementioned palace.

61. There was a certain young man among the king’s chamberlains, a Greek by nationality, named Drogo [Note: [Col. 0575D] I would scarcely believe that a Germanic name was brought from Greece; perhaps *Graecius* or *Graeciensis* should instead be read, meaning one born at Graecium in Styria.]. He had been seized by a fever and, whether through the negligence of his attendants or the ignorance of physicians, had suffered for several months from a long and serious illness.

After Abbot Hildoin had returned to us the relics of the blessed Marcellinus, as was demonstrated in the second book, Drogo was admonished in a dream to come to our oratory, light there a candle purchased for four denarii, and invoke the holy martyr Marcellinus, whose head was said to be there, for his assistance. He was also told that, if he did this in that place, he would soon be rid of the illness from which he had long suffered.

He believed the one who gave him this admonition and fulfilled the command with all possible speed. Immediately he was made well, recovered the strength of his limbs, and returned home on his own feet.

### 62

There was also another man there, equally young, named Gerlacus, from the city of Rheims, among those who had been ordered to come from that city for the construction of the palace buildings. About half a year earlier, in that same village, he had been afflicted by such a severe and dreadful contraction of the nerves that his feet were joined to his buttocks and his knees to his chin. His companions and relatives carried him in their arms to the oratory mentioned above; and, since he could not be placed otherwise, they laid him face down and prayed with great devotion to the holy martyr that health might be restored to him.

It was Sunday, at the third hour of the day, when he was brought there. He lay there until the ninth hour. When the office of that hour had been solemnly completed by the clerics, behold, such a fragrance of an exceedingly sweet and unfamiliar odor came forth from the chest containing the sacred relics of the blessed martyr and filled the entire little cell of the oratory, that all who were present rose up in wonder without hesitation and carefully asked one another whether they all perceived it equally.

Suddenly they saw the man who was lying nearby being dragged as though by certain persons holding him, and the limbs that had been contracted by the disease being stretched out. Understanding that divine power was present, they lifted the man and placed him before the altar. When he had been set there and was imploring divine aid with many tears, everyone looking on, he was so completely restored that he who had come into the oratory borne on others’ hands went out of it on his own feet.

Nevertheless, he is known still to carry on his body evidence of the affliction he endured. For afterward he limped so badly with his left leg and foot that he always needed a staff to guide his walking. Let those who wish say why this was not completely healed. For my part, I see no other way to conjecture about it than to suppose that it suited his inward salvation that some traces of outward weakness should remain in him.

### 63

Juliacum [Note: [Col. 0576D] Juliacum is a very strongly fortified town with a castle and the chief place of the distinguished duchy of Jülich, under the archdiocese of Cologne.] is the name of an ancient municipal town, eight leagues distant from the village of Aachen. From its territory a certain girl, afflicted by a similar disease and in a similar manner, was brought by her mother and other relatives to the oratory mentioned above. Since she could not be carried inside because of the crowd of people who had happened at that time to gather there to hear the solemn Masses, they placed her outside, beside the eastern window of the oratory, awaiting an opportunity when, after the crowd had dispersed, she could more easily be brought into the oratory.

But when the service had reached approximately its middle, and, after the Gospel had been completed, the offering of the saving Host had been made, they saw her suffering distress and, as sweat broke out over her entire body, sinking as if into sleep. Reasonably conjecturing from these signs that divine power was present, they lifted her from that place and laid her, like someone asleep, upon a squared stone that happened to be lying nearby. There, before all who had gathered to witness this miracle, with the Lord’s help she recovered the perfect health of all her limbs in the space of one hour.

Among the other spectators were Jews. One of them, named David, after this sign had been completed, quickly ran to the window of the room where I then was and addressed me, reporting the miracle he had witnessed and giving thanks to God, who had deigned to perform such great miracles through his martyrs for the salvation of mortals.

### 64

In the same village there was a blind man of advanced age who, as he himself asserted, had been struck by sudden blindness three years earlier and used to beg alms from door to door among the other poor. While he was sleeping in his little hut, he saw in a dream someone standing beside him and saying that, if he wished to see, he should go to our oratory; there was a physician there who could restore his sight if he asked.

He refused and rejected the sight that was being offered:

> “What,” he said, “do I now have to do with sight, which I lost long ago? It is better for me to lack it than to have it. Now everyone listens to a beggar and provides what is necessary; but it is not fitting for a sighted man to beg. I am old and weak and cannot work.”

Then the one who was speaking with him said:

> “Go,” he said, “and do not delay; for whether you wish it or not, you will recover your sight.”

He obeyed the command, went to the oratory, and spent the night there. When nothing happened that night, he returned to his hut. Then the one who had earlier appeared to him in sleep appeared again and ordered him, in the same way as before, to go to the oratory. He did as he had been ordered, but even then nothing happened.

On the third occasion, however, he came after being warned, and when he prostrated himself before the altar to pray, he recovered his sight. While he was still blind, we had seen him many times begging in our house among the other poor and infirm. Therefore we did not seek another witness to his restoration of sight, because we believed that the testimony of our own unlying conscience was sufficient for us.

### 65

As a beneficial reputation spread through the surrounding villages and settlements on account of these and many other manifestations of miraculous power, a woman from the district of the Ripuarians [Note: [Col. 0577D] The Ripuarii, or Ripuarians, were so called from the guarding of the bank of the Rhine; their royal city was once Cologne. Thus below, in no. 93, it is said that this metropolis lies in the territory of the Ripuarians, situated on the Rhine.], who had long been blind and possessed both the desire and the confidence of recovering her sight, asked to be brought to the oratory mentioned above.

When she arrived there, she continued for three full days and an equal number of nights in prayer and fasting. But when she felt no sign of the desired healing at that time, she was taken home. After a few days had passed, having conceived—by no empty hope—the expectation of recovering the light, she again asked to be led to the sacred relics.

She was taken there by a single boy, for those who had previously led her there, judging her hope empty and futile, were unwilling to go with her any farther. When she reached, with this boy accompanying and guiding her, the cemetery of the palace of Aachen, which lies on the hill overlooking the same village on its eastern side, she received there the light she had long desired, as though divine grace had come to meet her.

Then, amazed and astonished, she stopped and ordered the boy guiding her to follow:

> “Until now,” she said, “I followed where you led the way; but now I do not need your guidance, because I see the road by which we must go, and, with the Lord’s help, I see this village in which the sacred relics are located and to which I have decided to come. You need only see to it and take care that you lead me by the direct road to the martyrs’ oratory in the village itself.”

After saying this, she went to the oratory, gave thanks, and informed us of the miracle that had taken place in her. Seeing and rejoicing, she returned home.

### 66

Ascvilare [Note: [Col. 0577D] This place is situated approximately this distance away in the territory of Jülich, near Linnich, and is commonly called Wiler. It may formerly have been distinguished by the addition of *Asc*, meaning “ashes,” from another place two leagues farther away, commonly called Holtzwiler, “the hamlet of the woods.”] is the name of a royal estate four leagues distant from the palace of Aachen. A certain man there was held and afflicted by a long-standing illness of the entrails. His people had already despaired of him to such an extent that he seemed curable only by cautery.

A physician was sought for this purpose, and a day was appointed for an operation that would prove of no benefit. Meanwhile, a woman living on the same estate was shown in a dream that the man ought not to submit to such a treatment for his cure—a treatment scarcely tolerable because of its painfulness and, since it would be useless, incapable of bringing health to the sufferer.

But if he wished to become well, he was to go to the palace of Aachen, seek out our oratory, have himself placed there, and not leave it before three days had been completed. In this way he would obtain complete health.

When this was announced to him, he summoned his friends and relatives and asked them to carry out toward him the instructions of that revelation. They immediately placed him on a beast of burden and brought him to the oratory. Having placed him there as they had been ordered, they departed, intending to return after three days.

Left there, he spent three days and nights earnestly imploring the Lord to restore his health, and he was so perfectly healed that he declared that no trace remained in his entrails of the disease by which he had been afflicted for so long. When his people returned to him as they had promised and found him well as they had hoped, he went back home—not on the back of the beast on which he had come, but by the use of his own feet—with immense rejoicing and happiness both for himself and for them.

### 67

There is likewise a royal estate in the district of the Meuse, about eight leagues distant from the village of Aachen, whose inhabitants call it Gangluden [Note: [Col. 0578D] Gangelt is a town in the territory of Jülich. Jacobus Krietzradt, who came from there, informed us that *Gangluden* had been a particular district around that town and was often called by that name—*het landt van mille, Gangelt, ende Vucht*—and that those places were called the “triple cord.”].

A woman there had a daughter of about eight years who was so wasted by the dreadful disease of paralysis that for a long time she had scarcely been able to move any limb for its proper function. Having heard of the miracles, the mother conceived in a pious heart the hope of recovering her daughter’s health and immediately arranged to carry her in her own arms to the oratory mentioned above.

When she arrived there before midday, at the hour of the meal, she found none of the clerics present, for they had gone away shortly before to eat. Nevertheless, she entered and placed her daughter beside her on the floor. Lighting a very small candle that she had brought as an offering, she set it on the same floor before the girl and prostrated herself with the utmost devotion to pray before the sacred ashes.

As soon as this had been done, without any delay, the girl, through heavenly grace, recovered the health and strength of all her limbs. Without her mother noticing, she rose, picked up the candle that lay before her, and stood behind her mother’s back.

When the mother, having completed her prayer, lifted her head from the floor and saw that neither the candle nor her daughter was in the place where she had put them, she rose and turned around. She saw her daughter standing behind her with the candle, praising God and full of joy.

Since she saw that no one was present to whom she could report the miracle that had occurred—for apart from the poor who were keeping watch there in order to beg, no one was inside the walls of the oratory except herself and her daughter when the miracle took place—she paid her vows with thanksgiving and returned home with her daughter healthy and unharmed.

[Col. 0579A]

I shall briefly explain how news of this miracle was brought to us. [Note: [Col. 0579D] Writing to this Gerwardus in Letter 14, Eginhard says among other things: “You urge—indeed, you give counsel—that, abandoning the martyrs’ vigils, at which I have been ordered unceasingly to be present and to take part, I should go to the palace.”] Gerwardus, the palace librarian, who at that time had also been entrusted by the king with responsibility for the palace works and construction, was coming from Nijmegen and making his way to the palace of Aachen.

When he had spent one night at the estate mentioned above, he asked his host whether he had recently heard anything new about the palace. The man replied:

> “Nothing is now more famous among the courtiers than the signs and miracles that are taking place in Eginhard’s house through certain saints whose relics he is said to possess in the oratory of his house. All our neighbors hasten there every day to venerate them, and anyone who is brought there sick is immediately healed.”

He began to tell him how the daughter of that woman had been healed a few days earlier. Then Gerwardus said:

> “Go and bring that same woman to me, so that she herself may tell me what I wish to hear.”

The woman came and clearly related everything as it had happened. When Gerwardus went to the king on the following day, he informed him of what he had learned concerning this miracle from the woman’s account [Ms., “report”].

When I entered and stood before the king, as was my custom, he told both me and the other persons standing beside him what Gerwardus had reported to him about this miracle, expressing his admiration for and praise of the divine mercy and power.

Thus it happened that we learned, through such an account, of a sign that had occurred in our own house while we knew nothing of it.

---

## CHAPTER VII

Miracles performed at Valenciennes in Hainaut at the relics of these saints. Ten blind persons restored to sight; others healed of illness.

### 68

It is enough for the present work to have recalled these miracles of the blessed martyrs that took place at the palace. We must now turn to those manifestations of miraculous power that occurred in places to which, at the request of religious men and by my granting them, the venerable relics of those same martyrs came, and where they have until now been worshiped with great reverence.

The first of all to receive them from me was Georgius, priest and rector of the monastery of Saint Salvius the martyr [Note: [Col. 0579D] Saint Salvius is commemorated on 26 June. There we shall show that it was a monastery of clerics, which Baldericus, in book II, chapter 31 of his *Chronicle of Cambrai*, calls the canonical monastery of Saint Salvius, bishop and martyr. It is now a priory of the Cluniac order, founded in 1103, near Valenciennes and practically in its suburbs; Mabilio notes that the place is commonly called Famars.], situated in the district of Fanumartis, in a village called Valenciennes, on the bank of the river Scheldt. He received them from me and sent them through a certain deacon from the palace of Aachen to the monastery mentioned above.

When the deacon, having only one companion with him, had come in the district of Hesbaye to a royal village called Vuasidium [Note: [Col. 0580D] Vuasidium may perhaps be Weset, or Veltweset, between Maastricht and Bilsen, which may have been called Wased.], and had dismounted in a meadow close to the village in order to rest the animals, behold, one of the inhabitants of the place, bowed down by a hump and with his jaws swollen by excessive swelling from a severe toothache—which, as he himself said, he had suffered for a long time—entered the meadow in a fury carrying an iron fork around his neck and angrily demanded why they were grazing in his meadow.

The deacon, who was carrying the martyrs’ relics and was then preparing to suspend them at the top of the staff that he had fixed in the ground there for this purpose, said to him:

> “It is better for you to prostrate yourself before these relics of the saints, which I hold here in my hands, and ask God to deign, through the merits of these same saints, to free you from the pain you are suffering. For the swelling visible on your face testifies that you have a severe pain in your mouth.”

At these words the man threw down the fork he had been carrying, fell prostrate before the relics, and, as the deacon had advised him, implored the Lord for his health.

Before long he rose from prayer so completely healed that neither the swelling in his face, nor the pain in his teeth, nor the hump that had weighed upon him remained on his back. Accordingly, he entered the village at a quick pace and invited all his relatives and neighbors who lived there to praise God and give thanks to Christ the Lord.

A great multitude of people poured into the meadow, and a crowd from the surrounding region gathered to give thanks for the man who had been healed. They all asked the deacon to remain there that night. He could not refuse them, since they were prepared, if he did not consent, to detain him even against his will.

They then kept an all-night vigil, and the entire region resounded with praises of God. On the following day, when the deacon began his journey, all the assembled crowd accompanied him as he departed with immense devotion. They were unwilling either to stop or to disperse before he had been met and welcomed by others who, moved by the fame of this miracle, were coming to meet him.

In this way, on the occasion of this miracle, the sacred relics of the martyrs were received by the peoples of those regions and, under God’s guidance, brought to the basilica of Saint Salvius, to which the aforementioned Georgius had sent them.

I know this sign from the account of Georgius himself. As for the other events that are now to be related, I received from him a little book, whose order or sequence is evidently as follows.

### 69

In the fourteenth year [Note: [Col. 0580D] This is the year of Christ 827, most probably in June, when these events occurred.] of the reign of Louis Augustus, with Christ propitious, when the Lord deigned to display signs and wonders in the king’s own palace through the merits of his saints, for the strengthening of the faith of the Christian people, just as at the beginning of the nascent Church, Georgius the priest requested and obtained from Eginhard the abbot, at the palace of Aachen, the relics of the blessed martyrs of Christ Marcellinus and Peter, whose bodies Eginhard had recently received after having them brought from Rome by his men.

He arranged for them, enclosed in a reliquary that he had suitably adorned with gold and gems, to be sent through his deacon, a man named Theothardus, to the basilica of Saint Salvius the martyr, which he then held by royal benefaction.

When this deacon had come to the royal estate called Vuasidium, a humpbacked man met him. He was so afflicted and exhausted by toothache that for fifteen days he had been unable to take any food other than water alone.

At the deacon’s urging, he prostrated himself in prayer before the relics he was carrying and devoutly and humbly called upon Christ the Lord to have mercy on him. Through the intercession of the saints Marcellinus and Peter, every bodily affliction was driven away, and he rose from prayer healed.

This miracle occurred on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July. I have related it more fully above, because I took care to write it down according to the account of the aforementioned Georgius.

### 70

On the third day the deacon arrived at Valenciennes with the relics. As he was reverently and honorably bringing them into the basilica of Saint Salvius, as he had been ordered, a certain young man from the king’s estate called Listina [Note: [Col. 0581D] Perhaps Lessines, a town of Hainaut, or Liptines near Laubium, where a synod was held at a royal estate under Carloman.], named Dominicus, had already been afflicted for an entire year by the disease that the Greeks call *spasmós* (“spasm”), to such a degree that his right hand could not be held still at all but moved in a continuous circular motion, as though he were turning a millstone.

At the very entrance, through the merits of the blessed martyrs and before the entire people, he was so completely healed that thereafter he suffered no further trouble from that dreadful movement.

On the fourth day thereafter, namely on the feast of the blessed John the Baptist, an old woman named Gerrada, who testified that she had been blind for one year [Ms., “blind”], received the light she had sought in faith by invoking the blessed martyrs, while the solemn Mass was being celebrated [Ms., “is celebrated”], before the eyes of all who were present and through the merits of the martyrs.

Likewise, on the feast of Saint Salvius, which falls on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, a certain deaf and mute man deserved, during the solemn Mass, through the martyrs’ assistance, to recover both hearing and speech.

On that same day an old woman from the district of Laon, named Rodeltrudis, who had not seen the light of heaven for three years, recovered her sight during the same celebration of Mass.

On the fifth day before the Kalends of July, a boy of about seven years, named Donitianus [Note: [Col. 0581D] I think it should be written Domitianus or Donatianus.], who had been blind from birth, was given sight through the merits of the blessed martyrs while the divine office was being celebrated.

### 71

On the vigil of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, namely on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, a little girl named Theotbalda, believed to be about nine years old, who had seen nothing for three years, was standing amid a great crowd of people at the time of the saving office. With the merits of the martyrs interceding, she received through divine mercy the sight she had lost.

On the same day a certain man named Dado, from a village called Ponticulus [Note: [Col. 0581D] There are indeed, in nearby French Flanders around Valenciennes, between Douai and Tournai, Pont-à-Rache and Pont-à-Marcy; but it would be rash to say that either place is designated here by the name Ponticulus.], had been bent over for six years and could not raise himself toward heaven. He therefore walked hunched over, supported beneath the armpits by short crutches placed there to sustain him. At that same hour and in the same place, through the mercy of God and the merits of the blessed martyrs, he was made upright and healthy.

### 72

On the fourth day before the Nones of July, a widow named Adalrada, who had been deprived of the light of her eyes for four years and could see nothing, heard of the miracles and conceived a hope of recovering her sight, not in vain faith. Taking up a staff, she set out alone, without a guide, to go to Valenciennes.

When she began to approach the village, it seemed to her that she could see something like a single ray of the sun with her right eye. Accordingly, she entreated divine clemency with a pure heart, asking that, through the intercession of his saints, he might allow her to see the church of Saint Salvius.

She was immediately heard, and, through the Lord’s mercy, obtained without delay what she had desired.

On that same day another woman from the district of Noyon, named Ruoitla, who had been blind for five years, recovered during the solemn Mass the light she had lost, Christ the Lord granting it through the merits of his saints.

### 73

On the octave of the apostles, namely on the day before the Nones of July, a certain man named Gunthardus from the same district, as though struck by paralysis, was brought by his family to the basilica of Saint Salvius. They said that he had already suffered from the same illness for a year and that the left side of his body had been so severely weakened that he could neither bring his hand to his mouth nor wash or put on his shoes.

Through the mercy of God and the merits of the saints, he was healed during the morning office on the very solemnity itself.

### 74

Likewise another man, named Hildebonus, coming from the monastery called Ad-duos-Gemellos [Note: [Col. 0582D] The monastery called “At the Two Twins” seems to be the one commonly called Saint-Martin des Jumeaux near Amiens in Picardy, later restored by Bishop Guido around the year 1073.], who had been blind from infancy and had never seen the light of heaven throughout his life, recovered his sight on the same day, during the celebration of Mass, in the same basilica, through the same saints, with the same Lord showing mercy and giving aid. He deserved to see clearly all the things he had not previously seen.

On the day of the Nones of July, a small girl named Reginlindis, who seemed to be no more than seven years old and had lacked the light of her eyes for three years, was standing among the others in the basilica to hear the divine office. Through the intervention of the saints’ merits, she was given sight before the entire crowd.

On the fourth day before the Ides of July, a blind woman named Alagia, who had been without sight for nearly two years, was illuminated by the Lord Jesus Christ during the sacred solemnities of Mass, with the prayers of the saints assisting her.

On the same day a very old blind man from the village of Gauliacas [Note: [Col. 0583C] I still do not know how to locate Gauliacas around Valenciennes.], named Ermenwardus, who had been unable to see anything for fourteen years, entered the church for the evening office and invoked the blessed martyrs. His blindness immediately departed, and, with the Lord’s help, he recovered the light he had long desired.

### 75

On the seventh day before the Kalends of August, a certain girl who was tormented by an unclean spirit was brought into the basilica. While the office of the sacred offering was being celebrated, through the power of Christ and the merits of the blessed martyrs, the demon was driven away and she deserved to recover perfect health of mind and body.

These are the miracles and manifestations of power that our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to perform, through the merits of his holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, in the village of Valenciennes for the salvation of the human race. The aforementioned Georgius the priest [Note: [Col. 0583C] In the Pithoean *Annals of the Franks* under the year 826, the following is recorded: “A certain priest named Georgius, coming from Venice with Balderic, count of Friuli, made a hydraulic organ at Aachen.” After it was completed, he became rector of the monastery of Saint Salvius, and in 827 obtained the relics mentioned here.] collected these events in a brief booklet and arranged to send it to us; we judged that they ought to be inserted into this work.

This Georgius is the Venetian who came from his homeland to the emperor and, at the palace of Aachen, constructed with extraordinary skill an organ called in Greek *hydraulikē* (“hydraulic,” that is, water-powered).

---

## CHAPTER VIII

Miracles at Ghent, in the monastery of Saint Bavo, at the relics of these saints.—Eight blind persons restored to sight; other sick persons assisted.

### 76

Another little book was given to me concerning the monastery of Saint Bavo, situated beside the Scheldt in a place called Ghent, where that river joins the river Lys. It was supplied by the brothers serving God there [Note: [Col. 0583C] Meyerus writes in the *Annals of Flanders* that Eginhard was abbot of these brothers, or monks, from the year 826, adding that he, “the priest of the emperor Louis, restored the monastery, which had been disfigured by fire, and brought the wandering monks together into one community.” Sanderus adds in book IV, chapter 4 of his *History of Ghent*, that he “obtained from the emperor Louis confirmation of the privileges of the monastery of Ghent and other new privileges”—which, if only they still existed, would confirm Eginhard’s appointment to this abbacy. As for the claim that he wrote in the *Life of Charlemagne* that the two of them were frequently together at Ghent, this is not found in that *Life*, which we discussed under 28 January. But Eginhard himself writes above, in no. 4, that he was at the monastery of Saint Bavo at Ghent in 826. Lupus, his associate, was abbot of Ferrières in the diocese of Sens and simultaneously of Saint-Josse-sur-Mer in Ponthieu. Thus Eginhard could have held some responsibility for the monastery of Saint Bavo while living at Seligenstadt. In letter 12 he likewise asks for the rent owed to him at Saint Bavo and at Blandinium.] at whose request I sent the relics of the aforementioned martyrs of Christ to that same monastery. In it, the following events were found recorded in order.

[Note: [Col. 0583D] These details correspond exactly to the year 828, solar cycle 25, with Sunday letters E and D.]

In the year 828 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, the relics of the holy martyrs of Christ Marcellinus and Peter came to the monastery of Saint Bavo on the fifth day before the Nones of July, a Friday, in the sixth indiction.

On the third day, namely the following Sunday, which was the third day before the Nones of July, a blind girl named Hartlinda from a village called Fursenum [Note: [Col. 0583D] Whether Fursenund was called Furnas in a shortened form in the twelfth century, I leave for another to conjecture until something more directly relevant is found.] was brought before the altar on which the sacred relics of the martyrs had been placed. Her father and mother testified that she had been without the use of her eyes for eight years. Before all who were present, she recovered her sight through the Lord’s mercy.

Eight days later, namely on the fourth day before the Ides of July, another blind girl named Helmrada was brought there from a village called Magle [Note: [Col. 0584C] This seems to be modern Machelen, approximately halfway by road between Courtrai and Ghent.
