The relics of these saints remained in the monastery of Saint Bavo until the year 1070, when Baldwin of Mons, count of Flanders and Hainaut, introduced Benedictine monks into the monastery of Hasnon on the Scarpe, three leagues from Valenciennes, for the secular canons, and restored their church. He arranged for the relics of Saint Marcellinus and Peter to be transferred there from the church of Saint Bavo, placed in a gilded reliquary and adorned with precious gems, as Guillaume Gazet reports in his *Ecclesiastical History of Belgium*, in the account of Lietbert, the thirty-second bishop of Cambrai and Arras, p. 162; as do Henricus Doutremannus, book I, chapter 8 of his *History of Valenciennes*, Locrius, and others. Concerning these relics, Razzius notes the following in his *Belgian Sacred Treasury*: “I judge that what Molanus asserts—that the reliquary and nearly all their sacred bones were destroyed by the fury of the iconoclasts—was written on the basis of the false report of certain persons. For, concealed at Valenciennes through the zeal of certain pious men, they are still preserved today, and the ascetics of Hasnon piously display them in a most beautiful and precious chest embossed in gold and silver. I know this with complete certainty from the solemn inquiry made and presented to Georgius Colvenerius, chancellor of the University of Douai and doctor and ordinary professor of sacred theology.” Thus far Razzius.], whose parents reported that eight days after she had been baptized she had been struck by sudden blindness.

She too immediately recovered, before the sacred ashes of the martyrs, the light she had lost long before, the Lord restoring it to her.

On the third day thereafter, which was the day before the Ides of July, a certain crooked girl named Bildrada came there from a village called Boderetium [Note: [Col. 0584D] I find no trace of Boderetium anywhere in Flanders.], which belonged to the monastery of Saint Vedast. When she had humbly invoked Christ the Lord before the relics of the saints mentioned above for the restoration of her health, she was made upright before all who were present and deserved, in an instant, to recover the sound condition of her body.

### 77

Afterward, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, a woman named Eddela, a servant of Saint Amandus, from a village called Baceroda [Note: [Col. 0585C] Baceroda is now commonly Baefroy on the Scheldt in Brabant, at the head of the road leading to Aalst, under the bishop of Ghent in the deanery of Termonde.], who was said to have been without the light of her eyes for many years, recovered her sight there, praying happily [Ms., “faithfully”].

On the same day a servant of Saint Bavo named Eberaldus, from a village called Millinium [Note: [Col. 0585C] Millinium: perhaps Melle, also on the Scheldt in Flanders, two leagues below Ghent; or rather Mullem in the district of Oudenaarde?], who likewise had not seen the light of heaven for many years, was granted the long-desired light in the same place, all who were present looking on.

On that same day two widows who had been blind for many years were given sight there. One of them, named Blidwara, is said to have come from a village called Accinium [Note: [Col. 0585C] Accinium is probably Eessene, near Diksmuide, under the bishopric of Ypres]; the other, named Ricberta, from a village called Vuerminium [Note: [Col. 0585C] Vuerminium may now perhaps have changed into Wormhout, as though “forest of Werminius,” in the castellany of Bergues.].

### 78

Then, twenty-five days later, on the feast of the Assumption of Saint Mary, a woman named Angarihilda from a village called Gojacum [Note: [Col. 0585D] Gojacum is perhaps modern Coyegem, one of the parishes of the castellany of Courtrai.], before the sacred relics of the martyrs, with the whole people looking on and marveling at what had happened, became so bent over that she could not raise herself at all to look toward heaven.

On the following day, namely the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, in the same church, while the Gospel was being read, with the same people bearing witness, she was so completely straightened and restored to her former condition that it was as though she had never been bent toward the ground by any injury to her body.

Afterward, on the twenty-second day of the month of September, namely the tenth day before the Kalends of October, a man named Liodoldus from the district of Texandria [Note: [Col. 0585D] Texandria, also called Taxandria, is called in modern usage Campine or Brabantine Campania; yet I have not been able to find Apennium there.], from a village called Apennia, had supported himself while walking with two staffs because of weakness in his left leg and foot.

There he was so perfectly healed in the sight of the people that thereafter he no longer needed the assistance of staffs when walking.

[Col. 0585C]

79. On the fourth day after the accomplishment of this miracle, that is, on the seventh day before the Kalends of October, a certain young man who was deaf and mute, and whose left hand was also contracted, named Hunwald, from a village called Corvio [Note: Corvium: I have not yet been able to determine where it should be sought], came before the sacred relics of the martyrs and prayed there devoutly. Immediately, through the power of Christ, all the afflictions from which he had suffered were driven away, and he was made so completely well that he seemed never to have been deaf, mute, or in any way disabled by contraction of the nerves in his hand.

On the following day, that is, the sixth day before the Kalends of October, a certain woman named Engilgarda, who for many years had been afflicted with a dreadful paralysis, was cured in the same basilica through the merits of the blessed martyrs, before all the people. She was a servant belonging to the bishopric of Tournai, from a village called Vuerecundia [Note: Verecundia, in the diocese of Tournai, commonly Warcoin on the Scheldt, between Courtrai and Tournai, though closer to the latter than to the former].

On the next day, that is, the fifth day before the Kalends of October, another woman named Ramburga, from the village of Bertingaheim [Note: Bertingaheim, perhaps contracted to Bernem, in the deanery of Aardenburg under the bishop of Bruges], who had been severely disabled in the lower part of her body by a similar affliction, received perfect strength in her limbs before the same sacred relics, while all who were present looked on. By God’s will she was freed in an instant from the illness with which she was said to have suffered for ten years.

80. On the same day, a certain blind man named Germarus, from the village of Schaltheim [Note: Schaltheim, probably now hidden beneath—or washed away by—the waters of the Scheldt, whose estuary has changed greatly over so many centuries], situated near the mouth of the Scheldt, a river in the maritime region of the Frisians, invoked the Lord’s mercy and the blessed martyrs on account of the calamity he suffered there, and was granted the joyful recovery of the light long denied him.

On the fourth day after this sign occurred by the Lord’s will, that is, on the day before the Kalends of October, a certain servant of Saint Bavo named Gundrada, from the village of Aldingaheim [Note: Aldingaheim, perhaps Maldingaheim, so that it is the present-day Maldegem, three leagues from Bruges and five from Ghent], who had not seen the sun for nearly three years, prostrated herself before the altar to pray. Christ the Lord, granting it through the merits of his saints, restored to her the light she had lost.

[Col. 0586C]

## CHAPTER IX

### The blind, deaf, mute, contracted, and paralytic healed at the relics deposited at Maastricht

81. The brothers from the monastery of Saint Servatius the Confessor, situated on the bank of the River Meuse in the settlement still called Maastricht, about eight leagues from the palace at Aachen, and frequented by a great multitude of inhabitants, especially merchants, also brought me a third little book [Note: Concerning these relics discovered there, the following was sent to us, out of his kindness, by the Reverend Lord Alardus Laurentius van Eyll, canon of the church of Maastricht:

“In the year of the Lord 1623, on 25 April, when the altar stone of Saint Peter the Apostle was raised slightly in the crypt of the collegiate church of Saint Servatius, and was tilted somewhat to one side, it was discovered that the body of the altar on which the stone rested was hollow inside and made from a single stone, hollowed out within like a vessel, with a capacity of two feet in length and one and a half feet in width and depth. In this hollow was placed a leaden box, nearly one foot long, whose lid bore the engraved and carved inscription:

**RELICS OF MARCELLINUS AND PETER, MARTYRS**

The ashes of the aforesaid martyrs were wrapped in a still-intact shroud, although it dissolved into ashes at the slightest touch. Those ashes filled as much space as the shroud could contain. These relics were seen at the said altar by the Reverend Lord Dean Winandus of Gelre, Guilielmus Tophius the cantor, and Joannes Stevart, canons of the aforementioned church of Saint Servatius.

Poem concerning the said altar of Saint Peter:

> Here the ashes of Marcellinus are enclosed in the altar,  
> And likewise the bones of Peter, renowned for the signs he accomplished.  
> The noble abbot Eginhard gave this treasure  
> When eight hundred and twenty-eight years  
> Had elapsed since the birth of the gracious Virgin.”

Thus far the material sent by the aforementioned canon van Eyll.]

Its text, if I remember correctly, seems to have been composed as follows:

The arrival of the holy martyrs of Christ, Marcellinus and Peter, at Maastricht took place on the day before the Nones of June. On that very day an immense multitude of people from the same settlement came out to meet them, gathered to receive them, praising and blessing God for his immeasurable and unspeakable mercy, by which he had deigned, through such great patrons, to visit a people believing and trusting in him.

When, amid these praises and spiritual joy, they had reached the basilica of Saint Servatius, and the solemn rites of Mass had been celebrated with great rejoicing by all, and everyone had returned to his own home, the bier on which the sacred ashes had been brought was placed to the right of the altar beside the chancel screen. The entire day was brought to an end amid the great exultation and joy of the people who remained assembled in the settlement.

82. When we had entered the same basilica to celebrate the evening office according to custom, there was among the others a certain boy named Berngisus. His relatives, who had come there a few days earlier from the district of Cundensium [Note: Condensium, or perhaps Condrusium? A part of the diocese of Liège, commonly called the Condroz?], had brought him, blind from birth [Manuscript: “blind”]. Suddenly he fell onto the pavement before everyone and lay there for some time as though overcome by sleep. Then, opening his eyes, he saw the light which he had never before seen, Christ the Lord granting it through the merits of his saints.

On the fifth day thereafter, that is, on the sixth day before the Ides of June, a certain man named Hildimarus, who was deaf and mute, received both hearing and speech through the power of Christ, before those same sacred relics of the saints.

83. On that same day, a certain girl named Adallinda, of the household of Saint Lambert, who was not only deaf and mute but also blind, and whose entire body had been so miserably twisted by contraction of the nerves that her knees were drawn up against her chest, was brought by her family and placed beside the sacred relics of the martyrs. Before all who were present, by a wondrously swift gift of God, she obtained sight, hearing, speech, the straightening of all her limbs, and health.

On the following day, that is, the fifth day before the Ides of June, a certain royal servant named Berohadus, from the village of Cresciacum [Note: Of the several places called Cresciacum, the more famous is that situated in the diocese of Melun in Gaul, which still enjoys royal jurisdiction], who had been weakened and rendered useless by contraction of the nerves throughout the right side of his body, came before the aforementioned relics of the saints. He was immediately raised upright and restored without delay to the health he desired.

Likewise, a certain girl from Maastricht itself, named Theothildis, whose right hand had been so contracted and twisted by a similar condition that it was useless for every purpose, was cured in the same way before the same relics of the saints on that day.

84. When these things had been seen, the people gathered in the basilica began, out of their excessive exultation and joy, to sing praises to the Lord in hymns and litanies, raising their voices on high.

Suddenly a certain deaf boy entered and stood astonished and seemingly bewildered in the midst of the crowd. Then, when he had reached the altar of the holy Savior, which stood in the middle of the church, blood burst forth from his nostrils—the flow of which he had long been deprived—and he was granted the faculty of hearing.

On the following day, that is, the fourth day before the Ides of June, it seemed to us that the bier containing the sacred ashes of the martyrs should be raised higher, so that it might stand somewhat above the altar beside which it had been placed and could more easily be seen by those approaching it.

As we were doing this, singing litanies with praise of God while we worked, a certain girl of the household of Saint Servatius was brought into the basilica shortly before and placed before the bier. From birth her feet had been twisted by contraction, her hands had likewise been rendered limp by relaxation of the nerves, and she was also mute. Suddenly she was restored to health, so that at that very hour she was able to speak, walk, and use her hands perfectly for every necessary purpose.

85. A certain woman from Maastricht itself, who had a blind servant named Adaigarda, entered the basilica and entrusted her to the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, so that she might merit to recover her sight through their intercession; then she left her there.

After the evening office had been completed, the servant remained in the same church. Suddenly, as though pushed by someone, she fell onto the pavement. After rolling about there for a long time, she eventually rose, seeing clearly, to the great astonishment and amazement of the people standing around her.

This occurred toward evening on the Ides of June, just as the twilight at the beginning of night was setting in.

A certain man from the province of Burgundy, from the territory of Gien [Note: Gena­bum, in the territory of the Aurelianenses on the Loire, today Gien, as some find plausible on the basis of a certain foundation in the name; Genabus in Lucan], named Theotgarius, suffering from a condition which physicians call *spasmos* in Greek, and which in Latin may appropriately be called “trembling,” because of the constant agitation of the limbs, came into the basilica and stood amid the crowd that had gathered, as is customary on Sunday, to hear the solemn Mass.

After the Gospel reading had been recited, when the symbol of Christian belief was being recited [Manuscript: “sung”], the trembling man suddenly collapsed to the ground. While the divine office was being performed, he lay almost motionless and more like a dead man than a living one. After a great deal of blood had continued to flow from his nostrils [Manuscript: “had flowed”], when the sacred office had been completed, he rose healthy and without the slightest trembling, to the great amazement of the watching people.

This miracle occurred on Sunday, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, as stated above [Note: Since this concurrence requires the Dominical Letter D, and this occurred in the year 828, with no such occurrence thereafter before the year 834, it seems likely that the relics were sent to Valenciennes and Maastricht at approximately the same time. The same may be conjectured concerning Ghent].

[Col. 0589A]

86. On Wednesday, that is, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, a certain boy named Folchardus, from the monastery called Meldradium [Note: Meldradium, commonly Meldert, in Brabant near Hoegaarden, where Blessed Pepin established nuns in honor of Saint Ermelindis], whose legs and feet were twisted by a grievous contraction, was cured in the same place before all the people.

On the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, a certain man came to the church and entered among the others. His right hand, together with his arm, was being moved in a remarkable circular motion, as though he were turning a millstone, and he did this incessantly.

He said that this restlessness had happened to him because he had ground grain on Sunday contrary to the prohibition, and that a full year had already passed since he had been punished with this affliction. When he approached the sacred relics of the martyrs and faithfully invoked them there, that mill-like movement was suddenly stilled in quiet.

This man said that he had come from the monastery of the Scots called Fossae [Note: Fossae, a town in the district of Liège], and that his name was Dothius.

87. On the vigil of Saint John the Baptist, which falls on the ninth day before the Kalends of July, a certain man came to Maastricht, to the basilica of Saint Servatius, saying that he was from the city of Tournai.

As he himself related, he had been deaf and mute from infancy. When his family took him to Saint Sebastian, he began there both to hear and to speak, but ineffectively, since his words could scarcely be understood; nor could he conceal the weakness of his hearing when others spoke to him.

When he came for the morning office, he fell asleep prostrate before the sacred relics. Not long afterward, as though awakened by someone who had struck him in the mouth with a fist, he asked the bystanders who had done it. When they all replied that no one had done so, he rose. At that very hour he was made well and heard and spoke perfectly, without any impediment.

88. On the same day, while the solemn Mass was being celebrated, a certain woman named Adallinda brought two candles to be lit in the church. She handed one of them to one of the attendants with her right hand so that it might be lit, while she held the other in her left hand, as though it would later be lit from the first.

But, astonishingly, while the attendant was lighting the candle given to him, the one that remained in the woman’s hand was kindled by divine power before everyone’s eyes.

89. There is a convent of nuns called Eike [Note: See the Life of Herlindis and Relindis, virgins and sisters, who built the said monastery with their father Adalhardus], situated on the River Meuse.

In it, a woman consecrated to God named Saliga lay paralyzed throughout her body, except for her right arm, by a dreadful disease. During sleep she seemed to see one of her neighbors standing beside her and addressing her in these words:

“What are you doing?”

When she answered that she was doing nothing other than resting in her bed, he said:

“Have you heard anything about the saints who have come to Maastricht, to Saint Servatius?”

When she replied that she had heard nothing about them, he said:

“Rise quickly and hasten to go there, for there you will recover the health of all your limbs.”

When she awoke, however, she took no steps to do this. On the following night she was again warned by the same man, in the same manner, to go to Maastricht. As before, she disregarded the voice of her admonisher and postponed setting out to the place to which she had been ordered to go.

On the third night she saw the same man standing beside her. With a certain severity he asked why she had despised his warnings; then he struck her side with a staff which he seemed at that moment to be holding in his hand and ordered her to go quickly to Maastricht.

Now she no longer dared resist the authority of the threefold vision. She summoned her relatives and friends, and was taken to Maastricht as she had been commanded. In the basilica of Saint Servatius she was placed beside the sacred ashes of the martyrs.

As she awaited the fulfillment of the promised healing, it was only on the fifth day after her arrival that she deserved, to the great amazement of all, to recover perfect health throughout her entire body.

[Col. 0590B]

## CHAPTER X

### Two miracles performed in the church of Saints Marcellinus and Peter through the intercession of Saints Protus and Hyacinthus and Saint Hermes

90. Two very remarkable miracles still remain. I do not think they should be concealed in silence; rather, I confidently believe that by writing them down I shall bring the fourth volume now in hand to a most fitting conclusion.

Although these signs might seem to be shared by the blessed martyrs Marcellinus and Peter together with the other saints, since one of them occurred at the arrival of the relics of Saints Protus and Hyacinthus and beside those very relics, while the other certainly took place on the feast day of Saint Hermes, beside his own relics [Note: Saints Protus and Hyacinthus are commemorated on 11 September, and Saint Hermes on 28 August], they nevertheless seem especially attributable to those saints because they occurred in the basilica where their most sacred bodies lie at rest.

The truth of these events concerns us, since we were present and divine mercy granted us to see them. Therefore, omitting a preface, let us proceed to the miracles themselves.

91. Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome, who succeeded Eugene and likewise Valentine in the honor of the pontificate [Note: Eugene II died on 27 August 827, and Valentine was appointed in his place; after dying about fourteen days later, he was succeeded by Gregory IV, who died on 11 January 844, according to our chronology. Baronius, however, assigns the events here related to the year 829], wished to enlarge the title of Saint Mark the Evangelist, in which he had been a presbyter, and to build a monastery there.

He therefore searched through cemeteries and churches situated farther from the city, to see whether he could find the bodies of holy martyrs; and when he found them, he had them transferred to the title he had built with magnificent workmanship.

It happened by chance that, at the time when he was about to open the tomb of the blessed Hermes and remove his sacred body from it, one of our men, who had come to Rome that same year to pray, as is customary for penitents, was among the multitude of pilgrims gathered at the martyr’s basilica.

After carefully observing what was being done, he conceived the hope of obtaining relics of the aforementioned martyr—though with a simple heart, yet not without reason. He approached the deacon Deusdona, whom we mentioned frequently in the first book, and earnestly begged him to obtain from the custodians of the place even the smallest portion of these relics and to arrange for it to be brought to me.

The deacon immediately granted his request and promised that he would do so without delay. After paying the custodians, he obtained not only relics of Saint Hermes but also those of Saints Protus and Hyacinthus, whose bodies had been placed in the same basilica.

He arranged for these to be sent through one of his retainers, whose surname was Sabbatinus, together with our own man, who had persuaded him to undertake the task. Whatever he was able to obtain from the body of the blessed Hermes, however, he himself brought to us when he came, as a most precious gift.

When we were informed of the arrival of the relics of Saints Protus and Hyacinthus, we went out to meet them. Receiving them honorably, as was proper, and bringing them into the basilica with hymns and prayers, we placed them beside the bodies of the blessed Marcellinus and Peter, together with the bier on which they had arrived.

On the following day, a certain woman from a nearby little estate called Baldradestat entered with the rest of the people, possessed by a demon. The evil spirit began to roar, beat her against the pavement after throwing her down, and publicly reveal his wickedness by confessing it.

When the priest who was exorcising him asked who he was, where he had come from, and when and why he had entered her, he answered each question. He testified that he was not merely a demon but the worst of all living beings.

When the priest further asked him the cause of such great wickedness, he admitted that an evil will had given it to him. When he was again asked whether he had ever been in heaven, he confessed that he had been in heaven and had been cast down from it because of pride.

When the same priest asked whether he had seen Christ the Lord, he replied that he had seen him in hell, at the time when Christ had deigned to die and descend there for the salvation of the human race.

92. When the questioning reached the point at which he was asked whether he knew the names of the martyrs whose relics had been brought into that church the day before, he said:

“Their names are very well known to me, because when they suffered I was present, and I was tortured by intense envy of their eternal glory. Even now I suffer them here as my most grievous enemies, for they torment me with an unbelievable torment and compel me, against my will, to leave this vessel in which I have long lain hidden.”

The priest said to him:

“When you have come out, where will you go?”

He replied:

“I shall go along an evil road and seek distant and deserted regions.”

After this, when he had explained, at the priest’s command, both the occasion and the manner of his entry, he turned to the woman and said:

“Unhappy woman, before I leave I shall crush and shatter your bones, and I shall leave you disabled and mindful of our fellowship.”

When she, as though conscious of her weakness, began in a humble and supplicating voice to implore the help of the saints, he immediately began to roar and rebuke her fiercely through her mouth, commanding her to be silent when she tried to speak.

For us who were present, it was an extraordinary sight: the unclean spirit spoke through the same little woman in such a different manner, and reproduced now a male voice, now a female one, so exactly that it seemed as though not one but two persons were fiercely arguing within her and hurling insults at one another.

And in truth there were two, differing from one another in will: one was the demon, desiring to beat the body he possessed; the other was the woman, desiring to be freed from the enemy who held her captive. This difference of wills could be understood clearly and plainly from the difference in their voices and the dissimilarity of the words they exchanged [Manuscript adds: “in alternation”].

When, therefore, the office of the heavenly mystery had been completed according to custom, and we had left the basilica to attend to bodily needs, we ordered the woman to wait there with the custodians until our return. We trusted that, through the power of Christ and the merits of his martyrs, her wicked possessor would soon depart.

Nor was our hope disappointed. After returning to the church following our meal and expelling the demon, we found her healthy and unharmed, fully in possession of her mind, and exulting in the praises of God.

This sign is known to have been completed at the arrival of the relics of the blessed martyrs of Christ, Protus and Hyacinthus, in the manner we have described. The event attributed to Saint Hermes will be made clear by the account that follows.

93. Cologne is a metropolitan city in the territory of the Ripuarians, situated on the Rhine. From there came a certain woman who had been so weakened from the loins downward by a longstanding relaxation of the nerves that, deprived of the use of her legs and feet, she could move only while seated, with her legs stretched out in front of her and her hands placed on the ground for support, propelling herself in this fashion and thus taking the place of walking.

When she heard of the miracles and powers that the Lord had worked through his holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter in healing the sick and infirm, she eagerly desired to come to their basilica. Since she could not conveniently travel by any other means, she was carried in a merchant ship by men who were going there for the feast of those same saints.

She arrived there on the feast day and remained for some time in the hope of recovering her health. But when she saw that her cure had been delayed—and indeed it had been delayed, not denied, because it was to occur not elsewhere but there, and not then but at another time—she decided to travel to Mainz.

The feast of Saint Alban the martyr was approaching there [Note: Saint Alban the martyr is commemorated at Mainz on 21 June], and in that city there is both a basilica and a very celebrated monastery dedicated to him.

When she arrived there and prayed to the Lord before the martyr’s memorial for the restoration of her health, she saw in sleep a certain young cleric standing beside her and carrying new shoes in his hand. He ordered her to take them and put them on her feet, and she did so.

He then ordered her, wearing those shoes, to return to the place from which she had come there and await the arrival of the physician who would undoubtedly heal her.

When she awoke, she believed the vision and returned as quickly as she could to the life-giving shrine of the holy martyrs. She remained there among the other poor for two months, awaiting the fulfillment of the promise made in the vision.

Meanwhile, around the middle of August, the deacon Deusdona, whom we mentioned frequently in the first book of this work, came from Rome and brought us, as a great gift, one joint of the finger of the blessed martyr Hermes.

We received it, placed it in a small reliquary, and set it in the upper part of the basilica, above the western entrance to the church itself.

But the woman who, as I have said, had come there after being divinely instructed by the vision, and who had now completed two months without seeing any of the promised assistance arrive, began to think that she had been deceived by an empty dream and started planning her return to her homeland.

She arranged with merchants who would take her back that on the following Sunday, which would fall on the fifth day before the Kalends of September together with the annual feast of Saint Hermes [Note: This was the year 830, with Dominical Letter B], she would board their ship as it returned to her region.

The night preceding without doubt the appointed day of departure had already arrived. After we had completed the nocturnal office according to custom and had gone out to rest [Manuscript adds: “from the church”], while the others were leaving, the woman, wishing to enter, sat down on the very threshold.

There, before everyone, she was overcome by a kind of stupor and remained silent for a short time. Then, when a considerable quantity of blood burst from all the toenails of her feet, she came to herself, extended her hand to those standing around, rose to her feet, and began to walk toward the martyrs’ tomb.

When she reached it, she prostrated herself in prayer before the altar and lay there until the hymn which the rejoicing and astonished multitude was singing most devoutly in praise of God had been completed.

When it ended, she rose healed, but she no longer wished to return to her homeland.

This miracle is therefore rightly attributed to the blessed Hermes, since it occurred on his feast day and beneath his relics. Yet the most holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter cannot in any way be excluded from sharing in the event, since it was performed in their basilica and since the woman who was healed had continually invoked them throughout the whole time of her pilgrimage, asking them to help her.

94. These are the events concerning the countless powers of the saints which we have decided to commit to writing and memory, either because we saw them ourselves or because we learned of them through the truthful report of the faithful.

I do not doubt that they will be agreeable reading to lovers of Christ and worshipers of his martyrs, since nothing seems impossible to them which Almighty God has been pleased to bring about.

But to unbelievers and those who detract from the glory of the saints, because I do not doubt that these things will be distasteful, I think it should be advised that they not read them at all. Otherwise, perhaps offended by the poverty of our language, they may be unable to avoid blasphemy and envy, and thus declare that they hate God and their neighbor, whom they are commanded to love.

[Col. 0593C]

[Note: This title is found in an old manuscript of the library of Saint Benedict on the Loire (Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, fourth century, part I).]

# RHYTHM OF EGINHARD, A MOST LEARNED MAN, ON THE PASSION OF CHRIST’S MARTYRS MARCELLINUS AND PETER

[*Acta Sanctorum*, Bollandists, volume I, June.]

[Col. 0593D]

### 1

There was a certain holy exorcist,  
Peter by name [Note: D. Teulet: “at Rome”],

Who followed the teaching of the great apostle Peter  
And preached the true faith of Jesus Christ to the nations.

This man was an adjurer of wicked demons  
And, powerful in speech, drove away the dark spirits;  
By the sign of the holy cross he made the sick well.

The pagans seized him and bound him in harsh chains;  
After mangling him through many kinds of torture,  
At last they committed him to a dark prison.

In their folly they thought that punishment inflicted on his bodily limbs  
Could prevail to remove the faith of Christ.  
But his heart, fixed upon heaven, remained unwilling to yield to whips.

A man named Arthemius was appointed his keeper.  
He bound the crowd of prisoners with dreadful chains  
And guarded the locks of the gloomy dungeon.

He had a daughter whom he loved dearly,  
A virgin by name, who, seized and tormented by a savage demon,  
Tortured her father’s heart with cruel suffering.

### 2

When Peter learned of this, he addressed Arthemius,  
The illustrious soldier of Christ both warning and exhorting him  
To obtain salvation for his daughter through holy faith:

“Believe,” he said, “in God Christ, who created all things,  
Who holds heaven and earth in his right hand  
And protects with gentle power what he possesses.”

While blessed Peter, the servant of Christ, was saying these things,  
Arthemius, the keeper of the dark prison,  
Replied at length against him, though his words were futile:

“Peter, it is neither true nor plausible  
That your Christ could save my daughter,  
When he offers no comfort to his worshipers.

I suppose he would bring aid to his servants if he could;  
But those blows disclose that he cannot do so—  
Those blows which, because of him, have long worn you out as you endure them.”

To this Peter replied with a cheerful expression:

“We confess Christ and believe in him,  
Who alone is the Savior and Lord of the ages.

He is able to do whatever pleases him,  
Powerful over heaven and earth as well as over the waves of the sea;  
The whole heaven with its stars serves him.

Whenever he wishes, he can break  
The hard bonds of the chains with which I am bound  
And make me safe from every punishment of torture.

But I believe that he does not wish to obstruct my reward;  
Rather, he wishes to cleanse me from sins  
And bring me through the torments of suffering to everlasting glory.

Nevertheless, Arthemius, I would like you to test  
Whether what we believe about Christ is true or false,  
And whether it is true that we say he is so powerful.”

[Col. 0595C]

### 3

At this, the keeper of the prison cave, still not believing, said:

“Let what you urge be done, and let it be clear today  
What your Christ, whom you ask me to believe in, can accomplish.

Behold, I shall now add chains to your chains;  
I shall leave you shut up in this dark prison  
And fasten the doors of the cave with stronger bolts.

If your Christ frees you from such heavy bonds,  
And, once released, restores you safe and sound,  
I shall believe in him and worship him as God without doubt—

Provided that I see my dear daughter redeemed,  
Through Christ himself, from the power of that demon  
By whom she is tormented.”

Then the strong Peter, the servant of Christ, smiled and said:

“A weak faith can be strengthened  
If you fulfill in deeds what you have promised in words;

If you see me, without human help or assistance,  
Freed from this dark prison in which I am confined,  
Entering the threshold of your house on foot.

You will verify that he whom you left shut up in the dark prison  
Is standing before you, not merely by looking at him  
But by examining him through the touch of your hands.”

At these words Arthemius repeatedly shook his head.  
Not believing that God could accomplish such great things,  
He answered Peter, the servant of Christ, in these words:

“Man, deranged in mind, you speak nonsense,  
Which I think has come upon you because of the many sufferings  
That you have long endured for the Christian sect.”

[Col. 0596A]

### 4

So he spoke and departed, making his way home.  
To his wife, whose name was Candida,  
He reported Peter’s words, greatly astonished and amazed.

His wife, with a believing heart despite his doubt, said  
That she was amazed he had wanted to call insane  
The man whom he had heard promise the restoration of their daughter’s health.

Nor, she said, could what he had promised be long delayed;  
He declared that he would accomplish it at the present time,  
And that what he had said and promised would become clear that very day.

But he, opposing her, rebuked his wife  
For believing these words and called her foolish,  
Because she believed that Peter’s Christ was so powerful a God.

“There is no divinity,” he said, “not even Jupiter himself,  
Who could release him, shut up as he is, from his chains  
Or let him go free from the dark pit of the cave.”

She, believing Peter’s words, by which he had promised  
That through the power of Jesus Christ he could perform wonders,  
Replied to her resisting husband in these terms:

“This is what will increase the glory of his God:  
That through him will be done what the great divinities  
Now worshiped by us are unable to accomplish.”

### 5

While they discussed these things together, taking turns in argument,  
And, as the sun sank beneath the horizon, the stars brought forth the night,  
Behold, Peter appeared, as he had promised, to the astonishment of all.

He carried the sign of the cross in his hand  
And shone in a radiant white garment.  
He showed himself to be a true servant of Christ and no impostor  
While he was handled by the hands of many.

When Arthemius saw this, immense astonishment seized him.  
Without delay he threw himself at Peter’s feet,  
Crying out in a loud voice that Christ was the one true God.

His wife and his entire household likewise declared  
That there was no one but Christ, all-powerful over creation,  
Whom blessed Peter had preached and worshiped.

At his arrival, the demon that had long possessed and tormented their daughter  
Fled immediately and, though unwillingly, proclaimed the man of God,  
So that the terrible evil might be heard aloud in the open air [Note: D. Teulet: “openly”]:

“The power of Christ,” he said, “remaining in you, Peter,  
Has driven me from the virgin whom I held until now.”

### 6

While Peter was doing these things through the power of the Spirit,  
Swift rumor immediately flew through the neighboring places  
And gathered a great number of men and women.

No fewer than three hundred men came together,  
And an even larger number of women streamed in.  
All alike marveled at the holy glory of Christ,

For they all saw that, in the name of Christ,  
Every illness was healed by heavenly grace  
And demons were driven away through Peter’s sacred commands.

Seeing this, they desired with pure hearts to receive  
The saving faith of Christ, and at the same time they begged  
To merit being washed in the sacred waters of the font.

At once, summoned by Peter, there came the servant of Christ,  
The great martyr and confessor, the presbyter Marcellinus.

To confirm the newly formed people by baptism.

When these things had been fulfilled in due order, fourteen days passed by God’s will,

during which the saints strengthened the nation of the new people,

so that, remaining in Christ, they might not wish to worship created things,

nor embrace this life as something of great importance;

rather, they might wish to lose it for his sake.

### 7

When these things had been completed, a cruel lictor, sent by the judge,

ordered all who had been shut up in the foul prison

to appear before the judge at the first hour of night.

As soon as the keeper of the dark prison heard this,

he addressed the prisoners who were present in gentle words,

telling them all to go wherever each one wished.

“Whoever,” he said, “thinks of attaining the palm of the kingdom,

let him not hesitate to go with me into the presence of the serene judge,

there to undergo punishment [Note: [Col. 0597D] D. Teulet: “let him hesitate”].

But if anyone is not yet able to despise worldly life,

and has been terrified by fear of torments,

let him go free wherever his own will leads him.”

But behold, at the first cockcrow of the night,

the judge rises watchful and, with raging voice, orders

that the guilty, all bound, be brought before his sight.

The keeper of the darkness of the prison stands ready before him and says:

“Peter the exorcist, whom you had ordered to be punished,

by the power of his Christ has released all the prisoners;

and, freed from their chains, he ordered them to go free.

He himself, however, retaining a certain Marcellinus with him,

remains in the custody into which he had once been sent.”

When he heard this, the furious deputy orders

that Arthemius, beaten with lead and bound,

be received into a dark and narrow confinement.

### 8

But the savage judge, intending to question

the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter about their deeds,

orders them to stand before his tribunal.

When he sees them standing before him with grim faces,

he first decides to address them in gentle words,

hoping thereby to change the purpose of their minds:

“I should say,” he declared, “that you could be punished with a lesser penalty,

if I did not see that all the criminals who had been confined with you

in the prison’s cavern had escaped,

and if I did not know that this had been done according to your Christian doctrine,

by which you wickedly deceive the minds of the wretched,

bewitching and misleading them through your cunning magical arts.”

To him the great martyr of Christ, the priest Marcellinus,

bearing in his breast a brave spirit full of devotion,

returned a few words, but words of no small weight:

“He is not a criminal, nor should he be called guilty,

who, having abandoned paganism, has begun to believe in Christ

and judges that he ought to serve him with a sound mind.

Whoever does this will be called a son of the Most High God,

and, freed from all the filth of sins,

will truly be seen, by God’s gift, to be what he is called.”

As Marcellinus said this, the savage judge threateningly orders

that he be beaten under the fists of two men and subdued,

and thrown into a place entirely deprived of light.

There he has glass scattered after it has been broken upon the ground,

and orders the naked defender of the truth to be laid upon it [Note: [Col. 0598D] D. Teulet: “to lay”],

and, bound, to be rolled over those fragments;

he orders Christ’s servant to be deprived of all food,

so that, killed by these punishments, he might perish quickly—

the man whose faith he had seen he could not extort.

### 9

Then, seeing Peter, he addresses him with these words:

“I do not want you to think,” he says, “that you will again be tortured on the rack

or burned with flaming torches.

Rather, know that, bound with stronger knots

and fastened to a stake, you will stand tomorrow in the daylight,

and will soon end your life by the tearing of wild beasts.”

Then blessed Peter, responding with a courageous heart,

wishing to stir up the anger of the stubborn judge,

provokes his raging madness with these words:

“Since you are called Serenus, I am astonished, most mighty man,

that you bear your face so darkened by a foul cloud

that you cannot discern your own measure.

For we all know that you are mortal;

yet, as though something great remained vigorous within you,

you threaten the Christian people with immense punishments,

trusting in a most foolish and savage boldness

that the immortal faith of Christ could ever be driven

from the hearts of believers by temporal punishments.

You took Christ’s priest—whom you could have asked

to pray for your many transgressions—

beat him with fists and delivered him to prison.

Yet concerning this sorrowful deed,

that great martyr of Christ, rejoicing with true joy,

now makes no complaint;

rather, he gives worthy thanks to the Creator of all things.”

When the arbiter of torments heard this,

enraged, he orders Peter to be seized

and weighed down with the burden of chains,

and received into a dark confinement.

In a most constricted stock he furiously orders

the soles and legs of the precious martyr

to be enclosed and held fast, so that he could not get away.

### 10

But while the martyrs were separated in this manner,

an angel, sent from the summit of heaven,

came to console the blessed witness of Christ.

When he found the holy Marcellinus lying upon glass,

bound, naked in body and without clothing,

praying to Christ God, as was his custom,

he immediately released him and, covering him with his own garments,

ordered him to follow wherever he went before him,

telling him to be led to the place where Peter had been.

When they had arrived there, the true messenger of God,

after immediately freeing Peter, commanded Marcellinus

that they both follow him together as he went before them.

Following him, they suddenly entered a certain house

in which a Christian people had assembled,

those who through them had come to divine instruction.

Then the great angel instructed the martyrs

to strive to strengthen the gathered multitude

through the course of seven successive days,

and only then to present themselves to the raging tyrant,

and to show how little his power could accomplish

against the providence of God, who contains all things.

### 11

Then, on the following day, the most savage judge ordered

that his attendants visit the places where he had commanded

the martyrs to be guarded, shut up and bound together.

When they reported that they had not been found there,

he ordered them to go and bring, together with Arthemius,

his wife also, named Candida,

and their daughter, called a virgin,

from whom Peter the exorcist had expelled a demon

and whom, cleansed, he had made a believer in Christ the King.

When these people had been brought before him,

he looked at them with a savage eye

and ordered them to sacrifice to the gods—

rather, to the dreadful little specters—

and to abandon the holy faith of Christ by denying it.

When he saw that they were unwilling to do what he had commanded,

the savage man ordered that they be killed together

in a huge heap of rubble [Note: [Col. 0599D] D. Teulet omits “in”],

in the manner of condemned criminals who are crushed.

As they were being led bound along the Via Aurelia,

they suddenly saw the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter,

and with them a very large crowd of people.

At the sight of them, those who had dragged

the blessed confessors to punishment,

weighed down and crushed beneath the burden of chains,

asserted that they had fled in terror.

When the devout crowd saw the fugitives,

it hastened ahead to forestall the frightened men

and began to soothe their raging hearts with gentle words.

But the pious multitude, unable to accomplish what it wished,

held them fixed in place until Christ’s servant Marcellinus

had offered the saving sacrifice.

For in the cave where the future passion was expected,

the martyr of Christ celebrated the solemn rites of Mass.

When these had been completed, those whom he had ordered to depart went away.

### 12

Then the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter turned around,

and both together addressed the faithless people,

speaking to the raging men with these words:

“Behold, you have seen that it was in our power

to harm you as we wished

and to carry away by force those whom you held bound.

But Christian patience refused to do this;

by instilling it into the hearts of his servants,

Christ, by his gift, makes them gentle and restrained.

And even now, with heavenly grace assisting us,

we could leave this place if our inclination moved us to do so.

You, on the other hand [Note: [Col. 0600D] D. Teulet: “you, conversely”],

tell us openly at last what you are able to do.”

Then the satellites of Satan, gnashing and snarling,

first slaughtered Arthemius himself, whom they were dragging,

striking him with a hard sword and making him a martyr.

They joined his wife and daughter to his death;

they threw them headlong over the threshold of the crypt

and buried them beneath stones and great masses of sand.

### 13

Then they bind the blessed defenders of the truth,

Marcellinus and Peter, eager for martyrdom,

and fasten them in chains to the trunks of trees,

until they could report to the dreadful arbiter of torments

and learn from the judge himself, once he had given his decision,

by what kind of death the great martyrs were to be destroyed.

When he had learned all the deeds that had been carried out

and everything he had ordered,

he commands that the holy martyrs be led into a black forest

and there receive their capital sentence.

When the satellites of the demons had led them there,

they, joyful and cheerful and praising the Lord,

made the place larger for their passion.

For with their own hands they pulled out thorns and brambles,

so that, clearing it, they might make the ground pure—

the ground that was to receive their sacred blood.

Then, praying and giving each other the kiss of peace,

with knee bent, they patiently endured the executioner

and, casting off the heavy burden of the flesh,

sought heaven.

The man who had been ordered to cut down

these great martyrs of Christ with the sword

himself confessed that he had seen their spirits,

released from the bonds of the flesh, fly upward,

covered in a radiant garment of almost virginal form,

shining also with gold and the light of jewels,

surrounded by a glittering throng of angels,

rejoicing amid an immense abundance of light,

and, penetrating above all the lofty stars of the world,

lifted up to ascend to the eternal realms of heaven.

### 14

Two women are reported to have been born at Rome:

one named Lucilla, the other Firmina.

They retained the true faith of Christ in pure hearts.

They were relatives of the blessed martyr Tiburtius,

and, sitting beside his most holy tomb,

they kept vigils there while watching in a manner pleasing to God.

He himself, accompanied by the blessed men who were with him,

Marcellinus and Peter, clearly revealed to them in sleep

where the sacred bodies of those chosen men had been laid,

and at the same time admonished them

to go without delay and immediately remove them,

and take care to place them near his own body in the crypt.

Obeying the command, they went to the black forest,

carried away from there the ashes of the blessed men,

and, placing them in the cave, buried them in the appointed place.

They are said to have been assisted in carrying this out

by two clerics of the apostolic holy see,

whom the sacred order calls acolytes.

### 15

When these events are reported to have taken place,

they assert that the account was related

by the very man who had killed those martyrs,

and that Pope Damasus learned it from him

when, still in childhood, during those same times,

he served under a teacher and was rising

toward the highest offices of affairs,

then serving as a reader in the Roman church.

Afterward, they say, he recalled all these things

and committed them to writing

when he held the chief position of that nourishing see

and exercised authority over the whole Church.

The man who had struck the blessed martyrs,

named Dorotheus,

is said by divine grace to have reached the sacrament of baptism

when the pontiff Julius was governing the holy see.

He also undertook a public and sincere penance,

and by the uprightness of his conduct deserved to attain

the saving grace of the eternal Savior,

through the wonderfully patient endurance

of those blessed martyrs whom he had struck—

an endurance worthy to be remembered now and forever.

They, triumphing over the devil, the prince of the world,

placed in the heavenly dwellings,

rejoice forever in the presence of Christ,

through eternal ages of ages.

[Col. 0601]

## EGINHARD’S CHARTERS

[Col. 0601A]

### I. Charter by which Eginhard, with the consent of his wife Imma, grants the cell of Michelstadt with its appurtenances to the monastery of Lorsch, while retaining its usufruct

(Ann. 819, 12 September.)

(Helvich, *Lauresham Antiquities*, p. 41.)

Our Lord and Redeemer, who dwelt bodily on earth,

deigned to admonish human beings, stained by various filths of sins,

saying: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you”;

and again: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity,

so that they may receive you into eternal dwellings.”

Therefore, in the name of that almighty God who both says this and commands it,

we, Eginhard and Imma, thinking together about the salvation of our souls

and the removal of our sins,

and considering with equal devotion the attainment

of the rewards of blessed and everlasting life,

have decided to draw up this testament.

By it, with spontaneous and complete willingness,

we give—and from this day wish to be considered to have given—

the cell belonging to us by right, called Michlenstat,

situated in the district of Plumgowe,

in the forest called Odenewalt above the river Mimiling,

which the most glorious prince, our lord Emperor Hludowicus,

granted to us with the greatest generosity,

transferred from his right to ours by solemn gift,

and confirmed as our property by the authority of his charter.

This cell, as we have said, in its entirety,

with all its appurtenances and boundaries,

and with everything belonging to it,

that is, basilicas, houses and other buildings,

lands, meadows, forests, fields, pastures,

waters and watercourses,

cultivated and uncultivated places,

movable, immovable and self-moving property,

and one hundred slaves of various sex and age,

we give and transfer to the basilica or monastery

of the venerable martyr of Christ Nazarius,

called Lorsch,

which has been built in the district of the Rhine,

on the bank of the river called Wisgoz,

where at the present time the venerable man Adalung

is known to be pastor and rector of the congregation serving God as abbot.

We make the aforesaid gift and transfer on this condition:

that, as long as by divine command we live in this mortal state,

we may keep the aforesaid cell in our power

and under our administration,

without contradiction or impediment from any person or authority,

both jointly and individually in succession,

if one of us should die before the other and one survive.

If it should happen that we have sons,

one of them may succeed us in the same possession by precarious right.

After our death, however,

the aforesaid cell, in its entirety,

shall be received by the aforementioned venerable monastery

without anyone’s contradiction,

and shall remain perpetually in its power and dominion.

If anyone should wish to oppose this testament of our gift,

or attempt to tear it down or invalidate it,

may he first experience Christ and his holy martyr Nazarius

as adversaries of his impious audacity,

and, moreover, under the compulsion of the fisc,

may he be forced to pay from his own property

to the party of the aforesaid venerable monastery

a fine of one pound of gold and twelve pounds of silver.

And may this testament and this gift of ours remain firm and inviolate.

If at any time any person should produce another document in our name

that is contrary to this testament,

bearing a date earlier or later,

even if it appears or is said to have been confirmed by our hand,

may it remain void and empty and have no effect.

Rather, as we have stated above,

may this gift of ours remain firm and inviolable

with perpetual stability, supported by formal stipulation.

And so that this testament may receive complete validity

according to legal custom,

we have decided to confirm it with our own subscriptions,

and we have had it strengthened by the marks of suitable witnesses

who saw the gift itself.

—This gift was made in the monastery of Lorsch,

on 12 September,

in the sixth year of the reign of our lord Hludowicus,

the most glorious emperor,

successfully, in the name of God.

I, Eginhard, sinner and donor, have acknowledged this and subscribed with my own hand.

I, Imma, have consented and subscribed.

+ Mark of Rabangarius.

+ Mark of Warboto.

+ Mark of Wolfbert and others.

[Col. 0602C]

I, Hirmimarus, deacon and imperial notary,

at Eginhard’s request, wrote and subscribed this testament.

[Col. 0602C]

### II. Description of the places and boundaries of the estate of Michelstadt, made by Eginhard himself

(Helvich, cited above.)

Since there are certain people who, swollen with worldly pride and loving themselves,

invade things given by the faithful of Christ to holy churches or monasteries,

either to retain them for themselves by hereditary right

or to divide them as a benefice by worldly tenure,

I, Eginhard, lest the hands of wicked men prevail

over the things that I acquired from the royal hand of Emperor Hludowicus

at Michlenstat,

beseech the memory of the faithful, both those to come and those present,

to note how they were collected into one whole

and by what names they were expressed.

After I had resolved to subject the aforesaid place

to the dominion of the men of Lorsch,

I summoned those who knew the matter,

carefully investigated the boundary and the names of the places,

and ordered my notary Luther to set them down in writing

while the matter was still fresh in memory.

I did this with particular care because the estates

of many monasteries are joined to theirs,

and the benefices of different lords

are bounded on every side.

The places of the boundaries and the names of the places

are therefore designated as follows:

They begin at Mount Mamenhart

and include the whole of that same mountain as far as the road;

from the road to the double oak;

from there, between Ulenbuch and Rumpheshusen, to the oak;

from the oak to the river Bramaha;

down this river into Willinebach;

up this river as far as the stony stream;

from there to Willineburch,

entering through one gate and going out through another.

From there to the bank of the Euterun;

down this river to Langenvirst,

where Langenvirst divides.

Along Langenvirst to Breitensol;

from there through Eichendal to the river Urtella.

Up this river to Vinsterbuch;

from there to Eginhard’s Phaphenstein.

From Phaphenstein above Richgeressneitten;

from there to the summit of Clophendal,

to Clophenberck;

from there to Cuningesbrunnen.

Down this river into the Mimelingen;

up this river to Manegoldescella;

from there into the river Mosaha.

Up this river to Geroldesbrunnen;

from there to Ellenbogen, at the river Branbach.

Down that river into the Mimelingen;

from it to the oak between Grascapht and Munitat;

from there once more to Mount Mamenhart.

[Col. 0603B]

### III. Charter of Eginhard, abbot of the monastery of St. Servatius the Confessor, by which he solemnly manumits Meginfrid, a servant of that monastery elected to holy orders

(Ann. 819 or 821.)

(Dom Bouquet, *Collection of Histories*, vol. VI.)

[Col. 0603C]

Ecclesiastical authority openly admonishes,

and royal majesty also agrees with the canons

with the utmost constancy of religious observance,

that whenever any church chooses someone from its own household

to be promoted to holy orders,

the person who is then rector of that church

shall, in the presence of priests and the other clergy living canonically,

as well as noble laymen,

release him by solemn manumission from the yoke of slavery,

and confirm the liberty granted to him before witnesses

by a charter of free status.

Therefore I, Eginhard, abbot in the name of God

of the venerable monastery of Saint Servatius the confessor of Christ,

have established this servant of our church,

named Meginfrid,

who was unanimously and concordantly elected by our venerable congregation

for holy orders,

as a Roman citizen at the altar’s horn,

in the presence of priests and noble men,

by the authority of the ecclesiastical and imperial decree,

as written above.

By the delivery of this document,

which I have written to confirm his free status,

I release him from the bond of slavery,

so that from this day and time onward

he may remain entirely free and secure from every bond of servitude,

as though he had been begotten and born of free parents.

Let him proceed, finally, into the rank

that the honor of canonical liberation has granted him,

with the doors open to him, as to the other Roman citizens.

Thus from now on he shall owe neither us nor our successors

any harmful or servile service,

nor any obligation of a freedman,

but throughout all the days of his life,

under a definite and complete free status,

as do the other Roman citizens,

by this title of manumission and free status,

let him always remain fully free and secure.

Regarding the property he has

or may acquire from now on,

let him freely do whatever he wishes

according to the authority of the canons.

And so that this authority of manumission and liberty

may possess unshaken and inviolable validity,

I have confirmed it below with my own hand.

I have also asked the priests and clergy of our church,

as well as the noble laymen who were present at this release,

to confirm it below in the same manner.

Done at Utrecht on this side of the Rhine,

in the monastery of Saint Servatius,

in the sixth year, with Christ favoring,

of the empire of our lord [Hludowicus],

in the fourteenth indiction.

—I, Eginhard, abbot, have confirmed this by subscribing with my own hand.

[Col. 0604C]

### IV. [Note: [Col. 0603D] D. Mabillon first published this charter of exchange from the original, *De re diplomatica*, book VI, p. 515. Eginhard did not make this exchange as abbot of Fontenelle—for Ansegis had already been appointed in his place—but rather as abbot of Bandinium; for the vice-dominus of Bandinium is the first to subscribe our charter, and he subscribed again to the diploma immediately following, in which Eginhard is called abbot of Saint Bandinius of Ghent.]

Exchange of slaves between Eginhard, abbot, and Theodrada, abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary of Argentogil

(Ann. 824.)

(Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*.)

With the assistance of the Lord Jesus Christ,

it pleased and was agreed between the most noble Theodrada,

abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary of Argentogil,

and the venerable abbot Eginhard,

together with the consent and will of the handmaids of God residing there

and the agreement of good men,

that they should exchange or trade slaves among themselves.

And so they did.

Therefore the most excellent abbess Theodrada,

from the property of Saint Mary,

gave to the party of Abbot Eginhard a certain man

named Gulfocus the priest [Note: [Col. 0603D] D. Mabillon calls this passage noteworthy because among the exchanged slaves the name Gulfocus the priest is read, although slaves were always manumitted before ordination, as is clear from the canons and from the wording of the preceding charter. Ducange, who cites this passage under the word “priest,” maintains that slaves sometimes assumed priestly character without their servile condition being altered. This was not entirely unheard of, and is established by the canons issued against such ordinations. But it is scarcely probable that this was tolerated in connection with the royal court. It should be noted, however, that the charter calls Gulfocus a priest, not a slave. Hence one may conjecture that he was manumitted before assuming the priesthood, though against the will of the abbess of Argentogil, who owned him and who accepted two slaves in Gulfocus’s place as compensation. This is provided for by the amended Salic Law (title XXVIII, section 2): “If anyone has released another’s slave . . . let him be judged liable for thirty-five solidi, and restore the principal in his place, and let the slave’s own master receive the slave’s property.” Here another slave is given in place of the principal, but nothing concerning property; presumably because a freedman has none.]

Likewise, in compensation for this matter,

the venerable lord Abbot Eginhard gave in return

to the party of Saint Mary two slaves,

named Imboldo and Vulframno,

so that from this day onward

each party might freely enjoy in every respect

whatever it chose to do, according to its own need,

with what each of us had received.

And, for the sake of firmness,

we inserted this agreement between ourselves and our successors:

that we should make or have made two documents

concerning this matter, written in identical terms.

And so we did.

Neither we nor our successors

shall ever presume to bring any accusation or claim

against the other party concerning what it received from its counterpart.

Whoever does so shall lose the thing he received

and, in addition, under compulsion of the fisc,

shall be forced to pay his counterpart

one pound of gold and six pounds of silver.

His claim shall have no effect,

but these present exchanges shall remain firm and stable.

—Done at Argentogil, before the basilica of Saint Mary,

in the eleventh year of the reign of our most pious lord Emperor Hludowicus.

+ Mark of Egisharius, vice-dominus.

+ Mark of Theotboldus.

+ Mark of Derulfus.

+ Mark of Berharius.

+ Mark of Anelo.

+ Mark of Anselucus.

[Col. 0605B]

### V. Charter of Eginhard, abbot of Saint Blandinium at Ghent, by which he grants Nordbert on lease certain property transferred by Nordbert to the monastery of Blandinium

(Ann. 830, 21 January.)

(Teulet, *Works of Eginhard*.)

The venerable Eginhard, abbot in Christ.

Since it is not unknown how you bought your property,

transferred it to our monastery,

assigned it and confirmed it for the use of our brothers,

but afterward you made a request

and our will did not refuse,

that we should grant you, Nordbert,

by our benefice,

that property and the land which Thiodsumda had possessed,

we have done so.

And, for your honor, whenever you should come to our monastery

after some time had passed,

we shall arrange to provide you with a portion.

And, in return for the usufruct,

you have undertaken to pay us a census from those properties,

so that every year, on the feast of Saint Martin,

you must give two denarii,

and the brothers must receive that census.

And this pleased and was agreed between us:

you shall have no license to sell, give away, alienate,

exchange, or otherwise put into jeopardy

the properties themselves,

except that, as long as you live,

you may use and improve them.

After your death,

the property that you bought and held as our benefice,

and the allod that you previously transferred,

from that day the brothers shall have

for their table and their use.

And Odbert may pay a census for this as a cleric,

at two denarii,

and the brothers who are within the monastery

shall receive that census on your anniversary,

for your soul.

—This lease was made in the public monastery of Blandinium,

on 21 January,

in the sixteenth year of the reign

of our most glorious lord Emperor Hludowicus.

+ I, Eginhard, abbot, have acknowledged and subscribed.

—Mark of Egesharius, vice-dominus.

—Mark of Baduricus, custodian, priest (thus).

—Mark of Wincgarius, dean, priest.

—Mark of Fletuualdus, priest.

—Mark of Ermenlandus, priest.

—Mark of Regenmundus, priest.

—Mark of Thegenlandus, priest.

—Mark of Hrodgarius, deacon.

—Mark of Johannus, subdeacon (thus).

—Mark of Odric, subdeacon.

—Mark of Teutmundus, cleric.

—Mark of Folcuuinzo, cleric.

—Mark of Sigebertus, cleric.

—Mark of Brunhardus, cleric.

—Mark of Adalgarius, deacon.

—Mark of Egelmundus, priest.

[Col. 0606B]

—Mark of Erchenmarus, priest.

—I, Rinhadus, priest, wrote this.

[Col. 0606B]

### VI. Charter of the same kind for Engelhard

(Ann. 830 or 839, 7 September.)

The venerable Eginhard, abbot of the monastery of Blandinium,

to our beloved friend Engelhard.

Since it is not unknown how you transferred

and confirmed an allod of yours to our monastery,

namely, in the district of Rodaninse [Note: [Col. 0605D] Later the march of Rhoden.],

at a place called Facum,

near the little river Absentia,

that is, there a house with a courtyard,

together with other buildings and a *watriscapud* [Note: [Col. 0605D] Kilian Dufflaens, in his *Etymological Dictionary of the Germanic Language*, interprets *waeter-schapp* as an aqueduct or watercourse. Hasselt, however, cites several passages from the customs of Belgium by which this interpretation appears to require some further extension, since the passages concern colonists living in the *waeter-schapp* of Sparendam. *Watriscapud* may therefore be understood as a canal or watercourse together with the estates lying along both banks, or as a small estate enclosed on every side by water and protected by embankments, of which many such examples can be seen in Belgium. See Ducange’s *Glossary*, under “Aquagium.”],

and arable land,

and in Vacheria an acre,

with fifteen measures for sowing,

and there, in a little meadow, four cartloads of hay to be gathered,

and in Wielingahem [Note: [Col. 0606D] Today Wieleghem or Wyleghem, near Oudenaarde],

a meadow yielding twelve cartloads of hay.

You transferred and confirmed all these things,

and everything belonging to that house,

to our monastery.

But afterward you made a request,

and our will did not refuse,

that we should grant that allod to you, Engelhard,

and to your wife Heletrada,

by our benefice.

We have done so,

and have released it to Heletrada and your sons,

so that you may be secure, without service or rent.

And, in return, by our benefice,

we grant you your inheritance,

the property that Engelramnus donated and confirmed

to the monastery of Blandinium,

namely, in the same district of Rodaninse

and in the same estate called Facum,

near the little river Absencia,

there a house with a courtyard,

together with other buildings,

and in the field called Facheria an acre,

where eleven measures can be sown,

and in the little meadow three cartloads of hay for mowing,

and in Wielingahem twelve cartloads for gathering hay.

All these things, and everything belonging to that house,

we grant to you, Engelhard and Heletrada,

for use,

and for both properties you shall pay rent:

every year, on the feast of Saint Martin,

you must give four denarii.

The one of you who outlives the other

may possess both properties and give the rent.

After their deaths, their sons may hold this property

subject to a rent of six denarii.

After the death of their sons,

their nearest relatives may hold it subject to rent.

—This lease was made on 7 September,

in the twenty-seventh year of the reign

of our most glorious lord Emperor Hludowicus.

+ I, Eginhard, abbot, have acknowledged and subscribed.

. . . . . . . hardus [notary], called [I] wrote.

[Col. 0607A]

## APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF EGINHARD

### ABBREVIATION [Note: [Col. 0607D] I believe the author of this abbreviation to have been Eginhart, chancellor of Emperor Charles the Great. By the Chronicle that he abbreviated are to be understood the two books of the venerable Bede entitled *On the Six Ages of the World* and *On Times*. LAMB. —Pertz, however, in the preface to the *Life of Charlemagne*, p. 429, says: “Lambecius’s attempt to attribute to him [Eginhard] the Abbreviation of the Chronicle from the Creation of the World up to the year 809 rests on no foundation whatsoever.” EDIT.]

### OF THE CHRONICLE

(Lambecius, *Commentaries on the Vienna Library*.)

[Col. 0607B]

When Adam was 130 years old, he begot Seth;

Seth, when he was 105 years old, begot Enos,

while Adam was alive and was 235 years old.

For Enos, when he was 90, begot Cainan,

while Adam was alive and was 325 years old.

Cainan, when he was 70, begot Mahalaleel,

while Adam was alive and was 395 years old.

Mahalaleel, when he was 65, begot Jared,

while Adam was alive and was 460 years old.

Jared, when he was 162, begot Enoch,

while Adam was alive and was 622 years old.

Enoch, when he was 65, begot Methuselah,

while Adam was alive and was 687 years old.

Methuselah, when he was 187, begot Lamech,

while Adam was alive and was 874 years old.

Lamech, when he was 172, begot Noah.

Noah, when he was 500 years old, begot Shem.

When Shem was 100 years old, the Flood occurred;

and here the total of 1,656 years is completed.

In the second year after the Flood,

Shem, being 102 years old, begot Arphaxad.

Arphaxad, when he was 35, begot Shelah.

Shelah, when he was 30, begot Eber.

Eber, when he was 24, begot Peleg.

Peleg, when he was 30, begot Reu.

Reu, when he was 32, begot Serug.

Serug, when he was 30, begot Nahor.

Nahor, when he was 29, begot Terah.

Terah, when he was 70, begot Abraham.

Here the total of the second age is completed,

having 292 years;

and the years of the two ages together amount to 1,948.

When Abraham was 100 years old, he begot Isaac.

Isaac, when he was 60, begot Jacob.

Jacob, when he was 90, begot Joseph,

who lived 110 years.

From Joseph until the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt

under Moses as leader were 145 years;

from Israel’s departure until Joshua were 40 years;

from Joshua until Othniel were 26 years;

from Othniel until Aoth [Al.: Ehud] were 40 years;

from Aoth until Deborah were 80 years;

from Deborah until Gideon were 40 years;

from Gideon until Abimelech were 40 years;

from Abimelech until Tola were 3 years;

from Tola until Jair were 23 years;

from Jair until Jephthah were 22 years;

from Jephthah until Abessan were 6 years;

from Abessan until Achialion were 7 years;

from Achialon until Labdon were 10 years;

from Abdon until Samson were 8 years;

from Samson until Eli were 20 years;

from Eli until Samuel were 40 years;

from Samuel until Saul were 12 years;

from Saul until David were 20 years.

Here the total of the third age is completed,

with 942 years;

and the years of the three ages together amount to 2,890.

From David to Solomon there are 40 years; from Solomon to Rehoboam 40 years are reckoned; from Rehoboam to Abijah there are 17 years [Col. 0608B]; from Abijah to Asa there are 3 years; from Asa to Jehoshaphat 41 years; from Jehoshaphat to Jehoram 25 years; from Jehoram to Azariah there are 8 years; and from Azariah to Athaliah there is 1 year. From Athaliah to Joash there are 6 years; from Joash to Amaziah 40 years; from Amaziah to Uzziah 29 years. From Uzziah to Jotham there are 52 years; from Jotham to Ahaz 16 years; from Ahaz to Hezekiah 16 years; and from Hezekiah to Manasseh 29 years. From Manasseh to Amon there are 55 years; from Amon to Josiah 2 years; from Josiah to Jehoiakim 31 years; from Jehoiakim to Zedekiah 11 years; from Zedekiah to Nebuchadnezzar 11 years. Here the reckoning of the fourth age ends, containing 473 years; the four ages together amount to 3,363 years.

The fifth age extends for 30 years to Cyrus; from Cyrus to Cambyses there are 30 years; from Cambyses to Darius 9 years; from Darius to Xerxes [Col. 0608C] 36 years; from Xerxes to Artaxerxes 21 years; and from Artaxerxes to Darius 40 years. From Darius to the later Artaxerxes there are 19 years; from Artaxerxes to the other Artaxerxes there are 40 years; from Artaxerxes to Arses there are 26 years; from Arses to Darius there are 4 years; from Darius to Alexander 6 years; from Alexander to Ptolemy 5 years; and from Ptolemy to Philadelphus 40 years. From Philadelphus to Euergetes there are 38 years [Bede incorrectly: 33]; from Philopator to Epiphanes 17 years; and from Epiphanes to Philometor 24 years. From Philometor to the other Euergetes there are 35 years; from Euergetes to Soter 29 years; from Soter to Alexander 17 years; from Alexander to Ptolemy there are 10 years; from Ptolemy to Dionysius 8 years; from Dionysius to Cleopatra 30 years; and from Cleopatra to Julius Caesar 2 years. [Col. 0608D] From Julius to Octavian Augustus there are 5 years; and from Octavian Augustus to Christ 42 years. Here the fifth age ends, containing 589 years; and the five ages together amount to 3,952 years.

From the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ to Tiberius 14 years are counted; from Tiberius to Christ’s Passion there are 18 years; from Christ’s Passion to Gaius 5 years; from Gaius to Claudius 4 years; and from Claudius to Nero 14 years [Bede: 13]. From Nero to Vespasian there are 14 years; from Vespasian to Titus 8 years [Bede: 10]; from Titus to Domitian 2 years; and from Domitian [Col. 0609A] to Nerva 16 years. From Nerva to Trajan there is 1 year; from Trajan to Hadrian 14 years [Bede, more correctly: 19]; from Hadrian to Antoninus there are 21 years; and from Antoninus to the other Antoninus 23 years [Bede: 22]. From Antoninus to Commodus there are 19 years; from Commodus to Helvius Pertinax 13 years [Bede, less correctly: 3]; from Helvius to Severus there is 1 year; from Severus to Antoninus Caracalla 18 years; from Antoninus Caracalla to Macrinus 7 years; from Macrinus to Aurelius there is 1 year; and from Aurelius to Alexander 4 years. From Alexander to Maximinus there are 13 years; from Maximinus to Gordian 3 years; from Gordian to Philip 6 years [Bede: 7]; from Philip to Decius 7 years; from Decius to Valerian 3 years [Bede: Decius, 1 year; Gallus Volusianus, 2 years]; from Valerian to Claudius 15 years; from Claudius to Aurelian 2 years; from Aurelian to [Col. 0609B] Probus 7 years [Bede: 5]; from Probus to Carus 5 years [Bede: 7]; and from Carus to Diocletian 2 years.

From Diocletian to Constantine there are 20 years [Bede adds: Maximian and Severus, 2 years]; from Constantine to Constantius 21 years [Bede, more correctly: 31]; from Constantius to Julian 24 years; and from Julian to Jovian 2 years. From Jovian to Valentinian there is 1 year; from Valentinian to Valens 11 years [Bede: 13]; and from Valens to Theodosius 4 years. From Theodosius to Arcadius there are 17 years; from Arcadius to Honorius 13 years; from Honorius to Theodosius 15 years; from Theodosius to Marcian 26 years; and from Marcian to Leo 17 years [Bede, more correctly: 7; and he adds: from the elder Leo to Leo his son, 17 years]. From Leo to Zeno there is 1 year; and from Zeno to Anastasius there are 16 years [Bede: 17].
