From Anastasius to [Col. 0609C] Justin there are 27 years [Bede: 26]; from Justin to Justinian 9 years; from Justinian to Justin 39 years; from Justin to Tiberius 16 years [Bede: 11]; from Tiberius to Maurice 4 years [Bede: 7]; and from Maurice to Phocas 20 years [Bede: 21]. From Phocas to [Col. 0610A] Heraclius there are 8 years; from Heraclius to Constantine there are 26 years [Bede adds: who was the son of Heraclius; from Constantine, son of Heraclius, to Heracleonas, 6 months; from Heracleonas and his mother Martina to Constans, Heraclius’s grandson, 2 years; from Constans to Constantine (Pogonatus), his son, 28 years]. From Constantine to Justinian there are 17 years; from Justinian to Pippin the Elder 2 years; from Pippin the Elder to Charles 27 years; from Charles to Pippin and Carloman 27 years; and from Pippin and Carloman until Pippin was established as king there are 10 years. From Pippin to Charles and Carloman there are 17 years; and from Charles and Carloman until Charles there are 4 years. From that point Lord Charles alone assumed the kingdom and, with God’s protection, governs happily to the present year [Note: [Col. 0609C] This was the year 809 of the common Christian era, as is clear from the following reckoning both of the years of the world and of the years of the reign and empire of Charlemagne. As for the preceding computation of the succession of the Roman emperors, it has been corrupted in many places, both in Bede and here, through the fault of unlearned and negligent scribes, and must be corrected with the aid of the more accurate chronology customary in our age.]—which is the forty-second year of his reign and the ninth of his empire. The total sum of the years from the origin of the world to the present year is 4,761. [Col. 0610B]

From Adam to the Nativity of Christ 3,952 years are reckoned; from that point to his Passion, 33 and a half years. If, in the first year in which Adam was made, you place the Easter term on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April and the concurrent on VII, it will fall on that very Wednesday on which people believe the stars were created, together with the full moon and the equinox. If, with such a term and such a concurrent, you begin the cycle and, by counting, carry the aforesaid number of years through to the Nativity or Passion of Christ, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity you will have the term on the Kalends and the concurrent on IV; and in the year of the Passion the term will be on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May and the concurrent on IV.

But if you wish to reckon 5,199 years from Adam to the Lord’s Nativity, and complete the computation of those years according to the aforesaid method by means of concurrents and terms, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity you will have the Easter term on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May and the concurrent on I; while in the year of the Passion the term will be on the fourth day before the Nones [Col. 0610C] of April and the concurrent on II. If, however, you declare that there were 5,500 years from Adam to Christ, and compute them according to that same rule, the result for the year of the Lord’s Nativity will be an Easter term on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April and the concurrent on VII, while in the year of the Passion the term will be on the Nones of April and the concurrent on VII.

[Col. 0609C]

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 840.

CLAUDIUS, BISHOP OF TURIN.

[Col. 0609C]

HISTORICAL NOTICE ON CLAUDIUS.

(In Antonio, *Bibliotheca veterum Hispanorum*.)

[Col. 0609D]

Claudius, bishop of Turin, the most obstinate Iconoclast, or enemy of sacred images, a disciple of Felix, bishop of Urgell, came from our Spain, where he had originated, to the Italians at the appointment of Louis the Pious, in order to teach the Italians the sacred doctrine in which he excelled. For this purpose he was made bishop of Augusta Taurinorum in Gaul, in the region of Subalpine Gaul or Piedmont.

Jonas, bishop of Orléans, whom Claudius had as his opponent, has left all these matters beyond doubt in the work he composed against Claudius’s blasphemies. He writes:

“While he [Louis, emperor and son of Charles] was happily ruling, the same Felix [of Urgell] was reborn in one of his disciples, named Claudius, just as—if I may use the words of blessed Jerome—Euphorbus was reborn in Pythagoras. Although this Claudius did not, like Felix his teacher, a Nestorian heretic, attack the rule of the Catholic faith, he nevertheless attempted through that same disciple of his to hurl poisoned weapons against the traditions of the Church.” [Col. 0611A]

Concerning Claudius’s homeland, education, journey to Italy, and episcopal appointment at Turin, Jonas says shortly afterward:

“He, therefore, of whom we are speaking, sprung from that same Spain and attached from early youth to the discipleship of that same Felix, served for some time in the office of the priesthood in the palace of the aforementioned most glorious and serene, God-beloved Augustus [Louis]. But in order to provide for the benefit of others through the teaching of evangelical preaching, which appeared to be present in him to a considerable degree, he was appointed bishop of the Church of Turin through the pious devotion of that most devout prince.”

Jonas goes on to say that Claudius rejected and seriously condemned the use of sacred images and of the cross and other salutary signs, as well as the relics and tombs of the saints. Upon hearing this, he says, Claudius was admonished by a certain father of monks, Theodemir, through a letter, to desist from these practices. Our pseudo-historians maintain that this Theodemir later became bishop of Calahorra (Luitprand, under the year 840; Julian, no. 431); but in truth he belonged to the Gallican Church, as the most learned man John Mabillon prudently recognized from the words of Jonas in Book I of his *Analecta vetera* (p. 45). [Col. 0611B]

Jonas continues that Claudius replied to these letters with such insolence that he boasted that all the Gauls and the faithful of Germany were ensnared in the traps of idolatry and empty superstitions. Yet Jonas himself was mistaken and departed from the straight path in the opposite direction, since he allowed the use of images—not for adoration, but only for instruction—in accordance with the synod of Frankfurt held in his time (Baronius, vol. IX, under the year 825, no. 61).

The following words of the same Jonas prove that Claudius’s letters grew into a large and lengthy work:

“Meanwhile, it is reported that, in attacking that same abbot and the entire Gallican Church, he vomited forth a book of such great length that in size it surpassed David’s Psalter by fifty psalms. Of it only a certain excerpt has reached the hands of our humble self, and this is its beginning: ‘Title of the book: Apology and Reply of Claudius, Bishop, against Theodemir, Abbot.’” [Col. 0611C]

Jonas refuted this work in three books, called in the older editions *On the Cult of Images*. In reality, the first was *On the Cult of Images and the Adoration of the Cross*; the second, specifically and again, *On the Cult of the Cross*; and the third, *On Pilgrimages Undertaken to the City*. Their entire contents, and especially the testimonies already mentioned, together with the complete preface of the first book addressed to King Charles the Bald, son of Louis the Pious, show that Claudius was the Church’s most pernicious enemy; Jonas had undertaken the work at Louis’s command. Yet Claudius was no longer alive when Jonas published these writings—he had died while Louis the Pious was still living, or shortly after Louis’s death, for Louis died in 860; nevertheless, Jonas says that he would eradicate the remnants of Claudius’s heresy, adding this concerning other works of Claudius, which were to be condemned to eternal infamy:

“But because, as I have learned from a truthful report” (he says in the preface to Book I), “not only does the error in question revive in the minds of his disciples, but, under his teaching, the Arian heresy is also found to be flourishing—of which he is said to have compiled certain written records and to have left them through secret cunning in the library of his bishopric [perhaps: episcopal residence], for the purpose of attacking the simplicity and purity of the Catholic and apostolic faith—I have not dared, at the admonition and encouragement of the sons of the holy Church of God, but to take up again for detailed examination the work I had set aside.”” [Col. 0611D]

Thus far Jonas.

Walafrid Strabo, a writer of the same period, likewise reports something concerning Claudius’s death, condemned by his own judgment even before he was pierced by the weapons of Catholic writers. But since the following words are found in Claudius’s own *Apology*, and are to be referred to a preceding letter of Theodemir:

“‘You said this,’ you ask, ‘about Paschal, bishop of the Roman Church, who has already fallen while life was still present’”—

it is necessary to conclude that Theodemir sent his admonitory letters to Claudius before the twenty-fourth year of this era, which was the last year of Paschal’s life, and that Claudius, shortly afterward, when Eugenius II was already pope, set himself to writing the wicked *Apology*.

Apart from Jonas, Dungalus, a presbyter of the same period [called Dugalus by others, including Barthius in Book XIX, chapter 12, of the *Adversaria*], and Einhard himself, the distinguished author of the *Life of Charlemagne*, also took care in their writings to demolish this man’s false doctrines. The former’s book, *For the Cult of Sacred Images, against the Insane and Blasphemous Rants of Claudius, Bishop of Turin*, dedicated to the emperors Louis the Pious and his son Lothar, once existed in the library of Pierre Pithou (Baronius, vol. IX, under the year 825, no. 62; Labbe, *On Writers*, under Dungalus), and has already been published among the *Monuments of the Ancient Fathers*, volume IV of the *Bibliotheca*. Einhard’s little book, now no longer extant, *On the Cross to Be Adored*, whose veneration Claudius rejected, is mentioned by Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, in Letter 4 addressed to Einhard himself. [Col. 0612B]

Thus far Claudius, an enemy of God and of the true faith. But did this same man also write certain Catholic works before he abandoned a sound mind? Certainly, if the most diligent scholar Philip Labbe is correct in his dissertation *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he departs from his Bellarmine. Labbe’s view is that this Claudius was Claudius Clement, whom Bellarmine praises as a Catholic writer of several works on the sacred books, and that he is the same as Claudius of Turin, the bishop now under discussion.

Labbe, however, is greatly mistaken. He acknowledges that this Claudius Clement was Scottish by nationality, whereas he should have recognized from Jonas’s writings that the other Claudius of Turin was most clearly from Spain. This Claudius Clement the Scot is commonly distinguished from Claudius, bishop of Turin (Sixtus of Siena, Book IV of the *Bibliotheca*; Possevinus in the *Apparatus*; Bulaeus, volume I of the *History of the University of Paris*, in the catalogue of its academics).

Whatever the truth may be, this gave rise to the error of many who, confusing Claudius the Iconoclast heretic—not Spanish, as he was, but English (Ambrose of Monte Cassino, *In Triumph of Catholic Truth*, under “Adoration”; Francis Augustine ab Ecclesia, *Chronological History of the Cardinal Bishops of Piedmont*; Prateolus, *On Heretics*)—and sometimes even Scottish (the aforementioned Labbe; Thomas Dempster, *Ecclesiastical History of the Scots*, chapter 304) with the other Claudius the Scot, call him by that name.

Philip Labbe also published in the first volume of his *New Manuscript Library* a certain short chronicle by a certain Claudius, extending from the beginning of the world to the Nativity of Christ, though incomplete; he suspected that it belonged to this Claudius of Turin.

Thomas Dempster, who was generous in assigning men illustrious for the fame of his Scottish nation, praised no fewer than three men of similar name, all from Scotland, of the same period, and authors of books. The first was Saint Claudius Clement, a Benedictine monk and colleague of Alcuin, who labored to establish the academies at Paris and Pavia. Trithemius (*Book II, On Illustrious Benedictine Men*, chapter 28), Paul Langius (*Chronicle of Città di Castello*, near the end), Possevinus, Arnold Wion (*Appendices to the Tree of Life*), and others cited by Dempster mention him; Caesar Egassius Bulaeus also mentions him more than once in his *History of the University of Paris* (volume I, under the year 815, p. 146; and in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Academics*, p. 568). In my judgment, the materials which Christopher Brower communicated to us from the manuscript catalogue of the abbots of Fulda, in his notes on Rabanus’s poem 13 concerning Bruno, Einhard, Modestus, and Candidus, sent to Clement the Scot to study grammar, belong to this man, although Dempster thought otherwise.

For these first restorers of reviving letters taught the whole circle of the liberal arts, like Bede, Alcuin, and others, who did not disdain to teach grammar, through which one must enter the citadel of knowledge and wisdom. What displeases Labbe in this matter is that many have called him one of the founders of the academy of Paris, although no such academy existed at that time and it did not arise until several centuries later. He is also displeased that the same sources call him both a Benedictine monk and bishop of Auxerre. We leave the French to debate the origins of their most celebrated school. In any case, the monastic status of Clement—if this is Claudius Clement—and of Alcuin seems to be indicated by the monk of Saint Gall who wrote *On the Deeds of Charlemagne under Charles the Bald*, his nephew, published by Heinrich Canisius (volume I of the *Ancient Readings*), in addition to the more recent authorities already mentioned. [Col. 0613A]

Since the same monk is the author of this eulogy, someone might readily believe that Clement, a Scot from Ireland, and Alcuin—or rather Albinus—who were incomparably learned in secular studies and the sacred Scriptures and were received with the highest honor by Charlemagne so that they might teach wisdom to the Frankish youth, was the author not of the Spanish Claudius of Turin—for whom no achievement in sacred letters has remained in human memory—but of whatever commentaries on the sacred Bible are praised under the name of Claudius. These include, namely, the commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, dedicated to Abbot Dructerannus (Bulaeus agrees in the cited *Catalogue of the Academics of Paris*), published at Paris in 1542 in octavo and thence in the *Bibliotheca of the Fathers*; likewise the commentary on Romans and on the two Epistles to the Corinthians; and the commentary on the Gospel of Saint Matthew (Bulaeus, in the same place), preserved in manuscripts in certain museums of Gaul. If Trithemius’s account of his works is true, they also include commentaries on Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Judges, Ruth, and Joshua, whether commentaries or explanations; and also a treatise on Leviticus, whose preface and epilogue Labbe reported that he had in his hands (*On Writers*, volume I, p. 228; and in the *Specimen of the New Library*, part I, [Col. 0613C] p. 24).

Nevertheless, we remain uncertain and can argue with Labbe that this work belongs to Claudius of Turin because it is said to have been addressed in the year 823 to Theodemir the abbot, who appears to be the same man with whom our Claudius of Turin shortly afterward disputed concerning the cult of images.

At this time there exists, published by John Mabillon, the Benedictine, a man of singular industry and learning, in the *Ancient Analecta*, the previously mentioned preface of Claudius, bishop of Turin, to the books of *Instructions on the Letter and the Spirit concerning Leviticus*, addressed to Theodemir the abbot. In my judgment our Claudius most clearly reveals himself in it as the author of the work. For he laments to the aforementioned Theodemir, whom he calls his most dear brother, that he is tormented by the perversity of evil men and is weary of living. In the work itself, to whose aforementioned preface a certain fragment is appended, after adducing the words of Saint Augustine from the book *On True Religion* concerning the fact that angels are not to be worshiped, the author adds:

“This most well-fortified and highest sacrament of our faith, and this firmest imprint stamped upon our heart: in asserting and defending this truth, I have become a reproach to my neighbors and a terror to my acquaintances, so much so that those who saw us not only mocked us but also pointed us out to one another with a finger.”

From this it already appears that he was hostile to the adoration or veneration of holy spirits. It seems that he wrote these things to the same Theodemir before the *Apology*, when he was beginning to form an improper opinion about the veneration of the blessed.

In the same preface he also states that two years earlier he had sent the same Theodemir four books of *Expositions and Instructions on the Letter and the Spirit concerning Exodus*, whose beginning was: “After the exposition of the Book of Genesis.” He also mentions there an exposition of the Book of Genesis, comprising three books drawn from the sayings of the holy Fathers concerning the letter and the spirit, completed eight years earlier. We have never heard that either of these two works still exists. [Col. 0614A]

Mabillon says in his notes on this *Analecta* (p. 46) that he possesses a commentary on Leviticus in the Remigius manuscript.

Why should we not also suspect that this same author wrote the commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, formerly published under his name, and likewise on the Epistles to the Ephesians and Philippians, whose preface, addressed to Louis Augustus himself, Mabillon also published? In this preface he mentions the preceding commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians as having been completed the previous year. Mabillon likewise testifies that expositions of these and perhaps all the other Epistles of Saint Paul are preserved in the library of Fleury. [Note: [Col. 0613D] I quickly examined *The Old Library of Fleury*, by John a Bosco Celestine, published at Lyons in 1605, in octavo; nevertheless, I did not come upon Claudius of Turin.]

He also reports that a fragment of the preface to Saint Matthew was brought to light by James Ussher among the Irish letters. Certainly, from the previously mentioned preface to the *Epistles to the Ephesians and Philippians*, the following words seem to concern the vexations which began to be inflicted upon Claudius because of his doctrines:

“Although I possess many excerpts from the remaining epistles, much still remains to be sought out. But because, my sins hindering me, you have heavily burdened me in the present year, and because I am given over to excessive anxieties, I do not wish to live, nor am I able to study the Scriptures.””

Thus far he.

In the Vatican manuscript numbered 5775, a *Treatise on the Epistle to the Corinthians* is also listed under the name of Claudius of Turin. It begins, “Admonished by the Lord’s command,” and on folio 97 a second treatise on the same recipients begins, with the words, “Knowing that the holy apostle.” A preface precedes each of them, with this title: “To Theodemir, abbot, venerable in Christ and to be loved with sincere charity: Claudius, bishop by the inspiration of God’s grace,” and so forth.

A letter of Theodulf, the unworthy bishop of the Church of Terdon, follows. He says that he had the work copied and continues:

“I offer it for the love of God and of my uncle John, the venerable bishop who presided as bishop over this Church in which I now preside, and for the remedy of my soul, to blessed Columbanus, confessor of Christ, so that both the monks presently dwelling there and those who will dwell there in the future may hold it under his authority,” and so forth. “It was executed in the year 862 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the tenth indiction. Theodulf, bishop.”

A note in a more recent hand follows:

“This book belongs to the monks of Saint Justina, of the observance of the Order of Saint Benedict, residing in the monastery of Saint Columbanus at Bobbio; it was written in year 47.”

From these facts it is clear that the book was written in this ninth century, while Claudius was alive, and that it could scarcely have been unknown that this was his genuine offspring.

Dempster’s second Claudius Clement the Scot is another man, to whom he assigns commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians, written in the time of Louis the Pious, and whom he identifies with the bishop of Turin torn apart in Jonas’s books. The author recalls in his preface the expedition undertaken against the Northmen. Dempster also says that this man was praised among Latin poets by Lilio Gyraldi of Ferrara. But, unless I am mistaken, Gyraldus mentions only one poet named Clement (*On the Poets*, Dialogue 4, p. 187 in my copy), and this is the associate of Apuleius whom Apuleius himself likewise praises in his *Florida*.

Dempster also says that he was the author of *Theological Sentences*, against which Dungalus wrote; likewise, of three books of commentaries on Matthew, “which, he says, Baronius was the first to explain in volume X of the *Annals*”; but all this is utter darkness to me. He then heaps upon the same man works on the Pentateuch, Judges, Ruth, the Psalter, all Paul’s Epistles, fourteen books *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, a *Memorial of Histories*, a certain *Summary*, and finally Homilies, which he says Boston transmitted. But we know what the most learned men thought of Thomas Dempster (Labbe, *Library of Libraries*, p. 159; Hallervord, *Specimen of Latin History*, p. 8):

“His familiar acquaintance,” Ussher says, “was an inventory of books that were never written, drawn from his idle brain” (*On the Antiquities of the British Churches*, chapter 13, p. 463); elsewhere he calls him “a man of much reading, but entirely lacking judgment” (ibid., chapter 1, p. 11). [Col. 0615A]

Now Dempster’s third and final Claudius Clement, himself of the same period and nation as the two preceding men, is that Clement the Scot in eastern Francia who was a heretic and troublesome opponent to Boniface, the martyr, bishop of Mainz, and apostle of the Germans, in spreading the seed of the Gospel (see Baronius, volume IX, under the year 745, nos. 21, 24, 28, 37). But he was not their contemporary; he was much earlier than the other two, for he was condemned by Pope Zacharias at the Roman Council of 745. Nor do the matters which Christopher Brower read in the catalogue of the abbots of Fulda pertain to him, but rather to that Clement, the colleague of Alcuin.

To bring the matter finally to a close: we do not deny that Claudius of Spain, bishop of Turin, whom we believe to have been the only man of this age so called, also composed other works—not merely those relating to his wicked heresies—however much Jonas, who wrote against him after his death, and likewise Dungalus omitted to mention certain Catholic works produced by him long before. They plainly ought to have mentioned them, in order that they might thereby press more forcefully upon the most unjust deserter of the camp of faith. [Note: [Col. 0615B] The surviving fragments of Claudius of Turin, both published and still in manuscript, and the places in which the individual pieces once existed or now exist, are indicated by John Albert Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae aetatis*, under “Claudius the Spaniard,” volume I, p. 388. There were also those who accused Claudius of Arianism, but Fabricius considers this to have been said against him calumniously; and he says that the new wound inflicted upon an otherwise learned man by Richard Simon, in his criticism of Du Pin’s *Ecclesiastical Library*, volume I, p. 286 and elsewhere, was wiped away and healed.] [Col. 0615B]

[Note: [Col. 0615D] No one has given a more certain testimony concerning Claudius, bishop of Turin, than Jonas, bishop of Orléans, both in the preface and at the beginning of Book I, *On the Cult of Images against Him*:

“He, therefore, of whom we are speaking,” he says, “sprung from that same Spain and attached from early youth to the discipleship of that same Felix, served for some time in the office of the priesthood in the palace of the aforementioned most glorious and serene, God-beloved Augustus [Louis]. But in order to provide for the benefit of others through the teaching of evangelical preaching, which appeared to be present in him to a considerable degree, he was appointed bishop of the Church of Turin through the mercy of that most devout prince.”

This refutes the widespread and common error that had prevailed for many years, namely, that Claudius was Scottish by race and originated in Ireland. Even the learned Ussher of Armagh fell into this error.

Theodemir was a Gallican abbot and presided over one hundred and forty monks under the rule of Saint Benedict, as he himself testifies in the letter written against Claudius, fragments of which Jonas reports in Book III of the work mentioned above. I conclude that he was abbot in Gaul, not in Spain, as I once suspected, from the following words of Jonas in Book I, speaking of the same Claudius:

“Meanwhile, it is reported that, in attacking that same abbot and the entire Gallican Church, he vomited forth a book of such great length,” and so forth.

But in what place he was abbot has so far remained unknown to me.

Claudius wrote many works, especially commentaries on the sacred books: three books on Genesis in 814; four on Exodus in 821; and a work on Leviticus in 825, all of which he undertook at the urging of Theodemir the abbot. He also commented on the Gospel of Matthew and dedicated his work to Justus, abbot of Carrofum, in 815. In addition, he expounded all Paul’s Epistles, among them dedicating his explanation of the Epistle to the Galatians to Dructerannus, abbot of Solignac; and he dedicated the work he composed on the Epistle to the Ephesians to Louis Augustus. He also wrote certain works on the cult of sacred images and pious pilgrimages, in which he held an incorrect opinion.

Of all these works, only the exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians has been published in print, in the *Bibliotheca of the Fathers*. Ussher brought a fragment of the preface to Matthew to light among the Irish letters. The rest, apart from these two prefaces, still lies in darkness.

I found an exposition on Matthew in the library of the cathedral church of Laon. We possess commentaries on Leviticus in the Remigius manuscript, and expositions on Paul’s Epistles in two volumes in the library of Fleury.

The abbot Theodemir, Dungalus the Recluse, and Jonas, bishop of Orléans, wrote against Claudius, defending in published books the cult of sacred images and pious pilgrimages.”]

PREFACE OF CLAUDIUS, BISHOP, TO THE BOOKS OF *INSTRUCTIONS ON THE LETTER AND THE SPIRIT CONCERNING LEVITICUS*, ADDRESSED TO THEODEMIR, ABBOT.

[Mabillon, *Ancient Analecta*]

[Col. 0615C]

You compel and force me, most dear brother Theodemir, abbot, and, so to speak, rebuke me with an indignant spirit for having remained silent so long and for not obeying your command concerning my exposition of Leviticus. It is now two years since I sent you the four books of *Expositions and Instructions on the Letter and the Spirit concerning Exodus*, whose beginning is “After the exposition of the Book of Genesis”; eight years ago I published three books drawn from the sayings of the holy Fathers concerning the letter and the spirit.

In reply, you say that what happened to you is what happened to Jacob, who served for Rachel and received Leah at night. In the same way, you requested an exposition of the Book of Leviticus and received one of Exodus. Nor do I truly acknowledge that I went sufficiently astray in this matter. For just as it was not customary among them for the younger daughters to be given in marriage before the elder, so it did not seem right to me [Col. 0615D] to expound the rites of sacrifice before the ministers of the sacrifices or the place in which they were performed.

As for my inability thus far to obey your command, it was not due to laziness or negligent sluggishness, but to the dreadful assault of public affairs and the excessive perversity of evil men. These two things torment me so greatly that I am now weary of living. My wings of virtue weakened, I am unable to flee into solitude, where I might rest a little and say to God:

“Leave me, so that I may mourn my sorrow for a little while and make known to you my sin, before I go away and do not return to the land of darkness, covered by the shadow of death, where everlasting horror dwells and no order.”

[Col. 0616C] But crawling upon the earth, weeping and groaning, I cry out to God:

“Why have you rejected me, and why do I walk sadly while the enemy afflicts me?”

The work you command is indeed a good one, but it bears a great burden beyond its own strength. I do not know how something that cannot be grasped by thought can worthily be completed. Just as it is difficult for anyone to touch heaven with his hand, so it is difficult to explain all the mysteries of the divine law as you command.

But you ought to have entrusted this task to those who possess within themselves a fountain of eloquence, from which whatever is assigned to them is explained most abundantly in a richly flowing poem. On the contrary, anyone of narrow understanding, such as I am, who lacks an abundance of speech by which either to refresh others or to temper the poverty of his own dryness—[Col. 0616D] such people not only desire to say something on their own, but also dread whatever may be imposed upon them.

I recognize this in myself, possessing only a small measure of understanding and eloquence. For I have neither learned the study of secular literature nor ever had a teacher in it. As much as the learned need to speak, so much is it useful for the unlearned to remain silent. They know how to discuss great matters from small beginnings; I do not know how to offer even some small things concerning great matters. Therefore I fear what must be sought from others.

As for your command that I should note in our expositions the opinion of each individual teacher on the pages, I have read of no one who did this, except the most blessed Bede [Col. 0617A]. He did so only in two books, namely in his exposition of the Evangelists Mark and Luke. I omitted doing this because, after carefully investigating certain opinions that I had noted under the names of some authors, I later discovered that they belonged to others.

For, as you know very well, just as in these last days the Word of God, clothed in flesh from Mary, came forth into the world, and what was seen in him was one thing while what was understood was another—the appearance of flesh was evident to all, but recognition of his divinity was granted to the few and elect—so also, when the Word of God is brought to human beings through the prophets or the lawgiver, it is not brought without appropriate garments. For just as there it is clothed in flesh, so here it is veiled in the covering of the letter: the letter is seen as flesh, while the spiritual sense hidden within is perceived as divinity [Col. 0617B].

Such, then, is what we now find as we examine the book of Leviticus, in which the rites of sacrifices, the variety of victims, and the ministries of priests are described. Yet these matters according to the letter—which is as the flesh and garment of the Word of God and of his divinity—may perhaps be seen or heard by the unworthy, while the blessed are those eyes that see, beneath the veil covering the letter, the divine Spirit within; and blessed are those who bring to the hearing of these things the pure ears of the inner person.

We therefore undertake this work, with divine mercy approving, during Lent, on the seventh day before the Ides of March, in the year 823 of the Incarnation of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ [Col. 0617C].

Here ends the preface of Claudius, bishop of Turin; and, after the chapters of the first book have been prefixed, the first book of *Expositions of the Letter and the Spirit* begins.

The book has been called *Leviticus* because it treats of the ministries of the Levites and the varieties of victims, and so forth.

## At the end of the work

Because you commanded these things to be written, I have undertaken them—not on account of our learning, but because of your gracious regard. It is yours to judge more truly and to urge us by your example toward true charity [Col. 0618A], which is the highest virtue of all virtues. With respect to this charity of which I speak, I trust more in what your prayers can accomplish for me than in my own strength.

Behold, dearest brother, I have answered, as I could, some of your inquiries. For this reason I earnestly beg you: if concerning these matters about which you question me you have found anything better, or are later able to find anything better, we shall be most grateful if you make it known to us, because I prefer learning to teaching.

For that beauty of truth and wisdom—which is common to all, provided only that there is a persevering will to enjoy it, for love of which we have completed this work—does not exclude those who approach it because of the crowd of hearers surrounding it; it is not completed in time, does not move from place to place, is not interrupted by night, is not shut out by shadow, and is not subject to bodily senses [Col. 0618B]. It is near to all who, from the whole world, turn toward it and love it; it is everlasting for all. It is in no place, yet is absent nowhere; outside it admonishes, within it teaches. It changes all who see it for the better, while it is changed for the worse by no one. No one judges it, and no one judges well without it.

By this faith I separate all mutability from eternity, and in eternity itself I perceive no intervals of time, because intervals of time consist in the past and future movements of things. But nothing passes away in the eternal, and nothing is future: for whatever passes away ceases to be, and what is future has not yet begun to be. Eternity merely is; it was not, as though it no longer existed, nor will it be, as though it did not yet exist. For it alone could most truly say to the human mind, “I am who I am,” and of it one could most truly say, “He who is has sent me” [Col. 0618C].

And because this is so, we are not commanded to strive toward a creature in order to become blessed, but toward the Creator himself. If we are persuaded of him in any way other than what is proper and accords with reality, we are deceived by a most destructive error. For by proceeding toward what either does not exist or, if it exists, does not make us blessed, no one can ever attain the blessed life.

By that truth and wisdom, which is common to all, all become wise and blessed by cleaving to it. One person’s blessedness does not make another person blessed: when someone imitates him in order to become blessed, he desires to become blessed from the same source from which he sees the other made blessed—namely, from the unchangeable and common truth.

Nor does one person’s prudence make another prudent, nor one person’s courage another courageous, nor one person’s temperance another temperate, nor one person’s justice make anyone else just. Rather, a person adapts his mind to those unchangeable rules and lights of the virtues that live incorruptibly in truth and wisdom themselves—those rules and lights to which the person whom he proposes to himself for imitation also adapted and fixed his mind.

Therefore, a will cleaving to the common and unchangeable good obtains the first and greatest goods of the human being, although the will itself is a certain intermediate good. But a will turned away from the unchangeable and common good, and turned toward its own good, or toward an external or inferior good, sins.

> **[Note: [Col. 0619C] From Augustine, *On True Religion*, chapter 55.]**
>
> Therefore, let our religion not be the worship of dead human beings. If they lived piously, they are not to be regarded as seeking such honors; rather, they wish us to worship the one by whom they were enlightened, and rejoice that we are partners in their merit. They are therefore to be honored for imitation, not adored as a matter of religion. If, however, they lived badly, they are not to be worshiped wherever they may be.
>
> Whatever the highest angel worships must also be worshiped by the least human being, because human nature itself became least by failing to worship it. The wise angel is not wise from one source and the human being from another; the angel is not truthful from one source and the human being from another, but both are so from one unchangeable wisdom and truth.
>
> For the very same thing was accomplished through a temporal dispensation for our salvation: the unchangeable, consubstantial, and coeternal Power and Wisdom of God, equal to the Father [Col. 0620A], deigned to assume human nature, so that through it he might teach us that human beings must worship what every intellectual and rational creature must worship.

> We should believe that even the best angels and the most excellent ministers of God desire this: that we worship with them the one God, by whose contemplation they are blessed. For we are not blessed, nor shall we ever be blessed, by seeing angels; rather, we are blessed by seeing the truth, through which we also love the angels and rejoice with them. We do not envy them because they enjoy it more readily and without any hindering troubles; instead, we love them all the more because we too have been commanded to hope for such a condition from the common God.
>
> For this reason we honor them with love, not servitude; nor do we establish temples for them. Consequently, they do not wish to be honored by us in this manner [Col. 0620B], because they know that we ourselves, when we are good, are temples of the highest God.

This is the most strongly fortified and most exalted mystery of our faith, and the firmest seal impressed upon our heart. In asserting and defending this truth, I became a reproach to my neighbors and a terror to those who knew me, so much so that those who saw us not only mocked us but also pointed us out to one another with their fingers.

But the Father of mercies and God of all consolation consoled us in all our tribulation, so that we too might console those who are in every kind of affliction, trusting in him and, through him, not failing in temptations. He arms and surrounds us with the weapons of righteousness and the helmet of salvation.

[Col. 0620C]

**The end.**

[Col. 0619c]

# To the Most Humane Reader  
## Dom Joannes Chrysostomus Trombelli

How valuable the book is that I present to you, most humane reader, is made sufficiently clear by the celebrated Franciscus Antonius Zacharias, when he teaches that it is “especially useful both for the history of ecclesiastical writers and for recognizing the sequence and origins of the events connected with the case of Claudius of Turin, the Iconoclast” [Col. 0619D]. For this reason he says that he would have published the same book if he had been able to remain longer at Pistoia. He adds that the outstanding Joannes Dominicus Mansi had long desired to publish it.

> **[Note: [Col. 0619D] *Bibliotheca Pistoriensis*, p. 13, no. 11.]**
>
> On the same page, note 12, he writes: “These are the biblical passages concerning which Theodemirus composed thirty questions. In this very codex he pursues them at length and shows what he wishes to have explained in them. For this reason this work of Theodemirus, which we have copied in our codex, is not to be despised. The distinguished Father Joannes Dominicus Mansi intended to publish it in full; whether he will actually do so, I do not know. If I had been permitted to remain longer at Pistoia, I would long ago have published the whole work myself, together with other liturgical books, and so forth.”

In fact, the distinguished Mansi had ordered it to be copied; but when he learned that we were publishing unpublished writings of ancient ecclesiastical authors, he sent me everything that had been copied, so that I might bring it into print. For this reason also I acknowledge that I owe a very great debt to that illustrious man, who has deserved so well of humane letters.

But, to say something about Claudius of Turin: he was, as suited the age—for, as everyone knows, he lived under the emperors Charlemagne and Louis the Pious [Col. 0620D]—eloquent and learned, but of the class of learned men whom knowledge puffs up and drives from the bosom of the Church. Such men wish to follow their own opinions rather than the things of Jesus Christ, who commands that the doctrines to be believed should not be measured according to our own ingenuity and judgment, but according to ancient tradition and the agreement and approval of the Church.

So that I may not be thought to have spoken rashly, consult the writers whom I cite in a note, lest I burden the reader with a lengthy discussion.

> **[Note: [Col. 0620D]** Jonas of Orléans, in his books *On the Worship of Images*, p. 533 and following, vol. IV, part I, of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris edition. In its preface, Theodemirus is praised as having become an adversary from a friend to Claudius in his error. Dungalus, p. 146, part II, vol. IV. Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 820. Labbe, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Cave, likewise under the year 820. Oudinus, likewise under that year. Ughelli, *On the Bishops of Turin*. Mabillon, p. 92, *Analecta*, Paris edition, 1723. Trombelli, *On the Worship of the Saints*, dissertations II and VI, §§6 and 7. Many other ancient and more recent writers are also cited by Oudinus, except Trombelli.]

In any case, Claudius has long enjoyed such a reputation among learned men that whatever books composed by him have been found—including those published by Catholic authors—have even been inserted into the *Great Library of the Ancient Fathers*, as it is called.

> **[Note: [Col. 0621C]** Petrus Pesselierus, a monk of Saint-Germain of Auxerre, published Claudius’s commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians; these were inserted into the second part of volume I of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, p. 795 of the Paris edition.
>
> Mabillon also published the preface to the books *Expositions of the Letter and the Spirit on Leviticus*, as well as the preface to the exposition on the Epistles to the Ephesians, pp. 90–92, *Analecta*, Paris edition, 1723 [Col. 0621D].
>
> Pesselierus valued Claudius’s commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians so highly that he wrote of it as follows:
>
> “When I was there a few days ago and was turning over various gems of learning—of which quite a number are carefully preserved in that very ancient library—this commentary of Claudius on nearly all the Epistles of Paul happened to come before me. After quickly running through it, as one does after brushing away the dust, I immediately marveled at the negligence of earlier generations and thought it utterly disgraceful that so precious and refined a treasure should lie neglected and remain hidden for so long, to the great loss of the Christian commonwealth. It is impossible to say how great an addition this would bring to every diligent student of sacred literature, especially since it sheds such brilliance upon the reading of Paul that it seems to provide an easy path toward explaining his hidden meanings and obscure passages.”]

Moved by the example of these outstanding men, I decided to publish Claudius’s still-unedited questions and answers on the books of Kings. They are contained in a codex owned by the Church of Pistoia, along with many other works listed and described by the celebrated Zacharias. Yet because of the copyist’s ignorance or negligence, it was so full of frequent and disgraceful errors that at first I thought it entirely impossible to correct these commentaries. For that reason I came close to abandoning altogether my plan to publish them: who would publish writings that he knew to be so corrupt?

But when I discovered from the style—which anyone can readily recognize—that certain passages had been drawn from Augustine and others from Gregory the Great and incorporated into Claudius’s solutions, I searched for them in the works of those teachers. Having found them, I compared them with our codex, and by this comparison corrected many passages.

I then suspected that the man who had incorporated so much from Augustine and Gregory into his work might easily have consulted others as well, from whose studies his commentaries could have been enlarged. I therefore turned to authors older than Claudius and clearly discovered—leaving aside for the moment what I shall later say about Eucherius—that he had drawn a great deal from Bede, Isidore, and even Rabanus, a contemporary of Claudius. Thus these commentaries that we are publishing are assembled from these teachers.

With regard to Rabanus, however, we do not rashly suspect that the passages we cite from Rabanus were taken from an older author by both Rabanus and Claudius.

The commentaries of Claudius that we now publish are not all of one kind. Some are fuller and more extensive—and these come first—while others, placed at the end, are shorter. The earlier ones are indeed more richly supplied with the labors of others; but although in the later and shorter commentaries Claudius incorporates foreign words into his own work much more sparingly, he nevertheless sometimes cites the very authors whom he had quoted in the earlier commentaries [Col. 0621C].

Claudius himself does not conceal this, for he acknowledges [Col. 0622A]:

> **[Note: [Col. 0622C] In the preface to the first commentary.]**
>
> In answering the questions proposed by Theutmirus, he had “satisfied them not from his own ingenuity, but from the judgment of illustrious teachers, and not from his own rashness, but from the authority of others.”

He also declares:

> **[Note: [Col. 0622C] In the preface to the second commentary.]**
>
> Some matters “remain undiscussed, because he had found nothing translated concerning them in the ancient translations, nor had he read anything explained in the little works of our predecessors.”

Then he adds:

> “I confess that I am ignorant of these matters too, because I do not remember having read anything about them. Therefore I am not ashamed of my lack of knowledge, because I have not been taught by reading; nor am I afraid of danger, because I do not presume to teach what I do not understand.”

Although many others in those times followed this practice, Claudius followed it above all—not only in the commentaries that we now publish, but also in those that he wrote and published on the Epistles of Paul.

> **[Note: [Col. 0622C] In the preface to the Epistle to the Ephesians, published by Mabillon, he writes:]**
>
> “With regard to the dullness of my understanding, I have composed the Epistles of the blessed apostle Paul to the Ephesians and Philippians not so much from the treatises of our predecessors as from the opinions of various treatises. Like a beggar who possesses no field of his own but gathers food from the field of those who reap behind them lest he perish from hunger in winter, so I too have gathered these Epistles into a brief composition from the sayings of others.”
>
> And in question 10 of the second kind of commentary:
>
> “What these things signify, however, has already been explained in the first book of this work from the sayings of our predecessors, as the Lord granted and as we were able to discover.”

Yet Claudius did not draw everything that he inserted into his commentaries from others; that he sometimes added some things of his own is shown by these words of his in the commentaries on the Epistle of the apostle Paul to the Galatians:

> “With God’s help, during this Lenten season I have undertaken to arrange the Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Galatians by combining passages from the treatises of the blessed Fathers Augustine and Jerome. When I saw that many things were lacking in these treatises for a suitable exposition, I turned to other books of the aforementioned Father Augustine and endeavored to complete from them the exposition that was lacking in those treatises. I also tried, as it seemed appropriate to me, to join some of my own words to theirs, so that the two expositions might be joined without separation, stimulate the reader’s understanding, and help avoid weariness.”]

From that comparison we therefore obtained this advantage: except for a few passages that we could not compare with our exemplar because we did not find them in the published books of earlier writers, Claudius’s writings could appear not uncorrected.

The comparison also brought another benefit. In the very exemplar that I have generally called defective, there is sometimes something of value by which passages already published from Isidore and Bede, which Claudius cites, can be improved.

I suspect that there will be some who condemn this labor of mine, since they will say that the commentaries of Claudius that I called “fuller and more extensive” are precisely those that were long ago published under the name of Eucherius. But they are not identical in every respect, for differences often occur. Even if one wishes to regard them as entirely identical, one will still derive no small benefit from my labor, since one will clearly discover from it that what has already been attributed to Eucherius belongs to Claudius, and perhaps was later published under another name by some much later writer who made Claudius’s labors his own.

Moreover, whoever these commentaries may ultimately belong to, if I publish them in a thoroughly corrected form and adorn them with Claudius’s prefaces and with quite a few notes, will this not be pleasing and welcome to the humane reader? Farewell.

[Col. 0623]

# Thirty Questions on the Books of Kings

[Col. 0623A]

## Greeting

To the beloved teacher, Lord Claudius, bishop of the see of Turin, Theutmirus [Col. 0623B], your son and the least of all abbots, sends eternal salvation in the Lord.

> **[Note: [Col. 0623B]** Concerning this Theutmirus, or Theodomirus, or Teuthmyrus, Mabillon records the following [p. 92, *Analecta*, Paris edition, 1723, note on Claudius’s prefaces]:
>
> “Theodomirus, to whom the first preface is addressed, was a Gallic abbot and presided over one hundred and forty monks under the rule of Saint Benedict, as he himself testifies in the letter written against Claudius, fragments of which Jonas reports in book III of the work mentioned above. I infer from Jonas’s book I, where he speaks of this Claudius as follows—‘He is said to have vomited forth a pamphlet of such great length against that same abbot and the whole Gallican Church in his denunciation’—that he was an abbot in Gaul, not in Spain, as I once suspected. But at what place he was abbot has so far remained unknown to me.”]
>
> That Claudius was in fact accused by Theuthmirus is clearly shown by the very preface of Claudius that he places before the second commentary on the books of Kings; we shall give that preface later. That Theuthmirus wrote against Claudius is shown by the passages cited by Dungalus from Claudius writing against Theuthmirus.

> **[Note: [Col. 0623C]** “*Abba* is found everywhere without inflection,” says the very learned Ducange [in his *Glossary*, under the word *Abbas*], and he gives these examples:
>
> “Abba Felix, in Facundus of Hermiane’s book against Mocianus. Yet the same author later writes: ‘Lampridius, priest and abbot of the monastery of Jerusalem.’
>
> Abbo, in book II of *On the Siege of Paris*.
>
> ‘In this storm Hugo the prince dies, an abbot.’
>
> Elsewhere:
>
> ‘Ebolus, a most powerful abbot.’
>
> Odo, in the *Life of Saint Majolus*: ‘And he is honored by all as lord and abbot.’
>
> Bernard of Morlaix, *On Contempt of the World*:
>
> ‘He who argues well and quickly calculates by scholastic art  
> Does not seek in deeds, but seeks by arts, to be made an abbot.’”
>
> He then adds other examples, which you may consult if you wish; there is no need to be more expansive in so obvious a matter.]

My father and teacher, I reread the book of Exodus that you sent, and I rejoiced with immense joy. Just as [Col. 0623D] you will recognize from the letter that I myself sent in another letter concerning the Epistles of Paul, the teacher of the nations. For the venerable Father Leidrath [Col. 0624B], formerly bishop of Lyon, also rejoiced when he heard this, and asked him to write to me at length. He was surprised that you had not sent him a letter for so long, and promised that he himself would send you a letter, for he greatly desires to see you, if that could be done. And if not a physical visit, at least a letter [Col. 0624C].

> **[Note: [Col. 0624C]** In the copy sent to me the text reads: “And if not a bodily visit or a letter.” But Baluzius and other learned men long ago taught us, from their experience in reading codices, that a small stroke placed above the final letter of a word indicates the *m* with which the word ends; through copyists’ negligence it is often absent, or has been erased by the age and condition of the codex. The reader must therefore supply it.]

> **[Note: [Col. 0623D]** The manuscript reads *sive* (“or”), clearly an error, which the distinguished Zacharias noted before me.]

> **[Note: [Col. 0623D]** The word *ipse* (“himself”) may refer either to Theutmirus, who was sending the letter, or to Claudius, who was receiving it. In that period they commonly addressed an eminent man with a plural verb, while sometimes retaining the singular noun referring to the person addressed. In this same sentence: “My father and teacher, you will recognize the book that you sent . . .”; and later: “He himself was surprised that you had not sent him your letter. Send it,” and again, more explicitly: “that they may be joined into one body, and as you yourself know, etc. . . . prayer is very powerful, as you yourself know.” In the letter also sent to Louis the Pious—which is itself a kind of preface to the exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians—he writes: “I beg your clemency not to be a harsh exactor toward me,” and so forth.]

> **[Note: [Col. 0624B]** The distinguished Zacharias reads *Teldrathus*. This is only a very slight variation. The names themselves, being drawn from Germanic languages, often occur very clearly in ancient letters and diplomas. Concerning this Leidrath, or, if you prefer, Teldrath, consult what is reported in the *Gallia Christiana* [concerning the archbishops of Lyon].]

> **[Note: [Col. 0624C]** The syntax is, in my judgment, somewhat entangled: nevertheless, it can easily be extracted that Leidrath asked Theutmirus to write to Claudius.]

And what shall I say about our father, Lord Nimbridius, archbishop of Narbonne [Col. 0624C]?

> **[Note: [Col. 0624C]** On the word *domnus*, consult what Ducange says in his lexicon. As for this Nimbridius, the other ancient writers are silent about him.] How filled with immense joy he was when I told him about the exposition of the aforementioned book! With what humility he asked me to let him read it or have it copied! He too was surprised that you had not sent him your letter. Please send frequent letters in these regions to bishops, abbots, and monks, especially, if it pleases you, to me, your son. I am always consumed by this desire and longing.

Among other things, I ask you to send me clarified those questions on the books of Kings [Col. 0624C] that he sent you on a short sheet—not only according to the historical sense, but also according to allegory or tropology.

> **[Note: [Col. 0624C]** Supply “book.”]

> **[Note: [Col. 0624C]** Leidrath—or, if you prefer, Nimbridius—of whom he had spoken a little earlier.]

The first should stand insofar as it can according to history; the second, if allegory admits it; the third, entirely according to moral interpretation.

As for those thirty questions that, at the request of Nothelinus [Col. 0624D], the priest Bede explained from the aforementioned book of Kings, I did not ask you to explain them because they are held among us in a single body together with the exposition of the Temple of Solomon, as it was explained by the aforementioned priest Bede.

Amid all this, please also correct the questions that I sent [Col. 0624D] and explain them in order; and whatever I may have expressed in an inept manner [Col. 0625D], correct as a teacher corrects a pupil. I did not send them in order because of a certain haste and the copyist’s negligence; but you should arrange them according to the historical sequence.

> **[Note: [Col. 0624D]** The copy sent to me reads *Nothelino*, but Zacharias, who inspected the codex itself, reads *Notelmo*. Ancient codices from those times would admit either reading, since no stroke was placed above the letter *i* and there was no dot. The same distinguished Zacharias believes that the Nothelm indicated here is the man who was first a priest of London and then archbishop of Canterbury.]

> **[Note: [Col. 0625D]** I am uncertain whether the reading should be *fuerit* or *fuerim*. The latter is preferred by the distinguished Zacharias. Indeed, Theutmirus speaks rather crudely of the bishop if he means the questions proposed by Leidrath or Nimbridius when he says: “Correct me as a teacher corrects a pupil.” Yet that these thirty questions were proposed by one of the two men mentioned above, whose solution Theutmirus demands, seems to be indicated by Theutmirus himself when he adds that these “thirty questions and their explanations, if it pleases your wisdom, together with those questions concerning the aforementioned book of Kings that I sent to your holiness for explanation, once they have been explained by you, should be joined in their proper order into one body.”
>
> He is therefore asking Claudius to combine in one body and return to Theutmirus, explained and illuminated, both these questions and those that he himself sent Claudius for solution and exposition. Whether one or the other proposed them, both these questions and the others he subsequently lists were, at his request, to be resolved and illuminated by Claudius.]

1. “And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest.” I Samuel 2:35.

2. “And not one of all his words fell to the ground.” I Samuel 3:19.

3. “And he struck seventy men of the people, and fifty of the common people.” I Samuel 6:19. (The Vulgate translator, however, has: “fifty thousand of the common people.”)

4. “From the day on which the ark remained in Cariathiarim, its days were multiplied,” and so forth. I Samuel 7:2.

5. What Jonathan said to David: “If I live, you will show me mercy,” and so forth. I Samuel 20:14.

6. “Solomon held a solemn feast, and all Israel with him.” III Kings 8:65.

> **[Note: [Col. 0626D]** I follow exactly the copy sent to me. In the edition published by Father Zacharias, this question and the following three are placed after the one that begins, “When the bars projected,” and is numbered XIX. Here, however, we follow chronology and the sequence of ecclesiastical history. Yet Theutmirus himself asserts that this order was not preserved when the questions were proposed. Recall what was said above: “Explain them in order . . . for I did not send them in order,” and so forth.]

7. “In his days Hiel of Bethel built Jericho.” III Kings 16:34. (The Vulgate has: “Hiel of Bethel.”)

8. “May the gods do this to me, and may they add this, if the dust of Samaria shall suffice by the handful for all the people who follow me.” III Kings 20:10. (But the Vulgate has “by handfuls.”)

9. “A third part of you shall enter on the Sabbath and keep watch over the king’s house.” IV Kings 11:6. (In our version, however, it reads “keep the watches.”) [Col. 0625C]

10. What Abigail said to David: “For if a man should ever rise up pursuing you,” and so forth. I Samuel 25:29.

11. “And he commanded that they teach the sons of Judah the bow.” II Samuel 1:18.

12. “And he struck Moab and measured them with a cord.” II Samuel 8:2.

13. “He was like the most tender little worm of wood.” II Samuel 23:8. (The Vulgate has “he is.”)

14. “He went down and struck the lion in the middle of the cistern.” II Samuel 23:20.

15. Concerning the Temple, which had thirty cubits in height; whereas in the book of Chronicles it had one hundred and twenty. III Kings 6:2; II Chronicles 3:4.

16. “The door of the middle side-chamber was on the right side of the house.” III Kings 6:8 [Col. 0625D].

17. “And he covered the house with cedar panels.” III Kings 6:9. (The Vulgate has “and he also covered.”) [Col. 0626A]

18. “When the bars projected and their ends appeared outside the sanctuary,” and so forth. III Kings 8:8. (But it should be read *eminerent*, “projected,” as the common reading has.)

19. “And he brought out the king’s son, and placed upon him the diadem and the testimony.” IV Kings 11:12.

20. “And no account was required from those men who received the money.” IV Kings 12:15.

21. “He struck Edom in the Valley of Salt.” IV Kings 14:7.

22. “He will restore the boundaries of Israel from the entrance of Hamath.” IV Kings 14:25.

23. “And every nation made its own god.” IV Kings 17:29. (The Vulgate correctly offers this reading, and the distinguished Zacharias follows it; but the copy sent to me reads “its own house.”) [Col. 0626B]

24. “Where is the god of Hamath and Arphath? Where is . . .?” IV Kings 18:34. (The Vulgate has “Arphad.”)

25. “The shadow went up ten lines.” IV Kings 20:9. (But, with the Vulgate, it should be read: “Do you wish the shadow to go up?” unless one wishes to indicate that in verse 11 it had already descended.)

26. “Who dwelt in Jerusalem in the second.” IV Kings 22:14.

27. “He also defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hennom.” IV Kings 23:10.

28. “He also removed the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the Sun.” IV Kings 23:11.

29. “And the high places that were in Jerusalem, on the right side of the mountain of Offense,” and so forth. There, verse 15.

30. “And he carried away all Jerusalem and all the princes,” and so forth. IV Kings 24:14. [Col. 0626C]

These thirty questions and their explanations, if it pleases your wisdom, should be joined in their proper order into one body with those questions concerning the aforementioned book of Kings that I sent to your holiness for explanation, once you have explained them. As you yourself know, place both your preface and my petition at the head of the explanations of the aforementioned questions, as introductory prefaces. And in all the writings that you send to these regions, do not forget me; rather, always deign to admonish me concerning what I ought to do.

Above all, I beg you in your prayers to ask the Lord for me, and by your devotion to have others ask as well. For if the prayer of one righteous person has great power (James 5:16), as you yourself know, how much more the constant prayer of many? Farewell, my father, and always flourish in the prosperity of your spiritual sons.

[Col. 0627A]

1. **[Note: [Col. 0627D] Recall annotation 11.]** There was a certain man from Ramatha in Sophin, from the hill country of Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah. And a little later: “He had two wives: the name of one was Hannah, and the name of the second was Peninnah.” I Samuel 1:1–2. What this man signifies, and what his two wives signify—one fertile, the other infertile. And why it is written concerning Hannah: “Her rival also afflicted her and tormented her greatly.” And so forth, verse 6.

2. “When they went up to the temple of the Lord at the appointed time, and she provoked her in this way. But she wept and did not eat,” until it says: “And her countenance was no longer turned this way and that.” And so forth, verse 7 and following.

3. “My heart exults in the Lord,” until it says: “The Lord will judge the ends of the earth, and will give power to his king, and will exalt the horn of his Christ.” Chapter 2:1, through verse 11.

4. “Now Samuel ministered before the Lord, a boy girded with an *ephot*.” What the *ephot* was, down to the words, “They went away to their place.” I Samuel 2:18–20.

> **[Note: [Col. 0627D]** *Ephod* and similar words, written somewhat differently from the form found in the Vulgate and required by the Hebrew language, should be attributed either to the speech of the regions inhabited by Theutmirus or, if you prefer, to the copyist. Inexperienced copyists—especially those who write from dictation—often represent words in writing as they pronounce them. Many use the letters *t* and *d* interchangeably, employing one in place of the other.]

5. “The Lord visited Hannah, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters.” (The same chapter, verse 21.) Yet above, speaking prophetically, she says: “The barren woman has borne many.” (Verse 5.) Elsewhere she bore seven [Col. 0628D]. What does this mean?

> **[Note: [Col. 0628D]** See what I gave in the ninth annotation to the sermon of Saint Antipater.]

6. Why is it said through the man of God to Eli: “Why have you rejected my offerings and my sacrifice, which I commanded you to offer in the temple,” until it says: “Those who despise me shall be dishonored.” The same passage, verses 29–30.

> **[Note: [Col. 0627C]** The Vulgate translates it with some difference: “Why have you spurned my sacrifice and my offerings, which I commanded to be offered,” and so forth.]

7. “Behold, the days are coming, and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, so that there will be no old man in your house. And you will see Christ, your rival, amid all the prosperity of Israel,” until it says: “I will eat a morsel of bread.” The same passage, verse 31, through the end of the chapter.

> **[Note: [Col. 0627D]** The Vulgate differs somewhat, for it has: “And you will see your rival in the temple,” and so forth.]

8. “Now the boy Samuel ministered to the Lord before Eli,” until it says: “Nor could he see the lamp of God before it was extinguished; and Samuel was sleeping in the temple of the Lord, where the ark was,” and so forth. Chapter 3, verses 1 through 3.

> **[Note: [Col. 0627D]** This too is included, but with the difference that the Vulgate has these words: “Nor could he see; the lamp of God, before it was extinguished, Samuel,” and so forth.

9. What does it signify that, after the ark of God had been transported by the Philistines and placed in the temple of Dagon, Dagon was found the next day before the ark of God? On the third day his head and both palms had been cut off and were lying on the threshold, while only the trunk itself remained. And so forth. Chapter 5, verses 1–5. (If you want this expressed more clearly, correct it as follows: “Dagon is found lying before the ark [Col. 0628A] of God—and afterward, on the third day ….”)

10. “The men who had not died were struck in the more secret part of the buttocks,” up to where it says: “But the lords of the Philistines also followed the ark of the Lord as far as the boundaries of Beth-shemesh.” The final verse of the same chapter, or verse 12, through the end of verse 12 of the following chapter, that is, chapter 6.

11. “The men of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat,” up to where it says: “From the fortified city to the village that had no wall, and as far as great Abel, upon which they placed the ark of the Lord.” Why does it say “great Abel”? And so forth. The verses indicated here are verse 13 and the following verses through verse 18 inclusive of chapter 6.

12. Why is it written of Samuel that he judged Israel all the days of his life, when during his lifetime he lost the leadership? (Consult verse 15 and the following verses of chapter 7.)

13. When Samuel had anointed Saul king, he said to him: “When you leave me today, you will find two men beside Rachel’s tomb, at the border of Benjamin, jumping about at midday in great pits. And you will deliver his people from the hand of his enemies.” Chapter 10:2. (But this manuscript’s interpretation differs greatly from the Vulgate, which I want you to consult.) Why is Saul anointed twice, and David three times? And so forth.

14. Why is it written of Saul: “Saul was the son of one year when he began to reign, and he reigned two years over Israel,” chapter 13:1, when above it is read that he stood out above all the people from the shoulder upward, chapter 9:2? [Col. 0628C]

15. Why is it written in the same book: “No blacksmith was found throughout the whole land of Israel,” and that the edges of the plowshares, mattocks, forks, and axes had been blunted, even down to the goad that needed sharpening? And so forth, 13:20–21. How could these things exist without a smith?

16. Why is it written of Jonathan that he stretched out his hand and dipped it into a honeycomb; and when he had eaten, his eyes were enlightened? 14:27. How did he dip into it if he did not see? If he saw, how were his eyes enlightened? And so forth.

17. When the Lord sent Saul to strike the sinners of Amalek, why did he spare the Kenite, saying shortly afterward: “For you showed mercy to all the children of Israel when they came up from Egypt”? And so forth. [Col. 0628D] 15:1, 6. Who is this Kenite, and where is it recorded that he showed this mercy?

18. Why did Samuel say to King Agag: “Does bitter death separate in this way?” up to where it says: “Samuel cut Agag in pieces before the Lord.” 15:32 and following.

19. Why is it written of David that, at the time when Saul saw David going out against the Philistines, he said to Abner, the commander of the army: “From what family does this young man descend, Abner?” And so forth. 17:55. This is despite the fact that above it is read that David had previously been Saul’s armor-bearer and played the harp in his presence. And so forth, 16:21, 23. And why was Goliath called illegitimate? 17:4, 23. And Jonathan added an oath to David. 20:17.

20. Why, when David went to fight the Philistine, did he refuse to wear Saul’s armor, but take five stones from the stream in a pouch, yet throw only one and strike the Philistine? And so forth. 17:39–40 and 49.

21. Why did Saul angrily say to his son Jonathan: “Son of a woman who seizes a man of her own accord”? 20:30.

22. When David was fleeing before Saul, he came to Abimelech at Nob. And so forth, up to where it says: “Moreover, this way is polluted.” 21:1–5. How had it been polluted? And it is added: “Today it will be sanctified in my vessels,” verse 5.

23. Concerning the city of Keilah, which David attacked: whether it had another name or not. For I do not at all recall Scripture mentioning this city except in the prophet, where it reads: “Woe to Keilah, the city of Keilah, which David attacked.”

24. How is what is said of Saul to be understood: that, at the end of his life, he consulted a woman who had a pythonic spirit? It is written that she raised Samuel for him, and Samuel said to him: “Tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me.” Can it stand literally that the woman with the pythonic spirit raised Samuel? 28:7 and following.

25. Why did David curse the mountains of Gilboa at the death of Saul and his sons? II Samuel 1:21. Whether this can stand literally. [Col. 0629C]

26. How is this to be understood, that David, mourning Abner and cursing Joab, said: “May there never fail from the house of Joab one who suffers a discharge of semen, and a leper; one who holds a spindle, and one who falls by the sword, and one who lacks bread”? II Samuel 3:29. And so forth.

27. What does it signify that the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, entered the house of Ish-bosheth in the heat of the day, while he was sleeping on his bed at noon, up to where it says: “David commanded his young men to kill them; but they took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in the tomb of Abner at Hebron”? II Samuel 4:5. And so forth.

28. “David went on, and all the men who were with him, to Jerusalem, against the Jebusite, the inhabitant of the land.” [Col. 0629D] They said to David: “You shall not enter here unless you remove the blind and the lame,” saying: “David shall not enter here.” And so forth. II Samuel 5:6 and following.

29. “David captured the stronghold of Zion; this is the city of David.” What is “the stronghold”?

30. “For on that day they offered a reward to whoever struck the Jebusite and touched the channels of the roofs.” (In my opinion, one should read, in accordance with the Vulgate: “the pipes,” and “he removed the lame and the blind who hated David’s life,” up to where it says: “The Lord of hosts was with him.”) There, verses 7 and following.

31. When the Philistines had once come against David in the valley of Rephaim, and he consulted the Lord, the Lord answered him: “Go around behind the pear trees; [Col. 0630A] and when you hear the sound of one walking on the tops of the pear trees, then enter into battle,” up to where it says: “He struck the Philistines from Geba until you come to Jazer.” And so forth. Verse 32 and following.

32. Why was Uzzah struck, when he held the ark of the Lord with his hand so that it would not slip from the cart onto the ground? And what does his rashness signify, or the kicking of the oxen that were pulling it? And so forth. 6:6–7 and following.

33. When the ark of the Lord had entered the city of David, Michal, Saul’s daughter, looking through the window, saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord and despised him in her heart, up to where it says: “I shall be humble in my own eyes.” And so forth. 6:16 through verse 22 inclusive.

[Col. 0630B]

34. Why did Nathan tell David to build a house for the Lord, and afterward forbid him to do so? And so forth, up to where it says: “According to all these words.” And shortly afterward: “Thus Nathan spoke to David.” And so forth. 7:3 and following.

35. “After this David struck the Philistines and humbled them, and took the bridle of tribute from the hand of the Philistines; and he struck Moab and measured them with a cord, making them equal with the ground.” And so forth. 8:1–2 and following.

36. “Joab, son of Zeruiah, was over the army; Jehoshaphat, son of Ahilud, was recorder. Zadok, son of Ahitub, and Ahimelech, son of Abiathar, were priests; and Seraiah was secretary. Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, was over the Cherethites and Pelethites; and David’s sons were priests.” 8:16–18. Who were the Cherethites [Col. 0630C] and Pelethites? Or how could David’s sons be priests, since they were not of the tribe of Levi? And so forth.

37. Why is it written of Absalom that he had erected a monument for himself, saying: “I have no son”? 18:18. This is despite the fact that it is written above in the same book that he had three sons and one daughter named Tamar, of elegant appearance. And so forth. 14:27.

38. Why, among David’s mighty men, is it written of each one that he did this or that, but that he did not attain the rank of the three? Who were these three, or why is this written? 23:19 and following.

39. Why is David blamed for numbering the people? II Samuel 24:1. When Jehoshaphat and the other kings numbered the people and remained blameless and without punishment? And the rest through the end. IV Kings [Col. 0630D] 3:6. (But what is said here about Jehoshaphat should be said about Joram, with whom Jehoshaphat had entered into an alliance. Scripture says: “Therefore King Joram went out on that day from Samaria and counted all Israel, and sent to Jehoshaphat,” etc. Yet from Amaziah, king of Judah, who was by no means wicked, we learn that his subjects were counted, from II Chronicles 21:5.)

40. Why is it written of David that he had grown old, although he had not exceeded seventy years, and that, though covered with clothing, he could not become warm? And that, when a beautiful young woman, Abishag the Shunammite, had been found, she slept with the king and ministered to him, but the king did not know her? III Kings 1:3. This is despite the fact that we read and see men having intercourse with women at a more vigorous age. And so forth.

[Col. 0631A]

41. What does it mean that, at the end of his life, David commanded his son Solomon concerning Joab and Shimei—whom he had previously spared—not to let them go unpunished, but to bring their gray hairs down with blood into Sheol? There, 2:5, 8.

42. What did he mean when he said of Joab: “He put the blood of battle on his belt, which was around his loins, and on his sandal, which was on his feet”? There, verse 5.

43. What does Adonijah signify, who asked Abishag in marriage, for which reason Solomon ordered him to be killed? There, verse 20 and following. And what does it mean that it is frequently written in this book: “May God do these things to me, and may he add these others”? There, verse 23 and following. Was this an oath, or not?

[Col. 0631B]

44. “Solomon loved the Lord, walking in the commandments of David his father, except that he walked on the high places and burned incense.” 3:3. What were the high places, which are frequently mentioned in this book? And why is Samuel not blamed, when he is said to have sacrificed on a high place? (I Samuel 9:12, 14.) III Kings 3:2.

45. What do those two prostitute women who came before King Solomon signify? III Kings 3:16.

46. “The men of Gebal also prepared wood and stones for building the house.” III Kings 5:18.

47. Since it is stated more explicitly in the Book of Kings, III Kings 8:9, and apart from II Chronicles 5:10, that there was nothing else in the ark except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed in it—and so forth—while the Apostle writes to the Hebrews, 9:4, that in the ark were the tablets, [Col. 0631C] Aaron’s rod, and manna: if they were not there, why did the Apostle say this? And if they were there, who put them there? And if this was Aaron’s rod, was it the same one by which signs were performed in Egypt, at the sea, and in the wilderness, or another? And what became of the ark itself? Or whether it will ever be seen—by all, as I suppose it should be seen.

48. When the cloud filled the house of the Lord, Solomon said: “The Lord said that he would dwell in a cloud.” 8:10–12. Where is it recorded that the Lord had said this?

49. Were the bread of the Presence placed in the Temple, where there was the altar of incense, the lampstand, and the lamps? Did anyone enter there except the order of priests and Levites? And was there an assembly of the common people there? Or, if only priests or Levites [were there—supply: “dwelling” or “entering there”?]

[Col. 0631D]

50. Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in the land of Galilee. Since they did not please him, he called them the land of Cabul “to this day.” What does this mean? I want to know. 9:11–13.

51. What does it mean that Moses, in the wilderness, employed Hebrew builders for the construction of the tabernacle, not foreigners? Exodus 35:30 and following.
