(The second part of the question seems to be missing: namely, why Solomon brought a Syrian man for the construction of the Temple and its sacred furnishings. “King Solomon also sent and brought Hiram from Tyre.” III Kings 7:14.)

52. “Solomon made of thyine wood the supports of the house of the Lord and of the king’s house.” What kind of wood was thyine? [Col. 0632A] And shortly afterward he says: “Such algum wood had not been brought or seen to the present day.” 10:11–12. And what is Ophir, and where is it, and from where was the wood brought? 5:11.

53. Why was the altar of burnt offering in the tabernacle and in the Temple made of wood but covered with bronze? Exodus 38:1. Since fire was continually burning on that altar, why was it not consumed by the fire?

54. Solomon made two hundred shields of pure gold. 10:16. And shortly afterward: “The king placed them in the house of the forest of Lebanon.” Verse 17. If the forest of Lebanon belonged to Solomon, why did he not cut cedar wood from Lebanon?

55. “Silver became as plentiful in Jerusalem as stones, and he supplied cedar wood in abundance like the sycamores that grow in the lowlands.” And so forth. 10:27.

56. “The rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom—behold, are they not all written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon?” 11:41. What sort of book is this? I want to know.

57. When Elijah was fleeing from Jezebel and came to the mountain of God, Horeb, and remained in a cave, and the word of the Lord came to him, Scripture shortly afterward reports, 19:2–8: “Behold, the Lord passes by, and a great and strong wind overturning mountains and crushing rocks,” up to where it says: “I alone am left, and they seek my life to take it.” 19:11–14 and following.

58. When Elijah said concerning Ahab: “If he dies in the city, the dogs shall eat him; but if he dies in the field, the birds of the air shall eat him,” 21:24, how is this true, when he is said to have been carried to Samaria and buried in his own tomb? 22:37—unless only that the dogs licked the reins, there, verse 38, and did not eat him.

59. Why did Elisha, sending his servant to raise the Shunammite’s son, command him, saying: “If a man meets you, do not greet him; and if anyone greets you, do not answer him”? IV Kings 4:29.

60. “Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria.” And shortly afterward: “For through him the Lord gave salvation to Syria.” 5:1. What was that salvation?

61. “There was a great famine in Samaria, and it was besieged for so long that a donkey’s head was sold for eighty pieces of silver, and a fourth part of a cab of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver.” 6:21. What is “a cab of dung”? (But the Vulgate correctly has “a fourth part of a cab of dung”; therefore it should be said: What is a fourth part of a cab of dung?)

62. What is meant by the fact that Ben-hadad, king of Syria, sent Asahel to Elisha to inquire whether he could be healed of his illness or not? When he had received an answer from him and returned to his lord, Scripture reports: “He took the blanket, poured water over it, and spread it over his face.” 8:7, 15 and following.

63. Why did Jehoash, king of Israel, send word to Amaziah, king of Judah, saying: “The thistle of Lebanon sent to the cedar that is in Lebanon, saying: Give your daughter to my son as a wife; but the wild beasts of the forest, which are in [Col. 0633A] Lebanon, passed by and trampled down the thistle”? IV Kings 14:9.

64. Why is it written of Jeroboam, son of Joash: “He restored the boundaries of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Wilderness, according to the word of the Lord, which he spoke through his servant Jonah, son of Amittai, the prophet”? Jonah 1:1. Where did Jonah speak these words? 14:25.

65. Why is it written of Jotham, king of Judah: “He built the highest gate of the house of the Lord”? 15:35. Had it not previously been built by Solomon, or did he construct a new one?

66. Why is it written of Hezekiah: “After he destroyed the high places and broke the statues, he cut down the groves and broke the bronze serpent that Moses had made; and he called it Nehushtan” (the Vulgate has Nohestan)? 18:4. [Col. 0633B] And so forth. What does this mean?

67. Why is it said through Isaiah to King Hezekiah: “Behold, the days are coming, and they shall take away” (the Vulgate has “shall be transferred”) “everything that is in your house, and what your fathers have stored up, to Babylon; nothing shall remain, says the Lord. And of the sons whom you shall beget, they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon”? 20:17–18. Who were these eunuchs?

68. What does it mean that, after many other matters, it is written of Josiah: “He had the grove carried out of the house of the Lord, outside Jerusalem, into the valley of Kidron, and burned it there, reduced it to dust, and threw it upon the graves of the common people”? What is this grove, or what were the graves of the common people? 23:6.

69. “He also destroyed the idols” (the Vulgate has “the little houses”) “of the effeminate men that were in the house of the Lord, for which the women wove something like little houses for the grove.” Verse 7.

70. “He also destroyed the altars of the gates at the entrance of the gate of Josiah, the governor of the city,” up to where it says of the priests of the high places: “They ate unleavened bread among their brothers.” 5:8–9.

71. “He took the commanders of the army, Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and three gatekeepers; and from the city, one eunuch.” And [Col. 0634B] shortly afterward: “And Sopher, the commander of the army, who tested the recruits from the people of the land.” Why does it say “the chief priest” and “the second,” or “one eunuch” and “three gatekeepers,” or who are the recruits? 25:18–19.

72. “In the year in which he began to reign, Evil-merodach, king of Babylon, lifted up the head of Jehoiachin, king of Judah, from prison, and spoke kindly to him,” up to where it says: “All the days of his life.” There, verse 27 and following.

[Col. 0633]

THUS FAR THEUTMIRUS; CLAUDIUS RESPONDS IN THE FOLLOWING MANNER.

Your timely and many-sided inquiry, most Christian brother Theutmirus, compels and constrains me [Note: At [Col. 0633D] the editor thinks *importuna* (“importunate”) should be read.] to come forth before the public and fearful judgment of many—not by necessity, but, what is more powerful, by charity. I mean those who know how to judge according to appearance and not with righteous judgment. This is especially because you order me to place at the beginning of our little works, in the exposition of the Pentateuch and the Book of Kings, both your request and my preface—something that seems presumptuous and ridiculous to many in our time.

If they knew the true name of “preface,” I do not think they could say such things. [Note: At [Col. 0633D] the editor corrects an obvious scribal error: the manuscript has *veri nominis praefationis*; he prints *verum nomen praefationis*. If anyone prefers to read *veritatem nominis praefationis*—that is, “the true etymology of the name ‘preface’”—he does not object.] For a preface is the speech of a first work, and a preliminary discourse of books, [Note: The exemplar sent to the editor reads *prolocutio*; he substitutes *praelocutio* to agree with *praefatio*. He permits retention of *prolocutio*, observing that *prologus*, not *praelogus*, is the usual form.] fitted before the narratives of their subjects to prepare the ears of the hearers. It is called a preface as though it were a preliminary discourse, that is, a first discourse; in another term, a prologue—that is, the preface of the work that follows. It is both the beginning of speech and the head of a composition, which is also called by another name, a proem. For a proem is the beginning of teaching and the opening sections of books, fitted before the narrative of their subject to prepare the ears of the hearers. Most learned Latins have assigned this meaning to the word.

Let anyone know that what is lacking in our time is not knowledge, but time for writing: that is, there is time to expound all the Scriptures if the grace of the Holy Spirit deigns to be present to anyone. One must not prejudge the time at which someone writes; one must distinguish only whether what he writes is true and catholic or false and heretical.

And because you often ask me for the resolution of many matters, especially in the Pentateuch and the Book of Kings—which are both older and more obscure than the other books of the divine law and require a great interpreter—and because in them I have answered your questions not from my own ingenuity but from the judgment of distinguished teachers, not from personal rashness but on the authority of others, I have satisfied you not as much as I ought, but as much as I could, preserving not so much the scope of exuberant eloquence as the measure of necessary brevity. [Note: The exemplar has *tanquam*; it must certainly be *tam*, corresponding to *quam* in “than the measure of necessary brevity.” P. Zacharias had already noted this.] Thus your innumerable inquiries can be answered, and I shall also be free to insert in other books matters from elsewhere that I judge useful to your knowledge, if you find these things acceptable.

But I want you to know, brother, that this discourse does indeed open paths to understanding; it does not, however, discuss and resolve individually every single thing that has been written. As I was able, I answered your inquiries. If you have found, or are able to find, something better concerning these matters about which you questioned me, we shall be most grateful if you make it known to us. For this reason I beseech you, by the grace of God—which, as I believe, abounds in you—not to reject my request, but willingly to teach me if you can anything that I confess I do not know.

And if you have either read or heard, or are still able to hear, read, or devise, anything here that has been resolved and defined by a reasonable and complete discussion, I ask you not to hesitate to send it to me. For—to confess what is owed to your charity—it is more beneficial for me to learn than to teach. For this is what we are admonished by the Apostle James (1:19): “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak.” And as the most learned Father Augustine says: “The sweetness of truth should invite us to learn; the necessity of charity should compel us to teach.” Rather, one should pray that this necessity may pass away, by which one human being teaches another human being, and that we may all be taught by God (John 6:45; Isaiah 54:13), although we are taught by God even when we speak of matters pertaining to true devotion, even when a human being appears to teach them.

For, as the Apostle says (I Corinthians 3:7): “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth.” Since, if God did not give the growth, the apostles who planted and watered would be nothing, how much more insignificant am I, or you, or any people of this age, who seem to be teachers in this final age?

I have also added to this work a brief allegorical exposition of the Book of Ruth, which you did not request and which seems to belong more to the Book of Judges than to the Book of Kings. For this reason I beg you, although I am far away in body yet near in mind, not to cease commending me to the Creator of all in your prayers. May it be through the power of your tears and the merits of your prayers that, even if I am detained beside the river Chebar—that is, beside the heaviness [Note: Jerome, in his book *On Hebrew Names*, renders Chobar as “heaviness”; he also calls the same river “most heavy” in Haggai, with reference to this meaning. Again, in his translation of Origen’s first homily on Ezekiel: “I was beside the river Chobar, which is interpreted ‘heaviness’”; and afterward, “beside this most heavy river of the age.” This interpretation, however, displeases Bochart and other critical scholars.] [Col. 0635C] of this age—I may nevertheless desire to see our Lord in the majesty of his glory and hear from him that our dwelling is in the midst of scorpions. Ezekiel 2:6.

[Col. 0635D]

Concerning Elkanah, Elcana, and his two wives, and the birth of Samuel. Chapter 1. Concerning Hannah’s song. [Note: The copy has “concerning the prophet sent to Eli, and the evil of his sons and their death.” I have corrected these and other similar obvious scribal errors whenever they occur, and shall continue to do so, without informing the reader, for why should he need to be warned about such trifles? I have retained and shall retain the others that can to some extent be tolerated or may be attributed to Claudius himself, usually informing the reader.]

Concerning the prophet sent to Eli, the wickedness of his sons, and their death. Concerning the faithful priest whom God promises will be according to his heart. Concerning the dimness of Eli’s eyes and the growth of Samuel, and the words of the Lord that did not fall to the ground. Concerning the captivity of the ark and the idol Dagon, as well as the death of Eli and his daughter-in-law. Concerning the evil spirit that rushed upon Saul. Concerning David and his anointing. [Col. 0636A] Concerning the contest between David and Goliath. Concerning the fact that Saul promised to give David his daughter in marriage in exchange for one hundred Philistine foreskins. Concerning David’s flight and deliverance, and the image found in his bed. Concerning David’s arrival at Samuel’s house, and Saul’s messengers who were sent to seize David and who, after receiving the spirit of God, prophesied. Concerning the return of the Lord’s ark to the land of the Israelites and the striking of the men of Beth-shemesh. Concerning what is written: “From the day when the ark of the Lord remained at Kiriath-jearim, the days were multiplied.” Concerning what is written: “When all the people of Israel had assembled, Samuel prayed to the Lord, and he heard him.” [Col. 0636B] Concerning Samuel’s sons, who turned aside after greed and accepted gifts. Concerning the anointing of Saul as king and Samuel’s arrival at Gilgal. Concerning the fast imposed by Saul. Concerning Saul’s battle against Amalek and King Agag, and concerning what is written: “The Lord repented that he had made Saul king.” Concerning Samuel’s rebuke of Saul, because he had not obeyed the voice of the Lord, and the tearing of Samuel’s garment, as well as the death of King Agag. Concerning the oath of David and Jonathan. Where David came to Abimelech the priest and took Goliath’s sword, or received the bread of the Presence. [Note: Who does not know that *seu*, *vel*, and similar particles often have the force of “and” in ecclesiastical writers? Many have noted this; among them, without enumerating many, Benedict XIV, in his annotations on the Mass, at the words “*vel qui tibi offerunt*.”] [Col. 0636C] Where David fled to King Achish and changed his expression. Where David, in the cave, cut off Saul’s cloak. Concerning David’s descent into the wilderness of Maon, where Nabal lived, and where David, while Saul and his army slept, took away the spear and cup. Concerning David’s battle against Amalek. Concerning the woman with a pythonic spirit whom Saul consulted, and the raising of Samuel. Concerning the battle of the Philistines, the defeat of Israel, and the death of Saul and his son Jonathan. Concerning David’s lament for the death of Saul and Jonathan, and the slaughter of Israel, and the cursing of the mountains of Gilboa.

[Col. 0636D]

[Note: Isidore taught these very things before Claudius, though sometimes in different words and with the order somewhat altered.]

The period of the kings begins after the judges, when David, after Saul had been rejected, began to reign. Hence the book in which the events are contained—the book we are now undertaking—is called *Malachim*, that is, “Kings,” and is contained in the third and fourth volumes. It is much better to say *Malachim*, that is, “Kings,” than *Malachot*, that is, “Kingdoms.” For it does not describe the kingdoms of many nations, but that of the one Israelite people, which consists of twelve tribes. Nevertheless, in earthly Jerusalem the tribe of Judah, one of the twelve, reigned through a long succession. In that city, after Saul had been rejected, David first reigned.

“In those times [Note: In many and various ways. There.] many and various mysteries of Christ and the Church [Note: Are revealed.] are represented. For [Note: From the very beginning.] at the very beginning of the Book of Kings, when the priesthood was changed in Samuel after Eli had been rejected, and the kingdom was changed in David after Saul had been rejected, it cries out that a new priesthood and a new kingdom are foretold as coming in the Lord Jesus Christ, the old one having been rejected because it was a shadow of what was to come. [Note: Christ is often proclaimed the author of the age to come, that is, the author of the new kingdom, which is rightly said here to be coming in comparison with the Jews, whose kingdom has long since been desolated and overthrown. Eucherius has “of the coming one,” namely, of Christ.] Was not David himself, when he ate the bread of the Presence—which no one was permitted to eat except the priests—in one and the same person representing both things that were to come, namely, kingship and priesthood in the one Lord Jesus Christ? And consider the times of the Kings: first the time of the Judges, afterward that of the Kings. So there will first be judgment, and afterward the kingdom.”

“There was a certain man from Ramathaim-zophim, from the hill country of Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, son of Jeroboam, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.” Elkanah was not descended from Aram—that is, Amram—but from Izhar, who himself was a son of Kohath, and Kohath was a son of Levi. (Exodus 6:18–19 and following.)

“This Izhar was the father of Korah [Note: The sons of Izhar were Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri. Exodus 6:21.], whose sons remained after he perished. (Numbers 26:10–11 and following.) Samuel was from his lineage [Note: “His,” or, if you prefer, “that man’s,” that is, Elkanah’s or Izhar’s]; afterward, in the time of David and Solomon, their descendants were singers and prophets among the people and in the Temple of God. (I Chronicles 6:28, 32–33 and following.) The families of this Kohath received cities and their suburbs for habitation—as the Book of Joshua testifies—in the hill country of Ephraim (Joshua 20:7 and 21:21–22 and following), where the cities of Shechem, Gezer, Cethsaim, and Beth-horon were located.

“Elkanah was the son of Jeroboam, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, son of Elkanah, son of Joel, son of Azariah, son of Zephaniah, son of Tahath, son of Assir, son of Abiasaph, son of Korah, son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Israel,” as the Book of Chronicles relates. [Note: I Chronicles 6, but with some difference in the transcription of the names.] “And he had two wives: the name of one was Hannah, and the name of the second was Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children,” and so forth.

This therefore was a praiseworthy man who had two wives: the name of one was Hannah, and the name of the second was Peninnah. He had children by the second, Peninnah; but the first, who was also the nobler, was barren. You will find similar things in Genesis, for divine Scripture is related to itself. There you will find Abraham’s first wife, Sarah, the nobler, and the second, the Egyptian Hagar, of lowly status; and Abraham became a father by the lowly woman before he did so by the noble one. (Genesis 16:1; 17:19; 18:10; 21:1 and following.) Yet afterward he also became a father by his noble wife.

So now, too, Elkanah—whose name means “possession of God”—first becomes a father by his second wife rather than by the first, because God had closed Hannah’s womb, just as earlier he had closed Sarah’s womb. But after Peninnah had given birth many times, Hannah’s womb is opened through prayers and petitions, and she too becomes the mother of a son whom she offered to God. (I Samuel 1:11, 24 and following.)

Let us therefore see what mystery these things contain. Peninnah is interpreted as “conversion,” while Hannah is interpreted as “grace.” [Note: The exemplar has *unde quisque ergo*; either *unde* or *ergo* is redundant. The editor removes *ergo*, but permits removal of the equally redundant *unde* instead.] Therefore, whoever among us wishes to become God’s possession should join these two wives to himself. But when he celebrates marriage with them, he should first join to himself the one who is nobler and more distinguished—grace. For grace is joined to us first through faith, as the Apostle also says: “You have been saved by grace through faith.” [Note: Romans 5:1; Galatians 2:16; and more explicitly Ephesians 2:8.]

But we are joined second to Peninnah, that is, to conversion, because through the grace of faith correction of morals and conversion of life take place. Yet although this is the order of the marriage, another order of procreation results. For Peninnah first bears children for us, because we produce our first fruits from conversion and bring forth the first buds of righteousness through actions and works. The first work of righteousness is to turn away from sins; for unless we first turn and depart from evil, we shall not be able to become fathers through Hannah or generate children through grace.

“Let us therefore examine the differences of each. Peninnah has children, but they do not stand before God. For such children cannot belong to conversion in such a way that they stand before and cling to God; yet they are not empty or wholly alien to the things of God. For they receive portions of the divine sacrifices and eat from the offerings of God. Thus each of us first turns away from sin, so that from conversion he may produce works of righteousness. Afterwards Hannah, stirred up within us by zeal and emulation of what is good, pours out a prayer to God so that she too may bear children.

“What kind of children, then, does Hannah, who is grace, bear? Those who sit beside God. For grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. This, then, is the son of grace: the one who is free for God and for the word of God.”

After this Hannah prayed and said [Note: Chapter 2, verse 1. But this interpretation differs greatly from our Vulgate, and indeed from the Vulgate and the version that Augustine presents below, which is to be cited from Book XVII, chapter 4, of *The City of God*]:

“My heart has been established in the Lord, and my horn has been exalted in my God my Savior. My mouth has been enlarged over my enemies. I have rejoiced in your salvation,” and so forth. [Note: Everything that follows is copied from chapter 4 of Book XVII of *The City of God*; Claudius himself does not conceal this afterward.]

“Will these words really be thought to belong merely to a little woman rejoicing over the son born to her? Has the human mind been so turned away from the light of truth that it does not perceive that the words she poured forth surpass the measure of a woman?”

« Moreover, whoever is appropriately moved by the very events that had already begun to be fulfilled even in this pilgrimage—does he not turn his attention, look, and recognize in this woman, whose name (that is, Hannah) is interpreted as “his grace,” the Christian religion itself, the very City of God, whose king and founder is Christ, and finally the grace of God itself, by whose prophetic spirit she spoke in this manner? By this grace the proud are estranged, so that they may fall; by it the humble are filled, so that they may rise—precisely what this hymn chiefly proclaims. Unless someone should perhaps say that this woman prophesied nothing, but merely praised God in exultant proclamation on account of the son for whom she had prayed and whom she obtained.

What, then, does she mean when she says: “He has made the bow of the mighty weak, and the weak have girded themselves with strength. Those who were full of bread have been reduced, and the hungry have crossed the land, because the barren woman has borne seven, while she who had many children has grown weak”? Had she herself borne seven, although she had been barren? When she said this, she had only one; nor did she later bear seven—or six, with Samuel as the seventh—but three sons and two daughters.

Finally, speaking of the people, when no one yet reigned, she placed at the end [Note: “That he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory” (verse 8).]: “He gives strength to our kings, and has exalted the horn of his Christ.” Whence did she say this, if she was not prophesying?

Let the Church of Christ speak—the City of the great King, full of grace and fruitful in offspring. Let it say what it recognizes as having been prophesied about itself so long beforehand through the mouth of this devout mother: “My heart has been established in the Lord, and my horn has been exalted in my God.” Truly the heart has been established and the horn exalted, because it is not in itself but in the Lord its God. “My mouth has been enlarged against my enemies”: because even amid the straits of afflictions the word of God has not been bound.

[Note: II Timothy 2:9; in the edition of Augustine published by the Fathers of Saint-Maur, the words “nor in preachers who are bound” are added.]

“I have rejoiced,” she says [Note: The manuscript reads inquid, both here and shortly below. Elsewhere I have observed that t and d are often interchanged in ancient codices, so that one reads inquid, capud, ed, and conversely set, Davit, etc. See the ninth annotation on the sermon of St. Antipater.], “in your salvation.” This is Christ Jesus, whom that old man Simeon, as we read in the Gospel (Luke 2:25 and following), embraced as a little child while recognizing him as great: “Now dismiss your servant in peace,” he said, “for my eyes have seen your salvation.” Let the Church therefore say: “I have rejoiced in your salvation.”

« [Note: 1 Samuel 2:2, but with some distinction, as also occurs below.] “For there is none holy like the Lord, and there is none just like our God.” He is both holy and sanctifying; just and justifying. “There is none holy besides you,” because no one becomes holy except through you.

Then it follows (verse 3): “Do not boast, you proud, and do not speak lofty things; let not arrogance come forth from your mouth, for the Lord is a God of knowledge.” He knows you himself, even where no one else knows; for “whoever thinks that he is something, when he is nothing, deceives himself.” These words are spoken to the adversaries belonging to the City of God’s Babylon, who presume upon their own strength and glory in themselves rather than in the Lord. Among them are also the carnal Israelites, earthly citizens of earthly Jerusalem, who, as the Apostle says (Romans 10:3), “being ignorant of God’s righteousness”—that is, the righteousness which God gives to human beings, since he alone is just and justifies—and wishing to establish their own, that is, as though prepared by themselves for themselves rather than bestowed by him, have not submitted to God’s righteousness.

They are proud because they think, on the basis of what is their own rather than God’s, that they can please God—who is the God of knowledge and therefore also the judge of consciences. In him he sees the thoughts of human beings, “for they are vain” (Psalm 93:11; 35). If they are human thoughts, they are not from him (1 Samuel 2:3). “And preparing,” she says, “his own devices.” What devices can we suppose these to be except that the proud should fall and the humble rise? He carries out these devices when he says: “The bow of the mighty has been weakened, and the weak have girded themselves with strength.” The bow has been weakened—that is, the purpose of those who seem so powerful to themselves that, without God’s gift and assistance, they think they can fulfill the divine commandments by human sufficiency. And those are girded with strength whose inward cry is: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak” (Psalm 6:3).

« “Those who were full of bread,” she says, “have been reduced, and the hungry have crossed the land.” Who are to be understood as those full of bread except those same people who are, as it were, powerful—namely, the Israelites, to whom the oracles of God were entrusted (Romans 3:2)? But among that people the sons of the maidservant have been reduced. Although expressed in less classical Latin, this is nevertheless well conveyed: those who were greater have become lesser, because even from those breads—that is, from the divine words, which at that time the Israelites alone among all nations had received—they savor earthly things.

But the nations, to whom that law had not been given, after they came to those oracles through the New Testament, crossed the land while greatly hungering, because in them they savored not earthly but heavenly things. And this is given as though in answer to the question why it happened.

« “Because the barren woman has borne seven, while she who had many children has grown weak.” Here everything that was being prophesied shone forth for those who recognized the number seven, by which the perfection of the universal Church is signified. For this reason the Apostle John also writes to seven churches (Revelation 2:4), thereby showing that he is writing to the fullness of one Church. And in the Proverbs of Solomon, Wisdom, prefiguring this beforehand, “built her house and hewed out her seven pillars” (Proverbs 9:1).

The City of God was barren among all the nations before this offspring, which we behold, arose. We also see that earthly Jerusalem, which had many children, has now grown weak, because whoever were sons of the free woman in it constituted its strength. But now, since there is the letter there and not the Spirit, it has lost its strength and become weak.

(Verse 6.) « “The Lord puts to death and gives life; he leads down to the underworld and brings back.” He put to death that woman who had many children and gave life to this barren woman who bore seven; although it may more appropriately be understood that he gives life to the same people whom he had put to death, for he repeated the thought as though by addition: “He leads down to the underworld and brings back.”

Those to whom the Apostle says (Colossians 3:1), “If you have died with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God,” are beneficially put to death by the Lord. He adds to them (ibid., verse 2): “Taste the things that are above, not the things that are on earth,” so that they may be the very ones who “crossed the land while hungry” (verse 3). “For you have died,” he says. See how God beneficially puts them to death.

Then it follows: “And your life is hidden with Christ in God.” See how God gives life to these same people. But did he lead these same people down to the underworld and bring them back? We see both of these things, beyond any dispute among the faithful, fulfilled rather in him, our head, with whom the Apostle said that our life is hidden in God.

For he who “did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Romans 8:32), in this manner certainly put him to death; and because he raised him from the dead, he gave life to that same one again. And because his voice is recognized in prophecy—“You will not abandon my soul in the underworld” (Psalm 15:10; Acts 2:27)—he led that same one down to the underworld and brought him back.

By this poverty of his we have been enriched. “For the Lord makes poor and makes rich.” To know what this means, let us hear what follows: “He humbles and exalts”—certainly, he humbles the proud and exalts the humble. For what is read elsewhere (James 4:6; Proverbs 3:34), “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble,” is contained throughout this entire speech of Hannah, whose name is interpreted as “his grace.”

Now, when it adds: “He raises the poor from the earth,” I understand this better of no one than of him who, though rich, became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might be enriched, as was said shortly before. He raised him from the earth so quickly that his flesh did not see corruption.

Nor will I exclude from him what is added: “And he lifts the needy from the dung.” The needy man is plainly the poor man; and the dung from which he was raised is rightly understood as the Jewish persecutors, among whose number the Apostle said that he had been: “I persecuted the Church” (1 Corinthians 15:9; Philippians 3:6). “The things that were gain to me,” he says (ibid., verse 8), “I considered loss for Christ; indeed, I considered them not merely losses but dung, so that I might gain Christ.”

He was raised from the earth, poor above all the rich, and from that dung the needy man was raised above all the wealthy, so that he might sit with the powerful of the people, to whom he said: “You will sit upon twelve thrones” (Matthew 19:28), while giving them the inheritance of the throne of glory. For those powerful men had said (Matthew 19:27): “Behold, we have left everything and followed you.”

These most powerful men had made this vow; but from whom did they receive it, unless from the one of whom it is immediately said here [Note: The published Augustine reads “to the one making a vow,” but the Fathers of Saint-Maur do not indicate the scriptural passage in which these words occur.]: “Granting the gift of making a vow”? Otherwise they would have belonged to those powerful men whose bow was weakened. “Granting,” he says, “the gift of making a vow”; for no one would make a proper vow to the Lord unless he received from him what he was to vow (verse 8).

It follows:

[Note: Here Claudius follows Augustine’s Septuagint interpreters, who read: “giving a vow to the one who vows, and he blessed the years of the just”—διδοὺς εὐχὴν τῷ εὐχομένῳ, καὶ εὐλόγησεν ἔτη δικαίου. Why these same Septuagint interpreters differ so greatly from the Hebrew and the Vulgate is a question for interpreters, to whom I refer the reader; for that matter does not belong to the present work.]

“And he blessed the years of the just.” Thus, of course, he may live without end with the one to whom it was said (Psalm 101:28): “Your years will not fail.” There the years stand; here they pass away—or rather, they perish. Before they come, they do not exist; when they have come, they will not remain, because they come together with their end.

Of these two things—“granting the gift of making a vow” and “blessing the years of the just”—one is what we do and the other what we receive. But this second thing cannot be received from God the giver unless, with his assistance, the first has been accomplished, because “a man is not powerful by his own strength” (verse 9).

“The Lord will make his adversary weak”—that is, the one who envies and resists the person making a vow, so that he may not be able to fulfill what he vowed. From the ambiguity of the Greek it may be understood as “and his adversary.” For when the Lord begins to possess us, the adversary who had been ours certainly becomes his and will be overcome by us; but not by our own strength, because “a man is not powerful by his own strength.” The Lord, therefore, will make his adversary weak.

[Note: In the interpretation of this verse, Claudius plainly follows Augustine’s version of the Septuagint: Κύριος ἀσθενοποιήσει τὸν ἀντίδικον αὐτοῦ· Κύριος ἅγιος—that is, “The Lord makes his adversary weak [or feeble]; the Lord is holy.”]

« “The Lord is holy,” so that he may be overcome by the holy ones whom the Lord of the saints makes holy.

« Through these things [Note: In Eucherius this reads “through this”; in the edition of Augustine by the Fathers of Saint-Maur, it reads “he shall not boast,” here and below. There are also other differences at this point between our manuscript and the published Augustine and Eucherius.] the wise man shall be disregarded in his wisdom; the powerful man shall be disregarded in his power; and the rich man in his riches. But let the one who boasts, boast in this: to understand and know the Lord, and to practice judgment and righteousness in the midst of the earth.

[Note: All that Claudius—or rather Augustine, from whom Claudius wrote this—now inserts as words taken from Hannah’s song is found neither in the Hebrew nor in most Greek manuscripts. Accordingly, it is found neither in the Complutensian edition nor in nearly all the other editions. Nevertheless, it appears in the Greek Bibles published by Aldus, in the following form:

Μὴ καυχάσθω ὁ φρόνιμος ἐν τῇ φρονήσει αὐτοῦ· καὶ μὴ καυχάσθω ὁ δυνατὸς ἐν τῇ δυνάμει αὐτοῦ· καὶ μὴ καυχάσθω ὁ πλούσιος ἐν τῷ πλούτῳ αὐτοῦ· ἀλλ’ ἐν τούτῳ καυχάσθω ὁ καυχώμενος ἐν τῷ συνιεῖν καὶ γινώσκειν τὸν Κύριον καὶ ποιεῖν κρίμα καὶ δικαιοσύνην ἐν μέσῳ τῆς γῆς.

Our Mingarellius translated it as follows: “Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the powerful man boast in his power, nor the rich man in his riches; but let the one who boasts boast in this, if he understands and knows the Lord, and if he practices judgment and righteousness in the midst of the earth.”

After quoting these words, that same Mingarellius, whom I cited, adds: “The Hebrew exemplar does not contain these words here either, and they seem to have been transferred here from the ninth chapter of Jeremiah.” And indeed, in verses 23 and 24 of Jeremiah’s ninth chapter, these words occur: “Thus says the Lord: Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man boast in his strength, nor the rich man boast in his riches; but let the one who boasts boast in this: to understand and know me, that I am the Lord who practices mercy, judgment, and righteousness in the midst of the earth.”

From this passage of Augustine, and therefore of Eucherius and Claudius, it is plainly evident that the verses I have mentioned had long before been read in Hannah’s song and customarily recited by the churches. Whether Paul has these words in view when he says, “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (2 Corinthians 10:17), the reader may judge.]

A person understands and knows the Lord in no small measure when he understands and knows that even these things are given to him by the Lord, so that he may understand and know the Lord. For what do you have, the Apostle says (1 Corinthians 4:7), that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it—that is, as though you possessed from yourself the basis for your boasting?

He practices judgment and righteousness who lives rightly. He lives rightly who obeys God, who commands; and the end of the commandment (1 Timothy 1:5)—that is, the goal toward which the commandment is directed—is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. This love, as the Apostle John testifies (1 John 4:7), is from God. Therefore, to practice judgment and righteousness is from God.

But what does “in the midst of the earth” mean? Surely those who dwell at the ends of the earth are not forbidden to practice judgment and righteousness. Who could say such a thing? Why, then, was “in the midst of the earth” added?

If it had not been added, and the text had said only “to practice judgment and righteousness,” this great commandment would have applied to both kinds of people, those living inland and those living by the sea. But so that no one might suppose that after the end of the life lived in this body there remains time to practice judgment and righteousness—things he did not practice while in the flesh—and thus think he could evade divine judgment, “in the midst of the earth” seems to me to mean while each person lives in the body.

In this life each person carries his own earth, which, when the human being dies, the earth receives [Note: The word “common” is added in the published Augustine; it is absent in Eucherius.] and will certainly return when he rises. Therefore, “in the midst of the earth”—that is, while our soul is enclosed in this earthly body—judgment and righteousness must be practiced, for our future benefit, when each person will receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil (2 Corinthians 5:10).

For when the Apostle says “through the body,” he means the time during which one lived in the body. If someone blasphemes with a wicked mind and impious thought, but does not carry this out through any bodily members, will he therefore not be guilty because he did not perform it through bodily movement, even though he did it during the time in which he also possessed a body?

In this sense what is read in the Psalm may also be fittingly understood (Psalm 75:12): “But God our king before the ages has worked salvation in the midst of the earth.” The Lord Jesus is to be understood as our God, who is before the ages (John 1:5; Hebrews 1:2), because through him the ages were made. He worked salvation in the midst of the earth when “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14) and dwelt in an earthly body.

[Note: The expression “the divine Word dwelt in an earthly body,” if taken strictly, will rightly displease Catholics. For the divine Word not only dwelt in an earthly body; by assuming human nature and uniting it to himself, he also hypostatically united the body to himself. Theologians have treated this subject extensively, and they also note that this and similar expressions were not infrequently used before the rise of the errors of Nestorius and Eutyches by Fathers who were undoubtedly orthodox and opposed to those errors.]

Then, after Hannah’s words had prophesied how the one who boasts ought to boast—not in himself, but in the Lord—because of the retribution that will occur on the day of judgment (verse 10), she says: “The Lord has ascended into the heavens and thundered; he himself will judge the ends of the earth, because he is just.”

She has followed exactly the order of the confession of the faithful. The Lord Jesus Christ ascended into heaven, and from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. For who ascended, as the Apostle says (Ephesians 4:9–10), except the one who also descended into the lower parts of the earth? The one who descended is himself the one who ascended above all the heavens, so that he might fulfill all things.

Therefore, he thundered through his clouds, because after he had ascended he filled them with the Holy Spirit. Concerning these clouds, he threatened Jerusalem the handmaid—that is, the ungrateful vineyard—through the prophet Isaiah, that they should not rain upon her (Isaiah 5:6).

As it is said, “He himself will judge the ends of the earth,” as though it meant “the ends of the human being” [Note: Augustine’s published text reads “the ends of the earth,” but incorrectly; for he would not otherwise explain what he had set out to explain. This passage should therefore be corrected on the basis of Eucherius and our manuscript, and “the ends of the human being” should be read.]. For he will not fail to judge other parts, since without doubt he will judge all human beings. But “the ends of the earth” are better understood as “the ends of the human being,” because what changes for better or worse during the intervening period will not be judged, but rather the condition in which the one being judged is found at the end.

[Note: Do not understand these words as though the Lord judges only our final actions. It is written: “And I will search Jerusalem with lamps” (Zephaniah 1:12). Rather, he judges us as he finds us when death snatches us from the world. If God finds us pleasing to him, he will no longer remember our iniquities (Isaiah 43:25). But if he finds us hateful to him and overtaken by mortal sin, “the righteousness of the righteous will not deliver him on whatever day he sins” (Ezekiel 25:12). The same point is expressed more explicitly elsewhere (Ezekiel 18:24): “If the righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity … will he live? None of his righteous deeds that he has done will be remembered; in the transgression by which he transgressed and in the sin that he committed, in these he shall die.”]

Therefore, what will be judged is not the changing condition itself, but the state in which the one being judged is found. Hence it is said (Matthew 10:22): “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.” Whoever therefore perseveringly practices judgment and righteousness in the midst of the earth will not be condemned when the ends of the earth are judged (verse 10).

“And he gives strength to our kings,” she says, so that, by judging them, he does not condemn them, but gives them the strength by which, as kings, they may rule the flesh and, in him, conquer the world—the one who shed his blood for them (ibid.).

« “And he has exalted the horn of his Christ.” How has Christ exalted the horn of his Christ? The one of whom it was said above, “The Lord has ascended into the heavens,” is understood to be the Lord Christ; he himself, as it is said here, has exalted the horn of his Christ. Who, then, is Christ’s Christ? Or will he exalt the horn of each one of his faithful, just as this same woman said at the beginning of the hymn: “My horn has been exalted in my God”? For we may rightly call all those who have been anointed with his chrism “Christs.” Yet the whole body together with its head is one Christ.

This is what Hannah, the mother of Samuel, a holy and greatly praised man, prophesied. In him the transformation of the old priesthood was then prefigured, and now fulfilled, because she who had many children has grown weak, so that the barren woman who bore seven might have a new priesthood in Christ.

We have been compelled to insert this song according to the translation of the Seventy interpreters [Note: You have the song itself and the exposition given by Augustine in chapter 4 of book 17 of The City of God, as I have already said; please consult it. Claudius copied a substantial part of what Augustine explained at that place.], as it was expounded by blessed Augustine, because that translation contains a fuller and more truthful account of the history [Note: What follows concerning the interpretation of this verse was taken entirely from Isidore, on this passage.] ».

« Meanwhile (chapter 2:18), Samuel was ministering in the temple of God, girded with the ephod (chapter 1:12–13, and again verse 17). But the sons of Eli, violating the divine sacrifices, were sinning before the Lord; and through them many mocked the sacrifice of God (ibid., verse 27 and following, and again chapter 2:11 and following). Therefore Eli the priest was condemned because of their wickedness (chapter 2:23 and following), because he punished them with insufficient severity [Note: “Poor me” is added, though I do not know why.]. He did restrain them, and he did reprove them, but with the gentleness and mildness of a father, not with the severity and authority of a high priest. By this judgment priests may learn how they are punished on account of the conduct of their sons—that is, on account of the crimes of the people—and how, even if they themselves are holy, the fault of their subjects is nevertheless reckoned to them if they do not restrain them (chapter 2:27 and following).

« But this is stated more explicitly to Eli the priest himself by the man of God who was sent to him. His name is not given, but from his office and ministry it is understood without doubt that he was a prophet. For it is written:

[Note: The interpretation found here differs greatly from that of Augustine, whom Claudius is copying; Claudius’s version here is almost entirely that of the Vulgate. Is this to be attributed to the copyist, or rather to Claudius himself? I await the judgment of others.]

“Then a man of God came to Eli and said to him: Thus says the Lord. Was I not plainly revealed to the house of your father when it was in Egypt, in the house of Pharaoh? And I chose him out of all Israel for myself as priest, to ascend my altar, burn incense to me, and carry the ephod before me. And I gave to the house of your father all the sacrifices of the children of Israel.

“Why have you kicked away my victim and my offerings, which I commanded to be offered in the temple, and honored your sons more than me, so that you might eat the first portions of every sacrifice of my people Israel? Therefore thus says the Lord God of Israel: Speaking, I spoke that your house and the house of your father should minister in my sight forever.

“But now the Lord says: Far be this from me. Rather, whoever glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me shall be held of no account. Behold, the days are coming, and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, so that there will be no old man in your house. And you will see your rival Christ in the temple amid all the prosperity of Israel, and there will be no old man in your house throughout all your days.

“Nevertheless, I will not utterly remove a man from you from my altar, but so that your eyes may fail and your soul may waste away; and the greater part of your house shall die when it reaches manhood. This will be a sign for you: what will happen to your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas. On one day both shall die, and I will raise up for myself a faithful priest who will act according to my heart and my soul.”

« This prophecy cannot be said to have been fulfilled in Samuel, in whom the transformation of the old priesthood was so clearly foretold. Although Samuel belonged to a different tribe from the one appointed by the Lord to serve at the altar, he was nevertheless not a son of Aaron, whose descendants had been designated to furnish the priests.

Thus, in that historical event too, the same transformation that was to occur through Christ Jesus was foreshadowed. It belonged properly to the Old Testament, but figuratively to the New: it was a prophecy in deed as well as in word, signifying by the event itself what had been said in words to Eli the priest through the prophet.

For afterward there were priests from the line of Aaron, such as Zadok (2 Samuel 15:24 and following) and Abiathar (1 Samuel 20 and 22; again 22:6, 9, and 30:7; 2 Samuel 15:24 and following), during the reign of David, and others thereafter, before the time came when what had been foretold so long beforehand concerning the change of the priesthood had to be accomplished through Christ.

But who, now looking upon these things with faithful eyes, would not see that they have been fulfilled? For no tabernacle, no temple, no altar, no sacrifice, and therefore no priest remains among the Jews, although God’s law had commanded that priests be appointed for them from the seed of Aaron.

This too is recalled here when the prophet says (chapter 2:30):

[Note: Numbers 25:12–13: “Behold, I give him—Phinehas, son of Eleazar—the peace of my covenant; and it shall be for him and for his seed after him a perpetual covenant of priesthood.”]

“Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Speaking, I spoke that the house of your father should minister in my sight forever. But now the Lord says: Far be this from me. Rather, whoever glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me shall be held of no account.”

[Note: These words too are taken from the Vulgate. Augustine presents a much different interpretation, which is also maintained below.]

For when he names “the house of his father,” he is not speaking of his immediate father, but of that Aaron who was first appointed priest, from whose descendants the others would follow. The preceding words demonstrate this, where he says (Exodus 4:28; verse 1 and following): “I was revealed to the house of your father when it was in Egypt, in the house of Pharaoh” (Leviticus 21:22; Numbers 3:10), “and I chose him from all the tribes of Israel for myself as priest.”

Who was this man’s father in the Egyptian bondage, from which, after they had been freed, he was chosen for the priesthood, except Aaron? Of his stock, therefore, he said in this passage that there would no longer be priests—a fact which we now see fulfilled.

Let faith keep watch; the realities are at hand. They are seen, held, and thrust before the eyes of those who refuse to see.

“Behold,” he says, “the days are coming, and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your house, so that there will be no old man in your house, and you will see your rival Christ in the temple amid all the prosperity of Israel” (Numbers 25:13 and following).

[Note: Verse 31. At this point Claudius follows neither the Vulgate nor Augustine entirely, but some other interpretation.]

Behold, the days that were foretold have now come. There is no priest according to the order of Aaron. Whenever a man from his race sees the Christian sacrifice prevailing throughout the whole world, while that honor has been taken away from him, his eyes fail and his soul wastes away with the decay of grief.

But what follows belongs specifically to the house of this Eli, to whom these words were spoken (verses 33–34): “And the greater part of your house shall die when they reach manhood. This will be a sign for you concerning what will happen to your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas: on one day both shall die.”

This sign, therefore, was made as a sign of the transfer of the priesthood from this house; by that sign the change of the sacrifice of the house of Aaron was signified [Note: The published Augustine reads “priesthood,” but the two words have the same reference.]. For the death of his sons signified the death not of human beings but of the priesthood itself among the sons of Aaron.

« What follows also concerns that priest whose figure Samuel represented [Note: That is, Eli.], succeeding him. Therefore what follows is said of Christ Jesus, the true priest of the New Testament (verse 35): “I will raise up for myself a faithful priest who will act according to my heart and my soul.”

[Note: The material I have noted up to this point is found in Augustine. Seek what follows in Question 1 of Bede’s book of thirty questions on the Books of Kings.]

« Under the figure of Samuel, the Lord and Savior, the supreme and true high priest, ought to be understood. He, like Samuel, succeeded the deceased Eli in the priesthood, not from the line of Aaron but chosen from another family of Levi.

For he was [Note: This parenthesis is absent from the published editions.]—as we have already mentioned—the son of Elkanah, son of Jeroboam, son of Elihel, son of Thau, son of Suth, son of Elkanah, son of Joel, son of Azariah, son of Zephaniah, son of Thahath, son of Assir, son of Abiasaph, son of Korah, son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Israel, as the Books of Chronicles relate.

Thus the mediator of God and human beings, in order to be our high priest, took the origin of his flesh not from Levi but from another tribe, namely Judah. He offered the Father for us a sacrifice other than the legal one, namely his very own flesh. And he left as heirs of his priesthood others than those descended from Aaron—namely, the children of the grace of the New Testament, gathered from every nation of the Gentiles.

As for God’s statement, speaking in a human manner (ibid., that is, verse 35), “who will act according to my heart and my soul,” it may rightly be understood of Samuel, in that as a human being he obeyed God in everything according to his will. But it is more rightly understood of the Lord and Savior, because, as the only-begotten Son [Note: The manuscript reads patronorum, “of patrons,” which I judge to be a copyist’s error. Bede has patris, “of the Father.”], he is in all things conscious of the Father’s mysteries, in accordance with what he himself plainly testifies about himself, saying (John 8:28): “I do nothing of myself, but as the Father taught me, so I speak. And he who sent me is with me; he has not left me alone, because I always do what pleases him.”

[Note: Augustine transmitted what follows again in section 3 of chapter 5 of book 17 of The City of God.]

« But when God says, “because he will do everything that is in my heart and in my soul,” let us not suppose that God has a soul, since he is the creator of the soul. Rather, this is said figuratively of God, not properly, just as are “hand,” “foot,” and the other members of the body. And so that no one may believe that human beings were made in the image of God according to the bodily form of this flesh, wings are also attributed to him, although human beings certainly do not possess them. Thus it is said to God (Psalm 16:8): “Protect me under the shadow of your wings,” so that human beings may understand that such things are spoken of that ineffable nature not through proper but through transferred names.

[Note: Thus far Augustine. For what follows, seek again in Bede at the place recently cited—that is, Question 1 among the thirty questions—although certain things have been altered and added, which I attribute to Claudius himself.] »
And I will build him a faithful house, and he shall walk before my Christ all his days.

“This is the house which the Father builds, of which the Apostle says (Heb. 3:6): ‘whose house we are, if we hold fast the confidence and the glory of hope firm to the end.’ And this house shall walk before his Christ, namely, before the supreme Pontiff himself. ‘He shall walk,’ he said—that is, he shall conduct himself—as he had earlier said concerning the house of Aaron (v. 30): ‘Speaking, I have spoken, so that your house and your father’s house might minister in my sight forever.’ But when he says, ‘he shall walk before my Christ,’ this must certainly be understood of the house itself, not of that priest who is Christ himself, the Mediator and Savior. His house, therefore, shall walk before him.

“‘He shall walk’ may also be understood as referring to the passage from death to life, throughout all the days in which this mortality continues until the end of the present age. Otherwise, how could it be understood of Samuel that a faithful house was built for him, which would walk before Christ the Lord—that is, before Samuel himself—throughout all days, when we read later (chap. 8:3) that his sons, having turned aside from his ways, inclined toward greed and perverted judgment? Unless perhaps in this passage we understand his house to mean the Israelite people, who throughout all the days of his priesthood served the Lord, concerning whom it is written (1 Sam. 7): ‘And all Israel rested after the Lord.’ And shortly afterward (ibid., v. 4): ‘And the children of Israel removed the Baals and the Astartes, and served the Lord alone.’

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Chapter 1, verse 36. Here Augustine is again copied, but with a substantially different interpretation of Scripture.]

“But what follows—‘It shall come to pass that whoever remains in your house shall come, that prayer may be made for him’—is not properly said of the house of this Eli, but of the house of that Aaron from which men remained until the coming of Jesus Christ, and from which such men are not lacking even now. For concerning the house of this Eli it had already been said above [Note: [Col. 0649D] A version from Augustine is cited here.]: ‘And everyone who remains of your house shall fall by the sword.’ How, then, could it truly be said here, ‘There shall be one who remains in your house; let him come, that prayer may be made for him’? If the former statement is true, namely, that no one would survive the avenging sword, this can only be because he wished those to be understood who belong to the stock of that entire priesthood according to the order of Aaron.

“Therefore, if this concerns those predestined remnants of which another Prophet said (Isa. 10:21–22; Rom. 9:27), ‘The remnant shall be saved,’ whence the Apostle also says (Rom. 11:5), ‘So therefore at this present time also there is a remnant saved according to the election of grace,’ then it is rightly understood of such remnants that the one of whom it was said, ‘whoever remains in your house,’ certainly believes in Christ. Thus in the time of the Apostles many from that very people believed (Acts 2:41 and elsewhere). Nor are there now lacking those who, although very rarely, nevertheless believe. And in such a person is fulfilled what this man of God immediately went on to say:

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Chapter 2, verse 36. Most of what follows is copied from Augustine, though not entirely. Isidore has it in full, chapter 2 of his book on 1 Kings; Claudius therefore copies him here almost verbatim.]

“‘And let him offer a silver coin and a round loaf of bread, and say: “Dismiss me, I beg you, to one priestly portion, that I may eat a morsel of bread.”’ What is signified by the silver coin except the confession of the mouth (Rom. 10:10), which is made by believers unto salvation? Silver is customarily used to signify speech, as the Psalmist testifies where it is sung:

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Psalm 11:7. There is some variation here between the printed edition and our manuscript.]

‘The words of the Lord are pure words,
silver tested in fire,
approved by the earth,
purified sevenfold.’

“But what does this one who comes say? ‘Dismiss me, I beg you, to one priestly portion, that I may eat a morsel of bread.’ He calls the priestly portion the body of Christ, that is, the Church, whose priest is that mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. To this people the Apostle Peter says (1 Pet. 2:9): ‘A holy people, a royal priesthood.’ Into this priestly portion he asks to eat a morsel of bread. In these words the sacrifice of Christians is elegantly expressed, concerning which the priest himself says: ‘The bread which I will give’ (John 6:52) ‘is my flesh for the life of the world.’ For this is the sacrifice, not according to the order of Aaron (Heb. 5:6; 7:11 and elsewhere), but according to the order of Melchizedek.”

[Note: [Col. 0649D] 1 Kings 3:2. With some distinction, which is also found in other editions. See Calmet on this passage.]

Now it happened one day that Eli was lying in his place, and his eyes had grown dim, so that he could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished. In the tabernacle of the covenant there was a lampstand, where from evening until morning (Exod. 27:20–21; Lev. 24:3, 8), after the high priest had arranged the lamps in the evening, they burned continually, prepared outside the veil, as the Lord had commanded (ibid.). When this priest entered the tabernacle, already worn down by great old age, his eyes had grown so dim that he could not even look upon a lighted lamp—how much less an extinguished one? Figuratively, however, Eli had been the lamp of God when, possessing the dignity of the priesthood, he shone with the brightness of righteousness. The Prophet declares that this lamp was extinguished when, on account of the crimes of his sons, he lost both the authority of the priesthood and the light of his merits.

(Cap. 3:19.) “Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him, and none of his words fell to the ground.”

[Note: [Col. 0650D] The explanation of this passage is taken entirely from Bede’s second question.]

“This signifies that nothing of what he said was ineffective, but that everything happened just as he had spoken. For idle words fall to the ground—words that are to be regarded as worthless and trampled under universal contempt—just as blessed Job also said (Job 29:24): ‘And the light of my face did not fall to the ground.’ For he was accustomed to maintain and preserve such gravity in his countenance that he was never relaxed into contemptible cheerfulness. But whenever he showed himself more cheerful to those present, he did so and acted always for a definite reason connected with their benefit.”

“Accordingly,

[Note: [Col. 0650D] Isidore teaches us (chapter 3 on 1 Kings) that the passages which follow are marked off with lines.]

after these things had been foretold by that Prophet to Eli as a figure of the change from the Old Testament—when Israel offended the Lord—

[Note: [Col. 0650D] Chapter 4, verses 2 and following.]

“the Philistines drew up their battle line against them, and so forth. The Israelites took up the ark as a defense for their position; the ark was captured by the enemies, and they themselves were not merely defeated and put to flight, but a great slaughter of the slain also took place. This event signifies “something” (nonnihil), or rather “several things” (nonnulla), concerning the future. For in prophecy (with the variant prophetice, “prophetically”), the capture of that ark by foreigners indicated that the covenant of God would pass to the nations (gentibus; corrected gentes).

[Col. 0650D]

“When Eli the priest was told that the ark of the Lord had been captured, he fell from his seat and died (chap. 4:16–18). As the ark of the Lord passed to the nations, the priesthood of the Jews perished and came to an end.

[Note: [Col. 0650D] The words ‘perished and came to an end’ should not, I would have you understand, be taken to mean that it truly perished at that time; for in reality Abiathar and Zadok are recorded as priests a few years later. Rather, because Samuel, while Eli’s only surviving son was still a young child and therefore unable to perform the priestly office, fulfilled the functions of a priest, he even offered the solemn sacrifices. 1 Sam. 7:6, 10; 9:12, 16; 2, etc.]

“Two sons also fell, and one wife was widowed; and she soon died in childbirth (chap. 5:20), because of the same upheaval. This was prefigured by an evident sign: after the Jewish priesthood had been extinguished, the carnal Synagogue, clinging to it in a carnal manner, would be overthrown; and when Eli had fallen from his seat, the seat of the Jewish priests would remain vacant, and the glory of the priesthood and kingdom would be extinguished.”

[Note: [Col. 0651D] “Of the high priest” (pontificis) is preferable to our reading.]

(Cap. 5:2 and following.) “But what does it mean that, when the Philistines had placed the ark of the Lord in the temple of Dagon their god, they entered the temple and found their god fallen and broken, with his head and both his hands cut off? As soon as the covenant of the Lord reached the nations, the idols that possessed the deceived world were immediately destroyed, and all the error of images collapsed together, unable to endure the presence of God.

“For in the severed hands of Dagon, the work of idolatry was being cut off.

[Note: [Col. 0651D] ‘Amputated.’ Some things are lacking in the printed edition of Eucherius.]

“And in the severing of his head the pride of the devil is signified (significatur; the variant significabatur means “was signified”), from whom sin had its beginning. As for the fact that this occurred at the threshold, it was so that they might recognize (agnoscere; corrected agnoscerent) the definite and predetermined end of their idolatry; for a threshold signifies the limits of a road.

“That also has great significance which occurred in the very fall and breaking of Dagon their god: they found only his back, all his other limbs having been broken (v. 5). For the back signifies flight. Whoever flees gives his back to those pursuing him. Hence it is written concerning enemies (Ps. 20:13): ‘For you will make them turn their backs.’ Where are the idols? They have perished. And if some remain, they are hidden by certain people—and they have fled.

“(Verses 6 and Ps. 77:66.) But the fact that those who captured the ark of God were struck in their hindquarters appears to be a sign of punishment. For if there are any who have received the covenant (susceperint; variants susceperunt, “received,” and dilexerunt, “loved”) and have loved the things behind them in life, they are most justly tormented by those very things which, as the Apostle says (Phil. 3:8), they ought to have regarded as refuse. Those who receive the divine covenant in such a way that, looking back, they do not strip themselves of their former vanity are like those enemies who placed the captured ark of the covenant beside their idols.

“And indeed the other old things fall even against the will of those who possess them, because (Isa. 40:6) ‘all flesh is grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass; the grass withers, and the flower falls.’ But the ark of the Lord remains forever: namely, the hidden covenant, the kingdom of heaven, where the eternal Word of God is.”

(6:1 and following.) When the ark of the Lord returned from the land of the Philistines to the land of the Israelites, it was placed upon a cart, and cows were harnessed to the cart; they are said to have been nursing calves.

[Col. 0652A]

(V. 10.) Their calves they shut up at home, as it is written. (V. 12.) The cows went straight along the road that leads to Beth-shemesh; they proceeded along one road, going forward and lowing, and did not turn aside either to the right or to the left.

[Note: [Col. 0651D] All that follows our Claudius took from Gregory the Great, who touches on it in book 7, number 42, of the Moralia on Job, but states it most explicitly in Homily 37 on the Gospels, number 3. I have therefore distinguished these passages with lines so that the reader may separate them from Claudius’s words.]

“What, then, do the cows signify except the faithful in the Church, who, while they consider the commands of sacred speech, carry the ark of the Lord as though it had been placed upon them? It should also be noted concerning them that they are said to have been nursing calves, because there are many who, inwardly established in the way of God, are bound outwardly by carnal affections; nevertheless, those who carry the ark of God in their minds do not turn aside from the straight path.

“For behold, the cows are proceeding to Beth-shemesh. Beth-shemesh is interpreted as ‘House of the Sun.’ And the Prophet says (Mal. 4:2): ‘But for you who fear God, the sun of righteousness shall rise.’ If, therefore, we are making for the dwelling of the eternal Sun, it is altogether fitting that we should not turn aside from God’s path on account of carnal affections.

“For it must be weighed with all our strength that the cows, placed beneath God’s cart, proceed, uttering groans from their inmost parts, and yet do not turn their steps from the road.

[Note: [Col. 0652D] The printed editions read: ‘they signify.’]

[Note: [Col. 0652D] What follows is drawn partly from Homily 37 on the Gospels and partly from Book 7 of St. Gregory’s Moralia. Reader, please compare it with the printed editions.]

“They feel love through compassion, but do not turn their necks backward.

[Note: [Col. 0652D] The printed editions read: ‘who.’]

“So, surely, the preachers of God and all the faithful within the holy Church ought to act: they should sympathize with their neighbors through charity, and yet not depart from the way of God through compassion. For the ark proceeding to Beth-shemesh means that heavenly knowledge is drawing near to the dwelling of inward light. But we truly make for Beth-shemesh when, walking along the path of righteousness, we do not turn toward the neighboring sides of error, not even for the sake of affection for our children.

“This is how those must walk who, having been placed beneath sacred things, now carry the ark of the Lord through inward knowledge: by grieving over the needs of their relatives, they must not turn aside from the path of righteousness that they have received.

“For their sake affection ought to hold our mind, but it ought not to bend it, lest the same mind be either hard because it is untouched by affection, or, once touched, become excessively lax because it bends.”

[Note: [Col. 0652D] Chapter 6:19. Bede teaches that the explanation of this passage was given by Claudius, specifically in chapter 3 of the Questions on the Books of Kings.]

The men of Beth-shemesh were struck because they had looked upon the ark of the Lord; he struck seventy men of the people and fifty thousand of the populace.

“The words ‘people’ and ‘populace’ are used indifferently for one and the same thing. For both are customarily translated from the one Greek word λαός (laos, ‘people’). But there appears to be a difference in this respect: in the first clause of the verse the word ‘men’ has been added. ‘Men’ signifies elders, so that the meaning is that seventy of the people’s nobles were struck, while fifty thousand men from the common crowd were struck.

“So that this might not happen, in Exodus (Exod. 2) the people stood at a distance and prayed, while Moses alone ascended to the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0653C] These additions are not found in Bede.]

“These men were struck because they not only approached but also, as another translation reports, despised it—which is more consistent with reason. For in Exodus they saw and heard, and beheld the evident manifestations of divine power, yet they did not perish. Therefore these men were punished not for seeing but for despising and acting rashly.”

[Note: [Col. 0653C] I am entirely unfamiliar with the translators whom Claudius indicates. I do know those who translated the passage as ‘had examined’: that is, they looked at it closely and in detail; or, if you prefer, they searched to discover what had been placed in the ark. The Hebrew words themselves appear to support this interpretation, for they can suitably be rendered, ‘because they had looked into the ark of the Lord.’ Yet who does not know that the very same Hebrew words can also be translated favorably, as the Vulgate actually translates them: ‘because they had seen the ark’? Could fifty thousand of the common people, with no one restraining them, conveniently have searched out whatever had been placed in the ark and hidden from the eyes of those standing around? Furthermore, interpreters of considerable authority offer highly plausible reasons why God punished the Beth-shemites with death for looking freely upon the ark. If someone wishes to regard this free gaze as a kind of irreverence, and therefore as contempt in interpretation, we may certainly admit the ‘despising and rashness’ mentioned here by Claudius.]

(Cap. 7:2.) From the day on which the ark remained in Kiriath-jearim, the days multiplied. For it was the twentieth year, and all the house of Israel rested after the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Repeat this passage from Bede, number 4.]

“This should not be understood as though the twenty years during which the ark remained (maneret; corrected manserit) in Kiriath-jearim were to be counted all the way to the eighth year of David’s reign, when he brought it to Jerusalem with a great gathering of the people (2 Sam. 6). For it is found later (1 Sam. 14:8) that in Saul’s time it was taken from this city and brought into the camp while he was fighting against the Philistines.”

[Note: [Col. 0653D] ‘Removed.’ Our reading is preferable.]

“For thus it is written (ibid.): ‘And Saul said to Ahijah, “Bring the ark of God near”; for the ark of God was there on that day with the children of Israel.’ And since it is clear (2 Sam. 7) that David brought it to Jerusalem, it remains to be understood that it was taken from the house of Aminadab, into which it is said to have been brought at that time,

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Unless you attribute this word to an erring copyist—for the printed Bede reads tulitque—it is among those words which, departing from Latin, either formed or augmented the vernacular languages. Italians say tolto and tolta, where Latin has ablatum and ablatam.]


[Note: [Col. 0653D] We learn from chapter 8 of the First Book of Kings that previously it had also been placed in the house of Abinadab at Gibeah.]

“and that, after being brought back from the camp in Saul’s days, it was carried into the aforementioned city; from there it was brought again to Jerusalem under David’s reign.

“Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that, from the time the ark remained in Kiriath-jearim, it was the twentieth year when it happened to be transferred from there in Saul’s time on account of the war. Or certainly it was the twentieth year when all the house of Israel still rested after the Lord, having cast away their idols and serving him alone. This they did throughout the entire period of Samuel’s leadership, which, according to Josephus, lasted twelve years,

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Josephus, chapter 13 of book 6 of the Antiquities [no. 9], has this in Havercamp’s edition: ‘Under this one, and after the prophet Samuel had died … he ruled, and alone governed the people after the death of Eli the high priest for twelve years, and together with King Saul for eighteen.’]

“and during the first period of Saul’s reign, which,

[Note: [Col. 0654C] ‘As the history has it,’ though certainly incorrectly.]

“as the same historian affirms,

[Note: [Col. 0654C] Chapter 14, or the last chapter, of the same sixth book of Josephus [no. 9]. In Havercamp’s edition it reads: ‘This was the end of Saul … He reigned while Samuel was alive for eighteen years, but after his death for twenty-two years.’ Yet Peter Comestor explains this passage of Josephus so that Saul’s years of reign total twenty: ‘Saul reigned eighteen years while Samuel was alive, and two years after his death.’ Havercamp cites Clement and Eutychius, Alexandrian followers of Josephus, who assign Saul exactly twenty years of reign. This opinion of our Claudius can be most properly confirmed against Zonaras, who reports the following at the very end of the first book of his Annals: ‘Saul reigned while Samuel was still alive for eighteen years; after Samuel’s death, twenty-two.’ The same may also be taught by that ancient translation of Josephus attributed to Rufinus, which reads: ‘Saul therefore reigned eighteen years while Samuel was alive, and two more after his death.’ Nevertheless, consult, I beg you, the interpreters on these two passages of Scripture: 1 Sam. 13:1, ‘Saul was a year old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years’; and Acts 13:21, ‘He gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years.’]

“was maintained for twenty years, as no student of sacred history is unaware. For afterward, when the spirit of the Lord had departed from Saul and an evil spirit troubled him (1 Sam. 16:14), especially in his pursuit of the innocent and righteous David (chap. 18:10 and following), it was necessary that some part either of his army or of his people should have become accomplices in his wickedness.”

Kiriath-jearim is the same place that is elsewhere called Kiriath-baal, “the city of forests” (Josh. 15:60; 18:14), one of the cities of the Gibeonites belonging to the tribe of Judah, nine miles from Jerusalem on the road to Diospolis.

[Col. 0654B]

The Prophet Uriah, whom Jehoiakim killed in Jerusalem, was from this place, as Jeremiah writes.

[Note: [Col. 0654D] Jeremiah 26:20–21. Isidore relates this in chapter 4 of his book on 1 Kings.]

“Samuel governed Israel after the death of Eli. (1 Sam. 7 and following.) When all the people had been gathered, he cried to the Lord for Israel, and the Lord heard him. When he offered a burnt offering, the foreigners approached to fight against the people of God; the Lord thundered against them, and they were thrown into confusion. They fell before Israel and were defeated. (V. 12.) Then Samuel took one stone and placed it between Mizpah and Shen.

[Note: [Col. 0654D] The Vulgate reads ‘between Shen’; others, ‘Tooth’; Bede’s printed edition has ‘in Sichilech.’]
