“And, as the Seventy translators rendered it, ‘between New Mizpah and Old Mizpah.’ He called its name Stone of Help and said, ‘Thus far the Lord has helped us.’

[Col. 0654C]

“Mizpah is interpreted as ‘expectation’ or ‘watchfulness.’ That Stone of Help is a figure of the Savior as Mediator (medietas; the reading is materially uncertain); through it (quam; variant quem) one must pass from the old Mizpah to the new—that is, from the expectation placed in a carnal kingdom, which was a false blessedness, to the expectation placed through the New Testament in the kingdom of heaven, where blessedness is utterly true.

[Note: [Col. 0655D] “Spiritual” is added.]

[Col. 0655A]

“For because nothing is better, God helps us even to this point (chap. 12:17–18).

“This Samuel called upon the name of the Lord, and God heard him; and at the time of harvest he obtained rain. For in the Holy Scriptures rain signifies the words of the Gospel or of the law, as Moses says:

[Note: [Col. 0655D] Deut. 32:2: ‘Let my speech flow down like dew; like rain upon the grass,’ and so forth.]

‘Let my speech be awaited like rain,
and let my words descend like dew.’

“Christ therefore gave this rain to the world at the time of harvest, that is, when the nations had to be gathered, so that (ut; reading unde) they might be collected into the bosom of the Church like grain into the granaries.

[Col. 0655B]

[Note: [Col. 0655D] 7:15. Bede continues.]

“Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life, and before him there had been judges and rulers over Israel. (8:3.) But Samuel’s sons turned aside after greed and accepted gifts (v. 4 and following); and they became such unjust judges that the people, unable to endure them, asked for a king like the other nations. The Lord gave them Saul as king.”

(Chapters 9 and 10.) When Saul was seeking his father’s asses and came to Samuel at Ramah, Samuel foretold to him, among the other things they said to one another, the signs that would happen to him that day when he departed from him.

(Chapter 10:5 and 10.) When he had departed from him, he came to the hill of the Lord, where there was a Philistine garrison. The first sign had already occurred, just as the man of God had said; and behold, a band of prophets came to meet him. The spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied in their midst. (V. 11 and following.) When all who had known him yesterday and the day before saw that he was with the prophets and prophesied, they said to one another: “What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?”

[Note: [Col. 0655D] Claudius took what follows from Augustine’s Book 2 of Questions to Simplicianus, specifically from the first question.]

“And I do not think that this presents any difficulty: ‘The Spirit blows where he wills’ (John 3:8). For no contact with souls can defile the spirit of prophecy; ‘because of his purity he pervades and penetrates all things’ (Wis. 7:24). Yet he affects all people in different ways: some through the formation of their spirit, when images of things are shown to them; others through the mind’s fruitfulness for understanding; others through both forms of inspiration; and still others without their knowing it.

“Through the formation of the spirit there are two modes: either through dreams, as not only many saints but also Pharaoh (Gen. 45:2) and King Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. 2:1; 4:1) saw things that none of them was able to understand, although they were certainly able to see them; or through a manifestation in ecstasy, which some Latins interpret as ‘terror.’

[Note: [Col. 0655D] Augustine’s printed edition, by the Maurist Fathers, reads ‘stupor.’]

“Whether this is the proper meaning is doubtful, though it is near to it. Nevertheless, when the mind is separated from the senses, so that the human spirit, taken up by the divine Spirit, is free to receive and contemplate images—as was shown to Daniel, who did not understand it, and as the vessel was lowered from heaven to Peter by its four corners—

[Note: [Col. 0656D] Acts 10:11, but the Vulgate reads ‘by the corners.’]

“for Peter himself later learned what that manifestation signified.

“Through the mind’s fruitfulness for understanding there is one mode: when what is shown in images is revealed—what it signifies and to what it pertains.

[Note: [Col. 0656D] Augustine’s printed edition reads ‘is revealed,’ but I prefer the reading of our manuscript.]

“This is the more certain prophecy. For the Apostle calls this more properly prophecy (1 Cor. 3:2), just as Joseph deserved to understand what Pharaoh merely saw, and Daniel explained to the king what the king perceived but did not know.

“But when the mind is affected so that it does not understand images of things through conjectural examination, but contemplates the things themselves—as wisdom, justice, and every immutable and divine form are understood—that does not belong to the prophecy of which we are now speaking.

“Those who receive both prophetic gifts see images of things in the spirit and at the same time understand what they mean, or else they are instructed by clear utterances in the manifestation itself, as certain things are explained in the Apocalypse.

“Yet the spirit of prophecy also affects those who do not know what they are saying, as when Caiaphas, being high priest, prophesied concerning the Lord that it was expedient for one man to die for the whole nation (John 11:49), while he had another meaning in the words he spoke and did not know that he was not speaking them from himself. Examples abound in the holy books.

[Note: [Col. 0656D] Augustine inserts other material here, which Claudius omits.]

“By the expression ‘the spirit rushed upon him,’ a sudden inspiration is signified, as though it came from the hidden sanctuary of divinity.

“Of these modes, which should we understand Saul to have experienced? This becomes sufficiently clear from what is written there: ‘God changed Saul’s heart’ (1 Sam. 10:9). In this way he signifies another affection of the heart, which God produced by changing it, so that it might become capable of prophetic divination through images that signify and prefigure.

[Note: [Col. 0656D] The words ‘How far does Saul’s prophecy differ from that of the prophets?’ do not occur in Augustine’s printed book.]

“But how far does Saul’s prophecy differ from that of the prophets? The difference is as great as that between the prophecy of the prophets—such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, and others of this kind—and the temporary prophecy that appeared in Saul; it is like the difference between human speech when human beings speak and that same speech when, because of a necessary prodigy, the she-ass on which the prophet Balaam was sitting spoke (Num. 22:28).

“For that animal received this gift for that moment, so that God might reveal what he had determined; it was not that the beast would speak perpetually among human beings. Or, if this example is too remote because of the greater difference, it is much less surprising that a reprobate man was given prophecy for a moment, through a temporary affection, since it was given by the one who, whenever he wished, made the ass speak.

“For the difference between an animal and a human being is greater than that between a reprobate human being and even elect human beings. If someone says something that pertains to wisdom, he is not immediately to be considered wise. Nor, if someone prophesies at some time, is he thereby numbered among the prophets, since the Lord also says in the Gospel (Matt. 13:20) that some receive the word with joy and have no depth of root, but are temporary.

“Therefore, as the following reading indicates, this happened as a proverb: ‘Is Saul also among the prophets?’ (1 Sam. 10:12). Let us cease, then, to wonder when something divinely given appears in people and exceeds either their merit or their habitual character, whenever God happens to wish such a thing to be displayed for the sake of some signification.

“If it troubles anyone that afterward Saul was oppressed when an evil spirit attacked him (1 Sam. 16:14), although he had previously received the spirit of prophecy, this too should cause no wonder. The former occurred as part of a dispensation for signifying something; the latter resulted from the merit by which he was judged.

“Nor should these alternations within the human soul—that is, within a changeable creature—trouble us, especially while it bears corruptible and mortal flesh. Do we not see in Peter himself, as the Gospel shows, such a great confession that he deserved to hear (Matt. 16:17): ‘Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven’? And shortly afterward (ibid., v. 23), he understood the Lord’s passion so carnally that he immediately heard: ‘Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, for you do not understand the things of God, but those of human beings.’

[Col. 0657C]

“And perhaps, for those who understand somewhat more deeply, the difference between these two visions of the mind—the fact that Peter first understood, by revelation from God the Father, that the Son was the Christ, and afterward feared that he should die—has as much force for distinguishing visions that arise imaginatively in the human spirit when the mind is separated from the senses as does the revelation of prophecy with which Saul was first inspired and the mixture of the evil spirit by which he was afterward oppressed.”

[Note: [Col. 0657D] Thus far are Augustine’s words. What follows was handed down by Isidore in chapter 5 of his book on 1 Kings.]

“After this, at the Lord’s command, the first king is anointed by a Prophet for the kingdom. In what he was anointed to be, he himself bore the image of Christ. Hence blessed David, who was also called Christ, said to the man who claimed to have killed Saul (2 Sam. 1:14): ‘How were you not afraid to stretch out your hand against the Lord’s Christ?’

“This is why he rose above everyone from the shoulders upward (1 Sam. 9:2): our head is above us, and that head is Christ. But in the fact that he was later rejected and cast aside, while David succeeded to the kingdom, he represented the people of Israel, as had been foretold: that people had obtained a kingdom which it would lose when Christ our Lord came to reign through the New Testament, not carnally but spiritually.”

Saul was one year old when he began to reign; and he reigned two years over Israel.

One year after he had been chosen king by Samuel, he sat in his domestic house and concealed the fact that he was king. (1 Sam. 13:1.) For the remaining two years he publicly judged all Israel, maintaining obedience with humility. This was the period before he transgressed the Lord’s command concerning Amalek. For the rest of the time that he lived and ruled, he remained a transgressor of the Lord’s command.

(1 Sam. 10:26 and chapter 11.) Afterward, while Saul was awaiting Samuel at Gilgal and saw that he was delaying, he offered a burnt offering. When Samuel came, he said to Saul, among other things (1 Sam. 15–16):

“You have acted foolishly and have not kept the commandment of the Lord your God, which he commanded you. If you had not done this, the Lord would by now have established your kingdom over Israel forever. But your kingdom shall certainly not continue. The Lord has sought for himself a man after his own heart, and the Lord has commanded him to be leader over his people, because you did not keep what the Lord commanded.”

This should not be understood as though God had prepared Saul himself to reign forever and afterward had been unwilling to preserve this arrangement because Saul sinned. For God did not fail to know that Saul would sin. Rather, he prepared his kingdom as a figure of the eternal kingdom. Therefore he added (1 Sam. 13:13): “And now your kingdom shall not stand for you.”

What was signified in Saul stood and shall stand, but not for Saul himself, because he was not destined to reign forever, nor was his offspring, so that the statement “forever” might at least appear to be fulfilled through descendants succeeding one another.

(1 Sam. 2:14.) “And the Lord will seek for himself a man according to his heart,” signifying either David or the mediator himself of the New Testament, who was prefigured also in the chrism with which David himself and his descendants were anointed.

“God does not seek a man as though he did not know where he was; rather, he speaks through a human being in the human manner, because by speaking in this way he seeks us. For not only were we known to God the Father, but also to his Only-begotten Son, who came to seek what had perished—we were known to such an extent that we were chosen in him before the foundation of the world.

“Thus he said, ‘He will seek for himself,’ meaning, ‘he will make him his own.’ Hence in the Latin language this verb receives a preposition and becomes adquiri, ‘to acquire.’ This makes its meaning sufficiently clear, although even without the added preposition quaerere, ‘to seek,’ can be understood as ‘to acquire,’ from which profits and gain are named (Eph. 1:4).”

[Note: [Col. 0657D] “Nor is it a lesser virtue to guard the gate than to seek it,” says Ovid.]

Moreover, no ironworker was found throughout the whole land of Israel. For the Philistines had taken precautions lest the Hebrews perhaps make a sword or a spear, and lest they have ironworkers who could make weapons for fighting back. (Chapter XIII, 19) “Thus the Chaldeans, after destroying Jerusalem and laying waste the whole Promised Land, took pains [Note: [Col. 0658D] The following passage is taught by Bede in Question 30 on the Books of Kings.] so that no craftsman, no smith, should remain in it who could either repair the city’s defiled walls or mend what had been torn down. Rather, whatever skill they had found among the exterminated people, they transferred entirely to Babylonia, so that it might either be of no further use or serve the needs of that city.” [Col. 0659A] [Note: [Col. 0659D] Something is missing here, by which the transition from the literal to the allegorical sense would be made and the two connected. Bede has much else, which I shall place before the reader when the passage at IV Kings 24:14, “And he transferred all Jerusalem,” is explained.]

What else are the weapons with which, while fighting against the devil, we defend the freedom given us by God, except the utterances of the Scriptures, in which, through the examples both of the Lord himself and of his saints, we learn with the utmost clarity by what order the battles against vices ought to be overcome? But the Philistines deprive the children of Israel of weaponsmiths when evil spirits, by inserting worldly occupations into them, hinder the minds of the faithful from meditating on sacred reading, so that they may neither themselves gain confidence for resistance through this exercise nor perhaps kindle others who do not know how to read to resist vices by exhorting or reproving them [Note: [Col. 0659D] “Kindle” [accendant]. Our reading is preferable.]. They remove the weaponsmiths when they overwhelm those who know the sacred utterances with such great crimes that they are utterly ashamed to speak the good things they had learned.

[Col. 0659B]

[Note: [Col. 0659D] You have an explanation of the following passage in chapter 6 of Isidore’s book on I Kings.]

“Saul, however, after these events, when he was proceeding to fight against the Philistines, imposed a fast on the whole army until they returned from the battle. (V. 25 and 27) But Jonathan his son, seeing honey on the surface of the field, extended the tip of his staff, dipped it into the honeycomb, and tasted it, and his eyes were enlightened. They were not enlightened so as to see—for he had seen beforehand—but so as to discern, because he had touched what was forbidden. For that fall, just as it did Adam, made him attentive and rendered him confused. By this event we are warned that all the allurements of worldly pleasures ought to be despised by one who strives to serve God. For he cannot engage with manly courage against the spiritual foreigners, that is, against the rulers of darkness, who still neglects to turn away from the sweetness of this world. [Col. 0659C] (Prov. 5:3) For the lips of the adulteress drip honey, which is the delight of carnal pleasure; according to mystical interpretations, Jonathan is thought to have eaten of this, and, having been detected by lot, to have been freed only with difficulty through the prayers of the people.”

(I Kings 15:7.) Saul undertook battle against Amalek and killed all the enemies from Havilah to Shur. There is one region called Havilah, which the river Pishon encircles (Gen. 2:11), flowing out of paradise; today it is called India. Havilah was named after a certain grandson of Noah. There is also another Havilah, a wilderness opposite Egypt: this one ought to be called Havilah, while the former should be called Evilath. Shur likewise is a wilderness between Kadesh and Barath, extending the desert as far as the Red Sea from the border of Egypt (Gen. 16:7).

(Again, 20:1; 25:18; Exod. 15:22; I Kings 27:8.) Having struck as far as this boundary [Note: [Col. 0660D] Isidore gives the following in chapter 7.] “he spared Agag the king (I Kings 15:7) and did not wish to destroy everything according to the Lord’s command; and the Lord became angry with him.” [Note: [Col. 0660D] Isidore gives many other matters here in explaining this passage, which Claudius omits—I do not know for what reason.]

The word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying: “I regret that I made Saul king, because he has abandoned me and has not fulfilled my words in deed.” (V. 10) For God does not regret one of his deeds [Col. 0660A] as a human being does, since his judgment concerning absolutely all things is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain. How, then, does the Lord regret anything, in whom there is complete foreknowledge?

[Note: [Col. 0660D] Here again Augustine is copied by Claudius; almost the whole of his second question in Book II to Simplicianus is set down here. Augustine’s words are marked with quotation lines in the usual manner.]

“We, however, when we hear this about God in the divine Scriptures, consider it unworthy to think this about him. Yet something must be said by which this may in some way be demonstrated. Since, however, all the words by which human conversations are carried on are wonderfully and unquestionably surpassed by that eternal power and divinity, whenever something is said about him in human terms that would even appear contemptible to human beings, human weakness itself is admonished that even those things which it considers to have been fittingly said about God in the holy Scriptures are more suited to human capacity than to divine sublimity—and therefore that these too must be transcended—just as all such things must be transcended by a [Col. 0660B] sounder understanding.

“For what human being does not realize that, since God knows all things beforehand, repentance cannot exist in him? Yet these are two words, repentance and foreknowledge. Because we believe that one of them—foreknowledge—fits God, we deny that repentance exists in him. But when another person, examining these matters with clearer consideration, asks how even foreknowledge itself can fit God, and discovers that the meaning of this word too is far surpassed, in every direction, by his ineffable divinity, he is not surprised that both expressions could be spoken of him on account of human beings, although both would improperly be spoken of him on his own account.

“For what is foreknowledge except knowledge of future things? But what is future for God, who transcends all times? [Col. 0660C] If God’s knowledge possesses the things themselves, they are not future for him but present; and therefore it can no longer be called foreknowledge, but only knowledge. If, however, just as in the order of temporal creatures, things that are future are not yet present with him, but knowledge anticipates them, then he experiences them twice: once according to foreknowledge of future things, and again according to knowledge of present things. Something temporal, therefore, occurs in God’s knowledge, which is utterly absurd and false. For he who foreknows what is to come cannot know it when it has come unless it becomes known twice: by foreknowing it before it exists and by knowing it when it already exists.

“Thus it follows that—something far removed from truth—something temporal occurs in God’s knowledge, since temporal things that are foreknown are also experienced as present, although they were not experienced before they came to be, but only foreknown. If, when the things foreknown as future have arrived, nothing new occurs in God’s knowledge, then that foreknowledge will remain as it was even before the things foreknown arrived. How, then, will it now be called foreknowledge, since the things are no longer future? [Col. 0661A] They are already present, though they had been seen as future, and shortly afterward they will be past. But foreknowledge of past things, any more than of present things, cannot in any way be spoken of.

“We are therefore brought back to the conclusion that knowledge of things now present arises in place of what was foreknowledge when those same things were future. And if what was previously foreknowledge later becomes knowledge in God, this admits mutability and temporality, although God truly and supremely is neither mutable in any respect nor temporal through any novel movement.

“Let us therefore not speak of God’s foreknowledge, but only of his knowledge. Let us ask how this too may be understood. For among ourselves we ordinarily speak of knowledge only when we retain in memory what we have sensed and understood, when we remember that we have sensed or understood something, so that we may recall what we wish. [Col. 0661B] But if this is so in God, so that it can properly be said, ‘He understands and has understood; he senses and has sensed,’ then time is admitted and steals in. That mutability, which is far from God’s substance, must nevertheless be removed.

“And yet God both knows and foreknows in an ineffable manner; so too he repents in an ineffable manner. For although God’s knowledge is so far removed from human knowledge that comparison itself would be laughable, both are nevertheless called knowledge. Human knowledge, moreover, is such that the Apostle says of it: (I Cor. 13:8) ‘Knowledge will be destroyed,’ which certainly cannot in any way be said of God’s knowledge.

“Likewise, human anger is turbulent and not without mental anguish, whereas God’s anger—of which it is said in the Gospel, (John 3:36) ‘But the wrath of God remains upon him,’ and the Apostle says, (Rom. 1:18) ‘The wrath of God is revealed [Col. 0661C] from heaven against all ungodliness’—exercises vengeance with wondrous equity upon the subject creature, while he himself remains continually tranquil. Human mercy also contains a certain misery of the heart, which is why it has received its name in Latin. Hence the Apostle urges us not only (ibid. 12:15) ‘to rejoice with those who rejoice,’ but also to ‘weep with those who weep.’ Yet who in his right mind would say that God is touched by any misery, whom Scripture nevertheless everywhere testifies to be merciful? Thus we understand human jealousy as involving the disease of envy, but God as jealous not in that way: the word is the same, but not the manner.

“[Col. 0661D] It would take too long to go through the rest, and there are innumerable examples showing that many divine things are called by the same names as human things, although they are separated by incomparable difference. Nor have the same names been assigned to both classes of things without purpose: these familiar things, which are encountered in daily life and become known through more ordinary experiences, provide some path toward understanding those sublime realities. If I remove from human knowledge its mutability and the transitions from thought to thought that occur when we recall something, so that we may see in the mind what was not present to our gaze a moment before, and thus leap repeatedly in memory from one part to another—for this reason the Apostle says in part that our knowledge is incomplete (I Cor. 13:9)—if, then, I remove all these things and leave only the vitality of certain and unshaken truth, surveying all things in one eternal contemplation [Col. 0662A]—or rather, if I do not leave it, since human knowledge does not possess this, but conceive it as far as my powers allow—then God’s knowledge is somehow suggested to me. Yet this name could be common to both realities because, by knowing something, it does not remain hidden from a human being.

“Furthermore, even among human beings knowledge is customarily distinguished from wisdom, as the Apostle also says: (I Cor. 12:8) ‘To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit.’ In God, however, these are plainly not two things but one. Among human beings they are usually distinguished plausibly in this way: wisdom pertains to the understanding of eternal things, while knowledge pertains to things we experience through the bodily senses. But although someone else may offer another distinction, unless the two were different, the Apostle would not distinguish them in this way.

[Col. 0662B]

“If, then, the name knowledge is properly assigned to things we experience through the bodily senses, there is no knowledge of God at all. For God is not composed of body and soul in himself, as a human being is. It is better to say that God’s knowledge is of another kind, not of the same kind as that which is called human knowledge. Likewise, the very thing called ‘God’ is altogether different from what is meant when it is said that (Ps. 81:1) ‘he stood in the assembly of the gods.’ Yet the sharing of the name pertains in some way to the fact that the thing is not hidden.

“Similarly, from human anger I remove turbulent motion [Col. 0662C], so that the strength of vengeance remains; thus I rise, as far as possible, toward an awareness of what is called God’s anger. Likewise, if from mercy you remove compassion with the person whose misery you share in showing mercy, so that the tranquil goodness of helping and freeing from misery remains, some sort of knowledge of divine mercy is suggested. Nor should we reject or disdain God’s jealousy when we find it written of him. Rather, let us remove from human jealousy the pallid wasting of pain and the sick disturbance of the mind; let only that judgment remain by which corruption of chastity is not permitted to go unpunished, and we rise toward beginning, in some way, to grasp God’s jealousy.

“Therefore, when we read God himself saying, ‘I regret,’ let us consider what the act of repenting usually involves in human beings. It plainly involves a will that something be changed, but in a human being it is accompanied by mental pain, for he reproaches himself for having acted [Col. 0662D] rashly. Let us therefore remove those features that arise from human weakness and ignorance, and let only the willing remain that something should not be as it was.

“By this means it can be intimated to our minds, to some extent, by what rule we should understand God’s repentance. When he is said to repent, he wills that something not be as he had made it to be; yet, when it was so, it ought to have been so. When it is no longer permitted to remain so, it ought no longer to be so—according to a certain perpetual and tranquil judgment of equity, by which God arranges all mutable things with an immutable will.

“But because we customarily speak of foreknowledge and knowledge with praise when referring to human beings, and the human race is accustomed to tremble before anger in great powers rather than to censure it [Col. 0663A], we think that such expressions are more suitably used of God. One who is jealous, however, and one who repents, is ordinarily either blamed or correcting a fault in himself; and therefore such language is used of human beings with reproach. For this reason it troubles us when we read that something of this kind exists in God.

“Yet Scripture, in caring for everyone, includes these expressions precisely so that what pleases us may not be understood in God in the way it is customarily understood in human beings. Through those things that displease us—when we do not dare to understand them in God as they are found in human beings—we also learn to seek in the same way those things that we had thought suitable and fitting. For if something is not to be said of God because it is displeasing in a human being, let us not call God immutable, since it was said of human beings with reproach: (Ps. 54:20) ‘For there is no change in them.’

[Col. 0663B]

“There are also things praiseworthy in human beings that cannot exist in God, such as modesty, which is a great adornment of younger people, and the fear of God. For it is not only praised in the ancient books; the Apostle also says: (II Cor. 7:1) ‘Perfecting holiness in the fear of God,’ which certainly does not exist in God. Therefore, just as human qualities that are praiseworthy are rightly understood in God—not as they exist in human beings, but by common names according to an altogether different reason and manner—so certain human qualities that are blameworthy are understood in God, though not in the same way.

[Note: [Col. 0663D] The printed edition has “of younger ages” [quod aetatum]; this is, I think, an error.]

[Note: [Col. 0663D] The edition of the Maurist Fathers has this reading: “are not rightly understood in God; thus certain blameworthy human qualities are understood in God, not in the same way.”]

“For shortly afterward the same Samuel, to whom the Lord had said, ‘I regret that I made Saul king,’ says to Saul concerning God (I Kings 15:29): ‘For he is not like a human being, that he should repent.’ Here he plainly shows that even when God says, ‘I regret,’ it is not to be understood in the human [Col. 0663C] manner, as we have already discussed as far as we were able.”

(V. 18, etc.) When Samuel came to Saul, he said to Saul: “Stop, and I will tell you what the Lord said to me during the night.” He said to him, “Speak.” And Samuel said: “Were you not small in your own eyes when you were made head of the tribes of Israel?” [Note: [Col. 0663D] The following words, marked with quotation lines, have been copied from chapter 22 [no. 42] of Book XXXIV of St. Gregory’s Commentary on Job.]

“One is small in his own eyes when, in considering himself, he judges himself inferior to the merits of others. For whoever extends himself above the merits of others through the pride of his thoughts sees himself as great. But Saul, rejected, did not remain in the good work he had begun, because he swelled with the pride of the power he had received. David, on the other hand, always thinking humbly of himself and placing himself below Saul by comparison, after he found an opportunity to strike, spared that raging enemy and prostrated himself in a humble confession, saying: (I Kings 24:15) ‘Whom are you pursuing, king of Israel? Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog and a single flea.’

“And certainly he had already been anointed king (I Kings 16:1, 12, 13, etc.); already, when Samuel pleaded for him and poured the oil from the horn over him, he had learned that divine grace, after Saul’s rejection, was reserving him to possess the governance of the kingdom. [Col. 0664A] Yet he humbly subjected himself in mind to the enemy who persecuted him, although he knew that by divine judgment he had been placed above him. He therefore humbly put himself below the one whom, through the grace of election, he knew himself to be incomparably better than.”

(Chapter 15.) Samuel rebuked Saul for not having obeyed the voice of the Lord, but, turning to the spoil, for having done what was evil in the sight of the Lord by sparing Amalek and not killing it. Samuel said: (V. 22–23) “Does the Lord desire holocausts and sacrifices, and not rather that the voice of the Lord be obeyed? For obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams. For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to comply is like the crime of idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you, so that you shall not be king.” [Col. 0664B] [Note: [Col. 0664D] You will find this in numbers 28 and 29 of Book XXXV of the Moralia.]

“Obedience is rightly placed before sacrifices, because through sacrifices another’s flesh is slaughtered, whereas through obedience one’s own will is put to death. Therefore, each person appeases God more quickly in proportion as, with the pride of his own will restrained before God’s eyes, he offers himself to the sword of the commandment. Conversely, disobedience is called the sin of divination so that the greatness of the virtue of obedience may be demonstrated.

“Thus, by contrast, the nature of its praise is better shown. If rebellion is like the sin of divination and refusal to comply like the crime of idolatry, obedience alone possesses the merit of faith, without which everyone is shown to be unbelieving, even if he appears faithful. Hence Solomon says, in displaying obedience: (Prov. 21:28) ‘An obedient man speaks of victories.’ Indeed, an obedient man speaks of victories because, when we humbly submit to another’s voice, we overcome ourselves in our hearts.

“Hence Truth says in the Gospel: (John 6:37–38) ‘Whoever comes to me I will not cast out, because I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me.’ What does this mean? If he did his own will, would he have rejected those who come to him? Who does not know that the Son’s will does not differ from the Father’s will? But because the first human being, wishing to do his own will, departed from the joy of paradise, the second, coming for the redemption of humankind, showed that he was doing the Father’s will and not his own, and taught us to remain within. Therefore, when he does not his own will but the Father’s, he does not cast out those who come to him, because, by subjecting us through the example of his obedience, he closes the way by which we might depart.”

(V. 27.) Samuel turned to leave, but Saul seized the edge of his cloak, and it was torn. Samuel said to him: “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbor, who is better than you.” We are compelled to set down this sentence according to the translation of the Seventy interpreters, because it contains much more there. [Note: [Col. 0664D] Here Augustine is again copied, from chapter 7 of Book XVII of The City of God.] For there it is written as follows:

[Col. 0665A] “I will not return with you, because you have rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord will reject you, so that you shall not be king over Israel. And Samuel turned his face to leave, and Saul seized the flap of his double cloak, and tore it. Samuel said to him: ‘The Lord will tear the kingdom from Israel out of your hand today and will give it to your neighbor, who is good above you. And Israel will be divided in two, and he will not turn back, nor will he repent, for he is not like a human being, that he should repent. He threatens, and he does not remain.’

“This man, to whom it is said, ‘The Lord will reject you, so that you shall not be king over Israel,’ and ‘The Lord will tear the kingdom from Israel out of your hand today,’ reigned forty years over Israel, for exactly as long a period of time as David himself. He heard this at the beginning of his reign, so that we may understand it to have been said because no one of his lineage was going to reign.

“And let us look to David’s lineage, [Col. 0665B] from which, according to the flesh, arose the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. Scripture does not have the reading found in many Latin manuscripts, ‘dirumpet Dominus regnum Israel de manu tua’ (‘The Lord will tear the kingdom of Israel from your hand’), but, as we have set it down and found it in the Greek, ‘dirumpet Dominus regnum ab Israel de manu tua’ (‘The Lord will tear the kingdom away from Israel from your hand’). Thus ‘from your hand’ is to be understood as meaning ‘away from Israel.’

“This man therefore figuratively bore the person of the people of Israel, the people that was going to lose the kingdom, while Christ Jesus our Lord would reign through the New Testament, not carnally but spiritually. When it is said of him, ‘He will give it to your neighbor,’ this refers to kinship according to the flesh. For Christ was from Israel according to the flesh, and so was Saul.

“But what has been added, ‘who is good above you,’ may indeed be understood as ‘better than you,’ and some have interpreted it in that way. But it is better understood as ‘good above you’: because he is good, he is therefore above you, in accordance with the prophetic statement: (Ps. 109:1) ‘Until I place all your enemies beneath your feet.’ Among these is Israel, from which Christ took the kingdom away, its own persecutor.

“Nevertheless, there was also an Israel in whom there was no deceit (John 1:47), something like the grain among that chaff. For the apostles were from there, as were so many martyrs, whose first was Stephen; from there were the many churches whom the Apostle mentions (Gal. 1:24), glorifying God at his conversion.

[Col. 0665D]

“Concerning this, I have no doubt that what follows is to be understood: ‘And Israel will be divided in two’—namely, into Israel hostile to Christ and Israel adhering to Christ; into Israel belonging to the slave woman and Israel belonging to the free woman. For these two kinds were at first together, as Abraham was still cleaving to the slave woman, until the barren woman, made fruitful by God’s grace, cried out: (Gen. 21:10) ‘Cast out the slave woman and her son.’

“Because of Solomon’s sin, when his son Rehoboam was reigning (III Kings 12), we know that Israel was divided in two and continued in that state, with each part having its own kings, until that entire nation was overthrown and carried away by the Chaldeans in a great devastation. But what does this have to do with Saul? If something of that kind had been threatened, it ought rather to have been threatened to David himself, [Col. 0666A] whose son Solomon was. Finally, the Hebrew nation is not now divided among itself, but is scattered throughout the lands indiscriminately in association with the same error.

“That division, however, which God, under the figure of Saul as representing that kingdom and people, threatened against the kingdom and people, was signified as eternal and immutable by the addition: ‘And he will not turn back, nor will he repent, for he is not like a human being, that he should repent. He threatens, and he does not remain.’ That is: a human being threatens and does not remain, but not God, whom it is said not to repent like a human being. Wherever he is read to repent, a change in affairs is signified while divine foreknowledge remains immutable. Wherever, therefore, he is said not to repent, he is understood not to change.

“Through these words we plainly see that a divinely pronounced judgment concerning this division of the people [Col. 0666B] of Israel was irrevocable and entirely perpetual. For whoever from among them have passed over to Christ, or are passing over, or will pass over, were not of that people according to God’s foreknowledge, though they were according to the one and same nature of the human race.

“Again, whoever among the Israelites adhere to Christ and persevere in him will never be with those Israelites who persist in being his enemies to the end of this life; they will remain perpetually in the division foretold here. For the Old Testament, (Gal. 4:24) which generates slavery from Mount Sinai, profits nothing, except insofar as it bears witness to the New Testament. Otherwise, as long as Moses is read (II Cor. 3:15–16), a veil is placed over their hearts; but whenever anyone turns to Christ [Col. 0666C], the veil will be removed. For the intention of those who turn is itself changed from the old covenant to the new, so that each person seeks to receive not carnal but spiritual happiness.”

(Chapter 15:33.) Samuel therefore took a sword and cut Agag into pieces. In doing this Samuel sinned so little that he would have sinned by not doing it. God had commanded the Amalekites to be killed, and he certainly knows not only according to deeds but also according to the heart of a human being what each person ought to suffer, and through whom. Saul was therefore worthy to have such commands imposed upon him, and the Amalekites deserved to suffer them, since they had not honored the divine name but had attempted to destroy the people of God who had crossed the sea on dry ground (Exod. 17:8).

Therefore, when the Lord withdrew from Saul because of his disobedience, he was seized by an evil spirit from the Lord, and the evil spirit of the Lord rushed upon him. [Col. 0666D]

[Note: All these not inconsiderable passages, which will shortly be marked, as usual, by small lines, are taken from Augustine, writing in no. 4 of Question 1 of Book II, *To Simplicianus*.] [Col. 0665D]

> Now, the fact that it is also called “the evil spirit of the Lord” is understood in the same way as it is said, “The earth is the Lord’s”—that is, as a creature belonging to him and placed under his power. Or, if that example of expression is not suitable because the earth is not evil—for “every creature of God is good” (1 Tim. 4:4)—then the following may be suitable: Saul himself, already rejected, wicked, ungrateful, and a persecutor of holy David, although he was driven by the flames of the fiercest envy, was nevertheless still called “the Lord’s Christ,” as David himself called him when he avenged the man who had been slain (2 Sam. 1:24). [Col. 0667A]
>
> Yet I think rather that the evil spirit by whom Saul was tormented was called “the spirit of the Lord” because, by God’s hidden judgment, he tormented Saul. For God uses even evil spirits as ministers, either for the punishment of the wicked or for the testing of the good—using one for one purpose and another for another. However evil a spirit may be, because he desires to do harm with an evil will, he does not receive the power to harm except from him under whom all things have been arranged according to definite and just degrees of merit (Rom. 13:1). For just as an evil will is not from God, so power is not except from God. Although each person has it in his power what he wishes, it is not in each person’s power what he can do to anyone or what he can suffer from anyone. [Col. 0667B]
>
> Even the only Son of God, when he was humbly about to suffer for a time, said to the man who spoke arrogantly and claimed that he had the power to kill or release him: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11). The devil also, when he wished to harm the righteous Job, was indeed a devil in his desire to do harm, but he nevertheless asked the Lord God for the power to harm him, saying: “Send your hand and touch his flesh” (Job 11:5), although, if permitted, he himself would have done this. For in this way he was asking that very permission, and he called his own hand, permitted by the Lord, “the Lord’s hand”—that is, the very power that he wished to receive. [Col. 0667C]
>
> The saying in the Gospel agrees with this, where the Lord says to his disciples: “This night Satan asked to sift you as wheat” (Luke 22:31). Thus he is called the evil spirit of God—that is, God’s minister for doing to Saul what the all-powerful Judge judged that he ought to suffer. For that spirit, in the will by which he was evil, was not God’s; but as a creature, insofar as he had been created, and in the power that he had received not from himself but by the equity of the Lord of all, he was God’s. [Col. 0667D]

> The very words of Scripture also have this form: “And Samuel went,” it says, “and departed to Ramatha, and the spirit of God departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord seized him and suffocated him. And Saul’s servants said to him: ‘Behold, an evil spirit of the Lord is suffocating you.’” [Col. 0667D]
>
> How, then, this was said by his servants—“the evil spirit of God”—is shown by the preceding words of the narrative Scripture, which says: “An evil spirit from the Lord.” In this respect it is “of the Lord,” because it was from the Lord; for the spirit had the will, by himself, to harm Saul—that is, to seize him—but he did not have the power unless supreme justice permitted it.
>
> [Note: The printed edition reads *to harm*; earlier it had said *to suffocate*. Below, however, he speaks of those wishing to harm.]
>
> If God justly takes vengeance, as the Apostle himself says when he speaks of God handing people over to the desires of their hearts (Rom. 1:24), there is nothing surprising if, while always preserving his unchangeable equity, he also justly hands them over to the desires of others who wish to harm them. [Col. 0668A]
>
> It should certainly be observed that the spirit of God is called evil when the qualification is added; but when only “the spirit of God” is said, even if “good” is not added, he is understood to be good. Hence it appears that the spirit of God is called good according to substance, but evil according to ministry.
>
> Nevertheless, it may still be asked whether, when “the spirit of God” is said—and by this expression alone, even without an added qualification, a good spirit is understood—the reference is to the one who is consubstantial with the Father and the Son in the Trinity, the Holy Spirit, of whom it is said: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17). And again: “God has revealed it to us through his Spirit” (1 Cor. 2:10). And also: “Thus no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (ibid., v. 11). [Col. 0668B]
>
> In many passages he is called “the Spirit of God” in this way, and the Holy Spirit is understood even when nothing is added, because the surrounding context sufficiently indicates whom the words concern. Sometimes even “of God” is not added, yet that Spirit of God, pre-eminently holy, is still understood. For whom else does he mention when he says: “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. 8:16)? And: “The Spirit himself helps our weakness” (ibid., v. 26). And: “All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11). And: “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit” (ibid., v. 4).
>
> In all these statements neither “of God” nor “holy” is added, yet he himself is understood. But I do not know whether any clear example can be produced in which “the Spirit of God” is said without qualification and does not signify the Holy Spirit, but some other spirit—created and formed, although good. The passages brought forward are uncertain and require clearer evidence, such as the statement: “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:2). [Col. 0668C]
>
> For I find nothing that prevents us from understanding the Holy Spirit there also. When, under the name of “waters,” that formless matter is indicated which was made from nothing so that all things might be made from it, who forbids us to understand the Holy Spirit of the Creator as moving over that matter—not by spatial degrees and intervals, which cannot properly be said of anything incorporeal, but by the excellence and eminence of the will that rules over all things, so that all things might be created? [Col. 0668D]
>
> This is especially so because that expression, in accordance with the custom of those Scriptures, also gives forth a certain prophetic mystery, by which the water of the future baptism and the people to be born through the Holy Spirit are prefigured.
>
> Therefore, when it is said, “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters,” it does not compel us to understand that spirit—as some understand it—as the one by whom the entire corporeal mass of the world is, as it were, animated for the service of whatever is generated and for the preservation of corporeal creatures within their proper forms. For whatever is of this kind is a creature.
>
> Nor are there lacking those who wish to understand the same spirit in the statement: “Because the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wis. 1:7)—namely, an invisible creature that gives life to and sustains all visible things by a kind of universal harmony.
>
> But here, too, I see nothing that prevents us from understanding the Holy Spirit, since God himself says through the Prophet: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24). For God does not fill heaven and earth without his Holy Spirit. Why, then, should it be surprising if it is said of his Holy Spirit that he “has filled the world”? [Col. 0669A]
>
> He fills it in one way by sanctifying, as it is said of Stephen and others of this kind: “He was filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 6:5; 7:55). Thus he fills in one way by sanctifying grace, as he does certain holy people; in another way by being present and ordering things, as he does all things.

[Note: The printed editions add several things here that really seem to be repetitions of what precedes.] [Col. 0669D]

> Therefore, I do not know whether it can be shown by any definite scriptural evidence that, when “the Spirit of God” or “the Spirit of the Lord” is said without any qualification, anything other than the Holy Spirit is signified. [Col. 0669B]
>
> But even if there is perhaps some passage that does not presently come to mind, I certainly think it can safely be said that whenever the Spirit of God is mentioned in the sacred writings and nothing is added—whether the Spirit understood is the Holy Spirit consubstantial with the Father and the Son, or some invisible creature—evil cannot nevertheless be understood unless “evil” is also added.
>
> For because God makes good use of the evil spirit for the ministry of his judgment, he too is called the spirit of God, for the punishment of the wicked, the discipline of the good, or the testing of the good.

> Nor should the fact that Saul is later said to have prophesied when the spirit of God came upon him disturb us (1 Sam. 19:23). How can the evil spirit come after the good spirit, and the good again after the evil? [Col. 0669C]
>
> This happens not through any changeability in the Holy Spirit, who is immutable with the Father and the Son, but through the changeability of the human mind, while God distributes all things either to the wicked according to the merit of their condemnation or correction, or to the good according to the abundance of his grace.
>
> It might even appear that the Spirit of God had always been the same in Saul, but that he was evil for him because Saul was incapable of sharing in his holiness. Yet this view is not correct. The safer and truer interpretation is that, according to the changeability of human affection, the good Spirit of God moves a person to what is good—whether to prophecy or to any other work in the divine service—whereas the evil spirit affects him; because of the ministry of divine equity, which distributes all things and makes good use of all things, that spirit too is called the Spirit of God.
>
> [Note: The printed edition reads *good*.]
>
> [Note: The printed editions add *evil*.]
>
> This is especially clear because it is said: “The Spirit of God departed from him, and an evil spirit from the Lord seized him” (1 Sam. 16:14). It is impossible in any way for the same spirit to be understood as both having departed and having seized him. [Col. 0669D]
>
> Moreover, in certain copies—especially those that appear to have been rendered word for word from the Hebrew language—the Spirit of God is found without a qualification, and is understood to be evil, from the fact that it seized Saul, while David restored him by touching the lyre.
>
> It is nevertheless clear that “evil” was not added because it had already been said a little earlier, and could be supplied and understood from the proximity of the Scriptural passage. For in copies of this kind we read:
>
> “Therefore, whenever the spirit of God seized Saul, David took the lyre and struck it with his hand; Saul was refreshed and felt better, for the evil spirit departed from him” (ibid., v. 23). [Col. 0670A]
>
> Thus either what is not said here—“the spirit of God”—but is said only as “the evil spirit,” appears to have been supplied as an equivalent for what had been expressed less fully there; or, because the passage above had been worded in this way:
>
> “And Saul’s servants said to him: ‘Behold, an evil spirit of God is troubling you. Let our lord command, and let your servants who are before you seek a man skilled in playing the lyre, so that, whenever the evil spirit of God seizes you, he may play with his hand and you may feel better’” (ibid., vv. 15–16). [Col. 0670B]
>
> There was no need to say again, “Whenever the spirit of God seized Saul,” and add “evil,” because it was known which spirit was meant at that point.

[Note: These passages are taken from chapter 9 of Isidore’s *Book I on Samuel*.] [Col. 0669D]

> Thus, after Saul had been rejected because of his disobedience, the Lord sent Samuel to Jesse, and, taking a horn of oil, he anointed David as king. But let us see how this same David prophetically signified Christ.
>
> For David is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable.” And what is stronger than that lion from the tribe of Judah, who conquered the world (Rev. 5:5)? And what is more desirable than the one of whom it is said: “The desired one of all the nations will come” (Hag. 2:8)?
>
> This David is anointed as king, announcing through that anointing the Christ who was to come; for Christ is named from *chrism*, anointing. David is transferred from the pastoral office of tending sheep to the kingship of human beings. But our David, Jesus himself, was taken from the sheep of the Jewish people and transferred to kingship over the nations. For Christ is no longer among the Jewish people; he has been taken away and now feeds the flocks of the nations. [Col. 0670C]
>
> David was skilled in musical songs. For the rational and measured harmony of diverse sounds, joined together in concordant variety, suggests the unity of the ordered Church, which daily resounds in various modes and modulates with mystical sweetness.
>
> This David, still a boy, singing sweetly—or rather, powerfully—on the lyre, restrained the evil spirit that was working in Saul.

[Note: Compare this with what Augustine says in no. 1 of Sermon 1 on Psalm 34. The words “David is interpreted as strong of hand” through “this David is anointed” are taken from chapter 87 of Book XXII *Against Faustus*. From this we infer that much of what follows, in which this passage is explained, was also taken from Augustine.] [Col. 0669D]

> For what power could that lyre possess? It was a figure of the cross of Christ, mystically represented by the wood and the stretching of the strings; and the passion itself was sung. By this means let us morally set forth an example and, through humble speech, call the pride of the rich toward some good. [Col. 0670D]

[Note: Seek what follows on page 3 of Gregory the Great’s *Pastoral Rule* [Admonition 3].]

> Often, too, a proud rich man must be soothed by the charm of exhortation, because hard wounds are often softened by gentle applications. [Note: The printed editions read “hard and wounds.”] The fury of madmen is frequently brought back to health when the physician soothes them. When one accommodates oneself to them with sweetness, the sickness of insanity is calmed. [Col. 0671A]
>
> For it should not be carelessly overlooked that, when an evil spirit attacked Saul, David took up the lyre and calmed his madness. What is signified by Saul except the arrogance of the powerful? And what is suggested by David except the humble life of the saints?
>
> Therefore, when Saul is seized by an unclean spirit, his madness is tempered as David sings. So, when the minds of the powerful are turned by pride toward frenzy, it is fitting that, as though by the sweetness of a lyre, they should be recalled to the health of their minds by the tranquility of our speech.

(1 Samuel 17.) After this, David defeated the giant in battle. [Col. 0671D]

[Note: Here too Augustine teaches us; Claudius transcribed Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 143, though not consistently—as elsewhere he usually does—word for word, or, as the expression goes, literally. He excerpts some passages from it and presents them more briefly, while copying others exactly. I ask you to compare what Claudius has here with Augustine’s *Exposition of the Psalm* I mentioned, Psalm 143. But, as I think, Claudius copied this material from Isidore, Question 10 on 1 Samuel.]

> When foreigners were fighting against the people of God, pride challenged humility; the devil challenged Christ. Holy David took up weapons of war in order to advance against Goliath. Because of his age and the small stature of his body, he could not carry these weapons; he cast off what burdened him, took five stones from the stream, and placed them in a shepherd’s pouch. Armed with these, he advanced and conquered. [Col. 0671B]
>
> This is what that David did; but let us investigate the mysteries. In David, Christ is understood. At the time when the New Testament was revealed, he provided for the presentation and commendation of grace, laid down his weapons, and took five stones.
>
> He therefore laid down the bodily sacraments of the Law, which were not imposed upon the nations; he laid down what we do not observe. For we read the old Law but do not observe it. Nevertheless, we understand it as having been promised and established for some symbolic purpose.
>
> Thus he laid down these weapons as the burdens of the sacraments of the old Law, and he took up the Law itself. For the five stones signify the five books of Moses. He took those five stones from the stream—that is, from the world. Mortal time flows onward, and whatever comes into the world passes away.
>
> The stones were in the stream, as though in that first people. They were there useless and idle; they passed over the streams. But what did David do so that the Law itself might become useful? He received grace. For “the Law cannot be fulfilled without grace” (Rom. 3:10); the fullness of the Law is love.
>
> Since grace makes it possible to fulfill the Law, grace is signified by milk. For this is what is freely given in the flesh: the mother does not seek to receive but strives to give. The mother gives this freely and is saddened if there is no one to receive it.
>
> How, then, did David show that the Law cannot operate without grace? He took the five stones, signifying the Law in its five books, and, wishing to join them to grace, placed them in the shepherd’s pouch in which he was accustomed to milk the sheep. [Col. 0671C]
>
> Armed with these, he advanced against Goliath, who proudly presumed upon himself. He took one stone and struck down the devil. [Col. 0671D]

[Note: The printed edition of Augustine reads: “He struck the enemy in the forehead.”]

> He struck him in the forehead, and he fell from that part of the body where he did not bear the sign of Christ. You may also observe this: he placed five stones, but threw one. There are five books of the Law, but unity conquered. [Col. 0672A]

[Note: The printed edition reads *of the Law*. I think this should certainly be read with Claudius.]

> “The fullness of the Law is love,” as the Apostle says (Rom. 13:10): “Bearing with one another in love, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:2–3).
>
> Finally, after striking and bringing him down, David took his sword and immediately cut off his head. Our David does this too: he casts down the devil through his own people. When his great ones, whom the devil held in his hand and through whom he slaughtered other souls, come to believe, they turn their tongues against the devil; and thus Goliath’s head is cut off by his own sword. [Col. 0672D]

[Note: This is taken from no. 24 [elsewhere chapter 16] of Book XVIII of St. Gregory’s *Moral Expositions on Job*.]

> This also applies to the man who, with sound faith—which is usually counted by most saints as righteousness—gathers from the very sacred testimonies that the heretic brings forward and immediately refutes the obstinacy of his error. [Col. 0672B]

[Note: The printed edition reads *from there*.]

> For when they bring us testimonies from the sacred Law, they bring with them the means by which they may be defeated. Thus David, as a type of the Lord—for his name is interpreted as “strong of hand”—and Goliath, signifying the pride of heretics, expressed through events what we assert in words. [Col. 0672C]

[Note: The material enclosed in parentheses is not found in Gregory.]

> Goliath came to battle with a sword, while David came with a shepherd’s pouch. But David, overcoming that same Goliath, killed him with his own sword. This is what we too do: we, who by the gracious favor of the promised David have deserved to become his members, defeat proud heretics when they bring forward the statements of sacred Scripture by conquering them with the very words and statements that they themselves produce. Thus we cut down the exalted Goliath with his own sword.

(1 Samuel 18:7.) [Col. 0672D]

> Meanwhile, David’s victory offended King Saul, who was indignant that public acclamation should resound with “a thousand for Saul, and ten thousand for David.”

[Note: Seek this in chapters 11 and following of Isidore’s *Book I on Samuel*.] [Col. 0672D]

> Hence Saul’s envy and the seed of hatred against David. The crafty plotter, so that he might expose him to danger without appearing to do so through his own ambushes, decided to bind him to the marriage of his daughter Michal, if David would bring him one hundred foreskins of the Philistines as a victor. Instead of one hundred, David gave two hundred; and thus, where he was believed likely to perish in fulfillment of the royal demand, he was immediately increased by a more glorious triumph.
>
> In the same way, when the Jews attempt to kill Christ against the will of God, they brought about the salvation of the nations through the very act by which they believed they would extinguish him.
>
> The fact that David first brought the foreskins of foreigners and then joined himself in marriage to Saul’s daughter signified that Christ would not first promise the synagogue to himself in marriage until he had become glorious among the nations. For first, among the nations, he cut away the pollution of the flesh, and afterward he was joined to the synagogue. [Col. 0673A]
>
> For after, as it is written, “the fullness of the nations has entered,” then “all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26).
>
> He brought twice as many foreskins—that is, two hundred—either on account of the Jews and the nations acquired, or because the number acquired from the nations is greater than the number of believing Jews.
>
> Saul then increased his hatred of David to such an extent that, when the spirit hostile to him invaded Saul, the king tried to pin David with a spear as David customarily played music to restore his spirit (1 Sam. 19:10). [Col. 0673B]
>
> But what does it mean that, when the hostile spirit invaded Saul, David took up the lyre and calmed his madness? Saul signifies the arrogance of the Jews, while David signifies humility.
>
> Therefore, when Saul is seized by an unclean spirit, his madness is tempered as David sings. So, when the minds of the Jews are turned toward frenzy through blasphemy, it is fitting that their minds should be recalled to salvation, as though by the sweetness of a lyre, through the tranquility of evangelical speech.

(1 Samuel 19:14 and following.) Saul sent guards to David’s house to watch him and kill him. But David departed by night, fled, and was saved. When Saul’s messengers came, they found a statue placed in David’s bed, with a goatskin at its head. [Col. 0673B]

> Let us therefore hear what this means: Saul sent men to guard David’s house in order to kill him. This does not refer to the Lord’s cross, but nevertheless pertains to his passion; for Christ was crucified, died, and was buried.
>
> That burial was like a house, to guard which the kingdom of the Jews sent men when guards were stationed at Christ’s tomb (Matt. 28). [Col. 0673C]
>
> How, then, was the house guarded, if David represented Christ and Christ was to be killed, when Christ was not killed in the burial but on the cross?
>
> The passage is therefore referred to the body of Christ, because to kill Christ was to remove the name of Christ. For no one would have believed in Christ if the lie of the guards who had been bribed had prevailed—namely, their claim: “While we were sleeping, his disciples came and stole him” (ibid. 28:13).
>
> Thus to wish to kill Christ is to extinguish the memory of his resurrection, so that a lie might be preferred to the Gospel. But just as Saul could not accomplish his purpose of killing David, so the kingdom of the Jews could not erase the memory of Christ.
>
> Those who, relying on Saul’s power—that is, on the kingdom of the Jews—wished to presume against Christ stumbled against the stone of stumbling, as against a statue. His kid appeared to be a lamb, because they persecuted him as a sinner in whom they had found no sin. [Col. 0673D]

Therefore David, avoiding the act of the royal hand and escaping his persecution, came to Samuel (1 Sam. 19:18 and following). Saul sent messengers to seize David, but Samuel was among the prophets and the company of prophets who prophesied at that time. The messengers who were sent, having received that same Spirit, prophesied; the same happened when others were sent, and likewise when a third group was sent. Later, when Saul himself had come, the spirit of God came upon him, and he walked along, entering and prophesying. [Col. 0674A]

[Note: You will find what follows in number 7 and those following of Question 1 of Book II, *On Various Questions to Simplicianus*.] [Col. 0673D]

> Here, the spirit can only be understood as a good spirit, through whom the holy prophets saw images and visions of future events.
>
> This is not merely because it is said, “and he prophesied.” For in copies derived from the Hebrew, this too is found said of an evil spirit:
>
> “On the following day an evil spirit of God seized Saul, and he prophesied in the midst of his house” (1 Sam. 18:10). [Col. 0674B]
>
> In other places of the divine Scriptures it is often found that prophecy is spoken of not only as good but also as evil. The prophets of Baal are mentioned, and certain people are reproached because they prophesied in Baal (1 Kings 18:16, 18, 22, 25, 40).
>
> Therefore, it is not necessary to understand that the spirit who later came upon Saul was good merely because it is said: “He walked along, entering, and he prophesied.” Rather, it is because the statement “the spirit of God came upon him” is given without qualification. For it was not said there, as it had been said above, “an evil spirit of God,” so that the same qualification could be supplied in what follows.
>
> On the contrary, the preceding circumstances testify more and more strongly that the spirit of God was good and genuinely prophetic. David was with Samuel. Saul sent messengers to seize David while Samuel was among the prophets and the company of prophets who were prophesying at that time. The messengers who were sent, having received that same Spirit, prophesied; the same happened when others were sent, and likewise with a third group. Later, when Saul himself had come, the Spirit of God also came upon him, and he walked along, entering, and prophesied. [Col. 0674C]
>
> For when it is said that the spirit of God also came upon them and that they too prophesied, it was clearly the same spirit who was in the prophets, among whom Samuel was found. From this it is necessary to understand that the spirit was good.
>
> For this reason the question must be carefully examined: how did those men, when sent to seize a man and lead him to his death, deserve to be affected by such a spirit? And how did Saul himself, who had sent them, when he came in person seeking to shed innocent blood, deserve to receive that spirit and prophesy?

> Here we encounter something astonishing, which the Apostle Paul explains most clearly when he points out the surpassing way: [Col. 0674D]
>
> “If I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love, I have become sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions, and if I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:1 and following).
>
> Here it is clear that he mentioned those gifts that are given through the distributions of the Holy Spirit, as he says above:
>
> “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healings in the one Spirit; to another, workings of powers; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues. But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one his own gifts as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:7 and following). [Col. 0675A]
>
> It is therefore sufficiently clear that prophecy is among the gifts of the Spirit. Yet if someone has prophecy and does not have love, he is nothing.
>
> From this it is understood that it can happen that some who are unworthy of eternal life and the kingdom of heaven are nevertheless sprinkled with certain gifts of the Holy Spirit, while they do not have love. Without love, those gifts are not merely insignificant; they profit such people nothing.
>
> For prophecy without love, as has been shown, does not lead to the kingdom of God; but love without prophecy certainly does lead there.
>
> When he speaks of the members of Christ, saying, “Are all apostles? Are all prophets?” (ibid. 12:29), he unmistakably shows that even one who does not have prophecy can be counted among the members of Christ. What place would such a person have there if he did not have love, without which a human being is nothing?
>
> He would never have spoken in this way when he was discussing the members by whom the body of Christ is filled: “Do all have love?” Instead he said: “Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all powers? Do all have gifts of healings?”—and other questions of this kind. [Col. 0675B]

> But someone may say that it is indeed possible for a person not to have prophecy and yet to have love, and therefore to be counted among and remain attached to the members of Christ; but that it is impossible for someone to have prophecy and not have love. For a person who has prophecy without love is nothing. [Col. 0675C]
>
> Perhaps this is like saying that a person who has a soul without a mind is nothing—not because a person who has a soul but no mind can be found, but because, if such a person could be found, he would be nothing.
>
> Similarly, it may be said that a body has shape but no color and cannot be seen—not because there is a body lacking color, but because, if color were absent, it could not be seen.
>
> Thus perhaps it was said that if someone has prophecy and does not have love, he is nothing—not because prophecy can exist in anyone without love, but because, if it did exist, it could not be beneficial.
>
> To solve this question, then, we must show that some reprobate possessed the gift of prophecy. If we find no one, this Saul himself would sufficiently demonstrate it. [Col. 0675D]
>
> Yet Balaam also appears to have been reprobate (Num. 22:5, 24 and following). Scripture does not conceal that he was condemned by divine judgment, and yet he had prophecy. Because he lacked love, he possessed the will to curse the people of Israel—a will that the enemy had purchased, hiring him for a fee to pronounce the curse. Nevertheless, by the gift of prophecy with which he was sprinkled, he blessed them against his will.
>
> The words written in the Gospel also testify strongly to this view:
>
> “Many will say on that day: ‘Lord, Lord, in your name we ate and drank, and in your name we prophesied, and in your name we performed many mighty works.’ Yet he will say to them: ‘I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity’” (Matt. 7:22 and following). [Col. 0676A]
>
> We will not suppose that they are lying when they say these things in that judgment, where there will be no opportunity for deception. Nor do we read that any of such people say: “We loved you.”
>
> They will therefore be able to say: “In your name we prophesied,” even though they are wicked and reprobate. But they will not be able to say: “We kept the love that you commanded.” For if they said this, they would not receive the answer: “I do not know you.”
>
> “By this,” he says, “it will be known that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John 13:35).

> This example of Saul therefore resists certain proud heretics who either deny that anything good from the gifts of the Holy Spirit can be given to those who do not belong to the lot of the saints, or who object when we say that such people can possess the sacrament of baptism. [Col. 0676B]
>
> When they come to the Catholic Church, that sacrament is in no way to be violated in them or administered to them as though they did not possess it. Nevertheless, they must not for that reason place their confidence in salvation—not because we reject what we acknowledge that they received, but because they ought to recognize that the fellowship of unity, bound by love, must be joined to the same sacrament.
>
> Without love, whatever they may have—however holy and venerable it may be in itself—makes them nothing. They are all the more unworthy of the reward of eternal life because they have not used well the gifts they received in this life, which is passing away. [Col. 0676C]
>
> No one uses them well except through love (1 Cor. 13:7), and love endures all things; therefore it does not divide unity, of which it is the strongest bond.
>
> For that servant also received a talent; nor is a talent understood as anything other than some divine gift. “To the one who has, more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away” (Matt. 25:29).
>
> What he does not have cannot be taken away; rather, he does not have something else, and therefore what he does have is rightly taken away. He does not have the love by which he might use his gift, and so whatever else he has, which is useless without love, is taken away.

> It is therefore not surprising that King Saul received the spirit of prophecy at the time when he was first anointed. Afterward, when he had been rejected because of his disobedience and the Spirit of the Lord had departed from him, he was seized by an evil spirit from the Lord. That spirit too was called the Spirit of the Lord because of its ministry, since the Lord makes good use even of evil spirits—either for the condemnation of some, for the correction of others, or for their testing. [Col. 0676D]
>
> Although evil does not come from the Lord, power nevertheless comes only from the Lord (Rom. 13:1).
>
> It is also called “the sleep of the Lord” (1 Sam. 26:12), the sleep that had overcome Saul’s soldiers when David took the spear and cup from beside the head of the sleeping king. This is not because the sleep was in the Lord, as though he himself were sleeping, but because the sleep that had then seized the men had been infused by God’s will, so that David’s presence would not be perceived in that place. [Col. 0677A]
>
> Nor is it surprising that Saul again received the spirit of prophecy when he was pursuing the righteous man and, intending to seize and kill him, came to the place where the assembly of the prophets was (1 Sam. 19:24).
>
> Thus it has been sufficiently demonstrated that no one should henceforth feel secure because of such a gift, as though he were especially pleasing to the Lord if he does not have love. For that gift could indeed be given to Saul because of the hidden purpose of some sacrament; nevertheless, it could be given to one who was reprobate, envious, ungrateful, returning evil for good, and who, even after receiving the Spirit, was not corrected or changed for the better.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] For XX:14–15, consult what follows in question 5 of book XXX of Bede’s *Questions on the Books of Kings*.]

For Jonathan said to David—whom he grieved to see wearied by the unjust persecutions of his father—“If I live, you shall show me the mercy of the Lord; but if I die, you shall not remove your mercy from my house forever, when the Lord has uprooted the enemies of David, each one from the earth.” When Scripture added, “So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David” (verse 16), it immediately continued: “The Lord required it from the hand of David’s enemies.”

[Note: [Col. 0677D] The Vulgate reads *requiret*.]

“He did this by anticipation, inserting into the narrative beforehand what happened much later, when, after Saul had been killed, the kingdom was transferred to David by the Lord, and those who had unjustly persecuted the innocent man were punished by divine vengeance. Then the Lord required it from the hand of David’s enemies, asking why they had afflicted the holy man. Then they were compelled to give an account of the hatred with which they had raged against him for so long. The same may likewise be understood of Absalom, Sheba son of Bichri, and David’s other enemies.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] The same is lacking.]

“Alternatively, if you wish to know what the Lord required from the hand of David’s enemies, it can, unless I am mistaken, be clearly understood from the preceding statement, where it was said that Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David. He required this from the hand of David’s enemies: namely, why they themselves had not wished to enter into a covenant of peace with him, when they saw that the Lord was with him.

“Scripture seems to have inserted this statement in advance for this reason: to prove true Jonathan’s testimony, in which he had said, ‘When the Lord uproots David’s enemies, each one from the earth.’ For David’s enemies were indeed uprooted from the earth—not because David himself took vengeance on his adversaries, but because the Lord judged on his behalf.

“It is rightly added: ‘And Jonathan continued to make David swear, because he loved him; for he loved him as his own soul’ (verse 17). Thus the man who embraced David with such perfect love according to the law of the Lord might be shown to be free from the destruction of his enemies.
