Although, if sudden death had snatched him away, he could not have shared with David the earthly kingdom he had hoped for, nevertheless, without any opposition, he received a share in the heavenly kingdom with him whom he had loved for the glory of his virtues, however briefly—himself also being full of virtues.”

[Note: [Col. 0677D] Both our manuscript and the printed editions have *ita* (“thus”); nevertheless, I think *subita* (“sudden”) should be read, as I have printed it.]

### (Chapter XX, 45, and XXI, 1)

[Note: [Col. 0677D] What follows is taken from Isidore.]

“Then David arose again and fled that day from Saul’s presence. He came to Abimelech the priest, from whom he also took Goliath’s sword and received the loaves of the Presence. This event brought death upon the priest and punishment upon the religious city.

“This, then, is the historical account; but insofar as it concerns the mystery of prophecy, it was fulfilled in Christ our Lord, who, having taken flesh—”

[Note: [Col. 0677D] *Domini* (“of the Lord”) is erroneous.]

“—while avoiding Jewish persecution, went over to the peoples—”

[Note: [Col. 0677D] *Apostolos* (“the Apostles”) is also erroneous. When does he pass over to the Apostles? He fled instead to Galilee of the Gentiles, and to the Tyrians and Sidonians, not to the Apostles. I therefore think that this passage of Isidore was corrupted long ago by an ancient copyist, and that something—certainly only a little—is missing here.]

“—with whom he took the food he desired. ‘With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you’ (Luke 22:15), he said. From them he took Goliath—that is, the weapons of the devil—for he himself, being strong, tore away the spoils. Against those, therefore, by whom Christ was received, the devil brought tribulations and death. For, as the Apostle says, all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution. And the Lord says, ‘If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you’ (John 15:20).”

[Note: [Col. 0678D] Thus far Isidore.]

But the fact that in the Gospel the Lord calls Abiathar the high priest, rather than Abimelech, creates no discrepancy. Both were there when David came and asked for the loaves, and Abimelech, the high priest, gave them to him, together with Abiathar his son (1 Samuel 22:16 and following). After Saul killed Abimelech, along with eighty-five men of his priestly household, Abiathar fled to David and became his companion throughout his exile. Later, when David was reigning, he too received the office of high priest; and, remaining in the priesthood throughout the whole period of David’s reign, he became a man of much greater distinction than his father. Therefore he was worthy that the Lord should mention him, even while his father was still alive, as though he were already high priest.

[Note: [Col. 0678D] Here again Isidore teaches us, and Rabanus follows him.]

“In Doeg the Edomite, however, who betrayed the priests of the Lord,” the person of Judas the betrayer is signified—

[Note: [Col. 0678D] The words “who betrayed the priest of the Lord” are absent from the printed editions.]

“—through whom the devil brought these things about, so that, after his destruction had been accomplished in Christ, the Church would thereafter suffer persecution, many disciples of Christ would be killed, and priests would undergo the disasters of persecution for his name.”

[Note: [Col. 0678D] *Consistit* (“is signified”) is the reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0678D] *Ita* (“thus”) is the reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0678D] “Very many.”]

[Note: [Col. 0678D] “Would endure the most severe persecutions.”]

Some say that Doeg signified the Antichrist, of whom Judas was a member, because just as Doeg killed eighty-five priests, so the Antichrist will kill the martyrs who hold to faith in the resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0679D] On 1 Samuel 21:10. Isidore also teaches this, in chapter 16; Rabanus follows him.]

“Meanwhile, while David was fleeing from Saul, he wished to hide with a certain king of Gath named Achish. But when David’s glory had been recounted, he pretended madness, lest the king to whom he had fled should, through envy, plot something against him. As though seized by a fit of insanity, he changed his mouth: his saliva ran down upon his beard, he collapsed into their hands, and he fell at the doors of the gate. King Achish said to his servants, ‘Why have you brought this man to me? Were madmen lacking among us?’ And so he dismissed him.

“Achish is interpreted as ‘How is he?’—which signifies ignorance, and the speech of one who marvels without recognizing. This was fulfilled among the Jewish people: when they saw Christ, they did not recognize him. Before them he changed his mouth and departed.

“For there were there the carnal commandments of the law, and a sacrifice according to the order of Aaron; afterward he himself instituted a sacrifice from his body and blood according to the order of Melchizedek. He therefore changed his mouth in the priesthood; he changed it in the commandments, giving another covenant and rendering the carnal observance void. Then he collapsed into their hands, when they seized him and crucified him.

“‘And he went out to the door of the gate’ (verse 13)—that is, he humbled himself. [Note: [Col. 0679D] The reading is *procidere* (“to fall prostrate”).]

This means that he proceeded as far as the door of our faith. For the door of the gate is the beginning of our faith. From there the Church begins and reaches the vision, so that, when it believes what it does not see, it may deserve to enjoy it when it begins to see him face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12).

“But the fact that during that apparent madness saliva ran down upon his beard is explained by the Apostle, who says: ‘The Jews demand signs, and the Greeks seek wisdom; but we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling block and to the Gentiles foolishness. But to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God, because the foolishness of God is wiser than men.’”

[Note: [Col. 0679D] “And what is weak in God is stronger than men.” The saliva signifies foolishness and weakness; but what is foolish in God is stronger than men—not in the sense that …]

“Not that the saliva is offensive; but observe that it runs down upon the beard. For just as weakness is shown in the saliva, so strength is shown in the beard. He therefore concealed his strength beneath the body of his weakness. What was weak outwardly appeared as saliva, while inwardly divine power was hidden as though beneath a beard.”

### (Chapter XXIV)

“Afterward, in the wilderness of Engedi, when Saul was seeking to pursue David, David entered a cave and hid there.”

[Note: [Col. 0679D] This too is taken from Isidore, from whom Rabanus also drew it.]

[Note: [Col. 0679D] What follows may likewise be found in Isidore, and in large part in Augustine’s *Exposition of Psalm 56*, section 4.]

“But the king, unexpectedly caught in the ambush he had prepared for the innocent man, fell into the very trap he had devised. For it is written: ‘He who digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it’ (Proverbs 26:27). David, however, returning good for evil, did not kill his enemy; instead, as testimony to what had happened, he cut off the edge of the royal cloak, although it would have been easier to destroy the adversary caught in the ambush than merely to deceive him.

“What, then, does it mean that this man, fleeing from Saul’s presence, hid in a cave? Why did he hide, except so that he might be concealed and not found? What is it to be covered by a cave except to be covered by earth? For whoever flees into a cave is covered by earth, so that he may not be seen.

“Jesus carried the earth: the flesh that he had received from the earth. In it he concealed himself, so that God would not be found by the Jews. ‘For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory’ (1 Corinthians 2:8). Why, then, did they not find the Lord of glory? Because he had hidden himself in a cave—that is, he presented the weakness of his flesh to their eyes and concealed the majesty of his divinity beneath the covering of his body, as in the recess of a cave.”

[Note: [Col. 0680D] The printed editions have *enim* (“for”).]

[Note: [Col. 0680D] “Was.”]

“They therefore persecuted a man without recognizing God. He could die only in man; he could be crucified only in man; he could be seized only in man. To those who sought him wrongly, therefore, he presented earth; to those who sought him rightly, he preserved life.

“According to the flesh, then, he fled into a cave from Saul’s presence, because he suffered himself to be so hidden from the Jews that he died.”

[Note: [Col. 0680D] Isidore and Claudius omit several things here. See the Augustine passage cited.]

“But why did he wish to remain patient even unto death, fleeing from Saul’s presence into a cave? For a cave may be understood as the lower part of the earth. And certainly, as is manifest and known to all, his body was placed in a tomb that had been cut out of rock. That tomb, therefore, was a cave; there our David fled from Saul’s presence. For the Jews persecuted him until he was placed in the cave.”

[Note: [Col. 0680D] The preceding material is also found in Isidore, but is absent from Augustine.]

“But what does it mean that Saul the persecutor entered the cave to relieve his bowels, except that the Jews emitted, like a foul odor, the malice they had conceived against Christ, and displayed by worse deeds—the killing of Christ—the harmful thoughts they had harbored? Yet David did not wish to kill Saul. Although he had him in his power, hidden in the recess of the cave, he preferred to spare him rather than kill him.

[Note: [Col. 0680D] *Potius* (“rather”) is added, but is redundant.] So Christ, while he was in the cave of the flesh, had the persecuting people in his power, yet did not kill them. For it had been written of them by the Prophet: ‘Do not kill them’ (Psalm 58:12).

“David merely cut off the upper edge of Saul’s cloak in silence, to show prophetically that Christ did not kill the Jews, but merely took away from them the glory of the kingdom. For the cutting off of the cloak signifies the amputation of the kingdom.”

[Note: [Col. 0680D] Thus far Isidore.]

But in the fact that David so revered Saul that, when he was hidden in the dark cave into which Saul had also entered under the pressure of bodily necessity, his heart struck him with fear, and he secretly cut off a small piece of Saul’s garment from behind, so that he might have something with which to demonstrate how he had spared him when he could have killed him, and thus remove from Saul’s mind the suspicion with which he had vehemently persecuted holy David, thinking him his enemy—

[Note: [Col. 0681D] Something is missing here.]

—the future kingdom was symbolized as something that would endure eternally. For Christ is called “Christ” from that oil with which he was anointed with chrism. Therefore, lest he be guilty of violating so great a sacrament in Saul, he feared even to touch his garment in this way. For it is written: “David’s heart struck him because he had cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak” (1 Samuel 24:6). His men, who urged him to kill Saul, since he had been delivered into his hands, he answered: “Far be it from me, from the Lord, that I should do this thing to my lord, the Lord’s anointed, or lay my hand upon him, for he is the Lord’s anointed” (1 Samuel 24:7).

The great reverence shown to this future symbol was not for its own sake, but for the sake of what it prefigured.

[Note: [Col. 0681D] We learned what follows from Gregory the Great, who transmits it in the third part of the *Pastoral Rule*, admonition 5.]

“Morally understood, whom does Saul signify except wicked rulers, and whom does David signify except good subjects? Saul’s relieving his bowels therefore signifies wicked superiors extending the malice conceived in their hearts into deeds of foul odor, and demonstrating by outward actions the harmful thoughts they have entertained.

“Yet David feared to strike him, because the devout minds of subjects, refraining from every plague of detraction, do not strike the lives of their superiors with the sword of the tongue, even when they criticize their imperfections. If, because of weakness, they can scarcely restrain themselves from speaking—humbly—of certain extreme and outward faults of their superiors, they cut the edge of the cloak silently, as it were. For when they diminish, even harmlessly and secretly, the dignity placed over them, they seem to cut the garment of the king set above them. Yet they return to themselves and reproach themselves most severely even for the slightest tearing of a word.

“Therefore it is rightly written there also: ‘Afterward David struck his heart because he had cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak.’ For the deeds of superiors are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, even when they are rightly judged worthy of criticism.

“If the tongue ever slips against them, even in the smallest matter, it must be restrained by the affliction of repentance—

[Note: [Col. 0681D] The printed editions have: “the heart must be restrained.”]

—so that the person may return to himself and, having sinned against the authority placed over him, may dread the judgment of the one by whom that authority was placed over him.

“For when we sin against superiors, we oppose the order of the one who set them over us. Thus Moses too, when he learned that the people were murmuring against him and Aaron, said: ‘What are we? Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord’ (Exodus 16:8).”

### (25:2)

After this David went down into the wilderness of Maon, where Nabal lived; his wife’s name was Abigail. David sent his young men to him, asking that whatever his hand found should be sent by Nabal to David and his young men. Nabal foolishly repelled them, and they reported this to David.

[Note: [Col. 0681D] What follows is explained by Bede in question 6 on the Books of Kings.]

“Then David girded himself with weapons and wished to plunder him (verse 13). But Abigail went out to meet David (verses 18, 23), interceding for herself and for her household, whom her husband had offended while overcome by folly and drunkenness. ‘For,’ she said, ‘if a man ever rises up pursuing you and seeking your life, the soul of my lord shall be kept as in a bundle of the living, with the Lord your God. But the soul of your enemies shall be whirled about as by the force and circle of a sling’ (verse 29).

“By a beautiful comparison she distinguishes the condition of the righteous from the lot of the reprobate. She calls the souls of the former ‘living,’ thereby implying that the souls of the latter have been overtaken by spiritual death. In accordance with the Prophet’s statement, ‘The soul that sins shall itself die’ (Ezekiel 18:4), she compares the former to a bundle and the latter to a stone in a sling. A bundle is tied together so that it may remain whole and be preserved; a stone is placed loose in a sling so that it may be cast away.

“So in this world the elect are constricted by the pressures of tribulations, so that, warned by these things, they may bind themselves more closely to one another in mutual love and, united with one another, be preserved forever by the hand of their Redeemer. But the more freely the reprobate are released in this life into their own pleasures, the farther they will be cast away in the future from the glory of the divine vision, so that it may rightly be said of them: ‘They indeed have been rejected from your hand’ (Psalm 87).”

[Note: [Col. 0682D] “Cast out.”]

[Note: [Col. 0682D] *Connectent* (“they may bind together”) is, I think, incorrect.]

“He wonderfully describes the almighty providence of the heavenly protector when he says that the soul of the holy man is guarded with him as in a bundle of the living. For just as it is very easy for anyone to preserve in his hand a bundle of grass or hay, so the power of our Lord and Savior watches over all the elect throughout the world, from the beginning to the end of the age, without difficulty, lest any of them perish in any way.

“In accordance with this, he himself speaks in the Gospel under the figure of sheep: ‘They follow me, and I give them eternal life; and they shall never perish, nor shall anyone snatch them from my hand’ (John 10:27–28). Just as a single bundle is tied with whatever bonds may be used, so the whole assembly of the saints is bound together by one and the same faith, hope, and love, and is surrounded by the one protection of God.

[Note: [Col. 0682D] “Both.”]

“The literal sense is also clear: David’s soul, although enemies pursued him, was always preserved among the living. His enemies, however, as adversities pressed upon them, were to be disturbed by unstable motion like a stone whirled in a sling, and were to be expelled from their territories or even removed from human affairs.”

[Note: [Col. 0682D] Thus far Bede.]

[Note: [Col. 0683D] Consult what follows in the third part of Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule*, admonition 17.]

And in this deed of Abigail, what does she indicate to us by her speech except that we correct angry people more effectively if, in the very act of admonishing them about their anger, we defer correction? For disturbed people do not know what they are hearing; but once they have returned to themselves, they receive words of exhortation all the more willingly because they are ashamed that they were tolerated so calmly.

To a mind drunk with fury, everything right that is said appears wrong. Hence Abigail rightly and commendably kept silent about Nabal’s fault while he was drunk, and spoke of it commendably after the wine had been digested (chapter 25:37). For he was able to recognize the evil he had done precisely because he had not heard of it while drunk.

### (Chapter 26:5 and following)

[Note: [Col. 0683D] What follows is transmitted by Isidore in question 18.]

“David, still fleeing from Saul’s presence, entered the king’s camp. When he found Saul sleeping, he did not strike or kill him; he took only the spear fixed near his head and the cup of water that was near Saul’s head. All the others being asleep, he went out from the camp and crossed to the summit of the mountain.”

[Note: [Col. 0683D] The printed edition of Isidore reads *lenticulam* (“little bowl”), which is plainly wrong, since Scripture itself says “the cup of water that was at Saul’s head,” and the cup is mentioned again afterward.]

“What, then, does this mean? The Jews were persecuting Christ, but by persecuting him they were sleeping, because they were not watchful in heart. Hardness of heart is a kind of slumber. They slept in the old life and did not awaken to the new.

“Christ came; he did not kill them, but took from them the cup of water—that is, the grace of the law. He also took away the royal scepter, namely, the power of the kingdom, which they regarded as a great thing and by which they protected themselves temporally, and which they wielded against God through unbelief.

[The reading *qua* is certainly wrong.] Then our victorious David returned from their camp and rose beyond it to the height of the heavenly mountain.”

[Note: [Col. 0683D] The word “entered” is added, but is redundant.]

### (Chapter 28)

“Meanwhile, while David was fleeing and going to Achish, king of the Philistines, to fight against Israel, the Amalekites rose up, attacked Ziklag, set it on fire, and took captive everything belonging to David and his young men (chapter 30:1).

“When David returned to pursue the Amalekites (verses 8 and 11 and following), he found an Egyptian boy, exhausted on the way—the Amalekites had abandoned him there when he became ill. David restored the boy with food and made him the guide of his journey. Thus he followed the Amalekites, found them feasting, and utterly destroyed them.”

[Note: [Col. 0683D] These words are also found in Isidore; consult number 73, otherwise chapter 41, of Gregory the Great’s fifth book of the *Moralia*.]

[Note: [Col. 0683D] *Lacessentem* (“harassing”) is certainly wrong.]

[Note: [Col. 0683D] The words “he made him the guide of his journey,” which are nevertheless found in both Isidore and Gregory, are missing.]

[Note: [Col. 0684D] “The Amalekite while feasting.” Our reading is preferable.]

“What does it mean that the Egyptian Amalekite boy, exhausted on the road, sits there, except that the lover of the present age, covered by the blackness of his sin, is often abandoned by that same age when he becomes weak and despised, so that he can no longer run with it, but, broken by adversity, grows numb?

“God chooses those whom the world despises, because contempt itself often recalls a person to himself. The one who abandoned his father and squandered prodigally the portion of his substance that he had received, after he began to hunger, came to himself and said: ‘How many hired servants of my father have an abundance of bread?’ (Luke 15:13, 17). He had gone far from himself when he sinned; and if he had not hungered, he would not have returned to himself. Once he had become needy in earthly matters, he then began to consider what he had lost in spiritual things.”

[Note: [Col. 0684D] What follows may be found in no. 7 of homily 36 of Gregory the Great’s *Homilies on the Gospels*; Isidore has other material, though apt material.]

[Note: [Col. 0684D] Gregory inserts other material here.]

“Thus the weak and those despised in this world often hear the voice of God all the more quickly because they have nothing in this world in which to delight.

“The Amalekites’ boy mentioned above aptly represents this. While the Amalekites were plundering and running about, he remained sick on the road and withered from hunger and thirst. David nevertheless found him and gave him food and drink. Immediately recovering, he became David’s guide, found the Amalekites feasting, and with great strength struck down those who had abandoned him.

“Amalekite means ‘the people who lick.’ What, then, does a licking people signify except worldly minds? They circle around and, as it were, lick everything earthly, delighting only in temporal things. A licking people makes its plunder, as it were, when, loving earthly things, it gathers profits from the losses of others.”

[Note: [Col. 0684D] The printed editions have “increases” or “exaggerates.”]

“But the sick Egyptian boy is abandoned on the road, because every sinner, once he begins to grow weak in the condition of this world, immediately becomes despised by worldly minds. Yet David finds him and gives him food and drink, because the Lord, strong of hand, does not despise the outcasts of the world. Often he converts to the grace of his love those who are entirely unable to follow the world and who, as it were, remain on the road; he offers them the food of his word and directs them along the way as guides for himself, making them his preachers.

“For when they bring Christ into the hearts of sinners, they lead him against his enemies like David. They strike down the feasting Amalekites with the sword like David, because by the Lord’s power they overthrow the proud, whoever they may be, who had despised themselves in the world.

“Thus the Egyptian boy who had remained on the road killed the Amalekites, because often those who could not previously run with worldly people in this world overcome worldly minds by preaching.”

### (Chapter 28:3 and following)

[Note: [Col. 0684D] All of this is taken from Isidore, who thereafter likewise cites Augustine. Rabanus also has the same material.]

“After Samuel’s death, the Philistines gathered against Israel. Saul consulted the Lord, but he did not answer him (verse 6). Saul sought a woman skilled in divination who would raise Samuel for him; and when he had been raised, he immediately said to him: ‘Why have you disturbed me, so that I should be raised?’ and so forth (verse 15).

“Historically, the question is whether the woman skilled in divination actually summoned the prophet himself from the underworld, or whether it was some imaginary apparition produced by the deception of demons. On this question Augustine, bishop of blessed memory, wrote the following to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan:”

[Note: [Col. 0685D] Book 2 of the *Questions to Simplicianus*, question 4, section 1.]

“You ask, I say, whether the unclean spirit who was in the woman skilled in divination could have acted so that Samuel would appear to Saul and speak with him. But it is a far greater miracle that Satan himself, the prince of all unclean spirits, could speak with God and ask that Job, a most righteous man, be put to the test (Job 1:11), or that he could ask that the Apostles also be put to the test (Luke 12:31). If this presents no difficult question because truth, present everywhere, speaks through whatever creature it wishes to whatever creature it wishes, and because it is therefore no sign of great merit to the one to whom God speaks—for what matters is what he says, since an emperor does not speak with many innocent people for whom he provides most prudently for salvation, while he does speak with many guilty people whom he orders to be killed—then there should likewise be no question about how an unclean spirit could speak with the soul of a holy man.

“For God the Creator and Sanctifier is unquestionably far greater than all the saints. But if it troubles us that an evil spirit was permitted to raise the soul of a righteous man and, as it were, call it back from the hidden repositories of the dead, is it not more remarkable that Satan took up the Lord himself and placed him upon the pinnacle of the Temple? In whatever manner he did this, the manner in which Samuel was raised is likewise hidden.

“Unless perhaps someone should say that the devil had an easier permission to take up the living Lord from wherever he wished and place him wherever he wished than to raise the spirit of the dead Samuel from its dwelling place. But if the Gospel does not disturb us in that matter because the Lord willed and permitted it to happen without any diminution of his power and divinity—just as he permitted himself to be seized, bound, mocked, crucified, and killed by the Jews themselves, although they were perverse and unclean, doing the devil’s works—it is not absurd to believe that, by some dispensation of the divine will, the spirit of the prophet consented to appear before the king, not unwillingly or under the domination and subjugation of magical power, but willingly and obediently to God’s hidden arrangement, unknown both to the woman skilled in divination and to Samuel, in order to strike him with the divine sentence.

“For why should the soul of a good man, summoned by evil living people, seem to lose its dignity if it comes, when good people who are alive often come when summoned to evil people and deal with them as the duty of justice requires, preserving and keeping unshaken the dignity of their virtue, while treating the vices of the others according to the use or necessity of present circumstances?”

“Nevertheless, this event may admit of another, easier solution and a more accessible interpretation: we need not believe that Samuel’s spirit was truly raised from its rest, but rather that some phantom or imaginary illusion was produced by the devil’s machinations. Scripture calls it by Samuel’s name for this reason: images are accustomed to be called by the names of the things whose images they are. Thus everything painted or fashioned from some material—metal, wood, or any substance suitable for such works—and nearly all images are customarily called by the names of the things whose images they are.

“For who would hesitate to call a painted man a man? Indeed, when we look at paintings of individual people, we readily use their proper names—for example, when, looking at a panel or wall, we say, ‘That is Cicero; that is Sallust; that is Achilles; that is Hector; this is the river Simois; that is Rome,’ when they are nothing other than painted images.

“Therefore, although the cherubim are heavenly powers, those figures fashioned from the metal that God commanded to be placed above the Ark of the Covenant to signify a great reality are nevertheless called ‘cherubim.’”

[Note: [Col. 0685D] The printed edition has “those images.”]

“Likewise, whoever sees a dream does not say, ‘I saw an image of Augustine’ or ‘an image of Simplicianus,’ but ‘I saw Augustine’ or ‘Simplicianus,’ although, at the time when he sees such a thing, we are unaware. Thus it is perfectly clear that it is not the people themselves but their images that are seen. Pharaoh too said that in his dream he had seen ears of grain and cattle, not images of ears of grain or cattle (Genesis 41:18).

“If, then, it is clearly established that among human beings images are called by the names of the things whose images they are, it is not surprising that Scripture says that Samuel was seen, even if perhaps an image of Samuel appeared through the contrivance of him who ‘transforms himself into an angel of light’ and his ministers into ministers of righteousness (2 Corinthians 11:14).”

“If it troubles us how true predictions were also made to Saul by an evil spirit, it may likewise seem remarkable how the demons recognized Christ (Matthew 8:29), whom the Jews did not recognize. When God wishes even the lowest and infernal spirits to know some truth—only matters temporal and pertaining to this mortal life—it is easy

[Note: [Col. 0686D] Our manuscript has *infirmos, summosque* (“weak, highest”), certainly by error, as the printed Augustine passage and what follows show.]

and not inappropriate and not inappropriate for almighty God, being just, to grant such spirits some power of divination through the hidden arrangement of his mysteries, for the punishment of those to whom these things are foretold, so that they may suffer in advance, by knowing beforehand, the evil that threatens them before it arrives.

“Thus they foretell to human beings what they hear from angels. But they hear only as much as the Lord and governor of all either commands or permits. Hence the spirit of divination in the Acts of the Apostles also bears witness to the Apostle Paul and attempts to become an evangelist (Acts 16:17).

“Yet these spirits mix deceptions with what they know to be true, and they foretell the truth less for the purpose of teaching than of deceiving. Perhaps this is why, when that image of Samuel predicted Saul’s death, it also said that he would be with Samuel (1 Samuel 28:19)—which is certainly false. For in the Gospel we read that the good are separated from the wicked after death by a great interval. The Lord testifies that a great chasm was fixed between the proud rich man, who was already suffering torments in the underworld, and the one who had lain ulcerated at his gate and was now established in rest (Luke 16:26).

“Or, if Samuel said to Saul, ‘You will be with me’ in the sense not of equality of blessedness but of a common condition of death—because both were human, both could die, and the dead man was announcing death to the living—your prudence, I think, perceives that, under either interpretation, the reading can be given an acceptable meaning that does not contradict the faith.”

[Note: [Col. 0687D] The printed editions have *eam* or *illam* (“it” or “that one”).]

“Unless perhaps, through a deeper and more perplexing inquiry, which exceeds either my abilities or the limits of my time, it may be discovered with certainty whether a human soul, after it has departed this life, can be summoned by magical incantations and appear before the eyes of the living

[Note: [Col. 0687D] The printed editions have *vivorum* (“of the living”).]

bearing even the features of a body, so that it may not only be seen but recognized.

“And if this is possible, whether the soul of a righteous person also—though not compelled by magical rites

[Note: [Col. 0687D] The printed editions add *sacris* (“sacred rites”).]

—might deem it worthy to appear, obeying the more hidden commands of the supreme law. If it should become clear that this cannot happen, then both interpretations should not be admitted in the treatment and exposition of this Scripture; rather, with that interpretation excluded, the imaginary simulation of Samuel produced by a diabolical rite should be understood.

“But since, whether such a thing can happen or cannot happen, the deceit of Satan and the cunning operation by which images are fabricated remain constantly active in many forms for deceiving human senses, let us proceed cautiously, so as not to prescribe limits to more careful inquiries. Nevertheless, for the present, let us rather believe that something of this kind was brought about by the evil spirit through the ministry of that woman skilled in divination, so long as we are not granted the ability to devise and explain anything more.”

(31.) “Then, when battle had broken out, the Philistines struck Israel with a great slaughter; and Saul and his son Jonathan died.” (2 Samuel 1:2) But a certain man escaped and came to David at Ziklag, reporting to David the great slaughter that had taken place among the people; (verse 6) moreover, he added falsely that he himself had killed Saul and his son. (verse 15) But David, avenging the Lord’s Anointed, ordered him to be killed. (verse 17) David lamented this lament over Saul and over his son Jonathan. (verse 18) “And he ordered them to teach the sons of Judah the bow, as it is written in the Book of the Just.”

[Note: [Col. 0687D] Bede taught what follows, customarily marked with lines (Question 7); consult him. Rabanus has the same material on this passage.]

He did this because he already knew that the Philistines had an abundance of archers, and Saul in particular had perished from their missiles; thus he wanted his own soldiers also to learn the same art of warfare, so that they might defeat them. As for what follows, “as it is written in the Book of the Just,” they assert that this book can now be found nowhere, not even among the Hebrews themselves; nor can the Book of the Wars of the Lord be found, which is mentioned in the Book of Numbers (Numbers 21:14), nor Solomon’s songs, nor his very wise discussions concerning the nature of trees and of all herbs, and likewise concerning cattle, birds, reptiles, and fish; nor what is said in the Book of Chronicles (2 Chronicles 9:29). “The rest of Solomon’s works, both earlier and later, are written in the words of Nathan the prophet, and in the books of Ahijah the Shilonite; also in the vision of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam son of Nebat”; and many volumes of this kind, whose existence Scripture indeed proves, but which plainly do not exist today.

For when Judea was devastated by the Chaldeans, the library assembled in ancient times was also consumed by the enemy’s fire along with the other wealth of the province. From it, the few books now contained in Holy Scripture were later restored through the diligence of Ezra the priest and scribe. Hence it is written of him: “Ezra went up from Babylon, and he was a ready scribe in the Law of Moses” (Ezra 7:6–7)—“ready,” that is, because he discovered more expeditious forms of writing than the Hebrews had possessed up to that time. And in the letter of the king of the Persians it is written: “Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, the most learned scribe of the law of the God of heaven, greetings.” (Ezra 7:12)

(2 Samuel 1:21.) “Mountains of Gilboa, may neither dew nor rain come upon you, nor fields of firstfruits; for there the shield of the mighty was cast away, the shield of Saul, as though he had not been anointed with oil.”

It must be understood that Saul truly signifies the death of the true Christ: after having been anointed with the holy chrism—because of which he was also called “the Lord’s Anointed”—Saul deserved to be killed by his enemies, and thus prefigured the death which the true Christ, without guilt, deigned to undergo. The mountains of Gilboa, on which he perished, signify the proud designs of the Jewish people, by which they rebelled against the victor of life.

Accordingly, Gilboa is rightly interpreted as “rolling” or “descent.” For they rolled about in the filth of sins, in accordance with that proverb.

[Note: [Col. 0688D] 2 Peter 2:22. For it happened to them according to the true proverb: “A dog returned to its vomit, and a washed sow to wallowing in the mire.”] And, straying from the straightness of the way of salvation, they were already rushing downward—toward the foul desires of this world—for the sake of which they did not hesitate to hand over the King of heaven and earth to death. Therefore it is rightly wished for them that they should receive neither dew from heaven nor rain. We see this fulfilled in them today by the facts themselves: when heavenly grace abandoned them, it was transferred to the people of the Gentiles. Isaiah also threatened that this would happen to them under the figure of a vineyard, speaking in the person of the Lord: “And I will command the clouds not to rain upon it.” (Isaiah 5:6)

This is plainly to say: “I will command the apostles and all apostolic men not to preach the word of life to them any longer, but to leave them, unworthy and empty in their barrenness, to the eternal fire, deprived of the irrigation of the heavenly word which they rejected.”

[Note: The following passage is quoted by Paterius, who took it from chapter 4 of the preface to Book IV of the *Moralia*.]

“Concerning these people it is also rightly said: ‘so that they cannot be fields of firstfruits.’ For the proud minds of the Hebrews do not bear first fruits, because, remaining for the most part in unbelief at the coming of the Redeemer, they did not wish to follow the beginnings of faith. For Holy Church, made fruitful in her beginnings by the multitude of the Gentiles, will scarcely receive the Jews whom she finds at the end of the world; gathering the last of them, she will set them aside like gleanings of the harvest. Isaiah speaks of these remnants: ‘Though the number of the sons of Israel be like the sand of the sea, the remnant shall be saved.’” (Isaiah 10:22; Romans 9:27)

“The mountains of Gilboa may therefore have been cursed by the prophet’s mouth so that, when no fruit arises from the withered earth, the landowners may be struck by the penalty of barrenness; thus the sentence of the curse may fall upon those who, compelled by their iniquity, deserved to receive among themselves the death of the king.”

[Note: Thus far Gregory; Rabanus also takes this passage from him in his commentary on this place.]

You should not think it absurd that the evil deeds of the reprobate should signify something good, or, conversely, that the good works of the righteous should be placed in an opposite signification. Read, therefore, the *Moralia* of the holy Pope Gregory, where he explains how blessed Job cursed his own day, saying: “May the day perish on which I was born,” and so forth.

[Note: See Saint Gregory’s letter to Saint Leander, prefixed to his exposition of the Book of Job, and Book IV, chapter 1, of that same exposition. Add also what Claudius later reports concerning Bathsheba from Gregory the Great.]

You will see that it is exceedingly common in Scripture for good things to be understood as signifying evil, and evil human deeds to be taken in the sanctification of good things. Thus interpreters explain that Uriah, David the king’s most faithful soldier, is to be understood in an evil signification with respect to his most devout and innocent deeds or words, whereas David himself, in his greatest crime, is to be understood in a good signification.

For if good could not be signified through evil, and evil through good, it would never be permissible to write the name of God in black ink, but it would always have to be written in shining gold, because “God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all.” Nor, conversely, would it be proper for the names of Absalom and Doeg—wicked men—to be written in the titles of the Psalms in shining red pigment, but only in the color of ink.

Therefore, just as on the pages of books we can depict both evil and good in any color without reproach, so also, in the realm of signification, good and evil can rightly be expressed through any human deeds. Nevertheless, it happens much more often, and is heard much more agreeably, that good is represented by good and evil by evil.

But just as in wall painting it is not fitting to depict a dark-skinned Ethiopian in white, or a Saxon of white body or hair in a dark color, so in the recompense of merits each person will receive according to his own work; and as he was in conduct, so he will appear in judgment. It will not matter at all what each person represented, but what he actually did.

# BOOK II

[Col. 0689C]

## HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTER HEADINGS OF BOOK II

Concerning what is written: after the death of Saul, the men of Judah came and anointed David king in Hebron; and concerning Abner son of Ner, who appointed Ish-bosheth son of Saul king over Israel.

Concerning the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, who killed Ish-bosheth.

Concerning the praise of David, who gathered thirty thousand chosen men from Israel to bring up the ark of God, and concerning the death of Uzzah.

Concerning David’s admonition, when he was instructed by the prophet that he himself should not build the Lord’s temple, but his son should do so, and concerning his thanksgiving.

Concerning the messengers of David whom he sent to Hanun, king of the Ammonites.

Concerning David’s sin with Bathsheba and the death of Uriah, when Nathan came to David and proposed to him the parable of the rich man and the poor man.

Concerning David’s flight because of Absalom, when he left the city of Jerusalem walking barefoot.

Concerning the battle with Absalom, and his being struck and killed.

Concerning the Seventeenth Psalm.

Concerning the names of David’s mighty men.

Concerning David’s battle against the Philistines, when, being thirsty, he desired water from Bethlehem.

Concerning David’s sin, when he sinned by numbering the people.

[Col. 0689C]

## HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE TO BOOK II

[Note: This entire preface is taken from chapters 1, 2, and 3 of Book XVII of *The City of God*, with a few minor omissions. I ask the reader to compare this preface with those chapters and with what I have said.]

“The promises of God made to Abraham, whose seed, as we have learned by God’s pledge, was to include both the Israelite nation according to the flesh and all nations according to faith—how these promises are fulfilled, the City of God has shown as it advances through the ordered succession of times.

Since, therefore, the preceding book has been brought to an end with the reign of David, we now take up, beginning with that reign, the remaining events that follow, insofar as seems sufficient for the work undertaken.

This entire period—from the time when holy Samuel began to prophesy until the people of Israel were led captive into Babylon, and from there, according to the prophecy of the holy Jeremiah (Jeremiah 25:11), until the Israelites returned after seventy years and the house of God was restored—is the whole period of the prophets.

Although we may also rightly call the patriarch Noah himself, in whose days the whole earth was destroyed by the Flood, and others before and after him, down to the time when kings began to exist among the people of God, prophets—because through them certain future events, or events signifying something in one way or another, or predictions relevant to the City of God and the kingdom of heaven were given—especially since we read that some of them were expressly called by this name, such as Abraham (Genesis 20:7) and Moses (Deuteronomy 34:10), nevertheless the days of the prophets are chiefly and especially understood to begin from the time when Samuel began to prophesy. At God’s command, he first anointed Saul (1 Samuel 10:1), and after Saul had been rejected, David himself (1 Samuel 16:13) as king; from David’s stock the other kings were to succeed one another for as long as it was fitting that they should succeed.

If I wished to recall everything that was foretold by the prophets concerning Christ, while the City of God passed through these times by the dying of some of its members and the birth of others to succeed them, the task would extend into immensity.

First, the very Scripture which, by arranging in order the kings, their deeds, and their fortunes, appears to be occupied with narrating events with the diligence of history—if it is considered with the help of God’s Spirit—will be found to be concerned no less, or even more, with announcing future events than with declaring past ones. Who does not know, if he thinks about these matters even moderately, how laborious and lengthy it would be to investigate this by careful searching and to demonstrate it through exposition, and how unworthy of any limited number of volumes?

Second, those very passages which unquestionably belong to prophecy are so numerous in their references to Christ and to the kingdom of heaven, which is the City of God, that a fuller discussion would be required to disclose this than the scope of the present work allows.

Therefore, if I can, I shall so moderate my pen that, while carrying out this work according to God’s will, I shall neither say what may be omitted nor omit what is sufficient.”

[Note: Claudius omits much here that is unrelated to the present subject and that Augustine most appropriately inserted in order to connect the preceding material with what he immediately goes on to discuss.]

The seed of Abraham was already in the promised land—that is, the people of Israel according to the flesh—and there it had begun to reign, not only by using and possessing the cities of its enemies but also by having kings. The promises of God concerning that people had already been fulfilled to a considerable extent: not only those made to the three patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and whatever other promises had been made in their times, but also those made through Moses, by whom that same people was freed from Egyptian slavery and through whom all the events of earlier times were revealed when he led the people through the wilderness.

The promise of God concerning the land of Canaan, from a certain river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates, had not, however, been fulfilled either through the distinguished leader Joshua son of Nun, by whom that people was brought into the promised land, who conquered the nations, divided the land among the twelve tribes as God had commanded, and then died, or throughout the whole period of the Judges after him. Nor was the future fulfillment yet being prophesied; rather, it was awaited.

It was fulfilled through David and his son Solomon. The kingdom of David and his son Solomon was extended over as great an expanse as had been promised, for they subdued all those nations and made them tributary.

Thus the seed of Abraham according to the flesh—that is, in the land of Canaan—had been established under kings in the promised land, so that nothing remained for the earthly promise of God to be fulfilled except that the Hebrew nation should remain in that same land, insofar as temporal prosperity was concerned, in an unshaken condition through a succession of prosperity until the end of this mortal age, if it obeyed the laws of the Lord its God.

But because God knew that it would not do this, he also made use of temporal punishments to exercise his few faithful servants within it and to admonish those who were later to exist among all the nations—those who needed to be admonished. Among these nations he was going to fulfill another promise through the Incarnation of Christ, when the New Testament was revealed.

Accordingly, just as those divine oracles made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and all the other signs or prophetic sayings given in the preceding sacred writings were made, so too the remaining prophecies from this period of the Kings pertain partly to the nation descended from Abraham according to the flesh, and partly to that seed of his in whom all nations are blessed as fellow heirs of Christ through the New Testament, for the possession of eternal life and the kingdom of heaven.

Some refer to the slave woman who gives birth in slavery—that is, to the earthly Jerusalem, which is in slavery with her children—and others to the free City of God, that is, the true and eternal Jerusalem in heaven, whose children are human beings living according to God while they journey on earth. Yet some passages are understood to belong to both: properly to the slave woman, figuratively to the free woman.

The utterances of the prophets are therefore found to be threefold: some concern the earthly Jerusalem, some the heavenly Jerusalem, and some both.”

(2 Samuel 2:4–6.) “After the death of Saul, the men of Judah came and anointed David in Hebron, so that he might reign over the house of Judah. And it was reported to David that the men of Jabesh-gilead had buried Saul. Therefore David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them: ‘Blessed are you by the Lord, because you have shown this mercy toward your lord Saul and have buried him; and now the Lord will indeed repay you with mercy and faithfulness.’”

[Note: Augustine transmitted the following in chapter 9, section 11, of *On the Care for the Dead*, also called *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*.]

“Why, then, are these men who buried Saul and his son said to have shown mercy, and why are they blessed for this reason by the pious king, unless it is because the hearts of those who show compassion are rightly moved when they grieve over what happens to the bodies of the dead—things which, with that affection by which no one ever hates his own flesh, they do not wish to happen to their own bodies after death, and which they take care to provide for others who do not feel them, while they themselves still feel?”

After David had been anointed king over Judah, Abner son of Ner made Ish-bosheth son of Saul king over all Israel. Abner son of Ner went out from the camp at Gibeon with the young men of Ish-bosheth. Joab son of Zeruiah, together with David’s young men, went out from Hebron. They stirred up a battle beside the pool of Gibeon, and Asahel pursued Abner.

Abner spoke to Asahel, saying: “Turn aside; do not follow me, lest I be forced to pierce you through to the ground.” But Asahel despised the warning and would not turn aside. Therefore Abner struck him in the groin with the butt end of his spear, pierced him through, and he died.

[Note: The following was transmitted by Gregory the Great in the sixteenth chapter of the third part of the *Pastoral Rule*, admonition 17.]

“Whom did Asahel represent except those whom furious passion seizes and drives headlong? Such people must be avoided with as much care as they are violently carried away by their madness.

Thus Abner—whose name in our language means ‘lamp of the father’—fled, because when the tongue of teachers, which reveals the light of the heavenly God, sees someone’s mind being carried away along the precipices of fury, it refrains from returning the darts of words against the enraged person. It does not wish to strike the pursuer.

But when the angry do not calm themselves through any reflection, and, like Asahel, do not cease to pursue and rage, those who attempt to restrain the furious must not raise themselves up in anger. Instead, they should display whatever tranquility they possess and should bring forward certain words subtly, by which they may prick the mind of the enraged person obliquely.

Thus, when Abner stopped before his pursuer, he did not pierce him with the point of the spear, but with its butt end. To strike with the point is to confront someone with the force of open rebuke; to strike the pursuer with the butt end is to touch the angry person calmly with certain words and, as though sparing him, to overcome him.

Asahel immediately fell dead, because disturbed minds, when they perceive that they are being spared and yet are touched inwardly by the reasoning of the replies in a tranquil manner, immediately fall from the position into which they had raised themselves. Those who recoil from the violence of their own anger under the blow of gentleness die, as it were, without iron.”

(2 Samuel 4–6.) Then the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, came. They entered the house of Ish-bosheth in the heat of the day, while he was sleeping on his bed at noon. They entered the house, and the woman guarding the door of the house was cleaning wheat and fell asleep. Taking ears of wheat, they entered secretly and struck him in the groin.

[Note: Gregory transmitted what follows, as usual, in section 49—elsewhere chapter 36—of Book I of the *Moralia on Job*.]

“The woman guarding the door cleans the wheat when the guardianship of the mind separates virtues from vices by discernment. If she falls asleep with respect to the death of her own lord, she admits the plotters, because when the vigilance of discernment ceases, it opens a path for evil spirits to kill the soul.

They enter and take away the ears of wheat because they immediately remove the seeds of good thoughts; and they strike in the groin because they destroy the virtue of the heart through the pleasure of the flesh. To strike in the groin is to pierce the life of the mind with the pleasure of the flesh.

Ish-bosheth would certainly not have succumbed to this death if he had not assigned a woman—that is, a soft and weak guard—to the entrance of the house, the access to the mind.

[Note: [Col. 0694D] The printed edition reads: “to this death.”] A strong and vigilant understanding must be placed at the doors of the heart, one which neither the dreams of negligence overwhelm nor the error of ignorance misleads.

Thus Ish-bosheth is rightly named the one who is stripped by hostile swords while a woman is his guard. For Ish-bosheth means ‘man of shame.’ A man of shame is one who is not fortified by a strong guardianship of the mind: while he supposes that he is practicing virtues, vices that enter secretly kill him unawares.

The entrance to the mind must therefore be fortified with every virtue, lest at any time the enemies lying in wait penetrate it through the opening of neglected thought.”

(Chapter 6.) David gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand. He arose and went forth, and all the people who were with him from among the men of Judah, to bring up the ark of God, upon which the name of the Lord of hosts was invoked, who sits upon the cherubim above it.

[Note: I also find what follows in Rabanus when he explains this passage.]

David gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand, because the Lord established the primitive Church from Israel—not indeed from all Israel, but by joining to himself those who were chosen. For “not all who are of Israel are Israelites” (Romans 4:12; 9:4, 6, 7, 8), but “the children of the promise are counted as the seed.”

“They are reported to have numbered thirty thousand, that is, to have been perfected in the steadfastness of faith, works, and hope. Three refers to faith because of the confession of the Holy Trinity; ten refers to works because of the Decalogue of the Law; a thousand refers to hope because of its perfection in the hope of eternal life, than which nothing is higher, just as no number is greater than a thousand.

Even if you say ten thousand, thirty thousand, or a thousand thousand, you do not go beyond the number one thousand by counting; rather, you multiply it either by itself or by repeatedly combining it with smaller numbers. Therefore multiply three by ten, so that faith may not be dead without works. Likewise multiply thirty by a thousand, so that faith, which works through love, may hope for its reward nowhere but in heaven.

The chosen men of Israel therefore signify peoples who rightly believe, work, and hope. The men of Judah who were with David signify those peoples and teachers who clung familiarly to Christ’s side. Surrounded by this twofold army, he rejoices to bring up the Lord’s ark—that is, to extend the Church and implant it in the hearts of those who did not believe.

The ark is placed upon a new cart so that the grace of the New Testament may be poured into minds renewed in baptism, and new wine may be entrusted for preservation to new wineskins.”

(1 Samuel 7:1 and 2 Samuel 6:4.) “The ark had previously been in the house of Abinadab, which was in Gibeah, because the same faith of the Church that is now preached also flourished before the time of the Lord’s Incarnation in those who followed the devotion of the patriarchs and prophets.

Abinadab, whose name is interpreted as ‘my spontaneous father,’ signified either Abraham, the father of faith, or Moses, the lawgiver. Both of them certainly guard the ark in Gibeah, because by the lofty example of their virtue they fortify the breasts of believers.

Thus Gibeah is interpreted as ‘hill’; it is a place in the city of Kiriath-jearim.

When the ark had been brought outside, David and all Israel danced before the Lord with various kinds of musical instruments, because as soon as the proclamation of the new grace began, the Lord invited everyone to offer praises to God the Father in humility, saying: ‘Whoever serves me, let him follow me.’ (John 12:26) One receives through the Spirit the word of wisdom, another the word of knowledge, another kinds of tongues, another the grace of healings, and so forth. (1 Corinthians 12:8–10)

But as the ark advanced—that is, as the primitive Church grew—with these and similar kinds of spiritual gifts, it came to the threshing floor of Nachon, that is, to the prepared threshing floor, namely, the Church of the Gentiles, which was to be consecrated by the truth of faith. Concerning this John says: ‘He will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor.’ (Matthew 3:12)

There the priest who touched the ark incautiously, as though to correct it, was immediately struck down by the Lord, because the Jewish people, while envying the Gentiles, deprived themselves of the gift of salvation; and while wishing to mix the Law with the Gospel, it deprived itself of the grace of both.

‘And he held it,’ the text says, ‘because the oxen were kicking.’ For the oxen to kick is for the preachers of the Gospel to act with greater freedom concerning the faith and not to proceed according to the custom of the Law, but to interpret spiritually the sabbaths, new moons, circumcision, and sacrifices.

Those who came down from Judea to teach the brothers attempted to correct them as though they were straying, saying: ‘Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.’ (Acts 15:1) And James said concerning them to Paul: ‘You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the Law.’” (Acts 21:20)

[Col. 0695C]

“Therefore, because of the priest who had been killed, David did not wish to bring the ark of the Lord to himself in the city of David, but turned it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. For when the Jews rejected the word, lest preaching that had been heard but not received should do further harm, the apostles were taken away from them and sent to instruct the Gentiles.

Therefore the place called the threshing floor of Nachon, which demonstrates the faith of the Gentiles prepared for the Lord’s grace, is called the striking of Uzzah, because ‘through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles.’ (Romans 11:11)

Obed-edom is interpreted as ‘serving man.’ He is the one of whom the Lord says to the Father: ‘You will appoint me as head of the nations, and a people whom I did not know will serve me.’ (Psalm 18:43)

There, also anticipating the rejection of the Jews, as though in the death of Uzzah, he says: ‘You will deliver me from the contradictions of the people.’ (Psalm 18:44)

The name of the city also fits: Gath is interpreted as ‘winepress,’ signifying the cross, in which the true vine deigned to be trodden and pressed. From this the whole people of the Gentiles may rightly be called Gittite, to whom it is said: ‘But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.’” (Galatians 6:14)

[Note: See what Augustine says in section 3 of his exposition of Psalm 55.]

“The three months during which the ark remained there are faith, hope, and love. Just as a month is completed by its days, so each virtue reaches perfection by its own stages. These months do not cease to run until the fullness of the Gentiles enters.

At last David will return and bring the ark into the city of David, because the Lord, when Enoch and Elijah preach, will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children.” (Luke 1:17)

“Sacrificing oxen and rams—that is, crowning with the blood of martyrdom those who thresh the Lord’s threshing floor and exercise leadership over his sheep—and openly revealing the example of his own Incarnation and Passion, which the Jews had not believed until then, he also makes this clear by the fact that David himself was girded with a linen ephod.

For linen, which is produced from the earth and reaches the whiteness of a garment through much labor, displays the truth of human flesh triumphing amid the blows of suffering.

But while everyone rejoiced and resounded with hymns at the entrance of the heavenly ark, Michal alone, the daughter of Saul, was absent from those who carried the ark. Indeed, she looked down upon David humbled from the watchtowers.

This signifies that, among the Jews who will believe at the end of the world, there will be some who will follow Christ in profession but Antichrist in conduct. Accordingly, that same Michal, to signify the instability of carnal people, is interpreted as “all water”; she is called not David’s wife but Saul’s daughter, because those who serve Christ only in faith, without corresponding conduct, will not be crowned in his kingdom but condemned by the anathema of his persecutors, whom they imitated.

Let the perverse be angry and despise the humility of the Church; nevertheless, the ark of the Lord enters its appointed place.

It is placed in the middle of the tabernacle that David had pitched for it—that is, the faith of the Church is preached, advances, and is implanted in the hearts of all whom the Lord had predestined for eternal life. (Acts 13:48)

David offers burnt offerings and peace offerings before the Lord—that is, Christ, who is at the right hand of God and intercedes for us, commends the faith and devotion of the Church to the Father. (Romans 8:34)

Following David’s example, he blesses the humble and faithful and feeds them with the nourishment of a saving mystery. To each he distributes one cake of bread (2 Samuel 6:19), namely, the bread that descended from heaven and gives life to this world. (John 6:35, 48)

He also gives one portion of roasted beef, namely, that fatted calf which was slaughtered for the younger son returning to his father and roasted in the fire of suffering, saying: ‘My strength has dried up like a potsherd.’ (Psalm 22:15; 2 Samuel 6:19)

And he gives flour fried in oil, that is, flesh utterly cleansed from the stain of sin but roasted in the frying pan of the cross because of its abundant love for human salvation.

It is rightly that one cake of bread and one portion of meat are given, because ‘there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.’ (Ephesians 4:5–6)

In another sense the faithful receive these gifts when ‘we, though many, are one bread and one body in Christ.’ (1 Corinthians 10:17) Each of them chastises the wantonness of his flesh, subjects it to service, and cooks it in the fire of the Holy Spirit. They also make the fruits of good works boil through compassion for their neighbor in the richest oil of mercy.

But, by contrast, the daughter of Saul enters the king’s chamber in vain and produces no fruits from the seed she has conceived, because those who receive the word of God only through the ear, without the offspring of good works, await the day of everlasting death.”

[Note: Thus far also Rabanus.]

In this history of the blessed king and prophet David, in which he is said to have brought up the ark of God, humility is morally commended, pride condemned, and rashness punished. David himself was not ashamed to dance humbly before the ark of the Lord (verse 14), and immediately afterward he was deemed worthy to receive the promise of the Son of God who was to be born from his line. His wife, however, who despised that humility, was not deemed worthy to be made fruitful by his seed and suffered the punishment of perpetual barrenness.

It is pleasing to consider how great are the gifts of virtue that David receives, and in all these things how firmly he preserved himself in humility.

[Note: What follows is found explicitly in chapter 46—elsewhere sections 77 and 78—of Book XXVII of the *Moralia on Job*, composed by Saint Gregory.]

“Who would not be lifted up by breaking the jaws of lions and scattering the arms of bears (1 Samuel 17:38); by being chosen while his elder brothers were passed over (1 Samuel 16:12; 18:28); by being anointed to govern the kingdom after the king’s rejection; by striking down Goliath with a single stone (1 Samuel 16:50); by bringing back the numerous foreskins required by the king after killing the Philistines (1 Samuel 18:27); by finally receiving the promised kingdom; and by possessing the whole Israelite people without any opposition? (2 Samuel 5:1)

And yet, when he brings the ark of God back to Jerusalem, as though he had forgotten that he had been set above everyone else, he dances before the ark amid the people. And because dancing before the ark was, as is believed, the custom of the common people, the king whirls about in the dance in divine service.

Behold: the one whom the Lord had placed above all others in a singular way humbles himself beneath the Lord, making himself equal to the least and displaying himself as lowly. He does not recall the power of the kingdom; he does not fear becoming contemptible in the eyes of his subjects by dancing. He does not recognize himself as superior to the others in honor before the ark of the one who had bestowed that honor.

Before the Lord he performed what was weak or lowly, so that, through humility, he might strengthen what he had done bravely before men.

[Note: The printed edition reads *vilia* (‘lowly things’), but I think *debilia* (‘weak things’) should be retained, since humility would strengthen them.]

I do not know what others may think of his deeds; I am more astonished by David dancing than by David fighting. By fighting he subdued the enemy, but by dancing before the Lord he conquered himself.

Michal, the daughter of Saul, still mad with the swelling pride of royal lineage [Note: [Col. 0698D] The printed edition reads: “of royal descent.”], looked down upon him in his humility and said: ‘How glorious was the king of Israel today, uncovering himself before the maidservants of his servants, as one of the buffoons might uncover himself!’ (verse 20)

She immediately heard the reply: ‘As the Lord lives, I will dance before the Lord, who chose me rather than your father.’ A little later he said: ‘I will dance, and I will make myself even more contemptible than I have become; and I will be humble in my own eyes.’ (verse 22)

It is as though he plainly said: ‘I desire to become contemptible before human beings, because through humility I seek to preserve myself noble before the Lord.’

There are, however, some who think humbly of themselves because, although placed in positions of honor, they recognize that they are nothing but dust and ashes; yet they refuse to appear lowly before other people and, contrary to what they think inwardly about themselves, cover themselves externally with a rigid dignity.

There are also some who desire to appear lowly to others and, by displaying themselves as degraded, despise everything they are; yet inwardly, within themselves, they swell up as though because of the very merit of the lowliness they have displayed. They are all the more elevated in heart the more they suppress pride in outward appearance.

David detected and overcame both these battles of a single pride with great vigilance and remarkable strength. Because he thinks humbly of himself inwardly and does not seek outward honor, he declares: ‘I will dance, and I will become more contemptible.’ And because, by presenting himself as lowly outwardly, he does not swell up inwardly, he adds: ‘And I will be humble in my own eyes.’

It is as though he says: ‘As I show myself outwardly, despising myself, so I regard myself inwardly.’

What, then, will those do whom learning elevates, if David knew the Redeemer who was to come from his own flesh, announced his joys by prophesying, and yet pressed down the neck of his heart with the strong heel of discernment, saying: ‘And I will be humble in my own eyes’?”

“[Note: [Col. 0698D] Understand ‘priest’ in the broader sense.] The priest also, who touched the ark with heedless presumption, expiated the guilt of his audacity by a premature death”—[Note: [Col. 0698D] Claudius transcribes this from Gregory’s Book V of the *Moralia* [no. 24, elsewhere chapters 9 or 10], although he has altered some things.]—“shows that those who are lesser and inferior are unable to understand and despise either the deeds or the words of their betters; yet these should not rashly be censured by them, since they cannot truly grasp them. Often something is done by those in authority as a matter of administrative accommodation which is judged an error by those beneath them; often many things are said by the strong which the weak condemn precisely because they do not understand them.

This was well signified by the ark of the covenant, which was tilted when the oxen kicked. The Levite who, believing it about to fall, wished to steady it immediately received the sentence of death. For what is the mind of the righteous except the ark of the covenant, which, carried by oxen that kick, is tilted? For sometimes even one who governs well, shaken by the confusion of the peoples subject to him, is moved by love alone to accommodate himself to their condition for the sake of administration. But in what is done by such accommodation, that very inclination of strength is judged a fall by the inexperienced. Hence some subjects raise against this hand of theirs the hand of censure, but through their very presumption they immediately fall away from life.

The Levite therefore stretched out his hand as though to help; but, transgressing, he lost his life, because whenever the weak criticize the deeds of the strong, they themselves are rejected from the company of the living. At times holy men, accommodating themselves to the least, say certain things, while contemplating the highest they utter others; and when fools do not understand the force either of accommodation or of elevation, they boldly criticize these things. And what is it to wish to correct the righteous for his accommodation except to raise the tilted ark with the proud hand of censure? What is it to censure the righteous for [Note: [Col. 0698D] The printed edition has ‘unknown.’] an unpolished manner of speaking except to regard the movement of his strength as a lapse into error?

But the one who presumptuously raises the ark of God loses his life, because no one would dare to correct the saints in what is right unless he had first formed a better judgment of himself. Hence that same Levite is rightly called Uzzah, which is interpreted as ‘strong of the Lord’; for presumptuous people would never judge the deeds or words of their betters to be weak unless they believed themselves strong in the Lord.” 

## (Chapter 7)

After these events, when many prosperous things had happened to King David, he conceived the plan of building a house for God—that is, the famous temple which was later constructed by his son, King Solomon. While he was considering this, the word of the Lord came to Nathan the prophet, to be conveyed to the king. When the Lord had said that David himself would not build a house for him, and that for so long a time he had not commanded anyone among his people to build him a cedar house, [Col. 0699B] he continued:

> “And now this is what you shall say to my servant David. Thus says the Lord: [vers. 12] When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come forth from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom. He himself shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me.”

[Note: [Col. 0699D] Having transcribed so much from Augustine in his explanation of the First Book of Kings, he again transcribes from Augustine what he presents in chapters 8 and 9 of Book XVII of *The City of God*.]

> “Whoever thinks that this very great promise was fulfilled in Solomon is greatly mistaken. He notices what was said—‘He shall build me a house’—because Solomon built that famous temple, but he fails to notice: ‘His house and his kingdom shall be faithful before me forever.’
>
> “Let him therefore attend and observe Solomon’s house, full of foreign women worshiping false gods, and Solomon himself, once wise, seduced and overthrown by them into that same idolatry; and let him not dare to suppose either that God promised this falsely or that he could not have foreknown that such a Solomon and such a house would come to be.
>
> “Nor should we doubt this even if we did not already see these things fulfilled in Christ our Lord, who was made [Rom. 1:3] from the seed of David according to the flesh, lest we search vainly and fruitlessly for someone else here, like the carnal Jews. For they themselves understand that the son whom they read as having been promised to King David in this passage was not Solomon, to such an extent that, although the one who was promised has already been revealed with such clarity, they still profess to await another with astonishing blindness.
>
> “A certain image of the future reality was indeed formed in Solomon, in that he built the temple, enjoyed peace in accordance with his name—for *Solomon* means ‘peaceful’ in Latin—and was remarkably praiseworthy at the beginning of his reign. Yet, through the shadow of what was to come, his very person also announced Christ the Lord; it did not present him. Hence certain things are written about him as though they had been foretold about him, while Holy Scripture, prophesying through historical events as well, in a certain way [Col. 0700A] sketches in him the outline of future things.

> “For, besides the books of sacred history, where he is reported to have reigned, the seventy-second psalm is also inscribed with his name in its title. In it many things are said which cannot possibly apply to him, but which apply with perfect clarity to Christ the Lord, so that it is plainly evident that in the one there was some kind of shadowy figure, while in the other the reality itself was presented.
>
> “It is known within what limits Solomon’s kingdom was confined; yet in that psalm we read, to say nothing of other passages: [Ps. 71:8] ‘He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth’—something we see fulfilled in Christ. For he began his rule from the river, where, after being baptized by John, he began to be recognized by the disciples when John pointed him out. They called him not only Teacher but also Lord.
>
> “Nor was there any other reason why Solomon began to reign while his father David was still alive—a thing that happened to none of the other kings—except that this too might make it sufficiently clear that Solomon is not the one designated by this prophecy, which speaks to his father and says: ‘And when your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come forth from your womb, and I will prepare his kingdom.’
>
> “How, then, on account of what follows—‘He shall build me a house’—could this be thought to have been prophesied of Solomon, and not rather on account of what precedes it: ‘When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you’? Another peaceful one is understood to have been promised, one who, unlike Solomon, was foretold as being raised up after David’s death.
>
> “However long an interval may have elapsed, Jesus Christ plainly had to come after the death of King David, to whom he was promised: he was the one who would build a house for God, not from wood and stones but from human beings—the kind of house whose construction we rejoice in. For to this house, that is, to Christ’s faithful, the Apostle says: [1 Cor. 3:17] ‘For the temple of God is holy, which you are.’
>
> “For this reason, in the eighty-ninth psalm, whose title is ‘Understanding, by Ethan the Israelite,’ the promises of God made to King David are recalled, just as they are set down in this Book of Kings. Similar things are said there, including: [ibid., that is, Ps. 88:5] ‘I have sworn to David my servant: I will prepare your offspring forever,’ and so forth.”

[Note: [Col. 0699D] In the printed edition of Augustine, many other passages from the same psalm are quoted, ending with the words: ‘and his throne as the days of heaven.’]

> “As for what he says: [Note: [Col. 0700D] There is here some difference between the printed text of Augustine and ours; ours agrees almost completely with Eucherius’s Vulgate text.] ‘If he commits any iniquity, I will chastise him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men; but I will not remove my mercy from him, as I removed it from Saul, whom I removed from before my face’—he did not say ‘from them,’ but ‘from him.’ No sins can be found in Christ himself, who is the head of the Church, for which he would need to be corrected by human chastisements and divinely disciplined while mercy was preserved; but this applies to his body and members, which is his people.”

[Col. 0701A]

[Note: [Col. 0701D] The following material should be sought at the end of chapter 12 and in the following chapter, that is, chapter 13.]

> “What God spoke through Nathan to David must by no means be passed over, where he says: [2 Sam. 7:10–11] ‘And I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and I will plant them, and they shall dwell apart, and shall no longer be troubled, and the son of iniquity shall not again humble them, as from the beginning, from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel.’
>
> “Whoever hopes for so great a good in this world and in this land acts foolishly. [Note: [Col. 0701D] The printed edition reads ‘thinks.’] Or will someone think that this was fulfilled in the peace of King Solomon? Scripture indeed commends that peace with lofty praise as a shadow of what was to come. But this suspicion is carefully forestalled, since after saying, ‘The son of iniquity shall not again humble them,’ it immediately adds, ‘as from the beginning, from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel.’
>
> “Judges had been appointed over that people before kings began to rule there, from the time when it received the land of promise.
