And certainly the son of iniquity—namely, a foreign enemy—humbled it at intervals, during which the people are recorded to have alternated peace with wars. There one finds periods of peace longer than Solomon had, although he reigned for forty years. Under the judge called Ehud, there were eighty years of peace.
>
> “Far be it, then, that Solomon’s times should be thought to have been foretold in this promise, and still less the times of any other king. None of them reigned in such great peace as he did; nor did that nation ever hold its kingdom in such security that it was not anxious about being subjected to enemies. For amid such instability in human affairs, no people has ever been granted such security that it would not fear the hostile incursions of this life.
>
> “The place, therefore, that is promised as a dwelling so peaceful and secure is eternal, and is owed to the eternal, in the mother Jerusalem that is free, where Israel will truly be the people. For this name is interpreted as ‘seeing God.’ In desire for this reward, a devout life must be led by faith during this troubled pilgrimage.”

When Nathan had announced these words to David, [2 Sam. 7:18] “King David entered and sat before the Lord.”

[Note: [Col. 0701D] Here too Claudius follows Augustine his teacher, adapting to his purpose what the holy doctor teaches in Question 4 of Book II of the *Questions to Simplicianus*.]

> “What else should be understood by this sitting except that he sat in the presence of the Lord—either where the ark of the covenant was, through which a holier and more specially marked presence of the Lord may be understood, or because he sat down to pray? This is not rightly done except in the presence of God, that is, in the innermost part of the heart.
>
> “For ‘before the Lord’ may also be understood as meaning in a place where no human being was present to hear him praying. Whether, then, because of the ark of the covenant, or because of a secret place removed from observers, or because of the innermost heart where the feeling of the one praying was located, it was appropriately said: ‘He sat before the Lord.’
>
> “Unless perhaps it is the fact that he prayed while sitting that causes difficulty, since the spirit of Elijah also did this when he obtained rain by praying. [Note: [Col. 0702D] The printed edition has ‘Saint Elijah,’ 1 Kings 18:42.] These examples teach us that no particular posture of the body has been prescribed for prayer, provided that the mind, present to God, carries out its intention.
>
> “For we also pray standing, as it is written: [Luke 18:13] ‘But the tax collector stood at a distance’; and on our knees, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles; [Acts 7:59; 20:36] and sitting, as David and Elijah did here. If we also prayed lying down, it would not be written in the Psalms: [Ps. 6:6] ‘Every night I wash my bed; I drench my couch with my tears.’
>
> “Whenever someone seeks an occasion for prayer, he arranges his limbs in whatever bodily position seems appropriate at the time for moving the mind. But when the desire to pray is not sought but arises spontaneously—when something suddenly comes to mind that stirs the feeling of supplication with inexpressible groanings—prayer should not be postponed, no matter how it finds the person, so that we may search for somewhere to withdraw, or somewhere to stand, or somewhere to prostrate ourselves. For the mind’s concentration creates solitude for itself, and often even forgets which part of heaven, or in what bodily posture, found the limbs at that moment.”

> “David also made a name for himself when he returned after Syria had been captured in the Valley of Salt, with twelve thousand slain. [Note: [Col. 0702D] 2 Samuel 8:13. From this point Claudius transcribes Gregory the Great teaching; namely, what Gregory presents as no. 45 [elsewhere chapter 14 or 18] of Book III of the *Moralia*.]
>
> “What is signified by the multitude struck down for David in the Valley of Salt except that our Redeemer, by the scrutiny of his severity, extinguishes the folly of uncontrolled taste in those who hold false opinions about him?”

[Col. 0702C]

## (2 Samuel 10:1 and following)

After this, the king of the Ammonites died, and Hanun his son reigned in his place. David said: “I will show kindness to Hanun the son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me.” So David sent his servants to console him over the death of his father.

When David’s servants came into the land of the Ammonites, the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun their lord: “Do you think that David has sent comforters to you out of respect for your father, and not because he sent his servants to you in order to investigate and spy out the city and overthrow it?”

So Hanun took David’s servants, shaved off half of each man’s beard, cut their garments in half as far as their buttocks, and sent them away. [Col. 0702D] When this was reported to David, he sent to meet them, for the men were horribly disgraced. David commanded them: “Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown, and then return.”

Just as Hanun king of the Ammonites—[Note: [Col. 0702D] The manuscript incorrectly has ‘Moab.’]—disfigured David’s servants who had been sent to him and sent them back to David shamefully mutilated, so too the devil, the prince of this world, is accustomed to disfiguring many religious people through vices that creep in. When he exposes their hidden evils as open and shameful deeds and accomplished lust, he leaves them naked of the dignity of chastity, as though their garments had been cut away as far as their buttocks; and when he strips them of their former strength, he shaves them, as it were, like a beard.

Yet the true David, namely the Lord and our Savior, does not exclude them in his merciful regard from the pardon of repentance. He commands them also to remain in Jericho—that is, under the ban of repentance—until, by making satisfaction, they recover the spiritual mysteries and strength of mind that they lost by sinning; and only then may they stand in his presence.

## (2 Samuel 11:2)

It happened, when David rose from his bed in the afternoon and walked on the roof of the royal palace, that he saw a woman bathing. He sent for her and took her, and slept with her, and she conceived. When David learned this, he sent to Joab, saying: “Send Uriah the Hittite to me.”

When Uriah came to David . . . . . . David sent a letter by Uriah to Joab, instructing him to place Uriah where the fiercest battle was. Joab did so, and Uriah the Hittite died.

[Note: [Col. 0703D] Search for this at no. 55 [elsewhere chapter 28] of Book III of Gregory’s *Moralia on Job*.]

> “Often something is a virtue in its historical sense but a fault in its symbolic sense. Sometimes an event that occurred is a cause of condemnation [Note: [Col. 0703D] The printed edition reads: ‘in the deed it is a cause of condemnation.’], while in the written account it is a prophecy of virtue. We can quickly demonstrate both points [Note: [Col. 0703D] The printed edition reads ‘true.’] by bringing forward the testimony of this sacred Scripture to establish each.
>
> “Who, hearing the story—not only among the faithful but even among unbelievers—would not assert without hesitation that David, walking on the roof, desired Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah? Yet when Uriah returned from battle, David urged him to go home and wash his feet. He immediately replied: [vers. 11] ‘The ark of the Lord is under tents, and shall I rest in my own house?’ David received him at his own table and gave him the letter by which he was to die.
>
> “But whose type does David represent as he walks on the roof except the one of whom it is written: [Ps. 18:6] ‘He set his tabernacle in the sun’? And what does bringing Bathsheba to himself signify except joining the law of the letter, united to the carnal people, to himself through spiritual understanding?
>
> “Bathsheba is said to mean ‘the seventh well,’ because through knowledge of the law, by the infusion of spiritual grace, perfect wisdom is supplied to us. Whom, then, does Uriah signify except the Jewish people? His name is interpreted as ‘my light [Note: [Col. 0703D] Lord].’ The Jewish people, because it is lifted up by the knowledge of the law it has received, glories as though in the light of God.
>
> “But David [Note: [Col. 0703D] The printed editions add ‘of Uriah.’] took Uriah’s wife from him and joined her to himself, because our Redeemer, appearing in the flesh—he is called ‘strong of hand,’ which is what David means—made it known that the law spoke spiritually about him. By the fact that the law was held according to the letter, he showed it to be estranged from the Jewish people and joined it to himself, since he declared that he was preached through it.
>
> “David nevertheless urges Uriah to go home and wash his feet, because the incarnate Lord, coming among the Jewish people, commanded them to return to their conscience and wipe away the filth of their deeds with tears, so that they might understand the commandments of the law spiritually; and, after so much hardness in the commandments, finding the font of baptism, return to the water after their labor.
>
> “But Uriah, remembering that the ark of the Lord was under tents, replied that he could not enter his house—as though the Jewish people were saying: ‘I see the commandments of God in carnal sacrifices, and I do not seek to return to conscience through spiritual understanding.’ For he says, as it were, that the ark is under tents because he understands the commandments of God only as providing the service of carnal sacrifice.
>
> “Although Uriah refuses to return home, David calls him to his table, because, although the Jewish people scorns returning to conscience, the coming Redeemer nevertheless preaches spiritual commandments to it, saying: [John 5:46] ‘If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me.’ The Jewish people therefore holds the law, which speaks of his divinity, yet refuses to believe in him.
>
> “Hence Uriah is sent to Joab with the letter by which he is to be killed, because that same Jewish people carries the law by which it is convicted and condemned to death. For while retaining the commandments of the law [Note: [Col. 0704D] The printed edition has ‘while holding fast’] and resisting their fulfillment, it itself bears the judgment by which it is condemned.
>
> “What, then, could be more wicked than David in this deed? What could be purer than Uriah? Yet again, in the mystery, what is more sacred [Note: [Col. 0704D] The printed edition has ‘more holy.’] than David? What is found more unbelieving than Uriah? For the one, through the fault of his life, signifies the innocence of prophecy, while the other, through the innocence of his life, expresses guilt in prophecy. . . . .
>
> “The power of sacred speech narrates past events in such a way as to express what is to come; it approves a matter in the event itself without contradicting it in the mystery; it condemns the deeds as historical events while urging that they be performed mystically.”

> “[Note: [Col. 0704D] The following is found at no. 23, elsewhere chapter 12 or 15, of Book XXXIII of the *Moralia*.] For this reason the sins of such men in sacred Scripture, namely David and Peter, were indicated [Note: [Col. 0704D] Gregory’s Vulgate text has ‘were set forth’], so that the fall of the great might be a warning to the lesser; but the repentance and forgiveness of both are also presented there, so that the recovery of those who have been lost may be the hope of those who are perishing.
>
> “Therefore, when David falls from his standing, let no one grow proud; and when David rises after his fall, let no one despair. See how wonderfully Scripture uses the same word to crush the proud by which it raises up the humble. It reported one and the same event, but in different ways recalled the proud to fear and the humble to confidence.
>
> “O immeasurable medicine of a new kind! Set forth in one and the same arrangement, it both dries up what is swollen by pressing it down and pours strength into what is parched by lifting it up. It frightened us by the fall of the great, but strengthened us by their restoration. Thus, always thus, the mercy of divine providence both restrains us when we are proud and supports us lest we fall into despair.

[Note: [Col. 0705D] Claudius omits some of Gregory’s admonitions and transcribes what follows from Gregory [no. 25].]

> “But since the occasion required that, with David brought forward, we recall the memory of so great a crime, the reader’s mind may perhaps be troubled about why almighty God does not preserve from bodily vices those whom he has chosen forever and whom he raises even to the summit of spiritual gifts.
>
> “We therefore answer briefly, since we believe that the matter can quickly be settled. Some people, through the virtues they have received and the grace bestowed for good works, fall into the vice of pride, yet do not recognize how [Note: [Col. 0705D] The printed edition reads: ‘that they have fallen.’] they have fallen. Therefore the ancient enemy, who already rules within them, is also permitted to rage against them outwardly, so that those who are lifted up in thought may be cast down through the lust of the flesh.
>
> “We know that at times it is a lesser thing to fall into bodily corruption than to sin through silent thought and deliberate pride. But when pride is believed to be less shameful, it is avoided less carefully. People are more ashamed of lust because everyone recognizes it as disgraceful. Thus it often happens that some, falling into lust after pride, become ashamed of the hidden fault because of their public fall; and then they correct greater faults when, having been cast down by lesser ones, they are more deeply confounded. They see themselves guilty in lesser matters who had believed themselves free in more serious ones.
>
> “Therefore, by the gracious dispensation of the Lord, the evil spirit [Note: [Col. 0705D] The printed edition reads ‘Behemoth.’] is sometimes released and drags a person from one fault to another; yet, by striking harder, he loses the one whom he had captured, and by the very means through which he appears to have conquered, he is overcome.
>
> “It is pleasing to consider within the fortified shelter of grace how greatly God holds us by the favor of his mercy. Behold: one who exalts himself over virtue returns to humility through vice. The one who is lifted up by the virtues he has received is wounded not by a sword but, so to speak, by medicine.
>
> “For what is virtue except medicine? And what is vice except a wound? Since we make a wound out of medicine, he makes medicine out of a wound, so that we who are struck by virtue may be healed by vice. We turn the gifts of virtues toward the use of vices; he takes the enticements of vices and turns them into an instrument of virtue. He strikes the condition of our salvation in order to preserve it, so that we who flee humility while running [Note: [Col. 0705D] The printed edition reads ‘to it.’] may cling to salvation when we fall.
>
> “Yet in all this we must know that most people, the more things in which they fall, are bound more tightly. When the ancient enemy [Note: [Col. 0705D] ‘Behemoth.’] strikes them with one vice so that they collapse, he binds them with another as well, so that they may not rise.
>
> “Let a person therefore consider against what adversary [Note: [Col. 0705D] ‘Enemy.’] he is waging war; and if he realizes that he has already [the text also reads: ‘already in some respect’] sinned in some respect, let him at least fear being dragged from one fault to another. Thus he should diligently avoid wounds by which people are often killed, because it is exceedingly rare for our enemy to preserve the salvation of the elect even through wounds. [Note: [Col. 0705D] This is found at no. 28, elsewhere chapter 14 [or 13].]
>
> “For, as we have said, the Lord often subjects his elect to the tempter in order to instruct them. Thus, after the barriers of paradise and after the secrets of the third heaven, lest the Apostle Paul become proud because of the greatness of his revelations, [2 Cor. 12:7] an angel of Satan was given to him.
>
> “But, as we have already stated, through this very temptation it is arranged that those who could have perished in their pride may be saved through humility. Thus, by the hidden order of providence, from the very point where the devil’s iniquity is permitted to rage, the goodness of God is piously brought to completion; for our adversary obeys the commands of heavenly grace precisely where he exercises the anger of his most wicked will.”

## (Chapter 12, verse 1)

After these events, the Lord sent Nathan to David. When Nathan came, he presented a parable about a rich man and a poor man: one possessed sheep and cattle, while the other had only one ewe. The rich man took the poor man’s one ewe.

When David heard this, he was angry with that man and said: “As the Lord lives, the man who did this is a son of death.” Nathan said to David: “You are that man.” David said to Nathan: “I have sinned against the Lord.” Nathan then said to David: “The Lord has also taken away your sin; you shall not die.”

> “[Note: [Col. 0706D] Search for this in Rabanus.] If the Lord took away David’s sin, which was so detestable, why did he afterward endure all the things that were spoken by the Lord’s prophet concerning that same sin?
>
> [Note: [Col. 0706D] What follows was transcribed by Rabanus and Claudius from Book IX of Gregory’s *Moralia* [no. 54, chapter 34; formerly chapter 27].]
>
> “Without doubt, however, the Lord does not leave a crime without punishment; either the person himself punishes it in himself through repentance, or God strikes him by avenging it together with him. Sin is therefore never simply spared, because it is never released without retribution.
>
> “Thus David deserved to hear after his confession, ‘The Lord has taken away your sin,’ and yet, afterward afflicted by many torments and fleeing, he paid the penalty for the guilt he had committed.
>
> “So the water of salvation absolves us from the guilt of our first parent; nevertheless, even after we have been absolved, we still suffer the penalty of that same guilt while living in the flesh, because he cuts away our sins—whether through us or through himself—even when he releases them. For he strives to wipe away the stains of iniquity from his elect through temporal affliction, since he does not wish them to be punished in them forever.”

[Note: [Col. 0706D] The following seems to have been taken from Augustine, but I have been unable to locate the passage.]

[Note: [Col. 0706D] This passage is corrupt in the received Eucherius.]

> “When he says that there were two men in one city, Uriah and David are understood; and learn to distinguish the persons. He calls the poor man’s ewe a woman—that is, his wife, who had been violated, who ate from his table, drank from his cup, and slept in his lap.
>
> “Consider that the poor man possessed incentives to compassion, whereas the rich possessed many supports for pride. Among the poor, a wife is also a servant and attendant; she bears children and is herself both mother and nurse. Among the rich, it is not so. As soon as a rich woman has given birth to a son, she immediately hands him over to someone else; pride cuts away the signs of compassion. She is ashamed to become a nurse, though she has become a mother. How, then, did the ewe sleep in his lap? He enlarged the parable by his account of compassion.
>
> “A traveler therefore came to that king. Who, then, is the traveler? Desire, naturally. In order to show the other man’s chastity, he called the desire ‘foreign.’ For he had never violated another man’s marriage, nor looked upon it with wicked eyes; but, struck by that woman, he lost his chastity, because he had made himself somewhat less watchful through the security of peace.
>
> “The traveler came—an unjust and savage desire—to the rich man. He did not take from his flocks or herds to prepare a feast for the traveler; instead, he sent for and seized the poor man’s ewe, which slept in his lap and ate from his table.
>
> “When King David heard this, he was very angry against that man and said to Nathan: ‘As the Lord lives, the man who did this is a son of death. He shall repay the ewe fourfold, and he himself shall be punished by the sword.’
>
> “O justice overflowing the bounds of judgment! There was no fiber of love in him that would have prevented him from speaking justly. He indeed orders a fourfold repayment according to the law—for the law commands that a thief be bound to restore fourfold—but he also went beyond the law, ordering that the man himself be killed and held liable for fourfold restitution. [Note: [Col. 0707D] ‘Beyond the bounds’: that is, exceeding the limits of the law, which did not prescribe the thief’s death.]
>
> “He therefore pronounced the sentence, and the judgment exceeded the limits. When the prophet heard this, he cast off every shadow of the image, brought forth the sword into the midst, and confidently said: ‘You are the king who did this.’ O secure man, not cutting through the meaning of his grief with a sword, but striking briefly with an accusation!
>
> “When it was necessary, he concealed the narrative; but when the time came, he immediately struck and cut without inflicting a great wound, saying only: ‘You are the king.’ The king quickly returned to his conscience and, like a faithful and capable servant, simply confessed his guilt, saying: ‘I have sinned against the Lord.’ The prophet replied: ‘The Lord has taken away your sin.’
>
> “A swift confession, a swifter cure: he sinned by an act, repented by a word, God assented, and correction was accomplished. The wound was opened, and health returned. But the prophet was not content with this. After the correction, after the repentance, after the amendment, after the absolution of sins, he composed a psalm for this reason, so that his suffering might become medicine even for a later generation; so that his shipwreck might be a harbor for others; and so that those who fell into the same wounds by which he had been wounded might themselves use the medicine and be healed through amendment.”

## (Chapter 16)

David was fleeing from his son Absalom. Walking barefoot, he crossed the torrent of Kidron, and all the people were with him; they came as far as Bahurim. Behold, Shimei, son of Gera, from the family of Saul’s house, came out, threw stones, and cursed the king, saying: “Go away, go away, man of blood and man of Belial.”

[Note: [Col. 0707D] Here Claudius transcribes Paterius and therefore adds some things that are not found explicitly in Book XXX of the *Moralia*, which Paterius cites. Perhaps Paterius inserted some material of his own, although it is very closely joined to Gregory’s words so as to adapt the explanation to the Books of Kings; or perhaps the ancient manuscripts read by Paterius differed somewhat from ours. I prefer the former explanation to the latter.]

> “Whoever among the faithful is pierced by the illumination of divine grace and hastens on the wings of heavenly contemplation to be lifted by holy desire from the depths to the heights should place before the eyes of his mind these deeds of the blessed King David and of the other holy Fathers who preceded him, wherever they suffered something unjustly. By practicing imitation in these examples, let him advance; and let whatever presently pricks him through vice be restrained either by the memory of past evils, or by the consolation of former gifts, or also, as has been said, by imitation, so that he may be summoned to what is better by the example of the Fathers who preceded him.
>
> “We must demonstrate this by clearer examples, as we proposed. [Note: [Col. 0708D] The following is found at no. 37, elsewhere chapter 10, formerly chapter 17, of Book XXX of Saint Gregory’s *Moralia*.] To speak of one among many, so that the diligent reader may understand many things in one: whoever, oppressed by insulting words, is unable to preserve the virtue of patience should recall David’s action.
>
> “When Shimei pressed him with abuse and the armed nobles sought to avenge him, David said: [vers. 10] ‘What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him alone, so that he may curse; for the Lord commanded him to curse David. And who is there who would dare to ask, “Why has he done so?”’ A little later he says: ‘Let him alone, so that he may curse according to the Lord’s command, if perhaps the Lord may look upon my affliction and repay me good for this day’s cursing.’
>
> “By these words he clearly indicates that, after committing the crime against Bathsheba and fleeing from the son who had risen against him, he recalled to mind the evil he had committed. He considered the insulting words not so much insults as aids, by which he believed he could be cleansed and receive mercy.
>
> “We tolerate insults well when, in the secrecy of our minds, we return to the evils we have committed. What seems slight is the injury with which we are struck when we perceive in our conduct that what we deserve is worse. Thus it comes about that, by the intervention of insults, which we trust can avert a graver punishment under the judgment of God, gratitude rather than anger is owed to them.”

[Note: [Col. 0708D] Claudius copied this from Isidore [in Book II of *The Books of Kings*, chapter 3].]

“Now what does this signify: that the parricidal son Absalom was pursuing his father, while his father at first, confident of victory, avoided him and fled before his face, even though he saw his kingdom perishing? He also mourned him with great lamentation and grieved over the death of the parricide. For it is written that David fled from the face of his son who was waging war against him (the edition reads: ‘against himself’). And since it is written concerning the people of Jerusalem: ‘I nourished sons and exalted them, but they themselves despised me’ (Isaiah 1:2), therefore his impious son is understood tropologically, that is, as the Jewish people who betrayed him. Absalom, however, as some interpret the name, is understood as ‘the father’s peace.’ This seems strange in the historical account: how can he be understood as the father’s peace, when he persecuted his father in war?

“But those who attend carefully to the allegory observe that Absalom is Jerusalem, whose name also means ‘peace’; from its face Christ fled when, abandoning it through his suffering, he succeeded among the Gentiles through faith.

[Note: [Col. 0709C] See what Augustine says, no. 1 of his *Exposition on Psalm III*.]

“Others understand Absalom as Judas the betrayer, whom Christ endured with such great and indeed wondrous patience as though he were good, although he was not ignorant of his thoughts. He admitted him to the meal at which he commended and handed over to the disciples the figure of his body and blood,

[Note: [Col. 0709C] This passage alarmed many of our writers, so much so that some suspected it to be corrupt and thought it should be read in another way. But the reading we have proposed must in fact be retained, for, if properly understood, this passage causes us no fear. Bellarmine carefully examines the passage, which we said was taken from Augustine [*On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, Book II, chapter 24, §55, from volume seven]. There he raises against himself these words of Augustine, taken from the *Commentary on Psalm III*: ‘Christ admitted Judas to the meal at which he commended the figure of his body to the disciples.’ He observes that ‘Augustine is speaking of the figure of the body suspended on the cross, that is, of the representation of the Lord’s passion. For Augustine called the Eucharist a figure of the body in the same way that the ancient Greeks called it *antitypa* [ἀντίτυπα]; we have discussed this term in the testimonies of Basil.’ Thus far Bellarmine. Earlier, in chapter 15 of Book II, after he had raised against himself the fact that Basil—since in Bellarmine’s time the liturgy bearing Basil’s name was attributed to Basil—called the Eucharist *antitypa* [ἀντίτυπα], he replies that the body and blood of the Lord, as they are under the appearances of bread and wine, are signs of that same body and blood as they were on the cross: for the Eucharist represents Christ’s passion. Hence Chrysostom, in Homily 17 on the Epistle to the Hebrews, says that the Eucharist is a type, or figure, of the sacrifice of the cross, and nevertheless asserts there that the same Christ is now offered who was offered then. Bellarmine pursues this argument at length in this passage and also discusses it near the beginning of chapter 24. To spare the reader, we select only this: ‘Lanfranc illustrates the whole matter by a striking comparison [Luke, final chapter]. The Lord pretended that he was going farther; Augustine explains this in Book *Against Lying*, chapter 13, where he says that by this pretense Christ signified that he would ascend above all the heavens.’

[Note: [Col. 0710D] Ambrose offers another related and no less clear example in Book II of his commentary on Luke, chapter 2, no. 63, in these words: ‘After three days, once raised from that triumphant passion, he will present himself to our faith in the heavenly seat and divine honor, he who was believed to have died.’]

“The same Christ, therefore, was a figure of himself, and it could most correctly be said that Christ pretended to go farther, and in a certain sense that Christ was ascending into heaven.’ I wished to note this, lest the reader tremble with fear where there is no fear, or criticize Claudius concerning a matter for which he certainly should not be criticized.”

“Finally, in the very act of betrayal he also received a kiss. This is rightly understood to mean that Christ offered peace to his betrayer, although Judas was being ravaged within by the warfare of such a wicked thought. Therefore Absalom is called ‘the father’s peace,’ because the father possessed the peace that Judas did not possess.”

[Note: [Col. 0710C] Claudius also took this from Isidore, but from the immediately preceding chapter, that is, chapter 2. From this fact one may suspect that perhaps a different order of chapters was preserved in ancient manuscripts of Isidore.]

“But perhaps someone may say: If David bore the image of Christ, how is it written that he had many wives and concubines, since Christ both abhors and condemns such things? This was happening prophetically. David’s many wives signified the image of the many peoples and nations that would be joined through faith to the fellowship of Christ. His concubines, however, signify the churches of heretics, which boast that they remain under the title of Christ’s name. But because they pursue Christ for carnal profit, they are called not wives but concubines.

“Accordingly, today, if kings have several wives or concubines, it is a crime, because the figures for which permission was granted to have wives or concubines have now passed away. But now, because the figures have passed away, no permission is granted.”

(Chapter 20, verse 4, and following.) After Absalom had been struck down and David had returned to Jerusalem, he told Amasa to assemble all the men of Judah by the third day and appointed him commander in place of Joab. When Amasa delayed beyond the appointed time, David ordered Joab and Abishai to go and seize Sheba son of Bichri. When Joab found Amasa at Gibeon, Joab took Amasa by the chin with his right hand, as though to kiss him, and struck him in the side, and he died.

[Note: [Col. 0710D] The continuation is also found in Paterius, who took it from Book XV of Gregory the Great’s *Moralia* [no. 23].]

“What does it mean that Joab held Amasa’s chin with his right hand, while secretly moving his left hand to the sword and spilling out his entrails? Nothing other than what is plainly understood. To hold the chin with the right hand is, as though out of kindness, to flatter; but he moves his left hand to the sword who secretly strikes out of malice.

“[Note: [Col. 0710D] Chapter 22, no. 2, and following; also Psalm XVII. Claudius took the passages marked with lines from Isidore. Seek them, therefore, in chapter 6 of Book II of *The Books of Kings*. Rabanus Maurus also has them; from this you can see how highly Isidore’s commentaries were valued.] The seventeenth Psalm follows, and it is rightly asked why this one Psalm alone is found written in the Books of Kings. Nor is it without reason that this Psalm alone is found in the Books of Kings, because it signifies that kingdom where we have no adversary. Its title is: ‘On the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.’

“Who is represented in David except the one who came according to the flesh from David’s seed, who in his body, which is the Church, still suffers enemies? Hence he spoke from heaven to the persecutor whom he slew with his voice and, transferring him into his own body, in a certain sense consumed: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ (Acts 9:4) When does he deserve to deliver this body from the hand of its enemies, except when that last enemy, death, is also destroyed, so that one may come to the kingdom of God?”

[Note: [Col. 0710D] This entire interpretation is taken from Augustine, whose *Exposition on this Psalm* [that is, Psalm 17] Claudius copied.]

**“I will love you, my strength.”**  
“I will love you, Lord, through whom I am strong.”

**“Lord, my firm foundation, my refuge, and my deliverer.”**  
“Lord, who strengthened me, because I fled to you; and I fled because you delivered me.”

[Col. 0710C]

**“My God, my helper, and I will hope in him.”**  
“My God, who first granted me help through your calling, so that I might be able to hope in you.”

[Col. 0711A]

**“My protector, the horn of my salvation, and my redeemer.”**  
“My protector, because I did not presume upon myself, as though I were raising against you the horn of pride; rather, I found you yourself to be the horn, that is, the firm height of salvation. To find this, you redeemed me.”

**“Praising, I called upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies.”**  
“Seeking not my own glory but the Lord’s, I will call upon the Lord, and there will be no source from which errors of impiety can harm me.”

**“The pains of death surrounded me.”**  
“That is, the pains of the flesh surrounded me. ‘And torrents of iniquity troubled me’: wicked crowds, stirred up for a time like rain-swollen rivers that will soon subside, acted so as to trouble me.”

**“The pains of hell surrounded me.”**  
“Among those who surrounded me in order to destroy me were the pains of envy, which bring about death and lead to the hell of sin. ‘The snares of death overtook me’: they overtook me, wishing to harm me first, so that what they later deserved might be returned to them. Such people are caught for destruction—people who persuaded others to do evil by boasting of righteousness, whose righteousness they glorify against the Gentiles in name, not in reality.”

**“And in my distress I called upon the Lord, and I cried to my God; and he heard my voice from his holy temple.”**  
“And he heard my voice from my heart, in which he dwells. ‘And my cry is in his presence’: my cry, which I have within me before him, not in the ears of human beings, entered his ears.”

**“And the earth was shaken and trembled.”**  
“Once the Son of Man was glorified, sinners were shaken and trembled. ‘And the foundations of the mountains were troubled’: the hopes of the proud, which had existed in this age, were troubled. And they were shaken because God was angry with them, so that the hope of temporal goods would no longer have a firm foundation in human hearts.”

**“Smoke rose in his anger.”**  
“The tearful prayer of penitents rose when they had understood what God threatens against the impious. ‘And fire burns from his face’: the ardor of charity, after repentance, burns forth from knowledge of him. ‘Coals were kindled by him’: those who had already died—abandoned by the fire of good desire and the light of righteousness, and who had remained cold and dark—were kindled and illuminated again and came to life.”

[Col. 0711D]

**“He bowed the heavens and came down.”**  
“And he humbled the righteous one, so that he might descend to human weakness. ‘And darkness was under his feet.’

[Note: [Col. 0711D] Let the reader know that what I have enclosed here in parentheses, and likewise what I shall enclose in parentheses from this point onward, is not found in Augustine’s *Exposition*, but has been inserted from Gregory, cited by Paterius at this passage. The reader may consult him if he wishes.]

“‘His darkness was under his feet,’ because he is not seen by those below with the same brightness with which he rules above. For the impious, who savor earthly things, did not know him because of the darkness of their malice. ‘The earth was under his feet,’ like the footstool of his feet.”

[Col. 0712A]

**“He mounted upon the cherubim and flew.”**  
“(For he is said to have mounted and flown upon the cherubim—that is, upon the fullness of knowledge—because no knowledge comprehends the height of his majesty. He therefore flew because he snatched himself far away from our understanding into the heights.)

[Note: [Col. 0711D] The words beginning “so that no one” are found again in Augustine.]

“So that no one might come to God except through love; ‘for love is the fullness of the law’ (Romans 13:10). For he quickly showed himself to be incomprehensible to those who love him, lest they suppose that they could comprehend him by bodily imaginings.

“[Note: [Col. 0711D] Seek these words again in Gregory.] ‘The Lord mounted upon the cherubim and flew,’ because he deigned to exalt the glory of his Incarnation above the fullness of knowledge that could exist in human beings. His flying, then, is his withdrawing the mystery of his power from human understanding. For however fully the life of spiritual people may shine with knowledge, it cannot comprehend how it came about that the one who existed was conceived, that the author of humanity before the ages was born as a human being at the end of the ages, that God became flesh, and that the Word became an infant.

“Hence it is rightly added there also: ‘He flew upon the wings of the winds,’ because he transcends all the understanding of souls. We may appropriately understand the soul to be represented by wind, on account of the swiftness of its thought.) That speed by which he showed himself to be incomprehensible is above the virtues of souls, by which they raise themselves, as if on wings, from eternal fears into the breezes of freedom.”

**“He made darkness his hiding place.”**  
“And he made the obscurity of the mysteries and the hidden hope in the hearts of believers his hiding place, where he might remain concealed without abandoning them.

[Col. 0712C]

[Note: [Col. 0712D] The material that follows, until the words ‘among these also,’ is found neither in Augustine nor in Gregory.]

“‘Because, while we are darkened by the cloud of our weakness through our ignorance, he is hidden from us, lest he now be seen by us in eternal and steadfast charity.’

[Note: [Col. 0712D] Augustine teaches us this again.]

“Among these darknesses also, where we still walk by faith and not by sight, as long as we hope for what we do not see and await it with patience.

[Note: [Col. 0712D] Claudius carefully copied this, as was his custom, from Paterius and therefore from Gregory.]

“Because our author, having cast us down into this exile, has withdrawn from us the light of his vision, he has hidden himself from our eyes, as it were in a hiding place of darkness. When we diligently contemplate these darknesses of our blindness, we are recalled to lamentation. Weep for the blindness suffered outwardly if you humbly remember that you have been deprived of the inner light. When the darkness surrounding you is considered, the mind torments itself with burning desire for the inner splendor; with every effort of attention it shakes itself, and, having abandoned the upper light from which it was created, seeks it again after rejection. Hence it often happens that, amid these very devout tears, the brightness of inner joy breaks forth, and the mind that had previously lain blind in time is strengthened by being nourished above for the contemplation of the inner radiance.)

“‘His tabernacle is around him.’ Yet those who believe in him, having been converted to him, surround him, because he is in their midst, favoring all equally—those in whom, as in a tabernacle, he dwells at this time.

“‘Dark water in the clouds of the air.’ Nor should anyone therefore suppose that he is already in that light which is to come, when we pass from faith to sight, if he understands the Scriptures correctly. For in the prophets and in all preachers of the divine word the teaching is obscure.

[Note: [Col. 0713D] Paterius, and therefore Gregory, supplies what follows.]

“‘Because before the Lord’s coming, while they bore within themselves immense mysteries, pregnant with hidden sacraments, the meaning of those mysteries was darkened to the eyes of those who contemplated them.’”

**“Before the brightness of his presence”:**  
“In comparison with the brightness that is in the presence of his manifestation.

“‘His clouds passed by.’ The preachers of his word are no longer confined within the boundaries of Judea, but have passed over to the Gentiles.

“(They traverse all the regions of the world with the splendor of miracles.)

“‘Hail and coals of fire.’ These are figurative rebukes by which hard hearts are beaten as though by hail. But if cultivated and gentle earth, that is, a devout soul, receives them, the hardness of hail is dissolved into water: the terror of rebuke, struck by lightning and as if frozen, is dissolved into nourishing instruction. Hearts kindled by the fire of charity come back to life. All these things passed in his clouds to the Gentiles.

“(For holy men both strike the hearts of their hearers with fear and pour themselves into them with gentleness. The prophet testifies to how they strike when he says: ‘They shall speak of the power of your terrible acts, and they shall tell of your greatness’ (Psalm 144:6); and, following, he adds how they flourish in gentleness: ‘They shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness’ (ibid., verse 7). ‘And they shall exult in your righteousness.’)”

**“The Lord thundered from heaven.”**  
“And the Lord sounded forth from the heart of the righteous with evangelical confidence. ‘And the Most High gave his voice,’ so that we might possess it and hear heavenly things in the depths of human affairs.”

**“He sent out his arrows and scattered them.”**  
“And he sent out the Evangelists, flying along straight paths on the wings of virtues—not by their own strength, but by the strength of him by whom they were sent. ‘And he scattered them,’ among those to whom they were sent, so that to some they might be the fragrance of life leading to life, and to others the fragrance of death leading to death. ‘And he multiplied his lightnings and troubled them’: he multiplied his miracles and troubled them.”

**“And the springs of waters appeared.”**  
“And those who had become in the preachers springs of ‘water welling up to eternal life’ (John 4:14) appeared. ‘And the foundations of the earth were revealed’: the prophets, who had not been understood, were revealed, upon whom the believing world was to be built. ‘At your rebuke, Lord,’ who cries: ‘The kingdom of God has drawn near to you’ (Luke 10:9); ‘at the rebuke of the spirit of your anger,’ which says: ‘Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish’ (Luke 13:5).”

**“He sent from on high and received me.”**  
“Calling me from the Gentiles into a glorious inheritance, the Church without spot or wrinkle, he took me up from the multitude of waters. He took me up from the multitude of peoples.”

**“He rescued me from my strongest enemies.”**  
“He rescued me from my enemies, who prevailed in afflicting and corrupting this temporal life of mine. ‘And from those who hated me, because they were strengthened against me,’ as long as I remained under them, ignorant of God.”

**“They overtook me on the day of my affliction.”**  
“They harmed me first during the time when I bear a mortal and laborious body. ‘And the Lord became my firm foundation.’ Because the foundation of earthly will had been bruised and shaken by the bitterness of miseries, the Lord became my firm foundation.”

[Note: [Col. 0713D] The edition reads: “of earthly pleasure.”]

**“And he led me out into a broad place.”**  
“Because I was suffering carnal narrowness, he led me out into the spiritual breadth of faith. ‘He rescued me because he desired me.’ Before I desired him, he rescued me from my most powerful enemies, who envy me now that I desire him, and from those who hate me because I desire him.”

**“And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness.”**  
“The Lord will repay me according to the righteousness of good will—he who first granted mercy before I possessed good will. ‘And according to the purity of my hands he will repay me’: according to the purity of my deeds he will repay me, he who granted me the ability to do good by leading me out into the breadth of faith.”

**“For I have kept the ways of the Lord.”**  
“So that I may attain the breadth of good works, which are through faith, and perseverance through endurance.”

[Note: [Col. 0713D] The edition reads: “into the breadth.”]

**“Nor have I acted impiously against my God, because all his judgments are always before my eyes.”**  
“Because I continually contemplate all his judgments—that is, the mercy of the righteous, the punishments of the impious, the chastisements of those being corrected, and the trials of those being tested. ‘And I have not thrust his righteousness away from me,’ as those do who collapse under its burden and return to their vomit.”

[Note: [Col. 0714D] The edition reads: “and the rewards of the righteous.”]

**“And I shall be blameless before him, and I shall keep myself from my iniquity. And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness.”**  
“Therefore the Lord will repay me not only on account of the breadth of faith, which works through love, but also on account of the length of perseverance, according to my righteousness.”

[Col. 0714D]

**“And according to the purity of my hands he will repay me in the sight of his eyes.”**  
“Because the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal; this pertains to the height of hope.”

**“With the holy you will be holy.”**  
“There is also a hidden depth in which you are understood to be holy with the holy, because you sanctify. ‘And with the innocent man you will be innocent’: because you harm no one, but each person is bound by the cords of his own sins.”

**“And with the chosen you will be chosen.”**  
“And you will be chosen by the one whom you choose. ‘And with the perverse you will be overturned.’ And with the perverse you will appear perverse,

[Note: [Col. 0715D] The words ‘because, since you do not favor them, you appear perverse’ are absent from the printed editions.]

“because you do not favor them, since they say: ‘The way of the Lord is not straight,’ while their own way is not straight.”

[Note: [Col. 0715D] The edition reads: “you will be perverse.”]

**“For you will save the humble people.”**  
“What appears perverse to the perverse is that you will save those who confess their sins. ‘And you will humble the eyes of the proud’: those who, ignorant of God’s righteousness, wish to establish their own righteousness—you will humble.”

**“For you will illumine my lamp, O Lord.”**  
“Because our light does not come from ourselves, but you will illumine my lamp, O Lord. ‘My God, illumine my darkness.’ For we are darkness because of our sins, but my God will illumine my darkness.”

[Note: [Col. 0715D] The edition reads: “you illumine.” In what follows, however, it repeats “you will illumine.”]

**“For by you I shall be delivered from temptation.”**  
“For I shall be delivered from temptation not by myself but by you. ‘And in my God I shall leap over a wall’: not in myself but in my God I shall leap over the wall that sins have raised between human beings and the heavenly Jerusalem.”

[Note: [Col. 0715D] The edition reads: “I shall be delivered.”]

**“My God, his way is immaculate.”**  
“My God does not come into human beings unless they have cleansed the way of faith by which he may come to them, because his way is immaculate. ‘The words of the Lord have been tested by fire’: the words of the Lord are proved by the fire of testing. ‘He is the protector of all who hope in him.’ All who hope not in themselves but in him will not be consumed by that same tribulation, for hope follows faith.”

[Note: [Col. 0715D] The edition reads: “of tribulation.”]

**“For who is God besides the Lord?”**  
“To whom we are servants. And who is God besides the Lord, whom, after good service, we shall possess as sons, as a hoped-for inheritance?”

[Note: [Col. 0715D] The edition reads: “whom we serve.”]

**“God who girded me with strength.”**  
“God who girded me so that I might be strong, lest the flowing folds of desire impede my works and my steps. ‘And he made my way immaculate’: he made the way of charity immaculate, by which I shall come to him, just as the faith by which he comes to me is immaculate.”

**“Who made my feet like those of a stag.”**  
“He perfected my love so that it might pass beyond the thorny and shadowy entanglements of this age.

[Note: [Col. 0715D] The words ‘he calls stags spiritual men because of their eagerness in swift running’—that is, ‘in swift running,’ or, if you prefer, ‘of swift running’—belong to Claudius. The rest is from Gregory the Great, cited by Paterius from Book XVI of the *Moralia* [no. 24, formerly chapter 16, previously 10].]

“‘He calls stags spiritual men because of their eagerness in swift running. For the minds of the strong, fixed immovably in God, look down upon all adversities the more as they see what grows up against the commandments of the Creator. Awaiting the rewards of eternity, they draw strength from adversities, because they do not doubt that a more glorious victory remains for them as the struggle increases. Thus the desires of the elect, while pressed by adversity, make progress, just as fire is pressed by the blast so that it may grow; and from the point where it seems almost to be extinguished, it is strengthened.

“In this way we show how greatly we burn with desire for God if we pass to him not only through calm and gentle things but also through harsh and difficult ones. Thus the Psalmist rightly says: ‘He made my feet like those of a stag.’ For when a stag climbs the ridges of mountains, it leaps over whatever rough things confront it, whatever things entangled in thorns oppose it, and without any obstacle to its course it is raised into the heights.

[Note: [Col. 0716D] So Paterius has it, but in the printed book of Saint Gregory the words belong to the preceding section.]

“Likewise the minds of the elect leap by contemplation over whatever they see obstructing and opposing them in this world; and, like stags despising the thorns of earthly things, they raise themselves to the things above.”

**“And he will set me upon the heights.”**  
“And he will fix my intention upon the heavenly dwelling, so that I may be filled with ‘all the fullness of God’ (Ephesians 3:19).”

**“Who teaches my hands for battle.”**  
“He teaches me to act so as to overcome the enemies who try to block the heavenly kingdoms from us. ‘And you made my arms like a bronze bow’: you established the tireless intention of my good works.”

**“And you gave me the protection of my salvation, and your right hand received me.”**  
“That is, the favor of your grace received me. ‘And your discipline guided me to the end.’ Your correction, not allowing me to go astray, guided me so that whatever I do I may refer it to the end for which I am to be crowned. ‘And your discipline itself will teach me’: that same correction will teach me to reach the goal toward which it guided me.”

[Note: [Col. 0716D] The edition reads: “correction.”]

[Note: [Col. 0716D] The edition reads: “which is joined to you.”]

**“You enlarged my steps beneath me.”**  
“Carnal narrowness will not impede me, because you have made my charity broad, so that it acts joyfully even through those mortal things and limbs that are beneath me. ‘And my footsteps were not weakened’: neither my ways nor the signs impressed for imitation by those who follow me have been weakened.”

**“I will pursue my enemies and overtake them.”**  
“I will pursue my carnal affections, lest I be overtaken by them; rather, I will overtake them so that they may be consumed. ‘And I will not turn back until they fail’: I will not turn from this intention to rest until those who obstruct me have failed.”

**“And I will crush them, and they will not be able to stand.”**  
“I will crush them, and they will not endure against me. ‘They will fall beneath my feet.’ Once they have been cast down, I will place before me the loves by which I walk into eternity.”

**“And you girded me with strength for battle.”**  
“You restrained the flowing desires of my flesh by your strength, so that I would not be hindered in such a battle. ‘You brought down beneath me those who rose up against me’: you deceived those who were pursuing me, so that those who wished to be above me would become beneath me.”

**“And you gave me the backs of my enemies.”**  
“You turned my enemies and made them a back for me, that is, so that they would follow me. ‘And you destroyed those who hated me’: you destroyed others of them who persisted in hatred.”

**“They cried out, and there was no one to save them.”**  
“For who could save those whom you would not save? ‘They cried to the Lord, and he did not hear them.’ They cried not to just anyone but to the Lord, yet he judged those who did not depart from their wickedness unworthy of being heard.”

**“And I will grind them like dust before the face of the wind.”**  
“I will grind them, for they are dry, not receiving the rain of God’s mercy, so that, lifted up and inflated by pride, they may be swept away from the firm and unshaken hope that is like the solidity and stability of earth. ‘Like the mud of the streets I will wipe them out’: along the broad ways of destruction on which many walk, I will wipe out those who luxuriate and slip.”

[Note: [Col. 0717D] The edition reads: “before.”]

[Col. 0717B]

**“You will rescue me from the disputes of the people.”**  
“You will rescue me from the disputes of those who said: ‘If we let him live, the whole world will follow him’ (John 11:48).”

[Note: [Col. 0717D] The words “alive” are absent from the printed editions.]

**“He will appoint me as head of the nations. A people whom I did not know will serve me.”**  
“The people of the Gentiles, whom I did not visit in bodily presence, served me. ‘At the hearing of the ear it obeyed me’: it obeyed me without seeing me with its eyes, receiving my preachers and obeying me at the hearing of the ear.”

[Note: [Col. 0717D] The edition reads: “served.” In the explanation it is indeed “served.”]

**“The sons of strangers lied to me.”**  
“The sons who should not be called mine, but rather strangers, to whom it is rightly said, ‘You are of your father the devil,’ lied to me. ‘The sons of strangers grew old’: the sons of strangers, to whom I brought the new covenant so that they might be renewed, remained in the old man.

[Note: [Col. 0717D] The edition reads: “in the old man.”]

“‘And they limped from their paths.’ Like men weak in one foot, because they held to the old and rejected the new covenant, they became lame, following even in the old law their own traditions rather than God’s. (Matthew 15:2) For they accused him concerning unwashed hands, because such were the paths they themselves had made and worn down through custom, wandering from the way of God’s commandments.”

[Note: [Col. 0717D] The edition reads: “from the ways.”]

**“The Lord lives, and blessed is my God.”**  
“To set one’s mind on things according to the flesh is death (Romans 8:6). ‘The Lord lives, and blessed is my God.’ ‘And let the God of my salvation be exalted’: let me not think of the God of my salvation according to earthly custom, nor hope for an earthly salvation itself from him, but hope for him in the heights.”

**“God who gives me vengeance and subjects peoples beneath me.”**  
“God who vindicates me by subjecting peoples beneath me. ‘My deliverer from my enemies,’ the Jews who cry, ‘Crucify, crucify!’”

**“You will exalt me above those who rise up against me.”**  
“Above those Jews who rose against me while I was suffering, you will exalt me when I rise again. ‘You will rescue me from the unjust man’: you will rescue me from their unjust kingdom.”

[Note: [Col. 0717D] The edition reads: “you will rescue.”]

**“Therefore I will confess to you among the nations, O Lord.”**  
“Therefore the nations will confess to you through me, O Lord. ‘And I will sing psalms to your name’: you will become more widely known through my good works.”

**“Magnifying the salvations of his king.”**  
“God who makes the salvations given by his Son to believers admirable. ‘And showing mercy to his Christ’: God who shows mercy to his Christ, David and his seed forever—to the deliverer with the mighty hand who conquered this world, and to those whom he begot in the Gospel for ever.”

[Note: [Col. 0717D] The edition reads: “to those whom he begot as believers in the Gospel.”]

“Whatever has been said in this Psalm that cannot properly apply to the Lord himself, that is, to the head of the Church, must be referred to the Church. For the whole Christ speaks here, in whom all his members are present.”

(2 Samuel, chapter 23, verse 1.) “These are the last words that David son of Jesse spoke.” He calls David’s last words not words that are to be ended but words that are to be fulfilled—not words to be exhausted, but words that confer upon all the faithful the fullness of perfection.

(Verse 2.) “The Spirit of the Lord spoke through me” [the Vulgate reads: “by me”], “and his word was through my tongue.” By “the Spirit of the Lord” he means the Holy Spirit; by “the word of God” Christ, the Son of God, is understood. For Christ himself is the Christ of God, the Christ of Jacob.

(Verse 6.) “But transgressors will all be plucked out like thorns.” The transgressors, Jews and heretics, are like thorns torn from the Church, which is the land of the living; they will perish, consumed by eternal fire.

[Col. 0718C]

(Verse 8.) “These are the names of David’s mighty men: the one seated in the chair, the wisest prince among the three, is himself like the tenderest worm of wood, who killed eight hundred at one assault.”

[Note: [Col. 0718D] Compare this with what Bede relates [in Question 9], and you will plainly see that Claudius took it from this distinguished teacher.]

“It was not Gesbæa [Jeshbaam, 1 Chronicles 9:11], as some think, but David himself who was called ‘like the tenderest worm of wood.’

“Through him both martial valor and the man’s civil modesty are signified. For just as a woodworm appears tender and fragile throughout its body, and also very small, yet nevertheless eats through the strongest substance of wood, consuming it and making it worm-eaten, so called from wearing away wood and named *teredenis*, so he appeared affable to all at home, peaceful and humble, but in public combat he displayed himself as strong and intolerable to his enemies.”

It is not absurd for these three very mighty men—David, Eleazar, and Shammah—to be understood as the Trinity: God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The other mighty men did not attain to their equality.

(Verses 14 and following.) “Likewise, when David was engaged in battle with the Philistines, he became thirsty in the fighting and sought water. ‘Who will give me a drink,’ he said, ‘from the well that is in Bethlehem?’ The road to the cistern was at the gates. David was surrounded by enemies [Note: [Col. 0718D] I think *interclusus* (“shut in” or “surrounded”) should be read.], and the hostile camp had enclosed him in its midst.

[Note: [Col. 0719D] “They came before.” But the reading of our manuscript is preferable.]

“Three men cut through the multitude of their adversaries, drew water from the well that was in Bethlehem, and offered it to the king to drink. But the king refused to drink it and [Note: [Col. 0719D] I think *perfudit* (“he poured it over”) should be read.] poured it out to the Lord. He said: ‘Far be it from me to do this, that I should drink the blood of the men who went there, or drink the peril of their lives.’

[Note: [Col. 0719D] The Vulgate reads: “and the peril of their souls.” There appears to be some error here.]

“He therefore overcame nature, refusing to drink while thirsty, and gave the whole army an example by which it might learn to endure thirst. But if you wish to look more deeply and inspect the mystery, David was thirsty—not for the water that is in Bethlehem, but in the spirit he foresaw Christ, born in that same Bethlehem from the Virgin. Therefore he wished to drink not the water of a stream but the cleansing flow issuing from Christ’s side.

[Note: [Col. 0719D] Flowing.]

“That is, he was not thirsty for the element of water but for the blood of Christ. Hence he did not drink the water that was offered but poured it out to the Lord, signifying that he thirsted for Christ’s sacrifice—not a stream flowing from nature, but that sacrifice in which there would be remission of sins; he thirsted for that eternal spring, not one sought amid the dangers of others, but one that would erase the dangers of others.”

« In this event [Note: [Col. 0719D] Claudius took what follows from Paterius, and therefore from Gregory. See, I beg you, Gregory’s Homily 34 on the Gospels [no. 16].] one must consider very carefully, so far as human conduct is concerned, that whoever remembers having committed unlawful acts should strive to abstain even from certain lawful ones, so that by this he may make satisfaction to his Creator: whoever has committed what was forbidden ought to cut himself off even from what was permitted, and should rebuke himself in small matters who remembers that he strayed in great ones [Note: [Col. 0719D] The edition reads “to have sinned.”] (Exod. 20:17). Certainly, the Law of the Old Testament forbids coveting another man’s wife, but it does not prohibit the king, under penalty, from issuing brave commands to soldiers or from desiring water. And we all know that David, pierced by the sword of desire, both coveted and took another man’s wife, and that worthy wounds followed his fault; he corrected the evil he had committed by the lamentations of repentance. Later, when he was sitting opposite the enemy ranks, he wished out of longing to drink water from the cistern of Bethlehem; his chosen soldiers burst through the midst of the opposing troops and brought back unharmed the water the king had desired. But the man trained by scourges immediately rebuked himself for having desired the water at the risk of his soldiers and, pouring it out to the Lord, offered it as a libation, as it is written: “He offered it as a libation to the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0720D] The edition reads “sacrifice.”] For the water poured out was changed into the Lord’s sacrifice, because through the penitential rebuke of himself he slaughtered the fault of desire. Thus he who once had not feared coveting another man’s wife later shrank even from having coveted water. For because he remembered that he had committed unlawful acts, he was now strict against himself and abstained even from lawful ones. »

[Col. 0720A]

(Verses 16 and following.) Three mighty men, Abishai, Joab’s brother, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada, broke through the Philistine camp to draw this water. (Verse 20.) This Benaiah struck down two lions of Moab; he also went down and struck a lion in the middle of a cistern on a snowy day. [Note: [Col. 0720D] Bede taught this in Question 10.] « Josephus gives a clearer account of how this happened: namely, that the cistern was exceedingly deep and, when everything was full of snow in winter, it too had been leveled by a great accumulation of snow. When a lion, unaware of the danger, came upon it and fell in, it was trapped there and cried out with a great roar. People ran to see what it was; and when Benaiah also came with the others to witness the spectacle, he immediately leapt into the cistern and, attacking the lion in the midst of the snow, killed it. »

[Col. 0720B]

(Verses 23, 24, and following.) Thereafter [Note: [Col. 0720D] Claudius takes some material from Isidore, but so reverses and alters it that it has an entirely different meaning. See chapter 7 in Book II of Isidore’s Kings.] the catalog of the mighty men is woven as a figure of the saints, who, strengthened by the fortitude of virtuous works and by knowledge of the divine Trinity, not only defend themselves from wicked enemies but also protect any who are weak.

[Note: [Col. 0720D] II Kings, chapter 24.] After this David sinned by numbering the people. For David commanded Joab to pass through all Israel (verse 2) and bring him the number of the people. Scripture says this happened because (verse 1) the anger of the Lord began to burn against Israel. [Note: [Col. 0720D] What follows is found in Paterius [chapter 25] and therefore in Gregory, from whose Commentary on Job [Book XXV, no. 35] Paterius took it.] « What else is demonstrated in this event than that the actions of rulers are arranged according to the qualities of their subjects, so that often, because of the evil of the flock, even the life of a truly good shepherd may fall into sin? That David, whom God himself commended, that prophet David, who knew the mysteries of heavenly things, was puffed up by sudden elation and sinned by numbering the people; yet, while David sinned, the people received punishment. Why was this? Clearly, because the hearts of rulers are disposed according to the merit of their peoples. The just Judge punished the fault of the sinner in accordance with the conduct of those on whose account he sinned; but because he himself, sinning in his own will through pride, was not free from guilt, he too suffered the punishment of the fault. For the raging anger that afflicted the people bodily also struck down the ruler of the people with inward grief of heart.

It is certain, however, that the merits both of rulers and of peoples are so mutually connected that often, through the fault of shepherds, the life of the people becomes worse, and often, through the merit of the people, the life of shepherds is changed. But since rulers have their own Judge, it is a matter of great caution for subjects not rashly to judge the lives of their rulers. For the Lord did not, without reason, himself cast out the money changers’ coins and overturn the seats of those selling doves (Matt. 21:12): clearly signifying that through teachers he judges the life of the people, but by himself examines the deeds of teachers. The vices of subjects, however, which are either overlooked by teachers or cannot be judged by them at the present time, are undoubtedly reserved for his judgment.

Therefore, while the matter is conducted in sound faith, it is a virtue deserving merit if whatever belongs to one’s superior is tolerated. Yet one should humbly suggest, if perhaps it may be corrected, whatever is displeasing. But one must take the greatest care that the disordered defense of justice does not turn into pride; lest, while uprightness is directed without caution, humility—the very teacher of uprightness—be lost; and lest anyone despise having as his superior one whom he happens to find fault with in some action.

Against this swelling of pride, the mind of subjects is subdued for the preservation of humility if one constantly attends to one’s own weakness. For we neglect to examine our own strength truthfully; and because we believe ourselves capable of great things, we therefore judge those who have been placed over us severely. The less we know ourselves, the more we see those whom we strive to rebuke. All these are evils that are often committed by subjects against superiors and often by superiors against subjects: those who rule consider all their subjects less wise than they themselves are, while those who are subject judge the actions of their rulers and think that, if they themselves had happened to hold authority, they could have acted better.

Consequently, it often happens that rulers see less wisely what ought to be done, because the very cloud of exaltation darkens their eyes; and sometimes the one who was subject, once he has become a superior, does what, while still subject, he had formerly reproved as something that ought not to be done. Since he commits the very things he had judged, let him at least be ashamed because he judged them.

Therefore, just as superiors must take care lest the position of their singular wisdom lift their hearts too high [Note: [Col. 0722B] The edition reads “higher.”], so subjects must take care lest the deeds of their rulers displease them. But if the life of teachers is rightly reproved, subjects ought nevertheless to honor them even when they are displeased with them. This, however, must be carefully observed: do not desire to imitate one whom it is necessary to honor, nor refuse to honor one whom you disdain to imitate. For a subtle path of uprightness and humility must be held, so that the reprehensible deeds of teachers may displease while the minds of subjects do not depart from preserving reverence for the teaching office. »

[LIBER III.]

THE CHAPTERS OF BOOK III BEGIN.

[Col. 0721B] [Col. 0721C] On David’s old age, and Solomon’s succession, and his name. On the vision Solomon saw at Gibeon, and the wisdom bestowed upon him, and the judgment concerning the two women. On what is written, that Solomon produced three thousand proverbs, that his songs numbered five thousand, and that he discussed matters from the cedar to the hyssop. How King Hiram helped Solomon in the work of the Temple. How many laborers Solomon had in the work of the Temple. From what stone the Temple was made. When and where the Temple was built. What its measurements were. On its windows and boards all around. On the ascent and the construction of the second and third chambers. That the walls should be paneled with cedar and the floor interwoven with fir. On the distinct measurement of the Temple itself and of the inner sanctuary. That the whole house should be covered with cedar and gold. That the altar of the inner sanctuary should be of cedar and gold. On the making of the cherubim. That the carved wall and the floor should be covered with gold. On the entrance to the inner sanctuary, or Temple. On the courts of the house of the Lord. How many years the Temple was built. [Col. 0721D] On the bronze pillars. [Col. 0722C] On the bronze Sea. On the ten bases and basins. That the vessels of the house of the Lord were made in the region of the Jordan. On both altars. On the ten golden tables of the house of the Lord. On the ten lampstands. On the hinges of the doors and the completion of the house of the Lord. Where all the elders of Israel came to King Solomon and to Jerusalem, and brought the ark from Zion; and the priests carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord into the inner sanctuary of the Temple; and afterward it says that the poles projected and their ends appeared outside the sanctuary before the inner sanctuary. It also says that there was nothing else in the ark of the covenant except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed in it at Horeb. On the cloud that appeared in the house of the Lord. On Solomon’s and Hiram’s fleet, which went every year to Ophir to bring back gold, apes, peacocks, and algum wood. On Solomon’s throne and the abundance of silver and gold in Jerusalem. [Col. 0722D] On Solomon’s fall and the end of his misfortunes.

BOOK III BEGINS.

(III Kings 1.) David grew old, and Solomon was anointed king over all Israel at Gihon, so that the promise made to David might be fulfilled in him (II Kings 7:5, 12, 13): “You shall not build a house for me, but your son, who will come forth from your womb.” In this, indeed, an image of a future event was formed, in that he built the Temple and had peace according to his name. [Note: [Col. 0721D] What follows is taken from Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 71 [at the very beginning].] « Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful,” and therefore that name most truly suits him through whom we, once enemies, having received remission of sins, are reconciled to God. For “when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Rom. 5:10). He himself is the peaceful one, “who made both one, and by abolishing in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility, and by annulling the law of commandments expressed in decrees, created the two in himself as one new man, making peace.” And coming, he preached peace to those who were far away and peace to those who were near. He himself says in the Gospel (John 14:27): “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you.” By these and many other testimonies the Lord Christ is shown to be the peaceful one. [Note: [Col. 0722D] Isidore copies this in chapter 2 of his commentary on III Kings.] For the fact that he built a most excellent Temple for the Lord also signifies Christ, who built a house for God in the heavens—not of wood and stones, but of holy human beings, that is, believers, to whom the Apostle says (I Cor. 3:17): “For the temple of God is holy, which you are.” » [Note: [Col. 0723D] What follows, moreover, is found only in Isidore.]

Scripture very clearly teaches that Solomon was called by three names: “peaceful,” that is, Solomon; and Jedidiah, that is, “beloved of the Lord”; and Koheleth (Eccl. 1:1), that is, Ecclesiastes. Ecclesiastes is called in Greek the one who gathers an assembly, that is, the Church; we may call him a preacher, that is, one who speaks to the people, and whose speech is directed not specifically to one person but generally to all. He was called “peaceful” and “beloved of the Lord” because there was peace in his kingdom and the Lord loved him. For both Psalm 44 and Psalm 71 are prefaced by the title “of the Beloved and the Peaceful.” Although, as belonging to the prophecy of Christ and the Church, they surpass Solomon’s prosperity and strength, nevertheless historically they were written concerning Solomon.

(Chapters 3–4.) Solomon therefore went to Gibeon and offered a burnt offering there to the Lord. There the Lord appeared to him by night, heard the petition he made, and gave him wisdom and knowledge, so that no one before him had been like him, nor would anyone arise like him after him. After receiving wisdom from God, however, he was immediately tested in judgment because of wicked women. [Note: [Col. 0723D] Claudius took these passages, marked in the usual manner with lines, from Paterius and therefore from Gregory the Great. See, I beg you, what he relates in Book VIII of the Moralia [no. 48, chapter 29, elsewhere 17].] « Here one must observe that, after the Lord has illumined the darkness of our error with the light of his knowledge, he immediately tests us by visiting us with the goad of temptation, because by kindling our hearts he advances us in virtue, while by withdrawing he permits us to be shaken by temptation. For if, after the gifts of virtues, the soul were shaken by no temptation, it would then boast that it possessed these things from itself. Thus, so that it may possess both the firmness of gifts and humbly recognize its weakness, it is lifted to high places by the approach of grace, and by grace’s withdrawal it is tested as to what it is from itself. This is well suggested to us by the history of this sacred reading. Solomon is remembered as having received wisdom from God and yet, after receiving that same wisdom, as immediately being assailed by the case of the prostitutes. For as soon as he received the grace of so great a revelation, he endured the contest of wicked women; because often, when the inward radiance of generosity [Note: [Col. 0723D] The edition reads “of abundance.”] illumines our mind with the virtues granted to us, slippery thoughts immediately disturb it, so that the mind which exults because it has been raised up by an immense gift may also, when struck by temptation, discover what it is.

Thus Elijah, visited from above, opened the heavens with his word, and yet, when tested, suddenly became weak and, fleeing through the deserts, feared a single woman exceedingly [Note: [Col. 0723D] “One.”]. Thus Paul is taken up to the third heaven [Note: [Col. 0724D] “Caught up.”] and looks into the secrets of Paradise; yet, returning to himself, he struggles against the battle of the flesh, bears another law in his members, and grieves that the law of the spirit is wearied by its rebellion within him (Rom. 7:21). After the bestowal [Note: [Col. 0724D] “The giving.”] of the gift, therefore, God tests a person because by the gift bestowed he raises him up, and by withdrawing it for a little while he reveals the person to himself. Without doubt, we suffer this until, our stain of sin having been completely wiped away, we are refashioned into the substance of the incorruption that was promised. »

[Col. 0724B]

[Note: [Col. 0724D] This is where Paterius ends, and therefore Gregory. What follows Claudius learned from Isidore. See chapter 3 of Book III of Kings, verse 17.] « In this judgment of Solomon, where he is first described as having judged between two women contending over their affection, love burned in one while pretense had stolen into the other, there was a figure of Christ. The wicked woman—that is, the people of the synagogue or of the heretics—desired the son of the true mother, that is, the Church; she wanted him not in order to preserve him but in reality to kill him [Note: [Col. 0724D] The edition reads “unless she might preserve him,” but this is incorrect.]. But just as, when Solomon’s sword divided him [Note: [Col. 0724D] “Tearing apart,” but this too is incorrect.], the true child was revealed through the groan of his own mother, so also, when the Spirit of Jesus Christ teaches, those who have been seduced and taken captive by the error of heretics or of the synagogue sometimes deserve to recognize the Church, their mother, mourning for them on their behalf. Thus it appears sufficiently and appropriately that this woman represented the wickedness of the heretics or of the synagogue: they wickedly nourish their own and destroy them, while they entice and persuade others in order to ruin them.

In the moral sense, however, what else is signified by the names of nursing mothers except the order of teachers? And what else by their sons except the person of disciples? Teachers who are watchful in knowledge but asleep in life nourish their hearers through the vigils of preaching; yet, while they neglect to do what they say, they kill through the sleep of their sluggishness and oppress through negligence those whom they seemed to feed with the milk of words.
