Hence, while they themselves live reprehensibly and cannot have disciples of laudable life, they try to draw others to themselves, so that, while they display good followers, they may excuse before human judgment the evil they do and, as it were, cover their deadly negligence through the life of their subjects.

Thus the woman who had killed her own son sought another’s. Yet Solomon’s sword found the true mother, because the strict Judge’s anger at the final examination reveals whose offspring lives and whose perishes. Here one must carefully observe also that the living son is first ordered to be divided, so that afterward he may be returned to his mother alone: for in this life the life of a disciple is, as it were, permitted to be divided, when one person sometimes receives merit before God and another praise before human beings.

But the false mother did not fear that the child she had not borne should be killed, because arrogant teachers, ignorant of charity, if they cannot obtain the fullest title of praise through other people’s disciples, cruelly persecute their lives. Inflamed by the torch of envy, they do not want those whom they see they cannot possess to live for others. Hence the perverse woman cries out (verse 26): “Let him be neither mine nor hers.” For, as we said, those whom they do not see obeying them for temporal glory they begrudge to others, that they may live in the truth.

The true mother, however, strives that her son may at least be with a stranger and live. Thus truthful teachers allow others to receive the praise of teaching from their disciples, provided that those same disciples do not lose the integrity of life. By these entrails of compassion this true mother is recognized, because every teaching office is approved in the examination of charity, and she alone deserved to receive the whole who, as it were, yielded the whole [the text reads “conceded”]. For faithful superiors, because they not only do not begrudge others praise arising from their good disciples but also pray that those disciples may be useful to others, receive their children whole and living when, at the supreme examination, the joys of perfect recompense follow from their lives. »

[Col. 0725C]

[Note: [Col. 0725D] Chapter 4:32. Seek what follows in Isidore, who illustrates Book III of Kings with commentary.] « Solomon also spoke three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered five thousand. [Note: [Col. 0725D] The Vulgate reads “one thousand and five.”] What else is signified by the three thousand proverbs except the fullness of faith handed down by Christ in the Law and the Gospels? Since it is expounded in its entirety in many ways through the meanings of allegories under the mystery [Note: [Col. 0725D] “In a ministry.”] of the Trinity, it is, as it were, called three thousand proverbs. His five thousand songs are understood through the five bodily senses. Whoever governs these senses well in different virtues is blessed and, through them, sings, as it were, five thousand songs to the Lord.

(Verse 33.) « Solomon discussed matters from the cedar to the hyssop. By the name of cedar the height of glory in the elect is understood, as the Prophet also testifies, saying (Ps. 91:13): “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree and will multiply like a cedar in Lebanon.” Hyssop, however, is a lowly herb clinging to a rock, by which Christ’s humility is signified. Our Redeemer discussed matters from the cedar to the hyssop because he descended from the lofty excellence of heavenly glory to the humility of the flesh. Indeed, by the name of cedar the proud exaltation of the wicked is also signified, as it is said through David (Ps. 28:5): “The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars.”

Thus Christ discusses matters from the cedar to the hyssop [Col. 0726A] [Note: [Col. 0725D] The edition reads “discussed.” I prefer the reading of our manuscript, since it has “judges” below.], because he judges the hearts of the wicked and the humble. He discussed matters concerning wood when he hung on the cross. Then, in the cedar, he bent down the arrogance of the world, which he also brought down to the humility of hyssop—that is, to the foolishness of the cross and the contemptible faith. »

(Chapter 5.) [Note: [Col. 0726D] What follows, marked in the usual manner with lines, is also found in Rabanus.] The history follows: « When Solomon was about to build a house for the Lord, he sought assistance from Hiram, king of Tyre, who had always been a friend of David and who, after Solomon had obtained the kingdom, had also begun to keep peace with Solomon. Solomon soon found that Hiram was eager to help him in everything, so that he gave him craftsmen, wood, and gold as the work required. In return for this favor, Solomon gave him every year many cors of wheat and oil as food for his household.

There is no doubt that Solomon, who is interpreted as “peaceful,” signifies by both his name and the serene condition of his kingdom the one of whom Isaiah said (9:7): “His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace.” Hiram, however, whose name in Latin means “living on high,” figuratively expresses believers from the nations, glorious in life together with faith. Nor does anything prevent Hiram, who was a king and who by royal power helped Solomon—that is, the Peaceful One—in the construction of the house of the Lord, from typologically proclaiming those converted to the faith who were themselves lords of worldly affairs, by whose aid the Church is known often to have been assisted and nobly increased, and by whose authoritative decrees she has been raised up against heretics, schismatics, and pagans.

Solomon therefore asks Hiram for assistance in the work of the Temple because, when the Lord came in the flesh and planned to build the house he loved, namely the Church, he chose helpers for the work not only from the Jews but also from the nations; for he took ministers of the word from both peoples. Hiram sent Solomon cedar and fir wood cut from Lebanon, to be placed in the house of the Lord, because the converted Gentile world sent to the Lord men once distinguished in worldly affairs, already cast down and humbled from the mountain of their pride by the axe of the Lord’s rebuke, men who, formed according to the rule of evangelical truth, were to be placed in the building of the Church, each according to his merit and time.

« He also sent craftsmen, because the Gentile world offered to the Lord philosophers converted to true wisdom, who, by the grace of their learning, might rightly be appointed also to govern peoples. Such were Dionysius the Areopagite in the times of the apostles, and afterward the most eloquent teacher and courageous martyr Cyprian, along with very many others. He sent gold, which is understood in almost the same sense. For he displayed men distinguished in wisdom and intellect [Note: [Col. 0726D] Perhaps it should be read “offered.”], for whom the Gentile world awaits from the Lord the gifts of heavenly grace in return for all these offerings: namely, the wheat of the word of God, and the oil of charity, anointing, and illumination by the Holy Spirit.

It aptly accords with the affairs of the Church that Solomon, asking for assistance in holy work, says to Hiram (III Kings 5:6): “Command your people to cut cedars for me from Lebanon, and let my servants be with your servants.” The servants of Hiram who cut cedars for Solomon from Lebanon are the chosen teachers from the nations. Their task is to correct and overthrow in the service of their Redeemer those who rejoiced in the possessions and glory of this world, transferring their desires from the pride of arrogance to that service.

With these servants there were also Solomon’s servants, and together they devoted themselves to the work mentioned. For the first teachers from the nations necessarily had to be instructed in the word of faith by the teaching of the apostles themselves, who had learned from the Lord, lest, if they began to teach without teachers, they should become teachers of error.

Solomon therefore wished Hiram’s servants to cut wood for him from Lebanon because they were more skilled than his own servants at cutting. But he also wished his own servants to be present, so that they might show the cutters what size the wood ought to be. The figure of this matter is clear: the apostles knew with greater certainty the word of the Gospel that they had heard from the Lord. But Gentiles freed from error [Note: [Col. 0727D] “Or converted” is added; these words do occur in Rabanus himself, but the word “freed” is absent. If the reader wishes, let him delete it.] and transformed to the truth of the Gospel knew the errors of the nations better; and the more certainly they knew them, the more skillfully they learned to overthrow and abolish them. » [Note: [Col. 0727D] Thus far Rabanus. I found what follows only in Claudius, who followed the practice he explained elsewhere in these words: “I have also striven to join some of my own words below their discourse, as seemed appropriate to me, so that the two interpretations might be joined without division.” [In the Epistle to the Galatians.]]

Paul indeed knew the mystery of the Gospel, which he had learned through revelation, better; but Dionysius was better able to refute the false doctrines of the pagans, whose syllogisms and every argument he had known from childhood together with their errors. What follows agrees aptly with this interpretation (chapter 6, verse 6): “For you know that there is not among my people a man who knows how to cut wood like the Sidonians.” For there was no one among the Jewish people, where the Lord was teaching bodily present, who knew how to refute the errors of the Gentiles as learnedly as the Gentiles themselves who had been converted to the faith and had become Christians from among the nations. Since the Sidonians and Tyrians were peoples of the Gentiles, they are rightly understood as a figure of the nations.

That our Solomon sent servants to this work is indicated in mystical language in what follows, when it says (verses 13–14): “Solomon chose laborers from all Israel, and the levy was thirty thousand men; he sent them to Lebanon, ten thousand each month in rotation, so that they might be two months in their homes.” » [Note: [Col. 0728D] Rabanus appears again.] « Here one must first observe that Solomon did not choose laborers from all Israel without reason, nor was there any part of the people from which men worthy of so great a work were not taken. For priests are not to be chosen from one lineage of Aaron alone, but are to be sought from the whole Church—those who may be sufficient to build the house of the Lord either by their example or by their word. Wherever such men are found, they are immediately promoted to the office of teachers without any acceptance of persons. When they are ordained to instruct unbelievers and call them into the fellowship of the Church, they are sent, like strong and chosen men, to cut the materials for the Temple in Lebanon.

The number of thirty thousand, by which these cutters of wood were counted, may appropriately be referred as a figure to those who are perfected in the faith of the Holy Trinity, which is especially fitting for teachers. Yet, since the thirty thousand were arranged so that ten thousand devoted themselves to the holy work in each month, we must consider more carefully the mystery of the number ten.

For ten thousand men from Israel are sent to cut wood for the work of the house of the Lord because all teachers and instructors of the ignorant who are to be ordained ought themselves in every respect to observe the ten commandments of the Law and to show their hearers that they must be observed. They ought also to hope for the future rewards in heaven, which are commonly represented by the denarius, and should always proclaim them as objects of hope to their hearers.

The three months, whose intervals were assigned to each of the woodcutters, figuratively proclaim the perfection of the three evangelical virtues: almsgiving, prayer, and fasting. » [Note: [Col. 0728D] These passages marked here are absent from the published copies of Rabanus. Did Claudius insert them from his own material, or did the negligence of copyists remove them? Let the reader decide.]

He mentioned these because they were to be performed not for human display but solely for the glory of the inward Judge; otherwise they would remain empty of eternal fruit. By these words he clearly taught that all the fruits of the virtues are indicated by these three branches, as it were, growing from one root of charity. « By almsgiving are understood all the things we benevolently do for our brothers in order to fulfill love of neighbor; by prayer, everything through which, by inward contrition, we are joined to our Creator; by fasting, everything through which we guard ourselves from the contagion of vices and the allurements of the world, so that with a free mind and chaste body we may always be able to cling to the love both of our Creator and of our neighbor. These are the three months of the Temple’s laborers. Since a month is completed by the fullness of the days of the lunar cycle, the fullness of every spiritual virtue is shown through it, in which the mind of the faithful is regarded by the Lord’s daily illumination as the moon is regarded by the sun. »

[Note: [Col. 0728D] These passages do not occur in the published works of Rabanus. I leave it to the reader to decide why this happened.]

One month, in which they cut wood for the work of the Temple, is almsgiving, that is, the work of mercy, by which we labor for the salvation of our neighbor to bring him successfully into the unity of the holy Church: by teaching, rebuking, supplying temporal necessities, and displaying examples of life. The two remaining months, during which they were permitted to remain in their homes and attend to their own needs, are prayer and fasting. Through these, while we work outwardly for the needs of our brothers, we turn inwardly to the Lord and care especially for our own salvation.

And since only those perfectly care for either their own salvation or that of their brothers who humbly submit themselves to the contemplation of divine grace, it rightly follows (verse 14): “And Adoniram was over this levy.” Adoniram, whose name in Latin means “My exalted Lord,” whom does he indicate better than the one whom his name imitates, namely the Lord and Savior? Adoniram is placed over the laborers of the Temple so that, by his provision, he may properly arrange in which months each should go out to work and in which they should return to care for their own household, when the Lord and our Savior more familiarly enlightens the minds of holy preachers, teaching them to discern when it is appropriate to undertake the work of building the Church—by preaching or by performing other works of piety—and when it is again fitting to return, as if to inspect their own house, to examine their own conscience and make it worthy of the heavenly Inspector and Visitor through prayers and fasts. »

(Verses 15–16.) Solomon therefore had seventy thousand men who carried burdens and eighty thousand stonecutters in the mountain, besides the superintendents who directed each work: three thousand three hundred officers commanding the people and those who performed the work, and so forth. « [Note: [Col. 0729D] Rabanus appears again; you will find him teaching where the passages are marked with lines.] Stonecutters are called cutters of stones. These cutters of stones figuratively signify the same as the cutters of wood: namely, holy preachers, who exercise the minds of the ignorant through the labor of the word of God and strive to transform them from the shamefulness and deformity in which they were born, carefully fitting them, once regularly instructed, to the unity of the faithful, that is, to the building of the house of God.

The fact that both wood and stones were cut in the mountain, and that both materials, cut and prepared, were transferred to the mountains of the house of the Lord, has an evident meaning: all human beings are born on the mountain of pride, because we derive the origin of our flesh from the transgression of the first man, which pride caused. Whoever by the grace of God has been predestined to life is cut away through catechesis and the reception of the sacraments of faith, and is transferred from the mountain of pride to the mountain of the house of the Lord. Freed from the power of darkness, we reach the stronghold of the virtues that exists in the unity of the holy Church.

It should also be noted that these laborers were distributed so that some cut stones in the mountain while others carried burdens. The gifts of the Spirit are diverse. Some possess greater constancy in speaking and reproving the insolent; some are gentler in comforting the fainthearted and supporting the weak; some, endowed with both virtues, devote themselves to the work of the Lord. Such are those of whom the Apostle speaks, saying [Note: [Col. 0729D] What lacks the line markings is absent from the published Rabanus.]: “Reprove the unruly, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient with everyone” (I Thess. 5:14).

The superintendents who directed each work are the authors of Sacred Scripture, whose teaching instructs us in all things: how we should teach the ignorant and rebuke the contemptuous; how it is fitting for us to bear one another’s burdens, so that we may fulfill the law of Christ (Gal. 6:2). »
[Note: The passages lacking line markings are absent from Rabanus’s printed edition.]

The more each person labors either in supporting the needs of his neighbors or in correcting their errors, the more certain are the rewards he awaits in the future—whether the repose of souls after death or the blessed immortality of bodies. [Note: Something seems to be missing here, such as “after the final judgment,” or something similar. Muratori explains how such expressions, which attribute rest to the dead, should be understood in his book entitled *On the State of the Dead*.] [Note: Rabanus resumes here.]

“Accordingly, the workers mentioned above are rightly said to number seventy thousand and eighty thousand. Seventy thousand, namely, on account of the sabbath-rest of souls (for the seventh day was consecrated as the Sabbath, that is, as rest). Eighty thousand, on account of the hope of the resurrection, which preceded us in the Lord on the eighth day (that is, after the Sabbath), and which is likewise hoped for in us on the eighth day, that is, in the eighth age.

“The overseers numbered three thousand three hundred, clearly on account of faith in the holy Trinity, which the sacred writings preach to us. But the fact that, instead of three thousand three hundred overseers, the Book of Chronicles records three thousand six hundred (II Chronicles 2:18) refers precisely to the same perfection of exalted men. For since the Lord completed the adornment of the world in the number six, good works that are perfect are rightly represented by it. And because Holy Scripture teaches that works of righteousness must be possessed together with faith in the truth, the overseers of the temple’s works are rightly said to have numbered three thousand six hundred.

“We must not pass over the fact that these seventy thousand and eighty thousand burden-bearers and stonecutters, together with their overseers, were not Israelites but proselytes—that is, resident foreigners who lived among them. For it is written in the Book of Chronicles (II Chronicles 2:17): ‘So Solomon numbered all the proselyte men who were in the land of Israel, after the numbering with which David his father had numbered them; and they were found to be one hundred and fifty thousand and three thousand six hundred. And he made seventy thousand of them bearers of burdens on their shoulders,’ and so forth. [Note: Rabanus and the Vulgate edition read “from among them.”]

“Proselytes were so called in Greek because they were born from other nations and, after receiving circumcision, had passed over into the faith and fellowship of the people of God. Thus the workers of the Lord’s house came from the children of Israel, from the proselytes, and from the nations. From the children of Israel there were thirty thousand, who were sent to cut cedars from Lebanon; from the proselytes came those of whom we have just spoken, the hewers of stone; and from the nations came Hiram himself and his servants, who cut timber from Lebanon together with Solomon’s servants. Thus every kind of human being through whom the Church was to be built was represented beforehand in the construction of the temple: Jews, proselytes, and Gentiles converted to the truth of the Gospel build one and the same Church of Christ, whether by living rightly or also by teaching.”

### Verse 27

“And the king commanded that they bring great and precious stones for the foundation of the temple and shape them.”

Mystically, no other foundation of the temple is to be understood than that which the Apostle points out when he says (I Corinthians 3:11): “For no one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.” He can rightly be called the foundation of the Lord’s house because, as Peter says (Acts 4:12): “There is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved.”

Great and precious stones are placed upon this foundation when men distinguished in deeds and holiness cling to their Creator with the intimate holiness of their minds, so that the more firmly they place their hope in him, the more powerfully they may guide the lives of others—which is to bear the breadth of the structure.

The stones that were placed in the foundation of the temple to support the whole building are properly the prophets and apostles, who received the word and sacraments of the truth from the Wisdom of God itself, whether visibly or invisibly. [Note: The passages not marked with line strokes are absent from Rabanus.]

Hence the Apostle also says of us, who strive according to our measure to imitate their life or teaching (Ephesians 2:20), that we are “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets.” More generally, all who have learned both to cling faithfully to the Lord himself and to bear courageously the burdens of their brothers imposed upon them may be represented by great and precious stones.

[Note: These are again the words of Rabanus.]

“These stones are rightly ordered to be shaped first and then placed in the foundation, for everything square customarily stands firm, whichever way it is turned. The hearts of the elect are likened to this figure: they have learned to stand so firmly in faith that no adversity arising from circumstances, not even death itself, can make them depart from their upright state.” [Note: The passages not marked here are not found in Rabanus’s printed edition.]

The Church has received such teachers not only from Judea but also from the nations. Therefore, concerning the great, precious, and square stones of this world, it is rightly added:

### Verse 18

“Which Solomon’s masons and Hiram’s masons shaped.”

Precious stones are shaped when each of the elect, through the instruction and diligence of the saints who preceded them, abandons whatever harmful or useless thing they possess within themselves and displays before the sight of their Creator only the rule of innate righteousness, like the stable form of squareness. The stones were shaped not only by Solomon’s masons but also by Hiram’s, because from both peoples there were some who became not merely disciples of those exalted teachers but teachers themselves. [Note: These passages too are absent from Rabanus.]

It was as though they prepared them as squared stones for raising the building of the Lord’s house. For it was not only Jeremiah and Isaiah and the other prophets from the circumcised people who supplied the teachers of the following age with the greatest model of life or endurance and with proclamations of saving doctrine; blessed Job also, with his children, who were from the nations, did so. Thus, after useless words, deeds, and thoughts had been cast aside, they were found worthy and fit to bear the burden of the holy Church.

[Note: Rabanus again.]

“Moreover, the Gibliites prepared timber and stones for building the house.”

“Giblus is a city in Syria of Phoenicia, from which the Gibliites received their name. Ezekiel mentions it, saying (27:8): ‘Your wise men, Tyre, became your pilots; the elders of Giblus and its wise men.’ In Hebrew the word is *Gobel* or *Gebal*, which is interpreted as ‘defining’ or ‘delimiting.’ This name appropriately suits those who prepare human hearts for the spiritual building constructed from the virtues of the soul. For they are able to teach their hearers faith and works of righteousness only because they themselves, first instructed by the sacred pages, have diligently learned by a firm definition of truth what faith must be held and along what path of virtue one must walk.

“For the person who does not know the discernment of the catholic faith uselessly claims for himself the office of teacher; and those who try to teach others a rule they themselves have not learned build not a sanctuary for the Lord but a ruin for themselves.

“In building the Lord’s house, therefore, timber and stones must first be cut from the mountain, because those whom we seek to instruct in the faith of the truth must first be taught to renounce the devil and to be rescued through rebirth from the lot of the first transgression in which we were born. Then precious and great stones are to be sought and placed in the foundation of the temple, so that, having rejected their former manner of life, we may remember to examine in everything the life and conduct of those whom we know to cling especially to the Lord through the virtue of humility, and to set them before our hearers for imitation.” [Note: The passages lacking line markings are not found in Rabanus.]

We see such people enduring with invincible steadfastness of mind, in a certain sense squared, immovable against every assault of temptation; we discover them to be precious and great in merit and reputation.

After the foundation has been composed of such great stones, the Lord’s house must be built with timber and stones carefully prepared and placed in fitting order. These had once been removed from their former position [or “root”; this wording indicates another reading, but I have not wished to remove it. Let the Reader remove it if he wishes.] For after the first rudiments of faith and after the foundations of humility have been placed in us according to the example of exalted men, [Note: The following passage is found in Rabanus.] “a wall of good works must be added upward, as though upon rows of stones set one upon another, so that we may walk and advance from virtue to virtue” (Psalm 83:8).

Or certainly, the great, precious, and square foundation stones are, as we said above, the first teachers of the churches (Ephesians 2:20), who heard the word of salvation from the Lord himself. The rows of stones or timber placed above them are the priests who follow in their own time, through whose preaching and ministry the structure of the Church grows or is ordered (or “adorned”) by virtues.

What color the stones were with which the temple was built is clearly stated in the Book of Chronicles. David said to Solomon, when he showed him the temple expenses and what he had prepared (I Chronicles 29:2): “I have prepared in abundance every precious stone and Parian marble.” Parian marble is called white marble, such as that island customarily produces. [Note: Rabanus’s printed edition reads: “Its height was sixty cubits.”]

[Note: The passages lacking line markings are not found in Rabanus.]

Hence the poet says of it (Virgil, *Aeneid* 3):

> Olearon, and snowy Paros, and the Cyclades  
> Scattered across the sea; but we sail through straits  
> Stirred up by frequent winds.

Paros is therefore called snowy because it sends forth marble of the whitest kind.

“It is one of the Cycladic islands, and Josephus indicates that the temple was made from this stone, saying: ‘He therefore raised the temple as far as the roof, constructed of white stone; its height was twenty-five cubits, and one hundred [reading uncertain].’” [Note: Rabanus’s printed edition reads: “Its height was one hundred and twenty-five cubits.”]

“The meaning of the mystery is not hidden. It is evident to everyone that the white marble from which the Lord’s house was constructed signifies the pure action of the elect and, at the same time, their conscience cleansed from every blemish of corruption. Such people the wise architect wished to place upon the foundation of Christ as precious stones, redeemed with gold and silver (II Corinthians 7:1): ‘Beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.’” [Note: Rabanus also extends to this point.]

In the earlier part of this volume you have the building explained by blessed Bede. [Note: Our manuscript omits many passages found in the published Eucherius, taken from Bede; the manuscript refers the Reader to that work. Certain passages are certainly missing here, as is indicated in the sequence of chapters.]

### Chapter 8:1; II Chronicles 5:2

“All the elders of Israel came to King Solomon in Jerusalem to bring up the ark of the covenant of the Lord from the city of David, that is, from Zion. The priests brought the ark of the covenant of the Lord and carried it into its place, into the inner sanctuary of the temple, the holy of holies, beneath the wings of the cherubim. For the cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark and covered the ark and its poles from above.

“When the poles projected and their ends appeared outside the sanctuary before the inner sanctuary, they could no longer be seen farther out. They have remained there to the present day.”

[Note: Bede, in chapter or question 14, transmits the following line-marked material; Rabanus has it likewise.]

“This is written more explicitly in the Book of Chronicles (the same passage, verse 9): ‘The ends of the poles by which they carried the ark, because they were somewhat longer, appeared before the inner sanctuary. But if anyone had been outside for a little while, he could not see them.’

“Here we must observe that although the ends of the poles appeared before the inner sanctuary to those who approached more closely and looked more attentively, it could not happen that the ends themselves projected beyond the inner sanctuary. For it was necessary that, when the inner sanctuary was closed and a veil was hung before its doors, the poles too, together with the ark and the cherubim, should be concealed inside. This could not happen if the projecting poles did not leave space for the doors to be extended and closed.

“Scripture took such care to explain the placement of the poles not without reason but in view of a great sacrament. For it is clear that the outer house of the temple signifies the Church journeying on earth, while the holy of holies signifies the inner happiness of the heavenly homeland. The ark brought into the holy of holies signifies the humility assumed by Christ and brought within the veil into the royal heaven. The poles by which the ark was carried typologically proclaim the preachers of the word, through whom he himself was made known to the world. [Note: Here Claudius omits certain passages found in the published books of Bede and Rabanus. Did the Reader judge them less suitable to what he had proposed to explain?]

“For the ends of the poles appeared outside before the inner sanctuary not always, but when it happened that the doors of that inner sanctuary were opened; and even then they appeared not to everyone but only to those who approached more closely and strove to observe attentively what was inside. But the ark itself—what it was like and how it had been placed—could be seen only by those who had entered the inner sanctuary. For no saint still living in this life, even if he raises his mind very high, sees the glory of his Redeemer there fully; only the citizens of that homeland do so.

“The poles also remained hidden in the inner sanctuary with the ark, because all the perfected elect who preceded us from the world are even now hidden in the secret place of God’s face, away from the disturbance of human beings. Yet their ends are sometimes seen, when the inner sanctuary is opened, by those who draw near, whenever divine grace grants the more perfect and those who cleanse the eye of their hearts with complete devotion to contemplate something of the joy of the heavenly citizens.

“This contemplation is not granted to those who have withdrawn somewhat farther away, because the more they remain outside with wandering minds, the less they see what the inner joys are.” [Note: Some passages found in the published books of Bede and Rabanus are omitted here by Claudius.]

### Verse 10

Then it continues:

“Now there was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed there at Horeb, when the Lord made a covenant with the children of Israel as they came out of the land of Egypt.”

One may ask how this passage can say that there was nothing in the ark except the two tablets of the testimony, when the Apostle Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth, writes to the Hebrews, that is, to the children of Israel (Hebrews 9:2):

“For a tabernacle was prepared, the first one, in which were the lampstand, the table, and the presentation of the loaves, which is called the holy place. Behind the second veil was the tabernacle called the holy of holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant covered on every side with gold, in which was a golden urn containing the manna, and Aaron’s staff that had blossomed, and the tablets of the covenant.”

Behold, from the testimony of the Apostle we have learned that these things too were there. He would not have dared to write anything else to them except what they held with certainty: that all these things were in the ark. Yet it does not appear clearly when they were brought into it, except that it is written in the Book of Numbers (17:9–10):

“Moses brought out all the staffs from before the Lord to all the children of Israel. They saw them, and each one received his own staff. And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Bring Aaron’s staff back into the tabernacle of the testimony, to be kept there as a sign for the rebellious children of Israel, so that their complaints may cease from me and they may not die.’”

Likewise concerning the manna, it is written in Exodus (16:33–34):

“Moses said to Aaron: ‘Take one vessel and put there as much manna as an omer can contain, and place it before the Lord to be kept throughout your generations, as the Lord commanded Moses.’ And Aaron placed it in the tabernacle to be preserved.”

There was in the ark a golden urn containing manna, because in the man Christ “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9). There was Aaron’s staff, which, after being cut off, blossomed again, because all authority to judge belongs to him from whom judgment seemed to have been taken away in the humility of his passion (John 5:22, 27, 29, 30, and elsewhere).

There were also the tablets of the covenant, because in him are hidden “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 3:3). The poles by which it was carried were attached to it, because the teachers who once labored in the word of Christ now rejoice in the glory of Christ through the present vision. What one of them said—“I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23)—he left to be understood of all his fellow workers.

### Chapter 8:10

“It happened that when the priests had come out of the sanctuary, a cloud filled the house of the Lord, and the priests could not stand and minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the Lord had filled the house of the Lord.” [Note: The following passages, which explain this verse, are taken entirely from chapter 2 of Isidore’s commentary on the Third Book of Kings.]

“The glory of the Lord is understood as Christ, whose faith has filled the whole world. Concerning this glory, when Moses was pleading with the Lord to spare the sinful people after the worship of the calf, the Lord replied (Numbers 14:19–20 and elsewhere): ‘I will be merciful to them; nevertheless, as I live and as my name lives, the whole earth shall be filled with my glory.’ The seventy-first Psalm also sings (verse 19): ‘The whole earth shall be filled with his glory.’ Hence the angels also cried out to the shepherds (Luke 2:14): ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.’

“But the fact that a cloud filled the house of the Lord and the priests could not minister because of the cloud indicates the proud priests and teachers of the Jews. While they disdained to investigate the mysteries of Christ’s Nativity, they lost the ministry owed by their faith through the cloud of error. The darkness of unbelief so filled their minds that, as their own merits required, they did not recognize the worship of belief.” [Note: The material that follows and explains this passage is taken entirely from chapter 2 of Isidore’s commentary on the Third Book of Kings.]

After the whole work of the Lord’s house had been completed, and after Solomon’s long prayer and the divine oracles addressed to him, Scripture reports among other things (I Kings 9:26) that King Solomon made a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber.

Ezion-geber is a harbor of the Red Sea (Numbers 33:35) and was the thirty-first encampment of the children of Israel when they departed from Egypt. At the same place, as Scripture testifies, Jehoshaphat’s fleet was later shattered by the force of a storm (I Kings 22:49). A fleet is a group of ships of the sea; *classis* also means a multitude of ships.

### I Kings 9:27–28

After this Scripture again reports that Hiram’s servants came with Solomon’s servants in the same ships to Ophir, and brought from there to King Solomon in Jerusalem four hundred and twenty talents of gold.

Ophir, from which, as we have already said, gold was brought to Solomon, was one of the descendants of a man named Heber, Ophir by name (Genesis 10:25, 29). Josephus reports that descendants of his stock lived from the river Cophena as far as the region of India called Hieria, and that the region itself received this name from him. Hence the translators of the Septuagint, deriving the name, translated it not as *Ophir* but as *Ophira*.

### I Kings 10:1

The queen of Sheba also, having heard of Solomon’s fame, came in the name of the Lord to test him with riddles.

Just as this queen came from the ends of the earth—that is, from India, as some say—to hear Solomon’s wisdom, so the Church came after many ages to the Redeemer and teacher, in order to receive from him the teaching of truth instead of the foolishness of error.

She is that queen of whom it is said to the Lord (Psalm 44:10): “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment of gold and surrounded with variety”—that is, surrounded by the precious beauty of diverse virtues. She is also the mother of all believers, who regenerates for salvation those born for death. Through her Christ restored more in grace than was lost in nature; he took the degenerate offspring of the transgressor Adam into the adoption of divine sonship and made citizens of heaven out of those disinherited from paradise.

She was called after the synagogue, but promised before the synagogue. For she was already prefigured in the first human being. Just as Eve was fashioned from Adam’s side, so the Church, redeemed from Christ’s body and wound, grew.

### Chapter 10:2

“The queen of Sheba entered Jerusalem with a very great retinue and riches, with camels carrying spices, an exceedingly great quantity of gold, and precious gems. She came to Solomon and spoke to him about everything that was in her heart.”

Thus, in the figure of this queen, the Church comes from the nations and, putting an end to earthly desires and vices at the ends of the earth, comes to hear the wisdom of Solomon—that is, of the peaceful man, our Lord Jesus Christ (Ephesians 2:14), “who made both one, abolishing hostility between God and humanity in his flesh.”

After the ancient and profane superstitions, she comes to hear and learn about the illumination of faith, the future judgment, the immortality of the soul, the hope of resurrection, and glory.

She therefore came to Jerusalem with a very great retinue—that is, no longer with only one people, the Jews, as the synagogue formerly possessed only Hebrews, but with the peoples and diverse nations of the whole world.

She came bearing gifts worthy of Christ: gold and precious gems, carried by camels—that is, by people coming from the Gentiles, who had previously been twisted by the foulness of vices, bent beneath the burden of evil deeds, and disfigured by the crookedness of sins.

With these gifts, as it were, this queen enters to Christ the peaceful king, bringing with her the spices of faith, the gold of purity, precious incense, and the brilliance of gems—that is, the marks of good conduct and the adornments of virtues.

### I Kings 10:2; II Chronicles 9:1

“And she spoke to him about everything that was in her heart.”

That is, she opened her heart to him, revealed her hidden conscience in confession, and expressed repentance for her former offenses.

Let us see what this queen does.

### Verse 4

“When the queen of Sheba saw all Solomon’s wisdom, and the house that he had built, and the food of his table, and the holocausts that he offered in the house of the Lord, she no longer had any spirit left in her.”

What reason was there for a powerful queen to marvel so greatly at a house, expenses, and royal food? We must therefore seek something greater in this passage.

The Church gathered from the nations saw the wisdom of Christ. After the carnal institutions of the Gentiles and the human and animal teaching of the philosophers, she received an understanding of salvation and life; she perceived the spiritual wonders of good things and recognized the true Maker of heaven and earth and the most powerful Creator of the human race.

Concerning his wisdom it is said (Wisdom 11:21): “You have ordered all things by measure and number and weight.”

She also saw the house he had built—that is, the incarnation of the man he assumed. Concerning this house the Apostle says (Colossians 2:9): “In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.”

She also saw Solomon’s foods, namely those of which he said (John 4:34): “My food is to do the will of my Father who sent me.”

Christ’s food is our salvation; he is refreshed by heavenly banquets through our progress. We are his food when, acquired by the Church, we pass into his members and body. Or his food is the heavenly sacrament of the altar, concerning which it is said (Psalm 77:24; John 6:50 and elsewhere): “He gave them bread from heaven; human beings ate the bread of angels.”

She also saw his holocausts—that is, undoubtedly, the mystery of prayers and supplications—and she was astonished. There she saw the immeasurable riches of her Lord.

### Verses 6 and following

“And she said to the king: ‘The word is true that I heard in my land concerning your words and your wisdom. I did not believe those who told me until I came myself and saw with my own eyes and proved that they had not told me even half. Your wisdom and works are greater than the report that I heard.’”

When this queen—or any holy soul—reaches the eternal Jerusalem, that is, the vision of peace, and enters blessed rest and the glory of the heavenly promises, she will perceive far more and far more magnificent things than were announced to her on earth through the sacred writings, through the prophets and apostles.

For now she sees “through a mirror in an enigma,” but then she will see with her own eyes, that is, “face to face” (I Corinthians 13:12).

When, I say, each faithful and holy soul is presented in that age before the divine sight, full of the fruits of good works, offering itself—or rather, itself as a gift—to its God, bringing forth things worthy of heaven and manifold gifts capable of attaining heaven, gems of mercy, pearls of righteousness, and ornaments of diverse merits—that is, spices of compunction and sweet-smelling balsams of chastity—bringing forth, as I said, an exceedingly great quantity of gold, that is, restoring intact within itself to its gracious Redeemer an inestimable price, pleasing him with spiritual offerings of heart and body, so that, joined to the wonders of heaven, it may take up the voice of prophetic exultation (Psalm 65:15): “I will enter your house with holocausts.”

Then the blessed and glorious soul, placed amid the astonishing riches of its rewarder, will be able to use the ineffable words of this queen toward God, saying: “The word is true that I heard in my land concerning your words. Your works are greater than the report that I heard.”

This means: “O Lord, I dared to hope for great things from my tribulations, but I have received a greater forgiveness. The greatness of the sweetness that I behold openly surpasses the understanding of my thought; the fulfillment of my expectation exceeds it.” [Note: “The price of the reward.” This is the reading of the published Eucherius.]

And truly, what God has prepared for those who love him is not comprehended by faith, is not reached by hope, and is not contained by charity; it surpasses desires and prayers. It can be acquired but cannot be measured. A person will see his merits increase through an unimagined generosity of rewards; he will have fruit from receiving, but no disgust from satiety.

King Solomon also made a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with exceedingly pure gold. It had six steps, and the top of the throne was rounded at the back.

The ivory throne undoubtedly represented the eternal power of the Judge, shining with the gold of divinity, which the Lordly man received from the Father. [Note: This expression is Nestorian in itself, but it can be softened in the manner in which some similar expressions of the Fathers are softened—expressions that are freer because they were uttered before the rise of the error of Nestorius. In any case, unless we are mistaken, it belongs among the expressions for which Claudius was censured and on account of which he was not without reason counted among the followers of Nestorius.]

The six steps of this throne typologically demonstrated every visible and invisible creature, which was made in six days and subjected by the Father to Christ the Lord.

As for the description of the throne itself as rounded at its rear, this undoubtedly signifies that the present world, which revolves through the boundaries of time, will be judged by the Lord at its end.

The twelve young lions standing in pairs on the six steps signify the authority of the holy apostles, to whom the Lord said (Matthew 19:28): “You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

After some intervening material Scripture again reports (verse 27) that Solomon made silver so abundant in Jerusalem that it was like stones.

This is a figurative, not a literal, expression. It is like what we read in Genesis, where God said to Abraham (13:16): “I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth.”

That expression is what the Greeks call *hyperbole*. It is figurative, not literal, and no one who has learned Scripture doubts that it regularly uses this and other figures.

This figure of speech occurs when what is said is far greater than what is signified by the statement. For who does not see that the number of stones in the city of Jerusalem was incomparably greater than the weight of silver?

### Chapter 11

“King Solomon loved many foreign women: the daughter of Pharaoh, Moabite women, Ammonite women, Edomite women, Sidonian women, and Hittite women, from the nations concerning which the Lord had said to the children of Israel: ‘You shall not enter among them, nor shall they enter among you; for they will certainly turn your hearts away, so that you follow their gods.’

“Solomon was joined to these women in an exceedingly ardent love. He had seven hundred wives who were like queens and three hundred concubines, and the women turned his heart away.”

Those who prosper in this world and are struck by none of its adversities must be warned by the example of Solomon. After receiving wisdom, he is described as falling even into idolatry, although we are told that before his fall he had suffered no adversity in this world. He entirely abandoned the wisdom granted to him because no discipline of even the slightest tribulation guarded him—until, after he abandoned God, he learned that he had been abandoned by God. [Note: See chapter 6 of Isidore’s commentary on the Third Book of Kings, and also Rabanus’s commentary on this passage.]

“Now what shall I say about his other works? Holy Scripture strongly reproves and condemns him, and says absolutely nothing about his repentance or about God’s indulgence toward him.

“Among his later evil deeds there is not even one that occurs to us which signifies anything good in allegory. [Note: The printed edition reads *occurrit, quid saltem in allegoria* (“there occurs what at least in allegory …”).] Hence his lamentable destruction—unless perhaps someone says that the foreign women, deceived by whose love he was, signified the elect churches from the nations.

“This could perhaps be understood without absurdity if those women had abandoned their gods on account of Solomon and worshiped his God. But since he offended his own God on their account and worshiped their gods, no good meaning can be inferred from it.

“Yet it should not be supposed that he could signify nothing good, but only evil. For in the person of this Solomon there appears a remarkable excellence and a terrifying overthrow.

“Thus what existed in him at different times—first good and later evil—is shown in the Church in this present age simultaneously and at one time. By his goodness I understand the good people of the Church, and by his evil the evil people of the Church, as though within the unity of one threshing floor.

“Thus, in that one man, the good are represented by the grains and the evil by the chaff; or, certainly, within the unity of one crop, the good by the wheat and the evil by the weeds.” [Note: The printed edition reads “weeds.”]

### Chapter 11:29

“It happened at that time that Jeroboam went out from Jerusalem, and the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite found him on the road, covered with a new cloak. They were alone in the field. Ahijah seized his new cloak with which he was covered, tore it into twelve pieces, and said to Jeroboam: ‘Take ten pieces for yourself, for thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I shall tear the kingdom from Solomon’s hand and give you ten tribes. One tribe will remain to him for the sake of my servant David, and another tribe for the sake of Jerusalem, which I chose from all the tribes of Israel.’”

[Note: These passages are taken from chapter 7 of Isidore’s commentary on the Third Book of Kings; perhaps the following passages too are taken from the same Isidore. But, unless we are mistaken, the rest of the commentary of Isidore cited here has since perished.]

“But the fact that after Solomon’s death ten tribes were separated from the temple and two remained clearly indicates what the Apostle says about that entire people (Romans 11:5): ‘A remnant has been saved according to the election.’”

The fact that the prophet’s single cloak was torn into twelve pieces, of which Jeroboam received ten, seems to have represented the following: the harmony of the Church is torn apart by heretics; the very teachers of error, by whom unity was divided, separate the people from the Catholics into, as it were, ten errors, and hold them tyrannically subject to themselves.

After many other matters, the Book of Kings reports and says (I Kings 11:41):

“The rest of the words of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom—behold, are all written in the Book of the Words of the Days of Solomon.”

In the Book of Chronicles—which we call by this Greek name, but which in Latin we may call the Book of Past Events—it is written as follows concerning Solomon (II Chron. IX, 29): “The rest of Solomon’s deeds, both the first and the last, are written in the words of Nathan the prophet, and in the books of Ahijah the Shilonite, and also in the vision of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam.” They assert that these books can now be found nowhere, not even among the Hebrews themselves; nor can the Book of the Wars of the Lord, which is mentioned in the Book of Numbers (XXI, 14), nor the Book of Jashar [the Upright] (Josh. X, 13), nor Solomon’s songs [Col. 0740D], nor his very wise discussions concerning the nature of trees and all plants, as well as animals, birds, reptiles, and fish. The same applies to what we have just quoted from the Book of Chronicles, where it says: “The rest of Solomon’s earlier and later works are written in the words of Nathan the prophet, in the books of Ahijah the Shilonite, and also in the vision of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam son of Nathan,” as well as to many volumes of this sort, which Scripture indeed attests to [Col. 0741A], but which plainly do not exist today. For when Judea was devastated by the Chaldeans, the library assembled in ancient times was also consumed by hostile fire along with the other wealth of the province [Col. 0742A]. From it, the few books that are now contained in Holy Scripture were later restored through the labor of Ezra, the pontiff and prophet.

# [BOOK IV]

## THE CHAPTERS OF BOOK IV BEGIN

[Col. 0741A]

Concerning the prophet of the Lord who came to Jeroboam at Bethel, and the false prophet who deceived him, for which reason he also died.

Concerning King Ahab and his wife Jezebel.

Concerning the rebuilding of Jericho, which Hiel of Bethel carried out.

Concerning Elijah and his miracles.

Concerning the death of the widow’s son, whom Elijah raised.

Concerning Elijah’s appearance before Ahab, the priests of the idols, the altar that Elijah built, the fire sent by God, and also the abundance of rain.

[Col. 0741B] Concerning Jezebel’s wickedness against Elijah and his flight.

Concerning his arrival at Mount Horeb, the mountain of God.

Concerning his departure for Damascus, and the anointing of Hazael as king in Syria; of Jehu son of Nimshi as king over Israel; and of Elisha the prophet to succeed him in Israel.

Concerning what is written: “May the gods do this to me, and more also, if a handful of the dust of Samaria will suffice for all the people who follow me.”

Concerning the vision of the prophet Micaiah, in which he saw the Lord sitting upon a lofty throne, and concerning the lie of the false prophets.

Concerning Ahab’s death and the succession of his son.

Concerning the two captains of fifty, who were burned with their soldiers by fire.

Concerning Elijah’s conversation with Elisha and his being carried up into heaven.

Concerning Elisha, who healed the barren and poisonous waters of Jericho.

Concerning the children cursed by him and devoured by bears.

Concerning the woman whose sons were being seized by a creditor but were freed through Elisha.

Concerning the man and woman who frequently received Elisha into their house when he passed by.

Concerning the raising of the child, when he sent his staff through his servant, but the dead child did not revive.

Concerning Naaman the Syrian’s cleansing from his leprosy.

Concerning the iron that sprang from the wood and sank into the depths, and concerning the king of Syria’s plan to seize Elisha.

Concerning the famine that occurred in Samaria while the Assyrians were besieging it, when a donkey’s head was sold for eighty silver pieces.

[Col. 0742B] Concerning the anointing of King Joash, son of Azariah, whom Jehoiada the pontiff appointed king, and concerning his deeds.

Concerning Amaziah, king of Judah, who struck Edom in the Valley of Salt.

Concerning Jeroboam, king of Israel, who restored Israel’s boundaries.

Concerning those who were brought to Samaria by the king of the Assyrians.

Concerning Hezekiah, king of Judah, and Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, and the blasphemy of Rabshakeh, as well as the striking down of Sennacherib’s army.

Concerning King Hezekiah’s illness and the fifteen years added to his life.

Concerning his riches, displayed to the Chaldeans in the disease of vainglory [Note: [Col. 0741C] Is something missing here?].

Concerning Manasseh and his wickedness.

Concerning King Josiah, Huldah the prophetess [Note: [Col. 0742C] The Vulgate has “Huldah”], and his deeds.

Concerning Nebuchadnezzar, his army, and the evil of the kings of Judah, on account of which Jerusalem was handed over to the Chaldeans to be destroyed.

## THE TEXT OF BOOK IV BEGINS

After the division of the kingdom of Israel between Rehoboam and Jeroboam, after Israel withdrew from the house of David, Scripture continues and says (III Kings XII, 20) [Note: [Col. 0741D] From this passage it is clear that the division formerly proposed for the Books of Kings was very different from the one we now follow. Claudius begins IV Kings here, whereas we have this material at verse 20 of chapter XII of III Kings. Nevertheless, while editing Claudius, we must retain the division that he proposed]:

“Now when all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent for him and summoned him; and when the assembly had gathered, they appointed him king over Israel.”

[Note: [Col. 0741D] You will find this passage for the most part in chapter 14, elsewhere numbered 45, of the book *On Correction and Grace*.]

“It must certainly not be doubted that human wills cannot resist the will of God, who in heaven and on earth has done whatever he wished, and who has also made those things that are still to come, so as to prevent him from doing what he wishes and when he wishes—unless, to cite one example among many, this account of Jeroboam is sufficient: when God wished to give him the kingdom on account of Solomon’s sin, it was in the power of the Israelites either to submit to the aforementioned king or not to submit. This, certainly, lay within their will, so that they could even resist God. Yet God accomplished this through the wills of those very people, unquestionably possessing omnipotent power by which human hearts are inclined in whatever direction pleases him.

“Thus, whenever God wishes to establish kings on earth, he has men’s wills more fully in his power than they themselves have their own.”

[Note: [Col. 0741D] The edition reads *itaque* (“therefore”).]

[Note: [Col. 0741D] Augustine has the following: “Unless perhaps, to mention one example among many, when God wished to give Saul the kingdom, it was in the power of the Israelites either to submit to that man or not to submit,” and so forth. Claudius has altered this somewhat, applying to Jeroboam what Augustine had said about Saul.]

[Note: [Col. 0742D] Augustine inserts several things here that Claudius omitted, as not particularly relevant to his subject.]

### (Chapter 13)

Then Scripture relates that a prophet came from Judah to Bethel to Jeroboam, the sacrilegious king, to rebuke him for the sacrileges of the idols he had made, by which he had turned the children of Israel away from the Lord, the God of their fathers. He was ordered not to eat or drink there; but because he was deceived by a false prophet and disobeyed the word of the Lord, he was killed by a lion on the road.

[Note: [Col. 0742D] Search for this passage in Paterius, and therefore in Gregory the Great; consult Book XXIII of his *Morals* [numbers 53 and 54].]

“What is a human being, whatever his merit may be, if he is abandoned by the protection of his Creator? That protection is thought less necessary if it is always possessed. Yet it is often withdrawn beneficially, so that a person may be shown [Note: [Col. 0742D] That is, “that.” The edition reads “than.”] that, without it, he is nothing.

“Therefore the hand of the Lord sometimes reveals us to ourselves through adversity—the same hand that, while we are unaware of it, carries us in prosperity. For when we are deprived of support and begin to fall, yet are held up by assistance, the fact that we trembled at falling becomes instruction, and the fact that we remain standing becomes protection.

“Let no one, therefore, consider himself possessed of any virtue, even when he is able [Note: [Col. 0743D] “Is able.”] to act courageously. For if divine protection withdraws, he is suddenly overwhelmed feebly in the very place where he boasts [Note: [Col. 0743D] “Boasted.”] of standing firmly.

“For what is the meaning of this? The man of God was sent to prophesy against the altar of Samaria; in the presence of the king he exercised the authority of a free voice, and miraculously stiffened the king’s outstretched arm into rigidity [Note: [Col. 0743D] *In rigore*, ‘into rigidity’]. Yet shortly afterward he mercifully restored it to health. Invited into the king’s house, he refused to eat; and, in order not to eat on the road, he observed the Lord’s prohibition. Yet on that same road he was both deceived and ate, and after eating he perished.

“What, then, do we gather from this matter upon careful reflection? What, so to speak, do we suspect must be feared, except that perhaps he silently boasted to himself that he had despised the king for the sake of the Lord’s commands [Note: [Col. 0743D] The edition reads *gloriatus ei*]. Then, shaken in his inner firmness, he was seized by fault in his action at the very point where glory had stolen into his heart [Note: [Col. 0743D] ‘Had arisen’]. He was deceived by the false prophet’s words, so that he might learn that what enabled him to resist the king’s command had not been his own strength.

“Yet rightly he received the sentence of death from the mouth of the one whose deception had caused him to depart from the command of life, so that he might truly receive punishment from the very source through which he had carelessly committed the fault.”

The text continues:

### (XIII, 21)

“Thus says the Lord: Because you were disobedient to the mouth of the Lord and did not keep the command that the Lord your God commanded you; because you returned, ate bread, and drank water in the place where he commanded you not to eat bread or drink water, your corpse shall not be brought into the tomb of your fathers,” and the rest.

[Note: [Col. 0743D] Augustine transmitted what follows, marked with lines in the usual manner, in chapter 7, elsewhere numbered 9, of the book *On the Care of the Dead* [elsewhere *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*].]

“How great this punishment should be reckoned, if we think according to the Gospel, where we have learned that after the body has been killed there is nothing to fear—that the lifeless limbs should suffer nothing [Note: [Col. 0744D] The edition reads *exanima*, ‘lifeless’]—and indeed it should not be called a punishment at all.

“But if we consider the human affection one has for one’s own flesh, he could be terrified or saddened while alive by what he would not experience once dead. This was the punishment: his spirit grieved that this would happen to his body, although when it happened he would feel no grief. The Lord wished to punish his servant only to this extent, since he had not refused to fulfill the command through his own stubbornness, but, deceived by another’s falsehood, believed that he was obeying when he was not.

“For one must not think that he was killed by the beast’s bite in such a way that his soul was then dragged away to Tartarus as a punishment. The very lion that had killed him guarded his body, while the animal on which he had ridden remained unharmed, and stood fearlessly together with that savage beast at its master’s funeral. By this wondrous sign it is evident that the man of God was restrained temporally even unto death rather than punished after death.

“Regarding this matter, when the Apostle had mentioned, on account of the offenses of certain people [Note: [Col. 0744D] The edition reads *quasdam*, ‘certain’], the illnesses and deaths of many (I Cor. XI, 31–32), he says: ‘If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord. But when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world.’

“The very man who had deceived him buried him with considerable honor in his own tomb and arranged to be buried beside his bones. In this way he hoped that his own bones might be spared when the time came when, according to the prophecy of that man of God (IV Kings XXIII, 16–17), Josiah, king of Judah, would bring out the bones of many of the dead in that land and defile with those same bones the sacrilegious altars that had been erected for graven images. For he spared the tomb in which the prophet lay, who had foretold these things more than four hundred years earlier; and on his account the burial of the man who had deceived him was not violated either.

“Indeed, through that affection by which no one has ever hated his own flesh (Eph. V, 29), the man who had killed his soul through falsehood had made provision for his own corpse. Thus, because everyone naturally loves his flesh, it was a punishment for him to learn that he would not be in the tomb of his fathers; and it was a matter of care for the other man to ensure that his bones would be spared if he lay beside one whose tomb no one would violate.

“The martyrs of Christ, striving for the truth, overcame this affection. It is no wonder that they despised what they would not feel after death had taken place, since they could not be overcome by the torments of those whom they perceived while alive.

“Certainly God, who did not permit the lion to touch again the prophet’s body—the body that the lion itself had killed—and who made the killer its guardian, could have prevented dogs from touching the bodies of his servants when they had been thrown before them. He could, I say, have restrained human savagery in countless ways, so that they would not dare to burn corpses or scatter their ashes into the air [Note: [Col. 0744D] The edition lacks *in aera* (‘into the air’), but reads: ‘nor scatter [them] as ashes.’]. But this trial too had to be added to the manifold variety of temptations, so that the strength of the confession which would not yield to the savagery of persecution for the sake of bodily safety would not tremble for the honor of the tomb; and finally, so that faith in the resurrection would not fear the destruction of bodies.

“Therefore these things too had to be permitted, so that, even after such examples of horror, the martyrs, burning with confession of Christ, might also become witnesses to this truth: they had learned that those who killed their bodies afterward had nothing left that they could do. For whatever they might do to dead bodies, they would in fact do nothing, since the one who had departed from the flesh, which lacked all life, could feel nothing, nor could the one who created it lose anything from it.”

Passing over much of the history in the Book of Kings, we hasten briefly toward the time of Ahab, the most wicked king, and his sacrilegious wife Jezebel, so that we may discuss, however slightly, the virtues of the holy prophets Elijah and Elisha.

### (III Kings XVI, 28)

Meanwhile Scripture relates that Ahab, son of Zambri, reigned over Israel in Samaria for twenty-two years after his father’s death, and did evil in the sight of the Lord more than all who had preceded him. It was not enough for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat; in addition he took as his wife Jezebel, daughter of Methbaal [Note: [Col. 0745D] “Ethbaal”], king of the Sidonians. He went and served Baal in the temple that he had built in Samaria, and planted a sacred grove there. Ahab also added to his deeds the provocation of the Lord, the God of Israel, more than all the kings of Israel who had preceded him.

A *lucus*—a sacred grove—is a dense, wooded place, so called because little light (*lux*) penetrates it: a place covered with many trees, a pleasant place where there are many trees. The word *lucus* is used by *catachresis* [Note: [Col. 0745D] “By antiphrasis”], because it lacks light, being enclosed by the dense trees and excessive shade of the groves and depriving the place of the sun’s light. It may also be derived from *conlucere*, “to shine together,” because the frequent lights used there for pagan religion and worship caused it to shine.

Pagans used to consult demons in such groves and received oracles from them through signs and voices. Hence they were also called *fana*—shrines—from *fari*, “to speak.” For in the days of Elijah, when the Jewish people had already been divided into two factions and Ahab, having seized the kingdom of the Israelites, held its summit, he took as his wife Jezebel, a woman of foreign race and profane mind. Through her care and persistence the worship of idols advanced so far that both king and people were led over into the sacrilegious rite.

[Col. 0745C] The ancient artificer of tyranny, the devil, grew fierce against the injury done to God, striving to destroy the manifold worship of God. He grew fierce in the heart of the woman, at whose instigation the divine law and its priesthood were despised. The prophets were killed, the altars removed; everything stood aghast and shuddered at so great a crime. I mean the world, wasting away in every part because human error ascribed the Creator’s name to its limbs and forms.

“But perhaps you ask that it be shown to you whether the elements fear sinful human beings. Hear Jeremiah, the great prophet, crying out with a divine voice (Jer. II, 12): ‘The heavens were horrified at this, and the earth was shaken, because my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cracked cisterns that cannot hold water.’

“Thus the elements were disturbed—not in their function but in their affection—because, as I said, human error imposed upon them the unique name of the Godhead and, in blind devotion, rendered to them the service owed to the Creator.

“Elijah stood in the midst of this great peril of souls; he stood amid the very shipwreck of the world, which had been brought upon the earth not by a flood of waters but by the punitive and blind rivalry of the devil. For while the others remained hidden, he alone, like a burning lamp, offered himself to those whom he saw submerged in the darkness of profound night—now warning, now rebuking, now healing, and now even threatening (Jer. I, 6).

“But light brought to the blind, and speech addressed to the deaf, are of no use. The disastrous error increased day by day, and the shadow of death covered every creature. The wretched human race bowed down before every form and every appearance.

“What, indeed, shall I say about the sun, moon, and stars, about the earth and the principal features of the sea, and the most splendid elements? Before all living creatures—flying creatures, quadrupeds, reptiles, and even flies and worms—the image of the eternal and only God was prostrated.

“How, then, could that mind bear it—the mind wholly devoted to piety and faith, I mean that of the prophet Elijah—seeing such a collapse and such destruction of souls? The body of that people lay bound by a royal disease; and, as though its members had already been torn apart from the soul and had lost sensation, thrown across crags and cliffs, through forests and sacred groves, it possessed no remnants of the divine image within itself.

“No cup, no kind of medicine would help it, even if one were offered, because its limbs pushed away whatever was applied. Iron had to be used; the wound had to be healed with blood. As Isaiah says, the disease had spread from the head to the feet (chapter XVI, 34).”

[Note: [Col. 0745D] You will find what follows in Bede’s *Questions on the Books of Kings*, question 16 of the thirty questions.]

In the days of Ahab’s reign, Hiel [Note: [Col. 0745D] “Hiel”] of Bethel built Jericho. He laid its foundations in Abiram [Note: [Col. 0745D] “In the firstborn”], his firstborn, and set up its gates in Segub, his youngest.

“The meaning is clear: when the aforementioned founder of the city began to lay its foundations, his firstborn, who was called Abiram, died; and when he attempted to fortify the gates after the city had been built, he lost the youngest of his sons, named Segub. Joshua had predicted that this would happen when, after destroying the city, he delivered it over to the ban: ‘Cursed before the Lord be the man who raises up and builds this city of Jericho. In his firstborn let him lay its foundations [Note: [Col. 0745D] The edition reads ‘let its foundations be laid’], and in his youngest child let him set up its gates.’

“Since Hiel [Note: [Col. 0746D] ‘Living’] is interpreted as ‘uniting with God,’ and Bethel as ‘house of God,’ Hiel of Bethel restores the walls of Jericho, which had been destroyed and placed under the ban by Joshua.

[Note: [Col. 0746D] Cornelius à Lapide here notes the same things that our writer, whom Eucherius believes and calls Angelomus, transmits. Yet Angelomus has so much in common with our writer!]

“When one of those who has assumed the religious habit in the Church returns to the crimes which the Lord Jesus had forgiven him [Note: [Col. 0746D] “Had forgiven.”] on the day of baptism, and, by living luxuriously, again pursues the pomp of the devil that he himself had renounced; when, leaving the ecclesiastical truth with which he has been imbued, he revives the doctrines of errors or the fables of the pagans, as though coming forth from Bethel, he raises up the ruins of Jericho.

“Such a person is rightly cursed before the Lord. He loses his firstborn in laying the foundations of the wicked city, and his youngest in setting up its gates, because he has lost both the foundations of faith, from which good buildings should begin [Col. 0747A] [Note: [Col. 0747D] ‘The house’], and the barriers of good action by which he ought to have been brought to completion [Note: [Col. 0747D] ‘He loses’].

“I have also expounded these things in an allegorical sense, so that you may remember how true is the Apostle’s statement (I Cor. X, 11): ‘All these things happened to them figuratively, but they were written for our sake.’”

The text continues.

Then Elijah the Tishbite, from the inhabitants of Gilead, said to Ahab: “As the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, in whose sight I stand.”

[Note: [Col. 0747D] You will find this in Paterius, who took it from Book XI of Gregory’s *Morals* [number 49].]

“We should know that we come into the sight of the Lord in two ways. In one way, by carefully weighing our sins here, we place ourselves in his sight and judge ourselves through weeping. In another way, we come into the sight of the Lord when at the final judgment we stand before the judge’s tribunal. For whenever we bring the power of our Creator back to our awareness, we stand in his sight.

“Thus it is rightly said now through the man of God, Elijah: ‘As the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, in whose sight I stand.’”

[Note: [Col. 0747D] The word *Christus* appears in the exemplar, but it is entirely inappropriate here. Thereafter Claudius either copied, in part, the old translation of the homily attributed to Chrysostom, which is read in Montfaucon’s edition, volume II, page 730 and following, and is entitled *On the Apostle Peter and the Prophet Elijah*, or at least consulted it. See number 2 of that homily.]

Elijah now approaches—not as he was accustomed to do, gentle and mild, but harsh and severe—the very head of the body; he approaches King Ahab himself and says to him: “As the Lord, the God of hosts, the God of Israel, lives, in whose sight I stand: there shall be neither rain nor dew during these years, except at the word of my mouth.”

Great is the power of prophetic dignity: the speech is human, but its effect is divine. A human being speaks on earth, and the heavenly powers obey his command. One word of the prophet moved all creation, and, sounding upon the ground, wonderfully shook the air.

The order of human service was disturbed, and the harmony of the elements established through the ages withered away, when moisture was denied to dryness and cold to heat. Yet the elements gladly accept their punishment, provided that it contributes either to human salvation or to the honor of the Creator.

Elijah is ordered to withdraw and hide. Food is supplied to him from heaven by birds. Then the torrent dries up, and his cups fail. For the sentence, proceeding like fire, penetrated in some manner into the earth’s vital parts and immediately dried everything.

There was no beauty in the fields, no loveliness in the meadows. Even the banks, once adorned with flowering shrubs, languished in the most wretched squalor when the springs were deprived of their waters and the rivers of their streams.

The prophet moves on from there and, at God’s command, goes to prepared storerooms, forgetting every other concern and thinking only of himself. He is not moved by human feeling or bent by any compassion. He does not look to the very laws of nature; he does not see the little child breathing out its life beneath its mother’s dried-up breast; he passes with a gloomy face by the profound hunger that has exhausted old and young, who are no longer bodies but corpses; he does not answer the farmer who pleads or the husbandman who begs. He has become more savage than wild beasts and, made more brutal than war itself, despises the entire human race.

And the word of the Lord came to Elijah, saying (III Kings XVII, 5): “Depart from here, go toward the east, and hide yourself by the torrent Cherith, which is opposite the Jordan. You shall drink from the torrent, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.”

So he went and acted according to the word of the Lord. The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning, and likewise bread and meat in the evening; and he drank from the torrent. After some days the torrent dried up, for there had been no rain upon the earth.

Elijah, therefore, is rightly compared with the Son of God, with whom both the authority and the name truly correspond. For *Elijah* is interpreted as “My God,” a name that belongs substantially to the Son of God, who originally claims for himself the authority to do whatever he wishes, since he testifies that everything belonging to the Father is also his. *Tishbite* is interpreted as “capturing” or “turning back.”

The Psalmist says of the Lord (Ps. LXVII, 19): “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive.” And again (Ps. CXXV, 4): “Turn back, O Lord, our captivity, as a torrent in the south.”

And lest anyone perhaps be troubled that I have compared Elijah with the Son of God, let him read the Epistle to the Hebrews; there he will find the Apostle saying (Heb. VII, 3): “In a certain manner this Melchizedek, made like the Son of God, remains a priest forever: without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end.”
