This could in fact correspond to no human being except the Son of God, whose origin—whence or from whom he derives it—Scripture nowhere indicates. Scripture likewise testifies the same concerning Elijah, when it suddenly introduces his name and does not at all state from what tribe or family he arose.

The torrent Cherith, which is interpreted as “division” or “cutting off,” most certainly corresponds to the Jewish people. That people is rightly compared with a torrent, because what had been divinely entrusted to it for observance through the Law was destined to be brought to an end at the appointed time of the Lord’s Incarnation, when the shadows and images of the Law are known to have been fulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 0748D] Claudius took the following marked passage from chapter 34 of Book XII *Against Faustus*, and the same interpretation is given by Isidore in chapter 8 of III Kings.]

“Afterward, during the time of famine, Elijah is fed by ravens, which bring bread in the morning and meat in the evening. Do not the Manichaeans understand Christ in those books—the Christ to whom sinners confess, as one who in some manner hungers for our salvation—now possessing the first fruits of faith [Note: [Col. 0748D] The edition reads *fidem*, ‘faith.’] in the Spirit, but at the end, as it were at the evening of the age, receiving also the resurrection of the flesh?”

Bread and meat, which Scripture declares the ravens brought to Elijah in the morning and evening, may also be understood as works of mercy, which the Lord testified are given to himself in strangers and the needy (Matt. X, 4). In the meat, however, one should understand the chastisement of the body, or the sufferings that all the saints are read to have inflicted upon themselves or endured from persecutors for the love or worship of God, in the morning and evening—that is, under the Old Testament and under the evangelical proclamation.

[Col. 0749A]

### (Chapter XVII, 7–8 and following)

When the brook had dried up, the Lord said to Elijah: “Rise and go to Zarephath of Sidon, and remain there; for I have commanded a widow there to feed you.” He rose and went to Zarephath. When he had come to the gate of the city, a widow appeared to him gathering sticks. He called her and said: “Give me, I pray you, a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to fetch it, he called after her and said: “Bring me also, I beg you, a morsel of bread in your hand.” She replied: “As the Lord your God lives, I have no bread except a handful of flour in a jar, and a little oil in a flask. Behold, I am gathering two sticks, so that I may go in and prepare it for myself and my son, that we may eat and die.” [Col. 0749B]

To her Elijah said: “Do not be afraid; but go and do as you have said. Nevertheless, first make for me from that little flour a small cake baked under the ashes, and bring it to me; but afterward you shall make one for yourself and your son. For thus says the Lord God of Israel: The jar of flour shall not fail, nor the flask of oil diminish, until the day when the Lord gives rain upon the face of the earth.” She went and did according to Elijah’s word, and he, she, her household, and her son ate; and from that day the jar of flour did not fail, and the flask of oil was not diminished, according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken through Elijah. [Col. 0749D]

[Note: I suspect that much has been taken from Augustine for the explanation of this passage; but I have not yet found the place which I should cite. Did Claudius consult some sermon that is now unavailable to us? Let the reader judge.] [Col. 0749D]

To pass over for the moment what sacramental meaning lies hidden in the fact that he is sent from the land of Israel to the region of Sidon, whence Jezebel, the source and cause of all evils, arose, let us briefly consider this: he goes to a widow suffering from poverty and situated at the very boundary between life and death, who had gone out to gather sticks and obtain the final means of sustenance both for herself and for her children. [Col. 0749C]

But Elijah, seeing the woman worn out by squalor, is neither moved nor delayed; he does not turn back his step, but thrusts himself upon her and immerses himself in her condition, becoming himself more burdensome to her than hunger. He says to her: “Give me a little water, that I may drink.” [Col. 0749D]

O blessed man, if the widow had answered you and, driving you away with justified words, had said: “Why do you ask from me what you have taken away from everyone? Why do you seek from a woman what you have denied to the world? This universal need, this poverty, has been brought about by the authority of your mouth. I ought to be satisfied by you—and you come to me?”

But the woman used none of these words, either in heart or in speech. At once her devoted mind, not unworthy of an evangelical reward, brings a cup of cold water to the thirsty prophet. [Col. 0749D]

Elijah adds and says: “Bring me also a morsel of bread in your hand.” But she replies: “As the Lord your God lives, I have no bread except a handful of flour in a jar. Behold, I am gathering two sticks, so that I may go in and prepare it for myself and my son; we shall eat and die.”

But what then? Elijah says to her: [Col. 0750A] “Have confidence,” he says, “and do according to my word. But first make me from it a small cake baked under the ashes; afterward you shall make one for yourself and your son.”

[Note: I ask that what follows be compared with number 3 of the homily entitled *On Saints Peter and Elijah*, which Montfaucon placed among the doubtful works of Chrysostom, volume II, page 729. For many passages are taken from it, though with some variation. From this fact it is quite clear that the homily had long ago been translated into Latin, and perhaps belongs among those which we learn Cassiodorus translated.] [Col. 0749D]

O magnificent spirit of the woman! O marvelous resolve of her mind! O deed truly made venerable throughout the ages! He asks for a drink, and she immediately offers it. What perhaps kings already lacked, what the rich did not possess, the widow distributed from her abundance. He asks for bread from one who, together with her son, was to die on the following day. She does not deny that she has it, although she plainly confesses what she possesses, and she is not afraid to disclose the truth. To the one who asks—indeed, in a certain sense, demands—she lays the whole matter before him: the quantity of her provisions and the number of persons, wishing him to be a guest no less than a judge.

She did not say: “I cannot do what you command.” She did not say: “Consider the widow, wasting away not so much from concern for herself as for her son. Consider the chorus of little children; do not take me away from them, and do not leave a mother deprived of so many children. You are the one who condemned the whole world by the sentence of famine. While you were angry, the entire human race perished. Then you passed through your homeland; you traversed almost the whole land and province of your people. Nowhere did a wealthy man meet you who would receive the hungry man and refresh the fasting one. [Col. 0750B]

“I alone have met you—or perhaps I alone remain—who, besides lacking money, am also weighed down by the burden of children, and suffer this multitude of offspring as a plague still heavier than all else. I leave the house not to gather ears of grain but sticks, not to bring food but fuel. Since I cannot free them from hunger, I try at least to protect them from the cold.

“Certainly, since you are so cruel that you do not consider what you impose, you ought at least to have been content to eat with us what remained, or first to have allowed the children to be filled, so that what was left might then be offered to you. But you command that food be prepared for you alone—and not merely alone, but you want to be filled first. You show no concern for the wretched, and even the reverence owed to nature does not restrain you. You want to take the final food from the very teeth of little children and infants.” [Col. 0750C]

But she neither did nor said any of these things. Rather, undaunted, she runs and completes what has been commanded.

[Note: Claudius transferred almost everything that follows, though with some variation, to his own work from the homily *On Saints Peter and Elijah*.]

At that time there was a spectacle most pleasing to angels and human beings: among the nations, and in a profane land, a widowed woman was already a daughter of Abraham, much more hospitable than her own father and much more humane than the father of the faith (Gen. XVIII, 2, etc.). [Col. 0750D]

Abraham was indeed hospitable and deeply devoted to strangers; but he was truly wealthy, he was rich, and he had the ability to do whatever he wished, because his spirit was less than his resources, and his feeling did not surpass his spirit. But this woman, who had been deprived not only of her husband but also of her resources, who was poor not only by birth but also constrained by the calamity of the time, had come to such poverty that she could possess nothing in the house except what increased her hunger. The crowd of children itself was a burden heavier than famine. Yet amid all these evils a generous spirit and devoted mind prevailed. [Col. 0751A]

She goes on and, as the man of God had commanded, faithfully completes the task; she receives the Prophet and welcomes him. With what face, with what words, shall I praise this woman?

“Nothing worthy comes to my mind that could equal the spirit of such virtue. For I consider how, out of zeal for kindness, she cast aside every natural affection, caring neither for herself nor for her little children. Nothing could recall her from her purpose of mind: neither the weakness of her sex nor the tenderness of a mother’s devotion toward her children.

“She killed the duties of nature for the sake of hospitality, and the devoted spirit of a mother became toward her guest a cruel tomb for her children.” [Col. 0751B]

[Note: Montfaucon’s translation has: “One could see her entrails cast out and the Prophet received; she made the whole crowd of her children into a tomb. For, as far as the widow’s intention went, they were dead; but by God’s kindness it came about that they lived and were unharmed.”] [Col. 0751D]

So far as it depended upon her, the children were dead and, in a certain sense, strangled and buried by their mother’s hands. But so far as God’s mercy was concerned, they did not truly die, nor were they consumed by hunger or starvation; for while all the others were perishing, they alone grew strong.

Immediately, the Prophet, rewarding such faith with a divine recompense, said: “As the Lord lives, your jar of flour shall not fail, and your vessel of oil shall not diminish.”

Thus the widow’s hand became an everlasting winepress and a mill continually pouring forth. And why do I speak of the woman’s hand? At the Prophet’s word, the widow’s whole house became a storehouse of the devout. There was no dew there, no rain, no breath of spring, no warm sunlight, no cloud, no plow, no farmer, no cultivator; rather, in every respect, the Prophet’s word abundantly supplied the widow’s needs.” [Col. 0751C]

It should nevertheless be known that, according to the Seventy translators, this widow is said to have had not one son only but several.

[Note: Berengaudus teaches many things similar to these in his commentary on the Apocalypse, at the words: “And when he had opened the fourth seal.”] [Col. 0752D]

The woman who is recorded as having lived in Zarephath bore the figure of the Church. Abandoned for a long time by her creator, she did not know the people of the true faith and, like a poor woman, nourished them with scant alms—that is, she taught the word without its fruit—until the prophetic word should come, which was suffering hunger in Judea because the fleece of Israel had been dried up, as it were, and the gate of heaven had been closed.

She is called a widow because, being a gentile, she had not yet been devoted to divine worship and did not possess knowledge of the sacred Law. Zarephath, moreover, is a city whose name is interpreted as “burning,” or “tribulation of bread,” or “distress of bread.” It must be understood as the present world, in which the burning of the worst desire blazes, where concern is devoted to acquiring superfluous possessions, as though to trapping birds. There, too, there had previously been the burning of dire desire and a scarcity of spiritual bread. [Col. 0751D]

Therefore, as Scripture declares concerning Elijah, when our Lord came to the Church of the nations and found her outside the gate of the city—that is, in her ancestral and ingrained error—he did not summon her to the confession of his name through signs, miracles, and mighty wonders, as he had done for Israel. Rather, he commanded her by his word alone, saying: [Col. 0752A]

“Give me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink, and a morsel of bread in your hand.”

Water in a vessel must be understood as faith of the heart (Rom. X, 10), by which one believes unto righteousness. A morsel of bread in the hand must be understood as the work of mercy, by which faith and works are joined to one another by a certain indissoluble bond. For when one of them fails, the other cannot stand at all. As the Apostle James said earlier (II, 26): “Faith without works is dead.” And works without faith become empty and futile.

Thus the Church, in the figure of that widowed woman, by going at the Lord’s command to bring him water, in a certain sense displays to the Lord the faith prepared in her heart. She confesses that she did not yet have bread—namely, works worthy of divine worship—but testifies that she has a little flour in a jar and a little oil in a flask. [Col. 0752B]

The handful of flour in the jar indicates the natural law, implanted in human nature by divine generosity, through which good and evil are distinguished and through which one does not do to another at any time what one does not wish done to oneself.

[Note: The exemplar reads: “not do it to another at any time.”] [Col. 0752D]

The little oil in the flask must be understood as rational understanding, through which the creature understands the Creator and strives to please him by pious works. She therefore said that she had little because she had not yet received the gift of spiritual grace through the sacrament of baptism.

Yet there the flour and oil are blessed by the prophetic word: that is, the fruit and joy of charity—or the grace of the Lord’s body and the anointing of chrism—are made fruitful by the unfailing word through the gift of heaven. Until now, the oil of spiritual joy and the flour of blessing have not failed in her vessels, while the other nations, which do not believe, suffer the want of divine bread and devote themselves to an unprofitable pursuit. [Col. 0752C]

As for her statement that she was gathering two sticks, with which she would bake the little flour she possessed and, after eating it with her children, await the end of death, it must be understood as follows: in the two sticks, not only by the name of wood but also by the number of the pieces of wood, she foreshadowed the mystery of the cross. Through it she believed that bread of eternal life would be given to herself and to her children—that is, to the people who would believe in Christ—and that they would die to past sins through the washing of baptism, according to what the Lord proclaimed in the Gospel (John XX, 29): “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”

By the small cake baked under the ashes she already foreshadowed that which, at the beginning of the faith, the nations are read as having determined to observe through the Apostle’s letter: that they should abstain only from the worship of idols, from fornication, and from things strangled. These requirements, granted by the Apostles in wise counsel to people still uncultivated and savage, were recognized as very slight and small in comparison with the preaching of the Gospel, into which they were afterward introduced. [Col. 0752D]

When he says, “Make it first for me,” he intended this for all believers from the nations: they were not to attribute to their own merits the fact that, while Israel was hardened and rejected, they themselves were saved, but to him who in his mercy enabled them to believe. [Col. 0753A]

As for what was said to Cain, “He does not offer rightly who does not divide rightly”—that is, he who attributes to himself rather than to God all the good that he possesses—

[Note: Gen. IV, 7, from the old version of the Septuagint, which Augustine follows in *The City of God*, book XV, chapter 10.]

—or, alternatively, the cake baked under the ashes must be understood historically as the Law, which contained spiritual understanding covered by the letter. The leavened bread, however, must be understood as the preaching of the Gospel, into which testimonies from the Old Testament have been inserted like leaven.

As for the statement that Elijah fed the one who was feeding him, it must be understood in this way: all the faithful indeed feed God by their faith and pious works; nevertheless, the fact that they have these things is granted to them by him. For, as it is written (James I, 17), “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights.” The divine gifts bestowed upon those who fear God are in no way wholly diminished. [Col. 0753B]

Again, in another sense: by the cake baked under the ashes which the true Elijah, our Lord, commands to be offered to him for food by the Church of the nations, what else should be understood but the satisfaction of penitents? The Psalmist sings the same thing in the person of a penitent when he says (Ps. CI, 10): “For I ate ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping.” By such satisfactions the Lord urges that he be fed.

After these events, the son of the woman, the mistress of the household, became ill, and his illness was extremely severe, so that no breath remained in him. She said to Elijah: “What have I to do with you, man of God? You have come to me so that my iniquities might be remembered and my son might be killed?” [Col. 0753C]

Elijah said to her: “Give me your son.” He took him from her bosom, carried him to the upper room where he stayed, and laid him upon his bed. He then stretched himself over the child and measured himself over him three times. The child’s soul returned to him, and he revived. Elijah brought him down from the upper room, gave him to his mother, and said: “Behold, your son lives.”

She replied: “Now by this I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of God in your mouth is true.”

The statement that the woman’s son was held by an excessive illness and brought even to the point of death is recognized as having the following meaning.

After someone has received knowledge of God or the preaching of the Gospel, and has tasted good works, he must necessarily languish in the most serious affliction because of crimes committed and errors of the past. For, as it is written: [Col. 0753D]

“He who increases knowledge increases” [the salutary pain of repentance] “sorrow.”

[Note: Eccles. I, 18: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow.”]

Through continual chastisement he does violence to his own perdition, so that he may escape everlasting death and attain the life of eternal blessedness. The Apostle Paul confirms this when he says (I Cor. XV, 9) that he is not worthy to be called an Apostle because he persecuted the Church of God and attacked it.

In the descent into the font, the one who has believed in Christ dies to original sin and former vices through baptism. Therefore, after being raised to the upper room of the sacred altar, it is clear that he is made alive through the anointing of chrism, the invocation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and communion in the Lord’s body and blood. [Col. 0754A]

Then from the whole Church, whose figure was represented by the child’s mother, this confession is uttered: that the Lord Jesus is the true Son of God and is seated in the Father’s bosom or at his right hand. Then, brought down again from the altar, he is restored alive to the assembly of the faithful, as to his mother.

Or, in another sense: after a believer has mortified his members, through repentance and satisfaction, with respect to his former vices, and after being raised above earthly desires and carnal longings, has merited life through meditation on the Law and the Prophets and through evangelical preaching, and has become a temple of God, he strives to direct the intention of his mind there where Christ sits at the right hand of the Father. Though still dwelling in the flesh, he already endeavors to have his manner of life in heaven. [Col. 0754B]

However much a person may strive to raise his mind to God, and may rejoice that through a certain rapture of contemplation he clings to Christ the Lord in the heights, the nature of the body, to which the soul is joined, nevertheless compels him to be drawn back from the heights to lower things.

As for the statement that Elijah stretched himself over the child and measured himself over him three times, it is evident that the Lord fulfilled this very thing when, through the Law and the prophecies of the Prophets, or through his own preaching, he brought salvation to the people of the nations.

The words of Elijah concerning the widow, already expounded figuratively above, are found very differently in ancient translations. In them Elijah entreats the Lord, saying. [Col. 0754C]

[Note: What follows was transmitted by Augustine in question 5 of book II of *On Various Questions to Simplicianus*.]

“O Lord, witness of this widow, with whom I dwell in her house, have you done evil by killing her son?”

Nothing in this statement would trouble the mind if the true pronunciation were preserved. For it is the voice of one who does not believe that God would have done such evil to the widow who had received the prophet so piously, especially at the time when he was there and she had brought him all her meager livelihood amid such great and utter poverty.

Thus it was said as though he were asking: “O Lord, witness of this widow, with whom I dwell in her house: have you not done evil by killing her son?” The implied meaning is that the Lord, who was indeed witness of the woman’s heart, saw how great her piety was, and for this reason had sent Elijah himself to her; he had not killed her son in order to do evil, but to display a miracle for the glory of his name, by which he might commend so great a prophet both to those then living and to posterity. [Col. 0754D]

As the Lord says (John XI, 4), Lazarus had not died unto death, but so that God might be glorified in his Son.

The subsequent events also prove this. Elijah himself trusted that the event had not occurred in order that his hostess might be afflicted with bitter grief, but rather so that God might show the widow more magnificently what sort of servant of God she had received.

Scripture continues and says:

“And he breathed upon your child, and called upon the Lord, and said: ‘O Lord my God, let the soul of this child return into him now.’ And it happened so.” [Col. 0755A]

This prayer, in which Elijah asked so briefly and faithfully that the child should rise again, sufficiently indicates with what feeling the preceding words were spoken. The woman herself also showed that her son had been killed for the purpose Elijah had presumed, when she uttered those words not in affirmation but in rejection.

For when she had received her son alive, she said (verse 24): “Behold, now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of God in your mouth is most certain.”

There are many things in Scripture which, unless they are pronounced in that manner, fall into the opposite meaning.

[Note: They should be pronounced.]

Such is the passage (Rom. VIII, 33): “Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect? God who justifies.” [Col. 0755D]

If you answer as though you were affirming this, you see what great perversity arises. Thus it must be pronounced as though it said: “Is it God who justifies?”—with the implication, certainly not. Accordingly, I think Elijah’s statement is clear, though the failure to preserve its pronunciation had made it obscure.” [Col. 0755B]

### (III Kings XVIII, 1, 7 and following)

The word of the Lord came to Elijah: “Go and show yourself to Ahab, so that I may give rain upon the face of the earth.”

He went, and on the way he met Obadiah, the steward of King Ahab, and said: “Go and announce to Ahab: Elijah is here.” He went and announced it to him. Ahab came to meet him and said to Elijah: “Are you the one who troubles Israel?” [Col. 0755C]

Elijah answered him: “I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father’s house, because you abandoned the commandment of the Lord and followed the Baals. Nevertheless, now send and gather all Israel to me on Mount Carmel, and the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the prophets of the sacred groves, who eat at Jezebel’s table.”

Ahab therefore sent for all the children of Israel and gathered the prophets on Mount Carmel.

Elijah approached all the people and said: “How long will you limp between two sides? If the Lord is God, follow him; but if Baal is God, follow him.” The people did not answer him a word.

Elijah said to them again: “I alone remain a prophet of the Lord, while the prophets of Baal are four hundred and fifty men. Let two oxen be given to us. Let them choose one ox for themselves, cut it into pieces, and place it upon the wood, but let them not put fire beneath it. I also shall prepare the other ox and place it upon the wood, but I shall not put fire beneath it.

“Let them invoke the names of their gods, and I shall invoke the name of the Lord. The God who answers by fire—he shall be God.”

All the people answered and said: “An excellent proposal.”

Elijah said to the prophets of Baal: “Choose one ox and prepare it first, because you are more numerous.”

They did so. They invoked the name of Baal from morning until midday, but there was neither a voice nor anyone who answered. [lacuna] They cut themselves with knives and lances according to their custom until they were covered with blood. [Col. 0755D]

When midday had passed and the time had arrived at which the true sacrifice ought to be offered—

[Note: I do not know why the word “true” has been added, unless perhaps it refers to the legitimate sacrifice which he was afterward to offer to God. On this matter see verse 36.]

—Elijah said to the people: “Come to me.” When the people had come to him, he repaired the altar of the Lord that had been destroyed. He took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, and built an altar in the name of the Lord. He made a channel around the altar, as large as would contain two measures of seed, placed the wood upon the altar, and said: “Fill four jars with water and pour it over the burnt offering and the wood.”

When they had done this, he ordered them to do the same a second and a third time. The trench and the channel were filled with water. [Col. 0756A]

[Note: What follows I found, with some slight variation, in the homily entitled *On Saints Peter and Elijah*, which, as I have already said, Montfaucon placed among the doubtful homilies of Chrysostom, volume II, page 729. See, I beg you, number 4 of that homily, page 737.] [Col. 0755D]

See why Elijah also does this, and pay close attention. Blessed Elijah possessed knowledge of everything that was done in the temples of demons, both through the grace of his prophetic dignity and through his devotion to divine worship. [Col. 0756B]

“He knew, among their other foolish rather than clever contrivances, a fraud of this kind that had been devised so that the souls of wretched people might more easily be ensnared: their altars were not simply set before the feet of the shrine, but a projecting platform was constructed above them, beneath which a pyre was supported by an underground vaulted passage. From the opposite side, through a hidden entrance in a hollow wall, one descended to it, and through open cavities the servant of deception secretly supplied prepared fires at the time of sacrifice.

“Thus, when the minds of the wretched were struck with amazement, and they saw no flames applied from above but observed the victim suddenly consumed, they believed that the fires had been brought from heaven by an invisible power. [Col. 0756C]

“Therefore, so that unbelieving minds might not suspect the same thing concerning divine altars, he ordered the trench that he had commanded to be made to be filled with water, so that, if there were any pit beneath the altar, it might be exposed, or so that the water descending downward might extinguish any hidden fires.

“Nor was it enough to wet the place once: this was done a third time. But the Prophet was not satisfied even with this; he ordered the very wood of the altar to be flooded, so that, when every suspicion of fraud had been removed, neither the king, nor the people, nor the priests of the demons themselves would doubt that the power was divine.” [Col. 0756C]

[Note: Verse 36, but with a considerable difference between the Vulgate and this interpretation. The homily which I have said is among the doubtful works of Chrysostom, and which is being copied here almost word for word, cites this interpretation.] [Col. 0756D]

When the time had come for the burnt offering to be presented, Elijah approached the altar and cried out, saying:

“O Lord my God, hear me today by fire, as you heard me by water, so that this people may know that you are the Lord God of Israel, and that I am your servant, and that I have done these things because of you. Hear me, Lord; hear me by fire, and let this people know that you are God, and that you have turned the heart of this people backward.”

And behold, while he was crying out, fire fell from heaven and devoured the burnt offering, the wood, and the stones, as well as the dust and the water that was in the trench of the channel, licking it up.

When all the people saw this, they fell upon their faces and said: “The Lord, he is God! The Lord, he is God!” [Col. 0757A]

Elijah said to them: “Seize all the infamous prophets, and let not one of them escape.” They seized them, and Elijah immediately led them to the brook Kishon, where he ordered them to be slaughtered.

The most merciful God, who does not forget to show mercy and does not restrain his mercies in anger, once again deigned to send Elijah to Israel his son, so that he might give them the rain of evangelical preaching.

The three years of famine foreshadowed that the knowledge of the Holy Trinity had been absent from the Jewish people, or from the whole world. Ahab, whose name is interpreted as “brother of the father,” and of whom Scripture also declares that he killed the prophets of God, bore the figure of the chief priests.

When Ahab says to Elijah—

[Note: These words were omitted in the preceding scriptural passage, but they occur at verse 17.] [Col. 0757D]

“Are you the one who troubles Israel?”—the chief priests are also read as having said the same thing about the Lord to Pilate (Luke XXIII, 2): “We have found this man subverting our nation.” [Col. 0757B]

For, as the Lord is recorded as having reproached them, they were sons of their father the devil, whose works they desired to do, wickedly proclaiming that the author of their life should be crucified: “You are of your father the devil,” the Lord says (John VIII, 44), “and you wish to do your father’s works. He was a murderer from the beginning and a liar” (I John III, 8), “and he never stood in the truth.”

Obadiah, whose name is interpreted as “servant of the Lord,” and who, at the time when Ahab had ordered the Lord’s prophets to be slaughtered, had hidden one hundred prophets in caves, supplying them with food each day, foreshadowed in a certain way those who, from among the leaders of the Jews, were secret disciples of the Lord (John XIX, 38), namely Nicodemus and the others whom the Evangelist mentions. [Col. 0757C]

The prophets of Baal and the prophets of the sacred groves bore the figure of the scribes and Pharisees, who neglected the precepts of the sacred Law and corrupted the people by their own traditions; against them the Lord is recorded to have pronounced a future “Woe.”

Mount Carmel, whose name is interpreted as “knowledge of circumcision,” foreshadowed the Church of Christ. In it we are commanded to understand that the circumcision of the foreskin is not to be accepted. For by circumcision of the foreskin one must understand that the lust of the flesh and sensual excess are to be cut away. By circumcision of the heart, unclean thoughts are to be understood as needing amputation.

The ox that Elijah slaughtered for a burnt offering and cut into pieces must be understood as the Old Testament. From it, in order to refute Jewish superstitions, the Lord Jesus manifestly brought forth through evangelical preaching the things written there in many places, as he is recorded to have said (Matt. XXI, 42): “Have you not read what was said: ‘The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone’?” And, he says, the scribes and Pharisees understood that he was speaking about them, and so forth, as is found in the Gospel. [Col. 0757D]

The other ox chosen by the false prophets signifies the reprobate people, offered by the Pharisees and scribes, or by heretics, not to God but to their author, the Devil. [Col. 0758A]

The passing of midday signified the course of the world as it hastened toward evening. At the world’s evening, the Lord Jesus Christ offered himself to the Father as the true sacrifice—which he himself is—for the removal of the sins of the human race.

The altar repaired by Elijah and restored from twelve stones must be understood as the confession of the Holy Trinity. This confession, once destroyed among the Jews or among heretics, was restored by the Lord through the Apostles in the Church.

The wood arranged upon the altar foreshadowed the gibbet of the cross, to which the Lord’s body was fastened and which was a true and acceptable burnt offering to God the Father.

[Note: Verse 34: “Fill four jars with water.”] [Col. 0757D]

The four jars filled with water, four in number, signified the four Gospels, in which the sacrament of baptism, given in the name of the Holy Trinity, is commanded. [Col. 0758B]

The fire that consumed the altar stones, everything upon it, and also the water foreshadowed the Holy Spirit, who takes up and sanctifies not only the Apostles but all believers, through the washing of regeneration, as a sacrifice to God.

The false prophets who are read as having been killed by Elijah must be understood as the opposing powers, concerning whom the Apostle declared that the Lord triumphed on the cross. Alternatively, they may be understood as those who are read as having impiously cried out against the Lord (Matt. XXVII, 25): “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

That this was fulfilled in the time of Vespasian and Titus will be beyond doubt for anyone who has read Josephus the historian. [Col. 0758C]

Then the history continues and says:

[Note: Verse 42, but with some difference between the Vulgate and this interpretation.] [Col. 0758D]

“Elijah went up to the summit of Carmel and, bending down to the earth, placed his face between his knees; and he entreated the Lord. [Note: These words, “he entreated the Lord,” do not occur in the Vulgate.] He said to his servant: ‘Go up and look toward the sea’—seven times.”

When he had done this, the seventh time a small cloud appeared, like the footprint of a man, rising from the sea. Suddenly the heavens were darkened, and there was a great rain.

The Evangelist declares that, when Elijah entreats God for rain to be given, the Lord likewise did this for his disciples and for those who were to believe through their word.

There is no doubt that Elijah’s servant, who was commanded to look toward the sea, bore the figure of all the prophets who lived before the Savior’s coming. Throughout the whole period preceding the Savior’s advent, they were granted, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, to await his incarnation. [Col. 0758D]

The small cloud which is described as rising from the sea like a man’s footprint must be understood as our Lord and Redeemer. For just as a footprint is the extremity of the body, so the Lord Jesus wished to exist in the world as humble, small, and poor, in order to cleanse us from sin.

The heavens were darkened because the holy preachers of the divine Word were filled with hidden sacraments. There was a great rain because the evangelical shower watered the boundaries of the whole world through the preaching of the Apostles. [Col. 0759A]

The chariot of Ahab, which Elijah preceded with girded loins, must be understood as the power of the Devil, to whom the Lord says (Matt. IV, 10): “Get behind me, Satan; you shall not tempt the Lord your God.”

For at the Lord’s advent the Devil’s power became so empty and weak that he did not even have permission to exercise dominion over swine unless it had been granted to him.

### (Chapter XIX)

“All these things that Elijah had done, and how he had killed the prophets of Baal, were reported to Jezebel. She immediately sent a messenger to him, saying: ‘May the gods do these things to me and add these things, unless by this hour tomorrow I make your life like the life of one of them.’

“When Elijah heard this, he was very afraid and went wherever his desire led him. He came to Beersheba of Judah and left his servant there. He himself went on into the wilderness for a day’s journey. When he had arrived there and sat beneath a juniper tree, he said: ‘It is enough for me, Lord; take my life.’” [Col. 0759B]

[Note: [Col. 0759D] What follows is supplied by Paterius; hence Gregory, *Moralium* XIX, nos. 9 and 10.]

“Holy men who, lifted up by the spirit, are carried away to lofty things are restrained by certain temptations as long as they remain in this life, lest they grow proud through some form of elation. Thus they are never able to advance as far as they wish; rather, lest they be lifted up by pride, a certain measure of their virtues is established in them. Hence Elijah, although he had advanced to great heights through so many virtues, was held back by a certain measure when he later fled from Jezebel, who, though a queen, was nevertheless only a little woman.

I consider this man of extraordinary virtue: bringing fire down from heaven and, at his sudden request, consuming two companies of fifty men with all their attendants; closing the heavens to rain by a word; opening the heavens to rain by a word; raising the dead; foreseeing whatever was to come. And yet again there comes to mind with what terror he fled before a single woman [Note: [Col. 0759D] He fled.]. I observe a man struck by fear asking death from the hand of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0759D] Of God.], but not receiving it; and fleeing death from the hand of a woman, thereby escaping it.

He was seeking death while he fled, saying: ‘It is enough for me, Lord; take my life, for I am no better than my fathers.’ Whence, then, was he so powerful as to perform all those virtues? Whence so weak as to fear a woman in such a way? It is because, by the dispensation of the heavenly will, measures are weighed out according to a hidden balance [Col. 0759D], so that the holy men of God may be very powerful through God’s power and yet, again, be moderated by a certain measure through their own weakness.

In those virtues Elijah recognized what he had received from the Lord; in these weaknesses he recognized what he himself could be. The former was the power of virtue; the latter was weakness guarding virtue.

“In those virtues he showed what he had received; in these weaknesses he guarded what he had received. Elijah was displayed in his miracles; in his weaknesses he was preserved.”

After this comes the following:

**(XIX, 5.)** “And he cast himself down and slept in the shade of a juniper tree. And behold, an angel of the Lord touched him and said to him: ‘Rise and eat.’ He looked, and behold, at his head there was a cake baked under the ashes and a vessel of water. He ate and drank, and again he slept. And the angel of the Lord touched him a second time and said: ‘Rise and eat, for a great journey remains before you.’ He arose, ate and drank, and walked in the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights, as far as the mountain of God, Horeb [Note: [Col. 0760D] Horeb.].”

What, then, of Jezebel? “May the gods do this to me and add this also, unless I set your life like the life of one of them.” And Elijah heard and fled a journey of forty days [Note: [Col. 0760D] What follows is found as no. 4 in the frequently cited homily on Saints Peter and Elijah, although the words are sometimes transposed and their order altered.].

“O violence of the word! O height of terror! When he heard a woman’s word, Elijah fled—and he fled not for one, nor two, nor three days. The woman’s word entered into him, and over so long a stretch of journey, driven on by fear and tossed about, he did not know what to do. It was as when a violent whirlwind, blowing against a ship driven forward by the breath of the west wind, seizes its mast and bends it back. So the woman’s word struck the mind of the Prophet, who had been sailing under the sails of his virtues, and tossed his whole ship amid every wave of fear, while its helmsman was bewildered.

What, then, Elijah? You are the one who by a word closed heaven and withheld the rains; who commanded the air and brought forth divine fires; who ordered the false priests to be put to death for the sake of healing; who steadfastly reproached the king to his face because he and his house were overthrowing the people of Israel; who had said: ‘The Lord lives: there shall be neither rain nor dew except at my word’ [Col. 0760C]; who had made the widow’s house a threshing floor of grain and a winepress of oil; who had commanded all the elements—yet now, hearing a harlot’s word, you were terrified, and one little woman made you a fugitive and a captive of fear.

O astonishing event! Look at these two men, Peter and Elijah, magnificent and brighter than the others, like two citadels of cities raised high into the heavens, worn down by women. Peter fears a girl; Jezebel terrifies Elijah. And because both were subject to the fault of the same weakness, the natural frailty of both found one betrayer.

Elijah therefore fled a journey of forty days. Where is the unrestrained ardor of your zeal? Where is the flame of your steadfastness? Where is the authority of your freedom, when you said: ‘The Lord lives, there shall be no rain upon the earth,’ or when you reproved the king face to face, and, performing so many wonders, could not endure one word from an adulteress?

But consider what is shown in these events: namely, that as long as the grace of the Lord cooperates with a human being, all things go well and all things are secure. The elements serve; rulers are cast down; kings bow down; peoples revere. But if, whether for the sake of perfection or correction, heavenly help once withdraws itself from a person, the frailty of nature is immediately revealed. At once those things that seemed subject rise up; those that formerly feared him as lord begin to become objects of terror.

Jezebel, whose name means ‘empty flow,’ represented the Synagogue. Serving empty superstitions, it refused to believe the evangelical preaching; and, persecuting the author of life, it preferred to extinguish him rather than believe, just as Jezebel persecuted Elijah.

Elijah’s servant, who was left at Beersheba—which is interpreted as ‘well of the oath’—is to be understood as the priestly ministry that was offered to the Lord’s temple in Jerusalem for divine worship.

The desert to which Elijah is said to have reached after a day’s journey, and beneath whose juniper tree he rested, is to be understood as the whole world, which had been placed in the power of the Evil One because of the worship of demons. To this world the Lord, having left Judea, deigned to pass through his preachers; and there he sleeps, as it were, while he rests through faith in the hearts of the faithful.

The juniper tree, wild and uncultivated, prefigured the Church from the Gentiles, which had not been cultivated by the precepts of the sacred Scriptures. The Evangelist declares that the Lord foretold that the kingdom of Israel would pass to it (Matthew XXI, 43): ‘The kingdom,’ he says, ‘will be taken from you [Jews] and given to a nation producing the will of God.’

The one day’s journey that Elijah is said to have made is to be understood as the unity of the Trinity, which evangelical preaching introduced to all nations.

What else do the cake baked under the ashes and the vessel of water signify except the repentance of the Gentiles and the pouring out of tears, by which the Lord is greatly refreshed?”

**(Verses 8, 9, etc.)** After this, it says, Elijah came to the mountain of God, Horeb [Note: [Col. 0761D] Horeb.], and remained in a cave. And behold, the word of the Lord came to him and said: “What are you doing here, Elijah?” He replied: “I have been very zealous for the Lord God of hosts, because the children of Israel have abandoned your covenant, demolished your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I alone have been left, and they seek my life in order to take it.”

[Note: [Col. 0761D] This too is found as no. 4 in the frequently cited homily on Saints Peter and Elijah.]

“Fleeing, then, Elijah came to a certain place and fell asleep there, and the Lord came to him. The Lord, that is, came to his servant and said (III Kings XIX, 13): ‘What are you doing here, Elijah?’—as though reproving him for fear and flight. ‘What are you doing here, Elijah?’ he says. ‘Do you think you have fled? Has the fury of one little woman made you a fugitive? Where is that steadfastness? Where is that freedom? Learn henceforth not to trust in yourself, nor, when matters proceed favorably, to attribute them to your own virtue.’

Nevertheless Elijah answers and says—retaining one thing in his mind but expressing another with his mouth—(verse 14): ‘The prophets have been killed; your altars have been demolished; I alone have been left, and they seek my life.’ This was the thought that cast the Prophet down from the very height of his merits and showed him to be an ordinary human being.

Accordingly, the divine word immediately rebukes him. ‘It is not so, Elijah,’ it says. ‘You are mistaken and entangled in the snares of human thought. You did not flee for that reason, nor did the queen terrify you because you were alone. For you are not the only one who has not worshiped Baal. I have faithful servants; I have many friends; I have the outstanding virtue of seven thousand chosen men, whom neither human error could bend nor the thought of empty glory exalt (verse 18). All these have not bent their knees before Baal, but, with steadfast knees, they worship me always, in the likeness of the heavenly host.

“You fled, therefore, not because the adulteress’s fury raged against you alone, but because the greatness of your virtues produced in you such a judgment about the human race that you bore so arrogant a sentence against it. For a little while you were destined to be abandoned by my grace; and unless I had loosened the reins of such great elation for you, you would have fallen into a more serious fall and learned to attribute good deeds not to your own virtue but to the divine.

“You fled, therefore, for no other reason than that, when my grace withdrew, a woman frightened you with threatening speech. Let us consider, then, how great was the force of the adulterous woman’s word when grace had withdrawn, and how great was the magnitude of Elijah’s strength.

For forty days Elijah wanders in flight through pathless places and deserts. Yet this man of such intelligence, stunned by fear, feels no hunger. What are you doing, Elijah? Where is that confidence, so often mentioned already, astonishing to everyone? Where is that fearsome mouth? Where is that terrible tongue commanding the elements by turns?

But, as I have said, these things stood firm for you while grace supplied them. See, then, how so great a Prophet is permitted to fall through the lightness of his fault, so that, corrected and reproved for the vice of elation, he may be wholly clothed in the garment of moderation and clemency.”

“We have now been instructed and taught, in Peter and Elijah, how the Lord permits them, for our sake, to be encompassed by sin; how he permitted those standard-bearers of faith and piety, those pillars of the human race, to be shaken when fear prevailed, so that they might be an example to peoples: namely, that God has by no means granted them the grace of not sinning, lest, while they themselves were free from faults and vices, they should prove harsh and cruel toward sinners.

Rather, when someone has been overtaken by sin, they should not immediately reject him or condemn the disposition of one lying fallen; they should show the compassion of charity, extend a hand, and raise up the fallen person, promising him hope of divine clemency. In this way they may also commend themselves to live by the example of such teachers.

We have said these things not to accuse the righteous, but to raise sinners up to hope. First we extolled their virtues; now we have brought forward their faults, so that we might show both to the righteous a pattern of caution and to sinners a most trustworthy harbor of salvation.”

It is rightly asked how Elijah could lawfully have offered sacrifice outside the temple of God, when he both obtained fire from heaven and convicted the prophets of the demons. This seems to me defensible by no other argument than the one by which Abraham’s deed is defended, when, commanded by God, he wished to sacrifice his son.

When the one who established the law commands something to be done that he prohibited in the law, the command itself is regarded as law, because he is the author of the law. Other miracles besides the sacrifice were certainly available by which the prophets of the sacred groves could have been overcome and convicted. But the Spirit of God, who was in Elijah, could not do anything in this matter contrary to the law, because he is the giver of the law.

Another question still troubles the mind: why did Elijah appeal to the Lord, saying that Israel, after abandoning God, had killed his prophets [Note: [Col. 0763D] “They demolished your altars and killed your prophets.”] and destroyed his altars, when the law had long before commanded that they could have no more altars than one—first in the tabernacle, then in the temple?

The clear meaning is that, after the ten tribes had been cut off from the house of David and separated from the temple and Jerusalem, those among the ten tribes called Ephraim who were worshipers of the divine name—who, as must be supposed, resorted to the altars that the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had once erected in suitable places where God had appeared to them—had recourse to those altars as worshipers of the divine name. Even if not for offering sacrifice, they nevertheless resorted there to pray to the God of their fathers.

When the sacrilegious Israelites and worshipers of idols saw this, they destroyed the altars, so that there would be no place where true worshipers could pray to the Lord. This is what was already stated above: that Elijah restored the altar of the Lord which had been destroyed.

**(Verse 11.)** And the Lord said to Elijah: “Go out and stand on the mountain before the Lord.” And behold, the Lord passed by, and a great and mighty wind overturned the mountains and shattered the rocks before the Lord.

By saying that the great wind preceded the Lord, and so forth, Scripture signifies that his coming would benefit the hearts of believers through certain hidden and ineffable signs [Col. 0763C]. For when it says, “Overturning the mountains and shattering the rocks before the Lord,” this is what the Apostle says (II Corinthians X, 4–5): “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal but spiritual, for the destruction of strongholds … and of every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God.”

**(Verses 11, 12.)** “The Lord was not in the wind; and after the wind, an earthquake. The Lord was not in the earthquake; and after the earthquake, a fire. The Lord was not in the fire; and after the fire, the sound of a gentle breeze.”

[Note: [Col. 0763D] Search out what follows, up to the words “he stood at the entrance of the cave,” marked with lines in Paterius; hence consult Gregory, Book V on Job, no. 66—formerly chapter 36, and earlier still chapter 26.]

“The wind before the Lord overturned the mountains and shattered the rocks, because the terror that bursts forth at his coming casts down the height of our hearts and melts their hardness.

But he says that God is not in the wind of the earthquake or in the fire. In the sound of the gentle breeze, however, he does not deny that God is present. For when the mind is lifted up to the height of contemplation, whatever it is able perfectly to behold is not the Lord. But when it perceives something subtly, this is what it hears concerning the incomprehensible substance of eternity. We perceive, as it were, the sound of a gentle breeze when, through sudden contemplation, we subtly taste the flavor of uncircumscribed truth.

It is therefore true that we know God when we recognize that we cannot fully know anything of him [Col. 0764A] [Note: [Col. 0763D] Of God.]—or rather, when we recognize that we cannot know him fully [Note: [Col. 0763D] More precisely: ‘fully’ is preferable.]. Hence it is rightly added there: ‘When Elijah heard this, he covered his face with his cloak and went out and stood at the entrance of the cave.’”

[Note: [Col. 0764D] You will also find this in Gregory, though transmitted elsewhere—namely, no. 18 of Homily 1 on Ezekiel.]

“What does it mean that, when the Prophet hears the voice of the Lord speaking with him, he stands at the entrance of his cave and veils his face? It means that, when the voice of heavenly understanding comes into the mind through the grace of contemplation, the whole human being is no longer inside the cave, because the soul [Note: [Col. 0764D] The mind.] is no longer possessed by concern for the flesh. But he stands at the entrance because he is preparing to leave the narrow confines of mortality.

Yet one who stands at the entrance of the cave and perceives the words of God in the ear of his heart must veil his face. For when, through heavenly grace, we are led to higher understanding, the more subtly we are lifted up, the more we must always press ourselves down through humility by our own understanding. We must not attempt to know more than we ought to know (Romans XII, 3), but to know with sobriety.

Otherwise, while we investigate invisible things too intensely, we may go astray; we may seek something belonging to bodily light in that incorporeal nature. To incline the ear and cover the face means to hear the voice of the inner substance through the mind and yet turn the eyes of the heart away from every bodily appearance, lest the mind imagine anything corporeal in that nature which is wholly everywhere and everywhere uncircumscribed.”

**(Verse 15.)** And the Lord said to Elijah: “Go, return on your way through the desert to Damascus. When you arrive, anoint Hazael as king over Syria; and Jehu son of Nimshi you shall anoint as king over Israel; and Elisha son of Shaphat, who is from Abel-meholah, you shall anoint as prophet in your place. And whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, Jehu shall kill; and whoever escapes the sword of Jehu, Elisha shall kill.”

[Note: [Col. 0764D] See Jerome’s book *On Hebrew Places*.]

Abel-meholah is one of the principal cities [Note: [Col. 0764D] One of the chief cities.] of Solomon. It is now a village—as we read in the book of places—in the Aulon, ten miles from Scythopolis toward the south, and is now called Bethaula [Note: [Col. 0764D] Others read Bethulia.], or Betula.

“Damascus, which is interpreted as ‘drinking blood’ or ‘offering blood to drink,’ represented the whole world. It is beyond doubt that its inhabitants, sacrificing their sons to demons, drank and offered their blood to drink. In Scripture, blood signifies sin and death, which the wretched seemed not only to inflict upon themselves but also to offer to their imitators.

Hazael, whose name is interpreted as ‘work of God,’ contained the figure of all the nations, and the interpretation suits him very well: ‘work of God.’ For it was a divine work that, when Israel had been hardened and had utterly refused to believe in the Lord’s signs and virtues, the peoples of the nations should believe in the crucified one with complete eagerness of mind.

Or, alternatively, ‘work of God’ means the image of God established among the Gentiles through faith in Christ. No one can doubt this. For just as in Jacob and Esau there had been a figure beforehand in which the primacy and blessing of the elder son were transferred to the younger brother, so also in these two, namely Hazael and Jehu, we understand that the divine dispensation brought about the following: the people of the Gentiles, who were younger, were placed before Israel, the firstborn, in the person of Jehu.

According to the testimony of Scripture, the people who had been at the head, because of continual transgressions and the crime committed against the Lord, became the tail; and, when the kingdom was transferred from that people—as the Lord had declared—it was given to the people of the Gentiles, who carried out the will of God.

But because it belongs to divine mercy that all human beings should be saved, just as Esau, although subjected to his younger brother, was by no means deprived of blessing, so here too God foretells to Elijah: ‘I will leave for myself seven thousand men whose knees have not bowed before Baal.’

By saying ‘I will leave,’ he wished it to be understood that this referred to a future time, which is known to have been fulfilled at the Lord’s coming. We must understand as certain that those from all Israel who received the faith through the apostles of Christ were anointed with the sevenfold Spirit of Christ.

Jehu, whose name is interpreted as ‘he himself’ or ‘he is,’ son of Nimshi—which is interpreted as ‘touching’ or ‘handling’—specially prefigured the person of the Apostles. The interpretation of these names fits them very well. For the blessed Apostles are truly said always to exist: because of their confession of the Trinity and their truthful preaching, they live perpetually for God and for the whole world.

John too, when writing in his epistle about the Word of life—that is, the Son of God who assumed flesh—spoke as follows (I John I, 1, 3): ‘What we have seen with our eyes, what we have heard with our ears, and what our hands have handled.’

When it is said to Elijah, ‘You shall anoint Elisha son of Shaphat, from Abel-meholah, as prophet in your place,’ it is to be understood as follows. Elisha is interpreted as ‘the salvation of my God’; Shaphat as ‘judging’; and Abel-meholah as ‘bringing forth mourning.’

The Son of God, who is the true salvation of the faithful (John V, 22), and to whom the Father has entrusted all judgment—a judgment in which there will be mourning for the impious and unbelieving, namely the pains of Gehenna—could not be contemplated by everyone in the splendor and power of his substance. Therefore, as the Apostle says (Philippians II, 7), ‘emptying’ his majesty, he deigned, in the prefiguration of Elisha, to assume the form of a servant. He was born a true human being from a virgin’s womb and anointed with the Holy Spirit.

As for what the historical account says—that whoever escaped the sword of Hazael would be killed by Jehu, and whoever escaped the sword of Jehu would be killed by Elisha—this may be understood as follows.

The sword of Hazael the Syrian is to be understood as the teaching of those inspired prophets from the Gentiles who arose through divine inspiration concerning the Lord’s Incarnation, Passion, and Resurrection, in order to refute the Jewish teachers who concealed this mystery from the peoples.

The sword of Jehu, who was anointed over Israel, is to be understood as the preaching of John, the Lord’s precursor. When the Sadducees and Pharisees came to his baptism, he rebuked them, and it is written that he said (Luke III, 7): ‘Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?’

The sword of Elisha is to be understood as the evangelical preaching, of which the Lord is recorded as saying (Matthew X, 34): ‘I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword.’ For it divides and separates the faithful and righteous, in a certain sense, from the unfaithful and unrighteous; and in the hearts of believers it kills harmful desires, every vice, and every sin.”

Meanwhile the Lord said to Elijah: “I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent their knees before Baal, and every mouth that has not worshiped him, kissing his hand.”

[Note: [Col. 0765D] See chapter 12 of Paterius, in Book III of *Kings*. He in turn took this from Gregory, Book XXXI on Job, no. 107.]

“It is certain that the person who, when acting rightly, neglects to consider the merits of those who are better extinguishes the eye of his heart through the darkness of elation. Conversely, the person who carefully weighs the good deeds of others illuminates himself with a great ray of humility. For when he sees outwardly, and sees accomplished by others, the things he himself has done, he suppresses the swelling of pride that strives to break forth inwardly from a sense of uniqueness.

Hence the voice of the Lord says to Elijah, who thought he alone remained: ‘I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent their knees before Baal.’ Thus, when he recognized that he had not alone remained, he might turn away from the glory of elation that could arise in him from his sense of uniqueness [Note: [Col. 0765D] From which it could arise.].

He was a Prophet and had often known heavenly mysteries. What, then, was difficult about recognizing that faithful servants of God had also remained in this world? Yet here we must carefully observe how wickedly elation closes the eye of the heart. For the one who had known humbly the hidden judgments of God [Note: [Col. 0766D] ‘Judgments’ is added.] did not know, when elated, the things that were evident.”

After this, he says (XIX, 19): “Elijah found Elisha son of Shaphat plowing with twelve yoke of oxen. He himself was one of those plowing with the twelve yoke. When Elijah came to him, he cast his cloak over him. Immediately he left the oxen, ran after Elijah, and said: ‘Let me kiss my father and my mother, I beg you, and then I will follow you.’ Elijah said to him: ‘Go back; for what was mine, I have done for you.’ Elisha then returned, took a yoke of oxen, slaughtered them, cooked their flesh with the wood of the oxen’s plow, and gave it to the people to eat.”

Figurally, the twelve yoke of oxen are to be understood as the twenty-four books of the Old Testament. The twelve plowmen are to be understood as the twelve Apostles. Yet the Lord deigned to be the worker among them all, for he said (John XV, 5): “Without me you can do nothing.”

The kiss of the father is recognized as a sign of reconciliation. In the two oxen, the law and the prophecy are to be understood. Our Lord killed their shadows and images in the letter through the mystery of his Incarnation and Passion, and cooked them on the plow of his cross; he also offered them to the faithful to eat, so that they might no longer live according to the letter but according to the spirit.

**(XX, 10.)** After this Scripture reports that Ben-hadad, king of Syria, while besieging Samaria and beginning to attack it, said: “May the gods do this to me and add this also, if the dust of Samaria will suffice by handfuls for all the people who follow me.”

This is the meaning.

[Note: [Col. 0767D] Claudius took the explanation of this passage from Bede, Question 17 of Book XXX of *Questions on the Books of Kings*, where Bede presents it.]

“Samaria, according to the custom of cities, had earth inside, near the walls, almost level with the walls themselves, lest the blows of a battering ram, striking repeatedly under the force of hostile hands, should knock them down when they had been erected without the support of the adjoining earth [Note: [Col. 0767D] ‘For the height of the walls is far above …’ But the reading of our manuscript is preferable.].

On the outside, however, the height of the walls rose far above the surface of the earth, especially since, as Scripture reports, the city itself had been situated on the summit of a mountain.

The proud king therefore terrified the besieged city by saying that he had such a multitude of troops with him that, if each of his soldiers brought only a stone, a clod of earth, or a piece of wood for constructing a ramp against the city, a ramp so high could be raised from it that it would appear level with the surface of the city inside the walls. Thus, fighting against the city from horseback, they could throw missiles or torches.

The king of Israel restrained the arrogance of his presumption with a moderate reply, saying (verse 11): ‘Tell him: Let not the one who is girded boast as the one who is ungirded.’”

One person is girded, another ungirded, and another not girded [Note: [Col. 0767C] One manuscript has a different reading, and so on.].

The girded person is one who goes about surrounded by a belt. The ungirded person is one who has recently removed his belt—for example, because he is about to enter a bath, climb into bed, or perhaps put on another tunic. The person not girded is one who has recently put on a tunic but has not yet secured himself by fastening a belt around it.

Thus, in a military campaign, the person who has been stationed for battle is rightly called girded, that is, clothed in armor. The person who has returned home victorious after the battle has been completed is rightly called ungirded, because, having laid aside his armor, he enjoys the leisure of the desired peace. But the person who has not yet begun to fight or to prepare himself for battle is rightly said to be not girded.

The king of Israel therefore said to the king of Syria, who was boasting as though he had already captured Samaria, which he had only begun to besiege: “Let the girded man be disregarded, equally as the ungirded” [Note: [Col. 0767D] “That”; our reading is preferable.]. It is as though he were saying plainly: ‘Do not boast as though you were already victorious in the hazard of war, while you are still stationed in battle and do not know whom victory will follow.’

He was speaking truly. For as soon as the battle began, Ben-hadad did not return home triumphing over defeated adversaries; rather, he fled home after his army had been slaughtered.

There is no doubt that Ben-hadad, king of Syria, represented the devil, who is the prince of this world. Together with thirty-two kings [Note: [Col. 0768D] Verse 6: thirty-two kings with him.], that is, with all his vices, he does not cease to fight against the human race. Ahab, whose name is interpreted as ‘brother of the father,’ represented here the person of the Jews, with whom the devil had previously contended.”

**(XXII, 19.)** Meanwhile Scripture continues with the vision of the prophet Micaiah, where he says to Ahab: “I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and all the army of heaven standing at his right and at his left. And it was said: ‘By what means shall I deceive Ahab, so that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ One spoke words of one kind, and another otherwise. Then one came forward and said: ‘I will deceive Ahab.’ And it was said to him: ‘By what means will you deceive him?’ He answered: ‘I will go forth and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’”

[Note: [Col. 0768D] Paterius includes what follows, and therefore Gregory also includes it (*Moralium* II, no. 38, chapter 20—formerly chapter 21). There is, however, a great difference between what the cited book of Gregory presents and what our manuscript contains; I follow the reading of our manuscript. Let the reader consult the Vulgate.]

“What do we understand by the Lord’s throne except the angelic powers, upon whose wings he sits while disposing all things below? And what is meant by the army of heaven except the multitude of ministering angels?

What, then, does it mean that the army of heaven is said to stand at his right and at his left? God is within all things in such a way that he is also outside all things; he is uncircumscribed. That truth, eternal blessedness which is called his right hand, has no left hand, because there is nothing that displeases it; it sees all things together and beholds all things together. But because there are things in which both a good spirit and an evil spirit exist, the army of heaven is described as being at his right and at his left.

By the right hand, therefore, we understand the elect angels; by the left, the rejected spirits. For not only the good serve God—those who help—but also the evil, who test. They serve not only because they lift up those who return from sin, but also because they burden those who refuse to return.

Nor should it seem strange that even rejected angels are called the army of heaven. Although they have been cast out from the ethereal heaven, they nevertheless still dwell in the aerial heaven. We call the birds of heaven those creatures that we know to be suspended in the air. Paul says of these same spirits (Ephesians VI, 12): ‘Against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.’ And, naming their head, he says (Ephesians II, 2): ‘According to the prince of the power of this air.’

The army stands at the right and at the left because the will of the elect spirits agrees with divine mercy, while the mind of the rejected spirits, serving its own wickedness, obeys the judgment of his severity.

Hence immediately afterward the deceitful spirit is described as leaping forth into the midst [Note: [Col. 0768D] Into the middle.], through whom King Ahab was to be deceived in accordance with his merits. For it is not right to believe that a good spirit wished to serve deceit by saying, ‘I will go forth and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’ Rather, because King Ahab was worthy, on account of his preceding sins, to be condemned by such a deception—so that he who had often fallen willingly into guilt might at last be seized unwillingly for punishment—by hidden justice permission is given to evil spirits, so that those whom they willingly strangle in the snare of sin they may also unwillingly drag into the punishment of sin.”

[Note: [Col. 0769D] Up to this point the passage is Gregory’s; the words that follow seem to belong to Claudius, not to the earlier writer.]

But how God brings these things about, being everywhere present, wholly present everywhere, and always present; how the holy angels and all the lofty and most pure spirits created by him consult his simple, immutable, and eternal truth; how they temporally carry out, according to the fitness of earthly things, what they see to be eternally just in him; how the fallen spirits, who did not remain in truth because of the uncleanness and weakness of their desires, and who are unable because of their punishments to contemplate and consult the truth inwardly present, await external signs through creation and are moved by them, whether to do something or not to do it; and how they are compelled and constrained by the eternal law by which the universe is governed, either being permitted by God to act or commanded to yield and submit—this would be difficult to comprehend and exceedingly lengthy to explain.

**(XXII, 40, 52, and following.)** After the death of Ahab, his son Ahaziah began to reign in his place. Scripture reports of him (IV Kings I, 2): “He fell through the lattice of his upper chamber, which he had in Samaria, and became ill.”

King Ahaziah of Samaria, who separated himself from the house of David and fell through a lattice, seems to signify the following: heretics or schismatics, even if they appear to climb some height of good action, nevertheless, because they do not possess the structure of ecclesial unity, continually fall back to the lowest depths of vices, as though relying on the open and unsolid supports of their sides. Deprived of divine help, they perish through the arrogant pride of obstinacy.

## (IV Kings 1:9)

Then the same Scripture reports that this same Ochozias sent two captains of fifty to Elias. Because they insolently called him a man of God, they were consumed by heavenly fire while he prayed; but the third who was sent was saved.

“Figuratively, however, the number fifty is a confession of repentance, through which the remission of sins is declared. For the Jews, unwilling to acknowledge that Christ is truly God or the prince who bestows forgiveness, say to him (John 8:57): ‘You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?’ Such men are extinguished by the future conflagration of divine fire (Col. 0769D); but the third captain of fifty, who, converted to faith in the Trinity, displays the mysteries of repentance, therefore deserved to attain forgiveness.

[Note: [Col. 0769D] Isidore, chapter 1 of his book on IV Kings, teaches most explicitly what Claudius presents here.]

[Note: [Col. 0769D] “Through which.”]

[Note: [Col. 0769D] “They say [that he is] of repentance,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0769D] “You have seen.”]

[Note: [Col. 0769D] “Those like these.”]

[Note: [Col. 0770D] “The third captain of fifty.”]

[Note: [Col. 0770D] “He acknowledged it.”]

It must be understood that Holy Scripture mentions a curse in two ways: one, namely, which it approves; the other, which it condemns. For a curse is pronounced in one way by a judgment of justice, and in another by the spite of vengeance. The curse pronounced by a judgment of justice was uttered against the first man when he sinned, when he heard (Gen. 3:17): “Cursed is the earth in your work.” A curse according to the judgment of justice is pronounced when it is said to Abraham (Gen. 12:3): “I will curse those who curse you.”

Again, because a curse not according to the judgment of justice, but from the spite of vengeance, is forbidden, we are warned by the voice of Paul preaching, who says (Rom. 12:14): “Bless, and do not curse.” And again the same Apostle says (1 Cor. 6:10): “Nor will cursers possess the kingdom of God.” Thus God is said to curse, and yet man is forbidden to curse, because what man does through the malice of vengeance, God does only with the examination and power of justice.

[Note: [Col. 0770D] “But when.”]

For holy men also, when they pronounce a sentence of cursing, do not burst forth into it from a desire for vengeance, but from the judgment of justice. Within themselves they behold the subtle judgment of God, and recognize that the evils arising outwardly deserve to be struck by a curse; and they do not sin in that curse because they do not dissent from the inward judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0770D] “Evil things.”]

Hence Peter hurled a sentence of cursing at Simon, who offered him money, saying (Acts 8:20): “May your money be with you unto perdition.” For by not saying “is,” but “may it be,” he indicated that he had spoken not in the indicative but in the optative mood. Hence Elias said to the two men of fifty who came to him: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you.” The outcome of the matter showed with how much truth their sentence prevailed. For Simon perished in eternal destruction, and the flame coming down from above consumed the two men of fifty.

Thus the power that follows bears witness to the intention with which a sentence of cursing is pronounced: the innocence of the one who curses remains, and yet the curse consumes the one who is cursed even unto destruction. Therefore, from the end of both parties it is gathered that the sentence against the guilty is hurled by one and the same inward Judge.” [Col. 0770C]

[Note: [Col. 0770D] Claudius took everything that follows in the explanation of this passage from chapter 1, elsewhere numbered 2, of Book IV of Saint Gregory’s Moralia.]

## (Chapter II, verses 2, 4, and following)

The fact that Elias, about to be taken away and raised to heaven, ordered Eliseus to remain at Gilgal, or at Bethel, or at Jericho, or at the Jordan, while Eliseus continually swore by the Lord that he would not leave him, appears to have signified that Elias bore in himself the figure of the Apostles, who, from the very revelation of faith—for this is how “Gilgal” is interpreted—adhered inseparably to Christ the Lord and did not withdraw from his company until the day of his ascension into heaven.

When they had crossed the Jordan (ibid., verse 9), Elias said to Eliseus: “Ask what you wish me to do for you before I am taken away from you.” Eliseus said: “I ask that your spirit be doubled in me.”

According to the truth of the historical account, a double portion of the spirit of Elias was bestowed upon Eliseus, because Eliseus performed many more miracles than Elias. Tropologically, however, a double portion of the spirit of Elias was attributed to Eliseus because, after the Lord’s ascension, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, a twofold gift of understanding—that is, of the Old and New Testaments—was bestowed upon the Apostles. [Col. 0770D–0771A]

## (Ibid., verse 11)

“As they went on and walked, speaking with one another, behold, a fiery chariot and fiery horses divided the two; and Elias went up into heaven in a whirlwind. But Eliseus saw it and cried out: ‘My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer!’ And he saw him no more.” [Col. 0771A]

The chariot of Israel—that is, the mind of those who see the Lord—is not incongruously understood as the Lord Jesus Christ, who, by patiently bearing with his elect, carries them as though in a chariot, and who, through his preaching and discipline, drives them as a charioteer.

Morally, however:

[Note: [Col. 0771D] What follows is found first in section 15 of Homily 7 on Ezekiel, and then in sections 5 and 6 of Homily 29 on the Gospel.]

“What does it mean that Elias is called the chariot of Israel and its charioteer, unless it is because the charioteer drives and the chariot carries? Therefore the teacher who both bears the conduct of the people through patience and instructs them with the words of sacred eloquence is called both chariot and charioteer. He is a chariot because he carries them by bearing with them; he is a charioteer because he exercises the people through good admonitions. [Col. 0771B]

[Note: [Col. 0771D] Thus far Homily 7 on Ezekiel; what follows is from the homily on the Gospel.]

“What does it mean that Elias is said to have been carried up to heaven? Do we perhaps believe that, while he was still placed in this corruptible flesh, he was brought into the bosom of that supreme rest before the resurrection and ascension of the Lord?
