But one heaven is airy, another ethereal. The airy heaven is close to the earth; hence we speak of the birds of heaven, because we see them flying through the air.

“Elias, therefore, was raised into the airy heaven so that he might suddenly be led into a certain hidden region of the earth [Note: [Col. 0771D] “A hidden region.”], where he would live already in great rest of flesh and spirit until he returns at the end of the world and pays the debt of death. For in being raised up, Elias designated the Lord’s ascension: he postponed death, but did not escape it.

“Our Redeemer, however, because he did not postpone death but conquered it, and consumed it by rising again, revealed the glory of his eternal resurrection by ascending. [Note: [Col. 0771D] “And of the resurrection.”]

“It should also be noted that Elias is read to have ascended in a chariot, so that it might plainly be shown that a mere human being needed assistance from another. For those aids were accomplished and displayed through angels, since he could not ascend even into the airy heaven by his own power, being weighed down by the weakness of his nature. [Note: [Col. 0771D] “Which is.”]

“Our Redeemer, however, is not read to have been lifted up by a chariot or by angels, because he who had made all things was carried above all things by his own power. He was returning there where he was, and returning from where he remained, because while he ascended into heaven through his humanity, through his divinity he continued to encompass earth and heaven alike.” [Note: [Col. 0771D] “Remained.”]

[Note: [Col. 0772D] Thus far Gregory at the cited passage. What follows is transmitted by Augustine in chapter 6, section 11, of Book IX of On the Literal Meaning of Genesis.]

Nor should it be supposed that Elias is already [Note: [Col. 0772D] The editions read: “are.”] in the condition in which the saints will be when, after the day’s work has been completed, they will receive the denarius together (Matt. 20:20), or in the condition of those human beings who have not yet departed from this life, although he departed from it not by death but by translation.

He therefore already possesses something better than he could have in this life, although he does not yet possess what he will rightly have at the end as a result of the good conduct of this life. For “they provided something better for us” (Heb. 11:40), lest they should be made perfect without us.

Or if anyone thinks that Elias could not have deserved this if he had taken a wife and begotten children—for he is believed not to have had any because Scripture does not say so, although it says nothing about his celibacy either—what will he answer concerning Enoch, who pleased God after begetting sons and was translated, not having died? (Gen. 5:21, 24.) Why, then, if Adam and Eve had lived justly and chastely begotten children, could they not have yielded their place to their descendants by translation rather than by death?

For if Enoch and Elias, having died in Adam and bearing in the flesh the succession of death—which they are believed to return to this life in order to discharge, and to die after what was delayed for so long—are nevertheless now in another life, where before the resurrection of the flesh, before the animal body is changed into a spiritual one, they do not fail through sickness or old age, how much more justly and probably would that have been granted to those first human beings, if they had lived without any sin of their own or of their parents, so that, after begetting children, they might yield to them a better state, from which, when the world had ended, they would be changed with all the blessedness of the saints into an angelic form—not through the death of the flesh, but through the power of God—and far more happily? [Col. 0772A–B]

## (IV Kings 2:12–13)

“He grasped his garments and tore them into two parts, and he lifted up the mantle of Elias, which had fallen to him.” [Col. 0772C]

For Eliseus bore the figure of the Lord and our Redeemer. His garments are to be understood as the Scriptures of the Old Testament, which were then torn—that is, revealed to human beings—when, through his passion, resurrection, or ascension into heaven, they were fulfilled. The mantle of Elias, collected by Eliseus, is to be understood as the power of the Word, which he left to the world for the glorification of his flesh.

## (Verses 19 and following)

“When Eliseus was living in Jericho, the men of the city came to him and said: ‘Behold, the situation of this city is very good, as you yourself, Lord, see; but the waters are bad, and the land is barren.’ He said: ‘Bring me a new vessel and put salt in it.’ When they had brought it, he went out to the spring of the waters, put salt into it, and said: ‘Thus says the Lord: I have healed these waters, and there shall no longer be death or barrenness in them.’ Thus the waters were healed to this day, according to the word of Eliseus which he spoke.” [Col. 0772D]

[Note: [Col. 0772D] Claudius took this explanation from Isidore, although he altered the order of the words somewhat. See chapter 2 of Isidore’s book on IV Kings.]

The city of Jericho prefigured the form of this world. Its habitation, according to the creation of the Creator, is not merely good but very good, as is evident to all. Its bad waters, however, are to be understood as the teaching of philosophers and poets, which provokes human minds to the worship of demons, to lust, and to wantonness.

The barren land indicates the whole human race, which, having abandoned God the Creator and having darkened its understanding, served all created things.

Whom else, then, did this miracle prefigure except the Lord Jesus Christ? After the Word became flesh and deigned to be baptized by his minister in the Jordan River, he transformed the barren waters of Jericho—that is, of this world—into the fruitfulness of the bath, so that whatever was regenerated from them might receive such a spirit. In the salt, wisdom is understood; in the unformed vessel, the flesh of the Lord. [Col. 0773A–B]

## (II, 23)

“Eliseus went up to Bethel. As he was going up by the way, little boys came out of the city and mocked him, saying: ‘Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead.’ When he had cursed them in the name of the Lord, two bears immediately came out of the forest and tore forty-two of the boys. From there he went to Mount Carmel.” [Col. 0773B]

[Note: [Col. 0773D] Claudius also took this explanation from Isidore, although he altered some things.]

There is no doubt that Eliseus, whose name is interpreted as “salvation of God,” bore the person of the Savior. The Savior, ascending to Bethel—that is, to the heavenly house of God—was mocked by the Jews as by foolish children. Those same Jews cried: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead”—“Crucify, crucify,” at the place of Calvary.

Because of this heinous crime, after forty-two years had passed following the Savior’s resurrection and ascension into heaven, the Jewish people was consumed by the Roman commanders, namely Vespasian and Titus, as though by two bears. Mount Carmel, however, is to be understood as the Church, to which the Lord transferred his kingdom after rejecting Israel. [Col. 0773C]

## (Chapter IV)

“A certain woman,” he says, “from the wives of the prophets came to Eliseus and said: ‘Your servant, my husband, is dead, and you know that he feared God. And now my creditor is coming and wishes to take my two sons into his service.’ Eliseus said to her: ‘What do you have in your house? Tell me.’ She replied: ‘I have a little oil with which I may anoint.’ Eliseus said to her: ‘Go and ask your neighbors for many vessels; then enter your room, take the oil, and pour it into the vessels. You pour, and your sons shall present the vessels. When they are full, sell them and pay your creditor; you and your sons shall live on what remains.’ She went and did as the man of God had commanded her.” [Col. 0773D]

[Note: [Col. 0773D] Paterius has a similar explanation; consequently, consult Gregory.]

This widow signified the ancient Church of the holy Fathers who were under the Law. At the Savior’s coming, she was left bereft of legal precepts as though of a lawful husband, together with her two surviving sons—that is, the twofold people.

The creditor of this Church is to be understood as the devil, who before the Savior’s coming held the human race subject through original sin and daily sins, because he kept within the letter of the Law and the prophecy of the Old Testament the grace of evangelical preaching, unrevealed among them. [Col. 0774A]

But after she deserved to arrive at knowledge of the true Eliseus—that is, our Savior—at his instruction she asked her neighbors for many empty vessels, because after the preaching of the Apostles she gathered into the house of faith a multitude of believers from the various nations.

She also poured the oil she possessed into the other little vessels, because through the mouths of preachers she distributed spiritual grace among all the nations. From that oil, that is, from divine grace, she redeemed her sons, because through the gift of the Holy Spirit and the anointing of charity she freed herself and all the faithful from perpetual slavery to sin. [Col. 0774B]

## (Verse 8)

“It happened that Eliseus passed by, and there was a prominent woman there who held him so that he might eat bread. Whenever he passed that way, he turned aside to her to eat bread. She said to her husband: ‘I perceive that this is a holy man of God who passes by us frequently. Let us make a small upper room and put in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a lampstand, so that whenever he comes to us he may remain there,’” and so forth. [Col. 0774B]

This woman, the Shunammite, represented the type of the Church. Before she received the true Eliseus—that is, our Savior—through faith, she was barren. But after she deserved to receive that same Lord in the lodging of her heart, she bore the faithful people as though an only son.

The upper room prefigures the height of faith; the bed, spiritual rest and the leisure of contemplation. The table signifies the unity of faith and harmony in preaching. The chair signifies the power of teaching; the lampstand, the illumination of faith or the brightness of virtues. [Col. 0774C]

After this, Scripture reports concerning the son of the Shunammite (verses 20 and following) that the servant of Eliseus, sent with a staff, did not raise him; but Eliseus himself, coming and applying himself to the child’s limbs, walking back and forth, and breathing seven times into the mouth of the dead man, immediately restored him to living light through the mystery of compassion:

[Note: [Col. 0774D] The following is taken from Paterius, and therefore from Gregory, who transmits it in section 63 of chapter 40 of Book IX of the Moralia.]

“Because God, the author of the human race, grieved as over a dead child when, in his mercy, he looked upon us extinguished by the sting of iniquity. And because through Moses he brought forth the terror of the Law, he sent the rod as though through a child. For through the Law God had held the rod when he said: ‘If anyone does this or that, let him die.’

“Thus the fear of the death of sin was unable to raise us up, but only the grace of gentleness breathed upon us restored us to the condition of life. [Note: [Col. 0774D] “To the condition.”] The child with the staff, however, was unable to raise the dead man, because, as Paul testifies (Heb. 7:19), the Law brought nothing to perfection.

“But he himself came and humbly stretched himself over the corpse, joining himself to the dead man’s limbs so as to make them equal, because, although he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a man (Phil. 2:6).

“He walks back and forth because he calls both Judea nearby and the nations situated far away. He breathes seven times over the dead man [Note: [Col. 0775D] “Breathes upon.”] because, through the opening of the divine will, the sevenfold grace of the Spirit breathes upon those lying in the death of sin; immediately the living man is raised, because the one whom the rod of terror could not raise returned to life through the spirit of love.” [Col. 0775A]

## (Chapter V)

Now the historical account of Naaman the Syrian must be pursued. We have shown above that Eliseus bore the figure of the Lord the Savior.

Naaman, however, commander of the army of Syria, who was a leper and came to the blessed Eliseus to be healed at the suggestion of a maidservant, represented the people of the nations. [Col. 0775B]

The little girl who had been captured from the land of Israel by the Assyrians, brought to Syria, and made to serve Naaman’s wife, and who told her mistress that if she went to the blessed Eliseus she would obtain healing, is to be understood as the fame of the Law.

She is called “little” for the reason given by the Apostle: it was unable to bring anyone to perfection (Heb. 7:19). For all perfection is in the Lord Jesus Christ. The fame of what the Scriptures contained in the Law concerning chastity, sobriety, patience, justice, hospitality, piety, and the other virtues had reached all nations. Although at that time prophecy flourished only in Judea, it could not happen that its blessed reputation failed to reach the neighboring nations as well.

Although they tried to preserve it, it served them like a captive, because they were devoted to the worship of idols. [Col. 0775C]

Nevertheless, Naaman listened to the girl and came to Eliseus to be cleansed from leprosy. So too the people of the nations, who heard the fame of the Law and prophecy, came to Christ to be cleansed from the leprosy of all sins.

But let us see what the blessed Eliseus said to Naaman through a messenger. For he said to him (verse 10): “Go and wash seven times in the Jordan.” When Naaman heard that he should wash seven times in the Jordan (verses 11 and following), he became indignant and wanted to refuse. But after receiving counsel from his friends, he agreed to wash and was cleansed.

This signified that, before Christ was crucified, the people of the nations did not themselves believe Christ speaking; but afterward, when the Apostles spoke, they came faithfully to the sacrament of baptism. [Col. 0775D]

Eliseus, in prefiguration of future things, did not wish to see Naaman the Syrian, and yet he did not despise him at all. Thus the Lord Jesus Christ did not make the people of the nations, who did not see him with bodily eyes, foreign to his salvation.

Eliseus therefore said to Naaman that he should wash. It should be noted that, just as Eliseus sends Naaman to the Jordan River, so the people of the nations were sent by Christ to baptism.

But the fact that Eliseus neither touched nor baptized Naaman himself signified that Christ did not come to the people of the nations in person, but through his Apostles, because he said to them (Matt. 28:19): “Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” [Col. 0776A]

It should also be observed that Naaman, who represented the people of the nations, received healing in that river which Christ later consecrated by his baptism.

When Naaman heard that he should wash seven times in the Jordan, he became indignant and said (verses 11–12): “Are not the rivers of my country, the rivers of Damascus, Abana and Pharphar, better, so that I may wash in them and be cleansed?” When he said this, his servants advised him to accept the prophet’s counsel.

What this signifies must now be considered.

[Note: [Col. 0775D] Augustine, among others, most explicitly transmitted that Eliseus was a type of the Lord Jesus in section 11—elsewhere chapter 9—of Sermon 11 on the Words of the Apostle [in the new series, 26].]

Saint Eliseus, as we have said, bore the type of the Lord and Savior; Naaman represented the people of the nations. The fact that Naaman believed he would receive healing from his own rivers indicated that the human race presumed upon free will and its own merits. [Col. 0776B]

But merits of their own, without the grace of Christ, may possess freedom; they cannot receive healing at all. Therefore, unless the human race had listened to the counsel of Eliseus after the example of Naaman—that is, unless it had humbly received the gift of baptism through the grace of Christ—it could not be freed from original and actual leprosy.

Or otherwise: the rivers of Damascus, whose waters Naaman the Syrian considered better than the waters of the Jordan, signify the wisdom of this world. Before the people of the nations received faith in Christ, they esteemed this wisdom highly, neglected the evangelical commandments, and despised them. [Col. 0776C]

“Wash,” he said, referring to seven times because of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, which rested in Christ the Lord. Finally, when the Lord was baptized in that river, the Holy Spirit came upon him in the form of a dove.

When Naaman therefore descended into the river as a figure of baptism, Scripture says (verse 14): “His flesh became like the flesh of a little child.”

We see this likeness fulfilled in the Christian people, because all who are baptized, whether old or young, are nevertheless called infants. Through Adam and Eve the old are born; through Christ and the Church the new are regenerated.

The first generation leads to death; the second generation leads to life. The first generation makes children of wrath; the second generation makes vessels of mercy, as the Apostle says: “In Adam all die; in Christ all will be made alive.”

Just as Naaman, an old man, became like a child by washing seven times, so the people of the nations, though old with ancient sins and covered with many stains of iniquity like leprosy, are renewed through the grace of baptism. In them neither original nor actual leprosy of sin remains. They who had been bent beneath the weight of crimes are renewed, after the example of Naaman, by the saving bath like little children, and are clothed in the first robe. [Col. 0776D]

Of this the Apostle says: “All you who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ.”

In the cleansing of Naaman the Syrian, the tenth virtue of Eliseus is set forth. For the number ten indicates completion or perfection, because the Lord is read to have come at the end of the world, in whom salvation is recognized as having been granted to all nations sprinkled with the leprosy of unbelief. [Col. 0777A]

But after Naaman had been cleansed, he offered gifts to the blessed Eliseus, and Eliseus refused to accept them. In this the grace of Christ is figured, which is called grace because it is given freely.

For the Lord himself said to his disciples in the Gospel (Matt. 10:8): “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons; you have received freely, give freely.”

Meanwhile Naaman said to Eliseus (verse 17): “I ask you to grant your servant permission to take away a load of earth carried by two mules; for your servant will no longer offer burnt offerings or sacrifices to foreign gods, but only to the Lord.” [Col. 0777B]

The load of earth carried by two mules prefigured the mystery of the Incarnation of Christ. Both peoples—the one from circumcision and the one from uncircumcision—did not refuse to bear this mystery in hope of eternal blessedness.

After this the same Scripture reports that Eliseus questioned his servant Giezi (verse 25): “Where have you come from, Giezi?” He replied: “Your servant went nowhere.” He said: “Was not my heart present when the man turned back from his chariot to meet you? Now you have accepted silver, and you have accepted garments in order to buy olive groves, vineyards, sheep, cattle, male servants, and female servants. But the leprosy of Naaman will also cling to you and to your descendants forever.” [Col. 0777C]

[Note: [Col. 0777D] Claudius took the passages marked in the customary small lines from Augustine, who transmits them in chapter 29 of Book XXII of The City of God.]

“For if the prophet Eliseus, while absent in body, saw his servant Giezi receiving the gifts given to him by Naaman the Syrian, whom the prophet had cleansed from the deformity of leprosy, and if that wicked servant thought he had done it secretly because his master did not see him, how much more will the saints, in that spiritual body, see everything—not only when they close their eyes, but even from places where they are absent in body!

“Then that which the Apostle mentions will be perfect: ‘We know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be abolished’ (1 Cor. 13:9–10).

“Then, to show by some likeness, insofar as he could, how far this life differs from that which is to come [Note: [Col. 0777D] “Which is to come.”]—not merely the life of ordinary people, but that of those who here possess outstanding holiness—he says (ibid., verses 11–12): ‘When I was a child, I understood as a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child. But when I became a man, I abolished the things of a child. Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know as I am known.’

“If, therefore, in this life—where the prophecy of extraordinary human beings must be compared with that life as a child is compared with a young man—Eliseus nevertheless saw his servant receiving gifts where he himself was not present, will the saints, when that which is perfect has come and the corruptible body no longer weighs down [Note: [Col. 0777D] “Will weigh down.”] the soul, but the incorruptible body offers no impediment, need those eyes to see what is to be seen by bodily eyes, when Eliseus did not need them to see his absent servant?

“For according to the interpreters of the Septuagint, these are the Prophet’s words to Giezi (verse 26): ‘Was not my heart with you when the man turned from his chariot to meet you? And you accepted the money,’ and so forth. [Note: [Col. 0777D–0778D] “Was” (erat) is added; variants read “turned back” (reversus) for “turned” (conversus), “man” (homo) for “man” (vir), and “to meet” (in occursum) for “toward” (in obviam). These words are absent from the printed editions.]

“But as the presbyter Jerome translated from the Hebrew, he says: ‘Was not my heart present when the man turned back from his chariot to meet you?’ Therefore the Prophet said that he had seen this with his heart, certainly aided in a miraculous way by divine power [Note: [Col. 0778D] “God.”]—no one doubts that—but how much more abundantly will all possess that gift then, when ‘the Lord will be all in all’ (1 Cor. 15:28)! [Col. 0778B]

“Nevertheless, those bodily eyes will also have their own function, and each of the two will have its proper place for them in the spiritual body. For because that Prophet did not need his eyes in order to see someone absent, it does not follow that he did not use them to see present things—things which he could nevertheless see by the spirit even if he closed them, just as he saw absent things when he himself was not present with them.

“Far be it from us, therefore, to say that the saints in that life will not see God with their eyes closed, whom they will always see with the spirit. But whether they will also see him through the eyes of the body when they have them open—that is the question. [Col. 0778C]

“For if they have been able [Note: [Col. 0778D] Variant: “will be able” (poterunt).] to do only so much in the spiritual body, then those spiritual eyes themselves will likewise be able to do only as much as these eyes can do, such as we now possess; and, without doubt, God cannot be seen through them. It will therefore require a power of an entirely different kind if through them that incorporeal nature is to be seen which is not contained in a place but is wholly everywhere.”

Giezi, the servant of Eliseus, who was deceived by his desire for silver, accepted money from Naaman the Syrian, and shortly afterward was struck with the contagion of leprosy. There is no doubt that he bore the type of Judas the betrayer.

For just as Giezi served the blessed Eliseus in order to acquire money, so Judas had joined himself to the Lord and Savior in order to commit fraud and gather earthly riches. Thus it is written of him in the Gospel (John 12:6): “Because he was a thief, and had the purse, and carried away the things that were put into it.”

Giezi, who could have earned the favor of his master, just as his master had obtained the favor of the blessed Elias, was overcome by greed and deserved to be covered forever with cruel leprosy. Judas, however, through his love of money, lost both the grace of the apostleship and his life by the noose.

Thus we understand that all wicked priests within the Church have been inwardly covered with the leprosy of sin: they do not administer freely the ministry they received freely, contrary to the Lord’s commandments. For every work they perform in the Church, they seek not a future reward but a present recompense. [Col. 0779A]

Giezi can also be taken as a figure of the Jewish people, which was struck by the leprosy of sin at the very time when the people of the nations was liberated from it.

Thus the unbelieving Jews cried out during the Lord’s passion: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25). They deserved to be covered with the leprosy of sin when they cried out with sacrilegious lips against the heavenly physician: “Take him away, take him away; crucify him” (John 19:15).

Therefore the leprosy remained in them at the time when grace passed over to us. Thus the Apostle Paul also spoke to them, saying (Acts 13:46): “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you have judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations.” [Col. 0779B]

When the Apostles’ teaching passed to the nations, the leprosy of sin remained in the wretched Jews.

## (6:4–5)

After this Scripture reports that, when the blessed Eliseus went with the sons of the prophets to the Jordan River, and they were cutting wood for themselves, an axe fell into the water. The man from whose hand it had fallen cried out to the blessed Eliseus (IV Kings 6:5): “Alas, alas! And I had borrowed this very thing.”

Afterward, at the place where the axe had fallen, the blessed Eliseus threw in a piece of wood, and the iron floated.

[Note: [Col. 0779D] The earlier part of this explanation is taken from Isidore’s commentaries on 4 Kings.]

“Lord Jesus Christ, whose figure Eliseus bore, when by the presence of his body he wished to cut down the impiety of the Jews like a fruitless tree, because John had said of him: [Col. 0779C] ‘Behold, the axe is laid at the root of the trees’ (Matt. 3:10). Likewise, when the Passion intervened, he left that body, as it were an axe-handle, and descended into the depths of hell. Once placed in the tomb, he rose again to life, when the spirit returned, as it were to its handle.”

Or otherwise: We have often already said above that Eliseus bore the type of the Lord and Savior. But in that boy, the son of the prophet, from whose hand the axe slipped, Christ the Lord may not incongruously be understood. That axe which fell seems to signify Adam, or the whole human race. The prophet’s son therefore held the axe in his hand; and our Lord and Savior held in the hand of his power the human race that he had created. But just as that axe slipped from the prophet’s hand and fell into the depths, so the human race, when through pride it tore itself away from the hand of almighty God, fell into the river of lust and submerged itself in the whirlpool of every sin.

That axe therefore lay in the depths, because the human race had fallen through an unhappy ruin into the abyss of every crime, as it is written: “I am stuck in the mire of the deep” (Ps. 68:2). Again: “I have come into the depth of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me” (ibid. 3). For the river [Col. 0780A] in which the axe fell signifies the passing, fleeing, and downward-flowing course of pleasure, or the luxurious course of this world; for a river takes its name from flowing. And because all sinners, clinging to passing pleasures, are said to flow, that axe therefore lay buried in the mud of the river.

But Eliseus came, cast in a piece of wood, and made the iron float.

[Note: [Col. 0779D] The following appears to present an ancient explanation taken from another writer.]

What does it mean to cast in wood and bring the iron up into the light, except to ascend the gallows of the cross and rescue the human race from the depths of hell, freeing it from the very bottom of all sins through the mystery of the cross? After the iron floated, the Prophet stretched out his hand, recovered it, and restored it to its master for useful service. So it has happened with us: we who had fallen from the Lord’s hand through pride are restored by the wood of the cross [Col. 0780B] to the Lord’s hand or power.

Likewise, morally:

[Note: [Col. 0779D] Gregory the Great transmitted the following at length in no. 9 and 10, elsewhere as chapter 5 of book XXII of the *Moralia*; Paterius also cites it.]

“‘The iron in the axe-handle is the gift of understanding in the heart; but to cut wood with it is to rebuke those who act wrongly. Sometimes, when this is done carelessly, when the fall of vainglory is not avoided in the knowledge that has been received, the iron is lost in the water, because understanding becomes foolish through disordered conduct. We know that this understanding is given for the purpose that it should be restored before the eyes of the giver through good action. Hence rightly the man who had lost the iron cried out: “Alas, alas, my lord, and I had borrowed this as well.” For the elect have this distinctive quality: if at any time, in their knowledge, the fault of vainglory secretly steals upon them, they quickly return to their heart and pursue with tears whatever they find condemnable in themselves before the eyes of the strict Judge.

“‘Weeping, they carefully examine not only the evils they have committed, but also the good deeds they ought to have returned from the gift they received. For they recognize themselves as sinners all the more deeply because, through the good things they neglected—things they were able to do—they are held as debtors. Rightly, therefore, the man who lost the iron cried: “Alas, alas, alas, and I had borrowed this as well,” as though he were saying: “Through the slackness of negligence I lost what I had received from the grace of the creditor in order to return it through good works.”

“‘Yet God never abandons the mind that truly acknowledges itself in sins. Hence Eliseus immediately comes, casts the wood downward, and brings the iron up to the surface: for our Redeemer, looking upon us with compassion, humbles the sinner’s heart and restores understanding to the one who had lost it. He submerges the wood and lifts up the iron, because he afflicts the heart and repairs knowledge.

[Note: [Col. 0780D] “Which.”]

“‘Hence another translation appropriately says that he broke the wood, threw it in, and thus lifted up the iron.

[Note: [Col. 0780D] “He raises it.”]

“‘To break the wood is to crush the heart’s pride. To throw the wood down to the depths is to humble the elevated heart in thought, as we have said, through recognition of its own weakness.

[Note: [Col. 0780D] “Elevated.”]

[Note: [Col. 0780D] “In knowledge.”]

“‘Then immediately the iron returns to the surface, because understanding returns to its former practice of active exercise.

[Note: [Col. 0780D] “To.”]

[Note: [Col. 0780D] “To its former use.”]

[Col. 0781A] “‘Therefore, since the gift of understanding that one receives is scarcely preserved amid so many difficulties, one must take great care lest it grow sluggish through idleness, and care must be taken lest it fade away in the practice of works through the fault of pride. For holy men do not rejoice when they recognize what they do, but when they do what they have recognized.

[Note: [Col. 0781D] “They do.”]

[Note: [Col. 0781D] “They had recognized.”]

“‘And although, in understanding, they rejoice in the more abundant gift of the giver, they nevertheless consider with sorrow the debt of works, so that by their action they may repay what has been extended to them in thought.

[Note: [Col. 0781D] “Granted.”]

[Note: [Col. 0781D] “In thought.”]

“‘For a debtor is foolish who gladly accepts borrowed money but does not consider the time when he ought to repay it.

[Note: [Col. 0781D] “Ought.”]

“‘The joy of receiving is moderated when, with diligent foresight, the appointed time for repayment is also kept in mind.’”

(Vers. 8.) “Now the king of Syria was fighting against Israel, and he took counsel with his servants, saying: ‘In that place and that place let us set an ambush,’” and so forth. The king of Syria, besieging Samaria, bore the type of the devil, who before the Savior’s coming had enclosed the Jewish people in his siege. His cruelty and the hidden snares that he set before the human race were frustrated by the foreknowledge and power of the true Eliseus, that is, the Lord and Savior.

The army of the king of Assyria, which was sent by him to capture Eliseus, represented the scribes and Pharisees, who were incited by the devil’s prompting to persecute God. Through the power of that same Lord and Savior they were struck with blindness by a just judgment; and again, through his mercy, they were fed with the bread of the word of God and refreshed with the water of knowledge.

It is rightly asked how those Syrians could have gone into Samaria if they had been struck with such blindness that they saw absolutely nothing. They too were struck with this blindness (*aurasia*) [Note: [Col. 0781D] The place may be somewhat corrupt; let others judge. The codex reads: “these auras.”]—and those who were seeking Lot’s door were struck in the same way. Thus, disturbed by their misfortune, they became deranged until they reached Samaria, and afterward they no longer sought to capture the Prophet in this manner.

(V. 24 and following.) “After this, Ben-hadad, king of Syria, gathered his entire army, went up, and besieged Samaria. A great famine arose in Samaria, and the city was besieged for so long that a donkey’s head was sold for eighty pieces of silver, and a quarter of a cab of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver,” and so forth.

The famine inflicted upon Samaria signifies the scarcity of the word of God, or the poverty of faith, by which the devil, before the Savior’s coming, had enclosed God’s people. The donkey’s head sold for eighty pieces of silver signifies pride, which is the beginning of every sin. For there is no doubt that by the donkey, an unclean animal, all the vices of the devil were prefigured; and, as has been said, their head is pride. All the reprobate, neglecting the Decalogue of the Law and the Gospel ogdoad, in which the image of God is found, preferred to consume this as food for themselves rather than the bread of the word of God.

But the quarter of a cab of dove’s dung, purchased for five pieces of silver and said to have been taken as food, seems to have signified this: the reprobate people, abandoning the worship of God and subjecting themselves to the five bodily senses, were fed, as though on some stench of sins, through the worship of idols and pretense, and satisfied the devil.

There is no doubt that the two women, one of whom, in the famine’s deprivation, cooked and ate her own son, signified the reprobate multitude from the Jews. Whatever good it could originally have possessed in itself, it consumed and exhausted through the poverty of faith. The other woman, who refused to consent to such a crime, undoubtedly represented the chosen people.

(Cap. 7:3.) “There were therefore four leprous men near the entrance of the gate, and they said to one another: ‘Why should we remain here until we die?’” and so forth.

The four lepers, who, placed outside the city, announce Israel’s future [Note: [Col. 0782D] “Liberation,” I believe.] deliverance, seem to have signified those from the Jewish people who first confessed the uncleanness of their sins before the others and deserved to attain such great grace that they might announce to the rest the devil’s defeat and flight through the victory of Christ’s cross.

The five horses, which are said to have remained in Samaria because of the extreme scarcity caused by the famine, certainly represented the carnal Jewish people abandoned under the five books of the Law.

That commander who, hearing through Eliseus of the future abundance of grain, refused to believe, represented the scribes and Pharisees. He saw the abundance of faith divinely bestowed upon the Church, but because he refused to believe, he died in his impiety and was trampled underfoot by the faithful.

[Col. 0782C]

(Cap. 8.) “Eliseus spoke to the woman whose son he had restored to life, saying: ‘Arise, go,’” and so forth.

The Shunammite woman, who, because of the scarcity caused by famine, crossed from Judea into the land of the Philistines at Eliseus’s advice, prefigured the primitive Church, which through the Apostles believed in Christ from the circumcision. Because of the Jews’ unbelief and the poverty of the word of God that had overtaken them, this Church, when the divine Spirit revealed it to her, migrated to the Gentile people.

At the end of the world, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, she will return to the former people. When Elias preaches, she will receive the elect from that same people, as though reclaiming the ancient possession of her patrons under her own right; and then all Israel will be saved.

(Cap. 11:4.) “In the seventh year Joiada sent for them and took the centurions and the soldiers . . . and commanded them, saying . . . ‘Let a third of you enter on the Sabbath,’” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0782D] Claudius borrowed this explanation of the passage entirely from Bede, who gives it in his explanation of the Books of Kings.]

“What the high priest Joiada said to the priests and Levites in the temple, when he brought out Joash, son of Azariah, whom he had secretly nourished in the temple during the six years of Athaliah’s reign, was this: ‘Let a third of you enter on the Sabbath and keep watch over the king’s house; another third shall be at the Gate of Seir; and another third at the gate that is behind the dwelling of the shield-bearers. You shall guard the watch of the house of Messa. But let the two parts of you, all who go out on the Sabbath, keep watch over the house of the Lord around the king, and surround him, bearing weapons in your hands,’” and so forth.

What is said and done there is better understood if something more extensive is repeated concerning the places in the temple where these things occurred.

The temple itself, apart from the porticoes by which it was surrounded and joined to it on every side, had within its walls—for this is the first measurement, which the Books of Chronicles call it—sixty cubits in length and twenty in width. Its entire circuit was surrounded by a courtyard three cubits high, with an entrance on the eastern side. Scripture mentions this in the Book of Kings: “He built the inner court with three rows of hewn stones and one row of cedar wood” (3 Kings 6).

It calls this the inner court because other courts had been constructed around it. In the Books of Chronicles it says: “He also made the court of the priests and the great basilica, and doors in the basilica, which he covered with bronze” (2 Chron. 4). It calls this the court of the priests because it had been made to keep others from entering the temple and to indicate that entry was permitted only to the priests.

[Note: [Col. 0783D] The edition has only the following: “which would indicate that entry was permitted to the priests.” The reading of our codex is preferable.]

This same court was closer to the temple wall on the southern, western, and northern sides. Toward the rising sun, where it also had its entrance by means of steps, it extended a great distance from the temple. On that side it contained the altar of holocausts; on another, ten basins in which the sacrifices were washed; on another, the bronze sea in which the priests entering upon their ministry washed themselves; and on another, the choirs of the Levites, the priests who offered sacrifice, and those who sang psalms.

This court was surrounded on every side by a very large building, exceedingly long and square. Its inner wall—that is, the wall facing the temple from the four regions of the world—was constructed below entirely in arches, whereas the outer wall was founded in solid masonry. It had bronze doors, as we mentioned above, and “doors in the basilica, which he covered with bronze.” It was also strengthened by very large porticoes and divided by suitable upper rooms.

Again, outside this building, another structure of similar design was built in a circuit.

[Note: [Col. 0784D] “Altar.”]

[Note: [Col. 0784D] “Made.”]

A third was likewise built around it in the same order, enclosing all the inner areas far and wide. It differed from the earlier buildings only in that its eastern and northern walls had no doors, since both belonged to the city walls.

These are the courts of which the Psalms sing: “You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Ps. 133 and 134). Since the house of the Lord itself had been built on a higher place, the courts were arranged so that, the farther outward they were, the higher their walls became, because their foundations were lower down.

[Note: [Col. 0784D] “They became so”: but the text is mistaken.]

Indeed, the outermost walls were four hundred cubits high, yet they did not even approach the height of the temple. A general reference to all these things is made in the Book of Chronicles:

“David gave Solomon his son the plan of the portico, the temple, the storerooms, the upper room, the inner rooms, and the house of the mercy-seat, as well as the plan of everything he had conceived: of the courts and chambers around the treasury of the house of the Lord and the treasuries of the holy things” (1 Chron. 28).

Josephus’s account, or the picture formed by the ancients, also distinguishes more fully the order in which these things were constructed (Antiq. 8.3).

Once these arrangements had been made, only the high priest entered the Holy of Holies, once a year, with the blood of sacrifices. Only purified priests entered the sanctuary before the oracle. [Col. 0784B] All the priests and Levites entered the inner court.

Around this court, under the open sky—or, if bad weather prevented it, in the buildings situated around it—the Israelite men gathered to pray or to hear the word of God.

[Note: [Col. 0784D] “Would customarily gather.”]

In the third order of courts, Israelite women stood under the open sky to pray. If the weather did not permit this, they entered the roofs of the nearby surrounding buildings. In the last order of courts, Gentiles who had happened to gather for prayer entered.

There also, after the time of the dispersion, those who had recently come from the Gentiles and had become Israelites, after being purified for seven days, finally proceeded into the inner holy places.

[Note: [Col. 0784D] The words “for seven days” are absent from the editions.]

All the pavements within or among the courts were laid with variegated stone. The doors in the buildings were placed opposite one another in such a way that even those standing in the outermost courts could see the temple.

There were twenty-four divisions of priests, Levites, and doorkeepers, who succeeded one another in order through as many weeks. On the Sabbath a new group entered upon its office, and after the Sabbath the group that had ministered during the preceding week returned home.

But here the high priest declares the necessity of increasing the forces around the new king. He retained those whose turn was to enter for the coming week, and he kept back those who had already completed their week of service, so that they would not depart.

He had also gathered from all the cities of Judah the other Levites and the heads of the Israelite families, sending centurions for this purpose to Jerusalem, as the Books of Chronicles relate (1 Chron. 23). He divided them in this way when he was about to bring out the king’s son: all who had completed their Sabbath duty and were about to depart were divided into two groups, and, armed, they surrounded the king in the inner areas of the court.

The rest of the multitude—that is, those who were not of the tribe of Levi—guarded the outer doors of the courts against the queen’s fury, in case she should attempt anything hostile.

The priests, Levites, and doorkeepers who had recently come for the Sabbath, however, were divided into three groups. They were to watch the king’s house, that is, the palace, lest the queen, having gathered an army, defend herself against the king.

They were also to guard the gate of the dwelling of the shield-bearers, by which one descended from the temple to the palace, as is said below: “They led the king out of the house of the Lord and came by way of the gate of the shield-bearers into the palace, and he sat upon the throne of the kings.” There also seem to have been the gate of Siref and the house of Messa, which are mentioned together with the gate of the shield-bearers.

He calls the shield-bearers the guardians of the kings, as the Book of Chronicles testifies. After it had related that Rehoboam had made bronze shields in place of golden ones, it added: “And he entrusted them to the commanders of the shield-bearers, who guarded the entrance to the palace” (2 Chron. 12).

All these matters are set out more distinctly in that book:

“Let a third of you who come on the Sabbath, of the priests, Levites, and doorkeepers, be at the gates; another third at the king’s house; and another third at the gate called the Foundation. Let all the remaining people be in the courts of the house of the Lord, and let no one enter the house of the Lord except the priests and those who minister among the Levites. Let only those who have been sanctified enter.

[Note: [Col. 0785D] “Because.”]

Let all the remaining people keep the watches of the Lord. Let the Levites surround the king, each carrying his weapons,” and so forth.

(Vers. 12.) “Concerning the same matter, what follows says:

[Note: [Col. 0785D] The explanation of this passage and of the one that follows is also taken from Bede, in the same work, nos. 20 and 21.]

[Note: [Col. 0785D] “He brought out the king’s son and placed upon him the diadem, and the testimony.”]

“He brought out the king’s son and placed upon him the diadem and the testimony, the royal insignia upon the diadem of his head.” By “the testimony” he designates the decrees of God’s law, which prescribe what a king ought to do and how he ought to live.

The Books of Chronicles state the matter more clearly: “They placed the diadem upon him and gave him the law to hold in his hand” (2 Chron. 23:11).

It was certainly a matter of great and salutary prudence that, through the death of the tyrannical and impious queen, when the son of the legitimate king succeeded to the throne, he should be entrusted at the same time with the royal attire and with the observance of God’s law; and that the man who saw himself placed above the people for ruling them should remember that he himself ought to be subject to the divine laws and to be ruled by them.”

(Cap. 12:13.) “No accounting was made with the men who received the money,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0785D] Rabanus likewise took this passage from Bede.]

“Concerning the restoration of the Lord’s temple in the time of the aforementioned King Joash, it says: ‘No accounting was made with the men who received the money to distribute it to the craftsmen, but they dealt with it in good faith.’ This demonstrates the devotion of those about whom the passage speaks: they showed such zeal in religion that no one doubted that they handled the Lord’s money without any suspicion of fraud, and that, having taken it from the treasury, they faithfully offered it to the craftsmen to strengthen the house according to the needs of each.”

(13:20.) “After this,” it says, “Eliseus died, and they buried him. But bands of Moabites came into the land in that very year. Now, some men who were burying a man saw the raiders, and they cast the corpse into the tomb of Eliseus. When it touched the bones of Eliseus, the man immediately came back to life and stood upon his feet.”

The Moabite raiders are to be understood figuratively as demons, who drive wretched minds toward incest and every detestable work by the goads of vices.

Those who were burying the dead are to be understood as those who, as the Apostle James says, “convert the ungodly and sinners from the error of their way” through continual exhortation to the path of devotion and chastity, saving their souls from eternal death and covering a multitude of sins (James 5:19).

Or otherwise: Those who bury the dead and flee from the raiders are rightly called those who, wishing to live devoutly in Christ, flee and avoid every vice and sin, which produce death, and cast their bodies into the fountain of baptism. In it, according to the Apostle, believers are buried with Christ (Rom. 6:4; Col. 2:12), so that thereafter, through communion in his body and blood, they may live with Christ.

(14:7.) “He himself”—namely, Amaziah—“struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, ten thousand men,” and so forth.

Concerning Amaziah, king of Judah, it is said: “He himself struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, ten thousand, and captured the Rock in battle, and called its name” [Note: [Col. 0785D] “Jectehel.”] “Jecethel.”

[Note: [Col. 0786D] Bede has this in Question 21 among the thirty questions on the Books of Kings.]

“‘The Valley of Salt’ was a place where salt was produced, either from salty grass, which was cut, dried, and burned in many places, or from well water heated with salt and boiled until it reached the consistency of salt, or by some other method through which salt is customarily made. It is also the place where Joab is said to have struck twelve thousand Idumeans.

“Nor should it be passed over that, instead of ‘the Valley of Salt,’ the old edition put *Gemela*, as though it were the name of a region.

[Note: [Col. 0786D] “Gemelach.”]

“The Rock is a famous city of Arabia in the same land of Edom. In the Book of Numbers it is called Rekem, and it is still called this by the Assyrians.

[Note: [Col. 0786D] “Jecthel.”]

“Jecethel, the name that Amaziah the victor gave it, is interpreted ‘assembly of God’ or ‘help of God.’ He acted faithfully so that it might be perpetually remembered that he had captured it either through the assembly of God’s people or with God’s help.”

(14:25.) “He restored the boundaries of Israel from the entrance of Emath,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0786D] This passage and the following one are likewise taken from Bede.]

“Concerning Jeroboam, king of Israel, it is said: ‘He restored the boundaries of Israel from the entrance of Emath to the Sea of the Arabah.’ Emath, now called Epiphania, was Israel’s northern boundary. The Sea of the Arabah, which in Hebrew is called *Araba*, designates the Dead Sea. It extends lengthwise for 580 stadia to Zoaras of the Arabah, and in breadth for 150 stadia toward the vicinity of Sodom.”

[Note: [Col. 0786D] “Zoaras.”]

[Note: [Col. 0786D] “Extends.”]

[Note: [Col. 0786D] 17:29.]

“Each nation made its own god,” and so forth.

[Col. 0787A]

“Concerning the nations that the king of Assyria brought into Samaria, it says: ‘Each nation made its own god and placed it in the high shrines that they had made,’ the people of Samaria, each nation in its cities where they dwelt.

“For the men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth; the men of Cuth made Nergal; the men of Hamath made Ashima. The Hivites made Nibhaz and Tartak.

[Note: [Col. 0787D] “Samaritans.”]

[Note: [Col. 0787D] “Hamath.”]

[Note: [Col. 0787D] “Nibhaz and Tartak.”]

“In the Book of Places it is read that Benoth and Nergal were cities that the Samaritans who had crossed over from Babylonia built in the region of Judea. Ashima was also a town that those who came there from Hamath built. Nibhaz and Tartak were likewise cities that the Hivites founded in the same land of Judea.

“Yet, according to the sequence of the passage, it also seems possible to understand here the names of the idols that these nations had previously worshiped in their own land. For after it had been said, ‘Each nation made its own god,’ the following was added as though completing the sentence: ‘The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth,’ that is, ‘the tabernacles of Benoth.’

[Note: [Col. 0787D] “These.”]

[Note: [Col. 0787D] “When.”]

“And, unless I am mistaken, the translator would have done better to translate *Succoth* into Latin as ‘tabernacles’ and to leave the name of the idol, *Benoth*, standing by itself. The same is plainly said in what follows: ‘Those who were from Sepharvaim burned their sons in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim’ (17:31). There it is shown that Adrammelech and Anammelech were the idols of the city of Sepharvaim. It therefore follows that Nergal was the idol of the Cuthaeans, Ashima the idol of the Hamathites, and Nibhaz and Tartak the idols of the Hivites.

[Col. 0787C]

(18:13.) “In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib, king of Assyria, came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them,” and so forth.

The historical account is clear and requires no interpretation.

[Note: [Col. 0787D] Verse 19: “Thus says the Great King, the king of Assyria.”]

In the words of the Rabshakeh, however, one must consider his arrogance. Like a kind of opposing power, he imitates the custom of the prophets. What they commonly place in their prologues—“Thus says the Lord”—to display the authority and greatness of the speaker, he now says: “Thus says the great king, the king of Assyria.”

Let us consider the words of the Rabshakeh.

[Note: [Col. 0787D] “These words were transmitted by Claudius. Rabanus likewise transmitted them in his treatment of this passage.]

“‘First, when he says: “Do you trust in this broken reed, in Egypt?” it is false. No history relates that Hezekiah sent to the Egyptians and sought the help of Pharaoh.

[Note: [Col. 0788D] “Do you hope in a staff,” and so forth.]

“‘But when he adds: “If you say to me, ‘We trust in the Lord our God’” (v. 22), he speaks the truth. Yet again he joins a lie to the truth when he says that Hezekiah removed his high places and altars. He had done this not against the Lord but for the Lord: after destroying idolatry and the ancient error, he commanded that the Lord be worshiped in Jerusalem, where his temple was.

“‘And when, wishing to display the small number of the besieged, he promises two thousand horses, which Hezekiah would be unable to provide with riders, this does not arise from the weakness of the Jewish people, who lacked the skill of riding.

[Note: [Col. 0788D] “As though unskilled in riding.”]

“It arises from the observance of God’s commandments. Through Moses, God had commanded concerning the king of Israel: “He shall not multiply horses for himself, nor shall he have many wives” (Deut. 17:16–17).

“‘But to what he had said, “If you say to me, ‘We trust in the Lord our God,’” he cunningly and prudently replied that he had come not by his own will but at the Lord’s command.

[Note: [Col. 0788D] Verse 25: “Have I come without the Lord’s will?”]

“‘And Eliakim and the others said to the Rabshakeh:

[Note: [Col. 0788D] Verse 26.]

“‘“Speak to your servants in the Syrian language, for we understand it,”’ and so forth.

“The Rabshakeh’s accusation is a testimony to Hezekiah: after all the cities of Judah had been captured, he trusted in the Lord and said to the people: “Do not fear or be afraid of the king of Assyria and all the multitude that is with him, for there are more with us than with him. With him is an arm of flesh; with us is the Lord our God, who is our helper and fights for us” (2 Chron. 32:7). And, it says, the people were strengthened by these words of Hezekiah.

“Therefore the Rabshakeh seeks to destroy what Hezekiah had built, and he says to the people: “Let not Hezekiah deceive you, and let him not give you confidence in the Lord God” (4 Kings 18:29).

“Again, adding threat and terror, he says: “They shall eat their own dung and drink the urine of their cattle with you” (v. 27).

[Note: [Col. 0788D] The Vulgate reads: “Their own urine.”]

“Through this he shows that they are to be overcome by hunger, scarcity, and thirst. At the same time he joins enticements to fear, so that those whom he had not conquered through terror he might deceive through promises and persuasion, saying: “Make with me what is advantageous” (v. 31).

“Thus the sense is: “Do,” he says, “what benefits you and advances your blessing.” Or he says this: “Bless the king of Assyria and praise him, just as you confess the Lord, so that you may obtain rewards. Until I return from Egypt, or return after capturing Lomna, live in your city and enjoy your possessions. Then I shall come and transfer you to a land like your own land” (v. 32).

“Some think that the land of Media is promised to them, since it resembled the land of Judah both in location and in crops.”

[Note: [Col. 0788D] Rabanus ends here; the following is supplied by Bede, Question 24 on the Books of Kings, and again by Rabanus.]

“What he adds—‘Where is the god of Emath, Arphad, Sepharvaim, Ana, and Ava? Have they delivered Samaria from my hand?’—shows that the Samaritans had served the gods of all these cities or peoples. Since they were not gods but idols, it was fitting that the worshipers of vanity should be overthrown.”

Emath is a city of Coele-Syria, now called Epiphania, near Emesa, as we mentioned above.

[Note: [Col. 0788D] “Emesa.”]

Arphat is a city of Damascus, which Jeremiah also says was conquered by the king of Assyria (Jer. 4:47).

[Note: [Col. 0789D] “Arphad.”]

Sepharvaim, which in the plural number denotes “books” or “letters,” is the name of the places from which the Assyrians migrated and dwelt in Samaria, as we find in the Books of Places. But in Isaiah this word also appears to be the name of a city, where it is plainly said: “Where is the god of the city of Sepharvaim?” (Isa. 36:19), although it is expressed in the plural, like Thebes and Athens.

For Ana and Ava, the old edition placed *Aneumgava*, as though it were the name of a single city.

[Note: [Col. 0789D] “Aneumgava.”]

This is indeed how it is written in Hebrew. But because the syllable *u*, placed in the middle of the name, signifies “and” among them, it can also be divided so that the names are Ane and Gave, as Aquila translated them, or Anua and Avua, as our translator rendered them.”

[Col. 0789B]

(Vers. 36.) “The people were silent and answered him nothing, for they had received the king’s command that they should not answer him.”

[Note: [Col. 0789D] Rabanus, and what follows, transmits almost verbatim.]

“Truly Hezekiah, being righteous, acted faithfully and with complete deliberation. For this reason he had ordered that they should not answer the blaspheming Assyrian, lest they provoke him to greater blasphemies.”

(Vers. 37.) “Eliakim and the others with him entered Hezekiah with their garments torn.”

“Leaving aside what is obvious, let us discuss only what contains a hidden meaning. He tears his garments because they had heard the Rabshakeh blaspheming.

(Cap. 19:1.) “The king himself also tears his garments because he believed that it was on account of his own sins and those of the people that the Rabshakeh had come as far as the gates of Jerusalem and had spoken such things against the Lord.

“Therefore he was wrapped in sackcloth instead of royal dress. From the palace he went up to the temple, and he sent Eliakim the high priest, Shebna the scribe,

[Note: [Col. 0789D] “Soboam.”]

“and the elders of the priests to Isaiah the prophet, son of Amos (v. 2).

“Here the king’s humility and prudence must be considered. He himself went to the temple, while he sent the leaders of the people and the elders of the priests to Isaiah the prophet, son of Amos, not clothed in priestly robes but covered with sackcloth.”

(Vers. 3.) “They said to him,” it says: “‘Thus says Hezekiah: This day is a day of tribulation, correction, and blasphemy.’”

He calls it the day of our tribulation, God’s correction, and the enemies’ blasphemy. He adds the likeness of a woman in labor, distressed because her children have come to the point of birth but she lacks the strength to give birth.

[Note: [Col. 0789D] Rabanus ends here. What follows is taken from Paterius, and therefore from Gregory the Great; Paterius does not indicate the passage of Gregory that he cites.]

“‘In the literal sense we see these things occurring because of sins: when enemies invade, our defenders prepare themselves, but in no way do they grow strong enough for the preparations.

“For it is written: “The spirit of counsel and fortitude shall rest upon him” (Isa. 11:2). These two are necessarily joined to one another, because neither strength without counsel can be useful, nor counsel without strength.

“What benefit, then, do those who prepare themselves through counsel provide, when they do not advance to battle through strength?

“Thus King Hezekiah, afflicted and troubled, says: “This is a day of tribulation and blasphemy; the children have come to the point of birth, and the woman in labor has no strength.”

“For the children come to the point of birth when sound counsels advance as far as the desire to accomplish the work; but the woman in labor has no strength because, while a weak person conceives counsels, he does not bring them forth through the birth of action for any useful purpose.’”

What follows:

(Vers. 4.) “Perhaps the Lord your God will hear all the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master, the king of the Assyrians, has sent. For we do not dare to call him the Lord of all of us, since, when he is angry, we suffer such things; but we call him your Lord, and in this we place our hope of vengeance: the living God is being blasphemed by a worshiper of dead idols.”

When the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah, Isaiah anticipated them. For by the same Spirit by which he knew the future, he had also heard of the absent king, and he tells them what they should answer their master, with confidence joined to humility of conscience. “Say,” he says, “to your master, whose Lord is my Lord also: For thus says the Lord: (vers. 6, 7) Do not fear the words by which not you but I have been blasphemed. Behold, I will send a spirit upon him, and he will hear a report and return to his own land, and I will strike him down with the sword in his own land.” Thus Hezekiah would hear two things he desired at once: that he would be delivered from the siege and danger, and that his hostile and enraged king would die in his own land.

(Vers. 8.) “Rabshakeh returned and found the king of the Assyrians attacking [Note: [Col. 0790D] The edition reads *Lobnam*.] Lomna, etc.” [Note: [Col. 0790D] Rabanus again teaches us these same things, though he transmits only this much: “When the city was about to be captured” [perhaps, “for the city about to be captured”]. Herodotus relates that Tharaca, king of the Ethiopians, came to its aid.] “Herodotus relates that Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, fought against the Egyptians and besieged Pelusium; and when the earthworks had already been constructed and the city was about to be captured, Tharaca, king of the Ethiopians, came to its aid. In a single night, near Jerusalem, one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrian army fell from pestilence.” [Note: [Col. 0790D] Book II, chapter 141. But with fables interwoven.] “Berosus, the writer of Chaldean history, relates this in fullest detail.” [Note: [Col. 0790D] We are wholly deprived of these books.]

[Col. 0790D]

(Vers. 14, 15.) “And so, when Hezekiah had received the letter from the hand of the messengers and had read it, he went up to the house of the Lord and spread it out before the Lord, etc.” Against the blasphemies of King Sennacherib, Hezekiah took up his customary weapons; again he goes to the temple and spreads out his letters before the Lord, boldly entreating him. He asserts that God alone is living; by him we understand idols to be images of the dead.

Isaiah sent word to Hezekiah (vers. 20), saying: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I have heard what you have entreated me concerning Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians. This is the word that the Lord has spoken concerning him: The virgin daughter of Zion has despised you and mocked you; the daughter of Jerusalem has shaken her head behind you.” [Note: [Col. 0791D] Rabanus also teaches nearly all that follows.] “Because Hezekiah entreated the Lord so boldly, and did not send to Isaiah as he had sent previously, the prophet himself does not go to him but sends messengers to tell him the word of God concerning Sennacherib, against whom he is praying: ‘This is the Lord’s sentence. The virgin daughter of Zion and the daughter of Jerusalem’—she is called virgin and daughter because, among all the nations that worship images, she alone preserves the chastity of the worship of God and the cult of the one divinity—‘has mocked and despised you. And she, lest she provoke you to greater blasphemies, did not answer you in your presence. After you have departed, she will shake her head.’ Certain of vengeance and secure of punishment, she has spoken thus: ‘You have acted proudly not against me but against the Lord; and not through yourself but through your servants, so that the arrogance of the blasphemer might be greater.’ [Note: [Col. 0791D] Verse 23, but here and thereafter an interpretation somewhat different from the Vulgate is presented.]

“For you have said that, with the multitude of your chariots, you have ascended to the heights of the mountains and cut down the lofty ridges of Lebanon. Its cedars and fir trees—which we may understand metaphorically either of all the nations and their rulers, or of Jerusalem, which is interpreted as ‘Lebanon’—may refer, as its cedars and fir trees, also to the powerful and nobles; its height to its summits; and the forest of Carmel to the temple. And when he adds: ‘I dug and drank water, and with the sole of my foot I dried up all the streams of the embankments,’ this may be understood historically to mean that, because of the multitude of his army, he dried up all the watercourses and was compelled to dig wells for himself; metaphorically, it may mean that he devastated with his army all the peoples who are sometimes represented under the name of waters.

(Vers. 25.) “‘Have you not heard what I did long ago? From ancient days I fashioned it, and now I have brought it about; and fortified cities of the warring hills shall become a ruin. Those who dwell in them, feeble of hand, trembled and were confounded like the grass of the field and the green herb of the roofs, which withered before it reached maturity. I knew your dwelling, your going out, your coming in, and your way; and your rage against me. You raged against me, and your pride has risen into my ears.’

“These words are to be understood as spoken by the Lord against the words of the Assyrian: the Lord answered his blasphemy in this way. ‘Do you not know that you did these things by my will, and that I foretold these future events and commanded that they be accomplished through you? Therefore what I had long ago decreed has been fulfilled in its appointed time: namely, that the hills—that is, the rulers—who were fighting among themselves, and the most strongly fortified cities, when I withdrew my hand and did not provide my customary aid, should be destroyed, tremble, perish, and be compared not with olive trees, vineyards, and fruitful trees, but with hay, grass, and the herbs of housetops, which hinder crops and wither before they reach maturity. Thus I knew beforehand your sitting, your going out, and your coming in; and I spoke through the prophets of the madness with which you were going to rage against me. Through them I knew long ago that you would say: (Isa. XIV, 14) “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne, and I will be like the Most High.” Thus your rage and your pride have reached my ears, and I will no longer endure you, so that you may understand that, although you were able to do these things, you could not do them by your own strength but by my decision. For the impious nations—[Note: [Col. 0791D] The edition reads “fruitful,” but incorrectly.] and unfruitful trees—deserved to be cut down and fall through you as through my axe and saw.’

(Vers. 28.) “‘Therefore I will put a ring in your nostrils and a bridle in your lips, so that I may restrain the mouths of blasphemers and you may no longer dare to speak such things; and I will place a bit upon your lips, which will tame your ferocity and lead you back to Assyria.

“‘But for you, Hezekiah, this will be the sign: Eat this year what you find, and in the second year what grows of itself. In the third year, sow and reap; plant vineyards and eat their fruit.’

“All this the prophet speaks through messengers to Hezekiah: what Sennacherib said and what the Lord answered him. He does not address him directly, lest he perhaps doubt that the things foretold would come to pass. For this reason especially the prophets had credibility among the people: they recalled not only what would happen many centuries later, but also what would be fulfilled immediately and after no great interval of time. ‘Within two years,’ he says, ‘the king of the Assyrians will perish and security will be restored to the city of Jerusalem. This will be the sign of the things I foretell: this year you shall eat what you find; in the second year, what grows of itself; but in the third year, once the Assyrian has been driven away and the siege relaxed, sow and reap; plant vineyards and eat their fruit.’ For the remnant of this city [Note: [Col. 0792D] The small remnant of the city.]—now surrounded by the hostile army and not believing that it will escape—will receive such abundance and prosperity in all things that, like a tree firmly established with a deep root, it will be filled with the thickest fruit.

[Note: [Col. 0792D] Verse 30. Rabanus also continues up to this point; what follows is taken from Paterius and therefore from Gregory. See no. 81, alternatively chapter 48, of Book VIII of the *Moralia*.]

“‘And whatever remains of the house of Judah will send roots downward and produce fruit upward.’ What do we understand by the name of roots in this passage except hidden thoughts, which emerge in secret but rise openly in the display of action? To send roots downward, therefore, is to multiply a good thought in hidden places; to produce fruit upward is to display through the effectiveness of right action what one has thought. Thus it sends roots downward in order to produce fruit upward. It is as though it were plainly said: thought is born in the depths so that reward may be given in the heights.

[Note: [Col. 0793D] Verse 31. Here again Rabanus teaches us.]

“‘For a remnant will go forth from Jerusalem and from Mount Zion, and they will fill the land of Judah, not by their own merit but by the mercy of God—indeed, by the zeal with which he has been zealous for his people against the ungodly. But when he finally adds: (vers. 34) “I will protect this city and save it for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant,” this signifies that they will be preserved not by their own merit but by God’s clemency—indeed, by the memory of their father David, through which they are reminded both of their own negligence and of his faith and justice. It also signifies that God loves justice so greatly that, even after the death of holy men, he protects their descendants not by their descendants’ own merit but by the virtue of their ancestors.

(Vers. 35.) “It came to pass, therefore, that on that night the angel of the Lord came and struck the camp of the Assyrians, one hundred and eighty-five thousand.” [Note: [Col. 0793D] “In the camp.”] Concerning this we also read in Chronicles: (II Chron. 32, 21) “And the Lord sent an angel, who struck every mighty man, warrior, and prince of the army of the king of Assyria; and he returned with disgrace to his own land.” One hundred and eighty-five thousand of the strongest men are slaughtered by one angel in a single night, and, though those slain had no wounds, cruel death sweeps through them, at the Lord’s will driving their souls from their bodies. The king of the Assyrians himself was preserved for this reason: that he might learn the power of God to silence blaspheming mouths and might become a witness to the majesty of the one whom he had shortly before despised. [Note: [Col. 0793D] Rabanus continues up to this point; what follows Claudius took for the most part from Augustine, though he altered some things to turn them to his own purpose. Consult, I beg you, what Augustine teaches in no. 22 [chapter 13] of Book XV *On the Trinity*.]

“Concerning such matters almighty God does many things through angels—not so that he himself may learn from them, but so that they may act or announce through his word what he wills, without bodily sound, sent by him to whomever he wills, hearing everything from him through that word of his—that is, finding in his truth what they must do, what they must announce, to whom, and when.” [Note: [Col. 0793D] Book 7 of *The City of God*, chapter 30.] “Yet he does not make human beings blessed from the angels but from himself, just as he makes the angels blessed from himself.” [Note: [Col. 0793D] This passage was copied entirely from the cited place in Book XV *On the Trinity*.] “Nor did he come to know anything from anyone at any time, whether from angels or from human beings, so that he might know it; rather, before all ages he foreknew all future temporal events, and within them also what we would ask from him, and when; whom he would hear, and concerning what matters; and whom he would not hear. He foreknew this without beginning. He knows all his creatures, spiritual and corporeal, not because they exist, but they exist because he knows them.”

[Col. 0794A]

(Vers. 35.) “When he rose at dawn, he saw all the bodies of the dead.” [Note: [Col. 0793D] “Departing.”] “And, gnashing his teeth, he departed. Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, returned and remained in Nineveh. While he was worshiping in the temple of Nesroch [Note: [Col. 0793D] *Nesroch*.] his god, Adrammelech and Sarasar, his sons, struck him with the sword. They fled to the land of Armenia, and his son Asorathan [Note: [Col. 0794D] Asarhaddon.] reigned in his place.”

[Note: [Col. 0794D] Rabanus resumes.] “When this king had returned to Nineveh, the first seat of his kingdom, and was worshiping in the temple of Nesroch his god as though he had returned victorious from his enemies, and entered the shrine of his idol in triumph and rejoicing, he—the despiser of the true God—was slaughtered in the sanctuary of a false divinity. He did not perish by an angel’s sword, which would have been common to many, but by the murder committed by his sons, who fled to the land of Ararath, where Scripture testifies that Asorathan, his son who reigned in his place, sent inhabitants of Samaria so that the land would not remain uncultivated. Ararath is a level region of Armenia through which the river Araxes flows, of astonishing fertility, at the foot of Mount Taurus, which extends as far as that place. Therefore the ark in which Noah and his children were delivered, when the Flood had ceased, was not carried generally to the mountains of Armenia, which is called Ararath, but to the highest mountains of Taurus, which overlook the plains of Ararath.

(Cap. 20.) “In those days Hezekiah became sick unto death, and Isaiah the son of Amoz, the prophet, came to him and said: Thus says the Lord: ‘Give orders to your household, for you shall die and shall not live.’”

[Col. 0794C]

“The Lord chastens the one whom he loves (Prov. III, 12), and disciplines every son whom he receives. So that Hezekiah’s heart might not be lifted up after his incredible triumphs and victory in the midst of captivity, he is visited by bodily illness and hears that he is going to die, so that, turning to the Lord, he might change his judgment.” [Note: [Col. 0794D] Rabanus continues up to this point; what follows Claudius took from Paterius and therefore from Gregory, who transmits it in no. 2 of Book XII of the *Moralia*.]

“But none of the things that happen to human beings in this world occur without the hidden counsel of almighty God. For God, foreknowing all future things, decreed before the ages how they would be ordered throughout the ages. It has already been determined for each human being how far the prosperity of this world will follow him and how far adversity will strike each one, lest either excessive prosperity raise up his elect or excessive adversity weigh them down. It has also been determined in the eternal truth [Note: [Col. 0794D] These words are absent from the *aeterna veritas*; they ought to be added from our exemplar.] how long each person is to live temporally in this mortal life [Note: [Col. 0794D] “In that very.”] [Note: [Col. 0794D] “Each person” is missing.] [Note: [Col. 0794D] “For.”] For although almighty God added fifteen years to the life of King Hezekiah, nevertheless, when he allowed him to die, he then foreknew that he would die.

“Here a question arises: how can the Prophet say to him, ‘Set your household in order, for you shall die and shall not live,’ when a sentence of death had been pronounced upon him, yet life was immediately added in response to his tears? The Lord spoke through the prophet at the time when Hezekiah deserved to die. By the abundance of his mercy, however, he postponed his death to the time which he himself had foreknown before the ages. The prophet was therefore not false, since he made known the time of death at which that man deserved to die; nor were the Lord’s decrees overturned [Note: [Col. 0795D] “Statutes” or “decrees.”], since the fact that the years of his life would increase through God’s generosity had also been fixed before the ages, and the span of life that was unexpectedly added outwardly had been established inwardly without any increase in divine foreknowledge.”

(Vers. 2.) “Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall.” [Note: [Col. 0795D] Here again Rabanus.] “Because he could not go to the temple, he turned toward the wall of the temple, beside which Solomon had built the palace; or simply toward the wall, so that he would not appear to display his tears to those sitting beside him. [Note: [Col. 0795D] Verse 3.
