In the Rabanus published elsewhere the following is added: “or, correctly, according to Jerome, toward his heart—since he calls what is round, that is, a wall, a “heart”—so that he might pray to the Lord with his whole mind.” Several other things are also added later that are absent from our exemplar.] And he said: ‘I beseech you, Lord; remember, I pray, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is pleasing in your sight.’”

“He now speaks of perfection of heart in that he destroyed the idols, opened the doors of the temple, broke the bronze serpent, and did the other things mentioned by the Scripture of the Books of Kings and Chronicles. And he wept with a great weeping because of the Lord’s promise to David, which he saw would perish with his death. At that time Hezekiah had no children; for after the third year of life granted to him, he fathered Manasseh. Thus all his weeping was because he had despaired that Christ would be born from his seed.” [Note: [Col. 0796D] What follows is taught from Gregory, Book XII of the *Moralia*, no. 36, through Paterius.]

“For the righteous are often compelled by certain necessities to confess their own works. But when the unrighteous hear their words, they think that these have been spoken out of pride rather than truth. They weigh the words of the righteous from their own hearts and do not believe that true good can be spoken humbly. For just as it is a grave fault for a person to claim for himself what he is not, so it is often no fault if he humbly declares the good that he is.

“Thus it frequently happens that the righteous and the unrighteous have similar words, while their hearts are always utterly different. And by the very words with which the Lord is offended by the unrighteous, he is also pleased by the righteous. For the Pharisee entered the temple and said: (Luke XVIII, 12) ‘I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess.’ Yet the tax collector went away more justified than he. Hezekiah too, when afflicted with bodily distress and brought to the extremity of life, said in compunction during his prayer: ‘I beseech you, Lord; remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart.’ Yet the Lord did not despise this confession of his perfection or reject it; rather, he immediately heard him in his prayers. Behold, the Pharisee justified himself in deed; Hezekiah asserted himself to be righteous even in thought; and from the point at which the former offended, the latter pleased the Lord. Why was this? Except because almighty God weighs the words and thoughts of each person, and in his ears those things are not proud which are spoken from a humble heart.” [Note: [Col. 0796D] “Pleased the Lord.”]

(Vers. 4 and 5.) “And the word of the Lord came to Isaiah, saying: ‘Return and say to Hezekiah, leader of my people: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears. Behold, I have healed you; on the third day you shall go up to the temple of the Lord.’”

Hezekiah, the leader of the people and son of David, whose works he followed—for he had done what was right according to all that David his father had done—is summoned, and his prayer is heard. His tears are seen, because he had walked before the Lord in truth and with a perfect heart, had wept with a great weeping, and had done what was pleasing in his sight.

(Vers. 6.) “And I will add fifteen years to your days. Moreover, I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of the Assyrians, and I will protect this city for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.” [Note: [Col. 0796D] This is taken from Augustine, who teaches it in no. 28, chapter 17, Book VI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*.]

“According to certain causes governing future events, Hezekiah was destined to die; God added fifteen years to his life, doing precisely what he knew before the foundation of the world that he would do and preserved in his will. He therefore did not do something that was not going to happen. Rather, what was more truly future was that which he foreknew he would do. Nevertheless, those years would not rightly be called ‘added’ unless they were added to something that, according to other causes, had stood otherwise.

“According to certain lower causes, therefore, he had already ended his life; but according to those causes that lie in the will and foreknowledge of God—who from eternity knew what he was going to do at that time—that was truly future, and he was then going to end his life when he did end it. For although it was granted to the one praying, and he also foreknew that he would pray in such a way that such a prayer ought to be granted, the one whose foreknowledge could not be deceived certainly knew this. Therefore what he foreknew had necessarily to occur.”

The fifteen years that, by God’s mercy, were prolonged for King Hezekiah from the time of his illness signify mystically that all who observe the fullness of both Testaments obtain the reward of eternal salvation and, through the perfection of the Law and the fullness of the Gospel, pass into the blessedness of eternal life.

(Vers. 7.) “Isaiah said: ‘Bring me a lump of figs.’ When they had brought it and placed it upon his ulcer, he was healed.” Hence medicine, when established by use and experience, is not to be despised, since God also made it.

After this Isaiah said: “This will be the sign from the Lord that the Lord will accomplish the word he has spoken. Do you want the shadow to advance ten lines, or to return ten degrees?” Hezekiah said: “It is easy for the shadow to increase by ten lines; I do not want this, but for it to return backward ten degrees.” The prophet Isaiah therefore called upon the Lord, and he brought the shadow back along the lines by which it had already descended on the sundial of Ahaz, backward ten degrees.

[Note: [Col. 0797D] The following, presented as an explanation of this passage, is transmitted by Bede. [Questions on the Books of Kings, question 25.]]

“The same term ‘degrees’ signifies what ‘lines’ does, namely, the division of the hours, which we customarily mark as twelve during the day on a sundial. Or, as Jerome says, the steps were constructed by mechanical art in such a way that, as the shadow descended one by one, it marked the intervals of the hours. It was the tenth hour of the day when he spoke these words to the king.

“‘Do you want,’ he says, ‘the shadow to advance ten lines as the sun proceeds over the earth through the northern regions toward the east’ [Note: [Col. 0797D] What follows below.]—which, according to the daily course of its movement, it was going to do beneath the earth—or ‘for the shadow to return by as many degrees,’ with the face of the sun turned backward and the sun itself returning through the southern region toward the east?

“But the king said: ‘It is easy for the shadow to increase by ten lines. I do not want this to happen, but for it to return backward ten degrees.’ For he saw that it could be a greater miracle if the sun pursued a course contrary to its accustomed movement than if, proceeding along its usual path, although much higher—that is, transported above the earth [Note: [Col. 0797D] ‘Raised above the lands.’]—it flew toward the east as though it were the morning of a second day, with no intervening night.

“For those who live on the island of Thule, which lies beyond Britain, or in the furthest regions of the Scythians, see this happen for several days every summer: while the sun is at its setting for the rest of the world and lies beneath the earth, it nevertheless appears above the earth throughout the entire night. And how it returns from the western region toward the east at a low altitude [Note: [Col. 0797D] ‘Returns.’] can plainly be seen, [Note: [Col. 0797D] The words ‘until at the proper time it is restored to the whole world by a common rising once again’ are absent from the printed editions.] until at the proper time it is restored to the whole world by a common rising once again. Both the histories of the ancients and people of our own age who come from those regions attest this most abundantly. But those who inhabit the inner southern regions never see the sun return from west to east through the southern skies.”

“To make the meaning clearer for readers, since this sign was both a figure of the present time and a type of the future, just as the sun returned to its beginning, so the years added to Hezekiah’s life would restore him; and so, for us who live within the hebdomad and the ogdoad, the spans of life might be extended through the resurrection of Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0797D] What follows Claudius borrowed from Isidore, chapter 6, *On the Books of Kings*.]

“Or certainly, the ten degrees in the sun’s descent are the successive periods through which the shadow of Christ had descended, and through which Christ, the Sun of justice, again ascended after the resurrection.

“The first degree of descent was from God into the angel, [Note: [Col. 0798D] The words ‘in whom he deigned to appear to the ancient fathers’ are absent from the printed editions, evidently through error.] in whom he deigned to appear to the ancient fathers, since he was the messenger of the great counsel. Thus he also speaks to Jacob: ‘The angel of God said, “I am the God to whom you anointed a pillar and made a vow,”’ so that he might show both an angel and God.

“The second degree of descent was in the patriarchs, because, as the Apostle says, he himself worked in them all. The third was in the giving of the Law, because he himself spoke in the Law. The fourth degree was in Joshua, who introduced the people into the promised land. The fifth was in the Judges, because through them he himself ruled that same people. The sixth was in the kings of the Jews, because he himself reigned in them. The seventh was in the prophets, because through them he was announced. The eighth was in the priests, because he himself is the supreme Priest of the Father. The ninth was in humanity. The tenth was in the Passion.

“Through these ten degrees, by which Christ himself descended through the shadow of the ancient Law, Christ, the Sun of justice, again ascended through the same degrees into heaven after his resurrection [Note: [Col. 0798D] “Upward” seems to be the reading of our copy.] and illumined that entire shadow of the Law with the rays of truth, revealing obscure things, opening what was closed, and laying bare everything that had been covered.”

(20, 12.) “At that time Merodach [Note: [Col. 0798D] *Berodach*.] Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah, for he had heard that Hezekiah had been sick, etc.” [Note: [Col. 0798D] Much of this appears in Rabanus. Claudius, however, presents more briefly some things that Rabanus explained at greater length.]

“‘At that time’—that is, in the same year in which the events narrated above took place—Merodach, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah. For among them the observation of the heavenly bodies and the courses of the stars were known through long practice and experience, as is also shown at the Lord’s birth. They understood that the sun had returned and that the divisions of the day had been doubled, and they thought that it served the one whom they regarded as the sole god [Note: [Col. 0798D] ‘That is, the sun’ is added.]. When they investigated the causes and explanation of this miracle, they learned—since the report flew through all the nations—that, because of the illness of the king of Judah, the course of the most conspicuous sign had also been altered.

“This is also fully attested by the Book of Chronicles, which says: (II Chron. 32, 30) ‘Hezekiah was the one who prospered in all his works and accomplished whatever he wished.’ Yet, when the princes of Babylon were sent to him to inquire about the sign that had occurred over the earth, God left him so that he might be tested and all that was in his heart might become known.

“He was left to temptation because, after such a great victory, the return of the sun, and the congratulations of the most powerful kingdom, his heart had been lifted up. Indeed, the same volume says: (ibid., vers. 23) ‘Many brought victims and sacrifices to the Lord in Jerusalem, and gifts to Hezekiah king of Judah; and he was exalted before all the nations.’ (Vers. 24.) ‘In those days he became sick unto death, prayed to the Lord, and he heard him and gave him a sign.’ But he did not repay according to the benefits he had received, because his heart was exalted; and wrath came against him, Judah, and Jerusalem. Again Holy Scripture says that the pride of his heart was softened through repentance, adding: ‘He humbled himself afterward, because his heart had been exalted, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and therefore the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah.’

“(IV Kings XX, 13, etc.) In those days Hezekiah rejoiced at the arrival of the messengers of Merodach Baladan, whom the Hebrews assert to have been the father of Nebuchadnezzar, and at the presentation of gifts and the congratulations on his recovery. He showed them his house of spices, his treasuries of silver, gold, perfumes, and finest ointment, and all the treasures of his vessels. There was nothing that he did not show them in his house and throughout his entire dominion. Hence he most justly deserved God’s anger: he showed them not only the treasures of his own possessions and palace but also those of the temple, since he had already removed the golden plates from its doors.

“(Vers. 14.) ‘The prophet Isaiah entered King Hezekiah.’ Again, after bodily recovery and the greatness of the sign, we see another occasion for pride presented to him, which a prudent worshiper of God ought to have avoided: he should not have shown foreigners his riches, which he possessed by God’s gift. From this, according to the rules of allegorical interpretation, we also learn not to cast pearls before swine or give what is holy to dogs. (Matt. VII, 6.) For the faithful person hides matters in the spirit; and whoever does not do this has all his virtue weakened [Col. 0799C] (and perishes), because posterity, having lost its masculine strength, is reduced to feminine softness.

“Isaiah therefore enters the king and, as though unaware, asks: ‘What did these men say, and from where did they come?’ He asks two questions: what they said and from where they came. He answered one and passed over the other. (Vers. 14.) ‘They came to me from a distant land, from Babylon.’ The more distant the land from which they came, the more glorious this king appeared, since they had come on his account. ‘They came,’ he says, ‘to me,’ whereas he ought to have said: ‘They came to glorify God because of the greatness of the sign, from Babylon, the most powerful city in the whole world.’

“Again Isaiah said: ‘What did they see in your house?’ He answered in part truthfully: they had seen everything in his house, and there was nothing that he had not shown them in his treasuries. But he concealed the other matter, fearing offense: he had shown them everything that he possessed in his dominion—clearly, also the vessels of the temple. Because of these things Isaiah, speaking the word of God, pronounced the sentence: (vers. 16) ‘Hear the word of the Lord of hosts. The time will come when everything that is in your house, and that was acquired not by your labor but by the labor of your fathers, will be carried away to Babylon, and some of your descendants will become eunuchs in the palace of the king.’

“From this the Hebrews wish to infer that Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, who were of royal descent, were made eunuchs, and there is no doubt that they served Nebuchadnezzar. (Dan. I, 6, 7. Rabanus also continues up to this point. What follows Claudius teaches.) We do not deny that some eunuchs—that is, castrated men—of royal descent were in the palace of the king of Babylon, according to the prophecy of blessed Isaiah. But it is in no way to be believed concerning Daniel and his companions. For if they had been eunuchs, that official who instructed them while they were still boys would not have feared their physical beauty and appearance (ibid., vers. 10), since the appearance of the face commonly deteriorates in castrated boys. Among the ancients, however, it was customary to call chamberlains and palace guards ‘eunuchs’; they had wives and had not been castrated in body.”

[Col. 0800B]

(Verse 19.) And Hezekiah said: “The word of the Lord which he has spoken is good; let there be peace only in my days.”

[Note: Rabanus again transmits only these few words.]

In this matter the Hebrews reproach him for not imitating the goodness of Moses, who said to God: “Either forgive them this offense, or, if you will not, erase me from the book which you have written.”

[Note: Everything that follows was transmitted by Paterius; therefore Claudius took it from Gregory, *Moralia*, Book VIII, nos. 81 and 82.]

What else does the Prophet’s judgment against King Hezekiah signify here than the thoughts of arrogant hypocrites, who seek the admiration of men? In everything that hypocrites do, because they seek human praise in their hidden thoughts, they cast, as it were, the roots of rushes into a heap of stones. For while they are about to perform their deeds, they think about their praises; once praised, they silently turn these praises over in their thoughts. They rejoice that they have shone forth as outstanding in human estimation.

And when they swell up within themselves, inflated by favor, they often silently marvel even at what they themselves are. They desire daily to appear greater than themselves, and they grow in their works through marvelous inventions.

[Note: “Intentions.”]

For just as virtues weaken every vice, so arrogance strengthens it.

[Note: “The virtue of humility weakens.”]

It forces the mind to grow young again and to be strong beyond its powers, because the love of praise commands even what bodily vigor denies.

[Note: “It attacks.”]

Hence, as we have said, they seek witnesses for their deeds. If witnesses happen to be lacking, they themselves recount what they have done. And when they begin to be lifted up by praise, they often add something by lying to those very deeds which they claim to have accomplished.

[Note: “To have accomplished.”]

But even when they tell the truth, by telling it they make these things alien to themselves, because, through the praises they have sought,

[Note: “Having been rewarded.”]

they are emptied of true and inward recompense.

[Note: “From their inmost part. Our reading is preferable.”]

For by making their good deeds known, they show the evil spirits, as though to lurking enemies, what they may plunder.

The life of such people, therefore, was represented by that universally known fault of Hezekiah. After he had struck down, through one prayer and within the space of a single night, one hundred and eighty-five thousand enemies by the blow of an angel; after he had brought the sun, already near its setting, back into the higher regions of the heavens; after he had prolonged a life shortened by its approaching end into a longer span—when he received the messengers of the king of Babylon, he showed them all the good things he possessed. But immediately he heard from the Prophet’s mouth: “Behold, the days are coming, and everything that is in your house shall be carried away to Babylon, and nothing shall be left, says the Lord.”

So indeed hypocrites, after they have grown through great virtues, because they neglect to beware of the snares of evil spirits and do not wish to conceal themselves within those same virtues, make their good deeds the property of their enemies by displaying them, and, by betraying them, suddenly lose whatever they have worked for through prolonged effort.

Hence the Psalmist says: “He delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hand of the enemy” (Ps. 77:71). The strength and beauty of the arrogant are delivered into the hands of the enemy, because every good that is displayed through the desire for praise

[Note: “Of praises.”]

is handed over to the power of the hidden adversary.

For they provoke enemies to plunder

[Note: “They summon.”]

because they expose their riches to their knowledge.

[Note: “He strips bare.”]

As long as we are separated from the security of our eternal homeland, we walk along a road beset by lurking robbers. Whoever fears being plundered on the journey must therefore hide the good things he carries.

O wretched people, who, by desiring human praise, scatter within themselves the fruits of their labors! When they desire to display themselves to the eyes of others, they condemn what they do. When evil spirits incite them to boastfulness, they strip them bare by capturing their works, as we have said.

[Note: With many passages inserted, he adds what follows. From this passage it is clear that Claudius plainly follows Paterius, who is doing the same thing.]

For this reason Truth says through the Gospel: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your alms may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. 6:3–4).

For this reason it is said of the Church of the elect through the Psalmist: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44:14).

For this reason Paul says: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12).

The Church, the daughter of kings, generated in good works through the preaching of spiritual rulers, has her glory within, because in what she does she does not possess the boastfulness of ostentation. Paul calls the testimony of his conscience his glory, because, since he does not seek praise from another’s mouth, he does not know how to place the joys of his life outside himself.

What we do must therefore be concealed, lest, carrying these things carelessly along the road of this life, we lose them through the assault of plundering spirits.”

### (21:1)

Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. He did evil in the sight of the Lord, according to the idols of the nations whom the Lord had destroyed from before the children of Israel. He turned back and rebuilt the high places which Hezekiah his father had demolished; he erected altars to Baal, made sacred groves as Ahab king of Israel had done, worshiped all the host of heaven, and served it. He built altars in the house of the Lord, concerning which the Lord had said:

[Col. 0802A] “In Jerusalem I shall place my name” (2 Kings 7:10).

He built altars for the entire host of heaven in the two courts of the temple of the Lord. He led his son through the fire; he practiced divination and observed omens; he made

[Note: “Python-spirits.”]

pythons and multiplied diviners, so that he might do evil before the Lord and provoke him.

I do not doubt, therefore, that all these practices—that is, divination, auspices, any kind of sacrifice, casting lots, any movement of birds or cattle, any examination of the entrails, or anything else that appears to disclose the future—are carried out through the operation of demons. They direct the birds, the cattle, the movements of the entrails, or the lots according to those signs which the same demons taught to be observed by the people to whom they handed down knowledge of this art.

The person who belongs to God and is counted among God’s portion must be wholly separated from all these things. He must have nothing in common with the hidden devices by which demons work, lest through them he again be joined to demons, be filled with their spirit and power, and be restored once more to the worship of idols.

[Note: I think *retrahatur*—“be drawn back”—should be read.]

Later (22:14) it is said that Josiah sent messengers to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum, who lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter, concerning the book of the divine law that had been found.

[Note: Bede gives an explanation of this passage, *Questions*, 26.]

What does it mean when it says that she lived in the Second Quarter? In the earlier part of this book it is written concerning King Hezekiah that he acted diligently and rebuilt the whole wall that had been destroyed. He also built towers upon it and another wall outside.

[Note: That is, 2 Chron. 32:5. In fact, Bede, from whom Claudius—as we have said—took this, has the following: the matter is explained in the Book of Chronicles, where it is written concerning the aforementioned King Hezekiah.]

Zephaniah mentions this place when he says: “A voice of crying from the Fish Gate, and a howling from the Second Quarter” (Zeph. 1:10). For this reason the old edition rendered it as the proper place-name *Masana*.

[Note: “Masana.”]

For *Masana* means “Second.” Therefore, when it is said that this prophetess lived in the Second Quarter, we should understand that she lived in the section of the second wall.

[Note: Understand this.]

### 2 Kings 22:18

“But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the Lord, you shall say this: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Because you heard the words of the book, and your heart was terrified, and you humbled yourself before the Lord when you heard the words against this place and its inhabitants—that they would become an astonishment and a curse—and because you tore your garments and wept before me, I also have heard you, says the Lord. Therefore I shall gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your tomb in peace, so that your eyes may not see all the evil which I am about to bring upon this place.”

[Note: Augustine transmitted what follows, *On the Care of the Dead*, Book I, nos. 16 and following, chapters 13 and following.]

“This man, terrified by the threats of God, had wept and torn his garments; and he became secure, through his prepared death, from all future evils. Why, then, would he rest in peace so that he would not see any of those things?

The spirits of the dead, therefore, are where they do not see whatever is done or happens in this life of human beings.

[Note: “To human beings.”]

How, then, do they see their tombs or their bodies—whether they lie abandoned or have been buried? How do they share in the misery of the living, when either they themselves suffer their own evils, if they have incurred such merits, or rest in peace, as was promised to this Josiah, where they endure no evils, either by suffering them or by sympathizing with them, having been freed from all the evils which, while they lived here, they endured by suffering and sharing in the sufferings of others?

Someone might say: If the dead have no concern for the living, how did the rich man who was tormented in Hades ask father Abraham to send Lazarus to his five brothers, who were not yet dead,

[Col. 0803B] and to warn them lest they too should come to that same place of torment?

[Note: “Act.”]

But because that rich man said this, did he therefore know what his brothers were doing or suffering at that time? He was concerned for the living, although he knew nothing at all of what they were doing, just as we are concerned for the dead, although we certainly do not know what they are doing.

For if we had no concern for the dead, we would surely not pray to God for them.

Finally, Abraham did not send Lazarus, but replied that they had Moses and the Prophets here, whom they ought to hear so that they would not come to those punishments. Here again the question arises how Abraham himself knew what was being done here, since he knew that Moses and the Prophets—their books—were there, through obedience to whom human beings might avoid the torments of hell.

Finally, he knew that the rich man had lived in luxury and the poor Lazarus in suffering.

[Note: The edition adds “and pains.”]

For he also said to him: ‘Remember, son, that you received good things during your life, while Lazarus received evil things’ (Luke 16:25).

He therefore knew things which had taken place among the living, not among the dead. Yet he could have learned these things from Lazarus—not while they were happening among the living, but after they had died—so that the prophet’s statement would not be false: ‘Abraham did not know us’ (Isa. 63:16).

Accordingly, we must admit that the dead do not know what is happening here while it is happening. Afterwards, however, they hear from those who come to them from here through death—not everything, but whatever they are permitted to disclose, and whatever they are also permitted to remember, and whatever those to whom they disclose these things ought to hear.

The dead may also hear something from angels who are present at the events taking place here, whatever the One to whom all things are subject judges that each of them ought to hear.

For unless there were angels able to be present both among the places of the living and among those of the dead, the Lord Jesus would not have said: ‘It happened that the poor man died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom’ (Luke 16:22).

Thus they could be present now here and now there—those who carried away from here the person whom God willed.

[Note: “There.”]

The spirits of the dead may also learn, by the revelation of the Spirit of God, certain things that are happening here—things which it is necessary for them to know and which it is necessary for certain others to know—not only present or past things, but also future things.

So, while they lived here, not all human beings knew such things, but the Prophets did; nor did the Prophets themselves know everything, but only what God’s providence judged should be revealed to them.

Divine Scripture also testifies that some of the dead may be sent to the living, just as, conversely, Paul was caught up from among the living into Paradise (2 Cor. 12:2).

For the prophet Samuel, though dead, foretold future things to the living King Saul (1 Sam. 28:15).

[Note: The printed edition reads, “to Saul, also living and a king.” Our reading is preferable.]

Although some think that it was not Samuel himself who could have been summoned by magical arts, but rather some spirit suited to such wicked practices, which assumed his likeness.”

We have brought forward these matters by way of digression so that people may know to seek eternal truth if they wish to be saved—the One by whom we were created, in whom we live, through whom we move and exist (Acts 17:28).

We believe that holy souls do not take part in human miseries, as Isaiah, who was a son of Abraham, says to God: “You, Lord, are our Father; Abraham did not know us, and Israel did not acknowledge us” (Isa. 63:16).

“After this follows the account of the deeds of Josiah, which says: ‘He also defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, so that no one might consecrate his son or daughter through fire to Moloch’ (23:10).”

[Note: Bede transmitted all this, *Questions*, 27, 28, 29, and 30.]

“The mention of these places is frequent in Scripture, especially in the Book of Kings and in the Prophet Jeremiah.

The valley of Hinnom, or of the son of Hinnom, lies beside the wall of Jerusalem, toward the east. In it there was a most beautiful grove, watered by the springs of Siloam.

Topheth,

[Note: The printed editions add “or Taph eth,” for both forms are written.]

was a place in the same valley, beside the Pool of the Fuller, which Scripture mentions, and near the field

[Note: “Acheldana.”]

of Acheldemach, which is still shown on the southern side of Mount Zion.

Because Topheth was a most pleasant place and still provides the delights of gardens today,

[Note: Hence, even to this day.]

people used to sacrifice to demons there at an altar which they had set up, and to consecrate their children to them with an unspeakable fire, or to offer them as a burnt offering. Thus it is written in the Book of Chronicles concerning King Ahaz: ‘He burned incense in the valley of Benennon and purified his sons in the fire of Benennon’ (2 Chron. 28:3), for it signifies “son of Ennon.”

The valley of Hinnom is called in Hebrew

[Note: “Gehenna.”]

*Gebenn* (probably *Gehenn*),

[Col. 0804D] and from its name the punishment of hell is called *Gehenna* in the New Testament. For just as those who served idols perished in the valley of Hinnom, as the Prophets testify, so sinners are punished with eternal condemnation because of the things they have committed.

Finally, when Jeremiah reported that the Lord had commanded him and said: ‘Go out to the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is beside the entrance of the Potsherd Gate’ (Jer. 19:2), he shortly afterwards says: ‘This place shall no longer be called Topheth or the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter; and I shall overthrow the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem in this place, and I shall strike them down with the sword.’

Isaiah also most plainly calls Topheth hell. When describing under the name of Assyria the everlasting destruction of the devil, he says: ‘For at the voice of the Lord Assyria shall be terrified, struck with the rod.’ And after saying, ‘The passage of the rod has been founded, which the Lord will cause to rest upon him,’ he immediately adds how and where Assyria would perish: ‘For Topheth has been prepared from yesterday, prepared by the king, deep and wide.’

He aptly says “wide,” because *Topheth* means “breadth.” “Its fuel,” he says, “is fire and abundant wood; the breath of the Lord, like a stream of sulfur, sets it ablaze.”

Josiah defiled Topheth either with the bones of the dead, as we read that he did in the case of other places of idols below, or by scattering whatever other unclean things there were, so that the place might appear to all who looked at it to be suited to abomination rather than to delight.”

“What follows concerning the same King Josiah says: ‘He also removed the horses which the kings of Judah had given to the Sun at the entrance of the temple of the Lord.’ And shortly afterwards: ‘He burned the chariots of the Sun with fire.’”

[Note: “To every kind of idolatry and superstition.”]

This shows that at that time the Jews were enslaved to the idolatry and superstition of all the nations. They believed the Sun to be a god in the manner of the Gentiles, and therefore dedicated to the image they had made of it chariots and horses, placing these in the courts of the temple of the Lord.

For the Gentiles commonly paint or fashion an image of the Sun by placing a beardless boy in a chariot and yoking horses to him, as though they were seeking heaven in the chariot. They give it the form of a boy because the Sun, being born each day in a new rising, never falls into old age throughout the ages.

John, Bishop of Constantinople, thinks that the chariots and horses were assigned to the Sun because of the miracle involving the prophet Elijah, who was carried into heaven in a fiery chariot and with fiery horses.

[Note: “This.”]

For since the Sun is called *hēlios* in Greek—just as Sedulius also shows when he sang of Elijah’s ascent—he says:

> How well the path of heaven, shining before the lightning,  
> accords with Elijah, who was radiant even in his name!  
> He was worthy of this privilege; for if in the Greek tongue  
> one letter is changed by the accent, it means “Sun.”

[Note: “Is changed.”]

[Col. 0805D] The Greeks, hearing from the Israelites—who, rumor reported, possessed the divine writings—that Elijah had been carried into the heavens in a fiery chariot and with fiery horses, or perhaps seeing this very scene depicted among other images on a wall, were deceived by the similarity of the names and believed that the passage of the Sun through the heavens was being represented. Through human folly they changed a divinely wrought miracle into an argument for error.

The Jews themselves imitated them, striving not to appear less foolish in any respect than the most foolish of the Gentiles.”

### 2 Kings 23:13–14

“King Josiah also polluted the high places that were in Jerusalem, on the right side of the Mount of Offense, which King Solomon had built for Astarte, the idol of the Sidonians, and for Chemosh, the offense of Moab, and for Moloch, the abomination of the children of Ammon. He smashed the statues and cut down the sacred groves, and filled their places with the bones of the dead.”

“It is clearer than daylight that Scripture commonly calls “high places” locations situated on leafy hills, where people either sacrificed to demons or, attracted by the pleasantness of the sites, offered sacrifices to the Lord contrary to the prohibition, having abandoned the altar that was in the temple.

For this reason, in this Book of Kings, it is often said of kings who were not perfectly just: ‘Nevertheless, he did not remove the high places.’

He calls the Mount of Offense the mountain of an idol, because it is the custom of Scripture to call idols “offenses”: either God is offended by them, or they bring offense and ruin upon their worshipers.

This is made clear in the same passage when it subsequently says: ‘What King Solomon of Israel had built for Astarte, the idol of the Sidonians, and for Chemosh, the offense of Moab, and for Moloch, the abomination of the children of Ammon’ (1 Kings 11:7).

Here it is also openly shown—would that it were not shown—that Solomon never fully repented of the crime of idolatry he had committed. For if he had produced worthy fruits of repentance, he would have taken care above all that the idols he had built should be removed from the holy city, rather than leaving, as though wisely and rightly made, what he himself, though most wise, had made in error, thereby making it a stumbling block to fools.

Scripture mentions this place above as well, saying: ‘Then Solomon built a shrine to Chemosh, the idol of Moab, on the mountain opposite Jerusalem, and to Moloch, the idol of the children of Ammon.’

It should not seem contradictory that there the mountain on which these idols were made is said to be opposite Jerusalem, while here it is asserted to be situated in Jerusalem. It was, in fact, located so near the city that it seemed to belong to the city itself

[Note: “And to defile the city itself with the filth gathered there. Our reading appears preferable.”]

and even to touch it with the filth that was heaped upon it.”

### 2 Kings 24:14–15

“Nebuchadnezzar carried away all Jerusalem and all the princes. He also carried Jehoiachin away to Babylon, and led the judges of the land into captivity from Jerusalem to Babylon, together with all the strong men,” and so forth.

In reporting that Nebuchadnezzar carried away all Jerusalem, all the princes, and all the strong armies—ten thousand into captivity—Scripture adds: “And every craftsman and smith.”

[Note: The following material, marked with lines, Paterius took from Gregory; Claudius therefore did likewise. See *Moralia*, Book VII, chapter 13, no. 37, formerly chapter 16.]

“This is what the Philistines are said to have done earlier to the same people of Israel when it says: ‘Now no blacksmith was found throughout all the land of Israel, for the Philistines had taken care lest the Hebrews make a sword or spear’ (1 Sam. 13).

Just as they then took care that the Hebrews should not have blacksmiths who could make weapons for resistance, so now the Chaldeans, after Jerusalem had been destroyed and the whole land of promise devastated,

[Note: “With Jerusalem laid waste and the entire land. Our reading appears preferable.”]

took pains that no craftsman should remain in it, no smith who could repair the damaged walls of the city or mend what had been torn down.

[Note: “They strive.”]

[Note: “Should remain.”]

Rather, whatever skill they had found among the exterminated nation, they transferred to all Babylon, so that it might either be useless thereafter or serve the needs of that city.

I do not think the allegory of this deeply lamentable history, which corresponds so closely to the negligence of our own time, should be withheld.

It is clear that Jerusalem and the land of Israel signify the city of Christ, that is, the holy Church; while Babylon and the Chaldeans, or Philistines, signify the city of the devil, that is, the entire multitude of evil beings, whether human or angelic.

Israel serves the Philistines or Chaldeans when the faithful, remaining in the Church in name only but deceived by unclean spirits or human beings, submit the necks of their minds either to avarice, lust, or any other sin.

Nebuchadnezzar leads Jerusalem, all its princes, and ten thousand strong armies into captivity when teachers of peoples, and those who seemed to serve the Lord with an unconquerable spirit and faithfully to preserve the law’s Decalogue in love of God and neighbor, are suddenly overcome either by the enticements of the world or by adversities, and pollute themselves with greater crimes,

[Note: “The reading with *a* is preferable.”]

or, by turning toward heresy, fall under the name of open apostasy.

[Note: “The mark.”]

What else are the weapons with which, while fighting against the devil, we defend the freedom given us by God, except the words of Scripture? In them we learn with the greatest clarity, through the examples of the Lord himself and of his saints, by what order the battles against vices are to be overcome.

But the Philistines deprive the children of Israel of weaponsmiths when evil spirits divert the minds of the faithful from meditation on sacred reading by inserting worldly affairs into their lives. They do this so that the faithful may neither gain confidence through the exercise of resistance nor perhaps kindle others who do not know how to read to resist vices by exhorting or reproving them.

They remove the weaponsmiths when they overwhelm those who know the sacred words with such crimes that they are utterly ashamed to speak the good things they have learned.

[Note: “Which they had learned.”]

They transfer every craftsman and smith from Jerusalem to Babylon when they turn away from their purpose those who used to benefit many through manifold virtuous activity and fortify the city of God against the attacks of temptation, compelling them to devote the talent which they ought to have spent in defense of the holy Church instead to the will of the king of vices.

If we understand “smith” here not as a worker in doors or walls but rather as a worker in gold and gems, the spiritual interpretation nevertheless reaches the same conclusion. It is said of Wisdom: “For there is gold and an abundance of gems” (Prov. 20:15). Therefore, we can understand “smiths” of these things most appropriately as teachers, who, as long as they live and teach rightly, devote the skill of their art to the adornment of the holy city.

But if they should fall into error, what happens except that they are carried away captive to Babylon by the king of the Chaldeans? For a craftsman and smith to migrate from Jerusalem to Babylon is for a talent of the word received from heaven to be buried in the earth—that is, for spiritual knowledge to be turned toward the works of sin.”

After this Scripture reports (25:5–6 and following) that the Chaldean army pursued King Zedekiah; they seized him and brought him to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where he pronounced judgment upon him. The king of Babylon killed Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes, put out his eyes, bound him with chains, and brought him to Babylon.

[Note: The passages that follow, marked with lines, Paterius took from Gregory, and Claudius therefore did likewise. See *Moralia*, Book VII, chapter 13, formerly chapter 16, no. 37.]

“While Holy Scripture narrates Zedekiah’s captivity, it announces the order of inward captivity. For the king of Babylon is the ancient

[Note: “Enemy” is added.]

possessor of inward confusion. He first slays the sons before the eyes of the one who sees, because he often kills good works in such a way that the person who has been captured sees with grief that he himself has lost them.

For the mind often groans and yet, overcome by the pleasures of its flesh, loses the good things it has produced while loving them; it considers the losses it suffers, yet does not raise the arm of virtue against the king of Babylon. While it sees itself struck by the perpetration of wickedness, it is eventually subjected to this further sin: it is deprived even of the light of reason.

[Note: “Through the habitual practice of sin.”]

Therefore the king of Babylon, after first killing the sons, puts out Zedekiah’s eyes, because the evil spirit first removes good works and then takes away the light of understanding—which Zedekiah rightly suffers at Riblah.

For *Riblah* means “many things.” The light of reason will eventually be closed to the person who is weighed down by the multitude of his iniquity through habitual wrongdoing.”

[Note: The following passages, not marked with lines, have not been found in any ancient writer; nevertheless, they contain something of Augustine’s style.]

Just as on the fourth day, at the beginning of creation, the heavens were adorned with lights, so in the fourth age of the world the Israelite people, renowned for heavenly faith, illuminated by the Prophets as by stars, glorified by the kingdom of David and Solomon, and ennobled throughout the whole world by the height of its most holy temple, received its evening when, as sins multiplied, that kingdom was destroyed by the Chaldeans, the temple demolished, and the entire nation transferred to Babylon.

[Note: See what Augustine transmits in Book XVI, chapter 43, of *The City of God*.]

This fourth age of the world, from David to the Babylonian captivity, comprises, according to the Hebrew truth, four hundred and seventy-three years.

[Note: The edition reads “four hundred and eighty-three.”]

According to the Septuagint interpreters, it comprises somewhat more. In both texts there are seventeen generations; nevertheless, for the sake of a particular mystery, the Evangelist Matthew gives fourteen, beginning from the youthful age when the times of the kings began among the people of God. For this is the age of human beings that is ordinarily suited to governance.

The aforementioned Zedekiah, son of Josiah, reigned for eleven years. In his eleventh year, and in the eighth year of the king of Babylon, according to lunar reckoning, on the fifth day of the fourth month—and according to solar reckoning, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, with the moon in its fifth phase, which they count as the fifth day, on the seventh day of the week—the city was opened. All the princes of the kings of Babylon entered and took possession of the city, and they led the people captive to Babylon.

Afterwards, in the fifth month, on the tenth day of the lunar month—and according to solar reckoning, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, with the moon in its tenth phase, which the Hebrews call the tenth day of the fifth month—Nebuzaradan, commander of the army of Babylon,

[Note: Something is missing here.]

the walls of the city were destroyed; the temple likewise was burned and laid waste, four hundred and thirty years after the year in which it had begun to be founded.

If I am asked how I know this, or how it could have happened that the city was captured or burned on such days, I reply that in that year the beginning of the year and the beginning of the first month fell, according to lunar reckoning, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April.

As for the captivity itself in Babylon—during which the Spirit of God also commands through the prophet Jeremiah that they should go and pray for those in whose kingdom they were living as strangers, since their peace would be their peace, and that they should build houses, renew vineyards, and plant gardens—who would fail to recognize what this prefigured, if he observed that the true Israelites, in whom there is no deceit, migrated through the apostolic dispensation, together with the gospel mystery, into the kingdom of the Gentiles?

Therefore the Apostle, as though repeating Jeremiah, says to us: “I urge, then, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all godliness and purity. For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:1–4).

For through this, once they too believed, dwellings of peace were built for them: the basilicas of Christian congregations, the renewed vineyards of faithful peoples, and the planted gardens in which, among all the vegetables, that mustard seed reigns. Beneath its far-reaching shade the lofty pride of the nations also finds refuge and rest, as though among the birds of heaven.

And since, after seventy years, according to the prophecy of the same Jeremiah, there is a return from captivity and the temple is renewed, what faithful Christian would not understand that, after the passing of the ages which run their course through the repetition of the number seven, we too—that is, the Church of God—must return from our pilgrimage in this world to the heavenly Jerusalem?

Through whom, except Jesus Christ, the true great Priest? His figure was borne by that Jesus, the great priest of that time when the temple was built after the captivity. The prophet Zechariah saw him in filthy clothing; after the devil, who stood accusing him, had been defeated, his filthy garment was removed and a garment of honor and glory was given him.

So the body of Jesus Christ, which is the Church, after the adversary has been overcome through judgment at the end of time, will be taken from the grief of pilgrimage into the glory of eternal salvation.

This too is sung most plainly in the psalm of the dedication of the house of God: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced with sorrow” (Ps. 29:12).

Who, taking the opportunity of another work, could touch upon all the things in those ancient laws and in the books of the Prophets which figuratively announce Christ, however briefly, unless perhaps someone should think that it happens through ingenuity that things which unfolded in their own times according to the order of events are turned, through interpretation, toward the meanings of Christ?

The Jews or the pagans may say this. But for those who wish to be thought Christians, the authority of the Apostle presses upon their necks, saying: “All these things happened to them as a figure” (1 Cor. 10:6). “And all these things were our figures.”

**Here ends the fourth book of the treatise on the Books of Kings.**

[Col. 0809D]

**HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE OF CLAUDIUS, BISHOP.**
Because, therefore, with God’s favor, I think that in the preceding books some of your questions have been sufficiently answered, dearest brother Theutmir, we now endeavor to join certain of your questions to the end of this book, since it seemed superfluous to me to intermingle bare questions about the letter among the flowers of spiritual allegory. Some matters, however, remain undiscussed, because I have found nothing translated concerning them in the ancient translations, nor have I read anything expounded in the little works of our predecessors. I confess that I am ignorant of these matters, since I do not remember having read anything about them. And therefore I am not ashamed of my lack of knowledge, because I have not been taught by reading; nor do I fear the danger, because I do not presume to teach what I do not understand.

While I held your questions in my hands, after the preceding books had already been completed, intending to write something in response to them, a letter from Aachen reached me, sent from the royal palace, reporting how you had caused my treatise on the Epistles to the Corinthians—which I had lent you two years earlier—to be presented at that same palace for condemnation by the judgment of the bishops and nobles. My friends there received that treatise not for condemnation, but for copying, and they received it not merely humbly but also affectionately [Note: humanely, as I think]. May the Lord forgive you—the witness of my life and giver of my work—for you did not fear to disparage the words of truth; sitting against me, you speak falsehood, and against a son of Mother Church you have set a stumbling-block. If you live in this way, you carry in your mind the death which Uzzah suffered in his body for his unlawful presumption. [Col. 0810D–0811B]

### I. (I Reg. 1:18)

Concerning what is written, “Her countenance also was no longer changed in different ways”: this is how it is written by the Seventy interpreters: “And the woman went on her way, and entered her lodging”—that is, while still at Shiloh—“and ate with her husband, and drank, and her face no longer fell”; that is, after she had poured out her prayer with her whole heart in the tabernacle of the Lord, and Eli the priest had said to her, “Go in peace. The God of Israel grant you the petition that you have asked of the Lord,” trusting in the Lord’s goodness and in the priest’s oracle, she returned to her home no longer anxious as before, but joyful in her confidence in the Lord. This is what is meant by: “And her face no longer fell.” [Col. 0811C]

### II. (Chapter 2:18)

Concerning what is written: “Now Samuel ministered before the face of the Lord, a boy girded with a linen ephod.” The ephod mentioned in Exodus (chapter 25:7) is called the shoulder-piece. Not all priests, however, wore such a shoulder-piece as the high priest Aaron and his descendants did—one made of gold, hyacinth-colored material, purple, scarlet, and fine linen. For it is one thing to have something woven from the aforesaid colors and gold, and another to have a simple linen garment resembling that of the priests. This kind of garment, which we call the shoulder-piece, is known among the Hebrews as an ephod and is appropriate only to high priests. [Col. 0811D]

But this immediately raises the difficulty that Samuel, who was a Levite, is said to have possessed, while still a boy, an ephod—that is, a linen shoulder-piece—made for him by his mother. It was certainly not such a garment, since when he was entrusted for upbringing while still a child, he was not the high priest. We have sufficiently explained this in the book *The Formation of the Letter and the Spirit*, namely in the treatise on Exodus, which we expounded some years ago.

### III. (6:18)

I was also asked what the “great Habel” was, upon which they placed the ark of the Lord when it returned from the land of the Philistines. I searched with great diligence in various translations, but I did not find “great Habel”; rather, I found “a great stone,” upon which they placed the ark of the covenant of the Lord [Note: Rabanus says that “great Abel” was a city on the border of Israel]. [Col. 0812A]

### IV. (7:15)

You also ask why Samuel is said to have judged Israel throughout all the days of his life, yet lost the principate during his lifetime. Judgment does not always pertain to domination, but also to instruction. For this reason judges are called teachers of the people. Thus Deborah is said to have judged Israel (Judges 4:4–5), that is, to have taught it. Samuel therefore judged Israel throughout all the days of his life because throughout all the days of his life he taught Israel the way of God’s commandments. [Col. 0812B]

### V. (10:2)

Concerning what is written: when Samuel had anointed Saul king, he said to him, “When you depart from me today, you will find two men beside Rachel’s tomb in the territory of Benjamin, leaping over great pits, and you will deliver the people of the Lord from the hand of their enemies.”

The great pits signified the affliction, humiliation, and tribulation of the Israelites, which they suffered at the hands of the Ammonites, the Philistines, and the other enemies who surrounded them. The two men leaping over them were a foreshadowing of the great victories that the Lord achieved through Saul’s hand over Nahash, king of the Ammonites, and the satraps of the Philistines. [Col. 0812C]

### VI. (Chapter 10)

You also ask why Saul is anointed king twice and David three times, when this is not actually so: Saul was anointed once, and David twice. David is nevertheless read as having been anointed by Samuel (I Reg. 16:13), first in his father’s house; then, afterward, in Hebron over the house of Judah (II Reg. 5:3); and third in Jerusalem. [Col. 0812D]

There is no doubt that David, whose name is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable,” bore a figure of the Lord Savior. He was anointed, as it were, in his father’s house because he was known in Judea only through the Law and the Prophets (Psal. 75:2), and his name was held in great regard among Israel.

But afterward he was anointed again in Hebron over all Judah, because through evangelical and apostolic preaching his name became renowned throughout the whole earth—that is, in the Church, where there is the true confession of faith, since *Judah* is interpreted as “confession.” [Col. 0813A]

A third time our David—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ in his body, which is the Church—will be anointed in Jerusalem, that is, in the vision of peace, when death has been conquered (I Cor. 15:54), death will be swallowed up in victory, and this mortal nature will put on immortality. For God will wipe every tear from the eyes of the saints, and death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor any pain. Rather, God will be all in all.

Our David—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ in his body, which is the Church—will receive this third anointing at the end of the age, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father and abolishes the principalities (I Cor. 15:24) [Note: The solution to the question concerning Saul is therefore missing]. [Col. 0813D]

### VII. (Chapter 15:1)

You also ask why, when the Lord sent Saul to strike the sinners of Amalek (verse 6), he spared the Kenite, saying shortly afterward, “For you showed mercy to all the children of Israel when they came up from Egypt.” From this you ask who this Kenite was and where it is written that he showed this mercy.

The Kenite was a family of the people descended from the stock of Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, who was also called by another name, Raguel. They had learned the wonders of the God of heaven through Moses and had themselves seen them during the forty years in the wilderness. They lived around that wilderness and therefore were always related to, well disposed toward, and friendly with the children of Israel—that is, the Hebrew people. Saul recalled the mercy that they had shown to the children of Israel when they came out of Egypt. [Col. 0813B]

From this stock came Heber (Aber in the text), the Kenite [Note: Haber the Kenite], the husband of the holy woman Jael, who in her tent killed Sisera, the enemy of the children of Israel and commander of King Jabin’s army (Judges 4:17) [Note: of Jabin, king of Azot]. [Col. 0813D–0814D]

### VIII

You further inquire why Samuel said to King Agag, “Does bitter death separate in this way?” (I Reg. 15:32), whereas it was not Samuel who said this to Agag, but Agag, who was about to be killed, who said it to Samuel.

The expression whose meaning you ask about—*siccine*, “in this way”—was made obscure not by its nature in the historical account, but by the translator’s preference. It means: “Does bitter death separate thus?” or “Does bitter death separate in such a manner?”

Something similar is found in the Song of Deuteronomy (32:5), where, among other things, it says: “Perverse and crooked generation, is this what you repay the Lord?” Whereas in the ancient translation it is written more appropriately and clearly: “Have you repaid the Lord in this way, foolish and senseless people?” [Col. 0813C]

### IX

We also add what you asked: why God did not say to Samuel (16:1), “Go and anoint David for me,” but rather, “Go and anoint for me one of the sons of Jesse,” and so forth. Why did he speak ambiguously instead of naming David specifically?

It was so that David might not suffer what Joseph suffered (Gen. 37:5 and following). For just as Joseph’s brothers, learning that he would one day be their king or lord, plotted against him and afterward sold him, after many injuries, so it was necessary to provide against the possibility that these men might perpetrate the same things. Thus ignorance became the mother of caution. [Col. 0813D]

### X. (I Reg. 17:39–40, 49)

Concerning what is written: David, going to fight the Philistine, refused to carry Saul’s armor, but put five stones from the stream into his bag, although he threw only one.

David came from tending the sheep after he had been anointed, at God’s command, with the oil of blessing—through the ministry of a man but by God’s direction. The horn of chrism placed upon his head was more precious than every diadem and purple garment [Note: Rather, I think]. Thus he went forth bearing divine anointing upon his head, not clothed in armor, not protected by a shield, and not armed with weapons, but possessing God’s blessing, stronger than everything. [Col. 0814A]

Since the king did not believe this, David was compelled to explain his former deeds. David said to the king (I Reg. 17:34–36): “Your servant was tending his father’s flock, and a lion or bear came and carried away a ram from the midst of the flock. I pursued them, struck them, and tore the prey from their mouths. They rose up against me, but I seized them by the jaw, strangled them, and killed them. Therefore this uncircumcised Philistine will also be like one of them.”

The king, provoked by the greatness of the sign, believed him and said to David, “Put on my armor and go forth thus.” When David had done so, he could not advance in the customary manner, because God did not permit it. He intended that David should conquer naked, and that Saul’s weapons should not share the credit for the victory, lest the king say, “My weapons won.” David therefore threw off the armor and put on confidence. [Col. 0814B]

He went forth unarmed, yet armored with faith. The shepherd and soldier went forth; he hurled a stone driven not by bodily strength but by the power of faith. With a single swing of the sling he struck the blasphemer on the forehead. When the man fell, David ran up, took his sword, and cut off his head, so that what is written might be fulfilled (Psal. 9:17): “The sinner is caught in the works of his own hands.”

Thus, in the name of the Lord, he carried away victory from the enemy and at that time removed reproach from the children of Israel. What these things signify, however, has already been expounded in the first book of this work from the writings of our predecessors, as the Lord granted us and as we were able to discover. [Col. 0814C]

### XI

Now I shall briefly undertake to address what we omitted in the earlier part of this work and what you did not ask about. Why did the Lord, who plainly knew the future, say (Acts 13:22), “I have found David son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will do all my wills,” when David himself committed such and so many offenses? [Col. 0814D]

If we understand this as spoken of David himself, who, after Saul had been rejected and killed, became king of Israel, the matter is perfectly clear. God knew the future and foresaw in David such great devotion and such truthful repentance that he would belong among those of whom he himself says (Psal. 31:1): “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin.” [Col. 0815A]

Since God foresaw that David would sin and would erase his sins through devout humility and sincere repentance, why should he not say, “I have found David, a man after my own heart,” to whom he would not reckon sin, because he did so many good things, lived with such devotion, and in that very devotion offered a sacrifice of a contrite spirit for his sins?

For all these reasons it was most truly said: “I have found David after my own heart.” Although what he sinned was not according to God’s heart, his making satisfaction for his sins through suitable repentance was according to God’s heart. Thus the only thing in him that was not after God’s heart was the thing that God did not reckon against him. Once this was removed—that is, not reckoned—what remained except the grounds for saying most truly, “I have found David after my own heart”?

If, however, we wish to understand this prophetically of Christ, no difficulty in the question arises. Unless perhaps someone asks how Christ could rightly be called by this name. We answer: because of the seed of David, from which Christ assumed flesh.

We have also explained the reason for this name in Christ without lack of precedent. We find that Christ Jesus was most openly called “David” by the prophet Ezekiel, where it is read from the person of God the Father (Ezek. 34:23): “And I will raise up over my sheep one shepherd who will feed them, my servant David. He himself will feed them, and he himself will be their shepherd. I, the Lord, will be their God. And my servant David will be prince among them. I, the Lord, have spoken.” [Col. 0815B]

And elsewhere (Ezek. 37:22): “And there will be,” he says, “one king ruling over them all. They will no longer be two nations, nor will they be divided into two kingdoms. They will no longer defile themselves with their idols, their abominations, or any of their iniquities. I will save them from all their dwelling places in which they sinned; I will cleanse them, and they will be my people, and I will be their God. And my servant David will be king over them, and there will be one shepherd over all of them.”

The prophet Hosea likewise, when he foretold the condition of the Jews as they now have it and their later belief in Christ, prophesied of the same Christ under the name of David, saying (Hos. 3:4): “For the children of Israel will sit many days without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without altar, without priesthood, without manifestations”—as no one now doubts is the condition of the Jews. [Col. 0815C]

But when the Apostle Paul, speaking to the Gentiles, says (Rom. 11:30), “For just as you once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy through their unbelief, so they also now have not believed through your mercy, so that they too may obtain mercy,” this prophet, foretelling the matter so long beforehand, confidently adds (Hos. 3:5): “And afterward the children of Israel will return, and they will seek the Lord their God and David their king; they will be astonished at the Lord and at his goodness in the last days.”

Behold: through the name of David, Christ was prophesied, since when these things were prophesied, David, the king of Israel, had long since fallen asleep. The Lord Jesus, however, was to come in the flesh from his seed; for this reason he was called David in the prophetic manner of speaking. [Col. 0815D]

The Apostle Paul, however, appears to have placed this testimony in the Acts of the Apostles in such a way that it can be understood only of that king David who succeeded Saul. For among other things he says there (Acts 13:21–22): “They asked for a king, and God gave them Saul son of Kish, a man from the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. After removing him, God raised up David as king for them. To him he also bore witness, saying: ‘I have found David son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my wills.’” [Col. 0816A]

But because he follows this by adding, “From this man’s seed, according to the promise, God brought Israel a Savior, Jesus,” he indicated more profoundly that this testimony should rather be understood of the Lord Jesus, who truly does all the wills of God the Father, than of that king David. For although, according to the preceding discussion, David may rightly be said to have been found after God’s heart because his sins were forgiven on account of his devout repentance, how did he do all God’s wills? Although Scripture praises him most highly when it recounts his times and deeds, it nevertheless censures him because he did not destroy the high places where God’s people sacrificed contrary to God’s command, since he had ordered sacrifice to be offered only at the tabernacle of testimony. Although God himself was also worshiped at those same high places, King Hezekiah, descended from David’s line, later destroyed them, to his great praise (IV Reg. 18:4) [Note: III Reg. 2:2–3: “Nevertheless, since the Temple had not yet been built, I do not think that sacrifice to the true God on the high places was expressly forbidden. There are also those who refer to Solomon what Claudius says about David.”]. [Col. 0816B]

### XII

You ask why Saul, in anger, said to his son Jonathan (I Reg. 20:30): “Son of a woman who voluntarily seizes a man.” The Greek language calls such women—of the kind Saul falsely accused Jonathan’s mother of being—*lupas*, that is, “she-wolves” or prostitutes, although she was not one.

A prostitute is called a “she-wolf” because of rapacity and because of the lust of that animal, which seizes and lays hold of those who come to it. Hence also the name *lupanaria* is given to places where prostitutes are found.

In the Septuagint, however, it is written: “And Saul became very angry with Jonathan in his anger and said to him: ‘Son of girls who voluntarily defile themselves.’” This has the same meaning as what is written above. [Col. 0816C]

### XIII. (21:1)

You inquire at length about David’s flight from Saul and his coming to Abimelech the priest to ask for bread. The priest replied that he had no bread except the holy bread, which had been removed from the altar and which no one but the priests was permitted to eat. He asked him whether the young men were pure, especially with regard to women. David answered: “If women are concerned, we have abstained from them since yesterday and the day before yesterday, and the vessels of the young men have been holy.”

By “the vessels of the young men” he meant holy—that is, chaste in mind or body from women—because in many places among the ancient people sanctification is used to mean abstinence from women. Thus we read in the Gospel (John 11:55): “Many went up to Jerusalem from the region before the day of Passover, to sanctify themselves,” that is, to be pure from women during the Passover solemnity. [Col. 0816D]

What follows—“Moreover, this way is polluted”—does not refer to a road for the feet or to the streets of the region, but to this mortal life, which truly is a way in which there is no one who does good and does not sin, and in which no one among the saints is without stain. Concerning this way the prophet prays: “Remove from me the way of iniquity.” And again: “Direct my steps according to your word, so that no iniquity may rule over me.”

Then follows: “But even today it will be sanctified in my vessels,” as though he were plainly saying: “Although we have been chaste from women since yesterday and the day before yesterday, after receiving the holy bread we will guard our life in chastity for at least as many days, and for much longer.” [Col. 0817A]

### XIV. (23)

Your question concerning the city of Keilah is exceedingly foolish: whether David conquered it, and whether it had another name. David did not conquer it; rather, he delivered it after it had been besieged and conquered by enemies.

You say that you do not remember Scripture mentioning this city except in the prophet Isaiah, where it is read: “Woe to Keilah, the city which David conquered.” This is entirely false, since Isaiah the prophet writes (29:1): “Woe to Ariel, Ariel, the city which David conquered.” This is understood to have been said of earthly Jerusalem. [Col. 0817B]

The Keilah mentioned above was a city in the tribe of Judah, where David once stayed when he was fleeing Saul. Now, as we read in the *Book of Places*, it is the village of Keilah, lying east of Eleutheropolis on the road to Hebron, about the eighth milestone, where the tomb of the prophet Habakkuk is shown [Note: Do these things satisfy you, excellent reader?]. [Col. 0817D]

### XV

As for your inquiry about Mount Gilboa, which David cursed at Saul’s death—whether the curse can stand according to the literal meaning—the words belong to an agitated spirit and excessive grief. Taken literally, they cannot mean that dew or rain never afterward fell there. What these things signify, however, has already been explained in the earlier part of this work. [Col. 0817C]

### XVI. (II Reg. 5:6)

When it says, “The king went, and all the men who were with him, to Jerusalem, to the Jebusite inhabitant of the land,” the name “Jerusalem” is used here by anticipation, just as in the Book of Judges it says (1:7–8), “Adonibezek, king of Jerusalem” [Note: This is stated most explicitly in Josh. 18:29]. What is now Jerusalem was then Jebus [Note: Jebus, which is Jerusalem], and it was called that name until David’s time. But the historian, by anticipation, wished to call it Jerusalem and Zion, the city of David—not because it was then so called, but because it became so after David captured it. [Col. 0817D]

The Jebusites were a people descended from the son of Canaan (Gen. 10:15–16), who was called Jebus, and Jerusalem was their possession. It later fell by lot to the tribe of Benjamin.

The Scripture then continues by saying that they said to David—that is, the Jebusites said (II Reg. 5:6): “David will not enter here.” Since the city was enclosed by a strong circuit of walls and fortified by the aid of warriors, the Jebusites said in their pride: “Unless you remove the blind and the lame, you will not enter here.” The meaning, or order, of the words is that David would not be able to capture by the right of war not only the city or its warrior men, but not even the blind or the lame stationed upon the wall. [Col. 0818A]

### XVII. (II Reg. 5:7)

Concerning what is written: “David captured the fortress of Zion.” After David captured it, he built its fortress, like the head of a body, and called it Zion.

[Note: I found *Archis* written. Was this through the ignorance of a copyist, or rather because the word displeased Claudius? Let the reader judge. If you wish, retain the word *Archis*.]

A fortress is the head and summit of a city, because a citadel is built at the highest point of a city for the sake of strength.

### XVIII. (8:16)

Concerning what is written: “Joab son of Zeruiah was over the army; Jehoshaphat son of Ailud was the recorder [Note: Ahilud]; Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests; Seraiah was the scribe; Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites; and David’s sons were priests.” [Col. 0818B]

After this you add and ask: Who were the Cherethites and Pelethites? Or how could David’s sons be priests when they were not from the tribe of Levi?

The Hebrews relate that the Cherethites and Pelethites came from the descendants of those of whom the Lord said to Moses (Num. 11:16): “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people, teachers and leaders. Bring them to the door of the tabernacle of the covenant and have them stand there with you, so that I may descend and speak with you. I will take from your spirit and give it to them, so that they may bear the burden of the people with you and you may not bear it alone.”

From their stock, as I have already said, came preserved descendants or families called Pherethi and Cerethi: the Cerethi being interpreted as “those who give judgment,” and the Phelethi as “those who punish,” so that those whom the former ordered to be killed by giving judgment might be punished by the latter. [Col. 0818C]

But a very perplexing difficulty arises: how could David’s sons be priests, as though they were sons of Aaron, when they are not said to have any kinship from the tribe of Levi? This was caused not by the authority of divine Scripture, but by the rashness of the interpreter.

While I myself was deeply doubtful about this in my heart, I turned to the ancient interpreters and found it written in various translations as follows:

“And David was administering judgment and justice among all his people. Joab son of Zeruiah was over the army; Jehoshaphat, son of another, was the recorder; Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests; Asa was the scribe; Benaiah son of Jehoiada was counselor; and Ochibi and Ophilit and the sons of David were princes of the royal court.” [Col. 0818D]

### XIX. (II Reg. 18:18)

You ask why Scripture says of Absalom after his death that he erected a monument for himself, saying, “I have no son,” when this book states above (14:27) that he had three sons and, in the same passage and at 13:1, one daughter named Tamar, of beautiful appearance. [Col. 0819A]

The historian recapitulates these matters after Absalom’s death. It was not something done then, but something that had been done earlier, before he had sons. Because he had despaired of being able to have children, he had erected a monument bearing his name in the manner of a capitol. As Scripture says, he called it “the hand of Absalom.”

The ancient translation supports our interpretation. It says that while Absalom was still alive, he set up a handmade star in the king’s valley, because he said, “I have no son to commemorate my name.” He called it a star—that is, the statue he had made in his own name—and named this star “the hand of Absalom” to this day.

It uses the diminutive term “star” for a statue, as though it meant “little statue” or “small statue,” in the manner of a capitol, which above it called a monument. [Col. 0819B]

### XX

[Note: There is no doubt that what follows up to number 21 should be placed here; it had been set at the end of the codex. Just as it is placed there in a wholly inappropriate location, so here it belongs in a most suitable one. This is not surprising, since such things are sometimes found in manuscripts; I previously cited an unquestionable example in Pope Hadrian’s letter to Charlemagne. Let the reader consult what I wrote in *On the Cult of the Saints*, dissertation 10, chapter 15.] [Col. 0819D]

You continue to ask why, among David’s mighty men, Scripture writes of each one that he did this or that, but does not reach the number three. Who were these three, or why is this written? (II Reg. 23:19 and following.)

First it introduces three who surpass the other men—that is, the thirty-three—in right of valor. Then it names another three who were inferior to the first three, yet surpassed the thirty in merit of courage. After these come the thirty in their proper order.

To make what we are saying clearer, we shall set out their names in order: David; second, Eleazar; third, Shammah [Note: Semma]. David was their leader. [Col. 0820D]

Then come another three: first Abishai, second Benaiah, third Asahel. Abishai was also leader of this second group of three. He is placed in this way as though it were said: just as David was leader among the first group, so Abishai was leader among the following group.

Therefore he was the most renowned among the three and illustrious among the three: second and their leader. He was second—that is, inferior to the first three—but leader over those who followed.
