He was one of the three, but he did not reach the first three, because in merit and courage he did not reach David, Eleazar, and Shammah, and so forth. [Col. 0819C]

### XXI. (II Reg. 24:1)

You also ask why David is blamed for numbering the people, when Jehoshaphat [Note: I find nowhere that Jehoshaphat numbered the people; Ahab, however, is recorded as having numbered them at III Reg. 20:15, 27; Joram, king of Israel, at IV Reg. 3:6; and Amaziah, king of Judah, likewise, and not to his disadvantage, at II Paral. 25:5; Solomon also did so while he was still acceptable to God.] and the other kings numbered God’s people and remained without blame or punishment, especially since before Jehoshaphat Moses numbered God’s people twice. [Col. 0820D]

For Jehoshaphat numbered God’s people out of necessity, and Moses did so at God’s command; but David acted through presumption and rashness, and because of the people’s iniquity. This has already been treated above, at the end of the second book of this work. [Col. 0820A]

### XXII. (III Reg. 2:5)

You ask this also: why is it written of David that he grew old, although he did not exceed seventy years, and that he was covered with garments but was not warmed, and that when a beautiful young woman, Abishag the Shunammite, was found, she slept with the king and ministered to him. “The king did not know her,” although in more advanced age we read and observe that men are unable to have intercourse with women. [Col. 0820B]

It is not surprising that a seventy-year-old man, who from his youth had been harassed and broken by many hardships and tribulations, became impotent in manhood, since we see many young men and young women whose blood is so sluggish in early youth that neither the men are moved by any sexual impulse nor the women can retain or vivify within their wombs, through any warmth, the seed they have received.

For melancholic blood—that is, blood of black bile, as physicians say—is extremely cold, and those whom it possesses excessively it renders sterile both in begetting and in conceiving.

Moreover, the same physicians say that men whose blood is colder are foolish, while those whose blood is warmer are more prudent. Hence old men, whose blood has already grown cold, and children, whose blood is not yet warm, are less wise and more stupid.

## XXIII. (1 Kings 2:5, 7)

You ask this also: Why did David say of Joab, “He put the blood of battle on his belt, which was around his loins, and on his footwear, which was on his feet,” and so forth? In the ancient translation it is written as follows:

“And now you know what Joab son of Zeruiah did to me, and what he did to the two commanders of the army of Israel, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether, commander of the army of Judah: he killed them and avenged the blood of war in peacetime, and put the blood of innocent men upon my life, and upon my belt, which was around my loins, and upon my footwear, which was on my foot. You shall deal with him according to your wisdom and bring his gray hairs down with blood to Sheol.”

For when God commands it, the law defines the right: “If anyone deliberately kills a person, drive him away from my altar, so that he may die” (Exodus 21:14). And again in Deuteronomy it says (19:11–13): “The land of your possession cannot otherwise be cleansed except by the blood of the one who shed blood.”

David himself said that Joab’s sin of homicide abounded because he did not avenge what he could and ought to have avenged by the authority of the law and the power of the king. Therefore, what he had not done earlier, he ordered his son Solomon to do near the time of his death, so that Joab might be punished here by the sentence of the law and not be punished forever by God.

But since we have mentioned Joab, we ought to repeat what was previously omitted above. When David cursed him on account of Abner son of Ner, among other things he said (2 Samuel 3:29): “May there not fail from the house of Joab one suffering from a discharge of semen, nor a leper, nor one holding a spindle, nor one falling by the sword,” and so forth.

This is found in a much different form among the Septuagint:

“David heard after Abner had died and said: ‘I am innocent, and my kingdom before the Lord is innocent from now and forever of the blood of Abner son of Ner. May it come upon the head of Joab and upon his father’s entire house. May there not fail from the house of Joab a gonorrheal sufferer, a leper, one holding a *sitalē*, one falling by the sword, and one lacking bread.’”

*Gonorrhea* is a disease of the bladder together with the penis. Afflicted by the discharge of semen, a man very frequently suffers without any erection, showing debility together with pallor of the body and wasting. In Greek they call this disease *gonorrhoia*. It is an exceedingly severe and very shameful condition, so that sufferers do not know how their genitals are discharging semen. The seminal passages are affected, so that, because of their weakness, they cannot retain the substance of the semen; they discharge a thin, reddish, and very sharp urine, and, because of the frequent abundance of moisture, it is expelled spontaneously at uncertain times.

If such people do not take care over this disease, death follows them. Some perish silently because of negligence and failure to apply remedies; they succumb to the illness.

We do not know what “holding a *sitalē*” means, because it is a foreign word. Our translation says “holding a spindle,” followed by “falling by the sword.” The sense may be that the one who, having considered himself nobler, killed another by deceit, and, weakened in manly strength, was reduced to feminine softness and effeminacy, should fall by the sword before his enemies, and, becoming poor and wretched, should lack bread.

Or perhaps “holding a spindle” means enduring the disease that some call *fusum*, which physicians call *phthisis*. *Phthisis* is an ulceration, a swelling in the lungs, which is more readily found among the young. It is called *phthisis* among the Greeks because it is a wasting of the whole body, produced by rheumatism of the throat together with a slight fever, continual discharge, and a catarrh dripping for a long time; thus the lungs are damaged. It is a very dangerous and malignant disease of the lungs. As has already been said, it generally occurs in youth.

Another translation reads as follows: “May there not fail from the house of Joab one suffering from rheumatism, and a leper,” and so forth. In Joab, however, we do not see this fulfilled literally: he lived in such honor throughout his life, until David’s death, and enjoyed such bodily health that he was always commander of the army of Israel and an exceedingly powerful warrior. David said this out of excessive anguish of spirit, just as he did regarding the mountains of Gilboa; taken literally, the statement does not stand, but it showed that he had not consented to the death of Abner, commander of Israel.

## XXIV. (1 Kings 3:2)

Concerning what is written: “Solomon loved the Lord, walking in the commandments of his father, except that he walked on the high places and burned incense.” After this you ask what the “high place” was, since the term is frequently read in this book, and you say: Why is Samuel not blamed, when he is said to have sacrificed on a high place?

After the people of God had left Egypt and come to Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:20 and following), they heard the Lord speaking to them from the midst of the fire. There, in a certain sense, they entered into a covenant with God and promised that they would do everything the Lord commanded. Just as there is one God and there was one people of God (Deuteronomy 12:5, 8, 12, 13, 14, 21, 26, 27), so he commanded that they should have one altar of God in the tabernacle, on which they would honor God with sacrifices and praises.

After a long time, because of their sins, the ark of God was also captured by foreigners. In it was the covenant written that they had made with God: that they would worship no other God besides the God of their fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whose unconquerable name remains forever, and whose memorial endures from generation to generation.

After this the tabernacle was destroyed. Without the ark, in which the covenant between God and the people had been written, it remained dishonored and empty. Thus it seemed good to certain holy men that, during the period between the destruction of the tabernacle and the building of the temple, they should honor the Lord their God—the God of heaven—with incense and sacrifices in pleasant, clean, and elevated places.

It was unlawful for that people to continue doing this after the ark had returned from captivity, the tabernacle had been erected, and the temple had been built for them. This is why Scripture so often reproves those who still burned incense on the high places and thought that they were doing this blamelessly, because they knew that Samuel, who had pleased God, and Solomon, and many other people of that time had acted in this way.

Indeed, among all those kings they are considered worthy of praise before God, with great commendation, who destroyed such places—namely, Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:4) and Josiah (2 Kings 23:5, 8, 13, 19, 20).

## XXV

When it is read in the Book of Kings (1 Kings 8) and in Chronicles (2 Chronicles 5:10) that there was nothing else in the ark except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed in it at Horeb, why does Paul write to the Hebrews that the ark contained the tablets, Aaron’s staff, and the manna? If they were not there, why did the Apostle say this? And if they were there, who put them there?

This was answered in the third book of this work. Only this remains from your question: whether it was the very staff of Aaron that blossomed—the staff through which signs were performed in Egypt and extraordinary wonders at the sea.

It was altogether one and the same staff: the one called “the staff of God” in Exodus, and at different times called Moses’ staff or Aaron’s staff according to the diversity of the works performed.

## XXVI

You ask also what became of the ark itself, or whether it will ever be seen—that is, become visible—by human beings.

Regarding this, I confess that I have read nothing else except what is written, among other things, in the Second Book of Maccabees (2:5 and following):

“Jeremiah came to the place and found a house in a cave, together with the tabernacle, the ark, and the altar of incense, and he brought them in there and blocked up the entrance. Some of those who followed him came near to mark the place for themselves, but they could not find it. When Jeremiah learned of their eagerness to search it out, he said to them that the place would remain unknown until God gathered together the assembly of his people and showed mercy to them. Then the Lord would reveal it, and the majesty of the Lord would appear, and a cloud, as in the time of Moses.”

From this it should be believed that the Lord will accomplish these things through Elijah.

Some people, distrusting and ignorant of the power of almighty God, say: How can it be that that tabernacle, made of wool and linen, could last through so many ages? We answer them that the same power by which, for forty years, no one among their tribes was weak, whose foot was not [Note: “loosed,” as I think], whose sandals were not torn apart, and whose garments were not consumed by age, continued in the garments and in the wood of the tabernacle for four hundred and eighty years, until the time of Solomon; and thereafter for another four hundred and thirty years, until the destruction of Jerusalem under Nebuchadnezzar. That same power will continue in the tabernacle itself until the end of the age.

But since the presbyter Bede, of blessed memory, in his exposition of the construction of the tabernacle and temple, says that the altar of incense was placed outside the veil [Note: See what Bede transmits in Book 2, *On the Tabernacle*, at the words: “The veil, however, will be inserted through rings … and the table outside the veil.”], this is why you asked me in your letter: Why, then, did I say in the *Book of Instructions* that the letter and the spirit in Exodus are beyond the veil?

For this reason, if that blessed Bede were alive in the body, I would wish to ask him whether, after the ark had been removed from the temple, he would seek to enter beyond the veil to the altar of incense, or where he would place the blood, or whose altar’s horns he would touch, or to whom he would offer incense, after the ark of the covenant was no longer there.

## XXVII. (1 Kings 9:11–13)

Here is another question concerning what is written: “King Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in the land of Galilee. Since they did not please him, he called them the land of Chabul to this day.”

If this question is hidden from you, it is not clear to me either. I only want you to know that it is found differently in the ancient translations. There it is written as follows:

“Then Solomon gave King Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee. Hiram went out from his city Tyre and proceeded to Galilee to see the cities that Solomon had given him, and they did not please him. And he said: ‘What are these cities that you have given me, brother?’ And he called them ‘the End’ to this day.”

What this means, however, or why he called them “the End,” I confess that I do not know—unless perhaps he said this because he would not seek any other cities from him thereafter.

This much we know: their mutual friendship was not broken between them until the day of their death, because afterward Hiram sent one hundred and twenty talents of gold (1 Kings 9:14). Later they both built a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber (1 Kings 10:11, 26, 27), which at appointed years would go to Ophir to bring Solomon gold, ivory, monkeys, and peacocks.

## XXVIII. (1 Kings 10:11–12)

You add that you wish to inquire about something which I confess I do not know: what King Solomon made from the *thyine* wood: a beautiful house of the Lord, a house of the queen, and zithers and lyres for the singers.

After this comes the statement: “Such *thyine* wood was neither brought nor seen to the present day.”

Among the Seventy translators, however, I find it written as follows:

“And Hiram’s ship, which had brought gold from Ophir, also brought a very great quantity of unworked beams and precious stones. The king made from these unworked beams the supports of the house of the Lord and of the king’s house, and nablas and *cinnurim* for the singers. Such unworked wood was not found in the lands, nor seen to this day.”

Another translation reads:

“And Hiram’s ship, which brought gold and *sephora*, brought a very great number of unworked beams and precious stones. The king made from the unworked wood the ceiling of the house of the Lord and of the king’s house, and nablas and *ambuci* for the songs. Such wood has not appeared to this day.”

That such wood came from India is attested by divine Scripture. But what can we say about the nature of that wood, when the prophets themselves who later wrote this history confess that they do not know it?

## XXIX. (1 Kings 10:16)

After this the same history continues and says:

“King Solomon also made two hundred shields of pure gold: six hundred shekels were used for the plating of one shield, and three hundred small shields of tested gold; three hundred minas of gold covered one small shield.”

Physicians say that a *pelta* is a crescent-shaped shield of the Amazons, shaped like half a moon, or perhaps a third or a quarter of one, or—what is more credible—a half-moon shield of the kind the Amazons once used in battle. It is not likely, however, that these were such shields, because Scripture does not indicate this.

A mina is called so in Greek; it contains sixty shekels, making one thousand two hundred obols. A shekel makes two *semisses*, or solidi—the Greek term is *stater*—and contains twenty obols. An obol contains seven siliquae and one-fifth of a siliqua. By weight, this makes a double drachma, which our people call a scruple. It was made of bronze in the shape of an arrow, which is why it received its name from the Greeks: *obolos* in Greek means “arrow.”

A mina is one pound. A talent contains sixty minas.

In the Septuagint it is written as follows:

“And Solomon made three hundred gold spears of beaten work. Three hundred gold pieces were in one spear, and three hundred beaten-gold shields. Each shield contained three hundred minas of gold.”

Another translation reads:

“And King Solomon made three hundred gold lances of beaten work. Two hundred and fifty gold pieces were in one lance, and three hundred gold shields, three hundred gold pieces in each shield.”

Then Scripture continues (verse 17): “And the king placed them in the house of the forest of Lebanon.”

If it belonged to Solomon, why did he request cedar wood from Hiram out of Lebanon? Scripture does not say that he placed them on Mount Lebanon’s forested heights, but in the house of the forest of Lebanon. This is an instance of a figure of speech in which the producer is named for the thing produced, and the container for what it contains.

Lebanon was called the temple together with its porticoes, vestibules, and great halls. Therefore it was already said literally above that these surrounded the temple in a square on every side. Since the building was truly immense and contained much wood from Lebanon—indeed, innumerable pieces of it—it was called “the forest of Lebanon.”

The temple itself is also called Lebanon in Scripture, as the prophet Zechariah says (2:1): “Open your doors, Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars.” Jeremiah likewise says against Shallum son of King Josiah, among other things (22:22):

“The wind will shepherd all your shepherds, and your lovers will go into captivity. Then you will be confounded and ashamed because of all your wickedness, you who sit in Lebanon and nest among the cedars.”

For them, to sit in Lebanon meant to have their hope of salvation in the temple. To nest among the cedars meant that, because of the buildings of the temple, the sinful people expected to be saved and not taken captive on account of the merit of that place.

Lebanon is also the name of a cold mountain and a valley in Syria Phoenicia, which was the possession of the Canaanites and overlooks the Great Sea; their capital was Tyre. Hence the Sidonians placed cedar, fir, and pomegranate wood on the Great Sea, and from there it came by rafts across the sea as far as Joppa; from there it was transported by compulsory ox-cart labor for forty miles to Jerusalem.

That mountain received the name Lebanon from the whiteness of its snows. *Lebanon* is interpreted as “whiteness” or “whitening.” In the same way, that temple acquired the name because of the height of its walls and their grandeur, brilliance, or whiteness.

## XXX

It is right to ask—although you did not ask this—what it means that in this book divine Scripture frequently says of the sacrilegious and wicked kings of Israel: “He did what was evil in the sight of the Lord.”

Although there are many evils among human beings, Scripture, passing over all the other evils, names one evil in particular, in comparison with which the other evils, though they are evils, seem almost not to be evils. Just as, in comparison with good things, God, who is good, is called the Good of goods, the Holy of holies, the God of gods, and the Lord of lords, so in human actions and deeds the worship of idols may be called the evil of evils, the crime of crimes, and the sin of sins.

In divine Scripture this is also commonly called iniquity, abomination, filth, sin, fornication, and hatred. It is called “sin” when Scripture frequently says of the already ruined kings of Israel: “He did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam, who sinned and caused Israel to sin.” Although there was one sin, he used the plural because of the two calves.

“Shame” and “filth” are used as Moses speaks concerning the children of Israel in Exodus (32:25): “For he had stripped them” —that is, Aaron had stripped the children of Israel—“for the shame of their filth and had set them naked among their enemies,” that is, deprived of the help of God.

The worship of idols is called “iniquity,” as the prophet Hosea names the two calves “two iniquities” (10:10).

“For­nication” is used in many ways by the prophets. Thus we read (Jeremiah 3:1): “But you have fornicated with your lovers”—that is, instead of serving the one God with whom you ought to have maintained a spiritual marriage in purity of mind, you served many gods and thus shamefully prostituted yourself in your heart with many lovers, that is, demons.

Although someone may appear to worship or adore one image, in that one image he serves the entire host of demons.

Since the subject has turned to the worship of images and idols, we should also explain the etymologies of these names, so that people of our time may know what evil human beings serve.

A *simulacrum* is a figure, example, likeness, image, form, countenance, appearance, aspect, or resemblance. The use of images began when, out of desire for the dead, images or likenesses were established of those thought to have been received into heaven (Wisdom 14:15). In their place, demons presented themselves on earth to be worshiped and persuaded deceived and ruined human beings to sacrifice to them.

Some of these had been brave men or founders of cities. When they died, the people who had loved them fashioned images of them, so that they might have some consolation from contemplating the images. Gradually, however, with the demons persuading them, this error entered into later generations, so that those whom their predecessors had honored merely in memory of their name, their successors regarded and worshiped as gods.

Images (*simulacra*) are named from resemblance (*similitudo*), as though they were “imitated,” because by the hand of an artist they imitate the faces of those in whose honor they are fashioned, whether from stone or another material. Thus they are called images either because they are like gods, or because they are fabricated and contrived as though they were gods; hence they are false.

Again, an idol (*idolum*) is an image made and consecrated in human form, according to the interpretation of its name. For *eidos* in Greek means “form,” and, with a diminutive ending, *eidōlion* means what in Latin is expressed by *formula*. Therefore every form or little form demands to be called an idol.

*Idolatry* is interpreted as the service or worship of idols. For *latreia* in Greek means “service” in Latin. As far as true religion is concerned, this service is owed only and exclusively to God.

Just as impious pride—whether of human beings or demons—either commands or desires such service for itself, so pious humility, whether of human beings or holy angels, refuses service offered to itself and shows to whom it is owed.

Some Latins, ignorant of the etymology of the Greek language, ineptly say that *idolum* derives its name from *dolus*, “deceit,” because the devil introduced the worship of the creature under the name of divine worship.

It must be understood with the utmost care that not only the person who worships visible images and representations, but also anyone who worships any creature—whether heavenly, earthly, spiritual, or bodily—in place of the name of God, and hopes from it for the salvation of his soul, which comes from God alone, belongs to those of whom the Apostle says [Note: What is taught here, if understood of worship strictly so called, is entirely true. If understood of worship in the broad sense, it belongs among the matters criticized in Claudius. See what I set out in nos. 24 ff. of chapter 3, dissertation 1, *On the Worship of Saints*, and also nos. 6 and 7 of chapter 6, dissertation 2, concerning the same Claudius.] (Romans 1:25): “They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is God, blessed forever.”

The same applies to those of whom the prophet says (Jeremiah 17:5): “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man and whose heart departs from the Lord.”

It should also be understood that the nations did not impose the name “image” or “idol” upon their gods; rather, the holy men of God, worshipers of the divine name and of the one God, imposed this name upon the gods of the nations.

## XXXI

Passing over certain of your minor questions, which have already been resolved in the preceding books, we come to what Elijah said about Ahab (1 Kings 21:24): “If he dies in the city, the dogs will eat him; but if he dies in the field, the birds of the air will eat him.”

After this you add (1 Kings 22:37): How is this true, when Ahab is said to have been carried to Samaria and buried in his sepulcher in Israel?

In the Septuagint Fathers there is something additional. After several intervening words it says:

“The king died in the evening, and the herald of the army stood in the camp at sunset, saying: ‘Let each man go to his city and to his land, because the king has died.’ And they came to Samaria and buried the king in Samaria. They washed his chariot in the pool of Samaria, and the dogs licked his blood, according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken; and the Spirit of God, which was in Elijah, could not have lied.”

The blood that flowed from his body and ran onto the bed of the chariot, which was made of leather, constituted a large part of his body. This coagulated like flesh, and the dogs ate it. Thus was fulfilled what Elijah, the servant of the Lord, had openly foretold in its entirety.

Or—and this is what should rather be believed—the dogs ate him when they ate his sons, who were also his flesh.

As for the statement that prostitutes washed themselves in his blood, they did this only in order to perform some magic.

## XXXII. (2 Kings 5:1)

You ask what the salvation was that God granted through Naaman the commander.

No salvation should be understood better than the one that he himself conceived in his mind through the cleansing of his leprosy, when he pledged that he would worship no other god except the God of Israel. Through the greatness of his healing and the proclamation of his tongue, many people, abandoning their idols, began to worship the God of Israel alone.

This was the salvation that God gave Syria through him, because there is truly no other salvation for human beings like knowledge of the Creator and the remedy for sins.

What these things signify, however, has been sufficiently explained in the preceding book.

## XXXIII. (2 Kings 6:21)

The same Scripture also says that so great and terrible a famine occurred in Samaria, and that the city was besieged for so long, that a donkey’s head was sold for eighty pieces of silver and a quarter of a *kab* of dove dung for five pieces of silver.

The “kab of dung” may be understood as a small bladder of the throat, except that the ambiguity of the word makes us uncertain, since the text does not say “head” or “of the head.”

The city, besieged by enemies for a long time, had no open exit for human beings. Free-flying doves therefore carried themselves by flight into the fields, or toward the army, and, finding grain, filled the small pouches of their throats. Returning to the city at that same time, before the grains had been consumed by digestion, they were caught; thus five pieces of silver bought a quantity of grain, not the stench of dung.

I have not read this anywhere, nor learned it from anyone else. I have said it as it seemed to me. If you can discover something better about this, you will do well to let us know.

## XXXIV. (2 Kings 14:9)

This is your question concerning King Joash. It is not impossible to understand, but it is difficult for us to express: Why did Joash king of Israel send back word to Amaziah king of Judah, saying:

“The thornbush of Lebanon sent to the cedar that is in Lebanon, saying: ‘Give your daughter to my son as a wife’”?

It was said figuratively, not literally.

A *trope* is an expression transferred from its proper meaning to an improper resemblance, for the sake of ornament or necessity. There are fourteen tropes, which in Latin may be interpreted as “modes” or “ways.” Having set them out, we bring one of them into discussion; its name is metaphor.

A metaphor is a transfer of things and words. It occurs in four ways.

The first is from an animate thing to an animate thing [Note: Either something is missing, or the text should read “that is,” or “likewise, as”]. Thus in the Book of Job (4:10): “The roar of the lion, the voice of the lioness, and the teeth of the lions’ cubs are broken,” so that by the metaphor already mentioned, Job is understood as the lion, his wife as the lioness, and their sons as the teeth of the lions’ cubs.

Likewise in the Psalm (11:1): “Why did the nations rage?” Human beings and beasts are both said to rage, and both have souls.

In the prophet Jeremiah (4:7): “A lion has come up from his lair”—that is, Nebuchadnezzar from Babylonia—“and the destroyer of the nations has risen.” Both the lion and the destroyer possess a soul.

The second is from an inanimate thing to an animate thing, as in the statement (Isaiah 55:12): “The mountains will sing praise before God, and all the trees of the forest will clap their hands.” Mountains and trees of the forest are inanimate, whereas singing and clapping hands belong to animate beings.

The third is from an inanimate thing to an inanimate thing, as in the prophet (Zechariah 11:1): “Open your doors, Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars.” This is a transfer from a city to a mountain, neither of which possesses a soul.

This is also the passage about which you ask: Joash king of Israel sent word to Amaziah king of Judah, saying: “Give your daughter to my son as a wife.” By the trope of allegory, Joash compared himself to a cedar, and the king of Judah to a thornbush. By the same figure he compared his own people to the beasts of the forest, saying: “The beasts of the forest that are in Lebanon passed over and trampled down the thornbush”—that is, Amaziah.

After this he adds (2 Kings 14:10): “You have indeed struck Edom and prevailed, and your heart has lifted you up. Be satisfied with your glory and sit in your house. Why do you provoke evil, so that you may fall, and Judah with you?” And so it happened.

## XXXV. (2 Kings 15:35)

This also troubles you: Why is it written concerning Jotham king of Judah: “He built the highest gate of the house of the Lord”?

After this you added: Had it not previously been built by Solomon? Or did he build a new one, and Israel as well?

It was not newly built. Rather, it was the same gate that had once been built by Solomon and called “the highest.” Jotham began its restoration and raised it up again by repairing it.

## XXXVI. (2 Kings 18:4)

You also ask concerning Hezekiah why divine Scripture says that, after he destroyed the high places, smashed the pillars, cut down the sacred groves, and broke the bronze serpent that Moses had made, he called it *Nabas* [Note: Vulgate: *Nohestan*], and so forth.

It should be believed that he did this under the instruction of the prophet Isaiah [Note: I do not find this in Isaiah]. You ask me about the very matter that I desire to know: if someone could show me the etymology of this name, since I have not found the name written differently even in the ancient translation—except that *Nabas* means “serpent” in their language. What the final syllable means, I confess that I do not know.

This is a great lesson, which can contribute to the edification of the Church, if there is someone able to observe why Hezekiah, with great praise and for the salvation of souls, destroyed what Moses had made at God’s command for the salvation of that people.

For who does not know that Moses possessed greater merit than King Hezekiah? Concerning Moses, the Lord said to Aaron and Miriam in the Book of Numbers (12:6):

“Hear my words: If there is a prophet among you, I will make myself known to him in a vision; I will speak to him in a dream. But not so with my servant Moses, who is faithful in all my house. Mouth to mouth I will speak with him; he sees the Lord in a form and not in riddles.”

The serpent that Moses, as has already been said, made at God’s command so that the people would not perish by a serpent’s death was ordered by God to be made. But the people began to venerate and worship it. Thus those who were going to die again received the death that their parents had escaped temporarily: they died forever in their souls.

Therefore Hezekiah destroyed what Moses had made at God’s command. Accordingly, this example ought to possess great authority in the Church: if some of our predecessors or ancestors did things that could be without fault in their own time, but later turned into error and superstition, their descendants should destroy them without delay and with great authority [Note: This is also among the passages in Claudius that is rightly regarded as suspect].

### XXXVII–XXXVIII

A necessary inquiry remains for us, although it was not part of your question: how divine Scripture resounds [in the words of 2 Kings 19:35]: “When the angel of the Lord went out, he struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand from the army of the Assyrians.” And the prophet Daniel says [Dan. 6:22]: “The Lord sent his angel and shut the lions’ mouths.” And in the thirty-second Psalm [Col. 0830B] [Ps. 33:8], according to the more accurate translation: “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and he will deliver them.” There are many other examples similar to and even greater than these. If we wished to review all of them in the order of divine Scripture, life would fail before speech.

> **Note [Col. 0829D]:** What follows Claudius excerpted from Augustine, but he did not take everything from a single book; rather, he gathered it from various works. I shall indicate some passages of Augustine for the reader to consult.

That angels are sent by him who is everywhere and fills heaven and earth—not by bulk, but by power—just as truth and wisdom reach “from end to end mightily and dispose all things sweetly” [Wis. 8:1], is something the Apostle proclaimed to the Athenians, saying [Acts 17:27–28; see also chapter 12, elsewhere no. 23, of Book IV of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*]:

> “In him we live and move and have our being.”

A clear consideration, insofar as the human mind is capable of it, supports this view: we believe and say that God works continually in the things he has created. For we are not in him as though we were his substance, as it is said [John 5:26] that he “has life in himself”; rather, since we are something other than he is, we are in him for no other reason than that he works this, and this is his work, which contains all things, and by which his Wisdom, as has already been said [Wis. 8:1], “reaches from end to end mightily and disposes all things sweetly.”

Through this ordering [Acts 17:28], “we live and move and have our being in him.” Hence it follows that, if he were to withdraw this work of his from things, we would neither live, nor move, nor exist.

> **Note [Col. 0830D]:** The edition reads *quo* (“by which” or “whereby”).

> **Note [Col. 0830D]:** I beg you to compare this passage with the printed text.

For even the devil himself is not outside the power of the Almighty. Indeed, how could the evil ones subsist anywhere, or possess life, except through him who gives life to all things? God certainly did not so abandon that same rejected angelic creature of his that he ceased to show himself to it as the God who creates and gives life, and who, even amid punitive evils, bestows many good things upon the wicked [no. 22].

The power of the Creator and Almighty, indeed of the One who holds all things together, is the cause of the subsistence of every creature.

> **Note [Col. 0830D]:** *Omni* (“all”).

If this power ever ceased to govern the things that have been created, their forms would cease at the same time, and all nature would collapse. For the world and every creature—visible or invisible, bodily or spiritual—could not stand even for the blink of an eye if God withdrew from it his governance.

> **Note [Col. 0831D]:** In the published passage of Augustine these words are lacking: “and every creature, whether invisible or visible, bodily or spiritual.” He knows how to act while resting and to rest while acting, and he can apply a not-new plan to a new work.

> **Note [Col. 0831D]:** No. 25, chapter 14. The remainder has been collected from other passages of Augustine. Compare this with what Augustine sets forth in chapter 30 of Book VII of *The City of God*.

> **Note [Col. 0831D]:** Book XV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 13, no. 22.

When he created, he did not grow weary; nor, when he ceased, was he refreshed. He is good without quality, great without quantity, Creator without need, present without location, containing all things without posture, wholly everywhere without place, eternal without time, performing wonders without any change in himself, and suffering nothing.

He does indeed have messengers, that is, angels; yet it is not the case that they announce to him something of which he is unaware. There is nothing that he does not know. Rather, it is their good to consult the Truth concerning his works.

> **Note [Col. 0831D]:** “Truth” is added here.

This is what is meant when they are said to announce certain things to him: not that he learns from them, but that, sent by him to whoever he wills, they announce through his Word, without bodily sound, what he wills. They hear everything from him through that Word of his—that is, in his Truth they find what they must do and what must be announced, to whom, and when.

We also pray to him, yet we do not teach him our necessities. For his Word says [Matt. 6:8, 32]: “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him.” He did not come to know these things at some point in time so that he might know them; rather, without beginning, he foresaw all future temporal things and, among them, what we would ask of him and when, and whom he would hear or not hear, and concerning what matters.

> **Note [Col. 0831D]:** Again, Book VI of *On the Trinity*, chapter 10, no. 11.

He knows all his creatures, spiritual and bodily, not because they exist, but they exist because he knows them. He did not fail to know what he had made when he was about to create it. Because he knew, he created; he did not know because he created. Nor did he know them as created otherwise than as things to be created.

> **Note [Col. 0832D]:** Claudius took what follows for the most part from the same Augustine. Compare this passage with chapter 30 of Book VII of *The City of God*.

For this is the God whom we worship, as divine Scripture teaches us: the God who established beginnings and ends for the natures he created, both of subsisting and of moving; who possesses, knows, and orders the causes of things; who fashioned the power of seeds; who bestowed the rational soul, which is called the mind, upon living beings as he willed; who granted the faculty and use of speech; who gave to spirits, as pleased him, the gift of foretelling the future; and through those whom he chooses drives away illnesses.

He also governs the beginnings, progress, and ends of wars themselves, whenever the human race must be corrected and chastised in this way. He both created and governs the most vehement and violent fire of this world in proportion to the vastness of nature. He is the creator and governor of all waters. He made the sun, the brightest light of bodily things, and gave it a fitting power and motion. He does not withdraw his dominion and power even from the realms below.

He established the seeds and nourishment of mortals, whether dry or liquid, assigning them to natures suited to them. He grounds and makes the earth fertile. He grants its fruits to animals and human beings. He knows and orders not only the primary causes but also those that follow from them. He set the moon’s appointed measure. He provides heavenly and earthly paths through changes of place.

He granted to human talents, which he created, knowledge of various arts to assist life and nature. He established the union of male and female for the propagation of offspring. To human communities he granted, for their easiest uses, the gift of earthly fire, which they might apply to hearths and lamps.

> **Note [Col. 0832D]:** *Quem* (“which” or “whom”).

All these things the one true God makes and accomplishes. Yet he does so as God—that is, wholly everywhere, confined by no places, bound by no chains, divisible into no parts, changeable in no respect, filling heaven and earth by the presence of his power, not by any need of his nature.

Thus he governs everything he created in such a way that he also permits the creatures themselves to exercise and perform their proper motions. For although they can exist without him in no way, they are not what he is. He also does many things through angels, but he makes the angels blessed only from himself. Thus, although he sends angels to human beings for certain purposes, he does not make human beings blessed through the angels, but through himself, just as he makes the angels blessed through himself.

From this one true God we hope for eternal life. For, in addition to the benefits that he bestows upon the good and the wicked through the administration of nature, of which we have mentioned some, we have from him a great and distinctive sign of great love.

Although we can never offer thanks sufficient for the fact that we are, that we live, that we behold heaven and earth, and that we possess mind and reason by which we seek him who created all these things, nevertheless he did not wholly abandon us when we were weighed down and overwhelmed by sins, turned away from contemplating his light, and blinded by love of darkness—that is, of iniquity. He sent us his Word, who is his only Son, born and suffering after assuming flesh for our sake, so that we might know how highly God valued the human being, and so that through that unique sacrifice we might be cleansed from all sins.

By his Spirit, love having been poured into our hearts, and every difficulty having been overcome, we might come to eternal rest and to the ineffable sweetness of contemplating him. What hearts, what tongues could claim to be sufficient for giving him thanks?

> **Note [Col. 0832D]:** “How many?”  
> **Note [Col. 0832D]:** The following appears to have been taken from Augustine, but I have not yet found the passage in which the holy Doctor presents it.

Thus the supreme and true God, with his Word and Holy Spirit—these three are one God—is one almighty God, creator and maker of every body. His creatures are blessed through participation in him.

> **Note [Col. 0833C]:** Sermon 43, elsewhere *On the Words of the Apostle* 27, nos. 3–4.

He made the human being rational, from soul and body. When the human being sinned, he neither permitted him to remain unpunished nor abandoned him without mercy. He gave to good and evil beings existence, together with the stones; seminal life, together with the trees; sensory life, together with animals; and intellectual life, together with the angels alone.

From him come every measure, every form, and every order; from him come measure, number, and weight; from him comes whatever naturally belongs to any genus or possesses any value. From him come the seeds of forms, the forms of seeds, and the motions of seeds and forms.

He gave the flesh its origin, beauty, health, fertility for propagation, arrangement of limbs, and health through harmony. He gave the irrational soul memory, sensation, and appetite; and to the rational soul he additionally gave mercy, understanding, and will.

He did not refuse not only heaven and earth, nor only angel and human being, but even the small and contemptible creature, so slight that it is despised, the little spine in its entrails; nor did he leave a flower of the grass or a leaf of a tree without the fitting arrangement of its parts and a kind of peace among them.

And afterward:

> **Note [Col. 0833C]:** Claudius again excerpted what follows from Augustine, copying the holy Doctor’s chapter 32 of Book VII of *The City of God*.

> “The mystery of eternal life was proclaimed from the very beginning of the human race through certain signs and sacraments appropriate to the times, by angels and at the times when it was fitting. Then the Hebrew people were gathered into a certain commonwealth, which enacted this sacrament. There, through some who knew and some who did not know, it was foretold that what has been brought about from the coming of Christ until now and onward was to come.

> “Afterward that same people was scattered among the nations, for the sake of the testimony of the Scriptures in which eternal salvation was proclaimed as destined to be in Christ. For not only all the prophecies that are expressed in words, nor merely the precepts of life that shape conduct and piety and are contained in those writings, but also the sacred rites, priesthoods, temple or tabernacle, altars, sacrifices, ceremonies, feast days, and everything else belonging to that service which is owed to God—and which in Greek is properly called *latria* [λατρεία]—

> **Note [Col. 0833D]:** *Latria* [λατρεία].

> —all these things signified and foretold what, for the sake of the eternal life of believers in Christ, we believe has been fulfilled, is being fulfilled before our eyes, and will yet be fulfilled.”

> **Note [Col. 0833D]:** “They signified and foretold.”

> **Note [Col. 0833D]:** What follows is not found in Augustine’s printed works. Whether it once existed there, whether Claudius took it from other passages of Augustine, or whether he substituted it from his own material, the reader may judge.

But while we wish to demonstrate the ministry of the angels, in a certain transport of mind we proclaim to the ignorant the manifestations of the goodness of the unchangeable God and of the truth of the divine work.

### XXXIX

You also ask who is the first priest and who the second. The first priest is the high priest, such as Aaron, Eleazar, and their successors, who were permitted to enter beyond the veil into the Holy of Holies every day.

The second priests were those who in our time are called presbyters. Concerning them the Apostle says [Heb. 9:6]: “The priests always entered the outer tabernacle, completing the services of the sacrifices.”

The others, who were called Levites because they were from the tribe of Levi, had permission to enter neither the inner nor the outer sanctuary. They were merely doorkeepers, singers, and ministers of the priests; at the outer altar of holocausts they were cutters of wood, attendants responsible for the fires, and distributors of the sacred meats among the people.

Concerning these two sons he says in the Psalm [Ps. 134:20–21]:

> “House of Aaron, bless the Lord;  
> house of Levi, bless the Lord.”

> **Note [Col. 0834D]:** I do not see how they can be called “two sons,” since Aaron himself was from the tribe of Levi.

### XL

You also ask what *tyrones* are. The *tyrones* took their name from Tyre,

> **Note [Col. 0834D]:** Tyro.

a Phoenician city that was once the metropolis of the Canaanites, where Hiram, the friend of Solomon, was king.

> **Note [Col. 0834D]:** I beg the reader to examine this etymology carefully.

*Tyrones* are called strong youths who are selected for military service and are capable of bearing arms. They are judged not merely from their declaration of birth, but from their appearance and bodily health.

It was the custom of the Roman military to train boys in arms first. Thus, at the age of sixteen, they served as *tyrones*; before that age they were kept under guardianship. It is clear that slaves never served among them unless they had first been freed from slavery.

**Claudius, bishop, has completed his work on the Books of Kings.**

---

## PREFACE OF CLAUDIUS, BISHOP, TO THE CHAIN ON THE HOLY MATTHEW

*(From Mai’s* Spicilegium*, vol. IV, p. 301.)*

### EDITOR’S NOTICE

I previously published the preface of Claudius, bishop of Turin—who will himself soon speak of his age—to his commentaries on the Epistles of Paul in the seventh volume of the Vatican collection, *Scriptorum veterum*, p. 274 [below, col. 837]. Now I am pleased to publish his preface to the *Catena* that he compiled, chiefly from Latin Fathers, on the Gospel of Matthew.

I have seen this work, still unpublished, in two manuscripts: one of such venerable antiquity that it seems to have been contemporary with Claudius himself, and the other dating approximately from the eleventh century. Since we are not as well supplied with Latin chains as with Greek ones, it would be useful to make this Claudian work publicly available; I do not despair of doing so at some point.

For the present, however, I gladly commit his learned prologue to print. Long ago Baronius published only two small portions of a few lines of it under the year 815, and Usserius transferred it from there into the Irish Epistles, as though Claudius had been Irish by birth—a belief held without justification. In every other respect this preface survived only in the older manuscript, because the other manuscript is acephalous.

### THE PREFACE BEGINS

**To the holy and most blessed father Justus, specially honored by me with singular devotion and affection, Claudius, a sinner.**

> “In the year 815 after the incarnation of our Savior Jesus Christ, our Lord, after the pious and most gentle prince, Hludowicus, son of the holy Catholic Church of God, had in the second year of his reign, supported by heavenly aid, moved an army against barbarian nations; and after your fatherly presence had departed and withdrawn from the palace of the aforesaid prince to the secure and beloved harbor of your monastery, which has always been dear to you, you instructed me to send the brothers of your monastery some little work worthy of remembrance, for reading, in exposition of the Gospel.”

> **Note [Col. 0835C]:** This is as far as Baronius published it in the cited place.

Would that my ability to speak were as great as my willingness to obey! Although my will had for some time been occupied with writing something else, I immediately strove to direct my will toward what you had commanded. I attempted, insofar as I was able, to investigate and explain the Gospel according to Matthew from the short works of the holy Fathers—not exhaustively, for that is difficult to accomplish—drawing from the treatises of our teachers and predecessors, who surpassed us in the study of this work both in knowledge and in time: Origen, Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Rufinus,

> **Note [Col. 0835D]:** *Rufini.* I believe this to be an error of an ancient copyist for *Rabani*. For I have discovered, by comparison with the passage “If anyone divorces his wife except on account of fornication,” which is entirely Rabanus’s, that wherever the letter R is written in the *Catena*, Rabanus rather than Rufinus is meant. I greatly wonder at this, since Claudius and Rabanus were indeed contemporaries, although Claudius was somewhat older. Claudius also seems to have learned the name Fortunatus only from Jerome’s preface to his Commentary on Matthew.

John, Fulgentius, Leo, Maximus, Gregory, and Bede. But just as, in the citadel of the head, the tongue sounds more loudly than all the other members, so in explaining the Gospel the most blessed Augustine is preeminent among them all.

In many places also, where the meaning or words of these authors were lacking, my poverty has tried, in whatever way it could, to fill the gap.

Since you commanded it, I know that my judgment will be spoken of by many who know how to judge only according to the flesh and not also with a just judgment, as though I had rashly attempted this work in attacking or criticizing my predecessors.

Let whoever he is read the apology of the blessed presbyter Jerome, which he wrote in the preface to this exposition of Matthew for a certain man named Eusebius. There he says:

> “I am sufficiently astonished, dearest Eusebius, that, when you were suddenly about to sail to Rome, you wished this little package to be given you by me, as though I were to compress Matthew by briefly explaining him in words while expanding him in meaning. If you remembered my reply, you would never have asked in a few days for a work of years.”

He promised that he would explain it to him most fully at a later time. He would certainly not have done this if the holy man had not known that many mysteries had been omitted there.

Let him also read the other Latin interpreters of that Gospel, Hilary and Fortunatus, and, following the order of the history, diligently seek out all the physical, allegorical, and even ethical meanings in their fullness. Then he will be able to know whether I have labored in this work idly or devoutly, superfluously or necessarily. And if the fruit of my labor does not please him, let him hear this answer, without offense to charity: let the one who is displeased disregard it.

I also beseech your fatherly affection and the benevolent charity of all the brothers not to be frightened by the lengthy exposition or the size of the volume. For truly the holy Gospel, which our Savior is said in many places to have compared with the kingdom of heaven, cannot be expressed in a few words or explained in a few thoughts.

It was fitting that the sacred sayings of our Savior should be distinguished from the other Scriptures both in merit and in form, lest the dignity of heavenly mysteries lie openly and indiscriminately before everyone, and holy things be exposed to dogs and pearls to swine. Therefore our Savior himself arranged that the purity of his words should be hidden from the indiscriminate eyes of all and covered, as it were, by a veil of modesty.

By a divine and excellent dispensation it was provided that the evangelical Scripture of our Lord should be veiled and overshadowed by heavenly mysteries, just as divinity itself was hidden in its secrecy. This is made clearer by the examples that follow.

As for the fact that many things in this book are found less orderly than they ought to be, do not attribute everything to ignorance. Forgive some things on account of poverty, and others on account of bodily weakness and the feebleness of my eyes. They were not taken down on tablets or arranged on sheets of paper; rather, they have been fixed in this book just as I was able to find or discern them.

Grant pardon, then, for my imprudence, which you compelled me to display. Your esteem forced me to become verbose for your ears, trusting that the length of the volume, if it displeases by its expression, will please by its affection, once you understand that it has been arranged not for eloquence of speech but for love of you.

I also knew that your kindness was more inclined to criticize the modesty of silence in my friendships than the boldness of loquacious familiarity. Read it, if you live [so the manuscript reads], and transcribe it.

I also beseech you, after it (that is, the book) has become well known to you, to send it back to our brothers to whom it is still unknown.

Finally, I possess your presence within the hidden places of my mind, and I behold your likeness in the mirror of my heart. There our love has painted it perfectly, so that it cannot be erased by the forgetfulness of any age; it is renewed every moment by continual remembrance.

There I converse with you more secretly about your habit of goodness. There too I reflect upon the conduct of a better life. There I kiss you with the lips of my mind and embrace you with the hands of my mind.

Thus true love, nourished alive in my inner being by the image of you and kindled by the spark of charity, promises me the bond of your love, and my soul serves as surety for your soul. I ask my breast, conscious of our mutual affection, how much I ought to presume concerning you.

And therefore I earnestly ask both you and all who practice the heavenly commandments and follow the divine words, to whomever knowledge of my name may come through this little work or through any other work: I humbly seek from all of you intercession for my sins, earnestly entreating you to beseech our most merciful Lord with continual petitions that, with your aid, he may erase all my transgressions and sins through his customary clemency and abundant goodness, and, even if not to the same reward, at least command us to reach the same harbor of rest.

> **Note [Col. 0837B]:** Baronius also published this passage.

So that, although here, because of the distances of intervening lands, we cannot often see one another with bodily eyes, we may rejoice there in one another’s presence. And when the crown of merits is bestowed upon you by the just Judge, may forgiveness for what has been entrusted to me not be denied by the most merciful Redeemer and most perfect Advocate.

Therefore may he deign, through the ineffable operation of grace and power, to grant us this: that those whom he joins here by the truth of faith he may not separate there by dwelling-place. May divine mercy grant that he preserve your fatherhood for many years in outward vigor and the cheerfulness of sound health. For I truly feel myself restored whenever I learn that your health, which I always desire, is secure.

I greet and venerate your sons and my brothers, and, venerating them, I greet them. Remember me, men of God.

---

## PREFACE OF CLAUDIUS, BISHOP, TO HIS COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF THE APOSTLE PAUL

> **Note [Col. 0837D]:** From an ancient Bobbio manuscript, now Vatican. Richard Simon also mentions that this preface was read in a Paris manuscript, *Critical History of the New Testament*, chapter 25. For the present I publish it without the commentaries, whose later publication I await having leisure to undertake.

*(From Mai’s* New Collection of Ancient Writings*, vol. VII, p. 274.)*

**To Theudemirus, venerable and sincerely beloved in Christ, the abbot whom I must honor with singular devotion and affection: Claudius, bishop, by the inspiration of God’s grace, wishes perpetual blessedness in the Lord.**

It was not through obstinate stubbornness that I long and greatly resisted your wish, most diligent little patron, not to send you the clarified Epistles of the teacher of the nations. Rather, hindered by the clamoring causes that arise in this fleeting world, I have not yet been able to do so.

I had resolved in my heart that, when I first approached the sweetness of the Scriptures, I would remain watchful and tireless in examining and meditating upon them, lest I allow the sharpness of my mind to fall asleep in sluggish torpor. I thought within myself that I would then truly be living on the bread of angels; and if I could not live as the greatest men did, at least, striving to live as a sick man does, I might be able to taste something with my tongue and urge others to follow my apostolic example.

Thus, forgetting what lies behind and stretching ourselves through understanding toward what lies within, we might grow in the spiritual mirror and not be held back by illicit desires.

As Cicero says:

> **Note [Col. 0838D]:** In fragments of his work *On Philosophy*, or in the *Hortensius*, cited by Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book XIV, at the end.

> “There is great hope for us,” he says, “when we spend our days and nights considering and sharpening our understanding, which is the edge of the mind, and taking care that it never become dull—that is, when we live in philosophy.”

A little later he adds:

> “And if, as was the view of the ancient philosophers, especially the greatest and most illustrious of them, we possess eternal and divine minds, then we must believe that the more these minds remain continually in their proper course—that is, in reason and the desire to investigate—and the less they mingle and become entangled with human vices and errors, the easier their ascent and return to heaven will be.”

Then, repeating this very conclusion and bringing his speech to an end, he says:

> “Therefore, to bring the discourse to an end at last, whether we wish to be peacefully extinguished after living in these limbs, or whether we wish to move without delay from this dwelling into another and somewhat better one, we must devote all our effort and care to these studies.”

> **Note [Col. 0838D]:** The editions of Cicero read *artibus* (“arts”) incorrectly here; the correct reading is *artubus* (“limbs”).

> **Note [Col. 0838D]:** The editions read *haud paulo* (“not a little”) here.

> **Note [Col. 0839B]:** This is where Cicero’s passage, as quoted by Augustine, ends. Let learned readers determine whether the following sentence belongs to Cicero or Claudius.

For this ardor, even if it does not instruct the mind of the seeker, at least exercises his intellect. It enables him to discover that he knows what he perhaps thought he did not know; and, once reminded, he knows what he previously did not know.

While I was earning my livelihood through labor and money, my attention was more freely occupied with the divine Scriptures. After I took up the care of the diocese, the more causes arose, the more anxieties they produced.

During the winter I wear out the palace roads going and returning, and I can fulfill less of the love mentioned above. After the middle of spring, traveling forward with weapons and carrying parchment together with arms, I proceed to the coastal watchposts, keeping guard in fear against the Agarenes and Moors. By night I hold a sword, and by day, with books and pen, I try to bring my begun desire to completion.

> **Note [Col. 0839B]:** The manuscript reads *pergameno* (“with parchment”) rather than *pergamenam* (“parchment”).

For unless that man presided over the spirit with preceding grace—the man whom the Apostle commends when he speaks of the head not being veiled—that which the Lord spoke concerning seed sown beside the road would have happened to my mind.

You also show that you are living this kind of life when you consider me without anxiety, and for that reason you are a troublesome exactor. Nor ought you to be troublesome to me, since, if I possessed the ability whenever I possessed the will, I would not have been your debtor. If I had not undertaken this work before these anxieties arose, when the brothers asked me—as you know—I could scarcely have accomplished anything from it even now.

I truly confess that I initially undertook both this work and the Pentateuch unwillingly. The brothers who were established in the school commanded me to do so, for I was teaching them the Scriptures by word of mouth. The pious prince, the emperor Hludowicus, also instructed me, and the aforesaid prince compelled me not merely to deliver words wandering away through forgetfulness, but to write them down with a pen so that they might endure, and to put into writing what I brought forth orally.

You asked me to write at the admonition and exhortation of the brothers, so that they might fulfill the vow they had vowed to the Lord. And it was a vow, as I say, not a purpose—the word you wrote, “purpose,” belongs to God alone.

I could find no better admonition than the First Epistle of the apostle Paul, which I sent, since its whole purpose is to remove human merit, whereas this is precisely what monks now chiefly boast of.

> **Note [Col. 0840B]:** This rash and false opinion of Claudius requires no refutation. We know, moreover, that Claudius, who also held erroneous opinions concerning the veneration of sacred images, was refuted by the abbot Theudemirus, whom Claudius is addressing here. I say nothing of the charge of Arianism brought against Claudius, from which critics otherwise acquit him.

Thus it commends the grace of God, through which everyone who has vowed may fulfill what he has vowed to the Lord.

---

## PREFACE OF CLAUDIUS, BISHOP, TO HIS EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS, ADDRESSED TO THE EMPEROR LOUIS THE PIOUS

*(Mabillon,* Vetera Analecta*, p. 91.)*

**To my own illustrious and glorious lord, whom I cherish above all mortals with special devotion and affection; by the grace of God, father of his country rather than merely emperor, whose imperial dignity arose from the fountain of piety; son of the holy Catholic Church of God, Hlodohicus: Claudius, a sinner.**

In our times, when studies have grown cold, scarcely anyone is found who is most ready through daily application not only to discuss matters that have not been discussed, but also to read what has already been discussed by our predecessors. It is therefore remarkable that your imperial authority, so great and sublime, demands such a work from me when it orders me to explain the Epistles of the teacher of the nations, the apostle Paul, from the treatises of our predecessors, who illuminated us and surpassed us in the study of this work both in knowledge and in time.

Your most sacred serenity, always most beloved by me, knows—for it is always devoted to pious works and instructed by holy readings—how, beneath the imperial diadem, you practice a contemplative life. It also knows what the blessed apostle Peter wrote concerning the praise of these same Epistles in his Second Epistle, where he says:

> “As also our beloved brother Paul wrote to you according to the wisdom given to him, as he does in all his Epistles when he speaks in them of these matters, among which there are certain things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction.”

Behold, with the blessed Peter, his fellow apostle, as our witness, we find that while the apostles themselves were still living in the flesh, various heresies arose because unlearned people did not understand the difficulty of their meaning correctly.

Who, then, could worthily or properly approach the exposition of writings which so great and eminent a first confessor in the flesh of the Lord and shepherd of the Church of the New Testament declares difficult to understand?

Nevertheless, although not relying upon my own strength but upon your merits, with the help of him who opened the mouth of the mute and made the tongues of infants eloquent; who is faithful in his words and holy in all his works; who said, “Ask and you will receive, seek and you will find, knock and it will be opened to you”—with his gracious aid I have gathered together, in a brief style, the Epistles of the blessed apostle Paul to the Ephesians and the Philippians.

I have drawn not so much from the treatises of our predecessors as from the statements of various treatises, like a beggar who possesses no field of his own but gathers food for himself from another’s harvest behind those who reap, lest he perish from hunger in winter.

Likewise, I too have composed these Epistles from the words of others. If your serenity judges this exposition suitable for reading, refer it to Christ, the author; for, as I said above, this very work is yours through the Lord’s gift.

But if it should be open to criticism because of the rusticity of its language, he whom we are discussing and whom we hold in our hands has taught us not to fear such people, provided their criticism is free from deceit that attacks the true faith. He taught that the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power, and he wrote of himself that he was unlearned in speech rather than in knowledge.

I have completely repudiated, insofar as I was able, the deadly and detestable doctrine of Pelagius, who proved an ungrateful preacher of divine grace, through the most blessed Augustine, the most gracious herald of heavenly grace, in his treatment of this Epistle.

I have likewise repudiated those who attempted to support their heresy from this Epistle to the Ephesians, where it says, “He chose us before the foundation of the world.” They understood this to mean that human souls existed before the beginning of the world and were coeternal with God the Creator. Others, from the Epistle to the Philippians, believed God the Father to be superior to the Son.

I proclaim all these doctrines to Catholic ears as things to be avoided, like a deadly precipice or lethal poison. For this reason I conceal their names, lest I seem to disparage my predecessors rather than speak the truth.

As for the Apostle’s Epistle to the Galatians, on which I worked most diligently last year insofar as I was able, I have recently added nothing to it. Rather, just as I previously composed it, I have joined it at the beginning of this work according to its proper order.

As for the remaining Epistles, although I have many excerpts in my possession, much still remains to be sought out. But because this year, with my sins hindering me, you have burdened me heavily, and because, given over to excessive anxieties, I have no desire to live, nor am I able to examine the Scriptures, I beg your Clemency not to be a troublesome exactor [Col. 0842B]. For if divine mercy assists me, I am devoted to repaying what I owe. May the almighty Lord, who is King of kings and Lord of lords, cause you, my lord, to overcome the snares of all enemies; and, granting you the reward of the purest charity, may he deign to let you live for the advancement and adornment of the whole Church, so that, when the term of mortal life is ended, he may make you stand free from the consciousness of sin before his holy throne. Here ends the work.

## HERE BEGINS THE TREATISE.

The Ephesians are Asians. Having received the word of truth, they persevered in the faith. The Apostle praises them highly, writing to them from Rome, from prison, and so forth.

[Col. 0841B]

# CLAUDIUS THE BISHOP’S EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PAUL TO THE GALATIANS

*(Bibliotheca maxima Patrum, vol. XIV.)*

[Col. 0841C]

## THE AUTHOR’S DEDICATORY LETTER

To the most devout lord Dructerannus, abbot, singularly worthy of the highest honor in Christ, Claudius, a sinner.

If I am not mistaken, three years and more have now passed since, while I was still detained in the turf-field of Aluenni, in the palace of the devout prince Lord Louis—then king, now emperor—you began, through your fervent affection, to rouse the sluggishness of my understanding, so that I might undertake some fruitful labor on the Epistles of the Apostle Paul, the teacher of the nations. But because, until now, I have been unable to obey your command, weighed down by the labors and storms of the world, now, by God’s generosity, during this season of Lent [Col. 0841D], I have arranged the Epistle of the blessed Apostle Paul to the Galatians, using the expositions of the blessed Fathers Augustine and Jerome, blended together according to their sentences.

When I saw that much was lacking in these treatises for a suitable exposition, I turned to other books of the aforementioned Father Augustine and endeavored from them to complete the exposition that was missing from those treatises. I also tried, as it seemed to me appropriate, to insert below their manner of expression some words of my own, which would join the two expositions without rupture, exercise the reader’s understanding, and help avoid weariness.

For the present, I joyfully strive to send this to your holiness as a kind of small trophy, so that whenever you hold it in your hand and read it, you may deign to remember me; and so that the immeasurable charity of Christ, present everywhere, may unite those whom the distances of the earth separate.

As for the remaining Epistles, many excerpts from them are already in our hands. If the Lord wills, and grants me life and health, and if you pray for us, I shall endeavor to undertake their exposition as quickly as I can [Col. 0842D]. May the gracious and merciful God deign to increase both the years and the merits of your reverend blessedness, so dear to me, for the advancement and adornment of his Church. Farewell in the Lord, man of God, and remember me.

[Col. 0843A]

## ARGUMENT OF THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PAUL TO THE GALATIANS

The Galatians are Greeks. Galatia was named from the ancient peoples of the Gauls, by whom it was occupied. For the Gauls, summoned to assist the king of Bithynia, divided the kingdom with him after the victory had been completed. Thereafter, mingling with the Greeks, they were first called Gallo-Greeks, but now, from the ancient name of the Gauls, they are called Galatians, and their region is called Galatia.

They first received the word of truth from the Apostle, but after his departure they were tempted by false apostles to turn toward the Law and circumcision. The Apostle calls them back to the faith of the truth, writing to them from Ephesus.

The chief argument by which the Galatians had been persuaded and led astray by the false apostles was that they heard that Paul, through whom they had believed the true Gospel [Col. 0843B], was not an apostle: namely, because he had neither been chosen from among the Twelve nor at any time followed Christ, as Peter and the others had. He therefore needed to refute this disparagement with sound arguments and the authority of the Holy Spirit, proving in due order that he had been sent neither by men nor through a man, but by the one who had chosen both him and the others for the apostolic office.

[Col. 0843B]

## ANOTHER ARGUMENT

The reason why the Apostle writes to the Galatians is this: they are to understand that the grace of God brings with it the consequence that they are no longer under the Law. For when the grace of the Gospel had been preached to them, certain people from the circumcision—although Christian in name, they had not yet embraced the very benefit of grace and still wished to remain under the burdens of the Law that the Lord God had imposed—not on those serving righteousness, but on those serving sin. That is, he gave the just Law to unjust people in order to demonstrate their sins, not to remove them.

For no one removes sins except the grace of faith that works through love. Thus, although the Galatians had already been established under this grace, those people wanted to place them under the burdens of the Law, asserting that the Gospel would profit them nothing unless they were circumcised and underwent the other carnal observances of the Jewish rite.

For this reason they began to regard the Apostle Paul, from whom the Gospel had been preached to them, with suspicion, as though he did not maintain the discipline of the other apostles, who compelled the Gentiles to Judaize. The Apostle Peter had yielded to the scandals caused by such people and had been led into their pretense, as though he too held that the Gospel profited the Gentiles nothing unless they fulfilled the burdens of the Law. The Apostle Paul recalled him from this pretense, as he teaches in this very Epistle.

A similar question also arises in the Epistle to the Romans. Nevertheless, there appears to be some difference: there he settles the dispute itself and suppresses the quarrel that had arisen between those who had believed from the Jews and those who had believed from the Gentiles. The former thought that the reward of the Gospel had been rendered to them as the merit of the works of the Law, and they did not want that reward given to the uncircumcised, whom they regarded as undeserving. The latter, by contrast, eagerly sought to place themselves above the Jews, as though above the murderers of the Lord.

In this Epistle, however, he writes to those who had already been disturbed by the authority of those who came from the Jews and who compelled observance of the Law [Col. 0844A]. For they had begun to believe them, as though the Apostle Paul had not preached the truth because he had not wished them to be circumcised. Therefore he began in this way: “I am astonished that you are so quickly transferring yourselves from him who called you into the glory of Christ to another Gospel.”

With this opening he briefly indicated the question at issue. Indeed, even in the greeting itself—when he says that he is an apostle “not from men nor through a man,” something he is not found to say in any other Epistle—he sufficiently shows that those who were persuading them of such things were not from God but from men, and that, as far as the authority of evangelical testimony is concerned, he ought not to be considered inferior to the other apostles.

For he knows himself to be an apostle “not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father.” Accordingly, beginning at the very threshold of the Epistle, with the Lord permitting and assisting our study, we have undertaken to consider and treat each point in this way.

[Col. 0844B]

## EXEGESIS OF THE FIRST CHAPTER

### “Paul, an apostle”

The fact that the Apostle Paul places his name and the title “apostle” at the beginning of almost all his Epistles is a mark of authority. Just as the judges of this age, in order to appear more noble, take their titles from the kings whom they serve and from the dignity with which they swell with pride, so the Apostle, claiming for himself great dignity among Christians, placed “apostle of Christ” before his name as a title, so that the authority of the name itself might terrify those who read it and he might judge that all who believed in Christ ought to be subject to him.

“Apostle,” that is, “one who has been sent,” is properly a Hebrew term; it is also what “Silas” signifies. His name was given from sending or being sent. The Hebrews say that among the prophets and holy men themselves there are some who are both prophets and apostles, while others are prophets only.

Thus Moses, to whom it is said, “And I will send you to Pharaoh,” and who himself replies, “Provide another whom you may send” (Exod. III), and Isaiah, to whom God says, “Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?” (Isa. VI), are both apostles and prophets. From this we too can understand that John the Baptist ought to be called both prophet and apostle. For Scripture says: “There was a man sent from God, whose name was John” (John I).

For this reason, in the Epistle to the Hebrews [Col. 0844D], Paul did not, according to the customary practice, place either his name or the title “apostle” at the beginning: he was going to speak about Christ—“Therefore, having Jesus, the high priest and apostle of our confession” (Heb. IV)—and it would not have been fitting that where Christ was to be called an apostle, Paul should also be designated an apostle.

There are four kinds of apostles. The first is one who is sent neither by men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father. The second is one who is indeed from God, but through a man. The third is one who is from a man and not from God. The fourth is one who is neither from God nor through a man, but from himself.

Isaiah and the other prophets can belong to the first kind, as can the Apostle Paul himself, who was sent neither by men nor through a man, but by God the Father and Christ [Col. 0845A].

Jesus, son of Nun, belongs to the second kind: he was indeed appointed an apostle by God, but through the man Moses.

The third kind occurs when someone is appointed through human favor and ambition, as we now see many people introduced into the priesthood not by God’s judgment but by having purchased the favor of the crowd.
