The fourth kind consists of the false prophets and false apostles about whom the Apostle says: “Such people are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ” (II Cor. XI). They say, “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord did not send them.

### “Not from men nor through a man”

Paul does not present himself as an apostle “not from men nor through a man” arrogantly, as some think, but necessarily. Rather, he says that he is an apostle through Jesus Christ and God the Father, so that by this authority he might confound those who were parading Paul outside the number of the Twelve and claiming that he had suddenly burst forth from I know not where or had been appointed by his elders.

The statement can also be understood as indirectly directed against Peter and the others: the Gospel had not been handed down to him by the apostles, but by Jesus Christ himself, who had also chosen those men as apostles.

All this is prepared so that no one, arguing against the burdens of the Law on behalf of the Gospel’s grace, could object: “But Peter said this”; “the apostles established this”; “your predecessors decreed something else.” Paul now closes off this objection, as it were, in hidden speech, and makes it clearer in what follows, when he reports that nothing was conferred upon him by those who seemed to be something; and he writes that he resisted Peter to his face, saying that Peter had been compelled by no necessity to yield to the hypocrisy of the Jews.

If this seems rash to some—that he spoke against the apostles, although indirectly—the explanation is that he went to Jerusalem precisely to confer the Gospel with them, lest he should be running, or should have run, in vain. He continues:

### “But through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead”

Because the operation of the Son and the Father is one, and so that you may know that Christ is God, through whom Paul was made an apostle, observe carefully that he named the Son before the Father, in opposition to the accusations of the Arians.

But when he added, “who raised him from the dead,” Christ is believed to have been raised according to that aspect in which he could die, namely, according to the flesh alone.

[Col. 0845D]

### “And all the brothers who are with me, to the churches of Galatia”

In other Epistles, Sosthenes and Silvanus, and sometimes Timothy, are placed at the beginning. In this one alone, because the authority of many was necessary, the name of all the brothers is assumed. They themselves perhaps came from the circumcision and were not held in contempt by the Galatians.

The judgment and agreement of many concerning one matter contributes greatly to correcting a people. After commending his own authority, Paul adds these men in order to show that everyone was disturbed against the Galatians, although his authority was sufficient and could not be refuted. Nevertheless, to show the gravity of their action, by which they had abandoned their original faith, he identifies many who were inflamed along with him to condemn their error [Col. 0846A].

For a person can easily understand that he is in error if he sees himself reproved by many.

The phrase “to the churches of Galatia” must also be noted. Here alone Paul writes generally, not to the church of a single city, but to the churches of the entire province. And he calls them “churches” even though he later accuses them of having been corrupted by error.

From this we must recognize that “church” can be understood in two ways: the church that has neither stain nor wrinkle and is truly the body of Christ, and the church that gathers in Christ’s name without possessing complete and perfect virtues.

### “Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ”

The grace of God is that by which sins are given to us for pardon, so that we may be reconciled to God. Peace is that by which we are reconciled to God.

In the other Epistles he places the grace and peace of God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, through which, without the merit of works, our former sins have been granted pardon and peace has been bestowed after forgiveness. Here, however, he wisely conducts his case against those who had been forestalled by the Law and thought that they could be justified by works, so that they might know that they had been saved by grace and ought to persevere in what they had begun.

### “Who gave himself for our sins, that he might rescue us from the present evil age”

Neither did the Son give himself for our sins without the Father’s will, nor did the Father hand over the Son without the Son’s will. But this is the Son’s will: to fulfill the Father’s will, as he himself says in the Psalm: “I desired to do your will, my God” (Ps. XXXIX).

He plainly shows that the Law profits nothing when he says that Christ offered himself to suffer for us and to justify us, whom the Law held guilty; so that, rescued from the Law through faith in Christ, we might no longer be sinners but justified, being called by a second birth the sons of God.

“The present evil age” is to be understood as referring to the evil people who are in it, just as we call a house evil because of the evil inhabitants within it. The age itself, which runs through day and night, years and months, is not thereby called evil; rather, the things done in the age are evil. Thus it is said, “Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matt. VI).

The days of Jacob are also written as “few and evil” (Gen. XLVII), not because the period of time in which Jacob lived was evil, but because the experiences he endured exercised him through various trials.

### “According to the will of our God and Father, to whom be glory”

How much more, then, ought human beings not arrogantly to attribute to themselves whatever good they accomplish, when even the Son of God himself said in the Gospel that he did not seek his own glory or come to do his own will, but the will of the one who sent him (John VIII).

The Apostle now recalls the Father’s will and glory so that he too, following the example of the Lord by whom he was sent, might signify that he did not seek his own glory or do his own will in preaching the Gospel, as he says shortly afterward: “If I were pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.”

To make firm and fully authoritative what he says—that Christ liberated us—he added that Christ did this according to the Father’s will.

[Col. 0847A]

### “Forever and ever”

Infinite glory is owed for infinite benefits.

### “Amen”

He concludes his prologue in the Hebrew language with “Amen.” The Septuagint translated it as γένοιτο (*genoito*), “let it be”; Aquila translated it as πεπιστωμένος (*pepistōmenos*), “made certain” or “confirmed.” We, however, can interpret it as “truly” or “faithfully,” which is also how the Savior always uses it in the Gospel, confirming his words with “Amen.”

### “I am astonished that you are so quickly transferring yourselves from him who called you into the glory of Christ to another Gospel, which is not another”

After enumerating the benefits, the Apostle says that he is astonished that they could be drawn away from the freedom of the Gospel by words alone and transferred into slavery to the Law, from which they ought not to have been separated by any tortures.

For if the Gospel is something other than what the Lord gave either directly or through someone, it can no longer be called the Gospel. He carefully said, “You are transferring yourselves from him who called you into the glory of Christ,” a glory which they wanted to empty of meaning, as though Christ had come in vain if circumcision of the flesh still had to be maintained and works of this kind of Law had such power that people could be saved through them. He added:

### “Unless there are some who are troubling you and want to pervert the Gospel of Christ”

“They want,” he says, “to change, pervert, and disturb the Gospel of Christ; but they cannot, because its nature is such that it cannot be anything other than what is true.”

Just as they trouble these people, so they cannot actually pervert the Gospel of Christ, because it remains most firm. Nevertheless, they want to pervert it because they recall the attention of believers from spiritual things to carnal ones [Col. 0847C]. When the believers have turned toward those carnal things, the Gospel itself remains unperverted.

Therefore, after saying “those who are troubling you,” he did not say “and perverting you,” but “who want,” he says, “to pervert the Gospel of Christ.”

### “But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a Gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be accursed”

Truth must be loved for its own sake, not because of the human being or angel through whom it is announced. For whoever loves it because of its announcers can also love lies if those announcers should happen to put forward some of their own.

For this reason he pronounced a curse both upon himself—he was accused of doing one thing in Judaea and teaching another among the Gentiles—and upon an angel, whom he declared to be even greater than his predecessors, the apostles. Thus no one would think the authority of Peter and John great, since neither Paul himself, whom he had previously taught, nor an angel was permitted to preach otherwise than they had once learned [Col. 0847D].

In this way he named the angel specifically, while leaving the others unnamed. “If anyone,” he says, “should preach a Gospel to you,” using a general designation so that he would neither insult his predecessors nor fail to indicate their names indirectly.

No one should be surprised that the Apostle, who softened the harshness of conduct, was moved in this way. For the salvation of the Galatians, he expresses indignation against the enemies of Christian discipline.

This indignation shows that it is no slight sin, after receiving the faith, to turn back to the Law. For he asserts that the Gospel he had preached to them was so firm and true that he taught that even they themselves—that is, the apostles, if they should perhaps preach differently after being changed—were not to be heard [Col. 0848A].

Their reputation as apostles of Christ had, of course, spread everywhere. Or, if perhaps the devil should appear from heaven, pretending to be an angel of God so that he might easily be heard, anyone preaching contrary to this would be known to be an opponent and would be regarded as an abomination.

If, therefore, he commands that the apostles of Christ—whose splendid reputation was established through the performance of signs and wonders—and an angel from heaven, whom spiritual reasoning could commend, be accursed if they teach differently from what they had learned from the Apostle Paul, how much more should those be accursed whom no testimony can commend for the purpose of leading others astray?

He repeats the warning in order to confirm them in the first tradition. A law repeated makes the negligent more attentive.

[Col. 0848B]

### “As we have said before, and now I say again: If anyone should preach to you a Gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed”

Either he had said this previously on the present occasion, or, because he repeated what he had said, he wished to say “as we have said before.” In any case, the repetition most beneficially directs the mind toward holding firmly to the faith that is commended in this way.

It can also be understood as a hyperbolic statement: not that the Apostle or an angel could preach anything other than what they had once proclaimed, but that even if it could happen that the Apostle and the angels were changed, one still ought not to depart from what had once been received.

He does this not only against the Galatians but also against all heretics who attempt to alter the apostolic traditions.

### “For now am I persuading human beings, or God? Or am I seeking to please human beings? If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ”

No one persuades God, because everything is manifest to him; one persuades human beings. He persuades well who does not seek to please them personally, but seeks to make them embrace the truth that he recommends.

Whoever pleases human beings, not seeking his own glory from them but the glory of God, so that they may be saved, pleases not human beings but God. Or rather, when he pleases both God and human beings, he does not in fact please human beings as such.

For it is one thing to please human beings, and another to please both God and human beings (II Cor. V). We must not think that the Apostle teaches us by his example to disregard human judgments, since elsewhere he says: “Knowing therefore the fear of the Lord, we persuade human beings, but we are manifest to God.”

And he also says: “Be without offense to Jews and Gentiles and the Church of God, just as I please everyone in everything, not seeking what is useful to myself but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved” (I Cor. X).

For if it is possible for us to please both God and human beings at the same time, then we should please human beings as well. But if we cannot please human beings except by displeasing God, we ought to please God rather than human beings.

Moreover, he himself explains why he pleases everyone in everything: “Not seeking,” he says, “what is useful to myself, but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved.”

Whoever pleases human beings out of that charity which does not seek its own interests but those of others, so that they may be saved, certainly pleases God first, for whom the salvation of human beings is dear.

The word “now,” added here in particular, also has its force: it may mean that one ought to please or displease human beings according to the circumstances, so that someone who now does not please them because of the truth of the Gospel may once have pleased them for the salvation of many.

Paul had once pleased the Jews when, being zealous for the traditions of his fathers, he lived blamelessly according to the Law. He possessed such ardor and faith in the ceremonies of his ancestors that he shared in the killing of Stephen and went to Damascus to bind those who had departed from the Law (Acts VIII, IX).

But after he was transformed from a persecutor into a chosen vessel and began to preach the faith that he had once attacked, he likewise began to displease the Jews whom he had previously pleased.

This, then, is what he says: “Am I now seeking to please the Jews, whom, by displeasing them, I have pleased God? If I were pleasing them, I would not be a servant of Christ.”

For then I would be asserting the Law and destroying the grace of the Gospel [Col. 0849B]. But now I am not even led into the pretense of observing the Law, because I cannot please both God and the Jews at the same time; whoever pleases them displeases God.

### “For I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel that was preached by me: it is not according to man. For I neither received it from a man nor learned it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ”

Now he opens the beginning of the Epistle. He wishes to make clear the very point at issue: he had not learned from a human being the things he taught, so that there might be doubt concerning his teaching; nor was his preaching adapted according to human judgment in such a way that it might seem unworthy of divine authority.

Rather, he says that he learned it from the Son of God through revelation, when Christ, after the resurrection, was already in heaven, as Paul mentioned above. What he learned corresponded to the will and majesty of the one from whom he testifies that he learned it.

The Gospel that is according to man is a lie: “Every man is a liar” (Ps. CXVI; Rom. III). For whatever truth is found in a human being comes not from the human being but from God through the human being.

Therefore, what is according to man ought not even to be called the Gospel. Such was the teaching asserted by those who were drawing into slavery from freedom those whom God was calling from slavery into freedom.

There is a difference between receiving and learning. The person who receives the Gospel is one to whom it is first announced and who is brought to its faith, so that he may believe that what is written is true. The person who learns is one who comes to know, once they have been explained and expounded, the things that are represented in it through riddles and parables—not through revelation by a human being, but through Christ [Col. 0849D].

As we said at the beginning, when we were expounding the words “Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through a man,” the present passage can also be understood as an indirect reference to Peter and Paul’s other predecessors: Paul is moved by no one’s authority in place of the Law, since Christ alone is his teacher of the Gospel.

By “that revelation” he means the occasion when, as he was going to Damascus, he heard the voice of Christ on the road: “Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX). Having been blinded in his eyes, he saw the true light of the world.

### “For you have heard of my former way of life in Judaism: how beyond measure I persecuted the Church of God and ravaged it, and how I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries in my own nation, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers”

He briefly recalls his former purpose, by which, according to the flesh, he flourished while opposing the Church; but he indicates that he abandoned it in order to become a servant of Christ. He shows that he had been more devoted than those others in defending the Law.

Yet he did not do this for human approval, but because he thought it useful before God. Through ignorance, while pleasing human beings, he thought that he was serving God, possessing a free conscience. For he did not know that the time for asserting the Law had already passed.

Therefore, following the teaching of the Jewish fathers, who were established either in error or in malice, he acted with every effort and fervor of mind so that he might appear superior in zeal for the Law to his other contemporaries. He was so insane against the discipline of Christ [Col. 0850B] that he spared no one who had obtained the covenant of faith.

But once God’s revelation taught him that this labor was empty and, indeed, opposed to the truth, he abandoned it and devoted himself to the grace of faith, so that his progress might be with God.

If this man, therefore, who was an Israelite and who possessed the dignity of a teacher among the Jews, educated by Gamaliel, a most prudent man, abandoned the Law even though he had held a place among the best people in life, how much more ought those who were outside the Law not to subject themselves to it?

And if he rejoices that he has come out from under the yoke of slavery, why have these people bound their freedom with the chains of the Law?

This account is highly beneficial to the Galatians: it shows how Paul, once a ravager of the Church and an ardent defender of Judaism, was suddenly converted to faith in Christ [Col. 0850C]. This occurred at the very time when the crucified Christ was first being proclaimed in the world, when the new doctrine was being driven out to the ends of the earth by both Gentiles and Jews.

For they could say: “If the man who was instructed in the disciplines of the Pharisees from his earliest age, who surpassed all his contemporaries in Jewish tradition, now defends the Church that he once persecuted with the greatest force, and prefers to embrace the grace and novelty of Christ amid the hatred of everyone rather than the beauty of the Law amid the praise of many, what ought we to do, who have begun to be Christians from paganism?”

He aptly added, “Beyond measure I persecuted the Church of God,” so that this too might give rise to wonder: it was not just anyone among those who lightly persecuted the Church, but the one who surpassed the others in persecution, who was converted to the faith [Col. 0850D].

And wisely, while narrating one matter, he inserts another: he had served not so much the Law of God as the traditions of his fathers—that is, the traditions of the Pharisees, who teach “doctrines that are the commandments of men” and reject the Law of God in order to establish their own traditions.

What an elegant observation, and what weight the words possess.

“You have heard,” he says, “of my former way of life in Judaism.”

He says “way of life,” not “through grace,” to show that he could not have separated himself from that way by human counsel, but only through divine revelation and mercy.

“Formerly,” not “now.”

“In Judaism,” not “in the Law of God.”

“Because beyond measure I persecuted the Church of God and ravaged it.”

I did not persecute it as the others did, but beyond measure [Col. 0851A]. Nor was the persecution, however violent, sufficient; like some marauder and plunderer, I ravaged the Church.

He does not say “the Church of Christ,” as he then believed—that is, the Church he despised and persecuted—but, as he now believes, “the Church of God.” Either he thereby signifies that Christ is God, or that the Church belongs to the same God who was formerly the teacher of the Law.

“And I advanced,” he says, “in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries in my own nation, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers.”

Again, he calls his advancement an advancement not in the Law of God but in Judaism. Nor does he say “beyond all,” but “beyond many”; nor “beyond the old,” but “beyond my contemporaries,” so that he might both report his zeal for the Law and avoid boasting.

By mentioning the traditions of his fathers rather than the commandments of the Lord, he showed that he was a Pharisee from Pharisees and that he possessed zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.

Even today, those who understand the Scriptures according to the Jewish sense persecute the Church of Christ and ravage it—not through zeal for God’s Law, but corrupted by human traditions.

### “But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the Gentiles”

In a certain sense, whoever is separated from the blind custom of carnal parents is set apart from his mother’s womb.

Or it may also mean that God set him apart from the womb in his foreknowledge, when he willed and brought about what he knew would happen.

Nor is it inappropriate to understand “his mother’s womb” as the Synagogue [Col. 0851C].

### “Immediately I did not yield to flesh and blood”

A person yields to flesh and blood whenever he assents to his carnal relatives and blood relations when they offer carnal counsel.

### “Nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me”

If, by saying, “Immediately I did not yield to flesh and blood,” he had spoken of the apostles, why was it necessary for him to repeat the same point by saying, “Nor did I go up to Jerusalem to the apostles who were my predecessors,” in order to learn something from them?

The sense that we explained above, therefore, must be retained.

But I went away to Arabia and returned again to Damascus. If he went from Damascus to Arabia in order to teach what had been revealed to him, the order of the narrative does not seem to agree with Luke’s account in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter IX). Luke reports that, after Paul had accepted the faith of Christ and had preached the Gospel boldly in Damascus for many days, a plot was made against him; that he was lowered by night through the wall in a basket; and that he came to Jerusalem, attempting to join himself to the disciples. When they avoided him and were afraid to approach him, Barnabas brought him to the apostles. There he related how he had seen the Lord on the road and had acted boldly in Damascus in the name of Jesus. “He was with them,” Luke says, “going in and coming out in Jerusalem, and acting boldly in the name of the Lord. He also spoke and disputed with the Greeks. But they were seeking to kill him. When the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him away to Tarsus.”

Here, however, Paul says that he first went to Arabia and returned again to Damascus; that after three years he came to Jerusalem, saw Peter, and remained with him fifteen days; and that, apart from James, the Lord’s brother, he saw no other apostle. In order that these statements might be believed as true—for in his absence they could have seemed doubtful—he confirms them under oath, saying: “As for what I am writing to you, behold, before God, I am not lying.”

We may therefore suppose that, according to Luke’s account, Paul did indeed go to Jerusalem, not as though he were going to the apostles who had preceded him in order to learn something from them, but to escape the assault of the persecution that had been stirred up against him in Damascus on account of Christ’s Gospel. He came to Jerusalem as he might have come to any other city. From there, because of the plots against him, he immediately withdrew and went to Arabia or Damascus. Then, after three years, he returned to Jerusalem to see Peter.

Or certainly, immediately after he had been baptized and strengthened by receiving food, he was with the disciples who were in Damascus for several days (Acts IX). While all were astonished, he preached at once in the synagogues of the Jews that Jesus was the Son of God. He then went to Arabia, returned from Arabia to Damascus, and remained there for three years. Scripture attests that those were many days, saying: “When many days had passed, the Jews took counsel to kill him. Their plot became known to Saul, and they guarded the gates day and night in order to kill him. Therefore his disciples took him by night and lowered him through the wall in a basket. When he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join himself to the disciples.”

Luke omitted Arabia because perhaps Paul had accomplished nothing there that was worthy of apostolic mention, and instead gave in his concise narrative those events that seemed worthy of Christ’s Gospel. Nor should this be attributed to the apostle’s negligence, as though he had gone to Arabia in vain; rather, some dispensation and command of God required him to do so. For later in the Acts of the Apostles we read that Paul, together with Silas, was forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.

Alternatively: “But I went away to Arabia and returned again to Damascus.” What benefit does this account offer me if I read that Paul went immediately to Arabia after Christ’s revelation and returned from Arabia to Damascus, yet do not know what he did there or what benefit his going and returning produced? In this same Epistle the Apostle himself provides an occasion for a higher understanding when he discusses Abraham, Sarah, and Hagar. “These things,” he says, “are spoken allegorically. For these are the two covenants: one indeed from Mount Sinai, generating slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, joined to the Jerusalem that now is” (Gal. IV).

He teaches that the Old Testament—that is, the son of the slave woman—was established in Arabia, which is interpreted as “humble” and “situated in the west.” Therefore, as soon as Paul believed, and turned toward the Law and the Prophets and toward the sacramental realities of the Old Testament, which had already been placed in the west, he sought Christ in them, the one whom he had been commanded to preach among the nations. Having found him, he did not remain there any longer, but returned to Damascus—that is, to the blood and passion of Christ. From there, strengthened by prophetic reading, he proceeded to Jerusalem, the place of vision and peace—not so much to learn anything from the apostles as to compare with them the Gospel that he had preached.

Then, after three years, I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter. If Paul evangelized in Arabia and afterward saw Peter, he did not do so in order to learn the Gospel through Peter, since he had already been teaching for three years, but in order to increase brotherly affection through personal acquaintance. If this does not seem convincing to someone, let him connect all these statements with the preceding interpretation: the apostles contributed nothing to him; he was commanded to go to Jerusalem for the purpose of seeing the apostle. He would then understand that Paul did not go there out of a desire to learn, since he too had the same source of preaching, but in order to show honor to the earlier apostle.

And I remained with him fifteen days. He specifies fifteen days in order to show that the period was not long enough for him to have learned anything from Peter, and thus to relate everything to the meaning with which he began: that he had not been taught by a human being, but by God.

But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord’s brother. He saw James at Jerusalem because James had been appointed bishop there by the apostles. We should understand “the Lord’s brother” to mean his cousin. Thus he denies that he saw any apostle besides these, so that no hidden contradiction might arise: “Even if you were not taught by Peter, you had other apostles as teachers.” He did not fail to see them out of contempt for them, but because they had been scattered throughout the whole world to preach the Gospel.

As for what I write to you, behold, before God, I am not lying. When he is about to speak of matters relevant to his commendation, he calls God as witness that what he is going to say is true, lest it seem fabricated, since it would not suit his character to invent anything. Yet by commending himself he seeks their advancement. This commendation benefits them, so that they may know that what he says is entirely true: “Behold, before God, I am not lying.”

He certainly swears; and what is holier than this oath? Yet this oath does not violate the Lord’s command, in which he says: “Let your speech be, Yes, yes; No, no. Whatever is more than this is from evil” (Matt. V). Therefore, as far as it depends on him, the Apostle does not swear. He does not desire an oath out of eagerness or delight in swearing—something that comes from evil—but the weakness and unbelief of those who are not otherwise moved to faith require it. This may be understood not only of what he is now writing to the Galatians, but also generally of all his Epistles: what he writes is not false, and his heart and words do not differ.

Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. After his vision at Jerusalem, he came to Syria, which is interpreted for us as “lofty” and “exalted,” and from there passed into Cilicia, which he desired to take up in the faith of Christ, evangelizing to it the call to repentance. Cilicia, indeed, is interpreted as “assumption” or “lamentable calling.”

But I was unknown by face to the churches of Judaea that are in Christ. We must observe that it was not only at Jerusalem that Jews believed in Christ, nor were they so few that they were absorbed into the churches of the nations. Rather, they were numerous enough for churches to be formed from them.

They had only heard that the one who once persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once attempted to destroy, and they glorified God in me. He says this because, while he defended Judaism against the faith, like those by whom the Galatians had been overthrown, he was chosen by God and taught to abandon Judaism and preach the new law. Thus the Jewish believers whom he had formerly persecuted rejoiced in him and gave thanks to God, who had made a defender out of a persecutor.

In this way the Galatians could understand that they had been deceived when, under Christ’s name, they professed themselves Jews, circumcising the flesh of their foreskin, although the law fulfilled something different in Christ from what Judaism did. There circumcision is of the flesh; here, of the heart. There one serves under the elements, through new moons and the Sabbath; here, one serves God alone in the spirit, because one believes with the heart. There servile condition is the cause of sin; here, freedom comes through the forgiveness of sins. There is therefore a great difference between them.

## Chapter II

Then, after fourteen years, I again went up to Jerusalem, taking Barnabas with me, and Titus. Thus, after fourteen years, he went up to Jerusalem. Whereas previously he had gone only to see Peter and had remained with him fifteen days, he now says that he went in order to confer the Gospel with the apostles, taking with him Barnabas, who was circumcised, and Titus, who was from the nations and had his foreskin, so that “in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word might stand” (Deut. XVII).

I went up according to revelation. He says this so that they would not wonder why he went up even then, after having remained away for so long. If he went up by revelation, then it was beneficial for him to go up at that time, since his reputation had been growing among all the Jews, although he was not seen in person. With his customary steadfastness he was traveling about establishing and strengthening the churches among the nations. But because of the law, the Jews formed a bad opinion of him, as though he disagreed with the preaching of the other apostles. This became a stumbling block to many, so that even the nations might be disturbed, fearing that he was leading them into something different from what the apostles who had been with the Lord had handed down.

For this very reason the Galatians were overthrown by Jews who said that Paul taught something different from Peter. Therefore, warned by a revelation from the Lord, he went up to Jerusalem with witnesses to his preaching, namely Barnabas and Titus—one from the Jews and the other from the nations. If they had any scandal or offense concerning him, it could be removed by the testimony of these men. He disclosed the meaning of his preaching to them, but privately conferred with the apostles so that they might know that he did not disagree with the rule of the Gospel—that is, so that they would not think that he was running or had run in vain, as some of the Jewish believers supposed.

He could not have learned anything from them, since he had been instructed by God. But for the sake of concord and the peace of God, it became known that he had gone up so that the brothers or fellow apostles might be relieved of their doubt or suspicion, and so that the nations might benefit by learning that his Gospel agreed with that of the apostles.

And I conferred with them the Gospel that I preach among the nations. To confer is one thing; to learn is another. Among those who confer, there is equality; between a teacher and a learner, the learner is inferior. At the beginning of his faith, Paul saw the apostles only in passing. After seventeen years, as he himself says, he speaks fully with them and humbles himself. He asks whether he might be running or might have run in vain, for two reasons: first, to display Paul’s humility, since he, a teacher throughout the whole world of the nations, went to the apostles who had preceded him; and second, so that the Galatians might learn that the churches in Judaea, too, had not rejected his Gospel.

At the same time he teaches that, for the sake of Christ’s faith and the freedom of the Gospel, he dared to bring Titus, an uncircumcised man, to those very people who had falsely learned many things about him—that he violated the law, destroyed Moses, and entirely abolished circumcision. Even amid such a great multitude of Jews and among his enemies, who, as though out of zeal for the law, desired to drink his blood, neither he nor Titus was overcome by fear or compelled to yield to necessity. Such necessity might have found an excuse either because of the place, or the authority of the elders, or the number of the churches composed of Jews who believed in Christ, or because of the time, lest they should endure such hostility all at once.

The whole point of what he says is that he teaches that, among those whom he had formerly persecuted, he could never have become glorious as a former persecutor unless his preaching had also been approved by the judgment of those who had previously misunderstood him. He secretly returns to his purpose by confirming that he spent so short a time in Judaea that he was unknown even by face to the believers. From this he shows that Peter, James, and John were not his teachers, but Christ, who had revealed the Gospel to him.

It should also be noted that above he says that he persecuted the Church, whereas here he says that he persecuted the faith: there, persons; here, a matter. Thus he could more appropriately say, “There he preaches the faith that he once attempted to destroy.” The same wording could not have been used in the same way of the Church.

But privately, before those who were regarded as leaders, lest I should be running or should have run in vain. He explained the Gospel privately to those who held prominence in the Church, after having already explained it publicly to everyone. He did not do this because he had said anything false and wished to tell the truth privately to the more important men, but because he had omitted certain matters that the little ones could not yet bear. Of such people he says that he gave the Corinthians milk, not solid food (1 Cor. III). It is never permissible to speak falsely.

What he says—“I conferred with them the Gospel that I preach among the nations, but privately with those who were regarded as leaders, lest I should be running or should have run in vain”—may also be understood in this way: he privately discussed with the apostles the evangelical freedom of the nations and the abolition of the old law, because of the multitude of Jewish believers who could not yet hear that Christ was the fulfillment and end of the law. Even in Paul’s absence, they had boasted at Jerusalem that he was running or had run in vain if he thought that the old law should not be followed.

Paul did not fear that he had preached a false Gospel among the nations for seventeen years. Rather, he wished to show his predecessors that he was not running or had run in vain, as those who were ignorant of the matter supposed.

But not even Titus, who was with me, although he was from the nations, was compelled to be circumcised, because of the false brothers who had infiltrated, who had slipped in to spy out our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus, in order to reduce us to slavery. To them we yielded in submission for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you.

If Titus, although he was from the nations, could not be compelled by any fear to be circumcised at Jerusalem, the capital city of the Jews, where such indignation at Paul’s blasphemy against Moses was burning that he was later almost killed by the Jews, when, after being rescued by the tribune, he was sent in chains to Rome to Caesar, what does it mean that you should be circumcised, when Titus was not compelled to be circumcised by the apostles who were regarded as important, but was accepted while uncircumcised?

Throughout the whole course of his argument Paul is teaching that he was a Hebrew of Hebrews, formerly observing every work of the law, circumcised on the eighth day, and a Pharisee according to the law; nevertheless, because of Christ’s grace, he despised everything. When he went to Jerusalem and the false brothers who had believed from circumcision wanted to compel him to circumcise Titus, neither Titus nor Paul yielded to violence, so that they might preserve the truth of the Gospel.

If he says that he was overcome by necessity and circumcised Titus, how does he recall the Galatians from circumcision, when he could not even excuse Titus, who had been with him from the nations, from being circumcised at Jerusalem? Therefore, either the Greek manuscripts should be read as follows: “To whom we did not yield even for an hour in submission,” so that the following words may be understood coherently—“so that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you”—or, if someone prefers the reading found in a Latin copy, we should understand the passage according to the preceding interpretation: that the yielding for an hour concerned not circumcising Titus, but going to Jerusalem.

That is, Paul and Barnabas yielded to submission by going to Jerusalem because a disturbance concerning the law had arisen at Antioch, so that their opinion might be confirmed by the apostles’ letter and the truth of the Gospel might remain with the Galatians. That truth was not in the letter but in the Spirit; not in a carnal sense but in spiritual understanding; not in manifest Judaism but in what is hidden.

Some say that Paul went up to Jerusalem after fourteen years at the time when, according to the Acts of the Apostles, disagreement arose at Antioch over questions concerning the observance or abandonment of the law, and it was decided to go to Jerusalem and await the judgment of the elders. Paul and Barnabas themselves were sent on that occasion. They say that this is what is read in the Latin manuscripts: “To whom we yielded for an hour in submission, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you.”

That is, Paul and Barnabas allowed themselves to be sent to Jerusalem concerning a matter that was manifest, as though it were doubtful, so that the grace of the Gospel might be confirmed by the judgment of the elders and approved by the believers. Thus no further doubt would remain concerning the abandonment of circumcision, since the apostles’ letter commanded that the yoke of the law be removed from those among the nations who had believed in Christ.

It should be known, however, that the conjunction “but,” which occurs here in the phrase “because of the false brothers who had infiltrated,” is superfluous. Even if it is read, it has nothing corresponding to it and brings the sentence to a close. The order and meaning of the reading should instead be this:

“But not even Titus, who was with me, although he was from the nations, was compelled to be circumcised.” Then the reason why he was unwillingly being urged toward circumcision is immediately added: “because of the false brothers who had infiltrated, who had slipped in to spy out our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus, in order to reduce us to slavery.”

That is, those who had infiltrated in order to spy out our freedom watched closely and vehemently desired that Titus be circumcised, so that they might then proclaim circumcision as necessary for salvation, even with Paul’s testimony and consent, and thus reduce them to slavery—that is, call them back under the burdens of the law.

Paul says that he did not yield to their submission even for an hour, that is, not even for a time, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain among the nations. Although they wished, by threats, intimidation, and numbers, to transfer us from the freedom of Christ into slavery to the law, we did not yield to them even temporarily by circumcising Titus, especially since some necessity connected with ecclesiastical peace might have excused us. We did all this so that no occasion would be given you to depart from the grace of the Gospel.

If, then, at Jerusalem, amid so many Jews, with false brothers pressing from every side and with those who were elders restraining us to some extent, we could not be compelled by force or reason to observe circumcision, which we knew had come to an end, how will you who are from the nations, you who are in Galatia, you against whom no force can be brought, voluntarily depart from grace and pass back into the antiquity of the law, which has already been abolished?

But from those who were regarded as important—whatever they once were—it makes no difference to me. God does not accept a person’s status. “Even if,” he says, “the Lord had Peter and John as apostles with him, and they saw him transfigured on the mountain, and the foundation of the Church was placed upon them, it makes no difference to me, because I am not speaking against those who followed the Lord at that time, but against those who now propose the law in place of grace.”

“I do not disparage my predecessors, nor do I accuse the elders in any respect. But I say this because God does not accept a person’s status: that is, without partiality he called them to salvation, not counting their offenses against them.”

Therefore, while those who had first become apostles were absent, Paul was perfected by the Lord, so that when he conferred with them there was nothing they could add to his perfection. Rather, they saw that the same Lord Jesus Christ, who saves without partiality, had given Paul the ministry among the nations, just as he had given Peter the ministry among the Jews.

They were not found to disagree with him in any respect, as though, when he said that he had received the perfect Gospel, they denied it and wished to add something to him as to an imperfect man. On the contrary, they were approving witnesses to his perfection and censurers of imperfection. They gave him and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship—that is, they consented to fellowship—and obeyed the Lord’s will, agreeing that Paul and Barnabas should go to the nations, while they themselves went to the circumcision, which seems contrary to the foreskin, that is, to the nations.

But from those who were regarded as important I received nothing. He says that he obtained nothing from the apostles, but from God. The one who gives the unlearned understanding of Christian teaching, he says, also graciously gave me, when I was learned in the law, an understanding of this kind of reasoning. How, then, could he have learned from them, when Christ’s grace found him learned and made him more learned?

Above he conferred with them and reported to them much of what he had accomplished among the nations. They contributed nothing to him; they merely approved what he said, gave the right hands of fellowship, and confirmed that his Gospel and theirs were one.

On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the Gospel of the foreskin, just as Peter had been entrusted with that of the circumcision. The whole meaning of what he says is that one and the same Gospel was entrusted to me for the foreskin and to Peter for the circumcision. He sent me to the nations and placed him in Judaea.

Those who were already adults among the nations could not easily be subjected to the pain of circumcision that lay before them, abstain from the foods to which they had always been accustomed, and refrain from foods that God had created for use. Nor could those who had believed from the Jews, who had been circumcised and who, through custom as though through a second nature, thought they possessed more than the other nations, easily despise the things in which they gloried.

Therefore, by God’s providence, one of the apostles was given to the circumcised, appearing to accept the shadows of the law, while another was established among the uncircumcised, so that he would not regard the grace of the Gospel as slavery but as free faith. Thus, under some pretext, no impediment to faith would arise, and because of circumcision or the foreskin people would not fail to believe in Christ.

For he who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision worked also through me among the nations. That is, I am not inferior to him, because both of us were ordained by one person to one ministry.

From this we perceive why Peter, James, and John gave the right hands of fellowship to Paul and Barnabas: so that the Gospel of Christ would not be thought different because of differing observances, but so that there might be one communion of the circumcised and of those who have the foreskin. Thus the nations would not be deterred from the faith of Christ and from believing by the burden and difficulty of the law.

A hidden question arises here. What, then? If Peter found people from the nations, did he not bring them to the faith? Or if Paul found some from the circumcision, did he not invite them to Christ’s baptism? The answer is this: each was given a principal commission concerning Jews and nations, so that those who defended the law would have someone to follow, while those who preferred the grace of the law would not lack a teacher and guide. But they shared the common purpose of gathering a Church for Christ from all nations.

For we read that the Gentile Cornelius was baptized by the holy Peter, and that Paul very frequently preached Christ in the synagogues of the Jews. Nevertheless, it is recognized that Peter was given full authority in preaching to Judaism, while Paul possessed perfect authority in preaching to the nations. Hence he also calls himself the teacher of the nations in faith and truth.

Each received a dispensation according to his strength. It was more difficult to draw and persuade those who were far from God to the faith than those who were near. He names Peter alone and compares himself with him because Peter received the primacy for founding the Church, while Paul too was chosen in a similar way to hold the primacy in founding the churches of the nations.

And when they recognized the grace that had been given to me, Peter, James, and John, who were regarded as pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship, so that we should go to the nations and they to the circumcision.

He says that the gift he had received from God was approved by the apostles who were more distinguished than the others. He calls them pillars for the sake of their firmness; they had always been with the Lord in secret places and were worthy to behold his glory on the mountain. Thus he says that these men approved the gift he had received from God, so that he might be worthy to hold the primacy in preaching to the nations, just as Peter held it in preaching to the circumcision.

Just as he gives Peter distinguished men among the apostles as companions, so he joins Barnabas to himself, who was associated with him by divine judgment. Yet he first claims for himself alone the grace granted by God, just as it was granted to Peter alone among the apostles. Thus the apostles of the circumcision extended the right hands of fellowship to the apostles of the nations, demonstrating concord and partnership. Both, knowing that they had received from the Lord the spirit of perfection for the administration of the Gospel, showed that they had no need of one another in any respect.

The apostles are therefore the pillars of the Church (Matt. XXVII), especially Peter, James, and John. Two of these were worthy to ascend the mountain with the Lord. One of them, in the Apocalypse, introduced the Savior speaking: “The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God” (Rev. III). He teaches that all believers who conquer the adversary can become pillars of the Church.

Writing to Timothy, Paul says: “So that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Tim. III). From these and other passages we are taught that Scripture calls the apostles and all believers pillars, and also calls the Church itself a pillar. It makes no difference whether this is said of the body or of its members, since the body is divided into members and the members belong to the body.

Therefore Peter, James, and John, who were regarded as pillars, gave Paul and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship. But they did not give the right hands of fellowship to Titus, who was with them. He had not yet reached the measure at which the commerce of Christ could be entrusted to him on equal terms with his elders, nor did he hold the same place in that enterprise that Barnabas and Paul held.

For this reason Paul makes known what took place between himself and the apostles, so that the Galatians may know that what they had received from him was true and approved.

So that we should go to the nations and they to the circumcision, provided only that we should remember the poor, which was the very thing I was eager to do. The holy poor, whose care was especially entrusted by the apostles to Paul and Barnabas, were those Jewish believers who brought the prices of their possessions to the apostles’ feet to be distributed to the needy. They also included those who, by their fellow tribesmen, relatives, and parents, were regarded with abhorrence and as accursed because they had deserted the law and believed in a crucified man.

The letters of Paul bear witness to how much labor the holy Apostle expended in ministering to them. He wrote to the Corinthians, the Thessalonians, and all the churches of the nations so that they might prepare this gift, either personally or through others whom they approved, and convey it to Jerusalem. Hence he now says confidently: “I was eager to do this very thing.”

All the apostles shared responsibility for the holy poor who were in Judaea, who had placed the prices of their possessions, after selling them, at the apostles’ feet. If Paul and Barnabas were sent to the nations so that the churches of the nations, which had not done this, might minister to them, sharing in the prayers of those who had done it—as he says to the Romans: “But now I am going to Jerusalem to minister to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have decided to make some contribution for the poor saints who are in Jerusalem. They have decided to do so, and they are their debtors. For if the nations have shared in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in material things” (Rom. XV).

But when Peter came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he was blameworthy. For before certain men came from James, he ate with the nations. But when they came, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were from the circumcision. The other Jews also joined in his pretense, so that even Barnabas was led into that pretense.

When Peter came to Antioch, Paul rebuked him—not because he observed the customs of the Jews, in which he had been born and brought up, although he did not observe them among the nations—but because he wished to impose them upon the nations after seeing that certain men had come from James, that is, from Judaea. James was in charge of the church at Jerusalem.

Therefore, fearing those who still thought that salvation was established in those observances, Peter separated himself from the nations, and the other Jews joined in his pretense, imposing those burdens of slavery upon the nations. Paul therefore opposed him to his face by the same device through which Peter was pretending. He spoke before everyone, not so much to rebuke Peter as to correct those for whose sake Peter had pretended.

This is sufficiently clear from the words of his rebuke. He does not say: “If you, though you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the nations to Judaize?” Rather, by an unanswerable argument he binds Peter—and through Peter those who were fighting among themselves.

“If you, Peter,” he says, “who are a Jew by nature, circumcised from childhood and observing all the precepts of the law, now know, because of Christ’s grace, that these things have no usefulness in themselves but are examples and images of future realities, and if you eat with those who are from the nations, living freely and without distinction rather than superstitiously as before, how can you now compel those from the nations who have believed to Judaize by withdrawing from them and separating yourself from them as though they were contaminated?”

He says all this not so much to rebuke Peter, as I have already said, but to correct those for whose sake Peter had pretended. If those from whom you withdraw are unclean, he says, and you withdraw because they do not have circumcision, then you compel them to be circumcised and become Jews, although you yourself, born a Jew, have lived as a Gentile.

He subtly reveals the reason why he argued against Peter: namely, that by his pretense Peter was compelling the nations to Judaize, since they wished to imitate him. Paul spoke to him before everyone because necessity required it, so that all might be healed by Peter’s rebuke. It was not useful to correct in private an error that was openly causing harm.

Moreover, Peter’s weakness and love—he to whom the Lord had said three times, “Do you love me? Feed my sheep”—gladly endured such a rebuke from a later shepherd for the salvation of the flock.

Someone may ask: Why did Paul oppose Peter to his face and declare him blameworthy, when Paul himself became a Jew to the Jews? He did so out of compassion, not deception. A person becomes like the one he wishes to help when he comes to the other’s aid with as much mercy as he would wish to receive if he himself were in the same misery. Thus he becomes like that person, not because he deceives him, but because he considers himself as though he were in the other’s condition.

Hence the Apostle says: “Brothers, if someone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted.”

If, because he said, “I became to the Jews as a Jew, and to those under the law as though I were under the law,” he is therefore thought to have deceitfully adopted the sacraments of the old law when he shaved his head at Cenchreae, offered a sacrifice after becoming bald at Jerusalem, circumcised Timothy, and practiced going barefoot—things that plainly belong to Jewish ceremonies—then, in the same way, he ought to have deceitfully adopted the idolatry of the nations, since he said that he became as one without the law to those who were without the law, in order to win them. Yet he certainly did not do this. He did not sacrifice to idols anywhere or worship those images; rather, as a martyr of Christ, he freely showed that they were to be detested and avoided.

As for what the Apostle Paul himself did—retaining and performing certain lawful observances according to Jewish custom, so that he might show himself not to be an enemy of the law and the prophets—far be it from us to believe that he did this deceitfully.

The following statement of his is sufficient on this matter: it had been established that Jews who at that time believed in Christ were not to be prohibited from their ancestral traditions, nor were Gentiles, when they became Christians, to be compelled to adopt them. Thus the rites that were clearly divinely commanded were not to be avoided as sacrilegious; yet, once the New Testament had been revealed, they were not to be regarded as so necessary that those who turned to God could not be saved without them. There were, however, people who thought and preached this, even though they had already accepted the Gospel of Christ; Peter and Barnabas had also pretended to agree with them. Therefore they compelled the Gentiles to Judaize. For to compel them meant to preach those practices as necessary, as though, even after receiving the Gospel, no one could be saved in Christ without them. This was the error of certain people; this was what Peter’s fear pretended; this was what Paul’s freedom rebuked. The weakness of the Galatians compelled him to relate that he had not spared Peter himself, because Peter was not openly defending the truth of the Gospel, just as, for the Corinthians’ advancement, he disclosed the revelation that he had concealed for fourteen years. He does all this in order to show that he had never been a supporter of circumcision, as the false apostles were boasting about him.

There are, however, some who understand not Peter, the chief of the apostles, but another man named Peter, who was reproved by Paul. If they had read the words of the Apostle Paul more carefully, they would not say this. For when Paul was about to say that, when Peter came to Antioch, he opposed him to his face, he prefaced the beginning of his account in order to show which Peter he meant, saying: “The Gospel of the uncircumcision was entrusted to me, just as the Gospel of the circumcision was entrusted to Peter. For he who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the Gentiles.” It is therefore clear which Peter Paul is discussing: the one whom he calls an apostle and whom he states to have been entrusted with the Gospel of the circumcision.

There were also some who said that the Second Epistle of Peter, in which Paul’s Epistles are praised, was not written by him. But if they had weighed the words of that same Epistle, they could have formed a quite different judgment. For it says there: “A voice came to him from the magnificent glory: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” And it continues: “And we ourselves heard this voice when we were with him on the holy mountain” (2 Peter 1).

[Col. 0862D]

Let them therefore read the Gospel, and they will immediately recognize that, when this voice came from heaven, the Apostle Peter stood with the Lord on the mountain. He, then, wrote this Epistle—the man who heard that voice on the mountain with the Lord.

“We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from the Gentiles.” The Jews, with an already ancient arrogance, gave the name “sinners” to the Gentiles, as though they themselves were righteous, seeing the speck in another’s eye but not the beam in their own. Speaking according to their custom, the Apostle says: “We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from the Gentiles”—that is, we are those whom they call sinners, although they themselves also are sinners. “We, therefore,” he says, “who are Jews by nature, although we were Gentiles”—not because they call them sinners, but because we too are sinners—“believed in Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified by the faith of Christ.” They would not have sought justification unless they had been sinners.

“Knowing that a person is not justified by works of the law, but through faith in Jesus Christ, we too believed in Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by works of the law.” We believe in Christ so that faith, which we have in Christ, might grant us what the law had not given us. But if, having departed from the law in which we could not be saved, we have passed over to faith, in which circumcision of the flesh is not sought but pure devotion of the heart, and if now, by withdrawing from the Gentiles, we act as though everyone who is not circumcised is unclean, then the faith in Christ in which we think we were formerly saved is a minister of sin rather than of righteousness—a faith that removes circumcision, without which a person is unclean. But far be it that I should reclaim what I once destroyed and know has not benefited me. Once having departed from the law, I have died to the law, so that I might live to Christ. I have been fastened to his cross and, reborn as a new person, have endured through faith rather than through the flesh; and having gone out of the world with Christ, I hold fast to what I once undertook. Christ did not die for me in vain; I believed in him to no purpose if I could have been saved without his faith under the old law.

For this reason “no flesh will be justified by works of the law.” Once, not every flesh was justified by the law, but only those people who were in the province of Palestine. Now every flesh is justified by faith in Jesus Christ, while his Churches are founded throughout the whole world.

[Col. 0863C]

The works of the law may also, without impropriety, be understood as circumcision, the Sabbath, feast days, baptisms, seasonal festivals, unleavened bread, and the other practices that were given as sacraments—not for righteousness, but for occupying the people and subduing their hardness.

“But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves have also been found to be sinners”—they would not have sought justification unless they had been sinners. Or did they sin because they wished to be justified in Christ? For if they were already righteous, then by seeking something else they certainly sinned. “But so it is,” he says; “therefore Christ is a minister of sin.” They cannot say this, since even those who wished to deliver the Gospel only to circumcised Gentiles had believed in Christ. Therefore, when he says, “Far be it,” he does not say it alone, but together with them.

He destroyed the pride that gloried in the works of the law—a pride that both ought and could be destroyed, lest the grace of faith appear unnecessary if people were believed to be justified by the works of the law even without it. Therefore he is a transgressor if he builds those things again, saying that the works of the law justify even without grace, so that Christ is found to be a minister of sin.

“Is Christ therefore a minister of sin? Far be it.” For if he does not save the Gentiles by faith alone, neither does he save us, since no one will be justified by works of the law. Then we too are still sinners, and Christ is a minister of sin, as though he were unable to forgive sins—just like the law given through Moses, which only displayed sins and did not remove them.

“For if I build again the things that I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor.” What then? Because you formerly attacked the faith of Christ, which you now build up, do you make yourself a transgressor? But I did not destroy that faith, because it cannot be destroyed. Rather, he had truly destroyed, and steadfastly continued to destroy, the pride in question, because it could be destroyed. Therefore the transgressor is not the person who attempted to destroy what was true and, after recognizing that it was true and could not be destroyed, held fast to it so that he might be built up in it. The transgressor is the one who, after destroying a false thing because it can be destroyed, builds it again.

“For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.”

[Col. 0864B]

He says that he died to the law so that he would no longer be under the law, yet through the law—either because he was a Jew and had received the law as a pedagogue, as he explains later, or because he died to the law understood spiritually, so that he would not live under it in a carnal manner. Through the same law understood spiritually, he died to the carnal observances of the law.

The work of a pedagogue is to make the pedagogue unnecessary, just as an infant is nourished by the breast so that later he no longer needs the breast, and one reaches one’s homeland by ship so that afterward the ship is no longer needed. Thus he died to the law through the law, so that he might live to God. For the person who is under God lives to God, while the person who is under the law lives to the law. A person lives under the law to the extent that he is a sinner—that is, to the extent that he has not been changed from the old person.

[Col. 0864C]

“I have been crucified with Christ.” Since he had said that he died to the law through the law, he shows how he died: “I have been crucified with Christ”—that is, I have died to all the sins for which the law was given, and therefore the law is no longer necessary for me.

“But I live—now no longer I; Christ, however, lives in me.” The one who once lived under the law no longer lives, because he was persecuting the Church. But Christ lives in him: wisdom, strength, the Word, peace, joy, and the other virtues. A person who does not possess these cannot say, “Christ lives in me.” Who, then, would dare impose the law upon Christ, who lives in Paul? No one would dare say that Christ does not live rightly, so that a law must be imposed upon him to restrain him. Throughout this whole passage he discusses Peter, speaking against Peter in his own person.

[Col. 0864D]

“But what I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God,” he says. It is one thing to be in the flesh and another to live in the flesh. “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Romans 8). Hence it is said to those who live rightly: “You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit.”

What he adds—“I live in faith in the Son of God”—is to be understood in this way: Christ also lives in the believer by dwelling in the inner person through faith, so that later, when mortality has been swallowed up by life, he may fill the believer through sight. For future life has been promised to Christians. Therefore the person who now lives in this life, fortified by God’s help, lives in faith in the promised life. In this life he contemplates the image of that future life, possessing it as a pledge.

[Col. 0865A]

To show that Christ lives in him and that, while living in the flesh, he lives by the faith of the Son of God—not through his own merit but through the grace of God, which was obtained for us through the love of Christ—he added:

“Who loved me and gave himself for me.” For whom, surely, if not for a sinner, did he give himself, in order to justify him? The person who says this was born and raised a Jew and had been an especially zealous defender of his ancestral traditions. Therefore, even if Christ gave himself for people of that kind, they too were sinners. I will not say, then, that this was given because of their merits of righteousness, since there was no need for it to be given to the righteous. For the Lord says: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matthew 9)—so that they might no longer be sinners.

The Apostle speaks of God to the Romans, saying that he “did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8). He does not say that Christ himself gave himself up, but that the Father gave him up in order to save the world that had been lost; Christ gave himself up in order to carry out the will of the Father and his own will. Judas, the priests, the elders of the people, and Pilate, not knowing what they were doing, handed life over to death. Therefore, since Christ himself also gave himself up for our salvation, blessed and exceedingly happy will be the person who, with Christ living in him, can say through each thought and deed: “I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.”

“I do not reject the grace of God, so as to say that righteousness comes through the law.” But the person who lives under the law after the Gospel, and who defiles himself with sins after baptism, rejects the grace of God.

“For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing”—that is, he died without cause, since righteousness could exist in human beings through the law, that is, through the works of the law in which the Jews trusted. Those whom he refutes do not themselves say that Christ died for nothing, since they wished to be regarded as Christians. Therefore they were not rightly persuading people that Christians are justified through those works of the law. Christ died precisely in order to provide what the law could not; consequently, he did not die for nothing. His death is the justification of sinners.

This far he has spoken against Peter; now he returns to the Galatians, to whom he rightly says:

[Col. 0865C]

## On Chapter 3

[Col. 0865D]

“O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you so that you do not obey the truth?”

This passage can be understood in two ways. The Galatians may be called foolish because they had come from greater things to lesser ones: they had begun with the Spirit but were bringing their course to completion in the flesh. Or the reason may be that each province has its own characteristics, and each people is said to possess either a good or a bad quality that another does not possess.

Avoiding such lofty interpretations, we shall pursue what lies above: either we shall say that they are accused of folly because they cannot distinguish the spirit of the law from its letter, or that they are reproved for the fault of their nation, because they are unteachable and senseless, slow to attain wisdom.

As for what follows—“Who has bewitched you?”—the evil eye is properly said to harm infants, tender children, and those who have not yet planted their feet firmly as they walk. Hence one of the Gentile poets says:

> “I do not know what eye bewitches my tender lambs.”

Whether both of these interpretations are true or not, God knows; let the reader decide. For it may be that demons also serve this sin and turn away from good works those whom they recognize as having either begun or advanced in God’s work.

The point at issue here is that we think the example was taken from popular belief: just as tender childhood is said to be harmed by the evil eye, so the Galatians, newly born and nourished in faith in Christ with milk rather than solid food, were as though poisoned by some bewitching substance. They had vomited out the food of the Holy Spirit, not because their stomach was sickened by faith. The words are those of someone angry and astonished, since they had been so corrupted that they did not even recognize that they had been deceived.

Everyone who is bewitched passes from good to evil. So these people had passed from freedom and security to servitude and anxiety.

“Before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed and crucified among you.” Christ was rightly publicly portrayed for us: the whole chorus of the prophets foretold his gallows and passion, his blows and scourging, so that we might know his cross not only from the Gospel, in which his crucifixion is reported, but also from long before he deigned to descend to earth and assume the human being who was crucified.

The Galatians’ faith is not a small distinction: they believed in the crucified one in such a way that he had already been publicly portrayed before them. In other words, by reading the prophets repeatedly and understanding all the sacraments of the old law, they had come to faith by a proper path and in proper order.

“This alone I wish to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit from works of the law, or from hearing with faith?” The answer is certainly: from hearing with faith. Faith had been preached to them by the Apostle, and in that preaching they had perceived the coming and presence of the Holy Spirit. At that time, when people were newly invited to faith, the presence of the Holy Spirit also appeared through perceptible miracles, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles. This had happened among the Galatians before those people came to corrupt and circumcise them.

The meaning, then, is this: if your salvation lay in those works of the law, the Holy Spirit would not have been given to you unless you had been circumcised.

[Col. 0866D]

“Are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being brought to completion by the flesh?” This is what he had said above at the beginning: “Unless there are some who are troubling you and wishing to overturn the Gospel of Christ.” Trouble is contrary to order. The order is to rise from carnal things to spiritual things, not to fall from spiritual things to carnal ones, as had happened to these people.

The Jews do not receive the Spirit except through faith; you, by contrast, think that the Spirit is not sufficient for you unless you are also subjected to the law. This is the Gospel turned backward; and because that is not good, it is not the Gospel when it is preached in this way.

“You suffered so many things in vain—if indeed in vain.”

[Col. 0867A]

They had already endured much for the faith, not through fear, as though they were placed under the law, but rather through love. In those very sufferings they had conquered fear, because “the love of God has been poured out in their hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5), which they had received.

“Therefore,” he says, “you suffered so many things in vain”—you who wish to fall back from the love that endured so much in you into fear—“if indeed you suffered so many things in vain.” Here “if indeed” does not express doubt but affirmation, as in: “If indeed it is righteous before God to repay tribulation to those who trouble you, and rest to you who are troubled along with us” (2 Thessalonians 1).

What is said to have happened “in vain” is superfluous. But what is superfluous neither benefits nor harms. We must see to it, however, that this may not prove destructive. For not rising is not the same as falling, although these people had not yet fallen but were already inclining toward a fall. The Holy Spirit was still at work in them, as he says next:

“Therefore, does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so from works of the law or from hearing with faith?”

“Supplies” means “administers”; it should be read as a present-tense expression, so that it may be shown that the Holy Spirit is continually ministered to those who are worthy, hour by hour and moment by moment. The more a person advances in God’s work and love, the more he possesses within himself the virtues of the Holy Spirit—virtues brought to completion by hearing with faith, not by works of the law.

This does not mean that the works of the law are to be despised and that a simple faith is to be sought without them; rather, the works themselves are to be adorned by the faith of Christ. For the wise man’s saying is well known: not that the faithful lives by righteousness, but that the righteous lives by faith (Habakkuk 2).

It is shown at the same time that, after receiving the Holy Spirit through faith, the Galatians possessed gifts of power: prophecy, kinds of tongues, healings of diseases, and the other gifts enumerated among the spiritual gifts in the Epistle to the Corinthians. Yet after such experiences, perhaps because they did not possess the grace of discerning spirits, they were ensnared by false teachers.

“Just as Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.”

This is especially victorious in Abraham: before he was circumcised, the faith of the Gentiles was counted as righteousness in him. For this reason what was said to him is most rightly recalled: “All nations will be blessed in you” (Genesis 22)—through imitation of his faith, by which he was justified even before the sacrament of circumcision, which he received as a seal of faith, and before the servitude of the law, which was given much later.

Such faith is rightly counted as righteousness: it has surpassed the works of the law and won God’s favor not through fear but through love.

“Therefore you know that those who are of faith are sons of Abraham.” It is true that believers are Abraham’s sons. If Abraham was first justified by faith, then all who believe after him are his sons, whether Jews or Gentiles.

He discussed this more fully in the Epistle to the Romans: faith was counted as righteousness to Abraham and to all who believe with this disposition, because Abraham believed while uncircumcised. He “rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8). Hence it is also said to the unbelieving Jews: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham.”

“Foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, Scripture announced the Gospel beforehand to Abraham: ‘All nations will be blessed in you.’ Therefore those who are of faith will be blessed with faithful Abraham.”

It is not that Scripture itself—the ink and parchment, which are insensible—could foresee the future. Rather, the Holy Spirit and the meaning hidden in the letters foretold what would come many centuries later.
