The example taken from Genesis is contained in its own book in this form: “All the nations of the earth will be blessed in your seed.” Interpreting this concerning Christ, the Apostle says: “It does not say ‘in seeds,’ as though in many, but as though in one: ‘and in your seed,’ who is Christ.”

Therefore, at times he either omitted words or added them. No one can doubt, however, that all nations were not blessed in Isaac, Jacob, or the twelve patriarchs, or in the others descended from Abraham’s line. Rather, through Christ Jesus all nations praised God, and the new name is blessed throughout the earth.

“For all who are of the works of the law are under a curse, for it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of this law, to do them.’”

He wishes this to be understood as fear, not freedom: those who did not remain in all that was written in the book of the law to do it were punished by bodily and present vengeance. To this was added the fear that, in the punishment of their bodies itself, they would suffer the disgrace of being accursed.

But the person who worships God freely is justified before God—not out of a desire to obtain something from him apart from him, nor through fear of losing something. In God alone is our true blessedness and perfection. Since he is invisible to bodily eyes, he is worshiped by faith for as long as we live in this flesh, just as he said above: “What I now live in the flesh, I live in faith in the Son of God.” This is the righteousness to which the statement refers: “The righteous lives by faith.”

He wished to show from this that no one is justified in the law, because it is written that the righteous lives by faith. In this matter, what he now calls “in the law” must be understood as referring to what is said about the works of the law. He is speaking to those who are occupied with circumcision of the flesh and similar observances. Whoever lives in these is so in the law that he lives under the law. But, as stated, he now uses “law” for the works of the law themselves; this is made clear by what follows.

“For the law is not from faith, but ‘the one who does these things will live by them.’” He does not say, “The one who does it will live in it,” so that you may understand that in this passage “law” is used for the works themselves. Those who lived in these works certainly feared that, if they did not perform them, they would suffer stoning, crucifixion, or something of that kind.

“Whoever does these things,” he says, “will live by them”—that is, he will receive a reward, so as not to be punished by this death. This is not life with God, for the person who lives by faith in this life will have the most immediate reward when he departs from it.

Whoever desires or fears present things that are seen does not live by faith, since faith in God concerns invisible things that will be given later. There is therefore a kind of righteousness in the works of the law, since those who perform them are not left without their reward. Hence he says to the Romans: “If Abraham was justified by works, he has glory—but not before God” (Romans 4).

It is one thing not to be justified and another not to be justified before God. The person who is not justified at all preserves neither the things that have a temporal reward nor those that have an eternal one. But the person who is justified by the works of the law is not justified before God, because he expects from them a temporal and visible payment.

Nevertheless, this too is, as I said, a kind of earthly and carnal righteousness. The Apostle himself calls it righteousness when he says elsewhere: “According to the righteousness that is in the law, I lived without reproach” (Philippians 3).

For this reason our Lord Jesus Christ, who was about to give freedom to believers, did not observe certain of these practices according to the letter. Thus, when his hungry disciples plucked ears of grain on the Sabbath, he replied to those who were indignant that the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath (Matthew 12).

By not observing those practices carnally, he set carnal envy ablaze and indeed accepted the punishment appointed for those who did not observe them. But he did so in order to free believers in him entirely from fear of such punishment. To this refers what he adds next:

“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, because it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.’”

A human being’s death results from the punishment of sin; hence death itself is also called sin. Not because a person sins while dying, but because it came about through sin that he dies.

In another sense, for example, “tongue” properly means the flesh that moves inside the teeth beneath the palate; in another sense, “tongue” means what is done through the tongue, as when we speak of the Greek tongue and the Latin tongue. Likewise, “hand” properly means the bodily limb that we move in order to work; in another sense, “hand” means writing produced by the hand. We say, “His hand was brought forth,” “his hand was read against him,” and “I have your hand”—where “hand” properly means a human limb.

I do not suppose that the writing itself is a human limb; nevertheless, it is called a “hand” because it was made by the hand. Similarly, sin means not only the evil deed itself, which deserves punishment, but also death itself, which exists because of sins and is therefore called sin.

Christ did not commit that sin by which he would be liable to death. But he accepted for us the other thing—that is, death, which was inflicted upon human nature because of sin. He hung this on the tree; this is what Moses called accursed. There death was condemned so that it would not reign, and was accursed so that it might perish.

Therefore, through Christ’s sin—sin so called in this sense—our sin too was condemned, so that we might be set free and not remain condemned while sin reigned.

Why, then, does Faustus wonder that sin is accursed, death is accursed, and the mortality of the flesh is accursed apart from Christ’s sin? Yet it came about from human sin even in Christ. For he assumed a body from Adam, since the virgin Mary, who bore Christ, descended from Adam.

God had said in paradise: “On the day when you touch it, you will surely die” (Genesis 2). This is the curse that hung on the tree.

Let the person who denies that Jesus was accursed deny also that he died. But the person who confesses that he died and cannot deny that death comes from sin—and that for this reason death itself was called sin—should hear the Apostle saying: “Our old person was crucified together with him” (Romans 6). Let him understand whom Moses called accursed, and therefore let the Apostle confidently say of Christ: “He became a curse for us,” just as he was not afraid to say, “He died for all.”

For “he died” means “he was accursed,” since death itself comes from the curse, and every sin is accursed—whether the sin itself that is committed so that punishment may follow, or the punishment itself, which is called sin in another sense because it comes from sin.

Christ accepted our punishment without guilt, so that from it he might release us from our guilt and also bring our punishment to an end. I would be saying this on my own authority if the Apostle did not repeat it so often that he both awakens the sleeping and confounds those who bring accusations.

“God sent his Son,” he says, “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8). He had not come from the transmission of mortality in Mary through a man, but because death comes from sin, the flesh, although from a virgin, was nevertheless mortal; and precisely because it was mortal, it bore the likeness of sinful flesh.

He also calls this sin, saying next: “In order to condemn sin in the flesh through sin.” Again, elsewhere he says: “The one who knew no sin he made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him” (2 Corinthians 5).

Why, then, would Moses have been afraid to say “accursed,” when Paul was not afraid to say “sin”? Clearly the prophet ought to have foreseen this and to have been prepared to be criticized by heretics together with the Apostle. For whoever criticizes the prophet for saying “accursed” is compelled to criticize the Apostle for saying “sin.”

The curse is certainly sin’s companion. Nor is the charge of envy any greater because he added the word “God,” saying: “Accursed by God is everyone who hangs on a tree.” Unless God hated sin and our death, he would not have sent his Son to undergo and abolish them.

What is surprising, then, if what God hates is accursed by God? The more mercifully he hates our death, which hung on the tree when Christ died, the more willingly he grants us immortality, which will come when Christ returns.

As for the addition of “everyone”—“Accursed is everyone who hangs on a tree”—Moses certainly did not fail to foresee that righteous people would be on crosses. Rather, he rightly foresaw that heretics would deny the Lord’s true death and would therefore wish to separate Christ from this curse, so that they might also separate him from the reality of death.

If that death was not real, no curse hung on Christ crucified on the tree, because he was not truly crucified. But against heretics who were to come long afterward, Moses cries out from afar:

“You equivocate in vain, you who dislike the truth of Christ’s death: accursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” Not this one or that one, but absolutely everyone—even the Son of God, indeed emphatically the Son of God. For this is what you do not want, and for this reason you exert yourselves and lead others astray. You dislike that he was accursed for us because you dislike that he died for us.

A person is outside the curse of that Adam only if he is outside Adam’s death. But when Christ accepted death from a human being and for a human being, he did not disdain to accept from that human being and for that human being the curse that accompanies death—indeed, he did so fully, he the Son of God, ever living in his righteousness but dead because of our sins in the flesh assumed from our punishment.

For this reason “everyone” was added, lest Christ be said not to belong to true death if, through a foolish reverence, he were separated from the curse joined to death.

The person who is faithful according to the truth of the Gospel understands that Christ’s being called accursed by Moses’ mouth is no insult to Christ. He was called accursed not according to the divinity of his majesty but according to the condition of our punishment, because he was suspended on the tree.

Why, then, is Christ not praised by the mouth of the Manichaeans when they deny that he had mortal flesh in which he could suffer true death? Through the prophetic curse, humility is understood as praiseworthy; through the heretical semblance of honor, a charge of falsehood is brought against him.

If you deny that he was accursed, you deny also that he died. If you deny that he died, you are no longer fighting against Moses but against the apostles. If you confess that he died, confess that he accepted the punishment of our sin without our sin.

Now, when you hear of the punishment of sin, believe that it came either from blessing or from a curse. If the punishment of sin comes from blessing, wish always to remain in the punishment of sin. But if you wish to be freed from it, believe that through the justice of the divine judgment it came from a curse.

Confess, then, that the one whom you confess to have died for us accepted a curse for the sake of those who were to receive good. Moses meant nothing else when he said, “Accursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,” except that everyone who hangs on a tree is mortal and dying.

He could have said, “Accursed is everyone who is mortal,” or, “Accursed is everyone who is dying.” But this is what the prophecy asserts. He knew that Christ’s death would take place on the cross and that heretics would arise who would say: “He did hang on the tree, but only in appearance, not so that he would truly die.”

By crying out, therefore, “Accursed,” he cried out nothing other than that he truly died. He knew that the death of sinful humanity, which Christ accepted without sin, came from the curse pronounced when it was said: “If you touch it, you will die.”

“So that we might receive the adoption of the Spirit through faith”—that is, so that what is not feared in the flesh but loved in the spirit might be announced to those who were to believe.

[Col. 0871D]

“Brothers, I speak in human terms: no one rejects or adds anything to a humanly confirmed testament.” When the testator changes his testament, he changes one that has not been confirmed. A testament is confirmed by the death of its testator.

The fact that the testator’s death serves to confirm his testament, because he can no longer change his intention, corresponds to the immutability of God’s promise, which confirms the inheritance of Abraham, whose faith was counted as righteousness.

“Promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed.” He does not say “to seeds,” as though to many, but as though to one: “and to your seed,” who is Christ.

The Apostle calls Christ the seed of Abraham to whom the promises were spoken—that is, all Christians who imitate Abraham’s faith. He reduces them to singularity by emphasizing that it was not said “to seeds” but “to your seed.” For faith is one, and those who live carnally by works cannot be justified together with those who live spiritually by faith.

It is evident that the law had not come into existence and could not have been given after so many years in such a way as to invalidate the ancient promises made to Abraham. If the law justifies, then Abraham, who lived long before the law, was not justified. Since they cannot say this, they are compelled to admit that a person is not justified by the works of the law but by faith.

At the same time, this compels us to understand that all the ancient fathers who were justified were justified by that same faith. We shall be saved by believing in what is partly past—that is, the Lord’s first coming—and partly future—that is, the Lord’s second coming. The whole of this was what they believed: both comings were future to them, as the Holy Spirit revealed them, so that they might be saved.

Hence also the statement: “Abraham desired to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John 8).

I say this: a testament confirmed by God is not annulled by the law, which came into being four hundred and thirty years later, so as to nullify the promise.

First, for the sake of those who do not understand, let us examine those years minutely and carefully. Then we shall explain what conclusion is to be drawn from them. Abraham, therefore, when he was seventy-five years old, received a divine oracle telling him to depart from his land. Twenty-five years later he fathered Isaac, when he was one hundred years old. Isaac, in the sixtieth year of his life, fathered Jacob and Esau. From Abraham’s first promise these amount to eighty-five years.

Finally, in the ninety-first year of his life Jacob fathered Joseph; and in the one hundred and thirtieth year of Jacob’s life—which was the thirty-ninth year of Joseph’s life—he went down into Egypt. From Abraham’s first promise these amount to two hundred and fifteen years. The children of Israel remained in Egypt for two hundred and fifteen years after Jacob’s entry. After Joseph’s death, however, they remained for one hundred and forty-four years.

Between Joseph’s death and Moses’ birth there were sixty years, because Moses was eighty years old when God appeared to him and sent him to Pharaoh. If anyone doubts these figures, or lacks the skill to calculate and find the total number of years, let him count from Jacob’s entry into Egypt, and he will find that until Joseph’s death there were seventy-one years. Add sixty-four years to these: the total is one hundred and thirty-five, because Moses is found to have been born in the sixty-fourth year after Joseph’s death. Add Moses’ eighty years of life, since he was that old when he was sent to Pharaoh. Add these to the preceding one hundred and thirty-five years, and the total is two hundred and fifteen.

From Abraham’s first promise, then, until Jacob’s entry into Egypt there were two hundred and fifteen years. From that point until the crossing of the Red Sea there were another two hundred and fifteen years. The total is four hundred and thirty. This is what the Apostle says in this passage. He does not say, however, “the testament confirmed by God, which came into being after four hundred and thirty years,” as though the law itself were the testament. Rather, he says that the testament was not annulled by what came into being after four hundred and thirty years.

But someone may say: How can it be that the children of Israel stayed so few years in the land of Egypt, when Scripture, in the book of Genesis, reports that God said to Abraham: “Know with certainty that your offspring will be strangers in a land not their own, and they will subject them to slavery and mistreat them for four hundred years” (Gen. XV)?

The statement that they would be reduced to slavery is therefore not to be referred to the four hundred years, as though they were enslaved for the whole of that period. Rather, the four hundred years are to be referred to what was said earlier: “Your offspring will be strangers in a land not their own.” For whether in the land of Canaan or in Egypt, that offspring was a stranger before receiving an inheritance in the land by God’s promise—something that happened only after they had been liberated from Egypt. The passage should therefore be understood as having been expressed through the figure of speech that grammarians call hyperbaton, that is, through an altered word order.

The sense, or order of the words, is: “Know with certainty that your offspring will be strangers in a land not their own for four hundred years.” The intervening words should be understood as: “And they will reduce them to slavery and harm them”; this insertion does not belong to the four hundred years. For it was toward the end of this total period—that is, after Joseph’s death—that the people of God underwent harsh slavery in Egypt.

A sufficiently necessary question follows. If faith justifies, and the earlier saints who were justified before God were justified through faith itself, why was it necessary for the law to be given?

The simple sense woven through this passage has this force: the Apostle was teaching that the promises previously made to Abraham could not be destroyed by the law given afterward, nor could what came later prejudice what came first. The promises were given to Abraham four hundred and thirty years earlier, namely, that all nations would be blessed in him; whereas the observance of the law—that the one who performed it would live by it—was given to Moses on Mount Sinai after four hundred and thirty years.

Conversely, one might ask here: Why, then, was it necessary for the law to be given after so long an interval following the promise, when the law’s promulgation could give rise to the suspicion that the pledge had been destroyed, and when, while the promise remained, the law had been given without being beneficial? Foreseeing this question, the Apostle himself raises and explains it in what follows, saying:

> What, then, is the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made; ordained through angels in the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not for one party alone, but God is one.

Since the promise made to Abraham remained, it seemed pointless that the law, given later through Moses, had been introduced. He explains why it was given: “Because of transgressions,” he says. For after the people's offense, after they worshiped the calf and murmured against the Lord, the law followed in order to prohibit transgressions.

The law was therefore imposed upon a proud people, so that, since they could not receive the grace of love unless humbled—and without this grace they could in no way fulfill the commandments of the law—they might be humbled by transgression, seek grace, and not suppose, in their pride, that they could be saved by their own merits. Thus they would be righteous not by their own power and strength, but in the hand of the mediator who justifies the ungodly.

All the administration of the Old Testament was ministered through angels, with the Holy Spirit working in them, and with the Word of truth himself—not yet incarnate, but never withdrawing from any truthful administration. For that administration of the law was arranged through angels, who sometimes acted in their own person and sometimes in God’s person, as is also the custom of the prophets.

Through that law, which displayed diseases without removing them, pride was crushed by the guilt of transgression. It was arranged through angels, but in the power of the mediator, so that he himself might free from sins those compelled by transgression of the law to confess that they needed the Lord’s grace and mercy, so that their sins might be forgiven and, in a new life, they might be reconciled to God through the one who had poured out his blood for them.

In these people, then, pride had to be broken through transgression of the law. They gloried in their father Abraham and boasted as though they possessed righteousness by nature; they placed their merits in circumcision above those of the other nations, all the more perniciously because they did so arrogantly.

The Gentiles, however, could be humbled much more easily even without this kind of transgression of the law. For the evangelical grace found people who, recognizing that they derived no origin of righteousness from their parents, were also servants of idols. The Jews could not be told, as the Gentiles could, that the righteousness of their parents in worshiping idols had been false, since they themselves considered it righteousness. Nor could the Jews be told that the righteousness of their father Abraham had been false.

Therefore it is said to them: “Produce fruit worthy of repentance, and do not say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Luke III).

To these others it is said:

> Therefore remember that formerly you were Gentiles in the flesh, called uncircumcision by what is called circumcision in the flesh, made by human hands; remember that at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope of the promise and without God in this world (Eph. II).

Finally, in the one case unbelievers are shown to have been broken off from their own olive tree; in the other, believers from the wild olive tree are shown to have been grafted into their olive tree.

Their pride, therefore, had to be worn down through transgression of the law. Thus, in Romans, after he had intensified their sins with words from Scripture, he says: “You know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become liable to God” (Rom. III). The Jews are liable through transgression of the law, and the Gentiles through ungodliness without the law.

Hence he says again: “God has enclosed all things in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all” (Rom. XIII).

Is the law therefore against the promises of God? Certainly not. The law was not given, then, in order to remove sin, but in order to enclose everything under sin. The law showed that there was sin where people, blinded by habit, might suppose there was righteousness. In this way, once humbled, they would recognize that their salvation was not in their own hand but in the hand of the mediator.

Certainly not: the law is not hostile to the promise, since it confirms it. For Moses first said: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers” (Deut. XVIII; Acts XIII). The Apostle Peter proves in the Acts of the Apostles that this was spoken about Christ.

> For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly have been from the law. But Scripture enclosed everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ. Before faith came, however, we were kept under the law, enclosed for the faith that was to be revealed.

Just as the mediator of God and human beings stood between the one who gave the law and those who received it, so the law itself, given after the promise, inserted itself between the promise and its fulfillment. It should not therefore be thought to exclude the promise because, following after it, it seems to abolish what came first. Rather, from the fact that it could not give life or bestow what the first promise had pledged, it is clear that it was given to guard the promise, not to overthrow it.

If a law had been given that could grant life and provide what the promise had pledged, then the promise would truly be thought to have been excluded by the law. But now, since the law was imposed because of transgressions, as we have said above, it rather proves them to be sinners—those to whom, after the promise, it was given as a guard and, so to speak, as a prison. Because they did not wish, through freedom of the will, to await the promise in innocence, they were restrained by legal bonds and reduced to the servitude of commandments, so that they might be kept until the coming of the faith that was to come in Christ and bring the promise to completion.

He calls this righteousness the righteousness that is reckoned as righteousness before God—that is, the righteousness of faith. The law, too, had a kind of righteousness, but only for the present age, not the kind that would justify before God. It could not forgive sins or make the sinners righteous; rather, it was given to serve as a terror provoking people to good conduct and punishing the irreverent.

Therefore the law was not given so that it could give life, but so that it could condemn. Nor should it be thought that Scripture is the author of sin because it is said to have enclosed everything under sin. A commandment enjoined by word of mouth rather displays and reproves sin than causes it. A judge, likewise, is not the author of crime because he binds wicked people; he encloses them and pronounces them guilty by the authority of his judgment, so that, if he later wishes, the sovereign may release them from the punishment they deserve through clemency.

When he says, “Before faith came, we were kept under the law, enclosed for the faith that was to be revealed,” he speaks as though he were saying plainly: The guilt of the law no longer binds us; we have already been freed by grace. Before we were humbled and received spiritual grace, the letter did nothing but kill us, commanding what we could not fulfill. Hence he says: “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (II Cor. III).

Their enclosure consisted only in fear of the one God. The fact that they were found to be transgressors of his law benefited those who believed—not to their destruction, but to their advantage. For knowledge of a greater illness made them desire the physician more intensely and love him more ardently. “For the one to whom much is forgiven loves much.”

Therefore the law was our pedagogue in Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified by faith. But when faith came, we are no longer under a pedagogue. For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus.

*Paedagogus* is Greek. A *paedagogus* is a personal attendant. We call a *paedagogus* an instructor or rearer of boys. The *paedagogus* is the person assigned to children, from the fact that he leads boys—that is, guides them—and restrains an age inclined to frivolity, so that their hearts, prone to vices, may be held in check while their tender childhood is trained in studies and, restrained by fear of punishment, prepared for the greater disciplines of philosophy and the governance of the state.

Yet the pedagogue is not the teacher and father, nor does the one being educated expect to receive the pedagogue’s inheritance or knowledge. Rather, the pedagogue guards another man’s son, intending to withdraw when the boy has reached the lawful age for receiving his inheritance. Indeed, the name *paedagogus* itself expresses this meaning, and it is compounded from the notion of leading boys—that is, teaching them.

Thus the law of Moses was placed over the wanton people like a stricter pedagogue, to guard them and prepare them for the future faith. Once that faith came and we believed in Christ, we are no longer under a pedagogue. The tutor and guardian withdraw from us, and, having reached the lawful age, we are truly called sons of God. It is not the abolished law that gives us birth, but faith, which is in Christ Jesus, as a mother.

If anyone, after completing the period of his youth, when he is already called heir, free, and son, wishes to remain under a pedagogue, let him know that he cannot live by the laws of a child. For where can the following now be fulfilled: “Three times a year every male of yours shall appear before the Lord your God” (Exod. XXXIV), with Jerusalem overthrown and the temple destroyed down to its ashes? Where are the salutary sacrifices and the sacrifices for sin? Where is the preparation of fine flour, the offering of burnt offerings, and the everlasting fire, when the altar has been entirely destroyed (Lev. IV, V, and VI)? What punishment can now be assigned to crimes when Scripture says, “You shall remove the evil from your midst” (Deut. XIII), while the Jews are serving and the Romans ruling?

Thus it comes about that they live neither under the Father nor under the pedagogue, since the law cannot be fulfilled after the succession of faith, while faith, when the law as pedagogue is disclosed, is not held fast.

> For all of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.

That Christ is the clothing of the faithful is proved not only from the present passage but also from another, where the same Paul exhorts: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. XIII). When they are changed, they put on Christ, since they are called what they believe.

If, therefore, those who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ, it is clear that those who have not put on Christ were not baptized into Christ. When he says that all are sons of God through the faith by which they have put on Christ—whoever has been baptized in him—he says this so that the Gentiles would not despair of themselves because they were not kept under a pedagogue, and therefore would not suppose themselves to be sons. By putting on Christ through faith, all become sons.

They do not become sons by nature, as the only Son does—the one who is also the Wisdom of God. Nor do they become sons by the power and singularity of assumption, so as to possess naturally and enact the person of Wisdom, as the mediator himself became one with the Wisdom that assumed him, without the intervention of any mediator. Rather, they become sons by participation in Wisdom—that is, through the faith prepared and bestowed by the mediator. This grace of faith he now calls clothing: those who have believed in Christ have put on Christ, and for this reason have become sons of God and brothers of the mediator.

> There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus.

A Jew is not better because he is circumcised, nor is a Gentile worse because he has a foreskin; rather, according to the quality of faith, a Jew or a Greek may be better or worse. Slave and free are likewise not separated by social condition but by faith, because a slave may be better than a free person, and a free person may surpass a slave in the quality of faith.

Similarly, male and female are distinguished by the strength and weakness of their bodies. Faith, however, is judged according to the devotion of the mind. Often a woman becomes the cause of salvation for a man, and a man surpasses a woman in religious devotion.

Since this is so, and the whole diversity of race, condition, and body is removed by Christ’s baptism and by putting him on, “we are all one in Christ Jesus.” Just as the Father and the Son are one in themselves, so we too may be one in them.

If faith accomplishes this—the faith by which one walks righteously in this life—how much more perfectly and fully will the very reality accomplish it when we see face to face? For now, although we possess the firstfruits of the Spirit, which is life because of the righteousness of faith, our body is still dead because of sin. Thus this distinction of nations, social condition, and sex has indeed already been removed from the unity of faith, but it remains in mortal conduct.

The order of these distinctions must be preserved during the journey of this life; the Apostles command this and hand down very salutary rules concerning how people are to live with one another: according to the difference of nation, Jews and Greeks; according to the difference of condition, masters and slaves; according to the difference of sex, husbands and wives; and likewise in other cases that may arise.

The Lord himself first said: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII).

Some things we preserve in the unity of faith without any distinction; other things we preserve in the order of this present life, as on a road, lest the name of God and the teaching of our Savior be blasphemed. We do this not only because of wrath, so that we may avoid offending people, but also for the sake of conscience, so that we do not act hypocritically, as though merely before human eyes, but with a pure conscience of love for God, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

When he says, “You are all one in Christ Jesus,” he adds: “And if you are one in Christ Jesus, then you are Abraham’s offspring.” Here he shows that the one offspring is Christ, who is to be understood not only as the mediator but also as the Church, of which he is the head. Thus all may be one in Christ and receive the inheritance according to the promise through faith.

The people were enclosed in this faith—that is, they were kept under a pedagogue until its coming—as though until the appropriate age, when those who had been called according to the purpose within that same people were to be called into freedom. They were the grain found in that threshing floor.

> But if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise.

For the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring, which is Christ Jesus. Consequently, those who are Christ’s children—that is, his offspring—are also called Abraham’s offspring, since they are his offspring from the offspring.

Whenever our Lord Jesus is called Abraham’s offspring, this must be understood bodily, because he was generated from Abraham’s stock. But whenever we, who have believed in him after receiving the Savior’s word, and who have received the nobility of Abraham’s race, to whom the promise was made, are called his offspring, we must understand this spiritually, as the offspring of faith and preaching.

One must also consider that when he speaks about the Lord, he says that the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring—that is, in Christ Jesus—and he uses the plural, “promises.” But when he speaks about those who through Christ are Abraham’s offspring, he names the promise in the singular, as in the present passage: “Then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise.” It was fitting that what was spoken plurally in the one Christ should be expressed singularly in the many human beings.

[Col. 0878C]

## ON CHAPTER FOUR

> I say, then, that as long as the heir is a child, he differs nothing from a slave, although he is lord of all; but he is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by his father.

Those who possess the spirit of fear and have not yet deserved to receive the spirit of freedom and adoption are rightly said to be under guardians and stewards. The age of infancy fears sins, dreads the pedagogue, and does not believe that it is free.

Although this child is lord by nature—and according to both interpretations under which we have called guardians and stewards either prophets or angels—he remains under stewards until he has completed the lawful time of a mature man. According to Roman law, the lawful age ends after a period of twenty-five years. Thus Christ’s coming was reckoned for the perfection of the human race.

As soon as he has come and we have all grown into a perfect man, the pedagogue and tutor withdraw from us. Then we shall enjoy the Lord’s authority and possess the inheritance in which, though born beforehand, we were in some sense regarded as strangers.

> So also, when we were children, we were enslaved under the elements of this world.

Some interpret “the elements of the world” as the law of Moses and the sayings of the prophets, because through these, as through the beginnings and rudiments of letters, we receive the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom.

Thus, to those who ought already to have been perfect but, having neglected the truth, still clung to the rudiments of instruction, the Apostle writes in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “For although by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need someone to teach you what are the elements of the beginning of the oracles of God” (Heb. V).

The law of Moses and the prophets can therefore, as we have said, be understood as the elements of letters, because through them syllables and names are joined together, and they are learned not so much for their own sake as for the usefulness of another matter. In this way we can read a connected sentence, in which the meaning and order of the words are considered more than the rudiments of the letters.

When we interpreted the law and the prophets as “the elements of the world,” “world” is customarily understood to mean those who are in the world. Paul says the same: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. V). And in the Gospel: “The world was made through him, and the world did not receive him” (John I).

One may ask how, according to this comparison, the Jews were under the elements of this world, since through the law they had received, the worship of the one God who made heaven and earth was commended to them.

There may, however, be another interpretation of this passage. Since above he made the law a pedagogue under whom the Jewish people were, he may now call the stewards and guardians under whom they served the elements of the world. The child—that is, the people belonging through one faith to the divine offspring of Abraham—was gathered from both Jews and Gentiles.

Part of this people, the part gathered from the Jews, was under the pedagogue of the law during the time of childhood; another part, the part gathered from the Gentiles, was under the elements of this world, serving them as stewards and guardians. Thus, when the Apostle takes on their person—not saying, “When you were children, you were enslaved under the elements of this world,” but saying, “When we were children, we were enslaved under the elements of this world”—this does not refer here to the Jews, from whom Paul derives his origin, but rather to the Gentiles, though he can appropriately join himself to those to whom he was sent to preach the Gospel.

The “elements of the world” may also signify the new moons and the Sabbath. New moons are lunar days observed by the Jews; the Sabbath is the day of rest.

Before the promise came—that is, the gift of God’s grace, which purifies and justifies believers—we were like imperfect children, subjected through the law of God to fellow servants, as to pedagogues. Our freedom was made subject to the cause of sin.

The Jews, however, hoped for nothing from the elements, as the pagans did; they worshiped the Creator God in the creature.

Then he says that, when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son to free the little heir who was partly serving the law as a pedagogue and partly serving the elements of this world as stewards and guardians.

> But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, he says, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law.

“The fullness of time” is the completion of the time appointed by God the Father, when he would send his Son, so that, made from a virgin and born as a human being, he might subject himself to the law until the time of baptism. In this way he gave the pattern by which sinners, washed and released from the yoke of the law, might by God’s condescension become sons and be adopted, having been redeemed by the blood of his Son.

He used “woman” instead of “female,” following the manner of expression of the Hebrews. For when it is said of Eve, “He formed her into a woman,” she had not yet experienced intercourse with a man; Scripture does not say that she experienced this until after they had been expelled from paradise.

He said “made” because of his assumption of created nature. Those who are born from females are not then born from God, but God nevertheless made them so that they might be born in this way, like every creature.

He said “made under the law” because Christ was circumcised and a lawful offering was presented for him. Nor is it surprising that he underwent the works of the law from which he would free those who were held by them in servitude. He also endured death in order to free those who were held by mortality.

> So that we might receive the adoption of sons.

He said “adoption” so that we might clearly understand the unique Son of God. We are sons of God by his benefit and the condescension of his mercy. He is the Son by nature, being what the Father is.

He does not say “that we may receive” but “that we may receive again,” signifying that we had possessed this in Adam, from whom we are mortal.

The statement, “to redeem those who were under the law,” therefore refers to the people who served as a child under the pedagogue. It also relates to the words, “made under the law.” But the statement, “so that we might receive the adoption of sons,” relates to the words, “made of a woman.” From this we receive adoption: the only-begotten Son did not disdain participation in our nature by being made of a woman. Thus he was not only the only-begotten Son, where he has no brothers, but also became the firstborn among many brothers.

He proposed two things: “made of a woman” and “made under the law.” But, changing the order, he answered by joining to him the people who served as a child under guardians and stewards—that is, under the elements of this world—so that they would not suppose themselves to be sons because they were not under a pedagogue.

> And because you are sons, he says, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, “Abba, Father.”

He used two words so that the latter might interpret the former. For *Abba* means “Father.” It is elegantly understood that he did not place two words from two languages meaning the same thing without reason, because the whole people, from Jews and Gentiles, had been called into the unity of faith: the Hebrew word refers to the Jews, the Greek word to the Gentiles, while the identical meaning of both words belongs to the unity of the same faith and Spirit.

In Romans, where a similar question concerning peace in Christ between Jews and Gentiles is discussed, he says: “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption of sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. VIII).

When the Apostle had said, “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive the adoption of sons,” it remained for him to show that the Gentiles, who were not under the law, nevertheless belonged to the same adoption of sons. He teaches this from the gift of the Holy Spirit, who was given to all.

Thus Peter also defended before the believing Jews the uncircumcised centurion Cornelius, who had been baptized, saying that he could not refuse them water (Acts IX), because it had become clear that they had received the Holy Spirit.

So here also he says: “Because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’” Then he most clearly shows that he is also speaking about those who had come to faith from the Gentiles, to whom he is writing the letter.

> Therefore you are no longer a slave but a son.

“Having,” he says, “the Spirit of the Son of God crying within you, ‘Abba, Father,’ you have begun to be not slaves but sons.” Previously you differed nothing from a slave, although by nature you were the Lord’s, since you lived as children under guardians and stewards.

He is not a slave because, removed from the power of the law, he has become a partner in the blessing of God’s proper Son. He is doing all this because of what he had said: “As long as the heir is a child, he differs nothing from a slave.”

[Col. 0881C]

> And if a son, then also an heir through God.

That is, through God’s mercy, not through the promise of the fathers, from whom he would not have been born bodily like the Jews, though he was Abraham’s son according to the imitation of faith. You have obtained the grace of this faith through the Lord’s mercy.

> But at that time, when you did not know God, you served those who by nature were not gods. But now, having come to know God—or rather, having been known by God—how can you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements, to which you wish to be enslaved once more?

Since previously they sinned through ignorance while serving idols, he signifies that they were easily forgiven. Thus Abimelech says to God in Genesis: “Lord, will you indeed destroy an ignorant nation?” (Gen. XX).

He also reproves the Galatians, whom he had transferred from the worship of idols to faith in the true God: having abandoned idols, which by nature were not gods, and having come to know God—or rather, having been known by him—and having received the Spirit of adoption, they nevertheless wished again, like children under guardians and a pedagogue, to return to the weak and most impoverished elements.

These had been given to a people weak and poor in understanding in the desert because they could not receive or endure greater things. The same elements that he now calls weak and beggarly he previously called merely the elements of the world. Where they were called the elements of the world, he did not add “weak and beggarly”; here again, where they are called weak, the designation “of the world” is omitted.

I therefore think that as long as someone is a child and has not completed the time appointed by the father, so that he can be called son and heir, he is under the elements of the world—that is, under the law of Moses.

But when, after freedom, adoption, and the inheritance owed to a son, he turns back again to the law, wishing to be circumcised and to follow the whole letter of Jewish superstition, then what had previously been merely the elements of the world for him are also called weak and beggarly beginnings.

They are so useless to their worshipers that they cannot even provide what they had provided before, once Jerusalem, the temple, and the altar have been destroyed.

The statement, “having come to know God, or rather having been known by God,” should not trouble us. It is clear that as long as we walk by faith and not by sight, we have not yet known God; rather, we are purified by that faith so that at the proper time we may be able to know him.

But if the expression “rather, having been known by God” is understood strictly, God might seem to know something in time that he had not known before. It was therefore said figuratively, so that we understand God’s eyes as his love itself—the love he commended by sending his only Son to be killed for the ungodly.

For we commonly say of those who are loved that they are held before someone’s eyes. This, then, is the meaning of “having come to know God,” or rather “having been known by God.” John says the same: “Not that we loved God, but that he first loved us.”

> You observe days, months, seasons, and years.

The Jews observe days, months, years, and seasons in a slavish fashion: the Sabbath, new moons, the month of new things, and every seventh year, which they call the Sabbath of Sabbaths.

Because these were shadows of things to come, they remained as superstition after Christ had arrived, being observed as though they were means of salvation by those who did not know to what they should be referred.

It is as though the Apostle had said this to the Gentiles: What benefit is it that you escaped the slavery in which you were held, when you served the elements of the world, if you now return to such practices, led astray by those who do not yet recognize the time of their freedom? Along with the other works of the law that they understand carnally, they also serve the seasons. You too wish to serve them again as before and to observe with them days, months, years, and seasons, which you served before you believed in Christ.

> I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored over you in vain.

He moderated his words quite carefully between the Apostle’s authority and the gentleness of a holy man when he added: “I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored over you in vain.”

Now, seeing that they possessed zeal for God but not according to knowledge, he did not altogether despair of the salvation of those who had been deceived by a pious error. Nor did he leave them entirely without reproof, lest he give them themselves an occasion to persist in error and others an occasion to imitate them.

He used “I fear for you” in place of “I fear concerning you.” A teacher labors in vain when he urges his disciples toward greater things, but they slip backward and turn again to lesser and lower things.

Be as I am, because I also was as you are. That is, I beseech you, brothers, to disregard the Jewish observances of days, months, seasons, and years, which are shadows of things to come. Imitate me, who, having lived blamelessly under the Law, regarded everything as refuse and rubbish so that I might gain Christ. For I too was once as you are now, held fast by these same observances; and because the Church of Christ did not practice them, I persecuted and ravaged it. Although I was born a Jew, I now reject these carnal things through spiritual discernment. Then, appropriately and fittingly, he reminds them of their former affection, lest they regard him as an enemy. He says this so that they may take pains to correct themselves, since it is not impossible for them to become like him: he too was what they were—that is, a human being. And although he had been in error and had persecuted the Church, he was corrected, converted, and says:

## Brothers, I beseech you, you have done me no wrong.

You know that it was because of an infirmity of the flesh that I formerly preached the gospel to you; and you did not despise or reject your trial, which was in my flesh. Rather, you received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.

He now deals more gently with them and begins to recall their good qualities, so that, after hearing severe reprimands, they might be refreshed by the recollection of their good works and deliberately reformed, lest, being oppressed too long by reproaches, they should become harsher and embittered. The sense is this: When I first announced the gospel to you, and because of the infirmity of your flesh—for you were not able to receive the greater mysteries—I preached to you as to little children. I pretended to be weak myself in order to win you, who were weak. Did you not receive me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus? Since at that time you did me no harm at all, and, for your sake, regarded me—humble and abject—as resembling the Son of God, how is it that, when I urge you toward greater things, I am now harmed by you, because you are causing my labor and that dispensation by which I had pretended to be little to be lost? For a disciple harms his teacher when, through negligence, he despises his commands and labor.

And you did not despise or reject your trial, which was in my flesh. They were tested when the Apostle was suffering persecution: whether they would abandon him through fear or embrace him through love. “You did not despise,” he says, “this trial as useless, nor reject it, so as not to share in my danger.” This passage may also be explained as follows: When I came to you, I did not come with a discourse of wisdom, but as a humble and despised man, bringing nothing great except the crucified one. When, therefore, you saw me afflicted in body by infirmities and promising the kingdoms of heaven, you did not mock me or consider me worthy of contempt. For you understood that the humility of my flesh and the lowliness of my appearance had become a test for you: whether you would despise one whom unbelievers regarded as pitiable. But, on the contrary, you received that humble, lowly, and despised man as an angel, and more than an angel.

When he says, “But you received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus,” he especially praises them because he was not disfigured in their eyes by his afflictions, but rather commended by them. Those who knew why he suffered believed that he endured these miseries for their sake. Therefore, just as they received the Apostle as an angel of God, believing that what he preached was God’s gift, so they showed him the honor due to the author, the Lord Jesus Christ. He also shows that Christ is greater than an angel—Christ whom the Psalmist had sung as made lower, according to the dispensation of the body, saying: “You made him a little lower than the angels.” And he demonstrates that his words at the beginning had been so powerful that they were regarded as both angelic and of Christ.

He recalls for them the time when he first preached God’s gospel to them. At that time the Apostle was being subjected to insults and weakened by blows; for one who is humbled and does not resist for the sake of God’s gospel appears weak. In this he praises their conscience, because they had not been drawn away from the faith. The Apostle’s humiliation was a test of the Galatians, in which they were found steadfast, not doubting the faith. For they might have been scandalized and said: “What power or hope is there in this faith, when its minister is so humiliated?” But because they had already fixed their minds upon future hopes, they did not fear present sufferings for Christ’s name. They were certain that our faith has its dignity not on earth but in heaven, and that great rewards are repaid for these tribulations. Thus he brings shame upon them: after such praiseworthy conduct, they had been deceived and had come to appear blameworthy.

## Where, then, is your blessedness?

For I bear you witness that, if it had been possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me.

He shows with what great love they had received him and how completely they had surrendered themselves to his teaching: they were willing to give him the members of their body that were most precious, so that, by surrendering their own eyes, they might somehow repay the light of the gospel. “Although,” he says, “at that time, when you received the gospel according to the flesh, I called you blessed because you were fervent at the beginning, now, because I do not see a summit placed upon the building and because the foundations have almost been laid in vain, I am compelled to say: Where, then, is your blessedness, by which I previously praised you, considering you blessed?”

Indeed, I myself confess that you loved me, when I preached humbly to you or was afflicted by persecutions, so greatly that, if it had been possible—for what he says is to be understood hyperbolically—you would have torn out your own eyes and given them to me, so that I might see more than all of you through your eyes. In your ineffable love for me, you wished to be blind so that the light of the gospel might arise more abundantly in my heart. You wished my gain to increase through your loss. This was at the time when, as to little children and infants—whether because of the infirmity of your flesh I announced small and humble things, or because of the injuries inflicted upon my flesh I seemed unworthy of faith—I preached to you as to the weak.

But now, because I have begun with elements and syllables and childish reading to summon you to greater studies, so that you may hold books in your hands and learn words full of instruction and meaning, you resist and become angry. The perfection of doctrine seems burdensome to you, and you have been so changed in your attitudes toward others that you now regard as an enemy the one whom you had received as an angel and as Christ, and to whom you had wished to give your eyes, because I announce the full truth to you. He fittingly concludes the thought, saying:

## So then, have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?

Such is the nature of truth: it is pursued by hostility, just as pernicious friendships are won through flattery. What delights is willingly heard; everything we do not want offends us. Thus these people had begun to love the Sabbath rest and festival days, proclaiming feasts against the Apostle, who taught every form of self-restraint by his own example.

## They court you, but not well.

That is, they envy you: they want to make you who are spiritual into carnal people. This is what “they court you, but not well” means. It signifies that they had been overthrown through the envy of the Jews. For when they saw them making such progress in the gospel and possessing such great love for the Apostle, they acted with the aim of deceiving them. They were hostile to the Apostle on account of the Law, and, while preserving the name of the Savior, they wanted to make the Galatians Jews, rejoicing in their overthrow. They could not bear to hear that the promised grace had been given to the uncircumcised Gentiles. Therefore they wanted the Galatians to become their imitators, so that they might be circumcised according to their custom.

“But they want to exclude you,” he says, “so that you may court them.” That is, imitate them. How else, except by being held under the yoke of servitude, as they themselves are held? He is therefore speaking to the Galatians, who had been induced by the advocates of the Law to imitate them, although the latter ought rather to have imitated the Galatians—for it is natural that the greater should come from the lesser, not the lesser from the greater.

## Court what is good, always in what is good.

That is, do not imitate the advocates of Jewish observance, but imitate what is good. For just as one who imitates riches, power, or dignity courts not so much what is good as what ought to be avoided, so you, on the contrary, should court what is good in what is good, seeking spiritual things more than carnal ones, so that you may teach not that they make you Jews, but that you make them Christians.

Do this always, so that you may reach the end of good works by a steadfast course. Court, then, what is good in what is good. Formerly, when I was with you, you did this; but after I departed from you, you lost everything that I had believed. You were carried away from a firm station and a safe harbor when the wave rolled back again into the deep. It is not surprising that, when the Apostle—the vessel of election and the one in whom Christ the Lord spoke—departed, the Galatians were changed, since even now we see the same thing happening in the churches.

Therefore, wishing to show the concern teachers have for their disciples and the emotions they endure lest their followers fall away from salvation, Paul says:

## My little children, for whom I am again in labor.

You were brought into the light through the gospel and begotten through instruction, yet you have made me endure labor again. He shows that they can be reborn through repentance. For elsewhere, speaking as a father, he had said: “Even if you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers” (I Cor. IV). Now he speaks in Christ not as a father but as a mother, so that they may recognize in him the anxiety and devotion of both parents.

## Until Christ is formed in you.

Christ is formed in the one who has received the form of Christ. He receives Christ’s form who clings to Christ through spiritual love. For this results in his becoming, through imitation of Christ, what Christ is, insofar as his own condition permits. “Whoever says that he remains in Christ,” John says, “ought to walk as he walked.”

But since human beings are conceived by mothers in order to be formed, and, once formed, are brought forth in labor so that they may be born, what is meant by the words, “for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you,” unless we understand this labor as referring to the anguish of concern by which he brought them forth so that they might be born in Christ? He is again in labor because of the dangers of deception by which he sees them disturbed. That solicitude and care for them—since he says that he is, in a certain sense, bringing them forth—can last until they attain “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ,” so that they may no longer be moved by every wind of doctrine.

The statement, then, “until Christ is formed in you,” does not concern the beginning of faith, since they had already been born, but their strength and perfection. Or, alternatively, Christ is formed in the hearts of believers when all the mysteries are disclosed to them and the things that had seemed obscure become clear.

## I wish I could be with you now and change my voice, because I am perplexed about you.

I do not see what else this can mean, except that, because he had called them his little children and was sparing them—perhaps lest, provoked by a harsher rebuke, they should easily transfer their hatred to those deceivers whom he could not resist while absent—he says: “I wish now to be present with you and to change my voice,” that is, to deny that you are children, because I am perplexed about you.

Parents often disown bad children so that they may not be ashamed of them. I cannot write as much as you deserve to hear, because a letter cannot reproduce the voice of one who is rebuking. It cannot make the cry of an angry person resound or express the pain of the heart through written characters. The disgrace and reproach of disciples are the teacher’s loss, just as their progress is the teacher’s glory. He is therefore perplexed about them because, having become children, they had ceased to be servants.

## Tell me, you who wish to be under the Law: do you not hear the Law?

It should be noted that “the Law” here means the history of Genesis, not, as people commonly think, merely what ought to be done or avoided. Rather, everything narrated about Abraham, his wives, and his children is called the Law. We also read elsewhere that the prophets are called the Law. Therefore, one hears the Law who, according to Paul, looks not merely at its surface but into its marrow. One does not hear the Law who, like the Galatians, follows only its external shell.

## For it is written that Abraham had two sons: one by a slave woman and one by a free woman.

What he says about Abraham’s two sons is readily understood, since the Apostle himself interprets this allegory. Through these two sons, the two covenants are signified. The sons whom Abraham fathered by another wife after Sarah’s death do not belong to this signification. Consequently, many who read the Apostle but do not know the book of Genesis suppose that Abraham had only two sons.

The Apostle mentions only these two because he had only these two when the events that he subsequently explains were being signified. The son born of the slave woman, who was called Hagar, signifies the Old Testament—that is, the people of the Old Testament—because of the servile yoke of carnal observances and the earthly promises by which they are entangled. Since they merely hope for these things from God, they are not admitted to the spiritual inheritance of the heavenly patrimony.

It is not sufficient, for the purpose of signifying the people who inherit the New Testament, that Isaac was born of a free woman; what matters more here is that he was born according to the promise. Ishmael, however, was born both of a slave woman and according to the flesh. Likewise, Abraham received children from Keturah, whom he later married, not according to the promise but according to the flesh.

Isaac was wonderfully born through the promise, when both parents had grown old. If, relying on the Apostle’s confidence by which he clearly shows that these two are to be understood allegorically, someone should wish also to discern in the children of Keturah some figure of future realities—for these events concerning such persons were not written without the administration of the Holy Spirit—he may perhaps find heresies and schisms signified. For those sons were born of a free woman, as these people are from the Church, but nevertheless they were born according to the flesh.

## But he who was born of the slave woman according to the flesh—he who was born of the free woman through the promise.

It is extremely difficult to demonstrate that only Isaac, who was born of Sarah, was generated through the promise, and not also Ishmael, who was born of Hagar, the Egyptian slave woman. Scripture relates that, when Hagar fled pregnant from Sarah’s persecution and an angel came to her in the desert and urged her to submit to her mistress’s authority, that same angel also said: “I will multiply your offspring exceedingly, and it shall not be numbered for multitude.”

Later, concerning Ishmael—words that no one would doubt were words of promise—the angel says: “He will be a wild man; his hand will be against everyone, and everyone’s hand against him, and he will dwell opposite all his brothers.” Yet it can be said that the angel or God spoke this about Ishmael after he had been conceived, whereas God promised Isaac before he was conceived in Sarah’s womb.

Ishmael was the son of the flesh; Isaac was the son of faith. Abraham fathered Ishmael according to the ordinary course of the flesh, but he received Isaac through the promise, believing against the nature of old age. Who are those born according to the flesh, if not lovers of the world? And who are those born through the promise, if not lovers of the kingdom of heaven—those to whom eternal life has also been promised, who worship God freely?

For the present, we must briefly strive toward higher things, so that we may say that each one of us is first born not according to the promise, when he is instructed in the simple words of Scripture and is still pleased with explanations. But when he has risen to higher things and understood the spiritual Law, then he is generated through the promise. To speak more plainly: those who do the works of Abraham are born daily from Abraham; but those who have the spirit of servitude, again in fear, are born from the Egyptian slave woman.

## These things are spoken allegorically.

“Allegory” properly belongs to the art of grammar: it is one thing represented through another. The Apostle gave us the rule for how we should allegorize, namely, that while the historical truth remains, we should understand the figures. For after saying that Abraham truly had two wives, he then showed what these women themselves signified.

He does the same wherever the honorable deeds of holy people are recounted, but not where sins are condemned. To abandon the mysteries and say that God was either incapable or ignorant is to accuse him either of being unable to display his mysteries in another way or of condemning in advance, without knowing what was necessary for him, the sins of certain people. Moreover, he would not have rebuked and punished those sins later if he himself had wished them to occur for the sake of his mysteries.

You will rarely find commandments interpreted in this way, lest their force should appear to be emptied.

## For these are the two covenants.

One is from Mount Sinai, generating for servitude, which is Hagar. Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, adjoining the Jerusalem that now exists, and it is in slavery with its children.

Nearly everyone explains this passage in the same way, interpreting Hagar, the slave woman, as the Law and the people of the Jews, and Sarah, the free woman, as the Church gathered from the Gentiles, who is the mother of the saints, as Paul says: “She is the mother of us all.”

For a long time this woman did not give birth, before Christ was born from a virgin, and she was barren before Isaac, the laughter of the world, had been recognized from the chosen father with the proclamation of sublime doctrines. For “Abraham” is rendered in our language as “chosen father,” with the sound of the name retained.

Hagar, however, whose name is interpreted as “sojourning,” “pilgrimage,” or “delay,” gives birth to Ishmael, who only hears the commandments and does not perform them: a rustic and bloodthirsty man, pursuing deserts, hostile to all his brothers born from the free woman, and standing opposite them with an adverse countenance.

Nor is it surprising that the Old Testament, established and written on Mount Sinai—which is in Arabia and adjoins the Jerusalem that now exists—is not perpetual, since a sojourn differs from permanent possession, the name of Mount Sinai signifies “temptation,” and Arabia signifies “decline” or “setting.”

## But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.

For this reason Sarah signifies the heavenly Jerusalem, which for a long time was deserted by intercourse with her husband because her barrenness was known. Although the people of the New Testament are new, their predestination with God—and the heavenly Jerusalem itself—is ancient.

He says that the earthly Jerusalem has a husband because she gives birth according to the flesh. But he calls the heavenly Jerusalem, which he says is our mother, barren because she does not give birth according to the flesh and does not suffer labor—that is, she does not travail. Rather, she gives birth spiritually, without suffering, crying out in joy.

The Jerusalem that exists in the present is below, lowly, and sunk in the lowest place.

It is written:

> Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband.

The synagogue had the Law as its husband and, according also to the prophecy of Hannah, was once fruitful in children. But the barren Church, without a husband—Christ—and without any address from the bridegroom’s word, lay for a long time in the desert.

But after the synagogue received the book of divorce into its hands and turned all her husband’s ornaments into the adornment of an idol, then, while the former husband’s single garment rotted away, he wove another belt around his loins and made another loincloth from the Gentiles. Hence, as soon as she was joined to this husband, she conceived and gave birth. Through the prophet Isaiah the Lord immediately cries out: “Was a nation born all at once?”—when, in one day in the Acts of the Apostles, three thousand and five thousand people believed (Acts VI).

I do not think it necessary to speak of the multitude of Christians and the small number of Jews, since throughout the whole world the standards of the cross shine brightly, while scarcely any Jew appears in the cities, and then only rarely and conspicuously.

## But we, brothers, are children of the promise according to Isaac.

We say, therefore, that the Apostle calls them children of the promise according to Isaac because he has not entirely despaired of their salvation, and because he believes that they will return again to the spirit with which they had begun. Let them become children of the free woman; if they have been perfected according to the flesh, they are children of the slave woman.

## But just as then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the spirit, so it is now.

But what does Scripture say?

> Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.

Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman, by whose freedom Christ set us free.

I do not think we can find a place where Ishmael actually persecuted Isaac, except that when the son of the Egyptian woman, who was older, played with Isaac, Sarah was indignant and said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with my son Isaac” (Gen. XXI). A simple game between children is certainly unworthy of expulsion and disinheritance.

But the Apostle, a Hebrew of Hebrews and instructed at the feet of Gamaliel—a teacher who once restrained the Pharisees raging against the Lord by his counsel—understood from Sarah’s words, “The son of the slave woman shall not inherit with my son Isaac,” that the game was not simple, since it is called persecution.

Perhaps Ishmael, being the older child and circumcised at a time when he could already understand and feel what he suffered, was claiming the privileges of the firstborn. Scripture therefore called the quarrel of the children a game. Sarah, unable to endure this and unwilling, from early childhood, to tolerate the son of the slave woman’s customary claim to the privileges of the firstborn, broke out in the words: “Cast out the slave woman with her son. For the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with my son Isaac.”

When this seemed harsh to Abraham—for greater things were always given to firstborn sons—not only that Ishmael should cease to be first, but that he should not even receive an equal portion with his younger brother, God, who wished the free woman to remain within and the slave woman to be expelled outwardly, confirmed Sarah’s words and said to Abraham (Gen. XXII): “Let it not be harsh in your sight concerning the boy and the slave woman. Whatever Sarah says to you, listen to her voice, for in Isaac shall your offspring be called.”

Therefore, just as then the older brother Ishmael persecuted Isaac, who was still nursing and a little child, claiming the privileges of the firstborn by the prerogative of circumcision, so now Ishmael according to the flesh rises up against his younger brother, the Christian people from the Gentiles; he is puffed up and exalts himself.

## Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman.

However much iniquity exalts itself, it is still a slave woman and must be subjected to the saints. However greatly they exalt themselves and boast that they are children of Abraham, as long as they remain children of the slave woman, understand the Law carnally, and live in servile submission under its terror, they cannot share the inheritance with you.

Therefore you must not abandon our mother and follow the slave woman. Although she was the wife of the same husband, she was so only for a time, because Sarah was not yet able to give birth—that is, because the New Testament had not yet been revealed.

## By this freedom Christ set us free.

This freedom must now be applied above all against the yoke of servitude under which those who were dragging these people toward circumcision were held in the works of the Law.

## Chapter V

### Stand firm, and do not again submit to the yoke of servitude.

When he says “stand firm,” he indicates that they have not yet fallen completely; otherwise he would more appropriately say, “Rise.” When he says, “Do not again be held under the yoke of servitude,” we can understand no other yoke here more correctly than circumcision and the other Jewish observances.

For the Galatians, who at the preaching of the Apostle Paul had immediately abandoned idols and passed over to the grace of the gospel, were not returning to the servitude of the Jewish Law, which they had never previously known. Rather, by wishing to observe seasons, to be circumcised in the flesh, and to offer bodily sacrifices, they were in a certain sense returning to the same forms of worship in which they had formerly served through idolatry.

### Behold, I, Paul, say to you:

I, Paul, speak boldly to you, fearing no one and not concealing my name, so that those who hear may be moved not so much by the authority of the one sent as by the authority of the one who sent him. It is as though he were saying: “Behold, imitate me, so that you may not be afraid”; or, “If you are afraid, place the responsibility upon me.”

### For if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.

How are we to understand his saying, “Do not again be held under the yoke of servitude,” when he is writing to people who had never been Jews? He is certainly acting so that they will not be circumcised. But here the interpretation we discussed above is both clarified and confirmed.

For what else can he say to the Gentiles in this passage than that they should benefit from having been freed through faith in Christ from the servitude of their superstition, and should not again wish to become servants under the yoke of carnal observances—observances that, although under God’s Law, bound a carnal people in servitude?

He says that Christ will profit them nothing if they are circumcised, but he means circumcision in the manner in which these people wanted them circumcised: that is, so that they would place the hope of salvation in circumcision of the flesh. For Christ did not profit Timothy nothing because Paul himself circumcised that young man, who was already a Christian. Paul did this because of the scandal that might arise among his own people, without pretending anything, but from the indifference expressed in the words: “Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing” (I Cor. VII).

That circumcision does no harm to one who does not believe salvation to be in it. Circumcision is then unprofitable when it is thought to confer some benefit by itself.

Only those who had already been formed by the revealed faith and whom that faith found already accustomed to such things were not to be prohibited from these observances. In them the prophetic action itself was to be completed: they had previously been held by these practices for the fulfillment of prophecy. If these practices were removed from them as well, the prophecy would seem to have been rejected rather than completed.

But if they were imposed upon the Gentiles, either they would be thought not to have been instituted to promise Christ, or Christ would be thought still to be promised by them.

Thus, before Christ came, the first people of God were commanded to fulfill the Law and the prophets and to observe all the things that these promised. Among them, those who understood what these things referred to were free; those who did not understand were servants.
