The later people, coming to faith because Christ was already proclaimed to have come, suffered, and risen again, were neither compelled to observe these practices nor prohibited from doing so if the same faith found them already instructed in such mysteries. But among those who were devoid of such practices and who believed without being restrained by any inherited condition, custom, or fitting necessity, these observances were also prohibited, so that their cessation might begin to become visible in them.

All those things had been instituted to promise Christ. When he came and fulfilled those promises, they ought now to cease.

### I testify again to every man who receives circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole Law.

God, who first commanded circumcision to Abraham and then to Moses in the Law, established not only circumcision but also many other things to be observed: festivals to be frequented at Jerusalem; burnt offerings of sacrifices every morning and evening; sacrifice at one place only; the fiftieth year of remission; and other matters that every reader can easily extract for himself from the Scriptures.

Therefore, we shall exhort Ebion and his followers, who, after believing in Christ through the gospel, think that people must be circumcised: either let them practice circumcision and all the other things commanded in the Law, or, if it is impossible to do everything, let circumcision also cease, since it was prescribed first among the others as though they were useless.

If they answer that they ought to do only what is possible—for God does not demand from us what we cannot do, but what we can fulfill—we shall say to them that it is not the same God who wishes them to keep the Law and yet abandons those who keep it. Or how will he make them guilty for neglecting the Law when, even if they wish to do so, they cannot fulfill everything?

But we follow the spiritual Law, which says: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deut. XXV). And with the Apostle we understand: “Is it oxen that God cares about? Surely he says this for our sake” (Rom. IX). We observe delicate Sabbaths—not so that our ox, donkey, and lowly animals may do so, of whom it is written: “You save humans and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. XXXV)—but rational human beings and spiritual men.

The animals are those who are slower in understanding and are trained by spiritual people to perform the Lord’s Sabbaths. Nor is this contrary to what was written above: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing,” and what follows: “I testify to every man who receives circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole Law.” He said this so that, through fear of the countless observances written in the works of the Law, they would not be compelled to fulfill them all—something that neither the Jews themselves nor their ancestors were able to do—as Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles. Thus they should abstain from those things to which these people wished to subject them.

### You have been severed from Christ, you who are justified in the Law; you have fallen away from grace.

Just as no one can serve two masters, so it is difficult to fulfill both the shadow and the truth of the Law at the same time. The shadow is in the old Law until the day dawns and the shadows are removed. The truth is in the gospel of Christ. “Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I).

Therefore, whoever thinks that he is justified by some observance of the Law loses the grace of Christ and abandons the gospel that he had held. Having lost grace, he is destroyed with respect to faith in Christ and rests in his own work.

The passage may also be understood as extending generally to the whole Law what he had previously commanded specifically concerning circumcision when he said: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.” He now embraces the whole Law by saying that those who believe they are to be justified by any observance make no progress in Christ’s work.

The meaning is: If you place your hope in the Law, you judge Christ’s grace to be weak. What you have already received freely, you wish to acquire through your own labors, as though you did not possess it.

This had not yet happened, but because their will had begun to move in that direction, he speaks in many places as though it had already happened.

### For through the Spirit, by faith, we await the hope of righteousness.

He uses “Spirit” to distinguish it from the letter. “The hope of righteousness” is to be understood as Christ, because he is himself truth, patience, hope, righteousness, and every virtue. We await his second coming, when he will judge all things. He will then come not in patience but in righteousness, to repay each person according to his works.

Awaiting the presence of that day, the Apostle and those like him say: “May your kingdom come” (Matt. IX), so that, when the Son has handed the kingdom over to God and the Father, and he himself has been subjected along with all things that are subject, the head may in a certain sense be subjected to the body, and God may be “all in all.” For he who is now present partially in individuals will then begin to be wholly present in everyone.

### For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any power, but faith working through love.

Those who wish to live in Christ Jesus must seek the virtues and flee the vices. The things that lie between virtues and vices are neither to be fled nor sought, such as circumcision, uncircumcision, and other things of this kind.

Circumcision is indeed beneficial if you keep the Law. It was therefore useful to those who lived under the Law—not because they were circumcised, but because the oracles of God were entrusted to them, and, by turning them into works, they were not excluded from salvation.

From the time when the gospel shone throughout the whole world, the injury of circumcision has become superfluous. It was effective, like the other matters of the Law, at the time when carnal blessings were also promised to those who kept the Law: if they fulfilled it, they would be blessed in the city and blessed in the field; their barns would be full; and many other things contained in the promises would be theirs (Deut. XXVIII).

But we wish to have power and strength in Christ Jesus—that is, in true circumcision, not Jewish circumcision. For it is not the one who is a Jew outwardly, nor circumcision that is outward in the flesh, but the one who is a Jew inwardly, and circumcision of the heart in the spirit, not in the letter. Circumcision of the flesh therefore profits nothing in Christ; what profits is circumcision of the heart and ears, which removes that reproach of the Jews.

### You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth?

The sense is this: Since you were running, serving the truth rather than images, by what perverse teacher have you been hindered, so that you follow the shadow of the Law and abandon the truth of the gospel?

This persuasion does not come from the one who called you. He does not say that this persuasion belongs to God, but to those who were asserting such things. For this persuasion is carnal, whereas he called them to freedom. He therefore urges them not to listen to any of those who came to persuade them of these things. “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5). Lest anyone say, “Why do you rebuke everyone, when not everyone has gone astray?” he foretells that a little leaven of malice can corrupt the whole lump of the Church. Do not suppose that the plots of a few men who come from Judea and teach something different are to be disregarded, because a little leaven corrupts the whole lump. He says this in another sense also: although they add something from the Law to faith, they nevertheless violate faith, so that it may bear no fruit or be acceptable. He added this lest they perhaps think that they retained the grace of faith intact if they observed a few precepts of the Law.

I have confidence in you in the Lord, that you will think nothing else. Since, therefore, he foresaw in the Spirit that they would believe nothing other than what they were being taught through the Epistle, he says: “I have confidence in you in the Lord, that you will think nothing else.” For the addition of the Lord’s name itself signifies this. If he had judged this merely by conjecture, he could have said only, “I have confidence in you.” But now, by adding “in the Lord,” he prophesied, trusting by a certain divine inspiration that he knew what would happen.

[Col. 0894A]

But the one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he is. They say that he is secretly attacking Peter, about whom he writes above that he resisted him to his face because he was not walking with a straight foot toward the truth of the Gospel. But neither would Paul have spoken with such shameless abuse against a leader of the Church, nor would Peter have deserved to be made responsible for a troubled Church. From this it must be judged that he is speaking of someone else—someone who had either been with the apostles, or had come from Judea, or had believed as one of the Pharisees, or who certainly was regarded as important among the Galatians—so that he would bear the judgment of the troubled Church, whoever he was. The Galatians had therefore been disturbed between spirit and letter, circumcision and mutilation, hidden and manifest Judaism, not knowing what they should do.

More briefly, however, the passage may be understood in this way: “Whoever he is who is drawing you toward the teaching of the Pharisees and desires to be circumcised in the flesh, even if he is eloquent and boasts of his observance of the Law, I say nothing more than what you yourselves cannot deny: that he will bear judgment for this work and will receive the reward due for his labor.” When they wanted to persuade them to accept this slavery and saw that the authority of the apostle Paul was turning them back, they also said that Paul himself held this view, but did not wish to disclose it openly to them. He therefore added his own judgment at the appropriate point.

But I, brothers, if I still preach circumcision, why am I still suffering persecution? We read in the Acts of the Apostles, and the apostle Paul himself often records in his Epistles, that he endured very frequent persecutions from the Jews because he taught that those from the Gentiles who had believed in Christ ought not to be circumcised. These men, then—of whom he said above, “But the one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he is”—added this as well in order to deceive the Galatians: “Not only Peter and James and John and the other apostles in Judea observe circumcision and the other precepts of the Law, but Paul himself also, who taught you otherwise, although the truth of the matter is different. He circumcised Timothy, and frequently became a Jew to the Jews, compelled by the truth.”

Paul now wishes to remove this opinion from the minds of the Galatians and says: “But I, brothers, if I still preach circumcision, why am I still suffering persecution?” All the hatred of the Jews against me, he says, and the madness with which they rage against me, arises from nothing other than the fact that I teach the Gentiles that they ought not to be circumcised or to observe the burdens of the Law, which are superfluous and have already been abolished. But since I suffer persecution, it is clear that I do not preach the circumcision which I destroy. For I do not suffer persecution from the Jews so much because I preach one who was crucified and declare that Jesus is the Christ whom the Law and the Prophets foretold, as because I teach that the Law has been fulfilled. Consequently, those who say that righteousness comes through the Law and not through the grace of faith are enemies of his cross.

Would that those who are troubling you would even mutilate themselves. It is asked how Paul could be the disciple of the one who says, “Bless those who curse you” (Luke 6), and who himself says, “Bless and do not curse” (Rom. 12), and elsewhere, “Nor will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 3); yet now he should both curse those who were troubling the churches of Galatia and curse them with an imprecatory wish: “Would that those who are troubling you would even mutilate themselves.”

The suffering of mutilation is so detestable that even one who inflicts it unwillingly is punished by public laws, while one who castrates himself is regarded as insane. He says, “Let them not merely be circumcised, but even mutilated.” For thus they will become eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven and will cease to sow carnal things. He saw that the whole province, which he himself had led from idolatry to faith in Christ by his own blood and dangers, had been disturbed by a sudden persuasion; and in apostolic grief, the grief of a father, he could not restrain himself. He changed his tone and became angry with those whom he had previously addressed with affection, so that those whom he had been unable to retain by gentleness he might at least hold back by rebuke.

Some say, “Would that they might be cut off from error and grafted into the truth.” Others say, “If they think that this benefits them, let them not merely be circumcised, but also mutilated.” According to this view, Paul did not so much curse them as pray for them, that they might lose those parts of the body through which they were compelled to sin. Just as the Gospel says that it is better for someone to enter the kingdom of heaven without an eye, without a hand, without a foot, or without any other part of the limbs, than to go whole into Gehenna, so now he wishes them rather to lose one part of the body than, on account of possessing an intact body, to be condemned to everlasting fire. For if the removal of a limb is beneficial, much more is the removal—

You, however, brothers, were called to freedom; only do not turn your freedom into an opportunity for the flesh. He says, “You, brothers, were called to freedom,” perhaps because not everyone was able to receive the call to freedom. For this reason you now hear only this warning: do not turn your freedom into an opportunity for the flesh. Through love, the lesser ought to serve the greater, because whoever wishes to be greater will be the servant of all. Nor should one, as a spiritual person, tear Christ’s flesh or give them an opportunity to provoke one another to bite, lest they be consumed by one another.

We may add this interpretation: they were called from the slavery of the Law to the freedom of the Gospel, and above they were told, “Stand firm and do not submit again to the yoke of slavery.” They are now also warned that, while pursuing Christ’s easy yoke and the delightful commands of the Gospel, they must not suppose that this freedom of life allows them to use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh—that is, to live according to the flesh and to be circumcised according to the flesh. Rather, they should stand firm in the spirit, cut away the foreskin of the flesh in the spirit, and, striving toward the higher things of the spirit, abandon the humility of the letter.

[Col. 0895D]

But through love serve one another. For the one who serves through love serves freely and obeys God without misery, doing with love what is taught, not with fear what is compelled. Love then makes us free from the yoke of guilt when, through love, it subjects us in turn to one another’s service; when we regard the goods of others as our own and offer and display our own goods to others as though they were theirs. Love is so great a good that the whole Law is recapitulated in it. Its power is so great that its name is exalted to the point that God himself is called Love.

[Col. 0896A]

For the whole Law is fulfilled in one saying. He now speaks of the whole Law with reference to those works that belong to good morals. For even the precepts concerning the sacraments, when they are properly understood by free people and not observed in a carnal manner by slaves, must be referred to those two commandments: love of God and love of neighbor. It is therefore rightly understood as pertaining to what the Lord also says: “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5). He was going to remove carnal fear and give spiritual love, by which alone the Law can be fulfilled. “Love is the fullness of the Law” (Rom. 13).

Since faith obtains the Holy Spirit, through whom the love of God has been poured into the hearts of those who practice righteousness, no one should in any way boast of good works before the grace of faith. Therefore the Apostle refutes those who boast of the works of the Law by showing that the ancient works of the sacraments were shadows of things to come, and that after the Lord’s coming they are no longer necessary for the free heir. But the works that belong to good morals are not fulfilled except through love, through which faith works.

Accordingly, if some works of the Law are superfluous after faith, while others are of no value before the end, let the righteous live from the end, casting off the heavy burden of slavery and strengthened by Christ’s light load; and let him not overstep the boundaries of righteousness, obeying the light yoke of love. Even the works of the Law that are required can be summed up in one saying and fulfilled in one commandment. Faith alone, therefore, is not sufficient for life, so that the many-fringed precepts of the Law may be gathered together under the one heading of love.

[Col. 0896C]

You shall love your neighbor as yourself. It may be asked why the Apostle here also mentions only love of neighbor, which he says fulfills the Law, and likewise in the Epistle to the Romans, when he was dealing with the same question: “The one who loves another,” he says, “has fulfilled the Law. For, ‘You shall not commit adultery; you shall not murder; you shall not steal; you shall not covet’; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Love of neighbor does no evil. Love, therefore, is the fullness of the Law” (Rom. 13).

Since perfect love consists in the two commandments, love of God and love of neighbor, why does the Apostle in both this Epistle and that one mention only love of neighbor? Is it not because people can lie about their love of God, since fewer occasions test it, whereas in love of neighbor they are more easily convicted of not possessing it, when they act unjustly toward other people?

It follows that whoever loves God with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his mind also loves his neighbor as himself, because this is commanded by the one whom he loves with all his heart, soul, and mind. Likewise, who can love his neighbor—that is, every human being—as himself unless he loves God, by whose command and gift he can fulfill love of neighbor? Since, therefore, the two commandments are such that neither can be kept without the other, it is often sufficient to mention one of them when the subject is works of righteousness, namely, the one by which a person is more readily convicted.

[Col. 0897A]

Hence John says: “The one who does not love his brother, whom he sees, how can he love God, whom he does not see?” (1 John 4). For some people claimed to possess love of God, but were shown not to possess it by their hatred of their brother. It is easy to judge this in daily life and conduct.

Love, or charity, is completed in four ways: first, God is to be loved; second, we are to love ourselves; third, our neighbors; fourth, our enemies. God is to be loved more than ourselves, our neighbor as ourselves, and our enemy as a neighbor. Unless we love God first, we cannot love ourselves. This is what it means not to sin. And if we do not love ourselves, according to what pattern will we love our neighbors? If we do not love our neighbor, how much less will we love our enemy?

If, then, we wish to possess love, let us first love God more than our own souls. This is proved if, for God’s sake, we disregard even our own salvation and our own souls. Faith alone, therefore, is not sufficient for life unless one loves one’s neighbor as oneself—not merely refraining from doing him the evil one does not wish for oneself, but also doing him the good one wishes another to do to oneself—and thus fulfilling the whole Law, which has two kinds of commandments: not doing evil and doing good.

[Col. 0897B]

But if you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another. Through this vice of quarrelsomeness and envy, destructive arrangements were especially being fostered among them: each speaking evil of the other and seeking his own glory and a vain victory through contention. For when you judge yourselves better than one another, when you disparage another, when you are tortured by another’s prosperity and turn another’s good into your own evil, then you bite one another. And when you think that you avenge yourselves by cursing, the fellowship of the people is consumed by these pursuits as it is divided into factions.

How, however, can they avoid these things unless they walk by the spirit and do not fulfill the desires of the flesh? It is better not to think that Paul suddenly breaks into extraordinary commandments contrary to the argument and sequence of the whole Epistle, but to understand everything as referring to circumcision and observance of the Law.

“If others trouble you,” he says, “and you yourselves are troubled, if, in reading the whole of the ancient Scripture, you understand it exactly as it is written—‘An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth’ (Deut. 19)—and anger desires vengeance, while vengeance inflicts pain, which the Law not only does not prohibit but even commands, restoring justice through retaliation, then it follows that the stripped must strip another, the wounded must wound again, the devoured must bite back, and what appears to be justice becomes destruction: it does not vindicate one person but consumes both.”

I say, then: walk by the spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh. If, therefore, one does not consent to the desires of the flesh, however strongly they may be stirred, they are nevertheless not brought to completion in deeds. Accordingly, when the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, so that we do not do the things we wish, neither are the desires of the flesh fulfilled, even though they act, nor are our good works fulfilled, even though they are performed.

Just as the desire of the flesh is fulfilled when the spirit consents to it in evil works, so that it does not desire against it but together with it, so our good works will be fulfilled when the flesh has consented to the spirit in such a way that it itself no longer desires against the spirit. When we desire the perfection of righteousness, this is what we wish, and we must wish it with uninterrupted intention. But because we cannot bring this to completion in this corruptible flesh, he therefore said to the Romans: “To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find” (Rom. 7). Or, as the Greek manuscripts have it: “To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good—not”; that is, accomplishing the good is not present with me.

He does not say “to do” but “to accomplish the good.” For to do good is not to follow the desires; to accomplish the good is not to desire. What he says to the Galatians, “You shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh,” corresponds inversely to what he says to the Romans: “I do not find how to accomplish the good.” For neither are those desires fulfilled in evil when the assent of our will does not join them, nor is our will fulfilled in good so long as the movement of those desires, to which we do not consent, remains.

This conflict, in which even the baptized struggle as in an athletic contest when the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, belongs not to Jews or to any others, but fully to Christians, to the faithful who live well.

[Col. 0898C]

For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. The flesh does not desire without the soul, although the flesh is said to desire, because the soul desires carnally. The flesh desires nothing except through the soul. But the flesh is said to desire against the spirit when the soul, through carnal desire, resists the spirit. Then the flesh desires adultery, while the spirit desires chastity.

We are all of this: even the flesh itself, which dies when the soul departs, is our weaker part. It is not to be fled from and abandoned, but is to be received and restored. A person will then be righteous without any sin at all, when no law in his members resists the law of his mind. Once received again, the flesh will not thereafter be abandoned. Hence he says: “It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body.”

Since above we had begun to explain this passage according to a twofold interpretation, what we omitted must now be supplied. “The flesh desires against the spirit” means that the fleshly understanding of history and Scripture resists allegory and spiritual teaching. “The spirit against the flesh” means that higher things resist lower things, eternal things resist temporal things, and truth resists shadow. The fleshly sense of Scripture, because it cannot be fulfilled—for we cannot do everything that has been written—shows that we are not placed in a position to fulfill the Law by our own power, since even if we wish to follow the letter, impossibility prevents it.

[Col. 0898D]

These are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever things you wish. Reason causes the result not to follow the will, because in this life the flesh fights against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh. Through perfect sanctification, however, it comes about that every carnal appetite is subjected to our enlightened and vivified spirit—that is, to our will.

Just as we now see ourselves deprived of many childish pleasures which, when denied to us as children, tormented us most sharply, so we must believe that the same will be true of every carnal pleasure when perfect holiness has restored the whole person. But now, so long as there is within us something that resists the good will, we need the help of God, of good people, and of good angels, so that, until our wound is healed, it is not so grievously troubled that it destroys even the good will.

We deserved this death through sin; and sin was entirely a matter of free choice. In paradise no pain denied pleasure to the good will, nor did anything resist the human being who was rightly ordered. But now pleasure gradually steals in and mortifies the soul, so that, if it wishes to abstain, it cannot do so without distress and anguish.

[Col. 0899B]

But if you are led by the spirit, you are not under the Law. We should understand those to be under the Law whose spirit desires against the flesh in such a way that they do not do the things they wish—that is, they do not keep themselves joined together in the love of righteousness, but are conquered by the flesh that desires against them. Not only does the flesh resist the law of their mind, it also takes them captive under the law of sin, which is in their mortal members.

For those who are not led by the spirit must consequently be led by the flesh. To suffer the opposition of the flesh is not itself condemnation; to be led by the flesh is condemnation. Therefore he says, “But if you are led by the spirit, you are no longer under the Law.”

Above also he did not say, “Walk by the spirit and do not have the desires of the flesh,” but “Do not fulfill them.” For not to have them at all is no longer the contest but the prize of the contest, if we obtain victory by persevering under grace. The transformation of the body into an immortal state alone will have no desires of the flesh.

And if you occupy yourselves entirely with spiritual things, you have no need of the Law; it was given for carnal people. “If you are led by the spirit,” he says, “you are not under the Law.” Certainly he is speaking of the Law, which instills fear but does not bestow love, because “the love of God has been poured into your hearts,” not through the letter of the Law but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5). This is the law of freedom, not of slavery.

To the extent that a person is led by the spirit, he is not under the Law, because to the extent that he delights in the Law of God, he is not under fear of the Law; for fear contains torment, not delight.

[Col. 0899D]

Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity, shamelessness, the service of idols, sorcery, enmities, contentions, rivalries, jealousies, angers, quarrels, dissensions, heresies, envies, drunkenness, revelries. Those who consent to carnal desires and decide that these things ought to be done commit them, even if they are not given the ability to carry them out.

Those, however, who are affected by such movements yet remain steadfast in greater love—who not only do not offer the members of their body for evil action, but do not even consent by a sign of assent to offer them—do not commit these things, and therefore will inherit the kingdom of God. For sin no longer reigns in their mortal body so as to obey its desires, even though sin dwells in that same mortal body, since the force of our natural habit has not yet been extinguished—the force in which we were born mortal and which we have increased by our own sins, adding to what we had carried from the condemnation arising from the origin of human sin.

It is one thing not to sin and another not to have sin. In the person in whom sin does not reign, there is no sinning—that is, he does not obey its desires. But in the person in whom these desires do not exist at all, there is not only no sinning; there is also no sin. Although this can be accomplished in many respects in the present life, it cannot be completed in every respect except in the resurrection of the flesh and its transformation.

Why, then, does the teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth call all these and similar things works of the flesh? Because, in the manner of speech by which the whole is signified by a part, he wishes the human being himself to be understood by the name “flesh.”

If someone says that the flesh is the cause of the evil conduct of every kind of vice, on the grounds that the soul, affected by the flesh, lives in this way, he plainly has not considered the whole nature of the human being carefully. The corruptible body does indeed burden the soul. But the corruption of the body, which burdens the soul, is not the cause of the first sin but its punishment. Nor did corruptible flesh make the soul sinful; rather, the sinful soul made the flesh corruptible.

Although certain incentives to vice and the vicious desires themselves arise from this corruption of the flesh, not every vice of an evil life is nevertheless to be attributed to the flesh, lest by this reasoning we absolve the devil from all these things, since he has no flesh.

Who would not understand the service rendered to idols, sorcery, enmities, contentions, jealousies, rivalries, dissensions, heresies, and envies to be vices of the mind rather than of the flesh? It can happen that someone abstains from bodily pleasures because of idolatry or the error of some heresy; yet even then, although he appears to despise and restrain the lust of the flesh, apostolic authority convicts him of living according to the flesh. He is shown to be committing the damnable works of the flesh precisely in abstaining from the pleasures of the flesh.

For if the devil does not do the things done by a fornicator or a drunkard, or whatever evil belongs to the pleasures of the flesh—he who has no flesh—he cannot nevertheless be said to be without guilt, since he is also the hidden persuader and instigator of such crimes. Yet he is especially proud and envious, and this viciousness has so taken possession of him that on account of it he was destined to eternal punishment in the prisons of this dark air.

The Apostle attributes these vices, which hold dominion in the devil, to the flesh, although it is certain that the devil has no flesh. For he says that enmities, contentions, rivalries, jealousies, dissensions, and envies are works of the flesh. The head and origin of all these evils is pride, which reigns in the devil without flesh.

Since he possesses all these things without flesh, how are they works of the flesh unless they are works of the human being, whom the Apostle calls “flesh”? If the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, and all false doctrines that resist God are hostile to him, then heresies are consequently referred to the works of the flesh as hostile to God. In Greek, heresy is named from “choice” (*hairesis*), because each person chooses for himself the discipline that he thinks better.

Therefore whoever understands Scripture otherwise than the sense of the Holy Spirit requires—the Spirit by whom it was written—may be called a heretic, even if he has not departed from the Church; and he belongs to the works of the flesh because he chooses what is worse.

[Col. 0901A]

And things like these, which I warn you about, as I warned you before: those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. It may cause difficulty that he says, “which I warn you about, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God,” if one asks where he warned them previously, since this is not found in this Epistle.

Therefore either he had warned them of this when he was present, or he had learned that the Epistle sent to the Corinthians had reached them. For there he says: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor those who curse, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6).

After listing the works of the flesh, which close the kingdom of God, he then added the works of the spirit, which he calls the fruit of the spirit.

[Col. 0901B]

The fruit of the spirit is love. The first of all the virtues is love, which, as we have noted, is divided into four parts: love of God, love of oneself, love of neighbor, and love of the enemy.

[Col. 0901C]

Spiritual joy, peace. This is when the mind is tranquil and disturbed by no passions.

Patience. To endure injuries inflicted upon one.

Goodness. Always to desire to do good.

Kindness. It injures no one and does not desire injury to be done.

It should be noted that faith too is given by God, and the Apostle placed it seventh among the fruits of the spirit. This also should be noted, because it comes from God.

Faith. Either believing in God or fulfilling promises made to human beings.

Moderation. Not becoming angry.

Self-control. Self-control is for a time.

Chastity. Everlasting: to restrain oneself not only from fornication but from every iniquity.

[Col. 0901D]

Against such things there is no law. For the Law did not prohibit these things, and whoever fulfills the New Testament is not under the Old Testament. From this we should understand those to be placed under the Law in whom these things do not reign. For in those in whom these things reign, they themselves use the Law lawfully, because the Law was not set over them for coercion. Their righteousness is a greater and more powerful delight.

He does not say, “Against these things there is no law,” but “against such things”—that is, whether these things or other things of the same kind. Nevertheless, for those who consider carefully, the opposition between carnal and spiritual works is not here entirely unordered and confused. The reason it is concealed is that fewer or individual virtues are set against several vices.

For when he placed fornications at the head of carnal vices and love at the head of spiritual virtues, who among those devoted to the divine writings would not be prompted to examine the rest? If fornication is love released and wandering from lawful marriage in pursuit of the pleasure of satisfying lust, what is joined together more lawfully for spiritual fruitfulness than the soul with God? The more firmly it adheres to him, the more incorruptible it is.

Let it adhere through love. Love is therefore rightly opposed to fornication, since in love alone chastity is guarded. Impurity consists in all the disturbances conceived from that fornication, and spiritual joy, which is tranquility, is opposed to it.

The service of idols is the final fornication of the soul. On its account the most furious war was waged against the Gospel by those reconciled to God; its remnants, although almost lulled to sleep, still remain warm. Peace, therefore, is opposed to it—the peace by which we are reconciled to God. When the same peace is preserved with human beings, it heals in us the vices of sorcery, enmities, contentions, rivalries, jealousies, and dissensions.

To conduct ourselves with proper moderation among those with whom we live, patience serves for enduring, kindness for caring, and goodness for forgiving. Against heresies faith is set; against envy, gentleness; against drunkenness and revelries, self-control.

Let no one suppose that envy is the same as rivalry. They are neighbors, and because of this proximity either is often used in place of the other: rivalry for envy, or envy for rivalry. But since both are mentioned here in their proper places, they plainly demand that we distinguish them.

Rivalry is grief of mind when someone else attains what two or more people desired and what cannot be possessed except by one. Peace heals this, because we desire that which, if all who desire it attain it, makes them one in one thing.

Envy, however, is grief of mind when someone appears unworthy of attaining something, even something that you did not desire. The difference between the envious person and the person who is envied is that the envious person envies someone more fortunate, whereas the envied person is the one who suffers envy from another. Gentleness heals this, when a person, submitting the matter to God’s judgment, does not resist his will, but trusts him more than himself and believes that what he had considered undeserved was rightly done.

These spiritual fruits therefore reign in the person in whom sins do not reign. These good things reign when they delight so greatly that, in temptations, they hold the mind fast and prevent it from falling into consent to sin.

[Col. 0902D]

Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. How have they crucified it except through that chaste fear which remains forever and ever, by which we take care not to offend the one whom we love with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind?

Therefore, if all the members have been crucified together in this way, and every work of sin has been destroyed in us, and the flesh, hanging as it were upon the cross, has been extinguished and mortified with respect to the desires of the world, so that it desires nothing in the world against God’s commandments, why should it be suitable for them to keep the Law according to the letter, which was given to restrain the vices of sinners?

At the same time, this should be noted: he says that those belong to Christ who have crucified their flesh with its vices. This statement refutes those who think that faith alone is sufficient for the salvation of their souls.

[Col. 0903A]

## ON CHAPTER 6

If we live by the spirit, let us also walk by the spirit. Let us serve one another not through the Law but through love.

We ought not to quarrel over the interpretation of the Scriptures and say, for example, “Circumcision is better.” No, rather, “The foreskin.” The historical sense should be despised and allegory followed.

Indeed, allegory is vain and shadowy, supported by no roots of truth; hence envy arises among them in turn. “They wish to exclude you,” he says, “so that you may rival them.” They did not so much wish to teach the truth of the Law as to prevail.

They were deceived in this respect: they could not deny that they ought to follow the Holy Spirit, the defender and leader of their freedom. But, having turned carnally toward servile works, they did not understand that they were trying to turn themselves backward.

For this reason he does not say, “If we live by the spirit, let us follow the spirit.” They admitted that they ought to serve the Holy Spirit, but they wanted to follow him not with their spirit but with their flesh—not spiritually possessing the grace of God, but placing their hope of salvation in carnal circumcision and other things of this kind.

He speaks to those who, through mutual rivalry, wished to put themselves above one another: “Through the spirit,” he says, “we have life, but only if we conduct ourselves spiritually and do not serve the Law in a carnal manner” (Rom. 8).

[Col. 0903B]

Let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another, envying one another. After he had instructed them magnificently and in a wholly divine order against those by whom they were being led into slavery to the Law, he cautiously added this warning, lest, having become better instructed and wishing to answer the accusations of carnal people, they should devote themselves to quarrels and, while refusing to serve the burdens of the Law, they should serve vain desires through their appetite for empty glory.

Nothing proves a spiritual person so clearly as the way he deals with another’s sin: whether he considers that person’s liberation rather than insult, and assistance rather than abuse. To the extent that ability permits, he takes the burden upon himself. Therefore he says:

Brothers, and if someone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness. He also exhorts the one who is spiritual not to cease, out of fear for himself, from extending a hand to the one who is falling. And appropriately he calls the person overtaken in an offense a *human being*, who can die; by that very designation he shows the frailty of our condition, so that one who, like a human being deceived by error and plunged into an abyss, cannot raise himself up without help and a helper, may be deemed worthy of pardon. But the word “human” is not added to “spiritual”; rather, as though speaking to God, he commands the spiritual person to restore the human being overtaken in an offense—or, as it is better expressed in Greek, “to perfect” him in a spirit of gentleness. Now one who is being perfected is not lacking in everything, but only in some things. Accordingly, if he has gone astray after being overtaken not by many sins but by some particular fault, the spiritual person should apply a spirit of gentleness and meekness in correcting the sinner, lest he wish to correct the erring person harshly, angrily, or sorrowfully. Instead, he should encourage him, promising salvation and pledging pardon; he should bring forward Christ’s testimony, that one weighed down beneath the heavy burden of the law and sins is invited to his gentle yoke and light burden, so that they may learn that he is humble, mild, and gentle of heart, and may find rest for their souls (Matt. XI). This passage must be explained more fully at the end of the Epistle to the Romans. There, when he was writing similarly about the Jews’ foods and observances, and was describing as strong and perfect those who disregarded the precepts of the law according to the letter, but as weak and childish those who were still guided by ancient custom, and when he saw that there was a quarrel between the spiritual and the carnal, he admonished the spiritual not to despise the carnal, and said: “Receive the one who is weak in faith, not for disputes about opinions; for one believes that he may eat all things, but the weak person eats alone. Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat, and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats. For God has received him. Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master. And he will stand, for God is able to make him stand” (Rom. XIV). And after discussing this meaning at length in the intervening passage, he added at the end: “Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food.” And again: “We who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each of you please his neighbor for his good, for his edification” (Rom. XV).

Considering yourself, lest you also be tempted. Nothing inclines one so greatly toward mercy as the thought of one’s own danger. When you consider yourself, because you too are human and may be overtaken by some sin and then need the help of God and of your neighbor—for the healthy must sustain the weak and bury the dead, because they undoubtedly believe that they too can become weak and die—

Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ. Because the observance of the Old Testament involved fear, he could not have indicated more openly that charity is the gift of the New Testament than in this passage, where the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ.” For this is understood to be the law of Christ, by which the Lord himself commanded that we love one another, establishing the whole weight of the command in this saying, when he declared: “By this it is known that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John XIII). The work of this love is to bear one another’s burdens. But this work is not everlasting; it does, however, lead to everlasting blessedness, in which there will be none of our burdens that we are commanded to bear for one another. For now, in this life—that is, while we are on this road—let us bear our burdens, so that you may reach that life which is free from every burden. Nothing so proves a friend as bearing the burden of a friend. Yet we would not bear one another’s burdens if both persons’ time of weakness were the same, or if the kind of weakness were the same; rather, different times and different kinds of weakness make it possible for us to bear one another’s burdens. For example, you will bear your brother’s anger when you are not angry against him, so that again, at the time when anger has overtaken you, he may support you with gentleness and tranquility. But let us also connect this passage with what precedes, for it admits of a twofold interpretation. If someone is weak in faith and is still nourished with the milk of infancy, and cannot so quickly pass from legal observance to spiritual mysteries, then you who are stronger should bear his burdens, lest your knowledge destroy the brother for whom Christ died. The one who assists a poor brother weighed down by the burden of want also bears his brother’s need.

For if anyone thinks that he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. His flatterers do not deceive him; he deceives himself instead, because, being more present to himself than they are, he prefers to seek himself in them rather than in himself. Therefore he says: “If anyone thinks that he is something”—in that very belief that he is something—and judges himself not by clemency toward his neighbor but by his own work and labor, relying solely on his own virtue, then by this very arrogance he becomes nothing, and he deceives himself. He deceives his mind who thinks himself wise. And according to Isaiah: “Wise in his own eyes and understanding in his own sight” (Isa. V). The meaning of this passage can be connected with circumcision and the law in this way: the spiritual person who has no mercy for his neighbor, despising the humble because he himself is higher, deceives himself, not knowing that this is the law of the Spirit: that we should love one another.

But let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another. For each person will bear his own burden. “And not in another”—that is, when another praises him. Our flatterers therefore do not lessen the burdens of our conscience; and would that they did not often increase them as well, lest, when they take offense, our praise be diminished, since we neglect to correct them through reproof or ostentatiously display something of our own to them rather than show it steadfastly. I pass over the things that people invent and falsely claim about themselves for the sake of human praise. What is more darkened by blindness than to hunt after human error in order to obtain the emptiest glory, and to despise God as witness in one’s heart? It is as though the error of the person who thinks you good could in any way be compared with your own error, when you strive to please a human being by a false good while displeasing God by an evil one.

For each person will bear his own burden. This appears to contradict what precedes, where he says: “Bear one another’s burdens.” For if each person will bear his own burden, one person cannot bear another’s burden. But we must observe that there he commanded us to support one another when we sin in this life and to help one another in the present age; here, however, he is speaking of the Lord’s judgment at the resurrection, when we will be judged as sinners or as saints according to our own work—not on account of another’s sin or by comparison with someone worse—and each person will receive according to his work. Although obscurely, this brief statement teaches us a new doctrine which lies hidden: while we are in the present age, we can help one another either by prayers or by counsels. But when we have come before Christ’s tribunal, neither Job, nor Daniel, nor Noah will be able to plead for anyone; each person will bear his own burden (Ezek. XIV).

Let the one who is being catechized share all good things with the one who catechizes him. The meaning, then, is this: above he had commanded the spiritual to instruct those who had been overtaken in some offense in a spirit of gentleness and to bear one another’s burdens, fulfilling the law of Christ. Now, conversely, he commands those who were still weaker, disciples, and carnal, that just as they reap spiritual things from their teachers, so they should provide teachers with carnal things. For the teachers, devoting themselves entirely to divine instruction and study, need the necessities of this life. Thus what is written concerning the manna may be fulfilled: “The one who gathered much did not have too much, and the one who gathered little did not have too little” (II Cor. VIII). In the present passage he calls “good things,” according to popular usage and common custom, food, clothing, and the other things that people count among good things. “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these things” (I Tim. VI). Nor is it surprising that Paul designated things necessary for the body by the name “good,” since our Savior also said to those who had not yet risen to the summit of the virtues but were still walking at a lower level and asking that faith be added to them: “If you, though evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him?” (Matt. VII).

Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap. Foreseeing in the Spirit that those who were being instructed and ought to provide their teachers with the expenses and necessities of life might plead poverty and say, “My field has dried up from drought this year; hail has destroyed my vineyard; the revenues that might have existed have been seized by taxes; I have no means by which to contribute what is commanded,” he added: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked.” He knows, he says, your hearts; he is not ignorant of your resources. An excuse that seems plausible may somehow please a human being, but it cannot deceive God. At the same time, he urges them to provide what has been commanded, calling it seed, so that no one may think lost what he will receive back with multiplied interest.

[Col. 0906D]

For the one who sows in his own flesh will reap corruption from the flesh. He says this about lovers of pleasure rather than of God. A person sows in his own flesh when he does everything he does—even if it appears good—so that he may fare well according to the flesh.

But the one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit. Sowing in the Spirit means serving righteousness from faith with charity, and not obeying the desires of sin, although these desires arise from mortal flesh. The harvest of eternal life will come when death, the final enemy, has been destroyed, when mortality has been swallowed up by life, and this corruptible nature has put on incorruption. Therefore, at this third stage, in which we are under grace, we ought to sow the good works already mentioned above. Alternatively: the one who understands the law carnally also expects carnal promises, things that are corrupted in the present age. But the spiritual hearer sows in the Spirit and will reap eternal life from the Spirit. The order of the discourse should also be noted and connected with what precedes: the person who sows in the Spirit is called a human being, although when he begins to reap eternal life he may perhaps cease to be a human being. It should likewise be observed that the one who sows in the flesh is described with the addition “his own flesh.” But the one who sows in the Spirit is not said to sow “in his own spirit,” but simply “in the Spirit.” For the one who sows good does not sow in anything of his own, but in the Spirit of God, from whom he will also reap eternal life.

But in doing good, let us not grow weary. An unfailing reward, therefore, will follow unfailing righteousness. He urges to perseverance those who expect the reward of good work in this life, not knowing that just as there is one season for sowing and another for harvest in the case of seed, so in the present life the works that are now sown either in the Spirit or in the flesh are the time of sowing. The harvest of works is the future judgment. [Sic: “so too, in the present life, the works which are reaped either in the Spirit or in the flesh are the sowing; but the harvest is the future judgment, and according to the quality or diversity of the sowing, etc.”] According to the quality of the seed, we produce different measures, a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit. No one can reap such a field while growing weary. “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X). How fitting is it, then, that while sinners increase daily in evil works, we should grow weary in good work?

For in due season we shall reap, if we do not grow weary. Now is the time for sowing, not for reaping. Let us not therefore seek to receive our reward here, lest, when the tender grass is abandoned in winter, it become unfruitful because of its bitterness, and nothing remain to be reaped in the future. For it will be said to us: “You received your good things during your lifetime.” And again: “They have received their reward” (Luke XVI; Matt. V).

Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all. The time of sowing, as we have said, is the present time, the life through which we are passing. In it we may sow whatever we wish; when this life has passed, the time for working will be taken away. Hence the Savior also says: “Work while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work” (John XI).

Especially to those who are members of the household of faith. Who are we to understand here except Christians? We ought to extend the work of mercy to all people—to Jews, pagans, and Christians, to the good and the bad—lest we appear to deny them what God does not deny us. Yet especially to those who, together with us, render God a particular faith and service. Eternal life should be desired for all with equal love, but the same works of love cannot be shown to all. It seems to me that this passage can also be connected with what precedes, so that he calls those who are members of the household of faith the teachers to whom he had commanded above that all the things regarded as good should be supplied by their hearers. Then, having taught that the works of the law themselves, which are beneficial and pertain to good conduct, can be fulfilled only through the love that belongs to faith and not through slavish fear, he returns to the subject on which the whole argument is concerned.

See with what large letters I have written to you with my own hand. Those who wanted to circumcise the Galatians had spread the claim that Paul did one thing and preached another, destroying his teaching by his conduct, since the one who asserted that the law had been abolished was himself found to be in the law. Because Paul could not personally overturn this opinion before everyone—he was prevented by the bonds he was enduring on account of Christ’s martyrdom—he makes himself present through the letter. And lest any suspicion arise that the Epistle had been forged, from this point to the end he wrote it himself by hand, showing that the preceding portion had been written by someone else. That letters were sent under his name by false teachers he also demonstrates to the Thessalonians, writing: “We ask you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering to him, that you not be quickly shaken from your understanding or terrified, either by spirit, or by word, or by a letter allegedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were imminent, lest anyone deceive you in any way” (II Thess. II). And in order to free the whole Epistle he was sending from suspicion of forgery, he subscribed it at the end in his own hand, saying: “The greeting is by the hand of Paul, which is the sign in every Epistle.” That is: understand how confidently I have written what I have added with my own hand, and that I have feared no one in writing the letter myself. Or, if we understand “works” as referring to the hands—for which reason it is frequently said even among the prophets, “The word of the Lord which came by the hand of Jeremiah,” or “of Haggai”—then we may know, by this analogy, that the word of God was also made by the hand of Paul.

All who want to make a good showing in the flesh compel you to be circumcised, only so that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ. The Jews greatly persecuted those who seemed to abandon the observances handed down by men. Paul shows clearly enough how much he feared them when he wanted to write such a letter with his own hand. He therefore teaches that fear was still at work in these people, as though they were subject to the law, since they compelled the Gentiles to be circumcised. For this reason he had already shown above the point from which he had written his subscription by hand, and now he repeats what he had subscribed. Gaius Caesar, Octavian Augustus, and Tiberius, Augustus’s successor, promulgated laws that the Jews dispersed throughout the whole Roman Empire should live according to their own rite and serve the ceremonies of their fathers. Therefore, whoever was circumcised, even if he believed in Christ, was regarded by the Gentiles as a Jew. But whoever, being uncircumcised, professed by his foreskin that he was not a Jew became liable to persecution from both Gentiles and Jews. Wishing to avoid these persecutions, those who had corrupted the Galatians persuaded the disciples to accept circumcision as a defense. The Apostle now calls this “confidence in the flesh,” because they proposed circumcision in persecution both to the Gentiles whom they feared and to the Jews whom they wanted to please. For neither could the Jews prosecute them, nor the Gentiles, who saw them circumcising even proselytes and themselves observing the precepts of the law.

For those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the law; but they want you to be circumcised. If circumcision caused the law to be kept, this persuasion would seem to have some rational basis. But it is motivated by earthly prosperity, whether by the desire to obtain it or the fear of losing it. Therefore they do not truly keep the law, because carnal desire—which changes the sinner rather than increases him—is not healed by another desire. Carnal fear and desire make slaves of those who think that they are observing everything carnally. Hence the whole of what they strive for, do, and attempt is this: to boast and exult among the Jews over the injury done to your flesh, and to boast that they have circumcised Gentiles through their own instruction. They do all this so that they may please the Jews and find rest while hostility toward the law assails them [or: “when hostility toward the law has been overcome, find rest”]. Alternatively:

For those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the law. By “keeping the law” he means not killing, not committing adultery, not bearing false witness, and whatever else is clearly seen to pertain to good conduct. For it has already been said that these things cannot be fulfilled except through charity and the hope of eternal goods received through faith.

So that they may boast in your flesh. That is, so that they may not only avoid persecution from the Jews, who could scarcely tolerate the law’s being betrayed by the uncircumcised, but also boast before them that they have made so many proselytes. For the Lord said that, in order to make one proselyte, the Jews would travel around sea and land (Matt. XXIII).

But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world. I boast not in my own righteousness or doctrine but in the faith of the cross, through which all my sins have been forgiven. I died to the world, so that I might not hold it—that is, so that the world could neither harm me nor I desire anything from the world. The one who boasts in the cross of Christ does not wish to please in the flesh, because he does not fear the persecutions of carnal people, which Christ first endured in order to be crucified and to provide an example for those who follow his footsteps. Or, alternatively, the world had been crucified to him because he no longer loved it, since it was dead to his heart; and he had also crucified himself to the world, because he strove to present himself to it in such a way that, as though dead, he could not be desired by it. For if one is dead and the other alive in one place, and the dead person does not see the living, the living nevertheless sees the dead. But if both are dead to each other, neither sees the other. Thus the person who no longer loves the world, yet is loved by it without seeing it, does not see the world as though he were dead; nevertheless, the world, still dead, sees him. But if he neither retains the world in his love nor is held in turn by the world’s love, then both are extinguished for each other, because, while neither desires the other, each, as though dead, pays no attention to the other. Since, therefore, Paul neither sought the world’s glory nor was himself sought by the world’s glory, he boasts that both he has been crucified to the world and the world to him. Because many desire this but do not rise to the height of complete extinction, he therefore says:

For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision. At the present time circumcision does not help, and uncircumcision does not harm; only this helps: that someone, reborn through a new circumcision, should live accordingly. Here the Apostle maintains to the end the principle of indifference, lest anyone think that he acted deceitfully in circumcising Timothy, or that he would circumcise anyone else if some such reason should arise. For he shows that circumcision itself does not harm believers, but that it is the placing of hope for salvation in such observances that does harm. In the Acts of the Apostles, too, they are found persuading people in this way, denying that those who had believed from among the Gentiles could be saved in any other manner. The Apostle therefore refutes not the deed itself but the destructive error associated with it when he says: “Neither circumcision is anything, nor uncircumcision.”

But a new creation. By “new creation” he means the new life through faith in Jesus Christ, in which the body of our humiliation will be transformed, conformed to the body of Christ’s glory, when the old things have passed away and all things have become new.

And upon all who follow this rule, peace and mercy, and upon the Israel of God. That is, upon those who are truly being prepared for the vision of God—not upon those who are called by this name but, through carnal blindness, do not wish to see God, since they reject his grace and desire to be slaves of temporal things. He is called “the Israel of God” in distinction from the one who has ceased to be God’s Israel. For they say that they are Jews, and are not, but lie, since they belong to the synagogue of Satan. Nor is it surprising that, to distinguish spiritual Israel, carnal Israel is mentioned—the Israel that possesses neither peace nor mercy, of which it is also written to the Corinthians: “Look at Israel according to the flesh” (I Cor. X).

From now on let no one trouble me. Let no one question me any longer as though in doubt, for I have now explained the whole truth. He says this because he does not want the weariness caused by turbulent disputes to be imposed upon him when the subject has been sufficiently explained, both in the Epistle he wrote to the Romans and in this one itself.

For I bear the marks of Jesus in my body. That is, I carry on my body signs and marks not of circumcision but of the cross, through suffering; I bear the wounds and scourging that I endure for Christ, and I have other struggles and conflicts with my flesh, which fight alongside me in the persecutions I suffer. “Marks” (*stigmata*) are certain signs of servile punishments. Thus, for example, if a slave has been placed in fetters because of an offense—that is, because of a fault—or has suffered something of this kind, he is said to bear marks. For this reason, in the law of manumission he belongs to an inferior order. The Apostle therefore wanted to call the signs of the punishments he suffered from persecution “marks.” He knew that these had been repaid to him because of the guilt of the persecution by which he had persecuted the churches of Christ, just as the Lord himself said to Ananias when that same Ananias feared him as a persecutor of Christians: “I will show him,” he said, “what he must suffer for my name.” Nevertheless, because of the forgiveness of sins in which he had been baptized, all those tribulations did not work for his destruction but for the crown of victory. The conclusion of the Epistle is evidently like a subscription. For he uses this formula in some other Epistles as well:

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.” This is Paul’s subscription. He wishes the Lord’s grace—not the works of the law—to accompany them. “With your spirit,” he says, not “with the flesh,” in whose circumcision carnal people boast. But you have been circumcised spiritually, and you live spiritually.

[Col. 0911A]

## EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON BY CLAUDIUS, BISHOP

(From Mai’s *Spicilegium*, vol. IX.)

[Col. 0911B]

## EDITOR’S NOTICE

The expositions of the Epistles of the Apostle Paul by Claudius, bishop of Turin, who lived under Louis the Pious, lie both elsewhere and in ancient codices of the Vatican Library. I once intended to publish them, at the time when I edited the prologue to the First Epistle to the Corinthians in *Script. vet.*, vol. VII, p. 274. Later, however, after reading these writings of Claudius more carefully, I finally realized that almost nothing is found there—apart from the prologues—except abbreviated excerpts from the known commentaries of other Fathers; a fault in Claudius’s work which Simonius and Trombellius had already perceived long ago. I have therefore selected Claudius’s sole commentary on the very brief Epistle to Philemon and present it here to readers, so that they may see with me that Claudius contains nothing that is treated more fully and splendidly in Saint Jerome’s commentary on the same Epistle.

[Col. 0911C]

## THE EXPOSITION BEGINS

He writes a familiar letter to Philemon on behalf of Onesimus, his slave. He wrote to him from prison in the city of Rome, and this is its beginning: “Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ.” In no Epistle did he use this designation, although in the body of the Epistles—namely, those to the Ephesians, Philippians, and Colossians—he testifies that he is in chains for his confession. It seems to me a mark of greater dignity to call himself a prisoner of Jesus Christ than an apostle. For the apostles gloried that they had been considered worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus. But the authority of his chains is necessary. Since he is going to make a request for Onesimus, the person asking had to be one who could obtain what he requested. Truly blessed is the one who glories not in wisdom, riches, eloquence, or worldly power, but in the sufferings of Christ! Yet not everyone who is imprisoned is a prisoner of Christ. Whoever is imprisoned for Christ’s name and confession is truly called a prisoner of Jesus Christ, just as the shedding of blood makes a martyr only when it is shed for Christ’s name.

And Timothy, the brother. This is included so that we may know that the letter too was dictated from prison and in chains, where Timothy always remained with him. It was at this time, apparently, that the Epistles to the Philippians, Colossians, and Ephesians were dictated.

(Vers. 2.) “To Philemon, our beloved and fellow worker, and to Appia, our most beloved sister.” Paul and Timothy therefore write to their beloved Philemon and fellow worker, who is called beloved because he is engaged in the same work of Christ. They also write to Appia, who is believed to have been either his sister or his wife. Between two men, both apostolic—between Paul’s fellow worker and his fellow soldier—the name of Appia is inserted in the middle, so that, supported by such companionship on both sides, she may not appear to possess merely the rank belonging to her sex, but that belonging to her merit. “And to Archippus, our fellow soldier.” We should suppose that this Archippus fought with Paul and Timothy against the adversaries for Christ’s name, emerged victorious, and is therefore now called a fellow soldier because he overcame in the same contest and warfare. “And to the church which is in your house.” He writes to the church that is in his house. But it is ambiguous whether this means the church that is in the house of Archippus or the one in the house of Philemon. Yet, as is considered more certain, it should be referred not to Archippus but to Philemon, to whom the Epistle itself is also addressed.

(Vers. 3.) “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” The letter is still being written from two persons to several, and in nearly all the Epistles the opening is the same: he prays that grace and peace may come from God the Father and Christ the Lord. From this it is shown that the Son and the Father have one nature, since the Son can grant the same thing as the Father, and what the Son grants is said to be granted by the Father. Grace is given because we are saved by no merit or work of our own. Peace is that by which we are reconciled to God through his Christ. Although Paul and Timothy write together to Philemon, Appia, and Archippus, what follows makes clear that Paul alone is writing to Philemon alone and conversing with one person.

(Vers. 4.) “I give thanks to my God, always making remembrance of you in my prayers.” Here it is no longer Paul and Timothy speaking to Philemon and the others, but Paul alone speaking to Philemon alone. We can find this manner of writing in his other Epistles as well: although one or more persons are addressed in the preface, afterward, throughout the body of the Epistle, one speaker is introduced as conducting the argument. But when he says, “I give thanks to my God always, making remembrance of you in my prayers,” it is ambiguous whether he always gives thanks to God or always makes remembrance of him in his prayers. Yet both may be understood: the one who commanded others to give thanks to God in all things could not be constrained by any distress so that he himself would not always give thanks to God. If Paul always prayed for the holy and the better ones, and Philemon was holy, possessing such faith and charity that he was known not merely by report but by his actions, it is also credible that Paul always prayed for Philemon, so that the faith and charity he possessed in Christ and toward all his saints might be preserved, through the fellowship of faith and the working knowledge of every good thing, by Christ’s mercy.

(Vers. 5.) “Hearing of your charity and the faith that you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints.” That Philemon had charity in the Lord is not difficult to interpret, since after God we are commanded to love our neighbors. Nor should we think that faith and charity toward God and his saints are sufficient for us unless what we believe is completed by our actions.

(Vers. 6.) “So that the fellowship of your faith may become evident in the knowledge of every good thing in Christ Jesus.” Through how many steps and advances the apostolic discourse reaches toward higher things! Whatever good is praised in Philemon is to be drawn from the example of the apostles, and is good because it is drawn from the fountain of Christ.

(Vers. 7.) “For I had great joy and consolation in your charity, because the hearts of the saints have found refreshment through you, brother.” He repeats and teaches more fully why he said, “I give thanks to my God, always making remembrance of you in my prayers.” It was indeed fitting always to give thanks to God for Philemon’s charity, since by receiving the inward affection of the heart and the deep recesses of the saints’ souls he had refreshed them.

(Vers. 8–9.) “Therefore, having great confidence in Christ Jesus to command you what concerns the matter, and because of charity I rather appeal to you, since you are such a person—Paul, an old man, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.” After first offering many praises of Philemon, and since the matter for which he was about to make his request was both useful to the distinguished person and beneficial to the one making the request, Paul could have commanded rather than asked. But this arose from that confidence: one who had accomplished such great works for Christ could not, in other matters, be unequal to himself. Yet he wishes rather to ask than to command, presenting the great authority of the petitioner by which the Apostle appeals as both an old man and a prisoner of Jesus Christ.

The whole matter for which he appeals is this. Onesimus, Philemon’s slave, having compounded flight with theft, had stolen certain items of household property. Going to Italy, so that he might not be more easily apprehended in the neighboring region, he had squandered his master’s money in dissipation. Let no one think that this has been rashly or arbitrarily invented by us; let him learn it from what follows. For Paul would never have said, “If he has harmed you or owes you anything, charge it to my account. I, Paul, have written this with my own hand; I will repay it,” nor would he have become surety for stolen property unless what had been taken had been squandered. While Paul was therefore in prison at Rome on account of the confession of Christ, Onesimus believed in the Lord Jesus and was baptized by him; through worthy repentance he wiped away the stains of his former life, to such an extent that the Apostle became a witness to his manner of life—the same Apostle who had once rebuked Peter for not walking with a straight step in the truth of the Gospel. Therefore, insofar as the sin and crime that had injured human beings are concerned, he does not deserve pardon. But insofar as the testimony of the Apostle, who knows that he has been fully converted, is concerned, the one being asked is pressed by a weighty consideration: for Onesimus, once a fugitive slave and thief, had become the Apostle’s minister. And what other ministry did the Apostle have except the Gospel of Christ Jesus? Thus the one who was a slave of Christ and likewise his minister was to be forgiven no longer as by a master, but as by a fellow slave and fellow evangelist.

### (Verse 10)

“I appeal to you for my son, whom I have begotten in chains, Onesimus.” Desiring to obtain what he requests, he now declares that he is pleading not for Philemon’s slave but for his own son—and for that son whom he had begotten in the bonds of the Gospel, that is, whom he was sustaining for the sake of Christ’s Gospel.

### (Verse 11)

“Who was once useless to you.” “To you,” he says, “alone, not to others.” Now, on the contrary, through the compensation of usefulness—for he is useful both to his master and to Paul [Col. 0914C], and through Paul to others—he deserves more love than he had previously deserved hatred. Hence he says, “but now he is useful both to you and to me” (verse 12), because, while Paul was detained in prison and in chains, Onesimus could minister to him in the Gospel.

“But receive him as my own heart.” “Heart” sometimes signifies the affection of the heart and a complete willingness from the soul, when everything that belongs to us is received by the person being entreated. Alternatively, all children are to be understood as the hearts of their parents.

“Whom I wished to keep with me, so that he might minister to me on your behalf in the bonds of the Gospel” (verse 13). For this reason he repeatedly emphasizes and reiterates that he is his son, the son of his bonds, and a minister of the Gospel while he himself is in chains, so that Philemon—prudently and strategically praised so highly in the preface—would not dare to refuse, lest he appear unworthy of his own praises [Col. 0914D].

### (Verse 14)

“But I wished to do nothing without your counsel,” so that your good deed might not be as though compelled by necessity, but voluntary. The apostle Paul could therefore have kept Onesimus as his minister without Philemon’s consent; but if he had done this without Philemon’s willingness, it would indeed have been his good deed, but not a voluntary one. What was not voluntary was, in another respect, shown not to be good. For nothing can be called good that is freely offered.

From this we should consider the apostle’s prudence: for this reason he sends the fugitive slave back to his master, so that he may benefit his master—something he could not do if he were kept apart from him.

### (Verse 15)

“Perhaps for this reason he departed.” By adding “perhaps,” he appropriately tempered his statement; for the judgments of God are hidden, and it is rash to pronounce as certain what is doubtful. “Perhaps,” he says, “for this reason he was separated from you.” He speaks cautiously, timidly, and hesitantly, without planting his foot firmly.
