If he had not added “perhaps,” all slaves would have had to flee in order to become disciples of the apostles.

“For an hour from you.” Since he joined the expression “for an hour,” we must understand “hour” as meaning a period of time. In comparison with eternity, every period of time is brief.

### (Verse 16)

“So that you might receive him forever, no longer as a slave, but in place of a slave, as a most beloved brother.” No master is eternal in relation to his slave; for his power and the condition of both come to an end through death. Onesimus, however, who through the faith of Christ has become eternal, is eternal to the eternal Philemon, because he too had believed in Christ. Having received the spirit of freedom, he began to be no longer a slave but, from being a slave, a brother—a most beloved brother, an eternal brother, and himself also an eternal brother to his eternal apostle and master. The condition of the flesh united Onesimus to him, but afterward the spirit united him much more closely.

At that time, when he was subject to him in the flesh, he was not united to him in the Lord. From this we understand that a slave who has believed in Christ is bound by a twofold law to his master: for a time he is joined to him by the necessity of the flesh, and forever he is united to him in the spirit.

### (Verse 17)

“Therefore, if you regard me as a partner, receive him as you would receive me.” What he says amounts to this: “If you wish to have me as a partner, have Onesimus also, whom I regard as my associate, my son, and my own heart. If you do not wish to receive and have him, you will yourself understand that you cannot have me either.”

[Col. 0915C]

### (Verse 18)

“But if he has wronged you in anything or owes you anything, charge it to my account.” He is an imitator of his master and has Christ speaking within him; therefore he ought, according to his ability, to do what Christ did. For if Christ bore our weaknesses and suffered our wounds, the apostle rightly interposes himself on behalf of Onesimus and guarantees what Onesimus owed.

As we said above, all that had been taken by theft and squandered in extravagance could not be discharged except through what Philemon compensated at great cost: in place of a fugitive slave and lost money, he would receive a most beloved brother, an eternal brother, and through him make the apostle himself his debtor.

“I, Paul, have written this with my own hand; I will repay it” (verse 19). “What Onesimus took away by theft, I pledge myself to repay. This letter and my own hand are witnesses to this pledge [Col. 0915D]; I did not dictate it according to my usual practice, but wrote it myself.”

“And I will not say to you that you owe me even your own self.” Because of the word of Christ that I preached to you, through which you also became a Christian, you owe your very self to me. But if you are mine, and everything that is yours is mine, then Onesimus also, who is yours, is mine. I could therefore use him as my own, but I leave the matter to your will, so that you may receive a reward by forgiving him.

“Yes, brother, may I enjoy you in the Lord” (verse 20). If he had not added “in the Lord,” but had said only, “May I enjoy you,” he would have placed the hope of his blessedness in him. Nevertheless, “to enjoy” is also used very nearly in the sense of using something with love. When the person loved is present, pleasure necessarily accompanies him; if you pass beyond that pleasure and refer it to the place where one ought to remain, you use it, and you are said to enjoy it only improperly and by an abuse of language. But if you cling to it and remain in it, placing the end of your joy in it, then you are properly said to enjoy it, since nothing is to be enjoyed except that Trinity, that is, the highest and unchangeable good.

“Refresh my heart in Christ.” Just as he wishes to enjoy Philemon in the Lord, so he wishes his own heart—Onesimus, whom he also called by this same name above—to be refreshed through Philemon.

“Confident in your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say” (verse 21). He who presumes upon the person whom he is about to ask in a way anticipates that very presumption, so that the person asked may not be permitted to refuse what is requested. Moreover, if the petitioner knows that the person asked will do more than he requests, he asks for less, so that the person asked may have a voluntary reward for granting the greater request. But if Philemon does this at the command of a human being, how much more will he do it out of love for God? Hence he is rightly praised in the apostle’s words because he carried out his commands in deed.

### (Verse 22)

“At the same time, prepare lodging for me.” He says this so that, while Philemon expects him to come to him, he may be more inclined to do what has been requested. He knew that, when he came to preach the new truth—that Christ had been crucified—and to bring unheard-of doctrines, very many people would flock to him. It was therefore necessary that the house should be in a prominent part of the city, where people could easily gather; next, that it should be free from every inconvenience, spacious enough to accommodate many hearers [Col. 0916C], and not near places of public spectacles, lest it be made detestable by a shameful neighborhood. Finally, it should preferably be situated on level ground. For this reason, consider that he also remained for two years in rented lodgings at Rome. Nor, I think, was the dwelling small, since crowds of Jews gathered there every day.

“For I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you.” God, when asked, grants a son to his father, and a brother is often preserved through his brother’s prayer; but an apostle is granted to the prayers of the whole Church for the benefit of those who are going to hear him. This gift is said to be granted not so much to the one who is being delayed from martyrdom, though prepared for martyrdom, as to those to whom the apostle is sent.

That Paul was often in prison and was released from his chains, he himself says elsewhere: “in prisons frequently.” From these prisons he was sometimes released, through the Lord’s repeated help, when his persecutors found nothing in him deserving death [Col. 0916D]. Nero’s sword had not yet consecrated itself through Christian blood; rather, because of the novelty of his preaching—whether by envious Jews or by those who saw their idols being destroyed—he was sent to prison when the crowds had been stirred to fury, and then, when the attack and fury had subsided, he was released again.

The Acts of the Apostles testify that this happened as we say. There Agrippa tells Festus that Paul could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar, since he had found no charge against him except certain questions concerning their own religion and concerning a certain Jesus whom Paul claimed to be alive. From this we may observe that they could likewise have been released by the other judges, since the Lord was directing matters [Col. 0917A] so that the new preaching might be spread throughout the whole world.

### (Verses 25, 24)

“Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you, as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers.” This confirms what we said at the beginning: that the Epistle to the Colossians was written at the same time and carried by the same bearer as the letter written to Philemon. The names of those greeted also demonstrate this, for the letter itself is written approximately as follows:

“Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, and Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ.” A little farther on: “Luke the beloved physician greets you, and Demas. And say to Archippus: See to the ministry that you received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it. And remember my chains.”

[Col. 0917B]

If someone does not think that the letters were written at the same time because the Epistle to the Colossians contains a few names that are not listed here, he should understand that not all people are friends or acquaintances of everyone else, and that a private letter to one person is composed differently from a public letter to the whole Church.

Who Epaphras, Paul’s fellow prisoner, was may be inferred from the addition here of “in Christ Jesus.” We may suspect that he endured at Rome, for Christ, the same chains that Paul did, and that, being Christ’s prisoner, he could therefore also be called Paul’s fellow prisoner. Or perhaps he is called this because he too was distinguished among the apostles, like Andronicus and Junia, concerning whom it is written to the Romans:

“Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and fellow prisoners, who are distinguished among the apostles and who were in Christ before me.”

This is what may be said about Epaphras.

[Col. 0917C]

Moreover, when he wrote the Epistle to Philemon, he lists as fellow workers in the Gospel and in his chains [Col. 0918A] Mark, whom I think to be the author of the Gospel; Aristarchus, whom we mentioned above; Demas, concerning whom he says elsewhere, “Demas has abandoned me”; and Luke the physician, who transmitted the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles to the churches by writing them down.

For just as the apostles, from being fishermen of fish, became fishers of human beings, so he was transformed from a physician of bodies into a physician of souls. Of him he also says elsewhere: “We sent with him the brother whose praise in the Gospel is spread throughout all the churches.” Whenever his book is read in the church, his healing does not cease.

### (Verse 25)

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.” For when divine grace is present in the spirit, it makes the whole person spiritual, so that he clings to the Lord in mind and body and what is written in him may be fulfilled: “He who clings to the Lord is one spirit.”

According to the Hebrews, the names are interpreted as follows: Paul, “admirable”; Timothy, “beneficent”; Philemon, “wonderfully gifted,” or “mouth of bread,” from *mouth*, not from *bone*; Appia, “self-controlled” or “freedom”; Archippus, “length of labor”; Onesimus, “answering”; Epaphras, “fruitful and seeing,” or “growing”; Mark, “sublime command”; Aristarchus, “mountain of labor”; Demas, “silent”; Luke, “himself rising.”

If we wish to understand these names according to their interpretations, the matter is not difficult: he writes especially to one who is admirable and beneficent, to whom all vices have been granted and whose mouth is open toward heavenly things; then to one who is self-controlled and free, and to “length.”

Here ends the work.

[Col. 0917C]

## CLAUDIUS THE CHRONOLOGER

Whom we do not rashly suspect to have been the bishop of Turin, who was writing in the year 814.

## A BRIEF CHRONICLE

*(In Labbe, New Library of Manuscripts, p. 309.) (G)*

[Col. 0917C]

Since, therefore, with God as our helper, we have already shown above, for the most part, the years from the creation of the world, recorded together with the sequence of generations according to the Hebrew truth, we shall now set them out more fully by recapitulating them.

When the omnipotent Creator had completed the entire adornment of the world, on the third day after adorning heaven he created man. The adornment of heaven—that is, the sun, moon, and stars—is found, according to a truthful reckoning, to have been created first at the spring equinox, which among us is now called 12 Kalends of April. By a corresponding calculation, on 10 Kalends of April, on the seventeenth day of the moon, the first-formed Adam is found to have been fashioned from the clay of the earth and likewise given life according to our reckoning.

The second Adam, Christ the Son of God, was God and man alike: God before the ages, man at the end of the ages; God from God, man from man; God from the Father, without beginning or mother; man, at a definite beginning, from a mother without a human father. At the same time—but not on the same weekday, that is, on 10 Kalends of April—he is found to have risen from the dead.

If anyone, less instructed in the study of the divine Scriptures, should attempt to doubt this work, let him return to the divine books written according to the Hebrew truth, and let him hold and believe whatever he finds there, and cease condemning me. For it is not lawful for Christians to attribute to human chronicles the authority that must be attributed to those books written by the prophets under the authority of the Holy Spirit. If anyone’s obstinate intention persists in this matter, let him go to the Jews, the enemies of the Church, and seek in their books written in the Hebrew language the total of the years. Whatever he finds there, let him believe and hold, because, as blessed Augustine says in Book XV of *The City of God*, greater credence should be given to the language from which the translation into another language was made through interpreters.

Adam, in the 130th year from the day of his creation, begot Seth.

[Col. 0919A]

When Seth was 105 years old, he begot Enos, and Adam’s days of life were completed at Enos’s birth: 235 years.

In the 90th year of his life, Enos begot Cainan, and Adam’s days of life were completed at Cainan’s birth: 325 years.

In the 70th year of his life, Cainan begot Malalehel, and Adam’s days of life were completed at Malalehel’s birth: 395 years.

In the 60th year of his life, Malalehel begot Jareth, and Adam’s years of life were completed at Jareth’s birth: 460 years.

In the 62nd year of his life, Jareth begot Enoch, and Adam’s years of life were completed at Enoch’s birth: 622 years.

In the 65th year of his life, Enoch begot Mathusalem, and Adam’s years of life were completed at Mathusalem’s birth: 687 years. After he begot Mathusalem, Enoch walked before God for 300 years, and he was no longer seen, because God took him, in the 57th year after Adam’s death.

[Col. 0919B]

In the 87th year of his life, Mathusalem begot Lamech, and the years from the creation of the world were completed at Lamech’s birth: 874. Adam lived 56 years after Lamech was born.

In the 182nd year of his life, Lamech begot Noah, 125 years after Adam’s death, and the years from the creation of the world were completed at Noah’s birth: 1,065.

In the 500th year of his life, Noah begot three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. In the 600th year of his life the flood came, according to lunar reckoning, in the first month, on the seventeenth day of the month; according to solar reckoning, however, on the Kalends of April, on the seventeenth day of the moon. The Hebrews, who calculate the months not by the sun but by the moon, called it the seventeenth day of the first month [Col. 0919C]. On the seventh day of the week, which we call the Sabbath, Noah entered the ark, and on that very day the flood came.

A wondrous judgment of almighty God upon the human race: through Adam the moon received its beginning on the seventeenth day, and through failure to keep God’s command the seventeenth day encountered the punishment of death in the flood.

In the 600th year of Noah’s life, the years from the creation of the world amounted to 1,656. In that year in which the flood occurred, it was a leap year. If weekdays or Kalends were calculated according to our custom, the Kalends of January in that year would have fallen on the fourth weekday. Since it was the fourth year of the solar cycle, there were therefore 11 days in the epact, and 13 Kalends of April was the new moon, that is, the beginning of the new moon and the beginning of the first month of that year according to lunar months. In that year there were completed 33 years of the Jubilee from the creation of the world, 82 nineteen-year cycles, and 414 leap days.

[Col. 0919D]

## II

In the second age of the world, on its first day—which is the seventeenth day of the second month—Noah, his wife, his sons, and his sons’ wives came out of the ark on the first day of the week, which we call the Lord’s Day because of the Lord’s resurrection. As I have already said above, if weekdays or Kalends had been calculated according to our custom at that time, the Kalends of January in the year in which they came out of the ark would have fallen on the fifth weekday, in the first year after the leap year. Since it was the fifth year of the solar cycle, which is nineteen years, and the fourth epactal year [Col. 0920A], there were 22 days in the epact, and 7 Ides of March was the new moon, that is, the beginning of the new moon. According to the Hebrews, this was the beginning of the first month and the beginning of the year.

According to our reckoning, which is made by solar days, Noah and his sons are found to have come out of the ark on the fifth day before the Nones of May, on the twenty-seventh day of the moon. They are found to have remained in the ark, according to solar days, for a complete year, which consists of 365 days and one quarter—that is, six hours—and four weeks, that is, 28 days; for four times seven is 28.

When Shem was 100 years old, he begot Arphaxad two years after the flood, because the flood came in the 98th year of his life.

In the 35th year of his life, Arphaxad begot Sale; at Sale’s birth, 37 years after the flood had been completed.

In the 31st year of his life, Sale begot Heber; at Heber’s birth, 67 years after the flood had been completed.

In the 34th year of his life, Heber begot Peleg; at Peleg’s birth, the 101st year after the flood had been completed. This was the 701st year of Noah’s life. By this calculation Noah is found to have lived 249 years after the division of the languages.

Peleg means “division.” His father gave him this name because, at the time of his birth, the earth was divided through the confusion of languages. In the 30th year of his life he begot Reu; at Reu’s birth, 131 years after the flood had been completed.

In the 32nd year of his life, Reu begot Serug; at Serug’s birth, 143 years after the flood had been completed.

[Col. 0920C]

In the 30th year of his life, Serug begot Nahor; at Nahor’s birth, 193 years after the flood had been completed.

In the 28th year of his life, Nahor begot Terah; at Terah’s birth, 222 years after the flood had been completed.

In the 70th year of his life, Terah begot Abram; at Abram’s birth, 292 years after the flood had been completed.

In the 892nd year of Noah’s life, Abraham was born. This was the 390th year of Shem’s life. Noah is found to have lived 58 years after Abraham’s birth.

Thus, according to the reckoning, from the flood to Abraham’s birth there were 292 years, and from the creation of the world 1,948 years.

[Col. 0920C]

## III

The third age of the world began with the birth of Abraham the patriarch [Col. 0920D]. When he was 75 years old, in the 17th year after Noah’s death—which was the 465th year of Shem’s life and the 145th year of his father Terah’s life—he left his people and his homeland and, in accordance with the divine oracle, came into the land of Canaan. He received the promise that a Savior would be born from his offspring, in whom all the nations that would believe in Christ would be blessed, and that he himself would become a great nation. Of these promises, one is spiritual and the other carnal.

At this time Ninus and Semiramis ruled in Assyria.

In the 100th year of Abraham’s life, and in the 170th year of his father Terah’s life and the 490th year of Shem’s life, Abraham begot Isaac, 42 years after Noah’s death [Col. 0921A]. Isaac is recorded as the first and only person in the entire sequence of the Old Testament to have been circumcised on the eighth day; this privilege was granted to the son of promise not without a great mystery.

In the 60th year of Isaac’s life, and the 160th year of his father’s life—which was the 550th year of Shem’s life—102 years after Noah’s death and 25 years after the death of his grandfather Terah, Isaac begot Esau and Jacob. Abraham lived 15 years after Esau and Jacob were born. Shem lived 35 years after Abraham’s death, and his days of life were completed at 600 years.

Before the flood he lived 98 years, and after the flood 502 years. He died in the 600th year of his life, which was the 101st year of Isaac’s life and the 50th year of Jacob’s life. At Jacob’s birth, the years of the third age were completed: 160, and from the creation of the world: 2,108.

[Col. 0921B]

In the 91st year of his life, Jacob begot Joseph, which was the 151st year of Isaac’s life. Joseph was sold when he was 16, which was the 107th year of Jacob’s life and the 167th year of his father’s life. He remained a slave for 14 years and was brought out of prison in the 30th year of his life, which was the 121st year of Jacob’s life and the 181st year of Isaac his father’s life.

According to this calculation, Isaac is found to have lived four years after Joseph was brought out of prison, since he was 185 years old when he died. This was the 125th year of Jacob’s life. In the fifth year after his father’s death, Jacob also went down into Egypt, in the 39th year of Joseph’s life and the 130th year of his own life, with 70 persons.

The children of Israel remained in Egypt for 215 years after Jacob’s entry, and for 144 years after Joseph’s death [Col. 0921C]. Between Joseph’s death and Moses’ birth there were 64 years, because Moses was 80 years old when the Lord appeared to him and sent him to Pharaoh.

If anyone doubts these figures, or lacks the knowledge required to calculate and find the total number of years, let him begin with Jacob’s entry into Egypt, and he will find 71 years up to Joseph’s death. Add 64 to these, making 135, because Moses is found to have been born 64 years after Joseph’s death. Add the 80 years of Moses’ life, since Moses was 80 years old, as I have already said, when he was sent to Pharaoh. Add 80 to 135, and the total is 215.

Thus, from Abraham’s first promise to Jacob’s entry into Egypt there were 215 years, and from there to the crossing of the Red Sea there were another 215 years. The total is [Col. 0921D] 430 years, which is what the apostle says in the Epistle to the Galatians: “But this I say: the covenant confirmed by God; after 430 years the law was made.”

Thus, from Abraham’s birth—the point at which the third age of the passing world began—to the crossing of the Red Sea there were 505 years; from the creation of the world to Jacob’s entry into Egypt there were 2,238 years; and from that point to the crossing of the Red Sea there were 2,451 years.

But someone may say: How can it be that the children of Israel remained in the land of Egypt for so few years, when Scripture in the book of Genesis reports that God said to Abraham: “Know with certainty that your offspring will be strangers in a land not their own, and they will enslave them for 400 years”?

Therefore, the words “they will reduce them to servitude” should not be referred to the 400 years, as though they had held them in slavery for that entire period. Rather, the 400 years must be referred to what was said: “Your offspring will be strangers in a land not their own.” Whether in the land of Canaan or in Egypt, that offspring was a stranger before it received the land as an inheritance through God’s promise, after it had been liberated from Egypt.

Thus, through the figure of speech that grammarians call *hyperbaton*, the statement should be understood to mean, or its word order should be: “Know with certainty that your offspring will be strangers in a land not their own for 400 years.” The intervening words should be read separately: “And they will reduce them to servitude, and they will harm them,” so that this insertion does not belong to the 400 years [Col. 0922B]. For it was at the end of this total period of years—that is, after Joseph’s death—that the people of God were made to undergo harsh slavery in Egypt.

The apostle testifies in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “By faith Moses celebrated the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn of Egypt might not harm them.” But since, by investigating the years or ages of time, we have reached from the beginning of the world to the present, let us now carefully inquire into the time or day of that very Passover, the first Passover celebrated in the entire period of the Old Testament.

If you wish to know the time, day, weekday, or moon of this Passover, take the years from the beginning of the world, which up to that time amount to 2,453. Divide them by four, and say: four times 600 is 2,400, with 53 remaining. Again say: four times ten is 40, with 13 remaining; four times three is 12, with 1 remaining. You will find that the first year after a leap year had then occurred.

Take, therefore, the leap days that occurred throughout all the preceding time, 613, add them to the preceding years, and you will find their total to be 3,066. Add to these the six days that we call intercalary, and the total will be 3,072.

To find the weekday of that year, divide the total stated above and say: seven times 400 is 2,800, with 272 remaining. Again say: seven times 30 is 210, with 62 remaining; then seven times eight is 56, with six remaining. You will find that the sixth weekday, according to solar days, was the beginning of the year that we, following the custom of the Gentiles, call the Kalends of January.

[Col. 0922D]

Again take the preceding number of years, 2,453, and divide it by nineteen. Say: nineteen times 100 is 1,900, with 553 remaining. Divide these again by the same number and say: nineteen times 20 is 380, with 173 remaining. Divide these once more in the same way and say: nineteen times nine is 171, with two remaining. Add one, making three, and you will find that it was the third year of the solar cycle, which is the nineteen-year cycle. Subtract one, leaving two: this is the second year of the lunar epact.

Again say: eleven times two is 22, for that is the number of days by which the solar course exceeds the lunar course in two solar years. Add eight to these, making 30. Since it was an embolismic year, that many days occurred in the epact.

Again take the total of the 122 years of thirty days that were in the epact; 102 remain. You will find that, according to solar days, the Passover itself fell on the day before the Ides of April, on the second weekday, with the moon on its fourteenth day. According to lunar days, however, the third day before the Kalends of April was the new moon, that is, the beginning of the new moon, the beginning of the first lunar month, and the beginning of the year.

According to our reckoning, which is made by solar days, the children of Israel are found to have left Rameses on the Ides of April, with the moon on its fifteenth day, the day after Passover. They came to Succoth, and from Succoth, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, with the moon on its sixteenth day, they came to Pi-hahiroth. On the sixth day before the Kalends of June, with the moon on its first day—the first day of the third lunar month—they came to Mount Sinai and received the law, with God speaking to them through an angel [Col. 0923B], on the day before the Kalends of June, the fiftieth day after the slaughter of the lamb, on the second weekday and the fourth day of the moon. On that same day they had celebrated the Passover in Egypt.

In the 80th year of his life, Moses, having led the people of God, Israel, out of Egypt, governed them in the wilderness for 40 years. In the first of these years he constructed the tabernacle for the Lord. Completing all the work in seven months, he erected it on the first day of the first month of the second year. According to solar days, in that year the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April was the first weekday and the new moon, that is, the beginning of the new moon and of the first month. The Passover of the Hebrews fell on the seventh weekday, the fourth day before the Nones of April, with the moon on its fourteenth day, which they customarily called, according to lunar days, the fourteenth day of the first month.

From this point onward, it does not seem necessary for us to linger in seeking the total number of years through the leaders and judges, since the history of the Book of Kings gives such clear testimony:

“It came to pass in the 480th year after the children of Israel had come out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of King Solomon over Israel, in the month Ziv—which is the second month—that he began to build the house of the Lord.”

From this, subtracting Solomon’s four years and David’s 40 years, the total number of years from the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt to the first year of David’s reign is found to be 436. From Abraham’s first promise to that first year of David’s reign there were 866 years; from Abraham’s birth to that same year there were 941 years.

[Col. 0923C]

## IV

The fourth age of the world begins with the first year of David’s reign [Col. 0923D] and continues until the Babylonian captivity, which was carried out by King Nebuchadnezzar. According to the Hebrew truth it comprises 474 years; according to the translation of the Seventy Interpreters, more. The generations according to both books number 17.

David, the first king from the tribe of Judah, reigned for 40 years.

Solomon, the son of David, reigned for 40 years. In the fourth year of his reign he began to build the temple for the Lord in Jerusalem, 480 years having elapsed since the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, as the Book of Kings also bears witness. This was plainly done as a figure of the whole body in which the Church of Christ is built in this age and perfected in the age to come: Solomon completed the temple in seven years and dedicated it in the seventh month of the eighth year [Col. 0924A], which was the twelfth year of his reign.

Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, reigned for 17 years. Abijah, the son of Rehoboam, reigned for three years. Asa, the son of Abijah, reigned for 41 years. Jehoshaphat, the son of Asa, reigned for 25 years. Jehoram, the son of Jehoshaphat, reigned for eight years. Azariah, the son of Jehoram, reigned for one year. Athaliah reigned for seven years. Joash, the son of Azariah, reigned for 40 years. Amaziah, the son of Joash, reigned for 29 years. Azariah, also called Uzziah, the son of Amaziah, reigned for 52 years. Jotham, the son of Uzziah, reigned for six years. Hezekiah reigned for 19 years [Col. 0924B]. Manasseh, the son of Hezekiah, reigned for 55 years. Amon, the son of Manasseh, reigned for two years. Josiah, the son of Amon, reigned for 31 years.

Jehoahaz, the son of Josiah, whom Pharaoh Necho, king of Egypt, led in chains into Egypt, reigned for three months.

[Col. 0924B]

## V

From the fleshly coming of the Lord and Savior—as reckoned from the book of Ezra the prophet, the history of the book of the Maccabees and Josephus, and the historian Africanus—up to Roman times, there are 589 years. Thus, from the creation of the world to the birth of the Lord and Savior in the flesh, which occurred in the 42nd year of Caesar Octavian [Col. 0924C], the total number of years is 3,952.

Moreover, in the book of Chronicles, which that same holy man composed with no less marvelous accuracy than speed, he likewise recorded the same number of years, according to the Hebrew truth, from the creation of the world to the Lord’s birth in the flesh.

Therefore, it must be known, believed with the greatest firmness, and in no way doubted that, according to the Hebrew truth, the total number of years from the creation of the world to the destruction of Jerusalem—which took place in the eleventh year of Zedekiah, at the hands of Nebuchadnezzar—cannot be either greater or less. Rather, they must be held as I have already demonstrated above.

Whatever time remains up to the coming of the Lord in the flesh, I leave to the judgment of our ancestors who wrote chronicles [Col. 0924D]. For if we are not mistaken in the years that were reckoned after the destruction of Jerusalem, the total number of years from the creation of the world to the present year—which is the 814th year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in which the glorious prince Charles, of pious and ever-memorable memory, departed from this mortal age and the pious prince Louis succeeded him in the imperial rule of the holy Catholic Church of God—is 4,766.

To make what we are saying clearer, calculate these same years by quarters and say: four times 1,000 is 4,000, with 766 remaining; four times 100 is 400 [Col. 0925A], with 366 remaining; four times 90 is 360, with six remaining. From these take four, leaving two: the present year is the second year after a leap year.

Again say: nineteen times 200 is 3,800, with 966 remaining; nineteen times 50 is 950, with 16 remaining; add one, making 17. The present year is the seventeenth year of the solar cycle, which is the nineteen-year cycle. Subtract one, leaving 16: this is the sixteenth year of the lunar epact.

Eleven times ten is 110; eleven times six is 66, making 176. Add eight to these, making 184. Divide these by thirty and say: six times thirty is 180, with four remaining. You will find that in the present year the lunar cycle is running its course.

[Col. 0925B]

If I am asked how long, or for how many years, the present mortal age is to endure, I confess that I do not know, because I do not remember having read it anywhere. Therefore, I am neither ashamed of my ignorance, since I have not been taught it by reading, nor afraid of danger, since I do not presume to state what I have not read, lest I be found to transgress the divine oracle that answered the apostles when they asked about this:

“But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, except the Father alone.”

But what is it that the Father could possess without his power or know without his wisdom, since both belong to the Father—that is, his power and his wisdom? Rather, the Son’s not knowing means that he wills us, who do not know, to remain ignorant of this.

Moreover, we advise all the faithful together that, whether one follows the Hebrew truth—which has plainly come down to us pure through the blessed translator Jerome, even in the judgment of its Jewish enemies—or the translation of the Seventy Interpreters, which, as many assert, was first published with insufficient care, or, as blessed Augustine believes, was corrupted by pagans, or certainly a work mixed from manuscripts of both traditions [Col. 0926B] . . . The rest is missing.

[Col. 0925B]

## SOME PASSAGES OF CLAUDIUS OF TURIN

Extracts from his Commentaries on the Epistles of Saint Paul.

*(Richard Simon, Critical History of the New Testament, Book III, chapter 25.)*

“He who, being in the form of God, etc.” (Philippians 2:6). In the form of God, equal to the Father; in the form of a servant, the mediator between God and human beings, Christ Jesus, a man . . . Therefore Scripture rightly says both that the Son is equal to the Father and that the Father is greater than the Son. The former is understood on account of the form of God; the latter on account of the form of a servant, without any confusion . . .

“He did not consider it robbery, etc.” (ibid.). What he naturally possessed was not an act of usurpation, so that it could be called robbery; rather, it belonged to his nature that he should be equal.

From the preface to the Commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

In wintertime, wearing away the palace roads by going and returning, I am less able to fulfill the love mentioned above; after mid-spring, proceeding armed and carrying parchment together with my weapons, I go to the maritime watch-posts, keeping watch in fear against the Hagarenes and Moors, holding a sword by night and books and a pen by day, striving to fulfill the desire I have begun [Col. 0925D] . . . [lacuna]

### From the same preface

I confess that at first I approached unwillingly both this work and the Pentateuch that you requested, when, at the command of the pious prince Emperor Louis, I was teaching the brothers assembled in the school the Scriptures by word of mouth. I was also compelled by that same prince, so that I should not merely pass on words orally, where they might wander into oblivion, but should write them with a pen so that they would endure for a long time, and should commit to writing what I expressed orally.

### “Who is over all, God,” etc. (Romans 9:5)

For Christ our Lord and Savior is the true Son of God according to his divinity, and the true son of man according to the flesh. He was not born from the seed of David according to that which is “God, who is over all, blessed for ever” [Col. 0926C], but according to that weakness which he assumed from us.

### “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 1:3)

So that he might not appear to have passed over either the name or the gift of the Father, and perhaps provide suspicion or occasion for union, he teaches that Christ is indeed rightly to be invoked, but that all grace belongs to the Father. Thus he shows the two who are one through divinity, and places the authority of the Father first . . . [lacuna]

### “God was in Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:19)

For the Son is by nature the ambassador of God the Father . . . The Father is understood to be in the Son because their substance is one. For there is unity where there is no dominion; and consequently they are mutually equal.

[Col. 0926D]

### On the Epistle to the Hebrews 7:17

He [Melchizedek] offered no animal sacrifices, but only bread and wine, just as Christ offers an oblation of bread and wine to God the Father—that is, his body and blood—which oblation we offer daily upon the altar and receive.

### On the Epistle to the Philippians

Someone may think that the statement that a bishop and a presbyter are one and the same is not the opinion of the Scriptures but ours, and that one is a name of age while the other is a name of office. Let him reread the Apostle’s words to the Philippians: “Paul and Timothy,” etc.

### Revision by Bishop Claudius concerning the authors of the explanations on the Epistle to the Hebrews

I also give this reminder in the preface, my dearest friend, so that you may know that Origen composed three volumes on this Epistle, and that we too have followed him in part. Apollinaris and Didymus also published certain little commentaries. From these, although we have selected only a few passages, we have explained this Epistle at greater length from the opinions of the holy man Augustine, which we were able to find throughout his various books; and we have added or removed certain things that seemed appropriate to us, so that the diligent reader may recognize at once, at the beginning, that this work is either another’s or our own.

## Eulogy of Saint Augustine

The most holy Augustine, most devoted to the Lord, the pen of the Trinity, the tongue of the Holy Spirit, an earthly man but a heavenly angel, keen in resolving questions, discerning in refuting heretics, cautious in explaining the canonical Scriptures, etc.

From the opinions of that holy man, which we were able to find in his various books, we have explained this Epistle [Note: [Col. 0927B] Namely, the Epistle to the Romans.]. We have also added there some material from Origen’s Exposition and have treated certain matters as they seemed to us appropriate. I could find no better admonition than that contained in the First Epistle of the Apostle Paul, which I sent, because the whole matter there is directed toward removing human merits, in which the monks especially glory at the present time, and toward commending the grace of God.

## In the year of the Lord 840

## Louis I, called the Pious, Emperor Augustus

[Col. 0927B]

### The Life of Louis the Pious

By an unknown author, who testifies that he was by profession an astronomer and lived in the palace of that emperor.

[Note: [Col. 0927D] This author states in the Prologue that he learned what he wrote up to the time of Louis’s empire from the account of Adhemar, a most noble and devoted monk, who was Louis’s contemporary and foster-brother. He indicates that he himself saw and learned the later events, since he was present at court affairs. This edition, moreover, has now been revised and corrected in various places against two manuscript codices: one, very ancient, was supplied by the Thuane Library; the other, somewhat more recent, is preserved in the library of Alexander Petavius.]

*(In Chesne, Historical Writers of the Franks.)*

[Col. 0927C]

## Prologue

When the good or evil deeds of ancient people, especially of rulers, are recalled to memory, they provide readers with a double benefit. Some are useful for their benefit and edification; others for their warning. Since rulers stand, as it were, upon an elevated watchtower and therefore cannot remain hidden, their fame spreads more widely in proportion as they are seen more broadly; and the more prominent they are, the more people are attracted to imitate them and glory in doing so.

The monuments of our ancestors reveal that this is so. By their accounts they strove to instruct posterity in the path by which each ruler had traversed the road of mortals. Imitating their zeal, we do not wish to be either negligent toward those now living or envious toward those yet to come; therefore, though in a style lacking refinement, we commit to writing the deeds and life of Louis, an emperor beloved of God and orthodox [Col. 0927D].

For I confess, and say without the disguise of flattery, that anyone’s talent—not merely mine, which is very small, but even that of great men—succumbs before so vast a subject. For by divine authority we learn that Holy Wisdom teaches sobriety, wisdom, justice, and courage, than which nothing is sweeter for human beings in life. He adhered to these qualities so inseparably that one could scarcely know which of them one ought rather to admire in him.

For what was more sober than his sobriety, which is also called frugality or temperance? He practiced it so well that the most ancient proverb, celebrated even to heaven, was especially familiar to him: “Let nothing be excessive.” He delighted in the wisdom that he had learned from the authority of Scripture, which says: “Behold, the fear of the Lord—that is wisdom.”

How ardently he cultivated justice is attested by those who knew his zeal: he wanted every order of human beings to render what was just to its own order, and to love the Lord above all things and his neighbor as himself.

Courage, moreover, had become so firmly established in him that, although struck by evils so numerous and so great and provoked by injuries both private and external, nevertheless, with God as his guardian, no weight of injuries could break his unconquerable heart [Col. 0928D]. His rivals charged him with having succumbed to only one fault: excessive mercy. But with the Apostle let us say to such people: “Forgive him this injury.”

Whether these things are true or not, each reader will be able to discover by reading the work through. What I wrote up to the time of the empire I learned from the account of Adhemar, a most noble and devoted monk, who was Louis’s contemporary and foster-brother. I have committed the later events to writing because I was present at court affairs and saw and learned them myself.

## Here begins the narrative of his life

Charles, the most famous of kings and second to none in his time, after the death of his father and the disastrous death of his brother Carloman had assumed sole control of the Frankish people and kingdom, considered that an invincible guarantee of safety and prosperity would be his support of the peace and harmony of the Church: binding the peaceful more closely together in fraternal unity, striking rebels with impartial severity, bringing aid to those oppressed by pagans, and also leading the enemies of the Christian name, by whatever means, to the recognition and confession of the truth.

Having dedicated the beginnings of his reign to these efforts and entrusted them to Christ for protection and strengthening, after arranging the affairs of Francia, with God’s assent, as he wished and judged useful, he crossed into Aquitaine. There he attacked in war a certain tyrant named Hunold, who was plotting renewed wars and was already rushing toward arms. Compelled by fear of him [Col. 0929B], Hunold was forced both to abandon Aquitaine and to preserve his life by hiding and wandering in flight.

After completing these matters and arranging both public and private affairs as circumstances required, Charles left the most noble and devout queen Hildegard at the royal estate called Cassinogilus, pregnant with twins. He crossed the Garonne, which borders Aquitaine and Gascony. He had long before received that region into submission, after its prince Lupo had surrendered himself and his possessions to Charles’s authority.

Having completed there whatever opportunity and usefulness required, he resolved, after overcoming the difficulties of the Pyrenees, to proceed to Spain and, with Christ’s help, aid the Church, which was suffering under the bitterest yoke of the Saracens. Although the mountain almost touches heaven in height, bristles with the harshness of its cliffs, is darkened by the density of its forests, and by the narrowness of its road—or rather its path—almost cuts off passage not merely to a large army but even to a few people, he nevertheless traversed it successfully with Christ’s favor.

For the king’s spirit, ennobled by God, did not wish to be less courageous than Pompey or less energetic than Hannibal, who in ancient times undertook to overcome that region with great exhaustion and loss to themselves and their men. But this fortunate crossing was, if it is lawful to say so, stained by an uncertain and faithless fortune and by changing success. For when everything that could be accomplished in Spain had been completed and the return journey was proceeding favorably, misfortune intervened: some of the last men in the royal column were killed on that same mountain. Since their names are widely known, I have refrained from listing them.

On his return, the king found that his wife Hildegard had given birth to two male children. One of them, snatched away by premature death, scarcely began to die before he began to live beneath the light of day. The other, born from his mother’s womb in a favorable delivery, was nourished with the care due to an infant. They were born in the year 778 of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

When the child who promised a vigorous character had been reborn through the sacrament of baptism, his father decided that he should be called Louis and granted him the kingdom that he had dedicated to himself by his birth.

The most wise and perceptive king Charles knew that a kingdom is like a body, tossed now by one ailment, now by another, unless its health is protected by counsel and strength, as by physicians [Col. 0930A]. He therefore bound the bishops to himself in the manner that was proper. Throughout Aquitaine he appointed counts, abbots, and many others—commonly called vassals—from the Frankish people. It would not have been safe to oppose their prudence and courage by trickery or force. He entrusted them with the administration of the kingdom according to his judgment, the defense of its borders, and the provision of the royal estates.

In the city of Bourges he first appointed Humbert, and shortly afterward Sturbius, as count; at Poitiers, Abbo; at Périgueux, Widbald; at Auvergne, Iterius; in Wallagia, Bullus; at Toulouse, Chorso; at Bordeaux, Siguinus; among the Albigeois, Aimo; and at Limoges, Rothgarius.

When these matters had been properly arranged, he crossed the Loire with the rest of his forces and withdrew to Paris, which is also called Lutetia (779) [Col. 0930B]. Not long afterward, he conceived the desire to see Rome, once mistress of the world, and to approach the thresholds of the prince of the apostles and teacher of the nations, and to commend himself and his offspring to them. Relying upon such intercessors, to whom authority over heaven and earth had been granted, he hoped to care for his subjects and to crush the insolence of rebels, should any arise.

He also considered it no small support if he and his sons should receive the royal insignia from their vicar, together with priestly blessing. By God’s favor this turned out according to his wish. There, his son Louis, still being carried in a cradle, was invested with a blessing appropriate to a future ruler and with a royal diadem by the hands of Adrian, the venerable bishop (780) [Col. 0930C].

After completing everything that seemed necessary to do at Rome, King Charles peacefully returned to Francia with his sons and army. He sent his son Louis, the future king, to Aquitaine, placing over him as guardian Arnold and appointing other ministers in an orderly and suitable manner for the child’s protection (781). He was carried in a cradle as far as the city of Orléans. There, having been girded with weapons appropriate to his age, mounted upon a horse, he was transported, with God’s assent, into Aquitaine.

While he remained there for only a few years—four, namely—King Charles was continually waging hard conflicts against the Saxons (785) [Col. 0930D]. Fearing that either the people of Aquitaine might grow insolent because of Louis’s long absence, or that the boy might learn some foreign customs in his tender years, from which an age once imbued is freed only with difficulty, Charles sent for his son, who was already an excellent rider, together with the entire military population. He left only the margraves behind to protect the borders of the kingdom and repel any enemy incursions that might arise.

Louis, obeying his father as wisely and capably as he could, met him at Paderborn (786), dressed in the Gascon fashion together with boys of his own age: a rounded cloak, a loose-sleeved shirt, tight-fitting trousers, spurs inserted into small boots, and a missile weapon in his hand. For this was what his father’s pleasure and command had arranged.

He therefore remained with his father from that time until Herisburg, accompanying him until the sun, declining from the high axis, moderated the heat of summer with the yielding of autumn [Col. 0931A]. At the end of that season, having received permission from his father, he returned to Aquitaine to spend the winter.

At that time Chorso, duke of Toulouse, was deceived by a certain Gascon named Adeleric, bound by oaths, and finally released by him. To avenge this disgrace, King Louis and the nobles by whose counsel the affairs of the Aquitanian kingdom were administered summoned a general assembly in a place in Septimania called Mors-Gothorum.

The Gascon in question, conscious of his deed, delayed coming until, relying upon the intervention of hostages, he finally appeared. But although the hostages suffered no harm, he was in addition presented with gifts: he returned our hostages, recovered his own, and departed [Col. 0931B].

In the following summer, King Louis came simply, not on campaign, to Worms at his father’s command and remained with him in winter quarters (788). There the aforesaid Adeleric, ordered to plead his case before the kings and having been heard, wished but was unable to clear himself of the charges. He was outlawed and carried away into irrevocable exile.

Chorso was removed from the duchy of Toulouse, since through his negligence such disgrace had befallen the king and the Franks, and William was appointed in his place (789). He found the Gascon people, naturally fickle, greatly elated by the outcome described above and excessively enraged by Adeleric’s punishment. Nevertheless, within a short time he subdued them by both action and force and imposed peace upon that nation.

In the same year (790), King Louis held a general assembly at Toulouse. While he was staying there, Abutaurus, a Saracen leader, sent messengers to him together with the other rulers bordering on the Aquitanian kingdom, seeking peace and sending royal gifts. After the gifts had been accepted according to the king’s will, the messengers returned home.

Meanwhile, in the following year (790), King Louis met his father the king at Ingelheim and went with him from there to Regensburg. There, as he was entering the years of adolescence, he was girded with a sword. He then accompanied his father, who was leading an army against the Avars, as far as Chunoburg, but was ordered to return and remain with Queen Fastrada until his father came back.

Thus he spent the approaching winter with her while his father remained on the campaign he had begun. When his father returned from the Avar expedition [Col. 0932A], Louis received from him the command to return to Aquitaine and proceed into Italy with as many troops as he could, to aid his brother Pippin.

Obeying him, he returned to Aquitaine in autumn. After arranging everything relevant to the kingdom’s protection, he crossed into Italy through the harsh and winding defiles of Mount Cenis. Celebrating Christmas at Ravenna (793), he came to his brother. Joining him, they entered the province of Benevento with their combined forces, ravaged everything in their path, and captured one fortress.

When winter had passed, they returned together successfully to their father. One report, however, clouded much of their joy: they learned that their natural brother Pippin was plotting rebellion against their common father, and that many nobles were implicated in, entangled in, and ruined by this crime [Col. 0932B].

They therefore hurried to their father, who was in Bavaria, and came to a place called Salz, where he received them most graciously. King Louis spent with his father whatever remained of summer, autumn, and winter (794). His royal father took great care that neither honorable instruction should be hidden from his son the king nor foreign attachments dishonor him in any way.

When Louis was dismissed by his father in early spring (795), his father asked him why, although he was a king, he was so poor in household resources that he could not even offer a gift unless it had first been requested. He learned from him that, because each of the leading men pursued private interests while neglecting public ones, and because public property was being turned into private property, a man was lord in name only but was in practice needy of almost everything [Col. 0932C].

Wishing to remedy this need, but fearing that his affection for his son might suffer in the estimation of the nobles if he prudently deprived them of something he had previously granted through ignorance, he sent his messengers to Louis—namely Willebert, later archbishop of Rouen, and Count Richard, administrator of his estates—and ordered them to restore to public service the estates that had hitherto served royal use. This was done.

Once these matters had been restored, the king immediately demonstrated his prudence and revealed the affection of his mercy, which was known to be innate in him (796) [Col. 0932D]. He arranged that he should spend the winter in four places, so that after three years had elapsed each place would receive him for the winter in the fourth year: the palace of Tehotuadum, Cassinogilus, Andiacum, and Eurogilum. When the fourth year returned, these places supplied sufficient provisions for royal service.

After making these arrangements with great prudence, he prohibited the further extraction from the common people of military grain supplies, commonly called fodrum. Although the military men bore this with difficulty, he, a man of mercy, considered both the poverty of those who supplied the provisions and the cruelty of those who demanded them, as well as the destruction of both parties. He judged it better to supply his men from his own resources than, by permitting such a demand for grain, to entangle his people in danger.

At that time he relieved the people of Albi from the tribute by which they were burdened in supplying wine and grain [Col. 0933A]. He then had with him Meginarius, sent by his father, a wise and energetic man who understood the usefulness and dignity of royal affairs.

It is said that these actions pleased the king his father so greatly that, following this example, he prohibited military grain supplies from being exacted in Francia and ordered many other abuses to be corrected, rejoicing in his son’s successful progress.

Afterward the king came to Toulouse and held a general assembly there. He received and peacefully dismissed the envoys of Alfonso, prince of Galicia, whom Alfonso had sent with gifts to strengthen their friendship. He likewise received and dismissed envoys of Bahaluc, a Saracen leader who ruled in the mountainous districts near Aquitaine; they sought peace and brought gifts.

At that time, fearing that he might be overcome by the natural heat of his body and swept into the many winding paths of lust, he, with the counsel of his advisers, took as his wife Hermengard, the future queen, a woman of distinguished birth, the daughter of Count Ingram.

He also arranged at that time for very strong protection throughout the borders of Aquitaine. He fortified and repopulated the city of Ausona, the fortress of Cardona, Castaserra, and the other towns that had long stood deserted, and entrusted their defense to Count Borrell with suitable reinforcements.

When winter had passed, his father the king sent word that he should come with whatever forces he could muster to join him as he marched against the Saxons. Not delaying, Louis came to him at Aachen and went with him to Framersheim, where the king held a general assembly on the bank of the Rhine. In Saxony he remained with his father until the feast of Saint Martin [Col. 0933C].

From Saxony he departed with his father and withdrew to Aquitaine after a considerable part of the winter had passed. In the following summer, King Charles sent to him ordering him to accompany him into Italy; but after changing his mind, he ordered Louis to remain at home.

When the king was traveling to Rome and receiving the imperial insignia there (800), King Louis went again to Toulouse and from there hastened into Spain. As he approached Barcelona, Zaddo, the duke of that city, came to meet him as though he were a subject, but nevertheless did not surrender the city.

The king passed it by and came to Lérida, which he subdued and destroyed. After demolishing it and ravaging and burning the other towns, he advanced as far as Huesca. His military force cut down, ravaged, and burned its fields full of crops, and whatever was found outside the city was consumed by the devouring fire [Col. 0933D].

When these actions had been completed and winter was already approaching, he returned home. In the following summer, the most glorious Emperor Charles went to Saxony (801), ordering his son to follow him, as though he too would spend the winter in that land.

Hastening to do so, Louis came to Neuss, crossed the Rhine there, and hurried to meet his father. Before he reached him, however, he encountered his father’s messenger at a place called Ostfaloa, with orders not to tire himself further by traveling, but rather to establish a camp in a suitable place and await Charles’s return there. For the victorious Emperor Charles, having subdued the entire Saxon people, was already returning [Col. 0934A].

When his son met him, Charles embraced and kissed him repeatedly, praised him highly with abundant thanks, and often declared that he was fortunate to possess such a son, praising the usefulness of Louis’s obedience.

At last, when the long and most bloody Saxon war had ended—a war said to have occupied thirty-three years—King Louis, dismissed by his father, withdrew with his men to his own kingdom for the winter.

When winter had passed (802), Emperor Charles, finding a suitable opportunity because he was resting from foreign wars, began to visit the regions of his kingdom adjoining the sea. When King Louis learned this, he sent an envoy, Adhemar, to Rouen and asked his father to turn aside into Aquitaine, visit the kingdom he had given him, and come to the place called Cassinogilus [Col. 0934B].

His father received the request honorably and thanked his son, but denied the request and ordered him to meet him at Tours. When the son came there, his father received him with great joy, and Louis accompanied him as far as Verneuil while he was returning to Francia. After parting from him, Louis returned to Aquitaine.

In the following summer (803), Zaddo, duke of Barcelona, was persuaded by someone whom he considered a friend to proceed as far as Narbonne. He was captured and brought to King Louis, and likewise taken to his father Charles.

At that time King Louis assembled the people of his kingdom at Toulouse and deliberated concerning matters that seemed necessary. Since Burgundio had died, his county of Fidentiacus was assigned to Liutard [Col. 0934C]. The Gascons took this badly and broke out into such insolence that they killed some of Liutard’s men with the sword and burned others with fire.

When summoned, they initially refused to come; but they were brought to trial by whatever means were necessary and paid the penalties deserved for such audacity. Some were burned according to the law of retaliation.

After these matters had been settled, in the following year (804) the king and his advisers decided that they should go to attack Barcelona. The army was divided into three parts. Louis himself retained one part with him in Roussillon; he assigned the siege of the city to another, under Count Rotstagnus of Gerona; and he sent the third to take up position beyond the city, lest the besiegers should be unexpectedly attacked by the enemy [Col. 0934D].

Meanwhile, the besieged inhabitants sent to Córdoba and requested assistance. The Saracen king immediately sent an army to aid them. When those who had been sent arrived at Zaragoza, they were told about an army stationed in their path. William, the chief standard-bearer, was there, together with Adhemar and a strong force.

On hearing this, the Saracens turned toward the Asturians and inflicted an unexpected defeat upon them, but suffered a much heavier one in return. When they withdrew, our men returned to their comrades besieging the city. Joining them, they harassed the city by surrounding it continually and allowing no one to enter or leave, until the inhabitants, driven by the severity of famine, were forced to strip even the oldest leather from their doors and turn it into the most miserable food [Col. 0935A].

Others, preferring death to a most wretched life, threw themselves headlong from the walls. Some were encouraged by a vain hope, thinking that the Franks would be driven away from the siege by the harshness of winter. But the counsel of prudent men cut off this hope. Bringing timber from every direction, they began to build huts as though they intended to remain there in winter quarters.

Seeing this, the inhabitants of the city abandoned hope and turned to utter despair. They surrendered their ruler, a relative of Zaddo, whom they had set over themselves, a man named Hamur, and surrendered themselves and the city, having been granted permission to depart, in the following manner.

When our men had held the city, exhausted by the long siege, and believed that it was just about to be captured or surrendered, they adopted an honorable plan, as was fitting. They summoned the king, so that, if it should happen that such a famous city were conquered in his presence, its glorious name might add to the king’s renown.

The king agreed to this entirely honorable suggestion. He came to his army surrounding the city, which had endured unceasing assault for six weeks, and at last, overcome, surrendered itself to the victor.

After the city had been handed over and opened, the king assigned guards to it on the first day but refrained from entering it himself until he had arranged how to dedicate the desired and obtained victory to God’s name with fitting thanksgiving.

On the following day, with the priests and clergy of his army preceding him in solemn procession and with hymns of praise, he entered through the city gate and proceeded to the church of the holy and most victorious Cross, intending to give thanks to God for the victory granted to him (805) [Col. 0935C].

Afterward he left Count Bera there with auxiliaries from the Goths to guard the city and returned home to spend the winter. When his father learned of the danger that seemed to threaten him from the Saracens, he sent his brother Charles to assist him.

While Charles was staying at Lyons and hastening to aid his brother, a messenger of King Louis met him, announced that the city had been captured, and ordered him not to tire himself by going farther. He therefore turned back from that place and returned to his father.

While King Louis was spending the winter in Aquitaine, his father the king ordered him to come to Aachen to meet him on the Feast of the Purification of Saint Mary, Mother of God. Louis met him there, remained with him as long as he wished, and returned during Lent [Col. 0935D].

In the following summer (806), he set out for Spain with as much military equipment as seemed appropriate. Proceeding through Barcelona and coming to Tarragona, he captured those whom he found there and put the others to flight. By military force he cut down and destroyed all the places, castles, and towns as far as Tortosa, and consuming fire devoured them.

Meanwhile, at a place called Saint Columba, he divided his forces into two. He led the larger part with him against Tortosa, while sending Isembard, Adhemar, Bera, and Borrell with the remainder as rapidly as possible toward the upper reaches, so that, after crossing the Ebro, they might unexpectedly attack the enemy while they were sitting secure in their dwellings, or at least throw the region into confusion and panic [Col. 0936A].

Thus, while the king was making for Tortosa, the men mentioned above traveled for a long time toward the upper parts of the Ebro, going by night and making their way through forest tracks by day, until they crossed both the Cinca and the Ebro by swimming. They spent six days on this journey and crossed on the seventh.

When all had escaped unharmed, they ravaged the enemy’s land far and wide and reached their principal village, called Villa-Rubea. From there they carried off an extremely large amount of booty, since the enemy had been taken by surprise and had never suspected anything of the kind.

After these events, those who had escaped carried the news of the attack far and wide. A considerable multitude of Saracens and Moors gathered and took up a position against them at the mouth of a valley called Vallis-Ibana [Col. 0936B].

The nature of this valley is such that, lying deep below, it is enclosed on both sides by precipitous and lofty mountains. Had God’s providence not prevented our men from entering it, they could almost certainly have perished beneath a hail of stones from the enemy without any labor on the enemy’s part, or fallen into their hands.

While the enemy blocked the road and our men sought another route, more open and level, the Moors supposed that our men were doing this not merely to protect themselves but rather out of fear of them, and pursued them from behind.

Our men, however, leaving the booty behind, exposed their faces to the enemy and stood their ground. With Christ’s help they forced the enemy to turn their backs. They killed those whom they caught and returned joyfully to the booty they had abandoned. Finally, twenty days after their departure, they returned cheerfully to the king, having lost very few of their men [Col. 0936C].

King Louis received his men gladly and returned home after ravaging the enemy’s land everywhere.

In the following period King Louis again prepared an expedition into Spain. But his father prevented him from going there in person. At that time he had ordered ships to be built against the incursions of the Northmen on all the rivers that flowed into the sea. He also assigned this task to his son on the Rhône, the Garonne, and the Sílida.

Nevertheless, he sent his messenger Ingobert to him, so that he might represent the son’s presence and lead an army against the enemy on behalf of them both.

Since the king remained in Aquitaine for the reason stated above, his army reached Barcelona by a favorable route. There they deliberated among themselves about how they might make a secret attack upon the enemy and devised the following plan: they would build transport ships, dividing each one into four sections, so that each quarter of a vessel could be carried by two horses or mules and, once prepared with nails and hammers, easily fitted together. They would also prepare pitch, wax, and tow, so that as soon as they reached the river, the joints of the assembled parts could be sealed.

Equipped in this way, most of the army, with the aforementioned messenger Ingobert, had gone toward Tortosa. Those assigned to the task described above—Adhemar, Bera, and the others—completed a three-day journey (for they had no pack saddles), using the sky as their roof and renouncing fire [Al., a hearth] so that they would not be detected by smoke. They concealed themselves in the forests by day and traveled as far as they could by night.

On the fourth day, after assembling the boats, they themselves crossed the Ebro, while they set the horses to swimming [Col. 0937A]. This undertaking would have achieved their purpose completely had it not been detected with the greatest keenness.

For when Abaidun, the duke of Tortosa, was guarding the banks of the Ebro, and the men mentioned above were transporting themselves upstream in the manner described, a certain Moor entered the river to bathe and saw horse dung being carried along by the current.

Seeing this, and being—as such people are—exceedingly shrewd, he swam toward it, seized the dung, brought it to his nose, and exclaimed:

“Look, comrades; I warn you, take heed. This dung is not that of a wild ass or of any animal accustomed to feed upon grass. It is clear that these are the droppings of horses. It is certain that the grain in them was barley, and thus fodder for horses or mules. So keep a more careful watch, for, as I perceive, an ambush is being prepared for us in the upper part of this river.”

Immediately they mounted two of their men on horses and sent them to reconnoiter. When they saw our men, they reported the truth to Abaidun.

The others, compelled by fear, abandoned and left behind everything belonging to a military camp and committed themselves to flight. Our men seized everything that had been left behind and spent that night lodging in their tents.

But on the following day Abaidun gathered a large force of the enemy and came to fight them. Our men, nevertheless, relying upon divine aid, although inferior and greatly outnumbered, forced the enemy to flee and filled the fugitives’ route with the slaughter of many of them [Col. 0937C].

They did not restrain their hands from killing them until the light of the sun and day had withdrawn, the shadow of night had occupied the earth, and the lights of the stars succeeded to console the night.

After these events, with Christ’s favor, they returned to their own people with great joy and wealth. After jointly besieging the city for a long time, they returned home.

Moreover, in the following year (808), King Louis decided to return to Tortosa in person, taking with him Heribert, Liutard, Isembard, and a strong contingent from Francia. When he arrived there, he battered and crushed the city walls with rams, mangonels, siege-shelters, and other instruments to such an extent that its citizens lost hope. Seeing their own people broken in battle, they surrendered the keys of the city. Louis brought these back to his father on his return, to great acclaim. This event struck great fear into the Saracens and Moors because of what had happened, since they feared that a similar fate might engulf each of their cities.

The king therefore withdrew from the city after forty days from the beginning of the siege and returned to his own kingdom. But after the passage of the following year (809), he organized an army and decided to send it against Huesca, together with his father’s envoy Heribert. When those who had been sent arrived there, they besieged the city, capturing all whom they encountered alive or forcing them to flee. But while they were sitting around the city and relaxing with less diligence than was appropriate, some thoughtless and reckless young men approached the walls. First they attempted to provoke the men stationed on the battlements with words, and then to attack them with missiles. The townsmen, despising the small number of those present and calculating the delayed arrival of those who were absent, opened the gates and rushed out.

A battle was fought on both sides. Men were killed on either side, and at last the former withdrew into the city, while the latter returned to the camp to remain there. The siege was therefore prolonged; after completing the devastation and doing whatever seemed necessary against the enemy to satisfy their anger, they returned to the king, who at that time was occupied with the pursuits of hunting in the forests. For it was the very end of autumn. After receiving his men on their return from the expedition just described, the king spent the following winter peacefully among his own people.

When summer followed (810), he summoned a general assembly of his people and reported to them a rumor that a certain part of the Basques, which had long ago been received into submission, was now contemplating defection and rising in rebellion. Public necessity, he said, required that he go to suppress their stubbornness. Everyone applauded the king’s intention and declared that such conduct in subjects was not to be disregarded, but rather cut off with the utmost severity.

Accordingly, after moving and arranging the army as circumstances required, he reached the village of Aquas and ordered those accused of disloyalty to come to him. When they delayed coming, he approached their neighborhood and permitted his army to devastate everything belonging to them. At last, after everything that seemed to belong to them had been consumed, they came as suppliants and finally earned pardon for the loss of all their possessions, as a great gift.

After crossing the difficult pass of the Pyrenees—almost the Alps—he descended to Pamplona. He remained in those regions as long as seemed appropriate and arranged whatever served both the public and private interest. But when it became necessary to return through the narrow passes of the same mountain, the Basques attempted to practice their native and habitual custom of deceit. They were immediately detected by prudent cunning; their plans were met with caution, and their stratagem was avoided.

One of them, who had advanced to provoke an encounter, was captured and hanged. From nearly all the others, wives or sons were taken away, until our men had reached a point where their deceit could inflict no harm upon the king or the army.

After these events, the king and his people returned to their own land, with God favorable to them (811). From his earliest age, but especially at that time, the king’s mind was most fervently moved toward divine worship and the exaltation of the holy Church. Thus people proclaimed him not merely a king, but rather a priest because of his works.

For the entire clergy of Aquitania, before being entrusted to him, had been known—since it lived under tyrants—to devote itself more to riding, military training, and the casting of missiles than to divine worship. But through the king’s efforts, teachers were brought in from every direction, and the study both of reading and singing, as well as understanding divine and secular literature, quickly flourished beyond what could have been believed.

Above all, however, he was guided by affection for those who, abandoning all that they possessed for the love of the Lord, took care to become participants in the contemplative life. Before Aquitania was governed under him, this order had collapsed there; under him it grew so strong that he himself, eager to imitate the memorable example of his grandfather Carloman, likewise strove to attain the heights of the contemplative life.

But his father’s opposition—or rather, the indication of the divine will—prevented him from fulfilling this desire. God did not wish such a pious man to remain hidden in the solitary pursuit of his own salvation; rather, through him and under him, He wished the salvation of many to flourish.

Indeed, as has been said, he restored many things within his dominion, and even built monasteries from their foundations. In particular, these included:

- the monastery of Saint Mary and Saint Peter at Ferrières, which in ancient times was called Bethlehem. In its courtyard his father Pippin killed a lion, and in the same church he himself was solemnly consecrated king by Pope Stephen of Rome;
- the monastery of Saint Philibert;
- the monastery of Saint Florentius;
- the monastery of Carroffi;
- the monastery of Conques;
- the monastery of Saint Maxentius;
- the monastery of Menat;
- the monastery of Magnilocus;
- the monastery of Musciacum;
- the monastery of Saint Savin;
- the monastery of Masciacum;
- the monastery of Noviliacum;
- the monastery of Saint Theotfridus;
- the monastery of Saint Pascentius;
- the monastery of Dosora;
- the monastery of Sollemniacum;
- the nunnery of Saint Mary;
- the nunnery of Saint Radegund;
- the monastery of Vera;
- the monastery of Utera in the district of Toulouse;
- the monastery of Valada in Septimania;
- the monastery of Aniane;
- the monastery of Galuna;
- the monastery of Saint Lawrence;
- the monastery of Saint Mary called at Rubine [Orubione];
- the monastery of Caunas;

and many others, by which the whole kingdom of Aquitania was adorned as though by lamps.

Many bishops, and also very many laymen, imitated this example of his. They restored what had fallen into decay and competed to establish new monasteries; this can be seen with one’s own eyes.

Finally, the commonwealth of the Aquitanian kingdom had advanced to such happiness that, whether a king was departing or residing in the palace, scarcely anyone could be found complaining that he had suffered any injustice. For the king attended to judicial affairs three days in every week.

On one occasion, he had sent Archambald, imperial chamberlain, on a mission, entrusting him with certain matters to be conveyed to his son and reported back. When Archambald returned and reported this arrangement to his father as he had observed it, the king is said to have rejoiced so greatly that tears flowed from excessive delight. Turning to those standing around him, he said: “O companions, let us rejoice that we have been surpassed by this young man’s aged wisdom.”

Thus, because he had been a faithful servant of the Lord in what had been entrusted to him and prudent in increasing the talent committed to him, he was appointed to possess authority over the whole household of the master.
