At about the same time (813), Pippin, king of Italy, having died some time before, and Charles, likewise his brother, having most recently departed this life, hope of acquiring the whole inheritance rose upon him.

Gerricus, bishop of Capua, had been sent to consult his father about certain necessary matters. While he was staying at the palace and awaiting the response of those who had carried the message, both Franks and Germans advised him that the king should go to his father and stand beside him. They said that, since his father was already advancing into old age and was suffering bitterly from the unfortunate defection of his children, these circumstances seemed to foretell his speedy bodily dissolution.

When Gerricus reported this to the king, and the king in turn reported it to his counselors, some, or almost all, regarded the advice as salutary. But the king, following a deeper plan, delayed acting, lest by doing so he should make himself suspect to his father.

Nevertheless, the Divinity—for whose fear and love he had refused to act—ordered matters more wisely, as is His custom, ennobling those who love Him more highly than can be imagined.

When those whom he had been accustomed to weary with war requested peace, the king willingly granted it for a fixed period of two years.

Meanwhile, Emperor Charles, considering that he had declined into old age and fearing that, if he were removed from human affairs, he might leave in confusion the kingdom which, by God’s gift, had been nobly ordered—lest it be shaken either by external storms or troubled by internal divisions—sent for his son and summoned him from Aquitania.

He received him kindly when he came and kept him with him throughout the summer. He instructed him in those matters which he thought he needed to know: how he ought to live, reign, order the kingdom, and preserve it once ordered. Finally, he crowned him with the imperial diadem and made known that, with Christ’s favor, supreme authority over affairs would rest with him. When this business had been completed, he granted him permission to return to his own lands.

In November, returning from his father, Louis went back to Aquitania. His father, however, as though near death, began to be oppressed by frequent and unusual ailments. Death, as if through certain messengers announcing that its arrival was imminent, already and almost immediately to come, foretold itself by such signs.

At length, as the disorders of his illnesses fought among themselves and attacked his strength, the weakness of nature gave way. He took to his bed; growing nearer to death with every day and hour, he distributed his possessions in writing as he wished, and closed his final day, leaving the kingdom of the Franks almost inconsolable grief.

But in his successor the truthful Scripture was proved, which, consoling the minds of those afflicted in such circumstances, says: “The righteous man has died, and it is as though he had not died, for he has left behind a son like himself as heir.”

The most pious Emperor Charles died on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the year 814 of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. At that time Emperor Louis had summoned a general assembly of the people, almost as though by a certain foreknowledge, for the Purification of holy Mary, Mother of God, at a place called Tehotuadus.

After the death of his father of blessed memory, Rampo was sent to him by those who had arranged the burial—namely, his children and the palace nobles—so that he might promptly learn of his death and in no way delay his arrival.

When Rampo reached the city of Orléans, Theodulf, bishop of that city, a man learned in every respect, perceived the reason for his arrival. He immediately sent a messenger and hastened to inform the emperor, ordering him to ask only whether he should await Louis’s arrival in the city or meet him somewhere on the road as he came toward it.

The emperor immediately understood the point of this inquiry and ordered Rampo to come to him. From then onward, as he received one sad report after another of this kind, he departed from that place on the fifth day and set out with as many people as the shortness of time permitted.

Wala was greatly feared, since he held the highest position under Emperor Charles, lest he might be plotting some evil against the emperor. Yet Wala came to him most quickly and, commending and submitting himself to his will with the deepest humility, surrendered himself according to Frankish custom.

After his arrival at the emperor’s court, all the Frankish nobles imitated him and strove, competing with one another and in groups, to go out to meet Louis. At last Louis reached Heristall by a prosperous journey and, on the thirtieth day after setting out from Aquitania, happily entered the palace at Aachen.

For some time, although he was naturally most gentle, his mind had been troubled by what his sisters practiced in their father’s household; this alone stained the paternal house with a blemish. Wishing to remedy this abuse and at the same time fearing that the scandal once caused by Odilo and Hiltrude might revive, he sent Wala, Warnarius, Lantbert, and Ingobert.

When they came to Aachen, they were to take precautions so that such things could not occur, and they were cautiously to keep under guard until Louis’s arrival certain people guilty of monstrous sexual misconduct and swollen with pride.

Some of these, however, had asked for pardon as they traveled and obtained it. Louis also ordered that the people staying there should await his arrival without fear.

Count Warnarius, however, without Wala’s or Ingobert’s knowledge, summoned his nephew Lantbert and ordered Hodoin, already implicated in the aforesaid crime, to come to him, supposedly so that he might be arrested and handed over to royal vengeance.

Hodoin, warned by the sharp bite of his conscience, foresaw the ambush. Since he did not refuse to confront it and chose to test the matter himself, he brought ultimate disaster upon Warnarius. Coming to him as Warnarius had commanded, he killed Warnarius and rendered Lantbert disabled for a considerable time by an injury to the leg. Finally, struck through with a sword, Hodoin himself died.

When this was reported to the emperor, the friend’s death turned his mind toward mercy, so much so that a certain Tullius [reading uncertain: *illius* in the supplied text], one of those involved in such matters and who already seemed almost worthy of pardon through the emperor’s clemency, was punished by the loss of his eyes.

The emperor therefore came to the palace at Aachen and was received with great acclaim by his relatives and many thousands of Franks. He was proclaimed emperor for the second time.

When these matters had been completed, he thanked those who had diligently arranged his father’s burial and brought fitting comfort to his relatives, who were crushed by the bitterness of mourning. He also promptly supplied whatever was lacking for his father’s funeral rites.

After his father’s testament had been read aloud, none of the paternal possessions was left undistributed; everything was divided according to its provisions. For nothing had been left by him without a testamentary disposition.

The property which he had decided should be distributed among the metropolitan churches he divided according to the headings of their names; there were twenty-one portions. Whatever was suitable for royal adornment he reserved for a later age.

He also determined what should be distributed, according to Christian custom, to his sons and grandsons, to his daughters, to the royal male and female servants, and to all the poor in common. The lord Emperor Louis completed all these arrangements in practice, just as he reread them in writing.

After this, the emperor decreed that the entire female community, which was very large, should be excluded from the palace, except for a very few whom he considered suitable for royal service. He allowed each of his sisters to retain what she had received from their father. Those who had not yet obtained such a provision received one from the emperor and turned themselves to his commands.

Afterward, he carefully listened to the embassies that had been sent to his father but now came to him and received them. He treated them generously and sent them back with costly gifts.

Among these, the most distinguished was the embassy of Michael, emperor of Constantinople. The lord Charles had sent Amalarius, bishop of Trier, and Peter, abbot of Nonantola, to him to confirm peace. On their return they brought with them the aforesaid Michael’s envoys: Christophorus, the protospatharius, and Gregory the deacon, who had been sent to Emperor Charles to respond concerning everything that had been written.

When the emperor sent them back, he sent his own envoys with them to Leo, the substitute emperor: Norbert, bishop of Reggio, and Richoinus, count of Poitiers. He requested a partnership and renewal of friendship, as well as confirmation of the treaty.

That same year he held a general assembly at Aachen and sent faithful and trustworthy men from his side throughout all parts of his kingdom. Since they upheld equitable justice, they were to correct wrongdoing and weigh out appropriate justice to everyone with an even balance.

He also summoned his nephew Bernard, already king of Italy, to himself. Bernard obeyed, and the emperor sent him back to his own kingdom with generous gifts.

Likewise, he bound Grimoald, prince of Benevento—not in person, but through his envoys—with a treaty and oaths, so that every year he would pay seven thousand gold solidi into the public treasury.

That same year he sent two of his sons, Lothar to Bavaria and Pippin to Aquitania; he kept the third, Louis, who was still a child, with him.

At the same time Heriold, to whom supreme authority in the Danish kingdom seemed to belong and who had previously been driven from the kingdom by the sons of Godefrid, fled for refuge to Emperor Louis and, according to Frankish custom, placed himself in the emperor’s hands.

The king received him, ordered him to go into Saxony, and instructed him to await there the time when he could provide assistance for the recovery of his principality.

At that same time, imperial clemency restored to the Saxons and Frisians the right of their paternal inheritance, which under his father they had legally lost because of their treachery. Some attributed this to generosity, others to lack of foresight, since these peoples, accustomed to natural ferocity, ought to have been restrained by such reins, lest, once unbridled, they should be carried into the insolence of rebellion.

The emperor, however, judged that they would be bound to him more tightly the more generously he bestowed benefits upon them, and he was not deceived in his expectation. For after this he always found these same peoples most devoted to him.

In this year (815), as the course of time advanced, it was reported to the emperor that certain powerful Romans had entered into wicked conspiracies against Leo the apostolic bishop. The same apostolic bishop had dragged them before him, convicted them, and condemned them to capital punishment, since Roman law supported such a sentence against conspirators.

When the emperor heard this, he took it badly, as though the first priest of the world had acted with excessive severity. Therefore he sent Bernard, king of Italy, there, so that Bernard might learn for himself what in this matter was true and what false rumor had spread, and report it to him through Gerold.

King Bernard himself came to Rome and reported through the aforementioned envoy what he had seen. But soon envoys of the same apostolic bishop Leo followed: John, bishop of Silva Candida; Theodore, the nomenclator; and Sergius, the duke. They cleared Leo the apostolic bishop of the charges brought against him.

The emperor had ordered that Saxon counts and the Abodrites, formerly subject to the lord Charles, should be supplied to Heriold, so that he might be restored to his own kingdom. For this very purpose he sent Baldric as envoy.

When they had crossed the Eider River, they came into the land of the Northmen, to a place called Sinlendi. But although the sons of Godefrid possessed abundant forces and two hundred ships, they refused to come to close quarters or entrust themselves to battle. The two sides therefore withdrew from one another. Everything that could be encountered was plundered and burned, and forty hostages were also received from that people.

After these events they returned to the emperor at the place called Paderborn, where the entire people had gathered for his general assembly. At that place all the princes and leading men of the eastern Slavs came.

That same year Abulat, king of the Saracens, requested a three-year peace from the emperor. It was initially granted, but afterward rejected as useless, and war was declared against the Saracens.

At that time Bishop Norbert and Count Richoinus returned from Constantinople and brought back a treaty of alliance between that emperor and the Franks, which was most welcome.

At the same time, while Leo the apostolic bishop was suffering from an adverse illness, the Romans attempted, without awaiting any judge, to seize and restore to themselves all the estates which they call *domocultae* and which had recently been established by that same apostolic bishop, as well as those which they claimed had been taken from them unjustly.

King Bernard resisted their efforts through Winigis, duke of Spoleto, and sent the emperor a trustworthy report concerning all these matters.

After the emperor had passed the severity of winter in sound health and tranquil prosperity (816), and the welcome mildness of summer had followed, he sent the men called Eastern Franks, together with counts of Saxon stock, against the Slavic Sorbs, who were said to have revolted from his authority. By Christ’s gift, their undertaking was suppressed very swiftly and easily.

At the same time the nearest Basques, who inhabit places close to the Pyrenean ridge, wholly revolted from us, in accordance with their inborn habit of fickleness. The cause of their rebellion was that the emperor had removed their count, Siguvinus, from his office because of his evil conduct, by which he had become almost intolerable. Yet they were so thoroughly subdued in two expeditions that they late regretted their undertaking and earnestly sought submission.

Meanwhile word reached the emperor of the death of Lord Leo, bishop of Rome, which occurred on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the twenty-first year of his episcopate; and of the appointment in his place of Stephen, a deacon. After his consecration, Stephen did not delay in coming to the lord emperor. For scarcely two months had elapsed when he hastened with the greatest speed to meet him. Nevertheless, he first sent an embassy to satisfy the emperor concerning his appointment.

When the emperor learned of his arrival, he ordered his nephew Bernard to accompany him. He also sent other envoys to meet the pope as he approached and conduct him with due honor. The emperor himself resolved to await his arrival at Rheims. He ordered Hildebald, archchaplain of the sacred palace, Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, John of Arles, and a great company of other ministers of the Church, clothed in priestly vestments, to go out to meet him.

Finally the emperor proceeded a mile from the monastery of Saint Remigius the confessor and received him, as the vicar of blessed Peter, with the greatest honor: he received him as he dismounted from his horse and supported him with his own hand as he entered the church. Various orders of the Church sang before them in such great rejoicing, “We praise thee, O God,” and the rest. When the hymn had ended, the Roman clergy cried out the praises due to the emperor, and the lord pope concluded them with a prayer.

When this had been done, they sat down in the inner rooms of the house. The reasons for the pope’s coming having been set forth, and the blessing of bread and wine having been shared together, the emperor returned to the city, while the lord pope remained there. On the following day the lord emperor summoned the lord pope, entertained him at a most lavish banquet, and honored him with the greatest gifts. Likewise, on the third day the lord emperor was invited by the lord pope and received many and varied gifts.

On the next day, which was Sunday, the emperor was crowned with the imperial diadem and marked by a blessing during the celebration of the masses. At last, after these matters had been completed and everything he had requested had been granted, the lord pope returned to Rome. The emperor withdrew to Compiègne, where he received and heard the envoys of Abd al-Rahman, son of King Abulat. Having remained there twenty days or more, he set out for Aachen to spend the winter.

(817.) The emperor had indeed ordered the envoys of the Saracen king to go on ahead of him there, since he himself would come. When they had arrived, they were detained for almost three months. Afterwards, when they had grown weary of awaiting his arrival, they returned with the emperor’s permission.

While he was staying in that palace, he received an envoy who came to him from Leo, emperor of Constantinople, named Nicephorus. Apart from friendship and alliance, the embassy concerned the borders of the Dalmatians, Romans, and Slavs. Since neither these parties nor Chadalo, prefect of the frontier, was present, and the matter could not be settled without them, Albigarius was sent to Dalmatia, together with Chadalo, ruler of those same frontier regions, to make peace and arrange these matters.

In that same year the sons of Godefrid, formerly king of the Northmen, being pressed by Heriold, sent envoys to the emperor requesting peace. He rejected the embassy as useless and feigned, and gave Heriold assistance against them. In that year the moon was eclipsed on the Nones of February in the second hour of the night. The portentous star of a comet appeared in the sign of Sagittarius.

Pope Stephen died in the third month after returning from Francia to Rome, and Paschal succeeded him in the see of the Roman pontificate. After completing his solemn consecration, Paschal sent envoys to the emperor with an apologetic letter and very great gifts, declaring that he had yielded to this dignity rather than seized upon it, not through ambition or his own will, but through election and the acclamation of the people. The bearer of this embassy was Theodore the nomenclator. When his business had been completed and his requests granted—namely, confirmation of the treaty and friendship in the manner of his predecessors—he returned.

In the same year, when the time of Lent was almost complete, on Thursday of the final week, the day on which the memorial of the Lord’s Supper is celebrated, the emperor, after everything required by the solemnity of so great a day had been completed, wished to return from church to the royal residence. The wooden portico through which he had to pass, weakened by decay and age and rotted by continual dampness, collapsed beneath the emperor’s feet and those of his companions when its lower parts gave way. Its crash struck great fear into the entire palace, each person fearing that the fall might have overwhelmed the emperor.

But God, by whom he was loved, protected him from the immediate danger. For although twenty or more counts fell with him all the way to the ground and suffered various injuries, he suffered no more serious harm than a blow from the pommel of a sword against the lower part of his breast, a slight stripping of the skin at the edge of his ear, and his leg striking a piece of timber near the groin; prompt aid was, however, given. With physicians’ care applied, he was restored to his former health very quickly. After twenty days had passed, he went hunting at Nijmegen.

When this business had been completed, the emperor held a general assembly at Aachen, in which he displayed with all his effort the ardor for divine worship that he bore in the treasury of his heart. Having assembled bishops and the most eminent clergy of the holy Church, he caused a book to be compiled and arranged containing the rule of canonical life, in which, as the recluse himself acknowledges, the entire perfection of that order is contained. He also ordered that the total provision of food, drink, and every necessity be inserted in it, so that all, both men and consecrated women, serving Christ under this rule, might remember to wage free service for the Lord of all without being hindered by any want.

He sent this book throughout all the cities and monasteries of the canonical order in his empire by the hands of prudent envoys, who were to have it copied in all the aforesaid places and require that the stipulated and prescribed provisions be supplied. This matter brought great rejoicing and celebration to the Church, and an immortal memorial, with due praise, to the most pious emperor.

Likewise the same emperor, beloved of God, appointed Abbot Benedict, and with him monks of vigorous life in every respect, to travel throughout all monasteries of monks and hand down to every monastery, both of men and of consecrated women, a uniform and unchangeable manner of life according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

The same most pious emperor also considered that Christ’s ministers ought not to be subject to human servitude, and that many people’s avarice abused ecclesiastical ministry for private gain. He therefore decreed that whoever from servile condition, aided by learning and proven character, should be admitted to service at the altar, must first be freed by his own masters, whether private or ecclesiastical, and only then be invested with the ranks of the altar.

Wishing also that every church should have resources of its own, so that divine worship should not be neglected through such poverty, he inserted in the aforesaid edict that one mansus, by lawful compensation, together with a male and a female slave, should be granted to each church. This was the holy emperor’s exercise, his daily sport, his athletic contest before God, by which his life might shine more brightly in holy teaching and action: established amid the height of pomp, he stood out more highly by humbly imitating Christ.

Accordingly, bishops and clerics then began to lay aside belts laden with golden and jeweled knives, costly garments, and spurs weighing down their ankles. For it was regarded as something like a monstrosity if one assigned to the ecclesiastical household tried to aspire to the adornments of secular glory.

But the enemy of humankind could not endure this holy and God-worthy devotion of the emperor, which assailed him on every side and declared war on him from every order of the Church. He began to attack one who was attacking him with all his strength, and through his own members to harass, by force and cunning as he could, Christ’s most valiant warrior.

For after these matters had been duly arranged, and after the emperor, in that same assembly, wished his eldest son Lothar to be called and to be emperor, and sent his two sons Pippin into Aquitania and Louis into Bavaria, so that the people might know whose authority they ought to obey, news immediately reached him of the revolt of the Abodrites. Joining friendship with the sons of Godefrid, they were ravaging Transalbian Saxony. The emperor sent sufficient forces against them and, with God’s favor, suppressed their movement.

He himself went hunting, intending to follow the game-coverts of the Vosges. Meanwhile, when the hunt there had been completed according to Frankish custom, and he was returning to spend the winter at Aachen, news was brought to him that his nephew Bernard, king of Italy—through whom he himself had been a principal cause that Bernard should become king before his father—had been so maddened by the counsels of certain wicked men that he had revolted from him. All the cities and princes of the kingdom of Italy had sworn together to this effect, and had barred with obstacles and guards all the entrances by which Italy is entered.

When he had learned this with certainty from trustworthy reports, especially those of Bishop Rathald and Suppo, he gathered forces from every direction, from both Gaul and Germany, and came as far as Chalon with the full strength of a great army. But Bernard, seeing himself unequal in strength and unable to carry out his undertaking, since very many of his followers were deserting him every day, came to the emperor in despair. Laying down his arms, he threw himself at the emperor’s feet and confessed that he had acted wrongly.

His leading men followed his example, laid down their arms, and submitted themselves to the emperor’s power and judgment. At the first interrogation they disclosed their schemes: how and why they had begun the rebellion, to what end they had wished to bring it when begun, and whom they had drawn in as accomplices. The authors of this conspiracy were Eggiddeo, foremost among the king’s friends; Reginherius, formerly count of the emperor’s palace, son of Count Reginherius [manuscript: Meginherius]; and Reginhard, provost of the royal chamber.

Very many clerics and laymen were aware of this crime, and the storm of that time involved some bishops among them: Anselm of Milan, Wulfold of Cremona, and Theodulf of Orléans (818). After the leaders of the revolt had been exposed and committed to custody, the emperor returned to Aachen, as he had decided, to spend the winter, and remained there until he celebrated the holy solemnity of Easter.

After the celebration of that feast had passed, although Bernard, hitherto king, and his supporters in the aforesaid crime ought by Frankish law and judgment to have been struck with capital punishment, the emperor withheld the harsher sentence and consented that they be deprived of their eyes, although many opposed him and wished legal severity to be inflicted upon them in its full extent.

Yet although the emperor acted more leniently, the punishment imposed was brought to its effect upon some. Bernard and Reginherius, bearing the loss and removal of their eyes too impatiently, brought upon themselves the bitterness of death. The bishops bound by this enormity, having been deposed by the other bishops, he committed to monasteries. Of the rest he ordered none to be deprived of life or punished by amputation of limbs; rather, as the offense seemed to require, he ordered some to be exiled and others to be shorn.

After this, the emperor was told of the insolence of the disobedient Bretons, who had broken out into such arrogance that they dared to call one of their own, named Marmonius [Marmanus], king and had refused subjection in every way. To punish their insolence, the emperor gathered military forces from every side and set out against the borders of the Bretons. Having held a general assembly at Vannes, he entered the province and, in a short time and with little effort, ravaged everything, until, after Marcon [Marmonius above] had been killed while he was attending to the baggage of the camp by a keeper of the royal horses named Choslo, all Brittany with him was conquered, submitted, and gave its hand to serve again under whatever conditions the emperor might wish. For the hostages ordered, both their number and their quality, were given and received, and the whole land was arranged according to his will.

From these frontiers of Britain, now so pacified, the emperor withdrew [Col. 0948B] and returned to the city of Angers. There, while Queen Ermengard was being worn down by a prolonged illness, she survived the emperor’s return by two days and died on the third, on the fifth day before the Nones of October. In that year an eclipse of the sun occurred on the eighth day before the Ides of July. After the queen’s burial had been arranged, the emperor traveled by way of Rouen and Amiens and proceeded by the direct route to Aachen for the winter. As he returned and entered the palace at Herstal, envoys sent by Sigo, duke of Benevento, came to meet him bearing very great gifts and clearing their lord of responsibility for the death of Grimoald, his predecessor. Envoys of other peoples were also present—namely, of the Obodrites, the Goduscans, and the Timocians, who, having abandoned their alliance with the Bulgars, had recently joined themselves to our people. Envoys of Liudevitus [Col. 0948C], ruler of Lower Pannonia, were also present there, accusing Cadol of wrongdoing—falsely, as later became clear—on the ground that his savagery was unbearable to them. After hearing these matters, settling them, and dismissing the envoys, the emperor withdrew to spend the winter in that same palace according to his own arrangements.

**(819.)** While he was staying there, Sclaomir, king of the Obodrites, was brought before him by the Saxon dukes. When he was accused of defection and could not refute the charges brought against him, he was carried into exile, and his kingdom was handed over to Ceadrag, son of Trascon. At the same time a certain Wasco Lupus, surnamed Centullus, rose in rebellion and challenged Werimus [Werinus], count of the Auvergnans, and Berengar the Toulousan in battle. There he also lost, together with many others, his German brother [Gersandus], and at that time escaped only by flight. Later he was brought before the emperor, ordered to plead his case, and defeated by the evidence; he was condemned to exile.

That winter the emperor held a public assembly of his people in the same palace. He heard the envoys who reported to him from throughout his kingdom—those whom he had sent to restore the condition of the holy Church where it had been overthrown, or to confirm it where it stood. Whatever he judged useful, he added under the prompting of holy devotion, leaving untouched nothing that seemed capable of advancing the honor of the holy Church of God. Meanwhile he added certain chapters to the laws, dealing with cases in which the judicial proceedings seemed to limp; these chapters have been preserved to the present as being of the utmost necessity.

At that time, prompted by his advisers, he was considering contracting a marriage. Many feared that he wished to abandon the reins of government, but he was being compelled to do so. At length, satisfying their wishes, and examining the daughters of nobles brought from every quarter, he took as his wife Judith, daughter of Welf, a most noble count. In the following summer his people assembled to him at the palace of Ingelheim. There he received the envoys of his army, who had been sent to suppress Liudevitus’s open rebellion. Yet that undertaking remained almost entirely unfinished. Liudevitus, puffed up with the arrogance produced by this situation, sent the emperor certain terms through his envoys: if the emperor fulfilled them, he too would obey the emperor’s commands as before. But these terms were despised and rejected by the emperor as useless. Liudevitus, however, resolved to remain in his treachery and joined to himself in rebellion everyone he could.

After the army had returned from the borders of Pannonia, while Liudevitus remained in his treachery, Cadolach [Cadolh], duke of Friuli, fell ill with fever and died; Baldric succeeded him. When Baldric first came into Provence and entered the regions of the Carantani, he routed Liudevitus’s forces near the river Drava with a small number of his own men. Driving the remainder away, he compelled them all to withdraw from their territories. Liudevitus, driven away by Baldric, encountered Borna, duke of Dalmatia, stationed at the river Kupa. Whether Borna was abandoned by the treachery of the Goduscans [Dunscans] or through fear is uncertain; nevertheless, aided by the domestic support of his own people, he escaped the danger that threatened him and later subdued his deserters.

Meanwhile, in the following winter Liudevitus again entered Dalmatia and strove to lay everything waste, killing with the sword whatever was alive and consigning whatever was lifeless to fire. Since Borna could not withstand his force in open confrontation, he sought by cunning a way to harm him. For Borna did not declare open war against Liudevitus, but by sudden attacks so wore down both Liudevitus and his army that Liudevitus was ashamed and regretted having undertaken such things. For, after three thousand men of Liudevitus’s army had been killed and many horses and various kinds of equipment plundered, Borna compelled him to leave his own region. The emperor, staying at Aachen, heard all this with joy.

Meanwhile the Basques, divided by the native plague of sedition, were so subdued by Pippin, the emperor’s son, in that same year that none of them dared to rebel. His father had sent him for this purpose. When these matters had been completed, the emperor dismissed the assembly. At the appropriate season he devoted himself to hunting in the Ardennes, and returned to the palace at Aachen to spend the winter.

**(820.)** When winter came on, the emperor caused a great gathering of his people to assemble in the same palace. At that time Borna complained of Liudevitus’s attacks and received from the emperor large forces of assistance capable of ravaging his land. Divided into three contingents, these forces, at the beginning of spring, had devastated almost the whole territory under Liudevitus’s authority with sword and fire, while Liudevitus himself protected himself in the height of a certain fortress and would come forward neither for battle nor for negotiation. When they had returned home, the Carniolans and certain of the Carantani who had gone over to Liudevitus surrendered to our duke Baldric.

At the palace, Count Bera of Barcelona, when he was challenged by a certain man named Sanila and accused of disloyalty, engaged him in mounted combat according to their own law, since both were Goths, and was defeated. Although the law required that punishment be inflicted upon him and that, as guilty of treason, he be struck down by a capital sentence, the emperor’s clemency spared his life, and he was ordered to remain at Rouen.

At that time it was reported that thirteen pirate ships had put out to sea from the settlements of the Northmen and were approaching our shores to plunder them. When the emperor’s vigilance ordered guards to be established against them, they were driven back both from the Flemish coast and from the mouth of the Seine. They turned toward Aquitaine, ravaged a village called Bouin, loaded themselves with much booty, and returned.

In this year (821) the lord emperor spent the winter at Aachen. In the same winter, in the month of February, an assembly was held at Aachen. Three divisions were sent to ravage Liudevitus’s territory, and, on the pretext of a peace that seemed to have been made with Abulath, king of the Saracens, war was declared against him.

In the same year, on the Kalends of May, the emperor held another assembly at Nijmegen. There he ordered the partition of the kingdom, which he had made long before among his sons, to be read aloud in the presence of all, and confirmed by all the nobles who were then present. There too he received, heard, and dismissed the envoys of Paschal [Col. 0950C], the apostolic lord—Peter, bishop of Centumcellae, and Leo the nomenclator.

Departing from there, he returned to Aachen. From there, by way of the Ardennes, as far as the height of Mount Rumeric and through the broad wilderness of the Vosges, he spent all that remained of half the summer and of autumn. Meanwhile, when Borna had been deprived of life, the emperor appointed as his successor his own nephew named Ladasdeus.

At that time he received news of the death of Leo, emperor of Constantinople, who had been killed by his own household, especially by Michael. Michael was also installed in his place, supported by his fellow conspirators and above all by the praetorian soldiers.

In the middle of October of that year a public assembly was held at the estate of Thionville. There, finally, the lord emperor joined his firstborn son Lothar in solemn marriage with Ermengard, daughter of Count Hugh. The envoys of the Roman pope were also present: Theodore the primicerius and Florus, bearing great and varied gifts.

The emperor’s clemency, which had always shone forth as admirable in other matters, was displayed most conspicuously at this assembly, revealing with complete clarity how great it was in his heart. For he recalled all who had conspired against his life and kingdom, and not only restored their lives and limbs but also returned, with a great demonstration of generosity, the possessions of which they had been legally deprived.

He also restored Adalhard, once abbot of the monastery of Corbie but then residing in the monastery of Saint Philibert [Col. 0951A], to his former office. Likewise, he recalled his brother Bernard from the monastery of Saint Benedict, reconciled him, and restored him with his brother to the same position. When these matters had been completed and the other business required for the common good had been settled, he sent his son Lothar to Worms for the winter, while he himself returned to Aachen.

In the following year (822), the lord emperor ordered a general assembly to meet at a place called Attigny. There, after bishops, abbots, spiritual men, and also the nobles of his kingdom had been summoned to the council, he first sought reconciliation with his brothers, whom he had compelled against their will to be tonsured, and then with all those whom he seemed to have injured in any way.

After this, he openly confessed that he had erred and, following the example of the emperor Theodosius, voluntarily undertook penance both for these acts and for what he had done against his own nephew Bernard. If he found that anything of this kind had been done either by himself or by his father, he sought to correct it. Through the distribution of very many alms, through the persistent prayers of Christ’s servants, and through his own satisfaction, he strove so earnestly to appease the Divinity as though the acts that had legally fallen upon each person had been carried out by his own cruelty.

At the same time he sent an army from Italy against Liudevitus in Pannonia. Unable to remain there, Liudevitus abandoned his own city and went to a certain prince of Dalmatia, who received him within his city. Liudevitus, however, in turn treacherously killed his host and subjected the city to his own rule. Although he neither attacked our men nor entered into negotiations with them, he nevertheless sent envoys, declared that he had erred, and promised to come to the lord emperor.

At the same time the emperor was informed that the guardians of the Spanish frontier had crossed the river Segre, penetrated into the interior of Spain, and, having ravaged and burned everything that confronted them, had returned successfully with great booty. Those who guarded the Breton frontier likewise entered Britain and ravaged the region with sword and fire because of the rebellion of a certain Breton named Wiomarchus. Having completed these operations, they returned successfully.

When this assembly had ended, the lord emperor sent his son Lothar to Italy, together with his kinsman Wala, a monk, and also Geruntius [Geruncus], the doorkeeper. With their counsel he was to organize, strengthen, and protect the affairs of the Italian kingdom, both public and private.

When the emperor had decided to send his son Pippin to Aquitaine, he first joined to him in marriage the daughter of Count Theotbert. Only then did he send him to govern the regions mentioned. Having arranged these matters, he spent the autumn, according to the custom of the Frankish kings, in hunting, and, to spend the winter, proceeded across the Rhine to a place called Frankfurt.

There he ordered an assembly of the neighboring peoples to be held (823)—namely, of all those who, dwelling beyond the waters of the Rhine, obey the rule of the Franks. Treating with them concerning everything that seemed conducive to the common good, he suitably attended to the affairs of each. At the same assembly an embassy of the Avars was present bearing gifts. Envoys of the Northmen, renewing and confirming peace, were also present. After hearing them and dismissing them appropriately, he spent the winter in the same place, where buildings had been prepared with new construction as befitted the occasion and the season.

In that same estate—Frankfurt, that is—after winter had passed, the emperor held an assembly in May for the Austrasian Franks, the Saxons, and the other peoples bordering them. There he brought to a suitable conclusion the conflict between two brothers, who were disputing the kingdom among themselves in a great quarrel. They were of the Wilzi people, the sons of Liubi, formerly their king. Their names were Mileguastus and Celeadragus.

When their father Liubi had declared war against the Obodrites, he was killed by them, and the kingdom was handed over to his firstborn son. But when the latter showed himself too sluggish in administering the kingdom for the circumstances to tolerate, the favor of the people turned toward the younger brother’s dignity. Coming before the emperor in the course of this dispute, they discovered what the people wished, and the younger prince was declared king. Nevertheless, the emperor gave both brothers rich gifts, bound them by oaths, and dismissed them as friends both to one another and to himself.

Meanwhile Lothar, the emperor’s son, having been sent by his father to Italy, as was said above, had arranged the affairs of the kingdom according to the advice of the men who had been sent with him. With some matters completed and others still unfinished, he was preparing to give an account of each and was considering returning to his father. At the request of Pope Paschal, as the solemn feast of holy Easter approached, he went to Rome. The pope received him with the greatest honor, and on the holy day itself, at Saint Peter’s, bestowed upon him the imperial diadem together with the name Augustus.

After this, when he had come to Pavia, he remained there for a while because various necessities detained him. He then reached his father in June, reporting what had been completed and asking about what had been begun. To complete what remained unfinished, Adalhard, count of the palace, was sent, with Mauring as his associate.

When Gundulf, bishop of Metz, died at that time, all the clergy and people of that Church, as though animated by one spirit, asked that Drogo, the emperor’s brother, who was living most nobly under the canonical habit, be given to them as priest. In a remarkable manner the agreement of both the emperor and his nobles, as well as of the whole people, joined together as though by a kind of bond, so that everyone was found to desire this and no one to oppose it. Therefore the emperor, with the greatest joy, consented to the Church’s petition and gave them the bishop they had requested.

At the same assembly the death of the tyrant Liudevitus was announced; he had been killed by a certain man through treachery. The emperor dissolved this assembly and summoned another at Compiègne for the autumn.

At about the same time it was reported to the emperor that Theodore, primicerius of the holy Roman Church, and Leo the nomenclator had been deprived of their sight and then beheaded in the episcopal house at the Lateran. Enmity had arisen among the killers because it was said that those who had been killed had suffered such things on account of their loyalty to Lothar. The reputation of the pontiff was also damaged by this affair, since the whole matter was attributed to his consent.

While the emperor was preparing to send Adalung, abbot of the monastery of Saint Vedast, and Count Hunfrid to investigate the matter with the greatest care, envoys of Pope Paschal arrived: John, bishop of Silva Candida, and Benedict, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church. They opposed an apology to the accusation and offered the emperor an inquiry into the matter.

After hearing them and dismissing them with an appropriate reply, he ordered the envoys appointed for the purpose to go to Rome, as had been commanded, to investigate the truth of the doubtful matters. He himself stayed in various places as seemed appropriate and, at the appointed time—that is, on the Kalends of November—came to Compiègne.

At that assembly the envoys sent to Rome returned, announcing that Pope Paschal had cleared himself by oath, together with many bishops, of involvement in the killing of the victims, but had been unable to produce the killers. He nevertheless asserted that those who had been killed had suffered such things because their merits demanded it. They also presented with them the envoys sent by the apostolic lord, who brought a similar report. The names of the envoys were John, bishop of Silva Candida; Sergius the librarian; Quirinus the subdeacon; and Leo, master of the soldiers.

The emperor, therefore, being by nature most merciful and unable—although he greatly wished to do so—to pursue the vengeance of the slain on his own initiative, judged that the investigation of such matters should be abandoned and released the Roman envoys with suitable replies.

At the same time certain prodigious signs appeared and troubled the emperor’s mind, especially earthquakes at the palace of Aachen; unheard-of sounds during the night; the fasting of a certain girl who abstained completely from all food for twelve months; frequent and unusual flashes of lightning; stones falling with hail; and pestilence among human beings and animals.

Because of all these things, the most devout emperor repeatedly ordered fasts, and through the persistent practice of prayer and the distribution of alms, through the ministry of priests he urged the Divinity to be appeased. He declared with complete certainty that these signs foretold a great future calamity for the human race.

In that same year, in June, a son was born to him by Queen Judith; at the time of his baptism it pleased them to call him Charles.

In the same year Counts Eblus and Asenarius were ordered to cross the height of the Pyrenees. They went with large forces as far as Pamplona and, when they were returning after completing their mission, experienced the customary treachery of the region and the native deceitfulness of its inhabitants. For they were surrounded by the people of that place, lost all their forces, and fell into the hands of their enemies. They sent Eblus to Cordoba, to the Saracen king; but they spared Asenarius, as one connected with them by blood relationship.

Meanwhile, when Lothar, as stated above, had come to Rome after being sent by his father, he was received most gladly by Pope Eugenius (824). When he complained about the events that had occurred—namely, why those who had been loyal to the emperor and to the Franks had been killed by an unjust death, while those who survived were made a mockery and treated as such, and why so many complaints were resounding against the Roman pontiffs and judges—it was discovered that, through the ignorance or negligence of certain pontiffs and through the blind and insatiable greed of the judges, the estates of many people had been unjustly confiscated.

By returning what had been unjustly taken away, Lothar therefore created great joy among the Roman people. It was also established, according to ancient custom, that men should be sent from the emperor’s side to exercise judicial authority and administer justice to the entire people, and that, whenever it seemed appropriate to the emperor, they should weigh matters on an even balance.

When his son returned and reported these things to his father, the emperor, as a lover of equity and a cultivator of truth, was filled with great joy, because pious relief had come to those unjustly oppressed.

[Col. 0954B]

In the following period the lord emperor ordered an assembly to be held by his people in the month of May at Aachen (825). While he was staying there, an embassy of the Bulgars who had remained for a long time in Bavaria according to his command was brought before him for hearing. Its chief concern was the establishment of peace regarding the boundaries of the territories that were to be maintained between the Bulgars and the Franks.

Many nobles of the Bretons were also present, expressing their submission and obedience at length. Among them was Winemarchus [above, Wiomarchus], who seemed to surpass the others in authority and who had advanced so far in mad recklessness and most foolish audacity that, because of his insolence, he had even provoked the emperor to undertake an expedition to those regions in order to suppress him.

When he said that he regretted his action and had entrusted himself to the emperor’s loyalty, the emperor, according to his custom and the clemency he always habitually exercised, received him mercifully, gave him gifts together with the other citizens, and allowed him to return to his native soil.

Yet later, not forgetful of his customary treachery, while forgetting all the good things he had promised and experienced, he continued to attack the emperor’s faithful subjects in his neighborhood and harass them with constant injuries. He eventually reached the point where, overcome by Lantbert’s men, he met the end of his life in his own house, together with the end of all his evil deeds.

After dismissing both the envoys of the Bulgars and the Bretons, the emperor devoted himself to hunting in the recesses of the Vosges. He believed that this should be done again until, in August, according to the general agreement, he returned to Aachen to meet the people.

At that time, in October, he ordered the peace requested by the Northmen to be confirmed. After all matters that seemed necessary to be carried out and settled at that assembly had been completed, he proceeded with his son Lothar to Nijmegen, leaving the younger Louis in Bavaria. After hunting during the autumn, he returned to the palace at Aachen.

When the envoys of the Bulgars returned from that assembly, carrying the emperor’s letters, their king received what had been written with little pleasure because he had not obtained what he had requested. Sending the same messenger back with some anger, he ordered that either a common boundary should be established or that, by whatever strength he could command, he should defend the limits of his own territories [Col. 0955A].

When rumor spread that the king who had issued such orders had been deprived of his kingdom, the emperor detained the envoy until he had sent Bertric, count of the palace, and discovered that what was being reported was false. After learning the truth, he sent the envoy back with the business unfinished.

In that same year (826), on the Kalends of February, Pippin, the emperor’s son, reached his father, who was wintering at Aachen. The emperor entrusted him with the task of being prepared to respond if anything new arose in the regions of Spain. He then returned.

On the Kalends of June the emperor came to Ingelheim, and there the assembly of his people met him according to his command. At that assembly, according to his custom, he gave many admonitions, decrees, and decisions useful to the Church. He received, heard, and dismissed the embassies brought both from the holy Roman see and from the Mount of Olives by the abbot Dominicus.

He also sent back to their own lands, after disciplining them, two dukes: Ceadrag of the Obodrites and Tunglo of the Sorabs. They had been accused, and the evidence against them was sufficiently clear.

Heriold also came from the regions of the Northmen with his wife and a considerable force of Danes. At Mainz, at Saint Alban’s, he and all his companions were washed in the water of holy baptism and received many gifts from the emperor.

The most devout emperor feared that, because of this act, Heriold might be denied possession of his native land. He therefore gave him a certain county in Frisia called Rüstringen, where he could safely take refuge with his people if necessity required.

Meanwhile, when Baldric and Gerald and the other guardians of the Pannonian frontiers were present, Baldric brought before the lord emperor a certain priest named Gregory, a man of good life, who said that he could construct an organ according to the Greek manner. The emperor received him gladly. Since God was granting him things previously unknown in the Frankish kingdom, he gave thanks and entrusted Gregory to Tanculf, superintendent of the sacred treasury. He ordered that Gregory be maintained at public expense and commanded that whatever was necessary for this work should be prepared.

In the middle of October of that year the emperor ordered a German assembly to meet across the Rhine, in an estate called Salz. While he was staying there, the treachery and defection of Aizo were reported. Aizo had fled from the lord emperor’s palace and come to the city of Ausona, where he was received; there he overthrew Roda and inflicted considerable harm on those who tried to resist him.

He strongly fortified the castles he was able to seize by placing guards in them. He also sent his brother to the Saracen king named Abdiraman and received from him a powerful army to use against us. These events moved the emperor’s mind. Nevertheless, thinking that nothing should be done hastily, he decided to await the judgment of his advisers concerning what ought to be done in such circumstances.

At about the same time Hilduin, abbot of the monastery of Saint Dionysius, sent monks carrying his petition to Rome, to Eugenius, bishop of the holy Roman see, asking that the bones of Saint Sebastian the martyr be sent to him. The apostolic lord fulfilled his desire and, through the envoys mentioned above, sent the relics of the most holy soldier of Christ.

The aforesaid man received them with the greatest reverence and, together with the traveling shrine in which they had been brought, placed them temporarily beside the body of Saint Medard. While they remained there, God granted mortals such an abundance of miracles through the presence of their arrival that the multitude surpasses all number. The nature of these miracles, moreover, exceeds belief unless one trusts ears persuaded that nothing resists the divine command and that all things are possible for the believer.

Furthermore, while Aizo was attacking those who lived within our frontiers and devastating everywhere, especially the regions of Cerdanya and Vallès, his savagery advanced so far, with the support of Moorish [Col. 0956B] and Saracen auxiliaries, that some of our men were compelled to abandon the castles and towns they had previously held, and many others defected from us and joined their alliance (827).

Among these was Willemund, son of Bera, who joined their rebellion together with many of their allies. While the emperor was organizing an army to suppress these disturbances and strengthen our people, he sent ahead Abbot Elisachar, Count Hildebrand, and Donatus.

Going before the army, they joined forces with troops of Goths and Spaniards and steadfastly resisted the insolence of the rebels, while Bernard, count of Barcelona, was doing his utmost to thwart their efforts. Seeing this, Aizo departed to request a praetorian army from the Saracens. After obtaining it, he led it with its commander [Col. 0956C], Abumarus [Amaruan], to Zaragoza and from there as far as Barcelona.

The emperor then sent his son Pippin, king of Aquitaine, against them, together with the counts Hugh and Matfrid, whom he sent from his own side. Since they met the enemy with more timidity than was proper, delays became entangled with delays until, after ravaging the region of Barcelona and Girona, the enemy withdrew to Zaragoza.

Before this disaster there had appeared those terrifying nocturnal battle-lines, gleaming with human blood and blazing with the pallor of fire.

The emperor, meanwhile, devoted himself to hunting in the forests adjoining Compiègne and Carisiac [Col. 0956D] until the winter season. [Variant: “The emperor, meanwhile, receiving the annual gifts at Compiègne, once he had learned these things, sent reinforcements to defend the aforesaid frontier and continued hunting, etc., until the winter season.”]

In August of that same year Pope Eugenius died. The deacon Valentine succeeded him. Since he survived in office scarcely one month, Gregory, a priest of the title of Saint Mark, was elected in his place, though his consecration was postponed until the emperor’s advice had been sought. When the emperor consented and approved the election of the clergy and people, Gregory was ordained in the place of his predecessor.

Envoys of the emperor Michael came to Compiègne in September of that year and brought gifts. They were received with honor, provided for most generously, presented with gifts, and returned successfully.

In that same year Heinardus [Eginhardus], the wisest of the men of his time, moved by the ardor of holy devotion, sent to Rome. With the pope’s consent, he had the bodies of the saints Marcellinus and Peter transported to Francia, and buried them very fittingly in his own territory and at his own expense. Through their merits the Lord has continued to perform many miracles there.

In February of the following winter (828), a public assembly was held at Aachen. There, among other matters, the affair recently and disastrously and shamefully conducted in the Spanish frontier region was especially heatedly debated. After it had been discussed and investigated with the greatest care, those who were found to be responsible were the commanders whom the emperor had appointed.

The emperor therefore ordered only these men to atone for the guilt of this negligence by depriving them of their honors. Likewise, when the negligence and carelessness of Baldric, duke of Friuli, were brought against him and it was proved that our territory had been ravaged by the Bulgars, he was removed from the dukedom, and his authority was divided among four counts.

The emperor’s disposition, most merciful by nature, had always sought to extend mercy to sinners. But how those to whom such clemency was shown abused it and turned it into cruelty will become clear shortly, when it is revealed how, in return for the gift of life, they brought upon him, as far as they were able, the greatest calamity.

At that time Bishop Halitcarius of Cambrai and Abbot Auffridus [Ansfridus] of the monastery of Nonantola returned from overseas regions and reported that they had been received most graciously by Michael.

In the following summer the emperor held a public assembly at Ingelheim. There he received and dismissed the envoys of the Roman pope, Quirinus the primicerius and Theophylact the nomenclator, who came with great gifts. When he came to the estate of Thionville, and rumor spread everywhere that Saracens were about to come against our frontiers, he sent his son Lothar to the same frontier, assigning to him strong and numerous Frankish forces.

When Lothar, obeying his father’s commands, had reached Lyon and was awaiting news from the Spanish regions, his brother Pippin arrived to confer with him. While they remained there, the envoy returned and said that the Saracens and Moors had indeed raised an exceedingly large army but had held their ground and would not at that time advance farther into our territories. After hearing this, Pippin returned successfully to Aquitaine, while Lothar returned to his father.

Meanwhile the sons of Godefrid, formerly king of the Danes, had expelled Heriold from the kingdom. Since the emperor wished to help Heriold and had entered into a treaty of peace with the sons of Godefrid, he sent Saxon counts to them with Heriold himself and ordered them to negotiate with the aforesaid men so that they would receive Heriold into their alliance as they had formerly done.

Heriold, however, impatient of these delays, and without the knowledge of our men, set fire to some of their estates and burned them, carrying away their property. Thinking that this had been done with the consent of our people, they suddenly attacked our men, who suspected nothing of the kind. They crossed the river Eider, drove them from their camp, forced them to flee, and, having taken possession of everything, withdrew into their own camp.

After this had happened, when they learned the truth and feared the punishment they deserved, they first sent to those against whom they had committed these acts and then to the emperor, confessing their error. They next offered an appropriate satisfaction for the vengeance due, leaving the manner of satisfaction to the emperor’s decision, provided only that the peace remain unshaken. The emperor consented to their request according to their wish.

Count Boniface, whom the emperor had appointed prefect of the island of Corsica, embarked with his brother Berald and others in a small fleet. He searched the seas for pirates but did not find them, and put in at the island of the Sardinians, who were friendly to him. Taking on other men experienced in maritime travel, he proceeded to Africa and crossed between Utica and Carthage.

A multitude of Africans gathered against him, and he fought them five times. Some of our men also happened to die in these engagements, driven either by excessive eagerness or by ill-considered recklessness to attempt too much. Boniface nevertheless gathered his companions, withdrew to the ships, and returned to his homeland, leaving the Africans with an unfulfilled and unprecedented fear.

In this year the moon was eclipsed twice, on the Kalends of July and on the night of the Nativity of the Lord. A certain kind of grain was also brought to the emperor from the region of the Basques. It was shorter than wheat, yet not smooth like peas; they said that it had descended from heaven. The lord emperor spent the winter at Aachen.

When winter had passed, the sacred days of Lent were being celebrated and the venerable solemnity of Easter was approaching (829), when, in the dead of night, an earthquake occurred so powerful that it threatened all the buildings with collapse. A violent wind followed, and its force shook not only the smaller structures but also the palace at Aachen itself, stripping to a great extent even the lead tiles with which the basilica of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God, was roofed.

He remained in that palace because of the many necessities that compelled him and because of public affairs. He planned to depart from there on the Kalends of July and hasten to Worms to celebrate a general assembly of the people. A rumor temporarily compelled him to change this plan: it was said that the Northmen intended to transgress the boundaries fixed by treaty and their own frontiers, and to ravage the region beyond the Elbe.

When matters proved otherwise, the emperor arrived according to his plan and the arrangements of place and time. He carefully dealt with the matters that seemed necessary, received the annual gifts, and sent his son Lothar to Italy.

At that assembly he also learned that clandestine plots against him by those whose lives he had spared were spreading like a cancer and troubling the minds of many as though through hidden tunnels. He therefore resolved to erect a kind of bulwark against them. He appointed Bernard, until then count of the Spanish regions and frontiers, to be head of his chamber.

This action did not extinguish the seedbed of discord but rather increased it. Since those who were infected by this plague were still unable to disclose their wound, having no opportunity to carry out what they desired, they decided to postpone these matters to another time.

After settling the matters that opportunity required, the emperor crossed the Rhine, went to the estate of Frankfurt, and, for as long as seemed good and the approaching winter cold permitted, indulged in hunting there. Then, around the feast of the Mass of Saint Martin, he turned toward Aachen and there celebrated both that festival and the feast of Saint Andrew, as well as the Nativity of the Lord, together with the other observances, with due solemnity.

Around the time of Lent, while the emperor was traveling through the regions bordering the sea, the leaders of the wicked faction, no longer able to endure their long-concealed wound, exposed it. First the leading men conspired among themselves in a kind of alliance; then they drew the lesser men into it. Some of these were always eager for change, like dogs and rapacious birds that seek to turn another’s loss into an increase of their own advantage. Relying, therefore, on their numbers and on the agreement of many, they approached the emperor’s son Pippin, alleging their own degradation, Bernard’s insolence, and the contempt shown by the others. They also asserted—an abomination to say—that Bernard was an incestuous violator of his father’s marriage-bed; moreover, that the father had been so deceived by certain enchantments that he could neither avenge nor even perceive these things.

They said, therefore, that a good son ought indignantly to bear his father’s disgrace, remove those men from the way, and restore his father both to his right mind and to his dignity. In doing this, they claimed, he would be followed not only by the reputation of virtue but also by an enlargement of his earthly kingdom; under this pretext they disguised their guilt.

The young man, attracted by these incitements, came with them and with a large force of his followers through the city of Orléans, after removing Odo from office and restoring Matfrid, and they reached Werimbri. But when the emperor learned that their conspiracy against himself, his wife, and Bernard was most obstinately armed for slaughter, he allowed Bernard to entrust himself to flight. He wished his wife to remain at Laon, staying in the monastery of Saint Mary; he himself went to Compiègne.

Those who had come with Pippin to Werimbri sent Werin [below, Warino] and Lantbert, together with many others, and had Queen Judith brought to them after she had been led out of the city and the basilica of the monastery. They subjected her to the threat of death through punishments of various kinds, driving her so far that she promised that, if she were given the opportunity to speak with the emperor, she would persuade him to lay down his arms, cut off his hair, and withdraw into a monastery; she herself would do likewise, placing a veil upon her head. The more they desired this outcome, the more readily they believed her.

They therefore sent some of their men with her and had her brought all the way to the emperor. When he had granted her permission to speak with him privately, and he allowed her to escape death, she placed a veil upon her head. As for having his own hair cut, the emperor asked for time to deliberate. For the emperor, who had always lived benevolently toward others, was suffering under such unjust hatred that they were weary of his life—although, had they not lived by his favor, they would justly and lawfully have been deprived of life themselves.

When the queen returned to them, they moderated the other punishments, but, yielding to the acclamation of the crowd, ordered that she be carried into exile and confined in the monastery of Saint Radegund.

Around the month of May, the emperor’s son Lothar came from Italy and found him at Compiègne. The entire faction hostile to the emperor came over to Lothar as he arrived. He himself, however, did not at that time appear to have inflicted any dishonor upon his father, but he approved what had been done.

Finally, Heribert, Bernard’s brother, was punished by the loss of his eyes, contrary to the emperor’s wish; Odo, his cousin, was deprived of his arms and carried into exile, as men who had been aware of and supporters of the acclamations against Bernard and the queen.

Remaining in such circumstances, emperor in name alone, he passed the summer. When the autumn weather was approaching, those who held views opposed to the emperor wished a general assembly to be held somewhere in Francia. The emperor secretly resisted this, distrusting the Franks and placing greater confidence in the Germans. Nevertheless, the emperor’s opinion prevailed that the people should assemble at Nijmegen.

Fearing that the multitude of his opponents might overwhelm the small number of his loyal supporters, he ordered that everyone coming to the same assembly should travel with only simple provisions. He also instructed Count Lambert to guard the frontiers assigned to him. He sent Abbot Helisachar there as well, to administer justice.

At last they came to Nijmegen, and all Germany converged there to provide assistance to the emperor. The emperor, still wishing to weaken the strength of his adversaries, accused Abbot Hilduin and asked why, although he had been ordered to come peacefully, he had arrived in a hostile manner. Since Hilduin could not deny this, he was immediately ordered to leave the palace and to winter with only a very few men near Paderborn, in a military tent.

Abbot Walach was ordered to return to the monastery of Corbie and to preside there according to the rule.

When those who had assembled to oppose the emperor perceived this, broken in strength, they turned to utter desperation. Finally, gathering throughout the whole night and coming together at the residence of Lothar, the emperor’s son, they urged either that they should fight a battle or withdraw somewhere without the emperor’s permission.

After they had spent the entire night in this deliberation, the emperor sent word in the morning to his son that he should not trust their common enemies, but should come to him as a son to his father. When Lothar heard this, although those around him discouraged him, he came to his father. The emperor did not attack him with harsh reproach but corrected him with measured gentleness.

When Lothar had entered the inner part of the royal residence, the populace, at the devil’s instigation, began to rage against him, and the fury would have proceeded to mutual slaughter had not the emperor’s prudence prevented it. For while they were making tumult among themselves and were almost rushing into madness, the emperor came forth with his son before the sight of everyone. At this, all that murderous agitation subsided. When the emperor’s speech had been heard, the entire popular tumult disappeared.

After this, the emperor ordered all the leaders of that wicked conspiracy to be held in private custody. Later they were brought to judgment, and all the assessors of the law, together with the emperor’s son, decided in a lawful judgment that, as guilty of treason against the sovereign, they should be put to death. He permitted none of them to be killed, however. Instead, showing, as many thought, a mercy more lenient than he ought to have shown, but following his accustomed practice of kindness and clemency, he ordered the laymen to be tonsured in suitable places, while the clerics were likewise confined in appropriate monasteries.

When these matters had been completed, the emperor withdrew to Aachen to spend the winter (831). During this same period he always kept his son Lothar with him. Meanwhile he sent to Aquitaine and recalled his wife, together with her brothers Conrad and Rudolf, who had long before been tonsured. He did not, however, honor her as his wife until she had cleared herself of the accusations according to the manner prescribed by law. After this had been done, on the Feast of the Purification of Saint Mary, he granted life to all those whose cases had been judged for death.

He permitted Lothar to go to Italy, Pippin to Aquitaine, and Louis to Bavaria. He himself celebrated Lent and the solemnity of Easter in that place. When the Easter ceremonies had been completed, the emperor went to Ingelheim.

At that time, not forgetting his customary mercy—which, as Job says of himself, grew with him from the beginning and seems to have come forth with him from his mother’s womb—he summoned those whom, on account of their deserts, he had long before assigned to various places, restored them to their own possessions, and granted those who had been tonsured the choice of whether they wished to remain so or return to their former appearance.

Then the emperor crossed through the Vosges toward the region of Mount Romeric. There he indulged in fishing and hunting for as long as he pleased, and sent his son Lothar to Italy.

In the autumn he ordered his entire people to assemble at the villa of Theodon. At that place three envoys from the Saracens came from overseas—two were Saracens, one was a Christian—bringing great gifts from their homeland, namely various kinds of perfumes and cloth. After requesting and receiving peace, they were sent back.

Bernard was also present. By the method mentioned above, he had saved himself by flight and had lived for a long time in exile on the borders of Spain. He therefore approached the emperor and sought from him a means of clearing himself, according to the customary practice of the Franks: he wished to present himself to the man bringing the charge and to clear the accusation by combat.

But although an accuser was sought, none was present; the weapons were therefore set aside, and the purge was completed by oaths. The emperor had ordered his son Pippin to attend this assembly. Pippin, however, kept himself away from the gathering and came only after it had ended.

The emperor, wishing to punish this disobedience as well as his son’s great insolence of conduct, ordered Pippin to remain with him and kept him at Aachen until Christmas. But Pippin, distressed that he was being kept longer than he wished, took flight and went to Aquitaine without his father’s knowledge. The emperor, for his part, remained at Aachen for the winter, as he had begun to do.

When the severity of winter had passed and spring had returned, the emperor was informed that certain disturbances had arisen in Bavaria (832). He hastened to suppress them, reached Augsburg, quieted the uprising, immediately returned, and ordered a public assembly to be held at Orléans. He also commanded Pippin to meet him there, and Pippin came, although unwillingly.

The emperor, however, observing the plans of certain wicked men who were hastening his son’s mind toward worse things by threats as well as promises—and especially fearing Bernard, whose counsel Pippin was then said to be following, although Pippin himself was at that time staying in Aquitaine—crossed the Loire and came with his retinue to the palace of Jocundiacum, situated in the territory of Limoges.

When the case of each had been examined there, Bernard was accused of disloyalty. Since he nevertheless did not wish to proceed as far as a formal confrontation, Bernard was deprived of his honors. Pippin, on account of the corruption of his depraved conduct, the emperor ordered to be taken under private guard to Trier.

While he was being led there and was being treated with excessive leniency, his men removed him secretly from custody by night. Until the emperor returned from Aquitaine, Pippin wandered wherever he was able and wished.

At that time the emperor established a certain division of the kingdom between his sons Lothar and Charles. This arrangement, however, did not proceed according to his desire because of the great obstacles that must be described.

At that time the emperor decided to withdraw from Aquitaine, but after a short while he summoned the people to the Mass of Saint Martin and wished by every means to recall his fugitive son Pippin to him. Pippin refused to do so, and the most severe winter weather descended: first came a flood of abundant rains; then the wetness of the ground was bound by icy cold. This was so destructive that, when the horses’ hooves had been worn away, scarcely anyone could use horses for transport.

After the army had been broken by great hardship, and after he had repeatedly and painfully endured the Aquitanians’ unexpected raids, the emperor decided to go to a villa called Restis and, after crossing the Loire there, return to Francia for the winter. He did so, although less honorably than was proper.

(833.) The devil, hostile to the human race and to peace, was not at all idle in troubling the emperor. Through the cunning of his agents he stirred up the sons, persuading them that their father wished to destroy them voluntarily. They did not consider that one who was gentler toward outsiders could not become savage toward his own.

But because evil conversations corrupt good morals, and because a soft drop of water, striking stone repeatedly, can gradually bore through even its hardness, matters finally reached the point where the emperor’s sons were made to assemble together with whatever forces they could, and to summon Pope Gregory under the appearance of one who alone ought and could reconcile the sons with their father. The truth of the matter, however, became clear afterward.

The emperor, on the other hand, came to Worms in May with a strong force and spent a long time there deliberating what he ought to do. He sent envoys, namely Bishop Bernard and the others, urging his sons to come to him and return to their allegiance. He also wished to meet the pope of the Roman See, asking why, if he had come according to the custom of his predecessors, he delayed so long instead of meeting him.

When rumor spread everywhere, reporting truthfully what concerned the others but alleging concerning the Roman pope that he had come in order to entangle both the emperor and the bishops in the bonds of excommunication, should any of them be disobedient to the will of the pope and of the emperor’s sons, the emperor’s bishops were seized by a small measure of presumptuous boldness. They asserted that they would in no way submit to the pope’s will. If he came intending to excommunicate, they said, he would depart excommunicated, since the authority of the ancient canons stood otherwise.

At last they assembled on the feast of Saint John the Forerunner of Christ at a place which, because of what happened there, was marked with everlasting dishonor in its name and came to be called the Field of Lies. Since those who promised faithfulness to the emperor had lied, the place where this occurred remained, in its name, a witness to their wickedness.

While they were standing not far from there with their battle lines arranged, and it was already thought that they were about to rush to arms, the emperor was informed that the pope of the Romans was arriving. The emperor, standing in the battle line, received him as he came, although less appropriately than he should have done. He charged the pope with having prepared such a reception for himself, since he had come to him in an unprecedented manner.

The pope was led into the military quarters and explained at length, with many assertions, that he had undertaken the journey for no other reason than that he had been told the emperor was engaged in irreconcilable discord with his sons, and that he therefore wished to sow peace between both sides.

After hearing the emperor’s side, the pope remained with him for several days. The emperor then sent him back to his sons to establish mutual peace.
