But when almost the entire populace flowed toward the sons and the people with them like a torrent—some drawn away by gifts, some enticed by promises, and some terrified by threats—the pope was by no means permitted to return as he had been ordered.

After so many forces had been brought there and detached from the emperor, the defection grew stronger day by day, until on the feast of Saint Paul the common people threatened to attack the emperor while flattering his sons.

Unable to resist these forces, the emperor ordered his sons not to expose themselves to popular plunder. They sent him word to leave the camp and come to them, promising that they themselves would come out to meet him as quickly as possible.

When they met one another from opposite directions, the emperor admonished his sons, who had dismounted from their horses and come to meet him, to remember their promise and preserve inviolate what they had formerly promised both to him, to his son, and to his wife. When they had given an appropriate answer, he kissed them and went to their camp.

On his arrival, his wife was taken away and conducted to Louis’s tents. Lothar himself took him, together with the very young Charles, to his own quarters and made him remain with a very few men in a tent assigned for this purpose.

When the people had already been bound by oaths, the kingdom was divided among the brothers in three portions. The father’s wife, received by King Louis, was again carried into exile, to the Italian city of Tortona.

Pope Gregory, seeing these things, returned to Rome in the deepest sorrow. Of the two brothers, Pippin returned to Aquitaine and Louis to Bavaria.

Lothar, taking his father with him, while he himself rode separately with the men assigned to him and remained in private, came to the villa of Merlegium. After staying there as he pleased, arranging what seemed appropriate, and releasing the people from their obligations, he announced an assembly at Compiègne. He then crossed the Vosges by way of Mauri-Monastery and reached Metz, which is also called Mediomatricum.

Leaving that city, he arrived at Verdun and proceeded to the city of Soissons. There, in the monastery of Saint Medard, he ordered his father to be held under strict guard. Having entrusted Charles to Prüm, though without tonsuring him, Lothar himself devoted himself to hunting until autumn, that is, the Kalends of October. As had been arranged, he then came to Compiègne, bringing his father with him.

When he was staying there, an embassy from the emperor of Constantinople arrived to meet the father: Marcus, archbishop of Ephesus, and the emperor’s protospatharius. The embassy presented the gifts assigned to itself and withheld those sent to the father.

Although the embassy had been sent to his father, Lothar received it when it came to him, heard the tragedy it reported, and sent it back bearing an almost unheard-of tale.

At the same assembly many people were accused of devotion toward the father and defection toward the son. Some cleared themselves of the charges with simple words, others by oaths. Nevertheless, with the authors of the deed excepted, everyone felt compassion for such a situation and for such an exchange of fortunes.

Therefore, fearing that the unheard-of conspirators might be overthrown and that the acts already accomplished might be reversed, they employed, as it seemed to them, a crafty argument with certain bishops. They sought to have the emperor, for the matters of which he had already repented, judged to satisfy the Church again by a public penance, laying down his arms and making an irrevocable submission of a sort.

Yet even secular laws do not impose punishment twice for one offense committed once, and our law says that God does not judge the same matter twice. A few opposed this judgment; more gave their agreement; the majority, as usually happens in such matters, consented only in words so as not to offend the leading men.

They therefore compelled the emperor, who was absent, unheard, neither confessing nor convicted, to lay down his arms before the body of Saint Medard the confessor and Saint Sebastian the martyr and to place them before the altar. They clothed him in black garments, surrounded him with a large guard, and confined him beneath a certain roof.

When this affair had been completed, after the Mass of Saint Martin, the people, having received permission to depart, returned sadly to their homes because of these events. Lothar, taking his father with him, returned to Aachen to winter.

During the course of that winter, groups of people from Francia, Burgundy, Aquitaine, and Germany gathered together and complained in sorrowful protests about the emperor’s misfortune.

In Francia, Count Eggebard and Count William, the master of the horse, gathered around themselves as many men as they could in a united determination to restore the emperor.

From Germany, Abbot Hugh was sent into Aquitaine by Louis. Together with those who had fled there—namely Bishop Drogo and the others—he urged Pippin toward this same undertaking.

Bernard and Warinus, for their part, stirred up the people staying in Burgundy with their appeals, attracted them with promises, bound them by oaths, and united them in a single purpose.

(834.) When winter had passed and spring was already displaying its rosy face, Lothar took his father with him, set out through the district of Hesbaye, and headed for the city of Paris, where he ordered all the faithful to meet him.

Count Eggebard and the other nobles of that district came out to meet him with a large force that they had assembled, intending to fight for the emperor’s liberation. The matter would have reached its intended result had not the most devout emperor, concerned both for the danger to many and for his own, restrained them from this undertaking by command and entreaty.

At last they reached the monastery of Saint Denis the martyr.

Pippin, however, departed from Aquitaine with a very large force and came as far as the Seine. Since the destroyed bridges and the ships sunk in deep water prevented the crossing, he halted.

The counts Warinus and Bernard, having gathered many of their allies from the regions of Burgundy, came as far as the Marne River. There they were delayed partly by the harshness and badness of the weather, and partly held back while gathering their allies. They remained for several days at the villa of Bonneuil and on the estates surrounding it.

The season of Lent was approaching. On its first week, Thursday, they sent envoys—Abbot Rebald and Count Gautselm—to Lothar, the emperor’s son. They demanded that the emperor, freed from the bonds of custody, be restored to them.

If Lothar complied with their request, they said, they too would have been formerly appointed to secure his safety and honor before his father. If he did not, then, even if it were necessary, they would seek him at the risk of their own lives; and if anyone resisted them in this matter with arms, they would meet him in battle, with God as judge.

Lothar replied to this demand that no one could either sympathize more deeply with his father’s calamity or rejoice more greatly in his prosperity. He should not be charged with the guilt of having received the elder man, since they themselves had abandoned and betrayed him. Nor should the stain of prison custody be lawfully imputed to him, since it was clear that the matter had been carried out by episcopal judgment.

With this answer, the envoys were sent back to those who had dispatched them. Count Guerinus, Odo, and the abbots Fulco and Hugh were ordered to come to Lothar, so that they might deliberate with him how their request could be fulfilled.

Lothar, the emperor’s son, also ordered that those sent by him should be dispatched to him on the following day. They were to learn from him the time of the aforesaid men’s arrival and thus meet him on the appointed day to discuss the matter mentioned above.

In fact, however, after changing his plan, Lothar left his father in the monastery of Saint Denis, together with those who were being led by his favor, and went to Burgundy. He reached Vienne and chose to establish his camp there.

Those who had remained with the emperor urged him to resume the imperial insignia. But although the emperor had been expelled from communion with the Church in the manner described above, he did not wish to submit to a hasty judgment. On the Sunday that followed, he wished to be reconciled through episcopal ministry in the church of Saint Denis, and he consented to be girded with arms by the hands of the bishops.

At this event the people’s rejoicing grew so great that even the elements themselves seemed to sympathize with the injured man and to rejoice with him after his restoration.

Until that time, such a force of storms and violence of rains had prevailed that an extraordinary excess of water had risen, while the settled winds made the channels of the rivers impassable. But at his absolution the elements somehow seemed to conspire together, so that immediately the raging winds grew calm and the face of the heavens returned to its former serenity, which had not been seen for a long time.

The emperor then set out from that place. Although many urged him to do so, he did not wish to pursue his departing son.

He went from there to Nantogilum and afterward came to the royal villa of Carisiacum. There he remained, awaiting his son Pippin and those who were staying across the Marne, as well as those who had fled across the Rhine to his son Louis, and Louis himself, who was coming to him.

While he was staying there, in the middle of Lent, the joy of the day itself also smiling upon them, and the ecclesiastical hymn urging the celebration and saying, “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and keep festival, all you who love her,” a very great multitude of his faithful came to meet him there, rejoicing together in their common happiness.

The emperor received them graciously and gave thanks for the integrity of their faith. He sent his son Pippin joyfully to Aquitaine, and allowed the others to return happily to the places appropriate to them.

He himself reached Aachen. There he received Judith Augusta, who was being brought back from Italy by Bishop Ratold and Boniface, and he also received his son Pippin. He had already had Charles with him for some time.

There he celebrated the solemnity of Easter with his customary devotion. After the celebration, he exercised himself by hunting through the Ardennes forest. After the feast of holy Pentecost, he devoted himself to hunting and fishing in the region of Mount Romeric.

When the emperor’s son Lothar had departed from his father and gone to the regions mentioned above, Count Lantbert, Matfrid, and many others remained in the regions of Neustria, attempting to retain those territories by their own strength.

Count Odo and many others who favored the emperor’s cause took this badly. They took up arms against them and tried either to drive them from those places or at least to engage them in battle.

Because this undertaking was carried out more sluggishly than it should have been and was considered with insufficient caution, it brought them no small disaster. For when the enemy unexpectedly came upon them, they used less vigilance than the circumstances demanded and exposed their backs as the enemy pressed them.

There Odo himself and his brother William perished, together with many others; the rest placed their hope of safety in flight.

When this affair had been completed, those who had won the victory, since it seemed unsafe for them to remain there and they were unable to join Lothar, feared that the emperor might come upon them while they stayed there or intercept them on the road if they hurried toward their own men. They therefore sent to Lothar as quickly as possible, asking him to bring aid to those surrounded by fear of so great a danger.

When Lothar heard of their peril and of what had happened, he deliberated about going to their assistance. At that time Count Warinus fortified the fortress of Chalon as best he could with many allies, so that, if the partisans of the opposing side attempted anything new, it might serve as a refuge and fortification for him and his men.

When Lothar learned this, he planned to arrive there unexpectedly, but he was unable to do so. Nevertheless, he came and surrounded the town, setting fire to the things that lay around the city.

They fought fiercely for five days. Finally, the city was first received into surrender. Then, in turn, according to the custom of cruel victors, the church was devastated by plunder, its treasures were robbed, and the common stores were seized. In the end, the city was consumed by voracious fire, except for one small basilica which, by an astonishing miracle, although surrounded on every side by raging and licking flames, nevertheless could not be burned.

It had been consecrated to God in honor of the blessed martyr George. Lothar had not, however, wished the city to be burned.

After the city had been captured, by the acclamation of the army Count Gotselin, Count Sanila, and the imperial vassal Madalelmus were beheaded. Gerberga, formerly the daughter of Count William, was also drowned in water as a sorceress.

While these events were taking place, the emperor had arrived with his son Louis at the city of Langres. In that city he received news of this kind, which made him very sorrowful.

His son Lothar set out from Chalon toward Autun, proceeded from there to the city of Orléans, and then came to the district of Le Mans, to a villa called Matualis.

The emperor followed him with his very large forces and with his son Louis. When Lothar heard this, and after he had already recovered his own men, he established his camp not far from his father. They remained there for four days, with envoys passing between them.

On the fourth night Lothar began to withdraw with his men. His father advanced against him by a shorter route until they reached the Loire near the fortress of Blois, where the Cisse River flows into the Loire.

After camps had been established on both sides, Pippin also came to his father with as much military equipment as he could muster.

Lothar, his strength broken, came humbly to his father. The emperor restrained him with words and bound both him and his nobles by whatever oaths he wished, then sent them back to Italy. He blocked the narrow passages of the roads leading into Italy, so that no one could cross without the permission of the guards.

When these matters had been completed, he reached Orléans with his son Louis. There he granted both his son and the others permission to return to their own lands, and he himself reached Paris.

At that time, around the Mass of Saint Martin, he held a general assembly at the palace of Attigny. Since he had decided to purge many abuses that had grown up in both ecclesiastical and public affairs, the following measures were especially taken.

Through Abbot Ermold he ordered his son Pippin to restore without delay to the churches the ecclesiastical properties in his kingdom, whether Pippin himself had assigned them to his own men or they had seized them for themselves.

He also sent envoys throughout the cities and monasteries and ordered the ecclesiastical order, which had almost completely collapsed, to be raised again to its former condition.

Likewise, he ordered envoys to travel through the individual counties to restrain the monstrous violence of robbers and brigands, which had arisen in an unprecedented manner. Wherever their force had become especially oppressive, the envoys were to enlist neighboring counts and the men of the bishops to defeat and crush such criminals. They were to report each of these matters to him at the next general assembly at Worms, which he summoned to take place after winter had passed and the favor of spring had returned.

(835.) The emperor therefore spent the greater part of the winter at Aachen. From there he set out for Theodonis Villa before the Nativity of the Lord, where the people who had been ordered to come also arrived. While staying there, he complained against certain bishops concerning his deposition. [Col. 0968B] But when some had fled to Italy and others, though summoned, had refused to obey, only Ebo among those accused appeared. When he was pressed to give an account of such matters, he pleaded that he alone was being pressed, after all those in whose presence these things had been done had been left behind. The other bishops, however, while alleging the necessity of their presence, excused themselves on the grounds of their innocence. At last Ebo, being distressed to be wearied by such proceedings, sought the advice of certain bishops, made a confession concerning himself, and declared that he was unworthy of the priesthood and judged himself irrevocably to abstain from it. He communicated this decision to the bishops and through them to the emperor.

After this, Agobard, archbishop of Lyon, who delayed coming when summoned to make satisfaction, was removed from the episcopal office after being summoned three times, [Col. 0968C] while the others, as we have said, fled to Italy. On the following Sunday, which preceded the beginning of the holy Lenten season, the lord emperor came to the city of Metz, as did the bishops and all the people of that assembly. During the celebration of Mass, seven archbishops sang over him the seven prayers of ecclesiastical reconciliation. When all the people saw this, they gave abundant thanks to God for the emperor’s complete restoration.

After all this, both the lord emperor and the people who belonged to him returned to Theodonis Villa; and, when the sacred season of Lent began, he ordered each man to return to his own place. He himself spent Lent there, but celebrated the solemnity of Easter [Col. 0968D] at Metz. After the Easter solemnity and the venerable day of Pentecost, he went to the city of the Vangiones, now called Worms, according to the agreement, to hold a general assembly. There his son Pippin also met him, nor was his other son Louis absent.

As was his custom, the emperor did not allow this assembly to be devoid of public usefulness. For he carefully sought to examine what each of the envoys sent into the various regions had done. And because some counts were found negligent in suppressing and exterminating robbers, he chastised their negligence with appropriate denunciation and various judgments. He admonished his sons and the people to love equity, suppress robbers, [Col. 0969A] and relieve good men and their possessions from oppression. He also threatened that he would pronounce a harsher judgment against those who did not obey this admonition.

When he dismissed the people from this assembly, and had appointed the next one at Theodonis Villa after Easter, he withdrew to Aachen to spend the winter. He instructed his son Lothair to send to that same place certain nobles of his realm, so that the basis of mutual reconciliation between himself and Lothair might be investigated.

The empress Judith, having taken counsel with the emperor’s advisers, thought that the emperor’s bodily strength would soon fail him, as it seemed, and that death was approaching; and that danger threatened both herself and Charles unless they associated one of the brothers with them. They conjectured that none of the emperor’s sons was so suitable for this purpose as [Col. 0969B] Lothair, and urged the emperor to send peaceful envoys to him and invite him to this undertaking.

Since he was always devoted to peace, always a lover and admirer of peace and steadfastness, and sought to unite not only his sons but also his enemies to himself in charity, he readily agreed. At the agreed estate and at the appointed time, many envoys from his son arrived, sent at Lothair’s command; among them Wala was the first to appear.

When the matter mentioned above had been debated and brought to its conclusion, the emperor wished to be reconciled with his wife. First, he forgave Wala himself all the offenses he had committed against them, with great eagerness and kindness of heart. Through him and the other envoys sent to his son, he ordered Lothair to come as quickly as possible. If he did so, he should know that it would be greatly to his advantage.

The envoys returned and reported the matter to Lothair. But, to prevent the emperor’s command from being carried out, illness and fever intervened: they carried Wala away from human affairs, while casting Lothair onto a sickbed and making him languish for a very long time. When the most merciful emperor by nature heard that his son had been struck by illness, he visited him through very trusted envoys, namely his brother Hugh and Count Adalgar, and took pains to learn all his troubles. In this he imitated blessed David, who, although repeatedly harassed by his son, nevertheless bore his death with the greatest grief.

But after Lothair recovered as the illness abated, the emperor was informed that he was violating the conditions of the oaths previously promised, and especially that his men were harassing with the cruelest devastation the church of Saint Peter, which both his grandfather Pippin and his father Charles, [Col. 0969D] as well as he himself, had undertaken to protect. This so exasperated the emperor’s exceedingly gentle spirit that, as it seemed, he dispatched envoys in an extraordinary manner, granting almost no time for so long a journey.

He sent legates to Lothair, warning him not to permit such things to happen. He reminded him that, when he had given him the kingdom of Italy, he had simultaneously entrusted him with the care of the holy Roman Church, and that he must not allow the Church, which he had undertaken to defend against its adversaries, to be plundered by his own men. He also reminded him of the oaths he had recently promised him, lest, forgetting or despising them, he offend the Divinity. He should not be unaware that this would not go unpunished.

At the same time, he ordered him to prepare provisions and suitable lodging for him along the entire route leading to Rome. For he said that he wished to visit the thresholds of the blessed apostles. But an incursion of the Northmen into Frisia prevented this.

To suppress their insolence, he set out and sent envoys to Lothair: namely Abbot Fulco, Count Richard, and Abbot Adrebald. Fulco and Richard were to bring back Lothair’s response, while Adrebald was to go to Rome to consult Pope Gregory about necessary matters and to convey the emperor’s wishes and the other instructions entrusted to him.

When Lothair was questioned about these matters, as well as about the property of certain churches in Italy that had been taken away, he agreed to some points but replied that he could not observe others. Fulco [Col. 0970B] and Richard reported such things to the emperor when he was returning from Frisia after the flight of the Northmen, at the palace of Frankfurt. From there, after conducting his autumn hunt, he turned toward Aachen to spend the winter.

Adrebald, however, reached Rome as he had been ordered. There he found Pope Gregory ill, suffering especially from a flow of blood which, although slowly, nevertheless continually ran from his nostrils. Yet he was so revived by the emperor’s words and sympathy, with such eagerness and joy, that he professed almost to have forgotten his own illness.

Accordingly, he treated the envoy who stayed with him most generously and richly rewarded him when he departed. He sent with him two bishops: Peter, of the city of Centumcellae, and George, the regional bishop of the city of Rome. [Col. 0970C]

When Lothair heard that the aforementioned bishops were making their way to the lord emperor, he sent Leo, who at that time held a position of great influence with him, to Bologna. By threatening the bishops with great terror, Leo prevented them from proceeding farther.

Adrebald nevertheless secretly received from them the letter intended for the emperor. He entrusted it to one of his men, under the guise of a beggar, to carry it until he crossed the Alps; afterward he delivered it to the emperor.

It is grievous to relate how great a deadly plague invaded the people who followed Lothair at that time. Within a short period—that is, from the Kalends of September until the Mass of Saint Martin—the following leading men died: Jesse, formerly bishop of Amiens; Elias, bishop of the city of Troyes; Wala, abbot of the monastery of Corbie; Matfrid; Hugh; Lambert; [Col. 0970D] Godfrey, and likewise his son Godfrey; Count Albert of the Perche; Burgaretus, formerly superintendent of the royal huntsmen. Richard barely escaped. Not long afterward he too died.

These were the men whose deaths were said to have left Francia deprived of its nobility, unmanned in its strength as though its sinews had been cut, and deprived of prudence when they had died. But when these supports had been overthrown, God demonstrated how salutary and praiseworthy it is to observe what is shown to proceed from his mouth:

> Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom,  
> nor the strong man in his strength,  
> nor the rich man in his riches.

Who, moreover, could worthily marvel at the emperor’s spirit, and at how greatly divine mercy governed him with restraint? When he received this news, he neither exulted in himself nor mocked the death of his enemies. Rather, striking his breast with his fist and filling his eyes with tears, he prayed with profound lamentation that God would become favorable to them.

At this time the attack of the Britons was stirred up, but it subsided as easily as the emperor had placed his hope in him to whom it is most truly said:

> For with you, Lord, whenever you will, there is power.

In those same days during which the Purification of the most blessed ever-virgin Mary is celebrated, a great assembly, especially of bishops, gathered at Aachen (836). At it, among other matters necessary for the welfare of the Church, complaint was made particularly concerning the properties that Pippin and his men had taken from many churches. For this reason an imperial decree and a warning of the common council were drawn up, by which Pippin and his men were admonished of the great danger they had incurred by seizing ecclesiastical property. The matter had a favorable outcome. For Pippin, willingly accepting the admonitions of his devout father and of the holy men, obediently complied and decreed, even by the impression of his ring, that everything he had seized should be restored. [Col. 0971B]

Soon after this assembly, the emperor held another in the county of Lyon, during the summer, at a place called Stramiacus, with his sons Pippin and Louis. Lothair was absent because of the illness mentioned above.

At this assembly he caused the case of the vacant churches of Lyon and Vienne to be debated: Agobard, the former bishop of Lyon, had been ordered to come and give an account but had not appeared; Bernard of Vienne had appeared, but had again taken flight. [Col. 0971C] The matter, however, remained unfinished because of the absence, as stated, of the bishops.

The case of the Goths was also debated there. Some of them favored Bernard’s party, while others were led by support for Beringar, son of the former Count Hunro[c]us [Huro(n)ic]. But when Beringar was taken away by premature death, the greatest part of the power of Septimania remained with Bernard. Envoys were sent there to restore to better condition whatever required correction.

When these matters had been completed and his sons and the people had already been dismissed, the emperor, after finishing his autumn hunt, returned to Aachen by the Mass of Saint Martin. He spent the winter there and, according to the proper custom always most familiar to him, celebrated the Nativity of the Lord and the Easter solemnity there. [Col. 0971D]

(837.) In the middle of the Easter festival, a dreadful and always sorrowful portent appeared: the star of a comet in the sign of Virgo, in that part of the sign which binds her cloak below, and at the same time the serpent’s tail and the raven. Unlike the seven wandering stars, it did not move toward the East. Over twenty-five days—a remarkable thing to relate—the same star passed through the signs of Leo, Cancer, and Gemini and finally, at the head of Taurus, beneath the feet of Auriga, laid aside its fiery globe and the great length of its rays, which previously it had extended in every direction.

As soon as the emperor, who was exceedingly interested in such matters, saw it, he stopped. Before committing his limbs to rest, he summoned a certain man and also me, who wrote this account and was thought to possess knowledge of such matters, and diligently asked what I thought about it.

When I asked for time to examine the appearance of the star, investigate the truth of the matter, and report what I had learned on the following day, the emperor—rightly judging that I wished to gain time so as not to be forced to give a gloomy answer—said:

“Go to the walls adjoining this house and report to us what you observe. I know that I did not see this star during the previous evening, nor was it pointed out to me by you. But I know that this is a cometary sign, about which we have already spoken in past days. Tell me what you think it portends.”

When I had said some things and remained silent about others, he said:

“There is one thing you are still suppressing in silence. They say that this portent signifies a change of kingdom and the death of a prince.”

When I brought forward the Prophet’s testimony, which says, “Do not fear the signs of heaven, which the nations fear,” he, displaying his customary courage and prudence, said:

“We ought to fear no one other than him who is the creator of us and of this star. Yet we cannot sufficiently praise and marvel at his mercy, since he deigns to warn us—though we are sinners and unrepentant—by such signs. Since this portent touches both me and all of us together, let us all hasten, as far as we are able and wise, toward better things, lest, while he offers mercy and our impenitence obstructs it, we be found unworthy of it.”

After saying this, he himself indulged in a little wine and ordered everyone to do the same; he then instructed each person to gather himself to his own quarters. He spent that night awake, as we were told, and presented it to the approaching light laden with praises and supplications to God.

At dawn he summoned the palace officials and ordered alms to be distributed most generously to the poor and to the servants of God, both monks and canons. He also arranged for the solemn celebration of Masses wherever he could—not fearing merely for himself, but looking to the welfare of the Church entrusted to him.

After these arrangements had been properly made as he had ordered, he went hunting in the Ardennes. As they said, the hunt turned out most successfully for him, beyond what was usual; and everything that pleased him at that time proceeded with a favorable outcome.

Moreover, at the insistence of the empress and the palace officials, the emperor granted his beloved son Charles a certain part of the empire at Aachen. But because the arrangement remained without effect, we too pass over it in silence. When his brothers heard of it, they were distressed and held a mutual conference. Seeing that they could accomplish nothing by opposing it, and concealing their original purpose, they very easily settled the movements of their father, which seemed to have arisen from this affair.

Remaining at this place throughout the summer, the emperor announced a general assembly to be held in the autumn, in the middle of September, at Quierzy. At that place and time his son Pippin came to him from Aquitaine and took part in the assembly.

There the lord emperor girded his son Charles with manly arms, that is, with a sword; he marked his head with a royal crown; and he assigned him the portion of the kingdom formerly held by his namesake Charles, namely Neustria. [Col. 0973A]

Thus the lord emperor, having strengthened as far as possible the bond of goodwill among his sons, sent Pippin to Aquitaine and Charles to the portion of the kingdom assigned to him. The leading men of the province of Neustria who were present gave their hands to Charles and bound themselves to him by an oath of fidelity; each of the absent men later did the same.

At the same place and time nearly all the nobles of Septimania were present, complaining against Bernard, duke of that region, because his agents were abusing both ecclesiastical and private property at will, without regard for God or man. They therefore asked the lord emperor to receive them under the protection of his safeguard and thereafter send such envoys into that land as would, with authority [Col. 0973B] and prudence, weigh what had been taken away in an equitable balance and preserve for them their ancestral law.

To accomplish this, at their request and by the emperor’s choice, Count Boniface and likewise Count Donatus were sent, together with Adrebald, abbot of the monastery of Flavigny. When these matters had been properly completed, the emperor withdrew from that place, devoted himself according to custom to the autumn hunt, and gathered himself at Aachen to spend the winter.

After that winter had passed, on the Kalends of January a fierce cometary fire appeared in the sign of Scorpio, not long after sunset. Its threatening appearance was soon followed by the death of Pippin.

Meanwhile the empress Judith, by no means forgetful of the plan she had previously formed with the palace advisers and the other nobles of the Frankish kingdom, persuaded the emperor to send envoys to his son Lothair. They were to invite him to his father on the condition that, if he wished to be the lover, helper, guardian, and protector of his brother Charles, he should come to his father and know that he would receive from him pardon for everything wrongly done, as well as half the empire, except Bavaria.

This arrangement appeared entirely advantageous both to Lothair and to his men. Accordingly, after the Easter solemnity, he came to Worms at the appointed time (838). His father received him with great eagerness, ordered his men to be generously cared for, and carried out everything he had promised. Indeed, after granting him a delay of three days, he allowed Lothair himself to divide the whole empire among them, if he wished, though the choice of the portions [Col. 0973D] was to remain with the emperor and Charles. Otherwise, if he judged it preferable, the division of the empire was to be made by the emperor and Charles.

Thus Lothair and his men entrusted the division of the kingdom to the lord emperor according to his judgment, declaring that they could not carry out the division themselves because they were ignorant of the regions. The emperor, therefore, with his men, divided his entire empire according to an equitable balance, as seemed right to him and to them, except for Bavaria, which he left to Louis and which therefore fell to none of their portions.

When this had been done, and his sons and the entire people had been summoned, the choice having been given to him, Lothair selected for himself the southern part from the river Meuse. He left the western part for his brother Charles and indicated before the whole people by his word [Col. 0974A] that he wished Charles to possess it.

The emperor rejoiced in these events, and all the people, applauding such actions, declared that everything pleased them. But these proceedings wounded Louis’s spirit considerably.

The emperor gave thanks to God for what had been done and admonished his sons to be united and protect one another. Lothair, he said, should care for his younger brother, remembering that he was his spiritual father; Charles, however, should render the honor owed to his spiritual father and elder brother.

Having carried this out as a true lover of peace, and having sown as far as he was able mutual affection among the brothers and reciprocal love between the people of each son, he joyfully sent Lothair, also joyful, to Italy, richly supplied with gifts and endowed with his fatherly blessings. He admonished him not to forget at least the promises recently made to him.

He celebrated the Nativity of the Lord and the Easter solemnity with the greatest splendor at Aachen.

(839.) When Louis heard of his father’s will concerning his brothers and of the division of the kingdom among them, he did not accept it. He therefore thought that everything beyond the Rhine ought to be assigned to him and determined to claim it.

When this was reported to the emperor, he judged that the matter should be postponed until the Easter festival had passed. When it was over, he did not think such matters should be delayed any longer. With a large force he crossed the Rhine near Mainz and came to Tribur, where he stayed for some time to gather an army.

When it had been assembled, he proceeded as far as Bedonnia [Hodomia]. There his son, although unwilling, came as a suppliant [Col. 0974C]. Rebuked by his father, he confessed that he had acted wrongly and declared that he would correct what he had done improperly.

The emperor, employing the gentleness customary and always dear to him, forgave his son. First he rebuked him, as was fitting, with somewhat harsh words; afterward he soothed him with gentler ones and left him in the kingdom.

On his return he crossed the Rhine at a place called Confluentes, intending to carry out his customary hunt in the Ardennes. While he was engaged in it, highly trustworthy messengers came to him, reporting what was true: some of the Aquitanians were awaiting his decision concerning how the affairs of the kingdom of Aquitaine should be arranged, while others were indignant because they had heard that the emperor had given the same kingdom to Charles.

While the emperor was concerned about these matters, Ebroin, the most noble bishop of Poitiers, came to Flatera, announcing that he and the other leading men of that kingdom were awaiting the emperor’s will and wished to carry out the command of the ruler.

For the greatest of the nobles were united in this purpose. The foremost among them were the venerable bishop Ebroin himself; Count Reginard; Count Gerard, formerly Pippin’s son-in-law; and Hiratarius [Ratharius], likewise a count and Pippin’s son-in-law. Many others who followed their will could not in any way be separated from them.

The other part of the people, whose principal leader was a certain Emenus, took with them the son of the former King Pippin, also named Pippin, and wandered wherever they could, [Col. 0975A] as men of such character are accustomed to do, devoting themselves to plundering and tyranny.

The aforesaid bishop Ebroin therefore begged the emperor not to allow this disease to spread further, but to cure the affliction promptly by his arrival, before so great a plague could infect many.

The emperor sent the aforementioned bishop back to Aquitaine with many thanks and entrusted to him instructions for his faithful men. He also ordered some of them to meet him at Chalon in the autumn. For he had announced a general assembly there.

Let no one therefore be angry with the emperor because, under the prompting of cruelty, he wished to deprive his nephew of the kingdom. He knew the native character of that people, having been brought up among them; and because they pursued frivolity and other vices, they had utterly renounced seriousness and stability. Moreover, in order to make his brother Pippin such a man, almost all those who had been sent to guard him—just as they had formerly been given to him by his father Charles—had driven them from the borders of Aquitaine.

After their departure, what and how many evils and monstrous vices arose, both public and private, in that kingdom, are also represented by the current concerns of the present time.

The most devout emperor wished the boy to be brought up piously and reasonably, so that, once abandoned to vices, he might not later be able either to rule or to benefit himself or others. He was thinking of the statement attributed to a certain man who was unwilling to hand over the kingdom while his sons were still at a tender age and is recorded as having excused himself in these words:

> I do not forbid those born from me to be held in honor because I begrudge them anything; rather, because I know that these pursuits provide nourishment for fierceness in the young.

Accordingly, as he had arranged, the emperor went to the city of Chalon in the autumn and, according to his custom, regulated both ecclesiastical and public affairs. Then he turned his attention to the organization of the kingdom of Aquitaine.

For he departed from that place with the empress, his son Charles, and a strong force. After crossing the river Loire, he proceeded to the city of the Arverni. There he received his faithful men, who came to meet him, kindly and according to his usual custom, and had them commend themselves to his son Charles with the customary oaths.

Some refused to offer him the meeting and fidelity that were owed. Worse, they prowled around the army as robbers and carried out whatever plunder they could. He ordered these men, once captured, to be subjected to lawful examination. [Col. 0975D]

(840.) While he was engaged in these affairs, the festival of the Nativity of the Lord returned, and he celebrated the same solemnity at Poitiers with the proper and customary honor. While he remained there and arranged whatever necessity required, a messenger arrived announcing that his son Louis, having taken certain Saxons and Thuringians with him, had invaded Alamannia.

This brought him the greatest distress. For he was already weighed down by old age, and the abundance of phlegm that increases in winter burdened his lungs beyond what was usual and shook his chest. This sad news was added to his condition. Its report affected him with such bitterness—although by nature he was exceedingly gentle, almost beyond human measure, magnanimous in courage, and most cautious in piety—[Col. 0976A] that the phlegm growing into an abscess hardened, and a deadly ulcer formed within his vital organs.

Yet his unconquered spirit, when he learned that the Church of God was being disturbed by such a pestilence and the Christian people afflicted, yielded neither to disgust nor, broken by grief, to weakness. After beginning the holy Lenten fast with his wife and his son Charles, he set himself against this storm in order to calm it.

He was accustomed to make the whole season solemn with the greatest devotion through the chanting of psalms, persistent prayer, the celebration of Masses, and generosity in almsgiving, scarcely allowing himself one or two days for riding exercises. Now, however, in order to drive away discord and restore peace, he did not wish to have a single day of rest.

Following the example of the good shepherd, he did not refuse, for the welfare of the flock entrusted to him, to bear even the loss of his own body. Hence there is no doubt that he received the reward which the supreme Father and prince of shepherds promised to give to those who labor in this way.

With the greatest fatigue, and with his strength already attacked by the events mentioned above, he reached Aachen as the most sacred Easter solemnity approached, and celebrated it there with his customary devotion. When it was concluded, he hastened to complete the undertaking he had begun.

After crossing the Rhine, he entered Thuringia by a continuous journey, where he learned that Louis was staying at that time. Since his conscience did not allow him to remain there, especially because his father was already approaching, and since he also distrusted his own circumstances, Louis placed his safety in flight. [Col. 0976C] Having retraced his route, he returned to his own territory through the land of the Slavs.

After Louis had returned there, the emperor ordered a general assembly to be convened in the city of the Vangiones, now called Worms. Since Louis’s affairs stood as they did, while his son Charles was in Aquitaine with his mother, the emperor sent his son Lothair to Italy, ordering him to attend the same assembly so that he might deliberate with him and the others about this matter.

At that time an eclipse of the sun occurred, in an unusual manner, on the third day of the Greater Litany. The withdrawal of the light was so great that darkness prevailed, and it seemed to differ in nothing from the reality of night. For the ordered array of the stars could be seen, and no star suffered from the sun’s dimmed light. Rather, the moon, which had positioned itself opposite the sun, gradually moved eastward and first restored to it a horn-shaped light on the western side, as happens when it is seen in its first or second phase, and then, by gradual stages, restored the sun’s entire beauty over its whole disk.

Although this prodigy may be attributed to nature, it was nevertheless fulfilled in a lamentable outcome. For it signified that the great light of mortals—the emperor of most devout memory, I mean, who had been placed above the lampstand in the house of God and shone for all—was soon to be taken from human affairs, and that the world, after his departure, would be left in the darkness of tribulations.

He therefore began to waste away with loathing, to force himself to take food and drink despite a nauseated stomach, to be oppressed by frequent sighs, shaken by hiccups, and [Col. 0977A] thereby deprived of strength. For when nature is abandoned by its companions, it must necessarily grow weary and be overcome.

Seeing this, he ordered summer quarters and expeditionary lodgings to be prepared for him on an island adjacent to the city of Mainz. There, deprived of his strength, he committed himself to a sickbed.

Furthermore, who could explain his concern for the condition of the Church, or his grief over its turmoil? Who could recount the streams of tears that he shed for the hastening of divine mercy? For he did not grieve that he was about to depart, but he lamented what he knew was going to happen, saying that he was wretched, since his final days were being closed amid such funeral woes [miseries]. Venerable bishops and very many other servants of God were present to console him. Among them were Hethi, venerable archbishop of Trier [Col. 0977B], Otgar, likewise archbishop of Mainz, and also Drogo, the emperor’s brother, bishop of Metz and archchaplain of the sacred palace. The more closely he knew Drogo to be related to him, the more familiarly he entrusted all his affairs and himself to him. Through him he offered daily the gift of his confession—the sacrifice of a contrite spirit and humbled heart, which God does not despise.

For forty days his only food was the Lord’s Body, while he praised God’s justice and said: “You are just, Lord, since, because I spent the season of Lent without fasting, at least under compulsion I am fulfilling that same fast for you.” He ordered his venerable brother Drogo to have the ministers of his chamber come before him and to command that his household property, which consisted [Col. 0977C] of royal ornaments—namely, crowns, weapons, vessels, books, and priestly vestments—be listed item by item. According to what seemed right to him, he declared what should be distributed to churches, what to the poor, and finally what to his sons, Lothar and Charles.

To Lothar he sent a crown, a sword, and a scepter encircled with gold and jewels, to be held on the condition that he preserve faith with Charles and Judith and consent to and defend for him the whole share of the kingdom which, with God and the palace nobles as witnesses, he had bestowed upon Charles along with Lothar and in Lothar’s presence. When these matters had been properly completed, he gave thanks to God because he recognized that nothing remained to him as his own.

Meanwhile, both the venerable bishop Drogo and the other bishops were giving thanks to God for everything that was being done. They saw that he whom a choir of virtues had always accompanied was now being followed by perseverance, which, like the tail of a sacrificial victim, was rendering the whole sacrifice of his life wholly acceptable to God. Yet one thing darkened their joy. They feared that he might perhaps wish to remain irreconcilable toward his son Louis, knowing that a wound repeatedly cut open, or burned with a cautery, inflicts more bitter pain upon the sufferer. Nevertheless, trusting in his unconquered patience, which he had always displayed, they gently appealed to his mind through his brother Drogo, whose words he did not wish to disregard.

At first he indeed showed the bitterness of his spirit. But after reflecting for a little while, and gathering what little strength he possessed, he tried to enumerate how many and how great were the wrongs [Col. 0978A] with which he had been afflicted by him, and what he had incurred by acting so contrary to nature and to the Lord’s command. “But since he,” he said, “cannot come to me to make satisfaction, I am doing what is mine to do, with you and God as witnesses: I forgive him everything in which he has sinned against me. It will be your task, however, to admonish him that, although I have forgiven him so many wrongful deeds, he must not forget himself—the one who is leading his father’s gray hairs down to death in sorrow and, in such conduct, has despised the commands and threats of our common Father, God.”

When these matters had been completed and these words spoken—it was the evening of Saturday—he ordered the nocturnal vigils to be celebrated before him and his breast to be fortified with the wood of the holy cross. As long as he had the strength, he marked both his forehead and his breast with that same sign with his own hand. Whenever he grew tired, he requested by a gesture through the hands of his brother Drogo that this be done.

Thus he remained throughout that entire night bereft of every bodily strength, but possessing only sobriety of mind. On the following day, which was Sunday, he ordered the altar service to be prepared and the solemnity of the Mass to be celebrated by the ministry of Drogo. He also ordered that, according to custom, holy communion be given him through Drogo’s hands, and afterward that he be provided with a draught of a little warm drink. After tasting a very small amount of it, he asked his brother and those standing by to attend to the care of their bodies, saying that he would wait as long as it took them to refresh themselves.

When the moment of his departure was approaching, he summoned Drogo by joining his thumb to his fingers—for he used to do this whenever he called his brother by a gesture. When Drogo and the other priests came, he commended himself to them with such words and gestures as he could manage, asked to be blessed, and requested that the rites customarily performed at the departure of the soul be carried out.

While they were performing these rites, as several people have reported to me, he turned his gaze toward the left and, as though expressing indignation, said twice with all the strength he could muster, “Hutz, Hutz,” which means, “Out, out.” It is therefore clear that he saw an evil spirit, whose company he wished to have neither while alive nor while dying.

But when he raised his eyes to heaven, the more threateningly he looked upon the one side, the more joyfully he fixed his gaze upon the other [the manuscript reads: “looking at the hosts of angels, he saw them coming to him; he fixed his gaze upon them more joyfully,” and so forth], so that he seemed to differ in no respect from one who was smiling.

Having thus reached the end of his present life, he passed happily, as we believe, into rest, since, as the truthful teacher truly said: “He cannot die badly who has lived well.” He died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the sixty-fourth year of his life. He ruled Aquitaine for thirty-seven years and held the empire for twenty-seven.

After his soul had departed, his brother Drogo, bishop of Metz, together with other bishops, abbots, counts, royal vassals, and a very large gathering of both clergy and people, had the emperor’s remains transported with great honor to Metz and buried him nobly in the basilica of Saint Arnulf, where his mother also had been laid to rest.

The Life and Deeds of the Glorious, Invincible, and Orthodox Prince, the Emperor Louis the Pious, End Here.

[Col. 0979A]

## Epitaph of King and Emperor Louis, Who Lies in the Monastery of Saint Arnulf of Metz

The thunderbolt of empire, the noble summit of the Franks,  
Freed from the world, is enclosed in this tomb.

King Louis, so great a friend of piety  
That by the people and by his title he is called Pious.

Offspring of Hildegard, pious descendant of Charlemagne,  
Piety gathers him into the boundaries of peace.

The estate of Rumilly, and whatever belongs to it,  
He bestowed upon Saint Arnulf and upon this place.

From him descends the line of nobles, kings, and emperors,  
By whose gifts this place is sustained.

## Another Epitaph of Louis

(From an old parchment of Saint Arnulf of Metz, in Baluze, *Capitularia*, vol. II, [Col. 0979B] p. 1566.)

Preeminent in merits and renowned in fame and name,  
Here stands the blessed Augustus Louis. [Col. 0980A] When his body’s limbs were closed, when he released his last breath  
Of human life, he sought the realms above the stars.

Faithful, strong, second to none in piety,  
He was merciful, patient, and kind.

He renewed the churches of Christ in an honorable manner,  
And everywhere he was their true servant.

Born of Caesar Charles and surviving Augustus,  
He succeeded to this kingdom, ruling the people with the scepter.

Now, because of his sacred merits, it is right to believe  
That he reigns with Christ the Lord in the heavenly realms.

His brother Drogo, both a priest of Christ and his own brother,  
Brought his body here and placed it in this tomb.

He died in the twenty-seventh year of his reign, on the twelfth  
Day before the Kalends of July; in the sixty-fourth year of his age, he rested in peace.

This altar, eternal God, Caesar Lothar [Col. 0980B] ordered to be prepared for you with devoted heart,  
So that there the sacred victim of your Body might duly be consecrated  
And become clean through your blood. [Col. 0979B]

# Ecclesiastical Diplomas of Louis I, Surnamed the Pious, August Emperor, and of His Sons, up to the Division of the Empire in the Year 840

[Col. 0979C]

## I. For the Monastery of Nouaillé (Year 793)

[Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. [lacuna], p. 715.]

Louis, by the grace of God king of the Aquitanians.

In the name of Christ, it seems right to us that whenever Catholic ecclesiastics and priests of God, clerics and poor people, seek our clemency in any matter, royal power should extend protection to them, since they faithfully desire to reach our magnificence. And, with Christ as our guide, we undoubtedly believe that divine mercy will hear us more fully if we lend favorable ears to the petitions of priests and bring to completion what they rightly request.

[Col. 0979D] Accordingly, a written disposition was presented before us by the magnificent man and our kinsman Ato, deacon and abbot, which he had received from the mouth of the most glorious king Charles, my father and progenitor, and supreme Catholic ruler. It stated how he had established, from the possessions of Saint Hilary, a small cell called Novaliacus, situated in a quiet place and highly suitable for the dwelling of servants of God and the poor, and had settled there, according to the capacity of that place, monks who were to live according to the rule of Saint Benedict.

And the venerable man already mentioned, Lord Ato the abbot, our kinsman, most faithful to my lord and father and to us, carefully suggested to us that this cell and the little properties which he had brought there, as well as what the priest Hermembert, rector of that little cell, had confirmed there, and also those donations which Ansaldus, Ebarcius, and Guozbertus had brought to that cell for the former bishop of Poitiers whom we recognize, together with whatever God-fearing people and Catholic men might afterward wish to confer, should always be joined together through our munificence and never be separated.

We therefore strictly command all our faithful—bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, centenarii, toll-collectors, all our traveling envoys, and those known to exercise public or private authority—that they never at any time presume to enter the properties of the aforesaid little cell, or the people of that cell living anywhere, who properly belong under its jurisdiction, in order to hear cases, exact fines from any quarter, make lodgings or requisitioned provisions, or demand any payments whatsoever. The aforementioned Lord Ato the abbot and his monks have asked us to confirm in every respect, by our authority, the protection of this cell of God; and you should know that, out of reverence for our lord and patron, the most blessed Hilary, we have granted and confirmed it with the greatest goodwill.

Whatever our fiscus might thereby be able to increase, once our confirmation has been inspected, just as it was declared and granted through the immunities of earlier kings, whether it consists of those possessions that at the present time lawfully come to that house of God or of those that God-fearing people may thereafter donate there, must perpetually contribute to the increase of the lights of that holy place and to the support of the monks. Thus the community may more eagerly implore the mercy of the Lord for the stability of our kingdom.

And so that this decree may have greater force and be better preserved, we have ordered it to be confirmed below.

In the name of God, Reginpertus, also called the unworthy bishop or chaplain, subscribed for Louis, king of the Aquitanians. Sign + Magnarius. Sign + Immo. Sign + Adalbert. Sign + Erlald. Sign + Garic. Sign + Witfred. Sign + Ademar. Sign + Raganfred. Sign + Bico. Sign + Gislemar. Also, sign of Gislemar. Charles subscribed. Sign + Hariald. Sign. Abbo. Jalinus, cleric, subscribed. Sign + Wado. Sign. Of the most glorious king Louis.

Given on the third day before the Nones of August, in the twenty-fifth year [of the most glorious king Charles] and the fourteenth year of our reign. Enacted at our palace of Jogundiacum. I, Hildigarius, subscribed in the place of Deodatus.

## II. For the Monastery of Cormery (Year 807)

[In Baluze, *Capitularia of the Kings of the Franks*, vol. II, p. [Col. 0981C] 401.]

Louis, by the grace of God king of the Aquitanians, to all bishops, abbots, counts, household officers, vicars, centenarii, and the rest of our faithful, present and future.

Let it be known that we have granted to Abbot Fridegisus of the monastery of Saint Martin, where Saint Martin himself rests bodily, that the monks of the monastery of Cormery, who appear to live monastically under the rule of Saint Benedict, father of monks, may send two vessels, or as many as they may need, along all rivers running through our kingdom, God willing, without paying any customary dues, for their necessities.

To strengthen the authority of this grant, we have ordered this present decree to be made. By it, with imperial authority, we command that none of our present or future officials dare contradict them in any respect concerning this royal sanction. And so that this decree may possess greater force, we have ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of April, in the twenty-seventh year of our reign. Enacted happily in God’s name at the palace of Cassanogilum. Amen.

I, Albo, wrote it in the place of Helisachar.

## III. For the Monastery of Gellone (Year 807)

[In D. Bouquet, *Collection of Histories*, vol. VI, p. 452.]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, most serene king of Aquitaine.

Since we must consider how, despite the weight of sins, we may not lose the love of the eternal King, it has pleased us to bestow suitable benefits upon places devoted to divine worship, for the sake of the eternal kingdom of our Savior and of those serving him there, so that, rewarded by him, we may deserve to enjoy never-ending joy.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful, present and future, that, at the request of Lord William the monk, who had been a very distinguished count in the court of our father, Charles Augustus, but who, for the love of God, strove to lead a better life and chose poverty by refusing high office, and because of his unalterable devotion and fidelity toward us, we have granted his petition.

For the increase of our reward and out of affection for him, we have decided to give to the monastery called Gellone [Note: [Col. 0981D] The monastery of Gellone, situated in Occitania in the district of Lodève by the little river Hérault, is now called Saint-Guillem-du-Désert.], situated in the district of Lodève beside the river Hérault, below the castle of Verdun, consecrated in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and of Saint Mary, Saint Michael, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, Saint Andrew, and all the apostles, built by the aforesaid Count William in the service of our [Col. 0982C] father, where Juliofredus appears to preside as rector and abbot [Note: [Col. 0981D] The cartulary of Gellone mentions Juliofredus in these words: “Abbot Juliofredus, a blood relative of Emperor Charles, had a testament written, in which is contained every benefice that Saint William, prince throughout the lands of all Gaul, acquired from the lords and most pious Emperors Charles and Louis.”], certain possessions of ours.

These are: a fiscus of ours in the district of Béziers called Miliacus, with its villa and the church of Saint Paragorius, together with the villa of Milicianus and that of Campanianus, with all their appurtenances and dependencies in their entirety, as it was delivered and assigned by our envoy, Count Gotcelmus [Note: [Col. 0982D] Gotcelmus was the son of Saint William, duke of Toulouse, and the brother of Bernard, later duke of Septimania.], by crosses carved in stones or by the courses of waters at the boundaries, and as it was possessed by our father and by us.

And in the aforesaid district of Lodève, a place called Gastrias, but commonly Castra-Pastura, for feeding their livestock, with the church of Saint Martin, its boundaries and dependencies, in its entirety, for their various uses.

And in the same district, a villa called Magaranciatis, with the church of Saint Felix, together with all its appurtenances and dependencies.

As for the entire property which Lord William or other faithful people have transferred to the aforesaid monastery by written charters, wherever it may be, and whatever divine goodness may thereafter wish to add to the rights of that holy place through us or through others, we grant all of it to the aforesaid monastery for eternal reward, so that it may perpetually contribute to the support of the poor and the maintenance of the monks serving God there.

All the possessions described above, with their churches, villas, hamlets, houses, buildings, fields, lands, vineyards, olive groves, woods, scrublands, meadows, pastures, mills, waters and watercourses, roads, entrances and exits, cultivated and uncultivated lands, together with all their dependencies, we grant wholly and entirely to the aforesaid monastery of Gellone by this deed of donation, to hold perpetually. Thus, from this day and time onward, the inhabitants of this place may enjoy complete freedom to do, order, and dispose of whatever they wish concerning the aforesaid possessions.

[Col. 0983B]

The notary Godolelmus recognized this in the place of Guigo.

This decree was given on the fifth day before the Kalends of January, Indiction 1, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of Lord Louis, publicly at Toulouse; and in the eighth year of Charles’s empire.

[Note: Mabillon incorrectly gives Indiction 10 when he published this diploma in *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, fourth century, part I, p. 90.]

[Note: William the monk was therefore already a monk in the year 807. Consequently, his entry into monastic life should not be postponed until the following year, as Cointius thought, but should be assigned to the year 806, in agreement with the anonymous author of his Life and with Orderic, who are supported by this diploma.]

And so that this authority may remain firm and unshaken in our own and future times, with the Lord’s protection, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it confirmed by the impression of our ring. In God’s name, happily. Amen.

Sign of Lord Louis, most serene king.

## IV. For the Monastery of Donzère (Year 814)

[In D. Bouquet, the same work, from Chifflet, in the proofs appended to *History of the Abbey of Tournus*, p. 260.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus [Col. 0983C] Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, Augustus emperor.

Let the discernment of all our faithful, present and future, know how Dexter, abbot of the monastery of Donzère [Note: Commonly Donzère on the Rhône], which was built in the territory of Orange in honor of the holy Virgin Mary, Saint Peter, and the other saints, came to us and brought to our attention a decree of Charles, our most serene emperor and father. It stated that he had granted to Abbot Norfidius or his successors, for the construction of that same monastery, the place itself, which had belonged to his own property, and had confirmed it to them to hold in perpetuity.

But the aforesaid abbot and his community asked our highness to confirm, by our authority and for the increase of our reward, those possessions with all their appurtenances and dependencies, so that they might meet the needs of that church; and they asked us to order a decree to be made for them by which they could quietly hold and possess forever, without anyone’s opposition, the aforesaid possessions and the others that God-fearing people had bestowed upon that holy place.

We did not wish to deny their request; rather, you should know that we have granted and confirmed it in every respect.

[Col. 0984A] Therefore, commanding, we order that no public judge, no one exercising judicial authority, and none of the faithful of the holy Church of God or of our own, ever dare enter the churches, places, fields, or remaining possessions of the aforesaid monastery—which it appears currently to possess justly and reasonably, through the donation of our lord and father or of other faithful people, in whatever districts and territories, or whatever has been donated there, or whatever divine goodness may thereafter wish to add to the rights of that holy place through us or through others—in order to hear cases, exact fines, make lodgings or requisitioned provisions, take sureties, or distrain the people of that church, whether free or slaves, who appear to dwell upon its land; nor may anyone enter or presume to exact any payments or seek unlawful pretexts at any time.

Whatever our fiscus might hope to obtain from the possessions of the aforesaid monastery, we grant entirely to that monastery for eternal reward, so that it may perpetually contribute to the support of the poor and the maintenance of the monks serving God there.

And whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this life, as long as the monks themselves can find among them men capable of governing that community according to the rule of Saint Benedict, they shall have permission, by this authority and consent of ours, to elect abbots. Thus may those servants of God who appear to serve God there take delight in continually imploring the Lord’s mercy for us, for our wife and children, and for the stability of our entire empire, granted and preserved for us by God.

And so that this authority may be better preserved inviolate in our own and future times, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it sealed below with our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Helisachar recognized and subscribed.

Given on the day before the Kalends of June, in the first year of our empire, Christ being propitious, Indiction 7. Enacted happily in God’s name at the royal palace of Aachen. Amen.

## V. For the Monastery of Saint Severinus of Bordeaux (Year 814)

[In D. Bouquet, the same work, p. 458, from Bessius, *Kings of Aquitaine*, p. 17.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, Augustus emperor.

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own, present and future, that, for the increase of our reward, it has pleased us to return to the monastery of Saint Severinus [Note: [Col. 0985D] This monastery was later subjected by the same emperor, together with Saint Romanus of Blaye, to the Church of Bordeaux at the request of Bishop Sicharius.] near the city of Bordeaux a villa called Miscaria, situated in the district of Saintes on the river Garonne, with all its appurtenances, for the support of the brothers residing in that monastery; and to confirm by these letters of our authority that henceforth the aforesaid monastery may possess it peacefully forever.

Accordingly, we ordered this decree of ours to be made for them. By it we make known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, that they should recognize that the aforesaid villa, with all its appurtenances and dependencies, its houses, buildings, lands, vineyards, meadows, woods, pastures, waters, watercourses, and everything that appears lawfully to belong there, wholly and entirely and without omission, has been returned and confirmed by us to that monastery through this authority.

Therefore we command that no one attempt to remove or unjustly diminish anything from the aforesaid possessions, which we have decided to return and confirm to the aforesaid monastery, or to cause any opposition or bring any unjust challenge. Rather, let the said church possess these possessions, and let them contribute forever to the support of the brothers serving God there.

And let no one ever thereafter attempt to remove them, if he wishes to have the Lord favorable to him. Let no public judge ever dare enter the aforesaid possessions, or presume to exact anything there, in order to hear cases, exact fines, make lodgings or requisitioned provisions, take sureties, distrain the people of that church, or seek any payments or unlawful pretexts; so that, through our defense, these possessions may remain safe and unharmed at all times in the future.

And so that this authority may be more firmly believed in our own and future times and may be inviolably observed by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it sealed below with our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of July, in the first year of our empire, Christ being propitious, Indiction 7. Enacted happily in God’s name at the royal palace of Aachen. Amen.

## VI. For the Church of Le Mans (Year 814)

[In Mabillon, *Ancient Analecta*, p. 296.]

In the name of the Lord God, our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, Augustus emperor.

Let the sagacity and diligence of all our faithful, both present and future, know that the venerable Franco, bishop of the city of Le Mans, presented to our serenity certain authorities of our predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks. They stated that, partly through the negligence and carelessness of men and partly through enemies laying waste and setting fires, certain written charters had once been burned or consumed. Through these charters, kings and queens and many other Catholic men had transferred possessions and slaves to the church built in honor of Christ’s martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, over which, by God’s will, he presides.

Those same authorities also stated that not only his predecessors, namely the rectors of that church, but he himself thereafter, had until now justly, legally, securely, and peacefully held and possessed the same possessions and slaves that had been recorded in those charters that were burned. He presented them to our serenity so that, as an act of confirmation, we might strengthen those authorities by our own authority.

Therefore, having examined those authorities, and for the increase of our reward, we were pleased to assent to the petitions of the aforesaid venerable [Col. 0986B] man and to join our own authority to those authorities. Through it we command and order that all possessions or slaves bestowed upon that church through the generosity of faithful people may, in our time and in future times, be held and possessed peacefully and securely by the aforesaid Bishop Franco and his successors, without any disturbance or unjust objection.

But if a dispute should arise concerning those same possessions, which had been lawfully possessed by the leaders of that city before the aforesaid burning, so that it becomes necessary to litigate on their behalf, then those possessions and slaves of that church are to be defended by this authority of ours just as they could have been defended legally by those same charters had they not been destroyed by fire.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved for future times, we have subscribed it with our own hand and sealed it with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the first year of our empire, Christ being propitious, Indiction 7. Enacted happily in God’s name at our palace of Aachen. Amen.

## VII. For the Monastery of Anisola (Year 814)

[In D. Bouquet, *Collection of Histories*, vol. VI, p. 460, from the archives of this monastery.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divine ordering of clemency, Augustus emperor, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, centenarii, actionarii, our traveling envoys, and all the faithful, etc.

Let the discernment of all our faithful know that the venerable Adalgisus, abbot of the monastery of Anisola, came to us and brought to our serenity a decree of Lord Charles, our most serene emperor and father. It stated that he, our grandfather King Pippin of blessed memory, and their predecessors, namely the earlier kings, had always held that monastery under the fullest defense and protection of immunity, out of love for God and for the tranquility of the brothers residing there.

But, in the interest of firm security, the aforesaid abbot asked that we should again grant and confirm such protection around that holy place, for the increase of our reward. We did not wish to reject his request, for the love of God. Rather, let both present and future faithful of the holy Church and of our own know that it has been granted and permanently confirmed by us in every respect.

Therefore we command that no public judge, no one exercising judicial authority, and none of the faithful of the holy Church or of our own, ever dare enter the churches, places, fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery—which it appears presently to possess justly and reasonably in whatever districts and territories lie under the authority of our empire—in order to hear cases, exact fines, impose or collect exactions, make lodgings or requisitioned provisions, take sureties, distrain the people of that church, or seek any payments or unlawful pretexts.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors be permitted to possess the possessions of that church peacefully under the protection of immunity, to serve us faithfully, and, together with their brothers, to implore the mercy of the Lord for our stability and for that of the entire empire granted and preserved for us by God.

And so that this confirmation of our authority may be held more firmly and securely and be preserved more diligently by all the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Helisachar recognized it.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the first year of our empire, Christ being propitious, Indiction 7. Enacted happily in God’s name at the palace of Aachen. Amen.

## VIII. For Betto, Bishop of Langres (Year 814)

[In D. Bouquet, the same work, p. 461; in the *Instruments* appended to vol. IV of *Gallia Christiana*, col. 129.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, Augustus emperor.

If we provide assistance by our authority to priests in whatever ecclesiastical necessities, and offer them support so that they may carry out their ministry more freely, we do not doubt that the rewards of eternal recompense will be bestowed upon us by the supreme Pontiff, our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own people, present and future, that the venerable Betto, bishop of the city of Langres, presented to us the charters of authority of our royal predecessors. In them we find inserted that formerly, because of the occupation by the Saracens, the documents of the charters, and also the royal immunities that had been there, had been lost or destroyed; and that those kings, by their authority and out of compassion, at the petitions of their predecessors, the bishops, [Col. 0988A] sought to remedy the same loss . . . namely, so that by their authority their predecessor bishops might securely and peacefully retain in the right and possession of the aforesaid church the property and dependents contained in those charter documents consumed by fire, as well as the same properties that were afterward granted to that church by Catholic men.

Moreover, our royal predecessors had held under their protection the holy see itself, together with its dependent cells and all the properties lawfully belonging to it: namely, the fortification of the city of Langres, where there is a church in honor of Saint Mamma, the illustrious martyr; the fortress of Dijon, in which is situated a church in honor of Saint Stephen, the protomartyr; and, beside the walls, the monastery of Blessed Benignus, with all their possessions intact; and, in the district of Tonnerre [the Tonnerrois, Col. 0988B], the monastery of Melun, and in the same district the fortress of Tonnerre, that is, the head of the county; and the small monastery of Saint Symphorianus at Ladiniacum, with its churches and other properties belonging to it; and, within the walls of the aforesaid Langres, the abbey of Saint Peter; and beside the same city, the monastery of the holy Twins; and, in the county of Port, together with all that belonged to it, the church of Saint Gengulf, martyr of Christ, which once had been taken away by the tyrannical and sacrilegious temerity, and unlawful presumption, of certain princes, without regard for Almighty God, but by the same decree had been restored and confirmed in that place; and, in the district of the Atoarii, the monastery of Bèze, which they had always held under the fullest protection and safeguard of immunity.
