Nevertheless, for the security of the matter, the aforesaid Bishop Betto asked that we confirm by our authority the charters of those kings, for the love of God and in reverence for Saint Mamma the martyr. We willingly consented to his petition, and decided that this charter of our authority concerning that place should be issued for love of Almighty God and of Saint James the Apostle and brother of the Lord, whose arm is buried in the church of Saint Mamma. By it we order and command that none of our faithful, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, dare at any time enter the churches, places, fields, or other possessions—whether those lawfully held by the rulers of that church before the aforesaid occupation by the Saracens under the aforementioned charter documents, and afterward confirmed to the church by the authority of our royal predecessors—in order to demand any payments or unlawful pretexts [Col. 0988D], nor presume in any way to exact the things mentioned above, in our time or in that of our successors.

Rather, let the aforesaid bishop and his successors be permitted to possess peacefully, under the protection of our immunity, the properties of the aforesaid church together with its dependent cells, and to serve us faithfully, and, together with the clergy and people subject to him, to implore God’s mercy for our stability and for that of the whole empire granted to us by God and to be preserved by Him. Whatever our fiscus ought consequently to exact, we grant in full to the aforesaid church, so that it may increase there for all time. And, so that this [Col. 0989A] authority may be held more firmly in God’s name and be more carefully preserved by the faithful of the holy Church and by our own people, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Helisachar examined and subscribed.

## IX. For Hildegrin, Bishop of Halberstadt (814)

[In Leibniz, *Scriptores Rerum Brunsvicensium*, vol. II, p. 111.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor Augustus by the divinely ordained providence of God.

If we bring to effect the petitions of priests and servants of God that have come to our attention concerning necessities [Col. 0989B], we not only exercise the imperial custom, but also believe that such acts of ours will contribute to the reward of blessed recompense. Therefore let it be known to the knowledge of all our faithful, present and future, that Hildegrin Catholanensis, venerable bishop of the church of Halberstadt, which is built in honor of Christ and his protomartyr Stephen beside the river Holtemme in the district of Hartingowe, whose parish was established and defined by our most pious father, the emperor Augustus Charles, as comprising these districts: Darlingowe, Northüringowe, Belinesheim, Hartingowe, Svavia, and Hassingowe, came to us and brought the immunities of our holy father, ever to be piously remembered [Col. 0989C], in which it was contained how he had held that see under the fullest protection and safeguard of immunity.

For the sake of security, the aforesaid bishop asked us to grant and confirm similar provisions anew for the increase of our reward. Out of divine love we consented to his petition, and in all matters that he requested justly and reasonably we have endeavored to confirm them by this authority of ours. Therefore we order and command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, nor any of our faithful of the holy Church of God, presume at any time to enter the church, places, fields, or other possessions that they are now seen to possess justly and reasonably in whatever districts and territories, or anything that may henceforth be granted to them for divine love [Col. 0989D], in order to hear cases, exact fines [*freda*], make lodgings or requisitions, take hostages, unjustly distrain the men of that church, whether free or enslaved, or demand any payments or unlawful pretexts, or to exact outright the things mentioned above.

Moreover, we order all the inhabitants of the aforesaid districts to pay their tithes faithfully to the aforesaid church for divine love; and we grant that these tithes may at all times serve as an increase for the nourishment of the poor and the stipends of the servants of God serving God there. Thus may those servants of God who are seen to serve God there continually take pleasure in imploring the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife and offspring, and for the stability of our entire empire, granted to us by God [Col. 0990A] and to be preserved by Him. No one of our faithful, moreover, may presume to take away or prohibit anything from that parish of his, situated here and there through various districts; rather, by this authority of ours, it shall be permitted him, with the Lord’s help, to exercise the word of preaching and to carry out his ministry fully. And, so that this authority may remain unshaken in our time and in that of our successors, under the Lord’s protection, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of September, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 814, indiction 8, year 1 of our empire. Done at the palace of Aachen, happily in God’s name. Amen.

## X. For Hildebold, Bishop of Mâcon (814) [Col. 0990B]

[In D. Bouquet, *Recueil des historiens*, vol. VI, p. 462; in the instruments to vol. IV of *Gallia Christiana*, col. 264.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor Augustus by the divinely ordained providence of God.

If, from the gift of our generosity, we confer something upon places dedicated to God from the benefits bestowed upon us by God, we clearly believe that this will benefit us both in passing happily through mortal life and in attaining eternal life forever. Therefore let it be known to the knowledge of all our faithful, present and future [Col. 0990C], that, for the increase of our reward and the benefit of our soul, we have decided to give to the church of Saint Vincent of Mâcon, where Bishop Hildebold presides, certain properties of our ownership situated in the district of Lyon, in a village called Rosarias. Formerly a certain religious woman of God, Anstrudis, had transferred them by a deed of gift to the lord and my father, Charles, of good memory, the most excellent emperor.

These properties, with everything belonging or pertaining to them, including two dependents, namely Elmengarius and Adgarius, together with the demesne house, estate, woods [*silvis*], meadows, roads, exits, and all appurtenances, and as much as that religious woman was seen to possess in that village, and which at the present time is part of our right and possession in the same village of Rosarias, we have granted in full [Col. 0990D], without reservation, to the aforesaid church of Saint Vincent the martyr and to the congregation serving God there, as our alms.

Therefore we wish and command that, by this authority of ours, both now and in future, the aforesaid church shall hold in our alms the aforesaid properties, with the dependents named above and all things belonging to them, and that they shall remain perpetually under the jurisdiction of that church. The condition is that whatever the rulers of that church or the congregation of that holy place may from this day and time wish to do with these properties for their usefulness and advancement, they shall enjoy complete freedom to do so in every respect. And, so that this [Col. 0991A] authority may possess fuller firmness in God’s name and retain an inviolable and unshaken effect through long ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Helisachar examined.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of September, in the first year of our empire, indiction 7. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, in God’s name.

## XI. For Wirundus, Abbot of Stavelot and Malmedy (814)

[In Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, p. 21.]

In the name of God and our Savior Jesus Christ [Col. 0991B], Louis, emperor Augustus by the divinely ordained providence of God.

Let it be known to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, centenarii, toll-collectors, officials, our traveling envoys, those administering public affairs, and all other faithful of the holy Church of God and our own people, present and future, that the venerable Wirundus, abbot, and the whole congregation of the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy, situated in the Ardennes forest and built in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and also Saint Martin, where Saint Remaclus rests bodily, asked our serenity to grant them exemption from tolls for their ships traveling on the Rhine and Meuse rivers to meet their needs, and likewise for carts and pack animals carrying their necessities.

For the love of God and in veneration of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and Saint Martin the confessor, we were pleased to grant their petitions and to issue this charter of our magnificence concerning them for the sake of security. By it we order and command that none of our faithful, nor any collector exercising judicial authority, presume to receive or demand at any place any toll from the carts or pack animals of that congregation, whatever the commerce from which the fiscus might be able to exact a toll.

As for the ships that travel on the aforesaid rivers for the usefulness and needs of that congregation, wherever they may gain access to cities, ports, or other places [Col. 0991D], no one may dare to receive or demand from them, or from the men responsible for them, any toll, riverbank toll, landing toll, bridge toll, greeting toll, meal toll, pasturage charge, passage toll, any other levy, any census, or any payment whatsoever. Rather, by this authority of ours, let them be permitted, without anyone’s unlawful opposition or detention, to travel freely and safely throughout our entire empire and return, together with the ships and the men responsible for them and with the goods they carry. If they remain for any time in any place, or buy or sell anything, nothing at all shall be demanded from them, as has been said.

And, so that this authority may be held more firmly and be more carefully preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own people [Col. 0992A], we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Given on the Kalends of October, in the first year, with Christ favorable, of the empire of the lord Louis Augustus, indiction 8.

Done at the palace of Clichy, happily in God’s name. Amen.

## XII. For the Monastery of Caunes (814)

[In D. Bouquet, *Recueil des historiens*, vol. VI, p. 463, from the proofs of the new *History of Occitania*, vol. I, p. 41.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ [Col. 0992B], Louis, emperor Augustus by the divinely ordained providence of God.

If, from the gift of our generosity, we confer some benefit upon places dedicated to God, relieve ecclesiastical necessities through the petitions of the servants of God with our assistance, and protect them with imperial defense, we clearly believe that this will benefit us in passing through mortal life temporarily and in attaining eternal life happily. Therefore let the knowledge and advantage of all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, know that the venerable Attala, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary, situated on the river Orbieu at the boundary of the districts of Narbonne and Carcassonne, presented to us the charters of immunity of our lord and father, Charles, of good memory [Col. 0992C], the most pious Augustus. In them it was inserted how that same father of ours had caused the monastery, together with its dependent cells, to remain always under the fullest protection and safeguard of immunity, for the love of God and the tranquility of the brothers residing in those places.

One of these cells is called Flexus; it is built in honor of Saint Cucufas in the territory of Carcassonne, on the river called the Atax, with all its appendages and appurtenances. The second is called Caput Spina; it is dedicated in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, in the territory of Narbonne, beside the stream called the Clamesitis, with all its appendages and appurtenances. The third is called Palma; it is situated in the same territory of Narbonne on the seashore, with everything belonging to it, together with the congregations serving God there [Col. 0992D].

For the security of the matter, however, the aforesaid abbot and his entire congregation asked us, following our father’s custom, to decide that such a charter of our immunity should be issued concerning the monastery and its dependent cells, for the love of God and in reverence for divine worship. We willingly consented to their petition and decided that this charter of our authority, granting immunity and protection, should be issued for the sake of security and the benefit of our soul. By it we order and command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, nor any of our faithful, present or future, presume in our time or that of our successors to enter the cells, churches, places, fields, or other possessions that they now possess in whatever districts and territories within the jurisdiction of our empire [Col. 0993A], or anything granted there for divine love, or anything that divine piety may thereafter wish to increase in the possession of that holy place, whether through us or through others, in order to hear cases, exact fines, make lodgings or requisitions, take hostages, distrain the men of that church, both free and enslaved, living on its land, or demand any payments or unlawful pretexts; nor may anyone presume to exact outright the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors be permitted to possess peacefully, under the protection of our safeguard and immunity, the properties of that monastery, together with its dependent cells and the properties and people belonging or pertaining to them, free from all disturbance by judicial authority. Whatever the right of the fiscus could exact from the aforesaid properties of the monastery, we have granted in full to that monastery as our alms, so that it may perpetually serve as an increase and supplement for carrying out the service of God.

And whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this life, so long as the monks can find among themselves men capable of governing that congregation according to the rule of Saint Benedict, they shall, by this authority and consent of ours, have permission to choose abbots [Col. 0993C]. Thus may those servants of God who are seen to serve God there continually take pleasure in imploring the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife and offspring, and for the stability of the entire empire granted to us by God and to be preserved through his most merciful compassion forever.

Therefore, so that this authority may possess fuller force in God’s name and be more carefully preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own people, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the first year, with Christ favorable, of the empire of the lord Louis, most serene emperor, indiction 8. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily in God’s name. Amen.

## XIII. For the Same Monastery of Caunes [Col. 0993D] (814)

[In D. Bouquet, *ibid.*, as above.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor Augustus by the divinely ordained providence of God.

Let it be known to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, centenarii, traveling envoys, all administrators of public affairs, and all other faithful of the holy Church of God and our own people, that the venerable Attala, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary, came to us and begged our highness to grant to that monastery and to the congregation living there in God’s service exemption from tolls on the carts and pack animals carrying the necessities of the monastery or of the congregation serving God there, and on their ships traveling by sea or river, and on everything from which the fiscus could exact a toll; and he asked that we give or confirm our authority to the same monastery.

For the love of God and in veneration of that holy place, we were pleased to grant his prayers and to issue this charter of our munificence concerning that congregation for the sake of security. By it we order and command that no one of our faithful, nor any collector exercising judicial authority, presume to receive or exact any toll from the carts, pack animals, or ships, or from any commerce whatsoever, from which the fiscus might be able to exact a toll [Col. 0994A].

Wherever their ships or any of their merchandise may gain access to any villages or places, no one may exact from their men any passage charge, census, or payment. Rather, by this authority of ours, let it be permitted them, without anyone’s unlawful opposition or detention, to travel freely and safely throughout our entire empire and return, together with the men responsible for their affairs and the goods they carry. If they remain for any time in any place, or buy or sell anything, nothing at all shall be demanded or exacted from them, as has been said.

To make this authority of ours more carefully believed and preserved, we ordered it to be sealed with our ring.

I, Durandus the deacon, acting in place of Helisachar, examined it.

Given . . . in the first year, with Christ favorable, of the empire of the lord Louis [Col. 0994C], most serene Augustus, indiction 8. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily in God’s name. Amen.

## XIV. For Christian, Bishop of Nîmes (814)

[In Baluze, *Miscellanea*, book IV, p. 420.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor Augustus by the divinely ordained providence of God.

When, for the love of divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of priests, we do not doubt that we are fortified by heavenly grace. Therefore let the usefulness of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable Christian, bishop of the city of Nîmes, presented to us the immunity of our lord and father Charles, of good memory, the most pious Augustus [Col. 0994D]. In it was inserted how that same father of ours and his royal predecessors had always held under the fullest protection and safeguard of immunity the aforesaid see, built in honor of holy Mary, ever-virgin, and also of Saint Baudelius, together with two cells: one called Tornagus, built in honor of Saint Stephen the protomartyr; and the other called Vallis Flaviana, built in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles; together with the other cells belonging to it there.

For the security of the matter, however, the aforesaid Bishop Christian asked us to confirm by our authority the charters of those kings, for the love of God and in reverence for that holy place. We willingly consented to his petition, granted everything accordingly, and confirm it by this charter of our authority.

Therefore we order and command that none of our faithful, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, dare in our time or that of our successors enter the churches, places, fields, or other possessions—whether those which the aforesaid see or its cells now justly and lawfully possess in whatever districts and territories within the jurisdiction of the empire, or those that good men may henceforth grant to the same churches—in order to hear cases, exact fines or taxes, make lodgings or requisitions, take hostages, unjustly distrain the men of that church, both free and enslaved, living on its land, or demand any payments or unlawful pretexts; nor may they presume to exact outright the things mentioned above [Col. 0995B].

Rather, let the aforesaid bishop and his successors be permitted to possess peacefully, under the protection of immunity, the properties of the aforesaid churches together with all their dependencies, and to serve us faithfully, and, together with the clergy and people subject to him, freely to implore the Lord’s mercy for our stability and for that of the entire empire granted to us by God and to be preserved by Him. Whatever our fiscus could consequently expect, we grant in full, so that it may serve for the increase of those serving God there perpetually. And, so that this authority may remain unshaken in our time and in that of our successors, under the Lord’s protection, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, in the first year, with Christ favorable, of the empire of the lord Louis, most serene Augustus, indiction 8. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily in God’s name. Amen.

## XV. Concerning the Fair of Saint Dionysius (814)

[In D. Bouquet, *ibid.*, p. 466, from Dublet, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*, p. 733.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor [Col. 0995D] Augustus by the divinely ordained providence of God.

It is fitting for imperial highness not only to preserve inviolate the pious acts of its predecessors, but also eagerly to confirm them by the authority of its judgment, so that a gift bestowed or confirmed by the authority of so many princes for the love of God may be held more firmly and possessed more securely by those to whom it was assigned.

Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own people, present and future, that the venerable Hildoinus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Dionysius, built in the territory of Paris, where that holy Dionysius and his companions rest bodily, brought before us a charter of authority of our lord and father Charles, of good memory, the most pious Augustus [Col. 0996A]. In it was inserted that he himself and our grandfather Pippin, formerly king, as well as their predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, by charters of their authority had granted to the aforesaid monastery and to the congregation serving God there all tolls from the market held annually on the feast of that same Saint Dionysius in the aforesaid territory of Paris, from all merchants who gathered there for trade from every direction, both from the Saxon nation and from the Frisian nation and from all other nations that came from different provinces and territories to that market for the purpose of trading.

They had likewise granted the tolls from all carts, ships, and other vehicles by which wine, honey, and various other commodities were brought there for trade [Col. 0996B], and also from all other merchandise traded at that time not only in the same market and within the same city of Paris, but also through the villages, fields, and other places situated around that market, and from everything whatsoever from which the right of the fiscus could receive a toll.

It was also contained in the same authority that certain men, with rash presumption, had taken that market away from the power of the monastery of Saint Dionysius, and that the rulers of the aforesaid monastery had lawfully vindicated it in full before Grimoald, Mayor of the Palace. It was further stated that Soanachildis and Gerfredus, formerly count of that city, driven by greed, had imposed an additional four denarii on every merchant—free and enslaved—who came there to trade, in addition to the other toll that they paid; and that many, burdened by this charge, withdrew from the same market.

Only a very small toll from that market was then exacted for the monastery of Saint Dionysius on this account [Col. 0996C]. The aforesaid father of ours, by the authority of his judgment, had cut off or abolished this superimposed charge, and, according to his authority and confirmation, the monastery of Saint Dionysius had thereafter held or received the toll in full.

For the security of the matter, however, the aforesaid abbot, together with the congregation entrusted to his governance, asked us, following our father’s custom, to issue our authority concerning this matter for that holy place. Out of love for God and in veneration of Saint Dionysius, our patron [Col. 0996D], we were pleased to listen graciously to their petitions.

Therefore we order and command that, just as that toll was granted or confirmed by the other kings of the Franks and by our grandfather Pippin, and was vindicated before Grimoald, Mayor of the Palace, for the benefit of that monastery, and afterward was more firmly granted to the same monastery by the aforesaid lord and father of ours, the emperor Charles, after abolishing the additional practices imposed by evil men, so from now on, in our time and that of our successors, it shall remain inviolably granted by this authority of ours.

The condition is that the rulers or congregation of the aforesaid monastery may claim for their own use, without anyone’s disturbance or unlawful opposition, all the toll from the same market, held each year on the feast of Saint Dionysius in the aforesaid district of Paris, both from the merchants of the Saxon and Frisian nations and from other nations that come there at that time from different provinces and territories for the purpose of trading, and also from the carts, ships, and other vehicles by which wine, honey, and many other commodities are brought there for trade [Col. 0997A].

This includes all other merchandise traded either in the same market, or within the city of Paris, or in any other villages, places, and fields surrounding that market, by merchants who come there at that time. From everything, that is, from which the fiscus can exact a toll, we grant the entire toll, by this authority of ours, to the aforesaid monastery, as has been said, so that it may perpetually accrue as our alms for the uses of the congregation serving God there and for maintaining the lamps of that church.

We also order and command that no one of our faithful, nor any collector exercising judicial authority, presume from this day and time to create or cause any opposition or disturbance concerning that toll against the rulers of the monastery or its congregation. Nor may anyone dare to impose upon the merchants coming there either the charge added by Soanachildis and Count Gerfredus and abolished by our lord and father, or any other charge.

Rather, once every obstacle of disturbance and the presumption of rash men has been removed, the monastery [Col. 0997C] shall, by this authority of ours, receive the aforesaid toll in full as our alms, both in our time and in that of our successors.

Therefore, so that this authority may be held more firmly in God’s name through many years, and be more readily believed and more carefully preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own people, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of the lord Louis, most serene emperor.

Helisachar examined.

Given on the Kalends of December, in the first year, with Christ favorable, of the empire of the lord Louis, most serene Augustus, indiction 7. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily in God’s name. Amen.

[Col. 0997D]

## XVI. Concerning the Fair of the Monastery of Dionysius (814)

[In the same authors, in the same place.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor Augustus by the divinely ordained providence of God, to Bego, illustrious count, and to all your successors, present and future, and to the administrators of public affairs, or collectors receiving tolls within the district of Paris, and to all those who appear to hold offices within the same district.

We believe that it is known to you, and we make known, how all toll from whatever merchandise, from the eve of the distinguished solemnity of blessed Dionysius until the end of his market, must be rendered and belong to the church of Saint Dionysius, according to the authority and charters of our grandfather Pippin, formerly king, and of our lord and father Charles, emperor of pious memory, and likewise by our confirmation. This applies to port toll (*portaticum*), bridge toll (*pontaticum*), riverbank toll (*ripaticum*), wheel toll (*rotaticum*), rudder toll (*timonaticum*), rolling toll (*volutaticum*), turf toll (*cispitaticum*), dust toll (*pulveraticum*), *fortaticum* [technical toll, uncertain], acclamation toll (*laudaticum*), and greeting toll (*salutaticum*), as well as to all other merchandise from which a public law permits or requires a toll to be exacted.

Therefore, having now learned that certain officials of ours appear, with rash presumption, to oppose those royal authorities in the most flagrant resistance, whether in rendering or exacting the same toll [Col. 0998B], we have again ordered this charter of our authority to be made for the aforesaid holy place and its rulers. By it we expressly command you and all your successors, by our express command, that none of you or your successors ever presume to violate the aforesaid law and decree of royal authority, as you care for the grace of God and of us, etc.

And so that this administrative directive may be more truly believed in our time and in that of our successors, and obeyed more devotedly by you and your successors, we ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

I, Helisachar, examined it.

## XVII. For the Greater Monastery [Col. 0998C] (814)

[In D. Bouquet, *ibid.*, p. 468, from the cartulary of the same monastery.]

Louis, emperor Augustus by the providence ordained by God.

If, for the love of God, we bestow suitable gifts upon places dedicated to divine worship and upon those serving God in them, we do not doubt that the reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us by God. Therefore let the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both present and future, know that the venerable man Hieremias, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin the Greater, which was built near the city of Tours on the bank of the Loire, presented to our sight the charter of immunity of our lord and father, the good-memory, most devout Augustus Charles. It contained a statement of how that same father of ours had always caused the monastery to remain under the fullest protection and defense of immunity, for the love of God and the tranquility of the brothers residing there.

But for the firmness of the matter, the aforesaid abbot petitioned us that, following our father’s custom, we should judge it proper to issue such a command of our immunity for the love of God and reverence for divine worship toward that monastery. We willingly granted his petition and decreed that this command of our authority be issued, for the sake of immunity and protection, the security of the institution, and the benefit of our soul. By it we command and order that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, nor any of our faithful, present or future, dare enter, in our time or in times to come, into the churches, places, lands, or other possessions that it presently owns in any counties or territories under our rule, or into anything that has been bestowed there for the supreme love of God, or that divine piety may thereafter wish to increase in the ownership of that holy place through God-fearing men residing there, in order to hear cases, exact fines, provide lodgings or provisions, take sureties, or distrain the men of that monastery, whether free or servile, living upon its land; nor may anyone seek any exactions or unlawful pretexts. No one may presume to exact any of the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors be permitted to possess the property of that monastery, together with the things and persons belonging or attached to it, under the protection and defense of our immunity, in peace and free from all interference by judicial authority. Whatever the right of the fisc could exact from the aforesaid properties of the monastery, we have granted in full to that monastery as our alms, so that it may perpetually serve as an increase and supplement for the performance of God’s service, and so that those servants of God who appear to serve God there may continually beseech God’s immeasurable mercy on behalf of us, our wife and children, and the stability of the whole empire granted to us by God and to be preserved through his most merciful compassion.

Therefore, so that this charter may possess fuller force in the name of God and be more diligently preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own faithful, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.**

I, Helisachar, have recognized it.

Given on the third day before the Nones of December, in the first year, Christ being favorable, in the eighth indiction. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XVIII. For Nefridius, archbishop of Narbonne. (Year 814)

[In D. Bouquet, same work, p. 169, from the *Histoire générale du Languedoc*, new proof, vol. I, p. 44.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

When, for the love of divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of priests, we do not doubt that we are fortified by heavenly grace. Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own, present and future, that the venerable man Nefridius, archbishop of the city of Narbonne, approaching our presence, appealed to the gentleness of our majesty, asking that we cause the mother church of that city, which is dedicated to Saints Justus and Pastor and to Saint Mary ever-virgin, together with the monastery of Saint Paul the Confessor, where that saint rests bodily, built not far from the same city, with all that presently belongs to it, to remain under our protection and the guardianship of our immunity.

For the love of God and reverence for those same saints, we were pleased to lend an ear to his prayers and to issue this command of our authority and immunity concerning that church. By it we decree and order that no one exercising judicial authority, nor any of our faithful, dare enter, in our time or in times to come, into the churches, places, lands, or other possessions that it presently owns, or into anything that divine mercy may thereafter wish to increase in the ownership and power of that church, in order to hear cases, exact fines and taxes, provide lodgings or provisions, take sureties, distrain the men of that church, whether free or servile, or seek any exactions or unlawful pretexts; nor may anyone presume to exact any of the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid bishop and his successors reside peacefully under our protection and obey our imperial authority. Whatever the right of the fisc could exact from that property, we grant entirely to the same church for eternal recompense, so that it may contribute perpetually to the increase of the clerics serving God there. Thus may the rectors of that church, with everything belonging to them, together with the clergy and people subject to them, gladly beseech the Lord’s mercy on behalf of us, our wife and children, and the stability of the whole empire immeasurably granted to us by God.

And so that this authority of our command may be more truly believed and more diligently preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most devout Augustus.**

Durandus the deacon, acting in place of Helisachar, recognized it.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the first year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of our lord Louis, most devout Augustus, in the eighth indiction. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XIX. [Note: This diploma has not yet been published anywhere; Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. II, p. 392, merely notes that it was incorrectly reported by the Chronicle of Novientum.] For the monastery of Ebersheim. (Year 814)

[In Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, vol. II, p. 156, from the forged original charter of the abbey of Aprimonasterium.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Louis, by the grace of almighty God king of the Franks and Lombards, and Augustus, emperor of the Romans.

Since, according to the testimony of the Prophet, we know that a king’s joy proceeds from the strength of God, we believe that we increase the joy and honors of our kingdom if we strive to establish or confirm the holy and venerable monasteries of God’s servants according to their petition, especially since they themselves frequently beseech God for our peace and stability.

Therefore we make known to the ears of all the faithful, especially of our princes, that the venerable Sambatius, abbot of the monastery called Novientum or Ebersheim, which the illustrious duke Etich and his wife Bersvinda built in the name of Christ and in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of the holy martyr Maurice and his companions, in the Alsatian county, on the bank of the river Ill, in the diocese of Strasbourg, upon their own property, approached our serenity with his brothers. He asked that we confirm the monastery—which the aforesaid duke and his venerable daughter Odilia had wholly transferred into the right and lordship of the kingdom—fortified by certain indications of royal authority.

We therefore, providing both for our own salvation and for the interests of the brothers serving God there under regular discipline, and at the same time for the remedy of the soul of our most Christian father Charles and of our most serene mother, the empress Augusta Hildegard, kindly received his petition and decreed that it be beneficially fulfilled.

We therefore will that the place of the aforesaid Novientum, or monastery of Ebersheim, and the whole boundary of its foundation be free under immunity; and from this time forward we wholly remit to it every right of our fisc, on the condition that no public judge, whether spiritual or secular—bishop, duke, count, advocate, or any judicial authority—presume to enter without the abbot’s consent, exact a fine, provide lodgings or provisions there, constrain any person there unless requested by the abbot, or hear cases.

Rather, the present abbot Sambatius and his successors shall possess that place with all its dependencies—roads and trackless places, exits and entrances, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, pastures, woods, forests, waters and watercourses, mills, fisheries, hunting rights, buildings, serfs of either sex, and utilities of whatever name—in full authority.

Whatever legal dispute, whether forensic or civil, may arise within that place or outside it, in the villages belonging to it, shall belong for judgment solely to the abbot or to the stewards appointed by him.

As for thefts, robberies, or *frevelae* committed outside the monastery precincts, one third shall belong to the church’s advocate appointed by us.

[Note: A *causidicus* is called a *Vogt* in the German records of the abbey of Ebersheim.]

The assessment shall be as follows: if anyone from the church’s household or from outside is accused of such an offense and, brought before the abbot or his advocate, is convicted, he shall pay six *firdones* of public weight, or thirty *sicli* of Strasbourg coinage.

[Note: A *firdo* was a fourth part of a mark, according to Cange, *Glossary*, vol. III, p. 401. Today we call *sicli* schillings, thirty of which make three florins. Thus a *firdo* of public weight is a French pound (*franc*), one fourth of the Strasbourg pound. See Schilter, *Teutonic Glossary*, p. 300.]

[Note: The *siclus* was a coin formerly well known among the Hebrews and the ancient English. Ducange, vol. VI, pp. 479–480. Hickes writes, in the preface to his Anglo-Saxon grammar, p. 21, that among the Anglo-Saxons a *siclus* was worth two silver denarii.]

If the offense occurred outside that place or its boundary, he shall pay one *firdo*, or three ounces of Strasbourg coinage. If he refuses to do this, he shall pay the judicial penalty.

At the abbot’s request, and with the brothers’ consent, we have also granted, from the church’s allodial lands, a benefice to Lord Wolfhald, the advocate, and to all his successors without opposition, so that he may devote himself more diligently and carefully to the utility and defense of the church and of the entire household. Further, so that the abbot or his brothers may not thereafter be burdened anywhere by his entry or approach, we grant: at Sulza one mansus; at Egesheim a lordly estate with *salic* land; at Lagelnheim one mansus; at Burgheim one; at Sigolsheim one; at Rechenhusen a lordly estate with *salic* land, namely vineyards, fields, and the chapel of that place; at Grusenheim one mansus; at Weisweiler one mansus; at Stotzenheim two; at Huttenheim one; and at Northausen two.

[Note: *Frevelae* were a type of fine for certain offenses or acts of insolence. The word is still known in German in Alsace. See Haltaus’s *German Glossary*, pp. 487–488.]

[Note: The town of Sulz, or Ober-Sulz.]

[Note: Egisheim.]

[Note: Free and exempt from every burden, as Schilter explains in his *Teutonic Glossary*, under the word *Freygut*.]

[Note: Lagelnheim.]

[Note: Burgheim.]

[Note: Sigolsheim.]

[Note: A place formerly situated between Ostheim and Hunawihr, now destroyed.]

[Note: Weisweiler.]

[Note: Stotzenheim.]

[Note: Huttenheim.]

[Note: Northausen.]

We have also judged that the following must by no means be omitted; indeed, we strictly forbid that either the present abbot, any of his successors, or any administrator of the monastery presume to transfer anywhere by right of ownership, or grant to anyone by right of inheritance, anything from the church’s estate within the fixed boundary—that is, from the forest called Standenbruch, or Breitenlacha, all the way to the place called Querchlacha, and onward to the middle channel of the river Ill; and in width, from the spring-stream to the middle channel of the Ill, at the place called Staffelgruba.

[Note: The Chronicle of Novientum tells fabulous stories about this forest. A district called Stanenbruh, or Standenbruch, is also mentioned in a parchment book of the rights of the abbey of Ebersheim, written in German in 1320, fol. 56.]

But if the utility of the monastery requires it, only servile fiefs may be granted to the church’s serfs.

[Note: A servile fief denotes what the Alsatians today call a *Hofflehn*: a fixed number of fields is left to a peasant and his heirs to cultivate and is attached to his dwelling, called a *Hoff*.]

[Note: The sole difference is that in a servile fief the peasants were serfs.]

If anyone from the church’s household dies, whether inside or outside, the best thing he possessed among his livestock or any other property shall be taken to the nearest lordly estate; and his younger son, if he belongs to the church’s household, shall be enfeoffed together with his mother. If not, he shall be in the abbot’s power.

[Note: Although this charter is spurious, it nevertheless recounts many matters useful for the feudal law of the Middle Ages, specifically of the century in which the forger of this diploma lived.]

It must also be known that if the present abbot or any of his successors, by God’s command, departs from this life, the brothers, assembling according to the rule of Saint Benedict, shall elect another from among themselves. The elected man shall be presented to us and invested by us, and shall be sent to the bishop of Strasbourg to be ordained.

Therefore we establish and decree by the authority of royal power that any judge, or any person of whatever rank, powerful or weak, who attempts to violate or infringe the authority or confirmation of this charter, or violently seize or remove any possessions of the aforesaid monastery, shall pay forty pounds of gold into our fisc.

And so that this may be more truly believed and henceforth preserved firm and unshaken, we subscribe it with our own hand and order it sealed or marked with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Lord Louis, unconquered Augustus, emperor of the Romans.**

I, Charles, archbishop of Mainz, have subscribed.

[Note: In the year 814 Atulf occupied the church of Mainz, not Charles, who was promoted to that see only in 856; he was the son of King Pippin of Aquitaine.]

I, Witghernus, bishop of Strasbourg, have subscribed.

[Note: Witghernus, bishop of Strasbourg, had already met his final fate at that time, having died in 729.]

I, Turbo, archchaplain, acting in place of Lord Ibbo, *protospatharius*, have recognized it.

[Note: Turbo is unknown among all the notaries of Louis the Pious, who at that time had not yet adopted the title archchaplain.]

[Note: Bouquet indeed counts Ibbo among the notaries of the emperor Louis under the chancellor Helisachar, in *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. VI, p. 451, but never among the chancellors of that prince, especially not under the title *protospatharius*. Among the Greeks in the Constantinopolitan Empire, a *protospatharius* was a person of the highest distinction: he was first and chief among the *spatharii*, that is, those who served as guards of the emperor’s person. Ducange, *Glossary*, vol. V, p. 932, and vol. VI, p. 630, states that Photius held the office of *protospatharius* at the court of the Greek emperors before being appointed patriarch of Constantinople in 856; this is also attested by D. Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. IX, book L, p. 6.]

Done at Ingelenheim, in the royal estate, happily, in the name of Christ. Given on the third day before the Nones of November, in the eight hundred and fourteenth year of the Lord’s incarnation, in the fifth indiction, in the tenth year of the reign of our lord Louis, unconquered Augustus, emperor of the Romans.

[Note: This is how it is read in the spurious original, although the year 824 (*DCCCXXIIII*) appears to have been erased so that 814 (*DCCCXIIII*) could be inserted. Neither year agrees with the fifth indiction, which was 827, nor with the tenth year of the reign of Louis the Pious, which was 823.]

[Note: In the monogram he is called Louis the Pious, an epithet never used by Louis I. The seal bears an image of Louis with the inscription “Louis, emperor of the Romans.” The form and size of the seal are not Carolingian but considerably larger.]

## XX. For the monastery of Saint Anthimus of Siena. (Year 814)

[In Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. III, p. 530.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, [“grandson/descendant” — the printed text reads *Procis*] of the emperor Charlemagne, by divinely ordained clemency, emperor Augustus.

When, for the love of divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants, we do not doubt that we are fortified by heavenly grace. Therefore let the greatness of all our faithful know that, at the petition of the venerable man Apollinaris, abbot of the monastery of Saint Anthimus, we have granted to that monastery the village called Cilcario, belonging to the territory of the city of Siena, with the boundaries and places to be named:

To the east, the river Axo; to the west, the river Ombrone; from the bridge to the ford called Ursi. To the south, from the ford of Ursi along the road that runs below Mount Lucinius to the road of Saint Anthimus. To the north, from Gessa through Ponigastaldi, then along the public road to the bridge over the Ombrone; together with the two oratories situated within that boundary, namely Saint Christina and the holy mother church, together with one estate near that holy church and everything belonging to that estate.

Also within the designated woodland, in the territory of Clusium, half of the fishery of the Amesa, with half of everything belonging to that fishery, which formerly belonged to the public authority of the city of Clusium, with the boundaries and places to be named:

To the east, the pool called Moreccia, where the church of Saint Pancratius stands. From there it proceeds across the field of Saint Peter, over the middle of the mountain above Cordoliarium; from there from Casseratas to Ampla. At Ampla it reaches the mountain called Marmianus of Marmiano. On the other side, toward the west, it proceeds along the summit of Mount Tili, descending as far as the mud; from the mud, through the valley Impia, to Laterbe. From Laterbe it reaches the sea. Then, along the seashore, it reaches the place where the pool flows into the sea. From that place it reaches the land of Saint Lawrence, together with the same *mortaria ex angularique* [reading uncertain], and with that pool and its boatmen, together with everything upon it and whatever belongs to that custody.

Within the defined places: cultivated and uncultivated land, with serfs and *aldiones*.

Therefore we ordered this charter of our command to be written in the same holy monastery, so that from this day onward Brother Apollinaris, the abbot, and his successors may freely enjoy the right to possess, hold, give, exchange, or do whatever they choose from these things at the feast of the aforesaid church.

Let none of our faithful, or anyone exercising judicial authority, presume at any time to trouble the aforesaid Abbot Apollinaris or his successors concerning the aforesaid boundaries, raise any claim against them, or remove or diminish anything that we have granted from our munificence to the aforesaid holy place for the remedy of our soul.

Rather, with God’s aid, may this grant, established there as our alms, prosper in future times as much as pleases those servants of God who appear to serve God there, so that they may continually and attentively beseech God’s mercy on behalf of us, our wife, and our children.

If anyone should presume in any way to violate this grant of ours—which we do not believe will happen—let him know that he must pay sixty solid gold pieces: half to our palace and half to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Anthimus.

And so that it may be held more genuine and secure and observed in due time, Christ being favorable, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it marked with the ring of our seal.

**Sign of Louis, most powerful emperor, who recognized it.**

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the first year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most devout Augustus, in the eighth indiction. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace. In the name of God. Amen.

## XXI. For the monastery of Saint Maximinus of Trier. (Year 814)

[In Hontheim, *Ecclesiastical History of Trier*.]

Louis, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans.

If we provide for the tranquility of monasteries, this will secure for us and for our kingdom enduring stability and will earn for us the spiritual reward of the blessed poor. Therefore let the unanimous body of our entire kingdom know that we have received the petition of our venerable familiar Helisachar and abbot of the monastery of the most holy confessor Maximinus, our protector: following the action of our pious father Charles, rightly called the Great, he asked that we strengthen the aforesaid monastery also with the privileges of our authority. We received this petition with gentleness and commanded it to be carried out with authority.

[Note: Helisachar was our familiar. Very many charters prove that he held the office of chief chancellor at Louis’s court. Here it is useful to read what Eckhart collected in *Rerum Francicarum*, book XXVIII, no. 147: “Thus far we have seen that various annals were either continued or committed to writing by royal notaries or chancellors. We suspected that part of the Moissac Chronicle had been composed by the notary Egilbert; now we conclude that, from the time when Egilbert ceased, the same Chronicle was continued down to this point by the imperial chancellor Elisachar. For it ends with events occurring at the end of 818 or the beginning of 819; and at the same time, namely after 819, Elizachar is no longer found in subscriptions to diplomas. I therefore think that in that year he became abbot of Saint Maximinus at Trier, or withdrew to his monastery of Saint Albin at Angers and took leave of the court. Miraeus, in his *Belgian Diplomas*, chapter 11, inserted a precept of Louis by which the protection of that emperor was obtained for this place by the distinguished man and Abbot Elisachar of the monastery of Saint Maximinus in the city called Trier; it was given in 821 and, although genuine, has been considerably corrupted by a copyist. Miraeus notes that Elisachar was also abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Jumièges and of Saint Richarius in Ponthieu, or Centula. Ardo, in the *Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane*, chapter 52, indicates that Helisachar was Saint Benedict’s most faithful friend, and the friend of the brothers of Inda. In recounting the death of Saint Benedict, which occurred in 821, he says: ‘Helisachar the abbot came to him first and remained with him until his death.’ Ardo had already said the same in chapter 3, where he asks the monks of Inda, after they have examined the *Life of Saint Benedict* which he composed, to share it with Abbot Elisachar. ‘For,’ he says, ‘when he was leaving this world, Abbot Helisachar clung to him with the affection of a singular love, as the letter sent to us by him, more precious than gold, testifies; after your examination, I judge that it should be presented to him in particular.’ The same Helisachar is praised by Amalarius in the preface to the *Antiphonary*, in book I of the *Chronicle of Centula*, in Agobard’s consultation concerning the baptism of Jewish slaves, and in the book *On Dispensation*. In 827 Louis sent him, with others, to suppress disturbances in the Spanish March, as the *Annals of Lorsch* testify. The year of his death is still unknown to me.” Add Heumann, *On Diplomatics*, p. 238. Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. II, book XXXI, no. 80, places his death about the year 837.]

We have decreed, and announce to all future rulers after us, that the aforesaid place shall remain under the dominion of us and of succeeding kings, just as it is known to have remained under the authority of kings in earlier times; that it shall never be subject to any other place or to the domination of any person.

We also grant the election of the abbot to the discretion of the monks, so that they may elect the man who is found, according to the rule, to be worthy by the merit of his life and wisdom.

[Note: This includes the election of the abbot and so forth. It is truly astonishing that this was granted at Helisachar’s request, since all the records of Saint Maximinus make it clear that Helisachar himself was not a monk but a secular cleric. What is written in these documents—that the election of the abbot was granted to the monks’ discretion, namely that of a man found worthy according to the rule by reason of life and wisdom—could therefore, if genuine, have had no other practical effect than to remain among the monastery’s privileges for possible future use.]

We also entrust the serfs, estates, and the entire substance of the monastery to the abbot’s authority, and grant him, solely for the brothers’ benefit, free permission under our authority to sell and exchange, lest the condition of holy religion fail.

[Note: *Conductum*: that is, utility or advantage.]

Thus, without want but in tranquility and peace, may they continually beseech the Lord for our salvation. And so that this authority may endure inviolate, we have confirmed it with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our seal.

[Note: The date, subscription, and seal of these documents—whose original prototype is otherwise preserved at Saint Maximinus—are missing; the year and the remaining material at the end of the diploma appear to have been rubbed away. Nevertheless, it seemed appropriate to report them under this year, in a reasonably suitable place, before Louis was proclaimed Augustus. Yet many features undermine the diploma’s authenticity, including the following: “king of the Lombards”; “our pious father, rightly called the Great”; “remain under the dominion of us and of succeeding kings, as it is known to have remained under the authority of kings in earlier times,” and so forth.]

[Col. 1007A]

## XXII. [Note: Observe how ecclesiastical men in former times, so that exchanges of estates—and especially of villages—made by them might be more secure in the future, took care to obtain imperial confirmation of them. I would also ask you not to pass over without notice those words in which Rodulf is called rector of the monastery built within the walls of the city of Brescia, in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, commonly called the New Monastery. In the city of Brescia there was, and still is, a very celebrated monastery of nuns, Saint Julia, built in honor of our Savior by King Desiderius and his wife Ansa. I too, being one who, after receiving permission from those holy and noble virgins, examined the archive of that convent, have published in this very work several documents excerpted from it.

The foundation of this monastery is reported by the illustrious Mabillon in the Benedictine Annals under the year of Christ 759. He then says: “The New Monastery was so called from a restoration, recorded as having been carried out in the year of the Lord 835. The Necrology of Reichenau (*Necrologium Augiense*) seems to be referring to it, where Austreberga is praised as being from the monastery called the New.” When I encountered this Rodulf, rector of the New Monastery of Brescia, I initially suspected that this monastery had been different from Saint Julia: the former perhaps cultivated by monks, the latter by holy virgins. This suspicion was strengthened by a diploma of Emperor Louis II, issued at the city of Brescia in 856, at the New Monastery, since the emperor seemed to have lived and issued the diploma not in a nunnery but in a monastery of monks.

The suspicion, however, was brought to an end after I examined a certain diploma published by Margarinus in volume II of the Cassinese Bullary. From it it is clear that the name “New” was in ancient times almost always joined to the monastery of Saint Julia. Therefore this Rodulf, rector of the New Monastery, should be regarded merely as the steward and administrator of the convent of Saint Julia.

Let us return to the words of the diploma: “A village called Reduddum, also known by the name Curticella, in the district of Persiceta.” That same village still retains among us the name Reddu; it is adorned with a parish church and is subject to the territory of the town of Nonantola, under the most serene duke of Modena.

The extent of the region or district of Persiceta was also indicated to us by Leo of Marsica in book I, chapter 54 of the Cassinese Chronicle, where, writing about Abbot John, he says: “He made a lease for Adelbert, son of Rainerius of Rastello—this same village is now called Rastellino, and it too was formerly situated in the district of Persiceta—of several estates of this monastery in the county of Modena, on land called Persiceta.”

Peter the Deacon likewise, in book IV, chapter 18 of the same Chronicle, states that the following belonged to the Cassinese monastery: “The Monastery of Saint Benedict, in the territory of Modena, within the boundaries of the river Fusculus and the district of Malmeniliacum.” In former times *curtes* signified not only extensive estates but also an entire village. I have often pointed this out and elsewhere confirmed it from ancient documents.

All these places in the same territory of Persiceta belonged to the county of Modena. Anyone can understand how far that region extended by recalling the town now called San Giovanni, subject to the Bolognese territory, which, because it was built within the boundaries of Persiceta, still retains the name San Giovanni in Persiceto.

In a diploma of Emperor Frederick II, published by Ughelli in volume II of *Italia Sacra*, in the section on the archbishops of Bologna, the castle of San Giovanni in Persiceto is confirmed to Henry, bishop of Bologna. In the old edition of the histories of Matteo Villani, book I, chapter 68 and following, San Giovanni in Cesena is mentioned. In the most recent edition of the same work, volume XIV of *Rerum Italicarum*, I noted that the Florentine manuscript has the reading San Giovanni in per Cesena. But the passage is corrupt in both places; it should be restored as San Giovanni in Persiceto.

There, then, were formerly the boundaries of the county of Modena. At least the little river Samodia, now called the Samozza, separated the Modenese territory from the Bolognese. Indeed, Bazzano—formerly Badianum—was left on the Modenese side, together with the entire district of Persiceta, comprising Nonantola, San Cesario, Zena Corte, Panzano, the castle of San Giovanni, and other villages and castles. The power of the Bolognese later gradually brought a considerable part of these under its control, diminishing not only the county but also the diocese of the Modenese, although the Modenese protested in vain.

I omit the fact that other documents indicate that our county once extended beyond Samodia into the higher regions. Thus, in establishing the former boundaries between Bologna and Modena—boundaries that are now so unequal—we see that a just measure was once observed.

When the Lombards first wrested Modena from the Greeks who ruled at Ravenna, they did not immediately subject the entire territory of that city to themselves. Rather, Liutprand—according to Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book VI, chapter 49—took from the Greeks the castles of Aemilia, Feronianum [read: Feronianum], and Mons Bellius, as well as Buxetum and Persiceta.

Feronianum is now called Fregnano or Frignano. It is a province of the Modenese duchy in the mountains, adjoining the Bolognese territory, and containing Sextula, the chief place of the district, Fanano, and many other castles and villages. The Ligurian Friniates mentioned by Livy should be sought there rather than where Cluverius thought. They seem either to have given their name to the region or to have received theirs from it.

Mons Bellius is now Monte Veglio, or Monte Vio. It formerly obeyed the Bolognese but was for some time also subject to the authority of the Modenese.

Regarding Buxetum, the distinguished Benedictine monk Gaspar Berettus writes in the chorographical dissertation prefixed to volume X of *Rerum Italicarum*, section 14: “The place must be sought in the territory of Modena or Bologna, according to Paul and Sigebert.” And rightly so: for it does not seem plausible that Buxetum, situated by the Po between Piacenza and Parma, is meant here. Why, I ask, would a place of such slight importance have escaped the power of the Lombards, when they had long before peacefully possessed the surrounding territory and cities? Among us, however, its name—as has happened with many others—disappeared several centuries ago.

In Anastasius’s *Life of Pope Gregory II* we read: “The castles of Aemilia, Feronianum, Montebelli, and Verablum with their towns, Buxo and Persiceta, and also the Pentapolis and the city of Auximana surrendered themselves to the Lombards.”

So much for the ancient boundaries of the county of Modena. Yet scarcely any city can be found that has retained the boundaries of its territory stable even in ancient times. And if it once did retain them, the appearance of the boundaries was later completely altered by the wars stirred up among the Italian cities and by the raging factions of Ghibellines and Guelfs. In ancient times some cities extended more widely the territory subject to themselves or to their counts, while others extended it less widely.

Casale Maggiore, Videliana, Pomponesco, Pangunedum, and Suzzara once belonged to the county of Brescia. This may seem strange to those who consider the distance of that city from those places and the present state of affairs; but it is not at all strange to anyone who recalls how great a transformation subsequently occurred in other regions.]

### CONFIRMATION OF THE EXCHANGE MADE BETWEEN PETER, ABBOT OF NONANTOLA, AND RODULF, RECTOR OF THE BRESCIAN MONASTERY OF SAINT SAVIOR  
*(Year 814.)*

*[From Muratori, Italian Antiquities, volume II, p. 201.]*

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, emperor Augustus.

If we confirm by our edicts those things that the faithful of our kingdom exchange or barter among themselves for their own advantage, we exercise the imperial custom and believe that the arrangement will thereafter remain established by the firmest legal right. Therefore let it be known to the knowledge of all our faithful, present and future, how the venerable Peter, abbot of the monastery of Nonantola, built in honor of the blessed apostles and Saint Sylvester the Confessor, came to our clemency and informed our serenity that he had exchanged certain properties with Rodulf, rector of the monastery built within the walls of the city of Brescia in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, commonly called the New Monastery.

Accordingly, the venerable Peter, the abbot mentioned above, gave from the property of his monastery to the aforesaid Rodulf, for the benefit of the said monastery, the villages called Castiglione, Calcinato, Silviniano, and Monticello, just as it pleased Rodulf to receive them for the advantage of the monastery.

In return, as compensation for this transaction, the said Rodulf gave to the aforesaid venerable Abbot Peter, for the benefit of his monastery and of the servants of God dwelling in that convent, a village called Reduddum, also known by the name Curticella, in the district of Persiceta, with all its integrity and entirety.

He therefore presented to our view the written instrument of exchange concerning the places mentioned above, so that it might be reread. But for complete security he asked our Highness to confirm that exchange anew, in our mercy, by a fuller precept of our gentleness. We did not wish to deny his request; rather, know that we have granted and confirmed it in every respect, just as we do for each of our faithful who makes a just and reasonable petition.

Therefore, after examining the exchange itself, as it is more fully set out in it, we order and command that whatever one party has justly and reasonably transferred to the other party, they shall henceforth hold and possess by the firmest legal right under this authority of ours; and whatever they wish to do with it, they shall enjoy complete freedom of action.

And so that this authority may be held more securely and preserved more fully for future times, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.**

I, Helisachar, have reviewed and subscribed.

Given on the Kalends of August, in the first year, with Christ favorable, of our empire, in the seventh indiction. Issued at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XXIII. THE TESTAMENT OF ABBOT ABBO, THE FOUNDER, AND OTHER RIGHTS OF THE SAME MONASTERY ARE CONFIRMED FOR FRODOINUS, ABBOT OF THE NOVALESE MONASTERY  
*(Year 814.)*

*[From Muratori, Italian Antiquities, volume III, p. 30.]*

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal God, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, emperor Augustus.

It is fitting for imperial majesty not only to preserve inviolate the pious acts of our predecessors but also to confirm them by the authority of its own judgment. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own, present and future, that the venerable Frodoinus, abbot of the monastery called Novalese, built in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, in the valley called Seusina, brought and presented before us the testament made concerning the aforesaid monastery by the former religious and devout lord Abbo, and renewed and confirmed by our lord and father, the most glorious Emperor Charles.

It contained the following: how the aforesaid patrician Abbo offered the above-named place, together with all its property, to the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, out of love for the heavenly homeland and the blessed life; and how, by divine judgment, eternal punishment, and divine anathema were imposed upon all rash destroyers and despoilers who should ever dare, seduced by greed, to oppose the written act and security of so great a devotion. Thus the house of God itself, and the monks who serve Christ the Lord there in the religion of holy devotion, as well as Christ’s poor and pilgrims traveling to and from the mountains, were to have provision for their needs in return for their merits; and those who had undertaken to make and confirm the donation were to take care that this should be so.

The aforesaid abbot asked our Highness that we too should strengthen by our authority the testament confirmed and fortified by our lord and father. But, considering God’s mercy and eternal reward for good deeds, we gladly assented to his petition and decreed that this confirmation of our authority should be made.

By it we order and command that whatever the aforesaid religious Abbo bestowed upon the true God and the most blessed Peter, and whatever our lord and father confirmed by his authority for the sake of the heavenly court, the aforesaid Abbot Frodoinus and his successors shall henceforth hold and possess freely forever, without anyone’s unjust invasion, interference, or disturbance—all the royal rights, namely, over everything they presently possess and everything they may acquire in the future;

*[Note: You have seen Louis the Pious grant to the abbot of Novalese a market, homicide (*omicidium*), and assassination committed in the midst of a city within our empire. I say that if the word “assassination” were genuinely found in the original, nothing further would be needed to destroy all confidence in this document. For the words *assassin* and *assassination* began to be heard in the East only after Jerusalem was recovered by the Christians in the year of Christ 1099, and then passed to us. Perhaps, however, this sort of word should be attributed to a badly stitched copy, as should the other words that follow and that we can never accept: “committed in the midst of a city within our empire,” to say nothing of other matters, since the diploma otherwise certainly bears the appearance of a legitimate offspring. See another diploma granted by Charlemagne to the same Frodoinus, abbot of Novalese, in volume IV of Ughelli’s *Italia Sacra*, in the catalogue of the bishops of Turin (*Patrologia Latina*, volume XCVII, column 997). You will recognize without hesitation that it is spurious.]*

—a market, homicide (*omicidium*), and assassination committed in the midst of a city within our empire; the public road from the aforesaid city as far as Fontana Vercinesca; and all other things that belonged either to us or to our subjects.

We also wish and expressly order by this document of ours that wherever properties belonging to the above-mentioned monastery lie, they be diligently defended and protected by our faithful as though they were our own special property, because, as is known to many, they were truly transferred by a deed of donation from our grandfather Pippin of blessed memory and likewise from our glorious and most excellent father, King Charles.

And so that this authority may be held more securely and preserved for long ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened by our own hand and ordered it sealed with our seal.

In the first year, with Christ favorable, of our empire, in the seventh indiction. Issued at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XXIV. FOR THE CHURCH OF VIENNE  
*(Year 814.)*

*[Baluz., Capitularies, volume II, p. 1404, from the chartulary of the church of Vienne.]*

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, emperor Augustus, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, centenarii, actionarii, our traveling envoys, and all the faithful of God’s holy Church and our own, present and future.

Let it be known that if we bring to fulfillment the petitions of priests and servants of God which they make known to us for their needs, we not only exercise the royal custom but also trust that such deeds will contribute to our blessedness and the reward of recompense. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, learn how the venerable Bernard, bishop of the city of Vienne and prelate of the church of Saint Maurice the Martyr, came to us and brought royal precepts of our predecessors. In them we found it inserted that they had held that see, together with its cells and the properties belonging to it, under the fullest protection and the safeguarding of immunity.

He therefore asked us, for the sake of security, that for the increase of our reward we should once again grant and confirm similar privileges concerning that holy place. We did not wish to deny his petition; rather, let both present and future faithful of God’s holy Church and our own know that we have granted and permanently confirmed it in every respect.

Moreover, it pleased us to restore there the cell of Saint Symphorian, formerly taken away from it, together with all the properties belonging to it. We also restore there a certain village called Fasiana, which we wish in future times to contribute to the reception of pilgrims and the support of the poor who will be there, provided only that no one at any time presume to take it away or grant it as a benefice. Rather, as we have assigned it, let the administrators of this Church allow it to remain for the needs of the needy.

We have also granted there certain cells, one called the Upper Monastery and another the Middle Monastery, built in honor of Saint Andrew, Saint Nicetius, and the other saints. We wish them, in our time and in future times, to contribute to the support of the canons serving God there.

Therefore we order and command that no public judge, no one belonging to the judicial authority, and none of our faithful ever dare to enter the churches, places, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid church of Saint Maurice—which it appears presently to possess justly and reasonably in whatever districts and territories—or anything bestowed there for the love of God, or anything that we have restored or granted there from our generosity as an act of charity, or anything that divine mercy may thereafter cause to be increased in the legal possession of that holy place, in order to hear cases, exact fines, impose lodging or provisions, take sureties, or unjustly constrain the men of that church, whether free or enslaved, who appear to reside upon its land; nor may anyone at any time enter or presume to exact any returns or unlawful exactions.

Whatever the treasury might have separated from the property of the aforesaid church, we grant entirely to that church for eternal recompense, so that through perpetual ages it may contribute to the alms of the poor and to the support of the servants of God serving God there. Thus may those servants of God who appear to serve God there gladly pray continually for us, for our wife and offspring, and for the stability of our entire empire, granted to us by God and to be preserved by him.

And so that this authority may remain unshaken in our time and in future times, with the Lord protecting it, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.**

I, Helisachar, have reviewed it.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the first year, with Christ favorable, of our empire, in the seventh indiction. Issued at the palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XXV. FOR THE HISPANIANS WHO REMAINED IN THE KINGDOM OF THE FRANKS  
*(Year 815.)*

*[Baluz., Capitularies, volume I, p. 550.]*

This is the precept of remission or concession that Emperor Louis made for the Hispani who had fled to him [because of the persecution of the Saracens].

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, emperor Augustus, to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and our own, present and future, residing in the regions of Aquitaine, Septimania, Provence, and Hispania.

We suppose that none of you is unaware of how certain men, because of the unjust oppression and most cruel yoke that the people most hostile to Christianity, the Saracens, imposed upon their necks, abandoned their own dwellings and possessions, which belonged to them by hereditary right, and fled to us from the regions of Hispania. They came to settle in Septimania and in that part of Hispania which had been reduced to desolation by our margraves; withdrawing themselves from the power of the Saracens, they submitted themselves to our dominion with free and willing purpose. Therefore we wish it to come to the knowledge of all of you that we have decided to receive these men under our protection and defense and preserve them in freedom.

### I

In such a manner that, like the other free men, they shall go to the army with their count; and in our march they shall not neglect, according to the reasonable ordering and admonition of that count, to conduct searches and watches, which in the customary language are called *wactae*. They shall provide provisions for our envoys or for those of our son whom we send to those regions as circumstances require, or for envoys who are sent to us from the regions of Hispania, and they shall furnish riding horses for their transport.

No other tax shall be exacted from them, either by the count or by his *juniores* and officials.

### II

For the greater cases—such as homicides, abductions, arsons, plundering, mutilation of limbs, thefts, robberies, seizures of the property of others, and any matter in which one is accused by a neighbor, whether criminally or civilly, and summoned to court—they shall in every way not refuse to come to the court of their count.

As for the other, lesser cases, they shall not be prohibited from settling them among themselves by their customary practice, as they are known to have done until now.

### III

If any one of them attracts other people, coming from wherever, to the portion that he has occupied for habitation, and makes them live with him in his portion, which they call an *aprisio*, he may use their service without anyone’s opposition or impediment. He shall also be permitted to constrain them to render justice in matters that they themselves can settle among themselves.
