The remaining judgments—that is, criminal actions—shall be reserved for the count’s tribunal.

### IV

If any one of these men, having been attracted by one of their number and settled in his portion, leaves the place, the place that has been abandoned shall nevertheless not pass out of the dominion of the person who formerly held him.

### V

If, because of the leniency and gentleness of their count, they should offer that count something from their property as a mark of honor and service, this shall not be reckoned to them as any kind of tribute or tax. Nor shall that count or his successors presume to turn it into a custom, or compel them to provide lodging or provisions for themselves or their men, to furnish riding horses, or to render any tax, tribute, or service beyond what has already been set out above.

But these Hispani who at the present time reside in the aforesaid places, as well as those who may yet flee from the power of the wicked and gather to our faith, build dwellings after settling in deserted and uncultivated places with our permission or that of our count, and cultivate the fields, shall be permitted to remain in freedom under our defense and protection according to the aforesaid arrangement. They shall also cheerfully and faithfully render to us, at the appropriate times, the services mentioned above, both with their count and with his envoys.

### VI

Nevertheless, let these Hispani know that we have granted them permission to commend themselves in the customary manner as vassals to our counts. If any one of them receives a benefice from the person to whom he has commended himself, he must know that he owes his lord such service for it as our native subjects customarily render to their lords for a similar benefice.

### VII

For this reason we have decided to give them these letters of our authority, by which we decree and order that this constitution of our liberality and gentleness toward them be inviolably preserved by all the faithful of God’s holy Church and our own forever.

In each city where the aforesaid Hispani are known to live, we wish there to be three copies of this document: one to be held by the bishop of that city, another by the count, and a third by the Hispani who reside in that place. A copy of them shall, however, be deposited in the archive of our palace, so that by examining it, whenever—as commonly happens—the Hispani themselves make a complaint, or the count or someone else has a case against them, the dispute may be decided.

Indeed, so that this constitution may be both more truly believed and more diligently preserved for long ages by the faithful of God’s holy Church and our own, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Lord Louis, most serene emperor.**

Durandus the deacon, in place of Helisachar, has reviewed it.

Given on the Kalends of January, in the first year, with Christ favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the seventh indiction. Issued at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XXVI. FOR THE MONASTERY OF MICIACUM  
*(Year 815.)*

*[Baluz., Capitularies, p. 1406, from the chartulary of the monastery of Miciacum.]*

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, emperor Augustus, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts or *vicedomini*, vicars, centenarii, toll collectors, actionarii, and all who administer public affairs, present and future.

Let it be known that Dutresindus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Maximinus of Miciacum, and his entire congregation asked our Highness to grant them permission, for meeting their needs, to operate three ships on the Loire, the Cher, the Vienne, the Sarthe, the Mayenne, the Taunucus or Lidon, the Hilary, or any other rivers on which they might travel for the various needs of the aforesaid monastery; and likewise to exempt their carts, pack animals, boats, and all their commerce, wherever the treasury might be entitled to exact a toll.

Because of the love of God and reverence for that holy place, we assented to their request and granted this precept of our authority for the security of the monastery and for the increase of our reward, as they had asked.

Therefore we ordered this precept of ours to be made, by which we order and command that no one of our faithful, nor any collector belonging to the judicial authority, presume to receive or exact any toll from carts, pack animals, boats, or any commerce whatsoever, wherever the treasury might be entitled to exact a toll.

As for the three ships that travel either on the Loire or on the other rivers for the utility and need of that monastery, no one, at whatever cities, castles, ports, or other places they may arrive, shall dare to receive or exact from them or from the men who supervise them any toll of any kind—whether riverbank toll, bridge toll, gate toll, welcome toll, turf toll, meal toll, commendation toll, ferry toll, dust toll, or any other charge—or any tax or return.

Rather, without anyone’s unlawful opposition or detention, let the three ships and the men who are responsible for supervising them, together with what they carry, travel freely and safely throughout our empire, going and returning. If they remain for any length of time in any place, or buy or sell anything, nothing at all shall be exacted from them, as has been stated.

And so that this authority may possess fuller force and be more certainly believed and more diligently preserved by our faithful, we have ordered it sealed below with the impression of our ring.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the first year, with Christ favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most serene Augustus, in the eighth indiction. Issued at the palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XXVII. FOR THE CHURCH OF VIENNE  
*(Year 815.)*

*[Baluz., from the chartulary of the church of Vienne.]*

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, emperor Augustus, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, centenarii, actionarii, toll collectors, and all who administer public affairs.

Let it be known that, at the request of Bernard, bishop of the church of Vienne, built in honor of Saint Maurice, and for the increase of our reward and the benefit of the brothers serving the Lord there, we have granted him five ships for transporting his goods on various rivers, namely the Rhône and the Saône.

Therefore we command and instruct you that neither you nor your *juniores* presume to exact or collect from the aforesaid number of ships any toll, riverbank toll, gate toll, turf toll, meal toll, welcome toll, or any other return. Thus, by this authority of our precept, as we have stated, the ships may, for the benefit of the brothers serving God there, carry on their business more freely and securely, supported at the same time by your assistance and protection.

And so that this authority may be more truly and certainly believed, we have ordered it sealed below with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most serene Augustus.**

Ibbo, in place of Helisachar, has reviewed it.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of June, in the second year, with Christ favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most serene Augustus, in the eighth indiction. Issued at the palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XXVIII. FOR THE IMMUNITY OF THE MONASTERY OF CARROFUM  
*(Year 815.)*

*[D. Bouquet, Collection of Histories, volume VI, p. 474, from Besly, proofs appended to the History of the Counts of Poitou, p. 164.]*

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, emperor Augustus.

If we bestow suitable benefits upon places devoted to divine worship, out of love for God and for those who serve him in those places, we do not doubt that an eternal reward will be repaid to us by God. Meanwhile, let the discernment—or practical concern—of all our faithful, both present and future, know that the venerable abbot Justus [Note: This is Justus, the abbot to whom Claudius, bishop of Turin, dedicated his Commentary on Matthew], from the monastery of Carrofense, which was built in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and is situated in the Poitevin district near the river Charente, presented to our consideration a charter of immunity belonging to our lord and father, Charles, of blessed memory, the most devout Augustus. It contained the statement that the monastery itself had once been built by a certain Count Rotger on his own property, and that he had transferred it to our aforesaid father, together with all its possessions and church ornaments, as well as all its appurtenances and dependencies, by a deed of gift; and that, at his request, he had caused it to remain under his protection and the safeguard of immunity, free from the disturbance of judicial authority.

For the sake, therefore, of securing this matter, the aforesaid Abbot Justus and the whole congregation serving God there entreated us, following our father’s custom, to decree that an immunity charter of this kind be made by us for that monastery. We willingly granted their request and decreed that a charter of our authority should be issued for that monastery, for the sake of immunity and protection, out of love for divine worship and for the remedy of our soul. By it we command and order that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, nor any of our faithful, present or future, dare enter, in our time or in times to come, the churches, places, lands, or other possessions that it presently and justly and lawfully possesses in any districts or territories under the authority of our empire, or those which divine piety may henceforth choose to add to the legal holdings of that holy place, in order to hear cases, exact fines or taxes, demand lodging or provisions, take sureties, or distrain the men of that monastery—whether free or enslaved—who reside upon its land; nor may anyone seek any repayments or unlawful pretexts, or presume to exact anything whatsoever of those matters mentioned above.

Whatever the royal treasury might have been able to exact from the aforesaid possessions of the monastery, we grant in full to that same monastery for eternal reward, so that throughout perpetual times it may contribute to the support of the poor and the allowances of the monks serving God there. And whenever, by divine summons, the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this world, so long as the monks themselves can find among their number men capable of governing that congregation according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, by this authority and consent of ours we grant them permission to elect abbots. Thus the monks who appear to serve God there, together with the possessions and people belonging or pertaining to that monastery, may, under the protection of our safeguard and immunity and with every disturbance by wicked authority removed, possess them in quiet order; and may they delight continually to entreat God’s immense mercy for the safety of our wife and offspring and of the whole empire granted to us by God and to be preserved forever by his most merciful compassion.

Therefore, so that this authority may obtain fuller force in God, be strengthened by the faithful of Holy Church and by our own faithful, be more truly believed, and be more carefully preserved, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Helisachar reviewed it.

Given on the second day before the Ides of February, in the eleventh year, with Christ favoring us, of the empire of our lord Louis; in the eighth indiction. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## XXIX. For the Monastery of Dervense. (Year 815)

[In D. Bouquet, *Collection of Histories*, volume VI, p. 476, from the cartulary of this monastery.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

When we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants for the love of divine worship, we believe that the gift of heavenly grace is bestowed upon us by the Lord. Therefore, let it be known to all the faithful of Holy God’s Church and to our own, present and future, that Hauto, abbot of the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul [Note: Commonly Moutier-en-Der, in the diocese of Châlons], which is situated in the forest called Dervo, where the river Alsmantia flows into the Vigera, in the district of Perthois, showed us the immunity of our grandfather, King Pippin. It contained the statement that he and his predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, had always held that monastery under the fullest protection and safeguard of immunity.

For the greater security of the matter, however, the aforesaid Hauto requested that we confirm the same authority by our authority, out of love for God and reverence for that holy place. We willingly agreed to his request and decreed that this charter of our authority should be made for that holy place. By it we command and order that none of our faithful, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, dare enter, in our time or in times to come, the churches, places, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery that it presently possesses justly and reasonably, or those which divine piety may henceforth choose to add to the legal holdings of that monastery, in order to hear cases, exact fines, demand lodging or provisions, take sureties, or unjustly distrain the men of that monastery; nor may anyone seek any repayments or unlawful pretexts, or presume to exact anything whatsoever of the matters mentioned above.

But let the aforesaid abbot and his successors be permitted to possess the possessions of that monastery in quiet order under the protection of our immunity. Whatever the treasury might thereby have been able to exact, we grant in full to the aforesaid monastery for eternal reward, so that throughout perpetual times it may contribute to the support of the poor and the allowances of God’s servants serving there; so that those servants of God who serve there may delight continually to entreat the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of the whole empire granted to us by God and to be preserved by him.

And so that this authority, with the Lord’s protection, may remain unshaken, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most devout emperor.

Durandus, deacon, reviewed it in place of Helisachar.

Given on the second day before the Kalends of March, in the eleventh year, with Christ favoring us, of the empire of our lord Louis, most devout Augustus; in the eighth indiction. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1019A]

## XXX. For the Monastery of Gorze. (Year 815)

[In D. Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, p. 298.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ. Amen. Louis, by the divinely ordained clemency, emperor Augustus.

Since it is plainly just that royal and imperial power bestow some gift upon those whose necessity is shown to require it, and since the order of equity appears no less to demand that the same power lend a freer ear to those whose faithful service is demonstrated by clear acts of devotion and bring their petitions to fulfillment, we therefore wish it to be known to the discernment of all our faithful, present and future, how, at the urging and request of our faithful Madefrid, certain possessions of Theodemar, his property, situated in the district of Scarponne, in the territory of Theodalciaga, in the territory of Scammuse, in the territory of Helimninciaga, in the territory of Audomaga, in the territory of Absolomaga, in the territory of Munalabuvicuse, in the territory of Halaricunise, in the territory of Cunholomaga, in the territory of Dodomaga, in the territory of Bedeonecuse, and in the territory of Banomaga—that is, manses, houses, cottages, with all buildings erected upon them, fields, meadows, vineyards, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, and everything that Hartmann was seen to possess and have authority over from this day—he donated entirely to Saint Stephen, Saint Peter, Saint Gorgonius, or to the monastery of Gorze, for a term, to Abbot Optarius; and it was received as a precarium in the district of Scarponne, in the territory of Banomaga, or in the very village of Banonocurte, entirely, as the precarium itself records.

Afterward Magulfus, bishop and abbot of that monastery, came and wished to terminate the precarium. Then Count Hartmann approached our clemency, asking that he might retain, by our protection and permission, for the days of his life, the precarium that he had received from the aforesaid Abbot Optarius, just as they had agreed between themselves. Considering the advantage of the house of God, and having taken the advice of our faithful, we granted his petitions. Therefore, at the request of our faithful Madefrid and of the others, we have decreed that this grant of our authority be made to our aforesaid faithful Hartmann.

By it we establish and sanction that he may securely possess, for the days of his life, the possessions written above, both those which Hartmann himself gave to that house of God and those which he received as a precarium, by this charter of our majesty and by the agreement mentioned. No bishop shall thereafter have the right to diminish anything among those possessions or properties; rather, whatever he wishes to increase, improve, or acquire there, let him strive to arrange that it be done as though he held free ownership of the aforesaid possessions. Nevertheless, each year he shall pay as a census, on the feast of the blessed martyr Gorgonius, which is the fifth day before the Ides of September, five solidi in denarii, or the equivalent value in wax purchased at that price.

But if he should prove negligent or late in paying that census, once the neglected payment has been made, let him retain what he holds. After his departure, whenever God so wills, the possessions, properly administered and improved, shall return to the aforesaid monastery without any opposition or assignment by a judge.

To ensure that this authority of our clemency remains immovable and unshaken, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our bull.

The sign of Louis, most serene king.

I, Durandus, deacon, reviewed it in place of Helisachar.

[Col. 1020B]

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 815, in the eighth indiction, with epact 7 and the concurrent 2; but in the second year of the reign of Louis, emperor. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## XXXI. For the Monastery of Aniane. (Year 815)

(See this and several other charters of Louis the Pious relating to the monastery of Aniane among the works of Saint Benedict of Aniane.)

## XXXII. For the Church of Viviers. (Year 815)

[In D. Bouquet, same work, from J. Columba’s *Deeds of the Bishops of Viviers*, book II, no. 30.]

[Col. 1020C]

In the name of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence [Note: The printed editions incorrectly read “by the divine ordering of providence”], emperor Augustus.

If we heed the just petitions of priests and servants of God, we confidently believe that this will contribute to our eternal blessedness. Therefore, let the discernment of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable Thomas, bishop of Alba or Viviers, came to us and entreated our Highness that, for the increase of our reward, we should receive the aforesaid see, together with the brothers serving the Lord there, under our protection and immunity. Granting his request, we have endeavored to confirm it by a charter of our authority.

Therefore we command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, nor any of the faithful of Holy God’s Church or of our own, dare ever enter the churches, places, lands, or other possessions that it presently appears justly and reasonably to possess in any districts or territories, or anything that may henceforth be bestowed there for the love of God, in order to hear cases, exact fines, demand lodging or provisions, take sureties, unjustly distrain the men of that church, whether free or enslaved, or seek any repayments or unlawful pretexts; nor may anyone presume to exact any of the matters mentioned above.

But let the servants of the Lord residing there remain forever in peace under our protection and the safeguard of our immunity, and let them delight continually to entreat the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of our whole empire, granted to us by the Lord and continually preserved by his most merciful compassion.

And so that this authority may be believed more truly and certainly, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of our lord Louis, most serene emperor.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, in the eleventh year of the empire of our lord Louis Augustus, in the eighth indiction. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1021B]

## XXXIII. For the Monastery of Saint-Maixent. (Year 815)

[In D. Bouquet, same work, p. 480, from the old cartulary of this monastery.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained clemency, emperor Augustus.

If we bestow suitable benefits upon places devoted to divine worship, out of love for God and for those serving him in those places, we do not doubt that an eternal reward will be repaid to us by the Lord. Therefore, let the prudence of all our faithful, present and future, know that we have received the venerable Abbot Tetbert from the monastery of Saint-Maixent the Confessor, where that saint rests bodily, situated in the district of Poitiers, together with the congregation serving God there and with all the possessions and people that the congregation presently appears to possess, under our protection and the safeguard of immunity.

Accordingly, by this charter of our authority we decree and order that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, dare enter, in our time or in times to come, the churches, places, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery that it presently possesses justly and reasonably within the authority of our empire, or those which divine piety may henceforth choose to add to the legal holdings of that monastery, in order to hear cases, exact fines or taxes, demand lodging or provisions, take sureties, or distrain the men of that monastery, whether free or enslaved, who reside upon its land; nor may anyone seek any repayments or unlawful pretexts, or presume to exact anything whatsoever of the matters mentioned above.

But let the aforesaid Abbot Tetbert and his successors be permitted to possess the possessions of that monastery in quiet order under the protection of our immunity. Whatever the treasury might be able to expect from them, we grant in full to the aforesaid monastery for eternal reward, so that it may contribute in perpetual increase to the support of the poor and the allowances of the monks serving the Lord there.

And whenever, by divine summons, the aforesaid abbot departs from this world, so long as the monks themselves can find among their number men capable of governing according to the holy order and regular norm, let them have permission, by our permission and consent, to elect an abbot; so that the servants of God serving the Lord there may delight continually to entreat the Lord for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of our whole empire, granted to us by the Lord and to be preserved by him.

Moreover, so that this authority of our immunity may retain inviolable and unshaken firmness through long ages, and so that it may be believed more truly and certainly by the faithful of Holy God’s Church and by our own faithful and be more carefully preserved, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

[Col. 1022B]

The sign of Louis, emperor.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the eleventh year, with Christ favoring us, of the empire of our lord Louis, most serene emperor; in the eighth indiction. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## XXXIV. For the Monastery of Farfa. (Year 815)

[In Chesne, *Writers of Frankish Affairs*, volume III, p. 654.]

Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

It is fitting for imperial Highness not only to preserve inviolate the deeds of its predecessors, but also eagerly to confirm them by the authority of its judgment. Accordingly, let the discernment and diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable Abbot Benedict of the monastery of Acutianum, situated in the Sabine territory and built in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, presented to our consideration certain charters of confirmation belonging to our lord and father Charles, of good memory, most serene Augustus. They contained the statement that he had caused that monastery to remain under such a privilege, like the other monasteries in Francia that follow the rule of Saint Benedict the Father: namely, that no bishop should presume to take anything from the treasures or possessions of that monastery, place them under any tribute, or exact or demand any census from them.

They also stated how Duke Hildeprand, by his charters, had confirmed the estate called Tancies and the court called Vallantis, with all their entirety and appurtenances; and the court of Tacianum; the monastery of Saint Mark the Evangelist, situated beside the walls of the city of Spoleto, which our lord and father himself had confirmed to that monastery by his charter; the monastery of Saint Savior, situated not far from that same city of Spoleto; the monastery of nuns called Saint George, beneath the walls of the city of Reate; and the church of Saint Michael the Archangel, situated on the river Mellinus near that same city of Reate, with all its entirety.

He had also confirmed, in the territory of Firmum, Saint Sylvester and Saint Marina, with all their entirety, as well as everything that had been lawfully confirmed to that monastery by the generosity of kings and queens, bishops, dukes, and gastalds, or by gifts from the people or from other faithful, through their charters.

The aforesaid abbot and his congregation also requested us, for the full security of the matter, to follow our father’s custom and decree that our authority likewise be issued concerning this affair. For the benefit of our soul and the fruit of eternal reward, we willingly granted their requests, and, having examined our father’s authority, we were pleased to issue this charter of our authority.

By it we decree and establish that no bishop may take anything from the places mentioned above, or from the other monasteries, cells, hospices, churches, courts, villages, fisheries with their fishermen, male or female servants, holders of *libelli*, charter-holders, *offertae*, woods, mills, or anything else legally subject to that monastery; nor from anything granted by the munificence of kings or queens, by the confirmation of bishops, dukes, or gastalds, or by the generosity of the people or other faithful; nor from anything brought by monks who entered that monastery desiring to save their souls, whether received by them through donations from kings and queens, bishops, dukes, or through their parents’ inheritance or any other acquisition, and transferred there by charters; nor from anything that came to them by sales, accessions, exchanges, or possessions from any source and that, as has been said, came to that monastery and is known to be presently possessed justly and lawfully, or that may henceforth be bestowed there by the Lord’s generosity.

No one of our faithful, present or future, shall attempt to disturb the aforesaid abbot and his congregation or their successors, raise a legal complaint against them, or make any unjust claim. Rather, just as it is known to have been confirmed by our father, and as it is established that the place has been enriched with various possessions by the faithful of Holy God’s Church, so let it remain forever without anyone’s prejudice, harassment, or diminution. By this charter of our confirmation, let it hold them by perpetual right, remain under our privilege and protection, and, under our defense, let the monks in that monastery reside in peace and entreat the Lord for us and for the stability of our whole empire.

We have also granted them that whatever, under Lombard law, might have been due to the public treasury from the union of the monastery’s male servants with free women shall, by this charter, be confirmed as our alms.

And whenever, by divine summons, the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this life, so long as the monks themselves can find among their number a man capable of governing them according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, let them have permission to elect an abbot.

And so that this authority of our confirmation may be more fully and truly believed by all and more carefully preserved, we have ordered it to be subscribed according to our custom and sealed with our bull.

Durandus, deacon, reviewed it in place of Helisachar.

Given on the second day before the Nones of August, in the eleventh year, with Christ favoring us, of our empire; in the eighth indiction. Done at Frankfurt, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God.

## XXXV. For the Monastery of Banyoles. (Year 815)

[Flórez, *Sacred Spain*, volume XLIII, treatise 81, on the Church of Girona.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

[Col. 1024B]

If we bestow suitable benefits upon places devoted to divine worship, out of love for God and for those serving him in those places, we do not doubt that an eternal reward will be repaid to us by the Lord. Therefore, we wish it to be known to the greatness of all our faithful, present and future, how the illustrious Count Rampo approached our serenity and reported to our gentleness that a certain religious man named Bonitus had received, with the permission of the late Count Odilo, a deserted place called Banyoles, situated in the district of Besalú, where a church had been founded in ancient times; and that he had labored there by his own exertions, building a church in honor of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, constructing dwellings for monks and shelters for the poor, and establishing monks who would dwell there perpetually under the rule of religion.

But when that same abbot departed from this world by divine command, the monks themselves elected Mercoral, a venerable man, as abbot of the same monastery, with the consent of the venerable Nibridius, archbishop. Rampo brought him into our presence, commended him into our hands, and requested our clemency that we place him, together with the aforesaid monastery and the monks dwelling there, under our protection, defense, and the safeguard of immunity, along with the possessions that they appear presently to possess justly and reasonably, whether they had drawn them from the wilderness, received them through settlement, obtained them by donations from counts, or acquired them by any lawful means.

We willingly granted his petitions, conceded everything accordingly, and confirmed it by this charter of ours. Therefore we command that the aforesaid Abbot Mercoral, with the monks entrusted to him for governance and with the possessions legally belonging to that monastery, remain under our protection and the defense of immunity; so that no one exercising judicial authority dare enter, in our time or in times to come, the churches, places, lands, or other possessions of that monastery that it presently possesses justly and lawfully within the authority of our empire, or those which divine piety may henceforth choose to add to the legal holdings of that holy place, in order to hear cases, exact fines, demand lodging or provisions, take sureties, distrain the men of that monastery, or seek any repayments or unlawful pretexts; nor may anyone presume to exact anything whatsoever of the matters mentioned above.

But let the aforesaid abbot and his successors possess the possessions of that monastery in quiet order. And whenever, by divine summons, the aforesaid abbot or his predecessors depart from this world, so long as they can find among themselves men capable of governing that congregation according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, let them have permission to elect abbots, so that the monks dwelling there may delight continually to entreat the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of our whole empire.

And so that this authority may remain unshaken in our time and in times to come, with the Lord’s protection, we have ordered it to be sealed beneath with our ring.

Durandus, deacon, reviewed it in place of Abbot Fibrugis.

Given on the third day before the Ides of September, in the ninth year, with Christ favoring us, of the empire of our lord Louis, most devout Augustus; in the first indiction. Done at the king’s palace at Attigny, happily in the name of God. Amen.

—Examples from the charter of the lord emperor.

## XXXVI. For the Monastery of Fontenelle. (Year 815)

[Marten, *Larger Collection*, volume I, p. 61, from a manuscript of Fontenelle.]

[Col. 1025C]

In the name of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

When we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants for the love of divine worship, we do not doubt that we are fortified by heavenly grace. Therefore, let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, and also to our successors, the faithful of Holy God’s Church, that the venerable Abbot Trasarius of the monastery called Fontenelle, built in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of the other saints, presented to our consideration the immunity of our lord and father Charles, of good memory, most devout Augustus. It contained the statement that he and his predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, had always held the aforesaid monastery under the fullest protection and safeguard of immunity, out of divine love and for the tranquility of the brothers residing there.

For the greater security of the matter, however, Abbot Trasarius requested that we confirm the same authority by our authority, out of love for God and reverence for that holy place. We willingly agreed to his request, conceded everything accordingly, and confirmed it by this charter of ours.

Therefore we command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, dare enter, in our time or in times to come, the churches, places, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery that it presently possesses justly and reasonably within the authority of our empire, or those which divine piety may henceforth choose to add to the legal holdings of that place, in order to hear cases, exact fines or taxes, demand lodging or provisions, take sureties, unjustly distrain the men of that monastery, whether free or enslaved, who reside upon its land, or seek any repayments or unlawful pretexts, exact bridge tolls, receive market tolls, or collect wheel-tolls in any places, cities, or markets; nor may anyone presume to exact anything whatsoever of the matters mentioned above.

But let the aforesaid abbot and his successors possess the possessions of that monastery in quiet order under the protection of our immunity. Whatever the treasury may be able to exact from them, we also grant to the aforesaid monastery for eternal reward, so that it may contribute throughout perpetual times to the support of the poor and the allowances of the monks serving God there. Thus may those servants of God who serve there delight continually to entreat divine mercy for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of the whole empire granted to us by God and to be preserved by him.

And so that this authority of ours [Possibly: “of ours” should read “in our time”] may remain unshaken in our time and in times to come, with the Lord’s protection, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

[Col. 1026C]

Durandus, deacon, reviewed it in place of Helisachar.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, in the second year, with Christ favoring us, of the empire of our lord Louis, most devout Augustus; in the ninth indiction. Done at Nijmegen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## XXXVII. For the Monastery of the Barbarian Island. (Year 815)

[In D. Bouquet, *Frankish Historical Writers*, volume VI, p. 483, from *The Ruins of the Island-Barbara*, p. 45.]

In the name, etc., Louis, by the providence of God [Note: Correction: “by the divinely ordained providence”], emperor Augustus.

Let it be known to bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, *vicedomini*, vicars, centenarii, toll-collectors, and all administrators of public affairs, present and future, that Campio, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin, called the Barbarian Island, situated on the river Saône not far from the city of Lyon, and his entire congregation petitioned our Highness for permission to send three ships at all times along the Saône, Rhône, and Doubs for the purpose of conducting trade.

We willingly received their petition and, for the increase of our reward, granted it as they requested by this authority of ours. Therefore we ordered this charter of ours to be made for them, by which we command everyone that, wherever the aforesaid number of ships enters territories or jurisdictions under our administration, you must not presume to take or cause to be exacted any toll, nor what is commonly called a *cespitaticum*, *salutaticum*, or *coenaticum*, nor any census or repayment whatsoever from them.

Rather, let those same ships travel at all times along the aforesaid rivers, as stated above, freely and without any opposition, conduct their business, and, whenever they reach any cities or ports responsible for providing for those ships, suffer no disturbance or detention from any of our faithful. Whatever part of the aforesaid rivers they navigate, let them be able to go and return peacefully and securely with the ships and the goods they carry, by this ordinance of ours.

And if they remain for any period in any place, or buy or sell anything, let nothing, as we have said, be demanded or exacted from them. If, however—God forbid—through some accident or the negligence of the sailors, or because of a driving wind, as frequently happens, any of the aforesaid ships should sink, break apart, or reach the shore damaged, let no one presume to destroy it, ravage what is inside it, or seize anything by force—unless perhaps those responsible for providing for the ships should voluntarily wish to give something to someone.

If anything should be done otherwise anywhere, the officials of those places who are known to administer public affairs shall strive to correct it lawfully without any delay. Indeed, so that this authority may remain unshaken in our time and in times to come, with the Lord’s protection, we have ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

Given on the third day before the Ides of November [Note: The year of the incarnation, 816, has been added improperly and contrary to usage. For in that year Louis could not have been present at Aachen on the eleventh of November; moreover, the indiction is placed incorrectly, since it should follow the year of the empire. Finally, if this charter is genuine, the second year of the empire should be corrected, or the third year should be reckoned from September of the year 813], in the ninth indiction, in the third year, with Christ favoring us, of the empire of our lord Louis, most serene Augustus. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God.

## XXXVIII. For the Monastery of Saint Zeno of Verona. (Year 815)

[Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, volume V, p. 705.]

In the name of the eternal Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

The emperor ought not only piously to preserve inviolate the good deeds of his predecessors [Col. 1027D], but also eagerly to confirm them by the authority of his judgment. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful subjects, both present and future, know that Rotald, venerable bishop of the holy Veronese Church, together with Austerbert, abbot of the monastery of Saint Zeno, brought before us, among other charters of our lord and father, Charles, the most pious Augustus, and of our royal predecessors, a certain privilege confirmed by our father. In it we found written how our most beloved brother Pippin, once glorious king, together with the aforementioned bishop, had rebuilt and restored, for the love of God and in reverence for the aforesaid patron, the monastery of Saint Zeno, confessor of Christ, situated in the suburb of the aforesaid city; and how, after it had formerly been burned by unfaithful men and almost entirely deprived of all the possessions once bestowed upon it, no monks could remain there to perform the canonical hours and divine praises. Unless the bishop of the aforesaid city sent priests there, there was no one to celebrate the divine office there as was fitting. Therefore, for the benefit of their souls, they determined that certain properties, by which the monks and the poor of Christ might in future have the necessities of life, should be assigned and permanently confirmed to the aforesaid [Col. 1028B] place.

This was to apply to whatever properties were located in the county of Verona, in their several places: first, a small monastery built in honor of Saint Peter, called Mauratica, with all its appurtenances and tithes; likewise, in another place called Ostelia, in the aforesaid county of Verona, the church of Saint Lawrence with all its appurtenances and tithes; and, in a third place in the same county of Verona, the church built in honor of the holy martyrs Firmus and Rusticus, with all its appurtenances and tithes; also a granary within the city of Verona, with the areas surrounding it; and other properties, both in the city of Verona and outside it, in various places, which Count Anselm had once assigned to the aforesaid [Col. 1028C] monastery; likewise the properties at Runco, which were offered by the priest Onipert [lacuna], as well as in other mountainous and level places, wherever it is known to possess and hold property.

And in the county of Vicenza, namely Mount Torcello in the district of Venetia; likewise in the counties of Treviso, Tridentum, Brescia, Bergamo, Mantua, Piacenza, Parma, Bologna, Clumacum, and also in all the places of Tuscany, or wherever anything is proved to belong or to have belonged to the aforesaid monastery. But for the sake of security he petitioned our serenity that we should once again confirm these things by our pious imperial decrees, following the authority of our father.

But since, because of our sins, the aforesaid monastery of Saint Zeno had again been burned and destroyed together with other people [reading uncertain], so that monks could no longer dwell there, we do not wish to deny the petition of the aforesaid bishop. Rather, just as it is declared to have been done by our father, so let the diligence of all our faithful subjects know that we have granted and confirmed it by these imperial letters of ours. Finally, we order and decree that whatever the aforesaid church of Saint Zeno is known to possess justly and legally through our gift, or that of our beloved brother, or of the aforesaid bishop Rotald, or through the conveyance of other faithful subjects, or through purchase, or through any other legitimate acquisition, and whatever may hereafter be bestowed and assigned to it through the generosity of good men [Col. 1029A]; likewise, whatever offerings are made to Saint Zeno of any movable or immovable property, or whatever is offered or presented there, the holy congregation of monks shall henceforth securely hold and possess in its entirety by this privilege of our authority, without disturbance from any person.

This shall be subject only to what it had in the earlier privilege of our father: for the honor of succeeding bishops, it was established that each year, on the feast of Saint Zeno himself, the bishop of that city, together with his clergy, should receive from the monks serving there either twenty mancuses or fifty solidi of silver, and that nothing more should be demanded from them by anyone. Let the monks also always be permitted [Col. 1029B] to choose an abbot for themselves from their own congregation. If it should happen that they cannot find such a man among themselves, then, with the consent of the bishop of that city, let them have permission to seek an abbot within the same diocese.

Moreover, for the sake of eternal reward, it has pleased our serenity to make a provision concerning the dependents of the same monastery: namely, free women, whom the Italians call *herimannas*, who have joined themselves to the dependents of that church and monastery, or likewise to those of other churches—that is, of major churches, matricular churches, dioceses, monasteries, or any other churches. In accordance with the statutes of the preceding emperors and by the authority of this privilege of ours, let the aforesaid holy place inviolably possess such women together with the aforesaid dependents, without any human opposition.

If anyone—which we do not believe will happen—whether archbishop, bishop, duke, margrave, count, viscount, public administrator, or private person, should attempt to rise against or violate in any respect all the provisions written above within the jurisdiction of our kingdom, let him know that he shall pay fifty pounds of the finest gold as a composition: half to the same church and half to our palace. [Col. 1029D] And so that this grant and confirmation of our authority may be believed with greater certainty and observed more carefully in future times [Col. 1030A], we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of the lord Louis, most serene emperor.

Issued on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the year—Christ being favorable—of the empire of the lord Louis, most pious Augustus [lacuna], indiction 8. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, successfully.

### XXXIX. For the Monastery of Psalmodi. (Year 815.)

[Note: [Col. 1029D] This privilege was extracted from the archives of the church of Alès, to which the monastery of Psalmodi is united, by the most illustrious abbot of Saint Maximin, provost and vicar-general of the chapter of Alès. The lord Claude Estiennot certainly saw another copy in the Psalmodi archive; so great is the difference in the same charter that he transcribed.]

[In D. Bouquet, ibid., p. 484, from the archives of the church of Alès.]

In the name of the Lord God and of our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence ordained, emperor Augustus.

[Col. 1030B]

If, for the love of God and of those serving him in places dedicated to divine worship, we bestow suitable benefits upon them, we do not doubt that an eternal reward will be repaid to us by the Lord. Let the discernment and advantage of all our faithful subjects, present and future, know that the venerable man Theodemir [Note: [Col. 1029D] In the year 815, Claude, bishop of Turin, dedicated to this Theodemir three books on Genesis; in 821, an exposition of Exodus; and in 823, Commentaries on Leviticus, as is clear from the preface by the same author prefixed to the Commentaries on Leviticus. Theodemir later wrote a lengthy letter against Claudius of Turin, who had attacked the veneration of sacred images; a large part of it is reproduced in the third book of Jonas, bishop of Orléans, against that same Claudius of Turin. In this letter Theodemir says that he presided over one hundred and forty monks under the Rule of Saint Benedict, although out of modesty he calls his monastery a “little monastery.” Jonas speaks honorably of this abbot in the first book, in these words: “A certain man venerable for his sound and holy religious purpose, to be imitated for his honorable life and named with due honor, Theodemir, father of the monks, now already removed from human affairs, had learned, as rumor spread far and wide, that such things were being done and preached by that same Claudius against ecclesiastical authority. Moved by the duty of charity and impelled solely by love of his people, he took care to send Claudius a letter filled with charity, urging him to restrain himself from those things that he was reprehensibly doing and teaching.”] abbot of the monastery situated in the district of Nîmes, on the island called Psalmodi, built in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, and of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and of other saints, approached the majesty of our eminence and begged that we receive the aforesaid monastery, with all its properties that justly belong to it at the present time, under our protection and establish it under the fullest safeguard of immunity, for the love of God and for the tranquility of the brothers dwelling there.

We willingly granted his petition and decreed that this privilege of our authority should be made for that monastery, as a grant of immunity and protection, out of love for divine worship and for the remedy of our soul. By it we order and command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, dare enter the churches, places, lands, or other possessions that the aforesaid monastery now justly and legally possesses in any counties or territories within the jurisdiction of our empire, or that divine piety may hereafter cause to be added to the property of that holy place, in order to hear cases, exact fines or taxes, demand lodging or provisions, take sureties [Col. 1030D], [Col. 1031A] or forcibly constrain the men of this monastery, whether free or enslaved, who dwell upon its land; nor may anyone seek any restitutions or illicit pretexts, either now or in future, or presume to exact any of the things mentioned above.

Whatever the treasury might hope to exact from the properties of the aforesaid monastery, we grant in its entirety to that monastery for eternal reward, so that it may perpetually increase the provision for the poor and the support of the monks serving God there. And whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this life, so long as the monks themselves are able to find among themselves men capable of governing that congregation according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, let them have permission, by this authority and consent of ours, to elect abbots [Col. 1031B], so that those servants of God who serve him there may delight in continually imploring his boundless mercy for us, for our wife and offspring, and for the stability of our entire empire.

Therefore, so that this authority may possess fuller force in the name of God, and may be more truly believed and more carefully preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own faithful subjects, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

The deacon Durand, in the place of Helisachar, recognized this.

Issued on the third day before the Nones of December, in the year—Christ being favorable—two of the empire of the lord Louis, most pious Augustus, [Note: [Col. 1031D] Incorrectly given by the lord Estiennot as indiction 8; copyists repeatedly err in this matter.] indiction 8. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

### XL. For the Monastery of Montolieu in the Diocese of Carcassonne. (Year 815.)

[In D. Bouquet, ibid., p. 485, from the original charter.]

In the name of the Lord God and of our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence ordained, emperor Augustus.

When we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants for the love of divine worship, we do not doubt that we are fortified by heavenly grace. Therefore let the discernment of all our faithful subjects, present and future, know that the venerable man Olomundus, abbot of the monastery called Malasti, situated in the territory of Carcassonne on the river Duranus [Col. 1031D], built in honor of Saint John the Baptist, brought before us a certain privilege of our lord and father, Charles, of blessed memory, most serene Augustus. In it was written how that same Olomundus had built the monastery anew and, for its protection and because of the unlawful attacks of wicked men, had commended himself, together with the monks dwelling there, into the hand of that same lord emperor, so that under his protection they might be permitted to live and remain peacefully with their property and dependents [Col. 1032A].

He also begged our clemency to receive under our protection and the safeguard of immunity the aforesaid monastery, together with the cell called Saint Martin, subject to the aforesaid monastery, situated in the same district below the stream of Lampius and built in honor of Saint Martin the Confessor, with its property, dependents, adjoining lands, and boundaries.

For the love of God and in reverence for divine worship, it pleased us willingly to lend an ear to his prayers, and we decreed that this privilege of our authority should be made as a grant of immunity and protection. By it we order and command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, dare enter the churches, places, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery, which it now justly and reasonably possesses, or which divine goodness may hereafter cause to be added to the property of that holy place, in order to hear cases, exact fines, demand lodging or provisions, take sureties, or unjustly constrain the men of the monastery, whether free or enslaved, who dwell upon its land; nor may anyone seek any restitutions or illicit pretexts, either now or in future, or presume to exact any of the things mentioned above [Col. 1032B].

Whatever the treasury might hope to exact from the properties of the aforesaid monastery, we grant in its entirety to that monastery for eternal reward, so that it may perpetually increase the provision for the poor and the support of the monks serving God there [Col. 1032C]. And whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this life, so long as the monks themselves are able to find among themselves men capable of governing that congregation according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, let them have permission, by this authority and consent of ours, to elect abbots, so that the monks serving God there may delight in continually imploring the boundless mercy of the Lord for us, for our wife and offspring, and for the stability of our entire empire, granted to us by God and to be preserved forever by his most merciful compassion.

Therefore, so that this authority may possess fuller force in the name of God and may be more truly believed and more carefully preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own faithful subjects [Col. 1032D], we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

The deacon Durand, in the place of Helisachar, recognized this.

Issued on the sixth day before the Ides of December, [Note: [Col. 1031D] Mabillon and Baluze associate this charter with the year 815. Pagi, who holds that in all charters issued by Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, and their sons before the death of Louis the Pious, the indictions always began on the Kalends of September, assigns it to the year 814 and derives the second year of Emperor Louis from 813, when he was named associate in the imperial title by his father Charlemagne. I, however, believe that the indiction should be corrected to 8.] in the year—Christ being favorable—two of the empire of the lord Louis, most pious Augustus, indiction 8. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1033A]

### XLI. For the Church of Vienne. (Year 815.)

[In D. Bouquet, ibid., p. 486, from Cointius, vol. VII of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, p. 360.]

In the name of the Lord God and of our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence ordained, emperor Augustus.

If, for the love of God, we bestow suitable benefits upon places dedicated to divine worship and upon those serving him in those places, we do not doubt that an eternal reward will be repaid to us by God. Therefore let the prudence of all our faithful subjects, present and future, know that, for the increase of our merit and the fruit of eternal recompense, it has pleased us to restore, for the love of God and in reverence for that holy place, certain properties that had formerly been taken away from the mother church of Vienne, where Archbishop Bernard now presides, built in honor of Saint Maurice the Martyr [Col. 1033B].

These properties are in the district of Vaison, in a villa called Dalforiana, with houses and buildings, dependents, resident tenants, lands, olive groves, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, with all their appurtenances and adjoining lands. All these properties, with everything belonging or pertaining to them, which at the present time belongs to the estate of that villa in the same province [is], we restore in full and without reservation to the aforesaid church of Vienne by this authority of ours.

Therefore we will and command [Col. 1033C] that, by this authority of ours, both now and in future, the aforesaid properties, as we have stated above, remain perpetually in the ownership and dominion of that church, so that its rectors may freely exercise in every respect whatever authority they wish over those properties for the church’s benefit and advancement. To make this authority more secure, and so that it may be more truly believed and more carefully preserved through perpetual times by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own faithful subjects, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene Augustus.

The deacon Durand, in the place of Helisachar, recognized this.

Issued on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the year—Christ being favorable—2 of the empire of the lord Louis, most pious Augustus, indiction [Col. 1033D] 8. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

### XLII. For the Monastery of Prüm. (Year 815.)

[Hontheim, *Ecclesiastical History of Trier*, vol. I, p. 166.]

In the name of the Lord and of our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence ordained, emperor Augustus.

When we bring to completion the petitions of priests and servants of God that have been made known to us on account of their needs, we not only exercise the imperial custom [Col. 1034A], but also trust that such actions will contribute to our blessedness in the reward of eternity. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful subjects, present and future, know that the venerable man Tancrad, abbot of the monastery called Prüm, which our lord and grandfather Pippin, glorious king, built as a new work in honor of the holy Savior and of the other saints [Note: [Col. 1033D] See the privilege of immunity above, under the year 775, in November (*Patrologia Latina*, vol. XCVII, col. 1053)], brought forward a privilege of immunity of our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, most serene emperor. In it was written how he had always held that monastery, for the love of God and the tranquility of the brothers dwelling there, under his fullest protection and defense of immunity. But for the sake of security the aforesaid abbot Tancrad petitioned [Col. 1034B] that, for the love of God, we should add our authority to the paternal authority concerning that place.

We willingly assented to his petition and granted everything accordingly, confirming it by this privilege of ours. Therefore we order and command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, dare enter the churches, places, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery that it now justly and legally possesses in any counties or territories within the jurisdiction of our empire, or whatever divine goodness may hereafter cause to be added to the property of that holy place, in order to hear cases, demand fines, require lodging or provisions, take sureties, exact *scarae* or *coniecta*, whether from carts or from pack animals [Col. 1034C], or unjustly constrain the men of that monastery, whether free or enslaved, who dwell upon its land; nor may anyone seek any restitutions or illicit pretexts, either now or in future, or presume to demand or exact any of the things mentioned above.

Whatever the right of the treasury could have exacted from those properties, we have granted in its entirety to that monastery, for eternal reward: namely, so that it may perpetually increase the provision for the poor and the support of the monks serving God there, so that those monks may delight in continually imploring God’s mercy for us, for our wife and offspring, and for the stability of the whole empire granted to us by God and to be preserved forever by his boundless [Col. 1034D] mercy.

And so that this authority may be held more securely and, with the Lord’s help, better preserved through the ages, we have signed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor. Heliosar recognized this.

Issued on the third day before the Nones of February, in the second year, Christ being favorable, of our empire, indiction 8. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1035A]

### XLIII. For the Hispani Who Remained in the Kingdom of the Franks

[In Baluze, *Capitularies*, vol. I, p. 569.]

This is the privilege of grant that the emperor Louis made for the Hispani who had fled to him [against the oppression of the counts].

In the name of the Lord God and of our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence ordained, emperor Augustus.

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own faithful subjects, present and future, and also to our successors, that after the Hispani who had withdrawn themselves from the power of the Saracens and had placed themselves under the faith of us and of our father, we ordered and gave them a privilege of our authority explaining how they were to live in our kingdom with their counts and perform our service.

Some of these Hispani then brought a complaint to our ears containing two points. The first was that, when those Hispani came into our kingdom and occupied an abandoned place for habitation, they obtained it, by a privilege of our lord and father and of us, for possession by themselves and their successors. Those among them who were greater and more powerful came to the palace and received royal privileges. After receiving them, they attempted, by the authority of those privileges, either to drive away those among them who were poorer and weaker, although they appeared to have cultivated their own lands well, or to subject them to their service [Col. 1035C].

The second point was that others, likewise coming from Hispania, commended themselves to our counts or vassals, or even to the vassals of our counts, and received deserted places for habitation and cultivation. Once these places had been cultivated by them, their lords wished, on various pretexts, to expel them, retain them for their own labor, or give them to others in exchange for a reward.

Neither of these practices appears just or reasonable to us. Therefore, by this authority of our privilege, we decree and command that those who have deserved to receive either our privilege or that of our lord and father shall possess, by our grant, whatever they themselves and their dependents have cultivated from the wilderness.

The others who came with them and occupied deserted places shall possess, without disturbance from anyone, whatever uncultivated land they have brought under cultivation, both they themselves and their descendants; provided only that they perform our service with the person who received the privilege, in proportion to the possession that he holds.

Those who came later and commended themselves either to counts, to our vassals, or to their own peers, and received lands from them for habitation, shall possess those lands in future under the agreement and condition on which they received them, and shall leave them to their descendants.

We establish that this decree of our authority is to be preserved not only for those of the past and present, but also for those of the future who will yet come from those regions to our allegiance. We ordered seven privileges to be written in one uniform text concerning this constitution [Col. 1036A]: one to be kept at Narbonne, another at Carcassonne, a third at Roussillon, a fourth at Empúries, a fifth at Barcelona, a sixth at Girona, and a seventh at Béziers. We also ordered a copy of them to be kept in the archive of our palace, so that the aforesaid Hispani might receive and possess copies of those seven documents, and so that, by the copy retained in the palace, any complaint brought before us again might more easily be resolved.

And so that this constitution of our authority may possess firmer force and be more fully preserved through the ages by the faithful of the holy Church of God, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of the lord Louis, most serene emperor.

Arnald, in the place of Helisachar, recognized this.

Issued on the fourth day before the Ides of February, in the year—Christ being favorable—three of the empire of the lord Louis, most pious Augustus, indiction 9. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

### XLIV. For the Church of Mâcon. (Year 816.)

[In D. Bouquet, ibid., p. 487, from the instrument in vol. IV of *Gallia Christiana*, col. 265.]

In the name of the Lord God and of our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence ordained, emperor Augustus.

Let the advantage of our faithful subjects—namely, our counts and vassals, and also the vicars, centenarii, and envoys traveling throughout the empire granted to us by God—know that the venerable man Hildebold, bishop of the church of Mâcon, petitioned the height of our majesty that all who held benefices from the church over which he presides by God’s authority, built in honor of Saint Vincent the Martyr, should give every year the ninths and tithes from those benefices and contribute according to their means to the restoration of the buildings of that church.

We ordered this for everyone long ago in accordance with the command of the lord emperor; now, by these letters, we order and confirm it, recommending that all who hold, by our gift, benefices from the lands of the aforesaid church should not neglect to give the ninths and tithes each year to the aforesaid Bishop Hildebold or to his successors, without opposition or negligence [Col. 1036D]. Each person should also hasten to provide assistance according to his means for restoring the houses of that church. Let none of you who hold benefices from the aforesaid church presume to act against this command of ours; rather, let everyone observe it in all respects as it has been ordered by us, and as he wishes to retain the grace of God and of us, and the benefice itself.

And so that you may believe more certainly that this is our command, and so that it may be better preserved by you, we have ordered it sealed with our ring.

Issued on the fourth day before the Ides of February, in the year—Christ being favorable—3 [Col. 1037A] of the empire of the lord Louis, most pious Augustus, indiction 9. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, in the name of God.

### XLV. For the Monastery of Saint-Hilaire in the Diocese of Carcassonne. (Year 816.)

[Baluze, *Capitularies*, vol. II, p. 1409, from the archive of Saint-Hilaire.]

In the name of the Lord God and of our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence ordained, emperor Augustus.

If, for the love of God, we bestow suitable benefits upon places dedicated to divine worship and upon those serving him in those places, we do not doubt that an eternal reward will be repaid to us by the Lord. Therefore let the discernment and advantage of all our faithful subjects [Col. 1037B], present and future, know that the venerable man Monellus, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Hilaire, situated in the district of Carcassonne on the stream called the Leuchus, built in honor of Saint Saturninus the Martyr, where the aforesaid Saint Hilaire the Confessor also rests bodily, approached our clemency and brought before us a certain privilege of our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, most pious Augustus. It stated how our father had received that same monastery, at the petition of his predecessor, Abbot Nampio, under his protection and defense, namely so that the monks dwelling in that monastery might be permitted to live peacefully with all their possessions, without anyone’s disturbance [Col. 1037C].

For the sake of security, the aforesaid Abbot Monellus therefore petitioned us to establish under our protection and the safeguard of immunity the same monastery, together with its dependent cells, one called Garelianus and another called Saint Martin, and the villa beside that monastery called Salas, where there is a church built in honor of Saint Mary, ever-virgin, which we also granted to that monastery, together with the adjoining lands and boundaries of the aforesaid places.

For the love of God and in reverence for divine worship, it pleased us willingly to lend an ear to his prayers, and we decree that this privilege of our authority be made as a grant of immunity and protection. By it we order and command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, dare enter the churches, places, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery that it now justly and reasonably possesses, or that divine goodness may hereafter cause to be added to the property of that holy place, in order to hear cases, exact fines, demand lodging or provisions, take sureties, or unjustly constrain the men of that monastery, whether free or enslaved, who dwell upon its land; nor may anyone seek any restitutions or illicit pretexts, either now or in future, or presume to exact any of the things mentioned above [Col. 1037D].

Whatever the treasury might hope to exact from the properties of the aforesaid monastery, we grant in its entirety to that monastery for eternal reward, so that it may perpetually increase the provision for the poor and the support of the monks serving God there [Col. 1038A]. And whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this life, so long as the monks themselves are able to find among themselves men capable of governing that congregation according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, let them have permission, by this authority and consent of ours, to elect abbots. Thus may those monks who serve God there delight in continually imploring the boundless mercy of the Lord for us, for our wife and offspring, and for the stability of our entire empire, granted to us by God and to be preserved forever by his most merciful compassion [Col. 1038B].

Therefore, so that this authority may possess fuller force in the name of God and may be more truly believed and more carefully observed by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own faithful subjects, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

### XLVI. For the Church of Orléans. (Year 816.)

[Baluze, ibid., from the cartulary of the church of Orléans.]

In the name of the Lord and of our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence ordained, emperor Augustus.

If we confer some benefit through the gift of our liberality upon places dedicated to God, relieve ecclesiastical necessities at the petition of priests by our assistance, and protect them with imperial defense, we clearly believe that this will profit us both in passing through mortal life temporally and in obtaining eternal life happily. Let the discernment—or, rather, the concern—of all the faithful of holy God’s Church and of our own, both present and future, know that the venerable man Theodulf, archbishop of the Church of Orléans, presented to our sight an instrument of the lord and our father, Charles of blessed memory, the most pious Augustus. It contained the statement that this same father of ours and his predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, had caused the church of the Holy Cross—which, by God’s authority, Theodulf himself presides over—to remain under their protection and defense, and that by the instruments of their immunities this church had until then been protected and defended from the disturbance of judicial authority.

For the security of the matter, however, the same Bishop Theodulf petitioned us to follow the custom of our father and decree that an instrument of our immunity be made for the same church. We willingly assented to his petition and decreed that this instrument of our immunity be made for that holy see, out of love for divine worship and for the remedy of our soul. By it we prescribe and command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, nor any of our faithful, present or future, dare enter, in our times or in those to come, the churches, places, fields, or remaining possessions that the aforesaid church now justly and lawfully holds or possesses in any counties or territories within the dominion of our empire [Col. 1039A], nor those things that thereafter may be granted to that church by Catholic men, in order to hear cases, exact fines or taxes, impose lodgings or provisions, take sureties, distrain the men of that church—both free and enslaved—who dwell upon its lands, or demand any payments or unlawful pretexts; nor may anyone presume at all to exact the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid bishop and his successors be permitted to possess, in quiet and free order, the possessions of the aforesaid church, together with its dependent cells and the things or men belonging or pertaining to it, under the protection of our guardianship and immunity [Col. 1039B], with all disturbance by judicial authority removed; let them faithfully obey our imperial authority, and, together with the clergy and people subject to them, continually beseech God’s boundless clemency for our safety, that of our wife and offspring, and the stability of the whole empire granted to us by God and to be preserved without end through his most merciful compassion.

Whatever the right of the fisc could demand from the possessions of the aforesaid church, we have granted in full to that church, so that for all time it may serve as an increase and supplement for those serving God in that place, for the performance of divine service. And so that this authority may obtain fuller force in God’s name and be preserved more diligently for long ages by the faithful of holy God’s Church and by our own, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring [Col. 1039C].

## XLVII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT GERMANUS OF AUXERRE (816)

[At Baluze, same work, p. 1411, from the chartulary of Saint Germanus of Auxerre.]

In the name of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, centenarii, toll-collectors, fiscal agents, and all administering the public affairs, as well as to the other faithful of holy God’s Church and of our own, both present and future.

Let it be known that the venerable Alegrerus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Germanus, which is built in the suburb of the city of Auxerre, where the saint himself rests bodily, brought before us an instrument of our grandfather, King Pippin, and of Charles of blessed memory, our most pious father, the Augustus, as well as of our predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks. These instruments stated that, for the fruit of eternal reward, they had granted to the same monastery the toll from four ships that traveled along the Loire and other rivers for salt and other commerce, wherever the fisc was able to exact toll.

For the sake of securing the matter, the aforesaid Abbot Alegrerus petitioned us to follow the custom of our father and of our predecessors, the kings, and grant or confirm to the same monastery a benefit of this kind through an instrument of our authority [Col. 1040A]. Because of his prayers, out of love for God and reverence for Saint Germanus the bishop, we were pleased to have this instrument of our munificence made for the security of the monastery. By it we order and prescribe that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, dare exact from the aforesaid four ships—which travel along the Loire or other rivers within the dominion of our empire for the utility and necessity of the monastery—when they reach any cities, forts, ports, or other places, or from the men who supervise them, any toll, riverbank duty, port duty, bridge duty, passage duty, grass duty, meal duty, pasture duty [Col. 1040B], market duty, ferry duty, dust duty, any other levy, any census, or any payment; but by this authority of ours it shall be lawful for the ships and the men who are to supervise them, with the goods they carry, to go and return freely and safely, without anyone’s unlawful opposition or detention. If they remain for any length of time in any place, or buy or sell anything, nothing at all shall be exacted from them, as stated above.

And so that this authority may obtain fuller force in God’s name and be more truly believed and more diligently preserved by the faithful of holy God’s Church and by our own, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Given on 10 March, in the third year, with Christ favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, the most pious Augustus, indiction 9. Enacted at the royal palace of Aachen, happily in God’s name. Amen.

## XLVIII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF CORMARICUM (816)

[At Baluze, same work, from the chartulary of Saint Martin of Tours.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the mercy of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.
