If we willingly assent to the petitions of God’s servants who knock at our ears concerning various ecclesiastical necessities, and extend assistance so that they may serve more abundantly the divine power in places dedicated to the Lord [Col. 1040D], we confidently believe that this will undoubtedly bring us advantage both in passing through temporal mortal life and in attaining the future life happily.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful—namely, bishops, abbots, illustrious men, dukes, counts, household officers, fiscal officials, vicars, centenarii and their subordinates, as well as our envoys traveling throughout our empire, and also the other faithful of holy God’s Church and of our own, present and future—that the venerable man Fredegisus, abbot of the monastery of our special patron Saint Martin, where the venerable body of that most illustrious man rests, came before our serenity carrying the immunities of the ancient kings of the Franks, of our grandfather, the former King Pippin, and also of our lord and father Charles, the most serene emperor of pious memory.

By these instruments they had decreed that the same monastery should dwell peacefully in God’s service, and had placed under the protection of their immunity all the possessions of the aforesaid monastery throughout our kingdom, with Christ’s generosity: in Austrasia, Neustria, Burgundy, Aquitaine, Provence, Italy, and the other parts of our kingdom; possessions granted not only by orthodox rulers but also by other faithful people, or legally transferred for its use through any contracts or documentary titles. They had rendered these possessions immune from every public service and judicial exaction under the protection of their immunity.

This gift, bestowed upon the same monastery and also upon the monastery of Cormaricum, built from the possessions of Saint Martin, is evidently preserved inviolate to the present by God’s assent. For the sake of securing the matter, he humbly petitioned with all the prayers at his command that a benefit of this kind be made by our authority for the aforesaid venerable monastery. Because of his petition, out of love for God and reverence for blessed Martin, we were pleased in every way to grant our assent [lacuna].

Therefore we wish and decree that all the possessions of the same monastery, together with the men subject to it, remain in every respect under the protection of our defense. We therefore prescribe and command that no public judge, nor any administrator of public affairs, of higher or lower rank, presume to enter, in order to hear cases according to judicial custom [Col. 1041C], the churches, villas, or remaining possessions that it now justly and lawfully possesses in certain provinces or territories of our empire, or those that thereafter divine piety may will to be increased in the right of the monastery; nor may anyone exact fines, tolls, lodgings, provisions, or taxes, as is contained in the instrument of our lord and father; take sureties; distrain men, both free and enslaved, dwelling upon the land of the monastery; or demand any public services, payments, or unlawful pretexts by which the same monastery and those subject to it might unjustly suffer harm. In our times or in those to come, let no rash person dare to claim for himself unlawful power to do this [Col. 1041D].

Whatever, therefore, was due from the possessions mentioned above of the same monastery by right of the fisc, and whatever we find to have been granted by our predecessors, we willingly wish to be granted in its entirety to the same monastery through the gift of our generosity, so that, with the fisc’s dominion removed, it may serve for the preparation of the lamps of the basilica of Saint Martin and for the support of the poor and clergy serving the Lord in that place as a supplement [lacuna].

If anyone should dare to break out into such audacity as to become a violator of this our decree, let him know that, as is contained in the decree of our lord and father [Col. 1042A], he will not only fall under our displeasure but will also be punished by a penalty of six hundred solidi of gold, smelted pure; of this, two parts shall be received by the administrators of the aforesaid monastery and the third by the right of the fisc. It is fitting and just that a violator of the decrees of so many pious kings, our predecessors, and of our own decree should have such a penalty, so that he may recognize that he is rightly accused of such presumption and that fear may be instilled in others, lest they attempt to do the same by any act of audacity—so that no one, of course, may dare to violate the royal benefits reverently bestowed upon places dedicated to God.

Therefore we wish and decree that, with all disturbance by judicial authority removed, the aforesaid abbot and his successors of the monastery, together with all the men subject or belonging to them [Col. 1042B], remain in quiet order under the protection of our immunity and defense; and that, faithfully obeying our imperial authority, they continually beseech God’s boundless clemency, together with the clergy entrusted to them, for our safety, that of our wife and offspring, and the stability of the whole empire granted to us by God and to be preserved forever through his most gracious compassion.

If anything has been taken away from the possessions of the aforesaid monastery through the lukewarmness or negligence of abbots or through the order of judges, we command that it be completely restored by our authority. And so that this authority may have inviolable effect and be more truly believed by the faithful of holy God’s Church and by our own, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring [Col. 1042C].

**Sign of Louis, most serene emperor [lacuna]; in place of Helisachar I have reviewed and subscribed.**

Given on 30 August, in the third year, with Christ favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, the most pious Augustus, indiction 10. Enacted at the royal palace of Aachen, happily in God’s name. Amen.

*(The seal is golden.)*

## XLIX. [Note: [Col. 1041D] Robert, bishop of Maclovium, testifies that he saw this decree, in these words: “Date of this viewing made by us, Robert, bishop of Maclovium, on the Monday before the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, in the year 1294.”] FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MEVENNUS (816)

[At D. Bouquet, *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. VI, p. 489, in the proofs of the *History of Brittany*, p. 20.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering [Col. 1042D], emperor Augustus.

When we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants out of inward love for divine worship [Note: [Col. 1042D] Perhaps read “out of love for divine worship.”], we believe that the gift of heavenly grace is bestowed upon us by the Lord. Therefore let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, that a certain man, Helogar, bishop of Aleth, brought before us an instrument that the lord and our father, Charles, the most serene Augustus of blessed memory, had ordered to be made at the petition of the church over which, by God’s authority, he presides.

It contained the statement that, at the time of the rebellion, when the houses of the churches of Saint Mevennus and Saint Judicael—which are in the place called Wadel, and also in another place on the island called Machuti—were devastated by enemies who set them on fire, not only the church treasury and the liturgical vessels required for ecclesiastical offices perished, but also the documents [lacuna] by which the aforesaid churches had been endowed were burned and destroyed. The same father of ours, at his supplication, had established through the same instrument that, without anyone’s contradiction or impediment, Bishop Helogar himself [lacuna] of those things that had belonged to the places of Saint Mevennus and Saint Judicael, as well as Saint Machuti, so that all the possessions of the aforesaid churches, wherever they had been justly and reasonably established in various places at that time, or whatever might thereafter be granted there through equity’s [lacuna], should not only remain perpetually in the dominion of the aforesaid churches. Moreover, no one should ever presume to remove or diminish anything from them contrary to justice, or dare to create any impediment or accusation.

For the security of this matter he implored our clemency to add our authority to the paternal instrument. We were pleased to lend a willing ear to his petition and, out of love for God and reverence for the aforesaid holy places, to have this instrument of our authority and confirmation made. By it we prescribe and command that, just as the aforesaid churches were confirmed and granted by the Lord and our father, so by this authority of ours they shall firmly and inviolably hold and possess whatever the aforesaid churches now justly and lawfully possess [Col. 1043C].

No public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, shall dare in our times or in those to come to enter the churches, places, fields, or remaining possessions that they now justly and reasonably possess within the dominion of our empire, or those that divine piety may thereafter will to be increased in the right of the same churches, in order to hear cases, exact fines, impose lodgings [or] provisions, impose (*ponendos*) [or take (*tollendos*)] sureties, unjustly distrain men, both free and enslaved, dwelling upon the land of those churches, or demand any payments or unlawful pretexts; nor shall anyone presume at all to exact the things mentioned above [Col. 1043D].

Rather, let the aforesaid bishop and his successors be permitted to possess in quiet order, under the protection of our immunity, the possessions of the aforesaid churches together with all the things and men subject to them; let them faithfully obey our imperial authority, and let them, together with the clergy and people subject to them, freely beseech the Lord’s mercy for our stability, that of our wife and offspring, and of the whole empire granted to us by the Lord and to be preserved by him.

If, however, a dispute should arise concerning those same possessions that had been legally held by the prelates of the aforesaid churches before the aforementioned burning, so that it became necessary to argue their case lawfully in any place, then by this authority of ours let them defend those possessions and the serfs in the same way as they could have been defended by law through those same documents, had they not been lost.

This authority, therefore, so that it may possess firmer force and be believed more truly and certainly by everyone, we have confirmed below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Louis the emperor.**

Given on 26 March, in the [third] year, with Christ favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, the most pious Augustus, indiction 9. Enacted at the royal palace of Aachen, happily in God’s name. Amen.

## L. FOR THE CHURCH OF CAMBRAI (816)

[At D. Bouquet, *Collection of Histories*, vol. VI, p. 490, from John Carpentier, in the proofs of the *History of Cambrai*, p. 1.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.

When we favor the just petitions of God’s servants, etc. Accordingly, we confirm by this instrument of our authority the immunities of our grandfather, King Pippin, and of our father Charles, the most excellent emperor of blessed memory. They stated that the same father of ours and the preceding kings had held the aforesaid see—which is dedicated to the honor of Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin—for the love of God and the tranquility of the brothers residing there under the fullest protection and defense of immunity, etc.

**Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.**

I, Durandus the deacon, have reviewed this in place of Helisachar.

Given on 14 April, in the third year, with Christ favorable, of our lord Louis, the most pious Augustus, indiction 9. Enacted at the royal palace of Aachen, in God’s name. Amen.

## LI. FOR THE MONASTERY OF FOSSATUM (816)

[At Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. II, p. 721, from the authentic Fossatum document.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.

When we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants out of love for divine worship [Col. 1044D], we do not doubt that heavenly grace protects us. Therefore let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, that our faithful Bego reported to our serenity that he had found a certain small monastery in the county of Paris, in the place called Fossatum, built in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of holy Mary ever-virgin, situated on the river Marne, where monks had once lived under the holy Rule, almost destroyed; and that, for the benefit of his soul, he had undertaken the place with labor and taken care to restore it and return it to its former state.

After completing these things, he came before our presence and commended the same monastery to us, together with an abbot named Benedict and the monks entrusted to that abbot for governance [Col. 1045A]. He implored us that thereafter, under our protection and the guardianship of our immunity, just as the other abbots of monks throughout the empire granted to us by God’s favor remain, so we should cause him, together with the monastery, its monks, and the possessions and men lawfully subject to that monastery, to remain as well.

Because we recognized his petition as reasonable, indeed pleasing to God, we willingly accepted it; and through these imperial letters of ours, just as he asked, so we granted it. Therefore we wish the aforesaid abbot and the monks dwelling in the aforesaid monastery to remain under our protection and the guardianship of our immunity, together with the possessions they are now known to have or may thereafter lawfully acquire.

We prescribe and decree in every way that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, dare at any time enter the churches, places, fields, or remaining possessions of the aforesaid monastery, which it appears now to possess justly and reasonably in any counties or territories, whatever was granted there for divine love, or whatever divine piety may thereafter will to be increased in the right of that holy place, in order to hear cases, exact fines, impose lodgings or provisions, take sureties, unjustly distrain the men of the monastery, both free and enslaved, [who] appear to dwell upon its land, or demand any petitions or unlawful pretexts; nor may anyone presume at all to exact the things mentioned above [Col. 1045C].

Whatever, therefore, the fisc could hope to obtain from the possessions of the aforesaid monastery, we grant entirely to the aforesaid monastery for eternal reward, so that throughout perpetual times it may serve as an increase for the support of the poor and the stipends of the monks serving God in that place.

And whenever the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this life through divine calling, as long as the monks themselves are able to find among themselves men capable of governing that community according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, let them have permission, by this authority and consent of ours, to elect abbots. Thus may it please them continually to beseech the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of our whole empire [Col. 1045D], granted to us by God and to be preserved by him [Col. 1046A].

And so that this authority may remain unshaken in our times and in those to come, with the Lord’s protection, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most pious emperor.**

I, Durandus the deacon, have reviewed and subscribed in place of Helisachar.

Given on 20 June, in the third year, with Christ favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, the most pious Augustus, indiction 8. Enacted at Aachen, at the royal palace, happily in God’s name. Amen.

## LII. [Note: [Col. 1045D] It appears in Schoepflin’s *Alsatian Diplomas*, vol. I, p. 62, but not sufficiently correctly.] FOR THE MONASTERY OF BODONIS, OR BON-MOUTIER (816)

[Col. 1046B] [At Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, vol. II, proofs, p. 159, from the ancient chartulary of the abbey of Andlau, fourteenth century.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.

If, out of love for God, we bestow suitable benefits upon places dedicated to divine worship and upon those serving him in those places, we do not doubt that the reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us by the Lord. Therefore let the discernment of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable man Doddo, abbot, who appears to govern the cell called the monastery of Bodonis [Note: [Col. 1045D] The monastery of Bodonis was founded in the Vosges mountains near Castellion and Badonisvillare, in the valley now called Val de Bon-Moutier. It received its name from Saint Bodo, also called Leudinus, bishop of Toul, who around the year 670 founded at that place a monastery of holy virgins and placed his daughter, named Teutberga, over them. See the history of the bishops of Toul in Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, vol. I, proofs, pp. 163 and 216 of the new edition, and Stilting, in the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. III, September, p. 841. Bodo subjected the monastery of Bodonis to his church of Toul, having obtained privileges concerning it from the supreme pontiffs Agapetus and Gregory. At first a monastery of nuns, it later became an abbey of men of the Order of Saint Benedict. King Lothair took it from the church of Toul under Bishop Arnulf; after Lothair’s death in 869, when his kingdom was divided the following year, the monastery of Bodonis was assigned to Louis the German. His son, Emperor Charles the Fat, granted the monastery of Bodonis in 884 to the abbey of Andlau. We shall give the charter in its proper place. Nor did that abbey retain it for long, since in 912 Charles the Simple restored the monastery of Bodonis to Drogo and his church of Toul. Calmet, same work, p. 334. The monastery of Bodonis was later called the Abbey of the Holy Savior, which in 1569 was transferred to Domèvre, near Blâmont.]—situated in the county of Albins [Note: [Col. 1046D] The county of Albins, also called Albegia, was a county of Lorraine situated near Blâmont, as Schoepflin proves against others, *Illustrated Alsace*, vol. I, p. 670. Its name perhaps derives from the little river Vizuzia, in whose name the German word *Wifs* means “white.”] on the river Vizuzia [Note: [Col. 1046D] Today the village of Vesouze.], built [Col. 1046C] in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, and of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, as well as of Saint Michael the archangel and the other saints, presented to our sight the immunity of our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, the most pious Augustus.

It contained the statement that the same father of ours and the preceding kings had always held the aforesaid cell under their fullest protection and the guardianship of immunity, out of love for God and for the tranquility of the handmaids residing there. For the security of the matter, the aforesaid Abbot Doddo petitioned us to follow the custom of our father and of our predecessors, the kings, and decree that an instrument of our immunity of this kind be made for that cell, out of love for God [Col. 1046D] and reverence for that holy place [Col. 1047A]. We willingly assented to his petition, granted everything in this way, and confirmed it all through this decree of ours.

Therefore, prescribing, we command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, dare in our times or in those to come enter the churches, places, fields, or remaining possessions that it now justly and reasonably possesses within the dominion of our empire, or those that divine piety may thereafter will to be increased in the right of that holy place, in order to hear cases, exact fines or taxes, impose lodgings or provisions, take sureties, unjustly distrain the men of the same cell, both free and enslaved, dwelling upon its land, or demand any payments or unlawful pretexts; nor may anyone presume at all to exact the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors be permitted to possess the possessions of the aforesaid cell in quiet order under the protection of our immunity. Whatever the fisc may be able to hope for from them, we grant entirely to the aforesaid cell for eternal recompense, so that throughout perpetual times it may serve as an increase for the support of the poor and the stipends of the handmaids serving God there. Thus may it please those handmaids of God who serve God there continually to beseech the Lord for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of our whole empire, granted to us by God and to be preserved by him.

And so that this authority may remain unshaken in our times and in those to come, with the Lord’s protection, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring [Col. 1047C].

**Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.**

I, Durandus the deacon, have reviewed this in place of Helisachar.

Given on 13 January, in the second year, with Christ favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, the most pious Augustus, indiction 9. Enacted at the royal palace of Aachen [Note: [Col. 1047D] Germanus, in Mabillon, *On Diplomatic Matters*, book IV, p. 246, and Besselius, in the *Gottweig Chronicle*, vol. II, p. 453, discuss at length the palace at Aachen.] happily in God’s name. Amen.

## LIII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF AMMIATUM (816)

[Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, p. 590, in the section on the bishopric of Chiusi.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence, emperor Augustus.

When we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants out of love for divine worship, we do not doubt that heavenly grace protects us. Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of holy God’s Church, present and future, that the venerable man Audoaldus, abbot of the monastery of the Holy Savior, situated on Mount Amiata in the territory of Chiusi, brought before our sight an instrument of immunity belonging to our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, the most pious Augustus. It contained the statement that he had always held the aforesaid monastery under the fullest protection and defense of immunity, out of love for God and for the tranquility of the monks residing there.

For the sake of securing the matter, he arranged that we should join our authority to the paternal authority. We were pleased to lend a willing ear to his petition and to have this decree of our authority made, by which we prescribe and command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, dare ever enter the churches, places, fields, or remaining possessions of the aforesaid monastery that it now justly and lawfully possesses, or those that divine piety may thereafter will to be increased in the right of that place, in order to hear cases, exact fines (*freda*; printed *feuda*), impose lodgings or provisions, take sureties, or distrain the men of the monastery, both free and enslaved, dwelling upon its land; nor may anyone enter to compel them to military expeditions, or demand any payments or unlawful pretexts; nor may anyone presume at all to exact the things mentioned above [Col. 1048B].

The same instrument also contained the statement that the lord emperor had confirmed to that monastery the possessions—namely, the church of Saint Peter at Carmarita, the cell of Saint Savinus, and those of Saint Restituta, Saint Peter, and Saint Stephen at Tarquinii, together with their appurtenances. We perpetually confirm these possessions to the aforesaid monastery, to hold them just as our lord and father confirmed them through his decree.

We have also granted to the same holy monastery, just as our lord and father granted, that whenever the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this life through divine calling, as long as the monks are able to find among themselves men capable of governing that community, they shall, by this authority and consent of ours—or by permission of our beloved son Bernard, the king—have the right to elect abbots. Thus may it please the monks who appear to serve the Lord there continually to beseech the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of the whole empire entrusted to us by the Lord and to be preserved by him.

And so that this authority may remain unshaken in our times and in those to come, with the Lord’s protection, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.**

[Col. 1048D]

Given on 17 November, in the third year, with Christ favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, the most pious Augustus, indiction 10.

Enacted at the palace of Compiègne, happily in God’s name. Amen.

## LIV. THE PACT MADE BETWEEN THE BISHOP OF CONSTANZ AND THE MONASTERY OF SAINT GALL IS CONFIRMED (816)

[Neutgart, *Alemannic Codex*, from the diplomatic collection of D. Emmanuel de Haller, provincial prefect of Neuwied, among the Bernese.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus [Col. 1049A] Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.

If we favor the just and reasonable petitions of the servants of God for the love of divine worship, we do not doubt that we are fortified by heavenly grace. Therefore let it be known to the diligence of all our faithful, both present and future, that, when the monks from the monastery of Saint Gall, situated in the Durgouve district on the river called Petrosa [Note: [Col. 1049D] Steinach.], approached our Serenity, they brought us a privilege of our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, the most devout Augustus. It contained the following provision: Sidonius, bishop of the city of Constance, and John, abbot of the aforesaid monastery, had established and confirmed in writing—also presenting the document to that same lord and father of ours—that, to prevent future disagreement and to ensure the peace of the monks serving God there, the aforesaid abbot and his successors were to pay each year to the aforesaid bishop or his successors one ounce of gold and one horse worth one pound, provided only that the monks serving God there might live and remain in peace, and that nothing further should be demanded by the bishops of the aforesaid church from the property of the aforesaid monastery. Once this census had been paid, the same monks were to be permitted to live securely, without anyone molesting them or diminishing their possessions.

For the sake of confirming this arrangement, and for the future peace of the monks serving God there, we have wished to confirm once again, by this imperial document of ours, the authority of our father. Therefore we order and decree that, just as it is contained in the letters of our father—which he ordered to be written and confirmed at the request of the bishop of the aforesaid city—so, with the Lord’s help, it shall henceforth be perpetually preserved by us, by our faithful, and by our successors. And so that this authority of our decree may obtain firmer force in God’s name and be more faithfully preserved by our faithful, we have ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

I, Durandus, deacon, have examined and subscribed it in the place of Helisachar.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February [Note: [Col. 1049D] The twenty-seventh of January, which was the final day of the eleventh year of Louis the Pious.], in the second year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most devout Augustus, [Col. 1049D] indiction 9 [Note: [Col. 1050D] Indiction 9 fell in the year 816.]. Enacted at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in God’s name. Amen.

## LV. FOR THE MONASTERY OF MORBACH (Year 816)

[At Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, p. 18, from the cartulary of Morbach.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, centenaries, toll-collectors, agents, our envoys traveling about, and all who administer public affairs, as well as to all other faithful of the holy Church of God and of ours, both present and future.

Since the venerable abbot Guntrammus of the monastery called the Vivarium of Pilgrims, situated in the duchy of Alsace on the river Morbach, constructed in honor of Saint Deodgar, Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, brought before us a privilege of our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, the most devout Augustus, it was contained therein that he had granted to that monastery and to the monks dwelling there exemption from tolls on ships traveling along any rivers, as well as on carts and pack animals carrying the necessities of that monastery and of the community serving God there, whether at Marsal and Iris or wherever they might go, conduct business, or sell goods; no one was to presume to exact or demand a toll from them.

For the sake of confirmation, the aforesaid abbot requested that, following the custom of our father, we grant or confirm this benefit of our authority to the same monastery. Because of the love of God and reverence for that holy place, we gladly assented to his petition and wished this privilege of our munificence to be issued for the sake of confirmation. By it we order and command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, shall presume to seek or exact any toll or exaction from ships, carts, pack animals, or other vehicles carrying the necessities of that monastery, in any kind of commerce from whatever source the fisc is entitled to collect a toll.

Rather, wherever, within the jurisdiction of our empire, they may have access for the utility and necessity of that monastery—to whatever cities, castles, ports, bridges, crossings, or other places—no one among them, nor any of the men responsible for supervising such matters, shall dare to receive or exact from them any toll, as we have said, or any levy, census, or payment. Instead, by this authority of ours, it shall be lawful for the ships, carts, pack animals, and other vehicles, and for the men responsible for supervising them, to go and return freely and securely with what they carry, without anyone unlawfully opposing or detaining them. If they remain anywhere for some time, or buy or sell anything, absolutely nothing shall be exacted from them, as has been stated.

And so that this authority may possess fuller force in God’s name and be more truly believed and preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by ours, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Durandus, deacon, examined it in the place of Elisachar.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, in the third year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most devout Augustus, [Col. 1051A] indiction 9. Enacted at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in God’s name. Amen.

## LVI. FOR THE SAME MONASTERY (Year 816)

[At Martène, ibid., from the cartulary of Morbach.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

Let it be known to all our faithful, both present and future, that the venerable abbot Guntrammus of the monastery called the Vivarium of Pilgrims, situated in the duchy of Alsace on the river Morbach, constructed in honor of Saint Leodegar, Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and holy Mary ever-virgin, brought us a privilege of our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, the most serene Augustus. It stated that the free men who had been subject to the aforesaid monastery in the time of our grandfather, King Pippin, were at that time attached to that house of God.

The same abbot Guntrammus requested that, just as in the time of our grandfather, King Pippin, and of our aforesaid lord and father Charles, those men had been subject to the monastery, so they might also be subject in our time. Therefore, ordering and commanding, we decree that, as is contained in that same privilege, no one exercising judicial authority, nor any of our envoys traveling about, shall presume to disturb, bring a charge against, or inflict any unjust opposition upon the aforesaid free men who served the aforesaid monastery in the time of our lord and father. Rather, let them be permitted, according to their custom and as well as they are able, to serve that monastery and to be obedient men.

And so that this order of ours may be believed with greater certainty, we have ordered it to be sealed below with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Durandus, deacon, have examined it in the place of Helisachar.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, in the third year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most devout Augustus, indiction 9. Enacted at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in God’s name. Amen.

## LVII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF FOSSATUM [Col. 1051D] (Year 816)

[At D. Bouquet, *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, p. 492, from Gérard Dubois, *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, p. 324.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

Let it be known to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, centenaries, toll-collectors, auction officials, and all who administer public affairs, as well as to all other faithful of the holy Church of God and of ours, both present [Col. 1052A] and future, that, at the petition of the illustrious count Bego, we have taken under our protection and defense the monastery situated in the Paris district, in the place called Fossatum, constructed in honor of blessed Mary, Mother of God, and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, on the river Marne, together with its abbot, named Benedict, and the brothers dwelling there, as well as the property and men lawfully subject to that monastery.

He asked that, whenever it pleased the monks dwelling in that monastery to send their agents to any part of our empire for the purpose of conducting business, with carts, pack animals, or by ship, or with any kind of merchandise, they should have permission to travel wherever they wished without anyone molesting or opposing them.

We gladly agreed to this petition as an act of our charity and ordered these letters of our authority to be issued. Through them we order, for the sake of all our faithful, present and future, that wherever the envoys of the aforesaid abbot or of his successors are sent within the jurisdiction of our empire for the purpose of conducting business, no one shall presume to receive or exact from them toll, or what is commonly called *ripaticum*, *rotaticum*, *pontaticum*, *portaticum*, or [Note: [Col. 1051D] Cointius, vol. VIII of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, reads *carvaticum*, which he considers incorrectly written for *carnaticum*. He nevertheless says that *carvaticum* is the same as *carraticum*, namely, a tax for passing carts, and interprets *carnaticum* as a kind of tax levied on animals. I, however, think that *tranaticum* should be read here.] *taritaticum* or *cispitaticum*, nor *salutaticum*, nor any census, levy, or compulsory payment, nor any other return or due.

Rather, let both them and their men, and all their goods, travel in peace and freely conduct their business. Wherever they have access—to whatever cities, ports, or places—[Col. 1052C] they shall suffer no disturbance, detention, or opposition from any of our faithful. Wherever they are sent, whether by ship or overland, they shall be able, by this authority of ours, to go and return safely and peacefully with everything they carry.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and observed more diligently by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by ours, we have ordered it to be sealed below with the impression of our ring.

Durandus, deacon, examined it in the place of Helisachar.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the third year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most devout Augustus, [Note: [Col. 1052D] Correct to “indiction 9”; Cointius reads it this way in the cited passage.] indiction 10. Enacted at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in God’s name. Amen.

[Col. 1052D]

## LVIII. FOR THE CHURCH OF SAINT MAURICE OF ANGERS (Year 816)

[At D. Bouquet, ibid., p. 496, from Sammarthanus, vol. II of *Gallia Christiana*, p. 216.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If by a gift of our generosity we confer some benefits upon places dedicated to God, relieve ecclesiastical needs at the petition of priests by our assistance, and protect them by imperial defense, we clearly believe that this will benefit us both in passing through mortal life temporally and in attaining eternal life happily.

Let the prudence and advantage of all our faithful, present and future, know meanwhile that the venerable Benedict, bishop of the city of Angers, presented to our sight a privilege of immunity and of transport by ship belonging to our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, the most devout Augustus. It contained the provision that not only that same father of ours, but also his predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, had established the church of Saint Maurice, over which that bishop presides by God’s will, under their name and protection, together with the monasteries and cells subject to it and the property and men belonging or pertaining to it. By the authority of their immunities, they had also ensured that three ships traveling along the channel of the Loire or along the other rivers flowing into the Loire had remained protected and defended from the interference of judicial authority.

For the confirmation of this matter, the aforesaid bishop Benedict requested that, following the custom of our father and of our royal predecessors, we decree such a privilege of immunity for the love of God and in reverence for the blessed martyr Maurice, in whose name and honor the church is dedicated. We gladly granted his petition and decreed that this privilege of our authority should be issued for that church, for the sake of immunity and protection, out of love for divine worship [Col. 1053C] and for the remedy of our soul.

By it we prescribe and command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, shall dare in our time or in future to enter the churches, places, or fields, or to approach the aforesaid ships or the remaining possessions that the aforesaid church now justly and lawfully holds or possesses in any districts or territories within the jurisdiction of our empire, or whatever divine piety may henceforth add to the rights of that church, for the hearing of cases, the exaction of fines, the provision of lodging or supplies, the taking of sureties, or the distraint of the men of that church; nor shall anyone seek any compulsory services or unlawful pretexts, or presume to exact anything mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid bishop and his successors be permitted to possess peacefully, under the protection and immunity of ours, the property of the aforesaid church of Saint Maurice, together with everything subject to it and the property and men belonging or pertaining to it, as well as the aforesaid three ships, with all interference by judicial authority removed; let them faithfully obey our empire and, together with the clergy and people subject to them, continually implore God’s immense mercy for the safety of us, our wife and offspring, and also of the whole empire entrusted to us by God and to be preserved forever by his most merciful compassion.

Whatever the fisc could have demanded from the property of the aforesaid church, we have granted to that church in full, so that it may forever serve as an increase and supplement for carrying out the service of God.

Therefore, so that this authority may possess fuller force in God’s name, and may be more truly believed and more diligently preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by ours, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

[Col. 1054B]

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Durandus, deacon, examined it in the place of Helisachar.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, in the [third] year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most serene emperor, indiction 10. Enacted at the palace of Salmunciacum, happily, in God’s name.

## LIX. FOR THE CHURCH OF TREVES (Year 816)

[Hontheim, *History of Treves*, p. 167.]

In the name of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If by a gift of our generosity we confer some benefit upon places dedicated to God [Col. 1054C], relieve ecclesiastical needs at the petition of priests by our assistance, and protect them by imperial defense, we clearly believe that this will benefit us both in passing through mortal life temporally and in attaining eternal life happily.

Therefore let the prudence of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable Henry [Hettinus], archbishop of the holy church of Treves, presented to our sight a privilege of immunity belonging to our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, the most devout Augustus. [Note: [Col. 1053D] The privilege of immunity, etc. We assigned that charter of immunity of Charles to the year 773 (*Patrologia*, vol. XCVII, col. 1049); it is certainly suspect, not so much in substance as in form. For it sometimes happened that, when genuine diplomas had been lost but their contents had been quoted by later generations, substitutes were fabricated, though made as close as possible to the wording of the lost originals.]

It contained the provision that not only that same father of ours, but also his predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, had established the church of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, over which that archbishop presides by God’s will, under their name and protection, together with the monasteries, cells, basilicas, villages, and castles belonging to that see, and the property and men belonging to it, under the title of immunity and the protection of defense.

Specifically, no one was to summon the men of that church to court through *malbobergi*, [Note: [Col. 1053D] *Malbobergi*: a type of court. For *malberg* means a judgment held in an elevated place, the judgment hill, the mountain court. Compare Eckhard on the Salic Law, p. 14, where he says: “It is well known that courts were formerly held on hills, including hills made by human labor, and in the open air, so that the judges could be seen by the whole people. Hills of this kind remain in our villages or districts, and usually have a lime tree or another kind of tree in the middle, providing shelter in rainy weather.” Charlemagne did indeed change the custom, bringing under cover the courts that had ordinarily been held in the open air. *Capitularies*, book III, chapter 57: “In places where they customarily hold public courts, a building should be constructed that can be used in winter and summer.” See also book IV, chapter 28, while retaining the meaning of *malberg*.] nor by any other means; nor was anyone to presume to exact fines or tolls, or to demand supplies at their public or private hearings.

For the confirmation of this matter, the aforesaid archbishop Heti requested that, following the custom of our father and of our royal predecessors, we decree such a privilege of immunity for that church, out of love for God and reverence for Saint Peter. We gladly assented to his petition and decreed that this privilege of our authority should be issued for that church, for the sake of immunity and protection, out of love for divine worship and for the remedy of our soul.

By it we prescribe and command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, shall dare in our time or in future to enter the monasteries, churches, castles, villages, estates, places, [Col. 1055B] fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid church, which that church now justly and lawfully holds and possesses both beyond and beside the Rhine, or around the Loire, in districts or territories within the jurisdiction of our empire, or whatever divine piety may henceforth add to the rights of that holy place, for the hearing of cases, the exaction of fines, taxes, or any *conjectus*, [Note: [Col. 1056D] “To exact any *conjectus*.” A *conjectus* is a contribution or collection, especially one paid by the people to the royal envoys while they were traveling.] the provision of lodging or supplies, the taking of sureties, or the distraint of the men of that church; nor shall anyone seek any compulsory services or unlawful pretexts, or presume to exact anything mentioned above, nor demand toll, as is contained in the privilege of our lord and father.

Rather, let the aforesaid archbishop and his successors be permitted to possess peacefully, under the protection and immunity of ours, the property of the aforesaid church of Saint Peter, together with everything subject to it and the property and men belonging or pertaining to it, with all interference by judicial authority removed; let them faithfully obey our empire and, together with the clergy and people subject to them, pray to God for the safety of us, our wife and children, and also of the whole empire entrusted to us by God and to be preserved forever by his most merciful compassion, etc.

Therefore, so that this authority may possess fuller force in God’s name and may be more truly believed and more diligently preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by ours, we have also confirmed it below with our own hand [Col. 1055D] and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Durandus, deacon, examined it in the place of Helisachar.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, in the third year, with Christ propitious, of Louis the most devout Augustus, indiction 10. Enacted at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in God’s name. Amen.

[Col. 1056A]

## LX. FOR THE MONASTERY OF FULDA (Year 816)

[Schannat, *Fulda Traditions*.]

In the name of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the grace of God emperor of the Romans, Augustus.

Since we know that it is our responsibility to care not only for the government of the kingdom but also for the administration of the holy Church, and especially to serve devotedly the needs of Christ’s faithful, we therefore do not dare to conceal in silence the things we do for the honor of God and the love of eternal life concerning the churches and monasteries of God’s servants, lest, through the ignorance of those who succeed us, they perhaps—God forbid—be violated by any importunate unbelievers. [Col. 1056B]

We therefore make known to your fidelity that our faithful secretary, Rabanus, venerable abbot of the holy church of Fulda, approached the excellence of our highness and explained to us the care and concern he devotes to acquiring the relics of the saints, both from the city of Rome and from various cities where many martyrs surrendered their bodies to sufferings so that they might deserve to have everlasting crowns in the heavenly kingdom.

The same venerable man, Abbot Rabanus, therefore asked the excellence of our highness that, by our authority, he might send his envoys wherever in the world he wished, and especially and above all to the city of Rome, and, bearing letters of our authority, request the most sacred ashes of the holy martyrs. Out of the generosity of our munificence, we granted him permission to write and send, by the authority of our decree, wherever in the world he wished, for the aforesaid business and request for sacred relics, both to the apostolic authority and to other faithful persons.

Since his labor of such devoted diligence was therefore not fruitless, we recently learned that he had acquired from distant regions the body of Saint Venantius the martyr and had placed it with the greatest honor in the church of Saint John the Baptist. The merits of this martyr have become widely celebrated in the church of Fulda through reports of miracles: the sick come and are healed; the demon-possessed, and they are delivered; the paralyzed, and they are cured; the blind, and they are given sight; and the human race is saved from every kind of infirmity by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1056D], through the help and intercession of Saint Venantius.

Moved by divine prompting by the report of this deed, we give thanks to God and to his holy martyr Venantius, who in our times and in our lands has deigned to visit his people and graciously to assist wretched mortals in their various needs and troubles.

Therefore, at the request and petition of our aforesaid secretary, Abbot Rabanus, we offer to God, to Saint Boniface, and to the holy martyr Venantius, in the aforesaid monastery of Saint John, certain property of ours: namely, the estate called Urespringen, with all its little estates and villages, indeed with all its appurtenances and dependencies—that is, lands, fields, meadows, woods, cultivated fields, pastures, garden plots, enclosures, houses, households, waters, orchards, cultivated and uncultivated lands, movable and immovable property, outgoings and revenues, roads and trackless places. We transfer and donate the whole of it, complete and intact, and wish it to remain transferred in perpetuity to the aforesaid place, for the remedy of our soul and in memory of our pious father, the emperor Charles.

We establish this conditionally: that remembrance of us be made among the brothers of the monastery of Fulda both more attentively and more frequently, so that those brothers may be seen to be sustained by our offerings.

It has therefore pleased us to secure this donation with a privilege of our imperial dignity and to mark it with the seal of our majesty. By this privilege and authority of ours we decree that no one shall presume to invalidate this decree and donation of ours, nor shall any judge or any other person presume to inflict injury or violence upon the aforesaid place or its settlers.

Given at Fulda on the Ides of May.

## LXI. FOR THE CHURCH OF RHEIMS (Year 816)

[Mabillon, *Annals of the Holy Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. II, from the cartulary of Der.]

[Col. 1057C]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus, to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of ours, namely present and future.

If by a gift of our generosity we grant some benefit to places dedicated to God, we clearly believe that this will benefit us both in passing through mortal life temporally and in attaining eternal life happily.

Therefore we wish it to be made known to all that the holy church of Rheims, in which our predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, received the faith and the grace of holy baptism, and in which we too received the imperial insignia through the laying on of the hand of Lord Pope Stephen, and which we have solemnly resolved to restore from its foundations, both for the honor of God and in memory of our parents and for the dignity of our consecration—

whereas formerly it stood solely in the ancient religious honor of Mary, Mother of God, we, adding the new grace of exaltation, have renewed it under the invocation of Saint Savior, God and our Lord Jesus Christ, enriching it with suitable possessions—

and, moreover, cultivating it with devoted intention for the salvation of ourselves and our successors, and wishing to confirm it in its proper state of dignity, have arranged to add a certain abbey situated in the county of Blesense (the county of Blaise), on the river called Vera (the Voire). There is a monastery there dedicated in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, in the forest called Ders. [Col. 1058A]

We grant that abbey, together with our royal forest and the total integrity of all its property—namely, estates, small estates, male and female dependents, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, and all its lawful boundaries—to the same church of Rheims forever. For the honorable completion of the entire structure of that church, and wherever it may subsequently be necessary to restore it, we transfer it as a possession, and by solemn deliberation transfer it from our right into its right and dominion.

In addition to all this, we grant to the aforesaid holy church of Rheims a certain place belonging to our fisc, highly necessary and suitable for digging a lead mine, in the district of Laon (Lomois, near Namur), also within the boundaries or dependencies of a place called the estate of Geminiacum. Around the entire excavation, on every side, there shall be a square area of thirty poles, the manual pole being measured at thirty feet.

Thus, while more confidently carrying out the needs of the aforesaid holy church of God there, in buildings and in all its abundant external dependencies—that is, roads, waters, pastures, and woods—let them possess those things that are ours in common there, without any opposition, by our generosity.

And so that these writings of our confirmation may benefit that consecrated place in our charity for perpetual times, we have confirmed them below with our own hand and resolved to strengthen them forever with the impression of our ring.

[Col. 1058C]

Given at Rheims on the Kalends of November, etc.

## LXII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF PRÜM (Year 816)

[At Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, p. 66, from the cartulary of Prüm.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

Let it be known to all our faithful, both present and future, that the monks from the monastery called Prüm, which our grandfather, Lord Pippin, of pious memory, constructed as a new work in honor of the holy Savior and richly endowed with his own property, approached our Serenity and reported how, among the other donations, he had confirmed a certain forest there.

They also said that our servants from our fisc, which is called Tumbas, had unjustly occupied part of that forest. When we heard this, we immediately sent our envoy named Adalbert, our seneschal, to investigate carefully through truthful and reputable men, namely the local inhabitants, whether this was so or not.

He, carrying out the most careful investigation according to our instructions, discovered that our servants had unjustly held part of that forest on our behalf. When this had been reported to us, so that the benefaction of our parents might be preserved inviolate, we sent another envoy of ours, namely Witharius, so that he too might identify the aforesaid forest by the boundaries and reliable signs, and restore the part thereof to the aforesaid monastery. This he did.

When he had reported to us that he had done all these things, we ordered this authority of ours to be issued as an increase to his reward, and ordered that first the boundaries of the aforesaid forest, as they had been marked out by our envoy, be inserted according to the places named, namely:

From the boundary of Romarisvilla, on the right-hand side of the monastery, to Lindinawinca; from there to Folkeffelt; and along the length of the Pyrumbach as far as Prüm. From there they proceed to Marisburias; from there by the Hundinesbach; by the road that leads to Steinbuhil; through the middle of Steinbuhil; from there to Sconenbach; from there to Sconensceid; from there to Firnibach; from there upward along the Alba to Hildibach; from there to Centbuzzi; from there to Garanbach, where it rises, along its length to Hura; and along the Hura to the mountain as far as Barbach, which lies on the left-hand side of the monastery; from there to Buocha; from there to Huochonloe; from there by the road to Sturenfelt; from there by the Sclusunbach to Gerbrchetesprunnon; from there to Suindinesbrath; from there by the Bodilenpath to Bodilenbrath; from there to the place where the stream Melana rises at Hurspringa; from there into Melana, along that stream; from there down Melana to the narrows; from there through the narrows to Deofansleid; from there to Hagana; from there to Merbach, where the boundary ends.

Therefore, ordering and commanding, we decree that henceforth no one among the faithful of the holy Church of God or among ours shall presume to disturb any part of the aforesaid forest belonging to the aforesaid monastery, oppose it in any way, or attempt to inflict any injury upon it. Rather, from this day forward and henceforth, with God propitious, they shall be able to possess the aforesaid forest peacefully and securely according to its boundaries, in our time and in future times, and to do whatever they choose for the needs of the common community, so that they may continually delight to implore the mercy of the Lord for us, our wife and offspring, and for the stability of our whole empire, granted to us by God and to be preserved forever by his most merciful compassion.

And so that this authority may be more truly believed and more diligently preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by ours, we have subscribed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Lord Louis, most serene Augustus.

[Col. 1059D]

I, Durandus, deacon, have examined it in the place of Helisachar.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of November, in the third year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most serene Augustus, indiction 10. Enacted at the royal palace of Compiègne, happily, in God’s name. Amen.

## LXIII. [Note: [Col. 1059D] There exists a diploma of King Pippin concerning the foundation of this monastery, given at Aachen in the seventh year of his reign; but Mabillon considers it insufficiently genuine, *Annals of Benedictine History*, book XXVIII, no. 65.] FOR THE MONASTERY OF SORICINIUM (Year 817)

[At D. Bouquet, *Collection of Histories*, vol. VI, p. 501, from the brief chronicle of the abbey of Saints Paul and Peter in the district of Blizentium.]

[Col. 1060A]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If, out of love for God, we contribute something to places devoted to divine worship, for the benefit of those serving in those places, we do not doubt that a reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us by the Lord. Therefore, let the diligence of all the faithful, present and future, know that it has pleased us, for the remedy of our soul and the fruit of eternal reward, to grant certain properties to the monastery called Suricinum, situated in the Toulouse region and built in honor of the Mother of God and the other saints, where Bertrand is now known to preside as abbot. These properties were formerly handed over to us by Count Ariacas [the author of the short chronicle and Mabillon, in the place cited shortly below, call him Arecatum] by formal enumeration in the Auch region: namely, the estate of Blizentia, with the churches founded there in honor of the Mother of God and Saint John, together with the lands of Peyrault [the French words that occur here and elsewhere in this diploma appear to have been inserted by the author of the chronicle], its buildings, and its dependants; and another estate called Montlieu, with all that is contained in the aforesaid donation and with its dependants; and the estate called Exartigas, with all its buildings and appurtenances; and the estate called Waccaria, with the church of Saint John and likewise the adjoining buildings; and the estate called Marcillanum, with its buildings and appurtenances, with houses and dependants, and whatever in that place is recognized as belonging to us by right of ownership, together with the church constructed in the same place in honor of Saint Martin; and a mill on the River Gers, and whatever we are seen to possess in that same place.

Moreover, in the Dagne region, and in the estate called Alamanni, and in the estate of Modolingo, with the churches constructed there in honor of the Mother of God and Saint Sulpicius, with dependants and tenant farmers, with their houses and inhabitants; and whatever there is recognized as belonging to us by right of ownership, with churches, male and female servants, and tenant farmers, with houses, buildings, lands, vineyards, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, movable and immovable property, cultivated and uncultivated, acquired and to be acquired—we give everything, wholly and in its entirety, to God and to the aforesaid monastery of Suricinum, for the salvation of our soul, as support for the brothers serving God there, for the giving of alms, and for the other needs of the aforesaid monastery; by this grant of our authority we perpetually assign it to them, so that the abbots and monks may freely and peacefully administer these properties.

And so that this charter of our donation may possess perpetual validity in future times and be more diligently observed by our faithful, we have confirmed it with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Deacon Durand, acting in the place of Helisachar, has recognized this.

Given on the third day before the Nones of May, in the fourth year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of our most devout lord Louis, with the tenth indiction. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

[Column 1061A]

### LXIV. FOR THE CANONS OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT STEPHEN OF LIMOGES. (Year 817.)

[In D. Bouquet, *Recueil des Histoires*, cited above, p. 502.]

In the name of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

If, out of love for divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of priests, we believe that the gift of heavenly grace is bestowed upon us by the Lord. Therefore, let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own, present and future, that the venerable Regimpertus, bishop of the city of Limoges, approached the serenity of our eminence and informed us that a certain deacon named Mathusalam, from the canonical community of the aforesaid city, which is built in honor of Saint Stephen, had long ago handed over to him certain properties belonging to him by right of ownership. These properties are in the same Limoges region, in a place called Carentenago: namely, a small monastery that he himself had built and dedicated in honor of the Lord and our Savior.

But afterward, with God’s generosity, both he and the aforesaid bishop enriched this small monastery more fully with acquired properties, and by their testament they assigned all these properties, as an act of charity on our part and theirs, for the support of the canons living in the aforesaid canonical community. For this reason he asked the clemency of our serenity to order that our decree concerning this matter be made for the sake of legal security, so that through it, in our time and in future times, the aforesaid small monastery, with everything lawfully belonging or pertaining to it, might serve the support and uses of the canons living in the aforesaid see.

Granting assent to his petition and confirming it by a decree of our authority, we prescribe and order that none of our faithful, present or future, presume through greed or any pretext to diminish any of the aforesaid properties. Rather, the aforesaid small monastery, with everything lawfully and reasonably belonging or pertaining to it, shall henceforth be inviolably preserved in the manner arranged and ordered by that bishop, in our time and in future times. Nor may any successor of the aforementioned bishop dare to give that same small monastery as a benefice to anyone or presume to divert it to other uses. Instead, as it was established by him and through him, and confirmed by this authority of ours, so shall it remain permanently undisturbed.

And so that this confirmation may be more truly believed by all the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own people, and may be more carefully preserved, we have ordered it to be sealed beneath with our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Deacon Durand, acting in the place of Helisachar, has recognized this.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourth year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of our most devout lord Louis Augustus, with the tenth indiction. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

[Column 1062A]

### LXV. FOR THE CHURCH OF SAINT STEPHEN OF LIMOGES. (Year 817.)

[In D. Bouquet, cited above.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

If, in imperial fashion, we grant appropriate benefits to places dedicated to God, relieve ecclesiastical needs at the petitions of priests by our assistance, and protect them by imperial defense, we plainly believe that this will benefit us both in passing through mortal life in time and in attaining eternal life happily. In the meantime, let the discernment and understanding of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable Regimpertus, bishop of the city of Limoges, presented to our sight a charter of immunity of our lord and father of blessed memory, Emperor Charlemagne. It contained the statement that not only that same father of ours, but also his predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, had caused the see of that city, which is built in honor of Saint Stephen the martyr and the other saints, and over which that bishop presides by God’s authority, to remain under their name and protection, together with its monasteries, small monasteries, dependent villages, and the properties and people belonging or pertaining to it; and that, by the authority of their immunities, this church had until then been protected and defended from the interference of judicial power.

But, for the security of the matter, the aforesaid Bishop Regimpertus asked us, following the custom of our father [margin: *parentum*, “of our parents”] or of the preceding kings, to decree that a privilege of immunity of this kind be made for that church, out of love for God and reverence for that holy place. We willingly granted his petition and decided that this decree of our authority should be made for that church, for the sake of immunity and protection, out of love for divine worship and for the remedy of our soul.

Through it we prescribe and order that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, dare enter, in our time or in future times, the churches, places, lands, or other possessions that the aforesaid church now justly and legally holds in any regions or territories within the jurisdiction of our empire, or those which divine mercy may henceforth increase in the right of that church, in order to hear cases, exact fines, impose lodging or provisions, take sureties, distrain the church’s people, or demand any exactions or unlawful services or pretexts. Nor may anyone presume to exact any of the matters mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid bishop and his successors be permitted to possess the properties of that church, with everything subject to it and with the properties and people belonging or pertaining to it, under the protection and immunity of our defense, free from all interference by judicial authority, in peaceful order; and let them faithfully obey our imperial authority and, together with the clergy and people subject to them, continually implore the immense mercy of God for the safety of ourselves, our wife and offspring, and also of the entire empire granted to us by God and to be preserved forever by his most merciful compassion.

Whatever the right of the treasury might be able to exact from the properties of the aforesaid church, we have granted in full to that same church, so that it may perpetually serve as an increase and supplement for carrying out God’s service. Therefore, so that this authority may possess fuller force in the name of God, and may be more truly believed and more carefully preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own people, we have confirmed it beneath with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Deacon Durand, acting in the place of Helisachar, has recognized this.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourth year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, most devout Augustus, with the tenth indiction. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

### LXVI. FOR THE MONASTERY OF CRUDAT. (Year 817.)

[In D. Bouquet, cited above, p. 503, from the new edition of the *History of Languedoc*, vol. I, p. 50.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

If, in imperial fashion, we generously grant suitable benefits to places dedicated to divine worship, we have no doubt that this will benefit us both for the stability of our empire and for the salvation of our soul. Therefore, let it be known to all the faithful, present and future, that Count Elpodorius approached our serenity and explained that formerly his father Eribertus, on the River Rhône in the county of Viviers, at a place called Crudat, which belonged by right to our treasury, found the place deserted and, undertaking the effort out of divine love, gathered monks there. With the assistance of that man and of other faithful people, they restored the same place, so that they might remain there under the monastic rule, as they have done until now with God’s favor.

Although he had restored quiet possessions to them from his own resources, provided them with suitable assistance according to his ability, and possessed the charitable devotion of his father, he asked our highness to receive those monks, together with their abbot Bonaldus, under our fullest protection, along with the properties belonging to that place by right of the treasury, so that henceforth they might live peacefully through our charity and his and observe their way of life without weariness.

Because we recognized his petition as just and pleasing to God, we willingly assented and received the monks, together with the aforesaid place and the properties lawfully belonging to it, under our fullest protection. And so that from now on they might remain peacefully in that place, we granted it to them through our generosity and by our authority.

Therefore, prescribing, we order that none of our faithful, nor any itinerant envoy, nor anyone performing a secular administrative office, presume to disturb the aforesaid monks in the aforesaid place, attempt to take away or diminish anything belonging lawfully to that place, or inflict any assault upon them. Rather, by these imperial letters of ours, let them be permitted to remain under our fullest protection and, living peacefully, continually to implore the Lord with unceasing prayers for us and for the stability of our entire empire.

We also prescribe and order that no public judge enter their properties at any time to hear cases, exact fines, impose lodging or provisions, take sureties, distrain their people, whether free or enslaved, or demand any exactions or unlawful services or pretexts; nor may anyone presume to exact any of the matters mentioned above from the properties that they justly possess at the present time or that the Lord may henceforth cause to increase.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors be permitted to possess the properties of the aforesaid monastery peacefully under the protection of our immunity. Whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this life, so long as the monks are able to find among themselves men capable of governing that community according to the rule of Saint Benedict, they shall, by this authority and consent of ours, have permission to elect abbots.

And so that this authority may remain undisturbed in our time and in future times, with the Lord’s protection, we have confirmed it beneath with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

[Note: In the papers of Dom Estiennot, where this decree is quoted, the following is added here: “Deacon Durand, acting in the place of Helisachar, has recognized this.”]

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourth year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, most devout Augustus, with the tenth indiction. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

### LXVII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SOLEMNIA. (Year 817.)

[In Baluze, *Capitularies*, vol. II, p. 1414, from the papers of J. Sirmond.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

When we bring suitable assistance to places dedicated to divine worship out of love for divine service, and properly fulfill the royal custom, we truly believe that this will help us to obtain the rewards of eternal recompense. Therefore, we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, and also to our successors, faithful of the holy Church of God, that the venerable man Agiulfus, abbot of the monastery called Solemniacus, approached the serenity of our eminence. This monastery was built by Saint Eligius in honor of Saint Peter and the other saints. He carried in his hands the immunities of our grandfather, King Pippin, and of our lord and father, Charlemagne, of blessed memory, the great emperor. These documents contained the statement that, out of divine love and reverence for divine worship, they had always caused the aforesaid monastery to remain under their fullest protection and had made it immune and free from every public service and judicial exaction.

This benefit granted to the same monastery has, with God’s favor, demonstrably been preserved inviolably until now. For the sake of securing the matter, he humbly asked with whatever prayers he could offer that a benefit of this kind toward the aforesaid venerable monastery be established by our authority. Because of our love for God and reverence for divine worship, we were entirely willing to grant his petition.

Therefore, we will and decree that all the properties of the same monastery, together with the people subject to it, both free and enslaved, shall in every respect remain under the protection of our defense. Accordingly, we prescribe and order that no public judge, nor any administrator of the state, of higher or lower rank, presume to enter the churches, estates, or other possessions that it justly and legally holds at the present time in any regions or territories of our empire, or those which divine mercy may henceforth increase in the right of that monastery, in order to hear cases according to judicial procedure.

Nor may anyone exact fines, taxes, lodging, provisions, or sureties; distrain the monastery’s people, whether free or enslaved; or demand any public services, exactions, or unlawful pretexts by which the monastery or those subject to it might suffer any disadvantage. In our time or in future times, no one may be so audacious as to claim unlawful authority to do such things.

Whatever, therefore, ought to have been exacted from the properties of the aforesaid monastery for the treasury, and whatever is known to have been granted by our predecessors, we willingly wish to be granted to that monastery in full as a gift of our generosity, so that, with the dominion of the treasury removed, it may serve as a supplement for preparing the lamps of the basilica of the aforesaid monastery and for supporting the poor and the clerics serving the Lord in that place.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved more carefully forever, we have confirmed it beneath with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

[Column 1065D]

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Deacon Durand, acting in the place of Helisachar, has recognized this.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourth year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, most devout Augustus, with the tenth indiction. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

### LXVIII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT-GERMAIN-DES-PRÉS. (Year 817.)

[Mabillon, *Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict*, part II, p. 118.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

Whatever we do out of love for God, for the benefit of God’s servants, we trust contributes to our attaining eternal blessedness. Therefore, let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, that, for the benefit of our soul, we have most willingly granted to the monastery of Saint Germanus, where his holy and venerable body rests and where the venerable man Hirminius performs the pastoral office, a fishery that formerly our great-grandfather, Charles of blessed memory, ordered to be constructed in the region of Pincerais, in the estate called Rioilus, namely on the River Seine, as support for the monks serving God in that holy place. We have confirmed it by these letters, on the following condition: the one-night right [that is, the right of fishing for one night] that the monastery of Saint Denis and the monastery of Saint Peter receive from it shall in no way be taken away from them by anyone. Rather, those monasteries shall at all times contribute, according to their share, assistance toward the restoration and repair of the fish-weir, as necessity requires.

The remainder, however, we have ceded in full to the venerable monastery of Saint Germanus. We also order and decree that no one presume, in our time or in future times, to disturb the aforesaid monastery or its administrators concerning the aforesaid fishery, to cause it any opposition on account of it, or attempt to remove anything from it.

Rather, from now on and thereafter, let the monks hold this Charles-weir as freely as our father Charles, most serene emperor and Augustus, our grandfather Pippin, and our great-grandfather Charles, who ordered the fishery to be constructed, held it; and as we ourselves have held it until now. Namely, the water shall always remain unobstructed on every side by everyone, as it still exists under our authority.
