No works shall ever be made, either before or behind it, that could harm this weir. Even if the banks belong to whatever authority, the water nevertheless belongs to the king.

Therefore, concerning this authority of cession, we ordered this royal decree of ours to be made. Through it we decree and order that no Christian dare or presume to violate the gift made for our salvation, whether by force or through any cunning prejudice harmful to the Charles-weir. Rather, without any subtraction, diminution, or damage, let the monks of Saint Vincent and Saint Germanus be permitted, in complete possession, perpetually to possess and enjoy this gift that we grant them, for our eternal rest.

Therefore, so that this command of our authority may retain the force of continuity firmly through the successive courses of years, we have strengthened it beneath with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Deacon Durand, acting in the place of Helisachar, has recognized this.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of September, in the third year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, most devout Augustus, with the tenth indiction. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen. (With a wax seal.)

### LXIX. FOR THE CHURCH OF SAINT MARTIN OF TOURS. (Year 817.)

[In Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, p. 63, from the cartulary of Saint Martin.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

If we willingly grant the petitions of God’s servants who knock at our ears concerning various ecclesiastical needs, and extend assistance so that they may serve divine power more abundantly in places dedicated to God, we trust that this will undoubtedly prove advantageous to us both in passing through mortal life in time and in attaining the future life happily.

Therefore, we wish it to be known to all our faithful—namely, bishops, abbots, illustrious men, dukes, counts, household officials, royal agents, vicars, centenarii and their subordinates, as well as our envoys traveling throughout our entire empire, and also the other faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own realm, present and future—that the venerable man Fridegisus, abbot of the monastery of our special patron Saint Martin, where the venerable body of that most illustrious man rests, approached the serenity of our eminence.

He carried in his hands the immunities of the ancient kings of the Franks, as well as of our grandfather, the former King Pippin, and of our lord and father Charles, most serene emperor, of pious memory. By these documents they had decreed that the same monastery should remain peacefully in God’s service, and that all the properties of the aforesaid monastery throughout their entire kingdom—namely, in Austrasia, Neustria, Burgundy, Aquitaine, Provence, Italy, and the other parts of their kingdom—which had been granted not only by orthodox rulers but also by other faithful people, or had been legally transferred to the right of that monastery through various contracts and documentary instruments, should remain under their protection of immunity and be free and exempt from every public service and judicial exaction.

This benefit granted to the same monastery has, with God’s favor, demonstrably been preserved inviolably until now. For the sake of securing the matter, he humbly asked with whatever prayers he could offer that such a benefit toward the aforesaid venerable monastery be established by our authority. Because of our love for God and reverence for the most blessed Martin, we were entirely willing to grant his petition.

Therefore, we will and decree that all the properties of the same monastery, together with the people subject to it, shall in every respect remain under the protection of our defense. Accordingly, we prescribe and order that no public judge, nor any administrator of the state of higher or lower rank, presume to enter the churches, estates, or other possessions that it justly and legally holds at the present time in any provinces or territories of our empire, or those which divine mercy may henceforth increase in the right of that monastery, in order to hear cases according to judicial procedure.

Nor may anyone exact fines, taxes, lodging, provisions, or tolls, as is contained in the decree of our lord and father; take sureties; distrain the people, whether free or enslaved, residing on the land of the monastery; or demand any public services, exactions, or unlawful pretexts by which the monastery or those subject to it might suffer any unjust disadvantage. In our time or in future times, no one may be so audacious as to claim unlawful authority to do such things.

[Note: From this passage it is clear that the monks of Saint Martin had already by that time been converted into canons when this diploma was issued. Mabillon indeed holds that they retained the monastic habit throughout the reign of Charlemagne; but after his death they immediately discarded it, especially with the encouragement of Abbot Fridugisus, who also attempted to introduce a more relaxed way of life in the monastery of Saint Bertin at Sithiu, over which he presided as abbot.]

Whatever, therefore, from the properties of the aforesaid monastery was due to be transferred to the treasury, and whatever we have learned was granted by our predecessors, we willingly wish to be granted to that monastery throughout its entire extent as a gift of our generosity, so that, with the dominion of the treasury removed, it may serve as a supplement for preparing the lamps of the basilica of Saint Martin and for supporting the poor and the clerics serving the Lord in that place.

But if anyone should have dared to advance to such audacity as to become a violator of this decree of ours, let him know that, as is contained in the decree of our lord and father, he will not only fall under our displeasure but will also be punished by a penalty of six hundred solidi of gold, refined to purity, of which two parts shall be received by the administrators of the aforesaid monastery and the third part by the treasury.

For it is worthy and just that a violator of the many pious kings who preceded us, and of our decree, should undergo such a penalty, so that he may recognize that he is rightly accused of such great audacity and that he may inspire fear in others, lest they attempt to do the same by any act of boldness. Thus no one should attempt to violate the royal benefits reverently granted to places dedicated to God.

Therefore, we will and decree that, with all interference by judicial authority removed, the aforesaid abbot and his successors, together with all the people subject or belonging to the aforesaid monastery, shall remain in peaceful order under the protection of our immunity and defense. Faithfully obeying our imperial authority, they shall, together with the clergy entrusted to them, continually implore the immense mercy of God for the safety of our wife and offspring and also of the entire empire granted to us by God and to be preserved forever by his most gracious compassion.

If anything belonging to the properties of the aforesaid monastery has been unjustly taken away through the sluggishness or negligence of abbots or through the presumption of judges, we command by this authority of ours that it be restored in full.

And so that this authority may inviolably achieve its effect and may be more truly believed and more diligently preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own people, we have confirmed it beneath with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Helisachar has recognized this. Given on the third day before the Kalends of September, in the third year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, most devout Augustus, with the tenth indiction.

Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

### LXX. FOR THE CHURCH OF SAINT MARTIN OF TOURS. (Year 817.)

[In Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, p. 65, from the cartulary of Saint Martin.]

[Column 1069B]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

If, in imperial fashion, we generously grant suitable benefits to places devoted to divine worship, we have no doubt that this will benefit us for the stability of our empire and for attaining the salvation of our soul. Therefore, let it be known to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, centenarii, toll-collectors, officials, our envoys traveling throughout our empire, all those administering the state, and also the other faithful of the holy Church of God and of our realm, present and future, that the venerable man Fridugisus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin, the outstanding confessor of Christ and our patron, where his venerable body rests, brought to us a decree of authority of our lord and father, Charles, most serene Augustus, of pious memory.

It contained the statement that, at the request of his predecessor, the former abbot Wlfardus, that same father of ours, out of love for God and reverence for Saint Martin, had decreed that the carts and pack-animals of the men mentioned above, which were sent to the various markets of his kingdom for the benefit and needs of the aforesaid monastery, should be immune and secure from every toll.

For the security of the matter, he also asked our serenity, following our father’s custom, to grant this kind of benefit to the same holy place. We willingly listened to his petition and decided that this decree should be made. Through it we prescribe and order that whenever the aforesaid abbot and his successors, and the clerics serving Christ in that place, for the sake of meeting their needs and benefit, send carts and pack-animals for commercial purposes to any markets of our empire, or to places in Austrasia, Neustria, Burgundy, Aquitaine, Provence, Italy, or any other regions of our empire, no one may exact from them, or from the men in charge of them, any toll, bridge toll, ferry toll, wheel toll, dust toll, or turf toll, or any other exactions, nor may anyone presume to cause them any opposition or detention.

Rather, by this authority of ours, let them be permitted to go and return freely and securely through all the places of our empire, as they deem convenient, and let them suffer no disadvantage from those who administer the state or from their subordinates.

The toll that could lawfully have been exacted from the aforesaid vehicles and men by right of the treasury, we have most willingly granted to the same holy place as an act of our charity, just as is also contained in the decree of our father, so that the aforesaid abbot and his successors, together with the clergy entrusted to him, may gladly pray continually to the Lord for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of our empire.

And so that this authority may achieve inviolable effect and may be more truly believed and more carefully preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own people, we have confirmed it beneath with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Deacon Durand, acting in the place of Helisachar, has recognized this.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of September, with the tenth indiction, in the third year of the reign of our lord Louis, emperor Augustus. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

### LXXI. FOR THE MONASTERY OF TOURNAI. (Year 817.)

[In D. Bouquet, *Recueil des Histoires*, vol. VI, p. 509, from Foppens, in the supplement to Miraeus’s *Diplomata*.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

Let it be known to the knowledge of all our faithful, present and future, that the venerable man Wendilmarus, bishop of the city of Tournai, asked us to grant him, as an act of our charity, certain lands belonging to our treasury in that city, for enlarging and extending the cloister of the canons.

Accordingly, to examine and oversee this matter, we sent the venerable abbot Irmio and our envoys Ingobertus and Hartmannus, so that they might inspect it and, in accordance with what the need for constructing that cloister required, assign land from our treasury to him by our authority.

They did so: namely, from our own treasury in that place, land measuring eighty-four perches around its circumference; and likewise in the same place, from our treasury held by Werimfredus as a benefice, ninety-nine perches; and similarly from our treasury held by Count Hruoculfus in office, thirty-two perches.

But so that the same church and its administrators might hold and possess the aforesaid places and the cloister to be enlarged and extended firmly and perpetually, he asked for our authority concerning this matter. Through it, the lands would remain firmly and inviolably in the right of the aforesaid church in our time and in future times.

We were pleased to grant his requests, for the increase of our reward and out of reverence for that holy place, and to hand over the aforesaid lands to the same church immediately, according to their measurement and boundaries.

Therefore, we will and order that, by this authority of ours, in our time and in future times, the aforesaid Bishop Wendilmarus, his successors, or the community of that holy place shall possess the aforesaid lands, granted as an act of our charity, according to the measurement and boundaries established by our envoys; and that they shall remain perpetually under the authority of that church. This condition alone shall apply: whatever they wish to do concerning or upon those lands, according to ecclesiastical law, for the benefit and advancement of that church, they shall enjoy complete freedom to do.

Therefore, so that this authority may possess fuller force in the name of God and may be more truly believed and more carefully preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own people, we have ordered it to be sealed beneath with our ring.

Roimundus [Faramundus], acting in the place of Helisachar, has recognized this.

Date: 20 November, in the fourth year of the empire of our lord, with Christ propitious, indiction 11. [Note: Indiction 11 was to begin in September.] Done at the royal palace of Aachen, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

[Note: Baluze, in volume I of the Capitularies, p. 591, published a diploma assigned to the year 817, in which Louis the Pious is said to confirm the donations made to the Roman Church by his grandfather Pippin and by his father Charles. Pagi, under the year 817, no. 7, considers this donation of Louis no less fictitious than the one attributed to Constantine the Great. For, he says, among so many Roman pontiffs who mentioned the gifts made by Pippin and Charlemagne, there is not one who mentions a donation by Louis the Pious—because, having the most just title to the properties possessed by the Church, they despised a fictitious one. Moreover, the emperors Otto I and Henry I enumerate individually what Pippin and Charlemagne donated to the Roman Church, and they confirm these gifts by their diplomas; but they made no mention of Louis’s donation. Leo of Ostia, who died at the beginning of the twelfth century, was the first to mention it, and therefore it had been devised not long before. In that donation Louis grants to the apostolic see the islands of Corsica, Sardinia, and Sicily in their entirety, with all the adjoining territories; yet Sicily was never under the power of Charlemagne or his successors. Finally, in that donation Louis establishes that, when the Roman pontiff dies, the person whom all the Romans have elected shall be consecrated according to canonical custom, without any ambiguity or contradiction. “And when he has been consecrated,” he says, “let legates be sent to us or to our successors, the kings of the Franks,” etc. This is sheer fabrication, since, while Louis the Pious was still alive, Pope Eugene II, at the request of Lothair, his colleague in the paternal empire, decreed that the Roman pontiff should not be consecrated except in the presence of imperial legates—a practice that remained in force throughout this century and beyond.]

## LXXII. FOR THE CHURCH OF RHEIMS. (Year 817)

[In D. Bouquet, in the same place, p. 510, from Flodoard, Book II of the Ecclesiastical History of Rome, chapter 19.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence, emperor Augustus.

[Col. 1071C]

If, out of religious generosity, we remit to venerable places what had previously been exacted from them by our royal or imperial predecessors for the uses of the state, so that it may be expended for the advantages and needs of those holy places; and if, concerning this same matter, we graciously grant favorable assent to the most salutary suggestions and petitions of our faithful, we provide greatly both for our soul and for the welfare of the kingdom and the realm. For nothing belonging to the state is seen to be diminished when anything from that same state is granted for pious works, religious places, the needs of God’s churches, or the benefit of God’s servants.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s Church, present and future, and especially to our successors who hold the summit of power in which, by the Lord’s authority, we have been established, and who thereafter are to be established by the Lord of lords, that the venerable Ebo, archbishop of the Church of Rheims, prelate of the most reverend see of Saint Remigius, the most glorious pontiff and our special patron, has made known to our Clemency that the holy mother Church of the aforesaid metropolitan city, consecrated in honor of holy Mary, ever-virgin and mother of God, had already been worn down by the old age of time.

In that church, by God’s agency and with Saint Remigius as co-worker, our Frankish people, together with our namesake king of that people, merited being washed in the baptismal font and illumined by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. That most noble king himself was also found worthy, by God’s mercy, to be anointed for royal power. There too, by divine favor, we merited being crowned by the hands of the lord Stephen, Roman supreme pontiff, for the dignity and power of the empire.

Since we desire to renew that church in return for so many benefits bestowed upon us there by God, and since we see the inconvenience of the place as an obstacle to carrying this out, we grant for this work, and for all the other structures to be built for the needs of God’s servants dwelling there, the entire wall with the gates of that city, together with all the labor and all the expenses that had customarily been carried out and paid at our royal palace in Aachen from the property and resources of that church and of the bishopric of Rheims. We grant this as our alms and for the salvation of the soul of our lord and father, as well as of our other predecessors, who for some time had held that bishopric to the detriment of their salvation and had spent its property and resources for their own uses contrary to ecclesiastical regulations; consequently, less benefit than ought to have accrued had come from them to the holy places established within that bishopric.

We also wish our vassals and all our faithful who possess anything from the property of that bishopric to serve the same work, as was established by our lord and father of blessed memory; and, as was decreed by our lord and grandfather Pippin of pious memory, let them pay to that church the tithes and ninths from the property they hold from it.

We also grant that all the public roads running around that same church, which may obstruct the construction of cloisters and dwellings for God’s servants, may be transferred and altered. And if anything belonging to our fisc is held there, by this decree of our authority we likewise grant it perpetually, so that no judge, count, envoy, or anyone exercising judicial power may ever presume to inflict upon the aforesaid holy Church of Rheims any disturbance or any obstacle of accusation concerning it.

We beseech our successors to remember their salvation, both present and eternal; to remember also the benefits bestowed upon us, our people, and our predecessors in that holy place through blessed Remigius by the merits of holy Mary; and, just as they will wish their own good deeds to be preserved by their successors, so let them take care that what we have granted to that holy place for the love of God, of his holy mother, and of our blessed protector Remigius be preserved perpetually and inviolably.

And so that this decree of our grant may, in future times and in the name of God, possess a fuller force of stability, we have decreed that it be authenticated below by the impression of our ring.

## LXXIII.

[Note: This mutilated diploma appears in Guillimann, *On the Bishops of Strasbourg*, p. 118; in Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, vol. VII, p. 481; and in Bouquet, *Writers of Frankish History*, vol. VI, p. 505. A complete version, though corrupt in certain places, was published by the editors of *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, among the documents, p. 462, and by Schoepflin, *Alsatian Diplomas*, vol. I, p. 65, no. 81, who reproduced it engraved on copper in plate 8. Here we present it transcribed from the original itself, in its genuine form.]

### FOR THE CHURCH OF STRASBOURG. (Year 817)

[In Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, documentary volume II, p. 165.]

In the name of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence, emperor Augustus.

When we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants [Note: This repetition of “God’s servants” occurs in the autograph itself, perhaps through the scribe’s carelessness.] out of love for divine worship, we do not doubt that we are fortified by heavenly grace. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable Adaloch, called bishop of the Church of Strasbourg, which was built in honor of holy Mary, mother of God and ever-virgin, brought before our presence [Note: The illustrious Abbot Godfrey of Bessel, in his *Chronicle of Göttweig*, vol. I, p. 76, seeks to prove from the formula customary in ancient imperial diplomas—“brought before our presence the decrees or authorities of our predecessors”—that imperial archives of Germany had already been established in the ninth century, from which the cited diplomas were drawn. But this is not proved by the aforesaid formula; rather, it demonstrates that such diplomas were produced not from the emperors’ chancery but from the archives of the churches themselves.] a certain charter of our lord and father, Charles, of blessed memory, the most pious Augustus, [Note: This charter or diploma of Charlemagne, dated 7 March 773, appears above, no. 63, p. CVI (*Patrologia*, vol. XCVII, col. 926).] in which it was inserted how, formerly, concerning a certain little place called Stilla [Note: Today the village of Still. Consult the notes on the aforesaid diploma of Charlemagne.], which the aforesaid church had possessed for a long time through royal confirmations, the rectors of that church had had a dispute with the royal judges; and how they had acquired the aforesaid place for the benefit of that church by the specified boundaries: namely, along the royal road that runs above the stream called Stilla [Note: The stream is still called Still today.], above Rummald’s house [Note: The village of Urmat.], then to the place called Paphinisnaida [Note: An unknown place], thence over the entire mountain called Arlegisbergo [Note: Heiligenberg], as far as the place where the stream called Hasla rises [Note: The Hasel stream]; then to the place where Wichia rises [Note: The Wich stream], as far as it enters the Brusca [Note: The Brusche River]; thence again along the Brusca for a long distance, until the Stilla enters it.

And our lord and father had confirmed by that same charter that it should belong perpetually to that see. He therefore asked that, following the custom of our father, we should confirm this by our authority; and let the diligence of all our faithful know that we have done so.

Therefore we command and order that, just as it is contained in the decree of our lord and father, and just as the aforesaid church possesses it at the present time, so thereafter it shall hold and possess it without anyone’s hindrance; and whatever the rectors of the aforesaid see may wish to do or decide concerning it or within it for the benefit and advantage of that see, let them enjoy full freedom to do so by ecclesiastical right in perpetuity.

And so that this charter may possess a firmer force in the name of God, and so that it may be more truly believed by the faithful of God’s holy Church and by our own faithful, and more diligently preserved, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring. [Note: In the original, these words, “of our ring,” have been erased by age.] [Note: Thegan notes, under the year 814, chapter 10, in Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 76, that Louis the Pious renewed all diplomas granted to churches by his predecessors and strengthened them with his own hand and signature.]

[Col. 1074C]

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Durandus, deacon, have examined and subscribed this in the place of Helisachar. [Note: Durandus the deacon was notary of the emperor Louis the Pious under the chancellors Helisachar, Fridugisus, and Theoto.] [Note: Helisachar, or Elisachar, was the first chancellor of Louis the Pious by rank. Many diplomas of this emperor survive to which he subscribed. Einhard and Agobard call him a priest and abbot; for he presided as abbot over the abbey of Saint Maximin at Trier and over many other monasteries in that period.]

Issued on 28 August, in the third year of the empire of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, with Christ propitious, indiction 10. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, successfully in the name of God. Amen. [Note: The seal of this diploma was lost after a long passage of time. A trace of one that formerly existed remains on a darkened membrane, cut crosswise in the form of a cross, with the four corners of the incision torn away.]

## LXXIV. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT GALL. (Year 817)

[In Neugart, *Alemannic Code*, p. 163.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence, emperor Augustus.

To all the counts in the regions of Alamannia, and to your successors and subordinates, and to all our faithful, let it be known that, for the salvation of our soul and for the attainment of the fruit of eternal reward, it has pleased us to grant to the monastery of Saint Gall, situated in the district of Thurgau, where the venerable abbot Gauzbert presides, and to the congregation of that monastery, a certain census from the manses written below—that is, what used to go out to the counts’ authorities—while preserving, however, the customary dues that ought to go from the census, tribute, or any other matter to the authorities of our palace.

For this reason we have ordered this document of our prescription to be made for the aforesaid monastery and its congregation. Through it we command all of you that, from the manses named below, namely:

In the district administered by Count Frumald: the manse of Weisarius at Huntingun [Note: Houdingen, near the fortress of Fürstenberg], and that of Puado at Chenigun [Note: Guningen, in the rural district of Wurmling];

In the district administered by Count Cunthard, at Pisingas [Note: Bisingen, between Bahlingen and the fortress of Hohenzollern]: the manse of Tato and Cuato, the manse of Geilo, the manse of Gozbert, the manse of Wolfo, and the manse of Altmann;

In the district administered by Count Karamann, at Seerzingas [Note: Scherzingen, in the rural district of Ebing]: the manses of Atolf and Liutbold; at Swanningas [Note: Schwenningen, near the sources of the Neckar, close to Villingen]: the manse of Liubolt; and at Wilaresbach [Note: Weilersbach, between Rottweil and the town so named]: the manses of Ratolt and Heriger;

In the district administered by Count Hhuadarius [Note: Alternatively, Count Ruadharius], at Teiningas [Note: Tuningen, toward the Föhn mountain]: the manses of Amalo, Gerhart, Luithar, Wolfoert, and Nilo; at Filingas [Note: The town of Villingen and the village of Haud]: the manses of Wito and Heimo; at Nordstetim [Note: Nordstetten, near Horb]: the manse of Oto and Reginker; at Forrum [Note: Pforzheim, on the Danube between the fortress of Warten]: the manse of Pruning and Waning; at Speichingas [Note: Spaichingen, in the county of Hohenberg]: the manse of Otto, Waramann, and Adalmar; and at Tanheim [Note: Tanheim, called Fürst]: the manse of Tuato;

In the district administered by Count Erchangar: the manse of Ruadleoz at Heimbak [Note: Heimbach, near the town of Dornhan], the manse of Frehotf at Talahusun [Note: Thalhausen, below Rottweil on the Neckar], and that of Otgar at Puahhein [Note: Bucchen, Bucheim, which, along with the other places listed so far, we assign to the ancient Bertholdsbar, as well as the counts Frumald, Cunthard, Karamann, Rhuadarius, and Erchangar];

In the district administered by Count Rihwin [Note: Rihwin, count of Thurgau]: the manse of Snizolf at Huttinvillare [Note: Uzwil near Toggenburg], the manse of Gundwin at Chezzinvillare [Note: Keswil in Thurgau]; between Kiselmari and Facco, one manse; the manse of Roatpert at Lanchasalachi [Note: Landschlacht, parish of Altnau, in the same district]; two manses at Zilleslata [Note: Zillschlact, parish of Sitterdorf, in the same district]; the manse of Amalric; the manse of Balduvin at Hebinhow [Note: Hennau, a village with a parish church near Toggenburg]; the manse of Puwon at Ifinwiltare [Note: Ifwil, parish of Bichelsee in Thurgau]; the manse of Hunepert; and the manse of Herirat at Tanninghouum [Note: Daenikon or Tennicken];

In the district administered by Count Odalric: the manse of Rihwin at Stetim [Note: Stetten near Meersburg in Linzgau, whose count was Odaric], at Mavacdorf [Note: A scribal error for Maracdorf, Markdorf], the manses of Isambert, Ruadbert, Ruatbald, and Arnolt; the manse of Walbert at Fisbach [Note: Fischbach]; and the manse of Theotramn at Chlusturnon [Note: Kluftern]—in all forty-seven manses—

you shall presume to exact or demand no census, tribute, labor, plowing, or any other dues, but, just as we have granted them in our alms, so let them remain perpetually.

And so that this document of our authority may be more firmly believed and preserved by all, we have ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

I, Durandus, deacon, have examined and subscribed this in the place of Helisachar.

[Col. 1076B]

Issued on 4 June, in the fourth year of the empire of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, with Christ propitious, indiction 10. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, successfully in the name of God. Amen. [Note: Indiction 10 was running in the year 817, Louis the Pious’s fourth year.]

## LXXV. FOR THE SAME MONASTERY. (Year 818)

[In Neugart, in the same place, p. 169.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence, emperor Augustus.

When we confer some gift of our generosity upon places devoted to divine worship, we clearly believe that this will benefit us both for the stability of our empire and for attaining the reward of eternal life. Therefore we wish it to be known to the understanding of all our faithful, present and future, that the venerable Gauzbert, abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, situated in the district of Thurgau, made known to our Serenity that a certain man named Isingrim had formerly, by means of written charters, legally transferred certain properties belonging to him, in the presence of noble men, to the monastery over which he, by God’s will, presides; and that, according to the law, the aforesaid monastery had obtained lawful possession of them.

But when the aforesaid Isingrim became unfaithful to us and was killed in that state of disloyalty, his own properties were confiscated to the fisc. Likewise, those which he had previously transferred to the aforesaid monastery in lawful order were added to the fisc.

We therefore ordered Count Richoin [Note: Richoin, alternatively Richwin, count of Thurgau] to investigate this matter carefully and report to us. He came to us and reported that, after careful investigation, the matter was as Gauzpert asserted.

Therefore it pleased our Excellency, for the benefit of our soul, not only to return the aforesaid properties which the aforementioned Isingrim had transferred to the aforesaid monastery, but also to make them belong to that monastery by this confirmation of our authority, so that its rectors may hold and possess them in present and future times.

We therefore decree and order that no one, in our time or in future times, presume to remove from that monastery the aforesaid properties which the said Isingrim justly and legally transferred to it, or to inflict or introduce against that monastery and its rectors any unjust accusation or disturbance. Rather, whatever the superiors of that monastery may wish to do with or within those properties for its benefit and advantage, let them enjoy complete freedom to do so.

And so that this charter may possess a firmer force, we have ordered it sealed below with our ring.

I, Durandus, deacon, have examined and subscribed this in the place of Helisachar.

Issued on 2 June, in the fifth year of the empire of our lord Louis, most serene Augustus, with Christ propitious, indiction 11. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, successfully in the name of God. Amen. [Note: In the year 818, indiction 11 was running.]

## LXXVI. [Col. 1077C] FOR THE SAME MONASTERY. (Year 818)

[In Neugart, in the same place, from the diplomatic collection of D. de Halle.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence, emperor Augustus.

When, out of love for divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants, we trust that the gift of heavenly grace is bestowed upon us by the Lord. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own faithful, present and future, that we have received under our protection and under the safeguard of our immunity the monastery of Saint Gall, situated in the district of Thurgau, where the venerable Gauzbert presides as abbot; it had been subject to the bishopric of the holy Church of Constance, where Wolfleoz is now bishop; together with the monks serving the Lord there, and with the properties and persons subject to it and legally belonging or pertaining to it.

Therefore we command and order that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial power, in our time or in future times, dare enter the churches, places, fields, or other possessions which it now justly and legally possesses in any counties or territories within the authority of our empire, or which divine piety may thereafter wish to increase as belonging to that holy place, in order to hear cases, exact fines [Note: A fine, a monetary penalty, or any kind of exaction], make lodgings [Note: Here “lodging” means the obligation to receive the prince’s envoys or legates, or other public persons, as guests and supply them with necessary food], or provisions [Note: “Provisions”: expenses incurred in receiving guests], take sureties, or unreasonably constrain the men of that monastery, whether free or enslaved, who dwell upon its land; nor may anyone seek any repayments or unlawful pretexts. Nor shall anyone presume to exact any of the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors be permitted to possess in peace, under the protection and defense of our safeguard and immunity, the property of the aforesaid monastery, with everything subject to it and with the properties and persons lawfully belonging or pertaining to it, free from all disturbance by judicial authority, and faithfully obey our imperial command. Thus may it please the monks who appear to serve God there, dwelling in peace, continually to entreat the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of the whole empire granted to us by God and to be preserved by his most merciful compassion throughout the immensity of the Lord’s mercy.

Accordingly, so that this charter may possess fuller firmness in the name of God, and so that it may be more truly believed by the faithful of holy Church and by our own faithful and more diligently preserved, we have ordered it sealed below with our ring.

I, Durandus, deacon, have examined and subscribed this in the place of Helisachar.

Issued on 3 June, in the fifth year of the empire of Louis, most pious Augustus, with Christ propitious, indiction 11. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, successfully in the name of God. Amen. [Note: Indiction 11 agrees with the year 818.]

## LXXVII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF FLEURY. (Year 818)

[In D. Bouquet, in the same place, p. 511, from Perard, *Documents for the History of Burgundy*, p. 46.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence, emperor Augustus.

When, out of love for divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants, we do not doubt that we are fortified by heavenly grace. Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own faithful, present and future, that the venerable Adalgandus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict of Fleury, which is built in the district of Orléans on the river Loire, where Saint Benedict himself rests in body, brought to us the charters of immunity of our grandfather, formerly King Pippin, and of our lord and father, Charles, the most pious Augustus. These charters contained the provision that they themselves, or their predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, had held the aforesaid monastery, together with the properties and persons belonging and pertaining to it, under their protection and defense, and that it had always been defended and secured by the authority of their immunities against disturbance by judicial power.

For the sake of securing the matter, the aforesaid abbot asked us, out of love for God and reverence for Saint Peter and Saint Benedict, to follow the custom of our father and predecessors and decree that a charter of our immunity be made concerning that holy place. [Note: Corruptly printed as “secundum” in Perard.] We granted his petition and decreed that this charter of our authority be made concerning that holy place. Through it we command and order that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial power, dare enter, in our time or in future times, the churches, places, fields, or other possessions which it now justly and legally possesses in any counties or territories within the authority of our empire, or which divine piety may thereafter wish to increase as belonging to that holy place, in order to hear cases, exact fines, make lodgings or provisions, take sureties, or constrain the men of that monastery dwelling upon its land; nor may anyone seek any repayments or unlawful pretexts, or presume to exact the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors be permitted to possess the property of the aforesaid monastery peacefully under the protection of our immunity. And whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid abbot and his successors have departed this life, so long as the monks themselves are able to find among themselves men capable of governing that congregation according to the rule of Saint Benedict, let them have permission, by this authority and consent of ours, to elect abbots. Thus may it please the monks who appear to serve God there continually to entreat the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of our whole empire, granted to us by God and to be preserved by him. [Note: Incorrectly printed by the same author as “they ought to.”]

And whatever the fisc could exact from the property of the aforesaid monastery, we have granted to that monastery and to its congregation serving God there, so that it may provide them with an increase or supplement for carrying out their service.

And so that this charter may remain unshaken in our time and in future times, with the Lord’s protection, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed below with the impression of our ring.

[Col. 1079D]

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Durandus, deacon, have examined this in the place of Helisachar.

Issued on 27 July, in the fifth year of the empire of our lord Louis, most serene Augustus, with Christ propitious, indiction 11. Done at the city of Orléans, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1080A]

## LXXVIII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF FLEURY. (Year 818)

[In D. Bouquet, in the same place, from the notes of D. Claude Estiennot.]

In the name of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence, emperor Augustus.

To all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, centenaries, toll-collectors, administrators, and all who administer the state, as well as to the other faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own faithful, present and future, let it be known that the venerable Adalgaud, abbot of the monastery of Fleury, which is built in the district of Orléans on the river Loire, in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and Saint Benedict the confessor, where Saint Benedict himself rests in body, brought to us a charter of decree of our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, the most pious Augustus.

It contained the provision that our grandfather Pippin, formerly king, and that same father of ours had granted to the monastery the toll from four ships which traveled along the river Loire and other rivers for salt and other commerce, and also from carts and pack animals carrying supplies for the monastery or for the congregation serving God there, and from villages or from anything whatsoever from which the fisc could exact toll.

For the sake of securing the matter, the aforesaid abbot asked us, following the custom of our father and predecessors, to grant or confirm this sort of benefit by a charter of our authority. [Note: Adrevald mentions this privilege in his *Book on the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapter 19, in these words: “By the royal munificence of the ancient kings of the Franks, this most sacred monastery had been granted, by the written charter of the decree itself, the right for four ships, free from every fiscal obligation, to travel freely along the channel of the Loire.” He then recounts a miracle that occurred in the time of Count Raho. Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, Book XXVIII, no. 79, would have wished Adrevald to provide a surety for a similar miracle. The same Mabillon further observes that literary studies flourished at Fleury around that time, as Theodulf testifies in a capitulary whose nineteenth chapter advises priests to send their relatives to school either at the Church of the Holy Cross, which is the cathedral, or at the monastery of Saint Aignan or Saint Benedict.]

And this we did, etc.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Durandus, deacon, examined this in the place of Helisachar.

Issued on 27 July, in the fifth year of the empire of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, with Christ propitious, indiction 11. Done at the city of Orléans, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

## LXXIX. FOR THE MONASTERY OF MAGNUS LOCUS. (Year 818)

[In D. Bouquet, in the same place, p. 513.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence, emperor Augustus.

When we bring fitting assistance to places devoted to divine worship for the honor of divine service, we properly fulfill the royal custom, and we truly believe that this will benefit us in attaining the rewards of eternal recompense.

Therefore we wish it to be known to the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own faithful, present and future, how we have received, as is contained in our other charters, the venerable abbot Heimo of the monastery called Magnus Locus (Manlieu), which is built in honor of Saint Sebastian in the district of Auvergne, together with his congregation and the properties lawfully belonging to them, under our fullest protection and the safeguard of our immunity.

Accordingly, we decree and enact by these imperial documents of ours that all the property of that monastery, as we have said, together with everything subject to it, shall remain under the immunity of our protection.

Therefore we command and order that no public judge, nor any administrator of the state of a higher or lower rank, presume to enter, in the manner of a judicial proceeding, the churches, villages, or other possessions which at the present time belong to that place in any provinces, or [which] divine piety may thereafter wish to increase as belonging to that monastery, whether through us or through anyone else; nor may anyone take fines, tributes, lodgings, provisions, tolls, or sureties; nor constrain men, whether free or enslaved, dwelling upon the land of that place; nor seek any public dues, repayments, or unlawful pretexts by which that monastery or those subject to it might in any way suffer unjust harm.

In our time or in future times, let no one be so rash as to presume to claim the power to do so.

And whatever the fisc could hope to obtain from the property of the aforesaid monastery, we grant all of it to the aforesaid monastery for eternal recompense, so that throughout perpetuity it may contribute to the support of the poor and the maintenance of the monks serving God there. Thus may those serving God there continually pray for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of the whole empire granted to us by God and to be preserved by him.

And so that this charter of our immunity may retain inviolable and unshaken firmness through the course of the years, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

[Col. 1082A]

I, Durandus, deacon, have examined this in the place of Helisachar.

Issued on 17 August, in the fifth year of the empire of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, with Christ propitious, indiction 11. Done at the palace of Angers, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

## LXXX. FOR LOTHAIR, CO-EMPEROR. (Year 818)

[Note: The date of this charter is uncertain, but it was issued after the year 817, when Lothair was designated emperor by his father. It predates October 821, when Lothair married Irmingard.]

[In Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, vol. II, p. 167, from manuscript codex no. 2718 of the Royal Library, written in Tironian notes [Note: [Col. 1081D] This charter, the twenty-fifth, is found in the capitulary of Louis the Pious, which P. Carpenter published from a royal codex written in Tironian notes, in *Tironian Alphabet*, p. 53. Bouquet, in *Collection of the Historians of France*, vol. VI, p. 646, and Heumann, in *Commentary on Diplomatic Matters*, vol. I, p. 413, transcribed it from Carpenter. The French authors of the *New Diplomatics*, vol. III, pp. 562–622, discuss Tironian notes at length. In the library of the principal church of Strasbourg there formerly existed an outstanding psalter written in Tironian notes and distinguished by golden capitals. Johannes Trithemius had seen that codex at Strasbourg in 1498 and greatly praises it in book five of his *Polygraphia*. That Strasbourg codex was previously said to have been written in Armenian letters [Col. 1082D], until the aforementioned abbot recognized in it Tironian notes, whose meaning Gruter sets out on p. 30.].]

In the name of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus [Note: [Col. 1082D] This initial formula is absent from the manuscript codex, but must unquestionably be supplied.]. Let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, that we grant to our beloved son Lothair Caesar [Note: [Col. 1082D] The designation “Caesar” here deserves notice. At this time, in the sense in which it is used here, it is exceedingly rare; Einhard and the other writers nowhere use it when they mention Lothair as appointed by his father as co-emperor.] and associate in our empire, as his own property, from one of our estates situated in the Alsatian district, called Herinstein, one royal demesne manor with all that is situated upon it, and only sixty other manors belonging to it, together with the unfree dependents residing upon them and attached to those same sixty manors.

These properties, then, as written above, with their houses, buildings, dependents, lands, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, movable and immovable property, we deliver to you, our beloved son Lothair the emperor, as your own property, by this grant of our authority, to possess; namely, so that whatever you may wish to do with or claim from those same properties and dependents, you may enjoy complete freedom in every respect to do so [Col. 1082C]. And so that this grant of our donation may retain inviolable permanence throughout future ages, we have confirmed it with our own hand . . . etc.

## LXXXI. For the Abbey of Aprimonastier. (Year 818.)

[Note: [Col. 1082D] Schoepflin records this diploma twice in vol. I of *Alsatian Diplomatics*: more correctly among the spurious documents, p. 105, though he also places it among the genuine documents, p. 66.]

[In Grandidier, ibid., from the manuscript codex of the *Chronicle of Novientum*, preserved at Sélestat in the library of Beatus Rhenanus [Note: [Col. 1082D] This charter is not preserved in the archive of Aprimonastier Abbey.].]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

If, for the love of God, we bestow suitable benefits upon places devoted to divine worship and upon those serving Him in those places [Col. 1083A], we do not doubt that a reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us by God. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable Theopaldus, abbot of the monastery called Novientum or Ebersheim, situated in the district of Illisacia, above the bank of the river Ill, in the county of Kirchheim [Note: [Col. 1083C] On the county of Kirchheim, also called the district of the Troningi, consult Schoepflin, *Illustrated Alsace*, vol. I, pp. 641 and 663.], which the illustrious man Duke Etich built in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of Saint Maurice the martyr and his companions, through the agency of the priest of Christ, the blessed Theodatus [Note: [Col. 1083C] See the *Chronicle of Novientum*.], presented to us the immunity and privileges of our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, Augustus.

When these had been read through and recited in the hearing of the nobles, they appeared to contain the statement that our same father, for love of the heavenly kingdom, but especially out of reverence for the Theban martyrs—for, after recovering his strength through their intercession following many losses and the difficulties of battle, he had triumphed over the barbarians on the feast of their passion—had always protected the aforesaid monastery with a special affection under the fullest protection of royal immunity.

Therefore the aforesaid abbot, together with his advocate, Lord Vulfhald, asked us, following our father’s custom, to receive the place of the aforesaid monastery and its principal estates under the protection of our imperial defense, excluding every comital or fiscal authority. We, therefore, moved by the example of our ancestors and at the same time providing for the advantage of that place and for our own salvation [Col. 1083C], have decided to grant their petition in every respect.

Accordingly, by imperial authority we command that no public judge and no judicial authority, now or in the future, presume to enter the aforesaid place or its estates by force of office; nor are they to impose provisions or lodging there, nor compel any of its people, nor demand anything there from the right of our fisc. Rather, the aforesaid abbot Theopaldus and all his successors are henceforth to possess those estates by force of office and in their entirety, with every protection [Note: [Col. 1083D] That is, guardianship and defense. See the glossaries of Wachter and Haltaus, pp. 1101 and 1373.]:

That is, at Sulza [Note: [Col. 1083D] The small town of Ober-Sulz.], the royal estate with all its appurtenances: namely, the church with its tithes; the gate estate with the entire tithe of royal land, whether in vineyards, fields, meadows, or forests, and of all their newly cleared lands, as well as of the animals raised on the royal estate.

The chapel also called the cell of Saint Peter belongs to the aforementioned gate estate, with everything pertaining to it; likewise the chapel in the village called Sarmenza [Note: [Col. 1083D] Today Sermersheim, situated above Benfeld. The ruins of an ancient chapel dedicated to Saint Ulrich still remain there beside the river Ill.], belonging to that gate estate.

In the ban of Regenesheim [Note: [Col. 1083D] Today Rexheim, near Ensisheim.], the tithes of two manors; at Gundolvesheim [Note: [Col. 1083D] Today Gundelsheim, a village near Rouffach.], the tithes of five manors; and at Bercholz [Note: [Col. 1083D] Today Bergholtz, near the town of Gebweiler.], the tithe of one vineyard belong to that estate.

At Balteresheim [Note: [Col. 1083D] Today Baltersheim, near Ensisheim.], Batenheim [Note: [Col. 1083D] Today the village of Battenheim, also near Ensisheim.], Ruoleichesheim [Note: [Col. 1084C] Today Rurelsheim, likewise near Ensisheim.], Hirzveit [Note: [Col. 1084C] Today Hirzvelt, a village between Ensisheim and Neuf-Brisach.], and Bollewilre [Note: [Col. 1084C] Today Bollweiler, two leagues above Rouffach.], whatever looks toward the aforesaid royal estate of Sulza pays tithes to the gate estate.

The entire household, whether military, tributary, or servile, with the whole ban of that village or district and with every free use, belongs to that royal estate. This district begins on the ridge of the mountain called Beleus [Note: [Col. 1084D] Beleus, or Mount Belus, in German Belchen and in French Ballon, is regarded as the highest of all the Vosges mountains. It lies two leagues from Murbach and must not be confused with another mountain of the same name in the borders of the county of Burgundy, near Belfort.], beyond the place called Breidenbrunno, and extends downward through the middle of the village called Reteresheim [Note: [Col. 1084D] Retersheim, somewhat above Rouffach]. In width it extends from the middle of the village called Alreswilre [Note: [Col. 1084D] Almswiler, near Sulzbach in Sundgau.] as far as the ancient bed of the river called Lorfaha [Note: [Col. 1084D] The river Lauch.]. It lies in the county of Illechik [Note: [Col. 1084D] See Schoepflin, *Illustrated Alsace*, vol. I, p. 661.] and in the diocese of Strasbourg.

At Egenesheim [Note: [Col. 1084D] Egisheim.], the royal estate, with one quarter of the ban and the tithes of that allodial property, together with its other appurtenances.

At Sigoltesheim [Note: [Col. 1084D] Sigolsheim.], the royal estate with all its appendages, vineyards, fields, and meadows; tributary and servile manors; dependents of both sexes; and the chapel of that estate with all the tithes of that property. The tithes of the royal land and of the servile benefices belong to the monastery gate. One half of the lordship, or ban, of the entire district, with its forest and every use, belongs to that royal estate.

That district begins at the little village called Mezeral [Note: [Col. 1084D] Today a village in the Gregorian Valley, also called Mezeral, belonging to the town of Munster.], and ends at the stream of the river called Vachonna [Note: [Col. 1084D] Today the stream Fachina or Fecht, formed from two streams joining near the town and Abbey of Munster.], beside the little village called Scottenwilre [Note: [Col. 1084D] Today the village of Stosswihr, not far from the town of Munster.] [Col. 1085A]. In width it extends beyond the Vachonna beside Lucelwilre [Note: [Col. 1085C] Today the small village of Wihr in the Gregorian Valley, commonly called Klein-Wihr; this later name is equivalent to Lucelwilre. *Lutzel* is an old Germanic word meaning something small.] as far as the stream called Mulibach [Note: [Col. 1085C] Today the stream Mühlbach, which the inhabitants call Kleinthalbach; the village of Mühlbach, belonging to the town of Munster, lies near it.], situated in the county of Illichick and in the diocese of Strasbourg.

At Olleswilre [Note: [Col. 1085C] Orschweiler or Orchweyer, near Sélestat.], the royal estate with the allodial property of vineyards and fields; tributary and servile manors. The tithes of that property belong entirely to the monastery gate for the use of the poor and guests. The ban of that allodial property, with all its protection, belongs to that estate, including roads and trackless ways, exits and returns. The common ban extends as far as the bed of the Eckenbach [Note: [Col. 1085C] The Eckenbach torrent, which separates Upper Alsace from Lower Alsace and the diocese of Strasbourg from that of Basel.] and the bed of the river Ill; the use of wood and pasture for fattening fifty pigs in Westerholz belongs to that estate. It is situated in the county of Kirchheim.

At Scerewilre [Note: [Col. 1085C] Scherweiler.], the royal estate with vineyards, fields, and meadows; tributary manors and their estates; and the ban of that property and its stewardship belong to the royal estate. The tithes of the royal land belong to the monastery gate.

At Chagenheim [Note: [Col. 1085C] Today the village of Kogenheim near Ebersheim Abbey, belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg, in which the abbey has a royal estate.], the royal estate with royal land, estates, estate buildings, servile and tributary manors, together with a mill and fisheries, the household, and other appurtenances and every free use.

At Sarmeresheim [Note: [Col. 1085C] Sermersheim.], the royal estate with royal land, estates, servile and tributary manors, and the church of that village with its tithes. The tithes of the royal land belong to the gate; the ban and stewardship of that property or household belong to that estate.

At Hittenheim [Note: [Col. 1085C] Huttenheim.], the royal estate with royal land and all its appurtenances, a mill, and fisheries; the parish church with all its tithes [Col. 1085C]; the tithes of the royal land belong to the gate. One half of the ban, with its appurtenances, belongs to that estate.

At Northus [Note: [Col. 1085C] Northausen, commonly Nartz.], the royal estate with all its appendages; royal land with its tithes, which belong to the gate.

In that village, and at Hundenesheim [Note: [Col. 1085D] Today Hindisheim, three leagues distant above Strasbourg, belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg in the bailiwick of Dachstein.], and at Lumeresheim [Note: [Col. 1085D] Today Leimersheim, near Hipsheim, belonging to the same bishop in the bailiwick of Benfeld.], one half of the ban also belongs to that estate.

At Utenheim [Note: [Col. 1085D] Utenheim, a village belonging to the people of Reinach, where Ebersheim Abbey divides the tithes with the parish priest. The full right of patronage formerly belonged to the same abbey; but by virtue of a settlement made in 1749, the bishop of Strasbourg exercises this right three times, and the abbot the fourth time.], the royal estate with royal land and its tithes, and the church with its tithes; one quarter of the ban belongs to that estate.

At Valva [Note: [Col. 1085D] Today Valff, situated between Benfeld and Obernai, a village belonging to the nobles of Andlau.], the royal estate and royal land with estates and meadows, and one quarter of the ban.

At Hiltesheim [Note: [Col. 1085D] Today Hiltzen, a village belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg, in which Aprimonastier Abbey enjoys all the tithes, a royal estate, and the right of patronage.], the royal estate, royal land with its tithes, the church with its tithes, and the ban in its entirety, with all protection and every use.

At Witenesheim [Note: [Col. 1086C] Today Wittisheim, commonly Witzen; in this village the aforesaid abbey still has the right of patronage and the tithes, which it divides with the parish priest.], the royal estate with all its appurtenances, royal land with its tithes, and the ban with complete lordship.

The chapel of Niveratesheim [Note: [Col. 1086C] Niffern, a village two leagues from Aprimonastier, now destroyed. Only the chapel of Saint Catherine remains, belonging to the aforesaid abbey, in the district of the parish of Schwabsheim.] with its tithes [Col. 1086B].

At Muoteresholz [Note: [Col. 1086C] Today Mietersholz, a league and a half from Sélestat toward the Rhine, belonging to the Rathsamhausen family, in which Ebersheim Abbey enjoys a royal estate, tithes, and the right of patronage.], the royal estate, royal land with its tithes, and the church with its tithes; one half of the ban belongs to that estate.

The chapel at Baldenheim [Note: [Col. 1086C] Baldenheim, a village belonging to the lord of Waldner. The abbey possesses half the tithes there. Baldenheim formerly had a chapel of Saint Oswald belonging to the same abbey; it is now destroyed, and its title is said to have been transferred to the church of Ebersheim Abbey [Col. 1086D].] with one half of the tithes of that village.

At Artolvesheim [Note: [Col. 1086D] Today Artelsheim, a village of Lower Alsace between the Rhine and Sélestat, belonging to the prince of Rohan-Soubise. There Aprimonastier Abbey divides the tithes with the parish priest, and also enjoys a royal estate and the right of patronage, as we said above concerning Utenheim.], the royal estate with all its appurtenances, royal land with its tithes, the church with its tithes, and the ban in its entirety with every use.

The chapel at Birenheim [Note: [Col. 1086D] Today the village of Bindern, near Ebersheim Abbey, belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg. Ebersheim Abbey possesses a royal estate there.] with the tithes of that village.

At Gruzenheim [Note: [Col. 1086D] Grusenheim.], the royal estate with royal land and its tithes, the church with all the tithes of its ban, and the ban in its entirety with complete lordship and free use.

At Wizwile [Note: [Col. 1086D] Weisweiler.], which lies in the Breisgau district, the royal estate with all its appendages, the church with all its tithes, and the ban with every free use [Col. 1086C].

At Burcheim [Note: [Col. 1086D] Burgheim.], the royal estate, royal land with its tithes, the church with [Col. 1087A] its tithes, and the ban with every free use.

At Lagelenheim [Note: [Col. 1087D] Lagelnheim.], the royal estate, royal land with its tithes, the church with its tithes, and the ban with all its lordship, from the bank of the Rhine to the bank of the river Ill.

Thus the aforesaid abbot Theopaldus and all his successors are to possess these aforesaid estates with all their appurtenances, without any contradiction, seizure, or diminution by any judicial authority, whether secular or spiritual, through the munificence and generosity of our imperial authority, with power to improve and enlarge them, so that the brothers serving God there may pray more frequently to Him for our salvation and for the stability of our empire.

And so that this imperial authority of ours may remain stable and unshaken, with Christ’s favor, in our time and in future ages, we have signed it below with our own hand and sealed it with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Lord Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Durandus, notary, have examined this at the instance of Lord Helias [Note: [Col. 1087D] Perhaps the chancellor Helisachar, mentioned in the charters of Louis.], archchancellor.

Given on the Kalends of May, in the third year, with Christ’s favor, of the most pious emperor Augustus. Done at Trhonie or Kilikhein [Note: [Col. 1087D] Besselius, in the *Gottweig Chronicle*, vol. II, book III, p. 487, and Schoepflin, *Illustrated Alsace*, vol. I, p. 704, have much to say about the royal palace at Kirchheim.] in the county of Count Wuorand, in the assembly of the emperor and the nobles, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 817, indiction 6 [Note: [Col. 1087D] The year of the Incarnation 817 does not agree with the fourth year of the empire of Louis the Pious, which fell in the year 818, nor with the sixth indiction, which was then the fifteenth. Moreover, indiction 11 was running in the year 818, or the fourth year of Louis. These and other defects make this diploma, if not spurious, at least interpolated.], successfully in the name of Christ.

## LXXXII. For the Monastery of Como. (Year 818, the day before the Kalends of August.)

[Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*,]

[Col. 1087C]

Louis, by divine providence, ever Augustus.

When we willingly grant the just petitions of priests and servants of God that they bring to our ears, and with God’s help cause them to reach fulfillment, we not only exercise a royal and imperial custom, but also show generosity for strengthening the condition of the earthly kingdom, which we trust will contribute to attaining eternal blessedness.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own faithful, present and future, that the entire order of the holy Church of Como, both priests and clerics, approached the serenity of our majesty and earnestly begged us to grant, for the love of the heavenly Requiter, and in consideration of our soul and that of our lord and father Charles, most excellent emperor of pious memory [Col. 1087D], a certain estate belonging to the right of our kingdom, called Anutium, beside Lake Lucan, with its appurtenances and legally attached dependencies, to be possessed in perpetuity.

We, therefore, who regarded their petition as well founded, gladly acceded to their prayers, granting to the aforesaid order and to the entire body of clerics, and to their descendants, the aforesaid estate of Anutium, with all its dependencies: namely, manors, jurisdictions, and bridges; lands, vineyards, and fields; fisheries; cultivated and uncultivated lands; mountains, valleys, and plains; rocks and rocky places; waters and watercourses; marshes; judicial rights; male and female slaves of both sexes; legal proceedings; courts; and water jurisdictions, from the boundary of Cadro to the bridge of Trasia, everything in its entirety, as it is known justly and lawfully to belong to it.

We command that the aforesaid congregation of priests and clerics of the holy Church of Como, who at the appointed time shall serve God, Saint Abundius the confessor, and the martyr Pelagia, have authority to hold and possess it, and to do with that estate and its lawful dependencies whatever they wish, by our fullest imperial authority [Col. 1088A].

Therefore we order and decree that no duke, count, or any administrator of the state, nor any person, great or small, of either sex, of whatever order or rank, presume to inflict any diminution or invasion upon the aforesaid estate of Anutium or its dependencies. Nor may anyone at any time molest the free or servile people dwelling in that estate or within the aforesaid boundaries by any public service, levy, or public watch, nor at any time presume to remove or diminish anything from what we have mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid congregation of priests and canons, and their successors who shall exist at the appointed time, be permitted to possess the aforesaid estate in its entirety, quietly and peacefully, for the praise and honor of the holy Roman Church, just as it has until now been possessed from the public domain.

If, however—which we absolutely do not believe—any rash person should act contrary to the provisions of this command of ours, let him know that he must pay one hundred pounds of the purest gold, half to our palace and half to the aforesaid congregation.

And so that it may be more truly believed and more diligently observed by all, we have approved it with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.

I, Durandus the deacon, acting in another’s stead, have verified it.

Given on the day before the Kalends of August, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 818, indiction 11, of Lord Louis, most serene emperor, in the fourth year of his empire [Col. 1088D] [Note: [Col. 1088D] “Fifth” should be written.]. Done at Como, at Saint Peter’s, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

## LXXXIII. For the Church of Saint Peter of Maguelone. (Year 819.)

[In D. Bouquet, *Collection of Histories*, vol. VI, p. 513, from Sammarthanus, vol. III of *Gallia Christiana*, p. 358.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus [Col. 1089A] Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained clemency, emperor Augustus.

It is evident that, by God’s ordained grace, we surpass other mortals; therefore it is fitting that, by whose gift we excel, we should strive in every way to aid ecclesiastical affairs.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, and to our faithful successors in the holy Church of God, that, for the increase of our reward and the fruit of eternal recompense, it pleased us to restore in its entirety to the church of Saint Peter of Maguelone, where Argerimus presides by God’s appointment, a certain estate situated in the territory of Maguelone, called Villanova, as Count Robert held it as a benefice—since it is established that it was among the aforesaid properties—with all its entirety [Col. 1089B].

This is granted on the sole condition that whatever the rulers and ministers of the aforesaid see may henceforth wish to do, for the advantage of that church, with the estate or with the things presently belonging to it, they may enjoy free authority to do so.

Therefore we command all people and establish by these letters that none of our faithful, present or future, presume to withdraw the aforesaid estate with everything belonging to it from the aforesaid see, diminish anything, or bring an unjust claim against it. Rather, just as it has been entrusted by us and confirmed to the aforesaid church by this authority of ours, so let it remain perpetually.

And so that this authority may be firmly held and better preserved for future ages, we have ordered it to be sealed below with our ring [Col. 1089C].

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Durandus the deacon examined this at the instance of Helisachar.

Given on the Ides of March, in the sixth year, with Christ’s favor, of the empire of Lord Louis, most excellent Augustus, indiction 12. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

## LXXXIV. For the Monastery of Déas. (Year 819.)

[In D. Bouquet, ibid., p. 516, from Chifflet, in the proofs appended to *History of the Abbey of Tournus*, p. 191.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence [Col. 1089D], emperor Augustus.

Let it be known to the understanding of all our faithful, present and future, that the venerable Arnulfus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Philibert, situated on the island called Herio, because of the incursions of the barbarians who frequently devastate that monastery, had built a new monastery outside it, in the district called Erbadellicus (Herbauge), at a place called Deas [Note: [Col. 1089D] Commonly Dée or Grand-Lieu; now a priory in the diocese of Nantes.], with our consent and assistance. For the convenience of that monastery and of the congregation dwelling there, he wished to bring water there from the river called Bedonia (the Bologne), and he begged the clemency of our excellence [Col. 1090A] to grant him passage for that water across the royal road, which is called a paved or chaussée road, so that it might reach the aforesaid monastery, in our time and in future ages, without anyone’s obstruction. He also wished to build a bridge at the same place, so that it would cause no hindrance to travelers.

Since his petition appeared just and useful to the aforesaid monastery, we gave our assent and granted permission for the watercourse to pass across the aforesaid road, provided only that a bridge be built over it in such a way that it would harm no travelers.

Therefore we command and order that no one, now or in future, presume to create or impose any obstacle, hindrance, or legal complaint against the rulers of the aforesaid monastery concerning the aforesaid watercourse. Rather, without anyone’s harassment, what we have granted shall remain ratified and stable forever.

And so that this command of ours may remain stable and unshaken forever, we have ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

I, Durandus the deacon, at the instance of Helisachar, have examined and subscribed it.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, in the sixth year, with Christ’s favor, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, indiction 12. Done at the palace of Aachen, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

## LXXXV. For the Monastery of Conques in the Diocese of Rodez. (Year 819.)

[In Baluze, *Capitularies*, p. 1416, from the archive of the [Col. 1090C] Monastery of Conques.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

We believe that many of our faithful, especially those established in the western regions, should know how a certain religious man named Dado, who in our time shone forth in religion and holiness, with divine grace assisting him, while he sought quiet and wished in leisure to see how sweet the Lord is, found a certain small place in the district of Rodez beside the stream Dourdou, called Conques, suitable for this purpose.

At that place some Christians, long ago fleeing there because of fear of the Saracens, who had devastated almost the whole land and reduced it to a desert, had built a very small oratory. Dado took up the labor and, with his own hands, cleaned and cleared that place as far as his strength allowed, and worked to make it suitable for his repose.

But after not many days, a religious man named Medraldus chose that same place as a dwelling, together with the aforesaid Dado. Because their true religious devotion had spread a reputation for good character among their neighbors, some, abandoning the world, likewise attempted to seek the quiet life which those men were leading. Wishing to become imitators of their religious example, they placed themselves under their instruction. As the congregation gradually grew, they built there a church [Col. 1091A] in honor of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ.

It was decided by common consent that Dado, in accordance with the desire divinely bestowed upon him, should seek an even more remote place called Grande Vabrum, as he did; that Medraldus should become abbot; and that the congregation itself should be regular, according to the ability and understanding granted to them by the Lord.

When these things had been accomplished, it happened that the same congregation came under our own special defense and protection. For, so that they might serve the Lord fully under the Rule of Saint Benedict, we strove, with the Lord’s help, to bring this about through the counsel of good monks and through our frequent admonition. To support their own needs, we also assigned to them certain properties of ours, namely the church of Cermangis, the church called Campus Hiacus, and the church of Saint Christopher built at Montiniac, with all their possessions [Col. 1091B].

Likewise, the church of Garcanga with the estate of Gammaleria; and again another church built at the port of Acri under the title of Saint Saturninus, with all their appurtenances.

We also similarly granted there the church of the Savior at Cicerniacum, and two other churches, one at Burnacellum and the other at Rucenniacum, with all their dependencies; and another church at Ruhilia, with all its possessions.

We also caused Selvaniacum and everything assigned there to stand fully under the protection of immunity by our authority, so that at all times [Col. 1091C] the aforesaid monastery, with that congregation and with the aforementioned place called Grande Vabrum, where the aforesaid Dado found the quiet he desired and brought his life to an end, together with all things justly belonging to it—whether those which it presently possesses or those which the Lord may thereafter wish to increase there—might remain inviolably, with all these things, under our special protection and that of our sons and successors, with God’s favor.

Thus the aforesaid place called Conques, together with that congregation, may always remain secure under imperial and royal defense, without anyone’s hindrance, so that, with God’s help, it may continually observe its purpose in peace and pray to the Lord for us and for the common stability of our empire [Col. 1092A].

And so that this authority may be more truly believed by all, we have caused it to be strengthened below with the mark of our hand and sealed with our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Durandus the deacon, at the instance of Helisachar, examined and subscribed it.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of April, in the sixth year, with Christ’s favor, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, indiction 12.

Done at the royal palace of Aachen, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

## LXXXVI. For the Monastery of Saint Bavo at Ghent [Note: [Col. 1091C] These diplomas of Louis the Pious, as well as those of the emperors Charles the Bald and Otto II, granted in favor of the monastery of Ghent or Saint Bavo, are still preserved intact, with their seals, at Ghent in the episcopal palace. The most reverend Lord Antonius Triestius, bishop of Ghent, kindly showed and communicated them to us. They are preserved intact, as they say, because they were never violated by the Normans—a rare circumstance among the monasteries of Belgium. When the Norman invasion of Belgium broke out, the monks of Ghent withdrew with the relics of the saints and the diplomas, first to Saint-Omer and then to Laon, a city of Picardy, to escape the storm. They remained in that region for approximately one hundred years, and when affairs had quieted, they returned from there to Ghent, their original monastery, by right of restoration.]. (Year 819.)

[In Miraeus, *Belgian Donations*, p. 55.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

If, for love of God, we bestow suitable benefits upon places devoted to divine worship and upon those serving Him in those places, we do not doubt that a reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us by the Lord.
