Therefore let the discernment of all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own people, present and future, know that the venerable man Einhardus, abbot of the monastery called Ganda, situated in the district of Brachbat, built in honor [Col. 1092C] of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, where also Saint Bavo, confessor of Christ, rests in body, brought before our sight the charter of immunity of our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, most excellent emperor. It contained the statement that he, for the love of God and the tranquility of the brothers dwelling in that monastery, had always kept it under the fullest protection and safeguard of immunity.

For the sake of securing its permanence, the aforesaid Einhardus asked us [Note: [Col. 1091D]

Einhard, or Eginhard, is the man who elegantly and faithfully wrote the life of Charlemagne, his foster father, as he himself calls him. Several letters of his are extant among the letters of Lupus of Ferrières, where they were published [but now separately. See the present volume, col. 509, among the Works of Einhard]. Einhard was the fifteenth abbot of the monastery of Ghent and the first abbot of Seligenstadt, in the diocese of Mainz, which he built and endowed at his own expense, as is recorded in the Chronicles of Lorsch and Ghent. The monastery of St. Peter at Ghent was built by St. Amandus—who, after relinquishing the episcopate of Tongeren or Maastricht, acted for many years as an apostle throughout Flanders and Brabant—chiefly with the resources of Bavo, whom he brought from secular military service to a sacred and ascetic life. In this monastery, clerics first lived together in common, and later Benedictine monks resided there. In 1537, by the authority of Pope Paul III, they changed their habit and became what are called secular canons, at the request of Emperor Charles V, who was also Count of Flanders. Three years later, when that place of St. Bavo, situated at the confluence of the Scheldt and the Lys, seemed to Charles V a suitable site for a fortress to defend the city, the college of canons was transferred from there to the parish basilica of St. John at Ghent; by decree of the same pope, its title was changed from St. John to St. Bavo. Thereafter, at the request of Philip II, the Catholic king and son of Charles, Paul IV raised the collegiate church of St. Bavo to cathedral rank in 1559.

St. Bavo was the son of Agilulf, count in Hasbania, and died at Ghent in the monastery he had founded in the year 630, according to Sigebert’s reckoning in his Chronicle, or in the following year.]

the abbot, so that, for the sake of confirmation, we might add our own authority to paternal authority [Col. 1093A]. We willingly granted his request and decreed that this our authority should be issued for the sake of the immunity and protection of the aforesaid monastery and its rulers. By it we prescribe and command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, in our present or future times dare enter the churches, places, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery—which at the present time it justly and lawfully possesses in whatever counties and territories lie within the jurisdiction of our empire, or which divine piety may thereafter cause to be increased for the benefit of that holy place—for the hearing of cases, the exaction of fines, the provision of lodging or transport, the taking of sureties, or the coercion of the monastery’s people, both free and enslaved, who live upon its land [Col. 1093B]; nor may anyone presume to demand any restitutions or unlawful pretexts, or to exact any of the matters mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors be permitted to possess peacefully, under the protection of our immunity, the property of the aforesaid monastery together with all the fines granted to it, as is contained in the charter of our lord and father; and let them faithfully obey our imperial authority, so that the servants of God who serve him there may take pleasure in continually imploring the Lord’s mercy on our behalf, on behalf of our wife and offspring, and for the stability of our entire empire, granted and preserved for us by God.

Therefore, so that this authority may obtain fuller validity in the name of God, and may be more truly and certainly believed and more diligently preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own people, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Given on the Ides of April, in the sixth year of our empire, Christ being favorable, indiction 12. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily in the name of God. Amen.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

## LXXXVII. FOR THE BUCHAU CONVENT OF WOMEN. ([Col. 1093D] Apograph. No one will fail to see that this Lunigian copy is extremely defective. We therefore took pains to obtain another, more faithful to the original, from the Buchau records, but without success. Year 819, June 22.)

[In Neugart, *Codex Alemannicus*, p. 17, from Lunig, *Spicilegium*, part III, ch. 7, concerning abbesses.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divinely inspiring clemency [Col. 1094D], emperor Augustus.

[An unusual formula. The more common formula before Louis the Pious was removed from the kingdom: “by divinely ordaining providence”; a rarer one: “by divinely ordaining clemency.” After the year 833 the customary formula was: “by the divinely propitiated clemency.”]

If we confer some gift upon places dedicated to God and fulfill the custom of imperial magnificence, and thereby trust that divine favor may more readily be won for us [Col. 1094A], therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both present and future, that, moved by divine love, we have given in perpetuity as property to the monastery called Buchau [Col. 1094D]—also Buchaugia or Buchau—which was built in honor of Saints Cornelius and Cyprian and is situated beside the lake called Federsee [or Phedersee, in Latin *lacus plumarius*, on the right bank of the Danube]—a certain estate belonging to us, situated in the hundred called Extagia [also Estagia or Stagia: a house, dwelling, or residence], named Sulgen [Sulgen or Saulgen, a town and the residence of the count of the aforesaid hundred], together with its boundaries and everything belonging to it, namely courtyards, buildings, households and slaves, demesne land, cultivated and uncultivated land, fields, meadows, open country, pastures, woods, tithes, waters and watercourses, mills, fisheries, roads and trackless places, accesses and exits, and all other things, great and small, that justly and lawfully belong to the same properties [Col. 1094B].

We also establish and confirm, by the fortification of our authority, that no public judge, nor duke, count, or anyone exercising judicial authority, dare enter at any time the churches, estates, places, lands, or other possessions presently subject to the aforesaid monastery, or those which may thereafter come into the right and lordship of that monastery through the increase of divine piety, in order to hear cases, exact fines, provide transport, take sureties, or distrain the people of the monastery, whether free or enslaved, living upon its land [*distringendos*], nor to demand any restitutions, bans, or unlawful pretexts, or to hold any public court; nor may anyone presume to exact the matters mentioned above [Col. 1094C].

Furthermore, the censual people belonging to its household, wherever they may be established, shall have peace and shall be governed before no judge, pay no fine [or ban], and conduct no secular business except before the abbess or the advocate of the monastery. The abbesses of the aforesaid monastery shall be permitted to possess everything peacefully under the protection of the lord’s immunity.

With regard to advocates, however, since we do not know what sort they may one day be, we establish and command by our imperial authority that the advocate himself shall have no right in the aforesaid place to hold court or exercise any judicial authority, unless he has come at the abbess’s summons and has then complied with her wishes or request. The advocate shall receive only such expenses or service from the abbess as is appropriate: whenever the advocate has held court once in a year at any particular place and has brought twelve horses, he shall be honorably provided for [Col. 1094D]. Let the advocate establish no court anywhere against the abbess’s will [Col. 1095A]. Whatever he acquires through holding court shall be divided into two parts for the abbess and a third for the advocate. Let him compel no servant of God to appear in court without the abbess or her consent; let him condemn or coerce no member of the household without the lawful deliberation of his associates; let him appoint no advocate or collector for himself; let him demand no private gift or service from any place, whether estate or cellars, as though it were owed to him by established right; let him refrain from frequenting lodgings or overnight stays anywhere. If he wishes to hold court at any place beyond what has been established and commanded, he himself shall provide from the third part falling to him there whatever he needs for expenses, unless he has been summoned there by the abbess for some reason; in that case, what is proper shall be suitably furnished to him [Col. 1095B].

Therefore, if any advocate should presumptuously transgress or violate these statutes with obstinate audacity, let him pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to our palace and half to the monastery, and let him be deprived forever of the advocacy and its other benefits after a proper examination of his transgression.

When the lady and mother of that monastery has departed this life, let no abbess coming from elsewhere be appointed there. Rather, let the nuns themselves, and thereafter the clergy and people, elect and appoint whom they know to be suitable. We strictly forbid her to grant any property of the aforesaid monastery to anyone as a benefice, or in any way to presume to alienate it through the abuse of the sisters or brothers serving God there.

And so that this authority of our grant may retain perpetual force [Col. 1095C], we have ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, in the sixth year of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, Christ being favorable, indiction 12 [Col. 1095D].

Indiction 12 corresponds to the year 819.

Done at the public palace of Angelhaim [an error of the copyist for Ingelheim, from which palace at Aachen the emperor departed in July and where he also held an assembly, as Einhard explicitly testifies in his *Annals* for this year, in D. Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 178 (and above, col. 367)], happily in the name of God. Amen.

Sign of Lord Louis, most pious emperor Augustus [Col. 1095D].

These words, which in other diplomas precede the chancellor’s name and the chronological notes, were perhaps moved to the end through the fault of the copyist. Bouquet nevertheless reports, at the place cited, p. 518, from Miraeus, *Codex Donationum Piarum*, p. 55, a fragment of another charter granted by Louis the Pious to Einhard, abbot of the monastery of Ghent, in which the emperor’s subscription is likewise finally read at the foot. See the preceding charter.]

## LXXXVIII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF GRAVACA. (Year 820.)

[In Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. II, p. 201.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divinely ordaining providence, emperor Augustus.

[Col. 1095D]

If we restore to holy churches and other venerable pious places property belonging to them which has been taken away through negligence or through the greed of people living according to the flesh, and recall it to their control, we confidently believe that this will contribute both to our more readily obtaining the rewards of eternal compensation and to the stability of the kingdom [Col. 1096A]. Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, that the venerable Podo, bishop of the church of Piacenza, through his messenger, the priest Reginold, showed us privileges containing donations of the Lombard kings Hilprand, Aistulf, and Desiderius, as well as of other good men. From these donations a certain monastery called Gravacus had been unjustly taken away, during the time of our lord and father Charles of pious memory, by certain persons, as Reginold, the aforesaid bishop’s messenger, asserted.

We therefore ordered our messengers, the venerable Bishop Adallaho and Count Artman, whom we sent to Italy to administer justice [Col. 1096B], to investigate the matter carefully and report to us whether it was indeed so. Our aforesaid messengers, having investigated the case thoroughly, brought it to our attention and explained it to us as carefully as they could. When we had considered and understood it attentively, we recognized that it was just for the aforesaid monastery, together with its cells and the property subject to it, to be restored to the church of the episcopate of Piacenza. Therefore we have decided, by this command of our authority, to restore and confirm the aforesaid monastery in its entirety to the venerable bishop and ruler of the church of Piacenza.

Accordingly, we prescribe and command that none of our faithful presume henceforth to disturb or bring any complaint against the aforesaid venerable Bishop Podo, the church of Piacenza, or his successors, concerning the aforesaid monastery of Gravaca, built in the county of Piacenza. Rather, let him and his successors be permitted, in our time and in that of our successors, to hold the aforesaid monastery peacefully, without opposition from any authority or unjust person, and to govern it according to the sacred canons; and let them have free and fully secure power to do whatever they may wish to do there according to equity and justice.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and be better believed and more diligently preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own people, we have ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

I, Gandulf, acting in the place of Fridugis, have examined and subscribed.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the seventh year of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, Christ being favorable, indiction 13. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1097A]

## LXXXIX. FOR THE MONASTERY OF FARFA. (Year 820.)

[In Mabillon, *Annales Ordinis S. Benedicti*, vol. II, p. 722.]

In the name of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divinely ordaining providence emperor Augustus, to all bishops, abbots, abbesses, dukes, counts, judges, gastalds, our vassals, vicars, actionaries, centenarii, and all other faithful, or our messengers traveling everywhere.

Know that the venerable Ingoald, abbot of the monastery of Holy Mary, ever Virgin and Mother of God, in the Sabine territory at a place called Acutianus, made known to the clemency of our kingdom that monks, or persons offered to Saint Mary according to the rule of Saint Benedict, whom he is bound to supervise according to due order, sometimes flee and appear throughout bishoprics, other monasteries, or various places; and he reported that he was in no way able to receive them, because various people unjustly prevented him or his messengers from doing so [Col. 1097B]. He therefore asked our Highness that, wherever he might find them, he himself, his messengers, and his successors should be prevented by no one from receiving them, but should have permission to receive them in person wherever they were found, without delay or opposition from anyone.

For this reason we ordered this authority to be issued to them, by which we absolutely command that none of you presume to place any impediment or opposition in the way of the aforesaid abbot, his successors, or their messengers concerning, as we have said, his monks or the fugitives offered to him according to the rule of equity [Col. 1097C]. Rather, wherever such persons are found, let them be received immediately and according to the rule. Whoever wishes to act otherwise shall know that he must answer before our presence on this matter; and you shall cause these letters, once read, to be returned to them.

And so that you may believe more certainly that this is our command, we have ordered it to be sealed beneath with our ring.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the seventh year of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, Christ being favorable, indiction 13. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily in the name of God.

## XC. FOR THE MONASTERY OF ARLES IN THE DIOCESE OF ELNE. [Col. 1097D] (Year 820.)

[In D. Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 522, from the Appendix to *Marca Hispanica*, p. 766.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Redeemer [Savior] Jesus Christ, Louis, by divinely ordaining providence, emperor Augustus.

If, for the love of God and of those who serve him in places dedicated to divine worship, we bestow suitable benefits, we do not doubt that a reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us by the Lord [Col. 1098A]. Therefore let the prudence of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable Castellanus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary, came to us and made known that he had built, with his brothers, a monastery among ancient buildings in the valley called Asperia; and that now, with God’s help, he serves there under the holy rule with a company of monks. He begged us to receive under our protection and guardianship the aforesaid monastery and the cells which they had built from the wilderness and which now belong to it; namely, the church of Saint Peter at Arulas, the church of Saint John at Riardo, the church of Saint Julian above the stream of Buciacum, and the other property belonging or pertaining to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary [Col. 1098B], so that those monks might live peacefully and freely with everything belonging to them.

For the love of God and reverence for divine worship, we were pleased to lend an ear to his prayers, and we have decided that these imperial letters of our authority should be issued. By them we prescribe and command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, presume to enter the aforesaid cells or the property lawfully pertaining to the aforesaid monastery, with rash intent, in order to provide lodgings or transport, take sureties, distrain the people of that monastery, demand any restitutions or unlawful pretexts, or exact anything. Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors live and reside peacefully under our protection, together with the property presently pertaining to the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1098C].

Whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid abbot departs this life, so long as the monks themselves find among them persons capable of governing them according to the rule of Saint Benedict, let them have permission to elect abbots, so that those monks may take pleasure in continually imploring the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of our entire empire.

And so that this authority may remain unshaken in our present and future times, under the protection of the Lord, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Durandus the deacon, acting in the place of Fridugis, has examined it.

[Col. 1098D]

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the seventh year of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, Christ being favorable, indiction 14. Done at the palace of Veru, happily in the name of God. Amen [Col. 1097D].

Indiction 14 was to begin in September.

Mabillon, book VI of *De Re Diplomatica*, p. 526, mentions a command of Louis dated on the fifth day before the Kalends of October in the same year and examined by the same Durandus, concerning an exchange between Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis, and Theodard. He also mentions another command concerning an exchange made by the same Hilduin with Hairradus, dated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November at the royal palace of Silviacum, in the same year and authenticated by the same notary Durandus.]

## XCI. FOR THE MONASTERY OF PRÜM (Year 820.)

[In Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis*, vol. I, p. 172.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divinely ordaining providence, emperor Augustus.

If, from the benefits granted to us by God, we confer something through the gift of our generosity upon places dedicated to God, we plainly believe that this will help us both to pass our mortal life successfully and to attain eternal life forever. Therefore let the prudence of all our faithful, present and future, know that, moved by divine inspiration and inflamed by love of the heavenly homeland, we have wished, for the salvation of our soul, to grant to the cell of Saint Goar [Col. 1099C]—and so forth.

[The cell of Saint Goar, etc. The manner in which the abbey of Prüm obtained the cell of Saint Goar from King Pippin at the assembly of Attigny is related by Wandelbert, a monk and deacon of that place, in his little book on the Miracles of this saint. It happened that Queen Bertrada, Pippin’s wife, while traveling from the monastery of Prüm toward the territory of Worms, turned aside to the cell of Saint Goar, where Erpingus was then in charge in the capacity of rector; but she found nothing there of the necessities of life. When the king learned that the hospitality that had once flourished there under the blessed man was lacking, at the general assembly held at Attigny he entrusted the same cell to Assuerus, abbot of Prüm, who was present, urging him to organize it properly and make it suitable for hospitality. At that time the cell was subject not to the monastery and its monks but only granted to the abbot by right of benefice.

During the reign of Charlemagne, a dispute arose between Weomad, bishop of Trier, and Assuerus the abbot concerning the same cell, the archbishop asserting that it belonged to the rights of his church. The case was entrusted to the royal messengers, and it was judged that the cell belonged to the king’s right; consequently, it had been lawfully handed over to Abbot Assuerus at the king’s command. Nevertheless, at the archbishop’s insistence, Charlemagne held a general assembly at the source of the Lippe in Saxony and, under oath by Ratbert, then advocate of the same monastery, and twelve witnesses, declared that the possession belonged not to the Church of Trier but solely to royal lordship. After this, the same king, with the consent of his people, transferred the cell to the monastery of Prüm by a royal charter, which, Wandelbert records, was kept in the monastery’s archives in his own time.

Today, however, the cell and lordship of Saint Goar are no longer in the power and right of the people of Prüm. Trithemius already wrote in his *Chronicon Hirsaugiense*, vol. I, p. 22: “The town of Saint Goar, with its toll, belonged to Prüm; but now it is the property of the provincial counts of Hesse, and the church there, once a provostship of our order, is now secular.”]

… the cell of Saint Goar, where the saint himself rests in body, which belongs to the estate of the monastery of Saint Savior at Prüm, formerly built from the foundations by our lord King Pippin, our grandfather, and Queen Bertrada, our grandmother, from their own property [Col. 1099B], where at the present time Abbot Tancradus appears to preside, a certain portion of the forest situated between Wesalia and Boppard, of our fiscal estates or what lies within them, and to grant it at present and transfer it from our right into the right and lordship of the aforesaid cell and monastery.

The forest itself has the following boundaries. It begins at the stream of Antiliolus, where it flows into the Rhine, and continues to the place where that stream rises; from there below Hoavelisa, then it comes to Winbach as far as Horon; from there to Moldeshart as far as the stream of Boucha, and upward along that stream to its source. From there it comes to the stream called Westerbeia, and downward along it as far as the road that leads to Trigorium [Col. 1100D].

[Where Saint Goar now is.]

From there it crosses that stream and comes to Heiswillari as far as the road that leads to Confluentes (Coblenz); from there to Basanbrunnus, and downward along it as far as the Great Stream; and along the Great Stream as far as the Rhine. Within these boundaries, whatever is contained there, together with the little village called Biberesheim, in which there are two hides and twelve residents.

The names of the slaves are these: Ruodland with his wife Helidim and their children, and so forth.

This forest, according to the measurement and adjoining boundaries set out above, together with cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows and pastures, exits and entrances, movable and immovable property—in its entirety and without reserve—we have perpetually granted by this donation of our authority to the aforesaid cell of Saint Goar and to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Savior at Prüm, for the support of the brothers serving God there and for meeting all the needs of that monastery; and we assign it perpetually to be held, so that the rulers and ministers of the aforesaid monastery may enjoy complete freedom in every respect to dispose of, regulate, or otherwise administer whatever they wish concerning it.

And so that this authority of our gift may be held more firmly and better preserved for future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

[Col. 1100B]

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Durandus the deacon, acting in the place of Fridugis, has examined it.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the sixth year of the empire of Louis Augustus, Christ being favorable, indiction 13. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## XCII. FOR THE CHURCH OF PARIS. (Year 820.)

[In Baluze, *Capitularia*, vol. II, p. 1418, from the small chartulary of the church of Paris.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divinely ordaining providence, emperor Augustus.

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own people, present and future, that the venerable Ynchadus, bishop of the Church of Paris, brought before our Serenity certain authorities which our lord grandfather Pippin and our father Charles, of blessed memory, most pious emperor, had ordered to be issued at the requests of his predecessors in that city. They contained the statement that, for the increase of eternal reward and for the sake of confirmation, they had established by their authorities for the aforesaid Church of Paris that the property, slaves, and tolls which had been handed over to that church through the generosity of kings or emperors or by written charters might thereafter be possessed more securely.

We, by this authority of ours [Col. 1101A], have confirmed and strengthened the same property, slaves, and tolls of that church, so that in the future its rulers may hold and possess them peacefully and securely, without disturbance or unjust summons from anyone.

Moreover, we have granted to the aforesaid Bishop Ynchadus and his successors, and have confirmed by our authority in the manner of a father, that no count or judicial authority shall receive any tax from the land of Saint Mary situated on the island itself, nor presume to do this concerning the household of that church or concerning other free men or inhabitants—commonly called Albani—living on that land of Saint Mary. Nor shall anyone attempt to inflict upon them any disturbance, lordship, ban contrary to law, or unlawful pretext [Col. 1101B]. No one shall dare to receive or exact from the land of Saint Mary or from those living upon it any tax called the road tax, riverbank tax, woodland tax, or any restitution.

Rather, let the aforesaid Bishop Ynchadus and his successors be permitted to arrange and govern the island peacefully according to their own will, and on that land of Saint Mary to operate taverns and conduct their other affairs without any restitution being demanded from anyone.

We further prescribe and command that, on the royal road on the side of Saint Germanus, from Saint Mederic as far as the place commonly called Tudella on the lane of Saint Germanus, and on the other smaller roads leading to the monastery of the aforesaid [Col. 1101C] Saint Germanus, no royal messenger exercise any judicial authority there, or receive any tax, riverbank tax, road tax, or toll. Rather, the bishop’s messenger shall regulate matters according to his own will; and the advocate of that church, both concerning the land of Saint Germanus itself and the aforesaid land of Saint Mary situated on the island, shall render a proper and lawful account there without any judicial authority or ban, except in a lawful court or royal assembly, as the law of the churches prescribes.

As for the free men who appear to reside on the land of the aforesaid Church of Paris and are known to serve it, we wish that, as is contained in the charter of our grandfather Pippin [Col. 1101D], none of them go to the army except together with the bishop of that church, or remain according to his arrangement. Nor may anyone presume to receive from those men living on the land of Saint Mary any tax or restitution from their persons, which they have been accustomed to pay for a long time and ought to pay in future. Whatever our fisc could demand or expect from them, we gladly grant in every respect, for the love of God and of holy Mary, Mother of God, to the aforesaid Bishop Ynchadus and his successors, and with a willing mind confirm it by our authority.

Nor may any judicial authority presume to exercise coercion over the men living on the land of Saint Mary, except, as we have said, in the lawful court of the count [Col. 1102A]. There they must come together with the advocate of the Church of Paris without delay and be compelled to render a proper account and fulfill lawful justice.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly in the name of God and be more diligently preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own people, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Durandus the notary, acting in the place of Frudigis, has examined and subscribed.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the seventh year of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious emperor, Christ being favorable. Done publicly at the palace of Aachen, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## XCIII. FOR THE CHURCH OF PARIS. [Col. 1102B] (Year 820.)

[In Baluze, at the same place.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divinely ordaining providence, emperor Augustus.

If, by our authority, we provide for the needs of priests in their various ecclesiastical necessities and offer assistance so that they may carry out their ministry more freely, we do not doubt that the Lord Jesus Christ, the supreme Pontiff, will grant us the rewards of eternal recompense.

Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own people, present and future, that the venerable Inchadus, bishop of the church of the city of Paris, brought before our Serenity a certain authority which our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, most glorious emperor, had ordered to be issued at the request of his predecessor Enchenradus, bishop of that city [Col. 1102C]. It stated that, through the carelessness and negligence of the custodians of that church, the written charters had been burned, consumed by fire, or lost—charters by which many noble men had, for the remedy of their souls, assigned property and slaves to that church—and that our same father had confirmed by the same authority that the property and slaves recorded in those documents, by which the aforesaid church was then legally endowed, should be held and possessed securely and peacefully by the rulers of that church under ecclesiastical right in future times [Col. 1102D].

The aforesaid Inchadus also asked our Serenity that, for the increase of our reward and for the sake of confirmation, we should order our authority concerning this matter to be issued to that church in the manner of a father, by which, in present and future times, the property and slaves that had been handed over to that church through the aforesaid written charters might be held or possessed firmly, peacefully, and securely by the church’s prelates.

Accordingly, having examined the authority of our lord and father, we were pleased to grant the requests of this venerable man and to join this authority of ours to our father’s authority.

Therefore we prescribe and command that all property and slaves granted to that church through generosity may, in our time and in future times [Col. 1103A], be held or possessed peacefully and securely by the rulers of that church through this authority of ours, without disturbance or unjust summons from anyone.

If, however, a dispute should arise concerning those same properties previously possessed lawfully by the prelates of that church before the aforesaid burning, so that it becomes necessary to argue the matter legally in court, then by this authority of ours the property and slaves of that church shall be defended in the same way in which they could have been defended by law through those same documents, had they not been destroyed by fire.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly in the name of God and preserved more diligently by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own people, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most pious emperor.

[Col. 1103B]

Durandus the deacon, acting in the place of Fridugis, has examined it.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, in the seventh year of the empire of Lord Louis the emperor, Christ being favorable. Done publicly at the palace of Carisiacum, in the name of God. Amen.

## XCIV. FOR THE MONASTERY OF NONANTOLA

A court held at Verona by Ratald, bishop of Verona and envoy of Louis the Pious Augustus, in which the monks of Nonantola prevail in their case against Hucpold, count of Verona. (Year 820.)

[From Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, vol. I, p. 461.]

While we had taken our seats in judgment at Verona, in the name of God, we, Retaldus, bishop and envoy of our lord the emperor for hearing the claims of all persons, Hucpuldus, count of that city, sitting with us, together with Andreas the judge, Bonifritus the official notary, Draco and Raginpertus, the scabini of that city, and the others, the same Bonifritus the notary, in accordance with what we had entrusted to him, began to inquire of the aforesaid Count Hucpuldus, on behalf of the monks of Nonantula, concerning the wood called Ostilia, which appears to be situated within the boundaries of the city of Verona: namely, that portion which once belonged to Anselm the abbot and Aidinus, his brother, whose properties had come from the aforesaid monastery—that is, one quarter of the whole of the aforesaid wood, and half of the other three quarters, which they had acquired from the royal share—except for one lot belonging to the cultivated estate of the royal chapel, whose title is Saint Lawrence, and another, Sorticella, which appears to belong to the estate of Roverscella of Count Anselm. And he said that the same Hucpuldus held it contrary to law.

When we heard this, we entrusted the matter to Hucpuldus himself, so that he might investigate whether he held it lawfully, come to the court, and defend it as best he could. When we had entrusted this to him by order of our lord the emperor, Hucpuldus himself entrusted it to the aforesaid Raginpertus, his scabinus and advocate, so that he might investigate the matter and give a full account of it in court.

When the court had been set, on the appointed day we came to the royal estate called Pociolo, on the bank of the river Mincio. After we had taken our seats there to hear cases, Andreas, bishop of Vicenza, Count Hucpuldus himself, Count Sevodo of Mantua, the aforementioned judge Andreas, Bonifritus, Lupus, Bodonicus, Draco himself, Raginpertus the scabinus, and the others sitting with us, Bonifritus himself reported this case to us [Col. 1104B] and said:

“Here now is the court. We wish to know what this Count Hucpuldus wishes to show concerning the wood called Ostilia, which belongs to the monastery of Nonantula, or for what reason he disputes its possession.”

Count Hucpuldus himself and the aforementioned Raginpertus, his advocate, replied that they had not found, nor could they find, any lawful or just basis by which he could legally dispute the quarter and the half on behalf of the aforesaid monastery of the three portions of the aforesaid wood Ostilia—apart from the two lots which we named above. Accordingly, there in the present court, Count Hucpuldus himself, by his own hands, through the hand of the same Bonifritus, reinvested the aforesaid monastery with the property. Therefore, for the security of the same monastery of Nonantula, we ordered this record to be drawn up [Col. 1104C].

I, Deusdedit, official notary, wrote this in the seventh year of the reign of our lord Emperor Louis, on the day before the Kalends of April, in the thirteenth indiction. I, Rataldus, bishop and envoy of our lord the emperor, have subscribed with my own hand. I, Andreas, bishop of Vicenza, in agreement, have subscribed. Andreas the judge has subscribed. Draco has subscribed. Raginpertus the scabinus has subscribed. I, Hucpuldus, count, have subscribed. I, Bonifritus the notary, have subscribed. I, Odo, count, have subscribed. Lupus has subscribed. [Col. 1104D] Bodonicus has subscribed. Brandolinus has subscribed.

[Note: [Col. 1103D] Observe in this court record words and phrases from the Italian or Frankish language, namely *comendavimus*, that is, Italian *comandammo* or French *commandâmes*; and *de parte monachorum*, which one would say in Italian *da parte de monaci*; and *veniret ad plaido*; and *racionem exinde donared*; and *per manicias suas*. As I observed in my dissertation on the counts palatine, in the year 853 Hucpuldus appears as count palatine. I do not know whether it could have happened that the same Veronese count mentioned in this charter was later advanced to and held that more important office; or whether, rather, one should call his nephew, or another count descended from him, count palatine. But although the authority of counts—that is, the ordinary judges of the people—and that of the royal envoys, that is, the extraordinary judges, was so great, nevertheless, whenever they wished to hold a court and establish a tribunal outside the king’s palace or outside their own residences, this was still forbidden to them, and they could not do so unless they had obtained permission from the lords of that house or land. This was established by law 22 of Louis the Pious Augustus, among the Lombard laws, part II, volume I of *Rerum Italicarum*, where we read: “The count shall hold minor courts within his jurisdiction, or wherever he is able to obtain permission.” Therefore, whenever courts were held in another person’s houses or lands—for this was sometimes done in the open countryside, under the open sky, and beneath trees—the counts and royal envoys customarily requested from the lord of the place permission to establish a tribunal there. Once permission had been obtained, it was also customary to express it in the very records of the proceedings with the words *per data licentia*, so that thereafter the public judges could not lawfully claim any right for themselves over that house or land.]

[Col. 1105A]

## XCV. For the Monastery of Inda

(Year 821.)

[In Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, from manuscript D of Louvrex.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus, to all bishops, abbots, counts, vicars, centenarii, toll-collectors, officials, and all who administer public affairs, and to the other faithful of the holy Church of God and of ours, both present and future:

Let it be known that we have granted to our monastery [Note: [Col. 1105D] He calls the monastery of Inda his own not only because it was close to his royal palace, but also because he had founded it.] called Inda, dedicated in honor of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ and built in our forest of Ardenne, [Col. 1105B] where the religious man Benedict is now abbot, [Note: [Col. 1105D] This is that famous Benedict, the reformer of our order, abbot of Aniane and Inda, through whose principal efforts the Council of Aachen had been assembled a few years earlier, namely in 817.] and to the entire congregation serving God there, every toll, both on ships traveling along the various rivers of our empire for any purpose, and on carts and pack animals necessary for that monastery [perhaps *necessaria*, “necessary things”] or of the congregation serving God there, as well as on any other merchandise from whatever source on which the treasury could exact a toll. We have granted it in full, so that no one may presume to receive or exact any toll or other levy.

Therefore we order this command of our authority to be issued to the aforesaid monastery and to the congregation dwelling there, so that ships, carts, pack animals, and every other vehicle engaged in the various business of that monastery or in supplying its needs may travel freely throughout our empire; and so that no public judge, no official exercising judicial authority, and no toll-collector may demand or exact from ships, or from any of the things mentioned above on which the treasury could exact a toll from any source, any toll, riverbank duty, port duty, bridge duty, safe-conduct duty, wheel duty, dust duty, ferry duty, transport duty, any exaction encountered, or any census or payment.

Rather, by this authority of ours, it shall be lawful, without anyone’s unlawful opposition or detention, for ships, carts, pack animals, and other vehicles, and for the men responsible for providing them, together with what they carry, to go and return freely and safely throughout our empire [Col. 1105D]. And if they remain for any length of time in any place, or buy or sell anything, nothing at all shall be exacted from them, as has been stated.

And so that this authority may possess fuller force in the name of God, and so that it may more truly be believed to be ours by all and be more diligently preserved, we ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

Durandus the deacon, in the place of Fridugisus, examined this.

[Col. 1106A]

Issued on the sixth day before the Ides of February, [Note: [Col. 1106D] This diploma was therefore issued and granted to the most holy abbot Benedict three days before his death; for on the third day before the Ides of February in the year 821, in the fourteenth indiction, he exchanged this present life for eternal life in his monastery of Inda.] in the eighth year, by the favor of Christ, of the reign of our lord Louis, most serene Augustus, in the fourteenth indiction. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XCVI. For the Monastery of Buchau

(Year 821.)

[In Schaten, *Annales Paderbornenses*, p. 67.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If we bring to fulfillment the petitions of priests and servants of God, which they make known on behalf of their needs, we not only exercise imperial clemency, but also confidently believe that such acts will benefit us toward the reward of blessed recompense [Col. 1106B]. Therefore, let it be known to the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, that the venerable man Castus, abbot of the church called Fiscbechi, with the churches subject to it in the same district of Leriga, and with the tithe from the forest of Annueri and Ponteburg, and with the other churches in Hesiga and Fenkiga—except for one church in Saxlinga, which we have granted to return to the parish of Saint Paul—came to us at the place called Mimigernaford, where Bishop Gerfridus appears to preside, and petitioned our highness that, for the increase of our reward, we should receive that holy place under our protection and the safeguard of our immunity.

Out of divine love we assented to his petition [Col. 1106C], and, since he had asked justly and reasonably, we have endeavored by this authority of ours to confirm everything accordingly.

Therefore we order and command that no public judge, no one exercising judicial authority, and none of the faithful of the holy Church of God or of ours, may at any time enter the churches, places, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid church—which it now appears to possess justly and reasonably, wherever they may be situated in districts and territories—or anything that may thereafter be bestowed upon it out of divine love, in order to hear cases, exact fines, provide lodging or requisitions, unjustly distrain the men of that church, whether free or enslaved, or demand any restitutions or unlawful services; nor may anyone presume to exact such things.

Whatever the treasury might have hoped to receive from the property of the aforesaid church, we grant entirely out of divine love, so that it may increase perpetually for the support of the poor and the maintenance of the servants of God serving God there [Col. 1106D]. Thus may those servants of God who appear to serve God there gladly entreat the Lord’s mercy continually on behalf of us, our wife and children, and the stability of our empire, which has been granted to us by God and must be preserved by him.

Let no one of our faithful presume to take away or prohibit anything from that abbey, situated throughout various surrounding districts [Col. 1107A]. Rather, by this authority of ours, let it be permitted to the abbot, with the Lord’s help, to exercise the ministry of preaching and fully perform his office.

And so that this authority may remain undisturbed in our times and in those of our successors, under the protection of the Lord, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Durandus the deacon, in the place of Helisachar, examined and subscribed this.

Issued on the fifth day before the Nones of September, in the eighth year of our reign, in the fourteenth indiction. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XCVII. [Col. 1107B] For the Monastery of Hornbach

(Year 821.)

[*History of Metz*, p. 23.]

In the name of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

We wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, that the illustrious Count Lantbertus came to our highness and reported that a royal official named Nantcarius had seized, from our fisc at Frankfurt, during the time of our lord and father, the emperor Charles of blessed memory, certain properties—namely, lands, woods, and meadows situated above the boundary—which belonged to his monastery called Orombach.

We ordered this matter to be investigated by our beloved son, the emperor Lothar, and also by the illustrious man Matfredus. Later Wyrundus, abbot of the aforesaid venerable monastery, came to us and reported the same case. We again ordered Matfredus and our other faithful to investigate the matter carefully.

As they reported to us, they found through Count Hruotbertus and the other noble and truthful men living in the vicinity that the aforesaid Nantcarius, together with the royal servants, had unjustly removed that property from the authority of the aforesaid monastery; and that, according to justice and certainty, it ought to belong between our share and that of the aforesaid monastery. They also found that the aforesaid boundary had been divided at the road called Talanweke [Col. 1107D], and from there by Gerold’s Path, then to Wisigartaweck.

Moreover, when our official Geroldus, who holds the aforesaid fisc in his administration, was questioned by them, he could demonstrate no legal basis by which he could have held it for our share. Therefore, in accordance with this investigation, it pleased us that the same boundary should be restored to the aforesaid monastery, as had been investigated and testified.

Accordingly, we ordered this authoritative command to be made, by which we order and command that, just as our faithful investigated and reported to us, so from this day onward it shall remain in the possession of the aforesaid monastery. Let the monastery have no fear that thereafter it will suffer any disturbance, accusation, or impediment whatsoever from the side of our fisc.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly, and be believed and preserved more truly and certainly by our faithful, we ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

Durandus the deacon, in the place of Fridugisus, examined this.

Issued on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the eighth year, by the favor of Christ, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus.

## XCVIII. For the Monastery of Saint Gall

[Col. 1108B] (Year 821, 15 February.)

[In Neugart, *Codex Alemannicus*, p. 179.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

When we willingly assent to the just petitions of the servants of God which they bring to our ears, and, with God’s help, bring them to fulfillment, we not only exercise royal and imperial custom, but also confidently believe that this will assuredly benefit us both in strengthening the condition of our earthly kingdom and in attaining the blessedness of eternal life.

Therefore, we wish it to be known to the understanding of all our faithful, present and future, that the venerable Cozbertus [Col. 1108C], abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, approached our clemency and made known to us that, during the time of John, bishop and abbot of that monastery, a villa called Uhcinriuda— which Gieta and her son Lantprehtus had bestowed upon the same monastery, together with its appurtenances, through a written testamentary donation—had been taken away and joined to our fisc at Zurich [Note: [Col. 1107D] In the charters of Beata and Lambertus, Uhcinriuda does not occur, but Tunriudde or Tunriude does; yet the difference between the two names is too great for them to be regarded as one and the same. Hence I infer that Beata and Lambertus assigned Uhcinriuda to Saint Gall by another charter. In the vicinity of the same places mentioned by the cited charters there is the village of Fischenried, in the parish of Busskirch above Rapperswil, on the stream called the Jona; its name is more readily reconciled with Uhcinriuda.], and he therefore entreated us to order a most just investigation into the matter, so that he might not unjustly lose what he ought to possess, according to the order of equity, from the property of the aforesaid monastery.

Granting our assent to his petition, we did as he had requested. We ordered our faithful Geroldus [Note: [Col. 1108D] Count Geroldus of the Zürichgau.] to investigate this case and report to us carefully what he had discovered [Col. 1108D]. When he returned, he reported that, as he had been able to discover through the local inhabitants, after calling upon those who were held in greatest trust among them, the aforesaid monastery had been unjustly deprived of the property concerning which Cozbertus had reported to us.

When we had heard this report and found it to be true, we ordered that the aforesaid villa, with all the property belonging to it, which had formerly been seized, should be restored to the same venerable monastery.

The same religious man, Abbot Cozbertus, also petitioned our clemency [Col. 1109A] that we should order a confirmation of our command to be given to him concerning the restored property. Since his petition appeared reasonable to us, we took care to bring it to fulfillment.

Therefore we decree and command that Cozbertus, abbot of the aforesaid monastery, and his successors, by this confirmation of our authority, henceforth hold and possess the above-named property with the greatest firmness; and that it may never be withdrawn from the right of the aforesaid monastery by any of the faithful of the holy Church of God or of ours, or by any person of whatever rank or power. Rather, through this confirmation of our authority, let it receive perpetual security.

And so that this authority may possess inviolable and unshaken firmness in our times and in those of our successors, we ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring [Col. 1109B].

Gundulfus [Note: [Col. 1109D] Bishop of Metz. He died in 823 and was succeeded by Drogo, the brother of Louis the Pious, as the ancient annals repeatedly testify.] examined and subscribed this in the place of Fridugisus.

Issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the eighth year, by the favor of Christ, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the fourteenth indiction. Done at the royal palace of Aachen [Note: [Col. 1110D] Where the emperor spent the winter and held an assembly in February, as Einhard testifies in his *Annals*, as do other chroniclers.] in the name of God. Amen.

## XCIX. For the Monastery of Saint Sulpitius at Bourges

(About the year 821.)

[In D. Bouquet, *Recueil des historiens*, vol. VI, p. 525, from the cartulary of the same monastery.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

[Col. 1109C]

It is the custom of imperial majesty willingly to grant the petitions of our faithful … so that they may more gladly devote themselves to services both private and public. Therefore, let the experience and diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know that one of our faithful, named Raninchus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Sulpitius, situated in the suburb of the city of Bourges, came before our imperial highness and presented many royal commands, strengthened by royal generosity and granted to the aforesaid place.

These documents stated that, at the petition of the abbots and rectors of the aforesaid monastery, princely generosity had granted that the reverence and dignity of Saint Father Sulpitius should continually remain under the protection of immunity [Col. 1109D], and that no judicial authority should in any way impose a penalty upon the property of the same monastery, or exact a foreigners’ toll or wheel duty within or outside the city, in the enclosures, churches, or villas, or distrain any slave or free person making a levy for the service of God [the text requires *praesumat*, “presume”].

He therefore humbly petitioned that what was contained in scattered documents, and was already in some way being weakened, should be collected by our command and, as if brought together into one, confirmed.

Accordingly, it pleased our clemency to assent to his salutary petitions, so that religion might increasingly flourish there and so that the servants of God dwelling there might more fervently pray for us, our wife and children, and the stability of our kingdom.

We ordered a command of our authority to be issued to them, by which, through our deliberation and decree, we confirmed everything that our predecessors had established for that place, both for as long as the monastic order should flourish there and thereafter: both the matters we have already mentioned and those contained in other commands concerning markets and ports, as well as concerning the enclosures of cities and the provisions to be observed in the villas by both male and female residents, so that, just as our predecessors and forefathers decreed, everything might remain undisturbed.

It is well established that all the principal possessions of the aforesaid monastery are donations of the faithful, who assigned their estates, together with their dependents, to that place out of love for the Lord [Col. 1110B] and Saint Sulpitius.

But since, as we have learned from the report of the abbot named above, through a sound indulgence certain members of the household are said, when judged, to observe servile law, some people in the church object whenever households are joined to them, refusing to observe the lawful division. Therefore, at the petition of our faithful Raninchus, we kindly grant that whenever the household of Saint Sulpitius is joined by marriage to the household of another church, this shall cause no prejudice, inasmuch as the servile condition is seen to evade the law applicable to colonists; rather, an equitable division shall be carried out everywhere according to law.

Moreover, we grant the same provision with regard to our fiscs that are known to have belonged to the church.

It has also pleased us to grant and add the following: since the property of that place is divided among scattered holdings, and since the many advocates cannot guard the courts in each place without the presence of the king … [Col. 1110C] they shall not suffer loss of property, nor within the city, so that they may more safely and securely be glad to serve the Lord.

Furthermore, we grant to the clothing and footwear provisions of the monk-brothers, as had formerly been the case, all the annual market fairs in full, together with their jurisdiction; and from the weekly market, the payment which we granted as belonging to that place.

Moreover, let no bishop, no authority, and not even any of our household officials presume to impose a penalty or take up residence within the enclosures and premises of the same monastery, so that, for their advancement and peace, our memory may in no way be torn away from them.

And so that the authority of our arrangement and concession may possess perpetual firmness in its full force [Col. 1110D], we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.

## C. For the Monastery of Fulda

[In Schaten, *Episcopatus Paderbornensis*, p. 70.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If, out of love for God and for those who serve him in places dedicated to divine worship, we bestow more substantial benefits, we do not doubt that a reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us by the Lord [Col. 1111A].

Therefore, we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, that the venerable Bishop Baderadus of the church constructed in honor of holy Mary ever-virgin and Saint Kilian, at the place called Paderborn, sent a petition and entreated us to place the aforesaid see, with everything justly and lawfully belonging or pertaining to it at the present time, under our protection and the defense of immunity, together with its property and dependents. Let the diligence of all our faithful know that we have done so.

Therefore we order and command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, may at any time enter the churches, places, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid church [Col. 1111B]—which it now possesses under the laws of our empire—or those which divine mercy may thereafter wish to increase in the right of that place, in order to hear cases judicially, exact fines, provide lodging or requisitions, take sureties, distrain the men of that church, or demand any restitutions or unlawful services; nor may anyone presume to exact any of the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid bishop and his successors possess in peace the property of the aforesaid church, together with everything they possess, and faithfully obey our imperial authority.

Whatever the treasury might be able to expect from it, we grant entirely, for the sake of eternal recompense, to the aforesaid church, for the support of the poor and the preparation of lights [Col. 1111C], so that the clerics dwelling in that see may more gladly entreat the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife, and our children.

And so that this authority may be better preserved for future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Hirminmaris the deacon, in the place of Abbot Fridugisus, examined this.

Issued on the fourth day before the Nones of April, in the ninth year of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the fifteenth indiction. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## CI. For the Monasteries in the City of Sens

[Col. 1111D] (Year 822.)

[In Mabillon, *Annales ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, vol. II, p. 476.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If, out of love for him by whose gift we have been placed above the other mortals, we procure earthly benefits of temporal support for those who, under holy religion, serve God alone, for his praise and honor and for the salvation of souls destined to be enrolled among the heavenly choirs of angels in eternal blessedness [Col. 1112A]—benefits without which the present life cannot be spent—so that they may serve him alone without impediment, insofar as the frailty of present mortality permits, since they are known to have devoted themselves to his praise and service for the whole course of their lives, we believe that the labor of our effort and the work of our piety will in no way be without fruit before God, without whom no one can even will what is good, much less accomplish it.

Therefore, let the sincerity of all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, learn that the venerable Hieremias, archbishop of the church of Sens, made known to our clemency by humble petition [Col. 1112B] that the monastic cells of the bishopric over which, by God’s authority, he presides—namely, the cell of Saint Peter, the cell of Saint John, and the cell of Saint Remigius—[Note: [Col. 1111D] Louis, or rather Hieremias, who obtained the command, calls these monasteries “cells,” a humbler designation, in order to indicate their greater subjection.] [Note: [Col. 1111D] Of these three monasteries two survive: Saint Peter’s, popularly called Vivi, and Saint John’s, now belonging to regular canons of the Order of Saint Augustine, but then, like the other two, inhabited by monks under the holy rule. The abbey of Saint Remigius was later transferred to Vallilias, then restored again to its first site, and is now wholly destroyed; its abbatial portion was assigned to missionary clerics and its conventual portion to the monastery of Saint Peter.] in which monks, under the discipline of the holy rule, ought to offer a religious life to divine piety with every exertion of labor, had formerly been subjected to various circumstances and diverse necessities by the hands and authority of his predecessors.

Driven by complete poverty, and straying far from their purpose, they had deviated, because the resources of the aforesaid cells had been diminished by an earlier division. The bishops who presided over them, having no other means from which to obtain the subsidies necessary for their own expenses, compelled the cells to give them as much as they could extort, since they could obtain sufficient resources nowhere else.

Thus it came about that those who ought, with devoted steadfastness of mind and body, to offer praises to the heavenly piety there, commend their lives to it, and intercede for the safety of us, our wife and children, for the preservation of the kingdom granted to us by divine mercy, and for the pardon of the whole Church and a blessed arrival at eternal beatitude, wandered far and wide from the cloisters of the monastery, shamefully seeking the means by which they might sustain their poverty.

With the proper order that they ought to preserve thrown into confusion, they could not only provide us with no benefit because of the matters mentioned above, but were also reasonably believed to be causing very great harm to themselves and to their prelates.

For this reason, prompted by the petitions of the aforesaid bishop, we judged it a worthy work to be undertaken [Col. 1112D], so that, while we still remain in this mortal body, we might provide not only for those who are now known to be devoted to divine worship in those places, but also for those who, in future times, enlightened by love of heavenly wisdom, may seek those same places in order to serve God.

Thus they may have from the same places temporal support for expenses appropriate to their order, by which they may meanwhile be sustained in this pilgrimage [Col. 1113A] until, called by divine mercy to the joys of their eternal homeland, they are able to arrive there.

Accordingly, establishing this command of our authority, we decreed, in accordance with the petition of the aforesaid bishop, that it should be made. From whatever property the above-named cells now possess as assigned to the needs of the monks serving God there, no bishop who may succeed over time by divine vocation may presume, under any pretext or occasion, to withdraw or diminish anything, or grant it as a benefice, or apply it to his own uses.

Rather, he shall endeavor to preserve everything in all respects just as the aforesaid bishop set out each place individually and in order in the text of his memorandum, subscribed it with his own hand, and requested the bishops who were present at the assembly to subscribe it as well [Col. 1113B], in order to prevent every kind of dispute that might arise in future times.

Nor may he at any time appropriate for himself any other service or larger gifts from them beyond what that same bishop thought fit to include in the same memorandum.

And lest, on account of this decree, the abbots or monks established in those monasteries begin to grow proud against their bishop, we have taken precautions to remove every occasion for this and to give no place to the devil, while preserving in all respects the bishop’s authority and power in every matter of ecclesiastical discipline.

That is, while always governing those cells under his own authority, he shall appoint abbots according to the institution of the holy rule, and change them if necessary; correct whatever is wrong, cut away what is superfluous, nourish virtues, [Col. 1113C] uproot vices, and, like a good farmer, tearing out the brambles and following the institutions of the Fathers, discern what kind of seed he ought to entrust to each field.

This authority of our constitution has been made so that the religious order in the places written above may not be thrown into confusion in our times or in those of our successors, but may be preserved inviolably and forever in every respect in the service of God, for whose praise and service we were created.

So that it may possess fuller firmness in the name of God for all time, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene Augustus.

Durandus the deacon, in the place of Fridugisus, examined this.

[Col. 1113D]

Issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the ninth year, by the favor of Christ, of the reign of our lord Louis, most serene Augustus, in the fifteenth indiction. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## CII. For the Monastery of Elnone

(Year 822.)

[In D. Bouquet, cited above, p. 530.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

When we provide appropriate assistance to places devoted to divine worship for the love of divine service, and properly fulfill the royal custom, we truly believe that this will benefit us in attaining the rewards of eternal recompense. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own, both present and future, that the venerable man Adaleodus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Amandus, approached the serenity of our majesty together with Aldric, our envoy whom we had sent to the aforesaid monastery to confirm the observance of the rule of Saint Benedict. They represented to our gentleness that we ought to assign and confirm certain properties and estates of that church’s possessions for the uses and necessities of the community of Christ’s confessor Amandus.

Accordingly, at the prayer and request of the aforesaid abbots—namely Adaleodus and Aldric—and indeed for the benefit of our own soul, that of our wife, and those of our children, we have decided to hand over and confirm the properties listed below to the aforesaid brothers and to the community of Saint Amandus for their food, clothing, and footwear, as well as for their other uses and necessities. We have therefore decided that these imperial letters of ours be made concerning this grant, and we command that henceforth and forever they be preserved by us and, by God’s dispensation, by our successors, in accordance with our pious decrees. Let your sagacity know that we have done and granted this for the sake of attaining eternal rewards and providing for the necessities of the aforementioned community, on the sole condition that whatever, by God’s gift and through diligent labor, can be obtained or acquired from these properties shall, without any subtraction, wholly accrue to the use of the brothers.

By the same imperial authority we further prescribe and command that no person belonging to God’s holy Church, whether present or future, attempt to inflict disturbance, opposition, prejudice, or violence upon the aforesaid and underspecified properties. Rather, without any concealment, subtraction, diminution, or division, let it be permitted to that same community of monks serving God to have, possess, and enjoy them securely and perpetually, in their entirety and inviolably, without any accusation or contradiction. They have been specially assigned and confirmed by us for this purpose alone, as stated above, for our reward, so that no human power may divert them without risking its own peril; instead, they shall always remain safely and inviolably under royal and imperial protection for the use of the brothers. Thus may the devout and God-beloved community of that place, aided by the gift of our piety, take greater delight in beseeching the Lord on our behalf and for the stability and peace of this entire empire.

These are the names of the properties which we have decided to give them: in the county of Brabant, at the places called Baceroth (Bassarode), Decla, Neonisio, and Securiaco, forty-eight manses; in the county of Ostrevant, at the place called Halciacus, with its dependencies, fifty-eight manses; in the county called Menpiscus, at the place called Roslar, with its dependencies, one hundred and eighteen manses; four mansioniles around the monastery, together with a fishery and Seoncurtis; and eight marshes in Flanders. Also, in the county of Laon, Barisiacum with all its dependencies.

Moreover, we have judged that they should receive a ninth part of all the movable property of that church throughout all its estates, and of the possessions of the rector of this monastery—that is, grain, legumes, hay, cheese, pigs, foals, *camsilis* [a term of uncertain meaning], food provisions (*pastis*), wine, and eggs.

And so that this authority may retain inviolable force for future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Durandus the deacon, have examined this on behalf of Fridugisus.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of July, in the eighth year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the fifteenth indiction. Done at the villa of Stratella, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1115D] It should be read “ninth,” not “eighth.”]

## CIII. For the Monastery of Saint Christina (Year 822)

[From Baluze, *Capitularia*, vol. II, p. 1422, from an old Lombard codex.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.

When, for the love of divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants, we believe that the gift of heavenly grace is bestowed upon us by the Lord. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own, both present and future, that the venerable man Peter, abbot of the monastery of Saint Christina, which is situated near our villa of Ollonna, presented to our sight the immunity charter of our lord and father, the most serene emperor Charles, of blessed memory. It stated that he had placed the aforesaid monastery, together with all its properties and dependants, which the same monastery at that time lawfully possessed either through the donations of kings and queens or through those of other God-fearing people, under his protection and defense; and that, by the authority of that immunity charter, the monastery had until then been protected and defended against interference by judicial authority.

For the sake of securing this arrangement, the abbot Peter requested our serenity to add our authority to that of our father. Granting his requests out of love for divine worship and reverence for that holy place, we ordered this charter of our immunity to be made for the same monastery. By it we prescribe and command that the aforementioned monastery, with all its properties and dependants presently and lawfully belonging or pertaining to it, shall in every respect remain under the protection of our immunity. No public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, shall dare in our time or in that of our successors to enter the churches, villas, courts, places, fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery—which it now lawfully possesses in any county or territory within the jurisdiction of our empire, or which divine piety may thereafter cause to be added to the right of that holy place—for the hearing of cases, the collection of fines, the provision of lodgings or transport, the taking of sureties, or the coercion of the monastery’s people; nor shall anyone presume to demand any of the other things mentioned above or to seek any unlawful pretext.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors quietly possess the properties of the aforementioned monastery [lacuna], as is contained in the charter of our lord and father, under the protection of our immunity, and faithfully obey our imperial authority. Thus may the community serving God there take delight in continually imploring the Lord’s mercy on our behalf, on behalf of our wife and children, and for the stability of our entire empire, which God has granted and entrusted to us to preserve.

And so that this authority may remain unshaken in our time and in that of our successors, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Durandus the deacon, have examined this on behalf of Fridugisus.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, in the ninth year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the first indiction. Done at Cispiacho in Ardna, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## CIV. For the Church of Saint Victor of Marseille (Year 822)

[Col. 1116C] [From D. Bouquet, *Collection of Historians*, vol. VI, p. 532, from the chartulary of this church.]

In the name of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus, to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own, and to all officials administering the public affairs, both present and future.

We wish your sagacity to know how the venerable Theodbert, bishop of Marseille, approached the serenity of our majesty, carrying in his hands a certain charter of our lord and father, Charles, most excellent emperor. It stated that he had granted to the church of Saint Victor the martyr, where his most sacred body is buried, the toll from the estate called Leonio—whatever the royal fisc customarily exacted from it, whether from salt or from other dues—as well as the toll from ships coming from Italy which appeared to put in at that same church, so that whatever custom had been accustomed to exact from there for public works or for the royal fisc should be granted to the aforesaid church of Saint Victor the martyr of Marseille or to its rectors.

Therefore he earnestly entreated our clemency, insofar as he was able, that, following our father’s custom, the aforesaid church, over which he presides as bishop by God’s authority, might likewise merit possessing our authority. Listening favorably to his requests, we ordered these imperial letters of ours to be made, by which we prescribe and command that, just as our lord and father granted to the aforesaid church, so thereafter and forever it shall remain firm and stable. No one exercising judicial authority shall presume to exact or demand any toll from the places mentioned above, or to inflict or impose any opposition upon the aforesaid church of Saint Victor and its rectors. Rather, this grant shall be preserved inviolably in our time and in that of our successors.

And so that this authority of our confirmation may remain inviolable for future times, we ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of our lord Louis, most serene emperor.

Given on the Kalends of November, in the ninth year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the first indiction. Done at the royal palace of Isemburg.

## CV. For the Monastery of Saint Amandus (Year 822)

[From Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, fourth century, part I, p. 66.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.

When, for the love of divine service, we provide suitable assistance to places devoted to divine worship, and properly fulfill the royal custom, we truly believe that this will benefit us in attaining the rewards of eternal recompense. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own, both present and future, that the venerable man Adaleodus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Amandus, approached the serenity of our majesty together with Aldric, our envoy whom we sent to the aforesaid monastery to confirm the observance of the rule of Saint Benedict. They represented to our gentleness that we ought to assign and confirm certain properties and estates of that church for the uses and necessities of the community of Christ’s confessor Amandus.
