Accordingly, at the prayer and request of the aforesaid abbots—namely Adaleodus and Aldric—and indeed for the benefit of our own soul, our wife, and our children, we have decided to hand over and confirm the properties listed below to the aforesaid brothers and to the community of Saint Amandus for their food, clothing, and footwear, as well as for their other uses and necessities. We have decided that these imperial letters of ours be made concerning this grant, and we command that henceforth and forever they be preserved by us and, by God’s dispensation, by our successors, in accordance with our pious decrees. Let your sagacity know that we have done and granted this for the sake of attaining eternal rewards and providing for the necessities of the aforementioned community, on the sole condition that whatever, by God’s gift and through diligent labor, can be obtained or acquired from these properties shall, without any subtraction, wholly accrue to the use of the brothers.

By the same imperial authority we prescribe and command that no person belonging to God’s holy Church, whether present or future, attempt to inflict disturbance, opposition, prejudice, or violence upon the aforesaid and underspecified properties. Rather, without any concealment, subtraction, diminution, or division, let it be permitted to that same community of monks serving God to have, possess, and enjoy them securely and perpetually, in their entirety and inviolably, without any accusation or contradiction. They have been specially assigned and confirmed by us for this purpose alone, as stated above, for our reward, so that no human power may divert them without risking its own peril; instead, they shall always remain safely and inviolably under royal and imperial protection for the use of the brothers. Thus may the devout and God-beloved community of that place, aided by the gift of our piety, take greater delight in beseeching the Lord on our behalf and for the stability and peace of this entire empire.

These are the names of the properties which we have decided to give them: in the county of Brabant, at the places called Baceroth (commonly Bassarode), Decla, Neonifio, and Securiaco, forty-eight manses; in the county of Ostrevant, at the place called Halciacus, with its dependencies, fifty-eight manses; in the county called Menpiscus, at the place called Roslar, with its dependencies, one hundred and eighteen manses; four mansioniles around the monastery, together with a fishery and Seoncurtis; and eight marshes in Flanders. Also, in the county of Laon, Barisiacum with all its dependencies.

Moreover, we have judged that they should receive a new share of all the movable property of that church throughout all its estates, and of the possessions of the rector of this monastery—that is, grain, legumes, hay, cheese, pigs, foals, *camsilis* [a term of uncertain meaning], food provisions (*pastis*), wine, and eggs.

And so that this authority may retain inviolable force for future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Durandus the deacon, have examined this on behalf of Fridugisus.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of July, in the eighth year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the fifteenth indiction. Done at the villa of Stratella, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1117D] From this charter it is clear that in the eighth year of Louis’s reign, A.D. 822, Adaleodus was already abbot of this monastery, contrary to what is stated in the Elnone Chronicle.]

## CVI. For the Bishop of Modena (Year 822)

[From Muratori, *Italian Antiquities*, vol. I, p. 771.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.

If, for the love of divine worship, we lend an ear to the petitions of priests and God’s servants, we are confident that this contributes greatly not only to the stability of our kingdom but also to attaining eternal rewards more readily. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own, both present and future, how the venerable Deusdedit, bishop of the church of Modena, unable to come to us because of old age and bodily infirmity, sent one of his priests named Willihianus. Through him he petitioned us concerning properties belonging to his church which the kings of the Lombards, for love and fear of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ and of his confessor Saint Geminianus, had either given to that church or confirmed as having been given by others. He asked that, after we had inspected the charters and confirmations of those kings, we confirm those properties and possessions to the same church by a charter of our authority.

Since his petition appeared just and grounded in reason, we were pleased willingly to lend an ear and give our assent. Accordingly, after inspecting and rereading the charters and confirmations of the aforesaid Lombard kings, we were pleased to confirm their donations, grants, and confirmations to the same church by this charter of our authority, in accordance with the petition of the aforementioned bishop.

First, the confirmation which King Cunipert made to the church of Saint Geminianus concerning Villa Poziolo, together with the tribute, the *succidiales*, and the *angariae* which the servants of Saint Geminianus were obliged to perform for working and cultivating that estate.

[Note: [Col. 1119D] I would by no means dare determine what *succidiales* were. Was it written for *socidiales*, designating revenues received from herds and flocks entrusted in partnership? Or does it derive from *succidere*, or, as they used to say, *runcare*—clearing forests—and from bringing previously uncultivated fields under cultivation? I am genuinely uncertain. Meanwhile, if you wish, consult the *Farfense Chronicle*, part II of volume I of the *Collection of Italian Affairs*, where servants are mentioned together with their property, namely an ox, a cow, a horse, and so forth. In our own times the custom still survives among the people of Milan of entrusting their estates to cultivators—now entirely free men—under nearly the same conditions I have just indicated: namely, that they return to the owner each year a certain quantity of produce and money.]

Likewise, the charter which King Liutprand made to the aforesaid church concerning the servants and *aldiones* belonging to the right of the church of Saint Geminianus and residing in the district of Salestina, in the villas whose names are Galaniticum and Gabellum Castellum, with their fisheries. This had been the Massa of Saint Geminianus from ancient times; concerning it, the charter of King Ratchis was shown to us. There is likewise the charter of Desiderius.

Also, the charter of King Hildeprand, which he made to the church of Saint Geminianus at the request of Bishop John, concerning the church of Saint Peter within the walls of the city of Geminiana, now called Nova, together with all the properties and dependencies belonging to that church or lawfully acquired there.

Likewise, the donation which our lord and father, the emperor Charles, of pious memory, made of the parish of Saint Thomas, situated at Gandaceto beside the river Lama, together with everything belonging to it, as well as its canonical revenues and tithe.

Likewise, the donation which our lord and father, the emperor Charles, made at the request of Geminianus, bishop of Modena, of the mill near the road, together with its intake or watercourse, which belonged to the royal estate of the city of Nova.

Also, the properties which two Roman men, namely Gondolus and Constantinus, and their wives Maria and Agnita, donated to the church of Saint Geminianus.

Likewise, the Oratory of Saint Apollinaris situated at Stagnano within the jurisdiction of Montebello; the Oratory of Saint Domninus built near Clusium on the river Niziana; and the olive grove situated beside the walls of the fortress of Montebello and belonging to the same church.

These properties and possessions of the aforesaid church of Modena, or of Saint Geminianus—which the kings either gave or confirmed, or which other devout and God-fearing people transferred to the same church by formal donation, and which are now held under the right of that church, or which may have been unjustly and violently taken away from it—we have been pleased to confirm to the same church by this charter of our authority, in accordance with the petition of the aforesaid venerable man and our petitioner, Bishop Deusdedit.

Therefore we prescribe and command that no public judge, count, *gastald*, or person of any authority shall presume to disturb or unjustly prosecute the aforementioned bishop or his successors, or the church of Saint Geminianus, concerning the aforesaid properties and possessions which the kings named above confirmed to that church and which we confirm by this authority of ours; nor shall anyone presume to take away or alienate anything from them contrary to the order of justice, or bring any accusation against them. Rather, let the aforementioned church and its rectors hold and possess them peacefully under our protection and that of our successors, without any unjust contradiction by anyone, as we have already said.

We have also granted this privilege to the aforementioned church: if, after the death of the bishops of that see, someone should be found among the clergy who, according to the canons, is capable of holding the honor and office of the episcopate, they shall have permission to choose him from among themselves.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and, with the Lord’s protection, remain unshaken in our time and in that of our successors, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed below with our ring, condemning anyone who violates it to a penalty of two pounds of refined gold.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Durandus the deacon, have examined this on behalf of Fridugisus.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of February, in the ninth year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, and in the fifteenth indiction. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## CVII. For the Monastery of Prüm (Year 823)

[From Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, p. 79, from the chartulary of Prüm.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.

If we confirm by our edicts those things which the faithful of our empire exchange among themselves for their own advantage, we exercise the imperial custom, and we wish them thereafter to remain established by the strongest legal right. Therefore let the discernment of all our faithful, both present and future, know that the venerable man Tancradus, abbot of the monastery called Prüm, founded in honor of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, represented to us that he had made an exchange with a certain man named Fulcbert, for the advantage of both parties.

The aforesaid venerable man Tancradus, abbot, from the property of the aforesaid monastery, with the consent and agreement of the monks residing there, gave to the aforementioned Fulcbert, to have as his own perpetually, certain properties situated in the county of Worms, in the villa called Flaconheim: two manses with houses, buildings, lands, vineyards, meadows, woods, pastures, appurtenances, right of exit and return, and whatever in the same villa the aforesaid monastery is presently recognized as lawfully possessing.

In return for these properties, the aforementioned Fulbert gave from his own property to the aforesaid monastery and to the entire community serving God there throughout the ages certain properties situated in the same county: one mansus in the villa called Glaolfesheim; one mansus in another villa called Villarie; also, in a third place, in the villa called Leiwrdesheim, one small estate; and, in a fourth place, in the villa called Huccunheim, two parts of a *jurnale*, with their boundaries and adjoining sides.

These properties likewise included houses, buildings, lands, vineyards, meadows, woods, pastures, appurtenances, right of exit and return, and whatever in the aforesaid places he is presently recognized as lawfully holding and possessing.

He declared that he had the two exchanges, written in identical form and strengthened by the hands of good men, in his possession. But for complete security he requested our highness to confirm those exchanges anew by a decree of our gentleness. We did not wish to deny assent to his requests; rather, know that just as we have granted and confirmed such requests to each of our faithful who petitions justly, so we have granted and confirmed them to these men.

Therefore we prescribe and command that whatever one party has justly and reasonably transferred to the other party shall henceforth, by this authority of ours, hold and possess it by the strongest legal right, and do whatever it wishes with it.

And so that this authority may retain inviolable force for future times and be more readily believed and preserved by all, we ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

I, Durandus the deacon, have examined this on behalf of Fridegisus.

Given on the Ides of October, in the tenth year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the first indiction. Done at the royal palace of Aristallium, prosperously in the name of God.

## CVIII. For the Same Monastery (Year 823)

[From Martène, same work, from the chartulary of Prüm.]

In the name of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.

If we confirm by our edicts those things which the faithful of our empire exchange among themselves for their own advantage, we exercise the imperial custom, and we wish this thereafter to remain established by the strongest legal right. Therefore let the discernment of all our faithful, both present and future, know that the venerable man Hildoinus, abbot and chief chaplain of our sacred palace, made known to our highness that the religious man Tancradus, abbot of the monastery of Prüm, had made an exchange of certain enslaved persons with a certain man named Opilo.

The aforesaid venerable man Tancradus, from the property of his aforesaid monastery of Prüm, which is founded in honor of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, with the consent of the community of that monastery, gave to the aforementioned Opilo seven enslaved persons, by these names: Theotharius, Grimoldus, Theotgaudus, Werintrudis, Goza, Hunlinda, and Bertruda.

In return for these enslaved persons, the aforementioned Opilo gave from his own property to the aforesaid monastery fourteen enslaved persons, by these names: Germundus, Reginerus, Nortbertus, Bernoldus, Thiedoldus, Hautmarus, Winigodus, Rotgerus, Wigiradus, Bumannus, Willisuinda, Thieodulfus, Theotlinda, and Anstila.

They declared that they had the two exchanges, written in identical form and strengthened by the hands of good men, in their possession. But for complete security they requested our highness to confirm those exchanges anew and more fully by a decree of our gentleness [perhaps: “of our gentle authority”]. We did not wish to deny assent to their requests; rather, know that just as we have granted and confirmed such requests in every respect to each of our faithful who petitions justly, so we have granted and confirmed them here.

Therefore we prescribe and command that whatever one party has justly and reasonably transferred to the other party shall henceforth, by this authority of ours, hold and possess it by the strongest legal right, and shall enjoy complete freedom to do with it whatever it chooses.

And so that this authority may be held firm and better preserved for future times, we ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

I, Durandus the deacon, have examined this on behalf of Fridegisus.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, in the tenth year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the first indiction. Done at Construentes [perhaps Confluentes], on the Moselle, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## CIX. Confirmation of the Exchange Made between Bernoldus, Bishop of Strasbourg, and Erchengarius, Count of Nordgau (Year 823)

[From Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, vol. II, p. 174, from the fourteenth-century parchment chartulary of the abbey of Andlau.]

[Note: [Col. 1123C] Edited by Schoepflin, *Alsatian Diplomatic Documents*, vol. I, p. 71, but not very accurately.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.

If we confirm by our edicts those things which the faithful of our empire have exchanged among themselves for their own advantage, we exercise the imperial custom, and we wish this thereafter to remain established by the strongest legal right. Therefore let the discernment of all our faithful, both present and future, know that the venerable Bernoldus, bishop of the church of Strasbourg, and the illustrious man Erchengarius, count, approached and made known to the ears of our clemency that, for the advantage of both parties, they had exchanged certain properties and enslaved persons.

[Note: [Col. 1123C] Schoepflin thinks that Erchengarius administered the county of Nordgau, or Lower Alsace. This charter of exchange, together with another involving Waldo, abbot of Schwarzach, proves him to have been a very powerful lord and possessor of many patrimonies. The memory of Count Erchengarius is recorded in the Schwarzach necrology under 2 March.]

The aforesaid Bishop Bernoldus therefore gave from the property of his aforesaid church to that same Erchengarius, to have as his own, in the county of Alsace, in the villa and territory called Bodolesvillare or Pleanungovillare, all the properties which he appeared to hold in that villa [lacuna] from the property of his bishopric, together with twelve enslaved persons, by these names: Ello, Fridalind, Hildim, Willaran, Engilbert, Odalgart, Antbert, Amalgart, Adalgart, Regingart, Adaltrud, and Willigart.

[Note: [Col. 1123D] Bodolesvillare, which is one and the same place as Pleanungovillare, is today the village of Blienswilre, between Sélestat and Andlau. Although the sense of this charter indicates that they are one and the same village, Schoepflin considers them two places, deriving Balschweiler from Bodolesvillare and Blienswilre from Pleanungovillare.]

In return for this property, the aforementioned Count Erchengarius gave from his own property to the aforesaid bishopric, for the benefit of his church, in the same county, at the places named below:

At Duminheim, two *areales* with houses and a granary, forty-six *jugera* of arable land, and meadows sufficient for ten wagonloads;

[Note: [Col. 1123D] Today the village of Dunnenheim, belonging to the abbey of Neubourg.]

in the villa of Liutpoleshaim, two *areales* with one house, thirty-two *jugera* of arable land, and meadows sufficient for two wagonloads;

[Note: [Col. 1123D] Today Lipsheim, a village belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg.]

in the villa of Wittinishaim, one *areale* with a lordly house and a granary, seventy-five *jugera* of arable land, meadows sufficient for ten wagonloads, approximately seven *jugera* of woodland, and one orchard;

[Note: [Col. 1123D] Today Wittisheim, commonly Witzen, a village belonging to the same bishop of Strasbourg.]

at Creacheshaim, one *hoba*;

[Note: [Col. 1123D] Today Criesheim, also a village of the bishopric of Strasbourg. A *hoba*, or *hube*, is a rural holding, or a measure of land with a tenant’s dwelling. Wachter gives the etymology of the word in his *Glossary*, p. 758. Potgiesser, *On the Status of Servants*, book I, chapter 4, §20, p. 227, and Haltaus, *German Glossary*, pp. 959 ff., have collected and explained its various meanings.]

at Platpoteshaim, one *areale* with one house, fifteen *jugera* of arable land, meadows sufficient for four wagonloads, and a *goldmarcha*;

[Note: [Col. 1124C] Today Plobsheim, belonging to the lords Kempffer and de Güntzer. *Goldmarcha* suggests gold-washing, or the right to collect gold, which the Germans call *goldwasche*. The nobles de Güntzer and Kempffer still exercise this right today in the village of Plobsheim by virtue of the fief which they hold from the king. Schoepflin reads *holzmarcha* in place of *goldmarcha*: a portion of woodland granted for gathering wood, as Haltaus’s *German Glossary*, p. 954, explains.]

and, in addition, twelve enslaved persons, by these names: Vulpot, Winigelt, Ratini, Radvich, Hunboldus, Frenkin, Freidin, Hucbert, Rinhart, Deganolt, Hitto, and Adalger.

They declared that they had the two exchanges, written in identical form and strengthened by the hands of good men, in their possession. But for complete security they requested our highness to confirm those exchanges anew and more fully by a decree of our gentleness. We did not wish to deny assent to their requests; rather, know that just as we have granted and confirmed such requests to each of our faithful who petitions justly and reasonably, so we have granted and confirmed them in every respect here.

Therefore we prescribe and command that whatever one party has justly and lawfully transferred to the other party shall henceforth, by this authority of ours, hold and possess it by the strongest legal right, and shall enjoy complete freedom to do with it whatever it wishes.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved for future times, we ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

I, Durandus the deacon, have examined this on behalf of Fridugisus.

[Note: [Col. 1124D] Fridugisus was an Englishman by birth, abbot of the church of Saint Martin of Tours and subsequently of Sithiu. At the same time as Helisachar, he held the office of chancellor at the court of Emperor Louis, and continued in it until the year 832.]

Given [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 1124D] The notation of the day and month has been erased. But the *Annals of Einhard*, in Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 182 (vol. I of this work, col. 430), attest that Louis the Pious held an assembly at Frankfurt in May 825; and the emperor’s charters for the abbeys of Gregoriana and Masoniana, reported by Schoepflin, *Alsatian Diplomatic Documents*, vol. I, pp. 69–70, prove that he was still staying there in June. Germanus, in Mabillon, *On Diplomatic Matters*, book IV, p. 283, and Besselius, in the *Gotwin Chronicle*, vol. II, p. 473, discuss the notable and splendid royal palace of Frankfurt on the Main.]

in the tenth year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the first indiction. Done at the royal palace of Frankfurt, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## CX. For the Monastery of Saint Grata in the Diocese of Urgell (Year 823)

[From Baluze, in the appendix to *Marcellinus Hispanus*, p. 767.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.

If, out of love for Him by whose gift we have been exalted above other mortals, we assent to the just and reasonable petitions of the servants of God, and if we assist places consecrated to divine service with suitable benefits of our generosity, so that they may carry out divine worship more abundantly, we faithfully believe that a reward will be bestowed upon us by the Lord. Therefore we wish it to be brought to the knowledge of our faithful, both present and future, [Col. 1125B] how Count Matfredus, an illustrious man, approached the serenity of our majesty, carrying in his hands certain charters which, while we were formerly established in Aquitaine, we had ordered to be issued to a certain venerable Possedonius, bishop of the see of Urgell. These contained the provision that we had granted certain deserted places for the construction of monasteries or the gathering of monks, specifically so that, after his death, the monks living in those places which he desired to build might have permission to choose an abbot from among themselves.

The aforesaid Bishop Possedonius, through the same Matfredus, our faithful servant, suggested that we receive under our power—or rather, protection and lordship—the monastery which that bishop had rebuilt, called Santa Grata, situated above the river Bosegia, [Col. 1125C] dedicated in honor of holy Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God, and the cell dependent upon that monastery, called Saint Fructuosus, together with all its appurtenances, as well as whatever the monks presently living in the aforesaid places held or possessed, or might thereafter construct from deserted and uncultivated places; and that the monks and the property belonging there should be our own in the same way as the other monasteries within Septimania are acknowledged to be ours. By our authority we would grant them permission from that time onward to elect whatever abbot they wished.

Because we recognized their petition as just and reasonable, we willingly gave our assent. We received the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1125D] with the aforesaid cell and its appurtenances, together with the monks living there and all the property presently belonging to that monastery, as well as whatever they should thereafter acquire from deserted and uncultivated places for their use, into our service, specifically so that they should remain under our—or rather, their own—lordship.

For this reason we ordered these letters of our authority to be drawn up for the monks [Col. 1126A] of the aforesaid monastery. Through them we wish to make known to our faithful that they should recognize the aforesaid monastery, with the aforementioned cell and its appurtenances and all its property, as our own, as stated above, and that it should remain under our protection and guardianship. No bishop, count, or itinerant royal envoy shall exercise any lordship, tyranny, or authority there, except as canonical authority commands.

And therefore, since it is established that the aforesaid monastery is ours, we grant to the monks living there under the holy Rule permission not only to have the right to elect an abbot at the present time, but also in the future: whenever, by divine calling, the appointed abbot or others who in the course of time [Col. 1126B] shall have departed from this world, they shall have permission, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, to elect abbots from among themselves. Thus the monks serving God there, living the monastic life more securely and peacefully, may pray more attentively for the mercy of the Lord on behalf of us, our wife, and our offspring.

And so that this authority may retain inviolate and unshaken permanence through the passage of the years, and so that it may be believed more truly and certainly and preserved more carefully by the faithful of God’s holy Church and by our own people, we ordered it to be sealed below with the impression of our ring.

[Note: [Col. 1125D] In the original document from which this charter is edited, the following formula came next: “The sign of Louis, most serene emperor,” according to the usual form. But that line was erased, and in its place the following words were written in another hand, though a very ancient one and perhaps contemporary: “Moreover, we give and grant that very se . . . whose name is Santa Maria, with its titles, and the house of Santa Grata, with its boundaries and limits.”]

Durandus, deacon, have examined this in place of Fridugisus.

Issued on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, in the tenth year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most serene Augustus, in the first indiction. Enacted at the royal palace of Frankfurt, successfully, in God’s name. Amen.

### CXI. FOR THE MONASTERY OF MASONIS. (Year 823.)

[In D. Bouquet, ibid., p. 535, from Ludovicus Laguille, in the proofs of his *History of Alsace*, p. 15.]

In the name of [the Lord God] and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divine clemency made favorable to him [Note: [Col. 1126D] Louis the Pious did not use this expression, *repropitiante*, until 834, when he was restored to the throne after his deposition in the preceding year. See Mabillon, Book II of *De re diplomatica*, chapter 2, no. 13.], emperor Augustus.

Since it is our responsibility to defend and establish all the places of our kingdom constructed for the praise and glory of God, we order that the abbey in the Vosges region, founded by a certain noble prince, from whom it also took its name—called the Valley of Masonis (Masmunster, [Col. 1126D] or Moisevaux)—namely, the brother of Duke Lutfrid and of Eberard, who built Morbach in honor of the precious martyr and bishop Leodegar, no human person shall henceforth presume to destroy or disturb it. Let no one demand or extort from the household or possessions of that enduring church any fines, military summonses, revisionary services, stipends, or any other exactions, nor remove or diminish anything from all that has been given or will be given to the aforesaid place. Rather, let everything there serve forever, freely, fully, and undisturbed, those who minister to God.

If, however, any person wishes to appropriate anything from the property of that church by a false assertion of legal claims, this shall in no way be permitted except in the presence of the leading men of the kingdom, lest the place be oppressed under a false pretext.

As for the advocates, whose future character we do not know, we command them on God’s behalf and ours not to appoint or maintain any sub-advocates, exactors, or other agents in that place or throughout any of its dependencies. Rather, the advocate himself, to whom we or our successors shall grant the royal ban over that abbey, shall kindly provide for the places belonging to that church, and once a year shall hold a public court at the village called Gowenheim, where the judicial seat of the whole abbey is situated, together with those who know and love what is just. There he shall render justice to all who have suffered injury, according to the judgment of suitable judges from that people and with the consent of the others.

No one from the entire household, rich or poor, shall be deprived of his land or his right except at the aforesaid common place, by the judgment of the wise. On the day of the public court, the abbess shall honorably provide and render service to the advocate and his men. Whatever, and wherever, the advocate acquires through holding court in the abbey, the abbess shall receive two parts and he the third.

The clerics and those laymen who preside over the household and the church by birth and moral integrity shall not be compelled to any servile service, either in their persons or in their property; rather, they shall serve the abbess faithfully and devotedly. She too must treat them not as slaves but as a mother treats her sons.

Furthermore, so that our royal or imperial successors may care for that church, we establish that whenever the Roman king or emperor comes to Basel, each *hoba* or *mansus* shall pay twelve coins for his service.

Therefore, whatever powerful person, advocate, or anyone else violates these decrees of ours, let him tremble before the wrath of God, of all the saints, of the dreadful judgment, and of us; and let him either leave the borders of the kingdom or pay thirty pounds of the finest gold to the royal treasury, after first restoring the church’s loss.

These are the names of the villages and places in which the aforesaid church has properties and possessions outside the valley—which, holding the ban and its obligations, extends from Gowenheim to the summit of Mount Grazon: Brunhobetum, Giltewillre, Dannemaria, Werza, Boyseigum, Rotbach, Balderchedorff, Spechbach, Rollingum, Morschviller, Zullensheim, Vespach, Stennenbrun, Bruchbach, Richenesheim, Mullenhusen, Enisigesheim, Uffholtz, Herlichesheim, Ongersheim, Sigoltesheim, Langenheim, Sigenesheim.

Simeon, deacon, have examined this in place of Fridugisus, arch-chancellor.

Issued on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, in the tenth year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our most pious lord Augustus, in the first indiction. Enacted successfully at the palace of Frankfurt. Amen.

[Col. 1128A]

### CXII. FOR THE NEW MONASTERY OF CORBIE. (Year 823.)

[In Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum of the Order of Saint Benedict*, fourth century, part I, p. 524.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence appointed emperor Augustus.

We believe that none of our faithful doubts how great a labor our lord and father, Charles, the most Christian emperor, once undertook among the Saxons in order to bring them to recognition of the true faith; and, with divine grace cooperating, he accomplished this as he desired.

We, raised by the gift of the heavenly Majesty to his throne, ordered a monastery to be built for the increase of our reward by a certain venerable man, Adalhard, [Col. 1128B] an aged abbot from the monastery called Corbie, in that province of Saxony. For the dedication of that monastery we sent from the sacred palace, through our chapel, the venerable and most sacred relics of the blessed Stephen, the protomartyr, to a royal estate above the Weser, at a place formerly called Huxori.

Thus, because, by God’s agency, our aforesaid lord and father of blessed memory had first established the faith of the Christian religion among that people, we too established there the first order of monastic religion, to be observed and maintained, in order to increase and strengthen the vigor of that same faith. With the help of Almighty grace this was brought to completion, and the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1128C] was given the name Corbie because, from a certain older monastery, Corbie, the aforesaid aged Abbot Adalhard, to whom we had entrusted this responsibility, [lacuna], having taken with him his brother Walon and as many other monks as were suitable and necessary, might choose an appropriate and fitting place within that same province and there, as circumstances best permitted, establish and construct the aforesaid monastery.

Therefore it pleased our excellence to grant by this authority, in perpetual right, the aforesaid estate called Huxori, with all its boundaries and limits, its woods, lands, waters and watercourses, and all its dependencies and appurtenances, to that monastery, and immediately to transfer it from our right into the right and lordship of the aforesaid monastery. We also confirm by this authority the property or possessions granted by Saxons who fear or love God within Saxony itself for beginning this work or providing assistance, as well as the property that had been given to the older Corbie within the aforesaid borders of Saxony: lands, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, whether private or common; houses and buildings, whether previously possessed or later constructed; and slaves of various kinds and conditions, movable and immovable. Whatever had been given or transferred, in its entirety, we have bestowed upon the aforesaid monastery, with the consent of the aforementioned abbot and congregation, by a solemn gift, and have granted and confirmed it perpetually for the monks serving God there, to possess and enjoy.

We judged that this ought reasonably to be done because it was evident that the aforesaid place had been constructed by monks of the earlier Corbie monastery; and because in every place one Lord is served and one King is served as soldiers, it was fitting that those possessions should be assigned to the service of the same monks, who are known to have been the first builders and perpetual inhabitants of that monastery within that province, appointed to the service of Almighty God under the holy Rule.

For if it should happen that the place could not subsist on the property granted to it within that province, it would have been fitting that a generous hand should be extended from the property of the earlier monastery, as far as could reasonably be done on both sides, out of kindness and charity. How much more ought those possessions that are known to have been granted earlier within the same province, as has been said, to be bestowed with every kindness and the most ardent affection of charity?

We also establish, decree, and sanction by these imperial letters that whenever, by divine calling, the abbot of the aforesaid monastery departs from this life, so long as the monks themselves are able to find among themselves persons capable of governing the congregation according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, they shall, by this authority and with our consent, have permission to elect abbots. Thus may it please those servants of God who serve there to pray continually for the mercy of the Lord on behalf of us, our wife, our offspring, and the stability [Col. 1129C] of our empire.

It has also pleased us to insert this into the present authority: that the rulers of this monastery may lawfully exchange property and slaves with any free persons, namely, so that whatever one party justly and reasonably transfers to the other, they may hold and possess with the firmest legal right by this authority of ours; and whatever they wish to do with it thereafter, they may freely exercise in every respect the discretion to do whatever they choose.

And so that this authority of our gift and confirmation may retain inviolate permanence in future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

[Col. 1129D]

Durandus, deacon, have examined and subscribed this in place of Fridugisus. Issued on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, in the tenth year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the first indiction. Enacted at the royal palace of Ingelheim, successfully, in God’s name. Amen.

### CXIII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF CORBIE IN SAXONY. (Year 823.)

[In Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 534.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine clemency appointed emperor Augustus.

When, out of love for divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of the servants of God, we do not doubt that the gift of the heavenly benefit will be bestowed. Therefore let the discernment of all our faithful, present and future, know that the most reverend man Adalard, abbot of the monastery of Corbie, which we formerly ordered him to build anew in the province of Saxony for the increase of our reward, above the river Weser, at a royal estate in the place formerly called Huxori, dedicated in honor of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, approached the serenity of our majesty. He suggested to our gentleness that we should place that monastery and the monks dwelling there through the years, together with their property and people, not only under our protection and defense, but also order an immunity to be made for them such as all [Col. 1130B] the churches in Francia possess.

Considering his petition worthy and beneficial, we ordered this charter of immunity to be made for the aforesaid monastery of Corbie and its rulers. By it we decree and command that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, shall ever dare to enter the churches, places, fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery—which it presently holds in any counties or territories, or which may thereafter be granted to it there—to hear cases according to judicial custom, exact fines, provide lodgings or transport services, take sureties, constrain the people of that monastery, whether free or dependent, or seek any returns or unlawful pretexts; nor shall anyone presume to exact any of the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors conduct their affairs, live, and reside in peaceful order under the protection of our immunity. Whatever the treasury might have been able to exact from the property of that monastery, we grant wholly and entirely, for eternal recompense, to feed the poor and provide lamps for that monastery, so that the monks dwelling there may gladly pray more attentively for the mercy of the Lord on behalf of us, our offspring, and the condition of our entire empire entrusted to us to govern.

It has also pleased us to insert this into the present authority: that the rulers of this monastery may lawfully exchange property and slaves with any free persons, namely, so that whatever one party justly and reasonably transfers to the other, they may hold and possess with the firmest legal right by this authority of ours; and whatever they wish to do with it thereafter, they may freely exercise in every respect the discretion to do whatever they choose.

And so that this authority of our immunity and confirmation may retain inviolate permanence in future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Durandus, deacon, have examined and subscribed this in place of Fridugisus.

Issued on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, in the tenth year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the first [Col. 1131A] indiction. Enacted at the palace of Ingelheim, successfully, in God’s name. Amen.

### CXIV. FOR THE MONASTERY OF TRAJECTUM. (Year 823.)

[In Heda, *Bishopric of Trajectum*, p. 45.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence appointed emperor Augustus.

It befits imperial greatness not only to preserve inviolate the pious acts of its predecessors but also to confirm them by the authority of its own judgment. Therefore let the diligence and discernment of all our faithful, present and future, know that Rixfridus [Rixfredus], a venerable man and bishop of the church of Old Trajectum, which was built in honor of Saint Martin the confessor and the other saints, brought to our gentleness certain charters of establishment. They showed how the Lord and our father Charles, of good memory, most pious emperor Augustus, and our grandfather Pippin, together with their predecessors, had granted to that church the entire tithe from slaves, lands, tolls, commerce, and every source from which the royal fiscus appeared to demand or receive a toll; and how the people of that church were to remain under the guardianship [Note: [Col. 1131D] *Mundeburde*, that is, protection or defense. The French call it *mambournie*; the Belgians call guardians *mambers*. It is read in the *Formulas of Marculf*, Book I, chapter 24, “Charter of the prince’s guardianship”; see Jerome Bignon’s notes on that passage. Add the capitulary of Charles and Louis, Book VI, chapter 223, with the notes there, and the Latin glosses of Baluze and Lydius on Clemangis, letter M.] and protection of that church.

Likewise, on the banks at Dorestad, no one was to presume to impose or exact the *ban* [Note: [Col. 1131D] That is, a judicial fine. See the glossary just cited and the notes on Marculf, Book I, chapter 40.] or the *fredum* [Note: [Col. 1131D] A composition owed to the treasury, from *vrevel*. M. Goldast, Lydius, II. Bignonius, in his notes on Marculf; Lindebrogius on the Salic Law, title 14, from Gregory of Tours.], or the *conjectum* [Note: [Col. 1132D] Lydius interprets *conjectum* as a contribution from people’s property in the glosses mentioned above. Flodoard, *On the Conjectum to Be Given to the Normans*. Gregory of Tours, Book VI, chapter 45, concerning King Chilperic: “A great apparatus of expenses was gathered from various cities along the journey; in it the king ordered nothing to be supplied from his treasury, but everything from the contributions of the poor.” Aimon, Book III, chapter 56, reports this in such a way that necessities were supplied on the journey from the property of the poor. In the Miropaeus manuscript the following is noted in the margin: “I saw *veerschat*, but I am uncertain.”], which they themselves call *verschât* [*geschot*], nor exact it from them.

Nor, if any merchant wished to enter their banks, should he cause them any dispute on that account; nor should anyone dare to take lodgings in their houses without their permission, or take away their property while they lived, or touch it after their death, or in any way bring a legal claim against them in any matter—those who belong to that tenth part or remain under the guardianship of the church of Saint Martin.

The purpose was that, just as those people neither wished nor were able to take or usurp anything from the remaining nine parts, so the agents of the commonwealth should not presume to take or usurp anything for the treasury from that tenth part. Thus the bishop of that church, with all the clergy and the people subject to him, might provide sustenance, maintain the lamps in that see, and feed and instruct the pagans who are converted to Christianity. [Col. 1131D]

For the firmness of this matter, the aforesaid bishop nevertheless requested that, following the custom of our father and of our predecessor kings, we should judge it appropriate to issue such a charter of our authority [Col. 1132A] for that church, out of love for God and reverence for Saint Martin.

We were pleased to lend a willing ear to his petition and to confirm by this authority of ours that the aforesaid church should possess forever, in free right, the entire tithe—whether from slaves, lands, tolls, commerce, or whatever source from which the right of the fiscus ought to demand a census on behalf of the royal treasury—and everything written above.

And so that no one may presume to interfere or make an unjust claim, but so that, just as it was established and confirmed for us by the lord emperor, our grandfather, and the predecessor kings, so it may be preserved and guarded inviolate for all time, may it please the servants of God who remain there with their bishop, and those whom they have converted from pagan practice to the true faith of Christ, to pray continually for the mercy of God on behalf of us, our wife, our offspring, and all the Christian people.

And so that this authority may be more readily believed by all and more carefully preserved, we have subscribed it with our own hand and caused it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Issued on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, in the eleventh year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the second indiction. Enacted at the royal palace of Aachen, successfully, in God’s name. Amen.

Helisachar has examined this.

### CXV. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT FLORENTIUS AT GLONN. [Col. 1132C] (Year 824.)

[In Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. II, p. 739, from the archive of Glonn.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence appointed emperor Augustus.

If, out of love for God and for those who serve Him in places consecrated to divine worship, we bestow suitable benefits, we do not doubt that a reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us by God. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own people, present and future, that we caused a certain venerable man, Frotbert, together with his monks whom we had sent to Italy, to return from there, and granted them a certain monastery situated in the territory of Poitiers above the bank of the Loire, called Glonn or Saint Florentius, where the body of that blessed confessor of Christ rests.

We granted it on the condition that they should live there a monastic life according to the Rule of the blessed Father Benedict. We received the aforesaid religious man Frotbert and his monks, as well as the aforementioned venerable monastery, with all the property and slaves presently belonging or pertaining to it, under our protection and the guardianship of our immunity, so that by this authority they may remain peaceful and unharmed, without anyone’s unjust disturbance.

Therefore we ordered these imperial letters to be drawn up, through which we command that no public judge, nor any agent of the commonwealth of higher or lower rank, shall ever dare to enter the churches, places, fields, or other possessions which at the present time they lawfully hold in any counties or territories under the authority of our empire, or which divine mercy may thereafter add to the right of that place, whether through us or through any free person, in order to hear cases according to judicial custom, exact fines, provide lodgings or transport services, take sureties, constrain the people of that monastery living on its land, or seek any returns or unlawful pretexts; nor shall anyone presume to exact any of the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors, together with all that is presently justly subject to them, live and reside peacefully under the protection of immunity. Whatever the treasury might hope to obtain from the property of the aforesaid monastery, we grant in its entirety, for eternal recompense, to that monastery, so that throughout perpetual times it may increase the sustenance of the poor and the provisions of the monks serving God there.

Whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this life, so long as the monks are able to find among themselves persons capable of governing the congregation according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, they shall, by this authority and with our consent, have permission to elect an abbot. Thus may it please those servants of God who serve Him there to pray continually for the mercy of God on behalf of us, our wife, our offspring, and the stability of our entire empire, granted and preserved for us by God.

And so that this authority may, with God’s protection, be held more firmly in our own and future times and be better preserved throughout the future, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most pious king.

Simeon, deacon, has examined this in place of Fridugisus.

Issued on the day before the Kalends of July, in the eleventh year, with Christ propitious, of our reign, in the twelfth indiction [read: twenty-first]. Enacted at the royal palace of Compiègne, successfully, in God’s name. Amen.

[Col. 1134A]

### CXVI. FOR THE MONASTERY OF FARFA. (Year 824.)

[In Chesne, *Writers of Frankish Affairs*, vol. II, p. 659.]

Louis, by divine providence appointed emperor Augustus.

If, with the grace of our God going before us, we strive to adapt the devotion of our hearts to divine service, and if we extend the assistance and consolation of our imperial generosity and protection to venerable places belonging to God and the saints, to the households of God, and to those serving the heavenly Majesty; if, finally, we lend an open and benevolent ear to those oppressed by various injustices and calamities, we believe that through these practices and pious endeavors we everywhere earn heavenly assistance, prosper in successful outcomes, and, though unarmed, rejoice in glorious triumphs; indeed, after the temporal insignia of empire, we may happily attain the starry kingdoms.

Therefore, when the manifold complaint of the guardians of many churches and venerable places, and of various people from the regions of Italy, had reached our ears, we were moved by piety at their tearful voices and, as duty required, sent our dearest and sweetest son Lothar to protect and defend the sacred and venerable places, and to uphold the rights of all the people whose grievous complaints, as we have said, had incessantly assailed our ears.

Accordingly, I, Lothar Augustus, agreeing with my father’s [Col. 1134C] will and obeying his commands, came—with God’s protection and in peaceful prosperity—to the threshold of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, for the sake of prayer and the exaltation of that holy Church of God. Among the others who, as we have said, were presenting many complaints, there came Ingoaldus, venerable abbot of the monastery of the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary, situated in the territory of Sabina. He asserted that his monastery, after its former liberty had been removed, had been bound by tribute and payment to the Roman pontiffs, and that many possessions had been forcibly taken from the same monastery.

We therefore carefully inquired by what means he hoped either to recover the aforesaid property or to escape the domination of the aforesaid authority. He immediately presented to our sight ancient charters of the Lombard [Col. 1134D] kings, stating how they had established by royal authority that the holy place should remain at all times under their protection and immunity.

In particular he showed the charter of confirmation of our lord grandfather Charles Augustus, of pious memory, and also the charter of our lord and father Louis, the unconquered emperor. They had issued these to the same monastery as a benefit and privilege, for the increase of their reward. They declared that the aforesaid monastery should remain forever under the privilege of their protection, like the other monasteries situated in the kingdom from the borders of Francia; specifically, that no pontiff, bishop, duke, or any other prince should ever be permitted to place the aforesaid monastery under tribute or any payment, take anything from it, or diminish anything from the property subject to that place.

After examining these documents, it seemed just and reasonable to us, to our nobles, and also to the Roman leaders that the writings of the pious kings, and especially the charters of our lord Charles and of our father, Lord Louis Augustus, should receive the strongest force through perpetual stability. We therefore ordered the possessions forcibly taken from the monastery to be restored, without any excuse being accepted.

Accordingly, it pleased us, father and son, and indeed the aforesaid princes, by concordant and common agreement, that the aforesaid nourishing place should remain under our protection and immunity and that of our successors forever. At the petition of the aforesaid Ingoaldus, venerable abbot of that monastery, we have likewise established by this present charter that those possessions, and others situated in the territory of Sabina or wherever else, which justly belong to the same monastery, shall remain there with unshaken stability, now and in future, without anyone’s violent disturbance. [lacuna]

### CXVII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MEDARD. (Year 824.)

[In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, fourth century, part I.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence [Col. 1135C] emperor Augustus.

Although what is offered by the faithful to the venerable places where their bodies are known to rest can contribute nothing to the increase of the saints’ glory, it must nevertheless be believed that it greatly benefits the salvation of those who, for the love of God, bring their possessions to the memorials of the martyrs: for from these offerings the poor are fed, as are the needy who have insufficient means of their own to live. It is certain that Christ is worshiped and honored in the veneration of those who did not hesitate to lay down their lives for him, and with whom he truthfully promised that he would be until the consummation of the age.

Therefore, when, through the zeal and earnest persistence of the venerable Hilduin, abbot of the monastery of Saint Medard and archchaplain of our sacred palace, the body of the most blessed and most precious martyr of Christ, Sebastian, had been transferred from the city of Rome to the city of Soissons, to the monastery of Saint Medard the confessor of Christ—which the venerable abbot Hilduin is known presently to govern—through the authority and generosity of our lord Eugene, our special [variant: spiritual] apostolic patron, such a multitude of signs and miracles of every kind of healing shines forth there through the merits of that most glorious martyr that, deservedly, the hearts of all the faithful are moved to venerate him.

For this reason, when we too had come to the aforesaid place for the sake of prayer, and were contributing toward the construction from the foundations and adornment of the church, in honor of Saint Medard and of the aforementioned most illustrious martyr of Christ Sebastian, as well as toward the celebration of the Mass, golden sacred furnishings [or: ministries] adorned with gems, it pleased us, for the completion of the work mentioned above, for the preparation of the lights, for the support of the poor, and for the reception of guests, to contribute from our own possessions by a solemn donation something to the memorial of the most blessed martyr of Christ Sebastian, so that through his intercession we might be worthy to receive the rewards of eternal life and happily govern, under divine protection, the kingdom entrusted to our care.

We therefore donate to that same most blessed saint and martyr Sebastian a certain monastery of ours called Cauciacum (Choisy), constructed in honor of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, situated in the county of Noyon on the river Aisne, together with all its treasure and furnishings, and with its churches, houses, buildings, estates, cultivated and uncultivated lands, vineyards, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, rights of access and return, and also the forest called Veruga, with its wild animals, together with all its appurtenances and dependencies, and whatever, in ancient or more recent times, appears to belong or be serviceable to the aforesaid monastery—in its entirety and without exception, as stated above—to the memorial of the often-mentioned most blessed martyr of Christ Sebastian, for preparing the lights, and for the reception of guests and support of the poor. From our right we transfer it into his right and lordship.

Nevertheless, the administrators of that monastery, where that most sacred body rests, shall not have the power to give the aforesaid monastery of Cauciacum or its appurtenances to anyone as a benefice or for any use. Rather, it shall always remain solely for the purpose to which we have devoted and transferred it: namely, for preparing the lights, receiving the poor, and receiving guests.

We have also wished to insert this into our charter of donation: that the abbots of the aforesaid monasteries of the most blessed saints Medard and Sebastian should have responsibility before God to ensure that in the aforesaid monastery of Cauciacum, which we have bestowed upon the aforementioned holy martyr Sebastian, there be such a community as can maintain holy religious observance and fully render the divine office to God.

And so that this authority of our donation may retain inviolable and unshaken force throughout the passing years, we have confirmed it below with our own hand, ordered it subscribed in our customary manner, and commanded it to be sealed with our bull.

### CXVIII. Lothar’s Privilege for the Monastery of Como. (Year 824.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. V, p. 266.]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal God, Lothar Augustus, son of the most invincible lord Emperor Louis.

It is fitting that whoever has suffered loss through fire or through any accidental occurrence, and has sought to be protected by imperial aid, should be relieved by the clemency of him from whom he believes he can obtain the help he has implored.

Therefore let the prudence and diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable man Leo, bishop of Como, made known to our serenity how, through a certain negligence and carelessness, all the documentary charters by which he ought to have held and defended by right of ownership the property handed over to him by his kin and by outsiders, or purchased or exchanged by him, had been burned or consumed by fire. For this reason he asked our serenity to order an imperial authorization to be made for him concerning this matter, for the increase of our reward and the strengthening of his legal security. Through it he might, in the present and future times, be able to hold and possess the property and dependants that had been transferred to him by the aforesaid documentary charters, or purchased or exchanged by him, or that had come to him by any writing lawfully and legally, both in the county [perhaps: district] of Como and in the territories of Sibrium [perhaps: Seprium], and that he is known to have possessed peacefully and securely.

We therefore wished to grant the petitions of that venerable man, and at his request decreed that this imperial authorization of ours be made. We therefore command and order that all property and dependants which were lawfully and legally granted to him by any writing by whatever persons, both relatives and outsiders, and which, up to the day of the execution written above, he appears to have held and ruled by proprietary right peacefully and securely, with no one disturbing or challenging him, he may, by this confirmation of our authority, properly and securely have and possess without anyone’s disturbance or unjust opposition.

But if, concerning those same possessions held by him lawfully and peacefully before the aforesaid execution, a dispute should arise such that it is necessary to argue their case legally in court, then, by this authority of ours, let the aforesaid property and dependants be defended in the same way as they could have been defended by law through those same documents, had they not been consumed by fire.

And so that this authority may be believed to be ours and may be preserved for future times by the faithful of the aforesaid holy Church and by our own faithful, we have wished it to be strengthened below by our own hand and by the image of our ring.

[Col. 1137D]

Sign of Lothar, most glorious emperor.

I, Maredo, have reviewed it in the place of Vitgagius.

Given on the second day before the Nones of June, in the tenth year, Christ being propitious, of the empire of our most serene lord Emperor Louis, and in the first year of the reign of Lothar, most glorious Augustus, in Italy, in the first indiction. Enacted at the villa of Venonica, belonging to Count Vilfred, happily in the name of God. Amen. In the year of the Lord 823.

### CXIX. Lothar’s Privilege for the Same Monastery. (Year 824.)

[In Ughelli, same work.]

In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal God, Lothar Augustus, son of the most invincible lord Emperor Louis.

If, out of regard for the love of the Judge who is to come and is to be feared, we, divinely moved, lend the ears of our clemency to the just and reasonable petitions of priests and servants of God—which they have taken care to make known to us for the peace of the holy and catholic Church and for the dignity of its present condition, whose governance they have received by God’s authority—and if, with God’s favor, we bring them to the fulfillment desired with ardent longing, we not only exercise the imperial custom and, by preserving the deeds of our predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, and by favoring our own deeds so that posterity may uphold them inviolate, strengthen them; we also confidently believe that such actions will avail us, without ambiguity, to obtain the rewards of the heavenly homeland.

Therefore let the fidelity of all our faithful, both present and future, know that Leo, the venerable man and bishop of the holy Church of Como, where the holy confessor of Christ Abundius rests in his precious body, approaching the magnificent height of our serenity, presented to our sight an authorization or confirmation of our lord and father Louis, most excellent Augustus. In it was contained a confirmation, according to imperial custom, of the charter of our glorious emperor and grandfather Charles of pious memory, or rather of the charter of confirmation of Cumpert, Aripert, Liutprand, Ratigis, Heistulf, Desiderius, and their predecessors, concerning everything that they had lawfully and legally given to that same venerable place, out of divine love, as well as whatever it might thereafter lawfully acquire.

It was also specifically inserted in the same document that, together with that place, we grant in perpetuity the toll, or market, and Gegis; and, for the canonical allowance of the clergy of Como, the Cluses and our bridge at Chiavenna.

Moreover, the same authority contained a ruling concerning the dispute that had arisen between Peter, his predecessor and rector of the holy Church of Como, and Waldo, abbot of Saint-Denis. It stated how our grandfather of devoted memory, the pious and glorious emperor Charles, had decreed concerning the same matter: namely, concerning the possessions that Abbot Waldo had claimed from the aforesaid Bishop Peter, situated in the Val Tellina in the duchy of Milan, that just as the Como Church had hitherto held those possessions through the confirmation of the earlier kings, so in the future it should hold them through his confirmation.

Those possessions were baptismal churches: one at Amatia, another at Burmis, and a third at Postlavo, as well as the small monastery of Saint Fidelis belonging to the bishopric of Como.

Therefore, for the security of this matter, the aforesaid venerable Bishop Leo asked for the peace of our serenity, so that we should not only confirm by our authority the charters of our lord and father and of our grandfather Charles of holy memory, but also include under our authority everything that the kings mentioned above, or their predecessors—namely the Lombard princes Ansprand, Cumbert, and Bertharius—had assigned or confirmed to the aforesaid Church by their authorities, and confirm and strengthen it for the aforesaid holy Church of Como through our charter, for the love of God and in reverence for Saint Abundius.

We granted his petition because of divine love. In accordance with his request, we confirmed the aforementioned charters of the ancient kings by our imperial charter, specifically decreeing that whatever is contained in the charters of our lord and father or of our magnificent grandfather, Emperor Charles, and whatever the aforementioned Lombard kings assigned or confirmed with justice to the aforesaid Church, and which it is permitted to possess peacefully and justly, should remain perpetually firm and stable, without any opposition.

We further decree and sanction that all the aforesaid possessions of the Church of Como shall remain perpetually under the protection and guardianship of our palace, just as they were in the time of our father and grandfather.

And if any dispute should arise concerning the possessions of the aforesaid Church that we have confirmed by this charter and for the increase of our reward, and it cannot be settled there, let it be reserved for our sacred palace, so that there it may receive its conclusion according to the path of justice.

And so that this authority may retain inviolable and unshaken force throughout the passing years, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Lothar, most glorious emperor.

I, Maredo, have reviewed it in the place of Vitharius.

Given on the third day before the Nones of January, in the eleventh year, Christ being propitious, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, and in the second year of the reign of his son Lothar, most glorious, in the second indiction, in the year 824.

Enacted at the royal palace of Compiègne, happily in the name of God. Amen.

### CXX. Concerning a Certain Exchange between Count Leibulf and Noto, Archbishop of Arles. (Year 825.)

[In D. Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 540, from the Cartulary of Aniane.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If we confirm by our edicts those things that the faithful of our empire exchange among themselves for their own advantage, we exercise the imperial custom and wish this to remain thereafter established by the firmest right.

Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know that the illustrious man Count Leibulf, through our archchaplain Hilduin, submitted to us that he might exchange certain possessions of his own property for possessions belonging to the bishopric of Arles, namely from his benefice.

We therefore ordered Noto, archbishop of Arles, by our letters to examine both properties, and, if the exchange should be appropriate and most advantageous to both parties, authorized them to exchange with one another and to draw up a charter between themselves, as is customary.

Accordingly, the aforementioned most reverend Archbishop Noto came into our presence and said that he had the exchange in his hands, asserting that the aforesaid exchange was appropriate and most advantageous. He entreated us, both on his own behalf and on behalf of the aforesaid Leibulf, to decree that our charter concerning these exchanges be made.

Granting his petition, we ordered it to be done as they themselves entreated. For the exchanges contained the following: the aforesaid Archbishop Noto, with the consent and will of his canons, had given from the possessions of his bishopric, namely from the benefice of the aforesaid Leibulf, to Leibulf as his own property and for his possession, certain possessions belonging to the estate of Saint Mary, Saint Stephen, or Saint Genesius in the county of Arles itself:

An island in the suburbs of that city, surrounded on both sides by the river Rhône, with two churches; three houses for habitation, together with three other small dwellings; twelve modia of vineyard, six modia of meadow, one modius of garden, and forty modia of cultivated and uncultivated land.

At a place called Rubinas: eight houses, two gardens, and four modia of vineyard.

At a place called Ferromannis: five dwellings, one garden, and 270 modia of land.

In the territory of that city, at Campo Lapideo, pasture belonging to the aforesaid churches, called Prinnannus, where a dug well is known to exist: twelve solidatae (assessed land-units), with their boundaries and side-measurements, as contained in the written exchanges.

In return, as compensation for these possessions, the aforesaid Count Leibulf gave to the representatives of the aforementioned churches of Saint Mary, Saint Stephen, and Saint Genesius, from his own property situated within the district called Argenteo, in the villa of Campo Publico:

A church with three altars, dedicated to Saint Mary, Saint Peter, and Saint John, with a sacristy; two cells with a courtyard, garden, and trees; fifteen modia of vineyard; sixty modia of arable land; and, in the same villa, two houses with courtyards and gardens.

In the villa called Rannessa and in the villa called Gelariano: four houses, four vineyards, one modius of garden, and ten modia of another vineyard.

In the villa called Occisianus: two houses with two plots.

In the villas called Gangiacus, Curicus, and Occisianus, and in the villa of Campo Publico: 400 modia of land and fourteen modia of vineyard, with their boundaries and side-measurements, as contained in the same exchanges.

Thus the aforesaid Archbishop Noto declared that he had in his hands two exchanges, drawn up in identical form as described above and strengthened by the hands of good men.

But for complete security they asked our majesty that we should confirm those exchanges anew, more fully, by a charter of our mildness.

We did not wish to deny their petitions. Know, therefore, that just as we have done for each of our faithful who petitions justly, so we have granted this to them and confirmed it in every respect.

Therefore we command and order that whatever one party has justly and reasonably transferred to the other party, each shall henceforth hold and possess by the firmest right through this authority of ours, so that each may freely enjoy the power to do whatever it wishes with what it has received.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved for future times, we have ordered it sealed below with our ring.

Sign of Louis, emperor Augustus.

[Col. 1141B]

I, Durandus the deacon, have reviewed it in the place of Fridugisus.

Given on the third day before the Nones of January, in the eleventh year, Christ being propitious, of the reign of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the third indiction. Enacted at the palace of Aachen, happily in the name of God. Amen.

### CXXI. For the Dionysian Monastery. (Year 825.)

A charter of the emperors Louis the Pious and Lothar by which the Dionysian monastery is exempted from the payment of two hundred modia of wine.

[Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, vol. II, p. 535.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothar, by the providence of God, emperors Augustus.

If, from those things which [lacuna] and are paid by annual custom to the churches of God’s saints, we remit anything, for the love of God, in the present and future times, and grant it for the needs and uses of those churches, we confidently believe that this will undoubtedly profit us toward everlasting reward.

Therefore let it be known to all present and future that the venerable man Hilduin, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Denis and archchaplain of our sacred palace, made known to our highness that, at some time under one of our predecessors, because of a shortage and need of wine, the person who then governed the public affairs had ordered that, because of the aforesaid [lacuna] of necessity and indigence, [lacuna] should be supplied from the monastery of Saint-Denis to our villa of Vern.

Therefore, when that same abbot, who at that time presided over the same holy church, had supplied two hundred modia of wine there on account of the petition mentioned above, and the other administrators who governed that place after him had acted similarly, it appeared that, because of this . . . [lacuna] . . . it was held by the royal officials in that villa as a legal obligation and due payment.

For this reason he asked us, for the love of God and in reverence for the saints resting there, to release that holy Church from this obligation and custom.

We granted to that holy place what he requested—indeed, what he implored—as useful to the salvation of our soul and . . . [lacuna] . . . and established it within its power and discretion: so that, just as it had been granted and bestowed by us through the intercession of that church, it might be assigned to whatever common benefit of that church . . . [lacuna] . . . it wished, in every respect . . . [lacuna] . . . [Col. 1142A]

And we command in every way that neither in our time nor ever in the time of any of our successors should anyone—neither judge, envoy, nor any other person—presume to exact or demand that wine from the authority of the aforesaid monastery. Rather, let our aforesaid faithful Hilduin [lacuna] be permitted to assign it perpetually, as ecclesiastical necessity may dictate. so that the grant of our alms concerning that payment may remain stable and inviolate in that place for future times, just as it is known to have been granted and confirmed for the love of God and in return for eternal reward . . . [lacuna] .

And so that this authority may obtain fuller force throughout future times, we ordered it sealed below with the impression of our ring.

I, Adalulf the deacon, have reviewed and subscribed it in the place of Fridugisus.

[Col. 1142B]

The date has been cut off.

### CXXII. The Monastery of Argentolium Is Restored to the Dionysian Monastery. (Year 825.)

[In D. Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 542, from Dublet, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*, p. 736.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothar, by the providence of God, emperors Augustus.

If we restore by our authority to their former condition those things that God-fearing people have bestowed or donated by solemn donation to places dedicated to divine worship, when they are later known to have been taken away from them on any pretext, and confirm them again by the decree of our command, we confidently believe that this undoubtedly pertains both to our attaining eternal blessedness and to strengthening the stability of our empire.

Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, both present and future, know that the illustrious woman, namely our sister Theodrada, consecrated to God, informed our mildness that she had learned that the monastery called Argentogilum, situated in the county of Paris on the river Seine, which she first held by benefice from our lord and father, the most serene Emperor Charles, and afterward by our generosity, ought to belong to the monastery of the blessed and glorious martyr of Christ, Dionysius, where at the present time the venerable man Hilduin, abbot and archchaplain of our sacred palace, appears to preside as rector.

She asked that, for the increase of our reward, we should cause it to be restored to its former condition, in such a way that, after her departure from this life, if we had not previously given her another monastery in exchange for it, or if she should not wish to relinquish it of her own will, the aforesaid monastery would be received into the authority of the monastery of Saint-Denis, without any opposition or anyone’s questioning.

After hearing her beneficial and religious petition, we questioned the aforementioned venerable man Hilduin, who was present, asking whether he knew anything about this matter. He immediately showed us for rereading the donation of a certain God-fearing and religious man named Ermenric and his wife Mumana, who had built the aforesaid monastery as their own property and had transferred it by a testamentary document, through solemn donation, to the monastery of the blessed martyr of Christ Dionysius; and also the charter of confirmation of Lothar, formerly king, which he had ordered to be written concerning the same donation.

Having examined these documents, it pleased us to assent to the petition of our beloved sister Theodrada and, as she requested, by our authority to restore the aforesaid monastery of Argentogilum to the authority of the holy and most precious martyr of Christ Dionysius.

Therefore we command this confirmation of our authority to be made, by which we decree and order in every respect that the aforementioned monastery of Argentogilum, after the departure from this life of our beloved sister, be received, without contradiction from anyone or questioning by us or our successors, into the monastery and authority of the aforesaid most blessed martyr of Christ Dionysius, to which it is known to have originally been given or donated by the aforesaid faithful for the love of God, in reverence for those saints, and through their pious intercession.

It shall be restored to the right and lordship of that monastery, in its entirety and with all its appurtenances, together with whatever is presently seen to belong there.
