And if it should happen that the same sister wishes to relinquish that monastery, as we have said, either voluntarily or in exchange for another monastery before the end of her life, then nevertheless, without any contradiction or waiting for a formal transfer, it shall be received perpetually for possession by the monastery of the martyr of Christ Dionysius, as set out above.

Henceforth, at no time shall any person endowed with any dignity or authority presume to make any demand of the rulers of the aforesaid monastery and of the most blessed martyr of Christ Dionysius, or bring any accusation against them. Rather, let them be permitted, without anyone’s unjust questioning, to hold and administer the aforesaid monastery of Argentogilum peacefully, in the same manner as the other possessions donated to and belonging to the authority of blessed Dionysius.

Whatever they wish to do for the advantage and benefit of that church, according to the rule of the Christian religion, let them have full power in every respect.

And so that this authority of our confirmation or restoration may retain inviolable and unshaken force throughout future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hands and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Sign of Lothar, most glorious Augustus.

I, Durandus the deacon, have reviewed it in the place of Fridugisus.

[Col. 1144A]

### CXXIII. For the Church of Rheims. (Year 825.)

[In D. Bouquet, same work, p. 543, from Flodoard, *History of the Church of Rheims*, book II, chapter 19.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothar, by the providence of God, emperors Augustus.

If we confer some benefit from the gift of our generosity upon places dedicated to God, and relieve ecclesiastical needs by our assistance, we clearly believe that this will help us both to pass through mortal life in time and to obtain eternal life happily.

Therefore we wish it to be made known to all our faithful, present and future, that we caused the holy Church of Rheims—in which our predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, received the faith and the grace of sacred baptism, and in which we too received the imperial insignia through the laying on of the hand of our lord Pope Stephen—to be built from its foundations out of reverence for the Christian faith and for the salvation of our soul. We decreed that it be consecrated in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, Savior of the world, and also in honor of that holy and undefiled mother, Mary.

Thus, moved by divine inspiration and kindled by love of the heavenly homeland, we ordered certain estates that had formerly been taken away from that holy see to be restored with devoted intent. These are:

In the suburbs of that holy Church, the church of Saint Sixtus, and also the church of Saint Martin, with their appurtenances;

Outside, in the same parish, in the castle of Vonz, a baptismal church, and in the same parish the baptismal church of Saint John, likewise with its appurtenances, and Bretiniacum;

Also the estate of Spernacum with its appurtenances, and in the estate called Lucida, as well as in Proviliacum, in the same county of Rheims;

In the county of Dulcom, the estate called Canera;

And also the estate called Verna in the county of Vertud.

And if thereafter we should decide in our time that anything further should be added to the possessions of the aforesaid holy Church, by this charter of our authority we establish that not only the possessions restored, but also those to be restored, together with whatever the rulers and ministers of the aforementioned Church choose concerning them or within them, they must perpetually possess, administer, and manage in whatever way they deem most advantageous, so that without anyone’s unjust opposition they may arrange, administer, and do whatever they perceive to be suitable and beneficial to the aforesaid Church.

And so that this confirmation of our authority may always possess firmer force in every respect, both in the present and in the future, we have confirmed it below with our own hands and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

[Col. 1145A]

**Note:** Marlot believes that this charter was issued after Ebo had been deprived of office, since the emperors make no mention of him in it and indicate that the construction of the cathedral church had been completed entirely.

### CXXIV. For the Monastery of Saint Maximin at Miciacum. (Year 825.)

[In D. Bouquet, *Collection of Historians*, vol. VI, p. 544; from Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, p. 736.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothar, by the providence of God, emperors Augustus.

When we accede to the petitions of Christ’s priests that concern the honor of divine worship, we fulfill imperial custom, and we faithfully believe, beyond doubt, that this will benefit us in attaining eternal recompense. Therefore we wish it to be known to the discernment of all our faithful, both present and future, and also to the greatness of our successors, that the venerable Jonas, bishop of the Church of Orléans, requested that we confirm by our imperial authority the privilege which he had recently made or ratified, with the concurrence of his metropolitan Jeremiah, archbishop, and of the canons of the church which, by God’s bounty, he serves, concerning the cell of Saint Maximin, which belongs to his episcopate, for the honor of divine service and for the monastic order to be faithfully and religiously observed. He presented this privilege to our attention. Since we perceived that its provisions had been made justly and reasonably, out of love for God and for the salvation of souls, we judged it equitable and worthy to grant assent to his petition.

Therefore, by this authority of our decree, we order and absolutely determine that, just as the same bishop established concerning that same cell through the aforesaid privilege, so it shall in every respect be observed in our times and in those of our successors by the rulers of the aforesaid church. This condition, however, shall apply: in the aforesaid cell, in which clear evidence testifies that men formerly lived commendably under the monastic order and pleased God—and through whose intercession that order is believed to have been restored in the same place, with the bishops of the aforesaid see taking care of it—the regular order shall always be most religiously maintained and guarded. When the abbot of that monastery has been removed from human affairs, an abbot shall be appointed by the bishop of the same see, who shall exercise pious and fatherly concern, in the manner contained in the same privilege.

The properties, too, whether those that justly and legally belong to the same cell, together with the two estates, namely Quasella and Castaneum Villare, or those which the same bishop subsequently added from the resources of his episcopate—specifically, from the possessions of the other cell of Saint Maximin—for the more honorable performance of divine office, shall, in their entirety and without any diminution, as he established, accrue to the use of the monks. If, perhaps, the bishop of that see should wish to add anything to these properties for the love of God, let him do so most willingly, with God’s grace and with the support of episcopal authority. But if both the will and the ability to do this should perhaps be denied him, let him not, driven by greed or inflamed by anyone’s persuasion, remove in any way anything from what has been collected. Rather, may the monks of that cell, supported by these and the other possessions bestowed upon them by God-fearing people, be able to serve the divine power more freely and devotedly, and continually implore divine mercy for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of the empire granted to us by God and to be preserved through his boundless and most gracious goodness, as well as for the rulers of the church whose place and possessions they use.

But if any of the prelates of the aforesaid see should in some way wish to invalidate and completely overturn the aforesaid arrangement contrary to this our decree, we wish and determine that the matter be brought to the attention of the metropolitan of Sens, so that he, having summoned the suffragan bishops of his diocese, may investigate and correct the matter with careful inquiry and endeavor to restore it to its former condition, while preserving the dignity and authority of the aforesaid see. If, however, it should happen that, because of some difficulty in the matter, he is unable to settle it, we wish the matter to become known through his report to us and to the ears of our successors, so that, by the sanction of our authority, the violator of this arrangement may be reprimanded and corrected at a general assembly of bishops, and so that, by their salutary judgment, the aforesaid arrangement may recover the vigor of its former status.

Let the prelate of the aforesaid church take the greatest care that the monks of that cell, who have been endowed with the possessions of the aforesaid mother church and have obtained, through the aforesaid privilege and this our authority, the leisure of holy repose, remain inviolably, with God’s help, in the commitments by which they have bound themselves to God. This means that they must neither deviate inwardly from their purpose nor, through their insolence or negligence, allow the possessions assigned to them to be neglected or taken away externally in any manner. Rather, they must remember to preserve in every respect toward the church, whose place and possessions they use, the faithfulness and humble, appropriate subjection that is fitting and necessary. Nor should they suppose that, because of our authority, they can withdraw themselves from the right and power of that church or alienate those same possessions by any contrivance—especially since both the place and the possessions they use belong to that church’s right and depend upon its authority.

And so that these provisions may possess fuller force in God’s name, and so that they may be believed more truly and certainly and preserved more securely, we ordered them to be fortified with our name’s mark and sealed with the impression of our ring.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the twelfth year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, indiction 3. Done happily at the royal palace of Aachen, in God’s name. Amen.

## CXXV. FOR ALBOIN, ABBOT OF ANISOLA. (Year 825.)

Grants permission to choose an abbot.

[In Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, vol. I, p. 23.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, emperor Augustus.

Let it be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to ours, and also, by God’s dispensation, to our successors, that the venerable Alboin, abbot of the monastery of Saint Carilef, which is called Anisola, approaching our clemency, represented to our gentleness that, just as canonical and regular authority commands, it would be useful for the monastery over which, by God’s authorization, he presides if, by our decree, we should confirm that, after his death, should someone be found in the aforesaid monastery who could preside according to the rule of Saint Benedict over the monks serving God there, they should have permission to choose an abbot from among themselves.

Since his petition appeared to us just and reasonable, we lent an ear to it and ordered these imperial letters to be made. Through them we decree and command that, after the departure of the aforesaid abbot, if someone from that same congregation is found there who can govern the others according to the rule of Saint Benedict, they shall have permission to choose an abbot from among themselves, so that it may please them joyfully to entreat the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife, our offspring, and the stability of our whole empire. And so that you may believe this authority made by us more truly and preserve it more carefully, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Durand, deacon, have reviewed this in place of Fridegisus.

Given on the day before the Kalends of June, in the twelfth year, Christ being favorable, of our lord Louis the emperor, indiction 3. Done at the royal palace of Aachen.

## CXXVI. CONCERNING THE ESTATE OF CLUNY. (Year 825.)

[From the Cluniac cartulary, in D. Bouquet, *Collection of Histories*, vol. VI, p. 546.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, emperor Augustus.

For if we confirm by our edicts those things which the faithful of our empire have exchanged among themselves for their own needs, we exercise imperial custom, and we wish this to remain thereafter established by the firmest right. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable man Hilduin, abbot and chief chaplain of the sacred palace, made known to our serenity that Hildebald, bishop of the Church of Mâcon, and the illustrious man Warin, count, had recently exchanged certain properties between themselves for their common advantage and benefit.

The aforesaid Bishop Hildebald therefore gave to the same Count Warin and to his wife Albana, to have perpetually as their own, from the property of his episcopate, in the same county of Mâcon, an estate called Anniacus, with the church in that estate, and with houses, dwellings, buildings, vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, rights of exit and return, with the dependents living there and with all their offspring—everything in its entirety, whatever appears to pertain to that estate.

He also gave, in the county of Nevers, an estate called Aptannacus, with the church built there, with manses, houses, buildings, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, woods, rights of exit and return, and with the dependents living there and all their offspring—everything in its entirety, as much as appears to pertain to that estate.

In exchange for this property, the aforesaid Count Warin and his wife Albana gave, from their own property, to Bishop Hildebald, for the benefit of his church, in the same county of Mâcon, an estate called Gemuliacus, with the church built there, with manses, houses, dwellings, buildings, vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, rights of exit and return, and the dependents living there with all their offspring—everything in its entirety, as much as appears to pertain to that church and is recognized as being their possession.

And in the county of Nevers, they gave an estate called Calda-Aqua, with houses, dwellings, buildings, manses, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, rights of exit and return, with the dependents living there and all their offspring—everything in its entirety, as much as appears there to be their own property.

They also gave, in the duchy of Auvergne, in the county of Donobrin, an estate called Lituinias, with houses, dwellings, buildings, manses, vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, and with the dependents living there and their offspring—everything in its entirety, as much as is recognized as their own property.

Accordingly, he declared that he had in hand two exchanges, written in identical form and strengthened by the hands of good men. But, for complete security, he asked our highness that we should confirm those exchanges anew and more fully by a decree of our gentleness. We did not wish to deny their petition; rather, know that, just as we have done for each of our faithful who asks justly, so we granted this to them and confirmed it in every respect.

Therefore, ordering, we command that whatever one party has justly and reasonably transferred to the other party, from now on, by this our authority, shall hold and possess by the firmest right; and whatever either party wishes to do or decide concerning it, let each enjoy full freedom to do whatever he chooses.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved for future times, we ordered it sealed below with our ring.

Durand, deacon, reviewed this in place of Fridugisus.

Given on the third day before the Nones of June, in the twelfth year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, indiction 3. Done happily at the royal palace of Aachen, in God’s name. Amen.

## CXXVII. A DONATION OF THE EMPERORS LOUIS AND LOTHAIR TO RICBOD, ABBOT OF SENS. (Year 825.)

[Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. II, p. 735.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, by the ordering of divine providence, emperors Augustus.

We wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, that we have granted as a benefice to a certain faithful of ours, Ricbod, abbot, a cell built in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ in the Vosges, at a place called Aluwini-Mons, on the river Prusia. Some time ago his uncle, Wicbod by name, transferred it by written documents to the bishopric of Metz, which was built in honor of Saint Stephen the protomartyr.

Accordingly, we grant this cell, with everything justly belonging to it, in its entirety, to the aforesaid faithful of ours, Abbot Ricbod, as a benefice through this grant of our authority, in such a way that throughout all the days of his life he may hold and possess it peacefully, without anyone’s unjust opposition. After his death, however, together with everything belonging to it, it shall in every respect return in its entirety to the right of the monastery of Sens, which also belongs to the aforesaid bishopric of Metz.

And so that this grant of our authority may be held more firmly, believed more securely in future times, and preserved more carefully, we have confirmed it below with our own hands and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Sign of Lothair, most glorious Augustus.

I, Hirminmaris, notary, have reviewed and subscribed this in place of Fridugisus.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the twelfth year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis and in the fourth year of the reign of our lord Lothair, indiction 4. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, in God’s name, happily.

[Note: [Col. 1149D] Thus in the authentic document; perhaps one should read “13.”]

## CXXVIII. LOUIS’S DECREE FOR THE CHURCH OF BRIOUDE. (Year 825.)

[Baluz., *Capitularies*, vol. II, p. 1426.]

In the name of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, emperor Augustus.

We wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to ours, and also, by God’s dispensation, to our successors, that after we granted the county of Brioude to our faithful Berengar, illustrious count, he, by whatever means he possessed, restored to its former condition a certain church where Saint Julian the martyr rests bodily. It had been built in the village of Brioude, not far from the fortress of Victoriacum, and had been destroyed and burned by the Saracens.

In that church he established thirty-four canons, and in the aforesaid fortress of Victoriacum, which he likewise rebuilt, twenty, so that they might serve the Lord according to canonical order and live canonically. He gave them property [read *res*, “property,” for *rex*, “king”] from his benefice—namely, from the possessions of the aforesaid church of Saint Julian—one hundred manses, from which they could meet their needs and obtain support: sixty manses in common for the aforesaid clerics, and forty manses for the abbot whom they jointly chose over themselves.

By every means at his disposal, the same faithful count Berengar entreated our clemency that, by a decree of our authority, we should establish that no one should presume to withdraw any of the aforesaid one hundred manses; that the canons established in the aforesaid places should have permission to choose an abbot over themselves from among their own number; and that the abbot or his congregation should be under no one’s jurisdiction and should render service for the aforesaid possessions to no one, except that each year they should present to the king’s representative one horse with shield and lance. Thereafter they should be immune and free from every public or private exaction or compulsory service.

Since his petition appeared to us just and reasonable, we were pleased to lend an ear to it and ordered these imperial [read *imperiales*] letters to be made. Through them we decree and command that, just as the aforesaid Berengar granted, established, and arranged concerning the places, abbot, canons, and possessions described above, and requested us to confirm, or just as has been stated above, so thereafter, in our times and those of our successors, with the Lord’s help, it shall remain fixed and stable.

We also wished to insert this provision: whatever from now on divine mercy may grant and bestow in the aforesaid places, whether through us, our successors, or any free and God-fearing persons, shall remain under the same condition stated above.

And so that this decree and confirmation of our authority [read: “this decree and confirmation of our authority”] may retain inviolable and unshaken stability through future times, we ordered it sealed below with our ring.

Given on the second day before the Nones of June, in the twelfth year of the reign of Louis, most serene Augustus, indiction 3.

## CXXIX. FOR THE MONASTERY OF NEW CORVEY. (Year 825.)

[In Schaten, *Paderborn Annals*, p. 83.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, by the ordering of divine providence, emperors Augustus.

Let it be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to ours, present and future, that, for the love of divine worship and for the remedy of our soul, we ordered a certain monastery called Corvey to be built in Saxony, in honor of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, above the river Weser, at a place called Höxter. We entrusted its construction and governance to the venerable man Adalhard, who was abbot of another, older monastery likewise called Corvey, from which the aforesaid new monastery is evidently known to have received its name.

Moved, therefore, by divine inspiration and inflamed by love of the heavenly homeland, for the salvation of our soul we have granted to the same monastery the chapel which our lord and father, the emperor Charles, long ago ordered to be built in the fortress called Heresburg, with all the properties, dependents, and tithes belonging to it, whatever our lord and father is known to have piously bestowed upon that chapel, in complete integrity, to the aforesaid monastery as support for the monks serving God there. Through this donation of our authority, we have granted it from the present day to be held and possessed perpetually, and we have transferred it into its jurisdiction.

This is to be understood in such a way that, from this day forward, whatever the rulers and ministers of the aforesaid monastery may wish to arrange and order concerning the aforesaid chapel or the things belonging to it, for the benefit of that monastery or of the brothers dwelling in it, they may arrange and order without anyone’s unjust opposition, and may do whatever they perceive to be suitable and advantageous to the interests of the aforesaid monastery.

And so that this authority of our grant may retain inviolable and unshaken stability through future times, and so that it may be believed more truly and certainly by our faithful, both present and future, and also by our successors, we have signed it below with our own hands and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Sign of Lothair, most glorious Augustus.

I, Durand, deacon, have reviewed and subscribed this in place of Fridugisus.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the thirteenth year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, indiction 4. Done happily at the royal palace of Ingelheim, in God’s name. Amen.

## CXXX. LOTHAIR’S PRIVILEGE FOR THE MONASTERY OF NOVALESA. (Year 825.)

[In Muratori, *Italian Antiquities*, vol. III, p. 577.]

In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, eternal God, Lothair, son of the most invincible lord Emperor Louis Augustus.

It is clear that no mortal can attain anything good in this wretched pilgrimage of mortality through his own merits. But since it is evident to all that all temporal goods have been freely given to us by God, it is fitting that they be handled and administered piously and prudently, so that through them, with God’s favor, we may be able to obtain the perpetual salvation of our soul.

Therefore let the diligence of all the faithful of God’s holy Church and of our own know that, while a certain hospital was being built at the command of our lord and father, Louis, most serene and religious Augustus, on Mont Cenis, in honor of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ and also of the most blessed ever-virgin Mary, for the reception of pilgrims, he wished to enrich it with such an abundance of his own property that it would suffice to sustain the daily influx of Christ’s poor.

[Note: [Col. 1151C] A hospital. Just as Saint Bernard of Menthon built a hospice on Mont Joux—now the Great Saint Bernard—for the convenience of travelers near Aosta around the year 980, so Christian mercy provided the same in other places of this kind. The Turks themselves now imitate this pious custom, raising such buildings to support pilgrims and travelers, for whom there would otherwise be no lodging. I could gather examples of this custom from all Italy. But it is useful to show the same practice in the one region where I live.

In the Modenese territory, on the river Scultenna—by which name it is still called by the inhabitants of the mountains, while the people of the plain call it the Panaro—Saint Anselm, founder of the monastery of Nonantola, built a hospice under the name of Saint Ambrose, of which no traces now remain.

On the river Gabellus, now called the Secchia, in the territory of Reggio, there was formerly established a very wealthy hospice at Rubiera, which still flourishes.

Again, in our region there is a road that leads from Sassuolo to Garfagnana and Tuscany across the intervening Apennines. There, on the mountain ridge, a house dedicated to hospitality was built in ancient times together with a church; it is still called the Hospice of Saint Peregrine. Yet all its revenues and alms, through the injustice of the times, now go to the advantage of a lay rector rather than to the feeding of the poor, for whose benefit they were and still are assigned.

The monastery of Frassinoro was likewise founded in these same mountains by the great countess Matilda and her mother Beatrice, and it is reasonable to believe that hospitality was practiced there.

Furthermore, from the territory of Reggio another road runs through Cerreto and Ligonchio, crosses the Apennines, and descends into Garfagnana at Silano. On both sides behind the mountain ridge, hospices were once built; they are still called *hospitaletti*, and charity is practiced there.

There are also other places in the Modenese mountains that retain not the institution but the name, being called *hospitaletti*. Thus the people of Bologna have a road that crosses the Apennines into the territory of Pistoia, and there too the name *hospitaletti* survives—perhaps referring to the one to which the celebrated Countess Matilda granted many estates for the benefit of pilgrims.]

But when he wished to honor that place with an abundance of possessions that would be more suitable because of their proximity, with the consent of our lord and father Louis, most glorious emperor, we confirmed by a decree of our authority the royal grants from our patrimony made to the aforesaid place under the monastery belonging to us, called Novalesa.

But so that this holy and venerable monastery, founded in honor of the most blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, should suffer no loss of the property transferred from it, but instead rejoice in the greater gift of a worthy recompense, we assigned to it, to make up for this, a certain monastery called Appanis, likewise built in honor of that prince of the apostles and subject to its own jurisdiction. We considered that both monasteries should serve God regularly under the governance of one abbot.

These matters having been arranged, it pleased our imperial excellence, in response to the petitions of the venerable man Ildrad, father of these monasteries, to confirm by a decree of our authority the aforesaid monastery called Appanis to its earlier monastery, Novalesa, together with all its possessions and appurtenances justly belonging to it. Let the discernment of all our faithful know that we have done this.

Therefore, ordering and establishing, by this our imperial decree we confirm that, as recompense for the aforesaid hospital, we grant to the monastery of Novalesa and to its future rulers, under the right of the monastery of Novalesa and our ownership, the monastery called Appanis, together with everything that is duly known to belong to it, for the aforesaid need. Thus, from now on and thereafter, it shall remain perpetually in the right of that oft-mentioned monastery and of its rulers, in God’s name, and shall benefit the servants of God dwelling daily in both places, so that they may be able with joyful hearts to entreat God’s mercy for the common salvation.

But so that this decree of our confirmation may be believed by everyone and better preserved through future times, we have decreed that it be fortified below with our own hand and the seal of our ring.

Sign of [lacuna] Lothair, most glorious Augustus.

I, Guitard, have written this in place of Vitgarius.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the eleventh year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, most serene emperor, and in the reign of Lothair, most glorious Augustus [lacuna], indiction 3. Done at Murinco from the royal palace, happily in God’s name. Amen.

## CXXXI. FOR VICTOR, BISHOP OF CHUR. (Year 825.)

[In Grandidier, *History of Strasbourg*, vol. II, p. 181, from the original charter of the archive of the Church of Chur.]

[Note: [Col. 1153B] That this diploma belongs correctly to the year 825 is indicated by Aegidius Tschudi, in the *Catalogue of the Bishops of Chur*, among the manuscript *Helvetico-Tugiensia* of D. L. B. de Zurlauben, manuscript vol. VI, p. 38, and in *Gallia Comata*, a posthumous work printed in 1758, book II, part I, chapter 3, p. 300; by Sprecherus, in *Rhaetia*, book III, p. 97; Bucelinus, in *Sacred and Secular Rhaetia*, p. 170; Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, vol. VII, p. 762; Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. III, no. 81, p. 501; and Eckart, *Commentary on the Affairs of Eastern Francia*, vol. II, p. 194. But all of them gave only a brief extract of the diploma. Schoepflin published the complete text, though not sufficiently accurately, under the year 822, *Alsatian Diplomas*, vol. I, p. 68, from a manuscript of Christian Urstisius, which belongs to Brucker, professor of history at Basel. Here we publish the corrected diploma as it was communicated to us from the original itself through the kindness of the illustrious prince of the Holy Roman Empire, the bishop of Chur, by the reverend and noble Monsieur de Jost, counselor to that prince-bishop. We here return public thanks to both for the benefit they conferred.]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, eternal God, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, emperor Augustus.

We wish it to be known to the faithful of God’s holy Church and to ours, present and future, that the venerable man Victor, bishop of the holy Church of Chur,

[Note: [Col. 1153D] Of Victor, Sprecherus gives the following account in *Rhaetia*, p. 97: “In the bishopric of Chur, Victor sits second after Remigius. He had a long dispute with Roderic, count of Langaro, whose territory extended around Chur from the river Lanquart to the Rhine and Mount Crispalt, on both banks of the Rhine. Therefore Emperor Louis sent Bishop Bernold of Strasbourg and Gottfrid, abbot of Gregory’s Valley, with Count Roger. Through their authority it was brought about that Roderic restored to Victor what he had seized. Concerning this matter a document exists, and so forth.”]

approached the serenity of our highness, reporting to us that a certain count of ours, Roderic,

[Note: [Col. 1153D] Roderic was count of Langaro—Count of the Lanquart, a river in the country of the Grisons—whose county boundaries Tschudi describes in *Gallia Comata*, p. 300. The same Tschudi calls Roderic count of Istria, brother of Adelbert, count of Rhaetia, and son of Hunfrid, count of Rhaetia and Chur and lord of Istria. See Tschudi’s manuscript diplomatic excerpts, whose original is preserved in the library of the Abbey of Saint Gall, while a copy is held by D. L. B. de Zurlauben, vol. IV of the *Helvetico-Tugiensian Monuments*. Thegan calls Hunfrid duke over Rhaetia, in Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 80, and Eginhard calls him count of Chur, ibid., p. 183.]

had inflicted many acts of oppression and injuries upon him and his church.

[Note: [Col. 1154C] The same man as Cothefrid, the abbot mentioned in the brief chronicle of the monastery of Münster under the year 815, when he succeeded Rachio, bishop of Strasbourg, in that monastery. (*Diplomatic Code of the Church of Strasbourg*, vol. I, no. 16, p. XXV.) Two diplomas survive in favor of this Gothefrid, or Gotafrid: one of Louis the Pious from the year 823, and another jointly issued by Louis and Lothair in 826, both originals, preserved in the archive of the monastery of Münster. Among others, Bouquet published them in vol. VI, pp. 534 and 551, and Schoepflin in *Alsatian Diplomas*, vol. I, pp. 69 and 72. The same man appears as Abbot Godefrid in a charter of Louis the Pious from 831, to be published below.]

To investigate this matter, we sent our faithful Bernold, venerable bishop of Strasbourg, and Cotafrid, abbot of the monastery of Saint Gregory,

and Roderic himself, the offender, together with our faithful Count Rothar,

[Note: [Col. 1154D] Count Rothar, who is called Retharius in the subsequent charter of the year 831, appears to be the same as Count Ratharius, who is called the son-in-law of Pippin, king of Aquitaine, by the Astronomer, author of the *Life of Louis the Pious*, in Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 122. It is established from the chronicle of Ademar of Chabannes, published by Labbe, vol. II of the *Manuscript Library*, p. 151, that in 839 Raterius was appointed by Emperor Louis as count of Limoges.]

into the province called Rhaetia,

[Note: [Col. 1154D] Today, the country of the Grisons, allied with the Swiss and divided into three large parts called leagues.]

so that they might investigate the truth of this complaint among the people through careful examination. On their return they reported that certain properties belonging by right to the church—properties which our predecessors, our father, our grandfather, our great-grandfather, and other God-fearing men had granted to that church for the remedy of their souls—had been unjustly taken away. These were the church of Saint Sisinnius and the estate of Zizers,

[Note: [Col. 1154D] Today Zizers, the principal and largest village in the jurisdiction called the Four Villages, situated in the League of the House of God, or Caddea, in Rhaetia, on the right bank of the Rhine, about three leagues from Chur. In Latin it is called *pagus Ciceronianus*. See Sprecherus, *Rhaetia*, book IX, p. 324; Tschudi, *Gallia Comata*, book II, part I, chapter 9, p. 314; and Leu, *Helvetisches Lexicon*, vol. XX, p. 122.]

and the hospice of Saint Peter,

[Note: [Col. 1155D] The hospice of Saint Peter appears to have been situated in the valley of Saint Peter—*Sant-Peters-Thal*—described by Leu, *Helvetisches Lexicon*, vol. XVIII, p. 406. That valley is a wilderness, although it contains several and varied settlements and mineral waters. It depends on the supreme jurisdiction of Lugnez, in the Upper Gray League.]

as well as the church of Saint Columbanus, with all the properties and dependents justly and lawfully belonging to it.

Accordingly, after examining the whole truth of the matter, it pleased us to restore those same properties to the church of Chur in their entirety by the authority of our decree. Through it we firmly wish and command that, in our times and in those of our successors, no person of any power should presume to bring any dispute concerning the aforesaid properties against that bishop or against those who will govern the same see after him.

Furthermore, because he complained to us that his episcopal right had been taken away, we command all who reside in his parish that no one should presume to offer any opposition or impediment to the episcopal ministry to be exercised by him and his successors. Rather, they shall have, as was granted to this holy see by our predecessors, full authority in their ministry—namely, over the monasteries situated in his parish, over the priests to be ordained, and over the tithe, which is to be administered according to canonical command—so that, for the remedy of our soul, it may please them to implore the Lord’s mercy more freely, together with all their clergy.

And so that this authority of ours may remain inviolable, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of our lord Louis, most pious emperor Augustus.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the twelfth year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious emperor Augustus, epact 28,

[Note: [Col. 1156D] Here is the ancient use of epacts in royal diplomas. According to the learned and dear-to-us Dom Clément, in the preliminary dissertation to *The Art of Verifying Dates*, p. XXXI, the practice first appears in a letter written in 821 by the monks of the monastery of Inda concerning the death of Saint Benedict of Aniane and addressed to Ardo; the latter inserted it in chapter 57 of his *Life of that Abbot*.]

indiction 3. Done happily in the city of Strasbourg, in God’s name. Amen.

## CXXXII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF ANIANE. (Year 826.)

[In Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. II, p. 724.]

In the name of the Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, by the ordering of divine providence, emperors Augustus.

If, out of love for God, we bestow suitable benefits upon places dedicated to divine worship and upon those serving Him in those places, we do not doubt that a reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us by the Lord. Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own people, present and future, [Col. 1155D] how Durandus, abbot in Septimania, specifically in the county of Narbonne, at a place called Vernodubrus (Vernazoubre), on property which we had granted him through the liberality of our munificence, began, by our undertaking, a monastery in honor and veneration of the most blessed Anianus, confessor of Christ, at the place called Holatianus. He gathered a considerable number of monks; he appointed over them an abbot named Woica; and by a testament of his confirmation he assigned certain properties and slaves there, as well as books and church furnishings, and bestowed various equipment. Together with all these things and the other specified possessions, he transferred them to us as his own property by a charter of conveyance, as is more fully established in that conveyance itself. At the same time he requested our Serenity that the work which he had most devoutly begun for the observance of the holy profession, and had vowed to God, and which he had transferred to us in perpetuity for its maintenance, should through our care and authority be preserved for this purpose: namely, that the same order might perpetually be observed in that place for our eternal remembrance and almsgiving. We gladly accept his gift, willingly grant his petition, and by this authority of ours, [Col. 1156B] as he requested, grant and confirm it.

Accordingly, we wish it to be known to all of you that we have most devoutly bestowed the aforesaid monastery, together with all its places, villages, islands, fisheries, and whatever other properties are seen to belong to it, together also with all their boundaries, limits, and appurtenances, with the slaves and other possessions, just as they are more fully contained in the charter of donation which he delivered to us, so that the holy profession may there be perpetually preserved through our almsgiving. Thus, whatever it appears to possess at the present time, or is recognized as belonging to it, and whatever hereafter, by divine prompting, shall be granted to them either by us or by our successors, or by any of the faithful of the holy Church of God, shall always be devoted to providing for the needs of the servants of God serving the Lord there, [Col. 1156C] and to caring for the poor, for the love of God and for His honor, by God’s mercy, as an expiation for our sins.

But so that the men of God may serve the Lord there more peacefully, and so that the possessions of this monastery, like those of our own property, may be defended and protected from evil men, we have ordered this imperial authority of ours to be issued for this purpose, so that no one may doubt that they stand under our special protection and the safeguard of immunity. Therefore we order and prohibit that no public judge, or anyone exercising judicial authority, or any person of greater or lesser rank, presume to enter the churches, places, villages, or other possessions which the monastery holds or possesses in the aforesaid counties and territories, or any others which divine piety may henceforth wish to increase as the property of that holy place, in order to hear cases according to judicial custom. Nor may anyone presume to exact tribute, requisition, or lodging; to demand tolls; to take sureties; to distrain the men of this monastery, whether free or enslaved, residing upon its land; or to seek or exact any public services, restitutions, or unlawful [Col. 1157A] pretexts. Rather, the aforesaid abbot and his successors shall be permitted to possess the property of the monastery, together with all those subject to it, in peaceful order under the protection of our guardianship and immunity, with all disturbance by judicial authority removed. Whatever the fisc could thereafter exact or expect from it shall instead be devoted to the support of the brothers, to the provision of lamps for that church, and to feeding the poor, as has been said.

We further establish that whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this light, the monks residing there shall have permission, with the consent of us and our successors, to choose from among themselves an abbot capable of governing and benefiting them according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, [Col. 1157B] so that it may please the servants of God serving the Lord there to implore the Lord’s mercy for us, for our offspring, and for the stability of our entire empire.

We also grant and confirm by this authority of ours, and we ask our successors to retain this monastery under their special protection, so that it may never be placed under a bishop or another monastery, nor granted as a benefice to anyone, but may remain solely under their jurisdiction and protection for all time, for the observance of the monastic order. Thus may they preserve this work of our donation immovably, just as they would wish their own agreements to be preserved by their successors.

And so that this authority may possess fuller force in the name of God, we have confirmed it below with our own hands [Col. 1157C] and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most pious emperor.

Sign of Lothair, most glorious Augustus.

I, Hirminmar, notary, have reviewed this in the place of Fridugisus.

Issued on the Kalends of August, in the thirteenth year, with Christ favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, and of Lothair, indiction 4. Done at the royal palace of Carisiac, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

### CXXXIII. FOR THE GREGORIAN MONASTERY. (Year 826.)

[In Mabillon, *Annales Ordinis S. Benedicti*, vol. II, p. 724, from the authentic Gregorian document.]

[Col. 1157D]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

If, from the benefits bestowed upon us by God, we confer something upon places dedicated to God as a gift of our liberality, we plainly believe that this will profit us both in passing our mortal life successfully and in attaining eternal life forever. Therefore let it be known to the knowledge of all our faithful, present and future, that the venerable man Gotafrid, abbot of the monastery of Saint Gregory, also called Confluens, requested us to grant to that monastery, as our almsgiving, for the benefit and needs of the brothers serving God there, a certain part of our forest adjoining the monastery, which appears to look toward or belong to our fisc under the name Columbarium (Colmar). For the increase of our reward and out of reverence for that holy place, we were pleased to heed his prayers, and we decided to grant to the same monastery, as our almsgiving, a certain part of the aforesaid forest, identified and delimited by the following places, for the needs and benefit of the brothers dwelling there in the service of God: namely, from the place where the stream Bredembach flows into the Fachina, upward to the place where that stream begins; then by the path called Isneida as far as the mountain called Swarzimberg; then across the middle of that same mountain as far as the Great Stone, [Col. 1158B] which lies at the foot of the mountain; and from there as far as the Fachina. Whatever part of our aforementioned forest appears to lie within the places enumerated and delimited below, we grant in its entirety to the same monastery as our almsgiving.

Therefore we wish and command that, by this authority of ours, within the places named above, both in our time and in future times, the aforesaid abbot Gotafrid, his successors, or the congregation of that holy place shall possess the aforesaid portion of woodland granted from our prescribed forest as our almsgiving, and that it shall remain perpetually under the control of that monastery. This provision shall apply, however, so that whenever they wish to do anything in or with it for the benefit and advancement of the monastery, they may enjoy complete freedom to act [Col. 1158C] in every respect.

And so that this donation and confirmation of our authority may be held more firmly and retain unshaken and inviolable force both in our time and in that of our successors, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Hirminmar, deacon, have reviewed this in the place of Fridugisus.

Issued on the day before the Ides of June, in the tenth year of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, with Christ favorable, [Note: [Col. 1157D] Or rather thirteen. EDITOR.] indiction 1. Done at the royal palace of Frankfurt, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

### CXXXIV. DIPLOMA OF LOUIS AND LOTHAIR FOR THE PRÜM MONASTERY. (Year 826.)

[Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis*, p. 175.]

In the name of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, by divinely ordained providence, emperors Augustus.

We wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own people, present and future, that the venerable man Tancrad, abbot of the monastery called Prüm, which is dedicated in honor of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ and of Saint Mary ever-virgin, sent to us through his monks the authority of the aforementioned lord Pippin, formerly king, our grandfather. It contained a record of how that same Pippin and our grandmother Bertrada had not only enriched the monastery with many possessions, which they had built from the foundations on their own property, but had also placed it under their protection and that of their heirs, namely kings. He likewise sent the authority of our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, most excellent emperor, in which it was written how he had confirmed and established the constitution of his pious father: in the villages and possessions of the aforesaid monastery, no public judge, without his command or that of his heirs, was to presume to hear cases, exact fines everywhere, take sureties, or exact or demand scaras, lodging dues, or requisitions, whether from vehicles or from packhorses. [Col. 1159B] Rather, whatever the fisc or the fines could expect from the free men [Note: [Col. 1159D] “From the free men”: that is, free laymen.] and ecclesiastical persons or servants who appeared to dwell within the fields, boundaries, or upon the land of the aforesaid monastery was, by his indulgence, to be devoted to the lamps of the monastery.

The aforesaid abbot further entreated us not only to add the authority of our confirmation to the guarantees granted by our grandfather and father, but also to place under our protection and the defense of immunity the monastery itself, together with the possessions and people which it presently holds in whatever counties and territories, whether through the grants of the aforesaid lord King Pippin or of our father, or through the liberality of free men—whether by grants, exchanges, sales, or any other lawful [Col. 1159C] procedure—or whatever divine piety might henceforth wish to increase as the property of that holy place.

We lend a favorable ear to his prayers and have ordered these imperial letters to be issued, by which we decree and command that whatever has lawfully and rightfully been accumulated for the same monastery through the gift of kings or the grant of free men, whatever the monastery legally holds or possesses at the present time, and whatever shall hereafter be justly and lawfully granted to it, shall be held and possessed in perpetuity by the rectors of the aforesaid monastery, without unjust opposition from anyone.

Moreover, we command and establish by this authority of ours that no public judge, or anyone exercising judicial authority, presume to enter the churches, places, fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery to hear cases according to judicial custom, or, as is contained in the diploma of our lord and father, to exact fines or take sureties, or to exact or demand scaras, lodging dues, or requisitions, whether from vehicles or packhorses; nor may anyone presume to exact a ban or military ban from the men of the monastery, whether free men, ecclesiastical persons, or servants who dwell within the fields, boundaries, or upon the land of the aforesaid monastery, [Col. 1160A] or to seek any restitutions or unlawful pretexts.

Rather, the rectors of the aforesaid monastery shall be permitted to live and reside peacefully, together with all possessions and slaves lawfully held by the monastery, as is contained in the authority of the aforementioned King Pippin and of our lord and father, as well as in this authority of ours, and faithfully to obey the command of us and our successors. Thus the monks dwelling there through successive generations may live in peace and earnestly implore the Lord’s mercy for us and our offspring.

Whatever the fisc could exact by right from the possessions of the aforesaid monastery, we grant entirely, as our almsgiving for eternal recompense, in perpetuity, for the lamps of the monastery, the sustenance of the poor, and the support of travelers. [Col. 1160B]

And so that this authority of our confirmation may retain inviolable force through the course of the years, we have also confirmed it below with our own hands and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, emperor +. Sign of Lothair, most glorious emperor +. [Note: [Col. 1159D] “Sign of King Louis.” Namely, of Bavaria, which encompassed a large part of Germany. See Struve, *Corpus Historiae Germanicae*, period IV, section 2, § 10.] Sign of King Louis. I, Megmgmar, notary, have reviewed this in the place of Fridugisus.

Issued on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, in the thirteenth year, with Christ favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, and in the fourth year of Lothair, most serene Augusti, indiction 4. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

### CXXXV. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MAXENTIUS. (Year 827.)

[Col. 1160C] [In D. Bouquet, vol. IV, p. 550, from the cartulary of this monastery.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, by divinely ordained providence, emperors Augustus.

We do not doubt that it is known to many throughout the empire, with the Lord’s assistance, how a certain monastery called Saint Maxentius, situated in the territory of Poitiers, where Saint Leodegarius rests bodily, together with all possessions rightfully belonging to it, had for some time been placed under the authority of counts through the benefaction of our predecessor kings. In our own time, however, by the inspiration of divine mercy, we restored that monastery, together with a certain portion of its possessions, to its former condition, and appointed a regular abbot who would live a monastic life according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and remain under no authority or jurisdiction except ours and that of our sons.

But because we are presently unable to return to the aforesaid monastery the portion of its possessions which is still held as a benefice, on account of a certain utility or necessity of our kingdom that now presses upon us, we therefore command that the monastery, with the portion of possessions it now holds, be entirely free and peaceful from all interference involving secular and public obligations, namely military expeditions, bans and military bans, public works, requisitions, and lodging duties. [Col. 1161A]

With regard to the portion of the aforesaid monastery’s possessions which, as stated above, is still held as a benefice under the authority of various men, we command and establish and decree by these imperial letters of ours that they shall fully pay the ninths and tenths to the often-mentioned monastery of Saint Maxentius and its rectors, until, with the Lord’s help, we ourselves, or our sons and successors, cause the aforesaid portion of possessions to be fully and completely returned or restored to the venerable monastery to which it rightfully belongs.

And so that this confirmation of ours may retain unshaken and inviolable force through the course [lacuna] of times, we ordered it to be sealed below with the impression of our ring.

[Note: [Col. 1161D] There is a similar diploma of King Pippin, issued in the same year on the Ides of January.]

Issued on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, in the thirteenth year [read: fourteenth] of the empire of Lord Louis the emperor and the sixth year of Lothair, with Christ favorable, indiction 5. Done at the royal palace of Compiègne, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

### CXXXVI. LOTHAIR AUGUSTUS BESTOWS MANY BENEFITS UPON THE NONANTULA MONASTERY. (Year 827.)

[In Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, vol. II, p. 197.]

To Lord Lothair Augustus, peaceful emperor Augustus, most serene patrician of the Romans, crowned by God, holding the peaceful seat and Roman blessedness, of the Lombards.

[Col. 1161C]

It has been reverently established that all the matters which ought to be carefully set forth for all the empire’s venerable places in every [law—reading uncertain] … a diploma has been presented to us in the venerable monastery for [a purpose—text corrupt]. Accordingly, concerning certain possessions granted and bestowed by us upon that venerable monastery, or concerning whatever men or persons may have paid dues, it appears that some properties, granted to that religious institution or to its patrimony and possessions, have been acquired. Therefore, in every respect [Note: [Col. 1161D] Carefully note those words in our Aemilian territory, that is, in the province or part of Emilia belonging to us and to the Italian kingdom, or in the region of Modena within the boundaries of the city of Geminiana. The same was Civitas Nova and Geminiana, as is also established by a diploma of Louis the Pious in Sillingardus and Ughelli. Below, the city of Geminiana is again mentioned, which is called the city of Flexiana. If this passage is to be punctuated in that way, the city seems to have borne, besides the name Geminiana, also the designation Flexiana. I nevertheless leave the matter uncertain. From this we may perhaps also infer why Riparia—now Rivara, a village in the territory of San Felice—was given that name: namely, because it was formerly the bank of the Scultenna, although it is now several stadia distant from that river. It is useful to record these points in order to clarify the affairs of Modena, and indeed also the final charters of Charlemagne, in which this Nova city is mentioned. Those who have cast suspicion of forgery upon those documents should reflect that it could scarcely have happened that an impostor of later centuries inserted into that testament a city of which, after so long a time, not even traces of ruins survive.] in our Aemilian territory, or in the region of Modena within the boundaries of the city of Geminiana, among our properties held as lordly estates or tenant holdings, whether public or private, belonging or adjoining to our royal household, let whatever is owed to our household be granted to the same venerable monastery, from the boundaries of Fossa Sclarola or Fossa Pavignana to the boundaries of Riparia, the bank of the Scultenna, and the river Moclena, and onward through the river Lama to Suleole, as far as Bagnone—that is, Tumba Rodiliana, the estate of Restanus, the estate of Grummolus, the Leguriana forest, the Agolaria forest, the house of Lautus, the field of Roviritius, the field of Rusco, Campolongo, Bruniana, the city of Geminiana, which is called Flexiana, Quarantola, Ureniana, Verminitica, Niratica, Calendatica, Pilliciana, Corniola; and, among the properties belonging to the aforesaid possessions along the river Moclena, the boundaries of the city of Geminiana, the estate of Menterionus, the estate of Firmanus, the estate of Alpertus, and the estate of Tassinaria; also every estate of Brixili and the estate of Bruxili, or Curlo, and Tumbole, and Fossa Bruxola, Corrigio Brancudo, Valle Alba, the estate of Fontanella, Corrigio Boni, the estate of Acus, and the estate of Tallolus.

In addition, let other landed estates or holdings, with everything generally or specifically belonging or adjoining to those possessions, whether tributary or rent-paying, lordly estates or tenant holdings, and the agents generally or specifically belonging or adjoining to those possessions, within their boundaries and sides, and belonging or adjoining to the aforesaid landed estates and holdings, or lordly estates or tenant holdings granted by that monastery, be placed in that venerable monastery by privilege, without any obstacle or opposition from anyone, through our fullest largesse. Therefore, let any person who attempts to violate or infringe what has been established by our diploma know that he shall be liable to pay a fine of one hundred mancuses of refined gold.

Accordingly, we command that our decrees be observed inviolably.

Issued under the date and month of August, indiction 5.

[Col. 1162C]

Lothair Augustus, emperor.

### CXXXVII. FOR THE DERVENSIS MONASTERY. (Year 827.)

[In Baluze, *Capitularia*, vol. I, p. 651.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ.

Louis and Lothair, by divinely ordained providence, emperors Augustus.

If we favor the just and reasonable petitions of the servants of God out of love for divine worship, we believe that the gift of heavenly grace is bestowed upon us by the Lord. Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own people, present and future, [Col. 1162D] that the religious man Hauto, abbot of the monastery called Puteolus, which was built at Dervo in honor of the blessed Peter and Paul, approached the majesty of our Serenity and represented to our gentleness [Col. 1163A] that the aforesaid monastery, where he, a worshiper of God, presided as abbot, was suitable to become a regular monastery. For not only did the place where the monastery had been founded, but also all its appropriate surroundings, provide what was suitable for servants of God wishing to live a monastic life. He also showed us privileges indicating that the monastery had been founded for the completion of the monastic order, and royal diplomas in which it clearly appeared that it had formerly been a regular monastery.

Wishing to learn the matter more carefully, we ordered the venerable man Hebo, archbishop of Reims, and some of his suffragans to go to the aforesaid place and examine carefully not only whether the place itself was suitable for observing the monastic order, but also [Col. 1163B] whether the clerics dwelling there lived in a monastic manner. They obeyed our commands, and, as the aforesaid Archbishop Hebo reported to us, they found the place suitable for maintaining the regular standard, and the clerics dwelling there declared voluntarily that they wished to undertake and observe a monastic life perpetually.

But so that the aforesaid monastic order might worthily be observed in that place, in our time and in future times, as an eternal almsgiving for us and our successors, and so that the monks dwelling there through the ages might live according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, the aforesaid Abbot Hauto, with every prayer at his disposal, requested that this monastery might deserve to have our diploma of confirmation, just as the other monasteries of monks in the kingdom are known, with God’s favor, to possess one from us. Judging his petition just and reasonable, by these imperial letters of ours we command and order that from now onward the aforesaid monastery remain under the monastic order, and that the monks dwelling there, with the Lord’s help, lead a monastic life perpetually under the Rule of Saint Benedict.

And whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid abbot departs from this world, the monks shall have permission by this authority of ours to elect abbots, provided that they are able to choose from among themselves one capable of governing and benefiting them according to the Rule, so that the monks dwelling there through the ages may gladly implore the Lord’s mercy without ceasing for us, our wives and children, and the stability of our entire kingdom. [Col. 1163D]

And so that this command and confirmation of our authority may retain inviolable and unshaken force through the course of the years, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most glorious emperor.

Sign of Lothair, most serene Augustus.

I, Durandus, deacon, have reviewed this in the place of Fredugisus.

Issued on the second day before the Ides of February, in the fourteenth year, with Christ favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, and in the fifth year of Lothair, indiction 5. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1164A]

### CXXXVIII. FOR THE DERVENSIS MONASTERY. (Year 827.) A dispute between the abbot and the royal fisc concerning the forest of Astenetum is settled.

[In Martène, *Thesaurus novus anecdotorum*, vol. II, p. 24.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, by divinely ordained providence, emperors Augustus.

We wish it to be known to the understanding of all our faithful, present and future, that Ando, abbot of the monastery called Stavelot and Malmedy, approached the ears of our clemency and petitioned us, saying that a certain dispute had arisen between himself and Albricus, the agent of our fisc, called Tectis, [Col. 1164B] concerning a certain forest which appears to lie at a place called Astanetum, between two streams, the Tailernion and the Dulnosus.

Wishing to learn the nature of this dispute and quarrel, we sent two of our faithful—namely, Jasto, count of our palace, and Wirnitus, tutor of our children—to inspect the place concerning which the dispute had arisen and to investigate the truth of the matter from those dwelling around it on both sides. When they returned, they reported to us that, although the aforesaid Abbot Ando, through the donation diplomas of the ancient kings of the Franks, and the household of our aforesaid fisc and its agents, on account of ancient custom, ought jointly to have their requirements and advantages in that forest, we nevertheless decided to define those rights and advantages in the following manner, so that disputes and disagreements might not arise from now on.

Namely, while the royal diplomas issued by the ancient kings of the Franks concerning the aforesaid forest in relation to the prescribed monastery remain inviolable, both parties—the monastery and our fisc—shall mutually and jointly enjoy, without any hindrance from the other party, the use of the same forest for pasturing animals and swine, for obtaining timber, and for fishing, with the payment of the pasturage dues shared equally between them. Neither party shall in any way presume to clear more of the aforesaid forest or to construct dwelling places in it. [Col. 1164D]

And so that this written act of our authority may be believed true and more carefully preserved, we ordered it to be sealed below with the impression of our ring.

I, Herminmar, notary, have reviewed this in the place of Fridugisus.

Issued on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, with Christ favorable, in the fourteenth year of the empire of Lord Louis and the fifth year of Lord Lothair, most pious Augusti, indiction 5.

Done at the royal palace of Tectis [Note: [Col. 1163D] No mention of this royal palace is found in Book IV of Mabillon’s *De re diplomatica.], prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1165A]

### CXXXIX. FOR THE MICIACENSIS MONASTERY OF SAINT MAXIMINUS. (Before the year 828.)

[From the cartulary of Miciacum, in D. Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 554.]

[Note: [Col. 1165D] An unusual invocation. Many other blemishes make this diploma suspect.]

In the name of the Lord God Almighty and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, his son, by divinely ordained providence, emperors Augustus.

We wish it to be known above all to our successors, and also to all the faithful, that Jonas, our faithful servant and bishop of the Church of Orléans, petitioned our greatness that, for the honor of divine service and so that the monastic order might truly and religiously be preserved, we should entrust to him by a privilege of our authority a certain monastery under royal jurisdiction, called Miciacum, in the diocese of Orléans. It was founded in honor of God and of the glorious protomartyr Stephen by Clovis I, the most Christian king of the Franks, and was magnificently elevated by the munificence of later kings.

The same venerable bishop Jonas, cherishing the aforementioned place of Miciacum with special affection because of the merit and reverence of the most holy Fathers Euspicus, Maximinus, Avitus, and many others, who are shown by the testimony of evident miracles to have lived and pleased God commendably in that same monastery, together with a large number of brothers under the monastic order, does not seek it out from ambitious desire or the arrogance of pride, but so that the regular monastic order may be maintained with the greatest religious devotion.

Therefore our piety entrusts the aforesaid place to him and to his successors on the following condition: that through them it should be increased more by spiritual and temporal growth than diminished; that they should exercise no tyrannical domination over the monks, household, bondsmen, or servants; and that neither he himself nor any of his successors should seize, in his own right and power, any of the movable or immovable property of the aforesaid monastery of Miciacum—whether what it now possesses, by Christ’s favor, or what it may acquire in the future—or in any way invade, steal, or remove it, or grant it to anyone.

For the information of those to come, we have thought it appropriate to record in this pragmatic document—which Bishop Jonas himself composed and drafted in our presence, with the concurrence of his metropolitan, Jeremiah, and which he presented to our excellence for confirmation in writing—the possessions of land contained in the royal charters, through whose munificence they were bestowed upon the aforesaid place and which, at present, by God’s grace, it securely and peacefully possesses.

First is the estate of Miciacum with its dependencies, together with the river Loire and the Ligerici. Continuously, the water of that same river Loire belongs to the aforesaid monastery on both banks, from the place where its land begins above the chapel of Saint Maximinus in the east, until it ends entirely toward the west at the river Rollenus.

Only as much of the Ligerici River belongs to the aforesaid monastery as is recorded here. The possession of the Ligerici River begins at the mill of a certain Dromedamius and runs along the bank of Saint Hilary until, at a village named after a certain Mortosius, it enters the bed of the Loire, eroding its boundaries over a considerable channel. It ends at a certain enclosure of land on the opposite bank belonging to the aforesaid monastery, opposite the place where there is also a public road. Between that road and the other land of the aforesaid monastery there extends for a short distance a small plot of Saint Cross, as well as the little river Rollenus, which at that place presently flows into the Loire.

The other bank of the aforesaid Ligerici River always remains under the authority of the aforesaid monastery, even though land belonging to another jurisdiction lies above it.

In the city of Orléans the aforesaid monastery of Miciacum possesses the cloister called the chapel of Saint Maximinus, and the land of that allod extends outside the walls. Elsewhere in the city it has the allod called Momberric, between Saint Stephen and Saint Mary of the Good Tidings. Beyond the Loire it has the estate of Berarius, called the chapel of Saint Maximinus, together with Censiacum and its forest, Mount Pastor, Mount Theobald, and the estate of Marmanios.

Elsewhere it has the estate of Cambiacum, with its church and everything belonging to it. Elsewhere it has an estate called Fontanas, where there is a stream of water; nearby it has an estate called Casellagi.

In Sologne it possesses the estate of Venuense, with a church, bondsmen, cultivated and uncultivated lands, and a forest called Tassimata; also the estate of Litimiacum, commonly called Monsteuranni, with servants, forests, and its other appurtenances; the estate of Dardi with everything belonging to it; and an estate called Fontenellas, with its forest, servants, and everything belonging to it.

It also has the church of Saint Peter at Gaudiacum and the church of Saint Hilary beyond the Ligerici. At Marogilum it possesses, in one place, twenty-four *prata* [meadows], and in another place called Ad Renas, four *aripennes* of allodial land; and opposite Orléans, at a place called Ad Portum (Le Portereau), eight *aripennes* of vineyard.

Clovis I, the first king of the Franks, gave these possessions to the place of Miciacum by hereditary right.

In the county of Bourges, below the castle of Saint Gundulf, it has the estate of Pauliacum, with a church, the water of Nostiusa, and everything belonging to it. It also has another estate there beside the aforesaid Pauliacum, called Ad Sanctum Martinum, with a church and everything belonging to it. Clodomir, the eldest son of the elder Clovis, granted these possessions to the aforesaid place.

It also has the estate called Vienna, with a church, a forest, and everything belonging to it, in which there is a *collalimilus*; and the estate called Villa Maria, with everything belonging to it; and a forest called Torsellis, extending for two leagues. King Clotarius granted these possessions to the aforesaid place.

In Belsica it has the estate of Ardreni puteus (Ampuys), with everything belonging to it—Bittiacum, Montemuicheth, Pirarium, Sancinum, Nocumentum—and the servants belonging to it; and in the county of Étampes two estates, Casellas and Castaneum Villare. King Chilperic gave these.

In the county of Beauvais it has an estate called Ad Sanctum Maximinum, with a church dedicated in his honor, near the diocese of Senlis. Opposite Orléans it has the estate of Bruerias, called Ad Sanctum Dionysium, with a church dedicated in honor of that martyr, together with its appurtenances: Albarias, Caventono, Asinarias, servants, lands, and meadows. Elsewhere it has the estate of Nemesis, with water, lands, meadows, and everything belonging to it.

King Dagobert bestowed these possessions.

Beside the Long Forest it has an estate called Villare Magnum, with a church dedicated in honor of Saint Maximinus. In the county of Dunois it has a cell at a place called Mount Letard (Montlitar), with the water of Conida, mills, forest, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated lands, pastures, vineyards, bondsmen, and servants.

King Theodoric transferred these possessions to the aforesaid place from the inheritance of Lupus, the most pious duke.

In the county of Limoges it has a church called Magniacum, with a church and water, mills, cultivated and uncultivated lands, vineyards, meadows, forests, pastures, small entrances and exits, servants, and bondsmen. Our father, the glorious Augustus, the emperor Charles the Great, transferred this estate to the place of Miciacum.

In the territory of Poitiers, at the port of Vitraria, in the county of Herbadelicum, on the river Tannacus, it has salt-producing areas for loading ships or for meeting its own needs. It possesses the aforesaid areas with vineyards, lands, meadows, pastures, forests, and everything belonging to them. These lands had been held by Garotholenus from the royal fisc; our grandfather Pippin and his son, our father Charles, bestowed them upon the monastery of Miciacum by royal munificence.

But we, so that we should not appear inferior to the aforesaid kings, have granted to the aforesaid place, at the petition of Dructesindus, abbot of that place, and confirm by the privilege of our authority, the passage of three ships through various rivers of our empire—namely, the Loire, the Seine, the Marne, the Cher, the Vienne, the Sarthe, the Mayenne, and the Layon—for any needs of the monastery, so that they may go and return securely and freely and pay no toll, customary due, or other impost.

Nor may any collector of the fisc demand or receive any customary due from carts, wagons, pack animals, or any vehicle traveling either by land or water, or from any commerce belonging to the aforesaid place. Nor, in any business conducted in the villages, lands, waters, or forests of the aforesaid monastery, may any judicial authority presume to demand anything, impose or exact any legal payment or customary due, or inflict any harassment.

When the abbot of that monastery dies, we wish no bishop or any minister of royal authority, under any pretext, to involve himself in listing or inspecting the property acquired or to be acquired by the same monastery.

We also wish no one other than the man whom the entire congregation, by common consent, has requested as worthy in character to be appointed abbot of that monastery. We grant the bishop permission to approach the aforesaid place solely for the purpose of prayer, or, if he has been invited to perform the sacred mysteries of the Mass and wishes to give something from his episcopal property to the aforesaid monastery, to do so with our royal and his episcopal authority. But if his will or means does not permit this, he must presume to seize nothing from the property that has been bestowed.

Furthermore, if some misfortune of any kind should occur which cannot at all be settled by the bishop, or if he should act wrongly toward that place, we order that it be reported to the ears of our royal successors, so that whatever has been corrupted may be corrected by royal judgment.

Nor, because of this commendation—which we have piously and mercifully made for the assistance and defense of the monastery of Miciacum and which we entrust to our faithful Bishop Jonas—should the bishops of the see of Orléans think that they may, by any scheme, alienate the property of the aforesaid monastery or disturb that place, especially since the aforesaid place was founded by royal benefaction and its property was bestowed by the abundant munificence of kings. This is all the more so because our presence is far removed from those regions.

Therefore, by an emphatic command, we wish the monks of the aforesaid place—enriched with the possessions mentioned above so that they may carry out divine service with greater honor, and having obtained, through the bishop’s assistance and this our authority, the regular leisure of holy repose—to remain immovably, with God’s help, in those duties to which they have bound themselves before God.

For this benefit bestowed by us, we earnestly ask the monks, the servants of God of the aforesaid place, always to pour forth prayers to almighty God for us, for our wife Judith and our offspring, for the stability of the empire granted to us by God, and for its preservation throughout all ages by our successors through His most gracious mercy.

And so that this charter may possess fuller force in the name of almighty Christ and be preserved in faith by our successors, we have wished it to be signed in our name and in that of those who were present, and we have ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the twenty-fourth year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, and in the fourteenth indiction. Enacted at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in God’s name.

[Note: [Col. 1167D] It should be corrected to “year 23,” so that the regnal year would agree with the fourteenth indiction and with the year of Christ 836. Yet this diploma is shown to have been issued before that time by: (1) its superscription, in which Louis and Lothair are jointly designated emperors, indeed “by divine ordering providence,” contrary to the practice adopted after Lothair’s secession; (2) the consent of Jeremiah, archbishop of Sens, who had died seven years before 836; and (3) the subscription of the chancellor Fridugisus, who had died two years earlier.
