Although this pragmatic document is blemished by so many defects, Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, book XXXI, no. 66, considers it not to be disregarded, because it states separately what Clovis the Great, his sons Clodomir and Clotarius, Chilperic son of Clotarius, Dagobert grandson of Chilperic, Theodoric III likewise grandson of Dagobert, and finally Pippin, Charlemagne, and Louis conferred upon the monastery of Miciacum.]

Durandus, deacon, recognized this in place of Fridugisus, chancellor.

[Note: [Col. 1169C] Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, book 6, no. 80, mentions a charter of Louis and Lothair concerning an exchange made by Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis, with a certain Lantfred. “Adalulfus, deacon, recognized [it] in place of Fridugisus. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, in the fifteenth year of the reign of Lord Louis and the sixth of Lothair; enacted at the royal palace of Aachen”; that is, in the year of Christ 828.]

CXL. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SCHWARTZACH. (Year 828.)

The exchange of properties made between Waldo, abbot of Schwartzach, and Erchengarius, count of the Nordgau, is confirmed.

[From the ancient cartulary of Andlau Abbey.]

[Note: [Col. 1169C] Schoepflin published it, *Alsatian Diplomatics*, vol. I, p. 72, not quite correctly.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, emperors Augustus by divine ordering providence.

[Note: [Col. 1169C–D] Although Lothair had been made partner in the empire on 31 July 817 and confirmed on 1 May 821 at the assembly of Noyon, nevertheless, in diplomas in which the names of Louis and Lothair occur together, the first year of Lothair’s empire is reckoned from 822, when, at the assembly of Attigny in August, he was sent into the kingdom of Italy. No diplomas of this sort are found in Alsace before 826; only two of this kind survive: ours of 828, and another, an autograph of 826, for the monastery of Saint Gregory.]

For if we confirm by our edicts those things which the faithful of our empire have exchanged among themselves for their respective advantage, we exercise an imperial custom, and we wish this henceforth to remain in the strongest legal force. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, present as well as future, know that Waldo, abbot of the monastery called Svarzhaha, and also the illustrious man Count Erkingarius, together with his mother and brothers, Rotdrudis, Vuoradus, Bernaldus, and Bernardus, coming before our clemency, made known to our highness that they had exchanged certain property and bondsmen with one another for the advantage of both parties.

[Note: [Col. 1169D] The same person as Wido: he was of a great family and, as Eckhart supposes (*On the Affairs of East Francia*, vol. II, p. 481), related to Louis the Pious; Eckhart asserts that he was nephew of Duke Ernest and kinsman of Count Adalard of the palace.]

Accordingly Count Erkingarius, with his mother and brothers Rotdrudis, Vuoradus, Bernaldus, and Bernardus, by the permission granted them by us, gave Waldo, abbot, for the use of his aforesaid monastery: in the estate of Creuhesheim, six mansi and seven *journals*; in Utilinhaim, four mansi; and between Fedinheim, Lampartheim, and Techinheim, two mansi and meadows sufficient for thirty-four cartloads; at Mustridisheim, one *sors*; at Fregistatt, two *sortes* and *Waltmasta* for fattening seven times sixty-two pigs; at Zeinhaim, two aripennes of vineyard; likewise at Wangon; and thirty-four bondsmen, by these names: Anno, Willigart and her daughter Feginbolt, Vuitbert, Duno, Wanahilt, Pallo, Trutger, Rahrud, Goltrut, Hildefrit, Theacla, Waldila, Meginfrit, Richilt, Winilind, Liuthari, Fridalind, Irmanhilt, Liapheri, Wolfarth, Willirat, Liudolf, Nortwib with three children, Waldgard, Ruadind, Helinsind, Antrat [lacuna].

[Notes: Creuhesheim is today Griesheim, a village belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg. Utilinhaim is today Utelnheim or Ittlenheim, two leagues from Strasbourg, where Schwartzach Abbey holds rights of tithes and patronage. Fedinheim is today Vendenheim, a fief of the bishopric of Strasbourg belonging to the lords of Wurmser. Lampartheim is today Lampertheim, half a league from Vendenheim, belonging to the cathedral chapter of Strasbourg. Techinheim is an unknown village, perhaps Eckwersheim near Vendenheim and Lampertheim. A *carrada* is a cartload, as much as can be carried in a cart; in French, *charretée* (Du Cange, vol. II, p. 347). Mustridisheim is today Meistersheim, four leagues from Strasbourg, a fief of the bishopric of Strasbourg belonging to the lords of Landsperg. A *sors* was a measure of land; it also meant a right of use, or the right to use a forest (Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. VI, pp. 609–10). Fregistatt is today Freystadt, across the Rhine, a large village belonging to the prince of Hesse-Darmstadt in the district of Lichtenau. *Waltmasta* means use of the forest for fattening pigs, from *mast*, which, according to Wachter, *Glossary*, p. 1056, means acorn or fodder; until now the word *Waltmasta* has been unknown to glossaries. Zeinhaim is today Zeinheim, near Wilgotheim, belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg. An *aripennis* is a measure of land, whence the French *arpent* (Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. I, pp. 624, 692). Wangon is today the village of Wangen, an ancient possession of Saint Stephen’s Abbey. Schoepflin wrongly reads *marleya* for *mancipia*.]

And conversely, in compensation for this property, the aforesaid Abbot Waldo, from the property of the said monastery, gave Count Erkingarius and his mother and brothers Rotdrudis, Vuoradus, Bernaldus, and Bernardus, by the permission granted them by us, in the Alsatian district, in the estate or *marka* of Erboldisvillare, at the place called Zinzila, seventeen mansi, meadows sufficient for fifty cartloads, and four aripennes of vineyard, with their boundaries and limits; and thirty-four bondsmen, named as follows: Adelbert, Watto, Dheganholt, Hildigun, Werinbold, Hugibold, Ingilbold, Otgunt, Weringunt, Willibert, Franco, Horslolf, Ruatber, Snelrath, Hiltrad, Ingilbert, Engitman, Niwrat, Trutlind with her son, Werhild, Ruathild, Willisind, Ratgunt, Ingilbrich, Lonico, Adalhild, Libold, Willigunt, likewise Deganbald, Lipsind, Liutsind, Werinbert, and Wacho.

[Note: [Col. 1170D] Zinzila is today Zinsweiler, a village half a league from Oberbronn. It was first called Erboldisweiler, but soon lost that name and was called Zinsweiler from the stream Zinzela which washes it. At Zinzila Count Odalric wrote, in 804, a charter donating the property of Heinhaim to Fulda Abbey; Schannat printed it in *Fulda Traditions*, p. 86, no. 181.]

Accordingly, they declared that they held before them two deeds of exchange drawn up in identical terms and strengthened by the hands of worthy men; but for complete security they requested our highness that, etc. The remainder is as in the diploma of 823, by which Louis the Pious confirms an exchange made between Bernold of Strasbourg and the aforesaid Erchengarius, above, no. CIX. And that this authority may be more firmly held, we ordered it sealed below with our ring.

Hirminmaris, notary, recognized [it] in place of Fridugisus.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of March, in the fifteenth year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of Lord Louis and the sixth of Lothair, most pious Augustus, in the sixth indiction. Enacted at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in God’s name. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1171D] The Astronomer, in the *Life of Louis the Pious*, in Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 109 (col. 927 of this volume), relates that in February 828 Louis the Pious and his son Lothair held a public assembly at Aachen. There also, in the same year and in March, the two emperors, father and son, granted Abbot Sigehard of the monastery of Kremsmünster a diploma dated the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.]

CXLI. FOR THE RESTORATION OF THE CHURCH OF BENIGNUS IN THE CITY OF DIJON. (Year 828.)

[In Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, vol. II, p. 516.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor Augustus by divine ordering providence, to Count Amadeus, Elias and Waldo, Isembard and Barbert, our vassals. Let it be known to you that we wish you to give assistance to Herlegaud the deacon in restoring and reroofing the church of Saint Benignus, martyr of Christ, for this reason: we have learned that you hold benefices from the endowment of that church. Cause ninths and tithes in everything to be given, because this is just. Therefore we direct you to provide assistance in restoring and roofing that church. See that you fulfill this entirely; and we expressly command you to show no negligence in this matter, if you wish to retain our favor. And so that you may know more certainly that this is our command, we have ordered it sealed with our ring.

CXLII. FOR THE CHURCH OF SAINT ANDREW OF BORDEAUX. (Before 828.)

[In Dom Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 557, from Lopes, *Metropolitan Church of Bordeaux*, p. 377.]

In the name of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor Augustus by divine ordering providence.

If by the bounty of our liberality we confer some benefit upon places dedicated to God, and at the petitions of priests relieve ecclesiastical needs by our aid, we clearly believe that this will profit us both for passing this mortal life in time and for happily attaining eternal life. Meanwhile, let the wisdom and advantage of all the faithful, present and future alike, know that the venerable man Sicharius, archbishop of Bordeaux, coming into our presence, offered for our inspection the immunity charter of our lord and father Charles, most serene Augustus of good memory. It contained how he, and indeed his predecessors the kings as well, had caused that see—which is in honor of the apostles Saint Andrew and Saint James, together with the monasteries subject to it, called Blavia, established in honor of Saint Romanus, where that saint rests in body, situated in the same district of Bordeaux on the river Garonne, and Saint Severinus, where he too rests, built in the suburb of that city—together with all their appendages and adjacent properties, should remain under his protection and defense, with the cells subject to it and the property and persons pertaining or belonging to it; and how that church had been secured and defended by the authorities of their immunities from the disturbance of judicial power.

[Note: [Col. 1172D] Read *adjacentiis* or *aspicientiis* instead of *assentiis*.]

But for the security of the matter, the aforesaid Archbishop Sicharius asked us, following the custom of our parents and predecessor kings, to order such a charter of our immunity to be made for that church, for the love of God and reverence for that holy place. We willingly assented to his petition and decreed that this charter of our authority, granting immunity and protection to that church, be made for the love of divine worship and the remedy of our soul. By it we command and order that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, nor any of our faithful, present or future, shall dare, either now or hereafter, to enter the churches, fields, or other possessions which the said church now lawfully and legally holds in any districts or territories within our empire, or those which divine mercy may hereafter increase in its right, for hearing cases, exacting *freda* or taxes, requiring lodgings or provisions, taking sureties, unjustly distraining the people of that church, free or servile, who dwell upon its land, or demanding any payments or unlawful exactions; nor shall any presume to exact the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid bishop and every successor possess in peaceful order the property of the said church, with its subject cells and the property or people belonging or pertaining to it, under the protection of our immunity and free from every disturbance of judicial power; let them faithfully obey our empire; and, together with the clergy and people subject to him, let them continually implore God’s boundless mercy for our safety and that of our wife and offspring, and for the whole empire bestowed upon us by God and to be preserved forever through his most merciful compassion. Whatever the fiscal right may be able to exact from the aforesaid property of the church, we have granted it all to this church by perpetual renunciation, so that in perpetual times it may serve to increase the support of the poor and the stipends of the clergy serving God there. And so that this authority may obtain fuller force in God’s name and be more diligently observed by our faithful, we confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our ring.

CXLIII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF KREMSMÜNSTER. (Year 828.)

[In Rettempacher, *Annals of Kremsmünster*, p. 30.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, emperors Augustus by divine ordering providence.

If, in imperial fashion, we bestow suitable benefits upon places devoted to divine worship, we do not doubt in the least that this will undoubtedly profit the stability of our empire and the salvation of our soul. Therefore we wish all the faithful of the holy Church of God and ours, present as well as future, to know that, at the request of our beloved son Louis, king of the Bavarians, and of Count Gerold, we granted to our monastery called Chremisa, constructed in honor and veneration of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, situated in the district of Trungau, where the venerable man Abbot Sigehard now presides and monks reside from time to time, a certain territory in the district of Grunzwiti, near Mount Sumerberch. Until now the servants or slaves of that monastery held it at a rent paid to the count; there the monks of the aforesaid monastery also built a church, houses, and other buildings.

That territory is bounded as follows: on the east it begins at Sumerberch, as the envoys of Count Gerold marked it out, as far as Draeisma, to the place called Hohoga, Plaettehinn, and thence upward as far as the territory of the bishopric of the church of Passau; thence on the south as far as Heribrunnum; then on the west as far as the place where Flinspach comes out of the forest; and on the north, as that forest extends, as far as the already-mentioned mountain called Sumerberch. The said territory, whatever lies within the aforesaid boundaries, saving nevertheless the property of free slaves, and all the rest that at present within these bounds belonged to the counts, we hereby transfer in its entirety to the aforesaid monastery of Chremisa, transferring it from our right into its right and lordship. Thus its governors and ministers may freely have full discretion to do or decide whatever they choose from the aforesaid territories for the utility and advancement of the said monastery. And that this authority, under the Lord’s protection, may remain unshaken in our own and future times, we confirmed it below with our own hands and ordered it marked with the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

The sign of Lothair, most glorious emperor Augustus.

Durandus, deacon, recognized [it] in place of Fridugisus.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the fifteenth year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of Lord Louis, most serene emperor, and the sixth of Lothair, in the sixth indiction. Enacted at Aachen, at the royal palace, happily, in God’s name. Amen.

CXLIV. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT GALL. (Year 828, 12 February.) Louis the Pious and Lothair, emperors, confirm a gift made by King Pippin to the monastery of Saint Gall.

[In Neugart, *Alemannic Codex*, p. 196, from the manuscript of the monastery of Saint Gall, p. 172.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, emperors Augustus by divine ordering providence.

Let all our faithful, present as well as future, know that Gauzbert, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, made known to us his authorization: our grandfather, King Pippin, had once granted to that monastery certain free men in the district of Brisichava, whose names are Williharius, Putico, Gauzbertus, Otarius, Pillinus, Haimo, Hundo, Wolfuvinus, Motharius, Chrodarius, Gangulffus, Zuppo, Gisalo, Drasamundus, Harimundus, Otini, Grotzeo, Swabulffus, Biritoldus, Griffo, and Wolantinus. This was on the condition that these free men and their posterity should render and pay to the aforesaid monastery the rent which they customarily paid to the fisc. But because they had no written charter of the grant of our grandfather King Pippin, we ordered Count Liutharius to investigate this case carefully, to see whether it was so.

[Notes: Brisichava is Breisgau. Ermoldus Nigellus, *Deeds of Louis the Pious*, verses 274 and 373, and the Astronomer, *Life of Louis the Pious*, chapters 13 and 16, in Bouquet, *Writers of Gallic Affairs*, vol. VI, pp. 18, 20, 91, 94 (col. 927 of this volume), mention Count Liuthard. I would not venture to determine whether he is the same man as the Count Lithuarius mentioned here.]

Having carefully examined the matter according to truth and equity, he reported to us that, as he had been able to establish by oath through the local people and truthful men, it was true as set out above. Therefore we decreed that this charter of our authority be made, by which we command and order that, just as the aforesaid free men rendered to the monastery of Saint Gall, by the enactment of our grandfather King Pippin, the rent which they customarily paid annually to the fisc, so henceforth all their posterity shall pay it in its entirety to the aforesaid monastery under this our charter. And let no disturbance or legal harassment in this matter be suffered by the monastery’s party from counts, centenaries, travelling envoys, or persons of any other rank; but just as it was granted by our grandfather King Pippin, so may it be inviolably preserved by all our faithful with respect to the aforesaid men and the rent owed by them. And that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved in future times, we ordered it sealed below with our ring.

Hirminmaris, notary, recognized and subscribed [it] in place of Fridugisus.

Given on the day before the Ides of February, in the fifteenth year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of Lord Louis, emperor, and the sixth of Lothair, in the sixth indiction. Enacted at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in God’s name. Amen.

[Notes: Pope Paschal placed the imperial crown upon Lothair at Rome on Easter Day in 823, as Einhard testifies in the annals for that year. Compare the Fulda Annals and the Saxon Chronicle, in Bouquet, *Writers of Gallic Affairs*, vol. VI, pp. 183, 208, 220. Therefore one must say that the writer of the diploma reckoned Lothair’s first year from Christmas Day or the Kalends of January, but began the second and subsequent years from that point. That the emperor was at Aachen at this time is readily gathered from Einhard’s words: “An assembly was held at Aachen in February.”]

CXLV. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT-GERMAIN. (Year 829.)

[In Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, vol. II, p. 521.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, emperors Augustus by divine ordering providence.

If we confirm by our edicts those things which the faithful of our empire have established faithfully and devoutly, out of love for God, [Col. 1175B] in the places entrusted to them, for the welfare and benefit of churches and servants of God, we believe without doubt that this will remain for us unto eternal blessedness and for the protection of the whole kingdom entrusted to us by God, and we confidently expect to have the Lord as our recompense in the future.

Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own, present as well as future, that the venerable man Hilduin, abbot of the monastery of Saint Vincent and Saint Germanus, and also archchaplain of our sacred palace, brought to our serenity the following matter: for the love of almighty God and to guard against future danger to that congregation, lest through any negligence or parsimony [perhaps: rapacity] of his successors the monastic order in it should in future be disturbed, he had established and assigned their allowances, which they were to receive annually in food and drink, as well as certain estates specifically intended to serve their needs; and by a written instrument and charter of his grant, confirmed by his own hand and those of other good men, he had granted and assigned these to them. Thus, on no account, not even for public service, could any of his successors in the future impose an impediment upon them by which they would necessarily deviate from the path of righteousness and regular observance; rather, content with the goods and allowances assigned to them, and free from want and poverty, they would be able to maintain the regular rule and observe it without transgression, insofar as human frailty permits.

Accordingly, he humbly begged and requested our highness [Col. 1175D] that, for the security of the matter, we should order an authoritative charter of ours to be issued concerning the same constitution, out of regard for God and reverence for those saints, by which it might henceforth remain stable and inviolate. We, lending an ear to his petition because it was necessary and reasonable, and clearly understanding with what intention and reason he had brought such matters before our clemency, decreed that it should be done just as he had requested.

Therefore we establish [Col. 1176A] and order, according to what is contained in his arrangement, that each year they be given 1,440 modii of pure wheat; and for the reception of guests, 180 modii, making together 1,620 modii; 2,000 modii of wine; 180 modii of legumes; 160 weights of cheese; and of fat, twenty modii or fifty pigs, of the best quality that can be found; four modii of butter; one cartload of honey, measured as eight modii, or as is paid from the census of the estate of Lucarias; and a monthly allowance from twelve estates of honey and wax, namely, four sextarii each month and two pounds of wax; 100 modii of salt; and poultry with eggs for the two feasts, namely Easter and Christmas.

For clothing [Col. 1176B] and all their other needs, to be provided according to the regular institution, we have assigned to them the same estates which he himself appears to have granted to them by his concession: namely, Antoniacum (Antony), with the chapel itself, and whatever he presently held there for his own use, as well as whatever people hold from it by precaria or whatever others still hold there by his benefice and which appears to belong to that place, so that after their departure it may return to the use of the brothers. The second, whose name is Cella (La Celle), which is called Villaris, with all its appurtenances, insofar as he presently held anything there for his own use, and whatever people hold by precaria or by his benefices and which appears to belong there. The third, called Matriolas (Marolles [Col. 1176C] near Montereau), in its entirety. The fourth, called Cati-cantus (Cachant). The fifth, whose name is Novigentus (Nogent-l’Artaud), in its entirety. The sixth, called Spinogilum (Espigneul), with the chapel itself and whatever he held there for his own use. The seventh, the little estate called Valedronis (Valenton). The eighth, called Agmantus (Esmant), together with the forest itself called Usta [another reading: Utta, Otte].

These estates, therefore, with their appurtenances and revenues, as we have said, for meeting all the needs of that congregation, both of the sick and of the old, and for providing the necessities of mortal life, we grant and confirm to them by imperial authority and favor through this charter of our confirmation, with stable right, just as the aforesaid venerable [Col. 1176D] abbot granted them in his aforesaid constitution. We command that no abbot in succession dare remove or diminish anything which he wisely established, divert it to his own uses, or grant it to anyone as a benefice. Nor shall he exact services from these estates, or receive paraveredi or expenses for the reception of guests; nor shall he demand any exactions from them for any purpose without unavoidable necessity, apart from the dues long ago established at the principal [Col. 1177A] church of Saint Germanus and at the long bridge of Paris. If he should judge that these should be increased, and should increase the number of monks, he shall have permission to enlarge them by a greater expenditure of money.

These provisions, as we think, are sufficient for the needs of 120 monks. But no one shall presume to alienate or diminish the estates which we have established out of love for God. If anyone should presume to do so and, after our departure, should wish to violate this confirmation which we have issued for the constitution of the aforesaid venerable man Hilduin, and if a complaint should reach our successors who shall survive us at that time, let them, having recognized our authority, defend our statutes and confirm them by a charter of their own authority, so that in future times [Col. 1177B] the brothers serving God in the aforesaid monastery and observing the Rule of Saint Benedict may serve Him freely and without disturbance, and so that a reward for this may be repaid to us in everlasting eternity.

And so that this authority, which we have established out of love for God and for the remedy of our soul, may possess firmer force and thereafter endure unshaken, we have confirmed it below with the subscription of our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Given on the Ides of January, in the sixteenth year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of the lord Louis, most serene Augustus, in the seventh indiction. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## CXLVI. FOR THE MONASTERY OF FARFA. [Col. 1177C] (Year 829)

[In Duchesne, *Writers of French Affairs*, vol. III, p. 658.]

Louis and Lothair, by divine providence, emperors Augustus.

Whenever we bestow something from our generosity upon places consecrated to divine worship, we clearly believe that this will benefit us for the stability of our empire and for attaining the reward of eternal life. Therefore we wish it to be known to the understanding of all our faithful, present as well as future, that, inflamed by heavenly love and for the salvation of our soul, we grant a certain small monastery situated in the territory of Teate or Voci, in a place called Lucana, and built in honor of Saint [Col. 1177D] Stephen the protomartyr, in its entirety, to our monastery of Saint Mary ever-virgin, situated in the Sabine district, where at the present time Abbot Ingoaldus is known to preside.

The aforesaid small monastery, in its entirety, with its churches, cells, territories, buildings, dependents lawfully belonging to it, houses, *amassaricia*, *aldiaricia*, *bouillicaria*, *vaccaricia*, the Gaii Alps, mills, waters, watercourses, pastures, marshes, and whatever is presently known to belong to it justly and legally, and which by right of ownership is under our jurisdiction and possession, we transfer wholly and in its entirety, without investigation, to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary, transferring it from our right into its right and lordship. [Col. 1178A]

Namely, whatever the rectors and ministers of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary ever-virgin may wish to do, order, and arrange concerning the aforesaid monastery of Saint Stephen, according to canonical and regular authority, they shall freely enjoy the discretion to do whatever they choose in every respect. And so that this authority of our gift may be held more firmly and better preserved in future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hands and ordered it authenticated by the impression of our ring.

Deacon Durandus, acting in the place of Fridugisus, recognized it.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the fifteenth year of the reign of Lord Louis and the seventh of Lothair, in the seventh indiction. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## CXLVII [Col. 1178B]. FOR FLODEGARIUS, BISHOP OF ANGERS (Year 829)

[In Baluze, *Capitularies*, vol. II, p. 829.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, by divine providence, emperors Augustus.

If we confirm by our edicts those things which the faithful of our empire have exchanged among themselves for their own needs, we exercise the imperial custom, and we wish this to remain thereafter established by the firmest right. Therefore let the discernment of all our faithful, present as well as future, know that our beloved son, Augustus Lothair, made known to our gentleness that Flodegarius, bishop of the city of Angers, had recently made an exchange concerning certain dependents with a certain man named Winnerad, for the common advantage and benefit. Accordingly, the aforesaid venerable man Flodegarius, bishop of the city of Angers, gave to the party of the aforementioned Winnerad, from the account of his church of Saint Maurice, from the estate called Chamberliacum, with the consent of Berta, who appears to hold that estate as a benefice, a dependent named Aredius, to be held as his own. In return, as compensation for this matter, the aforementioned Winnerad gave to the aforesaid venerable man Flodegarius, bishop, for the portion of the aforesaid estate or of the lady Berta, who at that time appears to have held the estate as a benefice, two dependents from his own property, named Restaldus and Ermenaldus.

He declared that he had these two exchanges, written in identical form and confirmed by the hands of good men, in his possession. But for their complete security he requested that we confirm the exchanges anew and more fully by a charter of our gentleness. We did not wish to deny his petition; rather, know that we have granted and confirmed everything to him just as we have done for each of our faithful who make a just request.

Therefore we command and order that whatever one party justly and reasonably transferred to the other party, that party shall henceforth hold and possess by the firmest right under this authority of ours, and shall do with it whatever it chooses. And so that this authority of ours may be held more firmly and better preserved in future times, we have ordered it sealed below with our ring.

[Col. 1179A]

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Meginarius, notary, acting in the place of Fridugisus, recognized and subscribed.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of . . . , in the fifteenth year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of Louis, most serene emperor, and the seventh of Lothair, in the seventh indiction. Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## CXLVIII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT ANDREW OF JURÉ, IN THE DIOCESE OF ELNE (Around the year 829)

[In D. Bouquet, same work, from the appendix to Marca Hispanica, col. 775.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence, emperor Augustus.

[Col. 1179B]

We wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own, present as well as future, how the illustrious Count Gaucelmus [Note: [Col. 1179D] Gaucelmus, count of Roussillon, son of Saint William and brother of Bernard, duke of Septimania, was beheaded by order of the emperor Lothair in the year 834.] approached our clemency and made known to our highness that a certain abbot named Miro had once built a monastery in the territory of Elne, beside the River Tech, in a certain place, in honor of Saint Andrew, and had established monks to live in that monastery according to the Rule of Saint Benedict; and that, after he had been taken from human affairs, Abbot Sisegutus had been appointed in his place and office.

The same illustrious man, Count Gaucelmus, entreated us to place the aforesaid Abbot Sisegutus, together with his monks, and his aforesaid monastery, with all the cells belonging to it in the aforesaid [Col. 1179C] district of Elne—namely, one situated in honor of Saint Martin, where that abbot first began to live with his monks, and the valley itself with the aforesaid cell and all its contents, as well as another cell built in honor of Saint Vincent, and also the estate called Garrericis, together with the fiscal lands themselves and with the properties or appurtenances which they presently appear to hold and possess justly and legally in the aforesaid places—to be established in our alms under our protection and defense, just as the other monasteries within Septimania are known to exist.

Granting assent to his entreaty, let the understanding of all our faithful know that we have done so. Therefore we ordered these letters of our authority to be made and given to him as a guarantee, by which we command and order that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial power, dare enter, in judicial fashion, the churches or places or lands, or the remaining possessions of the aforesaid monastery and the cells named above, or those which divine mercy may hereafter increase in the jurisdiction of that place, in order to hear cases, exact fines, demand lodging or provisions, or seek any other payments or unlawful pretexts; nor shall anyone presume to exact the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors be permitted, without unjust disturbance from anyone, to live and reside peacefully with all the properties presently belonging to them justly and legally, and together with their monks continually to implore the mercy of the Lord for us, for our wife and offspring, and for the stability of our entire empire. Whenever the aforesaid abbot and his successors depart this life by divine calling, so long as they are able to find among themselves men capable of governing and ordering them according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, let them have the freedom to choose abbots from among themselves. And so that these letters of our authority may be more truly believed by all and more diligently preserved, we have ordered them sealed below with our ring.

## CXLIX. FOR THE MONASTERY OF EBERSHEIM (Year 829) [Col. 1180B]

[In Grandidier, *History of Strasbourg*, vol. II, p. 190.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Louis, by the favor of divine grace king of the Franks and Lombards, and Augustus, Roman emperor.

If, out of love for God, we bestow suitable benefits upon places devoted to divine worship and upon those serving Him in those places, we do not doubt that an eternal reward will be repaid to us by God. Therefore let the discernment of all our faithful, both present and future, know that the venerable Theopaldus, abbot of the monastery called Novientum or Ebersheim, situated in the district of Alsace above the River Ill, in the county of Kirchheim, which the illustrious Duke Ethich built in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1180C] and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of Saint Maurice and his companions, presented to us the immunity and privileges of our lord and father, the Emperor Charles, of blessed memory.

When these had been read aloud in the presence of the princes, they appeared to state that the same father of ours, for love of the heavenly kingdom, but especially out of reverence for the Theban martyrs, had always protected the aforesaid monastery with a particular affection under the fullest protection of royal immunity. Therefore the aforesaid abbot, together with his advocate, Lord Vuifhald, asked us, following the custom of our father, to receive the aforesaid monastic place and its principal estates under the protection of our imperial defense, excluding every comital or fiscal authority.

We, therefore, moved by the example of our ancestors and at the same time providing for the welfare of that holy place and for our own salvation, have decided to assent to his petition in every respect. Accordingly, by imperial authority we command that no public judge and no judicial power, in our times or in those to come, presume to enter the aforesaid place or its estates by force of authority; nor shall anyone make provisions or lodging there, constrain any person, or seek anything there as belonging to our fisc. Rather, the aforesaid abbot Theopaldus and all his successors shall from now on possess these estates with full authority and entirely, together with all their immunity.

At Hiltesheim [Note: [Col. 1180D] Today Hiltzheim.], [the text as printed reads: “the estate of Lothair was beheaded by the emperor in 834”] the lord’s estate with all its appurtenances, the entire bann, and the church with its tithes; we have also retained for ourselves and our judges half a mansus in that village, so that the monastery may suffer no impediment in its estate; judicial authority, however, shall belong by right to the abbot and his judges. In Wittensheim [Note: [Col. 1181C] Wittisheim, or Witzen.], the lord’s estate with its appurtenances and the church with its tithes, retaining for ourselves a quarter of a mansus, under the terms stated above. In Gruzenheim [Note: [Col. 1181C] Grusenheim.], the lord’s estate with all its appurtenances, the church with its tithes, and three parts of the bann with judicial authority; but, so that the monastery may suffer no impediment in its estate, as we have said above, we have retained one mansus for ourselves and our judges. In Artolvesheim [Note: [Col. 1181C] Artelsheim.], the lord’s estate with all its appurtenances [Col. 1181B], the entire bann, and the church with its tithes. In Muttersholtz [Note: [Col. 1181C] Mietersholz.], the lord’s estate with all its appurtenances and the church with its tithes. In Svabesheim [Note: [Col. 1181C] Today the village of Schwabsheim, belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg, two leagues from Sélestat.], the lord’s estate with all its appurtenances. The church at Nivratesheim [Note: [Col. 1181C] Niffer.], with its tithes. In Beckensheim [Note: [Col. 1181C] A village unknown, unless it is perhaps Burgheim, mentioned in other charters of Ebersheim.], the lord’s estate. In Wilre [Note: [Col. 1181C] Today Weiler, or Viler, belonging to D. de Choiseul-Meuse.], the lord’s estate and the church with its tithes. In Binrenheim [Note: [Col. 1181C] Bindern.], the lord’s estate with the bann of that allod, and the church with its tithes. In Kagenheim [Note: [Col. 1181C] Kogenheim.], the lord’s estate. In Ebersheim [Note: [Col. 1181C] Today the village of Ebersheim, belonging to the chief chapter of Strasbourg.], the lord’s estate. In Utenheim [Note: [Col. 1181D] Utenheim.], the lord’s estate and the church with its tithes. In Valva [Note: [Col. 1181D] Valff.], the lord’s estate.

Thus may the aforesaid Abbot Theopaldus and all his successors possess the aforesaid estates, without any contradiction, seizure, or diminution by any judicial authority, whether secular or spiritual, improving and increasing them by the generosity of our imperial authority, with full authority, [Col. 1182A] so that the brothers serving the Lord there may pray more frequently for our salvation and for the stability of our empire.

And so that this imperial authority of ours may remain stable and unshaken, by Christ’s gift, in our times and in those to come, we have signed it with our own hand and sealed it with the impression of our seal.

Given on the Ides of June, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 829, in the seventh indiction, in the . . . year of the reign of Lord Louis, most serene king. Done at Forchheim [Note: [Col. 1181D] There is no diploma among those of Louis the Pious that was issued at Forchheim. Moreover, it is clear from the royal diploma of Louis and Lothair for Abbot Ingoaldus of Farfa, in Duchesne, vol. III of the *Scriptores of France*, p. 658, that this emperor was at Aachen in June of the year 829. It should also be observed that the diplomas of this year were never issued by Louis alone, but always jointly with his son Lothair.], in the royal estate, happily in the name of Christ. Amen.

The sign of Lord Louis, most serene king. Albert, chancellor, acting in the place of Diothmar, archchaplain [Note: [Col. 1181D] Albert and Diothmar are entirely unknown among the chancellors of Louis the Pious. Both are known from the charters of the Emperor Arnulf. Deotmar, or Theodmar, archbishop of Salzburg under Arnulf and his son Louis III, held the office of archchancellor, and Albert, more correctly written Aspertus, frequently recognized documents in the place of Theodmar. Mallinkrot, *On Archchancellors*, in Wencker, *Collections of the Archives*, pp. 243–244. There exists an authentic diploma of King Arnulf for the abbey of Ebersheim, to be cited below, ending as follows: “Given on the Ides of June, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 889, in the seventh indiction, in the second year of the reign of Lord Arnulf, most serene king. Done at Forchheim, in the royal estate, happily in the name of Christ. Amen. The sign of Lord Arnulf, most serene king. Albert, chancellor, acting in the place of Diothmar, archchaplain, recognized it.” Who does not see that the forger of Louis the Pious’s diploma had this charter of King Arnulf from the year 889 before his eyes? Hence we have strong suspicion that the spurious diploma of Louis the Pious from the year 829 was written on the very original of Arnulf’s charter from 889, which [Col. 1182D] was therefore destroyed. For only copies of it survive, both in the archive of the bishopric of Tabernae and in the archive of Aprimonasterium itself. The forger, however, deleted the whole diploma of Arnulf because it favored the rights of the bishops of Strasbourg too much, as he supposed, and in its place wrote a fictitious charter of Louis the Pious according to his own invention. But when the criminal hand thus corrupted it, artistry could not be employed in erasing the final formulas; hence the marks of the former Arnulfine diploma remain. Among other things, this is proved by the different characters, the different strokes of the letters, the more blackish ink, and the thicker letters. It is proved by the deleted letters LX following DCCCLXXXIX, so that the year DCCCXXIX could be made, in which Louis the Pious lived. It is proved by the deleted year that designated the reign. It is also proved by the seal itself, whose bust is elegantly impressed and well preserved in white wax, while the letters written around the head have been erased. The corruptor of the charter did this skillfully so that the name of Arnulf would not be discovered on the seal.]

## CL. FOR THE MONASTERY OF CENTULA, OR SAINT RICHARIUS [Col. 1182B] (Year 830)

[In D. Bouquet, same work, p. 562, from Achery, vol. IV of the *Spicilegium*, p. 478.]

In the name of the Lord [God] and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence, emperor Augustus.

We wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own, present as well as future, that when we came for the sake of prayer to the basilica of the most blessed confessor of Christ, Richarius, monks from that monastery approached our highness, asking that, for the sake of security, we should order our authority to be issued concerning the properties which at the present time they possess in various districts and territories within the jurisdiction of our empire, for their food and clothing. [Col. 1182C] By it we should decree that neither the abbots residing there over the course of time, nor the ministers, nor any other person of higher or lower rank [perhaps: dignity] should presume to take away, diminish, or divert to other uses anything from those properties.

Judging their petition just and reasonable, we ordered these imperial letters of ours to be issued, for the sake of security, concerning the servants of God who reside there as time passes. By them we decree and establish in every respect that no rector of the aforesaid monastery, nor his ministers, presume to take away, diminish, divert to other uses, or exact or demand provisions, *lidimonium*, military service, or any other payments from the properties which at the present time they possess in various districts and territories within the jurisdiction of our empire for their uses, food, and clothing. Their names are: Cininicurtem with Bronoilum, Aldulficurtem, Valles, Drusciacum, Novamvillam, Mons-Angelorum, Wiberentium, Bagardas, Curticellam, Crux, Langoratum, Altegiam, Sidrutem, Niviellam, Verculf, Concilium, [Col. 1183B] Rocconis-Montem, and Maris; or whatever now appears justly and legally to belong to the aforesaid places.

Rather, let them hold and possess these things in the manner and under the terms which we now establish, so that in our times and in those to come they may have and enjoy them securely and peacefully, and so that the servants of God serving in the aforesaid monastery may continually delight to implore God’s mercy for us, for our wife and offspring, and for the stability of our entire empire.

And so that this authority may possess inviolable and unshaken force in future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our ring. [Col. 1183C]

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Given on the third day before the Nones of April, in the twenty-seventh year, Christ being favorable, of the reign of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the eighth indiction. Done at the monastery of Saint Gualaricus, happily. Amen.

Deacon Durandus, acting in the place of Fridugisus, recognized and subscribed.

## CLI. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT PHILIBERT AT HERIO (Year 830)

[In D. Bouquet, same work, from manuscript materials of the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, by divine providence, emperors Augustus.

[Col. 1183D]

For if we employ the power granted to us by God in the service of divine worship, and, while we are placed in this wicked age, strive by our efforts to secure the repose of God’s servants, so that through our care, insofar as lies within us, they may dwell safely amid the storms of the world, freely maintain their profession, and continually cleave to God in devoted tranquility, with the disturbances of the age removed, through the holiest desires and pious endeavors, we do not doubt that this contributes to earning God’s mercy, to the absolution of our sins, and to the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own, present as well as future, how the venerable Atho, formerly a bishop [Col. 1184A], had obtained the monastery of Saint Philibert, our patron and most illustrious confessor of Christ, situated on the island of Herio and built by him, through the generosity of our lord and father, Charles, of holy memory and most excellent emperor, so that the regular order which had once been instituted in that place by the aforesaid most holy man, and which had thereafter been laudably and suitably maintained for many years, but had been corrupted partly through the negligence of its superiors and partly through the sloth of its subordinates, might be restored to its former condition.

Warned by divine inspiration and supported by the assistance of religious men, he took care to labor to the best of his ability, and with earnest prayers implored the help of our father and of us, so that his pious devotion might achieve its effect. But because, before his reasonable petition [Col. 1184B] and pious devotion and [lacuna] obtained the desired result, the same bishop closed his final day; and because various circumstances arose, the community of that place was hindered on many occasions from observing its purpose, [lacuna] inflamed with love and kindled with the most fervent desire, strove through, so to speak, spiritual force [lacuna] had begun and had vowed to God a regular profession, so that no disturbance or persecution of the world, however timely, could in any way compel them to deviate from their purpose [lacuna].

And since we had spiritual compassion for their tribulations, because they were striving, dead to the world, to live for God, we willingly provided them, for the love of Christ—whose footsteps they were striving most ardently to follow—with the assistance they required, and granted them the desired repose and freedom [Col. 1184C]. We appointed one of their own number as abbot, who might be able to govern them.

We also ordered our imperial authority to be issued, by which that monastery and all the property justly belonging to it, in its entirety, might perpetually remain under the fullest protection, immunity, and guardianship of us and our successors. Likewise, by our authority we prohibited any tribute, fine, census, lodging-tax, or any other exaction from ever being demanded from that place for any reason.

And whatever the fisc could demand or hope for, or whatever seemed to pertain from that place to our public service, we most willingly granted so that it might wholly be devoted to the support of the brothers, the feeding of the poor, repairs [lacuna], or the preparation of lights [Col. 1184D].

We further confirmed by our precept that they should always have the freedom to choose an abbot from among themselves who could preside over them according to the rule and benefit them, so that the place might remain perpetually under monastic discipline without any alteration over time.

We granted all these things to them with the utmost devotion for the love of God, so that, through the free mercy of the most gracious Lord, recompense might be made for us eternally in the heavenly homeland, and so that we might have them perpetually as helpers and intercessors before the divine clemency.

But when that place began to be very frequently harassed by pirate incursions, and the monks themselves consequently suffered many hardships and continual troubles [Col. 1185A]; and when this necessity compelled them every year to abandon the same place from the beginning of spring until the end of autumn, leaving it almost deserted and without divine worship, and to transport outside, at great expense and labor, all the church’s ministry and the entire equipment of the monastery; and to build another monastery anew, so that the aforesaid place might not be wholly abandoned or rendered void, and so that the monks’ devotion, shaken and impeded by such prolonged disturbance, might recover what it had partly lost through this stormy upheaval, they petitioned our Highness to permit them to construct a fortress around the new monastery, so that, protected within it, they might observe their way of life in the same place where they had made their regular profession, and, by God’s mercy, enjoy the repose they desired [Col. 1185B].

Since we knew their petition to be very necessary, we accepted it and permitted them to do so. Moreover, supported by the help of the faithful through divine assistance, and applying the most diligent effort according to their ability, they brought the work to completion with God’s cooperation.

But so that the completed work might be useful and remain safe from enemy incursions, they earnestly requested that our serenity grant that men of the same monastery, whether free or servile, be permanently assigned especially to defend it, and that through our generosity they remain exempt from other public services.

This we willingly granted for the repose of the aforesaid servants of God, and, so that it might be preserved in this way in the future, confirmed it by this authority of ours [Col. 1185C], because we judged it more useful that this be done, so that an equal number of our faithful might always be assigned to guard the same place [lacuna], and so that the place might not on this account be utterly destroyed.

Therefore we have decided that these imperial letters be issued, by which we make known to all, as stated above, that we wish—and earnestly ask that our successors preserve this—that the aforesaid monastery and its community remain under the special protection and defense of us and our successors, and in a certain manner be guarded as our particular charge; that everything which we have granted to it for the love of God and confirmed through our other documents be preserved inviolate; and that the men of the same monastery—whether free men who are known to hold benefices from it or to dwell upon its lands [Col. 1185D], or tenants and servants who justly belong to it—be exempt from all public services pertaining to us, and at all times be assigned and appointed for the defense of that place or the service of the aforesaid community, without anyone’s command [lacuna] or deprivation.

And since small gifts used to be paid from it each year before that order was established there, lest our pious devotion, donation, and settlement should perhaps appear burdensome for our successors to preserve, and so that every occasion for violating it might be entirely removed, we have established that six pounds of silver be paid from it each year to the royal treasury, on this condition, namely, that by this confirmation the same place be entirely freed forever from all gifts and services, and from every public and palatine obligation [Col. 1186A], and remain irrevocably established with all its property intact, without any disturbance, harassment, or exaction of any kind.

Thus the monks serving God there, made free and peaceful through our efforts from all the impediments of the world, may serve God with the utmost fervor and devotion, and may be able to beseech the Lord with inward vows and unceasing prayers for us and our offspring, and also for the stability of the entire kingdom.

And so that this authority may remain perpetually inviolate, we have confirmed it below with our own hands and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.

**The sign of Louis, most serene emperor, and Lothair, most glorious Augustus.**

[Col. 1186B]

Given on the third day before the Nones of August, in the seventeenth year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, and the eighth of Caesar Lothair. Issued at the palace of Silvacus.

Hirminmar, notary, recognized this in place of Fredugisus.

## CLII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF FONS BESUUS. (Year 830.)

[In D. Bouquet, same place, from Dacher’s *Spicilegium*.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, emperors Augustus, by the divinely ordained providence.

If, for love of divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants, we do not doubt that heavenly grace thereby protects us [Col. 1186C]. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, present as well as future, know that the venerable man Alberic, bishop of the Church of Langres, brought to our gracious attention how he had rebuilt from the foundations a certain abbey called Fons Besuus, from the property of his bishopric, where monks had once lived according to the rule but which in modern times had been utterly destroyed; how he had constructed suitable buildings, gathered monks together, and appointed as abbot a man named Seraphim.

And so that the monks gathered in that place might, with the Lord’s help, serve God more effectively and freely under the discipline of the holy rule, he not only restored there the property legally belonging to the aforesaid abbey, but also subjected to it other property from the aforesaid [Col. 1186D] bishopric. He also showed us a charter of foundation which he himself had confirmed with the consent of his metropolitan, Archbishop Agobard, of his suffragan bishops, of the clergy subject to him, and of certain noble laymen. In it was written at greater length that he had not only restored there the property legally belonging to the abbey already mentioned, but had also subjected to it certain property from his aforesaid bishopric.

These are their names: Pauliacum with its appurtenances; the village of Bellenavum with its appurtenances; and Arco with its appurtenances. He gave these estates, with all their dependencies and everything situated upon them—fields, meadows, woods, orchards, pastures, accessways, waters [Col. 1187A] and watercourses—and all revenues, in their entirety, together with the slaves, freedmen, and all their personal property (*peculium*), as well as the resident settlers, for the service of the monks, to possess by perpetual right.

He also gave the church situated in the village of Bellenavum, dedicated to Saint Stephen, entirely free from every customary exaction; likewise the church of the village called Danbrum with its appurtenances; the village of Danblim with its church and all its appurtenances; and the village of Trescasas with its church and all its appurtenances.

Likewise, the church of the village called Saint-Sequan, with its appurtenances; the church of the village of Morniacum with everything belonging to it; as well as the church in the valley of Verona, dedicated to Saint Maurice; and the church of the village of Beria, dedicated to Saint Lawrence [Col. 1187B], with all its appurtenances.

Moreover, in the territory of Dijon, he gave the tithes of those vineyards which Lord Amalgarius, duke and founder of this holy monastery, had donated to this church: at the village called Fiscinis, a considerable quantity of vineyards, with meadows, fields, and female servants to cultivate them; and likewise vineyards in the village of Fisciacum, and likewise in Marcennacum.

After making the donation of all these things, he earnestly implored our clemency with whatever prayers he could offer, asking that our authority might grant confirmation for the sake of firmness over the same foundation, so that the aforesaid place—which he had restored for the love of God and as an act of our almsgiving, and in which he had gathered monks who might perpetually implore the Lord’s mercy for us and for all the people subject to us [Col. 1187C]—might be confirmed by our authority.

Specifically, if it should occur to any of his successors that he wished to add other property there, he would retain the right and power to do so, subject to due discretion; but if not, his devotion [donation], made and confirmed on the advice of so many good men, would remain firm and stable by our grant.

Judging his petition worthy and reasonable, we ordered these imperial letters to be issued, by which we decree and command that the aforesaid form of organization, which the venerable Bishop Alberic established in the aforesaid place, remain inviolate; and that no rector who succeeds in that place have permission to alter the prescribed order or in any way remove the property which he restored or subjected to it [Col. 1187D]. Rather, his foundation shall remain firm and stable through this confirmation of ours.

And so that this authority of our confirmation may retain inviolable and unshaken firmness in times to come, we ordered it to be authenticated below with our ring.

**The sign of Emperor Louis.**

**The sign of Lothair, his son.**

Issued [Note: The year of the Incarnation has been added.] in the year 830 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction 7, epact 15.

[Col. 1188A]

## CLIII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF CARROF AT POITIERS. (Year 830.)

[In D. Bouquet, same place, from the cartulary of Carrof.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, emperors Augustus, by the divinely ordained providence.

If, for the love of God, we grant some benefit to places devoted to divine worship and to those serving God in them, we have no doubt that this will contribute to the stability of our empire and to the salvation of our souls. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of holy Church and to our own, present as well as future, that, at the urging of our aforesaid beloved son Lothair Augustus [Col. 1188B] and partner in our empire, by common will and equal consent, for the increase of our reward and the fruit of eternal recompense, we grant to the monastery of Carrof, situated in the county of Poitiers and built in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, where at the present time the venerable man Gunbald is known to preside as abbot, certain properties of ours situated in three places: in the county of Beauvais, an estate called Fraxindus; in the county of Reims, an estate called Dominica Villa; and in the county of Meaux, the estate of Montiniacum.

These properties written above, with their appurtenances, insofar as whatever at the present time justly and legally appears to belong to them, and is held by right of ownership and possession under our jurisdiction, we grant wholly and entirely, without exception, [Col. 1188C] with churches, houses, buildings, lands, vineyards, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, ways out and ways in, from our right into the right and power of the aforesaid venerable monastery by solemn donation. Thus, from this day and time onward, whatever the rectors and ministers of the aforesaid monastery may wish to do, dispose of, and arrange concerning the aforesaid properties or whatever legally appears to belong to them, they shall enjoy entirely free discretion to do whatever they choose.

And so that this authority of our gift may retain inviolable and unshaken firmness in times to come, we have confirmed it below with our hands and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.

[Col. 1188D]

**The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.**

**The sign of Lothair, most glorious Augustus.**

Durandus, deacon, recognized this in place of Fridugisus.

Given on the Ides of August, in the seventeenth year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most serene emperor, and the eighth of Augustus Lothair, indiction 8. Issued at the royal palace of Salmonciacum, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## CLIV. FOR THE MONASTERY OF CARROF AT POITIERS. (Year 830.)

[In D. Bouquet, same place, p. 567, from the cartulary of Carrof.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor Augustus by the divinely ordained providence [Col. 1189A].

If we willingly grant the petitions of God’s servants who strike upon our ears concerning various ecclesiastical necessities, and extend assistance so that divine power may be served more abundantly in places dedicated to God, we trust that this will undoubtedly prove advantageous to us both for passing through mortal life in time and for attaining the future life happily.

Therefore let it be known to all our faithful—namely, bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, household officials, *grafiones*, vicars, centenarii, toll-collectors, officials, our traveling envoys, and also the remaining faithful of holy Church, present as well as future—that the venerable Gunbald, abbot [Col. 1189B] of the monastery of Carrof, situated in the county of Poitiers on the river Charente and built in honor of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, sent a petition through the venerable Baldenus, a devout monk, beseeching our clemency to grant to that monastery and to the community serving God there, for the benefit of our soul, the toll from three ships which appear to travel along the river Loire, or along other rivers, and also by sea, for the uses and necessities of that community.

For the love of God and reverence for that most sacred place, we willingly assented to his prayers and ordered the benefit he requested of us to be granted to the monastery and its rectors. Accordingly, we command and strictly order all the faithful of holy Church and our own [Col. 1189C] that wherever the aforesaid three ships, which, as we have said, appear to travel along the river Loire and other rivers and also by sea, may arrive or have any landing, no one presume to receive or exact from them, or from the men responsible for their supervision, any toll, *ripaticum* [Note: [Col. 1189D] *Ripaticum*, “bank duty,” was a tax paid on riverbanks, either for maintaining the banks’ embankments, for goods displayed on the banks, or for the privilege of using the banks to transport small vessels.], *pontaticum* [Note: [Col. 1189D] *Pontaticum*, “bridge duty,” was a tax on bridges or a toll on ships passing beneath bridges.], *salutaticum* [Note: [Col. 1190D] *Salutaticum*, “duty of happy arrival,” was the right to demand greetings, gifts, or payments made beyond the prescribed census or required payment.], or any census or exaction whatsoever.

Rather, let the men responsible for supervising them travel about peacefully, conduct their business freely, and, wherever they may have access to cities, fortresses, ports, estates, or other places, or wherever they may have bought or sold anything, suffer no disturbance, detention, or opposition from anyone [Col. 1189D]. But, as we have said, let the men responsible for their supervision be permitted to go and return in every direction with complete security and tranquility; and let nothing at all, as stated, be demanded from them by any of our faithful.

And so that this authority of our command may be held more firmly and be more diligently preserved by the faithful of holy Church and by our own, we ordered it to be authenticated with the impression of our ring.

[Col. 1190A]

## CLV. FOR THE NUNNERY OF SAINT MARY AT FORUM JULII. (Year 830.)

[In Mabillon, *Annales Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, vol. II, p. 737, from a copy of the most illustrious Philippus a Turre, bishop of Adria.]

In the name of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, emperors Augustus by the divinely ordained providence.

If by a gift of our generosity we confer some assistance upon places dedicated to God, we clearly believe that this will undoubtedly contribute to the stability of our empire and to the benefit of our souls. Therefore let the experience of all the faithful of holy Church and of our own, both present and future, know that Maxentius, patriarch of the Church of Aquileia [Col. 1190B], appearing before our majesty, implored our clemency with all the prayers at his command, asking that we hand over the nunnery called Saint Mary, situated beside the basilica of Saint John, built within the walls of the city of Forum Julii, in the place called Vallis, to the aforesaid mother church of Saint Mark the Evangelist and Saint Hermachoras, martyr and bishop, where, by God’s authority, that patriarch presides. Let all your diligence know that we have done so.

Therefore, for the sake of firmness, we ordered these imperial letters of ours to be issued to the aforesaid mother church, by which we prescribe and command that the aforesaid nunnery, with the property and people justly and legally belonging to it at the present time, henceforth remain in the right and [Col. 1190C] power of the aforesaid church and its rectors. Thus, whatever the rectors and ministers of the aforesaid church may canonically wish to arrange and dispose of for its utility and advancement, they shall enjoy entirely free discretion to do whatever they choose.

And so that this authority of our gift may be held more firmly and better preserved in times to come, we have confirmed it below with our own hands and ordered it to be authenticated with the impression of our ring.

**The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.**

**The sign of Lothair, most serene Augustus.**

Durandus, deacon, recognized this in place of Fridogisus.

[Col. 1190D]

Given on the third day before the Ides of November, in the seventeenth year, with Christ propitious, of our lord Emperor Louis, most serene, and the ninth of Augustus Lothair. Issued at the royal palace of Nijmegen, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## CLVI. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SITHIU. (Year 830.)

[In Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 632.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor Augustus by the divinely ordained providence [Col. 1191A].

When we bring suitable aid to places devoted to divine worship for the love of divine service, we properly fulfill the imperial custom, and we truly believe that this will benefit us in attaining the rewards of eternal recompense. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of holy Church and to our own, present as well as future, that the monks from the monastery of Sithiu, situated in the county of Tarvanna and built in honor of holy Mary, God’s mother and ever-virgin, and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, in which the bodies of the blessed confessors of Christ Audomar and Bertin rest, and where at the present time, by God’s authority, the venerable [Col. 1191B] Fridugisus presides as abbot, presented to our view a charter of immunity of our lord and father Charles, emperor most serene and of good memory.

In it was inserted that not only he himself, but also his predecessors, namely the earlier kings of the Franks, had always held the aforesaid monastery, for the love of God and the tranquility of the brothers residing there, under their fullest protection and guardianship of immunity. But for the sake of firmness they requested that, following not only the custom of our father and predecessors who were kings, we order such a privilege of our authority to be made for that monastery as a grant of immunity and protection, but also that we determine that all the cells and estates, or other possessions, of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary and Saint Peter and Paul, and of the blessed Audomar and Bertin, situated in whatever counties and territories within the dominion of our empire, should not be divided by any of our successors or converted to other uses [Col. 1191C]; and that no person of any kind should demand *foderum* from the household of that monastery.

We willingly assented to their petitions, and so grant and confirm everything through this privilege. Therefore we admonish our successors that, just as we have granted the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary and Saint Peter and Paul, and of the blessed confessors of Christ Audomar and Bertin, to remain secure and stable, so they should permit it to remain ratified and stable; that they neither make nor permit anyone to make any division of the monasteries, cells, estates, or other possessions [Col. 1191D] situated in whatever counties or territories, nor turn those properties to other uses.

We also enact and decree by these imperial letters that no public judge, or anyone exercising judicial authority, may ever dare to enter the churches, places, fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery which it presently justly and legally possesses in whatever counties and territories within the dominion of our empire, or which divine mercy may thereafter increase in the right of that holy place, in order to hear cases according to judicial custom, exact fines, provide lodgings or provisions, demand *foderum*, take sureties, or distrain the men of that monastery [Col. 1192A], both free and enslaved; nor may anyone seek any exaction or unlawful pretext, or presume in any way to exact the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors be permitted to possess the properties of the aforesaid monastery—or, as is contained in the privilege of our lord and father, with all fines and banns granted to them—in quiet order under the protection of our immunity, so that those servants of God who serve him there may gladly beseech the Lord’s mercy continually for us and our offspring, and also for the stability of our entire empire, granted and preserved to us by God.

And so that this authority may remain unshaken in our times and in those of our successors, with the Lord’s protection, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring [Col. 1192B].

**The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.**

Durandus, deacon, recognized and subscribed this in place of Fridugisus.

## CLVII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF PRÜM. (Year 831.)

[In Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, p. 85, from the cartulary of Prüm.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor Augustus by the divinely ordained providence.

If we confirm by our edicts the things which the faithful of our empire have exchanged among themselves for their needs, we exercise the imperial custom, and we wish this to remain thereafter in law with the strongest force [Col. 1192C]. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, present as well as future, know that the venerable Marcoardus, abbot of our monastery of Prüm, brought to our serenity that he had made an exchange with a certain man named Liudold and his wife Irmbirga concerning certain properties and slaves, for their common benefit and advantage.

Accordingly, the aforesaid venerable man Marcoardus, abbot, with the consent and agreement of the brothers living in the same monastery, gave to the aforesaid Liudold and his wife Irmbirga, in the county of Speyer, in the estate or district called Mekkimheim, one church with its churchyard, curtilage, and [Col. 1192D] house, together with various dwellings around it and the slaves residing there, whose names are these: Grimbert, Rotgild, Ingirion, Liudbirga, Diutarius, Wolfarius, Willemann, Ricbert, Ricbald; ninety-five *jornales* of arable land; four and a half *jornales* of vineyards; six cartloads of hay from the meadow where hay can be gathered; and, in another place, in the estate or district called Fridolvesheim, one curtilage, seventy-three *jornales* of arable land, and a meadow yielding six cartloads.

Also, in the district of Wakkenheim, five *jornales* of vineyards in all, and one meadow situated between Altrip and Geginheim, at the bridge which Reginhard and Ekkibald held as a benefice, with their boundaries and side-lines, as is contained in the same exchanges [Col. 1193A].

In return, in compensation for these things, the aforesaid Liudold and his wife Irmbirga gave to the aforementioned abbot Marcoardus, for the benefit of his monastery of Saint Savior at Prüm, or of the rectors living in that monastery in times to come, their own properties situated in the county of Caroasco, in the estate called Huosa, namely whatever at the present time they appeared to possess in the aforesaid estate or in the district of that estate, and which was their own by right and possession, with houses, buildings, and the slaves residing upon it, whose names are these: Wulger, Wolfgoz, Raccholf, Lantfrid, Wicbolt, Beringer, Roduin, Walaburc, Adalbolt, Gomalint, Steingart, Liutgart, Ricolf, Willolf, Wieldrud, Reginfrid, Irmfrid, Guotrat [Col. 1193B], Berachtrat, Hildrat, Hordrat, Liutfrid, Liutran, Hildigart, Thiatgoz, Nitran, Gundila, Zeiza, Liutmun, Berahtran, Reginfrid, Liofgunt, Adaldrud, Rimidrud, Berahgunt, together with meadows, woods, pastures, woodland growth, waters, and watercourses—in every respect, wholly and entirely, without exception—which they transferred perpetually to the aforesaid monastery to possess.

He also declared that he had received in hand two exchanges written in identical form and confirmed by the hands of good men. But for complete security he petitioned our Highness that we should confirm those exchanges anew and more fully through a privilege of our gentleness in the name of God. We did not wish to deny his petition; rather, just as we have done for each of our faithful who petitions justly, know that we granted this to him and confirmed it in every respect [Col. 1193C].

Therefore, prescribing and commanding, we order that whatever one party has justly and reasonably transferred to the other, each shall henceforth hold and possess by the strongest legal right through this authority of ours, and that each shall enjoy entirely free discretion to do whatever he chooses with what he has received.

And so that this authority of our confirmation may retain inviolable and unshaken firmness through the course of the years, we ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

Durandus, deacon, recognized this in place of Fridugisus.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of January, in the seventeenth year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, and the ninth of Lothair, indiction 9. Issued at the royal palace of Aachen, happily in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1193D]

## CLVIII. FOR THE CELL OF BARISIACUS, SUBJECT TO THE MONASTERY OF ELNON IN THE DIOCESE OF LAON. (Year 831.)

[In Mabillon, *Acta Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, part I, fourth century, p. 67.]

In the name of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor Augustus by the divinely ordained providence.

Let it be known to all the faithful of holy Church and to our own, present as well as future, that our faithful Leo, who holds from our generosity the cell called Barisiacus, built in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, complained that the fiscal official of Barisiacus had, by force (*per fortiam* [= *vim*]) [Col. 1194A], in the time of our grandfather Pippin, taken away from the aforesaid cell a certain wood adjoining our wood called Columbarias and had joined it to our fisc.

Desiring to know the truth of this matter, we sent our envoy Haganus, a vassal, to investigate this case as an act of our almsgiving and report it to us. Carrying out our command, he found—as he reported to us—that by law and justice the said wood belonged by law to the aforesaid cell and had been taken away from it by force.

When the aforesaid vassal reported this to us, it pleased our serenity, for the increase of our reward and the fruit of eternal recompense, to restore immediately the aforesaid wood to the cell of Saint Peter named above, and to have these imperial letters issued concerning this restoration [Col. 1194B], by which we prescribe and command that no one acting on behalf of our fisc presume to take away or diminish the same wood from the aforesaid cell, or bring or inflict any claim upon the aforementioned cell; but, just as it has been restored by us and confirmed through this authority of ours, so let it remain unshaken for all time.

And so that this authority of our restoration may be held more firmly and better preserved in times to come, we ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

Durandus, deacon, in place of Fridugisus.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the seventeenth year, with Christ propitious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most serene emperor, and the eighth of Augustus Lothair, indiction 9. Issued at the royal palace of Aachen, happily in the name of God.

[Col. 1194C]

## CLIX. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT ANDREW OF VIENNE. (Year 831.)

[From the cartulary of the church of Vienne, in Baluze, *Capitularia*, vol. II, p. 1432.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor Augustus by the divinely ordained providence.

[The supplied source ends here, mid-charter.]

If we bring to completion the petitions of priests and servants of God which they have made known to us for their needs, we not only exercise royal custom but also trust that this will contribute to the blessedness of reward.
