Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, both present and future, know how the venerable man Bernard, bishop of the Church of Vienne, came before our serenity and presented to us documentary charters by which Ansemundus, his wife Ansleubana, and their daughter Remila, named Eugenia, donated and handed over the monastery of Saint Andrew the Lower to Saint Maurice; and how the aforesaid founders, for the sake of security, committed it to Saint Leonianus, and so that it might remain at all times under the power and administration of [lacuna] the bishop of the Church of Vienne and his successors, by their beneficial action. Moreover, he displayed the commands of pious kings, namely Theuderic and Guntram, by which they more firmly confirmed it to Saint Maurice for possession.

But the aforesaid Bishop Bernard reported to our Highness that the monastery itself had been taken away from that Church through the greed of wicked men. Since we judged his petition just, indeed reasonable, we restored the monastery to Saint Maurice and to Bernard, bishop of that place, by a command of our authority, for the sake of reward and the remedy of our soul and for the benefit of our whole empire, so that both he and his successors may, without anyone’s opposition, govern and dispose of the monastery according to the will of God and of blessed Maurice from this day forward, and so that it may remain under our immunity, just as the other property of Saint Maurice does.

Therefore, ordering, we command that no public judge or judicial authority ever dare enter to hear cases, exact fines, demand lodging or provisions, take sureties, distrain the men of the same monastery—both free men and slaves who appear to reside upon its land—or demand any dues; and whatever the fiscus might be able to exact from it, we grant in its entirety to the Church of Saint Maurice for eternal recompense. And so that this grant of our generosity may possess inviolable force, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of March, in the eighteenth year, Christ being favorable, of Lord Louis, most serene Augustus, in the ninth indiction. Done happily in the royal palace at Aachen, in the name of God.

[Col. 1195C]

I, Helisachar, have recognized it.

### CLX. FOR THE CORMARICIAN MONASTERY. (Year 831)

[From the cartulary of Saint Martin of Tours, in D. Bouquet, volume VI, p. 572.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

We wish it to be known to all our faithful, both present and future, that our faithful and venerable Fridugisus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin, made known to our gentleness that his predecessor, a certain Iterius, formerly abbot of the same monastery, had built from new work a certain monastery called Cormaricus [Col. 1195D] on the River Anger and had established monks there to live according to the rule of Saint Benedict; at the present time Jacob is known to be its abbot.

But because the dwellings of the brothers living there had not been built according to what the rule of Saint Benedict required, that same Fridugisus himself rebuilt those dwellings more suitably and honorably. For the adornment and dignity of the same monastery, he also had a church built there from new work, and endowed that church from the property of Saint Martin situated in the territory of Tours, namely from the estate called Mardoni (now Brunomium). For this reason he asked and entreated us to order that an authoritative document of our command be made concerning such an act. We were pleased to have it made according to his petition.

Through it we command and order that none of his successors [lacuna], namely the patrons of the same monastery, our most blessed Saint Martin, at any time or on any pretext presume to withdraw from the right of the aforesaid monastery of Cormaricus the same estate, or to diminish anything belonging to it justly; rather, in complete integrity, just as it was transferred and delivered to that monastery by the aforementioned venerable Fridugisus, let it remain in its right with perpetual stability. Whatever the abbots, brothers, and agents of the same monastery decide to do with those properties or in those properties by ecclesiastical right, let them enjoy free authority in every respect to do so.

And so that this authority of our confirmation may possess inviolable and unshaken firmness both in our time and in future ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene Augustus.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the eighteenth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the ninth indiction. Done happily in the royal palace at Aachen, in the name of God. Amen.

### CLXI. FOR EPIPHANIUS, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT VINCENT OF VULTURNO. (Year 831)

[In Chesne, *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, volume III, p. 686.]

In the name of the Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, [Col. 1196C] Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

Let it be known to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, castaldei, actionarii, vicars, centenarii, and our other faithful, both present and future, that the venerable Epiphanius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Vincent the Martyr, situated in the territory of Benevento on the River Volturno, sent to us through his representatives a certain confirmation which Lupus, formerly duke, had made for the monastery of the aforesaid Saint Vincent the Martyr concerning certain houses at Amiternum and Savinum, as well as four judgments concerning certain male and female slaves from the estate of Trita, who were attempting to withdraw themselves from their required service as though by commands of the dukes. These matters concerning the status of the aforesaid people had been conducted in the presence of Count Suppo and of the castaldei Benedict, Hilpianus, and Ansfrid, together with the other scabini.

He requested that, for the sake of security, we order an authoritative confirmation of ours to be made concerning these matters. Hearing his petition, we decreed that this command of our confirmation be made concerning the named confirmation and judgments. By it we determine and order that none of you, nor any of your successors, concerning the aforesaid places—where, according to the assertion of the aforementioned representatives, twenty-four houses are known to be situated, with an equal number of people residing in them, whose names are these: John, Theopo, another John, Cortulus, Peter, Theodobertus, Hiso, Maio, Acepertus, [Col. 1197A] Hisimundus Roppolus, Marinus, George, Halo, Audactus, Audebertus, Audoaldus, Hildulfus, Paulerissus, Robert son of Marta, with Barbano, Sico, Alaysius, Senepergas, and Gemula—presume to cause any disturbance or unjust opposition.

These people, whose status was mentioned above and who, as stated, were attempting to withdraw themselves from the required service of the aforesaid estate of Trita as though by commands of the dukes, have been restored to their former service. But let the agents and officers of the same monastery be permitted to possess peacefully the aforesaid houses with the people residing in them, as well as the slaves who were restored to required service at the estate of Trita by the authority of our father, Lord Charles, most excellent emperor. According to the need and advantage of the same monastery, let them enjoy complete freedom to do and arrange justly whatever they decide concerning those properties and people or within them, without hindrance from anyone’s opposition.

And so that this authority of our confirmation may be believed by everyone more truly and certainly and preserved more diligently, we have signed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Given on the Kalends of April, in the eighteenth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the indiction [lacuna]. Done in the royal palace, in the name of God. Amen.

### CLXII. FOR THE CHURCH OF STRASBOURG. (Year 831)

[Col. 1197C] [In Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, volume II, p. 195, from the original document in the episcopal archive of Taberna.]

[Note: An excerpt of this charter was published by Guillimannus, *On the Bishops of Strasbourg*, p. 121, and by Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, volume VIII, p. 181. La Guille, *History of Alsace*, proofs, p. 19; Bouquet, volume VI, p. 572; *Gallia Christiana*, volume V, instruments, p. 462; and Schoepflinus, *Alsatian Diplomatic Documents*, volume I, p. 74, reproduced it in full but inaccurately. We present it corrected from the original itself.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful, both present and future, that the venerable man Bernaldus, bishop of Strasbourg [Note: The city of Argentoratum is called *Strazpuruc* in a very ancient eighth-century manuscript of the abbey of Wessobrunn in Bavaria, transcribed by the most learned Christian Friedrich Pfeffel among the *Monumenta Boica*, volume VII, p. 376. The *Monumenta Boica*, comprising nine quarto volumes and compiled from charters and documents of various abbeys in the Munich tetrarchy, were published at Munich by the Electoral Bavarian Academy of Sciences, to which we were admitted by an electoral diploma dated 13 February 1777. Here we publicly acknowledge our grateful sense of this honor.] [Col. 1197D], approaching the serenity of our Highness, presented to our sight a certain authoritative document of Lord Charles, our father, most excellent Augustus [Note: The cited diploma of Charlemagne, from December 775, appears above, no. 68 [in *Patrologia Latina*, volume XCVII, column 937, among the works of Charlemagne].]. It stated [Col. 1198A] that the same Lord Charles, our father, had granted to the Church of Strasbourg, for the benefit of his soul, that wherever—through cities or villages, fortresses, crossings, or ports, except Quentowic, Dorestad, and the *clusae* [Note: See the notes to the aforesaid diploma [in the volume and column of the *Patrologia* indicated above].]—the men of the aforesaid Church traveled and returned by water or by land, that is, with carts and pack animals, for the purpose of trade, no administrator of the public authority should exact any toll from them.

For the sake of security, therefore, the same venerable Bishop Bernaldus requested that we add this authority of ours to the paternal authority. We very willingly assented to his petition and ordered this command of our authority to be made. Through it we command all counts [Note: The office of the counts was to administer justice and collect taxes and tolls; concerning these, see Schoepflin, *Illustrated Alsace*, volume I, p. 776.], vicars [Note: Vicars, or vice-counts, sat as deputies beside the count and presided over judgments in the count’s absence. The name of the vicariate still survives in Occitania under the designation *vigueries*.], centenarii [Note: Centenarii were lower judges who administered justice over a hundred households, or a *centena*. Schoepflin, *Illustrated Alsace*, volume I, p. 791. Among the Germans centenarii were called *hundreter*, just as counts and vicars were called *graven* and *schoeffen*.], and all administrators of the public authority, [Col. 1198B] or all our faithful, that none of you dare accept or exact any toll, river toll, port toll, bridge toll, *salutaticum* (a toll of uncertain kind), turf toll, wheel toll, meal toll, pasture tax, license fee, timber toll, dust toll, or any *occursus* (encounter due), any tax, or any payment from the goods which the men of the Church of Strasbourg may transport by water or land—that is, with carts and pack animals—through our kingdoms, God willing, for the purpose of trade [Note: Concerning the kinds of these tolls, see the notes to the aforesaid diploma of Charlemagne, cited page, note CXVII.]; nor presume to cause any disturbance or impediment to the men who oversee those wares.

Rather, by this authority of ours, let them be permitted to go and return freely and securely throughout our entire empire, wherever necessity requires, with ships and other vehicles, without anyone’s opposition or impediment [Col. 1198C]. And if they remain for any length of time in any place, or buy or sell anything, let absolutely no toll be exacted from them, as stated above.

And so that this authority may possess inviolable and unshaken firmness, we have ordered it to be sealed below with our seal.

I, Hirminmaris, notary, have recognized and subscribed it in the place of Fridugisus.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of June, in the eighteenth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the ninth indiction. Done happily in the royal palace at Ingelheim, in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1199A]

### CLXIII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF FABARIA. (Year 831)

[In Grandidier, cited above, p. 197, from the original document of the monastery of Fabaria, or Pfäfers in Switzerland [Note: Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, book XXX, no. 66, states that he read this diploma in a book on the antiquities of the monastery of Fabaria, written by Augustine Stoklin, abbot of Fabaria, who composed it in 1628. But Mabillon did not reproduce it.].]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained clemency, emperor Augustus.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful, present and future, that John, abbot of the monastery of Fabaria [Note: Fabarium, or Fabaria, in German Pfäfers, was founded in honor of the holy virgin Mary, Mother of God. The abbey of Fabaria owed its growth to Heddon, abbot of Reichenau and later bishop of Strasbourg. The year of its foundation must be derived from the Chronicle of Hermannus Contractus, who places it in the year 731. According to Brusch, *On the German Bishoprics*, volume I, p. 13, the monastery of Fabaria is situated near the Rhine in the Alps of Raetia, above Mariafeld. [Col. 1200D] The baths of Fabaria are also widely celebrated; D. Haller lists the writers who have written about them in *A Critical Catalogue of All Writings Concerning Switzerland*, volume II, pp. 186–209.], which was built in honor of Saint Mary in the territory of Raetia, together with his monks, made known to our gentleness, approaching the serenity of our Highness, that they had suffered such attacks, wrongs, and great losses from a certain former count named Rodericus, both he himself and his community, that they had not only been stripped of the property which God-fearing men had contributed to the monastery of the aforesaid place for the remedy of their souls, but that the same aforementioned abbot had also nearly lost all authority over his monastery.

To investigate this matter carefully and report it to us, we appointed as our envoys Bernoldus, the venerable bishop of Strasbourg, as well as Godefridus, abbot of Saint Gregory, and also Count Retharius [Note: This is an example of the royal envoys who were appointed by the king to investigate the conduct and actions of dukes, counts, and other provincial officials. Several charters of the monastery of Saint Gall, published by Goldastus in volume II of *Alemannic Writers*, part I, pp. 55 and following, provide the formulas according to which judgment was conducted by the envoys. See the excellent work of Francis de Roye, *On the Royal Envoys*, printed in 1672. An encyclical letter of the emperors Louis and Lothar, from the year 828, concerning envoys sent throughout the kingdom is found in Baluze, volume I of the *Capitularies*, column 653, and Bouquet, volume VI, p. 343.].

When they reached the aforesaid monastery according to our command and investigated with careful inquiry, they found not only—as was stated above—that the aforementioned Abbot John had lost his office in certain respects, but also that certain properties belonging to the aforesaid monastery in the territory of Chur had been removed from its authority: namely, an estate at Nezudre; five tenant holdings at Zurigos and Montanioli, with all their appurtenances; and on them a church of Saint Mary with a small estate and everything belonging to it; also the estate called Frastenestum; the church of Saint Sulpitius; a small estate and its people, with everything belonging or pertaining to it; the estate of Birmento; and land with all the properties and people belonging to the aforesaid [Col. 1200A] places.

When we learned from the report of those same envoys that this was indeed true, it pleased us to restore these properties in their entirety to the same monastery of Fabaria through this written authority of ours. By it we order and decree that these properties remain in the right of the aforesaid monastery in their entirety, and that none of our faithful presume to cause any impediment or opposition concerning them to the aforementioned Abbot John or his successors, but that everyone consent to them. Let them be permitted to hold and possess those properties peacefully.

We also command all the faithful of Holy Church, both present and future, through this command of our authority, [Col. 1200B] that no public judge, bishop, count, or anyone appointed to judicial authority exercise any power over the abbot or monks of the aforesaid monastery concerning their cases, or over their people, whether settled within or outside it; nor enter to hear cases, demand lodging or provisions, or seek any dues. Rather, let the abbot of the same monastery, with his monks and by his own authority, possess for their necessary uses the property which at the present time is evidently held by the aforesaid monastery.

And so that this authority of ours may be held more firmly, believed more truly by the faithful in future times, and observed more diligently, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.

[Col. 1200C]

Sign of Louis, emperor Augustus.

I, Hirminmaris, notary, have recognized it in the place of Fridugisus.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the eighteenth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the ninth indiction. Done in the palace at Ingelheim, in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1201A]

### CLXIV. FOR THE CHURCH OF SAINT MARTIN OF TOURS. (Year 831)

That the bishop of Tours may not presume to dominate at Saint Martin’s, and that the brothers may have free power to elect an abbot.

[In Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, volume I, p. 86, from the cartulary of Saint Martin.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

If we confer some honor upon places dedicated to God, care for the peace and tranquility of those serving God in them, and provide assistance so that they may carry out their ministry more freely, we undoubtedly believe that this will strengthen the condition of our earthly kingdom and help us attain the blessedness of eternal life. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of Holy Church and to our own faithful, both present and future, that, at the petition of the brothers who faithfully serve God in the monastery of Saint Martin, confessor and bishop of Christ, our beloved wife Judith, Augusta, represented to us through the privilege of our father, Lord Charles, emperor of pious memory and most serene, and through other royal privileges, as well as apostolic privileges, how the same monastery had until now been free from the domination of the bishop of the city of Tours, and how it had undoubtedly possessed the liberty to choose from among itself an abbot of the highest worth.

She asked the summit of our dignity that, for the love and honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and out of reverence for blessed Martin, bishop and our special patron, we should deign to confirm the same by our imperial authority. We, moved by the beneficial representation, encouragement, and intervention of our beloved wife Judith, and urged by our venerable advisers to carry this out, have drawn up and decreed to grant this confirmation of our authority to the aforesaid monastery and to the brothers serving God therein.

Through it we establish and decree that it shall remain perpetually firm that in the aforesaid monastery, or among its brothers, the bishop of the city of Tours may not presume to exercise greater domination or possess greater license to dominate than his predecessors exercised in the time of that same father of ours, Lord Charles, or of our glorious grandfather, King Pippin. Nor may he introduce anything new, or receive lodging dues [Col. 1201D] in the villages or estates; and whoever becomes successor in that city shall live with the aforementioned brothers in God in the same spirit and manner of charity and affection, without the vexation of any innovation.

Likewise, we establish without doubt and wish it to be perpetually most firm that the brothers of the aforesaid monastery have permission to choose from among themselves an abbot who can preside over them and benefit them in all moral excellence and learning in the Scriptures, [Col. 1202A] on the sole condition stated beforehand that, for as long as Abbot Fridegisus—whose advice also led us to order that this confirmation be made—holds the aforesaid monastery, he suffer no prejudice or disturbance concerning any matters whatsoever.

After his death, however, let the aforementioned brothers have the power to choose from among themselves an abbot whom they judge to be excellent in nobility of lineage, uprightness of conduct, and learning in the Scriptures. And if, which we do not wish, no such person can be found there, then we establish that the matter is to be reserved to imperial authority.

We also admonish all who will succeed us in the empire entrusted to us by God that, just as they will wish their enactments to be preserved by their successors, so they should strive to preserve this constitution in every respect and for all time, for the common salvation of themselves and of us.

And so that this command and constitutional privilege of our authority may be held more firmly and preserved better for future times, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed below with our bulla.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Hirminmaris, notary, have recognized it in the place of Fridugisus.

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of November, in the eighteenth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the tenth indiction. Done at the royal palace of Theodon’s estate, in the name of God. Amen.

### CLXV. FOR VICTOR, BISHOP OF CHUR, AND HIS CHURCH. (Year 831)

[Col. 1202C] [In Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, volume II, p. 199, from the original document in the archive of the Church of Chur [Note: This unpublished diploma was communicated by Monsieur de Jost, copied from the original itself.].]

In the name of the Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

If, for the love of God and of those serving Him in places dedicated to divine worship, we bestow greater benefits upon those places, we do not doubt that an eternal reward from the Lord will be granted to us. Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful, both present and future, that the venerable Victor, bishop of the holy Church of Chur [Note: From this it is clear that the error of Aegidius Tschudi, *Comata Gaul*, book II, part I, chapter 9, p. 316, and of Johann Jakob Leu, *Helvetisches Lexicon*, volume V, p. 263, who assign the death of this Victor to the year 825, is mistaken.], which is established [Col. 1202D] as having been built in honor of Saint Mary ever-virgin, sent a petition and entreated us to place that episcopal seat, with all that justly and legally belonged or pertained to it at the present time, under our protection and the defense of our immunity, together with its properties and dependents. Let all our people know that we have indeed done this.

Therefore, ordering, we command that no public judge or anyone exercising judicial authority dare enter the churches, places, fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid Church—those which at the present time it holds in the territory of Chur, in Alsace, and in the duchy of Alamannia, as well as what we restored to that Church by the authority of our written document [Note: See above the diploma of the Emperor Louis for the same Victor, bishop of Chur, from the year 825]—or the things which the aforesaid Church now justly and legally holds and possesses, or whatever divine mercy may thereafter cause to be added to the right of that Church, in order to hear cases according to judicial procedure, exact fines or taxes, demand provisions, take sureties, unjustly distrain the men of that Church residing upon its land, or seek any dues or illicit pretexts at any time; nor presume to exact at all any of the goods mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid bishop and his successors be permitted to hold and possess the properties of that Church, with everything justly belonging or pertaining to it, free from all disturbance by judicial authority [Col. 1203B], so that, with the congregation entrusted to him, he may more attentively delight in imploring the mercy of the Lord for us, for our wife and offspring, and for our entire empire granted to us by God.

And so that this authority may possess inviolable and unshaken firmness in our time and in future ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene Augustus.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the eighteenth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the ninth indiction. Done at Ingelheim, in the name of God. Amen.

### CLXVI. CONCERNING THE VILLAGE CALLED EPAONIS IN THE DIOCESE OF VIENNE. (Year 831)

[Col. 1203C] [In Baluze, *Capitularies*, volume II, p. 1433.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

If, for the love of God [and the saints] and out of reverence for them, we bestow suitable benefits upon places dedicated to divine worship, we clearly believe that this will undoubtedly help us attain the rewards of eternal recompense. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of Holy Church and to our own faithful, both present and future, that the illustrious Count Abbo, who voluntarily approached the serenity of our Highness, had received from our generosity, as a benefice, the village called Epaonis, which belonged to the property of Saint Maurice from the bishopric of Vienne, where Bernard is now known, by God’s favor, to be bishop [Col. 1203D]. There were churches there which had been destroyed and left without roofs, called the churches of Saint Andrew the Apostle and Saint Romanus the Martyr.

With whatever prayers he was able, he entreated our clemency [lacuna] that whatever he himself held there by benefice [lacuna] we should restore to the Church of Saint Maurice of Vienne. Let the diligence of our faithful know that we have done so [lacuna].

For the sake of security, so that the same Abbo’s holding in the aforesaid village, which at his entreaty we restored to the aforementioned Bernard, archbishop, or rather to his holy see, might be held and possessed perpetually by its rectors under ecclesiastical right, we ordered these imperial letters to be made. Through them we determine and establish that the same rectors shall hold and possess the village itself, and the properties which the aforesaid Abbo has hitherto held there, together with whatever belongs to that village and to the same churches which were dedicated there in honor and reverence of Saint Andrew the Apostle and Saint Romanus the Martyr, just as they hold the other properties belonging to the aforesaid bishopric. Let them do with them whatever they choose according to ecclesiastical right.

And so that this authority of our confirmation may possess inviolable and unshaken firmness for future ages, we have ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

I, Durandus, deacon, have recognized it in the place of Fridarius [Fridugisus] [Col. 1204B].

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of March, in the eighteenth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most serene Augustus, in the eighth indiction. Done happily in the royal palace at Aachen, in the name of Christ. Amen.

### CLXVII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF DERVES. (Year 832)

[In Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, volume II, p. 737, from the cartulary of Derves.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

If we restore a place where the monastic order once flourished by repairing its buildings, reform the same monastic life, and, from the benefits granted to us by God, contribute something through the gift of our generosity to that place, so that the servants of God living there may have some support in this mortal life, we clearly believe that this will help us both to pass this transitory life happily and to attain eternal life forever.

Therefore we wish the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, to know how the venerable Haudo, abbot of the monastery called Ders, which is established as having been built in the territory of Perthe on the River Viera, formerly called Puteolus, and dedicated in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and of Saint Bercharius, whose body rests there—and who had himself built that monastery anew and placed monks there living according to the rule of Saint Benedict—approached our serenity and made known to our gentleness that the same monastic life had been completely abolished in that place and had passed into a canonical order.

He asked and humbly entreated that, by our authority, we permit that monastic life to be reformed and that suitable dwellings for this life be repaired and adapted. As was proper, we thanked him and permitted him to do what he requested.

Moreover, so that he might carry out more effectively what he had requested, and so that the servants of God who are established or will be established to live there, having some support from our generosity, might be able to serve God more willingly, it pleased us, for the increase of our reward and the fruit of eternal recompense, to assign solemnly through this written authority of ours to the aforesaid monastery, which, as we have said, is called Ders, certain properties belonging to us, situated in the county of Breon: namely, the estate and benefice called Dodiniaca-curtis, containing twelve mansi, which our vassal named Hisimbertus is known hitherto to have held as a benefice by our generosity.

We assign it with complete integrity: with dependents of both sexes, houses, buildings, churches, cultivated and uncultivated lands, small woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, a mill, and whatever is justly and legally known to belong to the named estate and to be part of our right and proprietary possession—everything, in its entirety—on the condition that it be held and possessed in perpetual tenure by the prelates and monks serving God there.

And so that this authority of our concession and gift may possess unshaken and inviolable firmness, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the nineteenth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the tenth indiction. Done happily in the royal palace at Aachen, in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1205C]

### CLXVIII. FOR THE NEW MONASTERY OF CORBIA. (Year 832)

[In Schaten, *Annals of Paderborn*, p. 90.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence, emperor Augustus.

If we strive to provide for churches and places dedicated to divine worship through our gifts, and mercifully bestow assistance there upon those who continually serve God, we not only exercise the honorable custom of royal munificence, but also trust that, through the distribution of temporal gifts, we can earn the rewards of an everlasting recompense. Therefore, let it be known to the diligence of all our faithful, both present and future, that, for divine love and for the remedy of our soul, we have granted to the monastery called New Corbie, which we built in Saxony in honor of Saint Stephen the protomartyr [Note: [Col. 1205D] In another copy I read, “in honor of Saint Stephen and Vitus.” But the relics of Saint Vitus were brought there only after four years; hence the name Vitus may have intruded by another hand. Nor did Emperor Louis build Corbie in honor of Saint Vitus.], and which is now governed by our faithful kinsman Warinus, the first abbot appointed there, a certain fishery on the River Weser, in the district called Wimodia, adjoining a village called Luisci, in the county of Abbo. Since it is constructed in the likeness of the stakes which the inhabitants call *hocas*, it is known among the natives by the Germanic name Hoewar. It belonged to our jurisdiction, and the same Count Abbo had hitherto held it as a benefice.

But since this fishery, without the dependents assigned to its administration, could not be especially useful to the brothers of the aforesaid monastery, for that reason we grant in full and entirely to the property of the said monastery thirty-two households, and everything that the aforementioned Abbo held as a benefice belonging to that fishery, so that the monks serving there may gladly pray without ceasing to the divine mercy on our behalf.

And so that the authority of this grant may be held more firmly and, throughout future times, be more truly believed and more carefully observed by our faithful, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

[Col. 1206B]

I, Hirminmarus, notary, have authenticated it on behalf of Theogo.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the eighteenth year, with Christ’s favor, of the reign of Louis, most serene Augustus, in the tenth indiction. Done at Frankfurt, in the royal palace, successfully, in the name of the Lord. Amen.

CLXIX. FOR THE REFORM OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT DENIS. (Year 832.)

[In Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. II, p. 549.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordered providence of God, emperor Augustus.

We are urged on by divine commands and apostolic admonitions, and are also reminded by the duty of imperial government, so that we may always keep vigilant with unflagging zeal for the condition of the Church and the advancement of holy religion, and labor with the utmost necessity, fruitful purpose, and devotion; and if anything anywhere is found liable to blame, correct it through the concern of royal authority. Thus we may recall what has gone astray, cut away what is superfluous, and restore what has fallen into ruin; and, once restored and rightly established by ecclesiastical men and the successors of the Lord’s apostles under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, confirm it by imperial decrees.

For it is certainly fitting that whatever priestly dignity, illumined by the divine Spirit, has discovered for the salvation of the body of Christ, which is the Church redeemed by the blood of that same God, Lord, and Savior of ours, or has established in reformed form for the advancement of religion, imperial majesty should strive to strengthen inviolably and perpetually by the command of its power. For whatever labor has been undertaken in such matters, or whatever has been dedicated by us to pious worship, we undoubtedly believe will be especially beneficial to the kingdom of our gentleness and to the people entrusted to our rule.

Therefore, we wish it to be known to all the faithful, present and future, that after, with God’s favor, we assumed our paternal empire, it was always our foremost concern that the Church of the Lord—entrusted by divine commission to our humility to govern and protect—might flourish with fortunate success; that, insofar as it pertains to our august devotion, we might ceaselessly advance it toward better things, eradicate from it whatever was harmful, and plant within it the growth of virtues.

For this reason we very frequently took care to admonish the priests of the Lord, whose duty we knew this to be, and readily offered our principal authority as an aid to their ministry, so that, according to the will of God, they might correct without delay whatever they found worthy of amendment in the ecclesiastical orders or in any person, setting aside every negligent sluggishness and every acceptance of persons, and strive to bring it to a state of uprightness.

But when, prompted by our diligent exhortation and by their own careful vigilance concerning the condition and progress of the holy Church, the sacred orders, and those matters that appeared worthy of correction, they dealt with these issues at an assembly held at Paris by our command, they judged among other things that the monastery of the most illustrious and distinguished martyr of Christ, blessed Dionysius, and of his companions—which is known to have been dedicated to God under the name of so many martyrs and enriched with the greatest possessions by the kings of the Franks, our glorious forefathers, so that the monastic order might devoutly serve God there—needed major reform and correction. For that order had been entirely torn away from it, to the peril of many, although no necessity hindered it and no lack of resources stood in its way.

They brought this matter to the ears of our serenity both personally and through the venerable and prudent man Hilduin, the religious abbot of the aforesaid monastery, so that it might be corrected through their authority by our most pious imperial power. Accordingly, the dignity of our empire, gratefully and kindly receiving, in accordance with our customary tranquility, the most salutary admonition of such men and the very humble prayers of the same venerable Abbot Hilduin, and judging the entire matter worthy of correction, determined that the affair should be referred to those same bishops of the Churches, so that, by the authority of our principate and by the judgment of those to whom such great power had been granted by the Lord, the same order might be restored in that place without hesitation.

Accordingly, Aldric, metropolitan of Sens, came with his suffragans, as did Ebo, metropolitan of Reims, with his suffragans, to the aforesaid monastery. Having held an assembly, they first made it clear to everyone, through manifest evidence, the ancient and recent charters of the kings, the privileges of the bishops, and the donations of the faithful, that the same monastery had been built, dedicated, and endowed for the monastic order; that the order itself had flourished there until the time when, through heavenly grace, our clemency assumed the imperial scepters, and had continued there, however imperfectly, under the leadership of the aforesaid Abbot Hilduin.

Next, they conducted a careful inquiry into those who had made the regular profession in that place. Some of those who had made that same profession, having become deserters from their undertaking, had already departed from human affairs; their perdition cannot be borne without great anguish of heart. Others falsely claimed that they had not made the same profession; but, openly convicted by witnesses, they were subjected to canonical penance for their defiance.

Still others—indeed, the greater part—who had until then fallen into apostasy, came forward, prostrated themselves on the ground, and confessed that they had regularly promised to make the same profession in that place. They humbly begged that they might be shown mercy and that the Lord might grant them forgiveness for so great an offense. After making this confession, in the presence of the assembly of bishops and the other priests, and of the entire clergy of the order that followed them, while a considerable crowd of noblemen and others stood around, they clothed themselves in the cowls of their undertaking. And together they repeated their regular profession, lest at any time, as had already happened to themselves and others in that place, they should be driven by diabolical impulse from the purpose of their holy profession.

Finally, a certain portion of them—namely, those who, moved by the gift of divine inspiration and bound by love to the purpose and habit of holy religion, had chosen with exceptional firmness to remain in it without any resistance or interruption, and who, after the others had abandoned the monastic life and habit, had continued to live in the cell of the same greater monastery until this synod convened at our command—came before the aforementioned venerable fathers. They asked that the former place, in which they had made their promise and had lived according to the rule, though less perfectly, be restored to them and that they themselves be restored to that place.

Their removal had occurred for the following reason. As we said earlier, as soon as divine favor had willed that we, having received the paternal seat, should lean upon the imperial scepters, the concern of our pious intention took care that the religion, dignity, and every form of good order begun and established by our lord and father, Charles, of divine memory, should plainly and truly, with all pretense removed, remain and flourish in each of its proper orders.

For the correction of the monastic institution according to its rule, we therefore appointed two religious men of venerable life, the abbots Benedict and Arnulf, who, throughout our empire—governed and preserved by God—might diligently and zealously attend to this matter.

These good and devout, but exceedingly simple, fathers, led astray by the cunning and harshness of the aforementioned brothers and by their own simplicity, deceived those who had remained steadfast in the salvation they had professed and removed them from the monastery—not through deliberate intent, but through inadequate careful and necessary investigation and foresight—and placed them in the aforementioned cell. But those who had sought the desires of their own will, not through virtue but through cunning, and who, having cast off from their necks the strap beneath the yoke of the Rule and, freed for a more lax life, attempted to seek the heavenly homeland by a broader road, they left in the dwellings of the venerable habit and monastic life.

Yet these fathers, more commendably, complied with the worthy petition of the brothers whom we have said remained steadfast in the strength of their religion, acting with the authority of the Church; for this was what our assent and command had ordered. They therefore satisfied the matter reasonably and canonically. And, because it had been suggested that our exalted attention should be informed how and in what manner so devout an act had been carried out by those most religious men, they produced two documents on this matter, identical in legal form and wording, and confirmed them with their own hands. One of them was to be preserved in the archive of the monastery itself, for the remembrance and stability of this order there in future times; the other they sent to our greatness, so that we might order it to be deposited in the palace archives as a memorial and perpetual confirmation of this duly accomplished act.

But when, with God’s approval, the same order was proceeding happily in that place, insofar as it could be divinely perceived, the ancient enemy of human salvation used some of the brothers themselves as his instruments and so agitated them with the fury of his snares that, after forming a conspiracy and oath-bound plot, they renounced the monastic undertaking and, without the permission of their abbot, their own bishop, or their metropolitan, approached the representatives of our dignity. They dared to bring to the ears of our serenity a grievance concerning this matter, contrary to canon law and to the institution of their own undertaking.

They presented us with a written volume accusing and blaspheming the bishops who, through their paternal concern and by our authority, had corrected them in the apostasy in which they were involved and had persuaded them to return to the undertaking they had abandoned. They also added in the same document other matters that were not worthy of being inserted in our imperial writings.

Our vigilance, having heard their complaints, ordered through our clemency the aforementioned venerable man Hilduin to command those same bishops against whom they complained, as well as others free from accusation, to come to the monastery itself at our command.

And because the brothers had sent their loud cries to our attention, from which it is not lawful to depart without an unambiguous and duly determined judgment, we ordered the matter to be reexamined through the careful inquiry of several bishops, canonically determined, and brought to rest—not because we doubted in any respect the judgment of the aforementioned fathers, which was entirely known to our excellence, but so that a greater triumph might be won for Christ the Lord our God over the conquered enemy who had stirred up the aforesaid brothers, and so that the same order might be confirmed in that place more firmly because it had been reaffirmed.

And since any accusation brought before our imperial dignity against the shepherds of the Church could not be erased without a definite and reasonable judgment, they came at the appointed time and day to the monastery mentioned above. The written document which the accusers had brought before our clemency was produced in their presence, and they proved, through true assertions and suitable witnesses, that everything they had said or written in their accusation was false, as is shown in detail by the written record.

Because of this matter, a copy was sent from the second synod of our constitution to the archive of our palace, together with documents containing the names of the witnesses who had been present at both assemblies, so that a record of the proceedings might be preserved. Another copy is also retained in the archives of the monastery itself.

Afterward, the brothers themselves, when divine providence had touched their hearts in the course of time, became devoted executors of their vigorous undertaking and penitents for their former negligences. With salutary and prudent agreement, they drew up three documents: one was to be placed at the head of the most glorious martyrs of Christ; another was entrusted to be kept under the protection of our royal authority; and the third was to be held by the abbot of the monastery itself.

In these documents they professed that they wished to observe the rule set down by the blessed father Benedict under the instruction of the Holy Spirit. Each of them confirmed the same documents below with his own name, rank, and designation as a monk. They presented one of them to our benevolent presence, humbly requesting—as the aforementioned venerable fathers, by whom the synodal decisions had been made, had also earnestly petitioned our authority—that we confirm by the privilege of our greatness and by imperial writings what had been discovered through such subtle and careful investigation, determined by just reasoning, restored through salutary restitution, and established by canonical authority.

Thus, what canonical authority teaches, and what is demonstrated by the vows of all the kings and faithful who enriched that place with their possessions so that the monastic order might be preserved there—since it cannot be removed from that place without danger to both king and kingdom—might be safeguarded by our imperial power through confirmation. The same order should not be deprived of that place in our own and future times; rather, with Christ the Lord’s generosity, it should remain there, flourish, and prosper through fortunate success, for the increase of our reward, and that of our wife and offspring, and for the salvation of those whose restoration was accomplished after so great a fall, as well as of those through whom, with God’s approval, that restoration was carried out by our authority. It should also serve as instruction for those who, inspired by the Lord, will later gather at that place for the monastic order. With every pretense removed, let the regular order always remain in the same monastery, flourish, and, with God’s help, grow strong in blessed success.

And so that this authority, which we have established for the love of God, for the salvation of the soul of our wife and offspring, as we have said, and for the stability of our empire, may possess firmer force and remain unshaken thereafter, we ordered two confirmations to be written in identical form. One was to be preserved under the palace guards in the repository of the imperial court; the other was to be carefully maintained forever by the custodians of the monastery itself. We confirmed them below with the subscription of our hand and ordered them to be sealed with our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Hirminmaris, notary, have examined and subscribed on behalf of Theoto.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, in the nineteenth year, with Christ’s favor, of the reign of Lord Louis, most serene emperor, in the tenth indiction. Done at the monastery of Saint Denis, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1211A]

CLXX. FOR THE DISTRIBUTION OF THE PROPERTY OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT DENIS. (Year 832.)

[In Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, p. 408.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordered providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If we confirm by our decrees what the faithful of our empire have established faithfully and devoutly, for the condition and usefulness of the Churches and the servants of God, in the places entrusted to them, out of love for God, we undoubtedly believe that this will remain for us unto eternal blessedness and for the protection of the entire kingdom entrusted to us by God; and we trust that the Lord, who recompenses, will reward us for it in the future.

Therefore, let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own, present and future, that the venerable man Hilduin, abbot of the monastery of the Prince of the Apostles and of the most illustrious martyrs of Christ, Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, who appear to be our particular patrons, informed our serenity that, for the love of almighty God and to guard against future danger to the same community, lest through the negligence or parsimony of any of his successors the monastic order there should be disturbed in future times, as it is clearly known to have happened in earlier times—as the synodal documents concerning the restoration of this holy order in the same monastery, the confirmation of our imperial authority, and the charter of the aforesaid venerable Abbot Hilduin fully relate in detail (which we have omitted here because it is clearly and exactly set down in those same places, as almost everyone’s knowledge attests)—he had established and assigned the provisions which they were to receive annually for food, as well as certain villas specifically to serve their needs; and, by the wording of a letter and by a written record of his grant, confirmed by his own hand and those of other good men, he had conceded and assigned them these things, so that none of his successors might in future, on any pretext or for public service, impose an impediment upon them that would force them to stray from the path of rectitude and regular observance. Rather, content with the property and provisions assigned to them, they might observe the regular norm without necessity or want and, without transgression, keep it as far as human weakness permits.

For this reason he humbly asked our exalted dignity to order, for the sake of divine regard and in reverence for those saints, that a precept of our authority be issued concerning this same constitution, so that it might thereafter remain stable and inviolate.

We, listening to his petition because it was necessary and reasonable, adjudged that it should be done as he had requested.

Therefore, we establish and command, according to what is contained in his arrangement, that every year there be given to them, for their use and for that of guests coming to the refectory, two thousand one hundred *modii* of pure wheat. For the provision of the servants who attend them, nine hundred *modii* of rye; of pure wine, for them and the guests mentioned above and for all their needs, two thousand five hundred *modii*; thirty *bracia* of beer, of twelve *modii* each; and, besides these, three *bracia* of spelt beer, of thirty *modii* each, according to custom.

Between Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, and the Mass of Saint Dionysius: three hundred *modii* of legumes; three hundred and thirty pounds of cheese; thirty-five *modii* of fat; two hundred *modii* of salt, measured by the same *modius* in which payment is made at the saltworks.

For making their leather shoes and sandals: two hundred portions of grease. Of butter: thirty *sextarii*. Of poultry, between Easter and the Nativity of the Lord, from the villas—as it is written in the charter of the constitution of the aforementioned venerable man—everything in full, which over the course of the year is to be supplied from all those resources according to the terms in which it is written and arranged there, together with the render in poultry which is due from the mills and *cambae*, as has long been customary, whether those estates have been held as demesne or granted as benefices. We establish and confirm that these things are to be given.

We have also decreed by imperial confirmation that soap from those villas, as it is established in the aforementioned confirmation of the same man, is to be supplied for the use of the brothers.

Of wood, let them be given eleven hundred measures called *midi*; honey, according to custom; two wagonloads of *tribillum*; sixteen *modii*; vegetables; tree fruits; pitch; carpenters; hoops for preparing wine vessels; and coverings for roofs. The construction and restoration of workshops, according to what is contained in the aforesaid document of the aforementioned honorable man, shall likewise be supplied and carried out as necessity dictates.

For the provision of clothing and all their needs according to the regular institution, we confirm to them the same villas which he appears to have granted to them by his concession: Murnum, as it was anciently called, now the Cell of Saint Denis; Tosonisvalley with Flaviacum and all its appurtenances, except Temeriacum Court; the Cell of Saint Martin on Mount Jocundiacum, in its entirety; the Villa Prataria with all its appurtenances; Pratariola with Sichaldicourt and everything belonging to it; Upper Nucitum with its appurtenances; Francorum-villa; Maflare; half of Baliolum; Mucella; Bedolitum; Villare; Wascon-villa, in its entirety and with all its appurtenances; and all the toll and customary payment which is accustomed to come from the annual market on the feast of Saint Dionysius, just as our lord grandfather Pippin, of good and blessed memory, gave them by his own precept, whatever the fisc could exact from it.

Likewise, Trimlidum and Painted Villa, in their entirety and with all their appurtenances; Greater Villa, in its entirety; in the same settlement, two *mansi*; and a small dwelling on Mount Sautia with its adjacent lands.

Across the Seine, the Chapel of Saint Audoenus, for repairing or arranging fishing nets, with one *mansus* at Bonogilum in its entirety; in Auvergne, two *mansi*; and at Campiniacum, two *mansi* for fishing.

Villa Exona with its customary payment and in its entirety; also the *mansi* and vineyards at Belna which the Frankish men of that community assigned to the brothers; likewise at Vanicolas, as is contained in the aforementioned document; also the customary payment from the *venna* situated on the River Loch, and from the district of Pontiu; and the payment from Flanders, as was customary.

The villa called Brinevalley; also the mares and the fishery at Tellis, in their entirety, both in customary payment and in their appurtenances; and *mansi* at Bracium; and Gabaregium in Bagasinum, in its entirety and with its appurtenances, some of which lie in the district of Coutances for the catching of large fish.

These villas, therefore, with their appurtenances, revenues, and dependents, and with everything which people retain from them by lease or by benefice, are to revert after their death to the use of the brothers and the provisions mentioned above. By imperial authority and favor, through this precept of our confirmation, and just as the aforesaid venerable abbot confirmed in his constitution, we grant and confirm them to the brothers of the same community under stable right for their particular needs.

We command that none of the abbots, in succession, dare withdraw or diminish what he established by salutary counsel and what has been strengthened by our decree, turn it to his own use, or grant any part of it to anyone as a benefice. Nor may he exact services from these villas, receive post-horses or expenses for the reception of guests, or exact from them any charges or lodging dues for any matter without unavoidable necessity, except for the customary labor services described on the page of the aforementioned man’s constitution; no one may ever presume to add anything to them.

The foregoing provisions have been arranged for a total of one hundred and fifty monks. No abbot shall ever be permitted to subtract anything from them. If anyone should wish to increase their number, let him accumulate resources for their use and increase the worshipers of the divine service.

But if anyone should presume to act otherwise and, after our departure, wish to violate this confirmation which we have made concerning the constitution of the aforesaid venerable man Hilduin, let the complaint come before our successors who at that time survive us. Once they have recognized our authority, let them defend the provisions of our constitution and confirm them by a precept of their own authority, just as, with God’s favor, they will wish their successors to defend and confirm what they themselves have rightly done. Thus, in future times, the brothers in the aforesaid monastery, observing the rule of blessed Benedict, may serve God freely and without disturbance; and may a reward proportionate to this confirmation be repaid to us in everlasting eternity.

We have also earnestly and most devoutly urged all our successors, by almighty God, by the love of eternal recompense, and by reverent devotion toward these special protectors of ours in this holy place, to preserve inviolate this confirmation of the constitution which we have strengthened by imperial authority for the provision of the monks’ regular needs.

Let them also take special and diligent care that, through the cunning efforts of the ancient enemy, the sacred order is not removed from that place, or proceed there less perfectly than human weakness permits because negligence has prevailed. Rather, just as we too appear to have singular concern for it—just as our predecessors and forebears of exalted dignity are known to have had such concern, a concern embraced there by the pious memorial of their buried bodies—so let them also show concern for it with divine regard. Let them take care not to entrust the most sacred place to rulers whose cunning or negligence would cause religion to decline there and want or sluggish negligence to increase. Rather, let them treat that most sacred place with such careful piety that, with Christ’s help, the glory of eternal blessedness may remain and increase for us and for them.

And so that this authority, which we have established for the love of God and for the remedy of our soul, may possess firmer force and remain unshaken thereafter, we have confirmed it below with the subscription of our hand and ordered it to be sealed with our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Hirminmaris, notary, have examined and subscribed on behalf of Theoto.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, in the nineteenth year, with Christ’s favor, of the reign of Lord Louis, most serene emperor, in the tenth indiction. Done at the monastery of Saint Denis, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

CLXXI. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MARTIN OF TOURS. [Col. 1214C] (Year 832.)

[From the Chartulary of Saint Martin, in Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, vol. I, p. 29.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordered providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If we confer some honor upon places dedicated to God, care for the peace and tranquility of those who serve God in them, and provide assistance so that they may carry out their ministry more freely, we undoubtedly believe that this will help strengthen the stability of our kingdom and attain the blessedness of eternal life.

Therefore, we wish it to be made known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own, present and future, that the venerable Abbot Fridegisus of the monastery of our patron Saint Martin, who himself rests there bodily, informed our exalted dignity that, partly through ignorance and partly through the suggestion of certain men, he had granted as benefices to certain servants of his certain villas belonging to the same monastery, which had formerly been assigned for the use of the brothers living in that monastery. As a result, he could not fully provide them with clothing and the necessary expenses.

For this reason, he himself and the entire community of Saint Martin requested that an authority in the form of our written document be given to them, by which, with every pretext removed, the same abbot might, by our grant and permission, recall those villas into his own domain, and both he and his successors might supply the brothers with the provisions and clothing owed to them in the same manner in which they had been supplied in the time of his predecessors to the brothers who then lived there.

We most willingly assented to their petition and determined that this authority in the form of our written document should be made and given to those same brothers. By it we decree and command that the aforementioned abbot and his successors should hold those same villas for this purpose, and under this arrangement and administration: from them they are to cause food and clothing to be supplied fully to the brothers who now serve God there and to those who will serve him there in future, in the same way in which these were provided and supplied to them in the time of our father Charles by Wulfadus and Itherius, abbots of this monastery.

Concerning the other villas that have been granted as benefices, we command that one third of the poultry, together with the eggs, be supplied to those same brothers.

We also wish and grant to those same brothers—both those who now live there and those who in future wish to gather there to inhabit the place and serve God—that from everything which God-fearing people contribute to the tomb of our most blessed patron, Saint Martin, they may receive one third for meeting their needs, except for the clothing and articles among these gifts which, for the sake of the dignity and decorum of his tomb, are to be retained there permanently.

We decree that wax and oil for preparing the lights in the same church are to be retained.

Therefore, by this authority of ours, we establish and command that none of the prelates or administrators of this monastery of our most blessed patron Saint Martin presume to tear down or in any way alter this grant and these statutes of ours. Rather, let them preserve them inviolate forever and ensure that they are preserved.

And so that this authority of our grant and constitution may possess firm and inviolable force, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked, according to our custom, with the seal of the bull.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Hirminmarus, notary, have authenticated it on behalf of Theoto.

Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the nineteenth year, with Christ’s favor, of the reign of Louis, most pious Augustus, in the eleventh indiction. Done at Tours, at the monastery of Saint Martin, successfully, in the name of God.

CLXXII. [Col. 1215D] [Note: [Col. 1215D] Labbe mentions this precept, but incorrectly assigns it to the year 833 in *Miscellanea Curiosa*, p. 457. Cointius refers to it in vol. VIII of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, p. 185, under the year 831, from whose September the tenth indiction began; here he also reckons the beginning of Louis’s reign from the year 813.] FOR THE GREATER MONASTERY. (Year 832.)

[From the chartulary of the same monastery, in D. Bouquet, *Collection of Historians*, vol. IV, p. 583.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordered providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If, out of love for him by whose gift we have been placed above other mortals, we raise up places consecrated to divine worship through benefits befitting our munificence, so that divine worship may be carried out there more abundantly, we faithfully believe that we shall be rewarded by the Lord with the prize of worthy recompense.

Therefore we wish it to be known to the diligence of all our faithful, both present and future, how our beloved wife Judith Augusta petitioned us that we should grant, by the authority of our written charter, a certain estate named Cambon, which is in the county of Blésois or Dunois, to the monastery of Saint Martin, built in the county of Tours on the bank of the Loire and called the Major Monastery, in which that most illustrious confessor of Christ regularly served the Lord with a company of monks, for the purchase of clothing for the brothers serving God there. [Note: Thus it is read in the chartulary; *concederemus* should be read instead of *concedimus*.]

Accordingly, they produced before us an instrument of our presence, showing how long ago a certain woman consecrated to God, named Oda, wife of Duke Eudo, had donated the same estate, with its dependencies, to the aforesaid monastery by a deed of sale. We willingly assented to her petition because of the love, honor, and veneration owed to our aforesaid most blessed patron Saint Martin. We therefore donate and hand over the aforesaid estate of Cambon—which, as we have said, is situated in the aforementioned county of Blésois or Dunois—with the small estates known to belong to it, namely Galliacum, Bitarilias, Varennes, Cultures, the estate of Aitard, and also with its boundaries and everything belonging to it: basilicas, houses and other buildings, vineyards, woods, lands, meadows, fields, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, cultivated and uncultivated places, movable and immovable property, and property capable of moving itself, together with male and female slaves and dependants of various sexes and ages, to the aforesaid monastery of the venerable confessor of Christ Saint Martin, which, as we have said, was built in the aforesaid county of Tours on the bank of the Loire.

At the present time the venerable Abbot Theoto is known to be pastor and rector of the congregation serving God there. Through this authority of our largition we give and hand over the estate on the following condition: that it shall remain in perpetuity under the right of that monastery, for the purchase—as we have stated—of clothing for the brothers serving God there. None of our faithful, nor, by God’s arrangement, any of our successors, shall have the power to withdraw or diminish from the right of that monastery the same estate or anything known to belong to it. Rather, as has been inserted above, the aforesaid congregation and their successors shall have the power, for the purpose we have stated, to do, arrange, exact, dispose of, and administer, both now and in future, whatever can in any way be exacted from the same estate and its dependencies.

Moreover, if any of the faithful of our empire should wish to add or assign anything to them for the needs of this matter, we wish that no one be permitted to take it away from them, so that they may more freely delight in imploring the Lord’s mercy for the salvation of ourselves and our successors. And so that the authority of this donation and transfer may possess perpetual and inviolable force, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.**

I, Hirminmarus, notary, have examined this document on behalf of Theoto.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the nineteenth year, Christ being gracious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the tenth indiction. Done at the estate of Caduppa, prosperously in God’s name. Amen.

## CLXXIII. For the Abbey of Saint Vincent at Le Mans (832)

[In Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. I, p. 84.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

We wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own, present and future, how information came to us concerning three cells, one of which is situated within the walls of the city of Le Mans and dedicated in honor of Saint Albinus, while the other two are built in the suburb of the aforesaid city, one dedicated in honor of Saint Vincent and the other in honor of Saint Audoenus. At the present time Bishop Aldric possessed them under the jurisdiction of the aforesaid city, though it had been alleged that they ought to belong not to that city by right, but to our public domain.

To investigate this matter carefully through the better and more truthful men residing throughout the area around the aforesaid city, and to report it to us, we sent our faithful man named Wido. When he had returned to us, he reported that, according to the testimony under oath of good men living around the boundaries of the aforesaid city, he had discovered the matter to be as follows: the aforesaid cells did not belong to our public property, but ought justly and lawfully to remain under the jurisdiction of the aforesaid church of Le Mans.

When we had learned from the report of our aforesaid faithful Wido that this was entirely true, and wishing completely to repel and remove future pretexts and disputes, it pleased us to have this written record of our authority and remembrance drawn up concerning the matter. By it we order and command that, with all public and judicial authority entirely excluded, the aforesaid cells shall perpetually remain under the jurisdiction of the aforesaid church of Le Mans; and that the aforementioned Bishop Aldric and his successors shall hold, possess, and control them according to ecclesiastical law, and shall do with them whatever they decide ought to be done for the advantage or benefit of the aforesaid church of Le Mans. And so that this written enactment of our authority might be regarded as more secure, believed more readily by our faithful, and preserved more diligently, we ordered it sealed below with our ring.

I, Hirminmarus, notary, have examined and subscribed this document on behalf of Theoto.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the eighteenth year, Christ being gracious, of the reign of Louis, most pious Augustus, in the tenth indiction. Done at the city of Le Mans, prosperously in God’s name. Amen.

## CLXXIV. For the Same Abbey of Saint Vincent (832)

[In Baluze, at the same place.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If we kindly and willingly lend an ear to the petitions of priests whenever they wish to bring some matter before us concerning their own needs or those of the churches entrusted to them, and bring their just and reasonable petitions to the desired result, then in this we not only exercise royal and imperial custom but also make those same priests more ready and devoted to entreat the Lord’s mercy for us.

Therefore we wish it to be known to the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, how, when we were returning from Aquitaine and had reached the city of Le Mans, the venerable Aldric, bishop of that city, approached us and reported concerning an estate called Brogilus and also Novavilla. Many years earlier it had been taken away from the right of that church, together with its dependencies and everything belonging to it, and transferred to our public property; at the present time it was possessed as a benefice by Herembert, our vassal. Thus, at an earlier time, the same estate, with its dependencies and everything belonging to it, had slipped from the hands of the rulers of the aforesaid city.

When we sent our faithful men, Simon the priest and venerable abbot and Hildemannus, our vassal, to investigate the truth of the matter more carefully, they reported to us that it was entirely true. When we learned from their report that the aforesaid benefice of Herembert justly belonged not to our public property but to the right of the aforesaid church of Le Mans, it pleased our clemency that the aforesaid benefice of Herembert—namely, the forest called Gauciacum, together with the two small forests called Dovera and Tulpiacus, with the buildings constructed in it, called Brolius, and also Novavilla with everything belonging to it, namely Salvaria, Colonica, Cauqueriolas, the estate of Herilavan, Fetrarias, the farmstead of Saviniacum, Buxarias, one chapel at Monticelli with everything belonging to it, half a mansus at Caliniacum, one mansus at Vincaria, and at Cipidus and Belinus those whom they call horse-keepers (*jumentarii*), together with the census payment which they are known to pay each year, namely honey and wax, and at Cabanidum those whom they call swineherds (*porcarii*), and those known to dwell in that clearing which lies toward the east, as well as those known to reside beside the river called the Sarthe, likewise half the toll which is paid annually from that port—

just as the aforementioned Herembert was to return the aforesaid benefice in its entirety to the aforementioned venerable Bishop Aldric, for the benefit of his aforesaid church, as it was under the jurisdiction of our rule on the day when he is known to have received that benefice from our largition, for the benefit of our soul; so that it might perpetually belong to the uses and advantages of that church and of those serving God in it.

Therefore, at the suggestion and request of the aforesaid venerable bishop, we ordered this precept of our confirmation and restitution to be made for him and for the aforesaid city. By it we decree and command that none of our faithful shall at any time presume to cause the aforementioned venerable Bishop Aldric or his successors any disturbance or bring any accusation against them concerning the aforesaid estate or any of all those things known to belong to the places mentioned above. Rather, he and his successors shall be permitted peacefully to hold and possess the aforesaid places, with everything belonging to them, according to ecclesiastical law, and shall have full freedom in every respect to do whatever they decide should be done for the opportunity and benefit of the aforesaid church.

And so that this authority of ours may possess perpetual firmness, we ordered it sealed with our ring.

I, Hirminmarus, notary, have examined and subscribed this document on behalf of Theoto.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the seventeenth year, Christ being gracious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the tenth indiction. Done at Bes, prosperously in God’s name. Amen.

## CLXXV. For the Same Abbey of Saint Vincent (833)

[In Baluze, at the same place.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If we confer some honor upon those who render the service owed to God, and assist them so that they may carry out their ministry more freely, we confidently believe that this will undoubtedly help to strengthen the condition of our earthly kingdom and to attain the blessedness of eternal life.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, that when we were returning from Aquitaine and had reached the city of Le Mans, which the venerable Bishop Aldric appears to govern, the clerics and servants of God residing there came into our presence and complained that our faithful who possessed the property of Saint Gervasius as benefices either paid negligently, or entirely delayed paying, the ninths and tenths from which they ought to have their necessary expenses. They asked and humbly entreated us that our imperial power should ensure that, according to the ancient custom and command of our lord and father, the most excellent Augustus Charles, as well as our own, the ninths and tenths from the same property should be fully and without any delay paid to the aforesaid church of Saint Gervasius and to the brothers residing there, and that the buildings of that church, the episcopal house, and the dwellings of the brothers living there should be repaired and restored. [Note: See Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 157, and Book II, chapters 21 and 22.]

Moreover, they humbly and earnestly requested that we order the names of the estates from which the ninths and tenths ought to be paid to the aforesaid church to be written individually into our authoritative precept, so that in future these estates or properties might not be alienated from the right of that church through evil cunning, any deceit, or the power of some rich or powerful person, and so that the ninths, tenths, census payments, or restorations of the aforesaid church might not be taken away.

We willingly heard their petitions out of love for God, and, as they requested, we ordered the monasteries, cells, villages, and estates which our faithful are known to hold by our largition from the right of the aforesaid church to be individually inserted into this precept, so that in future they might remain in their entirety under the right and dominion of the aforesaid church. They are as follows:
