The monastery of Saint Peter, which Bishop Bertran built, together with the small monastery of Saint Martin at Ponteleuve; the small monastery of Saint Victurius, in which that lord Victurius rests bodily; the small monastery of Saint Mary, built between the city wall and the river Sarthe, together with the small monastery of Saint Ricomerus beyond the river Sarthe belonging to it; the monastery of Saint Scholastica; the small monastery of Saint Germanus beyond the river Sarthe; the small monastery or hospice of Saint Mary, in which Lord Paduinus rests bodily; the cell of Saint Victurius within the city; the monastery of Saint Carilefus, in which that lord rests bodily; the small monastery of Saint Julian, in which he rests bodily; the monastery of Saint George; the monastery of Illidi; the monastery of Tussiacum; the monastery of Saint John and Saint Trechius at Buxiolum; the small monastery of Saint Martin at Diablenticum; the monastery of Saint Mary at Aurionnum; the monastery of Buxidum; the cell of Semiliacum; and the monastery of Calado.

All these, together with everything belonging to them, as we have carefully investigated and found in the authentic documents of Saint Gervasius, justly and lawfully belong to the aforesaid church of Saint Gervasius. Therefore we command that on the feast days of those saints in whose memorials the monasteries themselves are known to be dedicated, each year the census payments from them shall be willingly paid to the aforesaid mother and city church by those who hold these monasteries by our benefaction, for the use of the bishop and the brothers residing there and for the restoration of the church, both now and in future. The abbot who at that time is seen to possess each monastery shall also willingly provide an excellent meal for the canons of Saint Gervasius on the aforesaid feast day, if they wish to have our favor and those benefices themselves.

Thus neither we nor our predecessors or fathers shall suffer any loss or danger to the kingdom through the removal or diminution of these properties from the aforesaid church; rather, they shall remain forever under the jurisdiction of that church.

[Note: The word *Divitis* is corrupt.] *Divitis* [corrupt]: for all the canons and baptismal churches residing in the parish of the aforesaid city, whatever their jurisdiction may be, we command that all census payments, whether in oil, wax, or money, be paid in full each year to the aforesaid church, as they are contained in the full registers and summaries of the same mother church, without any refusal or delay.

With regard to the public villages, private villages, or small estates of the aforesaid church which our faithful hold by our largition, we command absolutely that the ninths and tenths be willingly and fully paid by those same faithful to the aforesaid mother church, and that they cause the buildings of that church, or of the houses belonging to it within the city, to be rebuilt or restored. These are: the estate of Tavida; the estate of Lugdunum; the estate of Baladon; the estate called Brogilus or Novavilla; the estate of Pradellis; Murniacum; the estate of Guilis; one third of the cell of Saint Almirus; one third of the cell of Saint Ulfacius; one third of the cell of Saint Rigmirus; the estate of Boulidum; Angonum; Solemnis Villa; and the village and cell of Virmerus; the estate of Apiliacum; Aldrinum; Clausidum; Noviliacum; Fanisnonia; Campus Sigiricus; Luciacum; Mons; the cell of Saint Leodegarius at Commis; Angor; Boulir; Vinogabron with its dependencies; the public village of Ailinum; the public villages of Bruslor and Sogonna; Silviacum; the estate of Viliacum; Tricionum; Silgiacum; Sabololium; the public village of Vinonium; the long estate; the estate of Campaniacum; Tonedralium; the public villages of Geneda; the estate of Didas; Tredentum; Vitlena; Taurimiacum; Calsanum; the estate of Verno; Adillanitae; Vigra; Fontana; Sanmurum; Brafialum; Folcaria; Domnoiorium; part of Fraxinidum; Mandaria; Dirigetum; the estate of Verno; Clermicium; Camiliacum; Traximaria; the public village of Coxiacum; the estate of Antoniacum; the estate of Bonalfa; all the estates belonging to the cell of Saint Martin within the city walls; the public village of Caugiacum; the estate of Limbriacum; Verincella; Verniacum; the estate of Ferciacum; Ponciacum; Cariliacum; Priliacum; Vigra; the benefice of Hadingus; the estate and valley of Bovo; Breviacum; Carbonaria; Ruiliacum; Sidregum; the port of Paciacum on the Garonne; Gaurecum; the cell called Longolin; Gajurecum; Florecum; the village of Diablenticum; the cell of Arciaca; the estate of Camariacum; Eviriaco; Calla; Commoriacum; the estate of Andoliacum; the estate of Griniacum; Martiniacum; Liverola; Sisciacum; the cell of the King’s House; and the county of Ardun, in which are the inhabited estates of Saint Gervasius; the farm of Busana; Noviomum; Scomoiacum; Camiliacum; Comacum; Corma; Noviomor; and the public villages of Bostiliacum.

All these things which have been individually inserted above, as has already been stated, we have investigated with greater clarity and care, and, notwithstanding the clerics themselves, have found in the authentic writings of that church to belong justly and lawfully to it. We have also found that other estates, which because of the length of the list or ignorance of the estates’ names have not been inserted into this precept, likewise belong justly and lawfully to the aforesaid church.

Concerning these matters we have decided that these letters of our authority should be made. By them we decree for all who at the present time or in future have obtained, or may obtain, benefices from the aforesaid mother church: we command that from all the produce of the land, both hay and grain of every kind, both from their own domain and from that of their vassals; from fishponds and gifts; from pasturage and pasture dues; from grazing rights and young animals; from fisheries and pannage, that is, from mast-feeding; from honey; from the produce of gardens; from the feeding of animals and the cheeses that are made; from demesne cow-pastures; and from all payments received from the men of the aforesaid mother church, except the *hostilense* [uncertain levy]—that is, oxen and the contribution for constructing carts—you shall each year return to the aforesaid mother church the lawful census, the ninths, and the tenths, without any refusal or delay.

Moreover, do not neglect to provide, according to the resources of the properties which you hold there as benefices, repairs both in the aforesaid church and in the houses adjoining it, including roofing and restoration, if each of you wishes to retain our favor and those same benefices.

I wish our faithful to hold the aforesaid benefices, together with the aforesaid census, with the consent and goodwill of the bishop of that church, until we are able to exchange them with those things which they appear to hold from our gift, and until, with the Lord’s assistance, we may deserve to restore and return to the aforesaid church the properties which, as we have learned, are justly and lawfully owed to it.

Let this also be known to all of you: if any one of you should delay fulfilling this command of ours, whether through contempt or negligence—for we wish and command that the bishop of the aforesaid city cause the same properties to be recalled into the right, power, or dominion of his church, either himself or through his canons, until those who held the properties or benefices of the aforesaid church by our largition come into our presence to render an account for this negligence and contempt—then let each person beware lest he hear there the sentence: “He who neglects the census shall lose the estate,” and lest, by this authority, because of their negligence or contempt, they themselves lose the benefices. [Note: See the *Capitularies of Charles*, title 7, chapter 69.]

And so that this command of ours may be believed more certainly, preserved more diligently, carried out by you in every respect, and held more firmly in future, we ordered these letters of ours to be sealed below with our ring.

I, Hirminmarus, notary, have examined and subscribed this document on behalf of Theoto.

Given on the second day before the Kalends of January, in the nineteenth year, Christ being gracious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the tenth indiction. Done at the city of Le Mans, prosperously in God’s name. Amen.

## CLXXVI. Diploma of Lothar for the Monastery of Verona (833)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. V, p. 717.]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, Lothar Augustus, son of the most invincible lord Emperor Louis.

Whatever has been defined in our presence or that of our nobles by the straight path according to law ought to be confirmed by our pronouncements, so that it may remain unshaken with the strongest legal force.

Therefore let it be known to the sagacity of all our faithful, present and future, that when our envoys were sitting at Piscaria to hear everyone’s cases and settle judgments rightly, Leo the abbot came there, together with Garimbald, advocate of Saint Zeno, under whose authority Leo appeared to act through the appointment of the venerable Bishop Ratald. They brought a complaint against Ragileus and Ragipert, advocates of Count Gorad, saying that the party of the aforesaid Gorad had illicitly and unlawfully occupied the forest called Hostilia, together with the pasture belonging to it, which belonged by right to Saint Zeno.

Since our aforesaid envoys were entirely unable to settle the matter themselves, we ordered it to be brought fully into our presence for deliberation. When we investigated the truth of the matter with diligent inquiry, the aforesaid abbot presented to our favorable attention the precepts of the ancient kings, as well as those of our grandfather, the lord Charles, most excellent emperor, and also of our uncle, the late glorious King Pippin, and of our lord and father Louis, most serene Augustus.

When we had ordered these to be reread, we discovered that the agreements of the monastery of Saint Zeno justly and reasonably covered all pastures, *capuli*, tenths, and every exaction, without any obligation of repayment in any respect, while its full right remained over the territory where Hostilia is called by that name. Its boundaries are from the Po to the field of Turmion, from the Lubia ditch to the Royal Ditch, and to the *pollex* beside the fortress of Reveri.

Therefore we ordered these letters of our authority to be made for that holy and venerable place, by which, without any disturbance, it may henceforth hold and possess these things by our authority, justly enjoying them.

Moreover, Bishop Ratald, to whom the aforesaid monastery had been entrusted for governance by our authority, reported to us that Count Gorad was bringing certain counterclaims against him concerning some properties and slaves which Vulvinus, the predecessor of the aforesaid Gorad, had formerly exchanged with Chunibert, bishop of the Church of Brescia, receiving in return an exchange agreeable to himself.

When the same Ratald, then venerable bishop, had later learned that these properties were useful to the aforesaid Church of Saint Zeno, he acquired the agreement for the possession of that church by giving in compensation suitable properties and slaves exchanged by Peter, the former bishop of that same church. But since an envoy of royal authority had been absent during these exchanges, to prevent such occasions from being used to take the properties away from that church—since legally they could not be exchanged without a royal envoy—we were pleased to add this authority of ours concerning the aforesaid exchanges.

By it we order that the matter shall remain sound. We decree that henceforth none of the faithful of God’s holy Church or of our own shall presume to bring any opposition against any part of the agreement of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Zeno. Rather, since it acquired them by the lawful path, it shall be permitted to arrange and dispose of them peacefully through the rulers of the church, in whatever way the advantage of the aforesaid church shall dictate.

If, however—which we do not believe will happen—any duke, count, official of any kind, or private person should presume to plot anything against all that has been stated above, or should attempt to violate or corrupt it in part or in whole, let him know that he shall pay one thousand *mancusi* of refined gold, half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Zeno, if any violent opposition has been brought against it.

And so that this may be believed with complete certainty and observed more diligently, we have strengthened it with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our ring.

I, Dructemirius, subdeacon and notary, have written this on behalf of Hermenfred.

Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the twentieth year, Christ being gracious, of the reign of our lord Louis, most serene emperor, and the eleventh year of Lothar, in the eleventh indiction [or twelfth]. Done at Mantua, in the royal palace, prosperously in God’s name. Amen.

## CLXXVII. For the Monastery of Saint-Denis (833). Precept of Emperor Louis

Mintriacum in the county of Paris is granted to Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis. [Note: This donation was made by Louis Augustus for the benefit of the oratory of blessed Mary, which Hilduin had built before the feet of the blessed martyrs, namely in the underground crypt, where that oratory may still be visited. Mintriacum, Mitry, is mentioned in the little work *On the Translation of Saint Vitus*, no. 16, in part I of volume IV of the Benedictine century, p. 533.]

[In Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 541.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

We are admonished by imperial solicitude, Christian religious zeal, and devotion to divine worship to consider the increase and lasting establishment of venerable places, since it is a munificence bearing spiritual rewards when, with Christ as our guide, we hasten with the readiest generosity to contribute to God’s Church and to the most revered places entrusted to us by his authority [Col. 1225A]. We especially believe that nothing is diminished from the rights of the commonwealth whenever, with a bountiful hand—as befits imperial majesty—we bestow something as imperial gifts upon the saints of the Lord, by whose power, after the Lord’s mercy, mother earth appears to be sustained, the whole world mercifully governed, human frailty also raised up, and our empire, with God’s favor, directed. We bestow these gifts chiefly through his providence and to him, with eager spirit and due devotion: to him who, the Holy of Holies, redeemed our common captivity, crowned the sanctified with grace, and promised, as its author, to transfer our kingdom into an everlasting empire, if we persist in works commanded by him, according to his power.

For affairs advance with an increase all the more favorable to a king’s greatness, the more provision has been made from them for venerable places through zeal for piety [Col. 1225B]. For we have received what has been entrusted to us by the Lord’s mercy so that, through the excellent stewardship of his omnipotence, it may confidently be believed that these things will be restored, and so that, for what we have bestowed, we may gain the confidence of obtaining eternal rewards in the ages to come. It is indeed known that, because of our ancestral transgression, the human race was punished with the retribution of bodily death. Therefore, since the end that will one day come is certain, while its occurrence is feared because it is uncertain, in the ignorance of this sorrowful blindness time must be redeemed by many acts of generosity, the Lord must be appeased by our offerings, and his saints must be won over to us by devout donations. For although benefits frequently bestowed upon secular affairs are cheated of a worthy return by the smallest reversals [Col. 1225C], no one can rightly doubt that those things accomplished under heavenly regard are repaid with the reward of eternal life. Even in this age imperial piety does not fail to receive exalted praise when God’s Church advances through the enlargement of new works and the most abundant gifts for the love of Christ.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own people, present and future, that the venerable man Hilduin, abbot and religious head of the monastery of the holy chief of the apostles and of Christ’s most excellent martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, our special protectors, built before the feet of those same blessed martyrs a church to the praise [Col. 1225D] of God, our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, in honor of the holy and ever-inviolable Virgin, queen of all heaven and of the whole world, the most glorious mother of that same almighty Lord, and of Christ’s holy Forerunner, and of the holy Apostles, Martyrs, Confessors, Virgins, and all the elect of the Lord, out of reverence for God and veneration of the citizens of heaven, for the perpetual salvation of ourselves, our wife, our offspring, and himself. With the Lord’s help and through his praiseworthy labor he placed in it many most precious relics of the saints.

To this church, inspired by the grace of our Savior and after the fullest deliberation, we have transferred into perpetual possession, by this charter of our august authority, for the present and perpetual salvation of ourselves, our wife and offspring, and for the stability of the empire, the portion of the estate called Mintriacus, just as Fredebald once held it as our benefice [Col. 1226A], together with all dependents and everything else lawfully recognized as belonging to that portion, whether in that same estate or elsewhere. We have transferred it to our triumphant Lord Jesus Christ, to his mother, the mother of the eternal Lord God, to holy Peter the key-bearer, and to the holy and most precious martyrs of Christ Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, as well as to all God’s saints whose patronage is reverently preserved in that most sacred church.

This transfer excludes what we have undertaken to confirm by our decrees to the aforesaid most revered house from the property of the mother Church, together with the privilege of the aforesaid venerable man Hilduin [Col. 1226B]. Thus, from this gift of our property and from the goods confirmed as stated above, according to the arrangement which that man of God had established with our consent in his confirmation, everything is to be fully carried out: namely, the provision of lamps therefrom for that church, the furnishing of suitable and worthy adornment, and whatever may be necessary for its repair and improvement.

We also decree that on the feasts—the Purification of holy Mary, the day of the martyrdom of the blessed Peter and Paul, the honor of all the Apostles, the solemnity of the most glorious martyr of Christ Sebastian, and our anniversary and that of our beloved wife Judith, whenever God wills it—the monks of that holy community shall, from the aforesaid goods, have a meal in the love of almighty God, in honor of the saints, and in memory of us [Col. 1226C]. This is apart from the charitable provisions which, from the Church’s goods assigned for solemnities and confirmed for this purpose by our authority, they will receive. On those same days, according to their means, food shall also be provided for the poor.

Thus, just as the brothers of that congregation have customarily offered special and daily prayers, in a praiseworthy manner, for our royal predecessors through the benefit of private donations, so may they strive, by their prayers, to obtain for this special blessing of ours, while we live in the body, salvation for us, and after our death eternal blessing.

We decree, by the authority of the King of kings, who mercifully granted us as much power as he willed, and by the threat and solemn appeal of his future judgment—in whose hand are the hearts of kings—that none of our successors, nor the heads of that monastery, nor any other person, great or small, may in any way overturn what we have piously transferred, decreed, and promulgated; nor give the property itself as a benefice; nor alienate it anywhere; nor divert its payments, gifts, exactions, revenues, or dues to their own use or that of their associates; nor, by any device, cunning, artifice, or pretext, expend them for any other purpose than, as we have stated above, the benefit of that holy Church [Col. 1227A] and the increase of our almsgiving, and such reasonable provision for the service of our oft-mentioned faithful man as we have agreed.

Rather, under the administration and direction of a special guardian—who shall be faithful, religious, and observant, and who shall always be appointed to that divine house by the choice of the abbot and brothers—our donation shall be carefully managed and faithfully distributed for the designated and due purposes, with a view to eternal recompense. We earnestly ask our successors that, just as they wish their predecessors to observe the provisions they themselves establish for their salvation, so they may ensure that this constitution of ours, which we confirm for the prosperity of ourselves, our wife, our offspring, and the stability of the empire, remains firm and unshaken and is preserved inviolate to the end throughout perpetual ages.

[Col. 1227B] And so that it may possess fuller force of permanence, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.**

I, Hirminmarus, notary, have reviewed and subscribed this in the name of Theoto.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the nineteenth year, with Christ favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the eleventh indiction. Issued at the royal palace of Vern, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

## CLXXVIII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT COLUMBA AT SENS. (Year 833.)

[From the autograph, in D. Bouquet, volume VI.]

[Col. 1227C]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.

If, for love of divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants, we faithfully believe that the Lord will reward us with the prize of a worthy recompense. Therefore let all the diligence of our faithful, present as well as future, know that the venerable man Sulpicius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Columba, martyr of Christ, in which the bodies of that saint and of Saint Lupus, confessor of Christ, are venerated as buried, brought before our sight a certain charter of immunity belonging to our lord and father, the pious Augustus Charles of blessed memory. It contained a statement of how he himself and his predecessors, namely the kings [Col. 1227D] of the Franks, had held the aforesaid monastery under complete protection and defense of immunity, for the love of God and the tranquility of the brothers living there.

The same charter also stated that the former kings Lothar and Dagobert had granted certain estates to that monastery, whose names are Cersiacus and Grandis-Campus. By that same charter the lord emperor had confirmed those estates, and whatever the aforesaid monastery then rightly and reasonably possessed, so that they might be held in perpetual right, during his time and that of his successors, by the leaders and agents of that monastery.

For the sake of securing the matter, however, the aforesaid abbot Sulpicius asked us, out of reverence for the saints mentioned and for the fruit of eternal recompense, to confirm our father’s charter by our authority [Col. 1228A]. Gladly agreeing to his petition, we granted what he requested and confirm it by this our charter.

Therefore we command that no public judge, nor any other person endowed with judicial authority, may ever dare to enter the churches, places, lands, or remaining possessions of the aforesaid monastery which, at the present time, it rightly and lawfully possesses in any counties or territories under our rule, or which divine piety may thereafter cause to be increased in the right of that holy place, in order to hear cases according to judicial custom, exact fines, provide lodgings or transport services, take sureties, or unjustly distrain the men of that monastery [Col. 1228B], whether free or servile, who live upon its land; nor, as is contained in the aforesaid charter of the lord emperor, may anyone distrain them for customary obligations, collect tolls, or demand any payments or unlawful dues or pretexts. No one may ever enter for any of these purposes or presume to exact anything listed above.

But let the aforesaid abbot and his successors be permitted to possess the property of the aforesaid monastery peacefully under the protection of our immunity. Whatever the fisc may hope to obtain from it, we grant entirely to the aforesaid monastery for eternal recompense, so that it may perpetually increase the provision for the poor and the support of the monks serving God there.

As for the estates named above, and all the property lawfully possessed at the present time, let them remain perpetually under the control of that monastery, as is contained in the charter of our lord and father and of the preceding kings [Col. 1228C], so that the monks serving God there may continually delight in imploring the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of our entire empire, granted to us by God and to be preserved immeasurably by his most merciful compassion.

Therefore, so that this charter may have fuller force in the name of God, and so that it may be more truly believed and more carefully preserved by the faithful of God’s holy Church and by our own people, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.**

Maginarius, notary, reviewed it in the name of Theoto.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of June, in the twentieth year, with Christ favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, most serene emperor, in the eleventh indiction. Issued at the city of Worms, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

## CLXXIX. FOR THE NEW MONASTERY OF CORVEY. (Year 833.)

[In Schaten, *Annales Paderbornenses*, p. 91.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.

We wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own people [Col. 1229A], present and future, how, with the Lord’s favor and the consent of our faithful, we founded the monastery of Corvey in Saxony, with the most devoted intention, in honor of Saint Stephen, Christ’s protomartyr. There we bestowed upon the aforesaid place of sanctification, as our almsgiving, the appropriate resources and whatever we found immediately available, with due generosity.

Moreover, because that region needed a place of commerce, we established that a public mint under our authority should always operate there for the benefit of those serving Christ, so that, in complete integrity and without any occasion of contradiction or impediment, that holy place might possess all the public revenue from it under our authority, and so that this gift of our generosity, increased through all time, might benefit the monastery’s interests [Col. 1229B].

And so that it might enjoy and hold all these gifts of our authority with assured permanence, we resolved to confirm them below by sealing them with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.**

I, Hirminmarus, notary, have reviewed and subscribed this in the name of Theogo.

Given on the Kalends of June, in the twentieth year, with Christ favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the eleventh indiction. Issued at the city of Worms, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

## CLXXX. FOR THE SAME MONASTERY. (Year 831.)

[Col. 1229C] [In Schaten, *ibid.*, p. 92.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.

If, from the benefits bestowed upon us by God, we confer something through the gift of our generosity upon places dedicated to God, we clearly believe that this will benefit us both in passing our mortal life successfully and in obtaining eternal life forever. Therefore we wish it to be known to the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, that, when we had founded a monastery in Saxony, with the Lord’s favor and the consent of our faithful, with the most devoted intention in honor of Saint Stephen, Christ’s protomartyr, and had given it the name New Corvey [Col. 1229D], and when we had bestowed upon that place of sanctification, as our almsgiving, the appropriate resources and whatever we had found immediately available, Warinus, whom we had appointed abbot of that monastery, petitioned our highness by suggesting that in the aforesaid duchy of Saxony we provide a place where salt could be produced for salting and seasoning the food of the monks dwelling in that monastery from time to time.

By this charter of our authority we have therefore granted, in the duchy of Budinisvelt, whatever right we appeared to possess in that salt which is above the river Wisera, in the county of Logi [Alternative old manuscript: “whatever right we possessed in that salt and in the spring which is above the river Wisera”]. We establish and decree that, under the right of this monastery, whatever we are seen to possess in that salt shall remain perpetually, as we have said, to support the needs of God’s servants dwelling in the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1230A].

And so that this charter of our generosity may be held more firmly, we ordered it sealed below with our ring.

Maginarius, notary, reviewed it in the name of Theogo.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of June [Alternative old manuscript: sixth day before the Kalends of June], in the twentieth year, with Christ favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, most serene emperor, in the eleventh indiction, in the name of God. Amen.

## CLXXXI. THE MONASTERY OF GLANNAFOLIUM IS PLACED UNDER THE FOSSATIAN MONASTERY. (Year 833.)

[Col. 1230B] [Baluz., *Capitularia*, volume II, p. 1436, from the cartulary of the Fossatian monastery.]

In the name of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.

If, for love of divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants, we do not doubt that we are fortified by heavenly grace. Therefore let the diligence of all the faithful, present as well as future, know that the venerable Count Rorigo reported to our serenity how he had found a certain monastery in the county of Anjou, in a place called Glannafolium, situated on the river Loire, where the venerable body of Saint Maurus, disciple of Father Benedict, lies buried. There, in former times, that beloved man of God had lived under the holy Rule with many brothers subject to him [Col. 1230C]. Finding the place destroyed, and moved by divine admonition, he undertook, for the redemption of his soul, together with his wife Bilehild, to restore that same place through their labor and to return it, as far as possible, to its former condition.

Afterward he summoned the venerable abbot Engilbert of the Fossatian monastery and entrusted to him and to the brothers subject to him the task of ensuring that regular religious observance of divine things should be preserved perpetually, as before.

When these matters had thus been disclosed to us, he urged the excellence of our greatness to undertake that place under our protection and defense of immunity, and to make it stand, just as the other abbots of monks exist throughout the empire by the power divinely granted to us, together with its abbot, monks, property, and men lawfully subject to that monastery. He also asked us to grant, by our imperial letters, foresight, authority, and jurisdiction to the aforesaid abbot of the Fossatian monastery and to all his successors, so that it might not again fall away from the path of regular order [Col. 1230D].

Since we recognized his petition as reasonable and indeed pleasing to God, we gladly accepted it and granted it just as he requested.

We therefore wish the aforesaid abbot, or the leaders of the monastery mentioned above, and the devout brothers of that place, perpetually to have, hold, possess, and govern the place in question, namely Glanna. They shall always exercise great care over it, applying the vigilance of their solicitude both to the place and to the community [Col. 1231A].

They shall appoint there such overseers, leaders, masters, and superiors that, by their direction and arrangement, everything within and without may be accomplished according to God’s will and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict; that they may serve Christ God devoutly after the manner and likeness of the Fossatian monastery; and that they may follow its pattern in all things, so that, setting aside all private property, they may possess everything in common according to apostolic tradition, thereby deserving to acquire perpetual salvation for themselves. They shall always be subject and obedient to the authority, governance, and power of one abbot.

And since at the aforesaid Fossatian place no mortal, apart from those who serve Christ there, is able to demand any customary due or payment—unless unjustly—we command that this place likewise remain under the same arrangement.

Everything they are now known to possess, or may thereafter lawfully acquire, shall remain under our protection and the defense of our immunity. We command and decree in every way that no successor of ours—neither king, bishop, archdeacon, count, public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority—may presume to bring under his dominion anything that belongs or will belong to that place [Col. 1231B].

No one may ever enter the churches, places, lands, or remaining possessions of the aforesaid monastery, which it appears to possess lawfully and reasonably at the present time in any counties or territories, or anything that has been bestowed there for the love of God, or that divine piety may thereafter wish to increase in the right of that holy place, in order to hear cases, exact fines, provide lodgings or transport services, take sureties, unjustly distrain the men of that place, whether free or servile, who appear to reside on its land, or demand any payments or unlawful dues or pretexts. Nor may anyone presume to exact anything listed above.

Whatever the fisc might hope to obtain from the property of the aforesaid monastery, we grant entirely to that place for eternal recompense, so that it may perpetually increase the provision for the poor and the support of the monks serving God there. It shall always possess the freedom of our royal protection [Col. 1231D], without military service, from which we wholly release that place.

Whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid abbot Engilbert or his successors depart from this life, whoever is appointed in his place shall possess the same authority and jurisdiction which his predecessor had while he lived.

Therefore, commanding, we authorize and confirm that no judge—neither emperor, king, bishop, count, nor any judicial authority—dare violate this command of our excellence. But, having seen this charter, just as they wish their own acts to remain firm and stable, so they shall allow this our act to remain inviolate.

In particular, two documents shall be written in one version under this arrangement [Col. 1232A], so that one may be kept beneath the shrine of Saint Maurus and the other preserved by the aforesaid abbot Engilbert in the Fossatian monastery.

If, however, any madman and enemy of God should presume to violate this command of our authority, let him be expelled from the thresholds of God’s holy Church, excommunicated by all the bishops of Gaul, and separated from the assembly of Christ’s faithful. With Caiaphas, Pilate, and Judas, the Lord’s betrayer, let him suffer eternal punishments; and, when his soul has departed from his body, let him find prepared for himself a hellish seat with the prince of demons.

Therefore, so that this authority may retain its firmness throughout the ages, we ordered it sealed with our ring, confirming this document with our own hand [perhaps: “unshaken”].

[Col. 1232B]

**Sign of Emperor Louis.**

Glorius, notary, reviewed it in the name of Hugh.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the twentieth year, with Christ favorable, of the reign of our lord Louis, most serene emperor, in the eleventh indiction. Issued at the royal palace of Aachen, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

## CLXXXII. CHARTER OF LOTHAR FOR THE CHURCH OF AREZZO. (Year 833.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, volume I, p. 413.]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal God, Lothar, by the providence of God’s ordering, emperor Augustus.

Whatever we grant, guided by divine love, to places devoted to God, we have never doubted that it answers to true and eternal acts of generosity [Col. 1232C]. Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own people, present and future, that, at the petition of Peter, venerable bishop of the Church of Arezzo, we have granted to the church of Saint Donatus, where he rests bodily and where the bishop’s seat is known to be located, for the benefit of our soul, a certain church established in honor of Saint Peter, with all its appurtenances and dependencies, situated in a place called Castellus in the territory of Arezzo.

It is the church which Barbatianus, formerly a priest, had once transferred from his own property to our uncle Pippin, glorious king, for him to possess, and which at the present time the priest Aliprandus is known to hold under an annual payment and by our munificence. But, for the sake of security, we have ordered by our authority that it be transferred to that same holy and venerable place [Col. 1232D], so that no public person, whoever he or she may be, may at any time presume to inflict trouble or controversy upon the aforesaid church or its leaders concerning the aforesaid church, with all its appurtenances, dependencies, and attachments.

Rather, let the leaders of that church be permitted to possess the same church peacefully and securely, with all its appurtenances and dependencies, and to govern and dispose of it as they please, according to the usefulness of that place.

And so that this charter of our generosity may possess fuller force in the name of God, we have written below with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our ring.

[Col. 1233A]

**Sign of Lothar, most invincible emperor Augustus.**

I, Protomus, subdeacon and notary, have written this.

Given on the second day before the Nones of October, in the year 833, in the thirteenth year of the reign of the lord emperor Lothar, in the fourth indiction, at [lacuna]. Successfully, in the name of God.

## CLXXXIII. FOR THE BISHOP OF AREZZO. (Year 833.)

Proceedings of the dispute between Peter, bishop of Arezzo, and Vigilius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Anthemius, concerning the monastery of Saint Peter of Axo, before Agiprandus of Florence and other bishops and envoys of Emperor Lothar I, with judgment in favor of the bishop of Arezzo.

[In Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, volume V, p. 923.]

In the name of God, we had been sent by the most excellent lord and most pious, God-crowned Augustus Lothar, great emperor [Col. 1233B]: I, Agiprandus, bishop of the holy Church of Florence—[Note: Ughelli gives for this period a Florentine bishop named Aliprandus, or Rambaldus. From this charter we learn his Germanic name, namely Agiprandus. Furthermore, Anastasius of Siena, a bishop unknown to Ughelli, must in future be added to the catalogue of the bishops of that city, and perhaps Thomas, appointed bishop of that city in the year 830, must be removed from it. Thus, as we have seen, although that dispute was conducted between two ecclesiastical persons, its judges were envoys or legates of Lothar I Augustus. Nor should you reply that both judges were adorned with episcopal dignity; for they instituted that judgment and delivered sentence not by their own authority, but by the delegated authority of Lothar himself. This is clearly established by the often-repeated formula: “according to the command and written instruction of the lord emperor.”]—and Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Volterra, to investigate the case concerning the Church of blessed Donatus at Arezzo and Petronius, bishop of that same church, between Bishop Petronius himself and Vigilius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Anthemius in the territory of Chiusi.

When we had assembled in the city of Siena and were seated in judgment at the Lord’s [lacuna] and the Church of Siena, together with the venerable Anastasius, bishop of that city, and Count Adelricus [lacuna], Walcharius and [lacuna], officials of the aforesaid city, and Datus, Christianus, Alexander, and Odelfridus, officials of the city of Arezzo, as well as Ringo and Rodulfus, officials of Volterra, there were also present with us Wilerus and Anserum of Siena; Anseprand and Camarinus, vassals [Col. 1233C] of the lord emperor; Ansiprand and Theudicius, brothers; Perisindus and Lundifredus, brothers; Angelus, Franciconus, Al[lacuna], citizens of Arezzo; Guiprandus; and many other capable men, both Frankish and Lombard, from each of the aforesaid cities.

There before us all came Petronius, bishop of the Church of Arezzo, together with Wileriud, and Agimundus, son of the late Tachiprandus of Siena, and Agimundus, son of the late Ariprandus of Arezzo, his advocates, bringing a claim against the aforesaid Vigilius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Anthemius, situated in the Valley of Saint [lacuna], in the territory of Chiusi; and Furvus [lacuna] of Siena and Ursus of Chiusi, advocates of the aforesaid monastery and abbot.

Then Wileriud and Agimundus began to speak against the aforesaid advocates of Saint Anthemius:

“On behalf of the monastery of Saint Anthemius [lacuna] and its abbot, they have invaded and held, contrary to law and in an evil manner, the monastery of Saint Peter of Axo together with its dependencies. Therefore we ask that you give judgment between us concerning it and have justice done on behalf of Saint Donatus, since it belonged by law to Saint Donatus.”

In reply, Vigilius the abbot himself, together with Furvus and Ursus, his advocates, answered [Col. 1234A]:

“It is true that we have and hold the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter of Axo together with its dependencies, but not contrary to law or in an evil manner, because, behold, we have in our hands a charter of the late lord King Charles of blessed memory, stating how, for the sake of his reward, he granted to Cugio, which is called Cicilianus, on behalf of Saint Anthemius, within the places designated; and within those designated places the monastery was built.”

When we, the aforesaid envoys, had ordered that charter to be read aloud to us [lacuna], it stated how King Charles had granted the aforesaid Cugio to Saint Anthemius, within the places designated by name, and that whatever he had granted within the designated places he had granted by name. But it contained nothing there [Col. 1234B] concerning the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter of Axo, namely that he had granted it, as he had granted the other properties that were read in the same charter.

When the charter itself had been reread, Wileriud and Agimundus, the advocates, said:

“Certainly this charter neither obstructs us nor the party of Saint Donatus, because what he granted, he granted by name. And if the lord King Charles had then wished to grant that monastery, he would have granted it by name, just as he granted the other properties and rights.”

This was said.

Then we, the aforesaid envoys and judges, questioned Vigilius the abbot and his aforesaid advocate, and they said:

“[Lacuna] since, behold, after this charter, nothing prevents [lacuna] this matter, [lacuna], on account of which the matter should belong either to Saint Anthemius or to this abbot.” [Col. 1234C]

Then the abbot himself, when questioned, said:

“Certainly King Charles granted it as a benefice by his charter to Tanimundus, formerly abbot, and likewise to Apollenaris, of blessed memory, abbot. Thereafter the lords emperors Louis and Lothar granted it to me as a benefice, and also on behalf of Saint Anthemius.”

When he had spoken in this way, we questioned him whether the charters of those emperors had been issued to their successors or to Saint Anthemius; and he replied:

“Certainly they were not issued to their successors [lacuna], but only to both of their persons; and it was granted to me alone as a benefice. I have no other charter concerning it [lacuna] regarding that Cugio.”

Having said and rejected this, then Peter, bishop of the aforesaid Church, produced a memorandum of the most pious lord Emperor Lothair. When it had been read aloud before us, it contained how that same lord Augustus had instructed and informed us, Agiprandus and Petron, bishops, that Peter, bishop of Arezzo, had informed him how Abbot Vigilius, when the cell that had been built in honor of Saint Peter [Col. 1235A] above the river Axso belonged to his episcopate, held it for no other reason than that Abbot Apollenaris had possessed it as a benefice. Thus the aforesaid bishop, admitting this, said that he had writs and documents by which the same memorandum instructed us to have them come together with their advocates and to investigate carefully whether Abbot Vigilius could produce any document establishing that it belonged to the monastery entrusted to him. If we could not find this, and he claimed it by the authority of a benefice, then the memorandum instructed us, as directed by his decree and will, to have the aforesaid documents from Bishop Peter presented to us. And if we found that it belonged to the aforesaid bishopric, then [Col. 1235B] without any delay we were to restore him to possession of everything pertaining to the aforesaid cell—which is what we did, after he had shown us the documents.

Then Peter, bishop, together with his aforesaid advocates, produced the writs and documents. The first judgment, when produced and read aloud, stated how, in the time of King Liutprand, Bishop Luparcianus, before an envoy of that same King Liutprand, had claimed from Bishop Deodatus the monastery of Saint Peter at Axso, on behalf of Saint Donatus, together with the remaining parish and baptismal churches, as will be read in that judgment. After this he produced the writ of the aforesaid King Liutprand. When it had been read aloud, it stated that by his writ he had confirmed that judgment concerning the monastery and the parishes to the advantage of the Church of Arezzo. [Col. 1235C]

He also produced another judgment, which clearly indicated how the aforesaid King Liutprand had sent four bishops as his envoys to determine the aforesaid case, monastery, and parishes. In their presence and by their judgment, Bishop Luparcianus had claimed from the Sienese Church, for his own Church of Arezzo, the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter at Axso together with the remaining parishes, as was read in that judgment. Likewise, by a writ, King Liutprand had confirmed that judgment and the monastery together with those parishes to the Church of Arezzo.

For this reason he also produced a brief privilege of Stephen, of blessed memory, pope of the city of Rome, showing how, at the petition of Stavilius, formerly bishop of the Church of Arezzo, he had confirmed by his writ and brief privilege, to the advantage of the Church of Arezzo, both the aforesaid judgments from the time of King Liutprand and the aforesaid writs of that same King Liutprand, concerning both the aforementioned monastery of Saint Peter at Axso and the aforesaid parishes, just as these matters were contained in the judgments and writs themselves. [Col. 1235D]

For the same reason he produced a brief privilege of Pope Leo, showing how he too, by his brief privilege and writ, at the petition of Arepertus of the holy Church of Arezzo and with the consent of the lord and most pious Emperor Charles, had confirmed in his peaceful synod, between Andrew, bishop of the holy Church of Siena, and that same Arepertus, bishop of the Church of Arezzo, by his writ to the advantage of the Church of Arezzo, both the aforesaid parishes and the aforementioned monastery of Saint Peter at Axso, just as the judgments and writs issued from the time of the Lombard King Liutprand contained them. [Col. 1236A]

Finally, the most pious lord King Charles, of holy and glorious memory, confirmed by his writ that writ of Pope Leo, and everything, as noted above, to the advantage of the Church of Arezzo, just as the [lacuna] judgments, writs, and brief privileges contained [lacuna] the aforementioned parishes and monastery, just as from ancient times they had been claimed [lacuna] by the Church.

Therefore he also showed us the writ of the lord Emperor Louis Augustus, stating how he too, by his writ, had confirmed both that writ of Charles, his father, of glorious memory, and that of the aforesaid Pope Leo, [Col. 1236B] together with the other judgments and writs often mentioned [lacuna] to the advantage of the Church of Arezzo, concerning both the parishes and the aforesaid monastery together with the other monasteries, just as they had been claimed and possessed from ancient times.

When the judgments and writs had been produced and read aloud, as we have explained above in due order, we, the aforesaid envoys and bishops, questioned Abbot Vigilius and Furvo and Urso, advocates of the same, asking them to produce any writ, judgment, witness, or other document they might have showing that the monastery of Saint Peter belonged to Saint Antemus. They, together with the abbot, rejected the claim and said:

“Certainly we have neither judgment nor writ, nor any document, nor any other means by which we might claim that monastery of Saint Peter, or the property belonging to it, for Saint Antemus or defend it on Saint Antemus’s behalf, except, as we said previously, that we held it as a benefice from the lords Emperors Louis and Lothair.”

When they had rejected the claim in this way, we, the aforesaid envoys, said to the abbot:

“Certainly, on this basis you will no longer be able to retain it, because the lord Emperor instructed us by the aforesaid memorandum that, if you did not produce such evidence that it belonged to the monastery entrusted to you, and if we found through the documents of this Peter, bishop, that it belonged to the episcopate of the Church of Arezzo, we were to restore it to possession without any delay.”

After this had been said, and in order to investigate the matter carefully, [Col. 1236D] we diligently inquired according to law into what the abbot had said: that after the writs, no investiture of the monastery had been made on behalf of Saint Donatus and the Church of Arezzo.

Then we, the aforesaid envoys, had the reliable witnesses whom Peter, bishop, had named to us brought forward. We made all those laymen swear upon the Gospels of God [lacuna] and questioned them concerning that restoration of possession, asking them whether they knew the matter and could tell us the certain truth. Likewise, we adjured the priests by their priesthood and by the fidelity that they had sworn to the lord Emperor, so that if they knew the truth about it, they too might declare the truth concerning the aforesaid restoration of possession.

First of all, Gumprandus, archdeacon of the Church of Arezzo, came forward and, when questioned by us, said: [Col. 1237A]

“I know and remember well, and I was present there, when Angelbertus, envoy of the lord King Charles, restored Arepertus, bishop, to possession of the monastery of Saint Peter situated at Axso, after the confirmation of the lord Pope Leo. Then, at the time when the writ of that same lord King Charles was issued, that same Bishop Arepertus appointed abbots in the monastery, named Augustine, Arnicausus, John, and Landoarius.”

The archpriests likewise testified: Vanipert, Lucius, an old man, Romaldus, and Lampertus. All unanimously, individually and alike, gave testimony and said what Gumprandus the archdeacon had said above.

After the testimonies had been sought and the judgments and writs had been read aloud, and after everything had been done in due order as we explained above, and after we had investigated the matter according to true law and found it by a legally valid inquiry, we therefore, in accordance with the command and memorandum of the most pious lord Emperor, since we had found that the monastery of Saint Peter at Axso, together with the property belonging to it, belonged to the Church of Arezzo, acted according to that memorandum and the command of the lord Emperor. We, the envoys, caused the advocates Peter, Willeradus, and Agimundus to be restored to possession of the monastery of Saint Peter, with its appurtenances, on behalf of the Church of Arezzo. For this reason we caused this record to be made [lacuna].

[lacuna] of our lords, the Emperors Louis and Lothair, the twentieth and fourteenth years, in the month of October, in the twelfth indiction.

+ I, Agiprandus, bishop, by command of the lord [Col. 1237C] Emperor, conducted and attended this inquiry.  
+ I, Peter, bishop, by command of the lord Emperor, conducted this inquiry and subscribed.  
+ I, Anastasius, bishop, was present there.  
+ I, Adelrat, count, was present there. [Col. 1238A]  
+ I, Ansprandus, vassal of the lord Emperor, was present there.  
+ I, Camarino, vassal of the lord Emperor, was present there.  
+ I, Ringo, was present there.  
+ I, Perirendus, was present there.  
+ I, Gundifridus, was present there.  
+ I, Aliprandus, was present there.  
+ I, Urso, district judge and vassal of the lord Emperor, was present there.  
+ I, [lacuna], district judge [lacuna].  
+ I, Tato, district judge, was present there.  
+ I, [lacuna], vassal of the lord Emperor, attended.  
+ I, Rodulphus, was present there.

## CLXXXIV. For the monastery of Verona, Saint Zeno. (Year 823.) Against those occupying its rights.

[Muratori, same work, vol. I, p. 459.]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal God, Lothair Augustus, son of the most invincible lord Emperor Louis.

Whatever has been defined in our presence or that of our magnates by the right course and according to law ought to be confirmed by our pronouncements, so that it may remain undisturbed by the firmest legal authority. Therefore let it be known to the discernment of all our faithful, present and future, that when our envoys were sitting at Piscaria to hear everyone’s cases and conclude just judgments, Leo, abbot, came there, together with Garibaldus, advocate of Saint Zeno. Since Leo appeared to hold office by appointment of Rataldus, the venerable bishop, they brought a complaint against Ragileus and Ragimpertus, advocates of Count Goradus, saying that [Col. 1238C] the aforesaid Count Goradus’s party had illicitly and unlawfully occupied a forest called Hostilia and the pastures belonging by right to Saint Zeno.

[Note: [Col. 1237C] Here it is said that Count Goradus’s party had illicitly and unlawfully occupied that forest. Counts possessed allodial properties, but they also possessed their official rights and the regular revenues arising from the office of count of any city, distinct from the tributes and revenues owed to the royal fisc. It is uncertain whether he counted this forest among his allodial properties, or whether Count Goradus instead maintained that it belonged to the jurisdiction of his office. This charter further reveals that the distinguished monastery of Saint Zeno had been granted to Bishop Rataldus of Verona in commendam, as they now say, by Lothair I Augustus, in accordance with the custom of those times. Since it can be inferred quite plainly from this that Rataldus was then still alive, the chronology of the bishops of Verona in Ughelli, volume V of Italia Sacra, appears to require correction. For he seems to place the death of Rataldus—whom he calls Rotaldus—around the year 820, and says that Bishop Audon succeeded him. He then reports the final documents of that same Audon, written in the year 830 under Louis the Pious, and introduces another Rotaldus into the catalogue of the bishops of Verona in the year 840. Yet the diploma now produced can establish that Bishop Radaldus was still flourishing in the year 833. Nor should a second Rataldus be invented, since one man governed the Church of Verona before Audon, as Panvinius correctly observed. Ughelli is also mistaken in assigning Audon’s testament to the time of Louis the Pious, since it was written under “our lord Louis, the great emperor,” in his eleventh year, on 15 August, in the eighth indiction; it therefore belongs to the time of Emperor Louis II, namely the year 860. Hence you may see that after Rataldus, Aginus presided over the Church of Verona; Anastasius the Librarian testifies that Aginus was present at Rome in the year 844 when that same Louis II, son of Lothair I and later emperor, was anointed king of Italy. After Aginus, Bishop Audo must be placed. Moreover, since in a diploma published by Ughelli himself, where Audo is called the former bishop of Verona, the text in fact reads “Louis, emperor Augustus of the world,” everyone may reasonably regard that diploma as spurious. Perhaps, however, the charter is otherwise, and the document is genuine—one issued by Louis II Augustus after Audon’s death. Let us return to our subject. The forest of Hostilia was a very extensive tract, and it did not belong in its entirety to the Veronese monastery of Saint Zeno, since the Modenese monastery of Nonantola also possessed a share there. I have other documents, drawn from the Ferrara parchments by my distinguished friend, mentioned elsewhere, Joseph Antenor Scalabrinius, rector of the church of Saint Mary of the Mouth at Ferrara. From them we learn that the Nonantolan monks also suffered harassment on account of this share from Hucpold, count of Verona, in the year 820. But that same Rataldus, bishop of Verona, acting with authority received from Louis the Pious Augustus and as his envoy, brought the count before the assembly and ordered him to desist. This is an excellent document, since, together with the present one, it perhaps gives us a succession of several counts of Verona and also restores to the record the life and name of Andrew, bishop of Vicenza, whom Ughelli omitted from Italia Sacra. (See diploma 114 above.)]

Since our aforesaid envoys could not themselves decide this matter, we ordered it to be brought fully before our presence for deliberation. Accordingly, when we sought the truth of the matter through a careful investigation, [lacuna] the aforesaid abbot produced before our eyes the writs of the ancient kings, as well as those of our grandfather, the lord Charles, most excellent emperor, and also those of our uncle Pippin, formerly glorious king, and of our lord and father Louis, most serene Augustus. When we had ordered these to be read aloud, we found that all pasturage dues and *capulum*, or tithe, and every exaction, belonged justly and reasonably in their entirety to the monastery of Saint Zeno, without any obligation of payment in any part, while its full territorial right remained intact in the district called Hostilia. Its boundaries are from the Po to Caput Turnioni, and from the Fossa Lubia to the Royal Ditch and Pollicina, beside the fortress of Revere. [Col. 1239B]

Therefore we ordered these letters of our authority to be made for the aforesaid holy and venerable place, by which, without any disturbance, it may henceforth and forever hold and justly enjoy them by our authority.

Furthermore, Bishop Rataldus reported to us—he had been entrusted with the aforesaid monastery’s governance by our authority—that Count Goradus was bringing certain counterclaims against him concerning some properties and slaves which, in former times, Vulvinus, the predecessor of the aforesaid Goradus, had exchanged with Chunibertus, bishop of the Church of Brescia, and in return had received an exchange agreeable to himself. After the same venerable Bishop Rataldus had recognized, some days later, that these properties were useful to the aforesaid Church of Saint Zeno, he acquired them for possession by an exchange from Peter, formerly bishop of that same Church, giving suitable properties and slaves in compensation to the aforesaid Church of Brescia.

But because no envoy of royal authority had been present during these exchanges, and because such exchanges could not legally be made without a royal envoy, we have decided to add our authority to the aforesaid exchanges, so that they may not be taken away from that Church on this pretext. By this authority we order and establish that it shall remain in force: no one among the faithful of the holy Church of God, or among our own people, shall henceforth dare to bring any opposition against any part of the often-mentioned Church of Saint Zeno. Rather, let it be permitted to its rectors, in the proper manner in which it acquired them, peacefully to order and dispose of them as the usefulness of the aforesaid Church may dictate.

If, however—which we do not believe will happen—any duke, count, official of any administration, or private person should presume to undertake anything against all the foregoing, or should attempt to break or corrupt any part or the whole of it, let him know that he will pay one thousand mancuses of pure gold, half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid monastery, etc.

[Col. 1240A]

I, Dructemirus, subdeacon and notary, wrote this in the place of Hermenfredus.

Issued on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the twentieth year, by Christ’s favor, of the reign of the lord Emperor Louis the Most Serene, and the eleventh of Lothair, in the eleventh indiction. Enacted at Mantua, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## CLXXXV. For the monastery of the nuns of Ticinum, Dodosi. (Year 833.)

[In Muratori, same work, vol. V, p. 531.]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal God, Lothair Augustus, son of the most invincible lord Emperor Louis.

When, for the love of divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s male and female servants, we believe that the gift of heavenly grace is thereby bestowed upon us by the Lord. Therefore let it be known to the discernment of all the holy Church of God’s faithful, present and future, how Asia, venerable abbess of the monastery of Dodosi, situated within the walls of the city of Pavia, earnestly petitioned our clemency that we should place that monastery, together with everything belonging to it, under the protection and defense of our immunity, for the love of God and reverence for that holy place. We willingly granted her petition, granted it as she requested, and confirmed it by this imperial writ of ours. Therefore we command that no one, etc. Rather, let the aforesaid abbess and her successors be permitted to possess the property of the aforesaid monastery peacefully and in due order under the defense of our immunity. Whatever our fisc might otherwise have expected from it, we grant in full to the aforesaid monastery for eternal recompense, so that it may support the female servants of God serving God there under the rule of Saint Benedict, etc. We have also appointed the venerable Abbot Meramnus as inspector of the same place, so that throughout his life he may ensure that the rule of Saint Benedict is observed there in all respects, etc.

Sign of Lothair, most glorious Augustus.

I, Luithcasus, in the place of Ermenfredus, have reviewed this.

Issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the twenty-first year, by Christ’s favor, of the reign of the lord Louis, most serene emperor, and the eleventh year of the reign of Lothair, most glorious Augustus, in Italy, in the eleventh indiction.

Enacted in the city of Pavia, in the public palace.

[Col. 1240D]

## CLXXXVI. For Maxentius, patriarch of Aquileia. (Year 833.)

[In Muratori, same work, vol. V, p. 977.]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal God, Lothair Augustus, son of the most invincible lord Emperor Louis.

If, for the love of God, we bestow suitable benefits upon places devoted to divine worship and upon those serving Him in those places, we do not doubt that a reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us by the Lord. Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own people, present and future, that the venerable Maxentius, patriarch of the Church of Aquileia, [Note: [Col. 1241D] Here we have Maxentius, patriarch of Aquileia, receiving a privilege in the year 833; this document will therefore be useful for restoring or establishing the chronology of the bishops of Aquileia. Sacred places, I should add, customarily supplied the emperors and their envoys with fodrum and parata whenever they traveled there.] approached our serenity. He brought us certain writs of authority belonging to the lord Louis, our most excellent emperor and father, in which it was stated that Charles Augustus, of blessed memory, and likewise our lord and father, had caused the aforesaid Church, together with its cells and the property subject to it, to remain under the protection of his immunity. They also stated that he had granted the clergy and people of that city permission, in accordance with canonical institution, to choose a bishop for themselves and install him in the aforesaid see.

It was also contained in those documents that he had decreed that neither the men of that Church should pay a tenth of their grain and livestock to the fisc, nor should they pay any pasture tax on the livestock of that Church sent to the Istrian regions for pasture. Nor should mansionaticum or fodrum be received or exacted in any way from the men of the aforesaid Church, except when the emperor or his son came to that city, or when a garrison was stationed there to ward off enemy ambushes.

For the sake of firm security, that same venerable patriarch requested that, following the custom of his predecessors, we should also issue our authority concerning that holy place. Out of love for God and for the salvation of our soul, we willingly assented to his petition and ordered this writ of our authority to be made concerning that holy place.

By it we establish and wish to remain perpetually firm that the clergy and people of the aforesaid city shall have permission, in accordance with canonical institution, to choose a bishop for themselves. We also order and command that none of our faithful, no collector, and no one exercising judicial authority shall presume to receive or exact from the property of the aforesaid Church any pasture tax, or from the grain and livestock of the men of that Church any tenth, or from them any mansionaticum or fodrum, except perhaps when we or one of our sons comes there, or when a garrison is stationed there to repel enemy attacks.

Moreover, no one among our faithful, nor any public judge, shall ever dare to enter the monasteries subject to the aforesaid Church, its hospices, parish churches, and their titles, or the other properties that the aforesaid Church now justly and reasonably holds or possesses in any villages and territories within the jurisdiction of our Empire—whether received as gifts from kings or dukes, through the cession of other faithful persons, or through offerings, purchases, exchanges, or whatever properties Catholic men may henceforth grant to the Church—for the purpose of hearing cases, exacting fines or tributes, making lodgings or provisions, taking sureties, or distraining the men of that Church, both free and enslaved, who live upon its land; nor shall anyone enter to seek any payments or unlawful pretexts, or presume at any time to exact anything mentioned above. [Col. 1242A]

Rather, let the aforesaid bishop and his successors be permitted to possess the property of the aforesaid Church peacefully under the protection of our immunity, faithfully to obey our imperial authority, and, together with the clergy and people subject to him, continually to implore God’s mercy for the safety of ourselves, our wife and offspring, and the whole Empire granted to us by God and to be preserved by His immeasurable power. Whatever our fisc might have been able to exact from the property of the aforesaid Church, we have granted in full to that Church, so that in our time and in that of our successors it may serve as an increase and supplement for those serving God there and carrying out God’s service. [Col. 1242B]

And so that this authority may have fuller force in the name of God and may be believed more truly and certainly by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own people, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Lothair, most glorious Augustus.

I, Liuthardus, in the place of Ermenfredus, have reviewed this.

Issued on the second day before the Kalends of December, in the twentieth year, by Christ’s favor, of the reign of the lord Louis, most serene emperor, and the thirteenth year of the reign of Lothair, most glorious Augustus, in Italy, in the eleventh indiction.

Enacted in the city of Pavia, in the public palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1242C]

## CLXXXVII. Writ of Louis the German for Gozbert, abbot of Saint Gall. (Year 833, 19 October.)

[In Neugart, *Codex Alemannicus*, p. 212.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Louis, by the favor of divine grace, king.

If, for the love of God, we bestow suitable benefits upon places devoted to divine worship and upon those serving Him in those places, we trust that we shall receive from the Lord a reward in eternal blessedness. Therefore let the usefulness and diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable Gozbert, [Col. 1242D] abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, situated in the district of Thurgau on the river called Petrosa, brought to our excellence certain writs of our grandfather Emperor Charles, and also of our lord and father Louis Augustus. These contained the following provision: Sidonius, bishop of the city of Constance, and John, abbot of the aforesaid monastery, had established, for the sake of future disagreement and the peace of the monks, that every year the abbots of that monastery of Saint Gall should pay to the bishop’s see one ounce of gold and one horse worth one pound, and that the bishops of the aforesaid city should exact nothing more from the property of the aforesaid monastery. The monks were to be permitted to live securely, without anyone’s harassment or diminution of their property.

Afterward our grandfather, and our lord and father, confirmed this constitution by their pronouncements so that it would remain valid in the future. Our father also established the aforesaid monastery of Saint Gall, with the monks serving God there, and with the property and people lawfully and legally belonging or pertaining to it, under his protection and the safeguard of his immunity. When the abbot of that monastery departed this life by divine summons, the monks were to have permission, according to the rule of Saint Benedict, to choose an abbot, and they were not to give anything on that account to kings, unless the abbots who held office from time to time should freely offer something.

Nor should any bishop become an oppressor or collector beyond what was contained in their election and in the constitution of our father. If a definite necessity or the desire for pious devotion made it necessary for him to visit that venerable place, he was to come honorably with a moderate number of men, so that the monastery would not be burdened, carry out whatever had to be done with the same propriety pleasing to God, and immediately return home.

But so that the constitution and confirmations named above might remain unshaken forever, the aforesaid abbot earnestly implored our clemency, using every available appeal, to add our authority also to those confirmations. [Col. 1243C] Because of divine love we willingly gave ear to his petition and ordered this authority of our confirmation to be made concerning that monastery and its rectors. By it we decree and command that, after the authorities of our grandfather and father have been examined, everything shall remain perpetually unshaken, by God’s favor, just as those documents more fully declare, without anyone’s harassment or opposition.

And no public judge, nor any administrator of public affairs of higher or lower rank, shall dare to enter the churches, places, estates, fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery which it presently justly and reasonably possesses within the kingdom divinely granted to us, or which divine mercy may henceforth wish to increase there, in order to hear cases according to judicial procedure, exact fines, [Note: [Col. 1243D] *Fredum*, from the German word *friden*, means a fine which, once paid, secured the accused person’s peace from the prince. The *fredum* was sometimes paid both to the royal fisc and to judges.] make lodgings or provisions, take sureties, [Col. 1244A] or irrationally distrain the men of that monastery, both free and enslaved, who live upon its land; nor shall anyone enter to seek any payments or unlawful pretexts, or presume to exact any of the matters mentioned above, in our time or that of our successors.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors be permitted to possess the property of the aforesaid monastery, together with everyone subject to it and the properties and people lawfully belonging or pertaining to it, under the protection and immunity of our safeguard, free from all disturbance by judicial authority, to obey our imperial command faithfully. [Note: [Col. 1243D] The same formula is also found in another diploma of Louis the German in D. Grandidier, *Historia Ecclesiae Argentoratensis*, vol. II, documents, no. 115.] Whenever the aforesaid abbot or his successors should die by divine summons, so long as the monks themselves are able to find among them men capable of governing the congregation according to the rule of Saint Benedict, they shall, by this authority of ours and with our consent, and in accordance with what is contained in our father’s authority, have permission to choose an abbot. Thus the monks serving God there may continually implore the Lord’s mercy for us and for the stability of our kingdom.

And so that this authority may retain unbreakable force throughout long ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most glorious king.

I, Adalleodus, deacon, in the place of Grimaldus, have reviewed this. [Note: [Col. 1243D] Grimaldus was Louis the German’s archchaplain and later abbot of Saint Gall.]

Issued on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the first year, by Christ’s favor, of the reign of the lord King Louis in East Francia, [Col. 1244C] in the twelfth indiction. [Note: [Col. 1243D] After the deposition of his father, Louis the German counted the year 833 as the first year of his rule in East Francia. At that time the eleventh indiction, according to the pontifical reckoning, was running from the Kalends of January; from the eighth day before the Kalends of October, that is, 24 September, the twelfth indiction according to the Caesarean or Constantinopolitan reckoning was in force, the reckoning also used by Louis the Pious and his sons.]

Enacted at Frankfurt, [Note: [Col. 1244D] It is clear from this that Louis the German came to Frankfurt earlier than Thegan reports in *The Deeds of Louis the Pious*, no. 45, in Bouquet, *Recueil des historiens des Gaules et de la France*, vol. VI, p. 83, where he says: “From Compiègne, he continues, they afterward led the most pious prince, the emperor Louis, to the palace at Aachen. When his like-named son heard this, he departed from Bavaria, driven by great grief because of the injury to his father. Coming to the palace at Frankfurt, he immediately sent his envoys from there, etc.” For the author of the *Life of Louis the Pious*, in the cited place, p. 114, testifies that Emperor Lothair came with his father to Compiègne on the Kalends of October and departed from there for Aachen, once this matter had been completed, on the feast of Saint Martin, that is, 11 November.] in the royal palace, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## CLXXXVIII. For the monastery of New Corbie. (Year 834.)

[In Schaten, *Annales Paderbornenses*, p. 94.]

In the name of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divine favor of God’s mercy, Emperor Augustus.

If, through the gift of our liberality, we bestow upon places dedicated to God something from the benefits granted to us by God, we hope that this will profit us both in passing our mortal life happily and in obtaining eternal life forever. Therefore we wish it to be known to the discernment of all our faithful, present and [Col. 1244D] future, that, at the request of the venerable Abbot Warinus, who is known to hold in his governance by our grant the monastery called New Corbie, our highness was pleased to transfer by this authority of ours to the aforesaid monastery a certain cell belonging to us, called Meppia, built in the district of Adegringen, so that it might remain forever under its authority together with everything belonging to it.

As we have said, we make this cell subject in its entirety, together with all its property and appurtenances—that is, basilicas, houses and other buildings, lands, meadows, forests, cultivated and uncultivated places, movable and immovable property, and slaves of every sex and age—to the aforesaid monastery. By this authority of ours we grant and transfer it in such a way that it shall remain in the right of that monastery and of the monks serving God there in the course of time, for various needs and for carrying out divine worship with greater devotion, without diminution or retraction by anyone. No one among our faithful shall presume, on any pretext whatsoever, to take it away from their control and authority or transfer it to any other place.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors, and the monks residing in the aforesaid monastery in the course of time, be permitted to use the aforesaid cell and everything belonging to it more diligently in the service of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, without anyone’s opposition, and to arrange, dispose of, and justly administer whatever pertains to their uses and needs in the warfare of our Lord Jesus Christ. Thus they may more joyfully and continually implore the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife and offspring, and the peace and stability [Col. 1245C] of the whole Empire entrusted to us by God.
