Therefore we command that no public judge or anyone exercising judicial authority dare enter the churches, estates, places, fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid church which it possesses at the present time, or which divine piety may henceforth increase in the right of that place, in order to hear or investigate cases according to judicial custom, to exact fines, to impose lodging or transport obligations, to take sureties, or to constrain the men of that church contrary to reason; nor may anyone seek any restitutions or unlawful pretexts.

We further command that the properties which it justly and legally possesses at the present time, or which divine piety may wish to increase there, remain in their right and control without anyone’s disturbance or unlawful opposition, and that they suffer no unjust claim or demand concerning them from anyone at any time. Rather, let them be permitted to possess the aforesaid properties, with everything justly and legally belonging to them, in peaceful order and without anyone’s unjust opposition, and to dispose of them according to ecclesiastical law as they wish, so that, carrying out divine worship more abundantly with our assistance, they may gladly pray more earnestly for the mercy of the Lord on behalf of our safety, that of our wife and offspring, and the stability of our empire.

And so that this authority of ours may remain unshaken in the present and future, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Hirminmarus, notary, in place of Hugo, have reviewed this.

Given on the third day before the Nones of March, in the twenty-third year, with Christ’s favor, [Note: [Col. 1271D] In the corrupted exemplar, very badly, “year 20.” Dom Vaissetius, in volume I of his *History of Languedoc*, p. 745, col. 1, thinks that it should be corrected to “year 8,” so that the indiction may correspond, and refers the charter to the year 821; but that most learned man did not notice that Hugo, in whose place the charter was reviewed, did not succeed Theoto in the office of chancellor until the year 834.] of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the fourteenth indiction [Note: [Col. 1272D] We have restored this from the corrupted exemplar. In the printed edition it is incorrectly “indiction 13.”]. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## CCIX. LOUIS THE PIOUS’S DIPLOMA FOR THE CHURCH OF LE MANS (Year 836)

[In Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. I, p. 97.]

In the name of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, [Col. 1272A] Louis, by the clemency of God’s favor, emperor Augustus.

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own, present and future, that the venerable Aldricus, bishop of the city of Le Mans, fervent alike in divine honor and love, strove to build, through his own new work and sweat and labor, a small monastery in his parish, in honor of God and our Savior, and of His holy mother Mary, and of the blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius and Stephen, and of all the saints generally, in a place formerly called by the common people Broialus. He diligently brought it to the desired and fitting beauty and completion, solemnly dedicated it at the appropriate time, and did not delay enriching it sufficiently from the possessions of the aforesaid see divinely entrusted to him, so as abundantly to support and supply the various needs of the monks serving the Lord there.

Accordingly, presenting to the sight of our majesty a certain document strengthened by the hands of himself and the other venerable bishops, and of the remaining orders serving God, as well as of religious laymen and nobles alike, he humbly begged our clemency to decree that what he had done, touched by divine love, in pious and religious devotion and supported by heavenly assistance, should be strengthened by our imperial authority and remain perpetually most firmly established, without anyone’s overturning or evasion. He also asked that the monks dwelling there, with his consent and that of his successors, should have permission among themselves to choose abbots to govern them according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

Gladly lending the ear of favor to his most pious, God-loving, and most welcome supplications, we ordered this written instrument of our authority to be made and given to him. Through it we decree and sanction that the aforesaid work, brought about by his most religious efforts, remain firm and stable at all times, exactly as he set it out in the aforesaid document of his devotion, which he had presented to us for rereading. No one, at any time, shall diminish anything from the properties which he contributed to that same small monastery, nor shall anyone presume on any pretext to overturn or in any way neglect the conditions established there through his efforts. Rather, just as he piously [Col. 1272D] and religiously ordained them, so, through this authority of ours, they shall remain perpetually unshaken.

Moreover, whenever, by divine calling, the abbot who is in charge at the present time, or those who are to be appointed in future, depart from this life, they shall have permission, with the consent of that same Bishop Aldricus and his successors, namely the bishops of the aforesaid see, to choose abbots from among themselves, if men can be found among them who are able, by the merit of their life and knowledge, to preside over them according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and to be of service to them.

And so that this authority of our confirmation may retain perpetual firmness in our times and those of our successors, we ordered it to be sealed below with the impression of our ring.

I, Hincminmarus, notary, in place of Hugo, have reviewed and subscribed.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, in the twenty-third year, with Christ’s favor, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the fifteenth indiction. Done at Gundulf’s estate, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## CCX. FOR THE SAME CHURCH (Year 836)

[In Baluze, *ibid.*, p. 100.]

[Col. 1273B]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the clemency of God’s favor, emperor Augustus.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, that Aldricus, venerable bishop of the city of Le Mans, presented for rereading before the sight of our majesty a certain document of his devotion and disposition, in which he had established and religiously arranged how the properties found at the time of his death in the bishopric entrusted to him should faithfully be distributed as his alms, according to the will and manner ecclesiastically described by him. He humbly asked that what was clearly arranged by him in pious devotion and most religious intention should be made unshaken by our imperial authority.

Assenting to his venerable supplications, we ordered this written instrument of our authority to be made for him. Through it we decree and sanction that, just as it is established and distributed by him through the aforesaid document, so it shall be observed in every respect and held most firmly. No one’s greedy wickedness or wicked greed shall dare to overturn it by any trick or divert anything to personal use. Rather, just as it is clearly seen to have been established by him, as we have said, with the greatest religious care, so it shall be carried out without delay or fear by those whom he chooses to obtain that same distribution. Thus he himself may receive from the Rewarder of all the fruit of so great a disposition in eternal blessedness, and we may more abundantly merit to attain a share in that same blessedness.

Therefore, so that this authority of ours may be able to retain inviolable force, we ordered it to be sealed below with the impression of our ring.

I, Hirminmarus, notary, in place of Hugo, have reviewed and subscribed.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of September, in the twenty-fifth year, with Christ’s favor, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the first indiction.

Done at the royal palace of Quierzy, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## CCXI. FOR THE SAME CHURCH (Year 836)

[In Baluze, *ibid.*]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, [Col. 1274A] Louis, by the clemency of God’s favor, emperor Augustus.

If we lend an ear to the just and reasonable petitions of priests and servants of God, and bring their just and reasonable requests to the desired result, we not only exercise the royal and imperial custom, but also make them more devoted and ready to implore the Lord’s mercy for our transgressions; and through this we trust that God’s immeasurable mercy may more easily be reconciled to us.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own, present and future, that Aldricus, venerable bishop, presented to us certain charters of the kings of the Franks, namely of our predecessors, concerning his monastery, situated and consecrated outside the walls of that same city in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, and of the other saints. Through these charters they established it immune from every public obligation and placed it under their immunity and protection. He humbly requested that we sanction by imperial authority the pious acts of our predecessors, to be strengthened by the customary kindness and gentleness of our majesty.

Gladly lending the ear of favor to his prayers, we ordered these letters of our authority to be made concerning the aforesaid monastery. Through them we command and order that no one, whether of higher or lower rank, or anyone exercising judicial authority, presume at any time to enter the estates, villages, places, or fields of that monastery in order to hear cases according to judicial custom, impose or exact claims, demand tolls, collect fines or sureties, impose lodging or transport obligations, constrain the men of that monastery, whether free or servile, or seek or exact any restitutions.

Rather, whatever the treasury might have hoped to obtain from it shall perpetually be assigned and applied to the lights of the same church and to relieving and supporting the needs of the congregation serving the Lord there, so that that congregation may gladly pray more earnestly for the mercy of the Lord on behalf of us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of our entire empire.

If, however, anyone exercising judicial authority should prove so rash as to attempt to violate this command of ours and theirs, let him know that, as is contained in the immunities of our predecessors, he shall be fined 600 solidi, two-thirds of which the rectors of the aforesaid monastery shall receive, and one-third our treasury.

And so that this authority of ours may retain inviolable and unshaken firmness, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be authenticated below with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most pious emperor.

I, Hirminmarus, notary, in place of Hugo, have reviewed and subscribed.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twenty-third year, with Christ’s favor, of the reign of [Col. 1275A] our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the fourth indiction.

Done at the royal palace of Aachen, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## CCXII. FOR THE SAME CHURCH (Year 836)

[In Baluze, *ibid.*]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the clemency of God’s favor, emperor Augustus.

If we willingly assent to the petitions of priests and servants of God, to their just and reasonable requests concerning whatever affairs and needs of the churches entrusted to them, and with God’s help bring them to fulfillment, we not only exercise the royal and imperial custom, but clearly believe that this will benefit us in receiving the rewards of eternal recompense.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own, present and future, that Aldricus, venerable bishop of the city of Le Mans, approached our serenity and made known to us that the monastery of Anisola, situated within the boundaries of his parish, in which Saint Carilephus also rests bodily, had been given and established by the aforesaid lord Carilephus, with the authorization and arrangement of Lord Innocent, formerly bishop of the aforesaid city, from properties belonging both to his bishopric and to other good men, kings as well as other noblemen, which had been handed over to the aforesaid Lord Carilephus.

He himself later, through written charters and with the permission, authorization, and consent of Childebert, king of the Franks, at the urging and on the confirmed command of the aforesaid Childebert, king of the Franks, gave these properties to the mother church of the city, which is built in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, and confirmed them canonically and legally. Upon these properties the aforesaid monastery was founded and built by the holy men just mentioned, and for a long time was canonically and legally possessed and governed by the bishops of the aforesaid see. But after certain causes intervened, it was later withdrawn from the right of the aforesaid mother church [Col. 1275D] and unjustly alienated for a period of time.

All this, as it was truthfully reported and demonstrated to us in writing by Drogo, our brother and archchaplain, and by the other faithful envoys whom we ordered to investigate and inquire into the matter diligently, had formerly been thoroughly examined and carefully investigated, both personally and through his most faithful envoys, by the lord and our father of blessed memory, Charles, glorious king of the Franks. After the truth of the matter had been truthfully investigated and fully known in every respect, the monastery of Anisola had been canonically and legally restored to the right and authority of the aforesaid mother church of Le Mans, whose bishop was Franco, by his command, strengthened with his own hand and marked with the impression of his ring, to be possessed in future according to ecclesiastical law.

So that what he asserted might in every respect be made genuinely clear to us, he presented to the sight of our majesty certain documents strengthened by the subscriptions of holy men: namely, written records, the investigation of the aforesaid lord and our father Charles, most pious Augustus, and the aforementioned command by which, as has already been said, he solemnly and legally restored the aforesaid monastery of Anisola to the mother church.

Moreover, he brought before us several other charters of kings—many of them, namely, of our predecessors, the kings of the Franks—strengthened by their own hands and sealed below with their seals. When these had been examined and reread, it was clearly shown that the aforesaid monastery belonged by right to the aforesaid see of Le Mans entrusted to him, and that it ought to remain under its authority by the strongest legal right. Therefore he humbly implored our clemency that what was declared by such evident proofs might also be declared by our assent, indeed by our authority.

When we had learned these matters more clearly and judged it fitting to extend the favor of our high office to them for the love of God and out of reverence for that holy see, we ordered this command of our authority to be made and given to his successors for all time. Through it we decree and sanction that the aforesaid monastery of Anisola, which for some time had been withdrawn from their right and jurisdiction, shall henceforth and in future be held and possessed by them. They shall have free power to dispose of it according to ecclesiastical custom as they wish; nor shall it ever thereafter be separated from the right of the aforesaid see and its rectors by any pretext or violence. Rather, with everything belonging to it, it shall perpetually remain wholly and faithfully under the power, disposition, and will of that see and its rectors, for the more devoted performance of divine worship.

And so that this authority of our restoration may retain inviolable, unshaken, and perpetual firmness, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be authenticated below with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most pious emperor.

I, Hirminmarus, notary, in place of Hugo, have reviewed and subscribed.

[Col. 1276D]

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of September, in the twenty-fifth year, with Christ’s favor, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the first indiction.

Done at the royal palace of Quierzy, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## CCXIII. FOR ALDRICUS, BISHOP OF LE MANS (Year 836)

A privilege concerning coinage is granted to him and his successors.

[In Baluze, *ibid.*]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the clemency of God’s favor, emperor Augustus.

[Col. 1277A]

If we lend an ear to the just and reasonable petitions of priests and servants of God and bring them to the desired result, we not only exercise the royal and imperial custom, but also make them more devoted and ready to implore the Lord’s mercy for our transgressions; and through this we trust that God’s immeasurable mercy may more easily be reconciled to us.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own, present and future, that a venerable man named Aldricus, bishop of the city of Le Mans, made known to us that his predecessors, namely Merolus and Gauzciolenus, and their predecessors, had possessed in the aforesaid city a public mint, granted to them with full authority by charters of the lord and our father Charles, of blessed memory, and of our grandfather Pippin, as well as of King Theoderic and earlier kings.

Because the property of the aforesaid see had been taken away or devastated, that mint had ceased for a time, although only briefly, during our reign or toward the end of the reign of our aforesaid father; and because of the poverty and desolation of those properties, it had been abandoned. Neither we, nor the lord Charles our father, nor any of our envoys prohibited it by our authority or his, but it had been abandoned solely because of the aforesaid want.

The aforementioned bishop also presented to our sight charters of our predecessors, namely the Frankish kings, which stated that the aforesaid mint had been granted to the predecessors of the aforesaid Bishop Aldricus by the aforementioned kings in ancient and recent times.

When we reread these documents and saw in them the signs and seals of our royal predecessors as well, we recognized that what he had said was true. Therefore we command and order that no envoy of ours, nor the count of that province, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, presume at any time to bring against him or his successors any claim, annoyance, unjust summons, accusation, or contrivance concerning the aforesaid mint.

Rather, in our times and in those to come, the aforesaid mint shall remain in the aforesaid city with the aforementioned bishop and his successors. This condition shall apply, however: the aforesaid Aldricus and his successors shall ensure that no false coin appears in that mint.

And so that this grant of ours concerning the aforesaid mint, which we ordered to be made for the love of God and out of reverence for that place, may be preserved for future times, more truly believed, and more diligently maintained, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most pious emperor.

I, Hirminmarus, notary, in place of Hugo, have reviewed and subscribed.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the twenty-third year, with Christ’s favor, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the fourteenth indiction.

Done at the royal palace of Aachen, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1278A]

## CCXIV. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT CARILEPHUS (Year 836)

[In Baluze, *ibid.*]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the clemency of God’s favor, emperor Augustus.

If we lend an ear to the just and reasonable petitions of priests and servants of God, and bring their just and reasonable requests to the desired conclusion, we not only exercise the royal and imperial custom, but also make them more devoted and readier to beseech the Lord’s mercy for our transgressions; and through this we trust that God’s immense mercy may more easily be reconciled to us. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of holy God’s Church and to our own people, present and future, that Aldricus, venerable bishop of the city of Le Mans, brought before us certain charters of the kings of the Franks, our predecessors, concerning his monastery situated within the boundaries of the aforesaid city’s diocese, in a place called Anisola, where the body of Saint Carilephus rests, and which is situated and consecrated in honor of the aforesaid Saint Carilephus and other saints. Through these charters they established it exempt from all public obligations and placed it under their immunity and protection. He humbly requested that we should confirm by imperial authority the pious deeds of our predecessors, in accordance with the customary benevolence and gentleness of our majesty.

Gladly lending the ear of our favor to his requests, we ordered this charter of our authority concerning the aforesaid monastery to be drawn up. Through it we command and decree that no one, whether of higher or lower rank, or anyone exercising judicial authority, at any time presume to enter the courts, estates, villages, places, or lands of the same monastery in order to hear cases according to judicial custom, or to impose or exact levies, or to demand tolls, or to collect fines or sureties, or to require lodgings or provisions, or to distrain the men of that monastery, whether free or enslaved, or to seek or exact any repayments. Rather, whatever the fisc could have expected from there shall henceforth be assigned and applied entirely to the lighting of that church and to relieving and supporting the needs of the community serving the Lord there, so that the aforesaid community may gladly beseech the Lord’s mercy more attentively on behalf of us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of our entire empire.

If, however, anyone exercising judicial authority should be so rash as to attempt to violate this charter of ours or those of our predecessors, let him know that, as is contained in the immunities of our predecessors, he shall be fined 600 solidi, of which two parts shall be received by the administrators of the aforesaid monastery and the third by our fisc. And so that this authority of ours may retain perpetual and unshaken firmness, we confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be authenticated by the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most pious emperor.

I, Hirminmarus, notary, acting in the place of Hugo, have examined and subscribed.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of September, in the twenty-fifth year, by Christ’s favor, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the first indiction.

Done at the royal palace of Quierzy, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

## CCXV. THE VILLA OF LUGDUNUM IS GRANTED TO THE CHURCH OF LE MANS. (Year 836.)

*[In Baluze, the same work.]*

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the clemency of God’s renewed favor, emperor Augustus.

If we bring the just and reasonable petitions and requests of our faithful—requests which they make for the benefit and exaltation of holy God’s Church—to the desired conclusion, we not only exercise in this matter the royal and imperial custom, but also, as we believe, make them more ready and more devoted toward us. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of holy God’s Church and to our own people, present and future, that Count Banzlegbus, our margrave of the land of Saxony, informed us that he possessed, by our benefice, a certain villa situated in the district of Le Mans, called Lugdunum, under the legal right of the canonical mother church, and that every year he paid from it the ninths, lawful rents, and tithes to the aforesaid mother church and its administrators.

Considering the uncertainty of human frailty, therefore, and fearing the final day of his summons, and fearing that the aforesaid villa might, through some impulse of his greed or by any stratagem, be alienated from the right of the aforesaid mother church, the said Banzlegbus, burning with divine love, approached our clemency and humbly begged that we should now return the villa called Lugdunum, with all its appurtenances, to the church of the aforesaid see of Le Mans and to Aldricus, the venerable bishop of that city, by our imperial authority, and confirm by our charter this restitution, so that it might be possessed more securely by that church and its administrators in future times.

We gladly heard his petition, out of love for God and reverence for that holy place and for the servants of God serving the Lord there, and we deemed it right to fulfill his supplication and pious desire as requested. Therefore, by this written instrument of our authority, we establish, decree, and command that, just as the aforesaid Banzlegbus, our faithful man, held the aforesaid villa in its entirety—just as it was under our authority on the day when he is known to have received that benefice from our grant—we have now returned it, for the benefit of our soul and the stability of our empire, to the venerable Bishop Aldricus for the use of his church, so that it shall remain forever for the benefit and use of that church and of those serving God therein.

Accordingly, at the suggestion and humble request of our aforesaid faithful, namely the venerable Bishop Aldricus and the aforementioned Banzlegbus, our faithful, we ordered this charter of our confirmation and restitution to be made for the aforesaid Bishop Aldricus, or for the use of the aforesaid city. Through it we decree and command that no one living under the authority of our empire shall at any time presume to cause any disturbance or bring any charge against the aforesaid Bishop Aldricus or his successors concerning the aforesaid villa or anything belonging to it, in whatever districts or places they may be; rather, he and his successors shall be permitted peacefully to hold and possess the aforesaid villa, with all its places and territories, whether persons bound to it or anything else belonging to it, by ecclesiastical right. Whatever they decide to do from it for the advantage and benefit of the aforesaid church of the see, they shall have full power to do in every respect in future times.

And so that this authority of our restitution may retain perpetual firmness, we confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Hirminmarus, notary, acting in the place of Hugo, have examined and subscribed.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the twenty-fifth year, by Christ’s favor, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the first indiction.

Done at the royal palace of Aachen, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

## CCXVI. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT COLUMBA AT SENS. (Year 836.)

*[From manuscript records of the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, in D. Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 610.]*

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the clemency of God’s favor [renewed favor], emperor Augustus.

We wish it to be known to all the faithful of holy God’s Church and to our own people, present and future, that long ago, when it was evident that the monastic order had everywhere been corrupted, and when, in order to correct and amend it—or rather, with the Lord’s help, to restore it to its former proper order and rectitude—we sent through the monasteries of the empire entrusted to us by God a certain abbot of that order, exceedingly zealous, named Benedict, it happened that he came to the monastery called Saint Columba, not far from the city of Sens.

While he was endeavoring to arrange the other matters there according to rule, since at that time a canonical abbot named Jacob happened to preside there, he set apart certain villas which in former times had been assigned for the use of the brothers serving God there, so that they might serve their needs perpetually, without royal or public service, or any gift or exaction by an abbot. These were: the villa called Morus, with everything belonging to it; the villa called Sarmasia, with everything belonging to it; likewise the villa of Tauriaca, with everything belonging to it; likewise the villa of Patricius, with everything belonging to it; likewise the villa now called Longa-Aqua, with everything belonging to it; and likewise everything which the aforesaid monastery is known to possess in these villas. Their names are as follows:

The villa of Gromen, the villa of Aurosus, the villa of Messeriacus, the villa of Canapus, the villa of Coriacus, the villa of Gravunciacus, the villa of Floxus, the villa of Curtennis, the villa of Spiriacus, the villa of Abo, the villa of Bandricus, the villa of Paciacus, the villa of Lupon, the villa of Syncleriacus, the villa of Regniacus; also, above the river called Fullonis, two guesthouses; and likewise that property which Auffridus and Donatus, nephews of Jeremiah, formerly bishop of the city of Sens, lawfully transferred to the aforesaid monastery; likewise the vineyards, arable lands, and meadows known to lie around the aforesaid monastery of Saint Columba; and the guesthouses known to lie in the place called Canalis.

But because thereafter the aforesaid monastery had been subjected through the deceit of certain people to the Church of Sens, although, after learning the matter more clearly, we had restored it to its own right and lordship and to the administration of its proper abbots, the venerable man Supplicius, abbot of that monastery, came into the presence of our majesty and humbly begged our clemency that he might receive our charter by which our establishment might remain firm and inviolable in our time and in that of our successors.

Judging it right and reasonable to favor his petitions, we ordered these imperial letters of ours to be made concerning the aforesaid monastery. Through them we command and decree that, subject to no church, but living under the authority and administration of its own leaders, it shall never at any time pay, or be compelled to pay, any service, payment, or other obligation from the aforesaid villas. Rather, without any reduction of their possessions, they shall always serve the uses of the brothers serving God there and their various needs. Nor shall any abbot, whether of that or another order, presume to grant any of them as a benefice to anyone; rather, as we have said, they shall perpetually serve their uses and the reception of the poor.

As for whatever shall be necessary to repair the roofs of that monastery, we decree and command that it be irreproachably restored from the common resources of the monastery itself.

And so that this authority of our confirmation may be preserved inviolate in our time and in that of our successors, we confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be authenticated by the impression of our ring.

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of April, in the twenty-third year, by Christ’s favor, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the thirteenth indiction [Note: Correct: the fourteenth indiction.]. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

## CCXVII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT SALVATOR AT REDON. (Year 836.)

*[From the proofs of the History of Brittany, p. 30, in D. Bouquet, the same work.]*

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the clemency of God’s renewed favor, emperor Augustus.

“If, out of love for him, etc.” [Note: As above in the charter for the same monastery, col. 1251.] Moved by his request, and at the same time admonished by the exhortation and intervention of our faithful Nominoe, it pleased our serenity to hand over, by this authority of ours, to the aforesaid monastery and to the monks serving God there for a long time, the parish called Rannac, with all its integrity, as well as the small place called Plaz, and indeed the little parish called Ardon, etc. [Note: As above, in the same place.]

Given on the third day before the Kalends of September, in the twenty-third year, by Christ’s favor, of the reign of Lord Louis, in the fifteenth indiction [Note: Correction: in the fourteenth indiction.]. Done at the royal palace of Quierzy, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

## CCXVIII. FOR VERENDARIUS, BISHOP OF CHUR. [Note: Schoepflinus published this charter in *Alsatia diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 77, from the manuscript of Christian Urstisius, which is at Basel; but it is extremely faulty and mutilated. Here we give it as it was transcribed from the original and communicated to us by D. de Jost.] (Year 836.)

*[In Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, vol. II, p. 203.]*

In the name of the Lord God, our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the clemency of God’s renewed favor, emperor Augustus.

Let it therefore be known to all the faithful of holy God’s Church and to our own people, present and future, that our beloved brother Drogo, archbishop and chief chaplain of our sacred palace, and likewise Rataldus, also a bishop, approached our gentleness and informed us that, when, by divine judgment, we had been deprived of the honors bestowed upon us from heaven through the ill will and faction of certain people [Note: Emperor Louis the Pious alludes to his wicked deposition from the throne in 833], and when Verendarius [Note: Fortunatus Sprecher, in *Rhaetia*, book III, p. 98, relates the following: “Verendarius, most dear to Louis, succeeded Victor as bishop of Chur . . . . . He is deprived of the bishopric and prefecture by the sons of Louis . . . . . But, once restored, the emperor reinstated Verendarius and confirmed to him all privileges in Rhaetia, likewise those concerning the parish and possessions of Sélestat in Alsace and others,” etc. Bucelinus, in *Rhaetia Sacred and Profane*, p. 173, records the same grant at the year 835; as do Tschudi, *Gallia comata*, book I, part IV, chapter 6, p. 233, at the year 836; D. L. B. de Zurlauben’s manuscript *Helvetico-Tugiensian Monuments*, vol. VI, p. 37; and Leu, *Swiss Lexicon*, vol. V, p. 264, who places his death on 3 October 844], the venerable bishop of Chur, because of the loyalty he had preserved toward us, had been deprived of his proper honors and driven into exile, a certain charter of our lord and father, Charles, most serene emperor, by which he had solemnly granted to that church certain properties of his own, had been lost and entirely withdrawn from the right of that church.

[Note: Drogo, son of Charlemagne, was made bishop of Metz in 818 and always remained faithful to his brother Louis the Pious, as the *Annals of Bertin* prove, in Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 195. He was given the title of archbishop as an honor. In the Acts of the Council of Thionville, at which Ebbo of Reims was deposed in 835, Drogo, archbishop, subscribed first of all. Drogo is called “our brother and chief chaplain” in a charter of Louis the Pious by which, in 838, the emperor returned the monastery of Anisola to Aldricus, bishop of Le Mans, in Baluze, book III of the *Miscellany*, p. 96.]

[Note: Rataldus, or Rothadus, bishop of Soissons, also took part in the deposition of Ebbo of Reims and, at the emperor’s command, led him to the abbey of Fulda, as Flodoard relates in the *History of the Church of Reims*, book II, chapter 20. Eckard mentions Rataldus in the years 831, 837, and 838, *Eastern Francia*, vol. II, pp. 250, 299, and 309.]

But since it is established that the aforesaid bishop had been driven into exile because of us, and since, during that same interval, the aforesaid charter of our lord and father had been lost, until divine mercy restored us to our former honor and also returned the aforesaid bishop to his own church, they requested our highness likewise concerning the following matter: without imperial authority he could in no way securely retain under the firm legal right of his church the properties located in the district of Alsace, in the place called Selezistata—namely, a chapel with everything belonging to it—and the toll at the city of Chur collected from travelers.

[Note: Today, Sélestat, a town of Alsace.]

They therefore asked that he might receive from us a written charter concerning these properties, by which, without anyone’s unlawful opposition or disturbance, he might thereafter possess these portions of the aforesaid bishopric and administer them by legitimate right.

Agreeing to their reasonable requests, we decreed that these letters of our authority should be made and given to the aforesaid bishop and his successors throughout the passing ages. Through them we command and decree that henceforth the aforesaid properties in their entirety, and the toll from all travelers, shall perpetually remain with the church of holy Mary and its administrators, by Christ’s favor; and that they shall have full power in every respect to do with them whatever they wish by ecclesiastical right. Nor should they ever fear suffering from anyone any charge, diminution, or withholding on account of the loss of the authority of that lord and father of ours. Thus they may gladly beseech the Lord’s clemency more freely for our salvation and that of all our people, and for the stability of the empire divinely entrusted to us.

And so that our authority may retain indissoluble firmness, we ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the twenty-second year, by Christ’s favor, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the fourteenth indiction. Done at Frankfurt [Note: Schoepflinus wrongly read: “at the royal palace of Aachen, at the place Frankfurt.” He also adds: “I, Hirminmarus, notary, acting in the place of Hugo, have examined”; these words are not found in the original.], successfully in the name of God. Amen.

## CCXIX. FOR THE MONASTERY OF LONGOVILLE. (Year 836.)

*[D. Calmet, *History of Lorraine*.]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Louis, by God’s gracious favor, Roman emperor Augustus.

If we restore places devoted to divine worship and correct with pious intention what needs correction, we do not hesitate to do such things, since they undoubtedly contribute to the stability of our kingdom and empire and to the receipt of eternal recompense. Therefore let all our people and all faithful Christians know that the brothers of the church of Glandern, consecrated in honor of holy Mary, God’s mother, and of the holy confessors Martin, Dignus, Bodagislus, and Undo, came complaining into our presence. They said that their church had been deprived by the kings who existed before our ancestor Charlemagne of courts and villas, and of benefices granted to the church of Glandern by Lord Bodagislus, father of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz; and that these properties had been cruelly taken away by tyrants from the founders of the place themselves, Saints Dignus and Undo.

We therefore lent them the ear of our clemency, especially because that monastery itself belonged to the empire, and we sought the counsel of the princes of the empire concerning this matter. They judged that what had been unjustly taken from them ought to be returned to them by judgment of the court. We heard this judgment with willing and grateful mind.

Accordingly, through the intervention of our wife, Queen Gruingardis, and of our sons Lothair Caesar, Pippin, and Louis, and of Angilramnus, chief chaplain of the palace and bishop of the city of Metz, and of the princes of the court, we return to them a certain court called Grundstat, with its church and endowment, and two other churches, of Mertenshein and of Vettemberg, with their endowments. Just as our father, namely Charles, and we ourselves held them, so we return them in their entirety to God and his holy mother Mary, and to the blessed confessors of Christ, Martin, Dignus, Bodagislus, and Undo, with all their appurtenances: with their men and women, revenues, rents, lands and mills, those acquired and those yet to be acquired, movable and immovable property, outputs, springs, and all those customary rights by which we have used them. By imperial authority and by judgment of the princes, we return them to those brothers.

If, however, any of our successors, kings or emperors, or any powerful person, tyrant, or wrongdoer should attempt to take away, invade, exchange [perhaps “transfer by exchange”], give in precarious tenure, or alienate the court which we return, by power, violence, or pretext, or should obstruct it, may holy Mary regard him as her adversary, and may all the holy confessors of Christ—Martin, Dignus, Undo, and Bodagislus—be enemies and judges of his perversity.

In the presence of the princes of the entire empire and of the brothers of the church of Glandern, we therefore ordered this charter to be preserved in the sacristy of Saint Peter and to be marked with our seal.

The sign of Louis, most pious emperor.

I, Hubaldus, have subscribed in the place of Angilramnus, chief chaplain.

Done at Worms on the Ides of May, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 836, in the seventh indiction, while Louis the most pious was emperor, in the eighth year of his consecration, ruling in the kingdom of the Franks.

## CCXX. FOR THE MONASTERY OF HOHENBURG. [Note: The style and formulas, unusual for Louis the Pious, make this charter highly suspect, if not entirely false.] (Year 837.)

*[From a certified transcript of the year 1385, in the episcopal archive at Saverne, in Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, vol. II, p. 205.]*

[Note: This certified transcript of the charter is found in a parchment judicial document of the year 1487 in the archive of Saverne, whose title reads: “Acts and proceedings between the monastery of Hohenburg and that of Moersberg.” It is there said to have been certified on 4 October 1385 by a public notary. It was previously reported by Dionysius Albrecht, *History of Hohenburg*, among the proofs, p. 16, and by Schoepflinus, *Alsatia diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 106, who rightly lists it among interpolated charters; both, however, published it inaccurately. An authentic charter of immunity of Louis the Pious from the same day and year exists, and we give it below as the following number.]

Louis, by the grace of God Roman emperor, ever Augustus, for perpetual remembrance.

We consider it pious and consonant with reason that those things which our father, Charles, most pious emperor, prudently granted to ecclesiastical persons and those of religious status should be fortified by the strength of our confirmation, so that they may not suffer the inconveniences of anyone’s accusation. Our beloved wife Judith, ever Augusta, approached the presence of our majesty and devoutly requested that certain letters and privileges of the venerable duke, father of Saint Odilia, should be renewed.

Gladly fulfilling her petition, we ordered this charter of our authority and immunity to be made, and we decree and sanction that the monastery called Hohenburg, with all that belongs or pertains to it, shall remain under our protection, just as it is established that it remained under the protection and defense of our father.

That honorable prince, noble by birth, virtuous in mind, and glorious in devotion, Duke Adelricus, also called Ethicus, concerned for the salvation of his soul and seeking a place more withdrawn from human affairs in which to devote himself to God, chose the aforesaid mountain of Hohenburg as his dwelling, rather than a valley. There he founded and built, with all honor and propriety, a cloister for women or ladies who were to remain there perpetually in the service of God. With due thought and piety, he transferred to them every dignity, lordship, authority, and right belonging to such an institution; and, by endowment, he surrendered to the altar of the blessed Virgin Mary there all the immovable and other goods he possessed, especially Upper Ehenheim.

[Note: Today Oberehenheim, the sixth of the imperial cities of Alsace, situated at the foot of Mount Hohenburg and so called from the river Ehno flowing through it. This town came to the Hohenburg abbey through the munificence of Duke Adalricus, and formerly belonged entirely to that abbey, until it was taken from it by the emperors in the twelfth century.]

[Rodesheim,]

[Note: Today Rosheim, seventh in order among the imperial cities, one league distant from Oberehenheim, with which it shared the same fate in the twelfth century. The Hohenburg abbey retained from the ancient lordship of Rosheim a manorial court called Gutenhausen, with certain rights of immunity; this later passed from the abbey to the bishop of Strasbourg.]

with fifteen villas, which he wished to remain perpetually under the authority of the aforesaid ladies. He commended the church of the aforesaid villa to his holy daughter Odilia, and the aforesaid cloister or community of Hohenburg, with all its right and appurtenances, properties, and the other things listed above, for the benefit of the said ladies, just as he faithfully established and granted it.

He also transferred to his aforesaid daughter and her successors, to be possessed in perpetual right, jurisdiction in the upper manorial court of Ehenheim, and the hearing and examination of cases according to judicial custom, together with the church situated in that court, the right of patronage of that church, and the rights belonging to the said church, surrendering them with every right and liberty.

[Note: This right of patronage is today exercised by the bishop of Strasbourg, who possesses the Hohenburg properties. The church mentioned here stands in the middle of the city of Oberehnheim, near the senatorial court. Formerly it was the mother church; today it is called the Cappel-Kirch and is dedicated to blessed Mary.]

After these and many other things had been carried out by the aforesaid duke, and after his death, with much time and many years having passed, Saint Odilia the virgin, because of the suitability of the place, built a lower cloister in the valley.

[Note: Called Niedermünster.]

This did not in any way detract from the dignity, right, or piety of the abbess and the other ladies at Hohenburg. It must also be understood that Saint Odilia and many of the abbesses who followed her at Hohenburg, for many years and a long time, each alone faithfully governed and administered both cloisters after the completion of the aforesaid cloister.

And these facts prove and affirm that the same rights, powers, dignities, authorities, and lordships handed over by the father of Saint Odilia to the aforesaid cloister at Hohenburg remain and ought to remain inviolate.

The following are the properties and names of the villas which the aforesaid duke donated and granted to the church at Hohenburg:

Brunstatt,

[Note: Brunstatt, a village in Sundgau near Mulhouse, mentioned among the possessions of the lower monastery in Saint Odilia’s testament.]

Ilfurt,

[Note: A village above Mulhouse, situated on the left bank of the Ill.]

Hemmersdorf,

[Note: Today Heimersdorf, a village near Ferrette. The Odilian testament attests that Heimersdorf belonged to a court at Arlesheim assigned to the lower monastery.]

Limmiswiler,

[Note: Luemscheweiler in Sundgau.]

Hirsingen,

[Note: Hirschingen in Sundgau, situated between Ferrette and Altkirch, an appurtenance of the court of Arlesheim.]

Karoldespach,

[Note: Karstbach near Altkirch.]

Reiningen,

[Note: Reiningen, one league distant from Mulhouse.]

Kimmenheim,

[Note: Kunheim in the bailiwick of Kochersberg, belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg.]

Gundolfsheim,

[Note: Gundelsheim near Rouffach.]

Regesheim,

[Note: Rexheim near Ensisheim.]

Rulechescheim,

[Note: Rurelsheim, not far from Ensisheim.]

Baltersheim,

[Note: Baltersheim, likewise in the vicinity of Ensisheim.]

Hetwiler.

[Note: An unknown village, unless perhaps it is Gertweiler near Barr, badly written by a copyist; it is mentioned in Saint Odilia’s testament.]

All the people belonging to the church of Hohenburg, whether living far away or nearby, ought to give the church what is called in the vernacular *Val*,

[Note: *Val*, or *Fall-Zins*, was a medieval term for rents payable every year on a fixed day under penalty of forfeiture of the holding. See Haltaus, *German Glossary*, p. 422.]

and a rent from their persons, except for the ministeriales, who are bound to defend the honor and liberty of the church.

We, for our part, in order to advance the benefit and prosperity of the aforesaid cloister of Hohenburg, so that the handmaids of God serving God there may gladly beseech God’s immeasurable clemency continually on behalf of us, our aforesaid wife and offspring, and the stability and peace of the entire empire divinely entrusted to us, and so that this authority of ours may possess inviolable and unshaken firmness, have subscribed and confirmed it with our own hand and ordered it to be authenticated by the attachment of our seal.

Given in our palace, in the year of the Lord eightieth [Note: It should read “eight hundredth.” But the date does not fit the year of Christ 837: neither the tenth indiction, which occurred in the years 817 and 832, nor the twelfth year of Louis the Pious, which was 825. In the year 837 the fifteenth indiction coincided.] thirty-seventh, in the tenth indiction, on the seventh day before the Ides of March, in the twelfth year of our reigns.

## CCXXI. FOR THE ABBEY OF HOHENBURG. (Year 837.)

*[From an old ninth-century parchment copy in the episcopal archive at Saverne, in Grandidier, the same work.]*

[Note: The original does not survive; but the copy was evidently written in the ninth or at least the tenth century, as is clear from the form of the letters and the age of the parchment. It cannot be called an original, since no traces remain of the seal that once existed. “A document that claims to be sealed,” say the French authors of the *New Diplomatics*, vol. VI, p. 355, “and shows no trace of a seal, is ordinarily only a copy.” The charter was reported, though incorrectly, by *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, p. 463, and by Schoepflinus, *Alsatia diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 78.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the clemency of God’s renewed favor,

[Note: From the year 834, when Louis the Pious was restored to the throne after his deposition, he retained his customary formula, but used *repropitiante*—“having again shown favor”—instead of *ordinante* or *propitiante*, because at his restoration he again experienced the favor of God, whom he acknowledged as the author of his first elevation.]

emperor Augustus.

When we strive to provide for places dedicated to God wherever they may have need, we confidently believe that we thereby merit more abundantly the favor of Him for whose love we are known to undertake this.

Therefore we wish it to be known to the diligence of all the faithful of holy God’s Church and of our own, both present and future, that our most beloved wife Judith [Note: Louis, after the death of Queen Irmengard, married Judith, daughter of Count Welf, in 819; the annals of that period contain much concerning her.], ever Augusta, caused to be brought before our majesty a certain charter of authority which our lord and father, Charles, most pious emperor [Note: The cited charter of Charlemagne has perished.], had ordered to be made for the monastery called Hohenburg, established in honor of the Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, for the sake of protection and immunity. She requested that we order it to be renewed according to customary practice and granted to the aforesaid monastery.

Gladly fulfilling her petition, we ordered this charter of our authority and immunity to be made, by which we decree and sanction that the aforesaid monastery, with everything belonging or pertaining to it, shall remain under our defense and the protection of immunity. No public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, nor any other person, greater or lesser, shall dare in our time or in that of our successors to enter the churches, places, lands, or remaining possessions which it presently justly and legally possesses, in whatever counties or territories, by grant of our empire, or which divine mercy may thereafter will to be increased under its right, in order to hear or investigate cases according to judicial procedure, exact public services, take sureties, unjustly constrain its men, both free and enslaved, or those dwelling upon its land, or exact fines; nor shall anyone demand any returns or unlawful exactions [Note: That is, payments imposed on account of the occasions of wars or other necessities. Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. IV, p. 1311.]. No one shall dare to enter for any of these purposes, nor presume to exact anything stated above.

Rather, with every disturbance by judicial authority and wicked men removed, the same monastery, together with all its property and dependents belonging to it, shall, as has been said, always remain peaceful under our imperial protection and the defense of immunity.

Whatever the royal treasury could have exacted from those same properties, we have granted entirely to the same monastery as an act of our almsgiving, just as it is established that our lord and father did, so that it might be carried out for its benefit and advancement; in order that the women serving God there may continually delight in entreating God’s immense mercy for us, for our aforesaid wife and offspring [Note: That is, for Charles called the Bald, whom Louis the Pious had by his wife Judith in 822, and whom his father crowned king of Neustria in 838], and for the stability and peace of the whole empire divinely bestowed upon us.

And so that this charter of our authority may possess unviolated and unshaken permanence, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be authenticated by the impression of our ring.

[Col. 1289A]

Issued on the seventh day before the Ides of March, in the twenty-fourth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the fifteenth indiction. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen. [Note: Bouquet notes in *Scriptores rerum Gallicarum*, vol. VI, p. 450, that certain charters survive in which the subscriptions of both Louis and the notary and chancellor are omitted; the same is found in the original documents themselves. It is therefore not surprising that they are also absent from copies.]

## CCXXII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF NONANTULA

*(Year 837.)* Diploma of Lothair I Augustus, by which he orders that no one shall preside over the monastery of Nonantula except one whom the monks have chosen from their own congregation.

[In Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, vol. VI, p. 308.]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal God, Lothair, by the ordering of divine providence, emperor Augustus.

It is fitting that those placed at the head of imperial glory should pursue the abundance of divine services with all the greater zeal, inasmuch as the wealth of the Most High, sufficiently demonstrated by apostolic documents, shows them a way more excellent than others, so that by his mercy the blessings of the present may be increased and, through his ineffable goodness, they may happily be crowned with the joys of eternal things that endure without end. For love of him they should strive for the usefulness and salvation of their subjects.

Therefore, let the diligence of all the faithful of holy God’s Church and of our own, present and future, know that when, out of love for the most holy Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Mary, the perpetual virgin, and for the most holy confessor of Christ, Sylvester, and out of desire for the holy congregation dedicated to divine service in their monastery, we visited the monastery of Nonantula for the sake of prayer, we recognized there, by divine gift, such devotion in the divine offices that we judged without doubt that their prayers would contribute to the stability of the kingdom and to our perpetual happiness.

Therefore, with divine assistance breathing upon us, it pleased us to bestow, by our authority, such a gift for encouragement and for the peaceful continuance of goodness there: that, through the succession of times and years, an abbot should always be chosen from the same congregation of monks serving God there in harmony, one who would be able prudently to govern so great a congregation according to the rule of Saint Benedict, provide for the salvation of souls and the welfare of the Church, and do so by the prince’s ordinance. At no time shall the office be entrusted to anyone except by their election and consent; rather, by our ordinance and that of our successors, they shall always have from the same congregation a pastor and a prudent, provident ruler of their souls.

Therefore, for the sake of firmness, we decreed that this charter of our authority be made concerning the same holy place. By it we beseech our successors that, just as they wish their own pious deeds to be preserved by those who follow them, so, for the love of God and reverence for the saints, they should preserve this concession of ours forever. We expressly command our faithful and firmly establish that it shall remain permanent: just as it has been granted there by us above, so they shall allow it to remain valid and unimpaired, and no one shall rashly oppose it, so that, with every tranquility secured through our efforts, the same congregation may more attentively delight in imploring the Lord’s mercy for us, for the stability of our imperial dignity, for the salvation of our wife and offspring, and for the protection and defense of those resting in the bosom of our holy mother, the Catholic Church.

And so that this gift of our concession may be more truly believed by our successors and more carefully preserved by the faithful, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be authenticated below by the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Lothair, most glorious Augustus.**

I, Dructemirus, subdeacon and notary, have reviewed and subscribed this in place of Egilmar.

Issued on the third day before the Nones of February, in the eighteenth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of our lord Lothair the emperor, in the fifteenth indiction.

Done at Nonantula, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## CCXXIII. RECORD CONCERNING THE MONASTERY OF SAINT CARILEPHUS

Accepted in the general synod held at the royal palace of Quierzy from Aldric, the bishop, by the judgment of the bishops, as it is inserted in the record itself.

*(Year 838.)*

[Baluz, *Miscellanea*, vol. I, p. 109.]

When, in the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, lord Louis the emperor had publicly taken his seat at the palace of Quierzy in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 838, to hear the cases of all and bring just judgments to an end, and had there convened a general assembly of the entire people together with his sons Pippin and Charles, namely glorious kings, as well as a synod of bishops and the other priests, gathered generally to deal with ecclesiastical and secular affairs and also to support the welfare of holy God’s Church, monks came there from the monastery of Anisola, in which Saint Carilephus rests bodily. They appeared before the aforesaid lord Louis the emperor, more than twenty of them together with Sigemund, who had formerly been their abbot, and complained that they had been unjustly expelled from their monastery. The lord emperor ordered their case to be carefully examined and investigated in detail at the general assembly held there.

When, in the presence of the bishops, abbots, and the other priests, they complained that they had come on account of this matter, Aldric, their bishop and bishop of the diocese of Le Mans, and abbot of the same monastery, was asked whether he had expelled them from their monastery, or by whom they had been expelled and were wandering about in this fashion, having abandoned the place in which they had renounced the world and in which they ought to remain throughout the days of their lives in ecclesiastical or secular affairs.

He replied: “I neither expelled them nor knew that they had been expelled.”

Then the donation of Saint Carilephus was brought before the king and his nobles. He had made it to Saint Innocent, the bishop, with the permission and consent of King Childebert. Many other charters of authority were also produced, too numerous to list. Concerning these, the aforementioned bishop had sufficient witnesses before everyone present at the same council, both priests and truthful laymen—noble, good, and legally competent—who approved those same charter documents. They had seen that the documents had been duly authenticated within the lawful years and testified fully and according to law that, by both canon law and secular law, the aforesaid monastery of Anisola, with everything pertaining to it, belonged by right more to the mother church of Le Mans than it could belong elsewhere—to the royal treasury, to the private property of the lord emperor, or to any man.

But no one was found who wished to say or prove anything against these claims.

Then the aforesaid lord Drogo, archbishop and senior chaplain, and the others who had previously been at the palace of Aachen when this case had been argued, thoroughly investigated, and canonically and legally determined, replied:

“There is no need now to remove all these matters again or reconsider each one individually, because we know that you have canonically and legally acquired and vindicated possession of the aforesaid monastery. But the matter now concerns these monks, who presently complain that they have been expelled from their monastery, and whose case the lord emperor ordered us to investigate.”

After it had been thoroughly investigated, however, it was established that the aforesaid monks had not left their monastery because of any expulsion, need, fault, or act of the aforementioned Bishop Aldric, but had done so of their own will and through their obstinacy. They had perpetrated this in order somehow to take the said monastery away from the aforesaid bishop, withdraw or alienate it from the right of the church of his see, and vindicate it for themselves.

They were therefore ordered to return to their monastery, in which they had renounced the world, to devote themselves there to fasts and prayers, and to serve the Lord regularly. But they answered in anger that they did not wish to return there.

Then all the bishops and the other priests, seeing that they were guilty of such great folly and were disobedient in this manner to the lord emperor, to the entire holy synod, and to their own bishop, and that they resisted their commands and their pious and just counsels, ordered the Rule of Saint Benedict to be brought and its sentences to be read in the presence of everyone. They opposed every one of its provisions. Finally, they ordered the sentence concerning the degrees of humility to be read. They showed that they intended to observe none of these, but rather to serve and pursue their own desires.

Considering this Rule, they then said: “What cannot be healed by a light and gentle remedy must necessarily be cut away with the knife.”

They ordered the canons to be brought. From these, in the presence of everyone, the sentence of the Council of Chalcedon concerning clerics who preside over poorhouses or monasteries was read again, chapter 8, containing the following:

> “Clerics who are placed in charge of poorhouses, or who are appointed in monasteries and basilicas of martyrs, shall remain under the authority of the bishops who are in each city, according to the traditions of the holy Fathers, and shall not, through contumacy, separate themselves from their bishop. Those who dare in any way to overturn this arrangement and do not submit to their own bishop shall, if they are clerics, be subject to the corrections of the canons; but if they are laymen or monks, they shall be deprived of communion.”

After this sentence had been read, they were again asked whether they still remained as disobedient as before. Remaining in the same obstinacy, they were then, by the judgment of all the bishops and of the universal holy council, excluded by all the bishops and the other priests from the entire priestly order and from communion according to this sentence. If they persisted irrevocably, they were made outcasts from the Catholic Church.

Then all the bishops and the other servants of God, or the general assembly, judged that the aforementioned Bishop Aldric should receive his monks and do with them whatever he wished. Some of them were restored to him by the hands of the holy council.

The entire holy synod also judged that he had legally vindicated his case and had canonically and legally acquired the aforesaid monastery with everything pertaining to it, and had won it for the church entrusted to him and for his successors in future times. Whatever he might, with the Lord’s assent, decide to do and arrange concerning it in ecclesiastical order, he should have full power to do in every respect.

It was therefore necessary that the aforesaid bishop and the ministers of his see’s church receive this vindication and this record by the counsel and judgment of all the bishops and other priests who had assembled at the aforesaid synod. Thus, if after this day—which we very much do not believe will happen—any dispute, claim, or accusation concerning this matter should arise through the instigation of malicious men, this record and vindication might be shown and declared before everyone, so that the claimant might not be able to vindicate what he claimed, but this present document and record might remain firm and stable for all time.

In the presence of these witnesses this was enacted.

Drogo, archbishop and senior chaplain, subscribed.

Autcarius, archbishop, subscribed.

Agobardus, archbishop, subscribed.

Bernardus, archbishop, subscribed.

Bernegarius [Bartholomaeus], archbishop of Narbonne, subscribed.

Agiulfus, archbishop of the city of Bourges, subscribed.

Notho, archbishop of Arles, subscribed.

Abtadus, bishop of Geneva, subscribed.

Harinbertus, bishop of Bayeux, subscribed.

Freculfus, bishop of Lisieux, subscribed.

Theodoricus, bishop of Cambrai, subscribed.

Erardus, bishop of Tongeren, subscribed.

Ragenarius, bishop of Amiens, subscribed.

Eccardus, bishop of Noyon, subscribed.

Ebroinus, bishop of Poitiers, subscribed.

Gundacher, bishop of Limoges, subscribed.

Jonas, bishop of the city of Orléans, subscribed.

Moduinus, bishop of Autun, subscribed.

Heribaldus, bishop of Auxerre, subscribed.

Adalbertus, bishop of Troyes, subscribed.

Dodo, bishop of Angers, subscribed.

Herchenradus, bishop of the city of Paris, subscribed.

Humbertus, humble bishop, subscribed.

Fulcarius, humble bishop, subscribed.

Godofredus, bishop of Senlis, subscribed.

Favvo, bishop of Chalon, subscribed.

Hildi, bishop of Verdun, subscribed.

Lupus, bishop of Châlons, subscribed.

Stephanus, humble bishop, subscribed.

I, Walafridus, deacon, reviewed and subscribed at the request of others.

Issued on the eighth day before the Ides of September, in the twenty-fifth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the first indiction. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## CCXXIV. FOR THE CHURCH OF THE CITY OF LE MANS AND ALDRIC, ITS BISHOP

*(Year 838.)*

[In Baluz, same work.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the merciful favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus.

If we bring the just and reasonable petitions and requests of our faithful, which they present for the benefit and advancement of holy God’s Church, to their desired effect, we not only exercise in this the royal and imperial custom, but also, as we believe, make them more ready and devoted toward us.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of holy God’s Church and of our own, present and future, that Bavo, our vassal, informed us that he possessed, by our benefice, a certain estate situated in the county of Le Mans, called Tridentem, belonging by right to the mother church of Le Mans. From it he paid each year the ninths, tenths, and lawful dues to the said mother church and its rectors.

Reflecting on the condition of human frailty, fearing the final day of his summons, and afraid that the aforesaid estate might, through some impulse of his own greed or by any device, be alienated from the right of the aforesaid mother church, the aforementioned Bavo, therefore burning with divine love, approached our clemency and humbly begged that we return the aforesaid estate called Tridentem, with everything pertaining to it, to the aforesaid mother church of Le Mans and to Aldric, the venerable bishop of that city, by our imperial authority, and confirm by our charter this return so that the same church and its rectors might possess it more securely in future times.

We willingly heard his petition out of love for God and reverence for that holy place and the servants of God serving there, and we judged it proper to bring his prayer and pious desire to the desired effect.

Therefore, by this writing of our authority, establishing, decreeing, and ordering, we declare that, just as our faithful Bavo held the aforesaid estate in its entirety, as it was under our authority when he is known to have received that benefice from our grant, we have now restored it, for the benefit of our soul and the stability of our empire, to the venerable Bishop Aldric for the use of his aforesaid church, so that it may remain perpetually for the uses and benefit of that church, its bishop, and those serving God in it.

Therefore, at the urging and humble request of our aforesaid faithful—namely, the aforementioned Bishop Aldric and Bavo, our vassal—we ordered this charter of our confirmation and return to be made for the aforementioned Bishop Aldric or for the church of the aforesaid city. By it we decree and order that no one living under the authority of our empire shall ever presume to cause any disturbance or bring any accusation against the aforesaid Bishop Aldric or his successors concerning the aforesaid estate or anything belonging to it, in whatever counties or places; rather, he and his successors shall be permitted to hold and possess the aforesaid estate peacefully, by ecclesiastical right, with all its places, territories, dependents, and everything pertaining to it. Whatever they decide to do from it for the opportunity and advantage of the aforesaid church of the see, they shall have full power to do in every respect in future times.

And so that this authority of our return may possess perpetual firmness, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.**

I, Hirminmarus, notary, have reviewed and subscribed this in place of Hugo.

Issued on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the twenty-fifth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the first indiction.

Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## CCXXV. FOR THE SAME CHURCH

*(Year 838.)*

[In Baluz, same work, p. 117.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the merciful favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus.

If we willingly lend an ear to the petitions of priests when they wish to inform us of something concerning their own needs or those of the churches entrusted to them, and bring their just and reasonable requests and petitions to the desired effect, we not only exercise in this the royal and imperial custom, but also make those same priests more ready and devoted to imploring the Lord’s mercy for us.

Therefore we wish it to be known to the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, that Aldric, the venerable bishop of the city of Le Mans, approaching the ears of our piety, reported to us concerning certain benefices which, many years earlier, had been taken away from the right of his see together with their appurtenances and transferred to our public treasury. Ghermundus, Berthadus, Vulfardus, Bodo, and their associates, our vassals, now possess them as benefices, and thus, at an earlier time, the benefices with their appurtenances and everything pertaining to them had slipped from the hands of the rectors of the aforesaid city into the hands of the said vassals.

When we sent our faithful envoys, the venerable Abbot Helisachar and Count Wido, to investigate the truth of the matter more diligently, they reported to us that everything was indeed so.

When, through their report, we had recognized that the benefices of the aforesaid vassals belonged justly not to our public treasury but to the right of the aforesaid church of Le Mans, it pleased our clemency to return the benefices of the aforementioned vassals in their entirety for the benefit of our soul, to the venerable Bishop Aldric for the use of his aforesaid church, just as it is established that they had received them individually in the various places from our grant, so that they might remain perpetually for the uses and benefit of that church and of those serving God in it.

Therefore, at the suggestion and request of the aforesaid venerable bishop, we ordered this charter of our confirmation and return to be made for him or for the church of the aforesaid city. By it we decree and order that no one of our faithful shall ever presume to cause any disturbance or bring any accusation against the venerable Bishop Aldric or his successors concerning the aforesaid benefices or anything known to belong to the benefices of our aforesaid vassals, wherever they may be situated. Rather, he and his successors shall be permitted to hold and possess the aforesaid places peacefully, by ecclesiastical right, with everything pertaining to them, and whatever they decide to do from them for the opportunity and advantage of the aforesaid church, they shall have full power to do in every respect.

And so that this authority of ours may possess perpetual firmness, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most pious emperor.**

I, Hirminmarus, notary, have reviewed and subscribed this in place of Hugo.

Issued on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, in the twenty-second year, Christ being favorable, [Note: It seems that 24 should be read.] of the empire of our lord Louis, most pious emperor, in the thirteenth indiction.

Done at Stramiacum above the Rhône River, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## CCXXVI. FOR THE SAME CHURCH

*(Year 838.)*

[In Baluz, same work, p. 118.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the merciful favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus.

If we bring the just and reasonable petitions and requests of our faithful, which they present for the benefit and advancement of holy God’s Church, to their desired effect, we not only exercise in this the royal and imperial custom, but also, as we believe, make them more ready and devoted toward us.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of holy God’s Church and of our own, present and future, that Agbertus, count, doorkeeper, and our counselor, informed us that he possessed, by our benefice, a certain estate situated in the county of Le Mans, called Calisamen, belonging by right to the mother church of Le Mans. From it he paid each year the ninths, tenths, and lawful dues to the aforesaid mother church and its rectors.

Reflecting on the condition of human frailty, fearing the final day of his summons, and afraid that the aforesaid estate might, through some impulse of his own greed or by any device, be alienated from the right of the aforesaid mother church, the aforementioned Agbertus, therefore burning with divine love, approached our clemency and humbly begged that we return the aforesaid estate called Calisamen, with everything pertaining to it, to the church of the aforesaid see of Le Mans and to Aldric, the venerable bishop of that city, by our imperial authority, and confirm by our charter this return so that the same church and its rectors might possess it more securely in future times.

We willingly heard his petition out of love for God and reverence for that holy place and the servants of God serving the Lord there, and we judged it proper to bring his prayer and pious desire to the desired effect.

Therefore, by this charter of our authority, establishing, decreeing, and ordering, we declare that, just as our faithful Agbertus held the aforesaid estate in its entirety, as it was under our authority on the day when he is known to have received that benefice from our grant, we have now restored it, for the benefit of our soul and the stability of our empire, to the venerable Bishop Aldric for the use of the church of his aforesaid see, so that it may remain perpetually for the uses and benefit of that church and of those serving God in it.

Therefore, at the urging and humble request of our aforesaid faithful—namely, the venerable Bishop Aldric and the aforementioned Agbertus, our faithful—we ordered this charter of our confirmation and return to be made for the aforesaid Bishop Aldric or for the church of the aforesaid city. By it we decree and order that no one living under the authority of our empire shall ever presume to cause any disturbance or bring any accusation against the aforesaid Bishop Aldric or his successors concerning the aforesaid estate or anything belonging to it, in whatever counties or places. Rather, he and his successors shall be permitted to hold and possess the aforesaid estate peacefully, by ecclesiastical right, with all its places, territories, dependents, and everything pertaining to it, and whatever they decide to do from it for the opportunity and advantage of the church of the aforesaid see, they shall have full power to do in every respect in future times.

And so that this authority of our return may possess perpetual firmness, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.**

I, Maginarius, notary, have reviewed and subscribed this in place of Hugo.

Issued on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the twenty-sixth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the second indiction.

Done publicly at the city of Poitiers, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## CCXXVII. FOR BISHOP ALDRIC

*(Year 838.)*

[In Baluz, same work, p. 119.]

[Col. 1297B]
