In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the merciful favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus.

If we willingly lend an ear to the just and reasonable petitions of God’s priests and bring them to their desired effect, we not only exercise the royal and imperial custom, but also make those same men more devoted and ready to implore the Lord’s mercy for our transgressions; through this we confidently believe that we may more readily secure for ourselves God’s immense mercy.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of holy God’s Church and of our own, present and future, that Aldric, the venerable bishop of the city of Le Mans, informed our highness that many of the duties which he ought to perform in his diocese and which belonged to his ministry had been neglected because he had already been constantly detained for so long in our service or even in our company. These duties included preaching, confirmation, and instruction, the restoration of churches, the correction of wicked men, and various other matters beneficial to the church entrusted to him and necessary for the clergy and people.

He also informed us that the mother church within the aforesaid city, having been built many years earlier, was daily approaching collapse because of the weakness of its walls. For this reason, he said that he wished to found it anew and build it in a better condition and location.

With tearful countenance he also asserted before us and our faithful that, if he could not otherwise obtain from us leisure to perform his ministry, he would rather give up the honors conferred upon him than neglect the clergy and people entrusted to him and thereby, God forbid, bring about their destruction.

Therefore he humbly entreated our clemency that, in accordance with canonical authority, he might have an administrator to conduct external affairs on his behalf and perform our services and journeys in his place as best he could, while the aforesaid bishop devoted himself to the things of God and strove to complete his ministry.

He also entreated that, if he could not find within his own clergy and diocese an administrator of the kind he wanted or needed, one who would in every respect obey him according to the institution of the canons, he might have permission to choose for himself and for the church entrusted to him, from among our faithful, wherever he wished, whether within or outside the palace, an assistant and defender; to change him whenever necessary; and to appoint a better or more useful one.

We most willingly lent a favorable ear to his prayers, granted our assent to the petitions set forth above, and brought his requests to their full effect.

By these letters of our authority, which we ordered to be made for him, we grant to the aforesaid pontiff and wish it to be granted in the future that he may reside peacefully in his diocese for as long as he wishes, and pray to the Lord for us and for the people entrusted to us by God. He may send his own men, together with his administrator or whomever he chooses, as has been said, wherever our command or an urgent necessity requires.

Therefore, by this charter of our authority, we command and decree that, if the aforementioned bishop survives us, none of our sons, successors, or faithful shall presume to bring any disturbance or accusation against the aforesaid pontiff or the church entrusted to him, or consent to those who wish to do so. Rather, for the love of God and out of reverence for us, they shall provide him fully with protection and defense, so that, peacefully and securely, as has been prescribed and granted to him by us, he may reside in his church and perform his ministry without impediment from anyone. Thus the aforesaid pontiff may delight in praying more attentively for us and our children, and for the stability and peace of the empire entrusted by us to God.

And so that this authority of ours may possess unviolated and unshaken permanence, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be authenticated by the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most pious emperor.**

I, Maginarius, notary, have reviewed and subscribed this in place of Hugo.

Issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the twenty-seventh year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the third indiction.

Done publicly at the city of Poitiers, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## CCXXVIII. FOR THE CHURCH OF LE MANS

*(Year 838.)*

[In Baluz, same work.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the merciful favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus.

[Source ends here.]

If we bring the just and reasonable petitions and requests of our faithful, which they present for the benefit and exaltation of the holy Church of God, to their desired conclusion, we not only exercise in this the royal and imperial custom, but also, as we believe, make them more ready and more devoted toward us. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own, both present and future, [Col. 1299A] that Count Adalbert and our counsellor informed us that he possessed, by our benefaction, a certain villa situated in the Carmisian district, called Bonalla, belonging by right to the mother church of Le Mans; and that each year he paid from it the ninths, tenths, and lawful dues to the aforesaid mother church and to the rectors of that church. Reflecting upon this matter, therefore, and considering the frailty of human life, fearing the final day of his summons, and afraid lest the aforesaid villa might be alienated from the right of the aforesaid mother church by some impulse of his own greed or by any device whatsoever, he therefore, burning with divine love, approached our clemency and humbly entreated us that we should, by our imperial authority, presently restore the aforesaid villa, called Bonalla, with everything belonging to it, [Col. 1299B] to the aforesaid mother church of Le Mans and to Aldric, the venerable bishop of that city, and confirm by our precept that this restoration should be more securely possessed by that church and its rectors in future times.

We willingly heard his petition, out of love for God and reverence for that holy place and for the servants of God serving God there, and judged it worthy to bring his entreaty and pious desire to the desired conclusion. Therefore, by this precept of our authority, establishing, decreeing, and commanding, we declare that, just as the aforementioned Adalbert, our faithful man, possessed the aforesaid villa in its entirety, as it was under the right of our power on the day when it is established that he received that benefice from our gift, so we have now restored it, for the benefit of our soul and the stability of our empire, to the aforementioned venerable Bishop Aldric, for the use of the church of his aforesaid see, so that it may remain perpetually for the interests and uses of that church and of those serving God in it.

Therefore, at the prompting and humble request of our aforesaid faithful men—namely, the aforementioned Bishop Aldric and the aforesaid Adalbert, our faithful man—we ordered this precept of our confirmation and restoration to be made for the aforementioned Bishop Aldric and for the church of the aforesaid city. By it we decree and command that no one living under the authority of our empire shall at any time presume to cause any disturbance or bring any accusation against the aforesaid Bishop Aldric or his successors concerning the aforesaid villa or anything belonging to it, in whatever districts [Col. 1299D] and places they may lie. Rather, he and his successors shall be permitted to hold and possess the aforesaid villa peacefully, with all its places and territories, bondmen and bondwomen, and everything belonging to it, by ecclesiastical right; and whatever they may decide to do with it for the advantage and benefit of the church of the aforesaid see, they shall have full power to do in every respect for all future time. And so that this authority of our restoration may possess perpetual firmness, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be authenticated with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Herminmarus, notary, have reviewed and subscribed it on behalf of Hugh.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the twenty-seventh year, with Christ favoring us, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the first indiction.

Done at the palace of Aachen, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1300B]

### CCXXIX. [Note: Published from the most ancient cartulary of the Abbey of Kempten by R. P. Rassler in the Appendix to *Vindicatio contra Vindicantem*, p. 27.] THE EXCHANGE CONCLUDED BY TATTO, ABBOT OF KEMPTEN, WITH COUNT WANINGUS IS CONFIRMED. (Year 838, 14 June.)

[In Neugart, *Codex Alemannicus*, p. 231.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus.

If we confirm by our edicts those things which our faithful exchange among themselves for their own advantage, we exercise the imperial custom, and we wish this to remain henceforth established by the firmest right. Therefore let the discernment of all our faithful, present as well as future, know that our beloved son and namesake, the glorious King Louis, informed us that Tatto, venerable abbot of the monastery called Kempten, and Count Waningus [Note: I count Waningus among the counts of Nibelgau, since in other charters he is expressly connected with that district.] had exchanged certain properties for the advantage of both parties. Accordingly, with our permission, the aforementioned Abbot Tatto gave to Count Waningus, as his own property, from the possessions of his aforesaid monastery, whatever right that monastery held in the places called Plezza [Note: Bless, on the right bank of the Iller, below Memmingen.], Pazeinhova [Note: Batzenhofen, near Augsburg.], Horunanc [Note: Hurblingen, in the same area.], and Suntheim [Note: Sundheim, on the Günz River.], except for a woodland mark and a small estate, which had been assigned to the aforesaid monastery for Aldric [Note: Aldric the priest, whose cell is mentioned in another diploma of Louis.], and except for those meadows at Gundilensee [Note: Apparently a copyist’s error for Gundilensee; today Guntzeck, between the Iller and the Günz.], and at Cuttinwanc [Note: Gottenau near Sundheim. The places listed thus far belong to the diocese of Augsburg and lie beyond the Iller.]. He transferred to the aforesaid Count Waningus, by way of exchange, everything else that was possessed in the aforesaid places under the right of the said monastery, together with their woodland marks and all their appurtenances. [Col. 1300D]

Conversely, in compensation for these properties, the aforementioned Count Waningus gave from the possessions of his county to the aforesaid Abbot Tatto, for the use of his aforementioned monastery, whatever he is known to possess there by right of his county in the villa called Reoda [Note: Rieden, above the confluence of the Eitrach and the Iller], both lands and meadows, as well as woods, waters, and woodland marks, or any other property; and likewise whatever he possessed by right of his aforesaid county in the place called Eitraha [Note: Eitrach, a village in the same area, in the diocese of Constance.]. He declared that he held in his hands two deeds of exchange written in identical form and strengthened by the hands of his own men and of other good men. But, for complete security, he requested our Highness to confirm these exchanges anew and more fully by a precept of our mildness. We did not wish to deny his petition; rather, know that, just as we have granted and confirmed matters to each of our faithful who make just and reasonable requests, so we have granted and confirmed these matters to them in every respect.

Therefore, giving orders, we command that whatever one party has justly and reasonably transferred to the other party, it shall henceforth hold and possess under the firmest right by this authority of ours, and that it shall have complete freedom to do with it whatever it decides. And so that this authority of our confirmation may remain inviolable, we ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

Sign of Lord Louis, emperor Augustus.

I, Bartholomeus, notary, have reviewed and subscribed it on behalf of Hugh.

[Note: Schannat, *Traditiones Fuldenses*, p. 176, reports another diploma of Louis the Pious, dated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March in the twenty-sixth year of his reign, reviewed and subscribed by Bartholomeus, notary, on behalf of Hugh. I believe Bartholomeus was abbot of Saint Martin in Île-Barbe in the diocese of Lyon; he is mentioned in these words in the catalogue of the monasteries associated with Reichenau: “From the monastery of Saint Martin of Île-Barbe, Bartholomeus the abbot,” Mabillon, *Vetera Analecta*, fol. 426, col. 2.]

Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the twenty-fifth year, with Christ favoring us, of the reign of Lord Louis [Note: The cartulary scribe erroneously has *Ludovicii* for *Ludovici*; likewise above *marka* and *markis* for *marca* and *marcis*.], most pious Augustus, in the first indiction [Note: The year 838, the twenty-fifth year of Louis the Pious, was in the first indiction.]. Done at the royal palace of Noyon [Note: It is established from the *Annals of Saint-Bertin* for this year, and compare the *Annals of Metz* and of Fulda, that Louis the Pious and his namesake son were at Noyon during this month.] in the name of God, successfully. Amen.

### CCXXX. FOR THE MONASTERY OF CORMERY. (Year 838.)

[In Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, p. 28.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus.

If we take care of the servants of God and of their needs—those who are known to have abandoned the world entirely—and provide for them with pious concern and imperial foresight, we confidently believe that this undoubtedly contributes to the benefit of our soul and to the attainment of eternal blessedness. Therefore we wish it to be known, by God’s disposition, to our successors and to the rectors and administrators of the monastery of Saint Martin, our patron, where that most precious confessor of Christ rests bodily, both present and future, that, touched by divine love, it has pleased our Highness to issue a precept of our authority concerning a certain villa belonging by right to the same monastery, called Cusciacus, assigned to the cell of Saint Paul, which is called Cormery by its rustic name. The former abbot of that monastery, Itherius, built it as a new foundation from his own property and assigned it to the aforesaid monastery, so that the needs of that cell and of the monks serving God there might be supported. We have also decided, by the same authority, to transfer it so that it may remain perpetually under its right, with everything belonging to it: houses, buildings of every kind, lands, vineyards, woods, meadows, fields, pastures, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated places, movable and immovable property, and self-moving property, bondmen and bondwomen of every sex and age—in its entirety, or whatever, however extensive, is presently known to belong to it justly and legally.

Thus it has pleased our Highness to secure this munificence of ours by imperial authority and solemnly strengthen it by royal sanction. Therefore we have decided that this document of our majesty should be drawn up and given to Audacrus, who is now known to govern the same monastery, and to his successors, namely the fathers of that cell. By it we sanction and command in every respect that the aforesaid villa, in its entirety, shall from now onward remain under the right and authority of the aforesaid cell and of the monks who in succession serve God there; and that everything which it ought to provide in public or private services to the abbots and rectors of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Martin shall wholly contribute to the right and advancement of the aforesaid cell, which we have said is dedicated in honor of Saint Paul, so that it may serve its buildings and the needs of the monks serving God there, and may increase in prosperity; and so that, through the glorious intercessions of that blessed apostle of Christ, divine favor may be more gloriously [lacuna].

And so that this authority of our transfer may remain for all time [lacuna], we ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

I, Hirminmarus, notary, have reviewed and subscribed it on behalf of Hugh.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the twenty-fourth year, with Christ favoring us, of the reign of Lord Louis Augustus, in the fifteenth indiction. Done at the royal palace of the villa of Theodon, successfully, in the name of God.

### CCXXXI. THE EXCHANGE OF CERTAIN ESTATES BETWEEN HILDUIN, ABBOT OF SAINT-DENIS, AND ERMENTRUD, ABBESS OF JOUARRE, IS CONFIRMED. (Year 839.)

[In Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 545.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus.

For if we confirm by our edicts those things which the faithful of our empire exchange among themselves for their own advantage, we exercise the imperial custom, and we wish this to remain henceforth established by the firmest right. Therefore let the discernment of all our faithful, present as well as future, know that Hilduin, a venerable man and abbot of the monastery of Saint-Denis, informed us that he had made an exchange with Ermentrud, abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary of Jouarre, for the advantage of both parties.

Accordingly, with our permission, the aforesaid Abbess Ermentrud gave, from the possessions of Saint Mary entrusted to her, to the monastery of Saint-Denis and to Abbot Hilduin, in the district of Meaux and in the villa called Cuciacus, two small estates, containing between the estates themselves and the vineyard approximately one bunuarium and one arpent; and, between arable land and meadow, eleven bunuaria and one arpent.

In return for this property, the aforementioned venerable man, Abbot Hilduin, gave from the possessions of his monastery, for the use of the monastery of Saint Mary of Jouarre and of Abbess Ermentrud, in the same district and in the villa called Liniacus, three small estates belonging to Saint-Denis, containing between the estates themselves and the vineyard approximately one and a half bunuaria, and, between meadow and arable land, eleven bunuaria and one arpent.

He declared that he held in his hands two deeds of exchange written in identical form and strengthened by the hands of good men. But, for complete security, he requested our Highness to confirm these exchanges anew and more fully by a precept of our mildness. We did not wish to deny his petition; rather, know that, just as we have granted and confirmed matters to each of our faithful who make just and reasonable requests, so we have granted and confirmed these matters to them in every respect.

Therefore, giving orders, we command that whatever one party has justly and reasonably transferred to the other party, it shall henceforth hold and possess by this authority of ours, and shall have the right, under ecclesiastical law, to do with it whatever it chooses. And so that this authority of the exchange may be held more firmly and preserved more fully for future times, we ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

I, Glorius, notary, have reviewed and subscribed it on behalf of Hugh.

Done at the royal palace of Attigny, in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious emperor.

[Col. 1304A]

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, in the second indiction, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

### CCXXXII. FOR THE ABBEY OF KEMPTEN. (Year 839, 18 April.)

[Note: R.P. Rassler published the complete text from an old cartulary in the *Appendix to Vindicatio contra Vindicantem*, p. 29; Mabillon published a more accurate text from the original itself, *Vetera Analecta*, fol. 448. It also appears, with certain errors, in Lunig, *Spicilegium ecclesiasticum*, vol. III, p. 170, and in Daniel Eberhard Baring, *Clavis diplomatica*, p. 363.]

[In Neugart, *Codex Alemannicus*, p. 237.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus.

If [we do something] for places dedicated to God, etc. Therefore let the discernment of all our faithful, present and future, know that, at the entreaty of our beloved brother Drogo [Note: Drogo, bishop of Metz and brother of Louis the Pious, is also celebrated by the author of the *Annals of Saint-Bertin* under the year 835 with the title of archbishop, and by Hincmar in his later work against Gottschalk, chapter 36. He was also the first to subscribe the acts of the general assembly held at the palace of Quierzy in 838: “Drogo, archbishop and senior chaplain.” See Bouquet, vol. VI, pp. 197, 253, and 302.], venerable archbishop and chief chaplain of our sacred palace, we have decided, for the benefit of our soul and the fruit of eternal reward, to place under the authority of a certain monastery called Kempten, and by solemn donation to transfer from our right into the right and power of the aforesaid monastery, a certain cell called Aldric’s Cell [Note: Above and below Kempten, on the left bank of the Iller, there are two villages, one called Martiuszell and the other Krugzell. The former is more probably indicated here, since the names of possessors were sometimes transferred to the places associated with them.]. It was handed over to our lord and father, the most excellent Emperor Charles, and is situated in the duchy of Alamannia, in the district of Albigoi [Note: Today Algoria, Algen.], near the monastery called Kempten, where the venerable Abbot Tatto now presides.

In return for this favor and permission of ours, the aforementioned venerable Abbot Tatto gave from the property of his monastery to Ratulf, our priest and chaplain, who had previously held the same cell by our grant, to possess as a benefice for the days of his life, six fully equipped hides in the district of Keltenstein [Note: A district named from the stream Geltnach, which rises in the diocese of Augsburg above the town of Kaufbeuren. Compare the *Chronicon Gottwicense*, book IV, p. 649.], in the place called Hruodoldishova [Note: Rudertshofen near Kaufbeuren.], and, in another place in the district of Augustgoi [Note: The most reverend Besselius describes the boundaries of this district as follows: “The tract of land around Augsburg appears to be that which today stretches above Augsburg between the rivers Lech, Wertach, and Sinkel, and is called the Lechfeld.”], a certain cell called Herilescella [Note: Hirschzell near Kaufbeuren, in the same region], with everything belonging to it—on the condition that he possess the aforesaid property only during the days of his life, and that after his death it return to the aforementioned monastery to be possessed perpetually.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Hirminmaris [Note: Rassler incorrectly has “Hirminhardus.”], notary, have reviewed and subscribed it on behalf of Hugh.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the twenty-sixth year, with Christ favoring us, of the reign of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the second indiction. Done at the royal palace of Bodoma [Note: Bodama or Bodoma, today Bodman, on the lower shore of Lake Constance; formerly a royal villa and palace, omitted by Mabillon in *De re diplomatica*, book IV. It is called Bedonnia by the author of the *Life of Louis the Pious*, in Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 122. The *Annals of Saint-Bertin* and Hermannus Contractus for this year testify that Louis the Pious came to Bodoma during Lent and celebrated Easter there.] successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1305A]

### CCXXIII. FOR THE MONASTERY OF KEMPTEN. (Year 839, 1 September.)

[Note: It appears in Mabillon, *Vetera Analecta*, new edition, fol. 448, and in Lunig, *Spicilegium ecclesiasticum*, part III, chapter 5, p. 169. D. Bouquet gives a fragment in vol. VI, p. 626.]

[In Neugart, *Codex Alemannicus*, p. 239.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence, emperor Augustus [Note: This formula is indeed unusual after the year 833. Above we saw another diploma of Louis the Pious granted to the Abbey of Kempten, no. 232, in which the customary formula from that time onward appears: “by the favor of divine clemency”; Mabillon himself testifies that Louis the Pious thereafter used that formula, *De re diplomatica*, book II, chapter 3, no. 13. Nevertheless, in his *German Journey*, prefixed to the *Analecta*, the most learned man asserts that he saw several diplomas of this abbey, even authentic ones, some of which—including those between that diploma and the present one—are to be cited below. Thus the expert in distinguishing public documents had no grounds for doubting the complete authenticity of this diploma.].

If [we do something] for places devoted to divine worship, etc. Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, that we have granted to the monastery called Kempten, constructed in honor of holy Mary ever-virgin and of the holy martyrs Gordian and Epimachus [Note: Hermannus Continuatus testifies in his chronicle under the year 774 that the bodies of these saints were brought from Rome to Alamannia and specifically to the recently built monastery of Kempten.], whom our mother, of good memory, Hildegard [Note: It may be inferred with some clarity even from this passage that the Abbey of Kempten was founded by Hildegard, the wife of Charlemagne, although the diploma of that emperor published in Lunig’s *Spicilegium ecclesiasticum*, at the place cited, is not considered genuine; its conclusion gives the year 773 with the second indiction, contrary to the usage of that age. Daniel Eberhard Baring lists both its defenders and its opponents, *Clavis diplomatica*, p. 38, Hanover edition, 1754.], established at that same place [Col. 1305B] for the performance of divine offices on their behalf, where the venerable Abbot Tatto now presides, the right that, whenever the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this life by divine summons, the monks serving God there may, by this authority and consent of ours, have permission to elect abbots for as long as they can find among themselves men capable of governing that congregation according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, etc.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Hirminmaris, notary, have reviewed and subscribed it on behalf of Hugh.

Given on the Kalends of September, in the twenty-sixth year, with Christ favoring us, of the reign of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the second indiction [Note: The indiction agrees perfectly with the year of the reign of Louis the Pious.]. Done at the royal palace in the city of Cabillonum [Note: That is, Cabilonum, Chalon-sur-Saône. The author of the *Life of Louis the Pious*, chapter 61, agrees. After recounting what happened in this year, he adds: “The emperor therefore, as he had arranged, went to the city of Chalon in the autumn season, and, following his custom, set in order both ecclesiastical and public affairs.”], successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

### CCXXXIV. FOR THE MONASTERY OF DEAS. (Year 839.)

[Note: Commonly Dee or Grand-Lieu, now a priory in the diocese of Nantes.]

[In Chifflet, proofs for the *History of the Abbey of Tournus*, p. 194, and in D. Bouquet, *Collection of Histories*, vol. VI, p. 628.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus.

[Col. 1306A]

If, from the benefits bestowed upon us by God, we confer something from our generosity upon places dedicated to God, we clearly believe that this will help us both to pass our mortal life successfully and to attain eternal life forever. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own [both present and future], that, touched by divine love, we have bestowed upon the monastery of Deas, where Saint Philibert, confessor of Christ, rests bodily, constructed in honor of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and where the venerable man Hilbod is known to preside as abbot, a certain villa belonging to our right, called Scobrit, situated in the district of Poitiers, in the vicariate of Racinse, with everything belonging or pertaining to it, and with bondmen and bondwomen of every sex [Col. 1306B] and age.

Accordingly, we transfer the aforesaid villa, with the church of Saint Vitalis, houses and other buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, vineyards, meadows, pastures, woods, saltworks, mills, rights of exit and return, and whatever belongs to the aforesaid villa, and is by right of ownership under our right and possession, in its entirety or without exact specification, from our right into the right and authority of the aforesaid monastery. This is on the condition that, from this day forward, the rectors and ministers of the same monastery shall have full and firm power in every respect to do, arrange, and decide to do for the benefit of that monastery whatever they choose concerning the aforesaid villa or [the things] belonging to it.

And so that this authority of our gift and concession may retain unshaken and inviolable firmness through long ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be authenticated with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Meginarius, notary, have reviewed and subscribed it on behalf of Hugh.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of December, in the twenty-sixth year, with Christ favoring us, of the reign of Lord Louis, most serene emperor, in the third indiction. Done at Poitiers, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1307A]

### CCXXXV. FOR ABBESS ASIA. (Year 839.)

A privilege of the Emperor Lothar I by which he grants to Asia, abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary at Pavia, called Theodota, land situated between the wall and the outer wall of the city of Pavia.

[In Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, vol. I, p. 918.]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, eternal God, Lothar, by divine providence, emperor Augustus, etc.

Therefore let the discernment of all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own know how … Asia, abbess of the monastery called Theodote, which was established in honor of the ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, and lives under the rule of the eminent and most holy Father Benedict, requested our pious Highness that, out of reverence for God and for the reward of our soul, for the increase of the usefulness of that holy place and the relief of the needs of those serving God there, we should grant a certain necessary piece of land situated between the city wall and the outer wall.

Recalling that her petition was beneficial to the reward of our soul, we willingly assented and, after effective deliberation, completed it as an enduring grant by our authority. But so that no one might dare to bring any opposition concerning it in future times, we decided to insert in this authority both the account of the grant and the boundaries themselves. The boundaries of the aforesaid land are as follows: from the upper end, the gate called Marenca, as far as the tower of the same monastery, where there is an oratory in honor of the holy archangel Michael, with entrances and exits onto the public road. Moreover, from the lower side of the aforesaid tower as far as the territories of the aforesaid monastery; on one side it has the land of that monastery, and on the other side the public road. It measures in length eighty-eight feet and in width twenty-nine feet.

She also requested the serenity of our Highness that we should confirm under this present authority of ours the exchange which the aforesaid abbess, and likewise Teutberga, had made by our authority from the property of Saint Mary ever-virgin, belonging to the above-written monastery, with Deado and the new monastery situated in honor of Saint Agatha, as an appropriate and reasonable exchange, and strengthen it on both sides by the firmest right, just as we have done.

Therefore, giving orders, we command—and wish this to remain forever—that none of our faithful presume at any time to inflict any disturbance or opposition upon the party of the aforesaid monastery concerning any of all these properties. Rather, in their entirety, just as they have been granted and bestowed there by us and by our authority, they shall remain there perpetually for the benefit of that monastery, without anyone’s opposition or any disturbance.

If anyone should attempt to inflict any violence or bring any pretext against the security of this our precept, let him know that he must pay sixty pounds of the finest gold, half to our palace and half to the party of that monastery. And so that this authority of ours may obtain fuller force in the name of God, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Lothar, most serene Augustus.

Dructemirus, subdeacon and notary, reviewed it on behalf of Algimar.

Given on the day before the Nones of May, in the nineteenth year, with Christ favoring us, of the reign of Lord Lothar, pious emperor, in the second indiction.

Done at the royal palace of Pavia, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

### CCXXXVI. DIPLOMA OF THE EMPEROR LOTHAR FOR THE MONASTERY OF LUCERNE. (Year 839.)

[Note: Printed in Aegidius Tschudi, *Gallia Comata*, p. 149, and by Guillimann, *Rerum Helveticarum*, book III, chapter 4; Lunig, *Spicilegium ecclesiasticum*, part III, chapter 5, p. 178; Bouquet, *Rerum Gallicarum Scriptores*, vol. VIII, p. 366; and Schoepflin, at the place cited, from the authentic copy at Murbach.]

[In Neugart, *Codex Alemannicus*, p. 243.]

In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, eternal God, Lothar, by divine providence, emperor Augustus.

[Col. 1308C]

Let the discernment of all our faithful know that the venerable man Sigimarus [Note: Sigimarus of Murbach is to be placed sixth in the catalogue of the abbots of this monastery, which P. Bucelin published from papers communicated to him in *Germania Sacra*, part II, p. 238; there he is incorrectly called Sigismund.], abbot of the monastery called the Pilgrims’ Dwelling, situated in the duchy of Alsace on the river Murbach, brought before us an authority of our father Louis, of sacred memory. In it was inserted how our grandfather Pippin, formerly king, and later Louis himself, had granted, as an act of almsgiving, to the monastery of Lucerne [Note: Lucerna.] and to the monks living there five free men, named Waldon, Vulfarius, Vulfin, Wolfold, and Vulbert, with their sons and descendants, living in the place called Eman [Note: Read Eman (die Emmat), Emma, Emmeta, greater and lesser, in the district of Lucerne.], on the river Reuss [Note: Read Ruisa or Rusa, as Tschudi and Guillimann read it; commonly the Rüss or Reüss.], in the district of Aargau; namely, they had transferred to the aforesaid monastery whatever they had customarily rendered to the public authority. Therefore, giving orders, we command, etc.

And so that this authority of ours may be firmer and better preserved for future times, we ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

I, Eichardus, reviewed it on behalf of Agilmar.

[Col. 1309A]

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the twenty-first year, with Christ favoring us, of the reign of Lord Lothar, pious emperor [Note: The years of Lothar’s reign in Italy are counted from the year 820, when Lothar must have been declared king of that province; for in other diplomas of this emperor, where the years of the empire and of the kingship are specified separately, the former always exceeds the latter by twenty, although King Bernard of the Lombards had already died in 818. His subjects, however, who were attached to his party, were not immediately subdued, as Chifflet conjectures in the proofs to the *History of Tournus*, p. 268. Compare D. de Saint-Marc, *Chronological Summary of the General History of Italy*, vol. I, p. 467.], in the third indiction [Col. 1310A] [Note: The third indiction corresponds to the year 840.]. Done at the city of Strasbourg, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1309A]

## LETTERS OF LOUIS THE PIOUS

### FIRST LETTER OF LOUIS TO MAGNUS, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

He sends a copy of the rule for canons decreed at the Council of Aachen. (Year 816.)

[Note: The highly commendable policy of Louis the Pious, which the authors of that age praised exceedingly, was later condemned by some writers, who considered the matter less carefully. To lend greater authority to their opinion, certain writers invented a voice which, in a remarkable prodigy from heaven, reproached Louis for having added poison to the Church. Accordingly, in the year 817, no. 140 and following, Cointius examines the position of Peter Damian, who wrote a short work against canons who, although they were commonly supported by the revenues of the churches, possessed money and other goods separately; and that of John Mauburnus, who presided over the monastery of Livry in the diocese of Paris in the year 1500 and wrote against the Rule of Aachen and against Louis himself. He demonstrates that they were mistaken in this matter, as may be read there. See also Pagi under the year 816, nos. 16 and 17. Louis sent two other letters on the same subject: one to Sicharius, archbishop of Bordeaux, through Adalelmus; the other to Arno, archbishop of Salzburg, through Nothon.]

[Baluz., *Capitularia*, vol. I, p. 454.]

The most glorious Louis, ever-victorious Augustus by heavenly gift, sends greetings in the Lord to Magnus, venerable in Christ, archbishop of the city of Sens.

As we very recently promised you in the sacred assembly which, with God’s help, we convened at the palace of Aachen, where many things were enacted, with Christ’s favor, ecclesiastically—indeed, catholic­ally, we have sent to your venerable fatherhood, through our present envoys, namely Ermenfred and Haimo, the text of the canonical institution which that same sacred assembly undertook to collect and gather into one from the opinions scattered throughout the writings of the holy Fathers [Col. 1309C]. Since lack of time denied you the opportunity to copy it, it was our concern to order it carefully copied, so that its text might be conveyed to you intact, without any corruption or mutilation. Therefore we have sent this letter to your holiness, through which we command you—mindful of our admonition—to make every effort to summon the suffragan bishops of your diocese to you at a suitable place and time; to have the same Institution read aloud, chapter by chapter, before the ecclesiastical orders; to make plainly known how beneficially the sacred assembly took care to frame it for the profit of souls; and, in accordance with the ministry divinely entrusted to you [Col. 1309D] and the command of our authority, to declare before our aforementioned envoys that it must be observed by those who are reckoned under the name of the canonical profession.

As for those who are slower in understanding and perhaps cannot fully comprehend it, let its meaning be poured into their minds through your own diligence, or that of your fellow provincial bishops who possess the gift of knowledge. We also wish your prudent blessedness to ensure that the aforesaid envoys carefully warn everyone, as you shall indicate, to copy it without any corruption or mutilation [Col. 1310B]; for we have sufficiently instructed them how carefully, diligently, distinctly, and clearly it is to be copied. We had a copy of it deposited in the archive of our palace for this very reason: so that through it we could know and investigate whether it had been negligently copied by anyone. For, as we discovered, while it was being read aloud in that same sacred council, before it had been presented by the council in our presence, and while the measure of food and drink had not yet been fully established, certain envious men, mutilating it for the most part, imprudently copied certain chapters from it.

Therefore, if you find that anyone in your diocese has done such a thing, you must annul this action before the assembly of your provincial bishops [Col. 1310C] and before our aforesaid envoys, and you must declare that this authentic version is to be copied diligently, as we have already said, in the manner in which our envoys shall explain to them. We therefore wish all superiors of canons to copy it carefully, study it diligently, and strive to fulfill it effectively, insofar as the Lord grants them ability, for their own benefit and that of their subjects. Thus, when—as we stated generally to everyone in their sacred and venerable council—we send our envoys throughout our entire empire on the coming Kalends of September to investigate this matter, all of them, superiors and subjects alike, will be found vigorous doers of the same instruction, each according to his capacity and ability [Col. 1310D].

For we shall command that, with life as our companion, a diligent inquiry be made into how each superior fulfills his ministry; how they have obeyed our command concerning cloisters and the other necessary dwellings of the canons, the distribution of their stipends, and the preparation of lodging for the poor [Col. 1311A]; and who has taken pains to instruct his clergy according to the standard of this Institution and the other spiritual exercises—or whether anyone, out of avarice, has cast out one of those whom he could have governed reasonably in the service of God. Since, in order that the matters mentioned above might most suitably be carried out, without opposition from any difficulty, in places where they had not yet been implemented, we have granted a period of one year for their completion, as you know, anyone who during that year neglects to obey our command—or rather, God’s command—to the best of his ability will undoubtedly strike terror into the others, so that they will not dare to act likewise.

We have therefore sent you the text of the Institution which that same sacred and venerable council carefully excerpted from the opinions of the holy Fathers and declared should be observed by sanctimoniales living canonically in one community [Col. 1311B]. We wish it to be carefully prescribed, whether by you or by your fellow provincial bishops, in all the monasteries for girls throughout your diocese in which canonical life is practiced. We further decree that it be handed down by you both to the abbesses and to the other sanctimoniales, and that they be instructed by your diligence in how they ought to observe it.

Moreover, except for any abbess whom we order to come into our presence, we wish the abbesses at all other times to reside in their own monasteries and to strive to live according to this form of the Institution and govern those subject to them. They must not grant any of them permission to reside in villages, to wander outside for any reason whatsoever, or to devote themselves to their own pleasures [Col. 1311C].

Although some clerics possess monasteries of girls, and some laymen possess monasteries of men and even of girls, your most diligent care must nevertheless ensure that in all places established under your diocese, wherever communities of clerics and sanctimoniales exist, they live according to the form of this Institution, insofar as their resources and means permit. For there is absolutely no church possessing resources in which it is impossible to govern as many and such persons as can perform the divine office, and in which hospitality cannot be practiced according to its means.

We have also sent the aforesaid envoys to your holiness so that they might carefully and thoroughly observe your diligence, and that of the other ecclesiastics residing in your diocese, in this matter [Col. 1311D], and assist you in giving further admonitions. They are also to report to us how readily the superiors, male and female, have received it, how diligently they have tried to copy it, and how devoutly they have taken care to fulfill it according to their ability. For we have ordered them to remain and travel about in your diocese or that of your fellow provincial bishops, together with your envoy, until the aforementioned text has been copied by everyone. Thus, after arranging everything and carefully recording the assessments, when the time allows them to return to us after completing their work, they are to record in writing, from both sides, everything that has been done and, through their own agency and that of your envoy, report it to our knowledge [Col. 1312A], so that we may know to whom we should offer thanks and whom we ought to correct with deserved reprimands.

But if anyone in your diocese should insolently resist this Institution of ours and our admonition, and should disdain to observe, insofar as the Lord grants him ability, what has been established and decreed by that same sacred and venerable council, we command that, unless he corrects himself beforehand, whoever he may be, he hasten to appear before us at your admonition or that of our envoys, so that we may correct him worthily according to the measure of his fault.

We have also sent you a standard of weight and measure according to which bread and drink are to be distributed equally to clerics and sanctimoniales. We decree that it be held by everyone with the utmost firmness and inviolability [Col. 1312B] [Read, perhaps: “held by all”], and we prohibit by every means that anyone add to or diminish it.

At the end of this letter, therefore, we admonish your holiness that, in accordance with the ministry conferred upon you by divine gift, you obey our most salutary admonition in this matter obediently and without excuse, and provide the others with a good example by your obedience. It is indeed fitting that, the more exalted you are above others in the dignity of the priesthood and the more venerably you are loved by us, the more devoted and ready you should show yourself in carrying out the will of God and of us.

Farewell in the Lord, and pray for us.

## LETTER II. LOUIS TO THE MONKS OF ANIANE  
### (Year 821)

[In D. Bouquet, *Collection of Histories*, vol. VI, from the archives of Aniane.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, Emperor Augustus, to the venerable brothers established in the monastery of Aniane, or Gellone.

Recently Archbishop Agobard came into our presence [Note: [Col. 1311D] Agobard of Lyon was archbishop; Nibridius was archbishop of Narbonne], informing us that, while he and Archbishop Nibridius were present, you had all, with one accord and without delay, elected Tructesind as abbot over you. Since this action appeared reasonable to us, we did not delay giving our assent, desiring and hoping that divine mercy would cause it to prosper for his and your common salvation; that he might occupy among you the place of father and shepherd [Col. 1312D]; and that you, as Christ’s sheep, might submit to him in equal humility and devotion, as is worthy and right.

This obedience and submission in humility must be strengthened by the protection of charity. It must be practiced among you without the false outward display of pretense. You know very well with what zeal and toil this place was first begun and constructed by your father, the lord Benedict of blessed memory; and afterward with what diligence he strove that you—whom the grace of the heavenly Shepherd had gathered there through his devoted persistence—might conduct yourselves rightly according to the rule of monastic life. By God’s generosity he brought this to completion according to his desire [Col. 1313A].

Furthermore, from that same sacred examination, he adopted throughout the empire entrusted to us by God a standard of pious conduct, far and wide, and did not cease to disseminate it among you [Note: [Col. 1313D] Cointius corrects the reading to *coadunavit e vobis*, “he gathered together from among you,” and *disseminare*, “and disseminated it.”]. Since this is certainly how matters stand, we have deemed it fitting to admonish you to strive, with God’s cooperation, to ensure that during your days this work, so nobly begun and brought to growth, suffers no damage through any circumstance. Rather, by God’s mercy, always strive to be such that, as before, masters and teachers may be chosen from among you—not only of the holy regular life, but also of every spiritual discipline and the highest excellence—wherever necessity or willingness requires.

Moreover, we wish your abbot Tructesind to be admonished that he exercise fatherly love toward you, and consider, according to age, bodily health, or the affliction of any illness, what is suitable for each of those subject to him. He must take every precaution lest the fervor of zeal in correcting the negligent exceed proper measure and make them fainthearted [Col. 1313B]. Nor should he be such among those who observe God’s commandments that, through sluggishness and idleness, he weakens in them the rigor of perseverance. Rather, with the greatest discretion, following the Apostle, let him become all things to all people, so that he may be able to save all who belong to him.

But if it should happen—as we do not wish—that he deviates in anything outside the rule excellently handed down to you by the aforementioned Benedict, and prefers to do what must be done according to his own judgment and will rather than according to your common counsel, correct him, as beloved brothers and sons, with all gentleness and patience [Col. 1313C]. If he accepts your counsel and is corrected by you, attribute this to God’s gift. But if he should persist, God forbid, in his own opinion, then inform us of it before it becomes known outside among your neighbors; for although we exercise royal power over others, we always wish to maintain toward you the affection of a father.

Although we have granted you this permission, you must nevertheless take the greatest care not to become inflamed against your abbot over any matter through slight anger or minor agitation, and not to rise against him with stubborn audacity without cause. For if any one of you is inflamed against him without reason and knocks at our ears without cause, let him know that we shall be moved against him with strict punishment, so that one of this sort may serve as an example to the others [Col. 1313D], lest anyone in the future dare to rise unjustly against his master.

You also, elders, must assist him in everything, both in disciplining the younger brothers and in every other matter beneficial to the monastery. Do not allow him alone to be weighed down by so great a burden. Rather, “bear one another’s burdens,” as the Apostle says, “and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.”

Younger brothers, we have decided to admonish you also [Col. 1314A] to be obedient and humble in everything toward your abbot and your elders—not insolent, not murmurers—but to preserve your vocation with all humility and gentleness. For if you act otherwise, so that one of you becomes puffed up against the abbot and the brothers, becomes an encouragement to perverse transgression not only for himself but also for others, and refuses to endure the correction of his abbot and brothers, we command that he be sent to us without delay, so that we may send him to such a place that he will be wholly unable to cause you any scandal.

We have ordered these things to be written to you so that you may know how much care and concern we wish to have for you. For if you are willing to preserve his precepts in obedience, we wish to have with you the same intimacy which we appeared to have with your abbot Benedict, of pious memory, and always to care for you and for that monastery.

Since it is established by the charter of donation of your aforesaid father that the same monastery was first the allodial property of our father and afterward of us, we promise firmly to observe and inviolably preserve for all time the same permission which he first and we afterward appeared to grant through our immunities. Thus, whenever the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this life by divine calling, as long as you are able to find among yourselves men capable of governing that congregation according to the rule of Saint Benedict, you shall always have permission, by our often-mentioned and confirmed authority [Col. 1314C], to elect an abbot.

We wish you always good health as you pray for us and preserve your holy vocation.

Amen.

[Col. 1314C]

## LETTER III. MICHAEL AND THEOPHILUS, SONS OF THE EASTERN EMPERORS, TO LOUIS THE PIOUS  
### (Year 824)

[In D. Bouquet, ibid., from Baronius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*.]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, the one true God: Michael and Theophilus, faithful emperors of the Romans in that same God, to their beloved and honorable brother Louis, glorious king of the Franks and Lombards, and to him who is called their emperor [Note: [Col. 1313D] Here Louis the Pious is called emperor of the Franks, but not emperor of the Romans. For the Greeks never called Charlemagne, nor his successors in the Western Empire, Augusti or emperors of the Romans, however much they needed them.] [Note: [Col. 1314D] Michael recounts the movements stirred up by the seditious man Thomas and his death; he tells many falsehoods about the death of the emperor Leo and about his own acquisition of the empire.]

[The preceding text is lacunose.] [Note: [Col. 1314D] That is, after the victory won over the tyrant Thomas.]

From that time all the Christians of our empire [Col. 1314D] returned to unity of peace and their former harmony, glorifying and magnifying our champion, the Lord Jesus Christ, who deigned to gather his people into unity of faith, in submission to the empire which comes from him. Therefore we judged it fitting to make known to you, as to our peaceful friend and spiritual brother, and, as we believe, partner in the joy of the empire given by God to us, the things that have taken place among us [Col. 1315A], so that together, as is proper for worshipers of one and the same faith and religion, we may praise and glorify our Savior Jesus Christ with praises and hymns.

It would have been proper at the very beginning of our empire [Note: [Col. 1315D] Michael began to reign in the year 820], as to our spiritual brother and peaceful friend, to make known to you through our genuine letters what had happened to us. But, as stated above, the revolt of the aforementioned tyrant and rebel Thomas, condemned to a shameful death, prevented this. But now God has granted us this present and opportune time after his death and the restoration of unity and harmony among our people.

Therefore we considered it right to send to your glory our protospatharius and general Theodore; Nicetas, the most holy metropolitan of Myra in Lycia [Col. 1315B]; Fortunatus, archbishop of Venice [Note: [Col. 1315D] Fortunatus died in France while traveling to Rome with the emperor Michael’s ambassadors]; Theodore, the most reverend deacon and steward of this most holy, catholic, and great church of God, Saint Sophia; and our candidate Leo.

We announce to your glory through these written lines, and also through the men themselves, all that has been set forth, so that through them as well as through your envoys we may again learn of the health of your affection, the safety of your faithful, and the prosperity of all your affairs established among you.

Furthermore, through these genuine and faithful written lines we strengthen and confirm the former peace and friendship established between you and us. We beseech the mediator of that same peace, the Lord who said, “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27) [Col. 1315C], to make that peace more splendid and stronger, and to display it to former times and authorities, since we hold and hope that your most glorious power likewise agrees, just as ours does [lacuna].

We also make this known to your Christ-loving affection: many among ecclesiastical and lay men, having become alienated from the apostolic traditions and no longer preserving the boundaries of the Fathers, have become inventors of evil things [Note: [Col. 1315D] Later the emperor Michael slanders the Catholics and recounts many falsehoods which prove him a heretic.] [lacuna]. Therefore, seeking the honor of the Church of Christ, we wrote a letter to the most holy pope of ancient Rome and sent it to him through the aforementioned envoys [lacuna]. For the rest, may your spiritual affection arrange that they come to him with every honor and without harm [lacuna].

As a token of the affection that exists between us, we have sent through the aforementioned envoys one *prasinovultim*, one *milinovultim* [Note: [Col. 1315D] Cangius conjectures that these two words, *prasinovultim* and *milinovultim*, were formed from the Greek πρασινοβλάττην and μηλινοβλάττην. *Prasinum* means green; *melinum*, yellow; *blatta*, a worm or purple dye], two Tyrian [Note: [Col. 1316D] *Tyrium*: Tyrian purple, a purple cloth], two genuine purple garments, two *dirodina* [Note: [Col. 1316D] *Dirodinum*, for *diarhodinum*, a garment of rose color], and two *diventa* [Note: [Col. 1316D] *Diventum*, an unknown word].

Completed in the month of April, on the tenth day, in the second indiction, in the God-consecrated imperial city [Note: [Col. 1316D] “Imperial city,” that is, Constantinople].

[Col. 1316A]

## LETTER IV. LOUIS TO BADURADUS, BISHOP OF PADERBORN  
### For the Benefit of the Monastery of Corvey in Saxony  
### (Year 824)

[In D. Bouquet, ibid., from Schaten, *Paderborn Annals*, p. 78.]

In the name of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence emperor Augustus, to Baduradus, bishop and our envoy.

We do not doubt that you know how, at our command, Adelhard, formerly abbot, constructed from the foundations a certain monastery in Saxony, and how we endowed it by formal donation with certain properties through certain good men. Concerning all these properties, we ordered a precept of our authority to be made for that monastery [Col. 1316B], so that those properties might remain perpetually and securely in the legal possession of the same monastery.

But, as we have learned from the report of Warinus, the monastery’s venerable abbot, certain counts wish to violate and tear apart our aforementioned precept. Specifically, they wish to compel both free men and *liti*—who reside on the land of the same monastery—to go on military service and to subject them to judicial constraint. We do not wish them to do this.

Therefore, through this letter we command you to take up that precept which, as we have said, we made for the same monastery; to have it read again in the presence of those counts in whose jurisdictions the property of the aforesaid monastery is known to lie; and, by the authority of our command, to order them henceforth not to presume to violate the precept of our authority [Col. 1316C], but rather to strive to preserve it, as it is contained in that precept, if they wish to have our favor.

[Col. 1316C]

## LETTER V. THE BISHOPS ASSEMBLED IN THE COUNCIL OF PARIS TO LOUIS THE PIOUS AND LOTHAR  
### On the Worship of Images  
### (Year 825)

(See this letter in volume 98 of this *Patrologia*, col. 1299, among the works of Charlemagne.)

[Col. 1316C]

## LETTER VI. LOUIS TO HIEREMIAS, BISHOP OF SENS, AND JONAS, BISHOP OF ORLÉANS  
### Memorandum Given to Them When They Went as Legates to Pope Eugene II in the Matter of Images  
### (Year 824)

[Baluz., *Capitularies*, vol. I, from Goldast, *Imperial Constitutions*, and Sirmond, *Gallican Councils*.] [Col. 1316D]

To Hieremias and Jonas, venerable bishops, greetings in the Lord.

Bishops Halitgarius and Amalarius came into our presence on the eighth day before the Ides of December [Note: [Col. 1316D] Halitgarius was bishop of Cambrai; Amalarius was bishop of Trier], bringing collections from the books of the holy Fathers [Col. 1317A], which you had collected while assembled together at the council held at Paris [Note: [Col. 1317D] This council of Paris was held in the year 825, as is clear from the letter of the bishops assembled there to Louis Augustus; see Letter IV]. We had them read aloud before us also. Since they pleased us and were judged by us necessary and useful for the matter for which they had been collected, we decided that they should be sent to you with all speed.

Therefore, by way of admonition, we command your diligence to review them carefully before you report anything from them to the lord apostolic; to excerpt and write down whatever you find better and more appropriately suited to the present matter; and to take pains to offer it to him for reading. For, as you know, we asked him to grant permission for these collections to be made by our priests. Therefore it cannot be omitted that he be shown what has been collected with his permission [Col. 1317B].

Take the greatest care, however, to show him from these materials only what agrees in every respect with the reasonable position to be held concerning images, and what neither he nor his people can readily reject. You yourselves must also conduct the discussion with him on this matter patiently and moderately. Take the greatest care not to compel him, by resisting him too strongly, to fall into some irrevocable stubbornness [Note: [Col. 1317D] When Baronius cited this passage under the year 825, he added the following marginal note to soften it: “In this age, *pertinacia* is customarily used for steadfastness, as Saint Eulogius, among others, teaches in his writings.” Goldast did not let this convenient opportunity to attack Baronius pass him by: “Certainly Tully wrote somewhere that stubbornness is closely related to perseverance; but since the word *pertinacia*, wherever it is found, is always taken in a bad sense, it is difficult to suppose that it can have another meaning here, especially if one considers each part of the letter attentively. Thus Baluzius”] [Col. 1317C]. Rather, gradually, by appearing to comply with his words rather than openly resisting him, you should be able to lead him toward the measure that must be maintained in the veneration of images. Thus strive instead to bring it about that, with God’s help, the matter under discussion may be brought to a better rather than a worse condition.

After you have completed this discussion concerning the same images—if, indeed, Roman stubbornness permits it to come to nothing—so that the discussion held among you may be brought to some good and suitable conclusion, and if he tells you that he wishes to send his legates to Greece for this same reason, we wish you to ask him whether he would approve of our legates going to Greece together with his. If he considers this preferable and replies that he entirely wishes it, then we wish you to inform us of it with all haste by letters sent from you to us, and likewise to inform us of your arrival among us. Thus, when you come into our presence, you will find Halitgarius and Amalarius with us.

With the lord apostolic, consider where and when he wishes his and our legates to join together for boarding the ships; and, when you come, God willing, you can report this to us in person.

## LETTER VII. LOUIS TO POPE EUGENE II  
### Sent through Bishops Hieremias and Jonas with the Acts of the Synod of Paris  
### (Year 824)

[Baluz., ibid.]

To the most holy and most reverend lord and father in Christ, Eugene, supreme pontiff and universal pope, Louis and Lothar, by the ordering of divine providence emperors Augustus, your spiritual sons, eternal health in our Lord Jesus Christ.

Because we have truly recognized that we are debtors to those entrusted with the governance of the Churches and the care of the Lord’s sheep, and that we must offer them assistance and help in every matter pertaining to divine worship, according to the measure of our strength and the capacity of our understanding, we could not neglect, when the Greek legates made known to us what embassy they were to bring to you, to consider with the greatest care and concern what assistance we might be able, with God’s help, to provide you in this matter [Col. 1318B].

For this reason we asked your holiness to permit our priests to seek out and gather from the books of the holy Fathers those opinions which might suitably contribute to a true determination of the same matter about which those legates were going to consult you. When, with the permission granted by you as well, they diligently sought these opinions and, with divine grace assisting, collected whatever they were able to find in so short a time, they sent the material to us for reading.

After reading it, we have taken care to send it to your holiness for reading and examination through these envoys of ours, namely the venerable bishops Hieremias and Jonas. If your fatherhood deems it worthwhile, you may have with them a useful and indeed profitable discussion concerning the same embassy which you are to send to Greece [Col. 1318C], for they are highly learned in the sacred Scriptures and are also considerably practiced in disputational reasoning.

We have not sent them into the presence of your holiness with the aforementioned collection of opinions so that they might perform here some sort of teaching office, or so that they might be thought to have been sent here to teach. Rather, as we have already stated, since we are bound to offer assistance to this most sacred see in every matter, we deemed it fitting to send both these envoys and the writings they bring, in case they might provide you with any assistance.

We commend them to your holiness, so that they may find with you both a gracious reception and an opportunity to speak with you familiarly. Your holiness knows how divided the Greek people are in this matter of the veneration of images [Col. 1318D]. Therefore we ask that your holiness deign to apply care and diligence to the question of how, through your most salutary teaching and admonition, they may be recalled more to harmony and unity than driven by this matter into greater discord and dissension.

For this reason you must consider with the utmost caution that the embassy which you intend to send there be supported by such prudence and moderation that it may justly be reproached by no one, neither Greek nor Roman, but be such as ought always to proceed from that most sacred see in every matter [Col. 1319A].

If it pleases your holiness that our envoys be sent to those regions together with yours for this same embassy, allow us to know this at a suitable time. Let us know not only that, but also—if they are to go—where and when they should join your envoys.

We do not ask about sending our envoys there because it appears necessary to us, or because we doubt that your envoys can accomplish this embassy by themselves. Rather, we offer them to you so that you may know that we are prepared in every matter which the need or will of this most sacred see may require [Col. 1319B].

We wish your holy, venerable, and pious fatherhood always good health in Christ, and ask that you remember us and all our people in your most holy prayers, most holy and blessed Father.

## LETTER VIII. A LETTER TO BE READ PUBLICLY TO THE PEOPLE OF GOD  
### On the Summoning of Four Councils  
### (Year 828)

[Baluz., ibid., p. 654.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ. Louis and Lothar, by the ordering of divine providence emperors Augustus, to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own people.

[Col. 1319C]

We believe that you remember how this year, on the advice of the priests and other faithful men, we ordered a general fast to be celebrated throughout our entire kingdom, and how we called upon God with complete devotion to reveal to us in what matters we had most offended him, so that he might be propitious toward us, and to grant us a peaceful time in which to undertake the correction necessary for us.

We had indeed wished to hold our general assembly at a suitable time and to deal there with common correction. This would have been accomplished by God’s mercy, had not, as you know, the uprising of the enemies prevented it. But since it could not then be done according to our will, it seemed good to us to hold the present assembly with some of our faithful and to consider there, with the Lord’s help, how the matters left unfinished because of the aforementioned impediment might be brought to completion [Col. 1319D].

Therefore we wish your diligence to know that at this present assembly we considered first of all that the archbishops, with their suffragans, should meet at suitable places and at an appropriate time, and that there they should seek and discover, according to divine authority, both concerning their own affairs and concerning the correction and amendment of us all, and should announce their findings to us and to our faithful according to the ministry entrusted to them.

We likewise considered sending our envoys throughout our entire kingdom, who would strive with all possible diligence concerning every matter that appeared to pertain to correction, and who would correct immediately, by our authority, whatever they found possible [Col. 1320A] [Sirmond: “by themselves”]. If any difficulty opposed them in any matter, they were to take care to report it to our knowledge.

Therefore we wish all of you, for the sake of the common salvation, the honor of the kingdom, and the benefit of the people, not to neglect to be obedient and helpful to our envoys in every way within your power. You should also know that, for this reason, we intend to sit one day each week in our palace to hear cases, so that through this or that count, through the diligence of the envoys and the obedience of the people, matters may become more clearly known to us.

And so that all these things may succeed, we wish a general three-day fast to be proclaimed for the Monday after the octave of Pentecost and to be observed generally by everyone with the greatest devotion [Col. 1320B].

Since we know that enemies of God’s holy Church are being stirred up everywhere and wish to attack the kingdom entrusted to us by God, we command and order that all men throughout our kingdom who are liable for military service be well prepared with horses, weapons, clothing, carts, and provisions, so that whenever they are notified by us, they may depart without any delay and proceed wherever necessity requires, and remain there for as long as necessity requires.

These are the chapters concerning the instruction of the envoys.

They must be told that it is necessary for us to understand collectively what danger threatens us, especially because through our negligence such great and serious matters have occurred by which God could have been offended and the honor and dignity of the kingdom diminished. Moreover, we have identified another negligence arising from the earlier occasion [Sirmond: “originating from the earlier occasion”], namely, that the embassy itself was not carried out as the necessity itself required, although you say in part that we gave you the grounds for this by failing to give you a full command in every respect to investigate this necessity.

Therefore the greatest care must be taken to determine how, with the Lord’s help, the matters corrupted through negligence and carelessness may now be corrected, and how it may diligently be ensured that such things do not happen again. After this, the associates are to be designated, and then the nature of the embassy that must be imposed is to be stated.

### I.

First, the envoys must be instructed above all to take every precaution not to be a burden to the people on their journey, lest they inflict affliction upon those whom they ought to assist.

### II.

They must first announce to the people, through our letter, our will and purpose, and the intention with which they have been sent by us. They must also be instructed about what they are to investigate.

### III

[Col. 1321A]

Above all, let them inquire carefully how each of those who ought to govern the people keeps himself guarded in his own ministry, so that we may recognize those who deserve thanksgiving for doing well, while those who deserve correction and rebuke for their negligence may in every way be made known to us. The inquiry is to be conducted as follows.

Let the best and most truthful men in each county be chosen. If any one of them is found not yet to possess the fidelity he has promised us, let him make that promise. Then they are to be instructed how they must preserve that fidelity toward us: namely, that if any of them knows of some matter concerning those rulers and various ministers who ought to govern and preserve the people—matters about which they will be questioned—which affects the people’s loss or disadvantage, and through which danger to our souls and dishonor might come upon us, he must make it known without fail, if he wishes to keep his fidelity and promise intact. If, after such admonition and formal warning, anyone is discovered to have stated matters otherwise than the truth stands, let him know that he is to be counted among the unfaithful.

[Col. 1321B]

These are the chapters which we wish them to investigate diligently. (Compared with the very ancient Tilian manuscript, formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint Remigius at Reims.)

First, concerning the bishops: how they carry out their ministry; what their conduct is like; how they keep the churches and clergy entrusted to them ordered and properly arranged; and what matters they chiefly pursue, whether spiritual or secular business.

Next, what sort of assistants they have in their ministry—namely, chorepiscopi [archpriests [Note: [Col. 1321D] Absent from the manuscript]]; archdeacons; household stewards; and the priests throughout their dioceses—and what zeal they possess for teaching, or what reputation they truly have among the people.

Likewise, let them inquire concerning all monasteries according to the character and profession of each one; and similarly concerning the other churches granted in benefice by our authority.

Let them inquire whether the bishops, in making their circuits through their dioceses, burden the other smaller churches or impose a burden upon the people, and whether improper gifts (*exenia* [manuscript: *exsenia*]) are demanded from the priests by the bishops themselves or by their ministers.

In the same way, let them inquire concerning the counts, what diligence they show in their ministry, so that we may recognize whoever performs it well. If anyone acts otherwise, we emphatically wish to know this: namely, whether the people, through his negligence and indolence, lack justice and peace, or whether he has knowingly or unknowingly allowed something unjust to be done.

Next, what sort of ministers or agents he has for governing the people; whether they act justly or unjustly in those ministries; or whether, with the count’s consent or negligence, they deviate from truth and justice.

It must be determined which persons, and for what offenses, are required to come into our presence. Apart from bishops, abbots, and counts, who must always come to our assemblies, the following persons are to come if they are found guilty of such offenses and crimes as are listed below.

[Col. 1322A]

## Letter IX. The Imperial Letter to Be Read Generally to the People of God

Sent by Emperor Louis the Pious after the assembly at Aachen concerning councils of bishops to be convened in the four regions of the empire. (Year 828.)

[Baluz., same work, p. 658.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothar, emperors Augustus, by the providence of God, to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own faithful:

We believe that you remember how this year, on the advice of the priests and our other faithful, we ordered a general fast to be observed throughout our entire kingdom, and that God be entreated with complete devotion to show us mercy, to reveal to us in what matters we had especially offended him, and to grant us a peaceful period in which to undertake the correction necessary for us.

Indeed, we had wished to hold our general assembly at a suitable time and to deal there with a common correction; and this would have taken place, by God’s mercy, had the disturbance caused by our enemies not prevented it, as you know. But since it could not then be done according to our will, it seemed good to us to hold the present assembly with some of our faithful and to consider there, with the Lord’s help, how those matters which had remained unfinished because of the aforesaid obstacle might be brought to completion.

Therefore we wish your diligence to know that at this present assembly, together with our faithful, we considered that first of all the archbishops [Col. 1322C] should meet with their suffragans at suitable places and at an appropriate time, and that there they should investigate and discover, according to divine authority, matters concerning both their own correction and amendment and that of all of us, and should announce their findings to us and to our faithful in accordance with the ministry entrusted to them.

For who would not perceive that God has been offended by our most wicked deeds and provoked to anger, when he sees his anger raging for so many years in the kingdom committed to us by him through diverse scourges—namely, continual famine, the death of animals, pestilence among human beings, the barrenness of almost all crops, and, so to speak, the people of this kingdom miserably harassed and afflicted by the most varied disasters of disease [Note: [Col. 1321D] These disasters, which the Franks had been suffering for several years, were declared by the devil in that very year, 828, during exorcisms through the mouth of a possessed girl; see Einhard, *Book III of the Translation of the Holy Martyrs Marcellinus and Peter*, chap. 13. (Patrologia, vol. CIV.)], and almost wholly deprived of every abundance of goods?

Nor do we doubt that it also arises from his just vengeance that scandals often arise in this kingdom through tyrants who, by their wickedness, strive to tear apart the peace of the Christian people and the unity of the empire.

It must likewise be attributed to our sins that, in the preceding year, the enemies of Christ’s name entered this kingdom and boldly and with impunity—or rather cruelly—carried out plundering, the burning of churches, the capture of Christians, and the killing [Col. 1323A] of God’s servants [Note: [Col. 1322D] These words refer both to the Saracens, whom Aizo joined in the Spanish March, and to the Bulgarians, who ravaged Pannonia in the year 827].

It is being carried out, then, by God’s just judgment, that because we offend in every respect, we are scourged both inwardly and outwardly. For we are plainly ungrateful for God’s benefits, since we are found to use them not according to God’s will but according to our own carnal inclination.
