Therefore, deservedly, God’s creatures granted to us by him fight against us in our ingratitude, according to the saying: “The whole world will fight on behalf of him against the senseless” (Wisdom 5:21).

Yet because we are afflicted and struck in so many ways, it is right and necessary that we return with all our heart to him by whom we are struck, so that the prophetic saying may be fulfilled in us: “Affliction alone will give understanding to the hearing” (Isaiah 28:19).

But because the merciful and compassionate Lord moderates the scourge itself so that he appears to impose it not for our destruction but rather for our correction, we ought truly to humble ourselves before him, to anticipate his face in confession, and to implore his mercy with bowed minds. Thus, may he who has made us experience scourges by a most just dispensation know that we recognize our sins, for which we are justly scourged by him, and understand more clearly the matters in which we especially offended him and provoked his anger. Then, by his mercy, abandoning and correcting what is wrong, pursuing what is good, and carrying it out with complete devotion, may we be able through a spirit of humility and a contrite soul to offer to God the sacrifice owed to him, escape the anger of his indignation, and, through worthy and appropriate correction and the performance of good works, earn, although unworthy, the grace of his reconciliation.

But because we recognize that we have sinned more grievously in this respect—since we ought to have been an example of salvation to everyone, to care for all, and by imperial authority to correct the deeds of the wicked before they increased—we wish, with the Lord propitious toward us, to obtain pardon in the sight of his mercy through worthy satisfaction, and through the most salutary correction and the good diligence which until now our negligence and ignorance have left undone, to amend as diligently as we can, at the proper time and with the counsel of our faithful. We wish to make our intention in this matter manifest to everyone.

Therefore, with the advice of the priests and our other faithful, we have established and decreed that, for this purpose—namely, to appease the Lord’s fury against us and against those subject to us—assemblies of the same bishops should be held in the most suitable manner in four places of our empire.

First, in the city of Mainz, where Archbishop Otgar, Hadabald, Hetti, and Bernuinus are to meet with their suffragans [Sirmond: metropolitans].

Second, in the city of Paris, where the future bishop of Sens, Ebbo, Ragnoard, and Landramnus are to meet with their suffragans.

Third, at Lyon, where Agobard, Bernard, Andreas, Benedictus, and Agericus are likewise to meet with their suffragans.

Fourth, at Toulouse, where Notho, Bartholomew, Adalelmus, and Agiulfus are to meet together with their suffragans.

At these assemblies they must discuss, investigate, and, with God’s help, discover matters pertaining to the Christian religion and to their pastoral care: what is held by the princes and the rest of the people either as divine authority teaches or otherwise; and what has been partly or wholly abandoned so that it is no longer observed.

Next, they must discover what may be found in the morals, conduct, and actions of those who have been appointed pastors of the people that does not agree with divine rule and authority. They must likewise discover what circumstances in either order have caused deviation from the right path.

Whatever is discovered concerning these matters must be kept with such diligent care that they do not allow it to come to anyone else’s knowledge before the appointed time. For this reason, one notary is to be chosen from among them all to record what they discover; bound by oath, he is to preserve carefully and faithfully whatever has been found and arranged.

[Col. 1324C]

## Letter X. The Bishops Gathered in the Synod at Paris in the Year 829, to Emperors Louis and Lothar

(Year 829.)

[Note: [Col. 1323D] It is useful to report some passages from the preface to this synod:

“Since it is plainly evident that the Church—which Christ, who redeemed it with his own blood, in his hidden dispensation wished to entrust to his orthodox servants, the glorious emperors Louis and Lothar, to govern and protect—is afflicted by various kinds of sickness, crushed by manifold disasters, and, as our merits demand, experiences the divine sword raging against it inwardly and outwardly, continually suffering the blows which the Lord threatened against those unwilling to obey his commands and instead falling into the evils he forbade, those God-filled princes, inspired from heaven, wisely judged that a worthy conversion to God ought to be undertaken . . . . . Desiring to provide for their salvation according to the ministry entrusted to us, in the year 829 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the reign of Louis and his son Lothar, on the eighth day before the Ides of June, we unworthy bishops—namely, from the dioceses of Duyocoytoyum, Sens, Tours, and Rouen—assembled at the city of Paris. We have decided briefly to note, in chapters below, how we acted and deliberated concerning the matters set forth above, in accordance with the admonition of those same princes.”]

[Apud D. Bouquet, *Collection of Histories*, vol. VI, from Sirmond, vol. II of the Councils of Gaul, p. 542.]

To the most excellent lords, endowed with the grace of piety, Louis and Lothar, orthodox and most invincible emperors Augustus:

We, your servants, although unworthy, yet bishops, humbly render thanks to God and praise and proclaim his boundless mercy and kindness. He causes you to burn with such devotion as his servants in love for him that you continually think about the advancement and exaltation of his holy Church and, as faithful and beloved spiritual sons, always strive to raise her—like a spiritual mother—to better and higher things.

For when the divine sword, because of our iniquity, was wearing down inwardly and outwardly the empire divinely entrusted to you through manifold disasters, you wisely perceived that these things occurred only by God’s just judgment. Immediately, by letters expressing your serenity, you admonished all the pastors of the churches in the preceding year that, since it was clear that they were the Lord’s watchmen and that the divine sword was raging over the earth—that is, over sinners—they should remember their watchmanship. After everyone generally had observed a three-day fast, each person placed in whatever order should diligently examine his own conscience, and, wherever he recognized that he had offended God, should not delay correcting himself through the satisfaction of repentance.

In those same letters you also wished to insert that, if God granted you peace and leisure on every side, you intended to spend this general assembly in such a way that first, whatever in yourselves—that is, in your person and ministry—was found to require correction, you would correct with the Lord’s help. Then you would investigate whatever in all the orders of your empire displeased God and, according to his will and with the consent of your faithful, restore it to the path of righteousness, so that you might make him propitious toward yourselves and toward the people entrusted to you.

But because the desired time was obstructed by external incursions and you did not obtain it according to your wish, your serenity chose to hold an assembly with some of your faithful during the past winter, to deliberate carefully about the matters mentioned above, to seek God’s will, and to provide for the welfare of the Church entrusted to you.

Therefore, concerning all that appeared to require timely amendment, your serenity drew up suitable chapters and sent capable agents, so that through those chapters they might both punish the crimes of wicked men and make the praise of good men known to your highness.

Among other things, you also decreed that assemblies of bishops should be held at one and the same time in the four regions of your empire. At these assemblies they were to discuss, investigate, and, with God’s help, discover matters pertaining to the Christian religion and to their pastoral care: what was held by the princes and the rest of the people either as divine authority teaches or otherwise; and what had been partly or wholly abandoned so that it was no longer observed.

Next, they were to discover what might be found in the morals, conduct, and actions of those who had been appointed pastors of the people that did not agree with divine rule and authority. They were likewise to discover what circumstances in either order had caused deviation from the right path; and whatever they found concerning these matters they were to make known to your highness.

As God gave us the ability, we, your most faithful and devoted guardians of your salvation, according to the smallness of our understanding and as the brevity of the time allowed, have, in accordance with your holy devotion and ordinance, noted in chapters in the preceding booklets those matters pertaining to the Christian religion, to our ministry and danger, and also those which we perceived to concern our own correction and amendment, as well as those which we foresaw ought to be announced and enjoined upon peoples generally. We have offered these to your serenity to be read—or rather, to be approved.

Although we chose first to satisfy your most ardent desire concerning the matters set forth above, we have nevertheless not consigned to oblivion those things which we recognized as pertaining specifically to your person and ministry. Rather, looking to your salvation, we have diligently collected in the second booklet of this work certain necessary chapters concerning your name and ministry and the danger to be avoided. We have dedicated them to be presented to you familiarly as an admonition, so that by examining, reading, and hearing them carefully, your highness may clearly and distinctly recognize the matters about which and for which, in our aforementioned assemblies, we have acted faithfully and beneficially according to the measure of our strength.

From this point follow certain matters which we have briefly selected from the chapters of our assembly and recognized as necessary for the observance and salvation of ourselves and of your faithful laymen. Thereafter follow other matters which we have judged to be highly salutary for your piety to request.

[Col. 1326B]

## Letter XI. Louis to Aldric, Bishop of Le Mans

Concerning certain properties alienated from his church. (Year 835.)

[Baluz., Book III of the *Miscellanies*, p. 165.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor Augustus, by the clemency of God’s restored favor, to Aldric, venerable bishop and our faithful servant, greetings.

Let your diligence know that your agent has come into our presence and reported that certain of our vassals—Ghermundus, Vulfardus, Berchadus, Bodo, and his associate—hold benefices from your bishopric which were formerly alienated from it by leases.

Therefore we wish you to recover them by our authority until you come into our presence, and always take great care concerning your fidelity to us, as we know you have done until now. For your aforementioned agent entreated our mercy that we give you an agent who might transfer the aforesaid properties to you and to your Church and make the lawful investiture. Accordingly, we order Helisachar, our agent, to make the investiture of the aforesaid benefices for you when he has been sent by us to those parts.

We also wish you, as soon as you can, to send us a thoroughly trustworthy agent who will inform us how matters are now being conducted toward you and our other faithful, and what has been done concerning those matters which we ordered you to undertake.

Farewell, and pray for us.

## Letter XII. Louis to Hilduin, Abbot of Saint-Denis

Concerning the collection into a single work of whatever he had found scattered through the Greek histories about Saint Denis. (Year 835.)

[Apud D. Bouquet, same work, from Surius under 9 October, p. 716.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor Augustus, by the clemency of God’s restored favor, to Hilduin, venerable abbot of the monastery of the most holy martyrs and special protectors Denis the Precious and his companions, eternal salvation in Christ.

All the generations of Gaul throughout past times have perceived how great a gift and protection the providence of the Lord has repeatedly, indeed continually, bestowed through the most blessed Denis—not only upon us and our predecessors and ancestors, but also upon the peoples of our entire empire. Through his distinguished apostolate they received the beginnings of the faith and obtained the aids of salvation.

Our predecessors did not honor the glory of this outstanding witness and friend of God in vain. While on earth they honored his sacred remains, for love and honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whatever resources they could; through his most worthy prayers they deserved to obtain the privilege of honor both in earthly and heavenly matters.

Thus one of the ancient kings of the Franks, Dagobert, who had shown no ordinary reverence toward that most precious martyr of Christ, was exalted during mortal life and, as the celebrated divine vision reports, was freed from punishments through his assistance and established desirably in eternal life [Note: [Col. 1327D] The vision which a monk of Saint-Denis fabricated after Dagobert’s death, claiming that it had first been shown to John the Sicilian hermit, should be counted among the legends.]

Our ancestors likewise embraced the sweet-sounding name of Lord Denis—for that is how they were accustomed to call him in their words and writings—with pious love and most beloved devotion.

Our great-grandfather, Charles, illustrious prince of the Franks, rejoiced that through the prayers of that most excellent martyr he had obtained the height of princely authority. At the end of his mortal life (741), he faithfully entrusted to him what he could hold more dearly, namely his own body, to be raised on the great day of judgment and his soul to be presented to the Lord. In this way he especially displayed the devotion and confidence of his heart toward his special patron.

Our grandfather Pippin, likewise of holy memory, received the blessing of heavenly favor. Because of the altar before the tomb of the aforesaid and repeatedly mentioned Lord Denis—dedicated by divine and memorable revelation, at the command of that most holy martyr, in honor of God and the apostles Peter and Paul, who were shown to be present—he was anointed king of the Franks by the same apostolic pope Stephen, together with his two sons, namely Carloman and our lord and father, Charles of divine memory, rightly called the Great, during the solemn celebration of Mass (754).

The title of his own tomb also makes known with what humility he ordered himself to be buried before the threshold of the basilica of the holy martyrs, once the course of this life had ended (768).

We too have experienced the benefits of his aid through many and frequent gifts. Above all, however, in the event of human vicissitude, when—as must always be confessed—we were visited by God’s just judgment with the rod of his instruction, we were restored and renewed by divine power before the aforesaid altar through the merits and comfort of our lord and most pious father Denis, by the staff of his gracious mercy (834). By episcopal judgment and authority we resumed the military belt, and until the present we have been sustained by his gracious assistance.

Therefore, venerable guardian and devotee of that provider and helper of ours, our lord Denis, we wish to admonish you to gather into one body whatever knowledge of him has been taken through translation from Greek histories, or whatever has been explained into our language from books written by him in his native tongue, by the command of our authority and through your diligent effort and the labor of translators, insofar as it is suitable to insert into this work.

Also gather what you have already found in Latin books, together with the material contained in the little book of his passion, and with what you found when you brought forth and showed to our serenity the material discovered in the oldest volumes or documents of the library of the Paris church, his sacred see. Arrange all this according to what you know of the suitability of the matters, subjects, and periods, and compose from it a single body and uniform text, so that it may be made known more briefly, weariness may be relieved for the bored, the less capable, and students of reading, and the benefit of edification may likewise be provided for all.

When these matters have been arranged in this way, we wish you to append the revelation shown to the blessed Pope Stephen in the church of that same most holy Denis, as it was dictated by him, together with the events connected with it, and the hymns which you possess concerning this glorious martyr and pontiff, as well as the nocturnal office.

But also collect separately, and with their integrity preserved, whatever else has been found concerning him in another volume, and send it to us as soon as possible, transcribed distinctly and correctly, or bring it in person. For wherever we know him to be, we believe that we possess a most great and exceedingly sweet pledge of the desired presence of that lord and comforter of ours, if through prayer, conversation, or reading we converse with him, or about him, or with words spoken by him.

Farewell in Christ, man of God, and continually remember us in your holy prayers.

[Col. 1328D]

## Letter XIII. Hilduin, Abbot of Saint-Denis, to Louis the Pious

He sends together whatever memory and the books at hand supplied concerning Saint Denis. (Year 836.)

[Apud D. Bouquet, same work, from Cointius, vol. VIII of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, p. 395.]

[Note: [Col. 1327D] To this letter Hilduin added a rather lengthy work in which he maintained that Dionysius the Areopagite, having left the Athenian bishopric and had another bishop appointed in his place, came to Rome; and that the same Dionysius was sent by Clement, bishop of Rome, into Gaul, where he later completed his martyrdom. Cointius refutes Hilduin’s work under the year 835, no. 115 and following.]

To Louis the Pious, always Augustus, honored by admirable divine kindness and the reverence due to authority, Hilduin, humble servant of Christ and matricularius of my lord Denis the Precious and his companions, and in all things most devoted to your imperial lordship, wishes present prosperity in Christ, the blessing of eternal happiness, and glory.

“My heart exults in the Lord, and my horn is exalted in my God. My mouth is enlarged,” and my lips will rejoice, so that I may proclaim the praises of my most glorious lord and martyr Denis, at the command of my lord the outstanding emperor. I could not keep them silent even if I had perhaps been forbidden by someone.

Indeed, I have great reason for rejoicing, because divine favor has wished to grant my desire in fuller measure, so that I recognize that the conception of my mind pleases him, since your God-pleasing sublimity has cooperated in action by extending the hand of authority over what my humility had spontaneously planned to undertake.

It is therefore beyond doubt that he is the author of good works and of all spiritual pursuits, who stirs the minds of those whom he wishes and, according to his pleasure, assists their actions through their abilities.

My spirit also greatly rejoices in God my Savior because your Christian soul so clearly recognizes the benefits of divine goodness and the consolations of the saints toward itself, and shows itself so readily inflamed with reverence and service toward its author and restorer and toward its special intercessors.

For your pious soul would not confess from its depths the divine judgments as true and just in this way unless it recognized itself to have been enlightened by the Holy Spirit. Nor would your wisdom of the greatest discernment investigate so devotedly the deeds and words of God’s friends unless it loved the supreme good, from whom and through whom all good things exist.

Your religious devotion is recognized as inflamed by love of him, so that you might investigate the glorious triumphs of Christ’s soldiers. Once you know them, you will fight more strongly against vices and the authors of vices through their assistance, so that, following the examples of the martyrs who fought manfully and conquered faithfully, you too may reach the palm with which they were rewarded.

This further contributes to the encouragement of your vow and diligence: Ezra, the restorer of Holy Scripture, thereby earned a great reward from God and acquired for himself an honorable name among human beings.

Therefore, when the fame of this most holy Father of ours—so ancient in respect of his earthly origin, conversion, and death—has become known to almost the entire world through his remarkable holiness and miraculous wonders, while knowledge of him remains known to only a few of our people and still unknown to many, once it has been disclosed through your efforts you will, as you yourself know better, gain great merit and acquire an everlasting memorial.

May the Lord make us suitable fellow workers for the completion of your good will. We obey your commands without hesitation in proportion to the diligence with which you request those things which we willingly carry out as executors.

Therefore, since you ask us to send you as quickly as possible, collected into one, whatever we have found in both Greek and Latin books concerning our lord and patron Denis, which until now we have known only imperfectly, and since we consider it unfitting to delay what our service plainly owes to your authoritative desire, we shall, insofar as the brevity of time permits, commit quickly to the notaries’ pens whatever our swiftly recalling memory suggests to our lips, with the Lord’s favor.

We humbly ask your wisdom not to seek in what we undertake to write—out of reverence and love for the most holy martyr and in obedience to your command—ornateness of words or elegance of composition, but rather the sincerity of the purest truth, as we have taken it from the words of the ancients.

Do not criticize us concerning the force of cases, prepositions, and conjunctions, or concerning changes in letters below, or concerning the placement of punctuation according to grammatical art. For we have undertaken not to pursue such matters, but to hasten the service of our devotion and the duty of commending ourselves to you, especially since we shall weave together those things which we have expressed from another language in the sequence of their wording, just as they have been filtered from the press. Although in translation they may not retain the corresponding flavor of the language, they nevertheless convey the savory taste of truth and of their meaning.

Accordingly, as your lordship commanded, we shall set forth the order of the history gathered into one, and afterward disclose its fullness separately to all readers and hearers.

For the divine inspiration and execution of what we desire faithfully to make public—to demonstrate what is true and probable—will be involved. We do not think that much labor is required from us for this, since truthful statements from well-known and thoroughly approved persons make clear what ought to be held and believed concerning this most holy martyr of Christ.

[Col. 1330C]

## Letter XIV. Louis the Pious to Jonah, Bishop of Orléans

Concerning the monastery of Anisolus. (Year 838.)

[Apud D. Bouquet, same work, from Baluz., Book III of the *Miscellanies*, p. 131.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, emperor Augustus, by the clemency of God’s restored favor, to Jonah, venerable bishop, greetings.

We wish it to be known that word has reached us that monks from the monastery of Saint Carilephus, in their presumptuous departure, had stripped that same monastery of its ecclesiastical ornaments, both from its treasury and from its vessels and vestments, as well as from its books.

Therefore, we command you and Abbot Henry to investigate this with every diligence and to have the ecclesiastical goods restored to that church in their entirety.

Farewell. From this matter, know that we have confidence in you, just as in it you recognize our will.

[Col. 1330D]

## Letter XV. The Same to the Same

(Year the same.)

[Apud Baluz., same work.]

In the name of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, [Col. 1331A] emperor Augustus, by the clemency of God’s restored favor, to Jonah, venerable bishop, greetings.

We wish you to know that word has reached us that the monks from the monastery of Saint Carilephus have left their own monastery in search of other places, forgetful of their own promise, in which they promised obedience and stability of place and renounced their own wills according to the rule of Saint Benedict. They also forgot the Gospel saying in which we hear the Lord’s example: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). They have also forgotten the apostolic saying: “Be subject to every human institution, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him” [Col. 1331B] (1 Peter 2:13).

They did this for no other reason than that their abbot appeared disobedient to us. We therefore took the same monastery away from that abbot and lawfully returned it to Aldric, bishop, and to the Church entrusted to him, just as it had been possessed and built by his predecessors. The bearer of this letter will be able to tell you how this was done, since it would be lengthy for us to include everything in this letter concerning how the matter was reasonably handled and settled. We perceive no contradiction in the canonical authority that monks ought to be subject to bishops.

Therefore, we wish you to be our agent together with Abbot Henry, and by the full authority of the canons, the rule, and our own authority, compel those same monks to return to their own monastery.

But if any one of them does not obey you [the Latin text reads *non ab obaudierit*, an evidently corrupt or uncertain form], we wish you to compel him to come into our presence at the next assembly, which, with the Lord’s consent, we are going to hold at Quierzy.

Farewell, and pray to the Lord for us.

## Index of Saint Agobard

(This volume, columns 9–351.)

Analytical index of the subjects and words contained both in the text of Saint Agobard and in the notes attached to the text.

(The numbers in this index indicate our columns.)

### A
## A

Abbots, if they possess the totality of ecclesiastical property, are superior to bishops, 175. Those who abuse ecclesiastical property are censured, 247. Abbo of Fleury became renowned not for miracles but for holiness of life, 131. Abraham was a Christian, 172. Permission to depart, 101. To release envoys, 102. The Acephali heretics—that is, the Eutychians—hostile to the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, 56. —Clerics, 138. Adalard, abbot of Corbie, a man of great authority at the court of Louis the Pious, 100, 228, 230. Young boys placed in church to learn ecclesiastical singing, 334, 337 ff. Adoption concerns those who belong to another family, 50. The worship of images is impious, 199 ff. The history of the ordination of Adrian II is examined, 307. An adulterer does not seek the fruit of offspring, but to satisfy lust, 195. Adultery can neither be permitted nor prohibited, 187. —A widow who married after assuming the religious veil is said to have committed it, 317. Adultery is loving someone above Christ, 206. A sacristan does not commit embezzlement with respect to what has been entrusted to him, 239. Equity must be established not by killings but by wisdom and mercy, 253. The Africans trace their origin to Abraham, 96. The decree of the African council concerning prayers and orations to be sung in church, 334. Hagarenes—that is, Saracens—96.

Agobard, archbishop of Lyon, 29. He suffers persecution on account of the Jews, 70. His chapters against the Jews, 72. His modesty and reserve—or, as he calls it, timidity—99 ff., 113, 116, 198, 229 ff., 231. He is criticized for having said that interpreters of Sacred Scripture were ignorant of grammar, 162 ff. He took part in the Council of Compiègne, 324. He corrected the Antiphonary of the church of Lyon, 330. His times were exceedingly evil and troubled, 138 ff.

The hastened piety of the Alexandrians is commended, 214. An altar constructed over the holy body of a martyr for the honor and worship of God, 208. The Amalekites trace their origin to Abraham, 96. Amalarius, deacon, abbot, and chorepiscopus, 102, 325, 339.

[Col. 1332B] The noble and elevated deed of Ambrose, bishop of Milan, carried out in the matter of the Jews’ synagogue and the burning of the Valentinian grove, is related, 79. He is praised, 217. Love of bodily things, even good things, is harmful for contemplating spiritual realities, 211. The punishment of Ananias and his wife Sapphira is set before those who use ecclesiastical property unlawfully, 245. Angels do not wish to be worshiped, 203. They are to be loved and honored with charity, not servility, 224. That angels were customarily painted with wings is evident from Agobard, 225. God has placed angels over the judges and kings of the earth, 265. The human soul has no master except God, 103. How it is to be understood that the soul reaches the body, 168. It is not part of the divine substance or nature, ibid. The virginity of the soul is incorrupt faith, 36. Whole faith, firm hope, sincere charity, 206. God is the life of souls, 262. The governance of souls is greater than imperial governance, 299. The mind is better than the body, 212, 256. Unity of minds cannot exist amid quarrels, 261. The heresy of the Anthropomorphites, 225.

The Antichrist is the head of all those in whom… [materially uncertain], 69. He will say that he is Christ, while he will call Christ an impostor, 94. His shamelessness is depicted, 280. The Antiphonary, 325, 330, 308. Apollinaris, bishop of Valence, is praised, 82. The Apostles abstained from Jewish banquets, 93. They are teachers of the world, 114. The teachers of the Church are the rams of the flock, 224. Their images were made by the ancients solely out of love and for remembrance, 215.

The Apostolic Sees, 304. They are the foundation of the Church, 294. The great authority once possessed by the Apostolic Sees, 293. The Apostolic Canons were sometimes altered and corrected, 304. Formerly all bishops were called apostolic, 296. Great reverence is owed by everyone to the Apostolic See, 293. Whether, while the honor of the Apostolic See remains, the pope can be dishonored, 301. The judgment by hot and cold water, 120, 250 ff., 254.

Araboth: the heaven in which God dwells according to the Jews, 87. Arles, a city of Gaul, rich in its harbor, 76, 350. The perfidy of the Arians had not yet been entirely extinguished in Agobard’s age, 117. The body of the heretic Armand, who had long been venerated as a saint, was burned by public authority, 131.

[Col. 1333] Bodily armor cannot demonstrate that anyone is just or innocent, 264. A mill-ass, 121. The example of Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, concerning ecclesiastical singing is related, 335. The assembly at Attigny, 227. The Audiani, schismatics rather than heretics, 225. Augustine’s works against the Pelagians, 162. Levant winds, 147 ff. Gold is censured as a vain and harmful pleasure, even with regard to ecclesiastical singing, 335.

Avitus, bishop of Vienne, 67. His book on the incarnation of the Savior, 65. The most powerful opponent of the Photinian heretics, 67. He is praised, 82, 124. He converted Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, to the Catholic faith, 124. He detested the judgment they called “of God,” that is, trial by combat, 124, 254. His Dialogues and Disputations with King Gundobad, 124, 207. Azariah the priest is praised because he rebuked King Uzziah when he presumed to sacrifice, 136.

## B

Among the Hebrews, *Baalim* signifies idols and is plural in number, 213. Baptism is validly conferred even by wicked people, 142 ff. —Bodily baptism is not necessary for martyrs, 172. It renews the inner person, 177. Slaves may be baptized even against their masters’ wishes, ibid. To barbarize, 313. Barnabas and Paul reject the sacrifice of victims, 203. Bartholomew, bishop of Narbonne, 179. Bede, a man of the English nation, is praised, 216.

Private wars are strongly contrary to Christian simplicity and piety, 119. —Domestic wars are condemned, 250, 253. —Public wars are lawful, 254. A brotherly warrior, 264. Beneficed persons, 139. A benefice, that is, a fief, ibid. The Beneventans, 158. Their duke was Grimoald, ibid. Bera, count of Barcelona, deposed for the crime of high treason, 309. Berarius, archbishop of Narbonne, 179. Bernard, bishop of Vienne, 77, 127. Count Bernard is accused of adultery with Judith Augusta, 308 ff. Count Bertmund of Lyon, 188. Bethsaida, 95. To blaspheme, that is, to revile, 121. Bodo, a palace deacon converted to Judaism, 72.

The good are killed by the wicked, 254. The merits of justice are not always rewarded to the good in this life, 264, 267. A brief summary, 175. The Burgundians, 268. They are called Gundobad’s people, 116, 120.

## C

Caesarea Philippi, 215. Caesarius, bishop of Arles, 83. Caiaphas was honored by prophecy because of the chair, 301. We ought to sing in church more with the mind than with the voice, 334. The canons must be preserved inviolate, 229. The ancient manuscript Collection of the Canons is praised, 241. Some reject the Gallican Canons because the modern Romans did not commend them, although the ancients revered them religiously, 122; and because Roman legates, or the emperor’s representatives, did not participate in their formulation, 241. The sacred canons, 245. Canonical institutions should remain permanently firm, 112. Canonical, 157. The singers’ schools at Lyon; their pride and incompetence are censured, 338. Capernaum, 95.

Chapters established at Attigny, 227. Capitular sanctions, 71. Charles the Bald killed Count Bernard, 310. He was buried in the monastery of Nantua, 71. Charlemagne, called the bishop of bishops, 197. Of all Christian kings, he was the most powerful in war; he subjected the Saxons and other peoples to Christ, 103. On this basis he excuses the Gallican Church’s disagreement with the Roman Church in the celebration of the offices, because the custom of the Gallican Church was not contrary to the faith, 110. He was at odds with Grimoald, duke of Benevento, 158. His epitaph, 349.

[Col. 1334] Carts loaded with dust, 158. The ruin of the city of Carthage, 349. The Catalans place themselves under the faith and patronage of Louis XIII, king of the Franks, 81. Catalonia was formerly called the Spanish March, 309. The chair of the apostle James is preserved at Jerusalem to the present day, 215. Advocates who refer cases to the prince, 187. The heresies of Cerinthus, 85.

Single combats are strongly contrary to Christian simplicity and piety, 119. Their outcome is uncertain, 126. The Council of Chalcedon, 123. Charity is commended, 118. Its description, 261. Whoever rises up against his neighbor to engage in combat does not possess continuous charity, 259. The edict of King Childebert against the Jews, 83.

The Jews call Christians Nazarenes, 73. Christian cattle—that is, cattle rejected by the Jews as unclean and therefore sold to Christians—ibid. Christians were forbidden to live with Jews, 109. All Christians are brothers, 114, 116. All are one Christ, ibid. There were Christians even under the Old Law, 170. The Christian religion is not novel, 174. All together are the temple of God, and individually they are temples, 202. Members of the household of faith, 257. They ought to love one another, 257. Perfect Christians glory in tribulations, 284.

Christ is the true Son of God, not an adopted son, 41. Apostle and pontiff, 56 ff. Head of the Church, 62, 64. Bridegroom of the Church, 110, 189. For Christ and the Church are one person, 62. He adopted human nature, 66. The Jews’ ravings about Christ, 87. Christ is the truth, 113. He did not abandon the Church, 142. Christ was humble, but nevertheless did not acknowledge that he had erred, 159. For what purpose he came from heaven, 196. Fredegisus said that Christ did not exist before he was born, 169. Mediator between God and human beings, 174. He commends the lambs and sheep to blessed Peter, 189, 197. Head and bridegroom of the Church, 191. In assuming human nature, he did not cease to be God, 160. Shepherd of shepherds and bishop of bishops, 196. Supreme shepherd, 197. The sole mediator between God and human beings, 202. To love a human being above Christ is adultery, 206. The name “Christ” comes from *chrism*, 209. He drove the sellers from the temple, 236. He had treasures in purses, 239. By deeds and words he anticipated the form and ordering of his Church, 240. How he is God and human, 271. Whether he entered the world through the Virgin’s ear, 332. He died spontaneously and freely for us, ibid. He consisted of four elements, 344.

The city of God and the city of the devil, 116. The city of God consists of angels and human beings, 274. The apocryphal books of Clement, bishop of Rome, 92. Acephalous clerics, 138. *Clericiones*, 139. Clerics are forbidden to attend Jewish banquets, 83, 109. In Agobard’s time they had fallen into contempt, 147. They cannot marry unless the woman is a virgin, 232. The name “clerics” includes all who are enrolled in the clergy, 248.

Coadjutors could formerly not be given to infirm bishops except at a synod, 29. *Coelicolae*: whence the name derives, 201. Colonies: whence they received this name, ibid. Various types of colonists, ibid. The devil introduces feasts and drunkenness under the name of charity, 225. The communion of brotherhood, 245. The Council of Compiègne concerning the unlawful use of sacred things, 230. The palace of Compiègne, ibid. and 321.

Great reverence and authority belong to general councils, 123. Regional and provincial councils yield to the authority of general councils, convened and accepted by the consent of the whole world; nevertheless, they too possess great authority in matters not defined by those general councils, 123, 242. —Two are to be held each year, 242. The source of their authority, 229. A council is plenary when the metropolitan bishop has taken part, 242. —The ancient councils determined that popular psalms were not to be sung in church, 327.

Royal counselors, 311. Royal advisers, 74. The emperor Constantine the Great was called the common bishop, 198. He worshiped images of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, 217. The customs of each Church are to be retained, provided they are not contrary to the faith, 109, 326. What bishops’ banquets ought to be like, 193. Córdoba, a city of Spain and seat of the Saracens, 76. Chorazin, 95. The transfer of dead bodies arranged by the dying, 208.

[Col. 1335] Criminals ought not to be advanced to the priesthood, 144. The sign of the Lord’s cross, formerly placed everywhere by the Alexandrians recently converted to the faith of Christ, 215. The trial of the cross, 251, 252. The worship owed to God cannot be expressed in Latin by a single word, 201. Cyprian, blessed martyr, 187. The translation of his relics, 349. Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, 36, 43.

## D

The humility of King David is proclaimed, 161. Some never voluntarily give a tenth to priests, 157. Tithes enfeoffed as fiefs, 237. Tithes must be given, 243. For they were vowed from the beginning of the human race and delivered to priests, 232. Bodily beauty in a woman is naturally an incitement to lust, 314.

The Romans worshiped gods for a long period without images. Those who first set up images did so in order to remove fear from the peoples and add error, 219. What God is according to Lucius Balbus, 219. God is truth, 169; and charity, 256. He alone is good by nature, 137. He alone is to be worshiped, 204, 214 ff. We owe him honor and fear, 243. In him alone we ought to place the hope of our blessedness, 209, 224. He wishes all human beings to be saved, 176. Therefore he scourges people in various ways for instruction and conversion, 180.

God’s providence sometimes acquits the innocent and condemns the guilty, 119. His judgment is often hidden but never unjust, 121, 158, 177, 181, 254. God’s judgments are incomprehensible, 254, and unfathomable, 263. He reserves judgment and the consummation of the world for the end, 265. Nothing happens in the world except by God’s dispensation or permission, 254. God dwells in all Christians, 202. All things are present to God, 185, 230. It is impossible to escape God’s hand, 151. No one is God’s son except one who imitates God, 256.

The *Deuteroses* of the Pharisees, 88. The devil is prince and head of all evils, 155. He is always eager to do harm, 182, 184. Nevertheless, he can harm no one unless God permits it, 150, 181. The devil is the inventor and cause of every evil, 280. He and his angels are our enemies, 275.

Antiquity established deacons in the priesthood, 198. Deacons are forbidden to sing anything in church besides the Gospel, 336. The disciples of the Lord are recognized by love; the disciples of the devil are recognized by quarrels and conflicts, 258. Dissension drives the world toward perfidy, ibid. The order of the divine words must never be changed, 331. When wealth in a bishop is blameworthy, 192. A member of the household of faith, that is, a Christian, 257. The senior mistress of the palace, 313. Dominius, a hermit of Limoges, 104. To adorn the memories of martyrs with gifts while neglecting the poor is wrong, 183. Private duels are strongly contrary to Christian simplicity, 119. The fury and savagery of duels are forbidden by princely edicts and the canons of councils, 258. Duodena, the wife of Count Bernard, 309 ff., 323.

## E

Eaof, or Eaor, bishop of Chalon, 77. Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, deposed Jesse, bishop of Amiens, at the Council of Noyon, 312. He imposed public penance on Louis the Pious, 322. The letter on hope and fear written by Agobard to the same man, 323. Eberard, master of Charlemagne’s cupbearers, 70. The devil introduces drunkenness and feasting under the name of charity, 225.

The Church is the house of the true David, that is, Christ, 97. The house of God, 236, 312. It has been called a virgin, 206. Betrothed to one man, Christ, 110, 189. How the Church and Christ—that is, the bridegroom and bride—are to be treated by pastors, 196. The Church and Christ are one person, 62 ff. Its foundation is in the Apostolic Sees, 294. The Church was strong in earlier years but is now weak, 141. The gates of hell cannot prevail against it, 112, 296. Injury to the Church is injury to God, 236. Whoever does not listen to the Church is to be regarded as a pagan and a tax collector, 242. The Church has different members, 206. Each Church may retain its particular customs, provided they are not contrary to the faith, 109, 326. The Church has been enriched so that it can support its preachers, the choirs of ministers, crowds of poor people, and the multitude of pilgrims who flock to it, 245. The nursing Churches—that is, parish churches—140.

The ancient rites of the Churches are not easily changed, 330. Their property is divided four ways, 240. Its use must be proper, 247. It is unjustly possessed by laymen, 229. Churches were built for praising God, praying, and offering sacrifice, 237. They are sold together with their possessions, ibid.

Ecclesiastical statutes must be confirmed by apostolic acts, 85. They are worthless unless they agree with the holy Scriptures, 241. The administration of ecclesiastical property, 231. Ecclesiastical goods must not be used for luxury or lust, 247. They are the property of the poor, 245. Ecclesiastical treasures must remain untouched and sacred, 240.

Bishops are vicars of Christ, 128. Members of Christ’s body, 191. Princes of the Church, 267. They sit on a throne in the Church, 198. They ought to be learned, 32. Yet it often happens that the uneducated hold primacy in the Church, while learned and wise men sit in obscurity, 266. They are required to visit their dioceses annually, 107. They ought not to be accusers, 188. What bishops establish in synods in harmony with the sacred Scriptures is to be regarded as law, 242. They ought not to be devoted to worldly pleasures, 191. Nor should they be spectators of childish games, 313. They must abstain from feasting and drunkenness, 193. Those who abuse ecclesiastical property are censured, 248. They ought to use wealth well, 192. Whether their commands must always be obeyed, 135. Those who give an unjust judgment are censured, 267. Bishops who violate the faith pledged to the prince by oath are to be deposed, 304.

Human error cannot remain hidden, 65. A learned man generally lies concealed in obscurity and wastes away in poverty and want, 266. Pope Eugenius II gave Louis and Lothair Augustus a written oath of fidelity, 305. The error of Eutyches, 36. Evrard, royal envoy, 70. A teacher of the Jews, 112. Excommunication without cause is invalid and rebounds upon its author, 300. The ancient interpreters of the divine books were formerly little concerned with the rules of grammar, 163. They are not to be read as matters that must be believed, but with freedom of judgment, 165. Marks of burning appearing on human bodies, 179.

## F

Falangus, 173. Famine under the emperor Claudius, 93. Faova, bishop of Chalon, 78. The happiness of the wicked is temporary, 263. Felix, bishop of Urgell, a man of ancient character, 34. He was deposed from the honor of the episcopate, 33. He died near Lyon, 31, 37.

A woman converted from Judaism to Christianity suffers severe persecution from the Jews for that very reason, 175. Whether women are human beings was debated at the Council of Mâcon, 89. Ferreolus, holy bishop of Uzès, 109. The trial by hot iron, 119, 251, 254. On feast days the ancient Christians devoted themselves entirely to prayer, 75.

Those who are truly faithful are members of Christ, 127. Under the supreme head they are one priest, ibid. How someone is faithful to the prince, 287, 301. Fidentius, a Catholic teacher, 68. The Christian faith is explained, 267. How its truth is to be sought, 37. It is ineffective for human salvation without peace, 257. How one should fight against its enemies, 276. Faith must not be measured by people’s lives; rather, life must be tested by faith, 35. A member of the household of faith, 257. Faith is owed to the prince under God, 188, 287.

The body of Saint Firminus, bishop of Uzès, 179 ff. The fisc, 240. We ought to weep with those who weep, 260. Florus, deacon of Lyon, 180. Outsiders—that is, non-Christians—252.

The name of the Franks is famous throughout the world, 310. Their immense kingdom was enlarged under Charlemagne, 321. It included Gaul and Germany, 303. Its dangers, 313. It was divided among the sons of Louis the Pious, 289. Frankish law, 117, 126. Fraternal combat, 255. The communion of brotherhood, 245. Bishops call one another brothers, 297. Fredegisus, abbot of Saint Martin, 31, 159. Frederick, royal envoy, 70. Fulda, the monastery of Saint Boniface, 78. Fulrad, abbot of Saint-Denis, ibid. The funerals of the ancients were conducted with dutiful piety, 208. Three kinds of theft and thieves, 240. The word “thief” is general, ibid.

## G

The Gallican Church, 304. Its government is divided between kings and bishops, 76. The great reverence formerly accorded to the Gallican Canons, 121, 241. Some reject these canons because the modern Romans did not commend them, although the ancients revered them religiously, 122; or because Roman legates, or the emperor’s representatives, did not participate in their formulation, 241. The freedom of the Gallican bishops in writing to the Roman pontiff, 303. They threaten deposition if he acts outside the proper order, 304.

*Garizim* is interpreted as “division,” 98. Gideon, the bravest of men, 161, 212. Pope Gelasius wrote the Book of Sacraments, 223. The monastery of Gellone in the First Narbonnaise, 309. Count Gerard, 137. Gerric, head of the chapel and royal envoy, 70. The discovery of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius made to Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, 217. Synodal proceedings were formerly painted in churches to preserve the memory of what had been done and of the error that had been overthrown, 225. The proper measure of divine, angelic, and human glory, 207.

The Goths were at once pagans and heretics, 119. No one has ever seen hail without rain, 153. It is foolish to claim that hail and thunder are produced by human force, 147 ff. Gregory, bishop of Langres, is praised, 82. Pope Gregory the Great rebuked the bishop of Fréjus because he had erased images of the apostles from his basilica on account of the superstition of the common people, who worshiped them contrary to the rule of faith, 217. He removed certain abuses concerning singing from the Roman Church, 327, 336.

Pope Gregory IV came to France, 296. His letter to the bishops of the kingdom of the Franks, 297. At the beginning of his pontificate he made a pledge of fidelity to Louis the Pious, 302, 306. He later crossed over to Lothair’s party against Louis, 296, 303. Grimoald, duke of Benevento, 158. Grimoald, bishop of Pinna, 318. Guasto de Baerne, 251. Guido, bishop of Elne, 248. William, count and founder of the monastery of Gellone, 309. Gundi, a nun who fell into adultery, 318. The Gundobadian Law, 117, 120. It is not a law but a death-trap, 121. It was accepted throughout all the provinces, 258. Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, a heretical man and author of the Gundobadian Law, 117, 123, 207. His Dialogues with Avitus, bishop of Vienne, 124, 207, 254. Gundobad—that is, a Burgundian—116, 120. The Gunebodigni, 117.

## H

The woman with the hemorrhage, healed by Christ, was a citizen of Caesarea Philippi, 215. Heretics depart from the true house of David, that is, Christ, 140. At the time of the Apostles there were no others except Jews and Samaritans, 86. *Hebal* is interpreted as “ancient abyss,” 99.

Helisachar, abbot of Centula, a man of great dignity with the emperor Louis the Pious, 100, 230. The island of Hero, 101. Jerome, priest and teacher, 166. He knew the Jews inwardly and in their outward appearance, 73. His translation is praised, 164. Jerusalem was subject to the Saracens, 118.

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, avoided the profane associations of Jews and heretics, 79. His Life was written by Fortunatus, ibid. Although in exile, he governed his diocese through his priests, 108. Hildebald, archbishop of Cologne, 175. Hildigitus of Lyon, 179. Hilduin, prelate of the sacred palace, 174. Hillel the Jew, a highly learned man from whose school many great men emerged, 88.

The words “homicide” and “sacrilege” were added to older editions of the Apostolic Canons, 304. The inner person was created in the image and likeness of God, 177, 222, 263, 270. The mind owes its religion to God alone, 103. It can do nothing by itself but only with God’s help, 277. Human beings are called gods, 206. Holy people reject worship, 203. God wills all human beings to be saved, 176. They can do no evil without God’s permission, 150.

The honored prince, 228, 231, 316. We owe God honor and fear, 243. Hospitality was once greatly practiced in the Church, 183. Christ adopted human nature, 66. Human errors must be avoided above all, 232. The first law given to human beings forbids the shedding of human blood, 263. The person who is truly humble considers himself despicable; and whoever considers himself despicable does not doubt that he has erred, 159, 161. Hypocrites are marked out, 195.

## I

Idols and images in the time of the Law signified all errors, 317. The worship of images is condemned, 199. Images of God and the saints are neither to be worshiped nor venerated, 200 ff. For if any image were to be worshiped or venerated, the image of the Creator would be more appropriate than that of a creature, 222. Agobard is indignant that they are called holy, 212, 226. Images of the saints must be crushed in every way and scraped away into dust, 218. Ancient Christians possessed images, but for historical purposes and remembrance, not for worship, 225.

For a new emperor, the approval of the supreme pontiff was formerly not necessary, 289, 296. How emperors are happy, 299. The wives and children of emperors and consuls are converted to the faith of Christ, 175. An imperial command, 298. In Agobard’s time impiety had reached great security, 187. A brief bearing the king’s name, 70. Briefs, 175. A description and various names of hell, 281 ff. The sick are to be healed in the Church, while the healthy are to be preserved, 197. For the most part, the innocent are defeated by the guilty, 118. Innocence is not preserved even where it is defended, 187. To make known, that is, to insinuate, 69.

Interpreters and expositors of the divine books were formerly little concerned with the rules of grammar, 163 ff. The interpreters of Sacred Scripture do not all possess equal authority, 165. Irmingard, wife of Louis the Pious, 315. The Italians are above all contemptuous of the canons and scornful of clerics, 122.

## J

James was chosen by Christ and the Apostles as bishop of the Jerusalemite See, 215. A three-day fast instituted by Louis the Pious, 289. Jeroboam caused Israel to sin, 233. Jesse, bishop of Amiens, deposed by Ebbo at the Council of Noyon, 312. John XII, Roman pontiff, deposed at a Roman council for violating the faith pledged to the emperor Otto, 306. John, bishop of Antioch, disagreed with Cyril of Alexandria, 36. The story is told of the apostle John leaving the bath because of the heretic Cerinthus, 85. *Joculares*, a class of entertainers, 249. The descendants of Jonadab are blessed by the Lord, 244.

King Jehoshaphat offended God because he gave assistance to the impious and to those who hated God, 97. Christ bestowed great grace of virtue on Judas, a false disciple and true betrayer, 132, 144. He kept the Lord’s purses, 239. He was a sacrilegious thief, 239. He possessed the same power as the other Apostles, 132.

The Jews, 70 ff. They boast that they are the offspring of the patriarchs, the race of the just, and the descendants of the prophets, 111. They are worse than all unbelievers, 76, 86. They are called vessels of the devil, 78; children of the devil, 111; and [children] of Antichrist, 94. Their errors and ravings are listed, 86 ff. Formerly they abstained from the food and drink of unbelievers, 98. Their banquets and associations are to be avoided, 94, 109 ff. On the days of the Lord’s Passion the Church publicly prays for their salvation, 178. Their slaves may be baptized against their masters’ wishes, 176. Their wealth, 73. The judgment by hot water and glowing iron, 120. The judgment of the cross, 252. Judgments among human beings are necessary, ibid. Their integrity is necessary for kingdoms and peoples, 120. The truth of judgments and affairs must be sought from God, 254.

An oath that is appropriate and lawful, 290, 292. What the oath of fidelity formerly sworn by bishops to the prince included, 302. An oath on behalf of the faith, 30. Controversies are ended by oath where witnesses are lacking, 250.

## L

Laymen who possess the property of churches and turn it to wicked uses are censured, 248. They cannot be administrators of sacred things, 241. Therefore they handle such things and spend them for their own uses, contrary to the prohibition and the canons, 229.

The Lombards, 115, 119. Their law was very favorable to wives, 317. *Latria*: what it is, 200. The presence of Roman pontifical legates was formerly unnecessary at regional or provincial councils, 241. Leidrad, bishop of Lyon, 31, 326, 350. Pope Leo III gave Charlemagne a written oath of fidelity, 305. Leofoas, sister of the king of Navarre and wife of Gaston de Baërne, 251. Why lepers are sent to priests rather than physicians, 136. A Levant wind, 147 ff. Levity must be avoided in rendering divine praises, 329.

Frankish law, 117, 126. The Gundobadian Law, 117, 120; it is not a law but a death-trap, 121. Contempt for the laws is attacked, 187 ff. The diversity of laws obstructs Christian unity, 116 ff. A booklet issued at the Council of Compiègne by treacherous bishops and presented to the emperor Louis the Pious, 322. The Book of Mysteries, 338. The Book of Sacraments, 224. Whatever is public—that is, commonly done—seems lawful, 187.

The Litanies—that is, the Rogations—whether they can be performed without fasting and abstinence from meat, 340. Two of the twenty letters among the Hebrews, 133. Christ’s purses, on which expenditures were made, 239. Lothair becomes a partner in the empire, 287. His partnership with Louis is confirmed by the supreme pontiff, 289, 296. Bagged wines, 138. One priest under the supreme head, 127. No one suffering from any vice can become a priest, 128; nor anyone who is unlearned, 145; nor anyone who is criminal, 144; nor one who has married a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute rather than a virgin, 232. A priest must be irreproachable in life and teaching, 145. One must not obey a wicked and unlearned priest, same place. Priests who teach badly or give bad commands must not be listened to, 135. Bad priests are truly priests, 194; but bad priests can administer goods correctly, 143; for by administering goods they harm only themselves and do not stain the mysteries of the Church, 144. When priests are heard by God or benefit others by preaching, they must not attribute this to their own merits, 132. Four kinds of priests, 146. Priests of the higher order, 139. Holy persons are to be loved and honored, but with charity, not servile submission, 224. They are to be honored for imitation, but not worshiped as a religious observance, 220. To honor the memorials of the saints ambitiously in order to seek popular glory is reprehensible, 213. Sanctity cannot be attributed to images, since they are lifeless things, 212. Chapter I.—Envoys sent by Einhard to Rome to obtain relics. The relics of Saints Marcellinus and Peter obtained, same place.  
Chapter II.—The sacred relics were carried through various places to Michilinstadt and, after various visions, to Mulinheim, later called Seligenstadt, 543.  
Chapter III.—Some relics of Saint Marcellinus, formerly taken away, are obtained and transferred to other places. Miracles performed, 550.  
Chapter IV.—Miracles performed at Mulinheim on the deaf and mute, the crippled, and other sick persons. Beer changed into wine. A candle lit of its own accord, 557.  
Chapter V.—Other miracles performed at Mulinheim: the deaf and mute, paralytics, and mentally afflicted healed. Light granted to travelers journeying at night. A little book presented to the emperor, 564.  
Chapter VI.—Miracles performed at the emperor’s palace through the relics of these saints. Blindness, crippling, paralysis, and fever removed, 574.  
Chapter VII.—Miracles performed at Valenciennes in Hainaut through the relics of these saints. Ten blind persons given sight; other sick persons healed, 579.  
Chapter VIII.—Miracles at Ghent, in the monastery of Saint Bavo, through the relics of these saints. Eight blind persons given sight. Other sick persons helped, 583.  
Chapter IX.—At the relics deposited at Maastricht, the blind, deaf, mute, crippled, and paralytic were healed, 586.  
Chapter X.—Two miracles performed through the intercession of Saints Protus and Hyacinth and Saint Hermes in the church of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, 590.

## Letters of Louis the Pious

1309.

### Letter I

Louis to Magnus, Archbishop of Sens.—He sends a copy of the rule for canons decreed at the Council of Aachen. 1309.

### Letter II

Louis to the monks of Aniane. 1312.

### Letter III

Michael and Theophilus, his son, emperors of the East, to Louis the Pious. 1314.

### Letter IV

Louis to Badurad, Bishop of Paderborn.—On behalf of the Monastery of Corbie in Saxony. 1316.

### Letter V

The bishops assembled at the Council of Paris to Louis the Pious and Lothair, concerning the veneration of images. Same page.

### Letter VI

Louis to Jeremiah, Bishop of Sens, and Jonah, Bishop of Orléans.—A memorandum given to them when they were going to Rome to Pope Eugenius II concerning the matter of images. Same page.

### Letter VII

Louis to Pope Eugenius II.—Sent through the bishops Jeremiah and Jonah, together with the acts of the Synod of Paris. 1317.

### Letter VIII

A letter to be read generally to the people of God.—Concerning the convocation of four councils. 1319.

### Letter IX

An imperial letter to be read generally to the people of God.—Louis the Pious, Emperor, sent it after the decision at Aachen concerning the gathering of councils of bishops in the four parts of the Empire. 1322.

### Letter X

The bishops assembled at the Synod of Paris in the year 829 to the emperors Louis and Lothair. 1324.

### Letter XI

Louis to Aldric, Bishop of Le Mans.—Concerning certain possessions alienated from his church. 1326.

### Letter XII

Louis to Hilduin, Abbot of Saint-Denis.—Concerning the gathering into one work of the things he had found written here and there in Greek histories about Saint Denis. Same page.

### Letter XIII

Hilduin, Abbot of Saint-Denis, to Louis the Pious.—He sends, collected together, whatever memory and the books at hand supplied concerning Saint Denis. 1328.

### Letter XIV

Louis the Pious to Jonah, Bishop of Orléans.—Concerning the Monastery of Anisola. 1330.

### Letter XV

The same to the same. Same page.

1331.
